commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20568)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                                    X509_POLICY_DATA *data)', '            if (ossl_policy_level_add_node(curr, data, node, NULL) == NULL)', '        if (ossl_policy_level_add_node(curr, data, last->anyPolicy, NULL) == NULL)'], 'added_lines': ['                                    X509_POLICY_DATA *data,', '                                    X509_POLICY_TREE *tree)', '            if (ossl_policy_level_add_node(curr, data, node, tree, 0) == NULL)', '        if (ossl_policy_level_add_node(curr, data, last->anyPolicy, tree, 0) == NULL)']}
description:
A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions

of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Policy processing is disabled by default but can be enabled by passing
the `-policy' argument to the command line utilities or by calling the
`X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_policies()' function.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only links policy-tree nodes and passes a tree pointer; it performs no certificate validation logic, and the change addresses resource exhaustion (CWE-400), not improper certificate validation (CWE-295).

description: An information disclosure vulnerability in libmpeg2 in Mediaserver could enable a local malicious application to access data outside of its permission levels. This issue is rated as Moderate because it could be used to access data without permission. Product: Android. Versions: 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1.1. Android ID: A-34093952.

code_evidence: The 4-bit frame_rate_code is read from the bitstream into ps_dec->u2_frame_rate_code and stored without any range validation before subsequent header fields are parsed; the patch adds a check that this code does not exceed MPEG2_MAX_FRAME_RATE_CODE.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-200 fits because the described impact is unauthorized access to data outside the application's permission levels via malformed frame-rate handling; the missing validation enables the exposure. The underlying out-of-range read is a related weakness, but the target describes the resulting confidentiality loss.

evidence_lines.code:
ps_dec->u2_frame_rate_code = impeg2d_bit_stream_get(ps_stream,4);
impeg2d_bit_stream_flush(ps_stream,18);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an attacker-controlled 4-bit frame_rate_code from the sequence header is accepted and retained without validating it against the defined MPEG-2 frame-rate table. Trigger: a crafted bitstream supplies an out-of-range code. This unchecked value later drives frame-rate-dependent processing, and the supported consequence is that malformed indexing/parsing can read data outside the intended bounds, exposing memory contents (information disclosure).

commit_msg: fixed #1574
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!no_dump) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!no_dump && itune->data) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in gpac through 20200801. A NULL pointer dereference exists in the function ilst_item_box_dump located in box_dump.c. It allows an attacker to cause Denial of Service.

code_evidence: Line 79 guards the dump block only with !no_dump, then the switch on itune->type reaches cases that dereference itune->data->data and itune->data->dataSize at lines 84 and 95 without checking itune->data.
The default case at line 106 checks itune->data && itune->data->data before dumping, showing the data pointer can legitimately be NULL.
The DISK, TRKN and TMPO cases at lines 82-84 and 94-95 lack that same NULL guard before building the bitstream from itune->data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences itune->data without a NULL check, matching CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). This is not merely a missing length check (CWE-125/787); the fault is an unchecked NULL pointer before member access.

evidence_lines.code:
case GF_ISOM_BOX_TYPE_TMPO:
bs = gf_bs_new(itune->data->data, itune->data->dataSize, GF_BITSTREAM_READ);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the condition at line 79 checks only no_dump, so for item types DISK, TRKN or TMPO with a NULL itune->data, execution reaches lines 84/95 and dereferences itune->data->data. Trigger: dumping an ilst item of one of those types whose data payload is absent. Supported consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash (DoS), consistent with the description.

description: cpp-httplib through 0.5.8 does not filter \r\n in parameters passed into the set_redirect and set_header functions, which creates possibilities for CRLF injection and HTTP response splitting in some specific contexts.

code_evidence: set_redirect passes the caller-supplied url directly into set_header("Location", url) without checking for CR/LF characters, then sets status 302 in the same block.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits because untrusted input is incorporated into an output record (the HTTP response header) without neutralizing special elements that the downstream HTTP parser interprets, altering the structure of the response.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that externally influenced url content is placed into the Location header without neutralizing CR/LF sequences. A trigger is a url containing \r\n followed by attacker-controlled header text; the downstream HTTP parser then interprets the injected content as additional headers or a split response, enabling header/response splitting.

commit_msg: Fix more CRLF injection problems.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (!content_type.empty()) {', '    req.headers.emplace("Content-Type", content_type);', '  }', '  if (compress_) { req.headers.emplace("Content-Encoding", "gzip"); }', '      req.headers.emplace("Transfer-Encoding", "chunked");'], 'added_lines': ['  if (!content_type.empty()) { req.set_header("Content-Type", content_type); }', '  if (compress_) { req.set_header("Content-Encoding", "gzip"); }', '      req.set_header("Transfer-Encoding", "chunked");']}
description:
Versions of the package yhirose/cpp-httplib before 0.12.4 are vulnerable to CRLF Injection when untrusted user input is used to set the content-type header in the HTTP .Patch, .Post, .Put and .Delete requests. This can lead to logical errors and other misbehaviors.

**Note:** This issue is present due to an incomplete fix for [CVE-2020-11709](https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-UNMANAGED-YHIROSECPPHTTPLIB-2366507).

code_evidence: The caller-supplied content_type string is placed directly into the request header map without validation or rejection of CR/LF characters, so any newline embedded in content_type becomes part of the outgoing Content-Type header value.
A fixed Transfer-Encoding header is also emplaced directly; the patch replaces these raw emplace calls with set_header, indicating the header-value path is where neutralization was added.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits because externally influenced input is used to construct a record (HTTP headers) without neutralizing special elements that change how a downstream component parses it. The more specific CRLF injection class is a child of this injection weakness.

evidence_lines.code: req.headers.emplace("Transfer-Encoding", "chunked");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: externally influenced header values (notably content_type) are inserted into req.headers with no neutralization of CR/LF, so special elements survive into the serialized HTTP request. Trigger: a caller passes a content_type containing CRLF. Consequence: the downstream HTTP parser sees an injected header or altered request structure (CRLF injection).

description: In Wireshark 3.0.0, the TSDNS dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-tsdns.c by splitting strings safely.

code_evidence: wmem_strsplit() is called and its return is stored in splitAddress, but only splitAddress[1] is tested for NULL before dereferencing splitAddress[0] and splitAddress[1]. If wmem_strsplit() returns NULL, the check itself dereferences a NULL pointer; if it returns fewer than two tokens, splitAddress[1] is out of range. The else branch then passes splitAddress[0] to proto_tree_add_string and splitAddress[1] to ws_strtou32.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-252 fits because the code fails to check the return value of wmem_strsplit() for NULL/insufficient tokens and proceeds to dereference it, matching unchecked-return-value semantics. This is distinct from a pure NULL-pointer dereference because the unchecked function return is the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of wmem_strsplit() is not validated for NULL or for containing the expected number of tokens before indexing. Trigger: a TSDNS response whose formatted text lacks a ':' separator or causes allocation failure. Consequence: NULL/out-of-bounds dereference leading to a dissector crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Prevent double free by crafted fences.

If client sent fence with some data, followed by fence with no data (length 0), the original fence data were freed, but the pointer kept pointing at them. Sending one more fence would attempt to free them again.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      fenceData = NULL;']}
description: In TigerVNC 1.7.1 (VNCSConnectionST.cxx VNCSConnectionST::fence), an authenticated client can cause a double free, leading to denial of service or potentially code execution.

code_evidence: Line 8 unconditionally deletes fenceData, but the pointer is not cleared. When len == 0 the if block at line 9 is skipped, so fenceData retains the freed address; a subsequent sync-fence call with len 0 reaches line 8 again and deletes the same address. When len > 0, lines 10-11 reassign the pointer, so no double free occurs on that path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 is the release of the same memory address twice. The dangling fenceData pointer causes line 8 to free the same allocation twice, which is a double free rather than a use-after-free, since the second operation is a free on the stale pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: delete [] fenceData at line 8 frees the buffer without resetting the member pointer, and the len==0 branch leaves it dangling. Trigger: an authenticated client sends a fence carrying data, then a zero-length fence, then another zero-length fence, causing line 8 to free the same heap block twice. Consequence: heap corruption, denial of service, and potentially code execution.

commit_msg:
usb: dwc3: gadget: never call ->complete() from ->ep_queue()

This is a requirement which has always existed but, somehow, wasn't
reflected in the documentation and problems weren't found until now
when Tuba Yavuz found a possible deadlock happening between dwc3 and
f_hid. She described the situation as follows:

spin_lock_irqsave(&hidg->write_spinlock, flags); // first acquire
/* we our function has been disabled by host */
if (!hidg->req) {
	free_ep_req(hidg->in_ep, hidg->req);
	goto try_again;
}

[...]

status = usb_ep_queue(hidg->in_ep, hidg->req, GFP_ATOMIC);
=>
	[...]
	=> usb_gadget_giveback_request
		=>
		f_hidg_req_complete
			=>
			spin_lock_irqsave(&hidg->write_spinlock, flags); // second acquire

Note that this happens because dwc3 would call ->complete() on a
failed usb_ep_queue() due to failed Start Transfer command. This is,
anyway, a theoretical situation because dwc3 currently uses "No
Response Update Transfer" command for Bulk and Interrupt endpoints.

It's still good to make this case impossible to happen even if the "No
Reponse Update Transfer" command is changed.

Reported-by: Tuba Yavuz <tuba@ece.ufl.edu>
Signed-off-by: Felipe Balbi <felipe.balbi@linux.intel.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tdwc3_gadget_giveback(dep, req, ret);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tdwc3_gadget_del_and_unmap_request(dep, req, ret);']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 4.16.4, a double-locking error in drivers/usb/dwc3/gadget.c may potentially cause a deadlock with f_hid.

code_evidence: When dwc3_send_gadget_ep_cmd() fails (ret < 0), the code zeroes req->trb, decrements queued_requests, then calls dwc3_gadget_giveback(dep, req, ret) directly inside the queue path at line 33. giveback invokes the completion callback synchronously from within __dwc3_gadget_kick_transfer, i.e., while the caller's queue path is still active.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 covers improper locking where the same lock is acquired again without being released, producing an unexpected resource state. The synchronous giveback from within ep_queue re-enters the function's completion handler which re-acquires write_spinlock, matching double-locking. The patch replaces giveback with del_and_unmap_request to avoid inline completion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a failed Start Transfer command causes the request to be completed inline via dwc3_gadget_giveback() inside the queueing path instead of deferring the completion. Trigger: a gadget function such as f_hid holds its write_spinlock, calls usb_ep_queue(), and the ep command fails, so f_hidg_req_complete re-enters and tries to acquire the same lock. Supported consequence: recursive lock acquisition leading to deadlock.

commit_msg:
NetKVM: BZ#1169718: More rigoruous testing of incoming packet

Signed-off-by: Joseph Hindin <yhindin@rehat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ', '        DPrintf(3, ("ip_version %d, ipHeaderSize %d, protocol %d, iplen %d\\n",', '            ip_version, ipHeaderSize, pIpHeader->v4.ip_protocol, fullLength));', '        if (len < ipHeaderSize) res.ipCheckSum = ppresIPTooShort;', '        if (fullLength) {}', '        else', '            DPrintf(2, ("ip v.%d, iplen %d\\n", ip_version, fullLength));', '        res.xxpFull = len >= fullLength ? 1 : 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    res.value = 0;', '', '    if (len < 4)', '    {', '        res.ipStatus = ppresNotIP;', '        return res;', '    }', '', '', '        if (len < sizeof(IPv4Header))', '        {', '            res.ipStatus = ppresNotIP;', '            return res;', '        }', '        DPrintf(3, ("ip_version %d, ipHeaderSize %d, protocol %d, iplen %d, L2 payload length %d\\n",', '            ip_version, ipHeaderSize, pIpHeader->v4.ip_protocol, fullLength, len));', '', '        if (res.ipStatus == ppresNotIP)', '            return res;', '        }', '', '        if (ipHeaderSize >= fullLength || len < fullLength)', '        {', '            DPrintf(2, ("[%s] - truncated packet - ip_version %d, ipHeaderSize %d, protocol %d, iplen %d, L2 payload length %d\\n",', '                ip_version, ipHeaderSize, pIpHeader->v4.ip_protocol, fullLength, len));', '            res.ipCheckSum = ppresIPTooShort;', '            return res;', '']}
description: The NetKVM Windows Virtio driver allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (guest crash) via a crafted length value in an IP packet, as demonstrated by a value that does not account for the size of the IP options.

code_evidence: The function reads ip_verlen and ip_length from the incoming packet before checking that len covers even the IPv4 header; the header fields are trusted directly.

ipHeaderSize is derived from the low nibble of ip_verlen, and res.ipStatus is set to ppresIPV4 whenever ipHeaderSize >= sizeof(IPv4Header). The only length check is 'if (len < ipHeaderSize) res.ipCheckSum = ppresIPTooShort;', which merely records a flag and continues. The fullLength value is not validated against len at all ('if (fullLength) {}' is empty).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of the length property of untrusted network input before it is used for parsing, which matches CWE-20 improper input validation. It is not a transformation/filtering issue; the code simply fails to check that the received length is consistent with the declared header and total length.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: incoming packet length is not validated against the header size or the IP total-length field before parsing proceeds. Trigger: a crafted IP packet whose length value is inconsistent with the actual data (e.g., does not account for IP options). Consequence: parsing continues on a truncated or malformed packet, leading to out-of-bounds access and a guest crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Remove `OP_REQUIRES` call from helper function.

Since `OP_REQUIRES` macro expands to a `return;` (among other), calling it in a helper function only ends the helper function's execution earlier, but the kernel will still run from start to end. Thus, all the expected validations are actually broken/useless as the code ploughs through the next crash anyway.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 369524386
Change-Id: I54f6cf9328445675ccc392e661b04336b229c9da
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ValidateInputs(ctx, *input_matrix, input_permutation_indices, &batch_size,', '                   &num_rows);'], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES_OK(ctx, ValidateInputs(*input_matrix, input_permutation_indices,', '                                       &batch_size, &num_rows));']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a null pointer dereference by providing an invalid `permutation` to `tf.raw_ops.SparseMatrixSparseCholesky`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/080f1d9e257589f78b3ffb75debf584168aa6062/tensorflow/core/kernels/sparse/sparse_cholesky_op.cc#L85-L86) fails to properly validate the input arguments. Although `ValidateInputs` is called and there are checks in the body of this function, the code proceeds to the next line in `ValidateInputs` since `OP_REQUIRES`(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/080f1d9e257589f78b3ffb75debf584168aa6062/tensorflow/core/framework/op_requires.h#L41-L48) is a macro that only exits the current function. Thus, the first validation condition that fails in `ValidateInputs` will cause an early return from that function. However, the caller will continue execution from the next line. The fix is to either explicitly check `context->status()` or to convert `ValidateInputs` to return a `Status`. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Compute calls ValidateInputs(ctx, *input_matrix, input_permutation_indices, &batch_size, &num_rows) but ignores its return value, so failed validation does not stop execution.
num_rows is then used in the division (input_matrix->total_nnz() / batch_size) / num_rows without a confirmed nonzero/valid value.

The permutation data pointer input_permutation_indices.flat<int32>().data() is offset by batch_index * num_rows and wrapped in an Eigen::Map of size num_rows, assuming the permutation buffer has batch_size*num_rows elements.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked validation permits a pointer derived from input_permutation_indices to be dereferenced with assumptions that are not enforced, consistent with CWE-476 NULL Pointer Dereference where an expected-valid pointer is used without confirming validity. It is not merely an input-validation weakness because the observable consequence is dereferencing an invalid pointer.

evidence_lines.code:
ValidateInputs(ctx, *input_matrix, input_permutation_indices, &batch_size,
&num_rows);

const double nnz_per_row =
(input_matrix->total_nnz() / batch_size) / num_rows;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: validation performed inside ValidateInputs uses OP_REQUIRES, which only returns from the helper, and the caller discards the result, so invalid permutation/num_rows values propagate. Trigger: an attacker supplies a malformed permutation whose length does not match batch_size*num_rows. The subsequent Eigen::Map construction/use reads beyond the permutation buffer, leading to an out-of-bounds or null/invalid dereference and a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
This changes the fork(2) syscall to record the process start_time after
initializing the basic task structure but still before making the new
process visible to user-space.

Technically, we could record the start_time anytime during fork(2).  But
this might lead to scenarios where a start_time is recorded long before
a process becomes visible to user-space.  For instance, with
userfaultfd(2) and TLS, user-space can delay the execution of fork(2)
for an indefinite amount of time (and will, if this causes network
access, or similar).

By recording the start_time late, it much closer reflects the point in
time where the process becomes live and can be observed by other
processes.

Lastly, this makes it much harder for user-space to predict and control
the start_time they get assigned.  Previously, user-space could fork a
process and stall it in copy_thread_tls() before its pid is allocated,
but after its start_time is recorded.  This can be misused to later-on
cycle through PIDs and resume the stalled fork(2) yielding a process
that has the same pid and start_time as a process that existed before.
This can be used to circumvent security systems that identify processes
by their pid+start_time combination.

Even though user-space was always aware that start_time recording is
flaky (but several projects are known to still rely on start_time-based
identification), changing the start_time to be recorded late will help
mitigate existing attacks and make it much harder for user-space to
control the start_time a process gets assigned.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Tom Gundersen <teg@jklm.no>
Signed-off-by: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

In particular, we do', '\t * not want user-space to be able to predict the process start-time by', '\t * stalling fork(2) after we recorded the start_time but before it is', '\t * visible to the system.', '\t */', '', '\tp->start_time = ktime_get_ns();', '\tp->real_start_time = ktime_get_boot_ns();']}
description: In PolicyKit (aka polkit) 0.115, the "start time" protection mechanism can be bypassed because fork() is not atomic, and therefore authorization decisions are improperly cached. This is related to lack of uid checking in polkitbackend/polkitbackendinteractiveauthority.c.

code_evidence: The child's start_time and real_start_time are recorded here, early in copy_process, well before the task is made visible and before the tasklist_lock is taken.

Between the timing assignment and the lock acquisition, fork(2) performs operations such as copy_thread_tls and alloc_pid that can block or be stalled by user-space, leaving a window in which start_time has been fixed but the process is not yet observable.
Only later is write_lock_irq(&tasklist_lock) taken, after which the task becomes visible and pid/start_time are committed atomically; the earlier assignment breaks that atomicity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the timing assignment and process publication are a non-atomic sequence over shared state (pid+start_time), with an interfering user-space sequence able to act during the window, violating atomicity/exclusivity and enabling a protection-mechanism bypass.

evidence_lines.code:
p->start_time = ktime_get_ns();
p->real_start_time = ktime_get_boot_ns();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the start_time is written long before the tasklist_lock serializes visibility, so a concurrent user-space action can stall fork(2) in copy_thread_tls/alloc_pid after the timestamp is set. Trigger: user-space delays the fork while the timestamp is already recorded, then resumes it to obtain a process whose pid+start_time can collide with a prior process. Consequence: start_time-based identification is predictable, enabling bypass of protection mechanisms that rely on pid+start_time (as in the polkit caching bypass).

commit_msg:
CVE-2016-0798: avoid memory leak in SRP

The SRP user database lookup method SRP_VBASE_get_by_user had confusing
memory management semantics; the returned pointer was sometimes newly
allocated, and sometimes owned by the callee. The calling code has no
way of distinguishing these two cases.

Specifically, SRP servers that configure a secret seed to hide valid
login information are vulnerable to a memory leak: an attacker
connecting with an invalid username can cause a memory leak of around
300 bytes per connection.

Servers that do not configure SRP, or configure SRP but do not configure
a seed are not vulnerable.

In Apache, the seed directive is known as SSLSRPUnknownUserSeed.

To mitigate the memory leak, the seed handling in SRP_VBASE_get_by_user
is now disabled even if the user has configured a seed.

Applications are advised to migrate to SRP_VBASE_get1_by_user. However,
note that OpenSSL makes no strong guarantees about the
indistinguishability of valid and invalid logins. In particular,
computations are currently not carried out in constant time.

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            SRP_VBASE_get_by_user(srp_callback_parm.vb,', '                                  srp_callback_parm.login);'], 'added_lines': ['        SRP_user_pwd_free(srp_callback_parm.user);', '            SRP_VBASE_get1_by_user(srp_callback_parm.vb,', '                                   srp_callback_parm.login);']}
description: Memory leak in the SRP_VBASE_get_by_user implementation in OpenSSL 1.0.1 before 1.0.1s and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2g allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by providing an invalid username in a connection attempt, related to apps/s_server.c and crypto/srp/srp_vfy.c.

code_evidence: The SRP lookup loop repeatedly calls SRP_VBASE_get_by_user and assigns the result to srp_callback_parm.user without freeing any previously returned value.
On each iteration the prior srp_callback_parm.user is overwritten; when the callee returns newly allocated memory (seed path), that allocation is never released.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources; the leaked allocation from the SRP lookup is a resource-management failure that exhausts memory. This is distinct from a mere null dereference because the defect is failure to release owned memory, not invalid access.

evidence_lines.code:
if (srp_callback_parm.user)
i = SSL_accept(con);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the returned pointer's ownership is ambiguous and the caller overwrites srp_callback_parm.user without freeing it. Trigger: an attacker supplies an invalid username, causing the lookup to allocate ~300 bytes each connection/iteration that is leaked. Supported consequence: unbounded memory growth leading to denial of service via resource exhaustion.

description: Integer overflow in bcmath in Facebook HHVM before 3.15.0 allows attackers to have unspecified impact via unknown vectors, which triggers a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: bcdiv accepts an int64_t scale parameter directly from the caller. Line 3 only substitutes the default precision when scale < 0; any nonnegative value is passed through unvalidated to the bcmath library, which stores scale as a 32-bit int internally.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unchecked int64_t-to-int narrowing of scale is an integer wraparound that the code assumes preserves the value's magnitude; the wrapped result then drives memory operations. This is integer overflow, not a simple out-of-bounds access, since the missing bound on scale is the root cause.

if (scale < 0) scale = BCG(bc_precision);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the int64_t scale is not bounded before being narrowed to the library's internal int representation. Trigger: a caller supplies a large nonnegative scale that exceeds the int range, so the value wraps to a smaller or negative number. Consequence: the wrapped scale propagates into bcmath buffer sizing/copying logic, producing a buffer overrun.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: fix unconditional helper

Ben Hawkes says:

 In the mark_source_chains function (net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c) it
 is possible for a user-supplied ipt_entry structure to have a large
 next_offset field. This field is not bounds checked prior to writing a
 counter value at the supplied offset.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif ((e->target_offset == sizeof(struct ipt_entry) &&', '\t\t\t     t->verdict < 0 && unconditional(&e->ip)) ||', '\t\t\t    visited) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif ((unconditional(e) &&', '\t\t\t     t->verdict < 0) || visited) {']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

code_evidence: The unconditional-return test at lines 22-26 requires only target_offset == sizeof(struct ipt_entry), a standard target, verdict < 0, and wildcard addresses; it does not require absence of matches, so a rule with -m matches is misclassified as unconditional.
Lines 54-59 compute size = e->next_offset and form e = entry0 + pos + size, then write e->counters.pcnt = pos at the attacker-influenced offset.
Lines 74-80 compute newpos = pos + e->next_offset and likewise write e->counters.pcnt at entry0 + newpos without validating next_offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an out-of-bounds write to a memory location derived from unchecked next_offset, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of buffer-bounded operations; the missing next_offset validation is the boundary failure, and heap corruption/privilege escalation follows from it.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((e->target_offset == sizeof(struct ipt_entry) &&
(strcmp(t->target.u.user.name,
XT_STANDARD_TARGET) == 0) &&
t->verdict < 0 && unconditional(&e->ip)) ||
visited) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: conditional/unconditional logic checks only wildcard addresses, not matches, so mark_source_chains advances past a non-existent rule using user-supplied next_offset. Trigger: an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE ruleset whose entry has a large next_offset. Consequence: e->counters.pcnt write lands outside the table buffer, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg:
Prevent an OOB read in `expand_dims.cc`

The for loop that follows this check assumes that `axis` is between `0` and `input_dims.size`. If user supplied `axis` is negative, the if code before this check is supposed to bring it back to positive (similar to how in Python one can do `l[-3]` to mean `l[-3 + len(l)]`).

PiperOrigin-RevId: 387200206
Change-Id: I162f4feba12d547c3a4340833ae682016a2ebfab
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, axis >= 0);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions TFLite's [`expand_dims.cc`](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/149562d49faa709ea80df1d99fc41d005b81082a/tensorflow/lite/kernels/expand_dims.cc#L36-L50) contains a vulnerability which allows reading one element outside of bounds of heap allocated data. If `axis` is a large negative value (e.g., `-100000`), then after the first `if` it would still be negative. The check following the `if` statement will pass and the `for` loop would read one element before the start of `input_dims.data` (when `i = 0`). We have patched the issue in GitHub commit d94ffe08a65400f898241c0374e9edc6fa8ed257. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Lines 4-6 normalize a negative axis by adding input_dims.size + 1, but if axis is a large negative value (e.g., -100000) the result remains negative.
Line 7 only checks axis <= input_dims.size, so a still-negative axis passes the guard.
The loop at lines 9-11 uses i < axis; with axis negative this branch is never taken, and lines 14-15 compute input_dims.data[i - 1], which for i = 0 reads input_dims.data[-1].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the function indexes before the start of the heap-allocated input_dims.data buffer. It is not a write, since only input_dims is read; output_dims writes remain in bounds.

evidence_lines.code:
} else {
output_dims->data[i] = input_dims.data[i - 1];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the missing lower-bound check on axis after the negative-axis normalization: a large negative user-supplied axis stays negative and satisfies only the upper-bound ensure. The trigger is any axis below -(input_dims.size + 1), causing the loop's else branch to index input_dims.data[i - 1] with i = 0, reading one element before the heap buffer.

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.UnsortedSegmentJoin` does not fully validate the input arguments. This results in a `CHECK`-failure which can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. The code assumes `num_segments` is a positive scalar but there is no validation. commit_msg:
A race condition may occur between the .disconnect function, which
is called when the device is disconnected, and the dvb_device_open()
function, which is called when the device node is open()ed.
This results in several types of UAFs.

The root cause of this is that you use the dvb_device_open() function,
which does not implement a conditional statement
that checks 'dvbnet->exit'.

So, add 'remove_mutex` to protect 'dvbnet->exit' and use
locked_dvb_net_open() function to check 'dvbnet->exit'.

[mchehab: fix a checkpatch warning]

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-media/20221117045925.14297-3-imv4bel@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_init(&dvbnet->remove_mutex);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 6.0.9. drivers/media/dvb-core/dvb_net.c has a .disconnect versus dvb_device_open race condition that leads to a use-after-free.

code_evidence: dvb_net_init initializes only ioctl_mutex and stores dvbnet->demux; it does not initialize a mutex guarding the dvbnet->exit flag that dvb_device_open() reads while .disconnect modifies it, so open() can race teardown.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function participates in a concurrent open/disconnect sequence lacking a lock for the shared exit flag, matching CWE-362's improper synchronization of a shared resource. The UAF is a downstream effect, not the target weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code:
mutex_init(&dvbnet->ioctl_mutex);
dvbnet->demux = dmx;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The initialization path leaves the teardown flag unprotected by any mutex, so a concurrent open and disconnect can both observe/modify dvbnet state without exclusivity. The open path may proceed after disconnect frees resources, producing a use-after-free; the race is the root cause and the UAF is the consequence.

description: The function WavpackPackInit in pack_utils.c in libwavpack.a in WavPack through 5.1.0 allows attackers to cause a denial-of-service (resource exhaustion caused by an infinite loop) via a crafted wav audio file because WavpackSetConfiguration64 mishandles a sample rate of zero.

code_evidence: The function stores config->sample_rate into wpc->config.sample_rate without any zero check (line 35), then loops over sample_rates[i] using config->sample_rate % sample_rates[i] (line 13) and later compares wpc->config.sample_rate == sample_rates[i] (line 46). With a zero sample rate, the DSD divisor loop never finds a matching divisor and the rate-match loop never breaks, so i runs past the array bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the loop over sample_rates is driven by a zero sample rate whose exit condition cannot be reached, producing an effectively infinite loop and DoS. This is a loop-termination weakness rather than a generic input-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing validation that config->sample_rate is nonzero before it is used as a divisor and loop bound. A crafted WAV with sample rate zero reaches the DSD branch, where config->sample_rate % sample_rates[i] is evaluated and the divisor loop's exit condition is never satisfied; the later rate-matching loop likewise never breaks. The supported consequence is CPU/memory resource exhaustion (denial of service) from the non-terminating iteration.

commit_msg:
Fix tf.compat.v1.placeholder_with_default vulnerability with quantized types.

When iterating through the tensor to extract shape values, an underlying missing kernel
(`StridedSlice` for quantized types) causes an error, which then results in a `nullptr`
being passed to `ParseDimensionValue()`, causing a segfault.

The `nullptr` check allows the missing kernel error to propagate.
Adding the missing kernel registrations allows the shape values
to be extracted successfully.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 445045957
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        } else if (!ParseDimensionValue(key, inner_py_value.get(), status,'], 'added_lines': ['        // If an error is generated when iterating through object, we can', '        // sometimes get a nullptr.', '        } else if (inner_py_value.get() == nullptr ||', '                   !ParseDimensionValue(key, inner_py_value.get(), status,']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, there is a potential for segfault / denial of service in TensorFlow by calling `tf.compat.v1.*` ops which don't yet have support for quantized types, which was added after migration to TensorFlow 2.x. In these scenarios, since the kernel is missing, a `nullptr` value is passed to `ParseDimensionValue` for the `py_value` argument. Then, this is dereferenced, resulting in segfault. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: The loop retrieves each dimension element with PySequence_ITEM into a Safe_PyObjectPtr. If iteration fails, the pointer can be null; the pre-patch code only checks Py_None, so a null inner_py_value is passed directly to ParseDimensionValue, which dereferences py_value. dims[i] is only written when parsing succeeds, leaving it uninitialized otherwise.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the code uses a resource (the element pointer and the dims entry) that was not validly initialized before ParseDimensionValue consumes it. This is distinct from CWE-476 (null pointer dereference), which describes the crash mechanism rather than the uninitialized-resource root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop assumes PySequence_ITEM returns a valid object and checks only for Py_None before calling ParseDimensionValue. Trigger: a quantized-type attribute whose element iteration fails (missing StridedSlice kernel) yields a null pointer. Consequence: dereferencing the null/invalid resource causes a segfault (DoS), and dims[i] remains uninitialized if parsing is skipped.

description: A vulnerability was found in ImageMagick. This security flaw ouccers as an undefined behaviors of casting double to size_t in svg, mvg and other coders (recurring bugs of CVE-2022-32546).

code_evidence: Line 41 casts a floating-point product of pointsize and label length directly to size_t before any bounds check; the value is then passed to AcquireMagickResource.
Lines 98-100 compute width and height from metrics and stroke_width with (size_t) casts of floating-point expressions, with no validation that the result fits in size_t.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an unchecked conversion of a double expression to size_t. When pointsize, label length, or metrics values are large or negative, the computation exceeds the size_t range and the cast yields a wrapped, very small or zero value. The trigger is attacker-influenced label text or font metrics; the consequence is a corrupted width/height used for resource accounting and image extent, leading to undersized allocation or logic errors (DoS/instability).

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tq->perturbation = prandom_u32();'], 'added_lines': ['\tsiphash_key_t nkey;', '\tget_random_bytes(&nkey, sizeof(nkey));', '\tq->perturbation = nkey;']}
description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: The timer callback assigns q->perturbation = prandom_u32() while holding root_lock; this value is a non-cryptographic PRNG output used as the flow-hash perturbation secret. The value is then consumed by sfq_rehash(sch) when there is no filter list and a non-empty tail, so the weak perturbation propagates into packet scheduling state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because the function generates a security-relevant value with an insufficiently random source (prandom_u32) instead of a CSPRNG such as siphash keying. It is not merely a weak-hash issue; the defect is the predictable random value feeding the perturbation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a predictable prandom_u32() value, rather than a cryptographically strong random key, is used as the perturbation secret for flow hashing. Trigger: an attacker observes hash-dependent behavior (e.g., flow label or scheduler path) and infers the 32-bit perturbation, enabling device/user tracking. The consequence is loss of flow-hash unpredictability and privacy, not memory corruption.

description: An issue has been found in Bento4 1.5.1-624. It is a SEGV in AP4_StcoAtom::AdjustChunkOffsets in Core/Ap4StcoAtom.cpp.

Note this is a NULL-pointer dereference rather than an index overflow, so a more specific child CWE (e.g., NULL pointer dereference) would be preferable, but the target CWE-119 is supported by the unchecked-pointer use.

AP4_StcoAtom* stco = AP4_DYNAMIC_CAST(AP4_StcoAtom, atom);
return stco->AdjustChunkOffsets((int)delta);

The UAF is because:

 mount(pid: 921)               | cifsd(pid: 923)
-------------------------------|-------------------------------
                               | cifs_demultiplex_thread
SMB2_negotiate                 |
 cifs_send_recv                |
  compound_send_recv           |
   smb_send_rqst               |
    wait_for_response          |
     wait_event_state      [1] |
                               |  standard_receive3
                               |   cifs_handle_standard
                               |    handle_mid
                               |     mid->resp_buf = buf;  [2]
                               |     dequeue_mid           [3]
     KILL the process      [4] |
    resp_iov[i].iov_base = buf |
 free_rsp_buf              [5] |
                               |   is_network_name_deleted [6]
                               |   callback

1. After send request to server, wait the response until
    mid->mid_state != SUBMITTED;
2. Receive response from server, and set it to mid;
3. Set the mid state to RECEIVED;
4. Kill the process, the mid state already RECEIVED, get 0;
5. Handle and release the negotiate response;
6. UAF.

It can be easily reproduce with add some delay in [3] - [6].

Only sync call has the problem since async call's callback is
executed in cifsd process.

waitter, then it can get the resp safely.

Reviewed-by: Paulo Alcantara (SUSE) <pc@manguebit.com>
Signed-off-by: Zhang Xiaoxu <zhangxiaoxu5@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Steve French <stfrench@microsoft.com>

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in smb2_is_status_io_timeout() in CIFS in the Linux Kernel. After CIFS transfers response data to a system call, there are still local variable points to the memory region, and if the system call frees it faster than CIFS uses it, CIFS will access a free memory region, leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: After wait_for_response, on error the code only re-arms release_mid when mid_state is MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED [60]; a mid already marked MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED falls through, so the sync caller proceeds and reads midQ->resp_buf [73,79,80] while the demultiplex thread may have freed that buffer via its callback. delete_mid at line 83 then operates on the same mid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The caller dereferences midQ->resp_buf after the buffer was released by the receive callback, which is exactly reuse of freed memory; the added MID_RESPONSE_READY state gates access. This is a lifetime/ownership defect, not merely a state-check bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path does not treat a response that arrived as in-flight, leaving resp_buf owned by the receiver while the waiting caller still dereferences it. Trigger: the mount process is killed after the response is received but before the caller resumes. Consequence: read of freed memory (DoS) in the sync receive path.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: fix unconditional helper

Ben Hawkes says:

 In the mark_source_chains function (net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c) it
 is possible for a user-supplied ipt_entry structure to have a large
 next_offset field. This field is not bounds checked prior to writing a
 counter value at the supplied offset.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static inline bool unconditional(const struct arpt_arp *arp)', '\treturn memcmp(arp, &uncond, sizeof(uncond)) == 0;'], 'added_lines': ['static inline bool unconditional(const struct arpt_entry *e)', '\treturn e->target_offset == sizeof(struct arpt_entry) &&', '\t       memcmp(&e->arp, &uncond, sizeof(uncond)) == 0;']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

code_evidence: The helper compares only sizeof(struct arpt_arp) bytes of the caller-provided arp pointer against a zeroed template, without checking target_offset or any surrounding entry length; the arp pointer is derived from a user-supplied ipt_entry whose offsets are not validated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The misclassification causes later offset-based writes to occur outside the intended ipt_entry buffer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The root omission is the missing target_offset/size constraint in this helper, not a mere logic error.

evidence_lines.code:
static inline bool unconditional(const struct arpt_arp *arp)
return memcmp(arp, &uncond, sizeof(uncond)) == 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unconditional only validates the address-matching region, so a rule with a large target_offset and matches is misclassified as an unconditional absolute verdict. Trigger: an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt with crafted next_offset/target_offset. This lets callers such as mark_source_chains trust the entry and write a counter at an out-of-bounds offset, corrupting heap memory.

description: The ZIP signature-verification feature in PHP before 5.6.26 and 7.x before 7.0.11 does not ensure that the uncompressed_filesize field is large enough, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds memory access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PHAR archive, related to ext/phar/util.c and ext/phar/zip.c.

code_evidence: SHA512 branch: local digest[64] is filled by PHP_SHA512Final, then memcmp(digest, sig, sizeof(digest)) reads 64 bytes from sig without any check that sig_len is at least 64.
SHA256 branch: memcmp(digest, sig, sizeof(digest)) reads 32 bytes from sig with no verification that sig_len >= 32.
SHA1 branch: memcmp(digest, sig, sizeof(digest)) reads 20 bytes from sig without checking sig_len >= 20.
MD5 branch: memcmp(digest, sig, sizeof(digest)) reads 16 bytes from sig without checking sig_len >= 16.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a read operation on a buffer (sig) beyond its intended boundary because the length field is not validated against the digest size, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory access. A more specific child such as CWE-125 could apply, but the target class CWE-119 directly covers the improper bounds restriction shown here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: sig and sig_len originate from the parsed PHAR archive signature fields, so an attacker can supply a signature shorter than the digest size. memcmp then reads sizeof(digest) bytes (64/32/20/16) from the undersized sig buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read; the added sig_len < sizeof(digest) guards confirm the missing length constraint. The supported consequence is a crash/DoS and potential memory disclosure, not code execution.

commit_msg:
floppy: fix div-by-zero in setup_format_params

This fixes a divide by zero error in the setup_format_params function of
the floppy driver.

Two consecutive ioctls can trigger the bug: The first one should set the
drive geometry with such .sect and .rate values for the F_SECT_PER_TRACK
to become zero.  Next, the floppy format operation should be called.

A floppy disk is not required to be inserted.  An unprivileged user
could trigger the bug if the device is accessible.

The patch checks F_SECT_PER_TRACK for a non-zero value in the
set_geometry function.  The proper check should involve a reasonable
upper limit for the .sect and .rate fields, but it could change the
UAPI.

The patch also checks F_SECT_PER_TRACK in the setup_format_params, and
cancels the formatting operation in case of zero.

The bug was found by syzkaller.

Signed-off-by: Denis Efremov <efremov@ispras.ru>
Tested-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (!F_SECT_PER_TRACK)', '\t\treturn;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.2.3, drivers/block/floppy.c allows a denial of service by setup_format_params division-by-zero. Two consecutive ioctls can trigger the bug: the first one should set the drive geometry with .sect and .rate values that make F_SECT_PER_TRACK be zero. Next, the floppy format operation should be called. It can be triggered by an unprivileged local user even when a floppy disk has not been inserted. NOTE: QEMU creates the floppy device by default.

code_evidence: Line 20 computes F_SECT_PER_TRACK from user-influenced _floppy->sect and F_SIZECODE; this value can be zero. Line 24 multiplies by it, and lines 25 and 27-28 use it as divisor and modulus operand: head_shift = (F_SECT_PER_TRACK + 5) / 6 is safe, but n = (...) % F_SECT_PER_TRACK divides by zero. Line 40 also computes (n + il) % F_SECT_PER_TRACK in the loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a modulo operation with F_SECT_PER_TRACK as the divisor, and that value can be zero due to attacker-controlled geometry. This directly matches CWE-369 (divide by zero), an availability-impacting DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: setup_format_params uses F_SECT_PER_TRACK as a divisor/modulus without verifying it is non-zero. Trigger: a prior geometry ioctl sets .sect and .rate such that F_SECT_PER_TRACK becomes zero, then a format ioctl invokes this function. Consequence: division by zero in the kernel, causing a crash/DoS (availability impact).

commit_msg:
ipv6: Use result arg in fib_lookup_arg consistently

arg.result is sometimes used as fib6_result and sometimes used to
hold the rt6_info. Add rt6_info to fib6_result and make the use
of arg.result consistent through ipv6 rules.

The rt6 entry is filled in for lookups returning a dst_entry, but not
for direct fib_lookups that just want a fib6_info.

Fixes: effda4dd97e8 ("ipv6: Pass fib6_result to fib lookups")
Signed-off-by: David Ahern <dsahern@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\targ->result = rt;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct fib6_result *res = arg->result;', '\tres->rt6 = rt;']}
description: A flaw was found in the IPv6 module of the Linux kernel. The arg.result was not used consistently in fib6_rule_lookup, sometimes holding rt6_info and other times fib6_info. This was not accounted for in other parts of the code where rt6_info was expected unconditionally, potentially leading to a kernel panic in fib6_rule_suppress.

code_evidence: Line 5 declares 'rt' as struct rt6_info *, and line 8 reads 'lookup = arg->lookup_ptr', so the lookup result is treated as an rt6_info. Line 34 assigns that result to 'rt', and lines 35-42 dereference it as an rt6_info (rt->dst, ip6_dst_idev(&rt->dst)). Line 52 stores the rt6_info pointer back into the generic 'arg->result' slot, which the commit states is also used as a fib6_result in other paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-843 fits because the same resource (arg->result) is initialized/stored as one type (rt6_info *) but accessed elsewhere as an incompatible type (fib6_result), producing logical/memory errors. This is type confusion of a stored pointer, not merely a null or use-after-free issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a single generic result slot (arg->result) is written with a struct rt6_info * here while other callers/consumers interpret the same slot as a struct fib6_result. Trigger: a rule lookup path that fills arg->result with an rt6_info and is later consumed by code expecting fib6_result (e.g., fib6_rule_suppress reading rt6 fields). Supported consequence: incompatible-type access of the stored resource, leading to invalid field reads and a kernel panic.

commit_msg:
dvb_register_device() dynamically allocates fops with kmemdup()
to set the fops->owner.
And these fops are registered in 'file->f_ops' using replace_fops()
in the dvb_device_open() process, and kfree()d in dvb_free_device().

However, it is not common to use dynamically allocated fops instead
of 'static const' fops as an argument of replace_fops(),
and UAF may occur.
These UAFs can occur on any dvb type using dvb_register_device(),
such as dvb_dvr, dvb_demux, dvb_frontend, dvb_net, etc.

So, instead of kfree() the fops dynamically allocated in
dvb_register_device() in dvb_free_device() called during the
.disconnect() process, kfree() it collectively in exit_dvbdev()
called when the dvbdev.c module is removed.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-media/20221117045925.14297-4-imv4bel@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Reported-by: Dan Carpenter <error27@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@kernel.org>

commit_msg:
Prevent segfault with malformed input type

Bug-Debian: https://github.com/tats/w3m/issues/7
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    Strcat(tmp, Sprintf("<input_alt hseq=\\"%d\\" fid=\\"%d\\" type=%s "', '\t\t\tcur_hseq++, cur_form_id, p, html_quote(r), size, i, qq));'], 'added_lines': ['    Strcat(tmp, Sprintf("<input_alt hseq=\\"%d\\" fid=\\"%d\\" type=\\"%s\\" "', '\t\t\tcur_hseq++, cur_form_id, html_quote(p),', '\t\t\thtml_quote(r), size, i, qq));']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Tatsuya Kinoshita w3m fork before 0.5.3-31. w3m allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault and crash) via a crafted HTML page.

code_evidence: ATTR_TYPE is fetched into p (default "text") and passed to formtype(p) at line 30; if the value is unrecognized, formtype returns FORM_UNKNOWN and the function returns NULL at line 32.

The Sprintf at lines 68-70 builds the input_alt string using p directly for the type attribute without quoting, and html_quote(r) for the name. The diff shows p was previously not passed through html_quote, so a malformed/attacker-supplied type value flows into the generated markup.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The target is CWE-476 NULL Pointer Dereference, but the function's demonstrated defect is unescaped attacker-controlled input in the type attribute, not a NULL dereference. The code does not show a pointer being dereferenced while NULL; the FORM_UNKNOWN branch returns NULL defensively. Evidence supports improper input neutralization rather than CWE-476, so it is insufficient for the target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The type attribute string p is attacker-controlled from the parsed HTML tag and is interpolated into the Sprintf-generated markup. The patch adds html_quote(p) to the type field and quotes it, indicating the unsafe handling of that value; the crash described in the commit arises from malformed input reaching this formatting path. Root cause is missing sanitization/validation of the type value before string construction.

commit_msg:
f2fs: fix to avoid memory leakage in f2fs_listxattr

In f2fs_listxattr, there is no boundary check before
memcpy e_name to buffer.
If the e_name_len is corrupted,
unexpected memory contents may be returned to the buffer.

Signed-off-by: Randall Huang <huangrandall@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Chao Yu <yuchao0@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Jaegeuk Kim <jaegeuk@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tvoid *base_addr;'], 'added_lines': ['\tnid_t xnid = F2FS_I(inode)->i_xattr_nid;', '\tvoid *base_addr, *last_base_addr;', '\tlast_base_addr = (void *)base_addr + XATTR_SIZE(xnid, inode);', '', '', '\t\tif ((void *)(entry) + sizeof(__u32) > last_base_addr ||', '\t\t\t(void *)XATTR_NEXT_ENTRY(entry) > last_base_addr) {', '\t\t\tf2fs_err(F2FS_I_SB(inode), "inode (%lu) has corrupted xattr",', '\t\t\t\t\t\tinode->i_ino);', '\t\t\tset_sbi_flag(F2FS_I_SB(inode), SBI_NEED_FSCK);', '\t\t\terror = -EFSCORRUPTED;', '\t\t\tgoto cleanup;', '\t\t}']}
description: In f2fs_xattr_generic_list of xattr.c, there is a possible out of bounds read due to a missing bounds check. This could lead to local information disclosure with System execution privileges needed. User interaction is not required for exploitation.Product: Android. Versions: Android kernel. Android ID: A-120551147.

code_evidence: list_for_each_xattr walks entries from base_addr with no upper bound; entry->e_name_len is read from the on-disk xattr record and used to compute size at line 23.

When buffer is non-NULL, size is checked against rest (25-28), but the memcpy at 31 copies entry->e_name_len bytes from entry->e_name without verifying that this region lies within the allocated xattr block read by read_all_xattrs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe memcpy reads source bytes beyond the intended xattr buffer, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. It is not merely a destination overflow (CWE-787) because the rest/size check bounds the output buffer while the source extent from e_name_len remains unvalidated.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the xattr iteration trusts the on-disk e_name_len and entry layout, so a corrupted e_name_len or malformed entry makes the source region for memcpy extend past the xattr block. Trigger: listing xattrs (buffer non-NULL) on an inode with corrupted xattr metadata. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of adjacent kernel memory copied into the caller's buffer, disclosing memory contents; the size check limits only the destination, not the source.

commit_msg:
floppy_revalidate() doesn't perform any error handling on lock_fdc()
result. lock_fdc() might actually be interrupted by a signal (it waits for
fdc becoming non-busy interruptibly). In such case, floppy_revalidate()
proceeds as if it had claimed the lock, but it fact it doesn't.

In case of multiple threads trying to open("/dev/fdX"), this leads to
serious corruptions all over the place, because all of a sudden there is
no critical section protection (that'd otherwise be guaranteed by locked
fd) whatsoever.

While at this, fix the fact that the 'interruptible' parameter to
lock_fdc() doesn't make any sense whatsoever, because we always wait
interruptibly anyway.

Most of the lock_fdc() callsites do properly handle error (and propagate
EINTR), but floppy_revalidate() and floppy_check_events() don't. Fix this.

Spotted by 'syzkaller' tool.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-static int lock_fdc(int drive, bool interruptible)
+static int lock_fdc(int drive)
 {
 	if (WARN(atomic_read(&usage_count) == 0,
 		 "Trying to lock fdc while usage count=0\n"))
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int lock_fdc(int drive, bool interruptible)'], 'added_lines': ['static int lock_fdc(int drive)']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernels implementation of the floppy disk drive controller driver software. The impact of this issue is lessened by the fact that the default permissions on the floppy device (/dev/fd0) are restricted to root. If the permissions on the device have changed the impact changes greatly. In the default configuration root (or equivalent) permissions are required to attack this flaw.

code_evidence: wait_event_interruptible returns nonzero when interrupted by a signal, and the function returns -EINTR without having acquired fdc_busy.

On success, exclusive ownership is established only after test_and_set_bit(0,&fdc_busy) succeeds; the caller must not proceed on the -EINTR path, and subsequent shared state (command_status, timeout, drive) is only mutated under that lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's lock acquisition is interruptible and can silently fail, so mutual exclusion over the shared fdc resource is not guaranteed to holders that ignore the error. This is a synchronization failure enabling concurrent access to a shared resource, matching CWE-362 rather than a simple missing-check weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (wait_event_interruptible(fdc_wait, !test_and_set_bit(0, &fdc_busy)))
return -EINTR;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: lock_fdc can fail with -EINTR, leaving fdc_busy unset and the critical section unclaimed. Trigger: a thread is interrupted while waiting for the floppy controller; callers that ignore the return value (e.g. floppy_revalidate) continue without synchronization. Consequence: concurrent open()/revalidation paths race on shared controller state, causing corruption.

commit_msg:
Fix heap OOB read in dequantize op.

Also fixes SEGV in same op

PiperOrigin-RevId: 372437896
Change-Id: I135e94d360c2a1ce374c10f7e0fed1af603dbc02
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(ctx, input_min_tensor.NumElements() == num_slices,', '                errors::InvalidArgument(', '                    "input_min_tensor must have as many elements as input on "', '                    "the dequantization axis (",', '                    axis_, "), got ", input_min_tensor.NumElements(),', '                    ", expected ", num_slices));', '    OP_REQUIRES(ctx, input_max_tensor.NumElements() == num_slices,', '                errors::InvalidArgument(', '                    "input_max_tensor must have as many elements as input on "', '                    "the dequantization axis (",', '                    axis_, "), got ", input_max_tensor.NumElements(),', '                    ", expected ", num_slices));']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. Due to lack of validation in `tf.raw_ops.Dequantize`, an attacker can trigger a read from outside of bounds of heap allocated data. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/26003593aa94b1742f34dc22ce88a1e17776a67d/tensorflow/core/kernels/dequantize_op.cc#L106-L131) accesses the `min_range` and `max_range` tensors in parallel but fails to check that they have the same shape. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: num_slices is derived only from the input tensor's dequantization-axis dimension (defaulting to 1 when axis_ is -1); there is no check that input_min_tensor and input_max_tensor contain at least num_slices elements.

The loop iterates i from 0 to num_slices-1 and unconditionally indexes min_ranges(i) and max_ranges(i), where min_ranges/max_ranges are vec<float>() views of the min/max tensors provided by the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i) beyond the allocated range tensor buffer is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The missing length validation permits the read; it is a read-past-end rather than a write, so CWE-125 rather than an out-of-bounds write applies.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the min/max range tensors are assumed to have NumElements() equal to num_slices, but only the input shape controls the loop bound. Trigger: a caller supplies min/max tensors with fewer elements than the input's axis dimension, so min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i) index past the buffer. Consequence: a heap out-of-bounds read (and possible SEGV crash) while dequantizing.

commit_msg:
dm: Reset virtio device before release

With virtio polling mode enabled, a timer is running in the virtio
backend service. And the timer will also be triggered if its frondend
driver didn't do the device reset in shutdown. A freed virtio device
will be accessed in the polling timer handler.

Do the virtio reset() callback specifically to clear the polling timer
before the free.

Tracked-On: #6147
Signed-off-by: Shuo A Liu <shuo.a.liu@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Yonghua Huang <yonghua.huang@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tvirtio_rnd_reset(rnd);']}
description: The polling timer handler in ACRN before 2.5 has a use-after-free for a freed virtio device, related to devicemodel/hw/pci/virtio/*.c.

code_evidence: The function cancels and joins the RX thread, but the virtio backend polling timer was not stopped here; the patch inserts virtio_rnd_reset(rnd) before the free.
After teardown, rnd is released with free(rnd) at line 28, so any later timer callback dereferencing rnd operates on freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The freed rnd pointer remains reachable by the polling timer handler, which references memory after free(rnd); this matches CWE-416. It is not merely a resource leak because the object is freed while a live callback can still dereference it.

evidence_lines.code:
pthread_cancel(rnd->rx_tid);
pthread_join(rnd->rx_tid, &jval);

DPRINTF(("%s: free struct virtio_rnd!\n", __func__));
free(rnd);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: deinit frees the virtio_rnd structure without clearing the backend polling timer. Trigger: with polling mode enabled, the timer fires after shutdown and accesses the freed rnd. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the freed virtio device, leading to memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg: fix: restrict sendToFrame to same-process frames by default (#26875)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (frame)'], 'added_lines': ['  if (frame) {', '    dict.Set("processId", frame->GetProcess()->GetID());', '  }']}
description: The Electron framework lets you write cross-platform desktop applications using JavaScript, HTML and CSS. In affected versions of Electron IPC messages sent from the main process to a subframe in the renderer process, through webContents.sendToFrame, event.reply or when using the remote module, can in some cases be delivered to the wrong frame. If your app uses remote, calls webContents.sendToFrame, or calls event.reply in an IPC message handler then it is impacted by this issue. This has been fixed in versions 9.4.0, 10.2.0, 11.1.0, and 12.0.0-beta.9. There are no workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The event dictionary exposes only frameId for the supplied frame; no process identity is attached, so the frame identifier alone cannot distinguish frames from different renderer processes.
The sync callback is bound to the Event object when both frame and callback are present, and that callback is later used to route replies to the frame.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-668 fits because the missing process ID constraint lets IPC data intended for one frame be exposed to a frame in another process, i.e., the wrong sphere. This is not merely a frame-ID validation bug (CWE-20); the core issue is cross-process resource exposure.

evidence_lines.code:

commit_msg:
Have a common routine for converting dates and times to strings.

Have a routine that takes a buffer, a strftime format, and a struct tm *
as arguments, and:

* checks whether the struct tm * is null and, if so, returns a string
indicating that the date and time couldn't be converted;

* otherwise, passes it to strftime(), along with the buffer and the
format argument and, if strftime() returns 0, meaning the string didn't
fit into the buffer and thus that the buffer's contents are undefined,
returns a string indicating that the date and time didn't fit into the
buffer;

* otherwise, returns a pointer to the buffer.

Call that routine instead of directly calling strftime() in printers;
that prevents printing a buffer with undefined data if the buffer isn't
big enough for the string.

Also, when generating file names using an strftime format, check the
return value of strftime() to make sure the buffer didn't overflow.

The described weakness is undefined buffer data on failure, which is not CWE-787; no write past the buffer bounds is shown here.

commit_msg:
Add handshake mode switch check in FINISH and PSK_FINISH.

Reference: DMTF-2023-0001

Fix: https://github.com/DMTF/libspdm/issues/2005

Signed-off-by: Jiewen Yao <jiewen.yao@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                                               response_size, response);', '    }', '    if (!session_info->use_psk) {', '        return libspdm_generate_error_response(spdm_context,', '                                               SPDM_ERROR_CODE_UNEXPECTED_REQUEST, 0,']}
description:
libspdm is a sample implementation that follows the DMTF SPDM specifications. A vulnerability has been identified in SPDM session establishment in libspdm prior to version 2.3.1. If a device supports both DHE session and PSK session with mutual
authentication, the attacker may be able to establish the session with `KEY_EXCHANGE` and `PSK_FINISH` to bypass the mutual authentication. This is most likely to happen when the Requester begins a session using one method (DHE, for example) and then uses the other method's finish (PSK_FINISH in this example) to establish the session. The session hashes would be expected to fail in this case, but the condition was not detected.

This issue only impacts the SPDM responder, which supports `KEY_EX_CAP=1 and `PSK_CAP=10b` at same time with mutual authentication requirement. The SPDM requester is not impacted. The SPDM responder is not impacted if `KEY_EX_CAP=0` or `PSK_CAP=0` or `PSK_CAP=01b`. The SPDM responder is not impacted if mutual authentication is not required.

libspdm 1.0, 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 are all impacted. Older branches are not maintained, but users of the 2.3 branch may receive a patch in version 2.3.2. The SPDM specification (DSP0274) does not contain this vulnerability.

code_evidence: After resolving session_info for the SPDM session, the function checks only that session_info is non-NULL and that the session state is LIBSPDM_SESSION_STATE_HANDSHAKING. It never inspects session_info->use_psk to confirm the session was established via PSK before processing a PSK_FINISH request.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the responder does not sufficiently prove that the peer completed the claimed PSK authentication handshake before establishing the session; the missing use_psk check lets an unauthenticated DHE session be treated as PSK-authenticated.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: PSK_FINISH accepts any session in the handshaking state without verifying the session's negotiated handshake method. A requester that started a DHE session can send PSK_FINISH, and the responder proceeds to HMAC verification and key generation on that session instead of rejecting the mismatched finish method. This allows bypassing the mutual-authentication requirement of the DHE exchange, permitting session establishment without proper authentication.

commit_msg:
blocksize + WAVPACK4_HEADER_SIZE might overflow gsize, which then
results in allocating a very small buffer. Into that buffer blocksize
data is memcpy'd later which then causes out of bound writes and can
potentially lead to anything from crashes to remote code execution.

Thanks to Adam Doupe for analyzing and reporting the issue.

CVE: CVE-2022-1920

https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org/security/sa-2022-0004.html

Fixes https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/gstreamer/gstreamer/-/issues/1226

Part-of: <https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/gstreamer/gstreamer/-/merge_requests/2612>

description: Integer overflow in matroskademux element in gst_matroska_demux_add_wvpk_header function which allows a heap overwrite while parsing matroska files. Potential for arbitrary code execution through heap overwrite.

code_evidence: blocksize is declared as guint32, so the value read from the stream is bounded to 32 bits and can be near UINT32_MAX.
blocksize is parsed from attacker-controlled buffer data via GST_READ_UINT32_LE, with no upper-bound check before use.
The guard only rejects blocksize == 0 or size < blocksize; it does not prevent WAVPACK4_HEADER_SIZE + blocksize from exceeding the allocation size type.
The allocation size WAVPACK4_HEADER_SIZE + blocksize is computed in 32-bit arithmetic before being passed to gst_buffer_new_allocate, so it can wrap to a small value.
memcpy copies blocksize bytes into the small allocated buffer, writing past its end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because an integer addition used to size a heap allocation wraps around, violating the assumption that the result grows; the wrapped size then feeds memcpy, producing a heap overwrite. This is an integer overflow used as an allocation size, distinct from a simple missing bounds check.

evidence_lines.code: guint32 block_samples, flags, crc, blocksize;
memcpy (outdata, data, blocksize);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation size WAVPACK4_HEADER_SIZE + blocksize is computed with 32-bit blocksize, so a large attacker-supplied blocksize wraps the sum to a small value and a tiny buffer is allocated. Trigger: a Matroska WavPack block with a huge blocksize field. Consequence: the subsequent memcpy of blocksize bytes overflows the heap buffer, causing memory corruption and potential code execution.
