commit_msg:
Check for overflow when calculating on-disk attribute data size (#2459)

A bogus hdf5 file may contain dataspace messages with sizes
which lead to the on-disk data sizes to exceed what is addressable.
When calculating the size, make sure, the multiplication hasn't
overflown.
The test case was crafted in a way that the overflow caused the
size to be 0.

This fixes CVE-2021-37501 / Bug #2458.

Signed-off-by: Egbert Eich <eich@suse.com>
Co-authored-by: Allen Byrne <byrn@hdfgroup.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    /* Check if multiplication has overflown */', '    if ((attr->shared->data_size / dt_size) != ds_size)', '        HGOTO_ERROR(H5E_RESOURCE, H5E_OVERFLOW, NULL, "data size exceeds addressable range")']}
description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability in HDFGroup hdf5-h5dump 1.12.0 through 1.13.0 allows attackers to cause a denial of service via h5tools_str_sprint in /hdf5/tools/lib/h5tools_str.c.

code_evidence: Lines 65-70 derive dt_size and ds_size from the decoded datatype and dataspace, then compute the on-disk data size as ds_size * (hsize_t)dt_size with H5_CHECKED_ASSIGN, which performs a narrowing conversion but does not validate that the multiplication itself did not overflow.

Lines 71-76 use the resulting data_size as the allocation size for attr_buf and then H5MM_memcpy that many bytes from the message buffer p into attr->shared->data; the only guard is comparing data_size to p_size, which is also derived from the same overflowed value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked multiplication directly yields an incorrect buffer size that is then used to allocate and copy data, so the function writes past the intended buffer bounds, matching CWE-787. The root cause is the missing overflow check on the size computation, not merely a denial of service.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A crafted HDF5 file supplies a dataspace and datatype whose product overflows the hsize_t multiplication, so data_size becomes a small or zero value that passes the p_size check. The memcpy then copies based on this corrupted size while the source buffer is read according to the attacker-influenced message layout, producing an out-of-bounds read/write of the attribute buffer.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code builds a TensorShape from unvalidated user-provided dimensions (line 39) instead of using checked construction. The ByteDataOp handler computes offset from image->rows-y-1 and x, then checks offset+(operand*number_planes) > pixel_info_length; if the earlier allocation was undersized due to overflow, this bound check uses the same flawed length and does not protect the buffer.

commit_msg:
efi: capsule-loader: Fix use-after-free in efi_capsule_write

A race condition may occur if the user calls close() on another thread
during a write() operation on the device node of the efi capsule.

This is a race condition that occurs between the efi_capsule_write() and
efi_capsule_flush() functions of efi_capsule_fops, which ultimately
results in UAF.

So, the page freeing process is modified to be done in
efi_capsule_release() instead of efi_capsule_flush().

Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v4.9+
Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/all/20220907102920.GA88602@ubuntu/
Signed-off-by: Ard Biesheuvel <ardb@kernel.org>

The same cap_info and its page buffers are concurrently used by efi_capsule_write on another thread, so release can free them while a write is in progress.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: release() frees the shared cap_info buffers with no lock or in-progress guard, so a close() on one thread can free memory that efi_capsule_write() is still dereferencing. The allocation size for non-transparent files is (record_length+2)*record_count, but the loop can read more records than record_count and rv from sc_read_record may exceed rec_len, so offs can grow beyond the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing at *out + offs + 2 and offs+1 beyond the calloc'd region is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the missing record-count check is the mechanism, but the supported weakness is the write past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the record loop has no upper bound on the record number and trusts the returned record length rv when advancing offs, while the buffer was sized from record_count and record_length. Trigger: a card/file reporting more records or longer records than declared causes sc_read_record to write past the calloc'd *out buffer. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, memory corruption/crash.

commit_msg:
amd/iommu: fix flush checks

Flush checking for AMD IOMMU didn't check whether the previous entry
was present, or whether the flags (writable/readable) changed in order
to decide whether a flush should be executed.

Fix this by taking the writable/readable/next-level fields into account,
together with the present bit.

Along these lines the flushing in amd_iommu_map_page() must not be
omitted for PV domains. The comment there was simply wrong: Mappings may
very well change, both their addresses and their permissions. Ultimately
this should honor iommu_dont_flush_iotlb, but to achieve this
amd_iommu_ops first needs to gain an .iotlb_flush hook.

Also make clear_iommu_pte_present() static, to demonstrate there's no
caller omitting the (subsequent) flush.

This is part of XSA-275.

Reported-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* 4K mapping for PV guests never changes, ', '     * no need to flush if we trust non-present bits */', '    if ( is_hvm_domain(d) )', '        amd_iommu_flush_pages(d, dfn_x(dfn), 0);'], 'added_lines': ['    amd_iommu_flush_pages(d, dfn_x(dfn), 0);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x on AMD x86 platforms, possibly allowing guest OS users to gain host OS privileges because TLB flushes do not always occur after IOMMU mapping changes.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's missing flush for PV domains is a stale-IOMMU-mapping/TLB-coherence flaw enabling privilege escalation, not an explicit exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor; CWE-200 is not directly supported.

commit_msg: issue #91: filter out invalid negative sample rates to prevent encoder crash
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!config->sample_rate) {', '        strcpy (wpc->error_message, "sample rate cannot be zero!");'], 'added_lines': ['    if (config->sample_rate <= 0) {', '        strcpy (wpc->error_message, "sample rate cannot be zero or negative!");']}
description: WavPack 5.3.0 has an out-of-bounds write in WavpackPackSamples in pack_utils.c because of an integer overflow in a malloc argument. NOTE: some third-parties claim that there are later "unofficial" releases through 5.3.2, which are also affected.

code_evidence: config->sample_rate is read from the caller-supplied WavpackConfig and only validated against zero ([7,8,9]); a negative rate passes this guard and is stored into wpc->config.sample_rate at line 43.
In hybrid bitrate mode, bps is computed as config->bitrate * 256000.0 / config->sample_rate / config->num_channels, so a negative sample_rate yields a negative quotient that is then cast to uint32_t.

The resulting bps feeds wps->bits (line 174) and stream setup, where per-stream structures are allocated in the loop at lines 123-128 based on channel configuration; an inconsistent derived bitrate can drive later sample packing/allocation arithmetic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts a signed input that flows into a calculation whose result is cast to an unsigned integer, permitting wraparound to a small or huge value; this is CWE-190. It is not merely a missing-input-validation issue because the defect is the integer arithmetic assuming a positive denominator/size.

evidence_lines.code: bps = (uint32_t) floor (config->bitrate * 256000.0 / config->sample_rate / config->num_channels + 0.5);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sample-rate guard rejects only zero, not negative values, allowing an attacker-controlled negative rate into later size/bitrate computations. Trigger: a crafted WavpackConfig with sample_rate < 0 in hybrid bitrate mode. The unsigned cast of the negative quotient and inconsistent stream sizing can produce wrapped allocation sizes, leading to out-of-bounds writes during sample packing (as in WavpackPackSamples).

commit_msg:
When an ULP-enabled socket enters the LISTEN status, the listener ULP data
pointer is copied inside the child/accepted sockets by sk_clone_lock().

The relevant ULP can take care of de-duplicating the context pointer via
the clone() operation, but only MPTCP and SMC implement such op.

Other ULPs may end-up with a double-free at socket disposal time.

We can't simply clear the ULP data at clone time, as TLS replaces the
socket ops with custom ones assuming a valid TLS ULP context is
available.

Instead completely prevent clone-less ULP sockets from entering the
LISTEN status.

Fixes: 734942cc4ea6 ("tcp: ULP infrastructure")
Reported-by: slipper <slipper.alive@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Abeni <pabeni@redhat.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/4b80c3d1dbe3d0ab072f80450c202d9bc88b4b03.1672740602.git.pabeni@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\terr = -EINVAL;', '\tif (!ulp_ops->clone && sk->sk_state == TCP_LISTEN)', '\t\tgoto out_err;', '']}
description:
There is a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux Kernel which can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation. To reach the vulnerability kernel configuration flag CONFIG_TLS or CONFIG_XFRM_ESPINTCP has to be configured, but the operation does not require any privilege.

There is a use-after-free bug of icsk_ulp_data of a struct inet_connection_sock.

When CONFIG_TLS is enabled, user can install a tls context (struct tls_context) on a connected tcp socket. The context is not cleared if this socket is disconnected and reused as a listener. If a new socket is created from the listener, the context is inherited and vulnerable.

The setsockopt TCP_ULP operation does not require any privilege.

We recommend upgrading past commit 2c02d41d71f90a5168391b6a5f2954112ba2307c

code_evidence: The function rejects only when an ULP is already installed (icsk_ulp_ops set), otherwise it proceeds to call ulp_ops->init(sk) and then stores icsk_ulp_ops.

There is no check on sk->sk_state, so a ULP whose ops lack a clone callback can be attached to a socket already in TCP_LISTEN; init sets up the ULP context (e.g. icsk_ulp_data) that will be copied into accepted children by sk_clone_lock().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The inherited icsk_ulp_data pointer is freed at socket disposal and later reused/freed again by the other socket, matching CWE-416 use-after-free. The missing LISTEN-state guard is the enabling condition, not a separate weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: __tcp_set_ulp permits installing a clone-less ULP on a listening socket, so the listener's ULP context pointer is inherited by cloned child sockets without de-duplication. When either socket is disposed, the shared context is freed twice/used after free; the trigger is setsockopt(TCP_ULP) on a LISTEN socket plus accepting a child.

commit_msg:
Greg Kroah-Hartman says:

====================
Raw socket cleanups

Ori Nimron pointed out that there are a number of places in the kernel
where you can create a raw socket, without having to have the
CAP_NET_RAW permission.

To resolve this, here's a short patch series to test these odd and old
protocols for this permission before allowing the creation to succeed

All patches are currently against the net tree.
====================

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!capable(CAP_NET_RAW))', '\t\t\treturn -EPERM;']}
description: ax25_create in net/ax25/af_ax25.c in the AF_AX25 network module in the Linux kernel 3.16 through 5.3.2 does not enforce CAP_NET_RAW, which means that unprivileged users can create a raw socket, aka CID-0614e2b73768.

code_evidence: The SOCK_RAW case in the socket-type switch only breaks, so creation of a raw AX.25 socket proceeds without any privilege check.

The SOCK_DGRAM branch shows the same switch handling normal socket types; only SOCK_RAW reaches sk_alloc without a capability gate, so no CAP_NET_RAW authorization is enforced before the raw socket is created.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the function performs an action (raw socket creation) without an authorization check on the caller's capability. The missing CAP_NET_RAW gate is a missing authorization constraint, not an input-validation flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
case SOCK_RAW:
break;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SOCK_RAW branch lacks a CAP_NET_RAW capability check, unlike the fixed version that returns -EPERM. Trigger: an unprivileged local user calls socket(PF_AX25, SOCK_RAW, ...). Consequence: the user obtains a raw socket, bypassing the intended privilege restriction on raw protocol access.

commit_msg:
avformat/adtsenc: return value check for init_get_bits in adts_decode_extradata

As the second argument for init_get_bits (buf) can be crafted, a return value check for this function call is necessary.
'buf' is  part of  'AVPacket pkt'.
replace init_get_bits with init_get_bits8.

Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int off;', '    init_get_bits(&gb, buf, size * 8);'], 'added_lines': ['    int off, ret;', '    ret = init_get_bits8(&gb, buf, size);', '    if (ret < 0)', '        return ret;']}
description: adts_decode_extradata in libavformat/adtsenc.c in FFmpeg 4.4 does not check the init_get_bits return value, which is a necessary step because the second argument to init_get_bits can be crafted.

code_evidence: init_get_bits(&gb, buf, size * 8) is called with an attacker-influenced buf and size, but its return value is discarded; no error path exists.
The code immediately proceeds to avpriv_mpeg4audio_get_config2 and then skip_bits_long(&gb, off) and get_bits(&gb, 1) using gb, assuming initialization succeeded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-252 fits because the function omits a return-value check on init_get_bits and continues under the assumption of success. A related weakness such as CWE-20 concerns input validation, but the specific defect here is the unchecked return value enabling use of an invalid state.

evidence_lines.code: init_get_bits(&gb, buf, size * 8);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bit-reader initialization result is ignored, so a crafted buffer that makes init_get_bits fail leaves gb uninitialized or invalid. Trigger: attacker-supplied extradata reaching this function. Consequence: subsequent skip_bits_long/get_bits and ff_copy_pce_data operate on an invalid bit context, leading to unexpected state and possible crash/out-of-bounds reads.

commit_msg:
guest_physmap_remove_page() needs its return value checked

Callers, namely such subsequently freeing the page, must not blindly
assume success - the function may namely fail when needing to shatter a
super page, but there not being memory available for the then needed
intermediate page table.

As it happens, guest_remove_page() callers now also all check the
return value.

Furthermore a missed put_gfn() on an error path in gnttab_transfer() is
also being taken care of.

This is part of XSA-222.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    guest_physmap_remove_page(d, gfn, _mfn(mfn), 0);', '    return GNTST_okay;'], 'added_lines': ['    int rc;', '    rc = guest_physmap_remove_page(d, gfn, _mfn(mfn), 0);', '    return rc ? GNTST_general_error : GNTST_okay;']}
description: Xen through 4.8.x does not validate memory allocations during certain P2M operations, which allows guest OS users to obtain privileged host OS access, aka XSA-222.

code_evidence: Line 8 calls guest_physmap_remove_page() and discards its return value; line 9 unconditionally returns GNTST_okay regardless of whether the P2M removal succeeded (e.g., failure to shatter a super page due to memory allocation failure).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate the outcome/status of an operation whose result is required for safe processing, then returns success anyway—improper validation of a required property (success) leading to unsafe downstream use, matching CWE-20.

evidence_lines.code:
guest_physmap_remove_page(d, gfn, _mfn(mfn), 0);
return GNTST_okay;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return status of guest_physmap_remove_page() is never checked, so an allocation/P2M failure is silently treated as success. Trigger: a guest mapping replacement where the P2M operation fails. Consequence: the caller believes the page was removed and proceeds to free it, leaving a stale P2M mapping that can grant privileged host access.

commit_msg:
blk-mq: fix race between timeout and freeing request

Inside timeout handler, blk_mq_tag_to_rq() is called
to retrieve the request from one tag. This way is obviously
wrong because the request can be freed any time and some
fiedds of the request can't be trusted, then kernel oops
might be triggered[1].

Currently wrt. blk_mq_tag_to_rq(), the only special case is
that the flush request can share same tag with the request
cloned from, and the two requests can't be active at the same
time, so this patch fixes the above issue by updating tags->rqs[tag]
with the active request(either flush rq or the request cloned
from) of the tag.

Also blk_mq_tag_to_rq() gets much simplified with this patch.

Given blk_mq_tag_to_rq() is mainly for drivers and the caller must
make sure the request can't be freed, so in bt_for_each() this
helper is replaced with tags->rqs[tag].

description: In blk_mq_tag_to_rq in blk-mq.c in the upstream kernel, there is a possible use after free due to a race condition when a request has been previously freed by blk_mq_complete_request. This could lead to local escalation of privilege. Product: Android. Versions: Android kernel. Android ID: A-63083046.

code_evidence: The iteration finds busy bits in the tag bitmap and dereferences the request via blk_mq_tag_to_rq(tags, off + bit) at [14], then immediately passes that pointer to fn(rq, data, reserved) at [15]. No lock or reference is held across the lookup-and-call, so the tag-to-request mapping can change concurrently (e.g., timeout handler vs. request completion/free).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a concurrent access to shared tag state without synchronization: the bitmap-derived tag is used to fetch a request that another thread may free in the same window, which is a race condition (CWE-362). The use-after-free is the consequence of that race, not the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the busy-bit scan and the request lookup/callback are not atomic with respect to concurrent tag release, so blk_mq_tag_to_rq can return a request that is being freed. Trigger: a timeout or busy-tag iteration races with blk_mq_complete_request freeing the request. Consequence: the callback dereferences a stale request pointer, causing a kernel oops or use-after-free that may be exploitable for privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
wifi: wilc1000: validate length of IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_CHANNEL_LIST attribute

Validate that the IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_CHANNEL_LIST attribute contains
enough space for a 'struct wilc_attr_oper_ch'. If the attribute is too
small then it can trigger an out-of-bounds write later in the function.

'struct wilc_attr_oper_ch' is variable sized so also check 'attr_len'
does not extend beyond the end of 'buf'.

Signed-off-by: Phil Turnbull <philipturnbull@github.com>
Tested-by: Ajay Kathat <ajay.kathat@microchip.com>
Acked-by: Ajay Kathat <ajay.kathat@microchip.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@kernel.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20221123153543.8568-4-philipturnbull@github.com
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -19,7 +19,8 @@
 		if (index + sizeof(*e) + attr_size > len)
 			return;
 
-		if (e->attr_type == IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_CHANNEL_LIST)
+		if (e->attr_type == IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_CHANNEL_LIST &&
+		    attr_size >= (sizeof(struct wilc_attr_ch_list) - sizeof(*e)))
 			ch_list_idx = index;
 		else if (e->attr_type == IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_OPER_CHANNEL &&
 			 attr_size == (sizeof(struct wilc_attr_oper_ch) - sizeof(*e)))
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (e->attr_type == IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_CHANNEL_LIST)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (e->attr_type == IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_CHANNEL_LIST &&', '\t\t    attr_size >= (sizeof(struct wilc_attr_ch_list) - sizeof(*e)))']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.0.11. Missing validation of IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_CHANNEL_LIST in drivers/net/wireless/microchip/wilc1000/cfg80211.c in the WILC1000 wireless driver can trigger a heap-based buffer overflow when parsing the operating channel attribute from Wi-Fi management frames.

code_evidence: The original check accepts any IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_CHANNEL_LIST attribute regardless of attr_size and records its offset in ch_list_idx.

Later, ch_list is cast from that offset and attr_size is read from ch_list->attr_len; the loop then indexes ch_list->elem + i and calls memset(e->ch_list, sta_ch, e->no_of_channels) using unvalidated no_of_channels.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787): unvalidated length leads directly to memset writing past the allocated buffer. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read because the write in the loop modifies memory beyond bounds.

evidence_lines.code:
if (e->attr_type == IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_CHANNEL_LIST)
ch_list_idx = index;

description: A flaw was found in OpenEXR's Multipart input file functionality. A crafted multi-part input file with no actual parts can trigger a NULL pointer dereference. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

Trigger: a crafted multipart file with no parts. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and process crash, affecting availability.

description: A use-after-free vulnerability exists in NanoMQ 0.17.2. The vulnerability can be triggered by calling the function nni_mqtt_msg_get_publish_property() in the file mqtt_msg.c. This vulnerability is caused by improper data tracing, and an attacker could exploit it to cause a denial of service attack.

description: In libavformat/mov.c in FFmpeg 3.3.3, a DoS in read_tfra() due to lack of an EOF (End of File) check might cause huge CPU and memory consumption. When a crafted MOV file, which claims a large "item_count" field in the header but does not contain sufficient backing data, is provided, the loop would consume huge CPU and memory resources, since there is no EOF check inside the loop.

code_evidence: item_count is read directly from the file at line 29 and used to size the allocation at lines 30-31; there is no check that the file actually contains that many entries.
The loop at line 36 iterates i from 0 to index->item_count, with item_count attacker-controlled from the file.
Each iteration reads time/offset and skips fieldlength-dependent bytes via avio_r8 without any EOF check, so reads past end of stream still advance the loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits because the function performs an iteration whose count is attacker-influenced and not sufficiently limited, causing resource exhaustion. The missing EOF check confirms the loop bound is not tied to real input length, matching Excessive Iteration rather than a mere allocation-size issue.

evidence_lines.code:
for (i = 0; i < index->item_count; i++) {
int64_t time, offset;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound index->item_count comes from a file field and is not constrained by available data or an EOF check. Trigger: a crafted MOV declares a large item_count but supplies little backing data; the loop keeps iterating and calling avio_r8 on exhausted input. Consequence: excessive CPU/memory consumption (DoS), as the loop runs for the claimed count regardless of actual data.

description: ImageMagick 7.0.7-17 Q16 x86_64 has memory leaks in coders/msl.c, related to MSLPopImage and ProcessMSLScript, and associated with mishandling of MSLPushImage calls.

commit_msg:
Fix heap-buffer-overflow in getString

getString is allocating a 4-bytes buffer to store an 'R' and an
8-bit number.

t=malloc(4); /* Rdd */
sprintf(t,"R%d", act->p.RegisterNumber );
return t;

Since up to three digits can be required to store the 8-bit
number, the buffer has to be 5 bytes long.

In this commit we also fix the PUSH_DOUBLE case by dynamically
computing the required buffer size.

This commit fixes #116 (CVE-2018-7867).

commit_msg:

description: Out-of-bounds Read in r_bin_java_bootstrap_methods_attr_new function in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.7.0. The bug causes the program reads data past the end 2f the intented buffer. Typically, this can allow attackers to read sensitive information from other memory locations or cause a crash. More details see [CWE-125: Out-of-bounds read](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/125.html).

code_evidence: After the default attribute is created, offset is advanced by 6 (line 6) without any prior bounds check against sz. Line 9 then calls R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset), reading a two-byte value at offset 6. Because the only bounds check present is in the later loop (line 13), the buffer may be shorter than offset+2, so this read can go past the end of the intended buffer before any size validation occurs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads a ushort from buffer at an offset that can exceed the supplied sz, which is the direct definition of CWE-125 (reading data past the end of the intended buffer). This is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write or a null dereference, matching the target weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the num_bootstrap_methods field is read at a fixed offset before verifying that offset+2 (and the subsequent 8-byte region) fits within sz. Trigger: a crafted class file with a truncated bootstrap_methods attribute. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of buffer, which may crash the parser or disclose adjacent memory; the loop check at line 13 does not protect the earlier read.

commit_msg:
After commit cea0cc80a677 ("sctp: use the right sk after waking up from
wait_buf sleep"), it may change to lock another sk if the asoc has been
peeled off in sctp_wait_for_sndbuf.

However, the asoc's new sk could be already closed elsewhere, as it's in
the sendmsg context of the old sk that can't avoid the new sk's closing.
If the sk's last one refcnt is held by this asoc, later on after putting
this asoc, the new sk will be freed, while under it's own lock.

This patch is to revert that commit, but fix the old issue by returning
error under the old sk's lock.

Fixes: cea0cc80a677 ("sctp: use the right sk after waking up from wait_buf sleep")
Reported-by: syzbot+ac6ea7baa4432811eb50@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Neil Horman <nhorman@tuxdriver.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\terr = sctp_wait_for_sndbuf(asoc, &timeo, msg_len, &sk);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\terr = sctp_wait_for_sndbuf(asoc, &timeo, msg_len);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.14.16. There is a use-after-free in net/sctp/socket.c for a held lock after a peel off, aka CID-a0ff660058b8.

code_evidence: sctp_sendmsg holds sk's lock via lock_sock(sk) at line 82 and later calls sctp_wait_for_sndbuf(asoc, &timeo, msg_len, &sk) at line 235, passing the address of the local sk pointer so the callee may overwrite it after a peel off.
After the wait returns, the error path at lines 236-241 jumps to out_free; lines 284-288 free new_asoc and release_sock(sk), where sk may now reference a different, possibly closed socket.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function references and locks a socket pointer that can be freed by another context, then operates on it after release, which is CWE-416 (use after free). This is not merely a race on stale data; the object's memory can be reclaimed and reused.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sctp_wait_for_sndbuf is allowed to replace the caller's sk with the peeled-off association's new sk, but that new sk may be concurrently closed. Trigger: waiting for send buffer space on an association subject to peel off. Consequence: after the association is freed, the new sk's last reference drops while its lock is held, causing a use-after-free and potential crash or memory corruption.

An invalid encoding value triggers a failure inside the encoding setup path, causing the process to crash. description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.3.4. ksmbd has an out-of-bounds read in smb2_find_context_vals when create_context's name_len is larger than the tag length.

code_evidence: The function calls smb2_find_context_vals(req, SMB2_CREATE_SD_BUFFER) passing only the tag, with no tag length. The callee compares the create_context name_len against the tag using memcmp without a bounded length, so an attacker-controlled name_len larger than the tag causes an out-of-bounds read past the SMB2_CREATE_SD_BUFFER tag.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reading memory beyond the intended tag buffer due to an unbounded length in the comparison, which is a classic out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a write overflow, since no write past bounds occurs.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller does not supply a tag length, so the context-lookup comparison uses the attacker-controlled name_len as the read length. Trigger: a crafted create context whose name_len exceeds the fixed tag size. Consequence: out-of-bounds read in memcmp, leaking adjacent memory or causing a KASAN crash/DoS.

description: An issue was discovered in OpenCV before 4.1.1. There is a NULL pointer dereference in the function cv::XMLParser::parse at modules/core/src/persistence.cpp.

code_evidence: parse() calls skipSpaces(ptr) with the caller-supplied pointer before any NULL check; the subsequent guard at line 4 only validates the value returned by skipSpaces.
If ptr survives, fs->getFS() is invoked and *ptr is dereferenced at line 7 to select the '{' branch, then parseMap is called with the same pointer.
A later check at line 21 again tests ptr, but by then earlier dereferences at line 7 (and inside skipSpaces/parseMap) have already occurred.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function uses a pointer it expects to be valid without a prior NULL check, leading to a NULL dereference. The line-4 guard checks skipSpaces' return value rather than the original input, so it does not prevent the initial dereference.

if( !ptr || !*ptr )
CV_PARSE_ERROR_CPP( "Unexpected End-Of-File" );

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dereferences the incoming ptr (inside skipSpaces and at *ptr in line 7) without first verifying it is non-NULL. Trigger: a caller passing a NULL char* to parse. Supported consequence: a NULL pointer dereference causing a crash/DoS, consistent with the commit adding the missing null check.

commit_msg:
Restrict following symlinks to directories by ownership (CVE-2017-7500)

Only follow directory symlinks owned by target directory owner or root.
This prevents privilege escalation from user-writable directories via
directory symlinks to privileged directories on package upgrade, while
still allowing admin to arrange disk usage with symlinks.

The rationale is that if you can create symlinks owned by user X you *are*
user X (or root), and if you also own directory Y you can do whatever with
it already, including change permissions. So when you create a symlink to
that directory, the link ownership acts as a simple stamp of authority that
you indeed want rpm to treat this symlink as it were the directory that
you own. Such a permission can only be given by you or root, which
is just the way we want it. Plus it's almost ridiculously simple as far
as rules go, compared to trying to calculate something from the
source vs destination directory permissions etc.

In the normal case, the user arranging diskspace with symlinks is indeed
root so nothing changes, the only real change here is to links created by
non-privileged users which should be few and far between in practise.
Unfortunately our test-suite runs as a regular user via fakechroot and
thus the testcase for this fails under the new rules. Adjust the testcase
to get the ownership straight and add a second case for the illegal
behavior, basically the same as the old one but with different expectations.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int fsmVerify(const char *path, rpmfi fi)', '            if (S_ISDIR(dsb.st_mode)) return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['static int fsmVerify(const char *path, rpmfi fi, const struct stat *fsb)', '\t    uid_t luid = dsb.st_uid;', '\t    /* Only permit directory symlinks by target owner and root */', '            if (S_ISDIR(dsb.st_mode) && (luid == 0 || luid == fsb->st_uid))', '\t\t    return 0;']}
description: It was found that rpm did not properly handle RPM installations when a destination path was a symbolic link to a directory, possibly changing ownership and permissions of an arbitrary directory, and RPM files being placed in an arbitrary destination. An attacker, with write access to a directory in which a subdirectory will be installed, could redirect that directory to an arbitrary location and gain root privilege.

code_evidence: When the installed mode is a directory but the on-disk object is a symlink, the code re-stats the path with fsmStat(path, 0, &dsb), which follows the link, and then accepts the result if it resolves to a directory (line 26). The pre-patch logic returns 0 for any directory symlink without checking who owns the link.

The directory branch at lines 19-20 only accepts a real directory; the symlink sub-branch is reached when a symlink stands in for the expected directory, so resolution of the link to an attacker-chosen directory is the path taken.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the function accesses a file based on a path that resolves through a symlink to an unintended resource, and the fix adds an owner constraint (link uid must be root or the target directory owner) to prevent following untrusted links.

evidence_lines.code:
} else if (S_ISDIR(mode)) {
if (S_ISDIR(dsb.st_mode)) return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function resolves a directory symlink via fsmStat with follow enabled and accepts any target directory, without validating the link's owner. Trigger: an attacker who controls a directory in the install path places a symlink to a privileged directory owned by root; fsmVerify returns success, so rpm proceeds to treat the link target as the package directory and changes its ownership/permissions. Consequence: privilege escalation and modification of an arbitrary directory.

commit_msg: Fix a number-up crash bug (Issue #413)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['         i <= chapter_ends[c];'], 'added_lines': ['         i <= chapter_ends[c] && num_outpages < num_pages;']}
description: A flaw was found in htmldoc before v1.9.12. Heap buffer overflow in pspdf_prepare_outpages(), in ps-pdf.cxx may lead to execute arbitrary code and denial of service.

code_evidence: outpages is allocated with exactly num_pages entries (line 8) and num_outpages starts at 0 with outpage pointing to the base (lines 10-11).
The chapter loop at line 54 iterates from chapter_starts[c] to chapter_ends[c] without bounding num_outpages against num_pages; the patch adds that bound.

Inside the loop, outpage is advanced and num_outpages incremented (lines 62-63, 74-76) while outpage->nup and pspdf_transform_page are written for each page, so excess iterations push writes past the malloc'd array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to outpage fields after outpage has been advanced past the end of the malloc(sizeof(outpage_t)*num_pages) buffer, which is a write beyond the intended buffer bounds, matching CWE-787. The missing num_outpages < num_pages guard is the specific constraint whose absence permits the out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop over chapter pages can process more pages than num_pages, so outpage and num_outpages advance beyond the allocated outpages array. Trigger: a document whose chapter_ends span yields more output pages than num_pages. Consequence: outpage->nup and related outpage writes occur past the heap buffer, corrupting memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg: Catch FLI buffer overrun
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['       input buffer (on the other hand, the Python part of the driver', '       makes sure this is always the case) */'], 'added_lines': ['       input buffer */', '    if (bytes < 8) {', '        state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_OVERRUN;', '        return -1;', '    }']}
description: libImaging/FliDecode.c in Pillow before 6.2.2 has an FLI buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Only 4 bytes are guaranteed before reading I32(ptr) at line 12; a chunk shorter than a full header passes this guard.
The frame-type check at line 15 reads I16(ptr+4) and line 19 reads I16(ptr+6) without confirming the buffer holds the 8-byte header; the Python driver is assumed to guarantee this.
After ptr += 16 and bytes -= 16, the chunk loop reads I16(ptr+4) at line 29 and data = ptr+6, guarded only by bytes < 10 at line 24, so a truncated chunk header can be read past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads header fields (I16(ptr+4), I16(ptr+6)) past the end of the caller-provided buffer when the chunk is shorter than the header. This is an out-of-bounds read, not an out-of-bounds write, since the accesses are reads of input data.

evidence_lines.code:
if (bytes < 4)
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The decoder trusts that the input buffer always contains a complete chunk header and reads multi-byte header fields at ptr+4 and ptr+6 after only checking bytes >= 4. A truncated FLI chunk therefore causes I16 reads beyond the supplied buffer, so the root cause is a missing length check before header field access; the consequence is an out-of-bounds read that may crash the process or leak adjacent memory.

commit_msg: Fix for potential buffer overrun if JSON.stringify used with strangely crafted whitespace arg (fix #2114)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      unsigned int s = (unsigned int)jsvGetInteger(space);', '      jsvGetString(space, whitespace, sizeof(whitespace));'], 'added_lines': ['      int s = (int)jsvGetInteger(space);', '      if (s<0) s=0;', '      size_t l = jsvGetString(space, whitespace, sizeof(whitespace)-1);', '      whitespace[l]=0; // add trailing 0']}
description: Espruino 2v10.246 was discovered to contain a stack buffer overflow via src/jsutils.c in vcbprintf.

code_evidence: whitespace is a fixed 11-byte stack buffer (line 5). Numeric space is cast to unsigned int (line 8); a negative integer becomes a huge value, so the s>10 clamp at line 9 does not bound it, and whitespace[s]=0 at line 10 writes out of bounds. The else branch passes sizeof(whitespace)=11 to jsvGetString (line 13), which may fill all 11 bytes without leaving room for a terminator.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the fixed stack buffer whitespace, which is exactly CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The negative-cast and off-by-one are the concrete mechanisms; the resulting memory write beyond the array is the defining weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is missing bounds on the numeric whitespace count and an off-by-one in the string-copy size. Trigger: JSON.stringify with a negative numeric space yields an out-of-bounds write at whitespace[s]; a crafted long string space can fill the buffer with no terminator. Consequence: stack corruption and potential code execution or crash.

commit_msg: Fix #425
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  headers.emplace(key, val);'], 'added_lines': ['  if (!detail::has_crlf(key) && !detail::has_crlf(val.c_str())) {', '    headers.emplace(key, val);', '  }']}
description: cpp-httplib through 0.5.8 does not filter \r\n in parameters passed into the set_redirect and set_header functions, which creates possibilities for CRLF injection and HTTP response splitting in some specific contexts.

code_evidence: set_header accepts an externally influenced key and val and passes them unchanged into headers.emplace, with no check for CR/LF characters in either argument.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits because externally influenced input is incorporated into an output record (the HTTP header set) without neutralizing special elements that the downstream HTTP component interprets. The CRLF injection is a specific realization of this injection class; the function directly performs the unneutralized construction.

Trigger: a caller supplies a key or value containing \r\n. commit_msg:
Commit a23740ec43ba ("bpf: Track contents of read-only maps as scalars") is
checking whether maps are read-only both from BPF program side and user space
side, and then, given their content is constant, reading out their data via
map->ops->map_direct_value_addr() which is then subsequently used as known
scalar value for the register, that is, it is marked as __mark_reg_known()
with the read value at verification time. Before a23740ec43ba, the register
content was marked as an unknown scalar so the verifier could not make any
assumptions about the map content.

The current implementation however is prone to a TOCTOU race, meaning, the
value read as known scalar for the register is not guaranteed to be exactly
the same at a later point when the program is executed, and as such, the
prior made assumptions of the verifier with regards to the program will be
invalid which can cause issues such as OOB access, etc.

While the BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG map flag is always fixed and required to be
specified at map creation time, the map->frozen property is initially set to
false for the map given the map value needs to be populated, e.g. for global
data sections. Once complete, the loader "freezes" the map from user space
such that no subsequent updates/deletes are possible anymore. For the rest
of the lifetime of the map, this freeze one-time trigger cannot be undone
anymore after a successful BPF_MAP_FREEZE cmd return. Meaning, any new BPF_*
cmd calls which would update/delete map entries will be rejected with -EPERM
since map_get_sys_perms() removes the FMODE_CAN_WRITE permission. This also
means that pending update/delete map entries must still complete before this
guarantee is given. This corner case is not an issue for loaders since they
create and prepare such program private map in successive steps.

However, a malicious user is able to trigger this TOCTOU race in two different
ways: i) via userfaultfd, and ii) via batched updates. For i) userfaultfd is
used to expand the competition interval, so that map_update_elem() can modify
the contents of the map after map_freeze() and bpf_prog_load() were executed.
This works, because userfaultfd halts the parallel thread which triggered a
map_update_elem() at the time where we copy key/value from the user buffer and
this already passed the FMODE_CAN_WRITE capability test given at that time the
map was not "frozen". Then, the main thread performs the map_freeze() and
bpf_prog_load(), and once that had completed successfully, the other thread
is woken up to complete the pending map_update_elem() which then changes the
map content. For ii) the idea of the batched update is similar, meaning, when
there are a large number of updates to be processed, it can increase the
competition interval between the two. It is therefore possible in practice to
modify the contents of the map after executing map_freeze() and bpf_prog_load().

One way to fix both i) and ii) at the same time is to expand the use of the
map's map->writecnt. The latter was introduced in fc9702273e2e ("bpf: Add mmap()
support for BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY") and further refined in 1f6cb19be2e2 ("bpf:
Prevent re-mmap()'ing BPF map as writable for initially r/o mapping") with
the rationale to make a writable mmap()'ing of a map mutually exclusive with
read-only freezing. The counter indicates writable mmap() mappings and then
prevents/fails the freeze operation. Its semantics can be expanded beyond
just mmap() by generally indicating ongoing write phases. This would essentially
span any parallel regular and batched flavor of update/delete operation and
then also have map_freeze() fail with -EBUSY. For the check_mem_access() in
the verifier we expand upon the bpf_map_is_rdonly() check ensuring that all
last pending writes have completed via bpf_map_write_active() test. Once the
map->frozen is set and bpf_map_write_active() indicates a map->writecnt of 0
only then we are really guaranteed to use the map's data as known constants.
For map->frozen being set and pending writes in process of still being completed
we fall back to marking that register as unknown scalar so we don't end up
making assumptions about it. With this, both TOCTOU reproducers from i) and
ii) are fixed.

Note that the map->writecnt has been converted into a atomic64 in the fix in
order to avoid a double freeze_mutex mutex_{un,}lock() pair when updating
map->writecnt in the various map update/delete BPF_* cmd flavors. Spanning
the freeze_mutex over entire map update/delete operations in syscall side
would not be possible due to then causing everything to be serialized.
Similarly, something like synchronize_rcu() after setting map->frozen to wait
for update/deletes to complete is not possible either since it would also
have to span the user copy which can sleep. On the libbpf side, this won't
break d66562fba1ce ("libbpf: Add BPF object skeleton support") as the
anonymous mmap()-ed "map initialization image" is remapped as a BPF map-backed
mmap()-ed memory where for .rodata it's non-writable.

Fixes: a23740ec43ba ("bpf: Track contents of read-only maps as scalars")
Reported-by: w1tcher.bupt@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Andrii Nakryiko <andrii@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tbpf_map_write_active_inc(map);', '\tbpf_map_write_active_dec(map);']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernel's ebpf verifier between bpf_map_update_elem and bpf_map_freeze due to a missing lock in kernel/bpf/syscall.c. In this flaw, a local user with a special privilege (cap_sys_admin or cap_bpf) can modify the frozen mapped address space. This flaw affects kernel versions prior to 5.16 rc2.

code_evidence: The function obtains the map and validates write permission via map_get_sys_perms() & FMODE_CAN_WRITE at lines 17-20, then proceeds to copy the user value (line 37) and call bpf_map_update_value (line 39). The permission check and the actual map update are separated by copy_from_bpfptr, which can block on a userfaultfd page fault, widening the race window.
The err_put cleanup path at lines 44-45 releases the fd without any write-active accounting; the patch adds bpf_map_write_active_inc/dec to bracket the check-to-update window.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function checks the map's writability state before use but the state can change before the update is applied, exactly matching a TOCTOU race (CWE-367). The missing write-active accounting allows concurrent freeze/update interleavings, distinguishing it from a plain missing-authorization weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The permission check (FMODE_CAN_WRITE) occurs at line 17, but the map update at line 39 happens later after a user-copy that can sleep. A concurrent thread can freeze the map between check and use, so the update proceeds against a map the verifier later treats as read-only constant data, invalidating verifier assumptions and enabling out-of-bounds access.

commit_msg:
Prevent nullptr deref in SparseTensorSliceDataset

The arguments must determine a valid sparse tensor. This means that when indices are empty then the values must be empty too (and the reverse).

Also added test, by modifying existing test with empty sparse tensor to now run with an invalid sparse tensor input.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 388562757
Change-Id: Id8b54cd7c2316025b4f9a77292c8fb5344d17609
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    const auto num_indices = indices->NumElements();', '    const auto num_values = values->NumElements();', '    if (num_indices == 0 || num_values == 0) {', '      OP_REQUIRES(ctx, num_indices == num_values,', '                  errors::InvalidArgument(', '                      "If indices or values are empty, the other one must also "', '                      "be. Got indices of shape ",', '                      indices->shape().DebugString(), " and values of shape ",', '                      values->shape().DebugString()));', '    }']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. When a user does not supply arguments that determine a valid sparse tensor, `tf.raw_ops.SparseTensorSliceDataset` implementation can be made to dereference a null pointer. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/8d72537c6abf5a44103b57b9c2e22c14f5f49698/tensorflow/core/kernels/data/sparse_tensor_slice_dataset_op.cc#L240-L251) has some argument validation but fails to consider the case when either `indices` or `values` are provided for an empty sparse tensor when the other is not. If `indices` is empty, then [code that performs validation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/8d72537c6abf5a44103b57b9c2e22c14f5f49698/tensorflow/core/kernels/data/sparse_tensor_slice_dataset_op.cc#L260-L261) (i.e., checking that the indices are monotonically increasing) results in a null pointer dereference. If `indices` as provided by the user is empty, then `indices` in the C++ code above is backed by an empty `std::vector`, hence calling `indices->dim_size(0)` results in null pointer dereferencing (same as calling `std::vector::at()` on an empty vector). We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 02cc160e29d20631de3859c6653184e3f876b9d7. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function fetches the user-supplied indices and values tensors without checking whether either is empty relative to the other.
Only shape-rank validation is done on indices; an empty indices tensor still passes the IsMatrix check.
The loop reads indices->dim_size(0) and then dereferences indices->matrix<int64>()(i, 0), relying on indices being non-empty.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is a missing constraint that indices and values are both empty or both non-empty, allowing a dereference of an empty (null-backed) tensor. This directly matches CWE-476; it is not merely a validation bug because the supported consequence is a null pointer dereference causing a crash.

evidence_lines.code:
OP_REQUIRES(ctx, TensorShapeUtils::IsMatrix(indices->shape()),
errors::InvalidArgument(
"Input indices should be a matrix but received shape ",
indices->shape().DebugString()));

for (int64_t i = 0; i < indices->dim_size(0); ++i) {
int64_t next_batch_index = indices->matrix<int64>()(i, 0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When the user supplies an empty indices tensor together with a non-empty values tensor, the missing consistency check lets execution reach the loop. The empty indices tensor backs no elements, so dereferencing it via dim_size(0)/matrix access yields a null pointer dereference, crashing the process.

commit_msg:
Fix underscore lookahead in hex literal parsing

This patch fixes #4442.

JerryScript-DCO-1.0-Signed-off-by: Robert Fancsik frobert@inf.u-szeged.hu
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['          if (!lit_char_is_hex_digit (source_p[0]) || source_p == source_end_p)'], 'added_lines': ['          if (source_p == source_end_p || !lit_char_is_hex_digit (source_p[0]))']}
description: An issue was discovered in JerryScript 2.4.0. There is a heap-buffer-overflow in lexer_parse_number in js-lexer.c file.

code_evidence: After consuming an underscore at line 40, source_p is incremented. Line 41 evaluates lit_char_is_hex_digit(source_p[0]) before checking source_p == source_end_p; the bounds check is on the right of ||, so the short-circuit does not protect the read when source_p equals source_end_p, dereferencing one past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 covers out-of-bounds memory access caused by a missing/incorrect bounds constraint; here the check ordering permits reading past the intended buffer. The consequence is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write, but the defect is the same boundary-check failure the target CWE addresses.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the operand order in the compound condition dereferences source_p[0] before the end-of-buffer test. Trigger: a hexadecimal literal ending with an underscore, e.g. '0x1_', makes source_p reach source_end_p after line 40. The out-of-bounds read of source_p[0] follows, matching the reported heap-buffer-overflow in lexer_parse_number; the patch reorders the checks to test the bound first.

commit_msg:
xen/hypercall: Don't use BUG() for parameter checking in hypercall_create_continuation()

Since c/s 1d429034 "hypercall: update vcpu_op to take an unsigned vcpuid",
which incorrectly swapped 'i' for 'u' in the parameter type list, guests have
been able to hit the BUG() in next_args()'s default case.

Correct these back to 'i'.

In addition, make adjustments to prevent this class of issue from occurring in
the future - crashing Xen is not an appropriate form of parameter checking.

Capitalise NEXT_ARG() to catch all uses, to highlight that it is a macro doing
non-function-like things behind the scenes, and undef it when appropriate.
Implement a bad_fmt: block which prints an error, asserts unreachable, and
crashes the guest.

On the ARM side, drop all parameter checking of p.  It is asymmetric with the
x86 side, and akin to expecting memcpy() or sprintf() to check their src/fmt
parameter before use.  A caller passing "" or something other than a string
literal will be obvious during code review.

This is XSA-296.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            mcs->call.args[i] = next_arg(p, args);', '                arg = next_arg(p, args);', '                arg = next_arg(p, args);'], 'added_lines': ['            mcs->call.args[i] = NEXT_ARG(p, args);', '                arg = NEXT_ARG(p, args);', '                arg = NEXT_ARG(p, args);', '', ' bad_fmt:', '    gprintk(XENLOG_ERR, "Bad hypercall continuation format \'%c\'\\n", *p);', '    ASSERT_UNREACHABLE();', '    domain_crash(curr->domain);', '    return 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service via a VCPUOP_initialise hypercall. hypercall_create_continuation() is a variadic function which uses a printf-like format string to interpret its parameters. Error handling for a bad format character was done using BUG(), which crashes Xen. One path, via the VCPUOP_initialise hypercall, has a bad format character. The BUG() can be hit if VCPUOP_initialise executes for a sufficiently long period of time for a continuation to be created. Malicious guests may cause a hypervisor crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS). Xen versions 4.6 and newer are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.5 and earlier are not vulnerable. Only x86 PV guests can exploit the vulnerability. HVM and PVH guests, and guests on ARM systems, cannot exploit the vulnerability.

code_evidence: The function takes a caller-supplied `const char *format` (line 6), initializes va_list (line 11), and iterates `*p` through the format, calling next_arg(p, args) for each character (lines 15, 25, 41).

The iteration consumes format characters to pull variadic arguments and place them into guest registers; an unrecognized character reaches next_arg's default case (BUG in the pre-patch code), and the patched version routes to bad_fmt.

There is no validation that format is a trusted literal; the format drives argument interpretation and can be reached via guest hypercall continuations (e.g., VCPUOP_initialise), leading to a hypervisor crash.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-134 fits because the function treats its format argument as a control string that selects how variadic arguments are consumed; the weakness is unsafe interpretation of an externally-influenced format string, not merely a bad parameter value. The crash is the supported consequence of that format-string handling flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
va_end(args);
return op;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: hypercall_create_continuation interprets a format string via next_arg without constraining it to known characters, so a malformed externally-influenced format (e.g., 'u' vs 'i' from a guest-driven continuation) hits the unsupported-character path. Trigger: a guest causes a continuation with an unexpected format character. Consequence: BUG()/assertion crashes Xen, a denial of service.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.7-16 Q16, a memory leak vulnerability was found in the function GetImagePixelCache in magick/cache.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted MNG image file that is processed by ReadOneMNGImage.

code_evidence: The function clones the pixel cache into clone_image.cache (line 50) and opens it with OpenPixelCache (line 52). This is a resource-release defect rather than a use-after-free or out-of-bounds issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failure path after OpenPixelCache/ClonePixelCacheRepository does not release the newly cloned cache. Trigger: a crafted MNG image causes OpenPixelCache or the clone repository operation to fail. Consequence: the clone cache allocation is leaked, and repeated processing consumes memory leading to denial of service.

commit_msg:
x86: don't store possibly stale TLB flush time stamp

While the timing window is extremely narrow, it is theoretically
possible for an update to the TLB flush clock and a subsequent flush
IPI to happen between the read and write parts of the update of the
per-page stamp. Exclude this possibility by disabling interrupts
across the update, preventing the IPI to be serviced in the middle.

This is XSA-241.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        sp->tlbflush_timestamp = tlbflush_current_time();'], 'added_lines': ['        page_set_tlbflush_timestamp(sp);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to execute arbitrary code on the host OS because of a race condition that can cause a stale TLB entry.

code_evidence: Line 33 clears the shadow page's type/head fields and line 34 writes a new TLB-flush timestamp, updating shared per-page state without disabling interrupts. The commit replaces this with page_set_tlbflush_timestamp(), which performs the update atomically with respect to IPIs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the shared page state is updated in a sequence requiring exclusive access, but an interfering concurrent IPI can interleave within the timing window. This is a race condition rather than merely a stale-data bug, since the defect is the missing interrupt exclusion around the update.

evidence_lines.code:
sp->u.sh.type = sp->u.sh.head = 0;
sp->tlbflush_timestamp = tlbflush_current_time();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The read-then-write of tlbflush_timestamp is not atomic against a concurrent TLB-flush IPI; an interrupt serviced between reading the clock and storing it can cause a stale timestamp to be retained. The stale per-page stamp may allow reuse of a page whose TLB entry was not properly flushed, potentially enabling a guest to execute host code.

commit_msg:
Bug 757711: heap-buffer-overflow in xmlFAParsePosCharGroup <https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=757711>

* xmlregexp.c:
(xmlFAParseCharRange): Only advance to the next character if
there is no error.  Advancing to the next character in case of
an error while parsing regexp leads to an out of bounds access.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    NEXTL(len);'], 'added_lines': ['', '        NEXTL(len);']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the xmlFAParsePosCharGroup function in libxml2 before 2.9.4, as used in Apple iOS before 9.3.2, OS X before 10.11.5, tvOS before 9.2.1, and watchOS before 2.2.1, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted XML document.

code_evidence: After parsing the range end, the code calls CUR_SCHAR(ctxt->cur, len) at line 64 to decode a multibyte character and set len, then unconditionally executes NEXTL(len) at line 69 to advance the input pointer by len bytes. The function performs no check that the decoded character actually fits within the remaining regexp buffer before advancing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the unchecked pointer advance causes memory operations outside the intended buffer boundary. It is not merely a logic error in range ordering; the concrete consequence is an out-of-bounds memory access, which is the defining characteristic of CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pointer advancement NEXTL(len) occurs before validating the parsed range, so when the end character is a truncated/invalid multibyte sequence (or end < start), len can exceed the remaining buffer. Trigger: a crafted XML schema regexp char range such as [a-<truncated multibyte>. Consequence: ctxt->cur advances past the allocated buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read/write (heap-buffer-overflow).

commit_msg:

file_copy_fallback creates new files with default permissions and
set the correct permissions after the operation is finished. This
might cause that the files can be accessible by more users during
the operation than expected. Use G_FILE_CREATE_PRIVATE for the new
files to limit access to those files.

Fix an integer overflow issue in png.c

This aims to fix https://github.com/matthiaskramm/swftools/issues/13
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t', '    data2 = (unsigned char*)malloc(header.width*header.height*4);'], 'added_lines': ['', '    unsigned long long alloclen_64 = (unsigned long long)header.width * header.height * 4;', '    if (alloclen_64 > 0xffffffffl) {', '        return 0;', '    }', '    data2 = (unsigned char*)malloc((size_t)alloclen_64);']}
description: In SWFTools 0.9.2, an out-of-bounds write of heap data can occur in the function png_load() in lib/png.c:755. This issue can be triggered by a malformed PNG file that is mishandled by png2swf. Attackers could exploit this issue for DoS; it might cause arbitrary code execution.

code_evidence: Line 96 allocates data2 using malloc(header.width*header.height*4) with all operands as unsigned int; the multiplication is performed in 32-bit arithmetic and can wrap to a small value.

The later loops index data2 using the original width/height: dest = &data2[(y*header.width)*4] at 109 and 142, and the palette path writes at y*header.width*4+x*4 at 247, all beyond the truncated allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a buffer whose size is computed with a wrapped integer and then writes past that buffer's end, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The integer overflow is the enabling cause, but the directly supported weakness at this site is the resulting out-of-bounds heap write.

evidence_lines.code: data2 = (unsigned char*)malloc(header.width*header.height*4);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size computation header.width*header.height*4 overflows in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic before being passed to malloc, producing an undersized heap buffer. A malformed PNG declaring large dimensions triggers a small allocation, after which the decode loops write rows at width/height-derived offsets past the buffer end, corrupting heap memory and supporting DoS or code execution.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13690/IKEv2: Fix some bounds checks.

Use a pointer of the correct type in ND_TCHECK(), or use ND_TCHECK2()
and provide the correct length.

While we're at it, remove the blank line between some checks and the
UNALIGNED_MEMCPY()s they protect.

Also, note the places where we print the entire payload.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* Print the entire payload in hex */']}
description: The IKEv2 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isakmp.c, several functions.

code_evidence: ND_TCHECK(*p) validates only sizeof(*p) bytes at ext, while the subsequent UNALIGNED_MEMCPY copies sizeof(cert) bytes from ext into the local cert; the check does not cover the copied range.
rawprint reads item_len - 4 bytes starting at ext + 1 without any preceding bounds check on that region; item_len is taken from the packet rather than validated against the captured buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the intended buffer because ND_TCHECK validates fewer bytes than the subsequent copies/reads consume and rawprint reads item_len - 4 bytes unchecked. This is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), not a write or integer issue.

evidence_lines.code:
ND_TCHECK(*p);
UNALIGNED_MEMCPY(&cert, ext, sizeof(cert));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds checks use the wrong type/length and do not cover the bytes actually read. Trigger: a crafted IKEv1 CR payload whose declared item_len exceeds the captured data. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads via UNALIGNED_MEMCPY and rawprint, potentially leaking memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
gnttab: correct pin status fixup for copy

Regardless of copy operations only setting GNTPIN_hst*, GNTPIN_dev*
also need to be taken into account when deciding whether to clear
_GTF_{read,writ}ing. At least for consistency with code elsewhere the
read part better doesn't use any mask at all.

This is XSA-230.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( !(act->pin & GNTPIN_hstw_mask) )', '    if ( !(act->pin & GNTPIN_hstr_mask) )'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( !(act->pin & (GNTPIN_hstw_mask | GNTPIN_devw_mask)) )', '    if ( !act->pin )']}
description: Xen maintains the _GTF_{read,writ}ing bits as appropriate, to inform the guest that a grant is in use. A guest is expected not to modify the grant details while it is in use, whereas the guest is free to modify/reuse the grant entry when it is not in use. Under some circumstances, Xen will clear the status bits too early, incorrectly informing the guest that the grant is no longer in use. A guest may prematurely believe that a granted frame is safely private again, and reuse it in a way which contains sensitive information, while the domain on the far end of the grant is still using the grant. Xen 4.9, 4.8, 4.7, 4.6, and 4.5 are affected.

code_evidence: The write-side guard only tests GNTPIN_hstw_mask, so a grant pinned solely by a device (GNTPIN_devw_mask) is treated as unpinned and _GTF_writing is cleared.
The read-side guard only tests GNTPIN_hstr_mask; other pin bits (e.g. device read pins) are ignored, so _GTF_reading can be cleared while the grant remains in use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The premature clearing of in-use status lets a guest reclaim and reuse a frame still referenced by another domain, disclosing that domain's sensitive contents to the guest; this is a resultant confidentiality exposure matching CWE-200.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( !(act->pin & GNTPIN_hstw_mask) )
gnttab_clear_flag(_GTF_writing, status);

if ( !(act->pin & GNTPIN_hstr_mask) )
gnttab_clear_flag(_GTF_reading, status);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the status-fixup checks use incomplete pin masks, clearing _GTF_{read,writ}ing while a device-side pin still references the grant. Trigger: a copy operation on a device-pinned grant. Consequence: the guest is told the frame is no longer in use and may reuse it, exposing data still accessed by the far-end domain.

See https://github.com/wernsey/bitmap/issues/1

description: wernsey/bitmap before 2018-08-18 allows a NULL pointer dereference via a 4-bit image.

The loop body dereferences b->clip.x0/b->clip.x1/b->clip.y0/b->clip.y1 and passes b to BM_SET, which reads b->color, for every plotted pixel.

commit_msg:
PyACL - Fixing integer overflows that occur when resizing ACLs

Fixes #1700
CVE-2021-32559
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        unsigned short required_size =', '            pdacl->AclSize + sizeof(ACCESS_ALLOWED_OBJECT_ACE) + (unsigned short)GetLengthSid(psid);', '        pdacl_padded->AclSize = required_size;'], 'added_lines': ['        unsigned int required_size = pdacl->AclSize + sizeof(ACCESS_ALLOWED_OBJECT_ACE) + GetLengthSid(psid);', '        // max ACL size is USHRT_MAX', '        if (required_size > USHRT_MAX)', '            return PyErr_Format(PyExc_OverflowError, "%s: adding ACE would put ACL over size limit", funcname);', '        pdacl_padded->AclSize = (unsigned short)required_size;']}
description: An integer overflow exists in pywin32 prior to version b301 when adding an access control entry (ACE) to an access control list (ACL) that would cause the size to be greater than 65535 bytes. An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could crash the vulnerable process.

code_evidence: The required ACL size is computed as pdacl->AclSize + sizeof(ACCESS_ALLOWED_OBJECT_ACE) + GetLengthSid(psid) and stored in an unsigned short; both the addition and the GetLengthSid cast are truncated to 16 bits.
The truncated required_size is passed directly to malloc and later written into pdacl_padded->AclSize, so the allocated buffer and recorded size derive from the wrapped value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-190: a 16-bit size calculation wraps because the logic assumes the sum fits, and the wrapped value is then used for allocation and copying. It is not merely a buffer overflow (CWE-120), since the root cause is the unchecked integer wraparound in the size computation.

evidence_lines.code: pdacl_padded->AclSize = required_size;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: If the existing ACL size plus the ACE and SID lengths exceed 65535, the unsigned short computation wraps to a small value. malloc then allocates a buffer smaller than needed while pdacl_padded->AclSize records the wrapped size, and memcpy writes pdacl->AclSize bytes into it, causing a heap overflow that can crash the process.

commit_msg:
jfs: prevent NULL deref in diFree

Add validation check for JFS_IP(ipimap)->i_imap to prevent a NULL deref
in diFree since diFree uses it without do any validations.
When function jfs_mount calls diMount to initialize fileset inode
allocation map, it can fail and JFS_IP(ipimap)->i_imap won't be
initialized. Then it calls diFreeSpecial to close fileset inode allocation
map inode and it will flow into jfs_evict_inode. Function jfs_evict_inode
just validates JFS_SBI(inode->i_sb)->ipimap, then calls diFree. diFree use
JFS_IP(ipimap)->i_imap directly, then it will cause a NULL deref.

Reported-by: TCS Robot <tcs_robot@tencent.com>
Signed-off-by: Haimin Zhang <tcs_kernel@tencent.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Kleikamp <dave.kleikamp@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (JFS_SBI(inode->i_sb)->ipimap)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tstruct inode *ipimap = JFS_SBI(inode->i_sb)->ipimap;', '\t\t\tif (ipimap && JFS_IP(ipimap)->i_imap)']}
description: A NULL pointer dereference flaw in diFree in fs/jfs/inode.c in Journaled File System (JFS)in the Linux kernel. This could allow a local attacker to crash the system or leak kernel internal information.

code_evidence: The fileset-inode branch checks only that JFS_SBI(inode->i_sb)->ipimap is non-NULL before calling diFree(inode); it does not verify that JFS_IP(ipimap)->i_imap, the inner imap structure used inside diFree, has been initialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function passes an inode into diFree without validating the inner i_imap pointer that diFree dereferences, so a NULL pointer is used as valid. This matches CWE-476, a NULL pointer dereference; it is not merely a missing error return, since the flaw is the unchecked NULL used downstream.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: diFree is invoked based solely on the outer ipimap pointer being set, even though the inner i_imap may remain NULL after a failed diMount during jfs_mount. Trigger: eviction of a fileset inode in that partially initialized state reaches line 12. Consequence: diFree dereferences the NULL i_imap, causing a kernel NULL pointer dereference and crash (with possible memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
Prevent divisions by 0

PiperOrigin-RevId: 371003153
Change-Id: Idef56c95b9fcaeb97f87e18c7a674dbeb5173204
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  const int input_size = NumElements(input) / SizeOfDimension(input, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, batch_size != 0);', '  const int input_size = NumElements(input) / batch_size;']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The implementation of the `DepthwiseConv` TFLite operator is vulnerable to a division by zero error(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/1a8e885b864c818198a5b2c0cbbeca5a1e833bc8/tensorflow/lite/kernels/depthwise_conv.cc#L287-L288). An attacker can craft a model such that `input`'s fourth dimension would be 0. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 10 computes input_size by dividing NumElements(input) by SizeOfDimension(input, 0); the divisor is the input's batch dimension and is not checked to be nonzero before the division.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because the function performs a division whose divisor derives directly from model-controlled tensor dimensions and lacks a zero check; this is a divide-by-zero, not merely a bounds or shape error.

evidence_lines.code:
const int input_size = NumElements(input) / SizeOfDimension(input, 0);
const int batch_size = SizeOfDimension(input, 0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the batch dimension (SizeOfDimension(input, 0)) is used as a divisor without verifying it is nonzero. Trigger: an attacker crafts a model whose input tensor has a zero first dimension, so SizeOfDimension returns 0 and NumElements/0 is evaluated. Supported consequence: integer division by zero, causing a crash or undefined behavior (availability DoS).

commit_msg: added option to disable trivial auth methods
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcli_ses.is_trivial_auth = 1;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Dropbear through 2020.81. Due to a non-RFC-compliant check of the available authentication methods in the client-side SSH code, it is possible for an SSH server to change the login process in its favor. This attack can bypass additional security measures such as FIDO2 tokens or SSH-Askpass. Thus, it allows an attacker to abuse a forwarded agent for logging on to another server unnoticed.

code_evidence: cli_session_init resets authentication session state: lastprivkey is cleared and lastauthtype is set to 0, initializing the client-side auth bookkeeping before any server-driven authentication exchange occurs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the weakness is insufficient proof/validation of an authentication claim: the client's auth state is initialized and later trusted without properly verifying the server's advertised methods, letting an attacker alter the authentication process. It is not merely a credential-storage issue.

evidence_lines.code:
cli_ses.lastprivkey = NULL;
cli_ses.lastauthtype = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function initializes authentication-related session fields without any constraint tying them to server-advertised or previously completed authentication methods. In the client-side SSH flow, this state is subsequently used while processing the server's authentication method list; a non-RFC-compliant check allows the server to influence the login process, so an attacker-controlled server can steer authentication toward a weaker or unintended method, bypassing FIDO2 or SSH-Askpass protections and enabling agent-forwarding abuse.

commit_msg:
Clean up handling of counted blobs of bytes.

Don't treat the count+blob as itself a blob of bytes; use FT_NONE.
Create it with an unknown length (-1, meaning "to end of packet, for
now"), and set its length once we've finished dissecting it.  Dissect
the raw bytes of a prefixed-bytes item regardless of whether we're
building a protocol tree or not.

This means we do a better job of handling a too-large length; instead of
overflowing the offset, we throw an exception and stop dissecting, so we
don't run the risk of looping infinitely.

Bug: 14841

Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/28228
Reviewed-by: Guy Harris <guy@alum.mit.edu>
(cherry picked from commit a03eacc7aabd04a6fd0db978e0d7597220ac0515)
