commit_msg:
Fix invalid read in gdImageCreateFromTiffPtr()

tiff_invalid_read.tiff is corrupt, and causes an invalid read in
gdImageCreateFromTiffPtr(), but not in gdImageCreateFromTiff(). The culprit
is dynamicGetbuf(), which doesn't check for out-of-bound reads. In this case,
dynamicGetbuf() is called with a negative dp->pos, but also positive buffer
overflows have to be handled, in which case 0 has to be returned (cf. commit
75e29a9).

Fixing dynamicGetbuf() exhibits that the corrupt TIFF would still create
the image, because the return value of TIFFReadRGBAImage() is not checked.
We do that, and let createFromTiffRgba() fail if TIFFReadRGBAImage() fails.

This issue had been reported by Ibrahim El-Sayed to security@libgd.org.

CVE-2016-6911
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tTIFFReadRGBAImage(tif, width, height, buffer, 0);', '\tfor(y = 0; y < height; y++) {', '\t\tfor(x = 0; x < width; x++) {', "\t\t\t/* if it doesn't already exist, allocate a new colour,", '\t\t\t * else use existing one */', '\t\t\trgba = buffer[(y * width + x)];', '\t\t\ta = (0xff - TIFFGetA(rgba)) / 2;', '\t\t\tcolor = gdTrueColorAlpha(TIFFGetR(rgba), TIFFGetG(rgba), TIFFGetB(rgba), a);', '', '\t\t\t/* set pixel colour to this colour */', '\t\t\tgdImageSetPixel(im, x, height - y - 1, color);', '\treturn GD_SUCCESS;'], 'added_lines': ['\tint success;', '\tsuccess = TIFFReadRGBAImage(tif, width, height, buffer, 1);', '\tif (success) {', '\t\tfor(y = 0; y < height; y++) {', '\t\t\tfor(x = 0; x < width; x++) {', "\t\t\t\t/* if it doesn't already exist, allocate a new colour,", '\t\t\t\t * else use existing one */', '\t\t\t\trgba = buffer[(y * width + x)];', '\t\t\t\ta = (0xff - TIFFGetA(rgba)) / 2;', '\t\t\t\tcolor = gdTrueColorAlpha(TIFFGetR(rgba), TIFFGetG(rgba), TIFFGetB(rgba), a);', '\t', '\t\t\t\t/* set pixel colour to this colour */', '\t\t\t\tgdImageSetPixel(im, x, height - y - 1, color);', '\t\t\t}', '\treturn success;']}
description: The dynamicGetbuf function in the GD Graphics Library (aka libgd) before 2.2.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted TIFF image.

code_evidence: Line 17 calls TIFFReadRGBAImage() without checking its return value; on a corrupt TIFF the call can fail and leave buffer partially or wholly uninitialized. The nested loops at lines 18-25 then read buffer[(y * width + x)] for every pixel and pass the derived values to TIFFGetA/TIFFGetR/TIFFGetG and gdImageSetPixel, consuming data the decoder did not validly produce.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unchecked decode failure causes reads of buffer elements beyond the valid decoded data, i.e., data read outside the intended buffer contents. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder's failure status is ignored, so the pixel loop reads from a buffer whose contents were not populated by a failed TIFFReadRGBAImage(). Trigger: a crafted/corrupt TIFF image whose decode fails. Consequence: out-of-bounds or uninitialized reads during pixel extraction, leading to a crash/denial of service (as described for CVE-2016-6911).

commit_msg: [codec,nsc] fix input length validation
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcontext->PlanesSize = total;']}
description: FreeRDP is a free implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), released under the Apache license. Affected versions are subject to an Out-Of-Bounds Read in the `nsc_rle_decompress_data` function. The Out-Of-Bounds Read occurs because it processes `context->Planes` without  checking if it contains data of sufficient length. Should an attacker be able to leverage this vulnerability they may be able to cause a crash. This issue has been addressed in versions 2.11.0 and 3.0.0-beta3. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: Reads four PlaneByteCount values and accumulates them into total, but performs no per-field or overflow check before use.
Sets context->Planes to the stream pointer and only then validates that total bytes remain; the pointer is stored before the length check succeeds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function establishes a data pointer and size derived from untrusted length fields, enabling downstream reads beyond the intended buffer, which is CWE-125. It is not CWE-190 because no arithmetic overflow is demonstrated; the weakness is the unchecked read length.

evidence_lines.code:
context->Planes = Stream_Pointer(s);
return Stream_CheckAndLogRequiredLengthWLog(context->priv->log, s, total);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the plane pointer is captured and the aggregate size derived from attacker-controlled PlaneByteCount fields without validating that the remaining stream actually contains that many bytes before the pointer is trusted. Trigger: a crafted NSC stream with PlaneByteCount values exceeding the available data. Consequence: later decompression reads past the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and possible crash.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  registry_info=(RegistryInfo *) AcquireMagickMemory(sizeof(*registry_info));', '  if (registry_info == (RegistryInfo *) NULL)', '    ThrowFatalException(ResourceLimitFatalError,"MemoryAllocationFailed");'], 'added_lines': ['  registry_info=(RegistryInfo *) AcquireCriticalMemory(sizeof(*registry_info));']}
description: In the GetOpenCLCachedFilesDirectory function in magick/opencl.c in ImageMagick 7.0.7, a NULL pointer dereference vulnerability occurs because a memory allocation result is not checked, related to GetOpenCLCacheDirectory.

code_evidence: AcquireMagickMemory returns registry_info unguarded; the only NULL check calls ThrowFatalException, which is not a return path, so execution proceeds to ResetMagickMemory(registry_info,...) and later registry_info->type/value/signature assignments.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: A pointer expected to be valid is dereferenced after an unchecked allocation, matching CWE-476. The patch replaces the call with AcquireCriticalMemory, which enforces allocation success, confirming the missing NULL-handling constraint rather than a different memory-safety class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation result is not reliably validated before use, and the fatal-exception path does not halt execution in this flow, allowing a NULL registry_info to reach ResetMagickMemory and field writes. Trigger: memory allocation failure. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference, crashing the process (DoS).

description: Failure to Sanitize Special Elements into a Different Plane (Special Element Injection) in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.8.2.

code_evidence: DW_FORM_string copies attacker-controlled DWARF bytes directly into value->string.content via r_str_ndup without sanitizing escape sequences; this string is later rendered by downstream consumers.
DW_FORM_strp similarly strdup's content from the debug_str table at an offset read from the file, again storing raw bytes with embedded ANSI escapes intact.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 covers constructing output from externally-influenced input without neutralizing special elements that modify parsing/interpretation downstream. Here attacker-supplied DWARF strings flow unsanitized into a consumer that interprets ANSI escapes, matching the injection class. The added r_str_ansi_strip and newline/tab replacement confirm the intended neutralization of special elements.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function extracts string attribute values from an untrusted DWARF binary and stores them unmodified. When a downstream component (e.g., the disassembler/UI) prints these strings, embedded ANSI escape sequences or control characters are interpreted rather than shown literally, allowing terminal manipulation. The root cause is missing neutralization of special elements in output consumed by a renderer; the trigger is a crafted DWARF string attribute.

description: WebKit/Source/core/html/parser/HTMLPreloadScanner.cpp in Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.82, does not consider referrer-policy information inside an HTML document during a preload request, which allows remote attackers to bypass the Content Security Policy (CSP) protection mechanism via a crafted web site, as demonstrated by a "Content-Security-Policy: referrer origin-when-cross-origin" header that overrides a "<META name='referrer' content='no-referrer'>" element.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the preload scanner is constructed without validating or applying the document's referrer-policy metadata, so preload requests can proceed under a policy inconsistent with the document (e.g. a CSP referrer header overriding a no-referrer meta element). commit_msg: Fix stack size detection on Linux (fix #1427)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  return 1000000 - count; // give it 1 megabyte of stack'], 'added_lines': ['  const uint32_t max_stack = 1000000; // give it 1 megabyte of stack', '  if (count>max_stack) return 0;', '  return max_stack - count;']}
description: Espruino before 1.99 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) with a user crafted input file via an integer overflow during syntax parsing. This was addressed by fixing stack size detection on Linux in jsutils.c.

code_evidence: Line 9 computes count as a uint32_t difference between STACK_BASE and the address of a local; if STACK_BASE is below &ptr, the unsigned subtraction wraps to a huge value. Line 10 then returns 1000000 - count, so a large/wrapped count produces a negative result stored in the size_t return type, i.e. a very large free-stack value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because an unsigned arithmetic calculation wraps/produces a value outside the intended range, and the code assumes the result is a small positive remaining count. The patch adds the missing count>max_stack guard, confirming the weakness is the unguarded subtraction/wraparound rather than a generic bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unsigned subtraction on line 9 and the subtraction on line 10 have no guard ensuring count <= 1000000. Trigger: crafted input during syntax parsing causes stack layout where count exceeds 1000000 or the pointer difference wraps. Consequence: jsuGetFreeStack reports a huge free stack, so the parser's stack-depth check is bypassed and recursion continues until a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
sch_sfb: Don't assume the skb is still around after enqueueing to child

The sch_sfb enqueue() routine assumes the skb is still alive after it has
been enqueued into a child qdisc, using the data in the skb cb field in the
increment_qlen() routine after enqueue. However, the skb may in fact have
been freed, causing a use-after-free in this case. In particular, this
happens if sch_cake is used as a child of sfb, and the GSO splitting mode
of CAKE is enabled (in which case the skb will be split into segments and
the original skb freed).

Fix this by copying the sfb cb data to the stack before enqueueing the skb,
and using this stack copy in increment_qlen() instead of the skb pointer
itself.

Reported-by: zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com # ZDI-CAN-18231
Fixes: e13e02a3c68d ("net_sched: SFB flow scheduler")
Signed-off-by: Toke Høiland-Jørgensen <toke@toke.dk>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void increment_qlen(const struct sk_buff *skb, struct sfb_sched_data *q)', '\tsfbhash = sfb_hash(skb, 0);', '\tsfbhash = sfb_hash(skb, 1);'], 'added_lines': ['static void increment_qlen(const struct sfb_skb_cb *cb, struct sfb_sched_data *q)', '\tsfbhash = cb->hashes[0];', '\tsfbhash = cb->hashes[1];']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s networking code. A use-after-free was found in the way the sch_sfb enqueue function used the socket buffer (SKB) cb field after the same SKB had been enqueued (and freed) into a child qdisc. This flaw allows a local, unprivileged user to crash the system, causing a denial of service.

code_evidence: increment_qlen takes a const struct sk_buff *skb and derives the flow hashes via sfb_hash(skb, 0) and sfb_hash(skb, 1), which read the skb cb field. The function is called after the skb has been enqueued into a child qdisc; if that child (e.g. sch_cake in GSO split mode) frees the original skb, these sfb_hash reads dereference freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences an skb pointer whose lifetime ended at the child enqueue, which is exactly CWE-416 use-after-free. The patch confirms this by replacing skb-based hash reads with a stack copy of the cb, showing the stale pointer was the defect rather than a mere NULL or bounds issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: increment_qlen reads the skb cb hashes after enqueueing the skb to a child qdisc, without guaranteeing the skb is still alive. Trigger: a child qdisc frees or replaces the original skb during enqueue (CAKE GSO splitting). Consequence: use-after-free read of the cb field, leading to crash/denial of service (and potentially worse memory corruption).

commit_msg:
fix a fencepost error in pipe_advance()

The logics in pipe_advance() used to release all buffers past the new
position failed in cases when the number of buffers to release was equal
to pipe->buffers.  If that happened, none of them had been released,
leaving pipe full.  Worse, it was trivial to trigger and we end up with
pipe full of uninitialized pages.  IOW, it's an infoleak.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.9
Reported-by: "Alan J. Wylie" <alan@wylie.me.uk>
Tested-by: "Alan J. Wylie" <alan@wylie.me.uk>
Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tWARN_ON(pipe->nrbufs == pipe->buffers);']}
description: Off-by-one error in the pipe_advance function in lib/iov_iter.c in the Linux kernel before 4.9.5 allows local users to obtain sensitive information from uninitialized heap-memory locations in opportunistic circumstances by reading from a pipe after an incorrect buffer-release decision.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function iov_iter_pipe only initializes iterator fields and does not perform the buffer-release logic or off-by-one decision that causes the uninitialized-page infoleak; the added WARN_ON is a diagnostic, not the vulnerable operation.

description: ngiflib 0.4 has a heap-based buffer overflow in WritePixel() in ngiflib.c when called from DecodeGifImg, because deinterlacing for small pictures is mishandled.

code_evidence: For pass 1, curY advances by 8 and only resets to posY+4 when curY reaches p->height; for small heights this single check can leave curY at or beyond height before the row pointer is computed.
Pass 4 increments curY by 2 with no height check at all, so the final deinterlace pass can advance curY past p->height.
The row base pointer is computed as p->frbuff.p8 + curY*width (plus posX) without re-validating curY against p->height.
The 32-bit path similarly computes p->frbuff.p32 + curY*width + posX from the unchecked curY.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes an out-of-bounds framebuffer address from an unchecked curY and writes pixel data through it, matching CWE-787 (write past the end of the intended buffer). It is not merely a read or integer issue; the unchecked row index directly produces an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: deinterlace pass transitions advance context->curY by increments (8, 4, 2) and the pass logic can leave curY >= p->height for small pictures, especially pass 4 which lacks any bounds check. Trigger: decoding a small interlaced GIF image. The computed framebuffer pointer curY*width+posX then indexes past the allocated buffer, and subsequent WritePixel stores (lines 7/10/11) write out of bounds.

description: An integer overflow was found in QEMU 4.0.1 through 4.2.0 in the way it implemented ATI VGA emulation. src_x and src_y are likewise signed int computations from guest-controlled src_x and dst_width/dst_height, again wrappable when the reverse-direction bit is set.

commit_msg:
netrom: Fix use-after-free caused by accept on already connected socket

If you call listen() and accept() on an already connect()ed
AF_NETROM socket, accept() can successfully connect.
This is because when the peer socket sends data to sendmsg,
the skb with its own sk stored in the connected socket's
sk->sk_receive_queue is connected, and nr_accept() dequeues
the skb waiting in the sk->sk_receive_queue.

As a result, nr_accept() allocates and returns a sock with
the sk of the parent AF_NETROM socket.

And here use-after-free can happen through complex race conditions:
```
                  cpu0                                                     cpu1
                                                               1. socket_2 = socket(AF_NETROM)
                                                                        .
                                                                        .
                                                                  listen(socket_2)
                                                                  accepted_socket = accept(socket_2)
       2. socket_1 = socket(AF_NETROM)
            nr_create()    // sk refcount : 1
          connect(socket_1)
                                                               3. write(accepted_socket)
                                                                    nr_sendmsg()
                                                                    nr_output()
                                                                    nr_kick()
                                                                    nr_send_iframe()
                                                                    nr_transmit_buffer()
                                                                    nr_route_frame()
                                                                    nr_loopback_queue()
                                                                    nr_loopback_timer()
                                                                    nr_rx_frame()
                                                                    nr_process_rx_frame(sk, skb);    // sk : socket_1's sk
                                                                    nr_state3_machine()
                                                                    nr_queue_rx_frame()
```

To fix this issue, nr_listen() returns -EINVAL for sockets that
successfully nr_connect().

Reported-by: syzbot+caa188bdfc1eeafeb418@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <v4bel@theori.io>
Reviewed-by: Kuniyuki Iwashima <kuniyu@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (sock->state != SS_UNCONNECTED) {', '\t\trelease_sock(sk);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.1.11. In net/netrom/af_netrom.c, there is a use-after-free because accept is also allowed for a successfully connected AF_NETROM socket. However, in order for an attacker to exploit this, the system must have netrom routing configured or the attacker must have the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability.

code_evidence: nr_listen() locks the socket and only checks sk->sk_state != TCP_LISTEN before transitioning it to TCP_LISTEN; there is no check that the socket is still unconnected (sock->state). A socket that already completed nr_connect() is therefore accepted into the listening state, so accept() later dequeues the peer skb and returns a sock sharing the parent sk. That sk can be freed by nr_release() while the accepted socket still references it, and a later close()/sock_hold() on the accepted socket touches freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the accepted socket retains a reference to a sock object that nr_release() frees, and subsequent operations on that stale reference constitute use after free. This is not merely a state-validation flaw; the state confusion is the enabling cause of the dangling reference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nr_listen() permits an already-connected AF_NETROM socket to become a listener because it validates only sk_state, not sock->state. Trigger: listen() then accept() on a connected socket yields an accepted sock aliasing the parent sk; concurrent close frees that sk while the accepted sock still holds a reference. Consequence: use-after-free on the freed sock, enabling memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
KMSAN reported uninitialized data being written to disk when dumping core.
As a result, several kilobytes of kmalloc memory may be written to the
core file and then read by a non-privileged user.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20200419100848.63472-1-glider@google.com
Link: https://github.com/google/kmsan/issues/76
Signed-off-by: Alexander Potapenko <glider@google.com>
Reported-by: sam <sunhaoyl@outlook.com>
Acked-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
Cc: Alexey Dobriyan <adobriyan@gmail.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Stephen Rothwell <sfr@canb.auug.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tvoid *data = kmalloc(size, GFP_KERNEL);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tvoid *data = kzalloc(size, GFP_KERNEL);']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's implementation of Userspace core dumps. This flaw allows an attacker with a local account to crash a trivial program and exfiltrate private kernel data.

code_evidence: Line 21 allocates a buffer of size 'size' with kmalloc, which does not zero the memory. Line 24 calls regset->get to fill 'data'; if the regset implementation does not write every byte of 'size', the buffer retains uninitialized kmalloc contents. Lines 29-37 then attach 'data' to a core note via fill_note, and line 39 accounts its size in *total, so the full buffer, including uninitialized bytes, is emitted to the userspace-readable core file.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the code uses and exposes a resource (the kmalloc buffer) before all of it has been initialized, leading to leaked uninitialized memory. The fix replaces kmalloc with kzalloc, confirming the intended initialization constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the regset buffer is allocated with kmalloc and only partially populated by regset->get. Trigger: a local user crashes a program whose core dump includes a regset note, causing the uninitialized tail to be written to the core file. Consequence: disclosure of stale kernel heap data (confidentiality), matching CWE-908's read-memory impact.

commit_msg:
Fix valgrind problems with gdevbjca.c

2 problems here. Firstly, we could access off the end of a row
while looking for runs. Change the indexing to fix this.

Secondly, we could overrun our gamma tables due to unexpectedly
large values. Add some clamping.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    while ( exam < end_row ) {', '      test2 = *++exam;'], 'added_lines': ['    while ( ++exam < end_row ) {', '      test2 = *exam;', "    /* exam points to the byte that didn't match, or end_row", '     * if we ran out of data. */']}
description: A buffer overflow vulnerability in FloydSteinbergDitheringC() in contrib/gdevbjca.c of Artifex Software GhostScript v9.50 allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via a crafted PDF file. This is fixed in v9.51.

code_evidence: The inner run-detection loop condition is tested against `exam` before the pre-increment dereference `*++exam`; when `exam` equals `end_row - 1`, the increment moves `exam` to `end_row` and `*++exam` reads one byte past the row end.

`end_dis = exam - 1` and `next = exam + 1` derive pointers from the possibly-past-end `exam`; the subsequent run-length and copy logic (counts, `compr`, `next`) then operate on this out-of-bounds position.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the faulty pointer arithmetic causes writes past the intended compressed buffer, not merely a read overrun; the root cause is the mis-ordered bound check and dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop advances `exam` and dereferences it before re-checking the bound, so the last valid byte can be followed by an out-of-bounds read and derived pointers; this corrupts the run-length bookkeeping and can lead to out-of-bounds writes into the compressed buffer, causing a crash/DoS.

commit_msg: Use asserts on lengths to prevent invalid reads/writes.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    assert((num_properties+1) != 0);', '\t\t    assert((idx+(a->names[i].len*2)) <= len);', '\t\tassert(v->len + idx <= len);', '', '\t\t    assert(v->len != 0);']}
description: An issue was discovered in tnef before 1.4.13. Two OOB Writes have been identified in src/mapi_attr.c:mapi_attr_read(). These might lead to invalid read and write operations, controlled by an attacker.

code_evidence: The name-length field a->names[i].len is read from the buffer at line 30, used to size a heap allocation at line 32, and then the loop at lines 33-34 copies bytes from buf+idx without verifying idx + a->names[i].len*2 <= len, so a crafted length can drive reads past the input buffer.
For binary/string values, v->len is attacker-controlled from the buffer at line 107 and passed to unicode_to_utf8(v->len, buf+idx) at line 110 without confirming v->len + idx <= len.

In the non-unicode branch, CHECKED_XMALLOC at line 114 allocates v->len bytes and memmove at line 115 copies v->len bytes from buf+idx; the missing bound check means the copy can read beyond the input buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length lets copies write past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. It is not merely CWE-125 since the same unchecked lengths also feed heap writes through the allocation/copy path.

evidence_lines.code:
v->data.buf = CHECKED_XMALLOC(unsigned char, v->len);
memmove (v->data.buf, buf+idx, v->len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled length fields (a->names[i].len, v->len) are trusted without checking that idx plus the length stays within len. Trigger: a crafted MAPI attribute with an oversized length. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads/writes on buf and heap buffers, corrupting memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
settings: Add support for defaults to keyfile backend

Stacked databases and locks are dconf features that allow
management software like Fleet Commander to set system-wide
defaults and overrides centrally for applications.

This patch adds minimal support for the same to the keyfile
backend. We look for a keyfile named 'defaults' and a
lock-list named 'locks'.

Suitable files can be produced from a dconf database with
dconf dump and dconf list-locks, respectively.

The default location for these files is /etc/glib-2.0/settings/.
For test purposes, this can be overwritten with the
GSETTINGS_DEFAULTS_DIR environment variable.

Writes always go to the per-user keyfile.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  if (g_hash_table_contains (kfsb->system_locks, key))', '    return FALSE;']}
description: The keyfile settings backend in GNOME GLib (aka glib2.0) before 2.60.0 creates directories using g_file_make_directory_with_parents (kfsb->dir, NULL, NULL) and files using g_file_replace_contents (kfsb->file, contents, length, NULL, FALSE, G_FILE_CREATE_REPLACE_DESTINATION, NULL, NULL, NULL). Consequently, it does not properly restrict directory (and file) permissions. Instead, for directories, 0777 permissions are used; for files, default file permissions are used. This is similar to CVE-2019-12450.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function set_to_keyfile only writes key values into the in-memory GKeyFile and adds a lock check; it performs no directory or file creation and assigns no filesystem permissions, so it does not support the permission-assignment weakness CWE-732.

commit_msg:
Security fixes: expect final changes for release 1.75.3.
* Fixed a debian security issue with fscanf() reading a string with
  possible buffer overflow.
* There were also a few similar situations with sscanf().
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['char       typestr[128];', '    if (fscanf(fp, " Number of pts = %d; format = %s\\n", &n, typestr) != 2)'], 'added_lines': ['char       typestr[128];  /* hardcoded below in fscanf */', '    if (fscanf(fp, " Number of pts = %d; format = %127s\\n", &n, typestr) != 2)']}
description: Leptonica before 1.75.3 does not limit the number of characters in a %s format argument to fscanf or sscanf, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a long string, as demonstrated by the gplotRead and ptaReadStream functions.

code_evidence: Line 4 declares a fixed stack buffer typestr[128]. Line 15 uses fscanf with an unbounded %s conversion that writes the file-supplied format token into typestr with no width limit; the return-value check on line 16 only validates count, not length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unbounded %s write into typestr is a direct out-of-bounds write past the intended stack buffer, matching CWE-787. It is not merely a read overrun or integer issue; the unsafe write itself is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing field-width bound on %s while reading into the 128-byte stack buffer typestr. Trigger: an attacker-controlled PTA stream containing a format token longer than 127 characters causes fscanf to write past typestr, producing a stack-based buffer overflow and possible crash or code execution.

commit_msg: Json library: fix a number of potential buffer overflows
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void'], 'added_lines': ['static bool', '    return true;', '  } else {', '    return false;']}
description: Contiki-NG before 4.2 has a stack-based buffer overflow in the push function in os/lib/json/jsonparse.c that allows an out-of-bounds write of an '{' or '[' character.

code_evidence: modify() writes c into state->stack[state->depth - 1] whenever depth > 0. There is no check that depth - 1 is within the allocated size of state->stack, so a caller-controlled depth larger than the stack capacity causes an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing c to state->stack[depth - 1] without an upper-bound capacity check is a direct out-of-bounds write past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. The missing constraint is on the index, not merely an unvalidated input, so the weakness is the write itself rather than a generic improper input validation issue.

evidence_lines.code:
if(state->depth > 0) {
state->stack[state->depth - 1] = c;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the only guard is depth > 0, which validates a lower bound but not the stack's upper bound. Trigger: parsing nested '{' or '[' pushes increases depth past the stack capacity, and the subsequent modify call indexes state->stack out of range. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write of the pushed character, corrupting adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
dm: Reset virtio device before release

With virtio polling mode enabled, a timer is running in the virtio
backend service. And the timer will also be triggered if its frondend
driver didn't do the device reset in shutdown. A freed virtio device
will be accessed in the polling timer handler.

Do the virtio reset() callback specifically to clear the polling timer
before the free.

Tracked-On: #6147
Signed-off-by: Shuo A Liu <shuo.a.liu@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Yonghua Huang <yonghua.huang@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tvirtio_hdcp_reset(vhdcp);']}
description: The polling timer handler in ACRN before 2.5 has a use-after-free for a freed virtio device, related to devicemodel/hw/pci/virtio/*.c.

code_evidence: Line 4 retrieves the virtio_hdcp device pointer from dev->arg; lines 5 and 7 free that object without first stopping the backend polling timer that still references it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the freed virtio_hdcp allocation remains referenced by the polling timer, which can use it after free. The patch's virtio_hdcp_reset(vhdcp) before free confirms the missing teardown constraint; this is not a mere memory leak, since the object is later accessed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: deinit frees vhdcp while an active polling timer in the backend retains a reference to the same device. Trigger: shutdown with virtio polling mode enabled, so the timer fires after free. Supported consequence: the timer handler dereferences freed memory (use-after-free), causing crash or invalid memory access.

commit_msg:
Avoid using stale UserScript pointers

BUG=625393
TEST=Manually. Compile Chrome with ASAN and follow the steps from the bug report.

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2116923002
Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#403725}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  return run_location == UserScript::DOCUMENT_START &&'], 'added_lines': ['  return script_ && run_location == UserScript::DOCUMENT_START &&']}
description: Use-after-free vulnerability in extensions/renderer/user_script_injector.cc in the Extensions subsystem in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.82 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via vectors related to script deletion.

code_evidence: ShouldInjectCss dereferences script_ via script_->css_scripts() without checking whether script_ is still valid before use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function reads through a pointer to freed memory. This is a use-after-free (stale pointer) rather than a null-pointer dereference, since the missing validity/liveness check allows access to deallocated UserScript memory.

evidence_lines.code:
return run_location == UserScript::DOCUMENT_START &&
!script_->css_scripts().empty();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the injector holds a raw pointer to a UserScript that may be deleted, and this function dereferences it unconditionally. When script deletion occurs before ShouldInjectCss runs, the stale pointer is used to call css_scripts(), producing a use-after-free that can crash or corrupt memory.

commit_msg:
Early catch potential overflow issue #43

`m_width` and `m_height` are of `int` type in the OpenEXR library. We
currently keep the same types in our class but this may case issue
when mapping 1D memory. In the most favorable case, they are
multiplied together (Y framebuffer). For RGB(A) case, the required
memory can also be 4 time larger. We check if resp. `m_width *
m_height` and `4 * m_width * m_heigh` stay within the `int` higher
limit. Thanks to @GAP-dev for bringing this issue.

This commit also cleans a bit raw memory allocation in favor of

commit_msg:
[Security] Raise an exception when input to CompositeTensorVariantToComponents is not a valid CompositeTensorVariant tensor.

So TF won't crash.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 474594628
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(context, encoded != nullptr,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("The input `encoded` is not a valid "', '                                        "CompositeTensorVariant tensor, got ",', '                                        encoded_t.DebugString()));']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. An input `encoded` that is not a valid `CompositeTensorVariant` tensor will trigger a segfault in `tf.raw_ops.CompositeTensorVariantToComponents`. We have patched the issue in GitHub commits bf594d08d377dc6a3354d9fdb494b32d45f91971 and 660ce5a89eb6766834bdc303d2ab3902aef99d3d. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.11. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.10.1, 2.9.3, and TensorFlow 2.8.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 8 obtains a CompositeTensorVariant pointer from the first Variant element via get<CompositeTensorVariant>(), which may return nullptr when the variant does not actually hold a CompositeTensorVariant. Line 10 then dereferences that pointer (encoded->metadata()) without any null check, and later lines 19 and 26 similarly use encoded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the code dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but which can be NULL, matching the null-pointer-dereference definition. The prior size check only ensures the variant tensor is non-empty, not that the contained object is a valid CompositeTensorVariant, so the missing null constraint is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the result of get<CompositeTensorVariant>() is trusted to be non-null. Trigger: an input encoded tensor that is non-empty but not a valid CompositeTensorVariant. Consequence: dereferencing the null pointer at line 10 causes a crash/segfault, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
Bug 701843: avoid divide by zero in devices/gdevepsc.c:epsc_print_page().

Fixes:
    ./sanbin/gs -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dSAFER -r8 -dNOCIE -dFitPage -sOutputFile=tmp -sDEVICE=epsonc  ../bug-701843.pdf
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '    start_graphics = (char)', '        ((y_24pin ? graphics_modes_24 : graphics_modes_9)[x_dpi / 60]);', '    first_pass = (start_graphics & DD ? 1 : 0);', '    last_pass = first_pass * 2;', '    dots_per_space = x_dpi / 10;    /* pica space = 1/10" */', '    bytes_per_space = dots_per_space * y_mult;'], 'added_lines': ['    start_graphics = (char)', '        ((y_24pin ? graphics_modes_24 : graphics_modes_9)[x_dpi / 60]);', '    first_pass = (start_graphics & DD ? 1 : 0);', '    last_pass = first_pass * 2;', '    dots_per_space = x_dpi / 10;    /* pica space = 1/10" */', '    bytes_per_space = dots_per_space * y_mult;', '    if (bytes_per_space == 0) {', '        /* This avoids divide by zero later on, bug 701843. */', '        return_error(gs_error_rangecheck);', '    }', '']}
description: A divide by zero issue discovered in eps_print_page in gdevepsn.c in Artifex Software GhostScript 9.50 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via opening of crafted PDF file.

code_evidence: x_dpi is derived from pdev->x_pixels_per_inch at line 17; dots_per_space and bytes_per_space are computed at lines 48-49.
bytes_per_space = dots_per_space * y_mult can be zero when x_dpi/10 is zero (x_dpi < 10), since y_mult is 1 or 3.
bytes_per_space is later used as a divisor in tpos = (outp - out) / bytes_per_space and newp = out + tpos * bytes_per_space at lines 196-197.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function divides by bytes_per_space, a value derived from attacker-influenced device resolution that can be zero; this directly matches CWE-369, divide by zero. The consequence is an availability-impacting crash, consistent with the CWE scope.

evidence_lines.code:
dots_per_space = x_dpi / 10;    
bytes_per_space = dots_per_space * y_mult;

tpos = (outp - out) / bytes_per_space;
newp = out + tpos * bytes_per_space;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function computes bytes_per_space from device resolution without ensuring it is nonzero. When a crafted PDF yields an x_pixels_per_inch below 10, dots_per_space becomes 0 and bytes_per_space is 0. Triggering the zero-run compression branch in the pass loop then evaluates (outp - out) / bytes_per_space, causing a division-by-zero crash and denial of service.

of `T1_ToFixedArray'.

`t1_parse_font_matrix'.

* src/type42/t42parse.c (t42_parse_font_matrix): Synchronize with
`t1_parse_font_matrix'.
(t42_parse_encoding): Synchronize with `t1_parse_encoding'.

* src/psaux/psobjs.c (ps_parser_load_field) <T1_FIELD_TYPE_BBOX>,
<T1_FIELD_TYPE_MMOX>: Properly handle result of `ps_tofixedarray'.

description: The (1) t1_parse_font_matrix function in type1/t1load.c, (2) cid_parse_font_matrix function in cid/cidload.c, (3) t42_parse_font_matrix function in type42/t42parse.c, and (4) ps_parser_load_field function in psaux/psobjs.c in FreeType before 2.5.4 do not check return values, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (uninitialized memory access and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted font.

code_evidence: T1_ToFixedArray is asked to read 6 fixed values from font-matrix input; the return value is a count, but the code only rejects it when result < 0. A short parse (0..5) passes the check, leaving temp[3] and later entries uninitialized, and temp[3] is then consumed by FT_ABS at line 18.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate that the parsed font-matrix input has the required quantity of elements before using it, which is improper validation of input properties and matches CWE-20. The fix changes the guard to result < 6, confirming the missing count check rather than a distinct arithmetic or memory-safety root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser's partial/short result is not treated as invalid input because the guard tests only for a negative error code instead of the required count of 6. Trigger: a crafted font whose font-matrix array yields fewer than six values. Consequence: uninitialized stack values (temp[3] onward) are read, leading to undefined behavior and an application crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Read and write operations are capped to MAX_RW_COUNT. Some read ops rely on
that limit, and that is not guaranteed by the IORING_OP_PROVIDE_BUFFERS.

Truncate those lengths when doing io_add_buffers, so buffer addresses still
use the uncapped length.

Also, take the chance and change struct io_buffer len member to __u32, so
it matches struct io_provide_buffer len member.

This fixes CVE-2021-3491, also reported as ZDI-CAN-13546.

Fixes: ddf0322db79c ("io_uring: add IORING_OP_PROVIDE_BUFFERS")
Reported-by: Billy Jheng Bing-Jhong (@st424204)
Signed-off-by: Thadeu Lima de Souza Cascardo <cascardo@canonical.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tbuf->len = pbuf->len;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tbuf->len = min_t(__u32, pbuf->len, MAX_RW_COUNT);']}
description: The io_uring subsystem in the Linux kernel allowed the MAX_RW_COUNT limit to be bypassed in the PROVIDE_BUFFERS operation, which led to negative values being usedin mem_rw when reading /proc/<PID>/mem. This could be used to create a heap overflow leading to arbitrary code execution in the kernel. It was addressed via commit d1f82808877b ("io_uring: truncate lengths larger than MAX_RW_COUNT on provide buffers") (v5.13-rc1) and backported to the stable kernels in v5.12.4, v5.11.21, and v5.10.37. It was introduced in ddf0322db79c ("io_uring: add IORING_OP_PROVIDE_BUFFERS") (v5.7-rc1).

code_evidence: Line 11 stores the user-supplied pbuf->len directly into buf->len without any upper bound, and line 13 advances addr by the same uncapped pbuf->len for each of pbuf->nbufs buffers. The length is never clamped to MAX_RW_COUNT, so an oversized len is accepted and propagated into the buffer descriptors.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length becomes an out-of-bounds write when later used by mem_rw, matching CWE-787. The missing-bound root cause is CWE-190, but the supported consequence is writing past a buffer, so CWE-787 fits.

evidence_lines.code:
buf->len = pbuf->len;
addr += pbuf->len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: io_add_buffers accepts an attacker-controlled provide-buffers length without enforcing the MAX_RW_COUNT cap. Trigger: a large len value in the PROVIDE_BUFFERS request causes buf->len to exceed the intended limit, bypassing the read/write cap relied upon by /proc/<PID>/mem operations. Consequence: the uncapped length can lead to a negative length in mem_rw and a heap out-of-bounds write, potentially enabling kernel code execution.

commit_msg:
There is a potential UAF between the unregistration routine and the NFC
netlink operations.

The race that cause that UAF can be shown as below:

 (FREE)                      |  (USE)
nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev   |  nfc_genl_dev_up
  nci_close_device           |
  nci_unregister_device      |    nfc_get_device
    nfc_unregister_device    |    nfc_dev_up
      rfkill_destory         |
      device_del             |      rfkill_blocked
  ...                        |    ...

The root cause for this race is concluded below:
1. The rfkill_blocked (USE) in nfc_dev_up is supposed to be placed after
the device_is_registered check.
2. Since the netlink operations are possible just after the device_add
in nfc_register_device, the nfc_dev_up() can happen anywhere during the
rfkill creation process, which leads to data race.

This patch reorder these actions to permit
1. Once device_del is finished, the nfc_dev_up cannot dereference the
rfkill object.
2. The rfkill_register need to be placed after the device_add of nfc_dev
because the parent device need to be created first. So this patch keeps
the order but inject device_lock to prevent the data race.

Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Fixes: be055b2f89b5 ("NFC: RFKILL support")
Reviewed-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Krzysztof Kozlowski <krzysztof.kozlowski@canonical.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20211116152652.19217-1-linma@zju.edu.cn
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\trc = nfc_genl_device_added(dev);', '\tif (rc)', '\t\tpr_debug("The userspace won\'t be notified that the device %s was added\\n",', '\t\t\t dev_name(&dev->dev));', ''], 'added_lines': ['\tdevice_lock(&dev->dev);', '\tdevice_unlock(&dev->dev);', '', '\trc = nfc_genl_device_added(dev);', '\tif (rc)', '\t\tpr_debug("The userspace won\'t be notified that the device %s was added\\n",', '\t\t\t dev_name(&dev->dev));']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nci_request in net/nfc/nci/core.c in NFC Controller Interface (NCI) in the Linux kernel. This flaw could allow a local attacker with user privileges to cause a data race problem while the device is getting removed, leading to a privilege escalation problem.

code_evidence: device_add at [7] publishes the device under nfc_devlist_mutex, but the mutex is released at [8] before rfkill allocation at [18] and rfkill_register at [21]. Concurrent netlink paths can reach rfkill_blocked on the not-yet-created rfkill object between publication and initialization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes a shared device to concurrent code without exclusive synchronization of the rfkill field, matching CWE-362's timing-window/shared-resource race. The UAF is the downstream consequence, not the root weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: device_add makes the device visible to netlink operations while dev->rfkill is still unset, and no shared lock protects the rfkill setup. Trigger: a concurrent nfc_dev_up calls rfkill_blocked before or during rfkill_alloc/register. Supported consequence: race on the rfkill state, leading to a use-after-free or NULL dereference during device removal.

description: In the Linux kernel before 4.20.5, attackers can trigger a drivers/char/ipmi/ipmi_msghandler.c use-after-free and OOPS by arranging for certain simultaneous execution of the code, as demonstrated by a "service ipmievd restart" loop.

code_evidence: free_user() derives the ipmi_user from refcount, then immediately kfree(user) without tearing down user->release_barrier, the srcu_struct embedded in that allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function frees user and later code reads user->release_barrier.rda through the stale pointer; the missing cleanup_srcu_struct() leaves a live reference to freed memory. This is a use-after-free, not merely a memory leak or double free.

evidence_lines.code:
struct ipmi_user *user = container_of(ref, struct ipmi_user, refcount);
kfree(user);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the kref release callback frees the ipmi_user allocation while the embedded release_barrier srcu_struct is still live. Trigger: ipmi_destroy_user() drops the refcount to zero and free_user() runs kfree(user) even though acquire_ipmi_user() can still reach user->release_barrier. Consequence: __srcu_read_lock() on the freed barrier dereferences freed memory, causing an OOPS/use-after-free (availability crash and possible memory corruption).

description: Buffer Overflow Vulnerability exists in ajaxsoundstudio.com n Pyo < 1.03 in the Server_debug function, which allows remote attackers to conduct DoS attacks by deliberately passing on an overlong audio file name.

code_evidence: A fixed 256-byte stack buffer is declared at line 6, then formatted output is written into it by vsprintf at line 9 with no destination-size argument; the format/varargs supplied by the caller are copied unbounded. The result is then passed to PySys_WriteStdout at line 11.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the function performs a buffer copy (vsprintf into a fixed-size destination) without verifying that the input length is less than the output buffer size, which is the classic unchecked buffer copy. Out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125) are not the issue here; the defect is an unbounded write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: vsprintf copies the caller-controlled formatted string into buffer[256] without any size check. Trigger: a long format expansion, such as the overlong audio filename reported in the description, overflows the stack buffer. Supported consequence: memory corruption/stack overwrite leading to crash (DoS) and potentially code execution; the vsprintf write is the direct unsafe operation, not the subsequent logging call.

commit_msg:
Lion says:
-------
In the QFQ scheduler a similar issue to CVE-2023-31436
persists.

Consider the following code in net/sched/sch_qfq.c:

static int qfq_enqueue(struct sk_buff *skb, struct Qdisc *sch,
                struct sk_buff **to_free)
{
     unsigned int len = qdisc_pkt_len(skb), gso_segs;

    // ...

     if (unlikely(cl->agg->lmax < len)) {
         pr_debug("qfq: increasing maxpkt from %u to %u for class %u",
              cl->agg->lmax, len, cl->common.classid);
         err = qfq_change_agg(sch, cl, cl->agg->class_weight, len);
         if (err) {
             cl->qstats.drops++;
             return qdisc_drop(skb, sch, to_free);
         }

    // ...

     }

Similarly to CVE-2023-31436, "lmax" is increased without any bounds
checks according to the packet length "len". Usually this would not
impose a problem because packet sizes are naturally limited.

This is however not the actual packet length, rather the
"qdisc_pkt_len(skb)" which might apply size transformations according to
"struct qdisc_size_table" as created by "qdisc_get_stab()" in
net/sched/sch_api.c if the TCA_STAB option was set when modifying the qdisc.

A user may choose virtually any size using such a table.

As a result the same issue as in CVE-2023-31436 can occur, allowing heap
out-of-bounds read / writes in the kmalloc-8192 cache.
-------

We can create the issue with the following commands:

tc qdisc add dev $DEV root handle 1: stab mtu 2048 tsize 512 mpu 0 \
overhead 999999999 linklayer ethernet qfq
tc class add dev $DEV parent 1: classid 1:1 htb rate 6mbit burst 15k
tc filter add dev $DEV parent 1: matchall classid 1:1
ping -I $DEV 1.1.1.2

This is caused by incorrectly assuming that qdisc_pkt_len() returns a
length within the QFQ_MIN_LMAX < len < QFQ_MAX_LMAX.

Fixes: 462dbc9101ac ("pkt_sched: QFQ Plus: fair-queueing service at DRR cost")
Reported-by: Lion <nnamrec@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jamal Hadi Salim <jhs@mojatatu.com>
Signed-off-by: Pedro Tammela <pctammela@mojatatu.com>
Reviewed-by: Simon Horman <simon.horman@corigine.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Abeni <pabeni@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct qfq_aggregate *new_agg = qfq_find_agg(q, lmax, weight);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct qfq_aggregate *new_agg;', "\t/* 'lmax' can range from [QFQ_MIN_LMAX, pktlen + stab overhead] */", '\tif (lmax > QFQ_MAX_LMAX)', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '', '\tnew_agg = qfq_find_agg(q, lmax, weight);']}
description:
An out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Linux kernel's net/sched: sch_qfq component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

The qfq_change_agg() function in net/sched/sch_qfq.c allows an out-of-bounds write because lmax is updated according to packet sizes without bounds checks.

We recommend upgrading past commit 3e337087c3b5805fe0b8a46ba622a962880b5d64.

code_evidence: qfq_change_agg() receives an attacker-influenced lmax and passes it directly to qfq_find_agg() without any upper-bound check; when no matching aggregate exists, a new aggregate is allocated and qfq_init_agg() stores the unbounded lmax. The only failure path concerns kzalloc() returning NULL, not the magnitude of lmax.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits: the unchecked lmax flows into aggregate initialization and subsequent scheduling operations that index/write beyond the intended buffer, matching an out-of-bounds write. A pure integer-overflow label would only describe an intermediate cause; here the supported consequence is memory written past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The caller derives lmax from qdisc_pkt_len(), which a user can inflate via a TCA_STAB size table. Because qfq_change_agg() accepts arbitrary lmax and initializes the aggregate with it, downstream QFQ scheduling arithmetic and aggregate lookups use the oversized value, producing heap out-of-bounds reads/writes (e.g., in the kmalloc-8192 cache). Root cause is the missing lmax cap; the OOB memory corruption is the consequence.

commit_msg: Guard binary expressions from too much recursion.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tjs_Ast *a;', '\ta = newexp(J);', 'loop:', '\tDECREC();'], 'added_lines': ['\tjs_Ast *a = newexp(J);', '\tSAVEREC();', 'loop:', '\tPOPREC();']}
description: jsparse.c in Artifex MuJS through 1.0.2 does not properly maintain the AST depth for binary expressions, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive recursion) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 3 declares the AST node; line 4 increments the recursion counter before line 5 obtains the base expression; the counter is only decremented once at line 9 after the loop.
Lines 6-8 form a goto loop: each accepted '.' or '[' builds a new nested MEMBER/INDEX node and jumps back to loop without any depth check; the '[' branch also recurses into expression().
Line 9 performs a single DECREC() on exit, so the counter does not reflect the number of iterations actually taken.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits: the function fails to control recursion depth for binary/member expressions, allowing a crafted file to exhaust the stack. The missing per-iteration depth accounting is the cause; the DoS is the consequence.

evidence_lines.code: DECREC();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a single INCREC()/DECREC() pair brackets the whole member-expression loop, so long chains of '.' or '[' operators build arbitrarily deep AST and recursion without advancing the depth counter. Trigger: a crafted input file containing a very long member/access chain. Consequence: excessive recursion and resource consumption leading to a denial of service.

commit_msg: Fix out of bounds crash on evidence
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (is_int && idx <= area->evidence().size() && idx >= 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (is_int && idx < area->evidence().size() && idx >= 0) {']}
description: Akashi is an open source server implementation of the Attorney Online video game based on the Ace Attorney universe. Affected versions of Akashi are subject to a denial of service attack. An attacker can use a specially crafted evidence packet to make an illegal modification, causing a server crash. This can be used to mount a denial-of-service exploit. Users are advised to upgrade. There is no known workaround for this issue.

code_evidence: argv[0] is converted to int idx with toInt(&is_int); the guard checks is_int && idx <= area->evidence().size() && idx >= 0 before calling area->deleteEvidence(idx). The upper bound uses <=, so idx equal to size() passes validation and is forwarded as an index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-129 covers using untrusted input as an array index without correctly validating it references a valid position. Here the index is untrusted and the bound check is off by one, so the size index is accepted; this is the direct cause of the out-of-bounds access, not merely a generic crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The client-supplied evidence index is validated with an inclusive upper bound against evidence().size(). An attacker sending an index equal to the container size passes the check, and deleteEvidence receives an out-of-range index, causing the crash/DoS described in the commit.

description: KernelSU is a Kernel based root solution for Android. Starting in version 0.6.1 and prior to version 0.7.0, if a KernelSU installed device is infected with a malware whose app signing block specially constructed, it can take over root privileges on the device. The vulnerable verification logic actually obtains the signature of the last block with an id of `0x7109871a`, while the verification logic during Android installation is to obtain the first one. In addition to the actual signature upgrade that has been fixed (KSU thought it was V2 but was actually V3), there is also the problem of actual signature downgrading (KSU thought it was V2 but was actually V1). Find a condition in the signature verification logic that will cause the signature not to be found error, and KernelSU does not implement the same conditions, so KSU thinks there is a V2 signature, but the APK signature verification actually uses the V1 signature. This issue is fixed in version 0.7.0. As workarounds, keep the KernelSU manager installed and avoid installing unknown apps.

code_evidence: The function advances the file position with ksu_kernel_read_compat and *pos/*offset arithmetic but never validates that the APK signing-block id or version matches the expected scheme, so the caller's authorization decision rests on unchecked block contents.
Only *size4 == expected_size gates entry; the block id/type that determines V1/V2/V3 semantics is not compared here, allowing a differently typed block to reach the hash comparison.
The length check bounds the stack buffer, but there is no check that the parsed structure is actually the expected signature block type, so a crafted block passes length validation.

The function reads the certificate, hashes it, and returns true solely when strcmp(expected_sha256, hash_str)==0; success therefore attests only that some block's hash matches, not that the block is the correct signature scheme.
Returning false on mismatch is the only rejection path; a block with a matching hash but wrong scheme returns true, misrepresenting the verification result to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function implements a security decision (is this APK signature valid for root authorization) but omits the scheme/type constraint needed for that decision, so the check is performed incorrectly, matching CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization. It is not merely a hash-comparison bug; the authorization outcome is wrong because the wrong object is authorized.

evidence_lines.code:
if (*size4 == expected_size) {
*offset += *size4;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signature-block parser accepts any block whose size equals expected_size and whose certificate hash matches expected_sha256, without confirming the block id/version identifies the V2 scheme. Trigger: a malicious APK signing block constructed as V1/V3 but hash-compatible makes check_block return true. Consequence: KernelSU treats the APK as V2-verified, enabling signature-downgrade abuse and root-privilege takeover.

commit_msg: Guard binary expressions from too much recursion.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["\twhile (jsP_accept(J, '&'))"], 'added_lines': ['\tSAVEREC();', "\twhile (jsP_accept(J, '&')) {", '\t\tINCREC();', '\t}', '\tPOPREC();']}
description: jsparse.c in Artifex MuJS through 1.0.2 does not properly maintain the AST depth for binary expressions, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive recursion) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: bitand() calls equality() to parse an operand (line 3), then loops on any '&' token (line 4), recursively invoking equality() again for each right operand (line 5) and re-entering the recursive-descent parser without any depth or recursion limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs unchecked recursive descent where input-controlled operator count directly determines recursion depth, matching CWE-674's uncontrolled recursion consuming stack resources. The missing depth guard, not mere CPU cost of the loop, is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the binary-expression loop recursively descends into equality() for each accepted '&' with no recursion-depth accounting. A crafted input containing a long chain of '&' operators drives unbounded nested parser recursion, exhausting the program stack and crashing the process (DoS).

commit_msg: Add bound check in datafile.cpp anywhere m_ppDataPtrs is accessed as an array. Should fix #2073
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif(Index < 0)', '\t//'], 'added_lines': ['\tif(Index < 0 || Index >= m_pDataFile->m_Header.m_NumRawData)']}
description: In Teeworlds 0.7.2, there is a failed bounds check in CDataFileReader::GetData() and CDataFileReader::ReplaceData() and related functions in engine/shared/datafile.cpp that can lead to an arbitrary free and out-of-bounds pointer write, possibly resulting in remote code execution.

code_evidence: The guard only rejects negative indexes: `if(Index < 0) return;` (line 3-4). Any Index >= m_Header.m_NumRawData passes through to `mem_free(m_pDataFile->m_ppDataPtrs[Index]);` (line 5) and the subsequent write `m_pDataFile->m_ppDataPtrs[Index] = 0x0;` (line 6), both indexing the pointer array without an upper-bound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes 0x0 through m_ppDataPtrs[Index] beyond the intended buffer when Index exceeds m_NumRawData. The missing upper-bound constraint is the direct cause; the arbitrary free on line 5 is a related consequence, not a separate weakness type.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the upper bound of the m_ppDataPtrs array (m_Header.m_NumRawData) is never validated against Index. Trigger: a caller supplies an Index at or beyond m_NumRawData. Consequence: line 6 writes a null pointer past the end of the array (out-of-bounds pointer write), and line 5 frees an out-of-bounds pointer value read from beyond the array, enabling arbitrary free and possible code execution.

commit_msg:
Exit without asserting when helper process startup fails (#1543)

... to dup() after fork() and before execvp().

Assertions are for handling program logic errors. Helper initialization
code already handled system call errors correctly (i.e. by exiting the
newly created helper process with an error), except for a couple of
assert()s that could be triggered by dup(2) failures.

This bug was discovered and detailed by Joshua Rogers at
https://megamansec.github.io/Squid-Security-Audit/ipc-assert.html
where it was filed as 'Assertion in Squid "Helper" Process Creator'.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        x = dup(crfd);', '        assert(x > -1);', '    } while (x < 3 && x > -1);', '    t1 = dup(crfd);', '', '    t2 = dup(cwfd);', '', '    t3 = dup(fileno(debug_log));'], 'added_lines': ['', '    // A dup(2) wrapper that reports and exits the process on errors. The', '    // exiting logic is only suitable for this child process context.', '    const auto dupOrExit = [prog,name](const int oldFd) {', '        const auto newFd = dup(oldFd);', '        if (newFd < 0) {', '            const auto savedErrno = errno;', '            debugs(54, DBG_CRITICAL, "ERROR: Helper process initialization failure: " << name <<', '                   Debug::Extra << "helper (CHILD) PID: " << getpid() <<', '                   Debug::Extra << "helper program name: " << prog <<', '                   Debug::Extra << "dup(2) system call error for FD " << oldFd << ": " << xstrerr(savedErrno));', '            _exit(EXIT_FAILURE);', '        }', '        return newFd;', '    };', '', '        x = dupOrExit(crfd);', '    } while (x < 3);', '    t1 = dupOrExit(crfd);', '', '    t2 = dupOrExit(cwfd);', '', '    t3 = dupOrExit(fileno(debug_log));']}
description: Squid is a caching proxy for the Web supporting HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, and more. Due to an Incorrect Check of Function Return Value bug Squid is vulnerable to a Denial of Service attack against its Helper process management. This bug is fixed by Squid version 6.5. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: In the child branch after fork, a do/while loop calls dup(crfd) and guards the result with assert(x > -1); if dup fails and returns -1, the assertion aborts the helper process.
A second block performs three dup() calls and asserts t1 > 2 && t2 > 2 && t3 > 2; any dup failure yielding -1, or a low fd, triggers the assertion.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because reachable assert() statements depend on dup(2) results that can fail at runtime, terminating the process. This is a reachable assertion causing DoS, not merely an unchecked return value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The helper child process uses assert() to check dup(2) return values instead of handling system-call failure. If dup fails (e.g., fd exhaustion) in the newly forked helper, the assertion aborts that process, causing helper initialization failure and a denial of service rather than a clean error exit.

commit_msg:
9pfs: add cleanup operation in FileOperations

Currently, the backend of VirtFS doesn't have a cleanup
function. This will lead resource leak issues if the backed
driver allocates resources. This patch addresses this issue.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liq3ea@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Greg Kurz <groug@kaod.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kurz <groug@kaod.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (s->ops->cleanup && s->ctx.private) {', '            s->ops->cleanup(&s->ctx);', '        }']}
description: Memory leak in hw/9pfs/9p.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) allows local privileged guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host memory consumption and possibly QEMU process crash) by leveraging a missing cleanup operation in FileOperations.

code_evidence: Line 43 calls s->ops->init(&s->ctx), which may allocate driver-private resources stored in s->ctx.private. On failure, control jumps to out at line 46.

The cleanup block at lines 62-67 frees only s->tag, s->ctx.fs_root and path; it never invokes s->ops->cleanup, so any resources allocated by a successful init before a later failure (e.g. lines 48-59) are not released.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates backend resources via s->ops->init but the rc error branch omits s->ops->cleanup, so allocated memory is not released after its lifetime; this is a missing-release memory leak (CWE-401), not a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path lacks the driver cleanup call, so resources allocated by s->ops->init are never released on failed realization. Trigger: a guest/device configuration causing init to succeed but a subsequent step (name_to_path, lstat, or non-directory check) to fail. Supported consequence: host memory/backend resource consumption, potentially crashing the QEMU process.

commit_msg:
avcodec/xwddec: Check bpp more completely

Fixes out of array access
Fixes: 1399/clusterfuzz-testcase-minimized-4866094172995584

Found-by: continuous fuzzing process https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz/tree/master/targets/ffmpeg
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (pixdepth == 1) {', '        } else if (pixdepth == 8) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (bpp == 1 && pixdepth == 1) {', '        } else if (bpp == 8 && pixdepth == 8) {']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the xwd_decode_frame function in libavcodec/xwddec.c in FFmpeg before 2.8.12, 3.0.x before 3.0.8, 3.1.x before 3.1.8, 3.2.x before 3.2.5, and 3.3.x before 3.3.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted file.

code_evidence: For XWD_GRAY_SCALE/XWD_STATIC_GRAY, bpp is validated only to be 1 or 8 at line 108, but the pixel format is selected from pixdepth alone: pixdepth==1 sets MONOWHITE and pixdepth==8 sets GRAY8 regardless of whether bpp matches.

The decode loop at lines 176-180 reads rsize = FFALIGN(width*bpp,bpad)/8 bytes per row into p->data[0] using p->linesize[0]. If bpp=1 but pixdepth=8, GRAY8 is chosen (1 byte/pixel) while rsize is computed for 1 bit/pixel, so the buffer is sized for fewer bytes than the copy writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes rsize bytes per row into a buffer sized from the mismatched pixel format, producing a heap out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-119's operation outside a buffer's intended boundary. The patch tightens the bpp/pixdepth constraint; this is a buffer-boundary violation rather than a mere integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: inconsistent bpp/pixdepth pairing lets a 1-bpp stream select an 8-bpp pixel format, so the allocated frame buffer is smaller than the per-row copy. Trigger: a crafted XWD file with GRAY_SCALE, bpp=1, pixdepth=8. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write during bytestream2_get_bufferu, corrupting adjacent heap memory.

description: Python 3.x through 3.9.1 has a buffer overflow in PyCArg_repr in _ctypes/callproc.c, which may lead to remote code execution in certain Python applications that accept floating-point numbers as untrusted input, as demonstrated by a 1e300 argument to c_double.from_param. This occurs because sprintf is used unsafely.

code_evidence: A fixed 256-byte stack buffer is declared for formatting output.
For the 'd' tag, sprintf writes the '%f' representation of self->value.d into buffer with no bound on the produced length.
For the 'f' tag, sprintf similarly writes the '%f' representation of self->value.f into the same fixed buffer.
The formatted result is then copied out via PyUnicode_FromString(buffer).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because an input-derived formatted value is copied into a fixed-size output buffer without checking the input size, producing a classic stack buffer overflow via sprintf in the float cases. This is a size-unchecked copy, not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence_lines.code: char buffer[256];
return PyUnicode_FromString(buffer);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the float branches use sprintf with a fixed 256-byte destination and no length limit. Trigger: a c_double/c_float parameter whose '%f' rendering (e.g. 1e300) expands beyond 256 bytes; the value is attacker-controlled when untrusted floating-point input reaches from_param. Consequence: the write overflows the stack buffer, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially enabling code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
Prevent `CHECK`-fail when decoding resource handles from proto

In certain scenarios, the proto might contain tensors that have too many elements (overflow). This is a `CHECK`-fail in general, but we should prevent this, given how many CVEs caused by that we have received this year (a large fraction of 200).

commit_msg:
candump: check for a too-long frame length.

If the frame length is longer than the maximum, report an error in the
file.

Fixes #19062, preventing the overflow on a buffer on the stack (assuming
your compiler doesn't call a bounds-checknig version of memcpy() if the
size of the target space is known).

commit_msg:
mm: get rid of vmacache_flush_all() entirely

Jann Horn points out that the vmacache_flush_all() function is not only
potentially expensive, it's buggy too.  It also happens to be entirely
unnecessary, because the sequence number overflow case can be avoided by
simply making the sequence number be 64-bit.  That doesn't even grow the
data structures in question, because the other adjacent fields are
already 64-bit.

So simplify the whole thing by just making the sequence number overflow
case go away entirely, which gets rid of all the complications and makes
the code faster too.  Win-win.

[ Oleg Nesterov points out that the VMACACHE_FULL_FLUSHES statistics
  also just goes away entirely with this ]

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: Will Deacon <will.deacon@arm.com>
Acked-by: Davidlohr Bueso <dave@stgolabs.net>
Cc: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.18.8. The vmacache_flush_all function in mm/vmacache.c mishandles sequence number overflows. An attacker can trigger a use-after-free (and possibly gain privileges) via certain thread creation, map, unmap, invalidation, and dereference operations.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only increments a sequence number and flushes the cache on overflow; it contains no memory free or dereference, so it does not directly demonstrate a use-after-free within this function.

commit_msg:
x86/hvm: Fix the handling of non-present segments

In 32bit, the data segments may be NULL to indicate that the segment is
ineligible for use.  In both 32bit and 64bit, the LDT selector may be NULL to
indicate that the entire LDT is ineligible for use.  However, nothing in Xen
actually checks for this condition when performing other segmentation
checks.  (Note however that limit and writeability checks are correctly
performed).

Neither Intel nor AMD specify the exact behaviour of loading a NULL segment.
Experimentally, AMD zeroes all attributes but leaves the base and limit
unmodified.  Intel zeroes the base, sets the limit to 0xfffffff and resets the
attributes to just .G and .D/B.

The use of the segment information in the VMCB/VMCS is equivalent to a native
pipeline interacting with the segment cache.  The present bit can therefore
have a subtly different meaning, and it is now cooked to uniformly indicate
whether the segment is usable or not.

GDTR and IDTR don't have access rights like the other segments, but for
consistency, they are treated as being present so no special casing is needed
elsewhere in the segmentation logic.

AMD hardware does not consider the present bit for %cs and %tr, and will
function as if they were present.  They are therefore unconditionally set to
present when reading information from the VMCB, to maintain the new meaning of
usability.

Intel hardware has a separate unusable bit in the VMCS segment attributes.
This bit is inverted and stored in the present field, so the hvm code can work
with architecturally-common state.

This is CVE-2016-9386 / XSA-191.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

description: The x86 emulator in Xen does not properly treat x86 NULL segments as unusable when accessing memory, which might allow local HVM guest users to gain privileges via vectors involving "unexpected" base/limit values.

code_evidence: In the non-64-bit address-size path after adding reg->base, the code computes last_byte and branches on reg->limit and the access type, but never tests reg->attr.fields.p, so a non-present (NULL/unusable) segment is treated as usable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing present-bit constraint lets a guest bypass the intended segment permission/usability restriction, fitting CWE-264 permissions/access-control management. It is not merely an out-of-bounds computation; the unchecked attribute governs whether access is permitted.

Trigger: HVM guest memory access through a NULL data segment in 32-bit mode. Consequence: segmentation access controls are bypassed, allowing privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
KEYS: add missing permission check for request_key() destination

When the request_key() syscall is not passed a destination keyring, it
links the requested key (if constructed) into the "default" request-key
keyring.  This should require Write permission to the keyring.  However,
there is actually no permission check.

This can be abused to add keys to any keyring to which only Search
permission is granted.  This is because Search permission allows joining
the keyring.  keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring(KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_SESSION_KEYRING)
then will set the default request-key keyring to the session keyring.
Then, request_key() can be used to add keys to the keyring.

Both negatively and positively instantiated keys can be added using this
method.  Adding negative keys is trivial.  Adding a positive key is a
bit trickier.  It requires that either /sbin/request-key positively
instantiates the key, or that another thread adds the key to the process
keyring at just the right time, such that request_key() misses it
initially but then finds it in construct_alloc_key().

Fix this bug by checking for Write permission to the keyring in
construct_get_dest_keyring() when the default keyring is being used.

We don't do the permission check for non-default keyrings because that
was already done by the earlier call to lookup_user_key().  Also,
request_key_and_link() is currently passed a 'struct key *' rather than
a key_ref_t, so the "possessed" bit is unavailable.

We also don't do the permission check for the "requestor keyring", to
continue to support the use case described by commit 8bbf4976b59f
("KEYS: Alter use of key instantiation link-to-keyring argument") where
/sbin/request-key recursively calls request_key() to add keys to the
original requestor's destination keyring.  (I don't know of any users
who actually do that, though...)

Fixes: 3e30148c3d52 ("[PATCH] Keys: Make request-key create an authorisation key")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>	# v2.6.13+
Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
