A crafted FB Zero tag with offset_end < tag_offset, or mismatched tag lengths, yields a wrapped total_tag_len. Trigger: attacker-controlled packet fields. Consequence: the returned offset fails to advance (or moves backwards), causing the caller to loop and crash the dissector (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

In order to fail safe in the supported case, re-implement all the VT-x
instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int nvmx_handle_vmlaunch(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)'], 'added_lines': ['static int nvmx_handle_vmlaunch(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.9.x through 4.11.x, on Intel x86 platforms, allowing x86 HVM and PVH guests to cause a host OS denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) or possibly have unspecified other impact because nested VT-x is not properly restricted.

code_evidence: Line 5 derives nvmx from vcpu_2_nvmx(v) and the handler proceeds without verifying that nested-virt state was initialized; line 7 calls vmx_inst_check_privilege(regs, 0), passing vmxop_check=0, which skips the CR4.VMXE check and lets the instruction through when nested virt is disabled.
Lines 21-22 and 32-33 dereference nvmx->launched_list via vvmcs_launched/set_vvmcs_launched, and line 29 passes v/nvmx into nvmx_vmresume, all operating on the uninitialized nvmx structure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the reachable path dereferences pointers derived from the uninitialized nvmx structure (launched_list, resume state) that are expected valid but are NULL/uninitialized, causing a host crash. This is a NULL dereference consequence, not merely a missing privilege check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the handler lacks a guard ensuring nested virt is enabled and skips the VMXE privilege check, so a guest can invoke VMLAUNCH while nvmx state is uninitialized. Trigger: a guest executes VMLAUNCH; the uninitialized nestedvmx state is then used, leading to a NULL/uninitialized pointer dereference in the resume/launched-list path and host denial of service.

description: Sigil before 0.9.16 is vulnerable to a directory traversal, allowing attackers to write arbitrary files via a ../ (dot dot slash) in a ZIP archive entry that is mishandled during extraction.

code_evidence: The ZIP entry name is read into file_name at line 22 and converted to qfile_name at line 25; only the literal "../" is stripped at lines 30-31 before the target path is built at line 33 and opened for writing at line 50.

This is relative path traversal rather than mere resource exhaustion or a filename-encoding issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the archive-controlled entry name is sanitized by naive substring removal of "../" rather than by validating the resolved path stays under m_ExtractedFolderPath. A crafted entry (e.g. one whose removal leaves a remaining traversal sequence, or an absolute/backslash path) survives filtering, so the concatenated file_path or cp437_file_path at lines 33/72 resolves outside the extraction directory; the file is then written at line 50 or copied at line 73, allowing arbitrary file write.

description: A heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability exists in Academy Software Foundation OpenEXR 2.3.0 in chunkOffsetReconstruction in ImfMultiPartInputFile.cpp that can cause a denial of service via a crafted EXR file.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can cause a denial of service via a FPE runtime error in `tf.raw_ops.SparseMatMul`. The division by 0 occurs deep in Eigen code because the `b` tensor is empty. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Lines 10-11 derive n and k2 from b.dim_size(0)/dim_size(1) with no check that either dimension is nonzero; only shape rank and k==k2 are validated.
Lines 18-22 short-circuit only when k==0; if k is nonzero but n or k2 is zero, execution continues to the matmul path instead of returning.
Lines 60-74 transpose b when transpose_b is set, allocating a tensor of shape {right->dim_size(1), right->dim_size(0)} and shuffling; empty dimensions propagate here.
Lines 75-85 call DoMatMul with the possibly empty matrices, where Eigen's internal division by a zero dimension triggers the FPE.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The added OP_REQUIRES checks and the description confirm the root cause is a divide-by-zero deep in Eigen on empty b. CWE-369 directly matches an unhandled zero dimension causing an FPE denial of service, rather than an out-of-bounds or type-confusion weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The kernel validates matrix rank and k==k2 but never rejects a b tensor with a zero-sized dimension. When k is nonzero yet b is empty (e.g., n or k2 is 0), the k==0 guard at lines 18-22 is skipped and the tensor reaches DoMatMul, where Eigen divides by the zero dimension, causing a floating-point exception and process crash.

commit_msg:
x86/mm: Fix use-after-free of ldt_struct

The following commit:

  39a0526fb3f7 ("x86/mm: Factor out LDT init from context init")

renamed init_new_context() to init_new_context_ldt() and added a new
init_new_context() which calls init_new_context_ldt().  However, the
error code of init_new_context_ldt() was ignored.  Consequently, if a
memory allocation in alloc_ldt_struct() failed during a fork(), the
->context.ldt of the new task remained the same as that of the old task
(due to the memcpy() in dup_mm()).  ldt_struct's are not intended to be
shared, so a use-after-free occurred after one task exited.

Fix the bug by making init_new_context() pass through the error code of
init_new_context_ldt().

This bug was found by syzkaller, which encountered the following splat:

Here is a C reproducer:

    #include <asm/ldt.h>
    #include <pthread.h>
    #include <signal.h>
    #include <stdlib.h>
    #include <sys/syscall.h>
    #include <sys/wait.h>
    #include <unistd.h>

    static void *fork_thread(void *_arg)
    {
        fork();
    }

    int main(void)
    {
        struct user_desc desc = { .entry_number = 8191 };

        syscall(__NR_modify_ldt, 1, &desc, sizeof(desc));

        for (;;) {
            if (fork() == 0) {
                pthread_t t;

                srand(getpid());
                pthread_create(&t, NULL, fork_thread, NULL);
                usleep(rand() % 10000);
                syscall(__NR_exit_group, 0);
            }
            wait(NULL);
        }
    }

Note: the reproducer takes advantage of the fact that alloc_ldt_struct()
may use vmalloc() to allocate a large ->entries array, and after
commit:

  5d17a73a2ebe ("vmalloc: back off when the current task is killed")

it is possible for userspace to fail a task's vmalloc() by
sending a fatal signal, e.g. via exit_group().  It would be more
difficult to reproduce this bug on kernels without that commit.

This bug only affected kernels with CONFIG_MODIFY_LDT_SYSCALL=y.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tinit_new_context_ldt(tsk, mm);', '', '\treturn 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn init_new_context_ldt(tsk, mm);']}
description: The init_new_context function in arch/x86/include/asm/mmu_context.h in the Linux kernel before 4.12.10 does not correctly handle errors from LDT table allocation when forking a new process, allowing a local attacker to achieve a use-after-free or possibly have unspecified other impact by running a specially crafted program. This vulnerability only affected kernels built with CONFIG_MODIFY_LDT_SYSCALL=y.

code_evidence: init_new_context calls init_new_context_ldt(tsk, mm) but discards its return value and unconditionally returns 0. Thus a failed LDT allocation during fork is reported as success, leaving mm->context.ldt pointing at the parent's ldt_struct (shared via dup_mm's memcpy).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing error propagation causes a dangling pointer to freed ldt_struct memory, matching CWE-416 (reuse of memory after it is freed). The weakness is not a mere resource leak; the shared, freed structure is subsequently read or freed.

evidence_lines.code:
init_new_context_ldt(tsk, mm);
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error from init_new_context_ldt is ignored, so fork proceeds with a shared ldt_struct. When one task exits, destroy_context_ldt frees it; the other task's mm still references the freed ldt_struct, producing a use-after-free on later access or free. Trigger: a fork whose alloc_ldt_struct allocation fails (e.g., vmalloc failure under a fatal signal).

commit_msg: ExecHelperMain: fix privilege lowering code
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tfor (int i = 0; i < ngroups; i++) {', '\t\t\t\t\tgidset[i] = groups[i];', '\t\t\t\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in switchGroup() in agent/ExecHelper/ExecHelperMain.cpp in Phusion Passenger before 5.3.2. The set of groups (gidset) is not set correctly, leaving it up to randomness (i.e., uninitialized memory) which supplementary groups are actually being set while lowering privileges.

code_evidence: A scoped array gidset is allocated with new gid_t[ngroups] at line 24, then passed directly to setgroups(ngroups, gidset.get()) at line 25 without any element being assigned.
The source array groups is populated by getgrouplist at lines 14-15 and sized by ngroups, but those values are never copied into the newly allocated gidset buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-732 fits because the function assigns group-based permissions to the process using an incorrectly specified group set, allowing access by unintended actors rather than the intended restricted set. This is a permission-assignment flaw, not merely a missing authorization check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the supplementary group ID list passed to setgroups() is an uninitialized heap buffer, because gidset is allocated but never filled from groups[]. Trigger: switchGroup() runs on Linux/BSD during privilege lowering and setgroups() consumes the garbage gid values. Consequence: the process retains or acquires unintended supplementary group memberships, granting access beyond the intended privilege drop.

commit_msg: ADDED: Security check for `emscripten_run_script()` #2954
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    // Security check to (partially) avoid malicious code on PLATFORM_WEB', '    if (strchr(fileName, \'\\\'\') != NULL) { TRACELOG(LOG_WARNING, "SYSTEM: Provided fileName could be potentially malicious, avoid [\\\'] character");  return; }', '']}
description:
Versions of the package raysan5/raylib before 4.5.0 are vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting (XSS) such that the SetClipboardText API does not properly escape the ' character, allowing attacker-controlled input to break out of the string and execute arbitrary JavaScript via emscripten_run_script function.

**Note:** This vulnerability is present only when compiling raylib for PLATFORM_WEB. All the other Desktop/Mobile/Embedded platforms are not affected.

code_evidence: The function takes a caller-supplied fileName and concatenates it into path via TextFormat/strcpy without escaping.
On PLATFORM_WEB, path-derived names are interpolated into a JavaScript string passed to emscripten_run_script using single quotes, with no neutralization of quote characters.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-79 fits because user-controllable input is placed into generated web-page/script output without neutralization, enabling script injection. It is not merely a path-traversal issue; the supported consequence is script execution in the browser.

evidence_lines.code:
void TakeScreenshot(const char *fileName)
strcpy(path, TextFormat("%s/%s", CORE.Storage.basePath, fileName));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unescaped fileName content flows into a JavaScript string literal executed by emscripten_run_script. Trigger: a fileName containing a single quote breaks out of the quoted argument and injects arbitrary JavaScript. Consequence: attacker-influenced input executes script in the page context (XSS) on web builds.

commit_msg: rfadts: add size guard on dmx (#2400)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t'], 'added_lines': ['']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.3.0-DEV.

code_evidence: The index-growth block reallocs ctx->indexes to ctx->index_alloc_size entries, then writes ctx->indexes[ctx->index_size] before incrementing ctx->index_size. The guard only checks cur_dur > ctx->index * GF_M4ASampleRates[sr_idx], so index_size can reach index_alloc_size and the write lands one element past the heap allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The out-of-bounds write targets a heap buffer allocated by gf_realloc, matching CWE-122. CWE-787 is the generic base weakness; the heap allocation here makes the heap-based variant the correct label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the capacity check compares index_alloc_size == index_size but the write occurs at index_size before the increment, allowing a write at the allocation boundary. Trigger: crafted ADTS frames that repeatedly exceed the cur_dur threshold. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, memory corruption and potential code execution.

commit_msg: Fix for CVE-2023-28366
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '#ifdef WITH_BROKER', '\tif(mosq->out_packet_count >= db.config->max_queued_messages){', '\t\tmosquitto__free(packet);', '\t\tif(mosq->is_dropping == false){', '\t\t\tmosq->is_dropping = true;', '\t\t\tlog__printf(NULL, MOSQ_LOG_NOTICE,', '\t\t\t\t\t"Outgoing messages are being dropped for client %s.",', '\t\t\t\t\tmosq->id);', '\t\t}', '\t\tG_MSGS_DROPPED_INC();', '\t\treturn MOSQ_ERR_SUCCESS;', '\t}', '#endif', '']}
description: The broker in Eclipse Mosquitto 1.3.2 through 2.x before 2.0.16 has a memory leak that can be abused remotely when a client sends many QoS 2 messages with duplicate message IDs, and fails to respond to PUBREC commands. This occurs because of mishandling of EAGAIN from the libc send function.

code_evidence: After locking out_packet_mutex, the function unconditionally appends packet to the out_packet linked list via out_packet_last->next or out_packet, then increments out_packet_count. No check compares out_packet_count against a configured maximum before enqueueing, and the packet is never freed along this path; ownership transfers to the list. The diff adds exactly such a max_queued_messages check that frees packet and returns early.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because queued packet memory is allocated and, absent the queue-limit/free branch, never released during the connection, matching missing release of memory after effective lifetime. It is not a use-after-free (CWE-416): no freed memory is dereferenced; the defect is retained, unreleased allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pre-patch function lacks any bound on the outgoing packet queue, so each queued packet is retained on the linked list without release. Trigger: a remote client repeatedly causes packets (e.g., QoS 2 duplicate-ID messages) to be queued while not draining them. Consequence: unbounded growth of out_packet allocations, exhausting memory and enabling remote DoS.

commit_msg:
When using the basic authentication scheme, we wouldn't validate that
the authorization field of the credentials is not NULL and pass it on
to g_hash_table_lookup(). g_str_hash() however is not NULL-safe and will
dereference the NULL pointer and crash.
A specially crafted (read: invalid) RTSP header can cause this to
happen.

As a solution, check for the authorization to be not NULL before
continuing processing it and if it is simply fail authentication.

This fixes CVE-2020-6095 and TALOS-2020-1018.

Discovered by Peter Wang of Cisco ASIG.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if ((token ='], 'added_lines': ['      if ((*credential)->authorization && (token =']}
description: An exploitable denial of service vulnerability exists in the GstRTSPAuth functionality of GStreamer/gst-rtsp-server 1.14.5. A specially crafted RTSP setup request can cause a null pointer deference resulting in denial-of-service. An attacker can send a malicious packet to trigger this vulnerability.

code_evidence: For a Basic-scheme credential, the code passes (*credential)->authorization directly to g_hash_table_lookup() as the key. The field is not checked for NULL and is used as a hash key, which causes g_str_hash() to dereference it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer assumed valid but that can be NULL, matching CWE-476. This is a NULL-pointer dereference, not merely a missing input validation issue, because the crash arises from the NULL dereference inside the hash function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Basic-auth path uses the parsed authorization string as a hash key without verifying it is non-NULL. Trigger: a crafted RTSP Authorization header that parses into a Basic credential with a NULL authorization field. Consequence: g_str_hash() dereferences the NULL pointer, crashing the process (denial of service).

commit_msg: check max member count in class
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (_members->CountUsed() >= MEMBER_MAX_COUNT) {', '\t\treturn false;', '\t}']}
description: sqclass.cpp in Squirrel through 2.2.5 and 3.x through 3.1 allows an out-of-bounds read (in the core interpreter) that can lead to Code Execution. If a victim executes an attacker-controlled squirrel script, it is possible for the attacker to break out of the squirrel script sandbox even if all dangerous functionality such as File System functions has been disabled. An attacker might abuse this bug to target (for example) Cloud services that allow customization via SquirrelScripts, or distribute malware through video games that embed a Squirrel Engine.

code_evidence: NewSlot adds a new member without any bound on _defaultvalues: it pushes m into _defaultvalues and stores the index via _make_field_idx(_defaultvalues.size()). The patch inserts a MEMBER_MAX_COUNT check in the function (diff context), confirming the missing constraint is the root of the issue.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked member insertion permits indices that later drive reads beyond the allocated member buffer, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. This is not merely an integer overflow; the supported consequence is a read past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function allows unbounded growth of _defaultvalues/_methods and member indices. Once indices exceed the fixed member-count limit used by the interpreter, later member-index reads can access past the intended buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read that may crash or leak memory and enable sandbox escape.

commit_msg:
Fixed a buffer overrun problem in the QMFB code in the JPC codec
that was caused by a buffer being allocated with a size that was too small
in some cases.
Added a new regression test case.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!(buf = jas_alloc3(bufsize, JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE, sizeof(jpc_fix_t)))) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!(buf = jas_alloc3(bufsize, JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE,', '\t\t  sizeof(jpc_fix_t)))) {']}
description: A heap-buffer overflow vulnerability was found in QMFB code in JPC codec caused by buffer being allocated with too small size. jasper versions before 2.0.0 are affected.

code_evidence: bufsize is derived from numrows via JPC_CEILDIVPOW2(numrows,1), while the stack buffer joinbuf holds QMFB_JOINBUFSIZE*JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE elements. The heap path only triggers when bufsize exceeds QMFB_JOINBUFSIZE, allocating bufsize*JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE elements.
The first write loop copies hstartcol groups of JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE into buf, advancing dstptr by JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE each iteration, writing up to hstartcol*JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE elements.
The final loop rewinds srcptr to buf and reads hstartcol groups back out, consuming the same region that was written.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to and reads from a heap buffer beyond its allocated boundary, which is exactly an out-of-bounds memory buffer operation. This fits CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within memory buffer bounds; the specific allocation-size error is the underlying cause, but the observable weakness is the out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation size for the heap join buffer does not match the number of elements the copy loops write and later read. When bufsize is large, the size computation under-allocates relative to the hstartcol*JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE accesses, so the write loop stores past the heap buffer and the read loop reads out of bounds, causing heap corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
Change pairing_cb to assume temporary pairing by default

When pairing takes place, the pairing_cb.is_temp flag indicates whether
a pairing is temporary or permanent. Link keys are not stored for
temporary pairings. Since this is a "positive" flag, resetting the
pairing_cb control block (ex. memset to 0), it will assume persistent
pairing by default. Under certain circumstances, this can lead to a link
key being stored for temporarily secured connection.

This patch reverses the flag to be a "negative" flag. Renamed to
"persistent_bond", the default 0 meaning is now used to indicate a
temporary bond. If the lag is not properly set now, it will default to a
temporary bond and will not save the link key erronously.

This fix is for CVE-2014-7914

Bug: 18345373
Change-Id: I6e821595877ff30d64dc6e33602ac049cab3dd1e
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (pairing_cb.is_temp)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (pairing_cb.bond_type == BOND_TYPE_TEMPORARY)']}
description: btif/src/btif_dm.c in Android before 5.1 does not properly enforce the temporary nature of a Bluetooth pairing, which allows user-assisted remote attackers to bypass intended access restrictions via crafted Bluetooth packets after the tapping of a crafted NFC tag.

code_evidence: Line 5 gates the entire bond-state transition on pairing_cb.is_temp; when the flag is true the function forces state to BT_BOND_STATE_NONE (lines 6-8), suppressing the bonding callback that would otherwise persist the link key.
Lines 16-19: on any non-bonding state, the pairing_cb control block is memset to zero, resetting the is_temp flag to its zero default, which is interpreted as a permanent pairing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a security-relevant authorization decision—whether a pairing may be persisted—but the default-zero positive flag makes that check incorrect, allowing a temporary bond to be treated as authorized for permanent storage. This is a flawed authorization check (CWE-863), not merely a logic error, because the access restriction on link-key storage is bypassed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the temporary/permanent pairing decision is represented by a positive flag (is_temp) whose zero-initialized default means 'permanent,' so any reset or unset flag silently authorizes persistent bond storage. Trigger: a temporary pairing whose control block is zeroed (line 18) or whose flag is not explicitly set, after which line 5's check is false and the bonding state proceeds to store a link key. Consequence: temporary pairing is enforced as permanent, bypassing the intended restriction.

commit_msg:
mm: Tighten x86 /dev/mem with zeroing reads

Under CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM, reading System RAM through /dev/mem is
disallowed. However, on x86, the first 1MB was always allowed for BIOS
and similar things, regardless of it actually being System RAM. It was
possible for heap to end up getting allocated in low 1MB RAM, and then
read by things like x86info or dd, which would trip hardened usercopy:

usercopy: kernel memory exposure attempt detected from ffff880000090000 (dma-kmalloc-256) (4096 bytes)

This changes the x86 exception for the low 1MB by reading back zeros for
System RAM areas instead of blindly allowing them. More work is needed to
extend this to mmap, but currently mmap doesn't go through usercopy, so
hardened usercopy won't Oops the kernel.

Reported-by: Tommi Rantala <tommi.t.rantala@nokia.com>
Tested-by: Tommi Rantala <tommi.t.rantala@nokia.com>
Signed-off-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!range_is_allowed(p >> PAGE_SHIFT, count))', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * On ia64 if a page has been mapped somewhere as uncached, then', '\t\t * it must also be accessed uncached by the kernel or data', '\t\t * corruption may occur.', '\t\t */', '\t\tptr = xlate_dev_mem_ptr(p);', '\t\tif (!ptr)', '\t\t\treturn -EFAULT;', '\t\tremaining = copy_to_user(buf, ptr, sz);', '\t\tunxlate_dev_mem_ptr(p, ptr);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tint allowed;', '\t\tallowed = page_is_allowed(p >> PAGE_SHIFT);', '\t\tif (!allowed)', '\t\tif (allowed == 2) {', '\t\t\t/* Show zeros for restricted memory. */', '\t\t\tremaining = clear_user(buf, sz);', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t\t/*', '\t\t\t * On ia64 if a page has been mapped somewhere as', '\t\t\t * uncached, then it must also be accessed uncached', '\t\t\t * by the kernel or data corruption may occur.', '\t\t\t */', '\t\t\tptr = xlate_dev_mem_ptr(p);', '\t\t\tif (!ptr)', '\t\t\t\treturn -EFAULT;', '\t\t\tremaining = copy_to_user(buf, ptr, sz);', '\t\t\tunxlate_dev_mem_ptr(p, ptr);', '\t\t}', '']}
description: The mm subsystem in the Linux kernel through 3.2 does not properly enforce the CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM protection mechanism, which allows local users to read or write to kernel memory locations in the first megabyte (and bypass slab-allocation access restrictions) via an application that opens the /dev/mem file, related to arch/x86/mm/init.c and drivers/char/mem.c.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function checks and enforces access via range_is_allowed rather than assigning permissions; the flaw is an insufficient authorization check on /dev/mem, which maps to CWE-285/863, not incorrect permission assignment (CWE-732).

commit_msg: Use readOrThrow to check error conditions of iIo.read().
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        iIo.read(riff, len);', '        iIo.read(data, len);', '        iIo.read(webp, len);'], 'added_lines': ['        readOrThrow(iIo, riff, len, Exiv2::kerCorruptedMetadata);', '        readOrThrow(iIo, data, len, Exiv2::kerCorruptedMetadata);', '        readOrThrow(iIo, webp, len, Exiv2::kerCorruptedMetadata);']}
description: Exiv2 is a C++ library and a command-line utility to read, write, delete and modify Exif, IPTC, XMP and ICC image metadata. A read of uninitialized memory was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.3 and earlier. Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. The read of uninitialized memory is triggered when Exiv2 is used to read the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to leak a few bytes of stack memory, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. The bug is fixed in version v0.27.4.

code_evidence: Stack buffers webp, data, and riff are declared without initialization, then filled via iIo.read(riff, len), iIo.read(data, len), and iIo.read(webp, len).

The return value of each read is ignored; if a read returns fewer than len bytes, the corresponding buffer retains uninitialized stack bytes that are then passed to memcmp against RiffImageId and WebPImageId.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the function uses uninitialized stack buffers (riff, webp) in memcmp after a failed or partial read; the fix replaces bare reads with readOrThrow to enforce full initialization before use. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the buffers are within bounds but uninitialized.

evidence_lines.code:
bool matched_riff = (memcmp(riff, RiffImageId, len) == 0);
bool matched_webp = (memcmp(webp, WebPImageId, len) == 0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the short read is not detected because iIo.read's return value is discarded, leaving part of the local buffers uninitialized. Trigger: a crafted image whose size passes the <12 check but whose reads return short, so memcmp reads uninitialized stack memory. Supported consequence: uninitialized stack bytes are read and can influence the comparison result, enabling limited stack memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
Fix integer issues leading to out of bounds access in fx_ge_text.cpp.

- Using |-skew| to get positive index, which doesn't work when skew is
  INT_MIN
- Incorrect logic when determining when to use |-skew| as an index.

R=tsepez@chromium.org,weili@chromium.org
BUG=chromium:601362

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1875673004
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      // skew is nonpositive so -skew is used as the index.', '      skew = -skew <= static_cast<int>(ANGLESKEW_ARRAY_SIZE)', '                 ? -58', '                 : -g_AngleSkew[-skew];'], 'added_lines': ['      // |skew| is nonpositive so |-skew| is used as the index. We need to make', '      // sure |skew| != INT_MIN since -INT_MIN is undefined.', '      if (skew <= 0 && skew != std::numeric_limits<int>::min() &&', '          static_cast<size_t>(-skew) < ANGLESKEW_ARRAY_SIZE) {', '        skew = -g_AngleSkew[-skew];', '      } else {', '        skew = -58;', '      }']}
description: core/fxge/ge/fx_ge_text.cpp in PDFium, as used in Google Chrome before 51.0.2704.63, miscalculates certain index values, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted PDF document.

code_evidence: m_ItalicAngle is read into skew [9]; the ternary computes -skew and uses -skew directly as an index into g_AngleSkew [10,12] without any lower-bound check. When skew is negative, -skew is positive and can exceed ANGLESKEW_ARRAY_SIZE; the bound test only compares -skew <= size and chooses -58 otherwise, but for skew == INT_MIN, -skew overflows (undefined) and the index is still used.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code indexes a fixed-size memory buffer (g_AngleSkew) using a value that is not properly restricted, allowing a read past the buffer boundary, which matches CWE-119. The integer overflow/negation issue is the root cause enabling the out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the skew value from the substituted font is used as an array index with an incorrect bounds test and without excluding INT_MIN. Trigger: a crafted PDF supplies an italic angle whose negation overflows or exceeds the angle-skew table size. Consequence: g_AngleSkew is read out of bounds, producing an out-of-bounds read and denial of service.

commit_msg:
KVM: x86: Forbid VMM to set SYNIC/STIMER MSRs when SynIC wasn't activated

Setting non-zero values to SYNIC/STIMER MSRs activates certain features,
this should not happen when KVM_CAP_HYPERV_SYNIC{,2} was not activated.

Note, it would've been better to forbid writing anything to SYNIC/STIMER
MSRs, including zeroes, however, at least QEMU tries clearing
HV_X64_MSR_STIMER0_CONFIG without SynIC. HV_X64_MSR_EOM MSR is somewhat
'special' as writing zero there triggers an action, this also should not
happen when SynIC wasn't activated.

Signed-off-by: Vitaly Kuznetsov <vkuznets@redhat.com>
Message-Id: <20220325132140.25650-4-vkuznets@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!synic->active && !host)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!synic->active && (!host || config))']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s KVM when attempting to set a SynIC IRQ. This issue makes it possible for a misbehaving VMM to write to SYNIC/STIMER MSRs, causing a NULL pointer dereference. This flaw allows an unprivileged local attacker on the host to issue specific ioctl calls, causing a kernel oops condition that results in a denial of service.

code_evidence: stimer_set_config derives synic via to_hv_synic(vcpu) and, before the fix, only rejects the call when !synic->active && !host; host-originated calls with inactive SynIC proceed past the guard.

The function then continues to read hv_vcpu fields and later dereferences stimer->config; when SynIC was never activated, the SYNIC/STIMER state is not initialized, so these accesses operate on unset pointers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a NULL pointer dereference caused by missing validation of SynIC activation before using uninitialized SYNIC/STIMER structures; this matches CWE-476. It is not merely improper input validation because the demonstrated impact is dereference of an invalid pointer.

evidence_lines.code:
if (unlikely(!host && hv_vcpu->enforce_cpuid && new_config.direct_mode &&
!(hv_vcpu->cpuid_cache.features_edx &
HV_STIMER_DIRECT_MODE_AVAILABLE)))
return 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard permits MSR configuration when synic->active is false as long as host is true, so VMM writes reach stimer_set_config without SynIC activation. Trigger: a misbehaving VMM issues ioctl calls setting SYNIC/STIMER MSRs. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference leading to a kernel oops and denial of service.

commit_msg:
GCM: move look-up table to .data section and unshare between processes

* cipher/cipher-gcm.c (ATTR_ALIGNED_64): New.
(gcmR): Move to 'gcm_table' structure.
(gcm_table): New structure for look-up table with counters before and
after.
(gcmR): New macro.
(prefetch_table): Handle input with length not multiple of 256.
(do_prefetch_tables): Modify pre- and post-table counters to unshare
look-up table pages between processes.
--

GnuPG-bug-id: 4541
Signed-off-by: Jussi Kivilinna <jussi.kivilinna@iki.fi>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  prefetch_table(gcmR, sizeof(gcmR));'], 'added_lines': ['  /* Modify counters to trigger copy-on-write and unsharing if physical pages', '   * of look-up table are shared between processes.  Modifying counters also', '   * causes checksums for pages to change and hint same-page merging algorithm', '   * that these pages are frequently changing.  */', '  gcm_table.counter_head++;', '  gcm_table.counter_tail++;', '', '  /* Prefetch look-up tables to cache.  */', '  prefetch_table(&gcm_table, sizeof(gcm_table));']}
description: In Libgcrypt 1.8.4, the C implementation of AES is vulnerable to a flush-and-reload side-channel attack because physical addresses are available to other processes. (The C implementation is used on platforms where an assembly-language implementation is unavailable.) NOTE: the vendor's position is that the issue report cannot be validated because there is no description of an attack

code_evidence: The function only prefetches the GCM lookup tables (gcmM and gcmR) into cache; it performs no counter modification, copy-on-write trigger, or page-unsharing logic. The shared physical pages of these lookup tables remain shared across processes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-668 fits because the lookup-table memory resource is exposed to unintended actors (other processes) through shared physical pages rather than being restricted to the owning process's control sphere. The pre-patch function lacks the unsharing modification that the patch adds.

evidence_lines.code:
prefetch_table(gcmM, gcmM_size);
prefetch_table(gcmR, sizeof(gcmR));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the prefetch routine touches lookup-table data without modifying any page, so identical physical pages remain shared between processes (e.g., via same-page merging) and their physical addresses stay observable. Trigger: an attacker process on the same host observing cache/page behavior. Consequence: the lookup-table resource is exposed to a control sphere outside the owning process, enabling flush-and-reload side-channel observation.

(cherry picked from commit a12cc3e14ea6734c7efe76aa6a19239909830b28)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            fMemArray = sk_malloc_throw(fAllocCount * sizeof(T));'], 'added_lines': ['            fMemArray = sk_malloc_throw(fAllocCount, sizeof(T));']}
description: In SkSampler::Fill of SkSampler.cpp, there is a possible out of bounds write due to an integer overflow. This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation. Product: Android Versions: Android-7.0 Android-7.1.1 Android-7.1.2 Android-8.0 Android-8.1 Android ID: A-78354855

code_evidence: Line 2 only asserts count >= 0, and line 8 compares count against preallocCount. When count exceeds preallocCount, line 9 sets fAllocCount to the larger of count and kMinHeapAllocCount, and line 10 multiplies fAllocCount by sizeof(T) in int arithmetic before passing the product to sk_malloc_throw.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because an unchecked integer multiplication used to size a heap allocation can wrap, yielding a buffer smaller than the requested element count. This differs from a plain out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), which here is the consequence rather than the root cause; the patch replaces the product with a two-argument helper that performs a saturating overflow check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation-size multiplication fAllocCount * sizeof(T) is computed in a fixed-width integer type without any overflow check. Trigger: a large count (attacker-influenced) that makes the product wrap to a small value. The undersized allocation is then used with fAllocCount as the logical capacity, so subsequent writes past the wrapped size cause an out-of-bounds write.

it introduced null-ptr-deref in rds_tcp_kill_sock as below:

At line 19 the code unconditionally evaluates tc->t_sock->sk, so if a connection was queued with t_sock == NULL, the dereference of a NULL pointer occurs before disconnect or tcp_done are reached.

Trigger: a connection with t_sock set to NULL is moved into tmp_list, then the second loop dereferences tc->t_sock->sk. Supported consequence is a kernel NULL pointer dereference leading to denial of service (crash).

if (*(ml_get(lnum) + leader1_len) == NUL)

commit_msg:
dmg: prevent chunk buffer overflow (CVE-2014-0145)

Both compressed and uncompressed I/O is buffered.  dmg_open() calculates
the maximum buffer size needed from the metadata in the image file.

There is currently a buffer overflow since ->lengths[] is accounted
against the maximum compressed buffer size but actually uses the
uncompressed buffer:

  switch (s->types[chunk]) {
  case 1: /* copy */
      ret = bdrv_pread(bs->file, s->offsets[chunk],
                       s->uncompressed_chunk, s->lengths[chunk]);

We must account against the maximum uncompressed buffer size for type=1
chunks.

This patch fixes the maximum buffer size calculation to take into
account the chunk type.  It is critical that we update the correct
maximum since there are two buffers ->compressed_chunk and
->uncompressed_chunk.

Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Kevin Wolf <kwolf@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Max Reitz <mreitz@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                if (s->lengths[i] > max_compressed_size) {', '                    max_compressed_size = s->lengths[i];', '                }', '                if (s->sectorcounts[i] > max_sectors_per_chunk) {', '                    max_sectors_per_chunk = s->sectorcounts[i];', '                }'], 'added_lines': ['                update_max_chunk_size(s, i, &max_compressed_size,', '                                      &max_sectors_per_chunk);']}
description: Multiple buffer overflows in QEMU before 1.7.2 and 2.x before 2.0.0, allow local users to cause a denial of service (crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a large (1) L1 table in the qcow2_snapshot_load_tmp in the QCOW 2 block driver (block/qcow2-snapshot.c) or (2) uncompressed chunk, (3) chunk length, or (4) number of sectors in the DMG block driver (block/dmg.c).

code_evidence: The loop tracks max_compressed_size only from s->lengths[i] and max_sectors_per_chunk from s->sectorcounts[i], regardless of chunk type.
Type-1 (copy) chunks are read directly into s->uncompressed_chunk using s->lengths[chunk] as the byte count, but the uncompressed buffer is sized as 512 * max_sectors_per_chunk, not from lengths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The length accounting mismatch allows a read to write beyond the intended boundary of the allocated uncompressed buffer, directly matching CWE-119. This is a buffer-bounds error rather than merely an integer overflow, since the size computation and the actual write size use different metadata fields.

evidence_lines.code:
s->compressed_chunk = g_malloc(max_compressed_size + 1);
s->uncompressed_chunk = g_malloc(512 * max_sectors_per_chunk);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the maximum-buffer accounting ignores that type=1 chunks write s->lengths[i] bytes into the uncompressed buffer, which is sized only from sector counts. Trigger: a crafted DMG image with a type=1 chunk whose length exceeds 512 * max_sectors_per_chunk. Consequence: bdrv_pread writes past s->uncompressed_chunk, causing heap memory corruption, crash, or potential code execution.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.7-23 Q16 x86_64 2018-01-24, there is a heap-based buffer over-read in ReadSUNImage in coders/sun.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash in SetGrayscaleImage in MagickCore/quantize.c) via a crafted SUN image file.

For RMT_EQUAL_RGB, sun_colormap is allocated with image->colors bytes and ReadBlob reads image->colors bytes; the loop at 128 iterates i<image->colors writing image->colormap[i]. If colors==0 the colormap lacks entries, so later pixel lookups index an empty colormap.

commit_msg:
Excessive allocation of memory in dtls1_preprocess_fragment()

This issue is very similar to CVE-2016-6307 described in the previous
commit. The underlying defect is different but the security analysis and
impacts are the same except that it impacts DTLS.

A DTLS message includes 3 bytes for its length in the header for the
message.
This would allow for messages up to 16Mb in length. Messages of this length
are excessive and OpenSSL includes a check to ensure that a peer is sending
reasonably sized messages in order to avoid too much memory being consumed
to service a connection. A flaw in the logic of version 1.1.0 means that
memory for the message is allocated too early, prior to the excessive
message length check. Due to way memory is allocated in OpenSSL this could
mean an attacker could force up to 21Mb to be allocated to service a
connection. This could lead to a Denial of Service through memory
exhaustion. However, the excessive message length check still takes place,
and this would cause the connection to immediately fail. Assuming that the
application calls SSL_free() on the failed conneciton in a timely manner
then the 21Mb of allocated memory will then be immediately freed again.
Therefore the excessive memory allocation will be transitory in nature.
This then means that there is only a security impact if:

1) The application does not call SSL_free() in a timely manner in the
event that the connection fails
or
2) The application is working in a constrained environment where there
is very little free memory
or
3) The attacker initiates multiple connection attempts such that there
are multiple connections in a state where memory has been allocated for
the connection; SSL_free() has not yet been called; and there is
insufficient memory to service the multiple requests.

Except in the instance of (1) above any Denial Of Service is likely to
be transitory because as soon as the connection fails the memory is
subsequently freed again in the SSL_free() call. However there is an
increased risk during this period of application crashes due to the lack
of memory - which would then mean a more serious Denial of Service.

This issue does not affect TLS users.

Issue was reported by Shi Lei (Gear Team, Qihoo 360 Inc.).

CVE-2016-6308

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
(cherry picked from commit 48c054fec3506417b2598837b8062aae7114c200)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ((frag_off + frag_len) > msg_len) {', '         * msg_len is limited to 2^24, but is effectively checked against max', '         * above'], 'added_lines': ['    if ((frag_off + frag_len) > msg_len', '            || msg_len > dtls1_max_handshake_message_len(s)) {', '         * msg_len is limited to 2^24, but is effectively checked against', '         * dtls_max_handshake_message_len(s) above']}
description: statem/statem_dtls.c in the DTLS implementation in OpenSSL 1.1.0 before 1.1.0a allocates memory before checking for an excessive length, which might allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via crafted DTLS messages.

code_evidence: The sanity check only rejects the fragment when frag_off + frag_len exceeds msg_len; msg_len itself is not bounded against the implementation maximum.

After that check passes, the first-fragment branch calls BUF_MEM_grow_clean with msg_len + DTLS1_HM_HEADER_LENGTH, allocating memory based on the attacker-supplied 3-byte length before any excessive-size limit is enforced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 is the resource management category covering improper control of resource allocation/consumption. The function allocates attacker-influenced memory before enforcing a size limit, directly matching the category's resource-consumption concern.

evidence_lines.code:
if (s->d1->r_msg_hdr.frag_off == 0) { 
if (!BUF_MEM_grow_clean(s->init_buf, msg_len + DTLS1_HM_HEADER_LENGTH)) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the message-length limit check is missing before allocation, so the only bound is the 24-bit msg_len. Trigger: a peer sends a DTLS handshake message with a very large but internally consistent msg_len. The BUF_MEM_grow_clean call then allocates up to ~16MB per connection before the excessive-length rejection, enabling memory-exhaustion denial of service, especially with multiple pending connections or delayed SSL_free.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/1517
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (count != (ssize_t) length)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (length == 0)', '      break;', '    if (count != (ssize_t) extent)']}
description: ImageMagick 7.0.8-34 has a memory leak vulnerability in the WriteDPXImage function in coders/dpx.c.

code_evidence: The row loop calls ExportQuantumPixels into the buffer returned by GetQuantumPixels (line 512) and then WriteBlob. The original exit path breaks out of the loop when count != (ssize_t) length (line 523-524), where length is the exported byte count, not the per-row extent. When length differs from extent, the loop exits early; control reaches DestroyQuantumInfo at line 530, but the function then unconditionally throws via ThrowWriterException at line 532, which returns without CloseBlob(image) at line 533. The patch adds a length==0 break and compares count against extent instead of length, preventing the premature exit and ensuring the write comparison matches the actual bytes written.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to release the blob resources allocated by OpenBlob (line 64) when the write loop exits abnormally, matching CWE-401's missing release of memory after effective lifetime. This is a resource-lifetime error path, not a buffer overflow or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop compares WriteBlob's return against ExportQuantumPixels' returned length rather than the fixed per-row extent, so a mismatch (e.g., zero-length export or short write) breaks the loop early. Trigger: an image whose exported length differs from extent. The early break skips progress handling and reaches the error throw, which bypasses CloseBlob, leaving the blob's allocated resources unreleased for the lifetime of the operation.

commit_msg:
seas: safety check for target buffer size before copying message in encode_msg()

- avoid buffer overflow for large SIP messages
- reported by Stelios Tsampas

After header encoding, j holds the write offset and msg->len the SIP message size; line 102 copies msg->len bytes to &payload[j] without checking j + msg->len against len, so j can be near the buffer end and the copy overflows.

commit_msg:
ohci: allocate timer only once.

Allocate timer once, at init time, instead of allocating/freeing
it all the time when starting/stopping the bus.  Simplifies the
code, also fixes bugs (memory leak) due to missing checks whenever
the time is already allocated or not.

Cc: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Reported-by: Zuozhi Fzz <zuozhi.fzz@alibaba-inc.com>
Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>

description: The ohci_bus_start function in the USB OHCI emulation support (hw/usb/hcd-ohci.c) in QEMU allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and QEMU process crash) via vectors related to multiple eof_timers.

code_evidence: The function guards timer_del/timer_free with an if (ohci->eof_timer) check and then unconditionally sets ohci->eof_timer = NULL, so the pointer is dereferenced only after a NULL check and freed once.

The described crash from multiple eof_timers arises from allocation/free race conditions across start/stop elsewhere, not from an unguarded dereference in this function. description: libsixel before 1.10 is vulnerable to Buffer Overflow in libsixel/src/quant.c:867.

code_evidence: Line 6 computes pos = y*width+x with no bound check on x or y. Line 7 only guards pos < (height-2)*width-2, which does not constrain the right-edge offsets; calls at lines 8-9 add +1 and +2 to pos and lines 15-19 add width*2+1/+2, which can exceed the width*height buffer for pixels near the right/bottom edge. The fix passes width*height as a size argument so error_diffuse can reject out-of-range targets.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes indices that can point beyond the width*height buffer and passes them to error_diffuse for writing, which is an out-of-bounds write. The patch adding the width*height bound confirms the intended write target was not enforced; this is a spatial bounds error rather than an integer or pointer-arithmetic weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller computes neighbor indices with unconstrained x/y offsets and only checks a single pos threshold, so edge pixels produce indices beyond the buffer. Trigger: processing an image whose current pixel lies near the right or bottom edge. Consequence: error_diffuse writes past the allocated data buffer, corrupting memory (CWE-787).

commit_msg:
Bug 689699: Avoid buffer overrun.

When cleaning a pdf file, various lists (of pdf_xref_len length) are
defined early on.

If we trigger a repair during the clean, this can cause pdf_xref_len
to increase causing an overrun.

Fix this by watching for changes in the length, and checking accesses
to the list for validity.

This also appears to fix bugs 698700-698703.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t{', '\t\t\txref_len = pdf_xref_len(ctx, doc); /* May have changed due to repair */', '\t\t}', '\t\t{', '\t\t\txref_len = pdf_xref_len(ctx, doc); /* May have changed due to repair */', '\t\t}']}
description: pdf/pdf-write.c in Artifex MuPDF before 1.12.0 mishandles certain length changes when a repair operation occurs during a clean operation, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PDF document.

code_evidence: xref_len is cached once at line 17 before initialise_write_state/markobj, which may trigger a repair that grows pdf_xref_len; the loop at [29,30] then writes opts->use_list[num] up to the stale, smaller xref_len.
The truncation loop at [38,39] indexes opts->use_list[xref_len-1] using the same stale xref_len, which can exceed the current list length after a repair.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing and reading opts->use_list beyond its allocated bounds due to a stale length is an out-of-bounds memory buffer operation, directly matching CWE-119. The fix recomputes pdf_xref_len before each indexed loop; a mere off-by-one would be CWE-193, but here the length can diverge arbitrarily after repair.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: xref_len is captured before operations (initialise_write_state, markobj, preloadobjstms) that can perform a repair and increase pdf_xref_len, while use_list/gen_list/ofs_list were allocated at the old length. Trigger: a crafted PDF that causes a repair during cleaning. The stale length drives out-of-bounds writes in the [29,30] loop and out-of-bounds reads in the [38,39] truncation loop, causing buffer overflow and crash.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/770
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    SetImageProperty(image,"vips:metadata",metadata);'], 'added_lines': ['    {', '      SetImageProperty(image,"vips:metadata",metadata);', '      metadata=(char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(metadata);', '    }']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.0.7-4 Q16, a memory leak vulnerability was found in the function ReadVIPSImage in coders/vips.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption in ResizeMagickMemory in MagickCore/memory.c) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: metadata is initialized to NULL at [134] and grown inside the read loop via ConstantString at [139] and ConcatenateString at [141], allocating heap memory for the file-supplied metadata. After the loop, [143]-[144] pass metadata to SetImageProperty but never free the buffer; the function then closes the blob and returns the image at [145]-[148], losing the only pointer. The patch adds RelinquishMagickMemory after SetImageProperty, confirming the missing release.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because a heap resource (metadata) outlives its effective lifetime and is never released, matching the missing-release pattern and the reported memory-consumption impact. It is not CWE-401, which concerns freeing before all references are removed; here the allocation is simply never freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocated metadata string is not released after SetImageProperty consumes it. Trigger: any VIPS file reaching the metadata loop, with attacker-controlled size/content causing repeated ConcatenateString reallocations. Supported consequence: heap memory remains allocated per decoded image, causing memory consumption/DoS when many crafted files are processed.

commit_msg:
If the notification message length is 0, ignore the message (#4237)

Fixes #4234.

Signed-off-by: Jorge Niedbalski <jnr@metaklass.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        }', '        if (n == 0) {', '                log_debug("Got zero-length notification message. Ignoring.");', '                return 0;']}
description: The manager_invoke_notify_message function in systemd 231 and earlier allows local users to cause a denial of service (assertion failure and PID 1 hang) via a zero-length message received over a notify socket.

code_evidence: Line 33 receives attacker-influenced data via recvmsg from the notify socket; the negative-length branch at 34-38 only handles errors and returns, so a zero-length result n==0 falls through unhandled.
Lines 61-64 only reject oversized messages (n >= sizeof(buf)); a zero-length message passes this check and reaches buf[n]=0 at line 65, then is forwarded to manager_invoke_notify_message with n==0.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts externally supplied input and fails to validate a required property (nonzero length) before processing, which directly matches CWE-20 improper input validation. The added n==0 guard confirms the missing length constraint rather than a separate memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the receive path validates the upper bound of the message length but never validates that the length is nonzero, so a zero-length notify message is treated as valid input. Trigger: a local user sends a zero-length message over the notify socket. Supported consequence: the unvalidated zero-length input propagates into the notification handling path and causes an assertion failure and PID 1 hang (DoS).
