description: The aout_get_external_symbols function in aoutx.h in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29.1, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (slurp_symtab invalid free and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: Line 41 reads stringsize from the file's string table header. Line 48 allocates stringsize+1 bytes, but line 51 computes amt = stringsize - BYTES_IN_WORD without validating stringsize >= BYTES_IN_WORD. If stringsize is 0 or below the word size, the unsigned subtraction underflows to a huge value passed to bfd_bread at line 52, and line 59 writes strings[stringsize - 1], indexing outside the allocated buffer when stringsize is zero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs read/write operations outside the intended buffer boundary due to missing size validation, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within memory buffer bounds. The underflowed length and negative index are direct out-of-bounds accesses, not merely an integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an attacker-controlled string table size is used in unchecked subtraction and indexing. Trigger: a crafted aout/ELF file whose string size is zero or smaller than BYTES_IN_WORD. Consequence: out-of-bounds read/write via bfd_bread and strings[stringsize-1], leading to invalid free and crash (DoS) or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
MS-MMS: Use format_text_string()

The length of a string transcoded from UTF-16 to UTF-8 can be
shorter (or longer) than the original length in bytes in the packet.
Use the new string length, not the original length.

Use format_text_string, which is a convenience function that
calls strlen.

Fix #19086
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    format_text(pinfo->pool, (const guchar*)server_version, strlen(server_version)));'], 'added_lines': ['                    format_text_string(pinfo->pool, (const guchar*)server_version));']}
description: Due to failure in validating the length provided by an attacker-crafted MSMMS packet, Wireshark version 4.0.5 and prior, in an unusual configuration, is susceptible to a heap-based buffer overflow, and possibly code execution in the context of the process running Wireshark

code_evidence: The UTF-16 server version is decoded into server_version using an attacker-controlled byte count server_version_length*2; the resulting UTF-8 string can be shorter than that byte length.
format_text is then called with the original byte length strlen(server_version) as the length bound, while the actual transcoded string is shorter or longer.
The offset is advanced by server_version_length*2, so the packet length drives the read/write extent independently of the decoded string size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of an allocated buffer because a length derived from attacker input is not constrained to the actual string length, matching CWE-787. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the format_text operation produces the overflow write.

evidence_lines.code:
col_append_fstr(pinfo->cinfo, COL_INFO, " (version='%s')",
format_text(pinfo->pool, (const guchar*)server_version, strlen(server_version)));
offset += (server_version_length*2);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is using the packet-supplied UTF-16 byte length as the length passed to format_text instead of the actual transcoded string length. When the UTF-8 result length differs, format_text reads/writes beyond the allocated formatted buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds write (and possible code execution).

commit_msg:
ipsec: Fix aborted xfrm policy dump crash

An independent security researcher, Mohamed Ghannam, has reported
this vulnerability to Beyond Security's SecuriTeam Secure Disclosure
program.

The xfrm_dump_policy_done function expects xfrm_dump_policy to
have been called at least once or it will crash.  This can be
triggered if a dump fails because the target socket's receive
buffer is full.

This patch fixes it by using the cb->start mechanism to ensure that
the initialisation is always done regardless of the buffer situation.

Change-Id: Id41cdd41c4e43e0c3ac30c5d03c15b8046d70845
Fixes: 12a169e7d8f4 ("ipsec: Put dumpers on the dump list")
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct xfrm_policy_walk *walk = (struct xfrm_policy_walk *) &cb->args[1];', '', '\tBUILD_BUG_ON(sizeof(struct xfrm_policy_walk) >', '\t\t     sizeof(cb->args) - sizeof(cb->args[0]));', '\tif (!cb->args[0]) {', '\t\tcb->args[0] = 1;', '\t\txfrm_policy_walk_init(walk, XFRM_POLICY_TYPE_ANY);', '\t}', ''], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct xfrm_policy_walk *walk = (struct xfrm_policy_walk *)cb->args;']}
description: A vulnerability classified as problematic has been found in flar2 ElementalX up to 6.x on Nexus 9. Affected is the function xfrm_dump_policy_done of the file net/xfrm/xfrm_user.c of the component ipsec. The manipulation leads to denial of service. Upgrading to version 7.00 is able to address this issue. The name of the patch is 1df72c9f0f61304437f4f1037df03b5fb36d5a79. It is recommended to upgrade the affected component. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-217152.

code_evidence: The walk state is stored in cb->args[1], leaving cb->args[0] as a separate 'initialized' flag.

The guard at line 12 initializes the walk only when cb->args[0] is zero; if a prior dump invocation never reached this initialization (e.g., buffer-full abort), cb->args[0] stays zero and the walk is initialized later, but the reverse path—done handler called without initialization—is what the commit fixes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers improper resource shutdown/release; here the per-dump walk resource is not properly established/released across the dump lifecycle, yielding a crash. The fix makes initialization unconditional via cb->start, matching improper resource lifecycle management rather than a memory-safety class such as CWE-476.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the policy-walk resource (walk state in cb->args) is initialized lazily under a conditional flag rather than unconditionally per dump lifecycle. Trigger: a dump aborted before the initialization block runs, so xfrm_dump_policy_done later operates on an uninitialized walk. Supported consequence: crash/denial of service from using an improperly managed resource.

commit_msg:
bpf: Fix scalar32_min_max_or bounds tracking

Simon reported an issue with the current scalar32_min_max_or() implementation.
That is, compared to the other 32 bit subreg tracking functions, the code in
scalar32_min_max_or() stands out that it's using the 64 bit registers instead
of 32 bit ones. This leads to bounds tracking issues, for example:

  [...]
  8: R0=map_value(id=0,off=0,ks=4,vs=48,imm=0) R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  8: (79) r1 = *(u64 *)(r0 +0)
   R0=map_value(id=0,off=0,ks=4,vs=48,imm=0) R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  9: R0=map_value(id=0,off=0,ks=4,vs=48,imm=0) R1_w=inv(id=0) R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  9: (b7) r0 = 1
  10: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  10: (18) r2 = 0x600000002
  12: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  12: (ad) if r1 < r2 goto pc+1
   R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umin_value=25769803778) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  13: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umin_value=25769803778) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  13: (95) exit
  14: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=25769803777,var_off=(0x0; 0x7ffffffff)) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  14: (25) if r1 > 0x0 goto pc+1
   R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=0,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffff),u32_max_value=2147483647) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  15: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=0,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffff),u32_max_value=2147483647) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  15: (95) exit
  16: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umin_value=1,umax_value=25769803777,var_off=(0x0; 0x77fffffff),u32_max_value=2147483647) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  16: (47) r1 |= 0
  17: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umin_value=1,umax_value=32212254719,var_off=(0x1; 0x700000000),s32_max_value=1,u32_max_value=1) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  [...]

The bound tests on the map value force the upper unsigned bound to be 25769803777
in 64 bit (0b11000000000000000000000000000000001) and then lower one to be 1. By
using OR they are truncated and thus result in the range [1,1] for the 32 bit reg
tracker. This is incorrect given the only thing we know is that the value must be
positive and thus 2147483647 (0b1111111111111111111111111111111) at max for the
subregs. Fix it by using the {u,s}32_{min,max}_value vars instead. This also makes
sense, for example, for the case where we update dst_reg->s32_{min,max}_value in
the else branch we need to use the newly computed dst_reg->u32_{min,max}_value as
we know that these are positive. Previously, in the else branch the 64 bit values
of umin_value=1 and umax_value=32212254719 were used and latter got truncated to
be 1 as upper bound there. After the fix the subreg range is now correct:

  [...]
  8: R0=map_value(id=0,off=0,ks=4,vs=48,imm=0) R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  8: (79) r1 = *(u64 *)(r0 +0)
   R0=map_value(id=0,off=0,ks=4,vs=48,imm=0) R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  9: R0=map_value(id=0,off=0,ks=4,vs=48,imm=0) R1_w=inv(id=0) R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  9: (b7) r0 = 1
  10: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  10: (18) r2 = 0x600000002
  12: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  12: (ad) if r1 < r2 goto pc+1
   R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umin_value=25769803778) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  13: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umin_value=25769803778) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  13: (95) exit
  14: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=25769803777,var_off=(0x0; 0x7ffffffff)) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  14: (25) if r1 > 0x0 goto pc+1
   R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=0,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffff),u32_max_value=2147483647) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  15: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=0,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffff),u32_max_value=2147483647) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  15: (95) exit
  16: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umin_value=1,umax_value=25769803777,var_off=(0x0; 0x77fffffff),u32_max_value=2147483647) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  16: (47) r1 |= 0
  17: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umin_value=1,umax_value=32212254719,var_off=(0x0; 0x77fffffff),u32_max_value=2147483647) R2_w=inv25769803778 R10=fp0 fp-8=mmmmmmmm
  [...]

Fixes: 3f50f132d840 ("bpf: Verifier, do explicit ALU32 bounds tracking")
Reported-by: Simon Scannell <scannell.smn@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Reviewed-by: John Fastabend <john.fastabend@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ts32 smin_val = src_reg->smin_value;', '\tu32 umin_val = src_reg->umin_value;', '\t\tdst_reg->s32_min_value = dst_reg->umin_value;', '\t\tdst_reg->s32_max_value = dst_reg->umax_value;'], 'added_lines': ['\ts32 smin_val = src_reg->s32_min_value;', '\tu32 umin_val = src_reg->u32_min_value;', '\t\tdst_reg->s32_min_value = dst_reg->u32_min_value;', '\t\tdst_reg->s32_max_value = dst_reg->u32_max_value;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.8.15. scalar32_min_max_or in kernel/bpf/verifier.c mishandles bounds tracking during use of 64-bit values, aka CID-5b9fbeb75b6a.

code_evidence: Lines 7-8 initialize the 32-bit OR bound inputs smin_val/umin_val from the 64-bit src_reg->smin_value/umin_value fields rather than the 32-bit s32_min_value/u32_min_value subreg fields.
Lines 17-18, in the non-negative branch, set the 32-bit signed bounds dst_reg->s32_min_value/s32_max_value from the 64-bit dst_reg->umin_value/umax_value fields, again mixing widths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an incorrect conversion between numeric types: 64-bit values are stored into 32-bit fields, silently truncating data and yielding unexpected bound values that are then used in a sensitive verifier context. This matches CWE-681 (Incorrect Conversion between Numeric Types) rather than a pure logic error, since the truncating implicit conversion is the mechanism producing the wrong state.

evidence_lines.code:
s32 smin_val = src_reg->smin_value;
u32 umin_val = src_reg->umin_value;

dst_reg->s32_min_value = dst_reg->umin_value;
dst_reg->s32_max_value = dst_reg->umax_value;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the 32-bit subregister OR bound tracking reads 64-bit scalar bounds instead of the 32-bit subregister bounds. When a 64-bit value such as 25769803777 or 32212254719 is assigned to a u32/s32 field, it is truncated, producing a spuriously narrow range (e.g., [1,1] or max 1). The verifier then trusts incorrect 32-bit bounds for subsequent OR operations, enabling out-of-bounds speculation/access under the verifier's guarantees.

commit_msg: Make Disk Info Thread-Safe on Linux
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tthispct = device_space(mount, device, &dtotal, &dfree);', '\tDFcleanup();'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct nlist *DFhashvector[DFHASHSIZE] = {0};', '\t\tthispct = device_space(DFhashvector, mount, device, &dtotal, &dfree);', '\tDFcleanup(DFhashvector);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the sys-info crate before 0.8.0 for Rust. sys_info::disk_info calls can trigger a double free.

code_evidence: The loop calls device_space(mount, device, &dtotal, &dfree) for each parsed mount entry, passing no per-call state, so any heap allocation used to track device/space results is shared or global across iterations.

After the loop, DFcleanup() is invoked once with no argument, releasing that shared/global bookkeeping state; combined with device_space's per-iteration handling, the same allocation can be freed more than once.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the same address is freed more than once via the shared state freed by DFcleanup after per-iteration device_space calls. This is not a use-after-free (CWE-416), which would require dereferencing freed memory rather than a second free.

evidence_lines.code: thispct = device_space(mount, device, &dtotal, &dfree);
DFcleanup();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: device_space and DFcleanup operate on shared/global state rather than caller-owned per-invocation state, so multiple loop iterations and the final cleanup can release the same memory repeatedly. Trigger: parsing multiple mount entries followed by DFcleanup(). Supported consequence: double free, enabling memory corruption and potential code execution.

commit_msg: Fixed bug #70755: fpm_log.c memory leak and buffer overflow
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (len >= FPM_LOG_BUFFER) {', '\t\t\t\tzlog(ZLOG_NOTICE, "the log buffer is full (%d). The access log request has been truncated.", FPM_LOG_BUFFER);', '\t\t\t\tlen = FPM_LOG_BUFFER;', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t}']}
description: sapi/fpm/fpm/fpm_log.c in PHP before 5.5.31, 5.6.x before 5.6.17, and 7.x before 7.0.2 misinterprets the semantics of the snprintf return value, which allows attackers to obtain sensitive information from process memory or cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and buffer overflow) via a long string, as demonstrated by a long URI in a configuration with custom REQUEST_URI logging.

code_evidence: The loop now checks len >= FPM_LOG_BUFFER and breaks before appending more, capping len at FPM_LOG_BUFFER.

snprintf writes at most FPM_LOG_BUFFER - len bytes, but its return value (the would-be length) is stored in len2 and then added: b += len2; len += len2, so len and b can advance past the buffer end when output is truncated.
Later buffer[len] = '\n' and write(fpm_log_fd, buffer, len + 1) use the inflated len, indexing and reading beyond the FPM_LOG_BUFFER+1-byte buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The snprintf return-value misuse causes pointer/index arithmetic outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds read/write on a memory buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code treats snprintf's return value as bytes written, so after truncation len exceeds FPM_LOG_BUFFER and b points outside buffer. Trigger: a long URI or other long format value fills the buffer. Consequence: out-of-bounds write of the newline and out-of-bounds read in write(), leaking process memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
PR22209, invalid memory read in find_abstract_instance_name

This patch adds bounds checking for DW_FORM_ref_addr die refs, and
calculates them relative to the first .debug_info section.  See the
big comment for why calculating relative to the current .debug_info
section was wrong for relocatable object files.

	PR 22209
	* dwarf2.c (struct comp_unit): Delete sec_info_ptr field.
	(find_abstract_instance_name): Calculate DW_FORM_ref_addr relative
	to stash->info_ptr_memory, and check die_ref is within that memory.
	Set info_ptr_end correctly when another CU is refd.  Check die_ref
	for DW_FORM_ref4 etc. is within CU.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  unit->sec_info_ptr = stash->sec_info_ptr;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, miscalculates DW_FORM_ref_addr die refs in the case of a relocatable object file, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (find_abstract_instance_name invalid memory read, segmentation fault, and application crash).

code_evidence: info_ptr and end_ptr are derived from stash->info_ptr and unit_length without validating that the unit header and attributes stay within the buffer; subsequent reads use these bounds.

read_2_bytes/read_1_byte/read_4_bytes/read_8_bytes consume info_ptr and advance it (info_ptr += ...) relying on end_ptr; if unit_length or section placement is wrong the pointer can walk past the intended buffer.
unit->info_ptr_unit and sec_info_ptr are stored for later resolution of die refs; the removed sec_info_ptr assignment shows this unit's info pointer context is tracked but not bounds-checked here.

read_attribute is called with info_ptr and end_ptr; the return of NULL is checked, but attribute values (e.g. DW_FORM_ref_addr) are resolved later against a miscalculated base, enabling out-of-bounds reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function governs parsing of a memory buffer and its pointer bounds; the flaw permits reads outside the intended .debug_info buffer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. It is not merely a logic error because the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read leading to a crash.

evidence_lines.code:
bfd_byte *info_ptr = stash->info_ptr;
bfd_byte *end_ptr = info_ptr + unit_length;

version = read_2_bytes (abfd, info_ptr, end_ptr);
info_ptr += 2;

unit->info_ptr_unit = info_ptr_unit;
unit->sec_info_ptr = stash->sec_info_ptr;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: parse_comp_unit establishes buffer bounds from unit_length and stash pointers but does not ensure that attribute forms referencing other sections (DW_FORM_ref_addr) are resolved within the actual .debug_info memory. Trigger: a crafted relocatable object with a DW_FORM_ref_addr die reference causes find_abstract_instance_name to compute a wrong base and read outside the buffer. Consequence: invalid memory read, segmentation fault and crash (DoS).

commit_msg: Fix bug #69958 - Segfault in Phar::convertToData on invalid file
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tphp_stream_close(phar->fp);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (phar->fp) {', '\t\t\tphp_stream_close(phar->fp);', '\t\t}']}
description: The phar_convert_to_other function in ext/phar/phar_object.c in PHP before 5.4.43, 5.5.x before 5.5.27, and 5.6.x before 5.6.11 does not validate a file pointer before a close operation, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted TAR archive that is mishandled in a Phar::convertToData call.

code_evidence: After phar_rename_archive fails, the else branch at [106-108] destroys the manifest and directory hashes and then calls php_stream_close(phar->fp) at [109] without checking whether phar->fp is still a valid stream. The stream was set earlier by php_stream_fopen_tmpfile at [28], but the failure path assumes it remains openable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate a required property (a valid file pointer) of state derived from processing attacker-supplied archive input before using it in a close operation, matching CWE-20's missing input/state validation leading to a crash. It is not merely a NULL-pointer dereference artifact, since the unchecked precondition is the unvalidated pointer state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path closes phar->fp unconditionally, without validating that the pointer/stream is non-NULL before the close operation. Trigger: a crafted TAR archive processed through Phar::convertToData reaches the rename-failure branch, leaving phar->fp in an invalid state; the close is then performed on it. Consequence: segmentation fault / denial of service.

commit_msg:
[layout] Limit how far we skip when looking back

See comments.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '      /* When looking back, limit how far we search; this function is mostly', '       * used for looking back for base glyphs when attaching marks. If we', "       * don't limit, we can get O(n^2) behavior where n is the number of", '       * consecutive marks. */', '      stop = (unsigned) hb_max ((int) stop, (int) idx - HB_MAX_CONTEXT_LENGTH);', '']}
description: hb-ot-layout-gsubgpos.hh in HarfBuzz through 6.0.0 allows attackers to trigger O(n^2) growth via consecutive marks during the process of looking back for base glyphs when attaching marks.

code_evidence: prev() sets stop from num_items and only lowers it to 0 when HB_BUFFER_FLAG_PRODUCE_UNSAFE_TO_CONCAT is set [4,5,6]; otherwise the backward loop [7-9] scans arbitrarily far left, calling matcher.may_skip and matcher.may_match on every out_info entry [11,14] and only returning on a match or SKIP_NO [15-28]. With many consecutive marks that are skipped, each prev() call re-traverses the same long run of glyphs, so the work per call grows with the number of preceding marks and no bound constrains the scan.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs unbounded work (a scan whose length is not restricted) on behalf of attacker-controlled input, which is exactly a resource-consumption limit omission. CWE-770 covers allocation of a reusable resource (here CPU time/iterations) without throttling; the supported impact is CPU exhaustion DoS, consistent with the CWE scope.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the backward scan has no distance limit, so the number of iterations depends on the count of consecutive skippable marks rather than a fixed maximum. Trigger: a buffer containing a long run of consecutive marks that force repeated look-back for a base glyph. Consequence: quadratic CPU consumption (O(n^2)) leading to denial of service; the fix caps stop at idx - HB_MAX_CONTEXT_LENGTH.

commit_msg:
Fixed bug: barriers cannot be active during sweep

Barriers cannot be active during sweep, even in generational mode.
(Although gen. mode is not incremental, it can hit a barrier when
deleting a thread and closing its upvalues.)  The colors of objects are
being changed during sweep and, therefore, cannot be trusted.

commit_msg:
net: mqtt: Fix packet length decryption

The standard allows up to 4 bytes of packet length data, while current
implementation parsed up to 5 bytes.

Add additional unit test, which verifies that error is reported in case
of invalid packet length.

Signed-off-by: Robert Lubos <robert.lubos@nordicsemi.no>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int packet_length_decode(struct buf_ctx *buf, u32_t *length)', '\t\tif (bytes > MQTT_MAX_LENGTH_BYTES) {'], 'added_lines': ['static int packet_length_decode(struct buf_ctx *buf, u32_t *length)', '\t\tif (bytes >= MQTT_MAX_LENGTH_BYTES) {', '\tif (*length > MQTT_MAX_PAYLOAD_SIZE) {', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '']}
description: An off-by-one error in the Zephyr project MQTT packet length decoder can result in memory corruption and possible remote code execution. NCC-ZEP-031 This issue affects: zephyrproject-rtos zephyr version 2.2.0 and later versions.

code_evidence: The loop guard checks 'bytes > MQTT_MAX_LENGTH_BYTES' before reading each length byte, so when bytes equals the maximum it still performs one more iteration, allowing one extra continuation byte to be consumed and shifted into *length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The guard uses an incorrect maximum boundary value, permitting one more byte than the defined limit; this is a classic off-by-one (CWE-193). It is a boundary-comparison error rather than a generic integer overflow, though the extra shift contributes to an oversized length.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the off-by-one comparison '>' instead of '>=' against the maximum allowed length bytes. A packet with the maximum number of continuation-bit length bytes triggers an additional read and shift, producing an over-large length value that can drive subsequent buffer handling beyond intended bounds.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int          Read(void* pDestBuffer, int nSize)', '            if ( m_nPos + nSize >= m_nLen )', '                nSize = m_nLen - m_nPos - 1;'], 'added_lines': ['int          Read(void* pDestBuffer, unsigned int nSize)', '            if (m_nPos >= m_nLen)', '                nSize = 0;', '            else if (nSize > (m_nLen - m_nPos))', '                nSize = m_nLen - m_nPos;']}
description: Onlyoffice Document Server v6.0.0 and below and Core 6.1.0.26 and below were discovered to contain a heap overflow via the component DesktopEditor/fontengine/fontconverter/FontFileBase.h.

code_evidence: The bounds check computes m_nPos + nSize in signed int arithmetic; if nSize is large or m_nPos + nSize overflows, the condition can evaluate false and nSize is left unchanged.

The clamp nSize = m_nLen - m_nPos - 1 can itself produce a negative or oversized value when m_nPos >= m_nLen, and the memcpy then copies nSize bytes into pDestBuffer without any bound on the destination size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's memcpy writes attacker-influenced bytes beyond the destination buffer due to an ineffective size constraint, directly matching CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. CWE-125 is a related read-side weakness but here the overflow is a write via memcpy into pDestBuffer.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( m_nPos + nSize >= m_nLen )
nSize = m_nLen - m_nPos - 1;
memcpy( pDestBuffer, (m_sFile + m_nPos), nSize );

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length check is performed with signed arithmetic and a flawed clamp that does not guarantee nSize <= remaining source bytes or destination capacity. Trigger: a caller-supplied nSize that overflows m_nPos + nSize or an m_nPos at/after m_nLen. Consequence: memcpy writes past pDestBuffer, yielding a heap out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
Fix security vulnerability with FractionalMaxPoolGrad

PiperOrigin-RevId: 461722693
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        DCHECK_EQ(tensor_out_dup_mat(j, i), tensor_out_mat(j, i));', '      // According to maxpooling_op.cc, the performance impact below is small.', '      CHECK(input_backprop_index >= 0 &&', '            input_backprop_index < num_total_inputs)', '          << "Invalid input backprop index: " << input_backprop_index << ", "', '          << num_total_inputs;'], 'added_lines': ['        OP_REQUIRES(context, tensor_out_dup_mat(j, i) == tensor_out_mat(j, i),', '                    errors::InvalidArgument(', '                        "tensor_out_dup is not the same as tensor_out"));', '      OP_REQUIRES(', '          context,', '          input_backprop_index >= 0 && input_backprop_index < num_total_inputs,', '          errors::InvalidArgument(', '              "Invalid input backprop index: ", input_backprop_index, ", ",', '              num_total_inputs));']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. `FractionalMaxPoolGrad` validates its inputs with `CHECK` failures instead of with returning errors. If it gets incorrectly sized inputs, the `CHECK` failure can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 8741e57d163a079db05a7107a7609af70931def4. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over out_backprop_flat elements and reads input_backprop_index from out_arg_max_flat(index); the CHECK then aborts if that index is outside [0, num_total_inputs), before input_backprop_flat(input_backprop_index) is accessed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a CHECK assertion reachable via attacker-controlled input values, matching CWE-617's reachable assertion leading to exit. The DCHECK_EQ at line 100 is also an assertion, but CHECK is the aborting one; the weakness is the unconditional abort on invalid input, not an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a reachable CHECK (assertion) validates the backprop index derived from out_arg_max instead of returning an error. Trigger: malformed or incorrectly sized inputs cause an out-of-range index, firing the CHECK and terminating the process; consequence is a crash/denial of service rather than a handled InvalidArgument.

commit_msg:
Add support for different number of page table levels dependent
on the highest address used for a process. This will cause a 31 bit
process to use a two level page table instead of the four level page
table that is the default after the pud has been introduced. Likewise
a normal 64 bit process will use three levels instead of four. Only
if a process runs out of the 4 tera bytes which can be addressed with

commit_msg:

Currently, there is an out-of-bounds read on array ctrl->phys,
once variable i reaches the maximum array size of SERDES_MAX
in the for loop.

Fix this by changing the condition in the for loop from
i <= SERDES_MAX to i < SERDES_MAX.

Addresses-Coverity-ID: 1473966 ("Out-of-bounds read")
Addresses-Coverity-ID: 1473959 ("Out-of-bounds read")
Fixes: 51f6b410fc22 ("phy: add driver for Microsemi Ocelot SerDes muxing")
Reviewed-by: Quentin Schulz <quentin.schulz@bootlin.com>
Signed-off-by: Gustavo A. R. Silva <gustavo@embeddedor.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfor (i = 0; i <= SERDES_MAX; i++) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tfor (i = 0; i < SERDES_MAX; i++) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.20. drivers/phy/mscc/phy-ocelot-serdes.c has an off-by-one error with a resultant ctrl->phys out-of-bounds read.

code_evidence: The loop condition is i <= SERDES_MAX, so the final iteration uses i == SERDES_MAX, which is one past the last valid index of ctrl->phys. Line 15 passes &ctrl->phys[i] into serdes_phy_create, and line 16 returns ret on failure, but the out-of-bounds address is already taken on the last iteration.

commit_msg:
index: fix out-of-bounds read with invalid index entry prefix length

The index format in version 4 has prefix-compressed entries, where every
index entry can compress its path by using a path prefix of the previous
entry. Since implmenting support for this index format version in commit
5625d86b9 (index: support index v4, 2016-05-17), though, we do not
correctly verify that the prefix length that we want to reuse is
actually smaller or equal to the amount of characters than the length of
the previous index entry's path. This can lead to a an integer underflow
and subsequently to an out-of-bounds read.

Fix this by verifying that the prefix is actually smaller than the
previous entry's path length.

Reported-by: Krishna Ram Prakash R <krp@gtux.in>
Reported-by: Vivek Parikh <viv0411.parikh@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tsize_t varint_len;', '\t\tsize_t strip_len = git_decode_varint((const unsigned char *)path_ptr,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t     &varint_len);', '\t\tsize_t last_len = strlen(last);', '\t\tsize_t prefix_len = last_len - strip_len;', '\t\tsize_t suffix_len = strlen(path_ptr + varint_len);', '\t\tsize_t path_len;', '\t\tif (varint_len == 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tsize_t varint_len, last_len, prefix_len, suffix_len, path_len;', '\t\tuintmax_t strip_len;', '\t\tstrip_len = git_decode_varint((const unsigned char *)path_ptr, &varint_len);', '\t\tlast_len = strlen(last);', '', '\t\tif (varint_len == 0 || last_len < strip_len)', '', '\t\tprefix_len = last_len - strip_len;', '\t\tsuffix_len = strlen(path_ptr + varint_len);']}
description: Integer overflow in the index.c:read_entry() function while decompressing a compressed prefix length in libgit2 before v0.26.2 allows an attacker to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted repository index file.

code_evidence: strip_len is decoded from the attacker-controlled index path_ptr via git_decode_varint, while last_len is the previous entry's path length. prefix_len is computed as last_len - strip_len without first ensuring strip_len <= last_len; only varint_len == 0 is rejected. When strip_len exceeds last_len, the unsigned subtraction wraps to a huge size_t, which then feeds GITERR_CHECK_ALLOC_ADD and the git__malloc/memcpy at lines 64-67.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the prefix length from the crafted index entry is subtracted from last_len before any bound check, so an oversized strip_len wraps prefix_len to a very large value. Trigger: a malicious index v4 entry whose encoded strip_len exceeds the previous path length. Consequence: the wrapped size propagates into allocation/copy arithmetic, yielding an out-of-bounds read (and potential crash) when building the path, i.e. a denial of service.

commit_msg:
As reported by Jann, ihold() does not in fact guarantee inode
persistence. And instead of making it so, replace the usage of inode
pointers with a per boot, machine wide, unique inode identifier.

This sequence number is global, but shared (file backed) futexes are
rare enough that this should not become a performance issue.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tiput(key->shared.inode);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s futex implementation. This flaw allows a local attacker to corrupt system memory or escalate their privileges when creating a futex on a filesystem that is about to be unmounted. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to confidentiality, integrity, as well as system availability.

code_evidence: drop_futex_key_refs() selects on key->both.offset flags; in the FUT_OFF_INODE case it calls iput() on key->shared.inode, releasing the inode reference held by the futex key. Nothing in the function revalidates that the inode remains alive or that the key's stored inode pointer stays valid after the reference is dropped.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The key holds a pointer to an inode whose reference is released here without ensuring later users cannot reach it, matching CWE-416 (use after free): a freed inode is referenced through the futex key. This is a stale-pointer/lifetime flaw, not merely a reference-count imbalance.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The futex key stores a raw inode pointer and this function drops the reference via iput() when the key is released. Because ihold() did not actually guarantee inode persistence, the inode can be freed while a futex key still references it; subsequent key use dereferences the stale inode pointer, enabling memory corruption or privilege escalation when the filesystem is unmounted.

commit_msg:
x86: limit linear page table use to a single level

That's the only way that they're meant to be used. Without such a
restriction arbitrarily long chains of same-level page tables can be
built, tearing down of which may then cause arbitrarily deep recursion,
causing a stack overflow. To facilitate this restriction, a counter is
being introduced to track both the number of same-level entries in a
page table as well as the number of uses of a page table in another
same-level one (counting into positive and negative direction
respectively, utilizing the fact that both counts can't be non-zero at
the same time).

Note that the added accounting introduces a restriction on the number
of times a page can be used in other same-level page tables - more than
32k of such uses are no longer possible.

Note also that some put_page_and_type[_preemptible]() calls are
replaced with open-coded equivalents.  This seemed preferrable to
adding "parent_table" to the matrix of functions.

Note further that cross-domain same-level page table references are no
longer permitted (they probably never should have been).

This is XSA-240.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>

commit_msg:
We're holding the request reference, but we need to go one higher
to ensure that the ctx remains valid after the request has finished.
If the ring is closed with pending task_work inflight, and the
given io_kiocb finishes sync during issue, then we need a reference
to the ring itself around the task_work execution cycle.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v5.7+
Reported-by: syzbot+9b260fc33297966f5a8e@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tpercpu_ref_put(&ctx->refs);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.8.2. fs/io_uring.c has a use-after-free related to io_async_task_func and ctx reference holding, aka CID-6d816e088c35.

code_evidence: Line 4 copies req->ctx into a local ctx pointer; the callback then uses ctx in io_sq_thread_acquire_mm(ctx, req) at line 6 and, on the resubmit path, refcount_inc(&req->refs) and io_queue_async_work(req) at lines 8-9. The function takes no reference on ctx, so it relies on the ctx staying alive after the request completes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The callback accesses ctx after its lifetime may have ended, which is exactly CWE-416: use of memory after it has been freed. It is not merely a refcount bug, since the observable hazard is dereferencing the freed ring context.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the task_work callback dereferences req->ctx without holding a ctx reference. Trigger: if the ring is closed with task_work pending and the request completes synchronously during issue, the ctx may be torn down before this callback runs. Consequence: io_sq_thread_acquire_mm and io_queue_async_work operate on freed ring memory, a use-after-free (the patch adds percpu_ref_put, reflecting that a reference must be held across the callback).

commit_msg:
scsi: sg: fixup infoleak when using SG_GET_REQUEST_TABLE

When calling SG_GET_REQUEST_TABLE ioctl only a half-filled table is
returned; the remaining part will then contain stale kernel memory
information.  This patch zeroes out the entire table to avoid this
issue.

Signed-off-by: Hannes Reinecke <hare@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Bart Van Assche <bart.vanassche@wdc.com>
Reviewed-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Reviewed-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\trinfo = kmalloc(SZ_SG_REQ_INFO * SG_MAX_QUEUE,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\tGFP_KERNEL);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\trinfo = kzalloc(SZ_SG_REQ_INFO * SG_MAX_QUEUE,', '\t\t\t\t\tGFP_KERNEL);']}
description: The sg_ioctl function in drivers/scsi/sg.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.4 allows local users to obtain sensitive information from uninitialized kernel heap-memory locations via an SG_GET_REQUEST_TABLE ioctl call for /dev/sg0.

code_evidence: In the SG_GET_REQUEST_TABLE case, the ioctl allocates an sg_req_info_t table via kmalloc at [172,173] without zeroing it, then sg_fill_request_table(sfp, rinfo) at [177] fills only entries for currently queued requests. The full table size SZ_SG_REQ_INFO * SG_MAX_QUEUE is then copied to the user buffer with __copy_to_user at [179,180], so any unfilled slots retain stale heap contents and are exposed to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly transfers a partially initialized kernel buffer to an unprivileged user, exposing stale kernel memory contents; this is a direct exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor, matching CWE-200. The uninitialized-read nature is the mechanism, but the supported impact here is the information disclosure to userspace.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the request-info table is allocated uninitialized and only partially populated before being copied in full to userspace. Trigger: a local user issues the SG_GET_REQUEST_TABLE ioctl on /dev/sgN with fewer queued requests than SG_MAX_QUEUE. Consequence: uninitialized kernel heap memory is returned to the user, disclosing sensitive kernel data (confidentiality loss).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '                    /* To avoid divisions by zero / undefined behaviour on shift */', '                    if (rpx >= 31 || ((comp->dx << rpx) >> rpx) != comp->dx ||', '                            rpy >= 31 || ((comp->dy << rpy) >> rpy) != comp->dy) {', '                        continue;', '                    }', '']}
description: Division-by-zero vulnerabilities in the functions pi_next_pcrl, pi_next_cprl, and pi_next_rpcl in openmj2/pi.c in OpenJPEG through 2.3.0 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash).

code_evidence: rpx and rpy are derived from res->pdx/pdy plus levelno; the function then computes comp->dy << rpy and comp->dx << rpx and uses them as modulo divisors (and in 1 << rpy shifts) without validating that the shift stays in range, so a crafted resolution/level combination can yield zero or undefined shift values.
The loop increments pi->y and pi->x by pi->dy - (pi->y % pi->dy) and pi->dx - (pi->x % pi->dx), dividing by pi->dy and pi->dx, which are derived from comp->dx/dy shifted by resolution counts.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs modulo and division operations whose divisors depend on attacker-influenced component/resolution parameters, and can become zero, matching CWE-369 divide-by-zero. It is not merely an out-of-bounds index issue; the direct failure is division/modulo by a zero-valued shifted divisor.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: shift amounts rpx/rpy (and levelno) derived from image resolution parameters are not range-checked before being used as shift operands and modulo divisors. Trigger: a crafted codestream sets component dx/dy or resolution counts so a shifted value becomes zero or the shift is undefined. Consequence: modulo-by-zero / undefined shift causes a crash (DoS).

description: Race condition in the ALSA subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (use-after-free) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted /dev/snd/seq ioctl calls, related to sound/core/seq/seq_clientmgr.c and sound/core/seq/seq_ports.c.

code_evidence: snd_seq_create_port() returns a port pointer without holding a reference or lock; the caller then dereferences port->addr.port on line 12 and later lines 28-30 without any synchronization, so a concurrent delete via ioctl can free the object between creation and use.

After set_port_info, snd_seq_system_client_ev_port_start(port->addr.client, port->addr.port) reads the port's address and starts an event while no lock/refcount protects the port, allowing another thread to delete it concurrently.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code sequence requires exclusive access to the shared port object but lacks synchronization/refcount, so an interfering concurrent delete violates atomicity and yields a use-after-free. This is a race condition (CWE-362); the UAF is the consequence, not the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the create-port path does not take ownership/refcount or hold the port lock while using the freshly created port. description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-thrift.c had a large loop that was addressed by not proceeding with dissection after encountering an unexpected type.

code_evidence: The while loop at [12] iterates while offset < length, reading a type byte at [13] and advancing by one at [15]. At [23] the offset is overwritten with the return of dissect_thrift_type; if that call does not advance offset (or returns a value <= current offset), the loop condition remains true and the next iteration re-reads the same position. There is no iteration counter or progress check guarding the loop, so an unexpected type that causes dissect_thrift_type to return without advancing keeps the loop spinning.

This is not a simple off-by-one read but an iteration-control weakness enabling resource exhaustion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop trusts dissect_thrift_type to advance offset but never verifies forward progress. Trigger: a packet containing an unexpected/unknown Thrift type causes the callee to return without consuming bytes. Consequence: the while loop repeats indefinitely, consuming CPU (DoS) in the dissector.

description: An integer overflow issue exists in Godot Engine up to v3.2 that can be triggered when loading specially crafted.TGA image files. The vulnerability exists in ImageLoaderTGA::load_image() function at line: const size_t buffer_size = (tga_header.image_width * tga_header.image_height) * pixel_size; The bug leads to Dynamic stack buffer overflow. Depending on the context of the application, attack vector can be local or remote, and can lead to code execution and/or system crash.

code_evidence: tga_header.image_width and image_height are attacker-controlled 16-bit fields read from the file (lines 17-18). pixel_size is derived from pixel_depth (line 56). The multiplication at line 57 is performed in int before being assigned to size_t, so a large width*height can wrap to a negative/small int; that wrapped value then drives uncompressed_buffer.resize(buffer_size) at line 59.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the vulnerable operation is an integer multiplication whose wrapped result is used as an allocation size, exactly the 'size in memory allocation' critical case. It is distinct from a simple out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), which is the downstream consequence rather than the root cause here.

Trigger: a TGA file with large image_width/image_height. Consequence: an undersized uncompressed_buffer is allocated, and subsequent RLE decode/convert_to_image writes past it, yielding a stack/heap buffer overflow and crash or possible code execution.

commit_msg:
copy: CVE-2022-0485: Fail nbdcopy if NBD read or write fails

nbdcopy has a nasty bug when performing multi-threaded copies using
asynchronous nbd calls - it was blindly treating the completion of an
asynchronous command as successful, rather than checking the *error
parameter.  This can result in the silent creation of a corrupted
image in two different ways: when a read fails, we blindly wrote
garbage to the destination; when a write fails, we did not flag that
the destination was not written.

Since nbdcopy already calls exit() on a synchronous read or write
failure to a file, doing the same for an asynchronous op to an NBD
server is the simplest solution.  A nicer solution, but more invasive
to code and thus not done here, might be to allow up to N retries of
the transaction (in case the read or write failure was transient), or
even having a mode where as much data is copied as possible (portions
of the copy that failed would be logged on stderr, and nbdcopy would
still fail with a non-zero exit status, but this would copy more than
just stopping at the first error, as can be done with rsync or
ddrescue).

Note that since we rely on auto-retiring and do NOT call
nbd_aio_command_completed, our completion callbacks must always return
1 (if they do not exit() first), even when acting on *error, so as not
leave the command allocated until nbd_close.  As such, there is no
sane way to return an error to a manual caller of the callback, and
therefore we can drop dead code that calls perror() and exit() if the
callback "failed".  It is also worth documenting the contract on when
we must manually call the callback during the asynch_zero callback, so
that we do not leak or double-free the command; thankfully, all the
existing code paths were correct.

The added testsuite script demonstrates several scenarios, some of
which fail without the rest of this patch in place, and others which
showcase ways in which sparse images can bypass errors.

Once backports are complete, a followup patch on the main branch will
edit docs/libnbd-security.pod with the mailing list announcement of
the stable branch commit ids and release versions that incorporate
this fix.

commit_msg:
The SendEvent request holds xEvent which is exactly 32 bytes long, no more,
no less. Both ProcSendEvent and SProcSendEvent verify that the received data
exactly match the request size. However nothing stops the client from passing
in event with xEvent::type = GenericEvent and any value of
xGenericEvent::length.

In the case of ProcSendEvent, the event will be eventually passed to
WriteEventsToClient which will see that it is Generic event and copy the
arbitrary length from the receive buffer (and possibly past it) and send it to
the other client. This allows clients to copy unitialized heap memory out of X
server or to crash it.

In case of SProcSendEvent, it will attempt to swap the incoming event by
calling a swapping function from the EventSwapVector array. The swapped event
is written to target buffer, which in this case is local xEvent variable. The
xEvent variable is 32 bytes long, but the swapping functions for GenericEvents
expect that the target buffer has size matching the size of the source
GenericEvent. This allows clients to cause stack buffer overflows.

Signed-off-by: Michal Srb <msrb@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Peter Hutterer <peter.hutterer@who-t.net>
Signed-off-by: Peter Hutterer <peter.hutterer@who-t.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    /* Generic events can have variable size, but SendEvent request holds', '       exactly 32B of event data. */', '    if (stuff->event.u.u.type == GenericEvent) {', '        client->errorValue = stuff->event.u.u.type;', '        return BadValue;', '    }', '']}
description: In the X.Org X server before 2017-06-19, a user authenticated to an X Session could crash or execute code in the context of the X Server by exploiting a stack overflow in the endianness conversion of X Events.

code_evidence: Line 4 declares a fixed-size 32-byte stack buffer eventT. Line 11 selects a swap function using the client-controlled event type; for GenericEvent this is a variable-length swap routine. Line 14 invokes that routine with &eventT as the destination, so the routine writes a length determined by the GenericEvent payload into the fixed 32-byte buffer, overflowing the stack. Line 15 then copies the corrupted event back.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The swap writes beyond the bounds of the fixed-size eventT buffer, which is exactly the out-of-bounds memory operation described by CWE-119. The missing type/length check is the cause and the overflow is the supported effect; this is a buffer-bounds violation rather than a mere integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function performs endianness conversion of a client-controlled event without constraining the event type or its declared length to the fixed 32-byte destination. Trigger: an authenticated client sends a SendEvent request whose xEvent type is GenericEvent with a large xGenericEvent length. Consequence: the swap routine writes past eventT, causing a stack buffer overflow that may crash the server or enable code execution in its context.

commit_msg:
rar: file split across multi-part archives must match

Fuzzing uncovered some UAF and memory overrun bugs where a file in a
single file archive reported that it was split across multiple
volumes. This was caused by ppmd7 operations calling
rar_br_fillup. This would invoke rar_read_ahead, which would in some
situations invoke archive_read_format_rar_read_header.  That would
check the new file name against the old file name, and if they didn't
match up it would free the ppmd7 buffer and allocate a new
one. However, because the ppmd7 decoder wasn't actually done with the
buffer, it would continue to used the freed buffer. Both reads and
writes to the freed region can be observed.

This is quite tricky to solve: once the buffer has been freed it is
too late, as the ppmd7 decoder functions almost universally assume
success - there's no way for ppmd_read to signal error, nor are there
good ways for functions like Range_Normalise to propagate them. So we
can't detect after the fact that we're in an invalid state - e.g. by
checking rar->cursor, we have to prevent ourselves from ever ending up
there. So, when we are in the dangerous part or rar_read_ahead that
assumes a valid split, we set a flag force read_header to either go
down the path for split files or bail. This means that the ppmd7
decoder keeps a valid buffer and just runs out of data.

Found with a combination of AFL, afl-rb and qsym.

description: FreeRDP is a free implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). Prior to version 2.7.0, server side authentication against a `SAM` file might be successful for invalid credentials if the server has configured an invalid `SAM` file path. FreeRDP based clients are not affected. RDP server implementations using FreeRDP to authenticate against a `SAM` file are affected. Version 2.7.0 contains a fix for this issue. As a workaround, use custom authentication via `HashCallback` and/or ensure the `SAM` database path configured is valid and the application has file handles left.

code_evidence: SamOpen uses context->SamFile and returns -1 on failure without authenticating or rejecting the caller; a missing/invalid SAM path simply aborts the hash fetch.
SamLookupUserW is called with the user/domain from credentials; if no matching entry exists the function falls through to a second lookup with NULL domain.
The else branch closes the SAM and returns 0 after logging, so a failed lookup is reported as a return value rather than an enforced authentication failure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the weakness is insufficient proof of identity: the SAM-based credential check can fail open when the lookup fails, so the claimed identity is not reliably verified. This is improper authentication rather than a memory-safety issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function's return value conflates 'no SAM entry found' with other outcomes and the caller is not forced to treat a failed lookup as authentication failure. Trigger: a server configured with an invalid SAM path or a user absent from the SAM database causes SamOpen/SamLookupUserW to fail, returning -1/0 while no hash is produced. The supported consequence is that authentication against the SAM may succeed for invalid credentials if the caller misinterprets the failure code.

commit_msg:
Modify am_handler setup to run before mod_proxy

The way the ECP flow works is that when a client initiates the flow, the
SP's response is HTTP 200, but not the requested content, but a signed XML
document that contains the "samlp:AuthnRequest" element. The idea is that
the ECP client would then determine the IDP and send the document to the
IDP, get a samlp:Response and convey that to the SP to get access to the
protected resource.

Internally, the auth check which is normally done with am_check_uid() set to
apache's ap_hook_check_user_id() hook, just responds with OK, so it pretends
to authenticate the user. Then in the usual flow, the request reaches the
ap_hook_handler which handles the request. There in the pipeline, mellon
registers functions am_handler() which should run first (APR_HOOK_FIRST),
determine that this request is an ECP one and return the ECP AuthnRequest
document. But in case the proxy module is also in the picture, the proxy
module "races" for who gets to be the first to handle the request in the
pipeline and wins. Therefore, the request reaches the protected resource
via mod_proxy and returns it.

This fix modifies the ap_hook_handler() call to explicitly run before
handlers from mod_proxy.c

To reproduce the bug:
0) Have a SP with mellon connected to a Keycloak IDP (or any other IDP I
   guess). In the example below, my SAML SP is saml.federation.test
1) Set a Location protected by mellon that proxies requests to another
   URL. For example:

    ProxyPass         /sp-proxy  http://app.federation.test/example_app/
    <Location /sp-proxy>
        AuthType Mellon
        MellonEnable auth
        Require valid-user
    </Location>

2) call:
 curl -L -H "Accept: application/vnd.paos+xml" \
         -H 'PAOS: ver="urn:liberty:paos:2003-08";"urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:profiles:SSO:ecp"' \
          http://saml.federation.test/sp-proxy

Before the patch, you would see whatever is served from the proxied
page. With the patch, you should get back a XML document with a
samlp:AuthnRequest.

description: A vulnerability was found in mod_auth_mellon before v0.14.2. If Apache is configured as a reverse proxy and mod_auth_mellon is configured to only let through authenticated users (with the require valid-user directive), adding special HTTP headers that are normally used to start the special SAML ECP (non-browser based) can be used to bypass authentication.

code_evidence: The handler hook is registered with am_handler at APR_HOOK_FIRST but with NULL predecessors, so the ordering between am_handler and mod_proxy's handler is not constrained; the vulnerable version relies on hook priority alone to intercept ECP requests before the proxy handler runs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the authentication flow fails to prove the requester's identity before protected content is served; the ordering flaw lets the proxied resource be reached without completing SAML authentication. This is an authentication bypass, not merely a routing or ordering defect.

evidence_lines.code: ap_hook_handler(am_handler, NULL, NULL, APR_HOOK_FIRST);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the handler registration does not declare mod_proxy.c as a predecessor, so hook ordering between am_handler and the proxy handler is not guaranteed. Trigger: an unauthenticated request with ECP PAOS/Accept headers against a proxied location. Consequence: the proxy handler wins the race and serves the protected resource, bypassing the authentication check that am_check_uid only pretends to satisfy.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over jp2_image->numcomps and rejects components whose dx, dy, prec or sgnd differ from component 0, or whose data is NULL; dx/dy zero is also rejected.
After this geometry check, image->columns and image->rows are taken directly from comps[0].w and comps[0].h without further bounds validation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function receives attacker-controlled JP2 metadata and uses it without validating required properties (geometry consistency/bounds), matching CWE-20's improper input validation. The fix narrows the data==NULL check to non-ping mode, showing the validation path was incorrect for ping requests.

if ((jp2_image->comps[0].dx == 0) || (jp2_image->comps[0].dy == 0) ||

(jp2_image->comps[0].prec != jp2_image->comps[i].prec) ||

commit_msg:
passthrough: quarantine PCI devices

When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for
that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The
IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that
the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However,
when the guest domain is torn down the device is assigned back to dom0,
thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data.

This patch introduces a 'quarantine' for PCI devices using dom_io. When
the toolstack makes a device assignable (by binding it to pciback), it
will now also assign it to DOMID_IO and the device will only be assigned
back to dom0 when the device is made unassignable again. Whilst device is
assignable it will only ever transfer between dom_io and guest domains.
dom_io is actually only used as a sentinel domain for quarantining purposes;
it is not configured with any IOMMU mappings. Assignment to dom_io simply
means that the device's initiator (requestor) identifier is not present in
the IOMMU's device table and thus any DMA transactions issued will be
terminated with a fault condition.

In addition, a fix to assignment handling is made for VT-d.  Failure
during the assignment step should not lead to a device still being
associated with its prior owner. Hand the device to DomIO temporarily,
until the assignment step has completed successfully.  Remove the PI
hooks from the source domain then earlier as well.

Failure of the recovery reassign_device_ownership() may not go silent:
There e.g. may still be left over RMRR mappings in the domain assignment
to which has failed, and hence we can't allow that domain to continue
executing.

NOTE: This patch also includes one printk() cleanup; the
      "XEN_DOMCTL_assign_device: " tag is dropped in iommu_do_pci_domctl(),
      since similar printk()-s elsewhere also don't log such a tag.

This is XSA-302.

Signed-off-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing attackers to gain host OS privileges via DMA in a situation where an untrusted domain has access to a physical device. This occurs because passed through PCI devices may corrupt host memory after deassignment. When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However, when the guest domain is torn down, or the device is deassigned, the device is assigned back to dom0, thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data. An untrusted domain with access to a physical device can DMA into host memory, leading to privilege escalation. Only systems where guests are given direct access to physical devices capable of DMA (PCI pass-through) are vulnerable. Systems which do not use PCI pass-through are not vulnerable.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs IOMMU device reassignment and unity-map reservation; it contains no OS command construction or execution, so it does not support CWE-78.

commit_msg:
shell: utils: Fix buffer overrun in shell_spaces_trim

The third argument in memmove can possible be greater than remaining
buffer size. Just ensuring that memmove will changes bytes only inside
the string buffer and nothing else.

Signed-off-by: Flavio Ceolin <flavio.ceolin@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\t\tlen - shift + 1);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\t\tlen - j + 1);']}
description: The shell subsystem contains a buffer overflow, whereby an adversary with physical access to the device is able to cause a memory corruption, resulting in denial of service or possibly code execution within the Zephyr kernel. See NCC-NCC-019 This issue affects: zephyrproject-rtos zephyr version 1.14.0 and later versions. version 2.1.0 and later versions.

code_evidence: Inside the loop, when shift > 0, memmove copies from &str[j] into &str[i + 1], using length len - shift + 1. The destination is an in-place buffer of total length len, but the copy count is not bounded by the remaining destination capacity (len - (i + 1)); it depends on shift and the source index j, so the write can extend past str + len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies bytes with memmove without checking that the copy length fits the destination buffer, producing an out-of-bounds write. This is a buffer copy without input-size validation, matching CWE-120; the defect is the unchecked copy length, not merely an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the memmove length is computed from shift/j rather than the remaining destination size, so the copy count can exceed the buffer tail. Trigger: a shell string with a run of whitespace that makes shift large relative to i causes memmove to write beyond the string buffer, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially enabling crash or code execution.

Prevent division by zero in linkhash.

If a linkhash with a size of zero is created, then modulo operations
are prone to division by zero operations.

Purely protective measure against bad usage.

description: json-c through 0.14 has an integer overflow and out-of-bounds write via a large JSON file, as demonstrated by printbuf_memappend.

commit_msg: SA79000 advisory fix
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#ifdef LIBRAW_LIBRARY_BUILD', '  if(!image)', '    throw LIBRAW_EXCEPTION_IO_CORRUPT;', '#endif']}
description: An error within the "LibRaw::unpack()" function (src/libraw_cxx.cpp) in LibRaw versions prior to 0.18.7 can be exploited to trigger a NULL pointer dereference.

code_evidence: The function declares locals and immediately executes `ushort *ip = image[0];` at line 5 without any prior validation that the `image` pointer is non-NULL. The `image` global is dereferenced to obtain its first element, so a NULL `image` causes an invalid read at this initialization point, before the decoding loops begin.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the code dereferences the `image` pointer (through `image[0]`) without validating it, and the patch adds exactly an `if(!image) throw` guard confirming the missing NULL check. This is a direct NULL dereference, not an out-of-bounds or use-after-free issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: absence of a NULL check on the global `image` pointer before dereferencing it via `image[0]`. Trigger: a corrupt or malformed input path leaving `image` unset/NULL when `kodak_rgb_load_raw` is invoked. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference, causing a crash (DoS) during raw decoding.

commit_msg:
proc_pid_cmdline_read() and environ_read() directly access the target
process' VM to retrieve the command line and environment. If this
process remaps these areas onto a file via mmap(), the requesting
process may experience various issues such as extra delays if the
underlying device is slow to respond.

Let's simply refuse to access file-backed areas in these functions.
For this we add a new FOLL_ANON gup flag that is passed to all calls
to access_remote_vm(). The code already takes care of such failures
(including unmapped areas). Accesses via /proc/pid/mem were not
changed though.

This was assigned CVE-2018-1120.

Note for stable backports: the patch may apply to kernels prior to 4.11
but silently miss one location; it must be checked that no call to
access_remote_vm() keeps zero as the last argument.

Reported-by: Qualys Security Advisory <qsa@qualys.com>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Andy Lutomirski <luto@amacapital.net>
Cc: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\trv = access_remote_vm(mm, arg_end - 1, &c, 1, 0);', '\t\t\tnr_read = access_remote_vm(mm, p, page, _count, 0);', '\t\t\t\tnr_read = access_remote_vm(mm, p, page, _count, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['\trv = access_remote_vm(mm, arg_end - 1, &c, 1, FOLL_ANON);', '\t\t\tnr_read = access_remote_vm(mm, p, page, _count, FOLL_ANON);', '\t\t\t\tnr_read = access_remote_vm(mm, p, page, _count, FOLL_ANON);']}
description: A flaw was found affecting the Linux kernel before version 4.17. By mmap()ing a FUSE-backed file onto a process's memory containing command line arguments (or environment strings), an attacker can cause utilities from psutils or procps (such as ps, w) or any other program which makes a read() call to the /proc/<pid>/cmdline (or /proc/<pid>/environ) files to block indefinitely (denial of service) or for some controlled time (as a synchronization primitive for other attacks).

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function reads a remote process's command line via access_remote_vm with FOLL_ANON gating; the flaw is unbounded blocking on file-backed mappings (a FUSE DoS), not an out-of-bounds memory access, so CWE-119 is unsupported.

commit_msg:
Ensure the MakerNote data pointers are initialized with NULL.

This ensures that an uninitialized pointer isn't dereferenced later in
the case where the number of components (and therefore size) is 0.

This fixes the second issue reported at
https://sourceforge.net/p/libexif/bugs/125/

CVE-2020-13113
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tmemset(&n->entries[tcount], 0, sizeof(MnoteCanonEntry));']}
description: An issue was discovered in libexif before 0.6.22. Use of uninitialized memory in EXIF Makernote handling could lead to crashes and potential use-after-free conditions.

code_evidence: The loop allocates n->entries for c entries but only fills each entry's tag/format/components/order; the data pointer is assigned only inside the size>0 branch at line 67.
When format size is 0 (or components 0), the overflow check computes s=0; the continue at lines 47/56 skips both the data allocation at line 67 and the ++tcount at line 74.
Thus n->entries[tcount].data remains uninitialized from exif_mem_alloc, while the entry is later exposed via n->count and read by downstream consumers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the function exposes a resource (MnoteCanonEntry.data) that was allocated but never initialized on zero-size paths, and that resource is subsequently used. The missing initialization, not the zero-size check itself, is the weakness; an integer overflow or buffer overflow label would not describe this uninitialized-pointer state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: entries allocated by exif_mem_alloc are not zero-initialized, and paths that compute a zero tag size skip assigning the data pointer. Trigger: a MakerNote entry with format size 0 or components 0 causes continue before data is set. Consequence: later dereference of the uninitialized data pointer gives invalid memory access/crash, consistent with the reported use-after-free/crash behavior.

commit_msg: util-lib: use MODE_INVALID as invalid value for mode_t everywhere
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        return touch_file(path, false, USEC_INFINITY, UID_INVALID, GID_INVALID, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['        return touch_file(path, false, USEC_INFINITY, UID_INVALID, GID_INVALID, MODE_INVALID);']}
description: A flaw in systemd v228 in /src/basic/fs-util.c caused world writable suid files to be created when using the systemd timers features, allowing local attackers to escalate their privileges to root. This is fixed in v229.

code_evidence: touch() forwards a literal 0 as the final mode_t argument to touch_file(), instead of MODE_INVALID. The function itself sets no permissions and relies entirely on touch_file()'s interpretation of that argument.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw concerns incorrect specification of file permission attributes during creation, falling under CWE-264's permissions/access-control management category. It is not an injection or memory-safety issue; the defect is the wrong sentinel for mode, so permission handling is misapplied.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: passing 0 as the mode argument is ambiguous and may be treated as a real permission value rather than 'unspecified'. Trigger: callers invoking touch() (e.g., timer-created files) cause touch_file() to apply mode 0-derived permissions. Consequence: files may be created with unintended permissive or suid bits, enabling local privilege escalation; the fix uses MODE_INVALID to signal the default mode.

commit_msg:
crypto: ccp - fix resource leaks in ccp_run_aes_gcm_cmd()

There are three bugs in this code:

1) If we ccp_init_data() fails for &src then we need to free aad.
   Use goto e_aad instead of goto e_ctx.
2) The label to free the &final_wa was named incorrectly as "e_tag" but
   it should have been "e_final_wa".  One error path leaked &final_wa.
3) The &tag was leaked on one error path.  In that case, I added a free
   before the goto because the resource was local to that block.

Fixes: 36cf515b9bbe ("crypto: ccp - Enable support for AES GCM on v5 CCPs")
Reported-by: "minihanshen(沈明航)" <minihanshen@tencent.com>
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: John Allen <john.allen@amd.com>
Tested-by: John Allen <john.allen@amd.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tgoto e_ctx;', '\t\tgoto e_dst;', '\t\t\tgoto e_tag;', '\t\tif (ret)', '\t\t\tgoto e_tag;', 'e_tag:'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tgoto e_aad;', '\t\tgoto e_final_wa;', '\t\t\tgoto e_final_wa;', '\t\tif (ret) {', '\t\t\tccp_dm_free(&tag);', '\t\t\tgoto e_final_wa;', '\t\t}', 'e_final_wa:']}
description: A memory leak flaw was found in the Linux kernel in the ccp_run_aes_gcm_cmd() function in drivers/crypto/ccp/ccp-ops.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption). This vulnerability is similar with the older CVE-2019-18808.

code_evidence: On failure of ccp_init_data(&src) at line 117, control jumps to the e_ctx label (line 118), skipping the e_aad cleanup block at lines 212-214, so the previously initialized aad workarea is never freed.
When decrypting, ccp_init_dm_workarea(&tag) at line 193 fails, and the error path at line 196 jumps to the e_tag label without freeing final_wa.
After tag allocation succeeds, failure of ccp_set_dm_area(&tag) at line 197 jumps to e_tag at line 199, again bypassing ccp_dm_free(&tag) and leaking the tag workarea.
The e_tag label at line 204 only frees final_wa at line 205; it does not release tag, so the tag allocation is leaked on these error paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates DMA workareas and fails to release aad and tag on specific error branches, matching CWE-401 (missing release of memory after effective lifetime). This is a resource-lifetime leak, not a use-after-free or buffer overflow, because the memory is simply never freed.

evidence_lines.code:
if (ret)
goto e_ctx;

e_tag:
ccp_dm_free(&final_wa);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is incorrect error-path cleanup: the src-init failure uses goto e_ctx instead of e_aad, leaking the aad workarea, and the tag error paths jump to e_tag without freeing tag. Triggering these allocation or setup failures (e.g., malformed input causing DMA workarea init to fail) leaves allocated DMA memory unreleased, supporting memory-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg:
smart_pkt: treat empty packet lines as error

The Git protocol does not specify what should happen in the case
of an empty packet line (that is a packet line "0004"). We
currently indicate success, but do not return a packet in the
case where we hit an empty line. The smart protocol was not
prepared to handle such packets in all cases, though, resulting
in a `NULL` pointer dereference.

Fix the issue by returning an error instead. As such kind of
packets is not even specified by upstream, this is the right
thing to do.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t * TODO: How do we deal with empty lines? Try again? with the next', '\t * line?', '\t\t*head = NULL;', '\t\t*out = line;', '\t\treturn 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\t * The Git protocol does not specify empty lines as part', '\t * of the protocol. Not knowing what to do with an empty', '\t * line, we should return an error upon hitting one.', '\t\tgiterr_set_str(GITERR_NET, "Invalid empty packet");', '\t\treturn GIT_ERROR;']}
description: The Git Smart Protocol support in libgit2 before 0.24.6 and 0.25.x before 0.25.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via an empty packet line.

code_evidence: When the packet length equals PKT_LEN_SIZE (an empty packet line '0004'), the function sets *head to NULL, assigns *out, and returns success (0) without creating a packet object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function returns success with a NULL packet pointer that callers expect to be valid, leading to a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476). This is not merely a missing error check: the parser itself signals success for a state where no valid object exists.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an empty packet line is reported as successful while *head is set to NULL. Trigger: a remote peer sends an empty packet line '0004'. Callers that treat a zero return as success and dereference the returned packet pointer hit a NULL dereference, causing a crash/DoS.
