diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                if (TYPE(CHILD(n, i)) == COMMA)'], 'added_lines': ['                if (i < NCH(n) && TYPE(CHILD(n, i)) == COMMA)']}
description: typed_ast 1.3.0 and 1.3.1 has a handle_keywordonly_args out-of-bounds read. An attacker with the ability to cause a Python interpreter to parse Python source (but not necessarily execute it) may be able to crash the interpreter process. This could be a concern, for example, in a web-based service that parses (but does not execute) Python code. (This issue also affected certain Python 3.8.0-alpha prereleases.)

code_evidence: In the DOUBLESTAR case, after consuming the double star and the keyword name with `i += 2`, the code calls `CHILD(n, i)` in the comma test without first checking `i < NCH(n)`. When the keyword-only argument is the last child of the node, `i` equals `NCH(n)` and `CHILD` indexes past the end of the child array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads `CHILD(n, i)` at index `i == NCH(n)`, one past the last valid child, which is precisely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a buffer overflow write, since only a read of the child array occurs before the comma decision.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the comma check after `i += 2` lacks a bounds check against `NCH(n)`. Trigger: a parameter list ending in `**name` with no trailing comma or comment, so `i` is advanced to the child count. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of the node's child pointer array, which can crash the interpreter during parsing.

commit_msg: Add bounds check before length read
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if( (*p) > end - 2 )', '    {', '        MBEDTLS_SSL_DEBUG_MSG( 1, ( "bad server key exchange message "', '                                    "(psk_identity_hint length)" ) );', '        return( MBEDTLS_ERR_SSL_BAD_HS_SERVER_KEY_EXCHANGE );', '    }']}
description: ARM mbed TLS before 2.1.11, before 2.7.2, and before 2.8.0 has a buffer over-read in ssl_parse_server_psk_hint() that could cause a crash on invalid input.

code_evidence: Line 8 reads two bytes ((*p)[0] and (*p)[1]) to form len, and line 9 advances *p by 2, before any check that two bytes remain between *p and end.
The bounds check at line 10 compares (*p) + len to end only after the two-byte length field has already been consumed, so it cannot protect the line 8 read.
Line 16 advances *p by the attacker-controlled len, which only affects subsequent parsing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading (*p)[0] and (*p)[1] before the end-proximity check constitutes reading past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-125. The later length check addresses the identity hint body, not the initial length-field over-read, so it does not mitigate this weakness.

evidence_lines.code: *p += len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the two-byte PSK identity hint length is read at line 8 without first verifying that *p is at least two bytes before end. Trigger: a truncated or malformed ServerKeyExchange message supplying fewer than two bytes. This causes a 2-byte out-of-bounds read, potentially reading past the received buffer and crashing (DoS) on invalid input.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.5 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.13, epan/dissectors/packet-pcp.c has a memory leak.

code_evidence: On the first packet for a conversation, conversation_get_proto_data returns NULL and the code allocates pcp_conv_info with g_malloc at line 15, storing it via conversation_add_proto_data. Consequence: memory grows for each distinct conversation, enabling memory-consumption DoS during long capture sessions.

description: The DecodeGifImg function in ngiflib.c in MiniUPnP ngiflib 0.4 lacks certain checks against width and height, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (WritePixels heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted GIF file.

code_evidence: Sub-block posX, posY, width and height are read directly from the file with GetWord and stored without any bounds validation.
The frame buffer pointer is computed as frbuff.p8/p32 + posY*parent->width + posX (or the equivalent line_p + posX), using the attacker-controlled values as a raw offset into the canvas buffer.
npix is computed from width*height and drives the decode loop length, so oversized dimensions extend the number of pixels written.
WritePixels writes the decoded run at context.frbuff_p; with an offset or run beyond the canvas, the write lands past the allocated frame buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a write past the end of the intended frame buffer, matching CWE-787. The missing dimension/position constraint is the enabling cause; the out-of-bounds write in WritePixels is the supported consequence. This is not merely an integer overflow (CWE-190), since the unchecked values directly produce the out-of-range destination and write length.

evidence_lines.code: npix = (long)i->width * i->height;

WritePixels(i, &context, stackp, stack_top - stackp);
npix -= (stack_top - stackp);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: width, height, posX and posY parsed from the GIF sub-block are used to compute the destination pointer and pixel count without checking them against the parent canvas dimensions. Trigger: a crafted GIF declaring a sub-image that extends beyond the canvas (or oversized dimensions) makes the computed frbuff_p offset and/or npix exceed the buffer. Consequence: WritePixels writes past the end of the heap frame buffer, corrupting memory and crashing or potentially enabling further impact.

and because of that we could potentially leak code and data of a
previous loaded TA.

code and data"

commit_msg:
dm ioctl: fix out of bounds array access when no devices

If there are not any dm devices, we need to zero the "dev" argument in
the first structure dm_name_list. However, this can cause out of
bounds write, because the "needed" variable is zero and len may be
less than eight.

Fix this bug by reporting DM_BUFFER_FULL_FLAG if the result buffer is
too small to hold the "nl->dev" value.

Signed-off-by: Mikulas Patocka <mpatocka@redhat.com>
Reported-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Mike Snitzer <snitzer@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (len < needed) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (len < needed || len < sizeof(nl->dev)) {']}
description: An out-of-bounds (OOB) memory write flaw was found in list_devices in drivers/md/dm-ioctl.c in the Multi-device driver module in the Linux kernel before 5.12. A bound check failure allows an attacker with special user (CAP_SYS_ADMIN) privilege to gain access to out-of-bounds memory leading to a system crash or a leak of internal kernel information. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

code_evidence: get_result_buffer returns the user-supplied result buffer and its length len; the guard at line 17 only checks len < needed. When there are no dm devices, the loop leaves needed = 0, so any len >= 0 passes and line 22 writes nl->dev = 0 into the buffer without ensuring room for the dev field.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked write at line 22 places data beyond the intended result buffer, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. A missing size constraint is the root cause; the memory corruption is the consequence, not a separate weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size check compares len only against the computed needed, which is zero when no devices exist, omitting the mandatory sizeof(nl->dev) space. Trigger: a caller with a result buffer shorter than the dev field when the device list is empty. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write past the buffer end, corrupting memory or crashing the kernel.

commit_msg:
mp4: limit the recursion depth for boxes

Although the dissection of each box header consumes a couple of bytes,
it turned out that it's still possible to crash wireshark with a sample
file that contains a large number of nested boxes. The stack will fill
up before we reach the end of the data bytes.

Keep track of the recursion depth as we walk through the hierarchy of
boxes. Abort if we reach the (locally defined) upper limit.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        std::vector<char> new_base64_data(base64_data, base64_data + base64_len + 1);', '  xml_memory_writer writer;', '  writer.p_write = fp_;', '  doc_.save(writer, nullptr, pugi::format_raw | pugi::format_no_declaration, encoding_);', '  size_ = writer.p_write - fp_;'], 'added_lines': ['        vector<char> new_base64_data(base64_data, base64_data + base64_len + 1);', '  xml_vector_writer writer;', '  doc_.save(writer, nullptr, pugi::format_raw | pugi::format_no_declaration, encoding_);', '  if (writer.buf.size() < size_) {', '    size_ = writer.buf.size();', '    memcpy(fp_, writer.buf.data(), size_);', '  } else {', '    memmove(fp_, fp_ + size_leanified, size_);', '  }']}
description: formats/xml.cpp in Leanify 0.4.3 allows for a controlled out-of-bounds write in xml_memory_writer::write via characters that require escaping.

code_evidence: xml_memory_writer writer is initialized with p_write pointing at fp_ (after fp_ -= size_leanified). doc_.save serializes the document directly into that buffer, and size_ is computed as writer.p_write - fp_. The memory writer has no bound on how far p_write may advance, so escaped characters that expand output can push writes beyond the region allocated for the leanified result.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes serialized XML past the end of the intended buffer via an unbounded writer. It is not merely an off-by-one length miscalculation (CWE-193); the missing bound on writer advancement is the direct cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: serialization into a raw pointer buffer without a capacity limit. Trigger: XML content whose escaped form is larger than the space between fp_ and the buffer end. Consequence: out-of-bounds write past the intended buffer, corrupting adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
ALSA: control: code refactoring for ELEM_READ/ELEM_WRITE operations

ALSA control core handles ELEM_READ/ELEM_WRITE requests within lock
acquisition of a counting semaphore. The lock is acquired in helper
functions in the end of call path before calling implementations of each
driver.

ioctl(2) with SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_READ
...
->snd_ctl_ioctl()
  ->snd_ctl_elem_read_user()
    ->snd_ctl_elem_read()
      ->down_read(controls_rwsem)
      ->snd_ctl_find_id()
      ->struct snd_kcontrol.get()
      ->up_read(controls_rwsem)

ioctl(2) with SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_WRITE
...
->snd_ctl_ioctl()
  ->snd_ctl_elem_write_user()
    ->snd_ctl_elem_write()
      ->down_read(controls_rwsem)
      ->snd_ctl_find_id()
      ->struct snd_kcontrol.put()
      ->up_read(controls_rwsem)

This commit moves the lock acquisition to middle of the call graph to
simplify the helper functions. As a result:

ioctl(2) with SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_READ
...
->snd_ctl_ioctl()
  ->snd_ctl_elem_read_user()
    ->down_read(controls_rwsem)
    ->snd_ctl_elem_read()
      ->snd_ctl_find_id()
      ->struct snd_kcontrol.get()
    ->up_read(controls_rwsem)

ioctl(2) with SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_WRITE
...
->snd_ctl_ioctl()
  ->snd_ctl_elem_write_user()
    ->down_read(controls_rwsem)
    ->snd_ctl_elem_write()
      ->snd_ctl_find_id()
      ->struct snd_kcontrol.put()
    ->up_read(controls_rwsem)

Signed-off-by: Takashi Sakamoto <o-takashi@sakamocchi.jp>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (result >= 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (result >= 0) {', '\t\tdown_read(&card->controls_rwsem);', '\t\tup_read(&card->controls_rwsem);', '\t}']}
description: A use after free vulnerability exists in the ALSA PCM package in the Linux Kernel. SNDRV_CTL_IOCTL_ELEM_{READ|WRITE}32 is missing locks that can be used in a use-after-free that can result in a priviledge escalation to gain ring0 access from the system user. We recommend upgrading past commit 56b88b50565cd8b946a2d00b0c83927b7ebb055e

code_evidence: snd_ctl_elem_write_user() resolves card from file->card, takes snd_power_lock(card), waits for power state, then calls snd_ctl_elem_write(card, file, control) without holding card->controls_rwsem. The element write path performs snd_ctl_find_id() and invokes the driver's put() callback on kcontrol objects that are protected by controls_rwsem; here that lock is absent, so the lookup and callback run concurrently with control removal.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing lock allows a kcontrol to be freed and then used by snd_ctl_elem_write()'s lookup and put() callback, matching CWE-416 use after free. This is not merely a race on a live object; the supported consequence is reuse of freed memory. The added down_read/up_read around the call in the patch confirms the intended protection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the element-write helper accesses and invokes driver callbacks on snd_kcontrol objects without acquiring card->controls_rwsem, which normally serializes control lookup/use against removal. Trigger: a concurrent control-removal path frees the kcontrol while this write path is between snd_ctl_find_id() and the put() callback. Consequence: the callback dereferences freed kernel memory, supporting memory corruption or privilege escalation.

commit_msg: Bug 703791: Stay within hash table max key size in cached color converter.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tcached->hash = fz_new_hash_table(ctx, 256, n * sizeof(float), -1, fz_free);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (n * sizeof(float) <= FZ_HASH_TABLE_KEY_LENGTH)', '\t\t\tcached->hash = fz_new_hash_table(ctx, 256, n * sizeof(float), -1, fz_free);', '\t\telse', '\t\t\tfz_warn(ctx, "colorspace has too many components to be cached");']}
description: MuPDF through 1.18.1 has an out-of-bounds write because the cached color converter does not properly consider the maximum key size of a hash table. This can, for example, be seen with crafted "mutool draw" input.

code_evidence: Line 3 derives the key size from the source colorspace component count n = ss->n; line 15 passes n * sizeof(float) directly as the hash-table key length without any upper bound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing size constraint on n * sizeof(float) lets hash-table code write keys beyond the intended buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write. This is a buffer-bound error rather than an integer overflow: the multiplication itself is not shown to wrap, only to exceed the table's key capacity.

evidence_lines.code:
int n = ss->n;
cached->hash = fz_new_hash_table(ctx, 256, n * sizeof(float), -1, fz_free);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the key length passed to fz_new_hash_table is computed from an attacker-influenced colorspace component count with no check against FZ_HASH_TABLE_KEY_LENGTH. Trigger: a crafted input (e.g. via mutool draw) declaring a colorspace with many components causes a key size exceeding the fixed internal key buffer, and hash-table operations then write past that buffer. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds write, memory corruption, crash or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Check for integer overflow in xsltAddTextString

Limit buffer size in xsltAddTextString to INT_MAX. The issue can be
exploited to trigger an out of bounds write on 64-bit systems.

Originally reported to Chromium:

https://crbug.com/676623
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (ctxt->lasttuse + len >= ctxt->lasttsize) {', '\t    size = ctxt->lasttsize + len + 100;', '\t    size *= 2;'], 'added_lines': ['        int minSize;', '        /* Check for integer overflow accounting for NUL terminator. */', '        if (len >= INT_MAX - ctxt->lasttuse) {', '            xsltTransformError(ctxt, NULL, target,', '                "xsltCopyText: text allocation failed\\n");', '            return(NULL);', '        }', '        minSize = ctxt->lasttuse + len + 1;', '', '        if (ctxt->lasttsize < minSize) {', '            int extra;', '            /* Double buffer size but increase by at least 100 bytes. */', '            extra = minSize < 100 ? 100 : minSize;', '', '            /* Check for integer overflow. */', '            if (extra > INT_MAX - ctxt->lasttsize) {', '                size = INT_MAX;', '            }', '            else {', '                size = ctxt->lasttsize + extra;', '            }', '']}
description: The xsltAddTextString function in transform.c in libxslt 1.1.29, as used in Blink in Google Chrome prior to 57.0.2987.98 for Mac, Windows, and Linux and 57.0.2987.108 for Android, lacked a check for integer overflow during a size calculation, which allowed a remote attacker to perform an out of bounds memory write via a crafted HTML page.

code_evidence: The size calculation `size = ctxt->lasttsize + len + 100; size *= 2;` can overflow the signed int, yielding a small or negative allocation size passed to xmlRealloc.

The return value of xmlRealloc is stored into target->content and ctxt->lasttext, and ctxt->lasttsize is set to the overflowed `size`, so the recorded buffer capacity is smaller than the actual logical space needed.
memcpy writes `len` bytes at offset ctxt->lasttuse, then a NUL at lasttuse+len, without any bound check against the true allocated size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked integer overflow in the allocation size leads directly to a heap buffer that is too small, followed by memcpy writing past its end. This is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the integer overflow is the enabling condition, but the demonstrated consequence is the out-of-bounds write itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer growth computation `lasttsize + len + 100` doubled is performed in signed int without an overflow check. A crafted document drives len/lasttuse high enough that the arithmetic wraps, producing a tiny allocation while lasttsize and lasttuse advance beyond it. The subsequent memcpy and NUL terminator then write past the end of the heap buffer, corrupting memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

In create_bits() both height and stride are ints, so the result is
also an int, which will overflow if height or stride are big enough
and size_t is bigger than int.

This patch simply casts height to size_t to prevent these overflows,
which prevents the crash in:

    https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=972647

It's not even close to fixing the full problem of supporting big
images in pixman.

See also

    https://bugs.freedesktop.org/show_bug.cgi?id=69014

Trigger: attacker-supplied large height and stride. Consequence: buf_size wraps to a small value, and the subsequent calloc/malloc at lines 26/28 allocates too little for later use.

commit_msg:
Fix memory corruption in ephy_string_shorten()

This fixes a regression that I introduced in 232c613472b38ff0d0d97338f366024ddb9cd228.

I got my browser stuck in a crash loop today while visiting a website
with a page title greater than ephy-embed.c's MAX_TITLE_LENGTH, the only
condition in which ephy_string_shorten() is ever used. Turns out this
commit is wrong: an ellipses is a multibyte character (three bytes in
UTF-8) and so we're writing past the end of the buffer when calling
strcat() here. Ooops.

Shame it took nearly four years to notice and correct this.

Part-of: <https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/merge_requests/1106>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  /* +1 for ellipsis, +1 for trailing NUL */', '  new_str = g_new (gchar, bytes + 1 + 1);', '  strcat (new_str, "…");'], 'added_lines': ['  new_str = g_new (gchar, bytes + strlen ("…") + 1);', '  strncpy (new_str + bytes, "…", strlen ("…") + 1);']}
description: In GNOME Epiphany before 41.4 and 42.x before 42.2, an HTML document can trigger a client buffer overflow (in ephy_string_shorten in the UI process) via a long page title. The issue occurs because the number of bytes for a UTF-8 ellipsis character is not properly considered.

code_evidence: Line 14 computes bytes as the UTF-8 byte offset for target_length-1 characters. Line 15 allocates bytes + 1 + 1, reserving only one byte for the ellipsis plus a NUL. Line 16 copies bytes characters without a terminator, then line 17 strcat appends the three-byte UTF-8 ellipsis, writing past the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes beyond the end of a heap allocation due to an undersized buffer, which is exactly CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write). The arithmetic error in the size expression is the root cause; the resulting write past the allocation is the supported weakness, not merely a miscalculation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocation assumes the ellipsis occupies one byte, but "…" is three UTF-8 bytes. When the input title exceeds target_length, strcat writes the three-byte ellipsis plus a NUL into a buffer sized for only one ellipsis byte plus NUL, producing a heap out-of-bounds write. A long attacker-influenced page title triggers this path, causing memory corruption and potential crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix certauth built-in module returns

The PKINIT certauth eku module should never authoritatively authorize
a certificate, because an extended key usage does not establish a
relationship between the certificate and any specific user; it only
establishes that the certificate was created for PKINIT client
authentication.  Therefore, pkinit_eku_authorize() should return
KRB5_PLUGIN_NO_HANDLE on success, not 0.

The certauth san module should pass if it does not find any SANs of
the types it can match against; the presence of other types of SANs
should not cause it to explicitly deny a certificate.  Check for an
empty result from crypto_retrieve_cert_sans() in verify_client_san(),
instead of returning ENOENT from crypto_retrieve_cert_sans() when
there are no SANs at all.

ticket: 8561
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    return KRB5_PLUGIN_NO_HANDLE;']}
description: An authentication bypass flaw was found in the way krb5's certauth interface before 1.16.1 handled the validation of client certificates. A remote attacker able to communicate with the KDC could potentially use this flaw to impersonate arbitrary principals under rare and erroneous circumstances.

code_evidence: After verify_client_eku() sets valid_eku, the function rejects only when valid_eku is false (lines 16-19). When a PKINIT EKU is present, it falls through to the bare 'return 0;' at line 20, which certauth interprets as an authoritative authorization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the function improperly proves the claimed principal identity: an EKU check is treated as sufficient authorization without any cert-to-principal binding. Returning KRB5_PLUGIN_NO_HANDLE instead defers to other modules rather than asserting a successful authentication decision; this is an authentication-decision flaw, not merely a certificate-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the module returns success (0) after merely confirming an extended key usage, which only shows the certificate was issued for PKINIT client authentication and does not bind the certificate to the requested principal. Trigger: any client presenting a PKINIT-EKU certificate. Consequence: certauth treats the certificate as authoritatively authorizing the principal, enabling impersonation of arbitrary principals.

commit_msg:
DH_check(): Do not try checking q properties if it is obviously invalid

If  |q| >= |p| then the q value is obviously wrong as q
is supposed to be a prime divisor of p-1.

We check if p is overly large so this added test implies that
q is not large either when performing subsequent tests using that
q value.

Otherwise if it is too large these additional checks of the q value
such as the primality test can then trigger DoS by doing overly long
computations.

Fixes CVE-2023-3817

Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tom Cosgrove <tom.cosgrove@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Todd Short <todd.short@me.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/21550)

(cherry picked from commit 1c16253f3c3a8d1e25918c3f404aae6a5b0893de)
(cherry picked from commit 6a1eb62c29db6cb5eec707f9338aee00f44e26f5)

description:
Issue summary: Checking excessively long DH keys or parameters may be very slow.

Impact summary: Applications that use the functions DH_check(), DH_check_ex()
or EVP_PKEY_param_check() to check a DH key or DH parameters may experience long
delays. Where the key or parameters that are being checked have been obtained
from an untrusted source this may lead to a Denial of Service.

The function DH_check() performs various checks on DH parameters. After fixing
CVE-2023-3446 it was discovered that a large q parameter value can also trigger
an overly long computation during some of these checks. A correct q value,
if present, cannot be larger than the modulus p parameter, thus it is
unnecessary to perform these checks if q is larger than p.

An application that calls DH_check() and supplies a key or parameters obtained
from an untrusted source could be vulnerable to a Denial of Service attack.

The function DH_check() is itself called by a number of other OpenSSL functions.
An application calling any of those other functions may similarly be affected.
The other functions affected by this are DH_check_ex() and
EVP_PKEY_param_check().

Also vulnerable are the OpenSSL dhparam and pkeyparam command line applications
when using the "-check" option.

The OpenSSL SSL/TLS implementation is not affected by this issue.

The OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.1 FIPS providers are not affected by this issue.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no loop or iteration construct; the DoS arises from unbounded bignum computations (BN_check_prime, BN_mod_exp) on an oversized q, not from excessive iteration as defined by CWE-834.

commit_msg:
Airodump-ng: Fixed GPS stack overflow (Closes #13 on GitHub).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        \tif( recv( gpsd_sock, line + pos, sizeof( line ) - 1, 0 ) <= 0 )'], 'added_lines': ['        \tif( recv( gpsd_sock, line + pos, sizeof( line ) - pos - 1, 0 ) <= 0 )']}
description: Stack-based buffer overflow in the gps_tracker function in airodump-ng.c in Aircrack-ng before 1.2 RC 1 allows local users to execute arbitrary code or gain privileges via unspecified vectors.

code_evidence: line[256] is a fixed stack buffer; pos accumulates the JSON length (set from strlen at line 43, reused across loop iterations). At line 56 recv writes at line + pos with length sizeof(line) - 1, ignoring pos. The guard at line 52 only resets when pos == sizeof(line), so any pos in 1..255 leaves room computed as 255 bytes rather than 255 - pos, allowing bytes to be written past line's end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the recv call writes beyond the end of the stack array line; the fix subtracts pos from the size, confirming the missing bound. This is a direct out-of-bounds write, not merely an integer issue or read overrun.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the receive length omits the current offset pos, so the destination pointer line + pos is combined with a length that can exceed the remaining buffer. Trigger: a gpsd JSON response whose accumulated length pushes pos above zero while a large recv fills the full sizeof(line)-1 count. Consequence: out-of-bounds stack write, permitting memory corruption and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix vi_pci_write null vc_cfgwrite function pointer dereference (GHSL-2021-055)

This is a backport of what is done in bhyve.

Signed-off-by: Frederic Dalleau <frederic.dalleau@docker.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\terror = (*vc->vc_cfgwrite)(DEV_SOFTC(vs), ((int) newoff), size,', '\t\t\t((uint32_t) value));'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (vc->vc_cfgwrite != NULL)', '\t\t\terror = (*vc->vc_cfgwrite)(DEV_SOFTC(vs), ((int) newoff), size,', '\t\t\t\t((uint32_t) value));', '\t\telse', '\t\t\terror = 0;']}
description: HyperKit is a toolkit for embedding hypervisor capabilities in an application. In versions 0.20210107 and prior of HyperKit, ` vi_pci_write` has is a call to `vc_cfgwrite` that does not check for null which when called makes the host crash. This issue may lead to a guest crashing the host causing a denial of service. This issue is fixed in commit 451558fe8aaa8b24e02e34106e3bb9fe41d7ad13.

code_evidence: When offset >= virtio_config_size, the code computes newoff and bounds-checks it against max, then unconditionally calls the function pointer vc->vc_cfgwrite via (*vc->vc_cfgwrite)(...) without verifying that vc_cfgwrite is non-NULL. The patch adds a NULL check before this indirect call, confirming the pointer may legitimately be NULL for devices whose config space is not writable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences a pointer it expects to be valid but which can be NULL, and the resulting crash matches the availability/DoS scope. This is distinct from a bounds or type-confusion weakness; the defect is the missing NULL guard on the function pointer before the call.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the indirect call at line 36 dereferences vc->vc_cfgwrite without a NULL check. Trigger: a guest writes to a virtio config-space offset >= virtio_config_size for a device instance whose vc_cfgwrite is NULL. Consequence: a NULL function-pointer call crashes the host, enabling a guest to cause denial of service.

commit_msg:
When a client has a USB device attached over IP, the vhci_hcd driver is
locally leaking a socket pointer address via the

/sys/devices/platform/vhci_hcd/status file (world-readable) and in debug
output when "usbip --debug port" is run.

Fix it to not leak. The socket pointer address is not used at the moment
and it was made visible as a convenient way to find IP address from socket
pointer address by looking up /proc/net/{tcp,tcp6}.

As this opens a security hole, the fix replaces socket pointer address with
sockfd.

Reported-by: Secunia Research <vuln@secunia.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan <shuahkh@osg.samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tunsigned long socket;', '\t\tret = sscanf(c, "%2s  %d %d %d %x %lx %31s\\n",', '\t\t\t\t&devid, &socket, lbusid);', '\t\tdbg("socket %lx lbusid %s", socket, lbusid);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tint sockfd;', '\t\tret = sscanf(c, "%2s  %d %d %d %x %u %31s\\n",', '\t\t\t\t&devid, &sockfd, lbusid);', '\t\tdbg("sockfd %u lbusid %s", sockfd, lbusid);']}
description: The vhci_hcd driver in the Linux Kernel before version 4.14.8 and 4.4.114 allows allows local attackers to disclose kernel memory addresses. Successful exploitation requires that a USB device is attached over IP.

code_evidence: parse_status declares an unsigned long socket and parses a %lx field into it from the status text via sscanf.
The parsed socket value is emitted through dbg("socket %lx lbusid %s", socket, lbusid), placing the raw kernel socket pointer into debug output.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly forwards a sensitive kernel pointer into accessible debug output without scrubbing, which is an information exposure rather than a memory-safety error; CWE-200 covers such explicit leakage of sensitive internal state.

evidence_lines.code: dbg("socket %lx lbusid %s", socket, lbusid);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser reads a kernel socket pointer value from the status string and passes it unfiltered to dbg, so debug/status output discloses a kernel address. Trigger: a USB device attached over IP causes status text containing the socket pointer to be parsed and logged; consequence is kernel address disclosure to an unauthorized reader.

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Remove unsafe bits from the mod_l?_entry() fastpath

All changes in writeability and cacheability must go through full
re-validation.

Rework the logic as a whitelist, to make it clearer to follow.

This is XSA-182

Reported-by: Jérémie Boutoille <jboutoille@ext.quarkslab.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        /* Fast path for identical mapping and presence. */', '        if ( !l3e_has_changed(ol3e, nl3e, _PAGE_PRESENT) )'], 'added_lines': ['        /* Fast path for sufficiently-similar mappings. */', '        if ( !l3e_has_changed(ol3e, nl3e, ~FASTPATH_FLAG_WHITELIST) )']}
description: The PV pagetable code in arch/x86/mm.c in Xen 4.7.x and earlier allows local 32-bit PV guest OS administrators to gain host OS privileges by leveraging fast-paths for updating pagetable entries.

code_evidence: When the new L3 entry has _PAGE_PRESENT (line 19), the only flag validation is l3_disallow_mask (line 21). The fastpath at line 27 then accepts the entry if l3e_has_changed compares equal using only _PAGE_PRESENT as the ignored mask, so writeability/cacheability changes pass without re-validation of the referenced page before UPDATE_ENTRY installs nl3e.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is an enforcement error in the access-control check: the permission bits of an updated pagetable entry are not restricted before the update is applied, permitting an unauthorized privilege-bearing mapping. This matches improper access control (CWE-284) rather than a memory-corruption bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the fastpath's change-detection mask only ignores _PAGE_PRESENT, so modifications to other permission/cacheability flags are treated as unchanged and skip get_page_from_l3e re-validation. A local PV guest administrator can supply such an L3e and have it committed, letting the guest obtain writable/cacheable mappings it should not have, escalating to host privileges.

commit_msg:
Fix a potential integer overflow bug in the JPEG and PNG loaders (Issue #471)

All images are now limited to 4GiB of memory usage (37837x37837 pixels).

description: There is a vulnerability in htmldoc 1.9.16. In image_load_jpeg function image.cxx when it calls malloc,'img->width' and 'img->height' they are large enough to cause an integer overflow. So, the malloc function may return a heap blosmaller than the expected size, and it will cause a buffer overflow/Address boundary error in the jpeg_read_scanlines function.

code_evidence: Lines 47-48 assign img->width and img->height from the GIF image descriptor bytes, and lines 50-51 reject values outside 1..32767 before allocation.

Line 72 computes the allocation size as img->width * img->height * img->depth in int arithmetic before the (size_t) cast, so the multiplication itself can overflow even though the dimension checks bound each factor.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because an integer multiplication used to compute a memory-allocation size can overflow/wrap, yielding a smaller-than-expected buffer. This is distinct from CWE-122, which describes the resulting heap write; here the supported root cause is the unchecked integer arithmetic feeding malloc.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size expression img->width * img->height * img->depth at line 72 is evaluated in int before conversion to size_t, so with dimensions near the 32767 limit the product exceeds INT_MAX and wraps. Trigger: a crafted GIF whose descriptor yields large width/height passing the range checks. Consequence: malloc receives an undersized request, and subsequent pixel writes in gif_read_image can overflow the heap buffer.

commit_msg:
ALSA: control: Re-order bounds checking in get_ctl_id_hash()

These two checks are in the reverse order so it might read one element
beyond the end of the array.  First check if the "i" is within bounds
before using it.

Fixes: 6ab55ec0a938 ("ALSA: control: Fix an out-of-bounds bug in get_ctl_id_hash()")
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/YwjgNh/gkG1hH7po@kili
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfor (i = 0; id->name[i] && i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN; i++)'], 'added_lines': ['\tfor (i = 0; i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN && id->name[i]; i++)']}
description: An out-of-bounds access issue was found in the Linux kernel sound subsystem. It could occur when the 'id->name' provided by the user did not end with '\0'. A privileged local user could pass a specially crafted name through ioctl() interface and crash the system or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: Loop condition evaluates id->name[i] before checking i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN, so the bound check is short-circuited behind the array read. If id->name lacks a NUL terminator within the array, the read at index SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN occurs one element past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads id->name[i] past the intended array end when the bound check is evaluated too late, which is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not merely a missing length check; the read itself precedes the constraint.

evidence_lines.code:
for (i = 0; id->name[i] && i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN; i++)
h = MULTIPLIER * h + id->name[i];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the reversed operand order in the loop condition, which dereferences id->name[i] before validating the index. Trigger: a user-supplied id->name that is not NUL-terminated within SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read, potentially crashing the system or leaking adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
httplive: fix use-after-free

Implement a mutex to ensure secure multi-threaded
access to the KeyedVector in MetaDataBase.
Concurrent access by different threads can lead
to accessing the wrong memory location due to
potential changes in the vector

Bug: 298057702
Test: HTTP Live Streaming test
(cherry picked from https://partner-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:a2dfb31957a9d5358d0219a0eda7dcb5b0fff5fe)
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:90fb4ca425444429ada6ce0de1c13d35829bc196)
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:3c1d9613ef64e01d2e81c4aa44c90dcd8ca958b9)
Merged-In: I46b05c85d9c39f4ce549efc160c08a0646c9fd0a
Change-Id: I46b05c85d9c39f4ce549efc160c08a0646c9fd0a
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> guard(mInternalData->mLock);']}
description: In multiple functions of MetaDataBase.cpp, there is a possible UAF write due to a race condition. This could lead to remote escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: setData reads the shared mInternalData->mItems via indexOfKey, then conditionally adds a new entry and obtains a reference through editValueAt before writing with item.setData. No lock or synchronization guards this check-then-modify sequence on the shared KeyedVector, so the index i and the reference can be invalidated by a concurrent modification of mItems.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes a shared resource (mInternalData->mItems) accessed by concurrent code sequences without exclusive access, and a timing window allows another thread to modify it mid-sequence. This matches CWE-362's non-atomic concurrent access; the resulting UAF write is the consequence, not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an unsynchronized check-then-act on a shared container: indexOfKey and the subsequent add/editValueAt are not atomic with respect to other threads mutating mItems. A concurrent insert or reallocation between those calls can make i stale, so editValueAt returns a reference into relocated or freed storage, and item.setData writes through it, yielding a use-after-free write.

commit_msg:
evtchn: convert per-channel lock to be IRQ-safe

... in order for send_guest_{global,vcpu}_virq() to be able to make use
of it.

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    spin_lock(&chn->lock);', '    spin_unlock(&chn->lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned long  flags;', '    spin_lock_irqsave(&chn->lock, flags);', '    spin_unlock_irqrestore(&chn->lock, flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The function takes d->event_lock at line 15 and reads v->virq_to_evtchn[virq] under that lock, then allocates a port and initializes chn under the separate per-channel chn->lock.

The channel state and v->virq_to_evtchn[virq] are updated under different locks: chn->lock is released at line 36 before v->virq_to_evtchn[virq] is written at line 37 while only d->event_lock is held.
The out label at 38 and spin_unlock(&d->event_lock) at 39 release the domain event lock; the per-channel lock is not IRQ-safe, so an interrupt-context path can interleave with the critical section.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the bind sequence requires exclusive access to the shared event-channel and virq_to_evtchn state, but the non-IRQ-safe per-channel lock and split locking leave a timing window in which another code sequence modifies the shared resource.

evidence_lines.code:
out:
spin_unlock(&d->event_lock);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The per-channel lock is taken with plain spin_lock rather than spin_lock_irqsave, and the chn state is committed under chn->lock while the virq_to_evtchn binding is written later under only d->event_lock. An interrupting code sequence using the same channel lock or a concurrent reset can observe partially updated channel state, breaking exclusivity/atomicity of the bind sequence and allowing inconsistent internal state, out-of-bounds access or bug checks.

commit_msg:
USB: visor: fix null-deref at probe

Fix null-pointer dereference at probe should a (malicious) Treo device
lack the expected endpoints.

Specifically, the Treo port-setup hack was dereferencing the bulk-in and
interrupt-in urbs without first making sure they had been allocated by
core.

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (serial->num_bulk_in < 2 || serial->num_interrupt_in < 2) {', '\t\tdev_err(&serial->interface->dev, "missing endpoints\\n");', '\t\treturn -ENODEV;', '\t}']}
description: The treo_attach function in drivers/usb/serial/visor.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5 allows physically proximate attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by inserting a USB device that lacks a (1) bulk-in or (2) interrupt-in endpoint.

code_evidence: The guard only checks serial->num_interrupt_in == 0 and returns early for non-Treo/Kyocera vendors; it never verifies that two bulk-in endpoints exist before entering the port-swap logic.
COPY_PORT unconditionally assigns dest->interrupt_in_urb = src->interrupt_in_urb and immediately dereferences it via ->context; the macro also copies read_urbs entries without null checks.

treo_attach allocates swap_port and invokes COPY_PORT on serial->port[0] and serial->port[1], dereferencing their interrupt_in_urb pointers; a malicious Treo lacking the expected endpoints leaves these urbs unallocated (NULL).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly dereferences an urb pointer that can be NULL when the device lacks the expected endpoint, matching CWE-476's null-pointer-dereference definition. The added num_bulk_in/num_interrupt_in check is the missing constraint; this is not an out-of-bounds or use-after-free issue.

evidence_lines.code:
(serial->num_interrupt_in == 0))
return 0;

dest->interrupt_in_urb = src->interrupt_in_urb;\
dest->interrupt_in_urb->context = dest;\

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the missing endpoint-count validation lets a device with fewer than two bulk-in/interrupt-in endpoints reach COPY_PORT. Trigger: a physically proximate attacker plugs in a crafted Treo/Kyocera device lacking endpoints, so src->interrupt_in_urb is NULL. Consequence: dereference of that NULL pointer (and possibly read_urbs) crashes the kernel, causing denial of service.

commit_msg: safety checks for decoding/testing when the buffer size and block size are inconsistent, tentative CRC32 version for BE systems (needs further verification on SPARC?)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                if(old_size > block_size + 31) {', '                    fprintf(stderr, "Failed to decode a block: Inconsistent headers.\\n");', '                    return 1;', '                }', '                if(old_size > block_size + 31) {', '                    fprintf(stderr, "Failed to decode a block: Inconsistent headers.\\n");', '                    return 1;', '                }', '                    if(old_sizes[i] > block_size + 31) {', '                        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to decode a block: Inconsistent headers.\\n");', '                        return 1;', '                    }', '                    if(old_sizes[i] > block_size + 31) {', '                        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to decode a block: Inconsistent headers.\\n");', '                        return 1;', '                    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in libbzip3.a in bzip3 before 1.2.3. There is an xwrite out-of-bounds read.

code_evidence: In the sequential MODE_DECODE branch, old_size is read from the block header at line 79 and passed to bz3_decode_block at line 82 without an upper bound check, so a crafted header can drive decoding beyond the buffer.
In the multithreaded MODE_DECODE branch, old_sizes[i] is read at line 165 and passed to bz3_decode_blocks at line 169 (within block 165-169) with no bound on the header value.
The decoded output is then written using old_sizes[i] as the length at line 177, so an oversized header length propagates to xwrite, which reads past the end of buffers[j].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing upper-bound check on a header-derived length lets decode and xwrite read past the end of the buffer, matching CWE-125. This is a read overrun, not an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), because the oversized length is used to read/decode rather than to store attacker data past the buffer end.

evidence_lines.code:
xwrite(buffers[j], old_sizes[j], 1, output_des);
bytes_written += old_sizes[j];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the uncompressed block length (old_size/old_sizes[i]) is taken from an untrusted header and used as a decode/output length without validating it against the allocated buffer capacity. Trigger: a malformed input file whose header declares an old size larger than block_size+31. Consequence: bz3_decode_* and the subsequent xwrite read beyond the allocated buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read (crash or memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
teredo: be stricter on what to consider valid teredo

Invalid Teredo can lead to valid DNS traffic (or other UDP traffic)
being misdetected as Teredo. This leads to false negatives in the
UDP payload inspection.

Make the teredo code only consider a packet teredo if the encapsulated
data was decoded without any 'invalid' events being set.

description: Open Information Security Foundation Suricata prior to version 4.1.2 is affected by: Denial of Service - DNS detection bypass. The impact is: An attacker can evade a signature detection with a specialy formed network packet. The component is: app-layer-detect-proto.c, decode.c, decode-teredo.c and decode-ipv6.c (https://github.com/OISF/suricata/pull/3590/commits/11f3659f64a4e42e90cb3c09fcef66894205aefe, https://github.com/OISF/suricata/pull/3590/commits/8357ef3f8ffc7d99ef6571350724160de356158b). The attack vector is: An attacker can trigger the vulnerability by sending a specifically crafted network request. The fixed version is: 4.1.2.

code_evidence: When fewer than 2 bytes remain (plen < 2), the function returns without setting any invalid event, so a truncated extension header is silently accepted rather than flagged.
A routing-header length derived from packet byte *(pkt+1) is compared to plen; on overflow the code sets a non-invalid event and returns, leaving the malformed packet unmarked.
The hop-by-hop/destination-options header length (*(pkt+1)+1)<<3 is checked against plen but only a normal event is raised on truncation, not an invalid event.
An options length exceeding plen sets a non-invalid event while still advancing pkt/plen and continuing, so parsing proceeds on inconsistent length metadata.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is failure to validate attacker-supplied length metadata (header length, option length, remaining plen) against required properties before processing, matching CWE-20 improper input validation. The consequence is misclassification/detection bypass rather than a memory-safety flaw, so a lower-level memory CWE does not fit.

evidence_lines.code:
if (plen < 2) { 
SCReturn;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser derives extension-header lengths and remaining payload lengths directly from attacker-controlled packet bytes but only raises non-invalid events (or returns silently) when these lengths are inconsistent or truncated. Because these conditions are not marked invalid, the caller's Teredo/upper-layer validity check still treats the malformed packet as valid, allowing crafted packets to be misclassified and bypass protocol detection.

Use thread join to avoid thread exiting after instance

description: In run of MDnsSdListener.cpp, there is a possible memory corruption due to a use after free. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: The constructor launches a background thread bound to `this` via `threadLaunch(this)` and only logs when launch fails; it never stores the thread handle or joins it. The object's lifetime is therefore not synchronized with the monitor thread's execution, so the thread can run after the Monitor instance is destroyed/recycled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a lifetime/synchronization flaw where a thread continues to reference (and operate on) an object after it has been freed — the defining pattern of CWE-416. The fix (storing the thread and joining it) confirms the missing lifetime constraint rather than a different weakness such as a simple race without free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the spawned thread references the Monitor object (`this`) but the constructor keeps no ownership/handle and performs no join, so destruction of the instance can race with the thread's continued use of its members. Trigger: the Monitor instance is torn down while the thread is still executing; the thread then accesses freed memory, yielding use-after-free (crash or memory corruption).

commit_msg:
Bug 699665 "memory corruption in aesdecode"

The specimen file calls aesdecode without specifying the key to be
used, though it does manage to do enough work with the PDF interpreter
routines to get access to aesdecode (which isn't normally available).

This causes us to read uninitialised memory, which can (and often does)
lead to a segmentation fault.

In this commit we set the key to NULL explicitly during intialisation
and then check it before we read it. If its NULL we just return.

It seems bizarre that we don't return error codes, we should probably
look into that at some point, but this prevents the code trying to
read uninitialised memory.

description: In Artifex Ghostscript 9.23 before 2018-08-24, attackers able to supply crafted PostScript could use uninitialized memory access in the aesdecode operator to crash the interpreter or potentially execute code.

code_evidence: When state->ctx is NULL, gs_alloc_bytes_immovable allocates an aes_context but does not zero it; the allocation result is used directly at aes_setkey_dec(state->ctx, state->key, ...) with no initialization of the context memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the allocated aes_context resource is used before being initialized, matching use of an uninitialized resource. It is not merely a NULL-pointer dereference: the defect is that uninitialized bytes are consumed by aes_setkey_dec.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the freshly allocated aes_context is passed to aes_setkey_dec without being cleared, so the cipher routine reads the uninitialized key material/context. Trigger: a crafted PostScript stream reaching aesdecode with state->key NULL or otherwise unset. Consequence: uninitialized memory is read during decryption, causing a crash or potential disclosure/execution.

commit_msg:
in_mqtt: fix memory corruption on dropping packet (#1135)

This patch adds an extra verification to the buffer counters to
avoid corruption when memmove() an extra byte.

In addition this patch implement a linked list for the active
connections so when closing Fluent Bit we have a clean exit.

Signed-off-by: Eduardo Silva <eduardo@treasure-data.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['']}
description: An issue was discovered in the MQTT input plugin in Fluent Bit through 1.0.4. When this plugin acts as an MQTT broker (server), it mishandles incoming network messages. After processing a crafted packet, the plugin's mqtt_packet_drop function (in /plugins/in_mqtt/mqtt_prot.c) executes the memmove() function with a negative size parameter. That leads to a crash of the whole Fluent Bit server via a SIGSEGV signal.

code_evidence: buf_pos, buf_len and buf_frame_end are int fields; remaining-length bytes are accumulated into int length (line 34) and buf_frame_end is derived as conn->buf_pos + length (line 53). After the frame is handled, line 86 sets buf_pos = buf_frame_end and line 87 calls mqtt_packet_drop(conn). Line 89 assigns -1 to conn->buf_pos, which the drop routine later uses as a buffer offset/size, driving a negative memmove size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function stores buffer positions/lengths as int and assigns -1 to buf_pos, an incorrect numeric conversion/representation that yields an unexpected negative value later used as a size/offset. This matches CWE-681; an out-of-bounds write CWE would describe the consequence rather than the numeric-type cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: signed int frame counters and an explicit -1 assignment to buf_pos (line 89) produce a negative offset that reaches memmove in mqtt_packet_drop. Trigger: a crafted MQTT packet that leaves buf_len > 0 after frame processing. Consequence: negative-size memmove corrupts memory and crashes the server via SIGSEGV.

commit_msg:
video: fbdev: pxa3xx-gcu: Fix integer overflow in pxa3xx_gcu_write

In pxa3xx_gcu_write, a count parameter of type size_t is passed to words of
type int.  Then, copy_from_user() may cause a heap overflow because it is used
as the third argument of copy_from_user().

Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Helge Deller <deller@gmx.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint words = count / 4;'], 'added_lines': ['\tsize_t words = count / 4;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.19. In pxa3xx_gcu_write in drivers/video/fbdev/pxa3xx-gcu.c, the count parameter has a type conflict of size_t versus int, causing an integer overflow and bypassing the size check. After that, because it is used as the third argument to copy_from_user(), a heap overflow may occur. NOTE: the original discoverer disputes that the overflow can actually happen.

code_evidence: `count` is `size_t` but is narrowed into `int words = count / 4`; the subsequent guard `if (words >= PXA3XX_GCU_BATCH_WORDS) return -E2BIG;` compares this truncated/negative `int`, so a large `count` can bypass the size check.
`words * 4` is then passed as the length to `copy_from_user(buffer->ptr, buff, ...)`, and `buffer->ptr[words]` indexes with the same value, so the unchecked count governs a heap copy and store.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The narrowing of a size_t computation into int is an integer overflow/wraparound that defeats a size check before a memory copy, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a bounds-check omission because the arithmetic conversion is the cause of the bypassed constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the size_t-to-int conversion of count/4, which can wrap to a small or negative value and evade the PXA3XX_GCU_BATCH_WORDS limit. Trigger is an oversized count from the write caller; the unsupported consequence is a heap overflow in copy_from_user and the trailing buffer->ptr[words] store.

commit_msg:
tun: allow positive return values on dev_get_valid_name() call

If the name argument of dev_get_valid_name() contains "%d", it will try
to assign it a unit number in __dev__alloc_name() and return either the
unit number (>= 0) or an error code (< 0).
Considering positive values as error values prevent tun device creations
relying this mechanism, therefor we should only consider negative values
as errors here.

Signed-off-by: Julien Gomes <julien@arista.com>
Acked-by: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (err)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (err < 0)']}
description: In the tun subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.14, dev_get_valid_name is not called before register_netdevice. This allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and panic) via an ioctl(TUNSETIFF) call with a dev name containing a / character. This is similar to CVE-2013-4343.

code_evidence: dev_get_valid_name() may return a non-negative unit number when name contains "%d"; the check `if (err)` treats any nonzero return as failure and jumps to err_free_dev. On a successful positive return, the code is skipped and execution continues to dev_net_set(dev, net) with dev expected to be fully initialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function proceeds with a device pointer that was not successfully validated/initialized, leading to a NULL dereference and DoS. This is distinct from merely mishandling a return code; the supported consequence is a NULL pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the overly broad error test on dev_get_valid_name()'s return value, which conflates a valid positive unit number with an error. Triggering a TUNSETIFF with a name containing a slash (or otherwise failing name validation) leads to an error path that frees dev and returns; the missing correct handling of the return semantics allows later use of an invalid/freed device, producing a NULL pointer dereference and kernel panic.

commit_msg:
IORING_OP_MADVISE can end up basically doing mprotect() on the VM of
another process, which means that it can race with our crazy core dump
handling which accesses the VM state without holding the mmap_sem
(because it incorrectly thinks that it is the final user).

This is clearly a core dumping problem, but we've never fixed it the
right way, and instead have the notion of "check that the mm is still
ok" using mmget_still_valid() after getting the mmap_sem for writing in
any situation where we're not the original VM thread.

See commit 04f5866e41fb ("coredump: fix race condition between
mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and core dumping") for more background on
this whole mmget_still_valid() thing.  You might want to have a barf bag
handy when you do.

We're discussing just fixing this properly in the only remaining core
dumping routines.  But even if we do that, let's make do_madvise() do
the right thing, and then when we fix core dumping, we can remove all
these mmget_still_valid() checks.

Reported-and-tested-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Fixes: c1ca757bd6f4 ("io_uring: add IORING_OP_MADVISE")
Acked-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * We may have stolen the mm from another process', '\t\t * that is undergoing core dumping.', '\t\t *', "\t\t * Right now that's io_ring, in the future it may", '\t\t * be remote process management and not "current"', '\t\t * at all.', '\t\t *', '\t\t * We need to fix core dumping to not do this,', '\t\t * but for now we have the mmget_still_valid()', '\t\t * model.', '\t\t */', '\t\tif (!mmget_still_valid(current->mm)) {', '\t\t\tup_write(&current->mm->mmap_sem);', '\t\t\treturn -EINTR;', '\t\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in do_madvise in mm/madvise.c in the Linux kernel before 5.6.8. There is a race condition between coredump operations and the IORING_OP_MADVISE implementation, aka CID-bc0c4d1e176e.

code_evidence: The function selects locking from behavior via madvise_need_mmap_write() and then takes only mmap_sem (write or read) on current->mm. The mm may have been obtained by another process (io_uring) and be under core dumping.
After acquiring the lock, find_vma_prev() and the loop operate on current->mm VM state assuming exclusive ownership; no check validates that the mm is still valid for the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code sequence requires exclusive access to the shared mm/VM structures but relies on a lock that an interfering coredump sequence bypasses, permitting concurrent modification. That is a race condition on a shared resource with improper synchronization, matching CWE-362.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: do_madvise serializes VM modifications only with mmap_sem, but a concurrent core dump accesses VM state without that lock, so the lock does not establish exclusivity over current->mm. Trigger: IORING_OP_MADVISE causes do_madvise on a stolen mm racing coredump; the loop then reads/modifies vma/prev structures concurrently. Supported consequence: inconsistent VM state, potentially memory corruption or crash.

CVE-2017-12993/Juniper: Add more bounds checks.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kamil Frankowicz.

description: The Juniper protocols parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-juniper.c, several functions.

code_evidence: After juniper_parse_header succeeds, p is advanced by l2info.header_len and cast to a juniper_ipsec_header pointer ih; ih->type is dereferenced in the switch without verifying that the captured buffer actually contains the full header, so the read may fall past the end of the packet data.

Later, l2info.length is reduced by rewrite_len and p advanced by rewrite_len; the eflag branch then reads ih->sa_index, ttl, type, spi, src_ip and dst_ip via EXTRACT_*BITS/ipaddr_string. These accesses rely on l2info.length and the header extent, which are not checked against the actual captured bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading fields through ih and processing l2info.length without bounds validation against the captured buffer is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a write or integer issue; the unsafe operation is a read past the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dereferences the Juniper IPsec header (ih->type, then ih fields) and passes l2info.length to ip_print without confirming the captured data covers the header or the advertised length. Trigger: a truncated or malformed Juniper ES packet whose parse header succeeds but leaves fewer bytes than the header/rewrite length requires. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads of packet memory, potentially leaking or crashing.

commit_msg:
Don't allow scripts to run when a node is being adopted.

Running a script in the middle of rescoping nodes can break a lot of invariants and leave DOM in an inconsistent state.

This patch adds a ScriptForbiddenScope in TreeScope::adoptIfNeeded to ensure it never happens.

BUG=605766

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1910403003

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#389425}
(cherry picked from commit 146ff1bb11c88778d466bd7a49b544f2b5806ee0)

TBR=dominicc@chromium.org,esprehn@chromium.org

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1953323002 .

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/branch-heads/2661@{#665}
Cr-Branched-From: ef6f6ae5e4c96622286b563658d5cd62a6cf1197-refs/heads/master@{#378081}

description: The TreeScope::adoptIfNeeded function in WebKit/Source/core/dom/TreeScope.cpp in the DOM implementation in Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 50.0.2661.102, does not prevent script execution during node-adoption operations, which allows remote attackers to bypass the Same Origin Policy via a crafted web site.

code_evidence: TreeScopeAdopter adopter(node, *this) is constructed, then when adopter.needsScopeChange() is true, adopter.execute() performs the node-adoption rescoping with no ScriptForbiddenScope guarding the operation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to enforce the security policy that scripts must not execute during adoption, letting attacker-influenced script act across a boundary it should not cross. This is an enforcement failure in access control, matching CWE-284 rather than a memory corruption or input-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: adoptIfNeeded allows script execution during node adoption because adopter.execute() runs without a ScriptForbiddenScope. Trigger: a crafted page that causes a node to be adopted while script can run mid-operation. Supported consequence: rescoping invariants can be broken and the DOM left inconsistent, enabling a Same Origin Policy bypass.

commit_msg:
CVE-2019-3557: Fix OOB read in readRecord on BZ2Files/OutputFiles

Summary:
These File subclasses return -1 on read errors which is not what is
expected for readImpl--this made File::readRecord behave unusually if the read
fails, causing it to read (size_t)(-1) bytes from its stream buffer; which,
unsurprisingly produces a out-of-bounds heap read.

Reviewed By: leikahing, jjgriego

Differential Revision: D13659395

fbshipit-source-id: 359ed6e3ff9f9cf49b752b666f51c4e0b3ce4b8a

description: The implementations of streams for bz2 and php://output improperly implemented their readImpl functions, returning -1 consistently. This behavior caused some stream functions, such as stream_get_line, to trigger an out-of-bounds read when operating on such malformed streams. The implementations were updated to return valid values consistently. This affects all supported versions of HHVM (3.30 and 3.27.4 and below).

code_evidence: OutputFile::readImpl unconditionally returns -1 after raising a warning; it never returns a non-negative byte count for a read request.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The -1 return propagates into a size computation that indexes/reads past the buffer, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. It is not merely a return-value error; the supported consequence is reading memory beyond the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: readImpl returns -1, violating the non-negative contract for a read operation. Trigger: a caller such as readRecord or stream_get_line treats the result as a size and uses (size_t)(-1), causing a huge read from the stream buffer. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds heap read and possible crash or memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
This is a follow up of commit 915d975b2ffa ("net: deal with integer
overflows in kmalloc_reserve()") based on David Laight feedback.

Back in 2010, I failed to realize malicious users could set dev->mtu
to arbitrary values. This mtu has been since limited to 0x7fffffff but
regardless of how big dev->mtu is, it makes no sense for igmpv3_newpack()
to allocate more than IP_MAX_MTU and risk various skb fields overflows.

Fixes: 57e1ab6eaddc ("igmp: refine skb allocations")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/netdev/d273628df80f45428e739274ab9ecb72@AcuMS.aculab.com/
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: David Laight <David.Laight@ACULAB.COM>
Cc: Kyle Zeng <zengyhkyle@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Simon Horman <horms@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned int size = mtu;'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned int size;', '\tsize = min(mtu, IP_MAX_MTU);']}
description: An integer overflow flaw was found in the Linux kernel. This issue leads to the kernel allocating `skb_shared_info` in the userspace, which is exploitable in systems without SMAP protection since `skb_shared_info` contains references to function pointers.

code_evidence: Line 11 initializes size directly from the caller-supplied mtu with no upper bound, and line 13 computes size + hlen + tlen for alloc_skb.
Lines 17-19 only halve size after a failed allocation and bail below 256; they do not constrain the initial mtu, so a large mtu reaches the size + hlen + tlen addition unclamped.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an arithmetic wraparound in a size calculation used for memory allocation, matching CWE-190. It is not merely an unchecked resource limit; the overflowed sum defeats the allocation size check and enables memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: size is set to the unbounded mtu, so the allocation-size expression size + hlen + tlen can overflow unsigned int and request a small buffer. Trigger: a malicious user sets dev->mtu to an arbitrary large value. Consequence: the undersized skb is later filled with headers, causing out-of-bounds writes as skb_shared_info/subsequent data exceed the allocation.

commit_msg:
Fixes CVE-2023-3138: X servers could return values from XQueryExtension
that would cause Xlib to write entries out-of-bounds of the arrays to
store them, though this would only overwrite other parts of the Display
struct, not outside the bounds allocated for that structure.

Reported-by: Gregory James DUCK <gjduck@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Alan Coopersmith <alan.coopersmith@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (error_number < 0 ||', '\t    error_number > LastExtensionError) {', '\t   fprintf(stderr, "Xlib: ignoring invalid extension error %d\\n",', '\t\t    error_number);', '\t   return (WireToErrorType)_XDefaultWireError;', '\t}']}
description: A vulnerability was found in libX11. The security flaw occurs because the functions in src/InitExt.c in libX11 do not check that the values provided for the Request, Event, or Error IDs are within the bounds of the arrays that those functions write to, using those IDs as array indexes. They trust that they were called with values provided by an Xserver adhering to the bounds specified in the X11 protocol, as all X servers provided by X.Org do. As the protocol only specifies a single byte for these values, an out-of-bounds value provided by a malicious server (or a malicious proxy-in-the-middle) can only overwrite other portions of the Display structure and not write outside the bounds of the Display structure itself, possibly causing the client to crash with this memory corruption.

code_evidence: error_number is used directly as an index into dpy->error_vec at lines 16 and 17; the function performs no range check on error_number before these accesses.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing proc through dpy->error_vec[error_number] with an unvalidated index is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The missing bounds check is the root cause; the memory corruption is the consequence. This is an index-validation failure, distinct from an integer-overflow weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
oldproc = dpy->error_vec[error_number];
dpy->error_vec[error_number] = proc;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: error_number, an int supplied by the caller (from server-provided extension data), is used as an unchecked array index into the 256-element error_vec. A negative or oversized value causes the read at line 16 and the write at line 17 to fall outside the allocated buffer, corrupting adjacent Display memory; the supported consequence is memory corruption (and possible crash), not code execution outside the struct.

commit_msg:
The current CIPSO and CALIPSO refcounting scheme for the DOI
definitions is a bit flawed in that we:

1. Don't correctly match gets/puts in netlbl_cipsov4_list().
2. Decrement the refcount on each attempt to remove the DOI from the
   DOI list, only removing it from the list once the refcount drops
   to zero.

This patch fixes these problems by adding the missing "puts" to
netlbl_cipsov4_list() and introduces a more conventional, i.e.
not-buggy, refcounting mechanism to the DOI definitions.  Upon the
addition of a DOI to the DOI list, it is initialized with a refcount
of one, removing a DOI from the list removes it from the list and
drops the refcount by one; "gets" and "puts" behave as expected with
respect to refcounts, increasing and decreasing the DOI's refcount by
one.

Fixes: b1edeb102397 ("netlabel: Replace protocol/NetLabel linking with refrerence counts")
Fixes: d7cce01504a0 ("netlabel: Add support for removing a CALIPSO DOI.")
Reported-by: syzbot+9ec037722d2603a9f52e@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Paul Moore <paul@paul-moore.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!refcount_dec_and_test(&doi_def->refcount)) {', '\t\tspin_unlock(&calipso_doi_list_lock);', '\t\tret_val = -EBUSY;', '\t\tgoto doi_remove_return;', '\t}', '\tcall_rcu(&doi_def->rcu, calipso_doi_free_rcu);'], 'added_lines': ['\tcalipso_doi_putdef(doi_def);']}
description: The Linux kernel before 5.11.14 has a use-after-free in cipso_v4_genopt in net/ipv4/cipso_ipv4.c because the CIPSO and CALIPSO refcounting for the DOI definitions is mishandled, aka CID-ad5d07f4a9cd. This leads to writing an arbitrary value.

code_evidence: On the removal path, the function calls refcount_dec_and_test on doi_def->refcount; if the count does not reach zero it unlocks and returns -EBUSY without deleting the entry, so the DOI stays listed while its count is decremented on every failed removal attempt.

When the count does reach zero, list_del_rcu removes the DOI and call_rcu schedules calipso_doi_free_rcu, freeing the object after the grace period; but the premature decrements mean the object can be freed while other holders still reference it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the flawed refcount lets the DOI be freed via call_rcu while other code still holds a pointer to it, and subsequent access to that freed object is a use-after-free. The defect is in the refcount lifecycle, not merely a leak (CWE-401) or double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: removal decrements the DOI refcount unconditionally but only frees/unlists on the zero transition, so repeated remove attempts drive the count to zero while references remain. Trigger: concurrent or repeated DOI removal plus a holder (e.g., list/option generation) still using the DOI. Consequence: the object is freed by calipso_doi_free_rcu while the stale pointer is later dereferenced, yielding a use-after-free that can corrupt memory.

commit_msg: More reasonable fix https://github.com/unicorn-engine/unicorn/issues/1588
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    QLIST_SAFE_REMOVE(block, next);'], 'added_lines': ['    QLIST_REMOVE(block, next);']}
description: Unicorn Engine v2.0.0-rc7 and below was discovered to contain a NULL pointer dereference via qemu_ram_free.

code_evidence: The function only guards the incoming block parameter, returning early when block is NULL, so the pointer used in the list removal is assumed non-NULL.

QLIST_SAFE_REMOVE(block, next) is invoked on block; the macro reads block->next (and related fields) while performing the removal, and the patch replaces it with QLIST_REMOVE, indicating the prior macro's NULL-safety semantics were the source of the dereference.
