description: The mm_init function in kernel/fork.c in the Linux kernel before 4.12.10 does not clear the ->exe_file member of a new process's mm_struct, allowing a local attacker to achieve a use-after-free or possibly have unspecified other impact by running a specially crafted program.

code_evidence: mm_init initializes many mm_struct fields (mmap, mm_rb, vmacache_seqnum, etc.) but never initializes mm->exe_file to NULL.

The error paths fail_nocontext/fail_nopgd call free_mm(mm) and return NULL; because mm->exe_file was left uninitialized by mm_init, a stale ->exe_file reference from a prior memcpy in dup_mm() can be dropped by the caller's cleanup.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing initialization causes a reference to memory (struct file) to be used/dropped after it has been freed, matching CWE-416 use-after-free. The premature free is the root cause; later dereference of the freed file is the use.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mm_init fails to reset mm->exe_file, so a new mm_struct inherits/carries a stale file pointer. Trigger: fork error path (killable dup_mmap) reaches fail_nopgd/fail_nocontext and free_mm/cleanup drops a reference never taken; the struct file is freed prematurely. Consequence: use-after-free of the file (and associated vm_file), leading to NULL deref or arbitrary memory access.

commit_msg:
socket: close race condition between sock_close() and sockfs_setattr()

fchownat() doesn't even hold refcnt of fd until it figures out
fd is really needed (otherwise is ignored) and releases it after
it resolves the path. This means sock_close() could race with
sockfs_setattr(), which leads to a NULL pointer dereference
since typically we set sock->sk to NULL in ->release().

As pointed out by Al, this is unique to sockfs. So we can fix this
in socket layer by acquiring inode_lock in sock_close() and
checking against NULL in sockfs_setattr().

sock_release() is called in many places, only the sock_close()
path matters here. And fortunately, this should not affect normal
sock_close() as it is only called when the last fd refcnt is gone.
It only affects sock_close() with a parallel sockfs_setattr() in
progress, which is not common.

Fixes: 86741ec25462 ("net: core: Add a UID field to struct sock.")
Reported-by: shankarapailoor <shankarapailoor@gmail.com>
Cc: Tetsuo Handa <penguin-kernel@i-love.sakura.ne.jp>
Cc: Lorenzo Colitti <lorenzo@google.com>
Cc: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Signed-off-by: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (sock->ops) {', '\t\tstruct module *owner = sock->ops->owner;', '', '\t\tsock->ops->release(sock);', '\t\tsock->ops = NULL;', '\t\tmodule_put(owner);', '\t}', '', '\tif (rcu_dereference_protected(sock->wq, 1)->fasync_list)', '\t\tpr_err("%s: fasync list not empty!\\n", __func__);', '', '\tif (!sock->file) {', '\t\tiput(SOCK_INODE(sock));', '\t\treturn;', '\t}', '\tsock->file = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['\t__sock_release(sock, NULL);']}
description: In net/socket.c in the Linux kernel through 4.17.1, there is a race condition between fchownat and close in cases where they target the same socket file descriptor, related to the sock_close and sockfs_setattr functions. fchownat does not increment the file descriptor reference count, which allows close to set the socket to NULL during fchownat's execution, leading to a NULL pointer dereference and system crash.

code_evidence: sock_release() invokes sock->ops->release(sock) and then clears sock->ops without any synchronization, so a concurrent path operating on the same socket can observe or act on a partially torn-down socket.

After release, the function tests sock->file and either iput()s the inode or sets sock->file = NULL; these state changes to the shared socket structure are not serialized against other callers such as sockfs_setattr().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because two concurrent code sequences access the same shared socket resource without exclusivity, producing a timing window. The NULL dereference is the consequence of the race, not a separate memory-safety weakness in this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sock_release() mutates shared socket fields (ops, file) with no locking providing exclusive access. Trigger: a concurrent operation on the same socket (e.g., fchownat via sockfs_setattr) interleaves with close, which does not hold an fd reference. Consequence: the concurrent path sees NULLed state and dereferences it, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fixed a buffer overrun problem in the QMFB code in the JPC codec
that was caused by a buffer being allocated with a size that was too small
in some cases.
Added a new regression test case.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint hstartcol;', '\t\tif (!(buf = jas_alloc2(bufsize, sizeof(jpc_fix_t)))) {', '\t\thstartcol = (numrows + 1 - parity) >> 1;', '\t\t// ORIGINAL (WRONG): m = (parity) ? hstartcol : (numrows - hstartcol);', '\t\tm = numrows - hstartcol;', '\t\tdstptr = &a[hstartcol * stride];'], 'added_lines': ['\tint hstartrow;', '\t\tif (!(buf = jas_alloc3(bufsize, JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE,', '\t\t  sizeof(jpc_fix_t)))) {', '\t\thstartrow = (numrows + 1 - parity) >> 1;', '\t\t// ORIGINAL (WRONG): m = (parity) ? hstartrow : (numrows - hstartrow);', '\t\tm = numrows - hstartrow;', '\t\tdstptr = &a[hstartrow * stride];']}
description: A heap-buffer overflow vulnerability was found in QMFB code in JPC codec caused by buffer being allocated with too small size. jasper versions before 2.0.0 are affected.

code_evidence: The stack buffer splitbuf is sized QMFB_SPLITBUFSIZE * JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE elements; when bufsize exceeds QMFB_SPLITBUFSIZE, the heap buffer is allocated with only bufsize elements (jas_alloc2(bufsize, sizeof(jpc_fix_t))), omitting the JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE factor.
The save loop writes m * JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE elements into buf (dstptr advances by JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE each iteration), and the restore loop reads the same count from buf into a[hstartcol*stride].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The undersized allocation leads to out-of-bounds reads and writes on a heap buffer, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within memory buffer bounds; the allocation-size mismatch is the cause, the out-of-bounds access the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dynamic buffer is allocated with bufsize elements instead of bufsize * JPC_QMFB_COLGRPSIZE, while the copy loops store that many elements per row index. Trigger: numrows large enough that bufsize > QMFB_SPLITBUFSIZE, causing heap writes/reads past the allocation in the save and restore loops; consequence is heap corruption/overflow.

commit_msg:
This works just like close(2), unsurprisingly. We remove the file
descriptor and post the completion inline, then offload the actual
(potential) last file put to async context.

Mark the async part of this work as uncancellable, as we really must
guarantee that the latter part of the close is run.

Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (!req->ring_file)', '\t\treturn -EBADF;']}
description: A time-of-check to time-of-use issue exists in io_uring subsystem's IORING_OP_CLOSE operation in the Linux kernel's versions 5.6 - 5.11 (inclusive), which allows a local user to elevate their privileges to root. Introduced in b5dba59e0cf7e2cc4d3b3b1ac5fe81ddf21959eb, patched in 9eac1904d3364254d622bf2c771c4f85cd435fc2, backported to stable in 788d0824269bef539fe31a785b1517882eafed93.

code_evidence: The function enters an RCU read-side section and takes ctx->inflight_lock, then calls fcheck(req->ring_fd) and compares the returned file against req->ring_file inside the lock. On a match it records req->work.files = current->files and returns success. The check at line 7 validates the file descriptor-to-file mapping, but the lock protects only the inflight list, not the fd table entry, so the fd can be closed/reused by another thread after fcheck returns. The stored file pointer is then used by later close work without revalidation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-367 fits: the function checks the ring_fd-to-ring_file mapping and later uses the captured file state, with a window in which the resource state (fd table) can change. The patch adds a req->ring_file null guard, but the core issue is the check/use gap; a simple null check alone does not serialize the fd table, confirming the TOCTOU nature.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The fd table state is checked via fcheck while holding inflight_lock, but that lock does not serialize against fd close/reuse. A local user can race close() on ring_fd so the descriptor is reassigned between the check and the subsequent use of req->ring_file/req->work.files, causing the close operation to act on a file it did not validate, enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg: security: add a NULL pointer check to fix a server crash.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsecurity_decrypt(s->p, length, rdp);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!security_decrypt(s->p, length, rdp))', '\t\treturn FALSE;']}
description: FreeRDP before 1.1.0-beta1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via unspecified vectors.

code_evidence: security_decrypt(s->p, length, rdp) is called without checking its return value, so a decryption failure is ignored and execution continues to the MAC verification and return TRUE.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a missing validity check on a pointer-expecting operation leading to a NULL dereference and crash, matching CWE-476. It is not merely improper signature validation; the supported consequence is availability loss from dereferencing NULL.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The unchecked return of security_decrypt means a failed decryption (e.g., an invalid or NULL internal pointer) is not propagated; the function proceeds to security_mac_signature/memcmp and returns TRUE. The patch adds a NULL/failure check, indicating the missing constraint caused a NULL pointer dereference and remote server crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix tf.raw_ops.SaveSlices vulnerability with unsupported dtypes.

Check that given dtype is supported and emit a descriptive error if not.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 461660795
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  switch (dt) {', '    case DT_FLOAT:', '      return 4;', '    case DT_DOUBLE:', '      return 8;', '    case DT_INT32:', '      return 10;', '    case DT_UINT8:', '      return 2;', '    case DT_INT16:', '      return 10;', '    case DT_INT8:', '      return 10;', '    case DT_COMPLEX64:', '      return 8;', '    case DT_INT64:', '      return 10;', '    case DT_BOOL:', '      return 1;', '    case DT_QINT8:', '      return 10;', '    case DT_QUINT8:', '      return 2;', '    case DT_QINT32:', '      return 10;', '    case DT_QINT16:', '      return 10;', '    case DT_QUINT16:', '      return 3;', '    case DT_UINT16:', '      return 3;', '    case DT_COMPLEX128:', '      return 16;', '    case DT_HALF:', '      return 3;', '    case DT_INVALID:', '    case DT_STRING:', '    case DT_BFLOAT16:', '    default:', '      LOG(FATAL) << "MaxBytesPerElement not implemented for dtype: " << dt;', '  return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['  size_t max_bytes_per_element =', '      TensorSliceWriter::MaxBytesPerElementOrZero(dt);', '  if (max_bytes_per_element == 0) {', '    LOG(FATAL) << "MaxBytesPerElement not implemented for dtype: " << dt;', '  return max_bytes_per_element;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. If `Save` or `SaveSlices` is run over tensors of an unsupported `dtype`, it results in a `CHECK` fail that can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 5dd7b86b84a864b834c6fa3d7f9f51c87efa99d4. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: MaxBytesPerElement switches on the caller-supplied DataType dt. The default branch (line 40) covers unsupported dtypes including DT_INVALID, DT_STRING and DT_BFLOAT16, and executes LOG(FATAL) at line 41 before falling through to return 0 at line 43.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: LOG(FATAL) in the default branch is a reachable assertion-like abort that an attacker controls via the dtype argument, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion) with availability impact. It is not a memory-safety issue; the weakness is the fatal abort on attacker-reachable input, not a buffer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unsupported dtype reaches the default arm and triggers LOG(FATAL), an unconditional process-abort assertion rather than a recoverable error. The trigger is any Save/SaveSlices call passing an unsupported dtype; the supported consequence is a crash that can be used for denial of service.

commit_msg:
Kernel: User pointer validation should reject kernel-only addresses

We were happily allowing syscalls with pointers into kernel-only
regions (virtual address >= 0xc0000000).

This patch fixes that by only considering user regions in the current
process, and also double-checking the Region::is_user_accessible() flag
before approving an access.

Thanks to Fire30 for finding the bug! :^)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    auto* region = region_from_vaddr(process, vaddr);', '    return region && region->is_writable();'], 'added_lines': ['    auto* region = user_region_from_vaddr(const_cast<Process&>(process), vaddr);', '    return region && region->is_user_accessible() && region->is_writable();']}
description: Kernel/VM/MemoryManager.cpp in SerenityOS before 2019-12-30 does not reject syscalls with pointers into the kernel-only virtual address space, which allows local users to gain privileges by overwriting a return address that was found on the kernel stack.

code_evidence: validate_user_write resolves vaddr with region_from_vaddr and approves the write whenever the returned region is writable; it does not check is_user_accessible() and does not restrict resolution to user regions, so a vaddr in kernel-only space can yield a writable kernel region and pass validation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to constrain a memory access to the intended user buffer, so the write can land outside that buffer in kernel memory, matching CWE-119. It is not merely a missing privilege flag: the absent user-region restriction is what permits the out-of-bounds write.

evidence_lines.code:
auto* region = region_from_vaddr(process, vaddr);
return region && region->is_writable();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds/ownership check on the caller-supplied vaddr is incomplete, accepting any writable region rather than only user-accessible ones. Trigger: a local user passes a syscall pointer at or above 0xc0000000. Supported consequence: the kernel writes through that pointer into kernel memory, enabling corruption such as overwriting a return address on the kernel stack.

commit_msg:
fix a bunch of vsprintf -> vsnprintf

closes #1203
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t'], 'added_lines': ['']}
description: GPAC 0.7.1 has a buffer overflow issue in gf_import_message() in media_import.c.

code_evidence: Line 8 parses an arbitrary-length decimal string from the caller-controlled name into unsigned ID via sscanf. Line 9 declares a fixed 20-byte stack buffer szURL, and line 10 writes the formatted ID into it with unbounded sprintf; no width limit or size check constrains the output. The comparison at line 11 runs only after the write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a write past the end of an intended buffer, exactly CWE-787. The cause is the missing length constraint in sprintf, not merely reading out of bounds (CWE-125) or an integer overflow; the overflow is of the destination buffer itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sprintf into a fixed 20-byte stack buffer with an attacker-supplied numeric value. Trigger: a name matching the %u parse whose decimal form exceeds 19 digits, causing the write to run past szURL. Supported consequence: stack memory corruption, potentially crashing the parser or enabling control-flow hijack.

commit_msg:
Fix NULL pointer deref in outputSWF_TEXT_RECORD

fip and fip_current are static pointers to a linked list containing
fonts information. This list and the two pointers are initialized and
filled by saveFontInfo() (called by the outputSWF_DEFINEFONTxxxx()
functions when defining new fonts).

In the case where no font is defined, saveFontInfo() is never called
and the two list pointers are NULL.

This situation may trigger a NULL pointer dereference in
outputSWF_TEXT_RECORD. In this patch, we check for !fip_current
before dereferencing it. In the == NULL case, we print a warning and
continue.

This commit addresses CVE-2017-16883 (fixes #77).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['   id = fi->fontcodeID;\t\t\t\t\t/* trigger next if */'], 'added_lines': ['', '   if (!fi)', '      SWF_warn("outputSWF_TEXT_RECORD: can\'t process text record: fonts information list is NULL\\n");', '   else', '      id = fi->fontcodeID;\t\t\t\t\t/* trigger next if */']}
description: The outputSWF_TEXT_RECORD function in util/outputscript.c in libming <= 0.4.8 is vulnerable to a NULL pointer dereference, which may allow attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted swf file.

code_evidence: When StyleFlagHasFont is not set, fi is assigned fip_current and then dereferenced via fi->fontcodeID without any NULL check; fip_current is a static list pointer that remains NULL when no font was defined.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads a field through a pointer expected to be valid but which can be NULL, matching CWE-476's definition. The added guard in the patch confirms this exact dereference was the flaw; it is not a use-after-free or out-of-bounds issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the else-branch at line 32 unconditionally replaces fi with the potentially NULL fip_current and immediately reads fi->fontcodeID. Trigger: a crafted SWF text record lacking the has-font style flag in a file where no font was defined, so saveFontInfo never populated the list. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference, crashing the converter (denial of service).

commit_msg:
can: mcba_usb: mcba_usb_start_xmit(): fix double dev_kfree_skb in error path

There is no need to call dev_kfree_skb() when usb_submit_urb() fails
because can_put_echo_skb() deletes original skb and
can_free_echo_skb() deletes the cloned skb.

Fixes: 51f3baad7de9 ("can: mcba_usb: Add support for Microchip CAN BUS Analyzer")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/all/20220311080208.45047-1-hbh25y@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Hangyu Hua <hbh25y@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tdev_kfree_skb(skb);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: mcba_usb_start_xmit in drivers/net/can/usb/mcba_usb.c in the Linux kernel through 5.17.1 has a double free.

code_evidence: Line 33 hands skb ownership to the CAN echo buffer via can_put_echo_skb(); on mcba_usb_xmit() failure at line 34 the code jumps to xmit_failed.

At xmit_failed, can_free_echo_skb() (line 39) releases the cloned echo skb, mcba_usb_free_ctx() frees ctx, and line 41 then calls dev_kfree_skb(skb) on the same skb already owned/released through the echo path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the same skb memory is released through two paths (can_free_echo_skb and dev_kfree_skb). This is distinct from a simple leak: the second free is the core defect, matching double free rather than missing release.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path frees skb directly after ownership was transferred to the echo-skb mechanism, which also frees it. Trigger: usb_submit_urb/mcba_usb_xmit returns an error, causing the xmit_failed path to execute. Consequence: the skb is freed twice, corrupting the allocator and enabling use-after-free or arbitrary memory modification.

commit_msg:
The "ev->traffic_class" and "reply->ac" variables come from the network
and they're used as an offset into the wmi->stream_exist_for_ac[] array.
Those variables are u8 so they can be 0-255 but the stream_exist_for_ac[]
array only has WMM_NUM_AC (4) elements.  We need to add a couple bounds
checks to prevent array overflows.

I also modified one existing check from "if (traffic_class > 3) {" to
"if (traffic_class >= WMM_NUM_AC) {" just to make them all consistent.

Fixes: bdcd81707973 (" Add ath6kl cleaned up driver")
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (ev->traffic_class >= WMM_NUM_AC) {', '\t\tath6kl_err("invalid traffic class: %d\\n", ev->traffic_class);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.3. Out of bounds access exists in the functions ath6kl_wmi_pstream_timeout_event_rx and ath6kl_wmi_cac_event_rx in the file drivers/net/wireless/ath/ath6kl/wmi.c.

code_evidence: datap is cast to struct wmi_pstream_timeout_event and ev->traffic_class is read without any upper-bound validation.
ev->traffic_class is then used directly as an index into wmi->stream_exist_for_ac[] (line 9) and as a shift count (line 10); the only prior check (lines 5-6) validates len, not the field value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unchecked index ev->traffic_class is used to read wmi->stream_exist_for_ac[], accessing memory past the array's end. This is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write, since line 9 reads the array element for the &= operation.

evidence_lines.code:
if (len < sizeof(struct wmi_pstream_timeout_event))
return -EINVAL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The network-supplied ev->traffic_class is a u8 (0-255) but stream_exist_for_ac[] has only WMM_NUM_AC (4) elements. With no bounds check, an attacker-controlled packet with traffic_class >= 4 causes an out-of-bounds read of the array at line 9 (and out-of-range shift at line 10). The root cause is the missing upper-bound constraint; the consequence is an out-of-bounds memory read.

commit_msg:
e1000: fail early for evil descriptor

During procss_tx_desc(), driver can try to chain data descriptor with
legacy descriptor, when will lead underflow for the following
calculation in process_tx_desc() for bytes:

            if (tp->size + bytes > msh)
                bytes = msh - tp->size;

This will lead a infinite loop. So check and fail early if tp->size if
greater or equal to msh.

Reported-by: Alexander Bulekov <alxndr@bu.edu>
Reported-by: Cheolwoo Myung <cwmyung@snu.ac.kr>
Reported-by: Ruhr-University Bochum <bugs-syssec@rub.de>
Cc: Prasad J Pandit <ppandit@redhat.com>
Cc: qemu-stable@nongnu.org
Signed-off-by: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            if (tp->size >= msh) {', '                goto eop;', '            }', 'eop:']}
description: An infinite loop flaw was found in the e1000 NIC emulator of the QEMU. This issue occurs while processing transmits (tx) descriptors in process_tx_desc if various descriptor fields are initialized with invalid values. This flaw allows a guest to consume CPU cycles on the host, resulting in a denial of service. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

code_evidence: The do-while loop at lines 43-62 sets bytes = split_size (line 44), then line 45 clamps bytes to msh - tp->size when tp->size + bytes exceeds msh. If tp->size is already >= msh, msh - tp->size underflows as unsigned, so bytes stays large; after MIN at line 47, bytes may be nonzero and split_size is decremented at line 61, but the loop condition (bytes && split_size) can remain true indefinitely when sz never equals msh.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a loop whose termination depends on tp->size reaching msh, a condition that can become unreachable when tp->size >= msh; this is an unreachable exit condition producing an infinite loop (CWE-835). The added early check confirms the loop's exit was the flaw, not merely an out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop assumes tp->size < msh but never enforces it before computing msh - tp->size. A guest-controlled descriptor sequence can drive tp->size to or past msh (e.g., via header length/mss or chained descriptors), making the clamp ineffective and preventing the sz == msh exit path. Consequence: the host emulator spins in the do-while loop, consuming CPU and denying service.

commit_msg:
arm/mm: release grant lock on xenmem_add_to_physmap_one() error paths

Commit 55021ff9ab ("xen/arm: add_to_physmap_one: Avoid to map mfn 0 if
an error occurs") introduced error paths not releasing the grant table
lock. Replace them by a suitable check after the lock was dropped.

This is XSA-235.

Reported-by: Wei Liu <wei.liu2@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            else', '                return -EINVAL;', '            else', '                return -EINVAL;', '        d->arch.grant_table_gfn[idx] = gfn;', '        t = p2m_ram_rw;'], 'added_lines': ['        if ( !mfn_eq(mfn, INVALID_MFN) )', '        {', '            d->arch.grant_table_gfn[idx] = gfn;', '            t = p2m_ram_rw;', '        }', '', '        if ( mfn_eq(mfn, INVALID_MFN) )', '            return -EINVAL;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.4.x through 4.9.x allowing ARM guest OS users to cause a denial of service (prevent physical CPU usage) because of lock mishandling upon detection of an add-to-physmap error.

code_evidence: grant_write_lock(d->grant_table) is acquired, then the status-frame branch returns -EINVAL without releasing the lock.
The shared-frame branch similarly returns -EINVAL after the lock is held when idx exceeds nr_grant_frames.
Only the success path reaches grant_write_unlock(d->grant_table).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is failure to release a limited shared resource (the grant table lock) on error paths, matching CWE-400's 'not closing/returning a resource after processing' and error-condition scenarios. The consequence is CPU/resource exhaustion, not memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function acquires the grant table write lock, but error paths for out-of-range idx return before grant_write_unlock. A guest repeatedly issuing add-to-physmap with an invalid index leaves the lock held, blocking other CPUs from grant-table operations and consuming the physical CPU, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
dnn_backend_native: Add overflow check for length calculation.

We should not silently allocate an incorrect sized buffer.
Fixes trac issue #8718.

Signed-off-by: Reimar Döffinger <Reimar.Doeffinger@gmx.de>
Reviewed-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
Reviewed-by: Guo, Yejun <yejun.guo@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (output->length <= 0)', '        return DNN_ERROR;']}
description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability in FFMpeg 4.2.3 in dnn_execute_layer_pad in libavfilter/dnn/dnn_backend_native_layer_pad.c due to a call to memcpy without length checks, which could let a remote malicious user execute arbitrary code.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function dnn_execute_layer_math_binary contains no memcpy or other buffer copy; it performs element-wise arithmetic on float buffers, so it does not support the target CWE-120 buffer-copy weakness.

If the TCA_QFQ_LMAX value is not offered through nlattr, lmax is determined by the MTU value of the network device.
The MTU of the loopback device can be set up to 2^31-1.
As a result, it is possible to have an lmax value that exceeds QFQ_MIN_LMAX.

Signed-off-by: Gwangun Jung <exsociety@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Jamal Hadi Salim<jhs@mojatatu.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (tb[TCA_QFQ_LMAX]) {', '\t\tif (lmax < QFQ_MIN_LMAX || lmax > (1UL << QFQ_MTU_SHIFT)) {', '\t\t\tpr_notice("qfq: invalid max length %u\\n", lmax);', '\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t\t}', '\t} else'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (tb[TCA_QFQ_LMAX])', '\telse', '', '\tif (lmax < QFQ_MIN_LMAX || lmax > (1UL << QFQ_MTU_SHIFT)) {', '\t\tpr_notice("qfq: invalid max length %u\\n", lmax);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}']}
description: qfq_change_class in net/sched/sch_qfq.c in the Linux kernel before 6.2.13 allows an out-of-bounds write because lmax can exceed QFQ_MIN_LMAX.

code_evidence: When tb[TCA_QFQ_LMAX] is absent, lmax is taken from psched_mtu(qdisc_dev(sch)) without any bounds check; the range check (lmax < QFQ_MIN_LMAX || lmax > (1UL << QFQ_MTU_SHIFT)) only runs inside the tb[TCA_QFQ_LMAX] branch. A loopback MTU up to 2^31-1 can therefore set lmax beyond the valid range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked lmax leads to an index beyond QFQ_MAX_INDEX and a write past the allocated aggregate structure, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). Unlike CWE-125, the reported primary consequence includes an out-of-bounds write, not just a read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the lmax validation is nested only under the netlink attribute branch, so the MTU-derived fallback value is never constrained. Trigger: configuring qfq on a device with an oversized MTU. The unchecked lmax flows into qfq_find_agg/qfq_init_agg and later index computation, producing a slab-out-of-bounds write (and read) in qfq_activate_agg.

commit_msg:
httplive: fix use-after-free

Implement a mutex to ensure secure multi-threaded
access to the KeyedVector in MetaDataBase.
Concurrent access by different threads can lead
to accessing the wrong memory location due to
potential changes in the vector

Bug: 298057702
Test: HTTP Live Streaming test
(cherry picked from https://partner-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:a2dfb31957a9d5358d0219a0eda7dcb5b0fff5fe)
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:90fb4ca425444429ada6ce0de1c13d35829bc196)
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:3c1d9613ef64e01d2e81c4aa44c90dcd8ca958b9)
Merged-In: I46b05c85d9c39f4ce549efc160c08a0646c9fd0a
Change-Id: I46b05c85d9c39f4ce549efc160c08a0646c9fd0a
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> guard(mInternalData->mLock);']}
description: In multiple functions of MetaDataBase.cpp, there is a possible UAF write due to a race condition. This could lead to remote escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: remove() calls indexOfKey(key) to obtain index i, checks i < 0, then calls removeItemsAt(i) on the shared mInternalData->mItems vector without any lock. The lookup and removal are separate, non-atomic operations on a container shared across threads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits: a shared resource (mItems) is accessed by a code sequence lacking exclusivity/atomicity, allowing an interfering concurrent sequence to modify it mid-operation. This is a synchronization race, not merely a generic memory error; the added mutex in the patch confirms the missing-lock cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the check-then-act sequence on mItems is unsynchronized, so another thread mutating the vector between indexOfKey and removeItemsAt can invalidate the stored index. Trigger: concurrent access to MetaDataBase; consequence: removal at a stale index, i.e., a use-after-free write via the vector's memory.

commit_msg:
x86: don't store possibly stale TLB flush time stamp

While the timing window is extremely narrow, it is theoretically
possible for an update to the TLB flush clock and a subsequent flush
IPI to happen between the read and write parts of the update of the
per-page stamp. Exclude this possibility by disabling interrupts
across the update, preventing the IPI to be serviced in the middle.

This is XSA-241.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                 * page_set_tlbflush_timestamp() accesses the same union', '            page_set_tlbflush_timestamp(page);'], 'added_lines': ['                 * set_tlbflush_timestamp() accesses the same union', '            set_tlbflush_timestamp(page);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to execute arbitrary code on the host OS because of a race condition that can cause a stale TLB entry.

code_evidence: The loop updates page->u.inuse.type_info via cmpxchg at line 35, but the per-page TLB-flush timestamp is set at line 33 by page_set_tlbflush_timestamp(page) before that compare-and-swap. No interrupt disabling or other exclusion surrounds the timestamp update, so a TLB-flush IPI can be serviced between the timestamp read and write, storing a stale value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits: the timestamp is a shared resource accessed by a non-atomic read-modify-write sequence, and an interfering code sequence (the flush IPI) can modify it in the timing window, violating exclusivity. This is a race on shared state, not simply a logic or bounds error.

evidence_lines.code:
page_set_tlbflush_timestamp(page);
}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the TLB-flush timestamp update is not atomic with respect to concurrent flush IPIs because interrupts remain enabled during the read-modify-write. Trigger: an IPI serviced between the read and write parts of the timestamp update. Consequence: a stale TLB entry can persist, which Xen's advisory ties to potential privilege escalation on the host.

commit_msg:
Ensure that EXFLAG_INVALID_POLICY is checked even in leaf certs

Even though we check the leaf cert to confirm it is valid, we
later ignored the invalid flag and did not notice that the leaf
cert was bad.

Fixes: CVE-2023-0465
Reviewed-by: Hugo Landau <hlandau@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20588)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        int i;', '        for (i = 1; i < sk_X509_num(ctx->chain); i++) {'], 'added_lines': ['        int i, cbcalled = 0;', '        for (i = 0; i < sk_X509_num(ctx->chain); i++) {', '            cbcalled = 1;', '        if (!cbcalled) {', '            /* Should not be able to get here */', '            X509err(X509_F_CHECK_POLICY, ERR_R_INTERNAL_ERROR);', '            return 0;', '        }', '        /* The callback ignored the error so we return success */']}
description:
Applications that use a non-default option when verifying certificates may be
vulnerable to an attack from a malicious CA to circumvent certain checks.

Invalid certificate policies in leaf certificates are silently ignored by
OpenSSL and other certificate policy checks are skipped for that certificate.
A malicious CA could use this to deliberately assert invalid certificate policies
in order to circumvent policy checking on the certificate altogether.

Policy processing is disabled by default but can be enabled by passing
the `-policy' argument to the command line utilities or by calling the
`X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_policies()' function.

code_evidence: When X509_policy_check returns X509_PCY_TREE_INVALID, the loop starts at index 1 (line 22), skipping the leaf certificate at chain index 0. If the leaf carries EXFLAG_INVALID_POLICY, it is never matched, verify_cb_cert is never invoked for it, and the function returns 1 (line 30), silently accepting the invalid policy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the certificate policy verification step and returns success despite an invalid leaf certificate, i.e., incorrect certificate validation (CWE-295). It is not merely a policy-compliance gap; the validation routine itself fails to reject a bad certificate.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the invalid-policy notification loop excludes the leaf cert and returns success without confirming any flagged certificate was handled. Trigger: a malicious CA issues a leaf cert with invalid certificate policies while policy processing is enabled. Consequence: the invalid leaf passes verification, circumventing policy checks.

commit_msg:
security fixes

https://hhvm.com/blog/2021/02/25/security-update.html
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  m_cursor += length;', '  return length;'], 'added_lines': ['  assertx(m_cursor >= 0);', '    m_cursor += length;', '    return length;', '  return 0;']}
description: xbuf_format_converter, used as part of exif_read_data, was appending a terminating null character to the generated string, but was not using its standard append char function. As a result, if the buffer was full, it would result in an out-of-bounds write. This issue affects HHVM versions prior to 4.56.3, all versions between 4.57.0 and 4.80.1, all versions between 4.81.0 and 4.93.1, and versions 4.94.0, 4.95.0, 4.96.0, 4.97.0, 4.98.0.

code_evidence: Line 4 computes remaining = m_len - m_cursor with no lower-bound check on m_cursor; line 5 clamps length to remaining only when remaining < length, so a negative remaining leaves length unchanged. Line 7 then memcpy's length bytes into buffer from m_data + m_cursor, and lines 9-10 advance the cursor and return length even when length <= 0 (e.g., remaining negative), so the copy size is not constrained to the valid buffer region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because line 7 writes length bytes into buffer without ensuring length fits the destination, an out-of-bounds write. Related CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read) does not apply since the unsafe operation is the write via memcpy.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the read length is derived from unchecked cursor/remaining arithmetic and is not validated to be positive and within the buffer before memcpy. Trigger: a caller supplies a length and cursor state where remaining is negative, bypassing the clamp; the memcpy then writes past the buffer's end. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds write causing memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
coredump: fix race condition between mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and core dumping

The core dumping code has always run without holding the mmap_sem for
writing, despite that is the only way to ensure that the entire vma
layout will not change from under it.  Only using some signal
serialization on the processes belonging to the mm is not nearly enough.
This was pointed out earlier.  For example in Hugh's post from Jul 2017:

  https://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.LSU.2.11.1707191716030.2055@eggly.anvils

  "Not strictly relevant here, but a related note: I was very surprised
   to discover, only quite recently, how handle_mm_fault() may be called
   without down_read(mmap_sem) - when core dumping. That seems a
   misguided optimization to me, which would also be nice to correct"

In particular because the growsdown and growsup can move the
vm_start/vm_end the various loops the core dump does around the vma will
not be consistent if page faults can happen concurrently.

Pretty much all users calling mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and then
taking the mmap_sem had the potential to introduce unexpected side
effects in the core dumping code.

Adding mmap_sem for writing around the ->core_dump invocation is a
viable long term fix, but it requires removing all copy user and page
faults and to replace them with get_dump_page() for all binary formats
which is not suitable as a short term fix.

For the time being this solution manually covers the places that can
confuse the core dump either by altering the vma layout or the vma flags
while it runs.  Once ->core_dump runs under mmap_sem for writing the
function mmget_still_valid() can be dropped.

Allowing mmap_sem protected sections to run in parallel with the
coredump provides some minor parallelism advantage to the swapoff code
(which seems to be safe enough by never mangling any vma field and can
keep doing swapins in parallel to the core dumping) and to some other
corner case.

In order to facilitate the backporting I added "Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6"
however the side effect of this same race condition in /proc/pid/mem
should be reproducible since before 2.6.12-rc2 so I couldn't add any
other "Fixes:" because there's no hash beyond the git genesis commit.

Because find_extend_vma() is the only location outside of the process
context that could modify the "mm" structures under mmap_sem for
reading, by adding the mmget_still_valid() check to it, all other cases
that take the mmap_sem for reading don't need the new check after
mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm().  The expand_stack() in page fault
context also doesn't need the new check, because all tasks under core
dumping are frozen.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190325224949.11068-1-aarcange@redhat.com
Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6 ("userfaultfd: add new syscall to provide memory externalization")
Signed-off-by: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Peter Xu <peterx@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Rapoport <rppt@linux.ibm.com>
Reviewed-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@mellanox.com>
Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!mmget_still_valid(mm))', '\t\tgoto out_unlock;']}
description: The coredump implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10 does not use locking or other mechanisms to prevent vma layout or vma flags changes while it runs, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information, cause a denial of service, or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a race condition with mmget_not_zero or get_task_mm calls. This is related to fs/userfaultfd.c, mm/mmap.c, fs/proc/task_mmu.c, and drivers/infiniband/core/uverbs_main.c.

code_evidence: The function bumps the mm reference with mmget_not_zero() at [39] and then acquires mmap_sem for writing at [41], but before the fix it did not verify that the mm is still valid for coredump-consistent access after taking the lock.

After down_write(&mm->mmap_sem), find_vma_prev() at [42] walks the vma list; if no vma is found, [43,44] jumps to out_unlock. The patch inserts the mmget_still_valid() check between the lock acquisition and the vma lookup.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 covers improper lock acquisition/ordering that lets concurrent access interfere with shared resource state. Here the lock is taken after a reference that can race with coredump, and the missing validity check after locking means the lock does not fully serialize against the coredump path, matching the improper locking pattern rather than a pure use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The mm reference is taken before locking, so a concurrent core dump can invalidate the mm while userfaultfd_register() proceeds to read and modify the vma layout under mmap_sem. Without the validity check after lock acquisition, the function operates on an mm that may no longer be safe to traverse, allowing inconsistent vma state and the race described (sensitive information exposure or DoS).

This fix regression introduced by "monitor: Fix memory leaks".
J-Link shared library is in use if jlink_init() returns 0 and thus
handle shall not be closed.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tdlclose(so);'], 'added_lines': ["\t/* don't dlclose(so) here cause symbols from it are in use now */"]}
description: A vulnerability has been found in Linux Kernel and classified as problematic. This vulnerability affects the function jlink_init of the file monitor/jlink.c of the component BlueZ. The manipulation leads to denial of service. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211936.

code_evidence: dlopen() loads the J-Link shared library and stores the handle in so; the loop breaks once a library is successfully opened.
dlsym() resolves function pointers from the loaded library into the static jlink structure, making the library's symbols in use.
The function returns 0 while retaining the loaded library; the handle so is never closed, leaving the shared object resident.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers failing to properly release a resource. The function deliberately omits dlclose on the success path, leaving the loaded shared object unreleased; this is improper resource shutdown, distinct from a use-after-free because the handle is simply never closed.

evidence_lines.code:
dlclose(so);
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the successful path returns without releasing the dlopen handle, so the library stays loaded and its symbols remain referenced. Trigger: any caller invoking jlink_init() that reaches the success return. Supported consequence: repeated or long-lived initialization retains the shared library resource, a resource-release defect that can contribute to resource consumption/denial of service.

commit_msg:
Bug 701818: better handling of error during PS/PDF image

In the xps device, if an error occurred after xps_begin_image() but before
xps_image_end_image(), *if* the Postscript had called 'restore' as part of the
error handling, the image enumerator would have been freed (by the restore)
despite the xps device still holding a reference to it.

Simply changing to an allocator unaffected save/restore doesn't work because
the enumerator holds references to other objects (graphics state, color space,
possibly others) whose lifespans are inherently controlled by save/restore.

So, add a finalize method for the XPS device's image enumerator
(xps_image_enum_finalize()) which takes over cleaning up the memory it allocates
and also deals with cleaning up references from the device to the enumerator
and from the enumerator to the device.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    /* If an error occurs during an image, we can get here after the enumerator', "     * has been freed - if that's the case, just bail out immediately", '     */', '    if (xps->xps_pie == NULL)', '        return;']}
description: A use-after-free vulnerability in xps_finish_image_path() in devices/vector/gdevxps.c of Artifex Software GhostScript v9.50 allows a remote attacker to escalate privileges via a crafted PDF file. This is fixed in v9.51.

code_evidence: xps_finish_image_path dereferences the device's image-enumerator pointer xps->xps_pie at lines 11-13 (file_name, icc_name, width, height) and again at line 17 (xps->xps_pie->mat) without any null/liveness check before the first write at line 8. The function is reached during error handling after xps_begin_image() but before xps_image_end_image(); if the Postscript 'restore' freed the enumerator, xps->xps_pie is a dangling pointer and these reads use freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads fields through xps->xps_pie after the pointed-to object may have been freed, matching CWE-416's reuse of a dangling pointer. The fix's NULL check confirms the enumerator can be freed before this path executes; this is a use-after-free, not merely a null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the device retains xps->xps_pie across an image operation, but save/restore error handling can free the enumerator while the device still references it. Trigger: an error during image processing followed by 'restore' invokes xps_finish_image_path, which dereferences the stale pointer to build the ImageBrush/MatrixTransform output. Supported consequence: use-after-free read of freed enumerator fields (and possible write via gs_sprintf), enabling memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix segmentation fault in tf.image.crop_and_resize when boxes is inf or nan

This fix tries to address the issue raised in 42129 where segmentation fault
happened in tf.image.crop_and_resize when boxes is inf or nan.

This fix adds the check to make sure boxes is not inf or nan (isfinite)

This fix fixes 42129.

Signed-off-by: Yong Tang <yong.tang.github@outlook.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['']}
description: In Tensorflow before version 2.4.0, when the `boxes` argument of `tf.image.crop_and_resize` has a very large value, the CPU kernel implementation receives it as a C++ `nan` floating point value. Attempting to operate on this is undefined behavior which later produces a segmentation fault. The issue is patched in eccb7ec454e6617738554a255d77f08e60ee0808 and TensorFlow 2.4.0 will be released containing the patch. TensorFlow nightly packages after this commit will also have the issue resolved.

code_evidence: Box coordinates y1,x1,y2,x2 are read directly from the boxes tensor with no isfinite check.
height_scale and width_scale are computed from these values; inf/nan propagates into the scale factors.
in_y is derived from y1 and height_scale; the guard [35] compares in_y against image_height-1, but NaN comparisons are false, so the extrapolation branch is skipped.
in_y (NaN/inf) flows into floorf/ceilf, producing undefined int conversions for top_y_index/bottom_y_index.
The same pattern applies to in_x with left_x_index/right_x_index.
These unvalidated indices are used to index image(b_in, top_y_index, left_x_index, d) and the other three corner reads, yielding out-of-bounds reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs image tensor reads at indices derived from unvalidated floating-point box values, so operations occur outside the intended buffer boundaries, matching CWE-119. The underlying cause is missing input validation and undefined float-to-int conversion rather than a specific write primitive, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds memory access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: box coordinates are not validated as finite, so inf/NaN propagate through the scale and index computations. The bounds check at [35] fails for NaN, and float-to-int conversions of inf/NaN are undefined, producing arbitrary indices. Trigger: callers pass very large or NaN box values. Consequence: image is indexed with out-of-bounds coordinates, causing invalid memory reads and a segmentation fault.

commit_msg:
Security: Cross Protocol Scripting protection.

This is an attempt at mitigating problems due to cross protocol
scripting, an attack targeting services using line oriented protocols
like Redis that can accept HTTP requests as valid protocol, by
discarding the invalid parts and accepting the payloads sent, for
example, via a POST request.

For this to be effective, when we detect POST and Host: and terminate
the connection asynchronously, the networking code was modified in order
to never process further input. It was later verified that in a
pipelined request containing a POST command, the successive commands are
not executed.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["         * this flag has been set (i.e. don't process more commands). */", '        if (c->flags & CLIENT_CLOSE_AFTER_REPLY) break;'], 'added_lines': ["         * this flag has been set (i.e. don't process more commands).", '         *', '         * The same applies for clients we want to terminate ASAP. */', '        if (c->flags & (CLIENT_CLOSE_AFTER_REPLY|CLIENT_CLOSE_ASAP)) break;']}
description: networking.c in Redis before 3.2.7 allows "Cross Protocol Scripting" because it lacks a check for POST and Host: strings, which are not valid in the Redis protocol (but commonly occur when an attack triggers an HTTP request to the Redis TCP port).

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only checks the CLIENT_CLOSE_AFTER_REPLY/CLIENT_CLOSE_ASAP flags to stop processing further pipelined commands; it contains no check for POST or Host: strings, so it does not itself implement the missing cross-protocol input validation described by the target.

commit_msg: gnrc_sixlowpan_iphc: fix NULL pointer dereference
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (IS_USED(MODULE_GNRC_SIXLOWPAN_FRAG_MINFWD)) {', '            gnrc_sixlowpan_frag_fb_t *fb = ctx;', '', '            if (fb->pkt == pkt) {', '                /* free provided fragmentation buffer */', '                fb->pkt = NULL;', '            }', '        }']}
description: RIOT-OS, an operating system for Internet of Things (IoT) devices, contains a network stack with the ability to process 6LoWPAN frames. In versions 2023.01 and prior, an attacker can send a crafted frame which is forwarded by the device. During encoding of the packet a NULL pointer dereference occurs. This crashes the device leading to denial of service. A patch is available at pull request 19678. There are no known workarounds.

code_evidence: The function receives a packet pointer pkt and immediately dereferences it (pkt->data, pkt->next) to obtain the netif header, netif, and IPv6 header without any NULL check.

After _iphc_encode succeeds, the packet tmp is forwarded either via minfwd or multiplex_by_size; on the else path pkt is released but the fragmentation buffer ctx (fb) may still reference pkt, leaving a dangling pointer that is later dereferenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch adds clearing fb->pkt to NULL when it equals pkt, directly addressing a pointer that is later dereferenced while invalid, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference and its DoS impact.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dereferences pkt and pkt->next unconditionally and does not clear the fragmentation buffer's pkt reference when the buffer's packet is released in the else branch. Trigger: a crafted forwarded 6LoWPAN frame where encoding fails causes pkt release while fb->pkt still points to freed memory. Consequence: NULL/dangling pointer dereference crashes the device (DoS).

commit_msg:
Simplify the timerqueue code by using cached rbtrees and rely on the tree
leftmost node semantics to get the timer with earliest expiration time.
This is a drop in conversion, and therefore semantics remain untouched.

The runtime overhead of cached rbtrees is be pretty much the same as the
current head->next method, noting that when removing the leftmost node,
a common operation for the timerqueue, the rb_next(leftmost) is O(1) as
well, so the next timer will either be the right node or its parent.
Therefore no extra pointer chasing. Finally, the size of the struct
timerqueue_head remains the same.

Passes several hours of rcutorture.

Signed-off-by: Davidlohr Bueso <dbueso@suse.de>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190724152323.bojciei3muvfxalm@linux-r8p5

A kernel crash occurrs when defragmented packet is fragmented
in ip_do_fragment().
In defragment routine, skb_orphan() is called and

skb->ip_defrag_offset are same union member. so that

Hence crash occurrs in skb->sk check routine in ip_do_fragment() when
defragmented packet is fragmented.

v2:
 - clear skb->sk at reassembly routine.(Eric Dumarzet)

Fixes: fa0f527358bd ("ip: use rb trees for IP frag queue.")
Suggested-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Taehee Yoo <ap420073@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tfp->sk = NULL;']}
description: A security flaw was found in the ip_frag_reasm() function in net/ipv4/ip_fragment.c in the Linux kernel from 4.19-rc1 to 4.19-rc3 inclusive, which can cause a later system crash in ip_do_fragment(). With certain non-default, but non-rare, configuration of a victim host, an attacker can trigger this crash remotely, thus leading to a remote denial-of-service.

code_evidence: When the first fragment (head) differs from skb, skb is morphed from head and the old head is consumed; the reconstructed skb's union member sk/ip_defrag_offset is not reset.

The reassembly loop splices each fragment fp into head's frag_list, copying length and checksum state, but never clears fp->sk, so a reassembled skb can retain a non-NULL sk while ip_defrag_offset is also set.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate/normalize fragment state before merging, leaving an inconsistent skb->sk value that downstream code trusts; this improper handling of derived packet metadata leads to the crash, matching CWE-20's improper validation of input properties.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reassembled skb retains stale union state (sk aliased with ip_defrag_offset) because fp->sk is not cleared during splicing. Trigger: a fragmented packet is reassembled and then passed to ip_do_fragment(), whose skb->sk check fires on the stale pointer. Supported consequence: remote denial of service via kernel BUG crash.

commit_msg: Fix potential unsigned integer underflow
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\tif ( size_left < 4 ) {', '\t\t\tLogError("Process_ipfix [%u] Template withdraw size error at %s line %u" , ', '\t\t\t\texporter->info.id, __FILE__, __LINE__, strerror (errno));', '\t\t\tsize_left = 0;', '\t\t\tcontinue;', '\t\t}', '']}
description: nfdump 1.6.17 and earlier is affected by an integer overflow in the function Process_ipfix_template_withdraw in ipfix.c that can be abused in order to crash the process remotely (denial of service).

code_evidence: The loop continues while size_left is nonzero and unconditionally subtracts 4 from size_left after mapping the record pointer, without first verifying that at least 4 bytes remain.
After advancing DataPtr by 4, the remaining size is only checked against 4 to skip padding; a size_left below 4 that is nonzero re-enters the loop and is decremented again.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsigned subtraction size_left -= 4 wraps to a very large value when size_left < 4, matching CWE-190 integer wraparound. The consequence is an out-of-bounds read and crash, but the underlying defect is the unchecked arithmetic, not a separate memory-safety weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: size_left is a uint32_t decremented by 4 each iteration without a prior lower-bound check, so a value of 1–3 underflows to a huge value (0xFFFFFFFD–0xFFFFFFFF). Trigger: an IPFIX template-withdraw flowset whose length is not a multiple of 4. The loop then iterates over out-of-bounds DataPtr, causing reads past the buffer and a remote crash (DoS).

commit_msg: fix build
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!isalnum(page[0]))', '    if (strstr(page, ".."))'], 'added_lines': ['    if (!isalnum(page_name[0]))', '    if (strstr(page_name, ".."))']}
description: Directory traversal vulnerability in wiki.c in didiwiki allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via the page parameter to api/page/get.

code_evidence: Null guard returns FALSE when page_name is NULL, but there is no check that the name is confined to a restricted directory.
The first-character check uses the undefined identifier page instead of the parameter page_name, so it does not constrain the supplied name; in the patched version this becomes isalnum(page_name[0]).
The traversal filter also references page rather than page_name, so a name containing '..' is not rejected; the patch changes it to strstr(page_name, "..").
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-22 fits because external input is used to construct a pathname under a restricted directory without neutralizing '..' elements. The intended guards exist but are bypassed due to the wrong variable; this is path traversal rather than a mere input-validation bug because the consequence is escaping the restricted directory.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!page_name)
return FALSE;

if (!isalnum(page[0]))
return FALSE;

if (strstr(page, ".."))
return FALSE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the validation logic tests the wrong variable (page) instead of the caller-supplied page_name, so the alnum and '..' constraints never apply to the input used to build a file path. Trigger: an attacker supplies a page value containing '../' sequences; the checks pass, and the resulting path can resolve outside the intended wiki directory, allowing arbitrary file reads.

commit_msg:
DBUS notifications could crash the scheduler (Issue #5143)

- scheduler/ipp.c: Make sure requesting-user-name string is valid UTF-8.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '  attr = ippFindAttribute(job->attrs, "requesting-user-name", IPP_TAG_NAME);'], 'added_lines': ['  attr = ippFindAttribute(con->request, "requesting-user-name", IPP_TAG_NAME);', '', '  if (attr && !ippValidateAttribute(attr))', '  {', '    send_ipp_status(con, IPP_ATTRIBUTES, _("Bad requesting-user-name value: %s"), cupsLastErrorString());', '    if ((attr = ippCopyAttribute(con->response, attr, 0)) != NULL)', '      attr->group_tag = IPP_TAG_UNSUPPORTED_GROUP;', '    return (NULL);', '  }', '']}
description: The add_job function in scheduler/ipp.c in CUPS before 2.2.6, when D-Bus support is enabled, can be crashed by remote attackers by sending print jobs with an invalid username, related to a D-Bus notification.

code_evidence: The requesting-user-name attribute is located in con->request via ippFindAttribute at line 58 but is not validated here; the policy check at 59 does not inspect this string's content.

After cupsdAddJob, the attribute is fetched from job->attrs at 296 and, when con->username is empty, its string is copied into job->username at 308 and later logged at 305-307 and reused in ippSetName at 318.

No ippValidateAttribute check exists on this attribute before it is stored and propagated; only job-name (lines 262-281) receives validation, so a non-UTF-8 requesting-user-name flows into job state and D-Bus notification formatting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes untrusted request data and fails to check that it meets the required well-formedness (valid UTF-8) property before processing, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The crash is the consequence of missing validation, not a separate memory-safety flaw in this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the client-supplied requesting-user-name value is accepted without validating its string encoding. Trigger: a remote client submits a print job whose requesting-user-name contains invalid UTF-8. The unvalidated string is copied into job->username and used in job attributes/logging, and the malformed value reaches D-Bus notification handling, causing the scheduler to crash.

detected by @seviezhou via fuzzing. Fixes GH #251

code_evidence: In the generic-stride branch, wp and ip are advanced by n+stride-1 to point at the last element, then the loop writes wp[0] and wp[stride] while decrementing wp/ip. The final REPEAT at line 46 writes wp[0] after the loop has already moved wp back by stride per iteration, so the pointer arithmetic can place writes outside the intended output buffer bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs writes through wp[0]/wp[stride] whose computed addresses can fall outside the allocated output buffer, matching CWE-787 (write past the end or before the beginning of the intended buffer). This is a direct out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
Jonathan Looney reported that TCP can trigger the following crash
in tcp_shifted_skb() :

	BUG_ON(tcp_skb_pcount(skb) < pcount);

This can happen if the remote peer has advertized the smallest
MSS that linux TCP accepts : 48

An skb can hold 17 fragments, and each fragment can hold 32KB
on x86, or 64KB on PowerPC.

This means that the 16bit witdh of TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->tcp_gso_segs
can overflow.

Note that tcp_sendmsg() builds skbs with less than 64KB
of payload, so this problem needs SACK to be enabled.
SACK blocks allow TCP to coalesce multiple skbs in the retransmit
queue, thus filling the 17 fragments to maximal capacity.

CVE-2019-11477 -- u16 overflow of TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->tcp_gso_segs

Fixes: 832d11c5cd07 ("tcp: Try to restore large SKBs while SACK processing")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Looney <jtl@netflix.com>
Acked-by: Neal Cardwell <ncardwell@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Tyler Hicks <tyhicks@canonical.com>
Cc: Yuchung Cheng <ycheng@google.com>
Cc: Bruce Curtis <brucec@netflix.com>
Cc: Jonathan Lemon <jonathan.lemon@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\telse if (!skb_shift(skb, next_skb, next_skb_size))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\telse if (!tcp_skb_shift(skb, next_skb, 1, next_skb_size))']}
description: Jonathan Looney discovered that the TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->tcp_gso_segs value was subject to an integer overflow in the Linux kernel when handling TCP Selective Acknowledgments (SACKs). A remote attacker could use this to cause a denial of service. This has been fixed in stable kernel releases 4.4.182, 4.9.182, 4.14.127, 4.19.52, 5.1.11, and is fixed in commit 3b4929f65b0d8249f19a50245cd88ed1a2f78cff.

code_evidence: Line 6 reads next_skb->len into the int next_skb_size. Line 7 asserts both skbs have pcount 1 before the merge. Line 12 uses skb_shift() to merge next_skb into skb, which accumulates the segment count without bounding it to the 16-bit tcp_gso_segs field. Line 23 then adjusts the pcount by tcp_skb_pcount(next_skb), further mutating the accumulated count that is later checked by tcp_shifted_skb().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an unchecked integer accumulation that overflows a 16-bit counter (CWE-190): tcp_gso_segs is incremented past its maximum through skb coalescing. This is not merely a logic flaw in merging; the wraparound of the counter is what violates the invariant and triggers the BUG_ON.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: With SACK enabled, tcp_collapse_retrans coalesces many retransmit-queue skbs, each holding up to 17 fragments of maximal size. The per-skb fragment/segment count stored in TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->tcp_gso_segs is a 16-bit field, but the merge at line 12 and the pcount adjustment at line 23 never check it against 65535. Once enough skbs are merged the count wraps, and the later BUG_ON(tcp_skb_pcount(skb) < pcount) in tcp_shifted_skb fires, causing a remote denial of service (crash).

description: When processing certain files, PHP EXIF extension in versions 7.1.x below 7.1.29, 7.2.x below 7.2.18 and 7.3.x below 7.3.5 can be caused to read past allocated buffer in exif_process_IFD_TAG function. This may lead to information disclosure or crash.

commit_msg:
On 64-bit systems, struct bcm_msg_head has an added padding of 4 bytes between
struct members count and ival1. Even though all struct members are initialized,
the 4-byte hole will contain data from the kernel stack. This patch zeroes out
struct bcm_msg_head before usage, preventing infoleaks to userspace.

Fixes: ffd980f976e7 ("[CAN]: Add broadcast manager (bcm) protocol")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/trinity-7c1b2e82-e34f-4885-8060-2cd7a13769ce-1623532166177@3c-app-gmx-bs52
Cc: linux-stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Norbert Slusarek <nslusarek@gmx.net>
Acked-by: Oliver Hartkopp <socketcan@hartkopp.net>
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tmemset(&msg_head, 0, sizeof(msg_head));']}
description: net/can/bcm.c in the Linux kernel through 5.12.10 allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel stack memory because parts of a data structure are uninitialized.

code_evidence: msg_head is declared on line 4 as an uninitialized stack struct, and lines 8-14 assign only specific members (opcode, flags, count, ival1, ival2, can_id, nframes). The struct is then passed by pointer to bcm_send_to_user on line 15, so any padding bytes or unassigned members leave stack residue that is copied to userspace.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-909 fits because a critical resource (the msg_head struct) is used without full initialization before being exposed. This is distinct from a mere buffer-overflow; the defect is missing initialization of a resource that is then read and disclosed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bcm_msg_head stack object is never zeroed, so on 64-bit builds the 4-byte hole between count and ival1 (and any unassigned members) retains prior kernel stack data. Trigger: a local user causes the RX timeout handler to fire, which sends the partially initialized struct to userspace, leaking kernel stack memory.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/577
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ThrowWriterException(ResourceLimitError,"MemoryAllocationFailed");'], 'added_lines': ['    {', '      if (scanline != (unsigned char *) NULL)', '        scanline=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(scanline);', '      if (packed_scanline != (unsigned char *) NULL)', '        packed_scanline=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(', '          packed_scanline);', '      if (buffer != (unsigned char *) NULL)', '        buffer=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(buffer);', '      ThrowWriterException(ResourceLimitError,"MemoryAllocationFailed");', '    }']}
description: ImageMagick 7.0.6-2 has a memory leak vulnerability in WritePICTImage in coders/pict.c.

code_evidence: The function independently allocates three heap buffers—buffer, packed_scanline, and scanline—using AcquireQuantumMemory at lines 108-111. These allocations are performed sequentially, and each may succeed or fail independently. At lines 112-115 the function checks whether any allocation returned NULL; if one allocation fails while the others have succeeded, it immediately invokes ThrowWriterException without releasing the successfully allocated buffers, so the allocated memory remains unreleased on this error path.

The normal exit path releases all three buffers with RelinquishMagickMemory at lines 379-381. The exception thrown on allocation failure bypasses those calls, so the missing cleanup on the error path is what causes the leak.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 (Missing Release of Resource after Effective Lifetime) applies because the function fails to release successfully allocated memory resources when a subsequent allocation fails. The allocation failure triggers an immediate exception, bypassing the normal cleanup operations at lines 379-381, which release scanline, packed_scanline, and buffer. The defect is the missing resource cleanup on the allocation failure path, resulting in a memory leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: WritePICTImage allocates three independent heap buffers but does not release successfully allocated buffers when any allocation fails. Trigger: memory allocation failure during image processing, where at least one buffer allocation succeeds and another returns NULL. Consequence: ThrowWriterException exits through the error path without freeing the previously allocated buffers, causing a memory leak. Repeated failures can accumulate unreleased memory and contribute to resource exhaustion.

sLine.TrimRight("\n\r");

QuantumInfo
*quantum_info;
quantum_info=DestroyQuantumInfo(quantum_info);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: quantum_info is allocated via AcquireQuantumInfo but the only release path is the unconditional DestroyQuantumInfo after the row loops. Trigger: an early break from the row loop (ReadBlob returning -1 or QueueAuthenticPixels returning NULL) jumps past the destroy call and continues the outer while loop, where quantum_info is overwritten by a new AcquireQuantumInfo. commit_msg:
crypto: user - fix memory leak in crypto_report

In crypto_report, a new skb is created via nlmsg_new(). This skb should
be released if crypto_report_alg() fails.

Fixes: a38f7907b926 ("crypto: Add userspace configuration API")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (err)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (err) {', '\t\tkfree_skb(skb);', '\t}']}
description: A memory leak in the crypto_report() function in crypto/crypto_user_base.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering crypto_report_alg() failures, aka CID-ffdde5932042.

code_evidence: Line 16 allocates a new skb via nlmsg_new() and stores it in skb; if allocation fails, control jumps to drop_alg with err=-ENOMEM and no skb to free.

Line 23 calls crypto_report_alg() with the allocated skb; on failure err is set non-zero and control falls into drop_alg, which releases alg at line 25 but returns err at lines 26-27 without freeing skb.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the function allocates memory (skb) that is not released on an error path, matching the missing-release-after-effective-lifetime pattern. It is not a use-after-free or double-free: the skb is simply never freed, so the weakness is unreleased memory rather than dangling access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The skb allocated at line 16 is only handed to nlmsg_unicast() on the success path at line 28. When crypto_report_alg() fails, the error branch at lines 26-27 returns err while skb remains allocated and no longer referenced, leaking one skb per failing report request. Repeated triggering of crypto_report_alg() failures consumes kernel memory, supporting a denial-of-service resource exhaustion consequence.

commit_msg:
When an error occurs while rewriting the parser tree for window functions
in the sqlite3WindowRewrite() routine, make sure that pParse->nErr is set,
and make sure that this shuts down any subsequent code generation that might
depend on the transformations that were implemented.  This fixes a problem
discovered by the Yongheng and Rui fuzzer.

description: SQLite 3.30.1 mishandles certain parser-tree rewriting, related to expr.c, vdbeaux.c, and window.c. This is caused by incorrect sqlite3WindowRewrite() error handling.

code_evidence: Line 16 allocates pTab; if allocation fails, lines 17-19 return SQLITE_NOMEM without setting pParse->nErr, so the parser's error state is not updated.
Lines 77-84 handle a failed sqlite3ResultSetOfSelect by setting rc=SQLITE_NOMEM but continue executing VDBE operations at lines 85-88 and then free pTab at 93.
Line 92 sets rc on mallocFailed, and line 95 returns rc without ensuring pParse->nErr is set, so callers may proceed despite the exceptional condition.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to propagate an exceptional allocation condition into the parser's error state, so the exceptional condition is improperly handled rather than cleanly aborted. This matches CWE-755; CWE-476 is not the label because the flaw is the missing error-state handling, not a null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: allocation failure paths in sqlite3WindowRewrite return SQLITE_NOMEM or set rc without recording the error in pParse->nErr. Trigger: a memory allocation failure during parser-tree rewriting. Consequence: code generation continues or callers treat the rewrite as successful, producing an inconsistent parser tree and subsequent faulty behavior.

The recording of d->max_evtchns in evtchn_2l_init(), in particular with
the limited set of callers of the function, is insufficient. Neither for
PV nor for HVM guests the bitness is known at domain_create() time, yet
the upper bound in 2-level mode depends upon guest bitness. Recording
too high a limit "allows" x86 32-bit domains to open not properly usable
event channels, management of which (inside Xen) would then result in
corruption of the shared info and vCPU info structures.

Keep the upper limit dynamic for the 2-level case, introducing a helper
function to retrieve the effective limit. This helper is now supposed to
be private to the event channel code. The used in do_poll() and
domain_dump_evtchn_info() weren't consistent with port uses elsewhere
and hence get switched to port_is_valid().

Furthermore FIFO mode's setup_ports() gets adjusted to loop only up to
the prior ABI limit, rather than all the way up to the new one.

Finally a word on the change to do_poll(): Accessing ->max_evtchns
without holding a suitable lock was never safe, as it as well as
->evtchn_port_ops may change behind do_poll()'s back. Using
port_is_valid() instead widens some the window for potential abuse,
until we've dealt with the race altogether (see XSA-343).

This is XSA-342.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Fixes: 48974e6ce52e ("evtchn: use a per-domain variable for the max number of event channels")
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
