description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. Out of bounds event channels are available to 32-bit x86 domains. The so called 2-level event channel model imposes different limits on the number of usable event channels for 32-bit x86 domains vs 64-bit or Arm (either bitness) ones. 32-bit x86 domains can use only 1023 channels, due to limited space in their shared (between guest and Xen) information structure, whereas all other domains can use up to 4095 in this model. The recording of the respective limit during domain initialization, however, has occurred at a time where domains are still deemed to be 64-bit ones, prior to actually honoring respective domain properties. At the point domains get recognized as 32-bit ones, the limit didn't get updated accordingly. Due to this misbehavior in Xen, 32-bit domains (including Domain 0) servicing other domains may observe event channel allocations to succeed when they should really fail. Subsequent use of such event channels would then possibly lead to corruption of other parts of the shared info structure. An unprivileged guest may cause another domain, in particular Domain 0, to misbehave. This may lead to a Denial of Service (DoS) for the entire system. All Xen versions from 4.4 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.3 and earlier are not vulnerable. Only x86 32-bit domains servicing other domains are vulnerable. Arm systems, as well as x86 64-bit domains, are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The loop copies each guest-supplied port from sched_poll->ports into local port, then validates it against d->max_evtchns before calling evtchn_port_is_pending(d, port). d->max_evtchns is a per-domain limit recorded at domain creation, before 32-bit guest bitness is honored, so for 32-bit x86 domains it is too high relative to the 1023-channel shared-info limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the accepted out-of-range port drives indexing into the shared info / vCPU info structures past their valid bounds, writing/altering memory outside the intended buffer. The defect is the missing effective-limit check (port_is_valid), not merely a logic error; the resulting memory corruption is the out-of-bounds write consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the upper-bound check uses a stale/too-high d->max_evtchns, allowing ports above the 32-bit ABI limit to pass validation. Trigger: a 32-bit domain polling a port in the range beyond 1023 but below the recorded max. Consequence: evtchn_port_is_pending and later event-channel management index shared/vCPU info structures out of bounds, corrupting memory and causing DoS.

In dissect_compressed_beamforming_and_cqi, break out of a loop if our
bit offset doesn't advance.

description: In Wireshark 3.0.0, the IEEE 802.11 dissector could go into an infinite loop. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-ieee80211.c by detecting cases in which the bit offset does not advance.

code_evidence: The while loop calls next_he_scidx and dissect_he_feedback_matrix; the loop's only progress toward termination depends on scidx advancing and on bit_offset being updated by dissect_he_feedback_matrix. If that call returns a bit_offset that does not increase (e.g., malformed length makes it return the same or smaller offset), scidx still advances via next_he_scidx, but offset = bit_offset/8 stays fixed and the loop keeps iterating without consuming input.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the iteration's exit condition depends on next_he_scidx reaching SCIDX_END_SENTINAL while progress on the bit stream is not enforced, allowing an effectively unreachable exit. This is an infinite-loop availability weakness, not merely a length/validation error, though malformed length is the trigger.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop lacks a guard ensuring bit_offset advances each iteration. Trigger: a crafted 802.11 frame causes dissect_he_feedback_matrix to return a non-increasing bit_offset. Consequence: the loop never reaches its sentinel exit and spins, consuming CPU (DoS).

commit_msg:
show_opcodes() is used both for dumping kernel instructions and for dumping
user instructions. If userspace causes #PF by jumping to a kernel address,
show_opcodes() can be reached with regs->ip controlled by the user,
pointing to kernel code. Make sure that userspace can't trick us into
dumping kernel memory into dmesg.

Fixes: 7cccf0725cf7 ("x86/dumpstack: Add a show_ip() function")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Reviewed-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
Reviewed-by: Borislav Petkov <bp@suse.de>

Cc: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Cc: security@kernel.org
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20180828154901.112726-1-jannh@google.com

description: A missing address check in the callers of the show_opcodes() in the Linux kernel allows an attacker to dump the kernel memory at an arbitrary kernel address into the dmesg log.

code_evidence: Lines 10-13 build the segfault message using regs->ip directly as the faulting instruction pointer, with no check that this value is a userspace address.
Line 15 passes (u8 *)regs->ip to show_opcodes(), so the same unvalidated pointer is used as the start of a kernel memory dump.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an externally influenced address (regs->ip) and uses it without checking the required property that it is a userspace address, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The missing address constraint, not merely the logging, is the defect; CWE-200 describes the disclosure consequence rather than the root cause.

evidence_lines.code: show_opcodes((u8 *)regs->ip, loglvl);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: regs->ip originates from user-controlled register state (e.g., a userspace jump to a kernel address causing #PF) and is consumed without validating that it lies in the user address range. Trigger: userspace faults at a kernel address; the resulting ip is then used as the dump base in show_opcodes(), leaking kernel bytes into dmesg. The consequence is kernel memory disclosure to an unprivileged actor reading the log.

code_evidence: SFS_Expression reads an expression type from the bitstream and dispatches on it; there is no depth/stack counter or bound check before recursing.
Many cases recursively call SFS_Expression (unary, binary, assignment operators), and ET_CONDTEST/operator cases call it multiple times, so each input token can drive further recursion.
The default case only sets a parse error; it does not limit recursion depth, so a crafted stream of nested expression tokens keeps the function re-entering itself.

Trigger: a crafted BIFS/script bitstream containing deeply nested or chained operator/expression tokens. Consequence: unbounded stack growth leading to stack exhaustion/crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Patch series "Fix several device private page reference counting issues",
v2

This series aims to fix a number of page reference counting issues in
drivers dealing with device private ZONE_DEVICE pages.  These result in
use-after-free type bugs, either from accessing a struct page which no
longer exists because it has been removed or accessing fields within the
struct page which are no longer valid because the page has been freed.

During normal usage it is unlikely these will cause any problems.  However
without these fixes it is possible to crash the kernel from userspace. 
These crashes can be triggered either by unloading the kernel module or
unbinding the device from the driver prior to a userspace task exiting. 
In modules such as Nouveau it is also possible to trigger some of these
issues by explicitly closing the device file-descriptor prior to the task
exiting and then accessing device private memory.

This involves some minor changes to both PowerPC and AMD GPU code. 
Unfortunately I lack hardware to test either of those so any help there
would be appreciated.  The changes mimic what is done in for both Nouveau
and hmm-tests though so I doubt they will cause problems.


This patch (of 8):

When the CPU tries to access a device private page the migrate_to_ram()
callback associated with the pgmap for the page is called.  However no
reference is taken on the faulting page.  Therefore a concurrent migration
of the device private page can free the page and possibly the underlying
pgmap.  This results in a race which can crash the kernel due to the
migrate_to_ram() function pointer becoming invalid.  It also means drivers
can't reliably read the zone_device_data field because the page may have
been freed with memunmap_pages().

Close the race by getting a reference on the page while holding the ptl to
ensure it has not been freed.  Unfortunately the elevated reference count
will cause the migration required to handle the fault to fail.  To avoid
this failure pass the faulting page into the migrate_vma functions so that
if an elevated reference count is found it can be checked to see if it's
expected or not.

commit_msg:
netfilter: ebtables: CONFIG_COMPAT: don't trust userland offsets

We need to make sure the offsets are not out of range of the
total size.
Also check that they are in ascending order.

The WARN_ON triggered by syzkaller (it sets panic_on_warn) is
changed to also bail out, no point in continuing parsing.

Briefly tested with simple ruleset of
-A INPUT --limit 1/s' --log
plus jump to custom chains using 32bit ebtables binary.

Reported-by: <syzbot+845a53d13171abf8bf29@syzkaller.appspotmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>

description: A flaw was found in the Linux 4.x kernel's implementation of 32-bit syscall interface for bridging. This allowed a privileged user to arbitrarily write to a limited range of kernel memory.

code_evidence: match32->match_size is only validated against size_left (line 26), but this check bounds the match data relative to the remaining buffer count, not against the actual kernel buffer bounds; size_left is decremented from userland-derived sizes.
compat_mtw_from_user is invoked with match32 and may return a size ret that differs from match_size; only ret < match_size is rejected, but no upper bound ties ret to size_left or the buffer.

buf is advanced by sizeof(*match32) plus match32->match_size (lines 36-37) and then reused as match32 for the next iteration; the WARN_ON at line 40 only warns (does not bail) when a compat target leaves residual size_left, so parsing continues with a buf that may point past the intended buffer, and match_kern->match_size is written using ret.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes match_kern->match_size and advances buf based on unvalidated userland sizes, resulting in a write past the intended buffer. The missing ascending-order/range check on offsets is the enabling condition rather than a separate weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: userland-supplied match_size and offsets are trusted to advance buf and to size kernel writes without validating them against the total allocated buffer. Trigger: a 32-bit ebtables rule whose match/target sizes and offsets are inconsistent, especially a compat target leaving size_left nonzero. Consequence: buf advances out of range, producing out-of-bounds writes to kernel memory (match_kern->match_size assignment) and arbitrary limited-range kernel memory corruption.

commit_msg:
BACapp: Add a nesting / recursion check.

Track our recursion depth in fAbstractSyntaxNType. It calls several

Then it', "\t     * must be followed by either another label's octet length or", '\t     * a zero length octet (that terminates the sequence).', '\t     */', '\t    if (p+1+label_len+1 > max)']}
description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. A buffer overflow vulnerability in versions 2.12 and prior affects applications that use PJSIP DNS resolution. It doesn't affect PJSIP users who utilize an external resolver. This vulnerability is related to CVE-2023-27585. The difference is that this issue is in parsing the query record `parse_rr()`, while the issue in CVE-2023-27585 is in `parse_query()`. A patch is available in the `master` branch of the `pjsip/pjproject` GitHub repository. A workaround is to disable DNS resolution in PJSIP config (by setting `nameserver_count` to zero) or use an external resolver instead.

code_evidence: Line 30 reads label_len from *p; line 31 only checks pkt+label_len > max, which permits a label whose length byte plus following bytes extend past max. Line 33 advances p by label_len+1, line 35 dereferences *p, and line 38 checks p >= max only after that dereference, so the read at line 35 can occur beyond the packet end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 requires a buffer copy without input-size validation and a write past the destination. This function only computes name length from packet bytes; the flaw is a missing bound leading to an out-of-bounds read, which is better described by CWE-125.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The label-length bound omits the length octet and the terminating octet, so a crafted DNS name with a maximal label_len advances p to or past max; the subsequent *p read and length accounting then touch memory outside the packet. Consequence is an out-of-bounds read, not a write past a destination buffer.

Fix #587

Off by one error in common.c, CVE-2019-19906.

Thanks to Stephan Zeisberg for reporting
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  addlen=strlen(add); /* only compute once */'], 'added_lines': ['  addlen=strlen(add)+1; /* only compute once */']}
description: cyrus-sasl (aka Cyrus SASL) 2.1.27 has an out-of-bounds write leading to unauthenticated remote denial-of-service in OpenLDAP via a malformed LDAP packet. The OpenLDAP crash is ultimately caused by an off-by-one error in _sasl_add_string in common.c in cyrus-sasl.

code_evidence: Line 6 computes addlen as strlen(add) without room for the terminating NUL, so the buffer allocation on line 7 requests only (*outlen)+strlen(add) bytes.

Line 9 copies addlen bytes at offset *outlen, and line 10 advances *outlen by addlen; the copy itself stays within the allocated bytes, but no NUL terminator is written, leaving the string unterminated at *out.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The off-by-one in the size computation leads to a write/read past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds memory access. The fix adding +1 confirms the missing terminator byte; this is a boundary error rather than a separate length-inconsistency class.

evidence_lines.code:
addlen=strlen(add); 
if (_buf_alloc(out, alloclen, (*outlen)+addlen)!=SASL_OK)

strncpy(*out + *outlen, add, addlen);
*outlen += addlen;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length excludes the NUL terminator, so _buf_alloc reserves exactly the payload size and the resulting string is not NUL-terminated. A caller consuming the produced string via strlen or string functions reads one byte past the allocated region, causing an out-of-bounds access (the CVE-2019-19906 off-by-one) and remote crash/DoS in OpenLDAP.

description: Electron is a framework for writing cross-platform desktop applications using JavaScript, HTML and CSS. A vulnerability in versions prior to 11.5.0, 12.1.0, and 13.3.0 allows a sandboxed renderer to request a "thumbnail" image of an arbitrary file on the user's system. The thumbnail can potentially include significant parts of the original file, including textual data in many cases. Versions 15.0.0-alpha.10, 14.0.0, 13.3.0, 12.1.0, and 11.5.0 all contain a fix for the vulnerability. Two workarounds aside from upgrading are available. One may make the vulnerability significantly more difficult for an attacker to exploit by enabling `contextIsolation` in one's app. One may also disable the functionality of the `createThumbnailFromPath` API if one does not need it.

code_evidence: The function accepts an arbitrary caller-supplied path, converts it to a wide string, and builds an IShellItem via SHCreateItemFromParsingName with no check of the caller's privilege or the path's sensitivity.
It then instantiates CLSID_LocalThumbnailCache and calls GetThumbnail on that item, producing a bitmap of the file content to be resolved back to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the function performs a file-access action (thumbnail generation) without any authorization check on the requesting actor or resource. This is a missing check, not merely a path-traversal input-validation flaw, since no allowed-path or privilege constraint is enforced before the read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the native thumbnail operation trusts any path passed from the renderer without verifying that the caller is authorized to read that file or that the path is within an allowed scope. Trigger: a sandboxed renderer invokes createThumbnailFromPath with a sensitive path. Consequence: thumbnail content derived from the file is returned to the caller, disclosing file data.

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

In order to fail safe in the supported case, re-implement all the VT-x
instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>

description: There is a heap-based buffer over-read in libdwarf 0.4.0. This issue is related to dwarf_global_formref_b.

code_evidence: In the DW_FORM_ref_sig8 case, the code declares a local Dwarf_Sig8 sig8 and immediately calls memcpy(&sig8, attr->ar_debug_ptr, sizeof(Dwarf_Sig8)) at line 132, copying 8 bytes from the attribute data pointer without first verifying that 8 bytes remain before section_end. section_end is computed at lines 17-18 but is not used to bound this copy, unlike the READ_UNALIGNED_CK calls used for other forms.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing bounds check on the memcpy source leads directly to reading memory beyond the intended buffer. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write or an integer issue; the added guard confirms the fix targets the read overrun.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DW_FORM_ref_sig8 branch copies sizeof(Dwarf_Sig8) bytes from attr->ar_debug_ptr without checking the pointer against section_end. Trigger: a crafted DWARF attribute whose ar_debug_ptr is within 8 bytes of the section end. Consequence: the memcpy reads past the end of the section buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read that can crash the process (DoS) and expose adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
Fix integer addition overflow

As reported by https://github.com/tbeu/matio/issues/121
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    else', '                else'], 'added_lines': ['                    else if ( len < UINT32_MAX - 8 + (len % 8) )', '                    else {', '                        Mat_VarFree(matvar);', '                        matvar = NULL;', '                        break;', '                    }', '                else if ( len < UINT32_MAX - 8 + (len % 8) )', '                else {', '                    Mat_VarFree(matvar);', '                    matvar = NULL;', '                    (void)fseek((FILE*)mat->fp, fpos, SEEK_SET);', '                    break;', '                }']}
description: Integer overflow vulnerability in Mat_VarReadNextInfo5 in mat5.c in tbeu matio (aka MAT File I/O Library) 1.5.17, allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service or possibly other unspecified impacts.

code_evidence: len is read from the file as a 32-bit value; when len % 8 != 0, len_pad = len + 8 - (len % 8) is computed without an upper bound before malloc(len_pad + 1).
The same unbounded padding computation occurs in the MAT_T_MATRIX path, again feeding malloc(len_pad + 1).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer overflow in a size calculation used for memory allocation, matching CWE-190. It is distinct from a plain out-of-bounds write because the faulty constraint is the unchecked addition before allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the padding arithmetic len + 8 - (len % 8) can wrap when len is close to UINT32_MAX, producing a small len_pad. Trigger: a crafted MAT file supplying a large length triggers the non-multiple-of-8 branch. Consequence: the undersized allocation is followed by fread/InflateVarName of len_pad bytes and a write at name[len], so the wrapped size can cause a heap buffer overflow rather than merely a failed allocation.

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    // Refresh headers byte size before checking if allowed.', '    // TODO(asraa): Remove this when entries in HeaderMap can no longer be modified by reference and', '    // HeaderMap holds an accurate internal byte size count.', '    headers.refreshByteSize();', '    // Refresh headers byte size before checking if allowed.', '    // TODO(asraa): Remove this when entries in HeaderMap can no longer be modified by reference and', '    // HeaderMap holds an accurate internal byte size count.', '    headers.refreshByteSize();']}
description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

code_evidence: The shadow and enforced branches invoke shadow_engine->allowed(...) and engine->allowed(...) with the request headers, which drives the RBAC engine to iterate over all supplied header entries.
No limit, count, or size check is performed here before these calls; the function processes the full HeaderMap regardless of how many small headers the request contains.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function fails to control the CPU resource consumed when evaluating an unbounded number of request headers. The weakness is the missing constraint on how much header data is processed, not a parsing flaw (CWE-20) or a specific algorithmic-complexity bug.

evidence_lines.code:
if (engine != nullptr) {
if (engine->allowed(*callbacks_->connection(), headers, callbacks_->streamInfo(), nullptr)) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The filter passes an attacker-controlled header map directly into the RBAC engine's allowed() evaluation without bounding the number of headers. A request with many thousands of small headers stays under the max header size but forces repeated per-header work, consuming CPU and enabling denial of service. The refreshByteSize() additions only recompute a cached size; they do not throttle or cap processing.

commit_msg: If claiming from the same transport, do nothing
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t/* Previous transport may be gone, clear flag. */'], 'added_lines': ["\t\t\t/* If we're claiming from the same transport, ignore */", '\t\t\tif(session->source->instance == request->instance) {', '\t\t\t\tjanus_mutex_unlock(&session->mutex);', '\t\t\t\t/* Prepare JSON reply */', '\t\t\t\tjson_t *reply = json_object();', '\t\t\t\tjson_object_set_new(reply, "janus", json_string("success"));', '\t\t\t\tjson_object_set_new(reply, "session_id", json_integer(session_id));', '\t\t\t\tjson_object_set_new(reply, "transaction", json_string(transaction_text));', '\t\t\t\t/* Send the success reply */', '\t\t\t\tret = janus_process_success(request, reply);', '\t\t\t\tgoto jsondone;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t/* Previous transport may be gone, clear flag */']}
description: An issue was discovered in Janus through 0.9.1. janus.c has multiple concurrent threads that misuse the source property of a session, leading to a race condition when claiming sessions.

code_evidence: The 'claim' branch locks session->mutex, then checks session->source != NULL and, if set, calls session_over and janus_request_destroy on the old source before setting session->source = NULL. It then allocates a new source via janus_request_new and assigns it to session->source. Because session->source is shared across concurrent request threads, the check-then-act sequence on session->source is only protected by session->mutex, and any code path that reads or replaces session->source without holding that same mutex can interleave between the NULL check and the reassignment, or between the destroy and the new assignment.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function performs a non-atomic check-then-modify sequence on the shared session->source resource across concurrent threads, allowing an interfering sequence to interleave. This is improper synchronization of a shared resource, not merely a logic bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the claim path mutates the shared session->source pointer (destroy, NULL, reallocate, reassign) under session->mutex, but concurrent threads accessing the same session can observe or replace source outside that lock, so the check and update are not atomic. Trigger: two concurrent claim/request operations on the same session. Consequence: use-after-free or double-destroy of the request/transport, causing crash or instability.

description: Divide By Zero in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.3-DEV.

code_evidence: The sample rate sr is initialized to 0 at line 137 and only assigned when idx==0x1f (line 142) or idx<nb_usac_sr (line 144). If idx is 0x1f but the 24-bit read yields 0, or idx is out of range (>= nb_usac_sr and != 0x1f), sr remains 0.
The call to mhas_dmx_check_pid passes this possibly-zero sr onward (line 158); the patch guards the call with if(sr), confirming sr==0 was reachable and caused a division by zero downstream.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because a zero sample rate flows into downstream division. This is a divide-by-zero, not merely an uninitialized value, since the guarded call confirms sr==0 was consumed as a divisor.

evidence_lines.code: mhas_dmx_check_pid(filter, ctx, pl, sr, frame_len, CICPspeakerLayoutIdx, numSpeakers, start + pay_start, (u32) mhas_size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sr can remain 0 because the sample-rate index is either an out-of-range value or an explicit 0x1f read returning zero. Trigger: malformed MHAS type-1 header. Consequence: mhas_dmx_check_pid uses sr as a divisor, crashing the demuxer (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fixed recursive async function calls.

Previously, PromiseCapability record was stored (function->context)
directly in function object during a function invocation.  This is
not correct, because PromiseCapability record should be linked to
current execution context.  As a result, function->context is
overwritten with consecutive recursive calls which results in
use-after-free.

This closes #451 issue on Github.

commit_msg:
Free stderr_buffer when parsing plpgsql

Fixes #49
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tfree(parse_result.stderr_buffer);']}
description: An issue was discovered in libpg_query 10-1.0.2. There is a memory leak in pg_query_raw_parse in pg_query_parse.c, which might lead to a denial of service.

code_evidence: pg_query_raw_parse(input) returns parse_result, whose stderr_buffer is a heap-allocated resource. When the parse fails (result.error != NULL), the function returns early after only pg_query_exit_memory_context(ctx), without freeing parse_result.stderr_buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a resource (stderr_buffer via pg_query_raw_parse) and fails to release it on the error return path, matching CWE-772's missing release after effective lifetime. This is not a use-after-free or double-free, since the resource is simply never freed on that path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path at lines 11-14 exits before the resource owned by parse_result is released. Trigger: repeated calls with input that causes pg_query_raw_parse to return a non-null error. Consequence: stderr_buffer allocations accumulate, consuming memory and enabling denial of service, consistent with the issue description.

commit_msg:
Fix heap buffer overflow handler cgi (#1237)

* Address a memory leak

* Improve the CGI handler in case of header excess

In #1224 it was already pointed out that what issues arise when the number of headers exceed ENV_VAR_NUM. It seems also be the root cause of issue #1225. In addition I guarantee that the envp list always ends with NULL, a required terminal.

* Introduce a QA-test that would crash Cherokee if more than ENV_VAR_NUM are send in by a client towards Handler CGI.

Fix #1224 and #1225
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfor (i=0; i<ENV_VAR_NUM; i++)'], 'added_lines': ['\tfor (i=0; i<=ENV_VAR_NUM; i++)']}
description: In Cherokee through 1.2.104, remote attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds write in cherokee_handler_cgi_add_env_pair in handler_cgi.c by sending many request headers, as demonstrated by a GET request with many "Host: 127.0.0.1" headers.

code_evidence: Local index i is declared at line 4 and used to initialize the envp array in the loop at lines 17-18. The loop condition i<ENV_VAR_NUM limits initialization to indices 0..ENV_VAR_NUM-1, leaving the last slot of the envp array uninitialized rather than NULL-terminated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an incorrect bound in the array-initialization loop that leaves the terminator slot unset, enabling writes past the intended buffer end during header handling. This is a classic out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), not merely a missing NULL check, because the resulting memory access exceeds the allocated array.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The envp array has ENV_VAR_NUM+1 slots (needed for the NULL terminator), but this initializer only clears ENV_VAR_NUM entries. When many client headers are later added via cherokee_handler_cgi_add_env_pair, the code can write into the uninitialized last slot and beyond, causing an out-of-bounds write that corrupts memory and may crash or execute unintended code.

commit_msg:
There are multiple similar bugs implicitly introduced by the
commit c0cfa2d8a788fcf4 ("vsock: add multi-transports support") and
commit 6a2c0962105ae8ce ("vsock: prevent transport modules unloading").

The bug pattern:
 [1] vsock_sock.transport pointer is copied to a local variable,
 [2] lock_sock() is called,
 [3] the local variable is used.
VSOCK multi-transport support introduced the race condition:
vsock_sock.transport value may change between [1] and [2].

Let's copy vsock_sock.transport pointer to local variables after
the lock_sock() call.

Fixes: c0cfa2d8a788fcf4 ("vsock: add multi-transports support")
Signed-off-by: Alexander Popov <alex.popov@linux.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Garzarella <sgarzare@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Jorgen Hansen <jhansen@vmware.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210201084719.2257066-1-alex.popov@linux.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttransport = vsk->transport;'], 'added_lines': ['', '\ttransport = vsk->transport;']}
description: A local privilege escalation was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.10.13. Multiple race conditions in the AF_VSOCK implementation are caused by wrong locking in net/vmw_vsock/af_vsock.c. The race conditions were implicitly introduced in the commits that added VSOCK multi-transport support.

code_evidence: Line 16 reads the shared vsk->transport pointer into the local transport before acquiring the socket lock at line 18; line 19 then uses that stale local copy for the null/state check and later transport callbacks.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 fits because the function accesses a shared, lock-protected resource (vsk->transport) outside the lock_sock() critical section, violating the expected locking discipline. This is improper locking rather than a plain data race: the pointer is read before the lock is held, so the protected-state invariant is broken.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: vsk->transport is snapshotted before lock_sock(), so a concurrent transport change between the read and the lock leaves transport pointing at a stale or released transport. Trigger: racing transport reassignment during recvmsg. Consequence: subsequent transport-> callbacks (e.g. stream_rcvhiwat, notify_recv_init) dereference the wrong transport, leading to unexpected resource state or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
parsettf.c: Fix buffer overflow condition when reading CFF top dictionary

Closes #3087
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t// Space for at least 2 bytes is required', '\t\tif ((pt-buffer) > (sizeof(buffer) - 2)) {', '\t\t\t// The buffer is completely full; null-terminate truncate it', '\t\t\tif ((pt-buffer) == sizeof(buffer)) {', '\t\t\t\tpt--;', '\t\t\t}', "\t\t\t*pt++ = '\\0';", '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t}']}
description: FontForge 20161012 is vulnerable to a stack-based buffer overflow in addnibble (parsettf.c) resulting in DoS or code execution via a crafted otf file.

code_evidence: buffer is a fixed 50-byte stack array (line 2). The do-while loop (13-19) repeatedly reads bytes from the file and calls addnibble twice, advancing pt by up to 2 per iteration. The only guard is pt<buffer+44 on line 15, but once pt reaches buffer+44 the condition is false and the addnibble calls are skipped, leaving pt[-1] unchanged; the loop then checks pt[-1]!='\0' and may continue without appending a terminator, relying on attacker-controlled nibble data to stop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: addnibble writes through pt into the fixed stack buffer without a robust bound check, producing an out-of-bounds write, which is CWE-119. The added patch confirms the missing space-for-2-bytes constraint; this is a buffer-bounds write rather than a mere integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop termination depends on addnibble writing a '\0' terminator into buffer, but the guard at line 15 stops calling addnibble before a terminator is guaranteed, so pt can advance past the intended bound or the loop can iterate without writing. Trigger: a crafted otf/CFF top dictionary whose nibbles never yield a terminator. Consequence: writes via addnibble reach beyond buffer's 50-byte boundary (stack overflow), causing DoS or code execution.

commit_msg:
Don't invoke shutdown signal handler until JVM init completes

JVM init path: J9_CreateJavaVM.
JVM exit paths: protectedDestroyJavaVM and exitJavaVM.

A segfault or other side-effects can happen if the JVM init and
exit paths execute concurrently.

The exit path can be taken if a shutdown signal is raised and the
shutdown handler is invoked. JVM shutdown signals are SIGINT, SIGTERM
and SIGHUP.

Preventing invocation of the exit path from the shutdown signal handler
until the JVM initialization completes resolves the above side-effects.

Related:
- #17101
- #17438

Signed-off-by: Babneet Singh <sbabneet@ca.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tBOOLEAN shutdownStarted = FALSE;', "\t/* Don't invoke handler if JVM exit has started. */", '\tomrthread_monitor_enter(vm->runtimeFlagsMutex);', '\tif (J9_ARE_ANY_BITS_SET(vm->runtimeFlags, J9_RUNTIME_EXIT_STARTED)) {', '\t\tshutdownStarted = TRUE;', '\tomrthread_monitor_exit(vm->runtimeFlagsMutex);', '\tif (shutdownStarted) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tBOOLEAN invokeHandler = TRUE;', '\tU_32 runtimeFlags = 0;', "\t/* Don't invoke handler if JVM hasn't initialized or JVM exit has started. */", '\tissueReadBarrier();', '\truntimeFlags = vm->runtimeFlags;', '\tif (J9_ARE_NO_BITS_SET(runtimeFlags, J9_RUNTIME_INITIALIZED)', '\t|| J9_ARE_ANY_BITS_SET(runtimeFlags, J9_RUNTIME_EXIT_STARTED)', '\t) {', '\t\tinvokeHandler = FALSE;', '\tif (!invokeHandler) {']}
description: In Eclipse OpenJ9 before version 0.41.0, the JVM can be forced into an infinite busy hang on a spinlock or a segmentation fault if a shutdown signal (SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP) is received before the JVM has finished initializing.

code_evidence: predefinedHandlerWrapper is the shutdown-signal handler. It checks only J9_RUNTIME_EXIT_STARTED under vm->runtimeFlagsMutex (lines 15-19) and returns early only when shutdownStarted is set (lines 20-22). It never tests J9_RUNTIME_INITIALIZED, so the signal path can proceed to attach and signalDispatch while JVM initialization is still running.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a signal-handler code sequence accesses shared JVM runtime state concurrently with the init sequence without ensuring exclusivity/atomicity, allowing an interfering sequence to race and corrupt state. It is not merely a missing check; the defect is the unsynchronized concurrent execution window between init and exit paths.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the early-exit guard is incomplete, checking exit state but not initialization state, and the flag is read outside the initialization sequence's synchronization. Trigger: SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP arrives while J9_CreateJavaVM is still initializing. The handler proceeds into the exit path concurrently with init, causing a spinlock busy hang or segmentation fault (availability impact).

commit_msg:
Prevent KDC unset status assertion failures

Assign status values if S4U2Self padata fails to decode, if an
S4U2Proxy request uses invalid KDC options, or if an S4U2Proxy request
uses an evidence ticket which does not match the canonicalized request
server principal name.  Reported by Samuel Cabrero.

If a status value is not assigned during KDC processing, default to
"UNKNOWN_REASON" rather than failing an assertion.  This change will
prevent future denial of service bugs due to similar mistakes, and
will allow us to omit assigning status values for unlikely errors such
as small memory allocation failures.

CVE-2017-11368:

In MIT krb5 1.7 and later, an authenticated attacker can cause an
assertion failure in krb5kdc by sending an invalid S4U2Self or
S4U2Proxy request.

  CVSSv3 Vector: AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H/E:H/RL:O/RC:C

ticket: 8599 (new)
target_version: 1.15-next
target_version: 1.14-next
tags: pullup
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    assert(status != NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (status == NULL)', '        status = "UNKNOWN_REASON";']}
description: In MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) 1.7 and later, an authenticated attacker can cause a KDC assertion failure by sending invalid S4U2Self or S4U2Proxy requests.

code_evidence: The cleanup label asserts that status is non-NULL before using it in au_state->status and log_tgs_req.
status is initialized to 0 and only assigned on selected error paths; the S4U2Self call at line 140 can return errcode with status left unset, then line 159 jumps to cleanup.
The S4U2Proxy branch likewise calls kdc_process_s4u2proxy_req and can proceed to cleanup on errcode without guaranteeing status was assigned.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because an attacker-triggerable assertion in the KDC terminates the service. The weakness is the reachable assert on unvalidated status, not the S4U request parsing itself.

evidence_lines.code: assert(status != NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A malformed authenticated S4U2Self or S4U2Proxy request causes an error path that reaches cleanup while status is still NULL. The assert at the cleanup label then aborts the KDC process, producing a denial of service rather than a normal error response.

commit_msg:
Early catch potential overflow issue #43

`m_width` and `m_height` are of `int` type in the OpenEXR library. We
currently keep the same types in our class but this may case issue
when mapping 1D memory. In the most favorable case, they are
multiplied together (Y framebuffer). For RGB(A) case, the required
memory can also be 4 time larger. We check if resp. `m_width *
m_height` and `4 * m_width * m_heigh` stay within the `int` higher
limit. Thanks to @GAP-dev for bringing this issue.

This commit also cleans a bit raw memory allocation in favor of
`std::vector` container.

commit_msg:
When doing option parsing for standard type values of 1, 2 or 4 octets,
the value is converted directly into a variable instead of a pointer. To
avoid being tricked into being a pointer, check that for these option
types that sizes actually match. In L2CAP every option is fixed size and
thus it is prudent anyway to ensure that the remote side sends us the
right option size along with option paramters.

If the option size is not matching the option type, then that option is
silently ignored. It is a protocol violation and instead of trying to
give the remote attacker any further hints just pretend that option is
not present and proceed with the default values. Implementation
following the specification and its qualification procedures will always
use the correct size and thus not being impacted here.

To keep the code readable and consistent accross all options, a few
cosmetic changes were also required.

Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hedberg <johan.hedberg@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (olen == sizeof(rfc))', '\t\t\t\tmemcpy(&rfc, (void *)val, olen);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (olen != sizeof(rfc))', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\tmemcpy(&rfc, (void *)val, olen);', '\t\t\tif (olen != 2)', '\t\t\t\tbreak;']}
description: A heap data infoleak in multiple locations including L2CAP_PARSE_CONF_RSP was found in the Linux kernel before 5.1-rc1.

code_evidence: The loop consumes remote-supplied option data via l2cap_get_conf_opt, which sets type, olen and val from the untrusted response. For L2CAP_CONF_RFC, memcpy of olen bytes into the fixed-size struct rfc is guarded only by olen == sizeof(rfc) (lines 20-21), so a mismatched length silently skips the copy. For L2CAP_CONF_EWS, txwin_ext = val is assigned with no check that olen is the required 2 bytes (lines 23-24). The option length is thus not validated against the expected size for each option type.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function receives remote option data and fails to validate that its length property matches the required fixed size before using it. The missing size constraint is the direct input-validation defect, distinct from later memory-safety consequences.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser trusts the option length field and does not enforce per-type fixed sizes; the RFC path only rejects non-matching sizes implicitly, and EWS accepts any length while reading val. Trigger: a remote peer sends a configuration response with an option whose olen differs from the type's fixed size. Consequence: option data is misinterpreted, enabling the described heap infoleak and inconsistent protocol handling.

commit_msg:
Strengthen input verification for SpecializeType by replacing DCHECK with explicit test/status return.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 453436708
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  DCHECK_EQ(t.args_size(), 3);'], 'added_lines': ['  if (t.args_size() != 3) {', '    return Status(error::INVALID_ARGUMENT,', '                  absl::StrCat("illegal FOR_EACH type, expected 3 args, got ",', '                               t.args_size()));', '  }']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. When `tensorflow::full_type::SubstituteFromAttrs` receives a `FullTypeDef& t` that is not exactly three args, it triggers a `CHECK`-fail instead of returning a status. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 6104f0d4091c260ce9352f9155f7e9b725eab012. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: Before the patch, the function only guarded the argument count with DCHECK_EQ(t.args_size(), 3) at line 2, then unconditionally indexed t.args(0), t.args(1), and t.args(2) at lines 3-5. DCHECK is compiled out in release builds, so a FullTypeDef with fewer than three args reaches the indexed accessors without any runtime check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because the only guard on attacker-influenced input arity is a DCHECK, an assertion-like statement reachable from callers, whose failure terminates the process instead of returning INVALID_ARGUMENT. This is an availability impact from a reachable assertion, not a separate memory-corruption weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the arity constraint is enforced only by a debug assertion, not a runtime check. Trigger: a caller supplies a FullTypeDef whose args_size() is not 3. Consequence: in release builds the assertion is absent and the unchecked args(i) access proceeds, while in debug builds the DCHECK aborts the process, giving a reachable assertion/crash rather than a returned error status.

commit_msg:
usbip_host updates device status without holding lock from stub probe,
disconnect and rebind code paths. When multiple requests to import a
device are received, these unprotected code paths step all over each
other and drive fails with NULL-ptr deref and use-after-free errors.

The driver uses a table lock to protect the busid array for adding and
deleting busids to the table. However, the probe, disconnect and rebind
paths get the busid table entry and update the status without holding
the busid table lock. Add a new finer grain lock to protect the busid
entry. This new lock will be held to search and update the busid entry
fields from get_busid_idx(), add_match_busid() and del_match_busid().

match_busid_show() does the same to access the busid entry fields.

get_busid_priv() changed to return the pointer to the busid entry holding
the busid lock. stub_probe(), stub_disconnect() and stub_device_rebind()
call put_busid_priv() to release the busid lock before returning. This
changes fixes the unprotected code paths eliminating the race conditions
in updating the busid entries.

Reported-by: Jakub Jirasek
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan (Samsung OSG) <shuah@kernel.org>
Cc: stable <stable@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfor (i = 0; i < MAX_BUSID; i++)'], 'added_lines': ['\tfor (i = 0; i < MAX_BUSID; i++) {', '\t\tspin_lock(&busid_table[i].busid_lock);', '\t\t\tspin_unlock(&busid_table[i].busid_lock);', '\t\tspin_unlock(&busid_table[i].busid_lock);', '\t}']}
description: In the Linux Kernel before version 4.16.11, 4.14.43, 4.9.102, and 4.4.133, multiple race condition errors when handling probe, disconnect, and rebind operations can be exploited to trigger a use-after-free condition or a NULL pointer dereference by sending multiple USB over IP packets.

code_evidence: The loop scans busid_table entries and checks/clears/sets name and status fields (lines 11-15) without holding any per-entry lock; only the coarse busid_table_lock at line 5 is held, which does not protect the entry fields against probe/disconnect/rebind paths that access them without that lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a non-atomic check-then-write on a shared resource that other concurrent code sequences can modify, matching CWE-362's improper synchronization of a shared resource. It is a race condition rather than a simple NULL dereference, since the dereference is a downstream effect of the timing window.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: add_match_busid() reads and writes busid_table[i].name and .status while only the table-level lock is held, so concurrent probe, disconnect, and rebind paths that access the same entry unsynchronized can interleave. Trigger: multiple USB/IP import requests racing with those paths. Supported consequence: use-after-free or NULL-pointer dereference as entry state is corrupted.

commit_msg:
Check for multiplication overflow in sfconvert

Checks that a multiplication doesn't overflow when
calculating the buffer size, and if it overflows,
reduce the buffer size instead of failing.

This fixes the 00192-audiofile-signintoverflow-sfconvert case
in #41
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tconst int kBufferFrameCount = 65536;', '\tvoid *buffer = malloc(kBufferFrameCount * frameSize);'], 'added_lines': ['\tint kBufferFrameCount = 65536;', '\tint bufferSize;', '\twhile (multiplyCheckOverflow(kBufferFrameCount, frameSize, &bufferSize))', '\t\tkBufferFrameCount /= 2;', '\tvoid *buffer = malloc(bufferSize);']}
description: Integer overflow in sfcommands/sfconvert.c in Audio File Library (aka audiofile) 0.3.6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: frameSize comes from afGetVirtualFrameSize on the attacker-supplied input file; it is multiplied by the fixed kBufferFrameCount (65536) inside malloc without any overflow check, so the product can wrap to a small or negative value and the allocation size is wrong.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the code assumes the multiplication result is always a valid, larger allocation size, but wraparound yields a too-small value that feeds memory allocation and copying. This is the integer-overflow root cause; the heap overflow is its downstream consequence, not a separate target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer size computation kBufferFrameCount * frameSize is an unchecked int multiplication whose result is used directly for malloc. Trigger: a crafted file yielding a large frameSize causes the product to wrap. Consequence: an undersized buffer is allocated, and subsequent afReadFrames writes framesToRead frames into it, producing a heap overflow that can crash the process (DoS) and potentially corrupt memory.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/682
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  buffer=(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory((size_t) GetBlobSize(image),', '    sizeof(*buffer));'], 'added_lines': ['  buffer=(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory((size_t) GetBlobSize(image)+', '    MaxTextExtent,sizeof(*buffer));']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the ReadSFWImage function in coders/sfw.c in ImageMagick 7.0.6-8 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted file.

code_evidence: buffer is allocated with exactly GetBlobSize(image) bytes via AcquireQuantumMemory, then ReadBlob reads GetBlobSize(image) bytes into it. Later processing (e.g., CopyMagickMemory at header+6 and the SFWScan/marker walk) operates on this tightly sized buffer without slack.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs memory operations outside the allocated buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The patch adds MaxTextExtent slack, confirming the buffer-boundary restriction was the defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer is sized exactly to the input blob with no extra headroom, yet subsequent parsing writes/reads past the blob end (e.g., CopyMagickMemory(header+6,...) and marker traversal). A crafted SFW file drives those operations beyond the allocated region, causing a heap-based buffer overflow and crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Change pairing_cb to assume temporary pairing by default

When pairing takes place, the pairing_cb.is_temp flag indicates whether
a pairing is temporary or permanent. Link keys are not stored for
temporary pairings. Since this is a "positive" flag, resetting the
pairing_cb control block (ex. memset to 0), it will assume persistent
pairing by default. Under certain circumstances, this can lead to a link
key being stored for temporarily secured connection.

This patch reverses the flag to be a "negative" flag. Renamed to
"persistent_bond", the default 0 meaning is now used to indicate a
temporary bond. If the lag is not properly set now, it will default to a
temporary bond and will not save the link key erronously.

This fix is for CVE-2014-7914

Bug: 18345373
Change-Id: I6e821595877ff30d64dc6e33602ac049cab3dd1e
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            (p_auth_cmpl->key_type == HCI_LKEY_TYPE_CHANGED_COMB) || (!pairing_cb.is_temp))', '            BTIF_TRACE_DEBUG("%s: Storing link key. key_type=0x%x, is_temp=%d",', '                __FUNCTION__, p_auth_cmpl->key_type, pairing_cb.is_temp);', '            BTIF_TRACE_DEBUG("%s: Temporary key. Not storing. key_type=0x%x, is_temp=%d",', '                __FUNCTION__, p_auth_cmpl->key_type, pairing_cb.is_temp);', '            if(pairing_cb.is_temp)'], 'added_lines': ['            (p_auth_cmpl->key_type == HCI_LKEY_TYPE_CHANGED_COMB) || pairing_cb.bond_type == BOND_TYPE_PERSISTENT)', '            BTIF_TRACE_DEBUG("%s: Storing link key. key_type=0x%x, bond_type=%d",', '                __FUNCTION__, p_auth_cmpl->key_type, pairing_cb.bond_type);', '            BTIF_TRACE_DEBUG("%s: Temporary key. Not storing. key_type=0x%x, bond_type=%d",', '                __FUNCTION__, p_auth_cmpl->key_type, pairing_cb.bond_type);', '            if(pairing_cb.bond_type == BOND_TYPE_TEMPORARY)']}
description: btif/src/btif_dm.c in Android before 5.1 does not properly enforce the temporary nature of a Bluetooth pairing, which allows user-assisted remote attackers to bypass intended access restrictions via crafted Bluetooth packets after the tapping of a crafted NFC tag.

code_evidence: The storage branch is entered when the key type is a combination type OR when the pairing is not temporary; with the positive is_temp flag, a zeroed/reset pairing_cb defaults is_temp to false, so (!pairing_cb.is_temp) is true and the persistent-key path is taken.
Inside that branch, btif_storage_add_bonded_device stores the link key unconditionally, persisting credentials for a connection that should have been temporary.
The else branch only avoids storage and reports BT_BOND_STATE_NONE when pairing_cb.is_temp is true, so a default-false flag silently skips this temporary-pairing handling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is an incorrect authorization decision: the code fails to correctly enforce the temporary-bond restriction and grants persistent bonding, allowing protection-mechanism bypass. It is not just a data-exposure issue; the access-control check controlling whether credentials are stored is wrong.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((p_auth_cmpl->key_type < HCI_LKEY_TYPE_DEBUG_COMB)  || (p_auth_cmpl->key_type == HCI_LKEY_TYPE_AUTH_COMB) ||
(p_auth_cmpl->key_type == HCI_LKEY_TYPE_CHANGED_COMB) || (!pairing_cb.is_temp))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the temporary-pairing decision relies on a positive flag whose default (0 after reset) means persistent, so an unset flag authorizes link-key storage. Trigger: authentication completes with a key while pairing_cb.is_temp was never set true. Consequence: a link key is persisted for a temporarily secured connection, bypassing the intended temporary-bond restriction.

commit_msg:
Enhance validation of ngram op and handle case of 0 tokens.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 369940178
Change-Id: Ia82f42c09d14efe76e7dc013505b832a42282f0b
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      ngram->append(data[data_start_index + num_tokens - 1]);', '      for (int n = 0; n < right_padding; ++n) {', '        ngram->append(separator_);'], 'added_lines': ['      // Only output first num_tokens - 1 pairs of data and separator', '      // Handle case when there are no tokens or no right padding as these can', '      // result in consecutive separators.', '      if (num_tokens > 0) {', '        // If we have tokens, then output last and then pair each separator with', '        // the right padding that follows, to ensure ngram ends either with the', '        // token or with the right pad.', '        ngram->append(data[data_start_index + num_tokens - 1]);', '        for (int n = 0; n < right_padding; ++n) {', '          ngram->append(separator_);', '          ngram->append(right_pad_);', '        }', '      } else {', "        // If we don't have tokens, then the last item inserted into the ngram", '        // has been the separator from the left padding loop above. Hence,', '        // output right pad and separator and make sure to finish with a', '        // padding, not a separator.', '        for (int n = 0; n < right_padding - 1; ++n) {', '          ngram->append(right_pad_);', '          ngram->append(separator_);', '        }']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a dereference of a null pointer in `tf.raw_ops.StringNGrams`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/1cdd4da14282210cc759e468d9781741ac7d01bf/tensorflow/core/kernels/string_ngrams_op.cc#L67-L74) does not fully validate the `data_splits` argument. This would result in `ngrams_data`(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/1cdd4da14282210cc759e468d9781741ac7d01bf/tensorflow/core/kernels/string_ngrams_op.cc#L106-L110) to be a null pointer when the output would be computed to have 0 or negative size. Later writes to the output tensor would then cause a null pointer dereference. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The loop at [24,25,26,27] iterates while n < num_tokens - 1, indexing data[data_start_index + n]; when num_tokens is 0 this bound is -1 so the loop is skipped, but line 28 unconditionally appends data[data_start_index + num_tokens - 1], i.e. data[data_start_index - 1], reading before the intended data buffer.

The right-padding loop at [29,30,31,32] was not guarded by any num_tokens check, so with zero tokens the separator/right-pad output is emitted without the token, producing an inconsistent ngram layout.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 covers writes past/ before the intended buffer; here the same missing num_tokens constraint causes an out-of-range element access on the data array at line 28, which the fix wraps in a num_tokens > 0 guard. This is a buffer-bounds error rather than a null-pointer dereference (CWE-476), because the index is computed from data_start_index rather than a null base.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: num_tokens (derived from ngram_width and padding) can be zero, yet line 28 still computes index data_start_index + num_tokens - 1 = data_start_index - 1 and dereferences it. Trigger: a caller supplying ngram_width/data_splits yielding zero tokens for an ngram. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds access on the data buffer (the patch guards this with an if (num_tokens > 0) branch).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#ifdef LIBRAW_LIBRARY_BUILD', '  if(!image)', '    throw LIBRAW_EXCEPTION_IO_CORRUPT;', '#endif']}
description: An off-by-one error within the "LibRaw::kodak_ycbcr_load_raw()" function (internal/dcraw_common.cpp) in LibRaw versions prior to 0.18.7 can be exploited to cause a heap-based buffer overflow and subsequently cause a crash.

code_evidence: Nested loops iterate col from 0 to width-1 and unconditionally write image[row*width+col][c] at line 21. hpred[col & 1] and vpred[row & 1][col] are indexed by col; the write target depends on width/height from the file and the per-channel roff/width relationship, with no bounds check on col against the allocated image buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the code writes image data past the end of the intended allocation. This is an out-of-bounds write, not merely a read (CWE-125) or integer overflow, since the missing constraint directly permits the memory write beyond bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The per-channel loop uses the file-derived width to compute image[row*width+col][c] without validating that the computed index stays within the allocated image buffer. If width/height or channel layout are inconsistent, the write at line 21 lands outside the buffer, corrupting heap memory and potentially crashing or enabling code execution.

Adding check for min_width and min_height

Add check for min_wd and min_ht. Stride is updated if header
decode is done.

Bug: 74078669

(cherry picked from commit 84eba4863dd50083951db83ea3cc81e015bf51da)

description: In impeg2_fmt_conv_yuv420p_to_yuv420sp_uv_av8 of impeg2_format_conv.s there is a possible out of bounds write due to missing bounds check. This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation. Product: Android Versions: Android-7.0 Android-7.1.1 Android-7.1.2 Android-8.0 Android-8.1 Android-9.0 Android ID: A-74078669

code_evidence: Sequence header width/height are read from the bitstream (12 bits each) and only rejected when exactly zero; no minimum bound is enforced before being stored into ps_dec->u2_horizontal_size/u2_vertical_size.
The stored dimensions are persisted into decoder state and drive later stride/buffer sizing, so a tiny non-zero resolution passes this validation.
The only size check compares against u2_create_max_width/height (upper bound); there is no lower-bound rejection, so undersized dimensions flow into subsequent frame conversion.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing lower-bound check permits undersized dimensions to reach buffer-sizing/writing logic, causing writes beyond the intended frame buffer, which is exactly CWE-787. It is not merely an integer issue; the consequence is an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sequence-header parser accepts width/height values below the minimum supported resolution because it only rejects zero and enforces an upper bound. Trigger: a crafted sequence header with a small non-zero width/height. Consequence: downstream conversion writes past the allocated frame buffer, supporting memory corruption and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
security fixes

https://hhvm.com/blog/2021/02/25/security-update.html
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  result[outpos] = NUL;', '  return outpos;'], 'added_lines': ['  appendchar(&result, &outpos, &size, NUL);', '  return outpos - 1;']}
description: xbuf_format_converter, used as part of exif_read_data, was appending a terminating null character to the generated string, but was not using its standard append char function. As a result, if the buffer was full, it would result in an out-of-bounds write. This issue affects HHVM versions prior to 4.56.3, all versions between 4.57.0 and 4.80.1, all versions between 4.81.0 and 4.93.1, and versions 4.94.0, 4.95.0, 4.96.0, 4.97.0, 4.98.0.

code_evidence: The buffer result is malloc'd to size 240 with outpos tracking the next write position; appendchar(&result,&outpos,&size,...) is the helper that grows the buffer when full and is used for all incremental writes.
The terminating NUL was written directly via result[outpos] = NUL at line 470, bypassing appendchar, so no capacity check or reallocation occurs before this store.
If prior appendchar/appendsimplestring calls filled the buffer exactly to size, outpos == size and result[outpos] writes one byte past the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of the intended malloc'd buffer at result[outpos] when full, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. The patch confirms this by replacing the direct store with appendchar and adjusting the return value; this is a buffer-boundary violation rather than an integer or use-after-free issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the final NUL terminator is stored with a raw indexed write instead of the bounds-checking appendchar helper. Trigger: formatted output whose accumulated length reaches the allocated size (e.g., via exif_read_data using this converter), leaving outpos at size. Consequence: a one-byte out-of-bounds heap write, corrupting adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
proc_pid_cmdline_read() and environ_read() directly access the target
process' VM to retrieve the command line and environment. If this
process remaps these areas onto a file via mmap(), the requesting
process may experience various issues such as extra delays if the
underlying device is slow to respond.

Let's simply refuse to access file-backed areas in these functions.
For this we add a new FOLL_ANON gup flag that is passed to all calls
to access_remote_vm(). The code already takes care of such failures
(including unmapped areas). Accesses via /proc/pid/mem were not
changed though.

This was assigned CVE-2018-1120.

Note for stable backports: the patch may apply to kernels prior to 4.11
but silently miss one location; it must be checked that no call to
access_remote_vm() keeps zero as the last argument.

Reported-by: Qualys Security Advisory <qsa@qualys.com>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Andy Lutomirski <luto@amacapital.net>
Cc: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tretval = access_remote_vm(mm, (env_start + src), page, this_len, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tretval = access_remote_vm(mm, (env_start + src), page, this_len, FOLL_ANON);']}
description: A flaw was found affecting the Linux kernel before version 4.17. By mmap()ing a FUSE-backed file onto a process's memory containing command line arguments (or environment strings), an attacker can cause utilities from psutils or procps (such as ps, w) or any other program which makes a read() call to the /proc/<pid>/cmdline (or /proc/<pid>/environ) files to block indefinitely (denial of service) or for some controlled time (as a synchronization primitive for other attacks).

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only reads the target process's environment via access_remote_vm using env_start/env_end bounds; the flaw is missing FOLL_ANON to refuse file-backed mmap regions, causing blocking on slow FUSE devices, not an out-of-bounds memory buffer operation, so CWE-119 is unsupported.

commit_msg: Fix arbitrary heap exposure problem
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  memccpy(result, ptr, 0, len);'], 'added_lines': ['  memcpy(result, ptr, len);']}
description: Ruby through 2.2.7, 2.3.x through 2.3.4, and 2.4.x through 2.4.1 can expose arbitrary memory during a JSON.generate call. The issues lies in using strdup in ext/json/ext/generator/generator.c, which will stop after encountering a '\0' byte, returning a pointer to a string of length zero, which is not the length stored in space_len.

code_evidence: Line 4 allocates exactly len bytes with ALLOC_N(char, len). Line 5 copies with memccpy(result, ptr, 0, len), which stops at the first NUL byte before len; the remaining bytes in result are left uninitialized, and the caller treats the buffer as len bytes (returned without length tracking).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a len-byte buffer but fills it only partially, and the buffer is subsequently used as if fully initialized, so data beyond the copied region is read within the intended buffer size but outside the initialized content, yielding out-of-bounds/uninitialized memory exposure consistent with CWE-119. The defect is the copy operation not matching the allocation's intended boundary, not a length overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: memccpy stops copying at a NUL byte, so fewer than len bytes are written into the allocated buffer, leaving uninitialized heap content. Trigger: fstrndup is called on data containing an embedded NUL within len. Consequence: later use of the len-byte buffer exposes uninitialized heap memory; in the JSON.generate path this leaks arbitrary process memory. The fix uses memcpy to copy all len bytes.

We call skb_cow_data, which is good anyway to ensure we can actually
modify the skb as such (another error from prior). Now that we have the
number of fragments required, we can safely allocate exactly that amount
of memory.

Fixes: c09440f7dcb3 ("macsec: introduce IEEE 802.1AE driver")
Signed-off-by: Jason A. Donenfeld <Jason@zx2c4.com>
Acked-by: Sabrina Dubroca <sd@queasysnail.net>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treq = macsec_alloc_req(tx_sa->key.tfm, &iv, &sg);', '\tsg_init_table(sg, MAX_SKB_FRAGS + 1);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct sk_buff *trailer;', '\tret = skb_cow_data(skb, 0, &trailer);', '\tif (unlikely(ret < 0)) {', '\t\tmacsec_txsa_put(tx_sa);', '\t\tkfree_skb(skb);', '\t\treturn ERR_PTR(ret);', '\t}', '', '\treq = macsec_alloc_req(tx_sa->key.tfm, &iv, &sg, ret);', '\tsg_init_table(sg, ret);']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in drivers/net/macsec.c in the MACsec module in the Linux kernel through 4.10.12 allows attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging the use of a MAX_SKB_FRAGS+1 size in conjunction with the NETIF_F_FRAGLIST feature, leading to an error in the skb_to_sgvec function.

code_evidence: The scatterlist is allocated and initialized for a fixed MAX_SKB_FRAGS + 1 entries at line 76, but skb_to_sgvec at line 77 is called with the full skb->len. skb_to_sgvec can emit more scatterlist entries than MAX_SKB_FRAGS + 1 when the skb carries a fraglist (NETIF_F_FRAGLIST) or otherwise exceeds the assumed fragment count, so it writes past the end of the sg array. No count returned by skb_to_sgvec is checked against the initialized size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes scatterlist entries into a heap buffer sized by a fixed constant while the writer can produce more entries, an out-of-bounds write within a memory buffer, matching CWE-119. The fix computes the exact fragment count via skb_cow_data and sizes the table accordingly, confirming the boundary error rather than a separate logic flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the scatterlist array size is hardcoded to MAX_SKB_FRAGS + 1 instead of the actual number of fragments the skb will produce. Trigger: a transmitted skb whose fragment layout yields more sg entries than that constant. Consequence: skb_to_sgvec writes beyond the sg buffer, corrupting adjacent heap memory (heap overflow), enabling DoS or potential control-flow impact.

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

Fixes: c7aa12252f51 ("NFC: Take a reference on the LLCP local pointer when creating a socket")
Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Reviewed-by: Simon Horman <simon.horman@corigine.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tnfc_llcp_local_put(local);', '']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: Line 4 obtains 'local' via nfc_llcp_find_local(dev) without retaining a reference; lines 5-8 only check for NULL and free the skb on failure. Line 9 passes the unreferenced 'local' into __nfc_llcp_recv, and the function returns at line 10 without ever calling nfc_llcp_local_put, so no reference is held across the use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses a pointer to an object that can be freed concurrently because no reference is held, which is exactly CWE-416. A missing NULL check would be a different weakness; here the NULL check exists, but lifetime is unmanaged.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nfc_llcp_find_local returns a pointer without taking a kref, and this caller never acquires or releases one. Trigger: a concurrent nfc_llcp_unregister_device/local_release drops the last reference and frees the local between line 4 and line 9. Consequence: __nfc_llcp_recv dereferences freed memory (read/integrity impact), matching the reported UAF.

commit_msg:
CVE-2021-43825

Response filter manager crash

Signed-off-by: Yan Avlasov <yavlasov@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    ASSERT(!state_.remote_encode_complete_);', '    state_.remote_encode_complete_ = true;']}
description: Envoy is an open source edge and service proxy, designed for cloud-native applications. Sending a locally generated response must stop further processing of request or response data. Envoy tracks the amount of buffered request and response data and aborts the request if the amount of buffered data is over the limit by sending 413 or 500 responses. However when the buffer overflows while response is processed by the filter chain the operation may not be aborted correctly and result in accessing a freed memory block. If this happens Envoy will crash resulting in a denial of service.

code_evidence: maybeEndEncode conditionally invokes filter_manager_callbacks_.endStream() whenever end_stream is true, with no guard tracking whether encoding has already been terminated. The function itself contains no state check or completion flag, so repeated or late calls still reach endStream().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the missing completion guard permits endStream() to operate on freed filter-chain state, matching the commit's freed-memory access. It is not merely a double operation; the supported consequence is use of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function lacks a completion guard, so endStream() can be invoked after the encoding path has already ended or been aborted (e.g., a locally generated response during buffer overflow). Trigger: a second call with end_stream true reaches filter_manager_callbacks_.endStream() on an already-torn-down filter chain, yielding a use-after-free and crash. Consequence: denial of service.

commit_msg:
x86: limit GFNs to 32 bits for shadowed superpages.

Superpage shadows store the shadowed GFN in the backpointer field,
which for non-BIGMEM builds is 32 bits wide.  Shadowing a superpage
mapping of a guest-physical address above 2^44 would lead to the GFN
being truncated there, and a crash when we come to remove the shadow
from the hash table.

Track the valid width of a GFN for each guest, including reporting it
through CPUID, and enforce it in the shadow pagetables.  Set the
maximum witth to 32 for guests where this truncation could occur.

This is XSA-173.

Reported-by: Ling Liu <liuling-it@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif ( cpuid_eax(0x80000000) >= 0x80000008 )', '\t\tpaddr_bits = cpuid_eax(0x80000008) & 0xff;'], 'added_lines': ['\tif ( cpuid_eax(0x80000000) >= 0x80000008 ) {', '\t\teax = cpuid_eax(0x80000008);', '\t\tpaddr_bits = eax & 0xff;', '\t\thap_paddr_bits = ((eax >> 16) & 0xff) ?: paddr_bits;', '\t}']}
description: Integer overflow in the x86 shadow pagetable code in Xen allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host crash) or possibly gain privileges by shadowing a superpage mapping.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only reads CPUID leaves to set paddr_bits/hap_paddr_bits; it contains no permission, privilege, or access-control operation supporting the CWE-264 category, and the commit's truncation issue is not realized in this function.
