commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tprivate = t->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\tprivate = xt_table_get_private_protected(t);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: Under local_bh_disable(), the function reads the table's private pointer directly into 'private' via t->private, then immediately dereferences private->number at line 21 without any protected/ordered accessor. The patch replaces this raw read with xt_table_get_private_protected(t), indicating the direct load is the unsafe access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses a table-info pointer that can be freed concurrently by another thread, then dereferences it, which is precisely CWE-416 (use after free). The missing synchronization on the t->private load is the cause; the freed-memory dereference is the supported consequence, distinguishing it from a mere race without reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the private table pointer is loaded without the ordering/protection needed to synchronize with a concurrent rules replacement that may free the old table. Trigger: a replacement thread frees old table info while this path still holds/uses the stale pointer, so private->number and later private->entries dereference freed memory. Supported consequence: use-after-free in the packet/table processing context, with crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
bpf: fix incorrect sign extension in check_alu_op()

Distinguish between
BPF_ALU64|BPF_MOV|BPF_K (load 32-bit immediate, sign-extended to 64-bit)
and BPF_ALU|BPF_MOV|BPF_K (load 32-bit immediate, zero-padded to 64-bit);
only perform sign extension in the first case.

Starting with v4.14, this is exploitable by unprivileged users as long as
the unprivileged_bpf_disabled sysctl isn't set.

Debian assigned CVE-2017-16995 for this issue.

v3:
 - add CVE number (Ben Hutchings)

Fixes: 484611357c19 ("bpf: allow access into map value arrays")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Edward Cree <ecree@solarflare.com>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t__mark_reg_known(regs + insn->dst_reg, insn->imm);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (BPF_CLASS(insn->code) == BPF_ALU64) {', '\t\t\t\t__mark_reg_known(regs + insn->dst_reg,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t insn->imm);', '\t\t\t} else {', '\t\t\t\t__mark_reg_known(regs + insn->dst_reg,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t (u32)insn->imm);', '\t\t\t}']}
description: The check_alu_op function in kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.4 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging incorrect sign extension.

code_evidence: In the BPF_MOV|BPF_K immediate path, the destination register is set to SCALAR_VALUE and its known value is recorded via __mark_reg_known(regs + insn->dst_reg, insn->imm). The same treatment is applied regardless of whether the class is BPF_ALU64 or BPF_ALU, so a 32-bit ALU MOV of a negative immediate is tracked as a sign-extended 64-bit value rather than a zero-extended 32-bit value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The incorrect sign extension corrupts verifier-tracked register bounds, and the supported consequence is out-of-bounds reads/writes on a memory buffer, matching CWE-119. The root cause is the missing class-dependent masking, but the target weakness is the resulting out-of-bounds memory operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The verifier records an incorrect 64-bit known value for 32-bit BPF_ALU MOV immediates because insn->imm is not masked to u32 in the 32-bit case. This mis-tracks register bounds, so later ALU/memory operations can compute offsets the verifier believes are in range, allowing out-of-bounds map-value access and memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Add support for different number of page table levels dependent
on the highest address used for a process. This will cause a 31 bit
process to use a two level page table instead of the four level page
table that is the default after the pud has been introduced. Likewise
a normal 64 bit process will use three levels instead of four. Only
if a process runs out of the 4 tera bytes which can be addressed with
a three level page table the fourth level is dynamically added. Then
the process can use up to 8 peta byte.

commit_msg:
The server is failing to apply the umask when creating new objects on
filesystems without ACL support.

To reproduce this, you need to use NFSv4.2 and a client and server
recent enough to support umask, and you need to export a filesystem that
lacks ACL support (for example, ext4 with the "noacl" mount option).

Filesystems with ACL support are expected to take care of the umask
themselves (usually by calling posix_acl_create).

For filesystems without ACL support, this is up to the caller of
vfs_create(), vfs_mknod(), or vfs_mkdir().

Reported-by: Elliott Mitchell <ehem+debian@m5p.com>
Reported-by: Salvatore Bonaccorso <carnil@debian.org>
Tested-by: Salvatore Bonaccorso <carnil@debian.org>
Fixes: 47057abde515 ("nfsd: add support for the umask attribute")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: J. Bruce Fields <bfields@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!IS_POSIXACL(dirp))', '\t\tiap->ia_mode &= ~current_umask();', '']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.7.8, fs/nfsd/vfs.c (in the NFS server) can set incorrect permissions on new filesystem objects when the filesystem lacks ACL support, aka CID-22cf8419f131. This occurs because the current umask is not considered.

code_evidence: When ATTR_MODE is absent, iap->ia_mode is zeroed; otherwise the client-supplied mode is used unchanged.
iap->ia_mode is passed directly to vfs_create; the function never applies current_umask(), so for filesystems lacking POSIX ACL support the umask is not honored.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function assigns permissions to a newly created critical resource (a file) that are looser than intended because the umask constraint is omitted, matching CWE-732's incorrect permission assignment. It is not an authorization-check weakness (CWE-285), since the mode is set rather than a permission being validated.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!(iap->ia_valid & ATTR_MODE))
iap->ia_mode = 0;
host_err = vfs_create(dirp, dchild, iap->ia_mode, true);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: do_nfsd_create assigns the requested creation mode to the new file without masking it by the process umask. Trigger: an NFS client creates a file on an export whose filesystem lacks ACL support (so posix_acl_create does not apply the umask). Consequence: the new object receives broader permissions than the umask permits, allowing unintended actors to read or modify it.

commit_msg:
Fix invalid read in gdImageCreateFromTiffPtr()

tiff_invalid_read.tiff is corrupt, and causes an invalid read in
gdImageCreateFromTiffPtr(), but not in gdImageCreateFromTiff(). The culprit
is dynamicGetbuf(), which doesn't check for out-of-bound reads. In this case,
dynamicGetbuf() is called with a negative dp->pos, but also positive buffer
overflows have to be handled, in which case 0 has to be returned (cf. commit
75e29a9).

Fixing dynamicGetbuf() exhibits that the corrupt TIFF would still create
the image, because the return value of TIFFReadRGBAImage() is not checked.
We do that, and let createFromTiffRgba() fail if TIFFReadRGBAImage() fails.

This issue had been reported by Ibrahim El-Sayed to security@libgd.org.

CVE-2016-6911
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t/* 2.0.34: EOF is incorrect. We use 0 for', '\t\t\t * errors and EOF, just like fileGetbuf,', '\t\t\t * which is a simple fread() wrapper.', '\t\t\t * TBB. Original bug report: Daniel Cowgill. */', '\t\t\treturn 0; /* NOT EOF */'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (dp->pos < 0 || dp->pos >= dp->realSize) {', '\t\treturn 0;', '\t}', '', '\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t}', '', '\tif (dp->pos + rlen > dp->realSize) {', '\t\trlen = dp->realSize - dp->pos;']}
description: The dynamicGetbuf function in the GD Graphics Library (aka libgd) before 2.2.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted TIFF image.

code_evidence: Line 8 computes remain from dp->logicalSize - dp->pos without validating dp->pos, so a negative or oversized dp->pos yields an unchecked offset. Lines 9-16 only bound rlen by len/remain, and line 17 performs memcpy from dp->data + dp->pos with that rlen, reading outside the intended buffer when dp->pos is negative or dp->pos + rlen exceeds the real allocation.

commit_msg:
parse_tags: don't recurse for nested \t()

This fixes https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=4892
(stack overflow on deeply nested \t()).

This is possible because parentheses do not nest and the first ')'
terminates the whole tag. Thus something like \t(\t(\t(\t(\t() can be
read in a simple loop with no recursion required. Recursion is also
not required if the ')' is missing entirely and the outermost \t(...
never ends.

See https://github.com/libass/libass/pull/296 for more backstory.

description: An issue has been found in pdfalto through 0.2. It is a heap-based buffer overflow in the function TextPage::dump in XmlAltoOutputDev.cc.

code_evidence: A 10-byte heap buffer tmp is allocated once per word iteration via malloc(10*sizeof(char)); this fixed size is the destination for numeric formatting.
sprintf writes the formatted width and height of an inline image into tmp with no bound on the produced length, so a large coordinate value can exceed the 10-byte allocation.

sprintf formats X/Y/width/height of each image into this 10-byte buffer; long numeric output overflows the heap allocation before xmlNewProp reads tmp.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes formatted numeric data past the end of a heap-allocated buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is not merely a read overrun; the sprintf call modifies memory beyond the intended allocation.

char* tmp;
tmp=(char*)malloc(10*sizeof(char));

char* tmp;
tmp=(char*)malloc(10*sizeof(char));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fixed 10-byte heap buffers are used as sprintf destinations for attacker-influenced image geometry values. Trigger: a PDF whose image coordinates/dimensions format to more than 10 bytes (including sign and terminator) causes sprintf to write past the allocation; the consequence is heap memory corruption potentially leading to crash or code execution.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tlength = minus + ((integer)? (txSize)c_floor(c_log(integer) / c_log(radix)) : 0) + 1;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tlength = minus + ((integer)? (txSize)c_floor(c_log1p(integer) / c_log(radix)) : 0) + 1;']}
description: Moddable SDK v11.5.0 was discovered to contain an invalid memory access vulnerability via the component __asan_memmove.

code_evidence: Line 58 computes the integer-part buffer size from c_log(integer)/c_log(radix); for integer values near 1 the log is near 0, under-sizing length. Line 64 allocates length+1+mxFractionPartLength+1, line 93 writes the terminator at dot[i++], line 94 adds i to length, and line 95 rewinds string to dot. In the fractionless branch lines 99-101 allocate length and write backwards from the end. Lines 116-119 compute minus as the offset already consumed by backwards digit writes and memmove length bytes from string, so an underestimated length makes the source offset and copy length inconsistent with the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes digits and a terminator into a heap chunk sized by an underestimated length, then memmoves beyond the intended buffer bounds; this is an out-of-bounds memory buffer operation, fitting CWE-119. The patch replacing c_log with c_log1p corrects the size computation, consistent with a boundary error rather than an unrelated weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the integer-part length is derived from c_log(integer), which undercounts for integer values near 1, so the allocated chunk is too small for the digits/terminator actually written. Trigger: Number.prototype.toString with a non-10 radix and a value whose integer part is close to 1. Consequence: out-of-bounds writes and a memmove reading/writing past the chunk, matching the reported invalid memory access in __asan_memmove.

commit_msg:
Reject extraneous data after SSL or GSS encryption handshake.

The server collects up to a bufferload of data whenever it reads data
from the client socket.  When SSL or GSS encryption is requested
during startup, any additional data received with the initial
request message remained in the buffer, and would be treated as
already-decrypted data once the encryption handshake completed.
Thus, a man-in-the-middle with the ability to inject data into the
TCP connection could stuff some cleartext data into the start of
a supposedly encryption-protected database session.

This could be abused to send faked SQL commands to the server,
although that would only work if the server did not demand any
authentication data.  (However, a server relying on SSL certificate
authentication might well not do so.)

To fix, throw a protocol-violation error if the internal buffer
is not empty after the encryption handshake.

Our thanks to Jacob Champion for reporting this problem.

Security: CVE-2021-23214
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -112,6 +112,18 @@
 #endif
 
 		/*
+		 * At this point we should have no data already buffered.  If we do,
+		 * it was received before we performed the SSL handshake, so it wasn't
+		 * encrypted and indeed may have been injected by a man-in-the-middle.
+		 * We report this case to the client.
+		 */
+		if (pq_buffer_has_data())
+			ereport(FATAL,
+					(errcode(ERRCODE_PROTOCOL_VIOLATION),
+					 errmsg("received unencrypted data after SSL request"),
+					 errdetail("This could be either a client-software bug or evidence of an attempted man-in-the-middle attack.")));
+
+		/*
 		 * regular startup packet, cancel, etc packet should follow, but not
 		 * another SSL negotiation request, and a GSS request should only
 		 * follow if SSL was rejected (client may negotiate in either order)
@@ -142,6 +154,18 @@
 		if (GSSok == 'G' && secure_open_gssapi(port) == -1)
 			return STATUS_ERROR;
 #endif
+
+		/*

description: In parseInputs of ShimPreparedModel.cpp, there is a possible out of bounds read due to improper input validation. This could lead to local information disclosure with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: The input loop iterates over request.inputs and indexes model.getInputs()[i] without verifying that the caller-supplied request.inputs.size() does not exceed the model's input count.
The output loop similarly indexes model.getOutputs()[i] using the request.outputs index, again with no bound check against the model's output count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the model input/output vectors because request sizes are not validated against model sizes, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. This is a read overrun, not a write, so CWE-125 fits rather than an out-of-bounds write weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loops bound their iteration by the attacker-influenced request.inputs/outputs sizes while indexing the fixed-size model.getInputs()/getOutputs() vectors. A request whose inputs or outputs exceed the model's declared counts drives the index past the vector end, causing an out-of-bounds read of operand indices; the added commit check confirms this validation was missing. Consequence is out-of-bounds memory read leading to local information disclosure.

commit_msg:
commit c095508770aebf1b9218e77026e48345d719b17c upstream.

When args->nr_local is 0, nr_pages gets also 0 due some size
calculation via rds_rm_size(), which is later used to allocate
pages for DMA, this bug produces a heap Out-Of-Bound write access
to a specific memory region.

Signed-off-by: Mohamed Ghannam <simo.ghannam@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
Signed-off-by: Ben Hutchings <ben@decadent.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (args->nr_local == 0)', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;']}
description: In the Linux kernel through 3.2, the rds_message_alloc_sgs() function does not validate a value that is used during DMA page allocation, leading to a heap-based out-of-bounds write (related to the rds_rdma_extra_size function in net/rds/rdma.c).

code_evidence: tot_pages is initialized to 0 at line 5 and only incremented inside the loop at line 16; the loop at line 9 runs only while i < args->nr_local. With args->nr_local == 0 the loop body never executes, so tot_pages remains 0 and line 20 returns 0 as the extra-size value. No check rejects the zero-length local vector before this computation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The zero-size return drives an undersized allocation that is subsequently written beyond its end, which is precisely an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The weakness is the missing nr_local != 0 constraint enabling the bad size, not merely an integer overflow or NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: rds_rdma_extra_size returns 0 for an empty local vector because the accumulation loop is skipped, without validating nr_local. That zero size is later used to allocate DMA/scatterlist pages, and the caller proceeds to write scatterlist entries into the undersized allocation, producing a heap out-of-bounds write. Trigger: a user-supplied RDMA args with nr_local == 0; consequence: memory corruption past the allocated buffer.

Correct the guard to account for the size of the array of updates, as sizeof(nfts_upd) is always 2 bytes, regardless of how many updates there actually are.

description: In version 4.8.0 and earlier of The Sleuth Kit (TSK), there is a heap-based buffer over-read in ntfs_dinode_lookup in fs/ntfs.c.

code_evidence: The guard only checks upd_off + sizeof(ntfs_upd) against mft_rsize_b, ignoring how many update-sequence entries upd_cnt declares, so the check does not bound the upd array that is later indexed.
upd is placed at a_buf + upd_off and upd->upd_val is read immediately; the allowed region is only validated for a single ntfs_upd, not for upd_cnt entries.
The loop iterates i from 1 to upd_cnt-1 and reads &upd->upd_seq + (i-1)*2 at lines 188-189 and 200-203, indexing past the validated ntfs_upd when upd_cnt is large relative to the space after upd_off.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads update-sequence bytes through pointers derived from unvalidated upd_cnt, past the intended buffer. That is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); it is not a write, and the loop's offset guard does not constrain the upd array access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size check at 164 accounts only for one ntfs_upd (sizeof is fixed), not for the upd_cnt entries the loop dereferences. Trigger: a crafted MFT entry with a large upd_cnt and an upd_off near the buffer end passes the guard, then the loop reads upd->upd_seq beyond the intended buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read.

description: An issue was discovered in LINBIT csync2 through 2.0. It does not correctly check for the return value GNUTLS_E_WARNING_ALERT_RECEIVED of the gnutls_handshake() function. It neglects to call this function again, as required by the design of the API.

code_evidence: The return value of gnutls_handshake() is stored in err and dispatched through switch(err). The GNUTLS_E_WARNING_ALERT_RECEIVED case only logs the alert and breaks, so control falls to csync_conn_usessl = 1 without re-invoking gnutls_handshake().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-252 because the function mishandles the return value from gnutls_handshake(): the warning-alert return is not acted upon as the API requires, so the required follow-up call is skipped. It is not a simple missing-null check but an incomplete branch on a distinct return code, which still leaves the return value's required semantics unchecked.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code treats GNUTLS_E_WARNING_ALERT_RECEIVED as a terminal outcome, while the GnuTLS API requires the handshake to be called again after a warning alert. Trigger: a peer sends a warning alert during the handshake, causing gnutls_handshake() to return that value. The session is then marked as SSL-established despite an incomplete handshake, leaving the connection in an unexpected state rather than continuing or aborting the handshake.

commit_msg: Fix some pipelines to be safe if downstream write fails (fuzz issue 28262)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    this->offset = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    this->offset = 0;']}
description: QPDF 9.x through 9.1.1 and 10.x through 10.0.4 has a heap-based buffer overflow in Pl_ASCII85Decoder::write (called from Pl_AES_PDF::flush and Pl_AES_PDF::finish) when a certain downstream write fails.

code_evidence: After rijndael_process fills outbuf, bytes starts at buf_size and is decremented by last when padding strip succeeds (line 63). getNext()->write(outbuf, bytes) is called at line 67, and offset is reset only after that call at line 68.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an out-of-bounds write triggered by inconsistent decoder state after a failed downstream write, matching CWE-787. It is not merely a logic error because the stale offset directly enables writing beyond the intended buffer on the next operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The buffer length is computed and passed to the downstream write before this->offset is cleared. If the downstream write fails (throws or aborts), offset retains buf_size and the buffer state is inconsistent; a subsequent flush/decoder write can then operate on stale, over-long data, leading to an out-of-bounds write. The root cause is the ordering of state reset relative to the failing downstream call.

commit_msg:
(for 4.9.3) CVE-2018-16227/IEEE 802.11: add a missing bounds check

ieee802_11_print() tried to access the Mesh Flags subfield of the Mesh
Control field to find the size of the latter and increment the expected
802.11 header length before checking it is fully present in the input
buffer. Add an intermediate bounds check to make it safe.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Ryan Ackroyd.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (caplen < hdrlen + 1) {', '\t\t\tND_PRINT((ndo, "%s", tstr));', '\t\t\treturn hdrlen;', '\t\t}']}
description: The IEEE 802.11 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-802_11.c for the Mesh Flags subfield.

code_evidence: At lines 32-35, when the H flag is set and the frame is a QoS data frame, extract_mesh_header_length(p+hdrlen) dereferences p+hdrlen before any check that hdrlen is within caplen; hdrlen was computed from the frame control at line 26 and may equal or exceed caplen.

The only bounds check, lines 38-41, occurs after hdrlen has already been incremented by the mesh length, so it does not protect the read at line 34; the fix adds an intermediate caplen < hdrlen + 1 check before this access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads a byte at p+hdrlen before confirming hdrlen is within the captured buffer, directly matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. It is not a write or an integer overflow; the defect is a missing bounds check preceding a buffer access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mesh header length is read from p+hdrlen without first verifying that at least one byte at that offset is captured. Trigger: a truncated 802.11 QoS data frame with the H flag set, where hdrlen reaches the captured length. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of the packet buffer (information disclosure or crash), as fixed by the added check.

commit_msg:
Do not dereference PKCS7 object data if not set

Fixes CVE-2023-0216

Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (p7->d.ptr == NULL)', '        return NULL;']}
description:
An invalid pointer dereference on read can be triggered when an
application tries to load malformed PKCS7 data with the
d2i_PKCS7(), d2i_PKCS7_bio() or d2i_PKCS7_fp() functions.

The result of the dereference is an application crash which could
lead to a denial of service attack. The TLS implementation in OpenSSL
does not call this function however third party applications might
call these functions on untrusted data.

code_evidence: The function dereferences p7 through p7->d.signed_and_enveloped->recipientinfo and p7->d.enveloped->recipientinfo after only type checks, with no check that p7->d.ptr (the union data pointer) is non-NULL. The type macros inspect p7->type, so a malformed PKCS7 object can pass a type check while d.ptr remains NULL, causing the subsequent member dereference to read through a NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code dereferences a pointer it assumes valid without checking for NULL, matching CWE-476 NULL Pointer Dereference. This is not a generic invalid-pointer issue; the specific defect is the missing NULL check before dereferencing d.ptr, and the patch adds exactly that guard.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the union data pointer d.ptr is dereferenced without a NULL guard. Trigger: an application calls d2i_PKCS7()/d2i_PKCS7_bio()/d2i_PKCS7_fp() on malformed PKCS7 data whose type passes PKCS7_type_is_signedAndEnveloped or PKCS7_type_is_enveloped but whose d.ptr is NULL. Consequence: invalid pointer dereference on read, crashing the application (denial of service).

commit_msg:
Lossless decomp: Range-limit 12-bit samples

12-bit is the only data precision for which the range of the sample data
type exceeds the valid sample range, so it is possible to craft a 12-bit
lossless JPEG image that contains out-of-range 12-bit samples.
Attempting to decompress such an image using color quantization or merged
upsampling (NOTE: libjpeg-turbo cannot generate YCbCr or subsampled
lossless JPEG images, but it can decompress them) caused segfaults or
buffer overruns when those algorithms attempted to use the out-of-range
sample values as array indices.  This commit modifies the lossless
decompressor so that it range-limits the output of the scaler when using
12-bit samples.

Fixes #670
Fixes #672
Fixes #673
Fixes #674
Fixes #675
Fixes #676
Fixes #677
Fixes #678
Fixes #679
Fixes #681
Fixes #683
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#if BITS_IN_JSAMPLE == 12', '    *output_buf++ = (_JSAMPLE)((*diff_buf++) & 0xFFF);', '#else', '#endif']}
description: A heap-based buffer overflow issue was discovered in libjpeg-turbo in h2v2_merged_upsample_internal() function of jdmrgext.c file. The vulnerability can only be exploited with 12-bit data precision for which the range of the sample data type exceeds the valid sample range, hence, an attacker could craft a 12-bit lossless JPEG image that contains out-of-range 12-bit samples. An application attempting to decompress such image using merged upsampling would lead to segmentation fault or buffer overflows, causing an application to crash.

code_evidence: The loop copies each diff_buf sample to output_buf via a cast to _JSAMPLE with no range check: *output_buf++ = (_JSAMPLE)(*diff_buf++). For 12-bit precision, _JSAMPLE can hold values beyond the valid sample range, so out-of-range samples pass through unchanged to downstream consumers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked out-of-range sample propagates and is later used as an index, producing a write outside the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. The defect here is the missing constraint enabling the out-of-bounds write rather than an integer overflow itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing range limit on the scaler output; the cast does not constrain the value. Trigger: a crafted 12-bit lossless JPEG yields out-of-range samples that this noscale function forwards. Consequence: downstream merged upsampling/color quantization uses these values as array indices, causing out-of-bounds writes (segfault or buffer overrun).

description: Poppler prior to and including 22.08.0 contains an integer overflow in the JBIG2 decoder (JBIG2Stream::readTextRegionSeg() in JBIGStream.cc). Processing a specially crafted PDF file or JBIG2 image could lead to a crash or the execution of arbitrary code. This is similar to the vulnerability described by CVE-2022-38171 in Xpdf.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked addition numSyms += getSize() is an integer wraparound in a size computation used for allocation, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a bounds-check omission; the arithmetic itself can overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unbounded unsigned accumulation of segment symbol counts into numSyms. Trigger: a crafted JBIG2 file with many/large symbol dictionary references causes numSyms to wrap to a small value. Consequence: the allocation-size guard is defeated, leading to undersized allocation and later out-of-bounds writes when syms is filled.

commit_msg:
Simplify the timerqueue code by using cached rbtrees and rely on the tree
leftmost node semantics to get the timer with earliest expiration time.
This is a drop in conversion, and therefore semantics remain untouched.

The runtime overhead of cached rbtrees is be pretty much the same as the
current head->next method, noting that when removing the leftmost node,
a common operation for the timerqueue, the rb_next(leftmost) is O(1) as
well, so the next timer will either be the right node or its parent.
Therefore no extra pointer chasing. Finally, the size of the struct
timerqueue_head remains the same.

Passes several hours of rcutorture.

Signed-off-by: Davidlohr Bueso <dbueso@suse.de>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190724152323.bojciei3muvfxalm@linux-r8p5
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\thead->head = RB_ROOT;', '\thead->next = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['\thead->rb_root = RB_ROOT_CACHED;']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. A corrupted timer tree caused the task wakeup to be missing in the timerqueue_add function in lib/timerqueue.c. This flaw allows a local attacker with special user privileges to cause a denial of service, slowing and eventually stopping the system while running OSP.

code_evidence: timerqueue_init_head initializes the head's rb tree root and cached leftmost pointer. The pre-patch function sets head->head = RB_ROOT and head->next = NULL; the patch replaces these with head->rb_root = RB_ROOT_CACHED, initializing both the root node and the cached leftmost pointer in one assignment.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-665 (Improper Initialization) is the target; the function is exactly an initialization routine and its assignment initializes the cached rbtree root and leftmost cache. However, the code shown correctly initializes the resource, so it does not itself exhibit the improper initialization described. The evidence supports the initialization context but not a defect.

evidence_lines.code:
head->head = RB_ROOT;
head->next = NULL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cached-rbtree conversion must fully initialize the cached leftmost pointer stored in the rb_root struct. The function does so via RB_ROOT_CACHED; if the cached pointer were left uninitialized, timerqueue_add/remove navigating from the cached leftmost node could access a stale node, corrupting the timer tree and causing missed task wakeups (DoS). The trigger requires the initialization to be incomplete, which is not the case here.

commit_msg:
Fix small OOB reads.

In ssl3_get_client_certificate, ssl3_get_server_certificate and
ssl3_get_certificate_request check we have enough room
before reading a length.

Thanks to Shi Lei (Gear Team, Qihoo 360 Inc.) for reporting these bugs.

CVE-2016-6306

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
(cherry picked from commit ff553f837172ecb2b5c8eca257ec3c5619a4b299)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (nc + 3 > llen) {', '            al = SSL_AD_DECODE_ERROR;', '            SSLerr(SSL_F_SSL3_GET_SERVER_CERTIFICATE,', '                   SSL_R_CERT_LENGTH_MISMATCH);', '            goto f_err;', '        }']}
description: The certificate parser in OpenSSL before 1.0.1u and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2i might allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via crafted certificate operations, related to s3_clnt.c and s3_srvr.c.

code_evidence: The loop iterates while nc < llen over the server certificate message buffer. Each iteration calls n2l3(p, l) to read a 3-byte length from p without first checking that 3 bytes remain (nc + 3 <= llen). If fewer than 3 bytes remain, n2l3 reads past the end of the received message buffer. The subsequent check (l + nc + 3) > llen occurs only after the length has already been read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads memory past the end of the intended buffer due to a missing length check before n2l3. This is an out-of-bounds read, not an out-of-bounds write or integer overflow; the added nc + 3 > llen guard confirms the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser trusts that at least 3 bytes remain for each certificate length field, but a crafted certificate message with trailing 1–2 bytes leaves too few bytes. n2l3 then reads beyond the message buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read that can crash the process (DoS) or leak adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
MDEV-26561 mariabackup release locks

The previous threads locked need to be released too.

This occurs if the initialization of any of the non-first
mutex/conditition variables errors occurs.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\twhile (i > 0) {', '\t\tcomp_thread_ctxt_t *thd;', '\t\ti--;', '\t\tthd = threads + i;', '\t\tpthread_mutex_unlock(&thd->ctrl_mutex);', '\t}', '']}
description: MariaDB Server before 10.7 is vulnerable to Denial of Service. In extra/mariabackup/ds_compress.cc, when an error occurs (i.e., going to the err label) while executing the method create_worker_threads, the held lock thd->ctrl_mutex is not released correctly, which allows local users to trigger a denial of service due to the deadlock.

code_evidence: If mutex/condition initialization fails, control jumps to err without any lock held, but earlier iterations may have left ctrl_mutex locked.
After pthread_mutex_lock, a pthread_create failure unlocks only the current thread's ctrl_mutex and jumps to err; locks held by previously created threads remain locked.
The err label frees threads and returns NULL without releasing any ctrl_mutex held by earlier iterations, leaving locks held.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 covers improper acquisition/release of locks leading to unexpected state and DoS; the missing unlock of held ctrl_mutex on the err path directly matches this, distinct from a race on shared data.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path does not release ctrl_mutex locks acquired in earlier loop iterations (line 26) before jumping to err. Trigger: any init or pthread_create failure after at least one successful locked iteration. Consequence: worker threads block on ctrl_mutex, causing deadlock and denial of service.

description: Moonlight-common-c contains the core GameStream client code shared between Moonlight clients. Moonlight-common-c is vulnerable to buffer overflow starting in commit f57bd745b4cbed577ea654fad4701bea4d38b44c. A malicious game streaming server could exploit a buffer overflow vulnerability to crash a moonlight client. Achieving RCE is possible but unlikely, due to stack canaries in use by modern compiler toolchains. The published binaries for official clients Qt, Android, iOS/tvOS, and Embedded are built with stack canaries, but some unofficial clients may not use stack canaries. This vulnerability takes place after the pairing process, so it requires the client to be tricked into pairing to a malicious host. It is not possible to perform using a man-in-the-middle due to public key pinning that takes place during the pairing process. The bug was addressed in commit b2497a3918a6d79808d9fd0c04734786e70d5954.

code_evidence: Line 2 declares a fixed 128-byte stack buffer, and line 6 copies the caller-supplied 'string' into it with strcpy without any length check. Line 7 then points nextNumber at this copied buffer, so the unbounded copy is the operation feeding the later parsing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 directly matches a buffer copy without checking input size: strcpy writes the input into a fixed-size destination with no bound. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read, since the flaw is the unchecked write past versionString.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an attacker-controlled version string longer than 127 bytes is copied into a 128-byte stack buffer via strcpy with no size validation. Trigger: a malicious server sends such a version string during post-pairing parsing. Consequence: stack buffer overflow, causing a crash and potentially memory corruption; code execution is constrained by stack canaries.

commit_msg:
problem: zeromq connects peer before handshake is completed

Solution: delay connecting the peer pipe until the handshake is completed
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    //  Create the pipe if it does not exist yet.', '    if (!_pipe && !is_terminating ()) {', '        object_t *parents[2] = {this, _socket};', '        pipe_t *pipes[2] = {NULL, NULL};', '', '        const bool conflate = get_effective_conflate_option (options);', '', '        int hwms[2] = {conflate ? -1 : options.rcvhwm,', '                       conflate ? -1 : options.sndhwm};', '        bool conflates[2] = {conflate, conflate};', '        const int rc = pipepair (parents, pipes, hwms, conflates);', '        errno_assert (rc == 0);', '', '        //  Plug the local end of the pipe.', '        pipes[0]->set_event_sink (this);', '', '        //  Remember the local end of the pipe.', '        zmq_assert (!_pipe);', '        _pipe = pipes[0];', '', '        //  The endpoints strings are not set on bind, set them here so that', '        //  events can use them.', '        pipes[0]->set_endpoint_pair (engine_->get_endpoint ());', '        pipes[1]->set_endpoint_pair (engine_->get_endpoint ());', '', '        //  Ask socket to plug into the remote end of the pipe.', '        send_bind (_socket, pipes[1]);', '    }', '    zmq_assert (!_engine);', '    _engine = engine_;'], 'added_lines': ['    zmq_assert (!_engine);', '    _engine = engine_;', '    if (!engine_->has_handshake_stage ())', '        engine_ready ();']}
description: In ZeroMQ before version 4.3.3, there is a denial-of-service vulnerability. Users with TCP transport public endpoints, even with CURVE/ZAP enabled, are impacted. If a raw TCP socket is opened and connected to an endpoint that is fully configured with CURVE/ZAP, legitimate clients will not be able to exchange any message. Handshakes complete successfully, and messages are delivered to the library, but the server application never receives them. This is patched in version 4.3.3.

code_evidence: process_attach creates a pipe pair and immediately calls send_bind to attach the remote pipe to the socket whenever _pipe is absent, without checking whether the engine has completed its handshake.
The engine is stored and plugged in only after the pipe has already been created and bound, so the pipe becomes reachable before authentication/handshake state is established.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Premature pipe creation and binding without handshake gating lets unauthenticated connections consume limited pipe/session resources, producing a denial of service; this is uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400), distinct from a missing authentication check alone.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function binds and exposes a pipe to the socket as soon as an engine attaches, gated only on _pipe and termination, not on handshake completion. A raw TCP peer that connects to a CURVE/ZAP endpoint can therefore cause a pipe to be created and bound before authentication completes, consuming session/pipe resources and blocking legitimate clients from exchanging messages.

Both btrfs_find_device() and find_device() does the same thing except

commit_msg:
Disable sub frame loads more reliably in frame detach.

Previously, guarding against attaching a new frame in frame detach
was done by inspecting LoadEventProgress. There are certain
operations, such as document.open(), that can cause LoadEventProgress
to never advance, causing the guard to get skipped.

BUG=577105

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1659013003

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#373581}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ["    // Don't allow any new child frames to load in this frame: attaching a new", '    // child frame during or after detaching children results in an attached', '    // frame on a detached DOM tree, which is bad.', '    SubframeLoadingDisabler disabler(m_frame->document());']}
description: The DOM implementation in Google Chrome before 48.0.2564.109 does not properly restrict frame-attach operations from occurring during or after frame-detach operations, which allows remote attackers to bypass the Same Origin Policy via a crafted web site, related to FrameLoader.cpp, HTMLFrameOwnerElement.h, LocalFrame.cpp, and WebLocalFrameImpl.cpp.

code_evidence: stopAllLoaders() is called, then detachChildren() and document()->detach() tear down the current document tree, and clear() resets loader state. No SubframeLoadingDisabler or equivalent guard is established before detaching, so frame-attach operations remain permitted during/after detach.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing restriction on frame-attach during detach is an access-control/permission enforcement gap, matching CWE-264's permissions and security-feature management category; the fix adds SubframeLoadingDisabler to enforce that restriction.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: detaching children and the document without first disabling subframe loads allows a new child frame to be attached to a detached DOM tree. Trigger: script operations during document replacement (e.g., document.open()) can attach frames while detach proceeds. Supported consequence: an attached frame persists on a detached tree, enabling same-origin policy bypass.

commit_msg:
xen/arm: p2m: Don't check the return of p2m_get_root_pointer() with BUG_ON()

It turns out that the BUG_ON() was actually reachable with well-crafted
hypercalls. The BUG_ON() is here to prevent catch logical error, so
crashing Xen is a bit over the top.

While all the holes should now be fixed, it would be better to downgrade
the BUG_ON() to something less fatal to prevent any more DoS.

The BUG_ON() in p2m_get_entry() is now replaced by ASSERT_UNREACHABLE()
to catch mistake in debug build and return INVALID_MFN for production
build. The interface also requires to set page_order to give an idea of
the size of "hole". So 'level' is now set so we report a hole of size of
the an entry of the root page-table. This stays inline with what happen
when the GFN is higher than p2m->max_mapped_gfn.

The BUG_ON() in p2m_resolve_translation_fault() is now replaced by
ASSERT_UNREACHABLE() to catch mistake in debug build and just report a
fault for producion build.

This is part of XSA-301.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <Julien.Grall@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    BUG_ON(table == NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( !table )', '    {', '        ASSERT_UNREACHABLE();', '        level = P2M_ROOT_LEVEL;', '        goto out;', '    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing ARM guest OS users to cause a denial of service via a XENMEM_add_to_physmap hypercall. p2m->max_mapped_gfn is used by the functions p2m_resolve_translation_fault() and p2m_get_entry() to sanity check guest physical frame. The rest of the code in the two functions will assume that there is a valid root table and check that with BUG_ON(). The function p2m_get_root_pointer() will ignore the unused top bits of a guest physical frame. This means that the function p2m_set_entry() will alias the frame. However, p2m->max_mapped_gfn will be updated using the original frame. It would be possible to set p2m->max_mapped_gfn high enough to cover a frame that would lead p2m_get_root_pointer() to return NULL in p2m_get_entry() and p2m_resolve_translation_fault(). Additionally, the sanity check on p2m->max_mapped_gfn is off-by-one allowing "highest mapped + 1" to be considered valid. However, p2m_get_root_pointer() will return NULL. The problem could be triggered with a specially crafted hypercall XENMEM_add_to_physmap{, _batch} followed by an access to an address (via hypercall or direct access) that passes the sanity check but cause p2m_get_root_pointer() to return NULL. A malicious guest administrator may cause a hypervisor crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS). Xen version 4.8 and newer are vulnerable. Only Arm systems are vulnerable. x86 systems are not affected.

code_evidence: The sanity check uses a strict '>' comparison against p2m->max_mapped_gfn, so a gfn equal to 'highest mapped + 1' passes and is treated as valid.
After passing the check, p2m_get_root_pointer() is called and its NULL result is fatal via BUG_ON(table == NULL), crashing the hypervisor.
The out path dereferences level_orders[level] using the level value derived from the off-by-one path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-193 fits because the maximum mapped GFN is validated with an incorrect boundary (using '>' rather than '>='), allowing a value one greater than the intended maximum to be accepted. The BUG_ON then turns this off-by-one acceptance into a crash, matching the DoS scope of CWE-193.

evidence_lines.code:
table = p2m_get_root_pointer(p2m, gfn);
BUG_ON(table == NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The boundary comparison at line 19 admits a guest physical frame one past the highest mapped GFN. That frame can make p2m_get_root_pointer() return NULL, which the BUG_ON at line 28 converts into a hypervisor crash. Root cause is the off-by-one maximum check; trigger is a crafted XENMEM_add_to_physmap hypercall followed by an access; supported consequence is denial of service.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions an attacker can cause undefined behavior via binding a reference to null pointer in all operations of type `tf.raw_ops.MatrixSetDiagV*`. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/84d053187cb80d975ef2b9684d4b61981bca0c41/tensorflow/core/kernels/linalg/matrix_diag_op.cc) has incomplete validation that the value of `k` is a valid tensor. We have check that this value is either a scalar or a vector, but there is no check for the number of elements. If this is an empty tensor, then code that accesses the first element of the tensor is wrong. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit ff8894044dfae5568ecbf2ed514c1a37dc394f1b. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's defect is an unchecked empty diag_index tensor leading to out-of-bounds element access at line 14, not use of an uninitialized pointer; no pointer initialization issue is present.

description: stb stb_image.h 2.19, as used in catimg, Emscripten, and other products, has a heap-based buffer overflow in the stbi__out_gif_code function.

Trigger: a crafted GIF header with large dimensions. The undersized heap buffers are then written past their ends by the memset/allocations, corrupting heap memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

description: GPAC MP4Box 2.1-DEV-rev644-g5c4df2a67 is has an integer overflow in isomedia/isom_write.c

code_evidence: Line 10 subtracts the signed 32-bit offset_shift from each entry's decodingOffset in place, with no bound check on the result; the subtraction can wrap past the s32 minimum/maximum.
Lines 12-13 subtract offset_shift from the u32 mediaHeader duration only on a signed comparison guard, so the unsigned result can wrap to a very large value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs calculations whose results can overflow/wrap the associated integer representation (s32 and u32), matching CWE-190's wraparound description. It is not CWE-191 (underflow of unsigned subtraction) because the target is the representational overflow of signed/unsigned fields, not a size/count underflow used for allocation.

evidence_lines.code: trak->Media->information->sampleTable->CompositionOffset->entries[i].decodingOffset -= offset_shift;

if (trak->Media->mediaHeader->duration >= -offset_shift)
trak->Media->mediaHeader->duration -= offset_shift;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is unchecked signed/unsigned arithmetic on caller-supplied offset_shift: decodingOffset (s32) and duration (u32) are decremented directly. A large offset_shift drives either field past its representable range, wrapping the stored value; the comparison guard at line 12 does not prevent unsigned wraparound of duration. The supported consequence is corrupted timing metadata (integrity), which can later cause miscomputed sample offsets or a crash.

description: The parse_chunk_header function in libtorrent before 1.1.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a crafted (1) HTTP response or possibly a (2) UPnP broadcast.

code_evidence: The content-length header value is parsed with strtoll into m_content_length without checking that the result is non-negative; a crafted negative value flows directly into later body-length arithmetic.

The content-range header is parsed into m_range_start and m_range_end via strtoll; the code checks parse success and m_range_end < m_range_start, but a negative start/end still passes into m_content_length = m_range_end - m_range_start + 1, leaving a derived length that can be negative or inconsistent.

The chunked-body branch trusts parse_chunk_header's chunk_size and immediately computes chunk_range and m_cur_chunk_end += header_size + chunk_size without rejecting negative sizes, feeding them into subsequent position arithmetic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function accepts externally supplied numeric header fields and fails to validate the required property (non-negativity) before using them in memory/offset calculations. The missing constraint, not a transformation error, is the root cause; this distinguishes it from filtering/encoding weaknesses.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled HTTP headers (content-length, content-range) and chunk-size values are parsed into signed integers without rejecting negative results. Trigger: a crafted HTTP response or UPnP message supplies a negative length/range/chunk size. Consequence: the negative values propagate into body-offset arithmetic (m_cur_chunk_end, m_content_length, m_recv_pos), producing invalid buffer positions and a crash (DoS).

description: Istio 1.4.x before 1.4.9 and Istio 1.5.x before 1.5.4 contain the following vulnerability when telemetry v2 is enabled: by sending a specially crafted packet, an attacker could trigger a Null Pointer Exception resulting in a Denial of Service. This could be sent to the ingress gateway or a sidecar, triggering a null pointer exception which results in a denial of service. This also affects servicemesh-proxy where a null pointer exception flaw was found in servicemesh-proxy. When running Telemetry v2 (not on by default in version 1.4.x), an attacker could send a specially crafted packet to the ingress gateway or proxy sidecar, triggering a denial of service.

code_evidence: onResponseBody checks only wasm_->onResponseBody_ before invoking the VM callback with this and id_; nothing verifies that the in-VM context has been created. When the callback is registered but the VM context is not yet initialized, the callback is still entered, and the VM-side code dereferences a null context, producing the crash.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing guard permits a callback to run against an uninitialized/null VM context that is then dereferenced, matching CWE-476. This is not merely a missing-state check; the dereference of the null context is the direct cause of the crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the response-body path lacks a guard on in_vm_context_created_ before calling into the VM callback. Trigger: a crafted response/body causes onResponseBody to run with a registered callback but no initialized VM context. Consequence: null pointer dereference crashes the proxy (DoS).

commit_msg:
ASAN SFTP Fixes
When decoding SFTP messages, fix the size checks so they don't wrap. (ZD12766)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (sz + idx > maxSz) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (sz > maxSz - idx) {']}
description: WolfSSH v1.4.7 was discovered to contain an integer overflow via the function wolfSSH_SFTP_RecvRMDIR.

code_evidence: ato32 loads the attacker-controlled length sz from the SFTP message, then the bound check computes sz + idx in word32 arithmetic. If sz is near UINT32_MAX, the addition wraps to a small value, so the check passes and the oversized sz is used downstream.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an addition (sz + idx) whose result is assumed to exceed sz, but word32 wraparound can make it small, defeating the size check exactly as CWE-190 describes. The fixed form sz > maxSz - idx avoids the overflow, confirming the arithmetic wraparound is the target weakness rather than a simple off-by-one.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length validation adds sz and idx without guarding against word32 wraparound. Trigger: a crafted SFTP SETSTAT message with a large length field makes sz + idx wrap below maxSz, bypassing the bounds check. Consequence: the unchecked sz flows into WMALLOC(sz + 1) and WMEMCPY(name, data + idx, sz), enabling out-of-bounds reads/copies and memory corruption.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif ( (miniLen <= 4) || (miniLen > (boxEnd - boxPtr)) ) continue;\t// Ignore bad or empty values.'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif ( (miniLen <= 4) || (miniLen > (boxEnd - boxPtr)) )', '\t\t\t\tbreak;\t// Ignore bad or empty values.']}
description: An issue was discovered in Exempi before 2.4.4. The TradQT_Manager::ParseCachedBoxes function in XMPFiles/source/FormatSupport/QuickTime_Support.cpp allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via crafted XMP data in a .qt file.

code_evidence: The loop advances by boxPtr += miniLen, where miniLen = 4 + GetUns16BE(boxPtr). When the guard (miniLen <= 4) || (miniLen > (boxEnd - boxPtr)) is true, the body executes continue, skipping the increment's effect on progress: boxPtr is not advanced past the offending sub-box, so the same boxPtr is re-read on the next iteration with the same miniLen.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the loop's exit condition boxPtr < boxEnd-4 becomes unreachable when continue is taken with a non-advancing miniLen. The patch changes continue to break, confirming the intended exit. This is an unreachable-exit infinite loop, not merely a bounds-check weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the invalid-length guard uses continue, which re-evaluates the loop with boxPtr unchanged instead of terminating or advancing. Trigger: crafted .qt XMP data whose sub-box length is <= 4 or exceeds the remaining content, so miniLen never moves boxPtr. Consequence: the loop never reaches boxPtr >= boxEnd-4, causing an infinite loop and CPU-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg:
tipc: fix size validations for the MSG_CRYPTO type

The function tipc_crypto_key_rcv is used to parse MSG_CRYPTO messages
to receive keys from other nodes in the cluster in order to decrypt any
further messages from them.
This patch verifies that any supplied sizes in the message body are
valid for the received message.

Fixes: 1ef6f7c9390f ("tipc: add automatic session key exchange")
Signed-off-by: Max VA <maxv@sentinelone.com>
Acked-by: Ying Xue <ying.xue@windriver.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Acked-by: Jon Maloy <jmaloy@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tgoto exit;', '\t\tgoto exit;', '\tskey->keylen = ntohl(*((__be32 *)(data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME)));', '', '\t/* Sanity check */', '\tif (unlikely(size != tipc_aead_key_size(skey))) {', '\t\tkfree(skey);', '\t\tskey = NULL;', '\t\tgoto exit;', '\t}', 'exit:'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned int keylen;', '', '\t/* Verify whether the size can exist in the packet */', '\tif (unlikely(size < sizeof(struct tipc_aead_key) + TIPC_AEAD_KEYLEN_MIN)) {', '\t\tpr_debug("%s: message data size is too small\\n", rx->name);', '\t\tgoto exit;', '\t}', '', '\tkeylen = ntohl(*((__be32 *)(data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME)));', '', '\t/* Verify the supplied size values */', '\tif (unlikely(size != keylen + sizeof(struct tipc_aead_key) ||', '\t\t     keylen > TIPC_AEAD_KEY_SIZE_MAX)) {', '\t\tpr_debug("%s: invalid MSG_CRYPTO key size\\n", rx->name);', '\t\tgoto exit;', '\t}', '\t\tgoto exit_unlock;', '\t\tgoto exit_unlock;', '\tskey->keylen = keylen;', 'exit_unlock:', 'exit:']}
description: An issue was discovered in net/tipc/crypto.c in the Linux kernel before 5.14.16. The Transparent Inter-Process Communication (TIPC) functionality allows remote attackers to exploit insufficient validation of user-supplied sizes for the MSG_CRYPTO message type.

code_evidence: The message-derived size (msg_data_sz) and data pointer are taken directly from the received MSG_CRYPTO header without checking that the payload actually contains the fields being read.

Line 19 reads a 4-byte keylen from data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME and stores it into skey->keylen. The subsequent memcpy at lines 21-22 copies skey->keylen bytes from the message into skey->key, using the unvalidated length as the copy count.

The allocation at line 14 uses size, but the only consistency check (size != tipc_aead_key_size(skey)) occurs after the copy at lines 23-27, so the attacker-controlled keylen drives the memcpy before any validation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-1284 fits because the weakness is the failure to validate a specified quantity (the keylen/size in the message) before it is used to control a memory copy. The supplied length is not checked for consistency with the actual payload or against a maximum, so an attacker-specified quantity drives the unsafe operation.

evidence_lines.code:
u16 size = msg_data_sz(hdr);
u8 *data = msg_data(hdr);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function trusts the size field and the embedded keylen from a remote MSG_CRYPTO message. keylen is read from the packet and used directly as the length for memcpy into the kmalloc'd skey, while the size-vs-keylen consistency check runs only afterward. A crafted message with an oversized keylen therefore triggers an out-of-bounds write past the allocated skey buffer, causing memory corruption.

commit_msg:
evtchn: convert per-channel lock to be IRQ-safe

... in order for send_guest_{global,vcpu}_virq() to be able to make use
of it.

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    spin_lock(&lchn->lock);', '    spin_unlock(&lchn->lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned long flags;', '    spin_lock_irqsave(&lchn->lock, flags);', '    spin_unlock_irqrestore(&lchn->lock, flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The per-channel lock is acquired with plain spin_lock, which does not disable interrupts on the local CPU.
The lock is released with plain spin_unlock, leaving the interrupt-enabled critical section unchanged.
Inside the critical section the function reads lchn->state and lchn->u.interdomain fields and calls evtchn_port_set_pending on the remote channel.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the critical section relies on a spinlock that is not IRQ-safe, so an interfering interrupt context can access the shared event-channel resource concurrently, breaking atomicity of the state check and use.

evidence_lines.code: spin_lock(&lchn->lock);
spin_unlock(&lchn->lock);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The lock protecting the event-channel state is taken without disabling interrupts. An interrupt handler on the same CPU that re-enters event-channel code and acquires the same lock can deadlock or observe/modify the channel state between the check at line 8 and its use at lines 11-13, violating the exclusivity the critical section assumes.

commit_msg:
Fix DTLS buffered message DoS attack

DTLS can handle out of order record delivery. Additionally since
handshake messages can be bigger than will fit into a single packet, the
messages can be fragmented across multiple records (as with normal TLS).
That means that the messages can arrive mixed up, and we have to
reassemble them. We keep a queue of buffered messages that are "from the
future", i.e. messages we're not ready to deal with yet but have arrived
early. The messages held there may not be full yet - they could be one
or more fragments that are still in the process of being reassembled.

The code assumes that we will eventually complete the reassembly and
when that occurs the complete message is removed from the queue at the
point that we need to use it.

However, DTLS is also tolerant of packet loss. To get around that DTLS
messages can be retransmitted. If we receive a full (non-fragmented)
message from the peer after previously having received a fragment of
that message, then we ignore the message in the queue and just use the
non-fragmented version. At that point the queued message will never get
removed.

Additionally the peer could send "future" messages that we never get to
in order to complete the handshake. Each message has a sequence number
(starting from 0). We will accept a message fragment for the current
message sequence number, or for any sequence up to 10 into the future.
However if the Finished message has a sequence number of 2, anything
greater than that in the queue is just left there.

So, in those two ways we can end up with "orphaned" data in the queue
that will never get removed - except when the connection is closed. At
that point all the queues are flushed.

An attacker could seek to exploit this by filling up the queues with
lots of large messages that are never going to be used in order to
attempt a DoS by memory exhaustion.

I will assume that we are only concerned with servers here. It does not
seem reasonable to be concerned about a memory exhaustion attack on a
client. They are unlikely to process enough connections for this to be
an issue.

A "long" handshake with many messages might be 5 messages long (in the
incoming direction), e.g. ClientHello, Certificate, ClientKeyExchange,
CertificateVerify, Finished. So this would be message sequence numbers 0
to 4. Additionally we can buffer up to 10 messages in the future.
Therefore the maximum number of messages that an attacker could send
that could get orphaned would typically be 15.

The maximum size that a DTLS message is allowed to be is defined by
max_cert_list, which by default is 100k. Therefore the maximum amount of
"orphaned" memory per connection is 1500k.

Message sequence numbers get reset after the Finished message, so
renegotiation will not extend the maximum number of messages that can be
orphaned per connection.

As noted above, the queues do get cleared when the connection is closed.
Therefore in order to mount an effective attack, an attacker would have
to open many simultaneous connections.

Issue reported by Quan Luo.

CVE-2016-2179

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>

description: The DTLS implementation in OpenSSL before 1.1.0 does not properly restrict the lifetime of queue entries associated with unused out-of-order messages, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by maintaining many crafted DTLS sessions simultaneously, related to d1_lib.c, statem_dtls.c, statem_lib.c, and statem_srvr.c.

commit_msg:
Fix handling of symbolic link ACLs

On Linux ACLs on symbolic links are not supported.
We must avoid calling acl_set_file() on symbolic links as their
targets are modified instead.

While here, do not try to set default ACLs on non-directories.

Fixes #1565
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    struct archive_acl *abstract_acl,', '\telse if (acl_set_file(name, acl_type, acl) != 0)'], 'added_lines': ['    struct archive_acl *abstract_acl, __LA_MODE_T mode,', '\t}', '', '\tif (acl_type == ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT && !S_ISDIR(mode)) {', '\t\terrno = EINVAL;', '\t\tarchive_set_error(a, errno,', '\t\t    "Cannot set default ACL on non-directory");', '\t\treturn (ARCHIVE_WARN);', '\telse if (S_ISLNK(mode)) {', '\t    /* acl_set_file() follows symbolic links, skip */', '\t    ret = ARCHIVE_OK;', '\t} else if (acl_set_file(name, acl_type, acl) != 0)']}
description: An improper link resolution flaw while extracting an archive can lead to changing the access control list (ACL) of the target of the link. An attacker may provide a malicious archive to a victim user, who would trigger this flaw when trying to extract the archive. A local attacker may use this flaw to change the ACL of a file on the system and gain more privileges.

code_evidence: The name-based ACL path calls acl_set_link_np() when available, otherwise acl_set_file(); the commit notes acl_set_file() follows symbolic links, so on platforms without acl_set_link_np a symlink name resolves to its target and the ACL is applied to the target instead of the link.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the function accesses a filesystem object by name and, in the fallback path, does not prevent the name from being a link resolving to an unintended resource. The added S_ISLNK(mode) guard confirms the fix targets link-following; the weakness is link resolution before access, not a general ACL validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the fallback branch accesses the file by name via acl_set_file() without preventing symlink resolution. Trigger: a crafted archive containing a symbolic link whose ACL entry is processed on a system without acl_set_link_np. Consequence: the ACL of the link target is modified, potentially granting or revoking access on a file outside the extraction directory.

description: In Wireshark 2.6.0 to 2.6.1, 2.4.0 to 2.4.7, and 2.2.0 to 2.2.15, the ISMP dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-ismp.c by validating the IPX address length to avoid a buffer over-read.

code_evidence: Line 175 reads tuple_length from the packet, and line 176 uses it as the subtree length before any validation. The only bound check at line 183 compares remaining length against tuple_length, but the code then treats tuple_length as the data length although it includes the 4-byte type/length header.

In the EDP_TUPLE_IPX_ADDR case, lines 200-202 call tvb_get_string_enc with tuple_length-4 starting at offset+4 without verifying the IPX address is exactly 10 bytes; a short tuple_length still permits reads beyond the tuple's actual data.

case EDP_TUPLE_IPX_ADDR:
proto_tree_add_string(edp_tuples_leaf_tree, hf_ismp_interface_ipx_address ,tvb, offset, tuple_length,

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the tuple length field is used directly as data length and the IPX address length is not constrained. Trigger: a malformed ISMP EDP packet with a short or inconsistent tuple length for an IPX address tuple. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of packet buffer data, potentially crashing the dissector.

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only passes a perturbation value to skb_get_hash_perturb and scales the resulting hash; it contains no random-value generation or secret, so it does not itself demonstrate use of insufficiently random values.

description: An issue was discovered in Exiv2 0.27. There is infinite recursion at BigTiffImage::printIFD in the file bigtiffimage.cpp. This can be triggered by a crafted file. It allows an attacker to cause Denial of Service (Segmentation fault) or possibly have unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: printIFD takes an attacker-influenced recursion depth and only stops when depth > 200, printing a message and returning; otherwise depth is incremented and processing continues.

When option is kpsRecursive and a tag is an IFD pointer (0x8769, 0x014a, tiffIfd, tiffIfd8), the function loops over count entries and calls printIFD recursively with depth, using ifdOffset read from file data.
In the makernote branch, when the prefix is not "Nikon", the code seeks to 0 and calls printIFD recursively with the same depth value, so the depth increment from the caller is bypassed on this path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the function performs recursion whose depth is not reliably controlled, consuming the program stack. The depth > 200 guard is a mitigation, but attacker-controlled offsets and the same-depth recursive call at line 150 allow recursion to continue, supporting the uncontrolled-recursion classification.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: recursion depth is bounded only by a depth counter, but crafted TIFF/BigTIFF data controls IFD entries and offsets, and the non-Nikon makernote path recurses with an unchanged depth. Trigger: a malicious file that chains IFD pointers or forces the makernote branch causes repeated recursive calls. Consequence: stack exhaustion leading to crash/denial of service.

description: A vulnerability classified as critical has been found in Linux Kernel. Affected is the function btf_dump_name_dups of the file tools/lib/bpf/btf_dump.c of the component libbpf. The manipulation leads to use after free. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211032.

code_evidence: hashmap__find retrieves a prior dup count using orig_name as key; line 7 then stores orig_name itself as the hashmap key, retaining a pointer to the caller's string rather than a copy. The string backing orig_name is owned by the BTF string set, which is resized via realloc when new strings are added.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function stores a non-owning pointer as a persistent key and later reads through it after the underlying allocation is freed, directly matching CWE-416 use-after-free. A related double-free or buffer-overflow label does not fit: the defect is reuse of freed memory via a dangling key, not an out-of-bounds or duplicate free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: name_map keys alias orig_name, whose memory lives in a realloc-backed string set. Trigger: a later btf__add_str/btf__add_field reallocates that buffer, freeing the old region while name_map still holds the stale key. A subsequent hashmap lookup (e.g., strcmp in str_equal_fn via btf_dump_name_dups) dereferences the freed pointer, yielding a heap-use-after-free read.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>

description: An issue was discovered in the FUSE filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.10.6, aka CID-5d069dbe8aaf. fuse_do_getattr() calls make_bad_inode() in inappropriate situations, causing a system crash. NOTE: the original fix for this vulnerability was incomplete, and its incompleteness is tracked as CVE-2021-28950.
