commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13029/PPP: Fix a bounds check, and clean up other bounds checks.

For configuration protocol options, use ND_TCHECK() and
ND_TCHECK_nBITS() macros, passing them the appropriate pointer argument.
This fixes one case where the ND_TCHECK2() call they replace was not
checking enough bytes.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s), modified
so the capture file won't be rejected as an invalid capture.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tND_TCHECK2(*(p + 2), 4);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tND_TCHECK_32BITS(p + 2);']}
description: The PPP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-ppp.c:print_ccp_config_options().

code_evidence: ND_TCHECK2(*(p + 2), 4) is intended to verify that 4 bytes at p+2 are within the captured buffer before EXTRACT_32BITS(p + 2) reads them on the next line. The macro's first argument is the dereferenced byte value *(p + 2) rather than a pointer, so the bounds check does not validate the region that EXTRACT_32BITS subsequently reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads EXTRACT_32BITS(p + 2) without an effective preceding bounds check, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. The patch replaces it with ND_TCHECK_32BITS(p + 2), confirming the pointer argument was wrong; this is an over-read, not an over-write or integer issue.

evidence_lines.code:
ND_TCHECK2(*(p + 2), 4);
ND_PRINT((ndo, ": Magic-Num 0x%08x", EXTRACT_32BITS(p + 2)));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the truncation check dereferences p+2 and passes the resulting byte value to ND_TCHECK2, so the four bytes at p+2 are not confirmed present. Trigger: a BACP FPEER option with len==6 near the end of the capture; line 31 then reads 4 bytes that may lie past the captured buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read (buffer over-read).

commit_msg:
Bug 699927: don't include operator arrays in execstack output

When we transfer the contents of the execution stack into the array, take the
extra step of replacing any operator arrays on the stack with the operator
that reference them.

This prevents the contents of Postscript defined, internal only operators (those
created with .makeoperator) being exposed via execstack (and thus, via error
handling).

This necessitates a change in the resource remapping 'resource', which contains
a procedure which relies on the contents of the operators arrays being present.
As we already had internal-only variants of countexecstack and execstack
(.countexecstack and .execstack) - using those, and leaving thier operation
including the operator arrays means the procedure continues to work correctly.

Both .countexecstack and .execstack are undefined after initialization.

Also, when we store the execstack (or part thereof) for an execstackoverflow
error, make the same oparray/operator substitution as above for execstack.

commit_msg:
sixel_encoder_prepare_palette: kill use-after-free

The only place sixel_encoder_prepare_palette() is called
from is sixel_encoder_encode_frame(). If we have a
SIXEL_FAILED result inside the former, we unref the palette,
potentially freeing it. We then goto the error path for
sixel_encoder_encode_frame(), where we unref it again, in a
classic double-free. Remove the internal unref. As noted,
this is a single call site, so removing the unref can't
cause a memory leak.

Closes #27, reported by a4865g ("WuLearn").

description: libsixel 1.10.0 is vulnerable to Use after free in libsixel/src/dither.c:379.

code_evidence: When sixel_dither_initialize fails, the error branch calls sixel_dither_unref(*dither), releasing the caller-owned dither object, then jumps to end and returns the failed status to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The premature unref plus the caller's own unref on the same pointer yields reuse of freed memory, matching CWE-416. The fix removes the internal unref, confirming the flaw is improper freeing/ownership rather than mere resource exhaustion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function frees *dither on the initialize-failure path even though ownership of the returned pointer belongs to the caller. Trigger: a SIXEL_FAILED status from sixel_dither_initialize. The caller then unrefs the same dither again, causing a double-free and subsequent use-after-free/dangling reference to freed memory.

commit_msg:
coredump: fix race condition between mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and core dumping

The core dumping code has always run without holding the mmap_sem for
writing, despite that is the only way to ensure that the entire vma
layout will not change from under it.  Only using some signal
serialization on the processes belonging to the mm is not nearly enough.
This was pointed out earlier.  For example in Hugh's post from Jul 2017:

  https://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.LSU.2.11.1707191716030.2055@eggly.anvils

  "Not strictly relevant here, but a related note: I was very surprised
   to discover, only quite recently, how handle_mm_fault() may be called
   without down_read(mmap_sem) - when core dumping. That seems a
   misguided optimization to me, which would also be nice to correct"

In particular because the growsdown and growsup can move the
vm_start/vm_end the various loops the core dump does around the vma will
not be consistent if page faults can happen concurrently.

Pretty much all users calling mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and then
taking the mmap_sem had the potential to introduce unexpected side
effects in the core dumping code.

Adding mmap_sem for writing around the ->core_dump invocation is a
viable long term fix, but it requires removing all copy user and page
faults and to replace them with get_dump_page() for all binary formats
which is not suitable as a short term fix.

For the time being this solution manually covers the places that can
confuse the core dump either by altering the vma layout or the vma flags
while it runs.  Once ->core_dump runs under mmap_sem for writing the
function mmget_still_valid() can be dropped.

Allowing mmap_sem protected sections to run in parallel with the
coredump provides some minor parallelism advantage to the swapoff code
(which seems to be safe enough by never mangling any vma field and can
keep doing swapins in parallel to the core dumping) and to some other
corner case.

In order to facilitate the backporting I added "Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6"
however the side effect of this same race condition in /proc/pid/mem
should be reproducible since before 2.6.12-rc2 so I couldn't add any
other "Fixes:" because there's no hash beyond the git genesis commit.

Because find_extend_vma() is the only location outside of the process
context that could modify the "mm" structures under mmap_sem for
reading, by adding the mmget_still_valid() check to it, all other cases
that take the mmap_sem for reading don't need the new check after
mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm().  The expand_stack() in page fault
context also doesn't need the new check, because all tasks under core
dumping are frozen.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190325224949.11068-1-aarcange@redhat.com
Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6 ("userfaultfd: add new syscall to provide memory externalization")
Signed-off-by: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

description: The coredump implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10 does not use locking or other mechanisms to prevent vma layout or vma flags changes while it runs, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information, cause a denial of service, or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a race condition with mmget_not_zero or get_task_mm calls. This is related to fs/userfaultfd.c, mm/mmap.c, fs/proc/task_mmu.c, and drivers/infiniband/core/uverbs_main.c.

code_evidence: The function pins the mm with mmget_not_zero() and then acquires mmap_sem for writing, but there is no revalidation of mm state after the lock is taken.
find_vma_prev() runs under the write lock and its result vma is dereferenced immediately (vma->vm_start) without checking whether the mm is still valid; the patch inserts mmget_still_valid() here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 fits because the locking discipline is incomplete: the lock is acquired but the shared mm/vma state is not validated for consistency with the lock holder's assumptions, allowing unsynchronized modification. This is improper locking, not a plain race-only label, since the defect is the missing validity check under the held lock.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mm reference obtained via mmget_not_zero() is not revalidated after down_write(), so a concurrent core dump can complete and invalidate the mm while this path continues to walk and modify the vma tree. Trigger: another thread triggers core dumping (or equivalent mm teardown) between the mmget and the vma traversal. Consequence: use of a stale/inconsistent vma layout, leading to memory corruption or denial of service.

commit_msg:
Use correct origin when prompting for proxy authentication.

Since M49, Chrome has been prompting for proxy authentication
credentials using the target origin instead of the origin of the proxy
server. Even if the proxy origin was displayed correctly, a mischievous
network operator could still spoof the proxy server origin. To mitigate
these problems, this CL:

* Fixes the origin used in the proxy authentication login prompt to use
  the origin of the proxy server.

* Indicate if the proxy server connection is insecure.

* Always throw up an interstitial and clear the omnibox when showing a
  proxy auth prompt.

* Use the correct origin when saving proxy authentication credentials.

BUG=613626, 620737

commit_msg:
src/flac.c: Improve error handling

Especially when dealing with corrupt or malicious files.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tpflac->bufferbackup = SF_FALSE ;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: In libsndfile before 1.0.28, an error in the "flac_buffer_copy()" function (flac.c) can be exploited to cause a stack-based buffer overflow via a specially crafted FLAC file.

code_evidence: The callback stores the decoder-supplied frame and buffer into pflac, resets bufferpos to 0, clears bufferbackup, then calls flac_buffer_copy(psf) without validating frame channel count, block size, or buffer dimensions against the destination buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs memory-buffer operations driven by attacker-controlled frame parameters without restricting them to the buffer's intended boundary, directly matching CWE-119. The specific overflow sink lies in flac_buffer_copy, but this callback supplies the unvalidated inputs that enable it.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the callback trusts FLAC frame metadata (channels/block size) and the raw buffer pointer, then delegates copying to flac_buffer_copy with no bounds check. A crafted FLAC file yields frame values that drive writes beyond the intended buffer bounds, producing a stack-based buffer overflow. The consequence is out-of-bounds memory write; the cause is the missing dimension constraint before the copy.

description: The NetKVM Windows Virtio driver allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (guest crash) via a crafted length value in an IP packet, as demonstrated by a value that does not account for the size of the IP options.

commit_msg: Catch SGI buffer overruns
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int expandrow2(UINT8* dest, const UINT8* src, int n, int z)'], 'added_lines': ['static int expandrow2(UINT8* dest, const UINT8* src, int n, int z, int xsize)', '        if (count > xsize) {', '            return -1;', '        }']}
description: libImaging/SgiRleDecode.c in Pillow before 6.2.2 has an SGI buffer overflow.

code_evidence: count is taken from the encoded pixel byte (pixel & RLE_MAX_RUN) and only checked for zero; no upper bound on the run length is enforced before copying.
In the RLE_COPY_FLAG branch, count iterations each memcpy 2 bytes into dest and advance dest by z*2, so a large count writes far beyond the allocated destination row.
The else branch similarly loops count times copying 2 bytes into dest, again driven by the unvalidated count value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies src into dest in a loop whose iteration count comes from untrusted input, with no check that the copy fits the output buffer, matching CWE-120's buffer copy without input-size checking. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the writes to dest are the harmful operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoded run length count is trusted without comparison to the destination row size xsize. Trigger: a crafted SGI RLE stream whose pixel byte encodes a run longer than the row. Consequence: memcpy writes past the end of dest, corrupting heap memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
journalctl: verify sealed log epochs are continuous

Currently empty epochs are not sealed. This allows an attacker to truncate
a sealed log and continue it without any problems showing when verifying the
log.

This partially addresses CVE-2023-31438. One way to extend this change to
address CVE-2023-31438 completely, would be to verify that there is exactly
one seal per epoch (and not sealing when the epoch has not ended yet).

the change also adds a journal-file flag: HEADER_COMPATIBLE_SEALED_CONTINUOUS
this flag indicates that a journal file is sealed continuously and decides whether
any missing crypto epochs should trigger a warning or an error.

commit_msg:
Check sector and cluster size before use.

Otherwise malformed FS can cause heap corruption.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tfree(ef->sb);', '\t\treturn -EIO;', '\t}', '\t/* officially exFAT supports cluster size up to 32 MB */', '\tif ((int) ef->sb->sector_bits + (int) ef->sb->spc_bits > 25)', '\t{', '\t\tfree(ef->zero_cluster);', '\t\texfat_close(ef->dev);', '\t\texfat_error("too big cluster size: 2^%d",', '\t\t\t\t(int) ef->sb->sector_bits + (int) ef->sb->spc_bits);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* sector cannot be smaller than 512 bytes */', '\tif (ef->sb->sector_bits < 9)', '\t{', '\t\texfat_close(ef->dev);', '\t\texfat_error("too small sector size: 2^%hhd", ef->sb->sector_bits);', '\t\tfree(ef->sb);', '\t\treturn -EIO;', '\t}', '\t/* officially exFAT supports cluster size up to 32 MB */', '\tif ((int) ef->sb->sector_bits + (int) ef->sb->spc_bits > 25)', '\t{', '\t\texfat_close(ef->dev);', '\t\texfat_error("too big cluster size: 2^(%hhd+%hhd)",', '\t\t\t\tef->sb->sector_bits, ef->sb->spc_bits);', '\t\tfree(ef->sb);', '\t\treturn -EIO;', '\t}']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the verify_vbr_checksum function in exfatfsck in exfat-utils before 1.2.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted filesystem.

code_evidence: The boot sector is read from the untrusted filesystem into ef->sb at line 32; only the OEM name is validated before sector_bits and spc_bits are consumed.

At line 46 CLUSTER_SIZE(*ef->sb) is computed from the unvalidated sector_bits and spc_bits and passed to malloc, and at line 54 SECTOR_SIZE(*ef->sb) is passed to verify_vbr_checksum; line 61 then memsets CLUSTER_SIZE bytes.

The size check at lines 79-87 runs only after the allocation at line 46 and the verify/checksum and memset operations at lines 54 and 61, so oversized or malformed size fields are used before rejection.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an operation on a heap buffer outside its intended boundary: CLUSTER_SIZE-derived allocation size and subsequent writes disagree because unvalidated on-disk size fields control the buffer size. This is CWE-119 (out-of-bounds memory buffer operation); CWE-190 integer overflow is not required, since malformed size fields directly produce the mismatched allocation and write.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!verify_vbr_checksum(ef->dev, ef->zero_cluster, SECTOR_SIZE(*ef->sb)))
memset(ef->zero_cluster, 0, CLUSTER_SIZE(*ef->sb));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sector_bits and spc_bits from the crafted boot sector are used to compute allocation and buffer sizes without prior bounds checks. Trigger: a malformed exFAT image with a too-small sector_bits (<9) or a cluster size above 32 MB. Consequence: an undersized or incorrectly sized zero_cluster allocation is then written by verify_vbr_checksum and memset, causing a heap-based buffer overflow that may lead to heap corruption, denial of service or code execution.

commit_msg:
tjLoadImage: Fix issues w/loading 16-bit PPMs/PGMs

- The PPM reader now throws an error rather than segfaulting (due to a
  buffer overrun) if an application attempts to load a 16-bit PPM file
  into a grayscale uncompressed image buffer.  No known applications
  allowed that (not even the test applications in libjpeg-turbo),
  because that mode of operation was never expected to work and did not
  work under any circumstances.  (In fact, it was necessary to modify
  TJBench in order to reproduce the issue outside of a fuzzing
  environment.)  This was purely a matter of making the library bow out
  gracefully rather than crash if an application tries to do something
  really stupid.

- The PPM reader now throws an error rather than generating incorrect
  pixels if an application attempts to load a 16-bit PGM file into an
  RGB uncompressed image buffer.

- The PPM reader now correctly loads 16-bit PPM files into extended
  RGB uncompressed image buffers.  (Previously it generated incorrect
  pixels unless the input colorspace was JCS_RGB or JCS_EXT_RGB.)

The only way that users could have potentially encountered these issues
was through the tjLoadImage() function.  cjpeg and TJBench were
unaffected.

This is related to a heap-based buffer overflow in the get_word_rgb_row function in rdppm.c.

code_evidence: For 16-bit PGM (maxval > 255), the code unconditionally assigns get_word_gray_row as the row reader regardless of cinfo->in_color_space.
For 16-bit PPM (maxval > 255), it unconditionally assigns get_word_rgb_row, again without checking the destination colorspace.

The iobuffer is sized from w and maxval (3 bytes/pixel for PPM, 1 for PGM at 16-bit), and the output buffer in the else branch is sized by w * cinfo->input_components, which is derived from the requested in_color_space.

source->pub.get_pixel_rows = get_word_gray_row;

if (maxval > 255) {
source->pub.get_pixel_rows = get_word_rgb_row;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The row-reader selection ignores the requested destination colorspace, so a 16-bit grayscale read (get_word_gray_row) can feed an RGB buffer or a 16-bit RGB read can feed a grayscale buffer. The buffer sizing uses input_components from the destination colorspace while the reader writes per its own pixel layout, so the reader can write past the allocated output buffer. code_evidence: Line 10 calls the driver's setkeycode callback, which writes the previous keycode into old_keycode; the commit message notes this value can be garbage and exceed KEY_MAX.
Lines 14-16 pass that unvalidated old_keycode directly to __test_and_clear_bit, which computes a bit offset from it and writes into dev->key without any upper-bound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: __test_and_clear_bit performs a write indexed by an unvalidated offset, producing a write past the end of the key bitmap, which matches CWE-787. The flaw is an absent bounds check on the offset rather than a read-only out-of-bounds access (CWE-125) or an integer overflow itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: old_keycode returned by dev->setkeycode is trusted without validating it against KEY_MAX. Trigger: a crafted keycode table makes the callback return an out-of-range old_keycode; __test_and_clear_bit then clears a bit at an offset far outside dev->key's bitmap. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds write that corrupts adjacent memory within or beyond the input device structure.

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflows.

The data structures linkhash and printbuf are limited to 2 GB in size
due to a signed integer being used to track their current size.

If too much data is added, then size variable can overflow, which is
an undefined behaviour in C programming language.

Assuming that a signed int overflow just leads to a negative value,
like it happens on many sytems (Linux i686/amd64 with gcc), then
printbuf is vulnerable to an out of boundary write on 64 bit systems.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Prevent signed integer overflows with large buffers. */', '\tif (len > INT_MAX - offset)', '\t\treturn -1;']}
description: json-c through 0.14 has an integer overflow and out-of-bounds write via a large JSON file, as demonstrated by printbuf_memappend.

code_evidence: offset is taken from the caller (or pb->bpos when -1) and len is caller-controlled; size_needed is computed as offset + len in a signed int with no pre-check.
size_needed only feeds the size comparison and printbuf_extend; if offset + len wraps to a small or negative value, the buffer is not grown to the required size.
memset then writes len bytes at pb->buf + offset, so the wrapped size_needed permits an out-of-bounds write beyond the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size calculation (offset + len) that assumes the result is larger than its operands, which is false on signed integer wraparound; this directly matches CWE-190. The out-of-bounds write is the downstream consequence, not the labeled weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code: memset(pb->buf + offset, charvalue, len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signed int addition offset + len can overflow before any bound check, so size_needed no longer reflects the required buffer size. Trigger: a large len (or offset) supplied to printbuf_memset. Consequence: the buffer is not extended sufficiently and memset writes past the allocation, corrupting memory.

Weight shape: ",', '              weights.shape().DebugString(),', '              "; values shape: ", values.shape().DebugString()));', '    }', '', '', '    OP_REQUIRES(', '        context, num_batches > 0,', '        errors::InvalidArgument(', '            "Must provide at least 2 elements for the splits argument"));', '    OP_REQUIRES(context, splits_values(0) == 0,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("Splits must start with 0, not with ",', '                                        splits_values(0)));', '    OP_REQUIRES(context, splits_values(num_batches) == num_values,', '                errors::InvalidArgument(', '                    "Splits must end with the number of values, got ",', '                    splits_values(num_batches), " instead of ", num_values));']}
description: In Tensorflow version 2.3.0, the `SparseCountSparseOutput` and `RaggedCountSparseOutput` implementations don't validate that the `weights` tensor has the same shape as the data. The check exists for `DenseCountSparseOutput`, where both tensors are fully specified. In the sparse and ragged count weights are still accessed in parallel with the data. But, since there is no validation, a user passing fewer weights than the values for the tensors can generate a read from outside the bounds of the heap buffer allocated for the weights. The issue is patched in commit 3cbb917b4714766030b28eba9fb41bb97ce9ee02 and is released in TensorFlow version 2.3.1.

code_evidence: use_weights is set from weights.NumElements() > 0 without comparing weights.shape() to values.shape(); weight_values is a flat view of weights [9]. The loop iterates idx over num_values = values.NumElements() [11,15] and, when use_weights, indexes weight_values(idx) [24]. If weights has fewer elements than values, idx reaches beyond the weights buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked parallel indexing of weight_values by an index bounded only by num_values permits memory access past the intended weights buffer, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds memory operation. The shape check added in the patch confirms the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing shape validation between weights and values before the parallel access. Trigger: a caller passes a weights tensor with fewer elements than values while use_weights is true. Consequence: weight_values(idx) reads outside the heap buffer allocated for weights, yielding an out-of-bounds access; the corresponding write occurs into per_batch_counts using the out-of-bounds-derived weight value.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13027/LLDP: Fix a bounds check.

The total length of the OID is the OID length plus the length of the OID
length itself.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s), modified
so the capture file won't be rejected as an invalid capture.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (tlen < oid_len) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (tlen < 1U + oid_len) {']}
description: The LLDP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-lldp.c:lldp_mgmt_addr_tlv_print().

code_evidence: When remaining tlen is nonzero, oid_len is read from *tptr at line 38. The bounds check at line 39 compares tlen against oid_len only, ignoring the one byte already consumed by the OID length field itself. Line 44 then reads oid_len bytes starting at tptr + 1 via safeputs, so the check allows a length that exceeds the remaining buffer by up to one byte.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function validates a length then reads that many bytes from a pointer past the length field, allowing a read beyond the intended buffer. This is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), not merely an integer issue: the off-by-one check causes excess data to be read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check fails to account for the OID length byte, so it permits tlen == oid_len even though only tlen-1 bytes remain after tptr. Trigger: an LLDP management-address TLV whose OID length equals the remaining buffer length. Consequence: safeputs reads one byte past the TLV buffer, an out-of-bounds read that can leak memory or crash the parser.

commit_msg: Fix bug #73807
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!eof) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!eof && vars->str.c != vars->ptr) {']}
description: In PHP before 5.6.31, 7.x before 7.0.17, and 7.1.x before 7.1.3, remote attackers could cause a CPU consumption denial of service attack by injecting long form variables, related to main/php_variables.c.

code_evidence: Line 4-5 resets vars->ptr to the buffer start and vars->end to its end; the while loop at line 6 repeatedly calls add_post_var, advancing vars->ptr as variables are parsed, and caps only the count via max_vars at line 7. At line 15 the guard tests only !eof, so when parsing is incomplete the memmove at line 16 always shifts the remaining bytes (vars->end - vars->ptr) to the buffer start, even when vars->ptr already equals vars->str.c.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing constraint lets attacker-controlled input drive repeated redundant buffer copying, exhausting CPU without any limit on the work per request. This is uncontrolled resource consumption (CPU DoS) matching CWE-400, not a memory-safety or injection flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the incomplete-buffer branch lacks a check that there is actually unconsumed data to move. Trigger: input with long form variables causes repeated partial parsing where ptr equals the buffer start, so each iteration performs a memmove over the full remaining length. This quadratic re-scanning consumes CPU, producing a denial of service.

commit_msg:
Internal change

PiperOrigin-RevId: 411896058
Change-Id: Ia031058247e3cf382957a6662d3f9e1cbb481ca2
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  ConvolutionDimensions dims = OpDimensionsFromInputs(', '      op_info.inputs(0).shape(), op_info, &found_unknown_shapes);'], 'added_lines': ['  TF_ASSIGN_OR_RETURN(ConvolutionDimensions dims,', '                      OpDimensionsFromInputs(op_info.inputs(0).shape(), op_info,', '                                             &found_unknown_shapes));']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The estimator for the cost of some convolution operations can be made to execute a division by 0. The function fails to check that the stride argument is strictly positive. Hence, the fix is to add a check for the stride argument to ensure it is valid. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function obtains convolution dimensions via OpDimensionsFromInputs with the raw op_info, without validating stride values before use.
per_output_ops and ops are computed from dims.kx, dims.ky and output dimensions; if a stride-derived dimension is zero, downstream arithmetic can divide by zero.
The branch on dims.ky >= dims.sy and the input_size computation consume dimensions derived from the unvalidated stride argument.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because the estimator performs arithmetic on dimensions derived from an unchecked zero stride, triggering division by zero. This is a missing input-validation constraint leading to a division-by-zero crash, not merely an incorrect cost estimate.

evidence_lines.code:
ConvolutionDimensions dims = OpDimensionsFromInputs(
op_info.inputs(0).shape(), op_info, &found_unknown_shapes);

int per_output_ops = dims.kx * dims.ky == 1 ? 1 : dims.kx * dims.ky - 1;
int64_t ops = dims.batch * dims.ox * dims.oy * dims.oz * per_output_ops;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stride argument is not checked to be strictly positive before OpDimensionsFromInputs and subsequent size computations. A zero stride yields degenerate dimensions that feed division-based cost calculations, causing a divide-by-zero and a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
signal: Extend exec_id to 64bits

commit d1e7fd6462ca9fc76650fbe6ca800e35b24267da upstream.

Replace the 32bit exec_id with a 64bit exec_id to make it impossible
to wrap the exec_id counter.  With care an attacker can cause exec_id
wrap and send arbitrary signals to a newly exec'd parent.  This
bypasses the signal sending checks if the parent changes their
credentials during exec.

The severity of this problem can been seen that in my limited testing
of a 32bit exec_id it can take as little as 19s to exec 65536 times.
Which means that it can take as little as 14 days to wrap a 32bit
exec_id.  Adam Zabrocki has succeeded wrapping the self_exe_id in 7
days.  Even my slower timing is in the uptime of a typical server.
Which means self_exec_id is simply a speed bump today, and if exec
gets noticably faster self_exec_id won't even be a speed bump.

Extending self_exec_id to 64bits introduces a problem on 32bit
architectures where reading self_exec_id is no longer atomic and can
take two read instructions.  Which means that is is possible to hit
a window where the read value of exec_id does not match the written
value.  So with very lucky timing after this change this still
remains expoiltable.

I have updated the update of exec_id on exec to use WRITE_ONCE
and the read of exec_id in do_notify_parent to use READ_ONCE
to make it clear that there is no locking between these two
locations.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/kernel-hardening/20200324215049.GA3710@pi3.com.pl
Fixes: 2.3.23pre2
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -22,7 +22,7 @@
 		 * This is only possible if parent == real_parent.
 		 * Check if it has changed security domain.
 		 */
-		if (tsk->parent_exec_id != tsk->parent->self_exec_id)
+		if (tsk->parent_exec_id != READ_ONCE(tsk->parent->self_exec_id))
 			sig = SIGCHLD;
 	}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (tsk->parent_exec_id != tsk->parent->self_exec_id)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (tsk->parent_exec_id != READ_ONCE(tsk->parent->self_exec_id))']}
description: A signal access-control issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.6.5, aka CID-7395ea4e65c2. Because exec_id in include/linux/sched.h is only 32 bits, an integer overflow can interfere with a do_notify_parent protection mechanism. A child process can send an arbitrary signal to a parent process in a different security domain. Exploitation limitations include the amount of elapsed time before an integer overflow occurs, and the lack of scenarios where signals to a parent process present a substantial operational threat.

code_evidence: do_notify_parent compares tsk->parent_exec_id against tsk->parent->self_exec_id to decide whether the parent changed security domain during exec; on mismatch it downgrades the signal to SIGCHLD. The comparison reads the parent's exec_id counter directly, and the patch wraps only this read in READ_ONCE, confirming the check depends on the exec_id value being consistent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the protection hinges on an incrementing integer counter whose wraparound makes the comparison assume a stale value is current, enabling the access-control bypass. It is not merely a race or missing lock; the missing constraint is the bounded counter width.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: self_exec_id is a 32-bit counter incremented on each exec; it can wrap to a previously observed value. If a child records parent_exec_id and the parent execs enough times for self_exec_id to wrap back, the equality check at line 14 succeeds, the SIGCHLD downgrade is skipped, and the original signal is delivered to the parent. Root cause is the wrap-prone counter; the consequence is bypass of the exec_id-based access-control check, allowing signals across a security-domain change.

commit_msg:
[CSP] Don't check the path component of the URL when the response was fetched via ServiceWorker.

In ResourceFetcher::didReceiveResponse() we check the response URL when the response is fetched via ServiceWorker.
But the match algorithm should ignore the path component of the URL.

BUG=542060

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1454003003

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#360733}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['ResourceRequestBlockedReason FrameFetchContext::canRequestInternal(Resource::Type type, const ResourceRequest& resourceRequest, const KURL& url, const ResourceLoaderOptions& options, bool forPreload, FetchRequest::OriginRestriction originRestriction) const', '', '    // As of CSP2, for requests that are the results of redirects, the match', '    // algorithm should ignore the path component of the URL.', '    ContentSecurityPolicy::RedirectStatus redirectStatus = resourceRequest.followedRedirect() ? ContentSecurityPolicy::DidRedirect : ContentSecurityPolicy::DidNotRedirect;'], 'added_lines': ['ResourceRequestBlockedReason FrameFetchContext::canRequestInternal(Resource::Type type, const ResourceRequest& resourceRequest, const KURL& url, const ResourceLoaderOptions& options, bool forPreload, FetchRequest::OriginRestriction originRestriction, ContentSecurityPolicy::RedirectStatus redirectStatus) const']}
description: The Content Security Policy (CSP) implementation in Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 49.0.2623.75, does not ignore a URL's path component in the case of a ServiceWorker fetch, which allows remote attackers to obtain sensitive information about visited web pages by reading CSP violation reports, related to FrameFetchContext.cpp and ResourceFetcher.cpp.

code_evidence: The function computes redirectStatus only from resourceRequest.followedRedirect(), so a ServiceWorker-fetched response whose URL differs but was not a redirect is treated as DidNotRedirect.
CSP allow*FromSource calls pass this redirectStatus into the match algorithm; without DidRedirect the path component of the response URL is compared instead of ignored.
A violation from such a fetch is counted via ResourceLoadedAfterRedirectWithCSP, and the CSP report can reveal the differing path to a remote observer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is that path information from a visited page is exposed through CSP violation reports to an unauthorized remote actor, matching CWE-200's explicit exposure of sensitive metadata to an unauthorized party. It is not a generic confidentiality impact from another flaw; the CSP reporting path itself carries the leaked data.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!shouldBypassMainWorldCSP && !csp->allowScriptFromSource(url, redirectStatus, cspReporting))
return ResourceRequestBlockedReasonCSP;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: redirectStatus is derived solely from resourceRequest.followedRedirect(), ignoring responses fetched via ServiceWorker whose URL path differs. Trigger: a cross-origin page issues a ServiceWorker-fetched subresource whose response URL path differs from the request; the CSP match compares paths and reports a violation. Consequence: CSP violation reports leak the visited page's URL path to a remote party.

commit_msg:
bpv6: Fix possible infinite loop

display_extension_block is supposed to return the current offset,
not the number of bytes remaining. The number of bytes remaining
can be less than the current offset and cause an infinite loop.

In the case of an error, set lastheader and return the current
offset in order to break out of the main processing loop.

Fix #18711.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                offset = tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset);', '                break;'], 'added_lines': ['                *lastheader = TRUE;', '                return offset;']}
description: Excessive loops in multiple dissectors in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.2 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.10 and allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: In the ciphersuite result loop, when evaluate_sdnv_ei reports an error via ei, the handler adds an expert item and then sets offset = tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset) and breaks. This assigns a count of remaining bytes rather than the current absolute offset, so the returned offset can be smaller than the loop's starting offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits because malformed SDNV input drives repeated re-entry of the outer parsing loop without progress, an excessive iteration weakness affecting availability. The fix sets lastheader and returns the true offset to break the loop, confirming the loop-termination defect rather than a mere bounds error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path conflates 'bytes remaining' with 'current offset', so display_extension_block returns a value that does not advance past the block. The caller's main processing loop uses this return value as the next offset, and if the remaining-byte count is less than the current offset, the same block is re-parsed indefinitely, causing CPU exhaustion/DoS.

commit_msg:
run: Convert all environment variables into bwrap arguments

This avoids some of them being filtered out by a setuid bwrap. It also
means that if they came from an untrusted source, they cannot be used
to inject arbitrary code into a non-setuid bwrap via mechanisms like
LD_PRELOAD.

Because they get bundled into a memfd or temporary file, they do not
actually appear in argv, ensuring that they remain inaccessible to
processes running under a different uid (which is important if their
values are tokens or other secrets).

Signed-off-by: Simon McVittie <smcv@collabora.com>
Part-of: https://github.com/flatpak/flatpak/security/advisories/GHSA-4ppf-fxf6-vxg2
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (g_environ_getenv (bwrap->envp, "LD_LIBRARY_PATH") != NULL)', '    {', '      /* LD_LIBRARY_PATH is overridden for setuid helper, so pass it as cmdline arg */', '      flatpak_bwrap_add_args (bwrap,', '                              "--setenv", "LD_LIBRARY_PATH", g_environ_getenv (bwrap->envp, "LD_LIBRARY_PATH"),', '                              NULL);', '      flatpak_bwrap_unset_env (bwrap, "LD_LIBRARY_PATH");', '    }', '', '  if (g_environ_getenv (bwrap->envp, "TMPDIR") != NULL)', '    {', '      /* TMPDIR is overridden for setuid helper, so pass it as cmdline arg */', '      flatpak_bwrap_add_args (bwrap,', '                              "--setenv", "TMPDIR", g_environ_getenv (bwrap->envp, "TMPDIR"),', '                              NULL);', '      flatpak_bwrap_unset_env (bwrap, "TMPDIR");', '    }', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: Flatpak is a system for building, distributing, and running sandboxed desktop applications on Linux. A bug was discovered in the `flatpak-portal` service that can allow sandboxed applications to execute arbitrary code on the host system (a sandbox escape). This sandbox-escape bug is present in versions from 0.11.4 and before fixed versions 1.8.5 and 1.10.0. The Flatpak portal D-Bus service (`flatpak-portal`, also known by its D-Bus service name `org.freedesktop.portal.Flatpak`) allows apps in a Flatpak sandbox to launch their own subprocesses in a new sandbox instance, either with the same security settings as the caller or with more restrictive security settings. For example, this is used in Flatpak-packaged web browsers such as Chromium to launch subprocesses that will process untrusted web content, and give those subprocesses a more restrictive sandbox than the browser itself. In vulnerable versions, the Flatpak portal service passes caller-specified environment variables to non-sandboxed processes on the host system, and in particular to the `flatpak run` command that is used to launch the new sandbox instance. A malicious or compromised Flatpak app could set environment variables that are trusted by the `flatpak run` command, and use them to execute arbitrary code that is not in a sandbox. As a workaround, this vulnerability can be mitigated by preventing the `flatpak-portal` service from starting, but that mitigation will prevent many Flatpak apps from working correctly. This is fixed in versions 1.8.5 and 1.10.0.

code_evidence: Lines 136-142 read LD_LIBRARY_PATH from bwrap->envp and pass its caller-influenced value as a bwrap --setenv argument to a non-sandboxed helper.
Lines 143-149 do the same for TMPDIR. The value is forwarded verbatim into the argument list of the downstream setuid bwrap/flatpak run process without validation or neutralization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits because externally-influenced input is embedded in output (command arguments) consumed by a downstream component without neutralizing special elements that alter its interpretation. It is not merely a path-traversal issue; the weakness is the unneutralized injection into the downstream command's environment handling.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function forwards caller-supplied environment values (LD_LIBRARY_PATH, TMPDIR) into arguments of a host-side, non-sandboxed launcher. Trigger: a sandboxed app sets these variables to values trusted by the downstream command. Consequence: the downstream component interprets them, enabling arbitrary code execution outside the sandbox (sandbox escape).

commit_msg:
* tools/tiffcrop.c: fix readContigStripsIntoBuffer() in -i (ignore) mode so
that the output buffer is correctly incremented to avoid write outside bounds.
Reported by Agostino Sarubbo.
Fixes http://bugzilla.maptools.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2620
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                bufp += bytes_read;'], 'added_lines': ['                bufp += stripsize;']}
description: tools/tiffcrop.c in LibTIFF 4.0.7 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted TIFF image, related to "READ of size 1" and libtiff/tif_fax3.c:413:13.

code_evidence: The loop calls TIFFReadEncodedStrip with -1 (read full strip) writing at bufp, then advances bufp by bytes_read, the actual returned count, rather than the allocated stripsize. In ignore mode a short/negative read leaves the buffer pointer misaligned so subsequent strips write past the intended per-strip region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The miscomputed pointer leads to reads/writes outside the output buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The underlying arithmetic/pointer-increment error could be seen as CWE-787, but the demonstrated operation is a buffer boundary violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: buffer advancement uses the decoder's returned byte count instead of the fixed strip size, so a crafted TIFF yielding a short or negative read causes the write cursor to drift. Trigger: crafted TIFF processed in -i mode; consequence: out-of-bounds writes/reads on the output buffer (heap overflow).

description: A vulnerability, which was classified as critical, was found in PoDoFo 0.10.0. Affected is the function readXRefStreamEntry of the file PdfXRefStreamParserObject.cpp. The manipulation leads to heap-based buffer overflow. An attack has to be approached locally. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. The patch is identified as 535a786f124b739e3c857529cecc29e4eeb79778. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-thread.c had an infinite loop that was addressed by using a correct integer data type.

code_evidence: check_offset is declared guint8 (line 429) and masklen guint8 (line 430); check_len is gint32.

The while loop (431-440) reads masklen from check_offset, breaks only when masklen==0, then adds 2 and advances check_offset and decrements check_len. Because check_offset is 8-bit, it wraps at 256; masklen read from a wrapped position may be nonzero, so check_len can fail to reach 0 or check_offset may loop over the same bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits: the while loop's exit condition (check_len <= 0) can become unreachable due to integer wraparound of check_offset, producing an infinite loop. This is a loop-termination defect, not merely an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
double64_init: Check psf->sf.channels against upper bound

This prevents division by zero later in the code.

While the trivial case to catch this (i.e. sf.channels < 1) has already
been covered, a crafted file may report a number of channels that is
so high (i.e. > INT_MAX/sizeof(double)) that it "somehow" gets
miscalculated to zero (if this makes sense) in the determination of the
blockwidth. Since we only support a limited number of channels anyway,
make sure to check here as well.

CVE-2017-14634

Closes: https://github.com/erikd/libsndfile/issues/318
Signed-off-by: Erik de Castro Lopo <erikd@mega-nerd.com>

description: In libsndfile 1.0.28, a divide-by-zero error exists in the function double64_init() in double64.c, which may lead to DoS when playing a crafted audio file.

code_evidence: The only channel constraint is psf->sf.channels < 1; there is no upper bound check on the attacker-controlled channel count before it is used in arithmetic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a division whose divisor (blockwidth) can become zero due to a missing upper-bound validation on the channel count, matching CWE-369. This is a divide-by-zero, not merely an integer overflow, because the overflowed value is used as the divisor.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: psf->sf.channels comes from a crafted file header. Without an upper bound, a very large value makes sizeof(double)*psf->sf.channels overflow to zero when assigned to psf->blockwidth, so the later division psf->datalength / psf->blockwidth divides by zero, causing a crash/DoS.

PR29892, Field file_table of struct module is uninitialized

description: A flaw was found in Binutils. The use of an uninitialized field in the struct module *module may lead to application crash and local denial of service.

code_evidence: On a DECLFILE record, file_table is grown via bfd_realloc_or_free; realloc leaves the newly added slots (from old file_table_count up to the new count) uninitialized, and no memset clears them.
The new fileid slot is then written with name and srec, but other slots added by the growth remain uninitialized.
SETFILE reads module->file_table[data].srec, which can fall on an uninitialized slot when data refers to an index not yet declared.
SETREC_L/W similarly write module->file_table[curr_srec->sfile].srec, accessing potentially uninitialized fileinfo entries.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses file_table elements whose contents were never initialized, matching CWE-908 (use of uninitialized resource). The fix adds memset over the new range, confirming the uninitialized-resource cause rather than an out-of-bounds access.

evidence_lines.code:
module->file_table [fileid].name = filename;
module->file_table [fileid].srec = 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: after realloc growth, the extended file_table entries are not zero-initialized. Trigger: a SETFILE or SETREC command indexes a fileid whose slot was created by growth but never populated by a DECLFILE. Consequence: reading uninitialized .srec/.name fields yields garbage values, leading to crash or incorrect data use (local DoS).

description: The SSH transport protocol with certain OpenSSH extensions, found in OpenSSH before 9.6 and other products, allows remote attackers to bypass integrity checks such that some packets are omitted (from the extension negotiation message), and a client and server may consequently end up with a connection for which some security features have been downgraded or disabled, aka a Terrapin attack. This occurs because the SSH Binary Packet Protocol (BPP), implemented by these extensions, mishandles the handshake phase and mishandles use of sequence numbers. For example, there is an effective attack against SSH's use of ChaCha20-Poly1305 (and CBC with Encrypt-then-MAC). The bypass occurs in chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com and (if CBC is used) the -etm@openssh.com MAC algorithms. This also affects Maverick Synergy Java SSH API before 3.1.0-SNAPSHOT, Dropbear through 2022.83, Ssh before 5.1.1 in Erlang/OTP, PuTTY before 0.80, AsyncSSH before 2.14.2, golang.org/x/crypto before 0.17.0, libssh before 0.10.6, libssh2 through 1.11.0, Thorn Tech SFTP Gateway before 3.4.6, Tera Term before 5.1, Paramiko before 3.4.0, jsch before 0.2.15, SFTPGo before 2.5.6, Netgate pfSense Plus through 23.09.1, Netgate pfSense CE through 2.7.2, HPN-SSH through 18.2.0, ProFTPD before 1.3.8b (and before 1.3.9rc2), ORYX CycloneSSH before 2.3.4, NetSarang XShell 7 before Build 0144, CrushFTP before 10.6.0, ConnectBot SSH library before 2.2.22, Apache MINA sshd through 2.11.0, sshj through 0.37.0, TinySSH through 20230101, trilead-ssh2 6401, LANCOM LCOS and LANconfig, FileZilla before 3.66.4, Nova before 11.8, PKIX-SSH before 14.4, SecureCRT before 9.4.3, Transmit5 before 5.10.4, Win32-OpenSSH before 9.5.0.0p1-Beta, WinSCP before 6.2.2, Bitvise SSH Server before 9.32, Bitvise SSH Client before 9.33, KiTTY through 0.76.1.13, the net-ssh gem 7.2.0 for Ruby, the mscdex ssh2 module before 1.15.0 for Node.js, the thrussh library before 0.35.1 for Rust, and the Russh crate before 0.40.2 for Rust.

code_evidence: On rekey, the function only updates the local proposal and resends its KEXINIT (lines 9-13); it does not reset or bind the packet sequence numbers to the handshake, so the transcript state the integrity check depends on is not re-established.

The server's KEXINIT is parsed field-by-field and malformed trailing data (first_kex_packet_follows, reserved) is merely logged and skipped at lines 210-219, allowing a truncated or altered negotiation message to be accepted without an integrity failure.

commit_msg:
io_get_file_fixed will access io_uring's context. Lock it if it is
invoked unlocked (eg via io-wq) to avoid a race condition with fixed
files getting unregistered.

No single upstream patch exists for this issue, it was fixed as part
of the file assignment changes that went into the 5.18 cycle.

Signed-off-by: Jheng, Bing-Jhong Billy <billy@starlabs.sg>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\t     struct io_kiocb *req, int fd)', '\tstruct file *file;', '\t\treturn NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\t     struct io_kiocb *req, int fd,', '\t\t\t\t\t     unsigned int issue_flags)', '\tstruct file *file = NULL;', '\tio_ring_submit_lock(ctx, !(issue_flags & IO_URING_F_NONBLOCK));', '', '\t\tgoto out;', 'out:', '\tio_ring_submit_unlock(ctx, !(issue_flags & IO_URING_F_NONBLOCK));']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux Kernel io_uring system can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

The io_file_get_fixed function lacks the presence of ctx->uring_lock which can lead to a Use-After-Free vulnerability due a race condition with fixed files getting unregistered.

We recommend upgrading past commit da24142b1ef9fd5d36b76e36bab328a5b27523e8.

code_evidence: The function reads the fixed-file slot via io_fixed_file_slot(&ctx->file_table, fd)->file_ptr and extracts the struct file pointer at line 10, then stores it in req and returns it, all without acquiring ctx->uring_lock. Because no lock guards the file_table access, a concurrent fixed-file unregistration can free the file while this pointer is being read and subsequently returned.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the returned file pointer can reference memory freed by a concurrent unregistration, and the caller then operates on that stale pointer. The missing lock is the enabling condition; the supported weakness is the resulting use-after-free, not a generic race condition.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: io_file_get_fixed dereferences the fixed-file table and returns the resulting file pointer without holding ctx->uring_lock. Trigger: when invoked unlocked (e.g., via io-wq) concurrently with fixed files being unregistered, the slot's file can be freed between the read and use. Consequence: the returned dangling file pointer yields a use-after-free, enabling memory corruption or local privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fix invalid memory write on lua stack overflow {CVE-2021-32626}

When LUA call our C code, by default, the LUA stack has room for 20
elements. In most cases, this is more than enough but sometimes it's not
and the caller must verify the LUA stack size before he pushes elements.

On 3 places in the code, there was no verification of the LUA stack size.
On specific inputs this missing verification could have lead to invalid
memory write:
1. On 'luaReplyToRedisReply', one might return a nested reply that will
   explode the LUA stack.
2. On 'redisProtocolToLuaType', the Redis reply might be deep enough
   to explode the LUA stack (notice that currently there is no such
   command in Redis that returns such a nested reply, but modules might
   do it)
3. On 'ldbRedis', one might give a command with enough arguments to
   explode the LUA stack (all the arguments will be pushed to the LUA
   stack)

This commit is solving all those 3 issues by calling 'lua_checkstack' and
verify that there is enough room in the LUA stack to push elements. In
case 'lua_checkstack' returns an error (there is not enough room in the
LUA stack and it's not possible to increase the stack), we will do the
following:
1. On 'luaReplyToRedisReply', we will return an error to the user.
2. On 'redisProtocolToLuaType' we will exit with panic (we assume this
   scenario is rare because it can only happen with a module).
3. On 'ldbRedis', we return an error.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                if (!lua_checkstack(lua, 1)) {', '                    /* Notice that here we need to check the stack again because the recursive', '                     * call to redisProtocolToLuaType might have use the room allocated in the stack */', '                    serverPanic("lua stack limit reach when parsing redis.call reply");', '                }']}
description: Redis is an open source, in-memory database that persists on disk. In affected versions specially crafted Lua scripts executing in Redis can cause the heap-based Lua stack to be overflowed, due to incomplete checks for this condition. This can result with heap corruption and potentially remote code execution. This problem exists in all versions of Redis with Lua scripting support, starting from 2.6. The problem is fixed in versions 6.2.6, 6.0.16 and 5.0.14. For users unable to update an additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent users from executing Lua scripts. This can be done using ACL to restrict EVAL and EVALSHA commands.

code_evidence: In the RESP3 aggregate loop, each iteration calls redisProtocolToLuaType (which may recursively push elements onto the Lua stack) and then pushes an additional boolean for the '%' branch without first verifying stack capacity. The recursion on line 26 consumes stack room, and the push on line 28 follows with no lua_checkstack guard.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing lua_checkstack before lua_pushboolean lets writes exceed the Lua stack buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an unchecked length (CWE-125) because the consequence is writing past the buffer end, not reading.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop pushes values onto the Lua stack proportional to the attacker-controlled aggregate length and nesting depth, but never checks remaining stack space. A deeply nested or large RESP3 reply parsed via redisProtocolToLuaType drives the stack past its allocated capacity, causing an out-of-bounds write to the heap-based Lua stack and potential heap corruption or code execution.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13031/Check for the presence of the entire IPv6 fragment header.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s), modified
so the capture file won't be rejected as an invalid capture.

Clean up some whitespace in tests/TESTLIST while we're at it.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tND_TCHECK(dp->ip6f_offlg);'], 'added_lines': ['\tND_TCHECK(*dp);']}
description: The IPv6 fragmentation header parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-frag6.c:frag6_print().

code_evidence: dp is cast directly from the caller-supplied packet pointer bp without validating that a full struct ip6_frag header is present.
The only bounds check is ND_TCHECK(dp->ip6f_offlg), which validates just the 2-byte ip6f_offlg field, not the whole fragment header.
The verbose branch then reads EXTRACT_32BITS(&dp->ip6f_ident), a 4-byte field, which can lie beyond the validated region.
The non-verbose branch and the later EXTRACT_16BITS(&dp->ip6f_offlg) read fields that may also extend past the captured data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads packet data past the end of the validated buffer. It is not merely a length-arithmetic error; the unsafe operation is a direct out-of-bounds read of struct fields.

evidence_lines.code:
ND_PRINT((ndo, "frag (0x%08x:%d|%ld)",
EXTRACT_32BITS(&dp->ip6f_ident),
EXTRACT_16BITS(&dp->ip6f_offlg) & IP6F_OFF_MASK,
sizeof(struct ip6_hdr) + EXTRACT_16BITS(&ip6->ip6_plen) -
(long)(bp - bp2) - sizeof(struct ip6_frag)));

if ((EXTRACT_16BITS(&dp->ip6f_offlg) & IP6F_OFF_MASK) != 0)
return -1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the truncation check covers only ip6f_offlg rather than the entire IPv6 fragment header. Trigger: a truncated capture whose fragment header is shorter than sizeof(struct ip6_frag); the subsequent EXTRACT_32BITS on ip6f_ident (and other field reads) then access bytes beyond the validated buffer. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of packet memory, causing a crash or memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
net: rose: fix UAF bugs caused by timer handler

There are UAF bugs in rose_heartbeat_expiry(), rose_timer_expiry()
and rose_idletimer_expiry(). The root cause is that del_timer()
could not stop the timer handler that is running and the refcount
of sock is not managed properly.

such as rose_start_heartbeat() and so on to start timer,

Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Tested-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220629002640.5693-1-duoming@zju.edu.cn
Signed-off-by: Paolo Abeni <pabeni@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tsock_put(sk);']}
description: There are use-after-free vulnerabilities caused by timer handler in net/rose/rose_timer.c of linux that allow attackers to crash linux kernel without any privileges.

code_evidence: The timer callback derives sk from the timer and immediately calls bh_lock_sock(sk) without holding a reference to the socket.

After unlocking, the callback accesses sk state and invokes sk->sk_state_change(sk) when SOCK_DEAD is unset, but the function has no sock_put to balance a reference; the patch adds sock_put(sk) after bh_unlock_sock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function references a sock that can be freed concurrently by release paths while the timer handler is still executing, which is exactly CWE-416 use-after-free. It is not merely a race without memory reuse; the stale pointer is dereferenced after deallocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The timer handler runs asynchronously and uses the sock pointer without owning a reference. If rose_release/rose_destroy_socket drops the last reference while the timer is running, del_timer cannot stop the handler, so the callback's lock and state accesses operate on freed memory. Root cause is missing sock refcount management across timer start/handler; the supported consequence is use-after-free (crash, potential memory corruption).

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -1,5 +1,6 @@
 static inline u32 ___skb_get_hash(const struct sk_buff *skb,
-				  struct flow_keys *keys, u32 keyval)
+				  struct flow_keys *keys,
+				  const siphash_key_t *keyval)
 {
 	skb_flow_dissect_flow_keys(skb, keys,
 				   FLOW_DISSECTOR_F_STOP_AT_FLOW_LABEL);
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t  struct flow_keys *keys, u32 keyval)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t  struct flow_keys *keys,', '\t\t\t\t  const siphash_key_t *keyval)']}
description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: The function signature accepts a 32-bit integer `keyval` as the hash key/secret for flow hashing.
Line 6 passes this keyval directly to `__flow_hash_from_keys`, which derives the packet hash from attacker-observable flow fields; a 32-bit boot-time key is insufficiently unpredictable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because a security-relevant value (the flow-label/hash secret) is generated from insufficiently random, static 32-bit material, enabling inference. The patch replaces it with a siphash key, confirming the weakness is the weak key rather than a general hash collision issue.

evidence_lines.code:
static inline u32 ___skb_get_hash(const struct sk_buff *skb,
struct flow_keys *keys, u32 keyval)
return __flow_hash_from_keys(keys, keyval);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the flow-hash key is a 32-bit value (hashrnd) fixed at boot, and jhash over receiver-known fields lets an attacker infer it. Trigger: an attacker observes flow labels/hashes and solves for the key. Consequence: the device/user can be tracked across packets and networks because the secret is stable and inferable.

commit_msg: http://www.imagemagick.org/discourse-server/viewtopic.php?f=3&t=26861
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        (void) SeekBlob(image, offset, SEEK_CUR);', '        '], 'added_lines': ['        if (SeekBlob(image, offset, SEEK_CUR) < 0)', '          break;']}
description: coders/dds.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.0-4 Beta allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) via a crafted DDS file.

code_evidence: The loop iterates up to dds_info->mipmapcount times, computing a per-level byte offset from w, h and texel_size, then advancing the blob cursor with SeekBlob(image, offset, SEEK_CUR) while ignoring its return value (line 26). The iteration count and dimensions come from the crafted DDS header, so the loop's work is attacker-controlled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 covers improper management of system resources; here unbounded, input-driven mipmap iteration consumes CPU without a failure-based exit, matching the described CPU-consumption DoS. It is a resource-management error rather than a memory-corruption issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mipmap-skipping loop consumes CPU proportional to the attacker-supplied mipmapcount and dimensions, and the SeekBlob failure return is discarded, so an invalid or huge offset does not terminate processing early. Trigger: a crafted DDS file with a large mipmapcount reaches this loop. Supported consequence: prolonged CPU consumption (denial of service); the patched check breaks out when seeking fails.

commit_msg: fix #341
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    for (AP4_UI32 i=0; i<entry_count; i++) {'], 'added_lines': ['    // read the number of entries', '', '    // compute bounds', '    AP4_UI32 max_entries;', '    if (version == 0) {', '        max_entries = (size - (AP4_FULL_ATOM_HEADER_SIZE + 4)) / 12;', '    } else {', '        max_entries = (size - (AP4_FULL_ATOM_HEADER_SIZE + 4)) / 20;', '    }', '    //if (entry_count > max_entries) {', '    //    entry_count = max_entries;', '    //}', '    ', '    // read the entries', '    for (AP4_UI32 i=0; i < entry_count; i++) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in EnsureCapacity in Core/Ap4Array.h in Bento4 1.5.1-627. Crafted MP4 input triggers an attempt at excessive memory allocation, as demonstrated by mp42hls.

code_evidence: A 32-bit entry_count is read directly from the untrusted MP4 stream with no validation against the atom size or remaining bytes.
entry_count is passed unchanged to m_Entries.EnsureCapacity(entry_count), which preallocates capacity for that many AP4_ElstEntry elements, so a crafted value drives an arbitrarily large allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the function allocates a reusable resource (the entries container) on behalf of an untrusted actor without limiting the count to what the atom can legitimately hold. This is resource-exhaustion DoS, distinct from an out-of-bounds read/write (e.g., CWE-125/787) since no buffer index is exceeded here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The atom size and stream length are ignored when sizing the entry array; only the attacker-controlled entry_count is used. A crafted MP4 declaring a huge entry count triggers an excessive memory allocation in EnsureCapacity before any entry is read, causing memory exhaustion (DoS). The subsequent loop is unreachable for such inputs, so the cause is the unconstrained capacity request, not the parsing loop.

commit_msg:
dentry name snapshots

take_dentry_name_snapshot() takes a safe snapshot of dentry name;
if the name is a short one, it gets copied into caller-supplied
structure, otherwise an extra reference to external name is grabbed
(those are never modified).  In either case the pointer to stable
string is stored into the same structure.

dentry must be held by the caller of take_dentry_name_snapshot(),
but may be freely dropped afterwards - the snapshot will stay
until destroyed by release_dentry_name_snapshot().

Intended use:
	struct name_snapshot s;

	take_dentry_name_snapshot(&s, dentry);
	...
	access s.name
	...
	release_dentry_name_snapshot(&s);

Replaces fsnotify_oldname_...(), gets used in fsnotify to obtain the name
to pass down with event.

Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tconst char *old_name;', '\told_name = fsnotify_oldname_init(old_dentry->d_name.name);', '\t\tfsnotify_oldname_free(old_name);', '\tfsnotify_move(d_inode(old_dir), d_inode(new_dir), old_name,', '\tfsnotify_oldname_free(old_name);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct name_snapshot old_name;', '\ttake_dentry_name_snapshot(&old_name, old_dentry);', '\t\trelease_dentry_name_snapshot(&old_name);', '\tfsnotify_move(d_inode(old_dir), d_inode(new_dir), old_name.name,', '\trelease_dentry_name_snapshot(&old_name);']}
description: Race condition in the fsnotify implementation in the Linux kernel through 4.12.4 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted application that leverages simultaneous execution of the inotify_handle_event and vfs_rename functions.

code_evidence: Line 16 captures the old dentry name via fsnotify_oldname_init(old_dentry->d_name.name), returning a pointer into the dentry's name storage. Lines 17-18 perform simple_rename and line 23 d_move while the captured name is still in use; lines 24-26 then pass old_name to fsnotify_move. No lock or reference pins the name string across this window, so a concurrent vfs_rename on the same dentry can free or replace the name before fsnotify_move consumes it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a timing window where a shared dentry name resource is read without exclusive access while another concurrent sequence can modify it, matching CWE-362. It is a concurrency flaw, not merely a missing length check or use-after-free from normal lifetime handling.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the old name is snapshotted as a borrowed pointer rather than a stable copy or reference. Trigger: a concurrent rename of the same dentry between line 16 and line 24. Consequence: fsnotify_move reads freed/replaced name memory, yielding memory corruption or privilege escalation.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.6, the IPv6 dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-ipv6.c by validating an IPv6 address.

code_evidence: pinfo->dst.data and pinfo->src.data are cast directly to struct e_in6_addr pointers without checking that the address types are IPv6.
ip6_dst_addr is used as the memcpy source at line 59 and both pointers are passed to memcmp with IPv6_ADDR_SIZE, so if the underlying address is shorter than 16 bytes the reads overrun the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is missing validation of the input's type (AT_IPv6) before it is processed as an IPv6 address, which matches CWE-20's improper validation of required input properties; the consequence is a DoS crash.

evidence_lines.code:
ip6_dst_addr = (const struct e_in6_addr *)pinfo->dst.data;
ip6_src_addr = (const struct e_in6_addr *)pinfo->src.data;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function assumes pinfo->dst and pinfo->src always hold IPv6 addresses and reads IPv6_ADDR_SIZE bytes from them. When a packet causes a non-IPv6 address type to be present, the cast pointers reference a smaller buffer, and the memcpy/memcmp reads go out of bounds, crashing the dissector.

commit_msg:
drm/amd/display: memory leak

In dcn*_clock_source_create when dcn20_clk_src_construct fails allocated
clk_src needs release.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Alex Deucher <alexander.deucher@amd.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tkfree(clk_src);']}
description: Memory leaks in *clock_source_create() functions under drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc in the Linux kernel before 5.3.8 allow attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption). This affects the dce112_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce112/dce112_resource.c, the dce100_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce100/dce100_resource.c, the dcn10_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dcn10/dcn10_resource.c, the dcn20_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dcn20/dcn20_resource.c, the dce120_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce120/dce120_resource.c, the dce110_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce110/dce110_resource.c, and the dce80_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce80/dce80_resource.c, aka CID-055e547478a1.

code_evidence: clk_src is allocated with kzalloc and returned on the success path via &clk_src->base.
When dce110_clk_src_construct fails, the error path only calls BREAK_TO_DEBUGGER() and returns NULL without freeing clk_src, so the kzalloc'd object becomes unreachable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because an allocated buffer is not released after its effective lifetime ends on an error path, with the pointer lost when NULL is returned. This is a missing release on failure, not a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constructor-failure branch returns NULL without releasing the heap object allocated by kzalloc. Trigger: dce110_clk_src_construct returning nonzero, e.g., on resource/initialization failure. Consequence: the allocation is never freed, leaking memory and enabling resource consumption (DoS) if repeatedly triggered.

commit_msg: Fixed buffer overflow reported in #670
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if ((p+length) < q)', '    while (p < q)', '    {', '      for (i=0; i < (ssize_t) length; i++)', '        if (p[i] != target[i])', '          break;', '      if (i == (ssize_t) length)', '        return((unsigned char *) p);', '      p++;', '    }'], 'added_lines': ['  while ((p+length) < q)', '  {', '    for (i=0; i < (ssize_t) length; i++)', '      if (p[i] != target[i])', '        break;', '    if (i == (ssize_t) length)', '      return((unsigned char *) p);', '    p++;', '  }']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.0.6-6 and GraphicsMagick 1.3.26, a heap-based buffer over-read was found in the function SFWScan in coders/sfw.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: The outer loop condition is `(p+length) < q`, which only checks the start pointer plus length against q, not each inner read of `p[i]`.
Inside the loop, `p[i]` is read for i from 0 to length-1 while p advances via p++, so later iterations may read past q.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads memory beyond the intended buffer (past q) due to an insufficient bounds check before the `p[i]` reads, supporting a heap over-read and DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The guard `(p+length) < q` is evaluated once per outer iteration but the inner loop reads `length` bytes starting at the current p. Because p increments each iteration, the maximum read address `p+length` can exceed q, causing an out-of-bounds heap read when a crafted file makes the buffer boundary close.
