commit_msg:
staging/android/ion : fix a race condition in the ion driver

There is a use-after-free problem in the ion driver.
This is caused by a race condition in the ion_ioctl()
function.

A handle has ref count of 1 and two tasks on different
cpus calls ION_IOC_FREE simultaneously.

cpu 0                                   cpu 1
-------------------------------------------------------
ion_handle_get_by_id()
(ref == 2)
                            ion_handle_get_by_id()
                            (ref == 3)

ion_free()
(ref == 2)

ion_handle_put()
(ref == 1)

                            ion_free()
                            (ref == 0 so ion_handle_destroy() is
                            called
                            and the handle is freed.)

                            ion_handle_put() is called and it
                            decreases the slub's next free pointer

The problem is detected as an unaligned access in the
spin lock functions since it uses load exclusive
 instruction. In some cases it corrupts the slub's
free pointer which causes a mis-aligned access to the
next free pointer.(kmalloc returns a pointer like
ffffc0745b4580aa). And it causes lots of other
hard-to-debug problems.

This symptom is caused since the first member in the
ion_handle structure is the reference count and the
ion driver decrements the reference after it has been
freed.

To fix this problem client->lock mutex is extended
to protect all the codes that uses the handle.

Signed-off-by: Eun Taik Lee <eun.taik.lee@samsung.com>
Reviewed-by: Laura Abbott <labbott@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\thandle = ion_handle_get_by_id(client, data.handle.handle);', '\t\tif (IS_ERR(handle))', '\t\tion_free(client, handle);', '\t\tion_handle_put(handle);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tmutex_lock(&client->lock);', '\t\thandle = ion_handle_get_by_id_nolock(client, data.handle.handle);', '\t\tif (IS_ERR(handle)) {', '\t\t\tmutex_unlock(&client->lock);', '\t\t}', '\t\tion_free_nolock(client, handle);', '\t\tion_handle_put_nolock(handle);', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&client->lock);']}
description: Race condition in the ion_ioctl function in drivers/staging/android/ion/ion.c in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) by calling ION_IOC_FREE on two CPUs at the same time.

code_evidence: In the ION_IOC_FREE case, ion_handle_get_by_id() obtains a handle reference, then ion_free() and ion_handle_put() are called without holding client->lock. The get, free, and put sequence is not serialized against a concurrent ION_IOC_FREE call from another CPU.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in management of permissions and security features; here the ioctl path fails to enforce serialized access to a shared handle, allowing local users to corrupt kernel memory and gain privileges. The fix adds client->lock around the handle operations, confirming the missing access-control/serialization constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Two concurrent ION_IOC_FREE ioctls on the same handle both obtain references, but each independently frees and drops references; the second ion_handle_put() decrements the reference count of an already-destroyed handle, causing a use-after-free and potential memory corruption. The trigger is simultaneous ioctl calls on different CPUs; the missing lock is the root cause, and the use-after-free is the consequence.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121

commit_msg:
Generating strings for XKB data used a single shared static buffer,
which offered several opportunities for errors. Use a ring of
resizable buffers instead, to avoid problems when strings end up
longer than anticipated.

Reviewed-by: Michal Srb <msrb@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Keith Packard <keithp@keithp.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Cristau <jcristau@debian.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    char *str, buf[BUFFER_SIZE];', '                if ((str - (buf + len)) <= BUFFER_SIZE) {', '    if (len >= BUFFER_SIZE)', '        len = BUFFER_SIZE - 1;'], 'added_lines': ['    char *str, buf[VMOD_BUFFER_SIZE];', '                if ((str - (buf + len)) <= VMOD_BUFFER_SIZE) {']}
description: In X.Org Server (aka xserver and xorg-server) before 1.19.4, a local attacker authenticated to the X server could overflow a global buffer, causing crashes of the X server or potentially other problems by injecting large or malformed XKB related atoms and accessing them via xkbcomp.

code_evidence: buf is a fixed stack array of BUFFER_SIZE; the loop computes len from strlen(tmp) and writes via sprintf/strcpy at str, then advances str by len-1 (lines 41,44). The bounds check at line 31 compares (str - (buf + len)) <= BUFFER_SIZE, which is a pointer-difference test that does not reliably cap the remaining space, so writes into buf can exceed its boundary.

The final length is computed from strlen(str) and clamped to BUFFER_SIZE-1 (lines 56-58), then strncat copies len-i bytes into rtrn (line 77) and rtrn[len] is set (line 79); the clamp is against the wrong buffer size, so the destination tbGetBuffer(len+1) sizing and copy are not consistently bounded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs bounded buffer operations (buf writes and rtrn copy) whose boundary checks are incorrect, permitting reads/writes outside the intended buffer, which matches CWE-119. A more specific child such as CWE-787 could apply, but the supplied target is the buffer-bounds class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bounds checks use the wrong buffer size and an incorrect pointer-difference comparison, allowing sprintf/strcpy/strncat to write past the intended buffer. Trigger: large or malformed XKB atom strings make len/str exceed the allocated region. Consequence: out-of-bounds memory writes that can crash the X server or corrupt adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
Merge pull request from GHSA-cv8x-p47p-99wr

* - Avoid SSL socket parent/listener getting destroyed during handshake by increasing parent's reference count.
- Add missing SSL socket close when the newly accepted SSL socket is discarded in SIP TLS transport.

* - Fix silly mistake: accepted active socket created without group lock in SSL socket.
- Replace assertion with normal validation check of SSL socket instance in OpenSSL verification callback (verify_cb()) to avoid crash, e.g: if somehow race condition with SSL socket destroy happens or OpenSSL application data index somehow gets corrupted.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ssock->parent = ssock_parent;', '    if (!ssock->asock_rbuf)', '        return PJ_ENOMEM;', '        if (!ssock->asock_rbuf[i])', '            return PJ_ENOMEM;', '\tasock_cfg.grp_lock = ssock->param.grp_lock = glock;'], 'added_lines': ['    /* Set parent and add ref count (avoid parent destroy during handshake) */', '    ssock->parent = ssock_parent;', '    if (ssock->parent->param.grp_lock)', '\tpj_grp_lock_add_ref(ssock->parent->param.grp_lock);', '', '    if (!ssock->asock_rbuf) {', '\tstatus = PJ_ENOMEM;', '\tgoto on_return;', '    }', '\tif (!ssock->asock_rbuf[i]) {', '\t    status = PJ_ENOMEM;', '\t    goto on_return;', '\t}', '\tssock->param.grp_lock = glock;', '    asock_cfg.grp_lock = ssock->param.grp_lock;']}
description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In PJSIP before version 2.11.1, there are a couple of issues found in the SSL socket. First, a race condition between callback and destroy, due to the accepted socket having no group lock. Second, the SSL socket parent/listener may get destroyed during handshake. Both issues were reported to happen intermittently in heavy load TLS connections. They cause a crash, resulting in a denial of service. These are fixed in version 2.11.1.

code_evidence: The accepted socket stores a raw pointer to the listener (ssock->parent = ssock_parent) and later uses ssock_parent->param.grp_lock without holding a reference that keeps the parent alive.
A new group lock is created and attached to ssock->param.grp_lock with a destroy handler, but this lock is not installed on the active socket configuration here.

pj_activesock_cfg_default(&asock_cfg) resets the config; only async_cnt/concurrency/whole_data are set, so the accepted socket's activesock lacks the group lock that would serialize its destruction against callbacks.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits: concurrent callback and destroy sequences access shared socket state without exclusive synchronization, violating atomicity. Missing grp_lock is the synchronization defect; the crash is the consequence, not the cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The accepted SSL socket can be torn down concurrently with handshake/callback processing because it is created without a shared group lock and without holding a reference on its listener parent. Under heavy TLS load, the callback/destroy race frees or dereferences the socket (or destroyed parent) mid-handshake, causing a crash and denial of service.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttimer_stats_account_hrtimer(timer);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The time subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.9.9, when CONFIG_TIMER_STATS is enabled, allows local users to discover real PID values (as distinguished from PID values inside a PID namespace) by reading the /proc/timer_list file, related to the print_timer function in kernel/time/timer_list.c and the __timer_stats_timer_set_start_info function in kernel/time/timer.c.

code_evidence: __remove_hrtimer() deactivates the hrtimer, then timer_stats_account_hrtimer(timer) records start-time statistics for it. Those stats include the timer's start_pid, the real PID captured at timer start, which is later emitted by print_timer() in /proc/timer_list as '%s/%d'.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's call into timer_stats_account_hrtimer() is the data-collection point that lets real process identifiers reach a user-accessible proc file, so it directly supports exposure of sensitive information (CWE-200). The weakness is disclosure via an accounting interface, not a memory-safety flaw such as an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
__remove_hrtimer(timer, base, HRTIMER_STATE_INACTIVE, 0);
timer_stats_account_hrtimer(timer);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the hrtimer execution path feeds per-timer accounting data, including the real start_pid, into timer_stats, which is exposed through the world-readable /proc/timer_list without PID-namespace translation. Trigger: a local user reads /proc/timer_list while CONFIG_TIMER_STATS is enabled. Consequence: the user learns real PIDs that differ from namespace-local PIDs, exposing information about processes outside their namespace.

commit_msg:
avfilter/vf_tile: fix memory leak

Fixes #8313
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    av_frame_free(&tile->out_ref);']}
description: A Denial of Service vulnerability exists in FFmpeg 4.2 due to a memory leak in the filter_frame function in vf_tile.c.

code_evidence: uninit() frees only tile->prev_out_ref; the TileContext field tile->out_ref is never released here, and the patch adds the missing av_frame_free(&tile->out_ref).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to release an allocated/ref-counted frame during teardown, matching CWE-401 (missing release of memory after effective lifetime). It is not a use-after-free (CWE-416) because no freed memory is dereferenced; the defect is simply an unreleased reference.

evidence_lines.code:
TileContext *tile = ctx->priv;
av_frame_free(&tile->prev_out_ref);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the teardown path releases only one of the context's frame references, leaving out_ref allocated. Trigger: filter context destruction after out_ref has been populated with a frame reference; the unfreed allocation is never reclaimed, causing a memory leak that can accumulate into DoS resource consumption.

commit_msg:
journalctl: verify sealed log epochs are continuous

Currently empty epochs are not sealed. This allows an attacker to truncate
a sealed log and continue it without any problems showing when verifying the
log.

This partially addresses CVE-2023-31438. One way to extend this change to
address CVE-2023-31438 completely, would be to verify that there is exactly
one seal per epoch (and not sealing when the epoch has not ended yet).

the change also adds a journal-file flag: HEADER_COMPATIBLE_SEALED_CONTINUOUS
this flag indicates that a journal file is sealed continuously and decides whether
any missing crypto epochs should trigger a warning or an error.

description: An issue was discovered in systemd 253. An attacker can truncate a sealed log file and then resume log sealing such that checking the integrity shows no error, despite modifications. NOTE: the vendor reportedly sent "a reply denying that any of the finding was a security vulnerability."

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only reports unsupported journal header flags for diagnostics; it performs no integrity-check or checksum validation, so it does not support CWE-354.

commit_msg:
Fix oob memcpy in matrix_custom_frame methods

Adjust row_length if it exeeds the arguments array
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    struct razer_report report = get_razer_report(0x03, 0x0B, 0x46); // In theory should be able to leave data size at max as we have start/stop'], 'added_lines': ['    const size_t start_arg_offset = 4;', '    struct razer_report report = {0};', '', '    if (row_length > sizeof(report.arguments) - start_arg_offset) {', '        printk(KERN_ALERT "razerchroma: RGB data too long\\n");', '        row_length = sizeof(report.arguments) - start_arg_offset;', '    }', '', '    report = get_razer_report(0x03, 0x0B, 0x46); // In theory should be able to leave data size at max as we have start/stop']}
description: A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the razerkbd driver of OpenRazer up to version v3.3.0 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) and possibly escalate their privileges via a crafted buffer sent to the matrix_custom_frame device.

code_evidence: row_length is computed from attacker-influenced start_col and stop_col as ((stop_col + 1) - start_col) * 3, with no bound against the destination capacity.
report.arguments is a fixed-size field; only the first four bytes (indices 0-3) are written before the copy destination &report.arguments[4].
memcpy copies row_length bytes from rgb_data into &report.arguments[4] without checking that row_length fits within the remaining arguments space, allowing a write past the struct.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic buffer copy without input size checking: memcpy(&report.arguments[4], rgb_data, row_length) writes attacker-controlled length into a fixed-size destination. It is not merely a calculation error (CWE-131) because the core defect is the unchecked copy that overflows the destination.

evidence_lines.code:
size_t row_length = (size_t) (((stop_col + 1) - start_col) * 3);
struct razer_report report = get_razer_report(0x03, 0x0B, 0x46);
memcpy(&report.arguments[4], rgb_data, row_length);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy length derived from start_col/stop_col is not validated against the destination buffer size. Trigger: a crafted matrix_custom_frame buffer with a large stop_col or small start_col yields row_length exceeding the arguments array. Consequence: out-of-bounds write past report.arguments, corrupting adjacent stack memory and enabling crash/DoS or potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: fix checking node permissions

Today chk_domain_generation() is being used to check whether a node
permission entry is still valid or whether it is referring to a domain
no longer existing. This is done by comparing the node's and the
domain's generation count.

In case no struct domain is existing for a checked domain, but the
domain itself is valid, chk_domain_generation() assumes it is being
called due to the first node created for a new domain and it will
return success.

This might be wrong in case the checked permission is related to an
old domain, which has just been replaced with a new domain using the
same domid.

Fix that by letting chk_domain_generation() fail in case a struct
domain isn't found. In order to cover the case of the first node for
a new domain try to allocate the needed struct domain explicitly when
processing the related SET_PERMS command. In case a referenced domain
isn't existing, flag the related permission to be ignored right away.

This is XSA-417 / CVE-2022-42320.

Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\txc_dominfo_t dominfo;', '\tif (d)', '\t\treturn (d->generation <= gen) ? 1 : 0;', '\tif (!get_domain_info(domid, &dominfo))', '\t\treturn 0;', '', '\td = alloc_domain(NULL, domid);', '\treturn d ? 1 : -1;'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn (d && d->generation <= gen) ? 1 : 0;']}
description: Xenstore: Guests can get access to Xenstore nodes of deleted domains Access rights of Xenstore nodes are per domid. When a domain is gone, there might be Xenstore nodes left with access rights containing the domid of the removed domain. This is normally no problem, as those access right entries will be corrected when such a node is written later. There is a small time window when a new domain is created, where the access rights of a past domain with the same domid as the new one will be regarded to be still valid, leading to the new domain being able to get access to a node which was meant to be accessible by the removed domain. For this to happen another domain needs to write the node before the newly created domain is being introduced to Xenstore by dom0.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only validates domain generation counts and domain existence; it performs no allocation or cleanup of temporary/supporting resources, so CWE-459 (Incomplete Cleanup) is not supported by this code.

commit_msg:
stub_send_ret_submit() handles urb with a potential null transfer_buffer,
when it replays a packet with potential malicious data that could contain
a null buffer. Add a check for the condition when actual_length > 0 and
transfer_buffer is null.

Reported-by: Secunia Research <vuln@secunia.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan <shuahkh@osg.samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\tif (urb->actual_length > 0 && !urb->transfer_buffer) {', '\t\t\tdev_err(&sdev->udev->dev,', '\t\t\t\t"urb: actual_length %d transfer_buffer null\\n",', '\t\t\t\turb->actual_length);', '\t\t\treturn -1;', '\t\t}']}
description: The "stub_send_ret_submit()" function (drivers/usb/usbip/stub_tx.c) in the Linux Kernel before version 4.14.8, 4.9.71, 4.1.49, and 4.4.107 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via a specially crafted USB over IP packet.

code_evidence: When the URB is an input pipe with actual_length > 0, the code stores urb->transfer_buffer as an iovec base without checking it is non-NULL.
The isochronous branch performs pointer arithmetic on urb->transfer_buffer (offset added to it) with no NULL check either.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer it assumes valid (transfer_buffer) without a NULL check, matching CWE-476. This is not a buffer overflow (CWE-119) because no out-of-bounds access occurs; the defect is the missing NULL validation before use.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: transfer_buffer is used as a valid pointer whenever actual_length (or iso packet lengths) indicate data, but a crafted USB over IP packet can replay an URB with a non-zero length and a NULL buffer. Trigger: the host sends such a URB; the iovec points at NULL and kernel_sendmsg dereferences it. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a kernel crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
Do not ignore empty associated data with AES-SIV mode

The AES-SIV mode allows for multiple associated data items
authenticated separately with any of these being 0 length.

The provided implementation ignores such empty associated data
which is incorrect in regards to the RFC 5297 and is also
a security issue because such empty associated data then become
unauthenticated if an application expects to authenticate them.

Fixes CVE-2023-2975

Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/21384)

(cherry picked from commit c426c281cfc23ab182f7d7d7a35229e7db1494d9)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (inl == 0) {', '        *outl = 0;', '        return 1;', '    }', '    if (outsize < inl) {', '        ERR_raise(ERR_LIB_PROV, PROV_R_OUTPUT_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL);', '        return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    /* Ignore just empty encryption/decryption call and not AAD. */', '    if (out != NULL) {', '        if (inl == 0) {', '            if (outl != NULL)', '                *outl = 0;', '            return 1;', '        }', '        if (outsize < inl) {', '            ERR_raise(ERR_LIB_PROV, PROV_R_OUTPUT_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL);', '            return 0;', '        }']}
description:
Issue summary: The AES-SIV cipher implementation contains a bug that causes
it to ignore empty associated data entries which are unauthenticated as
a consequence.

Impact summary: Applications that use the AES-SIV algorithm and want to
authenticate empty data entries as associated data can be mislead by removing
adding or reordering such empty entries as these are ignored by the OpenSSL
implementation. We are currently unaware of any such applications.

The AES-SIV algorithm allows for authentication of multiple associated
data entries along with the encryption. To authenticate empty data the
application has to call EVP_EncryptUpdate() (or EVP_CipherUpdate()) with
NULL pointer as the output buffer and 0 as the input buffer length.
The AES-SIV implementation in OpenSSL just returns success for such a call
instead of performing the associated data authentication operation.
The empty data thus will not be authenticated.

As this issue does not affect non-empty associated data authentication and
we expect it to be rare for an application to use empty associated data
entries this is qualified as Low severity issue.

code_evidence: When inl == 0 the function immediately writes *outl = 0 and returns success without invoking ctx->hw->cipher, so an empty-input call (which the AES-SIV API uses to supply empty associated data) is treated as a no-op rather than being authenticated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to prove/authenticate a claimed associated-data identity (the empty AAD entry), so the integrity of that data is not established, matching CWE-287's insufficient authentication. This is an authentication-bypass of data rather than a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the zero-length early return bypasses the cipher/AAD authentication path for any empty call, regardless of whether out is NULL (AAD) or non-NULL. Trigger: an application passes an empty associated-data item via a zero-length update; the function returns 1 without authenticating it, so empty AAD entries are silently dropped, removing them from the authentication claim.

commit_msg:
avcodec/evc_ps: Check ref_pic_num and sps_max_dec_pic_buffering_minus1

Fixes: out of array write

Found-by: dongsookim@korea.ac.kr
Reviewed-by: James Almer <jamrial@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>

description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability in Ffmpeg before github commit 4565747056a11356210ed8edcecb920105e40b60 allows a remote attacker to achieve an out-of-array write, execute arbitrary code, and cause a denial of service (DoS) via the ref_pic_list_struct function in libavcodec/evc_ps.c

code_evidence: Line 81 parses attacker-controlled sps_max_dec_pic_buffering_minus1 with no upper-bound check before ref_pic_list_struct is invoked; the loop at lines 89-90 writes into sps->rpls[0][i] based on num_ref_pic_list_in_sps[0], which is bounded only by EVC_MAX_NUM_RPLS at line 85.

It is not merely an integer overflow because the unchecked count directly causes indexing beyond the buffer.

commit_msg:
Bug 790784 - (CVE-2017-17784) heap overread in gbr parser / load_image.

We were assuming the input name was well formed, hence was
nul-terminated. As any data coming from external input, this has to be
thorougly checked.
Similar to commit 06d24a79af94837d615d0024916bb95a01bf3c59 but adapted
to older gimp-2-8 code.
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -97,7 +97,8 @@
     {
       gchar *temp = g_new (gchar, bn_size);
 
-      if ((read (fd, temp, bn_size)) < bn_size)
+      if ((read (fd, temp, bn_size)) < bn_size ||
+          temp[bn_size - 1] != '\0')
         {
           g_set_error (error, G_FILE_ERROR, G_FILE_ERROR_FAILED,
                        _("Error in GIMP brush file '%s'"),
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if ((read (fd, temp, bn_size)) < bn_size)'], 'added_lines': ['      if ((read (fd, temp, bn_size)) < bn_size ||', "          temp[bn_size - 1] != '\\0')"]}
description: In GIMP 2.8.22, there is a heap-based buffer over-read in load_image in plug-ins/common/file-gbr.c in the gbr import parser, related to mishandling of UTF-8 data.

code_evidence: [80-83] bn_size is derived from the attacker-controlled header_size (bn_size = bh.header_size - sizeof(BrushHeader)) and a buffer temp of exactly bn_size bytes is allocated and filled by read(fd, temp, bn_size). The only check is that the read returned bn_size bytes; nothing guarantees a NUL terminator inside temp.

[92-94] gimp_any_to_utf8(temp, -1, ...) is called with length -1, so the string is treated as NUL-terminated. If the file's brush-name data lacks a '\0', the routine scans past the end of the heap allocation, producing the over-read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading past the end of the temp allocation matches CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read), which covers reads past the intended buffer. It is not CWE-787 or CWE-122, because the defect is an over-read of memory rather than an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser assumes the external brush-name field is NUL-terminated while only verifying that bn_size bytes were read. Trigger: a crafted .gbr file whose name bytes contain no NUL within bn_size. Consequence: gimp_any_to_utf8 with -1 length reads beyond the temp heap buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:

Found-by: AD-lab of venustech

commit_msg:
udf_expand_file_adinicb() calls directly ->writepage to write data
expanded into a page. This however misses to setup inode for writeback
properly and so we can crash on inode->i_wb dereference when submitting
page for IO like:

  #PF: supervisor read access in kernel mode

commit_msg:
Improve input validation for some parameters having a too small
reported length.

Thanks to Natalie Silvanovich from Google for finding one of these
issues in the SCTP userland stack and reporting it.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (plen == 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (plen < sizeof(struct sctp_paramhdr)) {', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tif (plen < sizeof(struct sctp_asconf_addrv4_param)) {', '\t\t\t\treturn (-101);']}
description: usrsctp before 2019-12-20 has out-of-bounds reads in sctp_load_addresses_from_init.

code_evidence: The parameter loop reads plen from the wire at line 125 and only rejects plen==0 (line 129); a plen of 1..3 passes, so the loop advances via SCTP_SIZE32(plen) and re-parses a truncated sctp_paramhdr-sized region with sctp_get_next_param at line 478.

For SCTP_SET_PRIM_ADDR, plen is only bounded above by sizeof(lstore) (line 289); the parameter is copied into lstore with length plen (lines 292-294), then fee is cast and fee->addrp.ph.param_type is read at line 299, and for the IPv4 case fii->addrp.addr is read at line 310, requiring the full sctp_asconf_addrv4_param size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads structure fields (fee->addrp.ph.param_type, fii->addrp.addr) after only validating plen against an upper bound, so a too-small reported length causes reads beyond the intended buffer, matching CWE-125. This is a read, not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: plen is trusted without a minimum-length check. A short SCTP parameter (plen below sizeof(struct sctp_paramhdr), or below the asconf addrv4 parameter size) is accepted, so the code reads param_type/addr fields past the end of the copied lstore/param buffer. Trigger: a crafted INIT/INIT-ACK with a truncated SET_PRIM_ADDR parameter. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
Don't feed anything but regular iovec's to blk_rq_map_user_iov

In theory we could map other things, but there's a reason that function
is called "user_iov".  Using anything else (like splice can do) just
confuses it.

Reported-and-tested-by: Johannes Thumshirn <jthumshirn@suse.de>
Cc: Al Viro <viro@ZenIV.linux.org.uk>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (!iter_is_iovec(iter))', '\t\tgoto fail;', 'fail:']}
description: The blk_rq_map_user_iov function in block/blk-map.c in the Linux kernel before 4.8.14 does not properly restrict the type of iterator, which allows local users to read or write to arbitrary kernel memory locations or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) by leveraging access to a /dev/sg device.

code_evidence: The function copies the caller-supplied iterator into local i (line 16) and loops calling __blk_rq_map_user_iov, storing the resulting bio in rq->bio and in the local bio (lines 17-23), without ever verifying the iterator type.
On error the unmap_rq label frees the mapped bio via __blk_rq_unmap_user(bio) and clears rq->bio (lines 27-30).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is reuse of a bio after __blk_rq_unmap_user frees it, matching CWE-416 (Use After Free). The missing iter_is_iovec check is the cause that lets a malformed mapping reach that free; the weakness itself is the stale reference, not merely improper input validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accepts any iov_iter type, including non-iovec iterators that __blk_rq_map_user_iov does not handle correctly, so the bio it builds is malformed. When a later mapping iteration fails, the error path calls __blk_rq_unmap_user(bio), releasing memory that the malformed mapping still references. Trigger: a local user supplies a non-regular iterator via splice on a /dev/sg device. Consequence: the freed memory can be reused, giving use-after-free reads/writes of kernel memory or a crash.

commit_msg: Fix arbitrary heap exposure problem
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        state->space_before = strdup(RSTRING_PTR(space_before));'], 'added_lines': ['        state->space_before = fstrndup(RSTRING_PTR(space_before), len);']}
description: Ruby through 2.2.7, 2.3.x through 2.3.4, and 2.4.x through 2.4.1 can expose arbitrary memory during a JSON.generate call. The issues lies in using strdup in ext/json/ext/generator/generator.c, which will stop after encountering a '\0' byte, returning a pointer to a string of length zero, which is not the length stored in space_len.

code_evidence: Line 6 computes len = RSTRING_LEN(space_before), the full byte length of the string including any embedded NUL bytes. Line 15 allocates a copy via strdup(RSTRING_PTR(space_before)), but strdup stops at the first NUL byte and allocates only up to that terminator, while line 16 records space_before_len = len, the original longer length. The two lengths therefore diverge whenever the string contains an embedded NUL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Recording a length that exceeds the actual allocated buffer causes subsequent operations to access memory beyond the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The defect is a length/truncation mismatch leading to out-of-bounds access, not merely a format or input-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: strdup truncates at the first NUL, so the allocated buffer is shorter than the space_before_len value stored on line 16. Trigger: setting a space_before string that contains an embedded NUL byte. Consequence: later code trusting space_before_len reads past the end of the shorter heap allocation, exposing adjacent memory (arbitrary heap read).

commit_msg:
For USB there is no separate channel being used to pass events
from firmware to the host driver and as such are passed over the
data path. In order to detect mock event messages an additional
check is needed on event subtype. This check is added conditionally
using unlikely() keyword.

Reviewed-by: Hante Meuleman <hante.meuleman@broadcom.com>
Reviewed-by: Pieter-Paul Giesberts <pieter-paul.giesberts@broadcom.com>
Reviewed-by: Franky Lin <franky.lin@broadcom.com>
Signed-off-by: Arend van Spriel <arend.vanspriel@broadcom.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbrcmf_fweh_process_skb(ifp->drvr, skb);'], 'added_lines': ['\tbrcmf_fweh_process_skb(ifp->drvr, skb, 0);']}
description: The Broadcom brcmfmac WiFi driver prior to commit a4176ec356c73a46c07c181c6d04039fafa34a9f is vulnerable to a frame validation bypass. If the brcmfmac driver receives a firmware event frame from a remote source, the is_wlc_event_frame function will cause this frame to be discarded and unprocessed. If the driver receives the firmware event frame from the host, the appropriate handler is called. This frame validation can be bypassed if the bus used is USB (for instance by a wifi dongle). This can allow firmware event frames from a remote source to be processed. In the worst case scenario, by sending specially-crafted WiFi packets, a remote, unauthenticated attacker may be able to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable system. More typically, this vulnerability will result in denial-of-service conditions.

code_evidence: brcmf_rx_event receives an skb and passes it to brcmf_rx_hdrpull; on success it invokes brcmf_fweh_process_skb(ifp->drvr, skb) with only the driver and skb, giving no indication of the frame's origin (host vs remote). The function performs no check on event subtype or source before dispatching the frame to firmware-event processing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts input (a firmware event frame) and processes it without validating the property that matters for safety—its origin/subtype—so remote frames are treated as trusted host events. This is improper input validation (CWE-20), not merely a parsing/transformation flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the event path forwards any received skb to firmware-event handling without distinguishing frames arriving from the host from those arriving over the USB data path. Trigger: a remote attacker sends crafted firmware event frames over USB; they are accepted as if host-originated and dispatched to the appropriate handler. Supported consequence: unvalidated event frames are processed, enabling denial-of-service or, in the worst case, code execution.

description: A privilege escalation to root exists in Eternal Terminal prior to version 6.2.0. This is due to the combination of a race condition, buffer overflow, and logic bug all in PipeSocketHandler::listen().

sanitise cache paths

Co-authored-by: JerikoOne <jeriko.one@gmx.us>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  return snprintf(dest, destlen, "%s.hcache", path);'], 'added_lines': ['  int count = snprintf(dest, destlen, "%s.hcache", path);', '', '  /* Strip out any directories in the path */', "  char *first = strchr(dest, '/');", "  char *last = strrchr(dest, '/');", '  if (first && last && (last > first))', '  {', '    memmove(first, last, strlen(last) + 1);', '    count -= (last - first);', '  }', '', '  return count;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Mutt before 1.10.1 and NeoMutt before 2018-07-16. pop.c does not forbid characters that may have unsafe interaction with message-cache pathnames, as demonstrated by a '/' character.

code_evidence: The function builds the cache pathname with snprintf(dest, destlen, "%s.hcache", path), writing into the caller-provided dest buffer. The only bound applied is destlen; the attacker-influenced path is copied verbatim with no constraint on characters such as '/', so the resulting pathname may contain directory separators that interact unsafely with message-cache path handling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing character restriction lets the formatted pathname exceed the intended cache-directory boundary and be used for file operations outside it, consistent with CWE-119's operation on a buffer outside its intended boundary. This is not a simple overflow: snprintf truncates to destlen, so the weakness is boundary escape rather than a write past dest.

evidence_lines.code: return snprintf(dest, destlen, "%s.hcache", path);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pathname is formatted into dest without validating or restricting path characters, so a path containing '/' yields a cache pathname that escapes the intended cache directory. Trigger: attacker-controlled path content reaching this namer. Consequence: the cache pathname is written to an unintended location, enabling unsafe cache-path interaction; the snprintf bound itself does not prevent this.

commit_msg:
evtchn: evtchn_reset() shouldn't succeed with still-open ports

While the function closes all ports, it does so without holding any
lock, and hence racing requests may be issued causing new ports to get
opened. This would have been problematic in particular if such a newly
opened port had a port number above the new implementation limit (i.e.
when switching from FIFO to 2-level) after the reset, as prior to
"evtchn: relax port_is_valid()" this could have led to e.g.
evtchn_close()'s "BUG_ON(!port_is_valid(d2, port2))" to trigger.

Introduce a counter of active ports and check that it's (still) no
larger then the number of Xen internally used ones after obtaining the
necessary lock in evtchn_reset().

As to the access model of the new {active,xen}_evtchns fields - while
all writes get done using write_atomic(), reads ought to use
read_atomic() only when outside of a suitably locked region.

Note that as of now evtchn_bind_virq() and evtchn_bind_ipi() don't have
a need to call check_free_port().

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    write_atomic(&d->active_evtchns, 0);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: evtchn_init() initializes the port table and spinlock, then calls get_free_port(d) to reserve port 0 and marks it ECS_RESERVED at line 15. The function performs no locking around this initialization sequence, and it does not initialize any active-port counter; the patch adds write_atomic(&d->active_evtchns, 0) after line 15, indicating this field is shared state consumed elsewhere.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a shared resource (the event-channel port table and active-port counter) is accessed without exclusive synchronization, leaving a timing window for concurrent modification. The root cause is the missing atomic/locked initialization, not merely a bounds check; the supported consequence is inconsistent state enabling OOB access or DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The initialization mutates shared domain event-channel state (d->evtchn, d->valid_evtchns and the new active_evtchns counter) without holding event_lock and without establishing the counter that later reset/bind paths rely on. A concurrent EVTCHNOP_reset or bind racing this setup can observe partially initialized state, so the active-port accounting is inconsistent and port validation assumptions can be violated, leading to out-of-bounds accesses or bug checks.

This is a direct null dereference rather than, e.g., an out-of-bounds read, since the defect is the missing NULL check on attr->name/attr->value.

Trigger: an attribute entry whose name or value member is NULL reaches this loop. description: GPAC 2.1-DEV-rev368-gfd054169b-master was discovered to contain a heap buffer overflow via the function FixSDTPInTRAF at isomedia/isom_intern.c.

code_evidence: The inner loop iterates over trun->nb_samples and reads traf->sdtp->sample_info[sample_index] using sample_index, which is only bounded by the check after the read/increment.

The guard `if (sample_index > traf->sdtp->sampleCount)` executes after the access at line 20 and after incrementing, so the read at line 20 can occur with sample_index equal to sampleCount, i.e., one past the sample_info array.

code_evidence: name_start and name_end point into eap->arg, the current command line buffer. define_function(eap, lambda_name) is called at line 47 and may free/reallocate that command line, leaving name_start/name_end dangling.

Later code still dereferences the stale pointers: line 81-82 calls vim_strnsave(name_start + 2, ...) and line 93 passes name_start to reserve_local, both after define_function has potentially freed the underlying buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function references memory (name_start/name_end) after the call that may free it, which is exactly CWE-416 use-after-free. The patch's comment and the added copy of the name before define_function confirm the freed-buffer dependency; this is not merely a double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pointers into the command-line buffer (name_start/name_end) are retained across define_function, which can free that buffer. Trigger: a nested :def whose define_function frees the current line. The use of the dangling name_start at lines 81-82 and 93 then reads freed memory, supporting a use-after-free with possible crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Fix a security vulnerability discovered by Qualys which can lead to a
privileges escalation on mbox deliveries and unprivileged code execution
on lmtp deliveries, due to a logic issue causing a sanity check to be
missed.

The empty-return-path exception at [26,27] also returns success.

commit_msg:
_bfd_clear_contents bounds checking

This PR shows a fuzzed binary triggering a segfault via a bad
relocation in .debug_line.  It turns out that unlike normal
relocations applied to a section, the linker applies those with
symbols from discarded sections via _bfd_clear_contents without
checking that the relocation is within the section bounds.  The same
thing now happens when reading debug sections since commit
a4cd947aca23, the PR23425 fix.

	PR 23770
	PR 23425
	* reloc.c (_bfd_clear_contents): Replace "location" param with
	"buf" and "off".  Bounds check "off".  Return status.
	* cofflink.c (_bfd_coff_generic_relocate_section): Update
	_bfd_clear_contents call.
	* elf-bfd.h (RELOC_AGAINST_DISCARDED_SECTION): Likewise.
	* elf32-arc.c (elf_arc_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-i386.c (elf_i386_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-metag.c (metag_final_link_relocate): Likewise.
	* elf32-nds32.c (nds32_elf_get_relocated_section_contents): Likewise.
	* elf32-ppc.c (ppc_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-visium.c (visium_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf64-ppc.c (ppc64_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf64-x86-64.c *(elf_x86_64_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* libbfd-in.h (_bfd_clear_contents): Update prototype.
	* libbfd.h: Regenerate.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t       contents + rel->r_offset);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t       contents, rel->r_offset);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.31. An invalid memory address dereference was discovered in read_reloc in reloc.c. The vulnerability causes a segmentation fault and application crash, which leads to denial of service, as demonstrated by objdump, because of missing _bfd_clear_contents bounds checking.

code_evidence: When the relocation's symbol section is discarded, the code calls _bfd_clear_contents with contents + rel->r_offset, computing a pointer from the untrusted relocation offset without validating that rel->r_offset lies within input_section's buffer. The patch changes this to pass contents and rel->r_offset separately so the callee can bounds-check the offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directs a memory operation to contents + r_offset without restricting the offset to the buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The root cause is a missing bounds check on the relocation offset rather than a null-pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a relocation r_offset from a malformed object file is used to form a buffer pointer without a bounds check. Trigger: a crafted relocation against a discarded section whose r_offset exceeds the section contents size. Consequence: _bfd_clear_contents performs an out-of-bounds memory access, causing a segfault/DoS (and potentially worse).

In kobject_get_path(), if kobj->name is changed between calls
get_kobj_path_length() and fill_kobj_path() and the length becomes
longer, then fill_kobj_path() will have an out-of-bounds bug.

The actual current problem occurs when the ixgbe probe.

In ixgbe_mii_bus_init(), if the length of netdev->dev.kobj.name
length becomes longer, out-of-bounds will occur.

cpu0                                         cpu1
ixgbe_probe
 register_netdev(netdev)
  netdev_register_kobject
   device_add
    kobject_uevent // Sending ADD events
                                             systemd-udevd // rename netdev
                                              dev_change_name
                                               device_rename
                                                kobject_rename
 ixgbe_mii_bus_init                             |
  mdiobus_register                              |
   __mdiobus_register                           |
    device_register                             |
     device_add                                 |
      kobject_uevent                            |
       kobject_get_path                         |
        len = get_kobj_path_length // old name  |
        path = kzalloc(len, gfp_mask);          |
                                                kobj->name = name;
                                                /* name length becomes

        fill_kobj_path /* kobj path length is
                        * longer than path,

                        */

do
    rmmod ixgbe
    sleep 0.5

When calling fill_kobj_path() to fill path, if the name length of

Signed-off-by: Wang Hai <wanghai38@huawei.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void fill_kobj_path(const struct kobject *kobj, char *path, int length)'], 'added_lines': ['static int fill_kobj_path(const struct kobject *kobj, char *path, int length)', '\t\tif (length <= 0)', '\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '', '\treturn 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in lib/kobject.c in the Linux kernel before 6.2.3. With root access, an attacker can trigger a race condition that results in a fill_kobj_path out-of-bounds write.

code_evidence: The function decrements length once, then loops over kobj and its parents. For each parent it computes cur = strlen(kobject_name(parent)) and subtracts cur from length, then does memcpy(path + length, kobject_name(parent), cur) and writes a '/' at the decremented length. There is no check that length stays positive before these writes, so the destination offset can become negative or the copy can extend beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the memcpy at line 8 and the byte write at line 9 can write past the intended buffer when the recomputed name length exceeds the allocated length. This is a direct out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read or information leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer size (length) is computed from kobject names before this call, but kobject_name(parent) is re-read and can grow concurrently (e.g., a netdev rename between length computation and fill). Trigger: a race in which a name length increases after allocation. Consequence: memcpy and the '/' write land outside the allocated path buffer, an out-of-bounds write (KASAN slab-out-of-bounds).

commit_msg:
Do not write after the end of the array and overwrite the stack when
colon-separated SGR sequences contain empty arguments. Reported by Sergey
Nizovtsev.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t} else'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t} else {', '\t\t\tif (n == nitems(p)) {', '\t\t\t\tfree(copy);', '\t\t\t\treturn;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t}']}
description: In tmux before version 3.1c the function input_csi_dispatch_sgr_colon() in file input.c contained a stack-based buffer-overflow that can be exploited by terminal output.

code_evidence: Fixed-size stack array p[8] is initialized and n is the write index into it.

The non-empty branch writes p[n++] before checking bounds; the guard n == nitems(p) returns only after the write, so the last valid slot is written and then further increments are not prevented in the else path.
The empty-argument branch at line 20-21 increments n without any bounds check, then line 22 reads p[n-1] and logs it, allowing n to exceed the array size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes and reads past the end of the fixed stack buffer p due to a missing bounds check on n, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). A pure read overrun would be CWE-125, but the unchecked index feeds array writes, so the write weakness fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Colon-separated SGR input with empty arguments (consecutive colons) repeatedly takes the else branch, incrementing n past nitems(p). Subsequent writes/reads at p[n-1] index beyond the stack array p[8], corrupting the stack; the trigger is attacker-controlled terminal output.

description: Directory Traversal in Zip Extraction built-in function in Kodi 17.1 and earlier allows arbitrary file write on disk via a Zip file as subtitles.

commit_msg:
x86/mm: Prevent some races in hypervisor mapping updates

map_pages_to_xen will attempt to coalesce mappings into 2MiB and 1GiB
superpages if possible, to maximize TLB efficiency.  This means both
replacing superpage entries with smaller entries, and replacing
smaller entries with superpages.

Unfortunately, while some potential races are handled correctly,
others are not.  These include:

1. When one processor modifies a sub-superpage mapping while another
processor replaces the entire range with a superpage.

Take the following example:

Suppose L3[N] points to L2.  And suppose we have two processors, A and
B.

* A walks the pagetables, get a pointer to L2.
* B replaces L3[N] with a 1GiB mapping.
* B Frees L2
* A writes L2[M] #

This is race exacerbated by the fact that virt_to_xen_l[21]e doesn't
handle higher-level superpages properly: If you call virt_xen_to_l2e
on a virtual address within an L3 superpage, you'll either hit a BUG()
(most likely), or get a pointer into the middle of a data page; same
with virt_xen_to_l1 on a virtual address within either an L3 or L2
superpage.

So take the following example:

* A reads pl3e and discovers it to point to an L2.
* B replaces L3[N] with a 1GiB mapping
* A calls virt_to_xen_l2e() and hits the BUG_ON() #

2. When two processors simultaneously try to replace a sub-superpage
mapping with a superpage mapping.

Take the following example:

Suppose L3[N] points to L2.  And suppose we have two processors, A and B,
both trying to replace L3[N] with a superpage.

* A walks the pagetables, get a pointer to pl3e, and takes a copy ol3e pointing to L2.
* B walks the pagetables, gets a pointre to pl3e, and takes a copy ol3e pointing to L2.
* A writes the new value into L3[N]
* B writes the new value into L3[N]
* A recursively frees all the L1's under L2, then frees L2
* B recursively double-frees all the L1's under L2, then double-frees L2 #

Fix this by grabbing a lock for the entirety of the mapping update
operation.

Rather than grabbing map_pgdir_lock for the entire operation, however,
repurpose the PGT_locked bit from L3's page->type_info as a lock.
This means that rather than locking the entire address space, we
"only" lock a single 512GiB chunk of hypervisor address space at a
time.

There was a proposal for a lock-and-reverify approach, where we walk
the pagetables to the point where we decide what to do; then grab the
map_pgdir_lock, re-verify the information we collected without the
lock, and finally make the change (starting over again if anything had
changed).  Without being able to guarantee that the L2 table wasn't
freed, however, that means every read would need to be considered
potentially unsafe.  Thinking carefully about that is probably
something that wants to be done on public, not under time pressure.

This is part of XSA-345.

Reported-by: Hongyan Xia <hongyxia@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Hongyan Xia <hongyxia@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        l3_pgentry_t *pl3e = virt_to_xen_l3e(v);', '', '        if ( !pl3e || !(l3e_get_flags(*pl3e) & _PAGE_PRESENT) )'], 'added_lines': ['    struct page_info *current_l3page;', '    L3T_INIT(current_l3page);', '', '        l3_pgentry_t *pl3e;', '', '        L3T_UNLOCK(current_l3page);', '', '        pl3e = virt_to_xen_l3e(v);', '        if ( !pl3e )', '            goto out;', '', '        current_l3page = virt_to_page(pl3e);', '        L3T_LOCK(current_l3page);', '', '        if ( !(l3e_get_flags(*pl3e) & _PAGE_PRESENT) )', '    L3T_UNLOCK(current_l3page);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x allowing x86 guest OS users to cause a host OS denial of service, achieve data corruption, or possibly gain privileges by exploiting a race condition that leads to a use-after-free involving 2MiB and 1GiB superpages.

code_evidence: Line 15-16 reads pl3e and checks presence without holding the L3 lock, so a concurrent mapping update can replace or free the L2 table between the check and later use.
Line 59 dereferences *pl3e to derive pl2e, and line 60 reads *pl2e, after the unlocked L3 entry walk.
Lines 130-140 walk l1t and free_xen_pagetable(l1t) after only map_pgdir_lock, without preventing another CPU from replacing L3[N] with a superpage.
Lines 160-170 read l2t and free_xen_pagetable(l2t) based on the same unsynchronized L3 walk.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The window between the unlocked read of the shared page-table entry and its later use/free violates exclusivity and atomicity, matching CWE-362. This is a synchronization race, not merely a stale-read logic error, because an interfering concurrent mapping update directly causes use-after-free and double-free consequences.

evidence_lines.code:
l3_pgentry_t *pl3e = virt_to_xen_l3e(v);
if ( !pl3e || !(l3e_get_flags(*pl3e) & _PAGE_PRESENT) )

pl2e = l3e_to_l2e(*pl3e) + l2_table_offset(v);
if ( !(l2e_get_flags(*pl2e) & _PAGE_PRESENT) )

l1t = l2e_to_l1e(*pl2e);
free_xen_pagetable(l1t);

l2t = l3e_to_l2e(*pl3e);
free_xen_pagetable(l2t);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function walks shared page tables and later frees lower-level tables based on entries it read without an exclusive lock over the L3 range. A concurrent map_pages_to_xen update can replace L3[N] with a 1GiB superpage and free the L2 table, leaving this sequence to write into or double-free freed page tables, causing host DoS, corruption, or privilege escalation.

description: async.c and dict.c in libhiredis.a in hiredis through 0.14.0 allow a NULL pointer dereference because malloc return values are unchecked.

code_evidence: Line 2 assigns the unchecked result of malloc(sizeof(*ht)) to ht; no NULL test follows. Line 3 immediately passes ht to _dictInit, which dereferences the struct, so an allocation failure yields a NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because a pointer expected to be valid is dereferenced while it may be NULL. This is a missing NULL check on allocation, not a buffer overflow or use-after-free.

dict *ht = malloc(sizeof(*ht));
_dictInit(ht,type,privDataPtr);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the malloc return value is used without a NULL check. Trigger: malloc fails (e.g., memory exhaustion) and returns NULL. Consequence: _dictInit dereferences a NULL pointer, causing a crash/DoS; the unchecked pointer is returned to callers as well.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['unsigned int GetU32BE (int nPos, bool *pbSuccess)', '            if ( nPos < 0 || nPos + 3 >= m_nLen )'], 'added_lines': ['unsigned int GetU32BE (const unsigned int& nPos, bool *pbSuccess)', '            if ( m_nLen < 4 || nPos > (m_nLen - 4) )']}
description: Onlyoffice Document Server v6.0.0 and below and Core 6.1.0.26 and below were discovered to contain a heap overflow via the component DesktopEditor/fontengine/fontconverter/FontFileBase.h.

code_evidence: The function checks bounds with `nPos < 0 || nPos + 3 >= m_nLen` at line 3, then reads m_sFile[nPos] through m_sFile[nPos + 3] at lines 8-11. The upper-bound test uses `>=` rather than `>`, so an index where nPos + 3 == m_nLen (i.e., nPos == m_nLen - 3) passes the check, and line 11 reads m_sFile[m_nLen], one element past the buffer. The signed int nPos and the `nPos + 3` arithmetic can also overflow for large values, bypassing the check entirely.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 covers accessing memory outside the intended buffer bounds; here the flawed check lets the code index m_sFile past its end, so the out-of-bounds access on lines 8-11 matches the target weakness. The cause is the incorrect boundary condition, not merely an integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The bounds check is off by one and uses signed arithmetic that can overflow, allowing nPos values near or beyond m_nLen to reach the four byte reads at lines 8-11. A caller-controlled position therefore causes reads past the end of m_sFile, yielding out-of-bounds memory access (heap over-read/overflow) and potential crash or information disclosure.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

commit_msg:
stb_image: Fix bug on JPEGs with malformed DC deltas

extend_receive implicitly requires n <= 15 (code length);
the maximum that actually makes sense for 8-bit baseline JPEG is
11, but 15 is the natural limit for us because the AC coding path
stores the number of magnitude bits in a nibble.

Check that DC delta bits are in range before attempting to call
extend_receive.

Fixes issue #1108.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if (t == -1) return stbi__err("can\'t merge dc and ac", "Corrupt JPEG");'], 'added_lines': ['      if (t < 0 || t > 15) return stbi__err("can\'t merge dc and ac", "Corrupt JPEG");']}
description: Buffer overflow vulnerability in function stbi__extend_receive in stb_image.h in stb 2.26 via a crafted JPEG file.

code_evidence: Line 8 decodes a DC Huffman symbol into t and line 9 only rejects t == -1, allowing large t values through; line 10 then passes t to stbi__extend_receive as the bit count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate t before using it to compute a DC coefficient that is written into the data buffer, directly enabling an out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-787. This is an input-validation gap leading to memory corruption, not merely an integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The decoded DC delta bit-length t is not upper-bounded before being used as the shift/count in stbi__extend_receive. A crafted JPEG yielding an oversized t lets that routine read/derive an out-of-range value that is combined with dc_pred and stored, producing an out-of-bounds write. The missing constraint (t <= 15) is the root cause; the write past the buffer is the consequence.

commit_msg: Fix more CRLF injection problems.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (!content_type.empty()) {', '    req.headers.emplace("Content-Type", content_type);', '  }'], 'added_lines': ['  if (!content_type.empty()) { req.set_header("Content-Type", content_type); }']}
description:
Versions of the package yhirose/cpp-httplib before 0.12.4 are vulnerable to CRLF Injection when untrusted user input is used to set the content-type header in the HTTP .Patch, .Post, .Put and .Delete requests. This can lead to logical errors and other misbehaviors.

**Note:** This issue is present due to an incomplete fix for [CVE-2020-11709](https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-UNMANAGED-YHIROSECPPHTTPLIB-2366507).

code_evidence: The caller-supplied content_type string is placed directly into the request headers via req.headers.emplace("Content-Type", content_type) whenever it is non-empty; no validation or CR/LF filtering occurs before the header is stored. The header value flows into send_ with the request.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits because untrusted input is used to construct an HTTP header record and special elements (CR/LF) are not neutralized, altering how a downstream HTTP parser interprets the message. A more specific child such as CRLF injection (CWE-93) is a refinement, but the target class is supported by the same unsafe construction.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the content_type parameter is externally influenced and is inserted into the Content-Type header without neutralizing CR/LF characters. Trigger: a caller passes a content_type containing \r\n sequences, which the header map stores verbatim. Consequence: the injected CRLF breaks out of the header line, allowing additional headers or request-line manipulation downstream, enabling logical errors or request smuggling-like misbehavior.

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>

The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

commit_msg:
internal redirect: fix a lifetime bug (#785)

Signed-off-by: Alyssa Wilk <alyssar@chromium.org>
Signed-off-by: Matt Klein <mklein@lyft.com>
Signed-off-by: Pradeep Rao <pcrao@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  ASSERT(!state_.remote_decode_complete_);', '  state_.remote_decode_complete_ = end_stream;', '  if (end_stream) {'], 'added_lines': ['  // If recreateStream is called, the HCM rewinds state and may send more encodeData calls.', '  if (end_stream && !remoteDecodeComplete()) {']}
description: Envoy is a cloud-native high-performance edge/middle/service proxy. In versions prior to 1.22.1 if Envoy attempts to send an internal redirect of an HTTP request consisting of more than HTTP headers, there’s a lifetime bug which can be triggered. If while replaying the request Envoy sends a local reply when the redirect headers are processed, the downstream state indicates that the downstream stream is not complete. On sending the local reply, Envoy will attempt to reset the upstream stream, but as it is actually complete, and deleted, this result in a use-after-free. Users are advised to upgrade. Users unable to upgrade are advised to disable internal redirects if crashes are observed.

code_evidence: On each call, the function asserts that remote_decode_complete_ is not already set (line 2), unconditionally overwrites it with end_stream (line 3), and if end_stream is true it records the last downstream byte timing and logs request end stream (lines 4-7). The guard depends solely on the end_stream argument; there is no check that the decode state was already marked complete, so a second call with end_stream=true re-executes the end-of-stream handling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-416: the completion bookkeeping fails to prevent a later operation from acting on an upstream stream object that was already freed. The weakness is the missing state guard enabling a post-free reset, not merely inconsistent state or a null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function has no completion guard, so repeated end-of-stream notification re-runs last-byte timing and end-stream processing on a stream that was already finalized. Trigger: during internal redirect replay, the recreated downstream state still allows encodeData/end_stream to reach this path after the original upstream stream was completed and deleted; a subsequent local reply then attempts to reset that already-deleted upstream stream. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the deleted upstream stream, causing a crash.

commit_msg: fixed #1975
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tvalues->laser_strings = 1;'], 'added_lines': ['\tvalues->laser_strings = 0;']}
description: An invalid free vulnerability exists in gpac 1.1.0 via the gf_svg_delete_attribute_value function, which causes a segmentation fault and application crash.

code_evidence: Line 13 sets values->laser_strings = 1, marking the parsed values as laser-string owned; line 14 then reads a count and lines 15-17 allocate and add each parsed value into values->values via gf_list_add. The laser_strings flag governs how these entries are later treated (e.g., freed as laser strings) by downstream code.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The incorrect laser_strings=1 causes the values list to be mishandled on later access/free, leaving a reference to freed memory that is subsequently used, matching CWE-416. The diff correcting it to 0 confirms the flag-driven ownership error rather than a simple double free (CWE-415).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the laser_strings flag is set to 1 even though the entries added by gf_list_add are not necessarily laser-string-allocated. When downstream code later processes or deletes the values based on this flag, it frees or reuses memory inconsistently, producing an invalid free and a dangling reference; the supported consequence is a crash/segmentation fault (CWE-416 use after free).

description: An issue was discovered in libredwg through v0.10.1.3751. A NULL pointer dereference exists in the function check_POLYLINE_handles() located in decode.c. It allows an attacker to cause Denial of Service.

commit_msg:
Fix remote code execution and privilege escalation vulnerability.

To trigger this, need to have a user already.

Thanks for Jeriko One <jeriko.one@gmx.us> for finding and reporting this.

CVE-2019-12816
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    for (unsigned int a = 0; a < sModule.length(); a++) {', "        if (((sModule[a] < '0') || (sModule[a] > '9')) &&", "            ((sModule[a] < 'a') || (sModule[a] > 'z')) &&", "            ((sModule[a] < 'A') || (sModule[a] > 'Z')) && (sModule[a] != '_')) {", '            sRetMsg =', '                t_f("Module names can only contain letters, numbers and "', '                    "underscores, [{1}] is invalid")(sModule);', '            return nullptr;', '        }'], 'added_lines': ['    if (!ValidateModuleName(sModule, sRetMsg)) {', '        return nullptr;']}
description: Modules.cpp in ZNC before 1.7.4-rc1 allows remote authenticated non-admin users to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code by loading a module with a crafted name.

code_evidence: Lines 4–13 iterate over each character of sModule and reject any character that is not a digit, lowercase/uppercase letter, or underscore, returning nullptr on the first invalid character. This is a lexical allowlist check on the module name.
Line 14 passes sModPath, not sModule, to dlopen(); the validated name is used only for error/translation strings, so the character filter does not constrain the path actually loaded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an input validation check that is incomplete relative to the operation it protects: the validated data (sModule) is not the data used in the dangerous dlopen() call (sModPath), so required properties of the input are not correctly validated. This is improper input validation (CWE-20) rather than a simple encoding/filtering issue.

evidence_lines.code: ModHandle p = dlopen((sModPath).c_str(), RTLD_NOW | RTLD_GLOBAL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates the module name but the path used to load code (sModPath) is not derived from or constrained by that validation, and the check is a per-character allowlist that does not reject path-like or crafted names reaching the load operation. Trigger: an authenticated non-admin user supplies a crafted module name/path. Consequence: arbitrary module loading, enabling privilege escalation and code execution.

commit_msg:
(uid_t) -1 is still used as placeholder to mean "unset". This is OK, since
there should be no users with such number, see
https://systemd.io/UIDS-GIDS#special-linux-uids.

(uid_t) -1 is used as the default value in class initialization.

When a user or group above INT32_MAX is created, the numeric uid or
gid wraps around to negative when the value is assigned to gint, and
polkit gets confused. Let's accept such gids, except for -1.

A nicer fix would be to change the underlying type to e.g. uint32 to
not have negative values. But this cannot be done without breaking the
API, so likely new functions will have to be added (a
polkit_unix_user_new variant that takes a unsigned, and the same for
_group_new, _set_uid, _get_uid, _set_gid, _get_gid, etc.). This will
require a bigger patch.

Fixes https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/polkit/polkit/issues/74.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  g_return_val_if_fail (gid != -1, NULL);', '']}
description: A flaw was found in PolicyKit (aka polkit) 0.115 that allows a user with a uid greater than INT_MAX to successfully execute any systemctl command.

code_evidence: polkit_unix_group_new accepts a signed gint gid and passes it directly to g_object_new as the "gid" property without any validation; the function body contains no check that rejects the (gid_t)-1 placeholder value or otherwise constrains the range of gid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function receives an input (gid) and fails to validate that it does not equal the reserved -1 value before processing it, which directly matches CWE-20 improper input validation; the missing constraint is on the input itself rather than a transformation or escaping issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constructor forwards an unchecked signed gid into the identity object, so the sentinel value -1 (and wraparound negatives from uids/gids above INT32_MAX) is accepted as a valid group. Trigger: a caller creates a Unix group identity with gid == -1. Consequence: downstream polkit logic treats the unset/placeholder value as a real identity, confusing authorization checks.

commit_msg:
Fix out-of-bounds read in parse_char_class() (Close #139)

/[\x{111111}]/ causes out-of-bounds read when encoding is a single byte
encoding. \x{111111} is an invalid codepoint for a single byte encoding.
Check if it is a valid codepoint.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['onigenc_single_byte_code_to_mbclen(OnigCodePoint code ARG_UNUSED, OnigEncoding enc ARG_UNUSED)'], 'added_lines': ['onigenc_single_byte_code_to_mbclen(OnigCodePoint code, OnigEncoding enc ARG_UNUSED)', '  if (code > 0xff)', '    return ONIGERR_INVALID_CODE_POINT_VALUE;']}
description: Onigmo through 6.2.0 has an out-of-bounds read in parse_char_class because of missing codepoint validation in regenc.c.

code_evidence: The function accepts a code point parameter and unconditionally returns 1, the multibyte length for any input. The parameter is annotated ARG_UNUSED, so no validation of the code point value occurs; even values exceeding 0xff are reported as one-byte encodable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing codepoint validation causes the caller to misjudge the encoded length of an invalid code point, leading to reading past the intended buffer, which directly matches CWE-125. The weakness is an unchecked input constraint rather than a write overflow, so CWE-125 fits over CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: onigenc_single_byte_code_to_mbclen performs no bounds check on the code point, so an invalid code point such as \x{111111} is treated as a valid single-byte character. Trigger: a regex containing an out-of-range code point in a character class reaches this function during parse_char_class, and the caller trusts the returned length of 1 while consuming data, reading past the buffer. description: Buffer overflow in the ReadVIFFImage function in coders/viff.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-5 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Lines 312-314 compute max_packets as ((columns+7)>>3)*rows for VFF_TYP_BIT, guarded by CheckMemoryOverflow.
Lines 318-320 compute max_packets as number_pixels*number_data_bands for other storage types, similarly guarded.
Lines 322-323 allocate pixels of size MagickMax(number_pixels,max_packets)*bytes_per_pixel, then line 326 reads bytes_per_pixel*max_packets bytes into it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic buffer copy without size validation: header-derived data is read into a heap buffer whose size can be smaller than the copy length. The root cause is the missing/incorrect size constraint between max_packets and the allocation, matching CWE-120 rather than an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocation size and the read size are derived from the same header-controlled values (columns, rows, number_data_bands) but through separate expressions; the overflow-check helper used here does not reliably prevent max_packets from exceeding the allocated pixel buffer. A crafted VIFF header can make the ReadBlob at line 326 write beyond the heap allocation, causing memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg: Fix bug #73768 - Memory corruption when loading hostile phar
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["\t\t\tbuffer[tmp_len] = '\\0';", '\t\t\t\tspprintf(error, 0, "cannot load phar \\"%s\\" with implicit alias \\"%s\\" under different alias \\"%s\\"", fname, buffer, alias);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tspprintf(error, 0, "cannot load phar \\"%s\\" with implicit alias \\"%.*s\\" under different alias \\"%s\\"", fname, tmp_len, buffer, alias);']}
description: Off-by-one error in the phar_parse_pharfile function in ext/phar/phar.c in PHP before 5.6.30 and 7.0.x before 7.0.15 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted PHAR archive with an alias mismatch.

code_evidence: tmp_len is read from the untrusted manifest at [263]. The bounds check at [264] rejects buffer + tmp_len > endbuffer, which permits the case buffer + tmp_len == endbuffer, i.e. the alias string ends exactly at the allocated buffer end. When the alias mismatch branch at [271] is taken, [273] writes buffer[tmp_len] = '\0', one byte past the manifest buffer end (and past endbuffer).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The write at [273] uses index tmp_len, one past the last valid byte, while the guard at [264] is off by one; this is a boundary value that is 1 more than the correct maximum, matching CWE-193. The patch removes the write and uses precision-limited %.*s, confirming the off-by-one root cause rather than a generic buffer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length check uses '>' instead of '>=' so a length that exactly reaches endbuffer is accepted, yet the code still writes a NUL at index tmp_len. Trigger: a crafted PHAR whose implicit alias length fills the manifest buffer exactly and whose alias mismatches the supplied alias. Consequence: an out-of-bounds heap write, producing memory corruption and possible code execution.

a sealed log and continue it without any problems showing when verifying the
log.

This partially addresses CVE-2023-31438. One way to extend this change to

one seal per epoch (and not sealing when the epoch has not ended yet).
