description: AP4_VisualSampleEntry::ReadFields in Core/Ap4SampleEntry.cpp in Bento4 1.5.0-617 uses incorrect character data types, which causes a stack-based buffer underflow and out-of-bounds write, leading to denial of service (application crash) or possibly unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: A 33-byte array compressor_name is declared as signed char and filled with 32 attacker-controlled bytes from stream.Read; compressor_name[0] is then read into a signed int name_length, so byte values >= 0x80 sign-extend to negative values.

The guard if (name_length < 32) admits negative name_length, and compressor_name[name_length+1] = 0 writes at an attacker-influenced negative offset, a stack-based buffer underflow/out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The buffer is populated as raw bytes but interpreted as a signed integer length; that incompatible interpretation of the same memory yields a negative index. This type-confusion-style misreading, not merely a missing bounds check, directly enables the out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-843.

evidence_lines.code: compressor_name[name_length+1] = 0;         m_CompressorName = &compressor_name[1];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a signed char element is promoted to signed int, so a length byte >= 0x80 becomes negative and passes the name_length < 32 check. Trigger: any sample entry whose first compressor-name byte has the high bit set. Consequence: the null-termination store indexes before the array, corrupting stack memory, causing denial of service or other impact.

commit_msg:
bpf: prevent out of bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic

Jann reported that the original commit back in b2157399cc98
("bpf: prevent out-of-bounds speculation") was not sufficient
to stop CPU from speculating out of bounds memory access:
While b2157399cc98 only focussed on masking array map access
for unprivileged users for tail calls and data access such
that the user provided index gets sanitized from BPF program
and syscall side, there is still a more generic form affected
from BPF programs that applies to most maps that hold user
data in relation to dynamic map access when dealing with
unknown scalars or "slow" known scalars as access offset, for
example:

  - Load a map value pointer into R6
  - Load an index into R7
  - Do a slow computation (e.g. with a memory dependency) that
    loads a limit into R8 (e.g. load the limit from a map for
    high latency, then mask it to make the verifier happy)
  - Exit if R7 >= R8 (mispredicted branch)
  - Load R0 = R6[R7]
  - Load R0 = R6[R0]

For unknown scalars there are two options in the BPF verifier
where we could derive knowledge from in order to guarantee
safe access to the memory: i) While </>/<=/>= variants won't
allow to derive any lower or upper bounds from the unknown
scalar where it would be safe to add it to the map value
pointer, it is possible through ==/!= test however. ii) another
option is to transform the unknown scalar into a known scalar,
for example, through ALU ops combination such as R &= <imm>
followed by R |= <imm> or any similar combination where the
original information from the unknown scalar would be destroyed
entirely leaving R with a constant. The initial slow load still
precedes the latter ALU ops on that register, so the CPU
executes speculatively from that point. Once we have the known
scalar, any compare operation would work then. A third option
only involving registers with known scalars could be crafted
as described in [0] where a CPU port (e.g. Slow Int unit)
would be filled with many dependent computations such that
the subsequent condition depending on its outcome has to wait
for evaluation on its execution port and thereby executing
speculatively if the speculated code can be scheduled on a
different execution port, or any other form of mistraining
as described in [1], for example. Given this is not limited
to only unknown scalars, not only map but also stack access
is affected since both is accessible for unprivileged users
and could potentially be used for out of bounds access under
speculation.

In order to prevent any of these cases, the verifier is now
sanitizing pointer arithmetic on the offset such that any
out of bounds speculation would be masked in a way where the
pointer arithmetic result in the destination register will
stay unchanged, meaning offset masked into zero similar as
in array_index_nospec() case. With regards to implementation,
there are three options that were considered: i) new insn
for sanitation, ii) push/pop insn and sanitation as inlined
BPF, iii) reuse of ax register and sanitation as inlined BPF.

Option i) has the downside that we end up using from reserved
bits in the opcode space, but also that we would require
each JIT to emit masking as native arch opcodes meaning
mitigation would have slow adoption till everyone implements
it eventually which is counter-productive. Option ii) and iii)
have both in common that a temporary register is needed in
order to implement the sanitation as inlined BPF since we
are not allowed to modify the source register. While a push /
pop insn in ii) would be useful to have in any case, it
requires once again that every JIT needs to implement it
first. While possible, amount of changes needed would also
be unsuitable for a -stable patch. Therefore, the path which
has fewer changes, less BPF instructions for the mitigation
and does not require anything to be changed in the JITs is
option iii) which this work is pursuing. The ax register is
already mapped to a register in all JITs (modulo arm32 where
it's mapped to stack as various other BPF registers there)
and used in constant blinding for JITs-only so far. It can
be reused for verifier rewrites under certain constraints.
The interpreter's tmp "register" has therefore been remapped
into extending the register set with hidden ax register and
reusing that for a number of instructions that needed the
prior temporary variable internally (e.g. div, mod). This
allows for zero increase in stack space usage in the interpreter,
and enables (restricted) generic use in rewrites otherwise as
long as such a patchlet does not make use of these instructions.
The sanitation mask is dynamic and relative to the offset the
map value or stack pointer currently holds.

There are various cases that need to be taken under consideration
for the masking, e.g. such operation could look as follows:
ptr += val or val += ptr or ptr -= val. Thus, the value to be
sanitized could reside either in source or in destination
register, and the limit is different depending on whether
the ALU op is addition or subtraction and depending on the
current known and bounded offset. The limit is derived as
follows: limit := max_value_size - (smin_value + off). For
subtraction: limit := umax_value + off. This holds because
we do not allow any pointer arithmetic that would
temporarily go out of bounds or would have an unknown
value with mixed signed bounds where it is unclear at
verification time whether the actual runtime value would
be either negative or positive. For example, we have a
derived map pointer value with constant offset and bounded
one, so limit based on smin_value works because the verifier
requires that statically analyzed arithmetic on the pointer
must be in bounds, and thus it checks if resulting
smin_value + off and umax_value + off is still within map
value bounds at time of arithmetic in addition to time of
access. Similarly, for the case of stack access we derive
the limit as follows: MAX_BPF_STACK + off for subtraction
and -off for the case of addition where off := ptr_reg->off +
ptr_reg->var_off.value. Subtraction is a special case for
the masking which can be in form of ptr += -val, ptr -= -val,
or ptr -= val. In the first two cases where we know that
the value is negative, we need to temporarily negate the
value in order to do the sanitation on a positive value
where we later swap the ALU op, and restore original source
register if the value was in source.

The sanitation of pointer arithmetic alone is still not fully
sufficient as is, since a scenario like the following could
happen ...

  PTR += 0x1000 (e.g. K-based imm)
  PTR -= BIG_NUMBER_WITH_SLOW_COMPARISON
  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= BIG_NUMBER_WITH_SLOW_COMPARISON
  [...]

... which under speculation could end up as ...

  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= 0 [ truncated by mitigation ]
  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= 0 [ truncated by mitigation ]
  [...]

... and therefore still access out of bounds. To prevent such
case, the verifier is also analyzing safety for potential out
of bounds access under speculative execution. Meaning, it is
also simulating pointer access under truncation. We therefore
"branch off" and push the current verification state after the
ALU operation with known 0 to the verification stack for later
analysis. Given the current path analysis succeeded it is
likely that the one under speculation can be pruned. In any
case, it is also subject to existing complexity limits and
therefore anything beyond this point will be rejected. In
terms of pruning, it needs to be ensured that the verification
state from speculative execution simulation must never prune
a non-speculative execution path, therefore, we mark verifier
state accordingly at the time of push_stack(). If verifier
detects out of bounds access under speculative execution from
one of the possible paths that includes a truncation, it will
reject such program.

Given we mask every reg-based pointer arithmetic for
unprivileged programs, we've been looking into how it could
affect real-world programs in terms of size increase. As the
majority of programs are targeted for privileged-only use
case, we've unconditionally enabled masking (with its alu
restrictions on top of it) for privileged programs for the
sake of testing in order to check i) whether they get rejected
in its current form, and ii) by how much the number of
instructions and size will increase. We've tested this by
using Katran, Cilium and test_l4lb from the kernel selftests.
For Katran we've evaluated balancer_kern.o, Cilium bpf_lxc.o
and an older test object bpf_lxc_opt_-DUNKNOWN.o and l4lb
we've used test_l4lb.o as well as test_l4lb_noinline.o. We
found that none of the programs got rejected by the verifier
with this change, and that impact is rather minimal to none.
balancer_kern.o had 13,904 bytes (1,738 insns) xlated and
7,797 bytes JITed before and after the change. Most complex
program in bpf_lxc.o had 30,544 bytes (3,817 insns) xlated
and 18,538 bytes JITed before and after and none of the other
tail call programs in bpf_lxc.o had any changes either. For
the older bpf_lxc_opt_-DUNKNOWN.o object we found a small
increase from 20,616 bytes (2,576 insns) and 12,536 bytes JITed
before to 20,664 bytes (2,582 insns) and 12,558 bytes JITed
after the change. Other programs from that object file had
similar small increase. Both test_l4lb.o had no change and
remained at 6,544 bytes (817 insns) xlated and 3,401 bytes
JITed and for test_l4lb_noinline.o constant at 5,080 bytes
(634 insns) xlated and 3,313 bytes JITed. This can be explained
in that LLVM typically optimizes stack based pointer arithmetic
by using K-based operations and that use of dynamic map access
is not overly frequent. However, in future we may decide to
optimize the algorithm further under known guarantees from
branch and value speculation. Latter seems also unclear in
terms of prediction heuristics that today's CPUs apply as well
as whether there could be collisions in e.g. the predictor's
Value History/Pattern Table for triggering out of bounds access,
thus masking is performed unconditionally at this point but could
be subject to relaxation later on. We were generally also
brainstorming various other approaches for mitigation, but the
blocker was always lack of available registers at runtime and/or
overhead for runtime tracking of limits belonging to a specific
pointer. Thus, we found this to be minimally intrusive under
given constraints.

With that in place, a simple example with sanitized access on
unprivileged load at post-verification time looks as follows:

  # bpftool prog dump xlated id 282
  [...]
  28: (79) r1 = *(u64 *)(r7 +0)
  29: (79) r2 = *(u64 *)(r7 +8)
  30: (57) r1 &= 15
  31: (79) r3 = *(u64 *)(r0 +4608)
  32: (57) r3 &= 1
  33: (47) r3 |= 1
  34: (2d) if r2 > r3 goto pc+19
  35: (b4) (u32) r11 = (u32) 20479  |
  36: (1f) r11 -= r2                | Dynamic sanitation for pointer
  37: (4f) r11 |= r2                | arithmetic with registers
  38: (87) r11 = -r11               | containing bounded or known
  39: (c7) r11 s>>= 63              | scalars in order to prevent
  40: (5f) r11 &= r2                | out of bounds speculation.
  41: (0f) r4 += r11                |
  42: (71) r4 = *(u8 *)(r4 +0)
  43: (6f) r4 <<= r1
  [...]

For the case where the scalar sits in the destination register
as opposed to the source register, the following code is emitted
for the above example:

  [...]
  16: (b4) (u32) r11 = (u32) 20479
  17: (1f) r11 -= r2
  18: (4f) r11 |= r2
  19: (87) r11 = -r11
  20: (c7) r11 s>>= 63
  21: (5f) r2 &= r11
  22: (0f) r2 += r0
  23: (61) r0 = *(u32 *)(r2 +0)
  [...]

JIT blinding example with non-conflicting use of r10:

  [...]
   d5:	je     0x0000000000000106    _
   d7:	mov    0x0(%rax),%edi       |
   da:	mov    $0xf153246,%r10d     | Index load from map value and
   e0:	xor    $0xf153259,%r10      | (const blinded) mask with 0x1f.
   e7:	and    %r10,%rdi            |_
   ea:	mov    $0x2f,%r10d          |
   f0:	sub    %rdi,%r10            | Sanitized addition. Both use r10
   f3:	or     %rdi,%r10            | but do not interfere with each
   f6:	neg    %r10                 | other. (Neither do these instructions
   f9:	sar    $0x3f,%r10           | interfere with the use of ax as temp
   fd:	and    %r10,%rdi            | in interpreter.)
  100:	add    %rax,%rdi            |_
  103:	mov    0x0(%rdi),%eax
 [...]

Tested that it fixes Jann's reproducer, and also checked that test_verifier
and test_progs suite with interpreter, JIT and JIT with hardening enabled
on x86-64 and arm64 runs successfully.

  [0] Speculose: Analyzing the Security Implications of Speculative
      Execution in CPUs, Giorgi Maisuradze and Christian Rossow,
      https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.04084.pdf

  [1] A Systematic Evaluation of Transient Execution Attacks and
      Defenses, Claudio Canella, Jo Van Bulck, Michael Schwarz,
      Moritz Lipp, Benjamin von Berg, Philipp Ortner, Frank Piessens,
      Dmitry Evtyushkin, Daniel Gruss,
      https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.05441.pdf

description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel before 4.20.6 performs undesirable out-of-bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic in various cases, including cases of different branches with different state or limits to sanitize, leading to side-channel attacks.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: push_stack only allocates a stack element, copies verifier state, and enforces a complexity limit; it performs no numeric calculation or conversion that could support CWE-189, and the speculative flag propagation is a state-tracking change unrelated to numeric errors.

commit_msg:
The purpose of this patch is to streamline error propagation and in particular
to propagate retrieve_ptr_limit() errors for pointer types that are not defining
a ptr_limit such that register-based alu ops against these types can be rejected.

The main rationale is that a gap has been identified by Piotr in the existing
protection against speculatively out-of-bounds loads, for example, in case of
ctx pointers, unprivileged programs can still perform pointer arithmetic. This
can be abused to execute speculatively out-of-bounds loads without restrictions
and thus extract contents of kernel memory.

Fix this by rejecting unprivileged programs that attempt any pointer arithmetic
on unprotected pointer types. The two affected ones are pointer to ctx as well
as pointer to map. Field access to a modified ctx' pointer is rejected at a
later point in time in the verifier, and 7c6967326267 ("bpf: Permit map_ptr
arithmetic with opcode add and offset 0") only relevant for root-only use cases.
Risk of unprivileged program breakage is considered very low.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.11.8. kernel/bpf/verifier.c performs undesirable out-of-bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic, leading to side-channel attacks that defeat Spectre mitigations and obtain sensitive information from kernel memory, aka CID-f232326f6966. This affects pointer types that do not define a ptr_limit.

code_evidence: The switch on ptr_reg->type rejects arithmetic only for enumerated pointer types; PTR_TO_CTX and PTR_TO_MAP fall through the default at [60,61] and proceed to arithmetic.
For PTR_TO_MAP_VALUE the mixed-signed-bounds guard at [54] applies only to that type; other unprotected types bypass it.
sanitize_ptr_alu at [71] is invoked for BPF_ADD but the rejection depends on the earlier type switch, which never constrained ctx/map pointers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw yields a state-dependent, externally observable difference (speculative access vs. rejection) that an unauthorized BPF program can exploit to read kernel memory, matching CWE-203's observable discrepancy enabling confidentiality impact. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the exploitable effect is the side-channel observable behavior.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The type switch permits pointer arithmetic on pointer types that define no ptr_limit (e.g., ctx, map), so the verifier's range tracking and speculation sanitization do not bound the resulting pointer. An unprivileged BPF program can then perform speculative out-of-bounds loads, and the resulting observable timing/cache discrepancy leaks kernel memory contents.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can cause a segfault and denial of service via accessing data outside of bounds in `tf.raw_ops.QuantizedBatchNormWithGlobalNormalization`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/55a97caa9e99c7f37a0bbbeb414dc55553d3ae7f/tensorflow/core/kernels/quantized_batch_norm_op.cc#L176-L189) assumes the inputs are not empty. If any of these inputs is empty, `.flat<T>()` is an empty buffer, so accessing the element at index 0 is accessing data outside of bounds. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no division operation; the described flaw is out-of-bounds access from empty scalar tensors, which does not support CWE-369 (divide by zero).

commit_msg:
mnt: Add a per mount namespace limit on the number of mounts

CAI Qian <caiqian@redhat.com> pointed out that the semantics
of shared subtrees make it possible to create an exponentially
increasing number of mounts in a mount namespace.

    mkdir /tmp/1 /tmp/2
    mount --make-rshared /
    for i in $(seq 1 20) ; do mount --bind /tmp/1 /tmp/2 ; done

Will create create 2^20 or 1048576 mounts, which is a practical problem
as some people have managed to hit this by accident.

As such CVE-2016-6213 was assigned.

Ian Kent <raven@themaw.net> described the situation for autofs users
as follows:

> The number of mounts for direct mount maps is usually not very large because of
> the way they are implemented, large direct mount maps can have performance
> problems. There can be anywhere from a few (likely case a few hundred) to less
> than 10000, plus mounts that have been triggered and not yet expired.
>
> Indirect mounts have one autofs mount at the root plus the number of mounts that
> have been triggered and not yet expired.
>
> The number of autofs indirect map entries can range from a few to the common
> case of several thousand and in rare cases up to between 30000 and 50000. I've
> not heard of people with maps larger than 50000 entries.
>
> The larger the number of map entries the greater the possibility for a large
> number of active mounts so it's not hard to expect cases of a 1000 or somewhat
> more active mounts.

So I am setting the default number of mounts allowed per mount
namespace at 100,000.  This is more than enough for any use case I
know of, but small enough to quickly stop an exponential increase
in mounts.  Which should be perfect to catch misconfigurations and
malfunctioning programs.

For anyone who needs a higher limit this can be changed by writing
to the new /proc/sys/fs/mount-max sysctl.

Tested-by: CAI Qian <caiqian@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t__touch_mnt_namespace(p->mnt_ns);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tstruct mnt_namespace *ns;', '\t\tns = p->mnt_ns;', '\t\tif (ns) {', '\t\t\tns->mounts--;', '\t\t\t__touch_mnt_namespace(ns);', '\t\t}']}
description: fs/namespace.c in the Linux kernel before 4.9 does not restrict how many mounts may exist in a mount namespace, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption and deadlock) via MS_BIND mount system calls, as demonstrated by a loop that triggers exponential growth in the number of mounts.

code_evidence: The loop detaches each mount from tmp_list and clears p->mnt_ns, but the original code only calls __touch_mnt_namespace(p->mnt_ns) and never decrements any per-namespace mount count. No bound or throttling on the number of mounts in a namespace is enforced here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 covers lack of throttling for the number of allocated resources. Here the mount namespace does not restrict how many mounts may exist, matching uncontrolled resource consumption; the change adds decrement accounting needed for the limit, not a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mount namespace maintains no accounting that would cap the number of mounts. Trigger: a local user repeatedly issues MS_BIND mounts (e.g., shared-subtree loops) causing exponential growth. Consequence: unbounded mounts consume memory and can deadlock, i.e., denial of service. The patch adds ns->mounts-- accounting in umount_tree, part of enforcing the limit.

description: An issue was discovered in l2cap_sock_release in net/bluetooth/l2cap_sock.c in the Linux kernel before 6.4.10. There is a use-after-free because the children of an sk are mishandled.

code_evidence: The release path unlinks sk via bt_sock_unlink, then shuts down and kills sk through l2cap_sock_kill(sk), which eventually frees sk. The function never disconnects or cleans up sk's listening children before this teardown; those children retain references to the freed sk.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's teardown order frees sk while references remain live, and those references are later used, which is precisely use-after-free. Contrast with a mere memory leak: the defect is stale-pointer reuse after deallocation, not failure to release memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: l2cap_sock_release frees sk without detaching its child sockets, which still hold pointers to it. Trigger: closing a listening socket while child channels are active; a later child callback such as l2cap_sock_ready_cb dereferences the stale sk pointer. Supported consequence: read of freed memory (KASAN use-after-free), with possible crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Split the xt_compat_match/xt_compat_target into smaller type-safe functions
performing just one operation. Handle all alignment and size-related
conversions centrally in these function instead of requiring each module to
implement a full-blown conversion function. Replace ->compat callback by
->compat_from_user and ->compat_to_user callbacks, responsible for
converting just a single private structure.

Signed-off-by: Patrick McHardy <kaber@trash.net>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (target->compat)', '\t\ttarget->compat(t, dstptr, size, COMPAT_FROM_USER);', '\telse', '\t\txt_compat_target(t, dstptr, size, COMPAT_FROM_USER);'], 'added_lines': ['\txt_compat_target_from_user(t, dstptr, size);']}
description: A heap out-of-bounds write affecting Linux since v2.6.19-rc1 was discovered in net/netfilter/x_tables.c. This allows an attacker to gain privileges or cause a DoS (via heap memory corruption) through user name space

code_evidence: origsize records the original user-provided entry size; de is placed at *dstptr and only sizeof(struct compat_ipt_entry) is advanced, while memcpy copies a full struct ipt_entry into de.

de->target_offset is recomputed as e->target_offset - (origsize - *size), then the target is copied via target->compat or xt_compat_target using the size-adjusted dstptr; de->next_offset is similarly adjusted.

After conversion, t = ipt_get_target(de) and xt_check_target is invoked using t->u.target_size - sizeof(*t), validating the converted target against a size that may not match the actual allocated layout.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The core defect is a write beyond the intended destination buffer during compat target conversion, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely an integer issue; the unchecked size/offset arithmetic directly enables the out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The compat conversion path writes the converted target data through dstptr into the destination buffer using offsets and sizes derived from the user-supplied entry (origsize, target_offset, next_offset) without bounding them against the allocated destination size. A crafted entry with large or inconsistent offsets/sizes causes the target copy to write past the end of the heap buffer, yielding heap memory corruption and potential privilege escalation or DoS.

commit_msg:
Fixed OOB read in update_read_cache_bitmap_v3_order

CVE-2020-11096 thanks @antonio-morales for finding this.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcache_bitmap_v2->bitmapBpp = CBR2_BPP[bitsPerPixelId];'], 'added_lines': ['\tBOOL rc;', '\tcache_bitmap_v2->bitmapBpp = get_cbr2_bpp(bitsPerPixelId, &rc);', '\tif (!rc)', '\t\tgoto fail;']}
description: In FreeRDP before version 2.1.2, there is a global OOB read in update_read_cache_bitmap_v3_order. As a workaround, one can disable bitmap cache with -bitmap-cache (default). This is fixed in version 2.1.2.

code_evidence: bitsPerPixelId is extracted from attacker-controlled flags (bits 3-6, range 0-15) and used directly to index the CBR2_BPP lookup table without a bounds check on the index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Indexing a fixed lookup table with an unvalidated value reads memory before/after the intended array, which is exactly CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read), not a write or integer issue.

evidence_lines.code:
bitsPerPixelId = (flags & 0x0078) >> 3;
cache_bitmap_v2->bitmapBpp = CBR2_BPP[bitsPerPixelId];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the flags-derived bitsPerPixelId is not validated against the size of CBR2_BPP before indexing. Trigger: a crafted cache bitmap order with an out-of-range bitsPerPixelId causes an out-of-bounds table read; the resulting value is stored in bitmapBpp and later consumed, potentially yielding a bad read or crash.

description: A heap buffer overflow in ExtractImageSection function in tiffcrop.c in libtiff library Version 4.3.0 allows attacker to trigger unsafe or out of bounds memory access via crafted TIFF image file which could result into application crash, potential information disclosure or any other context-dependent impact

code_evidence: The unaligned path loops j from 0 to full_bytes inclusive and writes sect_buff[dst_offset + j], so for j == full_bytes it writes one byte beyond the full_bytes region; the trailing-bits block then writes sect_buff[dst_offset] again after dst_offset += full_bytes.
The loop reads src_buff[offset1 + j + 1], one byte past the source region, and offset1/offset2 are derived from first_col/last_col without validating that the section lies within the image row.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of the destination buffer via the inclusive loop bound and trailing-byte store, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The out-of-bounds read is secondary; the supported consequence is memory corruption from writing beyond sect_buff.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the extraction loops and trailing-bit handling use inclusive bounds (j <= full_bytes, offset1 + full_bytes) without clamping the section to the image dimensions, so crafted TIFF section coordinates cause reads/writes past sect_buff and src_buff. Trigger: a crafted TIFF with a section at or beyond the row boundary, bps not multiple of 8. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write (and read), leading to crash or potential memory corruption.

commit_msg:
evtchn/x86: enforce correct upper limit for 32-bit guests

The recording of d->max_evtchns in evtchn_2l_init(), in particular with
the limited set of callers of the function, is insufficient. Neither for
PV nor for HVM guests the bitness is known at domain_create() time, yet
the upper bound in 2-level mode depends upon guest bitness. Recording
too high a limit "allows" x86 32-bit domains to open not properly usable
event channels, management of which (inside Xen) would then result in
corruption of the shared info and vCPU info structures.

Keep the upper limit dynamic for the 2-level case, introducing a helper
function to retrieve the effective limit. This helper is now supposed to
be private to the event channel code. The used in do_poll() and
domain_dump_evtchn_info() weren't consistent with port uses elsewhere
and hence get switched to port_is_valid().

Furthermore FIFO mode's setup_ports() gets adjusted to loop only up to
the prior ABI limit, rather than all the way up to the new one.

Finally a word on the change to do_poll(): Accessing ->max_evtchns
without holding a suitable lock was never safe, as it as well as
->evtchn_port_ops may change behind do_poll()'s back. Using
port_is_valid() instead widens some the window for potential abuse,
until we've dealt with the race altogether (see XSA-343).

This is XSA-342.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Fixes: 48974e6ce52e ("evtchn: use a per-domain variable for the max number of event channels")
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>

@@ -8,7 +8,7 @@

-    for ( port = 1; port < d->max_evtchns; port++ )
+    for ( port = 1; port < prev_evtchns; port++ )
     {
         struct evtchn *evtchn;

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. Out of bounds event channels are available to 32-bit x86 domains. The so called 2-level event channel model imposes different limits on the number of usable event channels for 32-bit x86 domains vs 64-bit or Arm (either bitness) ones. 32-bit x86 domains can use only 1023 channels, due to limited space in their shared (between guest and Xen) information structure, whereas all other domains can use up to 4095 in this model. The recording of the respective limit during domain initialization, however, has occurred at a time where domains are still deemed to be 64-bit ones, prior to actually honoring respective domain properties. At the point domains get recognized as 32-bit ones, the limit didn't get updated accordingly. Due to this misbehavior in Xen, 32-bit domains (including Domain 0) servicing other domains may observe event channel allocations to succeed when they should really fail. Subsequent use of such event channels would then possibly lead to corruption of other parts of the shared info structure. An unprivileged guest may cause another domain, in particular Domain 0, to misbehave. This may lead to a Denial of Service (DoS) for the entire system. All Xen versions from 4.4 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.3 and earlier are not vulnerable. Only x86 32-bit domains servicing other domains are vulnerable. Arm systems, as well as x86 64-bit domains, are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: setup_ports() iterates ports from 1 up to d->max_evtchns (line 4), a limit that for 32-bit x86 guests can exceed the 1023-channel capacity of the 2-level shared-info array. The loop bounds each iteration with port_is_valid() (line 7) and breaks on failure (line 8), but the pending-bit test at line 10 indexes shared_info(d, evtchn_pending) using port; once the effective limit exceeds the ABI array size, that indexing reaches beyond the array. Line 11 then records evtchn->pending and line 12 sets FIFO priority for the same out-of-range port.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the pending-bit access at line 10 writes to an array element indexed by a port that can exceed the array's bounds, i.e., an out-of-bounds write. A mere incorrect limit check (CWE-1284/1299) is the enabling cause; the concrete memory-writing operation past the buffer end is the out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound is the recorded d->max_evtchns rather than the guest-bitness-appropriate 2-level limit, so ports beyond the shared-info array size are visited. Trigger: a 32-bit x86 domain serviced by another domain allocates an out-of-range channel, and setup_ports() processes it. Consequence: shared-info/vCPU-info memory corruption and possible system-wide DoS.

description: An out-of-bounds (OOB) memory write flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s watch_queue event notification subsystem. This flaw can overwrite parts of the kernel state, potentially allowing a local user to gain privileged access or cause a denial of service on the system.

code_evidence: The first loop counts filters using the bound sizeof(wfilter->type_filter) * 8, which is a byte-size times 8 (bits per byte) rather than the bitmap's capacity in bits, so the limit is inconsistent with the actual bitmap width.

The second loop applies a different bound, sizeof(wfilter->type_filter) * BITS_PER_LONG, and for entries passing it calls __set_bit(q->type, wfilter->type_filter), writing into the type_filter bitmap indexed by the user-supplied tf[i].type.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: __set_bit(q->type, ...) writes to a bitmap whose index is attacker-controlled and insufficiently bounded, producing an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is not merely a read overrun or integer overflow; the supported consequence is memory modification past the buffer end.

evidence_lines.code:
if (tf[i].type >= sizeof(wfilter->type_filter) * 8)
continue;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the mismatched/incorrect filter type limit check: the counting loop and the population loop use different sizes, and neither reliably caps type to the bitmap's bit capacity. A local user supplies tf[i].type; values below the flawed bound reach __set_bit, which writes past the end of type_filter, corrupting adjacent kernel memory.

commit_msg:
(uid_t) -1 is still used as placeholder to mean "unset". This is OK, since
there should be no users with such number, see
https://systemd.io/UIDS-GIDS#special-linux-uids.

(uid_t) -1 is used as the default value in class initialization.

When a user or group above INT32_MAX is created, the numeric uid or
gid wraps around to negative when the value is assigned to gint, and
polkit gets confused. Let's accept such gids, except for -1.

A nicer fix would be to change the underlying type to e.g. uint32 to
not have negative values. But this cannot be done without breaking the
API, so likely new functions will have to be added (a
polkit_unix_user_new variant that takes a unsigned, and the same for
_group_new, _set_uid, _get_uid, _set_gid, _get_gid, etc.). This will
require a bigger patch.

Fixes https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/polkit/polkit/issues/74.

description: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command in the podcast playback function of Podbeuter in Newsbeuter 0.3 through 2.9 allows remote attackers to perform user-assisted code execution by crafting an RSS item with a media enclosure (i.e., a podcast file) that includes shell metacharacters in its filename, related to pb_controller.cpp and queueloader.cpp, a different vulnerability than CVE-2017-12904.

code_evidence: Line 6 appends the configured player command, then lines 7-9 append the externally supplied podcast filename wrapped in double quotes, escaping only embedded double quotes via replace_all.
Line 12 passes the assembled string to ::system(), which invokes a shell to interpret the command line.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-78 fits because externally influenced input is incorporated into an OS command executed via ::system() without adequate neutralization of shell special elements, allowing the input to alter the intended command. This is command injection, not merely an argument-injection variant, since the shell interprets the filename.

evidence_lines.code: ::system(cmdline.c_str());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The file argument (podcast filename from an RSS enclosure) is concatenated into a shell command with only double-quote escaping. Shell metacharacters such as $, backticks, or command separators that remain active inside double quotes are not neutralized, so a crafted filename is interpreted by the shell when ::system() runs, enabling command execution.

commit_msg:
Go into the error state if a fatal alert is sent or received

If an application calls SSL_shutdown after a fatal alert has occured and
then behaves different based on error codes from that function then the
application may be vulnerable to a padding oracle.

CVE-2019-1559

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            s->state = SSL_ST_ERR;']}
description: If an application encounters a fatal protocol error and then calls SSL_shutdown() twice (once to send a close_notify, and once to receive one) then OpenSSL can respond differently to the calling application if a 0 byte record is received with invalid padding compared to if a 0 byte record is received with an invalid MAC. If the application then behaves differently based on that in a way that is detectable to the remote peer, then this amounts to a padding oracle that could be used to decrypt data. In order for this to be exploitable "non-stitched" ciphersuites must be in use. Stitched ciphersuites are optimised implementations of certain commonly used ciphersuites. Also the application must call SSL_shutdown() twice even if a protocol error has occurred (applications should not do this but some do anyway). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.0.2r (Affected 1.0.2-1.0.2q).

code_evidence: On receiving a fatal alert (alert_level == SSL3_AL_FATAL), the function sets s->rwstate = SSL_NOTHING, records s->s3->fatal_alert, sets s->shutdown |= SSL_RECEIVED_SHUTDOWN, removes the session, and returns 0. The patch adds s->state = SSL_ST_ERR in this fatal-alert branch so the connection is marked errored rather than left in a usable state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-203 fits because the weakness is an observable behavioral discrepancy: error-state handling yields different externally visible outcomes for distinguishable input conditions, enabling a padding oracle. The added SSL_ST_ERR assignment addresses this state-dependent discrepancy, not memory corruption or a separate cryptographic flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a fatal protocol error did not transition the SSL state to error, so later SSL_shutdown() calls could still process records and return distinguishable results for invalid padding versus invalid MAC. Trigger: an application calls SSL_shutdown() twice after a fatal alert with non-stitched ciphersuites. Consequence: the differing observable responses form a padding oracle that can leak decrypted data.

commit_msg:
dm: validate inputs in vq_endchains

 inputs shall be validated to avoid NULL pointer access.

Tracked-On: #6129
Signed-off-by: Yonghua Huang <yonghua.huang@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (!vq || !vq->used)', '\t\treturn;']}
description: ACRN before 2.5 has a hw/pci/virtio/virtio.c vq_endchains NULL Pointer Dereference.

code_evidence: Line 8 dereferences vq->base and line 10 dereferences vq->used without any prior NULL check on vq or vq->used.
Lines 11-14 then read base->negotiated_caps, propagating the pointer obtained from vq->base; if vq or vq->used is NULL the dereference faults before reaching this point.
Lines 19-20 read vq->avail->flags, another unchecked pointer dereference reached when the EVENT_IDX branch is not taken.
Line 22-23 conditionally calls vq_interrupt(base, vq) using the pointers derived above, but the fault occurs earlier at the first unchecked dereference.

vq->save_used = new_idx = vq->used->idx;

intr = new_idx != old_idx &&
!(vq->avail->flags & VRING_AVAIL_F_NO_INTERRUPT);

Trigger: a caller passes a NULL vq or a vq whose used ring was never initialized. Consequence: a NULL pointer dereference causing a crash/DoS in the virtio device path.

commit_msg:
p2m: Always check to see if removing a p2m entry actually worked

The PoD zero-check functions speculatively remove memory from the p2m,
then check to see if it's completely zeroed, before putting it in the
cache.

Unfortunately, the p2m_set_entry() calls may fail if the underlying
pagetable structure needs to change and the domain has exhausted its
p2m memory pool: for instance, if we're removing a 2MiB region out of
a 1GiB entry (in the p2m_pod_zero_check_superpage() case), or a 4k
region out of a 2MiB or larger entry (in the p2m_pod_zero_check()
case); and the return value is not checked.

The underlying mfn will then be added into the PoD cache, and at some
point mapped into another location in the p2m.  If the guest
afterwards ballons out this memory, it will be freed to the hypervisor
and potentially reused by another domain, in spite of the fact that
the original domain still has writable mappings to it.

There are several places where p2m_set_entry() shouldn't be able to
fail, as it is guaranteed to write an entry of the same order that
succeeded before.  Add a backstop of crashing the domain just in case,
and an ASSERT_UNREACHABLE() to flag up the broken assumption on debug
builds.

While we're here, use PAGE_ORDER_2M rather than a magic constant.

This is part of XSA-247.

Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfns[i], INVALID_MFN, PAGE_ORDER_4K,', '                      p2m_populate_on_demand, p2m->default_access);', '', '            p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfns[i], mfns[i], PAGE_ORDER_4K,', '                types[i], p2m->default_access);', '            p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfns[i], mfns[i], PAGE_ORDER_4K,', '                          types[i], p2m->default_access);'], 'added_lines': ['        if ( p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfns[i], INVALID_MFN, PAGE_ORDER_4K,', '                           p2m_populate_on_demand, p2m->default_access) )', '            goto skip;', '            /*', "             * If the previous p2m_set_entry call succeeded, this one shouldn't", '             * be able to fail.  If it does, crashing the domain should be safe.', '             */', '            if ( p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfns[i], mfns[i], PAGE_ORDER_4K,', '                               types[i], p2m->default_access) )', '            {', '                ASSERT_UNREACHABLE();', '                domain_crash(d);', '                goto out_unmap;', '            }', '', '        skip:', '        map[i] = NULL;', '', '            /*', "             * If the previous p2m_set_entry call succeeded, this one shouldn't", '             * be able to fail.  If it does, crashing the domain should be safe.', '             */', '            if ( p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfns[i], mfns[i], PAGE_ORDER_4K,', '                               types[i], p2m->default_access) )', '            {', '                ASSERT_UNREACHABLE();', '                domain_crash(d);', '                goto out_unmap;', '            }', '    return;', '', 'out_unmap:', '    /*', '     * Something went wrong, probably crashing the domain.  Unmap', '     * everything and return.', '     */', '    for ( i = 0; i < count; i++ )', '        if ( map[i] )', '            unmap_domain_page(map[i]);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing HVM guest OS users to gain privileges on the host OS, obtain sensitive information, or cause a denial of service (BUG and host OS crash) by leveraging the mishandling of Populate on Demand (PoD) Physical-to-Machine (P2M) errors.

code_evidence: The code speculatively calls p2m_set_entry with INVALID_MFN to remove the guest mapping without checking the return value.

If the speculative unmap failed, the refcount check may still pass; the code then attempts to restore the original mapping but ignores that return value too, leaving the page unmapped while the page is still referenced.
The page is subsequently added to the PoD cache via p2m_pod_cache_add and its entry_count incremented, making the still-mapped page available for reallocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked failure leads the page to be freed to the hypervisor while the original domain still holds writable mappings, so later access uses memory that has been freed and possibly reallocated to another domain, matching CWE-416 Use After Free.

evidence_lines.code:
p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfns[i], INVALID_MFN, PAGE_ORDER_4K,
p2m_populate_on_demand, p2m->default_access);

p2m_pod_cache_add(p2m, mfn_to_page(mfns[i]), PAGE_ORDER_4K);
p2m->pod.entry_count++;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unchecked p2m_set_entry return values. If the speculative unmap fails (e.g., p2m pool exhaustion), the MFN may be inserted into the PoD cache and later remapped to another location while the original domain retains writable mappings. If the guest balloons out that memory, it is freed to the hypervisor and potentially reused by another domain, leaving the original domain with stale writable mappings to freed/reallocated memory.

commit_msg: Fix buffer overflow in ble-l2cap
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    payload_len = frame_len - 2;'], 'added_lines': ['    payload_len = frame_len - 2;', '', '    if(payload_len > BLE_L2CAP_NODE_MTU) {', '    \tLOG_WARN("l2cap_frame: illegal L2CAP frame payload_len: %d\\n", payload_len);', '    \t/* the payload length may not be larger than the destination buffer */', '    \treturn;', '    }', '', '    ', '    if(channel->rx_buffer.current_index + payload_len > BLE_L2CAP_NODE_MTU) {', '    \tLOG_WARN("l2cap_frame: illegal L2CAP frame payload_len: %d\\n", payload_len);', '    \t/* the current index plus the payload length may not be larger than ', '\t * the destination buffer */', '    \treturn;', '    }']}
description: A buffer overflow in os/net/mac/ble/ble-l2cap.c in the BLE stack in Contiki-NG 4.4 and earlier allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code via malicious L2CAP frames.

code_evidence: In the first-fragment branch, frame_len is read from the attacker-controlled frame at data[0], payload_len is computed as frame_len - 2 (line 13), and memcpy copies payload_len bytes from data[6] into channel->rx_buffer.sdu (line 14) with no comparison against the destination buffer size.

In the subsequent-fragment branch, frame_len is read from data[0], payload_len = frame_len (line 18), and memcpy writes payload_len bytes at offset current_index into channel->rx_buffer.sdu (line 19), then increments current_index (line 20) without any bound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs buffer copies (memcpy into sdu) with sizes taken from untrusted input and no size check against the destination, matching CWE-120's 'buffer copy without checking size of input.' The flaw is the missing length constraint on a copy, not a calculation error or out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: payload_len derived from the L2CAP frame header is copied into the fixed-size sdu buffer without validating it against BLE_L2CAP_NODE_MTU, in both the first and subsequent fragment paths. Trigger: a malicious L2CAP frame with an oversized length field. Consequence: out-of-bounds write past the sdu buffer, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially enabling code execution or crash.

description: The processRequest function in minissdpd.c in MiniSSDPd 1.2.20130907-3 allows local users to cause a denial of service (invalid free and daemon crash) via vectors related to error handling.

description: The xps_decode_font_char_imp function in xps/xpsfont.c in Artifex Ghostscript GhostXPS 9.21 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted document.

Consequence: the u16/s16 reads pass the buffer end, yielding an out-of-bounds read that can crash the application (DoS) or leak adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
core: set again TLS verification functions after GnuTLS options are changed (closes #1763)

When changing the options weechat.network.gnutls_ca_system or
weechat.network.gnutls_ca_user, the GnuTLS credentials are freed then allocated
again, but the verification function used to check the certificate on
connection is not set again.

As a consequence, any TLS connection is made without checking the certificate.

This regression was introduced in version 3.2, when the options were changed to
automatically load system certificates without having to give the path, and to
let user give an extra custom path with certificates.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '    gnutls_certificate_allocate_credentials (&gnutls_xcred);', ''], 'added_lines': ['    network_allocate_credentials ();']}
description: WeeChat (aka Wee Enhanced Environment for Chat) 3.2 to 3.4 before 3.4.1 does not properly verify the TLS certificate of the server, after certain GnuTLS options are changed, which allows man-in-the-middle attackers to spoof a TLS chat server via an arbitrary certificate. NOTE: this only affects situations where weechat.network.gnutls_ca_system or weechat.network.gnutls_ca_user is changed without a WeeChat restart.

code_evidence: Line 6 frees the existing GnuTLS credentials, and line 15 immediately reallocates them with gnutls_certificate_allocate_credentials. Line 16 then loads CA files, but the function never re-registers the certificate verification function on the new credential object. The removed call to gnutls_certificate_allocate_credentials is replaced by network_allocate_credentials, so this reload path leaves verification unset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-295 fits because the function's reload path results in TLS connections being made without validating the server certificate. This is improper certificate validation, not merely a missing CA file, since the verification function itself is not set on the fresh credentials.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: reloading frees and reallocates GnuTLS credentials without restoring the verification callback/trust state. Trigger: changing weechat.network.gnutls_ca_system or gnutls_ca_user, which invokes this reload. Consequence: subsequent TLS connections accept arbitrary server certificates, enabling man-in-the-middle spoofing.

commit_msg:
By validating length fields from server responses, out of boundary
accesses and endless loops can be mitigated.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    rlen = rep.length << 2;', '    dev = (XDevice *) Xmalloc(sizeof(XDevice) + rep.num_classes *', '\t\t\t      sizeof(XInputClassInfo));'], 'added_lines': ['    if (rep.length < INT_MAX >> 2 &&', '\t(rep.length << 2) >= rep.num_classes * sizeof(xInputClassInfo)) {', '\trlen = rep.length << 2;', '\tdev = (XDevice *) Xmalloc(sizeof(XDevice) + rep.num_classes *', '\t\t\t\t  sizeof(XInputClassInfo));', '    } else {', '\trlen = 0;', '\tdev = NULL;', '    }']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in X.org libXi before 1.7.7 allow remote X servers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds memory access or infinite loop) via vectors involving length fields.

code_evidence: rep.length and rep.num_classes are server-controlled reply fields used directly in arithmetic. rlen shifts rep.length left by 2 with no bound, and the allocation size adds sizeof(XDevice) to rep.num_classes * sizeof(XInputClassInfo), both of which can wrap on 32-bit long/int.

dlen recomputes rep.num_classes * sizeof(xInputClassInfo); _XRead uses dlen as read size into dev->classes, and rlen - dlen compares the wrapped length, so a wrapped rlen/dlen can misdirect the read or the _XEatData skip.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is exactly an integer overflow/wraparound in size computations (rep.length << 2, rep.num_classes * sizeof) feeding memory allocation and read lengths, matching CWE-190. The resulting out-of-bounds access is the downstream consequence, not a separate weakness class here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: untrusted reply length fields are multiplied/shifted without overflow checks before allocation and read sizing. Trigger: a malicious X server returns large rep.length or rep.num_classes so the products wrap to small values. Consequence: undersized allocation followed by an over-read or incorrect data consumption, causing out-of-bounds access or an infinite loop (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/traps: Use an Interrupt Stack Table for #DB

PV guests can use architectural corner cases to cause #DB to be raised after
transitioning into supervisor mode.

Use an interrupt stack table for #DB to prevent the exception being taken with
a guest controlled stack pointer.

This is part of XSA-260 / CVE-2018-8897

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -35,6 +35,7 @@
 			[IST_MCE - 1] = stack_top + IST_MCE * PAGE_SIZE,
 			[IST_DF  - 1] = stack_top + IST_DF  * PAGE_SIZE,
 			[IST_NMI - 1] = stack_top + IST_NMI * PAGE_SIZE,
+			[IST_DB  - 1] = stack_top + IST_DB  * PAGE_SIZE,
 
 			[IST_MAX ... ARRAY_SIZE(tss->ist) - 1] =
 				0x8600111111111111ul,
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t[IST_DB  - 1] = stack_top + IST_DB  * PAGE_SIZE,']}
description: A statement in the System Programming Guide of the Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual (SDM) was mishandled in the development of some or all operating-system kernels, resulting in unexpected behavior for #DB exceptions that are deferred by MOV SS or POP SS, as demonstrated by (for example) privilege escalation in Windows, macOS, some Xen configurations, or FreeBSD, or a Linux kernel crash. The MOV to SS and POP SS instructions inhibit interrupts (including NMIs), data breakpoints, and single step trap exceptions until the instruction boundary following the next instruction (SDM Vol. 3A; section 6.8.3). (The inhibited data breakpoints are those on memory accessed by the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction itself.) Note that debug exceptions are not inhibited by the interrupt enable (EFLAGS.IF) system flag (SDM Vol. 3A; section 2.3). If the instruction following the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction is an instruction like SYSCALL, SYSENTER, INT 3, etc. that transfers control to the operating system at CPL < 3, the debug exception is delivered after the transfer to CPL < 3 is complete. OS kernels may not expect this order of events and may therefore experience unexpected behavior when it occurs.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only initializes per-CPU TSS/IST stack pointers and loads GDT/IDT descriptors; it contains no concurrent code sequence or shared-resource timing window, so CWE-362 is not supported by this function.

In case of malformed packet, this can lead to an insane amount of
memory.
Instead let's use the automatic growth mecanism. This way the malformed
packet is caught by the dissection engine.

Bug: 14056
Change-Id: I7bf5b80a516210b341356f5d495f08d1dba05805
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/23537
Reviewed-by: Pascal Quantin <pascal.quantin@gmail.com>
Petri-Dish: Pascal Quantin <pascal.quantin@gmail.com>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot <buildbot-no-reply@wireshark.org>
Reviewed-by: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        pair_list = wmem_array_sized_new(wmem_packet_scope(), sizeof(struct mbim_pair_list), element_count);'], 'added_lines': ['        pair_list = wmem_array_new(wmem_packet_scope(), sizeof(struct mbim_pair_list));']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.1 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.9, the MBIM dissector could crash or exhaust system memory. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-mbim.c by changing the memory-allocation approach.

code_evidence: element_count is read directly from the packet as an attacker-controlled guint32. The if (element_count) guard at line 15 only checks for nonzero; it does not bound the value. Line 16 passes element_count to wmem_array_sized_new as the pre-allocated capacity, and line 17 multiplies it by 8 for the subtree length, so a malformed packet declaring a huge count forces a correspondingly huge allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function fails to throttle or constrain allocation of a limited resource (memory) based on untrusted input, enabling resource-consumption DoS. It is not a buffer overflow (CWE-119): the issue is the uncontrolled allocation size, not an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dissector pre-sizes a wmem array from an unvalidated, packet-supplied element_count, letting a malformed MBIM packet request an excessive allocation. Trigger: a crafted packet with a very large element count. Supported consequence: memory exhaustion or crash (DoS), since the allocation is driven by attacker-controlled size rather than the actual remaining data.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.1 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.7, the OpenFlow dissector could crash with memory exhaustion, triggered by network traffic or a capture file. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-openflow_v5.c by ensuring that certain length values were sufficiently large.

code_evidence: prop_len is read from the packet at line 12 and only used to set the item length; the code advances offset by 6 bytes (lines 13 and 17) without validating that prop_len is at least 8 before entering the switch.

In the OFPQDPT_EXPERIMENTER case, prop_len - 16 (line 45) is computed and added to offset (line 46) with no check that prop_len >= 16, so a small prop_len underflows the unsigned expression to a huge length and offset.
The default case similarly computes prop_len - 8 (line 50) and advances offset by that value (line 51), producing a large length/offset when prop_len < 8.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length leads to uncontrolled resource consumption and a crash, fitting the Resource Management Errors category (CWE-399). The fix adds a prop_len < 8 guard, confirming the missing constraint; this is resource-management failure rather than a pure bounds-check issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the property length field is trusted without a minimum-length check before it is used in unsigned subtraction and offset advancement. A crafted OpenFlow queue property with a small prop_len triggers subtraction underflow, yielding huge lengths and offsets that drive the dissector into excessive processing or out-of-bounds reads, causing memory exhaustion or a crash.

commit_msg:
x86/hvm: Fix the handling of non-present segments

In 32bit, the data segments may be NULL to indicate that the segment is
ineligible for use.  In both 32bit and 64bit, the LDT selector may be NULL to
indicate that the entire LDT is ineligible for use.  However, nothing in Xen
actually checks for this condition when performing other segmentation
checks.  (Note however that limit and writeability checks are correctly
performed).

Neither Intel nor AMD specify the exact behaviour of loading a NULL segment.
Experimentally, AMD zeroes all attributes but leaves the base and limit
unmodified.  Intel zeroes the base, sets the limit to 0xfffffff and resets the
attributes to just .G and .D/B.

The use of the segment information in the VMCB/VMCS is equivalent to a native
pipeline interacting with the segment cache.  The present bit can therefore
have a subtly different meaning, and it is now cooked to uniformly indicate
whether the segment is usable or not.

GDTR and IDTR don't have access rights like the other segments, but for
consistency, they are treated as being present so no special casing is needed
elsewhere in the segmentation logic.

AMD hardware does not consider the present bit for %cs and %tr, and will
function as if they were present.  They are therefore unconditionally set to
present when reading information from the VMCB, to maintain the new meaning of
usability.

Intel hardware has a separate unusable bit in the VMCS segment attributes.
This bit is inverted and stored in the present field, so the hvm code can work
with architecturally-common state.

This is CVE-2016-9386 / XSA-191.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    attr = ((attr & 0xf00) << 4) | (attr & 0xff);', '', '    /* Not-present must mean unusable. */', '    if ( !reg->attr.fields.p )', '        attr |= (1u << 16);'], 'added_lines': ['    /*', '     * Unfold Xen representation into VT-x representation.  The unusable bit', '     * is unconditionally set to the inverse of present.', '     */', '    attr = (!(attr & (1u << 7)) << 16) | ((attr & 0xf00) << 4) | (attr & 0xff);']}
description: The x86 emulator in Xen does not properly treat x86 NULL segments as unusable when accessing memory, which might allow local HVM guest users to gain privileges via vectors involving "unexpected" base/limit values.

code_evidence: The function translates a Xen segment register into VT-x VMCS fields. Lines 40-42 build the guest AR bytes: the present bit (reg->attr.fields.p) is only used to OR in the unusable bit (1u<<16) when the segment is non-present. When a NULL/non-present segment is loaded, the base and limit from reg are still written unchanged at lines 49-50, 55-56, etc.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in management of permissions and security features used for access control. Here the segment usability/present state, which gates memory access permissions, is mishandled, so the access-control mechanism is improperly maintained, matching the category.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: non-present (NULL) segments are not fully marked unusable; only the unusable bit is set while base/limit are forwarded unchanged. The guest can trigger this by loading a NULL data/LDT segment, and the stale base/limit values remain usable in the VMCS, allowing the guest to bypass segmentation checks and access memory beyond intended limits, supporting privilege escalation.

commit_msg: added  additional checks to datafile loading. Closes #2070
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned Size = 0;', '\tunsigned AllocSize = Size;'], 'added_lines': ['\tint64 Size = 0;', '\tint64 AllocSize = Size;', '\tif(Size > (int64(1)<<31) || Header.m_NumItemTypes < 0 || Header.m_NumItems < 0 || Header.m_NumRawData < 0 || Header.m_ItemSize < 0)', '\t{', '\t\tio_close(File);', '\t\tdbg_msg("datafile", "unable to load file, invalid file information");', '\t\treturn false;', '\t}']}
description: In Teeworlds 0.7.2, there is an integer overflow in CDataFileReader::Open() in engine/shared/datafile.cpp that can lead to a buffer overflow and possibly remote code execution, because size-related multiplications are mishandled.

code_evidence: Size is computed as an unsigned sum of Header.m_NumItemTypes, Header.m_NumItems, Header.m_NumRawData and Header.m_ItemSize multiplications; these header fields come from the file read at line 29 and are not bounded.
AllocSize is derived from Size plus fixed and Header.m_NumRawData-based additions, then passed directly to mem_alloc.
The allocation size and the later io_read length (Size) and mem_zero count (Header.m_NumRawData*sizeof(void*)) depend on the wrapped values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is integer overflow/wraparound in size calculations that feed memory allocation and copying, matching CWE-190. The resulting buffer overflow is a downstream consequence, not the target label.

evidence_lines.code: CDatafile *pTmpDataFile = (CDatafile*)mem_alloc(AllocSize, 1);

mem_zero(pTmpDataFile->m_ppDataPtrs, Header.m_NumRawData*sizeof(void*));
unsigned ReadSize = io_read(File, pTmpDataFile->m_pData, Size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size arithmetic at lines 48-54 is performed in unsigned 32-bit, so attacker-controlled header fields can wrap Size/AllocSize to a small value. Trigger: a crafted datafile with large count fields. Consequence: mem_alloc returns a small buffer while subsequent reads and pointer setup use the original or wrapped sizes, yielding a heap buffer overflow.

description: async.c and dict.c in libhiredis.a in hiredis through 0.14.0 allow a NULL pointer dereference because malloc return values are unchecked.

code_evidence: Line 6 allocates the redisLibeventEvents structure with malloc and stores the result in e without checking it against NULL. Line 7 immediately dereferences e by writing e->context = ac, so if malloc fails the NULL pointer is used.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer it expects to be valid after an allocation that can return NULL, matching CWE-476. This is distinct from a memory leak or integer overflow, since the direct fault is the unchecked NULL use.

e->context = ac;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unchecked malloc return value. Trigger: allocation failure returns NULL, and the very next statement dereferences e. Supported consequence: a NULL pointer dereference causing a crash (DoS) in redisLibeventAttach; the patch replaces malloc with hi_calloc to avoid the unchecked failure.

commit_msg:
af_key: Do not call xfrm_probe_algs in parallel

When namespace support was added to xfrm/afkey, it caused the
previously single-threaded call to xfrm_probe_algs to become
multi-threaded.  This is buggy and needs to be fixed with a mutex.

Reported-by: Abhishek Shah <abhishek.shah@columbia.edu>
Fixes: 283bc9f35bbb ("xfrm: Namespacify xfrm state/policy locks")
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_lock(&pfkey_mutex);', '\tmutex_unlock(&pfkey_mutex);', '']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernel's IP framework for transforming packets (XFRM subsystem) when multiple calls to xfrm_probe_algs occurred simultaneously. This flaw could allow a local attacker to potentially trigger an out-of-bounds write or leak kernel heap memory by performing an out-of-bounds read and copying it into a socket.

code_evidence: pfkey_register calls xfrm_probe_algs() and then compose_sadb_supported() without any lock in the original function. The commit adds a mutex around these two calls because namespace support made the previously single-threaded probe path reachable concurrently from multiple sockets.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function executes a code sequence (probe plus compose) that requires exclusive access to a shared resource, but no synchronization enforces atomicity, allowing an interfering concurrent sequence to modify the resource. This is exactly CWE-362; the missing mutex, not the later memory corruption, is the weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
xfrm_probe_algs();
supp_skb = compose_sadb_supported(hdr, GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_ZERO);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: xfrm_probe_algs() and the subsequent compose_sadb_supported() run on a shared algorithm/registration state without exclusive access, so concurrent pfkey_register invocations can interleave. The trigger is simultaneous register requests; the supported consequence is a race that corrupts shared state, enabling out-of-bounds read/write or kernel heap memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
NetKVM: BZ#1169718: Checking the length only on read

Signed-off-by: Joseph Hindin <yhindin@rehat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                                            ULONG ulDataOffset)', '    ppr = ParaNdis_CheckSumVerify(pPacketPages, ulPacketLength - ETH_HEADER_SIZE, ulDataOffset + ETH_HEADER_SIZE, flagsToCalculate, __FUNCTION__);'], 'added_lines': ['                                            ULONG ulDataOffset,', '                                            BOOLEAN verifyLength)', '    ppr = ParaNdis_CheckSumVerify(pPacketPages, ulPacketLength - ETH_HEADER_SIZE, ulDataOffset + ETH_HEADER_SIZE, flagsToCalculate,', '        verifyLength, __FUNCTION__);']}
description: The NetKVM Windows Virtio driver allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (guest crash) via a crafted length value in an IP packet, as demonstrated by a value that does not account for the size of the IP options.

code_evidence: The function accepts ulPacketLength and ulDataOffset as caller-supplied parameters and passes ulPacketLength - ETH_HEADER_SIZE directly to ParaNdis_CheckSumVerify without validating that the length is consistent with the actual packet, including IP options.
The return status is only checked for ppresIPTooShort or ppresXxpIncomplete after the length has already been used by the parser; there is no prior rejection of an inconsistent length value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function processes attacker-controlled packet metadata (length/offset) without validating its correctness before use, matching CWE-20 improper input validation. The weakness is the missing length constraint, not a separate memory-safety primitive such as CWE-125.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the packet length is used to drive checksum parsing without verifying it accounts for the real packet layout (e.g., IP option size), so a crafted length reaches the parser. Trigger: a remote IP packet with a length value inconsistent with its options. Consequence: incorrect parsing leading to a guest crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13028/BOOTP: Add a bounds check before fetching data

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s), modified
so the capture file won't cause 'tcpdump: pcap_loop: truncated dump file'
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tND_TCHECK(bp->bp_flags);']}
description: The BOOTP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-bootp.c:bootp_print().

code_evidence: At line 31-32, the function formats the BOOTP flags by calling EXTRACT_16BITS(&bp->bp_flags) without a preceding ND_TCHECK(bp->bp_flags) bounds check. The bp pointer is the raw captured packet (line 8), so bp_flags may lie beyond the captured snapshot end. The commit adds the missing ND_TCHECK(bp->bp_flags) before this access, confirming the unchecked read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the code reads data beyond the intended buffer boundary without a length check. It is not a write or integer issue; the added ND_TCHECK is precisely a bounds check against out-of-bounds reads.

evidence_lines.code:
ND_PRINT((ndo, ", Flags [%s]",
bittok2str(bootp_flag_values, "none", EXTRACT_16BITS(&bp->bp_flags))));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bp_flags field is read via EXTRACT_16BITS without verifying that two bytes remain in the capture. Trigger: a truncated BOOTP packet that still reaches this verbose path. Consequence: a buffer over-read of up to two bytes past the snapshot, potentially crashing tcpdump or leaking adjacent memory into output.

commit_msg: elf.c: Fix NULL deref on bad xsize expression
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            size_intn = yasm_intnum_copy(', '                yasm_expr_get_intnum(&entry->xsize, 1));', '            if (!size_intn) {', '            }', '        else'], 'added_lines': ['            yasm_intnum *intn = yasm_expr_get_intnum(&entry->xsize, 1);', '            if (!intn) {', '            } else', '                size_intn = yasm_intnum_copy(intn);', '        if (!size_intn)']}
description: Yasm v1.3.0.78 was found prone to NULL Pointer Dereference in /libyasm/intnum.c and /elf/elf.c, which allows the attacker to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: When entry->xsize is set, yasm_expr_get_intnum(&entry->xsize, 1) may return NULL for a non-integer size expression. The result is passed directly to yasm_intnum_copy without a NULL check. The subsequent if (!size_intn) test checks the copy's result, not the original intnum, and the error branch does not assign a fallback; size_intn remains NULL (only the else at 22-23 assigns a value, and it is skipped when xsize is set).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but NULL, matching CWE-476. It is not merely a missing error message: the NULL value flows into yasm_intnum_copy and is used without a valid guard, so the crash is a direct NULL dereference rather than an integer or bounds flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the NULL return of yasm_expr_get_intnum is dereferenced inside yasm_intnum_copy before any validity check, because the guard tests the wrong variable. Trigger: a crafted object file whose symbol has a size expression that is not an integer. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash/denial of service during ELF symbol table writing (and later size_intn use at 56/59).

commit_msg:
Blink-in-JS should not run micro tasks

If Blink-in-JS runs micro tasks, there's a risk of causing a UXSS bug
(see 645211 for concrete steps).

This CL makes Blink-in-JS use callInternalFunction (instead of callFunction)
to avoid running micro tasks after Blink-in-JS' callbacks.

BUG=645211

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2330843002
Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#417874}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!V8ScriptRunner::callFunction(v8::Local<v8::Function>::Cast(getter), scriptState->getExecutionContext(), holder, 0, 0, isolate).ToLocal(&result)) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (!V8ScriptRunner::callInternalFunction(v8::Local<v8::Function>::Cast(getter), holder, 0, 0, isolate).ToLocal(&result)) {']}
description: Blink in Google Chrome prior to 54.0.2840.59 for Windows, Mac, and Linux; 54.0.2840.85 for Android permitted execution of v8 microtasks while the DOM was in an inconsistent state, which allowed a remote attacker to inject arbitrary scripts or HTML (UXSS) via crafted HTML pages.

code_evidence: Lines 16-18 install a TryCatch and invoke the private-script DOM attribute getter via V8ScriptRunner::callFunction, which permits V8 microtasks to run after the callback; lines 19-21 rethrow any exception in the user script context. This function is the pre-fix version where the getter callback can trigger microtask execution while the DOM is in an inconsistent state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit and description tie the flaw to arbitrary script/HTML injection (UXSS) via crafted pages, which is the improper neutralization of dangerous input in generated web output that CWE-79 describes. The microtask execution is the enabling cause; the supported impact is cross-site script execution, fitting CWE-79 rather than a pure DOM-state or race weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DOM attribute getter is invoked with callFunction, allowing queued microtasks to execute while the DOM is mid-update and inconsistent. Trigger: a crafted HTML page causes a Blink-in-JS attribute getter to run, and microtasks scheduled by the callback execute against the inconsistent DOM. Supported consequence: script or HTML injection into the page, i.e., UXSS, because attacker-controlled script runs in the victim page's origin.

commit_msg:
scsi: libsas: fix a race condition when smp task timeout

When the lldd is processing the complete sas task in interrupt and set the
task stat as SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE, the smp timeout timer is able to be
triggered at the same time. And smp_task_timedout() will complete the task
wheter the SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE is set or not. Then the sas task may freed
before lldd end the interrupt process. Thus a use-after-free will happen.

Fix this by calling the complete() only when SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE is not
set. And remove the check of the return value of the del_timer(). Once the
LLDD sets DONE, it must call task->done(), which will call
smp_task_done()->complete() and the task will be completed and freed
correctly.

Reported-by: chenxiang <chenxiang66@hisilicon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Yan <yanaijie@huawei.com>
CC: John Garry <john.garry@huawei.com>
CC: Johannes Thumshirn <jthumshirn@suse.de>
CC: Ewan Milne <emilne@redhat.com>
CC: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
CC: Tomas Henzl <thenzl@redhat.com>
CC: Dan Williams <dan.j.williams@intel.com>
CC: Hannes Reinecke <hare@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Hannes Reinecke <hare@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: John Garry <john.garry@huawei.com>
Reviewed-by: Johannes Thumshirn <jthumshirn@suse.de>
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!del_timer(&task->slow_task->timer))', '\t\treturn;'], 'added_lines': ['\tdel_timer(&task->slow_task->timer);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.20. There is a race condition in smp_task_timedout() and smp_task_done() in drivers/scsi/libsas/sas_expander.c, leading to a use-after-free.

code_evidence: smp_task_done() calls del_timer() on the shared slow_task->timer and only calls complete() when del_timer() returns nonzero (timer was still pending). If the timer callback smp_task_timedout() has already fired, del_timer() returns 0 and this function returns early, so completion is never signaled here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a race condition (CWE-362): two concurrent code sequences (timer callback and done/interrupt path) share the task and timer without proper exclusive synchronization, producing a timing window. The use-after-free is the consequence of the race, not a separate primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The timer and the LLDD completion path concurrently access the same sas_task/slow_task. When the interrupt handler marks SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE while the timeout timer fires, smp_task_timedout() may complete and free the task, and the early return here leaves the two paths unsynchronized, allowing the task to be freed while the LLDD still references it (use-after-free).

description: David Brackeen ok-file-formats dev version is vulnerable to Buffer Overflow. When the function of the ok-file-formats project is used, a heap-buffer-overflow occurred in function ok_jpg_generate_huffman_table() in "/ok_jpg.c:403".

code_evidence: The loop iterates i=1..16 and, for each i, writes bits[i] entries via huff->size[k++] = i without any bound on k relative to sizeof(huff->size).
