commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflow in dcputs (buffer missing \0)

The dcputs function appends passed string at the end of the global
string buffer (dcstr), adapting the buffer's size if necessary.

Unfortunately, the strsize variable which holds the global buffer's
size is initialized to 0 in dcinit(), which means that no place for
the \0 character is reserved. Hence, whenever dcputs tries to strcat
a string to the global buffer, a byte may be missing leading to a
heap buffer overflow.

This commit addresses this issue (CVE-2017-11732, closes #80).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstrsize=0;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstrsize = 1; // We start with empty string, i.e. \\0']}
description: A heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability was found in the function dcputs (called from decompileIMPLEMENTS) in util/decompile.c in Ming 0.4.8, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: dcinit() sets strsize=0 while allocating strmaxsize=DCSTRSIZE bytes via calloc and pointing dcptr at dcstr. The buffer-size accounting variable strsize therefore does not reserve a byte for the terminating \0 that later dcputs/strcat operations require.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The incorrect size accounting leads to writes outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation within a buffer. The specific root cause is a size/terminator accounting error, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write to a heap buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: strsize is initialized to 0 instead of 1, so the tracked size omits the empty string's terminator. Trigger: a later dcputs call strcats a string into dcstr and uses strsize for sizing/reservation, causing a write one byte past the allocated region. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds write, potentially crash/DoS as described.

commit_msg:
Fix double-free/OOB-write while receiving IPC data

If a malicious client pretends to be the E17 window manager, it is
possible to trigger an out of boundary heap write while receiving an
IPC message.

The length of the already received message is stored in an unsigned
short, which overflows after receiving 64 KB of data. It's comparably
small amount of data and therefore achievable for an attacker.

When len overflows, realloc() will either be called with a small value
and therefore chars will be appended out of bounds, or len + 1 will be
exactly 0, in which case realloc() behaves like free(). This could be
abused for a later double-free attack as it's even possible to overwrite
the free information -- but this depends on the malloc implementation.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstatic unsigned short len = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstatic size_t len = 0;']}
description: In wallpaper.c in feh before v2.18.3, if a malicious client pretends to be the E17 window manager, it is possible to trigger an out-of-boundary heap write while receiving an IPC message. An integer overflow leads to a buffer overflow and/or a double free.

code_evidence: Line 4 declares the running message length as a 16-bit unsigned short, which wraps at 65536.
Lines 16-19 accumulate data: len += blen overflows, then erealloc(message, len + 1) allocates a small (or zero) buffer and strcat(message, buff) writes past it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The core defect is an integer overflow in a size computation that leads to writing data past the end of the allocated heap buffer, matching CWE-787. The double-free is a secondary consequence of the same overflow, not the primary weakness.

evidence_lines.code: static unsigned short len = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The accumulated length len is stored in an unsigned short and overflows after more than 64 KB of IPC data. On the next fragment, erealloc receives the wrapped len+1, yielding an undersized or freed buffer, and strcat then writes the new buff beyond the allocation (or into freed memory).

commit_msg:
fix autofs/afs/etc. magic mountpoint breakage

We end up trying to kfree() nd.last.name on open("/mnt/tmp", O_CREAT)
if /mnt/tmp is an autofs direct mount.  The reason is that nd.last_type
is bogus here; we want LAST_BIND for everything of that kind and we
get LAST_NORM left over from finding parent directory.

So make sure that it *is* set properly; set to LAST_BIND before
doing ->follow_link() - for normal symlinks it will be changed
by __vfs_follow_link() and everything else needs it set that way.

Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tnd->last_type = LAST_BIND;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The __do_follow_link function in fs/namei.c in the Linux kernel before 2.6.33 does not properly handle the last pathname component during use of certain filesystems, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (incorrect free operations and system crash) via an open system call.

code_evidence: path_put(&nd->path) releases the previous path reference at line 5 before any success is determined. On the access-allowed branch, proc_get_link stores a new path into nd->path at line 8, but nd->last_type is set to LAST_BIND only at line 9; the function returns without establishing last_type on the error path via 'goto out' at line 7.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The consequence is misuse of memory after it was released, matching CWE-416. This is not merely a missing-initialization issue (CWE-457) because the supported impact is an incorrect free leading to a crash, i.e., reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that nd->last_type is not initialized to LAST_BIND before the follow-link operation, so it retains a stale value from parent-directory lookup. The trigger is open() on a magic/autofs mountpoint; the caller then treats the stale type as a pathname component and frees nd.last.name, causing an incorrect free and system crash.

code_evidence: In the long-format-name branch, wszFormatName is taken from Stream_Pointer(s) and dereferenced via wszFormatName[0] without checking that any bytes remain; formatNameLength then comes from _wcslen, which scans until a NUL and can run past the stream buffer.

The second pass repeats the same pattern: Stream_Read_UINT32 consumes 4 bytes, then wszFormatName[0] and _wcslen scan unbounded memory, and Stream_Seek advances by a length derived from that out-of-bounds scan.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 directly matches: _wcslen and wszFormatName[0] read past the end of the intended stream buffer because remaining length is never validated. This is a read-overflow, not a write or integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is missing bounds checks on the clipboard format-name fields: the code trusts dataLen and the stream contents, dereferencing and NUL-scanning pointers without verifying remaining length. Trigger is a truncated or non-NUL-terminated long format name in attacker-controlled clipboard data; consequence is an out-of-bounds read (possibly crash or info disclosure).

commit_msg:
As the kcalloc may return NULL pointer,
it should be better to check the ishtp_dma_tx_map
before use in order to avoid NULL pointer dereference.

Fixes: 3703f53b99e4 ("HID: intel_ish-hid: ISH Transport layer")
Signed-off-by: Jiasheng Jiang <jiasheng@iscas.ac.cn>
Acked-by: Srinivas Pandruvada <srinivas.pandruvada@linux.intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn;', '\t}', '', '\tif (!dev->ishtp_dma_tx_map) {', '\t\tdev_err(dev->devc, "Fail to allocate Tx map\\n");']}
description: A null pointer dereference was found in the Linux kernel's Integrated Sensor Hub (ISH) driver. This issue could allow a local user to crash the system.

code_evidence: After computing the slot index i from msg_addr, the function takes ishtp_dma_tx_lock and iterates over acked_slots, indexing dev->ishtp_dma_tx_map[i+j] at line 17 and writing dev->ishtp_dma_tx_map[i+j] = 0 at line 22. The loop's only guard is the slot-range check (i + j) >= dev->ishtp_dma_num_slots; nothing verifies that ishtp_dma_tx_map itself was successfully allocated before these array accesses.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly dereferences dev->ishtp_dma_tx_map (read at line 17, write at line 22) with no validity check, matching CWE-476. This is a missing-constraint NULL dereference, not an out-of-bounds issue, since the slot-range check constrains indices but not the base pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ishtp_dma_tx_map is allocated with kcalloc, which can return NULL, and this function indexes and writes through it without a NULL check. Trigger: a DMA Tx ack is released while the map allocation failed or is NULL. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference, crashing the system (availability impact).

commit_msg:
x86/paravirt: Fix spectre-v2 mitigations for paravirt guests

Nadav reported that on guests we're failing to rewrite the indirect
calls to CALLEE_SAVE paravirt functions. In particular the
pv_queued_spin_unlock() call is left unpatched and that is all over the
place. This obviously wrecks Spectre-v2 mitigation (for paravirt
guests) which relies on not actually having indirect calls around.

The reason is an incorrect clobber test in paravirt_patch_call(); this
function rewrites an indirect call with a direct call to the _SAME_
function, there is no possible way the clobbers can be different
because of this.

Therefore remove this clobber check. Also put WARNs on the other patch
failure case (not enough room for the instruction) which I've not seen
trigger in my (limited) testing.

commit_msg:
nla: invalidate sec handle after creation

If sec pointer isn't invalidated after creation it is not possible
to check if the upper and lower pointers are valid.

This fixes a segfault in the server part if the client disconnects before
the authentication was finished.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!handle)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!handle || !SecIsValidHandle(handle))']}
description: FreeRDP before 1.1.0-beta+2013071101 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) by disconnecting before authentication has finished.

code_evidence: Line 4 checks only whether the handle pointer itself is non-NULL, then line 6 dereferences handle->dwLower without validating that the SecHandle contents are a valid security handle. A stale or invalidated SecHandle (e.g., after client disconnect before authentication completes) passes the NULL check and is dereferenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences a pointer it assumes is valid without an effective validity constraint; the patch adds SecIsValidHandle to prevent dereferencing an invalid handle. This is a NULL/invalid-pointer dereference availability issue rather than a use-after-free, since the problem is the missing validity check before the dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard validates the outer pointer but not the validity of the SecHandle's internal lower/upper values before dereferencing handle->dwLower. Trigger: a caller supplies a non-NULL but invalid SecHandle, as happens when the client disconnects before authentication finishes. Consequence: invalid dereference causing a server crash (DoS), matching the reported segfault.

description: ImageMagick 7.0.7-2 has a memory leak in ReadSGIImage in coders/sgi.c.

code_evidence: At [346,347] the PseudoClass path calls AcquireImageColormap and, on failure, throws via ThrowReaderException without releasing the pixel buffer allocated at [107-111].
The buffer is only released at [400] on the normal path, so the early exception path leaks it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the function fails to release an allocated resource (pixel_info) after its lifetime ends on an error path; this is a missing-release weakness, not a use-after-free or buffer overflow.

evidence_lines.code:
if (AcquireImageColormap(image,image->colors,exception) == MagickFalse)
ThrowReaderException(ResourceLimitError,"MemoryAllocationFailed");
pixel_info=RelinquishVirtualMemory(pixel_info);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch for a failed AcquireImageColormap aborts without freeing pixel_info, while the success path frees it at line 400. Trigger: a malformed SGI image whose depth < 3 forces the PseudoClass path and whose colormap allocation fails. Consequence: the allocated virtual-memory resource is never released, leaking memory on each such read.

commit_msg:
Change assert to release assert for BitArray to prevent out-of-bounds access.

R=inferno@chromium.org, mbarbella@chromium.org, ochang@chromium.org, tkent@chromium.org
BUG=574802

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1672603002

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#373745}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        ASSERT_WITH_SECURITY_IMPLICATION(index < arraySize);'], 'added_lines': ['        RELEASE_ASSERT(index < arraySize);']}
description: Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 50.0.2661.94, mishandles assertions in the WTF::BitArray and WTF::double_conversion::Vector classes, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted web site.

code_evidence: set() receives an unsigned index from its caller and only guards it with ASSERT_WITH_SECURITY_IMPLICATION(index < arraySize), a debug-only check that is compiled out in release builds. The unchecked index is then used directly to address m_data[index / 8] and shift by (index & 7).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The index is input to set() whose required property (index < arraySize) is not validated in production code, matching CWE-20's failure to check that input has properties needed for safe processing. The consequence is memory corruption/DoS rather than merely a logic bug, and the fix converts the check to RELEASE_ASSERT so validation always occurs.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds constraint on the externally supplied index is enforced only by a debug assertion, so release builds perform no validation. Trigger: a caller passing an index >= arraySize (reachable from crafted web content) makes m_data[index / 8] index past the backing store, producing an out-of-bounds write that can crash or corrupt memory.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (ptr->num_views) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (ptr->views) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in gpac through 20200801. A NULL pointer dereference exists in the function vwid_box_del located in box_code_base.c. It allows an attacker to cause Denial of Service.

code_evidence: Line 5 guards the loop and the free of ptr->views on ptr->num_views, not on ptr->views itself. If num_views is nonzero while views is NULL, the loop at lines 6-8 evaluates ptr->views[i].view_refs and dereferences the NULL views pointer.
Line 10 similarly calls gf_free(ptr->views) under the num_views guard, so the NULL views value reaches the free path whenever num_views is nonzero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences ptr->views (line 7) without verifying it is non-NULL, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. This is not a use-after-free or out-of-bounds issue; the defect is the missing NULL check on the array pointer itself.

gf_free(ptr->views);
}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a guard on the wrong field: num_views being nonzero is treated as proof that the views array exists. Trigger is a box with num_views > 0 but views == NULL, reached during deletion; the loop then dereferences NULL views, causing a crash (DoS). The free of views is a secondary NULL-related path.

commit_msg: Fixed oob read in ntlm_read_ntlm_v2_response
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (Stream_GetRemainingLength(s) < 16)', '\t\treturn -1;']}
description: In FreeRDP less than or equal to 2.0.0, there is an out-of-bound read in ntlm_read_ntlm_v2_client_challenge that reads up to 28 bytes out-of-bound to an internal structure. This has been fixed in 2.1.0.

code_evidence: Line 3 calls Stream_Read to copy 16 bytes into response->Response without first verifying that the stream has at least 16 bytes remaining. Line 4 then delegates to ntlm_read_ntlm_v2_client_challenge, which parses the Challenge field; both reads depend on the caller-supplied stream length, which this function never checks.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing length check causes data to be read past the end of the intended stream buffer. The related downstream challenge parse is the same class of weakness; the fixed Response read here is itself a direct out-of-bounds read, not a write or integer issue.

Stream_Read(s, response->Response, 16);
return ntlm_read_ntlm_v2_client_challenge(s, &(response->Challenge));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function reads a fixed 16-byte Response field from the stream without checking Stream_GetRemainingLength, so a truncated NTLMv2 response makes Stream_Read consume bytes beyond the buffer. Trigger: an attacker supplies a short/malformed NTLM message. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of internal stream memory, leaking or crashing.

commit_msg:
(for 4.9.3) CVE-2018-14881/BGP: Fix BGP_CAPCODE_RESTART.

Add a bounds check and a comment to bgp_capabilities_print().

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                    /* Restart Flags (4 bits), Restart Time in seconds (12 bits) */', '                    ND_TCHECK_16BITS(opt + i + 2);']}
description: The BGP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-bgp.c:bgp_capabilities_print() (BGP_CAPCODE_RESTART).

code_evidence: In the BGP_CAPCODE_RESTART branch, the code prints Restart Flags from opt[i+2] and reads a 16-bit Restart Time via EXTRACT_16BITS(opt+i+2) without first verifying that at least two bytes are available after opt+i.

The loop only checks the 2-byte capability header (ND_TCHECK2 at line 8) and a cap_len-sized region at line 17, but the restart branch accesses opt[i+2] and opt[i+3] before any check that cap_len covers those offsets.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads two bytes beyond the validated region of the packet buffer, which is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). This is a read of insufficiently checked data, not a write (CWE-787), so CWE-125 is the correct mapping.

evidence_lines.code:
case BGP_CAPCODE_RESTART:
ND_PRINT((ndo, "\n\t\tRestart Flags: [%s], Restart Time %us",
((opt[i+2])&0x80) ? "R" : "none",
EXTRACT_16BITS(opt+i+2)&0xfff));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the RESTART case dereferences opt[i+2] and opt[i+3] via EXTRACT_16BITS without a bounds check ensuring the capability payload is at least 2 bytes. Trigger: a crafted BGP capability with cap_type RESTART and a short/truncated cap_len. Consequence: a read past the captured buffer, causing a crash/DoS or disclosure of adjacent memory.

commit_msg: Fixed bug #69090 (check cached files permissions)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#ifndef ZEND_WIN32', '\thash_value ^= ZCG(root_hash);', '#endif']}
description: An issue was discovered in PHP 5.x and 7.x, when the configuration uses apache2handler/mod_php or php-fpm with OpCache enabled. With 5.x after 5.6.28 or 7.x after 7.0.13, the issue is resolved in a non-default configuration with the opcache.validate_permission=1 setting. The vulnerability details are as follows. In PHP SAPIs where PHP interpreters share a common parent process, Zend OpCache creates a shared memory object owned by the common parent during initialization. Child PHP processes inherit the SHM descriptor, using it to cache and retrieve compiled script bytecode ("opcode" in PHP jargon). Cache keys vary depending on configuration, but filename is a central key component, and compiled opcode can generally be run if a script's filename is known or can be guessed. Many common shared-hosting configurations change EUID in child processes to enforce privilege separation among hosted users (for example using mod_ruid2 for the Apache HTTP Server, or php-fpm user settings). In these scenarios, the default Zend OpCache behavior defeats script file permissions by sharing a single SHM cache among all child PHP processes. PHP scripts often contain sensitive information: Think of CMS configurations where reading or running another user's script usually means gaining privileges to the CMS database.

code_evidence: Line 13 computes the hash solely from the caller-supplied key and key_length; line 14 derives the bucket index from that hash.
Lines 17-19 declare a cache hit when hash_value, key_length and memcmp over key all match, returning the existing entry without any check of file ownership or permissions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission and privilege management; here cache lookup ignores the requesting process's identity/permissions, letting one user's cached script be reused by another. This is a permission-enforcement flaw in the caching access path, not a mere hash collision.

evidence_lines.code:
hash_value = zend_inline_hash_func(key, key_length);
index = hash_value % accel_hash->max_num_entries;

if (entry->hash_value == hash_value
&& !memcmp(entry->key, key, key_length)) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the opcode cache key is built only from the script filename (hash of key) and lookup accepts any matching entry, so cached bytecode is shared across child processes regardless of the EUID/user under which the script is being requested. Trigger: a shared-hosting child process under a different user requests a script whose filename is known or guessed. Consequence: the cached opcode for another user's script is returned and executed, defeating script file permissions.

commit_msg:
dm: rb: only free rb_entry when we remove this entry from the rb tree

Only free rb_entry when we remove this entry from the rb tree, otherwise, a
page fault would trigger when next rb itreation would access the freed rb_entry.

Tracked-On: #6056
Signed-off-by: Li Fei1 <fei1.li@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (entry)', '\t\tfree(entry);', ''], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t\tif (entry)', '\t\t\t\tfree(entry);']}
description: The Device Model in ACRN through 2.5 has a devicemodel/core/mem.c use-after-free for a freed rb_entry.

code_evidence: RB_REMOVE unlinks entry from the tree and clears mmio_hint if it points to entry.
After releasing mmio_rwlock, entry is freed unconditionally whenever non-NULL, even when lookup succeeded but the name/base/size/flags check failed (err=-1) and entry was never removed from the tree.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees an object still reachable through the rb tree and later accessed, matching CWE-416: reference to memory after free. It is not merely a double-free or leak, since the stale tree link is the use path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: free(entry) is placed outside the RB_REMOVE branch, so a non-matching lookup result (err set to -1 at line 14) leaves the entry still linked in rbt while it is freed. A later tree traversal or lookup dereferences the freed rb_entry, producing a use-after-free (crash or memory corruption); the fix moves the free inside the removal branch.

commit_msg:
ELF: added vn_next break condition (#3214)

if the dynamic section's verneednum mismatches the true number of entries then the for loop in get_gnu_verneed will continue to iterate on the last entry since vn_next will be 0 on the last entry. If verneednum is set to all 0xff's it will take a very long time to finish this loop naturally drastically hindering binary load time. The solution is simple, to check for when vn_next == 0 and break out of the loop since all entries have been iterated over regardless of what verneednum indicates.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!verneed_entry.vn_next) {', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t}', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in function get_gnu_verneed in rizinorg Rizin prior to 0.5.0 verneed_entry allows attackers to cause a denial of service via crafted elf file.

code_evidence: Loop bound is the untrusted DT_VERNEEDNUM value read from the ELF dynamic section at line 4 and stored as verneed_num. The for loop at line 22 iterates verneed_num times; each iteration advances verneed_offset only by the attacker-controlled vn_next at line 40, with no check that vn_next is nonzero or that the offset progresses. When vn_next is 0 on the final real entry, subsequent iterations re-read the same entry while verneed_num remains huge (e.g., 0xffff).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits because the function performs a loop whose execution count is driven by an attacker-controlled field and not bounded by the actual list length, enabling excessive iteration. This is resource-consumption via iteration count rather than an out-of-bounds access (e.g., CWE-125) or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the iteration count is taken from the file's verneed_num without validating it against the actual linked-list terminator (vn_next == 0). Trigger: a crafted ELF sets DT_VERNEEDNUM to a very large value while the verneed chain ends with vn_next 0. Consequence: the loop spins through the same entry up to verneed_num times, consuming excessive CPU and drastically stalling binary load (DoS).

commit_msg:
copy: CVE-2022-0485: Fail nbdcopy if NBD read or write fails

nbdcopy has a nasty bug when performing multi-threaded copies using
asynchronous nbd calls - it was blindly treating the completion of an
asynchronous command as successful, rather than checking the *error
parameter.  This can result in the silent creation of a corrupted
image in two different ways: when a read fails, we blindly wrote
garbage to the destination; when a write fails, we did not flag that
the destination was not written.

Since nbdcopy already calls exit() on a synchronous read or write
failure to a file, doing the same for an asynchronous op to an NBD
server is the simplest solution.  A nicer solution, but more invasive
to code and thus not done here, might be to allow up to N retries of
the transaction (in case the read or write failure was transient), or
even having a mode where as much data is copied as possible (portions
of the copy that failed would be logged on stderr, and nbdcopy would
still fail with a non-zero exit status, but this would copy more than
just stopping at the first error, as can be done with rsync or
ddrescue).

Note that since we rely on auto-retiring and do NOT call
nbd_aio_command_completed, our completion callbacks must always return
1 (if they do not exit() first), even when acting on *error, so as not
leave the command allocated until nbd_close.  As such, there is no
sane way to return an error to a manual caller of the callback, and
therefore we can drop dead code that calls perror() and exit() if the
callback "failed".  It is also worth documenting the contract on when
we must manually call the callback during the asynch_zero callback, so
that we do not leak or double-free the command; thankfully, all the
existing code paths were correct.

The added testsuite script demonstrates several scenarios, some of
which fail without the rest of this patch in place, and others which
showcase ways in which sparse images can bypass errors.

Once backports are complete, a followup patch on the main branch will
edit docs/libnbd-security.pod with the mailing list announcement of
the stable branch commit ids and release versions that incorporate
this fix.

Reported-by: Nir Soffer <nsoffer@redhat.com>
Fixes: bc896eec4d ("copy: Implement multi-conn, multiple threads, multiple requests in flight.", v1.5.6)
Fixes: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/2046194
Message-Id: <20220203202558.203013-6-eblake@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Richard W.M. Jones <rjones@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Nir Soffer <nsoffer@redhat.com>
[eblake: fix error message per Nir, tweak requires lines in unit test per Rich]
Reviewed-by: Laszlo Ersek <lersek@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (cb.callback (cb.user_data, &dummy) == -1) {', '    perror (rw->name);', '    exit (EXIT_FAILURE);', '  }'], 'added_lines': ['  cb.callback (cb.user_data, &dummy);']}
description: A flaw was found in the copying tool `nbdcopy` of libnbd. When performing multi-threaded copies using asynchronous nbd calls, nbdcopy was blindly treating the completion of an asynchronous command as successful, rather than checking the *error parameter. This could result in the silent creation of a corrupted destination image.

code_evidence: The return value of cb.callback(cb.user_data, &dummy) is compared against -1 and, on failure, perror(rw->name) is invoked and the process exit(EXIT_FAILURE). The function then returns true unconditionally.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-252 fits because the function fails to properly check and propagate the callback's return value; on failure it exits instead of returning an error to the caller, leaving the caller unable to detect the unexpected state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the completion callback's return value is only used to trigger perror/exit, and the function otherwise reports success. Trigger: a callback that returns -1 (e.g., an asynchronous NBD read or write failure) causes the process to exit rather than propagate the error to the caller. Consequence: the caller cannot detect the failed operation and may continue assuming success, risking silent corruption of the destination image.

commit_msg:
Reject zero length handshake records.

Summary:
Zero length (all padding) handshake are forbidden by RFC. Allowing
these was a regression in D13754697 (2c6f78a).

This is a partial fix for CVE-2019-11924

Reviewed By: xybu

Differential Revision: D16285100

fbshipit-source-id: 05a19d31ad74601ce89156a0e59517aaad8dd928
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (!msg.fragment) {'], 'added_lines': ['  if (!msg.fragment || msg.fragment->empty()) {']}
description: A peer could send empty handshake fragments containing only padding which would be kept in memory until a full handshake was received, resulting in memory exhaustion. This issue affects versions v2019.01.28.00 and above of fizz, until v2019.08.05.00.

code_evidence: Lines 22-25: after stripping zero padding, the code only rejects the record when no content-type byte was found; otherwise it moves the entire decrypted buffer into msg.fragment, which may be empty (all padding).

Lines 36-42: the only emptiness guard is the pre-patch `!msg.fragment`; an empty fragment still satisfies this check, so handshake and alert records with zero-length fragments pass through and are returned instead of throwing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function lets an actor supply an unbounded number of zero-length handshake fragments that are retained without a size/emptiness restriction, matching CWE-770's allocation of resources without limits. It is not a parsing confusion bug; the weakness is the missing constraint on retained empty fragments enabling memory exhaustion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the read path accepts a fully padded record whose fragment is empty, because the guard checks only for a null IOBuf, not for empty content. Trigger: a peer repeatedly sends handshake records containing only padding. Each accepted empty fragment is retained while awaiting a complete handshake, so buffered state accumulates and memory is exhausted (DoS).

description: An issue was discovered in Pure-FTPd 1.0.49. An uninitialized pointer vulnerability has been detected in the diraliases linked list. When the *lookup_alias(const char alias) or print_aliases(void) function is called, they fail to correctly detect the end of the linked list and try to access a non-existent list member. commit_msg:
mm, oom_reaper: gather each vma to prevent leaking TLB entry

tlb_gather_mmu(&tlb, mm, 0, -1) means gathering the whole virtual memory
space.  In this case, tlb->fullmm is true.  Some archs like arm64
doesn't flush TLB when tlb->fullmm is true:

  commit 5a7862e83000 ("arm64: tlbflush: avoid flushing when fullmm == 1").

Which causes leaking of tlb entries.

Will clarifies his patch:
 "Basically, we tag each address space with an ASID (PCID on x86) which
  is resident in the TLB. This means we can elide TLB invalidation when
  pulling down a full mm because we won't ever assign that ASID to
  another mm without doing TLB invalidation elsewhere (which actually
  just nukes the whole TLB).

  I think that means that we could potentially not fault on a kernel
  uaccess, because we could hit in the TLB"

There could be a window between complete_signal() sending IPI to other
cores and all threads sharing this mm are really kicked off from cores.
In this window, the oom reaper may calls tlb_flush_mmu_tlbonly() to
flush TLB then frees pages.  However, due to the above problem, the TLB
entries are not really flushed on arm64.  Other threads are possible to
access these pages through TLB entries.  Moreover, a copy_to_user() can
also write to these pages without generating page fault, causes
use-after-free bugs.

This patch gathers each vma instead of gathering full vm space.  In this
case tlb->fullmm is not true.  The behavior of oom reaper become similar
to munmapping before do_exit, which should be safe for all archs.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20171107095453.179940-1-wangnan0@huawei.com
Fixes: aac453635549 ("mm, oom: introduce oom reaper")

Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>
Acked-by: David Rientjes <rientjes@google.com>
Cc: Minchan Kim <minchan@kernel.org>

Cc: Roman Gushchin <guro@fb.com>
Cc: Konstantin Khlebnikov <khlebnikov@yandex-team.ru>
Cc: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttlb_gather_mmu(&tlb, mm, 0, -1);', '\t\tif (vma_is_anonymous(vma) || !(vma->vm_flags & VM_SHARED))', '\ttlb_finish_mmu(&tlb, 0, -1);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (vma_is_anonymous(vma) || !(vma->vm_flags & VM_SHARED)) {', '\t\t\ttlb_gather_mmu(&tlb, mm, vma->vm_start, vma->vm_end);', '\t\t\ttlb_finish_mmu(&tlb, vma->vm_start, vma->vm_end);', '\t\t}']}
description: The __oom_reap_task_mm function in mm/oom_kill.c in the Linux kernel before 4.14.4 mishandles gather operations, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (TLB entry leak or use-after-free) or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a copy_to_user call within a certain time window.

code_evidence: The function gathers the whole address space with tlb_gather_mmu(&tlb, mm, 0, -1) at line 24, which sets tlb->fullmm. It then unmaps eligible VMAs at lines 29-30 and finishes with tlb_finish_mmu(&tlb, 0, -1) at line 32. Because the gather spans the full mm, arch code such as arm64 skips the actual TLB invalidation when fullmm is set, so the pages freed after unmap_page_range may remain reachable through stale TLB entries.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale TLB entries let a thread access memory that has already been freed and possibly reallocated, which is precisely CWE-416 (use after free). This is not merely a resource leak: the unflushed entries preserve a usable reference to freed pages, enabling invalid access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: full-mm TLB gathering suppresses per-address TLB flushes on architectures where fullmm==1 elides invalidation. Trigger: the oom reaper unmaps and frees pages while another thread sharing the mm still has stale TLB entries and performs a copy_to_user within the race window. Consequence: that thread reads or writes freed pages without a page fault, yielding a use-after-free (DoS or memory corruption).

commit_msg:
mwifiex: Fix three heap overflow at parsing element in cfg80211_ap_settings

mwifiex_update_vs_ie(),mwifiex_set_uap_rates() and
mwifiex_set_wmm_params() call memcpy() without checking
the destination size.Since the source is given from
user-space, this may trigger a heap buffer overflow.

Fix them by putting the length check before performing memcpy().

This fix addresses CVE-2019-14814,CVE-2019-14815,CVE-2019-14816.

Signed-off-by: Wen Huang <huangwenabc@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Ganapathi Bhat <gbhat@marvell.comg>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (*(wmm_ie + 1) > sizeof(struct mwifiex_types_wmm_info))', '\t\t\treturn;']}
description: A vulnerability was found in Linux Kernel, where a Heap Overflow was found in mwifiex_set_wmm_params() function of Marvell Wifi Driver.

code_evidence: vendor_ie is located inside the user-supplied AP beacon tail buffer via cfg80211_find_vendor_ie using params->beacon.tail and tail_len; the returned pointer aliases attacker-controlled data.

When a vendor IE is found, wmm_ie points to it and memcpy copies *(wmm_ie + 1) bytes from wmm_ie + sizeof(struct ieee_types_header) into the fixed-size heap destination bss_cfg->wmm_info without any length check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-122 fits because the overflow writes past a heap-allocated destination (bss_cfg->wmm_info) using an attacker-controlled length. It is distinct from stack overflow since the overwritten buffer is heap-allocated; the missing bounds check on the element length is the specific cause.

evidence_lines.code:

WLAN_OUI_TYPE_MICROSOFT_WMM,
params->beacon.tail,
params->beacon.tail_len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is an unchecked length field: the element length byte *(wmm_ie + 1) comes from the user-space beacon tail and is used directly as the memcpy size into the fixed-size bss_cfg->wmm_info heap field. Triggering with an oversized WMM vendor IE overwrites adjacent heap memory, supporting memory corruption that can lead to code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
gnttab: correct locking on transitive grant copy error path

While the comment next to the lock dropping in preparation of
recursively calling acquire_grant_for_copy() mistakenly talks about the
rd == td case (excluded a few lines further up), the same concerns apply
to the calling of release_grant_for_copy() on a subsequent error path.

This is CVE-2022-33748 / XSA-411.

Fixes: ad48fb963dbf ("gnttab: fix transitive grant handling")
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['         * acquire_grant_for_copy() could take the lock on the', '         * remote table (if rd == td), so we have to drop the lock', '         * here and reacquire.'], 'added_lines': ['         * acquire_grant_for_copy() will take the lock on the remote table,', '         * so we have to drop the lock here and reacquire.', '            /*', '             * Like above for acquire_grant_for_copy() we need to drop and then', '             * re-acquire the locks here to prevent lock order inversion issues.', "             * Unlike for acquire_grant_for_copy() we don't need to re-check", "             * anything, as release_grant_for_copy() doesn't depend on the grant", '             * table entry: It only updates internal state and the status flags.', '             */', '            active_entry_release(act);', '            grant_read_unlock(rgt);', '', '', '            grant_read_lock(rgt);', '            act = active_entry_acquire(rgt, gref);', '']}
description: lock order inversion in transitive grant copy handling As part of XSA-226 a missing cleanup call was inserted on an error handling path. While doing so, locking requirements were not paid attention to. As a result two cooperating guests granting each other transitive grants can cause locks to be acquired nested within one another, but in respectively opposite order. With suitable timing between the involved grant copy operations this may result in the locking up of a CPU.

code_evidence: The recursive acquire path drops the remote table locks (active_entry_release/grant_read_unlock) before calling acquire_grant_for_copy() and reacquires them afterward, establishing nested lock acquisition across the transitive grant.

On the subsequent error/restart branch (rgt version mismatch, changed pin, or mismatched transitive fields), the function calls release_grant_for_copy() while still holding rgt and act locks, then only later reduces status and releases them.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The error path mishandles the exceptional condition (version/pin/field mismatch triggering ERESTART) by performing cleanup under held locks, violating the locking protocol used on the success path. This improper handling of an exceptional condition leads to the deadlock consequence, matching CWE-755.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error/restart path releases the transitive grant without first dropping the remote table lock, so two cooperating guests with mutual transitive grants can acquire the same locks in opposite nesting order. Trigger: suitable timing between grant copy operations causes lock order inversion and CPU lockup.

commit_msg:
In drm_load_edid_firmware(), fwstr is allocated by kstrdup(). And fwstr
is dereferenced in the following codes. However, memory allocation
functions such as kstrdup() may fail and returns NULL. Dereferencing
this null pointer may cause the kernel go wrong. Thus we should check
this kstrdup() operation.
Further, if kstrdup() returns NULL, we should return ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM) to
the caller site.

Signed-off-by: Gen Zhang <blackgod016574@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Jani Nikula <jani.nikula@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Jani Nikula <jani.nikula@intel.com>
Link: https://patchwork.freedesktop.org/patch/msgid/20190524023222.GA5302@zhanggen-UX430UQ
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!fwstr)', '\t\treturn ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM);']}
description: An issue was discovered in drm_load_edid_firmware in drivers/gpu/drm/drm_edid_load.c in the Linux kernel through 5.1.5. There is an unchecked kstrdup of fwstr, which might allow an attacker to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash). NOTE: The vendor disputes this issues as not being a vulnerability because kstrdup() returning NULL is handled sufficiently and there is no chance for a NULL pointer dereference

code_evidence: Line 8 assigns the result of kstrdup() to fwstr without checking for NULL; line 9 immediately copies that possibly-NULL pointer into edidstr.
Line 10 passes &edidstr to strsep(), which dereferences edidstr; line 11 and line 13 (and line 18 via edidname) then use the derived pointers, all reachable before any NULL check on fwstr.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because a pointer expected to be valid (fwstr/edidstr from kstrdup) is dereferenced while NULL. This is a missing NULL check, not an out-of-bounds issue: strsep on a valid buffer would be safe, so the weakness is specifically the unchecked allocation result.

evidence_lines.code:
fwstr = kstrdup(edid_firmware, GFP_KERNEL);
edidstr = fwstr;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unchecked return of kstrdup() at line 8 can be NULL, and the code proceeds to use it. Trigger: an allocation failure makes fwstr NULL; strsep() at line 10 then dereferences the NULL edidstr, causing a crash (DoS). The consequence is availability loss, not memory corruption.

commit_msg:
AutoarExtractor: Do not extract files outside the destination dir

Currently, a malicious archive can cause that the files are extracted
outside of the destination dir. This can happen if the archive contains
a file whose parent is a symbolic link, which points outside of the
destination dir. This is potentially a security threat similar to
CVE-2020-11736. Let's skip such problematic files when extracting.

Fixes: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gnome-autoar/-/issues/7
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (extracted_filename == NULL) {', '      archive_read_data_skip (a);', '      continue;', '    }', '        if (hardlink_filename == NULL) {', '          archive_read_data_skip (a);', '          continue;', '        }']}
description: autoar-extractor.c in GNOME gnome-autoar through 0.2.4, as used by GNOME Shell, Nautilus, and other software, allows Directory Traversal during extraction because it lacks a check of whether a file's parent is a symlink to a directory outside of the intended extraction location.

code_evidence: The loop reads each archive entry's pathname (line 27) and hardlink (line 28), then resolves them via autoar_extractor_do_sanitize_pathname (lines 29-30, 32-33).

The resolved extracted_filename and hardlink_filename are passed directly to autoar_extractor_do_write_entry (lines 66-67) without verifying that a parent component is a symlink pointing outside the destination.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the function accesses a file by name without preventing that name from resolving through a link to an unintended resource. The missing constraint is a symlink-parent check; the patch's NULL checks address sanitization failure, not this link-following gap, which is distinct from plain path traversal (CWE-22) since the escape occurs via link resolution.

evidence_lines.code:
autoar_extractor_do_write_entry (self, a, entry,
extracted_filename, hardlink_filename);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sanitized pathname is treated as safe based on string normalization, but the filesystem is not inspected for symlinked parent directories. Trigger: an archive entry whose parent path resolves through a symlink to a location outside the extraction directory. Consequence: autoar_extractor_do_write_entry writes the file to the symlink target, escaping the destination and enabling arbitrary file overwrite (directory traversal via link following).

commit_msg:
Split the xt_compat_match/xt_compat_target into smaller type-safe functions
performing just one operation. Handle all alignment and size-related
conversions centrally in these function instead of requiring each module to
implement a full-blown conversion function. Replace ->compat callback by
->compat_from_user and ->compat_to_user callbacks, responsible for
converting just a single private structure.

Signed-off-by: Patrick McHardy <kaber@trash.net>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (t->u.kernel.target->compat)', '\t\tt->u.kernel.target->compat(t, NULL, &off, COMPAT_CALC_SIZE);', '\telse', '\t\txt_compat_target(t, NULL, &off, COMPAT_CALC_SIZE);'], 'added_lines': ['\toff += xt_compat_target_offset(target);']}
description: A heap out-of-bounds write affecting Linux since v2.6.19-rc1 was discovered in net/netfilter/x_tables.c. This allows an attacker to gain privileges or cause a DoS (via heap memory corruption) through user name space

code_evidence: After resolving the target module, the code computes the target's compat size via the target's ->compat callback or xt_compat_target and accumulates it into off, then adds off to *size. The per-entry size accounting relies entirely on this callback-reported offset; no validation clamps off against the entry's actual next_offset or the destination buffer bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked size offset leads to writing data past the end of the intended heap buffer during compat translation. It is not merely an integer overflow; the write beyond the buffer boundary is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the compat size offset returned by the target's compat callback is trusted without checking it against the entry size or destination allocation. Trigger: a target module whose compat callback reports an offset larger than the real private structure, or a mismatch between the compat and native layout. Consequence: *size is inflated and later translation writes past the allocated table buffer, a heap out-of-bounds write enabling privilege escalation or DoS.

description: In wolfSSL before 5.2.0, certificate validation may be bypassed during attempted authentication by a TLS 1.3 client to a TLS 1.3 server. This occurs when the sig_algo field differs between the certificate_verify message and the certificate message.

Consequence: peer authentication/verification is bypassed because no matching verification path runs, allowing a mismatched peer to complete authentication.

commit_msg:
get_rock_ridge_filename(): handle malformed NM entries

Payloads of NM entries are not supposed to contain NUL.  When we run
into such, only the part prior to the first NUL goes into the
concatenation (i.e. the directory entry name being encoded by a bunch
of NM entries).  We do stop when the amount collected so far + the
claimed amount in the current NM entry exceed 254.  So far, so good,
but what we return as the total length is the sum of *claimed*
sizes, not the actual amount collected.  And that can grow pretty
large - not unlimited, since you'd need to put CE entries in
between to be able to get more than the maximum that could be
contained in one isofs directory entry / continuation chunk and
we are stop once we'd encountered 32 CEs, but you can get about 8Kb
easily.  And that's what will be passed to readdir callback as the
name length.  8Kb __copy_to_user() from a buffer allocated by
__get_free_page()

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 0.98pl6+ (yes, really)
Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif ((strlen(retname) + rr->len - 5) >= 254) {', '\t\t\tstrncat(retname, rr->u.NM.name, rr->len - 5);', '\t\t\tretnamlen += rr->len - 5;'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar *p;', '\tint len;', '\t\t\tlen = rr->len - 5;', '\t\t\tif (retnamlen + len >= 254) {', "\t\t\tp = memchr(rr->u.NM.name, '\\0', len);", '\t\t\tif (unlikely(p))', '\t\t\t\tlen = p - rr->u.NM.name;', '\t\t\tmemcpy(retname + retnamlen, rr->u.NM.name, len);', '\t\t\tretnamlen += len;', "\t\t\tretname[retnamlen] = '\\0';"]}
description: The get_rock_ridge_filename function in fs/isofs/rock.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5.5 mishandles NM (aka alternate name) entries containing \0 characters, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted isofs filesystem.

code_evidence: The NM branch bounds the concatenation using (strlen(retname) + rr->len - 5) >= 254, then calls strncat with rr->len - 5 and increments retnamlen by the claimed size. Because strncat stops at an embedded NUL in rr->u.NM.name, the bytes actually copied can be fewer than rr->len - 5, so retnamlen overstates the collected length. The return value at line 71 is this claimed retnamlen, not the real name length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The over-reported length causes kernel heap bytes to be returned to a local user, which is disclosure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor, matching CWE-200. The underlying copy error is the cause; the supported consequence is the information exposure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function tracks the claimed NM payload size rather than the actual bytes copied, because strncat truncates at a NUL inside the name. Trigger: a crafted isofs image with NM entries containing NUL characters (and CE continuations). Consequence: a length larger than the initialized buffer content is returned to the readdir callback, which copies that many bytes to user space, exposing uninitialized kernel memory.

writet1 protection against buffer overflow

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        alloc_array(t1_buf, strlen(t1_line_array) + strlen(t1_buf_array) + 1, T1_BUF_SIZE);', '        alloc_array(t1_line, strlen(t1_buf_array) + 1, T1_BUF_SIZE);']}
description: An issue was discovered in t1_check_unusual_charstring functions in writet1.c files in TeX Live before 2018-09-21. A buffer overflow in the handling of Type 1 fonts allows arbitrary code execution when a malicious font is loaded by one of the vulnerable tools: pdflatex, pdftex, dvips, or luatex.

code_evidence: Line 6 copies t1_line_array into t1_buf_array, line 7 trims the trailing char, line 8 reads a new line into t1_line_array, then line 9 concatenates it onto t1_buf_array without any capacity check, and line 10 copies the combined result back into t1_line_array. Neither destination buffer is resized to hold the concatenated length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs read/write operations (strcat/strcpy) beyond the intended bounds of t1_buf_array and t1_line_array, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. It is a buffer overflow caused by missing length constraints, not a format-string or integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: strcat and strcpy operate on fixed-size t1_buf_array/t1_line_array with no length validation against the merged string. Trigger: a malicious font whose charstring line causes sscanf to fail and whose subsequent line is long enough that the concatenation exceeds buffer capacity. Consequence: out-of-bounds writes to heap/static buffers that can corrupt adjacent memory and enable arbitrary code execution.

description: An issue was discovered in OpenCV before 4.1.1. There is a NULL pointer dereference in the function cv::XMLParser::parse at modules/core/src/persistence.cpp.

code_evidence: skipSpaces receives ptr and immediately does ptr-- then dereferences via *++ptr in each mode branch (lines 7,10,23,32) without any NULL check in this function body; line 49 reassigns ptr from fs->gets() and only breaks on NULL, but earlier iterations already dereferenced.
Indexed reads ptr[1], ptr[2], ptr[3] at lines 11,14,34 assume the pointer and following bytes are valid.

This is distinct from CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read), which would require evidence of reading beyond an allocated buffer rather than a NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dereferences the caller-supplied ptr (and neighboring bytes) unconditionally. Trigger: a caller passing NULL reaches the do/while dereference, or a buffer boundary leaves too few bytes for the multi-byte lookahead. commit_msg:
mnt: Update detach_mounts to leave mounts connected

Now that it is possible to lazily unmount an entire mount tree and
leave the individual mounts connected to each other add a new flag
UMOUNT_CONNECTED to umount_tree to force this behavior and use
this flag in detach_mounts.

This closes a bug where the deletion of a file or directory could
trigger an unmount and reveal data under a mount point.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\telse umount_tree(mnt, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\telse umount_tree(mnt, UMOUNT_CONNECTED);']}
description: fs/namespace.c in the Linux kernel before 4.0.2 does not properly support mount connectivity, which allows local users to read arbitrary files by leveraging user-namespace root access for deletion of a file or directory.

code_evidence: The loop walks each mountpoint entry in mp->m_list and selects mnt. For an already-unmounted mount (MNT_UMOUNT) it only detaches children, otherwise it calls umount_tree(mnt, 0), which lacks the UMOUNT_CONNECTED flag and thus detaches the mount tree rather than leaving mounts connected.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unsafe unmount directly exposes covered filesystem contents to an unauthorized actor, matching CWE-200's confidentiality impact. This is the resultant information exposure; the specific unmount-handling error is the mechanism, but the target label is the disclosure itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: detach_mounts unmounts a mount tree without preserving connectivity, so the underlying mount point becomes visible after the unmount during file or directory deletion. Trigger: a local user with user-namespace root deletes a file or directory under a mount, causing __detach_mounts to run. Consequence: data hidden beneath the mount point is revealed, allowing read of files the actor should not access.

commit_msg:
crypto: ccp - Release all allocated memory if sha type is invalid

Release all allocated memory if sha type is invalid:
In ccp_run_sha_cmd, if the type of sha is invalid, the allocated
hmac_buf should be released.

v2: fix the goto.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Gary R Hook <gary.hook@amd.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tgoto e_ctx;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tkfree(hmac_buf);', '\t\t\tgoto e_data;']}
description: A memory leak in the ccp_run_sha_cmd() function in drivers/crypto/ccp/ccp-ops.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.9 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption), aka CID-128c66429247.

code_evidence: Lines 225-228: the HMAC branch declares local pointer hmac_buf, which is later assigned the kmalloc result.
Lines 233-237: hmac_buf = kmalloc(block_size + digest_size, GFP_KERNEL) allocates memory; failure is handled with goto e_data.
Lines 258-260: the inner switch default sets ret = -EINVAL and jumps to e_ctx without freeing the already-allocated hmac_buf.
Lines 279-284: e_ctx only calls ccp_dm_free(&ctx) and returns; no kfree(hmac_buf) occurs on this path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits: an allocated buffer is not released on an error-handling path because the goto target bypasses cleanup. This is a leak of memory after its effective lifetime, not a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: After hmac_buf is allocated at line 233, the default case of the inner switch (lines 258-260) exits via e_ctx, skipping the kfree at line 277. Trigger: sha->final && sha->opad true and an unexpected sha->type reaching this switch. Consequence: the block_size+digest_size buffer is leaked, enabling memory-consumption DoS.

commit_msg:
[CVE-2022-40304] Fix dict corruption caused by entity reference cycles

When an entity reference cycle is detected, the entity content is
cleared by setting its first byte to zero. But the entity content might
be allocated from a dict. In this case, the dict entry becomes corrupted
leading to all kinds of logic errors, including memory errors like
double-frees.

Stop storing entity content, orig, ExternalID and SystemID in a dict.
These values are unlikely to occur multiple times in a document, so they
shouldn't have been stored in a dict in the first place.

Thanks to Ned Williamson and Nathan Wachholz working with Google Project
Zero for the report!
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (dict != NULL) {', '        if ((entity->name != NULL) && (!xmlDictOwns(dict, entity->name)))', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->name);', '        if ((entity->ExternalID != NULL) &&', '\t    (!xmlDictOwns(dict, entity->ExternalID)))', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->ExternalID);', '        if ((entity->SystemID != NULL) &&', '\t    (!xmlDictOwns(dict, entity->SystemID)))', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->SystemID);', '        if ((entity->URI != NULL) && (!xmlDictOwns(dict, entity->URI)))', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->URI);', '        if ((entity->content != NULL)', '            && (!xmlDictOwns(dict, entity->content)))', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->content);', '        if ((entity->orig != NULL) && (!xmlDictOwns(dict, entity->orig)))', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->orig);', '    } else {', '        if (entity->name != NULL)', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->name);', '        if (entity->ExternalID != NULL)', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->ExternalID);', '        if (entity->SystemID != NULL)', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->SystemID);', '        if (entity->URI != NULL)', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->URI);', '        if (entity->content != NULL)', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->content);', '        if (entity->orig != NULL)', '            xmlFree((char *) entity->orig);', '    }'], 'added_lines': ['    if ((entity->name != NULL) &&', '        ((dict == NULL) || (!xmlDictOwns(dict, entity->name))))', '        xmlFree((char *) entity->name);', '    if (entity->ExternalID != NULL)', '        xmlFree((char *) entity->ExternalID);', '    if (entity->SystemID != NULL)', '        xmlFree((char *) entity->SystemID);', '    if (entity->URI != NULL)', '        xmlFree((char *) entity->URI);', '    if (entity->content != NULL)', '        xmlFree((char *) entity->content);', '    if (entity->orig != NULL)', '        xmlFree((char *) entity->orig);']}
description: An issue was discovered in libxml2 before 2.10.3. Certain invalid XML entity definitions can corrupt a hash table key, potentially leading to subsequent logic errors. In one case, a double-free can be provoked.

code_evidence: When entity->doc has a dict, the function frees entity->content only when xmlDictOwns(dict, entity->content) is false; a content pointer owned by the dict is skipped.

In the else branch (dict == NULL), entity->content is freed unconditionally. The dict pointer is derived from entity->doc, so the branch depends on document state rather than on how the content was allocated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's ownership check on entity->content can lead to freeing memory that remains owned by the dict, matching CWE-415 (two frees of the same address). This is not merely a use-after-free: the defect is the second free of dict-owned memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the free of entity->content is governed by xmlDictOwns, which only reflects whether the pointer currently lies in the dict. If a dict-allocated content buffer is cleared in place (first byte zeroed) during entity-cycle handling, the pointer may no longer be recognized as dict-owned, so the branch at line 23-25 frees a buffer that the dict still references. The dict later frees or reuses that address, yielding a double-free and possible memory corruption.

commit_msg: Fixed head buffer overflow reported in: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/98
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    return((image->columns+7)/8);'], 'added_lines': ['    return(((image->columns+7)/8)*GetPSDPacketSize(image));']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in coders/psd.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted PSD file.

code_evidence: For depth==1, the row size is computed as ceil(columns/8) bytes, ignoring the per-packet size from GetPSDPacketSize(image). The else branch multiplies columns by the packet size, showing packet size must be accounted for. The depth==1 branch therefore under-allocates/under-computes the row length relative to the data actually read for multi-byte packets.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The undersized row length causes reads beyond the intended buffer, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not CWE-787 because the supported consequence here is reading past the buffer rather than writing; the diff fixes the size computation feeding those reads.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the 1-bit row-size calculation omits the packet size factor that the general branch applies. Trigger: a crafted PSD with depth==1 and a packet size greater than one leads callers to compute a row length smaller than the data read. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read past the intended buffer, causing DoS or memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
jbd2: fix use-after-free of transaction_t race

jbd2_journal_wait_updates() is called with j_state_lock held. But if
there is a commit in progress, then this transaction might get committed
and freed via jbd2_journal_commit_transaction() ->
jbd2_journal_free_transaction(), when we release j_state_lock.
So check for journal->j_running_transaction everytime we release and
acquire j_state_lock to avoid use-after-free issue.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/948c2fed518ae739db6a8f7f83f1d58b504f87d0.1644497105.git.ritesh.list@gmail.com
Fixes: 4f98186848707f53 ("jbd2: refactor wait logic for transaction updates into a common function")
Cc: stable@kernel.org
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+afa2ca5171d93e44b348@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Reviewed-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Signed-off-by: Ritesh Harjani <riteshh@linux.ibm.com>
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tDEFINE_WAIT(wait);', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: jbd2_journal_wait_updates in fs/jbd2/transaction.c in the Linux kernel before 5.17.1 has a use-after-free caused by a transaction_t race condition.

code_evidence: The function takes j_state_lock, increments j_barrier_count, and may release the lock at line 8 to wait on j_wait_reserved before reacquiring it at line 11. After reacquisition it calls jbd2_journal_wait_updates(journal) at line 13 and unlocks at line 14. The lock is dropped and reacquired within this sequence, so the shared journal state can change between lines 8 and 11.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the j_state_lock-protected sequence is not atomic: the lock is dropped at line 8 and reacquired at line 11, creating a window in which another code sequence modifies the shared transaction state. This is a synchronization race rather than an independent memory-safety flaw; the use-after-free is the downstream consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function releases j_state_lock to sleep on j_reserved_credits and then reacquires it without revalidating journal state. Trigger: while the lock is released, a concurrent commit path can complete and free the running transaction. Consequence: jbd2_journal_wait_updates operates on a stale transaction, yielding a use-after-free and possible crash or memory corruption.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.5 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.11, the PacketBB dissector could crash, triggered by packet injection or a malformed capture file. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-packetbb.c by restricting additions to the protocol tree.

code_evidence: head_length is read from the packet and checked (head_length > addressSize-1) before use; this is the validation present in the function.
tail_length is read and checked against addressSize-1-head_length before being used to bound the tail.
The full-tail branch repeats the tail_length check, showing length fields are attacker-controlled and validated explicitly.
block_length is computed from numAddr, midSize and prefix lengths and compared to maxoffset before the tree is built.
midSize bytes are copied per address into addr[head_length] and then addr[0..3] are combined into ipv4; addr is a fixed MAX_ADDR_SIZE buffer.
Case 3 adds bytes to the protocol tree using block_index + block_length - mid_index as the length, derived from validated packet fields.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs explicit bounds checks on attacker-controlled length fields, so the target CWE-20 (improper input validation) is not directly supported by the code shown; the change is a tree-formatting fix rather than a validation gap.

evidence_lines.code:
tvb_memcpy(tvb, &addr[head_length], mid_index + midSize*i, midSize);
ipv4 = (addr[3] << 24) + (addr[2] << 16) + (addr[1] << 8) + addr[0];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Lengths and counts (head_length, tail_length, numAddr, midSize) come from the packet and are validated against addressSize and maxoffset before use. The added/removed line changes a tree-formatting call, not the validation logic; the function already rejects over-long head/tail and blocks exceeding maxoffset. No unsafe operation tied to missing input validation is shown in the function body as provided.

description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An infinite loop was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The infinite loop is triggered when Exiv2 is used to print the metadata of a crafted image file. commit_msg:
Use new libostree APIs to reject world-writable/suid content

This uses the new libostree APIs that landed recently to ensure
that we reject any files with mode outside of `0775` for system
helper pulls, and we also mask directory modes during checkout.

However, this does *not* fix up any already downloaded content.
For that, one could uninstall/reinstall; or a future patch could
do a one-time fixup pass.

Note that I am not aware of a way for flatpak applications to escalate their
privileges directly with this flaw; the bubblewrap `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` turns
of setuid. However, in combination with code execution on the host via another
mechanism (e.g. unsandboxed app), a setuid app injected could be used to gain
full host privileges.

At this time we're not aware of any flatpak content exploiting this issue.

Closes: https://github.com/flatpak/flatpak/issues/845
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  options.bareuseronly_dirs = TRUE; /* https://github.com/ostreedev/ostree/pull/927 */']}
description: In Flatpak before 0.8.7, a third-party app repository could include malicious apps that contain files with inappropriate permissions, for example setuid or world-writable. The files are deployed with those permissions, which would let a local attacker run the setuid executable or write to the world-writable location. In the case of the "system helper" component, files deployed as part of the app are owned by root, so in the worst case they could be setuid root.

code_evidence: The checkout is performed with options.mode = OSTREE_REPO_CHECKOUT_MODE_USER, which applies the repository's stored file modes (including setuid/world-writable bits) to the deployed appstream content under the arch directory. No subsequent mode masking or permission validation is performed between checkout_at and the later move into place.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-732 fits because the function assigns/retains permissions for deployed critical resources without restricting them to intended actors. This is a permission-assignment flaw, not a missing authorization check on a caller, so CWE-285 is less apt.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ostree_repo_checkout_at is invoked with checkout mode USER, so file permission bits from the untrusted repository are carried into the deployed tree without being restricted to a safe mask. Trigger: a third-party repository supplies files with setuid or world-writable modes. Consequence: those permissions persist in the checkout, allowing a local attacker to run a setuid binary or write to world-writable locations (potentially as root under the system helper).

commit_msg:
Prevent OOB access in QuantizeV2 shape inference

PiperOrigin-RevId: 400309614
Change-Id: I31412c71b05b4f21b677f7fa715a61499cbee39d
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  }', '  if (axis < -1) {', '    return errors::InvalidArgument("axis should be at least -1, got ", axis);']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the shape inference code for `QuantizeV2` can trigger a read outside of bounds of heap allocated array. This occurs whenever `axis` is a negative value less than `-1`. In this case, we are accessing data before the start of a heap buffer. The code allows `axis` to be an optional argument (`s` would contain an `error::NOT_FOUND` error code). Otherwise, it assumes that `axis` is a valid index into the dimensions of the `input` tensor. If `axis` is less than `-1` then this results in a heap OOB read. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.7.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.6.1, as this version is the only one that is also affected.

code_evidence: GetAttr retrieves the optional axis attribute; when absent, s is NOT_FOUND and axis keeps its default -1, so no validation of the retrieved value occurs.
When axis != -1 the code passes axis + 1 to WithRankAtLeast and then indexes c->Dim(input, axis); axis is used directly as an index without any lower-bound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked negative axis is used as an array/dimension index, causing a read before the beginning of the allocated buffer, which matches CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). This is not a write or a mere integer overflow; the core defect is the missing lower-bound constraint enabling an out-of-range read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the axis attribute is accepted without validating that it is at least -1. Trigger: a model supplies a negative axis less than -1, so axis + 1 is non-positive and c->Dim(input, axis) accesses a dimension index before the buffer start. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds heap read during shape inference.

example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

Fixes: 52feb444a903 ("NFC: Extend netlink interface for LTO, RW, and MIUX parameters support")
Fixes: c7aa12252f51 ("NFC: Take a reference on the LLCP local pointer when creating a socket")
Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Reviewed-by: Simon Horman <simon.horman@corigine.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct nfc_llcp_local *local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct nfc_llcp_local *local = nfc_llcp_remove_local(dev);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: Line 3 obtains the local LLCP structure via nfc_llcp_find_local() without taking a kref reference, then checks it for NULL and, if present, calls local_cleanup(local) and nfc_llcp_local_put(local) on that unreferenced pointer. Because no reference is held between lookup and use, a concurrent unregister/release path can free the same local object while this function still operates on it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code accesses a heap object (local) after its lifetime may have ended, which is exactly CWE-416. The flaw is the missing reference/lifetime guarantee around the lookup, not a simple memory leak or double-free; the patch's switch to nfc_llcp_remove_local() confirms the use-after-free nature.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the lookup in line 3 returns a raw pointer to a list entry without acquiring a reference, so the object's lifetime is not pinned. Trigger: a concurrent nfc_llcp_unregister_device/local_release path drops the last reference and frees the local between line 3 and lines 8–9. Consequence: local_cleanup and nfc_llcp_local_put dereference freed memory, yielding use-after-free (potential memory corruption, crash, or information leak).

description: idn2_to_ascii_4i in lib/lookup.c in GNU libidn2 before 2.1.1 has a heap-based buffer overflow via a long domain string.

code_evidence: When idn2_lookup_u8 succeeds, the function copies output_u8 into the caller-supplied output buffer with strcpy at line 32, with no check that output_u8's length fits the buffer before the copy; the buffer is freed afterward at line 33.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because line 32 writes data beyond the intended output buffer's end via an unchecked strcpy. This is an out-of-bounds write; a related CWE-120 (classic buffer copy) would describe the unchecked copy, but the demonstrated consequence is the out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: strcpy copies the full, unbounded output_u8 string into the caller-provided output without a length check. Trigger: a long domain string that converts to an ASCII form exceeding the caller's buffer size. Consequence: a heap-based out-of-bounds write past the end of output, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg: Detect xref pointer infinite loop (fixes #149)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    std::set<qpdf_offset_t> visited;', '        visited.insert(xref_offset);', '        if (visited.count(xref_offset) != 0)', '        {', '            xref_offset = 0;', '        }']}
description: An issue was discovered in QPDF before 7.0.0. There is an infinite loop due to looping xref tables in QPDF.cc.

code_evidence: The while loop is controlled solely by xref_offset, which is reassigned from read_xrefTable (line 23) or read_xrefStream (line 27) each iteration.
Nothing tracks previously visited xref offsets, so if a table or stream points back to an already-processed offset, xref_offset remains nonzero and the loop never terminates.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the while loop's exit condition (xref_offset == 0) is unreachable when xref chains cycle; the added visited-set guard confirms the intended fix for this infinite loop, not a different weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop exit condition depends on xref_offset becoming zero, but a malformed PDF with looping xref tables makes read_xrefTable/read_xrefStream return a previously seen nonzero offset. Trigger: opening such a crafted PDF. Consequence: the loop iterates indefinitely, consuming CPU (denial of service).

description: Envoy is an open source edge and service proxy, designed for cloud-native applications. Sending a locally generated response must stop further processing of request or response data.
