commit_msg:
go7007_snd_init() misses a snd_card_free() in an error path.
Add the missed call to fix it.

Signed-off-by: Chuhong Yuan <hslester96@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab+huawei@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (ret < 0) {', '\t\tkfree(gosnd);', '\t\treturn ret;', '\t}', '\tif (ret < 0) {', '\t\tkfree(gosnd);', '\t\treturn ret;', '\t}', '\tif (ret < 0) {', '\t\tsnd_card_free(gosnd->card);', '\t\tkfree(gosnd);', '\t\treturn ret;', '\t}', '\tif (ret < 0) {', '\t\tsnd_card_free(gosnd->card);', '\t\tkfree(gosnd);', '\t\treturn ret;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (ret < 0)', '\t\tgoto free_snd;', '', '\tif (ret < 0)', '\t\tgoto free_card;', '', '\tif (ret < 0)', '\t\tgoto free_card;', '', '\tif (ret < 0)', '\t\tgoto free_card;', '', 'free_card:', '\tsnd_card_free(gosnd->card);', 'free_snd:', '\tkfree(gosnd);', '\treturn ret;']}
description: go7007_snd_init in drivers/media/usb/go7007/snd-go7007.c in the Linux kernel before 5.6 does not call snd_card_free for a failure path, which causes a memory leak, aka CID-9453264ef586.

code_evidence: snd_card_new() stores the allocated card in gosnd->card; on failure the code frees only gosnd and returns, so the card allocated by snd_card_new is never released via snd_card_free().
snd_device_new() is called on gosnd->card; on failure the code again frees only gosnd and returns, leaving the snd_card allocated at line 18 unreleased.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because memory allocated by snd_card_new() remains unreleased on error paths, matching missing release of memory after its effective lifetime. It is not a use-after-free, since no freed pointer is later dereferenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failure branches after snd_card_new() release only the gosnd structure and omit snd_card_free(gosnd->card). Trigger: snd_card_new() or snd_device_new() returns a negative error. Consequence: the snd_card allocation is leaked, reducing available memory; repeated init failures accumulate unreleased cards (CWE-401).

commit_msg:
CVE-2022-27239: mount.cifs: fix length check for ip option parsing

Previous check was true whatever the length of the input string was,
leading to a buffer overflow in the subsequent strcpy call.

Bug: https://bugzilla.samba.org/show_bug.cgi?id=15025

Signed-off-by: Jeffrey Bencteux <jbe@improsec.com>
Reviewed-by: David Disseldorp <ddiss@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t} else if (strnlen(value, MAX_ADDRESS_LEN) <=', '\t\t\t\tstrcpy(parsed_info->addrlist, value);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t} else if (strnlen(value, MAX_ADDRESS_LEN) <', '\t\t\t\tstrlcpy(parsed_info->addrlist, value,', '\t\t\t\t\tMAX_ADDRESS_LEN);']}
description: In cifs-utils through 6.14, a stack-based buffer overflow when parsing the mount.cifs ip= command-line argument could lead to local attackers gaining root privileges.

code_evidence: For OPT_IP, the guard uses strnlen(value, MAX_ADDRESS_LEN) <= MAX_ADDRESS_LEN, which is true for any value whose length is less than or equal to MAX_ADDRESS_LEN, including exactly MAX_ADDRESS_LEN. The subsequent strcpy(parsed_info->addrlist, value) copies the entire NUL-terminated value without a bound, so a value of length MAX_ADDRESS_LEN (or longer, since strnlen caps at MAX_ADDRESS_LEN and the comparison still passes when the cap is reached) overflows addrlist.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked strcpy writes beyond the bounds of the destination buffer. The weakness is the missing/inadequate length constraint before the copy, not merely incorrect length computation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the off-by-one length check permits a too-long ip= value to reach an unbounded strcpy into the fixed addrlist buffer. Trigger: a mount.cifs command-line ip= argument of sufficient length. Consequence: stack-based buffer overflow, potentially leading to code execution and privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
There is a potential UAF between the unregistration routine and the NFC
netlink operations.

The race that cause that UAF can be shown as below:

 (FREE)                      |  (USE)
nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev   |  nfc_genl_dev_up
  nci_close_device           |
  nci_unregister_device      |    nfc_get_device
    nfc_unregister_device    |    nfc_dev_up
      rfkill_destory         |
      device_del             |      rfkill_blocked
  ...                        |    ...

The root cause for this race is concluded below:
1. The rfkill_blocked (USE) in nfc_dev_up is supposed to be placed after
the device_is_registered check.
2. Since the netlink operations are possible just after the device_add
in nfc_register_device, the nfc_dev_up() can happen anywhere during the
rfkill creation process, which leads to data race.

This patch reorder these actions to permit
1. Once device_del is finished, the nfc_dev_up cannot dereference the
rfkill object.
2. The rfkill_register need to be placed after the device_add of nfc_dev
because the parent device need to be created first. So this patch keeps
the order but inject device_lock to prevent the data race.

Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Fixes: be055b2f89b5 ("NFC: RFKILL support")
Reviewed-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Krzysztof Kozlowski <krzysztof.kozlowski@canonical.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20211116152652.19217-1-linma@zju.edu.cn
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\trc = nfc_genl_device_removed(dev);', '\tif (rc)', '\t\tpr_debug("The userspace won\'t be notified that the device %s "', '\t\t\t "was removed\\n", dev_name(&dev->dev));', ''], 'added_lines': ['\trc = nfc_genl_device_removed(dev);', '\tif (rc)', '\t\tpr_debug("The userspace won\'t be notified that the device %s "', '\t\t\t "was removed\\n", dev_name(&dev->dev));', '', '\tdevice_lock(&dev->dev);', '\tdevice_unlock(&dev->dev);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nci_request in net/nfc/nci/core.c in NFC Controller Interface (NCI) in the Linux kernel. This flaw could allow a local attacker with user privileges to cause a data race problem while the device is getting removed, leading to a privilege escalation problem.

code_evidence: Lines 5-8 check and free dev->rfkill (rfkill_unregister/rfkill_destroy) with no device_lock held around the rfkill object.
Lines 16-19 call nfc_genl_device_removed before device_del at line 23; netlink operations remain possible until device_del, so nfc_dev_up can concurrently reach rfkill_blocked(dev->rfkill).
Line 23 device_del is the only later serialization point, but it occurs after the rfkill object is already destroyed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's rfkill teardown and the concurrent nfc_dev_up access are a shared-resource race violating exclusivity; the fix adds device_lock around the rfkill block, confirming improper synchronization (CWE-362). The UAF is the consequence of the race, not the target weakness.

evidence_lines.code: device_del(&dev->dev);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the rfkill object is destroyed in nfc_unregister_device without holding dev->dev's device_lock, while nfc_dev_up reaches rfkill_blocked(dev->rfkill) after only a nfc_get_device reference. Trigger: a netlink nfc_genl_dev_up racing nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev between the device_del and rfkill teardown. The unsynchronized concurrent access yields a use-after-free, enabling privilege escalation or crash.

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

commit_msg:
Ensure the MakerNote data pointers are initialized with NULL.

This ensures that an uninitialized pointer isn't dereferenced later in
the case where the number of components (and therefore size) is 0.

This fixes the second issue reported at
https://sourceforge.net/p/libexif/bugs/125/

CVE-2020-13113
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tmemset(&n->entries[tcount], 0, sizeof(MnotePentaxEntry));']}
description: An issue was discovered in libexif before 0.6.22. Use of uninitialized memory in EXIF Makernote handling could lead to crashes and potential use-after-free conditions.

code_evidence: n->entries is allocated for c elements at [47], but tcount is only reset to 0 at [52]; the loop at [53] fills entries incrementally and increments tcount only at [94].

Each iteration writes tag, format, components, order and size ([60-63],[76]), but the data pointer is set only inside the s!=0 branch ([77-92]); when s is 0 the data field remains whatever the allocator returned.
If the loop breaks early via CHECKOVERFLOW ([55-59]) or a size overflow ([67-73]), only tcount entries are finalized at [96], but entries beyond tcount were never initialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is that a resource field (entries[tcount].data) is used without being initialized on the zero-size path, which is exactly CWE-908 (Use of Uninitialized Resource). The missing memset/zeroing is the defect; the crash or invalid access is its consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocated MnotePentaxEntry array is not zero-initialized, and the data pointer is assigned only when the computed component size s is nonzero. For a tag whose format size times components is 0, no allocation or memcpy occurs, so later consumers read an indeterminate data pointer. The trigger is a crafted EXIF MakerNote with a zero-size component; the supported consequence is use of uninitialized memory, leading to invalid reads, crashes, or a dangling/use-after-free-like access when the garbage pointer is freed or dereferenced.

TIFFReadRGBATileExt(): fix (unsigned) integer overflow on strips/tiles > 2 GB

Fixes https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=53137
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        memmove( raster + (tile_ysize - i_row - 1) * tile_xsize,', '                 raster + (read_ysize - i_row - 1) * read_xsize,', '        _TIFFmemset( raster + (tile_ysize - i_row - 1) * tile_xsize+read_xsize,', '        _TIFFmemset( raster + (tile_ysize - i_row - 1) * tile_xsize,'], 'added_lines': ['        memmove( raster + (size_t)(tile_ysize - i_row - 1) * tile_xsize,', '                 raster + (size_t)(read_ysize - i_row - 1) * read_xsize,', '        _TIFFmemset( raster + (size_t)(tile_ysize - i_row - 1) * tile_xsize+read_xsize,', '        _TIFFmemset( raster + (size_t)(tile_ysize - i_row - 1) * tile_xsize,']}
description: A vulnerability was found in LibTIFF. It has been classified as critical. This affects the function TIFFReadRGBATileExt of the file libtiff/tif_getimage.c. The manipulation leads to integer overflow. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. The name of the patch is 227500897dfb07fb7d27f7aa570050e62617e3be. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier VDB-213549 was assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: In the row-copy loop, the destination offset is computed as (tile_ysize - i_row - 1) * tile_xsize and the source offset as (read_ysize - i_row - 1) * read_xsize, both in uint32_t arithmetic before being added to the raster pointer.
The memset destination adds read_xsize to the same uint32_t product, and the trailing loop repeats the (tile_ysize - i_row - 1) * tile_xsize computation.
All operands are uint32_t; the product overflows and wraps when tile dimensions make the tile exceed 2^32 bytes, so the computed pointer offsets are wrong.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs numeric calculation of array offsets with unsigned integer arithmetic that overflows, matching CWE-189 (Numeric Errors) as the target. The overflow is the cause; the resulting out-of-bounds memory access is the consequence, distinguishing it from a pure bounds-check weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
_TIFFmemset( raster + (tile_ysize - i_row - 1) * tile_xsize+read_xsize,
0, sizeof(uint32_t) * (tile_xsize - read_xsize) );

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unsigned 32-bit multiplication of tile/row dimensions to form pointer offsets without widening. Trigger: a TIFF tile or strip with dimensions such that (tile_ysize - i_row - 1) * tile_xsize or read_ysize * read_xsize exceeds 2^32. The wrapped offsets cause memmove/_TIFFmemset to operate on wrong raster locations, producing out-of-bounds writes/reads (memory corruption) rather than merely a wrong numeric result.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: fix unconditional helper

Ben Hawkes says:

 In the mark_source_chains function (net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c) it
 is possible for a user-supplied ipt_entry structure to have a large
 next_offset field. This field is not bounds checked prior to writing a
 counter value at the supplied offset.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!unconditional(&e->ipv6))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!unconditional(e))']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

code_evidence: check_underflow gates on unconditional(&e->ipv6), which only inspects the IPv6 address fields and does not account for the presence of match extensions in the entry.
After the gate, ip6t_get_target_c(e) and the target-name/verdict checks are performed, treating the entry as a valid standard-target rule.
The verdict is decoded and compared to NF_DROP/NF_ACCEPT, so an entry passing the gate is classified as an unconditional absolute-verdict rule.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the misclassification enables an out-of-bounds write to a user-influenced offset in the entry buffer. The root cause is the missing match-extension check in the unconditional test, not merely a bad verdict value.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!unconditional(&e->ipv6))
return false;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the 'unconditional' test is incomplete because it ignores match extensions, so a crafted user-supplied ipt_entry with matches but wildcard addresses passes as unconditional. This lets callers such as mark_source_chains treat the rule as terminal and follow a large next_offset, writing a counter at an offset that was never bounds-checked, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg:
Bug 698830: Don't drop unkept stream if running out of error stack.

Under normal conditions where fz_keep_stream() is called inside
fz_try() we may call fz_drop_stream() in fz_catch() upon exceptions.
The issue comes when fz_keep_stream() has not yet been called but is
dropped in fz_catch(). This happens in the PDF from the bug when
fz_try() runs out of exception stack, and next the code in fz_catch()
runs, dropping the caller's reference to the filter chain stream!

The simplest way of fixing this it to always keep the filter chain
stream before fz_try() is called. That way fz_catch() may drop the
stream whether an exception has occurred or if the fz_try() ran out of
exception stack.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfz_var(chain);', "\t\t/* don't close chain when we close this filter */", '\t\tchain2 = fz_keep_stream(ctx, chain);'], 'added_lines': ['\tchain = fz_keep_stream(ctx, chain);', '\t\tchain2 = chain;']}

commit_msg:
Fix DTLS buffered message DoS attack

DTLS can handle out of order record delivery. Additionally since
handshake messages can be bigger than will fit into a single packet, the
messages can be fragmented across multiple records (as with normal TLS).
That means that the messages can arrive mixed up, and we have to
reassemble them. We keep a queue of buffered messages that are "from the
future", i.e. messages we're not ready to deal with yet but have arrived
early. The messages held there may not be full yet - they could be one
or more fragments that are still in the process of being reassembled.

The code assumes that we will eventually complete the reassembly and
when that occurs the complete message is removed from the queue at the
point that we need to use it.

However, DTLS is also tolerant of packet loss. To get around that DTLS
messages can be retransmitted. If we receive a full (non-fragmented)
message from the peer after previously having received a fragment of
that message, then we ignore the message in the queue and just use the
non-fragmented version. At that point the queued message will never get
removed.

Additionally the peer could send "future" messages that we never get to
in order to complete the handshake. Each message has a sequence number
(starting from 0). We will accept a message fragment for the current
message sequence number, or for any sequence up to 10 into the future.
However if the Finished message has a sequence number of 2, anything
greater than that in the queue is just left there.

So, in those two ways we can end up with "orphaned" data in the queue
that will never get removed - except when the connection is closed. At
that point all the queues are flushed.

An attacker could seek to exploit this by filling up the queues with
lots of large messages that are never going to be used in order to
attempt a DoS by memory exhaustion.

I will assume that we are only concerned with servers here. It does not
seem reasonable to be concerned about a memory exhaustion attack on a
client. They are unlikely to process enough connections for this to be
an issue.

A "long" handshake with many messages might be 5 messages long (in the
incoming direction), e.g. ClientHello, Certificate, ClientKeyExchange,
CertificateVerify, Finished. So this would be message sequence numbers 0
to 4. Additionally we can buffer up to 10 messages in the future.
Therefore the maximum number of messages that an attacker could send
that could get orphaned would typically be 15.

The maximum size that a DTLS message is allowed to be is defined by
max_cert_list, which by default is 100k. Therefore the maximum amount of
"orphaned" memory per connection is 1500k.

Message sequence numbers get reset after the Finished message, so
renegotiation will not extend the maximum number of messages that can be
orphaned per connection.

As noted above, the queues do get cleared when the connection is closed.
Therefore in order to mount an effective attack, an attacker would have
to open many simultaneous connections.

Issue reported by Quan Luo.

CVE-2016-2179

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            dtls1_clear_received_buffer(s);']}
description: The DTLS implementation in OpenSSL before 1.1.0 does not properly restrict the lifetime of queue entries associated with unused out-of-order messages, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by maintaining many crafted DTLS sessions simultaneously, related to d1_lib.c, statem_dtls.c, statem_lib.c, and statem_srvr.c.

code_evidence: In the DTLS branch of tls_finish_handshake, the code resets the handshake sequence counters (handshake_read_seq, handshake_write_seq, next_handshake_write_seq) but does not clear the buffered out-of-order received-message queue at this point.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's missing queue cleanup lets orphaned buffered message entries accumulate, directly supporting resource mismanagement (memory consumption), which fits the target CWE-399 resource management errors category rather than a mere logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the finish-handshake path resets DTLS sequence state without releasing queued future/fragmented messages that will never be reassembled or consumed. Trigger: a peer sends fragments or future-sequence messages that become orphaned when the handshake completes; consequence: queue entries persist per connection until close, enabling memory exhaustion across many simultaneous sessions.

commit_msg:
mm: avoid setting up anonymous pages into file mapping

Reading page fault handler code I've noticed that under right
circumstances kernel would map anonymous pages into file mappings: if
the VMA doesn't have vm_ops->fault() and the VMA wasn't fully populated
on ->mmap(), kernel would handle page fault to not populated pte with
do_anonymous_page().

Let's change page fault handler to use do_anonymous_page() only on
anonymous VMA (->vm_ops == NULL) and make sure that the VMA is not
shared.

For file mappings without vm_ops->fault() or shred VMA without vm_ops,
page fault on pte_none() entry would lead to SIGBUS.

Acked-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (vma->vm_ops) {', '\t\t\t\tif (likely(vma->vm_ops->fault))', '\t\t\t\t\treturn do_fault(mm, vma, address, pte,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t\tpmd, flags, entry);', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\treturn do_anonymous_page(mm, vma, address,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t pte, pmd, flags);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (vma->vm_ops)', '\t\t\t\treturn do_fault(mm, vma, address, pte, pmd,', '\t\t\t\t\t\tflags, entry);', '', '\t\t\treturn do_anonymous_page(mm, vma, address, pte, pmd,', '\t\t\t\t\tflags);']}
description: mm/memory.c in the Linux kernel before 4.1.4 mishandles anonymous pages, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (page tainting) via a crafted application that triggers writing to page zero.

code_evidence: When pte_none(entry) holds, the code branches on vma->vm_ops; if vm_ops exists but vm_ops->fault is NULL (or the VMA is not anonymous), it falls through to do_anonymous_page() at lines 16-17 instead of rejecting the fault. The prior code only called do_fault when fault was non-NULL and otherwise also fell through, so the mapping-type precondition (anonymous, non-shared VMA) is never checked before installing an anonymous page.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts a fault context (VMA type/attributes) without validating the required properties before processing, matching CWE-20's improper input validation. The missing constraint is the VMA's mapping class, not a memory-safety primitive like an out-of-bounds access (CWE-125/787).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: handle_pte_fault does not validate that the VMA is an anonymous, non-shared mapping before calling do_anonymous_page(). Trigger: a page fault on a pte_none entry in a file-backed VMA lacking vm_ops->fault (or a shared VMA) reaches do_anonymous_page. Consequence: anonymous pages are mapped into file mappings, tainting page state and enabling privilege escalation or DoS rather than the expected SIGBUS.

commit_msg:
ASoC: SOF: ipc: Fix memory leak in sof_set_get_large_ctrl_data

In the implementation of sof_set_get_large_ctrl_data() there is a memory
leak in case an error. Release partdata if sof_get_ctrl_copy_params()
fails.

Fixes: 54d198d5019d ("ASoC: SOF: Propagate sof_get_ctrl_copy_params() error properly")
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20191027215330.12729-1-navid.emamdoost@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Mark Brown <broonie@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (err < 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (err < 0) {', '\t\tkfree(partdata);', '\t}']}
description: A memory leak in the sof_set_get_large_ctrl_data() function in sound/soc/sof/ipc.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.9 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering sof_get_ctrl_copy_params() failures, aka CID-45c1380358b1.

code_evidence: Line 13 allocates partdata with kzalloc; lines 14-15 return -ENOMEM only when allocation fails, so a successful allocation owns the buffer.
Lines 16-21 call sof_get_ctrl_copy_params, whose negative return is checked at line 22; the error branch at line 23 returns err without freeing partdata.
The only kfree(partdata) appears at line 50 after the loop, reachable only on the success path; the early return at line 23 bypasses it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory and fails to release it on an error return, matching CWE-401's missing release after effective lifetime. This is a leak on an error path, not a use-after-free or double-free, since the buffer is simply never freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path after the sof_get_ctrl_copy_params failure returns without releasing the kzalloc'd partdata. Trigger: sof_get_ctrl_copy_params returns a negative err. Consequence: the allocation is leaked, and repeated failures accumulate unreleased memory, supporting memory-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg:
DO NOT MERGE | libvpx: cherry-pick aa1c813 from upstream

Description from upstream:
vp9: Fix potential SEGV in decoder_peek_si_internal

decoder_peek_si_internal could potentially read more bytes than
what actually exists in the input buffer. We check for the buffer
size to be at least 8, but we try to read up to 10 bytes in the
worst case. A well crafted file could thus cause a segfault.
Likely change that introduced this bug was:
https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/#/c/70439 (git hash:
7c43fb6)

Bug: 30013856
Change-Id: If556414cb5b82472d5673e045bc185cc57bb9af3
(cherry picked from commit bd57d587c2eb743c61b049add18f9fd72bf78c33)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  uint8_t clear_buffer[9];', '    if ((profile >= 2 && data_sz <= 1) || data_sz < 1)', '      return VPX_CODEC_UNSUP_BITSTREAM;', '', '    if (data_sz <= 8)'], 'added_lines': ['  uint8_t clear_buffer[10];', '', '  // A maximum of 6 bits are needed to read the frame marker, profile and', '  // show_existing_frame.', '  if (data_sz < 1)', '    return VPX_CODEC_UNSUP_BITSTREAM;', '      // If profile is > 2 and show_existing_frame is true, then at least 1 more', '      // byte (6+3=9 bits) is needed.', '      if (profile > 2 && data_sz < 2)', '        return VPX_CODEC_UNSUP_BITSTREAM;', '    // For the rest of the function, a maximum of 9 more bytes are needed', '    // (computed by taking the maximum possible bits needed in each case). Note', '    // that this has to be updated if we read any more bits in this function.', '    if (data_sz < 10)']}
description: The decoder_peek_si_internal function in vp9/vp9_dx_iface.c in libvpx in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, 6.x before 2016-09-01, and 7.0 before 2016-09-01 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (buffer over-read, and device hang or reboot) via a crafted media file, aka internal bug 30013856.

code_evidence: clear_buffer is only 9 bytes; when a decrypt callback is supplied, data_sz is clamped to sizeof(clear_buffer) (9) and data is redirected to this 9-byte stack buffer.

The read-bit buffer rb is initialized over data/data_sz, then frame_marker, profile, and up to three more bits are read. The guard only rejects data_sz < 1 (or <=1 for profile>=2), and the later guard only rejects data_sz <= 8, so the worst-case reads (up to 10 bytes) can exceed the 9-byte buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads from a memory location outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The root cause is insufficient length validation before bit reads; the consequence is an over-read leading to SEGV.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The size checks are off by the number of bits consumed: a crafted stream with data_sz of 9 (or 1-2 for high profiles) passes validation, yet vpx_rb_read_literal/read_bit consume more bits than the buffer holds. Reading beyond data+data_sz (or beyond the 9-byte clear_buffer) yields an out-of-bounds read that can crash the decoder (SEGV), a denial of service.

commit_msg:
ext4: fix slab-use-after-free in ext4_es_insert_extent()

Yikebaer reported an issue:
==================================================================
BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in ext4_es_insert_extent+0xc68/0xcb0
fs/ext4/extents_status.c:894
Read of size 4 at addr ffff888112ecc1a4 by task syz-executor/8438

CPU: 1 PID: 8438 Comm: syz-executor Not tainted 6.5.0-rc5 #1
Call Trace:
 [...]
 kasan_report+0xba/0xf0 mm/kasan/report.c:588
 ext4_es_insert_extent+0xc68/0xcb0 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:894
 ext4_map_blocks+0x92a/0x16f0 fs/ext4/inode.c:680
 ext4_alloc_file_blocks.isra.0+0x2df/0xb70 fs/ext4/extents.c:4462
 ext4_zero_range fs/ext4/extents.c:4622 [inline]
 ext4_fallocate+0x251c/0x3ce0 fs/ext4/extents.c:4721
 [...]

Allocated by task 8438:
 [...]
 kmem_cache_zalloc include/linux/slab.h:693 [inline]
 __es_alloc_extent fs/ext4/extents_status.c:469 [inline]
 ext4_es_insert_extent+0x672/0xcb0 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:873
 ext4_map_blocks+0x92a/0x16f0 fs/ext4/inode.c:680
 ext4_alloc_file_blocks.isra.0+0x2df/0xb70 fs/ext4/extents.c:4462
 ext4_zero_range fs/ext4/extents.c:4622 [inline]
 ext4_fallocate+0x251c/0x3ce0 fs/ext4/extents.c:4721
 [...]

Freed by task 8438:
 [...]
 kmem_cache_free+0xec/0x490 mm/slub.c:3823
 ext4_es_try_to_merge_right fs/ext4/extents_status.c:593 [inline]
 __es_insert_extent+0x9f4/0x1440 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:802
 ext4_es_insert_extent+0x2ca/0xcb0 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:882
 ext4_map_blocks+0x92a/0x16f0 fs/ext4/inode.c:680
 ext4_alloc_file_blocks.isra.0+0x2df/0xb70 fs/ext4/extents.c:4462
 ext4_zero_range fs/ext4/extents.c:4622 [inline]
 ext4_fallocate+0x251c/0x3ce0 fs/ext4/extents.c:4721
 [...]
==================================================================

The flow of issue triggering is as follows:
1. remove es
      raw es               es  removed  es1
|-------------------| -> |----|.......|------|

2. insert es
  es   insert   es1      merge with es  es1     merge with es and free es1
|----|.......|------| -> |------------|------| -> |-------------------|

es merges with newes, then merges with es1, frees es1, then determines
if es1->es_len is 0 and triggers a UAF.

The code flow is as follows:
ext4_es_insert_extent
  es1 = __es_alloc_extent(true);
  es2 = __es_alloc_extent(true);
  __es_remove_extent(inode, lblk, end, NULL, es1)
    __es_insert_extent(inode, &newes, es1) ---> insert es1 to es tree
  __es_insert_extent(inode, &newes, es2)
    ext4_es_try_to_merge_right
      ext4_es_free_extent(inode, es1) --->  es1 is freed
  if (es1 && !es1->es_len)
    // Trigger UAF by determining if es1 is used.

We determine whether es1 or es2 is used immediately after calling
__es_remove_extent() or __es_insert_extent() to avoid triggering a
UAF if es1 or es2 is freed.

Reported-by: Yikebaer Aizezi <yikebaer61@gmail.com>
Closes: https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/CALcu4raD4h9coiyEBL4Bm0zjDwxC2CyPiTwsP3zFuhot6y9Beg@mail.gmail.com
Fixes: 2a69c450083d ("ext4: using nofail preallocation in ext4_es_insert_extent()")
Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Baokun Li <libaokun1@huawei.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230815070808.3377171-1-libaokun1@huawei.com
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\t/* es is pre-allocated but not used, free it. */', '\tif (es1 && !es1->es_len)', '\t\t__es_free_extent(es1);', '\tif (es2 && !es2->es_len)', '\t\t__es_free_extent(es2);'], 'added_lines': ["\t/* Free preallocated extent if it didn't get used. */", '\tif (es1) {', '\t\tif (!es1->es_len)', '\t\t\t__es_free_extent(es1);', '\t\tes1 = NULL;', '\t}', "\t/* Free preallocated extent if it didn't get used. */", '\tif (es2) {', '\t\tif (!es2->es_len)', '\t\t\t__es_free_extent(es2);', '\t\tes2 = NULL;', '\t}']}
description: The Linux kernel before 6.5.4 has an es1 use-after-free in fs/ext4/extents_status.c, related to ext4_es_insert_extent.

code_evidence: __es_remove_extent at line 37 may insert es1 into the extent tree; the subsequent __es_insert_extent at line 40 can merge es1 with a neighboring extent and free it. The code then dereferences es1->es_len at line 49 to decide whether to free it, reading a pointer that may already have been freed. The same pattern applies to es2 at line 51.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function dereferences es1 after it may have been freed by the merge path; the fix moves the check before the free can occur. This is a use-after-free, not merely a double-free or null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: es1/es2 are checked for reuse (es_len) after __es_insert_extent may have merged and freed them. Trigger: an extent insertion path where the preallocated extent gets merged into an adjacent extent, freeing it. Consequence: a slab-use-after-free read of es_len, potentially leading to corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
xbm: avoid stack overflow (read) with large names #211

We use the name passed in to printf into a local stack buffer which is
limited to 4000 bytes.  So given a large enough value, lots of stack
data is leaked.  Rewrite the code to do simple memory copies with most
of the strings to avoid that issue, and only use stack buffer for small
numbers of constant size.

This closes #211.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar buf[4096];'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar buf[1024];']}
description: gd_xbm.c in the GD Graphics Library (aka libgd) before 2.2.0, as used in certain custom PHP 5.5.x configurations, allows context-dependent attackers to obtain sensitive information from process memory or cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer under-read and application crash) via a long name.

code_evidence: A 4096-byte stack buffer 'buf' is declared at line 3. Line 7 calls vsnprintf with size sizeof(buf)-1, which bounds the write but returns the length the formatted output would have had if unbounded; that return value is stored in 'len'. Line 9 then passes 'len' to out->putBuf together with 'buf', so putBuf reads 'len' bytes from a buffer that actually holds at most 4095 bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The out-of-bounds read of the stack buffer is an operation outside the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. It is an under-read of the fixed-size buffer rather than a write overflow, but still a bounds violation on a memory buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the vsnprintf return value (untruncated length) is used as the read length instead of the actual bytes written. Trigger: a long name passed through the format produces len > sizeof(buf)-1. Consequence: putBuf reads past the end of 'buf', leaking stack memory or crashing.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In version 2.11.1 and prior, there are various cases where it is possible that certain incoming RTP/RTCP packets can potentially cause out-of-bound read access. This issue affects all users that use PJMEDIA and accept incoming RTP/RTCP. A patch is available as a commit in the `master` branch. There are no known workarounds.

code_evidence: Line 6 only asserts that the buffer pointer is non-null; line 7 uses PJ_ASSERT_RETURN to check length >= 12, but this assertion is compiled out in release builds, so no runtime length validation remains before the header is dereferenced.
Line 8 reads hdr->pt and hdr->count from the buffer without any validated minimum length, so a short packet causes an out-of-bounds read of the RTCP common header fields.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-125: the function dereferences a fixed-size header from an input buffer whose length is not enforced at runtime, reading before/within an undersized buffer. It is not merely an input-validation issue because the direct consequence is an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
PJ_ASSERT_RETURN(buf, PJ_EINVAL);
PJ_ASSERT_RETURN(length >= 12, PJ_ETOOSMALL);

if (hdr->pt != RTCP_PSFB || hdr->count != 1)
return PJ_ENOTFOUND;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the minimum-length check is a debug-only assertion (PJ_ASSERT_RETURN) rather than an unconditional runtime guard. Trigger: an incoming RTP/RTCP packet shorter than the 12-byte common header reaches this parser in a release build. Consequence: hdr->pt and hdr->count are read past the end of the supplied buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read (crash or memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.1848: [security] buffer-overflow in vim_regsub_both()

Problem:  buffer-overflow in vim_regsub_both()
Solution: Check remaining space

Signed-off-by: Christian Brabandt <cb@256bit.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    if (eval_result[nested] != NULL)'], 'added_lines': ['\t    if (eval_result[nested] != NULL &&', '\t\t    STRLEN(eval_result[nested]) < destlen)']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.1848.

code_evidence: When copy is set, eval_result[nested] (from expression evaluation) is copied into dest via STRCPY without any destlen bound check; the check on line 44 only tests for NULL, and dst is advanced by the string length. The patched guard adds STRLEN(eval_result[nested]) < destlen before copying.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked STRCPY writes data past the end of the intended dest buffer, which is precisely an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The missing length constraint is the cause; the overflow is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the evaluated substitution string is written to the destination buffer with STRCPY while only a NULL check gates it, with no check that its length fits within destlen. Trigger: a substitute expression returning a string longer than the destination buffer. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds write past dest, corrupting adjacent memory.

Added a bunch of `assert(b)`'s to address CVE-2018-17073
See https://github.com/wernsey/bitmap/issues/1
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tassert(b);']}
description: wernsey/bitmap before 2018-08-18 allows a NULL pointer dereference via a 4-bit image.

code_evidence: bm_rect accepts a Bitmap *b parameter and immediately passes it to bm_line at lines 2-5 without any NULL check or validation in the function body. The patch adds assert(b) at the top, confirming the developer recognized b may be NULL at entry and that downstream bm_line calls would dereference it.

It is not a buffer overflow or use-after-free; the defect is purely the missing NULL constraint before pointer use.

Trigger: a caller passes a NULL Bitmap (e.g., from a failed 4-bit image allocation/load). Consequence: bm_line dereferences the NULL pointer, causing a crash (DoS); the added assert converts this into an explicit abort in debug builds rather than a fix of the dereference path.

description: Botan 2.5.0 through 2.6.0 before 2.7.0 allows a memory-cache side-channel attack on ECDSA signatures, aka the Return Of the Hidden Number Problem or ROHNP, related to dsa/dsa.cpp, ec_group/ec_group.cpp, and ecdsa/ecdsa.cpp. To discover an ECDSA key, the attacker needs access to either the local machine or a different virtual machine on the same physical host.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function is ECDSA signature verification that only compares public signature values; the side-channel key-recovery weakness (ROHNP) resides in signing/scalar-multiplication and modular-reduction timing, not in this verification path, and the diff merely adds mod_order normalization with no sensitive-data exposure in this code.

commit_msg: GSSAPI server: Boundary check gss_wrap token (read OOB).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      if (bufdesc2.length < 4)', '\treturn GSASL_AUTHENTICATION_ERROR;', '']}
description: GNU SASL libgsasl server-side read-out-of-bounds with malicious authenticated GSS-API client

code_evidence: gss_unwrap fills bufdesc2 from attacker-supplied input; on success the code immediately dereferences bufdesc2.value[0] without checking bufdesc2.length.
Later, bufdesc2.value + 4 and bufdesc2.length - 4 are used to set the authzid, again assuming at least 4 bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads bufdesc2.value beyond its actual length due to a missing length check, not because of an arithmetic write or type confusion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unwrapped token length is never validated against the assumed 4-byte header before indexing. Trigger: an authenticated GSS-API client sends a wrapped token yielding a buffer shorter than 4 bytes (or zero length), so reading index 0 or offset 4 goes past the buffer; length-4 underflows. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of heap memory, potentially leaking data or crashing the server.

commit_msg:
evtchn/x86: enforce correct upper limit for 32-bit guests

The recording of d->max_evtchns in evtchn_2l_init(), in particular with
the limited set of callers of the function, is insufficient. Neither for
PV nor for HVM guests the bitness is known at domain_create() time, yet
the upper bound in 2-level mode depends upon guest bitness. Recording
too high a limit "allows" x86 32-bit domains to open not properly usable
event channels, management of which (inside Xen) would then result in
corruption of the shared info and vCPU info structures.

Keep the upper limit dynamic for the 2-level case, introducing a helper
function to retrieve the effective limit. This helper is now supposed to
be private to the event channel code. The used in do_poll() and
domain_dump_evtchn_info() weren't consistent with port uses elsewhere
and hence get switched to port_is_valid().

Furthermore FIFO mode's setup_ports() gets adjusted to loop only up to
the prior ABI limit, rather than all the way up to the new one.

Finally a word on the change to do_poll(): Accessing ->max_evtchns
without holding a suitable lock was never safe, as it as well as
->evtchn_port_ops may change behind do_poll()'s back. Using
port_is_valid() instead widens some the window for potential abuse,
until we've dealt with the race altogether (see XSA-343).

This is XSA-342.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Fixes: 48974e6ce52e ("evtchn: use a per-domain variable for the max number of event channels")
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    d->max_evtchns = BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d) * BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. Out of bounds event channels are available to 32-bit x86 domains. The so called 2-level event channel model imposes different limits on the number of usable event channels for 32-bit x86 domains vs 64-bit or Arm (either bitness) ones. 32-bit x86 domains can use only 1023 channels, due to limited space in their shared (between guest and Xen) information structure, whereas all other domains can use up to 4095 in this model. The recording of the respective limit during domain initialization, however, has occurred at a time where domains are still deemed to be 64-bit ones, prior to actually honoring respective domain properties. At the point domains get recognized as 32-bit ones, the limit didn't get updated accordingly. Due to this misbehavior in Xen, 32-bit domains (including Domain 0) servicing other domains may observe event channel allocations to succeed when they should really fail. Subsequent use of such event channels would then possibly lead to corruption of other parts of the shared info structure. An unprivileged guest may cause another domain, in particular Domain 0, to misbehave. This may lead to a Denial of Service (DoS) for the entire system. All Xen versions from 4.4 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.3 and earlier are not vulnerable. Only x86 32-bit domains servicing other domains are vulnerable. Arm systems, as well as x86 64-bit domains, are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: evtchn_2l_init() assigns d->max_evtchns as BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d) * BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d) unconditionally, so the limit is fixed at initialization time when the domain is still treated as 64-bit; it is never narrowed for 32-bit guests, permitting event-channel ports beyond the 1023-channel shared-info capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fixed over-large limit allows event-channel bookkeeping to write beyond the bounded shared-info buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The defect is an incorrect bound rather than a pure logic error, and the supported consequence is memory corruption from writing past the intended structure.

evidence_lines.code:
d->evtchn_port_ops = &evtchn_port_ops_2l;
d->max_evtchns = BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d) * BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the 2-level event-channel upper bound is recorded once in evtchn_2l_init() using the bitness assumed at domain creation, without accounting for later recognition of a 32-bit x86 guest. Trigger: a 32-bit domain servicing other domains allocates event channels above the shared-info limit. Consequence: subsequent management writes past the shared-info/vCPU-info structures, corrupting memory and causing DoS.

commit_msg:
usbip_host updates device status without holding lock from stub probe,
disconnect and rebind code paths. When multiple requests to import a
device are received, these unprotected code paths step all over each
other and drive fails with NULL-ptr deref and use-after-free errors.

The driver uses a table lock to protect the busid array for adding and
deleting busids to the table. However, the probe, disconnect and rebind
paths get the busid table entry and update the status without holding
the busid table lock. Add a new finer grain lock to protect the busid
entry. This new lock will be held to search and update the busid entry
fields from get_busid_idx(), add_match_busid() and del_match_busid().

match_busid_show() does the same to access the busid entry fields.

get_busid_priv() changed to return the pointer to the busid entry holding
the busid lock. stub_probe(), stub_disconnect() and stub_device_rebind()
call put_busid_priv() to release the busid lock before returning. This
changes fixes the unprotected code paths eliminating the race conditions
in updating the busid entries.

Reported-by: Jakub Jirasek
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan (Samsung OSG) <shuah@kernel.org>
Cc: stable <stable@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tint i;', '', '', '\tfor (i = 0; i < MAX_BUSID; i++)', '\t\tspin_lock_init(&busid_table[i].busid_lock);']}
description: In the Linux Kernel before version 4.16.11, 4.14.43, 4.9.102, and 4.4.133, multiple race condition errors when handling probe, disconnect, and rebind operations can be exploited to trigger a use-after-free condition or a NULL pointer dereference by sending multiple USB over IP packets.

code_evidence: init_busid_table() zeroes the shared busid_table and initializes only the table-wide busid_table_lock; the per-entry busid_lock fields are not initialized here in the before state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function establishes shared state whose concurrent access requires exclusive access, yet the before code provides only the coarse table lock and no per-entry lock, leaving a synchronization gap. This is a race-condition setup issue rather than a memory-safety weakness like CWE-416, which would describe the downstream consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
memset(busid_table, 0, sizeof(busid_table));
spin_lock_init(&busid_table_lock);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The shared busid table and its entries are set up without per-entry lock initialization, so later probe/disconnect/rebind paths that access entry status lack a dedicated synchronization primitive. Concurrent access to the same busid entry can interleave, producing NULL-pointer dereference or use-after-free consequences. The root cause is missing/improper synchronization setup for the shared resource, not the memset itself.

commit_msg: fixed invalid memory reads detected by the address sanitizer
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            memcpy(cp, qp->d_memory, memory_length);/* cp existing buffer   */'], 'added_lines': ['        size_t original_length = memory_length;', '', '', '            memcpy(cp, qp->d_memory, original_length);/* cp existing buffer   */']}
description: Yodl before 3.07.01 has a Buffer Over-read in the queue_push function in queue/queuepush.c.

code_evidence: Line 11 records the original allocation size as d_memory_end - d_memory, but line 22 then enlarges memory_length by extra_length - available_length + BLOCK_QUEUE before line 23 allocates the new, larger buffer cp.

In the else branch (d_read <= d_write), line 37 copies memory_length bytes from the old qp->d_memory into cp, although the old buffer is only original_length bytes; the copy over-reads the source past its allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a memcpy that reads beyond the intended boundary of the source buffer, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within memory buffer bounds. It is a read-side over-read rather than a write overflow, but still an out-of-bounds memory operation covered by this class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy length in the else branch uses the newly enlarged memory_length instead of the original buffer size. Trigger: queue_push is called with extra_length exceeding available_length, forcing reallocation, when d_read <= d_write. Consequence: memcpy reads past the end of the old d_memory allocation, an out-of-bounds read (buffer over-read) detectable by AddressSanitizer.

commit_msg: Fix buffer overflow in parseUrlAddrFromRtspUrlString (CVE-2023-42799)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static bool parseUrlAddrFromRtspUrlString(const char* rtspUrlString, char* destination) {', '    strcpy(destination, rtspUrlScratchBuffer + prefixLen);'], 'added_lines': ['static bool parseUrlAddrFromRtspUrlString(const char* rtspUrlString, char* destination, size_t destinationLength) {', '    PltSafeStrcpy(destination, destinationLength, rtspUrlScratchBuffer + prefixLen);', "    destination[destinationLength - 1] = '\\0';"]}
description: Moonlight-common-c contains the core GameStream client code shared between Moonlight clients. Moonlight-common-c is vulnerable to buffer overflow starting in commit 50c0a51b10ecc5b3415ea78c21d96d679e2288f9 due to unmitigated usage of unsafe C functions and improper bounds checking. A malicious game streaming server could exploit a buffer overflow vulnerability to crash a moonlight client, or achieve remote code execution (RCE) on the client (with insufficient exploit mitigations or if mitigations can be bypassed). The bug was addressed in commit 02b7742f4d19631024bd766bd2bb76715780004e.

code_evidence: Line 7 duplicates the caller-supplied RTSP URL into a heap scratch buffer; lines 11-27 locate and truncate the string at the port, IPv6 bracket, or path separator, but never bound the remaining substring length. Line 28 then calls strcpy to copy rtspUrlScratchBuffer + prefixLen into the caller's destination with no knowledge of destination's capacity, so a long attacker-controlled host/address portion overflows the fixed-size output buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the function performs a buffer copy operation (strcpy) without checking that the input length is less than the output buffer size, writing past the destination. This is a classic buffer copy overflow, not an out-of-bounds read or an integer size-calculation error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unchecked strcpy into a destination of unknown size. Trigger: a malicious game-streaming server returns an RTSP URL whose address component after the prefix exceeds the destination buffer. Consequence: memory corruption past the destination, enabling a client crash or, absent mitigations, remote code execution.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/617
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      if ((image != image2) && (image2 != (Image *) NULL))', '        image2=DestroyImage(image2);']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.0.6-3, a memory leak vulnerability was found in the function ReadMATImage in coders/mat.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service.

code_evidence: The MATLAB_KO label is reached from several error paths, including when ReadMATImageV4 returns NULL (lines 46-48). At the label only clone_info is destroyed before ThrowReaderException; image2 (assigned from ReadMATImageV4 at line 46) is not released, so the V4 image list allocated by the callee leaks on this error exit.
The patch adds the missing image2 release at the MATLAB_KO label, confirming the leak on this path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits: a resource (image2) is not released after its effective lifetime ends on the error path, producing a memory leak and resource-consumption DoS. It is not CWE-476 (NULL dereference) since the defect is the omitted release, not a bad pointer use.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error-handling label MATLAB_KO frees clone_info but not image2, even though image2 may hold an image returned by ReadMATImageV4. Trigger: a malformed/non-MATLAB header where ReadMATImageV4 returns NULL, causing goto MATLAB_KO. Consequence: the image2 resource is never released, leaking memory and enabling denial of service via repeated reads.

commit_msg:
KVM: x86: Introduce segmented_write_std

Introduces segemented_write_std.

Switches from emulated reads/writes to standard read/writes in fxsave,
fxrstor, sgdt, and sidt.  This fixes CVE-2017-2584, a longstanding
kernel memory leak.

Since commit 283c95d0e389 ("KVM: x86: emulate FXSAVE and FXRSTOR",
2016-11-09), which is luckily not yet in any final release, this would
also be an exploitable kernel memory *write*!

description: arch/x86/kvm/emulate.c in the Linux kernel through 4.9.3 allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) via a crafted application that leverages instruction emulation for fxrstor, fxsave, sgdt, and sidt.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs a bounded segmented read into a stack buffer and fxrstor; nothing in it frees or reuses freed memory, so CWE-416 use-after-free is not supported.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: make sure e->next_offset covers remaining blob size

Otherwise this function may read data beyond the ruleset blob.

Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    (unsigned char *)e + sizeof(struct arpt_entry) >= limit) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t    (unsigned char *)e + sizeof(struct arpt_entry) >= limit ||', '\t    (unsigned char *)e + e->next_offset > limit) {']}
description: The IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt implementation in the netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) or possibly obtain sensitive information from kernel heap memory by leveraging in-container root access to provide a crafted offset value that leads to crossing a ruleset blob boundary.

code_evidence: Lines 11-12 validate only that the entry header fits before limit; they do not verify that e->next_offset, the attacker-controlled size field, keeps the whole entry within the ruleset blob.
Lines 16-17 only enforce a minimum next_offset; no upper bound ties e + next_offset to limit, so iteration/parsing can advance past the blob.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing upper-bound check on e->next_offset allows operations beyond the intended memory buffer, which is CWE-119's out-of-bounds access class. The more specific out-of-bounds read is a child weakness, but the function directly supports the target class.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((unsigned long)e % __alignof__(struct arpt_entry) != 0 ||
(unsigned char *)e + sizeof(struct arpt_entry) >= limit) {

if (e->next_offset
< sizeof(struct arpt_entry) + sizeof(struct xt_entry_target)) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check ignores e->next_offset, so an entry whose size field exceeds the remaining blob passes validation. Trigger: a crafted IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE ruleset supplies an oversized next_offset. Consequence: subsequent processing reads memory beyond the ruleset blob, causing out-of-bounds read/DoS and possible kernel heap information disclosure.

commit_msg:
x86/fpu: Don't let userspace set bogus xcomp_bv

On x86, userspace can use the ptrace() or rt_sigreturn() system calls to
set a task's extended state (xstate) or "FPU" registers.  ptrace() can
set them for another task using the PTRACE_SETREGSET request with
NT_X86_XSTATE, while rt_sigreturn() can set them for the current task.
In either case, registers can be set to any value, but the kernel
assumes that the XSAVE area itself remains valid in the sense that the
CPU can restore it.

However, in the case where the kernel is using the uncompacted xstate
format (which it does whenever the XSAVES instruction is unavailable),
it was possible for userspace to set the xcomp_bv field in the
xstate_header to an arbitrary value.  However, all bits in that field
are reserved in the uncompacted case, so when switching to a task with
nonzero xcomp_bv, the XRSTOR instruction failed with a #GP fault.  This
caused the WARN_ON_FPU(err) in copy_kernel_to_xregs() to be hit.  In
addition, since the error is otherwise ignored, the FPU registers from
the task previously executing on the CPU were leaked.

Fix the bug by checking that the user-supplied value of xcomp_bv is 0 in
the uncompacted case, and returning an error otherwise.

The reason for validating xcomp_bv rather than simply overwriting it
with 0 is that we want userspace to see an error if it (incorrectly)
provides an XSAVE area in compacted format rather than in uncompacted
format.

Note that as before, in case of error we clear the task's FPU state.
This is perhaps non-ideal, especially for PTRACE_SETREGSET; it might be
better to return an error before changing anything.  But it seems the
"clear on error" behavior is fine for now, and it's a little tricky to
do otherwise because it would mean we couldn't simply copy the full
userspace state into kernel memory in one __copy_from_user().

This bug was found by syzkaller, which hit the above-mentioned
WARN_ON_FPU():

    WARNING: CPU: 1 PID: 0 at ./arch/x86/include/asm/fpu/internal.h:373 __switch_to+0x5b5/0x5d0
    CPU: 1 PID: 0 Comm: swapper/1 Not tainted 4.13.0 #453
    Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (i440FX + PIIX, 1996), BIOS Bochs 01/01/2011
    task: ffff9ba2bc8e42c0 task.stack: ffffa78cc036c000
    RIP: 0010:__switch_to+0x5b5/0x5d0
    RSP: 0000:ffffa78cc08bbb88 EFLAGS: 00010082
    RAX: 00000000fffffffe RBX: ffff9ba2b8bf2180 RCX: 00000000c0000100
    RDX: 00000000ffffffff RSI: 000000005cb10700 RDI: ffff9ba2b8bf36c0
    RBP: ffffa78cc08bbbd0 R08: 00000000929fdf46 R09: 0000000000000001
    R10: 0000000000000000 R11: 0000000000000000 R12: ffff9ba2bc8e42c0
    R13: 0000000000000000 R14: ffff9ba2b8bf3680 R15: ffff9ba2bf5d7b40
    FS:  00007f7e5cb10700(0000) GS:ffff9ba2bf400000(0000) knlGS:0000000000000000
    CS:  0010 DS: 0000 ES: 0000 CR0: 0000000080050033
    CR2: 00000000004005cc CR3: 0000000079fd5000 CR4: 00000000001406e0
    Call Trace:
    Code: 84 00 00 00 00 00 e9 11 fd ff ff 0f ff 66 0f 1f 84 00 00 00 00 00 e9 e7 fa ff ff 0f ff 66 0f 1f 84 00 00 00 00 00 e9 c2 fa ff ff <0f> ff 66 0f 1f 84 00 00 00 00 00 e9 d4 fc ff ff 66 66 2e 0f 1f

Here is a C reproducer.  The expected behavior is that the program spin
forever with no output.  However, on a buggy kernel running on a
processor with the "xsave" feature but without the "xsaves" feature
(e.g. Sandy Bridge through Broadwell for Intel), within a second or two
the program reports that the xmm registers were corrupted, i.e. were not
restored correctly.  With CONFIG_X86_DEBUG_FPU=y it also hits the above
kernel warning.

    #define _GNU_SOURCE
    #include <stdbool.h>
    #include <inttypes.h>
    #include <linux/elf.h>
    #include <stdio.h>
    #include <sys/ptrace.h>
    #include <sys/uio.h>
    #include <sys/wait.h>
    #include <unistd.h>

    int main(void)
    {
        int pid = fork();
        uint64_t xstate[512];
        struct iovec iov = { .iov_base = xstate, .iov_len = sizeof(xstate) };

        if (pid == 0) {
            bool tracee = true;
            for (int i = 0; i < sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN) && tracee; i++)
                tracee = (fork() != 0);
            uint32_t xmm0[4] = { [0 ... 3] = tracee ? 0x00000000 : 0xDEADBEEF };
            asm volatile("   movdqu %0, %%xmm0\n"
                         "   mov %0, %%rbx\n"
                         "1: movdqu %%xmm0, %0\n"
                         "   mov %0, %%rax\n"
                         "   cmp %%rax, %%rbx\n"
                         "   je 1b\n"
                         : "+m" (xmm0) : : "rax", "rbx", "xmm0");
            printf("BUG: xmm registers corrupted!  tracee=%d, xmm0=%08X%08X%08X%08X\n",
                   tracee, xmm0[0], xmm0[1], xmm0[2], xmm0[3]);
        } else {
            usleep(100000);
            ptrace(PTRACE_ATTACH, pid, 0, 0);
            wait(NULL);
            ptrace(PTRACE_GETREGSET, pid, NT_X86_XSTATE, &iov);
            xstate[65] = -1;
            ptrace(PTRACE_SETREGSET, pid, NT_X86_XSTATE, &iov);
            ptrace(PTRACE_CONT, pid, 0, 0);
            wait(NULL);
        }
        return 1;
    }

Note: the program only tests for the bug using the ptrace() system call.
The bug can also be reproduced using the rt_sigreturn() system call, but
only when called from a 32-bit program, since for 64-bit programs the
kernel restores the FPU state from the signal frame by doing XRSTOR
directly from userspace memory (with proper error checking).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (using_compacted_format())', '\t\telse'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (using_compacted_format()) {', '\t\t} else {', '', '\t\t\t/* xcomp_bv must be 0 when using uncompacted format */', '\t\t\tif (!err && state_size > offsetof(struct xregs_state, header) && fpu->state.xsave.header.xcomp_bv)', '\t\t\t\terr = -EINVAL;', '\t\t}']}
description: The x86/fpu (Floating Point Unit) subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.5, when a processor supports the xsave feature but not the xsaves feature, does not correctly handle attempts to set reserved bits in the xstate header via the ptrace() or rt_sigreturn() system call, allowing local users to read the FPU registers of other processes on the system, related to arch/x86/kernel/fpu/regset.c and arch/x86/kernel/fpu/signal.c.

code_evidence: In the ia32_fxstate path, when using_compacted_format() is false the code copies state_size bytes from userspace buf_fx directly into fpu->state.xsave with __copy_from_user, with no check that the user-supplied xcomp_bv header field is zero. The subsequent error handling at [42,43] only runs after this copy, and the added validation in the patched version is absent here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unvalidated xcomp_bv causes a failure path that leaks another task's FPU register state to an unprivileged actor, i.e., exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor, matching CWE-200. The underlying validation gap is the cause; the confidentiality loss is the supported impact.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the uncompacted-format branch accepts an arbitrary user-controlled xcomp_bv value from the XSAVE area without validating it is zero. Trigger: a local user sets reserved xcomp_bv bits via ptrace(NT_X86_XSTATE) or rt_sigreturn for a 32-bit task on hardware with xsave but not xsaves. Consequence: XRSTOR faults on task switch and the FPU registers of the previously running task are leaked, exposing other processes' register contents.

commit_msg:
Fix packet length handling.

Treat the packet length as unsigned - it shouldn't be negative in the
file.  If it is, that'll probably cause the sscanf to fail, so we'll
report the file as bad.

Check it against WTAP_MAX_PACKET_SIZE to make sure we don't try to
allocate a huge amount of memory, just as we do in other file readers.

Use the now-validated packet size as the length in
ws_buffer_assure_space(), so we are certain to have enough space, and
don't allocate too much space.

Bug: 12394
Change-Id: Ifa023ce70f7a2697bf151009b035a6e6cf8d5d90
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/15169
Reviewed-by: Guy Harris <guy@alum.mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint\tpkt_len, pktnum, hr, min, sec, csec;', '\tnum_items_scanned = sscanf(line+64, "LEN=%9d", &pkt_len);', '\tws_buffer_assure_space(buf, TOSHIBA_MAX_PACKET_LEN);'], 'added_lines': ['\tguint\tpkt_len;', '\tint\tpktnum, hr, min, sec, csec;', '\tnum_items_scanned = sscanf(line+64, "LEN=%9u", &pkt_len);', '\t\treturn FALSE;', '\t}', '\tif (pkt_len > WTAP_MAX_PACKET_SIZE) {', '\t\t/*', "\t\t * Probably a corrupt capture file; don't blow up trying", '\t\t * to allocate space for an immensely-large packet.', '\t\t */', '\t\t*err = WTAP_ERR_BAD_FILE;', '\t\t*err_info = g_strdup_printf("toshiba: File has %u-byte packet, bigger than maximum of %u",', '\t\t    pkt_len, WTAP_MAX_PACKET_SIZE);', '\tws_buffer_assure_space(buf, pkt_len);']}
description: wiretap/toshiba.c in the Toshiba file parser in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.12 and 2.x before 2.0.4 mishandles sscanf unsigned-integer processing, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: pkt_len is declared as a signed int, so a negative LEN value from the file is accepted as a negative packet length.
The LEN= field parsed at line+64 is stored into pkt_len via sscanf with %9d; the only check is that one item was scanned, not that the value is non-negative or within bounds.
The unvalidated pkt_len is copied directly into phdr->caplen and phdr->len, propagating the attacker-controlled length.

ws_buffer_assure_space is called with the fixed TOSHIBA_MAX_PACKET_LEN rather than the validated packet size, and hex_lines is derived from pkt_len, so an oversized or negative length is not constrained before use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts file metadata (packet length) without validating it against required properties (non-negative, bounded by WTAP_MAX_PACKET_SIZE), which is improper input validation of a specified quantity. The missing constraint directly enables the crash, matching CWE-20 rather than a lower-level transform/encoding issue.

evidence_lines.code: intpkt_len, pktnum, hr, min, sec, csec;

phdr->caplen = pkt_len;
phdr->len = pkt_len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the file-supplied LEN value is parsed into a signed int and only checked for sscanf success, not for non-negativity or an upper bound. A crafted Toshiba file with a negative or huge LEN yields an invalid packet length that is stored in the header and drives the hex-dump line count, leading to a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: Line 3 initializes the flow-hash secret via __flow_hash_secret_init(), but line 4 passes the global 32-bit hashrnd value directly into __flow_hash_from_keys as the key for hashing flow fields known to receivers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because a security-relevant value (the flowlabel cookie) depends on an insufficiently random, long-lived 32-bit secret that can be recovered. This is a predictability/insufficient-randomness weakness rather than a hash-collision or disclosure flaw per se.

evidence_lines.code:
__flow_hash_secret_init();
return __flow_hash_from_keys(keys, hashrnd);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the flow hash used for IPv6 auto flowlabels is keyed by a single boot-time 32-bit hashrnd value processed with jhash, a non-cryptographic function. Because the hashed input fields are observable on the wire, an attacker can infer the secret and derive stable per-device/per-user identifiers. The supported consequence is privacy loss via device tracking, not memory corruption.

commit_msg:
write_wakeup can happen in parallel with close/hangup where tty->disc_data
is set to NULL and the netdevice is freed thus also freeing
disc_data. write_wakeup accesses disc_data so we must prevent close from
freeing the netdev while write_wakeup has a non-NULL view of
tty->disc_data.

We also need to make sure that accesses to disc_data are atomic. Which can
all be done with RCU.

This problem was found by Syzkaller on SLCAN, but the same issue is
reproducible with the SLIP line discipline using an LTP test based on the
Syzkaller reproducer.

A fix which didn't use RCU was posted by Hillf Danton.

Fixes: 661f7fda21b1 ("slip: Fix deadlock in write_wakeup")
Fixes: a8e83b17536a ("slcan: Port write_wakeup deadlock fix from slip")

description: In the Linux kernel before 5.4.16, a race condition in tty->disc_data handling in the slip and slcan line discipline could lead to a use-after-free, aka CID-0ace17d56824. This affects drivers/net/slip/slip.c and drivers/net/can/slcan.c.

code_evidence: slcan_close reads tty->disc_data into sl and validates it, then clears tty->disc_data under sl->lock and later flushes work and unregisters the netdev. The clearing is a plain store, and the subsequent flush_work/unregister_netdev occur after the lock is released, so a concurrent write_wakeup that observed the old non-NULL disc_data can still access the freed netdev.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unsynchronized shared-state access (disc_data) with a concurrent reader is a race condition (CWE-362); the UAF is the downstream consequence, not the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the store to tty->disc_data and the teardown of sl->dev are not synchronized with concurrent readers of disc_data. Trigger: write_wakeup runs in parallel with close, reads a non-NULL disc_data, while close sets it to NULL and proceeds to free the netdev. Consequence: use-after-free of the netdevice/disc_data.

commit_msg:
x86/vpt: fix race when migrating timers between vCPUs

The current vPT code will migrate the emulated timers between vCPUs
(change the pt->vcpu field) while just holding the destination lock,
either from create_periodic_time or pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target if
the global target is adjusted. Changing the periodic_timer vCPU field
in this way creates a race where a third party could grab the lock in
the unlocked region of pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target (or before
create_periodic_time performs the vcpu change) and then release the
lock from a different vCPU, creating a locking imbalance.

Introduce a per-domain rwlock in order to protect periodic_time
migration between vCPU lists. Taking the lock in read mode prevents
any timer from being migrated to a different vCPU, while taking it in
write mode allows performing migration of timers across vCPUs. The
per-vcpu locks are still used to protect all the other fields from the
periodic_timer struct.

Note that such migration shouldn't happen frequently, and hence
there's no performance drop as a result of such locking.

This is XSA-336.

Reported-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Tested-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int on_list;', '', '    pt_lock(pt);', '    on_list = pt->on_list;', '    pt->on_list = 0;', '    pt_unlock(pt);', '', '    spin_lock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock);', '    pt->vcpu = v;', '    if ( on_list )', '    {', '        pt->on_list = 1;', '', '    spin_unlock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    write_lock(&pt->vcpu->domain->arch.hvm.pl_time->pt_migrate);', '    pt->vcpu = v;', '    {', '    write_unlock(&pt->vcpu->domain->arch.hvm.pl_time->pt_migrate);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There is a race condition when migrating timers between x86 HVM vCPUs. When migrating timers of x86 HVM guests between its vCPUs, the locking model used allows for a second vCPU of the same guest (also operating on the timers) to release a lock that it didn't acquire. The most likely effect of the issue is a hang or crash of the hypervisor, i.e., a Denial of Service (DoS). All versions of Xen are affected. Only x86 systems are vulnerable. Arm systems are not vulnerable. Only x86 HVM guests can leverage the vulnerability. x86 PV and PVH cannot leverage the vulnerability. Only guests with more than one vCPU can exploit the vulnerability.

code_evidence: The function reads pt->on_list and removes the timer from its list while holding only pt_lock(pt), then releases that lock at line 12.

After releasing pt_lock, the code acquires the destination vCPU's tm_lock, assigns pt->vcpu = v, and re-adds the timer to v's list; during this unlocked gap another vCPU operating on the same periodic_time can observe or modify pt->on_list/pt->vcpu, and the lock protecting the list is not the same object throughout the migration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code sequence requires exclusive access to the shared periodic_timer and its list membership, but a timing window exists between pt_unlock and spin_lock where an interfering code sequence can access the same resource, matching CWE-362's improper synchronization/race condition.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: timer migration between vCPUs is not performed under a single lock covering the pt->vcpu change and list operations; pt_lock is dropped between list_del and the destination-list insertion. Trigger: concurrent access by another vCPU of the same guest during the unlocked window. Consequence: locking imbalance where a vCPU releases a lock it did not acquire, leading to hypervisor hang or crash (DoS).
