description: An issue was discovered in libsndfile 1.0.28. There is a buffer over-read in the function i2ulaw_array in ulaw.c that will lead to a denial of service.

code_evidence: The loop indexes ptr[count] and buffer[count] using count derived from the caller's count. For a NaN input, both comparisons (ptr[count] >= 0 at line 4 and the else branch at line 7) take the else path, and lrint(normfact * NaN) produces an unspecified/undefined integer that is then used to index alaw_encode, causing an out-of-bounds read of the table. The patch adds an isfinite check to guard non-finite inputs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the computed index from lrint(NaN) is not bounded to the alaw_encode table size, so the function reads memory beyond the intended buffer. This is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write, since only the encode table is indexed and the result is stored in buffer[count] within bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function feeds lrint() of an unvalidated double (including NaN) directly into an array index without checking finiteness. Trigger: a caller supplies a NaN buffer element. Consequence: lrint returns an undefined value used to index alaw_encode, reading outside the table (out-of-bounds read, potentially crash/DoS).

The reference implementation of the `GatherNd` TFLite operator is vulnerable to a division by zero error(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/0d45ea1ca641b21b73bcf9c00e0179cda284e7e7/tensorflow/lite/kernels/internal/reference/reference_ops.h#L966). An attacker can craft a model such that `params` input would be an empty tensor. In turn, `params_shape.Dims(.)` would be zero, in at least one dimension. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Eval obtains the params input via GetInputSafe (line 3) and passes it to EvalGatherNd for both int32 and int64 index types (lines 11,13) without checking that params is non-empty. The added guard that would enforce NumElements(params) > 0 is absent from this function, leaving the empty-tensor case unblocked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a divide-by-zero (CWE-369): a zero-sized dimension is used as a divisor in the helper reached from this function. It is not a bounds/overflow issue; the missing non-empty constraint on params directly enables the zero divisor.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function forwards a params tensor of any size to EvalGatherNd, whose reference implementation divides by a dimension of params_shape. Trigger: a crafted model supplies an empty params tensor, making a Dims() entry zero. Consequence: division by zero, causing a crash/DoS in TFLite.

commit_msg:
bpf: don't let ldimm64 leak map addresses on unprivileged

The patch fixes two things at once:

1) It checks the env->allow_ptr_leaks and only prints the map address to
   the log if we have the privileges to do so, otherwise it just dumps 0
   as we would when kptr_restrict is enabled on %pK. Given the latter is
   off by default and not every distro sets it, I don't want to rely on
   this, hence the 0 by default for unprivileged.

2) Printing of ldimm64 in the verifier log is currently broken in that
   we don't print the full immediate, but only the 32 bit part of the
   first insn part for ldimm64. Thus, fix this up as well; it's okay to
   access, since we verified all ldimm64 earlier already (including just
   constants) through replace_map_fd_with_map_ptr().

Fixes: 1be7f75d1668 ("bpf: enable non-root eBPF programs")
Fixes: cbd357008604 ("bpf: verifier (add ability to receive verification log)")
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tprint_bpf_insn(insn);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tprint_bpf_insn(env, insn);']}
description: The do_check function in kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel before 4.11.1 does not make the allow_ptr_leaks value available for restricting the output of the print_bpf_insn function, which allows local users to obtain sensitive address information via crafted bpf system calls.

code_evidence: When log_level is set, do_check unconditionally calls verbose then print_bpf_insn(insn). The call passes only the instruction, not env, so print_bpf_insn cannot consult env->allow_ptr_leaks. For an ldimm64 instruction carrying a map file descriptor, the verifier log therefore renders the map address even for an unprivileged program, where allow_ptr_leaks is false. The env pointer is in scope at line 49 but is not forwarded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly emits sensitive information (a kernel map address) into a log accessible to an unauthorized actor. CWE-200 fits because this is an explicit information-exposure behavior in a component that manages sensitive data, not merely a downstream confidentiality impact of a separate memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the verifier-log path lacks the privilege gate needed to suppress pointer values in the printed instruction. Trigger: an unprivileged user submits a BPF program containing a map-address ldimm64 and requests a verification log. Consequence: the kernel map address is written into the user-readable log, leaking sensitive kernel pointer information.

commit_msg:
Update atyfb_base.c

Structure atyclk is copied to userland with padding bytes after
"vclk_post_div" field unitialized.  It leads to leaking of
contents of kernel stack memory.  We have to initialize them to zero. or it will allows local users to obtain potentially sensitive information from kernel stack memory by reading a copy of this structure
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t', '\t\t\tmemset( &clk, 0, sizeof(struct atyclk) );', '\t\t\t']}
description: The atyfb_ioctl function in drivers/video/fbdev/aty/atyfb_base.c in the Linux kernel through 4.12.10 does not initialize a certain data structure, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel stack memory by reading locations associated with padding bytes.

code_evidence: A stack-allocated struct atyclk clk is declared at line 31 and only its named fields are assigned (lines 35-47); any padding bytes between fields remain uninitialized. The whole structure is then copied to userland via copy_to_user at lines 48-49 with sizeof(clk), so padding contents reach the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly transfers uninitialized stack padding to an unprivileged user, which is a direct exposure of sensitive kernel memory, matching CWE-200's scope of confidentiality loss via information disclosure. The weakness is the missing initialization before copy_to_user, not a generic impact statement.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the local atyclk clk is not zero-initialized, leaving inter-field padding bytes holding residual kernel stack data. Trigger: a local user issues the ATYIO_CLKR ioctl on an integrated M64 device; the function fills named fields and copies the full structure, including padding, to the user buffer. Consequence: kernel stack memory contents are exposed to the caller.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    child->contents.serialised.ordered_offsets_up_to = s_child.ordered_offsets_up_to;']}
description: A flaw was found in GLib. GVariant deserialization is vulnerable to an exponential blowup issue where a crafted GVariant can cause excessive processing, leading to denial of service.

Lines 24-30: only a depth/recursion check is applied for untrusted data; there is no check that child element offsets are monotonic, so overlapping child elements are accepted.
Lines 31-41: the child GVariant is constructed from s_child.size/data and the new ordered_offsets_up_to field is copied, but no validation of offset ordering is performed here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function deserialises untrusted GVariant bytes and fails to sufficiently validate the resulting structure (offset ordering), matching CWE-502's deserialization of untrusted data with availability impact. The depth check alone does not validate structural integrity; the missing offset validation is the deserialization constraint.

GVariantSerialised serialised = g_variant_to_serialised (value);
s_child = g_variant_serialised_get_child (serialised, index_);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: g_variant_get_child_value builds a child GVariant from untrusted serialised data without ensuring that child element frame offsets are ordered, so overlapping elements can be deserialised. commit_msg:
Fix heap OOB / undefined behavior in `RaggedTensorToTensor`

PiperOrigin-RevId: 373244623
Change-Id: I2d6cbbc8c67b238a8815bf58097f7586d87c54f2
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void CalculateOutputIndexRowSplit(', '      OpKernelContext* context, const RowPartitionTensor& row_split,', '    if (row_split_size > 0) {', '      OP_REQUIRES(context, result->size() == row_split(row_split_size - 1),', '                  errors::InvalidArgument("Invalid row split size."));'], 'added_lines': ['Status CalculateOutputIndexRowSplit(', '      const RowPartitionTensor& row_split,', '    if (row_split_size > 0 && result->size() != row_split(row_split_size - 1)) {', '      return errors::InvalidArgument("Invalid row split size.");', '', '    return Status::OK();']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. Due to lack of validation in `tf.raw_ops.RaggedTensorToTensor`, an attacker can exploit an undefined behavior if input arguments are empty. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/656e7673b14acd7835dc778867f84916c6d1cac2/tensorflow/core/kernels/ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op.cc#L356-L360) only checks that one of the tensors is not empty, but does not check for the other ones. There are multiple `DCHECK` validations to prevent heap OOB, but these are no-op in release builds, hence they don't prevent anything. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick these commits on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: result is reserved using row_split(row_split_size - 1) as the expected total length, so the allocated size derives from the last row-split boundary value.
The loop indexes parent_output_index[i] for each i up to row_split_size-2 without validating that parent_output_index has at least row_split_size-1 elements.
The post-loop check validates result->size() against the same row_split boundary, but it runs after the loop has already written to result.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The buffer size for result is derived from row_split(row_split_size - 1) without ensuring it matches the iteration count and parent_output_index length, i.e., an incorrect size calculation that permits out-of-bounds writes, matching CWE-131 rather than a pure missing-bounds-check variant.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The size of result is computed from row_split's last boundary while parent_output_index indexing assumes a matching length; when the tensors' sizes are inconsistent (e.g., empty parent_output_index with non-empty row_split), the loop reads out of bounds and push_back writes exceed the reserved size. The only consistency check occurs after the writes, so it cannot prevent the heap out-of-bounds access in release builds.

commit_msg:
powerpc/tm: Block signal return setting invalid MSR state

Currently we allow both the MSR T and S bits to be set by userspace on
a signal return.  Unfortunately this is a reserved configuration and
will cause a TM Bad Thing exception if attempted (via rfid).

This patch checks for this case in both the 32 and 64 bit signals
code.  If both T and S are set, we mark the context as invalid.

Found using a syscall fuzzer.

Fixes: 2b0a576d15e0 ("powerpc: Add new transactional memory state to the signal context")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v3.9+
Signed-off-by: Michael Neuling <mikey@neuling.org>
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ["\t/* Don't allow reserved mode. */", '\tif (MSR_TM_RESV(msr))', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '']}
description: The signal implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.3.5 on powerpc platforms does not check for an MSR with both the S and T bits set, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (TM Bad Thing exception and panic) via a crafted application.

code_evidence: Line 18 reads the user-supplied MSR from the signal frame (sc->gp_regs[PT_MSR]); lines 19-20 then merge its TS and LE bits into regs->msr without checking for the reserved S+T combination.
The unvalidated msr is later passed to tm_recheckpoint() at line 89, so the reserved state propagates into the checkpoint/restore path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of untrusted userspace input (the MSR field) before it is used to restore processor state, matching CWE-20's improper input validation class; the validation gap is the cause, while the panic is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signal-return handler trusts the MSR value from userspace and never rejects the reserved configuration where both the T (transactional) and S (suspended) bits are set. Trigger: a local process crafts a signal frame with both bits set and returns from the signal handler. Consequence: the reserved MSR is restored via rfid, raising a TM Bad Thing exception and panicking the kernel (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/shadow: account for log-dirty mode when pre-allocating

Pre-allocation is intended to ensure that in the course of constructing
or updating shadows there won't be any risk of just made shadows or
shadows being acted upon can disappear under our feet. The amount of
pages pre-allocated then, however, needs to account for all possible
subsequent allocations. While the use in sh_page_fault() accounts for
all shadows which may need making, so far it didn't account for
allocations coming from log-dirty tracking (which piggybacks onto the
P2M allocation functions).

Since shadow_prealloc() takes a count of shadows (or other data
structures) rather than a count of pages, putting the adjustment at the
call site of this function won't work very well: We simply can't express
the correct count that way in all cases. Instead take care of this in
the function itself, by "snooping" for L1 type requests. (While not
applicable right now, future new request sites of L1 tables would then
also be covered right away.)

It is relevant to note here that pre-allocations like the one done from
shadow_alloc_p2m_page() are benign when they fall in the "scope" of an
earlier pre-alloc which already included that count: The inner call will
simply find enough pages available then; it'll bail right away.

This is CVE-2022-42332 / XSA-427.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ret = _shadow_prealloc(d, shadow_size(type) * count);'], 'added_lines': ['    count *= shadow_size(type);', '    /*', '     * Log-dirty handling may result in allocations when populating its', '     * tracking structures.  Tie this to the caller requesting space for L1', '     * shadows.', '     */', '    if ( paging_mode_log_dirty(d) &&', '         ((SHF_L1_ANY | SHF_FL1_ANY) & (1u << type)) )', '        count += paging_logdirty_levels();', '', '    ret = _shadow_prealloc(d, count);']}
description: x86 shadow plus log-dirty mode use-after-free In environments where host assisted address translation is necessary but Hardware Assisted Paging (HAP) is unavailable, Xen will run guests in so called shadow mode. Shadow mode maintains a pool of memory used for both shadow page tables as well as auxiliary data structures. To migrate or snapshot guests, Xen additionally runs them in so called log-dirty mode. The data structures needed by the log-dirty tracking are part of aformentioned auxiliary data. In order to keep error handling efforts within reasonable bounds, for operations which may require memory allocations shadow mode logic ensures up front that enough memory is available for the worst case requirements. Unfortunately, while page table memory is properly accounted for on the code path requiring the potential establishing of new shadows, demands by the log-dirty infrastructure were not taken into consideration. As a result, just established shadow page tables could be freed again immediately, while other code is still accessing them on the assumption that they would remain allocated.

code_evidence: shadow_prealloc() calls _shadow_prealloc() with only shadow_size(type) * count, reserving pages for shadow tables but not for the log-dirty tracking allocations that piggyback on the P2M allocation path during L1 shadow construction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing log-dirty page accounting causes shadow tables to be freed and then referenced, which is exactly the reuse of freed memory described by CWE-416. It is not merely a denial-of-service allocation failure; the freed shadow pages remain in use by other code paths.

evidence_lines.code: ret = _shadow_prealloc(d, shadow_size(type) * count);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The pre-allocation undercounts the pages needed when log-dirty mode is active and L1 shadows are being built. Subsequent log-dirty allocations can consume the reserved pool, causing just-created shadow page tables to be freed while other code still holds references to them, yielding a use-after-free.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/560
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (image_info->depth > 100)', '      bits_per_pixel=image_info->depth-100;', '    if (bits_per_pixel < 16)', '      (void) TransformImageColorspace(image,image->colorspace);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (bits_per_pixel > 16)', '      bits_per_pixel=16;', '    else', '      if (bits_per_pixel < 16)', '        (void) TransformImageColorspace(image,image->colorspace);']}
description: When ImageMagick 7.0.6-1 processes a crafted file in convert, it can lead to a Floating Point Exception (FPE) in the WritePALMImage() function in coders/palm.c, related to an incorrect bits-per-pixel calculation.

code_evidence: Line 70 derives bits_per_pixel from count, but lines 71-72 overwrite it with image_info->depth-100 whenever depth>100, an externally supplied value with no upper bound or validation.
Lines 89-90 compute bytes_per_row as (columns+(16/bits_per_pixel-1))/(16/bits_per_pixel)*2, so an attacker-chosen bits_per_pixel directly controls these divisions.
Lines 205,211-212,215 and 223 use bits_per_pixel in shifts and in 8/bits_per_pixel division, so a value of 0 or >8 breaks the calculation and can yield division-by-zero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an incorrect security-relevant calculation: an externally controlled depth is used without bounds checking to compute bits_per_pixel and derived row/bit arithmetic, producing a divide-by-zero. This matches CWE-682's incorrect calculation used in resource management; the crash is the consequence, not the weakness itself.

bytes_per_row=((image->columns+(16/bits_per_pixel-1))/(16/
bits_per_pixel))*2;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The bits-per-pixel calculation is overwritten by an unvalidated image_info->depth value, producing an out-of-range bits_per_pixel. That value then feeds integer divisions (16/bits_per_pixel and 8/bits_per_pixel) and shifts. When the crafted value yields a zero divisor, a floating point exception aborts the encoder, giving a denial of service.

description: In the Linux kernel through 6.3.1, a use-after-free in Netfilter nf_tables when processing batch requests can be abused to perform arbitrary read and write operations on kernel memory. Unprivileged local users can obtain root privileges. This occurs because anonymous sets are mishandled.

code_evidence: nft_lookup_activate dereferences priv->set and increments its use reference count via priv->set->use++ without validating that the referenced anonymous set is still active in the current generation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function operates on priv->set after the set may have been freed, which is exactly reuse of a dangling pointer (CWE-416). A mere reference-count bug would be CWE-911; here the actual defect is using freed memory during activation/commit.

evidence_lines.code:
struct nft_lookup *priv = nft_expr_priv(expr);
priv->set->use++;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: activation blindly takes a reference on priv->set even when that anonymous set was deleted earlier in the same transaction, so the set object may already be freed or scheduled for removal. Trigger: a batch request binds a lookup to an anonymous set and then deletes it. Consequence: the stale pointer is used during commit, yielding a use-after-free with wild-memory write, as shown in the KASAN splat.

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Don't have %cr4.fsgsbase active behind a guest kernels back

Currently, a 64bit PV guest can appear to set and clear FSGSBASE in %cr4, but
the bit remains set in hardware.  Therefore, the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE are usable
even when the guest kernel believes that they are disabled.

The FSGSBASE feature isn't currently supported in Linux, and its context
switch path has some optimisations which rely on userspace being unable to use
the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions.  Xen's current behaviour undermines this
expectation.

In 64bit PV guest context, always load the guest kernels setting of FSGSBASE
into %cr4.  This requires adjusting how Xen uses the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE
instructions.

 * Delete the cpu_has_fsgsbase helper.  It is no longer safe, as users need to
   check %cr4 directly.
 * The raw __rd{fs,gs}base() helpers are only safe to use when %cr4.fsgsbase
   is set.  Comment this property.
 * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}{base,shadow}() and read_msr() helpers are updated to use
   the current %cr4 value to determine which mechanism to use.
 * toggle_guest_mode() and save_segments() are update to avoid reading
   fs/gsbase if the values in hardware cannot be stale WRT struct vcpu.  A
   consequence of this is that the write_cr() path needs to cache the current
   bases, as subsequent context switches will skip saving the values.
 * write_cr4() is updated to ensure that the shadow %cr4.fsgsbase value is
   observed in a safe way WRT the hardware setting, if an interrupt happens to
   hit in the middle.
 * load_segments() is updated to use the VMLOAD optimisation if FSGSBASE is
   unavailable, even if only gs_shadow needs updating.  As a minor perf
   improvement, check cpu_has_svm first to short circuit a context-dependent
   conditional on Intel hardware.
 * pv_make_cr4() is updated for 64bit PV guests to use the guest kernels
   choice of FSGSBASE.

This is part of XSA-293.

Reported-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( cpu_has_fsgsbase )'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( read_cr4() & X86_CR4_FSGSBASE )']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges because a guest can manipulate its virtualised %cr4 in a way that is incompatible with Linux (and possibly other guest kernels).

code_evidence: The function chooses between two mechanisms for reading the GS base based on cpu_has_fsgsbase, a cached feature flag, rather than the actual current %cr4 state.
When the flag is set it executes swapgs and __rdgsbase(), which are only safe if %cr4.fsgsbase is actually set in hardware; otherwise it falls back to rdmsrl(MSR_SHADOW_GS_BASE).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate the actual required condition (current %cr4.fsgsbase) before using the FSGSBASE instruction, relying on an unverified assumption about hardware state, which is improper validation of the state governing safe processing.

evidence_lines.code:
else
rdmsrl(MSR_SHADOW_GS_BASE, base);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code validates the availability of the FSGSBASE instructions against a stale cached capability flag instead of the live %cr4 value that the guest kernel controls. Trigger: a 64-bit PV guest clears %cr4.fsgsbase while the hardware bit remains set, so the cached flag still selects the raw __rdgsbase path. Consequence: the GS base is read via a mechanism inconsistent with the guest's expectation, enabling privilege escalation or denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix tf.raw_ops.ResizeNearestNeighborGrad vulnerability with large dimensions.

Note: This fix will have to be cherry picked in r2.10, r2.9, and r2.8.
PiperOrigin-RevId: 479141644
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES_OK(', '        context,', '        context->allocate_output(', '            0, TensorShape({batch_size, out_height, out_width, channels}),', '            &output));'], 'added_lines': ['    TensorShape shape;', '    OP_REQUIRES_OK(context,', '                   TensorShape::BuildTensorShape(', '                       {batch_size, out_height, out_width, channels}, &shape));', '    OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, context->allocate_output(0, shape, &output));']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. When `tf.raw_ops.ResizeNearestNeighborGrad` is given a large `size` input, it overflows. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 00c821af032ba9e5f5fa3fe14690c8d28a657624. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.11. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.10.1, 2.9.3, and TensorFlow 2.8.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: out_height and out_width come directly from the user-controlled sizes vector (lines 27-28) with only a positivity check at line 14. The output shape is constructed inline as TensorShape({batch_size, out_height, out_width, channels}) and passed to allocate_output (lines 30-34), so the element-count/size computation for the buffer occurs without a checked dimension-product path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-131 fits because the defect is an incorrect calculation of the buffer size used for allocation, driven by unchecked dimensions. The patch replaces the inline shape with TensorShape::BuildTensorShape, which validates the dimension product, confirming the original code lacked this size-calculation check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the output tensor shape is built from unchecked int32-derived dimensions (out_height/out_width) via an inline TensorShape initializer, so the dimension product can overflow when computing the buffer size. Trigger: a large sizes input to ResizeNearestNeighborGrad. Consequence: incorrect/overflowed allocation size, leading to an undersized buffer that the resize-grad functor then writes into.

commit_msg: Fix heap buffer overflow. see #29
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    sprintf(tmp, ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->xMin);', '    sprintf(tmp, ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->yMin);', '    sprintf(tmp, ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->base);', '    sprintf(tmp, ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->xMax - word->xMin);', '    sprintf(tmp, ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->yMax - word->yMin);'], 'added_lines': ['    snprintf(tmp, sizeof(tmp),ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->xMin);', '    snprintf(tmp, sizeof(tmp),ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->yMin);', '    snprintf(tmp, sizeof(tmp),ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->base);', '    snprintf(tmp, sizeof(tmp),ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->xMax - word->xMin);', '    snprintf(tmp, sizeof(tmp),ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->yMax - word->yMin);']}
description: An issue has been found in pdfalto through 0.2. It is a heap-based buffer overflow in the function TextPage::dump in XmlAltoOutputDev.cc.

code_evidence: tmp is allocated as a fixed 10-byte heap buffer via malloc(10*sizeof(char)); no growth or bounds check follows.
sprintf writes the formatted xMin and yMin values into tmp without any size limit, so a numeric value whose formatted text exceeds 9 characters plus terminator overflows the allocation.
sprintf again writes word->base into the same 10-byte tmp, and the width computation word->xMax - word->xMin is likewise unbounded.
The height value word->yMax - word->yMin is formatted into tmp with sprintf, another unchecked write.
sprintf(tmp, "font%d", ...) also writes into tmp without a bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes formatted data past the end of the malloc'd tmp buffer. This is a direct out-of-bounds write; the underlying cause is the unbounded sprintf into a fixed-size allocation, not a read overrun (CWE-125) or mere buffer overflow without write semantics.

evidence_lines.code:
char *tmp;
tmp=(char*)malloc(10*sizeof(char));

sprintf(tmp, ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->xMin);
sprintf(tmp, ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->yMin);

sprintf(tmp, ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->base);
sprintf(tmp, ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->xMax - word->xMin);
sprintf(tmp, ATTR_NUMFORMAT, word->yMax - word->yMin);
sprintf(tmp, "font%d", fontStyleInfo->getId());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a 10-byte heap buffer is written with sprintf, which imposes no destination limit. Trigger: attacker-controlled PDF word coordinates or identifiers (xMin, yMin, base, width, height, font id) format to strings longer than the buffer. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write corrupting adjacent memory, potentially crash or code execution.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/591
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (EOFBlob(image) != MagickFalse)', '      {', '        ThrowFileException(exception,CorruptImageError,"UnexpectedEndOfFile",', '          image->filename);', '        break;', '      }']}
description: The ReadTXTImage function in coders/txt.c in ImageMagick through 6.9.9-0 and 7.x through 7.0.6-1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via a crafted file, because the end-of-file condition is not considered.

code_evidence: The outer do-while loop at line 51 continues while the last string read into text begins with MagickID (line 204). At line 189 ReadBlobString is called and its return value is discarded; the loop condition is then evaluated on text regardless of whether EOF was reached.

The inner pixel loop handles a NULL return from ReadBlobString by breaking at lines 101-102, but the outer loop has no such EOF check after line 189, so at end of file text retains its prior MagickID contents and the condition at line 204 stays true.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a loop whose exit condition cannot be reached because the EOF case is not considered, matching CWE-835's infinite-loop definition. It is not merely a missing input validation issue; the defect is the unreachable loop termination itself.

evidence_lines.code:
if (ReadBlobString(image,text) == (char *) NULL)
break;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the outer do-while loop re-reads a string at line 189 without checking for end-of-file, so the loop exit condition at line 204 is never reached once the file ends with a MagickID line. Trigger: a crafted TXT file whose final read leaves text equal to the MagickID prefix. Consequence: the loop iterates indefinitely, consuming CPU (denial of service).

commit_msg: Ignore exceptions when deserializing note plaintexts
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    CDataStream ss(SER_NETWORK, PROTOCOL_VERSION);', '    ss << pt.get();', '', '    ss >> ret;', '', '    assert(ss.size() == 0);'], 'added_lines': ['    try {', '        CDataStream ss(SER_NETWORK, PROTOCOL_VERSION);', '        ss << pt.get();', '        ss >> ret;', '        assert(ss.size() == 0);', '    } catch (const boost::thread_interrupted&) {', '        throw;', '    } catch (...) {', '        return boost::none;', '    }']}
description: Zcashd in Zcash before 2.0.7-3 allows discovery of the IP address of a full node that owns a shielded address, related to mishandling of exceptions during deserialization of note plaintexts. This affects anyone who has disclosed their zaddr to a third party.

code_evidence: The plaintext is serialized into a CDataStream and deserialized into SaplingNotePlaintext via ss >> ret, followed by assert(ss.size() == 0). Deserialization of attacker-influenced or corrupted plaintext can throw exceptions (e.g., stream errors or failed assertions) that are not caught here, so the exception propagates out of decrypt().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs deserialization that can raise exceptional conditions and does not handle them, matching CWE-755 (Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions). This is not merely a parsing/validation flaw; the defining issue is the absence of exception handling around the deserialization, causing an uncaught exception to propagate.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: deserialization of note plaintext occurs without guarding against exceptions. Trigger: a malformed or crafted ciphertext/plaintext causes ss >> ret or the size assertion to fail. Supported consequence: an uncaught exception escapes decrypt rather than returning boost::none, allowing an exception to propagate and be mishandled by callers, which the commit addresses by catching exceptions and returning boost::none.

commit_msg:
arm64: KVM: Tighten guest core register access from userspace

We currently allow userspace to access the core register file
in about any possible way, including straddling multiple
registers and doing unaligned accesses.

This is not the expected use of the ABI, and nobody is actually
using it that way. Let's tighten it by explicitly checking
the size and alignment for each field of the register file.

Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Fixes: 2f4a07c5f9fe ("arm64: KVM: guest one-reg interface")
Reviewed-by: Christoffer Dall <christoffer.dall@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Mark Rutland <mark.rutland@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Martin <Dave.Martin@arm.com>
[maz: rewrote Dave's initial patch to be more easily backported]
Signed-off-by: Marc Zyngier <marc.zyngier@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Will Deacon <will.deacon@arm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (validate_core_offset(reg))', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '']}
description: arch/arm64/kvm/guest.c in KVM in the Linux kernel before 4.18.12 on the arm64 platform mishandles the KVM_SET_ON_REG ioctl. This is exploitable by attackers who can create virtual machines. An attacker can arbitrarily redirect the hypervisor flow of control (with full register control). An attacker can also cause a denial of service (hypervisor panic) via an illegal exception return. This occurs because of insufficient restrictions on userspace access to the core register file, and because PSTATE.M validation does not prevent unintended execution modes.

code_evidence: off is derived from the userspace-supplied reg->id via core_reg_offset_from_id; the bounds check only rejects off >= nr_regs and off plus the register size >= nr_regs, allowing unaligned or multi-register spans that the ABI does not permit.
The unchecked off/size then feeds copy_to_user(uaddr, ((u32 *)regs) + off, KVM_REG_SIZE(reg->id)), copying register data to userspace using the unvalidated offset and size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts a userspace-controlled register id and offset without validating required properties (alignment, size, single-register containment) before using it in a copy, which is improper input validation of a metadata/offset value. A related out-of-bounds weakness is not the fit because the loose bounds check does prevent passing the end of the register array; the missing constraint is well-formedness of the requested access.

evidence_lines.code:
if (copy_to_user(uaddr, ((u32 *)regs) + off, KVM_REG_SIZE(reg->id)))
return -EFAULT;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the register offset and size taken from the userspace ioctl argument are not checked for alignment or single-register containment, only loosely bounded. Trigger: userspace issues KVM_GET_ONE_REG with an id that straddles registers or is unaligned. Consequence: reads spanning multiple core registers leak state that the ABI intends to keep per-register.

Trigger: malicious input causing many decode_data calls in sixpack_decode. Consequence: slab out-of-bounds write of one byte beyond cooked_buf, corrupting adjacent heap memory (KASAN slab-out-of-bounds).

description: The php_wddx_pop_element function in ext/wddx/wddx.c in PHP 7.0.x before 7.0.15 and 7.1.x before 7.1.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via an inapplicable class name in a wddxPacket XML document, leading to mishandling in a wddx_deserialize call.

code_evidence: When the class name is not found, pce falls back to PHP_IC_ENTRY and incomplete_class is set. The else branch then calls object_init_ex(&obj, pce) without checking success, and immediately passes Z_OBJPROP(obj) into zend_hash_merge. If instantiation fails, obj is not a valid object, so Z_OBJPROP(obj) dereferences an invalid/NULL object handle.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer/handle it expects to be valid but which may be NULL after failed object initialization, matching CWE-476. The missing SUCCESS/EG(exception) check is the specific cause, not a type-confusion or use-after-free issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of object_init_ex is ignored, so a failed instantiation leaves obj uninitialized while the code proceeds to use Z_OBJPROP(obj). Trigger: a wddxPacket with an inapplicable class name reaching this branch. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and application crash (denial of service).

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: remove nodes owned by destroyed domain

In case a domain is removed from Xenstore, remove all nodes owned by
it per default.

This tackles the problem that nodes might be created by a domain
outside its home path in Xenstore, leading to Xenstore hogging more
and more memory. Domain quota don't work in this case if the guest is
rebooting in between.

Since XSA-322 ownership of such stale nodes is transferred to dom0,
which is helping against unintended access, but not against OOM of
Xenstore.

As a fallback for weird cases add a Xenstore start parameter for
keeping today's way to handle stale nodes, adding the risk of Xenstore
hitting an OOM situation.

This is part of XSA-419 / CVE-2022-42322.

Fixes: 496306324d8d ("tools/xenstore: revoke access rights for removed domains")
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tret = _rm(conn, ctx, name);'], 'added_lines': ['\tret = rm_node(conn, ctx, name);']}
description: Xenstore: Cooperating guests can create arbitrary numbers of nodes T[his CNA information record relates to multiple CVEs; the text explains which aspects/vulnerabilities correspond to which CVE.] Since the fix of XSA-322 any Xenstore node owned by a removed domain will be modified to be owned by Dom0. This will allow two malicious guests working together to create an arbitrary number of Xenstore nodes. This is possible by domain A letting domain B write into domain A's local Xenstore tree. Domain B can then create many nodes and reboot. The nodes created by domain B will now be owned by Dom0. By repeating this process over and over again an arbitrary number of nodes can be created, as Dom0's number of nodes isn't limited by Xenstore quota.

code_evidence: do_rm canonicalizes the request name via get_node_canonicalized (line 8-9) and then deletes it with _rm (line 29). The deletion path is invoked for every successful write-permitted removal request; the function itself contains no ownership check or cleanup of nodes owned by a domain that may have written outside its home path. The commit changes this call site to rm_node, indicating the deletion/ownership handling is the relevant operation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the stale nodes are allocated in Xenstore and never released after the owning domain's lifetime ends, leading to memory exhaustion. This is a resource-lifetime/cleanup weakness, not an access-control flaw (which the ownership transfer already addressed).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: removal deletes only the addressed node path, without reclaiming nodes whose ownership was transferred to Dom0 after the owning domain was destroyed. Trigger: cooperating guests repeatedly create nodes in another domain's tree and reboot, leaving stale nodes owned by Dom0. Consequence: unbounded node accumulation not bounded by domain quota, causing Xenstore resource exhaustion/OOM.

commit_msg:
Anatoly has been fuzzing with kBdysch harness and reported a hang in
one of the outcomes:

  0: (b7) r0 = 808464432
  1: (7f) r0 >>= r0
  2: (14) w0 -= 808464432
  3: (07) r0 += 808464432
  4: (b7) r1 = 808464432
  5: (de) if w1 s<= w0 goto pc+0
   R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=808464432,umax_value=5103431727,var_off=(0x30303020;0x10000001f)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  6: (07) r0 += -2144337872
  7: (14) w0 -= -1607454672
  8: (25) if r0 > 0x30303030 goto pc+0
   R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=271581184,umax_value=271581311,var_off=(0x10300000;0x7f)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  9: (76) if w0 s>= 0x303030 goto pc+2
  12: (95) exit

  from 8 to 9: safe

  from 5 to 6: R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=808464432,umax_value=5103431727,var_off=(0x30303020;0x10000001f)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  6: (07) r0 += -2144337872
  7: (14) w0 -= -1607454672
  8: (25) if r0 > 0x30303030 goto pc+0
   R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=271581184,umax_value=271581311,var_off=(0x10300000;0x7f)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  9: safe

  from 8 to 9: safe
  verification time 589 usec
  stack depth 0
  processed 17 insns (limit 1000000) [...]

The underlying program was xlated as follows:

  # bpftool p d x i 9
   0: (b7) r0 = 808464432
   1: (7f) r0 >>= r0
   2: (14) w0 -= 808464432
   3: (07) r0 += 808464432
   4: (b7) r1 = 808464432
   5: (de) if w1 s<= w0 goto pc+0
   6: (07) r0 += -2144337872
   7: (14) w0 -= -1607454672
   8: (25) if r0 > 0x30303030 goto pc+0
   9: (76) if w0 s>= 0x303030 goto pc+2
  10: (05) goto pc-1
  11: (05) goto pc-1
  12: (95) exit

The verifier rewrote original instructions it recognized as dead code with
'goto pc-1', but reality differs from verifier simulation in that we're
actually able to trigger a hang due to hitting the 'goto pc-1' instructions.

Taking different examples to make the issue more obvious: in this example
we're probing bounds on a completely unknown scalar variable in r1:

  [...]
  5: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R10=fp0
  5: (18) r2 = 0x4000000000
  7: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R2_w=inv274877906944 R10=fp0
  7: (18) r3 = 0x2000000000
  9: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R10=fp0
  9: (18) r4 = 0x400
  11: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R4_w=inv1024 R10=fp0
  11: (18) r5 = 0x200
  13: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R4_w=inv1024 R5_w=inv512 R10=fp0
  13: (2d) if r1 > r2 goto pc+4
   R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffffff)) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R4_w=inv1024 R5_w=inv512 R10=fp0
  14: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffffff)) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R4_w=inv1024 R5_w=inv512 R10=fp0
  14: (ad) if r1 < r3 goto pc+3
   R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umin_value=137438953472,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffffff)) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R4_w=inv1024 R5_w=inv512 R10=fp0
  15: R0=inv1 R1=inv(id=0,umin_value=137438953472,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffffff)) R2=inv274877906944 R3=inv137438953472 R4=inv1024 R5=inv512 R10=fp0
  15: (2e) if w1 > w4 goto pc+2
   R0=inv1 R1=inv(id=0,umin_value=137438953472,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7f00000000)) R2=inv274877906944 R3=inv137438953472 R4=inv1024 R5=inv512 R10=fp0
  16: R0=inv1 R1=inv(id=0,umin_value=137438953472,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7f00000000)) R2=inv274877906944 R3=inv137438953472 R4=inv1024 R5=inv512 R10=fp0
  16: (ae) if w1 < w5 goto pc+1
   R0=inv1 R1=inv(id=0,umin_value=137438953472,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7f00000000)) R2=inv274877906944 R3=inv137438953472 R4=inv1024 R5=inv512 R10=fp0
  [...]

We're first probing lower/upper bounds via jmp64, later we do a similar
check via jmp32 and examine the resulting var_off there. After fall-through
in insn 14, we get the following bounded r1 with 0x7fffffffff unknown marked
bits in the variable section.

Thus, after knowing r1 <= 0x4000000000 and r1 >= 0x2000000000:

  max: 0b100000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x4000000000
  var: 0b111111111111111111111111111111111111111 / 0x7fffffffff
  min: 0b010000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x2000000000

Now, in insn 15 and 16, we perform a similar probe with lower/upper bounds
in jmp32.

Thus, after knowing r1 <= 0x4000000000 and r1 >= 0x2000000000 and
                    w1 <= 0x400        and w1 >= 0x200:

  max: 0b100000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x4000000000
  var: 0b111111100000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x7f00000000
  min: 0b010000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x2000000000

The lower/upper bounds haven't changed since they have high bits set in
u64 space and the jmp32 tests can only refine bounds in the low bits.

However, for the var part the expectation would have been 0x7f000007ff
or something less precise up to 0x7fffffffff. A outcome of 0x7f00000000
is not correct since it would contradict the earlier probed bounds
where we know that the result should have been in [0x200,0x400] in u32
space. Therefore, tests with such info will lead to wrong verifier
assumptions later on like falsely predicting conditional jumps to be
always taken, etc.

The issue here is that __reg_bound_offset32()'s implementation from
commit 581738a681b6 ("bpf: Provide better register bounds after jmp32
instructions") makes an incorrect range assumption:

  static void __reg_bound_offset32(struct bpf_reg_state *reg)
  {
        u64 mask = 0xffffFFFF;
        struct tnum range = tnum_range(reg->umin_value & mask,
                                       reg->umax_value & mask);
        struct tnum lo32 = tnum_cast(reg->var_off, 4);
        struct tnum hi32 = tnum_lshift(tnum_rshift(reg->var_off, 32), 32);

        reg->var_off = tnum_or(hi32, tnum_intersect(lo32, range));
  }

In the above walk-through example, __reg_bound_offset32() as-is chose
a range after masking with 0xffffffff of [0x0,0x0] since umin:0x2000000000
and umax:0x4000000000 and therefore the lo32 part was clamped to 0x0 as
well. However, in the umin:0x2000000000 and umax:0x4000000000 range above
we'd end up with an actual possible interval of [0x0,0xffffffff] for u32
space instead.

In case of the original reproducer, the situation looked as follows at
insn 5 for r0:

  [...]
  5: R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=808464432,umax_value=5103431727,var_off=(0x0; 0x1ffffffff)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
                               0x30303030           0x13030302f
  5: (de) if w1 s<= w0 goto pc+0
   R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=808464432,umax_value=5103431727,var_off=(0x30303020; 0x10000001f)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
                             0x30303030           0x13030302f
  [...]

After the fall-through, we similarly forced the var_off result into
the wrong range [0x30303030,0x3030302f] suggesting later on that fixed
bits must only be of 0x30303020 with 0x10000001f unknowns whereas such
assumption can only be made when both bounds in hi32 range match.

Originally, I was thinking to fix this by moving reg into a temp reg and
use proper coerce_reg_to_size() helper on the temp reg where we can then
based on that define the range tnum for later intersection:

  static void __reg_bound_offset32(struct bpf_reg_state *reg)
  {
        struct bpf_reg_state tmp = *reg;
        struct tnum lo32, hi32, range;

        coerce_reg_to_size(&tmp, 4);
        range = tnum_range(tmp.umin_value, tmp.umax_value);
        lo32 = tnum_cast(reg->var_off, 4);
        hi32 = tnum_lshift(tnum_rshift(reg->var_off, 32), 32);
        reg->var_off = tnum_or(hi32, tnum_intersect(lo32, range));
  }

In the case of the concrete example, this gives us a more conservative unknown
section. Thus, after knowing r1 <= 0x4000000000 and r1 >= 0x2000000000 and
                             w1 <= 0x400        and w1 >= 0x200:

  max: 0b100000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x4000000000
  var: 0b111111111111111111111111111111111111111 / 0x7fffffffff
  min: 0b010000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x2000000000

However, above new __reg_bound_offset32() has no effect on refining the
knowledge of the register contents. Meaning, if the bounds in hi32 range
mismatch we'll get the identity function given the range reg spans
[0x0,0xffffffff] and we cast var_off into lo32 only to later on binary
or it again with the hi32.

Likewise, if the bounds in hi32 range match, then we mask both bounds
with 0xffffffff, use the resulting umin/umax for the range to later
intersect the lo32 with it. However, _prior_ called __reg_bound_offset()
did already such intersection on the full reg and we therefore would only
repeat the same operation on the lo32 part twice.

Given this has no effect and the original commit had false assumptions,
this patch reverts the code entirely which is also more straight forward
for stable trees: apparently 581738a681b6 got auto-selected by Sasha's
ML system and misclassified as a fix, so it got sucked into v5.4 where
it should never have landed. A revert is low-risk also from a user PoV
since it requires a recent kernel and llc to opt-into -mcpu=v3 BPF CPU
to generate jmp32 instructions. A proper bounds refinement would need a
significantly more complex approach which is currently being worked, but
no stable material [0]. Hence revert is best option for stable. After the
revert, the original reported program gets rejected as follows:

  1: (7f) r0 >>= r0
  2: (14) w0 -= 808464432
  3: (07) r0 += 808464432
  4: (b7) r1 = 808464432
  5: (de) if w1 s<= w0 goto pc+0
   R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=808464432,umax_value=5103431727,var_off=(0x0; 0x1ffffffff)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  6: (07) r0 += -2144337872
  7: (14) w0 -= -1607454672
  8: (25) if r0 > 0x30303030 goto pc+0
   R0_w=invP(id=0,umax_value=808464432,var_off=(0x0; 0x3fffffff)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  9: (76) if w0 s>= 0x303030 goto pc+2
   R0=invP(id=0,umax_value=3158063,var_off=(0x0; 0x3fffff)) R1=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  10: (30) r0 = *(u8 *)skb[808464432]
  BPF_LD_[ABS|IND] uses reserved fields
  processed 11 insns (limit 1000000) [...]

  [0] https://lore.kernel.org/bpf/158507130343.15666.8018068546764556975.stgit@john-Precision-5820-Tower/T/

Fixes: 581738a681b6 ("bpf: Provide better register bounds after jmp32 instructions")
Reported-by: Anatoly Trosinenko <anatoly.trosinenko@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>

description: In the Linux kernel 5.5.0 and newer, the bpf verifier (kernel/bpf/verifier.c) did not properly restrict the register bounds for 32-bit operations, leading to out-of-bounds reads and writes in kernel memory. The vulnerability also affects the Linux 5.4 stable series, starting with v5.4.7, as the introducing commit was backported to that branch. This vulnerability was fixed in 5.6.1, 5.5.14, and 5.4.29. (issue is aka ZDI-CAN-10780)

code_evidence: Line 8 truncates val to 32 bits and line 9 derives sval via sign-extension when is_jmp32, so the bound values used below are 32-bit quantities.
After the main bound deduction, lines 88-91 invoke __reg_bound_offset32 on both branch registers when is_jmp32, applying a 32-bit range assumption that does not match the 64-bit bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The faulty 32-bit bound tracking yields incorrect register range assumptions that can allow subsequent memory operations to access beyond intended buffers, i.e., an out-of-bounds write. The defect is in range computation rather than a direct store, but the supported consequence is out-of-bounds memory modification, matching CWE-787; it is not merely an infinite loop, which is only the observed hang.

evidence_lines.code:
val = is_jmp32 ? (u32)val : val;
sval = is_jmp32 ? (s64)(s32)val : (s64)val;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: for 32-bit jumps the verifier refines register bounds using masked 32-bit values (lines 8-9) and then calls __reg_bound_offset32 (lines 88-91), which computes a tnum range from umin/umax masked with 0xffffffff even when the high 32 bits of the bounds disagree. This produces an incorrect var_off and overly tight bounds. Later instructions then rely on the wrong bounds, so a conditional jump the verifier believes always taken is not, and the program reaches instructions (including rewritten goto pc-1) that cause a hang; incorrect bounds can also permit out-of-bounds memory accesses.

code_evidence: The loop iterates i from 0 to ptr->layout.channels_count and indexes ptr->layout.layouts[i] without verifying that channels_count is within the bounds of the layouts array. The value of channels_count comes from the parsed box and is not clamped before this size calculation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads ptr->layout.layouts[i].position beyond the intended array bounds, which matches CWE-125 (reading past the end of a buffer). This is not a write or integer overflow; the defect is an unchecked index used in a read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts channels_count as an array bound for layouts[] without validating it against the actual array capacity. Trigger: a parsed ChannelLayoutBox with a large channels_count and definedLayout==0 causes the loop to read layouts[i] past the end of the buffer. commit_msg:
teredo: be stricter on what to consider valid teredo

Invalid Teredo can lead to valid DNS traffic (or other UDP traffic)
being misdetected as Teredo. This leads to false negatives in the
UDP payload inspection.

Make the teredo code only consider a packet teredo if the encapsulated
data was decoded without any 'invalid' events being set.

Bug #2736.

description: Open Information Security Foundation Suricata prior to version 4.1.2 is affected by: Denial of Service - DNS detection bypass. The impact is: An attacker can evade a signature detection with a specialy formed network packet. The component is: app-layer-detect-proto.c, decode.c, decode-teredo.c and decode-ipv6.c (https://github.com/OISF/suricata/pull/3590/commits/11f3659f64a4e42e90cb3c09fcef66894205aefe, https://github.com/OISF/suricata/pull/3590/commits/8357ef3f8ffc7d99ef6571350724160de356158b). The attack vector is: An attacker can trigger the vulnerability by sending a specifically crafted network request. The fixed version is: 4.1.2.

code_evidence: The function dispatches on the caller-supplied enum DecodeTunnelProto proto in a switch; DECODE_TUNNEL_IPV6 (line 9) is handled, but there is no case for DECODE_TUNNEL_IPV6_TEREDO, so such packets fall to the default branch (line 17), which only logs (line 18), breaks (line 19), and returns TM_ECODE_OK (line 21).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The proto input is not validated against the set of supported tunnel protocols; the unmatched value is accepted rather than rejected, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). Unlike a mere logging change, the missing case causes the packet to be accepted without processing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the switch does not recognize the DECODE_TUNNEL_IPV6_TEREDO protocol value, so a Teredo-encapsulated IPv6 packet is silently treated as successfully decoded (TM_ECODE_OK) without invoking DecodeIPV6. Trigger: an attacker sends a crafted packet whose tunnel protocol is classified as Teredo-IPv6. Supported consequence: the encapsulated payload is never inspected, enabling DNS/signature detection bypass (false negatives), consistent with the commit's Bug #2736.

commit_msg:
(for 4.9.3) CVE-2018-14462/ICMP: Add a missing bounds check

In icmp_print().

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry.

Add two tests using the capture files supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tND_TCHECK_16BITS(&dp->icmp_cksum);']}
description: The ICMP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-icmp.c:icmp_print().

code_evidence: When the computed checksum is nonzero, the code reads dp->icmp_cksum via EXTRACT_16BITS and prints it, but the preceding guard ND_TTEST2(*bp, plen) only validates plen bytes starting at bp; no ND_TCHECK_16BITS(&dp->icmp_cksum) bounds check protects this field access before the read.

The checksum path is entered only for verbose output on non-fragmented packets, and the field read occurs inside the sum != 0 branch, so a truncated capture whose advertised plen passes the 8-bit test but lacks the 2-byte icmp_cksum can reach the out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences dp->icmp_cksum without verifying that the 2-byte field is within the captured buffer, which is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). This is distinct from a write or integer issue: the defect is the missing read-side bounds check before EXTRACT_16BITS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a missing bounds check on the 16-bit icmp_cksum field before EXTRACT_16BITS. Trigger: a truncated ICMP capture where the checksum is nonzero and the field lies beyond the captured data. Consequence: the parser reads past the end of the captured buffer (CVE-2018-14462 buffer over-read), potentially crashing or leaking adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
Recently, we got two syzkaller problems because of oversize packet
when napi frags enabled.

One of the problems is because the first seg size of the iov_iter
from user space is very big, it is 2147479538 which is bigger than
the threshold value for bail out early in __alloc_pages(). And
skb->pfmemalloc is true, __kmalloc_reserve() would use pfmemalloc
reserves without __GFP_NOWARN flag. Thus we got a warning as following:

========================================================
WARNING: CPU: 1 PID: 17965 at mm/page_alloc.c:5295 __alloc_pages+0x1308/0x16c4 mm/page_alloc.c:5295
...
Call trace:
 __alloc_pages+0x1308/0x16c4 mm/page_alloc.c:5295
 __alloc_pages_node include/linux/gfp.h:550 [inline]
 alloc_pages_node include/linux/gfp.h:564 [inline]
 kmalloc_large_node+0x94/0x350 mm/slub.c:4038
 __kmalloc_node_track_caller+0x620/0x8e4 mm/slub.c:4545
 __kmalloc_reserve.constprop.0+0x1e4/0x2b0 net/core/skbuff.c:151
 pskb_expand_head+0x130/0x8b0 net/core/skbuff.c:1654
 __skb_grow include/linux/skbuff.h:2779 [inline]
 tun_napi_alloc_frags+0x144/0x610 drivers/net/tun.c:1477
 tun_get_user+0x31c/0x2010 drivers/net/tun.c:1835
 tun_chr_write_iter+0x98/0x100 drivers/net/tun.c:2036

The other problem is because odd IPv6 packets without NEXTHDR_NONE
extension header and have big packet length, it is 2127925 which is
bigger than ETH_MAX_MTU(65535). After ipv6_gso_pull_exthdrs() in
ipv6_gro_receive(), network_header offset and transport_header offset
are all bigger than U16_MAX. That would trigger skb->network_header
and skb->transport_header overflow error, because they are all '__u16'
type. Eventually, it would affect the value for __skb_push(skb, value),
and make it be a big value. After __skb_push() in ipv6_gro_receive(),
skb->data would less than skb->head, an out of bounds memory bug occurred.
That would trigger the problem as following:

==================================================================
BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in eth_type_trans+0x100/0x260
...
Call trace:
 dump_backtrace+0xd8/0x130
 show_stack+0x1c/0x50
 dump_stack_lvl+0x64/0x7c
 print_address_description.constprop.0+0xbc/0x2e8
 print_report+0x100/0x1e4
 kasan_report+0x80/0x120
 __asan_load8+0x78/0xa0
 eth_type_trans+0x100/0x260
 napi_gro_frags+0x164/0x550
 tun_get_user+0xda4/0x1270
 tun_chr_write_iter+0x74/0x130
 do_iter_readv_writev+0x130/0x1ec
 do_iter_write+0xbc/0x1e0
 vfs_writev+0x13c/0x26c

To fix the problems, restrict the packet size less than
(ETH_MAX_MTU - NET_SKB_PAD - NET_IP_ALIGN) which has considered reserved
skb space in napi_alloc_skb() because transport_header is an offset from
skb->head. Add len check in tun_napi_alloc_frags() simply.

Fixes: 90e33d459407 ("tun: enable napi_gro_frags() for TUN/TAP driver")
Signed-off-by: Ziyang Xuan <william.xuanziyang@huawei.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20221029094101.1653855-1-william.xuanziyang@huawei.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (it->nr_segs > MAX_SKB_FRAGS + 1)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (it->nr_segs > MAX_SKB_FRAGS + 1 ||', '\t    len > (ETH_MAX_MTU - NET_SKB_PAD - NET_IP_ALIGN))']}
description: An out-of-bounds memory access flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s TUN/TAP device driver functionality in how a user generates a malicious (too big) networking packet when napi frags is enabled. This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: The pre-patch check only bounds it->nr_segs; len (from user) is not validated.
linear = iov_iter_single_seg_count(it) can be a huge first-segment size; __skb_grow(skb, linear) then allocates/grows using that unchecked size.
skb->len and skb->data_len are set from len without any upper bound relative to ETH_MAX_MTU or header offsets.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing len upper bound leads to out-of-bounds memory access/write when skb headers overflow, matching CWE-787. It is not merely an allocation-size issue (CWE-770) because the supported consequence is writing/accessing past the intended buffer.

evidence_lines.code:
if (it->nr_segs > MAX_SKB_FRAGS + 1)
return ERR_PTR(-EMSGSIZE);

linear = iov_iter_single_seg_count(it);
err = __skb_grow(skb, linear);

skb->len = len;
skb->data_len = len - linear;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function trusts the user-supplied len and first iov segment size; with napi frags enabled, an oversized packet causes __skb_grow to allocate beyond limits and later header offsets (u16) to overflow, so __skb_push moves skb->data before skb->head. The trigger is a large iov_iter length reaching tun_napi_alloc_frags.

commit_msg:
Prevent infinite loop/stack overflow in TFLite `while` op.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 370800333
Change-Id: I6a2e4ff849da339545c449db2af7e11ce6ff02c3
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context,', '                 op_data->cond_subgraph_index != op_data->body_subgraph_index);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. TFlite graphs must not have loops between nodes. However, this condition was not checked and an attacker could craft models that would result in infinite loop during evaluation. In certain cases, the infinite loop would be replaced by stack overflow due to too many recursive calls. For example, the `While` implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/106d8f4fb89335a2c52d7c895b7a7485465ca8d9/tensorflow/lite/kernels/while.cc) could be tricked into a scneario where both the body and the loop subgraphs are the same. Evaluating one of the subgraphs means calling the `Eval` function for the other and this quickly exhaust all stack space. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range. Please consult our security guide(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/master/SECURITY.md) for more information regarding the security model and how to contact us with issues and questions.

code_evidence: Lines 7-8 only verify that the cond and body subgraph indices are in range; they do not reject the case where both indices are equal.
Lines 9-10 then resolve both indices to Subgraph pointers, so an attacker-supplied model can make cond_subgraph and body_subgraph refer to the same subgraph.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing inequality check permits self-referential subgraph evaluation, directly causing uncontrolled recursion and stack exhaustion, matching CWE-674. This is recursion control, not merely a generic loop bound (CWE-835), because the failure mode is recursive re-entry consuming stack space.

evidence_lines.code:
TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, op_data->cond_subgraph_index < subgraphs->size());
TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, op_data->body_subgraph_index < subgraphs->size());

Subgraph* cond_subgraph = (*subgraphs)[op_data->cond_subgraph_index].get();
Subgraph* body_subgraph = (*subgraphs)[op_data->body_subgraph_index].get();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The Prepare function validates index bounds but omits the constraint that the cond and body subgraph indices differ. When a crafted model sets both to the same subgraph, evaluation of the While op calls Eval on that subgraph, which re-enters the same op, producing unbounded recursion that exhausts the stack (or loops indefinitely).

commit_msg:
Fix UAF in comps_objmrtree_unite function

The added field is not used at all in many places and it is probably the
left-over of some copy-paste.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        char added;', '        pair->added = 0;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: A use-after-free flaw has been discovered in libcomps before version 0.1.10 in the way ObjMRTrees are merged. An attacker, who is able to make an application read a crafted comps XML file, may be able to crash the application or execute malicious code.

code_evidence: A Pair is heap-allocated and appended to tmplist; tmplist is initialized with &free as its destructor, so its items own their data.

Inside the loop, it is removed from tmplist and the pointed-to Pair is captured as parent_pair, then it is freed. The next statement dereferences pair->added, but pair may have been reassigned by malloc in the preceding iteration's for-loop body, so the write targets freed memory.
After the for-loop, parent_pair->key and parent_pair are freed, while stale pair pointers may remain in tmplist from appended children.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences freed heap memory (pair->added) after the prior node was freed, matching CWE-416. A double-free would require releasing the same pointer twice, which is not the demonstrated operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code writes pair->added after pair has been reassigned to a freshly malloc'd node, and the previously captured node was already freed. Trigger: a comps XML merge that populates subnodes so the for-loop runs. Supported consequence: use-after-free write, leading to memory corruption, crash, or possible code execution.

commit_msg:
Prevent KDC unset status assertion failures

Assign status values if S4U2Self padata fails to decode, if an
S4U2Proxy request uses invalid KDC options, or if an S4U2Proxy request
uses an evidence ticket which does not match the canonicalized request
server principal name.  Reported by Samuel Cabrero.

If a status value is not assigned during KDC processing, default to
"UNKNOWN_REASON" rather than failing an assertion.  This change will
prevent future denial of service bugs due to similar mistakes, and
will allow us to omit assigning status values for unlikely errors such
as small memory allocation failures.

CVE-2017-11368:

In MIT krb5 1.7 and later, an authenticated attacker can cause an
assertion failure in krb5kdc by sending an invalid S4U2Self or
S4U2Proxy request.

  CVSSv3 Vector: AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H/E:H/RL:O/RC:C

ticket: 8599 (new)
target_version: 1.15-next
target_version: 1.14-next
tags: pullup
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (code)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (code) {', '        *status = "DECODE_PA_S4U_X509_USER";', '    }']}
description: In MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) 1.7 and later, an authenticated attacker can cause a KDC assertion failure by sending invalid S4U2Self or S4U2Proxy requests.

code_evidence: decode_krb5_pa_s4u_x509_user parses attacker-supplied pa_data->contents (length/data set at lines 12-13); on a non-zero return code the function returns immediately at line 16 without assigning *status, leaving the caller's status pointer unset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unset status reaches an assert() in the KDC, and an invalid request from an authenticated attacker triggers it, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion). The weakness is the reachable assertion/DoS, not merely improper error handling; the missing status assignment is the cause, not the labeled weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decode-failure path returns without setting *status, so the KDC caller later hits an assertion on an unset status value. Trigger: an authenticated attacker sends an invalid S4U2Self/S4U2Proxy padata blob that fails decoding. Supported consequence: the krb5kdc process aborts (assertion failure), causing denial of service. The patch sets *status to DECODE_PA_S4U_X509_USER before returning, removing the reachable assertion.

commit_msg:
The hci_sock_dev_event() function will cleanup the hdev object for
sockets even if this object may still be in used within the
hci_sock_bound_ioctl() function, result in UAF vulnerability.

This patch replace the BH context lock to serialize these affairs
and prevent the race condition.

Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tbh_lock_sock_nested(sk);', '\t\t\tbh_unlock_sock(sk);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tlock_sock(sk);', '\t\t\trelease_sock(sk);']}
description: A use-after-free in function hci_sock_bound_ioctl() of the Linux kernel HCI subsystem was found in the way user calls ioct HCIUNBLOCKADDR or other way triggers race condition of the call hci_unregister_dev() together with one of the calls hci_sock_blacklist_add(), hci_sock_blacklist_del(), hci_get_conn_info(), hci_get_auth_info(). A privileged local user could use this flaw to crash the system or escalate their privileges on the system. This flaw affects the Linux kernel versions prior to 5.13-rc5.

code_evidence: Under only read_lock(&hci_sk_list.lock), the loop walks all sockets and takes bh_lock_sock_nested(sk) before touching hci_pi(sk)->hdev and calling hci_dev_put(hdev). bh_lock_sock_nested is a softirq-context spinlock that does not serialize against process-context paths such as hci_sock_bound_ioctl, which use the socket lock via lock_sock; those ioctls can still read or use the hdev reference concurrently while this handler clears it and drops the device reference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's cleanup sequence lacks proper exclusive synchronization over the shared socket/hdev state, so an interfering concurrent sequence can access the resource mid-update. That is the race-condition pattern of CWE-362; the UAF is the downstream consequence rather than the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the device-unregister cleanup path synchronizes sockets with a BH spinlock that is not mutually exclusive with the process-context socket-lock users of the same hdev. Trigger: a concurrent ioctl (e.g. HCIUNBLOCKADDR) races with hci_unregister_dev while the loop clears hci_pi(sk)->hdev and calls hci_dev_put(hdev). Consequence: the ioctl continues using a freed hdev, yielding a use-after-free that may crash or escalate privileges.

commit_msg:
WireGuard: fix null pointer crash

It was assumed that the WireGuard dissector is always called on the
first pass before the second pass. That might not be the case when the
heuristics dissector sets a conversation dissector later in the stream.
Be prepared to handle this case. Do not simply abort, the previous
packets may be valid data messages.

} else if (wg_pinfo->session) {
hs = wg_pinfo->session->hs;
