While b2157399cc98 only focussed on masking array map access
for unprivileged users for tail calls and data access such
that the user provided index gets sanitized from BPF program
and syscall side, there is still a more generic form affected
from BPF programs that applies to most maps that hold user
data in relation to dynamic map access when dealing with
unknown scalars or "slow" known scalars as access offset, for
example:

  - Load a map value pointer into R6
  - Load an index into R7
  - Do a slow computation (e.g. with a memory dependency) that
    loads a limit into R8 (e.g. load the limit from a map for
    high latency, then mask it to make the verifier happy)
  - Exit if R7 >= R8 (mispredicted branch)
  - Load R0 = R6[R7]
  - Load R0 = R6[R0]

For unknown scalars there are two options in the BPF verifier
where we could derive knowledge from in order to guarantee
safe access to the memory: i) While </>/<=/>= variants won't
allow to derive any lower or upper bounds from the unknown
scalar where it would be safe to add it to the map value
pointer, it is possible through ==/!= test however. ii) another
option is to transform the unknown scalar into a known scalar,
for example, through ALU ops combination such as R &= <imm>
followed by R |= <imm> or any similar combination where the
original information from the unknown scalar would be destroyed
entirely leaving R with a constant. The initial slow load still
precedes the latter ALU ops on that register, so the CPU
executes speculatively from that point. Once we have the known
scalar, any compare operation would work then. A third option
only involving registers with known scalars could be crafted
as described in [0] where a CPU port (e.g. Slow Int unit)
would be filled with many dependent computations such that
the subsequent condition depending on its outcome has to wait
for evaluation on its execution port and thereby executing
speculatively if the speculated code can be scheduled on a
different execution port, or any other form of mistraining
as described in [1], for example. Given this is not limited
to only unknown scalars, not only map but also stack access
is affected since both is accessible for unprivileged users
and could potentially be used for out of bounds access under
speculation.

In order to prevent any of these cases, the verifier is now
sanitizing pointer arithmetic on the offset such that any
out of bounds speculation would be masked in a way where the
pointer arithmetic result in the destination register will
stay unchanged, meaning offset masked into zero similar as
in array_index_nospec() case. With regards to implementation,
there are three options that were considered: i) new insn
for sanitation, ii) push/pop insn and sanitation as inlined
BPF, iii) reuse of ax register and sanitation as inlined BPF.

Option i) has the downside that we end up using from reserved
bits in the opcode space, but also that we would require
each JIT to emit masking as native arch opcodes meaning
mitigation would have slow adoption till everyone implements
it eventually which is counter-productive. Option ii) and iii)
have both in common that a temporary register is needed in
order to implement the sanitation as inlined BPF since we
are not allowed to modify the source register. While a push /
pop insn in ii) would be useful to have in any case, it
requires once again that every JIT needs to implement it
first. While possible, amount of changes needed would also
be unsuitable for a -stable patch. Therefore, the path which
has fewer changes, less BPF instructions for the mitigation
and does not require anything to be changed in the JITs is
option iii) which this work is pursuing. The ax register is
already mapped to a register in all JITs (modulo arm32 where
it's mapped to stack as various other BPF registers there)
and used in constant blinding for JITs-only so far. It can
be reused for verifier rewrites under certain constraints.
The interpreter's tmp "register" has therefore been remapped
into extending the register set with hidden ax register and
reusing that for a number of instructions that needed the
prior temporary variable internally (e.g. div, mod). This
allows for zero increase in stack space usage in the interpreter,
and enables (restricted) generic use in rewrites otherwise as
long as such a patchlet does not make use of these instructions.
The sanitation mask is dynamic and relative to the offset the
map value or stack pointer currently holds.

There are various cases that need to be taken under consideration
for the masking, e.g. such operation could look as follows:
ptr += val or val += ptr or ptr -= val. Thus, the value to be
sanitized could reside either in source or in destination
register, and the limit is different depending on whether
the ALU op is addition or subtraction and depending on the
current known and bounded offset. The limit is derived as
follows: limit := max_value_size - (smin_value + off). For
subtraction: limit := umax_value + off. This holds because
we do not allow any pointer arithmetic that would
temporarily go out of bounds or would have an unknown
value with mixed signed bounds where it is unclear at
verification time whether the actual runtime value would
be either negative or positive. For example, we have a
derived map pointer value with constant offset and bounded
one, so limit based on smin_value works because the verifier
requires that statically analyzed arithmetic on the pointer
must be in bounds, and thus it checks if resulting
smin_value + off and umax_value + off is still within map
value bounds at time of arithmetic in addition to time of
access. Similarly, for the case of stack access we derive
the limit as follows: MAX_BPF_STACK + off for subtraction
and -off for the case of addition where off := ptr_reg->off +
ptr_reg->var_off.value. Subtraction is a special case for
the masking which can be in form of ptr += -val, ptr -= -val,
or ptr -= val. In the first two cases where we know that
the value is negative, we need to temporarily negate the
value in order to do the sanitation on a positive value
where we later swap the ALU op, and restore original source
register if the value was in source.

The sanitation of pointer arithmetic alone is still not fully
sufficient as is, since a scenario like the following could
happen ...

  PTR += 0x1000 (e.g. K-based imm)
  PTR -= BIG_NUMBER_WITH_SLOW_COMPARISON
  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= BIG_NUMBER_WITH_SLOW_COMPARISON
  [...]

... which under speculation could end up as ...

  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= 0 [ truncated by mitigation ]
  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= 0 [ truncated by mitigation ]
  [...]

... and therefore still access out of bounds. To prevent such
case, the verifier is also analyzing safety for potential out
of bounds access under speculative execution. Meaning, it is
also simulating pointer access under truncation. We therefore
"branch off" and push the current verification state after the
ALU operation with known 0 to the verification stack for later
analysis. Given the current path analysis succeeded it is
likely that the one under speculation can be pruned. In any
case, it is also subject to existing complexity limits and
therefore anything beyond this point will be rejected. In
terms of pruning, it needs to be ensured that the verification
state from speculative execution simulation must never prune
a non-speculative execution path, therefore, we mark verifier
state accordingly at the time of push_stack(). If verifier
detects out of bounds access under speculative execution from
one of the possible paths that includes a truncation, it will
reject such program.

Given we mask every reg-based pointer arithmetic for
unprivileged programs, we've been looking into how it could
affect real-world programs in terms of size increase. As the
majority of programs are targeted for privileged-only use
case, we've unconditionally enabled masking (with its alu
restrictions on top of it) for privileged programs for the
sake of testing in order to check i) whether they get rejected
in its current form, and ii) by how much the number of
instructions and size will increase. We've tested this by
using Katran, Cilium and test_l4lb from the kernel selftests.
For Katran we've evaluated balancer_kern.o, Cilium bpf_lxc.o
and an older test object bpf_lxc_opt_-DUNKNOWN.o and l4lb
we've used test_l4lb.o as well as test_l4lb_noinline.o. We
found that none of the programs got rejected by the verifier
with this change, and that impact is rather minimal to none.
balancer_kern.o had 13,904 bytes (1,738 insns) xlated and
7,797 bytes JITed before and after the change. Most complex
program in bpf_lxc.o had 30,544 bytes (3,817 insns) xlated
and 18,538 bytes JITed before and after and none of the other
tail call programs in bpf_lxc.o had any changes either. For
the older bpf_lxc_opt_-DUNKNOWN.o object we found a small
increase from 20,616 bytes (2,576 insns) and 12,536 bytes JITed
before to 20,664 bytes (2,582 insns) and 12,558 bytes JITed
after the change. Other programs from that object file had
similar small increase. Both test_l4lb.o had no change and
remained at 6,544 bytes (817 insns) xlated and 3,401 bytes
JITed and for test_l4lb_noinline.o constant at 5,080 bytes
(634 insns) xlated and 3,313 bytes JITed. This can be explained
in that LLVM typically optimizes stack based pointer arithmetic
by using K-based operations and that use of dynamic map access
is not overly frequent. However, in future we may decide to
optimize the algorithm further under known guarantees from
branch and value speculation. Latter seems also unclear in
terms of prediction heuristics that today's CPUs apply as well
as whether there could be collisions in e.g. the predictor's
Value History/Pattern Table for triggering out of bounds access,
thus masking is performed unconditionally at this point but could
be subject to relaxation later on. We were generally also
brainstorming various other approaches for mitigation, but the
blocker was always lack of available registers at runtime and/or
overhead for runtime tracking of limits belonging to a specific
pointer. Thus, we found this to be minimally intrusive under
given constraints.

With that in place, a simple example with sanitized access on
unprivileged load at post-verification time looks as follows:

  # bpftool prog dump xlated id 282
  [...]
  28: (79) r1 = *(u64 *)(r7 +0)
  29: (79) r2 = *(u64 *)(r7 +8)
  30: (57) r1 &= 15
  31: (79) r3 = *(u64 *)(r0 +4608)
  32: (57) r3 &= 1
  33: (47) r3 |= 1
  34: (2d) if r2 > r3 goto pc+19
  35: (b4) (u32) r11 = (u32) 20479  |
  36: (1f) r11 -= r2                | Dynamic sanitation for pointer
  37: (4f) r11 |= r2                | arithmetic with registers
  38: (87) r11 = -r11               | containing bounded or known
  39: (c7) r11 s>>= 63              | scalars in order to prevent
  40: (5f) r11 &= r2                | out of bounds speculation.
  41: (0f) r4 += r11                |
  42: (71) r4 = *(u8 *)(r4 +0)
  43: (6f) r4 <<= r1
  [...]

For the case where the scalar sits in the destination register
as opposed to the source register, the following code is emitted
for the above example:

  [...]
  16: (b4) (u32) r11 = (u32) 20479
  17: (1f) r11 -= r2
  18: (4f) r11 |= r2
  19: (87) r11 = -r11
  20: (c7) r11 s>>= 63
  21: (5f) r2 &= r11
  22: (0f) r2 += r0
  23: (61) r0 = *(u32 *)(r2 +0)
  [...]

JIT blinding example with non-conflicting use of r10:

  [...]
   d5:	je     0x0000000000000106    _
   d7:	mov    0x0(%rax),%edi       |
   da:	mov    $0xf153246,%r10d     | Index load from map value and
   e0:	xor    $0xf153259,%r10      | (const blinded) mask with 0x1f.
   e7:	and    %r10,%rdi            |_

   f0:	sub    %rdi,%r10            | Sanitized addition. Both use r10
   f3:	or     %rdi,%r10            | but do not interfere with each
   f6:	neg    %r10                 | other. (Neither do these instructions

   fd:	and    %r10,%rdi            | in interpreter.)
  100:	add    %rax,%rdi            |_
  103:	mov    0x0(%rdi),%eax
 [...]

Tested that it fixes Jann's reproducer, and also checked that test_verifier
and test_progs suite with interpreter, JIT and JIT with hardening enabled
on x86-64 and arm64 runs successfully.

description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel before 4.20.6 performs undesirable out-of-bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic in various cases, including cases of different branches with different state or limits to sanitize, leading to side-channel attacks.

code_evidence: For BPF_ADD, signed bounds are computed via smin_ptr+smin_val and smax_ptr+smax_val; only signed_add_overflows triggers saturation to S64_MIN/S64_MAX, otherwise the sum is stored directly.
Unsigned bounds for BPF_ADD use umin_ptr+umin_val and umax_ptr+umax_val, but overflow is detected only by wrap comparison (sum < operand); the resulting bounds feed later access checks.
For BPF_SUB, signed bounds use smin_ptr-smax_val and smax_ptr-smin_val with signed_sub_overflows saturation.
Unsigned subtraction sets umin_value=0/umax_value=U64_MAX only when umin_ptr < umax_val; otherwise it computes umin_ptr-umax_val and umax_ptr-umin_val, which can underflow/wrap.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-189 (Numeric Errors) covers improper numeric calculation; the function's bound arithmetic and flawed overflow/underflow handling are exactly numeric-calculation weaknesses that corrupt range tracking.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pointer-arithmetic bound propagation performs arithmetic on scalar bounds and relies on incomplete overflow/underflow detection, so computed min/max values can be incorrect. Trigger: a BPF program adds or subtracts a register scalar with bounds near numeric limits to a map-value or stack pointer. Consequence: the verifier's derived bounds no longer reflect the actual runtime offset, weakening out-of-bounds checks and enabling out-of-bounds speculation/access.

description: Unicorn Engine v2.0.0-rc7 and below was discovered to contain a NULL pointer dereference via qemu_ram_free.

code_evidence: phys_mem_alloc returns new_block->host; on allocation failure the function returns immediately at line 10 without registering the block or setting any error state, leaving the caller to proceed with an uninitialized/failed mapping.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to propagate an allocation failure, allowing a NULL host pointer to reach later dereference paths such as qemu_ram_free, matching CWE-476. This is a missing-error-propagation cause rather than an improper resource-release issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an mmap/allocation failure is silently swallowed by the early return at line 10, so the caller believes the RAM block was added while no host mapping exists. Trigger: mapping a large memory region that makes phys_mem_alloc fail, then using/closing the region. Supported consequence: later dereference of the missing host pointer leads to a NULL pointer dereference crash (DoS).

description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An infinite loop was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The infinite loop is triggered when Exiv2 is used to modify the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. Note that this bug is only triggered when deleting the IPTC data, which is a less frequently used Exiv2 operation that requires an extra command line option (`-d I rm`). The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: The main while(!done) loop reads bufMinSize bytes at line 52, requires bufRead==bufMinSize (line 53), then computes marker length size (line 57). At line 165 it seeks size-bufRead relative to the current position; a crafted size smaller than bufRead causes a backward seek, and advanceToMarker() at line 170 may return the same marker again, so done never becomes true.

In the IPTC erase branch, the loop over segments computes start/length from attacker-controlled sizes; when length is zero the read/write at lines 216-219 is skipped but the loop still advances i, so this block itself terminates.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-835: the while(!done) iteration has an exit condition that crafted input can make unreachable because segment length is not constrained relative to bufRead. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the supported consequence is non-termination.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop's exit depends on reaching eoi_ or sos_. With a crafted segment whose declared size is less than the bytes already consumed, the relative seek at line 165 rewinds the stream and advanceToMarker re-reads the same marker, so done stays false and the loop repeats indefinitely, consuming CPU (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix heap buffer overflow in listfdb.c

listfdb reads nGlyphs + 1 glyphs and stores them in an array of size
nGlyphs*sizeof(int), resulting in a heap buffer overflow.

In this commit we replace for(i=0; i<=nGlyphs; ++i)
by for(i=0; i < nGlyphs; ++i) so that only nGlyphs glyphs are read.

This patch addresses CVE-2018-6358 (fixes #104).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  for(i=0; i<=nGlyphs; ++i)'], 'added_lines': ['  for(i=0; i<nGlyphs; ++i)']}
description: The printDefineFont2 function (util/listfdb.c) in libming through 0.4.8 is vulnerable to a heap-based buffer overflow, which may allow attackers to cause a denial of service or unspecified other impact via a crafted FDB file.

code_evidence: nGlyphs is read from the file (line 13), and offset is allocated with exactly nGlyphs*sizeof(int) bytes (line 15).

The loop condition i<=nGlyphs (line 17) allows nGlyphs+1 iterations, so the final iteration writes offset[nGlyphs] (line 23), one element past the allocated buffer. The off value read at lines 19-22 only supplies the stored value; the out-of-bounds index is what overflows.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes offset[i] beyond the malloc'd array, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is a write past the end of a heap buffer, not merely an out-of-bounds read; the fix changes the loop to i<nGlyphs, confirming the off-by-one write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound is inclusive (i<=nGlyphs) while the buffer holds only nGlyphs elements, so the last write at index nGlyphs lands past the heap allocation. Trigger: any FDB file processed by printDefineFont2, with the overflow occurring during the offset-reading loop. Supported consequence: heap corruption that can crash the process (DoS) or potentially enable code execution.

The gd image formats allow for a palette of 256 colors,
so if the transparent index is out of range, disable it.

(cherry picked from commit 0be86e1926939a98afbd2f3a23c673dfc4df2a7c)

description: In the GD Graphics Library (aka LibGD) through 2.2.5, there is a heap-based buffer over-read in tiffWriter in gd_tiff.c. NOTE: the vendor says "In my opinion this issue should not have a CVE, since the GD and GD2 formats are documented to be 'obsolete, and should only be used for development and testing purposes.'

code_evidence: In the non-GD2 branch, the palette transparent index is read from the stream into im->transparent via gdGetWord [28,29], then only a single magic value 257 is rejected [31,32]; all other values, including indices >= 256, are retained as the transparent index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing upper-bound check on a stream-controlled index permits subsequent reads beyond the palette arrays, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not CWE-787 because the supported consequence here is an out-of-range read, not a write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loaded transparent palette index is not constrained to the valid palette range (0..255). Trigger: a crafted GD/GD2 file supplies a transparent index above gdMaxColors. Consequence: later palette lookups using that index read past the end of the color arrays, supporting an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.

code_evidence: Multibyte offset handling computes off from mb_off_next/mb_head_off and adjusts offset, spaces and count; a negative or miscomputed spaces can reach allocation and copy logic.

newp is allocated as STRLEN(oldp)+s_len+count+1 using count, but the post-padding memset writes ts_val-spaces bytes at newp+offset+spaces, and STRMOVE copies the remainder; if count does not match the actual bytes written, the allocation is too small and the writes exceed newp.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of the heap buffer newp because its allocated length does not cover the memset/STRMOVE writes; this is a direct out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-787 rather than a read-only overrun.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation size is derived from count while subsequent memset/STRMOVE writes depend on spaces and ts_val, which can diverge when multibyte offsets or a non-TAB edge character are involved. Trigger: block insert/append over a line where the computed spaces/count mismatch. Consequence: heap buffer overflow (out-of-bounds write) corrupting memory.

commit_msg:
Fix MakerNote tag size overflow issues at read time.

Check for a size overflow while reading tags, which ensures that the
size is always consistent for the given components and type of the
entry, making checking further down superfluous.

This provides an alternate fix for
https://sourceforge.net/p/libexif/bugs/125/ CVE-2016-6328 and for all
the MakerNote types. Likely, this makes both commits 41bd0423 and
89e5b1c1 redundant as it ensures that MakerNote entries are well-formed
when they're populated.

Some improvements on top by Marcus Meissner <marcus@jet.franken.de>

CVE-2020-13112

With a wrapped s the bounds check passes for a small window while the true intended size is much larger, and later code consuming entry->size/entry->data can read past the intended region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unchecked size computation lets the function copy/accept data whose length exceeds the validated buffer extent, resulting in reads past the intended buffer. This is distinct from CWE-190 alone: the overflow is the root cause, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the format*components product at line 50 can overflow size_t, producing an undersized s that is stored as entry size and used for the bounds check at lines 56-57. Trigger: a crafted MakerNote entry with large components and a multi-byte format. Consequence: the check validates the wrong length, allowing the memcpy at line 68 and subsequent entry consumers to read past the buffer end (out-of-bounds read, possible crash/info disclosure).

commit_msg:
When we parse a multi-BSSID element, we might point some
element pointers into the allocated nontransmitted_profile.
However, we free this before returning, causing UAF when the
relevant pointers in the parsed elements are accessed.

Fix this by not allocating the scratch buffer separately but
as part of the returned structure instead, that way, there
are no lifetime issues with it.

The scratch buffer introduction as part of the returned data
here is taken from MLO feature work done by Ilan.

This fixes CVE-2022-42719.

Fixes: 5023b14cf4df ("mac80211: support profile split between elements")
Co-developed-by: Ilan Peer <ilan.peer@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Ilan Peer <ilan.peer@intel.com>
Reviewed-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
Signed-off-by: Johannes Berg <johannes.berg@intel.com>

description: A use-after-free in the mac80211 stack when parsing a multi-BSSID element in the Linux kernel 5.2 through 5.19.x before 5.19.16 could be used by attackers (able to inject WLAN frames) to crash the kernel and potentially execute code.

code_evidence: A separate scratch buffer is allocated with kmalloc(params->len); ieee802_11_find_bssid_profile parses into it, and element pointers in elems may point into this buffer.
A second parse pass reuses nontransmitted_profile as the start of the sub-element parse, so parsed element pointers can reference the scratch buffer.
The scratch buffer is freed with kfree(nontransmitted_profile) before the function returns elems, leaving any element pointers that reference it dangling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because memory is freed while still referenced by the returned elems structure, and those references are used afterward. This is a lifetime bug, not a simple out-of-bounds read, since the pointer remains valid but the backing allocation is released.

evidence_lines.code:
kfree(nontransmitted_profile);
return elems;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the parsed element structure outlives the separately allocated scratch buffer it points into. When a multi-BSSID element causes pointers to be stored into nontransmitted_profile, freeing that buffer at line 47 leaves dangling references; later access to those elements triggers a use-after-free, enabling crash or potential code execution.

description: In multiple functions of MetaDataBase.cpp, there is a possible UAF write due to a race condition. This could lead to remote escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

description: agent/Core/Controller/SendRequest.cpp in Phusion Passenger before 4.0.60 and 5.0.x before 5.0.22, when used in Apache integration mode or in standalone mode without a filtering proxy, allows remote attackers to spoof headers passed to applications by using an _ (underscore) character instead of a - (dash) character in an HTTP header, as demonstrated by an X_User header.

code_evidence: The header loop iterates over req->headers and only skips the three special headers (content-length, content-type, connection) when both the hash and key comparison succeed; at line 97 it continues past them.

For every other header, line 98 emits the literal prefix "HTTP_", then lines 99-105 copy the raw header key and convert it via httpHeaderToScgiUpperCase without checking that the key contains only alphanumeric characters or dashes. An attacker-supplied key such as X_User therefore becomes HTTP_X_USER, colliding with the environment name that a legitimate X-User header would produce.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function receives attacker-controlled header names and fails to validate their allowed character set before using them as symbolic keys, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The missing constraint is the character-class check on header keys, enabling spoofing through equivalent-but-different input names.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates only the three special headers and performs no character validation on general header names before mapping them to CGI/SCGI environment variable names. Trigger: a request containing a header whose name uses '_' instead of '-'. Consequence: the generated environment/header table entry collides with another header's name, allowing the attacker to spoof headers passed to the application.

 0 - -2147483648 cannot be represented in type 'int'

Add a sanity check to catch negative values of nr_wake and nr_requeue.

description: The futex_requeue function in kernel/futex.c in the Linux kernel before 4.14.15 might allow attackers to cause a denial of service (integer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a negative wake or requeue value.

code_evidence: Line 58 computes `task_count - nr_wake < nr_requeue`; if nr_wake is INT_MIN, `task_count - nr_wake` overflows a signed int (the exact UBSAN report).
Lines 90-92 use `task_count - nr_wake >= nr_requeue` as the loop bound; a negative nr_wake/nr_requeue makes this comparison meaningless, so the loop count is not constrained.
Line 101 uses `++task_count <= nr_wake` to decide wake-vs-requeue, relying on nr_wake being non-negative.
Line 133 decrements drop_count in `while (--drop_count >= 0)`, another signed arithmetic path dependent on validated counters.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs signed integer subtraction/addition on nr_wake and nr_requeue that can exceed int range, matching CWE-190's wraparound condition. The added guard `nr_wake < 0 || nr_requeue < 0` confirms the missing constraint was the cause; this is integer overflow rather than a pure logic flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
if (requeue_pi && (task_count - nr_wake < nr_requeue)) {
&key2, &pi_state, nr_requeue);
if (++task_count <= nr_wake && !requeue_pi) {
while (--drop_count >= 0)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nr_wake and nr_requeue are user-influenced int parameters that are used directly in signed arithmetic (`task_count - nr_wake`, `++task_count <= nr_wake`) without a lower-bound check. Trigger: a caller passes a negative value such as INT_MIN, causing signed overflow in `task_count - nr_wake` and skewed loop bounds. Supported consequence: undefined behavior and incorrect requeue/wake accounting, leading to denial of service (the UBSAN-reported overflow and possible instability).

commit_msg:
Validate the rank and number of elements of the `num_bits` tensor for QuantizeAndDequantizeV3.

QuantizeAndDequantizeV3Op, which accepts `num_bits` as a tensor, has a precondition that it should be rank <= 1 and the number of elements should be 1.
This change adds a validation for the Compute() method for this condition.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 463755293
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                errors::InvalidArgument("num_bits is out of range: ", num_bits_,', '                                        " with signed_input_ ", signed_input_));', '      OP_REQUIRES(', '          ctx, input_min_ <= input_max_,', '          errors::InvalidArgument("Invalid range: input_min ", input_min_,'], 'added_lines': ['                InvalidArgument("num_bits is out of range: ", num_bits_,', '                                " with signed_input_ ", signed_input_));', '      OP_REQUIRES(ctx, input_min_ <= input_max_,', '                  InvalidArgument("Invalid range: input_min ", input_min_,']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. If `QuantizeAndDequantizeV3` is given a nonscalar `num_bits` input tensor, it results in a `CHECK` fail that can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit f3f9cb38ecfe5a8a703f2c4a8fead434ef291713. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The constructor reads the num_bits_ attribute and enforces only a numeric range check (0 < num_bits_ < 62/63) via OP_REQUIRES, but never validates the rank or element count of the num_bits tensor.
Similarly, when range_given_ is true, only the ordering input_min_ <= input_max_ is checked; no constraint ties these to tensor shape/rank, so malformed tensor inputs pass construction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing rank/element-count constraint lets attacker-controlled input reach a CHECK/assert that terminates the process, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion). This is a missing-validation root cause distinct from a plain range error; the supported impact is availability loss via crash.

evidence_lines.code:
OP_REQUIRES(
ctx, input_min_ <= input_max_,
errors::InvalidArgument("Invalid range: input_min ", input_min_,
" > input_max ", input_max_));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the op constructor accepts num_bits without checking it is rank <= 1 and has exactly one element, so a nonscalar num_bits tensor passes validation. Trigger: a caller supplies a nonscalar num_bits input tensor to QuantizeAndDequantizeV3. Consequence: downstream code hits a CHECK failure, aborting the process and enabling denial of service.

description: An issue has been found in pdfalto through 0.2. It is a heap-based buffer overflow in the function TextPage::dump in XmlAltoOutputDev.cc.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.1 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.9, the MBIM dissector could crash or exhaust system memory. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-mbim.c by changing the memory-allocation approach.

Trigger: a malformed MBIM packet declaring a huge elem_count with little or no TFT list payload. Consequence: a single packet causes an enormous wmem allocation, exhausting memory or crashing the dissector (availability impact).

If we spot a data or prefetch abort bearing the ESR_EL2.EA bit set, we
know that this is an external abort, and that should crash the guest.

This is part of XSA-201.

description: An issue was discovered in slicer69 doas before 6.2 on certain platforms other than OpenBSD. On platforms without strtonum(3), sscanf was used without checking for error cases. Instead, the uninitialized variable errstr was checked and in some cases returned success even if sscanf failed. The result was that, instead of reporting that the supplied username or group name did not exist, it would execute the command as root.

code_evidence: parsegid first resolves the name via getgrnam and returns 0 on success; if lookup fails it falls through to the numeric conversion path.
On non-OpenBSD platforms the fallback uses sscanf(s, "%d", gid), but the return value is never checked; the subsequent test is on errstr, which is uninitialized on this branch.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-863 fits because a failed lookup/parse is incorrectly reported as an authorized successful resolution, letting execution proceed with an unvalidated group ID instead of rejecting the request. This is a faulty authorization/validation decision, not merely a parsing bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the numeric-ID fallback ignores sscanf's return status and instead checks an uninitialized errstr. Trigger: a supplied group name that is neither resolvable by getgrnam nor parseable as a number. The function returns 0 (success) with an indeterminate *gid, so the caller proceeds as though a valid group was found rather than reporting the missing group, enabling the operation to continue under an unintended identity/authorization context.

description: An out-of-bounds read flaw was found in libsndfile's FLAC codec functionality. An attacker who is able to submit a specially crafted file (via tricking a user to open or otherwise) to an application linked with libsndfile and using the FLAC codec, could trigger an out-of-bounds read that would most likely cause a crash but could potentially leak memory information that could be used in further exploitation of other flaws.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the weakness is reading data past the end of the intended buffer in flac_buffer_copy due to the missing blocksize update. This is an out-of-bounds read, not an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) or buffer reuse alone.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: wbuffer_size is not synchronized with the newly supplied frame's blocksize before flac_buffer_copy consumes pflac->wbuffer. Trigger: a crafted FLAC frame whose blocksize differs from the previously retained wbuffer_size, causing flac_buffer_copy to read beyond the current buffer. Consequence: out-of-bounds read, likely a crash and possible memory information disclosure.

code_evidence: The else-branch sets S.iwidth/S.iheight to S.width/S.height and IO.shrink=0, then allocates imgdata.image with calloc sized by S.raw_width*S.raw_height (line 91). The decoder writes into this buffer via raw_image aliasing (lines 92-95); later lines 110-121 rebind raw_alloc to imgdata.image, so the allocation size is the actual decoder buffer.

commit_msg:

The clump allocator has four allocation functions that use 'number of elements'
and 'size of elements' parameters (rather than a simple 'number of bytes').

Those need specific bounds checking.

description: The gs_alloc_ref_array function in psi/ialloc.c in Artifex Ghostscript 9.21 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PostScript document. This is related to a lack of an integer overflow check in base/gsalloc.c.

code_evidence: The allocation size passed to alloc_obj is computed as (ulong) num_elements * pstype->ssize directly in the call, with no prior range validation of num_elements against pstype->ssize.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's size computation is an unchecked integer multiplication whose wrapped result is then used as an allocation size, matching CWE-190's integer-overflow-in-memory-allocation pattern. A pure missing-bounds-check framing (CWE-1284) would not capture the arithmetic wraparound that produces the undersized allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the element count (uint num_elements) is multiplied by the element size (pstype->ssize) and cast to ulong without checking whether the product fits; a crafted count can wrap the multiplication to a small value. Trigger: a PostScript document supplying a large num_elements. Consequence: alloc_obj receives an undersized byte count, so the buffer is too small for the number of elements the caller believes were allocated, enabling a heap-based buffer overflow and crash.

description: The kernel in Amazon Web Services FreeRTOS before 10.4.3 has insufficient bounds checking during management of heap memory.

Consequence: the size wraps, passes the bounds check, and the returned pointer/split block are computed from a size inconsistent with the actual heap block, giving a buffer outside the intended bounds.

description: Buffer overflow in the PixarLogDecode function in tif_pixarlog.c in LibTIFF 4.0.6 and earlier allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted TIFF image, as demonstrated by overwriting the vgetparent function pointer with rgb2ycbcr.

commit_msg:
Bug#24388746: PRIVILEGE ESCALATION AND RACE CONDITION USING CREATE TABLE

During REPAIR TABLE of a MyISAM table, a temporary data file (.TMD)
is created. When repair finishes, this file is renamed to the original
.MYD file. The problem was that during this rename, we copied the
stats from the old file to the new file with chmod/chown. If a user
managed to replace the temporary file before chmod/chown was executed,
it was possible to get an arbitrary file with the privileges of the
mysql user.

This patch fixes the problem by not copying stats from the old
file to the new file. This is not needed as the new file was
created with the correct stats. This fix only changes server
behavior - external utilities such as myisamchk still does
chmod/chown.

No test case provided since the problem involves synchronization
with file system operations.

description: Race condition in Oracle MySQL before 5.5.52, 5.6.x before 5.6.33, 5.7.x before 5.7.15, and 8.x before 8.0.1; MariaDB before 5.5.52, 10.0.x before 10.0.28, and 10.1.x before 10.1.18; Percona Server before 5.5.51-38.2, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-78-1, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-8; and Percona XtraDB Cluster before 5.5.41-37.0, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-25.17, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-26.17 allows local users with certain permissions to gain privileges by leveraging use of my_copystat by REPAIR TABLE to repair a MyISAM table.

code_evidence: Repair paths are invoked with the new FALSE flag, so the temporary data file is no longer chmod/chown'ed to copy stats from the old file.
change_to_newfile renames the temporary data file into place; the prior stat-copying window is what the commit removes.
The recreated-index repair path also passes FALSE, avoiding stat copying on that temp file.
mi_sort_index is likewise called with FALSE, so no stat copy occurs during index sort.
The final rename of the new data file (with optional backup) is the operation the fix makes safe by removing the preceding stat copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because a shared filesystem resource (the temporary file) is accessed non-atomically: creation, stat copy and rename are separate steps, and an interfering sequence can replace the file between them. The window is a timing/exclusivity violation, matching concurrent execution on a shared resource; the privilege gain is the downstream consequence.

error=mi_repair_by_sort(param,info,filename,rep_quick);
error=mi_repair_parallel(param,info,filename,rep_quick);

error|=change_to_newfile(filename, MI_NAME_DEXT, DATA_TMP_EXT, MYF(0));
if (mi_open_datafile(info,info->s, NULL, -1))
error=mi_repair_by_sort(param,info,filename,1);
error=mi_sort_index(param,info,filename);

error|=change_to_newfile(filename,MI_NAME_DEXT,DATA_TMP_EXT,
MYF(MY_REDEL_MAKE_BACKUP) : MYF(0)));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: repair created a temporary .TMD file, then copied old-file stats onto it via chmod/chown before renaming it to the original .MYD. Trigger: a local user with permissions races to replace the temporary file between creation and the chmod/chown. Consequence: the attacker's file receives mysql-user privileges, enabling privilege escalation. The patch removes the stat copy (FALSE) so no privileged chmod/chown follows temp-file creation.

description: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in WebKit/Source/platform/v8_inspector/V8Debugger.cpp in Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 53.0.2785.89 on Windows and OS X and before 53.0.2785.92 on Linux, allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML into the Developer Tools (aka DevTools) subsystem via a crafted web site, aka "Universal XSS (UXSS)."

commit_msg:
crypto: fix af_alg_make_sg() conversion to iov_iter

Commit 1d10eb2f156f ("crypto: switch af_alg_make_sg() to iov_iter")
broke af_alg_make_sg() and skcipher_recvmsg() in the process of moving
them to the iov_iter interfaces.  The 'npages' calculation in the formar
calculated the number of *bytes* in the pages, and in the latter case
the conversion didn't re-read the value of 'ctx->used' after waiting for
it to become non-zero.

This reverts to the original code for both these cases.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

commit_msg: Fix bug #71637: Multiple Heap Overflow due to integer overflows

commit_msg:
x86: limit GFNs to 32 bits for shadowed superpages.

Superpage shadows store the shadowed GFN in the backpointer field,
which for non-BIGMEM builds is 32 bits wide.  Shadowing a superpage
mapping of a guest-physical address above 2^44 would lead to the GFN
being truncated there, and a crash when we come to remove the shadow
from the hash table.

Track the valid width of a GFN for each guest, including reporting it
through CPUID, and enforce it in the shadow pagetables.  Set the
maximum witth to 32 for guests where this truncation could occur.

This is XSA-173.

Reported-by: Ling Liu <liuling-it@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        {', '#if GUEST_PAGING_LEVELS == 2', '            /*', '             * Note that _PAGE_INVALID_BITS is zero in this case, yielding a', '             * no-op here.', '             *', '             * Architecturally, the walk should fail if bit 21 is set (others', "             * aren't being checked at least in PSE36 mode), but we'll ignore", '             * this here in order to avoid specifying a non-natural, non-zero', '             * _PAGE_INVALID_BITS value just for that case.', '             */', '#endif', '        }'], 'added_lines': ['', '    /* If this guest has a restricted physical address space then the', '     * target GFN must fit within it. */', '    if ( !(rc & _PAGE_PRESENT)', '         && gfn_x(guest_l1e_get_gfn(gw->l1e)) >> d->arch.paging.gfn_bits )', '        rc |= _PAGE_INVALID_BITS;', '']}
description: Integer overflow in the x86 shadow pagetable code in Xen allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host crash) or possibly gain privileges by shadowing a superpage mapping.

code_evidence: The 2MB superpage path extracts the GFN into start and only rejects it via _PAGE_INVALID_BITS when gfn_x(start) & GUEST_L2_GFN_MASK & ~0x1 is nonzero; there is no check that the resulting GFN fits the guest's valid physical address width.
The shadow L1 entry is then synthesized from a truncated GFN: start = (gfn_x(start) & ~GUEST_L2_GFN_MASK) + guest_l1_table_offset(va), and guest_l1e_from_gfn stores that value as the backpointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The description attributes host crash or possible privilege gain to a guest-controlled superpage mapping being shadowed without enforcing the GFN width limit, i.e., a failure to constrain a security-relevant resource (the GFN/backpointer) leading to privilege impact; this aligns with CWE-264's permissions/privileges scope. It is not merely a benign arithmetic error, since the missing width constraint enables the privilege-relevant consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
start = _gfn((gfn_x(start) & ~GUEST_L2_GFN_MASK) +
guest_l1_table_offset(va));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the superpage GFN is not constrained to the guest's gfn_bits width before being encoded into the shadow L1 entry's backpointer. Trigger: a guest maps a 2MB superpage whose GFN exceeds the shadow backpointer width (above 2^44 in non-BIGMEM builds), so the stored GFN is truncated. Consequence: the truncated backpointer no longer matches the original mapping, causing a host crash when the shadow is later removed from the hash table, or potentially privilege gain.

commit_msg:
XFS always inherits the SGID bit if it is set on the parent inode, while
the generic inode_init_owner does not do this in a few cases where it can
create a possible security problem, see commit 0fa3ecd87848
("Fix up non-directory creation in SGID directories") for details.

Switch XFS to use the generic helper for the normal path to fix this,
just keeping the simple field inheritance open coded for the case of the
non-sgid case with the bsdgrpid mount option.

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
Reported-by: Christian Brauner <christian.brauner@ubuntu.com>
Signed-off-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Reviewed-by: Darrick J. Wong <djwong@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Darrick J. Wong <djwong@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tinode->i_mode = mode;', '\tinode->i_uid = current_fsuid();', '\tif (pip && XFS_INHERIT_GID(pip)) {', '\t\tinode->i_gid = VFS_I(pip)->i_gid;', '\t\tif ((VFS_I(pip)->i_mode & S_ISGID) && S_ISDIR(mode))', '\t\t\tinode->i_mode |= S_ISGID;', '\t\tinode->i_gid = current_fsgid();'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct inode\t\t*dir = pip ? VFS_I(pip) : NULL;', '\tif (dir && !(dir->i_mode & S_ISGID) &&', '\t    (mp->m_flags & XFS_MOUNT_GRPID)) {', '\t\tinode->i_uid = current_fsuid();', '\t\tinode->i_gid = dir->i_gid;', '\t\tinode->i_mode = mode;', '\t\tinode_init_owner(inode, dir, mode);']}
description: A vulnerability was found in the fs/inode.c:inode_init_owner() function logic of the LInux kernel that allows local users to create files for the XFS file-system with an unintended group ownership and with group execution and SGID permission bits set, in a scenario where a directory is SGID and belongs to a certain group and is writable by a user who is not a member of this group. This can lead to excessive permissions granted in case when they should not. This vulnerability is similar to the previous CVE-2018-13405 and adds the missed fix for the XFS.

code_evidence: Line 27 sets the new inode's mode directly from the caller-supplied mode, and line 29 unconditionally sets i_uid to current_fsuid(). Lines 32-35 inherit the parent's group via XFS_INHERIT_GID and only add S_ISGID when the parent is SGID and the new mode is a directory; for non-directory creation the SGID bit inherited through the group is not cleared and the creator's own fsuid is retained.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to enforce the intended ownership/permission policy for inode creation, producing files with privileges the creator should not obtain; this is an incorrect restriction of access to a resource, matching CWE-284. It is not merely a resource-lifetime or memory issue, since the defect is in access-control specification/enforcement of inherited ownership and permission bits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the inode-creation path assigns ownership and mode bits without applying the generic SGID-directory constraint that forbids a non-member from creating a file in a group-writable SGID directory. Trigger: a local user who is not a member of the directory's group creates a file in an SGID, group-writable directory. Consequence: the new file receives the directory's group and SGID/group-execute bits, granting unintended privileges to unauthorized actors.

commit_msg: Fix bug #73192

commit_msg:
Prevent replicas from sending commands that interact with keyspace (#8868)

This solves an issue reported in #8712 in which a replica would bypass
the client write pause check and cause an assertion due to executing a
write command during failover.

The fact is that we don't expect replicas to execute any command other
than maybe REPLCONF and PING, etc. but matching against the ADMIN
command flag is insufficient, so instead i just block keyspace access
for now.

(cherry picked from commit 46f4ebbe842620f0976a36741a72482620aa4b48)

description: Redis before 6cbea7d allows a replica to cause an assertion failure in a primary server by sending a non-administrative command (specifically, a SET command). NOTE: this was fixed for Redis 6.2.x and 7.x in 2021. Versions before 6.2 were not intended to have safety guarantees related to this.

code_evidence: Lines 29-38 derive is_write_command and is_may_replicate_command from the client's command flags, including the EXEC/MULTI state, so the code classifies commands that touch the keyspace.
Lines 187-194 exempt clients with CLIENT_SLAVE from the client-pause blocking path, so a replica connection is never blocked by the pause check regardless of the command it issues.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit explicitly targets a replica bypassing the client pause check and causing an assertion failure in the primary, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion): an attacker-controlled input path (replica-issued SET) triggers an assert that exits the server. It is not merely an authorization weakness because the demonstrated impact is an assertion-driven crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: processCommand computes whether a command writes or may replicate, but the pause check at lines 187-194 skips blocking entirely for CLIENT_SLAVE clients. A replica can therefore submit a keyspace command (e.g., SET) that bypasses the client write pause; the primary then executes it during a failover window, reaching an assertion (serverAssert) that aborts the server. The root cause is the missing keyspace-access restriction for replica clients; the consequence is a reachable assertion causing a crash/DoS.

code_evidence: Case 16 reads the frame count from the file into Frames at line 119 without checking that it is nonzero; the value is used unchecked later.

The frame loop at 362-367 reuses the header state and jumps back to NEXT_FRAME, so an invalid zero frame count drives repeated processing rather than a clean exit.

Trigger: a crafted MAT file with DimFlag 16 and Frames=0. Because Frames is unsigned, --Frames underflows to a huge count, so the NEXT_FRAME loop is re-entered repeatedly, leading to a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
Avoid some undefined pointer arithmetic

A common idiom in the codebase is:

if (p + len > limit)
{
    return; /* Too long */
}

Where "p" points to some malloc'd data of SIZE bytes and
limit == p + SIZE

"len" here could be from some externally supplied data (e.g. from a TLS
message).

The rules of C pointer arithmetic are such that "p + len" is only well
defined where len <= SIZE. Therefore the above idiom is actually
undefined behaviour.

For example this could cause problems if some malloc implementation
provides an address for "p" such that "p + len" actually overflows for
values of len that are too big and therefore p + len < limit!

Issue reported by Guido Vranken.

CVE-2016-2177

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (data >= (d + n - 2))', '    if (data + length != d + n) {', '    while (data <= (d + n - 4)) {', '        if (data + size > (d + n))'], 'added_lines': ['    if ((d + n) - data <= 2)', '    if ((d + n) - data != length) {', '    while ((d + n) - data >= 4) {', '        if ((d + n) - data < size)']}
description: OpenSSL through 1.0.2h incorrectly uses pointer arithmetic for heap-buffer boundary checks, which might allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (integer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging unexpected malloc behavior, related to s3_srvr.c, ssl_sess.c, and t1_lib.c.

code_evidence: The bounds checks use pointer arithmetic on externally supplied data: line 22 tests data >= (d + n - 2), line 25 compares data + length to d + n, line 29 loops while data <= (d + n - 4), and line 32 tests data + size > (d + n). Here d+n is the end pointer of a malloc'd buffer of n bytes and length/size derive from the TLS message, so d+n and data+length/size are computed outside the array's valid range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked arithmetic on externally supplied length/size can wrap when computing the end address, defeating the boundary comparison — an integer overflow/wraparound (CWE-190). It is not a mere off-by-one (CWE-193) because the failure is the wrapped/undefined sum, not an incorrect boundary constant.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pointer arithmetic d + n, data + length and data + size is only well-defined when the offset stays within the allocation; oversized length/size from the peer violates that and is undefined behavior. A malloc address near the top of the address space can make the sum wrap to a small value, so the boundary check passes and parsing reads out of bounds, causing a crash or memory corruption (DoS).

description: mediaserver in Android 6.x before 2016-03-01 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, related to decoder/ih264d_parse_islice.c and decoder/ih264d_parse_pslice.c, aka internal bug 25928803.

code_evidence: After parsing a macroblock, u1_num_mbs is incremented and the total coded-MB counter u2_total_mbs_coded is incremented once per iteration, before the transfer/group-flush decision is evaluated.

The transfer block at lines 106-123 flushes u1_num_mbs macroblocks via ih264d_parse_tfr_nmb/ih264d_decode_recon_tfr_nmb and then resets u1_num_mbs to 0 when u1_tfr_n_mb is set; u1_mb_idx and ps_dec->u1_mb_idx are updated accordingly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function maintains buffer indices and counters that gate writes to ps_nmb_info/ps_deblk_mbn and the transfer buffers; mis-tracking u2_total_mbs_coded causes subsequent operations to exceed the intended buffer bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds read/write. This is a buffer-bounds consequence rather than, e.g., a pure integer-overflow label.

evidence_lines.code:
u1_num_mbs++;
ps_dec->u2_total_mbs_coded++;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the total-MB counter was advanced per parsed macroblock rather than by the number of macroblocks actually transferred, so the counter diverges from the buffer/group state maintained by u1_num_mbs and u1_mb_idx. Trigger: crafted slice data that causes group flushes (u1_tfr_n_mb) at varying counts. The stale count feeds later bounds checks (e.g., max_mb_addr comparisons) and can permit out-of-bounds writes into the MB/deblock buffers, resulting in memory corruption.

Do not share key mappings with JNI object

The key mapping information between the native key mappings and
the KeyCharacterMap object available in Java is currently shared,
which means that a read can be attempted while it's being modified.

(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:3d993de0d1ada8065d1fe561f690c8f82b6a7d4b)

description: In android_view_InputDevice_create of android_view_InputDevice.cpp, there is a possible way to execute arbitrary code due to a use after free. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: The function passes deviceInfo.getKeyCharacterMap() directly into android_view_KeyCharacterMap_create, handing a pointer to the shared KeyCharacterMap instance to JNI/Java without copying or ownership transfer. The commit message states this mapping is shared and can be read while it is being modified.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the exposed reference can outlive the shared KeyCharacterMap's allocation, and later Java-side access dereferences freed memory. This is a lifetime/ownership flaw, not merely a data race, which is why the fix copies the map before sharing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shared KeyCharacterMap object is exposed to Java without a private copy, so its lifetime is not controlled by the JNI wrapper. If the native side frees or replaces the shared instance while Java still references it, subsequent reads through the Java object access freed memory, enabling use-after-free that can lead to arbitrary code execution and local privilege escalation.

+++ func_after
@@ -1,6 +1,19 @@

-    return !memcmp(a, b, sizeof *a

description: In ovs versions v0.90.0 through v2.5.0 are vulnerable to heap buffer over-read in flow.c. An unsafe comparison of “minimasks” function could lead access to an unmapped region of memory. This vulnerability is capable of crashing the software, memory modification, and possible remote execution.

code_evidence: The function computes the comparison length as sizeof *a + MINIFLOW_VALUES_SIZE(miniflow_n_values(&a->masks)), i.e. the size derived solely from minimask 'a', and passes it to a single memcmp over both 'a' and 'b'. If 'b' has a smaller value array than 'a', memcmp reads past the end of 'b'.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the single memcmp reads data past the end of the intended buffer when 'b' is shorter than the length computed from 'a'; the consequence is a read of adjacent/unmapped memory. This is an out-of-bounds read, not an out-of-bounds write.

evidence_lines.code:
return !memcmp(a, b, sizeof *a
+ MINIFLOW_VALUES_SIZE(miniflow_n_values(&a->masks)));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the memcmp length is based only on 'a' and applied to 'b', with no check that the two minimasks have equal lengths. Trigger: comparing minimasks with differing numbers of values, as in strict flow deletion. Consequence: memcmp reads beyond the allocated region of the shorter object, causing an out-of-bounds read and possible crash.

description: KernelSU is a Kernel based root solution for Android. Starting in version 0.6.1 and prior to version 0.7.0, if a KernelSU installed device is infected with a malware whose app signing block specially constructed, it can take over root privileges on the device. The vulnerable verification logic actually obtains the signature of the last block with an id of `0x7109871a`, while the verification logic during Android installation is to obtain the first one. In addition to the actual signature upgrade that has been fixed (KSU thought it was V2 but was actually V3), there is also the problem of actual signature downgrading (KSU thought it was V2 but was actually V1). Find a condition in the signature verification logic that will cause the signature not to be found error, and KernelSU does not implement the same conditions, so KSU thinks there is a V2 signature, but the APK signature verification actually uses the V1 signature. This issue is fixed in version 0.7.0. As workarounds, keep the KernelSU manager installed and avoid installing unknown apps.

code_evidence: When the APK signing block contains an id of 0x7109871a, the loop overwrites v2_signing_valid with the result of check_block for that block; it records no count and does not reject additional matching blocks.

The signing-block loop reads each size/id pair and advances pos by (size8 - offset); the last v2 block encountered therefore determines v2_signing_valid, matching the described 'last block' selection rather than the first.
After the loop, the function only rejects v3/v3.1 schemes and returns v2_signing_valid; it performs no check that exactly one v2 block exists and no cross-check against a V1 signature file.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-863 fits because the function implements an authorization gate (manager signature verification) but performs the check incorrectly: the 'last block wins' selection and missing single-block/V1 constraints let an attacker bypass the intended signer restriction. This is an incorrect authorization check rather than a pure parsing flaw, since the defect directly defeats the signer-based privilege decision.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The signature-authorization decision is derived from whichever 0x7109871a block is processed last, and the function never verifies that exactly one such block exists or that no V1 signature is present. An attacker crafting an APK with a specially constructed signing block can make this verification accept a V2 result while Android's installer uses a different signature (first V2 block or V1), so the root-privilege authorization check is satisfied by the wrong signer.

commit_msg:
Prevent division by 0 in `resource_variable_ops.cc`

PiperOrigin-RevId: 387939939
Change-Id: Ib04902d63756633999959a70613f2eaa30c2c151
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void AddBatchOffsets(Tensor* indices, const Tensor& params) {'], 'added_lines': ['void AddBatchOffsets(OpKernelContext* ctx, Tensor* indices,', '                       const Tensor& params) {', '    OP_REQUIRES(', '        ctx, batch_size != 0,', '        errors::InvalidArgument(', '            "Inner size of indices would result in batch_size of 0 and a ",', '            "division by 0 in the implementation. This is illegal"));']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions an attacker can trigger a crash via a floating point exception in `tf.raw_ops.ResourceGather`. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/f24faa153ad31a4b51578f8181d3aaab77a1ddeb/tensorflow/core/kernels/resource_variable_ops.cc#L725-L731) computes the value of a value, `batch_size`, and then divides by it without checking that this value is not 0. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit ac117ee8a8ea57b73d34665cdf00ef3303bc0b11. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: AddBatchOffsets computes batch_size by multiplying params.dim_size(idx) over batch_dims_ starting from 1; if any batch dimension is zero, batch_size becomes 0. Line 6 then divides indices->NumElements() by batch_size without any guard.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 directly matches the unguarded division where the divisor batch_size can be zero. The pre-patch function lacks any check, unlike the patch which adds OP_REQUIRES batch_size != 0. This is a divide-by-zero, not merely an out-of-bounds index issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: batch_size is derived from attacker-influenced tensor dimensions and can be 0 when a batch dimension has size zero. Trigger: calling ResourceGather with such params reaches the unguarded division on line 6. Consequence: integer division by zero raises a floating point exception and crashes the process, an availability DoS.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                goto not_found;', '', '        if (e - p > HOST_NAME_MAX - 1)  /* -1 for the last dash */']}
description: Stack-based buffer overflow in the getpwnam and getgrnam functions of the NSS module nss-mymachines in systemd.

code_evidence: The name is parsed: strrchr finds the last dash, e==p is rejected, then strndupa(p, e - p) allocates a stack buffer whose length equals the machine-name length with no upper bound check.
The length of name drives the required buffer size l; if buflen is sufficient, memzero(buffer, sizeof(char*)) then strcpy(buffer + sizeof(char*), name) writes the full name into the caller buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies an unbounded attacker-influenced name into fixed/stack buffers, producing writes outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119. The missing length constraint is the cause; the out-of-bounds write is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the machine-name length extracted from name is not bounded by HOST_NAME_MAX before strndupa copies it to a stack buffer, and the downstream strcpy copies the full name. Trigger: a getgrnam request with an overlong vg-<machine>-<gid> name. Consequence: out-of-bounds stack writes via strndupa/strcpy, causing memory corruption.

A crafted pcap with an oversize caplen causes read(fd, &buf, caplen) to write past the 10000-byte stack buffer, and the subsequent checksum over caplen bytes operates on that out-of-bounds region. commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/524
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (ept_info.postscript_length > GetBlobSize(image))', '    ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"ImproperImageHeader");', '  if (ept_info.tiff_length > GetBlobSize(image))', '    ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"ImproperImageHeader");']}
description: The ReadEPTImage function in coders/ept.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.9-0 and 7.x before 7.0.6-1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Lines 33 and 37 read attacker-controlled 32-bit postscript_length and tiff_length directly from the file header with no bound check against the actual blob size.
Lines 39-44 allocate postscript_length+1 bytes via AcquireQuantumMemory and then zero that entire buffer; lines 45-54 do the same for tiff_length.
The allocated sizes are driven solely by the header fields, so a crafted file can request arbitrarily large allocations and full-buffer zeroing per image.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is uncontrolled consumption of the memory resource driven by unvalidated attacker input, which is the core of CWE-400; the missing size constraint allows allocation proportional to an unbounded header value rather than the actual file size.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reader trusts the declared postscript_length and tiff_length without comparing them to the available blob size or a resource limit. Trigger: a crafted EPT file with huge length fields causes AcquireQuantumMemory to allocate and ResetMagickMemory to touch gigabytes of memory, exhausting memory and causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow in build_read_multi_rsp

Local variables tracking structure size in build_read_multi_rsp are of
uint16 type but accept a full uint16 range from function arguments while
appending a fixed-length offset.  This can lead to an integer overflow
and unexpected behavior.

Change the locals to size_t, and add a check during reasssignment.

Bug: 273966636
Test: atest bluetooth_test_gd_unit, net_test_stack_btm
Tag: #security
Ignore-AOSP-First: Security
(cherry picked from commit 70a4d628fa016a9487fae07f211644b95e1f0000)
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:badb8ffce06b517cbcfdbfa68cb7b7e02d22494a)
Merged-In: I3a74bdb0d003cb6bf4f282615be8c68836676715
Change-Id: I3a74bdb0d003cb6bf4f282615be8c68836676715
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  uint16_t ii, total_len, len;', '            "multi read overflow available len=%d val_len=%d", len,', '        memcpy(p, p_rsp->attr_value.value, len);', '        if (!is_overflow) p += len;', '        p_buf->len += len;'], 'added_lines': ['  uint16_t ii;', '  size_t total_len, len;', '            "multi read overflow available len=%zu val_len=%d", len,', '        // check for possible integer overflow', '        if (p_buf->len + len <= UINT16_MAX) {', '          memcpy(p, p_rsp->attr_value.value, len);', '          if (!is_overflow) p += len;', '          p_buf->len += len;', '        } else {', '          p_cmd->status = GATT_NOT_FOUND;', '          break;', '        }']}
description: In build_read_multi_rsp of gatt_sr.cc, there is a possible out of bounds write due to an integer overflow. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: Local counters total_len and len are declared as uint16_t, so arithmetic on them wraps at 65536 rather than growing.

total_len is computed as p_buf->len + p_rsp->attr_value.len (plus 2 for variable length); the mtu comparison and the len = attr_value.len - (total_len - mtu) subtraction operate on this possibly-wrapped value.
p_buf->len is incremented by len after the memcpy(p, ..., len) at line 46; with wrapped len values the tracked length and the write offset p diverge from the real buffer extent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs size arithmetic in uint16_t and uses the wrapped result as a copy length and buffer-length update, matching CWE-190 integer overflow/wraparound. The resulting memory corruption is the downstream consequence, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code: uint16_t ii, total_len, len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: 16-bit total_len/len cannot represent the full sum of accumulated response length and attribute length, so the size computation wraps. Trigger: a multi-read request whose combined attribute lengths exceed 65535 causes the mtu check and len subtraction to use a wrapped value. Consequence: memcpy writes len bytes and p_buf->len advances inconsistently, producing an out-of-bounds write in the allocated buffer.

commit_msg: Suspend exception processing if there are too many exceptions
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (CheckMemoryOverflow(count,quantum) != MagickFalse)'], 'added_lines': ['  if (HeapOverflowSanityCheck(count,quantum) != MagickFalse)']}
description: magick/memory.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-5 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via vectors involving "too many exceptions," which trigger a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Line 6 calls CheckMemoryOverflow(count,quantum) to guard against integer overflow before computing the extent; if it reports overflow, lines 7-10 free the buffer and return NULL. Otherwise line 11 computes extent=count*quantum and line 12 passes it to ResizeMagickMemory. The guard is the only bound check between the multiplication and the resize.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes a buffer extent and reallocates based on it, so a missed integer-overflow guard leads directly to operations outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119. The underlying arithmetic flaw is integer overflow, but the supported consequence here is out-of-bounds buffer access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the overflow check (CheckMemoryOverflow) is replaced/relies on a weaker sanity check, so when count*quantum overflows the size_t multiplication the guard may not fire. The wrapped extent on line 11 is then used by ResizeMagickMemory on line 12, producing an undersized allocation relative to the intended buffer. Trigger: attacker-controlled count/quantum near the overflow threshold. Consequence: subsequent accesses exceed the allocated buffer, yielding out-of-bounds memory operations (crash/DoS, memory corruption).

commit_msg:
nl80211_set_rekey_data() does not check if the required attributes
NL80211_REKEY_DATA_{REPLAY_CTR,KEK,KCK} are present when processing
NL80211_CMD_SET_REKEY_OFFLOAD request. This request can be issued by
users with CAP_NET_ADMIN privilege and may result in NULL dereference
and a system crash. Add a check for the required attributes presence.
This patch is based on the patch by bo Zhang.

This fixes CVE-2017-12153.

References: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1491046
Fixes: e5497d766ad ("cfg80211/nl80211: support GTK rekey offload")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v3.1-rc1
Reported-by: bo Zhang <zhangbo5891001@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Vladis Dronov <vdronov@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Johannes Berg <johannes.berg@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!tb[NL80211_REKEY_DATA_REPLAY_CTR] || !tb[NL80211_REKEY_DATA_KEK] ||', '\t    !tb[NL80211_REKEY_DATA_KCK])', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;']}
description: A security flaw was discovered in the nl80211_set_rekey_data() function in net/wireless/nl80211.c in the Linux kernel through 4.13.3. This function does not check whether the required attributes are present in a Netlink request. This request can be issued by a user with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability and may result in a NULL pointer dereference and system crash.

code_evidence: The function only verifies that the outer NL80211_ATTR_REKEY_DATA attribute exists, then parses the nested attributes into tb; it never checks that the individual required entries tb[NL80211_REKEY_DATA_REPLAY_CTR], tb[NL80211_REKEY_DATA_KEK], and tb[NL80211_REKEY_DATA_KCK] are present.
nla_len() is called directly on each tb[...] entry without a prior NULL check; if a nested attribute is absent, its array slot remains NULL and nla_len dereferences it.
nla_data() similarly dereferences tb[NL80211_REKEY_DATA_KEK], tb[NL80211_REKEY_DATA_KCK], and tb[NL80211_REKEY_DATA_REPLAY_CTR] to build rekey_data, again assuming non-NULL entries.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is precisely a NULL pointer dereference: a pointer expected to be valid (the parsed nested attribute) is NULL and is dereferenced without a check. This is CWE-476 rather than a missing-validation category, since the supported consequence is the NULL dereference crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing presence validation of mandatory nested Netlink attributes after nla_parse_nested. Trigger: a CAP_NET_ADMIN user sends NL80211_CMD_SET_REKEY_OFFLOAD with NL80211_ATTR_REKEY_DATA lacking one of REPLAY_CTR/KEK/KCK. The absent slot is NULL, so nla_len()/nla_data() dereference it, causing a kernel NULL pointer dereference and system crash (DoS).
