commit_msg:
cuse: fix memory leak

The problem is that fuse_dev_alloc() acquires an extra reference to cc.fc,
and the original ref count is never dropped.

Reported-by: Colin Ian King <colin.king@canonical.com>
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <miklos@szeredi.hu>
Fixes: cc080e9e9be1 ("fuse: introduce per-instance fuse_dev structure")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v4.2+
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Base reference is now owned by "fud" */', '\tfuse_conn_put(&cc->fc);']}
description: Memory leak in the cuse_channel_release function in fs/fuse/cuse.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by opening /dev/cuse many times.

code_evidence: The function obtains fud from file->private_data and derives cc from fud->fc, tying the connection's lifetime to the file release path.
The only connection cleanup performed is fuse_dev_release(inode, file); no explicit fuse_conn_put(&cc->fc) is issued before returning.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 covers resource management errors, and here the resource (fuse_conn reference/memory) is acquired but not released on the release path. This is a reference-count leak rather than a use-after-free or double-free, matching improper resource lifetime handling.

evidence_lines.code:
struct fuse_dev *fud = file->private_data;
struct cuse_conn *cc = fc_to_cc(fud->fc);
rc = fuse_dev_release(inode, file);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The release path drops the device reference via fuse_dev_release but never releases the base connection reference held for cc->fc. Each open of /dev/cuse followed by close therefore leaves the fuse_conn reference count elevated, so the connection object is never freed; repeated opens accumulate unreleased memory, supporting a resource-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg:
NetLabel: correct CIPSO tag handling when adding new DOI definitions

The current netlbl_cipsov4_add_common() function has two problems which are
fixed with this patch.  The first is an off-by-one bug where it is possibile to
overflow the doi_def->tags[] array.  The second is a bug where the same
doi_def->tags[] array was not always fully initialized, which caused sporadic
failures.

Signed-off-by: Paul Moore <paul.moore@hp.com>
Signed-off-by: James Morris <jmorris@namei.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (iter > CIPSO_V4_TAG_MAXCNT)', '\tif (iter < CIPSO_V4_TAG_MAXCNT)', '\t\tdoi_def->tags[iter] = CIPSO_V4_TAG_INVALID;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (iter >= CIPSO_V4_TAG_MAXCNT)', '\twhile (iter < CIPSO_V4_TAG_MAXCNT)', '\t\tdoi_def->tags[iter++] = CIPSO_V4_TAG_INVALID;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 2.6.20, there is an off-by-one bug in net/netlabel/netlabel_cipso_v4.c where it is possible to overflow the doi_def->tags[] array.

code_evidence: The bounds check uses 'iter > CIPSO_V4_TAG_MAXCNT', so iter equal to CIPSO_V4_TAG_MAXCNT passes the check. The next line then writes doi_def->tags[iter++] with iter == CIPSO_V4_TAG_MAXCNT, one past the last valid index of the tags[] array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to doi_def->tags[] outside its intended boundary, which is a memory-buffer out-of-bounds write matching CWE-119. The missing constraint is the correct upper-bound comparison; this is not merely an uninitialized-read issue, as the same array is also written past its end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an off-by-one boundary check (strict > instead of >=) before indexing doi_def->tags[]. A nested NLBL_CIPSOV4_A_TAG attribute list containing CIPSO_V4_TAG_MAXCNT+1 tag entries drives iter to the array size and triggers an out-of-bounds write, corrupting adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
Bug 739133 - (CVE-2017-17785) Heap overflow while parsing FLI files.

It is possible to trigger a heap overflow while parsing FLI files. The
RLE decoder is vulnerable to out of boundary writes due to lack of
boundary checks.

The variable "framebuf" points to a memory area which was allocated
with fli_header->width * fli_header->height bytes. The RLE decoder
therefore must never write beyond that limit.

If an illegal frame is detected, the parser won't stop, which means
that the next valid sequence is properly parsed again. This should
allow GIMP to parse FLI files as good as possible even if they are
broken by an attacker or by accident.

While at it, I changed the variable xc to be of type size_t, because
the multiplication of width and height could overflow a 16 bit type.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tunsigned short xc, pc, pcnt, lpf, lpn;', '\t\t\txc+=skip;', '\t\t\t\twhile (ps>0) {', '\t\t\t\tfread(&(pos[xc]), ps, 2, f);', '\t\t\t\txc+=ps << 1;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tunsigned short pc, pcnt, lpf, lpn;', '\t\tsize_t n, xc;', '\t\tyc=MIN(yc, fli_header->height);', '\t\tn=(size_t)fli_header->width * (fli_header->height-yc);', '\t\t\txc+=MIN(n-xc,skip);', '\t\t\t\twhile (ps>0 && xc+1<n) {', '\t\t\t\tsize_t len;', '\t\t\t\tlen=MIN((n-xc)/2,ps);', '\t\t\t\tfread(&(pos[xc]), len, 2, f);', '\t\t\t\txc+=len << 1;']}
description: In GIMP 2.8.22, there is a heap-based buffer overflow in the fli_read_brun function in plug-ins/file-fli/fli.c.

code_evidence: xc is an unsigned short, so skip/ps arithmetic can wrap and exceed the frame buffer bounds.
pos is derived from framebuf plus width*yc with no check that yc stays within height.
skip is added to xc without any bound on xc relative to the row/frame size.
RLE run loop writes pos[xc++] twice per iteration without verifying xc against the allocated width*height buffer.
Literal run reads ps bytes*2 into pos[xc] and advances xc by ps<<1 with no capacity check.
Final lpf write pos[xc]=lpn occurs after the loop with no bounds validation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs unchecked writes at pos[xc] and fread into pos[xc], directly matching CWE-787 (write past the end of the intended buffer). This is a buffer-boundary error, not merely an integer truncation; the truncation only enables the OOB write.

evidence_lines.code: unsigned short xc, pc, pcnt, lpf, lpn;
if (lpf) pos[xc]=lpn;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The RLE decoder computes a write offset xc from attacker-controlled skip and run-length fields and writes into framebuf without constraining xc to width*height. A crafted FLI frame with large skip/pixel counts or a yc beyond height drives pos past the heap allocation, causing an out-of-bounds heap write.

commit_msg:
pkey: add support for PKCS #8 key serialization

OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#private_to_der, #private_to_pem are added to the
generic PKey class. They serialize the private key to PKCS #8
{Encrypted,}PrivateKeyInfo format, in DER- and PEM- encoding,
respectively. For symmetry, also add #public_to_der and #public_to_pem
that serialize the public key into X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo format.

OpenSSL::PKey.read now reads DER-encoded PKCS #8 keys as well as the
"raw" private keys. PEM-encoded PKCS #8 keys have been already handled
by PEM_read_bio_PrivateKey().

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overrun due to integer overflow in bcmath

Summary: scale gets passed around as an int inside the library.

Reviewed By: mxw

Differential Revision: D3624520

Line 10 passes that unvalidated scale into bc_sub, and lines 11-12 use the same scale to bound result->n_scale, so scale directly controls internal buffer/scale sizing.

The buffer overrun is the consequence; the missing scale constraint and integer wraparound are the root cause.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts an attacker-supplied scale value without upper-bound validation, so an oversized scale can overflow integer arithmetic in bcmath's scale handling. Supported consequence: an integer overflow/wraparound that leads to a buffer overrun, as described in the commit.

commit_msg:
Introduced time truncation to December 31, 9999 (ticket #1368).

Various buffers are allocated in an assumption that there would be
no more than 4 year digits.  This might not be true on platforms
with 64-bit time_t, as 64-bit time_t is able to represent more than that.
Such dates with more than 4 year digits hardly make sense though, as
various date formats in use do not allow them anyway.

As such, all dates are now truncated by ngx_gmtime() to December 31, 9999.
This should have no effect on valid dates, though will prevent potential
buffer overflows on invalid ones.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    /*', '     * no more than 4 year digits supported,', '     * truncate to December 31, 9999, 23:59:59', '     */', '', '    if (days > 2932896) {', '        days = 2932896;', '        sec = 86399;', '    }']}
description: NGINX before 1.13.6 has a buffer overflow for years that exceed four digits, as demonstrated by a file with a modification date in 1969 that causes an integer overflow (or a false modification date far in the future), when encountered by the autoindex module.

code_evidence: The function derives calendar fields arithmetically from time_t t: days = t / 86400 and sec = t % 86400 at lines 9-10, then shifts and scales days at lines 16-18 (days - 59 + 719527; year = (days + 2) * 400 / 146097; yday = days - (365*year + year/4 - year/100 + year/400)).

The computed year/month/day/hour/min/sec values are stored into narrow ngx_tm_* fields (lines 32-37), so a large time_t yields a multi-digit year and large field values that downstream fixed-size buffers do not accommodate.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the defect is an unchecked integer calculation whose result is assumed to stay within a bounded (four-digit-year) range; the diff's added truncation at days > 2932896 confirms the missing range constraint, distinguishing it from a pure out-of-bounds write in this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ngx_gmtime performs unbounded arithmetic on time_t without constraining the year range; with 64-bit time_t, days and the (days+2)*400 product can exceed intended four-digit-year assumptions, and the resulting year is cast into a narrow ngx_tm_year_t. Trigger: a time_t representing a date past year 9999 (e.g., a crafted file modification date reaching the autoindex module). Supported consequence: out-of-range year values propagate to callers whose buffers assume at most four year digits, enabling a buffer overflow.

description: An issue was discovered in drivers/scsi/qedi/qedi_dbg.c in the Linux kernel before 5.1.12. In the qedi_dbg_* family of functions, there is an out-of-bounds read.

code_evidence: Declares a fixed 32-byte nfunc buffer and copies sizeof(nfunc)-1 (31) bytes from func regardless of func's actual length.
Passes nfunc to pr_notice as a %s argument; the fixed-length copy can read past the end of the source string func.
Same nfunc used in the fallback pr_notice path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the func string because the copy length is fixed rather than bounded by the source length; that is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), distinct from a write overflow since the destination buffer is large enough.

evidence_lines.code:
pr_notice("[%s]:[%s:%d]:%d: %pV",
dev_name(&qedi->pdev->dev), nfunc, line,
pr_notice("[0000:00:00.0]:[%s:%d]: %pV", nfunc, line, &vaf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: memcpy copies a fixed 31 bytes from the caller-supplied func string without checking its length. Trigger: a func string shorter than 31 bytes, causing the read to extend past its terminating null. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of the source string, reported as a KASAN global-out-of-bounds read.

description: In libpixman in Pixman before 0.42.2, there is an out-of-bounds write (aka heap-based buffer overflow) in rasterize_edges_8 due to an integer overflow in pixman_sample_floor_y.

code_evidence: Line 6 derives i from pixman_fixed_floor(y); line 11 converts i to int and compares it against a sentinel; line 18 decrements i by pixman_fixed_1 when the fractional value is at the high end, so the integer part can be pushed below its original range.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a boundary check on a fixed-point-to-integer conversion that fails to recognize the wraparound value, allowing an integer overflow/wraparound to propagate; this matches CWE-190's integer wraparound logic error. It is not merely a wrong constant comparison, since the consequence depends on the wrapped value being used downstream.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the boundary guard compares the wrong sentinel value, so a legitimate minimum integer part is not saturated and instead falls into the else branch that subtracts pixman_fixed_1. Trigger: a caller supplying an extreme fixed-point y (as in the rasterizer) reaches this path. Supported consequence: the wrapped integer part flows back through the return value (i | f), producing an incorrect coordinate that can later drive out-of-bounds indexing in the rasterizer.

commit_msg:
Store a copy of each serialized shared_ptr within the archive to prevent the shared_ptr to be freed to early.

The archives use the memory address pointed by the shared_ptr as a
unique id which must not be reused during lifetime of the archive.
Therefore, the archives stores a copy of it.
This problem was also reported as CVE-2020-11105.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    uint32_t id = ar.registerSharedPointer( ptr.get() );'], 'added_lines': ['    uint32_t id = ar.registerSharedPointer( ptr );']}
description: An issue was discovered in USC iLab cereal through 1.3.0. It employs caching of std::shared_ptr values, using the raw pointer address as a unique identifier. This becomes problematic if an std::shared_ptr variable goes out of scope and is freed, and a new std::shared_ptr is allocated at the same address. Serialization fidelity thereby becomes dependent upon memory layout. In short, serialized std::shared_ptr variables cannot always be expected to serialize back into their original values. This can have any number of consequences, depending on the context within which this manifests.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only registers a shared_ptr for serialization and writes an id; it contains no memory release or deallocation call, so it does not support CWE-763.

commit_msg:
Fix memory leak with oneofs and PB_ENABLE_MALLOC (#615)

Nanopb would leak memory when all of the following conditions were true:
- PB_ENABLE_MALLOC is defined at the compile time
- Message definitions contains an oneof field,
  the oneof contains a static submessage, and
  the static submessage contains a pointer field.
- Data being decoded contains two values for the submessage.

The logic in pb_release_union_field would detect that the same
submessage occurs twice, and wouldn't release it because keeping
the old values is necessary to match the C++ library behavior
regarding message merges.

But then decode_static_field() would go to memset() the whole
submessage to zero, because it unconditionally assumed it to
be uninitialized memory. This would normally happen when the
contents of the union field is switched to a different oneof
item, instead of merging with the same one.

This commit changes it so that the field is memset() only when
`which_field` contains a different tag.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            *(pb_size_t*)iter->pSize = iter->pos->tag;', '            if (PB_LTYPE(type) == PB_LTYPE_SUBMESSAGE)', '                 * Then set any default values. */'], 'added_lines': ['            if (PB_LTYPE(type) == PB_LTYPE_SUBMESSAGE &&', '                *(pb_size_t*)iter->pSize != iter->pos->tag)', '                 * This is because the callbacks might otherwise have values', '                 * from some other union field. */', '            *(pb_size_t*)iter->pSize = iter->pos->tag;', '']}
description: Nanopb is a small code-size Protocol Buffers implementation. In Nanopb before versions 0.4.4 and 0.3.9.7, decoding specifically formed message can leak memory if dynamic allocation is enabled and an oneof field contains a static submessage that contains a dynamic field, and the message being decoded contains the submessage multiple times. This is rare in normal messages, but it is a concern when untrusted data is parsed. This is fixed in versions 0.3.9.7 and 0.4.4. The following workarounds are available: 1) Set the option `no_unions` for the oneof field. This will generate fields as separate instead of C union, and avoids triggering the problematic code. 2) Set the type of the submessage field inside oneof to `FT_POINTER`. This way the whole submessage will be dynamically allocated and the problematic code is not executed. 3) Use an arena allocator for nanopb, to make sure all memory can be released afterwards.

commit_msg:
syzbot reported a sequence of memory leaks, and one of them indicated we
failed to free a whole sk:

  unreferenced object 0xffff8880126e0000 (size 1088):
    comm "syz-executor419", pid 326, jiffies 4294773607 (age 12.609s)
    hex dump (first 32 bytes):
      00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 7d 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  ........}.......
      01 00 07 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  ...@............
    backtrace:
      [<000000006fefe750>] sk_prot_alloc+0x64/0x2a0 net/core/sock.c:1970
      [<0000000074006db5>] sk_alloc+0x3b/0x800 net/core/sock.c:2029
      [<00000000728cd434>] unix_create1+0xaf/0x920 net/unix/af_unix.c:928
      [<00000000a279a139>] unix_create+0x113/0x1d0 net/unix/af_unix.c:997
      [<0000000068259812>] __sock_create+0x2ab/0x550 net/socket.c:1516
      [<00000000da1521e1>] sock_create net/socket.c:1566 [inline]
      [<00000000da1521e1>] __sys_socketpair+0x1a8/0x550 net/socket.c:1698
      [<000000007ab259e1>] __do_sys_socketpair net/socket.c:1751 [inline]
      [<000000007ab259e1>] __se_sys_socketpair net/socket.c:1748 [inline]
      [<000000007ab259e1>] __x64_sys_socketpair+0x97/0x100 net/socket.c:1748
      [<000000007dedddc1>] do_syscall_x64 arch/x86/entry/common.c:50 [inline]
      [<000000007dedddc1>] do_syscall_64+0x38/0x90 arch/x86/entry/common.c:80
      [<000000009456679f>] entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x63/0xcd

We can reproduce this issue by creating two AF_UNIX SOCK_STREAM sockets,
send()ing an OOB skb to each other, and close()ing them without consuming
the OOB skbs.

  int skpair[2];

  socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, skpair);

  send(skpair[0], "x", 1, MSG_OOB);
  send(skpair[1], "x", 1, MSG_OOB);

  close(skpair[0]);
  close(skpair[1]);

Currently, we free an OOB skb in unix_sock_destructor() which is called via
__sk_free(), but it's too late because the receiver's unix_sk(sk)->oob_skb
is accounted against the sender's sk->sk_wmem_alloc and __sk_free() is
called only when sk->sk_wmem_alloc is 0.

In the repro sequences, we do not consume the OOB skb, so both two sk's
sock_put() never reach __sk_free() due to the positive sk->sk_wmem_alloc.
Then, no one can consume the OOB skb nor call __sk_free(), and we finally
leak the two whole sk.

Thus, we must free the unconsumed OOB skb earlier when close()ing the
socket.

Fixes: 314001f0bf92 ("af_unix: Add OOB support")
Reported-by: syzbot <syzkaller@googlegroups.com>
Signed-off-by: Kuniyuki Iwashima <kuniyu@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: A vulnerability, which was classified as problematic, has been found in Linux Kernel. This issue affects the function unix_sock_destructor/unix_release_sock of the file net/unix/af_unix.c of the component BPF. The manipulation leads to memory leak. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The associated identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211043.

code_evidence: After clearing the peer at [18,19,20], the function releases the receive queue skbs at [35,36,37,38,39,40] and then drops the socket reference at [43]; the OOB skb accounting referenced by the commit is not released here.
The receive-queue loop only dequeues sk->sk_receive_queue; the OOB skb held against sk_wmem_alloc is not part of that queue and remains unreleased.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function omits release of an allocated OOB skb during socket teardown, so memory stays allocated after its effective lifetime, matching CWE-401. This is a missing-free defect, not a use-after-free, since the leak arises from non-release.

commit_msg:
Fixes CVE-2023-3138: X servers could return values from XQueryExtension
that would cause Xlib to write entries out-of-bounds of the arrays to
store them, though this would only overwrite other parts of the Display
struct, not outside the bounds allocated for that structure.

Reported-by: Gregory James DUCK <gjduck@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Alan Coopersmith <alan.coopersmith@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (extension < FirstExtensionRequest ||', '\t    extension > LastExtensionRequest) {', '\t    fprintf(stderr, "Xlib: ignoring invalid extension opcode %d\\n",', '\t\t    extension);', '\t    return (WireToEventCookieType)_XUnknownWireEventCookie;', '\t}']}
description: A vulnerability was found in libX11. The security flaw occurs because the functions in src/InitExt.c in libX11 do not check that the values provided for the Request, Event, or Error IDs are within the bounds of the arrays that those functions write to, using those IDs as array indexes. They trust that they were called with values provided by an Xserver adhering to the bounds specified in the X11 protocol, as all X servers provided by X.Org do. As the protocol only specifies a single byte for these values, an out-of-bounds value provided by a malicious server (or a malicious proxy-in-the-middle) can only overwrite other portions of the Display structure and not write outside the bounds of the Display structure itself, possibly causing the client to crash with this memory corruption.

code_evidence: The extension argument is used directly as an array index into dpy->generic_event_vec, masked only with & 0x7F. No lower/upper bound check against FirstExtensionRequest/LastExtensionRequest exists in this function, so an arbitrary extension value from a malicious server indexes the array without validation, and line 11 writes proc into that slot.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function performs an unchecked indexed write (and read) into a fixed array, allowing memory past the intended buffer region to be modified. The write is the unsafe operation; the in-struct overwrite is its consequence, matching out-of-bounds write rather than a pure bounds-read or integer issue.

evidence_lines.code:
oldproc = dpy->generic_event_vec[extension & 0x7F];
dpy->generic_event_vec[extension & 0x7F] = proc;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation of the extension index before indexing generic_event_vec. PyACL - Fixing integer overflows that occur when resizing ACLs

Fixes #1700
CVE-2021-32559
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        unsigned short required_size =', '            psacl->AclSize + sizeof(SYSTEM_AUDIT_OBJECT_ACE) + (unsigned short)GetLengthSid(psid);', '        psacl_padded->AclSize = required_size;'], 'added_lines': ['       unsigned int required_size = psacl->AclSize + sizeof(SYSTEM_AUDIT_OBJECT_ACE) + GetLengthSid(psid);', '        // max ACL size is USHRT_MAX', '        if (required_size > USHRT_MAX)', '            return PyErr_Format(PyExc_OverflowError, "%s: adding ACE would put ACL over size limit", __FUNCTION__ );', '        psacl_padded->AclSize = (unsigned short)required_size;']}
description: An integer overflow exists in pywin32 prior to version b301 when adding an access control entry (ACE) to an access control list (ACL) that would cause the size to be greater than 65535 bytes. An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could crash the vulnerable process.

code_evidence: required_size is declared unsigned short, and the sum of psacl->AclSize, sizeof(SYSTEM_AUDIT_OBJECT_ACE) and GetLengthSid(psid) is computed and truncated into that 16-bit type before malloc.

The truncated value is used directly as the allocation size in malloc and as the length in ZeroMemory; then psacl_padded->AclSize is assigned that same truncated size, while memcpy copies psacl->AclSize bytes into the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size calculation and stores the result in a narrower integer type without a range check, so the value can wrap and become small. That wrapped size then drives allocation and copying, matching CWE-190's integer overflow with memory-safety consequences; it is not merely an off-by-one or bounds error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the required ACL size is stored in an unsigned short, so the addition wraparound truncates when the total exceeds 65535. Trigger: an ACL grown by an ACE whose combined size crosses the 16-bit boundary. The small truncated size is passed to malloc, and AclSize is set to it, so the memcpy of the original ACL size can overrun the undersized allocation, causing memory corruption or a crash.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.SparseReshape` can be made to trigger an integral division by 0 exception. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/8d72537c6abf5a44103b57b9c2e22c14f5f49698/tensorflow/core/kernels/reshape_util.cc#L176-L181) calls the reshaping functor whenever there is at least an index in the input but does not check that shape of the input or the target shape have both a non-zero number of elements. The [reshape functor](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/8d72537c6abf5a44103b57b9c2e22c14f5f49698/tensorflow/core/kernels/reshape_util.cc#L40-L78) blindly divides by the dimensions of the target shape. Hence, if this is not checked, code will result in a division by 0. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 4923de56ec94fff7770df259ab7f2288a74feb41. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1 as this is the other affected version.

code_evidence: When the target shape contains an unknown dimension (-1), the code checks product > 0 before computing 'missing = dense_size / product'. The patch adds a guard for dense_size > 0 && product > 0 before the reshape functor at line 85, but the division at line 50 relies on product being non-zero, which is the relevant divide-by-zero path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 directly matches the unsafe integral division at line 50 where the divisor product can be zero, causing a crash (availability impact). This is distinct from the patch's added guard on the functor call at line 85, which addresses a related empty-shape scenario; the in-function division is the concrete divide-by-zero supported by this code.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The code computes dense_size / product at line 50 to infer the unknown dimension. If the specified target dimensions multiply to zero (product == 0) while an unknown_index is present, this integral division by zero is executed. The patch's OP_REQUIRES at lines 44-49 guards this path by rejecting product == 0 when inference is needed, preventing the crash.

commit_msg:
pids: fix fork_idle() to setup ->pids correctly

copy_process(pid => &init_struct_pid) doesn't do attach_pid/etc.

It shouldn't, but this means that the idle threads run with the wrong
pids copied from the caller's task_struct. In x86 case the caller is
either kernel_init() thread or keventd.

In particular, this means that after the series of cpu_up/cpu_down an
idle thread (which never exits) can run with .pid pointing to nowhere.

Change fork_idle() to initialize idle->pids[] correctly. We only set
.pid = &init_struct_pid but do not add .node to list, INIT_TASK() does
the same for the boot-cpu idle thread (swapper).

commit_msg:
usbip_sockfd_store() is invoked when user requests attach (import)
detach (unimport) usb device from usbip host. vhci_hcd sends import
request and usbip_sockfd_store() exports the device if it is free
for export.

Export and unexport are governed by local state and shared state
- Shared state (usbip device status, sockfd) - sockfd and Device
  status are used to determine if stub should be brought up or shut
  down.
- Local state (tcp_socket, rx and tx thread task_struct ptrs)
  A valid tcp_socket controls rx and tx thread operations while the
  device is in exported state.
- While the device is exported, device status is marked used and socket,
  sockfd, and thread pointers are valid.

Export sequence (stub-up) includes validating the socket and creating
receive (rx) and transmit (tx) threads to talk to the client to provide
access to the exported device. rx and tx threads depends on local and
shared state to be correct and in sync.

Unexport (stub-down) sequence shuts the socket down and stops the rx and
tx threads. Stub-down sequence relies on local and shared states to be
in sync.

There are races in updating the local and shared status in the current
stub-up sequence resulting in crashes. These stem from starting rx and
tx threads before local and global state is updated correctly to be in
sync.

1. Doesn't handle kthread_create() error and saves invalid ptr in local
   state that drives rx and tx threads.
2. Updates tcp_socket and sockfd,  starts stub_rx and stub_tx threads
   before updating usbip_device status to SDEV_ST_USED. This opens up a
   race condition between the threads and usbip_sockfd_store() stub up
   and down handling.

Fix the above problems:
- Stop using kthread_get_run() macro to create/start threads.
- Create threads and get task struct reference.
- Add kthread_create() failure handling and bail out.
- Hold usbip_device lock to update local and shared states after
  creating rx and tx threads.
- Update usbip_device status to SDEV_ST_USED.
- Update usbip_device tcp_socket, sockfd, tcp_rx, and tcp_tx
- Start threads after usbip_device (tcp_socket, sockfd, tcp_rx, tcp_tx,
  and status) is complete.

Credit goes to syzbot and Tetsuo Handa for finding and root-causing the
kthread_get_run() improper error handling problem and others. This is a
hard problem to find and debug since the races aren't seen in a normal
case. Fuzzing forces the race window to be small enough for the
kthread_get_run() error path bug and starting threads before updating the
local and shared state bug in the stub-up sequence.

Tested with syzbot reproducer:
- https://syzkaller.appspot.com/text?tag=ReproC&x=14801034d00000

Fixes: 9720b4bc76a83807 ("staging/usbip: convert to kthread")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: syzbot <syzbot+a93fba6d384346a761e3@syzkaller.appspotmail.com>
Reported-by: syzbot <syzbot+bf1a360e305ee719e364@syzkaller.appspotmail.com>
Reported-by: syzbot <syzbot+95ce4b142579611ef0a9@syzkaller.appspotmail.com>
Reported-by: Tetsuo Handa <penguin-kernel@I-love.SAKURA.ne.jp>
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan <skhan@linuxfoundation.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/268a0668144d5ff36ec7d87fdfa90faf583b7ccc.1615171203.git.skhan@linuxfoundation.org
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.11.7. usbip_sockfd_store in drivers/usb/usbip/stub_dev.c allows attackers to cause a denial of service (GPF) because the stub-up sequence has race conditions during an update of the local and shared status, aka CID-9380afd6df70.

code_evidence: The stub-up path holds sdev->ud.lock only while checking status and looking up the socket, then publishes tcp_socket and sockfd before unlocking at line 35.

Lines 36-39 start the rx/tx kthreads via kthread_get_run with no error check, and status SDEV_ST_USED is set only afterward at lines 40-42, so the shared state and local thread pointers are inconsistent while threads run.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function updates shared usbip_device state and starts concurrent threads without holding exclusive access across the whole sequence, allowing an interfering sequence to observe stale or partial state. This is a concurrency race (CWE-362), not merely a missing error check; the error-handling gap worsens the race but the core weakness is improper synchronization of shared state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The status check and the publication of tcp_socket/sockfd/threads are not performed atomically: the lock is dropped and threads are started before status becomes SDEV_ST_USED, and kthread_get_run failures store invalid pointers. A concurrent stub-up/down or the started threads can observe mismatched state, leading to a GPF/crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86: don't leak ST(n)/XMMn values to domains first using them

FNINIT doesn't alter these registers, and hence using it is
insufficient to initialize a guest's initial state.

This is CVE-2015-8555 / XSA-165.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    else if ( v->fpu_initialised )', '    else', '        fpu_init();'], 'added_lines': ['    else']}
description: Xen 4.6.x, 4.5.x, 4.4.x, 4.3.x, and earlier do not initialize x86 FPU stack and XMM registers when XSAVE/XRSTOR are not used to manage guest extended register state, which allows local guest domains to obtain sensitive information from other domains via unspecified vectors.

code_evidence: When cpu_has_xsave is false and v->fpu_initialised is false, the original code called fpu_init() to reset the guest FPU state; the patched code instead calls fpu_fxrstor(v), restoring whatever ST(n)/XMMn register contents the host or another vCPU left in the physical FPU. The function then marks v->fpu_initialised = 1 (line 13), so the stale, uninitialized register content persists as the guest's state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an information exposure: stale FPU/XMM register contents from a prior context are made readable by an unauthorized guest domain. CWE-200 fits the confidentiality impact of leaking another domain's data, though the underlying flaw is uninitialized state; the disclosed information is the direct supported consequence of this function's failure to initialize.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on the non-XSAVE path, a fresh vCPU's FPU state is restored from uninitialized physical registers rather than being initialized, because the fpu_initialised branch was removed and fpu_init() no longer runs. Trigger: a guest domain first uses a vCPU without XSAVE, executing FPU/XMM instructions that read the restored registers. Consequence: the guest observes residual register data left by another domain, leaking sensitive information across domain boundaries.

commit_msg:
coredump: avoid deadlock when passing processed backtrace data

We would deadlock when passing the data back from the forked-off process that
was doing backtrace generation back to the coredump parent. This is because we
fork the child and wait for it to exit. The child tries to write too much data
to the output pipe, and and after the first 64k blocks on the parent because
the pipe is full. The bug surfaced in Fedora because of a combination of four
factors:
- 87707784c70dc9894ec613df0a6e75e732a362a3 was backported to v251.5, which
  allowed coredump processing to be successful.
- 1a0281a3ebf4f8c16d40aa9e63103f16cd23bb2a was NOT backported, so the output
  was very verbose.
- Fedora has the ELF package metadata available, so a lot of output can be
  generated. Most other distros just don't have the information.
- gnome-calendar crashes and has a bazillion modules and 69596 bytes of output
  are generated for it.

Fixes https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2135778.

The code is changed to try to write data opportunistically. If we get partial
information, that is still logged. In is generally better to log partial
backtrace information than nothing at all.

description: systemd 250 and 251 allows local users to achieve a systemd-coredump deadlock by triggering a crash that has a long backtrace. This occurs in parse_elf_object in shared/elf-util.c. The exploitation methodology is to crash a binary calling the same function recursively, and put it in a deeply nested directory to make its backtrace large enough to cause the deadlock. This must be done 16 times when MaxConnections=16 is set for the systemd/units/systemd-coredump.socket file.

code_evidence: The return and json pipes are created with O_CLOEXEC but without O_NONBLOCK, so writes into a full pipe block indefinitely.

The child writes the entire backtrace with loop_write(return_pipe[1], buf, strlen(buf), false); there is no size limit or non-blocking behavior, so a large backtrace exceeds the 64k pipe buffer and blocks.
json_variant_dump writes package metadata to the pipe without checking for a bounded or non-blocking write, which can likewise block on a full pipe.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to bound/throttle the data written to a limited kernel pipe resource and uses blocking writes, so attacker-triggered large output consumes the pipe capacity and deadlocks the service. This uncontrolled consumption of a limited resource causing denial of service matches CWE-400, rather than a mere logic bug.

evidence_lines.code:
r = RET_NERRNO(pipe2(return_pipe, O_CLOEXEC));
r = RET_NERRNO(pipe2(json_pipe, O_CLOEXEC));
json_variant_dump(package_metadata, JSON_FORMAT_FLUSH, json_out, NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parent forks a child and waits (FORK_WAIT) while the child writes backtrace/metadata into blocking pipes. When output exceeds the pipe capacity (e.g., a long backtrace with many modules), the child blocks on write while the parent blocks waiting for the child to exit, deadlocking the coredump processing and exhausting the service.

commit_msg:
Preserve GSS context on init/accept failure

After gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() has created a
context, don't delete the mechglue context on failures from subsequent
calls, even if the mechanism deletes the mech-specific context (which
is allowed by RFC 2744 but not preferred).  Check for union contexts
with no mechanism context in each GSS function which accepts a
gss_ctx_id_t.

CVE-2017-11462:

RFC 2744 permits a GSS-API implementation to delete an existing
security context on a second or subsequent call to
gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() if the call results
in an error.  This API behavior has been found to be dangerous,
leading to the possibility of memory errors in some callers.  For
safety, GSS-API implementations should instead preserve existing
security contexts on error until the caller deletes them.

All versions of MIT krb5 prior to this change may delete acceptor
contexts on error.  Versions 1.13.4 through 1.13.7, 1.14.1 through
1.14.5, and 1.15 through 1.15.1 may also delete initiator contexts on
error.

commit_msg:
xen: Check the alignment of the offset pased via VCPUOP_register_vcpu_info

Currently a guest is able to register any guest physical address to use
for the vcpu_info structure as long as the structure can fits in the
rest of the frame.

This means a guest can provide an address that is not aligned to the
natural alignment of the structure.

On Arm 32-bit, unaligned access are completely forbidden by the
hypervisor. This will result to a data abort which is fatal.

On Arm 64-bit, unaligned access are only forbidden when used for atomic
access. As the structure contains fields (such as evtchn_pending_self)
that are updated using atomic operations, any unaligned access will be
fatal as well.

While the misalignment is only fatal on Arm, a generic check is added
as an x86 guest shouldn't sensibly pass an unaligned address (this
would result to a split lock).

This is XSA-327.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned int align;', '        return -EINVAL;', '', '#ifdef CONFIG_COMPAT', '    if ( has_32bit_shinfo(d) )', '        align = alignof(new_info->compat);', '    else', '#endif', '        align = alignof(*new_info);', '    if ( offset & (align - 1) )']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.13.x, allowing Arm guest OS users to cause a hypervisor crash because of a missing alignment check in VCPUOP_register_vcpu_info. The hypercall VCPUOP_register_vcpu_info is used by a guest to register a shared region with the hypervisor. The region will be mapped into Xen address space so it can be directly accessed. On Arm, the region is accessed with instructions that require a specific alignment. Unfortunately, there is no check that the address provided by the guest will be correctly aligned. As a result, a malicious guest could cause a hypervisor crash by passing a misaligned address. A malicious guest administrator may cause a hypervisor crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS). All Xen versions are vulnerable. Only Arm systems are vulnerable. x86 systems are not affected.

code_evidence: The function only rejects an offset that overflows the end of the page frame (offset > PAGE_SIZE - sizeof(vcpu_info_t)); it never checks that offset is aligned to the natural alignment of vcpu_info_t.
new_info is computed as mapping + offset, so a guest-supplied misaligned offset yields a misaligned vcpu_info_t pointer.
write_atomic on the evtchn_pending_sel field then performs an atomic access through that misaligned pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The guest-controlled offset is used to form a pointer into a mapped frame without enforcing the structure's alignment constraint, so accesses target a memory location outside the structure's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The related alignment CWE is the underlying condition, but the supported operation is an out-of-bounds/misaligned access within the mapped buffer.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( offset > (PAGE_SIZE - sizeof(vcpu_info_t)) )
return -EINVAL;
new_info = (vcpu_info_t *)(mapping + offset);
write_atomic(&vcpu_info(v, evtchn_pending_sel), ~0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the offset supplied via VCPUOP_register_vcpu_info is bounds-checked but not alignment-checked. Trigger: a guest registers a gfn/offset where mapping+offset is not naturally aligned. Consequence: atomic operations on the resulting misaligned vcpu_info_t cause a fatal unaligned access/data abort, crashing the hypervisor (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix cwise dimension overflow issue again.

If resulting dimensions overflow an int32, we were seeing an overflow and
crash due to size mismatch during broadcast assignment.  The cause is a simple
dimension type mismatch.

Note that actual tests for this are currently impractical, since successful
operations require more than 2^32 elements and OOM on most machines.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 479336566
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['inline Eigen::IndexList<int, Eigen::type2index<1>> NByOne(int n) {', '    Eigen::IndexList<int, Eigen::type2index<1>> ret;'], 'added_lines': ['inline Eigen::IndexList<Eigen::DenseIndex, Eigen::type2index<1>> NByOne(', '      Eigen::DenseIndex n) {', '    Eigen::IndexList<Eigen::DenseIndex, Eigen::type2index<1>> ret;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. `tf.keras.losses.poisson` receives a `y_pred` and `y_true` that are passed through `functor::mul` in `BinaryOp`. If the resulting dimensions overflow an `int32`, TensorFlow will crash due to a size mismatch during broadcast assignment. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit c5b30379ba87cbe774b08ac50c1f6d36df4ebb7c. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.11. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.10.1 and 2.9.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range. However, we will not cherrypick this commit into TensorFlow 2.8.x, as it depends on Eigen behavior that changed between 2.8 and 2.9.

code_evidence: NByOne returns an Eigen::IndexList whose first dimension is stored as int, and its parameter n is also int. The dimension value is placed into the list via ret.set(0, n), so the computed dimension is held in a 32-bit int rather than Eigen::DenseIndex.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-131 fits because the dimension/size value is calculated in an int that can overflow, producing an incorrect size used by downstream allocation/assignment logic. This is a size-calculation flaw rather than an out-of-bounds access pattern itself (CWE-125/787), which are consequences of the bad size.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the broadcast dimension is computed and stored using int rather than Eigen's index type. Trigger: a shape whose product/dimension exceeds INT32_MAX. The truncated dimension then mismatches the actual buffer size during broadcast assignment, causing a crash; the commit describes exactly this size mismatch.

commit_msg:
Remove access to the root FS from lua

On linux / is mounted to /rootfs in RageFile, which allows access to the
_whole_ filesystem from lua. This means themes and mod files can
re-write user data and extract files via USB profiles.

/rootfs was only added for internal use by the alsa, oss and memory card
drivers, so it can be easily replaced with direct fstream file access.

description: The component /rootfs in RageFile of Stepmania v5.1b2 and below allows attackers access to the entire file system.

code_evidence: Under UNIX, the function unconditionally mounts the entire root filesystem "/" at virtual path "/rootfs" via FILEMAN->Mount, and also mounts "/proc" at "/proc". No access constraint, caller restriction, or path filtering limits which code can subsequently read these mounts through the virtual filesystem.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-732 fits because the function assigns overly permissive access to a security-critical resource: the whole root filesystem is exposed to a wider set of actors (untrusted Lua/mod content) than intended. It is not merely a missing authorization check in a request handler; the weakness is the permission/scope assignment made at mount time.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the initial filesystem setup grants the RageFile virtual filesystem broad read access to the host root (and /proc) by mounting them without restricting which consumers may use them. Trigger: any Lua theme or mod script that resolves paths through RageFile can read files under /rootfs (or /proc). Consequence: disclosure of arbitrary user files and system data, and potential modification of user data reachable through the mounted tree.

commit_msg:
Remove support for pre-authentication compression. Doing compression
early in the protocol probably seemed reasonable in the 1990s, but
today it's clearly a bad idea in terms of both cryptography (cf.
multiple compression oracle attacks in TLS) and attack surface.

Moreover, to support it across privilege-separation zlib needed
the assistance of a complex shared-memory manager that made the
required attack surface considerably larger.

Prompted by Guido Vranken pointing out a compiler-elided security
check in the shared memory manager found by Stack
(http://css.csail.mit.edu/stack/); ok deraadt@ markus@

NB. pre-auth authentication has been disabled by default in sshd
for >10 years.

commit_msg:
Add recursion limit for ASN.1 indefinite lengths

The libkrb5 ASN.1 decoder supports BER indefinite lengths.  It
computes the tag length using recursion; the lack of a recursion limit
allows an attacker to overrun the stack and cause the process to
crash.  Reported by Demi Obenour.

CVE-2020-28196:

In MIT krb5 releases 1.11 and later, an unauthenticated attacker can
cause a denial of service for any client or server to which it can
send an ASN.1-encoded Kerberos message of sufficient length.

commit_msg:
net: rose: fix UAF bugs caused by timer handler

There are UAF bugs in rose_heartbeat_expiry(), rose_timer_expiry()
and rose_idletimer_expiry(). The root cause is that del_timer()
could not stop the timer handler that is running and the refcount
of sock is not managed properly.

One of the UAF bugs is shown below:

                        |  rose_bind
                        |  rose_connect
                        |    rose_start_heartbeat
rose_release            |    (wait a time)
  case ROSE_STATE_0     |
  rose_destroy_socket   |  rose_heartbeat_expiry
    rose_stop_heartbeat |
    sock_put(sk)        |    ...
  sock_put(sk) // FREE  |
                        |    bh_lock_sock(sk) // USE

The sock is deallocated by sock_put() in rose_release() and
then used by bh_lock_sock() in rose_heartbeat_expiry().

Although rose_destroy_socket() calls rose_stop_heartbeat(),
it could not stop the timer that is running.

description: There are use-after-free vulnerabilities caused by timer handler in net/rose/rose_timer.c of linux that allow attackers to crash linux kernel without any privileges.

code_evidence: The function arms rose->timer with del_timer()/add_timer() and no reference on sk is taken. del_timer() cannot stop a handler already running on another CPU, so the timer callback can execute after the socket is freed by rose_release().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the timer callback accesses a sock object that may already be deallocated, i.e., memory reused after free. This is a lifetime/refcount flaw, not just a double-free or race by itself; the resulting use of freed memory is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the timer is started without holding a reference on the owning sock, and del_timer() does not synchronize with an in-flight timer handler. Trigger: rose_start_t1timer() schedules the timer, then rose_release() frees sk via sock_put() while the handler runs. Consequence: the handler dereferences freed memory (UAF), causing crash or memory corruption. The patch's sk_reset_timer()/sk_stop_timer() manage the refcount.

commit_msg:
Fix DTLS buffered message DoS attack

DTLS can handle out of order record delivery. Additionally since
handshake messages can be bigger than will fit into a single packet, the
messages can be fragmented across multiple records (as with normal TLS).
That means that the messages can arrive mixed up, and we have to
reassemble them. We keep a queue of buffered messages that are "from the
future", i.e. messages we're not ready to deal with yet but have arrived
early. The messages held there may not be full yet - they could be one
or more fragments that are still in the process of being reassembled.

The code assumes that we will eventually complete the reassembly and
when that occurs the complete message is removed from the queue at the
point that we need to use it.

However, DTLS is also tolerant of packet loss. To get around that DTLS
messages can be retransmitted. If we receive a full (non-fragmented)
message from the peer after previously having received a fragment of
that message, then we ignore the message in the queue and just use the
non-fragmented version. At that point the queued message will never get
removed.

Additionally the peer could send "future" messages that we never get to
in order to complete the handshake. Each message has a sequence number
(starting from 0). We will accept a message fragment for the current
message sequence number, or for any sequence up to 10 into the future.
However if the Finished message has a sequence number of 2, anything
greater than that in the queue is just left there.

So, in those two ways we can end up with "orphaned" data in the queue
that will never get removed - except when the connection is closed. At
that point all the queues are flushed.

An attacker could seek to exploit this by filling up the queues with
lots of large messages that are never going to be used in order to
attempt a DoS by memory exhaustion.

I will assume that we are only concerned with servers here. It does not
seem reasonable to be concerned about a memory exhaustion attack on a
client. They are unlikely to process enough connections for this to be
an issue.

A "long" handshake with many messages might be 5 messages long (in the
incoming direction), e.g. ClientHello, Certificate, ClientKeyExchange,
CertificateVerify, Finished. So this would be message sequence numbers 0
to 4. Additionally we can buffer up to 10 messages in the future.
Therefore the maximum number of messages that an attacker could send
that could get orphaned would typically be 15.

The maximum size that a DTLS message is allowed to be is defined by
max_cert_list, which by default is 100k. Therefore the maximum amount of
"orphaned" memory per connection is 1500k.

Message sequence numbers get reset after the Finished message, so
renegotiation will not extend the maximum number of messages that can be
orphaned per connection.

As noted above, the queues do get cleared when the connection is closed.
Therefore in order to mount an effective attack, an attacker would have
to open many simultaneous connections.

Issue reported by Quan Luo.

CVE-2016-2179

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    item = pqueue_peek(s->d1->buffered_messages);', '    if (item == NULL)', '        return 0;', '    frag = (hm_fragment *)item->data;'], 'added_lines': ['    do {', '        item = pqueue_peek(s->d1->buffered_messages);', '        if (item == NULL)', '            return 0;', '', '        frag = (hm_fragment *)item->data;', '', '        if (frag->msg_header.seq < s->d1->handshake_read_seq) {', '            /* This is a stale message that has been buffered so clear it */', '            pqueue_pop(s->d1->buffered_messages);', '            dtls1_hm_fragment_free(frag);', '            pitem_free(item);', '            item = NULL;', '            frag = NULL;', '        }', '    } while (item == NULL);']}
description: The DTLS implementation in OpenSSL before 1.1.0 does not properly restrict the lifetime of queue entries associated with unused out-of-order messages, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by maintaining many crafted DTLS sessions simultaneously, related to d1_lib.c, statem_dtls.c, statem_lib.c, and statem_srvr.c.

code_evidence: The function peeks only the head of buffered_messages and returns 0 if it is empty; it never inspects or evicts queued fragments whose sequence number is already behind handshake_read_seq.
If the head fragment is still being reassembled (reassembly != NULL), the function returns without consuming it, so a partially reassembled entry can remain indefinitely.
Only a fragment whose sequence equals handshake_read_seq is popped and freed; any other buffered entry, including stale/out-of-order messages, is left in the queue by the else return 0 path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 covers improper resource management; the queue entries are retained without lifecycle cleanup, directly causing memory exhaustion. This is a resource-management flaw rather than a data-corruption issue.

evidence_lines.code:
if (frag->reassembly != NULL)
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the retrieval path only removes a fragment exactly matching the current read sequence and never reaps stale or incomplete queue entries. Trigger: a peer sends future/out-of-order fragments or later sends a full message, orphaning buffered entries that are never freed. Consequence: unbounded accumulation of buffered handshake messages across many sessions consumes memory, enabling denial of service.

description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An out-of-bounds read was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The out-of-bounds read is triggered when Exiv2 is used to read the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: Line 90 sets value from parseEscapes(...line.substr(...)), which can yield an empty string. Line 91 computes last = value.length()-1, which underflows to a huge size_type when value is empty. Lines 92-93 then index value[0] and value[last] without any length check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads past the end of the intended buffer via unchecked std::string indexing. The fix replaces value[...] with value.at(...) to enforce bounds; a related weakness like CWE-120 (buffer overflow) would involve writes, not this read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no check that value is non-empty before indexing with value[0] and value[last], where last underflows for an empty string. Trigger: crafted command line whose value parses to an empty string. Consequence: out-of-bounds read (and potentially crash/DoS).

commit_msg:
If FI_EXTRA_ATTR is set in inode by fuzzing, inode.i_addr[0] will be
parsed as inode.i_extra_isize, then in __recover_inline_status, inline
data address will beyond boundary of page, result in accessing invalid
memory.

So in this condition, during reading inode page, let's do sanity check
with EXTRA_ATTR feature of fs and extra_attr bit of inode, if they're
inconsistent, deny to load this inode.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (!sanity_check_inode(inode)) {', '\t\tf2fs_put_page(node_page, 1);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in fs/f2fs/inode.c in the Linux kernel through 4.17.3. A denial of service (slab out-of-bounds read and BUG) can occur for a modified f2fs filesystem image in which FI_EXTRA_ATTR is set in an inode.

code_evidence: Line 40 derives inline flags from disk data via get_inline_info. Line 41-42 sets fi->i_extra_isize from ri->i_extra_isize when f2fs_has_extra_attr is set, without verifying that the filesystem superblock actually enables EXTRA_ATTR.

Line 51-52 invokes __recover_inline_status when inline data is flagged but no data exists; that routine computes an inline address using the unvalidated i_extra_isize, so a crafted image with FI_EXTRA_ATTR set can place the address past the page.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function trusts unvalidated on-disk metadata to compute an inline data address and then reads from it, which is exactly a read past the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-125. The weakness is the unbounded read, not merely a missing feature check.

evidence_lines.code:
if (f2fs_has_inline_data(inode) && !f2fs_exist_data(inode))
__recover_inline_status(inode, node_page);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is a missing consistency check between the on-disk FI_EXTRA_ATTR inode flag and the EXTRA_ATTR filesystem feature. A corrupted image sets the flag so i_addr[0] is parsed as i_extra_isize, and __recover_inline_status then reads inline data at an out-of-page address, producing a slab out-of-bounds read and crash.

commit_msg:
x86/shadow: Avoid overflowing sh_ctxt->seg_reg[]

hvm_get_seg_reg() does not perform a range check on its input segment, calls
hvm_get_segment_register() and writes straight into sh_ctxt->seg_reg[].

x86_seg_none is outside the bounds of sh_ctxt->seg_reg[], and will hit a BUG()
in {vmx,svm}_get_segment_register().

HVM guests running with shadow paging can end up performing a virtual to
linear translation with x86_seg_none.  This is used for addresses which are
already linear.  However, none of this is a legitimate pagetable update, so
fail the emulation in such a case.

This is XSA-187 / CVE-2016-7094.

Reported-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    struct segment_register *reg = hvm_get_seg_reg(seg, sh_ctxt);'], 'added_lines': ['    const struct segment_register *reg;', '', '    /*', '     * Can arrive here with non-user segments.  However, no such cirucmstance', '     * is part of a legitimate pagetable update, so fail the emulation.', '     */', '    if ( !is_x86_user_segment(seg) )', '        return X86EMUL_UNHANDLEABLE;', '', '    reg = hvm_get_seg_reg(seg, sh_ctxt);']}
description: Buffer overflow in Xen 4.7.x and earlier allows local x86 HVM guest OS administrators on guests running with shadow paging to cause a denial of service via a pagetable update.

code_evidence: Line 9 calls hvm_get_seg_reg(seg, sh_ctxt) with the caller-supplied segment value and stores the result without validating that seg is a user segment; hvm_get_seg_reg indexes sh_ctxt->seg_reg[] directly, so a non-user value such as x86_seg_none indexes outside that array. Lines 11-12 then pass the retrieved reg into hvm_virtual_to_linear_addr, continuing the translation with the out-of-bounds-derived segment register.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked segment value causes an array index outside sh_ctxt->seg_reg[]'s intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The crash is the consequence of that out-of-bounds access, not the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the segment index is used to index sh_ctxt->seg_reg[] without a bounds check. Trigger: a shadow-paging HVM guest performs a virtual-to-linear translation with a non-user segment (e.g. x86_seg_none). Consequence: an out-of-bounds array access hits the BUG() in the vendor get_segment_register path, causing a host denial of service.

commit_msg:
13242 parse_user_name in PAM is sloppy
Reviewed by: Alex Wilson <alex@cooperi.net>
Approved by: Gordon Ross <gordon.w.ross@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["\t\tif ((*ptr == ' ') || (*ptr == '\\t'))", '\t\telse {', '\tif ((*ret_username = malloc(index + 1)) == NULL)', '\t(void) strcpy(*ret_username, username);'], 'added_lines': ["\t\tif ((*ptr == ' ') || (*ptr == '\\t') ||", '\t\t    (index >= PAM_MAX_RESP_SIZE)) {', '\t\t} else {', '\tif (index >= PAM_MAX_RESP_SIZE ||', '\t    (*ret_username = strdup(username)) == NULL)']}
description: An issue was discovered in illumos before 2020-10-22, as used in OmniOS before r151030by, r151032ay, and r151034y and SmartOS before 20201022. There is a buffer overflow in parse_user_name in lib/libpam/pam_framework.c.

code_evidence: username is a fixed stack buffer of PAM_MAX_RESP_SIZE, but the loop copies each non-space/non-tab character from ptr into username[index] without any bound on index; the loop only stops at whitespace or NUL.
After the loop, malloc(index + 1) sizes the heap block from the attacker-influenced index and strcpy copies username into it; the copy length is derived from the same unbounded loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a buffer copy (username[index] = *ptr) without checking that the input length is less than the destination buffer size, matching CWE-120's classic buffer-copy overflow. This is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), and the root cause is the missing size constraint rather than a size calculation error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the character-copy loop lacks a check that index stays below PAM_MAX_RESP_SIZE, so a long whitespace-free user_input writes past the stack buffer username. Trigger: a caller-supplied string longer than PAM_MAX_RESP_SIZE with no space/tab/NUL early on. Consequence: stack buffer overflow, memory corruption and possible crash or code execution; the later malloc/strcpy also operates on the corrupted length.

commit_msg:
Detect recursion loops resolving objects (fixes #51)

During parsing of an object, sometimes parts of the object have to be
resolved. An example is stream lengths. If such an object directly or
indirectly points to the object being parsed, it can cause an infinite
loop. Guard against all cases of re-entrant resolution of objects.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (this->resolving.count(og))', '    {', '        // This can happen if an object references itself directly or', '        // indirectly in some key that has to be resolved during', '        // object parsing, such as stream length.', '\tQTC::TC("qpdf", "QPDF recursion loop in resolve");', '\twarn(QPDFExc(qpdf_e_damaged_pdf, this->file->getName(),', '\t\t     "", this->file->getLastOffset(),', '\t\t     "loop detected resolving object " +', '\t\t     QUtil::int_to_string(objid) + " " +', '\t\t     QUtil::int_to_string(generation)));', '        return new QPDF_Null;', '    }', '    ResolveRecorder rr(this, og);', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in QPDF before 7.0.0. Endless recursion causes stack exhaustion in QPDFTokenizer::resolveLiteral() in QPDFTokenizer.cc, related to the QPDF::resolve function in QPDF.cc.

code_evidence: Line 4 builds the object key og from objid/generation. Line 5 checks only the obj_cache; when the target is not cached, lines 19-21 call readObjectAtOffset and line 25 calls resolveObjectsInStream, both of which can re-enter resolve for the same og before obj_cache is populated, so no guard stops recursive resolution of a self-referencing object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to bound re-entrant resource use, matching the target's resource-management category: recursion is uncontrolled and exhausts the stack. CWE-674 (uncontrolled recursion) is the concrete descendant, but the target category CWE-399 is the requested label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: resolve() lacks any in-progress tracking, so parsing an object whose resolved parts (e.g. stream length) reference the same object re-enters resolve indefinitely. Trigger: a crafted PDF with a direct or indirect self-reference; consequence is unbounded recursion leading to stack exhaustion, a resource-management failure.

commit_msg: Defensive coding to avoid 0x80000000/0xFFFFFFFF FPE.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (ts != 0)'], 'added_lines': ['        if (ts > 0)']}
description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. A floating point exception (FPE) due to an integer divide by zero was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The FPE is triggered when Exiv2 is used to print the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. Note that this bug is only triggered when printing the interpreted (translated) data, which is a less frequently used Exiv2 operation that requires an extra command line option (`-p t` or `-P t`). The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: Line 4 obtains the type size ts from TypeInfo::typeSize(typeId()). Line 5 guards only against ts != 0, so a negative ts (e.g., -1/0xFFFFFFFF) passes the check. Line 6 then performs len % ts and len / ts with that negative divisor, and line 7 advances i += ts, so a negative ts also yields a non-terminating or degenerate loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs len % ts and len / ts with a divisor not constrained to be positive; a zero or otherwise invalid divisor causes division by zero, matching CWE-369. This is a divide-by-zero, not merely an out-of-bounds read, because the failure occurs in the division itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard tests ts != 0 rather than ts > 0, so a negative type size from crafted metadata reaches the modulo and division on line 6. The trigger is reading metadata whose typeId yields a negative size; the supported consequence is an FPE/crash (denial of service) during interpreted-data printing.

commit_msg:
Fix protocol parsing on 'ldbReplParseCommand' (CVE-2021-32672)

The protocol parsing on 'ldbReplParseCommand' (LUA debugging)
Assumed protocol correctness. This means that if the following
is given:
*1
$100
test
The parser will try to read additional 94 unallocated bytes after
the client buffer.
This commit fixes this issue by validating that there are actually enough
bytes to read. It also limits the amount of data that can be sent by
the debugger client to 1M so the client will not be able to explode
the memory.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        while((argv = ldbReplParseCommand(&argc)) == NULL) {'], 'added_lines': ['    char* err = NULL;', '        while((argv = ldbReplParseCommand(&argc, &err)) == NULL) {', '            if (err) {', '                lua_pushstring(lua, err);', '                lua_error(lua);', '            }', '            /* after 1M we will exit with an error', '             * so that the client will not blow the memory', '             */', '            if (sdslen(ldb.cbuf) > 1<<20) {', '                sdsfree(ldb.cbuf);', '                ldb.cbuf = sdsempty();', '                lua_pushstring(lua, "max client buffer reached");', '                lua_error(lua);', '            }']}
description: Redis is an open source, in-memory database that persists on disk. When using the Redis Lua Debugger, users can send malformed requests that cause the debugger’s protocol parser to read data beyond the actual buffer. This issue affects all versions of Redis with Lua debugging support (3.2 or newer). The problem is fixed in versions 6.2.6, 6.0.16 and 5.0.14.

code_evidence: The loop calls ldbReplParseCommand(&argc) and, when it returns NULL, reads up to 1024 bytes from the connection into buf and appends them to ldb.cbuf via sdscatlen. The parser is trusted to consume only bytes actually present in the buffer; no check validates that the declared payload length is available before parsing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reading memory past the end of the intended buffer during protocol parsing, which is exactly CWE-125. The commit adds a 1M cap and error propagation, but the target behavior is the out-of-bounds read condition, not an unbounded write or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ldbReplParseCommand parses a length-prefixed payload without confirming that enough bytes exist in ldb.cbuf, so a malformed request declaring a length larger than the buffered data causes the parser to read beyond the end of the allocated buffer. Trigger: a debugger client sends a bulk-length header exceeding the actual data. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of unallocated memory, potentially leaking data or crashing.

commit_msg:
x86/traps: Use an Interrupt Stack Table for #DB

PV guests can use architectural corner cases to cause #DB to be raised after
transitioning into supervisor mode.

Use an interrupt stack table for #DB to prevent the exception being taken with
a guest controlled stack pointer.

This is part of XSA-260 / CVE-2018-8897

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    set_ist(&idt[TRAP_debug],         IST_DB);']}
description: A statement in the System Programming Guide of the Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual (SDM) was mishandled in the development of some or all operating-system kernels, resulting in unexpected behavior for #DB exceptions that are deferred by MOV SS or POP SS, as demonstrated by (for example) privilege escalation in Windows, macOS, some Xen configurations, or FreeBSD, or a Linux kernel crash. The MOV to SS and POP SS instructions inhibit interrupts (including NMIs), data breakpoints, and single step trap exceptions until the instruction boundary following the next instruction (SDM Vol. 3A; section 6.8.3). (The inhibited data breakpoints are those on memory accessed by the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction itself.) Note that debug exceptions are not inhibited by the interrupt enable (EFLAGS.IF) system flag (SDM Vol. 3A; section 2.3). If the instruction following the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction is an instruction like SYSCALL, SYSENTER, INT 3, etc. that transfers control to the operating system at CPL < 3, the debug exception is delivered after the transfer to CPL < 3 is complete. OS kernels may not expect this order of events and may therefore experience unexpected behavior when it occurs.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only assigns IST stacks to IDT entries; it contains no concurrent sequence, shared-resource access, or synchronization window, so CWE-362 is not supported by this code.

commit_msg:
xen/page_alloc: Cover memory unreserved after boot in first_valid_mfn

On Arm, some regions (e.g Initramfs, Dom0 Kernel...) are marked as
reserved until the hardware domain is built and they are copied into its
memory. Therefore, they will not be added in the boot allocator via
init_boot_pages.

Instead, init_xenheap_pages will be called once the region are not used
anymore.

Update first_valid_mfn in both init_heap_pages and init_boot_pages
(already exist) to cover all the cases.

This is XSA-245.

Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
[Adjust comment, added locking around first_valid_mfn update]
Signed-off-by: Boris Ostrovsky <boris.ostrovsky@oracle.com>
Acked-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reported-and-Tested-by: Konrad Rzeszutek Wilk <konrad.wilk@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    /*', '     * Some pages may not go through the boot allocator (e.g reserved', '     * memory at boot but released just after --- kernel, initramfs,', '     * etc.).', '     * Update first_valid_mfn to ensure those regions are covered.', '     */', '    spin_lock(&heap_lock);', '    first_valid_mfn = min_t(unsigned long, page_to_mfn(pg), first_valid_mfn);', '    spin_unlock(&heap_lock);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x on the ARM platform allowing guest OS users to obtain sensitive information from DRAM after a reboot, because disjoint blocks, and physical addresses that do not start at zero, are mishandled.

code_evidence: The function initializes heap pages for a range but never updates first_valid_mfn for pages that bypass the boot allocator; the loop only computes node/range boundaries and frees pages via free_heap_pages. The added diff records that reserved-at-boot regions (kernel, initramfs) released afterward are not covered, so first_valid_mfn can remain above their MFNs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The XSA-245 issue is a confidentiality exposure: late-released DRAM regions are not tracked by first_valid_mfn and can be handed to guests without proper scrubbing, exposing sensitive information. This matches CWE-200's scope of unintended disclosure of sensitive data.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: init_heap_pages does not lower first_valid_mfn to include pages released after boot. Trigger: a region reserved at boot and later freed through this path. Consequence: first_valid_mfn stays high, so disjoint/late-released physical memory is mishandled and guest-visible DRAM may retain or expose prior data, leaking information across a reboot.

commit_msg:
knc: fix a couple of memory leaks.

One of these can be remotely triggered during the authentication
phase which leads to a remote DoS possibility.

Pointed out by: Imre Rad <radimre83@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tgss_release_buffer(&min, &in);', '', '\tgss_release_buffer(&min, &out);']}
description: The read_packet function in knc (Kerberised NetCat) before 1.11-1 is vulnerable to denial of service (memory exhaustion) that can be exploited remotely without authentication, possibly affecting another services running on the targeted host.

code_evidence: read_packet fills the GSS buffer `in`; the loop at the `again` label repeatedly reads packets and re-invokes gss_accept_sec_context without releasing the previous `in` buffer, so each iteration leaks the prior allocation.

gss_accept_sec_context allocates `out`; it is released only on the write_packet error path, and on the GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED path the code jumps back to `again` without releasing `out`, accumulating allocations per loop iteration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the implementation fails to bound and release a limited resource (memory) across repeated operations, allowing attacker-controlled iteration to consume resources without limit. This is resource exhaustion from missing buffer release, not a buffer overflow (CWE-119) or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function never releases the GSS buffers `in` and `out` on the normal loop path before re-reading and re-invoking gss_accept_sec_context. Trigger: a remote unauthenticated peer drives repeated GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED iterations during authentication. Consequence: each iteration retains buffers, exhausting memory and causing a denial of service.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.1847: [security] potential oob write in do_addsub()

Problem:  potential oob write in do_addsub()
Solution: don't overflow buf2, check size in for loop()

Signed-off-by: Christian Brabandt <cb@256bit.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    for (i = 0; bit > 0; bit--)'], 'added_lines': ['\t    for (i = 0; bit > 0 && i < (NUMBUFLEN - 1); bit--)']}
description: Out-of-bounds Write in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.1847.

code_evidence: buf2 is a fixed 10-byte (NUMBUFLEN) stack array [10]. In the binary branch, bits is set to the full width of uvarnumber_T (64) [293], and the loop iterates bit down from that width while writing buf2[i++] with no bound on i [296,297], then terminates buf2[i] with NUL [298]. The pre-patch loop condition only checked bit > 0, so i could reach up to 64, far exceeding NUMBUFLEN.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes beyond the end of the intended stack buffer buf2, which is the definition of CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. It is a write (not read) past the buffer, and the missing size constraint is the direct cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write index i into the fixed-size buf2 is not constrained by the buffer size; the loop bound depends only on the number of significant bits (up to 64). Trigger: a binary-mode number (pre == 'b'/'B') whose value has many significant bits causes the loop to write past buf2. Consequence: stack out-of-bounds write, memory corruption/crash; the patch adds i < (NUMBUFLEN - 1).

commit_msg:
In commit 73f156a6e8c1 ("inetpeer: get rid of ip_id_count")
I used a very small hash table that could be abused
by patient attackers to reveal sensitive information.

Switch to a dynamic sizing, depending on RAM size.

Typical big hosts will now use 128x more storage (2 MB)
to get a similar increase in security and reduction
of hash collisions.

As a bonus, use of alloc_large_system_hash() spreads
allocated memory among all NUMA nodes.

Fixes: 73f156a6e8c1 ("inetpeer: get rid of ip_id_count")
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
