joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function omits RelinquishMagickMemory on pcd_table allocations along exception and early-return paths, directly matching CWE-772's missing release of a resource after its effective lifetime. The patch adding cleanup at the default case confirms the leak pattern, though the cited paths in func remain unreleased.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: error/early-return paths abandon the pcd_table array and earlier table allocations. Trigger: crafted PCD data causing an allocation failure or an r->length > 16. Consequence: heap memory for pcd_table entries is never released, enabling memory-consumption DoS.

commit_msg:
USB: gadget: f_hid: fix deadlock in f_hidg_write()

In f_hidg_write() the write_spinlock is acquired before calling
usb_ep_queue() which causes a deadlock when dummy_hcd is being used.
This is because dummy_queue() callbacks into f_hidg_req_complete() which
tries to acquire the same spinlock. This is (part of) the backtrace when
the deadlock occurs:

  0xffffffffc06b1410 in f_hidg_req_complete
  0xffffffffc06a590a in usb_gadget_giveback_request
  0xffffffffc06cfff2 in dummy_queue
  0xffffffffc06a4b96 in usb_ep_queue
  0xffffffffc06b1eb6 in f_hidg_write
  0xffffffff8127730b in __vfs_write
  0xffffffff812774d1 in vfs_write
  0xffffffff81277725 in SYSC_write

Fix this by releasing the write_spinlock before calling usb_ep_queue()

Reviewed-by: James Bottomley <James.Bottomley@HansenPartnership.com>
Tested-by: James Bottomley <James.Bottomley@HansenPartnership.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 4.11+
Fixes: 749494b6bdbb ("usb: gadget: f_hid: fix: Move IN request allocation to set_alt()")
Signed-off-by: Radoslav Gerganov <rgerganov@vmware.com>
Signed-off-by: Felipe Balbi <felipe.balbi@linux.intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tgoto release_write_pending_unlocked;', '\tspin_unlock_irqrestore(&hidg->write_spinlock, flags);', 'release_write_pending_unlocked:'], 'added_lines': ['\tspin_unlock_irqrestore(&hidg->write_spinlock, flags);', '', '\t\tgoto release_write_pending;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 4.16.4, a double-locking error in drivers/usb/dwc3/gadget.c may potentially cause a deadlock with f_hid.

code_evidence: The write_spinlock is re-acquired at line 33, then usb_ep_queue() is called at line 43 while the lock is still held. On failure, line 47 jumps to release_write_pending_unlocked, which skips the spin_lock at line 54 and directly clears write_pending.
The normal path unlocks at line 51, but the error path label at line 55 assumes the lock is already held and clears write_pending before unlocking at line 57.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 covers improper acquisition/release of locks. Here the same spinlock is held across a callback that re-locks it, and an error path clears state and unlocks without owning the lock, directly matching improper locking rather than a generic race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The lock ordering is inconsistent: usb_ep_queue() is invoked with write_spinlock held, and its completion callback f_hidg_req_complete re-acquires the same lock, causing self-deadlock on dummy_hcd. Additionally, the error path enters release_write_pending_unlocked without holding the lock, so write_pending is modified and the lock is released while not held, corrupting lock state.

commit_msg:
io_uring: fix uninitialized field in rw io_kiocb

io_rw_init_file does not initialize kiocb->private, so when iocb_bio_iopoll
reads kiocb->private it can contain uninitialized data.

Fixes: 3e08773c3841 ("block: switch polling to be bio based")
Signed-off-by: Joseph Ravichandran <jravi@mit.edu>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tkiocb->private = NULL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.17.5. io_rw_init_file in fs/io_uring.c lacks initialization of kiocb->private.

code_evidence: In the IOPOLL path, kiocb->ki_flags, ki_complete and req->iopoll_completed are set, but kiocb->private is never assigned before the kiocb is used for polling. The diff adds 'kiocb->private = NULL;' at line 21, confirming the field was previously left uninitialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-909 covers missing initialization of a critical resource; kiocb->private is a resource field expected to hold a defined value before use. Unlike an out-of-bounds or type-confusion issue, the defect is purely the absent initialization, matching CWE-909.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: io_rw_init_file configures the kiocb for IOPOLL without initializing kiocb->private. Trigger: a request enters the IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL branch and later iocb_bio_iopoll reads kiocb->private. Consequence: the consumer reads uninitialized memory, yielding unpredictable data (read of stale/expired data).

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/1895
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    (void) memset(target,0,sizeof(target));', '    (void) memset(symbolic,0,sizeof(symbolic));']}
description: Stack-based buffer overflow and unconditional jump in ReadXPMImage in coders/xpm.c in ImageMagick 7.0.10-7.

code_evidence: length is clamped to MagickPathExtent-1 and CopyXPMColor(key,...) is checked, so key parsing is bounded.
target is initialized via CopyMagickString and ParseXPMColor(p+width,...) is called only when strlen(p) > width; the returned q is later used without validating that it lies within the line buffer.

The bound check (next-q) < 0 breaks only when q is past next; otherwise CopyXPMColor copies up to next-q bytes into target and symbolic, and ParseXPMColor(target,...) may return a pointer q outside target, so the subsequent CopyXPMColor(symbolic,q,...) reads/copies from an attacker-influenced location.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes into fixed-size stack buffers target and symbolic using a length and source pointer that are not constrained to those buffers, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. The absence of a memset is incidental; the missing valid range check on q and next-q is the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: q returned by ParseXPMColor may point outside the intended buffer; the (next-q) check does not establish that q is within target or symbolic. CopyXPMColor then copies from q with a length derived from next-q into fixed stack buffers target/symbolic, allowing writes past their bounds and corrupting stack state.

commit_msg:
Prevent undefined behavior

Fix #2068 in main branch.

Signed-off-by: Steven Bellock <sbellock@nvidia.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (spdm_request->header.spdm_version >= SPDM_MESSAGE_VERSION_11) {', '        if (spdm_request->ct_exponent > LIBSPDM_MAX_CT_EXPONENT) {', '            return libspdm_generate_error_response(spdm_context,', '                                                   SPDM_ERROR_CODE_INVALID_REQUEST, 0,', '                                                   response_size, response);', '        }', '    }']}
description:
libspdm is a sample implementation that follows the DMTF SPDM specifications. Prior to versions 2.3.3 and 3.0, following a successful CAPABILITIES response, a libspdm Requester stores the Responder's CTExponent into its context without validation. If the Requester sends a request message that requires a cryptography operation by the Responder, such as CHALLENGE, libspdm will calculate the timeout value using the Responder's unvalidated CTExponent.

A patch is available in version 2.3.3. A workaround is also available. After completion of VCA, the Requester can check the value of the Responder's CTExponent. If it greater than or equal to 64, then the Requester can stop communication with the Responder.

code_evidence: For SPDM v1.1+, the request-supplied ct_exponent is copied into connection_info.capability.ct_exponent at line 105 without any bounds check; the pre-patch function stores it verbatim. The surrounding version check only gates whether the field is used, not whether its value is valid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because untrusted input (ct_exponent) is stored without checking it against required domain constraints (a maximum exponent), so an out-of-range value is processed as if valid. The fix adds an explicit ct_exponent > LIBSPDM_MAX_CT_EXPONENT check returning INVALID_REQUEST, confirming the missing validation is the root cause rather than a transformation/filtering defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Responder's CTExponent from the CAPABILITIES request is accepted and persisted into the connection context with no range validation. Trigger: a malicious peer sends a CAPABILITIES response/request carrying an oversized ct_exponent; the Requester later uses this stored value to compute cryptographic-operation timeouts. Supported consequence: the derived timeout value is unbounded, leading to denial of service (excessive resource consumption or stalled operations).

commit_msg:
fixing string check

Signed-off-by: Daniel Wang <daniel.wang@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    char namebuf[128];', '        strcpy(namebuf, inet_ntoa(address->sin_addr));'], 'added_lines': ['    char namebuf[128] = {};', '        strncpy(namebuf, inet_ntoa(address->sin_addr), sizeof(namebuf)-1);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the ROS communications-related packages (aka ros_comm or ros-melodic-ros-comm) through 1.14.3. A buffer overflow allows attackers to cause a denial of service and possibly execute arbitrary code via an IP address with a long hostname.

code_evidence: A fixed 128-byte stack buffer namebuf is declared at line 50 and filled at line 60 with strcpy from inet_ntoa(address->sin_addr); the copy is unbounded and performs no size check against the destination.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the defect is a buffer copy operation (strcpy) with no check that the input fits the output buffer, matching the target's scope of memory modification and availability impact; it is not an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
char namebuf[128];
strcpy(namebuf, inet_ntoa(address->sin_addr));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: strcpy at line 60 copies the textual IPv4 address returned by inet_ntoa into the 128-byte namebuf without bounding the source length. Trigger: a resolved address whose dotted-decimal string exceeds the buffer size is copied, writing past namebuf; the consequence is stack memory corruption that can crash the process or potentially enable code execution.

commit_msg:
Prevent a memory exhaustion problem when trying to read in strings from a COFF binary with a corrupt string table size.

	PR 22507
	* coffgen.c (_bfd_coff_read_string_table): Check for an excessive
	size of the external string table.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (strsize < STRING_SIZE_SIZE)', ''], 'added_lines': ['  if (strsize < STRING_SIZE_SIZE || strsize > bfd_get_file_size (abfd))', '  ']}
description: The _bfd_coff_read_string_table function in coffgen.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29.1, does not properly validate the size of the external string table, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive memory consumption, or heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted COFF binary.

code_evidence: The external string-table size strsize is read directly from the untrusted COFF file via H_GET_32 (lines 29) with no upper-bound check against the actual file size.
The only validation (lines 34-40) rejects strsize only when it is smaller than STRING_SIZE_SIZE; any larger attacker-controlled value passes.

That unvalidated size drives bfd_malloc(strsize + 1) (line 41) and a subsequent bfd_bread of strsize - STRING_SIZE_SIZE bytes (line 45) into the allocated buffer, and strings[strsize] = 0 (line 53) indexes within the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the missing bound lets an attacker-influenced size govern memory allocation and buffer read operations, producing out-of-bounds or over-large memory operations. It is the class-level weakness; the specific memory-consumption outcome is a consequence of the unvalidated size driving buffer operations.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size field from the crafted COFF string table is trusted without an upper bound, so the check at lines 34-40 permits arbitrarily large values. Trigger: a corrupt string-table size in a malicious binary causes a huge allocation (line 41) and an oversized read (line 45), leading to excessive memory consumption/DoS or, where size arithmetic and reads exceed real file data, buffer-related failures.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#ifdef LIBRAW_LIBRARY_BUILD', '  else if(!image)', '    throw LIBRAW_EXCEPTION_IO_CORRUPT;', '#endif']}
description: An off-by-one error within the "LibRaw::kodak_ycbcr_load_raw()" function (internal/dcraw_common.cpp) in LibRaw versions prior to 0.18.7 can be exploited to cause a heap-based buffer overflow and subsequently cause a crash.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function sinar_4shot_load_raw contains no off-by-one out-of-bounds write; the added guard only checks a null image pointer, and the described kodak_ycbcr_load_raw weakness is not present here.

commit_msg:
Detect 0==DT_SYMTAB in invert_pt_dynamic()

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/333
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        unsigned const v_sym = get_te32(&dynp0[-1+ x_sym].d_val);', '        if (!nbucket', '        unsigned const v_sym = get_te32(&dynp0[-1+ x_sym].d_val);', '        if (!n_bucket || !n_bitmask'], 'added_lines': ['        unsigned const v_sym = !x_sym ? 0 : get_te32(&dynp0[-1+ x_sym].d_val);', '        if (!nbucket || !v_sym', '        unsigned const v_sym = !x_sym ? 0 : get_te32(&dynp0[-1+ x_sym].d_val);', '        if (!n_bucket || !n_bitmask || !v_sym']}
description: A Segmentaation fault was found in UPX in invert_pt_dynamic() function in p_lx_elf.cpp. An attacker with a crafted input file allows invalid memory address access that could lead to a denial of service.

code_evidence: DT_SYMTAB index x_sym is read from dt_table[DT_SYMTAB]; the code only enters the v_hsh/v_gsh blocks when the hash tables exist, but uses x_sym to index dynp0[-1+x_sym] at line 69 and 93 without verifying x_sym is nonzero.

When the crafted input has DT_HASH or DT_GNU_HASH but no DT_SYMTAB, x_sym is 0, so -1+x_sym underflows and get_te32 reads dynp0[-1], an out-of-bounds dynamic-entry access; the added !v_sym guard prevents this.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked index causes a read outside the dynamic-array buffer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation; the added !v_sym condition enforces the missing bound.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing check that DT_SYMTAB exists before computing dynp0[-1+x_sym].d_val. Trigger: a crafted ELF with DT_HASH/DT_GNU_HASH but no DT_SYMTAB. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of the dynamic table, leading to a segmentation fault/DoS.

commit_msg: fixed a few memory issues (#1249)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tp->eventTypeCount = gf_bs_read_int(bs, 8);'], 'added_lines': ['\tu8 count;', '\tp->eventTypeCount = 0;', '\tcount = gf_bs_read_int(bs, 8);', '\tif (count > ARRAY_LENGTH(p->eventType))', '\t\treturn GF_CORRUPTED_DATA;', '', '\tp->eventTypeCount = count;']}
description: An issue was discovered in GPAC 0.7.1. There is a NULL pointer dereference in the function GetESD at isomedia/track.c in libgpac.a, as demonstrated by MP4Box.

code_evidence: Line 5 reads an 8-bit attacker-controlled count from the bitstream directly into p->eventTypeCount with no bounds check. Line 6 then uses that count as the loop bound when writing p->eventType[i], so a count larger than the eventType array size writes past its end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked count drives indexed writes into a fixed-size array, directly producing an out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-787. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), since line 6 stores data beyond the buffer boundary.

evidence_lines.code:
p->eventTypeCount = gf_bs_read_int(bs, 8);
for (i=0; i<p->eventTypeCount; i++) p->eventType[i] = gf_bs_read_int(bs, 8);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parsed eventTypeCount is trusted as an array bound without validating it against the fixed capacity of p->eventType. Trigger: a crafted bitstream supplies a count exceeding the array length, and the loop at line 6 writes each read byte past the buffer end, corrupting adjacent memory (crash or potential code execution).

commit_msg:
x86,kvm,vmx: Preserve CR4 across VM entry

CR4 isn't constant; at least the TSD and PCE bits can vary.

TBH, treating CR0 and CR3 as constant scares me a bit, too, but it looks
like it's correct.

This adds a branch and a read from cr4 to each vm entry.  Because it is
extremely likely that consecutive entries into the same vcpu will have
the same host cr4 value, this fixes up the vmcs instead of restoring cr4
after the fact.  A subsequent patch will add a kernel-wide cr4 shadow,
reducing the overhead in the common case to just two memory reads and a
branch.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Allow g_variant_byteswap() to operate on tree-form variants

This avoids needing to always serialise a variant before byteswapping it.
With variants in non-normal forms, serialisation can result in a large
increase in size of the variant, and a lot of allocations for leaf
`GVariant`s. This can lead to a denial of service attack.

Avoid that by changing byteswapping so that it happens on the tree form
of the variant if the input is in non-normal form. If the input is in
normal form (either serialised or in tree form), continue using the
existing code as byteswapping an already-serialised normal variant is
about 3× faster than byteswapping on the equivalent tree form.

The existing unit tests cover byteswapping well, but need some
adaptation so that they operate on tree form variants too.

I considered dropping the serialised byteswapping code and doing all
byteswapping on tree-form variants, as that would make maintenance
simpler (avoiding having two parallel implementations of byteswapping).
However, most inputs to `g_variant_byteswap()` are likely to be
serialised variants (coming from a byte array of input from some foreign
source) and most of them are going to be in normal form (as corruption
and malicious action are rare). So getting rid of the serialised
byteswapping code would impose quite a performance penalty on the common
case.

Signed-off-by: Philip Withnall <pwithnall@endlessos.org>

Fixes: #2797

The serialised output is wrapped into new bytes and a new variant (line 25), consuming the allocated memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unconditional normalization path allows attacker-controlled input to drive unbounded allocation and processing; this is uncontrolled consumption of memory and CPU, matching CWE-400's scope of resource-consumption DoS. It is not a memory-safety flaw (e.g. CWE-787), since the issue is excessive resource use rather than out-of-bounds access.

Otherwise this function may read data beyond the ruleset blob.

Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>

description: The IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt implementation in the netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) or possibly obtain sensitive information from kernel heap memory by leveraging in-container root access to provide a crafted offset value that leads to crossing a ruleset blob boundary.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.5164: invalid memory access after diff buffer manipulations

Problem:    Invalid memory access after diff buffer manipulations.
Solution:   Use zero offset when change removes all lines in a diff block.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\toff = dp->df_lnum[idx] - lnum_deleted;', '\t\t\toff = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t    off = 0;', '\t\t\t    off = dp->df_lnum[idx] - lnum_deleted;']}
description: Out-of-bounds Write in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.

code_evidence: In the deleted>0 branch, when dp->df_lnum[idx] >= line1, the original code computed off = dp->df_lnum[idx] - lnum_deleted before testing last <= line2. The fix moves off=0 to the top of the branch and only assigns off = dp->df_lnum[idx] - lnum_deleted inside the else (lines 97-102) where line2 falls before the diff's last line.
The computed off is then applied to every other diff buffer at lines 132-133: dp->df_lnum[i] -= off and dp->df_count[i] += n, without any bound check tying the adjustment to the actual buffer size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect causes df_lnum[i]/df_count[i] to be adjusted with an unbounded offset, yielding an out-of-range diff range that leads to writes past the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. It is not merely an integer issue; the missing constraint on off directly permits memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: off is derived from lnum_deleted and the diff line numbers but is applied unconditionally to other buffers' df_lnum/df_count. When a change removes all lines of a diff block (last <= line2, count set to 0), the stale nonzero off shifts df_lnum[i] backward and inflates df_count[i], producing an invalid diff range. Subsequent diff-buffer manipulation then reads/writes outside the intended buffer range, causing the invalid memory access/out-of-bounds write. Trigger: deleting lines across a diff block boundary where the block is fully removed.

commit_msg:
proc: prevent accessing /proc/<PID>/environ until it's ready

If /proc/<PID>/environ gets read before the envp[] array is fully set up
in create_{aout,elf,elf_fdpic,flat}_tables(), we might end up trying to
read more bytes than are actually written, as env_start will already be
set but env_end will still be zero, making the range calculation
underflow, allowing to read beyond the end of what has been written.

Fix this as it is done for /proc/<PID>/cmdline by testing env_end for
zero.  It is, apparently, intentionally set last in create_*_tables().

This bug was found by the PaX size_overflow plugin that detected the
arithmetic underflow of 'this_len = env_end - (env_start + src)' when
env_end is still zero.

The expected consequence is that userland trying to access
/proc/<PID>/environ of a not yet fully set up process may get
inconsistent data as we're in the middle of copying in the environment
variables.

Fixes: https://forums.grsecurity.net/viewtopic.php?f=3&t=4363
Fixes: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=116461
Signed-off-by: Mathias Krause <minipli@googlemail.com>

Cc: Jarod Wilson <jarod@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

description: Race condition in the environ_read function in fs/proc/base.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5.4 allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory by reading a /proc/*/environ file during a process-setup time interval in which environment-variable copying is incomplete.

code_evidence: Only the mm pointer is validated before proceeding; env_end is not checked, so the function can run while the environment is only partially set up.
env_start and env_end are snapshotted under mmap_sem, but the setup path that populates them is not synchronized with this read; env_start may be set while env_end is still zero.

The range check and this_len computation use env_end - env_start and env_end - (env_start + src); with env_end==0 these underflow to huge size_t values, and access_remote_vm then reads beyond the written environment into kernel memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is a timing-dependent non-atomic access to a shared resource (the mm environment range) modified concurrently by the process-setup code, exactly the concurrent-execution/improper-synchronization pattern of CWE-362. The information disclosure is the consequence; the underlying weakness is the race window, not a separate info-exposure class.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!mm)
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: environ_read reads shared mm->env_start/env_end without ensuring the environment setup is complete (env_end nonzero), so a concurrent process-setup sequence leaves env_end zero. Trigger: a local user reads /proc/<PID>/environ during that window. The unsigned subtraction underflows, and access_remote_vm reads past the initialized environment, exposing kernel memory contents.

commit_msg:
Fix illegal client float (CVE-2020-11810)

There is a time frame between allocating peer-id and initializing data
channel key (which is performed on receiving push request or on async
push-reply) in which the existing peer-id float checks do not work right.

If a "rogue" data channel packet arrives during that time frame from
another address and  with same peer-id, this would cause client to float
to that new address. This is because:

 - tls_pre_decrypt() sets packet length to zero if
   data channel key has not been initialized, which leads to

 - openvpn_decrypt() returns true if packet length is zero,
   which leads to

 - process_incoming_link_part1() returns true, which
   calls multi_process_float(), which commits float

Note that problem doesn't happen when data channel key is initialized,
since in this case openvpn_decrypt() returns false.

The net effect of this behaviour is that the VPN session for the
"victim client" is broken.  Since the "attacker client" does not have
suitable keys, it can not inject or steal VPN traffic from the other
session.  The time window is small and it can not be used to attack
a specific client's session, unless some other way is found to make it
disconnect and reconnect first.

CVE-2020-11810 has been assigned to acknowledge this risk.

Fix illegal float by adding buffer length check ("is this packet still
considered valid") before calling multi_process_float().

Trac: #1272
CVE: 2020-11810

Signed-off-by: Lev Stipakov <lev@openvpn.net>
Acked-by: Arne Schwabe <arne@rfc2549.org>
Acked-by: Antonio Quartulli <antonio@openvpn.net>
Acked-by: Gert Doering <gert@greenie.muc.de>
Message-Id: <20200415073017.22839-1-lstipakov@gmail.com>
URL: https://www.mail-archive.com/openvpn-devel@lists.sourceforge.net/msg19720.html
Signed-off-by: Gert Doering <gert@greenie.muc.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                if (floated)'], 'added_lines': ['                /* nonzero length means that we have a valid, decrypted packed */', '                if (floated && c->c2.buf.len > 0)']}
description: An issue was discovered in OpenVPN 2.4.x before 2.4.9. An attacker can inject a data channel v2 (P_DATA_V2) packet using a victim's peer-id. Normally such packets are dropped, but if this packet arrives before the data channel crypto parameters have been initialized, the victim's connection will be dropped. This requires careful timing due to the small time window (usually within a few seconds) between the victim client connection starting and the server PUSH_REPLY response back to the client. This attack will only work if Negotiable Cipher Parameters (NCP) is in use.

code_evidence: After process_incoming_link_part1() succeeds, the code checks only the boolean floated flag before calling multi_process_float() and committing the peer-id float. The function does not verify that c->c2.buf.len is nonzero, so a packet that passed part1 while carrying an undecrypted/zero-length buffer still triggers the float.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is a timing-window condition: the check-and-commit sequence on the pending instance/peer-id is not atomic with respect to data-channel key initialization, allowing an interfering packet to modify the shared session state. This matches CWE-362; it is not merely a missing length check, since the length check is the guard that closes the race window.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the float decision relies solely on 'floated' without validating that the packet is still a valid, decrypted buffer. Trigger: a rogue P_DATA_V2 packet with the victim's peer-id arrives during the window between peer-id allocation and data-channel key initialization, when tls_pre_decrypt() zeroes the length and openvpn_decrypt() returns true. Consequence: multi_process_float() commits an illegal float, breaking the victim's session (availability DoS).

commit_msg:
Preserve GSS context on init/accept failure

After gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() has created a
context, don't delete the mechglue context on failures from subsequent
calls, even if the mechanism deletes the mech-specific context (which
is allowed by RFC 2744 but not preferred).  Check for union contexts
with no mechanism context in each GSS function which accepts a
gss_ctx_id_t.

CVE-2017-11462:

RFC 2744 permits a GSS-API implementation to delete an existing
security context on a second or subsequent call to
gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() if the call results
in an error.  This API behavior has been found to be dangerous,
leading to the possibility of memory errors in some callers.  For
safety, GSS-API implementations should instead preserve existing
security contexts on error until the caller deletes them.

All versions of MIT krb5 prior to this change may delete acceptor
contexts on error.  Versions 1.13.4 through 1.13.7, 1.14.1 through
1.14.5, and 1.15 through 1.15.1 may also delete initiator contexts on
error.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences via strdup a pointer that may legitimately be NULL, matching CWE-476's description of dereferencing a pointer expected to be valid but NULL. This is not merely an unchecked allocation result; the missing constraint is the NULL return from the locale lookup, which the patch later guards with an if (lang) check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return values of mobi_get_locale_string for the dictionary input and output language codes are assumed non-NULL. Trigger: a dictionary whose dict_input_lang or dict_output_lang holds a code not mapped to a locale string, so mobi_get_locale_string returns NULL. The NULL pointer is then passed to strdup, which dereferences it (undefined behavior / crash), giving a denial of service.

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s nouveau driver in how a user triggers a memory overflow that causes the nvkm_vma_tail function to fail. This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: Line 60 checks the candidate free region fits, then line 61 removes the node from vmm->free via rb_erase and line 62 saves the pointer in vma before breaking.

if (unlikely(!vma))

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: create_node: Don't defer work to undo any changes on failure

XSA-115 extended destroy_node() to update the node accounting for the
connection. The implementation is assuming the connection is the parent
of the node, however all the nodes are allocated using a separate context
(see process_message()). This will result to crash (or corrupt) xenstored
as the pointer is wrongly used.

In case of an error, any changes to the database or update to the
accounting will now be reverted in create_node() by calling directly
destroy_node(). This has the nice advantage to remove the loop to unset
the destructors in case of success.

Take the opportunity to free the nodes right now as they are not
going to be reachable (the function returns NULL) and are just wasting
resources.

This is XSA-414 / CVE-2022-42309.

Fixes: 0bfb2101f243 ("tools/xenstore: fix node accounting after failed node creation")
Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Reviewed-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int destroy_node(void *_node)', '\tstruct node *node = _node;', '\tdomain_entry_dec(talloc_parent(node), node);'], 'added_lines': ['static int destroy_node(struct connection *conn, struct node *node)', '\tdomain_entry_dec(conn, node);']}
description: Xenstore: Guests can crash xenstored Due to a bug in the fix of XSA-115 a malicious guest can cause xenstored to use a wrong pointer during node creation in an error path, resulting in a crash of xenstored or a memory corruption in xenstored causing further damage. Entering the error path can be controlled by the guest e.g. by exceeding the quota value of maximum nodes per domain.

code_evidence: The node is allocated in a separate context from the connection (see process_message()), but line 9 obtains the accounting owner via talloc_parent(node) and passes it to domain_entry_dec() instead of the actual connection.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function releases/updates a resource using the wrong pointer derived from the node's talloc parent instead of the connection, matching CWE-763 (release of an invalid pointer/reference); the consequence is crash or memory corruption.

evidence_lines.code:
struct node *node = _node;
domain_entry_dec(talloc_parent(node), node);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: domain_entry_dec() is called with talloc_parent(node) rather than the connection that owns the node accounting. On the error path (e.g., exceeding the per-domain node quota), this yields a wrong/invalid pointer that is dereferenced, causing xenstored to crash or corrupt memory.

This pointer is not copied before the regex execution, so any operation during vim_regexec that flushes or reallocates the current line buffer leaves p dangling; line 23 then performs pointer arithmetic on freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because a pointer to freed memory (p) is reused after the underlying buffer may have been released during regex execution. The fix confirms this by copying the line with vim_strsave before searching. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the defect is reuse of a previously valid pointer whose allocation was freed.

Trigger: the regex search (e.g. searching for a mark) causes the current line to be flushed or reallocated. commit_msg:
XRA: Fix an infinite loop

C compilers don't care what size a value was on the wire. Use
naturally-sized ints, including in dissect_message_channel_mb where we
would otherwise overflow and loop infinitely.

Fixes #19100
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  guint16 offset = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['  int offset = 0;']}
description: XRA dissector infinite loop in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.5 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.13 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: Line 3 declares offset as guint16, capping its range at 65535.
The while loop at line 9 continues while tvb_captured_length_remaining(tvb, offset) > 3, advancing offset by 3 each iteration at line 12.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loop's exit condition cannot be reached for large inputs because the guint16 counter wraps, matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. This is not merely an integer overflow; the overflow directly causes the non-terminating iteration.

The supported consequence is an infinite loop consuming CPU, i.e., denial of service.

commit_msg:
[folly] Add additional overflow checks to IOBuf - CVE-2021-24036

Summary:
As per title

CVE-2021-24036

Reviewed By: jan

Differential Revision: D27938605

fbshipit-source-id: 7481c54ae6fbb7b67b15b3631d5357c2f7043f9c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (minCapacity > kMaxIOBufSize) {', '    throw_exception<std::bad_alloc>();', '  }', '']}
description: Passing an attacker controlled size when creating an IOBuf could cause integer overflow, leading to an out of bounds write on the heap with the possibility of remote code execution. This issue affects versions of folly prior to v2021.07.22.00. This issue affects HHVM versions prior to 4.80.5, all versions between 4.81.0 and 4.102.1, all versions between 4.103.0 and 4.113.0, and versions 4.114.0, 4.115.0, 4.116.0, 4.117.0, 4.118.0 and 4.118.1.

code_evidence: Line 2 adds sizeof(SharedInfo) to the caller-supplied minCapacity without any upper-bound check; minSize is then rounded up on line 3 and passed to goodMallocSize on line 4. If minCapacity is attacker-controlled and near SIZE_MAX, the addition on line 2 wraps around, producing a small minSize that is ultimately used for allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the flaw is an unsigned integer addition whose result wraps around when the operand is near the type maximum, and the wrapped size drives memory allocation. This is an arithmetic wraparound in a size computation (CWE-190), not merely a generic buffer overflow (CWE-787), which is the downstream consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size calculation at line 2 assumes minCapacity + sizeof(SharedInfo) is larger than minCapacity, but an attacker-controlled near-SIZE_MAX minCapacity makes the unsigned addition wraparound to a small value. Trigger: a caller passing such a size when constructing an IOBuf. Supported consequence: an undersized external buffer is allocated relative to the intended capacity, enabling out-of-bounds heap writes and potential code execution (as described).

Return error from cabac init if offset is greater than range

When the offset was greater than range, the bitstream was read
more than the valid range in leaf-level cabac parsing modules.
Error check was added to cabac init to fix this issue. Additionally
end of slice and slice error were signalled to suppress further
parsing of current slice.

Bug: 34897036
Change-Id: I1263f1d1219684ffa6e952c76e5a08e9a933c9d2
(cherry picked from commit 3b175da88a1807d19cdd248b74bce60e57f05c6a)

description: A remote code execution vulnerability in libhevc in Mediaserver could enable an attacker using a specially crafted file to cause memory corruption during media file and data processing. This issue is rated as Critical due to the possibility of remote code execution within the context of the Mediaserver process. Product: Android. Versions: 5.0.2, 5.1.1, 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2. Android ID: A-34897036.

The function stores the initialized range/offset and returns IHEVCD_SUCCESS unconditionally, with no validation that u4_ofst stays within u4_range before returning to callers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing offset-vs-range check lets downstream parsing operate outside the intended bitstream buffer boundary, directly supporting CWE-119. The patch adds exactly this bounds constraint before success is returned.

DEBUG_RANGE_OFST("init", ps_cabac->u4_range, ps_cabac->u4_ofst);
return ((IHEVCD_ERROR_T)IHEVCD_SUCCESS);

commit_msg: Fix crash bug with bad GIFs (Issue #423)

description: Integer overflow in the htmldoc 1.9.11 and before may allow attackers to execute arbitrary code and cause a denial of service that is similar to CVE-2017-9181.

code_evidence: Width and height are read directly from the GIF header bytes (buf[6..9]) without bounds checking, so an attacker-supplied GIF can set either dimension up to 65535.
The image descriptor path overwrites img->width and img->height from buf[4..7] with the same unchecked 16-bit values and sets img->depth before allocation.

The pixel buffer size is computed as img->width * img->height * img->depth in int arithmetic before the cast to size_t; large dimensions can wrap/wrap-negative this product, producing a small allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the size calculation wraps within the integer representation, so the allocation does not match the intended pixel count. This is the arithmetic wraparound itself, not merely a heap overflow (CWE-122), which is the downstream consequence of the wrapped size.

evidence_lines.code:
img->width  = (buf[7] << 8) | buf[6];
img->height = (buf[9] << 8) | buf[8];

img->pixels = (uchar *)malloc((size_t)(img->width * img->height * img->depth));
return (gif_read_image(fp, img, cmap, buf[8] & GIF_INTERLACE, transparent));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the multiplication img->width * img->height * img->depth is evaluated as int before conversion to size_t, while width/height come from untrusted GIF fields with no upper bound in the before version. A crafted GIF with large dimensions makes the product overflow (or become negative), yielding an undersized malloc; subsequent gif_read_image writes pixel data into that buffer, causing heap corruption and a crash.

commit_msg: Fix a buffer overflow issue with fuzzer-generated code (Issue #5)

description: Codedoc v3.2 has a stack-based buffer overflow in add_variable in codedoc.c, related to codedoc_strlcpy.

code_evidence: A fixed 16384-byte stack array `buffer` is used as a destination with `bufptr` walking through it.

In the first loop, `bufptr += strlen(bufptr)` advances the pointer by the copied text length; the space is appended when `bufptr > buffer`, and `strlcpy` writes at `bufptr` with remaining size computed from `bufptr - buffer`.
The second loop repeats the same pattern: `bufptr += strlen(bufptr)`, append at line 50, and `strlcpy` at line 51.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through `bufptr` beyond the bounds of `buffer`, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The related CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read via `strlen(bufptr)`) is only a precursor; the supported consequence is the write past the buffer end.

evidence_lines.code:
charbuffer[16384],
*bufptr;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: `bufptr` can advance to or beyond the end of `buffer` because it is incremented by `strlen(bufptr)` and the space append at line 29/50 occurs without checking remaining capacity. Trigger: many whitespace-separated text nodes cause `strlcpy` to receive a zero or negative remaining size and the append to write past the array. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write to the stack buffer, potentially corrupting memory or crashing.

description: lldpd before 0.8.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (assertion failure and daemon crash) via a malformed packet.

If it returns NULL, line 173 executes assert(errno == ENOMEM). The allocation can fail for reasons other than ENOMEM (e.g., a malformed/oversized management address), so the assertion is reachable from a crafted packet and aborts the daemon instead of taking the existing goto malformed path at 175.

The current code silently returns on bad types. In case when we have an invalid data, we may get a container of a large size with a bad type, this would lead to us running long loop doing nothing (though we already can say that the data is invalid).

The new code would throw an exception as soon as we try to skip a value of invalid type.

Fixes CVE-2019-3552

description: C++ Facebook Thrift servers (using cpp2) would not error upon receiving messages with containers of fields of unknown type. As a result, malicious clients could send short messages which would take a long time for the server to parse, potentially leading to denial of service. This issue affects Facebook Thrift prior to v2019.02.18.00.

commit_msg:
qemu: Add missing lock in qemuProcessHandleMonitorEOF

qemuMonitorUnregister will be called in multiple threads (e.g. threads
in rpc worker pool and the vm event thread).  In some cases, it isn't
protected by the monitor lock, which may lead to call g_source_unref
more than one time and a use-after-free problem eventually.

Add the missing lock in qemuProcessHandleMonitorEOF (which is the only
position missing lock of monitor I found).

Suggested-by: Michal Privoznik <mprivozn@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Peng Liang <liangpeng10@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Michal Privoznik <mprivozn@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Michal Privoznik <mprivozn@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    virObjectLock(mon);', '    virObjectUnlock(mon);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in libvirt. The qemuMonitorUnregister() function in qemuProcessHandleMonitorEOF is called using multiple threads without being adequately protected by a monitor lock. This flaw could be triggered by the virConnectGetAllDomainStats API when the guest is shutting down. An unprivileged client with a read-only connection could use this flaw to perform a denial of service attack by causing the libvirt daemon to crash.

code_evidence: qemuProcessHandleMonitorEOF acquires only the domain lock (virObjectLock(vm)) at line 9 and calls qemuMonitorUnregister(mon) at line 24 without holding the monitor lock. The function's cleanup path at line 27 releases vm, never mon, so the monitor unregister path runs unprotected against other threads that also call qemuMonitorUnregister on the same mon.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the missing monitor lock allows a shared object to be freed twice, after which surviving references point to freed memory that is subsequently used. The weakness is the unsynchronized unregister leading to reuse of freed memory, not merely a generic race or resource leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: qemuMonitorUnregister(mon) is invoked without serializing access to the monitor object's registration state, while other threads (RPC worker pool, VM event thread) may concurrently unregister the same monitor. The concurrent path can cause g_source_unref to run more than once on the same source, freeing it while another thread still holds a reference and later dereferences it, yielding a use-after-free that crashes the libvirt daemon.

commit_msg:
virtio: properly validate address before accessing config

There are several several issues in the current checking:

- The check was based on the minus of unsigned values which can overflow
- It was done after .{set|get}_config() which can lead crash when config_len
  is zero since vdev->config is NULL

Fix this by:

- Validate the address in virtio_pci_config_{read|write}() before
  .{set|get}_config
- Use addition instead minus to do the validation

Cc: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>
Cc: Petr Matousek <pmatouse@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Petr Matousek <pmatouse@redhat.com>
Message-id: 1367905369-10765-1-git-send-email-jasowang@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Anthony Liguori <aliguori@us.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '    if (addr > (vdev->config_len - sizeof(val)))', '        return (uint32_t)-1;'], 'added_lines': ['    if (addr + sizeof(val) > vdev->config_len) {', '        return (uint32_t)-1;', '    }', '']}
description: A flaw was found in the way qemu v1.3.0 and later (virtio-rng) validates addresses when guest accesses the config space of a virtio device. If the virtio device has zero/small sized config space, such as virtio-rng, a privileged guest user could use this flaw to access the matching host's qemu address space and thus increase their privileges on the host.

code_evidence: Line 5 calls k->get_config before any bounds check, so a zero/small config_len still invokes the backend. Line 6 checks addr > (vdev->config_len - sizeof(val)); since both operands are unsigned, when config_len is 0 or less than sizeof(val) the subtraction underflows to a huge value, making the check pass. Line 8 then reads vdev->config + addr, which can point outside the device config buffer (or dereference NULL config).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The guest's unchecked config access crosses the device/host trust boundary, letting a privileged guest obtain host-level access—an unintended privilege sphere. CWE-269 fits as improper privilege management; the underflow is the mechanism, but the supported impact is privilege escalation across actors.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unsigned underflow in the bounds check combined with the get_config call occurring before validation. Trigger: a guest supplies an out-of-range config address on a virtio device with small/zero config_len. Consequence: the host reads memory outside the config buffer, giving the guest access to QEMU host address space and enabling host privilege escalation.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a dereference of a null pointer in `tf.raw_ops.StringNGrams`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/1cdd4da14282210cc759e468d9781741ac7d01bf/tensorflow/core/kernels/string_ngrams_op.cc#L67-L74) does not fully validate the `data_splits` argument. This would result in `ngrams_data`(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/1cdd4da14282210cc759e468d9781741ac7d01bf/tensorflow/core/kernels/string_ngrams_op.cc#L106-L110) to be a null pointer when the output would be computed to have 0 or negative size. Later writes to the output tensor would then cause a null pointer dereference. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The loop validates each split only as 0 <= split <= input_data_size, without enforcing monotonic ordering or that the last split equals the data size.

ngrams_splits_data[i] is accumulated from num_ngrams, where length = splits_vec(i) - splits_vec(i-1); non-monotonic or missing terminal splits yield zero/negative lengths and a possibly 0 or undersized total.
The output tensor is allocated with size ngrams_splits_data[num_batch_items], which can be 0 or too small for the computed ngram writes.
The write loop iterates over num_batch_items and writes via output_start = &ngrams_data[output_start_idx] using the accumulated offsets, so writes can exceed the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes ngram strings through ngrams_data using offsets derived from insufficiently validated splits, allowing writes beyond the allocated output buffer, which matches CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The null-pointer dereference described is a downstream effect of the same unchecked size computation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: data_splits is not fully validated (no monotonicity, no requirement that the final split equals input size), so computed ngram counts and total output size can be 0 or smaller than the offsets used. Trigger: a crafted data_splits tensor. Consequence: writes through ngrams_data past the allocated output tensor, corrupting memory or crashing.

commit_msg: MQTT parse_publish_vhdr: added missing check of topic length
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [''], 'added_lines': ['    /* Abort if topic is longer than our topic buffer */', '    if(conn->in_packet.topic_len > MQTT_MAX_TOPIC_LENGTH) {', '      DBG("MQTT - topic too long %u/%u\\n", conn->in_packet.topic_len, MQTT_MAX_TOPIC_LENGTH);', '      return;', '    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in the MQTT server in Contiki-NG before 4.2. The function parse_publish_vhdr() that parses MQTT PUBLISH messages with a variable length header uses memcpy to input data into a fixed size buffer. The allocated buffer can fit only MQTT_MAX_TOPIC_LENGTH (default 64) bytes, and a length check is missing. This could lead to Remote Code Execution via a stack-smashing attack (overwriting the function return address). Contiki-NG does not separate the MQTT server from other servers and the OS modules, so access to all memory regions is possible.

code_evidence: The two-byte topic length is assembled from attacker-controlled input_data_ptr bytes into conn->in_packet.topic_len (lines 10-15) and marked received at line 17 without any comparison against MQTT_MAX_TOPIC_LENGTH, so the declared length is unbounded.

copy_bytes is derived from topic_len minus topic_pos, capped only by the remaining input length (lines 22-23), and memcpy then writes that many bytes into conn->in_publish_msg.topic at the topic_pos offset (lines 26-28); the terminating write at line 35 also uses the unchecked topic_pos index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs a memcpy into a fixed-size buffer using a length value that is not constrained to the buffer's intended boundary, producing an out-of-bounds write. The more specific CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) is a child of CWE-119, but the target label is CWE-119, so it is used here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parsed PUBLISH topic length is accepted without validating it against the fixed size of the topic buffer. Trigger: a remote MQTT PUBLISH message declaring a topic length larger than MQTT_MAX_TOPIC_LENGTH causes memcpy to write past the end of conn->in_publish_msg.topic. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds stack/heap write that may corrupt adjacent memory, crash the server, or overwrite control data such as a return address, enabling code execution.

Avoid overflow in MDC2_Update()

Thanks to Shi Lei for reporting this issue.

CVE-2016-6303

Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>

description: Integer overflow in the MDC2_Update function in crypto/mdc2/mdc2dgst.c in OpenSSL before 1.1.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via unknown vectors.

code_evidence: i is loaded from c->num and, when nonzero, the guard checks i + len < MDC2_BLOCK. Because len is size_t, a very large len can wrap i + len; the addition is performed in size_t and the comparison can wrongly succeed. The branch then executes memcpy(&(c->data[i]), in, len), writing len bytes into the fixed-size c->data buffer at offset i.

Trigger: caller-supplied len large enough to wrap i + len. Consequence: memcpy writes past the end of c->data, an out-of-bounds write that can crash or corrupt memory.

commit_msg:
demux_mf: improve format string processing

Before this commit, the user could specify a printf format string
which wasn't verified, and could result in:
- Undefined behavior due to missing or non-matching arguments.
- Buffer overflow due to untested result length.

The offending code was added at commit 103a9609 (2002, mplayer svn):
git-svn-id: svn://svn.mplayerhq.hu/mplayer/trunk@4566 b3059339-0415-0410-9bf9-f77b7e298cf2

It moved around but was not modified meaningfully until now.

Now we reject all conversion specifiers at the format except %%
and a simple subset of the valid specifiers. Also, we now use
snprintf to avoid buffer overflow.

The format string is provided by the user as part of mf:// URI.

Report and initial patch by Stefan Schiller.
Patch reviewed by @jeeb, @sfan5, Stefan Schiller.

description: A format string vulnerability in mpv through 0.33.0 allows user-assisted remote attackers to achieve code execution via a crafted m3u playlist file.

code_evidence: Line 58 allocates a fixed buffer of strlen(filename)+32. Line 80 logs the raw user-supplied filename, and line 82 passes that same externally-controlled string as the printf format to sprintf with only one int argument (count++). Because the format string comes directly from the mf:// URI, any additional or mismatched conversion specifiers in filename are interpreted by sprintf, and the result is written into the fixed fname buffer without a length check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-134 fits because the format string originates from an external source (the mf:// URI) and is passed to sprintf at line 82. This is distinct from a plain buffer overflow, since the externally-controlled format string is the root cause enabling both argument mismatches and the overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: user-controlled filename is used as the sprintf format string with an unvalidated number of conversion specifiers. Trigger: a crafted mf:// URI containing extra or mismatched specifiers. Consequence: undefined behavior from missing/mismatched arguments and buffer overflow from an untested result length, potentially leading to memory corruption or code execution.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. A denial-of-service vulnerability affects applications on a 32-bit systems that use PJSIP versions 2.12 and prior to play/read invalid WAV files. The vulnerability occurs when reading WAV file data chunks with length greater than 31-bit integers. The vulnerability does not affect 64-bit apps and should not affect apps that only plays trusted WAV files. A patch is available on the `master` branch of the `pjsip/project` GitHub repository. As a workaround, apps can reject a WAV file received from an unknown source or validate the file first.

code_evidence: The do-while(1) loop at line 94 only exits via the break at line 106 when a LIST subchunk with a MOVI tag is found; otherwise it advances the file position by ch.len-read at line 108 and repeats. ch.len is a subchunk length read from the untrusted file at line 97, and there is no validation that ch.len >= read (read is 4 only when the chunk id is LIST).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains an iteration (do-while(1)) whose exit condition (finding the MOVI tag) can be made unreachable by malicious subchunk length values, matching CWE-835. The unchecked ch.len-read seek is the mechanism that prevents forward progress; this is an infinite loop rather than a simple out-of-bounds read.

Consequence: the parser spins indefinitely, causing CPU/resource consumption and denial of service.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4959: using NULL regexp program

Problem:    Using NULL regexp program.
Solution:   Check for regexp program becoming NULL in more places.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    if (regmatch.regprog == NULL)', '\t    {', '\t\tif (patc != pat)', '\t\t    vim_free(patc);', '\t\treturn FAIL;', '\t    }'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t{', '\t\t    if (regmatch.regprog == NULL)', '\t\t    {', '\t\t\t// invalid pattern, possibly after recompiling', '\t\t\tif (patc != pat)', '\t\t\t    vim_free(patc);', '\t\t\treturn FAIL;', '\t\t    }', '\t\t}']}
description: NULL Pointer Dereference in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.4959.

code_evidence: vim_regcomp() result is stored in regmatch.regprog and immediately checked for NULL before use; on failure it frees patc and returns FAIL, preventing a NULL program from reaching buflist_match().
In the non-fuzzy round==1 path, buflist_match() consumes regmatch, and vim_regfree(regmatch.regprog) is called on the allocation-failure path; the NULL guard ensures regprog is valid here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a NULL pointer dereference: a pointer expected to be valid (regmatch.regprog) is dereferenced after a failed allocation/compilation. CWE-476 fits directly; it is not a memory leak or double-free, which are the freeing concerns handled alongside the guard.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a NULL regexp program from vim_regcomp() could be passed onward when the check was misplaced. The trigger is an invalid pattern causing compilation failure; without the guard the NULL regprog reaches buflist_match()/regexec, dereferencing NULL and crashing (DoS). The guard converts this into a clean FAIL return.

commit_msg:
In sja1105_static_config_upload, in two cases memory is leaked: when
static_config_buf_prepare_for_upload fails and when sja1105_inhibit_tx
fails. In both cases config_buf should be released.

Fixes: 8aa9ebccae87 ("net: dsa: Introduce driver for NXP SJA1105 5-port L2 switch")
Fixes: 1a4c69406cc1 ("net: dsa: sja1105: Prevent PHY jabbering during switch reset")
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Vladimir Oltean <olteanv@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t\treturn -ENXIO;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\trc = -EINVAL;', '\t\tgoto out;', '\t\trc = -ENXIO;', '\t\tgoto out;']}
description: Two memory leaks in the sja1105_static_config_upload() function in drivers/net/dsa/sja1105/sja1105_spi.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.5 allow attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering static_config_buf_prepare_for_upload() or sja1105_inhibit_tx() failures, aka CID-68501df92d11.

code_evidence: config_buf is allocated with kcalloc and the only release is kfree at the out label.
If static_config_buf_prepare_for_upload fails (rc < 0), the function logs an error and returns -EINVAL directly, bypassing the out label, so config_buf is never freed.
Likewise, when sja1105_inhibit_tx fails (rc < 0), it returns -ENXIO directly, again skipping the kfree path.
The out block performs kfree(config_buf) before returning, showing the intended single cleanup path that these early returns evade.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated memory (config_buf) is not released after its effective lifetime when error conditions occur; the missing kfree on early returns is a classic leak, distinct from use-after-free since the buffer is simply never freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: error paths for static_config_buf_prepare_for_upload and sja1105_inhibit_tx return without releasing the kcalloc'd config_buf. Trigger: either helper returns a negative value. Consequence: config_buf remains allocated, leaking memory on each failure and enabling memory-consumption DoS.

description: In ImageMagick before 6.9.7-6 and 7.x before 7.0.4-6, the ReadMATImage function in coders/mat.c uses uninitialized data, which might allow remote attackers to obtain sensitive information from process memory.
