description: An improper link resolution flaw while extracting an archive can lead to changing the access control list (ACL) of the target of the link. An attacker may provide a malicious archive to a victim user, who would trigger this flaw when trying to extract the archive. A local attacker may use this flaw to change the ACL of a file on the system and gain more privileges.

code_evidence: archive_write_disk_set_acls forwards the caller-supplied pathname `name` to set_acl() for POSIX.1e ACLs without checking whether `name` refers to a symbolic link. The mode parameter is passed for the caller to decide, but this function itself performs no lstat/readlink check before the ACL-setting operation on the path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the function accesses a file via a pathname and fails to prevent that name from being a link resolving to an unintended resource; the fix's purpose is to avoid calling acl_set_file() on symlinks. This is link-following, not merely improper ACL handling.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ACL is applied by pathname with no link resolution guard, so a symlink at `name` causes the operation to follow the link and modify the target's ACL instead of the link. Trigger: an attacker-supplied archive containing a symlink entry, extracted by a victim. Consequence: ACLs of an unintended file are changed, potentially granting extra privileges (integrity/access-control impact).

commit_msg:
Add support for different number of page table levels dependent
on the highest address used for a process. This will cause a 31 bit
process to use a two level page table instead of the four level page
table that is the default after the pud has been introduced. Likewise
a normal 64 bit process will use three levels instead of four. Only
if a process runs out of the 4 tera bytes which can be addressed with
a three level page table the fourth level is dynamically added. Then
the process can use up to 8 peta byte.

Signed-off-by: Martin Schwidefsky <schwidefsky@de.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (tlb->mm->context.asce_limit <= (1UL << 31))', '\t\treturn;']}
description: The fork implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.5 on s390 platforms mishandles the case of four page-table levels, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted application, related to arch/s390/include/asm/mmu_context.h and arch/s390/include/asm/pgalloc.h.

code_evidence: pmd_free_tlb queues the pmd pointer into tlb->array[--tlb->nr_pxds] whenever !tlb->fullmm, without checking whether the mm's page-table configuration (tlb->mm->context.asce_limit) actually uses a pmd level. The pmd_free path is taken only in the fullmm case.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing guard on the mm's page-table-level metadata (asce_limit) before processing the pmd is improper validation of data that determines whether the pmd level applies, matching CWE-20; the added early return confirms the constraint was omitted.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function assumes a pmd level always exists, so for a 31-bit process whose asce_limit is at most 1<<31 the pmd is still pushed onto the pxds array, corrupting the tally/array state. Trigger: a crafted application forking under a two-level table configuration. Consequence: system crash (DoS) from the inconsistent mmu_gather state.

commit_msg:
ALSA: control: code refactoring for ELEM_READ/ELEM_WRITE operations

ALSA control core handles ELEM_READ/ELEM_WRITE requests within lock
acquisition of a counting semaphore. The lock is acquired in helper
functions in the end of call path before calling implementations of each
driver.

ioctl(2) with SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_READ
...
->snd_ctl_ioctl()
  ->snd_ctl_elem_read_user()
    ->snd_ctl_elem_read()
      ->down_read(controls_rwsem)
      ->snd_ctl_find_id()
      ->struct snd_kcontrol.get()
      ->up_read(controls_rwsem)

ioctl(2) with SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_WRITE
...
->snd_ctl_ioctl()
  ->snd_ctl_elem_write_user()
    ->snd_ctl_elem_write()
      ->down_read(controls_rwsem)
      ->snd_ctl_find_id()
      ->struct snd_kcontrol.put()
      ->up_read(controls_rwsem)

This commit moves the lock acquisition to middle of the call graph to
simplify the helper functions. As a result:

...
->snd_ctl_ioctl()
  ->snd_ctl_elem_read_user()
    ->down_read(controls_rwsem)
    ->snd_ctl_elem_read()

->snd_ctl_ioctl()
  ->snd_ctl_elem_write_user()
    ->down_read(controls_rwsem)
    ->snd_ctl_elem_write()
      ->snd_ctl_find_id()
      ->struct snd_kcontrol.put()
    ->up_read(controls_rwsem)

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = t->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = xt_table_get_private_protected(t);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: xt_find_table_lock returns table t, and line 16 reads t->private directly without any protection against concurrent replacement. The same pointer is then dereferenced at lines 17-19 (private->size and copy_entries_to_user), so a concurrent xt_replace_table that swaps and frees the old table info can leave this reader using freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences t->private and uses it after a concurrent free, matching CWE-416. This is not merely a race in the abstract; the concrete defect is a read of memory that the replacement path has already freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the private table-info pointer is fetched and used with no synchronization against the replacement path's sequence-count protocol. Trigger: a user with CAP_NET_ADMIN in a namespace runs concurrent iptables rules replacement while get_entries reads the table. Consequence: use-after-free read of freed xt_table_info, causing a crash or memory disclosure.

Fix tf.raw_ops.UnsortedSegmentJoin vulnerability with invalid num_segments.

Check that input is actually a scalar before treating it as such.

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.UnsortedSegmentJoin` does not fully validate the input arguments. This results in a `CHECK`-failure which can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. The code assumes `num_segments` is a scalar but there is no validation for this before accessing its value. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: The function reads num_segments_tensor from context->input(2) and checks only that NumElements() != 0. It then immediately calls num_segments_tensor.scalar<NUM_SEGMENTS_TYPE>()() to extract the value, assuming the tensor is a scalar without verifying its shape.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the code fails to validate a required property (scalar shape/rank) of an input before safely processing it, and the missing constraint directly enables the crash. The weakness is improper validation of input metadata, not a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the input tensor num_segments is dereferenced as a scalar without confirming rank 0. A non-scalar tensor with a nonzero element count passes the emptiness check and reaches scalar<>(), which triggers a CHECK-failure. Trigger: caller supplies a non-scalar num_segments tensor. Consequence: process abort, i.e., denial of service.

Add missing validations to reverse_sequence_op

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The implementation of `tf.raw_ops.ReverseSequence` allows for stack overflow and/or `CHECK`-fail based denial of service. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/5b3b071975e01f0d250c928b2a8f901cd53b90a7/tensorflow/core/kernels/reverse_sequence_op.cc#L114-L118) fails to validate that `seq_dim` and `batch_dim` arguments are valid. Negative values for `seq_dim` can result in stack overflow or `CHECK`-failure, depending on the version of Eigen code used to implement the operation. Similar behavior can be exhibited by invalid values of `batch_dim`. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The constructor reads the `batch_dim` and `seq_dim` attributes via GetAttr and stores them directly, with no check that either value is non-negative before the kernel uses them to index memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unvalidated negative dimension leads to memory being written past the intended buffer boundary. It is not merely an input-validation issue (CWE-20) or a pure availability bug: the underlying operation is an out-of-bounds write whose crash is the observable effect.

OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, context->GetAttr("batch_dim", &batch_dim_));
OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, context->GetAttr("seq_dim", &seq_dim_));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: `seq_dim`/`batch_dim` are accepted without a lower-bound constraint, so a negative value reaches the Eigen reverse-sequence implementation and is used in index arithmetic. Trigger: a caller supplies a negative `seq_dim` (or `batch_dim`). Consequence: the index computation writes outside the intended buffer, producing a stack overflow or CHECK-failure denial of service. The missing validation is the cause; the out-of-bounds write is the consequence.

commit_msg:
usb: max-3421: Prevent corruption of freed memory

The MAX-3421 USB driver remembers the state of the USB toggles for a
device/endpoint. To save SPI writes, this was only done when a new
device/endpoint was being used. Unfortunately, if the old device was
removed, this would cause writes to freed memory.

To fix this, a simpler scheme is used. The toggles are read from
hardware when a URB is completed, and the toggles are always written to
hardware when any URB transaction is started. This will cause a few more
SPI transactions, but no causes kernel panics.

Fixes: 2d53139f3162 ("Add support for using a MAX3421E chip as a host driver.")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Mark Tomlinson <mark.tomlinson@alliedtelesis.co.nz>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210625031456.8632-1-mark.tomlinson@alliedtelesis.co.nz
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['max3421_set_address(struct usb_hcd *hcd, struct usb_device *dev, int epnum,', '\t\t    int force_toggles)', '\tstruct max3421_hcd *max3421_hcd = hcd_to_max3421(hcd);', '\tint old_epnum, same_ep, rcvtog, sndtog;', '\tstruct usb_device *old_dev;', '\told_dev = max3421_hcd->loaded_dev;', '\told_epnum = max3421_hcd->loaded_epnum;', '', '\tsame_ep = (dev == old_dev && epnum == old_epnum);', '\tif (same_ep && !force_toggles)', '\t\treturn;', '', '\tif (old_dev && !same_ep) {', '\t\t/* save the old end-points toggles: */', '\t\tu8 hrsl = spi_rd8(hcd, MAX3421_REG_HRSL);', '', '\t\trcvtog = (hrsl >> MAX3421_HRSL_RCVTOGRD_BIT) & 1;', '\t\tsndtog = (hrsl >> MAX3421_HRSL_SNDTOGRD_BIT) & 1;', '', "\t\t/* no locking: HCD (i.e., we) own toggles, don't we? */", '\t\tusb_settoggle(old_dev, old_epnum, 0, rcvtog);', '\t\tusb_settoggle(old_dev, old_epnum, 1, sndtog);', '\t}', '\tmax3421_hcd->loaded_epnum = epnum;', '\tmax3421_hcd->loaded_dev = dev;'], 'added_lines': ['max3421_set_address(struct usb_hcd *hcd, struct usb_device *dev, int epnum)', '\tint rcvtog, sndtog;']}
description: drivers/usb/host/max3421-hcd.c in the Linux kernel before 5.13.6 allows physically proximate attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and panic) by removing a MAX-3421 USB device in certain situations.

code_evidence: The function loads cached pointers: old_dev = max3421_hcd->loaded_dev and old_epnum = max3421_hcd->loaded_epnum; same_ep compares the incoming dev with this cached old_dev, and if equal and not forced, returns early.
When old_dev is non-NULL and the endpoint differs, the code reads hardware toggles and calls usb_settoggle(old_dev, old_epnum, ...) on the cached device pointer without verifying it is still valid.
The cached references max3421_hcd->loaded_epnum and max3421_hcd->loaded_dev are refreshed here for later invocations, so a stale pointer persists across calls.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the code reuses a cached pointer to a usb_device after the device may have been freed, performing writes (usb_settoggle) on freed memory. This is a direct use-after-free rather than a mere null-pointer or race condition.

evidence_lines.code:
max3421_hcd->loaded_epnum = epnum;
max3421_hcd->loaded_dev = dev;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the driver caches a struct usb_device pointer (loaded_dev) and dereferences it via usb_settoggle when a new endpoint is loaded. Trigger: the previously loaded USB device is removed, freeing that usb_device, but loaded_dev is not cleared; a subsequent max3421_set_address call with a different endpoint passes the old_dev non-NULL check and writes toggles through the freed pointer. Supported consequence: use-after-free memory corruption leading to kernel panic/DoS.

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

In order to fail safe in the supported case, re-implement all the VT-x
instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.9.x through 4.11.x, on Intel x86 platforms, allowing x86 HVM and PVH guests to cause a host OS denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) or possibly have unspecified other impact because nested VT-x is not properly restricted.

commit_msg:
Made some changes to the I/O stream library for memory streams.
There were a number of potential problems due to the possibility
of integer overflow.
Changed some integral types to the larger types size_t or ssize_t.
For example, the function mem_resize now takes the buffer size parameter
as a size_t.
Added a new function jas_stream_memopen2, which takes a
buffer size specified as a size_t instead of an int.
This can be used in jas_image_cmpt_create to avoid potential
overflow problems.

description: Multiple integer overflows in the (1) jas_realloc function in base/jas_malloc.c and (2) mem_resize function in base/jas_stream.c in JasPer before 1.900.22 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted image, which triggers use after free vulnerabilities.

return m->pos_;

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. Incomplete validation in `SparseAdd` results in allowing attackers to exploit undefined behavior (dereferencing null pointers) as well as write outside of bounds of heap allocated data. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/656e7673b14acd7835dc778867f84916c6d1cac2/tensorflow/core/kernels/sparse_sparse_binary_op_shared.cc) has a large set of validation for the two sparse tensor inputs (6 tensors in total), but does not validate that the tensors are not empty or that the second dimension of `*_indices` matches the size of corresponding `*_shape`. This allows attackers to send tensor triples that represent invalid sparse tensors to abuse code assumptions that are not protected by validation. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: num_dims is taken solely from a_indices_t->dim_size(1) at [55], and both index matrices are bound at [56,57]. UnionSparseIndicesAndValues is then invoked at [59,60,61] with num_dims and the raw b_indices_mat without checking that b_indices_t->dim_size(1) equals num_dims.
The output loop at [70-74] copies a full row via chip<0>(idx) from a_indices_mat or b_indices_mat into output_indices_mat, whose row width is the a-derived num_dims.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing a row of width dim_size(1) of b_indices into a buffer sized with a_indices' dim_size(1) writes past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. The missing dimension-equality check is the root cause; the out-of-bounds write is the consequence, not merely an undefined-behavior/dereference issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the second dimension of b_indices is never constrained to match a_indices' second dimension, so num_dims reflects only a_indices. Trigger: a caller supplies a sparse tensor triple where b_indices has a larger second dimension than a_indices; the row-copy at [73,74] then copies more elements than the output row holds. Supported consequence: a heap out-of-bounds write into the allocated output_indices tensor.

commit_msg:
lib/node.c: Limit recursion in ri-records (CVE-2021-3622)

Windows Registry hive "ri"-records are arbitrarily nested B-tree-like
structures:

  +-------------+
  | ri          |
  |-------------|
  | nr_offsets  |
  |   offset[0] ------>  points to another lf/lh/li/ri block
  |   offset[1] ------>
  |   offset[2] ------>
  +-------------+

It is possible to construct a hive with a very deeply nested tree of
ri-records, causing the internal _get_children function to recurse to
any depth which can cause programs linked to hivex to crash with a
stack overflow.

Since it is not thought that deeply nested ri-records occur in real
hives, limit recursion depth.  If you hit this limit you will see the
following error and the operation will return an error instead of
crashing:

  \> ls
  hivex: _get_children: returning EINVAL because: ri-record nested to depth >= 32
  ls: Invalid argument

Thanks to Jeremy Galindo for finding and reporting this bug.

Reported-by: Jeremy Galindo, Sr Security Engineer, Datto.com
Signed-off-by: Richard W.M. Jones <rjones@redhat.com>
Fixes: CVE-2021-3622
Fixes: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1975489
(cherry picked from commit 781a12c4a49dd81365c9c567c5aa5e19e894ba0e)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (_get_children (h, subkey_lf, &children, &blocks, flags) == -1)'], 'added_lines': ['  if (_get_children (h, subkey_lf, &children, &blocks, flags, 0) == -1)']}
description: A flaw was found in the hivex library. This flaw allows an attacker to input a specially crafted Windows Registry (hive) file, which would cause hivex to recursively call the _get_children() function, leading to a stack overflow. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

code_evidence: The function reads the attacker-controlled subkey_lf offset from the nk record (line 28), validates only that it points to a valid block (line 30), then passes it to _get_children (line 35). The diff adds a depth argument 0 here, delegating recursion-depth limiting to the callee; this caller itself imposes no bound on the nested ri-record tree, so the recursion depth is controlled by the crafted hive content.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because untrusted input controls consumption of a limited resource (the call stack) without throttling, causing denial of service. The patch's added depth argument confirms the missing recursion limit was the resource-control flaw; it is not a memory-corruption or injection issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the hive file's nested ri-record offsets drive unbounded recursion in _get_children, and this caller only checks block validity, not nesting depth. Trigger: a specially crafted Windows Registry hive with deeply nested ri-records. Consequence: stack exhaustion from unbounded recursion, crashing processes linked to hivex (availability impact).

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: Fail a transaction if it is not possible to create a node

Commit f2bebf72c4d5 "xenstore: rework of transaction handling" moved
out from copying the entire database everytime a new transaction is
opened to track the list of nodes changed.

The content of all the nodes accessed during a transaction will be
temporarily stored in TDB using a different key.

The function create_node() may write/update multiple nodes if the child
doesn't exist. In case of a failure, the function will revert any
changes (this include any update to TDB). Unfortunately, the function
which reverts the changes (i.e. destroy_node()) will not use the correct
key to delete any update or even request the transaction to fail.

This means that if a client decide to go ahead with committing the
transaction, orphan nodes will be created because they were not linked
to an existing node (create_node() will write the nodes backwards).

Once some nodes have been partially updated in a transaction, it is not
easily possible to undo any changes. So rather than continuing and hit
weird issue while committing, it is much saner to fail the transaction.

This will have an impact on any client that decides to commit even if it
can't write a node. Although, it is not clear why a normal client would
want to do that...

Lastly, update destroy_node() to use the correct key for deleting the
node. Rather than recreating it (this will allocate memory and
therefore fail), stash the key in the structure node.

This is XSA-415 / CVE-2022-42310.

Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Reviewed-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>

description: IIPImage High Resolution Streaming Image Server prior to commit 882925b295a80ec992063deffc2a3b0d803c3195 is affected by an integer overflow in iipsrv.fcgi through malformed HTTP query parameters.

code_evidence: Line 7 allocates the output buffer using a 64-bit cast: (unsigned long long)resampled_width*resampled_height*channels, so the allocation itself is protected against 32-bit wraparound.
Line 34 computes resampled_index as a 64-bit value, and line 39 writes output[resampled_index+k]; this indexing is also widened.

Line 46, however, computes in.dataLength as resampled_width * resampled_height * channels * (in.bpc/8) with all operands of 32-bit type, so the multiplication is performed in 32-bit arithmetic before assignment to the (size_t) field.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size calculation whose result can exceed the integer representation and wrap, matching CWE-190; the patch's size_t casts confirm the intended fix. This is specifically a wraparound of the stored length, not an out-of-bounds index or a buffer overflow in the loop itself.

evidence_lines.code: unsigned char *output = new unsigned char[(unsigned long long)resampled_width*resampled_height*channels];

unsigned long long resampled_index = (unsigned long long)( (j*resampled_width + i) * channels );
output[resampled_index+k] = r;
in.dataLength = resampled_width * resampled_height * channels * (in.bpc/8);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size field in.dataLength is calculated in 32-bit arithmetic, while the actual buffer is allocated with a 64-bit product. Trigger: attacker-controlled resampled_width, resampled_height, or channels large enough that the product exceeds the 32-bit range. Consequence: in.dataLength wraps to a small value, so the metadata understates the real buffer size; downstream consumers trusting this length may under-allocate, over-read, or truncate, supporting the DoS and memory-integrity impacts.

description: curl 7.75.0 through 7.76.1 suffers from a use-after-free vulnerability resulting in already freed memory being used when a TLS 1.3 session ticket arrives over a connection. A malicious server can use this in rare unfortunate circumstances to potentially reach remote code execution in the client. When libcurl at run-time sets up support for TLS 1.3 session tickets on a connection using OpenSSL, it stores pointers to the transfer in-memory object for later retrieval when a session ticket arrives. If the connection is used by multiple transfers (like with a reused HTTP/1.1 connection or multiplexed HTTP/2 connection) that first transfer object might be freed before the new session is established on that connection and then the function will access a memory buffer that might be freed. When using that memory, libcurl might even call a function pointer in the object, making it possible for a remote code execution if the server could somehow manage to get crafted memory content into the correct place in memory.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only parses cipher strings into an ALG_ID array and sets Schannel credential fields; it contains no pointer lifetime management, free, or later dereference of freed memory, so it does not support CWE-416.

commit_msg:
pipe: limit the per-user amount of pages allocated in pipes

On no-so-small systems, it is possible for a single process to cause an
OOM condition by filling large pipes with data that are never read. A
typical process filling 4000 pipes with 1 MB of data will use 4 GB of
memory. On small systems it may be tricky to set the pipe max size to
prevent this from happening.

This patch makes it possible to enforce a per-user soft limit above
which new pipes will be limited to a single page, effectively limiting
them to 4 kB each, as well as a hard limit above which no new pipes may
be created for this user. This has the effect of protecting the system
against memory abuse without hurting other users, and still allowing
pipes to work correctly though with less data at once.

The limit are controlled by two new sysctls : pipe-user-pages-soft, and
pipe-user-pages-hard. Both may be disabled by setting them to zero. The
default soft limit allows the default number of FDs per process (1024)
to create pipes of the default size (64kB), thus reaching a limit of 64MB
before starting to create only smaller pipes. With 256 processes limited
to 1024 FDs each, this results in 1024*64kB + (256*1024 - 1024) * 4kB =
1084 MB of memory allocated for a user. The hard limit is disabled by
default to avoid breaking existing applications that make intensive use
of pipes (eg: for splicing).

Reported-by: socketpair@gmail.com
Reported-by: Tetsuo Handa <penguin-kernel@I-love.SAKURA.ne.jp>
Mitigates: CVE-2013-4312 (Linux 2.0+)
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tpipe->bufs = kzalloc(sizeof(struct pipe_buffer) * PIPE_DEF_BUFFERS, GFP_KERNEL);', '\t\t\tpipe->buffers = PIPE_DEF_BUFFERS;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tunsigned long pipe_bufs = PIPE_DEF_BUFFERS;', '\t\tstruct user_struct *user = get_current_user();', '', '\t\tif (!too_many_pipe_buffers_hard(user)) {', '\t\t\tif (too_many_pipe_buffers_soft(user))', '\t\t\t\tpipe_bufs = 1;', '\t\t\tpipe->bufs = kzalloc(sizeof(struct pipe_buffer) * pipe_bufs, GFP_KERNEL);', '\t\t}', '', '\t\t\tpipe->buffers = pipe_bufs;', '\t\t\tpipe->user = user;', '\t\t\taccount_pipe_buffers(pipe, 0, pipe_bufs);', '\t\tfree_uid(user);']}
description: fs/pipe.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5 does not limit the amount of unread data in pipes, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by creating many pipes with non-default sizes.

code_evidence: On each pipe allocation, the function allocates a full default buffer array (PIPE_DEF_BUFFERS) with no check of per-user or system-wide pipe memory usage.
The allocated buffer count is recorded as PIPE_DEF_BUFFERS, so every pipe carries the default capacity regardless of accumulated usage.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources; this function allocates pipe buffers with no resource limit or accounting, enabling memory exhaustion. The narrower CWE-770 (allocation without limits) is a member of this category and describes the same cause, but the target category fits the resource-management failure.

evidence_lines.code: pipe->buffers = PIPE_DEF_BUFFERS;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: alloc_pipe_info unconditionally allocates PIPE_DEF_BUFFERS buffers per pipe without any accounting or cap on unread pipe data. Trigger: a local user creates many pipes (optionally with non-default sizes) and fills them with data that is never read. Supported consequence: unbounded kernel memory consumption leading to OOM/denial of service; the missing limit, not the allocation itself, is the defect.

In the weighted single-prediction branch, put_weighted_pred is called unconditionally with pixels[1] and pixels[2] as destination pointers, with no chroma-format guard.
In the unweighted B-slice branch, put_unweighted_pred is likewise called unconditionally with the NULL chroma destination pointers.

description: Heap-based buffer overflow in libavformat/http.c in FFmpeg before 2.8.10, 3.0.x before 3.0.5, 3.1.x before 3.1.6, and 3.2.x before 3.2.2 allows remote web servers to execute arbitrary code via a negative chunk size in an HTTP response.

code_evidence: Line 9 stores s->off, a seek offset that can be attacker-influenced, in a signed int64_t; line 10 initializes the header-building length counter len to 0.
Line 70 resets s->filesize to -1 (signed sentinel) at request start, so downstream size/offset arithmetic treats the value as signed rather than an unsigned bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The signed offset/size handling leads to memory operations outside intended buffer bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory access within a buffer. It is the buffer-bounds class weakness; the signedness flaw is the root cause, not the classified weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code:
int64_t off = s->off;
int len = 0;
s->filesize         = -1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: offset and size state (s->off, s->filesize) are held as signed 64-bit values, so a negative or wrapped value from a malformed HTTP response (e.g. negative chunk size) can flow into length/size computations. Trigger: a remote server returns a negative chunk size, producing a negative offset/size that is later used to compute buffer positions. Consequence: arithmetic yields out-of-bounds accesses, enabling heap-based buffer overflow and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
This works just like close(2), unsurprisingly. We remove the file
descriptor and post the completion inline, then offload the actual
(potential) last file put to async context.

Mark the async part of this work as uncancellable, as we really must
guarantee that the latter part of the close is run.

Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcase IORING_OP_CLOSE:', '\t\tret = io_close_prep(req, sqe);', '\t\tbreak;']}
description: A time-of-check to time-of-use issue exists in io_uring subsystem's IORING_OP_CLOSE operation in the Linux kernel's versions 5.6 - 5.11 (inclusive), which allows a local user to elevate their privileges to root. Introduced in b5dba59e0cf7e2cc4d3b3b1ac5fe81ddf21959eb, patched in 9eac1904d3364254d622bf2c771c4f85cd435fc2, backported to stable in 788d0824269bef539fe31a785b1517882eafed93.

code_evidence: The switch dispatches IORING_OP_OPENAT to io_openat_prep(req, sqe), which resolves the path and prepares a file reference for later asynchronous execution.
The default branch rejects unhandled opcodes with -EINVAL; in the pre-patch function IORING_OP_CLOSE has no case, so close requests are not prepared here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The deferred prep/execution split means the resource state observed at submission is not re-validated at use, matching CWE-367's check-then-use gap. This is a TOCTOU race rather than a simple missing-validation error, since the weakness arises from the temporal separation between request preparation and asynchronous execution.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the deferred-request preparation path lacks a close handler, so close operations bypass the prep/validation stage and are resolved later against a resource whose state may already have changed. Trigger: a local user submits an IORING_OP_CLOSE whose target file or fd state is altered between submission and async execution. Consequence: the close acts on a stale or substituted resource, enabling the described privilege escalation.

OOB read memory can be written to a file,
if DataOffset is 0 and Length is too large
in SMB2_WRITE request of compound request.

To prevent this, when checking the length of

Fixes: e2f34481b24d ("cifsd: add server-side procedures for SMB3")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com # ZDI-CAN-17817
Signed-off-by: Hyunchul Lee <hyc.lee@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Namjae Jeon <linkinjeon@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Steve French <stfrench@microsoft.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif ((u64)le16_to_cpu(req->DataOffset) + length >', '\t\t    get_rfc1002_len(work->request_buf)) {', '\t\t\tpr_err("invalid write data offset %u, smb_len %u\\n",', '\t\t\t       le16_to_cpu(req->DataOffset),', '\t\t\t       get_rfc1002_len(work->request_buf));'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (le16_to_cpu(req->DataOffset) <', '\t\t    offsetof(struct smb2_write_req, Buffer)) {', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in ksmbd in the Linux kernel 5.15 through 5.19 before 5.19.2. There is an out-of-bounds read and OOPS for SMB2_WRITE, when there is a large length in the zero DataOffset case.

code_evidence: Length is taken from the untrusted SMB2_WRITE request at line 19 and only bounded against max_write_size at line 56. For the non-RDMA path, lines 66-67 validate DataOffset + length against the full request buffer length, but the resulting data_buf at lines 74-75 is computed from the SMB2 header pointer plus DataOffset; a zero DataOffset makes data_buf point before the write payload, and ksmbd_vfs_write at line 78 consumes length bytes from there.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes a data pointer from an attacker-controlled offset and reads Length bytes from it, reading outside the intended buffer. This is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), not a write overflow, because the vulnerable operation is reading request data into the VFS write path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: DataOffset is not required to be at least the size of the SMB2_WRITE header, so the data pointer can precede the buffer's data area. Trigger: a compound request with DataOffset 0 and a large Length passes the offset+length check but causes ksmbd_vfs_write to read Length bytes from before the intended buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read (and possible oops).

Instead of directly accessing the actions array without checks
for the value of n (which may lead to heap buffer overflow etc,
see #83 or #105), use the dedicated OpCode function.

commit_msg: tiffcrop: fix issue #380 and #382 heap buffer overflow in extractImageSection
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    ceil((width * image->bps + 7) / (double)8) * image->spp * length;'], 'added_lines': ['\t    ceil((width * image->bps * image->spp + 7) / (double)8) * length;']}
description: A heap buffer overflow in ExtractImageSection function in tiffcrop.c in libtiff library Version 4.3.0 allows attacker to trigger unsafe or out of bounds memory access via crafted TIFF image file which could result into application crash, potential information disclosure or any other context-dependent impact

code_evidence: Lines 21-22 derive width and length from section coordinates; line 24 computes sectsize as ceil((width * image->bps + 7)/8) * image->spp * length, multiplying samples-per-pixel after the per-row byte rounding and multiplying length after spp. This under-allocates when the rounding term is non-trivial, so the buffer created at line 25 is smaller than the data extractImageSection later writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The under-sized allocation leads directly to writes past the end of the intended section buffer, matching CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write). A pure integer-overflow explanation would fit CWE-190, but here the defect is the misordered size calculation causing an undersized buffer that is then overrun.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The size expression applies ceil rounding to width*bps only, then multiplies by spp; the correct row size is width*bps*spp rounded up. The resulting sectsize is too small, and extractImageSection writes a full section into sect_buff, overflowing the heap allocation.

description: epan/dissectors/packet-nbap.c in the NBAP dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.9 and 2.0.x before 2.0.1 does not validate conversation data, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: conversation is initialized to NULL (line 5) and only assigned by find_conversation (line 29). If no matching conversation exists, find_conversation returns NULL (line 32) and the code creates a new one via conversation_new (line 34).

The new conversation is then passed to conversation_set_dissector (line 37) and, for DL direction, umts_fp_conversation_info is built and stored with set_umts_fp_conv_data (lines 38-62), assuming the conversation pointer is valid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes conversation/message-derived data and fails to validate the resulting conversation pointer before using it, matching CWE-20's missing validation of input-derived state. The supported consequence is a NULL-pointer dereference denial of service; this is improper validation rather than a pure pointer-arithmetic or type-confusion issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The returned conversation pointer is used without validating that conversation_new succeeded; if conversation creation fails and returns NULL, subsequent calls such as conversation_set_dissector and set_umts_fp_conv_data dereference or store into an invalid conversation, causing a crash. The trigger is a crafted NBAP packet whose channel info leads to conversation lookup/creation failure.

commit_msg:
codecs: check OMX buffer size before use in (gsm|g711)dec

Bug: 27793163
Bug: 27793367
Change-Id: Iec3de8a237ee2379d87a8371c13e543878c6652c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (inHeader->nFilledLen * sizeof(int16_t) > outHeader->nAllocLen) {', '            ALOGE("output buffer too small (%d).", outHeader->nAllocLen);', '            android_errorWriteLog(0x534e4554, "27793163");', '', '            notify(OMX_EventError, OMX_ErrorUndefined, 0, NULL);', '            mSignalledError = true;', '            return;', '        }', '']}
description: libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-06-01 does not validate OMX buffer sizes for the GSM and G711 codecs, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, as demonstrated by obtaining Signature or SignatureOrSystem access, aka internal bug 27793163.

code_evidence: The input-length check only rejects nFilledLen > kMaxNumSamplesPerFrame, but sets mSignalledError without returning, so decoding proceeds even after the error.
inputptr is derived from the input header and passed to DecodeMLaw/DecodeALaw, which write decoded samples into outHeader->pBuffer.
The output length is computed as nFilledLen * sizeof(int16_t) with no comparison against outHeader->nAllocLen before the decode writes into the output buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs a write operation into the output memory buffer beyond its intended boundary due to the missing size constraint. This is a direct out-of-bounds write, not merely an integer issue, since the unchecked product drives the decode write.

evidence_lines.code: outHeader->nFilledLen = inHeader->nFilledLen * sizeof(int16_t);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder writes decoded 16-bit samples into the output buffer sized by nAllocLen without verifying that nFilledLen * sizeof(int16_t) fits. Trigger: a crafted input buffer whose length times two exceeds the output allocation. Consequence: a heap buffer overflow write past outHeader->pBuffer, enabling memory corruption and potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Avoid potentially dangerous signed to unsigned conversion

We make sure to never pass a negative `rlen` as size to memcpy(). See
also <https://bugs.php.net/bug.php?id=73280>.

Patch provided by Emmanuel Law.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif(remain == 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif(remain <= 0) {']}
description: Integer signedness error in the dynamicGetbuf function in gd_io_dp.c in the GD Graphics Library (aka libgd) through 2.2.3, as used in PHP before 5.6.28 and 7.x before 7.0.13, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted imagecreatefromstring call.

code_evidence: Line 8 computes remain = dp->logicalSize - dp->pos, which can be negative if pos exceeds logicalSize. The else branch at line 11 only guards remain == 0 (line 12), so a negative remain falls through to line 15, setting rlen = remain (negative). Line 17 then passes that negative rlen as the size argument to memcpy, converting it to a huge size_t.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The negative size passed to memcpy causes a write beyond the destination buffer's intended bounds, matching CWE-119. The signedness error is the root cause, but the directly supported weakness is the out-of-bounds memory write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the equality check remain == 0 fails to reject negative remain values, so a negative rlen reaches memcpy. Trigger: a crafted imagecreatefromstring call that drives dp->pos beyond dp->logicalSize. Consequence: memcpy interprets the negative length as a huge unsigned size, causing a stack-based buffer overflow (DoS or possible other impact).

commit_msg:
OSdep: Fixed segmentation fault that happens with a malicious server sending a negative length (Closes #16 on GitHub).

git-svn-id: http://svn.aircrack-ng.org/trunk@2419 28c6078b-6c39-48e3-add9-af49d547ecab
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tassert(plen <= *len); /* XXX */'], 'added_lines': ['\tassert(plen <= *len && plen > 0); /* XXX */']}
description: network.c in Aircrack-ng before 1.2 Beta 3 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault) via a response with a crafted length parameter.

code_evidence: Line 9 converts the attacker-supplied network header length nh.nh_len into plen without checking its sign. Lines 10-13 only print and assert plen <= *len; the assert does not reject a negative plen.
Line 14 assigns the unvalidated plen to *len, which is then used as the length argument to net_read_exact at line 15.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because untrusted network metadata (the length field) is accepted without validating the required property that it be non-negative. The missing check on line 13 is the root cause; the crash is the consequence of processing the invalid length.

evidence_lines.code:
*len = plen;
if ((*len) && (net_read_exact(s, arg, *len) == -1))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function trusts the length field from the remote peer and never enforces plen > 0 before storing it in *len. A malicious server sending a negative length passes the assert (since a negative value satisfies plen <= *len) and the negative value reaches net_read_exact, producing the segmentation fault described in the commit.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Reported-by: syzbot+f427adf9324b92652ccc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>

description: An issue was discovered in the FUSE filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.10.6, aka CID-5d069dbe8aaf. fuse_do_getattr() calls make_bad_inode() in inappropriate situations, causing a system crash. NOTE: the original fix for this vulnerability was incomplete, and its incompleteness is tracked as CVE-2021-28950.

commit_msg:
The cgroup release_agent is called with call_usermodehelper.  The function
call_usermodehelper starts the release_agent with a full set fo capabilities.
Therefore require capabilities when setting the release_agaent.

Reported-by: Tabitha Sable <tabitha.c.sable@gmail.com>
Tested-by: Tabitha Sable <tabitha.c.sable@gmail.com>
Fixes: 81a6a5cdd2c5 ("Task Control Groups: automatic userspace notification of idle cgroups")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v2.6.24+
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
Signed-off-by: Tejun Heo <tj@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/*', '\t\t * Release agent gets called with all capabilities,', '\t\t * require capabilities to set release agent.', '\t\t */', '\t\tif ((fc->user_ns != &init_user_ns) || !capable(CAP_SYS_ADMIN))', '\t\t\treturn invalfc(fc, "Setting release_agent not allowed");']}
description: A vulnerability was found in the Linux kernel’s cgroup_release_agent_write in the kernel/cgroup/cgroup-v1.c function. This flaw, under certain circumstances, allows the use of the cgroups v1 release_agent feature to escalate privileges and bypass the namespace isolation unexpectedly.

code_evidence: In the Opt_release_agent case, the code only rejects a respecified release_agent (lines 46-47) and then stores the user-supplied param->string into ctx->release_agent (line 48) without any capability or namespace check. The before-function has no capable(CAP_SYS_ADMIN) or fc->user_ns validation, so an unprivileged user in a non-initial user namespace can set the release agent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing capability/namespace authorization check before accepting the release_agent setting is a missing authorization weakness (CWE-862). It is not merely input validation: the operation is permitted to an actor lacking the required privilege, enabling privileged action execution.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the release_agent mount option is accepted from any caller without verifying CAP_SYS_ADMIN or restricting to the initial user namespace. Trigger: a user configures the cgroup v1 release_agent via a mount/filesystem context. Consequence: the kernel later invokes the release agent with full capabilities via call_usermodehelper, allowing privilege escalation and namespace-isolation bypass.

commit_msg:
avcodec/aacdec_template: add more checks to make sure only 22.2 gets to 22.2

Validates the set channel layout as well as verifies that the received
layout to the function matches the reference layout, so that it matches
the implemented re-ordering logic.

Fixes #8845
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (tags == 16 && i == 8) {', '    if (tags == 16 && total_non_cc_elements == 16) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (layout == PREFIX_FOR_22POINT2 && tags == 16 && i == 8) {', '        const uint8_t (*reference_layout_map)[3] = aac_channel_layout_map[12];', '        for (int j = 0; j < tags; j++) {', '            if (layout_map[j][0] != reference_layout_map[j][0] ||', '                layout_map[j][2] != reference_layout_map[j][2])', '                goto end_of_layout_definition;', '        }', '', 'end_of_layout_definition:', '', '    if (layout == AV_CH_LAYOUT_22POINT2) {']}
description: Buffer overflow vulnerability in sniff_channel_order function in aacdec_template.c in ffmpeg 3.1.2, allows attackers to execute arbitrary code (local).

code_evidence: At line 127 the special 22.2 path is entered solely on tags == 16 && i == 8, then e2c_vec[i] and subsequent layout_map[i] entries are written for a fixed 16-element layout; the pre-patch condition does not verify the actual channel layout.
Lines 173-175 set total_non_cc_elements = n = i and, when tags == 16 && total_non_cc_elements == 16, perform fixed-index FFSWAP operations assuming a 16-element 22.2 arrangement.
Lines 186-190 write back e2c_vec[i] into layout_map[i][0..2] for i < total_non_cc_elements, so any mismatch between the assumed and actual element count propagates into the layout_map writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes into fixed-size e2c_vec and layout_map based on an unvalidated layout assumption, matching CWE-120's unchecked-size copy/write into a destination buffer. The fix adds a reference-layout comparison and gates reordering on AV_CH_LAYOUT_22POINT2, confirming the missing size/layout check; this is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the 22.2 handling is selected by element count (tags == 16 && i == 8) rather than by the validated channel layout, so a differently ordered or malformed layout can reach the fixed 16-entry reordering and writeback logic. Trigger: crafted AAC channel configuration with 16 tags. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds writes to e2c_vec/layout_map and memory corruption.

description: There is a integer overflow in media_tools/av_parsers.c in the hevc_parse_slice_segment function in GPAC 1.0.1 which results in a crash.

code_evidence: pps_id is declared u32 at line 4, so it cannot hold a negative value; gf_bs_read_ue_log at line 11 returns an unsigned Exp-Golomb value into it. The guard at line 12 only rejects pps_id >= 64; line 14 then indexes vvc->pps[pps_id].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked index writes/reads outside the vvc->pps buffer. The missing upper-bound constraint on the u32 index is the direct cause of the out-of-bounds access; this is not merely a signedness issue (CWE-195) since the array indexing is the harmful operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check assumes pps_id is signed and only tests the upper bound, but the variable is u32, so a decoded value at or above 64 passes unchecked and is used directly as an array index at line 14. Trigger: a crafted bitstream supplying an oversized pps_id. Consequence: out-of-bounds access into the pps array (and a derived sps index at line 15), leading to memory corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
It turns out that currently we rely only on sysfs attribute
permissions:

  $ ll /sys/bus/rbd/{add*,remove*}
  --w------- 1 root root 4096 Sep  3 20:37 /sys/bus/rbd/add
  --w------- 1 root root 4096 Sep  3 20:37 /sys/bus/rbd/add_single_major
  --w------- 1 root root 4096 Sep  3 20:37 /sys/bus/rbd/remove
  --w------- 1 root root 4096 Sep  3 20:38 /sys/bus/rbd/remove_single_major

This means that images can be mapped and unmapped (i.e. block devices
can be created and deleted) by a UID 0 process even after it drops all
privileges or by any process with CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE in its user namespace
as long as UID 0 is mapped into that user namespace.

Be consistent with other virtual block devices (loop, nbd, dm, md, etc)
and require CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the initial user namespace for mapping and
unmapping, and also for dumping the configuration string and refreshing
the image header.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Ilya Dryomov <idryomov@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!capable(CAP_SYS_ADMIN))', '\t\treturn -EPERM;', '']}
description: The rbd block device driver in drivers/block/rbd.c in the Linux kernel through 5.8.9 used incomplete permission checking for access to rbd devices, which could be leveraged by local attackers to map or unmap rbd block devices, aka CID-f44d04e696fe.

code_evidence: rbd_config_info_show reads the device via dev_to_rbd_dev and returns rbd_dev->config_info through sprintf with no capability or privilege check; the only access gate is the sysfs attribute's file mode, not an in-function authorization decision.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-863 covers authorization checks that are performed incorrectly or, as here, omitted for a privileged resource access. The lack of a capable(CAP_SYS_ADMIN) constraint before returning config_info makes the access gate incomplete rather than a mere information-exposure bug.

evidence_lines.code:
struct rbd_device *rbd_dev = dev_to_rbd_dev(dev);
return sprintf(buf, "%s\n", rbd_dev->config_info);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the show handler exposes configuration data relying solely on sysfs attribute permissions. Trigger: any process that can open the attribute (e.g. UID 0 or CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE in a user namespace) invokes the read. Consequence: the rbd configuration string is disclosed without an explicit privileged check, bypassing the intended administrative-only access control.

commit_msg: * FIX [security] avoid data racing by clone retain msg
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tnng_msg_clone(r[i]->message);']}
description: A use-after-free vulnerability exists in NanoMQ 0.17.2. The vulnerability can be triggered by calling the function nni_mqtt_msg_get_publish_property() in the file mqtt_msg.c. This vulnerability is caused by improper data tracing, and an attacker could exploit it to cause a denial of service attack.

code_evidence: The loop reads each retained message pointer r[i]->message (line 75) and pushes it into work->msg_ret without cloning or taking ownership; then line 77 frees the dbtree_retain_msg vector r, dropping the references that owned those messages. The diff adds nng_msg_clone(r[i]->message) at line 75 so msg_ret holds an independent copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function retains references to nng_msg objects after their owning dbtree_retain_msg entries are freed, and those references are used later. The added clone shows the fix is to keep an independent reference rather than a stale one; this is use-after-free, not a simple memory leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: retained message pointers are stored in work->msg_ret while the source dbtree_retain_msg entries (r[i]) that reference them are freed by cvector_free(r), leaving msg_ret with dangling pointers. Trigger: a client subscribes to a topic with retained messages; later use of work->msg_ret dereferences freed message memory, causing a crash/DoS or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
arm64: KVM: Tighten guest core register access from userspace

We currently allow userspace to access the core register file
in about any possible way, including straddling multiple
registers and doing unaligned accesses.

This is not the expected use of the ABI, and nobody is actually
using it that way. Let's tighten it by explicitly checking
the size and alignment for each field of the register file.

Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Fixes: 2f4a07c5f9fe ("arm64: KVM: guest one-reg interface")
Reviewed-by: Christoffer Dall <christoffer.dall@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Mark Rutland <mark.rutland@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Martin <Dave.Martin@arm.com>
[maz: rewrote Dave's initial patch to be more easily backported]
Signed-off-by: Marc Zyngier <marc.zyngier@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Will Deacon <will.deacon@arm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (validate_core_offset(reg))', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;']}
description: arch/arm64/kvm/guest.c in KVM in the Linux kernel before 4.18.12 on the arm64 platform mishandles the KVM_SET_ON_REG ioctl. This is exploitable by attackers who can create virtual machines. An attacker can arbitrarily redirect the hypervisor flow of control (with full register control). An attacker can also cause a denial of service (hypervisor panic) via an illegal exception return. This occurs because of insufficient restrictions on userspace access to the core register file, and because PSTATE.M validation does not prevent unintended execution modes.

code_evidence: set_core_reg derives off from the userspace-supplied reg->id and only checks off >= nr_regs and off + size >= nr_regs; it never verifies that KVM_REG_SIZE(reg->id) matches the register field size or that reg->id is properly aligned, so arbitrary size/alignment combinations from userspace are accepted.

After copying the user value, only the pstate offset is range-checked against a fixed mode list; memcpy then writes KVM_REG_SIZE(reg->id) bytes at (u32 *)regs + off, using the unvalidated userspace-controlled size and offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The handler accepts input metadata whose properties (size, alignment, offset) are not validated before use, which is exactly CWE-20 improper input validation. The missing validate check and the unvalidated memcpy size make the weakness input-validation, not a separate memory-safety class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ioctl handler trusts the userspace-supplied register id metadata (offset, size, alignment) without validating it against the actual core-register layout. Trigger: a crafted KVM_SET_ONE_REG request with a mismatched or unaligned size/offset reaches memcpy, which writes beyond or across the intended register field, allowing userspace to control register contents including PSTATE.

commit_msg:
In the AEAD interface for AF_ALG, the reference to the "null skcipher"
held by each tfm was being dropped in the wrong place -- when each
af_alg_ctx was freed instead of when the aead_tfm was freed.  As
discovered by syzkaller, a specially crafted program could use this to
cause the null skcipher to be freed while it is still in use.

Fix it by dropping the reference in the right place.

Fixes: 72548b093ee3 ("crypto: algif_aead - copy AAD from src to dst")
Reported-by: syzbot <syzkaller@googlegroups.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v4.14+
Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Stephan Mueller <smueller@chronox.de>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcrypto_put_default_null_skcipher2();'], 'added_lines': []}
description: A flaw was found in the crypto subsystem of the Linux kernel before version kernel-4.15-rc4. The "null skcipher" was being dropped when each af_alg_ctx was freed instead of when the aead_tfm was freed. This can cause the null skcipher to be freed while it is still in use leading to a local user being able to crash the system or possibly escalate privileges.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's defect is a misplaced lifetime/reference release of the null skcipher (use-after-free), not missing or incorrect validation of input data; CWE-20 is unsupported.

commit_msg:
DO NOT MERGE: defensive parsing of mp3 album art information

several points in stagefrights mp3 album art code
used strlen() to parse user-supplied strings that may be
unterminated, resulting in reading beyond the end of a buffer.

This changes the code to use strnlen() for 8-bit encodings and
strengthens the parsing of 16-bit encodings similarly. It also
reworks how we watch for the end-of-buffer to avoid all over-reads.

Bug: 32377688
Test: crafted mp3's w/ good/bad cover art. See what showed in play music
Change-Id: Ia9f526d71b21ef6a61acacf616b573753cd21df6
(cherry picked from commit fa0806b594e98f1aed3ebcfc6a801b4c0056f9eb)

description: An information disclosure vulnerability in id3/ID3.cpp in libstagefright in Mediaserver could enable a local malicious application to access data outside of its permission levels. This issue is rated as Moderate because it could be used to access sensitive data without permission. Product: Android. Versions: 4.4.4, 5.0.2, 5.1.1, 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1. Android ID: A-32377688.

code_evidence: For 8-bit encodings, StringSize calls strlen on the caller-supplied start pointer without any bound on the buffer; the returned length (plus one) is then used to size or advance parsing of album-art strings.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unbounded strlen causes an out-of-bounds read whose supported impact is disclosure of memory outside the album-art buffer, matching the commit description of information disclosure. The root error is the missing length bound, but the target CWE-200 captures the resulting exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized local application.

evidence_lines.code:
if (encoding == 0x00 || encoding == 0x03) {
return strlen((const char *)start) + 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the string length is computed with strlen, which keeps reading until a NUL byte regardless of the actual buffer end. Trigger: a crafted mp3 whose album-art string lacks a NUL terminator within its buffer. Consequence: the function reads past the buffer and the oversized length propagates to callers, exposing adjacent memory contents beyond the intended field.

description: epan/dissectors/packet-gsm_cbch.c in the GSM CBCH dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.11 and 2.0.x before 2.0.3 uses the wrong variable to index an array, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds access and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: The loop bounds iteration with i<k, and new_slots is filled with k entries (line 47), so valid indices are 0..k-1.
In the 0x40 branch, new_slots[k] is read and passed to proto_tree_add_uint_format_value; k equals the populated count, so index k is one past the last valid entry.
The 0x41 branch likewise reads new_slots[k] at the out-of-bounds index.
The reserved-MDT else branch also reads new_slots[k] and formats it, while the same branch correctly writes other_slots[new_slots[i]-1] using i.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading new_slots[k] when k is the count of populated entries is an out-of-bounds buffer read, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. It is not an off-by-one write or integer overflow; the defect is a wrong index variable, so the buffer-boundary violation is the direct weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code uses the population counter k instead of loop index i to index new_slots inside the per-slot loop. Trigger: a crafted schedule packet whose octet1 is 0x40, 0x41, or a reserved value reaches these branches after k slots were populated, causing a read at new_slots[k]. Consequence: out-of-bounds stack read that can crash the dissector (DoS) or expose adjacent stack data in the formatted output.

commit_msg:
ALSA sequencer core initializes the event pool on demand by invoking
snd_seq_pool_init() when the first write happens and the pool is
empty.  Meanwhile user can reset the pool size manually via ioctl
concurrently, and this may lead to UAF or out-of-bound accesses since
the function tries to vmalloc / vfree the buffer.

A simple fix is to just wrap the snd_seq_pool_init() call with the
recently introduced client->ioctl_mutex; as the calls for
snd_seq_pool_init() from other side are always protected with this
mutex, we can avoid the race.

Reported-by: 范龙飞 <long7573@126.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint err = -EINVAL;', '\t\tif (snd_seq_pool_init(client->pool) < 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\tint err;', '\t\tmutex_lock(&client->ioctl_mutex);', '\t\terr = snd_seq_pool_init(client->pool);', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&client->ioctl_mutex);', '\t\tif (err < 0)', '\terr = -EINVAL;']}
description: The Linux kernel 4.15 has a Buffer Overflow via an SNDRV_SEQ_IOCTL_SET_CLIENT_POOL ioctl write operation to /dev/snd/seq by a local user.

code_evidence: On the first write, when the pool is empty (size > 0 but not allocated), snd_seq_pool_init(client->pool) is called without holding client->ioctl_mutex. The same pool can concurrently be resized/reset via the SNDRV_SEQ_IOCTL_SET_CLIENT_POOL ioctl, which takes that mutex and vmalloc/vfree's the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent sequence lacking proper synchronization over a shared resource (client->pool), matching CWE-362; the unsynchronized init call creates the timing window exploited by the concurrent ioctl.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The lazy pool initialization is not serialized against the ioctl path that resizes the pool. A local user racing write() against the pool-size ioctl can cause snd_seq_pool_init to vmalloc/vfree the buffer while the other path also mutates it, yielding use-after-free or out-of-bounds access. The fix wraps the init call in client->ioctl_mutex to restore exclusivity.

commit_msg:
Internal change

PiperOrigin-RevId: 411896058
Change-Id: Ia031058247e3cf382957a6662d3f9e1cbb481ca2
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  ConvolutionDimensions dims = OpDimensionsFromInputs(', '      op_info.inputs(0).shape(), op_info, &found_unknown_shapes);'], 'added_lines': ['  TF_ASSIGN_OR_RETURN(ConvolutionDimensions dims,', '                      OpDimensionsFromInputs(op_info.inputs(0).shape(), op_info,', '                                             &found_unknown_shapes));']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The estimator for the cost of some convolution operations can be made to execute a division by 0. The function fails to check that the stride argument is strictly positive. Hence, the fix is to add a check for the stride argument to ensure it is valid. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 9-10 computes ConvolutionDimensions via OpDimensionsFromInputs without validating that stride values (sx, sy) are strictly positive; the original function ignores any error returned by that helper.
Lines 11-20 derive compute ops using dims.sx and dims.sy in the branch conditions and dims.ox/dims.oy, which are derived from the stride; a zero stride propagates into these calculations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 (Divide By Zero) fits because the missing positive-stride constraint allows a zero divisor to reach the convolution dimension computation, matching the described division-by-zero. The fix wraps the call in TF_ASSIGN_OR_RETURN to propagate the validation error, confirming the unchecked-stride cause rather than a mere logic error.

evidence_lines.code:
ConvolutionDimensions dims = OpDimensionsFromInputs(
op_info.inputs(0).shape(), op_info, &found_unknown_shapes);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: stride fields from the op input are used to derive dimensions without a strictly-positive check, and the dimension helper's error status is discarded. Trigger: an op_info with stride sx or sy equal to zero. Consequence: downstream dimension/ops computation performs a division by the stride, yielding a division-by-zero that can crash the estimator (DoS).

commit_msg:
In btsdio_probe, &data->work was bound with btsdio_work.In
btsdio_send_frame, it was started by schedule_work.

If we call btsdio_remove with an unfinished job, there may
be a race condition and cause UAF bug on hdev.

Fixes: ddbaf13e3609 ("[Bluetooth] Add generic driver for Bluetooth SDIO devices")
Signed-off-by: Zheng Wang <zyytlz.wz@163.com>
Signed-off-by: Luiz Augusto von Dentz <luiz.von.dentz@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcancel_work_sync(&data->work);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in btsdio_remove in drivers\bluetooth\btsdio.c in the Linux Kernel. In this flaw, a call to btsdio_remove with an unfinished job, may cause a race problem leading to a UAF on hdev devices.

code_evidence: btsdio_remove obtains hdev from data->hdev and then frees it via hci_free_dev(hdev) after hci_unregister_dev. The work struct is bound to btsdio_work, which uses hdev; the remove path must synchronize with that work before freeing to avoid a dangling reference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees hdev and the race allows the work to reference it afterward, matching CWE-416 use after free. The fix adds cancel_work_sync, confirming the missing lifetime constraint rather than a separate weakness such as double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the teardown path frees the hci_dev while the associated scheduled work may still run and access it. Trigger: btsdio_remove is invoked with an unfinished job, so the work races with hci_unregister_dev/hci_free_dev. Supported consequence: use-after-free of hdev, leading to invalid memory access (crash or memory corruption).

commit_msg:
Better cleanup lines coming from network.

Thanks for Jeriko One <jeriko.one@gmx.us> for finding and reporting this.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    sLine.TrimRight("\\n\\r");'], 'added_lines': ['    sLine.Replace("\\n", "");', '    sLine.Replace("\\r", "");']}
description: ZNC before 1.7.1-rc1 does not properly validate untrusted lines coming from the network, allowing a non-admin user to escalate his privilege and inject rogue values into znc.conf.

code_evidence: Line 2 copies untrusted network data into sLine; line 3 only trims trailing newline/CR characters, so embedded CR/LF inside the line remain.
Lines 7-8: the unvalidated sLine is passed to OnRaw module hooks, and lines 9-13 construct CMessage from it and dispatch into per-type handlers.
Line 78 finally forwards the message via PutUser, so any rogue embedded line data propagates into downstream processing/config paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function receives untrusted network input and fails to enforce the required property (no embedded line separators) before processing and forwarding it, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The flaw is insufficient validation of input structure rather than an output-encoding issue.

evidence_lines.code:
CString sLine = sData;
sLine.TrimRight("\n\r");

IRCSOCKMODULECALL(OnRaw(sLine), &bReturn);
if (bReturn) return;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function strips only trailing CR/LF instead of removing all newline characters, so attacker-supplied IRC lines can carry embedded CR/LF. Trigger: a non-admin user sends crafted network data containing embedded line breaks. Consequence: the unvalidated line is parsed and forwarded (line 78), enabling privilege escalation and injection of rogue values into znc.conf as described in the advisory.

commit_msg:
vc2enc_dwt: pad the temporary buffer by the slice size

Since non-Haar wavelets need to look into pixels outside the frame, we
need to pad the buffer. The old factor of two seemed to be a workaround
that fact and only padded to the left and bottom. This correctly pads
by the slice size and as such reduces memory usage and potential
exploits.
Reported by Liu Bingchang.

Ideally, there should be no temporary buffer but the encoder is designed
to deinterleave the coefficients into the classical wavelet structure
with the lower frequency values in the top left corner.

Signed-off-by: Rostislav Pehlivanov <atomnuker@gmail.com>
(cherry picked from commit 3228ac730c11eca49d5680d5550128e397061c85)

description: The VC-2 Video Compression encoder in FFmpeg 3.0 and 3.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) because of incorrect buffer padding for non-Haar wavelets, related to libavcodec/vc2enc.c and libavcodec/vc2enc_dwt.c.

During encoding, the DWT filter reads neighboring samples beyond the allocated buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read and a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
cryp: prevent direct calls to update and final functions

With inconsistent or malformed data it has been possible to call
"update" and "final" crypto functions directly. Using a fuzzer tool [1]
we have seen that this results in asserts, i.e., a crash that
potentially could leak sensitive information.

By setting the state (initialized) in the crypto context (i.e., the
tee_cryp_state) at the end of all syscall_*_init functions and then add
a check of the state at the beginning of all update and final functions,
  we prevent direct entrance to the "update" and "final" functions.

[1] https://github.com/MartijnB/optee_fuzzer

Fixes: OP-TEE-2019-0021

Reported-by: Martijn Bogaard <bogaard@riscure.com>
Acked-by: Jerome Forissier <jerome.forissier@linaro.org>
Reviewed-by: Jens Wiklander <jens.wiklander@linaro.org>

snap-seccomp-blacklist: also disallow the use of ioctl + TIOCLINUX

Fixes CVE-2023-1523

Signed-off-by: Alex Murray <alex.murray@canonical.com>

Graphical terminal emulators like xterm, gnome-terminal and others are not affected - this can only be exploited when snaps are run on a virtual console.
