commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: fix unconditional helper

Ben Hawkes says:

 In the mark_source_chains function (net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c) it
 is possible for a user-supplied ipt_entry structure to have a large
 next_offset field. This field is not bounds checked prior to writing a
 counter value at the supplied offset.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!unconditional(&e->ip))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!unconditional(e))']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

code_evidence: check_underflow decides whether a rule is an 'unconditional' absolute verdict by calling unconditional(&e->ip), which only inspects the address match fields of the entry and ignores whether the entry carries match extensions. When the address check passes, it proceeds to ipt_get_target_c(e) and reads the target verdict.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit's actual out-of-bounds write stems from missing bounds validation of next_offset, which produces operations outside the buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. This function contributes by failing to reject the entry that reaches that path; the buffer-boundary defect is the supported weakness, not merely a logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an inconsistent definition of 'unconditional rule': check_underflow accepts entries that still have matches, so the caller's later mark_source_chains walk treats the entry as having a next entry and uses an unchecked user-supplied next_offset to write a counter outside the intended buffer. Trigger is an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt with a crafted ipt_entry; consequence is out-of-bounds memory access and heap corruption.

description: A Double Free vulnerability exists in filedump.c in GPAC 1.0.1, which could cause a Denail of Service via a crafted file in the MP4Box command.

commit_msg:
x86/mm: alloc/free_lN_table: Retain partial_flags on -EINTR

When validating or de-validating pages (in alloc_lN_table and
free_lN_table respectively), the `partial_flags` local variable is
used to keep track of whether the "current" PTE started the entire
operation in a "may be partial" state.

One of the patches in XSA-299 addressed the fact that it is possible
for a previously-partially-validated entry to subsequently be found to
have invalid entries (indicated by returning -EINVAL); in which case
page->partial_flags needs to be set to indicate that the current PTE
may have the partial bit set (and thus _put_page_type() should be
called with PTF_partial_set).

Unfortunately, the patches in XSA-299 assumed that once
put_page_from_lNe() returned -ERESTART on a page, it was not possible
for it to return -EINTR.  This turns out to be true for
alloc_lN_table() and free_lN_table, but not for _get_page_type() and
_put_page_type(): both can return -EINTR when called on pages with
PGT_partial set.  In these cases, the pages PGT_partial will still be
set; failing to set partial_flags appropriately may allow an attacker
to do a privilege escalation similar to those described in XSA-299.

Fix this by always copying the local partial_flags variable into
page->partial_flags when exiting early.

NB that on the "get" side, no adjustment to nr_validated_entries is
needed: whether pte[i] is partially validated or entirely
un-validated, we want nr_validated_entries = i.  On the "put" side,
however, we need to adjust nr_validated_entries appropriately: if
pte[i] is entirely validated, we want nr_validated_entries = i + 1; if
pte[i] is partially validated, we want nr_validated_entries = i.

This is part of XSA-310.

Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        page->nr_validated_ptes = i + 1;', '        page->partial_flags = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['        page->nr_validated_ptes = i + !(partial_flags & PTF_partial_set);', '        page->partial_flags = partial_flags;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to gain host OS privileges by leveraging race conditions in pagetable promotion and demotion operations, because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2019-18421. XSA-299 addressed several critical issues in restartable PV type change operations. Despite extensive testing and auditing, some corner cases were missed. A malicious PV guest administrator may be able to escalate their privilege to that of the host. All security-supported versions of Xen are vulnerable. Only x86 systems are affected. Arm systems are not affected. Only x86 PV guests can leverage the vulnerability. x86 HVM and PVH guests cannot leverage the vulnerability. Note that these attacks require very precise timing, which may be difficult to exploit in practice.

code_evidence: The function reads page->partial_flags and page->nr_validated_ptes into locals partial_flags and i, then iterates validating PTEs and mutating shared page state.
On -ERESTART the code stores i and PTF_partial_set back into the shared page_info.
On -EINTR the pre-fix code stores i + 1 and clears partial_flags to 0, discarding the retained partial state even though _put_page_type() can return -EINTR with PGT_partial still set.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper synchronization of shared page_info state across restartable type-change operations: the interrupted sequence leaves partial_flags inconsistent with the PTE, and a subsequent or concurrent sequence can observe and act on that stale state. This matches CWE-362's concurrent access to a shared resource without exclusivity/atomicity. It is not merely CWE-665 initialization, since the defect is the loss of state across an interleaved operation.

evidence_lines.code:
unsigned partial_flags = page->partial_flags,
i = page->nr_validated_ptes - !(partial_flags & PTF_partial_set);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the early-exit path for -EINTR overwrites page->partial_flags with 0 and advances nr_validated_ptes unconditionally, losing the partial-validation state of the PTE that another type-change sequence relies on. When the put operation is interrupted and later restarted, the page's partial state no longer matches the PTE, so a concurrent/interleaved pagetable promotion or demotion can operate on inconsistent state, allowing privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
sched/fair: Fix low cpu usage with high throttling by removing expiration of cpu-local slices

It has been observed, that highly-threaded, non-cpu-bound applications
running under cpu.cfs_quota_us constraints can hit a high percentage of
periods throttled while simultaneously not consuming the allocated
amount of quota. This use case is typical of user-interactive non-cpu
bound applications, such as those running in kubernetes or mesos when
run on multiple cpu cores.

This has been root caused to cpu-local run queue being allocated per cpu
bandwidth slices, and then not fully using that slice within the period.
At which point the slice and quota expires. This expiration of unused
slice results in applications not being able to utilize the quota for
which they are allocated.

The non-expiration of per-cpu slices was recently fixed by
'commit 512ac999d275 ("sched/fair: Fix bandwidth timer clock drift
condition")'. Prior to that it appears that this had been broken since
at least 'commit 51f2176d74ac ("sched/fair: Fix unlocked reads of some
cfs_b->quota/period")' which was introduced in v3.16-rc1 in 2014. That
added the following conditional which resulted in slices never being
expired.

if (cfs_rq->runtime_expires != cfs_b->runtime_expires) {
	/* extend local deadline, drift is bounded above by 2 ticks */
	cfs_rq->runtime_expires += TICK_NSEC;

Because this was broken for nearly 5 years, and has recently been fixed
and is now being noticed by many users running kubernetes
(https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/67577) it is my opinion
that the mechanisms around expiring runtime should be removed
altogether.

This allows quota already allocated to per-cpu run-queues to live longer
than the period boundary. This allows threads on runqueues that do not
use much CPU to continue to use their remaining slice over a longer
period of time than cpu.cfs_period_us. However, this helps prevent the
above condition of hitting throttling while also not fully utilizing
your cpu quota.

This theoretically allows a machine to use slightly more than its
allotted quota in some periods. This overflow would be bounded by the
remaining quota left on each per-cpu runqueueu. This is typically no
more than min_cfs_rq_runtime=1ms per cpu. For CPU bound tasks this will
change nothing, as they should theoretically fully utilize all of their
quota in each period. For user-interactive tasks as described above this
provides a much better user/application experience as their cpu
utilization will more closely match the amount they requested when they
hit throttling. This means that cpu limits no longer strictly apply per
period for non-cpu bound applications, but that they are still accurate
over longer timeframes.

This greatly improves performance of high-thread-count, non-cpu bound
applications with low cfs_quota_us allocation on high-core-count
machines. In the case of an artificial testcase (10ms/100ms of quota on
80 CPU machine), this commit resulted in almost 30x performance
improvement, while still maintaining correct cpu quota restrictions.
That testcase is available at https://github.com/indeedeng/fibtest.

Fixes: 512ac999d275 ("sched/fair: Fix bandwidth timer clock drift condition")
Signed-off-by: Dave Chiluk <chiluk+linux@indeed.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Reviewed-by: Phil Auld <pauld@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Ben Segall <bsegall@google.com>
Cc: Ingo Molnar <mingo@redhat.com>
Cc: John Hammond <jhammond@indeed.com>
Cc: Jonathan Corbet <corbet@lwn.net>
Cc: Kyle Anderson <kwa@yelp.com>

Cc: Peter Oskolkov <posk@posk.io>
Cc: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Cc: Brendan Gregg <bgregg@netflix.com>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/1563900266-19734-2-git-send-email-chiluk+linux@indeed.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static u64 distribute_cfs_runtime(struct cfs_bandwidth *cfs_b,', '\t\tu64 remaining, u64 expires)', '\t\tcfs_rq->runtime_expires = expires;'], 'added_lines': ['static u64 distribute_cfs_runtime(struct cfs_bandwidth *cfs_b, u64 remaining)']}
description: kernel/sched/fair.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.9, when cpu.cfs_quota_us is used (e.g., with Kubernetes), allows attackers to cause a denial of service against non-cpu-bound applications by generating a workload that triggers unwanted slice expiration, aka CID-de53fd7aedb1. (In other words, although this slice expiration would typically be seen with benign workloads, it is possible that an attacker could calculate how many stray requests are required to force an entire Kubernetes cluster into a low-performance state caused by slice expiration, and ensure that a DDoS attack sent that number of stray requests. An attack does not affect the stability of the kernel; it only causes mismanagement of application execution.)

code_evidence: distribute_cfs_runtime caps each cfs_rq's refill at the remaining bandwidth (runtime = -cfs_rq->runtime_remaining + 1, clipped to remaining) and decrements remaining, but then stamps cfs_rq->runtime_expires = expires, binding the refilled slice to the current period deadline so unused per-CPU quota cannot survive past the period.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function governs consumption of a limited CPU-bandwidth resource; the expiration assignment lets allocated quota be lost rather than maintained, so the product fails to properly control maintenance of a limited resource, matching CWE-400's resource-consumption scope. It is not a memory-safety issue, and the flaw is resource accounting/throttling rather than a separate memory weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: per-CPU bandwidth slices are coupled to a period deadline via runtime_expires, so quota allocated to a runqueue that does not consume it is discarded at the period boundary instead of being retained. Trigger: a high-thread-count, non-CPU-bound workload under cfs_quota_us causes slices to expire unused while periods are throttled. Consequence: degraded CPU throughput and quota mismanagement, enabling a workload-driven denial of service against such applications.

commit_msg:
Block a compromised renderer from reusing request ids.

BUG=578882

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1608573002

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#372547}

description: Race condition in the ResourceDispatcherHostImpl::BeginRequest function in content/browser/loader/resource_dispatcher_host_impl.cc in Google Chrome before 50.0.2661.102 allows remote attackers to make arbitrary HTTP requests by leveraging access to a renderer process and reusing a request ID.

code_evidence: BeginRequest derives child_id from the filter and request_id from the IPC, then validates several fields (lines 7-17) before looking up pending_loaders_ at lines 21-23 using transferred_request ids, not the incoming request_id. No check exists that the incoming GlobalRequestID(child_id, request_id) is unused before the loader is created and inserted into shared state. The missing constraint is the uniqueness check on the request id, which the patch adds before the transfer lookup.

This is not merely an input-validation flaw; the missing uniqueness constraint permits a timing/aliasing interference with in-flight shared resource state.

Trigger: a compromised renderer reuses a request id while another request with that id is still in flight. This violates exclusivity of the shared loader map, allowing the second request to interfere with the first, supported by the commit's intent to block renderer request-id reuse.

commit_msg:
There will be a crash if the guest destroy context 0. As the context 0 is
allocate in renderer init, not destroy in vrend_renderer_context_destroy.
The context will be freed in renderer fini by calling vrend_decode_reset.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liq3ea@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Airlie <airlied@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '   /* never destroy context 0 here, it will be destroyed in vrend_decode_reset()*/', '   if (handle == 0) {', '      return;', '   }']}
description: The vrend_decode_reset function in vrend_decode.c in virglrenderer before 0.6.0 allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and QEMU process crash) by destroying context 0 (zero).

code_evidence: The function validates only the upper bound: if handle >= VREND_MAX_CTX it returns, then loads ctx = dec_ctx[handle] and guards a NULL ctx.
It then sets dec_ctx[handle] = NULL, destroys/frees the context, and if handle != 0 switches hardware context using dec_ctx[0]->grctx, dereferencing the context-0 slot.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits a state where a pointer expected valid (dec_ctx[0]) becomes NULL and is dereferenced, matching CWE-476's NULL dereference with availability impact. The fix rejects handle 0, confirming the missing constraint rather than a bounds error (CWE-125/787).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: handle 0 is not excluded, so destroying context 0 nulls dec_ctx[0] and frees its grctx. Trigger: a guest requests destruction of context 0. Consequence: a later path dereferences the now-NULL dec_ctx[0] (e.g., the switch at line 14 or reset handling in vrend_decode_reset), causing a NULL pointer dereference and QEMU process crash.

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: skb_get_hash_perturb accepts a caller-supplied u32 perturb and passes it directly to ___skb_get_hash as the hash perturbation/secret; the function itself neither generates nor strengthens this value. The perturb is a 32-bit value used as the key material for flow hashing, so its unpredictability depends entirely on the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because a security-relevant value (flow hash perturbation used to derive on-wire flow labels) relies on an insufficiently random 32-bit secret that is stable across boots. This is not merely a weak hash algorithm (CWE-328); the defect is the insufficient entropy/unpredictability of the key material feeding the hash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the hash perturbation is a fixed 32-bit value (hashrnd set once at boot) rather than a cryptographically strong random key. Trigger: an attacker observes flow-label-derived hashes over traffic and infers the 32-bit secret. Consequence: device/user tracking via stable, predictable flow labels; the weak key space and persistence enable the inference.

commit_msg:
Serializing parsers with large amounts of buffered write data (e.g. in case of
a slow or blocked write destination) would cause "serialize_data" to reallocate
the state buffer whose default size is 64kB (USBREDIRPARSER_SERIALIZE_BUF_SIZE).
The pointer to the position for the write buffer count would then point to
a location outside the buffer where the number of write buffers would be written
as a 32-bit value.

As of QEMU 5.2.0 the serializer is invoked for migrations. Serializations for
migrations may happen regularily such as when using the COLO feature[1].
Serialization happens under QEMU's I/O lock. The guest can't control the state
while the serialization is happening. The value written is the number of
outstanding buffers which would be suceptible to timing and host system system
load. The guest would have to continously groom the write buffers. A useful
value needs to be allocated in the exact position freed during the buffer size
increase, but before the buffer count is written. The author doesn't consider it
realistic to exploit this use-after-free reliably.

[1] https://wiki.qemu.org/Features/COLO

Signed-off-by: Michael Hanselmann <public@hansmi.ch>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    uint8_t *write_buf_count_pos, *state = NULL, *pos = NULL;', '    write_buf_count_pos = pos;', '    memcpy(write_buf_count_pos, &write_buf_count, sizeof(int32_t));'], 'added_lines': ['    uint8_t *state = NULL, *pos = NULL;', '    ptrdiff_t write_buf_count_pos;', '    write_buf_count_pos = pos - state;', '    memcpy(state + write_buf_count_pos, &write_buf_count, sizeof(int32_t));']}
description: A use-after-free vulnerability was found in usbredir in versions prior to 0.11.0 in the usbredirparser_serialize() in usbredirparser/usbredirparser.c. This issue occurs when serializing large amounts of buffered write data in the case of a slow or blocked destination.

code_evidence: write_buf_count_pos is a raw uint8_t pointer into the state buffer that serialize_int/serialize_data may reallocate via realloc.
The pointer is saved as pos before serializing the write_buf_count field, then the loop serializes each write buffer's data, each call potentially reallocating state.
After the loop, memcpy writes through the stale write_buf_count_pos into the old (freed) allocation, not the reallocated state buffer.
The subsequent length computation uses the current pos/state, but the count was already written to freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The memcpy at line 55 dereferences a pointer to memory that may have been freed by realloc inside the serialization loop, matching CWE-416 use after free. It is not merely an out-of-bounds write because the stale pointer refers to the old allocation's region rather than exceeding the new buffer.

evidence_lines.code: uint8_t *write_buf_count_pos, *state = NULL, *pos = NULL;

memcpy(write_buf_count_pos, &write_buf_count, sizeof(int32_t));
len = pos - state;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an interior pointer into a growable buffer is cached across serialize_int/serialize_data calls that can realloc the buffer. Trigger: enough buffered write data to force a buffer growth between capturing write_buf_count_pos and the final memcpy. Consequence: the write_buf_count is written into freed memory (use-after-free), potentially corrupting reused heap memory or crashing.

set cinfo->output_components to 1, and if cinfo->out_color_space is not

commit_msg:
Defend against bad PT_DYNAMIC

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/391
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
	modified:   p_lx_elf.h

commit_msg:
Improve deep recursion detection in exif_data_load_data_content.

The existing detection was still vulnerable to pathological cases
causing DoS by wasting CPU. The new algorithm takes the number of tags
into account to make it harder to abuse by cases using shallow recursion
but with a very large number of tags.  This improves on commit 5d28011c
which wasn't sufficient to counter this kind of case.

The limitation in the previous fix was discovered by Laurent Delosieres,
Secunia Research at Flexera (Secunia Advisory SA84652) and is assigned
the identifier CVE-2018-20030.

code_evidence: The only recursion guard is a fixed depth cap (recursion_depth > 12); it bounds nesting depth but not the total number of recursive calls, so many tags at shallow depth each recurse freely.
The loop iterates up to n attacker-controlled entries read from the EXIF buffer, and each pointer tag in the loop triggers a recursive call.
EXIF_IFD_EXIF pointer recurses with recursion_depth + 1, so a large n at shallow depth produces many recursive invocations.
EXIF_IFD_GPS pointer recurses with recursion_depth + 1, another multiplicative fan-out point.
EXIF_IFD_INTEROPERABILITY pointer recurses with recursion_depth + 1, the path named in the advisory for CPU exhaustion.

commit_msg:
Fix possible stack overflows in decoder for illegal bit streams

Fixes CVE-2018-0429
A vulnerability in the Thor decoder (available at:
https://github.com/cisco/thor) could allow an authenticated, local
attacker to cause segmentation faults and stack overflows when using a
non-conformant Thor bitstream as input.
The vulnerability is due to lack of input validation when parsing the
bitstream. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause a
stack overflow and potentially inject and execute arbitrary code.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  decoder_info->log2_sb_size = clip(decoder_info->log2_sb_size, log2i(MIN_BLOCK_SIZE), log2i(MAX_SB_SIZE));']}
description: Stack-based buffer overflow in the Cisco Thor decoder before commit 18de8f9f0762c3a542b1122589edb8af859d9813 allows local users to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault) and execute arbitrary code via a crafted non-conformant Thor bitstream.

code_evidence: Line 4 reads log2_sb_size directly from the bitstream via get_flc(3, stream) with no bounds constraint, so any 3-bit value (0-7) is accepted as the superblock size exponent.
Lines 19-25 derive subsample and conditionally parse cfl_intra/cfl_inter; the parsed header fields, including the unconstrained log2_sb_size, feed downstream buffer/array sizing and addressing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because unvalidated header input leads to operations outside intended memory buffer boundaries. The patch's clip() confirms the missing restriction; the specific buffer overflow is a descendant weakness, but the target class CWE-119 is supported by the unconstrained size field driving out-of-bounds access.

evidence_lines.code: decoder_info->log2_sb_size = get_flc(3, stream);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sequence header parser accepts an out-of-range log2_sb_size without clamping it to the legal block-size range. Trigger: a non-conformant bitstream supplies an illegal 3-bit value. This propagates into downstream block/buffer geometry computations, producing out-of-bounds memory accesses (stack overflow) and possible code execution.

The patch is identified as b80f6d1893607c99e5113967592417d0fe310ce6. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-217614 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

commit_msg:
x86: limit GFNs to 32 bits for shadowed superpages.

Superpage shadows store the shadowed GFN in the backpointer field,
which for non-BIGMEM builds is 32 bits wide.  Shadowing a superpage
mapping of a guest-physical address above 2^44 would lead to the GFN
being truncated there, and a crash when we come to remove the shadow
from the hash table.

Track the valid width of a GFN for each guest, including reporting it
through CPUID, and enforce it in the shadow pagetables.  Set the
maximum witth to 32 for guests where this truncation could occur.

This is XSA-173.

Reported-by: Ling Liu <liuling-it@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        count = cpuid_eax(0x80000008);', '        count = (count >> 16) & 0xff ?: count & 0xff;'], 'added_lines': ['        count = d->arch.paging.gfn_bits + PAGE_SHIFT;']}
description: Integer overflow in the x86 shadow pagetable code in Xen allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host crash) or possibly gain privileges by shadowing a superpage mapping.

The same literal string is used as the identity token that later APIs (cholmod.diag, getfactor, solve, spsolve) compare against to validate a fake Capsule.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-697 applies because the security-relevant identity comparison uses predictable string literals as the comparison value, so the comparison is effectively incorrect and can be satisfied by forged input. The patch replaces literals with strCFDL/strCFDU/strCFZL/strCFZU tokens, consistent with fixing a flawed comparison token.

return (PyObject *) PyCapsule_New((void *) L, SP_ID(A)==DOUBLE ?
(uplo == 'L' ?  "CHOLMOD FACTOR D L" : "CHOLMOD FACTOR D U") :

commit_msg:
avcodec/cbs_jpeg: Check length for SOS

Fixes: out of array access
Fixes: 19734/clusterfuzz-testcase-minimized-ffmpeg_BSF_TRACE_HEADERS_fuzzer-5673507031875584
Fixes: 19353/clusterfuzz-testcase-minimized-ffmpeg_BSF_TRACE_HEADERS_fuzzer-5703944462663680

Found-by: continuous fuzzing process https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz/tree/master/projects/ffmpeg
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            if (length > end - start)', '                return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;', '']}
description: cbs_jpeg_split_fragment in libavcodec/cbs_jpeg.c in FFmpeg 4.1 and 4.2.2 has a heap-based buffer overflow during JPEG_MARKER_SOS handling because of a missing length check.

code_evidence: In the JPEG_MARKER_SOS branch, length is read from the fragment data at start (line 87), but end was set earlier by scanning for the next marker (line 45). The allocation at lines 89-90 uses end - start, yet memcpy at line 93 copies length bytes from frag->data + start without verifying that length <= end - start. If the SOS segment declares a length larger than the scanned region, the copy writes past the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe memcpy writes length bytes into a buffer sized end - start, so an attacker-controlled length exceeding that size writes past the buffer end, matching CWE-787. This is a write overflow, not merely an out-of-bounds read, so CWE-787 is the appropriate single label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SOS length field is trusted without checking it against the available span (end - start). Trigger: a crafted JPEG fragment whose SOS marker length exceeds the bytes before the next marker. Consequence: memcpy overflows the heap buffer allocated as end - start + padding, causing out-of-bounds write and potential crash or memory corruption.

The UAF is because:

 mount(pid: 921)               | cifsd(pid: 923)
-------------------------------|-------------------------------
                               | cifs_demultiplex_thread
SMB2_negotiate                 |
 cifs_send_recv                |
  compound_send_recv           |

    wait_for_response          |

1. After send request to server, wait the response until
    mid->mid_state != SUBMITTED;
2. Receive response from server, and set it to mid;

Add an extra state to mark the mid state to READY before wakeup the

Fixes: ec637e3ffb6b ("[CIFS] Avoid extra large buffer allocation (and memcpy) in cifs_readpages")
Reviewed-by: Paulo Alcantara (SUSE) <pc@manguebit.com>
Signed-off-by: Zhang Xiaoxu <zhangxiaoxu5@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Steve French <stfrench@microsoft.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t midQ->mid_state != MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED,'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t midQ->mid_state != MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED &&', '\t\t\t\t midQ->mid_state != MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED,']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in smb2_is_status_io_timeout() in CIFS in the Linux Kernel. After CIFS transfers response data to a system call, there are still local variable points to the memory region, and if the system call frees it faster than CIFS uses it, CIFS will access a free memory region, leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: wait_event_state() sleeps until midQ->mid_state != MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED. The predicate only tests for SUBMITTED, so it also returns true when the state is MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED, a state set by cifsd after it stores the response buffer in midQ->resp_buf and dequeues the mid. On a killable wait, error < 0 causes the caller to return -ERESTARTSYS and free the response buffer while the callback may still reference it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's incomplete wait predicate permits the response buffer to be freed while still referenced, which is exactly reuse of freed memory (CWE-416). This is a lifetime/ordering flaw, not merely a missing NULL check or an out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the wake condition treats MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED as a completed response and lets the sync caller proceed to free the response buffer before the receive-side callback has finished using it. Trigger: process kill during the wait after cifsd sets the mid to RECEIVED. Consequence: use-after-free read of the freed buffer by the callback (KASAN report in smb2_is_network_name_deleted), leading to DoS.

commit_msg: Path traversal bug in TarFileReader::extract() #115
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!String::startsWith(b, a))'], 'added_lines': ['    if (!String::startsWith(b, a + "/"))']}
description: tar/TarFileReader.cpp in Cauldron cbang before bastet-v8.1.17 has a directory traversal during extraction that allows the attacker to create or write to files outside the current directory via a crafted tar archive.

code_evidence: The extracted path is derived from the archive filename (getFilename()) appended to the caller-supplied _path, then canonicalized into a and b. The containment check uses String::startsWith(b, a) without a trailing separator, so a sibling directory sharing the prefix of a (e.g. a="/tmp/out" and b="/tmp/outside/...") passes the check.
After the flawed check, the path is passed to SystemUtilities::oopen(path, getMode()) for REG_FILE/NORMAL_FILE/CONTIGUOUS_FILE extraction, so the file is actually written at the unchecked location.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function limits an archive-derived pathname to a restricted directory but fails to properly neutralize the boundary, allowing resolution outside it, which is CWE-22. The weakness is the containment check rather than a generic path canonicalization issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the prefix test lacks a directory boundary, so canonical paths outside the extraction directory but sharing its string prefix satisfy startsWith. Trigger: a crafted tar entry whose name escapes into a sibling path with the same prefix. Consequence: file creation/overwrite outside the intended directory.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13007/PKTAP: Pass a properly updated struct pcap_pkthdr to the sub-dissector.

The sub-dissector expects that the length and captured length will
reflect the actual remaining data in the packet, not the raw amount
including the PKTAP header; pass an updated header, just as we do for
PPI.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Yannick Formaggio.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\thdrlen += printer(ndo, h, p);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct pcap_pkthdr nhdr;', '\t\t\tnhdr = *h;', '\t\t\tnhdr.caplen = caplen;', '\t\t\tnhdr.len = length;', '\t\t\thdrlen += printer(ndo, &nhdr, p);']}
description: The Apple PKTAP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-pktap.c:pktap_if_print().

code_evidence: After subtracting hdrlen, length and caplen describe only the remaining payload and p is advanced past the PKTAP header [27,28,29].

The PKT_REC_PACKET branch invokes the sub-dissector printer with the original header h and the advanced pointer p [35,36,37], so h->caplen and h->len still include the PKTAP header bytes that p no longer points to.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Passing a stale header length with an offset pointer lets the sub-dissector read beyond the intended buffer, directly matching CWE-125. This is an incorrect length/pointer pairing, not a write or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The sub-dissector trusts h->caplen/h->len to bound reads from p, but those values were not reduced by hdrlen while p was advanced. A crafted capture with a PKTAP header and a nested packet therefore causes the sub-dissector to read past the end of the remaining buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg: issue #30 issue #31 issue #32: no multiple format chunks in WAV or W64
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int is_rf64 = !strncmp (fourcc, "RF64", 4), got_ds64 = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    int is_rf64 = !strncmp (fourcc, "RF64", 4), got_ds64 = 0, format_chunk = 0;', '', '            if (format_chunk++) {', '                error_line ("%s is not a valid .WAV file!", infilename);', '                return WAVPACK_SOFT_ERROR;', '            }']}
description: An issue was discovered in WavPack 5.1.0 and earlier. The WAV parser component contains a vulnerability that allows writing to memory because ParseRiffHeaderConfig in riff.c does not reject multiple format chunks.

code_evidence: On the "fmt " branch, the function reads chunk_header.ckSize bytes into the fixed-size WaveHeader struct without tracking whether a format chunk was already processed; no guard prevents a second fmt chunk from re-entering this block.

The parsed WaveHeader fields (FormatTag, SubFormat, ValidBitsPerSample, NumChannels, BlockAlign, BitsPerSample, ChannelMask) are validated and then copied into config (bits_per_sample, channel_mask, float_norm_exp) and later used by WavpackSetConfiguration64 to size buffers.
A second fmt chunk overwrites these config values after the first pass, so downstream allocation and write sizes can be derived from inconsistent or attacker-controlled values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing multiple-format-chunk rejection lets attacker-influenced format parameters reach memory writes that can exceed the intended buffer. The added format_chunk counter rejects the second chunk, confirming the missing constraint is the root cause rather than a mere parsing/validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser accepts multiple format chunks, so WaveHeader/config fields can be overwritten with a second, differently sized format description. Trigger: a crafted WAV containing two "fmt " chunks. The consequence is that configuration derived from the last chunk drives later buffer sizing/writes, enabling an out-of-bounds write.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    offset_d_ += cudautils::align<size_t, 8>(output_size_ * sizeof(int8_t));', '        offset_d_ += cudautils::align<size_t, 8>(output_size_ * sizeof(int16_t));', '        offset_d_ += cudautils::align<size_t, 8>(output_size_ * max_sequences_per_poa_ * sizeof(uint8_t));'], 'added_lines': ['    offset_d_ += cudautils::align<int64_t, 8>(output_size_ * sizeof(int8_t));', '        offset_d_ += cudautils::align<int64_t, 8>(output_size_ * sizeof(int16_t));', '        offset_d_ += cudautils::align<int64_t, 8>(output_size_ * max_sequences_per_poa_ * sizeof(uint8_t));']}
description: Clara Genomics Analysis before 0.2.0 has an integer overflow for cudapoa memory management in allocate_block.cpp.

code_evidence: These three device-side offset advances compute output_size_ (and, for msa, max_sequences_per_poa_) multiplied by element sizes using size_t as the align template type, then add the aligned result to offset_d_. The host-side counterparts at lines 8, 12, 17 use plain arithmetic without alignment, so the device offset arithmetic is the localized site.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because an integer multiplication used to compute a memory offset can wrap, yielding a small offset and incorrect pointer placement into the device block buffer; this directly matches the overflow-in-offset-calculation scenario. The wrapped small offset is then added to offset_d_, so subsequent pointers (coverage, MSA, consensus) alias earlier regions of block_data_d_. commit_msg:
posix-timers: Sanitize overrun handling

The posix timer overrun handling is broken because the forwarding functions
can return a huge number of overruns which does not fit in an int. As a
consequence timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun can turn into
random number generators.

The k_clock::timer_forward() callbacks return a 64 bit value now. Make
k_itimer::ti_overrun[_last] 64bit as well, so the kernel internal
accounting is correct. 3Remove the temporary (int) casts.

Add a helper function which clamps the overrun value returned to user space
via timer_getoverrun(2) or siginfo::si_overrun limited to a positive value
between 0 and INT_MAX. INT_MAX is an indicator for user space that the
overrun value has been clamped.

Reported-by: Team OWL337 <icytxw@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Acked-by: John Stultz <john.stultz@linaro.org>
Cc: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Michael Kerrisk <mtk.manpages@gmail.com>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20180626132705.018623573@linutronix.de
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\ttimer->it_overrun += 1 << i;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\ttimer->it_overrun += 1LL << i;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.17.3. An Integer Overflow in kernel/time/posix-timers.c in the POSIX timer code is caused by the way the overrun accounting works. Depending on interval and expiry time values, the overrun can be larger than INT_MAX, but the accounting is int based. This basically makes the accounting values, which are visible to user space via timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun, random. For example, a local user can cause a denial of service (signed integer overflow) via crafted mmap, futex, timer_create, and timer_settime system calls.

code_evidence: Loop scales incr via `incr = incr << 1` and index i grows alongside; the overrun accumulation `timer->it_overrun += 1 << i` is an int-typed shift whose magnitude can exceed INT_MAX for large interval/expiry deltas.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly performs an integer increment/shift that can exceed the int representation, matching CWE-190's wraparound of an incremented value. The fix to `1LL << i` confirms the 32-bit overflow; this is not merely a logic flaw but representation-limited arithmetic.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: overrun accounting uses 32-bit int arithmetic where the shift `1 << i` and accumulation into ti_overrun can wrap for large deltas derived from user-controlled timer interval/expiry. Trigger: crafted timer_create/timer_settime values producing many expirations. Consequence: signed integer overflow yields random/negative accounting visible via timer_getoverrun and si_overrun, causing DoS/instability.

commit_msg:
rxrpc: Fix race between conn bundle lookup and bundle removal [ZDI-CAN-15975]

After rxrpc_unbundle_conn() has removed a connection from a bundle, it
checks to see if there are any conns with available channels and, if not,
removes and attempts to destroy the bundle.

Whilst it does check after grabbing client_bundles_lock that there are no
connections attached, this races with rxrpc_look_up_bundle() retrieving the
bundle, but not attaching a connection for the connection to be attached
later.

There is therefore a window in which the bundle can get destroyed before we
manage to attach a new connection to it.

Fix this by adding an "active" counter to struct rxrpc_bundle:

 (1) rxrpc_connect_call() obtains an active count by prepping/looking up a
     bundle and ditches it before returning.

 (2) If, during rxrpc_connect_call(), a connection is added to the bundle,
     this obtains an active count, which is held until the connection is
     discarded.

 (3) rxrpc_deactivate_bundle() is created to drop an active count on a
     bundle and destroy it when the active count reaches 0.  The active
     count is checked inside client_bundles_lock() to prevent a race with
     rxrpc_look_up_bundle().

 (4) rxrpc_unbundle_conn() then calls rxrpc_deactivate_bundle().

Fixes: 245500d853e9 ("rxrpc: Rewrite the client connection manager")
Reported-by: zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com # ZDI-CAN-15975
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Tested-by: zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com
cc: Marc Dionne <marc.dionne@auristor.com>
cc: linux-afs@lists.infradead.org
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tatomic_inc(&bundle->active);', '\t\t\tatomic_inc(&bundle->active);']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernel's RxRPC network protocol, within the processing of RxRPC bundles. This issue results from the lack of proper locking when performing operations on an object. This may allow an attacker to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the kernel.

code_evidence: rxrpc_look_up_bundle() searches local->client_bundles under client_bundles_lock (lines 14-31), drops the lock, allocates a candidate (line 33), then reacquires the lock and re-searches (lines 37-55). At found_bundle (lines 66-70) it takes a reference on the bundle and releases the lock, but does not increment bundle->active to pin the bundle against destruction. The patch adds atomic_inc(&bundle->active) at line 67, confirming the missing active-count protection.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The lookup and removal paths share the client_bundles resource; the lock is released before the active count protects the bundle, creating a timing window where an interfering sequence (unbundle) can destroy the object. This is a concurrent shared-resource synchronization defect, matching CWE-362 rather than a simple missing-lock bug, since locking is present but the lifetime/atomicity of the lookup-and-attach sequence is not preserved.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the lookup path returns a bundle reference without marking it active, so the bundle can be removed and freed by rxrpc_unbundle_conn()/rxrpc_deactivate_bundle() between lookup and later connection attachment. Trigger: a concurrent unbundle removes the bundle after the lookup's lock is released. Consequence: use-after-free of the bundle, potentially leading to kernel memory corruption and privilege escalation.

[Extensions] Rework inline installation observation

Instead of observing through the WebstoreAPI, observe directly in the TabHelper.
This is a great deal less code, more direct, and also fixes a lifetime issue
with the TabHelper being deleted before the inline installation completes.

BUG=613949

description: The Chrome Web Store inline-installation implementation in the Extensions subsystem in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.82 does not properly consider object lifetimes during progress observation, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted web site.

code_evidence: The function receives its parameters and then calls extension_reenabler_.reset() at line 4, destroying the ExtensionReenabler object before any further work.
After the switch, OnInlineInstallComplete is invoked at lines 22-26 using install_id, return_route_id and error with no reference to extension_reenabler_.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function explicitly releases the reenabler object and then continues processing the completion flow, matching a lifetime error where freed state is referenced afterward. This is a lifetime/ownership bug, not merely a logic error.

evidence_lines.code:
ExtensionReenabler::ReenableResult result) {
extension_reenabler_.reset();

OnInlineInstallComplete(install_id,
return_route_id,
result == ExtensionReenabler::REENABLE_SUCCESS,
error,
webstore_result);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: extension_reenabler_.reset() frees the ExtensionReenabler (and its curried callback state) too early, before the completion path that logically depends on it runs. The trigger is completing a re-enable flow, after which OnInlineInstallComplete executes against state whose owning object was already destroyed. This supports use-after-free leading to DoS or other memory corruption.

net/mlx5: DR, Fix NULL vs IS_ERR checking in dr_domain_init_resources

The mlx5_get_uars_page() function  returns error pointers.
Using IS_ERR() to check the return value to fix this.

Fixes: 4ec9e7b02697 ("net/mlx5: DR, Expose steering domain functionality")
Signed-off-by: Miaoqian Lin <linmq006@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Saeed Mahameed <saeedm@nvidia.com>

description: In the Linux kernel before 5.15.13, drivers/net/ethernet/mellanox/mlx5/core/steering/dr_domain.c misinterprets the mlx5_get_uars_page return value (expects it to be NULL in the error case, whereas it is actually an error pointer).

code_evidence: dmn->uar is assigned the return value of mlx5_get_uars_page(), which returns an error pointer rather than NULL on failure. The check at line 15 tests only for NULL, so an error pointer such as ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM) passes the guard and execution continues to line 20 with dmn->uar holding an invalid pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate a pointer before use because it checks only for NULL while the callee signals failure with error pointers. This is a pointer-validation defect leading to dereference of an invalid pointer, consistent with CWE-476; it is not a mere missing NULL check because the actual failure value is a non-NULL error pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error-return convention of mlx5_get_uars_page() (error pointers) is not matched by the NULL-only check. Trigger: an allocation failure in mlx5_get_uars_page() returns an error pointer, which is not detected. Consequence: the invalid dmn->uar is used by subsequent resource setup and cleanup paths, causing dereference of an invalid pointer (crash/DoS).

commit_msg:
synphasor: Use val_to_str_const

Don't use a value from packet data to directly index a value_string,
particularly when the value string doesn't cover all possible values.

Fix #19087

description: Due to failure in validating the length provided by an attacker-crafted IEEE-C37.118 packet, Wireshark version 4.0.5 and prior, by default, is susceptible to a heap-based buffer overflow, and possibly code execution in the context of the process running Wireshark.

code_evidence: The subtree label is built from conf_phasor_type[tvb_get_guint8(tvb, offset + 2)].strptr. The index comes directly from one packet byte at offset+2 without any bounds check against the size of conf_phasor_type.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The target CWE-787 requires writing data past the end of a buffer, but the shown operation only indexes and reads conf_phasor_type to obtain strptr. No out-of-bounds write occurs in this function; the defect is an unchecked array index leading to an out-of-bounds read, so CWE-787 is not directly supported.

commit_msg:
CIFS: Enable encryption during session setup phase

In order to allow encryption on SMB connection we need to exchange
a session key and generate encryption and decryption keys.

Signed-off-by: Pavel Shilovsky <pshilov@microsoft.com>

description: The Linux kernel before version 4.11 is vulnerable to a NULL pointer dereference in fs/cifs/cifsencrypt.c:setup_ntlmv2_rsp() that allows an attacker controlling a CIFS server to kernel panic a client that has this server mounted, because an empty TargetInfo field in an NTLMSSP setup negotiation response is mishandled during session recovery.

code_evidence: Line 7 gates signing-key generation on sign && generate_signingkey; line 8 invokes generate_signingkey(ses), and lines 9-10 free ses->auth_key.response and set it to NULL. If rc is nonzero, line 11's error path falls through to keygen_exit (line 28), where lines 29-31 free and NULL the response again when !sign.

The keygen_exit label at line 28 is reachable both from the rc error path and from the normal success path; the unconditional !sign cleanup at lines 29-31 can free ses->auth_key.response after it was already freed/NULLed at lines 9-10.

Trigger: a CIFS server response causing generate_signingkey to fail or produce empty key material. Consequence: kernel panic/DoS via NULL dereference or double free.

commit_msg:
openvswitch: fix OOB access in reserve_sfa_size()

Given a sufficiently large number of actions, while copying and
reserving memory for a new action of a new flow, if next_offset is
greater than MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE, the function reserve_sfa_size() does
not return -EMSGSIZE as expected, but it allocates MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE
bytes increasing actions_len by req_size. This can then lead to an OOB
write access, especially when further actions need to be copied.

Fix it by rearranging the flow action size check.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif ((MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE - next_offset) < req_size) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif ((next_offset + req_size) > MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE) {']}
description: An integer coercion error was found in the openvswitch kernel module. Given a sufficiently large number of actions, while copying and reserving memory for a new action of a new flow, the reserve_sfa_size() function does not return -EMSGSIZE as expected, potentially leading to an out-of-bounds write access. This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: req_size is size_t (NLA_ALIGN of int attr_len), while next_offset is an int computed from offsetof plus actions_len, mixing signed int and unsigned size_t arithmetic.

The size check (MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE - next_offset) < req_size mixes int and size_t; when next_offset exceeds MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE the subtraction underflows in unsigned arithmetic, so the comparison against req_size can be false and the -EMSGSIZE branch is skipped, falling through to new_acts_size = MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The check relies on implicit conversion between signed int (next_offset, MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE subtraction) and unsigned size_t req_size, producing an unexpected wrapped value used in a security-sensitive size check, matching CWE-681. It is a numeric conversion defect, not merely a missing bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard compares a signed int-derived difference against unsigned size_t req_size, so a large next_offset causes unsigned underflow and the overflow check fails. Trigger: enough accumulated actions that next_offset > MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE. Consequence: allocation is capped at MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE while actions_len is still incremented by req_size at line 29, yielding an out-of-bounds write during subsequent action copies.

commit_msg:
Revised handling of TIFFTAG_INKNAMES and related TIFFTAG_NUMBEROFINKS value

In order to solve the buffer overflow issues related to TIFFTAG_INKNAMES and related TIFFTAG_NUMBEROFINKS value, a revised handling of those tags within LibTiff is proposed:

Behaviour for writing:
    `NumberOfInks`  MUST fit to the number of inks in the `InkNames` string.
    `NumberOfInks` is automatically set when `InkNames` is set.
    If `NumberOfInks` is different to the number of inks within `InkNames` string, that will be corrected and a warning is issued.
    If `NumberOfInks` is not equal to samplesperpixel only a warning will be issued.

Behaviour for reading:
    When reading `InkNames` from a TIFF file, the `NumberOfInks` will be set automatically to the number of inks in `InkNames` string.
    If `NumberOfInks` is different to the number of inks within `InkNames` string, that will be corrected and a warning is issued.
    If  `NumberOfInks` is not equal to samplesperpixel only a warning will be issued.

This allows the safe use of the NumberOfInks value to read out the InkNames without buffer overflow

This MR will close the following issues:  #149, #150, #152, #168 (to be checked), #250, #269, #398 and #456.

It also fixes the old bug at http://bugzilla.maptools.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2599, for which the limitation of `NumberOfInks = SPP` was introduced, which is in my opinion not necessary and does not solve the general issue.

commit_msg:
The 32 bit field "rep.length" is not checked for validity, which allows
an integer overflow on 32 bit systems.

A malicious server could send INT_MAX as length, which gets multiplied
by the size of XRectangle. In that case the client won't read the whole
data from server, getting out of sync.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    nbytes = (long) rep.length << 2;', '    nrects = rep.length >> 1;', '    rects = Xmalloc (nrects * sizeof (XRectangle));'], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (rep.length < (INT_MAX >> 2)) {', '\tnbytes = (long) rep.length << 2;', '\tnrects = rep.length >> 1;', '\trects = Xmalloc (nrects * sizeof (XRectangle));', '    } else {', '\tnbytes = 0;', '\tnrects = 0;', '\trects = NULL;', '    }', '']}
description: Integer overflow in X.org libXfixes before 5.0.3 on 32-bit platforms might allow remote X servers to gain privileges via a length value of INT_MAX, which triggers the client to stop reading data and get out of sync.

code_evidence: rep.length comes from the server reply and is used unchecked: line 31 computes nbytes = (long) rep.length << 2 and line 32 computes nrects = rep.length >> 1, then line 33 allocates nrects * sizeof(XRectangle).

On 32-bit systems a large rep.length (e.g. INT_MAX) makes the shifted/multiplied size wrap, so the allocation is undersized relative to the data the reply claims; lines 41-45 then compute nread from nrects and read/eat data based on these wrapped values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The arithmetic on rep.length (shift, multiply by sizeof) can wrap on 32-bit platforms, which is exactly integer overflow/wraparound (CWE-190). The unchecked length is the trigger; the out-of-sync stream is the supported consequence, distinguishing it from a plain out-of-bounds write, which is not shown here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing range check on the server-controlled 32-bit rep.length before shifting and multiplying it to derive allocation and read sizes. With a malicious length, the size arithmetic wraps, producing a small allocation and inconsistent nbytes/nread, so the client stops reading the full reply and desynchronizes its X protocol stream.

commit_msg:
As Wenqing Liu reported in bugzilla:

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=215235

- Overview
page fault in f2fs_setxattr() when mount and operate on corrupted image

- Reproduce
tested on kernel 5.16-rc3, 5.15.X under root

1. unzip tmp7.zip
2. ./single.sh f2fs 7

Sometimes need to run the script several times

- Kernel dump
loop0: detected capacity change from 0 to 131072
F2FS-fs (loop0): Found nat_bits in checkpoint
F2FS-fs (loop0): Mounted with checkpoint version = 7548c2ee
BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffe47bc7123f48

The root cause is in __f2fs_setxattr(), we missed to do sanity check on

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org

Signed-off-by: Jaegeuk Kim <jaegeuk@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\twhile (!IS_XATTR_LAST_ENTRY(last))'], 'added_lines': ['\twhile (!IS_XATTR_LAST_ENTRY(last)) {', '\t\tif ((void *)(last) + sizeof(__u32) > last_base_addr ||', '\t\t\t(void *)XATTR_NEXT_ENTRY(last) > last_base_addr) {', '\t\t\tf2fs_err(F2FS_I_SB(inode), "inode (%lu) has invalid last xattr entry, entry_size: %zu",', '\t\t\t\t\tinode->i_ino, ENTRY_SIZE(last));', '\t\t\tset_sbi_flag(F2FS_I_SB(inode), SBI_NEED_FSCK);', '\t\t\terror = -EFSCORRUPTED;', '\t\t\tgoto exit;', '\t\t}', '\t}']}
description: In __f2fs_setxattr in fs/f2fs/xattr.c in the Linux kernel through 5.15.11, there is an out-of-bounds memory access when an inode has an invalid last xattr entry.

code_evidence: The loop initializes last = here and repeatedly advances with XATTR_NEXT_ENTRY(last) while only checking IS_XATTR_LAST_ENTRY(last). It never verifies that last stays within the buffer bounded by last_base_addr (computed at line 23), so a corrupted inode whose xattr entries lack a valid last entry causes last to be advanced past the allocated xattr block.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked pointer advancement in the loop reads xattr entry data beyond the intended buffer, which is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The later free-related crash is a downstream consequence; the direct weakness is reading memory outside the xattr block.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the xattr-walking loop lacks a bounds check against last_base_addr. Trigger: a mounted corrupted image supplies an inode with an invalid last xattr entry so IS_XATTR_LAST_ENTRY never becomes true. Consequence: XATTR_NEXT_ENTRY reads past the end of the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and eventual crash, as in the reported page fault during kfree/__f2fs_setxattr.

This issue might cause memory exhaustion, but is only relevant if the pickle format is used for serializing tens or hundreds of gigabytes of data. code_evidence: new_memo_size and i are declared as signed Py_ssize_t. In the error path, i is set to new_memo_size and the loop uses while (--i >= 0), relying on signed decrement to terminate at zero; with a large value this signed arithmetic can overflow/wrap, so the intended termination condition is not guaranteed.

Trigger: new_memo_size reaching a value where decrementing past the minimum signed range overflows. Consequence: the loop may not terminate as intended, leading to out-of-bounds Py_XDECREF/PyMem_FREE access and memory corruption or crash; the fix switches to size_t and a SIZE_MAX sentinel.

commit_msg:
Dmitry reported a struct pid leak detected by a syzkaller program.

Bug happens in unix_stream_recvmsg() when we break the loop when a
signal is pending, without properly releasing scm.

Fixes: b3ca9b02b007 ("net: fix multithreaded signal handling in unix recv routines")
Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Cc: Rainer Weikusat <rweikusat@mobileactivedefense.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tscm_destroy(&scm);']}
description: A flaw was found in the way memory resources were freed in the unix_stream_recvmsg function in the Linux kernel when a signal was pending. This flaw allows an unprivileged local user to crash the system by exhausting available memory. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

code_evidence: On a pending signal after unix_stream_data_wait, the function sets err and jumps to out without releasing scm.
scm is initialized at line 25 and may acquire references via scm_set_cred/unix_set_secdata during credential handling.
File descriptors are attached to scm through unix_detach_fds (non-peek) or scm_fp_dup (peek); scm.fp then breaks the loop.
The only cleanup path calls scm_recv or scm_destroy at the normal exit, which the signal goto out bypasses.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated resources referenced by scm are not released on an exceptional (interrupted) exit path, leaving them unavailable for reuse. This is a lifetime/release defect, not a use-after-free or double-free, since the memory is simply left allocated.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signal_pending branch jumps to out, skipping the scm_destroy/scm_recv cleanup that releases file descriptor references held in scm. Trigger: a signal interrupts a blocking unix stream recv after scm.fp was populated. Consequence: the referenced struct pid/file objects are never released, leaking memory and enabling resource-exhaustion DoS.

commit_msg:
The X protocol uses CARD16 values to represent the length so
this would overflow.

CVE-2021-31535

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (nbytes >= USHRT_MAX)', '                    return 1;']}
description: LookupCol.c in X.Org X through X11R7.7 and libX11 before 1.7.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The libX11 XLookupColor request (intended for server-side color lookup) contains a flaw allowing a client to send color-name requests with a name longer than the maximum size allowed by the protocol (and also longer than the maximum packet size for normal-sized packets). The user-controlled data exceeding the maximum size is then interpreted by the server as additional X protocol requests and executed, e.g., to disable X server authorization completely. For example, if the victim encounters malicious terminal control sequences for color codes, then the attacker may be able to take full control of the running graphical session.

code_evidence: Loop accumulates nbytes as sum of safestrlen(argv[i]) + 1 for each argument without any upper bound check, so a large argc or long argv strings can make nbytes arbitrarily large.
Xmalloc allocates nbytes, then the copy loop writes each argv[i] via strcpy and advances bp by strlen(argv[i]) + 1, then XChangeProperty is called with nbytes as the length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a buffer-copy operation where input sizes are not checked against the destination/protocol size limit before copying and writing, matching CWE-120's classic buffer copy without input size checking. The overflow here manifests as a protocol length overflow rather than a direct heap write, but the unchecked copy of input data into a size-constrained output remains the core weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The size computation in the first loop is not bounded against the protocol's CARD16 length limit, so the total length passed to XChangeProperty can exceed the maximum representable request length. The server then interprets the excess user-controlled bytes as additional protocol requests. The root cause is the missing size constraint on the computed length before the copy and property change, enabling request smuggling and potential arbitrary command execution on the server.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/196

description: The ReadGROUP4Image function in coders/tiff.c in ImageMagick before 7.0.1-10 does not check the return value of the fputc function, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a crafted image file.

code_evidence: The loop reads bytes from the image blob and writes each to the temporary TIFF file with fputc, but the return value is cast to void and discarded. No check confirms the byte was written or that the stream is still valid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-252 directly covers failing to check a function's return value, which is exactly the discarded fputc result at line 70. The patch confirms this by adding a comparison of fputc's return against c and setting a failure status.

for (length=0; (c=ReadBlobByte(image)) != EOF; length++)
(void) fputc(c,file);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of fputc is ignored, so a write failure (e.g., disk full or stream error) during processing of a crafted image is not detected. The loop continues and later code uses the partially written file; the supported consequence is an unexpected state leading to a crash/denial of service, as described by the commit.

commit_msg:
coders/png.c: Stop a memory leak in read_user_chunk_callback() (reference

https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/517).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['              profile=DestroyStringInfo(profile);', '', '      profile=DestroyStringInfo(profile);']}
description: The read_user_chunk_callback function in coders\png.c in ImageMagick 7.0.6-1 Q16 2017-06-21 (beta) has memory leak vulnerabilities via crafted PNG files.

code_evidence: Line 27 allocates a StringInfo via BlobToStringInfo and line 28 checks for NULL; if allocation fails, the function returns -1 at line 33 without any resource to free (profile is NULL), so this path is not the leak.
In the else branch, when the existing eXIf header bytes are malformed (lines 47-48), the function returns -1 at line 50 while the allocated profile from line 27 is still live and never released.
On the success path, SetImageProfile is called at lines 57-58 and the function returns 1 at line 59; in the pre-fix code the allocated profile is likewise not destroyed before returning.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the allocated StringInfo's effective lifetime ends at function return, yet the return paths omit DestroyStringInfo, leaving the resource unreleased. This is a missing-release defect rather than a use-after-free or buffer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: read_user_chunk_callback allocates a StringInfo profile for each recognized eXIf/exIf chunk but returns through the malformed-header branch (and the success branch) without releasing it. Trigger: a crafted PNG containing an eXIf chunk whose header bytes fail the p[1..5] checks, or any successful eXIf chunk. Consequence: repeated chunks leak memory, enabling resource-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg: Set pixel cache to undefined if any resource limit is exceeded
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      cache_info->type=UndefinedCache;', '      cache_info->type=UndefinedCache;', '      cache_info->type=UndefinedCache;', '              if (status == MagickFalse)', '                cache_info->type=UndefinedCache;', '  if (status == MagickFalse)', '    cache_info->type=UndefinedCache;']}
description: The WPG parser in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-4 and 7.x before 7.0.1-5, when a memory limit is set, allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via vectors related to the SetImageExtent return-value check, which trigger (1) a heap-based buffer overflow in the SetPixelIndex function or an invalid write operation in the (2) ScaleCharToQuantum or (3) SetPixelIndex functions.

code_evidence: At [74-85] the memory path is taken only when status from AcquireMagickResource(MemoryResource,...) is true or the cache type is already MemoryCache; on allocation success the type is set to MemoryCache and pixels are used by later writes.
At [186-193] SetPixelCacheExtent is checked and returns failure without invalidating cache_info->type, leaving a stale cache type after the extent operation fails.
At [250-255] ClonePixelCacheRepository runs and status is returned; on failure cache_info->type is not reset, so the cache remains marked as a usable type despite the failed clone.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The target CWE-119 covers writes outside a buffer's intended boundary. Here the missing cache-type invalidation on failure leads to out-of-bounds pixel writes; this is the buffer-boundary violation described by CWE-119 rather than a mere resource-exhaustion error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: OpenPixelCache can return failure while cache_info->type still indicates a valid memory/disk/map cache. Callers such as SetPixelIndex then treat the cache as usable and write through cache_info->pixels; when the resource-limited allocation or extent failed, those writes target a buffer that was never properly sized, producing the heap-based out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
Prevent the homeserver from inserting malicious secrets

Correctly verify that the reply to a secrets request is actually coming
from a verified device. While we did verify that it was us who replied,
we didn't properly cancel storing the secret if the sending device was
one of ours but was maliciously inserted by the homeserver and
unverified. We only send secret requests to verified devices in the
first place, so only the homeserver could abuse this issue.

Additionally we protected against malicious secret poisoning by
verifying that the secret is actually the reply to a request. This means
the server only has 2 places where it can poison the secrets:

- After a verification when we automatically request the secrets
- When the user manually hits the request button

It also needs to prevent other secret answers to reach the client first
since we ignore all replies after that one.

The impact of this might be quite severe. It could allow the server to
replace the cross-signing keys silently and while we might not trust
that key, we possibly could trust it in the future if we rely on the
stored secret. Similarly this could potentially be abused to make the
client trust a malicious online key backup.

If your deployment is not patched yet and you don't control your
homeserver, you can protect against this by simply not doing any
verifications of your own devices and not pressing the request button in
the settings menu.

description: nheko is a desktop client for the Matrix communication application. code_evidence: The handler only checks that msg.sender equals the local user before processing a SecretSend event; any device claiming that user identity passes this gate.
The sender_device_id is derived by matching msg.sender_key against cached device keys, but the original code never checks whether that device or key is verified before proceeding.
storeSecret is called with e->content.secret, persisting the secret without confirming the sending device is trusted.

if (msg.sender != local_user.to_string())

commit_msg:
scsi: lsi: exit infinite loop while executing script (CVE-2019-12068)

When executing script in lsi_execute_script(), the LSI scsi adapter
emulator advances 's->dsp' index to read next opcode. This can lead
to an infinite loop if the next opcode is empty. Move the existing
loop exit after 10k iterations so that it covers no-op opcodes as
well.

Reported-by: Bugs SysSec <bugs-syssec@rub.de>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
