description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-reload.c had an infinite loop that was addressed by validating a length.

code_evidence: Line 9 reads a 32-bit kind_responses_length from the packet; line 10 only checks 4 + kind_responses_length against length, so a large value can pass the truncation guard when the addition wraps or the loop bound is not otherwise constrained.
The while loop at line 19 iterates while kind_responses_offset < kind_responses_length, advancing by dissect_kinddata's return value; only a zero increment breaks the loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an iteration whose exit condition depends on an attacker-controlled length that can be too large to reach within bounded processing, i.e., an unreachable/impractical loop exit, matching CWE-835. It is not merely a buffer overflow: the guard at line 10 is a length validation that directly governs loop termination.

evidence_lines.code:
kind_responses_length = tvb_get_ntohl(tvb, offset);
if (4 + kind_responses_length > length) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: kind_responses_length is an unvalidated 32-bit packet field used directly as the loop termination bound. Trigger: a crafted StatAns length that passes the truncation check causes the loop to continue consuming offset increments until the bound is reached or wrap/overflow behavior prevents termination, producing CPU consumption. The added G_MAXUINT16 check constrains the length so the loop bound is reachable.

schema tree BUGFIX freeing nodes with no module set

Context must be passed explicitly for these cases.
Fixes #1452
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    lys_node_free(retval, NULL, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['    lys_node_free(ctx, retval, NULL, 0);']}
description: In function lys_node_free() in libyang <= v1.0.225, it asserts that the value of node->module can't be NULL. But in some cases, node->module can be null, which triggers a reachable assertion (CWE-617).

code_evidence: The error label calls lys_node_free(retval, NULL, 0) without passing ctx; in the vulnerable version this reaches lys_node_free with a NULL context.

retval is set to inout and its module is assigned, but the free path is invoked for numerous parse failures via goto error, including when node is NULL at [122,123] and on invalid statements at [59,61].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because attacker-supplied malformed schema input reaches an assert() in lys_node_free, producing a crash/exit rather than graceful error handling.

evidence_lines.code:
error:
lys_node_free(retval, NULL, 0);

retval = (struct lys_node *)inout;
retval->module = module;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path frees the partially built schema node without the required context argument, and lys_node_free asserts that node->module is non-NULL. A malformed YIN input/output statement that triggers goto error can reach this free with a node whose module is unset, causing a reachable assertion and abort.

description: json-c through 0.14 has an integer overflow and out-of-bounds write via a large JSON file, as demonstrated by printbuf_memappend.

code_evidence: Line 6 computes size_needed = offset + len using signed ints with no check that offset + len fits in INT_MAX. Consequence: memset writes len bytes past the undersized buffer, producing an out-of-bounds write and segmentation fault.

x86/mm: Refactor map_pages_to_xen to have only a single exit path

We will soon need to perform clean-ups before returning.

No functional change.

This is part of XSA-345.

Reported-by: Hongyan Xia <hongyxia@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Wei Liu <wei.liu2@citrix.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x allowing x86 guest OS users to cause a host OS denial of service, achieve data corruption, or possibly gain privileges by exploiting a race condition that leads to a use-after-free involving 2MiB and 1GiB superpages.

code_evidence: At [114-124], the code allocates l2t, then under map_pgdir_lock re-checks *pl3e and replaces it only if still present and PSE; l2t is freed if not consumed. This is the split/superpage conversion guarded by the lock.
At [199-212], the analogous l1t conversion re-checks *pl2e under map_pgdir_lock and frees l1t if the PSE superpage was already changed.

At [234-265], after writing leaf entries, the code re-reads ol2e under map_pgdir_lock, verifies all L1 entries are contiguous and identical, then collapses to a 2MiB superpage and frees the old L1 table.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the weakness is a concurrent check-then-act on shared page tables whose exclusivity depends on map_pgdir_lock; the lock's scope and the re-check window are the root cause. CWE-416 is only the consequence of the race, not the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function converts between 2MiB/1MiB and 4KiB mappings. The check-then-act sequences at [114-124], [199-212] and [234-265] rely on map_pgdir_lock to make the re-check and page-table replacement atomic. If a concurrent mapping path modifies the same page-table entries outside that lock, the re-check can pass on stale state, so the old table is freed while still referenced (use-after-free) or superpage/leaf entries are overwritten, causing host corruption or DoS.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.4+
Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (key_is_instantiated(key) &&'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (key_is_positive(key) &&']}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.10 does not correctly synchronize the actions of updating versus finding a key in the "negative" state to avoid a race condition, which allows local users to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only switches a state predicate from key_is_instantiated to key_is_positive and truncates a file; this is a race-condition synchronization fix (CWE-362), not input validation, so it does not support CWE-20.

commit_msg:
x86: don't allow page_unlock() to drop the last type reference

Only _put_page_type() does the necessary cleanup, and hence not all
domain pages can be released during guest cleanup (leaving around
zombie domains) if we get this wrong.

This is XSA-242.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        else if ( unlikely((nx & (PGT_locked | PGT_count_mask)) ==', '                           (PGT_locked | 1)) )', '        {', '            /*', '             * We must not drop the second to last reference when the page is', "             * locked, as page_unlock() doesn't do any cleanup of the type.", '             */', '            cpu_relax();', '            y = page->u.inuse.type_info;', '            continue;', '        }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service (memory leak) because reference counts are mishandled.

code_evidence: The loop derives nx = x - 1 and asserts a nonzero type count, then only performs special cleanup when the decremented count reaches zero (line 11). When the count does not reach zero, the code sets a TLB timestamp and attempts cmpxchg to store nx, releasing one type reference without invoking _put_final_page_type.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because a page/type resource is not released after its effective lifetime ends: the cleanup needed to free the final type reference is skipped. This is not a mere reference-count arithmetic error; the supported consequence is missing resource release leading to memory leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: decrementing the type count to a nonzero value bypasses the final-type cleanup path, and page_unlock() does not perform that cleanup. Trigger: a locked page reaches the second-to-last reference and a caller drops it via this path. Consequence: the final type reference/cleanup is lost, so the page type is never fully released, leaking domain pages and leaving zombie domains (DoS).

Fix PropertyDefinition parsing in ObjectInitializer

This patch fixes #3822 and fixes #3823 and fixes #3824 and fixes #3825.

JerryScript-DCO-1.0-Signed-off-by: Robert Fancsik frobert@inf.u-szeged.hu
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (context_p->token.type != LEXER_LITERAL', '      || context_p->token.lit_location.type != LEXER_IDENT_LITERAL)'], 'added_lines': ['  /* context_p->token.lit_location.char_p is showing the character after the string start,', '     so it is not suitable for reparsing as identifier.', "     e.g.: { 'foo' } */", '  if (context_p->token.lit_location.type != LEXER_IDENT_LITERAL)', '  {', '    parser_raise_error (context_p, PARSER_ERR_IDENTIFIER_EXPECTED);', '  }', '', '  if (context_p->token.type != LEXER_LITERAL)', '', '  JERRY_ASSERT (context_p->token.lit_location.type == LEXER_IDENT_LITERAL);']}
description: There is an Assertion 'context_p->token.type == LEXER_RIGHT_BRACE || context_p->token.type == LEXER_ASSIGN || context_p->token.type == LEXER_COMMA' failed at js-parser-expr.c:3230 in parser_parse_object_initializer in JerryScript 2.2.0.

code_evidence: The function rewinds the lexer to the token's literal start (char_p, which points after the opening quote for strings) and re-lexes via lexer_next_token, so the resulting token type depends on the original token's literal kind.

The guard only accepts LEXER_LITERAL with lit_location.type == LEXER_IDENT_LITERAL; otherwise parser_raise_error is called. A string literal like 'foo' is re-lexed into a non-identifier token, which the guard must reject before constructing a literal.

The guard in this function is the missing constraint that prevents the invalid token from reaching the assertion; this is not merely a parsing-logic error since the impact is an assertion-triggered crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: reparsing assumes the token's char_p can be re-lexed as an identifier, but for string literals char_p starts after the quote, so re-lexing yields a different token. Trigger: an object initializer such as { 'foo' } reaches this path; without the literal-type guard the subsequent code/assert is reached with an unexpected token, producing the reachable assertion failure and parser crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
net: mpls: fix stale pointer if allocation fails during device rename

lianhui reports that when MPLS fails to register the sysctl table
under new location (during device rename) the old pointers won't
get overwritten and may be freed again (double free).

Handle this gracefully. The best option would be unregistering
the MPLS from the device completely on failure, but unfortunately
mpls_ifdown() can fail. So failing fully is also unreliable.

Another option is to register the new table first then only
remove old one if the new one succeeds. That requires more
code, changes order of notifications and two tables may be
visible at the same time.

sysctl point is not used in the rest of the code - set to NULL
on failures and skip unregister if already NULL.

Reported-by: lianhui tang <bluetlh@gmail.com>
Fixes: 0fae3bf018d9 ("mpls: handle device renames for per-device sysctls")
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (!mdev->sysctl)', '\t\treturn;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 6.1.13, there is a double free in net/mpls/af_mpls.c upon an allocation failure (for registering the sysctl table under a new location) during the renaming of a device.

code_evidence: The function unconditionally dereferences mdev->sysctl (line 6), unregisters it (line 7), and frees the associated table (line 8) without checking whether mdev->sysctl is NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the same table pointer is freed on repeated unregister calls without a guard ensuring it is still valid. This is a double-free of a specific allocation, not merely a null-pointer dereference, so CWE-415 is the appropriate label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When sysctl registration under a new location fails during device rename, mdev->sysctl is left stale or NULL; a subsequent unregister call still reads mdev->sysctl->ctl_table_arg and frees that table, so the same allocation can be freed again. The missing NULL/stale-pointer guard is the root cause, and the supported consequence is a double free of the ctl_table allocation.

commit_msg:
Fix encrypt overflow

An overflow can occur in the EVP_EncryptUpdate function. If an attacker is
able to supply very large amounts of input data after a previous call to
EVP_EncryptUpdate with a partial block then a length check can overflow
resulting in a heap corruption.

Following an analysis of all OpenSSL internal usage of the
EVP_EncryptUpdate function all usage is one of two forms.

The first form is like this:
EVP_EncryptInit()
EVP_EncryptUpdate()

i.e. where the EVP_EncryptUpdate() call is known to be the first called
function after an EVP_EncryptInit(), and therefore that specific call
must be safe.

The second form is where the length passed to EVP_EncryptUpdate() can be
seen from the code to be some small value and therefore there is no
possibility of an overflow.

Since all instances are one of these two forms, I believe that there can
be no overflows in internal code due to this problem.

It should be noted that EVP_DecryptUpdate() can call EVP_EncryptUpdate()
in certain code paths. Also EVP_CipherUpdate() is a synonym for
EVP_EncryptUpdate(). Therefore I have checked all instances of these
calls too, and came to the same conclusion, i.e. there are no instances
in internal usage where an overflow could occur.

This could still represent a security issue for end user code that calls
this function directly.

CVE-2016-2106

Issue reported by Guido Vranken.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The TFLite computation for size of output after padding, `ComputeOutSize`(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/0c9692ae7b1671c983569e5d3de5565843d500cf/tensorflow/lite/kernels/padding.h#L43-L55), does not check that the `stride` argument is not 0 before doing the division. Users can craft special models such that `ComputeOutSize` is called with `stride` set to 0. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: ComputeOutSize takes stride as a caller-supplied int and performs integer division by stride in both the kTfLitePaddingSame branch (line 6) and the kTfLitePaddingValid branch (line 8) without checking stride against 0; the divisor is the raw parameter, not a computed value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 is divide-by-zero: the function divides image_size-dependent values by stride, and stride can be 0, directly matching the weakness. This is a specific arithmetic fault rather than a generic input-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: stride is used directly as a divisor with no zero guard. Trigger: a crafted model causes ComputeOutSize to be called with stride == 0. Consequence: integer division by zero, a crash/undefined behavior, supporting a denial-of-service impact.

commit_msg:
rpmsg: char: release allocated memory

In rpmsg_eptdev_write_iter, if copy_from_iter_full fails the allocated
buffer needs to be released.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Bjorn Andersson <bjorn.andersson@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!copy_from_iter_full(kbuf, len, from))', '\t\treturn -EFAULT;'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!copy_from_iter_full(kbuf, len, from)) {', '\t\tret = -EFAULT;', '\t\tgoto free_kbuf;', '\t}']}
description: A memory leak in the rpmsg_eptdev_write_iter() function in drivers/rpmsg/rpmsg_char.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering copy_from_iter_full() failures, aka CID-bbe692e349e2.

code_evidence: kbuf is allocated with kzalloc(len, GFP_KERNEL); failure to allocate returns -ENOMEM without a buffer to free.
After successful allocation, if copy_from_iter_full fails, the function returns -EFAULT directly, abandoning the kbuf pointer without releasing it.
The free_kbuf label and kfree(kbuf) exist and are reachable from the mutex_lock_interruptible error path, showing cleanup is expected but bypassed by the copy failure path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory and fails to release it on an error path, matching CWE-401's missing release of allocated memory after its effective lifetime. This is a leak, not a use-after-free or double-free, because the pointer simply becomes unreachable without being freed.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!copy_from_iter_full(kbuf, len, from))
return -EFAULT;

free_kbuf:
kfree(kbuf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy_from_iter_full failure branch returns -EFAULT before reaching the cleanup label, so the kzalloc'd buffer is never freed. Trigger: a caller supplies an iov_iter that cannot be fully copied, causing repeated write_iter calls to leak len bytes each time. Consequence: unbounded kernel memory consumption leading to denial of service.

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x allowing x86 guest OS users to cause a host OS denial of service, achieve data corruption, or possibly gain privileges by exploiting a race condition that leads to a use-after-free involving 2MiB and 1GiB superpages.

code_evidence: The superpage-shatter path allocates a new l2t, then takes map_pgdir_lock and re-checks *pl3e for PRESENT|PSE before atomically replacing it; if the page-table entry changed or was no longer a superpage, the freshly allocated l2t is left non-NULL and freed after unlocking.
The analogous L2 (PSE) shatter path allocates l1t, re-checks *pl2e under map_pgdir_lock, and only installs l1t if the entry is still a present superpage; otherwise l1t is freed after unlock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 requires a timing window in which an interfering sequence can modify a shared resource without exclusivity. Here the shared page-table entries are re-checked and written under map_pgdir_lock, and the patch is explicitly non-functional; the function does not directly exhibit the race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Concurrent page-table modification is mediated by map_pgdir_lock and re-validation of the PTE flags, so the allocation and installation sequence is serialized. The refactor only routes allocation failures through a single exit path and does not remove or narrow the lock/re-check window; no unsynchronized shared-resource access is introduced by this function.

commit_msg:
FileURLToFilePath:  Don't unescape '/' and '\\'.

GURL leaves these escaped, and unescaping them in paths changes the
meaning of the path.

Added two values to the UnescapeRule enumeration:
PATH_SEPARATORS and URL_SPECIAL_CHARS_EXCEPT_PATH_SEPARATORS.

In followup CLs, I intend to replace all uses of URL_SPECIAL_CHARS,
in favor of one or both the two new values, and eventually remove
the value, as it's easily to use in an unsafe manner.

BUG=586657

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1704163003

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#377013}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      path, UnescapeRule::SPACES | UnescapeRule::URL_SPECIAL_CHARS);'], 'added_lines': ['      path, UnescapeRule::SPACES |', '                UnescapeRule::URL_SPECIAL_CHARS_EXCEPT_PATH_SEPARATORS);']}
description: Google Chrome before 50.0.2661.102 on Android mishandles / (slash) and \ (backslash) characters, which allows attackers to conduct directory traversal attacks via a file: URL, related to net/base/escape.cc and net/base/filename_util.cc.

code_evidence: Line 26-27: the URL path is passed to UnescapeURLComponent with SPACES | URL_SPECIAL_CHARS, which decodes percent-encoded '/' and '\\' before the path is used as a file path.
Lines 13-15: only leading slashes/backslashes are stripped, so encoded separators later in the path survive to form traversal sequences.
Line 21: on Windows all '/' are converted to '\\', so an unescaped encoded separator becomes a native directory separator.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-22 fits because external URL input is used to construct a file pathname without neutralizing path separators that allow escaping a restricted directory. The function's own unescaping of separators is the missing constraint, not merely a related encoding weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
path = UnescapeURLComponent(
path, UnescapeRule::SPACES | UnescapeRule::URL_SPECIAL_CHARS);
std::replace(path.begin(), path.end(), '/', '\\');

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: FileURLToFilePath unescapes URL-special characters including path separators, so percent-encoded '/' or '\\' in a file: URL become literal separators in the resulting file path. Trigger: an attacker supplies a crafted file: URL whose encoded separators encode '..' traversal. Consequence: the resolved path can escape the intended directory, enabling directory traversal file access.

commit_msg:
Before this patch, function read_rindex_entry would set a rgrp
glock's gl_object pointer to itself before inserting the rgrp into
the rgrp rbtree. The problem is: if another process was also reading
the rgrp in, and had already inserted its newly created rgrp, then
the second call to read_rindex_entry would overwrite that value,
then return a bad return code to the caller. Later, other functions
would reference the now-freed rgrp memory by way of gl_object.
In some cases, that could result in gfs2_rgrp_brelse being called
twice for the same rgrp: once for the failed attempt and once for
the "real" rgrp release. Eventually the kernel would panic.
There are also a number of other things that could go wrong when
a kernel module is accessing freed storage. For example, this could
result in rgrp corruption because the fake rgrp would point to a
fake bitmap in memory too, causing gfs2_inplace_reserve to search
some random memory for free blocks, and find some, since we were
never setting rgd->rd_bits to NULL before freeing it.

This patch fixes the problem by not setting gl_object until we
have successfully inserted the rgrp into the rbtree. Also, it sets
rd_bits to NULL as it frees them, which will ensure any accidental
access to the wrong rgrp will result in a kernel panic rather than
file system corruption, which is preferred.

Signed-off-by: Bob Peterson <rpeterso@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\trgd->rd_gl->gl_object = rgd;', '\trgd->rd_gl->gl_vm.start = (rgd->rd_addr * bsize) & PAGE_MASK;', '\trgd->rd_gl->gl_vm.end = PAGE_ALIGN((rgd->rd_addr + rgd->rd_length) * bsize) - 1;', '\tif (!error)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!error) {', '\t\trgd->rd_gl->gl_object = rgd;', '\t\trgd->rd_gl->gl_vm.start = (rgd->rd_addr * bsize) & PAGE_MASK;', '\t\trgd->rd_gl->gl_vm.end = PAGE_ALIGN((rgd->rd_addr +', '\t\t\t\t\t\t    rgd->rd_length) * bsize) - 1;', '\t}', '\trgd->rd_bits = NULL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in fs/gfs2/rgrp.c in the Linux kernel before 4.8. A use-after-free is caused by the functions gfs2_clear_rgrpd and read_rindex_entry.

code_evidence: Lines 33-35 publish the new rgrp to the glock (gl_object = rgd) and set gl_vm before the insertion attempt, so the object is visible to other readers prior to being validated.

Lines 41-44 call rgd_insert under sd_rindex_spin; if insertion fails because another process already inserted an rgrp, line 45 clears the error and line 46 releases the glock while gl_object still points at this rgd.
Lines 47-49 free rd_bits and the rgd object without clearing gl_object or rd_bits, leaving the glock's gl_object dangling to freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees the rgrp at lines 47-49 but leaves gl_object pointing at that freed allocation, and subsequent glock users can dereference it; this is exactly a use-after-free. A simple leak would omit the free, whereas here the stale pointer outlives the object.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the rgrp is attached to the glock's gl_object before rgd_insert confirms it is the canonical instance. Trigger: a concurrent read_rindex_entry inserts the same rgrp first, so rgd_insert returns nonzero; this path then gfs2_glock_put and frees rgd while gl_object still references it. Supported consequence: later users dereference freed rgrp memory (e.g., double rgrp release or bitmap access), leading to kernel panic or corruption.

commit_msg:
Security fix for AC flag poisoning and MCDT

This PR does the following
- Ensuring the AC flag along with other system/control flags are always cleared upon enclave enter
- Update the inital MXCSR value to 0x1FBF and put lfence after MXCSR load (via LDMXCSR, XRSTOR, or FXRSTOR)
  for the MCDT mitigation

Signed-off-by: Ming-Wei Shih <mishih@microsoft.com>

+++ func_after
@@ -14,15 +14,17 @@
     td->oret_arg = arg;
 
     /* Restore the FXSTATE and flags */
-    asm volatile("pushq %[rflags] \n\t" // Restore flags.
-                 "popfq \n\t"
-                 "fldcw %[fcw] \n\t"     // Restore x87 control word
-                 "ldmxcsr %[mxcsr] \n\t" // Restore MXCSR
-                 : [mxcsr] "=m"(callsite->mxcsr),
-                   [fcw] "=m"(callsite->fcw),

description: Open Enclave is a hardware-agnostic open source library for developing applications that utilize Hardware-based Trusted Execution Environments, also known as Enclaves. There are two issues that are mitigated in version 0.19.3. First, Open Enclave SDK does not properly sanitize the `MXCSR` register on enclave entry. This makes applications vulnerable to MXCSR Configuration Dependent Timing (MCDT) attacks, where incorrect `MXCSR` values can impact instruction retirement by at most one cycle, depending on the (secret) data operand value. Please find more details in the guidance from Intel in the references. Second, Open Enclave SDK does not sanitize x86's alignment check flag `RFLAGS.AC` on enclave entry. This opens up the possibility for a side-channel attacker to be notified for every unaligned memory access performed by the enclave. The issue has been addressed in version 0.19.3 and the current master branch. Users will need to recompile their applications against the patched libraries to be protected from this vulnerability. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function restores previously saved MXCSR, FCW, and RFLAGS values via popfq/fldcw/ldmxcsr; it does not initialize a resource, and the diff only adds an lfence mitigation, so improper initialization (CWE-665) is not directly supported by this code.

commit_msg:
ASAN SFTP Fixes
When decoding SFTP messages, fix the size checks so they don't wrap. (ZD12766)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (sz > maxSz - WOLFSSH_SFTP_HEADER - UINT32_SZ - idx) {', '        return WS_BUFFER_E;', '    }']}
description: WolfSSH v1.4.7 was discovered to contain an integer overflow via the function wolfSSH_SFTP_RecvRMDIR.

code_evidence: Line 27 reads attacker-controlled sz from the SFTP message with ato32, and line 28 immediately uses sz in the allocation size expression sz + WOLFSSH_SFTP_HEADER + UINT32_SZ without any bound check against maxSz or a maximum.
That allocation result feeds the read at line 33 and the outSz computation at line 41, which also adds sz-derived values; there is no guard ensuring sz cannot wrap the addition.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the weakness is unchecked integer arithmetic on an attacker-supplied length that can wrap when computing an allocation size and packet size, exactly the size-calculation overflow pattern described. This is distinct from a simple bounds check failure; the core defect is the wraparound in the addition.

evidence_lines.code:
ret = WPREAD(fd, out + UINT32_SZ + WOLFSSH_SFTP_HEADER, sz, ofst);
outSz = (word32)ret + WOLFSSH_SFTP_HEADER + UINT32_SZ;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length field sz is trusted in arithmetic used for buffer sizing and offset math without a wraparound-safe check. Trigger: a crafted SFTP read request with a very large sz makes sz + WOLFSSH_SFTP_HEADER + UINT32_SZ wrap to a small value, so WMALLOC under-allocates; the subsequent WPREAD/outSz use can then overflow or mis-size the buffer. Supported consequence: memory corruption or crash from a too-small allocation.

commit_msg:
Greg Kroah-Hartman says:

====================
Raw socket cleanups

Ori Nimron pointed out that there are a number of places in the kernel
where you can create a raw socket, without having to have the
CAP_NET_RAW permission.

To resolve this, here's a short patch series to test these odd and old
protocols for this permission before allowing the creation to succeed

All patches are currently against the net tree.
====================

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\trc = -EPERM;', '\tif (sock->type == SOCK_RAW && !kern && !capable(CAP_NET_RAW))', '\t\tgoto out;', '']}
description: ax25_create in net/ax25/af_ax25.c in the AF_AX25 network module in the Linux kernel 3.16 through 5.3.2 does not enforce CAP_NET_RAW, which means that unprivileged users can create a raw socket, aka CID-0614e2b73768.

code_evidence: Only the socket type is validated; SOCK_RAW is accepted with no capability check, so creation proceeds for any caller.
After the type check, the function allocates the socket unconditionally (sk_alloc with kern) and returns success, setting up atalk_dgram_ops without any authorization gate on the raw-socket path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the function omits an authorization check (CAP_NET_RAW) before granting access to a privileged resource. The missing capability gate is an authorization omission, not a memory-safety defect, so it contrasts with validation weaknesses that reject malformed input.

evidence_lines.code:
if (sock->type != SOCK_RAW && sock->type != SOCK_DGRAM)
goto out;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the raw-socket branch performs no CAP_NET_RAW capability check before allocating and installing the socket. Trigger: an unprivileged process calls socket(AF_APPLETALK, SOCK_RAW, ...) with a non-kernel context. Consequence: the raw socket is created and usable, bypassing the intended privilege restriction.

commit_msg: Fixed handling of empty JPEG-LS scans.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  ', '  assert(lines > 0);'], 'added_lines': ['', '  if (lines == 0)', '    return false;']}
description: There is an assertion failure in SingleComponentLSScan::ParseMCU in singlecomponentlsscan.cpp in libjpeg before 1.64 via an empty JPEG-LS scan.

code_evidence: lines 4-8: lines is initialized from m_ulRemaining[0]; when frame height is 0, lines is asserted to be 0 and then forced to 8.
lines 11-13: lines is only clamped down to a maximum of 8, never raised, so a remaining count of 0 stays 0.
lines 14-16: when frame height is positive, the subtraction leaves lines unchanged (0) and assert(lines > 0) is reached with a zero value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because a reachable assert() in ParseMCU is triggered by malformed input, causing process termination. The fix replaces the assertion with a return false, confirming the assertion itself was the reachable failure point, not a memory-safety weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: For an empty JPEG-LS scan, m_ulRemaining[0] can be 0 while frame height is positive, so lines remains 0 and the assert(lines > 0) at line 16 fires. The trigger is attacker-controlled empty scan data; the consequence is an assertion-driven abort (denial of service) rather than graceful rejection.

commit_msg:
revert most of d7a0084bf99d618d1dc26a54fd413db7ae8b8e63

See php-memcached-dev/php-memcached#531
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (memcached_fatal(rc) && rc != MEMCACHED_TIMEOUT) {'], 'added_lines': ['  if (memcached_fatal(rc)) {']}
description: libmemcached-awesome is an open source C/C++ client library and tools for the memcached server. `libmemcached` could return data for a previously requested key, if that previous request timed out due to a low `POLL_TIMEOUT`. This issue has been addressed in version 1.1.4. Users are advised to upgrade. There are several ways to workaround or lower the probability of this bug affecting a given deployment. 1: use a reasonably high `POLL_TIMEOUT` setting, like the default. 2: use separate libmemcached connections for unrelated data. 3: do not re-use libmemcached connections in an unknown state.

code_evidence: Lines 10-13 read a binary response via binary_read_one_response, looping while the status is MEMCACHED_FETCH_NOTFINISHED, so the returned result comes from the current request.
Lines 17-19 reset the connection only when memcached_fatal(rc) is true; the pre-change guard also excluded MEMCACHED_TIMEOUT, leaving a timed-out connection unreset and its stale state reusable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Returning a prior request's response to a later caller exposes data not authorized for that caller, matching CWE-200's confidentiality scope. The root mistake is the missing reset on timeout, not an out-of-bounds read, so CWE-200 fits the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a fatal timeout is not treated as fatal, so memcached_io_reset is skipped and the connection retains unread/stale response state. Trigger: a request times out under a low POLL_TIMEOUT, then the same connection is reused. Consequence: a later read in lines 10-13 can return data belonging to the earlier request, exposing another request's value.

commit_msg:
Fixed recursive async function calls.

Previously, PromiseCapability record was stored (function->context)
directly in function object during a function invocation.  This is
not correct, because PromiseCapability record should be linked to
current execution context.  As a result, function->context is
overwritten with consecutive recursive calls which results in
use-after-free.

This closes #451 issue on Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['njs_function_lambda_call(njs_vm_t *vm)', '    ret = njs_vmcode_interpreter(vm, lambda->start);'], 'added_lines': ['njs_function_lambda_call(njs_vm_t *vm, void *promise_cap, void *async_ctx)', '', '    njs_assert(function->context == NULL);', '    ret = njs_vmcode_interpreter(vm, lambda->start, promise_cap, async_ctx);']}
description: njs through 0.7.0, used in NGINX, was discovered to contain a heap use-after-free in njs_await_fulfilled.

code_evidence: The function obtains the current function via frame->native.function and, at line 63, invokes the interpreter on lambda->start without carrying per-invocation async state (promise_cap/async_ctx); the pre-patch signature takes only vm.
After the interpreter returns, lines 64-66 restore saved level pointers (cur_local, cur_closures, cur_temp) that were captured before the nested call at lines 29-31.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the root cause is reuse of per-invocation state overwritten by a recursive call and later accessed after being freed/reallocated. This is memory lifetime confusion, distinct from a simple null dereference or bounds error.

evidence_lines.code:
frame = (njs_frame_t *) vm->top_frame;
function = frame->native.function;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: During recursive async function calls, per-invocation PromiseCapability state is stored on the shared function object rather than tied to the execution context. A recursive invocation overwrites the outer call's state, so when the outer call resumes after the nested interpreter call, it references freed/reused data, yielding use-after-free. The trigger is recursion into an async function; the supported consequence is invalid memory access (read/write) after free.

commit_msg:
can: kvaser_usb: kvaser_usb_leaf: Fix some info-leaks to USB devices

Uninitialized Kernel memory can leak to USB devices.

Fix this by using kzalloc() instead of kmalloc().

Signed-off-by: Xiaolong Huang <butterflyhuangxx@gmail.com>
Fixes: 7259124eac7d ("can: kvaser_usb: Split driver into kvaser_usb_core.c and kvaser_usb_leaf.c")
Cc: linux-stable <stable@vger.kernel.org> # >= v4.19
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcmd = kmalloc(sizeof(*cmd), GFP_KERNEL);'], 'added_lines': ['\tcmd = kzalloc(sizeof(*cmd), GFP_KERNEL);']}
description: In the Linux kernel through 5.4.6, there are information leaks of uninitialized memory to a USB device in the drivers/net/can/usb/kvaser_usb/kvaser_usb_leaf.c driver, aka CID-da2311a6385c.

code_evidence: Line 5 allocates a kvaser_cmd with kmalloc, which does not zero memory. Lines 8-11 initialize only id, len, and the flush_queue subfields; the remainder of the sizeof(*cmd) buffer stays uninitialized. Line 12 passes the full cmd buffer to kvaser_usb_send_cmd for transmission to the USB device.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses and transmits a resource (the kmalloc'd command buffer) that has not been fully initialized, matching CWE-908. The confidentiality impact (kernel memory disclosure) is consistent with the entry's scope; the fix to kzalloc confirms the uninitialized-resource root cause rather than a separate out-of-bounds issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: kmalloc leaves the command buffer partially uninitialized, and only a few header/subfields are written before the whole structure is sent to the USB device. Trigger: calling kvaser_usb_leaf_flush_queue causes the uninitialized tail bytes to be transmitted, leaking kernel memory to the device.

commit_msg: Fix bug #71498: Out-of-Bound Read in phar_parse_zipfile()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t'], 'added_lines': ['']}
description: The phar_parse_zipfile function in zip.c in the PHAR extension in PHP before 5.5.33 and 5.6.x before 5.6.19 allows remote attackers to obtain sensitive information from process memory or cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and application crash) by placing a PK\x05\x06 signature at an invalid location.

code_evidence: When user_stub is a resource and len<0, len is set to PHP_STREAM_COPY_ALL or -len and php_stream_copy_to_mem fills user_stub with the stream contents, giving a length derived from external stream data.

tmp = estrndup(user_stub, len) copies that length, php_stristr searches within it, and pos = user_stub + (pos - tmp) rebases the found halt_stub pointer; len = pos - user_stub + 18 then computes a stub length from that pointer arithmetic.
entry.uncompressed_filesize = len + 5 and php_stream_write(entry.fp, user_stub, len) write len bytes from user_stub without any independent bound check on the original buffer size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads from user_stub beyond its intended boundary because the computed len is not constrained to the buffer size, which is a memory-buffer bounds violation as described by CWE-119. It is not merely an integer issue: the actual out-of-bounds read operation on the buffer is what the weakness classifies.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the write length is computed from a searched pointer offset (pos - user_stub + 18) rather than from the validated size of the user_stub buffer; if the halt_stub match sits near the buffer end, the +18 extension exceeds the allocated content, causing an out-of-bounds read during php_stream_write. The trigger is an attacker-supplied stub stream whose halt_stub occurrence leaves fewer than 18 bytes remaining; the consequence is reading process memory past the buffer, potentially disclosing memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
Bug#24388746: PRIVILEGE ESCALATION AND RACE CONDITION USING CREATE TABLE

During REPAIR TABLE of a MyISAM table, a temporary data file (.TMD)
is created. When repair finishes, this file is renamed to the original
.MYD file. The problem was that during this rename, we copied the
stats from the old file to the new file with chmod/chown. If a user
managed to replace the temporary file before chmod/chown was executed,
it was possible to get an arbitrary file with the privileges of the
mysql user.

This patch fixes the problem by not copying stats from the old
file to the new file. This is not needed as the new file was
created with the correct stats. This fix only changes server
behavior - external utilities such as myisamchk still does
chmod/chown.

No test case provided since the problem involves synchronization
with file system operations.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int mi_sort_index(MI_CHECK *param, register MI_INFO *info, char * name)', '\t\t\tMYF(0)) ||'], 'added_lines': ['int mi_sort_index(MI_CHECK *param, register MI_INFO *info, char * name,', '                  my_bool no_copy_stat)', '\t\t\tno_copy_stat ? MYF(MY_REDEL_NO_COPY_STAT) : MYF(0)) ||']}
description: Race condition in Oracle MySQL before 5.5.52, 5.6.x before 5.6.33, 5.7.x before 5.7.15, and 8.x before 8.0.1; MariaDB before 5.5.52, 10.0.x before 10.0.28, and 10.1.x before 10.1.18; Percona Server before 5.5.51-38.2, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-78-1, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-8; and Percona XtraDB Cluster before 5.5.41-37.0, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-25.17, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-26.17 allows local users with certain permissions to gain privileges by leveraging use of my_copystat by REPAIR TABLE to repair a MyISAM table.

code_evidence: The function closes the temporary index file and then calls change_to_newfile() to rename it over the original index file, passing MYF(0) so the rename helper copies stat data (chmod/chown) from the old file to the new file. The temporary file name is derived from the table name at [18,19,20,21,22], so it is predictable and can be replaced by another process between the close at [58] and the rename/stat copy at [59,60].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the rename-then-stat-copy sequence requires exclusive access to the temporary file path, but a timing window allows a concurrent interfering sequence to substitute the file, violating exclusivity. The privilege escalation is the consequence; the weakness itself is the unsynchronized shared-resource access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: change_to_newfile() performs a rename followed by a stat copy (chmod/chown) on the new file without holding exclusive access to that path. Trigger: a local user replaces the predictable temporary .TMD file before the stat copy runs. Consequence: chmod/chown is applied to an attacker-chosen file, granting it mysql-user privileges (privilege escalation).

Fix undefined behavior in `tf.raw_ops.Switch` in eager mode.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 332578058
Change-Id: I9727571d2f21476b10d8aa27c1b7176564b76ac9
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      outputs->push_back(Tensor(*context.mutable_output(i)));'], 'added_lines': ['      const auto* output_tensor = context.mutable_output(i);', '      if (output_tensor != nullptr) {', '        outputs->push_back(Tensor(*output_tensor));', '      } else {', '        outputs->push_back(Tensor());', '      }']}
description: In Tensorflow before versions 1.15.4, 2.0.3, 2.1.2, 2.2.1 and 2.3.1, the `tf.raw_ops.Switch` operation takes as input a tensor and a boolean and outputs two tensors. Depending on the boolean value, one of the tensors is exactly the input tensor whereas the other one should be an empty tensor. However, the eager runtime traverses all tensors in the output. Since only one of the tensors is defined, the other one is `nullptr`, hence we are binding a reference to `nullptr`. This is undefined behavior and reported as an error if compiling with `-fsanitize=null`. In this case, this results in a segmentation fault The issue is patched in commit da8558533d925694483d2c136a9220d6d49d843c, and is released in TensorFlow versions 1.15.4, 2.0.3, 2.1.2, 2.2.1, or 2.3.1.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function dereferences a possibly-null output tensor pointer (missing null check, a NULL-pointer dereference), which is not input validation; the target CWE-20 does not fit the demonstrated root cause.

commit_msg: Fixed another problem with incorrect cleanup of JP2 box data upon error.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbox->ops = &boxinfo->ops;', '\t\t\t// Mark the box data as never having been constructed', '\t\t\t// so that we will not errantly attempt to destroy it later.', '\t\t\tbox->ops = &jp2_boxinfo_unk.ops;'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t// Mark the box data as never having been constructed', '\t// so that we will not errantly attempt to destroy it later.', '', '', '\t\t// From here onwards, the box data will need to be destroyed.', '\t\t// So, initialize the box operations.', '\t\tbox->ops = &boxinfo->ops;']}
description: The jp2_colr_destroy function in jp2_cod.c in JasPer before 1.900.13 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) by leveraging incorrect cleanup of JP2 box data on error. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2016-8887.

code_evidence: The box is allocated and its ops is initially set to jp2_boxinfo_unk.ops, then boxinfo is looked up and box->ops is overwritten with &boxinfo->ops before the data-copy/parse path.
On a jas_stream_copy failure, box->ops is reset to jp2_boxinfo_unk.ops and control jumps to error, where jp2_box_destroy(box) is called; the parse path then dereferences box->ops->getdata.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's error handling can hand a partially initialized box to jp2_box_destroy, which dereferences box->ops; this matches CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). It is not merely a resource leak because the supported consequence is a crash from dereferencing an invalid/NULL pointer during cleanup.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The box's operations pointer is set to the looked-up boxinfo ops before the box data is successfully copied/parsed, so an error during data handling leaves the box in a partially constructed state. The error path then invokes jp2_box_destroy on that box, which can dereference an uninitialized or inappropriate ops pointer, causing a NULL pointer dereference and crash (DoS).

Fix DoS in PE/QNX/DYLDCACHE/PSX parsers ##crash

* Reported by lazymio
* Reproducer: AAA4AAAAAB4=
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (r_buf_fread_at (buf, QNX_HEADER_ADDR, (ut8 *) lmfh, "iiiiiiiicccciiiicc", 1) < QNX_HDR_SIZE) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (r_buf_fread_at (buf, QNX_HEADER_ADDR, (ut8 *) lmfh, "iiiiiiiicccciiiicc", 1) != QNX_HDR_SIZE) {']}
description: Denial of Service in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.6.4.

code_evidence: The size pre-check at [2] compares r_buf_size(buf) against sizeof(lmf_header), but the actual read at [5] starts at QNX_HEADER_ADDR. The return value of r_buf_fread_at is only tested with '<' against QNX_HDR_SIZE at [5]; a partial read that is smaller than the full header is rejected, but a read returning a value larger than QNX_HDR_SIZE (or the mismatch between the required offset read and the header size) is not caught before the parsed lmfh fields are consumed at [9]-[20].

This is an input-validation defect enabling DoS rather than a memory-safety write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the header read's success condition is checked with '<' instead of an exact size match, so a short/inconsistent read can pass validation. Trigger: a crafted QNX LMF file whose header read returns an unexpected byte count. The parsed lmfh fields are then used by the sdb_set calls, leading to malformed parsing and a crash/DoS.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failed __ethtool_get_link_ksettings error path leaves msec and div zero, producing a zero timeout. commit_msg:
Use Int64 in dataWindowForTile to prevent integer overflow

Signed-off-by: Peter Hillman <peterh@wetafx.co.nz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    V2i tileMax = tileMin + V2i (tileDesc.xSize - 1, tileDesc.ySize - 1);', '    tileMax = V2i (std::min (tileMax[0], levelMax[0]),', '\t\t   std::min (tileMax[1], levelMax[1]));'], 'added_lines': ['    Int64 tileMaxX = Int64(tileMin[0]) + tileDesc.xSize - 1;', '    Int64 tileMaxY = Int64(tileMin[1]) + tileDesc.ySize - 1;', '    V2i tileMax = V2i (std::min (tileMaxX, Int64(levelMax[0])),', '\t\t   std::min (tileMaxY, Int64(levelMax[1])));']}
description: A flaw found in function dataWindowForTile() of IlmImf/ImfTiledMisc.cpp. An attacker who is able to submit a crafted file to be processed by OpenEXR could trigger an integer overflow, leading to an out-of-bounds write on the heap. The greatest impact of this flaw is to application availability, with some potential impact to data integrity as well.

code_evidence: tileMin is computed as minX + dx * tileDesc.xSize (and similarly for Y) using int arithmetic on attacker-influenced tile coordinates and tile sizes; no bounds check precedes it.
tileMax is derived directly from tileMin plus (tileDesc.xSize - 1); the addition can wrap to a negative or small value before any clamping.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs signed integer arithmetic whose result is assumed to grow beyond the operands; wraparound produces a smaller value, matching CWE-190 (Integer Overflow or Wraparound). It is the root cause here, distinct from the resulting out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: tileMin and tileMax are computed in 32-bit int with attacker-controlled dx/dy and tile dimensions, so the multiplication and subsequent addition can overflow and yield a wrapped, small or negative tileMax. Trigger: a crafted file specifying large tile coordinates/sizes. Consequence: the returned Box2i has an incorrect (too small) extent, so downstream heap allocation/copy sizing is under-computed, leading to an out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg: Ignore exceptions when deserializing note plaintexts
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    CDataStream ss(SER_NETWORK, PROTOCOL_VERSION);', '    ss << pt.get();', '', '    ss >> ret;', '    assert(ss.size() == 0);', ''], 'added_lines': ['    try {', '        CDataStream ss(SER_NETWORK, PROTOCOL_VERSION);', '        ss << pt.get();', '        ss >> ret;', '        assert(ss.size() == 0);', '    } catch (const boost::thread_interrupted&) {', '        throw;', '    } catch (...) {', '        return boost::none;', '    }']}

commit_msg:
nfc: replace improper check device_is_registered() in netlink related functions

The device_is_registered() in nfc core is used to check whether
nfc device is registered in netlink related functions such as
nfc_fw_download(), nfc_dev_up() and so on. Although device_is_registered()
is protected by device_lock, there is still a race condition between
device_del() and device_is_registered(). The root cause is that
kobject_del() in device_del() is not protected by device_lock.

   (cleanup task)         |     (netlink task)
                          |
nfc_unregister_device     | nfc_fw_download
 device_del               |  device_lock
  ...                     |   if (!device_is_registered)//(1)
  kobject_del//(2)        |   ...
 ...                      |  device_unlock

The device_is_registered() returns the value of state_in_sysfs and
the state_in_sysfs is set to zero in kobject_del(). If we pass check in
position (1), then set zero in position (2). As a result, the check
in position (1) is useless.

This patch uses bool variable instead of device_is_registered() to judge
whether the nfc device is registered, which is well synchronized.

Fixes: 3e256b8f8dfa ("NFC: add nfc subsystem core")
Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!device_is_registered(&dev->dev)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (dev->shutting_down) {']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel's NFC core functionality due to a race condition between kobject creation and delete. This vulnerability allows a local attacker with CAP_NET_ADMIN privilege to leak kernel information.

code_evidence: device_lock is taken, then device_is_registered(&dev->dev) is checked as a gate before proceeding to operate on dev (dev_up state and dev->ops->dev_down). The registration state is not a stable invariant under device_lock because device_del()'s kobject_del() clears state_in_sysfs without holding device_lock, so the check can pass and the resource be torn down before the subsequent use.

commit_msg:
repodata_schema2id: fix heap-buffer-overflow in memcmp

When the length of last schema in data->schemadata is
less than length of input schema, we got a read overflow
in asan test.

Signed-off-by: Zhipeng Xie <xiezhipeng1@huawei.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if (!memcmp(data->schemadata + data->schemata[cid], schema, len * sizeof(Id)))', '        if (!memcmp(data->schemadata + data->schemata[cid], schema, len * sizeof(Id)))'], 'added_lines': ['      if ((data->schemata[cid] + len <= data->schemadatalen) &&', '\t\t\t  !memcmp(data->schemadata + data->schemata[cid], schema, len * sizeof(Id)))', '        if ((data->schemata[cid] + len <= data->schemadatalen) &&', '\t\t\t\t!memcmp(data->schemadata + data->schemata[cid], schema, len * sizeof(Id)))']}
description: repodata_schema2id in repodata.c in libsolv before 0.7.6 has a heap-based buffer over-read via a last schema whose length is less than the length of the input schema.

code_evidence: memcmp reads len*sizeof(Id) bytes starting at data->schemadata + data->schemata[cid] without verifying that the stored schema extends that far; when the stored last schema is shorter than the input len, the read runs past the allocated schemadata region.
The slow-search loop repeats the same unchecked memcmp for every cid, so the out-of-bounds read can also occur on non-hash-matching entries.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a read beyond the intended schemadata buffer, matching CWE-125. It is not CWE-787 (write) since no out-of-bounds write occurs; the missing length check directly enables the over-read.

evidence_lines.code: if (!memcmp(data->schemadata + data->schemata[cid], schema, len * sizeof(Id)))

for (cid = 1; cid < data->nschemata; cid++)
if (!memcmp(data->schemadata + data->schemata[cid], schema, len * sizeof(Id)))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code trusts the input-derived len and compares against stored schemas without bounding schemata[cid]+len by schemadatalen. Trigger: a stored last schema shorter than the caller-supplied schema. Consequence: memcmp reads past the heap buffer, giving an out-of-bounds read (crash or ASan-detected overflow).

commit_msg:
Prevent leak of SecurityServer and ClientServer.

They are created in SConnection's and CConnection's constructors but never destroyed.

There is no reason for the indirection, so lets make them direct members.

description: In TigerVNC 1.7.1 (CConnection.cxx CConnection::CConnection), an unauthenticated client can cause a small memory leak in the server.

code_evidence: Line 4 initializes the security pointer to 0 in the member-initializer list, and line 12 allocates a new SecurityServer with `security = new SecurityServer();` inside the constructor. No corresponding delete appears in this constructor or elsewhere in the function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 covers failing to release a resource after its lifetime ends. Allocating SecurityServer with new and leaving it un-freed matches missing release of a heap resource; this is not a dangling-pointer or double-free issue, which would be distinct memory-safety weaknesses.

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  const uint64_t size_to_subtract = entry->entry_->key().size() + entry->entry_->value().size();', '  subtractSize(size_to_subtract);']}
description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

code_evidence: removeInline obtains the HeaderEntryImpl pointer, nulls the caller's pointer, and erases the underlying header entry from headers_. The added lines compute the removed entry's key+value size and call subtractSize before erasure, keeping the cached total byte size accurate as entries are removed. Without this bookkeeping the cached size would drift from the actual header bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fix maintains accurate accounting of a limited resource (the header byte budget), which is the resource-tracking control underlying CWE-400. However, the O(n^2) CPU exhaustion described in the commit arises from repeated full iteration in the add path, not from removeInline; this function only supports the accounting side, so it does not directly demonstrate the uncontrolled CPU consumption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cached byteSize must be incremented on add and decremented on remove; if removeInline fails to subtract the removed entry's key and value sizes, the cached total overstates actual header bytes. Trigger: a request that adds and removes many small headers while staying under the max-header-size check. Consequence: the inflated cached size causes premature limit rejection or incorrect accounting, degrading availability rather than bounding attacker-driven CPU consumption.

description: mpeg2ts/ATSParser.cpp in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 6.x before 2016-07-01 does not validate a certain section length, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, aka internal bug 28333006.

commit_msg:
arm64: dma-mapping: always clear allocated buffers

Buffers allocated by dma_alloc_coherent() are always zeroed on Alpha,
ARM (32bit), MIPS, PowerPC, x86/x86_64 and probably other architectures.
It turned out that some drivers rely on this 'feature'. Allocated buffer
might be also exposed to userspace with dma_mmap() call, so clearing it
is desired from security point of view to avoid exposing random memory
to userspace. This patch unifies dma_alloc_coherent() behavior on ARM64
architecture with other implementations by unconditionally zeroing
allocated buffer.

Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v3.14+
Signed-off-by: Marek Szyprowski <m.szyprowski@samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Will Deacon <will.deacon@arm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (flags & __GFP_ZERO)', '\t\t\tmemset(addr, 0, size);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tmemset(addr, 0, size);']}
description: arch/arm64/mm/dma-mapping.c in the Linux kernel before 4.0.3, as used in the ION subsystem in Android and other products, does not initialize certain data structures, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory by triggering a dma_mmap call.

code_evidence: In the CMA allocation path, a page is obtained via dma_alloc_from_contiguous and its kernel address computed as addr = page_address(page) [21]. The buffer is only zeroed when the caller passes __GFP_ZERO [22,23], so without that flag the freshly allocated pages retain their prior contents and are returned to the caller [24].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function returns a buffer whose contents are not scrubbed, and the commit notes such buffers can be exposed to userspace through dma_mmap, so the missing unconditional memset directly enables disclosure of kernel memory to an unauthorized local actor. This is the information-exposure mistake itself, matching CWE-200 rather than a mere downstream confidentiality impact.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the CMA coherent-allocation path conditionally clears pages based solely on the caller-supplied __GFP_ZERO flag, leaving stale kernel memory in the buffer otherwise. Trigger: a driver or ION-style consumer allocates a coherent buffer without __GFP_ZERO and later exposes it to userspace via dma_mmap. Consequence: uninitialized kernel heap contents are disclosed to the mapping user, leaking potentially sensitive kernel data.

commit_msg:
Add several missing validations in SDCA

PiperOrigin-RevId: 372172877
Change-Id: Id366da962432e18dcbfac847d11e98488bebb70a
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      if (example_indices.size() != feature_indices.size()) {', '        mutex_lock l(mu);', '        result = errors::InvalidArgument(', '            "Found mismatched example_indices and feature_indices [",', '            example_indices, "] vs [", feature_indices, "]");', '        return;', '      }']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The implementation of `tf.raw_ops.SdcaOptimizer` triggers undefined behavior due to dereferencing a null pointer. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/60a45c8b6192a4699f2e2709a2645a751d435cc3/tensorflow/core/kernels/sdca_internal.cc) does not validate that the user supplied arguments satisfy all constraints expected by the op(https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/raw_ops/SdcaOptimizer). The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function obtains example_indices and feature_indices as flat tensors from the sparse_example_indices_inputs and sparse_feature_indices_inputs lists; it never checks that these two per-feature tensors have equal length before indexing them together.

The loop advances end_id only while it is within example_indices.size(), then indexes feature_indices(start_id) at line 28 using that same start_id. If feature_indices is shorter than example_indices, the bound check on example_indices does not protect the feature_indices access.

The commit adds exactly this size check, confirming the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation that example_indices and feature_indices have matching sizes. Trigger: user-supplied SdcaOptimizer inputs where feature_indices is shorter than example_indices (or empty). The loop's size check is based only on example_indices, so a start_id valid for example_indices can exceed feature_indices' extent, causing an out-of-bounds/null data access and undefined behavior (crash).

data, not the remaining length of the record (which may include

description: The ngsniffer_process_record function in wiretap/ngsniffer.c in the Sniffer file parser in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.9 and 2.0.x before 2.0.1 does not validate the relationships between record lengths and record header lengths, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: The record length read from the file is truncated into a guint16 (line 8) and used directly; for REC_FRAME2 the code reads sizeof frame2 bytes (line 32) and then subtracts sizeof frame2 from length (line 41) without first checking that length >= sizeof frame2, so a short record causes underflow or an over-read.

For REC_FRAME4 the code reads sizeof frame4 bytes (line 50) and then conditionally subtracts sizeof frame4 or sizeof frame2 (lines 59-66) without validating that length is at least that large, allowing the subtraction to underflow the length.
REC_FRAME6 similarly reads sizeof frame6 bytes (line 70) and subtracts sizeof frame6 (line 79) with no prior length check.

The resulting length is passed to fix_pseudo_header (line 108) as the buffer length, so an incorrect length can drive an out-of-bounds read.

phdr->pkt_encap = fix_pseudo_header(wth->file_encap,
buf, length, &phdr->pseudo_header);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled record length from the capture file is used to read and subtract fixed header sizes without validating that length is at least the header size, and the later size > length check uses the already-decremented value. commit_msg:
(for 4.9.3) CVE-2018-16228/HNCP: make buffer access safer

print_prefix() has a buffer and does not initialize it. It may call
decode_prefix6(), which also does not initialize the buffer on invalid
input. When that happens, make sure to return from print_prefix() before
trying to print the [still uninitialized] buffer.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Wang Junjie of 360 ESG
Codesafe Team.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).

code_evidence: Line 5 declares char buf[] uninitialized. Line 26 calls decode_prefix6() to fill buf; on invalid input it returns a negative value without initializing buf. Lines 27-28 then pass buf to ND_PRINT regardless, reading uninitialized/out-of-bounds contents.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because ND_PRINT reads past the initialized region of buf when decode_prefix6() fails. This is an out-of-bounds/uninitialized read, not a write (CWE-787) or integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of decode_prefix6() is not checked, so a negative error return leaves buf uninitialized while ND_PRINT still consumes it. commit_msg:

Prevent reading past end of message in MSG_ReadBits. If read past
end of msg->data buffer (16348 bytes) the engine could SEGFAULT.
Make MSG_WriteBits use an exact buffer overflow check instead of
possibly failing with a few bytes left.

Check that ecall [user_check] pointers and ocall_malloc result pointer are outside enclave (#67)

This should reduce the enclave's attack surface by preventing an attacker from invoking ecalls on or triggering unexpected writes to arbitrary enclave memory, which could potentially leak information about that memory or lead to incorrect results.

Fixes #36. Fixes #66.

description: An issue was discovered in UC Berkeley RISE Opaque before 2018-12-01. There is no boundary check on ocall_malloc. The return value could be a pointer to enclave memory. It could cause an arbitrary enclave memory write.

code_evidence: The ecall forwards caller-supplied pointers input_rows, join_row, output_rows and output_rows_length directly to non_oblivious_sort_merge_join without validating that they lie outside the enclave or that the output pointer refers to writable non-enclave memory.

The missing boundary check on ocall_malloc's result is the root cause of the write; this is not merely an information disclosure issue.

Trigger: a malicious host invokes the ecall with a pointer into enclave memory, so the merge-join writes its output there. Consequence: arbitrary enclave memory corruption/out-of-bounds write, potentially leaking enclave data or corrupting results.

commit_msg:
The X protocol uses CARD16 values to represent the length so
this would overflow.

CVE-2021-31535

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (strlen(name) >= USHRT_MAX)', '        return NULL;']}
description: LookupCol.c in X.Org X through X11R7.7 and libX11 before 1.7.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The libX11 XLookupColor request (intended for server-side color lookup) contains a flaw allowing a client to send color-name requests with a name longer than the maximum size allowed by the protocol (and also longer than the maximum packet size for normal-sized packets). The user-controlled data exceeding the maximum size is then interpreted by the server as additional X protocol requests and executed, e.g., to disable X server authorization completely. For example, if the victim encounters malicious terminal control sequences for color codes, then the attacker may be able to take full control of the running graphical session.

code_evidence: Line 18 truncates strlen(name) into a CARD16 nbytes without bounding the actual string length; lines 20-21 then size the request and copy nbytes bytes from name based on that truncated value, so a name longer than USHRT_MAX produces an inconsistent length and over-copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies an input string (name) into the request buffer without verifying the input size against the output size, matching CWE-120's buffer copy without size check. The 16-bit truncation is the mechanism enabling the over-copy; the missing length constraint is the core weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the user-controlled font name length is cast to a 16-bit protocol field (CARD16) with no check that it fits, so an overlong name yields a truncated nbytes while the copy/request sizing uses the same value, allowing the excess name data to be interpreted as additional X protocol requests. Trigger: a client passes a color/font name exceeding the protocol maximum; consequence: attacker data is executed as extra requests by the server.

commit_msg:
crypto: replace rwlocks with simple mutexes

It was pointed out by Zhou Ran that the Windows XP implementation of
uv_rwlock_rdlock() and friends may unlock the inner write mutex on a
different thread than the one that locked it, resulting in undefined
behavior.

The only place that uses rwlocks is the crypto module.  Make that use
normal (simple) mutexes instead.

OpenSSL's critical sections are generally very short, with exclusive
access outnumbering shared access by a factor of three or more, so
it's not as if using rwlocks gives a decisive performance advantage.

PR-URL: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/2723
Reviewed-By: Fedor Indutny <fedor@indutny.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  CHECK((mode & CRYPTO_LOCK) || (mode & CRYPTO_UNLOCK));', '  CHECK((mode & CRYPTO_READ) || (mode & CRYPTO_WRITE));', '  if (mode & CRYPTO_LOCK) {', '    if (mode & CRYPTO_READ)', '      uv_rwlock_rdlock(locks + n);', '    else', '      uv_rwlock_wrlock(locks + n);', '  } else {', '    if (mode & CRYPTO_READ)', '      uv_rwlock_rdunlock(locks + n);', '    else', '      uv_rwlock_wrunlock(locks + n);', '  }'], 'added_lines': ['  CHECK(!(mode & CRYPTO_LOCK) ^ !(mode & CRYPTO_UNLOCK));', '  CHECK(!(mode & CRYPTO_READ) ^ !(mode & CRYPTO_WRITE));', '  if (mode & CRYPTO_LOCK)', '    uv_mutex_lock(locks + n);', '  else', '    uv_mutex_unlock(locks + n);']}
description: The uv_rwlock_t fallback implementation for Windows XP and Server 2003 in libuv before 1.7.4 does not properly prevent threads from releasing the locks of other threads, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (deadlock) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging a race condition.

code_evidence: crypto_lock_cb maps OpenSSL lock callbacks onto per-index locks. In the LOCK branch it acquires a read (line 6) or write (line 8) rwlock; in the else branch it releases a read (line 11) or write (line 13) rwlock. Unlock does not verify the calling thread owns the lock, so the release path can target another thread's lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function implements shared-resource synchronization whose exclusivity/atomicity can be violated when an interfering thread releases another thread's lock, matching CWE-362. It is not merely an incorrect lock flag check; the race is in the ownership of the lock operations.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the callback delegates to uv_rwlock_rdlock/wrlock and rdunlock/wrunlock without binding lock ownership to the acquiring thread. Trigger: on the libuv Windows XP/2003 fallback, a thread releases a lock held by a different thread, which can unlock the inner write mutex from the wrong thread. Supported consequence: undefined behavior leading to deadlock or instability (DoS).

SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS can be enabled and disabled
while packets are collected on the error queue.
So, checking SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS in sk->sk_tsflags
is not enough to safely assume that the skb contains
OPT_STATS data.

Add a bit in sock_exterr_skb to indicate whether the
skb contains opt_stats data.

Reported-by: JongHwan Kim <zzoru007@gmail.com>

commit_msg:
x86/HVM: guard against emulator driving ioreq state in weird ways

In the case where hvm_wait_for_io() calls wait_on_xen_event_channel(),
p->state ends up being read twice in succession: once to determine that
state != p->state, and then again at the top of the loop.  This gives a
compromised emulator a chance to change the state back between the two
reads, potentially keeping Xen in a loop indefinitely.

Instead:
* Read p->state once in each of the wait_on_xen_event_channel() tests,
* re-use that value the next time around,
* and insist that the states continue to transition "forward" (with the
  exception of the transition to STATE_IOREQ_NONE).

This is XSA-262.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        switch ( state )', '        case STATE_IOREQ_NONE:', '            wait_on_xen_event_channel(sv->ioreq_evtchn, p->state != state);', '            break;'], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned int prev_state = STATE_IOREQ_NONE;', '', '', '    recheck:', '        if ( unlikely(state == STATE_IOREQ_NONE) )', '        }', '', '        if ( unlikely(state < prev_state) )', '        {', '            gdprintk(XENLOG_ERR, "Weird HVM ioreq state transition %u -> %u\\n",', '                     prev_state, state);', '            sv->pending = false;', '            domain_crash(sv->vcpu->domain);', '            return false; /* bail */', '        }', '', '        switch ( prev_state = state )', '        {', '            wait_on_xen_event_channel(sv->ioreq_evtchn,', '                                      ({ state = p->state;', '                                         smp_rmb();', '                                         state != prev_state; }));', '            goto recheck;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.10.x allowing x86 HVM guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host OS infinite loop) in situations where a QEMU device model attempts to make invalid transitions between states of a request.

code_evidence: The outer while loop at lines 3-7 continues while sv->pending; there is no iteration counter or timeout.

For STATE_IOREQ_READY/INPROCESS, line 18 waits on the event channel with condition p->state != state, then breaks to re-read p->state at line 5; if the emulator restores the same state between reads, the loop repeats with sv->pending unchanged.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the while loop's exit condition (sv->pending becoming false) cannot be reached when the emulator keeps p->state at READY/INPROCESS across iterations, producing an unbounded loop. This is a loop-termination flaw, not merely a race condition, since the missing forward-state check permits the non-terminating iteration.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop trusts a shared p->state value read at line 5 and re-reads it inside wait_on_xen_event_channel at line 18; there is no forward-transition constraint, so a compromised emulator can toggle the state back between the two reads. Trigger: emulator sets p->state to READY/INPROCESS, then restores it during the wait. Consequence: sv->pending is never cleared, so hvm_wait_for_io spins indefinitely, causing host CPU DoS.
