commit_msg:
Bug 699927: don't include operator arrays in execstack output

When we transfer the contents of the execution stack into the array, take the
extra step of replacing any operator arrays on the stack with the operator
that reference them.

This prevents the contents of Postscript defined, internal only operators (those
created with .makeoperator) being exposed via execstack (and thus, via error
handling).

This necessitates a change in the resource remapping 'resource', which contains
a procedure which relies on the contents of the operators arrays being present.
As we already had internal-only variants of countexecstack and execstack
(.countexecstack and .execstack) - using those, and leaving thier operation
including the operator arrays means the procedure continues to work correctly.

Both .countexecstack and .execstack are undefined after initialization.

Also, when we store the execstack (or part thereof) for an execstackoverflow
error, make the same oparray/operator substitution as above for execstack.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['do_execstack(i_ctx_t *i_ctx_p, bool include_marks, os_ptr op1)'], 'added_lines': ['do_execstack(i_ctx_t *i_ctx_p, bool include_marks, bool include_oparrays, os_ptr op1)', '            case t_array:', '            case t_shortarray:', '            case t_mixedarray:', '                if (!include_oparrays && errorexec_find(i_ctx_p, rq) < 0)', '                    make_null(rq);', '                break;']}
description: Artifex Ghostscript allows attackers to bypass a sandbox protection mechanism by leveraging exposure of system operators in the saved execution stack in an error object.

code_evidence: The loop copies every e_stack entry into the caller-supplied ref array via ref_assign_old, with no check on what type of object is being copied out.
Only t_operator entries are sanitized: internal operators (op_def_is_internal) have a_executable cleared, but the operator's array contents are never examined.
The default branch is a no-op, so array/oparray entries pass through unchanged and are exposed to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is failure to scrub sensitive internal-only operator definitions from a resource (the saved execstack) that is intentionally made accessible to unauthorized PostScript actors, matching CWE-200's explicit exposure of sensitive information. It is not merely an indirect confidentiality loss; the code directly emits the sensitive objects.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function transfers execution-stack contents, including operator arrays holding internal-only operator definitions, into an array returned to PostScript callers (e.g. via execstack and error objects). Because only t_operator is checked and array types fall through the empty default case, the internal operator data is disclosed rather than replaced by its referencing operator.

commit_msg:
nfsd: encoders mustn't use unitialized values in error cases

In error cases, lgp->lg_layout_type may be out of bounds; so we
shouldn't be using it until after the check of nfserr.

This was seen to crash nfsd threads when the server receives a LAYOUTGET
request with a large layout type.

GETDEVICEINFO has the same problem.

Reported-by: Ari Kauppi <Ari.Kauppi@synopsys.com>
Reviewed-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: J. Bruce Fields <bfields@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tconst struct nfsd4_layout_ops *ops =', '\t\tnfsd4_layout_ops[lgp->lg_layout_type];'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst struct nfsd4_layout_ops *ops;', '\tops = nfsd4_layout_ops[lgp->lg_layout_type];']}
description: The NFSv4 server in the Linux kernel before 4.11.3 does not properly validate the layout type when processing the NFSv4 pNFS GETDEVICEINFO or LAYOUTGET operand in a UDP packet from a remote attacker. This type value is uninitialized upon encountering certain error conditions. This value is used as an array index for dereferencing, which leads to an OOPS and eventually a DoS of knfsd and a soft-lockup of the whole system.

code_evidence: Line 6-7 unconditionally indexes nfsd4_layout_ops[lgp->lg_layout_type] while initializing ops, before any error check or validation of lg_layout_type.
Line 10-11 then return on nfserr, but the out-of-bounds array access at line 7 has already occurred.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-129 fits because an untrusted value is used as an array index without validating it references a valid position. The missing constraint is the bounds/validation of lg_layout_type; the unchecked index is the cause, while the crash is only the consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
const struct nfsd4_layout_ops *ops =
nfsd4_layout_ops[lgp->lg_layout_type];

if (nfserr)
goto out;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: lgp->lg_layout_type, a client-controlled layout type from the GETDEVICEINFO/LAYOUTGET operand, is used as an array index without bounds validation, and this dereference happens before the error path. Trigger: a request with a large layout type reaches this encoder; the index reads outside nfsd4_layout_ops. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds pointer dereference causing an OOPS and knfsd DoS/soft-lockup.

commit_msg: Fix strncat/cpy bounding issues (fix #1425)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    strncpy(str, "ID:", len);', '    strncat(str, jslGetTokenValueAsString(), len);', '    strncpy(str, "String:\'", len);', '    strncat(str, jslGetTokenValueAsString(), len);', '    strncat(str, "\'", len);'], 'added_lines': ['    espruino_snprintf(str, len, "ID:%s", jslGetTokenValueAsString());', '    espruino_snprintf(str, len, "String:\'%s\'", jslGetTokenValueAsString());']}
description: Espruino before 1.99 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) and a potential Escalation of Privileges with a user crafted input file via a Buffer Overflow during syntax parsing, because strncat is misused.

code_evidence: strncpy(str, "ID:", len) writes the prefix but does not guarantee NUL-termination when len is small; strncat then appends jslGetTokenValueAsString() using len as the append limit rather than the remaining space, so it can write up to len bytes past the current terminator.

The LEX_STR branch repeats the same pattern: strncpy of "String:'", then two strncat calls each bounded by len instead of remaining capacity, compounding the overflow with the token value and trailing quote.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs buffer writes that can land outside str's intended bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds write within a memory buffer. The misuse of strncat is the mechanism; the supported consequence is memory corruption beyond the buffer.

evidence_lines.code:
strncpy(str, "ID:", len);
strncat(str, jslGetTokenValueAsString(), len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: strncat's third argument is treated as total buffer size rather than remaining free space, and the preceding strncpy may leave no terminator. Trigger: parsing a crafted identifier or string token whose value length approaches or exceeds len. Consequence: writes past str's intended boundary, corrupting adjacent memory and causing crash or potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fix bug in OPENSSL_LH_flush

Fixes #18139.

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/18141)

(cherry picked from commit e5da68183410c06f7b350a0721bc2bd6057e438e)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    lh->num_items = 0;']}
description: The OPENSSL_LH_flush() function, which empties a hash table, contains a bug that breaks reuse of the memory occuppied by the removed hash table entries. This function is used when decoding certificates or keys. If a long lived process periodically decodes certificates or keys its memory usage will expand without bounds and the process might be terminated by the operating system causing a denial of service. Also traversing the empty hash table entries will take increasingly more time. Typically such long lived processes might be TLS clients or TLS servers configured to accept client certificate authentication. The function was added in the OpenSSL 3.0 version thus older releases are not affected by the issue. Fixed in OpenSSL 3.0.3 (Affected 3.0.0,3.0.1,3.0.2).

code_evidence: The loop frees every node in each bucket and sets lh->b[i] = NULL, but after the loop the function returns without resetting the table's item counter or other bookkeeping state. The function therefore clears the buckets while leaving the hash table's accounting inconsistent with its now-empty contents.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-459 covers incomplete cleanup of temporary or supporting resources after use. Here the flush routine removes the nodes but fails to fully clean up the table's associated state (num_items), which is the incomplete-cleanup weakness that enables the described resource-consumption DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: OPENSSL_LH_flush frees all nodes and nulls the buckets but does not reset lh->num_items. Trigger: a long-lived process repeatedly decodes certificates or keys, calling flush between uses. Because the counter is not reset, the table's state no longer reflects the freed entries, so memory/bookkeeping is not properly cleaned up and reuse degrades, supporting unbounded resource consumption and denial of service.

commit_msg:
ipv6: do not free rt if FIB_LOOKUP_NOREF is set on suppress rule

Commit 7d9e5f422150 removed references from certain dsts, but accounting
for this never translated down into the fib6 suppression code. This bug
was triggered by WireGuard users who use wg-quick(8), which uses the
"suppress-prefix" directive to ip-rule(8) for routing all of their
internet traffic without routing loops. The test case added here
causes the reference underflow by causing packets to evaluate a suppress
rule.

Fixes: 7d9e5f422150 ("ipv6: convert major tx path to use RT6_LOOKUP_F_DST_NOREF")
Signed-off-by: Jason A. Donenfeld <Jason@zx2c4.com>
Acked-by: Wei Wang <weiwan@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tip6_rt_put(rt);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!(arg->flags & FIB_LOOKUP_NOREF))', '\t\tip6_rt_put(rt);']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.3.4, a reference count usage error in the fib6_rule_suppress() function in the fib6 suppression feature of net/ipv6/fib6_rules.c, when handling the FIB_LOOKUP_NOREF flag, can be exploited by a local attacker to corrupt memory, aka CID-ca7a03c41753.

code_evidence: Line 6-7 returns early when rt is NULL, so the suppress path only runs with a non-NULL rt reference.

Lines 15-17 unconditionally call ip6_rt_put(rt) on the suppress_route label without checking whether the lookup was performed under FIB_LOOKUP_NOREF, in which case the caller owns no reference to release.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the code releases a resource (the rt reference) it does not own, i.e., the effective lifetime/ownership is mishandled, producing an improper refcount decrement. This is an ownership/refcount error rather than a simple missing-release leak.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!rt)
return false;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a lookup carries FIB_LOOKUP_NOREF, no reference is taken on rt; the suppress path still calls ip6_rt_put(rt), decrementing an unowned reference and causing a reference-count underflow. Triggered by packets evaluating a suppress rule with the NOREF flag, this corrupts the rt refcount and can lead to use-after-free/memory corruption.

Fix issue of listen before chmod on Unix sockets (CVE-2023-45145) (#12671)

Before this commit, Unix socket setup performed chmod(2) on the socket
file after calling listen(2). Depending on what umask is used, this
could leave the file with the wrong permissions for a short period of
time. As a result, another process could exploit this race condition and
establish a connection that would otherwise not be possible.

We now make sure the socket permissions are set up prior to calling
listen(2).

(cherry picked from commit 1119ecae6fd8796fa337df2212f09173ab6c7b0a)

Co-authored-by: Yossi Gottlieb <yossigo@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (anetListen(err,s,p->ai_addr,p->ai_addrlen,backlog) == ANET_ERR) s = ANET_ERR;'], 'added_lines': ['        if (anetListen(err,s,p->ai_addr,p->ai_addrlen,backlog,0) == ANET_ERR) s = ANET_ERR;']}
description: Redis is an in-memory database that persists on disk. On startup, Redis begins listening on a Unix socket before adjusting its permissions to the user-provided configuration. If a permissive umask(2) is used, this creates a race condition that enables, during a short period of time, another process to establish an otherwise unauthorized connection. This problem has existed since Redis 2.6.0-RC1. This issue has been addressed in Redis versions 7.2.2, 7.0.14 and 6.2.14. Users are advised to upgrade. For users unable to upgrade, it is possible to work around the problem by disabling Unix sockets, starting Redis with a restrictive umask, or storing the Unix socket file in a protected directory.

code_evidence: The loop creates a listening socket (socket, then anetListen at line 24) and immediately proceeds to end without any chmod or permission-setting step on the socket path. The function exposes the socket to connection before any access restriction is applied; the patch adds a trailing 0 argument to anetListen, deferring permission setup to callers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-668 fits because the socket resource is exposed to a control sphere (other local users) beyond the intended one during the pre-chmod window. It is a resource-exposure/access-boundary issue rather than a memory-safety flaw; the incomplete ordering of listen and permission setup is the specific mistake.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The listening socket is activated via anetListen before file permissions are restricted, so under a permissive umask another process can connect during the window before chmod. Root cause is ordering of listen before permission setup; trigger is permissive umask; consequence is unauthorized connection to the resource.

description: UnRAR 5.6.1.2 and 5.6.1.3 has a heap-based buffer overflow in Unpack::CopyString (called from Unpack::Unpack5 and CmdExtract::ExtractCurrentFile).

commit_msg:
ocfs2: subsystem.su_mutex is required while accessing the item->ci_parent

The subsystem.su_mutex is required while accessing the item->ci_parent,
otherwise, NULL pointer dereference to the item->ci_parent will be
triggered in the following situation:

add node                     delete node
sys_write
 vfs_write
  configfs_write_file

    o2nm_node_local_write
                             do_rmdir
                              vfs_rmdir

                                mutex_lock(&subsys->su_mutex);
                                unlink_obj

	 to_o2nm_cluster_from_node
	  node->nd_item.ci_parent->ci_parent

Lines 17-19 dereference cluster->cl_has_local and cluster->cl_local_node; if the node's ci_parent was concurrently cleared by a configfs rmdir/unlink, the derived cluster is NULL and this dereference faults.

description: A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the handling of wildcard backend hosts of SNIProxy 0.6.0-2 and the master branch (commit: 822bb80df9b7b345cc9eba55df74a07b498819ba). A specially crafted HTTP or TLS packet can lead to arbitrary code execution. An attacker could send a malicious packet to trigger this vulnerability.

code_evidence: When the input begins with '[' and contains ']', len is computed from the attacker-controlled bracket position and used directly in strncpy into the fixed-size stack buffer ip_buf without any bounds check against sizeof(ip_buf).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code performs a buffer copy (strncpy) of attacker-controlled length without checking the input size against the output buffer, matching CWE-120 Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read or a size-calculation bug; the missing size constraint directly enables the overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bracketed IPv6 literal path copies (port - hostname_or_ip - 1) bytes into ip_buf[ADDRESS_BUFFER_SIZE] with no check that len is smaller than the destination. Trigger: a crafted HTTP/TLS hostname such as '[AAAA...]' with a ']' far beyond the buffer size. Consequence: stack buffer overflow, potentially leading to memory corruption and code execution.

commit_msg:
fru: Fix buffer overflow vulnerabilities

Partial fix for CVE-2020-5208, see
https://github.com/ipmitool/ipmitool/security/advisories/GHSA-g659-9qxw-p7cp

The `read_fru_area_section` function only performs size validation of
requested read size, and falsely assumes that the IPMI message will not
respond with more than the requested amount of data; it uses the
unvalidated response size to copy into `frubuf`. If the response is
larger than the request, this can result in overflowing the buffer.

The same issue affects the `read_fru_area` function.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tuint32_t off = offset, tmp, finish;'], 'added_lines': ['\tuint32_t off = offset;', '\tuint32_t tmp, finish;', '\tuint32_t size_left_in_buffer;', '\t\tmemset(frubuf + fru->size, 0, length - fru->size);', '\t\tlength = finish - offset;', '', '\tsize_left_in_buffer = length;', '\t\tif(rsp->data_len < 1', '\t\t   || tmp > rsp->data_len - 1', '\t\t   || tmp > size_left_in_buffer)', '\t\t{', '\t\t\tprintf(" Not enough buffer size");', '\t\t\treturn -1;', '\t\t}', '\t\tsize_left_in_buffer -= tmp;']}
description: It's been found that multiple functions in ipmitool before 1.8.19 neglect proper checking of the data received from a remote LAN party, which may lead to buffer overflows and potentially to remote code execution on the ipmitool side. This is especially dangerous if ipmitool is run as a privileged user. This problem is fixed in version 1.8.19.

code_evidence: finish is computed as offset+length and clamped to fru->size, but the original length variable is not updated, so the destination frubuf capacity is not tracked against the response size.

tmp is derived from the unvalidated remote response byte rsp->data[0]; memcpy copies tmp bytes from rsp->data+1 into frubuf at (frubuf+off)-offset with no check that tmp fits the remaining buffer or matches the requested msg_data[3].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a buffer copy (memcpy) of remote-controlled length into frubuf without verifying the input size against the destination capacity, which is exactly CWE-120. It is not an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) since the primary issue is the unchecked write, and the missing validation is on the copy size, not an integer calculation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop trusts the size field returned by the remote IPMI LAN party rather than the size requested. A malicious or malformed response can report a tmp larger than the requested length, causing memcpy to write past the frubuf buffer. Root cause is the missing size check on the response; the supported consequence is a heap/stack buffer overflow and potential memory corruption or code execution.

Fix VD-1301 and VD-1302 vulnerabilities

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (nb < 1 || MODBUS_MAX_WRITE_BITS < nb) {', '        int mapping_address = address - mb_mapping->start_registers;', '', '        if (nb < 1 || MODBUS_MAX_WRITE_REGISTERS < nb) {'], 'added_lines': ['        int nb_bits = req[offset + 5];', '        if (nb < 1 || MODBUS_MAX_WRITE_BITS < nb || nb_bits * 8 < nb) {', '        int nb_bytes = req[offset + 5];', '        int mapping_address = address - mb_mapping->start_registers;', '', '        if (nb < 1 || MODBUS_MAX_WRITE_REGISTERS < nb || nb_bytes * 8 < nb) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in libmodbus before 3.0.7 and 3.1.x before 3.1.5. There is an out-of-bounds read for the MODBUS_FC_WRITE_MULTIPLE_COILS case, aka VD-1302.

code_evidence: In MODBUS_FC_WRITE_MULTIPLE_COILS, nb is taken from req[offset+3..4] and checked only against nb<1 and MODBUS_MAX_WRITE_BITS<nb. The byte-count field req[offset+5] is never compared to nb. The else branch then calls modbus_set_bits_from_bytes(mb_mapping->tab_bits, mapping_address, nb, &req[offset+6]), which reads ceil(nb/8) bytes from req starting at offset+6 without verifying that the request actually contains that many bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads beyond the intended request buffer due to an unchecked length relationship. This is a read overrun, not a write overflow, so CWE-125 rather than CWE-787 is appropriate.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing constraint that the declared byte count (req[offset+5]) must be at least ceil(nb/8). A crafted request with a small byte count but a large nb passes the value check and causes modbus_set_bits_from_bytes to read past the end of the req buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read (possible crash or info leak).

commit_msg:
Fix empty batch issue in svd.

If there are zero batches, the GPU kernel previously failed with a `work_element_count > 0`
check failure.  In the zero batch case, there is no output, so simply return.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 462210670
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    // If there are zero batches, we are done.', '    if (shapeRaw.num_elements() == 0) {', '      done();', '      return;', '    }', '']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. When `tf.linalg.matrix_rank` receives an empty input `a`, the GPU kernel gives a `CHECK` fail that can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit c55b476aa0e0bd4ee99d0f3ad18d9d706cd1260a. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: shapeRaw is derived from the input shape after removing the last two dimensions, so an empty batch dimension yields a zero-element shape; shapeS/U/V inherit this zero-batch shape.
The only early-return guard checks n == 0 || m == 0, i.e. zero matrix dimensions, not zero batch count; with nonzero m and n but an empty batch, execution falls through to the SVD dispatch.
PerformSVD_MgeqN / PerformSVD_MlessN are then invoked with a zero-element input, reaching the GPU kernel that enforces work_element_count > 0.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The GPU kernel's CHECK assertion is reachable via attacker-controlled empty-batch input, and its failure terminates the process rather than returning an error, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion). This is a reachable-assertion DoS, not merely an invalid-shape input validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing check for zero-batch shapes before launching the SVD kernel. Trigger: tf.linalg.matrix_rank (or SVD) called with an empty batch input where m and n are nonzero. The kernel's work_element_count > 0 CHECK fails, aborting the process and causing denial of service.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a `CHECK` fail in PNG encoding by providing an empty input tensor as the pixel data. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/e312e0791ce486a80c9d23110841525c6f7c3289/tensorflow/core/kernels/image/encode_png_op.cc#L57-L60) only validates that the total number of pixels in the image does not overflow. Thus, an attacker can send an empty matrix for encoding. However, if the tensor is empty, then the associated buffer is `nullptr`. Hence, when calling `png::WriteImageToBuffer`(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/e312e0791ce486a80c9d23110841525c6f7c3289/tensorflow/core/kernels/image/encode_png_op.cc#L79-L93), the first argument (i.e., `image.flat<T>().data()`) is `NULL`. This then triggers the `CHECK_NOTNULL` in the first line of `png::WriteImageToBuffer`(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/e312e0791ce486a80c9d23110841525c6f7c3289/tensorflow/core/lib/png/png_io.cc#L345-L349). Since `image` is null, this results in `abort` being called after printing the stacktrace. Effectively, this allows an attacker to mount a denial of service attack. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Compute reads image from input(0) and only validates dims==3 and that NumElements fits in int32; it never rejects a zero-element tensor, so an empty image passes these checks.
With an empty tensor, image.flat<uint8>().data() (or the uint16 branch) returns nullptr, which is passed as the first argument to png::WriteImageToBuffer; that callee's CHECK_NOTNULL aborts.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code fails to check an unusual but attacker-reachable condition (empty tensor) and relies on a downstream assumption, causing a crash — matching CWE-754's improper check for exceptional conditions. It is not a bounds overflow (CWE-190) since the overflow check exists; the gap is the missing empty-input check.

evidence_lines.code:
OP_REQUIRES(context, image.dims() == 3,
errors::InvalidArgument("image must be 3-dimensional",
image.shape().DebugString()));
OP_REQUIRES(
context,
FastBoundsCheck(image.NumElements(), std::numeric_limits<int32>::max()),
errors::InvalidArgument("image cannot have >= int32 max elements"));

if (desired_channel_bits_ == 8) {
OP_REQUIRES(context,
png::WriteImageToBuffer(
image.flat<uint8>().data(), width, height,
width * channels, channels, desired_channel_bits_,
compression_, &output->scalar<tstring>()(), nullptr),
errors::Internal("PNG encoding failed"));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation that the image has at least one element. Trigger: attacker supplies an empty 3-D tensor to EncodePng; the buffer pointer becomes null and the downstream CHECK_NOTNULL fires, aborting the process. Consequence is a denial of service (crash) rather than wrong output.

commit_msg: antelope,storage-cfs: Fix length of filename array
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  char filename[INDEX_NAME_LENGTH];'], 'added_lines': ['  char filename[INDEX_NAME_LENGTH + 1];']}
description: Contiki-NG is an operating system for Internet of Things devices. An off-by-one error can be triggered in the Antelope database management system in the Contiki-NG operating system in versions 4.8 and prior. The problem exists in the Contiki File System (CFS) backend for the storage of data (file os/storage/antelope/storage-cfs.c). In the functions `storage_get_index` and `storage_put_index`, a buffer for merging two strings is allocated with one byte less than the maximum size of the merged strings, causing subsequent function calls to the cfs_open function to read from memory beyond the buffer size. The vulnerability has been patched in the "develop" branch of Contiki-NG, and is expected to be included in the next release. As a workaround, the problem can be fixed by applying the patch in Contiki-NG pull request #2425.

code_evidence: filename is declared with exactly INDEX_NAME_LENGTH bytes, but merge_strings(filename, rel->name, INDEX_NAME_SUFFIX) concatenates rel->name and the suffix into it; the merged result can require INDEX_NAME_LENGTH + 1 bytes including the terminating NUL. The resulting filename buffer is then passed to cfs_open, which reads past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-193 fits because the declared maximum buffer size is one less than the correct value needed for the merged string, an off-by-one sizing error. It is not a general buffer-overflow variant; the root cause is the incorrect size constant in the array declaration.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The fixed-size array is one byte too small for the maximum merged string plus its terminator, so merge_strings writes the NUL (and potentially more) beyond the buffer. The subsequent cfs_open call reads a non-terminated filename past the allocation, giving an out-of-bounds read whose consequence depends on adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
bgpd: Flowspec overflow issue

According to the flowspec RFC 8955 a flowspec nlri is <length, <nlri data>>
Specifying 0 as a length makes BGP get all warm on the inside.  Which
in this case is not a good thing at all.  Prevent warmth, stay cold
on the inside.

Reported-by: Iggy Frankovic <iggyfran@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Donald Sharp <sharpd@nvidia.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\tif (psize == 0) {', '\t\t\tflog_err(EC_BGP_FLOWSPEC_PACKET,', '\t\t\t\t "Flowspec NLRI length 0 which makes no sense");', '\t\t\treturn BGP_NLRI_PARSE_ERROR_PACKET_OVERFLOW;', '\t\t}', '']}
description: bgpd/bgp_flowspec.c in FRRouting (FRR) before 8.4.3 mishandles an nlri length of zero, aka a "flowspec overflow."

code_evidence: The loop reads a length byte psize = *pnt++ and, for extended lengths, consumes a second byte; pnt + psize > lim is the only bound check before validation and allocation.
After validation, temp = XCALLOC(MTYPE_TMP, psize) and memcpy(temp, pnt, psize) allocate and copy psize bytes, so a zero psize produces a zero-size allocation and copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-755 fits because the function fails to handle the exceptional zero-length NLRI condition, instead accepting and processing it as normal data. This is an input-validation/exceptional-condition handling flaw, not a bounds-overflow weakness such as CWE-787, since the pnt + psize > lim check addresses overruns.

evidence_lines.code:
temp = XCALLOC(MTYPE_TMP, psize);
memcpy(temp, pnt, psize);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser does not treat a flowspec NLRI length of zero as an exceptional/invalid condition. With psize == 0, the loop advances only by the length byte, the zero-size checks pass, and zero-length NLRI data reaches XCALLOC/memcpy and downstream update/withdraw processing. The missing zero-length rejection is the root cause; the supported consequence is improper handling of this malformed exceptional input rather than a memory-safety overflow.

commit_msg:
xkbcomp: fix stack overflow when evaluating boolean negation

The expression evaluator would go into an infinite recursion when
evaluating something like this as a boolean: `!True`. Instead of
recursing to just `True` and negating, it recursed to `!True` itself
again.

Bug inherited from xkbcomp.

Caught with the afl fuzzer.

Signed-off-by: Ran Benita <ran234@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        ok = ExprResolveBoolean(ctx, expr, set_rtrn);'], 'added_lines': ['        ok = ExprResolveBoolean(ctx, expr->unary.child, set_rtrn);']}
description: Endless recursion exists in xkbcomp/expr.c in xkbcommon and libxkbcommon before 0.8.1, which could be used by local attackers to crash xkbcommon users by supplying a crafted keymap file that triggers boolean negation.

code_evidence: For EXPR_INVERT/EXPR_NOT, line 42 calls ExprResolveBoolean(ctx, expr, set_rtrn) passing the same expr rather than its operand; the function then re-enters the same case with an unchanged expression.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect lets attacker-controlled input drive unlimited recursive resource consumption (stack), producing a crash, which matches CWE-400 uncontrolled resource consumption. It is not ordinary incorrect boolean logic because the demonstrated impact is exhaustion-driven denial of service.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the negation case recurses on the identical expression node instead of the unary child, so evaluation of any boolean negation never reaches a base case. Trigger: a crafted keymap containing a boolean expression such as !True. Consequence: unbounded recursion consumes stack until exhaustion, crashing xkbcommon users (DoS).

commit_msg: Make Disk Info Thread-Safe on Linux
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void DFcleanup()'], 'added_lines': ['void DFcleanup(struct nlist **DFhashvector)']}
description: An issue was discovered in the sys-info crate before 0.8.0 for Rust. sys_info::disk_info calls can trigger a double free.

code_evidence: The loop iterates the global hash table DFhashvector, freeing each node's name and the node itself, then sets the bucket to 0 after the inner loop. The function takes no argument and relies on the global DFhashvector, so concurrent callers operate on the same buckets. Two threads can both read the same np before either reaches free(np), leading both to free the same node and its name.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the same heap allocation is released twice due to unsynchronized shared-state traversal. This is distinct from a simple use-after-free: the second release is of an already-freed node, not a use of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cleanup routine frees shared hash-table nodes without any synchronization and only clears the bucket pointer after the inner loop completes. If two disk_info calls run DFcleanup concurrently, both traverse the same non-null bucket and call free() on the same np and np->name, causing a double free and possible heap corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Handle a special grappler case resulting in crash.

It might happen that a malformed input could be used to trick Grappler into trying to optimize a node with no inputs. This, in turn, would produce a null pointer dereference and a segfault.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 369242852
Change-Id: I2e5cbe7aec243d34a6d60220ac8ac9b16f136f6b
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  if (node.input_size() < 1) {', '    // Node lacks input, is invalid', '    return false;', '  }', '']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The implementation of TrySimplify(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/c22d88d6ff33031aa113e48aa3fc9aa74ed79595/tensorflow/core/grappler/optimizers/arithmetic_optimizer.cc#L390-L401) has undefined behavior due to dereferencing a null pointer in corner cases that result in optimizing a node with no inputs. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: After confirming the node is an Identity/IdentityN whose fetch status is known, the function unconditionally indexes node.input(0) and passes the result to node_map_->GetNode. No check guarantees the node has at least one input, so a malformed node with zero inputs is dereferenced out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked access produces an invalid pointer that is subsequently dereferenced, matching CWE-476's null-pointer dereference. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the crash stems from dereferencing the resulting null/invalid pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: node.input(0) is accessed without verifying node.input_size() >= 1. Trigger: a malformed graph node with no inputs reaches this path. Consequence: an out-of-range input access yields an invalid pointer that is dereferenced/checked, causing a crash (null-pointer dereference/segfault).

commit_msg:
proc_pid_cmdline_read() and environ_read() directly access the target
process' VM to retrieve the command line and environment. If this
process remaps these areas onto a file via mmap(), the requesting
process may experience various issues such as extra delays if the
underlying device is slow to respond.

Let's simply refuse to access file-backed areas in these functions.
For this we add a new FOLL_ANON gup flag that is passed to all calls
to access_remote_vm(). The code already takes care of such failures
(including unmapped areas). Accesses via /proc/pid/mem were not
changed though.

This was assigned CVE-2018-1120.

Note for stable backports: the patch may apply to kernels prior to 4.11
but silently miss one location; it must be checked that no call to
access_remote_vm() keeps zero as the last argument.

Reported-by: Qualys Security Advisory <qsa@qualys.com>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Andy Lutomirski <luto@amacapital.net>
Cc: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn -EFAULT;', '', '\tif (gup_flags & FOLL_ANON && !vma_is_anonymous(vma))']}
description: A flaw was found affecting the Linux kernel before version 4.17. By mmap()ing a FUSE-backed file onto a process's memory containing command line arguments (or environment strings), an attacker can cause utilities from psutils or procps (such as ps, w) or any other program which makes a read() call to the /proc/<pid>/cmdline (or /proc/<pid>/environ) files to block indefinitely (denial of service) or for some controlled time (as a synchronization primitive for other attacks).

code_evidence: The function validates a VMA before remote memory access but, in the changed version, the VM_IO|VM_PFNMAP check returns -EFAULT; the added FOLL_ANON guard rejects non-anonymous (file-backed) VMAs only when the caller sets FOLL_ANON.

The write path checks VM_WRITE, FOLL_FORCE and is_cow_mapping; the read path checks VM_READ, FOLL_FORCE and VM_MAYREAD. Nothing here bounds the length of the access_remote_vm() copy itself; this function only gates which VMAs are eligible.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 requires operations reading/writing outside an intended buffer boundary. This function performs no buffer copy and the patch adds a VMA-type eligibility check; the described issue is availability delay from file-backed mappings, not out-of-bounds memory access. The evidence does not support CWE-119.

evidence_lines.code:
if (vm_flags & (VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP))
return -EFAULT;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pre-patch code permitted GUP/remote reads against file-backed VMAs (e.g. FUSE mappings) because no anonymous-only constraint existed. Trigger: a caller reading /proc/pid/cmdline or environ with FOLL_ANON now hits the new check and gets -EFAULT for non-anonymous VMAs. The supported consequence is refusal/error rather than an out-of-bounds buffer operation; the reported impact is delay/blocking from slow backing devices, not memory corruption.

commit_msg:
[ Upstream commit ad0f75e5f57ccbceec13274e1e242f2b5a6397ed ]

When we clone a socket in sk_clone_lock(), its sk_cgrp_data is
copied, so the cgroup refcnt must be taken too. And, unlike the
sk_alloc() path, sock_update_netprioidx() is not called here.
Therefore, it is safe and necessary to grab the cgroup refcnt
even when cgroup_sk_alloc is disabled.

sk_clone_lock() is in BH context anyway, the in_interrupt()
would terminate this function if called there. And for sk_alloc()
skcd->val is always zero. So it's safe to factor out the code
to make it more readable.

The global variable 'cgroup_sk_alloc_disabled' is used to determine
whether to take these reference counts. It is impossible to make
the reference counting correct unless we save this bit of information
in skcd->val. So, add a new bit there to record whether the socket
has already taken the reference counts. This obviously relies on
kmalloc() to align cgroup pointers to at least 4 bytes,
ARCH_KMALLOC_MINALIGN is certainly larger than that.

This bug seems to be introduced since the beginning, commit
d979a39d7242 ("cgroup: duplicate cgroup reference when cloning sockets")
tried to fix it but not compeletely. It seems not easy to trigger until
the recent commit 090e28b229af
("netprio_cgroup: Fix unlimited memory leak of v2 cgroups") was merged.

Fixes: bd1060a1d671 ("sock, cgroup: add sock->sk_cgroup")

description: The Linux kernel 4.9.x before 4.9.233, 4.14.x before 4.14.194, and 4.19.x before 4.19.140 has a use-after-free because skcd->no_refcnt was not considered during a backport of a CVE-2020-14356 patch. This is related to the cgroups feature.

code_evidence: sock_copy(newsk, sk) copies sk_cgrp_data, including its cgroup reference state, from the original socket. Line 30 clears only sk_memcg; line 31 then calls cgroup_sk_alloc on the copied sk_cgrp_data without first accounting for the already-inherited reference count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits: the clone reuses cgroup state whose reference was not properly acquired, so later access can occur after the underlying cgroup memory is freed. This is a lifetime/reference-counting defect rather than a simple memory leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Because the cloned socket copies the cgroup reference fields without taking a new reference, the cgroup refcount is not incremented for the clone. When one socket releases the cgroup, the shared cgroup can be freed while the other socket still references it, yielding a use-after-free on the cgroup data.

description: Podofo v0.10.0 was discovered to contain a heap-use-after-free via the component PoDoFo::PdfEncrypt::IsMetadataEncrypted().

code_evidence: When the parser reports encryption, line 17 calls parser.TakeEncrypt() and stores the result in m_Encrypt. TakeEncrypt transfers ownership of the PdfEncrypt object away from the parser, so the parser no longer holds a reference to it. The commit message states this ownership transfer causes a heap-use-after-free when PdfMemDocument::SetEncrypt is used before the object's delay load.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function stores a pointer obtained through ownership transfer and later code dereferences it after the parser releases the object, which is exactly reuse of freed memory (CWE-416). The fix switches to GetEncrypt, retaining shared ownership. This is not merely a memory leak, since the object is freed while still referenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: m_Encrypt receives a raw pointer whose ownership was removed from the parser via TakeEncrypt, leaving the stored pointer dangling after the parser's copy is released. Trigger: later use of the encryption object (e.g., IsMetadataEncrypted) after the underlying allocation is freed. Consequence: heap-use-after-free, enabling invalid memory reads or writes and potential crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\thash = skb_get_hash_perturb(skb, q->perturbation);'], 'added_lines': ['\thash = skb_get_hash_perturb(skb, &q->perturbation);']}
description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: Line 17 derives the packet hash from skb_get_hash_perturb(skb, q->perturbation), using the qdisc's perturbation value as the key/secret for the hash; line 18 then uses the low HHF_BIT_MASK bits of that hash to index the flow table. The hash feeds flow identification (seek_list at line 19 and flow->hash_id at line 48), so the perturbation value acts as a security-relevant secret that determines observable flow state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because the function's security-relevant hashing depends on an insufficiently random secret (q->perturbation) whose predictability undermines the intended unpredictability of flow hashes. It is not merely a hash-collision issue; the weakness is the use of a weak/insufficient random value as a key.

evidence_lines.code:
hash = skb_get_hash_perturb(skb, q->perturbation);
flow_pos = hash & HHF_BIT_MASK;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that flow-hash secrecy relies on a static, low-entropy perturbation value passed into a jhash-based perturb function. Because the secret is small and fixed, an observer who can see resulting flow behavior can infer it, and the derived hash becomes predictable; the supported consequence is that flow/device identity can be tracked or distinguished rather than remaining unpredictable.

Cancel 9cdf439

Should not free the pointer in `realloc` since it can cause
use-after-free problem.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    mrb_free(mrb, p);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: mruby 2.1.2 has a double free in mrb_default_allocf (called from mrb_free and obj_free).

code_evidence: Line 5 obtains p2 from mrb_realloc_simple, which on failure returns NULL without freeing p. When p2 == NULL (line 7), line 8 calls mrb_free(mrb, p), freeing the original buffer; line 10 then raises a nomemory exception. If the caller retains p (or a realloc-based wrapper also frees p on failure), the same address is freed again.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the same allocation address can be released twice: once in the failure branch and again by the owner. This is a double free rather than merely a use-after-free, since the defect is the duplicate deallocation itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path frees the caller-owned original pointer p after realloc fails, breaking the realloc contract and leaving p dangling. Trigger: allocation failure in mrb_realloc_simple. Consequence: a later free of p, including via obj_free/mrb_free, produces a double free, enabling memory corruption and potentially code execution.

commit_msg:
Preserve GSS context on init/accept failure

After gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() has created a
context, don't delete the mechglue context on failures from subsequent
calls, even if the mechanism deletes the mech-specific context (which
is allowed by RFC 2744 but not preferred).  Check for union contexts
with no mechanism context in each GSS function which accepts a
gss_ctx_id_t.

CVE-2017-11462:

RFC 2744 permits a GSS-API implementation to delete an existing
security context on a second or subsequent call to
gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() if the call results
in an error.  This API behavior has been found to be dangerous,
leading to the possibility of memory errors in some callers.  For
safety, GSS-API implementations should instead preserve existing
security contexts on error until the caller deletes them.

All versions of MIT krb5 prior to this change may delete acceptor
contexts on error.  Versions 1.13.4 through 1.13.7, 1.14.1 through
1.14.5, and 1.15 through 1.15.1 may also delete initiator contexts on
error.

ticket: 8598 (new)
target_version: 1.15-next
target_version: 1.14-next
tags: pullup
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (ctx->internal_ctx_id == GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT)', '        return (GSS_S_NO_CONTEXT);']}
description: Double free vulnerability in MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) allows attackers to have unspecified impact via vectors involving automatic deletion of security contexts on error.

code_evidence: After casting the handle, the function dereferences ctx->mech_type to look up the mechanism; the patched guard against a union context with no internal_ctx_id is absent here.
The internal_ctx_id is passed straight to the mechanism's gss_wrap_size_limit without any check that it is GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT.
The iov-length shim path likewise forwards ctx->internal_ctx_id unchecked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit's fix pattern (reject union contexts with no mechanism context) targets use of a context already freed by another GSS function, consistent with CWE-415's double-free/memory-reuse class. This function lacks that guard; the weakness is the missing no-context check before dispatch.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accepts a union context whose mechanism-specific context may have been deleted on an earlier gss_init/accept error, and forwards the dangling internal_ctx_id. Trigger: a caller reuses such a context in gss_wrap_size_limit. Consequence: the mechanism operates on freed context memory, supporting memory corruption/double free as described.

commit_msg:
xfs: fix missing ILOCK unlock when xfs_setattr_nonsize fails due to EDQUOT

Benjamin Moody reported to Debian that XFS partially wedges when a chgrp
fails on account of being out of disk quota.  I ran his reproducer
script:

# adduser dummy
# adduser dummy plugdev

# dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=100 of=test.img
# mkfs.xfs test.img
# mount -t xfs -o gquota test.img /mnt
# mkdir -p /mnt/dummy
# chown -c dummy /mnt/dummy
# xfs_quota -xc 'limit -g bsoft=100k bhard=100k plugdev' /mnt

(and then as user dummy)

$ dd if=/dev/urandom bs=1M count=50 of=/mnt/dummy/foo
$ chgrp plugdev /mnt/dummy/foo

and saw:

================================================
WARNING: lock held when returning to user space!
5.3.0-rc5 #rc5 Tainted: G        W
------------------------------------------------
chgrp/47006 is leaving the kernel with locks still held!
1 lock held by chgrp/47006:
 #0: 000000006664ea2d (&xfs_nondir_ilock_class){++++}, at: xfs_ilock+0xd2/0x290 [xfs]

...which is clearly caused by xfs_setattr_nonsize failing to unlock the
ILOCK after the xfs_qm_vop_chown_reserve call fails.  Add the missing
unlock.

Reported-by: benjamin.moody@gmail.com
Fixes: 253f4911f297 ("xfs: better xfs_trans_alloc interface")
Signed-off-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Dave Chinner <dchinner@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Salvatore Bonaccorso <carnil@debian.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\txfs_iunlock(ip, XFS_ILOCK_EXCL);']}
description: An issue was discovered in xfs_setattr_nonsize in fs/xfs/xfs_iops.c in the Linux kernel through 5.2.9. XFS partially wedges when a chgrp fails on account of being out of disk quota. xfs_setattr_nonsize is failing to unlock the ILOCK after the xfs_qm_vop_chown_reserve call fails. This is primarily a local DoS attack vector, but it might result as well in remote DoS if the XFS filesystem is exported for instance via NFS.

code_evidence: Line 43 acquires XFS_ILOCK_EXCL on ip, then lines 54-56 call xfs_qm_vop_chown_reserve; if it returns an error, line 58 jumps to out_cancel.
The out_cancel path at lines 110-115 cancels the transaction and releases dquots but never calls xfs_iunlock(ip, XFS_ILOCK_EXCL), so the inode lock acquired at line 43 stays held on this error path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a missing lock release on an error path, leaving a limited synchronization resource held indefinitely and exhausting availability of the inode. This is exactly the CWE-400 scenario of not returning/releasing a resource due to mishandled error conditions, causing resource-consumption DoS. It is not CWE-667 (improper locking) as the primary frame, since the supported impact is unavailability from the unreleased lock.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch taken when xfs_qm_vop_chown_reserve fails (e.g., EDQUOT on chgrp) exits without releasing the ILOCK taken at line 43. Trigger: a chgrp/chown that changes gid or uid while quota is enabled and the reserve call fails. Consequence: the inode lock is never released, so subsequent operations on that inode block and the task returns to userspace holding the lock, wedging the filesystem (local, or remote via NFS, DoS).

commit_msg:
Implement a validity check for firstSN

Following 8.3.8.6.3 of DDS-RTPS 2.5.
This fixes issue #3236.

Signed-off-by: Seulbae Kim <squizz617@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    SequenceNumber_t zeroSN;', '    if (fisrtSN <= zeroSN)', '    {', '        EPROSIMA_LOG_WARNING(RTPS_MSG_IN, IDSTRING "Invalid Heartbeat received (" << firstSN << " <= 0), ignoring");', '        return false;', '    }']}
description: eprosima Fast DDS is a C++ implementation of the Data Distribution Service standard of the Object Management Group. Prior to versions 2.9.1 and 2.6.5, improper validation of sequence numbers may lead to remotely reachable assertion failure. This can remotely crash any Fast-DDS process. Versions 2.9.1 and 2.6.5 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: firstSN and lastSN are read directly from the network message via CDRMessage::readSequenceNumber without validating firstSN against zero. The only guard checks the relationship between lastSN and firstSN, so a remote sender can supply firstSN <= 0 (e.g., zero or negative) while satisfying lastSN == firstSN - 1, passing this check and propagating the invalid sequence numbers to findAllReaders/processHeartbeatMsg.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a remotely reachable assertion: attacker-controlled firstSN bypasses validation and later triggers an assert() in reader processing, causing abnormal termination. This matches CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion) rather than a generic input-validation weakness, because the supported impact is the reachable assertion leading to DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing constraint that firstSN must be positive before the heartbeat is accepted. Trigger: an attacker sends a crafted Heartbeat submessage with a non-positive firstSN and a consistent lastSN. Consequence: the unvalidated sequence number flows into reader processing, where a downstream assertion on sequence numbers can be reached, remotely crashing the process (DoS).

commit_msg:
Bug 706057: Fix use-after-free in getOwnPropertyDescriptor.

getOwnPropertyDescriptor should create the descriptor object by
using [[DefineOwnProperty]], and not by looking through the prototype
chain where it may invoke getters and setters on the Object.prototype.

If there exists an Object.prototype.get property with a setter, that method is
invoked when it shouldn't. A malicious getter here can delete the property
currently being processed in getOwnPropertyDescriptor, and we'll end up
with a use-after-free bug.

Avoid this problem by following the spec and use js_defproperty rather than
js_setproperty to define own properties in getOwnPropertyDescriptor and
related functions.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tjs_setproperty(J, -3, name);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tjs_defproperty(J, -3, name, 0);']}
description: A logical issue in O_getOwnPropertyDescriptor() in Artifex MuJS 1.0.0 through 1.3.x before 1.3.2 allows an attacker to achieve Remote Code Execution through memory corruption, via the loading of a crafted JavaScript file.

code_evidence: When the descriptor has a 'value' property, the function calls js_setproperty(J, -3, name) to store the value. js_setproperty performs a normal [[Set]], which walks the prototype chain and can invoke an inherited setter on Object.prototype instead of defining an own property; the fix replaces it with js_defproperty.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The reentrant deletion frees the backing object while getOwnPropertyDescriptor still holds and writes to it, producing a use-after-free that corrupts memory; that write to freed/reused storage is the out-of-bounds write the target CWE describes. A pure type-confusion or logic label would not capture the memory-write consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: using a prototype-chain-aware set operation to define an own property. Trigger: a crafted descriptor plus an attacker-controlled setter on Object.prototype; the setter reentrantly deletes the property or object being processed, leaving stale references that are later written through. Supported consequence: memory corruption and potential remote code execution.

commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20568)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (ossl_policy_level_add_node(curr, data, node, tree) == NULL) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (ossl_policy_level_add_node(curr, data, node, tree, 1) == NULL) {']}
description:
A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions

of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Policy processing is disabled by default but can be enabled by passing
the `-policy' argument to the command line utilities or by calling the
`X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_policies()' function.

code_evidence: tree_add_unmatched inherits the anyPolicy qualifier_set into a new policy data node (lines 11-12), then calls ossl_policy_level_add_node to insert it into the policy tree. The call at line 13 lacks the additional argument (the '1' flag added by the patch) that controls how the node is added to the level. This is the pre-patch form of the policy-tree construction used during X.509 certificate policy verification.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness lies in the X.509 certificate chain policy-verification path: malformed certificate policy data is processed without a bound, causing verification to consume excessive resources. This is improper handling during certificate validation (CWE-295), differing from CWE-400 resource exhaustion in that the defect is in the certificate-validation logic itself rather than generic resource accounting.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the policy-node insertion during certificate policy processing does not carry the flag that bounds node reuse/duplication, so the tree can grow exponentially as policy constraints are evaluated. Trigger: a malicious certificate chain with crafted policy constraints, when policy processing is enabled. Consequence: excessive computational resource consumption leading to denial of service during chain verification.

commit_msg:
Validate `data_splits` for `tf.StringNGrams`.

Without validation, we can cause a heap buffer overflow which results in data leakage and/or segfaults.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 332543478
Change-Id: Iee5bda24497a195d09d122355502480830b1b317
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    // Validate that the splits are valid indices into data', '    const int input_data_size = data->flat<tstring>().size();', '    const int splits_vec_size = splits_vec.size();', '    for (int i = 0; i < splits_vec_size; ++i) {', '      bool valid_splits = splits_vec(i) >= 0;', '      valid_splits = valid_splits && (splits_vec(i) <= input_data_size);', '      OP_REQUIRES(', '          context, valid_splits,', '          errors::InvalidArgument("Invalid split value ", splits_vec(i),', '                                  ", must be in [0,", input_data_size, "]"));', '    }']}
description: In Tensorflow before versions 1.15.4, 2.0.3, 2.1.2, 2.2.1 and 2.3.1, the `data_splits` argument of `tf.raw_ops.StringNGrams` lacks validation. This allows a user to pass values that can cause heap overflow errors and even leak contents of memory In the linked code snippet, all the binary strings after `ee ff` are contents from the memory stack. Since these can contain return addresses, this data leak can be used to defeat ASLR. The issue is patched in commit 0462de5b544ed4731aa2fb23946ac22c01856b80, and is released in TensorFlow versions 1.15.4, 2.0.3, 2.1.2, 2.2.1, or 2.3.1.

code_evidence: Splits are used directly as indices: length is splits_vec(i)-splits_vec(i-1) at [24]; a negative or oversized split yields an invalid/negative length, and num_ngrams (from get_num_ngrams at [27]) is accumulated into ngrams_splits_data[i] at [31] without validating splits in [0, data_size].

data_start = &input_data[splits_vec(i)] at [40] dereferences an attacker-controlled split index; length at [44] and num_ngrams at [45] then drive CreateNgrams at [46], which writes past the output buffer.
The output tensor is sized from the unvalidated ngrams_splits_data[num_batch_items] at [37]; ngrams_data at [38] and output_start at [43] provide the destination pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked splits lead directly to writes past the end of the ngrams output buffer via CreateNgrams, matching out-of-bounds write. The pointer corruption is the cause; the out-of-bounds write is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: data_splits values are consumed as array indices and as the basis for output-size computation without bounds checking. Trigger: a user supplies splits outside [0, input_data_size] (negative or too large), producing a bad data_start pointer and inconsistent length/num_ngrams values. Consequence: CreateNgrams writes beyond the allocated ngrams buffer, causing heap out-of-bounds writes and possible memory disclosure.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.3.3. There is an out-of-bounds read in crc16 in lib/crc16.c when called from fs/ext4/super.c because ext4_group_desc_csum does not properly check an offset. NOTE: this is disputed by third parties because the kernel is not intended to defend against attackers with the stated "When modifying the block device while it is mounted by the filesystem" access.

code_evidence: The legacy gdt_csum path computes a CRC16 over gdp+offset with length le16_to_cpu(sbi->s_es->s_desc_size) - offset. The bound is taken from the on-disk superblock field s_es->s_desc_size, not the validated in-memory sbi->s_desc_size, and it is compared via a signed int offset. The read length is thus derived from an unvalidated on-disk value, so a corrupted/oversized s_desc_size makes crc16 read past the group descriptor buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The CRC length exceeds the actual buffer, causing a read beyond the intended group-descriptor object, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not CWE-190 (integer overflow) because the defect is a missing upper bound on the read length, not arithmetic wrap.

evidence_lines.code:
if (ext4_has_feature_64bit(sb) &&
offset < le16_to_cpu(sbi->s_es->s_desc_size))
crc = crc16(crc, (__u8 *)gdp + offset,
le16_to_cpu(sbi->s_es->s_desc_size) -
offset);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the read length for the trailing group-descriptor CRC is computed from the raw on-disk s_desc_size rather than the kernel's validated s_desc_size, with only a lower-bound check offset < desc_size. Trigger: a mounted filesystem whose on-disk descriptor size is larger than the allocated descriptor buffer, modified while mounted. Consequence: crc16 reads past the end of the descriptor (slab-out-of-bounds read), observable as KASAN report/crash.

commit_msg:
Since server IDs are basically indistinguishable from really big client
IDs at many points in the source, it's theoretically possible to overflow
a map and either overflow server IDs into the client ID space, or grow
client IDs into the server ID space. This would currently take a massive
amount of RAM, but the definition of massive changes yearly.

Prevent this by placing a ridiculous but arbitrary upper bound on the
number of items we can put in a map: 0xF00000, somewhere over 15 million.
This should satisfy pathological clients without restriction, but stays
well clear of the 0xFF000000 transition point between server and client
IDs. It will still take an improbable amount of RAM to hit this, and a
client could still exhaust all RAM in this way, but our goal is to prevent
overflow and undefined behaviour.

Fixes #224

Signed-off-by: Derek Foreman <derek.foreman@collabora.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn (entry - start) + base;'], 'added_lines': ['\tuint32_t count;', '\t/* wl_array only grows, so if we have too many objects at', "\t * this point there's no way to clean up. We could be more", '\t * pro-active about trying to avoid this allocation, but', "\t * it doesn't really matter because at this point there is", '\t * nothing to be done but disconnect the client and delete', '\t * the whole array either way.', '\t */', '\tcount = entry - start;', '\tif (count > WL_MAP_MAX_OBJECTS) {', "\t\t/* entry->data is freshly malloced garbage, so we'd", "\t\t * better make it a NULL so wl_map_for_each doesn't", '\t\t * dereference it later. */', '\t\tentry->data = NULL;', '\t\treturn 0;', '\t}', '\treturn count + base;']}
description: An internal reference count is held on the buffer pool, incremented every time a new buffer is created from the pool. The reference count is maintained as an int; on LP64 systems this can cause the reference count to overflow if the client creates a large number of wl_shm buffer objects, or if it can coerce the server to create a large number of external references to the buffer storage. With the reference count overflowing, a use-after-free can be constructed on the wl_shm_pool tracking structure, where values may be incremented or decremented; it may also be possible to construct a limited oracle to leak 4 bytes of server-side memory to the attacking client at a time.

code_evidence: The function computes the new object's ID as '(entry - start) + base', where 'entry - start' is the index within the growing wl_array and 'base' is 0 or WL_SERVER_ID_START. The array can grow without bound as clients insert objects, so the index (and hence the returned uint32_t ID) can grow arbitrarily large. The patch's added count check is the guard against this unbounded index; without it, the arithmetic in line 26 can wrap past the server/client ID transition point.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the defect is an integer calculation ('count + base') whose result is assumed to grow monotonically but can overflow/wrap when the index becomes large. This is distinct from a simple resource-exhaustion issue: the security-relevant effect is the wrapped ID value, not merely high memory use.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ID is derived from an unbounded array index plus a base offset, with no upper bound before the addition. Trigger: a client creates a very large number of map entries, making 'entry - start' grow until 'count + base' exceeds the uint32_t range or crosses the server/client ID boundary. Consequence: integer wraparound yields a small/aliased ID, corrupting map bookkeeping and potentially causing undefined behavior or memory corruption rather than a clean failure.

commit_msg:
Harden CMD_SUBMIT path to handle malicious input that could trigger
large memory allocations. Add checks to validate transfer_buffer_length
and number_of_packets to protect against bad input requesting for
unbounded memory allocations. Validate early in get_pipe() and return
failure.

Reported-by: Secunia Research <vuln@secunia.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan <shuahkh@osg.samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int get_pipe(struct stub_device *sdev, int epnum, int dir)', '\tdev_err(&sdev->udev->dev, "get pipe() invalid epnum %d\\n", epnum);'], 'added_lines': ['static int get_pipe(struct stub_device *sdev, struct usbip_header *pdu)', '\tint epnum = pdu->base.ep;', '\tint dir = pdu->base.direction;', '', '\t/* validate transfer_buffer_length */', '\tif (pdu->u.cmd_submit.transfer_buffer_length > INT_MAX) {', '\t\tdev_err(&sdev->udev->dev,', '\t\t\t"CMD_SUBMIT: -EMSGSIZE transfer_buffer_length %d\\n",', '\t\t\tpdu->u.cmd_submit.transfer_buffer_length);', '\t\treturn -1;', '\t}', '', '\t\t/* validate packet size and number of packets */', '\t\tunsigned int maxp, packets, bytes;', '', '\t\tmaxp = usb_endpoint_maxp(epd);', '\t\tmaxp *= usb_endpoint_maxp_mult(epd);', '\t\tbytes = pdu->u.cmd_submit.transfer_buffer_length;', '\t\tpackets = DIV_ROUND_UP(bytes, maxp);', '', '\t\tif (pdu->u.cmd_submit.number_of_packets < 0 ||', '\t\t    pdu->u.cmd_submit.number_of_packets > packets) {', '\t\t\tdev_err(&sdev->udev->dev,', '\t\t\t\t"CMD_SUBMIT: isoc invalid num packets %d\\n",', '\t\t\t\tpdu->u.cmd_submit.number_of_packets);', '\t\t\treturn -1;', '\t\t}', '\tdev_err(&sdev->udev->dev, "CMD_SUBMIT: invalid epnum %d\\n", epnum);']}
description: The "stub_recv_cmd_submit()" function (drivers/usb/usbip/stub_rx.c) in the Linux Kernel before version 4.14.8, 4.9.71, and 4.4.114 when handling CMD_SUBMIT packets allows attackers to cause a denial of service (arbitrary memory allocation) via a specially crafted USB over IP packet.

code_evidence: get_pipe() takes epnum and dir directly and indexes udev->ep_in[epnum & 0x7f] or udev->ep_out[epnum & 0x7f] using the caller-supplied endpoint number; the only pre-index guard is the range check on lines 6-7, and the endpoint descriptor epd is then dereferenced without any validation of the transfer_buffer_length or number_of_packets fields that the CMD_SUBMIT path will later use to size allocations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs buffer-adjacent operations (endpoint array indexing and descriptor dereference) with insufficient bounds validation on caller-controlled values, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within memory buffer bounds; the missing length/packet checks are the direct cause of the out-of-bounds/oversized memory use.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: get_pipe() validates only epnum/dir and returns a pipe without constraining the CMD_SUBMIT transfer_buffer_length or number_of_packets, so those attacker-controlled values flow into downstream allocation and packet processing; trigger: a crafted USB over IP CMD_SUBMIT packet with oversized length or packet count; consequence: unbounded memory allocation leading to denial of service, and the unchecked endpoint indexing can reach out-of-bounds memory locations.

scheduler/cert.c: Fix string comparison (fixes CVE-2022-26691)

The previous algorithm didn't expect the strings can have a different
length, so one string can be a substring of the other and such substring
was reported as equal to the longer string.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  return (result);'], 'added_lines': [' /*', "  * The while loop finishes when *a == '\\0' or *b == '\\0'", "  * so after the while loop either both *a and *b == '\\0',", '  * or one points inside a string, so when we apply logical OR on *a,', "  * *b and result, we get a non-zero return value if the compared strings don't match.", '  */', '', '  return (result | *a | *b);']}
description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. This issue is fixed in Security Update 2022-003 Catalina, macOS Monterey 12.3, macOS Big Sur 11.6.5. An application may be able to gain elevated privileges.

code_evidence: The while loop at line 6 continues only while both *a and *b are non-NUL; line 8 accumulates XOR differences into result, then lines 9-10 advance both pointers. Line 12 returns only result, discarding whether either string still has remaining characters after the loop terminates.

commit_msg:
Preserve GSS context on init/accept failure

After gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() has created a
context, don't delete the mechglue context on failures from subsequent
calls, even if the mechanism deletes the mech-specific context (which
is allowed by RFC 2744 but not preferred).  Check for union contexts
with no mechanism context in each GSS function which accepts a
gss_ctx_id_t.

CVE-2017-11462:

RFC 2744 permits a GSS-API implementation to delete an existing
security context on a second or subsequent call to
gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() if the call results
in an error.  This API behavior has been found to be dangerous,
leading to the possibility of memory errors in some callers.  For
safety, GSS-API implementations should instead preserve existing
security contexts on error until the caller deletes them.

All versions of MIT krb5 prior to this change may delete acceptor
contexts on error.  Versions 1.13.4 through 1.13.7, 1.14.1 through
1.14.5, and 1.15 through 1.15.1 may also delete initiator contexts on
error.

ticket: 8598 (new)
target_version: 1.15-next
target_version: 1.14-next
tags: pullup
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (ctx->internal_ctx_id == GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT)', '\treturn (GSS_S_NO_CONTEXT);']}
description: Double free vulnerability in MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) allows attackers to have unspecified impact via vectors involving automatic deletion of security contexts on error.

code_evidence: After val_inq_ctx_args validates the handle, the function casts context_handle to gss_union_ctx_id_t and dereferences ctx->mech_type and ctx->internal_ctx_id without checking whether internal_ctx_id is GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT. The patch adds exactly that guard before gssint_get_mechanism, so the original code passes a union context whose mechanism context was already deleted into mech->gss_inquire_context.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The underlying defect is that a dangling mechanism context can be passed to another GSS call and freed again, matching CWE-415 double free. It is not merely a missing NULL check; the consequence is repeated deallocation of the same address.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: gss_inquire_context does not verify that the union context still owns a live mechanism context before forwarding it to the mechanism. Trigger: a caller invokes gss_inquire_context on a context that a prior gss_init_sec_context/gss_accept_sec_context error left with internal_ctx_id == GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT. The mechanism then operates on a freed context, supporting use-after-free/double-free memory corruption.

commit_msg:
compose: fix infinite loop in parser on some inputs

The parser would enter an infinite loop if an unterminated keysym
literal occurs at EOF.

Found with the afl fuzzer.

Signed-off-by: Ran Benita <ran234@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["        while (peek(s) != '>' && !eol(s))"], 'added_lines': ["        while (peek(s) != '>' && !eol(s) && !eof(s))"]}
description: An infinite loop when reaching EOL unexpectedly in compose/parser.c (aka the keymap parser) in xkbcommon before 0.8.1 could be used by local attackers to cause a denial of service during parsing of crafted keymap files.

code_evidence: After consuming '<', the loop at line 17 appends next(s) while peek(s) is not '>' and eol(s) is false; the condition lacks an eof(s) check. If the input ends with an unterminated keysym literal at EOF, neither '>' nor EOL is ever seen, so the loop keeps calling next(s)/buf_append without a terminating condition. The subsequent unterminated-literal error at line 20 is only reached after the loop exits.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the loop's exit condition is unreachable for EOF-terminated input, producing an infinite loop and resource-consumption DoS. This is not merely an error-handling omission: the loop itself cannot terminate on the triggering input.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the keysym-literal scan loop has no EOF exit condition, so an unterminated '<...' at end of input never satisfies the '>' or EOL tests. Trigger: parsing a crafted keymap whose keysym literal reaches EOF. Supported consequence: the parser spins indefinitely, consuming CPU and denying service.
