description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions an attacker can cause denial of service in applications serving models using `tf.raw_ops.NonMaxSuppressionV5` by triggering a division by 0. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/core/kernels/image/non_max_suppression_op.cc#L170-L271) uses a user controlled argument to resize a `std::vector`. However, as `std::vector::resize` takes the size argument as a `size_t` and `output_size` is an `int`, there is an implicit conversion to unsigned. If the attacker supplies a negative value, this conversion results in a crash. A similar issue occurs in `CombinedNonMaxSuppression`. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 3a7362750d5c372420aa8f0caf7bf5b5c3d0f52d and commit [b5cdbf12ffcaaffecf98f22a6be5a64bb96e4f58. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 9 reads the user-controlled max_output_size tensor as a signed int output_size with no non-negativity check in the before version.

Line 44 uses output_size as the loop bound compared against selected.size(), and lines 73-74 pass output_size to std::vector::resize in the pad_to_max_output_size path, where the signed int is implicitly converted to size_t.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an implicit signed-to-unsigned numeric conversion of a size argument producing an unexpected huge value used in a sensitive allocation context, matching CWE-681. It is not CWE-190 (integer overflow) because no arithmetic overflow occurs; the defect is the conversion itself.

evidence_lines.code: const int output_size = max_output_size.scalar<int>()();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a user-supplied int is used as a container size without validating it is non-negative. Trigger: max_output_size is negative and pad_to_max_output_size is set, so selected.resize(output_size, 0) converts the negative int to a huge size_t, causing a crash/heap OOB. Consequence is denial of service, not memory corruption of attacker-chosen data.

The defect is a wrong validation target, not a transformation/filtering issue, so CWE-20 fits rather than encoding/escaping weaknesses.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the validation on line 14 checks the pointer rather than the parsed length, so a crafted negative chunk-size value passes unchecked. Trigger: a remote HTTP response or UPnP broadcast containing a negative chunk length. Consequence: the invalid size flows into subsequent chunk handling, leading to a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix #340: System frozen

gdImageCreate() doesn't check for oversized images and as such is prone
to DoS vulnerabilities. We fix that by applying the same overflow check
that is already in place for gdImageCreateTrueColor().

CVE-2016-9317
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['']}
description: The gdImageCreate function in the GD Graphics Library (aka libgd) before 2.2.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (system hang) via an oversized image.

code_evidence: The function checks overflow2(sx, sy) for the width/height product and returns NULL on overflow.
It separately checks overflow2(sizeof(unsigned char *), sy) for the row-pointer allocation size.
It checks overflow2(sizeof(unsigned char), sx) for the per-row pixel allocation size.
The validated sizes then drive gdMalloc(sizeof(unsigned char *) * sy) and gdCalloc(sx, sizeof(unsigned char)), so the inputs sx and sy are attacker-controlled dimensions consumed by allocations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function accepts caller-supplied dimensions and must validate that they are safe to process; the overflow checks are the input-validation constraints that reject unsafe size values. This is improper validation of input size properties, distinct from a memory-corruption-only weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
im->pixels = (unsigned char **) gdMalloc (sizeof (unsigned char *) * sy);
im->pixels[i] = (unsigned char *) gdCalloc (sx, sizeof (unsigned char));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the image dimensions sx and sy are external inputs, and the function relies on explicit overflow checks before using them as allocation sizes. Trigger: an oversized width/height whose product or per-dimension allocation arithmetic overflows. Supported consequence: without these guards the allocation size computation could be wrong, leading to resource exhaustion or a hang (DoS) rather than safe rejection of the oversized image.

commit_msg: Resolve #767
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  for (size_t i = 0; i < fat->size(); ++i) {', '    Binary* binary = fat->at(i);', '  c_macho_binaries[fat->size()] = nullptr;'], 'added_lines': ['  size_t nb_bin = fat->size();', '  for (size_t i = 0; i < nb_bin; ++i) {', '    Binary* binary = fat->take(i).release();', '  c_macho_binaries[nb_bin] = nullptr;', '  delete fat;']}
description: LIEF commit 365a16a was discovered to contain a heap-buffer overflow via the function print_binary at /c/macho_reader.c.

code_evidence: Allocation sizes the array using fat->size() + 1 at the time of malloc, treating the result as the maximum indexable slot count.

The loop bound and the terminating write both re-evaluate fat->size() after the allocation; line 12 writes c_macho_binaries[fat->size()], and line 8 writes index i up to that same value, so the array's last valid index is exceeded whenever the current size equals the allocated size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing c_macho_binaries[fat->size()] and indexed entries beyond the malloc'd capacity is an out-of-bounds write to a heap buffer, matching CWE-787. It is not merely a read overflow or NULL dereference, since the faulting operations store pointers past the intended allocation.

evidence_lines.code:
auto** c_macho_binaries = static_cast<Macho_Binary_t**>(
malloc((fat->size() + 1) * sizeof(Macho_Binary_t**)));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer capacity is frozen from an earlier fat->size() value, but loop and terminator indices are derived from a later, possibly larger fat->size(). Trigger: a FatBinary whose reported size grows or differs between the malloc and the writes. The consequence is an out-of-bounds heap write at c_macho_binaries[fat->size()] and at loop index i, corrupting adjacent heap memory.

commit_msg:
f2fs: fix potential panic during fstrim

As Ju Hyung Park reported:

"When 'fstrim' is called for manual trim, a BUG() can be triggered
randomly with this patch.

I'm seeing this issue on both x86 Desktop and arm64 Android phone.

On x86 Desktop, this was caused during Ubuntu boot-up. I have a
cronjob installed which calls 'fstrim -v /' during boot. On arm64
Android, this was caused during GC looping with 1ms gc_min_sleep_time
& gc_max_sleep_time."

Root cause of this issue is that f2fs_wait_discard_bios can only be
used by f2fs_put_super, because during put_super there must be no
other referrers, so it can ignore discard entry's reference count
when removing the entry, otherwise in other caller we will hit bug_on
in __remove_discard_cmd as there may be other issuer added reference
count in discard entry.

Thread A				Thread B
					- issue_discard_thread
- f2fs_ioc_fitrim
 - f2fs_trim_fs
  - f2fs_wait_discard_bios
   - __issue_discard_cmd
    - __submit_discard_cmd
					 - __wait_discard_cmd
					  - dc->ref++
					  - __wait_one_discard_bio
   - __wait_discard_cmd
    - __remove_discard_cmd
     - f2fs_bug_on(sbi, dc->ref)

Fixes: 969d1b180d987c2be02de890d0fff0f66a0e80de
Reported-by: Ju Hyung Park <qkrwngud825@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Chao Yu <yuchao0@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Jaegeuk Kim <jaegeuk@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tf2fs_wait_discard_bios(sbi);'], 'added_lines': ['\tf2fs_wait_discard_bios(sbi, false);']}
description: The f2fs implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.14 mishandles reference counts associated with f2fs_wait_discard_bios calls, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (BUG), as demonstrated by fstrim.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only passes a new boolean argument to f2fs_wait_discard_bios; the root cause is a reference-count mishandling/concurrency bug in discard command removal, not improper input validation of range or other input, so the function does not directly support CWE-20.

commit_msg:
evtchn: convert per-channel lock to be IRQ-safe

... in order for send_guest_{global,vcpu}_virq() to be able to make use
of it.

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    spin_lock(&chn->lock);', '    spin_unlock(&chn->lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned long  flags;', '    spin_lock_irqsave(&chn->lock, flags);', '    spin_unlock_irqrestore(&chn->lock, flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The channel state and unbound fields are mutated and evtchn_port_init() is called while holding chn->lock via plain spin_lock/spin_unlock. The diff shows this lock is not IRQ-safe, so an interrupt handler acquiring the same per-channel lock can interleave with this sequence.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function provides temporary exclusive access to shared channel state via a lock that does not exclude concurrent interrupt-context access, breaking exclusivity/atomicity. The fix converts to spin_lock_irqsave/irqrestore, confirming the missing synchronization constraint rather than a different memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-channel lock is taken without disabling interrupts, so an IRQ-context code sequence can access the same channel state. Trigger: concurrent interrupt handling while evtchn_alloc_unbound updates chn->state and remote_domid. Consequence: violated internal assumptions and non-atomic channel state updates, enabling the race conditions described (out-of-bounds access, bug checks, privilege escalation).

commit_msg:
Default initialize fixed point Eigen types.

In certain cases, tensors are filled with default values of the type. But, for these fixed point types, these values were uninitialized. Thus, we would have uninitialized memory access bugs, some of which were caught by MSAN.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 344101137
Change-Id: I14555fda74dca3b5f1582da9008901937e3f14e2
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['QInt32() {}'], 'added_lines': ['QInt32() : value(0) {}']}
description: In affected versions of TensorFlow under certain cases a saved model can trigger use of uninitialized values during code execution. This is caused by having tensor buffers be filled with the default value of the type but forgetting to default initialize the quantized floating point types in Eigen. This is fixed in versions 1.15.5, 2.0.4, 2.1.3, 2.2.2, 2.3.2, and 2.4.0.

code_evidence: The only declaration is the default constructor QInt32() {}, which constructs a QInt32 without initializing its underlying 'value' member; no member initializer list or assignment is present.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 covers use/access of a resource that has not been initialized. Here the constructor produces an object whose value is never initialized, so subsequent reads use uninitialized memory. This is the initialization defect itself, not a separate out-of-bounds or type-confusion weakness.

evidence_lines.code: QInt32() {}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the default constructor leaves the quantized fixed-point storage uninitialized. Trigger: code that default-constructs QInt32 (e.g., tensor buffers filled with the type's default value) then reads the value. Supported consequence: use of uninitialized memory, producing indeterminate reads (reported by MSAN) and potentially invalid data or crashes.

commit_msg:
x86: don't wrongly trigger linear page table assertion (2)

_put_final_page_type(), when free_page_type() has exited early to allow
for preemption, should not update the time stamp, as the page continues
to retain the typ which is in the process of being unvalidated. I can't
see why the time stamp update was put on that path in the first place
(albeit it may well have been me who had put it there years ago).

This is part of XSA-240.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Tested-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        set_tlbflush_timestamp(page);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service (unbounded recursion, stack consumption, and hypervisor crash) or possibly gain privileges via crafted page-table stacking.

code_evidence: On the -EINTR path, free_page_type exited early for preemption; the code then asserts the page's type_info is still unvalidated and updates its timestamp before re-marking PGT_validated. This path runs while the page retains the type being unvalidated, so its state is re-entered repeatedly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's failure to bound repeated page-type revalidation enables unbounded recursion and resource consumption, matching CWE-400's uncontrolled consumption leading to DoS. The weakness is the missing restriction on repeated processing, not merely a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the preemption/restart path revalidates the page and refreshes its timestamp without completing type teardown, allowing repeated re-entry into page-type handling. A PV guest crafting page-table stacking can drive this recursion, consuming hypervisor stack and crashing the host.

commit_msg:
canvas: fix an integer overflow in caca_resize().

Fixes: #52 (CVE-2021-3410)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                caca_set_canvas_size(cv, width = x + wch, height);', '                caca_set_canvas_size(cv, width, height = y + 1);', '        caca_set_canvas_size(cv, width, height = y);'], 'added_lines': ['                if (caca_set_canvas_size(cv, width = x + wch, height) < 0)', '                    return -1;', '                if (caca_set_canvas_size(cv, width, height = y + 1) < 0)', '                    return -1;', '        if (caca_set_canvas_size(cv, width, height = y))', '            return -1;']}
description: A flaw was found in libcaca v0.99.beta19. A buffer overflow issue in caca_resize function in libcaca/caca/canvas.c may lead to local execution of arbitrary code in the user context.

code_evidence: x and y are signed ints, while width and height are unsigned; wch is a small positive int added to x to form a size argument.
The growx branch passes width = x + wch to caca_set_canvas_size without any bound check; the fix adds a return-value check, but the addition itself can wrap.
The growy branch passes height = y + 1 similarly unchecked.
After the loop, height = y is again passed unchecked when growy is set.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the arithmetic producing the canvas dimensions (x + wch, y + 1) can overflow/wrap before being used as a size, and the commit itself is titled an integer-overflow fix. The returned error check addresses downstream consequences but the wraparound in the size computation is the underlying weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: x, y (signed int) are incremented by escape-sequence parameters and character widths and then combined with unsigned width/height to compute new canvas dimensions, with no overflow check before the size is used for allocation/copying in caca_set_canvas_size. Trigger: a crafted ANSI input drives x or y to a large value, causing x + wch or y + 1 to wrap to a small or negative value. Consequence: an undersized canvas is allocated, leading to out-of-bounds memory access and possible code execution.

commit_msg:
media: ov519: add missing endpoint sanity checks

Make sure to check that we have at least one endpoint before accessing
the endpoint array to avoid dereferencing a NULL-pointer on stream
start.

Note that these sanity checks are not redundant as the driver is mixing
looking up altsettings by index and by number, which need not coincide.

Fixes: 1876bb923c98 ("V4L/DVB (12079): gspca_ov519: add support for the ov511 bridge")
Fixes: b282d87332f5 ("V4L/DVB (12080): gspca_ov519: Fix ov518+ with OV7620AE (Trust spacecam 320)")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>     # 2.6.31
Cc: Hans de Goede <hdegoede@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab+huawei@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn;', '\t}', '', '\tif (alt->desc.bNumEndpoints < 1) {', '\t\tsd->gspca_dev.usb_err = -ENODEV;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.6.1. drivers/media/usb/gspca/ov519.c allows NULL pointer dereferences in ov511_mode_init_regs and ov518_mode_init_regs when there are zero endpoints, aka CID-998912346c0d.

code_evidence: Line 9 resolves the altsetting via usb_altnum_to_altsetting and lines 10-14 reject a NULL alt. However, no check exists that alt->desc.bNumEndpoints is at least 1 before line 15 unconditionally reads alt->endpoint[0].desc.wMaxPacketSize. With zero endpoints, endpoint[0] is an invalid/NULL array entry dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked endpoint[0] access dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but NULL when no endpoints exist, matching CWE-476. It is not merely an out-of-bounds index issue because the missing constraint is endpoint presence, and the added commit check confirms the NULL-dereference fix.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates the altsetting pointer but not the endpoint count, then indexes endpoint[0]. Trigger: a USB device/configuration whose selected altsetting reports bNumEndpoints == 0, reached on stream start. Consequence: NULL/invalid pointer dereference in ov511_mode_init_regs, crashing the kernel (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fixed a buffer overrun problem in the QMFB code in the JPC codec
that was caused by a buffer being allocated with a size that was too small
in some cases.
Added a new regression test case.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!(buf = jas_alloc2(bufsize, sizeof(jpc_fix_t)))) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!(buf = jas_alloc3(bufsize, numcols, sizeof(jpc_fix_t)))) {']}
description: A heap-buffer overflow vulnerability was found in QMFB code in JPC codec caused by buffer being allocated with too small size. jasper versions before 2.0.0 are affected.

code_evidence: bufsize is derived from numrows via JPC_CEILDIVPOW2; when it exceeds QMFB_SPLITBUFSIZE, the heap buffer is allocated with jas_alloc2(bufsize, sizeof(jpc_fix_t)), sizing it only by bufsize and ignoring numcols.
The first copy loop writes into buf via *dstptr2 and advances dstptr by numcols per row, so the buffer must hold m * numcols elements.
The final copy loop reads from buf via *srcptr2 and advances srcptr by numcols per row, consuming m * numcols elements.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The allocation is smaller than the buffer region actually accessed by the copy loops, producing reads/writes outside the intended heap buffer boundary, which is exactly CWE-119. The underlying sizing error is an allocation-size miscalculation, but the demonstrated operation is an out-of-bounds buffer access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dynamic allocation multiplies only bufsize by the element size, omitting numcols, while the copy loops index buf as a numcols-wide, m-row array. Trigger: numcols > 1 with bufsize > QMFB_SPLITBUFSIZE. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds writes (and subsequent reads) past the allocation, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg:
llrp: limit recursion depth

LLRP defines fairly complex parameter nesting which we handle via recursion,
however this means a large crafted packet could cause very deep stacks and
potentially stack overflows. Limit our recursive depth to an arbitrary, which
should be more than enough for any legitimate packet (I hope).

Bug: 12048
Change-Id: I9ac31bddfa4ffd1a79809387d10d2261749b95e7
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/13794
Reviewed-by: Evan Huus <eapache@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    return dissect_llrp_parameters(tvb, pinfo, param_tree, suboffset, param_end);'], 'added_lines': ['    return dissect_llrp_parameters(tvb, pinfo, param_tree, suboffset, param_end, 0);']}
description: The dissect_llrp_parameters function in epan/dissectors/packet-llrp.c in the LLRP dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.10 and 2.0.x before 2.0.2 does not limit the recursion depth, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption or application crash) via a crafted packet.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only recurses via dissect_llrp_parameters without any buffer bounds operation; the shown code does not demonstrate an out-of-bounds read/write, and unbounded recursion causing stack exhaustion is not a CWE-119 buffer boundary violation.

commit_msg: Prevent HTTP pipelining which Crow doesn't support.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                    parser_.clear();']}
description: HTTP applications (servers) based on Crow through 1.0+4 may allow a Use-After-Free and code execution when HTTP pipelining is used. The HTTP parser supports HTTP pipelining, but the asynchronous Connection layer is unaware of HTTP pipelining. Specifically, the Connection layer is unaware that it has begun processing a later request before it has finished processing an earlier request.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only starts the adaptor and calls parser_.clear() on a successful start; it contains no free, pointer reuse, or object lifetime operation demonstrating a use-after-free, and the pipelining state issue described lies in the Connection/parser layers, not this start() callback.

commit_msg:
drm/amd/display: memory leak

In dcn*_clock_source_create when dcn20_clk_src_construct fails allocated
clk_src needs release.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Alex Deucher <alexander.deucher@amd.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tkfree(clk_src);']}
description: Memory leaks in *clock_source_create() functions under drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc in the Linux kernel before 5.3.8 allow attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption). This affects the dce112_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce112/dce112_resource.c, the dce100_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce100/dce100_resource.c, the dcn10_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dcn10/dcn10_resource.c, the dcn20_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dcn20/dcn20_resource.c, the dce120_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce120/dce120_resource.c, the dce110_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce110/dce110_resource.c, and the dce80_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce80/dce80_resource.c, aka CID-055e547478a1.

code_evidence: Lines 8-9 allocate clk_src with kzalloc and store the only pointer to the heap block.
Lines 12-16: when dcn20_clk_src_construct fails, control skips the success return and reaches line 17 (BREAK_TO_DEBUGGER) then line 18 returns NULL without freeing clk_src.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because an allocated object's effective lifetime ends on the error path without a corresponding release, matching missing release of memory. This is not a use-after-free (CWE-416) since the block is neither freed nor dereferenced after the failure.

evidence_lines.code:
struct dce110_clk_src *clk_src =
kzalloc(sizeof(struct dce110_clk_src), GFP_KERNEL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch after a failed dcn20_clk_src_construct returns NULL while the kzalloc'd clk_src pointer goes out of scope, so the allocation is never released. Trigger: repeated calls where the construct step fails. Consequence: memory consumption, a supported denial of service; the leak is the cause, resource exhaustion the effect.

Anatoly has been fuzzing with kBdysch harness and reported a hang in
one of the outcomes:

  0: (b7) r0 = 808464432
  1: (7f) r0 >>= r0

   R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=271581184,umax_value=271581311,var_off=(0x10300000;0x7f)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0

  from 8 to 9: safe

  from 5 to 6: R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=808464432,umax_value=5103431727,var_off=(0x30303020;0x10000001f)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  6: (07) r0 += -2144337872
  7: (14) w0 -= -1607454672
  8: (25) if r0 > 0x30303030 goto pc+0
   R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=271581184,umax_value=271581311,var_off=(0x10300000;0x7f)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  9: safe

  from 8 to 9: safe
  verification time 589 usec
  stack depth 0
  processed 17 insns (limit 1000000) [...]

The underlying program was xlated as follows:

  # bpftool p d x i 9
   0: (b7) r0 = 808464432
   1: (7f) r0 >>= r0
   2: (14) w0 -= 808464432
   3: (07) r0 += 808464432
   4: (b7) r1 = 808464432
   5: (de) if w1 s<= w0 goto pc+0
   6: (07) r0 += -2144337872
   7: (14) w0 -= -1607454672
   8: (25) if r0 > 0x30303030 goto pc+0
   9: (76) if w0 s>= 0x303030 goto pc+2
  10: (05) goto pc-1
  11: (05) goto pc-1
  12: (95) exit

The verifier rewrote original instructions it recognized as dead code with
'goto pc-1', but reality differs from verifier simulation in that we're
actually able to trigger a hang due to hitting the 'goto pc-1' instructions.

Taking different examples to make the issue more obvious: in this example
we're probing bounds on a completely unknown scalar variable in r1:

  [...]
  5: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R10=fp0
  5: (18) r2 = 0x4000000000
  7: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R2_w=inv274877906944 R10=fp0
  7: (18) r3 = 0x2000000000
  9: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R10=fp0
  9: (18) r4 = 0x400
  11: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R4_w=inv1024 R10=fp0
  11: (18) r5 = 0x200
  13: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R4_w=inv1024 R5_w=inv512 R10=fp0
  13: (2d) if r1 > r2 goto pc+4
   R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffffff)) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R4_w=inv1024 R5_w=inv512 R10=fp0
  14: R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffffff)) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R4_w=inv1024 R5_w=inv512 R10=fp0
  14: (ad) if r1 < r3 goto pc+3
   R0_w=inv1 R1_w=inv(id=0,umin_value=137438953472,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffffff)) R2_w=inv274877906944 R3_w=inv137438953472 R4_w=inv1024 R5_w=inv512 R10=fp0
  15: R0=inv1 R1=inv(id=0,umin_value=137438953472,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7fffffffff)) R2=inv274877906944 R3=inv137438953472 R4=inv1024 R5=inv512 R10=fp0
  15: (2e) if w1 > w4 goto pc+2
   R0=inv1 R1=inv(id=0,umin_value=137438953472,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7f00000000)) R2=inv274877906944 R3=inv137438953472 R4=inv1024 R5=inv512 R10=fp0
  16: R0=inv1 R1=inv(id=0,umin_value=137438953472,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7f00000000)) R2=inv274877906944 R3=inv137438953472 R4=inv1024 R5=inv512 R10=fp0
  16: (ae) if w1 < w5 goto pc+1
   R0=inv1 R1=inv(id=0,umin_value=137438953472,umax_value=274877906944,var_off=(0x0; 0x7f00000000)) R2=inv274877906944 R3=inv137438953472 R4=inv1024 R5=inv512 R10=fp0
  [...]

We're first probing lower/upper bounds via jmp64, later we do a similar
check via jmp32 and examine the resulting var_off there. After fall-through
in insn 14, we get the following bounded r1 with 0x7fffffffff unknown marked
bits in the variable section.

Thus, after knowing r1 <= 0x4000000000 and r1 >= 0x2000000000:

  max: 0b100000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x4000000000
  var: 0b111111111111111111111111111111111111111 / 0x7fffffffff
  min: 0b010000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x2000000000

Now, in insn 15 and 16, we perform a similar probe with lower/upper bounds
in jmp32.

Thus, after knowing r1 <= 0x4000000000 and r1 >= 0x2000000000 and
                    w1 <= 0x400        and w1 >= 0x200:

  max: 0b100000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x4000000000
  var: 0b111111100000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x7f00000000
  min: 0b010000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x2000000000

The lower/upper bounds haven't changed since they have high bits set in
u64 space and the jmp32 tests can only refine bounds in the low bits.

However, for the var part the expectation would have been 0x7f000007ff
or something less precise up to 0x7fffffffff. A outcome of 0x7f00000000
is not correct since it would contradict the earlier probed bounds
where we know that the result should have been in [0x200,0x400] in u32
space. Therefore, tests with such info will lead to wrong verifier
assumptions later on like falsely predicting conditional jumps to be
always taken, etc.

The issue here is that __reg_bound_offset32()'s implementation from
commit 581738a681b6 ("bpf: Provide better register bounds after jmp32
instructions") makes an incorrect range assumption:

  static void __reg_bound_offset32(struct bpf_reg_state *reg)
  {
        u64 mask = 0xffffFFFF;
        struct tnum range = tnum_range(reg->umin_value & mask,
                                       reg->umax_value & mask);
        struct tnum lo32 = tnum_cast(reg->var_off, 4);
        struct tnum hi32 = tnum_lshift(tnum_rshift(reg->var_off, 32), 32);

        reg->var_off = tnum_or(hi32, tnum_intersect(lo32, range));
  }

In the above walk-through example, __reg_bound_offset32() as-is chose
a range after masking with 0xffffffff of [0x0,0x0] since umin:0x2000000000
and umax:0x4000000000 and therefore the lo32 part was clamped to 0x0 as
well. However, in the umin:0x2000000000 and umax:0x4000000000 range above
we'd end up with an actual possible interval of [0x0,0xffffffff] for u32
space instead.

In case of the original reproducer, the situation looked as follows at
insn 5 for r0:

  [...]
  5: R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=808464432,umax_value=5103431727,var_off=(0x0; 0x1ffffffff)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
                               0x30303030           0x13030302f
  5: (de) if w1 s<= w0 goto pc+0
   R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=808464432,umax_value=5103431727,var_off=(0x30303020; 0x10000001f)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
                             0x30303030           0x13030302f
  [...]

After the fall-through, we similarly forced the var_off result into
the wrong range [0x30303030,0x3030302f] suggesting later on that fixed
bits must only be of 0x30303020 with 0x10000001f unknowns whereas such
assumption can only be made when both bounds in hi32 range match.

Originally, I was thinking to fix this by moving reg into a temp reg and
use proper coerce_reg_to_size() helper on the temp reg where we can then
based on that define the range tnum for later intersection:

  static void __reg_bound_offset32(struct bpf_reg_state *reg)
  {
        struct bpf_reg_state tmp = *reg;
        struct tnum lo32, hi32, range;

        coerce_reg_to_size(&tmp, 4);
        range = tnum_range(tmp.umin_value, tmp.umax_value);
        lo32 = tnum_cast(reg->var_off, 4);
        hi32 = tnum_lshift(tnum_rshift(reg->var_off, 32), 32);
        reg->var_off = tnum_or(hi32, tnum_intersect(lo32, range));
  }

In the case of the concrete example, this gives us a more conservative unknown
section. Thus, after knowing r1 <= 0x4000000000 and r1 >= 0x2000000000 and
                             w1 <= 0x400        and w1 >= 0x200:

  max: 0b100000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x4000000000
  var: 0b111111111111111111111111111111111111111 / 0x7fffffffff
  min: 0b010000000000000000000000000000000000000 / 0x2000000000

However, above new __reg_bound_offset32() has no effect on refining the
knowledge of the register contents. Meaning, if the bounds in hi32 range
mismatch we'll get the identity function given the range reg spans
[0x0,0xffffffff] and we cast var_off into lo32 only to later on binary
or it again with the hi32.

Likewise, if the bounds in hi32 range match, then we mask both bounds
with 0xffffffff, use the resulting umin/umax for the range to later
intersect the lo32 with it. However, _prior_ called __reg_bound_offset()
did already such intersection on the full reg and we therefore would only
repeat the same operation on the lo32 part twice.

Given this has no effect and the original commit had false assumptions,
this patch reverts the code entirely which is also more straight forward
for stable trees: apparently 581738a681b6 got auto-selected by Sasha's
ML system and misclassified as a fix, so it got sucked into v5.4 where
it should never have landed. A revert is low-risk also from a user PoV
since it requires a recent kernel and llc to opt-into -mcpu=v3 BPF CPU
to generate jmp32 instructions. A proper bounds refinement would need a
significantly more complex approach which is currently being worked, but
no stable material [0]. Hence revert is best option for stable. After the
revert, the original reported program gets rejected as follows:

  1: (7f) r0 >>= r0
  2: (14) w0 -= 808464432
  3: (07) r0 += 808464432
  4: (b7) r1 = 808464432
  5: (de) if w1 s<= w0 goto pc+0
   R0_w=invP(id=0,umin_value=808464432,umax_value=5103431727,var_off=(0x0; 0x1ffffffff)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  6: (07) r0 += -2144337872
  7: (14) w0 -= -1607454672
  8: (25) if r0 > 0x30303030 goto pc+0
   R0_w=invP(id=0,umax_value=808464432,var_off=(0x0; 0x3fffffff)) R1_w=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  9: (76) if w0 s>= 0x303030 goto pc+2
   R0=invP(id=0,umax_value=3158063,var_off=(0x0; 0x3fffff)) R1=invP808464432 R10=fp0
  10: (30) r0 = *(u8 *)skb[808464432]
  BPF_LD_[ABS|IND] uses reserved fields
  processed 11 insns (limit 1000000) [...]

  [0] https://lore.kernel.org/bpf/158507130343.15666.8018068546764556975.stgit@john-Precision-5820-Tower/T/

Fixes: 581738a681b6 ("bpf: Provide better register bounds after jmp32 instructions")
Reported-by: Anatoly Trosinenko <anatoly.trosinenko@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/bpf/20200330160324.15259-2-daniel@iogearbox.net
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (is_jmp32) {', '\t\t__reg_bound_offset32(false_reg);', '\t\t__reg_bound_offset32(true_reg);', '\t}'], 'added_lines': []}
description: In the Linux kernel 5.5.0 and newer, the bpf verifier (kernel/bpf/verifier.c) did not properly restrict the register bounds for 32-bit operations, leading to out-of-bounds reads and writes in kernel memory. The vulnerability also affects the Linux 5.4 stable series, starting with v5.4.7, as the introducing commit was backported to that branch. This vulnerability was fixed in 5.6.1, 5.5.14, and 5.4.29. (issue is aka ZDI-CAN-10780)

code_evidence: For unsigned JGE/JGT, false_umin/true_umax are derived from val, then when is_jmp32 the code adds gen_hi_min/gen_hi_max of var_off before clamping umin_value/umax_value; the 32-bit comparison only constrains the low 32 bits, yet the added high-bits term can produce bounds inconsistent with the actual u32 interval.

The JLE/JLT branch mirrors this: false_umax/true_umin are adjusted by gen_hi_max/gen_hi_min and then folded into umax_value/umin_value, allowing the recorded 64-bit bounds to disagree with the true 32-bit range.

After deduction and __reg_bound_offset, the is_jmp32 block calls __reg_bound_offset32 on both registers, rewriting var_off from these possibly incorrect bounds; the resulting tnum can mark bits as fixed that are actually variable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The faulty bound tracking lets the verifier accept a program whose runtime memory access exceeds the intended buffer, so the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The weakness is in verifier range computation, not in the memory-access instruction itself; the miscomputed var_off is the cause, and the OOB access is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the verifier's 32-bit jump handling mixes low-32-bit comparison values with high-bit terms from var_off, producing register bounds/var_off that do not reflect the real value range. Trigger: a crafted BPF program uses jmp32 comparisons on an unknown scalar; later the verifier relies on the over-restrictive var_off to treat a conditional jump as always taken. Consequence: verifier-approved instructions can access memory out of bounds, enabling out-of-bounds reads/writes in kernel memory.

description: In Exiv2 0.26, Exiv2::IptcParser::decode in iptc.cpp (called from psdimage.cpp in the PSD image reader) may suffer from a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read) caused by an integer overflow via a crafted PSD image file.

Trigger: a crafted PSD whose resource entry yields a zero accounting increment while still passing isIrb. Consequence: the loop never terminates, causing CPU resource consumption (denial of service).

commit_msg:
Fix EinsumHelper::ParseEquation to avoid uninitialized accesses.

EinsumHelper::ParseEquation is supposed to return true or false in
input_has_ellipsis and output_has_ellipsis to indicate whether there is
ellipsis in the inputs and output. Previously, when there is no ellipsis in the
inputs or output, the routine doesn't assign false to the variables. This
change initializes the two variables with false to fix the problem.
PiperOrigin-RevId: 391772004
Change-Id: I17b6c88aadef4131470378e48cced054bf252e86
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      input_has_ellipsis->at(i) = false;', '    *output_has_ellipsis = false;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affeced versions during execution, `EinsumHelper::ParseEquation()` is supposed to set the flags in `input_has_ellipsis` vector and `*output_has_ellipsis` boolean to indicate whether there is ellipsis in the corresponding inputs and output. However, the code only changes these flags to `true` and never assigns `false`. This results in unitialized variable access if callers assume that `EinsumHelper::ParseEquation()` always sets these flags. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.7.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.6.1, TensorFlow 2.5.2, and TensorFlow 2.4.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: input_has_ellipsis is resized to num_inputs at line 21, but each element is only assigned true when a kEllipsisLabel is found (line 28); elements without an ellipsis remain uninitialized.
output_has_ellipsis is dereferenced and set to true only in the else branch at line 36; when output_labels contains no kEllipsisLabel, the pointed-to bool is never written.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function leaves a pointer-targeted output flag (and vector elements) uninitialized on a non-ellipsis path, and callers consume that value, matching CWE-824's access of an uninitialized pointer/value. It is not merely a missing-default logic bug because the uninitialized memory is subsequently read through the output parameter.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: ParseEquation is documented to set every flag in input_has_ellipsis and *output_has_ellipsis, but it only writes true on the ellipsis path. When an input or the output has no ellipsis, the resized vector elements or the caller-provided bool remain uninitialized, so callers reading these flags access uninitialized memory and may take incorrect control flow.

commit_msg:
Bug 739133 - (CVE-2017-17785) Heap overflow while parsing FLI files.

It is possible to trigger a heap overflow while parsing FLI files. The
RLE decoder is vulnerable to out of boundary writes due to lack of
boundary checks.

The variable "framebuf" points to a memory area which was allocated
with fli_header->width * fli_header->height bytes. The RLE decoder
therefore must never write beyond that limit.

If an illegal frame is detected, the parser won't stop, which means
that the next valid sequence is properly parsed again. This should
allow GIMP to parse FLI files as good as possible even if they are
broken by an attacker or by accident.

While at it, I changed the variable xc to be of type size_t, because
the multiplication of width and height could overflow a 16 bit type.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tunsigned short xc, pc, pcnt;', '\t\t\txc+=skip;', '\t\t\t\tmemset(&(pos[xc]), val, ps);', '\t\t\t\txc+=ps;', '\t\t\t\tfread(&(pos[xc]), ps, 1, f);', '\t\t\t\txc+=ps;'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (numline > fli_header->height || fli_header->height-numline < firstline)', '\t\treturn;', '', '\t\tunsigned short pc, pcnt;', '\t\tsize_t n, xc;', '\t\tn=(size_t)fli_header->width * (fli_header->height-firstline-yc);', '\t\t\txc+=MIN(n-xc,skip);', '\t\t\t\tsize_t len;', '\t\t\t\tlen=MIN(n-xc,ps);', '\t\t\t\tmemset(&(pos[xc]), val, len);', '\t\t\t\txc+=len;', '\t\t\t\tsize_t len;', '\t\t\t\tlen=MIN(n-xc,ps);', '\t\t\t\tfread(&(pos[xc]), len, 1, f);', '\t\t\t\txc+=len;']}
description: In GIMP 2.8.22, there is a heap-based buffer overflow in the fli_read_brun function in plug-ins/file-fli/fli.c.

code_evidence: Line 7 reads numline and line 8 iterates yc over it without bounding numline against fli_header->height, so firstline+yc can exceed the allocated framebuffer rows. Line 12 computes pos=framebuf+(width*(firstline+yc)) with unsigned short arithmetic. Line 17 accumulates xc+=skip and lines 22/25 write pos[xc] via memset/fread with attacker-controlled ps and no check against the row/allocation limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs writes through memset and fread to pos[xc] beyond the intended framebuffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The missing boundary constraints are the cause; the heap corruption is the consequence, distinct from a mere out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the RLE decoder derives framebuf offsets from header width/height and per-frame skip/length bytes without validating them against the allocated buffer size. A crafted FLI frame with large firstline/numline or skip/ps values drives xc and row offset past the width*height allocation, and memset/fread then write out of bounds, corrupting heap memory (potential code execution or crash).

commit_msg:
BLIP: Fix decompression buffer bug

Until now, mistakenly, the buffer for decompressing compressed BLIP messages
has been statically allocated as 16 Kb, but that is not valid behavior.
16 Kb is the maximum size of a _compressed_ frame.  In theory, due to the
ability to zipbomb, there is virtually no upper bound on what the maximum
size of an uncompressed frame could be.  However, to keep sanity, it has
been made into a preference with a reasonable default that is not likely to
be exceeded (64 Kb).  The behavior before for this was that wireshark would
crash because the dissector would return NULL for a decompressed buffer due
to error and then try to deference it later.  A null check has been added,
so that the behavior is now that the packet will show
'<Error decompressing message>' instead, and log why it couldn't handle the
compressed message.  Closes #16866.

description: In Wireshark 3.2.0 to 3.2.6 and 3.0.0 to 3.0.13, the BLIP protocol dissector has a NULL pointer dereference because a buffer was sized for compressed (not uncompressed) messages. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-blip.c by allowing reasonable compression ratios and rejecting ZIP bombs.

code_evidence: On a revisited frame the saved proto data pointer is fetched and dereferenced at saved_data->buf and saved_data->size without any NULL check before constructing the child tvb.

The decompression output buffer is a fixed BLIP_INFLATE_BUFFER_SIZE allocation with avail_out set to that size; inflate() returns an error when the uncompressed data exceeds it, and the function returns NULL without saving state.
On the first pass the decompressed child tvb is built from the fixed buffer with bodyLength, and the same buffer pointer is stored in the saved slice_t for later reuse.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (saved_data) that is expected to be valid but can be NULL due to the earlier decompression failure path, matching CWE-476. The root cause is the missing NULL check, with the fixed-size buffer as the trigger; this is not a buffer overflow since the write is bounded by avail_out.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A zipbomb-style compressed frame inflates beyond the fixed 16 Kb buffer, making inflate() fail and decompress() return NULL. No proto data is stored, so on the revisited frame p_get_proto_data returns NULL and the code dereferences it at saved_data->buf, causing a NULL pointer dereference and dissector crash.

commit_msg:
sched/fair: Fix low cpu usage with high throttling by removing expiration of cpu-local slices

It has been observed, that highly-threaded, non-cpu-bound applications
running under cpu.cfs_quota_us constraints can hit a high percentage of
periods throttled while simultaneously not consuming the allocated
amount of quota. This use case is typical of user-interactive non-cpu
bound applications, such as those running in kubernetes or mesos when
run on multiple cpu cores.

This has been root caused to cpu-local run queue being allocated per cpu
bandwidth slices, and then not fully using that slice within the period.
At which point the slice and quota expires. This expiration of unused
slice results in applications not being able to utilize the quota for
which they are allocated.

The non-expiration of per-cpu slices was recently fixed by
'commit 512ac999d275 ("sched/fair: Fix bandwidth timer clock drift
condition")'. Prior to that it appears that this had been broken since
at least 'commit 51f2176d74ac ("sched/fair: Fix unlocked reads of some
cfs_b->quota/period")' which was introduced in v3.16-rc1 in 2014. That
added the following conditional which resulted in slices never being
expired.

if (cfs_rq->runtime_expires != cfs_b->runtime_expires) {
	/* extend local deadline, drift is bounded above by 2 ticks */
	cfs_rq->runtime_expires += TICK_NSEC;

Because this was broken for nearly 5 years, and has recently been fixed
and is now being noticed by many users running kubernetes
(https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/67577) it is my opinion
that the mechanisms around expiring runtime should be removed
altogether.

This allows quota already allocated to per-cpu run-queues to live longer
than the period boundary. This allows threads on runqueues that do not
use much CPU to continue to use their remaining slice over a longer
period of time than cpu.cfs_period_us. However, this helps prevent the
above condition of hitting throttling while also not fully utilizing
your cpu quota.

This theoretically allows a machine to use slightly more than its
allotted quota in some periods. This overflow would be bounded by the
remaining quota left on each per-cpu runqueueu. This is typically no
more than min_cfs_rq_runtime=1ms per cpu. For CPU bound tasks this will
change nothing, as they should theoretically fully utilize all of their
quota in each period. For user-interactive tasks as described above this
provides a much better user/application experience as their cpu
utilization will more closely match the amount they requested when they
hit throttling. This means that cpu limits no longer strictly apply per
period for non-cpu bound applications, but that they are still accurate
over longer timeframes.

This greatly improves performance of high-thread-count, non-cpu bound
applications with low cfs_quota_us allocation on high-core-count
machines. In the case of an artificial testcase (10ms/100ms of quota on
80 CPU machine), this commit resulted in almost 30x performance
improvement, while still maintaining correct cpu quota restrictions.
That testcase is available at https://github.com/indeedeng/fibtest.

Fixes: 512ac999d275 ("sched/fair: Fix bandwidth timer clock drift condition")

description: In writeToParcel of CursorWindow.cpp, there is a possible information disclosure due to uninitialized data. This could lead to local information disclosure with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: The buffer is sized as compactedSize = mAllocOffset + slotsSize, then rounded up to a 4-byte multiple via (compactedSize + 3) & ~3, and allocated with writeInplace(compactedSize).

Only two regions are copied: mAllocOffset bytes at the start and slotsSize bytes at offset compactedSize - slotsSize. The padding gap introduced by the rounding between mAllocOffset and compactedSize - slotsSize is never written.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a resource (the parcel buffer region) and later serializes it while part of it was never initialized, matching CWE-908's use of an uninitialized resource. This is not CWE-416 (use-after-free) because no freed memory is referenced; the defect is missing initialization of the padding bytes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the alignment rounding inflates compactedSize beyond the data actually copied, leaving an unwritten gap in the parcel buffer. Trigger: writeToParcel on a non-ashmem window serializes this padded region. Supported consequence: the uninitialized padding is transmitted, disclosing stale heap contents to the receiving side.

Fixes: use of uninitialized variables

description: aa_read_header in libavformat/aadec.c in FFmpeg before 3.2.14 and 4.x before 4.1.4 does not check for sscanf failure and consequently allows use of uninitialized variables.

code_evidence: Line 12 declares header_key_part[4] without initializing it. Line 33 enters the HeaderKey branch on attacker-controlled dictionary input val. Line 34-35 call sscanf with four %u conversions into those elements but the return count is not checked. Line 36-37 then iterate all four elements and pass each to AV_WB32, reading uninitialized stack slots whenever sscanf matched fewer than four values (e.g. empty or short HeaderKey).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the function reads and uses stack variables (header_key_part) that were never initialized. This is distinct from CWE-457 (use of uninitialized variable) only in abstraction; the resource-usage pattern here is a direct uninitialized-resource read, matching the target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the number of successful sscanf conversions is ignored, so header_key_part entries remain uninitialized when the HeaderKey string has fewer than four numeric fields. Trigger: a crafted .aa header whose HeaderKey value is empty or partial. Consequence: uninitialized stack contents are read and written into header_key, propagating into the derived file key and causing nondeterministic output or invalid memory reads.

description: RIOT-OS 2021.01 contains a buffer overflow vulnerability in sys/net/gnrc/routing/rpl/gnrc_rpl_validation.c through the gnrc_rpl_validation_options() function.

code_evidence: The loop is bounded only by expected_len < len, but before advancing the pointer it reads opt->type (line 6) and opt->length (line 62) and then computes the next pointer opt + 1 + opt->length (line 63) without verifying that sizeof(gnrc_rpl_opt_t) bytes remain or that the declared opt->length fits within the remaining len.

It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the malformed length drives memory bounds violations during option processing.

Because it dereferences the option header and advances by the declared length without checking the remaining buffer, a truncated or oversized option causes reads/writes past the supplied len, and the loop/pointer arithmetic can run beyond the buffer.

commit_msg:
Bug 701818: better handling of error during PS/PDF image

In the xps device, if an error occurred after xps_begin_image() but before
xps_image_end_image(), *if* the Postscript had called 'restore' as part of the
error handling, the image enumerator would have been freed (by the restore)
despite the xps device still holding a reference to it.

Simply changing to an allocator unaffected save/restore doesn't work because
the enumerator holds references to other objects (graphics state, color space,
possibly others) whose lifespans are inherently controlled by save/restore.

So, add a finalize method for the XPS device's image enumerator
(xps_image_enum_finalize()) which takes over cleaning up the memory it allocates
and also deals with cleaning up references from the device to the enumerator
and from the enumerator to the device.

description: A use-after-free vulnerability in xps_finish_image_path() in devices/vector/gdevxps.c of Artifex Software GhostScript v9.50 allows a remote attacker to escalate privileges via a crafted PDF file. This is fixed in v9.51.

code_evidence: The exit label unconditionally frees pie->pcs via rc_decrement, pie->buffer and pie->devc_buffer via gs_free_object, and releases pie->icc_link, then returns code. The function does not clear the pointers or detach the device's reference to the enumerator after freeing, and the error path (code < 0 at line 10) reaches the same cleanup. A 'restore' during error handling can free the enumerator while the xps device still holds a reference, so these frees act on memory that may already be freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the code frees and then allows the same enumerator/pointers to be referenced after release, matching use-after-free. It is not merely a double free: the defect is continued reference to freed memory, not just repeated release.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the enumerator's resources are freed in xps_image_end_image without transferring ownership or clearing dangling references, while save/restore error handling can free the enumerator first. Trigger: an error between begin_image and end_image combined with a PostScript restore. Consequence: use-after-free when the enumerator or its members are later accessed, leading to memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
The length value is interpreted as signed char on many systems
(depending on default signedness of char), which can lead to an out of
boundary write up to 128 bytes in front of the allocated storage, but
limited to NUL byte(s).

Casting the length value to unsigned char fixes the problem and allows
string values with up to 255 characters.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    length = *ch;', '\t\t    length = *ch;'], 'added_lines': ['\t    length = *(unsigned char *)ch;', '\t\t    length = *(unsigned char *)ch;']}
description: An issue was discovered in libX11 through 1.6.5. The function XListExtensions in ListExt.c interprets a variable as signed instead of unsigned, resulting in an out-of-bounds write (of up to 128 bytes), leading to DoS or remote code execution.

code_evidence: Line 33 reads the length prefix into signed int length; if char is signed, a value >=128 becomes negative. Line 35 checks ch + length < chend, which a negative length passes, so line 37 advances ch by length+1 (backwards) and line 38 re-reads a length before the buffer. Line 39 then writes a NUL through *ch at that out-of-range position.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The signed length lets ch advance before the buffer and the NUL write at line 39 lands outside the allocation, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The signedness flaw is the root cause; the write outside the buffer is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length byte is interpreted as signed, so large values become negative and bypass the upper-bound check. Trigger: a server reply with a length byte >=128. Consequence: ch moves before the allocated buffer and line 39 writes a NUL out of bounds, corrupting memory (DoS or potential code execution).

Before this patch an uv_mutex_t (backed by a critical section) could be
released by a tread different from the thread that acquired it, which is
not allowed. This is fixed by using a semaphore instead.

Note that the affected code paths were used on Windows XP and Windows
Server 2003 only.

85adf43 and bd1777f from the v1.x branch.

commit_msg:
Remove `OP_REQUIRES` call from helper function.

Since `OP_REQUIRES` macro expands to a `return;` (among other), calling it in a helper function only ends the helper function's execution earlier, but the kernel will still run from start to end. Thus, all the expected validations are actually broken/useless as the code ploughs through the next crash anyway.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a null pointer dereference by providing an invalid `permutation` to `tf.raw_ops.SparseMatrixSparseCholesky`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/080f1d9e257589f78b3ffb75debf584168aa6062/tensorflow/core/kernels/sparse/sparse_cholesky_op.cc#L85-L86) fails to properly validate the input arguments. Although `ValidateInputs` is called and there are checks in the body of this function, the code proceeds to the next line in `ValidateInputs` since `OP_REQUIRES`(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/080f1d9e257589f78b3ffb75debf584168aa6062/tensorflow/core/framework/op_requires.h#L41-L48) is a macro that only exits the current function. Thus, the first validation condition that fails in `ValidateInputs` will cause an early return from that function. However, the caller will continue execution from the next line. The fix is to either explicitly check `context->status()` or to convert `ValidateInputs` to return a `Status`. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: OP_REQUIRES(ctx, rank == 2 || rank == 3, ...) only returns from ValidateInputs on failure; the caller continues with an invalid rank.
row_dim is derived from the unchecked rank, then dense_shape_vec(row_dim) and dense_shape_vec(row_dim + 1) index the shape without confirming rank is 2 or 3.
OP_REQUIRES(ctx, perm_shape.dims() + 1 == rank, ...) again only exits this helper, so a permutation rank mismatch does not stop the caller.
OP_REQUIRES(ctx, perm_shape.dim_size(rank - 2) == *num_rows, ...) computes rank - 2 and indexes permutation shape after the failed validation returned early.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The broken validation allows invalid shape/rank inputs to flow into dereferences/indexing that can fault on a null or invalid pointer, matching CWE-476's null pointer dereference. The defect is missing enforcement of the constraint, not merely a logic error.

evidence_lines.code:
OP_REQUIRES(
ctx, perm_shape.dims() + 1 == rank,
errors::InvalidArgument(
"sparse matrix must have the same rank as permutation; got: ", rank,
" != ", perm_shape.dims(), " + 1."));

OP_REQUIRES(
ctx, perm_shape.dim_size(rank - 2) == *num_rows,
errors::InvalidArgument(
"permutation must have the same number of elements in each batch "
"as the number of rows in sparse matrix; got: ",
perm_shape.dim_size(rank - 2), " != ", *num_rows));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: validations use OP_REQUIRES inside a void helper, so a failed check returns only from ValidateInputs and the caller proceeds with invalid rank/permutation data. Trigger: an invalid permutation or matrix rank reaching this helper. Consequence: out-of-range shape indexing/dereference leading to a crash (null pointer dereference/DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix the race condition between the following two flows that run in
parallel:

1. l2cap_reassemble_sdu -> chan->ops->recv (l2cap_sock_recv_cb) ->
   __sock_queue_rcv_skb.

2. bt_sock_recvmsg -> skb_recv_datagram, skb_free_datagram.

An SKB can be queued by the first flow and immediately dequeued and
freed by the second flow, therefore the callers of l2cap_reassemble_sdu
can't use the SKB after that function returns. However, some places
continue accessing struct l2cap_ctrl that resides in the SKB's CB for a
short time after l2cap_reassemble_sdu returns, leading to a
use-after-free condition (the stack trace is below, line numbers for
kernel 5.19.8).

Fix it by keeping a local copy of struct l2cap_ctrl.

description: A vulnerability classified as critical was found in Linux Kernel. Affected by this vulnerability is the function l2cap_reassemble_sdu of the file net/bluetooth/l2cap_core.c of the component Bluetooth. The manipulation leads to use after free. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The associated identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211087.

code_evidence: At line 22 skb_in_use is set, then line 23 passes skb and the control pointer into l2cap_reassemble_sdu, which can queue the skb for a concurrent recvmsg path that dequeues and frees it. After the call returns, lines 26-30 still dereference control->final and pass control to l2cap_retransmit_all, reading memory inside the freed skb's control block.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent execution race: two threads share the skb without exclusive/atomic access, and the window between reassembly and the later control access violates exclusivity, matching CWE-362. The use-after-free is the consequence of the race, not the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: control points into skb->cb and the function keeps using it after l2cap_reassemble_sdu may have handed skb to another thread that frees it via skb_free_datagram. Trigger: an SDU is reassembled and queued while a concurrent bt_sock_recvmsg dequeues and frees it before this thread reads control->final. Consequence: a use-after-free read of the freed control block, causing KASAN-detected instability/crash.

commit_msg:
If for any reason a directory passed to do_split() does not have enough
active entries to exceed half the size of the block, we can end up
iterating over all "count" entries without finding a split point.

In this case, count == move, and split will be zero, and we will
attempt a negative index into map[].

Guard against this by detecting this case, and falling back to
split-to-half-of-count instead; in this case we will still have
plenty of space (> half blocksize) in each split block.

Fixes: ef2b02d3e617 ("ext34: ensure do_split leaves enough free space in both blocks")
Signed-off-by: Eric Sandeen <sandeen@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Andreas Dilger <adilger@dilger.ca>
Reviewed-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/f53e246b-647c-64bb-16ec-135383c70ad7@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* Split the existing block in the middle, size-wise */', '\t/* map index at which we will split */', '\tsplit = count - move;'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Ensure that neither split block is over half full */', '\t/*', '\t * map index at which we will split', '\t *', "\t * If the sum of active entries didn't exceed half the block size, just", '\t * split it in half by count; each resulting block will have at least', '\t * half the space free.', '\t */', '\tif (i > 0)', '\t\tsplit = count - move;', '\telse', '\t\tsplit = count/2;', '']}
description: A memory out-of-bounds read flaw was found in the Linux kernel before 5.9-rc2 with the ext3/ext4 file system, in the way it accesses a directory with broken indexing. This flaw allows a local user to crash the system if the directory exists. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

code_evidence: The loop from line 40 walks map[] backward while size+map[i].size/2 <= blocksize/2, incrementing move. If no entry exceeds half the block, the loop runs to i == -1, so move == count. Line 46 then computes split = count - move = 0, and line 48 reads map[split - 1], i.e. map[-1], before the buffer start.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because line 48 reads map[split - 1] with split == 0, accessing memory before the intended buffer. This is an out-of-bounds read affecting availability (crash), distinct from an out-of-bounds write since no data is stored past the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: split is derived from the loop count without guarding the case where the loop exhausts all entries (i goes negative, move == count). Trigger: a directory whose active entries do not exceed half the block size. Consequence: map[split-1] is a negative-index read before the allocated map buffer, an out-of-bounds read that can crash the system.

fix CVE-2019-9278

avoid the use of unsafe integer overflow checking constructs (unsigned integer operations cannot overflow, so "u1 + u2 > u1" can be optimized away)

check for the actual sizes, which should also handle the overflows
document other places google patched, but do not seem relevant due to other restrictions

fixes https://github.com/libexif/libexif/issues/26

description: In libexif, there is a possible out of bounds write due to an integer overflow. This could lead to remote escalation of privilege in the media content provider with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation. Product: AndroidVersions: Android-10Android ID: A-112537774

code_evidence: s is computed as format size times component count; the guard only checks s < components or s == 0, which does not catch a multiplication wraparound producing a small nonzero s.
doff is taken from file data when s > 4; the bounds check uses doff + s, which can itself wrap, and doff >= size is not checked before this arithmetic.
entry->data is allocated with s and memcpy copies s bytes from d + doff, so a miscomputed s or doff leads to an out-of-bounds read/copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the weakness is an integer overflow in the size and offset calculation whose wrapped result is then used for allocation and copying. The pre-patch checks assume doff+s > doff and similar, which fail under wraparound; this is distinct from a pure bounds-check omission since the arithmetic itself is the defect.

evidence_lines.code:
entry->data = exif_data_alloc (data, s);
memcpy (entry->data, d + doff, s);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is unchecked unsigned integer arithmetic: the format-size-times-components product and the doff+s offset can wrap to small values. A crafted EXIF entry with large components or a large offset passes the flawed sanity checks, and the subsequent allocation and memcpy use the wrapped size/offset, causing out-of-bounds memory access.

commit_msg: Fixed an array overflow problem in the JPC decoder.

description: Stack-based buffer overflow in the jpc_tsfb_getbands2 function in jpc_tsfb.c in JasPer before 1.900.30 allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via a crafted image.

code_evidence: Line 41 declares a fixed-size stack buffer bnds[64] for band descriptors.
Lines 71-75 call jpc_tsfb_getbands, which fills bnds based on the component's resolution levels derived from the crafted image; the write count is not bounded by the local array size.
Lines 135-137 compute bndno from rlvlno and index bnds[bndno], assuming the buffer covers all bands.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes beyond the end of the intended stack buffer bnds, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since jpc_tsfb_getbands populates the array; the fix enlarges the buffer to JPC_MAXBANDS.

evidence_lines.code: jpc_tsfb_band_t bnds[64];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the number of resolution levels/bands from the image is not constrained to the fixed 64-element stack array before jpc_tsfb_getbands writes into bnds. A crafted image with many resolution levels triggers an out-of-bounds write on the stack, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially enabling code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix issue of listen before chmod on Unix sockets (CVE-2023-45145) (#12671)

Before this commit, Unix socket setup performed chmod(2) on the socket
file after calling listen(2). Depending on what umask is used, this
could leave the file with the wrong permissions for a short period of
time. As a result, another process could exploit this race condition and
establish a connection that would otherwise not be possible.

We now make sure the socket permissions are set up prior to calling
listen(2).

(cherry picked from commit 1119ecae6fd8796fa337df2212f09173ab6c7b0a)

Co-authored-by: Yossi Gottlieb <yossigo@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int anetListen(char *err, int s, struct sockaddr *sa, socklen_t len, int backlog) {'], 'added_lines': ['static int anetListen(char *err, int s, struct sockaddr *sa, socklen_t len, int backlog, mode_t perm) {', '', '    if (sa->sa_family == AF_LOCAL && perm)', '        chmod(((struct sockaddr_un *) sa)->sun_path, perm);']}
description: Redis is an in-memory database that persists on disk. On startup, Redis begins listening on a Unix socket before adjusting its permissions to the user-provided configuration. If a permissive umask(2) is used, this creates a race condition that enables, during a short period of time, another process to establish an otherwise unauthorized connection. This problem has existed since Redis 2.6.0-RC1. This issue has been addressed in Redis versions 7.2.2, 7.0.14 and 6.2.14. Users are advised to upgrade. For users unable to upgrade, it is possible to work around the problem by disabling Unix sockets, starting Redis with a restrictive umask, or storing the Unix socket file in a protected directory.

code_evidence: anetListen binds the socket and, in the pre-fix code, the function takes no perm argument and never restricts the socket file's permissions.
bind(s,sa,len) creates the Unix socket file on disk using the process umask; the function performs no chmod before the socket becomes reachable.
listen(s, backlog) immediately activates the socket, so any local process able to connect during the window before external permission adjustment can establish a connection.
The function then simply returns; permission hardening is left to the caller after listen, creating the exposed interval.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-668 fits because the socket resource becomes accessible to parties outside the intended control sphere due to insecure permissions during a race; the weakness is resource exposure to the wrong sphere, not the race itself.

evidence_lines.code: static int anetListen(char *err, int s, struct sockaddr *sa, socklen_t len, int backlog) {

return ANET_OK;
}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the socket file's access permissions are not constrained before it is made connectable. Trigger: a permissive umask at bind time combined with listen before chmod. Consequence: an unintended local process can connect to the Unix socket during the race window, exposing the resource to the wrong control sphere.

commit_msg:
Fix tensor shape overflow in FusedResizeAndPadConv2D.

Replaced TensorShape constructor by Factory method with status.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 477742686
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    TensorShape resized_shape(', '        {input.dim_size(0), st.out_height, st.out_width, input.dim_size(3)});'], 'added_lines': ['    TensorShape resized_shape;', '    OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, TensorShape::BuildTensorShape(', '                                {input.dim_size(0), st.out_height, st.out_width,', '                                 input.dim_size(3)},', '                                &resized_shape));']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. When `tf.raw_ops.FusedResizeAndPadConv2D` is given a large tensor shape, it overflows. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit d66e1d568275e6a2947de97dca7a102a211e01ce. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.11. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.10.1, 2.9.3, and TensorFlow 2.8.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Constructs resized_shape directly from input.dim_size(0), st.out_height, st.out_width, and input.dim_size(3) without any overflow or bounds checking; a large shape makes this constructor compute an overflowing element count.
padded_shape.AddDim(before + resized_shape.dim_size(d) + after) accumulates dimensions derived from the unvalidated resized_shape, propagating the overflow into the padded size.
in_depth = padded_shape.dim_size(3) is later compared against filter.dim_size(2), so the corrupted dimension feeds subsequent shape logic and allocation decisions.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t} else {', '\t\t\t\tsize++;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: Integer overflow in the ftp_genlist function in ext/ftp/ftp.c in PHP before 5.4.42, 5.5.x before 5.5.26, and 5.6.x before 5.6.10 allows remote FTP servers to execute arbitrary code via a long reply to a LIST command, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow.  NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2015-4022.

code_evidence: The loop at [47,54] increments `size` for every received byte that is not part of a CRLF pair, while `size` was already advanced by `rcvd` at [46]. Thus `size` accumulates roughly twice the received byte count, and the guard at [42] checks only `rcvd` against `size`, so the inflated `size` can overflow `size_t` across iterations. The over-large `size` is then passed to `safe_emalloc` at [58] as the extra allocation size, and the later copy loop at [63,71] writes bytes into the buffer based on the same contents.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes an incorrect buffer length and then writes received data into the allocated region, so operations fall outside the intended bounds, matching CWE-119. The described consequence is a heap-based out-of-bounds write; the integer overflow is the cause rather than the labeled weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-byte `size++` inside the scan loop double-counts bytes already counted by `size += rcvd`, and the overflow check at [42] does not account for this growth. Trigger: a remote FTP server returns a long LIST reply, allowing `size` to wrap. Consequence: allocation and subsequent writes at [58] and [63,71] operate on an undersized buffer, producing a heap-based buffer overflow.

WireGuard: fix null pointer crash

It was assumed that the WireGuard dissector is always called on the
first pass before the second pass. That might not be the case when the
heuristics dissector sets a conversation dissector later in the stream.
Be prepared to handle this case. Do not simply abort, the previous
packets may be valid data messages.

Issue #522: Dir loop in malformed ISO causes segfault

Github Issue #522 revealed that we could blow the stack
when recursing to assemble ISO paths.  I saw this happen
at 130,000 dir levels.  This patch addresses this by limiting
the directory recursion to 1,000 elements.

TODO:  It would be even better to track and detect the dir loop
directly.

Lines 8-11 concatenate the current file's name (or '.') into the archive string; this is the per-level work repeated by the unbounded recursion, growing the path and call stack.

The fix adds a depth limit, confirming the missing constraint on input-derived recursion; this is distinct from output encoding or filtering.

A malformed ISO whose directory is a member of itself creates a cyclic parent chain, so the recursion never terminates, exhausting the stack and crashing (segfault) — a denial of service. Root cause is missing validation of the input's structural property (acyclic, bounded depth); the crash is the consequence.

commit_msg:
If an empty string is received from an x-server, do not underrun the
buffer by accessing "rep.nameLen - 1" unconditionally, which could end
up being -1.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["\t    (*name)[rep.nameLen - 1] = '\\0';", "\t    (*busID)[rep.busIDLen - 1] = '\\0';"], 'added_lines': ["\t    (*name)[rep.nameLen == 0 ? 0 : rep.nameLen - 1] = '\\0';", "\t    (*busID)[rep.busIDLen == 0 ? 0 : rep.busIDLen - 1] = '\\0';"]}
description: Buffer underflow in X.org libXvMC before 1.0.10 allows remote X servers to have unspecified impact via an empty string.

code_evidence: Lines 76-77: strncpy copies rep.nameLen bytes into *name (allocated with Xmalloc(rep.nameLen)), then unconditionally writes (*name)[rep.nameLen - 1]. If the X server returns nameLen == 0, the index becomes -1, a write before the allocated buffer. Lines 78-79 repeat the same pattern for busID with rep.busIDLen. Both lengths come directly from the server reply rep, so the server controls the boundary.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The write at [rep.nameLen - 1] with nameLen == 0 lands outside the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The specific underflow is a child of this class; the target label remains the provided CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes rep.nameLen and rep.busIDLen are at least 1 and computes index length-1 without a lower-bound check. Trigger: a malicious X server returns an empty string (length 0). Consequence: writes occur at index -1, outside the heap buffer, causing a buffer underflow on memory adjacent to the allocation.

commit_msg:
Zheyu Ma reported this crash in the sm712fb driver when reading
three bytes from the framebuffer:

  do_syscall_64+0x43/0x90

Fix it by removing the open-coded endianess fixup-code and
by moving the pointer post decrement out the fb_readl() function.

Reported-by: Zheyu Ma <zheyuma97@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Helge Deller <deller@gmx.de>
Tested-by: Zheyu Ma <zheyuma97@gmail.com>
