diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbuffer = kmalloc((count > PAGE_SIZE) ? PAGE_SIZE : count, GFP_KERNEL);', '\t\tfor (i = c >> 2; i--;) {', '\t\t\t*dst = fb_readl(src++);', '\t\t\t*dst = big_swap(*dst);', '\t\t}', '\t\tif (c & 3) {', '\t\t\tu8 *dst8 = (u8 *)dst;', '\t\t\tu8 __iomem *src8 = (u8 __iomem *)src;', '', '\t\t\tfor (i = c & 3; i--;) {', '\t\t\t\tif (i & 1) {', '\t\t\t\t\t*dst8++ = fb_readb(++src8);', '\t\t\t\t} else {', '\t\t\t\t\t*dst8++ = fb_readb(--src8);', '\t\t\t\t\tsrc8 += 2;', '\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tsrc = (u32 __iomem *)src8;'], 'added_lines': ['\tbuffer = kmalloc(PAGE_SIZE, GFP_KERNEL);', '\t\tfor (i = (c + 3) >> 2; i--;) {', '\t\t\tu32 val;', '', '\t\t\tval = fb_readl(src);', '\t\t\t*dst = big_swap(val);', '\t\t\tsrc++;']}
description: The Linux kernel was found vulnerable out of bounds memory access in the drivers/video/fbdev/sm712fb.c:smtcfb_read() function. The vulnerability could result in local attackers being able to crash the kernel.

code_evidence: Line 22 allocates a buffer of size min(count, PAGE_SIZE) based on the user-requested count. Line 29 sets c to min(count, PAGE_SIZE), and lines 31-35 write c>>2 words (each 4 bytes) into buffer via dst++. For c not a multiple of 4, lines 36-47 handle the trailing bytes using pointer arithmetic on src8, including a pre-decrement (--src8) and a post-increment (++src8) that can move the read pointer backwards relative to the buffer end. The trailing-byte loop writes at most c&3 bytes, but the combination of word writes and byte writes into a buffer sized to c can exceed the allocation when the endianness fixup reads/writes misaligned or when the pre-decrement reads before the intended framebuffer region. The subsequent copy_to_user at line 49 copies c bytes from buffer, so any overrun in the write loop corrupts adjacent heap memory before being copied out.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes past the end of the intended heap buffer (allocated to c bytes) during the endianness-fixup byte loop. The root cause is the incorrect pointer arithmetic in the trailing-byte handling, not merely an out-of-bounds read; the writes to *dst8 can exceed the buffer, matching out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop writes words and then trailing bytes into a heap buffer sized to c, but the trailing-byte logic uses a pre-decrement on the source pointer and can cause the destination pointer to advance past the allocated c bytes when c is not word-aligned. This out-of-bounds write into the kmalloc buffer corrupts kernel heap memory, and the crash reported (page fault at an address near the framebuffer end) is a consequence of the read/write pointer mismatch.

commit_msg: [FIX] revisit CVE-2015-8080 vulnerability
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int getnum (const char **fmt, int df) {'], 'added_lines': ['static int getnum (lua_State *L, const char **fmt, int df) {', "      if (a > (INT_MAX / 10) || a * 10 > (INT_MAX - (**fmt - '0')))", '        luaL_error(L, "integral size overflow");']}
description: An integer overflow in the getnum function in lua_struct.c in Redis before 6.0.3 allows context-dependent attackers with permission to run Lua code in a Redis session to cause a denial of service (memory corruption and application crash) or possibly bypass intended sandbox restrictions via a large number, which triggers a stack-based buffer overflow. NOTE: this issue exists because of a CVE-2015-8080 regression.

code_evidence: Line 5 initializes the accumulator a to 0; the do-while loop at lines 6-8 parses consecutive decimal digits without any bound check, computing a = a*10 + digit on line 7. Because a is a signed int and the digit count is attacker-controlled (the number of digits in the format string), a*10 can exceed INT_MAX and wrap to a small or negative value before being returned on line 9.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The parsing loop directly performs a*10 + digit on a signed int without overflow checking, so a large digit string causes wraparound, matching CWE-190's integer overflow/wraparound definition. It is the missing constraint in the arithmetic itself, not merely a downstream buffer error, that constitutes the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unbounded integer accumulation in the digit-parsing loop, with no check that a*10 + digit stays within INT_MAX. Trigger: a format string containing a sufficiently long run of digits, which the attacker controls via Lua struct calls. Consequence: signed integer wraparound yields a small or negative size value that later drives buffer sizing, enabling memory corruption, crash, or sandbox bypass.

struct dbus_info *info = handler ? handler->opaque : NULL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: find_handler_by_subtype can return an internal handler whose opaque field is NULL, making info NULL. The function then proceeds through dbus_unexport_handler and tcmur_unregister_handler and dereferences info->watcher_id, triggering a crash (DoS) when UnregisterHandler is invoked with an internal subtype such as qcow. The patch adds an _is_dbus_handler check to reject internal handlers before this path.

commit_msg:
Limit the number of HTTP requests processed from a connection in I/O cycle

Signed-off-by: Yan Avlasov <yavlasov@google.com>

Signed-off-by: Ryan Northey <ryan@synca.io>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  requests_during_dispatch_count_ = 0;']}
description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

code_evidence: onData initializes requests_during_dispatch_count_ to 0 before codec creation, then enters a do/while loop that repeatedly calls codec_->dispatch(data) and only redispatches on HTTP/1.1 conditions.
The loop has no per-cycle cap on the number of dispatch iterations; the added counter reset is not enforced here, so dispatch can process many requests/streams from one I/O cycle.
The while(redispatch) loop continues without any throttle tied to requests_during_dispatch_count_.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the code fails to throttle resource consumption (dispatch iterations) in onData, matching lack of throttling for allocated resources; it is not a memory-safety or protocol-parsing flaw.

evidence_lines.code: } while (redispatch);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function lacks a bound on work performed per I/O cycle, and the reset of requests_during_dispatch_count_ is not accompanied by enforcement in this function. Trigger: a client sends many HTTP/2 streams/cancellations that codec_->dispatch processes in one cycle. Consequence: unbounded CPU/memory consumption per connection cycle, enabling denial of service.

commit_msg: disable CNAME uncloaking when a proxy extension with a socks fallback is enabled
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        net::ProxyConfig::ProxyRules::Type::PROXY_LIST) {'], 'added_lines': ['            net::ProxyConfig::ProxyRules::Type::PROXY_LIST ||', '        (config.value().proxy_rules().type ==', '             net::ProxyConfig::ProxyRules::Type::PROXY_LIST_PER_SCHEME &&', '         !config.value().proxy_rules().fallback_proxies.IsEmpty())) {']}
description: In Brave Desktop 1.17 through 1.33 before 1.33.106, when CNAME-based adblocking and a proxying extension with a SOCKS fallback are enabled, additional DNS requests are issued outside of the proxying extension using the system's DNS settings, resulting in information disclosure. NOTE: this issue exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2021-21323 and CVE-2021-22916.

code_evidence: The function reads the current proxy configuration and sets can_uncloak=false only when the rules type equals PROXY_LIST. The patched condition now also disables uncloaking for PROXY_LIST_PER_SCHEME with non-empty fallback_proxies; before the fix, a per-scheme config with a SOCKS fallback left can_uncloak true.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is confidentiality loss: DNS lookups escape the intended proxy path, revealing sensitive network/request metadata to unauthorized parties. CWE-200 fits the direct information-disclosure behavior; the function gates that exposure rather than causing memory corruption or code execution.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the uncloaking gate recognized only one proxy-rules type, so a proxying extension configured per-scheme with a SOCKS fallback was not treated as protecting DNS. Trigger: CNAME-based adblocking plus such a proxy configuration. Consequence: CNAME resolution/DNS requests are issued using system DNS settings outside the proxy, disclosing queried names and network configuration to observers.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsch->q.qlen--;', '\tagg_dequeue(in_serv_agg, cl, len);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsch->q.qlen--;', '', '\tskb = agg_dequeue(in_serv_agg, cl, len);', '', '\tif (!skb) {', '\t\tsch->q.qlen++;', '\t\treturn NULL;', '\t}', '']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's net/sched: sch_qfq component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

When the plug qdisc is used as a class of the qfq qdisc, sending network packets triggers use-after-free in qfq_dequeue() due to the incorrect .peek handler of sch_plug and lack of error checking in agg_dequeue().

We recommend upgrading past commit 8fc134fee27f2263988ae38920bc03da416b03d8.

code_evidence: qfq_peek_skb() only peeks the skb; len may be nonzero while the peeked skb is NULL (e.g., plug qdisc's .peek handler), so the len==0 check does not guarantee skb validity.
After the !skb guard, the code decrements q.qlen and calls agg_dequeue(), whose return value is ignored; the function returns the stale peeked skb even if agg_dequeue() failed and freed/dropped it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function returns a pointer to an skb that agg_dequeue() may have freed, and callers then access it, matching CWE-416 use after free. The missing check on agg_dequeue()'s return value is distinct from a mere NULL dereference.

evidence_lines.code:
skb = qfq_peek_skb(in_serv_agg, &cl, &len);
if (len == 0 || in_serv_agg->budget < len) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: qfq_dequeue trusts qfq_peek_skb and ignores the return value of agg_dequeue(). Trigger: a plug qdisc used as a qfq class causes agg_dequeue() to fail and free the skb, yet qfq_dequeue returns that pointer. Consequence: subsequent use of the freed skb yields a slab use-after-free, as reported in qfq_dequeue.

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: remove nodes owned by destroyed domain

In case a domain is removed from Xenstore, remove all nodes owned by
it per default.

This tackles the problem that nodes might be created by a domain
outside its home path in Xenstore, leading to Xenstore hogging more
and more memory. Domain quota don't work in this case if the guest is
rebooting in between.

Since XSA-322 ownership of such stale nodes is transferred to dom0,
which is helping against unintended access, but not against OOM of
Xenstore.

As a fallback for weird cases add a Xenstore start parameter for
keeping today's way to handle stale nodes, adding the risk of Xenstore
hitting an OOM situation.

This is part of XSA-419 / CVE-2022-42322.

Fixes: 496306324d8d ("tools/xenstore: revoke access rights for removed domains")
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (domain_adjust_node_perms(conn, node))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (domain_adjust_node_perms(node))']}
description: Xenstore: Cooperating guests can create arbitrary numbers of nodes T[his CNA information record relates to multiple CVEs; the text explains which aspects/vulnerabilities correspond to which CVE.] Since the fix of XSA-322 any Xenstore node owned by a removed domain will be modified to be owned by Dom0. This will allow two malicious guests working together to create an arbitrary number of Xenstore nodes. This is possible by domain A letting domain B write into domain A's local Xenstore tree. Domain B can then create many nodes and reboot. The nodes created by domain B will now be owned by Dom0. By repeating this process over and over again an arbitrary number of nodes can be created, as Dom0's number of nodes isn't limited by Xenstore quota.

code_evidence: read_node allocates node via talloc(ctx, struct node) at line 8 and returns NULL on allocation failure.
After loading the record, domain_adjust_node_perms result is checked at line 43; on failure it jumps to the error label at line 44.
The error path saves errno, talloc_free(node) at line 54, and returns NULL, so the node allocation is released on this path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 requires allocated memory to remain unreleased after its lifetime. Since the only allocation at line 8 is freed at line 54 on every error jump and returned on success, the function does not exhibit an unreleased-memory condition; the described node-accumulation issue stems from cross-domain ownership handling, not from a leak in this function.

evidence_lines.code:
if (domain_adjust_node_perms(conn, node))
goto error;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function allocates a node and frees it via the shared error label on the adjust-perms failure path; the changed call at line 43 only drops the unused conn argument. No path in this function abandons the allocation without talloc_free, so there is no missing release here.

commit_msg:
write_wakeup can happen in parallel with close/hangup where tty->disc_data
is set to NULL and the netdevice is freed thus also freeing
disc_data. write_wakeup accesses disc_data so we must prevent close from
freeing the netdev while write_wakeup has a non-NULL view of
tty->disc_data.

We also need to make sure that accesses to disc_data are atomic. Which can
all be done with RCU.

This problem was found by Syzkaller on SLCAN, but the same issue is
reproducible with the SLIP line discipline using an LTP test based on the
Syzkaller reproducer.

A fix which didn't use RCU was posted by Hillf Danton.

Fixes: 661f7fda21b1 ("slip: Fix deadlock in write_wakeup")
Fixes: a8e83b17536a ("slcan: Port write_wakeup deadlock fix from slip")
Reported-by: syzbot+017e491ae13c0068598a@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Richard Palethorpe <rpalethorpe@suse.com>
Cc: Wolfgang Grandegger <wg@grandegger.com>
Cc: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
Cc: "David S. Miller" <davem@davemloft.net>
Cc: Tyler Hall <tylerwhall@gmail.com>
Cc: linux-can@vger.kernel.org
Cc: netdev@vger.kernel.org
Cc: linux-kernel@vger.kernel.org
Cc: syzkaller@googlegroups.com
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct slcan *sl = tty->disc_data;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct slcan *sl;', '', '\trcu_read_lock();', '\tsl = rcu_dereference(tty->disc_data);', '\tif (!sl)', '\t\tgoto out;', 'out:', '\trcu_read_unlock();']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.4.16, a race condition in tty->disc_data handling in the slip and slcan line discipline could lead to a use-after-free, aka CID-0ace17d56824. This affects drivers/net/slip/slip.c and drivers/net/can/slcan.c.

code_evidence: Line 3 reads the shared tty->disc_data into sl without any lock or RCU protection, then line 4 immediately dereferences sl to schedule work. Another concurrent code sequence (close/hangup) can set disc_data to NULL and free the netdev, making this read-then-use non-atomic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because concurrent execution of write_wakeup and close/hangup violates exclusivity/atomicity on the shared tty->disc_data resource. The missing synchronization (no lock/RCU) is the race; the use-after-free is the resulting consequence rather than a separate weakness class.

evidence_lines.code:
struct slcan *sl = tty->disc_data;
schedule_work(&sl->tx_work);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unsynchronized read of tty->disc_data and subsequent dereference are not atomic with respect to close/hangup freeing the structure. Trigger: write_wakeup runs in parallel with close/hangup, which NULLs disc_data and frees the netdev. Consequence: use-after-free/dereference of a freed sl pointer, causing instability or crash.

commit_msg:
checkpath: fix CVE-2018-21269

This walks the directory path to the file we are going to manipulate to make
sure that when we create the file and change the ownership and permissions
we are working on the same file.
Also, all non-terminal symbolic links must be owned by root. This will
keep a non-root user from making a symbolic link as described in the
bug. If root creates the symbolic link, it is assumed to be trusted.

On non-linux platforms, we no longer follow non-terminal symbolic links
by default. If you need to do that, add the -s option on the checkpath
command line, but keep in mind that this is not secure.

This fixes #201.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tinode_t type, bool trunc, bool chowner, bool selinux_on)', '\treadfd = open(path, readflags);', '\t\t\tfd = open(path, flags, mode);', '\t\t\treadfd = open(path, readflags);', '\t\t\treadfd = open(path, readflags);'], 'added_lines': ['\tinode_t type, bool trunc, bool chowner, bool symlinks, bool selinux_on)', '\tchar *name = NULL;', '\tint dirfd;', '\txasprintf(&name, "%s", basename_c(path));', '\tdirfd = get_dirfd(path, symlinks);', '\treadfd = openat(dirfd, name, readflags);', '\t\t\tfd = openat(dirfd, name, flags, mode);', '\t\t\treadfd = openat(dirfd, name, readflags);', '\t\t\treadfd = openat(dirfd, name, readflags);']}
description: checkpath in OpenRC through 0.42.1 might allow local users to take ownership of arbitrary files because a non-terminal path component can be a symlink.

code_evidence: do_check opens the caller-supplied path directly with open(path, readflags) and open(path, flags, mode); the path is used as-is without resolving or validating each component, so a non-terminal component that is a symlink is followed to the link target.
The mkdir/mkfifo branches also re-open the same path afterward (open(path, readflags)) rather than operating on a verified descriptor, so the object acted on can differ from the one created.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper link resolution before file access: path-based open/create/mkdir/mkfifo calls follow attacker-controlled symlinks. This is link following (CWE-59), not merely a race condition, because the defect is that link resolution is not prevented at all.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the whole path and performs file creation, opening, chmod and chown through path-based calls that follow symbolic links. Trigger: a local user makes a non-terminal path component a symlink pointing at a file they do not own. Consequence: the privileged process creates/modifies/chowns the link target, allowing ownership or mode changes on arbitrary files.

description: ImageMagick is free software delivered as a ready-to-run binary distribution or as source code that you may use, copy, modify, and distribute in both open and proprietary applications. In affected versions and in certain cases, Postscript files could be read and written when specifically excluded by a `module` policy in `policy.xml`. ex. <policy domain="module" rights="none" pattern="PS" />. The issue has been resolved in ImageMagick 7.1.0-7 and in 6.9.12-22. Fortunately, in the wild, few users utilize the `module` policy and instead use the `coder` policy that is also our workaround recommendation: <policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="{PS,EPI,EPS,EPSF,EPSI}" />.

code_evidence: The module name is resolved via GetCoderInfo and normalized to the canonical coder name (lines 16-18), then the authorization check uses rights=ReadPolicyRights (line 19) and rejects only when IsRightsAuthorized returns MagickFalse (line 20). With ReadPolicyRights, a policy granting read but denying other rights (e.g. module pattern PS with rights=none) is not fully honored, so the module registration proceeds for coder names that the policy intended to exclude.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The insufficient rights check lets the module coder escape the control sphere defined by policy.xml, exposing Postscript read/write to unintended parties, which matches CWE-668's exposure of a resource to the wrong sphere. It is not merely improper authorization of a single user; the resource (module capability) is exposed beyond the intended policy boundary.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the policy check evaluates only read rights rather than the full set of module rights, so a module excluded by a module-domain policy (rights=none) still passes IsRightsAuthorized. Trigger: a policy.xml restricting a coder such as PS. Consequence: PostScript coders remain registered and usable, exposing file read/write to actors the policy meant to block.

commit_msg:
misc: update: fix buffer overflow in updater

On 32 bit builds, parsing of update status files with a size of
4294967295 or more lead to an integer truncation in a call to malloc
and a subsequent buffer overflow. This happened prior to checking the
files' signature. The commit fixes this by disallowing overly large
status files (above 65k in practice)

Signed-off-by: Jean-Baptiste Kempf <jb@videolan.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if( i_read < 0 || i_read >= UINT16_MAX)', '    {', '        msg_Err(p_update->p_libvlc, "Status file too large");', '        goto error;', '    }', '']}
description: The GetUpdateFile function in misc/update.c in the Updater in VideoLAN VLC media player before 2.1.6 performs an incorrect cast operation from a 64-bit integer to a 32-bit integer, which allows remote attackers to conduct buffer overflow attacks and execute arbitrary code via a crafted update status file, aka an "integer truncation" vulnerability.

code_evidence: i_read is a signed 64-bit size obtained from the remote stream; it is passed to malloc after adding 1 without any upper-bound or negative check.
stream_Read copies i_read bytes into the heap buffer sized from the possibly truncated malloc argument, and i_read is later used to write the '\0' terminator at psz_update_data[i_read].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a buffer copy (stream_Read and terminator write) into an undersized output buffer without validating that the input size fits the allocation, matching CWE-120's classic buffer copy without size checking. The integer truncation at malloc is the mechanism enabling the out-of-bounds write rather than a separate CWE.

evidence_lines.code:
const int64_t i_read = stream_Size( p_stream );
psz_update_data = malloc( i_read + 1 );

if( stream_Read( p_stream, psz_update_data, i_read ) != i_read )
psz_update_data[i_read] = '\0';

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the 64-bit i_read is implicitly truncated when used as a 32-bit malloc size, so malloc allocates a much smaller buffer than i_read. Trigger: a crafted status file with size 4294967295 or more (e.g. i_read+1 wrapping to 0). The subsequent stream_Read and terminator write then copy/write past the allocation, corrupting heap memory before signature checks occur.

commit_msg:
Don't change the state of the ETM flags until CCS processing

Changing the ciphersuite during a renegotiation can result in a crash
leading to a DoS attack. ETM has not been implemented in 1.1.0 for DTLS
so this is TLS only.

The problem is caused by changing the flag indicating whether to use ETM
or not immediately on negotiation of ETM, rather than at CCS. Therefore,
during a renegotiation, if the ETM state is changing (usually due to a
change of ciphersuite), then an error/crash will occur.

Due to the fact that there are separate CCS messages for read and write
we actually now need two flags to determine whether to use ETM or not.

CVE-2017-3733

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    s->s3->flags &= ~TLS1_FLAGS_ENCRYPT_THEN_MAC;', '            s->s3->flags |= TLS1_FLAGS_ENCRYPT_THEN_MAC;'], 'added_lines': ['    s->tlsext_use_etm = 0;', '            s->tlsext_use_etm = 1;']}

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function parses the encrypt_then_mac extension and sets a flag without any input validation flaw; the defect is premature state change before CCS processing, a state-management/timing issue not improper input validation.

commit_msg:
md_rollback: Do not touch TABLECELLBOUNDARIES chain.

This chain is not normal opener/closer inline mark chain.

Fixes #42.

', '     * (start at 1 to not touch PTR_CHAIN.) */', '    for(i = 1; i < SIZEOF_ARRAY(ctx->mark_chains); i++) {'], 'added_lines': ['    /* Cut all unresolved openers at the mark index. */', '    for(i = OPENERS_CHAIN_FIRST; i < OPENERS_CHAIN_LAST+1; i++) {']}
description: md_build_attribute in md4c.c in md4c 0.2.6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (Segmentation fault and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted file.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over every entry of ctx->mark_chains from index 1 to SIZEOF_ARRAY-1, including the TABLECELLBOUNDARIES chain which is not an opener/closer inline mark chain. For each such chain it walks chain->tail backward via ctx->marks[chain->tail].prev (lines 8-9) and then writes ctx->marks[chain->tail].next = -1 (line 11). Because the table-cell chain is not managed as an opener chain, its tail/prev links are not valid mark indices, so the index used to dereference ctx->marks[] can be out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs memory operations on ctx->marks[] using indices derived from a chain it should not touch, i.e. operations outside the intended buffer boundary. This matches CWE-119; the more specific out-of-bounds child weakness is consistent with it, and the crash is the resultant impact.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: md_rollback treats all mark chains as opener chains and mutates their tail/next links. Trigger: a crafted document producing a table-cell-boundaries chain, followed by a rollback call. Consequence: ctx->marks[chain->tail] is accessed with an invalid index, causing an out-of-bounds read/write and a segmentation-fault crash (DoS).

description: Buffer Overflow found in Nginx NJS allows a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the njs_object_property parameter of the njs/njs_vm.c function.

code_evidence: array is allocated with capacity length (line 14) and the copy loop is entered whenever length != 0 (line 19). For the array branch, source values are copied element-by-element into array->start[n++] (line 24) with no check that the source array actually holds length elements from start.

The object branch writes into array->start[n++] (line 58) and calls njs_value_property for each index, decrementing length; an invalid property sets njs_value_invalid (line 61). Writes are bounded by the allocated length, but the source read extent depends on start/length.

Here the destination is sized to length and the loops are bounded by length, so the missing check concerns source read bounds rather than destination overflow; the patch addresses uncopied primitive types. This is closer to an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) than a classic unchecked destination buffer copy, so the evidence does not directly support CWE-120.

commit_msg:
mnt: Honor MNT_LOCKED when detaching mounts

Modify umount(MNT_DETACH) to keep mounts in the hash table that are
locked to their parent mounts, when the parent is lazily unmounted.

In mntput_no_expire detach the children from the hash table, depending
on mnt_pin_kill in cleanup_mnt to decrement the mnt_count of the children.

In __detach_mounts if there are any mounts that have been unmounted
but still are on the list of mounts of a mountpoint, remove their
children from the mount hash table and those children to the unmounted
list so they won't linger potentially indefinitely waiting for their
final mntput, now that the mounts serve no purpose.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tumount_tree(mnt, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (mnt->mnt.mnt_flags & MNT_UMOUNT) {', '\t\t\tstruct mount *p, *tmp;', '\t\t\tlist_for_each_entry_safe(p, tmp, &mnt->mnt_mounts,  mnt_child) {', '\t\t\t\thlist_add_head(&p->mnt_umount.s_list, &unmounted);', '\t\t\t\tumount_mnt(p);', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t}', '\t\telse umount_tree(mnt, 0);']}
description: fs/namespace.c in the Linux kernel before 4.0.2 processes MNT_DETACH umount2 system calls without verifying that the MNT_LOCKED flag is unset, which allows local users to bypass intended access restrictions and navigate to filesystem locations beneath a mount by calling umount2 within a user namespace.

code_evidence: The loop detaches every mount on mp->m_list by calling umount_tree(mnt, 0) unconditionally; it never inspects mnt_flags for MNT_LOCKED before removing the mount.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to enforce an access restriction (MNT_LOCKED) during mount detachment, which is precisely an enforcement failure of the intended access-control policy, matching CWE-284. It is not a memory-safety issue; the weakness is missing restriction of a resource operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: __detach_mounts force-unmounts and detaches locked mounts without checking MNT_LOCKED, so the lock intended to protect a mount from removal by a user namespace is not enforced. Trigger: a local user in a user namespace issues umount2 with MNT_DETACH against a parent mountpoint, reaching this detach path. Consequence: the access restriction is bypassed, letting the user navigate beneath a mount that should have remained locked.

commit_msg:
Fix GPU/CPU Conv2DBackpropInputOp check error.

For empty `out_backprop` inputs (e.g. `[3, 1, 0, 1]`), the current
CPU/GPU kernels fail (one with dnnl, the other with cudnn). Added
a shortcut path to return a zero input.

Note that the XLA test currently fails due to an incorrect result
size bug (b/239598470), so it is currently disabled.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 462217998
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    // If shapes are valid but `out_backprop` is empty, in_backprop should be', '    // set to all zeros.  Otherwise, cudnn/dnnl fail with an empty input.', '    if (out_backprop.NumElements() == 0) {', '      functor::SetZeroFunctor<Device, T> set_zero;', '      set_zero(context->eigen_device<Device>(),', '               in_backprop->template flat<T>());', '      return;', '    }', '']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. When `Conv2DBackpropInput` receives empty `out_backprop` inputs (e.g. `[3, 1, 0, 1]`), the current CPU/GPU kernels `CHECK` fail (one with dnnl, the other with cudnn). This can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 27a65a43cf763897fecfa5cdb5cc653fc5dd0346. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: Lines 32-34 only short-circuit when the computed input_shape has zero elements, not when out_backprop is empty; with an empty out_backprop (e.g. [3,1,0,1]) execution continues past this guard.
Lines 105-108 then enforce work_unit_size > 0 via OP_REQUIRES, but dims derived from the empty out_backprop yield work_unit_size == 0, so this check fails.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because an attacker-controlled empty out_backprop triggers a fatal assertion-style check (work_unit_size > 0) that aborts the process rather than returning a normal error/zero result. The fix adds an explicit empty-input path, confirming the assertion was reachable and the cause of the DoS.

evidence_lines.code:
OP_REQUIRES(
context, work_unit_size > 0,
errors::InvalidArgument("input, filter_sizes and out_backprop tensors "
"must all have at least 1 element"));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function derives convolution dimensions from a caller-supplied out_backprop shape but only guards on input_shape.num_elements()==0. An empty out_backprop with valid shapes slips past that guard, reaching the work_unit_size>0 check which fails, terminating the op (CHECK/OP_REQUIRES failure) and crashing the process — a reachable assertion leading to denial of service.

commit_msg:
x86: avoid leaking PKRU and BND* between vCPU-s

PKRU is explicitly "XSAVE-managed but not XSAVE-enabled", so guests
might access the register (via {RD,WR}PKRU) without setting XCR0.PKRU.
Force context switching as well as migrating the register as soon as
CR4.PKE is being set the first time.

For MPX (BND<n>, BNDCFGU, and BNDSTATUS) the situation is less clear,
and the SDM has not entirely consistent information for that case.
While experimentally the instructions don't change register state as
long as the two XCR0 bits aren't both 1, be on the safe side and enable
both if BNDCFGS.EN is being set the first time.

This is XSA-220.

Reported-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    /*', '     * {RD,WR}PKRU are not gated on XCR0.PKRU and hence an oddly behaving', '     * guest may enable the feature in CR4 without enabling it in XCR0. We', '     * need to context switch / migrate PKRU nevertheless.', '     */', '    if ( (value & X86_CR4_PKE) && !(v->arch.xcr0_accum & XSTATE_PKRU) )', '    {', '        int rc = handle_xsetbv(XCR_XFEATURE_ENABLED_MASK,', '                               get_xcr0() | XSTATE_PKRU);', '', '        if ( rc )', '        {', '            HVM_DBG_LOG(DBG_LEVEL_1, "Failed to force XCR0.PKRU: %d", rc);', '            return X86EMUL_EXCEPTION;', '        }', '', '        if ( handle_xsetbv(XCR_XFEATURE_ENABLED_MASK,', '                           get_xcr0() & ~XSTATE_PKRU) )', '            /* nothing, best effort only */;', '    }', '']}
description: The vCPU context-switch implementation in Xen through 4.8.x improperly interacts with the Memory Protection Extensions (MPX) and Protection Key (PKU) features, which makes it easier for guest OS users to defeat ASLR and other protection mechanisms, aka XSA-220.

code_evidence: After hvm_update_cr(v, 4, value) commits the guest CR4, the only conditional context-switch/migration path is gated on changes to PSE, PGE, PAE, SMEP, or clearing PCIDE; CR4.PKE is absent from this mask, so setting CR4.PKE does not force PKRU state to be switched or migrated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing CR4.PKE handling lets one vCPU observe another context's PKRU value, i.e., sensitive internal state exposed to an unauthorized guest actor, matching CWE-200. The weakness is the disclosure of another context's register state, not merely a policy bypass.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the CR4-change handler does not treat enabling CR4.PKE as requiring PKRU context switch/migration, because PKRU is not gated on XCR0.PKRU. Trigger: a guest sets CR4.PKE without XCR0.PKRU and accesses PKRU. Consequence: stale PKRU state from another vCPU can be observed, leaking cross-context register contents and weakening protection keys/ASLR.

commit_msg: [http2] delay processing requests upon observing suspicious behavior

description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

commit_msg:
Do not use "/bin/sh" to run external commands.

Picocom no longer uses /bin/sh to run external commands for
file-transfer operations. Parsing the command line and spliting it into
arguments is now performed internally by picocom, using quoting rules
very similar to those of the Unix shell. Hopefully, this makes it
impossible to inject shell-commands when supplying filenames or
extra arguments to the send- and receive-file commands.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\trun_cmd(tty_fd, xfr_cmd, fname, NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\trun_cmd(tty_fd, xfr_cmd, fname);']}
description: picocom before 2.0 has a command injection vulnerability in the 'send and receive file' command because the command line is executed by /bin/sh unsafely.

code_evidence: In the KEY_SEND/KEY_RECEIVE handler, xfr_cmd is taken from opts.send_cmd/opts.receive_cmd (line 103), and fname comes from read_filename() (line 108). Both flow into run_cmd(tty_fd, xfr_cmd, fname, NULL) at line 113, which the commit states executes via /bin/sh; the function passes the filename without neutralization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-77 fits because externally-influenced filename data becomes part of a command executed downstream without neutralization of special elements. The patch removing the /bin/sh invocation and the NULL argument confirms the command-construction weakness; this is the general command-injection class rather than a mere argument-parsing bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: do_command forwards the user-supplied filename (and configured transfer command) to run_cmd, which builds and executes a shell command string. Trigger: a filename or extra argument containing shell metacharacters (e.g., ;, $(), backticks) is entered at the send/receive prompt. Consequence: arbitrary shell command execution with the privileges of the picocom process.

commit_msg:

description: libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-06-01 allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, as demonstrated by obtaining Signature or SignatureOrSystem access, aka internal bug 27833616.

commit_msg: Extend stack when pushing arguments that does not fit in; fix #4038
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (resume && c->status == MRB_FIBER_TRANSFERRED) {', '  if (c->status == MRB_FIBER_RUNNING || c->status == MRB_FIBER_RESUMED) {', '  if (c->status == MRB_FIBER_TERMINATED) {', '  mrb->c->status = resume ? MRB_FIBER_RESUMED : MRB_FIBER_TRANSFERRED;', '  if (c->status == MRB_FIBER_CREATED) {', '    if (len >= c->stend - c->stack) {', '      mrb_raise(mrb, E_FIBER_ERROR, "too many arguments to fiber");', '    }', '  fiber_switch_context(mrb, c);'], 'added_lines': ['  enum mrb_fiber_state status;', '  status = c->status;', '  if (resume && status == MRB_FIBER_TRANSFERRED) {', '  if (status == MRB_FIBER_RUNNING || status == MRB_FIBER_RESUMED) {', '  if (status == MRB_FIBER_TERMINATED) {', '  old_c->status = resume ? MRB_FIBER_RESUMED : MRB_FIBER_TRANSFERRED;', '  fiber_switch_context(mrb, c);', '  if (status == MRB_FIBER_CREATED) {', '    mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2); /* for receiver and (optional) block */']}
description: An issue was discovered in mruby 1.4.1. There is a heap-based buffer over-read associated with OP_ENTER because mrbgems/mruby-fiber/src/fiber.c does not extend the stack in cases of many arguments to fiber.

code_evidence: In the MRB_FIBER_CREATED branch, the function only checks whether len exceeds the fiber stack capacity (c->stend - c->stack) and raises an error if so; it never extends the stack. It then sets b = c->stack+1 and copies len values from a into the fiber stack via *b++ = *a++. When len is smaller than the capacity check but the destination region is not actually allocated/large enough, the copy reads/writes beyond the intended stack buffer, supporting an out-of-bounds access associated with OP_ENTER.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch replaces the fixed 'too many arguments' guard with mrb_stack_extend, indicating the prior code performed the argument copy without ensuring the destination stack was large enough, i.e., an out-of-bounds read/access. This matches CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read) as the target weakness; the essential defect is missing bounds/extension before reading/copying into the stack.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the fiber stack is not extended for the incoming argument count before the copy loop; the code relies on a size comparison rather than allocating adequate space. Trigger: resuming a created fiber with many arguments so the destination stack region is insufficient. Consequence: out-of-bounds memory access (read/write) on the fiber stack, consistent with the reported heap-based buffer over-read.

commit_msg:
fix segfault in "lru" command

fixes #474 - off by one in token count.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    } else if (strcmp(tokens[1].value, "mode") == 0 && ntokens >= 3 &&', '    } else if (strcmp(tokens[1].value, "temp_ttl") == 0 && ntokens >= 3 &&'], 'added_lines': ['    } else if (strcmp(tokens[1].value, "mode") == 0 && ntokens >= 4 &&', '    } else if (strcmp(tokens[1].value, "temp_ttl") == 0 && ntokens >= 4 &&']}
description: In memcached before 1.5.14, a NULL pointer dereference was found in the "lru mode" and "lru temp_ttl" commands. This causes a denial of service when parsing crafted lru command messages in process_lru_command in memcached.c.

code_evidence: The "mode" branch checks ntokens >= 3, then dereferences tokens[2].value; the "temp_ttl" branch likewise gates on ntokens >= 3 but reads tokens[2].value.
With the off-by-one guard, a crafted lru command can satisfy the ntokens >= 3 condition while tokens[2] is not a valid populated token, so the dereference targets a NULL or absent token value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (tokens[2].value) expected to be valid but NULL due to the insufficient length check. This is a direct NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476); the token-count error is the cause, the NULL dereference the supported weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an incorrect token-count boundary (ntokens >= 3 instead of >= 4) before accessing tokens[2]. A crafted lru mode/temp_ttl message with too few tokens reaches strcmp/safe_strtol on an unpopulated token, dereferencing NULL and crashing the server (DoS).

commit_msg:
xen/hypercall: Don't use BUG() for parameter checking in hypercall_create_continuation()

Since c/s 1d429034 "hypercall: update vcpu_op to take an unsigned vcpuid",
which incorrectly swapped 'i' for 'u' in the parameter type list, guests have
been able to hit the BUG() in next_args()'s default case.

Correct these back to 'i'.

In addition, make adjustments to prevent this class of issue from occurring in
the future - crashing Xen is not an appropriate form of parameter checking.

Capitalise NEXT_ARG() to catch all uses, to highlight that it is a macro doing
non-function-like things behind the scenes, and undef it when appropriate.
Implement a bad_fmt: block which prints an error, asserts unreachable, and
crashes the guest.

On the ARM side, drop all parameter checking of p.  It is asymmetric with the
x86 side, and akin to expecting memcpy() or sprintf() to check their src/fmt
parameter before use.  A caller passing "" or something other than a string
literal will be obvious during code review.

This is XSA-296.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* All hypercalls take at least one argument */', "    BUG_ON( !p || *p == '\\0' );", '', '            mcs->call.args[i] = next_arg(p, args);', '                arg = next_arg(p, args);', '                arg = next_arg(p, args);'], 'added_lines': ['            mcs->call.args[i] = NEXT_ARG(p, args);', '                arg = NEXT_ARG(p, args);', '                arg = NEXT_ARG(p, args);', '', ' bad_fmt:', '    gprintk(XENLOG_ERR, "Bad hypercall continuation format \'%c\'\\n", *p);', '    ASSERT_UNREACHABLE();', '    domain_crash(current->domain);', '    return 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service via a VCPUOP_initialise hypercall. hypercall_create_continuation() is a variadic function which uses a printf-like format string to interpret its parameters. Error handling for a bad format character was done using BUG(), which crashes Xen. One path, via the VCPUOP_initialise hypercall, has a bad format character. The BUG() can be hit if VCPUOP_initialise executes for a sufficiently long period of time for a continuation to be created. Malicious guests may cause a hypervisor crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS). Xen versions 4.6 and newer are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.5 and earlier are not vulnerable. Only x86 PV guests can exploit the vulnerability. HVM and PVH guests, and guests on ARM systems, cannot exploit the vulnerability.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function interprets a hard-coded format string supplied by hypervisor callers, not an externally-controlled format string; the described flaw is a BUG() crash on an unexpected format character, not CWE-134.

commit_msg:
iwlwifi: Sanity check for sta_id

On my testing, I saw some strange behavior

[  421.739708] iwlwifi 0000:01:00.0: ACTIVATE a non DRIVER active station id 148 addr 00:00:00:00:00:00
[  421.739719] iwlwifi 0000:01:00.0: iwl_sta_ucode_activate Added STA id 148 addr 00:00:00:00:00:00 to uCode

not sure how it happen, but adding the sanity check to prevent memory
corruption

Signed-off-by: Wey-Yi Guy <wey-yi.w.guy@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: John W. Linville <linville@tuxdriver.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tiwl_sta_ucode_activate(priv, sta_id);', '\t\tret = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tret = iwl_sta_ucode_activate(priv, sta_id);']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 3.4, a buffer overflow occurs in drivers/net/wireless/iwlwifi/iwl-agn-sta.c, which will cause at least memory corruption.

code_evidence: sta_id is taken from addsta->sta.sta_id and used as an index into priv->stations[sta_id] without a bounds check against the station table size.
After the ADD_STA_SUCCESS_MSK path calls iwl_sta_ucode_activate(priv, sta_id) and sets ret=0, execution continues to the debug block that reads priv->stations[sta_id].sta.mode and .sta.addr.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked sta_id causes reads and writes outside the intended priv->stations buffer, which is the out-of-bounds memory operation described by CWE-119. This is not merely an integer issue; the defect is missing bounds restriction on the array index.

evidence_lines.code:
IWL_DEBUG_INFO(priv, "%s station id %u addr %pM\n",
priv->stations[sta_id].sta.mode ==
STA_CONTROL_MODIFY_MSK ?  "Modified" : "Added",
sta_id, priv->stations[sta_id].sta.sta.addr);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the response handler trusts the firmware-supplied sta_id and indexes the fixed station array with it, and the success path unconditionally proceeds to read array fields. Trigger: a malformed or unexpected REPLY_ADD_STA response with an out-of-range sta_id (e.g., 148) reaches the success or default path. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads/writes on the station table, leading to memory corruption as described.

commit_msg: v1.0.5: fix buffer overrun when reading bad WebPs
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if(l <= 12', '#ifdef SSIZE_MAX', '    || l - 12 > SSIZE_MAX', '#endif', '  ) {', '    PF("ERROR reading %s: %s", IP, k[2]);', '    goto w2p_close;', '  }']}
description: png2webp v1.0.4 was discovered to contain an out-of-bounds write via the function w2p. This vulnerability is exploitable via a crafted png file.

code_evidence: Line 19 computes the allocation length l from attacker-controlled RIFF bytes i[4..7] as a uint32 value plus 8; line 20 allocates exactly l bytes into x.

Line 25 copies 12 bytes into x, then calls fread(x + 12, l - 12, 1, fp). When l < 12, the size expression l - 12 underflows as size_t, and the destination x + 12 is already past the small malloc(l) buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing past the end of the malloc(l) buffer via the unchecked l - 12 size is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The integer underflow is the enabling cause, but the supported consequence is memory written outside the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the header-derived length l is used for malloc and for the fread size/offset without validating that l exceeds the 12-byte RIFF header. A crafted WebP with a tiny RIFF size field makes l - 12 wrap to a huge size_t, so fread writes beyond the allocated buffer, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg:
x86: Check for valid PLT section size

Update x86 get_synthetic_symtab to check for valid PLT section size
before examining PLT section contents.

	PR binutils/22018
	* elf32-i386.c (elf_i386_get_synthetic_symtab): Check for valid
	PLT section size.
	* elf64-x86-64.c (elf_x86_64_get_synthetic_symtab): Likewise.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if (plt == NULL)', '      if (plts[j].type == plt_unknown)', '\t  && (plt_type == plt_unknown || plt_type == plt_non_lazy))'], 'added_lines': ['      if (plt == NULL || plt->size == 0)', '      if (plts[j].type == plt_unknown', '\t  && (plt->size >= (lazy_plt->plt_entry_size', '\t\t\t    + lazy_plt->plt_entry_size)))', '\t  && (plt_type == plt_unknown || plt_type == plt_non_lazy)', '\t  && plt->size >= non_lazy_plt->plt_entry_size)', '\t      && plt->size >= non_lazy_bnd_plt->plt_entry_size', '\t\t   && plt->size >= non_lazy_ibt_plt->plt_entry_size', '', '  if (count == 0)', '    return -1;']}
description: The Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, does not validate the PLT section size, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted ELF file, related to elf_i386_get_synthetic_symtab in elf32-i386.c and elf_x86_64_get_synthetic_symtab in elf64-x86-64.c.

code_evidence: The section is fetched and its full size is allocated into plt_contents; the original code only checks plt == NULL before using the contents.
For a .plt section, memcmp reads lazy_plt->plt0_got1_offset bytes from plt_contents without confirming plt->size is at least that large; a tiny section yields an out-of-bounds read.
Non-lazy matching performs memcmp over non_lazy_plt->plt_got_offset bytes with no prior size check.
The BND non-lazy memcmp similarly reads plt_contents with no size validation.
The IBT non-lazy memcmp reads plt_contents without checking plt->size against the entry size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe memcmp operations read beyond the PLT buffer because the section size is not checked against the layout entry offsets, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read rather than an out-of-bounds write.

evidence_lines.code:
if (non_lazy_bnd_plt != NULL
&& (memcmp (plt_contents, non_lazy_bnd_plt->plt_entry,
non_lazy_bnd_plt->plt_got_offset) == 0))

else if (non_lazy_ibt_plt != NULL
&& (memcmp (plt_contents,
non_lazy_ibt_plt->plt_entry,
non_lazy_ibt_plt->plt_got_offset) == 0))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing validation of PLT section size before memcmp on plt_contents. A crafted ELF with a truncated PLT section triggers reads past the allocated buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read and crash (denial of service).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (current->active_mm == mm)', '\t\tset_user_asce(mm);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* we must change all active ASCEs to avoid the creation of new TLBs */', '\tif (current->active_mm == mm) {', '\t\tS390_lowcore.user_asce = mm->context.asce;', '\t\tif (current->thread.mm_segment == USER_DS) {', '\t\t\t__ctl_load(S390_lowcore.user_asce, 1, 1);', '\t\t\t/* Mark user-ASCE present in CR1 */', '\t\t\tclear_cpu_flag(CIF_ASCE_PRIMARY);', '\t\t}', '\t\tif (current->thread.mm_segment == USER_DS_SACF) {', '\t\t\t__ctl_load(S390_lowcore.user_asce, 7, 7);', '\t\t\t/* enable_sacf_uaccess does all or nothing */', '\t\t\tWARN_ON(!test_cpu_flag(CIF_ASCE_SECONDARY));', '\t\t}', '\t}']}
description: In the Linux kernel 4.19 through 5.6.7 on the s390 platform, code execution may occur because of a race condition, as demonstrated by code in enable_sacf_uaccess in arch/s390/lib/uaccess.c that fails to protect against a concurrent page table upgrade, aka CID-3f777e19d171. A crash could also occur.

code_evidence: The function reads current->active_mm and, if it equals the target mm, calls set_user_asce(mm), which updates S390_lowcore.user_asce and loads control registers 1/13 to point at the new page table. This register/ASCE update is performed without any synchronization against another thread on the same CPU that is executing in secondary-space mode (enable_sacf_uaccess / strnlen_user_srst).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a shared per-CPU resource update (user_asce/CR1) that requires exclusive, atomic access relative to the concurrent secondary-space user-access sequence, but no synchronization is enforced, exactly matching CWE-362. It is not merely a missing bounds check; the defect is an unsynchronized timing window between concurrent code sequences.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-CPU control-register/ASCE switch is not coordinated with a concurrently running user-access sequence that has temporarily switched the CPU into secondary address mode. Trigger: an IPI-driven page-table upgrade calls __crst_table_upgrade on a CPU whose current thread is inside enable_sacf_uaccess, so CR1 is changed while instruction fetch still relies on the old mapping. Consequence: after interrupt return the CPU fetches kernel instructions through a stale/mismatched ASCE, enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
Patch OOB write in content-line analyzer.

A combination of packets can trigger an out of bound write of '0' byte
in the content-line analyzer.

This bug was found by Frank Meier.

Addresses BIT-1856.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t// Weird corner-case:', '\t\t\t\t// this can happen if we see a \\r at the end of a packet where crlf is', '\t\t\t\t// set to CR_as_EOL | LF_as_EOL, with the packet causing crlf to be set to', '\t\t\t\t// 0 and the next packet beginning with a \\n. In this case we just swallow', '\t\t\t\t// the character and re-set last_char.', '\t\t\t\tif ( offset == 0 )', '\t\t\t\t\t{', '\t\t\t\t\tlast_char = c;', '\t\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t\t\t}']}
description: Bro before Bro v2.5.2 is vulnerable to an out of bounds write in the ContentLine analyzer allowing remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) and possibly other exploitation.

code_evidence: On a '\n' following a prior '\r', the code decrements offset before EMIT_LINE; when offset is 0 (the \r was consumed at a previous packet boundary), --offset underflows.
EMIT_LINE then writes buf[offset] = '\0' and forwards offset bytes, so the underflowed offset indexes/writes outside the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a direct out-of-bounds write: an unchecked boundary (offset == 0) allows buf[offset] to be written before the buffer start. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read or integer overflow; the faulty index is used by the write in EMIT_LINE.

evidence_lines.code:
buf[offset] = '\0'; \
ForwardStream(offset, buf, IsOrig()); \
offset = 0; \

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the '\n' branch assumes a buffered '\r' exists and unconditionally does --offset without checking offset > 0. Trigger: a packet ending in '\r' followed by a packet starting with '\n' leaves offset == 0 with last_char == '\r'. The decrement wraps offset, and EMIT_LINE writes the '\0' terminator and forwards out-of-bounds data, causing memory corruption/DoS.

Patch for Heap Buffer Overflow in EscapeShell

Proposed patch for bug #71270
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcmd = zend_string_alloc(2 * l, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['\tcmd = zend_string_safe_alloc(2, l, 0, 0);']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in ext/standard/exec.c in PHP 7.x before 7.0.2 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via a long string to the (1) php_escape_shell_cmd or (2) php_escape_shell_arg function, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: l is a signed int from strlen; the allocation size 2*l and estimate (2*l)+1 are computed with plain int arithmetic, so overflow can occur before allocation.
The loop writes into ZSTR_VAL(cmd) at index y; for multibyte sequences memcpy writes mb_len bytes and advances y, with no check that y stays within the allocated buffer.

Each escaped character writes one or two bytes (backslash plus character, or '^' on Windows) via y++, and the terminating NUL is written at ZSTR_VAL(cmd)[y] without any bound check against the allocated length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-189 (Numeric Errors) covers the improper integer calculation: 2*l can overflow in signed int arithmetic, producing an undersized allocation that the subsequent unchecked writes in the loop overrun. This numeric miscalculation is the direct cause of the heap overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the output buffer length is derived from a signed 2*l calculation and the destination index y is never validated against the allocation. A sufficiently long input, or multibyte/escape sequences expanding the output, causes writes past the heap buffer, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow and possible denial of service or code execution.

Detect bad e_shstrtab better.

	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                || (u32_t)file_size <= sh_name  // FIXME: weak', '                    throwCantPack("bad e_shstrndx");'], 'added_lines': ['                || (u32_t)file_size <= (sizeof(".shstrtab")', '                    + sh_name + (shstrtab - (const char *)&file_image[0]))', '                    throwCantPack("bad e_shstrtab");']}
description: An out-of-bounds read access vulnerability was discovered in UPX in PackLinuxElf64::canPack() function of p_lx_elf.cpp file. An attacker with a crafted input file could trigger this issue that could cause a crash leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: At line 75 sh_name is read from the attacker-controlled section header sec_strndx. Lines 77-78 only check that file_size > sh_name before calling strcmp on &shstrtab[sh_name]; they do not verify that sh_name plus the string length stays within file_image, so the strcmp at line 78 can read past the end of the mapped file buffer. The fix strengthens the bound to include sizeof(".shstrtab") and the shstrtab offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function dereferences &shstrtab[sh_name] via strcmp without a complete bounds check, reading memory beyond the intended buffer. It is not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bound check at line 77 compares only the raw sh_name against file_size and ignores the shstrtab base offset and the string length. Trigger: a crafted ELF64 with e_shstrndx pointing to a section whose sh_name is large but still less than file_size. Consequence: strcmp at line 78 reads past the end of file_image, causing an out-of-bounds read and a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
settings: Add support for defaults to keyfile backend

Stacked databases and locks are dconf features that allow
management software like Fleet Commander to set system-wide
defaults and overrides centrally for applications.

This patch adds minimal support for the same to the keyfile
backend. We look for a keyfile named 'defaults' and a
lock-list named 'locks'.

Suitable files can be produced from a dconf database with
dconf dump and dconf list-locks, respectively.

The default location for these files is /etc/glib-2.0/settings/.
For test purposes, this can be overwritten with the
GSETTINGS_DEFAULTS_DIR environment variable.

Writes always go to the per-user keyfile.

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementations of `Sparse*Cwise*` ops are vulnerable to integer overflows. These can be used to trigger large allocations (so, OOM based denial of service) or `CHECK`-fails when building new `TensorShape` objects (so, assert failures based denial of service). We are missing some validation on the shapes of the input tensors as well as directly constructing a large `TensorShape` with user-provided dimensions. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 25 materializes user-controlled sp_shape values into shape_vec, and line 26 constructs a TensorShape from them without validating element count or non-negativity.
Lines 44-49 use nnz = indices_t->dim_size(0) directly as the size for two allocations (output_values and dense_gathered) with no upper-bound or overflow check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing validation lets user-controlled dimensions produce integer overflow/wraparound in size calculations used for allocations and TensorShape construction, matching CWE-190. const auto shape_vec = shape_t->vec<int64_t>();
const auto lhs_dims = BCast::FromShape(TensorShape(shape_vec));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: user-provided sp_shape and indices dimensions are converted into TensorShape objects and allocation sizes without bounds/overflow validation. commit_msg:
Fix multiple vulnerabilities in `tf.experimental.dlpack.to_dlpack`.

We have a use after free caused by memory coruption, a segmentation fault caused by memory corruption, several memory leaks and an undefined behavior when taking the reference of a nullptr.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 332568894
Change-Id: Ife0fc05e103b35325094ae5d822ee5fdea764572
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '  dlm_tensor->dl_tensor.ctx = GetDlContext(h, status);', '  dlm_tensor->dl_tensor.data = TFE_TensorHandleDevicePointer(h, status);', '  dlm_tensor->dl_tensor.dtype = GetDlDataType(data_type, status);', '  dlm_tensor->dl_tensor.shape = &(*shape_arr)[0];', '  dlm_tensor->dl_tensor.strides = &(*stride_arr)[0];'], 'added_lines': ['  auto tf_dlm_context = GetDlContext(h, status);', '  if (!status->status.ok()) {', '    return nullptr;', '  }', '', '  auto* tf_dlm_data = TFE_TensorHandleDevicePointer(h, status);', '  if (!status->status.ok()) {', '    return nullptr;', '  }', '', '', '  auto tf_dlm_type = GetDlDataType(data_type, status);', '  if (!status->status.ok()) {', '    return nullptr;', '  }', '', '  dlm_tensor->dl_tensor.ctx = tf_dlm_context;', '  dlm_tensor->dl_tensor.data = tf_dlm_data;', '  dlm_tensor->dl_tensor.dtype = tf_dlm_type;', '  dlm_tensor->dl_tensor.shape = shape_arr->data();', '  dlm_tensor->dl_tensor.strides = stride_arr->data();', '']}
description: In Tensorflow before versions 2.2.1 and 2.3.1, if a user passes an invalid argument to `dlpack.to_dlpack` the expected validations will cause variables to bind to `nullptr` while setting a `status` variable to the error condition. However, this `status` argument is not properly checked. Hence, code following these methods will bind references to null pointers. This is undefined behavior and reported as an error if compiling with `-fsanitize=null`. The issue is patched in commit 22e07fb204386768e5bcbea563641ea11f96ceb8 and is released in TensorFlow versions 2.2.1, or 2.3.1.

code_evidence: GetTensorFromHandle(h, status) is called and status is never inspected; the returned pointer is immediately dereferenced via tensor->dtype() at line 3, so a failed lookup yielding nullptr is dereferenced.

GetDlContext, TFE_TensorHandleDevicePointer and GetDlDataType are each invoked with status, but their return values are stored directly into dl_tensor fields without any status->status.ok() check; on failure these helpers return nullptr or invalid values that are propagated into the exported DLPack tensor.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is precisely failure to check return values/error status from called functions (CWE-252); the resulting nullptr dereference and corrupted DLPack fields are consequences of the unchecked results, not the root cause itself. Contrast with CWE-476 (null pointer dereference), which describes the symptom rather than the missing check.

evidence_lines.code:
const Tensor* tensor = GetTensorFromHandle(h, status);
TF_DataType data_type = static_cast<TF_DataType>(tensor->dtype());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function relies on helper routines that signal failure through the out-parameter status, but it never checks that status before using their results. Trigger: an invalid tensor handle or unsupported dtype makes a helper return nullptr/failure while setting status to an error. Consequence: the null tensor is dereferenced (undefined behavior, crash) and null context/data/type values are published in the DLPack struct, leading to memory corruption and use-after-free downstream.

commit_msg: Fixed oob read in irp_write and similar
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif ((packetLength > INT_MAX) || !Stream_EnsureCapacity(s, packetLength))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif ((packetLength > INT_MAX) || !Stream_EnsureCapacity(s, packetLength) ||', '\t    (packetLength < header))']}
description: In FreeRDP before 2.1.0, there is an out-of-bound read in irp functions (parallel_process_irp_create, serial_process_irp_create, drive_process_irp_write, printer_process_irp_write, rdpei_recv_pdu, serial_process_irp_write). This has been fixed in 2.1.0.

code_evidence: packetLength is read from the attacker-influenced packet header via Stream_Read_UINT32 and is only checked against INT_MAX and Stream_EnsureCapacity; no lower bound relative to header is enforced.
The subsequent rdg_read_all computes (int)packetLength - (int)header as the read length and Stream_SetLength uses packetLength, so a packetLength smaller than header yields a negative read length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads data based on an unchecked length derived from untrusted input, allowing the read to go past/outside the intended buffer; this is a buffer read overrun, matching CWE-125 rather than a write overflow.

if (!rdg_read_all(rdg->tlsOut, Stream_Buffer(s) + header, (int)packetLength - (int)header))
Stream_SetLength(s, packetLength);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the missing constraint packetLength < header allows a header-declared length smaller than the fixed header size to pass validation. Trigger: a crafted packet whose length field is less than sizeof(RdgPacketHeader). commit_msg:
ovl: verify upper dentry before unlink and rename

Unlink and rename in overlayfs checked the upper dentry for staleness by
verifying upper->d_parent against upperdir.  However the dentry can go
stale also by being unhashed, for example.

Expand the verification to actually look up the name again (under parent
lock) and check if it matches the upper dentry.  This matches what the VFS
does before passing the dentry to filesytem's unlink/rename methods, which
excludes any inconsistency caused by overlayfs.

Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct dentry *upper = ovl_dentry_upper(dentry);', '\tif (upper->d_parent == upperdir) {', "\t\t/* Don't let d_delete() think it can reset d_inode */", '\t\tdget(upper);', '\t\tdput(upper);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct dentry *upper;', '\tupper = lookup_one_len(dentry->d_name.name, upperdir,', '\t\t\t       dentry->d_name.len);', '\terr = PTR_ERR(upper);', '\tif (IS_ERR(upper))', '\t\tgoto out_unlock;', '', '\tif (upper == ovl_dentry_upper(dentry)) {', '\tdput(upper);', 'out_unlock:']}
description: fs/overlayfs/dir.c in the OverlayFS filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.6 does not properly verify the upper dentry before proceeding with unlink and rename system-call processing, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) via a rename system call that specifies a self-hardlink.

code_evidence: The upper dentry is obtained once via ovl_dentry_upper(dentry) before any locking, then used directly in vfs_rmdir/vfs_unlink after the parent lock is taken.

The only staleness check is upper->d_parent == upperdir; it does not re-lookup the name, so an unhashed or otherwise stale dentry whose d_parent still matches passes the check and is passed to the unlink/rmdir methods.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to properly validate the identity/consistency of the upper dentry (input metadata) before using it in a destructive operation; the flawed d_parent-only check is an insufficient validation of input properties, matching CWE-20. It is not merely a logic error, since the missing constraint is a validation of the dentry's current state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts a cached upper dentry and validates only its parent pointer instead of verifying the dentry still corresponds to the requested name under the parent lock. Trigger: a rename/unlink where the upper dentry has become stale (e.g., self-hardlink rename), so the check at line 9 succeeds despite inconsistency. Consequence: the VFS receives a mismatched dentry, leading to a system crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/paging: don't unconditionally BUG() on finding SHARED_M2P_ENTRY

PV guests can fully control the values written into the P2M.

This is XSA-251.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    BUG_ON(SHARED_M2P(pfn_x(pfn)));'], 'added_lines': ['    BUG_ON(paging_mode_translate(d) && SHARED_M2P(pfn_x(pfn)));']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host OS crash) if shadow mode and log-dirty mode are in place, because of an incorrect assertion related to M2P.

code_evidence: paging_mark_pfn_dirty first returns unless log-dirty mode is enabled, then executes BUG_ON(SHARED_M2P(pfn_x(pfn))) on the caller-supplied pfn without confirming that the domain uses translated (shadow) paging.
The pfn is only checked for VALID_M2P after the assertion; a PV guest controls P2M values, so a pfn mapping to a shared M2P entry reaches the unconditional BUG_ON and crashes the host.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The pfn is guest-controlled input whose properties are not validated before an unsafe assertion; the added paging_mode_translate(d) guard is the missing validation. This matches CWE-20's improper input validation leading to a crash (availability impact), rather than a memory-safety flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( unlikely(!VALID_M2P(pfn_x(pfn))) )
return;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the caller-supplied pfn and asserts a shared-M2P property as an invariant without validating it against the domain's paging mode. Trigger: a PV guest under shadow plus log-dirty mode causes paging_mark_pfn_dirty to be invoked with a guest-controlled pfn that is a shared M2P entry. Consequence: the BUG_ON fires, producing a host OS denial of service rather than safely returning.

Bug: 11821
