description: The mp2t_open function in wiretap/mp2t.c in the MP2T file parser in Wireshark 2.0.x before 2.0.1 does not validate the bit rate, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero error and application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: bitrate is declared at line 11 and populated by mp2t_bits_per_second at lines 60-61; the return status is checked at line 62, but the value of bitrate itself is never validated before being stored at line 78.
After the status check, the function proceeds to file_seek and allocates mp2t, storing the unvalidated bitrate at line 78 for later use in mp2t_read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function receives a derived numeric property of the input (bitrate) and fails to validate that it satisfies the required nonzero constraint before using it, matching CWE-20's improper input validation of derived quantities such as rate. The consequence is a DoS crash via divide-by-zero.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mp2t_open accepts the bitrate produced by mp2t_bits_per_second without checking that it is nonzero. A crafted MP2T file can make the parser derive a zero bitrate, which is stored in mp2t->bitrate. Downstream processing that divides by this bitrate triggers a divide-by-zero crash, giving a denial of service. The missing constraint is the zero check on the derived rate.

commit_msg:
[CVE-2022-23308] Use-after-free of ID and IDREF attributes

If a document is parsed with XML_PARSE_DTDVALID and without
XML_PARSE_NOENT, the value of ID attributes has to be normalized after
potentially expanding entities in xmlRemoveID. Otherwise, later calls
to xmlGetID can return a pointer to previously freed memory.

ID attributes which are empty or contain only whitespace after
entity expansion are affected in a similar way. This is fixed by
not storing such attributes in the ID table.

The test to detect streaming mode when validating against a DTD was
broken. In connection with the defects above, this could result in a
use-after-free when using the xmlReader interface with validation.
Fix detection of streaming mode to avoid similar issues. (This changes
the expected result of a test case. But as far as I can tell, using the
XML reader with XIncludes referencing the root document never worked
properly, anyway.)

All of these issues can result in denial of service. Using xmlReader
with validation could result in disclosure of memory via the error
channel, typically stderr. The security impact of xmlGetID returning
a pointer to freed memory depends on the application. The typical use
case of calling xmlGetID on an unmodified document is not affected.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    xmlChar *ret, *dst;', '    const xmlChar *src;', '    src = value;', '    dst = ret;', '    while (*src == 0x20) src++;', '    while (*src != 0) {', '\tif (*src == 0x20) {', '\t    while (*src == 0x20) src++;', '\t    if (*src != 0)', '\t\t*dst++ = 0x20;', '\t} else {', '\t    *dst++ = *src++;', '\t}', '    }', '    *dst = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    xmlChar *ret;', '    xmlValidNormalizeString(ret);']}
description: valid.c in libxml2 before 2.9.13 has a use-after-free of ID and IDREF attributes.

code_evidence: The function duplicates the attribute value into ret, then normalizes whitespace by copying from src=value into dst=ret. The loop collapses runs of 0x20 and copies non-space characters, terminating with *dst = 0; the returned buffer is a freshly allocated, normalized copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the described defect lets a stored ID reference point to memory that has been freed, and later use of that pointer is invalid. The fix normalizes the value before storage, preventing stale references.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the normalization logic here builds a new string but, per the commit, the ID attribute value must be normalized after entity expansion in xmlRemoveID; otherwise xmlGetID can later return a pointer into freed memory. Trigger: parsing with XML_PARSE_DTDVALID without XML_PARSE_NOENT, causing entity expansion and re-normalization of ID values. Consequence: use-after-free when xmlGetID is called, leading to DoS and possible memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
dm: Reset virtio device before release

With virtio polling mode enabled, a timer is running in the virtio
backend service. And the timer will also be triggered if its frondend
driver didn't do the device reset in shutdown. A freed virtio device
will be accessed in the polling timer handler.

Do the virtio reset() callback specifically to clear the polling timer
before the free.

Tracked-On: #6147
Signed-off-by: Shuo A Liu <shuo.a.liu@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Yonghua Huang <yonghua.huang@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tvirtio_rpmb_reset(dev->arg);']}
description: The polling timer handler in ACRN before 2.5 has a use-after-free for a freed virtio device, related to devicemodel/hw/pci/virtio/*.c.

code_evidence: virtio_rpmb_deinit checks dev->arg and then frees the backend object with free((struct virtio_rpmb *)dev->arg); this is the last operation on the object in the function, and the pointer is not cleared afterward.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function releases dev->arg while a separate timer handler can still access the same allocation, which is precisely the use-after-free pattern of CWE-416. This is not merely a double free or missing NULL assignment, since the defect is continued use of the freed object by another execution path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the deinit path frees the virtio_rpmb object without first stopping the backend's polling timer, so the timer handler retains a reference to memory that has been released. Trigger: polling mode is enabled and the device is shut down without a reset, leaving the timer armed; the handler then fires and dereferences the freed device. Supported consequence: use-after-free, with potential crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = table->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = xt_table_get_private_protected(table);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: Line 9 reads table->private into private without any protection against a concurrent rules replacement; line 12 then allocates counters and line 15 dereferences private->entries.
The loop starting at line 16 walks the rule set through loc_cpu_entry (derived from private) and line 20 computes each entry pointer from that freed-suspect buffer.
Lines 21-22 copy the entry data to user space via copy_to_user using the stale pointer, so the read occurs after a concurrent replacement could have freed the old table info.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences and copies data through a pointer to table-private memory that can be freed concurrently, which is exactly CWE-416 (use of memory after it is freed). It is not merely a race condition or NULL dereference: the consequence is a read of freed rule memory, matching the UAF variant.

evidence_lines.code:
for (off = 0, num = 0; off < total_size; off += e->next_offset, num++){
e = loc_cpu_entry + off;

if (copy_to_user(userptr + off, e, sizeof(*e))) {
ret = -EFAULT;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unprotected table->private load and subsequent dereferences are not synchronized with the sequence-count check used by xt_replace_table, so the compiler/CPU may reorder the assignment and the replacement thread frees the old table while this function still uses it. Trigger: concurrent iptables rules replacement (CAP_NET_ADMIN) while copy_entries_to_user reads the rules. Consequence: use-after-free read of freed table/entry memory, leading to crash or memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.0017: accessing memory beyond the end of the line

Problem:    Accessing memory beyond the end of the line.
Solution:   Stop Visual mode when closing a window.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t    reset_VIsual_and_resel();\t// stop Visual mode', '']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.

code_evidence: In win_close, when the window being closed is curwin and the alternate window wp uses a different buffer, the code sets other_buffer, marks win->w_closing, and triggers BUFLEAVE autocmds without first terminating Visual mode. The fixed version adds reset_VIsual_and_resel() before this block. The function itself contains no bounds check or heap buffer operation; the overflow occurs in code operating on the Visual selection state that this path fails to reset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit fixes a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) caused by stale Visual-mode state after window close; the added reset_VIsual_and_resel() call prevents the overflow. The function is the trigger site, not the buffer operation itself, but it directly supports the target weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: closing the current window while Visual mode is active leaves a stale Visual selection (line/column state) that later code uses to index the buffer. Trigger: user closes a window in Visual mode with a different alternate buffer. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds memory access beyond the end of the line, i.e. a heap buffer overflow.

commit_msg:
avformat/rtpdec_h264: Fix heap-buffer-overflow

Fixes: rtp_sdp/poc.sdp

Found-by: Bingchang <l.bing.chang.bc@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["        if (value[strlen(value) - 1] == ',') {"], 'added_lines': ["        if (*value == 0 || value[strlen(value) - 1] == ',') {"]}
description: The sdp_parse_fmtp_config_h264 function in libavformat/rtpdec_h264.c in FFmpeg before 3.3.4 mishandles empty sprop-parameter-sets values, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted sdp file.

code_evidence: In the sprop-parameter-sets branch, the code indexes value[strlen(value) - 1] without first checking that value is non-empty. When value is an empty string, strlen(value) is 0, so the index becomes -1 and the read occurs one byte before the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code performs a read at a memory location outside the intended buffer boundary, which directly matches CWE-119 (out-of-bounds memory operation). It is an underflow of the index rather than a length mismatch, but the resulting out-of-bounds access is the supported weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing empty-string guard before computing strlen(value)-1 as an index. Trigger: a crafted SDP file providing an empty sprop-parameter-sets value. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read before the value buffer, yielding a heap buffer overflow/crash (DoS) and potentially other impact.

commit_msg:
Add PSS parameter check.

Avoid seg fault by checking mgf1 parameter is not NULL. This can be
triggered during certificate verification so could be a DoS attack
against a client or a server enabling client authentication.

Thanks to Loïc Jonas Etienne (Qnective AG) for discovering this bug.

CVE-2015-3194

Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            && param->type == V_ASN1_SEQUENCE) {'], 'added_lines': ['            && param && param->type == V_ASN1_SEQUENCE) {']}
description: crypto/rsa/rsa_ameth.c in OpenSSL 1.0.1 before 1.0.1q and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2e allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via an RSA PSS ASN.1 signature that lacks a mask generation function parameter.

code_evidence: pss->maskGenAlgorithm is non-NULL, so param is assigned the possibly-NULL parameter field of the maskGenAlgorithm X509_ALGOR. The condition evaluates OBJ_obj2nid(...) == NID_mgf1 first and then dereferences param->type without first testing param for NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code reads through param without ensuring it is non-NULL, which is a direct NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476), matching the fixed check added for param. This is distinct from a missing-type-validation issue because the crash occurs solely from the NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mgf1 parameter pointer param is dereferenced (param->type) before any NULL check. Trigger: an RSA PSS ASN.1 signature whose maskGenAlgorithm is present and uses mgf1 but lacks the mask generation function parameter, leaving param NULL. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and application crash (DoS) during certificate verification.

commit_msg:
x86/speculation: Allow enabling STIBP with legacy IBRS

When plain IBRS is enabled (not enhanced IBRS), the logic in
spectre_v2_user_select_mitigation() determines that STIBP is not needed.

The IBRS bit implicitly protects against cross-thread branch target
injection. However, with legacy IBRS, the IBRS bit is cleared on
returning to userspace for performance reasons which leaves userspace
threads vulnerable to cross-thread branch target injection against which
STIBP protects.

Exclude IBRS from the spectre_v2_in_ibrs_mode() check to allow for
enabling STIBP (through seccomp/prctl() by default or always-on, if
selected by spectre_v2_user kernel cmdline parameter).

  [ bp: Massage. ]

Fixes: 7c693f54c873 ("x86/speculation: Add spectre_v2=ibrs option to support Kernel IBRS")

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230221184908.2349578-1-kpsingh@kernel.org

description:
The Linux kernel allows userspace processes to enable mitigations by calling prctl with PR_SET_SPECULATION_CTRL which disables the speculation feature as well as by using seccomp. We had noticed that on VMs of at least one major cloud provider, the kernel still left the victim process exposed to attacks in some cases even after enabling the spectre-BTI mitigation with prctl. The same behavior can be observed on a bare-metal machine when forcing the mitigation to IBRS on boot command line.

This happened because when plain IBRS was enabled (not enhanced IBRS), the kernel had some logic that determined that STIBP was not needed. The IBRS bit implicitly protects against cross-thread branch target injection. However, with legacy IBRS, the IBRS bit was cleared on returning to userspace, due to performance reasons, which disabled the implicit STIBP and left userspace threads vulnerable to cross-thread branch target injection against which STIBP protects.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function is mitigation-selection logic for STIBP/IBPB; it contains no observable behavioral discrepancy or response difference exposed to an unauthorized actor, so it does not directly support CWE-203.

commit_msg:
Restrict the depth of the protocol tree.

Limit the the protocol tree to 500 levels. This keeps us from running
out of stack space in proto_tree_traverse_{pre,post}_order.

commit_msg: Fix for CVE-2023-28366
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmsg = mosquitto__malloc(sizeof(struct mosquitto_client_msg));'], 'added_lines': ['\tmsg = mosquitto__calloc(1, sizeof(struct mosquitto_client_msg));', '\t}else if(dir == mosq_md_in && msg->qos > 0 && state != mosq_ms_queued){', '\t\tutil__decrement_receive_quota(context);']}
description: The broker in Eclipse Mosquitto 1.3.2 through 2.x before 2.0.16 has a memory leak that can be abused remotely when a client sends many QoS 2 messages with duplicate message IDs, and fails to respond to PUBREC commands. This occurs because of mishandling of EAGAIN from the libc send function.

code_evidence: db__message_insert allocates a mosquitto_client_msg via mosquitto__malloc at line 101 and links it into msg_data->inflight or msg_data->queued (lines 119-125); it also allocates stored->dest_ids and a strdup'd context id at lines 127-131. When the strdup fails, lines 132-133 return MOSQ_ERR_NOMEM without removing the already-linked msg from the inflight/queued list or freeing it, so the allocated client message and its store reference become unreachable for the caller.

The function only decrements the send quota for outgoing messages at lines 146-148; incoming QoS 2 messages with duplicate IDs are still inserted and linked, so repeated inserts accumulate entries. The missing receive-quota decrement (added in the patch) combined with the early-return leak path leaves allocated messages permanently linked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the function allocates memory whose lifetime is not terminated on error paths; the allocation remains linked and is never released after its effective lifetime. This is a memory-lifetime/release defect, not a use-after-free or double-free, which would require later access or duplicate release rather than simple non-release.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation at line 101 is linked into the inflight/queued list before error returns at lines 132-133 and 135-137, which free nothing and do not unlink the message. Trigger: a client that repeatedly causes dest_ids strdup failure or duplicate-ID QoS 2 insertion. Consequence: each failed insertion leaks a mosquitto_client_msg and its msg-store reference, growing broker memory until exhaustion (DoS).

commit_msg:
Add IsScalar (rank == 0) check to min/max input tensors for QuantizedAdd/Relu/Relu6 op.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 461902847

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. If `QuantizedAdd` is given `min_input` or `max_input` tensors of a nonzero rank, it results in a segfault that can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 49b3824d83af706df0ad07e4e677d88659756d89. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The function reads the min/max bound tensors (inputs 2–5) and immediately indexes element 0 via flat<float>()(0) without verifying that these tensors are rank-0 scalars; a nonzero-rank input still yields element 0, so the bound values are taken from an unvalidated tensor shape.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of an input's required property (rank/scalar shape) before use, matching CWE-20's improper input validation class. It is not a transformation/filtering issue, and the missing shape constraint is the direct cause of the crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the expected scalar property (rank 0) of min_x/max_x/min_y/max_y is never checked before element access. Trigger: a caller supplies a nonzero-rank min/max input tensor to QuantizedAdd. The unchecked shape leads to a segfault, giving a denial-of-service consequence; the crash is the consequence, not the cause.

description: In SkSampler::Fill of SkSampler.cpp, there is a possible out of bounds write due to an integer overflow. This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation. Product: Android Versions: Android-7.0 Android-7.1.1 Android-7.1.2 Android-8.0 Android-8.1 Android ID: A-78354855

code_evidence: Line 3 computes the allocation size as count * sizeof(T) in size_t arithmetic and passes it directly to sk_malloc_flags. No overflow check (e.g., SkSafeMath::Mul) guards this multiplication before allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the multiplication that determines the allocation size can overflow before the allocation, and the result is trusted as the buffer size. This is the size-calculation flaw, distinct from the downstream out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) that it enables.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size computation count * sizeof(T) can wrap when count is large, producing a small byte count. Trigger: a caller supplies an attacker-influenced count. Consequence: a smaller-than-expected buffer is allocated, and subsequent writes indexed by count go out of bounds, enabling memory corruption or code execution as described in the advisory.

commit_msg:
Muyu Yu provided a POC where user root with CAP_NET_ADMIN can create a CAN
frame modification rule that makes the data length code a higher value than
the available CAN frame data size. In combination with a configured checksum
calculation where the result is stored relatively to the end of the data
(e.g. cgw_csum_xor_rel) the tail of the skb (e.g. frag_list pointer in
skb_shared_info) can be rewritten which finally can cause a system crash.

Michael Kubecek suggested to drop frames that have a DLC exceeding the
available space after the modification process and provided a patch that can
handle CAN FD frames too. Within this patch we also limit the length for the
checksum calculations to the maximum of Classic CAN data length (8).

CAN frames that are dropped by these additional checks are counted with the
CGW_DELETED counter which indicates misconfigurations in can-gw rules.

This fixes CVE-2019-3701.

Reported-by: Muyu Yu <ieatmuttonchuan@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Marcus Meissner <meissner@suse.de>
Suggested-by: Michal Kubecek <mkubecek@suse.cz>
Tested-by: Muyu Yu <ieatmuttonchuan@gmail.com>
Tested-by: Oliver Hartkopp <socketcan@hartkopp.net>
Signed-off-by: Oliver Hartkopp <socketcan@hartkopp.net>
Cc: linux-stable <stable@vger.kernel.org> # >= v3.2
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* check for checksum updates when the CAN frame has been modified */', '\t\tif (gwj->mod.csumfunc.crc8)', '\t\tif (gwj->mod.csumfunc.xor)'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Has the CAN frame been modified? */', '\t\t/* get available space for the processed CAN frame type */', '\t\tint max_len = nskb->len - offsetof(struct can_frame, data);', '', '\t\t/* dlc may have changed, make sure it fits to the CAN frame */', '\t\tif (cf->can_dlc > max_len)', '\t\t\tgoto out_delete;', '', '\t\t/* check for checksum updates in classic CAN length only */', '\t\tif (gwj->mod.csumfunc.crc8) {', '\t\t\tif (cf->can_dlc > 8)', '\t\t\t\tgoto out_delete;', '', '\t\t}', '\t\tif (gwj->mod.csumfunc.xor) {', '\t\t\tif (cf->can_dlc > 8)', '\t\t\t\tgoto out_delete;', '', '\t\t}', '', '\treturn;', '', ' out_delete:', '\t/* delete frame due to misconfiguration */', '\tgwj->deleted_frames++;', '\tkfree_skb(nskb);', '\treturn;']}
description: An issue was discovered in can_can_gw_rcv in net/can/gw.c in the Linux kernel through 4.19.13. The CAN frame modification rules allow bitwise logical operations that can be also applied to the can_dlc field. The privileged user "root" with CAP_NET_ADMIN can create a CAN frame modification rule that makes the data length code a higher value than the available CAN frame data size. In combination with a configured checksum calculation where the result is stored relatively to the end of the data (e.g. cgw_csum_xor_rel) the tail of the skb (e.g. frag_list pointer in skb_shared_info) can be rewritten which finally can cause a system crash. Because of a missing check, the CAN drivers may write arbitrary content beyond the data registers in the CAN controller's I/O memory when processing can-gw manipulated outgoing frames.

code_evidence: Modification functions run in the loop at [33,34] and can raise cf->can_dlc beyond the frame's actual data size. Lines [35,36,37,38,39,40] then invoke the crc8/xor checksum functions whenever csumfunc is set, without verifying that can_dlc fits the available frame data before those functions write relative to the data end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the checksum operation writes beyond the intended CAN frame data buffer due to the missing length constraint. This is an out-of-bounds write rather than a mere improper input validation issue, since the unchecked DLC directly drives the write extent.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: after modfunc changes can_dlc, the code performs checksum writes using a length that may exceed the allocated CAN frame data. Trigger: a privileged user (CAP_NET_ADMIN) configures a bitwise rule raising the DLC plus a relative checksum function. Consequence: the checksum store writes past the data buffer, corrupting skb tail data such as frag_list and causing a crash.

commit_msg: Add out-of-bounds check in getCode. Fixes #78
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  const mz_uint8 *pIn_buf_cur = pIn_buf_next,', '                 *const pIn_buf_end = pIn_buf_next + *pIn_buf_size;', '  mz_uint8 *pOut_buf_cur = pOut_buf_next,', '           *const pOut_buf_end = pOut_buf_next + *pOut_buf_size;'], 'added_lines': ['  const mz_uint8 *pIn_buf_cur = pIn_buf_next, *const pIn_buf_end =', '                                                  pIn_buf_next + *pIn_buf_size;', '  mz_uint8 *pOut_buf_cur = pOut_buf_next, *const pOut_buf_end =', '                                              pOut_buf_next + *pOut_buf_size;']}
description: tinyexr 0.9.5 has a heap-based buffer over-read in tinyexr::DecodePixelData in tinyexr.h, related to OpenEXR code.

code_evidence: Lines 25-28 compute pIn_buf_end as pIn_buf_next + *pIn_buf_size and pOut_buf_end similarly, but never validate that *pIn_buf_size accurately bounds the actual readable input buffer.
Line 220 only checks that fewer than 4 bytes remain before taking the fast path; otherwise the else branch runs.
In the 64-bit path, lines 232-236 call MZ_READ_LE32(pIn_buf_cur) and advance pIn_buf_cur by 4 after only checking num_bits < 30, without verifying (pIn_buf_end - pIn_buf_cur) >= 4.
The 16-bit path at lines 239-243 reads MZ_READ_LE16(pIn_buf_cur) and advances by 2 based solely on num_bits < 15, not on remaining input length.
Lines 263-267 perform a second MZ_READ_LE16 and advance pIn_buf_cur by 2 without re-checking the input end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads input bytes beyond the intended buffer end, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. This is a read-only over-read of input, not a write past pOut_buf_end, so CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) does not apply.

evidence_lines.code:
if (((pIn_buf_end - pIn_buf_cur) < 4) ||
((pOut_buf_end - pOut_buf_cur) < 2)) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The fast decode path refills the bit buffer by dereferencing pIn_buf_cur and advancing it, gated only by bit-count thresholds rather than by the remaining input length. When the input buffer is nearly exhausted, these reads can pass pIn_buf_end, producing an out-of-bounds heap read (the over-read described).

commit_msg: Adds better sanity checks around the method IX
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (method_wksidx != -1) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (method_wksidx >= 0 && method_wksidx < HTTP_WKSIDX_METHODS_CNT) {']}
description: Adding method ACLs in remap.config can cause a segfault when the user makes a carefully crafted request. This affects versions Apache Traffic Server (ATS) 6.0.0 to 6.2.2 and 7.0.0 to 7.1.3. To resolve this issue users running 6.x should upgrade to 6.2.3 or later versions and 7.x users should upgrade to 7.1.4 or later versions.

code_evidence: Line 9 obtains the request method's well-known index from the client request; line 10 derives method_wksidx as method - HTTP_WKSIDX_CONNECT, or -1 when the method is unknown.

Lines 15-17: when method restriction is enabled, the guard only checks method_wksidx != -1 before indexing rp->standard_method_lookup[method_wksidx], so any non-negative derived index, including one beyond the lookup table size, is used directly as an array index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because input-derived metadata (the method's well-known index) is not validated against the required range before indexing an array. The patch adds the missing bounds check (method_wksidx >= 0 && method_wksidx < HTTP_WKSIDX_METHODS_CNT), confirming improper validation of an index into a data structure as the root cause rather than a transformation error.

evidence_lines.code:
int method               = s->hdr_info.client_request.method_get_wksidx();
int method_wksidx        = (method != -1) ? (method - HTTP_WKSIDX_CONNECT) : -1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The derived method_wksidx is only checked against -1, not against the upper bound of standard_method_lookup. A crafted request method that yields a wksidx outside the table's valid range causes an out-of-bounds array read, which the commit describes as a segfault. Root cause is missing validation of the derived index's upper bound; the consequence is a crash (availability impact).

commit_msg:
drm/vc4: Fix an integer overflow in temporary allocation layout.

We copy the unvalidated ioctl arguments from the user into kernel
temporary memory to run the validation from, to avoid a race where the
user updates the unvalidate contents in between validating them and
copying them into the validated BO.

However, in setting up the layout of the kernel side, we failed to
check one of the additions (the roundup() for shader_rec_offset)
against integer overflow, allowing a nearly MAX_UINT value of
bin_cl_size to cause us to under-allocate the temporary space that we
then copy_from_user into.

Reported-by: Murray McAllister <murray.mcallister@insomniasec.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Anholt <eric@anholt.net>
Fixes: d5b1a78a772f ("drm/vc4: Add support for drawing 3D frames.")
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -14,7 +14,8 @@
 					  args->shader_rec_count);
 	struct vc4_bo *bo;
 
-	if (uniforms_offset < shader_rec_offset ||
+	if (shader_rec_offset < args->bin_cl_size ||
+	    uniforms_offset < shader_rec_offset ||
 	    exec_size < uniforms_offset ||
 	    args->shader_rec_count >= (UINT_MAX /
 					  sizeof(struct vc4_shader_state)) ||
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (uniforms_offset < shader_rec_offset ||'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (shader_rec_offset < args->bin_cl_size ||', '\t    uniforms_offset < shader_rec_offset ||']}
description: Integer overflow in the vc4_get_bcl function in drivers/gpu/drm/vc4/vc4_gem.c in the VideoCore DRM driver in the Linux kernel before 4.9.7 allows local users to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted size value in a VC4_SUBMIT_CL ioctl call.

code_evidence: shader_rec_offset is computed as roundup(bin_offset + args->bin_cl_size, 16) using attacker-controlled bin_cl_size; a near-MAX_UINT value wraps the 32-bit addition/roundup.

The guard only checks uniforms_offset < shader_rec_offset, exec_size < uniforms_offset, shader_rec_count bound, and temp_size < exec_size; it never verifies shader_rec_offset >= bin_cl_size, so a wrapped small offset passes.
temp_size derives from the wrapped offsets, so drm_malloc_ab under-allocates; bin, shader_rec_u and uniforms_u are then placed within this undersized buffer.
copy_from_user copies args->bin_cl_size bytes into bin, exceeding the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a 32-bit integer wraparound in size/offset computation used for allocation and copying, matching CWE-190. The added check specifically guards the missing overflow condition; a mere undersized-buffer copy would be CWE-787, but the wrapping arithmetic is the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
if (uniforms_offset < shader_rec_offset ||
exec_size < uniforms_offset ||
args->shader_rec_count >= (UINT_MAX /
sizeof(struct vc4_shader_state)) ||
temp_size < exec_size) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unchecked 32-bit addition/roundup of the user-supplied bin_cl_size produces a wrapped shader_rec_offset, and the validation omits the shader_rec_offset >= bin_cl_size check. Trigger: a VC4_SUBMIT_CL ioctl with a near-MAX_UINT bin_cl_size. Consequence: the temporary buffer is under-allocated, and the subsequent copy_from_user of bin_cl_size bytes overflows the heap allocation, enabling memory corruption or denial of service.

commit_msg:
Avoid division by zero in opj_pi_next_rpcl, opj_pi_next_pcrl and opj_pi_next_cprl (#938)

Fixes issues with id:000026,sig:08,src:002419,op:int32,pos:60,val:+32 and
id:000019,sig:08,src:001098,op:flip1,pos:49
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '                    /* To avoid divisions by zero / undefined behaviour on shift */', '                    /* in below tests */', '                    /* Fixes reading id:000019,sig:08,src:001098,op:flip1,pos:49 */', '                    /* of https://github.com/uclouvain/openjpeg/issues/938 */', '                    if (rpx >= 31 || ((comp->dx << rpx) >> rpx) != comp->dx ||', '                            rpy >= 31 || ((comp->dy << rpy) >> rpy) != comp->dy) {', '                        continue;', '                    }', '', '                    /* See ISO-15441. B.12.1.5 Component-position-resolution level-layer progression */']}
description: Division-by-zero vulnerabilities in the functions opj_pi_next_cprl, opj_pi_next_pcrl, and opj_pi_next_rpcl in pi.c in OpenJPEG before 2.2.0 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via crafted j2k files.

code_evidence: rpx and rpy are computed from res->pdx/pdy plus levelno (lines 48-49). Line 50 then divides pi->y by (comp->dy << rpy), and line 54 divides pi->x by (comp->dx << rpx); line 51 also computes 1 << rpy and line 55 computes 1 << rpx. When rpy or rpx reaches 31 or more, the shift is undefined and the divisor becomes zero, so the modulo in lines 50 and 54 divides by zero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs modulo by an expression that can evaluate to zero, causing a division-by-zero error (CWE-369). This is distinct from a generic shift issue: the supported consequence is the divide-by-zero on lines 50/54, which the target CWE directly describes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the divisor expressions comp->dy << rpy and comp->dx << rpx are not bounded before use in modulo operations. A crafted j2k file with large component sampling or resolution parameters makes rpx/rpy large, so the shift yields zero (or undefined behavior) and the modulo divides by zero, crashing the decoder.

commit_msg:
dir: Reserve the whole @@ prefix

If we add new features analogous to file forwarding later, we might
find that we need a different magic token. Let's reserve the whole
@@* namespace so we can call it @@something-else.

Signed-off-by: Simon McVittie <smcv@collabora.com>
(cherry picked from commit 1e7e8fdb24b51078f4c48e0711e24a14930ba1f0)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['              else if (strcmp (arg, "@@") == 0 || strcmp (arg, "@@u") == 0)'], 'added_lines': ['              else if (g_str_has_prefix (arg, "@@"))']}
description: Flatpak is a system for building, distributing, and running sandboxed desktop applications on Linux. In Flatpack since version 0.9.4 and before version 1.10.2 has a vulnerability in the "file forwarding" feature which can be used by an attacker to gain access to files that would not ordinarily be allowed by the app's permissions. By putting the special tokens `@@` and/or `@@u` in the Exec field of a Flatpak app's .desktop file, a malicious app publisher can trick flatpak into behaving as though the user had chosen to open a target file with their Flatpak app, which automatically makes that file available to the Flatpak app. This is fixed in version 1.10.2. A minimal solution is the first commit "`Disallow @@ and @@U usage in desktop files`". The follow-up commits "`dir: Reserve the whole @@ prefix`" and "`dir: Refuse to export .desktop files with suspicious uses of @@ tokens`" are recommended, but not strictly required. As a workaround, avoid installing Flatpak apps from untrusted sources, or check the contents of the exported `.desktop` files in `exports/share/applications/*.desktop` (typically `~/.local/share/flatpak/exports/share/applications/*.desktop` and `/var/lib/flatpak/exports/share/applications/*.desktop`) to make sure that literal filenames do not follow `@@` or `@@u`.

code_evidence: Line 121-122 reads an attacker-controlled Exec value from the .desktop file and parses it into arguments.

Lines 138-148 iterate over those arguments and copy each into new_exec; the guard only skips exact matches for "@@" or "@@u", so arguments like "@@foo" or "@@u/path" pass through the else branch and are embedded verbatim.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits because externally-influenced Exec arguments are inserted into a downstream-parsed command line without neutralizing special @@ elements. The incomplete equality check is the injection-enabling flaw; a prefix check would block the token family.

evidence_lines.code:
old_exec = g_key_file_get_string (keyfile, groups[i], "Exec", NULL);
if (old_exec && g_shell_parse_argv (old_exec, &old_argc, &old_argv, NULL) && old_argc >= 1)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the filter compares whole arguments for equality rather than rejecting the @@ prefix, so attacker-supplied tokens such as @@something are copied into the rewritten Exec field. Trigger: a malicious app publisher places a crafted @@ token in the desktop file's Exec. Consequence: flatpak later interprets the token and grants file access beyond the app's permissions.

commit_msg:
Bug #484 CVE-2018-17582 Check for corrupt PCAP files

* Check for packets that are larger than 262144 bytes
* Check for capture lengths that are greater than packet length

Example of a corrupt PCAP file ...

sudo src/tcpreplay -i ens33 --unique-ip -t --loop 4 get_next_paket_01
safe_pcap_next ERROR: Invalid packet length in send_packets.c:get_next_packet() line 1054: 8388670 is greater than maximum 262144
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    while ((pktdata = pcap_next(pcap, &pkthdr)) != NULL) {'], 'added_lines': ['    while ((pktdata = safe_pcap_next(pcap, &pkthdr)) != NULL) {']}
description: Tcpreplay v4.3.0 beta1 contains a heap-based buffer over-read. The get_next_packet() function in the send_packets.c file uses the memcpy() function unsafely to copy sequences from the source buffer pktdata to the destination (*prev_packet)->pktdata. This will result in a Denial of Service (DoS) and potentially Information Exposure when the application attempts to process a file.

code_evidence: Line 15 obtains pktdata and pkthdr from pcap_next without validating caplen against packet length or a maximum; the patch replaces this with safe_pcap_next. That untrusted caplen then drives header parsing at lines 33/36 (get_ipv4/get_ipv6) and line 47 (get_l2len), and the MAC_MODE path at line 90 only checks caplen < sizeof(*eth_hdr) before dereferencing eth_hdr->ether_shost at line 95.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reading data beyond the intended packet buffer due to an unchecked captured length; this is precisely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a write overflow, since the defect is in reading header fields based on caplen.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop accepts corrupt PCAP records whose captured length exceeds the available packet data or a sane bound, and downstream parsing trusts pkthdr.caplen. Trigger: a crafted/corrupt capture file. Consequence: parsers read past the packet buffer, yielding out-of-bounds reads (DoS, potential information exposure).

commit_msg: - fixed - Bug in presentation layer parser can cause infinite loop (LIB61850-302)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '            if (bufPos < 0)', '                return -1;', '']}
description: A denial of service vulnerability exists in the parseNormalModeParameters functionality of MZ Automation GmbH libiec61850 1.5.0. A specially-crafted series of network requests can lead to denial of service. An attacker can send a sequence of malformed iec61850 messages to trigger this vulnerability.

That callee can return a negative value on malformed input; the loop then re-tests bufPos < endPos with a negative bufPos and no progress, so the exit condition is never reached.
The original code returns -1 immediately when the sub-parser fails, terminating the loop; the patched guard at the a4 case prevents the negative index from re-entering the loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loop's exit condition bufPos < endPos becomes unreachable once bufPos is negative and never advances, matching CWE-835's infinite loop. This is not merely a length-validation flaw (CWE-20) because the observable fault is a non-terminating iteration causing resource exhaustion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the a4 case assigns the sub-parser result to bufPos without validating it, so a malformed presentation context definition list yields a negative bufPos. Trigger: a crafted network message containing tag 0xa4 with malformed length/content. Consequence: the while condition stays true and the loop iterates without advancing, consuming CPU (denial of service).

commit_msg:
outline: fix overflows in outline processing

This commit enforces strict invariant on ASS_Outline
to contain point coordinates into predetermined range.

Fixes https://github.com/libass/libass/issues/431.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if(abs(pt.x) > OUTLINE_MAX || abs(pt.y) > OUTLINE_MAX)', '        return false;', '']}
description: In libass 0.14.0, the `ass_outline_construct`'s call to `outline_stroke` causes a signed integer overflow.

code_evidence: The function grows the point buffer by computing new_size = 2 * outline->max_points (a size_t multiplication with no overflow check) before reallocating.
After reallocation, the incoming coordinate pt is written unconditionally into outline->points[outline->n_points] and n_points is incremented; pt is never range-checked against OUTLINE_MAX.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an unchecked arithmetic result (2 * max_points and downstream coordinate math) that can exceed the representable integer range, matching CWE-190's wraparound description. It is not merely an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the missing coordinate constraint enables the overflow that precedes the memory effects.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: point coordinates are accepted and stored without any bound, so downstream outline/stroke arithmetic on pt.x and pt.y can exceed the signed integer range and wrap. Trigger: a caller passes a large coordinate through outline_add_point; the doubled capacity computation (2 * max_points) is a second unchecked multiplication. Supported consequence: the wrapped values corrupt subsequent geometry computations, leading to memory corruption or a crash as described in the commit's overflow report.

commit_msg: Restrict packet kinds that can be sent through onion path.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        return 1;', '    }', '', '    if (len <= SIZE_IPPORT) {', '        return 1;', '    }', '', '    if (plain[SIZE_IPPORT] != NET_PACKET_ANNOUNCE_REQUEST &&', '            plain[SIZE_IPPORT] != NET_PACKET_ONION_DATA_REQUEST) {']}

commit_msg:
f2fs: fix race condition in between free nid allocator/initializer

In below concurrent case, allocated nid can be loaded into free nid cache
and be allocated again.

Thread A				Thread B
- f2fs_create
 - f2fs_new_inode
  - alloc_nid
   - __insert_nid_to_list(ALLOC_NID_LIST)
					- f2fs_balance_fs_bg
					 - build_free_nids
					  - __build_free_nids
					   - scan_nat_page
					    - add_free_nid
					     - __lookup_nat_cache
 - f2fs_add_link
  - init_inode_metadata
   - new_inode_page
    - new_node_page
     - set_node_addr
 - alloc_nid_done
  - __remove_nid_from_list(ALLOC_NID_LIST)
					     - __insert_nid_to_list(FREE_NID_LIST)

This patch makes nat cache lookup and free nid list operation being atomical
to avoid this race condition.

Signed-off-by: Jaegeuk Kim <jaegeuk@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Chao Yu <yuchao0@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Jaegeuk Kim <jaegeuk@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct free_nid *i;', '\tint err;', '\tif (build) {', '\t\t/* do not add allocated nids */', '\t\tne = __lookup_nat_cache(nm_i, nid);', '\t\tif (ne && (!get_nat_flag(ne, IS_CHECKPOINTED) ||', '\t\t\t\tnat_get_blkaddr(ne) != NULL_ADDR))', '\t\t\treturn false;', '\t}', '', '\tif (radix_tree_preload(GFP_NOFS)) {', '\t\tkmem_cache_free(free_nid_slab, i);', '\t\treturn true;', '\t}', '\tif (err) {', '\t\treturn true;', '\t}', '\treturn true;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct free_nid *i, *e;', '\tint err = -EINVAL;', '\tbool ret = false;', '\tif (radix_tree_preload(GFP_NOFS))', '\t\tgoto err;', '', '\tif (build) {', '\t\t/*', '\t\t *   Thread A             Thread B', '\t\t *  - f2fs_create', '\t\t *   - f2fs_new_inode', '\t\t *    - alloc_nid', '\t\t *     - __insert_nid_to_list(ALLOC_NID_LIST)', '\t\t *                     - f2fs_balance_fs_bg', '\t\t *                      - build_free_nids', '\t\t *                       - __build_free_nids', '\t\t *                        - scan_nat_page', '\t\t *                         - add_free_nid', '\t\t *                          - __lookup_nat_cache', '\t\t *  - f2fs_add_link', '\t\t *   - init_inode_metadata', '\t\t *    - new_inode_page', '\t\t *     - new_node_page', '\t\t *      - set_node_addr', '\t\t *  - alloc_nid_done', '\t\t *   - __remove_nid_from_list(ALLOC_NID_LIST)', '\t\t *                         - __insert_nid_to_list(FREE_NID_LIST)', '\t\t */', '\t\tne = __lookup_nat_cache(nm_i, nid);', '\t\tif (ne && (!get_nat_flag(ne, IS_CHECKPOINTED) ||', '\t\t\t\tnat_get_blkaddr(ne) != NULL_ADDR))', '\t\t\tgoto err_out;', '', '\t\te = __lookup_free_nid_list(nm_i, nid);', '\t\tif (e) {', '\t\t\tif (e->state == NID_NEW)', '\t\t\t\tret = true;', '\t\t\tgoto err_out;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '\tret = true;', 'err_out:', 'err:', '\tif (err)', '\treturn ret;']}
description: The add_free_nid function in fs/f2fs/node.c in the Linux kernel before 4.12 does not properly track an allocated nid, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (race condition) or possibly have unspecified other impact via concurrent threads.

code_evidence: The build-path NAT cache lookup and allocated-nid rejection check at lines 9-14 run before any locking, so another thread can insert the same nid into the free nid list between this check and the insertion below.

The free nid list insertion at lines 22-24 is protected by nid_list_lock, but that lock is not held during the preceding NAT cache lookup, so the lookup and list operation are not atomic with respect to concurrent add_free_nid callers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a concurrent sequence where the shared free nid list and NAT cache state are checked and modified without exclusive access across the whole operation, matching CWE-362's improper synchronization of a shared resource. This is a race condition rather than a simple missing bounds check because the defect is the non-atomic check-then-insert window.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the NAT cache lookup deciding whether a nid is already allocated is performed outside nid_list_lock, while the related free-list insertion holds the lock. A concurrent build_free_nids thread can add the same nid to the free nid list after the lookup, allowing an allocated nid to be loaded into the free nid cache and allocated again. The supported consequence is a race condition causing denial of service or other unspecified impact.

commit_msg:
crypto: mcryptd - Check mcryptd algorithm compatibility

Algorithms not compatible with mcryptd could be spawned by mcryptd
with a direct crypto_alloc_tfm invocation using a "mcryptd(alg)" name
construct.  This causes mcryptd to crash the kernel if an arbitrary
"alg" is incompatible and not intended to be used with mcryptd.  It is
an issue if AF_ALG tries to spawn mcryptd(alg) to expose it externally.
But such algorithms must be used internally and not be exposed.

We added a check to enforce that only internal algorithms are allowed
with mcryptd at the time mcryptd is spawning an algorithm.

Link: http://marc.info/?l=linux-crypto-vger&m=148063683310477&w=2
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Mikulas Patocka <mpatocka@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Tim Chen <tim.c.chen@linux.intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static inline void mcryptd_check_internal(struct rtattr **tb, u32 *type,', '\t\treturn;', '\tif ((algt->type & CRYPTO_ALG_INTERNAL))', '\t\t*type |= CRYPTO_ALG_INTERNAL;', '\tif ((algt->mask & CRYPTO_ALG_INTERNAL))', '\t\t*mask |= CRYPTO_ALG_INTERNAL;'], 'added_lines': ['static inline bool mcryptd_check_internal(struct rtattr **tb, u32 *type,', '\t\treturn false;', '', '\t*type |= algt->type & CRYPTO_ALG_INTERNAL;', '\t*mask |= algt->mask & CRYPTO_ALG_INTERNAL;', '', '\tif (*type & *mask & CRYPTO_ALG_INTERNAL)', '\t\treturn true;', '\telse', '\t\treturn false;']}

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only reads type/mask attributes from tb and sets flags; it performs no pointer dereference that can be NULL, so CWE-476 is not directly supported by this function's code.

commit_msg: Fix the Rijndael timing attack counter measure
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tword32 u = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\tvolatile word32 u = 0;']}
description: The timing attack protection in Rijndael::Enc::ProcessAndXorBlock and Rijndael::Dec::ProcessAndXorBlock in Crypto++ (aka cryptopp) before 5.6.4 may be optimized out by the compiler, which allows attackers to conduct timing attacks.

code_evidence: A local accumulator u is declared non-volatile and initialized to zero, then used only to be ANDed with table entries and ORed into the state words.

The loop iterates over Te cache lines, ANDing u with each line and with Te[255], then ORs u into s0..s3. Because u is never read externally and always zero, a compiler may legally eliminate the entire loop and the OR operations as dead code.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-200 fits because the removed countermeasure lets an unauthorized observer infer secret key-dependent information through timing, i.e., exposure of sensitive information. The flaw is the ineffective protection enabling observation, not a memory-safety error; the fix makes u volatile to preserve the accesses.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the timing-attack countermeasure relies on a non-volatile accumulator whose loop has no observable effect, so the optimizer can remove the table-touching accesses. Trigger: compiling with optimization enabled. Consequence: memory-access timing no longer depends on secret table indices, enabling cache-timing recovery of key-dependent state (confidentiality loss).

commit_msg:

  possible buffer overflow.
* There were also a few similar situations with sscanf().

Line 30 uses sscanf with an unbounded %s conversion that writes an arbitrarily long prestring argument into buf; the length check on line 35 occurs only after the write, and lines 38-39 then append a space and terminator.

commit_msg:
An privileged attacker can cause a crash by mounting a crafted ext4
image which triggers a out-of-bounds read in the function
ext4_valid_block_bitmap() in fs/ext4/balloc.c.

This issue has been assigned CVE-2018-1093.

BugLink: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=199181
BugLink: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1560782
Reported-by: Wen Xu <wen.xu@gatech.edu>
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!ext4_test_bit(EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset), bh->b_data))', '\tif (!ext4_test_bit(EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset), bh->b_data))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (offset < 0 || EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset) >= sb->s_blocksize ||', '\t    !ext4_test_bit(EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset), bh->b_data))', '\tif (offset < 0 || EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset) >= sb->s_blocksize ||', '\t    !ext4_test_bit(EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset), bh->b_data))', '\tif (offset < 0 || EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset) >= sb->s_blocksize ||', '\t    EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset + sbi->s_itb_per_group) >= sb->s_blocksize)', '\t\treturn blk;']}
description: The ext4_valid_block_bitmap function in fs/ext4/balloc.c in the Linux kernel through 4.15.15 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and system crash) via a crafted ext4 image because balloc.c and ialloc.c do not validate bitmap block numbers.

code_evidence: blk is taken from the on-disk group descriptor via ext4_block_bitmap and offset is computed as blk - group_first_block; offset is passed to EXT4_B2C and then ext4_test_bit without checking that the resulting bit index is within bh->b_data.
The inode bitmap block number is read the same way: offset = blk - group_first_block, then ext4_test_bit(EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset), bh->b_data) with no lower or upper bound check.

The inode table block number feeds EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset + sbi->s_itb_per_group) and EXT4_B2C(sbi, offset) directly into ext4_find_next_zero_bit over bh->b_data, again without validating offset or the end index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads bh->b_data at attacker-influenced bit indices that are not constrained to the buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read. The added checks (offset < 0 and EXT4_B2C(...) >= sb->s_blocksize) confirm the missing bounds are the defect; an integer overflow alone would not describe the observed read past the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bitmap block numbers from a crafted ext4 image are used to compute bit offsets without validating that offset >= 0 or that the converted bit index stays below the buffer size. Trigger: a privileged mount of a crafted image with bad block-bitmap, inode-bitmap, or inode-table block numbers. Consequence: ext4_test_bit/ext4_find_next_zero_bit read past bh->b_data, causing an out-of-bounds read and a system crash.

commit_msg:
bpf: fix branch pruning logic

when the verifier detects that register contains a runtime constant
and it's compared with another constant it will prune exploration
of the branch that is guaranteed not to be taken at runtime.
This is all correct, but malicious program may be constructed
in such a way that it always has a constant comparison and
the other branch is never taken under any conditions.
In this case such path through the program will not be explored
by the verifier. It won't be taken at run-time either, but since
all instructions are JITed the malicious program may cause JITs
to complain about using reserved fields, etc.
To fix the issue we have to track the instructions explored by
the verifier and sanitize instructions that are dead at run time
with NOPs. We cannot reject such dead code, since llvm generates
it for valid C code, since it doesn't do as much data flow
analysis as the verifier does.

Fixes: 17a5267067f3 ("bpf: verifier (add verifier core)")
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Acked-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tenv->insn_aux_data[insn_idx].seen = true;', '\t\t\t\tenv->insn_aux_data[insn_idx].seen = true;']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.8 ignores unreachable code, even though it would still be processed by JIT compilers. This behavior, also considered an improper branch-pruning logic issue, could possibly be used by local users for denial of service.

code_evidence: is_state_visited() prunes exploration when a prior state is found; on err==1 the verifier jumps to process_bpf_exit and never records or validates the skipped instruction path.
The loop only validates instructions it actually reaches; instructions bypassed by branch pruning are never passed through the class/mode checks (e.g. BPF_LD reserved-field checks at 205-207).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The verifier accepts attacker-supplied BPF bytecode without validating all of its instructions (reserved fields, modes) because pruned/dead code is never checked; this is improper input validation of program input, leading to the described DoS via JIT.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the verifier treats state-equivalence as proof a path is safe and skips it, without marking or sanitizing instructions that are unreachable at verification time. A crafted BPF program can contain constant comparisons whose dead branch holds instructions never validated; JIT compilation later processes those instructions, potentially hitting reserved fields and misbehaving.

commit_msg:
Fix `tf.raw_ops.RaggedTensorToTensor` failing CHECK in `tensor.cc`.

Tensor "', '                                        "requires at least one element."));']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. Due to lack of validation in `tf.raw_ops.RaggedTensorToTensor`, an attacker can exploit an undefined behavior if input arguments are empty. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/656e7673b14acd7835dc778867f84916c6d1cac2/tensorflow/core/kernels/ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op.cc#L356-L360) only checks that one of the tensors is not empty, but does not check for the other ones. There are multiple `DCHECK` validations to prevent heap OOB, but these are no-op in release builds, hence they don't prevent anything. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick these commits on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The loop derives each multiplier[i] as multiplier[i+1] * output_size[i+1] without validating that output_size has the expected ragged_rank_+1 length or that the products stay within INDEX_TYPE.
full_size is computed as multiplier[0] * output_size[0]; if output_size is empty or too short, these indexed reads are out of bounds, and the product can overflow.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-131 fits because the code computes buffer-related sizes (multiplier and full_size) from an unvalidated output_size vector, so the size calculation can be wrong or overflow. The missing length check, not merely a missing null check, is the sizing defect; the resulting OOB access is the consequence.

evidence_lines.code: const INDEX_TYPE full_size = multiplier[0] * output_size[0];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: output_size is produced by CalculateOutputSize and then indexed at [i+1] and [0] with no check that it contains ragged_rank_+1 elements, so an empty argument set yields an undersized vector. Trigger: calling RaggedTensorToTensor with an empty first partition/related input. Consequence: out-of-bounds indexing and integer overflow in the size computation, leading to undefined behavior or heap OOB rather than a correctly sized output buffer.

commit_msg:
arm64: perf: reject groups spanning multiple HW PMUs

The perf core implicitly rejects events spanning multiple HW PMUs, as in
these cases the event->ctx will differ. However this validation is
performed after pmu::event_init() is called in perf_init_event(), and
thus pmu::event_init() may be called with a group leader from a
different HW PMU.

The ARM64 PMU driver does not take this fact into account, and when
validating groups assumes that it can call to_arm_pmu(event->pmu) for
any HW event. When the event in question is from another HW PMU this is
wrong, and results in dereferencing garbage.

This patch updates the ARM64 PMU driver to first test for and reject
events from other PMUs, moving the to_arm_pmu and related logic after
this test. Fixes a crash triggered by perf_fuzzer on Linux-4.0-rc2, with
a CCI PMU present:

commit_msg:
The current CIPSO and CALIPSO refcounting scheme for the DOI
definitions is a bit flawed in that we:

1. Don't correctly match gets/puts in netlbl_cipsov4_list().
2. Decrement the refcount on each attempt to remove the DOI from the
   DOI list, only removing it from the list once the refcount drops
   to zero.

This patch fixes these problems by adding the missing "puts" to
netlbl_cipsov4_list() and introduces a more conventional, i.e.
not-buggy, refcounting mechanism to the DOI definitions.  Upon the
addition of a DOI to the DOI list, it is initialized with a refcount
of one, removing a DOI from the list removes it from the list and
drops the refcount by one; "gets" and "puts" behave as expected with
respect to refcounts, increasing and decreasing the DOI's refcount by
one.

Fixes: b1edeb102397 ("netlabel: Replace protocol/NetLabel linking with refrerence counts")
Fixes: d7cce01504a0 ("netlabel: Add support for removing a CALIPSO DOI.")
Reported-by: syzbot+9ec037722d2603a9f52e@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Paul Moore <paul@paul-moore.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!refcount_dec_and_test(&doi_def->refcount)) {', '\t\tspin_unlock(&cipso_v4_doi_list_lock);', '\t\tret_val = -EBUSY;', '\t\tgoto doi_remove_return;', '\t}', '\tcipso_v4_cache_invalidate();', '\tcall_rcu(&doi_def->rcu, cipso_v4_doi_free_rcu);'], 'added_lines': ['\tcipso_v4_doi_putdef(doi_def);']}
description: The Linux kernel before 5.11.14 has a use-after-free in cipso_v4_genopt in net/ipv4/cipso_ipv4.c because the CIPSO and CALIPSO refcounting for the DOI definitions is mishandled, aka CID-ad5d07f4a9cd. This leads to writing an arbitrary value.

code_evidence: On removal, refcount_dec_and_test is called while holding the DOI list lock; if the count does not reach zero the function returns -EBUSY without removing the entry, so each failed removal attempt still decrements the reference count.
When the count reaches zero, list_del_rcu is followed by cache invalidation and call_rcu(cipso_v4_doi_free_rcu), freeing the DOI object via RCU while other holders may still reference it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The DOI object is freed by call_rcu while surviving references remain, and those references are subsequently used, which is exactly CWE-416 (use after free). This is not merely a double free or refcount leak: the supported consequence is use of memory after it has been released.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The remove path drops the DOI refcount on every attempt rather than only on actual deletion, so concurrent or repeated removals can drive the count to zero and free the cipso_v4_doi object while other users still hold pointers obtained from cipso_v4_doi_search. A later access through such a stale pointer, e.g. in cipso_v4_genopt, dereferences freed memory.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    }', '    if (epoll_context != NULL) {', '        epoll_context->_ctx_status = CONTEXT_READ_OVER;']}
description: ehttp 1.0.6 before 17405b9 has an epoll_socket.cpp read_func use-after-free. An attacker can make many connections over a short time to trigger this.

code_evidence: The callback on_readable is invoked with the epoll_event whose data.ptr holds epoll_context, and its return value determines whether the context is later used.
On READ_CONTINUE, the code writes into event.events and calls epoll_ctl with the same fd obtained from epoll_context; the context's lifetime is not revalidated after the callback.
On READ_OVER, the same fd from the possibly freed context is reused in epoll_ctl, again without checking whether the callback released the context.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences and reuses data (fd, event.data.ptr) associated with an epoll context that may have been freed by the callback, matching CWE-416's reuse of freed memory. This is not merely a null dereference (CWE-476) because the object's lifetime ends after release, not its pointer being NULL.

evidence_lines.code:
} else if (ret == READ_OVER) {         event.events = EPOLLOUT | EPOLLONESHOT;
ret = epoll_ctl(_epollfd, EPOLL_CTL_MOD, fd, &event);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on_readable can close and release the epoll context (as the READ_CLOSE path acknowledges), but the read/over branches continue to use fd and event derived from that context. Trigger: many rapid connections cause the callback to release the context while handle_readable_event still proceeds; the freed context's fd is then passed to epoll_ctl, yielding a use-after-free that can crash or corrupt state.

Turns out a malicious server can register itself with a dangerous URL in
an attempt to attack a user's machine.

User interaction is required, as the URL has to be opened by
right-clicking on the server entry and clicking on "Open Webpage".

This commit introduces a client-side whitelist, which only allows "http"
and "https" schemes. We will also implement it in our public list.

In future we should probably add a warning QMessageBox informing the
user that there's no guarantee the URL is safe (regardless of the
scheme).

Thanks a lot to https://positive.security for reporting the RCE
vulnerability to us privately.

commit_msg:
mnt: Add a per mount namespace limit on the number of mounts

CAI Qian <caiqian@redhat.com> pointed out that the semantics
of shared subtrees make it possible to create an exponentially
increasing number of mounts in a mount namespace.

    mkdir /tmp/1 /tmp/2
    mount --make-rshared /
    for i in $(seq 1 20) ; do mount --bind /tmp/1 /tmp/2 ; done

Will create create 2^20 or 1048576 mounts, which is a practical problem
as some people have managed to hit this by accident.

As such CVE-2016-6213 was assigned.

Ian Kent <raven@themaw.net> described the situation for autofs users
as follows:

> The number of mounts for direct mount maps is usually not very large because of
> the way they are implemented, large direct mount maps can have performance
> problems. There can be anywhere from a few (likely case a few hundred) to less
> than 10000, plus mounts that have been triggered and not yet expired.
>
> Indirect mounts have one autofs mount at the root plus the number of mounts that
> have been triggered and not yet expired.
>
> The number of autofs indirect map entries can range from a few to the common
> case of several thousand and in rare cases up to between 30000 and 50000. I've
> not heard of people with maps larger than 50000 entries.
>
> The larger the number of map entries the greater the possibility for a large
> number of active mounts so it's not hard to expect cases of a 1000 or somewhat
> more active mounts.

So I am setting the default number of mounts allowed per mount
namespace at 100,000.  This is more than enough for any use case I
know of, but small enough to quickly stop an exponential increase
in mounts.  Which should be perfect to catch misconfigurations and
malfunctioning programs.

For anyone who needs a higher limit this can be changed by writing
to the new /proc/sys/fs/mount-max sysctl.

Tested-by: CAI Qian <caiqian@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>

description: epan/dissectors/packet-wbxml.c in the WBXML dissector in Wireshark 2.x before 2.0.5 does not restrict the recursion depth, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted packet.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.8-43 Q16, there is a heap-based buffer overflow in the function WriteSGIImage of coders/sgi.c.

code_evidence: Lines 39-40 reject columns/rows above 65535 before the raster loop, so the writer's dimensions are bounded before header fields are written.
Lines 64-65 cast image->columns and image->rows to unsigned short for the SGI header, so the header carries truncated 16-bit dimensions.
Lines 100-105 compute number_pixels from the full image->columns*image->rows and allocate the pixels buffer using that product, not the truncated header values.
Lines 109-113 iterate y over the full image->rows and fetch a full-width row of image->columns pixels.
Lines 119-124 compute the destination offset with iris_info.rows/iris_info.columns (the truncated unsigned-short header values) rather than the full dimensions, and write four bytes per pixel.

This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read; the unsafe operation modifies memory past the buffer end.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((image->columns > 65535UL) || (image->rows > 65535UL))
ThrowWriterException(ImageError,"WidthOrHeightExceedsLimit");

iris_info.columns=(unsigned short) image->columns;
iris_info.rows=(unsigned short) image->rows;

When dimensions exceed 65535, the check at lines 39-40 aborts, but the mismatch between allocation size and index arithmetic means writes can land outside the intended buffer. commit_msg:
When kmem_cache_alloc_bulk() attempts to allocate N objects from a percpu
freelist of length M, and N > M > 0, it will first remove the M elements
from the percpu freelist, then call ___slab_alloc() to allocate the next
element and repopulate the percpu freelist. ___slab_alloc() can re-enable
IRQs via allocate_slab(), so the TID must be bumped before ___slab_alloc()
to properly commit the freelist head change.

Fix it by unconditionally bumping c->tid when entering the slowpath.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: ebe909e0fdb3 ("slub: improve bulk alloc strategy")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -20,6 +20,15 @@
 		void *object = c->freelist;
 
 		if (unlikely(!object)) {
+			/*
+			 * We may have removed an object from c->freelist using
+			 * the fastpath in the previous iteration; in that case,
+			 * c->tid has not been bumped yet.
+			 * Since ___slab_alloc() may reenable interrupts while
+			 * allocating memory, we should bump c->tid now.
+			 */
+			c->tid = next_tid(c->tid);
+
 			/*
 			 * Invoking slow path likely have side-effect
 			 * of re-populating per CPU c->freelist
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t/*', '\t\t\t * We may have removed an object from c->freelist using', '\t\t\t * the fastpath in the previous iteration; in that case,', '\t\t\t * c->tid has not been bumped yet.', '\t\t\t * Since ___slab_alloc() may reenable interrupts while', '\t\t\t * allocating memory, we should bump c->tid now.', '\t\t\t */', '\t\t\tc->tid = next_tid(c->tid);', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in kmem_cache_alloc_bulk in mm/slub.c in the Linux kernel before 5.5.11. The slowpath lacks the required TID increment, aka CID-fd4d9c7d0c71.

code_evidence: The loop reads c->freelist into object [12] and, on the fastpath, advances c->freelist via get_freepointer [22]; the per-CPU tid is bumped only once after the loop [26]. When the freelist is empty [13], ___slab_alloc is called [14,15], and it may re-enable IRQs via allocate_slab, then c is re-read [18]. The fastpath removal in a prior iteration has already changed the freelist head without committing it via tid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent-execution synchronization flaw: an interruptible code sequence modifies a per-CPU shared freelist without first committing the change, violating atomicity/exclusivity against the interrupting sequence. CWE-362 fits; the missing tid bump is the improper synchronization, not merely a memory-safety bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-CPU freelist head change is not committed by bumping c->tid before entering the slowpath, which can re-enable interrupts. Trigger: bulk allocation where N > M > 0, so an object is removed on the fastpath and then ___slab_alloc runs. An interrupt handler on the same CPU can observe the modified freelist with a stale tid, causing inconsistent slab state and possible corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20569)

description:
A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions

of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Policy processing is disabled by default but can be enabled by passing
the `-policy' argument to the command line utilities or by calling the
`X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_policies()' function.

code_evidence: When last->anyPolicy is set, level_add_node is called with a NULL fourth argument instead of the policy tree and a depth/flag value, so the anyPolicy node is linked without tree bookkeeping that bounds or tracks policy processing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is part of X.509 policy-constraint validation during certificate chain verification; the flawed anyPolicy linkage prevents correct, bounded validation of the certificate chain. This fits CWE-295, though the demonstrated impact is DoS rather than identity spoofing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the anyPolicy link omits the tree pointer and depth parameter, so the policy tree cannot account for this node during certificate chain verification. A malicious chain with policy constraints can then cause unbounded/exponential node processing; the supported consequence is resource exhaustion (DoS), not certificate acceptance bypass.

commit_msg:
Avoid infinite recursion in the ALTER TABLE code when a view contains an unused CTE that references, directly or indirectly, the view itself.

FossilOrigin-Name: 1d2e53a39b87e364685e21de137655b6eee725e4c6d27fc90865072d7c5892b5
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if( pSelect->selFlags & SF_View ) return WRC_Prune;']}
description: alter.c in SQLite through 3.30.1 allows attackers to trigger infinite recursion via certain types of self-referential views in conjunction with ALTER TABLE statements.

code_evidence: Line 4 reads pSelect->pSrc and line 5 dereferences it without checking selFlags; the callback then iterates every source item (lines 9-11), and line 15 calls renameWalkWith, which walks the WITH/CTE clauses of the select and re-enters this callback for any nested Select. Because there is no guard on SF_View, a view whose unused CTE references the view itself causes the walker to revisit the same view Select repeatedly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits: the function performs recursive selection walking with no depth or self-reference guard, so the recursion is uncontrolled and exhausts resources. This is not merely a NULL-deref or logic bug; the missing termination condition is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: renameTableSelectCb recurses through renameWalkWith into CTE sub-selects without terminating on view selects, so a self-referential view CTE creates an unbounded walk. Trigger: ALTER TABLE on a table used by such a view. Consequence: unbounded recursion consuming stack/CPU until crash (DoS).

If the server sends a reply in which even the first string would
overflow the transmitted bytes, list[0] (or flist[0]) will be set to
NULL and a count of 0 is returned.

If the resulting list is freed with XFreeExtensionList or
XFreeFontPath later on, the first Xfree call:

    Xfree (list[0]-1)
 turns into
    Xfree (NULL-1)

which will most likely trigger a segmentation fault.

I have modified the code to return NULL if the first string would
overflow, thus protecting the freeing functions later on.

The existing code can potentially cause a SEGV due to an out of bounds write.

This fixes CVE-2019-11921.

code_evidence: Boost transform_width/binary_from_base64 decodes the whole input into a std::string with no bounds check on the computed output size.

decoded.erase(decoded.end() - numPadding, decoded.end());
