commit_msg:
x86/mm: fully honor PS bits in guest page table walks

In L4 entries it is currently unconditionally reserved (and hence
should, when set, always result in a reserved bit page fault), and is
reserved on hardware not supporting 1Gb pages (and hence should, when
set, similarly cause a reserved bit page fault on such hardware).

This is CVE-2016-4480 / XSA-176.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Tested-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    pse1G = (gflags & _PAGE_PSE) && guest_supports_1G_superpages(v); '], 'added_lines': ['    if ( gflags & _PAGE_PSE )', '    {', '        rc |= _PAGE_PSE | _PAGE_INVALID_BIT;', '        goto out;', '    }', '    pse1G = !!(gflags & _PAGE_PSE);', '        if ( !guest_supports_1G_superpages(v) )', '            rc |= _PAGE_PSE | _PAGE_INVALID_BIT;']}
description: The guest_walk_tables function in arch/x86/mm/guest_walk.c in Xen 4.6.x and earlier does not properly handle the Page Size (PS) page table entry bit at the L4 and L3 page table levels, which might allow local guest OS users to gain privileges via a crafted mapping of memory.

code_evidence: L3 entry flags are fetched and presence checked, but the PS bit is only honored when guest_supports_1G_superpages(v) is true; otherwise the code falls through to map the L3 GFN as a page-table pointer.
With pse1G false, the walk proceeds to l2p mapping and set_ad_bits for l2/l1, treating a superpage-marked entry as an ordinary table reference.
set_ad_bits writes accessed/dirty bits into the guest page tables based on pse1G, so the misclassified PS entry affects memory the guest did not intend to expose.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission and privilege management. The flawed page-table walk lets a guest influence which memory the hypervisor treats as its page tables, bypassing the intended privilege separation between guest and host, which is an access-control failure rather than a mere bounds issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the walker does not treat _PAGE_PSE at L3 as a reserved-bit violation when 1G pages are unsupported, so a guest-crafted L3 entry with PS set is interpreted as a pointer to an L2 table. Trigger: a local guest OS maps memory with PS set at L3 on hardware without 1G support. Consequence: the guest can steer the hypervisor's walk to attacker-chosen memory, undermining the access-control boundary between guest and hypervisor memory.

commit_msg:
netfilter: conntrack: Make global sysctls readonly in non-init netns

These sysctls point to global variables:
- NF_SYSCTL_CT_MAX (&nf_conntrack_max)
- NF_SYSCTL_CT_EXPECT_MAX (&nf_ct_expect_max)
- NF_SYSCTL_CT_BUCKETS (&nf_conntrack_htable_size_user)

Because their data pointers are not updated to point to per-netns
structures, they must be marked read-only in a non-init_net ns.
Otherwise, changes in any net namespace are reflected in (leaked into)
all other net namespaces. This problem has existed since the
introduction of net namespaces.

The current logic marks them read-only only if the net namespace is
owned by an unprivileged user (other than init_user_ns).

Commit d0febd81ae77 ("netfilter: conntrack: re-visit sysctls in
unprivileged namespaces") "exposes all sysctls even if the namespace is
unpriviliged." Since we need to mark them readonly in any case, we can
forego the unprivileged user check altogether.

Fixes: d0febd81ae77 ("netfilter: conntrack: re-visit sysctls in unprivileged namespaces")
Signed-off-by: Jonathon Reinhart <Jonathon.Reinhart@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["\t/* Don't allow unprivileged users to alter certain sysctls */", '\tif (net->user_ns != &init_user_ns) {', '\t\ttable[NF_SYSCTL_CT_HELPER].mode = 0444;', '#ifdef CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK_EVENTS', '\t\ttable[NF_SYSCTL_CT_EVENTS].mode = 0444;', '#endif', '\t\ttable[NF_SYSCTL_CT_BUCKETS].mode = 0444;', '\t} else if (!net_eq(&init_net, net)) {'], 'added_lines': ["\t/* Don't allow non-init_net ns to alter global sysctls */", '\tif (!net_eq(&init_net, net)) {']}
description: net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_standalone.c in the Linux kernel before 5.12.2 allows observation of changes in any net namespace because these changes are leaked into all other net namespaces. This is related to the NF_SYSCTL_CT_MAX, NF_SYSCTL_CT_EXPECT_MAX, and NF_SYSCTL_CT_BUCKETS sysctls.

code_evidence: The sysctl table is duplicated and per-entry data pointers are bound to per-netns structures (lines 11-26). Only three global-data entries (NF_SYSCTL_CT_MAX, NF_SYSCTL_CT_EXPECT_MAX, NF_SYSCTL_CT_BUCKETS) are forced read-only. The condition at line 31 uses net->user_ns != &init_user_ns, so a non-init netns owned by init_user_ns skips the read-only assignments for NF_SYSCTL_CT_MAX and NF_SYSCTL_CT_EXPECT_MAX; only the else-if at line 39 covers buckets. Those entries still point to global variables, so a writable sysctl in one netns mutates state shared by all namespaces.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-203 fits because writes in one netns produce observable differences in other namespaces' conntrack limits, exposing information/state across an isolation boundary. It is not merely a missing access check; the weakness is the observable cross-namespace discrepancy caused by shared global variables, which the fix removes by marking them read-only for every non-init netns.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the read-only guard keys on user namespace ownership instead of net namespace identity, leaving global-backed sysctls writable in non-init netns. Trigger: an actor with sysctl write access in such a netns changes NF_SYSCTL_CT_MAX or NF_SYSCTL_CT_EXPECT_MAX. Consequence: the change is observable in all other net namespaces, leaking cross-namespace state and allowing interference with other tenants.

commit_msg:
x86/vpt: fix race when migrating timers between vCPUs

The current vPT code will migrate the emulated timers between vCPUs
(change the pt->vcpu field) while just holding the destination lock,
either from create_periodic_time or pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target if
the global target is adjusted. Changing the periodic_timer vCPU field
in this way creates a race where a third party could grab the lock in
the unlocked region of pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target (or before
create_periodic_time performs the vcpu change) and then release the
lock from a different vCPU, creating a locking imbalance.

Introduce a per-domain rwlock in order to protect periodic_time
migration between vCPU lists. Taking the lock in read mode prevents
any timer from being migrated to a different vCPU, while taking it in
write mode allows performing migration of timers across vCPUs. The
per-vcpu locks are still used to protect all the other fields from the
periodic_timer struct.

Note that such migration shouldn't happen frequently, and hence
there's no performance drop as a result of such locking.

This is XSA-336.

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There is a race condition when migrating timers between x86 HVM vCPUs. When migrating timers of x86 HVM guests between its vCPUs, the locking model used allows for a second vCPU of the same guest (also operating on the timers) to release a lock that it didn't acquire. The most likely effect of the issue is a hang or crash of the hypervisor, i.e., a Denial of Service (DoS). All versions of Xen are affected. Only x86 systems are vulnerable. Arm systems are not vulnerable. Only x86 HVM guests can leverage the vulnerability. x86 PV and PVH cannot leverage the vulnerability. Only guests with more than one vCPU can exploit the vulnerability.

code_evidence: pt_intr_post takes v->arch.hvm.tm_lock, looks up the periodic timer via is_pt_irq, and if no timer matches, releases the same lock and returns.
After pt_irq_fired and copying cb/cb_priv, the lock is dropped before invoking the callback, and the lock is only ever the per-vCPU tm_lock, not a domain-level lock protecting timer migration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a check-then-act sequence on a shared periodic_timer under a lock that does not exclude concurrent migration, a timing window where another code sequence modifies the shared resource. This matches CWE-362 rather than a simple missing-lock defect, since the lock is present but insufficiently scoped.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: timer lookup and callback extraction are protected only by the per-vCPU tm_lock, while pt->vcpu migration between vCPU lists is guarded elsewhere. A concurrent migration can move the periodic_timer to another vCPU between the lookup and unlock, so this code sequence operates on a timer no longer owned by v. The resulting lock imbalance/unstable timer state can hang or crash the hypervisor (DoS).

Stopping."), lCurrentFilePath);', '            lError = 1;', '            break;', '        }', '        // Security: ensure full, non-relative path, under destdir/', '        lCurrentFilePath = destdir + wxFileName::GetPathSeparator() + lCurrentFilePath;', '        wxString lCurrentDirectory = lCurrentFilePath.substr(0, lCurrentFilePath.find_last_of("/\\\\"));']}
description: Directory traversal issues in the D-Mod extractor in DFArc and DFArc2 (as well as in RTsoft's Dink Smallwood HD / ProtonSDK version) before 3.14 allow an attacker to overwrite arbitrary files on the user's system.

code_evidence: Archive entry name from the tar record is decoded into lCurrentFilePath and only its directory portion is computed; no check rejects '..' segments or absolute paths.
The derived directory is created with Mkdir and the file is opened for write at the archive-supplied path, so a malicious name writes wherever it resolves.
The working directory is set to destdir, which constrains relative names but does not stop '../' escapes or absolute paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function constructs a pathname from external archive input intended to stay under destdir but fails to neutralize traversal elements, matching CWE-22. It is not merely an encoding bug; the missing path constraint is the weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
wxString lPreviousWorkingDirectory(::wxGetCwd());
::wxSetWorkingDirectory(destdir);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: untrusted tar entry names are used directly as output paths without neutralizing '..' or absolute components. Trigger: an archive containing an entry such as '../../x' or '/abs/x'. Consequence: arbitrary file overwrite outside destdir, potentially leading to code execution or data destruction.

commit_msg: Guard binary expressions from too much recursion.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["\twhile (jsP_accept(J, '^'))"], 'added_lines': ['\tSAVEREC();', "\twhile (jsP_accept(J, '^')) {", '\t\tINCREC();', '\t}', '\tPOPREC();']}
description: jsparse.c in Artifex MuJS through 1.0.2 does not properly maintain the AST depth for binary expressions, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive recursion) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: bitxor() parses a left operand via bitand() and then repeatedly consumes '^' tokens, rebuilding the AST in a loop with EXP2(BITXOR, a, bitand(J, notin)). The while loop at line 4 has no recursion-depth accounting or bound; each iteration invokes bitand(), which descends into the expression grammar for the right operand. A crafted input containing many '^' operators drives this descent without any depth guard.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the function permits recursion to grow unbounded through expression parsing, exhausting the program stack. This is uncontrolled recursion causing resource consumption, not merely a logic error in operator precedence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the binary-expression parser does not track or limit recursion depth while consuming '^' operators. Trigger: a crafted file with a long chain of XOR expressions causes repeated nested parser calls through bitand(). Consequence: excessive stack recursion leading to resource exhaustion and denial of service.

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
Reported-by: Kyle Zeng <zengyhkyle@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jamal Hadi Salim <jhs@mojatatu.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tcase TC_ACT_SHOT:', '\t\t\treturn NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (result == TC_ACT_SHOT)', '\t\t\treturn NULL;']}
description: cbq_classify in net/sched/sch_cbq.c in the Linux kernel through 6.1.4 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (slab-out-of-bounds read) because of type confusion (non-negative numbers can sometimes indicate a TC_ACT_SHOT condition rather than valid classification results).

code_evidence: After tcf_classify, only negative results are rejected; non-negative results such as TC_ACT_SHOT pass to line 22, where res.class is cast to struct cbq_class * and then dereferenced at line 31 (cl->level) without validating that res holds a class pointer.
The TC_ACT_SHOT case is handled only inside the switch at line 40, after cl has already been dereferenced at line 31, so the drop action does not prevent the invalid access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function interprets res as holding a struct cbq_class pointer based solely on a non-negative result, although the same res field may instead carry an action code such as TC_ACT_SHOT. Accessing that resource through an incompatible type is exactly CWE-843; the out-of-bounds read is the consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return code from tcf_classify is checked only for negativity, so a non-negative action code like TC_ACT_SHOT is treated as a successful classification and res.class is used as a pointer. Trigger: a TC filter action returning TC_ACT_SHOT with res.class unset or non-pointer. Consequence: cl->level reads memory at an invalid address, causing a slab-out-of-bounds read and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix a memory exhaustion bug when attempting to allocate room for an impossible number of program headers.

	* elfcode.h (elf_object_p): Check for corrupt input files with
	more program headers than can actually fit in the file.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      /* Check for a corrupt input file with an impossibly large number', '\t of program headers.  */', '      if (bfd_get_file_size (abfd) > 0', '\t  && i_ehdrp->e_phnum > bfd_get_file_size (abfd))', '\tgoto got_no_match;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils through 2.31. There is a heap-based buffer overflow in bfd_elf32_swap_phdr_in in elfcode.h because the number of program headers is not restricted.

code_evidence: The e_phnum guard only exists under #ifndef BFD64, so in 64-bit builds the count is unchecked before the allocation size is computed.
amt is computed as e_phnum * sizeof(*i_phdr) and passed to bfd_alloc; a corrupt e_phnum drives the allocation size directly.
The loop iterates i over e_phnum, reading a program header into x_phdr and writing through elf_swap_phdr_in into i_phdr, which advances each iteration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-influenced data into a heap buffer sized from an unchecked count, producing writes beyond the intended buffer. This is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the memory-exhaustion aspect is secondary to the buffer overrun.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the number of program headers from the untrusted ELF header is not validated against the actual file size in 64-bit builds. Trigger: a crafted ELF file with an impossibly large e_phnum. Consequence: the loop writes program headers past the allocated phdr buffer, corrupting heap memory (and exhausting memory during allocation).

commit_msg: fixed #1738
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!entry || !entry->av1_config) return NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!entry || !entry->av1_config|| !entry->av1_config->config) return NULL;']}
description: The AV1_DuplicateConfig function in GPAC 1.0.1 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via a crafted file in the MP4Box command.

code_evidence: Line 15 retrieves entry from the sample-description child_boxes list; line 16 validates only entry and entry->av1_config before line 17 passes entry->av1_config->config to AV1_DuplicateConfig. The nested config pointer is never checked against NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid without a NULL check, matching the described NULL pointer dereference DoS. The patch adds the missing !entry->av1_config->config guard, confirming the unchecked nested pointer as the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function assumes av1_config->config is always populated for an AV1 sample entry. A crafted MP4 can supply an av1_config whose config pointer is NULL, so the unchecked dereference at line 17 propagates NULL into AV1_DuplicateConfig, causing a NULL pointer dereference and crash (DoS). The missing constraint on config is the root cause; the crash is the consequence.

commit_msg:
VT-d: correct ordering of operations in cleanup_domid_map()

The function may be called without any locks held (leaving aside the
domctl one, which we surely don't want to depend on here), so needs to
play safe wrt other accesses to domid_map[] and domid_bitmap[]. This is
to avoid context_set_domain_id()'s writing of domid_map[] to be reset to
zero right away in the case of it racing the freeing of a DID.

For the interaction with context_set_domain_id() and did_to_domain_id()
see the code comment.

{check_,}cleanup_domid_map() are called with pcidevs_lock held or during
domain cleanup only (and pcidevs_lock is also held around
context_set_domain_id()), i.e. racing calls with the same (dom, iommu)
tuple cannot occur.

domain_iommu_domid(), besides its use by cleanup_domid_map(), has its
result used only to control flushing, and hence a stale result would
only lead to a stray extra flush.

This is CVE-2022-26357 / XSA-399.

Fixes: b9c20c78789f ("VT-d: per-iommu domain-id")
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        iommu->domid_map[iommu_domid] = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['        /*', '         * Update domid_map[] /before/ domid_bitmap[] to avoid a race with', '         * context_set_domain_id(), setting the slot to DOMID_INVALID for', '         * did_to_domain_id() to return a suitable value while the bit is', '         * still set.', '         */', '        iommu->domid_map[iommu_domid] = DOMID_INVALID;']}
description: race in VT-d domain ID cleanup Xen domain IDs are up to 15 bits wide. VT-d hardware may allow for only less than 15 bits to hold a domain ID associating a physical device with a particular domain. Therefore internally Xen domain IDs are mapped to the smaller value range. The cleaning up of the housekeeping structures has a race, allowing for VT-d domain IDs to be leaked and flushes to be bypassed.

code_evidence: cleanup_domid_map() reads the shared iommu->domid_bitmap and iommu->domid_map without holding a lock; the commit states it may run without locks besides domctl. It clears the bitmap bit (line 9) and then writes domid_map[iommu_domid] = 0 (line 10) as two separate non-atomic operations on shared per-iommu state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a concurrent sequence on shared domid_map[]/domid_bitmap[] lacks exclusive access, and the ordering of the two updates violates atomicity, allowing an interfering writer to be reset. It is not merely a missing check; the defect is the timing window between the two shared-state updates.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bitmap clear and map reset are unordered and unsynchronized, so a concurrent context_set_domain_id() writing domid_map[] can be overwritten by the zeroing in line 10. Trigger: cleanup races another access to the same (dom, iommu) structures. Supported consequence: leaked VT-d domain IDs and bypassed flushes, since did_to_domain_id() may observe inconsistent map/bitmap state.

commit_msg: fix: more robust address range checks in svhandler_flash_*
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  // Protect from overflow.', '  if (beginAddr + length < beginAddr) return;', '', '  // Do not allow firmware to erase bootstrap or bootloader sectors.', '  if (((beginAddr >= BSTRP_FLASH_SECT_START) &&', '       (beginAddr <= (BSTRP_FLASH_SECT_START + BSTRP_FLASH_SECT_LEN - 1))) ||', '      (((beginAddr + length) >= BSTRP_FLASH_SECT_START) &&', '       ((beginAddr + length) <=', '        (BSTRP_FLASH_SECT_START + BSTRP_FLASH_SECT_LEN - 1)))) {', '    return;', '  }', '', '  if (((beginAddr >= BLDR_FLASH_SECT_START) &&', '       (beginAddr <= (BLDR_FLASH_SECT_START + 2 * BLDR_FLASH_SECT_LEN - 1))) ||', '      (((beginAddr + length) >= BLDR_FLASH_SECT_START) &&', '       ((beginAddr + length) <=', '        (BLDR_FLASH_SECT_START + 2 * BLDR_FLASH_SECT_LEN - 1)))) {', '    return;', '  }'], 'added_lines': ['  // Verify requested address range is allowed.', '  if (!allow_svhandler_flash_range(beginAddr, beginAddr + length)) return;']}
description: In the KeepKey firmware before 7.3.2,Flaws in the supervisor interface can be exploited to bypass important security restrictions on firmware operations. Using these flaws, malicious firmware code can elevate privileges, permanently make the device inoperable or overwrite the trusted bootloader code to compromise the hardware wallet across reboots or storage wipes.

code_evidence: beginAddr, data and length are taken directly from supervisor-call parameters with no trust boundary check.
The only remaining guard is an integer-overflow check on beginAddr + length; it does not constrain the range to permitted flash regions.

The bootstrap and bootloader exclusion checks only test whether the start or end address falls inside each protected sector; a range that fully spans a protected sector satisfies neither condition and passes.
flash_program then writes to the caller-supplied beginAddr for length bytes, reaching protected sectors.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function processes caller-supplied address and length without validating that the whole range lies in allowed flash, so improper input validation (CWE-20) directly describes the weakness; the missing containment check is the validation gap, distinct from the resulting memory overwrite.

evidence_lines.code: if (beginAddr + length < beginAddr) return;
flash_program(beginAddr, (uint8_t *)data, length);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the range validation is incomplete, so a request whose span encloses a protected sector is accepted. Trigger: supervisor caller supplies a beginAddr/length covering BSTRP or BLDR sectors. Consequence: flash_program overwrites the bootstrap/bootloader region, enabling persistent firmware compromise.

Fix leak with ASN.1 combine.

When parsing a combined structure pass a flag to the decode routine
so on error a pointer to the parent structure is not zeroed as
this will leak any additional components in the parent.

This can leak memory in any application parsing PKCS#7 or CMS structures.

CVE-2015-3195.

Thanks to Adam Langley (Google/BoringSSL) for discovering this bug using
libFuzzer.

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>

Consequence: parent components are leaked and stale memory may be exposed, allowing sensitive process memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
Excessive allocation of memory in tls_get_message_header()

A TLS message includes 3 bytes for its length in the header for the message.
This would allow for messages up to 16Mb in length. Messages of this length
are excessive and OpenSSL includes a check to ensure that a peer is sending
reasonably sized messages in order to avoid too much memory being consumed
to service a connection. A flaw in the logic of version 1.1.0 means that
memory for the message is allocated too early, prior to the excessive
message length check. Due to way memory is allocated in OpenSSL this could
mean an attacker could force up to 21Mb to be allocated to service a
connection. This could lead to a Denial of Service through memory
exhaustion. However, the excessive message length check still takes place,
and this would cause the connection to immediately fail. Assuming that the
application calls SSL_free() on the failed conneciton in a timely manner
then the 21Mb of allocated memory will then be immediately freed again.
Therefore the excessive memory allocation will be transitory in nature.
This then means that there is only a security impact if:

1) The application does not call SSL_free() in a timely manner in the
event that the connection fails
or
2) The application is working in a constrained environment where there
is very little free memory
or
3) The attacker initiates multiple connection attempts such that there
are multiple connections in a state where memory has been allocated for
the connection; SSL_free() has not yet been called; and there is
insufficient memory to service the multiple requests.

Except in the instance of (1) above any Denial Of Service is likely to
be transitory because as soon as the connection fails the memory is
subsequently freed again in the SSL_free() call. However there is an
increased risk during this period of application crashes due to the lack
of memory - which would then mean a more serious Denial of Service.

This issue does not affect DTLS users.

Issue was reported by Shi Lei (Gear Team, Qihoo 360 Inc.).

CVE-2016-6307

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
(cherry picked from commit c1ef7c971d0bbf117c3c80f65b5875e2e7b024b1)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (l && !BUF_MEM_grow_clean(s->init_buf, (int)l)) {', '            SSLerr(SSL_F_TLS_GET_MESSAGE_HEADER, ERR_R_BUF_LIB);', '            goto err;', '        }', '        if (l && !BUF_MEM_grow_clean(s->init_buf,', '                                     (int)l + SSL3_HM_HEADER_LENGTH)) {', '            SSLerr(SSL_F_TLS_GET_MESSAGE_HEADER, ERR_R_BUF_LIB);', '            goto err;', '        }', ' err:'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The state-machine implementation in OpenSSL 1.1.0 before 1.1.0a allocates memory before checking for an excessive length, which might allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via crafted TLS messages, related to statem/statem.c and statem/statem_lib.c.

code_evidence: n2l3(p, l) decodes the attacker-supplied 3-byte length field into l. Only after this decode is the excessive-length check l > (INT_MAX - SSL3_HM_HEADER_LENGTH) performed.
BUF_MEM_grow_clean(s->init_buf, (int)l + SSL3_HM_HEADER_LENGTH) allocates the buffer sized from the peer-controlled l before the size limit is enforced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to constrain how much memory is allocated in response to an untrusted length, matching CWE-400's uncontrolled resource consumption. It is a logic-ordering flaw (allocation precedes the limit check), not a classic integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The peer-controlled TLS handshake length is used to size an allocation before the excessive-message-length check runs. A crafted message forces a large buffer allocation; the later check rejects the message, but the memory has already been consumed, enabling transitory memory exhaustion and denial of service.

commit_msg:
There is a small race window in the card disconnection code that
allows the registration of another card with the very same card id.
This leads to a warning in procfs creation as caught by syzkaller.

The problem is that we delete snd_cards and snd_cards_lock entries at
the very beginning of the disconnection procedure.  This makes the
slot available to be assigned for another card object while the
disconnection procedure is being processed.  Then it becomes possible
to issue a procfs registration with the existing file name although we
check the conflict beforehand.

The fix is simply to move the snd_cards and snd_cards_lock clearances
at the end of the disconnection procedure.  The references to these
entries are merely either from the global proc files like
/proc/asound/cards or from the card registration / disconnection, so
it should be fine to shift at the very end.

Reported-by: syzbot+48df349490c36f9f54ab@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* phase 1: disable fops (user space) operations for ALSA API */', '\tmutex_lock(&snd_card_mutex);', '\tsnd_cards[card->number] = NULL;', '\tclear_bit(card->number, snd_cards_lock);', '\tmutex_unlock(&snd_card_mutex);', '\t', '\t/* phase 2: replace file->f_op with special dummy operations */', '\t', '\t/* phase 3: notify all connected devices about disconnection */'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* replace file->f_op with special dummy operations */', '\t/* notify all connected devices about disconnection */', '', '\t/* disable fops (user space) operations for ALSA API */', '\tmutex_lock(&snd_card_mutex);', '\tsnd_cards[card->number] = NULL;', '\tclear_bit(card->number, snd_cards_lock);', '\tmutex_unlock(&snd_card_mutex);', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10. There is a use-after-free in the sound subsystem because card disconnection causes certain data structures to be deleted too early. This is related to sound/core/init.c and sound/core/info.c.

code_evidence: Disconnect clears snd_cards[card->number] and the snd_cards_lock bit under snd_card_mutex at the start of teardown, before the file f_op replacement and device/info unregistration below complete.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The premature clearing of the card slot allows another object to take over the identity while the original disconnection still references it, matching CWE-416's reuse of freed/reassigned memory via a stale pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The card slot is released early, so a concurrent registration can reuse the same card id and publish procfs entries while this card's disconnection is still in progress. The stale/duplicated slot association then lets the teardown path operate on structures no longer uniquely owned, causing the reported use-after-free and procfs name-conflict warning.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.3.9. ksmbd does not validate the SMB request protocol ID, leading to an out-of-bounds read.

code_evidence: After copying the 4-byte RFC1002 header into request_buf, the function now calls ksmbd_smb_request(conn) to validate the SMB protocol ID before proceeding; previously this validation happened after reading the full PDU.
The protocol-ID check at line 55-56 reads the ProtocolId field from smb2_get_msg(conn->request_buf), and only then does line 57-58 enforce SMB2_MIN_SUPPORTED_HEADER_SIZE.
pdu_size is derived from the attacker-controlled header at line 21; line 38 allocates pdu_size+5 bytes and line 45 reads pdu_size bytes into request_buf+4.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits reading smb2_hdr fields such as ProtocolId and downstream header fields from a buffer that may be shorter than SMB2_MIN_SUPPORTED_HEADER_SIZE, which is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). This is not a write overflow, since the issue is reading beyond the intended buffer bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the protocol ID is inspected and the SMB2 header size is only checked after the full attacker-sized PDU is read into a buffer sized from the untrusted length. Trigger: a request whose pdu_size is smaller than the SMB2 header size but whose buffer is later interpreted as an smb2_hdr (e.g. in init_smb2_rsp_hdr). Consequence: a read past the end of the allocated request buffer, as reported by KASAN.

commit_msg:
dccp_disconnect() sets 'dp->dccps_hc_tx_ccid' tx handler to NULL,
therefore if DCCP socket is disconnected and dccp_sendmsg() is
called after it, it will cause a NULL pointer dereference in
dccp_write_xmit().

This crash and the reproducer was reported by syzbot. Looks like
it is reproduced if commit 69c64866ce07 ("dccp: CVE-2017-8824:
use-after-free in DCCP code") is applied.

Reported-by: syzbot+f99ab3887ab65d70f816@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Alexey Kodanev <alexey.kodanev@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (sk->sk_state == DCCP_CLOSED) {', '\t\trc = -ENOTCONN;', '\t\tgoto out_discard;', '\t}', '']}
description: Linux kernel before version 4.16-rc7 is vulnerable to a null pointer dereference in dccp_write_xmit() function in net/dccp/output.c in that allows a local user to cause a denial of service by a number of certain crafted system calls.

code_evidence: After the connect-state check, the code proceeds to queue and transmit the skb without rechecking sk->sk_state after lock_sock() is reacquired.
dccp_qpolicy_push() followed by dccp_write_xmit() transmits the skb; on a disconnected socket the tx CCID handler dccps_hc_tx_ccid is NULL, so dccp_write_xmit() dereferences it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allows a send path on a disconnected socket whose tx CCID handler is NULL, and that NULL pointer is dereferenced downstream. This is a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476), not a use-after-free, since no freed object is accessed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dccp_sendmsg() does not reject a DCCP_CLOSED socket before pushing and transmitting the skb. Trigger: a caller invokes sendmsg() after dccp_disconnect() set the tx CCID handler to NULL. Consequence: dccp_write_xmit() dereferences the NULL handler, causing a kernel crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
blf: don't assume that app text is null-terminated in the file.

When reading the text from an app text message, allocate a buffer one
byte larger than the size of the message, and set that byte to '\0'
after reading the message text, to ensure that the text is
null-terminated and can be safely handed to routines that process C
strings.

Fixes #19084.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    gchar *text = g_try_malloc0((gsize)apptextheader.textLength);'], 'added_lines': ["    /* Add an extra byte for a terminating '\\0' */", '    gchar *text = g_try_malloc((gsize)apptextheader.textLength + 1);', "    text[apptextheader.textLength] = '\\0'; /* Here's the '\\0' */"]}
description: BLF file parser crash in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.5 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.13 allows denial of service via crafted capture file

code_evidence: The buffer is sized to exactly apptextheader.textLength bytes via g_try_malloc0, with no room for a terminator.
blf_read_bytes fills exactly apptextheader.textLength bytes read from the file; the file-controlled textLength determines the allocation size and copy length.
g_strsplit_set treats text as a NUL-terminated C string, but no terminator was written within the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a missing bound on the buffer relative to string-processing requirements, i.e., the allocated buffer is too small for the NUL terminator that downstream code assumes. This matches CWE-787's out-of-bounds write/memory boundary scope; the observable effect here is an out-of-bounds read, but the root cause is the undersized buffer lacking the required terminator byte.

evidence_lines.code: gchar *text = g_try_malloc0((gsize)apptextheader.textLength);

if (!blf_read_bytes(params, data_start + sizeof(apptextheader), text, apptextheader.textLength, err, err_info)) {
}
gchar **tokens = g_strsplit_set(text, ";", -1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation lacks space for a terminating '\0' and the file-sourced text is not guaranteed to contain one. Trigger: a crafted BLF app-text message whose textLength bytes contain no NUL causes g_strsplit_set to read past the buffer. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read leading to crash/DoS; the fix adds one byte and writes text[textLength] = '\0'.

commit_msg:
Prevent instability and crash due to message flood

This patch adds a rate limiting to selected patches. The underlying rate limiter
used is the Leaky-Bucket algorithm. It allows for a burst of messages, but
limits them after a specified amount of messages within a time frame.

Sonivox: sanity check numSamples.

description: Sonivox in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-04-01 does not check for a negative number of samples, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, related to arm-wt-22k/lib_src/eas_wtengine.c and arm-wt-22k/lib_src/eas_wtsynth.c, aka internal bug 26366256.

code_evidence: numSamples is loaded from pWTIntFrame->numSamples and used directly; pOutputBuffer and pSamples/loopEnd are derived from frame/voice pointers without validating that numSamples is positive.
The while(numSamples--) loop writes *pOutputBuffer++ on each iteration; a negative numSamples is nonzero and the decrementing loop runs a huge number of iterations, writing far past the audio buffer.

Inside the loop, pSamples is advanced by acc0 (phaseFrac >> NUM_PHASE_FRAC_BITS) and wrapped relative to loopEnd; with an invalid sample count the read of pSamples[0]/pSamples[1] can also fall outside the intended sample region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a write (and read) beyond the intended audio buffer boundary caused by an unbounded negative count, which directly matches CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory access. The integer sign error is the enabling root cause, but the supported weakness is the resulting improper buffer-bounds restriction.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the frame-provided numSamples without checking its sign. Trigger: a crafted media file yields numSamples <= 0, so while(numSamples--) continues for a very large iteration count. Consequence: out-of-bounds writes through pOutputBuffer and out-of-bounds reads via pSamples, causing memory corruption and potential code execution or denial of service.

description: A vulnerability has been found in Linux Kernel and classified as problematic. This vulnerability affects the function kcm_tx_work of the file net/kcm/kcmsock.c of the component kcm. The manipulation leads to race condition. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-211018 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: sock_orphan(sk) and kfree_skb(kcm->seq_skb) run before lock_sock(sk), so they mutate sk state and the socket association without holding the socket lock.
The queue purge and kcm->tx_stopped assignment then occur under lock_sock(sk)/release_sock(sk), establishing that the earlier orphan/kfree operations are the ones outside the exclusive section.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a shared resource (sk and its sk_socket) is modified by kcm_release outside the lock that kcm_tx_work relies on, allowing an interfering concurrent sequence. The missing exclusivity, not a simple NULL check, is the defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: kcm_release performs sock_orphan(sk) before acquiring the socket lock, while kcm_tx_work concurrently reads sk->sk_socket and clears SOCK_NOSPACE. Trigger: another thread runs kcm_tx_work while kcm_release clears sk->sk_socket via sock_orphan. Consequence: kcm_tx_work dereferences a NULL sk->sk_socket, causing a null-pointer write and kernel crash.

commit_msg:
xt_compat_match/target_from_user doesn't check that zeroing the area
to start of next rule won't write past end of allocated ruleset blob.

Remove this code and zero the entire blob beforehand.

Reported-by: syzbot+cfc0247ac173f597aaaa@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Reported-by: Andy Nguyen <theflow@google.com>
Fixes: 9fa492cdc160c ("[NETFILTER]: x_tables: simplify compat API")
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint pad, off = xt_compat_target_offset(target);', '\tpad = XT_ALIGN(target->targetsize) - target->targetsize;', '\tif (pad > 0)', '\t\tmemset(t->data + target->targetsize, 0, pad);'], 'added_lines': ['\tint off = xt_compat_target_offset(target);']}
description: A heap out-of-bounds write affecting Linux since v2.6.19-rc1 was discovered in net/netfilter/x_tables.c. This allows an attacker to gain privileges or cause a DoS (via heap memory corruption) through user name space

code_evidence: Line 14 copies tsize - sizeof(*ct) bytes from ct->data into t->data, where tsize comes from the user-controlled ct->u.user.target_size. Lines 15-17 then compute pad = XT_ALIGN(target->targetsize) - target->targetsize and memset t->data + target->targetsize for pad bytes, without checking that this zeroing region lies within the destination allocation (t = *dstptr).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because line 17 performs a memset past the end of the intended destination buffer; the missing bound check on the padding region is the out-of-bounds write. It is not merely an integer issue, since the write itself crosses the allocation boundary.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the padding memset at line 17 writes up to XT_ALIGN(target->targetsize) bytes at t->data, but the destination blob in *dstptr may not have room for that alignment padding before the next rule. Trigger: a user-namespace caller supplies a compat target whose size/offset causes the aligned zeroing to extend past the allocated ruleset blob. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially enabling privilege escalation or a DoS crash.

    (ir_preauth): parse a PREAUTH greeting the same as an OK greeting.

Fixes https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/balsa/issues/23

description: In GNOME Balsa before 2.6.0, a malicious server operator or man in the middle can trigger a NULL pointer dereference and client crash by sending a PREAUTH response to imap_mbox_connect in libbalsa/imap/imap-handle.c.

code_evidence: imap_cmd_step returns IMR_UNTAGGED for a PREAUTH greeting, so the error branch at 37-41 is skipped and control reaches 42. At 43, strncmp dereferences handle->last_msg without a prior NULL check; last_msg is only populated for OK greetings, so it remains NULL for PREAUTH.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly dereferences handle->last_msg at line 43 without validating it against NULL, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. The patch's addition of a (handle->last_msg != NULL) guard confirms the missing constraint; this is distinct from a buffer overread, since the pointer itself is NULL.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes last_msg is non-NULL whenever the initial response is IMR_UNTAGGED. A malicious or MITM server sending a PREAUTH greeting satisfies that branch condition while leaving last_msg unset, so strncmp reads through a NULL pointer. The supported consequence is a client crash (DoS); no write or memory corruption is shown.

It is always allocated,', '    // because recursive calls may make the returned string invalid.', '    reg_prev_sub = vim_strsave(newsub);', '']}
description: Use After Free in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0046.

code_evidence: When a '~' expansion occurs, line 23 frees the previously allocated newsub and line 24 replaces newsub with the newly allocated tmpsub.
At the end, line 39 frees reg_prev_sub, then line 40 stores the live newsub pointer directly into reg_prev_sub instead of an independent copy; line 41 only copies when newsub still equals source.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees a buffer (line 23) and later stores/uses a pointer to memory whose lifetime it does not control, matching CWE-416 use after free. newsub = tmpsub;

A recursive substitute call re-enters regtilde while an outer invocation still holds that buffer; the recursive invocation frees or replaces it, leaving reg_prev_sub dangling. The subsequent use of reg_prev_sub (e.g. STRLEN/mch_memmove at lines 15/20) reads freed memory, supporting crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
XRA: Fix an infinite loop

C compilers don't care what size a value was on the wire. Use
naturally-sized ints, including in dissect_message_channel_mb where we
would otherwise overflow and loop infinitely.

Fixes #19100
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  guint32 tlv_index =0;'], 'added_lines': ['  unsigned tlv_index = 0;']}
description: XRA dissector infinite loop in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.5 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.13 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: tlv_index is a 32-bit guint32 incremented by 1 for type and length and by length at line 96. With attacker-controlled length bytes, tlv_index can wrap past tlv_length, so the while condition at line 11 never becomes false. The patch changes the type to unsigned, matching the wire-size assumption and preventing the overflow that made the exit condition unreachable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the loop's exit condition (tlv_index < tlv_length) becomes unreachable when the counter overflows, producing an infinite loop. This is a reachability failure of the loop guard, not merely an out-of-bounds read, so the infinite-loop classification is the direct weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: tlv_index is a fixed-width counter advanced by attacker-controlled length values without overflow checks. Trigger: a crafted TLV whose length causes tlv_index to wrap around rather than reach tlv_length. Consequence: the while loop iterates indefinitely, consuming CPU and causing denial of service during dissection of a crafted capture or injected packet.

commit_msg:
Use looks_like_pbl() to disallow .pbl file inclusion (bug #23504)

This function is implemented using case-insensitive pattern matching,
unlike filesystem::ends_with(). I missed this when writing my original
fix, so the vulnerability still applied to .pbl files on a
case-insensitive filesystem (e.g. NTFS and FAT* on Windows) by using
different case to bypass the check.

NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2015-5069.

descriptors for a device. If the received hid descriptor is smaller than

commit_msg: Don't inflate more than ~16mb, drop connection on inflate error
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    } while (err == Z_BUF_ERROR);', '    if (err != Z_BUF_ERROR && err != Z_OK) {'], 'added_lines': ['', '    } while (err == Z_BUF_ERROR && dynamicInflationBuffer.length() <= INFLATE_LESS_THAN_ROUGHLY);', '    if ((err != Z_BUF_ERROR && err != Z_OK) || dynamicInflationBuffer.length() > INFLATE_LESS_THAN_ROUGHLY) {']}
description: uws is a WebSocket server library. By sending a 256mb websocket message to a uws server instance with permessage-deflate enabled, there is a possibility used compression will shrink said 256mb down to less than 16mb of websocket payload which passes the length check of 16mb payload. This data will then inflate up to 256mb and crash the node process by exceeding V8's maximum string size. This affects uws >=0.10.0 <=0.10.8.

code_evidence: The do-while loop at lines 9-14 repeatedly calls ::inflate into the fixed LARGE_BUFFER_SIZE inflationBuffer and appends output to dynamicInflationBuffer, continuing while err == Z_BUF_ERROR. There is no bound on the total decompressed size, so a small compressed payload that inflates to hundreds of MB accumulates without limit.

Lines 16-19 only reject on inflate error codes; a successful but oversized decompression passes this check and is returned via lines 20-23, so the decompressed length is never validated against a maximum.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts attacker-controlled compressed input and fails to validate the derived property (actual decompressed size) before processing, which is improper input validation. The fix adds a length bound to the loop and error check, confirming the missing size constraint is the target weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
err = ::inflate(&inflationStream, Z_FINISH);
} while (err == Z_BUF_ERROR);

if (err != Z_BUF_ERROR && err != Z_OK) {
}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decompressed output size is never validated; the loop only checks the inflate error code. Trigger: a client sends a large WebSocket message whose compressed form is under the 16MB payload length check but inflates far beyond it (e.g., 256MB). Consequence: dynamicInflationBuffer grows past V8's maximum string size, crashing the Node process (DoS).

commit_msg:
FTP/TFTP: Fix directory traversal regression, reported by Aaron Esau

Signed-off-by: Joachim Nilsson <troglobit@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!chrooted && strncmp(dir, home, strlen(home))) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!chrooted && strncmp(rpath, home, strlen(home))) {']}
description: There are multiple unauthenticated directory traversal vulnerabilities in different FTP commands in uftpd FTP server versions 2.7 to 2.10 due to improper implementation of a chroot jail in common.c's compose_abspath function that can be abused to read or write to arbitrary files on the filesystem, leak process memory, or potentially lead to remote code execution.

code_evidence: User-supplied path is appended to ctrl->cwd into dir; when path begins with '/', no separator is added, but '..' segments are never normalized before use.
For non-chrooted servers, home is prepended to dir via memmove/memcpy, producing dir that may contain traversal sequences.
dir is then passed to stat/realpath; realpath resolves the traversal, and the resulting rpath (or dirname(dir) plus basename) is returned without re-validating containment.
The containment check compares strncmp(dir, home, strlen(home)) on the unresolved dir rather than the resolved rpath, so a dir like home/../../etc passes the prefix check while rpath escapes home.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: External input constructs a pathname intended to stay under home, but '..' elements are not neutralized before resolution, letting the pathname escape the restricted directory — exactly CWE-22 path traversal. The defect is the mismatch between the checked dir and the resolved rpath, not merely a missing chroot.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the jail containment check runs against the pre-resolution dir string, while the returned path rpath is the realpath-resolved location. Trigger: an unauthenticated FTP client supplies a path containing '..' segments (or crafted cwd); dir keeps the home prefix so strncmp passes, but realpath collapses '..' and rpath points outside home. Consequence: read/write access to arbitrary filesystem locations outside the intended jail.

commit_msg:
IB/rxe: Fix mem_check_range integer overflow

Update the range check to avoid integer-overflow in edge case.
Resolves CVE 2016-8636.

Signed-off-by: Eyal Itkin <eyal.itkin@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Leon Romanovsky <leonro@mellanox.com>
Signed-off-by: Doug Ledford <dledford@redhat.com>

--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -6,9 +6,11 @@
 
 	case RXE_MEM_TYPE_MR:
 	case RXE_MEM_TYPE_FMR:
-		return ((iova < mem->iova) ||
-			((iova + length) > (mem->iova + mem->length))) ?
-			-EFAULT : 0;
+		if (iova < mem->iova ||
+		    length > mem->length ||
+		    iova > mem->iova + mem->length - length)
+			return -EFAULT;
+		return 0;
 
 	default:
 		return -EFAULT;
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\treturn ((iova < mem->iova) ||', '\t\t\t((iova + length) > (mem->iova + mem->length))) ?', '\t\t\t-EFAULT : 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (iova < mem->iova ||', '\t\t    length > mem->length ||', '\t\t    iova > mem->iova + mem->length - length)', '\t\t\treturn -EFAULT;', '\t\treturn 0;']}
description: Integer overflow in the mem_check_range function in drivers/infiniband/sw/rxe/rxe_mr.c in the Linux kernel before 4.9.10 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory corruption), obtain sensitive information from kernel memory, or possibly have unspecified other impact via a write or read request involving the "RDMA protocol over infiniband" (aka Soft RoCE) technology.

code_evidence: The bounds check computes `iova + length` and `mem->iova + mem->length` using u64/size_t arithmetic without verifying they cannot wrap. The comparison `(iova + length) > (mem->iova + mem->length)` is the only range guard before returning 0 (in-range).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the guard relies on an addition that can wrap, defeating the bounds check. The fixed code avoids it via `length > mem->length` and subtraction, confirming the overflow is the flaw; a simple off-by-one or missing check (CWE-125/787) would not require this rewording.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the addition `iova + length` can wrap around for attacker-controlled iova/length. Trigger: a read/write request whose iova+length overflows past 2^64 yields a small sum that passes the `>` comparison, so the range check incorrectly reports in-range. Consequence: out-of-bounds access to the memory region, enabling memory corruption or kernel-memory disclosure.

commit_msg: Add an HTTP/2 related rate limiting
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (item.http2_max_settings_frames_per_minute.has_value()) {', '      ai->actions.push_back(std::make_unique<HTTP2MaxSettingsFramesPerMinute>(item.http2_max_settings_frames_per_minute.value()));', '    }', '    if (item.http2_max_ping_frames_per_minute.has_value()) {', '      ai->actions.push_back(std::make_unique<HTTP2MaxPingFramesPerMinute>(item.http2_max_ping_frames_per_minute.value()));', '    }', '    if (item.http2_max_priority_frames_per_minute.has_value()) {', '      ai->actions.push_back(std::make_unique<HTTP2MaxPriorityFramesPerMinute>(item.http2_max_priority_frames_per_minute.value()));', '    }', '    if (item.http2_max_rst_stream_frames_per_minute.has_value()) {', '      ai->actions.push_back(', '        std::make_unique<HTTP2MaxRstStreamFramesPerMinute>(item.http2_max_rst_stream_frames_per_minute.value()));', '    }']}
description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

code_evidence: The function only conditionally installs an HTTP/2 buffer water-mark action when item.http2_buffer_water_mark is set; no rate-limiting actions for SETTINGS, PING, PRIORITY or RST_STREAM frames are attached to the per-SNI action list.

After the HTTP/2-related actions, only SNI_IpAllow is added; the action list that governs the connection lacks any per-minute frame limits, so an HTTP/2 peer can send excessive control frames (including rapid RST_STREAM cancellations) without throttling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function fails to install throttling actions that restrict the number of HTTP/2 control frames consumed per unit time, leaving resource consumption uncontrolled. The weakness is missing rate limiting (CWE-770-style throttling) manifesting as uncontrolled resource consumption.

evidence_lines.code: ai->actions.push_back(std::make_unique<SNI_IpAllow>(item.ip_allow, item.fqdn));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-SNI action list is populated with HTTP/2 buffer limits but no frame-rate limits. Trigger: a remote HTTP/2 client sends many SETTINGS/PING/PRIORITY/RST_STREAM frames. Consequence: server CPU/memory consumption is not bounded by a rate limit, supporting denial of service.

commit_msg:
USB: uas: fix bug in handling of alternate settings

The uas driver has a subtle bug in the way it handles alternate
settings.  The uas_find_uas_alt_setting() routine returns an
altsetting value (the bAlternateSetting number in the descriptor), but
uas_use_uas_driver() then treats that value as an index to the
intf->altsetting array, which it isn't.

Normally this doesn't cause any problems because the various
alternate settings have bAlternateSetting values 0, 1, 2, ..., so the
value is equal to the index in the array.  But this is not guaranteed,
and Andrey Konovalov used the syzkaller fuzzer with KASAN to get a
slab-out-of-bounds error by violating this assumption.

This patch fixes the bug by making uas_find_uas_alt_setting() return a
pointer to the altsetting entry rather than either the value or the
index.  Pointers are less subject to misinterpretation.

Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Tested-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
CC: Oliver Neukum <oneukum@suse.com>
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint alt;', '\tif (alt < 0)', '\t\treturn alt;', '\treturn usb_set_interface(udev,', '\t\t\tintf->altsetting[0].desc.bInterfaceNumber, alt);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct usb_host_interface *alt;', '\tif (!alt)', '\t\treturn -ENODEV;', '\treturn usb_set_interface(udev, alt->desc.bInterfaceNumber,', '\t\t\talt->desc.bAlternateSetting);']}
description: The uas driver in the Linux kernel before 4.13.6 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted USB device, related to drivers/usb/storage/uas-detect.h and drivers/usb/storage/uas.c.

code_evidence: alt is declared as int and receives the return of uas_find_uas_alt_setting(intf), which yields a bAlternateSetting number rather than an array index; the only validation is alt < 0. The value is then passed to usb_set_interface as the interface number argument position alongside intf->altsetting[0].desc.bInterfaceNumber.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unchecked descriptor-derived alternate-setting value leads to reading memory outside the intended altsetting buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read and crash. It is not merely an integer-validation issue; the supported impact is out-of-bounds memory access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the alternate-setting number from the USB descriptor is treated as a valid index/selector without bounding it against the interface's altsetting array. Trigger: a crafted USB device supplies a bAlternateSetting value that is not a valid array index, so downstream usb_set_interface reads out of bounds. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read, KASAN slab-out-of-bounds, and system crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
ipv6: fix out of bound writes in __ip6_append_data()

Andrey Konovalov and idaifish@gmail.com reported crashes caused by
one skb shared_info being overwritten from __ip6_append_data()

Andrey program lead to following state :

copy -4200 datalen 2000 fraglen 2040
maxfraglen 2040 alloclen 2048 transhdrlen 0 offset 0 fraggap 6200

The skb_copy_and_csum_bits(skb_prev, maxfraglen, data + transhdrlen,
fraggap, 0); is overwriting skb->head and skb_shared_info

Since we apparently detect this rare condition too late, move the
code earlier to even avoid allocating skb and risking crashes.

Once again, many thanks to Andrey and syzkaller team.

Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Tested-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Reported-by: <idaifish@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tcopy = datalen - transhdrlen - fraggap;', '', '\t\t\tif (copy < 0) {', '\t\t\t\terr = -EINVAL;', '\t\t\t\tkfree_skb(skb);', '\t\t\t\tgoto error;', '\t\t\t} else if (copy > 0 && getfrag(from, data + transhdrlen, offset, copy, fraggap, skb) < 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tcopy = datalen - transhdrlen - fraggap;', '\t\t\tif (copy < 0) {', '\t\t\t\terr = -EINVAL;', '\t\t\t\tgoto error;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tif (copy > 0 &&', '\t\t\t    getfrag(from, data + transhdrlen, offset,', '\t\t\t\t    copy, fraggap, skb) < 0) {']}
description: The __ip6_append_data function in net/ipv6/ip6_output.c in the Linux kernel through 4.11.3 is too late in checking whether an overwrite of an skb data structure may occur, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) via crafted system calls.

code_evidence: datalen is derived from length+fraggap and clamped to maxfraglen-fragheaderlen-trailer_len, then adjusted by trailer_len when datalen != length+fraggap (lines 109-111,118-119).
When fraggap is nonzero, skb_copy_and_csum_bits copies fraggap bytes from skb_prev at maxfraglen into the new skb buffer before any bound on the resulting copy count is checked (lines 154-161).
Only after that copy does the code compute copy = datalen - transhdrlen - fraggap and reject copy < 0 (lines 163-168), so a negative copy is detected after the overwrite already occurred.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is validating a derived length too late: the computed copy count is not checked against required bounds before it drives a memory copy, which is improper validation of input-derived properties. CWE-20 fits as insufficient validation of derived size/offset metadata; the concrete consequence is an out-of-bounds write rather than mere malformed-input rejection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The derived copy length (datalen - transhdrlen - fraggap) can become negative because datalen is clamped independently of fraggap; the negative value is checked only after skb_copy_and_csum_bits has written fraggap bytes into the newly allocated skb, so the derived size is not validated before use. Triggering with crafted sendmsg parameters causes an out-of-bounds write into skb head/shared_info, leading to a kernel crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fixed ngx_gmtime() on 32-bit platforms with 64-bit time_t.

In ngx_gmtime(), instead of casting to ngx_uint_t we now work with
time_t directly.  This allows using dates after 2038 on 32-bit platforms
which use 64-bit time_t, notably NetBSD and OpenBSD.

As the code is not able to work with negative time_t values, argument
is now set to 0 for negative values.  As a positive side effect, this
results in Epoch being used for such values instead of a date in distant
future.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ngx_uint_t  n, sec, min, hour, mday, mon, year, wday, days, leap;', '    n = (ngx_uint_t) t;', '    days = n / 86400;', '    n %= 86400;', '    hour = n / 3600;', '    n %= 3600;', '    min = n / 60;', '    sec = n % 60;'], 'added_lines': ['    ngx_uint_t  sec, min, hour, mday, mon, year, wday, days, leap;', '    if (t < 0) {', '        t = 0;', '    }', '    days = t / 86400;', '    sec = t % 86400;', '    hour = sec / 3600;', '    sec %= 3600;', '    min = sec / 60;', '    sec %= 60;']}
description: NGINX before 1.13.6 has a buffer overflow for years that exceed four digits, as demonstrated by a file with a modification date in 1969 that causes an integer overflow (or a false modification date far in the future), when encountered by the autoindex module.

code_evidence: Line 5 declares the working value n as ngx_uint_t and line 6 casts the time_t argument t into it; for a 64-bit time_t on a 32-bit platform this truncates the value before any date math.

Line 7 derives days by dividing the truncated n, and lines 14-16 then compute year and yday from days using multiplications such as (days + 2) * 400, which can wrap in the unsigned ngx_uint_t type and yield a bogus far-future year.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs unsigned integer arithmetic on a truncated time value without range checks, allowing wraparound in the date computation, matching CWE-190's integer overflow/wraparound. The downstream buffer overflow is a consequence of the bad year, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the time_t argument is narrowed to ngx_uint_t before conversion, so large (or negative) timestamps are truncated and the subsequent unsigned arithmetic in year/yday calculation can overflow. Trigger: a file modification time outside the 32-bit range (e.g. 1969) processed by the autoindex module. Consequence: a nonsensical year (beyond four digits) is stored in tp, which callers format into a fixed buffer.

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.histogram_fixed_width` is vulnerable to a crash when the values array contain `Not a Number` (`NaN`) elements. The implementation assumes that all floating point operations are defined and then converts a floating point result to an integer index. If `values` contains `NaN` then the result of the division is still `NaN` and the cast to `int32` would result in a crash. This only occurs on the CPU implementation. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: The function reads the `values` input as a flat tensor and passes it unchanged to the histogram functor; no check rejects NaN elements in `values`.
The only validation on `value_range` checks that element 0 is less than element 1; this does not constrain the `values` array.
The values tensor is forwarded to HistogramFixedWidthFunctor::Compute, which computes bin indices from the floating-point division and casts to an integer index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function receives raw input (`values`) and fails to validate that its elements are finite before processing, directly matching CWE-20's improper input validation leading to a crash. This is not a transformation/filtering defect; the missing validation of input properties (finitude) is the root cause.

OP_REQUIRES(
ctx, (value_range(0) < value_range(1)),
errors::InvalidArgument("value_range should satisfy value_range[0] < "
"value_range[1], but got '[",
value_range(0), ", ", value_range(1), "]'"));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the CPU histogram path accepts unvalidated floating-point `values`; when an element is NaN, the bin-index computation yields NaN and the subsequent cast to int32 is undefined/likely crashes. Trigger: calling histogram_fixed_width with a values array containing NaN. Consequence: process crash (availability DoS). The patch's parenthesization changes are cosmetic and unrelated to the NaN handling.

commit_msg:
Bug 698158: prevent trying to reloc a freed object

In the token reader, we pass the scanner state structure around as a
t_struct ref on the Postscript operand stack.

But we explicitly free the scanner state when we're done, which leaves a
dangling reference on the operand stack and, unless that reference gets
overwritten before the next garbager run, we can end up with the garbager
trying to deal with an already freed object - that can cause a crash, or
memory corruption.

Avoid assert when drawing arcs with NaN angles

Closes #352

See merge request cairo/cairo!515

description: An issue was discovered in cairo 1.16.0. There is an assertion problem in the function _cairo_arc_in_direction in the file cairo-arc.c.
