commit_msg:
cdrom: fix improper type cast, which can leat to information leak.

There is another cast from unsigned long to int which causes
a bounds check to fail with specially crafted input. The value is
then used as an index in the slot array in cdrom_slot_status().

This issue is similar to CVE-2018-16658 and CVE-2018-10940.

Signed-off-by: Young_X <YangX92@hotmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif ((int)arg >= cdi->capacity)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (arg >= cdi->capacity)']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.19. An information leak in cdrom_ioctl_select_disc in drivers/cdrom/cdrom.c could be used by local attackers to read kernel memory because a cast from unsigned long to int interferes with bounds checking. This is similar to CVE-2018-10940 and CVE-2018-16658.

code_evidence: The bounds check compares (int)arg, a signed 32-bit truncation of the unsigned long ioctl argument, against cdi->capacity. A crafted arg with a high bit set (e.g., 0x100000000 or 0xFFFFFFFF) becomes negative or wraps below capacity after the cast, so the guard at line 8 passes for a value that is actually out of range. The unchecked arg then flows to select_disc()/cdrom_select_disc() at lines 12 and 14.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-200 fits because the flawed bounds check enables an out-of-bounds read that exposes kernel memory to a local attacker, i.e., confidentiality loss via unauthorized information disclosure. The underlying indexing error is the cause; CWE-200 captures the supported disclosure consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the signed truncation cast in the capacity check, which lets an oversized unsigned long bypass validation. Trigger is a local caller passing a specially crafted ioctl argument; the out-of-range value is used as an index into the slot array, causing an out-of-bounds access whose result is returned to userspace, leaking kernel memory contents.

commit_msg:
virtio: validate num_sg when mapping

CVE-2013-4535
CVE-2013-4536

Both virtio-block and virtio-serial read,
VirtQueueElements are read in as buffers, and passed to
virtqueue_map_sg(), where num_sg is taken from the wire and can force
writes to indicies beyond VIRTQUEUE_MAX_SIZE.

To fix, validate num_sg.

Reported-by: Michael Roth <mdroth@linux.vnet.ibm.com>
Signed-off-by: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>
Cc: Amit Shah <amit.shah@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Juan Quintela <quintela@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (num_sg >= VIRTQUEUE_MAX_SIZE) {', '        error_report("virtio: map attempt out of bounds: %zd > %d",', '                     num_sg, VIRTQUEUE_MAX_SIZE);', '        exit(1);', '    }']}
description: The virtqueue_map_sg function in hw/virtio/virtio.c in QEMU before 1.7.2 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary files via a crafted savevm image, related to virtio-block or virtio-serial read.

code_evidence: The loop bound is the caller-supplied num_sg, so the number of iterations over sg[] and addr[] is entirely attacker-controlled.

Within each iteration, addr[i] and sg[i] are dereferenced and passed to cpu_physical_memory_map without any prior check on num_sg; the only failure check is on the returned len/base, not on the index bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes an externally supplied quantity (num_sg) and fails to validate its size before using it to index buffers, which is precisely improper input validation (CWE-20). The downstream out-of-bounds access is the consequence; the weakness is the absent bound check on the input, not a transformation or encoding flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: num_sg arrives from the wire (VirtQueueElement) and is used directly as the array iteration bound without validating it against VIRTQUEUE_MAX_SIZE. Trigger: a crafted savevm image supplies an oversized num_sg, causing reads/writes of addr[] and sg[] past their allocated VIRTQUEUE_MAX_SIZE bounds, leading to out-of-bounds memory access; the diff adds the missing size check before the loop.

commit_msg:
rxrpc: Fix race between conn bundle lookup and bundle removal [ZDI-CAN-15975]

After rxrpc_unbundle_conn() has removed a connection from a bundle, it
checks to see if there are any conns with available channels and, if not,
removes and attempts to destroy the bundle.

Whilst it does check after grabbing client_bundles_lock that there are no
connections attached, this races with rxrpc_look_up_bundle() retrieving the
bundle, but not attaching a connection for the connection to be attached
later.

There is therefore a window in which the bundle can get destroyed before we
manage to attach a new connection to it.

Fix this by adding an "active" counter to struct rxrpc_bundle:

 (1) rxrpc_connect_call() obtains an active count by prepping/looking up a
     bundle and ditches it before returning.

 (2) If, during rxrpc_connect_call(), a connection is added to the bundle,
     this obtains an active count, which is held until the connection is
     discarded.

 (3) rxrpc_deactivate_bundle() is created to drop an active count on a
     bundle and destroy it when the active count reaches 0.  The active
     count is checked inside client_bundles_lock() to prevent a race with
     rxrpc_look_up_bundle().

 (4) rxrpc_unbundle_conn() then calls rxrpc_deactivate_bundle().

Fixes: 245500d853e9 ("rxrpc: Rewrite the client connection manager")
Reported-by: zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com # ZDI-CAN-15975
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Tested-by: zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com
cc: Marc Dionne <marc.dionne@auristor.com>
cc: linux-afs@lists.infradead.org
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct rxrpc_local *local = bundle->params.local;', '\tbool need_drop = false, need_put = false;', '\t/* If there are no more connections, remove the bundle */', '\tif (!bundle->avail_chans) {', '\t\t_debug("maybe unbundle");', '\t\tspin_lock(&local->client_bundles_lock);', '', '\t\tfor (i = 0; i < ARRAY_SIZE(bundle->conns); i++)', '\t\t\tif (bundle->conns[i])', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tif (i == ARRAY_SIZE(bundle->conns) && !bundle->params.exclusive) {', '\t\t\t_debug("erase bundle");', '\t\t\trb_erase(&bundle->local_node, &local->client_bundles);', '\t\t\tneed_put = true;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\tspin_unlock(&local->client_bundles_lock);', '\t\tif (need_put)', '\t\t\trxrpc_put_bundle(bundle);', '', '\tif (need_drop)', '\t\trxrpc_put_connection(conn);', '\t_leave("");'], 'added_lines': ['\tbool need_drop = false;', '\tif (need_drop) {', '\t\trxrpc_deactivate_bundle(bundle);', '\t\trxrpc_put_connection(conn);']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernel's RxRPC network protocol, within the processing of RxRPC bundles. This issue results from the lack of proper locking when performing operations on an object. This may allow an attacker to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the kernel.

code_evidence: After releasing channel_lock at line 20, the code checks bundle->avail_chans without holding it, then takes local->client_bundles_lock and scans bundle->conns to decide whether to rb_erase the bundle and rxrpc_put_bundle it. This check-then-destroy sequence is not atomic with respect to rxrpc_look_up_bundle(), which can obtain the same bundle under client_bundles_lock and attach a connection only later, outside the lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a shared-resource check and destruction without holding exclusivity over the whole sequence, allowing an interfering concurrent code path to modify bundle state between check and free, which is the definition of CWE-362. The missing constraint is atomicity between lookup and removal, not merely a missing lock.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decision to remove and destroy a bundle is made under client_bundles_lock, but a concurrent rxrpc_look_up_bundle() can fetch the bundle and attach a connection after that lock is dropped, so the bundle is freed while a connection is being attached. Trigger: racing bundle lookup against unbundle_conn when avail_chans reaches zero; consequence is use-after-free of the bundle, supporting kernel memory corruption and privilege escalation.

if (p->index && ((p->index & XFRM_POLICY_MAX) != p->dir))
return -EINVAL;

commit_msg:
tmpfiles: refuse to chown()/chmod() files which are hardlinked, unless protected_hardlinks sysctl is on

Let's add some extra safety.

Fixes: #7736
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '        if (hardlink_vulnerable(&st)) {', '                log_error("Refusing to set ACLs on hardlinked file %s while the fs.protected_hardlinks sysctl is turned off.", path);', '                return -EPERM;', '        }']}
description: systemd-tmpfiles in systemd before 237 attempts to support ownership/permission changes on hardlinked files even if the fs.protected_hardlinks sysctl is turned off, which allows local users to bypass intended access restrictions via vectors involving a hard link to a file for which the user lacks write access, as demonstrated by changing the ownership of the /etc/passwd file.

code_evidence: open() uses O_NOFOLLOW and O_PATH, but O_NOFOLLOW only rejects a final symlink; it does not reject a hard link, and the resulting fd is then fstatat()'ed.
The only link-type check is S_ISLNK(st.st_mode), which skips symlinks but has no branch for regular files that are hardlinked to a file the user does not own.
The fd is re-exposed as /proc/self/fd/N and passed to path_set_acl(), so ACL changes are applied to the inode reached via the opened path without verifying its link count or ownership.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because path_set_acls() accesses a file via a name that can resolve to an unintended resource (a hardlinked inode) and applies ACL changes to it; the missing hardlink guard is the improper link resolution. This is link following, not a simple permission-check omission, since the attack uses the link to redirect the modification.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function resolves and modifies a file through a path/fd without rejecting hardlinked regular files, relying only on O_NOFOLLOW and an S_ISLNK check. Trigger: a local user creates a hard link to a file they lack write access to (e.g. /etc/passwd) and tmpfiles processes it, so ACLs are set on the shared inode, bypassing intended access restrictions.

commit_msg:
Bug 697453: Avoid divide by 0 in scan conversion code.

Arithmetic overflow due to extreme values in the scan conversion
code can cause a division by 0.

Avoid this with a simple extra check.

  dx_old=cf814d81
  endp->x_next=b0e859b9
  alp->x_next=8069a73a

leads to dx_den = 0
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (dx_den <= dx_old)', '        ((dy | dx_old) < 1L << (size_of(fixed) * 4 - 1) ?'], 'added_lines': ['    if (dx_den <= dx_old || dx_den == 0)', '        (((ufixed)(dy | dx_old)) < (1L << (size_of(fixed) * 4 - 1)) ?']}
description: The intersect function in base/gxfill.c in Artifex Software, Inc. Ghostscript 9.20 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero error and application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Lines 5-6 compute dx_old and dx_den from caller-supplied fixed-point fields; line 7 only rejects dx_den <= dx_old, so a dx_den of 0 can still pass when dx_old is negative (0 <= dx_old).
Lines 14-16 then use dx_den as the divisor in dy * dx_old / dx_den or fixed_mult_quo(dy, dx_old, dx_den) with no zero check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs division by dx_den without ensuring it is nonzero, directly matching CWE-369. The signed comparison bug is the enabling cause, but the supported weakness is the divide-by-zero, not a general integer-overflow issue.

evidence_lines.code:
y_new =
((dy | dx_old) < 1L << (size_of(fixed) * 4 - 1) ?
dy * dx_old / dx_den :

+ y;

description: In several functions of xmlregexp.c, there is a possible out of bounds write due to a heap buffer overflow. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: xmlRegGetCounter(ctxt) returns a counter index that is stored in counter; the return value is not checked before it is used to index ctxt->counters[counter].
The same unchecked counter value is used to write ctxt->counters[counter].min and .max at a second call site inside the else branch.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked negative index causes a write outside the bounds of the counters array, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds Write). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read: the faulty index is used as the destination of min/max assignments.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: xmlRegGetCounter can return a negative error value (e.g., on allocation failure), but the return is used directly as an array index. Trigger: a heap allocation failure while generating range-quantifier transitions. Consequence: ctxt->counters[counter] with a negative index writes before the intended buffer, corrupting heap memory (out-of-bounds write).

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4219: reading before the start of the line

Problem:    Reading before the start of the line.
Solution:   Check boundary before trying to read the character.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\twhile (VIM_ISWHITE(*(bd->textstart + s - 1)) && s > 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\twhile (s > 0 && VIM_ISWHITE(*(bd->textstart + s - 1)))']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.

code_evidence: Line 7 allocates a heap buffer pnew of size startspaces+endspaces+textlen+1; failure returns FAIL.
Lines 19-25 trim trailing whitespace: s = textlen+endspaces, and line 20 dereferences bd->textstart + s - 1 while testing VIM_ISWHITE before checking s > 0.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an ordering bug in a boundary check that permits an out-of-bounds access on a heap-backed buffer, matching CWE-122's heap buffer overflow scope. It is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write, but the heap allocation and missing pre-access boundary constraint fit the variant; a generic CWE-125 would describe the read more precisely but the target label is CWE-122.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop condition evaluates the whitespace test before the s > 0 boundary check. When the trim loop drives s to 0 (e.g., textlen+endspaces is 0 or all trailing bytes are multi-byte whitespace), the next iteration reads *(bd->textstart + s - 1), i.e. one byte before the start of the line buffer. Because textstart points into block data that may sit at the start of a heap allocation, this is an out-of-bounds heap read, potentially causing a crash.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        while (start != end)'], 'added_lines': ['        while (start < end)']}
description: In LibSass prior to 3.5.5, the function handle_error in sass_context.cpp allows attackers to cause a denial-of-service resulting from a heap-based buffer over-read via a crafted sass file.

code_evidence: The loop condition tests start != end while the body dereferences and advances the iterator via utf8::next(start, end). If start passes end (e.g., an incomplete or malformed UTF-8 sequence causes the iterator to advance beyond end), start != end remains true and utf8::next reads past the end of the input buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is reading beyond the intended buffer end, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. The fix changes the guard to start < end, confirming the missing bound constraint.

evidence_lines.code:
while (start != end)
(*result++) = utf8::next(start, end);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the inequality comparison start != end instead of a bounded start < end, so the loop does not terminate when the iterator overshoots end. Trigger is crafted UTF-8 input that advances the iterator past end; the consequence is an out-of-bounds read (heap over-read), potentially a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
nfsd: check for oversized NFSv2/v3 arguments

A client can append random data to the end of an NFSv2 or NFSv3 RPC call
without our complaining; we'll just stop parsing at the end of the
expected data and ignore the rest.

Encoded arguments and replies are stored together in an array of pages,
and if a call is too large it could leave inadequate space for the
reply.  This is normally OK because NFS RPC's typically have either
short arguments and long replies (like READ) or long arguments and short
replies (like WRITE).  But a client that sends an incorrectly long reply
can violate those assumptions.  This was observed to cause crashes.

Also, several operations increment rq_next_page in the decode routine
before checking the argument size, which can leave rq_next_page pointing
well past the end of the page array, causing trouble later in
svc_free_pages.

So, following a suggestion from Neil Brown, add a central check to
enforce our expectation that no NFSv2/v3 call has both a large call and
a large reply.

As followup we may also want to rewrite the encoding routines to check
more carefully that they aren't running off the end of the page array.

We may also consider rejecting calls that have any extra garbage
appended.  That would be safer, and within our rights by spec, but given
the age of our server and the NFS protocol, and the fact that we've
never enforced this before, we may need to balance that against the
possibility of breaking some oddball client.

Reported-by: Tuomas Haanpää <thaan@synopsys.com>
Reported-by: Ari Kauppi <ari@synopsys.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reviewed-by: NeilBrown <neilb@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: J. Bruce Fields <bfields@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (nfs_request_too_big(rqstp, proc)) {', '\t\tdprintk("nfsd: NFSv%d argument too large\\n", rqstp->rq_vers);', '\t\t*statp = rpc_garbage_args;', '\t\treturn 1;', '\t}']}
description: The NFSv2/NFSv3 server in the nfsd subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.10.11 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (system crash) via a long RPC reply, related to net/sunrpc/svc.c, fs/nfsd/nfs3xdr.c, and fs/nfsd/nfsxdr.c.

code_evidence: The function derives the procedure from the request (line 10) and immediately invokes the decoder xdr on rq_arg with rq_argp (lines 13-14), returning rpc_garbage_args only when decoding fails. There is no check that the total argument length is within the size expected for the procedure before decoding is attempted. The added guard in the patch is absent from this function, so oversized NFSv2/v3 arguments pass straight into decoding and later processing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of an input length property before processing untrusted RPC data, matching CWE-20's improper input validation of derived size. It is not a transformation/filtering issue (CWE-790), since no sanitization occurs; the code simply fails to enforce the size constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dispatcher never validates that the incoming RPC argument length matches the procedure's expected size before decoding. Trigger: a remote client appends extra data to an NFSv2/v3 call. Because arguments and replies share the page array, the oversized call leaves inadequate space for the reply, and decode routines advance rq_next_page past the page array, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
make the dump directories owned by root by default

It was discovered that the abrt event scripts create a user-readable
copy of a sosreport file in abrt problem directories, and include
excerpts of /var/log/messages selected by the user-controlled process
name, leading to an information disclosure.

This issue was discovered by Florian Weimer of Red Hat Product Security.

Related: #1212868

Signed-off-by: Jakub Filak <jfilak@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!dump_dir_accessible_by_uid(dirname, client_uid))'], 'added_lines': ['    if (g_settings_privatereports)', '    {', '        struct stat statbuf;', '        if (lstat(dirname, &statbuf) != 0 || !S_ISDIR(statbuf.st_mode))', '        {', '            error_msg("Path \'%s\' isn\'t directory", dirname);', '            return 404; /* Not Found */', '        }', "        /* Get ABRT's group gid */", '        struct group *gr = getgrnam("abrt");', '        if (!gr)', '        {', '            error_msg("Group \'abrt\' does not exist");', '            return 500;', '        }', '        if (statbuf.st_uid != 0 || !(statbuf.st_gid == 0 || statbuf.st_gid == gr->gr_gid) || statbuf.st_mode & 07)', '        {', '            error_msg("Problem directory \'%s\' isn\'t owned by root:abrt or others are not restricted from access", dirname);', '            return 403;', '        }', '        struct dump_dir *dd = dd_opendir(dirname, DD_OPEN_READONLY);', '        const bool complete = dd && problem_dump_dir_is_complete(dd);', '        dd_close(dd);', '        if (complete)', '        {', '            error_msg("Problem directory \'%s\' has already been processed", dirname);', '            return 403;', '        }', '    }', '    else if (!dump_dir_accessible_by_uid(dirname, client_uid))']}
description: The event scripts in Automatic Bug Reporting Tool (ABRT) uses world-readable permission on a copy of sosreport file in problem directories, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from /var/log/messages via unspecified vectors.

code_evidence: The pre-patch access gate is dump_dir_accessible_by_uid(dirname, client_uid); when the client uid lacks access the code returns 403 unless errno is ENOTDIR. There is no check that the problem directory is root-owned, group-restricted, or free of world/group access bits before the post-create handler runs and produces user-readable artifacts, so a directory with permissive ownership/permissions is accepted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This function governs whether a problem directory is processed; its missing ownership/permission constraint allows sensitive data in that directory to become readable by unauthorized local users, matching CWE-200's exposure of sensitive information. The underlying permission weakness is the enabling condition, but the supported consequence here is information disclosure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the access check only verifies accessibility by the requesting uid and never enforces restrictive ownership or mode on the dump directory. Trigger: a problem directory that is world-readable or owned by an unauthorized user passes the check. Consequence: the post-create event handler operates on it and user-readable copies/excerpts of sensitive logs are exposed to local users.

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in Linux kernel before 5.19.2. This issue occurs in cmd_hdl_filter in drivers/staging/rtl8712/rtl8712_cmd.c, allowing an attacker to launch a local denial of service attack and gain escalation of privileges.

code_evidence: For _Read_MACREG and _Write_MACREG commands, the handler read_macreg_hdl/write_macreg_hdl is invoked on pcmd, and then pcmd is stored in pcmd_r and returned to the caller. The caller later frees the returned command object; the handler has already freed or consumed the same object, so the returned pointer and any later use of pcmd_r reference freed memory. The other cases return NULL or a still-live command, so only these two branches create the dangling return.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function returns and causes reuse of a pointer to memory already released by the handler, which is the defining pattern of CWE-416. This is not merely a double free; the stale pointer escapes the switch and is referenced afterward, so the use-after-free mapping fits directly.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The MAC-register handlers free the command object internally, but the filter still returns that same pointer as pcmd_r. The returned stale pointer is subsequently used or freed again by the caller, producing a use-after-free that can corrupt memory or crash the driver.

commit_msg: fixed #1575
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar devName[255];'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar devName[256];']}
description: An issue was discovered in gpac through 20200801. A stack-buffer-overflow exists in the function DumpRawUIConfig located in odf_dump.c. It allows an attacker to cause code Execution.

code_evidence: devName is a fixed 255-byte stack buffer [3]. len is read from the bitstream as a single byte [10], controlling the loop that writes len bytes into devName [11], then terminates with devName[i] = 0 [12] at index len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The terminating assignment writes past the end of the intended stack buffer, which is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the write occurs due to a missing upper-bound constraint on the loop index.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the attacker-controlled length byte is used to index a fixed 255-byte stack array without a bounds check. When len is 255, the loop fills all bytes and the terminating write devName[255] = 0 writes one byte past the buffer (the patch enlarges it to 256). Trigger: a crafted UIConfig descriptor whose length byte is 255. Consequence: stack-buffer overflow corrupting adjacent stack memory, potentially leading to code execution or crash.

commit_msg: more room for ljpeg row
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  jh->row = (ushort *)calloc(jh->wide * jh->clrs, 4);'], 'added_lines': ['  jh->row = (ushort *)calloc(jh->wide * jh->clrs, 16);']}
description: In LibRaw, an out-of-bounds read vulnerability exists within the "LibRaw::adobe_copy_pixel()" function (libraw\src\decoders\dng.cpp) when reading data from the image file.

code_evidence: jh->high, jh->wide and jh->clrs are parsed directly from the JPEG/SOF marker bytes read from the file (lines 30-32); no bound is placed on their product beyond the per-field checks at line 51.

The row buffer is sized as jh->wide * jh->clrs * 4 bytes (line 64), a product derived from attacker-controlled dimensions; the allocation is only null-checked, not validated against the later read extent.
Downstream LJPEG decoding fills/reads this row using the same wide/clrs values, so the allocated extent can be smaller than the amount of pixel data the decoder expects to access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reading past the end of the jh->row heap buffer, which matches CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). It is not an allocation-size overflow per se; the consequence is an out-of-bounds read during decoding, consistent with the target CWE.

evidence_lines.code:
jh->row = (ushort *)calloc(jh->wide * jh->clrs, 4);
merror(jh->row, "ljpeg_start()");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the row buffer size is computed from unvalidated image dimensions (wide*clrs) with a fixed element multiplier, while the decoder later reads a full row of pixel data based on those same dimensions. A crafted DNG/JPEG with large or inconsistent dimensions triggers reads beyond the calloc'd buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read (crash or memory disclosure).

commit_msg: Fix a crash in the TGA loader with malformed input
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['Error ImageLoaderTGA::convert_to_image(Ref<Image> p_image, const uint8_t *p_buffer, const tga_header_s &p_header, const uint8_t *p_palette, const bool p_is_monochrome) {'], 'added_lines': ['Error ImageLoaderTGA::convert_to_image(Ref<Image> p_image, const uint8_t *p_buffer, const tga_header_s &p_header, const uint8_t *p_palette, const bool p_is_monochrome, size_t p_output_size) {', '\t\t\t\t\tif (i > p_output_size) {', '\t\t\t\t\t\treturn ERR_PARSE_ERROR;', '\t\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t\t\tif (i > p_output_size) {', '\t\t\t\t\t\treturn ERR_PARSE_ERROR;', '\t\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t\tif (i + 2 > p_output_size) {', '\t\t\t\t\treturn ERR_PARSE_ERROR;', '\t\t\t\t}', '', '\t\t\t\tif (i + 3 > p_output_size) {', '\t\t\t\t\treturn ERR_PARSE_ERROR;', '\t\t\t\t}', '']}
description: A stack overflow issue exists in Godot Engine up to v3.2 and is caused by improper boundary checks when loading .TGA image files. Depending on the context of the application, attack vector can be local or remote, and can lead to code execution and/or system crash.

code_evidence: The destination buffer is sized as width*height*sizeof(uint32_t) and written via image_data_w at index (y*width+x)*4..3.
The 8-bit loops read p_buffer[i] and call TGA_PUT_PIXEL without any bound check on i or x/y against width/height.
The 24-bit loop reads p_buffer[i+2] and writes pixels while incrementing i by 3, again without validating i against the buffer length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fix adds p_output_size checks immediately before the p_buffer reads and TGA_PUT_PIXEL writes, confirming the original code wrote/read past the intended buffer. This is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); an out-of-bounds read alone would be CWE-125, but the pixel macro writes past image_data_w.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The TGA header-controlled width/height and pixel depth drive the loop bounds, but pixel data is read and written without checking that the source buffer contains enough bytes. A malformed/short TGA causes out-of-bounds reads of p_buffer and, because the loop bounds come from the header while the destination is sized from the same width/height, inconsistent or truncated data can produce out-of-bounds writes through TGA_PUT_PIXEL, leading to memory corruption and crash/code execution.

commit_msg:
mm: migrate dirty page without clear_page_dirty_for_io etc

clear_page_dirty_for_io() has accumulated writeback and memcg subtleties
since v2.6.16 first introduced page migration; and the set_page_dirty()
which completed its migration of PageDirty, later had to be moderated to
__set_page_dirty_nobuffers(); then PageSwapBacked had to skip that too.

No actual problems seen with this procedure recently, but if you look into
what the clear_page_dirty_for_io(page)+set_page_dirty(newpage) is actually
achieving, it turns out to be nothing more than moving the PageDirty flag,
and its NR_FILE_DIRTY stat from one zone to another.

It would be good to avoid a pile of irrelevant decrementations and
incrementations, and improper event counting, and unnecessary descent of
the radix_tree under tree_lock (to set the PAGECACHE_TAG_DIRTY which
radix_tree_replace_slot() left in place anyway).

Do the NR_FILE_DIRTY movement, like the other stats movements, while
interrupts still disabled in migrate_page_move_mapping(); and don't even
bother if the zone is the same.  Do the PageDirty movement there under
tree_lock too, where old page is frozen and newpage not yet visible:
bearing in mind that as soon as newpage becomes visible in radix_tree, an
un-page-locked set_page_dirty() might interfere (or perhaps that's just
not possible: anything doing so should already hold an additional
reference to the old page, preventing its migration; but play safe).

But we do still need to transfer PageDirty in migrate_page_copy(), for
those who don't go the mapping route through migrate_page_move_mapping().

Cc: Christoph Lameter <cl@linux.com>
Cc: "Kirill A. Shutemov" <kirill.shutemov@linux.intel.com>

Cc: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>

Cc: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: KOSAKI Motohiro <kosaki.motohiro@jp.fujitsu.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

commit_msg:
openjpeg: Prevent overflows when using opj_aligned_malloc()

BUG=628304
R=thestig@chromium.org, ochang@chromium.org

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2218783002
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (((OPJ_UINT32)-1) / (OPJ_UINT32)sizeof(OPJ_INT32) < (OPJ_UINT32)h.mem_count) {', '\t\treturn OPJ_FALSE;', '\t}']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in OpenJPEG, as used in PDFium in Google Chrome before 53.0.2785.89 on Windows and OS X and before 53.0.2785.92 on Linux, allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted JPEG 2000 data that is mishandled during opj_aligned_malloc calls in dwt.c and t1.c.

code_evidence: h.mem_count is computed from opj_dwt_max_resolution(tr, numres) and then multiplied by sizeof(OPJ_INT32) directly inside the opj_aligned_malloc argument without any bound check on h.mem_count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the size passed to the allocator is an unchecked integer product that can overflow/wrap before allocation. This is the arithmetic root cause; the heap overflow is the downstream consequence, not a separate memory-corruption label.

evidence_lines.code:
h.mem_count = opj_dwt_max_resolution(tr, numres);
h.mem = (OPJ_INT32*)opj_aligned_malloc(h.mem_count * sizeof(OPJ_INT32));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation size h.mem_count * sizeof(OPJ_INT32) is a 32-bit multiplication whose result can wrap when h.mem_count is large, producing a small buffer. Trigger: crafted JPEG 2000 data yielding a large max-resolution count. Consequence: undersized heap allocation followed by writes through h.mem in the DWT loops, causing heap-based buffer overflow.

commit_msg: Use "length", which has been limited in size
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmemcpy(hashed, password, strlen(password));'], 'added_lines': ['\tmemcpy(hashed, password, length);']}
description: add_password in pam_radius_auth.c in pam_radius 1.4.0 does not correctly check the length of the input password, and is vulnerable to a stack-based buffer overflow during memcpy(). An attacker could send a crafted password to an application (loading the pam_radius library) and crash it. Arbitrary code execution might be possible, depending on the application, C library, compiler, and other factors.

code_evidence: length is computed from strlen(password) and clamped to MAXPASS, so the intended copy size is bounded by MAXPASS.

hashed is a fixed 256+AUTH_PASS_LEN stack buffer; memset zeroes only length bytes, but memcpy copies strlen(password) bytes from password, which may exceed the clamped length and the buffer's capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a direct out-of-bounds write: the copy destination has fixed capacity while the copy length is attacker-influenced and not bounded to that capacity. It fits CWE-787; CWE-125 (over-read) does not apply because the flaw is a write past the destination buffer.

evidence_lines.code:
memset(hashed, 0, length);
memcpy(hashed, password, strlen(password));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is using strlen(password) as the memcpy size instead of the already-bounded length variable. When an attacker supplies a password longer than the hashed buffer, memcpy writes past the stack buffer's end, corrupting adjacent stack data and potentially causing a crash or code execution depending on the environment.

commit_msg:
prevent /0 in eye for width/height 1

see https://github.com/libvips/libvips/issues/1236
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tdouble c = eye->factor * VIPS_PI / (2 * (point->width - 1));', '\tdouble h = ((point->height - 1) * (point->height - 1));'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* VIPS_MAX to prevent /0.', '\t */', '\tint max_x = VIPS_MAX( point->width - 1, 1 );', '\tint max_y = VIPS_MAX( point->height - 1, 1 );', '', '\tdouble c = eye->factor * VIPS_PI / (2 * max_x);', '\tdouble h = max_y * max_y;']}
description: Division-By-Zero vulnerability in Libvips 8.10.5 in the function vips_eye_point, eye.c#L83, and function vips_mask_point, mask.c#L85.

code_evidence: Line 5 computes the divisor (2 * (point->width - 1)) from point->width; when width is 1 the divisor becomes zero. Line 6 computes h from (point->height - 1) squared, which is zero when height is 1. Line 7 divides by h and uses c in the cosine argument, so both dimension-derived zero divisors reach the division.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because the function divides by a value derived from dimensions that can be zero, exactly the size/width/height case described for this weakness. It is not merely an out-of-bounds or integer overflow issue; the unsafe operation is a zero divisor reaching the division.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: image dimensions are used directly to form divisors without clamping. Trigger: a caller requests an eye image with width or height equal to 1, making (width - 1) or (height - 1) zero. Consequence: division by zero in the float calculation, yielding a crash/exit (availability DoS) in the image generation path.

commit_msg:
Simplified _libssh2_check_length

misc.c : _libssh2_check_length()

Removed cast and one-lined check.

description: In libssh2 before 1.9.0, kex_method_diffie_hellman_group_exchange_sha256_key_exchange in kex.c has an integer overflow that could lead to an out-of-bounds read in the way packets are read from the server. A remote attacker who compromises a SSH server may be able to disclose sensitive information or cause a denial of service condition on the client system when a user connects to the server. This is related to an _libssh2_check_length mistake, and is different from the various issues fixed in 1.8.1, such as CVE-2019-3855.

code_evidence: Line 3 compares len against buf->len and returns 0 if len exceeds the buffer, so the earlier guard bounds len to at most buf->len.
Line 5 computes (int)(buf->len - len) and casts the pointer difference (buf->dataptr - buf->data) to int, then compares them as signed ints.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function narrows size_t quantities to int before comparing, producing a wraparound that defeats the length validation; this is the integer overflow/wraparound described by CWE-190, not a simple off-by-one bounds check.

evidence_lines.code:
if(len > buf->len)
return 0;
return ((int)(buf->dataptr - buf->data) <= (int)(buf->len - len)) ? 1 : 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the signed int casts of size_t values in the length check: buf->len - len and the dataptr offset are narrowed to int. If either value exceeds INT_MAX, the cast wraps to a negative or small value, so the comparison can wrongly report that len bytes are available. Trigger: a large buffer length or pointer offset; consequence: the packet reader trusts an invalid length and performs an out-of-bounds read.

Fixes CVE 2017-3735

((f->addressFamily->data[0] << 8) | (f->addressFamily->data[1]))', '            : 0);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (f == NULL', '            || f->addressFamily == NULL', '            || f->addressFamily->data == NULL', '            || f->addressFamily->length < 2)', '        return 0;', '    return (f->addressFamily->data[0] << 8) | f->addressFamily->data[1];']}
description: While parsing an IPAddressFamily extension in an X.509 certificate, it is possible to do a one-byte overread. This would result in an incorrect text display of the certificate. This bug has been present since 2006 and is present in all versions of OpenSSL before 1.0.2m and 1.1.0g.

code_evidence: The guard only checks f, f->addressFamily and f->addressFamily->data for NULL before dereferencing data[0] and data[1]; it never verifies that the ASN1_STRING has length >= 2, so a one-byte addressFamily buffer is read one byte past its boundary.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads f->addressFamily->data[1] without confirming the buffer holds two bytes, performing a read beyond the buffer's intended boundary, which is the core of CWE-119. This is a bounds-check omission rather than a NULL-pointer dereference, since NULL is already checked.

evidence_lines.code:
return ((f != NULL &&
f->addressFamily != NULL && f->addressFamily->data != NULL)
? ((f->addressFamily->data[0] << 8) | (f->addressFamily->data[1]))
: 0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length of f->addressFamily is not constrained before indexing data[1]. Trigger: parsing an X.509 IPAddressFamily extension whose addressFamily contains fewer than two bytes. Consequence: a one-byte out-of-bounds read, yielding incorrect AFI display; the memory read is outside the intended buffer.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.5-5, the ReadPCXImage function in pcx.c allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory leak) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: The ThrowPCXException macro unconditionally calls RelinquishMagickMemory(scanline) and RelinquishVirtualMemory(pixel_info); before the fix these pointers are not guarded and page_table is never freed, so error paths leak allocations.
At this point page_table is set to NULL, but only after the DCX branch may allocate it; the macro does not release page_table, so any ThrowPCXException after allocation leaks the 1024-entry table.

scanline and pixel_info are allocated here; if either allocation fails, the error branch only frees the non-NULL ones before throwing, and subsequent ThrowPCXException calls rely on the macro to release them.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the function fails to release allocated resources (notably page_table) on error exits, so their effective lifetime ends without deallocation. This is a missing-release resource-consumption weakness, not a use-after-free or double-free.

evidence_lines.code:
#define ThrowPCXException(severity,tag) \
{ \
scanline=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(scanline); \
pixel_info=RelinquishVirtualMemory(pixel_info); \
ThrowReaderException(severity,tag); \
}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error-handling macro ThrowPCXException frees scanline and pixel_info but omits page_table, and it is invoked on many crafted-input error paths (bad magic, header, EOF) after resources have been allocated. Trigger: a crafted PCX/DCX file that fails validation after page_table, scanline, or pixel_info allocation. Consequence: the allocated buffers are not released, causing a memory leak and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflows in TGA and troff exports (addresses #53, #54)

These were all caused by sprintf() appending a null char that was not actually used.
Fixes CVE-2021-30498 and CVE-2021-30499.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    cur += sprintf(cur, "%c", (uint8_t)linechar[x + len]);'], 'added_lines': ['                    cur += write_u8(cur, (uint8_t)linechar[x + len]);']}
description: A flaw was found in libcaca. A heap buffer overflow in export.c in function export_tga might lead to memory corruption and other potential consequences.

code_evidence: Line 5 computes the malloc size as 1000 + height*(7 + width*(47+83+10+7)), a fixed worst-case estimate; line 6 allocates that many bytes and cur walks forward.

Line 60 uses sprintf(cur, "%c", ...) for each printable character, and sprintf always appends a terminating NUL byte that is counted in the returned value but is then overwritten by the next write; the size estimate did not reserve room for these extra NUL bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of the malloc'd buffer because the size computation undercounts the bytes written by sprintf. That is an out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787), not merely an integer issue or a read overrun.

evidence_lines.code:
*bytes = 1000 + cv->height * (7 + cv->width * (47 + 83 + 10 + 7));
cur = data = malloc(*bytes);
cur += sprintf(cur, "%c", (uint8_t)linechar[x + len]);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The heap buffer is sized by a per-cell constant that omits the NUL byte sprintf appends on each character emission. With enough canvas cells the accumulating cur pointer advances past the allocation end, so sprintf writes a NUL (and following data) out of bounds, corrupting heap memory.

The cgroup release_agent is called with call_usermodehelper.  The function
call_usermodehelper starts the release_agent with a full set fo capabilities.
Therefore require capabilities when setting the release_agaent.

Tested-by: Tabitha Sable <tabitha.c.sable@gmail.com>

description: A vulnerability was found in the Linux kernel’s cgroup_release_agent_write in the kernel/cgroup/cgroup-v1.c function. This flaw, under certain circumstances, allows the use of the cgroups v1 release_agent feature to escalate privileges and bypass the namespace isolation unexpectedly.

code_evidence: The function obtains the target cgroup via cgroup_kn_lock_live and returns -ENODEV only if it cannot be locked; no credential, capability, or user-namespace check gates the operation.

After locking, the caller-supplied buf is copied with strlcpy into cgrp->root->release_agent_path under release_agent_path_lock, directly modifying the release-agent path without any authorization test.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the function omits an authorization check on an action that modifies privileged kernel state; the missing check, not the string copy, is the weakness. A buffer/length issue (CWE-120) is not indicated since strlcpy bounds the copy.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write path performs no authorization check before overwriting the cgroup root's release_agent_path. Trigger: a caller able to open the release_agent file writes a path, and the stored agent is later executed with full capabilities. Supported consequence: privilege escalation and bypass of namespace isolation via the release-agent mechanism.

description: An issue was discovered in ytnef before 1.9.2. There is a potential out-of-bounds access with fields of Size 0 in TNEFParse() in libytnef.

code_evidence: The loop reads an attacker-controlled size at line 45, allocates a buffer of that size with calloc at line 48, then reads size bytes into it at line 50 and passes data plus size to a handler at line 78. A size of 0 yields a zero-length allocation, so the handler receives a pointer to a zero-byte buffer while still being told the field has data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the flow allows handlers to read beyond the intended zero-length allocation, i.e., past the end of a buffer. This is not CWE-787 (write) since the weakness manifests as reading data beyond the allocated field buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: TNEFParse accepts a field size of 0 without validation, allocating a zero-length buffer and passing it with the size to type-specific handlers. A handler that parses fields (such as a Version field) may read past this zero-length buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and potential crash or memory disclosure. The missing size==0 check is the trigger; the OOB read in handlers is the supported consequence.

commit_msg:
IB/security: Restrict use of the write() interface

The drivers/infiniband stack uses write() as a replacement for
bi-directional ioctl().  This is not safe. There are ways to
trigger write calls that result in the return structure that
is normally written to user space being shunted off to user
specified kernel memory instead.

For the immediate repair, detect and deny suspicious accesses to
the write API.

For long term, update the user space libraries and the kernel API
to something that doesn't present the same security vulnerabilities
(likely a structured ioctl() interface).

The impacted uAPI interfaces are generally only available if
hardware from drivers/infiniband is installed in the system.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jann@thejh.net>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgunthorpe@obsidianresearch.com>
[ Expanded check to all known write() entry points ]
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Doug Ledford <dledford@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (WARN_ON_ONCE(!ib_safe_file_access(filp)))', '\t\treturn -EACCES;']}
description: The InfiniBand (aka IB) stack in the Linux kernel before 4.5.3 incorrectly relies on the write system call, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (kernel memory write operation) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a uAPI interface.

The selected command handler is invoked directly with user-controlled offset and sizes, and on success the raw length is returned to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers failures in permission and access-control management. Here the missing access-context check lets an untrusted caller exercise the write() command path, which is an access-control weakness rather than a memory-safety flaw in itself.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ucma_write dispatches privileged command handling without verifying that the caller's file access is safe, so a write() call can reach kernel-side command processing on behalf of an untrusted context. Trigger: a local user issuing write() on the uAPI interface with a valid command header. Consequence: access-control bypass permitting kernel memory writes or denial of service.

commit_msg: Bug #717 avoid assertion in get_layer4_v6
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            if (next == NULL)', '                done = true;', '']}
description: tcprewrite in Tcpreplay 4.4.1 has a reachable assertion in get_layer4_v6 in common/get.c.

code_evidence: assert(ip6_hdr) aborts if the caller passes a NULL IPv6 header; no validation precedes it.

The while(!done) loop recurses on TCPR_IPV6_NH_IPV6 via get_layer4_v6((ipv6_hdr_t *)next, l3len - min_len), where next derives from packet bytes, so nested v6-in-v6 headers control recursion depth and the l3len passed down.
Only after the loop does the code test !next or bounds against ip6_hdr + l3len, returning NULL; this guard is downstream of the recursive call and assert.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because a reachable assert() in get_layer4_v6 terminates the application on malformed/attacker-supplied packet input; the added NULL check after recursion mitigates the crash path. This is not merely a NULL dereference (CWE-476) since the impact is assertion-driven abort.

evidence_lines.code: assert(ip6_hdr);

if (!next || (u_char*)next > (u_char*)ip6_hdr + l3len)
return NULL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function asserts a precondition on ip6_hdr and recurses on attacker-controlled nested IPv6-in-IPv6 headers without bounding recursion before the assert. A crafted packet with nested v6 headers, or a NULL header reaching the assert, triggers abort() in tcprewrite, causing process exit (DoS) rather than graceful NULL return.

commit_msg:
The functions XGetFontPath, XListExtensions, and XListFonts are
vulnerable to an off-by-one override on malicious server responses.

The server replies consist of chunks consisting of a length byte
followed by actual string, which is not NUL-terminated.

While parsing the response, the length byte is overridden with '\0',
thus the memory area can be used as storage of C strings later on. To
be able to NUL-terminate the last string, the buffer is reserved with
an additional byte of space.

For a boundary check, the variable chend (end of ch) was introduced,
pointing at the end of the buffer which ch initially points to.
Unfortunately there is a difference in handling "the end of ch".

While chend points at the first byte that must not be written to,
the for-loop uses chend as the last byte that can be written to.

Therefore, an off-by-one can occur.

I have refactored the code so chend actually points to the last byte
that can be written to without an out of boundary access. As it is not
possible to achieve "ch + length < chend" and "ch + length + 1 > chend"
with the corrected chend meaning, I removed the inner if-check.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    chend = ch + (nbytes + 1);'], 'added_lines': ['\t    chend = ch + nbytes;']}
description: An issue was discovered in libX11 through 1.6.5. The function XListExtensions in ListExt.c is vulnerable to an off-by-one error caused by malicious server responses, leading to DoS or possibly unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: Line 21 allocates nbytes+1 bytes for ch to allow NUL-terminating the last string. Line 32 sets chend = ch + (nbytes + 1), one past the first byte that must not be written. The loop at line 34 uses the condition ch + length < chend and at line 39 writes *ch = '\0' after advancing ch += length + 1 (line 37), so the write can land at chend, the out-of-bounds byte.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The buffer bound is computed one greater than the correct maximum writable offset, and the loop/termination logic uses that value as inclusive, producing exactly a one-byte overrun. This matches CWE-193 (off-by-one). A plain missing length check would be CWE-120, but here the boundary itself is off by one.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: chend is computed as ch + nbytes + 1 while the loop treats chend as an inclusive last writable byte; the NUL write at line 39 can therefore occur one byte beyond the allocated buffer. Trigger: a malicious server reply whose last string length places ch at chend-1. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, leading to crash/DoS or possible memory corruption.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.4+
Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (test_bit(KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE, &key->flags)) {', '\t\tret = -ENOKEY;', '\t\tgoto error2;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tret = key_read_state(key);', '\tif (ret < 0)', '\t\tgoto error2; /* Negatively instantiated */']}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.10 does not correctly synchronize the actions of updating versus finding a key in the "negative" state to avoid a race condition, which allows local users to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls.

commit_msg:
fix deinterlacing for small pictures

fixes #12
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif(context->curY >= p->height) {', '\t\t\t\t\tcontext->pass++;', '\t\t\t\t\tcontext->curY = i->posY + 4;', '\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t\tif(context->curY >= p->height) {', '\t\t\t\t\tcontext->pass++;', '\t\t\t\t\tcontext->curY = i->posY + 2;', '\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t\tif(context->curY >= p->height) {', '\t\t\t\t\tcontext->pass++;', '\t\t\t\t\tcontext->curY = i->posY + 1;', '\t\t\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t}', '\t\t\twhile(context->pass > 0 && context->pass < 4 &&', '\t\t\t      context->curY >= p->height) {', '\t\t\t\tswitch(++context->pass) {', '\t\t\t\tcase 2:\t/* 2nd pass : every eighth row starting from 4 */', '\t\t\t\t\tcontext->curY = i->posY + 4;', '\t\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t\tcase 3:\t/* 3rd pass : every fourth row starting from 2 */', '\t\t\t\t\tcontext->curY = i->posY + 2;', '\t\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t\tcase 4:\t/* 4th pass : every odd row */', '\t\t\t\t\tcontext->curY = i->posY + 1;', '\t\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t\t}']}
description: ngiflib 0.4 has a heap-based buffer overflow in WritePixel() in ngiflib.c when called from DecodeGifImg, because deinterlacing for small pictures is mishandled.

code_evidence: For deinterlace pass 1, curY is advanced by 8; the bounds check only fires when curY >= p->height, then sets curY = i->posY + 4 without re-validating that this row is still within the image.
Same pattern in pass 2: curY += 8, then on overflow curY is reset to i->posY + 2 without checking against p->height.
Same pattern in pass 3: curY += 4, then reset to i->posY + 1 without bounds re-check, so curY can remain >= p->height after the pass transition.
The line buffer pointer is then computed as p->frbuff base + curY*p->width (+ posX), using the possibly out-of-range curY for indexed mode.
The true-color branch computes the same curY*p->width offset, so both modes derive the write destination from the unvalidated row.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The destination pointer is derived from an unchecked row index and then written by memcpy/pointer stores, producing a write past the allocated framebuffer, which is CWE-787. It is not merely a read overrun or integer wrap; the missing height constraint directly yields an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pass-transition logic resets curY to i->posY + offset but never verifies the new row is < p->height, so for small images the 'every odd row' pass can leave curY beyond the image height. Trigger: a small interlaced GIF decoded through DecodeGifImg. Consequence: fbuff_p is computed past the framebuffer, and subsequent WritePixels memcpy/assignment writes out of bounds (heap overflow).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    buffer = sizeof(small) < size ? small : g_malloc(MIN(65536, size));'], 'added_lines': ['    buffer = sizeof(small) >= size ? small : g_malloc(MIN(65536, size));']}
description: A stack buffer overflow flaw was found in the Quick Emulator (QEMU) before 2.9 built with the Network Block Device (NBD) client support. The flaw could occur while processing server's response to a 'NBD_OPT_LIST' request. A malicious NBD server could use this issue to crash a remote NBD client resulting in DoS or potentially execute arbitrary code on client host with privileges of the QEMU process.

code_evidence: A fixed stack buffer `char small[1024]` is declared, and line 6 selects the destination with `sizeof(small) < size ? small : g_malloc(...)`; the comparison is inverted, so the stack buffer is chosen when `size` is at least 1024.

The loop reads `MIN(65536, size)` bytes into that selected buffer per iteration; with `size >= 1024` the read target is `small`, and the `assert(count <= size)` at line 12 does not bound `count` to 1024.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The overflow target is a stack-allocated local array written past its bounds, matching CWE-121's definition. It is distinguished from a heap overflow because the incorrectly selected destination is `small`, not the `g_malloc` buffer.

evidence_lines.code:
char small[1024];
buffer = sizeof(small) < size ? small : g_malloc(MIN(65536, size));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the reversed size comparison, which routes large requests into the 1024-byte stack buffer instead of heap allocation. A server response causing `size >= 1024` makes `read_sync` write up to 65536 bytes into `small`, overflowing the stack frame; the consequence is memory corruption, crash/DoS, or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
There is a current use after free possible on a gatt server if a client
disconnects while a WriteValue call is being processed with dbus.

This patch includes the addition of a pending disconnect callback to handle
cleanup better if a disconnect occurs during a write, an acquire write
or read operation using bt_att_register_disconnect with the cb.

commit_msg: fixed theoretical stack overflow identified in #195)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if(iptreet<uint64_t,32>::bit(addr1,i)) iptreet<uint64_t,32>::setbit(addr,i*2);', '            if(iptreet<uint64_t,32>::bit(addr2,i)) iptreet<uint64_t,32>::setbit(addr,i*2+1);'], 'added_lines': ['            if(iptreet<uint64_t,32>::bit(addr1,i))', '                iptreet<uint64_t,32>::setbit(addr,sizeof(addr),i*2);', '            if(iptreet<uint64_t,32>::bit(addr2,i))', '                iptreet<uint64_t,32>::setbit(addr,sizeof(addr),i*2+1);']}
description: A stack-based buffer over-read exists in setbit() at iptree.h of TCPFLOW 1.5.0, due to received incorrect values causing incorrect computation, leading to denial of service during an address_histogram call or a get_histogram call.

code_evidence: addr is a fixed 32-byte stack buffer (line 2). The loop runs while i < addrlen*8 (line 4) and calls setbit(addr,i*2) and setbit(addr,i*2+1) (lines 5-6), indexing up to 2*addrlen*8-1 bits. No bound ties addrlen to sizeof(addr), and the call on line 8 adds addr with addrlen*2, so a large addrlen drives setbit/add past the 32-byte buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads memory past the end of the intended stack buffer via oversized indexing/length. It is a read overrun rather than CWE-787 (write), since the weakness manifests as reading beyond addr; the fixed-size buffer with unvalidated length is the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: addrlen from the caller is not validated against the fixed 32-byte addr buffer. Trigger: a large addrlen makes the loop index setbit beyond addr's bounds, and add(addr,addrlen*2,val) then reads the buffer with an oversized length. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds stack read, potentially crashing during address_histogram or get_histogram (DoS) and possibly disclosing adjacent stack memory.

commit_msg:
Merge pull request from GHSA-25j7-9gfc-f46x

cpdb-libs uses the fscanf() and scanf() functions to parse command
lines and configuration files, dropping the read string components
into fixed-length buffers, but does not limit the length of the
strings to be read by fscanf() and scanf() causing buffer overflows
when a string is longer than 1023 characters.

As all buffers have a length of 1024 characters we limit the maximum string
length to be read to 1023 by replaceing all occurences of "%s" by "%1023s"
in all calls of the fscanf() and scanf() functions.

Simply done by

perl -p -i -e 's/(scanf\(.*?".*?)%s/\1%1023s/' cpdb/cpdb-frontend.c tools/cpdb-text-frontend.c

and verifying with

grep scanf */*.c

description: cpdb-libs provides frontend and backend libraries for the Common Printing Dialog Backends (CPDB) project. In versions 1.0 through 2.0b4, cpdb-libs is vulnerable to buffer overflows via improper use of `scanf(3)`. cpdb-libs uses the `fscanf()` and `scanf()` functions to parse command lines and configuration files, dropping the read string components into fixed-length buffers, but does not limit the length of the strings to be read by `fscanf()` and `scanf()` causing buffer overflows when a string is longer than 1023 characters. A patch for this issue is available at commit f181bd1f14757c2ae0f17cc76dc20421a40f30b7. As all buffers have a length of 1024 characters, the patch limits the maximum string length to be read to 1023 by replacing all occurrences of `%s` with `%1023s` in all calls of the `fscanf()` and `scanf()` functions.

code_evidence: buf is a stack array of BUFSIZE (1024) bytes, and scanf("%s", buf) copies an unbounded whitespace-delimited token from stdin into it with no field-width limit.

printer_id and backend_name are stack arrays of BUFSIZE, and scanf("%s%s", printer_id, backend_name) writes each input token without a maximum width, so a longer token overflows the adjacent stack storage.
final_file_path is a stack array of BUFSIZE; the second scanf("%s", final_file_path) likewise copies an arbitrarily long user-supplied path with no bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The overwritten buffers are local stack variables written past their bounds by scanf, which is precisely a stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121). It is not merely a missing-input-validation issue, since the concrete consequence is an out-of-bounds write on the stack.

evidence_lines.code:
char buf[BUFSIZE];
scanf("%s", buf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the unbounded %s conversion in scanf writing attacker-controlled stdin tokens into fixed 1024-byte stack arrays. A token longer than the buffer overflows into adjacent stack memory, corrupting saved data and potentially control flow, causing crash or code execution.
