commit_msg:
Unfortunately, we ended up merging an old version of the patch "fix info
leak with DMA_FROM_DEVICE" instead of merging the latest one. Christoph
(the swiotlb maintainer), he asked me to create an incremental fix
(after I have pointed this out the mix up, and asked him for guidance).
So here we go.

The main differences between what we got and what was agreed are:
* swiotlb_sync_single_for_device is also required to do an extra bounce
* We decided not to introduce DMA_ATTR_OVERWRITE until we have exploiters
* The implantation of DMA_ATTR_OVERWRITE is flawed: DMA_ATTR_OVERWRITE
  must take precedence over DMA_ATTR_SKIP_CPU_SYNC

Thus this patch removes DMA_ATTR_OVERWRITE, and makes
swiotlb_sync_single_for_device() bounce unconditionally (that is, also
when dir == DMA_TO_DEVICE) in order do avoid synchronising back stale
data from the swiotlb buffer.

Let me note, that if the size used with dma_sync_* API is less than the
size used with dma_[un]map_*, under certain circumstances we may still
end up with swiotlb not being transparent. In that sense, this is no
perfect fix either.

To get this bullet proof, we would have to bounce the entire
mapping/bounce buffer. For that we would have to figure out the starting
address, and the size of the mapping in
swiotlb_sync_single_for_device(). While this does seem possible, there
seems to be no firm consensus on how things are supposed to work.

Signed-off-by: Halil Pasic <pasic@linux.ibm.com>
Fixes: ddbd89deb7d3 ("swiotlb: fix info leak with DMA_FROM_DEVICE")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reviewed-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!(attrs & DMA_ATTR_SKIP_CPU_SYNC) &&', '\t    (!(attrs & DMA_ATTR_OVERWRITE) || dir == DMA_TO_DEVICE ||', '\t    dir == DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL))', '\t\tswiotlb_bounce(dev, tlb_addr, mapping_size, DMA_TO_DEVICE);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/*', '\t * When dir == DMA_FROM_DEVICE we could omit the copy from the orig', '\t * to the tlb buffer, if we knew for sure the device will', "\t * overwirte the entire current content. But we don't. Thus", '\t * unconditional bounce may prevent leaking swiotlb content (i.e.', '\t * kernel memory) to user-space.', '\t */', '\tswiotlb_bounce(dev, tlb_addr, mapping_size, DMA_TO_DEVICE);']}
description: A memory leak flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s DMA subsystem, in the way a user calls DMA_FROM_DEVICE. This flaw allows a local user to read random memory from the kernel space.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs a DMA bounce copy to prevent stale swiotlb buffer contents from leaking to userspace; it contains no memory allocation/release tracking, so it does not demonstrate CWE-401 missing release of memory.

commit_msg:
gfs2: Don't deref jdesc in evict

On corrupt gfs2 file systems the evict code can try to reference the
journal descriptor structure, jdesc, after it has been freed and set to
NULL. The sequence of events is:

init_journal()
...
fail_jindex:
   gfs2_jindex_free(sdp); <------frees journals, sets jdesc = NULL
      if (gfs2_holder_initialized(&ji_gh))
         gfs2_glock_dq_uninit(&ji_gh);
fail:
   iput(sdp->sd_jindex); <--references jdesc in evict_linked_inode
      evict()
         gfs2_evict_inode()
            evict_linked_inode()
               ret = gfs2_trans_begin(sdp, 0, sdp->sd_jdesc->jd_blocks);
<------references the now freed/zeroed sd_jdesc pointer.

The call to gfs2_trans_begin is done because the truncate_inode_pages
call can cause gfs2 events that require a transaction, such as removing
journaled data (jdata) blocks from the journal.

This patch fixes the problem by adding a check for sdp->sd_jdesc to
function gfs2_evict_inode. In theory, this should only happen to corrupt
gfs2 file systems, when gfs2 detects the problem, reports it, then tries
to evict all the system inodes it has read in up to that point.

Reported-by: Yang Lan <lanyang0908@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Bob Peterson <rpeterso@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Andreas Gruenbacher <agruenba@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tgoto out;', '', '\t/*', '\t * In case of an incomplete mount, gfs2_evict_inode() may be called for', '\t * system files without having an active journal to write to.  In that', '\t * case, skip the filesystem evict.', '\t */', '\tif (!sdp->sd_jdesc)']}
description: A NULL pointer dereference issue was found in the gfs2 file system in the Linux kernel. It occurs on corrupt gfs2 file systems when the evict code tries to reference the journal descriptor structure after it has been freed and set to NULL. A privileged local user could use this flaw to cause a kernel panic.

code_evidence: The only preconditions before proceeding to eviction are nlink, read-only sb, and i_no_addr; there is no check that sdp->sd_jdesc is non-NULL.
When the inode is not flagged for deletion, control reaches evict_linked_inode(inode), which uses the journal descriptor.
The out label is where the function returns; the guard is placed before any journal-dependent eviction path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function lacks a NULL check on sd_jdesc and then passes control to code that dereferences it, matching CWE-476's pointer-dereference-of-NULL pattern. The availability impact (kernel crash) is consistent with the weakness scope; this is not a use-after-free because the pointer is NULL, not stale.

evidence_lines.code:
if (inode->i_nlink || sb_rdonly(sb) || !ip->i_no_addr)
goto out;

else
ret = evict_linked_inode(inode);
out:

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: gfs2_evict_inode proceeds into linked-inode eviction without validating sdp->sd_jdesc. Trigger: on a corrupt or incomplete mount, the journal descriptor has been freed and set NULL while system inodes are still evicted. Consequence: evict_linked_inode dereferences the NULL journal descriptor (via jd_blocks), causing a kernel NULL-pointer dereference and panic.

commit_msg: Restrict packet kinds that can be sent through onion path.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        return 1;', '    }', '', '    if (packet[1 + RETURN_2] != NET_PACKET_ANNOUNCE_RESPONSE &&', '            packet[1 + RETURN_2] != NET_PACKET_ONION_DATA_RESPONSE) {']}
description: The Onion module in toxcore before 0.2.2 doesn't restrict which packets can be onion-routed, which allows a remote attacker to discover a target user's IP address (when knowing only their Tox Id) by positioning themselves close to target's Tox Id in the DHT for the target to establish an onion connection with the attacker, guessing the target's DHT public key and creating a DHT node with public key close to it, and finally onion-routing a NAT Ping Request to the target, requesting it to ping the just created DHT node.

code_evidence: Only a length check guards the payload; any packet kind beyond RETURN_2 is accepted and forwarded.

The function copies the attacker-chosen tail of the packet (packet + 1 + RETURN_2) into data and sends it via sendpacket to the decrypted send_to address, so the packet type is never validated before onion routing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing packet-kind constraint lets an unauthorized remote actor cause the node to route a request that exposes the target's IP address, which is sensitive location information. This is an explicit information-exposure weakness rather than a memory-safety error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: handle_recv_2 forwards onion-routed packets without restricting packet[1 + RETURN_2] to onion response types. Trigger: an attacker positioned near the target's DHT key sends an onion-routed NAT Ping Request; the target decrypts it and relays it to the attacker's DHT node, revealing its IP. Consequence: disclosure of the target's IP address.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.0765: with a Visual block a put command column may go negative

Problem:    With a Visual block a put command column may go negative.
Solution:   Check that the column does not become negative.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (curbuf->b_op_end.col < 0)', '\t    curbuf->b_op_end.col = 0;']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0765.

code_evidence: After a block put, b_op_end.col is set to bd.textcol + totlen - 1 with no lower-bound check, so a Visual-block put can make the column negative.
With PUT_CURSEND, the cursor is copied from b_op_end and then incremented, propagating the possibly negative column.
STRLEN(ml_get_curline()) is used only to clamp an upper bound; a negative col passes this check unchanged and is later used as an index/offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked negative column propagates into heap line-buffer indexing, causing an out-of-bounds access/write on heap-allocated storage, matching CWE-122. It is not merely an integer underflow; the underflowed value is used as a heap buffer offset.

evidence_lines.code:
curbuf->b_op_end.col = bd.textcol + totlen - 1;
curbuf->b_op_end.coladd = 0;

curwin->w_cursor = curbuf->b_op_end;
curwin->w_cursor.col++;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the block-put path computes b_op_end.col from bd.textcol + totlen - 1 without ensuring it stays non-negative. Trigger: a Visual-block put where the computed column goes below zero. The negative column is retained as the cursor/op-end position and used as a buffer offset, producing an out-of-bounds write on heap-allocated line data (CWE-122).

commit_msg: GIF loader: check bad image separator, ensure left/top offset of image don't reach image margins (#122)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    g->out[g->cur_x + g->cur_y * g->line_size] = g->codes[code].suffix;'], 'added_lines': ['    g->out[g->cur_x + g->cur_y * g->max_x] = g->codes[code].suffix;']}
description: An issue was discovered in libsixel 1.8.4. There is a heap-based buffer overflow in the function gif_out_code at fromgif.c.

code_evidence: Line 13 writes to g->out at index g->cur_x + g->cur_y * g->line_size; the guard at lines 10-12 only checks g->cur_y against g->max_y and does not bound g->cur_x or validate the resulting index against the allocated buffer size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a direct array store into g->out without verifying the computed index is within the buffer's allocated bounds, producing a write past the end of the intended buffer, which is exactly CWE-787. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the unsafe operation is the memory write at line 13.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination index uses g->line_size as the row stride while the buffer is sized by g->max_x, and cur_x is only reset at line 21 against max_x. If cur_x or the row stride exceeds the allocated width, the computed index points past the end of g->out; the unchecked store at line 13 then writes the suffix byte out of bounds, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tprivate = READ_ONCE(table->private); /* Address dependency. */'], 'added_lines': ['\tprivate = rcu_access_pointer(table->private);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: Line 28 loads table->private into a local pointer, and lines 30-31 immediately dereference it to obtain entries and jumpstack, which are then used throughout the rules walk.

The per-CPU sequence begin (line 27) and end (line 99) bracket the dereference, but the load at line 28 is an ordinary READ_ONCE with only an address dependency, so the compiler/CPU may reorder the private load after the sequence check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function dereferences table->private after the corresponding table info may already have been freed by the replacement thread. The root cause is the missing memory-ordering constraint at the line-28 load, not merely a NULL check, and the supported consequence is use-after-free access to freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The packet path loads table->private without an ordering guarantee that prevents the load from being moved after the sequence-count check. A concurrent rules replacement can therefore observe the sequence as even, free the old table info, and this thread then dereferences the stale private pointer at lines 30-31, causing a use-after-free in packet processing.

commit_msg:
WBXML: add a basic sanity check for offset overflow

This is a naive approach allowing to detact that something went wrong,
without the need to replace all proto_tree_add_text() calls as what was
done in master-2.0 branch.

Bug: 12408
Change-Id: Ia14905005e17ae322c2fc639ad5e491fa08b0108
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/15310
Reviewed-by: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
Reviewed-by: Pascal Quantin <pascal.quantin@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tguint32 off     = offset;'], 'added_lines': ['\tguint32 off     = offset, last_off;', '\tlast_off = off;', '\t\tif (off < last_off) {', '\t\t\tTHROW(ReportedBoundsError);', '\t\t}', '\t\tlast_off = off;']}
description: epan/dissectors/packet-wbxml.c in the WBXML dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.12 mishandles offsets, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (integer overflow and infinite loop) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: off is a guint32 initialized from the caller-supplied offset and only bounded by the while (off < tvb_len) check; tvb_get_guint8(tvb, off) then reads at that offset.
In the ENTITY case, tvb_get_guintvar(tvb, off+1, &len) returns attacker-influenced values; off += 1+len can wrap past tvb_len, so the loop guard no longer constrains off.
LITERAL/STR_T cases compute str_tbl+idx and pass it to tvb_strsize/tvb_format_text; a large idx from tvb_get_guintvar yields an out-of-range table offset.
OPAQUE case: off += 1+len+idx with attacker-controlled len and idx can wrap the guint32 off, so subsequent iterations read at wrapped, out-of-bounds offsets.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs buffer reads (tvb_get_guint8, tvb_strsize, tvb_format_text) at offsets derived from untrusted packet fields without bounds validation, i.e., operations outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119. The offset wrap is the mechanism; the memory read outside the buffer is the weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
ent = tvb_get_guintvar (tvb, off+1, &len);
off += 1+len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: off is advanced by attacker-controlled length/index values (len, idx) without checking that off+1+len or str_tbl+idx stays within tvb bounds. When the sum wraps guint32 or exceeds tvb_len, the loop condition no longer reflects the real offset, so tvb_get_guint8/tvb_strsize read past the buffer and the loop may spin, giving DoS or out-of-bounds reads.

commit_msg:
* ext/dl/dl.c (rb_dlhandle_initialize): prohibits DL::dlopen
  with a tainted name of library.
  Patch by sheepman <sheepman AT sheepman.sakura.ne.jp>.

* ext/dl/dl.c (rb_dlhandle_sym): ditto

git-svn-id: svn+ssh://ci.ruby-lang.org/ruby/branches/ruby_1_9_1@23405 b2dd03c8-39d4-4d8f-98ff-823fe69b080e
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    name = StringValuePtr(sym);'], 'added_lines': ['    name = SafeStringValuePtr(sym);']}
description: DL::dlopen in Ruby 1.8, 1.9.0, 1.9.2, 1.9.3, 2.0.0 before patchlevel 648, and 2.1 before 2.1.8 opens libraries with tainted names.

code_evidence: Line 16 converts the caller-supplied symbol name with StringValuePtr, which only coerces to a C string and does not reject a tainted Ruby string. The resulting name is then used at line 22 as the symbol argument to dlsym on the already-opened handle.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an untrusted symbol name and proceeds without validating its safety property (taint), matching CWE-20 improper input validation. The consequence is unauthorized native symbol resolution rather than mere string malformation, but the underlying cause remains missing validation of the input before use.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the symbol name input is not validated for taint before being used to resolve a native symbol. Trigger: an attacker supplies a tainted string as the symbol name to rb_dlhandle_sym. Because StringValuePtr does not enforce safety, the tainted name reaches dlsym, permitting resolution of attacker-influenced native symbols; the patch replaces it with SafeStringValuePtr to reject tainted input.

commit_msg:
While a stack of states is a good way to maintain graphics contexts, if
the command stream you are interpreting is untrusted, we must place
appropriate guards to be sure that, not only do we not pop past the end
of the stack, but we do not pop past the stack as it was when we began
rendering.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (stackHeight <= bottomGuard() || !state->hasSaves()) {', '    error(-1, "Restoring state when no valid states to pop");', '    return;', '  }']}
description: poppler before 0.16.3 has malformed commands that may cause corruption of the internal stack.

code_evidence: The function unconditionally calls state->restore(), forwards the restored state to out->restoreState(state), and decrements stackHeight without checking that a saved state exists or that the stack bottom guard is respected. The shown body has no validation of the command-driven stack depth before popping.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The malformed command stream acts as externally-influenced input that is interpreted without neutralizing the special 'restore' operation, so command elements modify downstream interpreter state. This matches CWE-74's injection pattern of unneutralized special elements affecting parsing/interpretation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the state-pop operation trusts the interpreter's command stream to supply a valid saved state and stack depth. Trigger: malformed commands cause restore() to be invoked when the stack is empty or below the render-time bottom guard. Consequence: the internal graphics-context stack is corrupted, potentially altering execution logic through attacker-influenced command data.

commit_msg:
x86: Check for valid PLT section size

Update x86 get_synthetic_symtab to check for valid PLT section size
before examining PLT section contents.

	PR binutils/22018
	* elf32-i386.c (elf_i386_get_synthetic_symtab): Check for valid
	PLT section size.
	* elf64-x86-64.c (elf_x86_64_get_synthetic_symtab): Likewise.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if (plt == NULL)', '      if (plts[j].type == plt_unknown)', '\t\t  && (memcmp (plt_contents + lazy_ibt_plt->plt_entry_size,', '\t\t  && (memcmp (plt_contents + lazy_ibt_plt->plt_entry_size,', '\t  && (plt_type == plt_unknown || plt_type == plt_non_lazy))', '\t  && (plt_type == plt_unknown || plt_type == plt_second))'], 'added_lines': ['      if (plt == NULL || plt->size == 0)', '      if (plts[j].type == plt_unknown', '\t  && (plt->size >= (lazy_plt->plt0_entry_size', '\t\t\t    + lazy_plt->plt_entry_size)))', '\t\t  && (memcmp (plt_contents + lazy_ibt_plt->plt0_entry_size,', '\t\t  && (memcmp (plt_contents + lazy_ibt_plt->plt0_entry_size,', '\t  && (plt_type == plt_unknown || plt_type == plt_non_lazy)', '\t  && plt->size >= non_lazy_plt->plt_entry_size)', '\t  && (plt_type == plt_unknown || plt_type == plt_second)', '\t  && plt->size >= non_lazy_ibt_plt->plt_entry_size)', '', '  if (count == 0)', '    return -1;']}
description: The Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, does not validate the PLT section size, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted ELF file, related to elf_i386_get_synthetic_symtab in elf32-i386.c and elf_x86_64_get_synthetic_symtab in elf64-x86-64.c.

code_evidence: The .plt section is located and its size is used to allocate plt_contents, but there is no minimum-size check before the section bytes are examined.
When plts[j].type is plt_unknown, memcmp reads lazy_plt->plt0_got1_offset bytes from plt_contents; if the .plt section is smaller than that, the read extends past the allocated buffer.
The nested IBT comparison reads at plt_contents + lazy_ibt_plt->plt_entry_size, adding a further offset that can exceed a short .plt section.
The non-lazy and non-lazy IBT branches similarly call memcmp on plt_contents with plt_entry/plt_got_offset lengths without confirming plt->size is at least that large.
Later, plt->size / plts[j].plt_entry_size derives a count; a too-small size yields zero or inconsistent counts, but the over-read occurs earlier in the memcmp calls.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads beyond the allocated PLT buffer via memcmp on attacker-influenced section size, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. It is not CWE-787 because no out-of-bounds write occurs; the impact is read-based crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the synthetic-symbol routine trusts the ELF-provided PLT section size and compares fixed-layout byte patterns against plt_contents without checking that the section is large enough. Trigger: a crafted ELF with a truncated .plt section. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read and application crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Check that ecall [user_check] pointers and ocall_malloc result pointer are outside enclave (#67)

This should reduce the enclave's attack surface by preventing an attacker from invoking ecalls on or triggering unexpected writes to arbitrary enclave memory, which could potentially leak information about that memory or lead to incorrect results.

Fixes #36. Fixes #66.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  // Guard against encrypting or overwriting enclave memory', '  assert(sgx_is_outside_enclave(plaintext, plaintext_length) == 1);', '  assert(sgx_is_outside_enclave(ciphertext, cipher_length) == 1);', '  sgx_lfence();', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in UC Berkeley RISE Opaque before 2018-12-01. There is no boundary check on ocall_malloc. The return value could be a pointer to enclave memory. It could cause an arbitrary enclave memory write.

code_evidence: ecall_encrypt receives plaintext, plaintext_length, ciphertext and cipher_length directly from the caller. Line 4 only checks cipher_length >= plaintext_length + IV_SIZE + MAC_SIZE, which constrains the destination size but does not validate that ciphertext or plaintext lie outside enclave memory. Line 7 passes the caller-supplied ciphertext pointer to encrypt(), which writes the IV, ciphertext and MAC into it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked destination pointer allows encrypt() to write beyond the intended output buffer, into enclave memory. This is a missing-boundary-check write, not merely a pointer-validation issue, so the out-of-bounds write label is appropriate.

evidence_lines.code:
assert(cipher_length >= plaintext_length + SGX_AESGCM_IV_SIZE + SGX_AESGCM_MAC_SIZE);
encrypt(plaintext, plaintext_length, ciphertext);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the absence of an enclave-boundary check on the destination pointer. A caller can supply a ciphertext pointer into enclave memory; encrypt() then writes the IV, encrypted data and MAC there, corrupting enclave memory. The trigger is an ecall invocation with an in-enclave ciphertext address, and the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds/arbitrary enclave-memory write.

FROMLIST: binder: fix UAF caused by faulty buffer cleanup

In binder_transaction_buffer_release() the 'failed_at' offset indicates
the number of objects to clean up. However, this function was changed by
commit 44d8047f1d87 ("binder: use standard functions to allocate fds"),
to release all the objects in the buffer when 'failed_at' is zero.

This introduced an issue when a transaction buffer is released without
any objects having been processed so far. In this case, 'failed_at' is
indeed zero yet it is misinterpreted as releasing the entire buffer.

commit_msg: Block GIF images with a code size > 12 (Issue #463)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  if (code_size > 12)', '  {', '    progress_error(HD_ERROR_READ_ERROR, "Bad GIF file \\"%s\\" - invalid code size %d.", img->filename, code_size);', '    return (-1);', '  }']}
description: A vulnerability was found in htmldoc version 1.9.15 where the stack out-of-bounds read takes place in gif_get_code() and occurs when opening a malicious GIF file, which can result in a crash (segmentation fault).

code_evidence: Line 19 reads an attacker-controlled code size byte from the GIF file and passes it unvalidated to gif_read_lzw at line 20; the function's only prior constraint is the implicit uchar range, allowing values up to 255.

Line 23 decodes pixels using that same code_size, and lines 25-30 index cmap[pixel] using the returned pixel value; pixel is only bounded by pixel < 256, so a larger code_size can let the LZW decoder yield pixel values beyond the color map's actual size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe operation is a read past the end of the color-map buffer driven by an unchecked decoded index. It is distinct from CWE-787, since the primary defect is an over-read rather than a write past bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the GIF code size byte is used as the LZW code width without an upper bound, so an oversized code size lets the decoder produce pixel indices exceeding the color map capacity. Trigger: opening a malicious GIF with code_size > 12. Consequence: out-of-bounds read in cmap indexing (per the report, in gif_get_code), causing a crash; the patch rejects code_size > 12 to prevent it.

commit_msg:
crypto: hmac - require that the underlying hash algorithm is unkeyed

Because the HMAC template didn't check that its underlying hash
algorithm is unkeyed, trying to use "hmac(hmac(sha3-512-generic))"
through AF_ALG or through KEYCTL_DH_COMPUTE resulted in the inner HMAC
being used without having been keyed, resulting in sha3_update() being
called without sha3_init(), causing a stack buffer overflow.

This is a very old bug, but it seems to have only started causing real
problems when SHA-3 support was added (requires CONFIG_CRYPTO_SHA3)
because the innermost hash's state is ->import()ed from a zeroed buffer,
and it just so happens that other hash algorithms are fine with that,
but SHA-3 is not.  However, there could be arch or hardware-dependent
hash algorithms also affected; I couldn't test everything.

Fix the bug by introducing a function crypto_shash_alg_has_setkey()
which tests whether a shash algorithm is keyed.  Then update the HMAC
template to require that its underlying hash algorithm is unkeyed.

Here is a reproducer:

    #include <linux/if_alg.h>
    #include <sys/socket.h>

    int main()
    {
        int algfd;
        struct sockaddr_alg addr = {
            .salg_type = "hash",
            .salg_name = "hmac(hmac(sha3-512-generic))",
        };
        char key[4096] = { 0 };

        algfd = socket(AF_ALG, SOCK_SEQPACKET, 0);
        bind(algfd, (const struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof(addr));
        setsockopt(algfd, SOL_ALG, ALG_SET_KEY, key, sizeof(key));
    }

Make sure we advance our offset in various places. Clarify a macro name.

Bug: 14412
Change-Id: I9b2af4bb57d039febe16f0c6d74ebb12fa34693c
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/25965

Petri-Dish: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    NOTE_EATEN_LENGTH(capability_length);'], 'added_lines': ['    CHECK_LENGTH_ADVANCE_OFFSET(capability_length);']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-wccp.c had a large loop that was addressed by ensuring that a calculated length was monotonically increasing.

code_evidence: The while loop at line 6 continues as long as length >= 8. Inside, line 7 calls dissect_wccp2_capability_element and assigns its return value to capability_length, but neither offset nor length is advanced by that value. Line 8's NOTE_EATEN_LENGTH macro does not update the loop variable length, so the loop condition remains unchanged across iterations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 (Excessive Iteration) fits because the while loop lacks a sufficient bound on iterations and does not advance its controlling length, allowing attacker-influenced packet data to cause excessive looping. Contrast with CWE-835 (infinite loop): here the defect is the missing monotonic length advance rather than a provably infinite loop, matching the commit's fix.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop's controlling variable length is never decremented by the per-iteration consumed capability_length, so the iteration count is unbounded. Trigger: a WCCP capability info packet with length >= 8 that returns a non-advancing or zero capability_length. Consequence: excessive iteration consuming CPU (DoS), since the loop never terminates or terminates only via external bounds.

commit_msg:
libvncclient: handle half-open TCP connections

When a connection is not reset properly at the TCP level (e.g. sudden
power loss or process crash) the TCP connection becomes half-open and
read() always returns -1 with errno = EAGAIN while select() always

commit_msg:
Fix FLI DOS -- CVE-2021-28676

* FliDecode did not properly check that the block advance was
  non-zero, potentally leading to an infinite loop on load.
* This dates to the PIL Fork
* Found with oss-fuzz
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (advance == 0 ) {', "            // If there's no advance, we're in in infinite loop", '            state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;', '            return -1;', '        }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Pillow before 8.2.0. For FLI data, FliDecode did not properly check that the block advance was non-zero, potentially leading to an infinite loop on load.

code_evidence: The chunk loop at line 27 iterates over 'chunks'. At line 184 'advance' is read from the chunk header via I32(ptr); the only guard (line 185) rejects advance<0 or advance>bytes. A zero advance passes this guard, so lines 189-190 leave ptr and bytes unchanged, and the loop condition c<chunks advances only by c++, continuing until chunks is exhausted; the loop is not infinite itself but the chunk pointer never advances, so subsequent chunks are reread from the same location. The fix adds an explicit advance==0 check returning IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the loop lacks a reachable progress/exit condition for zero-advance chunks: the pointer update that would terminate iteration is skipped, matching an unreachable exit condition. This is not an out-of-bounds issue; the missing zero check causes non-terminating/looping behavior rather than memory overrun.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the progress value 'advance' is validated only for negative or oversized values, not for zero. Trigger: a crafted FLI chunk whose advance field is 0. Because ptr and bytes are not advanced, the decoder repeatedly processes the same chunk data, consuming CPU and preventing forward progress, leading to a load-time denial of service.

commit_msg:
gbytearray: Do not accept too large byte arrays

GByteArray uses guint for storing the length of the byte array, but it
also has a constructor (g_byte_array_new_take) that takes length as a
gsize. gsize may be larger than guint (64 bits for gsize vs 32 bits
for guint). It is possible to call the function with a value greater
than G_MAXUINT, which will result in silent length truncation. This
may happen as a result of unreffing GBytes into GByteArray, so rather
be loud about it.

(Test case tweaked by Philip Withnall.)

(Backport 2.66: Add #include gstrfuncsprivate.h in the test case for
`g_memdup2()`.)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  g_return_val_if_fail (len <= G_MAXUINT, NULL);']}
description: An issue was discovered in GNOME GLib before 2.66.7 and 2.67.x before 2.67.4. If g_byte_array_new_take() was called with a buffer of 4GB or more on a 64-bit platform, the length would be truncated modulo 2**32, causing unintended length truncation.

code_evidence: The function accepts len as a gsize (64-bit on 64-bit platforms) but stores it into real->len and real->alloc, which are guint (32-bit) fields of GRealArray.
No check ensures len fits within guint before the narrowing assignment, so a len greater than G_MAXUINT is silently truncated modulo 2**32 when assigned to real->len and real->alloc.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-681 covers incorrect conversion between numeric types where data is omitted or translated unexpectedly. Here the gsize-to-guint assignment silently truncates the length, exactly the narrowing conversion described by CWE-681, rather than an integer overflow (CWE-190) or buffer bounds issue.

evidence_lines.code:
g_byte_array_new_take (guint8 *data,
gsize   len)

real->len = len;
real->alloc = len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the implicit narrowing conversion from gsize len to the 32-bit guint length/alloc fields without a range check. Trigger: calling g_byte_array_new_take with a buffer of 4GB or more on a 64-bit platform. Consequence: the stored length is truncated, so the GByteArray reports a smaller length than the actual buffer, leading to unintended length truncation and inconsistent state.

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tq->perturbation = prandom_u32();'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tget_random_bytes(&q->perturbation, sizeof(q->perturbation));']}
description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: When perturb_period is set, the timer is re-armed and q->perturbation is assigned prandom_u32(), a non-cryptographic PRNG output used as the SFQ perturbation secret.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because a security-relevant secret is generated with insufficient randomness. The patch replaces prandom_u32() with get_random_bytes(), confirming the weakness; this is not merely a hash-collision issue (CWE-328) but the weak source of the secret.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the perturbation value, which seeds flow hashing, is produced by prandom_u32() rather than a CSPRNG. Trigger: an attacker configures or observes the perturb period and can collect hashed flow outputs to recover the 32-bit state; consequence is predictable perturbation, enabling flow tracking/de-anonymization across the device.

commit_msg:
There are two sites that calls queue_work() after the
destroy_workqueue() and lead to possible UAF.

The first site is nci_send_cmd(), which can happen after the
nci_close_device as below

nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev   |  nfc_genl_dev_up
  nci_close_device           |
    flush_workqueue          |
    del_timer_sync           |
  nci_unregister_device      |    nfc_get_device
    destroy_workqueue        |    nfc_dev_up
    nfc_unregister_device    |      nci_dev_up
      device_del             |        nci_open_device
                             |          __nci_request
                             |            nci_send_cmd
                             |              queue_work !!!

Another site is nci_cmd_timer, awaked by the nci_cmd_work from the
nci_send_cmd.

  ...                        |  ...
  nci_unregister_device      |  queue_work
    destroy_workqueue        |
    nfc_unregister_device    |  ...
      device_del             |  nci_cmd_work
                             |  mod_timer
                             |  ...
                             |  nci_cmd_timer
                             |    queue_work !!!

For the above two UAF, the root cause is that the nfc_dev_up can race
between the nci_unregister_device routine. Therefore, this patch
introduce NCI_UNREG flag to easily eliminate the possible race. In
addition, the mutex_lock in nci_close_device can act as a barrier.

Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Fixes: 6a2968aaf50c ("NFC: basic NCI protocol implementation")
Reviewed-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Krzysztof Kozlowski <krzysztof.kozlowski@canonical.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20211116152732.19238-1-linma@zju.edu.cn
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* Clear flags */', '\tndev->flags = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* This mutex needs to be held as a barrier for', '\t * caller nci_unregister_device', '\t */', '\t/* Clear flags except NCI_UNREG */', '\tndev->flags &= BIT(NCI_UNREG);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nci_request in net/nfc/nci/core.c in NFC Controller Interface (NCI) in the Linux kernel. This flaw could allow a local attacker with user privileges to cause a data race problem while the device is getting removed, leading to a privilege escalation problem.

code_evidence: The function locks req_lock but the early-exit path only clears NCI_UP and returns; the lock does not prevent a concurrent nci_unregister_device from destroying workqueues while nci_send_cmd/nci_cmd_timer later queue work.

The final block flushes cmd_wq and deletes cmd_timer, then resets ndev->flags = 0, discarding the NCI_UNREG state; this allows the device-up path to race with unregistration and queue work onto a destroyed workqueue.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a concurrent shared-resource race: flags and workqueues are accessed without proper synchronization/atomicity between nci_close_device and unregistration. This fits CWE-362; the UAF is the downstream consequence rather than the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nci_close_device clears all flags (ndev->flags = 0) and does not coordinate with nci_unregister_device, so the NCI_UNREG marker is lost and no barrier prevents a concurrent nfc_dev_up/nci_open_device from calling nci_send_cmd after destroy_workqueue. Trigger: racing device up with device removal. Supported consequence: queue_work on a destroyed workqueue, leading to use-after-free.

commit_msg: Prevent arithmetic overflow on bounds check
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if( (*p) + len > end )'], 'added_lines': ['    if( (*p) > end - len )']}
description: ARM mbed TLS before 2.1.11, before 2.7.2, and before 2.8.0 has a buffer over-read in ssl_parse_server_psk_hint() that could cause a crash on invalid input.

code_evidence: len is read from the two-byte field at (*p)[0]<<8 | (*p)[1] [14], then *p advances by 2 [15]. The bounds check compares (*p) + len > end [16]; since len is attacker-controlled, the addition can wrap, so an oversized len passes the check. *p += len [22] then advances beyond end, and later reads via *p over-read the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The direct consequence is reading memory beyond the intended buffer, matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). The integer wrap is only the bypass mechanism; the supported impact is an over-read, not a write, so CWE-125 fits rather than an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length check uses pointer addition (*p)+len, which can overflow when len is large, so the 'fits in buffer' test is bypassed. Trigger: a server PSK hint length near SIZE_MAX that wraps the sum. Consequence: subsequent use of *p reads past the end of the received message buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read/crash on invalid input.

(for 4.9.3) CVE-2018-14882/ICMP6 RPL: Add a missing bounds check

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [' trunc:', '\tND_PRINT((ndo, "[ndp opt]"));'], 'added_lines': ['trunc:', '\tND_PRINT((ndo, "%s", icmp6_tstr));']}
description: The ICMPv6 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-icmp6.c.

code_evidence: Loop walks options while cp < ep; op is cast to nd_opt_hdr and ECHECK(op->nd_opt_len) only verifies the 2-byte length field, not the full declared option body.

Zero-length option jumps to trunc; options whose declared size (nd_opt_len<<3) exceeds ep also jump to trunc, but the trunc label at 0137-0138 merely prints and returns without distinguishing a true over-read.

For link-layer address options, l=(nd_opt_len<<3)-2 and print_lladdr reads cp+2 for l bytes; the earlier bound check uses ep but l can exceed the actual captured data when nd_opt_len is large relative to ep.

RDNSS loop computes l=(nd_opt_len-1)/2 and iterates reading nd_opt_rdnss_addr[i]; per-iteration ND_TCHECK only aborts if the address crosses snapend, but the lifetime read and iteration bound rely on the option length being consistent with captured data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory beyond the intended captured buffer boundary due to insufficient length validation, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. It is not an out-of-bounds write, since operations are reads/prints; the trunc label handling is the missing bounds check fixed by the commit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: option parsing trusts nd_opt_len to size sub-structure reads without ensuring the declared option body lies within the capture, so reads of link-layer addresses and RDNSS addresses can extend past the captured buffer. Trigger is a crafted ICMPv6 ND option with an inflated length field; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read (buffer over-read).

description: Memory leak in RTPS protocol dissector in Wireshark 3.4.0 and 3.2.0 to 3.2.8 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file.

code_evidence: Line 2 declares a GBytes pointer; line 3 allocates a new GBytes via g_bytes_new wrapping the key data; line 4 returns g_bytes_hash of that object without ever calling g_bytes_unref, so the allocation is never released.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory whose reference is discarded after use, matching CWE-401's missing release of memory after effective lifetime. It is not a use-after-free (CWE-416), since the memory is leaked rather than accessed after being freed.

commit_msg:
base64: Fixed decode buffer size estimation

Fixed required result buffer size underestimation in base64_estimate_decode_size() function.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    return ((base64_in_size / 4) * 3);'], 'added_lines': ['    return (((base64_in_size + 3) / 4) * 3);']}
description: RIOT 2020.04 has a buffer overflow in the base64 decoder. The decoding function base64_decode() uses an output buffer estimation function to compute the required buffer capacity and validate against the provided buffer size. The base64_estimate_decode_size() function calculates the expected decoded size with an arithmetic round-off error and does not take into account possible padding bytes. Due to this underestimation, it may be possible to craft base64 input that causes a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Line 3 computes the decoded-size estimate as (base64_in_size / 4) * 3, using integer division that truncates any partial 4-character group before multiplying by 3. For input sizes not divisible by 4, this underestimates the capacity needed by the decoder that consumes this estimate.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The underestimated size feeds buffer allocation/validation, enabling writes outside the buffer's intended boundary, which is the out-of-bounds memory operation CWE-119 describes. The arithmetic truncation is the root cause; the out-of-bounds write is the resultant weakness.

evidence_lines.code: return ((base64_in_size / 4) * 3);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: integer truncation in the size estimate discards the remainder group, so callers sizing or validating an output buffer via this value allocate too little space. Trigger: a base64 input whose length is not a multiple of 4 (including padding cases) makes the real decoded output exceed the estimate. Consequence: the decoder writes beyond the intended output buffer, an out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
Fix #77270: imagecolormatch Out Of Bounds Write on Heap

At least some of the image reading functions may return images which
use color indexes greater than or equal to im->colorsTotal.  We cater
to this by always using a buffer size which is sufficient for
`gdMaxColors` in `gdImageColorMatch()`.

(cherry picked from commit 7a12dad4dd6c370835b13afae214b240082c7538)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbuf = (unsigned long *)safe_emalloc(sizeof(unsigned long), 5 * im2->colorsTotal, 0);', '\tmemset( buf, 0, sizeof(unsigned long) * 5 * im2->colorsTotal );'], 'added_lines': ['\tbuf = (unsigned long *)safe_emalloc(sizeof(unsigned long), 5 * gdMaxColors, 0);', '\tmemset( buf, 0, sizeof(unsigned long) * 5 * gdMaxColors );']}
description: gdImageColorMatch in gd_color_match.c in the GD Graphics Library (aka LibGD) 2.2.5, as used in the imagecolormatch function in PHP before 5.6.40, 7.x before 7.1.26, 7.2.x before 7.2.14, and 7.3.x before 7.3.1, has a heap-based buffer overflow. This can be exploited by an attacker who is able to trigger imagecolormatch calls with crafted image data.

code_evidence: Line 20 allocates buf sized for 5 * im2->colorsTotal entries and line 21 zeroes it. Line 24 reads color = im2->pixels[y][x]; line 26 computes bp = buf + (color * 5), then lines 27-31 write five unsigned longs through bp. The indexing depends solely on the pixel value, not on colorsTotal, and no check bounds color against im2->colorsTotal.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of a heap buffer via an unchecked index, matching CWE-787. The weakness is the missing bound on color versus the allocation size, not merely integer overflow, so CWE-787 fits directly.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: buffer sizing and index computation both derive from the palette count, but the write index derives from arbitrary pixel data. If a crafted image contains an index >= colorsTotal, buf + color*5 points past the allocation and the increments on lines 27-31 write out of bounds, corrupting heap memory (potential crash or code execution).

Mach-o defend against bad crafted input

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/146
	modified:   p_mach.cpp
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            memcpy(&msegcmd[j], ptr, 2*sizeof(unsigned)); // cmd and size', '        ptr += (unsigned) ((const Mach_segment_command *)ptr)->cmdsize;'], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned headway = file_size - sizeof(mhdri);', '    if (headway < sz_mhcmds) {', '        char buf[32]; snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), "bad sizeofcmds %d", sz_mhcmds);', '        throwCantPack(buf);', '    }', '        if (headway < ((Mach_command const *)ptr)->cmdsize) {', '            char buf[64]; snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf),', '                "bad Mach_command[%d]{%#x, %#x}", j,', '                (unsigned)segptr->cmd, (unsigned)((Mach_command const *)ptr)->cmdsize);', '            throwCantPack(buf);', '        }', '        headway -= ((Mach_command const *)ptr)->cmdsize;', '            memcpy(&msegcmd[j], ptr, 2*sizeof(unsigned)); // cmd and cmdsize', '        ptr += (unsigned) ((Mach_command const *)ptr)->cmdsize;']}
description: p_mach.cpp in UPX 3.94 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (invalid memory access and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted Mach-O file, related to canPack and unpack functions. NOTE: the vendor has stated "there is no security implication whatsoever.

code_evidence: Line 12 takes sz_mhcmds from the untrusted Mach-O header and line 13 only rejects values above 16384; it never checks that the value is consistent with the actual file size. Line 15 allocates sz_mhcmds bytes, line 16 reads mhdri.sizeofcmds bytes into it, and lines 21-23 then walk that buffer, casting each position to Mach_segment_command and dereferencing cmd/cmdsize.

The loop at lines 22-58 advances ptr by the attacker-supplied cmdsize at line 57 and never verifies that ptr stays within the sz_mhcmds allocation, so segptr->cmd, the section loop at lines 27-37, and the memcpy calls at lines 41/45/51/54 can read past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs reads and memcpy operations on rawmseg at offsets derived from attacker-controlled command sizes without restricting them to the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The added headway checks in the patch target exactly this missing bound, confirming the out-of-bounds operation is the root cause rather than a mere consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Mach-O command buffer is sized from the header's sizeofcmds but the per-command cmdsize and ncmds are trusted without bounding ptr against the allocation. A crafted file with an oversized or inconsistent cmdsize makes the loop dereference and memcpy beyond rawmseg, causing out-of-bounds reads and an invalid memory access crash (availability impact).

commit_msg:
Bug 706506: Fix infinite recursion in mutool info.

2 separate problems here.

Firstly, pdf_mark_list_push fails to copy the pushed data
from local_list to the newly malloced block when we first
move from local storage to malloced storage.

(Also, while we are here, there is no point in storing
0 entries in the list as they will never be checked!)

Secondly, while gatherresourceinfo is supposed to be
called with indirected objects, it can (as is the case
with the given fuzzed file) be called with direct
references. These don't put anything sane in the cycle
checker.

Thus by using (legal) indirections from (say) the Font
resource entry back to something that contains the
original resource entry, we can get cycles that we don't
detect.

Fix this by pushing such entries onto the mark list.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (show & FONTS && font)', '\tif (show & (IMAGES|XOBJS) && xobj)', '\tif (show & SHADINGS && shade)', '\tif (show & PATTERNS && pattern)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (show & FONTS && font && !pdf_mark_list_push(ctx, mark_list, font))', '\tif (show & (IMAGES|XOBJS) && xobj && !pdf_mark_list_push(ctx, mark_list, xobj))', '\tif (show & SHADINGS && shade && !pdf_mark_list_push(ctx, mark_list, shade))', '\tif (show & PATTERNS && pattern && !pdf_mark_list_push(ctx, mark_list, pattern))']}
description: MuPDF v1.21.1 was discovered to contain an infinite recursion in the component pdf_mark_list_push. This vulnerability allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via a crafted PDF file.

code_evidence: The function recurses into font entries at line 25 after only checking the resource object itself (lines 11-12); the Font dictionary at line 17 is not pushed onto mark_list, so font entries containing indirect references back to the enclosing resource bypass cycle detection.
XObject entries are similarly recursed at line 42 while xobj (line 28) is never marked, permitting a Font/XObject indirection to re-enter gatherresourceinfo on an already-visited resource.
Shading and Pattern resources (lines 45-49) are gathered/recurred (line 56) without being pushed on the mark list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing push of nested resource objects defeats the recursion guard, so attacker-controlled indirect references drive unbounded recursion. This matches CWE-674 (Uncontrolled Recursion) rather than mere resource exhaustion, since the cycle check is bypassed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mark_list only records the top-level resource object, while nested Font/XObject/Shading/Pattern objects reached via legal indirect references are not marked. A crafted PDF whose font or xobject dictionary refers back to an enclosing resource causes gatherresourceinfo to re-enter indefinitely, exhausting the call stack and crashing (DoS).

commit_msg:
bpf: Fix leakage of uninitialized bpf stack under speculation

The current implemented mechanisms to mitigate data disclosure under
speculation mainly address stack and map value oob access from the
speculative domain. However, Piotr discovered that uninitialized BPF
stack is not protected yet, and thus old data from the kernel stack,
potentially including addresses of kernel structures, could still be
extracted from that 512 bytes large window. The BPF stack is special
compared to map values since it's not zero initialized for every
program invocation, whereas map values /are/ zero initialized upon
their initial allocation and thus cannot leak any prior data in either
domain. In the non-speculative domain, the verifier ensures that every
stack slot read must have a prior stack slot write by the BPF program
to avoid such data leaking issue.

However, this is not enough: for example, when the pointer arithmetic
operation moves the stack pointer from the last valid stack offset to
the first valid offset, the sanitation logic allows for any intermediate
offsets during speculative execution, which could then be used to
extract any restricted stack content via side-channel.

Given for unprivileged stack pointer arithmetic the use of unknown
but bounded scalars is generally forbidden, we can simply turn the
register-based arithmetic operation into an immediate-based arithmetic
operation without the need for masking. This also gives the benefit
of reducing the needed instructions for the operation. Given after
the work in 7fedb63a8307 ("bpf: Tighten speculative pointer arithmetic
mask"), the aux->alu_limit already holds the final immediate value for
the offset register with the known scalar. Thus, a simple mov of the
immediate to AX register with using AX as the source for the original
instruction is sufficient and possible now in this case.

description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 5.12.1 performs undesirable speculative loads, leading to disclosure of stack content via side-channel attacks, aka CID-801c6058d14a. The specific concern is not protecting the BPF stack area against speculative loads. Also, the BPF stack can contain uninitialized data that might represent sensitive information previously operated on by the kernel.

code_evidence: The ALU64 add/sub fixup reads the verifier's aux->alu_state and alu_limit for the current instruction, then emits a mask derived from aux->alu_limit around the register-based offset. The mask construction (MOV32 alu_limit, SUB/OR/NEG/ARSH/AND) is applied to a runtime register value without distinguishing whether the offset source was a known scalar or an immediate. When the pointer arithmetic uses a bounded immediate scalar, the verifier's aux->alu_limit is already the final immediate, but the fixup still treats it as a register source and masks a register value, so the speculative sanitization does not constrain the actual pointer offset to the intended immediate bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-863 fits because the verifier is the authorization mechanism that decides which BPF stack accesses are permitted, and this fixup fails to correctly enforce that check for immediate-based pointer arithmetic, allowing a restricted access under speculation. It is not merely a missing bounds check; the existing authorization logic is applied incorrectly, yielding a protection bypass.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the fixup rewrites immediate-based pointer arithmetic as if it were register-based, so the speculative mask is computed against a register rather than the fixed immediate limit. Trigger: an unprivileged BPF program performs stack-pointer add/sub with a known bounded scalar that the verifier records as an immediate. Consequence: speculative execution can use an intermediate out-of-bounds stack offset to disclose uninitialized kernel stack bytes via side channel, because the intended bound is not correctly enforced.

commit_msg:
(uid_t) -1 is still used as placeholder to mean "unset". This is OK, since
there should be no users with such number, see
https://systemd.io/UIDS-GIDS#special-linux-uids.

(uid_t) -1 is used as the default value in class initialization.

When a user or group above INT32_MAX is created, the numeric uid or
gid wraps around to negative when the value is assigned to gint, and
polkit gets confused. Let's accept such gids, except for -1.

A nicer fix would be to change the underlying type to e.g. uint32 to
not have negative values. But this cannot be done without breaking the
API, so likely new functions will have to be added (a
polkit_unix_user_new variant that takes a unsigned, and the same for
_group_new, _set_uid, _get_uid, _set_gid, _get_gid, etc.). This will
require a bigger patch.

Fixes https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/polkit/polkit/issues/74.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  unix_user->uid = -1;  /* (uid_t) -1 is not a valid UID under Linux */']}
description: A flaw was found in PolicyKit (aka polkit) 0.115 that allows a user with a uid greater than INT_MAX to successfully execute any systemctl command.

code_evidence: polkit_unix_user_init only sets unix_user->name = NULL and initializes no uid field, leaving the uid member with whatever value the allocated object holds; the patch adds an explicit uid = -1 sentinel. The function performs no validation of the uid value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of the uid property before it is used for authorization, which matches CWE-20's improper input validation; the fix constrains accepted values to exclude -1. It is not a type-conversion or encoding issue, so CWE-20 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constructor fails to establish a defined, validated uid state, so a caller-supplied or uninitialized uid (including a wrapped negative value from a uid above INT32_MAX) reaches polkit's authorization logic unchecked. Trigger: an object whose uid is not properly constrained. Consequence: the -1 sentinel/negative uid is treated as a valid identity, letting a high-uid user bypass authorization and execute privileged systemctl commands.

description: mm-video-v4l2/vidc/venc/src/omx_video_base.cpp in mediaserver in Android 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-08-01 allocates an incorrect amount of memory, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka internal bug 28816964.

This directly matches CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation class; the incorrect allocation length is the root cause, and the supported consequence is out-of-bounds memory access.

commit_msg:
This fixes CVE-2017-7482.

When a kerberos 5 ticket is being decoded so that it can be loaded into an
rxrpc-type key, there are several places in which the length of a
variable-length field is checked to make sure that it's not going to
overrun the available data - but the data is padded to the nearest
four-byte boundary and the code doesn't check for this extra.  This could
lead to the size-remaining variable wrapping and the data pointer going
over the end of the buffer.

Fix this by making the various variable-length data checks use the padded
length.

Reported-by: 石磊 <shilei-c@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Marc Dionne <marc.c.dionne@auristor.com>
Reviewed-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned int toklen = *_toklen, len;', '\t\tlen = (len + 3) & ~3;', '\t\ttoklen -= len;', '\t\txdr += len >> 2;'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned int toklen = *_toklen, len, paddedlen;', '\tpaddedlen = (len + 3) & ~3;', '\tif (paddedlen > toklen)', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t\ttoklen -= paddedlen;', '\t\txdr += paddedlen >> 2;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before version 4.12, Kerberos 5 tickets decoded when using the RXRPC keys incorrectly assumes the size of a field. This could lead to the size-remaining variable wrapping and the data pointer going over the end of the buffer. This could possibly lead to memory corruption and possible privilege escalation.

code_evidence: toklen is the caller-supplied remaining-buffer count, reduced by 8 after the tag/length words; the only bound check on the declared field length is len > max_data_size against a separate limit, not against toklen.

The padded length computed only inside the len>0 branch is subtracted from toklen and shifted into the xdr pointer without any check that the padded value fits within toklen; kmemdup copies len bytes from xdr before the pointer is advanced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an unchecked arithmetic operation on an unsigned length: toklen -= paddedlen underflows/wraps because the code assumes the result stays positive. That is exactly CWE-190 (integer wraparound used as a size/offset), not merely an off-by-padding bug; the wrap is what defeats the length accounting and yields the out-of-bounds pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the padded field length (len rounded up to a 4-byte boundary) is subtracted from the unsigned toklen and used to advance xdr without verifying paddedlen <= toklen. When the declared len is close to or exceeds the remaining bytes, toklen wraps to a huge unsigned value and xdr advances past the buffer end. The consequence is an out-of-bounds pointer that is returned to the caller via _xdr/_toklen, enabling subsequent over-reads/over-writes (memory corruption).

commit_msg:
can: ems_usb: ems_usb_start_xmit(): fix double dev_kfree_skb() in error path

There is no need to call dev_kfree_skb() when usb_submit_urb() fails
beacause can_put_echo_skb() deletes the original skb and
can_free_echo_skb() deletes the cloned skb.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/all/20220228083639.38183-1-hbh25y@gmail.com
Fixes: 702171adeed3 ("ems_usb: Added support for EMS CPC-USB/ARM7 CAN/USB interface")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Cc: Sebastian Haas <haas@ems-wuensche.com>
Signed-off-by: Hangyu Hua <hbh25y@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tdev_kfree_skb(skb);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: ems_usb_start_xmit in drivers/net/can/usb/ems_usb.c in the Linux kernel through 5.17.1 has a double free.

code_evidence: Line 56 hands the skb to the CAN echo buffer via can_put_echo_skb(). On the usb_submit_urb() failure path (line 59), line 60 calls can_free_echo_skb(), which releases the cloned skb, and line 63 then calls dev_kfree_skb(skb) on the same skb that was already stored and freed through the echo mechanism.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function releases the same skb memory address twice in the error path, matching CWE-415's double free. It is not merely a use-after-free because the defect is the repeated release itself, not a later dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch frees the skb through two ownership paths. Trigger: usb_submit_urb() returns an error after can_put_echo_skb() has taken ownership. Consequence: the skb is freed twice, corrupting the slab allocator and potentially enabling memory modification or code execution.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>

description: bluetoothd from bluez incorrectly saves adapters' Discoverable status when a device is powered down, and restores it when powered up. If a device is powered down while discoverable, it will be discoverable when powered on again. This could lead to inadvertent exposure of the bluetooth stack to physically nearby attackers.

code_evidence: The loop scans adapter->discovery_list for any client whose discovery_filter->discoverable is true, breaking on the first match.

set_discovery_discoverable(adapter, l ? true : false) then unconditionally overwrites the adapter's discoverable state based on whether a discovery client requested discoverability, without checking adapter->current_settings.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an authorization-relevant state change (enabling discoverability) without correctly verifying the actor's authority to change that setting, matching CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization. The client's filter is not an authorization to persist discoverability.

evidence_lines.code: set_discovery_discoverable(adapter, l ? true : false);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a discovery client's temporary discoverable filter is treated as authoritative and written to the adapter's persistent discoverable setting, ignoring whether the user configured discoverability. Trigger: a discovery client sets a discoverable filter, causing set_discovery_discoverable to enable discoverability and persist it. Consequence: the adapter remains discoverable after power-down/power-up, exposing the Bluetooth stack to nearby attackers.

without calling setkey first.  This patch adds a check so that
the accept(2) call will fail with -ENOKEY if setkey hasn't been
done on the socket yet.

sctp: Prevent soft lockup when sctp_accept() is called during a timeout event

A case can occur when sctp_accept() is called by the user during
a heartbeat timeout event after the 4-way handshake.  Since
sctp_assoc_migrate() changes both assoc->base.sk and assoc->ep, the
bh_sock_lock in sctp_generate_heartbeat_event() will be taken with
the listening socket but released with the new association socket.
The result is a deadlock on any future attempts to take the listening

description: net/sctp/sm_sideeffect.c in the Linux kernel before 4.3 does not properly manage the relationship between a lock and a socket, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock) via a crafted sctp_accept call.

code_evidence: Line 6 reads asoc->base.sk into a local only for net lookup, but lines 7-8 lock and test asoc->base.sk directly.

Line 23 unlocks asoc->base.sk, re-reading the association field after sctp_do_sm() has run; sctp_accept()/sctp_assoc_migrate() can change asoc->base.sk during that window, so the unlock targets a different socket than the one locked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a race condition (CWE-362): a concurrent sctp_accept()/migration interleaves with the timeout handler's lock/unlock sequence, violating exclusivity on the shared socket lock. The snapshot fix confirms the missing constraint that lock and unlock must reference the same object, not merely a generic locking bug.

evidence_lines.code: bh_unlock_sock(asoc->base.sk);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The lock and unlock are not bound to the same socket object: the socket pointer is re-fetched from asoc->base.sk at unlock time. If sctp_accept() migrates the association concurrently, bh_unlock_sock() releases a socket that was never locked, leaving the listening socket permanently locked; subsequent lock attempts deadlock and cause a soft lockup/DoS.

commit_msg:
Fix an integer underflow in build_read_multi_rsp

When p_buf->len is mtu - 1 and p_cmd->multi_req.variable_len
evaluates to true, integer underflow is triggered
in the following line, resulting OOB access.

```
 len = p_rsp->attr_value.len - (total_len - mtu);
```

Bug: 273874525
Test: manual
Ignore-AOSP-First: security
Tag: #security
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:85f4d53c7bf90b806639a3a302f0007ffb3b9f23)
Merged-In: Ia60dd829ff9152c083de1f4c1265bb3ad595dcc4
Change-Id: Ia60dd829ff9152c083de1f4c1265bb3ad595dcc4
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      total_len = (p_buf->len + p_rsp->attr_value.len);', '        /* just send the partial response for the overflow case */', '        len = p_rsp->attr_value.len - (total_len - mtu);', '      } else {', '        len = p_rsp->attr_value.len;', '        UINT16_TO_STREAM(p, len);', '        // check for possible integer overflow', '        if (p_buf->len + len <= UINT16_MAX) {', '          memcpy(p, p_rsp->attr_value.value, len);', '          if (!is_overflow) p += len;', '          p_buf->len += len;', '        } else {', '          p_cmd->status = GATT_NOT_FOUND;', '          break;', '        }'], 'added_lines': ['      total_len = p_buf->len;', '        VLOG(1) << "Buffer space not enough for this data item, skipping";', '        break;', '      }', '', '      len = std::min((size_t) p_rsp->attr_value.len, mtu - total_len);', '', '      if (len == 0) {', '        VLOG(1) << "Buffer space not enough for this data item, skipping";', '        break;', '      }', '', '      if (len < p_rsp->attr_value.len) {', '        UINT16_TO_STREAM(p, (uint16_t) len);', '        ARRAY_TO_STREAM(p, p_rsp->attr_value.value, (uint16_t) len);', '        p_buf->len += (uint16_t) len;']}
description: In build_read_multi_rsp of gatt_sr.cc, there is a possible out of bounds write due to a heap buffer overflow. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: total_len is computed as p_buf->len + attr_value.len (+2 if variable_len); when total_len > mtu, len = attr_value.len - (total_len - mtu) is computed with size_t and can underflow when total_len - mtu exceeds attr_value.len, yielding a huge len.
len is then written as a 16-bit length prefix via UINT16_TO_STREAM for variable_len responses, and p_buf->len is advanced by 2.

memcpy(p, attr_value.value, len) copies len bytes into the buffer; the only guard is p_buf->len + len <= UINT16_MAX, which does not bound len against the allocated buffer size (mtu + offsets), so an underflowed len causes an out-of-bounds heap write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a memcpy into a heap buffer whose length is derived from an underflowed size_t, producing a write beyond the allocated buffer. This directly matches CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write); the integer underflow is the root cause, but the supported consequence is the OOB heap write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the overflow branch subtracts (total_len - mtu) from attr_value.len using unsigned size_t without checking that the subtrahend is smaller, so when p_buf->len == mtu-1 and variable_len is true the subtraction underflows to a very large value. Trigger: a multi-read request whose accumulated response length exceeds mtu. Consequence: memcpy writes far past the osi_calloc'd heap buffer, corrupting heap memory (OOB write).

commit_msg:
Older kernels lack io_uring POLLFREE handling. As only affected files
are signalfd and android binder the safest option would be to disable
polling those files via io_uring and hope there are no users.

Fixes: 221c5eb233823 ("io_uring: add support for IORING_OP_POLL")
Signed-off-by: Pavel Begunkov <asml.silence@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (req->file->f_op->may_pollfree)', '\t\treturn -EOPNOTSUPP;']}
description: There exists a use-after-free in io_uring in the Linux kernel. Signalfd_poll() and binder_poll() use a waitqueue whose lifetime is the current task. It will send a POLLFREE notification to all waiters before the queue is freed. Unfortunately, the io_uring poll doesn't handle POLLFREE. This allows a use-after-free to occur if a signalfd or binder fd is polled with io_uring poll, and the waitqueue gets freed. We recommend upgrading past commit fc78b2fc21f10c4c9c4d5d659a685710ffa63659

code_evidence: The function performs no check on the polled file's poll-free capability before proceeding; the patched guard rejecting may_pollfree is absent, so any file including signalfd/binder is accepted.
vfs_poll(poll->file, &ipt.pt) registers io_poll_wake on the file's waitqueue via io_poll_queue_proc, storing the waitqueue head in poll->head.

The completion path dereferences poll->head under poll->head->lock and manipulates poll->wait.entry; if the underlying waitqueue was freed and POLLFREE was not handled, these accesses operate on freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function retains and later dereferences waitqueue/list state after the waitqueue lifetime ends. The missing may_pollfree rejection is the enabling condition, not a separate race or NULL-deref weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (unlikely(req->ctx->flags & IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL))
return -EINVAL;
mask = vfs_poll(poll->file, &ipt.pt) & poll->events;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: io_poll_add accepts files whose waitqueue may be freed (signalfd/binder) without handling POLLFREE, leaving poll->head and poll->wait.entry pointing into freed memory. Trigger: an io_uring poll on such a fd while the task waitqueue is torn down. Consequence: use-after-free when the completion path locks poll->head and touches list entries, risking memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix memory leak with bad options.

Option processing can allocate memory. Encountering a bad option was
returning and error without freeing that memory. This adds the necessary
calls to free the memory to fix #425.

Signed-off-by: Scott Bertin <sbertin@telular.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        coap_free_header(coap_pkt);', '          coap_free_header(coap_pkt);']}
description: In Eclipse Wakaama (formerly liblwm2m) 1.0, core/er-coap-13/er-coap-13.c in lwm2mserver in the LWM2M server mishandles invalid options, leading to a memory leak. Processing of a single crafted packet leads to leaking (wasting) 24 bytes of memory. This can lead to termination of the LWM2M server after exhausting all available memory.

code_evidence: At [69,70,71,72,73] the invalid-length check returns BAD_REQUEST_4_00 without releasing memory already allocated for the packet header/options.
Option parsing at [139,143,147,150] allocates multi-option storage (e.g., via coap_add_multi_option/coap_merge_multi_option) before later options are examined.
At [186,187,188,189,190] an unsupported critical option returns BAD_OPTION_4_02 without freeing the previously allocated packet state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory while parsing options and returns on malformed/invalid option conditions without releasing it, which is missing release of memory after its effective lifetime (CWE-401). The leak is a resource-consumption consequence, not a buffer overflow or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: error-return paths after option allocation exit without a coap_free_header call, so the allocated packet/option memory is orphaned. Trigger: a crafted packet whose option has an invalid length, or that carries an unsupported critical (odd-numbered) option after earlier allocating options. Consequence: repeated packets leak memory, exhausting the LWM2M server's available memory and causing denial of service.

description: ext/wddx/wddx.c in PHP before 5.6.25 and 7.x before 7.0.10 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a malformed wddxPacket XML document that is mishandled in a wddx_deserialize call, as demonstrated by a tag that lacks a < (less than) character.
