joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences ent->data without verifying it is non-NULL, directly matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. The consequence is a crash/DoS rather than memory corruption, distinguishing it from out-of-bounds or use-after-free issues.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: php_wddx_deserialize_ex assumes the top stack entry's data pointer is non-NULL after parsing. Trigger: a malformed wddxPacket XML (e.g., a tag lacking '<') leaves stack.top == 1 with ent->data NULL. The unconditional dereference at line 16 then causes a NULL pointer dereference and application crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.2109: [security]: overflow in nv_z_get_count

Problem:  [security]: overflow in nv_z_get_count
Solution: break out, if count is too large

When getting the count for a normal z command, it may overflow for large
counts given. So verify, that we can safely store the result in a long.

Signed-off-by: Christian Brabandt <cb@256bit.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t{', '\t    if (n > LONG_MAX / 10)', '\t    {', '\t\tclearopbeep(cap->oap);', '\t\tbreak;', '\t    }', '\t}']}
description: Vim is an open source command line text editor. When getting the count for a normal mode z command, it may overflow for large counts given. Impact is low, user interaction is required and a crash may not even happen in all situations. This issue has been addressed in commit `58f9befca1` which has been included in release version 9.0.2109. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: The function accumulates a numeric count in the signed long variable n. Inside the infinite loop, when a digit key is received, line 22 executes n = n * 10 + (nchar - '0') with no upper-bound check before the multiplication or addition.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the code performs an arithmetic accumulation that can exceed the signed long range and wrap around, assuming the result is always larger. The patch adds a LONG_MAX/10 guard, confirming the overflow is the root cause rather than a downstream bounds error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a signed long count is repeatedly multiplied by 10 and incremented for each digit without verifying it stays within LONG_MAX. Trigger: a user enters a z command with a very large digit count. Consequence: n wraps to a small or negative value, so the count used later (e.g., win_setheight or cap->count1) is wrong, causing instability or a crash.

description: An issue was discovered in Janus through 0.9.1. plugins/janus_voicemail.c in the VoiceMail plugin has a race condition that could cause a server crash.

code_evidence: Line 5 reads session->stopping and session->started with plain (non-atomic) accesses while other threads may concurrently update these fields, so the guard can observe a torn or stale value.
Line 9 performs a plain store session->started = FALSE while RTP callbacks for the same session may run concurrently, making the check-and-set non-atomic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because a shared resource (the session's started/stopping flags) is accessed concurrently without proper synchronization, creating a timing window in which one code sequence can modify state another is using. The fix's conversion to g_atomic_int_get/set confirms the weakness is improper synchronization rather than a simple logic error.

evidence_lines.code:
if(!session || g_atomic_int_get(&session->destroyed) || session->stopping || !session->started || session->start_time == 0)
return;

if((now-session->start_time) >= 10*G_USEC_PER_SEC) {
session->started = FALSE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function reads and writes shared session state (stopping, started) without atomic operations, so concurrent RTP callbacks can interleave between the guard at line 5 and the store at line 9. Two threads may both pass the guard and both enqueue a stop message, or observe an inconsistent state; the resulting unsynchronized access can crash the server.

commit_msg:
memory: properly check guest memory ranges in XENMEM_exchange handling

The use of guest_handle_okay() here (as introduced by the XSA-29 fix)
is insufficient here, guest_handle_subrange_okay() needs to be used
instead.

Note that the uses are okay in
- XENMEM_add_to_physmap_batch handling due to the size field being only
  16 bits wide,
- livepatch_list() due to the limit of 1024 enforced on the
  number-of-entries input (leaving aside the fact that this can be
  called by a privileged domain only anyway),
- compat mode handling due to counts there being limited to 32 bits,
- everywhere else due to guest arrays being accessed sequentially from
  index zero.

This is CVE-2017-7228 / XSA-212.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( !guest_handle_okay(exch.in.extent_start, exch.in.nr_extents) ||', '         !guest_handle_okay(exch.out.extent_start, exch.out.nr_extents) )'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( !guest_handle_subrange_okay(exch.in.extent_start, exch.nr_exchanged,', '                                     exch.in.nr_extents - 1) )', '', '        if ( !guest_handle_subrange_okay(exch.out.extent_start,', '                                         exch.nr_exchanged >> in_chunk_order,', '                                         exch.out.nr_extents - 1) )', '        {', '            rc = -EFAULT;', '            goto fail_early;', '        }', '', '        if ( !guest_handle_subrange_okay(exch.out.extent_start,', '                                         exch.nr_exchanged << out_chunk_order,', '                                         exch.out.nr_extents - 1) )', '        {', '            rc = -EFAULT;', '            goto fail_early;', '        }']}
description: An issue (known as XSA-212) was discovered in Xen, with fixes available for 4.8.x, 4.7.x, 4.6.x, 4.5.x, and 4.4.x. The earlier XSA-29 fix introduced an insufficient check on XENMEM_exchange input, allowing the caller to drive hypervisor memory accesses outside of the guest provided input/output arrays.

code_evidence: The pre-patch check validates only the base guest handle with guest_handle_okay() over the full extent counts, not the subrange actually accessed.
Input extents are read via __copy_from_guest_offset() starting at (i<<in_chunk_order)+j, an offset derived from guest-controlled exch.nr_exchanged and extent orders.
Output extents are read via __copy_from_guest_offset() at (i<<out_chunk_order)+j, likewise derived from guest-controlled fields.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes array indices from untrusted input (nr_exchanged, extent_order) without validating that the resulting index/subrange lies within the guest-provided array; the fix adds guest_handle_subrange_okay(). This matches CWE-129's improper validation of an array index, distinct from a simple buffer-length check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: guest-controlled exch.nr_exchanged is used with extent orders to compute array indices for the input/output extent_start arrays, but validation only checks the whole-array handle rather than the subrange beginning at nr_exchanged. Trigger: a caller sets nr_exchanged and mismatched extent orders so the computed index skips past validated memory. Consequence: hypervisor reads/writes guest memory outside the provided arrays (out-of-bounds access).

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/571
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      write_info=DestroyImageInfo(write_info);', '      write_info=DestroyImageInfo(write_info);']}
description: ImageMagick 7.0.6-2 has a memory leak vulnerability in WriteCALSImage in coders/cals.c.

code_evidence: write_info is allocated by CloneImageInfo at line 112 and used for ImageToBlob. If CloneImage at line 115 returns NULL, the early return at line 119 closes the blob but never destroys write_info.
If ImageToBlob at line 121 returns NULL, the early return at line 127 likewise leaks write_info.
Only the success path releases the ImageInfo at line 129, so the two error paths omit the required release.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because a resource (write_info) is not released after its effective lifetime ends on the early-return paths. This is a missing-release resource leak, not a use-after-free or double-free; the allocation is simply abandoned.

evidence_lines.code: write_info=DestroyImageInfo(write_info);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: write_info is allocated at line 112 but the error branches at lines 116-119 and 124-127 return without DestroyImageInfo, unlike the normal path at line 129. Trigger: CloneImage or ImageToBlob fails (e.g., allocation failure). commit_msg:
unix: correctly track in-flight fds in sending process user_struct

The commit referenced in the Fixes tag incorrectly accounted the number
of in-flight fds over a unix domain socket to the original opener
of the file-descriptor. This allows another process to arbitrary
deplete the original file-openers resource limit for the maximum of
open files. Instead the sending processes and its struct cred should
be credited.

To do so, we add a reference counted struct user_struct pointer to the
scm_fp_list and use it to account for the number of inflight unix fds.

Fixes: 712f4aad406bb1 ("unix: properly account for FDs passed over unix sockets")
Reported-by: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Hannes Frederic Sowa <hannes@stressinduktion.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: The Linux kernel before 4.5 allows local users to bypass file-descriptor limits and cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by leveraging incorrect tracking of descriptor ownership and sending each descriptor over a UNIX socket before closing it. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incorrect fix for CVE-2013-4312.

code_evidence: unix_detach_fds reads the in-flight descriptor list from the skb (scm->fp = UNIXCB(skb).fp) and then, for every entry, calls unix_notinflight(scm->fp->fp[i]) using only the file pointer. No user_struct/cred of the sending process is passed, so the decrement of the in-flight fd counter is not attributed to the sender that was charged when the descriptor was queued.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function mishandles release of a counted resource (in-flight file descriptors), leaving per-user accounting inconsistent, which directly matches CWE-399 resource management errors leading to uncontrolled resource consumption. It is not a memory-safety flaw; the defect is improper resource accounting.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: detach/release of in-flight fds decrements accounting without identifying the owning user_struct, so the counter credited at send time is not the one debited. Trigger: a local process repeatedly sends descriptors over a UNIX socket and closes them, with detach occurring in another context. Consequence: the sender's open-file resource limit is not restored, enabling bypass of fd limits and memory-consumption DoS.

commit_msg:
Add support for mount options to restrict access to /proc/PID/
directories.  The default backward-compatible "relaxed" behaviour is left
untouched.

The first mount option is called "hidepid" and its value defines how much
info about processes we want to be available for non-owners:

hidepid=0 (default) means the old behavior - anybody may read all
world-readable /proc/PID/* files.

hidepid=1 means users may not access any /proc/<pid>/ directories, but
their own.  Sensitive files like cmdline, sched*, status are now protected
against other users.  As permission checking done in proc_pid_permission()
and files' permissions are left untouched, programs expecting specific
files' modes are not confused.

hidepid=2 means hidepid=1 plus all /proc/PID/ will be invisible to other
users.  It doesn't mean that it hides whether a process exists (it can be
learned by other means, e.g.  by kill -0 $PID), but it hides process' euid
and egid.  It compicates intruder's task of gathering info about running
processes, whether some daemon runs with elevated privileges, whether
another user runs some sensitive program, whether other users run any
program at all, etc.

gid=XXX defines a group that will be able to gather all processes' info
(as in hidepid=0 mode).  This group should be used instead of putting
nonroot user in sudoers file or something.  However, untrusted users (like
daemons, etc.) which are not supposed to monitor the tasks in the whole
system should not be added to the group.

hidepid=1 or higher is designed to restrict access to procfs files, which
might reveal some sensitive private information like precise keystrokes
timings:

http://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2011/11/05/3

hidepid=1/2 doesn't break monitoring userspace tools.  ps, top, pgrep, and
conky gracefully handle EPERM/ENOENT and behave as if the current user is
the only user running processes.  pstree shows the process subtree which
contains "pstree" process.

Note: the patch doesn't deal with setuid/setgid issues of keeping
preopened descriptors of procfs files (like
https://lkml.org/lkml/2011/2/7/368).  We rely on that the leaked
information like the scheduling counters of setuid apps doesn't threaten
anybody's privacy - only the user started the setuid program may read the
counters.

description: fs/proc/base.c in the Linux kernel through 3.1 allows local users to obtain sensitive keystroke information via access to /proc/interrupts.

code_evidence: The readdir loop iterates over tasks returned by next_tgid and directly writes each PID entry into the caller's buffer via proc_pid_fill_cache using the caller-supplied filldir callback, with no per-task permission check.
The namespace and iteration state are initialized from the file position; every task in the namespace is enumerated regardless of the reader's credentials.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes process metadata (PIDs/directory entries) to actors not authorized to view them, matching CWE-200's exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor. The patch's hidepid/fake_filldir gating confirms the missing access check; this is an explicit information-disclosure behavior rather than a generic memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: proc_pid_readdir enumerates all tasks in the pid namespace and emits their /proc/PID directory entries without verifying whether the reading user may access them. Trigger: a local user reads the /proc directory; the loop walks every tgid and fills directory entries. Consequence: the existence and PIDs of other users' processes are disclosed, enabling information gathering about running processes, daemons and privileges.

commit_msg: A crafted packet from UE can crash SGW-U/UPF
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (gtp_h->type != OGS_GTPU_MSGTYPE_END_MARKER &&', '        pkbuf->len <= len) {', '        ogs_error("[DROP] Small GTPU packet(type:%d len:%d)", gtp_h->type, len);', '        ogs_log_hexdump(OGS_LOG_ERROR, pkbuf->data, pkbuf->len);', '        goto cleanup;', '    }']}
description: In Open5GS 2.4.0, a crafted packet from UE can crash SGW-U/UPF.

code_evidence: The received buffer is trimmed to the actual datagram size and cast to ogs_gtp_header_t; only the GTP version is checked, not that the buffer holds the full header.
ogs_gtpu_header_len(pkbuf) returns a length derived from the packet; the code checks only len < 0 and then calls ogs_pkbuf_pull(pkbuf, len) without confirming pkbuf->len >= len.
For GPDU packets, pkbuf->data is cast to struct ip after the pull, assuming an inner IP header exists even though the outer packet length may be too small.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts a length quantity from network input and pulls/consumes that many bytes without verifying it is consistent with the available packet size, matching CWE-1284's improper validation of a specified quantity in input. The resulting availability impact (crash) is the consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length value computed from the untrusted GTP-U packet is not validated against the actual received buffer length before ogs_pkbuf_pull and subsequent header access. Trigger: a UE sends a crafted short GTP-U packet whose computed header length exceeds the buffer. Consequence: the pull/assert path can fail and crash SGW-U/UPF (denial of service).

commit_msg:
evtchn: evtchn_reset() shouldn't succeed with still-open ports

While the function closes all ports, it does so without holding any
lock, and hence racing requests may be issued causing new ports to get
opened. This would have been problematic in particular if such a newly
opened port had a port number above the new implementation limit (i.e.
when switching from FIFO to 2-level) after the reset, as prior to
"evtchn: relax port_is_valid()" this could have led to e.g.
evtchn_close()'s "BUG_ON(!port_is_valid(d2, port2))" to trigger.

Introduce a counter of active ports and check that it's (still) no
larger then the number of Xen internally used ones after obtaining the
necessary lock in evtchn_reset().

As to the access model of the new {active,xen}_evtchns fields - while
all writes get done using write_atomic(), reads ought to use
read_atomic() only when outside of a suitably locked region.

Note that as of now evtchn_bind_virq() and evtchn_bind_ipi() don't have
a need to call check_free_port().

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    ASSERT(!d->active_evtchns);', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: evtchn_destroy() invokes spin_barrier(&d->event_lock) at line 5, then iterates and closes all ports via evtchn_close(d, i, 0) at lines 6-7 without holding the event lock.

The teardown continues with clear_global_virq_handlers(d), evtchn_fifo_destroy(d) and the closing brace at lines 8-10, with no active-port counter check or lock protecting these shared evtchn structures.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because shared evtchn state is modified without proper synchronization, allowing an interfering code sequence to interleave with the close/teardown sequence. This is a concurrency/atomicity defect rather than a simple bounds check; the missing lock and counter check directly permit the race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the port-closing loop and subsequent FIFO/global-virq teardown run without exclusive access to the domain's event-channel state, so a concurrent EVTCHNOP_reset or port-binding request can open new ports during the sweep. Trigger: racing requests issued while evtchn_destroy() iterates. Consequence: internal assumptions about port validity and counters are violated, enabling out-of-bounds accesses, BUG_ON checks, host/guest crashes, and potential privilege escalation.

Ensure the MakerNote data pointers are initialized with NULL.

This ensures that an uninitialized pointer isn't dereferenced later in
the case where the number of components (and therefore size) is 0.

This fixes the second issue reported at
https://sourceforge.net/p/libexif/bugs/125/

CVE-2020-13113
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tmemset(&n->entries[tcount], 0, sizeof(MnoteOlympusEntry));']}
description: An issue was discovered in libexif before 0.6.22. Use of uninitialized memory in EXIF Makernote handling could lead to crashes and potential use-after-free conditions.

code_evidence: n->entries is allocated with exif_mem_alloc (line 119) without zeroing, so each MnoteOlympusEntry's data pointer and size begin uninitialized. In the loop, tag, format, components and order are assigned (lines 132-135) and size is set at line 147, but data is only assigned when s != 0 (line 148). If exif_format_get_size(format) is 0, s is 0, the if(s) block is skipped, yet ++tcount at line 175 still records the entry, leaving its data pointer uninitialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function stores an entry whose data pointer was never initialized, directly matching CWE-908 use of uninitialized resource. It is distinct from CWE-476 null dereference because no NULL is assigned here; the value is indeterminate.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: entries allocated without initialization and the data field only written inside the s != 0 branch. Trigger: a parsed entry whose format size times components is 0 (e.g., zero components). Consequence: a later consumer dereferences the uninitialized entry data pointer, causing a crash or use-after-free-like invalid access.

commit_msg:
NetKVM: BZ#1169718: More rigoruous testing of incoming packet

Signed-off-by: Joseph Hindin <yhindin@rehat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    tChecksumCheckResult res, resIp;', '    resIp.value = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    tChecksumCheckResult res;', '', '    if (ppr.ipCheckSum == ppresIPTooShort || ppr.xxpStatus == ppresXxpIncomplete)', '    {', '        res.flags.IpOK = FALSE;', '        res.flags.IpFailed = TRUE;', '        return res;', '    }']}
description: The NetKVM Windows Virtio driver allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (guest crash) via a crafted length value in an IP packet, as demonstrated by a value that does not account for the size of the IP options.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.0011: reading beyond the end of the line with put command

Problem:    Reading beyond the end of the line with put command.
Solution:   Adjust the end mark position.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\telse', "\t\t    totlen -= spaces;  // didn't use these spaces"]}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.

code_evidence: totlen is computed as count * (yanklen + spaces) + bd.startspaces + bd.endspaces and used to size the heap allocation newp = alloc(totlen + oldlen + 1).

In the inner loop, spaces padding is only written when (j < count - 1 || !shortline) && spaces, so for a short line on the last iteration the trailing spaces are not emitted, yet totlen still counted them.
The end mark is set with curbuf->b_op_end.col = bd.textcol + totlen - 1, overstating the written extent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch adds an else branch subtracting the unused spaces from totlen, confirming a size/offset mismatch on a heap buffer allocated by alloc(). This is a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122): an incorrect computed length drives access beyond the heap allocation. It is not merely an off-by-one integer error but a heap buffer bound violation.

evidence_lines.code:
totlen = count * (yanklen + spaces) + bd.startspaces + bd.endspaces;
newp = alloc(totlen + oldlen + 1);

curbuf->b_op_end.col = bd.textcol + totlen - 1;
curbuf->b_op_end.coladd = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: totlen over-counts bytes when the last repetition suppresses padding on a short line, so the accounting no longer matches the actual buffer content. Trigger: a block put where the destination line is shorter than the block width (shortline true) and count reaches its final iteration. Consequence: the recorded end position extends past the allocated/initialized region, leading to out-of-bounds reads/access on the heap buffer.

commit_msg:
exif_process_APP12: Fix length calculation for second tag to prevent information leak

Summary:
buffer + 2+l1+1 points to the second tag. The maximum length of the buffer is length. Hence, the max length of the tag is length - (2+l1+1). Instead, the length passed is length - 2 - l1 + 1 which leads to a 2 byte overflow. If the last character of buffer is not null, this would lead to an out of bounds read of size 2.

Fixes CVE-2019-11925

Reviewed By: fredemmott

Differential Revision: D16930333

fbshipit-source-id: aad9cccaef3c678abc53bfd549aff6b582082a90
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      l2 = php_strnlen(buffer+2+l1+1, length-2-l1+1);'], 'added_lines': ['      l2 = php_strnlen(buffer+2+l1+1, length-2-l1-1);']}
description: Insufficient boundary checks when processing the JPEG APP12 block marker in the GD extension could allow access to out-of-bounds memory via a maliciously constructed invalid JPEG input. This issue affects HHVM versions prior to 3.30.9, all versions between 4.0.0 and 4.8.3, all versions between 4.9.0 and 4.15.2, and versions 4.16.0 to 4.16.3, 4.17.0 to 4.17.2, 4.18.0 to 4.18.1, 4.19.0, 4.20.0 to 4.20.1.

code_evidence: Line 7 checks length > 2+l1+1 before entering the branch, but line 8 passes the count length-2-l1+1 to php_strnlen while starting at buffer+2+l1+1. The available bytes from that offset to the end of the buffer are length-(2+l1+1) = length-2-l1-1, so the count overstates the bound by 2. Line 9-10 then add a tag using l2, which may reflect bytes read beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the intended buffer via an incorrect length bound, directly matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. This is a read overrun, not a write overflow, so CWE-787 does not apply.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an off-by-two in the length argument to php_strnlen for the second APP12 tag: the start offset is 2+l1+1 but the limit subtracts only 2+l1, permitting a scan two bytes past the buffer end. Trigger is a crafted APP12 block whose trailing bytes are not null-terminated; consequence is an out-of-bounds read (information leak or crash).

description: In libssh2 v1.9.0 and earlier versions, the SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT logic in packet.c has an integer overflow in a bounds check, enabling an attacker to specify an arbitrary (out-of-bounds) offset for a subsequent memory read. A crafted SSH server may be able to disclose sensitive information or cause a denial of service condition on the client system when a user connects to the server.

The check message_len < datalen-13 uses size_t arithmetic; when datalen is small (e.g., 9..12), datalen-13 wraps to a huge value, so the bound passes. Then data+9+message_len is used to read language_len and compute language pointer, yielding an out-of-bounds offset/read.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: subtraction datalen-13 on an unsigned size_t underflows when datalen<13, producing a huge bound that the attacker-chosen message_len satisfies. Trigger: crafted SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT packet with small datalen and large message_len. Consequence: out-of-bounds offset used for subsequent reads, enabling information disclosure or DoS on the client.

commit_msg: fixed redis-cli security issue with world readable history file
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    chmod(filename, S_IRUSR|S_IWUSR);', '    ']}
description: linenoise, as used in Redis before 3.2.3, uses world-readable permissions for .rediscli_history, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information by reading the file.

code_evidence: fopen(filename,"w") creates the history file with default process umask permissions, and the loop writes each history entry via fprintf(fp,"%s\n",history[j]) before fclose. No permission constraint is applied to filename, so the sensitive command history is stored in a file whose access mode is left to the environment.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-200 fits because the function stores sensitive history in a resource unintentionally accessible to unauthorized local actors, directly exposing information. The underlying permission mistake is an insecure-defaults issue, but the supported consequence here is information exposure to unauthorized readers.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the history file is created without restricting its mode, so under a permissive umask it becomes world-readable. Trigger: a local user reads .rediscli_history after the file is written. Consequence: disclosure of sensitive information such as commands and credentials typed into redis-cli.

Summary:
Fix handling of invalid union data in the table-based serializer. Previously if the input contained duplicate union data, previous active member of the union was overwritten without calling the destructor of the old object, potentially causing a memory leak. In addition to that, if the second piece of data was incomplete the wrong destructor would be called during stack unwinding causing a segfault, data corruption or other undesirable effects.

Fix the issue by clearing the union if there is an active member.

Also fix the type of the data member that holds the active field id (it's `int`, not `FieldID`).

Reviewed By: yfeldblum

Differential Revision: D26440248

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    const auto* fieldInfo = findFieldInfo(iprot, readState, structInfo);', '    // Found it.', '    if (fieldInfo) {', '      void* unionVal = getMember(*fieldInfo, object);', '      // Default construct and placement new into the member union.', '      structInfo.unionExt->initMember[fieldInfo - structInfo.fieldInfos](', '          unionVal);', '      read(iprot, *fieldInfo->typeInfo, readState, unionVal);', '      const_cast<FieldID&>(activeUnionMemberId(', '          object, structInfo.unionExt->unionTypeOffset)) = fieldInfo->id;'], 'added_lines': ['    if (const auto* fieldInfo = findFieldInfo(iprot, readState, structInfo)) {', '      auto& activeId = const_cast<int&>(getActiveId(object, structInfo));', '      if (activeId != 0) {', '        structInfo.unionExt->clear(object);', '      }', '      void* value = getMember(*fieldInfo, object);', '      structInfo.unionExt->initMember[fieldInfo - structInfo.fieldInfos](value);', '      read(iprot, *fieldInfo->typeInfo, readState, value);', '      activeId = fieldInfo->id;']}
description: An invalid free in Thrift's table-based serialization can cause the application to crash or potentially result in code execution or other undesirable effects. This issue affects Facebook Thrift prior to v2021.02.22.00.

code_evidence: When a field is found, the code placement-constructs the union member (initMember) and reads into it, then unconditionally overwrites activeUnionMemberId. There is no check for an already-active member, so a duplicate union field re-initializes a different member over the live one without clearing/destroying the old object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code overwrites the active union member id and re-initializes storage while the prior member remains live, so teardown releases the wrong object. This wrong-release behavior matches CWE-763. It is not merely a leak (CWE-401) because the incorrect active id drives an invalid destructor call.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the active union member is overwritten without first clearing the previous member, so the old object is never destroyed and the active id is set to the new field. Trigger: input containing duplicate union fields, or a second field whose read fails. Consequence: wrong destructor runs during unwinding (invalid release) causing crash, corruption, or leak.

commit_msg:
ath10k: fix memory leak

In ath10k_usb_hif_tx_sg the allocated urb should be released if
usb_submit_urb fails.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tusb_free_urb(urb);']}
description: A memory leak in the ath10k_usb_hif_tx_sg() function in drivers/net/wireless/ath/ath10k/usb.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering usb_submit_urb() failures, aka CID-b8d17e7d93d2.

code_evidence: Line 18 allocates a URB with usb_alloc_urb; on failure the code jumps to err_free_urb_to_pipe (lines 19-21), where only the pipe context is released.

On usb_submit_urb failure (line 33-34), the error path unanchors the URB (line 37) and jumps to err_free_urb_to_pipe (line 39); the allocated urb is never freed, and the success path frees it at line 41.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory in usb_alloc_urb and fails to release it on an error path, which matches CWE-401 (missing release of memory after its effective lifetime). It is not a double-free or use-after-free, because the object is simply orphaned and never freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the usb_submit_urb error branch unanchors the URB but does not call usb_free_urb before taking err_free_urb_to_pipe, losing the only reference to the allocated urb. Trigger: repeated usb_submit_urb failures cause each loop iteration to leak one URB, exhausting kernel memory and causing a denial of service.

commit_msg:
n_tty: fix EXTPROC vs ICANON interaction with TIOCINQ (aka FIONREAD)

We added support for EXTPROC back in 2010 in commit 26df6d13406d ("tty:
Add EXTPROC support for LINEMODE") and the intent was to allow it to
override some (all?) ICANON behavior.  Quoting from that original commit
message:

         There is a new bit in the termios local flag word, EXTPROC.
         When this bit is set, several aspects of the terminal driver
         are disabled.  Input line editing, character echo, and mapping
         of signals are all disabled.  This allows the telnetd to turn
         off these functions when in linemode, but still keep track of
         what state the user wants the terminal to be in.

but the problem turns out that "several aspects of the terminal driver
are disabled" is a bit ambiguous, and you can really confuse the n_tty
layer by setting EXTPROC and then causing some of the ICANON invariants
to no longer be maintained.

This fixes at least one such case (TIOCINQ) becoming unhappy because of
the confusion over whether ICANON really means ICANON when EXTPROC is set.

This basically makes TIOCINQ match the case of read: if EXTPROC is set,
we ignore ICANON.  Also, make sure to reset the ICANON state ie EXTPROC
changes, not just if ICANON changes.

Fixes: 26df6d13406d ("tty: Add EXTPROC support for LINEMODE")
Reported-by: Tetsuo Handa <penguin-kernel@i-love.sakura.ne.jp>
Reported-by: syzkaller <syzkaller@googlegroups.com>
Cc: Jiri Slaby <jslaby@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!old || (old->c_lflag ^ tty->termios.c_lflag) & ICANON) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!old || (old->c_lflag ^ tty->termios.c_lflag) & (ICANON | EXTPROC)) {']}
description: drivers/tty/n_tty.c in the Linux kernel before 4.14.11 allows local attackers (who are able to access pseudo terminals) to hang/block further usage of any pseudo terminal devices due to an EXTPROC versus ICANON confusion in TIOCINQ.

code_evidence: Line 4 resets canonical state only when the ICANON bit differs, ignoring EXTPROC changes; lines 5-7 zero read_flags and reset line_start/canon_head when ICANON is off, while lines 10-14 set canon_head and push when canonical input is active. Line 20 then stores ldata->icanon from L_ICANON(tty). Because the guard does not account for EXTPROC, a termios change that toggles EXTPROC while ICANON remains set leaves ldata->icanon and read_flags stale, desynchronizing the driver's internal canonical state from the actual termios flags.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code fails to correctly reinterpret the termios flag structure when EXTPROC overrides ICANON, leaving the stored canonical state (ldata->icanon) as an incorrect conversion of the effective terminal mode, matching CWE-704's incorrect type/state conversion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard at line 4 compares only ICANON, so an EXTPROC transition with unchanged ICANON skips reinitialization of ldata->icanon and canonical bookkeeping. Trigger: a local user changes EXTPROC on a pty and then queries TIOCINQ. Consequence: n_tty state is inconsistent with termios, leading to hang/block of pty usage.

commit_msg: apply patch from Robert Scott to fix - shifting some bounds checking
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                diffPtr + x > diffBlock + diffBlockLength ||', '                extraPtr + y > extraBlock + extraBlockLength) {'], 'added_lines': ['                diffPtr + x > diffBlock + diffBlockLength) {', '        if (newpos + y > newDataLength ||', '                extraPtr + y > extraBlock + extraBlockLength) {', '            PyMem_Free(newData);', '            PyErr_SetString(PyExc_ValueError, "corrupt patch (overflow)");', '            return NULL;', '        }']}
description: A buffer overflow in the patching routine of bsdiff4 before 1.2.0 allows an attacker to write to heap memory (beyond allocated bounds) via a crafted patch file.

code_evidence: The bounds check at lines 37-43 validates newpos+x against newDataLength and diffPtr+x against diffBlock+diffBlockLength, but it no longer validates the extra-block write (extraPtr+y) before the memcpy at line 51.

Line 51 copies y bytes from extraPtr into newData+newpos without any preceding check that newpos+y <= newDataLength or extraPtr+y <= extraBlock+extraBlockLength; y and the control tuples come from the attacker-supplied control list parsed at line 8.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked memcpy writes beyond the allocated newData buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read: the destination newData+newpos is written with attacker-controlled length y, so the write-past-end weakness fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard for the extra-data copy was removed from the combined check, so the memcpy at line 51 runs with unvalidated y. Trigger: a crafted control tuple whose y makes newpos+y exceed newDataLength (or extraPtr+y exceed the extra block). Consequence: heap memory past the newData allocation is written, corrupting the heap.

commit_msg:
USB: serial: console: fix use-after-free after failed setup

Make sure to reset the USB-console port pointer when console setup fails
in order to avoid having the struct usb_serial be prematurely freed by
the console code when the device is later disconnected.

Fixes: 73e487fdb75f ("[PATCH] USB console: fix disconnection issues")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>	# 2.6.18
Acked-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tinfo->port = NULL;']}
description: The usb_serial_console_disconnect function in drivers/usb/serial/console.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted USB device, related to disconnection and failed setup.

code_evidence: The setup path stores the acquired port in the global console info at line 57 (info->port = port) and increments the port count, then enters the open/setup sequence. On the kzalloc failure path (lines 61-64) it jumps to reset_open_count.

The error path at lines 100-106 resets port->port.count, releases the interface autopm reference and drops the serial reference via usb_serial_put(serial), but the function shown does not clear info->port. The patch adds info->port = NULL in this block, confirming the stale global pointer is the defect.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function retains a reference to port memory after the owning serial object is put and potentially freed, and that stale pointer is later reused by console code, matching CWE-416 Use After Free. This is not merely a missing NULL check; the pointer refers to freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a failed console setup leaves the global info->port pointing at a port whose serial reference is released by usb_serial_put. Trigger: setup fails (e.g., kzalloc returns NULL) and the device is later disconnected; the console code dereferences the stale info->port after the struct usb_serial may have been freed. Supported consequence: use-after-free leading to crash/DoS or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Keep minimum size when shrinking a stack

When shrinking a stack (during GC), do not make it smaller than the
initial stack size.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int goodsize = inuse + (inuse / 8) + 2*EXTRA_STACK;', '  if (inuse <= (LUAI_MAXSTACK - EXTRA_STACK) &&', '      goodsize < L->stacksize)'], 'added_lines': ['  int goodsize = inuse + BASIC_STACK_SIZE;', '  if (inuse <= (LUAI_MAXSTACK - EXTRA_STACK) && goodsize < L->stacksize)']}
description: Lua through 5.4.0 mishandles the interaction between stack resizes and garbage collection, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow, heap-based buffer over-read, or use-after-free.

code_evidence: Line 3 computes the shrink target goodsize as inuse + (inuse/8) + 2*EXTRA_STACK, without enforcing a minimum size; the only bound applied is the upper clamp to LUAI_MAXSTACK at lines 4-5. Lines 6-7 then authorize luaD_reallocstack(L, goodsize, 0) whenever inuse is within the limit and goodsize < L->stacksize, so the stack can be reallocated down to a size that lacks the required EXTRA_STACK headroom above the live usage.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the undersized reallocation from lines 3-8 leaves insufficient stack capacity, and later writes to that stack exceed its allocated bounds. This is an out-of-bounds write rather than a mere read (CWE-125) because the supported consequence is memory modification past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shrink computation lacks a lower bound (BASIC_STACK_SIZE), so goodsize can fall below the space needed for the stack's extra slots. Trigger: garbage collection calls luaD_shrinkstack while the stack is near full, and the condition at lines 6-7 permits reallocation to that undersized value. Consequence: subsequent stack pushes write past the end of the reallocated stack, an out-of-bounds write; the missing minimum is the cause, not the overflow itself.

code_evidence: session_new initializes session state from the caller-supplied nghttp2_option. The option block gates each field on opt_set_mask and copies values such as max_outbound_ack (89-91), max_settings (92-95), and max_send_header_block_length (78-81) directly into the session without validating bounds or enforcing a maximum. There is no throttle or rate limit applied to these per-session resource parameters.

Here the session's resource-tracking fields are set without a ceiling, matching the 'lack of throttling for the number of allocated resources' scenario. It is not CWE-770 (allocation without limits) alone because the weakness is the absence of a control on maintained per-session resource counters.

commit_msg:
Add limits to the size of received {A,I}XFR, in megabytes

This prevents memory exhaustion in case the master is sending a
very large amount of data in an update.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['shared_ptr<SOARecordContent> loadRPZFromServer(const ComboAddress& master, const DNSName& zone, DNSFilterEngine& target, const std::string& polName, boost::optional<DNSFilterEngine::Policy> defpol, int place,  const TSIGTriplet& tt)', '  AXFRRetriever axfr(master, zone, tt, &local);'], 'added_lines': ['shared_ptr<SOARecordContent> loadRPZFromServer(const ComboAddress& master, const DNSName& zone, DNSFilterEngine& target, const std::string& polName, boost::optional<DNSFilterEngine::Policy> defpol, int place,  const TSIGTriplet& tt, size_t maxReceivedBytes)', '  AXFRRetriever axfr(master, zone, tt, &local, maxReceivedBytes);']}
description: PowerDNS (aka pdns) Authoritative Server before 4.0.1 allows remote primary DNS servers to cause a denial of service (memory exhaustion and secondary DNS server crash) via a large (1) AXFR or (2) IXFR response.

code_evidence: loadRPZFromServer takes no maximum-received-bytes parameter, so the transfer size is unbounded at this call boundary.
AXFRRetriever axfr is constructed with only master, zone, TSIG and local address; no byte limit is supplied, so the retriever cannot cap incoming transfer data.
The while loop repeatedly calls axfr.getChunk and iterates every received record, accumulating processing per chunk without any check on total bytes received.

The fix adds maxReceivedBytes and passes it to AXFRRetriever, confirming the intended constraint was absent rather than an out-of-bounds or parsing weakness.

evidence_lines.code: shared_ptr<SOARecordContent> loadRPZFromServer(const ComboAddress& master, const DNSName& zone, DNSFilterEngine& target, const std::string& polName, boost::optional<DNSFilterEngine::Policy> defpol, int place,  const TSIGTriplet& tt)
ComboAddress local= master.sin4.sin_family == AF_INET ? ComboAddress("0.0.0.0") : ComboAddress("::");   AXFRRetriever axfr(master, zone, tt, &local);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function streams an AXFR/IXFR from a remote master and processes chunks in a loop with no limit on the amount of data accepted. A malicious or compromised primary can send an arbitrarily large response, causing the retriever and per-record processing to consume memory until the secondary crashes. The root cause is the missing size constraint at the retriever construction; the consequence is memory-exhaustion denial of service.

commit_msg:
In saa7134_initdev, it will call saa7134_hwinit1. There are three
function invoking here: saa7134_video_init1, saa7134_ts_init1
and saa7134_vbi_init1.

All of them will init a timer with same function. Take
saa7134_video_init1 as an example. It'll bound &dev->video_q.timeout
with saa7134_buffer_timeout.

In buffer_activate, the timer funtcion is started.

If we remove the module or device which will call saa7134_finidev
to make cleanup, there may be a unfinished work. The
possible sequence is as follows, which will cause a
typical UAF bug.

Fix it by canceling the timer works accordingly before cleanup in
saa7134_finidev.

CPU0                  CPU1

                    |saa7134_buffer_timeout
saa7134_finidev     |
  kfree(dev);       |
                    |
                    | saa7134_buffer_next
                    | //use dev

Fixes: 1e7126b4a86a ("media: saa7134: Convert timers to use timer_setup()")
Signed-off-by: Zheng Wang <zyytlz.wz@163.com>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tdel_timer_sync(&dev->vbi_q.timeout);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.3.2. A use-after-free was found in saa7134_finidev in drivers/media/pci/saa7134/saa7134-core.c.

code_evidence: saa7134_vbi_fini performs no synchronization on dev->vbi_q.timeout; it simply returns 0. The patched version adds del_timer_sync(&dev->vbi_q.timeout) before the cleanup returns, showing that the pre-fix function left the vbi queue timer running while teardown proceeded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the fini sequence lacks exclusive synchronization against a concurrent timer callback sharing dev->vbi_q.timeout, creating a timing window where the shared resource is accessed after release. The UAF is the downstream impact of this improper synchronization, so the target remains CWE-362 rather than a memory-safety label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the vbi fini path does not stop the timer bound to dev->vbi_q.timeout before the device is freed. Trigger: saa7134_finidev frees dev while a concurrently firing saa7134_buffer_timeout callback still runs against the same dev. The unsynchronized teardown permits the callback to use freed memory, producing a use-after-free (consequence), not merely a benign race.

commit_msg:
cryp: prevent direct calls to update and final functions

With inconsistent or malformed data it has been possible to call
"update" and "final" crypto functions directly. Using a fuzzer tool [1]
we have seen that this results in asserts, i.e., a crash that
potentially could leak sensitive information.

By setting the state (initialized) in the crypto context (i.e., the
tee_cryp_state) at the end of all syscall_*_init functions and then add
a check of the state at the beginning of all update and final functions,
  we prevent direct entrance to the "update" and "final" functions.

[1] https://github.com/MartijnB/optee_fuzzer

Fixes: OP-TEE-2019-0021

Signed-off-by: Joakim Bech <joakim.bech@linaro.org>
Reported-by: Martijn Bogaard <bogaard@riscure.com>

commit_msg:
9pfs: handle walk of ".." in the root directory

The 9P spec at http://man.cat-v.org/plan_9/5/intro says:

All directories must support walks to the directory .. (dot-dot) meaning
parent directory, although by convention directories contain no explicit
entry for .. or . (dot).  The parent of the root directory of a server's
tree is itself.

This means that a client cannot walk further than the root directory
exported by the server. In other words, if the client wants to walk
"/.." or "/foo/../..", the server should answer like the request was
to walk "/".

This patch just does that:
- we cache the QID of the root directory at attach time
- during the walk we compare the QID of each path component with the root
  QID to detect if we're in a "/.." situation
- if so, we skip the current component and go to the next one

Signed-off-by: Greg Kurz <groug@kaod.org>
Reviewed-by: Eric Blake <eblake@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Maydell <peter.maydell@linaro.org>

description: Directory traversal vulnerability in hw/9pfs/9p.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) allows local guest OS administrators to access host files outside the export path via a .. (dot dot) in an unspecified string.

code_evidence: The walk loop passes the client-supplied wnames[name_idx].data directly to v9fs_co_name_to_path without checking for the ".." component or confining the result to the exported root. For each component it then lstat's the resulting path and copies it into dpath, so a sequence such as ".." or "foo/../.." resolves to a parent of the export and the walk continues from there.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-22 fits because externally supplied path elements ("..") are used to build a pathname intended to stay under the exported root, but the parent-directory element is not neutralized, so resolution escapes the restricted directory. This is relative path traversal, not an absolute-path or symlink issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the path component from the 9P walk request is joined to the current directory path with no neutralization of "..". Trigger: a local guest administrator sends a walk request containing ".." components. Consequence: the resolved path and returned QIDs point outside the server's exported tree, letting the guest access host files outside the export.

commit_msg:
_bfd_clear_contents bounds checking

This PR shows a fuzzed binary triggering a segfault via a bad
relocation in .debug_line.  It turns out that unlike normal
relocations applied to a section, the linker applies those with
symbols from discarded sections via _bfd_clear_contents without
checking that the relocation is within the section bounds.  The same
thing now happens when reading debug sections since commit
a4cd947aca23, the PR23425 fix.

	PR 23770
	PR 23425
	* reloc.c (_bfd_clear_contents): Replace "location" param with
	"buf" and "off".  Bounds check "off".  Return status.
	* cofflink.c (_bfd_coff_generic_relocate_section): Update
	_bfd_clear_contents call.
	* elf-bfd.h (RELOC_AGAINST_DISCARDED_SECTION): Likewise.
	* elf32-arc.c (elf_arc_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-i386.c (elf_i386_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-metag.c (metag_final_link_relocate): Likewise.
	* elf32-nds32.c (nds32_elf_get_relocated_section_contents): Likewise.
	* elf32-ppc.c (ppc_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-visium.c (visium_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf64-ppc.c (ppc64_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf64-x86-64.c *(elf_x86_64_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* libbfd-in.h (_bfd_clear_contents): Update prototype.
	* libbfd.h: Regenerate.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t       contents + (rel->r_vaddr - input_section->vma));'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t       contents, rel->r_vaddr - input_section->vma);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.31. An invalid memory address dereference was discovered in read_reloc in reloc.c. The vulnerability causes a segmentation fault and application crash, which leads to denial of service, as demonstrated by objdump, because of missing _bfd_clear_contents bounds checking.

code_evidence: When a relocation's symbol resolves to a discarded section, the code calls _bfd_clear_contents with the pointer contents + (rel->r_vaddr - input_section->vma). The offset rel->r_vaddr - input_section->vma comes straight from the input file's relocation entry and is never validated against the size of contents or input_section before being added to the base pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes an unchecked offset from file-controlled relocation data and performs a write through the resulting pointer, an out-of-bounds memory buffer operation. That is the buffer-bounds weakness described by CWE-119; the concrete form is an off-by-anything write, not a type confusion or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the relocation virtual address r_vaddr is attacker-controlled and the derived offset into the section contents is not bounds-checked before _bfd_clear_contents writes to that location. Trigger: a crafted COFF object with a relocation against a discarded section whose r_vaddr lies outside the section. Consequence: an out-of-bounds memory write, causing a segfault or memory corruption (DoS).

description: The grub_ext2_read_block function in fs/ext2.c in GNU GRUB before 2013-11-12, as used in shlr/grub/fs/ext2.c in radare2 1.5.0, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive stack use and application crash) via a crafted binary file, related to use of a variable-size stack array.

code_evidence: The extent path declares a stack buffer whose size is derived from EXT2_BLOCK_SIZE(data) on the non-MSVC build, so the buffer length depends on on-disk filesystem parameters rather than a fixed compile-time constant.

commit_msg:
x86/spec-ctrl: Mitigate the Zen1 DIV leakage

In the Zen1 microarchitecure, there is one divider in the pipeline which
services uops from both threads.  In the case of #DE, the latched result from
the previous DIV to execute will be forwarded speculatively.

This is an interesting covert channel that allows two threads to communicate
without any system calls.  In also allows userspace to obtain the result of
the most recent DIV instruction executed (even speculatively) in the core,
which can be from a higher privilege context.

Scrub the result from the divider by executing a non-faulting divide.  This
needs performing on the exit-to-guest paths, and ist_exit-to-Xen.

Alternatives in IST context is believed safe now that it's done in NMI
context.

This is XSA-439 / CVE-2023-20588.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

commit_msg:
Correctly calculate the length of SM2 plaintext given the ciphertext

Previously the length of the SM2 plaintext could be incorrectly calculated.
The plaintext length was calculated by taking the ciphertext length and
taking off an "overhead" value.

The overhead value was assumed to have a "fixed" element of 10 bytes.
This is incorrect since in some circumstances it can be more than 10 bytes.
Additionally the overhead included the length of two integers C1x and C1y,
which were assumed to be the same length as the field size (32 bytes for
the SM2 curve). However in some cases these integers can have an additional
padding byte when the msb is set, to disambiguate them from negative
integers. Additionally the integers can also be less than 32 bytes in
length in some cases.

If the calculated overhead is incorrect and larger than the actual value
this can result in the calculated plaintext length being too small.
Applications are likely to allocate buffer sizes based on this and therefore
a buffer overrun can occur.

CVE-2021-3711

Issue reported by John Ouyang.

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Nicola Tuveri <nic.tuv@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (!sm2_plaintext_size(ec, md, inlen, outlen))'], 'added_lines': ['        if (!sm2_plaintext_size(in, inlen, outlen))']}
description: In order to decrypt SM2 encrypted data an application is expected to call the API function EVP_PKEY_decrypt(). Typically an application will call this function twice. The first time, on entry, the "out" parameter can be NULL and, on exit, the "outlen" parameter is populated with the buffer size required to hold the decrypted plaintext. The application can then allocate a sufficiently sized buffer and call EVP_PKEY_decrypt() again, but this time passing a non-NULL value for the "out" parameter. A bug in the implementation of the SM2 decryption code means that the calculation of the buffer size required to hold the plaintext returned by the first call to EVP_PKEY_decrypt() can be smaller than the actual size required by the second call. This can lead to a buffer overflow when EVP_PKEY_decrypt() is called by the application a second time with a buffer that is too small. A malicious attacker who is able present SM2 content for decryption to an application could cause attacker chosen data to overflow the buffer by up to a maximum of 62 bytes altering the contents of other data held after the buffer, possibly changing application behaviour or causing the application to crash. The location of the buffer is application dependent but is typically heap allocated. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1l (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1k).

code_evidence: When out is NULL, the function calls sm2_plaintext_size(ec, md, inlen, outlen) to compute the required plaintext buffer size, ignoring the ciphertext content in 'in' that determines the actual C1x/C1y encoding lengths. The computed *outlen is returned to the caller, who allocates a buffer of that size and calls again with non-NULL out; line 14 then passes that undersized buffer to sm2_decrypt.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The size-computation error leads directly to copying decrypted data into a buffer whose size was not verified against the actual input, matching CWE-120's unchecked-size buffer copy. CWE-131 is the upstream calculation flaw, but here the supported consequence is the classic overflow write, so the target CWE fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size query derives plaintext length from a fixed overhead assumption rather than parsing the actual ciphertext, so *outlen can be smaller than the real plaintext. Trigger: an attacker supplies SM2 ciphertext with longer/padded C1 integers; the two-call API then hands sm2_decrypt a too-small application buffer, and the plaintext copy overflows it (up to 62 bytes).

commit_msg:
Fix l2cap_channels OOB in get_channel_for_cid

While the bounds check is performed on `l2cap_channel_count`, only the lower byte is checked due to the uint8_t data type. Afterwards, the expression for `i` is re-calculated without the explicit data type, which means without truncation into 8 bits. Instead, the full 16-bit value is used as the channel index. This pointer will point out-of-bounds of the channel array.

This leads to a large 16 out-of-bounds channel id to be used as an index into the array for large CID inputs.

Sample value: 0xff41 -> 0xff41 - 0x41 = 0xff00 == 0x00 (as uint8_t)

This results in out-of-bounds memory to be interpreted as a channel object, and this memory to potentially be corrupted in the following call to `input_l2cap_frame_flow_channel`, which fills the out-of-bounds memory (the supposed channel object) with user-supplied data.

The fix here is to re-use the `i` variable as an index, which was used to perform the bounds check, and is truncated to 8 bits.

As a side note, due to the unsignedness of the data type `uint8_t i`, the check `i >= 0` is always true. Instead, a signed data type such as `int16_t` could be used to make the check take effect.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  uint8_t i = own_cid - L2CAP_FLOW_CHANNEL;', '    return &l2cap_channels[own_cid - L2CAP_FLOW_CHANNEL];'], 'added_lines': ['  int16_t i = own_cid - L2CAP_FLOW_CHANNEL;', '    return &l2cap_channels[i];']}
description: Contiki-NG is an open-source, cross-platform operating system for Next-Generation IoT devices. Versions prior to 4.9 are vulnerable to an Out-of-bounds read. While processing the L2CAP protocol, the Bluetooth Low Energy stack of Contiki-NG needs to map an incoming channel ID to its metadata structure. While looking up the corresponding channel structure in get_channel_for_cid (in os/net/mac/ble/ble-l2cap.c), a bounds check is performed on the incoming channel ID, which is meant to ensure that the channel ID does not exceed the maximum number of supported channels.However, an integer truncation issue leads to only the lowest byte of the channel ID to be checked, which leads to an incomplete out-of-bounds check. A crafted channel ID leads to out-of-bounds memory to be read and written with attacker-controlled data. The vulnerability has been patched in the "develop" branch of Contiki-NG, and will be included in release 4.9. As a workaround, Users can apply the patch in Contiki-NG pull request 2081 on GitHub.

code_evidence: Line 4 stores own_cid - L2CAP_FLOW_CHANNEL into a uint8_t, truncating the 16-bit difference to the low byte. Line 5 checks that truncated i against l2cap_channel_count, but line 6 re-computes the full 16-bit own_cid - L2CAP_FLOW_CHANNEL as the array index, so the bound actually validated differs from the index used.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function returns &l2cap_channels[own_cid - L2CAP_FLOW_CHANNEL] without validating the full index, causing an out-of-bounds read of the channel array, which matches CWE-125. The truncation is the cause; the out-of-bounds read is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check applies to the truncated uint8_t i while the array subscript uses the untruncated 16-bit value. Trigger: a crafted own_cid such as 0xff41 whose low byte passes the check but whose full difference exceeds the array size. Consequence: l2cap_channels is indexed out of bounds, returning a pointer to memory beyond the array that is then read and later written as a channel object.

commit_msg:
Kafka: Be more strict when dissecting varints.

The Kafka dissector uses the return value of tvb_get_varint to advance
the packet offset in many places. If tvb_get_varint fails it returns 0,
which means our offset isn't guaranteed to advance. Stop dissection
whenever that happens. Fixes #17811.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        return offset;'], 'added_lines': ['        return tvb_captured_length(tvb);']}
description: Large loop in the Kafka dissector in Wireshark 3.6.0 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: tvb_get_varint returns len; len is used as the item length and as the offset advance in the success path.
When len == 0 the function reports a bad varint but returns offset unchanged, so the caller's cursor does not advance.
The success path returns offset + len, showing the caller relies on a positive return to make progress.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's non-advancing return lets a caller loop without progress, matching CWE-834 (Excessive Iteration) as a resource-consumption cause. It is not merely an input-validation issue: the missing termination signal is what enables the unbounded iteration.

evidence_lines.code:
len = tvb_get_varint(tvb, offset, FT_VARINT_MAX_LEN, &value, ENC_VARINT_PROTOBUF);
pi = proto_tree_add_uint64(tree, hf_item, tvb, offset, len, value);
return offset + len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on a malformed/zero-length varint the function returns the unchanged offset instead of signaling termination. Trigger: a crafted Kafka packet yields len == 0. Because callers use the return value to advance the offset, dissection can re-enter the same position repeatedly, producing an unbounded loop and CPU exhaustion (DoS).

patch 9.0.2111: [security]: overflow in get_number

Problem:  [security]: overflow in get_number
Solution: Return 0 when the count gets too large

[security]: overflow in get_number

When using the z= command, we may overflow the count with values larger
than MAX_INT. So verify that we do not overflow and in case when an
overflow is detected, simply return 0

Signed-off-by: Christian Brabandt <cb@256bit.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t    if (n > INT_MAX / 10)', '\t\treturn 0;']}
description:
Vim is an open source command line text editor. When using the z= command, the user may overflow the count with values larger
than MAX_INT. Impact is low, user interaction is required and a crash may not even happen in all situations. This vulnerability has been addressed in commit `73b2d379` which has been included in release version 9.0.2111. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: get_number accumulates user-typed digits in int n. safe_vgetc() reads one character per loop iteration; when it is a digit, line 21 computes n = n * 10 + c - '0' and line 22 echoes it. There is no upper bound on n before or after this multiplication, so an unbounded count of typed digits is accepted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because line 21 performs an arithmetic calculation whose result can exceed the int representation and wrap, with no constraint on the input length. This is specifically integer overflow/wraparound, not a buffer overrun or truncation: the unsafe operation is the multiplication and addition on the accumulated count.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the digit-accumulation expression n * 10 + (c - '0') on line 21 is performed in signed int without checking whether n exceeds INT_MAX/10, so repeated digit input wraps n to a small or negative value. Trigger: a user entering a very long numeric count (e.g. for the z= command). Supported consequence: the returned count is corrupted, altering execution logic; the advisory notes a crash may occur, consistent with CWE-190 availability impact.

commit_msg:
Fix type confusion in nc_match_single()

This function assumes that if the "gen" is an OtherName, then the "base"
is a rfc822Name constraint. This assumption is not true in all cases.
If the end-entity certificate contains an OtherName SAN of any type besides
SmtpUtf8Mailbox and the CA certificate contains a name constraint of
OtherName (of any type), then "nc_email_eai" will be invoked, with the
OTHERNAME "base" being incorrectly interpreted as a ASN1_IA5STRING.

Reported by Corey Bonnell from Digicert.

CVE-2022-4203

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Hugo Landau <hlandau@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>

GEN_EMAIL : gen->type;', '        if (effective_type != sub->base->type)', '        r = nc_match_single(gen, sub->base);', '        if (effective_type != sub->base->type)', '        r = nc_match_single(gen, sub->base);'], 'added_lines': ['    int effective_type = gen->type;', '', '    if (effective_type == GEN_OTHERNAME &&', '        (OBJ_obj2nid(gen->d.otherName->type_id) == NID_id_on_SmtpUTF8Mailbox)) {', '        effective_type = GEN_EMAIL;', '    }', '        if (effective_type != sub->base->type', '            || (effective_type == GEN_OTHERNAME &&', '                OBJ_cmp(gen->d.otherName->type_id,', '                        sub->base->d.otherName->type_id) != 0))', '        r = nc_match_single(effective_type, gen, sub->base);', '        if (effective_type != sub->base->type', '            || (effective_type == GEN_OTHERNAME &&', '                OBJ_cmp(gen->d.otherName->type_id,', '                        sub->base->d.otherName->type_id) != 0))', '        r = nc_match_single(effective_type, gen, sub->base);']}
description:
A read buffer overrun can be triggered in X.509 certificate verification,
specifically in name constraint checking. Note that this occurs
after certificate chain signature verification and requires either a
CA to have signed the malicious certificate or for the application to
continue certificate verification despite failure to construct a path
to a trusted issuer.

The read buffer overrun might result in a crash which could lead to
a denial of service attack. In theory it could also result in the disclosure
of private memory contents (such as private keys, or sensitive plaintext)
although we are not aware of any working exploit leading to memory
contents disclosure as of the time of release of this advisory.

In a TLS client, this can be triggered by connecting to a malicious
server. In a TLS server, this can be triggered if the server requests
client authentication and a malicious client connects.

code_evidence: effective_type is set to GEN_EMAIL when gen is an OtherName with SmtpUTF8Mailbox type_id, otherwise gen->type.
The permitted-subtree filter only compares effective_type to sub->base->type; it never checks that the OtherName type_id of gen matches the constraint's OtherName type_id.
nc_match_single(gen, sub->base) is invoked for any OtherName whose effective_type equals the constraint base type, regardless of the actual otherName type.
The excluded-subtree loop repeats the same type-only comparison.
The second nc_match_single call likewise passes gen and sub->base without validating matching otherName type identifiers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flawed type check permits a later routine to read an OtherName value as an ASN1_IA5STRING, accessing memory outside the intended buffer. That is a read past the intended buffer, matching CWE-125. The type confusion is the mechanism; the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
if (effective_type != sub->base->type)
continue;
r = nc_match_single(gen, sub->base);

if (effective_type != sub->base->type)
continue;
r = nc_match_single(gen, sub->base);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: matching an OtherName SAN against an OtherName name constraint uses only the GENERAL_NAME type tag, not the specific otherName type_id. Trigger: an end-entity certificate with an OtherName SAN of a type other than SmtpUtf8Mailbox plus a CA OtherName constraint causes nc_match_single to treat the constraint as an email/IA5STRING. The mismatched interpretation reads beyond the intended buffer, yielding out-of-bounds read (crash/DoS or memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
HID: cp2112: fix sleep-while-atomic

A recent commit fixing DMA-buffers on stack added a shared transfer
buffer protected by a spinlock. This is broken as the USB HID request
callbacks can sleep. Fix this up by replacing the spinlock with a mutex.

Fixes: 1ffb3c40ffb5 ("HID: cp2112: make transfer buffers DMA capable")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>	# 4.9
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Benjamin Tissoires <benjamin.tissoires@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned long flags;', '\tspin_lock_irqsave(&dev->lock, flags);', '\tspin_unlock_irqrestore(&dev->lock, flags);', '\tspin_unlock_irqrestore(&dev->lock, flags);'], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_lock(&dev->lock);', '\tmutex_unlock(&dev->lock);', '\tmutex_unlock(&dev->lock);']}
description: drivers/hid/hid-cp2112.c in the Linux kernel 4.9.x before 4.9.9 uses a spinlock without considering that sleeping is possible in a USB HID request callback, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock) via unspecified vectors.

code_evidence: Line 9 acquires dev->lock with spin_lock_irqsave, disabling IRQs and holding the lock across the following calls.
Lines 10-12 invoke hid_hw_raw_request, a USB HID request callback that can sleep while the spinlock is held.
Line 26 releases the lock only after a second blocking hid_hw_raw_request at lines 19-21; line 30 releases it on the fail path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers improper resource shutdown/release; here the spinlock resource is acquired but cannot be released because the sleeping call blocks the holder, preventing release and causing DoS. This is a lock/resource-lifetime defect rather than a generic input-validation issue.

evidence_lines.code:
spin_unlock_irqrestore(&dev->lock, flags);
cp2112_gpio_set(chip, offset, value);
spin_unlock_irqrestore(&dev->lock, flags);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function holds a spinlock across hid_hw_raw_request, which may sleep; sleeping while holding a spinlock is illegal and can deadlock. A local user triggering the GPIO direction-output path causes the lock to remain held, leading to denial of service via deadlock.

commit_msg:
ALSA: msnd: Optimize / harden DSP and MIDI loops

The ISA msnd drivers have loops fetching the ring-buffer head, tail
and size values inside the loops.  Such codes are inefficient and
fragile.

This patch optimizes it, and also adds the sanity check to avoid the
endless loops.

Bugzilla: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=196131
Bugzilla: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=196133
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\twhile (readw(chip->DSPQ + JQS_wTail) != readw(chip->DSPQ + JQS_wHead)) {', '\t\tu16 wTmp;', '', '\t\tsnd_msnd_eval_dsp_msg(chip,', '\t\t\treadw(pwDSPQData + 2 * readw(chip->DSPQ + JQS_wHead)));', '', '\t\twTmp = readw(chip->DSPQ + JQS_wHead) + 1;', '\t\tif (wTmp > readw(chip->DSPQ + JQS_wSize))', '\t\t\twritew(0, chip->DSPQ + JQS_wHead);', '\t\telse', '\t\t\twritew(wTmp, chip->DSPQ + JQS_wHead);'], 'added_lines': ['\tu16 head, tail, size;', '\thead = readw(chip->DSPQ + JQS_wHead);', '\ttail = readw(chip->DSPQ + JQS_wTail);', '\tsize = readw(chip->DSPQ + JQS_wSize);', '\tif (head > size || tail > size)', '\t\tgoto out;', '\twhile (head != tail) {', '\t\tsnd_msnd_eval_dsp_msg(chip, readw(pwDSPQData + 2 * head));', '\t\tif (++head > size)', '\t\t\thead = 0;', '\t\twritew(head, chip->DSPQ + JQS_wHead);', ' out:']}
description: The snd_msnd_interrupt function in sound/isa/msnd/msnd_pinnacle.c in the Linux kernel through 4.11.7 allows local users to cause a denial of service (over-boundary access) or possibly have unspecified other impact by changing the value of a message queue head pointer between two kernel reads of that value, aka a "double fetch" vulnerability.

code_evidence: The loop condition re-reads JQS_wTail and JQS_wHead on every iteration, and line 8 re-reads JQS_wHead to index pwDSPQData. Because the head value is fetched again at use time, a changed head (or an unvalidated head/tail/size) is used directly as the ring-buffer index without any bound check against JQS_wSize.
Line 9 also re-reads JQS_wHead to compute wTmp, and lines 10-13 compare against a re-read JQS_wSize, so the wrap decision is based on values that may differ from the one used for the array access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unchecked, double-fetched head index drives a read beyond the intended DSPQ buffer. It is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write, since the out-of-range index is used in the readw data fetch, not in the writew head update.

evidence_lines.code:
writew(0, chip->DSPQ + JQS_wHead);
writew(wTmp, chip->DSPQ + JQS_wHead);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DSP queue head is fetched multiple times per iteration and used as an index (readw(pwDSPQData + 2 * head)) without validating it against the queue size. Trigger: the head pointer changes between kernel reads or is set out of range, causing the computed address to fall outside the DSPQ data buffer. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read of mapped memory (over-boundary access), potentially leading to a crash or information exposure.

commit_msg:
In commit 6a53b7593233 ("xfrm: check id proto in validate_tmpl()")
I introduced a check for xfrm protocol, but according to Herbert
IPSEC_PROTO_ANY should only be used as a wildcard for lookup, so
it should be removed from validate_tmpl().

And, IPSEC_PROTO_ANY is expected to only match 3 IPSec-specific
protocols, this is why xfrm_state_flush() could still miss
IPPROTO_ROUTING, which leads that those entries are left in
net->xfrm.state_all before exit net. Fix this by replacing
IPSEC_PROTO_ANY with zero.

This patch also extracts the check from validate_tmpl() to
xfrm_id_proto_valid() and uses it in parse_ipsecrequest().
With this, no other protocols should be added into xfrm.

Fixes: 6a53b7593233 ("xfrm: check id proto in validate_tmpl()")
Reported-by: syzbot+0bf0519d6e0de15914fe@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Cc: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
Cc: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tswitch (ut[i].id.proto) {', '\t\tcase IPPROTO_AH:', '\t\tcase IPPROTO_ESP:', '\t\tcase IPPROTO_COMP:', '#if IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_IPV6)', '\t\tcase IPPROTO_ROUTING:', '\t\tcase IPPROTO_DSTOPTS:', '#endif', '\t\tcase IPSEC_PROTO_ANY:', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tdefault:', '\t\t}', ''], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!xfrm_id_proto_valid(ut[i].id.proto))']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.19. The XFRM subsystem has a use-after-free, related to an xfrm_state_fini panic, aka CID-dbb2483b2a46.

code_evidence: The protocol validation switch accepts IPSEC_PROTO_ANY as a valid template protocol, alongside IPPROTO_AH/ESP/COMP and IPv6 routing/dstopts, and only rejects other values via default.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The permissive protocol check permits state objects that escape lifecycle cleanup, leaving references to freed state/net memory; this is CWE-416, not merely improper input validation, because the supported consequence is a use-after-free at teardown.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: validate_tmpl() admits IPSEC_PROTO_ANY as a template id.proto, so states with this wildcard are created and later inserted into net->xfrm.state_all. Because xfrm_state_flush()/fini only matches the three IPSec-specific protocols, states using IPPROTO_ROUTING (or other accepted values) are not flushed during net exit, leaving stale state entries referenced after their net is torn down, producing the reported use-after-free and xfrm_state_fini panic.
