description: Directory traversal vulnerability in abrt-dbus in Automatic Bug Reporting Tool (ABRT) allows local users to read, write to, or change ownership of arbitrary files via unspecified vectors to the (1) NewProblem, (2) GetInfo, (3) SetElement, or (4) DeleteElement method.

commit_msg: Fixes #507
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if (z > 4 || (x + (z - 1) > inlen)) {'], 'added_lines': ['      if (z == 1 || z > 4 || (x + (z - 1) > inlen)) {']}
description: In LibTomCrypt through 1.18.2, the der_decode_utf8_string function (in der_decode_utf8_string.c) does not properly detect certain invalid UTF-8 sequences. This allows context-dependent attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and crash) or read information from other memory locations via carefully crafted DER-encoded data.

code_evidence: Line 27 counts leading 1-bits in the first byte, capped at z<=4. Line 28's guard only rejects z>4 or x+(z-1)>inlen; a single-byte value with high bit set yields z==1, passing the check. Line 31 shifts tmp by z, then line 32 only decrements z when z>1, so z stays 1. The loop at lines 33-37 then dereferences in[x] and in[x++] once more for what should be a single-byte sequence.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an unchecked index advancing beyond the validated input length, so the loop dereferences in[x] outside the intended buffer. That is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), distinct from an out-of-bounds write since only reads occur.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length guard does not reject a continuation-byte count of one (z==1), which is invalid UTF-8. Trigger: a DER-encoded UTF-8 string whose character begins with a byte like 0x80-0xBF (high bit set, no valid multi-byte lead). Because z is not decremented, the loop reads in[x] past the consumed byte, and at buffer end reads beyond inlen, causing an out-of-bounds read/crash or disclosure of adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
binding: Moves the check for the first access to the initial document into BindingSecurity.

Checks the access to the initial document and reports it not only at
securityCheck() in V8Window.cpp but also at every call to
BindingSecurity::shouldAllowAccessTo() because V8 only calls back
securityCheck() on property lookups, and not for function invocation.

BindingSecurity::shouldAllowAccessTo() is called with every possible
cross-origin window, which means every possible new window.  Thus,
shouldAllowAccessTo() should be the right place to check the access
to the initial document.

BUG=630662
TBR=benwells@chromium.org

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2209303002
Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#412195}

The function is the security gate for cross-origin window access and the patch modifies this access check, so the missing initial-document validation fits directly. It is not a memory-safety issue; the weakness is in the authorization feature itself.

commit_msg:
Fix heap overflow in the ultra.c decoder

The Ultra type tile decoder does not use the _safe variant of the LZO
decompress function, which allows a maliciuous server to overwrite parts of the
heap by sending a larger-than-specified LZO data stream.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  inflateResult = lzo1x_decompress(', '  ', '      rfbClientLog("Ultra decompressed too little (%d < %d)", (rw * rh * (BPP / 8)), uncompressedBytes);'], 'added_lines': ['  inflateResult = lzo1x_decompress_safe(', '  /* Note that uncompressedBytes will be 0 on output overrun */', '      rfbClientLog("Ultra decompressed unexpected amount of data (%d != %d)\\n", (rw * rh * (BPP / 8)), uncompressedBytes);']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in rfbproto.c in LibVNCClient in LibVNCServer before 0.9.11 allows remote servers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted FramebufferUpdate message containing a subrectangle outside of the client drawing area.

code_evidence: Line 37 sets uncompressedBytes to the allocated raw_buffer_size, then line 38-41 calls the unsafe lzo1x_decompress with client->raw_buffer as output and &uncompressedBytes as the output length.
raw_buffer is allocated at line 24 sized by the expected rectangle bytes, and CopyRectangle at line 46 reads it; the decompressor is not bounded by that allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe decompressor writes past the bounds of the raw_buffer allocation, directly matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory buffer write. The fix switches to lzo1x_decompress_safe, confirming the missing boundary constraint rather than an unrelated logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unsafe lzo1x_decompress variant writes decompressed data into client->raw_buffer without enforcing the output buffer capacity, only updating uncompressedBytes after the fact. A malicious server sends an oversized LZO stream in the FramebufferUpdate; decompression overruns the heap allocation, enabling memory corruption, crash, or code execution.

commit_msg:
Correctly load/initialize classes when using ConstantPool

- do not load classes in the "ifLoaded" calls
- never intitialize classes in the natives
- do not update the constant pool when querying from the natives

Fixes: #12016

[ci skip]

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (stringRef != NULL) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif ((NULL != stringRef) && J9_ARE_NO_BITS_SET(resolveFlags, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE)) {']}
description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: Line 11 creates the interned string object, and lines 12-17 write it into the RAM constant pool slot (stringObjectP) via J9STATIC_OBJECT_STORE. The before-version guard only checked stringRef != NULL, so the write occurred regardless of resolveFlags; the patch adds the J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE condition to suppress this store when the caller requested no constant-pool update.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is failure to respect the no-update flag, leaving the resource (constant-pool entry) in a state populated outside the proper initialization sequence; this aligns with CWE-909 Missing Initialization of Resource. It is not a mere null-dereference (CWE-476) since the guard on NULL already existed; the missing constraint is the resolveFlags check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the resolve path unconditionally published a resolved value into the constant pool, so querying via ConstantPool API (NO_CP_UPDATE) still modified shared state. Trigger: caller uses jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool, causing pre-resolution of a String entry. Consequence: the constant pool entry becomes populated without the class-initialization path running, allowing static members to be accessed or uninitialized values observed.

commit_msg:
evtchn: avoid NULL derefs

Commit fbbd5009e6 ("evtchn: refactor low-level event channel port ops")
added a de-reference of the struct evtchn pointer for a port without
first making sure the bucket pointer is non-NULL. This de-reference is
actually entirely unnecessary, as all relevant callers (beyond the
problematic do_poll()) already hold the port number in their hands, and
the actual leaf functions need nothing else.

For FIFO event channels there's a second problem in that the ordering
of reads and updates to ->num_evtchns and ->event_array[] was so far
undefined (the read side isn't always holding the domain's event lock).
Add respective barriers.

This is XSA-221.

Reported-by: Ankur Arora <ankur.a.arora@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    struct evtchn *evtchn;', '                evtchn = evtchn_from_port(d, info->evtchn);', "                       (evtchn_port_is_pending(d, evtchn) ? 'P' : '-'),", "                       (evtchn_port_is_masked(d, evtchn) ? 'M' : '-'),"], 'added_lines': ["                       evtchn_port_is_pending(d, info->evtchn) ? 'P' : '-',", "                       evtchn_port_is_masked(d, info->evtchn) ? 'M' : '-',"]}
description: Xen through 4.8.x does not validate the port numbers of polled event channel ports, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and host OS crash) or possibly obtain sensitive information, aka XSA-221.

code_evidence: The port comes from info->evtchn, where info = pirq_info(d, pirq); pirq_info may return NULL for a port lacking a backing pirq, and no NULL check guards the subsequent use.
evtchn = evtchn_from_port(d, info->evtchn) dereferences info->evtchn, then the evtchn pointer is passed to evtchn_port_is_pending/evtchn_port_is_masked, which dereference it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences pointers (info, evtchn) that are expected valid but may be NULL, matching CWE-476's NULL Pointer Dereference definition. The fix removes the unnecessary evtchn_from_port dereference and passes the port number directly, confirming the unsafe dereference as the root cause rather than a generic bounds/validation issue.

evidence_lines.code:
(evtchn_port_is_pending(d, evtchn) ? 'P' : '-'),
(evtchn_port_is_masked(d, evtchn) ? 'M' : '-'),

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the lookup via pirq_info(d, pirq) is not validated before info->evtchn is read, and evtchn_from_port's result is used without a NULL check. Trigger: dumping IRQs for a guest event channel port with no valid bucket/pirq entry. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference crashing the host (DoS), and the commit also notes undefined read ordering for FIFO channels.

commit_msg:
Add a one-word sentinel value of 0x0 at the end of each buf_t chunk

This helps protect against bugs where any part of a buf_t's memory
is passed to a function that expects a NUL-terminated input.

It also closes TROVE-2016-10-001 (aka bug 20384).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  CHUNK_SET_SENTINEL(ch, alloc);']}
description: Tor before 0.2.8.9 and 0.2.9.x before 0.2.9.4-alpha had internal functions that were entitled to expect that buf_t data had NUL termination, but the implementation of or/buffers.c did not ensure that NUL termination was present, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (client, hidden service, relay, or authority crash) via crafted data.

code_evidence: chunk_new_with_alloc_size allocates a chunk via tor_malloc(alloc) and sets ch->memlen to CHUNK_SIZE_WITH_ALLOC(alloc), but ch->data = &ch->mem[0] exposes the payload area without writing any terminating byte. The added CHUNK_SET_SENTINEL call is absent from this version, so the chunk's usable memory is left without a guaranteed NUL terminator.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing terminator allows operations on the buffer to read beyond its intended boundary, which is the class-level out-of-bounds access described by CWE-119. It is not merely a missing-constraint logic error, because the concrete effect is an out-of-bounds memory read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the chunk constructor returns buffer memory with no sentinel byte written at the end of the usable region. Trigger: callers pass chunk data to functions expecting NUL-terminated strings, causing reads past the intended boundary. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read leading to crash (DoS) of client, hidden service, relay or authority.

commit_msg:
The syzbot fuzzer has found two (!) races in the USB character device
registration and deregistration routines.  This patch fixes the races.

The first race results from the fact that usb_deregister_dev() sets
usb_minors[intf->minor] to NULL before calling device_destroy() on the
class device.  This leaves a window during which another thread can
allocate the same minor number but will encounter a duplicate name
error when it tries to register its own class device.  A typical error
message in the system log would look like:

    sysfs: cannot create duplicate filename '/class/usbmisc/ldusb0'

The patch fixes this race by destroying the class device first.

The second race is in usb_register_dev().  When that routine runs, it
first allocates a minor number, then drops minor_rwsem, and then
creates the class device.  If the device creation fails, the minor
number is deallocated and the whole routine returns an error.  But
during the time while minor_rwsem was dropped, there is a window in
which the minor number is allocated and so another thread can
successfully open the device file.  Typically this results in
use-after-free errors or invalid accesses when the other thread closes
its open file reference, because the kernel then tries to release
resources that were already deallocated when usb_register_dev()
failed.  The patch fixes this race by keeping minor_rwsem locked
throughout the entire routine.

Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+30cf45ebfe0b0c4847a1@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/Pine.LNX.4.44L0.1908121607590.1659-100000@iolanthe.rowland.org
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tup_write(&minor_rwsem);', '\tif (intf->minor < 0)', '\t\tdown_write(&minor_rwsem);', '\t\tup_write(&minor_rwsem);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (intf->minor < 0) {', '\t\tup_write(&minor_rwsem);', '\t}', '\tup_write(&minor_rwsem);']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.2.10, there is a race condition bug that can be caused by a malicious USB device in the USB character device driver layer, aka CID-303911cfc5b9. This affects drivers/usb/core/file.c.

code_evidence: Minor allocation writes usb_minors[minor] and intf->minor under minor_rwsem, but the lock is released at line 29 before device_create() runs at line 33; intf->minor is checked and the class device built without holding the lock.

On device_create() failure, lines 37-40 reacquire the lock, clear usb_minors[minor] and reset intf->minor, but the window between line 29 and line 37 already exposes the allocated minor to concurrent openers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allows an interfering concurrent sequence to access the shared minor table between release and reacquisition of minor_rwsem, violating exclusivity/atomicity of the registration sequence. This is precisely CWE-362; it is not merely a duplicate-name issue, which is the separate deregistration race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the minor number is published in usb_minors and intf->minor while minor_rwsem is dropped before the class device is successfully created. A concurrent opener can find and use the minor during that window; if device_create() then fails, the cleanup path releases resources the opener still references, yielding use-after-free or invalid accesses.

commit_msg:
Fixed Error() instance dumping when "name" prop is not primitive.

Previously, njs_error_to_string2() might be invoked with error argument
pointing to vm->retval.  When "name" prop was not primitive vm->retval
might be overwritten.  As a result error pointer might be referencing a
primitive value.  In turn the second call of njs_object_property()
received an invalid object pointer because it expects only object value
types.

The fix is to ensure that error object pointer is never overwritten.

This closes #615 issue on Github.

commit_msg:
ALSA: pcm: Move rwsem lock inside snd_ctl_elem_read to prevent UAF

Takes rwsem lock inside snd_ctl_elem_read instead of snd_ctl_elem_read_user
like it was done for write in commit 1fa4445f9adf1 ("ALSA: control - introduce
snd_ctl_notify_one() helper"). Doing this way we are also fixing the following
locking issue happening in the compat path which can be easily triggered and
turned into an use-after-free.

64-bits:
snd_ctl_ioctl
  snd_ctl_elem_read_user
    [takes controls_rwsem]
    snd_ctl_elem_read [lock properly held, all good]
    [drops controls_rwsem]

32-bits:
snd_ctl_ioctl_compat
  snd_ctl_elem_write_read_compat
    ctl_elem_write_read
      snd_ctl_elem_read [missing lock, not good]

CVE-2023-0266 was assigned for this issue.

Cc: stable@kernel.org # 5.13+
Signed-off-by: Clement Lecigne <clecigne@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Jaroslav Kysela <perex@perex.cz>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230113120745.25464-1-tiwai@suse.de
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>

description: A use after free vulnerability exists in the ALSA PCM package in the Linux Kernel. SNDRV_CTL_IOCTL_ELEM_{READ|WRITE}32 is missing locks that can be used in a use-after-free that can result in a priviledge escalation to gain ring0 access from the system user. We recommend upgrading past commit 56b88b50565cd8b946a2d00b0c83927b7ebb055e

code_evidence: snd_ctl_find_id() looks up kctl in the card's control list and the result is dereferenced without any lock held; early returns on failure paths leave no synchronization protecting the object.
kctl is dereferenced via snd_ctl_get_ioff() and kctl->vd[index_offset] and kctl->get, all without holding controls_rwsem, so the object could be freed concurrently.
kctl->get(kctl, control) is invoked on the unlocked kctl pointer; a concurrent control removal can free kctl between lookup and this call, yielding a use-after-free.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses kctl and calls kctl->get after the object may have been freed by a concurrent path, which is exactly reuse of freed memory. A mere race or missing lock is the enabling condition; the supported consequence is CWE-416.

Trigger: a concurrent control removal/update frees the kcontrol while this unlocked read path still holds and uses its pointer. Consequence: use-after-free, allowing memory corruption or privilege escalation.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.1 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.9, the MBIM dissector could crash or exhaust system memory. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-mbim.c by changing the memory-allocation approach.

commit_msg:
mwifiex: Fix possible buffer overflows in mwifiex_cmd_802_11_ad_hoc_start

mwifiex_cmd_802_11_ad_hoc_start() calls memcpy() without checking
the destination size may trigger a buffer overflower,
which a local user could use to cause denial of service
or the execution of arbitrary code.
Fix it by putting the length check before calling memcpy().

Signed-off-by: Zhang Xiaohui <ruc_zhangxiaohui@163.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20201206084801.26479-1-ruc_zhangxiaohui@163.com

description: mwifiex_cmd_802_11_ad_hoc_start in drivers/net/wireless/marvell/mwifiex/join.c in the Linux kernel through 5.10.4 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a long SSID value, aka CID-5c455c5ab332.

code_evidence: Line 25 clears adhoc_start->ssid for IEEE80211_MAX_SSID_LEN bytes, then line 26 copies req_ssid->ssid_len bytes from req_ssid->ssid into that fixed-size destination with no length check.
Lines 29-30 similarly clear and copy into bss_desc->ssid.ssid using the same unvalidated req_ssid->ssid_len, and line 31 stores the oversized length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a direct buffer copy of input-controlled length into a fixed-size destination without a size check, matching CWE-120's 'Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input' definition. It is a write overflow, not an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

memset(adhoc_start->ssid, 0, IEEE80211_MAX_SSID_LEN);
memcpy(adhoc_start->ssid, req_ssid->ssid, req_ssid->ssid_len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: req_ssid->ssid_len is attacker-influenced and never compared against IEEE80211_MAX_SSID_LEN before memcpy into fixed-size SSID buffers. When ssid_len exceeds the destination capacity, the copy writes past adhoc_start->ssid and bss_desc->ssid.ssid, corrupting adjacent memory and enabling denial of service or code execution.

description: epan/dissectors/packet-nbap.c in the NBAP dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.9 and 2.0.x before 2.0.1 does not validate the number of items, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (invalid read operation and application crash) via a crafted packet.

When crcn_context_present is set, the decoded id is used directly as a GINT_TO_POINTER key in g_tree_lookup and g_tree_insert; if no entry exists, a new record is allocated and inserted with no check that the decoded value is a valid context identifier.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of an input-derived identifier before it is used to index and populate a data structure, matching CWE-20's improper validation of an input property. The crash is a downstream consequence of accepting the unvalidated id, not a separate memory-safety defect in this function.

evidence_lines.code:
offset = dissect_per_constrained_integer(tvb, offset, actx, tree, hf_index,
0U, 1048575U, &node_b_com_context_id, FALSE);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoded node_b_com_context_id is accepted without validating that it corresponds to a legitimate Node-B communication context before being used as a tree key and stored. Trigger: a crafted NBAP packet supplies an id (within the PER range but not a real context), with crcn_context_present set. The unchecked value flows into the context map, enabling inconsistent state that the commit message ties to a SIGSEGV/invalid read crash (availability impact).

commit_msg:
Since the tee subsystem does not keep a strong reference to its idle
shared memory buffers, it races with other threads that try to destroy a
shared memory through a close of its dma-buf fd or by unmapping the
memory.

In tee_shm_get_from_id() when a lookup in teedev->idr has been
successful, it is possible that the tee_shm is in the dma-buf teardown
path, but that path is blocked by the teedev mutex. Since we don't have
an API to tell if the tee_shm is in the dma-buf teardown path or not we
must find another way of detecting this condition.

Fix this by doing the reference counting directly on the tee_shm using a
new refcount_t refcount field. dma-buf is replaced by using
anon_inode_getfd() instead, this separates the life-cycle of the
underlying file from the tee_shm. tee_shm_put() is updated to hold the
mutex when decreasing the refcount to 0 and then remove the tee_shm from
teedev->idr before releasing the mutex. This means that the tee_shm can
never be found unless it has a refcount larger than 0.

Fixes: 967c9cca2cc5 ("tee: generic TEE subsystem")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reviewed-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Reviewed-by: Lars Persson <larper@axis.com>
Reviewed-by: Sumit Garg <sumit.garg@linaro.org>
Reported-by: Patrik Lantz <patrik.lantz@axis.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Wiklander <jens.wiklander@linaro.org>

+++ func_after

 {
-	/*
-	 * dma_buf_put() decreases the dmabuf reference counter and will
-	 * call tee_shm_release() when the last reference is gone.
-	 *
-	 * In the case of driver private memory we call tee_shm_release
-	 * directly instead as it doesn't have a reference counter.
-	 */
-	if (shm->flags & TEE_SHM_DMA_BUF)
-		dma_buf_put(shm->dmabuf);
-	else
-		tee_shm_release(shm);
+	tee_shm_put(shm);

description: A use-after-free exists in drivers/tee/tee_shm.c in the TEE subsystem in the Linux kernel through 5.15.11. This occurs because of a race condition in tee_shm_get_from_id during an attempt to free a shared memory object.

code_evidence: tee_shm_free() releases shared memory without any locking: for dma-buf-backed objects it calls dma_buf_put(shm->dmabuf), which only drops the dma-buf reference and defers tee_shm_release(); for private memory it calls tee_shm_release() directly. No teedev mutex or tee_shm refcount is held, so the teardown of the tee_shm is not atomic with respect to concurrent lookups.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the free sequence lacks exclusive access to the shared tee_shm/IDR state, allowing an interfering concurrent sequence to observe and use the resource during teardown. The weakness is improper synchronization of a shared resource, not the memory-safety consequence itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the tee_shm lifetime is tied to the dma-buf reference count and freed without synchronization, while tee_shm_get_from_id() can still find the object in teedev->idr. Trigger: one thread frees or unmaps the shared memory while another concurrently looks it up, so the lookup succeeds on an object already in the teardown path. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the tee_shm.

commit_msg: Fixed incorrect call to WriteBlob reported in #490.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        (void) WriteBlob(color_image,length,chunk);', '', '          chunk=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(chunk);'], 'added_lines': ['          {', '            (void) WriteBlob(color_image,length,chunk);', '            chunk=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(chunk);', '          }']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.0.5-7 Q16, a crafted file could trigger an assertion failure in the WriteBlob function in MagickCore/blob.c because of missing checks in the ReadOneJNGImage function in coders/png.c.

code_evidence: Chunk length is read from the file into `length` and the type is read into `type`; the only validation is `length > PNG_UINT_31_MAX || count == 0`, which does not constrain the length to the actual remaining blob data.

When `length != 0`, a buffer of `length` bytes is allocated and filled by reading `length` bytes via `ReadBlobByte`; the loop does not check for EOF or read errors, so short/truncated input yields a partially filled buffer with indeterminate contents.

For a JDAT chunk, `WriteBlob(color_image,length,chunk)` writes the attacker-controlled `length` bytes from `chunk`; the length is not validated against the amount actually read or the blob's real size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function processes attacker-supplied file metadata (the chunk length) and contents without validating that the declared length is consistent with the actual data available, which is improper validation of input properties (size/consistency) per CWE-20. The resulting crash is the consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the JNG chunk length field is trusted without validating it against the actual available input, and the read loop does not detect truncated/short reads. Trigger: a crafted JNG file declaring a JDAT length larger than the remaining data causes `chunk` to be partially filled while `length` remains the declared value. Consequence: `WriteBlob` writes `length` bytes from an incompletely populated buffer, driving the assertion failure/crash in WriteBlob.

commit_msg:
dm: Reset virtio device before release

With virtio polling mode enabled, a timer is running in the virtio
backend service. And the timer will also be triggered if its frondend
driver didn't do the device reset in shutdown. A freed virtio device
will be accessed in the polling timer handler.

Do the virtio reset() callback specifically to clear the polling timer
before the free.

Tracked-On: #6147
Signed-off-by: Shuo A Liu <shuo.a.liu@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Yonghua Huang <yonghua.huang@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tvirtio_audio_reset(virt_audio);']}
description: The polling timer handler in ACRN before 2.5 has a use-after-free for a freed virtio device, related to devicemodel/hw/pci/virtio/*.c.

code_evidence: Lines 10-12 only stop and reset the kernel backend when kstatus is VIRTIO_DEV_STARTED; the virtio device's polling timer reset is not performed on this teardown path.
Lines 23-25 destroy the mutex, log, and free dev->arg (the virtio_audio object) without first clearing the polling timer that the backend runs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the freed dev->arg object can be accessed by the still-running polling timer handler after free() at line 25. The missing reset before free is the cause; the stale-pointer access is the use-after-free, not merely a resource leak or missing cleanup.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: deinit frees the virtio_audio device (line 25) without resetting the virtio backend's polling timer, so a timer still armed in the backend service can fire after the object is freed. Trigger: polling mode active and the frontend driver does not reset the device at shutdown; the timer handler then dereferences freed memory. Consequence: use-after-free read/write on the freed virtio device, causing crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
passthrough: quarantine PCI devices

When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for
that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The
IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that
the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However,
when the guest domain is torn down the device is assigned back to dom0,
thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data.

This patch introduces a 'quarantine' for PCI devices using dom_io. When
the toolstack makes a device assignable (by binding it to pciback), it
will now also assign it to DOMID_IO and the device will only be assigned
back to dom0 when the device is made unassignable again. Whilst device is
assignable it will only ever transfer between dom_io and guest domains.
dom_io is actually only used as a sentinel domain for quarantining purposes;
it is not configured with any IOMMU mappings. Assignment to dom_io simply
means that the device's initiator (requestor) identifier is not present in
the IOMMU's device table and thus any DMA transactions issued will be
terminated with a fault condition.

In addition, a fix to assignment handling is made for VT-d.  Failure
during the assignment step should not lead to a device still being
associated with its prior owner. Hand the device to DomIO temporarily,
until the assignment step has completed successfully.  Remove the PI
hooks from the source domain then earlier as well.

Failure of the recovery reassign_device_ownership() may not go silent:
There e.g. may still be left over RMRR mappings in the domain assignment
to which has failed, and hence we can't allow that domain to continue
executing.

NOTE: This patch also includes one printk() cleanup; the
      "XEN_DOMCTL_assign_device: " tag is dropped in iommu_do_pci_domctl(),
      since similar printk()-s elsewhere also don't log such a tag.

This is XSA-302.

Signed-off-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        ret = hd->platform_ops->reassign_device(d, hardware_domain, devfn,', '    ret = hd->platform_ops->reassign_device(d, hardware_domain, devfn,'], 'added_lines': ['    struct domain *target;', '    /* De-assignment from dom_io should de-quarantine the device */', '    target = (pdev->quarantine && pdev->domain != dom_io) ?', '        dom_io : hardware_domain;', '', '        ret = hd->platform_ops->reassign_device(d, target, devfn,', '    ret = hd->platform_ops->reassign_device(d, target, devfn,', '    if ( pdev->domain == hardware_domain  )', '        pdev->quarantine = false;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing attackers to gain host OS privileges via DMA in a situation where an untrusted domain has access to a physical device. This occurs because passed through PCI devices may corrupt host memory after deassignment. When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However, when the guest domain is torn down, or the device is deassigned, the device is assigned back to dom0, thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data. An untrusted domain with access to a physical device can DMA into host memory, leading to privilege escalation. Only systems where guests are given direct access to physical devices capable of DMA (PCI pass-through) are vulnerable. Systems which do not use PCI pass-through are not vulnerable.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs PCI device deassignment and IOMMU ownership reassignment; it contains no OS command construction or execution, so CWE-78 is unsupported.

commit_msg:
Perform deep copy in pushdup (instead of shallow)

Until now, the element duplication in pushdup was performed via
t->val = Stack->val.

While this is perfectly fine for integer/double/register values,
this may create nasty, hard to debug issues with Strings. In fact,
when called with a String at the top of the stack, pushdup would
only push *a reference* to the same String element (shallow copy),
later allowing to modify several stack elements at once, which may
potentially lead to NULL pointer dereferences or any other
unspecified impact.

In this patch we implement deep copy in pushdup:
* If the type of the stack element is 's' (for String), we
  allocate a new buffer and copy the String into it.
* Otherwise we simply proceed as before, that is we do t->val = Stack->val
  which is perfectly fine since we are not dealing with pointers.

This patch is the last part of the patch for #121 (fixes #121), which
should now be completely fixed.

description: The pushdup function in util/decompile.c in libming through 0.4.8 does not recognize the need for ActionPushDuplicate to perform a deep copy when a String is at the top of the stack, making the library vulnerable to a util/decompile.c getName NULL pointer dereference, which may allow attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted SWF file.

code_evidence: pushdup allocates a new stack node t and copies only the pointer Stack->val into t->val, aliasing the same SWF_ACTIONPUSHPARAM (and its p.String buffer) across two stack entries. No deep copy or NULL check on Stack->val is performed before aliasing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit and description tie the shallow-copy aliasing to a getName NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): the dereferenced pointer is expected valid but becomes NULL. The function's aliasing is the enabling condition; the NULL dereference itself occurs in getName, so this is a root-cause-level fit rather than a use-after-free (CWE-416).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: duplicated stack entries share one heap-allocated value/string instead of independent storage. Trigger: a crafted SWF pushes a String and duplicates it; later modification or freeing of the shared String leaves the other stack entry's pointer dangling or NULL. Consequence: downstream getName dereferences the invalid pointer, causing a NULL pointer dereference and denial of service.

commit_msg: Fix bug #68819 (Fileinfo on specific file causes spurious OOM and/or segfault)

description: The mget function in softmagic.c in file 5.x, as used in the Fileinfo component in PHP before 5.4.40, 5.5.x before 5.5.24, and 5.6.x before 5.6.8, does not properly maintain a certain pointer relationship, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted string that is mishandled by a "Python script text executable" rule.

code_evidence: bytecnt is derived from m->str_range (line 20) and clamped only to nbytes; offset is never constrained relative to bytecnt before use.
buf is computed as s + offset while end/last are computed as s + bytecnt; when offset exceeds bytecnt, buf points past end.
The newline-scanning loop compares b (starting at buf) against end; with buf past end the pointer relationship is violated, and last - buf at line 47 can underflow to a huge size_t.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts offset and str_range-derived bounds without checking that offset <= bytecnt, i.e. it fails to validate an offset/position property of input before using it in pointer arithmetic — directly the improper input validation described by CWE-20. The added offset>bytecnt clamp is precisely that missing validation.

evidence_lines.code:
buf = RCAST(const char *, s) + offset;
end = last = RCAST(const char *, s) + bytecnt;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the FILE_REGEX branch fails to validate that the caller-supplied offset does not exceed the bytecnt bound derived from str_range/nbytes. Trigger: a crafted string matched by a regex rule whose offset surpasses bytecnt. Consequence: buf/end pointers become inconsistent, the scan misbehaves and s_len underflows, leading to OOM or a crash (and potentially memory corruption).

commit_msg: Fix a small memory leak
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  draw_info->geometry=AcquireString(geometry);'], 'added_lines': ['  (void) CloneString(&draw_info->geometry,geometry);']}
description: Multiple memory leaks in the caption and label handling code in ImageMagick allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via unspecified vectors.

code_evidence: In the gravity-undefined branches the code calls CloneString(&draw_info->geometry,geometry), which frees the previous geometry buffer before duplicating the new string; the loop at line 51 can execute repeatedly and the binary-search loop at line 71 also re-enters these branches.
At line 134 the code instead assigns draw_info->geometry=AcquireString(geometry), overwriting the pointer without freeing the buffer previously allocated by CloneString, so that allocation is leaked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function mismanages a heap resource by losing the only reference to an allocated buffer, matching CWE-399 (resource management errors, memory consumption). It is a memory leak rather than a use-after-free or overflow, since the orphaned block is simply unreachable.

evidence_lines.code:
(void) CloneString(&draw_info->geometry,geometry);
(void) CloneString(&draw_info->geometry,geometry);
draw_info->geometry=AcquireString(geometry);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unconditional assignment at line 134 replaces an already-allocated draw_info->geometry pointer with a fresh allocation, orphaning the prior buffer. Trigger: any path where the geometry was populated earlier (lines 56/77) reaches line 134. Consequence: each such call leaks memory, enabling resource exhaustion/DoS over repeated reads.

The specific defect is the incorrect loop condition, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds buffer operation.

Trigger: a source string whose first character is nonzero is copied into a destination buffer; the copy proceeds up to len regardless of s's actual length, reading and writing outside the buffer's intended boundary. commit_msg:
posix-timer: Properly check sigevent->sigev_notify

timer_create() specifies via sigevent->sigev_notify the signal delivery for
the new timer. The valid modes are SIGEV_NONE, SIGEV_SIGNAL, SIGEV_THREAD
and (SIGEV_SIGNAL | SIGEV_THREAD_ID).

The sanity check in good_sigevent() is only checking the valid combination
for the SIGEV_THREAD_ID bit, i.e. SIGEV_SIGNAL, but if SIGEV_THREAD_ID is
not set it accepts any random value.

This has no real effects on the posix timer and signal delivery code, but
it affects show_timer() which handles the output of /proc/$PID/timers. That
function uses a string array to pretty print sigev_notify. The access to
that array has no bound checks, so random sigev_notify cause access beyond
the array bounds.

Add proper checks for the valid notify modes and remove the SIGEV_THREAD_ID
masking from various code pathes as SIGEV_NONE can never be set in
combination with SIGEV_THREAD_ID.

Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers3@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Reported-by: Alexey Dobriyan <adobriyan@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: John Stultz <john.stultz@linaro.org>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsig_none = (timr->it_sigev_notify & ~SIGEV_THREAD_ID) == SIGEV_NONE;'], 'added_lines': ['\tsig_none = timr->it_sigev_notify == SIGEV_NONE;']}
description: The timer_create syscall implementation in kernel/time/posix-timers.c in the Linux kernel before 4.14.8 doesn't properly validate the sigevent->sigev_notify field, which leads to out-of-bounds access in the show_timer function (called when /proc/$PID/timers is read). This allows userspace applications to read arbitrary kernel memory (on a kernel built with CONFIG_POSIX_TIMERS and CONFIG_CHECKPOINT_RESTORE).

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only computes sig_none and selects timer readout values; it performs no buffer indexing or memory read past bounds, so the out-of-bounds read in show_timer is not directly supported here.

Trigger: a crafted string whose length makes the addition overflow. commit_msg:
usb: ehci: fix memory leak in ehci_process_itd

While processing isochronous transfer descriptors(iTD), if the page
select(PG) field value is out of bands it will return. In this
situation the ehci's sg list is not freed thus leading to a memory
leak issue. This patch avoid this.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liqiang6-s@360.cn>
Reviewed-by: Thomas Huth <thuth@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Michael Tokarev <mjt@tls.msk.ru>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                    qemu_sglist_destroy(&ehci->isgl);']}
description: Memory leak in the ehci_process_itd function in hw/usb/hcd-ehci.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a large number of crafted buffer page select (PG) indexes.

code_evidence: Line 27 initializes the scatter-gather list ehci->isgl via qemu_sglist_init before the page-crossing check. When off + len > 4096 and pg == 6, line 30 returns -1 without reaching the qemu_sglist_destroy at line 54, leaving the initialized sglist unreleased.
Line 54 is the normal cleanup path that frees ehci->isgl; the early return bypasses it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the resource (the sglist initialized at line 27) is not released after its effective lifetime ends on the error path at line 30, and the normal release at line 54 is bypassed. This is a missing-release weakness, not an out-of-bounds access; the PG bound check itself is present, but its cleanup is absent.

evidence_lines.code: qemu_sglist_destroy(&ehci->isgl);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an early error return after qemu_sglist_init skips the matching qemu_sglist_destroy. Trigger: a crafted iTD transaction whose PG index is 6 and whose offset plus length crosses a page boundary. Each such processing leaks the sglist resources, so repeated crafted descriptors accumulate memory and cause a denial of service.

commit_msg:
memory: prevent dma-reentracy issues

Add a flag to the DeviceState, when a device is engaged in PIO/MMIO/DMA.
This flag is set/checked prior to calling a device's MemoryRegion
handlers, and set when device code initiates DMA.  The purpose of this
flag is to prevent two types of DMA-based reentrancy issues:

1.) mmio -> dma -> mmio case
2.) bh -> dma write -> mmio case

These issues have led to problems such as stack-exhaustion and
use-after-frees.

Summary of the problem from Peter Maydell:
https://lore.kernel.org/qemu-devel/CAFEAcA_23vc7hE3iaM-JVA6W38LK4hJoWae5KcknhPRD5fPBZA@mail.gmail.com

Resolves: https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/issues/62
Resolves: https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/issues/540
Resolves: https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/issues/541

Resolves: https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/issues/827
Resolves: https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/issues/1282
Resolves: CVE-2023-0330

Reviewed-by: Thomas Huth <thuth@redhat.com>
Message-Id: <20230427211013.2994127-2-alxndr@bu.edu>
[thuth: Replace warn_report() with warn_report_once()]
Signed-off-by: Thomas Huth <thuth@redhat.com>

description: A DMA reentrancy issue was found in the USB EHCI controller emulation of QEMU. EHCI does not verify if the Buffer Pointer overlaps with its MMIO region when it transfers the USB packets. Crafted content may be written to the controller's registers and trigger undesirable actions (such as reset) while the device is still transferring packets. This can ultimately lead to a use-after-free issue. A malicious guest could use this flaw to crash the QEMU process on the host, resulting in a denial of service condition, or potentially execute arbitrary code within the context of the QEMU process on the host. This flaw affects QEMU versions before 7.0.0.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only records a dynamically-cast device pointer during MemoryRegion initialization; it contains no free, reference, or later use of freed memory, and the reentrancy/UAF behavior described is implemented elsewhere (handler gating), not in this function.

commit_msg:
Prevent an illegal memory access in readelf when attempting to parse a corrupt ELF file.

	PR 22510
	* readelf.c (load_debug_section): Fail if there are no section
	headers available.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  /* Without section headers we cannot find any sections.  */', '  if (filedata->section_headers == NULL)', '    return FALSE;']}
description: The load_debug_section function in readelf.c in GNU Binutils 2.29.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (invalid memory access and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via an ELF file that lacks section headers.

code_evidence: When string_table is NULL, the code computes strs = filedata->section_headers + filedata->file_header.e_shstrndx without verifying section_headers is non-NULL; with no section headers this is a pointer derived from NULL (or out-of-bounds) and strs->sh_size is then dereferenced.
find_section_in_set is called using filedata with no section headers available, so the lookup operates without a valid section-header buffer.
The compressed-name fallback repeats the same lookup, extending the unchecked path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs pointer arithmetic and a field read on a section-header buffer that may not exist, i.e., an out-of-bounds read of an intended buffer, matching CWE-119. It is not merely a NULL-pointer dereference because the offset e_shstrndx is attacker-controlled; the missing bounds/existence constraint is the core issue.

evidence_lines.code: sec = find_section_in_set (filedata, section->uncompressed_name, section_subset);
sec = find_section_in_set (filedata, section->compressed_name, section_subset);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: load_debug_section assumes section_headers points to a valid array and indexes it by e_shstrndx from the file. Trigger: a corrupt ELF lacking section headers yields a NULL/absent array, so the pointer arithmetic and sh_size dereference access memory outside any valid buffer. Supported consequence: invalid memory access and application crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overrun due to integer overflow in bcmath

Summary: scale gets passed around as an int inside the library.

Reviewed By: mxw

Differential Revision: D3624520

fbshipit-source-id: d39927413cec24fda2e475a296ad5d9019ccef0a
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (scale < 0) scale = BCG(bc_precision);'], 'added_lines': ['  scale = adjust_scale(scale);']}
description: Integer overflow in bcmath in Facebook HHVM before 3.15.0 allows attackers to have unspecified impact via unknown vectors, which triggers a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Line 3 normalizes a negative scale to the global bc_precision but applies no upper bound to the caller-supplied int64_t scale; the patched adjust_scale presumably adds that constraint.

The validated scale flows directly into bc_sqrt(&result, scale) at line 11 and then into the n_scale comparison/assignment at lines 12-13, so an extreme scale reaches bcmath's internal scale arithmetic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unchecked scale is used in arithmetic whose result is assumed valid but can wrap; the buffer overrun is the downstream consequence, not the root cause.

evidence_lines.code: if (scale < 0) scale = BCG(bc_precision);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing upper-bound check on the int64_t scale, which is passed into bcmath internals that treat scale as a plain int. A very large scale value triggers an integer overflow/wraparound there, and the wrapped small value is then used in size computations, leading to a buffer overrun as stated in the commit message.

commit_msg: Fixed out of bounds memory access from malformed DNS queries that have an invalid length label. Introduced in a6a07de0daa353bcd29056a4535a9c4784c113c8.

description: inspircd in Debian before 2.0.7 does not properly handle unsigned integers.  NOTE: This vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix to CVE-2012-1836.

commit_msg:
spnego: CVE-2021-44758 send_reject when no mech selected

This fixes a DoS where an initial SPNEGO token that has no acceptable
mechanisms causes a NULL dereference in acceptors.

send_accept() when called with a non-zero 'initial_response' did
not handle the case of gssspnego_ctx.preferred_mech_type equal
to GSS_C_NO_OID.

The failure to handle GSS_C_NO_OID has been present since the
initial revision of gssapi/spnego,
2baa7e7d613c26b2b037b368931519a84baec53d but might not have
been exercised until later revisions.

The introduction of opportunistic token handling in
gss_accept_sec_context(), 3c9d3266f47f594a29068c9d629908e7000ac663,
introduced two bugs:

 1. The optional mechToken field is used unconditionally
    possibly resulting in a segmentation fault.

 2. If use of the opportunistic token is unsuccessful and the
    mech type list length is one, send_accept() can be called
    with 'initial_response' true and preferred mech set to
    GSS_C_NO_OID.

b53c90da0890a9cce6f95c552f094ff6d69027bf ("Make error reporting
somewhat more correct for SPNEGO") attempted to fix the first
issue and increased the likelihood of the second.

This change alters the behavior of acceptor_start() so it calls
send_reject() when no mechanism was selected.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (preferred_mech_type == GSS_C_NO_OID) {', '\t    HEIMDAL_MUTEX_unlock(&ctx->ctx_id_mutex);', '\t    free_NegotiationToken(&nt);', '\t    return ret;', '\t}', '', '\tctx->preferred_mech_type = preferred_mech_type;'], 'added_lines': ['    }', '', '    ctx->preferred_mech_type = preferred_mech_type;', '', '    if (preferred_mech_type == GSS_C_NO_OID) {', '        send_reject(minor_status, output_token);', '        HEIMDAL_MUTEX_unlock(&ctx->ctx_id_mutex);', '        free_NegotiationToken(&nt);', '        return ret;']}
description: Heimdal before 7.7.1 allows attackers to cause a NULL pointer dereference in a SPNEGO acceptor via a preferred_mech_type of GSS_C_NO_OID and a nonzero initial_response value to send_accept.

code_evidence: The loop tries alternative mechanisms starting at index 1, leaving preferred_mech_type equal to GSS_C_NO_OID if no later mechanism succeeds.
When no mechanism was selected, the function returns without invoking send_accept; the patch adds send_reject here to avoid the accept path with a null preferred mechanism.
send_accept is called with initial_response set to 1 and the negotiated context; if preferred_mech_type remained GSS_C_NO_OID, send_accept dereferences the null mechanism.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a NULL pointer dereference: a pointer expected to reference a selected mechanism is used while null. The patch prevents the dereference by rejecting the token instead of proceeding to send_accept, directly supporting CWE-476 rather than a generic input-validation issue.

evidence_lines.code:
ret = send_accept (minor_status,
ctx,

commit_msg:
Bug#24388746: PRIVILEGE ESCALATION AND RACE CONDITION USING CREATE TABLE

During REPAIR TABLE of a MyISAM table, a temporary data file (.TMD)
is created. When repair finishes, this file is renamed to the original
.MYD file. The problem was that during this rename, we copied the
stats from the old file to the new file with chmod/chown. If a user
managed to replace the temporary file before chmod/chown was executed,
it was possible to get an arbitrary file with the privileges of the
mysql user.

This patch fixes the problem by not copying stats from the old
file to the new file. This is not needed as the new file was
created with the correct stats. This fix only changes server
behavior - external utilities such as myisamchk still does
chmod/chown.

No test case provided since the problem involves synchronization
with file system operations.

description: Race condition in Oracle MySQL before 5.5.52, 5.6.x before 5.6.33, 5.7.x before 5.7.15, and 8.x before 8.0.1; MariaDB before 5.5.52, 10.0.x before 10.0.28, and 10.1.x before 10.1.18; Percona Server before 5.5.51-38.2, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-78-1, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-8; and Percona XtraDB Cluster before 5.5.41-37.0, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-25.17, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-26.17 allows local users with certain permissions to gain privileges by leveraging use of my_copystat by REPAIR TABLE to repair a MyISAM table.

code_evidence: mi_repair_parallel is invoked with a quick flag and, in the vulnerable version, implicitly copies file stats from the old .MYD to the newly renamed temporary file.
mi_repair_by_sort is likewise invoked and performs the same old-to-new file-stat copy during the repair rename sequence.
mi_repair (keycache path) is invoked and also copies stats from the old file to the new file.
mi_sort_index is invoked and similarly copies file stats onto the repaired file.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The four repair calls expose a shared filesystem resource (the temporary/repaired file) whose stats are applied non-atomically relative to the rename, allowing an interfering sequence to replace it. This timing window is exactly CWE-362; it is not merely an incorrect permission setting, since the defect is the unsynchronized old-to-new stat copy.

evidence_lines.code:
error = mi_repair_parallel(&param, file, fixed_name,
param.testflag & T_QUICK);

error = mi_repair_by_sort(&param, file, fixed_name,
param.testflag & T_QUICK);

error=  mi_repair(&param, file, fixed_name,
param.testflag & T_QUICK);
error=mi_sort_index(&param,file,fixed_name);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the repair routines copy file statistics from the old .MYD to the temporary file after it is renamed into place, leaving a window where an attacker can swap the temporary file. Trigger: a local user with write access to the table directory races the rename against the chmod/chown. Consequence: the attacker-controlled file receives mysql-user privileges, enabling privilege escalation or arbitrary file modification.

commit_msg:
More checks for correct header sizes

Reported-by: "P. Amsuo, Purdue University"
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (f->buffer + f->buffer_len > f->transport_hdr + f->transport_len)', '        return -1;', '']}
description: VirtualSquare picoTCP (aka PicoTCP-NG) through 2.1 lacks certain size calculations before attempting to set a value of an mss structure member.

code_evidence: opt is derived from transport_hdr + PICO_SIZE_TCPHDR without verifying that transport_len actually covers the TCP header. The loop bound i < (transport_len - PICO_SIZE_TCPHDR) and the payload bound (opt + i) > f->payload are computed from transport_len/payload; if transport_len is smaller than PICO_SIZE_TCPHDR, the unsigned subtraction underflows to a huge value. A later default branch advances i = i + len - 2, and len can be 1, making i wrap/underflow further.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes loop and pointer bounds from transport_len and option lengths using unsigned arithmetic that can underflow or produce unintended values, then uses those results in parsing decisions and memory access. That is an incorrect security-critical calculation, matching CWE-682.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: size arithmetic on transport_len (unsigned subtraction) and option advancement (i + len - 2) is performed without validating header/option sizes. Trigger: a crafted TCP packet whose transport_len is below PICO_SIZE_TCPHDR or whose option lengths are inconsistent causes underflow/large loop bounds and out-of-range opt access. Consequence: out-of-bounds read/parse of option data, potentially a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
Fix segmentation fault in shape inference logic.

When running shape functions, some functions (such as `MutableHashTableShape`)
produce extra output information in the form of a `ShapeAndType` struct.  The
shapes embedded in this struct are owned by an inference context that is
cleaned up almost immediately; if the upstream code attempts to access this
shape information, it can trigger a segfault.

`ShapeRefiner` is mitigating this for normal output shapes by cloning them
(and thus putting the newly created shape under ownership of an inference
context that will not die), but we were not doing the same for shapes and
types.  This commit fixes that by doing similar logic on output shapes and
types.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 384761124
Change-Id: I07c0c42d29dfbb55bfa13ec1f09ef825fb0a1a1d
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    auto* resource = node_context->input_handle_shapes_and_types(0);', '      outer_context->set_output_handle_shapes_and_types(index, *resource);'], 'added_lines': ['    const std::vector<ShapeAndType>* resource =', '        node_context->input_handle_shapes_and_types(0);', '      // `ShapesAndType`s contain `ShapeHandle`s.  These `ShapeHandle`s point', '      // to `Shape`s that are owned by a different inference context too.  We', '      // need to copy them to the outer context to prevent them from being', '      // destroyed before they are used.', '      std::vector<ShapeAndType> copied_shapes_and_types;', '      for (auto& shape_and_type : *resource) {', '        ShapeHandle handle;', '        TensorShapeProto proto;', '        node_context->ShapeHandleToProto(shape_and_type.shape, &proto);', '        TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR(', '            outer_context->MakeShapeFromShapeProto(proto, &handle));', '        copied_shapes_and_types.push_back(', '            ShapeAndType(handle, shape_and_type.dtype, shape_and_type.type));', '      }', '', '      outer_context->set_output_handle_shapes_and_types(', '          index, copied_shapes_and_types);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions when running shape functions, some functions (such as `MutableHashTableShape`) produce extra output information in the form of a `ShapeAndType` struct. The shapes embedded in this struct are owned by an inference context that is cleaned up almost immediately; if the upstream code attempts to access this shape information, it can trigger a segfault. `ShapeRefiner` is mitigating this for normal output shapes by cloning them (and thus putting the newly created shape under ownership of an inference context that will not die), but we were not doing the same for shapes and types. This commit fixes that by doing similar logic on output shapes and types. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit ee119d4a498979525046fba1c3dd3f13a039fbb1. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The kRetvalOp branch retrieves the input's handle shapes and types via node_context->input_handle_shapes_and_types(0) and stores the dereferenced vector directly into outer_context with set_output_handle_shapes_and_types(index, *resource). The ShapeAndType entries contain ShapeHandle values that reference Shape objects owned by node_context's inference context, not by outer_context; no copy or re-homing into outer_context occurs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function passes references to memory owned by a context that can be freed, and later access uses that freed memory. The fix confirms this by cloning each ShapeHandle into outer_context via ShapeHandleToProto/MakeShapeFromShapeProto before storing; a mere dangling-pointer/null issue (CWE-476) would not require re-homing ownership.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the output handle shapes/types are propagated by shallow reference, so the embedded ShapeHandles remain owned by node_context's inference context. Trigger: when node_context is destroyed shortly after shape inference while outer_context or upstream code still holds these handles, the referenced Shape memory is freed. Supported consequence: dereferencing the stale ShapeHandle yields a use-after-free, observed as a segmentation fault.

description: Buffer overflow vulnerability in function AP4_MemoryByteStream::WritePartial in mp42aac in Bento4 v1.6.0-639, allows attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: The constructor computes the destination size as (AP4_Size)size-GetHeaderSize() and immediately calls stream.Read into m_Data.UseData() for that many bytes, with no check that size exceeds the header size. If size is smaller than the header size, the subtraction underflows and yields a huge AP4_Size, so SetDataSize allocates a huge/incorrect buffer and Read writes from the stream into it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the function copies stream data into a buffer sized from an unchecked, underflowing length calculation without verifying the input size against the destination, resulting in a classic buffer overflow write. This is a write-side size-check failure rather than a mere out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

stream.Read(m_Data.UseData(), m_Data.GetDataSize());

Trigger: a crafted file declaring an atom size smaller than its header. Consequence: integer underflow produces an oversized allocation and out-of-bounds write during stream.Read, causing memory corruption or denial of service.

commit_msg:
Integer Overflow in RAND commands can lead to assertion (CVE-2023-25155)

Issue happens when passing a negative long value that greater than
the max positive value that the long can store.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (getLongFromObjectOrReply(c,c->argv[2],&l,NULL) != C_OK) return;'], 'added_lines': ['    if (getRangeLongFromObjectOrReply(c,c->argv[2],-LONG_MAX,LONG_MAX,&l,NULL) != C_OK) return;']}
description: Redis is an in-memory database that persists on disk. Authenticated users issuing specially crafted `SRANDMEMBER`, `ZRANDMEMBER`, and `HRANDFIELD` commands can trigger an integer overflow, resulting in a runtime assertion and termination of the Redis server process. This problem affects all Redis versions. Patches were released in Redis version(s) 6.0.18, 6.2.11 and 7.0.9.

code_evidence: Line 10 parses argv[2] with getLongFromObjectOrReply into a signed long without any lower bound, so LONG_MIN is accepted. Line 11 branches on l>=0; for a negative value line 14 computes count = -l. Negating LONG_MIN overflows the signed long, and the result is stored in the unsigned long count, producing a huge value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a signed negation that can wrap for an extreme negative input and then uses the wrapped value in size logic, which is exactly integer overflow/wraparound (CWE-190). The later assertion failure is the consequence, not a separate weakness; the missing input constraint on the parsed long is the direct cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the count argument is not range-checked before negation, so a negative long beyond the positive range (e.g. LONG_MIN) overflows when negated at line 14. Trigger: an authenticated client issues SRANDMEMBER with such a count. The wrapped count then flows into size/count comparisons and loops, reaching the serverAssert at line 51 or driving large allocations, causing a runtime assertion and server termination (DoS).

commit_msg:
tls: clear data after a starttls acknowledgement

After a starttls acknowledgement message, clear the buffers of any
incoming data / commands.  This will ensure that all future data is
handled securely.

Co-authored-by: Pietro Cerutti <gahr@gahr.ch>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      // Clear any data after the STLS acknowledgement', '      mutt_socket_empty(adata->conn);']}
description: Mutt before 1.14.4 and NeoMutt before 2020-06-19 have a STARTTLS buffering issue that affects IMAP, SMTP, and POP3. When a server sends a "begin TLS" response, the client reads additional data (e.g., from a man-in-the-middle attacker) and evaluates it in a TLS context, aka "response injection."

code_evidence: After sending the STLS command via pop_query at [30], the code proceeds directly to mutt_ssl_starttls at [37] without discarding any extra data already buffered on adata->conn. The condition at [33] only checks the query return code; it does not verify that no residual server bytes remain before TLS negotiation begins. This is the exact location where the fix inserts mutt_socket_empty.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The buffered external input is not neutralized before being fed into the downstream TLS parser, so special elements from the server/attacker alter how that downstream component interprets the stream. This matches CWE-74's injection pattern; the missing buffer flush is the neutralization failure, distinct from a mere TLS configuration flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the client sends STLS, reads the acknowledgement, then upgrades to TLS while unread attacker-supplied bytes remain in the socket buffer. Trigger: a man-in-the-middle appends data after the "+OK begin TLS" response. Consequence: the injected bytes are consumed and interpreted in the TLS context, enabling response injection that can bypass protection mechanisms.

commit_msg:
Sanity check size passed to malloc...

Add sanity check before calling malloc in af_get_page() function to
avoid undefined behavior (e.g., seg fault) when dealing with a corrupt
AFF image with an invalid pagesize.

Issue found by Luis Rocha (luiscrocha@gmail.com).

description: The af_get_page() function in lib/afflib_pages.cpp in AFFLIB (aka AFFLIBv3) through 3.7.16 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault) via a corrupt AFF image that triggers an unexpected pagesize value.

code_evidence: The bad-block fill loop bounds its iterations by af->image_pagesize and af->image_sectorsize and memcpy's into caller buffer data without checking those image-derived values.
When data is NULL, malloc(af->image_pagesize) is called and *bytes is set to image_pagesize; memset later trusts the same value.
The tail-padding loop derives end_of_data from *bytes and iterates to image_pagesize-SECTOR_SIZE, memcpy'ing into data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The image pagesize is untrusted input used directly in allocation bounds and buffer indexing without validating its size; the root cause is missing size validation of input metadata, matching CWE-20. This is not a mere transform/encoding issue, since the value is accepted as-is and trusted.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: af->image_pagesize (and image_sectorsize) are populated from an AFF image without a range check, so a corrupt image yields an invalid/negative page size. Trigger: a crafted AFF file with an unexpected pagesize drives allocation and indexing using that value. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds writes or an undersized allocation, causing memory corruption or the reported segmentation fault.

commit_msg:
net: shell: dns: Properly manage lifetime of callback data

DNS callback needs "struct shell *shell" data structure to pass as
a parameter to shell print. How it was achieved previously is that
it was packaged together with cosmetic "bool first" param into
"struct net_shell_user_data" on the stack, and passed to the
callback. The problem was that the original command handler then
returned, so the "struct net_shell_user_data" on the stack was
overwritten, and the callback crashed on accessing it.

An obvious solution was to make that structure static, but that would
leave to issues still, as turns out we allow system shell to be run
as more than one concurrent instances.

Next solution was to keep this structure on the stack, but block the
command handler until callback is finished. However, that hit a
deadlock due to not well thought out use of a mutex in the shell
printing routines.

The solution presented here is due to @nordic-krch, who noticed that
"bool first" param is indeed cosmetic and not really required. Then
we have only "struct shell *shell" to pass to the callback, and can
do that in callback's pointer param directly, ditching
"struct net_shell_user_data" which needs to be stored on the stack.

Signed-off-by: Paul Sokolovsky <paul.sokolovsky@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct net_shell_user_data user_data;', '\tbool first = true;', '\tuser_data.shell = shell;', '\tuser_data.user_data = &first;', '', '\tret = dns_get_addr_info(host, qtype, NULL, dns_result_cb, &user_data,', '\t\t\t\tDNS_TIMEOUT);'], 'added_lines': ['\tret = dns_get_addr_info(host, qtype, NULL, dns_result_cb,', '\t\t\t\t(void *)shell, DNS_TIMEOUT);']}
description: Use After Free vulnerability in the Zephyr shell allows a serial or telnet connected user to cause denial of service, and possibly remote code execution. This issue affects: Zephyr shell versions prior to 1.14.0 on all.

code_evidence: The function declares a stack-local `struct net_shell_user_data user_data` at line 6 and a stack-local `bool first` at line 9. Lines 32-33 store `shell` and `&first` into this stack structure, then line 34-35 pass `&user_data` as the callback context to `dns_get_addr_info`, which returns without waiting for the asynchronous DNS callback. The stack frame is reclaimed when the handler returns, yet `dns_result_cb` later dereferences the dangling `&user_data` (and its nested `&first`).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the callback dereferences memory whose lifetime ended when `cmd_net_dns_query` returned; the pointer is not freed via free() but the stack object is invalidated, i.e., use after the storage's lifetime. This is a lifetime/dangling-reference flaw, not a simple null-deref or buffer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a pointer to stack-allocated callback data escapes the function's lifetime because the DNS resolution is asynchronous. Trigger: the command handler returns while resolution is still pending, so the stack frame is overwritten; the callback then reads `user_data.shell`/`user_data.user_data` from stale stack memory. Supported consequence: crash/DoS and, since the reused stack contents are attacker-influenced through a serial/telnet shell, possible memory corruption or code execution.

commit_msg:
tcp: take care of truncations done by sk_filter()

With syzkaller help, Marco Grassi found a bug in TCP stack,
crashing in tcp_collapse()

Root cause is that sk_filter() can truncate the incoming skb,
but TCP stack was not really expecting this to happen.
It probably was expecting a simple DROP or ACCEPT behavior.

We first need to make sure no part of TCP header could be removed.
Then we need to adjust TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->end_seq

Many thanks to syzkaller team and Marco for giving us a reproducer.

Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Marco Grassi <marco.gra@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Vladis Dronov <vdronov@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (sk_filter(sk, skb))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (tcp_filter(sk, skb))']}
description: The TCP stack in the Linux kernel before 4.8.10 mishandles skb truncation, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) via a crafted application that makes sendto system calls, related to net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c and net/ipv6/tcp_ipv6.c.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's use of sk_filter() reflects an skb-truncation handling flaw causing a crash (DoS), not an access-control restriction failure; no authorization, privilege, or resource-access boundary is present to support CWE-284.

description: An integer overflow and buffer overflow issues were found in the ACPI Error Record Serialization Table (ERST) device of QEMU in the read_erst_record() and write_erst_record() functions. Both issues may allow the guest to overrun the host buffer allocated for the ERST memory device. A malicious guest could use these flaws to crash the QEMU process on the host.

code_evidence: record_length is read from the NVRAM record header (lines 27-30) and is guest-controlled. The bounds check at line 34 computes s->record_offset + record_length in unsigned arithmetic; a large record_length can wrap the sum, bypassing the exchange_length comparison. The subsequent memcpy at line 38 copies record_length bytes into the exchange buffer at exchange + record_offset, overflowing the fixed memory region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The memcpy copies a guest-controlled input length into a fixed-size output buffer without a valid size constraint, matching CWE-120's buffer copy without checking size of input. The overflowed comparison is the missing constraint enabling the classic buffer copy overflow, not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an integer overflow in the offset+length validation lets an oversized record_length pass the check. Trigger: a guest-written record header with a large length value. Consequence: the host buffer backing the ERST exchange memory region is overrun, corrupting host memory and potentially crashing the QEMU process.

commit_msg:
Bug 697015: Avoid object references vanishing during repair.

A PDF repair can be triggered 'just in time', when we encounter
a problem in the file. The idea is that this can happen without
the enclosing code being aware of it.

Thus the enclosing code may be holding 'borrowed' references
(such as those returned by pdf_dict_get()) at the time when the
repair is triggered. We are therefore at pains to ensure that
the repair does not replace any objects that exist already, so
that the calling code will not have these references unexpectedly
invalidated.

The sole exception to this is when we replace the 'Length' fields
in stream dictionaries with the actual lengths. Bug 697015 shows
exactly this situation causing a reference to become invalid.

The solution implemented here is to add an 'orphan list' to the
document, where we put these (hopefully few, small) objects. These
orphans are kept around until the document is closed.

description: The pdf_to_num function in pdf-object.c in MuPDF before 1.10 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and application crash) via a crafted file.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only wraps pdf_dict_put with fz_try/fz_always and drops val; it contains no free of obj/key/val followed by reuse, and the use-after-free described stems from repair replacing objects elsewhere, not from this wrapper.

commit_msg:
Prevent CHECK-fail/heap OOB in UpperBound and LowerBound

PiperOrigin-RevId: 387738073
Change-Id: Iee74de95ddad18440d052a75a5a1cb67544f490a
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    // inputs must be at least a matrix', '    OP_REQUIRES(', '        ctx, sorted_inputs_t.shape().dims() >= 2,', '        errors::InvalidArgument("sorted input argument must be a matrix"));']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions an attacker can read from outside of bounds of heap allocated data by sending specially crafted illegal arguments to `tf.raw_ops.UpperBound`. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/core/kernels/searchsorted_op.cc#L85-L104) does not validate the rank of `sorted_input` argument. A similar issue occurs in `tf.raw_ops.LowerBound`. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 42459e4273c2e47a3232cc16c4f4fff3b3a35c38. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function reads input tensors sorted_inputs_t and values_t and only checks that their leading dimensions match; it never verifies that sorted_inputs_t has rank >= 2 before calling dim_size(1).
dim_size(1) is accessed on sorted_inputs_t only inside the int32-output guard; for non-int32 output the trailing-dimension check is skipped entirely.
The flat views and dim_size(1) of sorted_inputs_t (and values_t.dim_size(1)) are passed to LowerBoundFunctor::Compute, which indexes into the flattened buffers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The consequence is an out-of-bounds read of heap memory, matching CWE-125. The absent rank constraint permits indexing beyond the intended buffer, not a write or type-confusion weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
FastBoundsCheck(sorted_inputs_t.dim_size(1),
std::numeric_limits<int>::max()),
errors::InvalidArgument("trailing dim_size must less than "
"INT_MAX for int32 output type, was ",
sorted_inputs_t.dim_size(1)));

OP_REQUIRES_OK(
ctx, functor::LowerBoundFunctor<Device, T, OutType>::Compute(
ctx, sorted_inputs, values, sorted_inputs_t.dim_size(0),
sorted_inputs_t.dim_size(1), values_t.dim_size(1), &output));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing rank validation of sorted_inputs_t; a rank-0 or rank-1 tensor makes dim_size(1) and the trailing-dimension bound check operate on a nonexistent dimension. The trigger is a crafted call to LowerBound with insufficient-rank sorted_inputs; the functor then indexes the flat buffer using an invalid trailing dimension, reading past the allocated heap data.
