commit_msg:
ipsec: Fix aborted xfrm policy dump crash

An independent security researcher, Mohamed Ghannam, has reported
this vulnerability to Beyond Security's SecuriTeam Secure Disclosure
program.

The xfrm_dump_policy_done function expects xfrm_dump_policy to
have been called at least once or it will crash.  This can be
triggered if a dump fails because the target socket's receive
buffer is full.

This patch fixes it by using the cb->start mechanism to ensure that
the initialisation is always done regardless of the buffer situation.

Fixes: 12a169e7d8f4 ("ipsec: Put dumpers on the dump list")
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t.start = link->start,']}
description: The XFRM dump policy implementation in net/xfrm/xfrm_user.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.11 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) via a crafted SO_RCVBUF setsockopt system call in conjunction with XFRM_MSG_GETPOLICY Netlink messages.

code_evidence: For GETSA/GETPOLICY with NLM_F_DUMP, the code builds a netlink_dump_control containing only .dump and .done, then calls netlink_dump_start. No .start callback is set, so the dump state is not initialized before netlink_dump_start may allocate or fail based on socket receive buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing .start initialization leaves dump state uninitialized so the done path references memory that was not properly set up, matching CWE-416 use-after-free rather than a mere null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dump control omits the start callback, so initialization is skipped when netlink_dump_start fails early (e.g., receive buffer full). The done callback later runs against uninitialized/freed dump state, causing a use-after-free crash; trigger requires CAP_NET_ADMIN and a crafted SO_RCVBUF with XFRM_MSG_GETPOLICY dump.

There is logic to focus the location bar for editing if the URL is about:blank.
However, if the page transition type is PAGE_TRANSITION_LINK, bypass that logic;

commit_msg: Fixed #5645: realloc return handling

description: libfreerdp/codec/region.c in FreeRDP through 1.1.x and 2.x through 2.0.0-rc4 has memory leaks because a supplied realloc pointer (i.e., the first argument to realloc) is also used for a realloc return value.

code_evidence: Line 55 assigns the result of realloc(newItems, newItems->size) directly to dst->data, overwriting the original pointer. Line 56 tests !dst->data, and lines 57-59 free(newItems) and return FALSE on failure. Because realloc already freed or invalidated newItems when it returns NULL, free(newItems) is a double free, and the previously allocated dst->data is lost.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-252 fits because the unchecked assumption is the realloc failure state: the code does not correctly handle the NULL return and instead frees an already-invalid pointer. It is a failure-handling defect rather than a missing NULL test alone, so the misused return value is the core weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function checks the realloc result but mishandles the failure path: on NULL it frees the same pointer it passed to realloc, which realloc already released. Triggered by allocation failure, this yields a double free and a memory leak of the old dst->data buffer, supporting a crash or memory corruption.

nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121

commit_msg:
Fix security vulnerability with SpaceToBatchNDOp.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 445527615
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    const int64_t product = first_value * second_value;'], 'added_lines': ['    const int64_t product = MultiplyWithoutOverflow(first_value, second_value);']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.SpaceToBatchND` (in all backends such as XLA and handwritten kernels) is vulnerable to an integer overflow: The result of this integer overflow is used to allocate the output tensor, hence we get a denial of service via a `CHECK`-failure (assertion failure), as in TFSA-2021-198. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: Lines 4-5 read both dimension values as int64_t. Line 17 computes product = first_value * second_value with a raw signed multiplication, which can overflow/wrap. Lines 18-22 only detect overflow post hoc by checking product < 0, which misses wraparound to a positive value and is not a sound guard. Line 23 then uses the possibly wrapped product via MakeDim(product), propagating a corrupted dimension.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the function performs an arithmetic calculation (multiplication of dimension sizes) whose result can overflow the int64_t representation and wrap, and the wrapped value is then used as a dimension. The negative-result check does not prevent all overflow cases, so the weakness is the unchecked integer overflow itself, not merely a missing validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dimension product is computed by unchecked signed int64 multiplication in a path reachable with large known input dimensions. Trigger: first_value and second_value large enough that the product exceeds INT64_MAX and wraps. Consequence: the wrapped product is used as an output dimension, leading to invalid allocation sizes and denial of service via CHECK/assertion failures in downstream kernels.

commit_msg:
[bug] Division by 0

Early return when mh.group1_samplerate (Sample rate of first substream) is 0, to avoid division by 0 error.

Solves issue #417 .
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (mh.group1_samplerate == 0)', '            return false;', '        if (mh.group1_samplerate == 0)', '            return false;']}
description: Divide-by-zero bug in tsMuxer 2.6.16 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by running the application with a crafted file.

code_evidence: ratebits is read from the input (getBits(4)) and mapped through mlp_samplerate into mh.group1_samplerate; this value comes from attacker-controlled file data.
The TRUEHD branch likewise derives mh.group1_samplerate from an input nibble via mlp_samplerate.
mh.frame_duration_nano is computed by dividing mh.access_unit_size * 1000000000ll by mh.group1_samplerate; if mlp_samplerate returns 0 for a ratebits value, the divisor is zero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a division whose divisor is derived from input without a zero check, matching CWE-369 (divide by zero). This is a missing-constraint arithmetic flaw, not an out-of-bounds access or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no validation that mlp_samplerate(ratebits) is non-zero before it is stored in mh.group1_samplerate. Trigger: a crafted DTS-HD/TrueHD header whose ratebits maps to a zero sample rate. Consequence: the division at line 44 divides by zero, causing a crash/DoS.

description: Istio 1.4.x before 1.4.9 and Istio 1.5.x before 1.5.4 contain the following vulnerability when telemetry v2 is enabled: by sending a specially crafted packet, an attacker could trigger a Null Pointer Exception resulting in a Denial of Service. This could be sent to the ingress gateway or a sidecar, triggering a null pointer exception which results in a denial of service. This also affects servicemesh-proxy where a null pointer exception flaw was found in servicemesh-proxy. When running Telemetry v2 (not on by default in version 1.4.x), an attacker could send a specially crafted packet to the ingress gateway or proxy sidecar, triggering a denial of service.

code_evidence: The guard checks only wasm_->onDone_ before invoking wasm_->onDone_(this, id_). It does not verify that the VM context has been created (in_vm_context_created_), so the callback can run against a context that was never initialized, where internal VM state is null.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Calling a callback on an uninitialized context leads to dereferencing a NULL pointer, matching CWE-476's null dereference pattern. It is not merely a missing check on wasm_->onDone_ (a different nullability issue); the distinct fault is invoking VM code before its context exists.

evidence_lines.code:
if (wasm_->onDone_) {
wasm_->onDone_(this, id_);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: onDone() dispatches the Wasm callback without confirming the VM context exists. Trigger: a crafted packet causes onDone to run before the in-VM context is created. Consequence: the callback dereferences null VM state, crashing the proxy (DoS); the missing guard is the cause, the crash the consequence.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Reported-by: syzbot+f427adf9324b92652ccc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    AP4_Atom(AP4_ATOM_TYPE_FTYP, size)', '    while (size) {', '        stream.ReadUI32(compatible_brand);'], 'added_lines': ['    AP4_Atom(AP4_ATOM_TYPE_FTYP, size),', '    m_MajorBrand(0),', '    m_MinorVersion(0)', '    if (size < 16) return;', '    while (size >= 4) {', '        AP4_Result result = stream.ReadUI32(compatible_brand);', '        if (AP4_FAILED(result)) return;']}
description: The AP4_FtypAtom class in Core/Ap4FtypAtom.cpp in Bento4 1.5.1.0 has an Infinite loop via a crafted MP4 file that triggers size mishandling.

code_evidence: Line 6 subtracts 16 from the attacker-controlled size without validating size >= 16, so a small size underflows to a huge unsigned value. Line 7 loops while size is nonzero, and line 11 decrements by 4 each iteration; with an underflowed value the loop count becomes enormous, and the exit condition only nears zero after billions of iterations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loop's exit condition is not practically reachable for a malformed size because the counter underflows to a near-maximum value, matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition and availability impact. This is distinct from a simple integer overflow because the exploitable effect is the non-terminating iteration.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constructor trusts the atom size and subtracts 16 before checking it, so a crafted MP4 with size < 16 causes unsigned underflow. The while(size) loop then iterates an effectively unbounded number of times, appending brands and consuming CPU, supporting a denial-of-service consequence.

description: In Wireshark through 2.0.13 and 2.2.x through 2.2.7, the WBXML dissector could go into an infinite loop, triggered by packet injection or a malformed capture file. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-wbxml.c by adding validation of the relationships between indexes and lengths. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-7702.

code_evidence: tvb_get_guintvar derives idx and len directly from attacker-controlled WBXML bytes; the code then uses 1 + len + idx both as the reported length in proto_tree_add_bytes_format and as the advance for off without checking idx or len against tvb_len. A malformed varint can yield an oversized idx, making off jump past tvb_len or wrap, and the loop condition off < tvb_len may fail to terminate as intended.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The decoded idx/len are input data used without validating required properties (bounds relative to tvb_len), exactly the improper input validation of CWE-20. The fixed version adds the missing sanity checks; the infinite loop is the downstream consequence, not the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoded uintvar index/length are trusted as offsets without validating them against the buffer size. Trigger: a crafted WBXML packet whose opaque-data uintvar encodes an unrealistic idx/len. Consequence: off advances by an attacker-controlled amount, causing the dissector to loop indefinitely (DoS) or read out of bounds.

description: A heap-based buffer overflow in the vrend_renderer_transfer_write_iov function in vrend_renderer.c in virglrenderer through 0.8.0 allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service, or QEMU guest-to-host escape and code execution, via VIRGL_CCMD_RESOURCE_INLINE_WRITE commands.

Callback function rtrs_clt_dev_release() for put_device() calls kfree(clt)

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. The `GatherNd` function takes arguments that determine the sizes of inputs and outputs. If the inputs given are greater than or equal to the sizes of the outputs, an out-of-bounds memory read is triggered. This issue has been patched in GitHub commit 595a65a3e224a0362d7e68c2213acfc2b499a196. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The function computes num_indices as indices->bytes / sizeof(IndicesT) and scans indices_values[i] for each i; the only constraint checked is that each index is non-negative.

Each non-string branch dispatches to GatherNd<..., IndicesT>(params, indices, output), which uses those index values to read from the params buffer; the function itself performs no upper-bound check against the params dimensions before dispatching.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing upper-bound constraint on attacker-influenced indices allows a read beyond the intended params buffer. This is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write, since the index values only select data to be read and copied to output.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the validation loop rejects negative indices but never verifies that each index is less than the corresponding dimension of params. Trigger: a crafted indices tensor containing a value greater than or equal to the params dimension passes the positivity check and is forwarded to GatherNd. Supported consequence: GatherNd reads past the end of the params buffer, an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg: Add more bounds checks in Jp2Image::encodeJp2Header
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        enforce(sizeof(Jp2BoxHeader) <= static_cast<size_t>(output.size_), Exiv2::kerCorruptedMetadata);', '        enforce(length <= static_cast<size_t>(output.size_), Exiv2::kerCorruptedMetadata);', '            enforce(sizeof(Jp2BoxHeader) <= length - count, Exiv2::kerCorruptedMetadata);']}
description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An out-of-bounds read was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.3 and earlier. The out-of-bounds read is triggered when Exiv2 is used to write metadata into a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service by crashing Exiv2, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. Note that this bug is only triggered when writing the metadata, which is a less frequently used Exiv2 operation than reading the metadata. For example, to trigger the bug in the Exiv2 command-line application, you need to add an extra command-line argument such as insert. The bug is fixed in version v0.27.4.

code_evidence: output is sized from boxBuf.size_ + iccProfile_.size_ + 100, but length is read from the box header at line 4 and used to bound the loop at line 8 without being validated against boxBuf's actual size; pSubBox = (p+count) then dereferences p+count at line 10.

subBox.length is read from attacker-controlled bytes at line 13 and only checked against length-count at line 18, not against the real buffer extent, so count += subBox.length can advance past boxBuf; the loop condition count<length then permits reading further sub-box headers.

The else branch copies subBox.length bytes from boxBuf.pData_+inlen at line 51, relying on newlen <= output.size_-outlen (line 50) rather than the source buffer bound, allowing a read past the end of boxBuf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads box headers and copies sub-box data using lengths derived from the input without validating them against the source buffer's extent, which is exactly reading past the end of the intended buffer (CWE-125). The checks compare against output size, not the source buffer, so they do not prevent the out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
enforce(newlen <= static_cast<size_t>(output.size_ - outlen), Exiv2::kerCorruptedMetadata);
::memcpy(output.pData_+outlen,boxBuf.pData_+inlen,subBox.length);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the header length and each sub-box length come from the crafted JP2 box buffer but are never constrained to boxBuf.size_. Trigger: writing metadata on a crafted image where length or subBox.length exceeds the real buffer. Consequence: p+count and boxBuf.pData_+inlen dereferences/memcpy read past the buffer, crashing Exiv2 (DoS).

commit_msg: Guard binary expressions from too much recursion.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tSAVEREC();', '\tINCREC();', '\tPOPREC();']}
description: jsparse.c in Artifex MuJS through 1.0.2 does not properly maintain the AST depth for binary expressions, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive recursion) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: shift() parses a sequence of binary shift operators using a goto loop, and each iteration recurses into additive() while building a new AST node via EXP2; the function contains no recursion-depth accounting or limit check around this loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's uncontrolled recursive parsing of binary expressions, with no depth guard, matches CWE-674 (Uncontrolled Recursion) and its availability impact. It is not merely a length/size issue; the weakness is missing recursion control in the parser.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser tracks no AST/recursion depth for chained binary expressions, so a crafted input with deeply nested or long binary expressions drives unbounded recursive descent. Trigger: a remote attacker supplies a crafted file; the consequence is excessive stack consumption and a denial of service (crash or resource exhaustion).

commit_msg:
This fixes CVE-2017-7482.

When a kerberos 5 ticket is being decoded so that it can be loaded into an
rxrpc-type key, there are several places in which the length of a
variable-length field is checked to make sure that it's not going to
overrun the available data - but the data is padded to the nearest
four-byte boundary and the code doesn't check for this extra.  This could
lead to the size-remaining variable wrapping and the data pointer going
over the end of the buffer.

Fix this by making the various variable-length data checks use the padded
length.

Reported-by: 石磊 <shilei-c@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Marc Dionne <marc.c.dionne@auristor.com>
Reviewed-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned int toklen = *_toklen, n_parts, loop, tmp;', '\t\tif (tmp > toklen)', '\t\ttmp = (tmp + 3) & ~3;', '\t\ttoklen -= tmp;', '\t\txdr += tmp >> 2;', '\tif (tmp > toklen)', '\ttmp = (tmp + 3) & ~3;', '\ttoklen -= tmp;', '\txdr += tmp >> 2;'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned int toklen = *_toklen, n_parts, loop, tmp, paddedlen;', '\t\tpaddedlen = (tmp + 3) & ~3;', '\t\tif (paddedlen > toklen)', '\t\ttoklen -= paddedlen;', '\t\txdr += paddedlen >> 2;', '\tpaddedlen = (tmp + 3) & ~3;', '\tif (paddedlen > toklen)', '\ttoklen -= paddedlen;', '\txdr += paddedlen >> 2;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before version 4.12, Kerberos 5 tickets decoded when using the RXRPC keys incorrectly assumes the size of a field. This could lead to the size-remaining variable wrapping and the data pointer going over the end of the buffer. This could possibly lead to memory corruption and possible privilege escalation.

code_evidence: The name-part length check compares the unpadded length tmp against toklen (line 28), but the subsequent decrement subtracts the padded length (tmp+3)&~3 (lines 35-36) and advances xdr by the padded word count (line 37).
The realm length check has the same pattern: line 45 checks tmp against toklen, while lines 52-54 subtract and advance by the padded length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsigned toklen subtraction of a padded length that was not validated against toklen produces an integer wraparound (CWE-190), which is the root cause enabling the out-of-bounds pointer. This is distinct from a simple missing bounds check because the check exists but uses the wrong (unpadded) length.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: validation uses the unpadded length while consumption uses the padded length, so a field whose padded size exceeds the remaining toklen passes the check. Subtracting the larger padded value from the unsigned toklen wraps it to a huge value, and the padded xdr advance moves the pointer past the buffer end; later reads/copies then operate out of bounds, enabling memory corruption.

commit_msg: Fix conversion from GDB register profile to rizin profile
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar name[16], groups[128], type[16];', '\t\tret = sscanf(ptr, " %s %d %d %d %d %s %s", name, &number, &rel,', '\t\t\t&offset, &size, type, groups);'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar name[GDB_NAME_SZ + 1], groups[GDB_GROUPS_SZ + 1], type[GDB_TYPE_SZ + 1];', '\t\tret = sscanf(ptr, " %" RZ_STR_DEF(GDB_NAME_SZ) "s %d %d %d %d %" RZ_STR_DEF(GDB_TYPE_SZ) "s %" RZ_STR_DEF(GDB_GROUPS_SZ) "s",', '\t\t\tname, &number, &rel, &offset, &size, type, groups);']}
description: Rizin is a UNIX-like reverse engineering framework and command-line toolset. In version 0.5.1 and prior, converting a GDB registers profile file into a Rizin register profile can result in a stack-based buffer overflow when the `name`, `type`, or `groups` fields have longer values than expected. Users opening untrusted GDB registers files (e.g. with the `drpg` or `arpg` commands) are affected by this flaw. Commit d6196703d89c84467b600ba2692534579dc25ed4 contains a patch for this issue. As a workaround, review the GDB register profiles before loading them with `drpg`/`arpg` commands.

code_evidence: Fixed-size stack buffers name[16], groups[128] and type[16] are declared for destination fields.
Each line from the untrusted GDB profile is isolated and passed to sscanf; the '\n' is replaced with '\0' but the field lengths are not checked.
sscanf with unbounded "%s" conversions writes name, type and groups from the input line into the fixed-size buffers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic buffer copy without input size checking: sscanf copies input into fixed buffers without validating length, matching CWE-120. It is a write overflow from an unchecked copy, not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence_lines.code: char name[16], groups[128], type[16];

ret = sscanf(ptr, " %s %d %d %d %d %s %s", name, &number, &rel,
&offset, &size, type, groups);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unbounded %s conversions copy attacker-controlled tokens from the GDB register profile into fixed-size stack arrays with no width limit. Trigger: a name, type, or groups token longer than its buffer (16, 16, or 128 bytes) in a file loaded via drpg/arpg. Consequence: stack-based buffer overflow, corrupting adjacent stack memory and potentially enabling code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
RTPS: Add offset overflow checking.

Add and use check_offset_addition, which adds an expert item and throws
an exception if we're about to overflow our offset.

Fixes #18737
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    offset += member_length;'], 'added_lines': ['    offset = check_offset_addition(offset, member_length, tree, NULL, tvb);']}
description: Excessive loops in multiple dissectors in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.2 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.10 and allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: The loop at [11] continues while deserialized_size < size, where size is a caller-supplied length and deserialized_size is incremented by attacker-controlled member_length at [38] (and by 12/4 at [23],[33]). member_length is read from the packet at [14] or [17] without any upper bound or validation against the remaining tvb length. The offset advances by offset += member_length at [37] and offset += 12 at [22] without overflow checking, so a crafted member_length or repeated members can drive iteration and offset advancement far beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's while loop at [11] is bounded only by deserialized_size versus size, with per-iteration progress supplied by untrusted packet fields and no limit on iteration count, matching CWE-834 Excessive Iteration. The missing offset-overflow check (fixed in the patch) reinforces that loop progress is not constrained, enabling resource exhaustion rather than a memory-corruption weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop termination depends on deserialized_size, which is advanced by unvalidated, attacker-controlled member_length values, and the offset is incremented without overflow/remaining-length checks. Trigger: a crafted RTPS serializedData packet with large or repeated member lengths causes many iterations and out-of-range offset arithmetic. Consequence: excessive CPU consumption and likely crash/DoS during dissection.

commit_msg:
If sctp_destroy_sock is called without sock_net(sk)->sctp.addr_wq_lock
held and sp->do_auto_asconf is true, then an element is removed
from the auto_asconf_splist without any proper locking.

This can happen in the following functions:
1. In sctp_accept, if sctp_sock_migrate fails.
2. In inet_create or inet6_create, if there is a bpf program
   attached to BPF_CGROUP_INET_SOCK_CREATE which denies
   creation of the sctp socket.

The bug is fixed by acquiring addr_wq_lock in sctp_destroy_sock
instead of sctp_close.

This addresses CVE-2021-23133.

Reported-by: Or Cohen <orcohen@paloaltonetworks.com>
Reviewed-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Fixes: 610236587600 ("bpf: Add new cgroup attach type to enable sock modifications")
Signed-off-by: Or Cohen <orcohen@paloaltonetworks.com>
Acked-by: Marcelo Ricardo Leitner <marcelo.leitner@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* Nothing can fail after this block, otherwise', '\t * sctp_destroy_sock() will be called without addr_wq_lock held', '\t */'], 'added_lines': []}
description: A race condition in Linux kernel SCTP sockets (net/sctp/socket.c) before 5.12-rc8 can lead to kernel privilege escalation from the context of a network service or an unprivileged process. If sctp_destroy_sock is called without sock_net(sk)->sctp.addr_wq_lock then an element is removed from the auto_asconf_splist list without any proper locking. This can be exploited by an attacker with network service privileges to escalate to root or from the context of an unprivileged user directly if a BPF_CGROUP_INET_SOCK_CREATE is attached which denies creation of some SCTP socket.

code_evidence: Under default_auto_asconf, the function takes addr_wq_lock, adds sp->auto_asconf_list to net->sctp.auto_asconf_splist, sets sp->do_auto_asconf=1, then releases the lock. The lock protects only this list insertion; nothing here ties the flag/list membership to the later destroy path's locking.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits: a shared resource (auto_asconf_splist) is accessed by concurrent code sequences without consistent exclusive synchronization, permitting an interfering sequence to modify it. The weakness is improper synchronization, not a memory-safety bug itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: do_auto_asconf and auto_asconf_splist membership are established here, but the corresponding removal in sctp_destroy_sock can run without addr_wq_lock, so list mutation races with concurrent list operations. Trigger: a socket is created with default_auto_asconf and destroyed via a path (accept-migrate failure or BPF-denied create) that skips the lock. Consequence: concurrent list corruption, potentially leading to privilege escalation.

description: The ISO IS-IS parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isoclns.c, several functions.

code_evidence: The loop reads stlv_type and stlv_len from tptr without first verifying that two bytes are captured, and only checks len > 2 before dereferencing.

For ISIS_SUBTLV_SPB_INSTANCE, ND_TCHECK2(*tptr, ISIS_SUBTLV_SPB_INSTANCE_MIN_LEN) is the only length guard; it does not confirm stlv_len is at least the minimum length, so EXTRACT_32BITS/EXTRACT_16BITS and the tmp-driven VLAN tuple loop read past the subTLV boundary.

For ISIS_SUBTLV_SPBM_SI, ND_TCHECK2(*tptr, 8) is checked but stlv_len is not validated against 8 before the fixed reads, and the while (stlv_len >= 4) loop reads 4 bytes per iteration against the captured data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads packet fields (EXTRACT_32BITS, EXTRACT_16BITS, *(tptr)) past the end of the intended subTLV/buffer due to missing length validation, which is exactly CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. It is not merely an integer issue; the direct consequence is reading memory beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser trusts attacker-controlled stlv_len and the tmp tree count to bound subTLV field reads. ND_TCHECK2 only verifies capture length, not that reads stay within the declared subTLV or TLV, so a crafted IS-IS packet with short subTLVs causes reads beyond the intended buffer, yielding a buffer over-read (disclosure or crash).

commit_msg:
tls: clear data after a starttls acknowledgement

After a starttls acknowledgement message, clear the buffers of any
incoming data / commands.  This will ensure that all future data is
handled securely.

Co-authored-by: Pietro Cerutti <gahr@gahr.ch>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      // Clear any data after the STARTTLS acknowledgement', '      mutt_socket_empty(conn);']}
description: Mutt before 1.14.4 and NeoMutt before 2020-06-19 have a STARTTLS buffering issue that affects IMAP, SMTP, and POP3. When a server sends a "begin TLS" response, the client reads additional data (e.g., from a man-in-the-middle attacker) and evaluates it in a TLS context, aka "response injection."

code_evidence: After sending STARTTLS, the function reads a single reply line into buf and checks for "382". On success it calls mutt_ssl_starttls(conn) without first discarding any bytes that the peer appended after the acknowledgement; the diff adds mutt_socket_empty(conn) precisely to clear that buffered data, confirming the pre-patch read path retained attacker-influenced bytes for the subsequent TLS session.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The trailing externally supplied bytes are special elements that modify how the downstream TLS/protocol parser interprets subsequent data, matching CWE-74's injection structure. It is not a lower-level buffer flaw: the data is validly read but not neutralized before being passed to the downstream TLS context.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the client consumes only the STARTTLS reply line and leaves trailing bytes in the connection buffer. Trigger: a malicious or man-in-the-middle server sends "382" plus injected data. Those bytes remain queued and are evaluated after the TLS handshake, letting an attacker alter the protocol stream (response injection) and potentially bypass the protection mechanism.

commit_msg:
Fixed bug in 'lua_upvaluejoin'

Bug-fix: joining an upvalue with itself could cause a use-after-free
crash.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static UpVal **getupvalref (lua_State *L, int fidx, int n, LClosure **pf) {', '  if (pf) *pf = f;'], 'added_lines': ['static UpVal **getupvalref (lua_State *L, int fidx, int n) {']}
description: Lua 5.3.5 has a use-after-free in lua_upvaluejoin in lapi.c. For example, a crash outcome might be achieved by an attacker who is able to trigger a debug.upvaluejoin call in which the arguments have certain relationships.

code_evidence: getupvalref resolves fidx to a stack slot, requires it to be a Lua closure, then stores the closure pointer f in the caller-supplied out-parameter *pf (line 7) while also returning a pointer into that same closure's upvals array (line 8). Both the returned UpVal** and the exposed LClosure* alias the closure's internal upvalue storage; nothing here copies or pins the upvalue, so the caller can hold a reference to memory tied to the closure's lifetime.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the exposed upvalue pointer can be dereferenced after the underlying upvalue/closure storage is freed, which is exactly reuse of freed memory. A mere null-pointer or bounds issue (CWE-476/CWE-787) does not capture the lifetime violation; the defect is that a reference outlives its allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the helper hands out an interior pointer (&f->upvals[n-1]) plus the owning closure pointer, letting a caller like lua_upvaluejoin operate on an upvalue reference without ensuring it stays live. Trigger: debug.upvaluejoin with arguments whose relationships make the target upvalue alias the closure being modified, so the upvalue storage is freed/replaced while the stale pointer is still used. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the upvalue slot, leading to memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Jann Horn reported a problem with commit eb1231f73c4d ("selinux:
clarify task subjective and objective credentials") where some LSM
hooks were attempting to access the subjective credentials of a task
other than the current task.  Generally speaking, it is not safe to
access another task's subjective credentials and doing so can cause
a number of problems.

Further, while looking into the problem, I realized that Smack was
suffering from a similar problem brought about by a similar commit
1fb057dcde11 ("smack: differentiate between subjective and objective
task credentials").

This patch addresses this problem by restoring the use of the task's
objective credentials in those cases where the task is other than the
current executing task.  Not only does this resolve the problem
reported by Jann, it is arguably the correct thing to do in these
cases.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: eb1231f73c4d ("selinux: clarify task subjective and objective credentials")
Fixes: 1fb057dcde11 ("smack: differentiate between subjective and objective task credentials")
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Eric W. Biederman <ebiederm@xmission.com>
Acked-by: Casey Schaufler <casey@schaufler-ca.com>
Signed-off-by: Paul Moore <paul@paul-moore.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tu32 sid = task_sid_subj(target);'], 'added_lines': ['\tu32 sid = task_sid_obj(target);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.14.8. A use-after-free in selinux_ptrace_traceme (aka the SELinux handler for PTRACE_TRACEME) could be used by local attackers to cause memory corruption and escalate privileges, aka CID-a3727a8bac0a. This occurs because of an attempt to access the subjective credentials of another task.

code_evidence: task_sid_subj(target) dereferences target's subjective credentials; target is the passed-in task_struct, which may differ from the current task, so its subjective cred pointer can be stale or concurrently freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Accessing another task's subjective credentials yields a use-after-free of the cred structure, matching CWE-416. The fix switches to task_sid_obj(target), which uses the objective creds that remain valid for other tasks; this contrasts a mere permission-check bug rather than a lifetime issue.

evidence_lines.code: u32 sid = task_sid_subj(target);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function reads the subjective credentials of a non-current task via task_sid_subj(target). Subjective credentials are only valid for the task itself; for another task they may reference freed memory, so the resulting sid read (and its use in avc_has_perm at lines 14-20) can touch freed memory, causing memory corruption or privilege escalation.

Fixes #76

FossilOrigin-Name: 1a370f5a3fc952b9f433f5607a68f83871294222452b85a5092bde44c309a7ce
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (Jsi_ObjArraySizer(interp, obj, n) <= 0)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (Jsi_ObjArraySizer(interp, obj, n+1) <= 0)']}
description: Jsish v3.5.0 was discovered to contain a heap-use-after-free via jsi_ValueCopyMove in src/jsiValue.c. This vulnerability can lead to a Denial of Service (DoS).

code_evidence: n is set from arrayindex and passed directly to Jsi_ObjArraySizer, which is only asked to guarantee capacity for index n rather than n+1; the return is checked before continuing.
The slot obj->arr[n] is then read and, if non-null, its reference count decremented via Jsi_DecrRefCount, potentially freeing the value.
The same slot is then overwritten with obj->arr[n] = value, and the assertion only checks arrCnt against arrMaxSize, not that n was within the resized capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because obj->arr[n] is dereferenced after the underlying array storage may have been freed by the sizer/reallocation path when the wrong size bound was requested. This is a use-after-free rather than a plain out-of-bounds write because the stale slot access occurs after memory management.

evidence_lines.code:
if (obj->arr[n])
Jsi_DecrRefCount(interp, obj->arr[n]);

Assert(obj->arrCnt<=obj->arrMaxSize);
obj->arr[n] = value;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sizer is invoked with n instead of n+1, so the array may not be grown to cover index n, leaving obj->arr[n] outside the valid allocation. The access at obj->arr[n] (read, decref, and write) then touches memory that may have been freed or reallocated, giving a heap use-after-free that can crash or corrupt memory.

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

In order to fail safe in the supported case, re-implement all the VT-x
instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int nvmx_handle_vmptrld(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)'], 'added_lines': ['static int nvmx_handle_vmptrld(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)']}

crypto: rng - Remove old low-level rng interface

Now that all rng implementations have switched over to the new
interface, we can remove the old low-level interface.

Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct crypto_rng *rng = __crypto_rng_cast(tfm);', '\tstruct rng_alg *alg = crypto_rng_alg(rng);', '\tstruct old_rng_alg *oalg = crypto_old_rng_alg(rng);', '', '\tif (oalg->rng_make_random) {', '\t\trng->generate = generate;', '\t\trng->seed = rngapi_reset;', '\t\trng->seedsize = oalg->seedsize;', '\t\treturn 0;', '\t}', '', '\trng->generate = alg->generate;', '\trng->seed = alg->seed;', '\trng->seedsize = alg->seedsize;', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: The rngapi_reset function in crypto/rng.c in the Linux kernel before 4.2 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference).

code_evidence: crypto_old_rng_alg(rng) is retrieved and immediately dereferenced as oalg->rng_make_random without a NULL check.
When oalg->rng_make_random is false, the code falls through and dereferences alg->generate, alg->seed and alg->seedsize without verifying alg is non-NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs direct member dereferences on pointers that may be NULL, matching CWE-476. The weakness is the missing NULL validation before use, not a type confusion or bounds error; the supported consequence is a crash/DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The init routine assumes both the old and new algorithm descriptors returned from the tfm are valid and dereferences their members unconditionally. If either descriptor lookup yields NULL (e.g., a transform lacking the corresponding algorithm data), the member access crashes the kernel, causing a denial of service.

commit_msg:
win: fix unsavory rwlock fallback implementation

Before this patch an uv_mutex_t (backed by a critical section) could be
released by a tread different from the thread that acquired it, which is
not allowed. This is fixed by using a semaphore instead.

Note that the affected code paths were used on Windows XP and Windows
Server 2003 only.

Fixes: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/issues/515
PR-URL: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/pull/516
Reviewed-By: Ben Noordhuis <info@bnoordhuis.nl>
Reviewed-By: Saúl Ibarra Corretgé <saghul@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  uv_mutex_unlock(&rwlock->fallback_.write_mutex_);'], 'added_lines': ['  if (!ReleaseSemaphore(rwlock->fallback_.write_lock_.sem, 1, NULL))', '    uv_fatal_error(GetLastError(), "ReleaseSemaphore");']}
description: The uv_rwlock_t fallback implementation for Windows XP and Server 2003 in libuv before 1.7.4 does not properly prevent threads from releasing the locks of other threads, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (deadlock) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging a race condition.

code_evidence: The function releases the write lock by calling uv_mutex_unlock on rwlock->fallback_.write_mutex_ without verifying that the calling thread is the one that acquired the lock; the mutex is a process-wide object stored in the shared rwlock, so any thread reaching this function can release it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent shared-resource access with improper synchronization: the unlock operation is not exclusive to the owning thread, creating a timing window in which an interfering code sequence modifies lock state, matching CWE-362.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write lock is a mutex whose ownership is not enforced at unlock time, so an interfering thread can release a lock held by another thread. Trigger: concurrent threads in the fallback rwlock path where one thread calls wrunlock while another owns the write_mutex_. Consequence: lock state corruption leading to deadlock or other unspecified impact.

commit_msg:
adapter: Fix storing discoverable setting

discoverable setting shall only be store when changed via Discoverable
property and not when discovery client set it as that be considered
temporary just for the lifetime of the discovery.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tset_discovery_discoverable(adapter, false);']}
description: bluetoothd from bluez incorrectly saves adapters' Discoverable status when a device is powered down, and restores it when powered up. If a device is powered down while discoverable, it will be discoverable when powered on again. This could lead to inadvertent exposure of the bluetooth stack to physically nearby attackers.

code_evidence: adapter_stop() tears down the adapter's discovery state: it cancels scanning, removes the discovery list, clears filtered_discovery and no_scan_restart_delay, and sets adapter->discovering = false. The function never clears the adapter's persistent Discoverable setting, so the discoverable state set through the discovery client survives the power-down and is restored on the next power-up.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to enforce the intended constraint that discovery-client discoverability must not persist, so a temporary authorization/visibility state survives teardown and is restored—an incorrect authorization/state check (CWE-863), not merely a missing input validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: adapter_stop() resets discovery-related fields but leaves the Discoverable setting untouched, so a temporary discoverable state established by a discovery client is persisted. Trigger: the adapter is powered down while discoverable. Consequence: on power-up the adapter is again discoverable, exposing the Bluetooth stack to physically nearby attackers.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Allow g_variant_byteswap() to operate on tree-form variants

This avoids needing to always serialise a variant before byteswapping it.
With variants in non-normal forms, serialisation can result in a large
increase in size of the variant, and a lot of allocations for leaf
`GVariant`s. This can lead to a denial of service attack.

Avoid that by changing byteswapping so that it happens on the tree form
of the variant if the input is in non-normal form. If the input is in
normal form (either serialised or in tree form), continue using the
existing code as byteswapping an already-serialised normal variant is
about 3× faster than byteswapping on the equivalent tree form.

The existing unit tests cover byteswapping well, but need some
adaptation so that they operate on tree form variants too.

I considered dropping the serialised byteswapping code and doing all
byteswapping on tree-form variants, as that would make maintenance
simpler (avoiding having two parallel implementations of byteswapping).
However, most inputs to `g_variant_byteswap()` are likely to be
serialised variants (coming from a byte array of input from some foreign
source) and most of them are going to be in normal form (as corruption
and malicious action are rare). So getting rid of the serialised
byteswapping code would impose quite a performance penalty on the common
case.

description: A flaw was found in GLib. GVariant deserialization is vulnerable to a slowdown issue where a crafted GVariant can cause excessive processing, leading to denial of service.

code_evidence: g_variant_deep_copy takes a GVariant value and recursively rebuilds it, with no depth or size bound on the input.

For MAYBE/TUPLE/DICT_ENTRY/VARIANT, the loop walks every child (g_variant_n_children) and recursively calls g_variant_deep_copy on each child, so work scales with the full tree of the attacker-supplied variant.

The ARRAY branch loops over the array children, calling g_variant_get_child_value/g_variant_maybe_get_child_value and recursing per child; each child is deep-copied, so cost is proportional to the number of children and their nesting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function fails to bound the resources (CPU time, memory, recursion depth) consumed while processing input, allowing resource exhaustion. It is not a memory-safety bug such as CWE-787; the defect is uncontrolled consumption of processing resources.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursive deep-copy has no limit on nesting depth or total number of children, so a crafted, deeply nested or wide GVariant drives unbounded recursion and per-child allocation. Trigger: deserializing/byteswapping an attacker-controlled variant in non-normal form. Consequence: excessive CPU and memory consumption, leading to denial of service.

description: Memory leak in Kafka protocol dissector in Wireshark 3.4.0 and 3.2.0 to 3.2.8 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file.

code_evidence: Each loop iteration allocates a new output buffer via wmem_alloc and appends a child real-data tvb wrapping output.dst; on ZSTD_isError the code jumps to end before ret is set.
The end label finalizes composite_tvb and frees zds, but the per-iteration allocations are only released if the composite tvb is attached to decompressed_tvb.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated memory is not released after its effective lifetime when the error path discards the only reference. This is a missing-release leak, not an out-of-bounds write or double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: allocated decompression buffers are only retained through composite_tvb, and on error ret stays 0, so *decompressed_tvb is never set. Trigger: a malformed or crafted zstd payload causing ZSTD_decompressStream to return an error. Consequence: composite_tvb and its appended child buffers become unreachable, leaking packet-scope memory across repeated packets (DoS).

commit_msg:
PR22169, heap-based buffer overflow in read_1_byte

The .debug_line header length field doesn't include the length field
itself, ie. it's the size of the rest of .debug_line.

	PR 22169
	* dwarf2.c (decode_line_info): Correct .debug_line unit_length check.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (unit->line_offset + lh.total_length > stash->dwarf_line_size)', '\t(_("Dwarf Error: Line info data is bigger (%#Lx) than the space remaining in the section (%#Lx)"),', '\t lh.total_length, stash->dwarf_line_size - unit->line_offset);'], 'added_lines': ['  if (lh.total_length > (size_t) (line_end - line_ptr))', '\t(_("Dwarf Error: Line info data is bigger (%#Lx)"', '\t   " than the space remaining in the section (%#lx)"),', '\t lh.total_length, (unsigned long) (line_end - line_ptr));']}
description: decode_line_info in dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, mishandles a length calculation, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted ELF file, related to read_1_byte.

code_evidence: The length guard checks unit->line_offset + lh.total_length against stash->dwarf_line_size, but lh.total_length excludes the length field itself, so the bound permits a unit that extends past the section end.
lh.total_length is read from attacker-controlled .debug_line bytes and only zero-extended; the check at line 56 uses the raw field without accounting for the 4/8/12 bytes already consumed.
line_end is then set to line_ptr + lh.total_length at line 64, so line_end can point beyond the buffer, and subsequent reads such as read_1_byte at line 188 use this over-extended line_end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads one byte past the intended buffer because the length check fails to constrain line_end to the section; this is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.

evidence_lines.code:
op_code = read_1_byte (abfd, line_ptr, line_end);
line_ptr += 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unit_length bound check omits the length field size, so a crafted ELF with a large total_length passes validation and line_end is computed beyond the allocated .debug_line buffer. The decode loop then calls read_1_byte with the invalid line_end, causing a heap out-of-bounds read and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
xen/events: avoid removing an event channel while handling it

Today it can happen that an event channel is being removed from the
system while the event handling loop is active. This can lead to a
race resulting in crashes or WARN() splats when trying to access the
irq_info structure related to the event channel.

Fix this problem by using a rwlock taken as reader in the event
handling loop and as writer when deallocating the irq_info structure.

As the observed problem was a NULL dereference in evtchn_from_irq()
make this function more robust against races by testing the irq_info
pointer to be not NULL before dereferencing it.

And finally make all accesses to evtchn_to_irq[row][col] atomic ones
in order to avoid seeing partial updates of an array element in irq
handling. Note that irq handling can be entered only for event channels
which have been valid before, so any not populated row isn't a problem
in this regard, as rows are only ever added and never removed.

This is XSA-331.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Marek Marczykowski-Górecki <marmarek@invisiblethingslab.com>
Reported-by: Jinoh Kang <luke1337@theori.io>
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tevtchn_to_irq[row][col] = -1;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tWRITE_ONCE(evtchn_to_irq[row][col], -1);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.9.1, as used with Xen through 4.14.x. drivers/xen/events/events_base.c allows event-channel removal during the event-handling loop (a race condition). This can cause a use-after-free or NULL pointer dereference, as demonstrated by a dom0 crash via events for an in-reconfiguration paravirtualized device, aka CID-073d0552ead5.

code_evidence: The loop writes each element of the shared array evtchn_to_irq[row][col] with a plain assignment to -1. This array is concurrently read in the event-handling loop (evtchn_from_irq), so the non-atomic store can race with a reader observing a partially updated element. The patch converts this store to WRITE_ONCE, confirming the writer-side plain access was the concern.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because two concurrent code sequences access the same shared resource (evtchn_to_irq array) without proper synchronization/atomicity. The plain store in clear_evtchn_to_irq_row violates atomicity relative to concurrent readers, which is the race condition this patch addresses via WRITE_ONCE.

evidence_lines.code:
for (col = 0; col < EVTCHN_PER_ROW; col++)
evtchn_to_irq[row][col] = -1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: evtchn_to_irq array elements are modified with a non-atomic plain store while other code concurrently reads the same elements. Trigger: an event-channel row is cleared while the event-handling loop reads evtchn_to_irq[row][col]. Supported consequence: the reader can observe a partial/inconsistent value, leading to a race-induced NULL dereference or crash in evtchn_from_irq.

description: Stack-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.

code_evidence: Stack arrays arridx, curi and word are each sized MAXWLEN, and depth indexes all three.
In the else branch, word[depth++] = c writes at the current depth and then increments depth; arridx[depth] and curi[depth] are written at the new depth.

word[depth] = NUL writes the terminator at the current depth. The loop only stops when curi[depth] exceeds the node count, so depth can grow with each trie level until it reaches MAXWLEN, and the next write occurs one past the end of the arrays.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The overflowed buffers (word, arridx, curi) are local stack arrays, and the out-of-bounds writes stem from missing length validation, matching CWE-121. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, because the writes at lines 132-134 and 114 modify adjacent stack memory.

commit_msg:
Adding Error Check for f_code Parameters

In MPEG1, the valid range for the forward and backward f_code parameters
is [1, 7]. Adding a check to enforce this. Without the check, the value
could be 0. We read (f_code - 1) bits from the stream and reading a
negative number of bits from the stream is undefined.

description: LookupCol.c in X.Org X through X11R7.7 and libX11 before 1.7.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The libX11 XLookupColor request (intended for server-side color lookup) contains a flaw allowing a client to send color-name requests with a name longer than the maximum size allowed by the protocol (and also longer than the maximum packet size for normal-sized packets). The user-controlled data exceeding the maximum size is then interpreted by the server as additional X protocol requests and executed, e.g., to disable X server authorization completely. commit_msg:
Avoid some undefined pointer arithmetic

A common idiom in the codebase is:

if (p + len > limit)
{
    return; /* Too long */
}

Where "p" points to some malloc'd data of SIZE bytes and
limit == p + SIZE

"len" here could be from some externally supplied data (e.g. from a TLS
message).

The rules of C pointer arithmetic are such that "p + len" is only well
defined where len <= SIZE. Therefore the above idiom is actually
undefined behaviour.

For example this could cause problems if some malloc implementation
provides an address for "p" such that "p + len" actually overflows for
values of len that are too big and therefore p + len < limit!

Issue reported by Guido Vranken.

CVE-2016-2177

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (p + SSL3_RANDOM_SIZE + session_length + 1 >= d + n) {', '    if (p + j > d + n) {', '        if (p + 1 > d + n) {', '        if (p + cookie_len > d + n) {', '    if (p + 2 > d + n) {', '    if ((p + i + 1) > (d + n)) {', '    if ((p + i) > (d + n)) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (SSL3_RANDOM_SIZE + session_length + 1 >= (d + n) - p) {', '    if ((d + n) - p < j) {', '        if ((d + n) - p < 1) {', '        if ((d + n ) - p < cookie_len) {', '    if ((d + n ) - p < 2) {', '    if ((d + n) - p < i + 1) {', '    if ((d + n) - p < i) {']}
description: OpenSSL through 1.0.2h incorrectly uses pointer arithmetic for heap-buffer boundary checks, which might allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (integer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging unexpected malloc behavior, related to s3_srvr.c, ssl_sess.c, and t1_lib.c.

code_evidence: At lines 50-53, the bound check computes 'p + SSL3_RANDOM_SIZE + session_length + 1 >= d + n' where session_length is attacker-controlled from the TLS message; pointer addition past the buffer is undefined and can wrap.
At lines 62-65, 'p + j > d + n' uses attacker-supplied j as a pointer offset before validating it; oversized j can overflow the pointer arithmetic and yield a false pass.
At lines 90-93, 'p + 1 > d + n' is a pointer-addition comparison that is only well defined if p+1 stays within the allocation.
At lines 96-99, 'p + cookie_len > d + n' adds attacker-controlled cookie_len to p, which can wrap and bypass the length check.
At lines 151-154, 'p + 2 > d + n' performs pointer arithmetic before the remaining-length comparison, relying on undefined behavior.
At lines 162-165, '(p + i + 1) > (d + n)' adds the externally supplied cipher-list length i to p, risking pointer wraparound.
At lines 207-210, '(p + i) > (d + n)' again adds attacker-controlled i to p for a boundary check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the flawed checks rely on integer/pointer addition that can overflow or wrap, defeating the boundary comparison. This is integer overflow enabling a bypassed length check, distinct from a simple off-by-one or missing check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: boundary checks add externally supplied lengths (session_length, j, cookie_len, i) to a heap pointer p before comparing, so 'p + len' is only defined when len <= remaining size. Trigger: a remote TLS ClientHello with oversized length fields. Consequence: pointer arithmetic can wrap, making the check pass and leading to out-of-bounds reads/doS.

commit_msg:
Don't treat the packet length as unsigned.

The scanf family of functions are as annoyingly bad at handling unsigned
numbers as strtoul() is - both of them are perfectly willing to accept a
value beginning with a negative sign as an unsigned value.  When using
strtoul(), you can compensate for this by explicitly checking for a '-'
as the first character of the string, but you can't do that with
sscanf().

So revert to having pkt_len be signed, and scanning it with %d, but
check for a negative value and fail if we see a negative value.

description: A vulnerability was found in ImageMagick. This security flaw ouccers as an undefined behaviors of casting double to size_t in svg, mvg and other coders (recurring bugs of CVE-2022-32546).

code_evidence: Percent-based width/height are computed as floor(scale.x*stasis_width/100.0+0.5) and floor(scale.y*stasis_height/100.0+0.5), then cast directly to size_t with no bound check on the double value.
Aspect-ratio branch likewise computes *height via floor(PerceptibleReciprocal(geometry_ratio)*stasis_height*image_ratio)+0.5 and casts to size_t.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an unchecked numeric conversion where a computed value can exceed the destination integer's range, matching CWE-190's integer overflow/wraparound from an assumed-bounded calculation. This is distinct from CWE-681's general conversion error because the concrete risk is size_t wraparound from oversized geometry products.

*width=(size_t) floor(scale.x*stasis_width/100.0+0.5);
*height=(size_t) floor(scale.y*stasis_height/100.0+0.5);

*height=(size_t) floor((double) (PerceptibleReciprocal(
geometry_ratio)*stasis_height*image_ratio)+0.5);

commit_msg:
Make verification match the new restricted directory symlink behavior

Only follow directory symlinks owned by target directory owner or root
during verification to match the behavior of fsmVerify() in the new
CVE-2017-7500 world order.

The code is klunkier than it should and the logic should use common code
with fsmVerify() instead of duplicating it here, but that needs more
changes than is comfortable to backport so starting with this.

Also worth noting that the previous "follow the link" logic from
commit 3ccd774255b8215733e0bdfdf5a683da9dd10923 was not quite right,
it'd fail with RPMVERIFY_LSTATFAIL on a broken symlink when it should've
ran verification on the symlink itself. This behavior is fixed here too.

Finally, once again fakechroot gets in the way and forces the related
verify testcase to be changed to be able to create a valid link. Reuse
the replacement testcase for the purpose and add another case for
verifying an invalid link.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (S_ISDIR(fmode) && S_ISLNK(sb.st_mode) && stat(fn, &sb) != 0) {', '\tvfy |= RPMVERIFY_LSTATFAIL;', '\tgoto exit;'], 'added_lines': ['    if (S_ISDIR(fmode) && S_ISLNK(sb.st_mode)) {', '\tstruct stat dsb;', '\t/* ...if it actually points to a directory  */', '\tif (stat(fn, &dsb) == 0 && S_ISDIR(dsb.st_mode)) {', '\t    uid_t fuid;', '\t    /* ...and is by a legit user, to match fsmVerify() behavior */', '\t    if (sb.st_uid == 0 ||', '\t\t\t(rpmugUid(rpmfilesFUser(fi, ix), &fuid) == 0 &&', '\t\t\t sb.st_uid == fuid)) {', '\t\tsb = dsb; /* struct assignment */', '\t    }', '\t}']}
description: It was found that rpm did not properly handle RPM installations when a destination path was a symbolic link to a directory, possibly changing ownership and permissions of an arbitrary directory, and RPM files being placed in an arbitrary destination. An attacker, with write access to a directory in which a subdirectory will be installed, could redirect that directory to an arbitrary location and gain root privilege.

code_evidence: lstat() records the link itself, then stat(fn,&sb) unconditionally follows a directory symlink and overwrites sb with the target's metadata, so later checks inspect the referenced directory rather than the link.
After following, S_ISLNK(sb.st_mode) is false, so the RPMVERIFY_LINKTO block is skipped and readlink()/flink comparison never runs; only RPMVERIFY_MODE is cleared.
Verification therefore validates digest, size, mode, owner and group of the symlink target, letting an attacker-controlled link redirect checks to an arbitrary directory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 covers accessing a file via a name that resolves through a link to an unintended resource. Here stat() follows the directory symlink and subsequent checks use the resolved target, exactly the improper link resolution before file access; it is not merely a TOCTOU race (CWE-367) because the link is followed by design.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function resolves fn through stat() before performing attribute verification, without constraining the link target to the expected directory. A symlink planted where a directory is expected makes verification operate on the arbitrary target, so mismatched ownership/permissions or content are attributed to the installed path, enabling redirection of install/verify operations to attacker-chosen locations.

commit_msg:
libceph: harden msgr2.1 frame segment length checks

ceph_frame_desc::fd_lens is an int array.  decode_preamble() thus
effectively casts u32 -> int but the checks for segment lengths are
written as if on unsigned values.  While reading in HELLO or one of the
AUTH frames (before authentication is completed), arithmetic in
head_onwire_len() can get duped by negative ctrl_len and produce
head_len which is less than CEPH_PREAMBLE_LEN but still positive.
This would lead to a buffer overrun in prepare_read_control() as the
preamble gets copied to the newly allocated buffer of size head_len.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: cd1a677cad99 ("libceph, ceph: implement msgr2.1 protocol (crc and secure modes)")
Reported-by: Thelford Williams <thelford@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Ilya Dryomov <idryomov@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Xiubo Li <xiubli@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tBUG_ON(front_len < 0 || front_len > CEPH_MSG_MAX_FRONT_LEN ||', '\t       middle_len < 0 || middle_len > CEPH_MSG_MAX_MIDDLE_LEN ||', '\t       data_len < 0 || data_len > CEPH_MSG_MAX_DATA_LEN);', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in net/ceph/messenger_v2.c in the Linux kernel before 6.4.5. There is an integer signedness error, leading to a buffer overflow and remote code execution via HELLO or one of the AUTH frames. This occurs because of an untrusted length taken from a TCP packet in ceph_decode_32.

code_evidence: __tail_onwire_len computes the on-wire tail length from front_len, middle_len and data_len without validating their sign or upper bounds. Lines 7-8 and 9-10 add these raw values into the returned length; a negative or oversized value propagates directly into the size computation used for later allocation and copying.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The size calculation feeds an allocation and subsequent copy of frame data, and the missing length validation permits a buffer overrun, matching CWE-120's buffer copy without checking input size. The signedness/arithmetic error is the root cause, but the supported weakness is the unchecked copy driven by the computed size.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length arguments are used in arithmetic without checking that they are non-negative and within CEPH_MSG_MAX_* limits. Trigger: an untrusted frame descriptor supplies negative or oversized lengths (e.g., via signedness conversion from u32). Consequence: a miscalculated head/tail length leads to an undersized buffer that is later overrun by a copy.

commit_msg:
analysisd: fix possible null ptr deref in OS_CleanMSG.

If the `msg` provided to `OS_CleanMSG` has a `(` after the ID, but
doesn't not contain a `->` or `:` it should be rejected with
a `FORMAT_ERROR`.

Prev. to this commit nesting `strstr` for `->` as the first argument to
`strchr` for `:` results in a null ptr deref when the message is
malformed.

description: In OSSEC-HIDS 2.7 through 3.5.0, the server component responsible for log analysis (ossec-analysisd) is vulnerable to a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via crafted messages written directly to the analysisd UNIX domain socket by a local user.

code_evidence: When msg begins with '(', line 14 nests strstr(msg, "->") as the first argument to strchr. If the message lacks "->", strstr returns NULL and strchr(NULL, ':') dereferences it before the line 15 NULL check can run. The NULL check guards the wrong pointer, so the defect is the unchecked inner strstr, not an out-of-bounds or format-string issue.

Trigger: a crafted message from a local user that starts with '(' but contains no "->" separator. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference crashes ossec-analysisd, causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
sched/fair: Fix low cpu usage with high throttling by removing expiration of cpu-local slices

It has been observed, that highly-threaded, non-cpu-bound applications
running under cpu.cfs_quota_us constraints can hit a high percentage of
periods throttled while simultaneously not consuming the allocated
amount of quota. This use case is typical of user-interactive non-cpu
bound applications, such as those running in kubernetes or mesos when
run on multiple cpu cores.

This has been root caused to cpu-local run queue being allocated per cpu
bandwidth slices, and then not fully using that slice within the period.
At which point the slice and quota expires. This expiration of unused
slice results in applications not being able to utilize the quota for
which they are allocated.

The non-expiration of per-cpu slices was recently fixed by
'commit 512ac999d275 ("sched/fair: Fix bandwidth timer clock drift
condition")'. Prior to that it appears that this had been broken since
at least 'commit 51f2176d74ac ("sched/fair: Fix unlocked reads of some
cfs_b->quota/period")' which was introduced in v3.16-rc1 in 2014. That
added the following conditional which resulted in slices never being
expired.

if (cfs_rq->runtime_expires != cfs_b->runtime_expires) {
	/* extend local deadline, drift is bounded above by 2 ticks */
	cfs_rq->runtime_expires += TICK_NSEC;

Because this was broken for nearly 5 years, and has recently been fixed
and is now being noticed by many users running kubernetes
(https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/67577) it is my opinion
that the mechanisms around expiring runtime should be removed
altogether.

This allows quota already allocated to per-cpu run-queues to live longer
than the period boundary. This allows threads on runqueues that do not
use much CPU to continue to use their remaining slice over a longer
period of time than cpu.cfs_period_us. However, this helps prevent the
above condition of hitting throttling while also not fully utilizing
your cpu quota.

This theoretically allows a machine to use slightly more than its
allotted quota in some periods. This overflow would be bounded by the
remaining quota left on each per-cpu runqueueu. This is typically no
more than min_cfs_rq_runtime=1ms per cpu. For CPU bound tasks this will
change nothing, as they should theoretically fully utilize all of their
quota in each period. For user-interactive tasks as described above this
provides a much better user/application experience as their cpu
utilization will more closely match the amount they requested when they
hit throttling. This means that cpu limits no longer strictly apply per
period for non-cpu bound applications, but that they are still accurate
over longer timeframes.

This greatly improves performance of high-thread-count, non-cpu bound
applications with low cfs_quota_us allocation on high-core-count
machines. In the case of an artificial testcase (10ms/100ms of quota on
80 CPU machine), this commit resulted in almost 30x performance
improvement, while still maintaining correct cpu quota restrictions.
That testcase is available at https://github.com/indeedeng/fibtest.

Fixes: 512ac999d275 ("sched/fair: Fix bandwidth timer clock drift condition")
Signed-off-by: Dave Chiluk <chiluk+linux@indeed.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Reviewed-by: Phil Auld <pauld@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Ben Segall <bsegall@google.com>
Cc: Ingo Molnar <mingo@redhat.com>

Cc: Kyle Anderson <kwa@yelp.com>
Cc: Gabriel Munos <gmunoz@netflix.com>

Cc: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Cc: Brendan Gregg <bgregg@netflix.com>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/1563900266-19734-2-git-send-email-chiluk+linux@indeed.com

description: kernel/sched/fair.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.9, when cpu.cfs_quota_us is used (e.g., with Kubernetes), allows attackers to cause a denial of service against non-cpu-bound applications by generating a workload that triggers unwanted slice expiration, aka CID-de53fd7aedb1. (In other words, although this slice expiration would typically be seen with benign workloads, it is possible that an attacker could calculate how many stray requests are required to force an entire Kubernetes cluster into a low-performance state caused by slice expiration, and ensure that a DDoS attack sent that number of stray requests. An attack does not affect the stability of the kernel; it only causes mismanagement of application execution.)

code_evidence: assign_cfs_rq_runtime snapshots cfs_b->expires_seq and cfs_b->runtime_expires under the bandwidth lock, then after unlocking copies them into the per-CPU cfs_rq when the sequence differs. This local expiration bookkeeping controls when a CPU-local runtime slice is considered expired.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function governs allocation/expiration of the limited CPU bandwidth resource; its expiration bookkeeping fails to correctly release and re-use the quota, causing sustained resource mismanagement and reduced service availability, matching CWE-400. A pure race would be CWE-362, but the supported issue is uncontrolled consumption/maintenance of the quota resource.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The per-CPU runtime slice is stamped with the global expiration sequence/deadline, and the drift-extension logic lets slices outlive the period without being properly accounted against the global quota. Trigger: a high-thread-count, non-CPU-bound workload under a small cpu.cfs_quota_us keeps requesting slices whose local expiration is misaligned, so periods throttle while allocated quota remains unused. Consequence: CPU bandwidth quota is mismanaged, degrading throughput of the constrained applications (DoS-like availability impact).

code_evidence: Line 15 casts STRLEN(reg_prev_sub) to int, and line 16 sizes the destination buffer as alloc(STRLEN(newsub) + prevlen) with no bound check on the sum.

Lines 19-22 then copy prefixlen bytes, prevlen bytes of reg_prev_sub, and the postfix via STRCPY at tmpsub + len + prevlen; line 25 sets p = newsub + len + prevlen, so the computed sizes and offsets drive the copy destinations.

The out-of-bounds write is the consequence; a plain buffer-copy CWE would not capture the wrapping arithmetic that causes it.

tmpsub = alloc(STRLEN(newsub) + prevlen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocation size and copy offsets are computed as an int sum of the current substitute length and the previous replacement length, both attacker-influenced through the substitute text and prior match. When the sum exceeds INT_MAX it wraps, alloc returns a too-small buffer, and the subsequent memmove/STRCPY writes past it, causing the crash.
