commit_msg: postpone stream shutdown by H3 frame parsers
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if ((err = stream->recvbuf.handle_input(stream, &src, src_end, &err_desc)) != 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['            if ((err = stream->recvbuf.handle_input(stream, &src, src_end, in_generator, &err_desc)) != 0) {']}
description: h2o is an open source http server. In code prior to the `8c0eca3` commit h2o may attempt to access uninitialized memory. When receiving QUIC frames in certain order, HTTP/3 server-side implementation of h2o can be misguided to treat uninitialized memory as HTTP/3 frames that have been received. When h2o is used as a reverse proxy, an attacker can abuse this vulnerability to send internal state of h2o to backend servers controlled by the attacker or third party. Also, if there is an HTTP endpoint that reflects the traffic sent from the client, an attacker can use that reflector to obtain internal state of h2o. This internal state includes traffic of other connections in unencrypted form and TLS session tickets. This vulnerability exists in h2o server with HTTP/3 support, between commit 93af138 and d1f0f65. None of the released versions of h2o are affected by this vulnerability. There are no known workarounds. Users of unreleased versions of h2o using HTTP/3 are advised to upgrade immediately.

code_evidence: handle_buffered_input derives src and src_end from quicly_recvstate_bytes_available and asserts only that bytes_available <= buffer size, then loops while src != src_end calling stream->recvbuf.handle_input. The patched call passes in_generator, so the frame parser can defer stream shutdown; the pre-patch call did not, allowing the parser to continue over buffer bytes that had not been validated as received frames.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes buffer regions whose initialization is not established before parsing, matching use of an uninitialized resource (CWE-908). This is not merely a length/overflow issue: the weakness is reliance on uninitialized memory as valid frame input.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the receive loop trusts the QUIC recvstate byte count as the extent of initialized frame data. When frames arrive in a certain order, handle_input can treat uninitialized bytes within the receive buffer as parsed HTTP/3 frames. Consequence: the server may act on attacker-influenced uninitialized memory, leaking internal state to attacker-controlled backends or reflectors.

commit_msg:
crypto: user - fix leaking uninitialized memory to userspace

All bytes of the NETLINK_CRYPTO report structures must be initialized,
since they are copied to userspace.  The change from strncpy() to
strlcpy() broke this.  As a minimal fix, change it back.

Fixes: 4473710df1f8 ("crypto: user - Prepare for CRYPTO_MAX_ALG_NAME expansion")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v4.12+
Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstrlcpy(rkpp.type, "kpp", sizeof(rkpp.type));'], 'added_lines': ['\tstrncpy(rkpp.type, "kpp", sizeof(rkpp.type));']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.19.3. crypto_report_one() and related functions in crypto/crypto_user.c (the crypto user configuration API) do not fully initialize structures that are copied to userspace, potentially leaking sensitive memory to user programs. NOTE: this is a CVE-2013-2547 regression but with easier exploitability because the attacker does not need a capability (however, the system must have the CONFIG_CRYPTO_USER kconfig option).

code_evidence: Line 3 declares stack struct rkpp uninitialized; line 4 copies the 4-byte string "kpp" with strncpy into rkpp.type, which has a larger size, leaving the remainder of type and all other struct members uninitialized; lines 5-6 then put the whole sizeof(struct crypto_report_kpp) into the netlink skb copied to userspace.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The uninitialized stack bytes are copied verbatim to userspace, exposing sensitive kernel memory to an unauthorized actor, matching CWE-200's confidentiality impact. The underlying error is uninitialized-memory disclosure rather than an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: strncpy zero-pads only up to the copy count and the stack struct is never memset, so bytes beyond the literal remain uninitialized. Trigger: any crypto_report_kpp call sends the full struct via nla_put to an unprivileged userspace netlink reader, leaking kernel stack memory.

commit_msg:
Limit the number of HTTP requests processed from a connection in I/O cycle

Signed-off-by: Yan Avlasov <yavlasov@google.com>

Signed-off-by: Ryan Northey <ryan@synca.io>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  filter_manager_.decodeTrailers(*request_trailers_);'], 'added_lines': ['  if (!state_.deferred_to_next_io_iteration_) {', '    filter_manager_.decodeTrailers(*request_trailers_);', '  }']}
description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing per-cycle throttling of decodeTrailers allows a bounded input (connection) to drive unbounded resource consumption, matching CWE-400's lack of throttling for allocated work. filter_manager_.decodeTrailers(*request_trailers_);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: trailer decoding proceeds for each stream even when processing has been deferred to the next I/O cycle, so many cancelled/reset streams can each trigger filter-chain work in a single cycle. commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttable->private = bootstrap;', '\tprivate = table->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\trcu_assign_pointer(table->private, bootstrap);', '\tprivate = xt_table_get_private_protected(table);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: Line 21 publishes the bootstrap table info via a plain store to table->private without any release/ordering barrier. Line 22 then calls xt_replace_table, which synchronizes with the packet path using the per-CPU sequence counter; the packet path may observe the stale private pointer because the store is not ordered before the sequence check. Line 24 then reads table->private directly to obtain the private info.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unsynchronized publication of table->private enables the replacement path to free table info still in use, i.e., memory is referenced after being freed. This directly matches CWE-416; the ordering defect is the cause, and use-after-free is the supported consequence rather than a separate race-only weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the new table->private assignment lacks store-release ordering relative to the sequence-count check, so another CPU's packet path can still use the old table info. The replacement thread sees an even sequence count, proceeds to free the old table info, and the packet path dereferences freed memory, producing a use-after-free (observed as NULL pointer dereference in ip6t_do_table).

commit_msg:
signal: Extend exec_id to 64bits

commit d1e7fd6462ca9fc76650fbe6ca800e35b24267da upstream.

Replace the 32bit exec_id with a 64bit exec_id to make it impossible
to wrap the exec_id counter.  With care an attacker can cause exec_id
wrap and send arbitrary signals to a newly exec'd parent.  This
bypasses the signal sending checks if the parent changes their
credentials during exec.

The severity of this problem can been seen that in my limited testing
of a 32bit exec_id it can take as little as 19s to exec 65536 times.
Which means that it can take as little as 14 days to wrap a 32bit
exec_id.  Adam Zabrocki has succeeded wrapping the self_exe_id in 7
days.  Even my slower timing is in the uptime of a typical server.
Which means self_exec_id is simply a speed bump today, and if exec
gets noticably faster self_exec_id won't even be a speed bump.

Extending self_exec_id to 64bits introduces a problem on 32bit
architectures where reading self_exec_id is no longer atomic and can
take two read instructions.  Which means that is is possible to hit
a window where the read value of exec_id does not match the written
value.  So with very lucky timing after this change this still
remains expoiltable.

I have updated the update of exec_id on exec to use WRITE_ONCE
and the read of exec_id in do_notify_parent to use READ_ONCE
to make it clear that there is no locking between these two
locations.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/kernel-hardening/20200324215049.GA3710@pi3.com.pl
Fixes: 2.3.23pre2
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcurrent->self_exec_id++;'], 'added_lines': ['\tWRITE_ONCE(current->self_exec_id, current->self_exec_id + 1);']}
description: A signal access-control issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.6.5, aka CID-7395ea4e65c2. Because exec_id in include/linux/sched.h is only 32 bits, an integer overflow can interfere with a do_notify_parent protection mechanism. A child process can send an arbitrary signal to a parent process in a different security domain. Exploitation limitations include the amount of elapsed time before an integer overflow occurs, and the lack of scenarios where signals to a parent process present a substantial operational threat.

code_evidence: Line 21 unconditionally increments current->self_exec_id, the per-task exec generation counter consumed by do_notify_parent's signal access check; line 22 flushes signal handlers after the increment. The patch converts this increment to WRITE_ONCE but does not widen the counter.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer increment whose result can exceed the counter's representable range and wrap to a small value, which is exactly CWE-190. It is not merely a logic error: the access-control bypass arises because the arithmetic result no longer grows monotonically, so the comparison in the signal path becomes unreliable.

evidence_lines.code:
current->self_exec_id++;
flush_signal_handlers(current, 0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: self_exec_id is a bounded counter that is incremented on every exec without any wraparound guard. Trigger: a process execs enough times (or times execs to hit a specific value) that the counter wraps back to a prior value. Consequence: do_notify_parent's protection that compares exec generations can be satisfied for a parent in a different security/credential domain, allowing an arbitrary signal to be delivered across that boundary.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.16-rc6. ef100_update_stats in drivers/net/ethernet/sfc/ef100_nic.c lacks check of the return value of kmalloc().

code_evidence: Line 5 allocates mc_stats via kmalloc with GFP_ATOMIC and stores the pointer without checking for NULL.
Lines 11-13 pass mc_stats into efx_nic_copy_stats and efx_nic_update_stats, which consume the buffer; if the allocation failed, these calls operate on a NULL pointer.
Line 14 frees the possibly-NULL pointer, which is permitted, but the preceding dereference is the unsafe use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but which can be NULL after a failed allocation, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. This is distinct from an unchecked-return weakness alone: the concrete harm is the NULL dereference in the stats-copy path.

evidence_lines.code: __le64 *mc_stats = kmalloc(array_size(efx->num_mac_stats, sizeof(__le64)), GFP_ATOMIC);
kfree(mc_stats);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of kmalloc() is used without a NULL check. Trigger: memory pressure causes the GFP_ATOMIC allocation to fail, yielding NULL. Consequence: efx_nic_copy_stats/efx_nic_update_stats dereference the NULL buffer, causing a kernel crash (availability impact).

commit_msg:
tls: clear data after a starttls acknowledgement

After a starttls acknowledgement message, clear the buffers of any
incoming data / commands.  This will ensure that all future data is
handled securely.

Co-authored-by: Pietro Cerutti <gahr@gahr.ch>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  if (flags & IMAP_CMD_SINGLE)', '  {', '    // Process any existing commands', '    if (adata->nextcmd != adata->lastcmd)', '      imap_exec(adata, NULL, IMAP_CMD_POLL);', '  }', '    // The queue is empty, so the single command has been processed', '    if ((flags & IMAP_CMD_SINGLE) && (adata->nextcmd == adata->lastcmd))', '      break;']}
description: Mutt before 1.14.4 and NeoMutt before 2020-06-19 have a STARTTLS buffering issue that affects IMAP, SMTP, and POP3. When a server sends a "begin TLS" response, the client reads additional data (e.g., from a man-in-the-middle attacker) and evaluates it in a TLS context, aka "response injection."

code_evidence: The do/while loop repeatedly calls imap_cmd_step(adata) while the result is IMAP_RES_CONTINUE, consuming server responses until a terminal status or continuation; it does not clear or bound data received after a STARTTLS acknowledgement before those bytes are processed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function processes externally influenced server response data without neutralizing special elements, so injected content alters how the downstream protocol exchange is interpreted, matching CWE-74 injection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the command-execution loop treats all buffered incoming server data as part of the current IMAP exchange without discarding pre-TLS bytes after the STARTTLS acknowledgement. Trigger: a server or MITM appends extra data after the 'begin TLS' response. Consequence: injected responses are evaluated in the TLS context, enabling response injection.

commit_msg:
Add bound check for rfc_parse_data

Bug: 78288018
Test: manual
Change-Id: I44349cd22c141483d01bce0f5a2131b727d0feb0
(cherry picked from commit 6039cb7225733195192b396ad19c528800feb735)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  RFCOMM_PARSE_LEN_FIELD(eal, len, p_data);'], 'added_lines': ['', '  eal = *(p_data)&RFCOMM_EA;', '  len = *(p_data)++ >> RFCOMM_SHIFT_LENGTH1;', '  if (eal == 0 && p_buf->len < RFCOMM_CTRL_FRAME_LEN) {', '    len += (*(p_data)++ << RFCOMM_SHIFT_LENGTH2);', '  } else if (eal == 0) {', '    RFCOMM_TRACE_ERROR("Bad Length when EAL = 0: %d", p_buf->len);', '    android_errorWriteLog(0x534e4554, "78288018");', '    return RFC_EVENT_BAD_FRAME;', '  }']}
description: In rfc_process_mx_message of rfc_ts_frames.cc, there is a possible out-of-bounds read due to a missing bounds check. This could lead to remote information disclosure in the Bluetooth service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation. Product: Android Versions: Android-7.0 Android-7.1.1 Android-7.1.2 Android-8.0 Android-8.1 Android-9.0 Android ID: A-111936792

code_evidence: Only p_buf->len < RFCOMM_CTRL_FRAME_LEN (a fixed minimum) is checked before parsing; the length field's actual value is not validated against p_buf->len before further reads.
RFCOMM_PARSE_LEN_FIELD consumes the length octet(s) from p_data and advances p_data; when eal==0 a second octet is read. No constraint ties the parsed len to the remaining buffer size at this point.

p_data was advanced by the parsed length fields, then fcs = *(p_data + len) dereferences at offset len without confirming len stays within p_buf->len; the equality check p_buf->len != len occurs only after this read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences *(p_data + len) before validating len against the buffer, which is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), matching the described remote information disclosure. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds write, since only a read is performed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the frame's declared length is parsed and used to compute an FCS read offset without first confirming that the buffer contains len+1 bytes. Trigger: a remote RFCOMM frame whose length field is larger than the actual remaining payload. Consequence: p_data + len reads past the buffer end, disclosing adjacent memory; the length check at line 26 happens too late to prevent the read.

commit_msg:
Pass origin clean flag of ImageBitmap when structure clone

In this CL, we pass the origin clean flag of an ImageBitmap when this
ImageBitmap is being structure cloned, so that the receive of the
ImageBitmap is aware of this flag.

BUG=623406

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2097393002
Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#402204}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ImageBitmap* imageBitmap = ImageBitmap::create(imageData, IntRect(0, 0, imageData->width(), imageData->height()), options, true);'], 'added_lines': ['    uint32_t isOriginClean;', '    if (!doReadUint32(&isOriginClean))', '        return false;', '    ImageBitmap* imageBitmap = ImageBitmap::create(imageData, IntRect(0, 0, imageData->width(), imageData->height()), options, true, isOriginClean);']}
description: Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.116, does not ensure that a taint property is preserved after a structure-clone operation on an ImageBitmap object derived from a cross-origin image, which allows remote attackers to bypass the Same Origin Policy via crafted JavaScript code.

code_evidence: The function deserializes an ImageData and reconstructs an ImageBitmap from it, but the origin-clean/taint state is not read from the serialized stream or propagated to the created bitmap.
ImageBitmap::create is called with a hardcoded 'true' argument, unconditionally marking the resulting bitmap as origin-clean regardless of the source image's cross-origin taint.
The reconstructed bitmap is then exposed to script via toV8, so the tainted image reaches JavaScript with its security flag cleared.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-254 is the security-features category covering access-control/SOP enforcement failures; the function fails to preserve a security-relevant taint flag during serialization, enabling an SOP bypass. This is a concrete security-feature failure rather than a memory-safety issue.

evidence_lines.code: ImageBitmap* imageBitmap = ImageBitmap::create(imageData, IntRect(0, 0, imageData->width(), imageData->height()), options, true);
*value = toV8(imageBitmap, m_scriptState->context()->Global(), isolate());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the deserialization path drops the origin-clean taint property and hardcodes the bitmap as clean. Trigger: a structure-clone of an ImageBitmap derived from a cross-origin image. Consequence: the receiving context obtains a bitmap that bypasses the Same Origin Policy restriction on tainted canvas/image data.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.0286: using freed memory when location list changed in autocmd

Problem:    Using freed memory when location list changed in autocmd.
Solution:   Return QF_ABORT and handle it. (Yegappan Lakshmanan,
            closes #10993)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    return NOTDONE;', '\treturn NOTDONE;', '\treturn NOTDONE;'], 'added_lines': ['\t    return QF_ABORT;', '\treturn QF_ABORT;', '\treturn QF_ABORT;']}
description: Use After Free in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0286.

code_evidence: After buflist_getfile()/do_ecmd() may switch buffers and trigger autocommands, the code re-validates the saved location-list context via win_id2wp(prev_winid) and curwin->w_llist; on mismatch it only returns NOTDONE.
The quickfix branch likewise checks qflist_valid(NULL, save_qfid) and returns NOTDONE on change.
The changedtick/entry-presence check returns NOTDONE when the list was modified, but all three paths use the ordinary NOTDONE value rather than an abort indicator.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the root cause is continued use of a quickfix/location-list structure after an autocmd freed or replaced it; the insufficient abort signal allows the stale pointer to be referenced. This is a use-after-free, not merely a logic error, since the consequence is access to freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function holds pointers qfl/qf_ptr obtained before buffer/edit operations that can run autocommands. Those autocommands can change or free the location list, leaving qfl/qf_ptr dangling; the mismatch checks detect the change but return NOTDONE, so the caller may continue using the stale list. The fix returns QF_ABORT so the caller aborts instead of dereferencing freed memory.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (offset > max_offset)', '            return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['        if ((offset + (segment_count * 16)) < offset ||', '            (offset + (segment_count * 16)) > max_offset)', '            return 0;']}
description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.5 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.11, the RPC over RDMA dissector could go into an infinite loop, triggered by packet injection or a malformed capture file. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-rpcrdma.c by correctly checking for going beyond the maximum offset.

code_evidence: The while(1) loop only exits via break when value_follows is zero; otherwise segment_count is read and the offset is advanced.
Before the fix, offset += (segment_count * 16) can wrap a guint when segment_count is large, so the subsequent offset > max_offset check may not detect the overflow.
If offset wraps back below max_offset, the loop continues, reads attacker-controlled value_follows again, and may never reach the break or return 0.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the while(1) loop's exit conditions (break or return 0) can be bypassed when the offset wraps, making the exit condition unreachable. This is a loop-termination flaw, not merely an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code: offset += (segment_count * 16);

if (offset > max_offset)
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the offset advance by segment_count*16 is performed without first checking that the multiplication/addition stays within max_offset, allowing unsigned wraparound. Trigger: a malformed RPC-over-RDMA packet with a large segment_count. Consequence: the loop can iterate indefinitely, consuming CPU (DoS).

description: An error in BigInt conversion to Number in Hermes prior to commit a6dcafe6ded8e61658b40f5699878cd19a481f80 could have been used by a malicious attacker to execute arbitrary code due to an out-of-bound write. Note that this bug is only exploitable in cases where Hermes is used to execute untrusted JavaScript. Hence, most React Native applications are not affected.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function reuses references (resX/resY) whose lifetime has ended rather than the valid handles, so memory backing them may be freed and reused before the BigInt add consumes it. Trigger: x and y are both BigInt primitives, so control reaches the add call. The resulting dangling references feed BigIntPrimitive::add, matching the reported out-of-bound write and potential arbitrary code execution when untrusted JavaScript is executed.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. A denial-of-service vulnerability affects applications on a 32-bit systems that use PJSIP versions 2.12 and prior to play/read invalid WAV files. The vulnerability occurs when reading WAV file data chunks with length greater than 31-bit integers. The vulnerability does not affect 64-bit apps and should not affect apps that only plays trusted WAV files. A patch is available on the `master` branch of the `pjsip/project` GitHub repository. As a workaround, apps can reject a WAV file received from an unknown source or validate the file first.

code_evidence: Line 81 computes size_to_read = wave_hdr.fmt_hdr.len - 16 as a 32-bit unsigned/long value; a fmt_hdr.len with the high bit set yields a negative size passed to pj_file_setpos on 32-bit systems.

The for(;;) loop at line 88 reads an 8-byte subchunk, and on any non-DATA chunk sets size_to_read = subchunk.len at line 102 and seeks forward at line 103. A negative/overflowed subchunk.len causes the seek to move backward or fail to advance, so the same subchunk is re-read indefinitely.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unbounded for(;;) loop lacks a guaranteed exit because the negative/overflowed seek never advances past the malformed chunk, directly matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. This is distinct from CWE-190: the integer issue is the mechanism, while the supported weakness is the resulting infinite loop.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: WAV chunk lengths (fmt_hdr.len, subchunk.len) are trusted as signed/32-bit values and used directly as seek offsets without overflow/range validation. Trigger: a crafted WAV with a chunk length having the high bit set on a 32-bit build. Consequence: pj_file_setpos seeks backward or fails to advance, so the for(;;) loop at line 88 never reaches the DATA_TAG break and spins forever, causing a CPU denial of service.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    len = FFMIN(FFMAX(len, 0), sizeof(color_name) - 1);']}
description: Stack-based buffer overflow in the color_string_to_rgba function in libavcodec/xpmdec.c in FFmpeg 3.3 before 3.3.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 5 declares a fixed stack buffer char color_name[100].

Lines 35-37 enter the non-'#' branch and use the caller-supplied len directly in strncpy(color_name, p, len), then index color_name[len] to null-terminate, without any bound on len against the 100-byte buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an operation on a memory buffer that writes outside its intended boundary, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer. The specific out-of-bounds stack write could also be described as CWE-121, but the target label CWE-119 correctly captures the out-of-bounds buffer operation.

commit_msg:
Fix jpeg_skip_scanlines() segfault w/merged upsamp

The additional segfault mentioned in #244 was due to the fact that
the merged upsamplers use a different private structure than the
non-merged upsamplers.  jpeg_skip_scanlines() was assuming the latter, so
when merged upsampling was enabled, jpeg_skip_scanlines() clobbered one
of the IDCT method pointers in the merged upsampler's private structure.

For reasons unknown, the test image in #441 did not encounter this
segfault (too small?), but it encountered an issue similar to the one
fixed in 5bc43c7821df982f65aa1c738f67fbf7cba8bd69, whereby it was
necessary to set up a dummy postprocessing function in
read_and_discard_scanlines() when merged upsampling was enabled.
Failing to do so caused either a segfault in merged_2v_upsample() (due
to a NULL pointer being passed to jcopy_sample_rows()) or an error
("Corrupt JPEG data: premature end of data segment"), depending on the
number of scanlines skipped and whether the first scanline skipped was
an odd- or even-numbered row.

Fixes #441
Fixes #244 (for real this time)

commit_msg:
x86: Guard against corrupted PLT

There should be only one entry in PLT for a given symbol.  Set howto to
NULL after processing a PLT entry to guard against corrupted PLT so that
the duplicated PLT entries are skipped.

	PR binutils/22170
	* elfxx-x86.c (_bfd_x86_elf_get_synthetic_symtab): Guard against
	corrupted PLT.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* There should be only one entry in PLT for a given', '\t\t   symbol.  Set howto to NULL after processing a PLT', '\t\t   entry to guard against corrupted PLT.  */', '\t\tp->howto = NULL;']}
description: The *_get_synthetic_symtab functions in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, do not ensure a unique PLT entry for a symbol, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted ELF file, related to elf32-i386.c and elf64-x86-64.c.

code_evidence: Only when got_vma matches p->address, p->howto is non-NULL and the relocation type is valid does the code emit a synthetic symbol; the added p->howto = NULL is not present in this function but the guard p->howto != NULL at [119,120,121] is what prevents a duplicate PLT entry from being processed again.

For each accepted entry the code copies the symbol name into the names buffer sized from the earlier loop over dynrelbuf, advances names by len plus the "@plt" suffix, and increments the symbol pointer s and count n.

offset advances by plt_entry_size each iteration while the inner loop is bounded by plt_p->count; if a corrupted PLT causes more than one match for a symbol, the names buffer and symbol array can be overrun because the size accounting assumes one entry per relocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes symbol names and asymbol structures into a buffer sized by an assumption that corrupted input violates, producing writes outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operations.

evidence_lines.code:
if (got_vma == p->address
&& p->howto != NULL
&& valid_plt_reloc_p (p->howto->type))
offset += plt_entry_size;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer size is computed assuming a unique PLT entry per symbol, but a crafted ELF with duplicated PLT entries can cause multiple writes past the allocated asymbol/names region. Trigger: corrupted PLT data where the same relocation matches several PLT slots. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds write and crash or potential memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Since the tee subsystem does not keep a strong reference to its idle
shared memory buffers, it races with other threads that try to destroy a
shared memory through a close of its dma-buf fd or by unmapping the
memory.

In tee_shm_get_from_id() when a lookup in teedev->idr has been
successful, it is possible that the tee_shm is in the dma-buf teardown
path, but that path is blocked by the teedev mutex. Since we don't have
an API to tell if the tee_shm is in the dma-buf teardown path or not we
must find another way of detecting this condition.

Fix this by doing the reference counting directly on the tee_shm using a
new refcount_t refcount field. dma-buf is replaced by using
anon_inode_getfd() instead, this separates the life-cycle of the
underlying file from the tee_shm. tee_shm_put() is updated to hold the
mutex when decreasing the refcount to 0 and then remove the tee_shm from
teedev->idr before releasing the mutex. This means that the tee_shm can
never be found unless it has a refcount larger than 0.

Fixes: 967c9cca2cc5 ("tee: generic TEE subsystem")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reviewed-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Reviewed-by: Lars Persson <larper@axis.com>
Reviewed-by: Sumit Garg <sumit.garg@linaro.org>
Reported-by: Patrik Lantz <patrik.lantz@axis.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Wiklander <jens.wiklander@linaro.org>

This will guarantee that', '\t\t * the refcount_inc() in tee_shm_get_from_id() never starts', '\t\t * from 0.', '\t\t */', '\t\tif (shm->flags & TEE_SHM_DMA_BUF)', '\t\t\tidr_remove(&teedev->idr, shm->id);', '\t\tdo_release = true;', '\t}', '\tmutex_unlock(&teedev->mutex);', '', '\tif (do_release)', '\t\ttee_shm_release(teedev, shm);']}
description: A use-after-free exists in drivers/tee/tee_shm.c in the TEE subsystem in the Linux kernel through 5.15.11. This occurs because of a race condition in tee_shm_get_from_id during an attempt to free a shared memory object.

code_evidence: tee_shm_put() unconditionally releases the shared-memory buffer via dma_buf_put(shm->dmabuf) without taking the teedev mutex or checking any refcount; nothing serializes this release against concurrent lookup/teardown of the same tee_shm in tee_shm_get_from_id().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is improper synchronization over a shared resource (the tee_shm buffer) with a timing window in which another code sequence frees or accesses it concurrently, matching CWE-362. The use-after-free is the downstream consequence, not the primary weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (shm->flags & TEE_SHM_DMA_BUF)
dma_buf_put(shm->dmabuf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Because the buffer is dropped without synchronization, a concurrent thread can look up the same tee_shm through teedev->idr while tee_shm_put() is tearing it down, so the object can be freed while still reachable, yielding a use-after-free. The trigger is concurrent close/unmap of the dma-buf versus a lookup; the consequence is memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
copy: CVE-2022-0485: Fail nbdcopy if NBD read or write fails

nbdcopy has a nasty bug when performing multi-threaded copies using
asynchronous nbd calls - it was blindly treating the completion of an
asynchronous command as successful, rather than checking the *error
parameter.  This can result in the silent creation of a corrupted
image in two different ways: when a read fails, we blindly wrote
garbage to the destination; when a write fails, we did not flag that
the destination was not written.

Since nbdcopy already calls exit() on a synchronous read or write
failure to a file, doing the same for an asynchronous op to an NBD
server is the simplest solution.  A nicer solution, but more invasive
to code and thus not done here, might be to allow up to N retries of
the transaction (in case the read or write failure was transient), or
even having a mode where as much data is copied as possible (portions
of the copy that failed would be logged on stderr, and nbdcopy would
still fail with a non-zero exit status, but this would copy more than
just stopping at the first error, as can be done with rsync or
ddrescue).

Note that since we rely on auto-retiring and do NOT call
nbd_aio_command_completed, our completion callbacks must always return
1 (if they do not exit() first), even when acting on *error, so as not
leave the command allocated until nbd_close.  As such, there is no
sane way to return an error to a manual caller of the callback, and
therefore we can drop dead code that calls perror() and exit() if the
callback "failed".  It is also worth documenting the contract on when
we must manually call the callback during the asynch_zero callback, so
that we do not leak or double-free the command; thankfully, all the
existing code paths were correct.

The added testsuite script demonstrates several scenarios, some of
which fail without the rest of this patch in place, and others which
showcase ways in which sparse images can bypass errors.

Once backports are complete, a followup patch on the main branch will
edit docs/libnbd-security.pod with the mailing list announcement of
the stable branch commit ids and release versions that incorporate
this fix.

description: A flaw was found in the copying tool `nbdcopy` of libnbd. When performing multi-threaded copies using asynchronous nbd calls, nbdcopy was blindly treating the completion of an asynchronous command as successful, rather than checking the *error parameter. This could result in the silent creation of a corrupted destination image.

The callback result is otherwise ignored, and the function returns void with no error propagation. The dummy value passed as the completion status is never inspected.

commit_msg:
bpf: force strict alignment checks for stack pointers

Force strict alignment checks for stack pointers because the tracking of
stack spills relies on it; unaligned stack accesses can lead to corruption
of spilled registers, which is exploitable.

Fixes: f1174f77b50c ("bpf/verifier: rework value tracking")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* The stack spill tracking logic in check_stack_write()', '\t\t * and check_stack_read() relies on stack accesses being', '\t\t * aligned.', '\t\t */', '\t\tstrict = true;']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging the lack of stack-pointer alignment enforcement.

code_evidence: For PTR_TO_STACK the switch only sets pointer_desc = "stack " and breaks; it does not set strict. Thus stack pointer accesses inherit strict from env->strict_alignment, which may be false unless the environment is in strict mode.
The final call passes this non-forced strict value to check_generic_ptr_alignment, so stack pointer offset/size alignment is not enforced when strict_alignment is off.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing alignment constraint allows out-of-bounds memory operations on stack slots, matching CWE-119's operation outside intended buffer boundaries. The alignment-check gap is the cause; the resulting stack memory corruption is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: stack-pointer alignment is not forced for PTR_TO_STACK, so unaligned stack accesses pass the verifier when strict alignment is not globally enabled. Trigger: a local user loads a BPF program performing an unaligned stack access. Consequence: stack spill tracking in check_stack_write()/check_stack_read() is defeated, corrupting spilled registers and memory, enabling memory corruption or DoS.

description: In AMediaCodecCryptoInfo_new of NdkMediaCodec.cpp, there is a possible out-of-bounds write due to an integer overflow. This could lead to remote code execution in external apps with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation. Product: Android Versions: Android-7.0 Android-7.1.1 Android-7.1.2 Android-8.0 Android-8.1 Android-9.0 Android ID: A-111603051

code_evidence: Line 9 computes cryptosize as sizeof(AMediaCodecCryptoInfo) + sizeof(size_t) * numsubsamples * 2 using attacker-influenced numsubsamples without any overflow check. Line 10 allocates that possibly-wrapped size. Lines 21-23 then place clearbytes/encryptedbytes arrays and memcpy numsubsamples * sizeof(size_t) bytes into the undersized allocation.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size arithmetic on line 9 can wrap for large numsubsamples, producing a small cryptosize. The trigger is a large numsubsamples; malloc returns a small buffer, and the memcpy calls on lines 22-23 write numsubsamples-sized data past the allocation, yielding an out-of-bounds heap write.

commit_msg:
Fix security vulnerability with SpaceToBatchNDOp.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 445527615
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    block_num_elems *= block_shape[i];', '  const int64_t batch_size = input_shape[0];', '  output_shape[0] = batch_size * block_num_elems;'], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(ctx, block_shape[i] >= 1,', '                errors::InvalidArgument(', '                    "All values in block_shape must be positive, got value, ",', '                    block_shape[i], " at index ", i, "."));', '    block_num_elems = MultiplyWithoutOverflow(block_num_elems, block_shape[i]);', '  const int64_t batch_size = input_shape[0];', '  const int64_t output_dim =', '      MultiplyWithoutOverflow(batch_size, block_num_elems);', '  if (output_dim < 0) {', '    OP_REQUIRES(', '        ctx, output_dim >= 0,', '        errors::InvalidArgument("Negative output dimension size caused by "', '                                "overflow when multiplying ",', '                                batch_size, " and ", block_num_elems));', '  }', '  output_shape[0] = output_dim;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.SpaceToBatchND` (in all backends such as XLA and handwritten kernels) is vulnerable to an integer overflow: The result of this integer overflow is used to allocate the output tensor, hence we get a denial of service via a `CHECK`-failure (assertion failure), as in TFSA-2021-198. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: block_num_elems starts at 1 and is multiplied by each block_shape[i] in a loop with no overflow check; block_shape values come from the caller-supplied block_shape span, so a large product can wrap.

The unchecked product feeds the output dimension computation output_shape[0] = batch_size * block_num_elems, another unguarded multiplication that can wrap to a negative or small value; only a >0 check on block_num_elems exists, not on the final product.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the code performs integer multiplications on externally supplied dimensions that can exceed int64_t range, and the wrapped result is used as an allocation/shape size. The patch confirms this by introducing MultiplyWithoutOverflow and a block_shape>=1 check, which are precisely integer-overflow mitigations rather than a different weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function accumulates block_shape[i] into block_num_elems with plain multiplication and then multiplies by batch_size to size the output shape. With large user-controlled block_shape values, either multiplication overflows int64_t, producing a negative or truncated dimension. The wrapped dimension is then used to construct the output tensor, leading to a CHECK-failure/denial of service.

commit_msg:
upstream commit

Unregister the KEXINIT handler after message has been
received. Otherwise an unauthenticated peer can repeat the KEXINIT and cause
allocation of up to 128MB -- until the connection is closed. Reported by
shilei-c at 360.cn

Upstream-ID: 43649ae12a27ef94290db16d1a98294588b75c05
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tssh_dispatch_set(ssh, SSH2_MSG_KEXINIT, NULL);']}
description: The kex_input_kexinit function in kex.c in OpenSSH 6.x and 7.x through 7.3 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by sending many duplicate KEXINIT requests.  NOTE: a third party reports that "OpenSSH upstream does not consider this as a security issue."

code_evidence: The handler logs receipt, validates kex, then copies the peer packet payload into kex->peer via sshbuf_put without any dispatch-level guard preventing re-entry. Nothing in this function unregisters the SSH2_MSG_KEXINIT handler, so each received KEXINIT appends dlen bytes to the same buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is improper management of a system resource: repeated allocation without release or limit, matching CWE-399's resource-management category. It is not a parsing bug; the weakness is the missing lifecycle control over the handler and its buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function processes every KEXINIT packet and repeatedly appends attacker-controlled payload to kex->peer, while the dispatcher keeps invoking it. Trigger: an unauthenticated peer sends many duplicate KEXINIT messages on one connection. Consequence: unbounded buffer growth and memory exhaustion (denial of service), bounded only by connection lifetime.

description: The IKEv2 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isakmp.c, several functions.

code_evidence: ND_TCHECK(*ext) validates only a single byte of the isakmp_gen header, then UNALIGNED_MEMCPY copies sizeof(e) bytes from ext, reading past the validated region.
When verbose output is enabled and the length field exceeds 4, rawprint reads ntohs(e.len) - 4 bytes from ext + 1 without verifying that many bytes exist within the captured buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads beyond the intended captured buffer via an unchecked length, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. This is a read overrun, not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.

UNALIGNED_MEMCPY(&e, ext, sizeof(e));

if (2 < ndo->ndo_vflag && 4 < ntohs(e.len)) {
if (!rawprint(ndo, (const uint8_t *)(ext + 1), ntohs(e.len) - 4))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The header length field e.len is attacker-controlled and used to size a rawprint read, while the preceding ND_TCHECK only checks one byte rather than the full header or payload. description: ext/wddx/wddx.c in PHP before 5.6.28 and 7.x before 7.0.13 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via crafted serialized data in a wddxPacket XML document, as demonstrated by a PDORow string.

code_evidence: pdo_stmt_init registers the internal PDORow class and sets create_object to pdo_row_new and serialize to pdo_row_serialize, but assigns no serialize-deny or unserialize handler; the class therefore remains eligible for generic unserialization that would instantiate a PDORow lacking the internal handler state pdo_row_new expects.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a missing unserialize guard on an internal class, allowing an object whose internal pointers are NULL to reach code that dereferences them unconditionally, matching CWE-476. It is not merely improper input validation; the supported consequence is a NULL pointer dereference crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: PDORow objects can be created through the generic unserialize path rather than pdo_row_new, so internal fields that downstream handlers dereference are left NULL. Crafted serialized data (e.g., a PDORow string inside a wddxPacket) triggers this path, and dereferencing the missing pointer crashes the process (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix Null pointer deref in X509_issuer_and_serial_hash()

The OpenSSL public API function X509_issuer_and_serial_hash() attempts
to create a unique hash value based on the issuer and serial number data
contained within an X509 certificate. However it fails to correctly
handle any errors that may occur while parsing the issuer field (which
might occur if the issuer field is maliciously constructed). This may
subsequently result in a NULL pointer deref and a crash leading to a
potential denial of service attack.

The function X509_issuer_and_serial_hash() is never directly called by
OpenSSL itself so applications are only vulnerable if they use this
function directly and they use it on certificates that may have been
obtained from untrusted sources.

CVE-2021-23841

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
(cherry picked from commit 8130d654d1de922ea224fa18ee3bc7262edc39c0)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (f == NULL)', '        goto err;']}
description: The OpenSSL public API function X509_issuer_and_serial_hash() attempts to create a unique hash value based on the issuer and serial number data contained within an X509 certificate. However it fails to correctly handle any errors that may occur while parsing the issuer field (which might occur if the issuer field is maliciously constructed). This may subsequently result in a NULL pointer deref and a crash leading to a potential denial of service attack. The function X509_issuer_and_serial_hash() is never directly called by OpenSSL itself so applications are only vulnerable if they use this function directly and they use it on certificates that may have been obtained from untrusted sources. OpenSSL versions 1.1.1i and below are affected by this issue. Users of these versions should upgrade to OpenSSL 1.1.1j. OpenSSL versions 1.0.2x and below are affected by this issue. However OpenSSL 1.0.2 is out of support and no longer receiving public updates. Premium support customers of OpenSSL 1.0.2 should upgrade to 1.0.2y. Other users should upgrade to 1.1.1j. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1j (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1i). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.0.2y (Affected 1.0.2-1.0.2x).

code_evidence: X509_NAME_oneline() can return NULL when the issuer field is malformed, and the result is stored in f without any NULL check. The next statement passes f to strlen(f) inside the EVP_DigestUpdate() call, dereferencing the possibly-NULL pointer before any error handling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (f) that it assumes is valid but can be NULL, matching CWE-476 exactly. This is a NULL dereference rather than an out-of-bounds read, since the failure is a missing NULL check on a returned pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation of the X509_NAME_oneline() return value. Trigger: a certificate with a maliciously constructed issuer field makes the call fail and return NULL. Consequence: strlen(f) dereferences NULL, causing a crash and denial of service.

commit_msg:
ucma_destroy_id() assumes that all things accessing the ctx will do so via
the xarray. This assumption violated only in the case the FD is being
closed, then the ctx is reached via the ctx_list. Normally this is OK
since ucma_destroy_id() cannot run concurrenty with release(), however
with ucma_migrate_id() is involved this can violated as the close of the
2nd FD can run concurrently with destroy on the first:

                CPU0                      CPU1
        ucma_destroy_id(fda)
                                  ucma_migrate_id(fda -> fdb)
                                       ucma_get_ctx()
        xa_lock()
         _ucma_find_context()
         xa_erase()
        xa_unlock()
                                       xa_lock()
                                        ctx->file = new_file
                                        list_move()
                                       xa_unlock()
                                      ucma_put_ctx()

                                   ucma_close(fdb)
                                      _destroy_id()
                                      kfree(ctx)

        _destroy_id()
          wait_for_completion()
          // boom, ctx was freed

The ctx->file must be modified under the handler and xa_lock, and prior to
modification the ID must be rechecked that it is still reachable from
cur_file, ie there is no parallel destroy or migrate.

To make this work remove the double locking and streamline the control
flow. The double locking was obsoleted by the handler lock now directly
preventing new uevents from being created, and the ctx_list cannot be read
while holding fgets on both files. Removing the double locking also
removes the need to check for the same file.

Fixes: 88314e4dda1e ("RDMA/cma: add support for rdma_migrate_id()")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/0-v1-05c5a4090305+3a872-ucma_syz_migrate_jgg@nvidia.com
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+cc6fc752b3819e082d0c@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@nvidia.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tctx = ucma_get_ctx(f.file->private_data, cmd.id);', '\tcur_file = ctx->file;', '\tif (cur_file == new_file) {', '\t\tmutex_lock(&cur_file->mut);', '\t\tresp.events_reported = ctx->events_reported;', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&cur_file->mut);', '\t\tgoto response;', "\t * Migrate events between fd's, maintaining order, and avoiding new", '\t * events being added before existing events.', '\tucma_lock_files(cur_file, new_file);', '\txa_lock(&ctx_table);', '\tlist_move_tail(&ctx->list, &new_file->ctx_list);', '\tucma_move_events(ctx, new_file);', '\tctx->file = new_file;', '\tresp.events_reported = ctx->events_reported;', '\txa_unlock(&ctx_table);', '\tucma_unlock_files(cur_file, new_file);', '', 'response:'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct ucma_event *uevent, *tmp;', '\tLIST_HEAD(event_list);', '\tcur_file = f.file->private_data;', '\tctx = ucma_get_ctx(cur_file, cmd.id);', '\t/*', '\t * ctx->file can only be changed under the handler & xa_lock. xa_load()', "\t * must be checked again to ensure the ctx hasn't begun destruction", '\t * since the ucma_get_ctx().', '\t */', '\txa_lock(&ctx_table);', '\tif (_ucma_find_context(cmd.id, cur_file) != ctx) {', '\t\txa_unlock(&ctx_table);', '\t\tret = -ENOENT;', '\t\tgoto err_unlock;', '\tctx->file = new_file;', '\txa_unlock(&ctx_table);', '\tmutex_lock(&cur_file->mut);', '\tlist_del(&ctx->list);', '\t * At this point lock_handler() prevents addition of new uevents for', '\t * this ctx.', '\tlist_for_each_entry_safe(uevent, tmp, &cur_file->event_list, list)', '\t\tif (uevent->ctx == ctx)', '\t\t\tlist_move_tail(&uevent->list, &event_list);', '\tresp.events_reported = ctx->events_reported;', '\tmutex_unlock(&cur_file->mut);', '\tmutex_lock(&new_file->mut);', '\tlist_add_tail(&ctx->list, &new_file->ctx_list);', '\tlist_splice_tail(&event_list, &new_file->event_list);', '\tmutex_unlock(&new_file->mut);', 'err_unlock:']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.10. drivers/infiniband/core/ucma.c has a use-after-free because the ctx is reached via the ctx_list in some ucma_migrate_id situations where ucma_close is called, aka CID-f5449e74802c.

code_evidence: ucma_get_ctx() obtains ctx from f.file->private_data, then rdma_lock_handler() is taken and cur_file is read from ctx->file without revalidating ctx against cur_file's xarray. The migration path then moves ctx and events and sets ctx->file while holding ucma_lock_files and xa_lock, but ucma_close on the second fd can concurrently reach _destroy_id via ctx_list and kfree(ctx). After the migration branch, the code jumps to response and dereferences ctx->cm_id and ctx in rdma_unlock_handler()/ucma_put_ctx().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function references ctx after it may have been freed by a concurrent destroy, which is CWE-416. This is not merely a missing lock; the supported consequence is use of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ctx->file is changed without rechecking under the handler and xa_lock that ctx is still reachable from cur_file, so a concurrent ucma_close can destroy and free ctx. Trigger: ucma_migrate_id racing with close of the second fd via ctx_list. Consequence: use-after-free when the handler unlock and put dereference the freed ctx.

commit_msg: Better handling corrupted CFF charstrings. Fix #59.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsds out = sdsnewlen("", bytesNeeded);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsds out = sdsnewlen(NULL, bytesNeeded);']}
description: lib/support/unicodeconv/unicodeconv.c in libotfcc.a in otfcc v0.10.3-alpha has a buffer over-read.

code_evidence: The first pass reads two bytes per code unit via tmp = (uint8_t *)in; c = *tmp++; c = c << 8; c = c | *tmp; then advances in++. Input length is only normalized for odd bytes at line 7, so inb must provide inlenb bytes.
High-surrogate handling at lines 19-20 checks in >= inend before reading the next unit, but the check occurs after in++ advanced past the first unit.
The second pass repeats the same two-byte read and surrogate consumption at lines 56-64 using the same inend bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 matches because the function reads past the end of the intended input buffer. The change to sdsnewlen only affects allocation, not these reads, so the over-read is the directly supported weakness rather than a write overflow.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((c & 0xFC00) == 0xD800) {
if (in >= inend) { break; }

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder trusts that inb contains inlenb bytes and performs two-byte reads at the end of the buffer; the surrogate path consumes an extra code unit after a bounds check that can be reached with in already at inend. Trigger: a truncated or corrupted UTF-16BE charstring whose length ends mid-code-unit or on a lone high surrogate. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of adjacent memory during conversion.

This issue might cause memory exhaustion, but is only relevant if the pickle format is used for serializing tens or hundreds of gigabytes of data. This issue is fixed in: v3.4.10, v3.4.10rc1; v3.5.10, v3.5.10rc1, v3.5.7, v3.5.7rc1, v3.5.8, v3.5.8rc1, v3.5.8rc2, v3.5.9; v3.6.10, v3.6.10rc1, v3.6.11, v3.6.11rc1, v3.6.12, v3.6.7, v3.6.7rc1, v3.6.7rc2, v3.6.8, v3.6.8rc1, v3.6.9, v3.6.9rc1; v3.7.1, v3.7.1rc1, v3.7.1rc2, v3.7.2, v3.7.2rc1, v3.7.3, v3.7.3rc1, v3.7.4, v3.7.4rc1, v3.7.4rc2, v3.7.5, v3.7.5rc1, v3.7.6, v3.7.6rc1, v3.7.7, v3.7.7rc1, v3.7.8, v3.7.8rc1, v3.7.9.

code_evidence: The loop counter `i` is declared as `Py_ssize_t` (signed) but is compared against `self->unpickler->memo_size` in the loop condition `i < ...memo_size`.
`i` is passed to `PyLong_FromSsize_t(i)` to construct the memo key, so the counter's type directly governs the produced key value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the function's index variable can wrap when incremented toward the signed representation limit, and the fix changes it to `size_t` to avoid relying on signed overflow. This is an integer wraparound issue, not a mere bounds-check omission (CWE-125/787).

Py_ssize_t i;
for (i = 0; i < self->unpickler->memo_size; i++) {
key = PyLong_FromSsize_t(i);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is a signed `Py_ssize_t` counter used to iterate and index a memo whose size can grow very large; relying on this signed type risks signed-overflow/wraparound semantics as the index approaches the type limit. The trigger is a pickle stream with a large LONG_BINPUT memo size causing the memo to be resized to twice its size; the supported consequence is memory exhaustion / incorrect memo handling rather than direct corruption.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. The 9p filesystem did not protect i_size_write() properly, which causes an i_size_read() infinite loop and denial of service on SMP systems.

code_evidence: Mount path fetches root attributes via p9_client_getattr_dotl and passes the result to v9fs_stat2inode_dotl on the root inode without holding inode->i_lock.
Non-dotl branch similarly calls v9fs_stat2inode on the root inode from p9_client_stat without i_lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This supports CWE-835 because the unprotected i_size_write lets a concurrent reader's seqcount loop never observe a stable value, producing an unreachable exit condition and CPU-consuming DoS. It is not merely a race with benign data corruption; the demonstrated effect is a non-terminating loop.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The mount function populates root inode attributes through stat2inode helpers that perform i_size_write() without the inode lock. Concurrent i_size_read() callers, such as getattr, can then spin in read_seqcount_begin() indefinitely, causing a soft lockup and denial of service. The root cause is the missing locking around the size write; the infinite loop is the consequence.

commit_msg:
gif: avoid out-of-bound reads of masks array #209

When given invalid inputs, we might be fed the EOF marker before it is
actually the EOF.  The gif logic assumes once it sees the EOF marker,
there won't be any more data, so it leaves the cur_bits index possibly
negative.  So when we get more data, we underflow the masks array.

Flag it so we don't try to output anything more.  The image is invalid,
so we shouldn't be truncating any valid inputs.

This fixes #209.

description: The output function in gd_gif_out.c in the GD Graphics Library (aka libgd) allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted image.

code_evidence: Line 3 indexes masks with ctx->cur_bits before any lower-bound check; the preceding diff guard shows cur_bits can be CUR_BITS_FINISHED (negative) on re-entry.
Lines 28-34: on EOFCode, the while loop drains cur_bits while it is > 0, subtracting 8 each iteration, so cur_bits can end negative after emitting the final partial byte.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading masks at a negative cur_bits index accesses memory before the array's start, matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read) rather than an out-of-bounds write, since the value is only loaded and used in a bitwise AND.

ctx->cur_accum &= masks[ctx->cur_bits];
if(ctx->cur_bits > 0) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the EOF drain loop leaves ctx->cur_bits negative, and output() is re-entered with more data without a guard, so masks[ctx->cur_bits] at line 3 underflows the array. Trigger: crafted/truncated GIF data that emits the EOF marker early and is then followed by more data. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of the masks array, causing a crash/DoS.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void rdp_read_flow_control_pdu(wStream* s, UINT16* type)'], 'added_lines': ['BOOL rdp_read_flow_control_pdu(wStream* s, UINT16* type)', '\tif (!type)', '\t\treturn FALSE;', '\tif (Stream_GetRemainingLength(s) < 6)', '\t\treturn FALSE;', '\treturn TRUE;']}
description: In FreeRDP after 1.0 and before 2.0.0, there is an out-of-bounds read. It only allows to abort a session. No data extraction is possible. This has been fixed in 2.0.0.

code_evidence: The function unconditionally calls Stream_Read_UINT8 at line 4 and then four Stream_Seek_UINT8/Stream_Seek_UINT16 calls at lines 6-9 without first verifying that the stream has enough remaining bytes. Stream_Read_UINT8 consumes one byte and sets *type; the subsequent seeks advance the stream position by five more bytes. If the input stream is shorter than six bytes, these operations read/advance past the end of the intended buffer.

Trigger: a malformed or truncated flow-control PDU shorter than six bytes reaches this function. commit_msg:
fix vulnerability in bspatch

Patches with control data tuples with negative numbers in the first
and/or second can cause bspatch to write to arbitrary locations in the
heap.

Change-Id: Ibfccf222dbc24328ce7593476da36212d9052e12
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t// android local change (start)', '\t\tif (ctrl[0]<0||ctrl[1]<0)', '\t\t\terrx(1,"Corrupt patch\\n");', '\t\t// android local change (end)', '']}
description: Integer signedness error in bspatch.c in bspatch in bsdiff, as used in Apple OS X before 10.11.6 and other products, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow) via a crafted patch file.

code_evidence: Control tuples are read from attacker-controlled patch data into ctrl[0..2] as off_t via offtin; there is no sign check before use.

The only guard is newpos+ctrl[0]>newsize. If ctrl[0] is negative, this comparison can pass, and the subsequent BZ2_bzRead writes ctrl[0] bytes from new+newpos, a negative count causing out-of-bounds heap writes.
newpos+=ctrl[0] then moves newpos backwards, and the oldpos+i loop uses the negative ctrl[0] as a bound, further corrupting state and memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The logic assumes ctrl[0] is a positive length; a negative value makes the size/offset calculation wrap and is then used as a buffer length/offset, which is exactly CWE-190 integer wraparound feeding memory corruption. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the attacker-controlled signed value is used as a write length.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is missing signedness validation of ctrl[0]/ctrl[1] read from the patch. A crafted patch with a negative tuple value bypasses the newpos+ctrl check, so the decompression write and position arithmetic operate on negative sizes/offsets, causing heap-based out-of-bounds writes and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.3902: Vim9: double free with nested :def function

Problem:    Vim9: double free with nested :def function.
Solution:   Pass "line_to_free" from compile_def_function() and make sure
            cmdlinep is valid.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (cmdline != NULL)', '    if (cmdline != NULL)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (eap.nextcmd != NULL)', '    if (eap.nextcmd != NULL)', '\t    if (cmdline == line_to_free)', '\t\tline_to_free = NULL;']}
description: vim is vulnerable to Use After Free

code_evidence: line_to_free is initialized NULL and passed to get_function_body, which may set it to an allocated buffer later freed via vim_free(line_to_free) at line 145; cmdline is filled through eap.cmdlinep (line 33).

When cmdline is non-NULL, it is appended to evalarg->eval_tofree_ga for later freeing, but line_to_free is not cleared, so the same buffer can be freed twice: once by vim_free(line_to_free) at line 145 and again via the tofree array.
The cleanup at line 145 unconditionally frees line_to_free, which may alias cmdline already handed off to eval_tofree_ga.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a double free of the same heap buffer, causing the memory to be reused while still referenced (cmdline/line_to_free), matching CWE-416's description of referencing memory after it has been freed.

evidence_lines.code: vim_free(line_to_free);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: cmdline is stored for deferred freeing in eval_tofree_ga while line_to_free may reference the same allocation, and the cleanup still frees line_to_free. Trigger: a nested :def/lambda body where get_function_body sets line_to_free equal to the cmdline pointer. Consequence: the buffer is freed twice, leading to use-after-free/double-free of the command line memory.

commit_msg: misc oom and possible memory leak fix
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    \tperror("malloc");', '\treturn NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tperror("malloc");', '\t\treturn NULL;']}
description: Boa through 0.94.14rc21 allows remote attackers to trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) condition because malloc is mishandled.

code_evidence: The allocation size is computed as 4 * strlen(inp) + 1 without checking whether the multiplication overflows size_t; the only guard is a NULL check on the malloc result.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The wrapped allocation leads directly to writes outside the intended buffer boundary in the escaping loop, which is the out-of-bounds write pattern of CWE-119. The integer-overflow root cause is not itself the target label; the resulting buffer-bound violation is.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size expression 4 * strlen(inp) + 1 can wrap for very long input, so malloc returns a small buffer while the loop in lines 13-20 writes up to four bytes per input character. Trigger: an attacker-supplied pathname whose length makes the multiplication overflow. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds writes, memory corruption, and potentially code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
transport/server.cc: Return correct size of decompressed lz4 buffer

An incorrect size is returned from the function, which could lead to
crashes or undefined behavior. Fix by erroring out in these cases.

Fixes #11476
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    return out.size();'], 'added_lines': ['                    if (ret != out.size()) {', '                        throw std::runtime_error("Malformed CQL frame - provided uncompressed size different than real uncompressed size");', '                    }', '                    return static_cast<size_t>(ret);']}
description: Scylla is a real-time big data database that is API-compatible with Apache Cassandra and Amazon DynamoDB. When decompressing CQL frame received from user, Scylla assumes that user-provided uncompressed length is correct. If user provides fake length, that is greater than the real one, part of decompression buffer won't be overwritten, and will be left uninitialized. This can be exploited in several ways, depending on the privileges of the user. 1. The main exploit is that an attacker with access to CQL port, but no user account, can bypass authentication, but only if there are other legitimate clients making connections to the cluster, and they use LZ4. 2. Attacker that already has a user account on the cluster can read parts of uninitialized memory, which can contain things like passwords of other users or fragments of other queries / results, which leads to authorization bypass and sensitive information disclosure. The bug has been patched in the following versions: Scylla Enterprise: 2020.1.14, 2021.1.12, 2022.1.0. Scylla Open Source: 4.6.7, 5.0.3. Users unable to upgrade should make sure none of their drivers connect to cluster using LZ4 compression, and that Scylla CQL port is behind firewall. Additionally make sure no untrusted client can connect to Scylla, by setting up authentication and applying workarounds from previous point (firewall, no lz4 compression).

code_evidence: The user-provided uncompressed length is read into uncomp_len and only checked for being negative; no upper bound or consistency check against actual decompressed data exists.
uncomp_len is used to size the output buffer via make_fragmented_temporary_buffer, so the buffer's extent is attacker-controlled.

LZ4_decompress_safe writes only the real decompressed bytes into out; when uncomp_len exceeds the real size, the remainder of out is never written, yet the callback returns out.size() (the full claimed length), and the buffer is returned as if fully initialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the function accesses and exposes a resource (the output buffer) whose tail region was never initialized by LZ4_decompress_safe, and the missing ret != out.size() check lets uninitialized bytes be used. This is distinct from CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read) since the read stays within the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the client-supplied uncompressed length and returns the full claimed buffer size without verifying that decompression filled it. Trigger: a malicious CQL frame declares an uncompressed length larger than the actual LZ4 payload. Consequence: the returned fragmented buffer contains uninitialized memory that is later read, enabling information disclosure, authentication bypass, or crashes.

commit_msg:
manager.c: Prevent path traversal with GetConfig.

When using AMI GetConfig, it was possible to access files outside of the
Asterisk configuration directory by using filenames with ".." and "./"
even while live_dangerously was not enabled. This change resolves the
full path and ensures we are still in the configuration directory before
attempting to access the file.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (restrictedFile(fn)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tint ret = 0;', '\tret = restrictedFile(fn);', '\tif (ret == 1) {', '\t\treturn 0;', '\t} else if (ret == -1) {', '\t\tastman_send_error(s, m, "Config file not found");']}
description: Asterisk is an open source private branch exchange and telephony toolkit. In Asterisk prior to versions 18.20.1, 20.5.1, and 21.0.1, as well as certified-asterisk prior to 18.9-cert6, it is possible to read any arbitrary file even when the `live_dangerously` is not enabled. This allows arbitrary files to be read. Asterisk versions 18.20.1, 20.5.1, and 21.0.1, as well as certified-asterisk prior to 18.9-cert6, contain a fix for this issue.

code_evidence: The Filename header is read directly from the manager message into fn (line 4) with no sanitization, then only checked with ast_strlen_zero (line 13) before being passed to restrictedFile (line 17) and ast_config_load2 (line 21). The pre-fix restrictedFile return value is treated as a boolean; only a nonzero result blocks the request, so a filename containing '..' or './' that restrictedFile fails to reject reaches ast_config_load2 and is opened relative to the config directory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses external input (Filename header) to construct a pathname intended to reside under the configuration directory, and the pre-fix code does not properly neutralize '..'/'./' elements before opening the file, matching CWE-22 path traversal. The fix resolves the full path and verifies containment, confirming the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled Filename flows unchecked into config file loading, and the path restriction relies solely on restrictedFile without resolving the final path. Trigger: a manager GetConfig action supplying a traversal filename such as '../foo'. Consequence: arbitrary files outside the configuration directory can be read and returned in the response, violating confidentiality.

commit_msg:
BT-DHT: Fix endless loop

The correct return value for an error condition is 0, which will
cause the caller to then report an error. Fix #17754.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      return tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset);'], 'added_lines': ['      return 0;']}
description: Infinite loop in the BitTorrent DHT dissector in Wireshark 3.6.0 and 3.4.0 to 3.4.10 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: The while loop at [14] is driven by offset, which advances by string_len at [48]. When bencoded_string_length returns 0 at [16], the error branch at [17] reports the invalid length but returns tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset) at [20] instead of a distinct error value, and offset is never advanced, so the loop condition can keep re-evaluating the same byte.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-835: the while loop's exit condition is not reached on the zero-length-string path, producing an infinite loop. The fix returns 0 so the caller aborts, confirming the loop-progress defect rather than a separate memory-safety issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path returns a nonzero length to the caller rather than signaling failure, and the loop makes no progress when string_len is 0. A crafted or injected DHT packet containing a zero-length bencoded string triggers repeated iteration on the same offset, causing CPU exhaustion and denial of service.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tsas_port_delete(phy->port);', '\t\tphy->port = NULL;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.1.13, there is a memory leak in drivers/scsi/libsas/sas_expander.c when SAS expander discovery fails. This will cause a BUG and denial of service.

code_evidence: Line 21 allocates the SAS port via sas_port_alloc() and stores it in phy->port; line 22 registers it with sas_port_add().

In the error path when sas_discover_expander(child) returns nonzero (lines 58-59), the cleanup only deletes the rphy, removes the device from the list and drops the device reference (lines 60-64); phy->port is never released and the pointer remains dangling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because memory allocated by sas_port_alloc() is not released on the error path, making it unavailable for reuse; the later BUG is the downstream consequence, not the weakness itself. A use-after-free (CWE-416) does not apply since there is no premature free here, only a missing release.

evidence_lines.code:
phy->port = sas_port_alloc(&parent->rphy->dev, phy_id);
BUG_ON(sas_port_add(phy->port) != 0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failure branch of sas_discover_expander() omits sas_port_delete(phy->port) and clearing phy->port, so the port allocated at line 21 is leaked and phy->port keeps a stale reference. Trigger: discovery of an expander fails after the port was allocated and added. Consequence: leaked port resources accumulate and the stale phy->port later causes sas_port_add_phy to hit the BUG in scsi_transport_sas.c, leading to kernel panic/denial of service.

description: The IKEv1 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-isakmp.c:ikev1_n_print().

code_evidence: Line 90 computes cp just past the SPI field; line 91 sets ep2 from item_len and line 92 only checks cp < ep (capture end), not cp + 4 <= ep2.
For IPSECDOI_NTYPE_REPLAY_STATUS (lines 109-112), EXTRACT_32BITS(cp) reads four bytes without verifying that four bytes remain within the notify payload.
