diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct ipv6_opt_hdr *exthdr =', '\t\t\t\t(struct ipv6_opt_hdr *)(ipv6_hdr(skb) + 1);', '\twhile (offset + 1 <= packet_len) {', '\t\texthdr = (struct ipv6_opt_hdr *)(skb_network_header(skb) +', '\t\t\t\t\t\t offset);', '\treturn offset;'], 'added_lines': ['\twhile (offset <= packet_len) {', '\t\tstruct ipv6_opt_hdr *exthdr;', '\t\tif (offset + sizeof(struct ipv6_opt_hdr) > packet_len)', '\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '', '\t\texthdr = (struct ipv6_opt_hdr *)(skb_network_header(skb) +', '\t\t\t\t\t\t offset);', '\treturn -EINVAL;']}
description: The IPv6 fragmentation implementation in the Linux kernel through 4.11.1 does not consider that the nexthdr field may be associated with an invalid option, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and BUG) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted socket and send system calls.

code_evidence: Loop guard only requires offset + 1 <= packet_len, so it can enter when fewer than sizeof(struct ipv6_opt_hdr) bytes remain. Line 28 calls ipv6_optlen(exthdr) reading the option header, and lines 30-31 recompute exthdr from skb_network_header + offset without validating offset against packet_len, so subsequent iterations dereference beyond the linear buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads option-header bytes past the end of the skb linear data, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The missing length constraint on offset before dereferencing exthdr is the root cause; the crash is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The header-option parser trusts the attacker-controlled nexthdr chain and advances offset by ipv6_optlen without checking that a full ipv6_opt_hdr remains. A crafted raw IPv6 packet with an invalid/oversized option makes offset exceed packet_len, causing out-of-bounds reads (KASAN slab-out-of-bounds) in ip6_find_1stfragopt and downstream fragmentation, leading to a kernel crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
FLACExtractor: copy protect mWriteBuffer

Bug: 30895578
Change-Id: I4cba36bbe3502678210e5925181683df9726b431
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (getChannels() == 0 || getChannels() > 8) {', '            void (*mCopy)(short *dst, const int *const *src, unsigned nSamples, unsigned nChannels);'], 'added_lines': ['        if (getChannels() == 0 || getChannels() > kMaxChannels) {', '            void (*mCopy)(short *dst, const int * src[kMaxChannels], unsigned nSamples, unsigned nChannels);']}
description: A remote code execution vulnerability in FLACExtractor.cpp in libstagefright in Mediaserver could enable an attacker using a specially crafted file to cause memory corruption during media file and data processing. This issue is rated as Critical due to the possibility of remote code execution within the context of the Mediaserver process. Product: Android. Versions: 4.4.4, 5.0.2, 5.1.1, 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2. Android ID: A-34970788.

code_evidence: Lines 31-34 reject channel counts of 0 or greater than 8, bounding getChannels() before any copy routine is selected.
Lines 61-75 define the copy dispatch table whose mCopy signature takes a fixed-size array of channel source pointers, and whose entries only cover 1, 2, or 8 channels.
Lines 76-82 select the first table entry whose mChannels is at least getChannels(), so a valid channel count maps to a copyMultiCh routine.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fix enforces the maximum channel constraint (kMaxChannels) and sizes the mCopy source-pointer parameter accordingly, directly preventing operations outside the intended buffer boundary during channel copying, which fits CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the channel-count bound that must constrain the number of source channel pointers passed to the multi-channel copy routines. The trigger is a crafted FLAC stream with an out-of-range channel count in STREAMINFO; without the bound, the multi-channel copy would index beyond the expected source pointer array. The supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read/write leading to memory corruption.

description: libyara/re.c in the regex component in YARA 3.5.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and application crash) via a crafted rule that is mishandled in the yr_re_exec function.

code_evidence: Forward match calls exec with data + offset and length data_size - offset; the previous code passed no explicit size and relied on flags to infer start position, so the buffer length consumed by the regex engine was not bounded by the remaining bytes.
Backward match calls exec with data + offset and length offset; this bounds the backward scan to bytes before offset, but the wide/ASCII forward path is where the remaining-size bound matters.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function passes buffer pointers and sizes into the regex executor; the defect is a read beyond the intended input buffer, matching CWE-125. It is not a write or arithmetic overflow: the consequence is an out-of-bounds read leading to availability impact.

commit_msg:
The total cork length created by ip6_append_data includes extension
headers, so we must exclude them when comparing them against the
IPV6_CHECKSUM offset which does not include extension headers.

Reported-by: Kyle Zeng <zengyhkyle@gmail.com>
Fixes: 357b40a18b04 ("[IPV6]: IPV6_CHECKSUM socket option can corrupt kernel memory")
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct ipv6_txoptions *opt;', '\topt = inet6_sk(sk)->cork.opt;', '\ttotal_len -= opt ? opt->opt_flen : 0;', '']}
description: A NULL pointer dereference flaw was found in rawv6_push_pending_frames in net/ipv6/raw.c in the network subcomponent in the Linux kernel. This flaw causes the system to crash.

code_evidence: When the cork has more than one skb, csum_skb starts NULL and is only assigned inside the skb_queue_walk when offset < len (lines 33-37). If offset is never less than any skb's transport length, the loop ends without assigning csum_skb; line 39 then sets skb = csum_skb (NULL) and line 41/42 dereference it via skb_transport_offset and skb_copy_bits.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (skb) that it expects to be non-NULL but can be NULL on the multi-skb path, matching CWE-476. This is a null-dereference availability issue, not an out-of-bounds read, since the failure occurs before any buffer access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the multi-skb path assumes the walk always finds a skb containing the checksum offset, leaving csum_skb NULL otherwise. Trigger: a checksum offset that falls beyond the transport lengths of all queued skbs (e.g., offset >= total_len - 1 was not reached but per-skb lengths are shorter). Consequence: NULL skb is passed to skb_transport_offset/skb_copy_bits, causing a crash (DoS).

Doing so, we save one call to get data we already have in the struct.

Also, since there is no guarantee that getname use sockaddr_ll
parameter beyond its size, we add a little bit of security here.
It should do not do beyond MAX_ADDR_LEN, but syzbot found that
ax25_getname writes more (72 bytes, the size of full_sockaddr_ax25,
versus 20 + 32 bytes of sockaddr_ll + MAX_ADDR_LEN in syzbot repro).

Fixes: 3a4d5c94e9593 ("vhost_net: a kernel-level virtio server")
Reported-by: syzbot+f2a62d07a5198c819c7b@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Eugenio Pérez <eperezma@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct {', '\t\tstruct sockaddr_ll sa;', '\t\tchar  buf[MAX_ADDR_LEN];', '\t} uaddr;', '\tr = sock->ops->getname(sock, (struct sockaddr *)&uaddr.sa, 0);', '\tif (r < 0)', '\t\tgoto err;', '', '\tif (uaddr.sa.sll_family != AF_PACKET) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (sock->sk->sk_family != AF_PACKET) {']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.5.8, get_raw_socket in drivers/vhost/net.c lacks validation of an sk_family field, which might allow attackers to trigger kernel stack corruption via crafted system calls.

code_evidence: The function declares a stack buffer uaddr sized as struct sockaddr_ll plus MAX_ADDR_LEN, then passes (struct sockaddr *)&uaddr.sa to sock->ops->getname with a length of 0.

getname may write the full size implied by the socket's address family; for an AF_AX25 socket this is sizeof(full_sockaddr_ax25) (72 bytes), exceeding the 20+MAX_ADDR_LEN stack object. The family check at line 18 occurs only after getname has already written.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The operation writes past the end of the intended stack buffer uaddr, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. The missing family/size validation is the enabling cause, but the supported weakness is the resulting memory write beyond bounds, not merely an incorrect check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code calls the socket's getname before constraining the address family, so the write size is not bounded by the small uaddr buffer. Trigger: an attacker supplies an fd for a non-AF_PACKET socket whose getname writes more than the allocated stack size. Consequence: kernel stack out-of-bounds write, causing stack corruption/crash and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Greg Kroah-Hartman says:

====================
Raw socket cleanups

Ori Nimron pointed out that there are a number of places in the kernel
where you can create a raw socket, without having to have the
CAP_NET_RAW permission.

To resolve this, here's a short patch series to test these odd and old
protocols for this permission before allowing the creation to succeed

All patches are currently against the net tree.
====================

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (sock->type == SOCK_RAW)', '\telse'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (sock->type == SOCK_RAW) {', '\t\tif (!capable(CAP_NET_RAW))', '\t\t\treturn -EPERM;', '\t} else {', '\t}']}
description: ax25_create in net/ax25/af_ax25.c in the AF_AX25 network module in the Linux kernel 3.16 through 5.3.2 does not enforce CAP_NET_RAW, which means that unprivileged users can create a raw socket, aka CID-0614e2b73768.

code_evidence: The function accepts SOCK_RAW as a valid socket type alongside SOCK_STREAM and SOCK_DGRAM, returning only -ESOCKTNOSUPPORT for other types.
When sock->type is SOCK_RAW, the code assigns llcp_rawsock_ops and proceeds to allocate the socket via nfc_llcp_sock_alloc, with no permission or capability check gating this branch.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a privileged action (raw socket creation) without any authorization check, which is exactly CWE-862 Missing Authorization. It is not merely an incorrect capability comparison; the capability enforcement is entirely absent.

evidence_lines.code:
if (sock->type != SOCK_STREAM &&
sock->type != SOCK_DGRAM &&
sock->type != SOCK_RAW)
return -ESOCKTNOSUPPORT;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SOCK_RAW branch selects raw-socket operations and allocates a socket without verifying that the caller holds CAP_NET_RAW. Trigger: an unprivileged user requests a SOCK_RAW NFC LLCP socket. Consequence: the raw socket creation succeeds, granting access to raw protocol operations that should require privilege.

commit_msg:
bgpd: Limit flowspec to no attribute means a implicit withdrawal

All other parsing functions done from bgp_nlri_parse() assume
no attributes == an implicit withdrawal.  Let's move
bgp_nlri_parse_flowspec() into the same alignment.

Reported-by: Matteo Memelli <mmemelli@amazon.it>
Signed-off-by: Donald Sharp <sharpd@nvidia.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/*', "\t * All other AFI/SAFI's treat no attribute as a implicit", '\t * withdraw.  Flowspec should as well.', '\t */', '\tif (!attr)', '\t\twithdraw = 1;']}
description: An issue was discovered in FRRouting FRR through 9.0. bgp_nlri_parse_flowspec in bgpd/bgp_flowspec.c processes malformed requests with no attributes, leading to a NULL pointer dereference.

code_evidence: The function receives an attribute pointer 'attr' that may be NULL; the signature at lines 1-2 does not require it to be non-NULL.
When 'withdraw' is false, line 86's check falls through to bgp_update at lines 87-89, which is passed 'attr' directly without a NULL guard.
The alternative branch at lines 90-92 calls bgp_withdraw and does not use attr, so the unsafe path is specifically the update path with a NULL attr.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the defect is an unguarded NULL pointer passed into a callee that dereferences it, leading to a crash. It is not merely a missing validation (CWE-20); the direct consequence is a NULL dereference.

evidence_lines.code:
int bgp_nlri_parse_flowspec(struct peer *peer, struct attr *attr,
struct bgp_nlri *packet, int withdraw)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bgp_nlri_parse_flowspec treats a no-attribute NLRI as an update (withdraw false) and forwards the NULL attr into bgp_update. Trigger: a malformed flowspec NLRI arriving with no path attributes. Consequence: downstream attribute processing dereferences the NULL pointer, crashing bgpd (DoS).

description: In Mcrouter prior to v0.41.0, a large struct input provided to the Carbon protocol reader could result in stack exhaustion and denial of service.

code_evidence: In the FieldType::Struct case, skip() calls itself recursively at line 46 for each nested field returned by readFieldHeader(). The loop at lines 41-47 keeps recursing until a Stop field is encountered, with no depth counter or nesting limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 (Uncontrolled Recursion) directly matches: user-controlled struct nesting drives self-recursion in skip() with no limiting condition, exhausting the program stack. The missing depth constraint, not merely large data, is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: recursive descent over Struct fields without any depth bound. Trigger: a crafted input containing a deeply nested or long chain of struct fields causes skip() to recurse once per field. Supported consequence: unbounded stack growth leading to stack exhaustion and denial of service (crash).

commit_msg:
x86/mm: alloc/free_lN_table: Retain partial_flags on -EINTR

When validating or de-validating pages (in alloc_lN_table and
free_lN_table respectively), the `partial_flags` local variable is
used to keep track of whether the "current" PTE started the entire
operation in a "may be partial" state.

One of the patches in XSA-299 addressed the fact that it is possible
for a previously-partially-validated entry to subsequently be found to
have invalid entries (indicated by returning -EINVAL); in which case
page->partial_flags needs to be set to indicate that the current PTE
may have the partial bit set (and thus _put_page_type() should be
called with PTF_partial_set).

Unfortunately, the patches in XSA-299 assumed that once
put_page_from_lNe() returned -ERESTART on a page, it was not possible
for it to return -EINTR.  This turns out to be true for
alloc_lN_table() and free_lN_table, but not for _get_page_type() and
_put_page_type(): both can return -EINTR when called on pages with
PGT_partial set.  In these cases, the pages PGT_partial will still be
set; failing to set partial_flags appropriately may allow an attacker
to do a privilege escalation similar to those described in XSA-299.

Fix this by always copying the local partial_flags variable into
page->partial_flags when exiting early.

NB that on the "get" side, no adjustment to nr_validated_entries is
needed: whether pte[i] is partially validated or entirely
un-validated, we want nr_validated_entries = i.  On the "put" side,
however, we need to adjust nr_validated_entries appropriately: if
pte[i] is entirely validated, we want nr_validated_entries = i + 1; if
pte[i] is partially validated, we want nr_validated_entries = i.

This is part of XSA-310.

Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        page->nr_validated_ptes = i + 1;', '        page->partial_flags = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['        page->nr_validated_ptes = i + !(partial_flags & PTF_partial_set);', '        page->partial_flags = partial_flags;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to gain host OS privileges by leveraging race conditions in pagetable promotion and demotion operations, because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2019-18421. XSA-299 addressed several critical issues in restartable PV type change operations. Despite extensive testing and auditing, some corner cases were missed. A malicious PV guest administrator may be able to escalate their privilege to that of the host. All security-supported versions of Xen are vulnerable. Only x86 systems are affected. Arm systems are not affected. Only x86 PV guests can leverage the vulnerability. x86 HVM and PVH guests cannot leverage the vulnerability. Note that these attacks require very precise timing, which may be difficult to exploit in practice.

code_evidence: The loop calls put_page_from_l2e(pl2e[i], pfn, partial_flags) and can break with rc == -EINTR from hypercall_preempt_check() at line 21; the per-entry partial_flags is reset to 0 at line 16 after each successful entry.

On the -EINTR exit at line 36, the function sets page->nr_validated_ptes = i + 1 and page->partial_flags = 0, discarding the fact that pte[i] may still have PGT_partial set, so the resumed operation loses the partial state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The vulnerability arises from a restartable, preemptible sequence that fails to preserve exclusive partial state across a timing window where another code sequence can observe or modify the shared page metadata. This improper synchronization of shared page state across concurrent/interleaved operations matches CWE-362 rather than a simple bounds or validation flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the early -EINTR exit overwrites page->partial_flags with 0 instead of retaining the local partial_flags, so a page whose PTE was left partially validated is resumed as if fully un-validated. Trigger: a hypercall preemption between page-table demotion steps on a PGT_partial page. Consequence: inconsistent page type/refcount state enables privilege escalation from a PV guest to the host.

commit_msg:
RPCoRDMA: Set an upper bound for our chunk size.

Make sure our write chunk size doesn't exceed our tvbuff. Adjust a few
length checks.

Bug: 14449
Change-Id: If9dd8a6094830c5b47adfff0acb3ff726168e801
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/25945
Petri-Dish: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if ((offset + chunk_size) < offset)'], 'added_lines': ['        if (chunk_size == 0)']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-rpcrdma.c had an infinite loop that was addressed by validating a chunk size.

code_evidence: The while(1) loop only exits when value_follows is zero (line 9-10) or when the overflow check on line 13 triggers. If get_write_chunk_size returns a nonzero chunk_size that does not overflow offset+chunk_size, the loop advances offset by only 4 bytes per iteration (line 8) and never re-checks that offset stays within the tvbuff. A malformed chunk_size/offset combination that keeps value_follows nonzero and avoids the overflow condition lets the loop iterate indefinitely.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loop's exit condition on line 13 is effectively unreachable for valid non-overflowing chunk sizes, matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. The fix bounds chunk_size==0, confirming the loop could not terminate; this is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop's termination depends on chunk_size overflowing offset, not on a valid upper bound or bounds check against the tvbuff. Trigger: attacker-supplied packet data yielding nonzero value_follows and a chunk_size that never causes wraparound. Consequence: unbounded iteration consuming CPU (DoS).

Fix issue #2855

description: Integer overflow in the getnum function in lua_struct.c in Redis 2.8.x before 2.8.24 and 3.0.x before 3.0.6 allows context-dependent attackers with permission to run Lua code in a Redis session to cause a denial of service (memory corruption and application crash) or possibly bypass intended sandbox restrictions via a large number, which triggers a stack-based buffer overflow.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an integer overflow/wraparound in the parsed size calculation, matching CWE-190. The size check at line 13 only compares against MAXINTSIZE and does not validate overflow of the parsed value, so it is not a CWE-190 mitigation.

case 'c': return getnum(fmt, 1);
int sz = getnum(fmt, sizeof(int));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: getnum converts an attacker-controlled number from the Lua format string into an int/size_t without detecting overflow. commit_msg:
A number of userspace utilities depend on making calls to RTAS to retrieve
information and update various things.

The existing API through which we expose RTAS to userspace exposes more
RTAS functionality than we actually need, through the sys_rtas syscall,
which allows root (or anyone with CAP_SYS_ADMIN) to make any RTAS call they
want with arbitrary arguments.

Many RTAS calls take the address of a buffer as an argument, and it's up to
the caller to specify the physical address of the buffer as an argument. We
allocate a buffer (the "RMO buffer") in the Real Memory Area that RTAS can
access, and then expose the physical address and size of this buffer in
/proc/powerpc/rtas/rmo_buffer. Userspace is expected to read this address,
poke at the buffer using /dev/mem, and pass an address in the RMO buffer to
the RTAS call.

However, there's nothing stopping the caller from specifying whatever
address they want in the RTAS call, and it's easy to construct a series of
RTAS calls that can overwrite arbitrary bytes (even without /dev/mem
access).

Additionally, there are some RTAS calls that do potentially dangerous
things and for which there are no legitimate userspace use cases.

In the past, this would not have been a particularly big deal as it was
assumed that root could modify all system state freely, but with Secure
Boot and lockdown we need to care about this.

We can't fundamentally change the ABI at this point, however we can address
this by implementing a filter that checks RTAS calls against a list
of permitted calls and forces the caller to use addresses within the RMO
buffer.

The list is based off the list of calls that are used by the librtas
userspace library, and has been tested with a number of existing userspace
RTAS utilities. For compatibility with any applications we are not aware of
that require other calls, the filter can be turned off at build time.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Daniel Axtens <dja@axtens.net>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Donnellan <ajd@linux.ibm.com>
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20200820044512.7543-1-ajd@linux.ibm.com

description: A flaw was found in the way RTAS handled memory accesses in userspace to kernel communication. On a locked down (usually due to Secure Boot) guest system running on top of PowerVM or KVM hypervisors (pseries platform) a root like local user could use this flaw to further increase their privileges to that of a running kernel.

commit_msg:
hfs: fix keylen check in hfs_cat_traverse()

If key->key_len is 65535, calculating "uint16_t keylen' would
cause an overflow:

   uint16_t keylen;
   ...
   keylen = 2 + tsk_getu16(hfs->fs_info.endian, key->key_len)

so the code bypasses the sanity check "if (keylen > nodesize)"
which results in crash later:

    ./toolfs/fstools/fls -b 512 -f hfs <image>
    =================================================================
    ==16==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x6210000256a4 (pc 0x00000054812b bp 0x7ffca548a8f0 sp 0x7ffca548a480 T0)
    ==16==The signal is caused by a READ memory access.
        #0 0x54812a in hfs_dir_open_meta_cb /fuzzing/sleuthkit/tsk/fs/hfs_dent.c:237:20
        #1 0x51a96c in hfs_cat_traverse /fuzzing/sleuthkit/tsk/fs/hfs.c:1082:21
        #2 0x547785 in hfs_dir_open_meta /fuzzing/sleuthkit/tsk/fs/hfs_dent.c:480:9
        #3 0x50f57d in tsk_fs_dir_open_meta /fuzzing/sleuthkit/tsk/fs/fs_dir.c:290:14
        #4 0x54af17 in tsk_fs_path2inum /fuzzing/sleuthkit/tsk/fs/ifind_lib.c:237:23
        #5 0x522266 in hfs_open /fuzzing/sleuthkit/tsk/fs/hfs.c:6579:9
        #6 0x508e89 in main /fuzzing/sleuthkit/tools/fstools/fls.cpp:267:19
        #7 0x7f9daf67c2b0 in __libc_start_main (/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6+0x202b0)
        #8 0x41d679 in _start (/fuzzing/sleuthkit/tools/fstools/fls+0x41d679)

Make 'keylen' int type to prevent the overflow and fix that.
Now, I get proper error message instead of crash:
    ./toolfs/fstools/fls -b 512 -f hfs <image>
    General file system error (hfs_cat_traverse: length of key 3 in leaf node 1 too large (65537 vs 4096))
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                uint16_t keylen;', '                uint16_t keylen;'], 'added_lines': ['                int keylen;', '                int keylen;']}
description: The Sleuth Kit 4.6.0 and earlier is affected by: Integer Overflow. The impact is: Opening crafted disk image triggers crash in tsk/fs/hfs_dent.c:237. The component is: Overflow in fls tool used on HFS image. Bug is in tsk/fs/hfs.c file in function hfs_cat_traverse() in lines: 952, 1062. The attack vector is: Victim must open a crafted HFS filesystem image.

code_evidence: In the index-node branch, keylen is declared uint16_t [81], then assigned 2 + a 16-bit value read from the on-disk key [94,95]; the sanity check keylen > nodesize [96] follows.

The leaf-node branch mirrors this: uint16_t keylen [162], computed from key->key_len at [175,176] and checked at [177]. When key->key_len is 65535, 2 + 65535 wraps to 1 in 16 bits, so the length check passes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a calculation whose result exceeds the storage type, producing a small wraparound value that defeats a length/offset check, which is exactly integer overflow/wraparound (CWE-190). The downstream out-of-bounds read is the consequence, not the root cause; the type change to int prevents the wrap.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the key length is computed in a 16-bit unsigned variable, so a crafted key_len of 65535 wraps the sum to a small value and the bounds check against nodesize is bypassed. The wrapped keylen then flows into the callback/index-record offset computation, leading to an out-of-bounds read and crash on a crafted HFS image.

commit_msg:
Jann Horn reported that SO_PEERCRED and SO_PEERGROUPS implementations
are racy, as af_unix can concurrently change sk_peer_pid and sk_peer_cred.

In order to fix this issue, this patch adds a new spinlock that needs
to be used whenever these fields are read or written.

Jann also pointed out that l2cap_sock_get_peer_pid_cb() is currently
reading sk->sk_peer_pid which makes no sense, as this field
is only possibly set by AF_UNIX sockets.
We will have to clean this in a separate patch.
This could be done by reverting b48596d1dc25 "Bluetooth: L2CAP: Add get_peer_pid callback"
or implementing what was truly expected.

Fixes: 109f6e39fa07 ("af_unix: Allow SO_PEERCRED to work across namespaces.")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Cc: Eric W. Biederman <ebiederm@xmission.com>
Cc: Luiz Augusto von Dentz <luiz.von.dentz@intel.com>
Cc: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!sk->sk_peer_cred)', '\t\tn = sk->sk_peer_cred->group_info->ngroups;', '\t\tret = groups_to_user((gid_t __user *)optval,', '\t\t\t\t     sk->sk_peer_cred->group_info);'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\tspin_lock(&sk->sk_peer_lock);', '\t\tspin_unlock(&sk->sk_peer_lock);', '', '\t\tconst struct cred *cred;', '\t\tcred = sk_get_peer_cred(sk);', '\t\tif (!cred)', '\t\tn = cred->group_info->ngroups;', '\t\t\tput_cred(cred);', '\t\tret = groups_to_user((gid_t __user *)optval, cred->group_info);', '\t\tput_cred(cred);']}
description: A use-after-free read flaw was found in sock_getsockopt() in net/core/sock.c due to SO_PEERCRED and SO_PEERGROUPS race with listen() (and connect()) in the Linux kernel. In this flaw, an attacker with a user privileges may crash the system or leak internal kernel information.

code_evidence: In the SO_PEERCRED branch, sk->sk_peer_pid and sk->sk_peer_cred are read directly and passed to cred_to_ucred() without holding sk_peer_lock, so the read is not synchronized against concurrent writers of these fields.

In the SO_PEERGROUPS branch, sk->sk_peer_cred is dereferenced for the NULL check, then its group_info->ngroups is read and group_info is passed to groups_to_user(), all without any lock or reference taken on the cred.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The target CWE-362 fits because the unsafe operation is a concurrent access to a shared resource (sk_peer_cred) without exclusive access, creating a timing window in which an interfering code sequence frees or modifies the object. The race is the cause; the use-after-free read is the supported consequence, not a separate label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function reads shared sk->sk_peer_pid/sk_peer_cred without synchronization, while af_unix can concurrently replace or release these fields. Trigger: a local user calls getsockopt(SO_PEERCRED/SO_PEERGROUPS) while the peer credentials are changed, causing the cred to be freed between the read and use. Consequence: use-after-free read, leading to a kernel crash or leak of internal kernel memory.

commit_msg:
By validating length fields from server responses, out of boundary
accesses and endless loops can be mitigated.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    char *data = NULL;', '\t    if (any->length > rlen)'], 'added_lines': ['    char *data = NULL, *end = NULL;', '\t    end = data + rlen;', '\t    if ((char *)any + sizeof(XInputClass) > end ||', '\t\tany->length == 0 || any->length > rlen)', '\t\tif ((char *)any + sizeof(xValuatorState) > end)', '\t\t    goto out;']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in X.org libXi before 1.7.7 allow remote X servers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds memory access or infinite loop) via vectors involving length fields.

code_evidence: rlen is derived from the server-controlled rep.length via a left shift; the guard only rejects rep.length >= (INT_MAX>>2), so the multiplication itself has a bounded check but data allocation size still depends on untrusted length.
The loop trusts any->length to advance rlen and the pointer any, with no check that any has sizeof(XInputClass) bytes remaining before dereferencing any->length.
For ValuatorClass, v->num_valuators is attacker-controlled and multiplied by sizeof(int) in the size accumulation and in the V->valuators loop; no bound ties num_valuators to the remaining buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-190 because the code performs integer calculations (num_valuators * sizeof(int), size accumulation and pointer arithmetic) on untrusted values without ensuring the results stay within representable/allocation bounds, allowing wraparound that leads to out-of-bounds access. It is not merely a missing length check; the unchecked multiplication and addition are the core weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that arithmetic on server-supplied length/count fields (rep.length, any->length, v->num_valuators) is not constrained against the actual received buffer size. A malicious X server can send a small reply whose class length is zero or whose num_valuators is large, so pointer advancement and size computations wrap or exceed the allocation, causing out-of-bounds reads and an unbounded loop rather than a safely rejected reply.

* tools/tiffcp.c: fix read of undefined variable in case of missing
required tags. Found on test case of MSVR 35100.
* tools/tiffcrop.c: fix read of undefined buffer in
readContigStripsIntoBuffer() due to uint16 overflow. Probably not a
security issue but I can be wrong. Reported as MSVR 35100 by Axel

description: tools/tiffcrop.c in libtiff 4.0.6 reads an undefined buffer in readContigStripsIntoBuffer() because of a uint16 integer overflow. Reported as MSVR 35100.

code_evidence: Line 5 stores TIFFNumberOfStrips(in) in a uint16 nstrips; a strip count above 65535 wraps to a small value.
Line 14 loops strip < nstrips using that truncated count, and lines 15-16/26 read each strip into bufp based on bytes_read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The narrowing of an integer strip count to uint16 is exactly an integer overflow/wraparound (CWE-190) whose wrapped value drives buffer indexing and pointer advancement. This is not merely a bounds check omission; the wrap is the cause.

evidence_lines.code:
uint16 strip, nstrips   = TIFFNumberOfStrips(in);
for (strip = 0; strip < nstrips; strip++) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the strip count is narrowed to uint16, so a large TIFFNumberOfStrips value wraps. The loop then iterates a truncated count, and bytes_read-derived pointer arithmetic (bufp += bytes_read) advances inconsistently with the true strip layout, producing reads of an undefined/incorrect buffer region.

scsi: target: Fix XCOPY NAA identifier lookup

When attempting to match EXTENDED COPY CSCD descriptors with corresponding
se_devices, target_xcopy_locate_se_dev_e4() currently iterates over LIO's
global devices list which includes all configured backstores.

This change ensures that only initiator-accessible backstores are
considered during CSCD descriptor lookup, according to the session's
se_node_acl LUN list.

To avoid LUN removal race conditions, device pinning is changed from being
configfs based to instead using the se_node_acl lun_ref.

commit_msg:
tvbuff_composite: fix buffer overflow due to wrong offset adjustment

The tvb_offset method should return the offset of the buffer within the
backing tvb (ds_tvb). The currently returned non-zero offset is valid
for tvbuff_subset.c, but not for the composite TVB. The backing tvb is
the tvb itself, so the offset should be zero (or "counter" for
consistency with tvbuff_real.c and others).

This bug is observable with the capture from the bug. In tshark, the
data field in the PDML output has value "field length invalid!" and the
position attribute ("pos") is too large. With the -V option it even
crashes with a buffer overflow (read). In the GUI, the bytes tab shows
range 3199-19642 even if the data source is only 16444 bytes while the
selection should have been 0-16443.

Bug: 14466
Change-Id: I01399ff500321dba262eb60b67c4cddb173b4679
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/30124
Petri-Dish: Peter Wu <peter@lekensteyn.nl>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Anders Broman <a.broman58@gmail.com>
(cherry picked from commit ec5adb0ce98c37c8119feb972a5207e0e1721d9b)

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['composite_offset(const tvbuff_t *tvb, const guint counter)', '\tconst struct tvb_composite *composite_tvb = (const struct tvb_composite *) tvb;', '\tconst tvbuff_t *member = (const tvbuff_t *)composite_tvb->composite.tvbs->data;', '', '\treturn tvb_offset_from_real_beginning_counter(member, counter);'], 'added_lines': ['composite_offset(const tvbuff_t *tvb _U_, const guint counter)', '\treturn counter;']}
description: In Wireshark 2.6.0 to 2.6.4 and 2.4.0 to 2.4.10, the dissection engine could crash. This was addressed in epan/tvbuff_composite.c by preventing a heap-based buffer over-read.

code_evidence: composite_offset casts the tvb to struct tvb_composite, dereferences composite_tvb->composite.tvbs->data to get the first member tvb, then returns tvb_offset_from_real_beginning_counter(member, counter), deriving the offset from that member rather than returning counter for the composite tvb itself.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The incorrect offset causes reads indexed beyond the intended composite buffer, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. A wrong-offset/wrapping defect is the cause; the read past the buffer end is the supported weakness consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the offset for a composite tvb is computed relative to its backing member tvb, producing a non-zero offset that is invalid for the composite buffer whose backing tvb is itself. Trigger: a caller uses this offset to index into the composite tvb, so the position exceeds the buffer's real length. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds read past the end of the buffer, reported as a read crash.

commit_msg:
x86/fpu: Don't cache access to fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx

The state/owner of the FPU is saved to fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx by pointing
to the context that is currently loaded. It never changed during the
lifetime of a task - it remained stable/constant.

After deferred FPU registers loading until return to userland was
implemented, the content of fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx may change during
preemption and must not be cached.

This went unnoticed for some time and was now noticed, in particular
since gcc 9 is caching that load in copy_fpstate_to_sigframe() and
reusing it in the retry loop:

  copy_fpstate_to_sigframe()
    load fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx and save on stack
    fpregs_lock()
    copy_fpregs_to_sigframe() /* failed */
    fpregs_unlock()
         *** PREEMPTION, another uses FPU, changes fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx ***

    fault_in_pages_writeable() /* succeed, retry */

    fpregs_lock()
	__fpregs_load_activate()
	  fpregs_state_valid() /* uses fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx from stack */
    copy_fpregs_to_sigframe() /* succeeds, random FPU content */

This is a comparison of the assembly produced by gcc 9, without vs with this
patch:

| # arch/x86/kernel/fpu/signal.c:173:      if (!access_ok(buf, size))
|        cmpq    %rdx, %rax      # tmp183, _4
|        jb      .L190   #,
|-# arch/x86/include/asm/fpu/internal.h:512:       return fpu == this_cpu_read_stable(fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx) && cpu == fpu->last_cpu;
|-#APP
|-# 512 "arch/x86/include/asm/fpu/internal.h" 1
|-       movq %gs:fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx,%rax      #, pfo_ret__
|-# 0 "" 2
|-#NO_APP
|-       movq    %rax, -88(%rbp) # pfo_ret__, %sfp
…
|-# arch/x86/include/asm/fpu/internal.h:512:       return fpu == this_cpu_read_stable(fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx) && cpu == fpu->last_cpu;
|-       movq    -88(%rbp), %rcx # %sfp, pfo_ret__
|-       cmpq    %rcx, -64(%rbp) # pfo_ret__, %sfp
|+# arch/x86/include/asm/fpu/internal.h:512:       return fpu == this_cpu_read(fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx) && cpu == fpu->last_cpu;
|+#APP
|+# 512 "arch/x86/include/asm/fpu/internal.h" 1
|+       movq %gs:fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx(%rip),%rax        # fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx, pfo_ret__
|+# 0 "" 2
|+# arch/x86/include/asm/fpu/internal.h:512:       return fpu == this_cpu_read(fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx) && cpu == fpu->last_cpu;
|+#NO_APP
|+       cmpq    %rax, -64(%rbp) # pfo_ret__, %sfp

Use this_cpu_read() instead this_cpu_read_stable() to avoid caching of
fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx during preemption points.

The Fixes: tag points to the commit where deferred FPU loading was
added. Since this commit, the compiler is no longer allowed to move the
load of fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx somewhere else / outside of the locked
section. A task preemption will change its value and stale content will
be observed.

 [ bp: Massage. ]

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn fpu == this_cpu_read_stable(fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx) && cpu == fpu->last_cpu;'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn fpu == this_cpu_read(fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx) && cpu == fpu->last_cpu;']}
description: fpregs_state_valid in arch/x86/include/asm/fpu/internal.h in the Linux kernel before 5.4.2, when GCC 9 is used, allows context-dependent attackers to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact because of incorrect fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx caching, as demonstrated by mishandling of signal-based non-cooperative preemption in Go 1.14 prereleases on amd64, aka CID-59c4bd853abc.

code_evidence: fpregs_state_valid() compares the caller's fpu pointer against this_cpu_read_stable(fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx), treating the per-CPU owner context as a stable value that may be cached. The function is a validity predicate used inside the FPU lock/retry path; the cached read can be reused after a preemption point even though fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx was changed by another task.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale validity check causes the caller to copy FPU register state that does not belong to the current context into a signal frame buffer, producing out-of-bounds/incorrect memory writes and memory corruption. This matches CWE-119's operation on a memory buffer outside its intended boundary; the caching defect is the root cause, the buffer corruption is the resulting out-of-bounds memory operation.

evidence_lines.code:
static inline int fpregs_state_valid(struct fpu *fpu, unsigned int cpu)
return fpu == this_cpu_read_stable(fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx) && cpu == fpu->last_cpu;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: this_cpu_read_stable() lets the compiler hoist/cache the fpu_fpregs_owner_ctx load outside the locked section. Trigger: preemption between a failed copy_fpregs_to_sigframe() and the retry changes the owner context; the stale cached value makes fpregs_state_valid() incorrectly report the state as valid. Consequence: copy_fpregs_to_sigframe() proceeds with mismatched FPU state, leading to corruption of FPU/signal frame memory (memory corruption, DoS).

description: An information disclosure vulnerability in visualizer/EffectVisualizer.cpp in libeffects in Mediaserver could enable a local malicious application to access data outside of its permission levels. This issue is rated as Moderate because it could be used to access sensitive data without permission. Product: Android. Versions: 4.4.4, 5.0.2, 5.1.1, 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1. Android ID: A-31781965.

code_evidence: VISUALIZER_PARAM_CAPTURE_SIZE stores the caller-supplied captureSize directly into pContext->mCaptureSize with no upper bound; this value later sizes the memcpy at [166,167,168] and the reply buffer check at [131,132].
VISUALIZER_PARAM_LATENCY likewise stores an unbounded mLatency, which feeds latencyMs and the deltaSmpl computation at [151,152].

capturePoint = mCaptureIdx - captureSize - deltaSmpl can underflow; if capturePoint < 0, the memcpy at [159,160,161] reads from mCaptureBuf + CAPTURE_BUF_SIZE + capturePoint, i.e. a location that can be outside the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function returns capture data read from outside the intended buffer to the requesting app, an explicit exposure of process memory to an unauthorized local actor, matching CWE-200's confidentiality impact. The underlying out-of-bounds read is the mechanism; the observable result is sensitive data disclosure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled capture size and latency parameters are accepted without range limits, so the derived capturePoint and copy offsets are not constrained to the capture buffer. Trigger: a local app sends EFFECT_CMD_SET_PARAM with oversized values, then issues VISUALIZER_CMD_CAPTURE. Consequence: the memcpy reads out-of-bounds memory and returns it in the reply, exposing data outside the caller's permission level.

description: An issue was discovered in gpac 0.8.0. The strdup function in box_code_base.c has a heap-based buffer over-read.

code_evidence: Line 7 allocates exactly size bytes (ptr->size) for str. The loop at lines 9-15 copies bytes into str[i] and increments i, but only stops early when a NUL byte is read (line 12). If the box data contains no zero byte, the loop writes size bytes then size reaches 0, leaving no terminator. Line 16 then calls gf_strdup(str), which scans for a NUL past the end of the size-byte allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because gf_strdup reads beyond the intended buffer boundary of str, directly matching out-of-bounds read. This is not a write overflow (CWE-787): the copy loop stays within bounds; the unsafe access is the unbounded string scan in strdup.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer is filled with exactly ptr->size bytes and never explicitly NUL-terminated, so it is only terminated by chance when input contains a zero byte. Trigger: a txtc box whose payload lacks a NUL byte. Consequence: gf_strdup reads past the heap allocation (over-read) until it finds a zero, potentially crashing or leaking adjacent heap memory.

No upstream commit exists.

This imports the io_uring codebase from 5.15.85, wholesale. Changes
from that code base:

- Drop IOCB_ALLOC_CACHE, we don't have that in 5.10.
- Drop MKDIRAT/SYMLINKAT/LINKAT. Would require further VFS backports,
  and we don't support these in 5.10 to begin with.
- sock_from_file() old style calling convention.
- Use compat_get_bitmap() only for CONFIG_COMPAT=y

Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>

description:
There is a logic error in io_uring's implementation which can be used to trigger a use-after-free vulnerability leading to privilege escalation.

In the io_prep_async_work function the assumption that the last io_grab_identity call cannot return false is not true, and in this case the function will use the init_cred or the previous linked requests identity to do operations instead of using the current identity. This can lead to reference counting issues causing use-after-free. We recommend upgrading past version 5.10.161.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only conditionally invokes a cancellation helper; it contains no memory reuse or free logic, and the described identity/reference-counting use-after-free is in io_prep_async_work, not this function.

commit_msg: fixed #2284
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (mov->emsgs)', '\t\tgf_isom_box_array_del(mov->emsgs);']}
description: GPAC v2.1-DEV-rev368-gfd054169b-master was discovered to contain a memory leak via the component gf_list_new at utils/list.c.

code_evidence: The teardown function frees several fragment-related members (block_buffer, last_producer_ref_time) but the pre-patch code had no release for mov->emsgs; the patch adds that release after block_buffer is freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits: a heap allocation owned by the movie object is not released during its effective lifetime teardown, leaving memory unavailable for reuse. This is a missing-free defect in cleanup, not a double-free or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: gf_isom_delete_movie is the destructor for GF_ISOFile and must release all owned allocations. Because mov->emsgs (an array of boxes) was never freed, its allocated memory became unreachable once mov was freed, so each movie deletion leaked the emsgs array. Trigger is any lifecycle path that allocates emsgs and then deletes the movie; supported consequence is unbounded memory consumption over repeated open/close cycles.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12894/In lookup_bytestring(), take the length of the byte string into account.

Otherwise, if, in our search of the hash table, we come across a byte
string that's shorter than the string we're looking for, we'll search
past the end of the string in the hash table.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Forcepoint's security
researchers Otto Airamo & Antti Levomäki.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static inline struct enamemem *', '\tstruct enamemem *tp;', '\twhile (tp->e_nxt)', '\t\tif (tp->e_addr0 == i &&', '\t\t    tp->e_addr1 == j &&', '\t\t    tp->e_addr2 == k &&', '\t\t    memcmp((const char *)bs, (const char *)(tp->e_bs), nlen) == 0)', '\t\t\ttp = tp->e_nxt;', '\ttp->e_addr0 = i;', '\ttp->e_addr1 = j;', '\ttp->e_addr2 = k;', '\ttp->e_bs = (u_char *) calloc(1, nlen + 1);', '\tif (tp->e_bs == NULL)', '\tmemcpy(tp->e_bs, bs, nlen);', '\ttp->e_nxt = (struct enamemem *)calloc(1, sizeof(*tp));', '\tif (tp->e_nxt == NULL)'], 'added_lines': ['static inline struct bsnamemem *', '\tstruct bsnamemem *tp;', '\twhile (tp->bs_nxt)', '\t\tif (nlen == tp->bs_nbytes &&', '\t\t    tp->bs_addr0 == i &&', '\t\t    tp->bs_addr1 == j &&', '\t\t    tp->bs_addr2 == k &&', '\t\t    memcmp((const char *)bs, (const char *)(tp->bs_bytes), nlen) == 0)', '\t\t\ttp = tp->bs_nxt;', '\ttp->bs_addr0 = i;', '\ttp->bs_addr1 = j;', '\ttp->bs_addr2 = k;', '\ttp->bs_bytes = (u_char *) calloc(1, nlen + 1);', '\tif (tp->bs_bytes == NULL)', '\tmemcpy(tp->bs_bytes, bs, nlen);', '\ttp->bs_nbytes = nlen;', '\ttp->bs_nxt = (struct bsnamemem *)calloc(1, sizeof(*tp));', '\tif (tp->bs_nxt == NULL)']}
description: Several protocol parsers in tcpdump before 4.9.2 could cause a buffer over-read in addrtoname.c:lookup_bytestring().

code_evidence: The hash-table walk compares stored entries only by bs_addr0/1/2 and then calls memcmp(bs, tp->e_bs, nlen) without checking the stored entry's length.
Entries are allocated as calloc(1, nlen + 1) and filled with memcpy(tp->e_bs, bs, nlen), so a previously stored entry may be shorter than the current nlen.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read) fits because the memcmp at line 22 reads beyond the end of the allocated tp->e_bs buffer when the stored length is smaller than nlen. The length guard on stored bs_nbytes is what prevents this; without it, only the address fields gate the read, so the read length is not bounded by the buffer size.

evidence_lines.code:
while (tp->e_nxt)
if (tp->e_addr0 == i &&
tp->e_addr1 == j &&
tp->e_addr2 == k &&
memcmp((const char *)bs, (const char *)(tp->e_bs), nlen) == 0)

tp->e_bs = (u_char *) calloc(1, nlen + 1);
memcpy(tp->e_bs, bs, nlen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a lookup with a longer nlen collides on the same (i,j,k) hash key as an earlier shorter stored byte string, the memcmp reads nlen bytes from the shorter tp->e_bs buffer, reading past its allocated end. The missing length equality check is the root cause; the trigger is a hash collision with a shorter prior entry, and the consequence is an out-of-bounds read of heap memory.

commit_msg:
Kafka: Be more strict when dissecting varints.

The Kafka dissector uses the return value of tvb_get_varint to advance
the packet offset in many places. If tvb_get_varint fails it returns 0,
which means our offset isn't guaranteed to advance. Stop dissection
whenever that happens. Fixes #17811.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        return offset;'], 'added_lines': ['        return tvb_captured_length(tvb);']}
description: Large loop in the Kafka dissector in Wireshark 3.6.0 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: Line 12 fetches a varint; when it fails, len is 0 and the function returns the unchanged offset (line 15), so the caller's packet offset does not advance.

The record bytes/value/header dissectors are called sequentially (lines 26-32) and the function returns end_offset only after them; if the caller re-enters with an unadvanced offset, dissection repeats.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits because the non-advancing return lets the caller's record loop iterate without progress on attacker-controlled data, exhausting resources. The fix returning tvb_captured_length(tvb) shows the missing bound; this is iteration amplification, not a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on tvb_get_varint failure the function returns the same offset instead of a bounded value, so the caller's dissection loop cannot advance. Trigger: a crafted/injected Kafka packet with a malformed varint. Consequence: repeated dissection of the same bytes, causing excessive iteration and CPU consumption (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix a potential crash issue discovered by Alexander Cherepanov:

It seems bsdtar automatically handles stacked compression. This is a
nice feature but it could be problematic when it's completely
unlimited.  Most clearly it's illustrated with quines:

$ curl -sRO http://www.maximumcompression.com/selfgz.gz
$ (ulimit -v 10000000 && bsdtar -tvf selfgz.gz)
bsdtar: Error opening archive: Can't allocate data for gzip decompression

Without ulimit, bsdtar will eat all available memory. This could also
be a problem for other applications using libarchive.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint number_bidders, i, bid, best_bid;', '\tfor (;;) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tint number_bidders, i, bid, best_bid, n;', '\tfor (n = 0; n < 25; ++n) {', '\tarchive_set_error(&a->archive, ARCHIVE_ERRNO_FILE_FORMAT,', '\t    "Input requires too many filters for decoding");', '\treturn (ARCHIVE_FATAL);']}
description: libarchive before 3.2.0 does not limit the number of recursive decompressions, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption and application crash) via a crafted gzip file.

code_evidence: The function loops unconditionally with `for (;;)`, so nothing bounds how many decompression filter layers are accepted.

Inside the loop each iteration allocates a new filter via `calloc`, links it as `a->filter`, and initializes the bidder; then the loop repeats and re-bids on the newly stacked filter, allowing unbounded recursive decompression and memory growth.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to manage a system resource (memory) by allowing unlimited recursive filter allocation, matching CWE-399's resource-management-error category. It is not an integer overflow or buffer overflow; the weakness is unbounded resource consumption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the filter-selection loop has no cap on stacked decompression layers. Trigger: a crafted gzip file that repeatedly passes a bidder's bid test causes another filter allocation. Supported consequence: unbounded memory consumption and eventual application crash (denial of service).

commit_msg: Fix #79099: OOB read in php_strip_tags_ex
description: When using fgetss() function to read data with stripping tags, in PHP versions 7.2.x below 7.2.27, 7.3.x below 7.3.14 and 7.4.x below 7.4.2 it is possible to supply data that will cause this function to read past the allocated buffer. This may lead to information disclosure or crash.

code_evidence: At the quote case, the condition dereferences *(p-1) before any lower-bound check; p starts at buf (line 15) and is only advanced at line 227, so on the first iteration p-1 points before the estrndup buffer.
The '!' case (line 166) and '?' case (line 190) likewise evaluate *(p-1) without verifying p > buf, so a leading '!' or '?' in state 1 reads before the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code reads memory before the beginning of the intended buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The patch adds p >= buf + 1 guards, confirming the missing lower-bound constraint; this is not a write overflow (CWE-787) because only reads occur.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pointer p can still equal buf when the quote, '!' or '?' branches evaluate *(p-1), reading one byte before the buffer start. Trigger: attacker-supplied input to php_strip_tags_ex/fgetss whose first character (or a character reached while p == buf) enters these branches. Consequence: out-of-bounds read, leading to information disclosure or crash.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tunsigned int len;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tguint8 len;', '', '\t\tif (offset - base_offs + len > length) {', '\t\t\texpert_add_info(pinfo, gsup_ti, &ei_gsup_ie_len_invalid);', '\t\t\treturn offset - 2;', '\t\t}']}
description: In Wireshark 3.0.0, the GSUP dissector could go into an infinite loop. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-gsm_gsup.c by rejecting an invalid Information Element length.

code_evidence: The while loop at line 6 continues while offset - base_offs < length. Each iteration reads tag and len at lines 16-17, then advances offset by len at line 138; the loop condition is re-evaluated at line 139. If the caller-supplied length is smaller than the bytes actually consumed (or len is inconsistent), offset can jump past length without the loop terminating correctly, and recursive calls at line 26 pass len as the new length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the while loop's exit condition depends on offset reaching length, and the unchecked IE length can prevent that condition from being reached, producing an infinite loop. This is a loop-termination flaw rather than a simple out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop advances offset by the attacker-controlled IE length without validating that offset - base_offs + len stays within the caller-provided length. Trigger: a malformed GSUP packet whose IE length causes offset to overshoot or misalign with the boundary. Consequence: the dissection loop can fail to reach its exit condition, causing an infinite loop and CPU consumption (DoS).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\t\twhile (COMPARE(i) < 0) i++;', '\t\t\t\t\t\twhile (COMPARE(j) > 0) j--;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\t\twhile ((COMPARE(i) < 0) && (i <= j)) i++;', '\t\t\t\t\t\twhile ((COMPARE(j) > 0) && (i <= j)) j--;']}
description: Moddable SDK v11.5.0 was discovered to contain a heap-buffer-overflow via xs/sources/xsDataView.c in fxUint8Getter.

code_evidence: Partition loop initializes i = lo+1 and j = hi-1, then advances i while COMPARE(i) < 0 and decrements j while COMPARE(j) > 0 without any bound check against j or i.
When elements are already ordered, i can pass j and run past hi; PUSH(i) and MOVE(j,i) then index beyond the typed array length via the getter/setter.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe index reaches MOVE, which writes bytes at data->value.arrayBuffer.address + offset + INDEX*delta past the intended buffer, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write; the missing i<=j constraint is the root cause, distinct from a mere read overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The partition scan lacks a bound condition, so the increment/decrement loops can walk indices outside [lo,hi]; COMPARE/PUSH/MOVE use these indices to read/write the array buffer. Triggered by sorting data whose pivot ordering lets a scan run off the end, causing an out-of-bounds write (and read) in the buffer.

commit_msg:
pegasus: Use heap buffers for all register access

Allocating USB buffers on the stack is not portable, and no longer
works on x86_64 (with VMAP_STACK enabled as per default).

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
References: https://bugs.debian.org/852556
Reported-by: Lisandro Damián Nicanor Pérez Meyer <lisandro@debian.org>
Tested-by: Lisandro Damián Nicanor Pérez Meyer <lisandro@debian.org>
Signed-off-by: Ben Hutchings <ben@decadent.org.uk>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t      indx, &data, 1, 1000);'], 'added_lines': ['\tu8 *buf;', '', '\tbuf = kmemdup(&data, 1, GFP_NOIO);', '\tif (!buf)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\t\t\t      indx, buf, 1, 1000);', '\tkfree(buf);']}
description: drivers/net/usb/pegasus.c in the Linux kernel 4.9.x before 4.9.11 interacts incorrectly with the CONFIG_VMAP_STACK option, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash or memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging use of more than one virtual page for a DMA scatterlist.

code_evidence: usb_control_msg is passed &data, the address of a stack-allocated __u8 parameter, as its 1-byte data buffer; the USB core may DMA into/out of this buffer, which is not valid when the stack spans multiple virtual pages (CONFIG_VMAP_STACK).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stack buffer is treated as a DMA target, so the transfer can operate outside its intended single-byte boundary, matching CWE-119 (operations outside buffer bounds). The fix moves the buffer to the heap, confirming the boundary/placement flaw rather than a pure NULL-dereference or integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a DMA-capable USB transfer uses a stack buffer whose physical/virtual layout is unsuitable for scatter-gather DMA under VMAP_STACK. Trigger: any set_register call causing usb_control_msg to map the stack address. Consequence: system crash or memory corruption from out-of-bounds DMA access to the buffer.

commit_msg:
Don't allow too many consecutive warning alerts

Certain warning alerts are ignored if they are received. This can mean that
no progress will be made if one peer continually sends those warning alerts.
Implement a count so that we abort the connection if we receive too many.

Issue reported by Shi Lei.

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    /*', "     * Reset the count of consecutive warning alerts if we've got a non-empty", "     * record that isn't an alert.", '     */', '    if (SSL3_RECORD_get_type(rr) != SSL3_RT_ALERT', '            && SSL3_RECORD_get_length(rr) != 0)', '        s->rlayer.alert_count = 0;', '', '            s->rlayer.alert_count++;', '            if (s->rlayer.alert_count == MAX_WARN_ALERT_COUNT) {', '                al = SSL_AD_UNEXPECTED_MESSAGE;', '                SSLerr(SSL_F_SSL3_READ_BYTES, SSL_R_TOO_MANY_WARN_ALERTS);', '                goto f_err;', '            }', '']}
description: A denial of service flaw was found in OpenSSL 0.9.8, 1.0.1, 1.0.2 through 1.0.2h, and 1.1.0 in the way the TLS/SSL protocol defined processing of ALERT packets during a connection handshake. A remote attacker could use this flaw to make a TLS/SSL server consume an excessive amount of CPU and fail to accept connections from other clients.

code_evidence: Warning-level alerts are handled by recording the alert and marking the record read, then falling through to `goto start` to fetch the next record; each such alert consumes CPU without terminating the connection.
The alert fragment fields are copied from the record, and after processing the code loops back to `start`, so a peer can repeatedly send warning alerts that are ignored.
The `goto start` at line 283 continues the read loop, allowing unbounded repeated processing of warning alerts and sustained CPU consumption.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function lacks throttling of a resource-consuming operation (repeated alert processing), enabling remote resource exhaustion. This is uncontrolled consumption rather than a memory-safety corruption.

evidence_lines.code: goto start;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function processes each warning alert and returns to the read loop without limiting how many consecutive warning alerts a peer may send. Trigger: a remote peer continuously sends warning alerts that are ignored. Consequence: the server repeatedly reads and processes records, consuming CPU and failing to accept other clients (DoS).

commit_msg:
Bug 699661: Avoid sharing pointers between pdf14 compositors

If a copdevice is triggered when the pdf14 compositor is the device, we make
a copy of the device, then throw an error because, by default we're only allowed
to copy the device prototype - then freeing it calls the finalize, which frees
several pointers shared with the parent.

Make a pdf14 specific finish_copydevice() which NULLs the relevant pointers,
before, possibly, throwing the same error as the default method.

This also highlighted a problem with reopening the X11 devices, where a custom
error handler could be replaced with itself, meaning it also called itself,
and infifite recursion resulted.

Keep a note of if the handler replacement has been done, and don't do it a
second time.

description: In Artifex Ghostscript before 9.24, attackers able to supply crafted PostScript files to the builtin PDF14 converter could use a use-after-free in copydevice handling to crash the interpreter or possibly have unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: When the component count changes, the code frees p14dev->ctx via pdf14_ctx_free but does not clear the pointer; open_device(tdev) is then called on the same device, which may reuse the freed context/device state.

Earlier, the function adjusts and reuses profile pointers from p14dev->icc_struct->device_profile[0] and cl_icc_profile, showing shared pointer state that copydevice/finalize could free while still referenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The freed ctx pointer remains reachable and may be used after pdf14_ctx_free, matching CWE-416. This is not merely a memory leak (CWE-401) because the stale pointer can be dereferenced or freed again, not just lost.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: p14dev->ctx is freed without being set to NULL, leaving a dangling pointer that open_device may later dereference or that a copied device's finalize may free again. Trigger: a PostScript/PDF14 push-device path where the component count changes. Consequence: use-after-free/double-free, crash, or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Make sure binding security checks don't pass if the frame is remote.

Blink assumes that remote frames will always fail the security origin
check. Unfortunately, reality is not that simple. There are several
instances where this assumption fails to hold. For example:

  1. Navigate to a.com.
  2. a.com opens a new window.
  3. Navigate the new window to b.com via the omnibox.
  4. Click a link to c.com in both windows.

Because browser-initiated navigations go cross-process but
renderer-initiated navigations do not [1], the two c.com windows will
end up in different renderer processes.

Both windows have the same origin but see each other as RemoteFrames.
This means that SecurityOrigin's canAccess check will pass… but this
ends up violating many assumptions in Blink that passing the security
check implies a local frame.

[1] https://www.chromium.org/developers/design-documents/process-models#Caveats

BUG=601629
CQ_INCLUDE_TRYBOTS=tryserver.chromium.linux:linux_site_isolation

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1887553002

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#387087}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (isOriginAccessibleFromDOMWindow(targetFrameOrigin, accessingWindow))'], 'added_lines': ["    // It's important to check that targetWindow is a LocalDOMWindow: it's", '    // possible for a remote frame and local frame to have the same security', '    // origin, depending on the model being used to allocate Frames between', '    // processes. See https://crbug.com/601629.', '    if (targetWindow->isLocalDOMWindow() && isOriginAccessibleFromDOMWindow(targetFrameOrigin, accessingWindow))']}
description: Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 50.0.2661.94, does not ensure that frames satisfy a check for the same renderer process in addition to a Same Origin Policy check, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted web site, related to BindingSecurity.cpp and DOMWindow.cpp.

code_evidence: The access decision relies solely on isOriginAccessibleFromDOMWindow(targetFrameOrigin, accessingWindow) and returns true without verifying that targetWindow is a local DOMWindow.

When that origin check passes but targetWindow is a remote frame sharing the same security origin, the function skips the security error path and returns false only at the end; the missing local-frame constraint lets the caller proceed on an invalid assumption.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the code fails to validate a required property of its input (targetWindow being local) before granting access. It is a missing-constraint validation flaw, not just an authorization check, since the origin is verified but the frame-type property is not.

evidence_lines.code:
if (isOriginAccessibleFromDOMWindow(targetFrameOrigin, accessingWindow))
return true;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates the frame's security origin but does not validate the frame type (local vs. remote) as a required property. Trigger: a remote frame whose origin is accessible to accessingWindow. Consequence: the binding security check passes, violating caller assumptions that a passed check implies a local frame, enabling memory corruption/DoS.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    unsigned long outlen, loid[16];', '    if ((digestinfo[0].size == hash_descriptor[hash_idx].OIDlen) &&'], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned long outlen, loid[16], reallen;', '    if ((err = der_length_sequence(siginfo, 2, &reallen)) != CRYPT_OK) {', '       XFREE(out);', '       goto bail_2;', '    }', '', '    if ((reallen == outlen) &&', '        (digestinfo[0].size == hash_descriptor[hash_idx].OIDlen) &&']}
description: The rsa_verify_hash_ex function in rsa_verify_hash.c in LibTomCrypt, as used in OP-TEE before 2.2.0, does not validate that the message length is equal to the ASN.1 encoded data length, which makes it easier for remote attackers to forge RSA signatures or public certificates by leveraging a Bleichenbacher signature forgery attack.

code_evidence: pkcs_1_v1_5_decode writes the recovered message into out and sets outlen to the decoded length; der_decode_sequence then parses out as siginfo (SEQUENCE{digestinfo, OCTET_STRING}) without ever comparing the parsed sequence length against the actual decoded length outlen.
The signature is accepted when OID, hash length and hash bytes match; there is no check that the ASN.1 sequence consumed exactly outlen bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts attacker-controlled signature input whose derived structural property (ASN.1 sequence length) is not validated against the actual length, letting malformed data be treated as valid; this is improper input validation (CWE-20). Contrast with CWE-347 (improper signature verification): the flaw is the missing length-consistency check, not the verification algorithm itself.

if ((err = pkcs_1_v1_5_decode(tmpbuf, x, LTC_PKCS_1_EMSA, modulus_bitlen, out, &outlen, &decoded)) != CRYPT_OK) {
if ((err = der_decode_sequence(out, outlen, siginfo, 2)) != CRYPT_OK) {

if ((digestinfo[0].size == hash_descriptor[hash_idx].OIDlen) &&
*stat = 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the verifier derives the signed content via ASN.1 parsing but never validates that the encoded-sequence length equals the actual decoded message length outlen. Trigger: an attacker appends extra bytes after a valid DigestInfo structure inside the PKCS#1 v1.5 block. The parser accepts the prefix and the hash comparison succeeds, so *stat is set to 1, enabling forged RSA signatures/certificates (Bleichenbacher).

commit_msg:
The length checking code validates PutImage height and byte width by
making sure that byte-width >= INT32_MAX / height. If height is zero,
this generates a divide by zero exception. Allow zero height requests
explicitly, bypassing the INT32_MAX check.

Signed-off-by: Keith Packard <keithp@keithp.com>
Reviewed-by: Alan Coopersmith <alan.coopersmith@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (lengthProto >= (INT32_MAX / stuff->height))'], 'added_lines': ['    if (stuff->height != 0 && lengthProto >= (INT32_MAX / stuff->height))']}
description: The ProcPutImage function in dix/dispatch.c in X.Org Server (aka xserver and xorg-server) before 1.16.4 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero and crash) via a zero-height PutImage request.

code_evidence: Line 34 derives tmpImage from the request; line 35 copies the computed scanline length into lengthProto. Line 36 then divides INT32_MAX by the client-controlled stuff->height without checking for zero. When height is zero, the division at line 36 raises a divide-by-zero, aborting the length validation before lines 38-40 compare the request length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 precisely describes dividing a value by zero. Here the divisor is an unchecked request field used in an arithmetic validation, and the resulting exception yields a server crash, matching the Divide By Zero definition. It is not an integer overflow: the issue is the zero divisor itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length check divides by stuff->height, which comes directly from the PutImage request and may be zero. Trigger: a client sends a PutImage request with height 0, reaching line 36; the division by zero faults and crashes the server. Supported consequence is denial of service (crash), not memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Call setsid() before executing sandboxed code (CVE-2017-5226)

This prevents the sandboxed code from getting a controlling tty,
which in turn prevents it from accessing the TIOCSTI ioctl and hence
faking terminal input.

Fixes: #142

Closes: #143
Approved by: cgwalters

description: When executing a program via the bubblewrap sandbox, the nonpriv session can escape to the parent session by using the TIOCSTI ioctl to push characters into the terminal's input buffer, allowing an attacker to escape the sandbox.

The TIOCSTI tty-injection escape is a session/terminal isolation issue, not improper input validation.

commit_msg:
mp4: limit the recursion depth for boxes

Although the dissection of each box header consumes a couple of bytes,
it turned out that it's still possible to crash wireshark with a sample
file that contains a large number of nested boxes. The stack will fill
up before we reach the end of the data bytes.

Keep track of the recursion depth as we walk through the hierarchy of
boxes. Abort if we reach the (locally defined) upper limit.

description: The ehci_process_itd function in hw/usb/hcd-ehci.c in QEMU allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (infinite loop and CPU consumption) via a circular isochronous transfer descriptor (iTD) list.

code_evidence: The loop at line 15 iterates over the 8 transaction slots and only clears ITD_XACT_ACTIVE at line 83 when an active transaction is processed (line 16). If no transaction slot is active, the body is skipped, nothing is cleared, and the function returns 0 at line 86, signaling success without making progress.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the descriptor-processing loop/scheduler never reaches a terminating condition due to the missing progress check; the fix adds an xfers counter and returns -1 when no transfer occurred, breaking the loop. This is not a memory-safety issue but an unreachable exit condition causing resource consumption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function always returns success even when it processed zero active transactions, so the caller cannot detect a non-progressing iTD. Trigger: a guest supplies an iTD chain whose active bits are never set/cleared, forming a circular descriptor list. Consequence: the periodic scheduler retries the same descriptors indefinitely, consuming CPU (DoS).
