File has wrong header");']}
description: ClickHouse is an open-source column-oriented database management system that allows generating analytical data reports in real-time. A heap buffer overflow issue was discovered in ClickHouse server. An attacker could send a specially crafted payload to the native interface exposed by default on port 9000/tcp, triggering a bug in the decompression logic of Gorilla codec that crashes the ClickHouse server process. This attack does not require authentication. This issue has been addressed in ClickHouse Cloud version 23.9.2.47551 and ClickHouse versions 23.10.5.20, 23.3.18.15, 23.8.8.20, and 23.9.6.20.

code_evidence: bytes_to_skip is derived from uncompressed_size % bytes_size with no check that it is smaller than uncompressed_size; memcpy then copies bytes_to_skip bytes into dest, whose capacity is uncompressed_size, so an oversized skip count can write past dest.

Each switch case forwards source_size_no_header and &dest[bytes_to_skip] to decompressDataForType without passing the remaining destination capacity, so the decoder can write beyond dest when the header-derived skip value and compressed stream are attacker-controlled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of the destination buffer, which is exactly CWE-787's out-of-bounds write; the missing size constraint is the root cause and memory corruption/crash is the consequence, not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decompressor trusts header-derived values (bytes_size, bytes_to_skip) without ensuring bytes_to_skip < uncompressed_size or bounding the decompressed output to the remaining destination size. A crafted native-protocol payload reaching this function triggers the copy/decode, causing a heap out-of-bounds write and server crash.

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = table->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = xt_table_get_private_protected(table);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: Line 5 reads table->private into 'private' without any synchronization against a concurrent xt_replace_table that may free the old table info. Line 6 then dereferences private->number, and line 10 passes the same pointer to get_counters to snapshot counters, so the table info is used after it may have been freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences and iterates a table info pointer that a concurrent replacement can free, matching CWE-416 (use after free). A plain race condition (CWE-362) describes the concurrency, but the supported consequence here is reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the snapshot pointer is loaded and dereferenced without synchronizing with the replacement thread's sequence-count protocol, so the compiler/CPU can order the load after the replacement has freed the old table info. Trigger: concurrent iptables rules replacement while alloc_counters runs. Consequence: use-after-free reads of the freed xt_table_info (NULL-pointer crash as in the report, or memory corruption).

description:
There exists an vulnerability causing an abort() to be called in gRPC. 
The following headers cause gRPC's C++ implementation to abort() when called via http2:

te: x (x != trailers)

:scheme: x (x != http, https)

grpclb_client_stats: x (x == anything)

On top of sending one of those headers, a later header must be sent that gets the total header size past 8KB. We recommend upgrading past git commit 2485fa94bd8a723e5c977d55a3ce10b301b437f8 or v1.53 and above.

code_evidence: HttpSchemeMetadata::Encode switches on the ValueType x; only kHttp and kHttps are handled, while the default branch calls abort(). Parse (lines 60-69) returns kInvalid for any scheme other than "http"/"https", so a header like ':scheme: x' produces kInvalid, which Encode then routes into abort().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The default branch's abort() is an assertion-like termination reachable from attacker-controlled header input via the kInvalid path from Parse, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion). This is a cause of DoS, not a buffer or type confusion issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: Encode has no safe handling for the kInvalid value that Parse deliberately produces for unrecognized schemes. Trigger: an attacker sends an HTTP/2 ':scheme' header with a value other than http/https, causing Parse to return kInvalid; if encoding is later invoked (e.g. when headers are re-encoded), the default branch executes abort(). Consequence: process termination, a reachable-assertion denial of service.

Consequence: an oversized or overflowing allocation request, exhausting memory or failing allocation, a resource-consumption DoS.

commit_msg:
win: fix unsavory rwlock fallback implementation

Before this patch an uv_mutex_t (backed by a critical section) could be
released by a tread different from the thread that acquired it, which is
not allowed. This is fixed by using a semaphore instead.

Note that the affected code paths were used on Windows XP and Windows
Server 2003 only.

Fixes: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/issues/515
PR-URL: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/pull/516
Reviewed-By: Ben Noordhuis <info@bnoordhuis.nl>
Reviewed-By: Saúl Ibarra Corretgé <saghul@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  uv_mutex_destroy(&rwlock->fallback_.read_mutex_);', '  uv_mutex_destroy(&rwlock->fallback_.write_mutex_);'], 'added_lines': ['  DeleteCriticalSection(&rwlock->fallback_.read_lock_.cs);', '  CloseHandle(rwlock->fallback_.write_lock_.sem);']}
description: The uv_rwlock_t fallback implementation for Windows XP and Server 2003 in libuv before 1.7.4 does not properly prevent threads from releasing the locks of other threads, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (deadlock) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging a race condition.

code_evidence: The destroy function tears down the two fallback lock primitives: it destroys read_mutex_ and write_mutex_ via uv_mutex_destroy without any ownership or synchronization check. The prior fallback used a critical-section-backed mutex for the write lock, which could be released/destroyed by a thread other than the acquiring thread; this destroy path participates in that same unsynchronized teardown of shared lock state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the defect is improper synchronization over a shared resource (the fallback lock), allowing an interfering concurrent sequence to violate exclusivity/atomicity. It is not merely a resource-leak or cleanup bug; the missing ownership constraint on the shared lock is the concurrent-execution weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a fallback rwlock built on mutex primitives that do not enforce owner-only release, so concurrent threads can operate on shared lock state across acquisition and destruction without exclusive ownership. Trigger is a race where one thread destroys/releases while another holds or uses the lock; the supported consequence is deadlock or instability (DoS).

resovle BUGFIX handle cyclic typedefs with unions

Fixes #724
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                if (!strcmp(tpdf[i].name, name) && tpdf[i].type.base > 0) {', '                    goto check_leafref;', '        if (!strcmp(module->tpdf[i].name, name) && module->tpdf[i].type.base > 0) {', '            goto check_leafref;', '            if (!strcmp(module->inc[i].submodule->tpdf[j].name, name) && module->inc[i].submodule->tpdf[j].type.base > 0) {', '                goto check_leafref;', 'check_leafref:', '    if (match->type.base == LY_TYPE_LEAFREF) {', '        while (!match->type.info.lref.path) {', '            match = match->type.der;', '            assert(match);', '        }', '    }'], 'added_lines': ['                if (!strcmp(tpdf[i].name, name)) {', '                    goto check_typedef;', '        if (!strcmp(module->tpdf[i].name, name)) {', '            goto check_typedef;', '            if (!strcmp(module->inc[i].submodule->tpdf[j].name, name)) {', '                goto check_typedef;', 'check_typedef:', '    if (resolve_superior_type_check(&match->type)) {', '        return EXIT_FAILURE;', '    }', '']}
description: A stack consumption issue is present in libyang before v1.0-r1 due to the self-referential union type containing leafrefs. Applications that use libyang to parse untrusted input yang files may crash.

code_evidence: Typedef lookup only matches entries whose type.base > 0, so a typedef still being resolved (base not yet set) is skipped; the loop then advances to the parent and may return failure or a different match, obscuring the self-reference.

The check_leafref block follows the leafref derivation chain via match = match->type.der inside a while loop guarded only by !match->type.info.lref.path, with assert(match) as the sole termination guard.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unbounded while loop over a cyclic derivation chain is uncontrolled recursion/iteration consuming stack, matching CWE-674. It is not merely a NULL dereference (CWE-476) because the assert guards NULL; the failure is the missing cycle/recursion limit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a typedef resolves to a leafref whose path is not yet set and the derivation chain is cyclic (self-referential union/leafref), the while loop repeatedly follows type.der without a visited-set or depth bound. The assert only fires if der becomes NULL; a cycle keeps der non-NULL, so the loop recurses indefinitely and consumes stack, crashing the parser on untrusted YANG input.

 ffff8881dc7ae080: fb fb fb fb fb fb fb fb fb fb fb fb fb fb fb fb

There are already cleanup handlings in serial_ir_init error path,
no need to call serial_ir_exit do it again in serial_ir_init_module,
otherwise will trigger a use-after-free issue.

Fixes: fa5dc29c1fcc ("[media] lirc_serial: move out of staging and rename to serial_ir")

Reported-by: Hulk Robot <hulkci@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: YueHaibing <yuehaibing@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Sean Young <sean@mess.org>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab+samsung@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint result;', '', '\tresult = serial_ir_init();', '\tif (!result)', '\t\treturn 0;', '', '\tserial_ir_exit();', '\treturn result;'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn serial_ir_init();']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.1.6, there is a use-after-free in serial_ir_init_module() in drivers/media/rc/serial_ir.c.

code_evidence: After calling serial_ir_init(), the function checks the returned result. When serial_ir_init() fails (non-zero), it invokes serial_ir_exit() at line 30 even though serial_ir_init() already performed its own cleanup on its error path, then returns the original error code.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The double cleanup causes memory to be freed and then referenced again, which is exactly CWE-416 (use after free). This is not merely a memory leak or double-free label; the reported access occurs after the free, matching CWE-416.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path calls serial_ir_exit() a second time after serial_ir_init() has already released its resources on failure. Trigger: serial_ir_init() returns a non-zero value, causing redundant teardown of already-freed driver/kobject structures; subsequent access (e.g. sysfs removal in the reported trace) dereferences freed memory. Consequence: use-after-free read/write, crash or potential memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Bug 702857: Detect/avoid overflow when calculating sizes of pixmaps.

Throw an error when trying to allocate an overly large pixmap.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!samples)', '\t\t\tif (pix->stride - 1 > INT_MAX / pix->n)', '\t\t\t\tfz_throw(ctx, FZ_ERROR_GENERIC, "overly wide image");'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!samples && pix->h > 0 && pix->w > 0)', '\t\t\tif (pix->stride > INT_MAX / pix->h)', '\t\t\t\tfz_throw(ctx, FZ_ERROR_GENERIC, "Overly large image");']}
description: Artifex MuPDF before 1.18.0 has a heap based buffer over-write when parsing JBIG2 files allowing attackers to cause a denial of service.

code_evidence: When samples is NULL, line 44 checks only stride against INT_MAX/pix->n, not the product pix->h * pix->stride used at line 46. The guard omits the height factor, so a large h with a stride that passes the check can make h*stride overflow, causing fz_malloc to allocate a smaller buffer than the requested pixmap dimensions imply.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the integer overflow leads to an undersized allocation followed by writes past its end. This is an out-of-bounds write rather than merely an integer overflow (CWE-190), which here is only the enabling root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation-size overflow check at line 44 validates stride relative to n rather than the actual h*stride multiplication at line 46. Trigger: a JBIG2-derived pixmap with a large height and a stride that satisfies stride <= INT_MAX/n makes h*stride wrap around. Consequence: an undersized heap buffer is allocated and later pixmap writes exceed it, yielding a heap buffer overflow (DoS and potential memory corruption).

commit_msg:
MS-MMS: Use format_text_string()

The length of a string transcoded from UTF-16 to UTF-8 can be
shorter (or longer) than the original length in bytes in the packet.
Use the new string length, not the original length.

Use format_text_string, which is a convenience function that
calls strlen.

Fix #19086
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    format_text(pinfo->pool, (const guchar*)player_info, strlen(player_info)));'], 'added_lines': ['                    format_text_string(pinfo->pool, (const guchar*)player_info));']}
description: Due to failure in validating the length provided by an attacker-crafted MSMMS packet, Wireshark version 4.0.5 and prior, in an unusual configuration, is susceptible to a heap-based buffer overflow, and possibly code execution in the context of the process running Wireshark

code_evidence: The string is retrieved from the packet with a caller-controlled length (length_remaining-12) and transcoded from UTF-16 to UTF-8 into player_info; the resulting UTF-8 length can differ from the original byte length.
The original code passed strlen(player_info) as the length to format_text, so the copied length is derived from the string rather than the packet-declared length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fix replaces the mismatched length with format_text_string, which uses strlen, directly addressing a length mismatch that can write past the intended buffer. This supports CWE-787 rather than a read-only weakness because the wrong length drives a memory write.

evidence_lines.code:
col_append_fstr(pinfo->cinfo, COL_INFO, " (%s)",
format_text(pinfo->pool, (const guchar*)player_info, strlen(player_info)));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code used the UTF-16 packet length/transcoding assumptions rather than the actual UTF-8 string length when formatting. Trigger: an attacker-crafted MSMMS packet whose transcoded string length differs from the declared length. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds write when the wrong length is used for the destination buffer.

commit_msg: rosbag/record: fix signed int overflow
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        opts.max_size = 1048576 * S;'], 'added_lines': ['        opts.max_size = 1048576 * static_cast<uint64_t>(S);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the ROS communications-related packages (aka ros_comm or ros-melodic-ros-comm) through 1.14.3. parseOptions() in tools/rosbag/src/record.cpp has an integer overflow when a crafted split option can be entered on the command line.

code_evidence: Line 70 parses the deprecated --split value as a signed int S from the command line. Lines 74-75 reject only negative values; line 76 multiplies 1048576 * S in signed 32-bit arithmetic before assigning to opts.max_size. A large positive S (e.g., 4096 or more) makes the product exceed INT_MAX, producing a wrapped value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size calculation whose signed result can wrap to a small or negative number, matching CWE-190. The negative check at line 74 does not prevent positive overflow, and the wrapped value feeds max_size, not merely an unrelated field.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the multiplication 1048576 * S is performed in signed int without an upper-bound check, so the logic assumes the result grows with S. Trigger: a crafted large positive --split argument. Consequence: opts.max_size receives a wrapped, possibly negative value, corrupting split-size logic and enabling denial of service or altered recording behavior. The fix casts S to uint64_t before multiplying.

Merge pull request from GHSA-cv8x-p47p-99wr

* - Avoid SSL socket parent/listener getting destroyed during handshake by increasing parent's reference count.
- Add missing SSL socket close when the newly accepted SSL socket is discarded in SIP TLS transport.

* - Fix silly mistake: accepted active socket created without group lock in SSL socket.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In PJSIP before version 2.11.1, there are a couple of issues found in the SSL socket. First, a race condition between callback and destroy, due to the accepted socket having no group lock. commit_msg:
Trap for overly large input to XmlRPCPP which could cause problems with int <-> size_t conversions.

 - In XmlRpcClient, XmlRpcServerConnection and XmlRpcSocket, recognize when incoming or outgoing data is too large, generate an error and discard the data when practical.
 - Use the safe strtol() rather than atoi() to decode an incoming content-length header, and generate an error if the length is invalid or too large.
 - In XmlRpcUtil, prevent attempts to parse overly large XML input.
 - Add tests where they can reasonably be inserted into existing test routines.

Although this fix could be cleaner the update is written to make the update ABI compatible.

This fix addresses CVE-2020-16124 / Integer overflow in ros_comm.

Signed-off-by: Sid Faber <sid.faber@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  // Limit the size of the request to avoid integer overruns', '  if (_request.length() > size_t(__INT_MAX__)) {', '    XmlRpcUtil::error("XmlRpcClient::generateRequest: request length (%u) exceeds maximum allowed size (%u).",', '                      _request.length(), __INT_MAX__);', '    _request.clear();', '    return false;', '  }']}
description: Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability in the XML RPC library of OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages allows unauthenticated network traffic to cause unexpected behavior. This issue affects: OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages Noetic and prior versions. Fixed in https://github.com/ros/ros_comm/pull/2065.

code_evidence: generateRequest concatenates header and body into _request at [29], where body length is derived from params.toXml() and header from generateHeader(body.length()) at [26]; the log at [27,28] passes length() values as %d. Oversized params can make the request length exceed int range, and the function returns true without any size check before the fix.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer overflow/wraparound: the length of the concatenated request is assumed to fit int, and the fix adds a __INT_MAX__ check. This is CWE-190 rather than a mere buffer issue, since the unsafe operation is the size conversion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: request length is computed and later used as an int-sized content-length without validating it against __INT_MAX__, so a very large body from a large XmlRpcValue array produces a length that can wrap when converted to int. Trigger: an attacker-supplied or oversized parameter set. Supported consequence: malformed content-length and inconsistent size handling leading to unexpected behavior/DoS.

commit_msg:
adapter: Fix storing discoverable setting

discoverable setting shall only be store when changed via Discoverable
property and not when discovery client set it as that be considered
temporary just for the lifetime of the discovery.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only persists the Discoverable setting when it changes; it performs no authorization check, so CWE-863 (Incorrect Authorization) is not supported. in another subsystem]
Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190124063514.8571-2-houtao1@huawei.com
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: 7549ae3e81cc ("9p: Use the i_size_[read, write]() macros instead of using inode->i_size directly.")
Reported-by: Xing Gaopeng <xingaopeng@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Hou Tao <houtao1@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Dominique Martinet <dominique.martinet@cea.fr>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\ti_size_write(inode, iocb->ki_pos);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t/*', '\t\t\t * Need to serialize against i_size_write() in', '\t\t\t * v9fs_stat2inode()', '\t\t\t */', '\t\t\tv9fs_i_size_write(inode, iocb->ki_pos);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. The 9p filesystem did not protect i_size_write() properly, which causes an i_size_read() infinite loop and denial of service on SMP systems.

code_evidence: After a successful write, the function reads i_size with i_size_read() into a local, compares iocb->ki_pos against it, and if larger calls inode_add_bytes() then i_size_write() to update the inode size. The i_size_write() at line 26 is performed without holding inode->i_lock, while other writers such as v9fs_stat2inode() may update i_size concurrently.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is an unreachable exit condition in the seqcount read loop, matching CWE-835's infinite loop causing resource-consumption DoS. The missing lock is the cause; the infinite loop is the effect, so CWE-835 fits rather than a pure race-condition label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size update via plain i_size_write() is not serialized with concurrent i_size_write() callers under inode->i_lock. On 32-bit SMP, a writer interleaving between the seqcount increment and update can leave the seqcount state inconsistent, so a concurrent i_size_read() spins forever in read_seqcount_begin(). Trigger: simultaneous v9fs_vfs_getattr()/v9fs_vfs_getattr_dotl() and writes. Consequence: soft lockup/CPU exhaustion, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
evtchn: avoid NULL derefs

Commit fbbd5009e6 ("evtchn: refactor low-level event channel port ops")
added a de-reference of the struct evtchn pointer for a port without
first making sure the bucket pointer is non-NULL. This de-reference is
actually entirely unnecessary, as all relevant callers (beyond the
problematic do_poll()) already hold the port number in their hands, and
the actual leaf functions need nothing else.

For FIFO event channels there's a second problem in that the ordering
of reads and updates to ->num_evtchns and ->event_array[] was so far
undefined (the read side isn't always holding the domain's event lock).
Add respective barriers.

This is XSA-221.

Reported-by: Ankur Arora <ankur.a.arora@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static bool_t evtchn_2l_is_masked(struct domain *d,', '                                  const struct evtchn *evtchn)', '    return test_bit(evtchn->port, &shared_info(d, evtchn_mask));'], 'added_lines': ['static bool_t evtchn_2l_is_masked(struct domain *d, evtchn_port_t port)', '    unsigned int max_ports = BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d) * BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d);', '', '    ASSERT(port < max_ports);', '    return port >= max_ports || test_bit(port, &shared_info(d, evtchn_mask));']}
description: Xen through 4.8.x does not validate the port numbers of polled event channel ports, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and host OS crash) or possibly obtain sensitive information, aka XSA-221.

code_evidence: The function takes a struct evtchn pointer `evtchn` and unconditionally dereferences it via `evtchn->port` in the test_bit call, with no NULL check on `evtchn` before the access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function performs a pointer dereference (evtchn->port) on a pointer that may be NULL when the port is unvalidated, directly matching NULL Pointer Dereference. The fix removes the pointer dereference entirely by passing the port number, confirming the dereference was the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller can pass a NULL struct evtchn pointer (e.g. do_poll for an invalid/unbound port), and evtchn_2l_is_masked dereferences evtchn->port without validation. Trigger: polling an event channel port whose bucket/evtchn lookup yields NULL. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a host OS crash (DoS).

nfunc, line, qedi->host_no, &vaf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: memcpy(nfunc, func, 31) copies a fixed 31 bytes from func even when func is a shorter string literal. commit_msg:
seatd-launch: Remove socket path command line arg

This should not need to be configured, so remove the argument. If
downstream prefers a different folder, the location can be made
compile-time configurable like for seatd itself.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t    "  -h\t\tShow this help message\\n"', '\t\t\t    "  -s <path>\tWhere to create the seatd socket\\n"', '\t\t\t    "  -v\t\tShow the version number\\n"', '\tchar *sockpath = NULL;', '\twhile ((c = getopt(argc, argv, "vhs:")) != -1) {', "\t\tcase 's':", '\t\t\tsockpath = optarg;', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\tchar sockbuf[256];', '\tif (sockpath == NULL) {', '\t\tsprintf(sockbuf, "/tmp/seatd.%d.sock", getpid());', '\t\tsockpath = sockbuf;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t    "  -h\tShow this help message\\n"', '\t\t\t    "  -v\tShow the version number\\n"', '\twhile ((c = getopt(argc, argv, "vh")) != -1) {', '\tchar sockpath[256];', '\tsprintf(sockpath, "/tmp/seatd.%d.sock", getpid());']}
description: seatd-launch in seatd 0.6.x before 0.6.4 allows removing files with escalated privileges when installed setuid root. The attack vector is a user-supplied socket pathname.

code_evidence: sockpath is taken directly from the user-controlled -s option (optarg) with no validation of the path.
When absent, a fixed /tmp path is built with sprintf; the caller-supplied path bypasses this default.
The attacker-chosen sockpath is passed to seatd as its socket path and to the target environment (SEATD_SOCK).
Privileged chown and chmod operate on whatever path the attacker supplied, before privileges are dropped.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function lets an unprivileged caller choose a resource path that a setuid-root process then operates on, exposing files to the wrong security sphere. CWE-668 fits as the exposure-of-resource-to-wrong-sphere class; the specific privileged file operation is the concrete mechanism.

evidence_lines.code: char *command[] = {"seatd", "-n", pipebuf, "-s", sockpath, NULL};

if (chown(sockpath, uid, gid) == -1) {
if (chmod(sockpath, 0700) == -1) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When seatd-launch runs setuid root, the user-supplied socket pathname is not validated. The privileged process passes it to seatd and then calls chown/chmod on it while still root, so the attacker can direct privileged file operations at an arbitrary path, exposing or altering files outside the intended control sphere.

commit_msg:
FROMLIST: binder: fix UAF caused by faulty buffer cleanup

In binder_transaction_buffer_release() the 'failed_at' offset indicates
the number of objects to clean up. However, this function was changed by
commit 44d8047f1d87 ("binder: use standard functions to allocate fds"),
to release all the objects in the buffer when 'failed_at' is zero.

This introduced an issue when a transaction buffer is released without
any objects having been processed so far. In this case, 'failed_at' is
indeed zero yet it is misinterpreted as releasing the entire buffer.

This leads to use-after-free errors where nodes are incorrectly freed
and subsequently accessed. Such is the case in the following KASAN
report:

  Read of size 8 at addr ffff4faf037cfc58 by task poc/474

commit_msg:
bigben_worker() checks report_field to be non-NULL.
The check has been added in commit
918aa1ef104d ("HID: bigbenff: prevent null pointer dereference")
to prevent a NULL pointer crash.
However, the true root cause was a missing check for output
reports, patched in commit
c7bf714f8755 ("HID: check empty report_list in bigben_probe()"),
where the type-confused report list_entry was overlapping with
a NULL pointer, which was then causing the crash.

Fixes: 918aa1ef104d ("HID: bigbenff: prevent null pointer dereference")
Signed-off-by: Pietro Borrello <borrello@diag.uniroma1.it>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230125-hid-unregister-leds-v4-2-7860c5763c38@diag.uniroma1.it
Signed-off-by: Benjamin Tissoires <benjamin.tissoires@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (bigben->removed || !report_field)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (bigben->removed)']}
description: The Linux kernel through 6.1.9 has a Use-After-Free in bigben_remove in drivers/hid/hid-bigbenff.c via a crafted USB device because the LED controllers remain registered for too long.

code_evidence: Line 5 caches report_field = bigben->report->field[0]; lines 11-12 only bail out when bigben->removed is set, so a stale/non-NULL report_field is still dereferenced.
When work_led is set, lines 21-23 write into report_field->value and line 29 calls hid_output_report with the cached field.
The work_ff branch similarly writes report_field->value at lines 40-43 and outputs the report at line 48, using the same cached pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses memory through a pointer that can outlive the freed report structure, matching CWE-416 use after free. The removed flag guards only device teardown state, not the lifetime of report_field; a NULL check would not prevent the stale-pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the worker dereferences the cached report_field pointer without verifying it still belongs to the live report; the removal path can free the report/field while queued work remains. Trigger: bigben_remove frees the HID report and associated fields while bigben_worker is still scheduled. Consequence: writes to freed field->value and hid_output_report on freed memory cause use-after-free (memory corruption or crash).

commit_msg:
binding: Moves the check for the first access to the initial document into BindingSecurity.

Checks the access to the initial document and reports it not only at
securityCheck() in V8Window.cpp but also at every call to
BindingSecurity::shouldAllowAccessTo() because V8 only calls back
securityCheck() on property lookups, and not for function invocation.

BindingSecurity::shouldAllowAccessTo() is called with every possible
cross-origin window, which means every possible new window.  Thus,
shouldAllowAccessTo() should be the right place to check the access
to the initial document.

description: There is an Assertion 'v->d.lval != v' failed at src/jsiValue.c in Jsish v3.5.0.

code_evidence: Line 3 short-circuits when the value is already a number. Otherwise line 4 calls Jsi_ValueToNumberInt and treats its result as a Jsi_Number, ignoring any error status. Lines 5-6 then reset and rewrite v unconditionally as a number, and line 7 returns JSI_OK.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The description reports an Assertion 'v->d.lval != v' failure reached through this conversion path, matching CWE-617: an attacker-reachable assert() causing application exit. The missing error check is the enabling cause; the assertion is the observable consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the conversion result is consumed without checking the return status, so a failed/converted value still reaches Jsi_ValueReset and Jsi_ValueMakeNumber. Triggering a value whose numeric conversion fails or is self-referential reaches the assertion in Jsi_ValueReset/MakeNumber; the supported consequence is an assertion-triggered crash (DoS), not memory corruption.

description: An issue was discovered in fs/f2fs/super.c in the Linux kernel through 4.17.3. There is an out-of-bounds read or a divide-by-zero error for an incorrect user_block_count in a corrupted f2fs image, leading to a denial of service (BUG).

main_segs and blocks_per_seg are read at [30,31] and used in bounds checks at [32], but user_block_count is not among them.
sit_bitmap_size and nat_bitmap_size are compared at [42-46] using log_blocks_per_seg, yet no guard ensures user_block_count is nonzero before the checkpoint is accepted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a missing nonzero constraint on a divisor used later, matching CWE-369 (Divide By Zero). It is not a generic out-of-bounds issue; the omitted check directly permits a zero divisor.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sanity check accepts a corrupted checkpoint whose user_block_count is zero (or otherwise invalid), so a later utilization computation divides by sbi->user_block_count. Trigger: mounting a crafted f2fs image. Consequence: divide-by-zero in the discard/GC path, crashing the kernel (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fixed arrays expansion.

There were two problems with njs_array_expand():

 1. It checked that the requred size with the appended elements wasn't bigger
    then the array size and then did nothing.  If there were elements removed
    from the beggining (by shift() operation), then "size <= array->size" can
    be true even if there wasn't enought free space after the array.

 2. After allocating more space to prepend elements, it set array->size without
    counting those elements.

Probably, the original idea was to decrement array->size while removing
elements from the beginning, but it wasn't done right.  Even if so, the
new version of the function looks cleaner.

This closes #152 and closes #153 issues on Github.

description: Memory Corruption was discovered in the cmsgpack library in the Lua subsystem in Redis before 3.2.12, 4.x before 4.0.10, and 5.x before 5.0 RC2 because of stack-based buffer overflows.

code_evidence: The loop repeatedly calls mp_decode_to_lua_type(L,&c), which pushes decoded values onto the Lua stack, iterating while c.left > 0 && cnt < limit; when decode_all is true limit is INT_MAX (line 15), so the number of pushes is bounded only by input size.
After the loop, lua_pushinteger and lua_insert add another stack slot; the function never checks remaining Lua stack capacity before pushing, so a large input causes unbounded stack growth.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing stack-capacity check before repeated lua_push* operations leads to writes past the Lua stack boundary, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write; the patch adds luaL_checkstack to prevent it. A CWE-400 resource-exhaustion label would not capture the memory-corruption consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unpack loop pushes one Lua value per decoded element without reserving/checking stack space, and decode_all removes the practical limit. Trigger: unpacking attacker-supplied cmsgpack data with many small elements. Consequence: the Lua stack is overrun, producing a stack-based buffer overflow and memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Avoid some undefined pointer arithmetic

A common idiom in the codebase is:

if (p + len > limit)
{
    return; /* Too long */
}

Where "p" points to some malloc'd data of SIZE bytes and
limit == p + SIZE

"len" here could be from some externally supplied data (e.g. from a TLS
message).

The rules of C pointer arithmetic are such that "p + len" is only well
defined where len <= SIZE. Therefore the above idiom is actually
undefined behaviour.

For example this could cause problems if some malloc implementation
provides an address for "p" such that "p + len" actually overflows for
values of len that are too big and therefore p + len < limit!

Issue reported by Guido Vranken.

CVE-2016-2177

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (session_id + len > limit) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (limit - session_id < len) {']}
description: OpenSSL through 1.0.2h incorrectly uses pointer arithmetic for heap-buffer boundary checks, which might allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (integer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging unexpected malloc behavior, related to s3_srvr.c, ssl_sess.c, and t1_lib.c.

code_evidence: The boundary check computes session_id + len and compares it to limit. session_id is an attacker-influenced pointer into a TLS message buffer and len is the externally supplied session-id length. The check assumes session_id + len cannot wrap past limit; if len is large enough, pointer arithmetic becomes undefined/overflows and the comparison may pass, so the guard fails.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the check performs an arithmetic/pointer computation whose result can wrap, invalidating the logic that assumed session_id + len stays greater than session_id. This is an integer/pointer overflow in a size/offset check, not merely a generic out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length/pointer calculation session_id + len can overflow or be undefined before the comparison, so the size constraint is evaluated on a wrapped value. Trigger: externally supplied len large enough to overflow the pointer arithmetic. Consequence: the boundary check is bypassed, allowing later use of the oversized length (e.g., memcpy at line 42) and possible crash/DoS or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
unix: properly account for FDs passed over unix sockets

It is possible for a process to allocate and accumulate far more FDs than
the process' limit by sending them over a unix socket then closing them
to keep the process' fd count low.

This change addresses this problem by keeping track of the number of FDs
in flight per user and preventing non-privileged processes from having
more FDs in flight than their configured FD limit.

commit_msg:
sctp: Prevent soft lockup when sctp_accept() is called during a timeout event

A case can occur when sctp_accept() is called by the user during
a heartbeat timeout event after the 4-way handshake.  Since
sctp_assoc_migrate() changes both assoc->base.sk and assoc->ep, the
bh_sock_lock in sctp_generate_heartbeat_event() will be taken with
the listening socket but released with the new association socket.
The result is a deadlock on any future attempts to take the listening
socket lock.

Note that this race can occur with other SCTP timeouts that take
the bh_lock_sock() in the event sctp_accept() is called.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct net *net = sock_net(asoc->base.sk);', '\tbh_lock_sock(asoc->base.sk);', '\tif (sock_owned_by_user(asoc->base.sk)) {', '\tbh_unlock_sock(asoc->base.sk);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct sock *sk = asoc->base.sk;', '\tstruct net *net = sock_net(sk);', '\tbh_lock_sock(sk);', '\tif (sock_owned_by_user(sk)) {', '\tbh_unlock_sock(sk);']}
description: net/sctp/sm_sideeffect.c in the Linux kernel before 4.3 does not properly manage the relationship between a lock and a socket, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock) via a crafted sctp_accept call.

code_evidence: Line 5 re-reads asoc->base.sk to derive net, line 6 locks asoc->base.sk and line 7 checks ownership of that same expression, but line 20 unlocks asoc->base.sk again; the sock pointer is never captured once, so concurrent sctp_assoc_migrate() can change asoc->base.sk between the lock and the unlock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a concurrent code sequence requires exclusive access to the shared socket, but the lock/unlock pair resolves different resources across a timing window, violating exclusivity and atomicity. A plain deadlock label would miss the underlying race on the shared field that creates the imbalance.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the socket locked at line 6 and the socket unlocked at line 20 are each resolved from the mutable field asoc->base.sk instead of a single saved pointer. Trigger: sctp_accept() calls sctp_assoc_migrate() during a protocol-unreach timer event, changing asoc->base.sk after the lock is taken. The unlock then releases a different socket's lock, leaving the listening socket permanently locked while the new socket is unlocked without being held, causing deadlock/soft lockup (DoS).

commit_msg:
rsi: release skb if rsi_prepare_beacon fails

In rsi_send_beacon, if rsi_prepare_beacon fails the allocated skb should
be released.

Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tdev_kfree_skb(skb);']}
description: A memory leak in the rsi_send_beacon() function in drivers/net/wireless/rsi/rsi_91x_mgmt.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering rsi_prepare_beacon() failures, aka CID-d563131ef23c.

code_evidence: Line 5 allocates skb via dev_alloc_skb; lines 6-7 return -ENOMEM only when allocation itself fails, so ownership of a valid skb begins here.

Trigger: rsi_prepare_beacon returns nonzero, an error path reachable on malformed or failed beacon preparation. Each occurrence leaks MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE bytes, and repeated failures exhaust kernel memory, causing DoS. The leak is the cause; memory exhaustion is the consequence.

commit_msg:
nfc: replace improper check device_is_registered() in netlink related functions

The device_is_registered() in nfc core is used to check whether
nfc device is registered in netlink related functions such as
nfc_fw_download(), nfc_dev_up() and so on. Although device_is_registered()
is protected by device_lock, there is still a race condition between
device_del() and device_is_registered(). The root cause is that
kobject_del() in device_del() is not protected by device_lock.

   (cleanup task)         |     (netlink task)
                          |
nfc_unregister_device     | nfc_fw_download
 device_del               |  device_lock
  ...                     |   if (!device_is_registered)//(1)
  kobject_del//(2)        |   ...
 ...                      |  device_unlock

The device_is_registered() returns the value of state_in_sysfs and
the state_in_sysfs is set to zero in kobject_del(). If we pass check in
position (1), then set zero in position (2). As a result, the check
in position (1) is useless.

This patch uses bool variable instead of device_is_registered() to judge
whether the nfc device is registered, which is well synchronized.

Fixes: 3e256b8f8dfa ("NFC: add nfc subsystem core")
Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!device_is_registered(&dev->dev)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (dev->shutting_down) {']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel's NFC core functionality due to a race condition between kobject creation and delete. This vulnerability allows a local attacker with CAP_NET_ADMIN privilege to leak kernel information.

code_evidence: device_lock is taken and the registration state is checked via device_is_registered(&dev->dev); on failure the function jumps to error and returns -ENODEV.
If the check passes, the code later dereferences dev->ops and invokes dev->ops->dev_up(dev), using the device after the state check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function checks a resource state (device registration) and then uses the device, with a window in which the state can change between check and use, matching CWE-367. The race is enabled by unsynchronized kobject_del() rather than by a missing lock in nfc_dev_up itself.

evidence_lines.code:
if (dev->ops->dev_up)
rc = dev->ops->dev_up(dev);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the registration check relies on device_is_registered(), whose state_in_sysfs is cleared by kobject_del() outside device_lock, so the check can pass and then be invalidated concurrently by nfc_unregister_device/device_del. Trigger: a netlink caller invokes nfc_dev_up while another task unregisters the device. Consequence: the subsequent dev->ops dereference/use operates on a device being torn down, supporting use-after-free/information leak rather than a mere logic error.

commit_msg:
i2c: fix stack buffer overflow vulnerability in i2c md command

When running "i2c md 0 0 80000100", the function do_i2c_md parses the
length into an unsigned int variable named length. The value is then
moved to a signed variable:

    int nbytes = length;
    #define DISP_LINE_LEN 16
    int linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;
    ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);

On systems where integers are 32 bits wide, 0x80000100 is a negative
value to "nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN" is false and linebytes gets assigned
0x80000100 instead of 16.

The consequence is that the function which reads from the i2c device
(dm_i2c_read or i2c_read) is called with a 16-byte stack buffer to fill
but with a size parameter which is too large. In some cases, this could
trigger a crash. But with some i2c drivers, such as drivers/i2c/nx_i2c.c
(used with "nexell,s5pxx18-i2c" bus), the size is actually truncated to
a 16-bit integer. This is because function i2c_transfer expects an
unsigned short length. In such a case, an attacker who can control the
response of an i2c device can overwrite the return address of a function
and execute arbitrary code through Return-Oriented Programming.

Fix this issue by using unsigned integers types in do_i2c_md. While at
it, make also alen unsigned, as signed sizes can cause vulnerabilities
when people forgot to check that they can be negative.

Signed-off-by: Nicolas Iooss <nicolas.iooss+uboot@ledger.fr>
Reviewed-by: Heiko Schocher <hs@denx.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint alen;'], 'added_lines': ['\tuint\talen;']}
description: In Das U-Boot through 2022.07-rc5, an integer signedness error and resultant stack-based buffer overflow in the "i2c md" command enables the corruption of the return address pointer of the do_i2c_md function.

code_evidence: alen is declared as signed int and assigned get_alen() at line 16; it is only checked against > 3 at line 17, so a negative value such as -1 passes the check. length is parsed from argv[3] via hextoul at line 19 and passed directly as the size to dm_i2c_read at line 26 (or i2c_read at line 28) with memaddr, a caller-supplied destination pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked size passed to dm_i2c_read/i2c_read writes beyond the intended destination buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The signedness flaw is the root cause, but the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The signed alen from get_alen bypasses the >3 bound check when negative, and the attacker-controlled length is used as the read size into memaddr without a bounds check. An oversized or truncated length causes the i2c driver to write past the destination buffer, corrupting memory and potentially enabling return-address overwrite and code execution.

commit_msg:
Correctly load/initialize classes when using ConstantPool

- do not load classes in the "ifLoaded" calls
- never intitialize classes in the natives
- do not update the constant pool when querying from the natives

Fixes: #12016

[ci skip]

Signed-off-by: Graham Chapman <graham_chapman@ca.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t} else {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t} else if (J9_ARE_NO_BITS_SET(resolveFlags, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE)) {']}
description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: When method is non-NULL and CHECK_CLINIT is set but the class's initializeStatus is not the current vmStruct (lines 8-9), the code returns -1 only in that branch; the else on line 12 unconditionally writes ramStaticMethodRef->method into the constant pool entry at ramCP[cpIndex]. The patch gates this write with J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE, so before the fix the pool entry was updated even for callers that requested no constant-pool update.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe CP update lets static members be resolved without the class initialization method running, so the class's static state is used before initialization—a missing-initialization-of-resource weakness (CWE-909). This is not merely a stale-cache issue; it directly skips required initialization.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the else branch updates the resolved constant pool entry regardless of resolveFlags, ignoring the NO_CP_UPDATE request. Trigger: a caller resolving a static method ref with NO_CP_UPDATE (e.g. ConstantPool API) reaches this else path. Consequence: the entry is pre-resolved/cached, so subsequent static access may bypass class initialization and expose uninitialized values.

It is not merely a config-parsing bug since the defect disables the authentication mechanism itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: authentication setup is conditioned on the presence of an authfile rather than on whether authentication is required (is_auth_req). Trigger: a config that requires authentication but omits/empties the authfile directive. Consequence: read_authkey is skipped, so nodes lacking the correct key are not rejected from communicating, weakening node-to-node authentication.

commit_msg:
f2fs: fix potential panic during fstrim

As Ju Hyung Park reported:

"When 'fstrim' is called for manual trim, a BUG() can be triggered
randomly with this patch.

I'm seeing this issue on both x86 Desktop and arm64 Android phone.

On x86 Desktop, this was caused during Ubuntu boot-up. I have a
cronjob installed which calls 'fstrim -v /' during boot. On arm64
Android, this was caused during GC looping with 1ms gc_min_sleep_time
& gc_max_sleep_time."

Root cause of this issue is that f2fs_wait_discard_bios can only be
used by f2fs_put_super, because during put_super there must be no
other referrers, so it can ignore discard entry's reference count
when removing the entry, otherwise in other caller we will hit bug_on
in __remove_discard_cmd as there may be other issuer added reference
count in discard entry.

Thread A				Thread B
					- issue_discard_thread
- f2fs_ioc_fitrim
 - f2fs_trim_fs
  - f2fs_wait_discard_bios
   - __issue_discard_cmd
    - __submit_discard_cmd
					 - __wait_discard_cmd
					  - dc->ref++
					  - __wait_one_discard_bio
   - __wait_discard_cmd
    - __remove_discard_cmd
     - f2fs_bug_on(sbi, dc->ref)

Fixes: 969d1b180d987c2be02de890d0fff0f66a0e80de
Reported-by: Ju Hyung Park <qkrwngud825@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Chao Yu <yuchao0@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Jaegeuk Kim <jaegeuk@kernel.org>

description: The f2fs implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.14 mishandles reference counts associated with f2fs_wait_discard_bios calls, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (BUG), as demonstrated by fstrim.

commit_msg:
KVM: x86: Reload pit counters for all channels when restoring state

Currently if userspace restores the pit counters with a count of 0
on channels 1 or 2 and the guest attempts to read the count on those
channels, then KVM will perform a mod of 0 and crash.  This will ensure
that 0 values are converted to 65536 as per the spec.

This is CVE-2015-7513.

Signed-off-by: Andy Honig <ahonig@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tkvm_pit_load_count(kvm, 0, ps->channels[0].count, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['\tint i;', '\tfor (i = 0; i < 3; i++)', '\t\tkvm_pit_load_count(kvm, i, ps->channels[i].count, 0);']}
description: arch/x86/kvm/x86.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 does not reset the PIT counter values during state restoration, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero error and host OS crash) via a zero value, related to the kvm_vm_ioctl_set_pit and kvm_vm_ioctl_set_pit2 functions.

code_evidence: The function copies the user-supplied kvm_pit_state ps into the PIT state under lock, then calls kvm_pit_load_count only for channel 0 with ps->channels[0].count. Channels 1 and 2 counts are copied but never reloaded, so a restored zero count on those channels remains in state and later reads can reach a division/modulo by the zero count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because the supported consequence is a divide-by-zero from an unvalidated, unnormalized zero counter value, leading to host crash. The missing constraint (zero counts not converted to 65536) is the enabling cause; the division by zero is the resulting weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the restore path fails to reload/convert all three PIT channel counts, so a guest-supplied zero count on channels 1 or 2 is stored unchanged. Trigger: userspace restores state with a zero count, then the guest reads that channel count, causing a divide-by-zero in the host kernel and a denial of service crash.

commit_msg:
posix-timers: Sanitize overrun handling

The posix timer overrun handling is broken because the forwarding functions
can return a huge number of overruns which does not fit in an int. As a
consequence timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun can turn into
random number generators.

The k_clock::timer_forward() callbacks return a 64 bit value now. Make
k_itimer::ti_overrun[_last] 64bit as well, so the kernel internal
accounting is correct. 3Remove the temporary (int) casts.

Add a helper function which clamps the overrun value returned to user space
via timer_getoverrun(2) or siginfo::si_overrun limited to a positive value
between 0 and INT_MAX. INT_MAX is an indicator for user space that the
overrun value has been clamped.

Reported-by: Team OWL337 <icytxw@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Acked-by: John Stultz <john.stultz@linaro.org>
Cc: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Michael Kerrisk <mtk.manpages@gmail.com>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20180626132705.018623573@linutronix.de
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tnew_timer->it_overrun = -1;'], 'added_lines': ['\tnew_timer->it_overrun = -1LL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.17.3. An Integer Overflow in kernel/time/posix-timers.c in the POSIX timer code is caused by the way the overrun accounting works. Depending on interval and expiry time values, the overrun can be larger than INT_MAX, but the accounting is int based. This basically makes the accounting values, which are visible to user space via timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun, random. For example, a local user can cause a denial of service (signed integer overflow) via crafted mmap, futex, timer_create, and timer_settime system calls.

code_evidence: Line 25 initializes new_timer->it_overrun to -1 before the timer is registered; line 51 calls kc->timer_create(new_timer), which sets up and arms the timer whose overrun accounting is later maintained by the clock callbacks. The patch changes this initializer from -1 to -1LL, indicating it_overrun is a 64-bit field whose value flows into the overrun accounting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits: the overrun value is incremented beyond the representable int range, wrapping to a small/negative number. The 64-bit -1LL initializer and removal of (int) casts are the fix context for that overflow; the consequence is incorrect/random overrun reporting rather than a separate out-of-bounds issue.

evidence_lines.code:
new_timer->it_overrun = -1;
error = kc->timer_create(new_timer);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that the kernel-internal overrun counter is accumulated by timer_forward() callbacks and can exceed INT_MAX while the accounting/storage type is too narrow. Trigger: a local user creates an interval timer via timer_create with crafted interval/expiry values, causing repeated expirations and large overrun accumulation. Consequence: signed integer overflow/wraparound makes timer_getoverrun() and siginfo::si_overrun report random values, yielding a signed-overflow denial of service (and incorrect accounting visible to userspace).

code_evidence: Loop bound i < bin->ne_header->SegCount comes from the untrusted NE header; the loop indexes bin->segment_entries[i] without verifying that SegCount matches the number of allocated segment entries.
The derived pointer se is then dereferenced for length, minAllocSz, flags and offset, so an out-of-range i yields reads beyond the segment_entries allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-129 fits because an untrusted count is used directly as an array index bound without validating it against the array's real size, producing the out-of-bounds access. This is index validation, not a generic buffer overflow from a size calculation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: SegCount from the parsed NE file is trusted as the array length, with no bound check against the actual size of segment_entries. Trigger: a crafted NE header declaring a SegCount larger than the allocated entries. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of NE_image_segment_entry fields, causing a crash/segfault and potential memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
Make sure element data type and length do not mismatch the one specified
by the set declaration.

Fixes: 7d7402642eaf ("netfilter: nf_tables: variable sized set element keys / data")
Reported-by: Hugues ANGUELKOV <hanguelkov@randorisec.fr>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (desc->type != NFT_DATA_VERDICT && desc->len != set->dlen) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tu32 dtype;', '\tif (set->dtype == NFT_DATA_VERDICT)', '\t\tdtype = NFT_DATA_VERDICT;', '\telse', '\t\tdtype = NFT_DATA_VALUE;', '', '\tif (dtype != desc->type ||', '\t    set->dlen != desc->len) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.18.9. A type confusion bug in nft_set_elem_init (leading to a buffer overflow) could be used by a local attacker to escalate privileges, a different vulnerability than CVE-2022-32250. (The attacker can obtain root access, but must start with an unprivileged user namespace to obtain CAP_NET_ADMIN access.) This can be fixed in nft_setelem_parse_data in net/netfilter/nf_tables_api.c.

code_evidence: nft_data_init parses the attribute into data/desc, then the check at line 10 only rejects when desc->type != NFT_DATA_VERDICT AND desc->len != set->dlen. Since the condition is a conjunction, a parsed value whose type differs from what the set expects is accepted whenever its length coincidentally equals set->dlen; conversely a verdict-typed element bypasses the length check entirely, and no comparison of desc->type against the set's declared dtype (value vs verdict) occurs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts a resource (set element data) initialized with one type while the set later accesses it as an incompatible type, which is exactly CWE-843. The fix confirms this by comparing a derived dtype against desc->type; the flaw is type mismatch, not merely a length check (CWE-197).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the validation conflates type and length into one AND-condition and never checks desc->type against the set's declared data type. Trigger: a user with CAP_NET_ADMIN submits a set element whose attribute type (value vs verdict) mismatches the set declaration but whose length matches. The mismatched element is stored and later interpreted as the set's declared type, yielding type confusion and a buffer overflow in nft_set_elem_init.

commit_msg:
Handle null return from iniparser_getstring

Fix handling of NULL returns from iniparser_getstring in
iniparser_getboolean, iniparser_getlongint and iniparser_getdouble,
avoiding a crash.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (c==INI_INVALID_KEY) return notfound ;'], 'added_lines': ['    if (c==NULL || c==INI_INVALID_KEY) return notfound ;']}
description: iniparser v4.1 is vulnerable to NULL Pointer Dereference in function iniparser_getlongint which misses check NULL for function iniparser_getstring's return.

code_evidence: iniparser_getstring is called with INI_INVALID_KEY as default; the returned pointer c is only checked against INI_INVALID_KEY, not against NULL.
The very next statement dereferences c[0] without any intervening NULL check, so a NULL return reaches the dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer expected valid while returning NULL is possible, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. This is not merely a missing-input-validation issue; the defining flaw is the unchecked NULL used in a dereference.

evidence_lines.code:
c = iniparser_getstring(d, key, INI_INVALID_KEY);
if (c==INI_INVALID_KEY) return notfound ;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return of iniparser_getstring may be NULL, but the guard at line 6 only tests the sentinel INI_INVALID_KEY. Trigger: a key whose lookup yields NULL. Consequence: c[0] at line 7 dereferences NULL, causing a crash (DoS).

Fix crash in vtable analysis on UB ##crash

* BountyID 0730a95e-c485-4ff2-9a5d-bb3abfda0b17
* Reproducer: minified_crash
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tut64 curAddressValue;'], 'added_lines': ['\tut64 curAddressValue = UT64_MAX;']}
description: Access of Uninitialized Pointer in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.7.0.

code_evidence: Line 2 declares curAddressValue without an initializer; lines 3-5 pass its address to context->read_addr and only guard on the boolean return value, not on whether the callee actually wrote a value.

Line 6 then passes curAddressValue to vtable_addr_in_text_section, and lines 7-9 store it through *value, so the uninitialized contents are consumed whenever read_addr returns true without initializing the out-parameter.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-824 directly matches: a pointer variable is declared without initialization and then dereferenced/consumed on the success path. The fix initializing it to UT64_MAX confirms the defect was the missing initialization rather than a bounds or type-confusion issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: curAddressValue is uninitialized and read_addr's success return does not guarantee the out-parameter was populated. Trigger: a call path where read_addr succeeds without writing to the pointer, after which line 6 uses the indeterminate value. Supported consequence: use of an uninitialized pointer value leads to invalid memory access and a crash (denial of service).

commit_msg: added option to disable trivial auth methods
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (sent)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (sent) {', '\t\t\tauthctxt->is_trivial_auth = 0;', '\t\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in OpenSSH before 8.9. If a client is using public-key authentication with agent forwarding but without -oLogLevel=verbose, and an attacker has silently modified the server to support the None authentication option, then the user cannot determine whether FIDO authentication is going to confirm that the user wishes to connect to that server, or that the user wishes to allow that server to connect to a different server on the user's behalf. NOTE: the vendor's position is "this is not an authentication bypass, since nothing is being bypassed.

code_evidence: send_pubkey_test() and sign_and_send_pubkey() both return a sent value that is assigned to the local sent variable; the added block sets authctxt->is_trivial_auth = 0 only when sent is true, then returns sent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness concerns insufficient proof/confirmation of the authentication claim: the client cannot verify that the server's identity and the intended authentication method are what they claim. This matches CWE-287's scope of improper authentication. It is not a credential comparison flaw (CWE-287 class rather than a lower-level child), because the defect is in tracking/confirming the authentication method state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function tracks whether a non-trivial public-key authentication attempt was actually sent. If a client uses public-key auth but the server silently offers the None method and the client never sends a key test (sent stays 0), is_trivial_auth is never cleared, so the caller cannot distinguish a real FIDO/public-key confirmation from a trivial-auth connection. The cause is the conditional flag update; the consequence is that the user cannot tell whether the server is being authenticated or agent-forwarding is being authorized.

commit_msg: Fix bug #72663 - destroy broken object when unserializing
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ["\t    /* We've got partially constructed object on our hands here. Wipe it */", '\t    zend_hash_clean(Z_OBJPROP_PP(rval));', '\t    ZVAL_NULL(*rval);']}
description: ext/standard/var_unserializer.c in PHP before 5.6.25 and 7.x before 7.0.10 mishandles certain invalid objects, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted serialized data that leads to a (1) __destruct call or (2) magic method call.

code_evidence: process_nested_data populates properties of the attacker-supplied object; on failure at line 8 the function returns 0 without cleaning the partially constructed object or resetting *rval.

For successfully deserialized objects, the function looks up and invokes the magic method __wakeup (lines 11-16) via call_user_function_ex, so a crafted serialized payload triggers object magic-method execution.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the object-deserialization path: it reconstructs objects from untrusted serialized input and invokes magic methods without fully validating the resulting object, matching CWE-502. This is not merely memory corruption; the weakness is deserializing untrusted data into executable object state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled serialized data is turned into a live object whose properties are populated before validity is confirmed, and on failure the object is left partially constructed rather than destroyed. Trigger: crafted serialized data that fails process_nested_data or reaches __wakeup. Supported consequence: magic method calls (__wakeup) and __destruct calls on broken objects, leading to DoS or unspecified impact.

commit_msg: Avoid a crash (double-free) when SSH connection fails
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        sshu->session = NULL;']}
description: nse_libssh2.cc in Nmap 7.70 is subject to a denial of service condition due to a double free when an SSH connection fails, as demonstrated by a leading \n character to ssh-brute.nse or ssh-auth-methods.nse.

code_evidence: When libssh2_session_handshake returns a nonzero rc on line 12, line 13 frees sshu->session but does not clear the pointer before returning via luaL_error on line 14. The struct member retains its dangling address, so any later path that frees or uses sshu->session again operates on already-freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the same allocation reachable through sshu->session can be freed more than once: the handshake-failure branch frees it and leaves the pointer live. This is a use-after-free-adjacent dangling-pointer issue, but the directly supported consequence is the double free, so CWE-415 is the precise label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch frees sshu->session without invalidating the stored pointer. Trigger: a failed SSH handshake (e.g., a leading newline input) drives rc nonzero and leaves a dangling session pointer in the userdata. Consequence: a subsequent free of the same address is a double free, causing memory corruption and a denial-of-service crash, with possible further exploitation.

commit_msg: misc oom and possible memory leak fix
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [''], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!now) {', '\t\treturn -1;', '\t}', '\tfree(now);']}
description: Boa through 0.94.14rc21 allows remote attackers to trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) condition because malloc is mishandled.

code_evidence: now = strdup(asctime(timeptr)); stores a heap copy of the time string, then now[strlen(now) - 1] = '\0' writes to the last character without checking that the string is non-empty. asctime always yields a non-empty string, but the code's safety depends entirely on this unchecked assumption rather than any explicit bound or length test.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the operation now[strlen(now)-1] can read/write outside the strdup'd buffer's intended boundary when the length is zero, an improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer. It is not merely an OOM/leak issue; the unchecked index is the buffer-bounds weakness, though the zero-length path is not demonstrated by the code alone.

evidence_lines.code:
now = strdup(asctime(timeptr));
now[strlen(now) - 1] = '\0';

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the terminating write indexes strlen(now)-1 with no guard that strlen(now) >= 1. If the copied string were empty (asctime returning an empty buffer, or any future change to the source), strlen(now)-1 underflows to SIZE_MAX and the write lands far outside the allocated buffer. Trigger: an empty time string reaching strdup; consequence: out-of-bounds heap write, corrupting adjacent heap metadata or data.

commit_msg:
check e2ee public key against private one

should ensure we have matching private/public keys

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Gallien <matthieu_gallien@yahoo.fr>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if (!_privateKey.isNull()) {'], 'added_lines': ['            if (!_privateKey.isNull() && checkPublicKeyValidity(account)) {']}
description: The Nextcloud Desktop Client is a tool to synchronize files from Nextcloud Server with a computer. Clients using the Nextcloud end-to-end encryption feature download the public and private key via an API endpoint. In versions prior to 3.3.0, the Nextcloud Desktop client fails to check if a private key belongs to previously downloaded public certificate. If the Nextcloud instance serves a malicious public key, the data would be encrypted for this key and thus could be accessible to a malicious actor. This issue is fixed in Nextcloud Desktop Client version 3.3.0. There are no known workarounds aside from upgrading.

code_evidence: The function derives _privateKey from user-supplied mnemonic via decryptPrivateKey (lines 27-28), then gates writePrivateKey/writeCertificate/writeMnemonic solely on !_privateKey.isNull() (line 30). No check binds the decrypted private key to the previously downloaded public key/certificate before persisting both.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-295 fits because the client fails to validate that the private key corresponds to the public key/certificate it trusts, breaking the key-pair integrity assumption. This is improper certificate/public-key validation, not generic key storage.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decrypted private key is accepted and stored without verifying it matches the account's downloaded public certificate. Trigger: a malicious server serves a mismatched public key; the client encrypts data for that key while never confirming the private key pairing. Consequence: confidentiality compromise, as data is encrypted for an attacker-controlled key the client does not own.

Fixes: 7549ae3e81cc ("9p: Use the i_size_[read, write]() macros instead of using inode->i_size directly.")
Reported-by: Xing Gaopeng <xingaopeng@huawei.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tv9fs_stat2inode_dotl(st, d_inode(dentry));'], 'added_lines': ['\tv9fs_stat2inode_dotl(st, d_inode(dentry), 0);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. The 9p filesystem did not protect i_size_write() properly, which causes an i_size_read() infinite loop and denial of service on SMP systems.

code_evidence: p9_client_getattr_dotl returns st, which is passed to v9fs_stat2inode_dotl(st, d_inode(dentry)) at line 21 before generic_fillattr(d_inode(dentry), stat) at line 22. The changed call omits the i_size_write() lock argument (0), so the inode size update is not serialized with the concurrent i_size_read() inside generic_fillattr.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is an unbounded loop (read_seqcount_begin retry) whose exit condition is not reached, matching CWE-835. The missing lock is the cause; the infinite loop is the weakness consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: v9fs_stat2inode_dotl updates inode->i_size without holding inode->i_lock, while generic_fillattr's i_size_read() uses a seqcount. Concurrent getattr calls on 32-bit SMP can observe an in-progress write and spin in read_seqcount_begin() without a guaranteed retry exit, causing a soft lockup/CPU DoS.

commit_msg: Fix memleak in tcp server by wiping priority queues on deletion
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int add_accepted(TCP_Server *tcp_server, const Mono_Time *mono_time, const TCP_Secure_Connection *con)', '        if (realloc_connection(tcp_server, tcp_server->size_accepted_connections + 4) == -1) {', '    memcpy(&tcp_server->accepted_connection_array[index], con, sizeof(TCP_Secure_Connection));'], 'added_lines': ['static int add_accepted(TCP_Server *tcp_server, const Mono_Time *mono_time, TCP_Secure_Connection *con)', '        if (alloc_new_connections(tcp_server, 4) == -1) {', '    move_secure_connection(&tcp_server->accepted_connection_array[index], con);', '']}
description: The TCP Server module in toxcore before 0.2.8 doesn't free the TCP priority queue under certain conditions, which allows a remote attacker to exhaust the system's memory, causing a denial of service (DoS).

code_evidence: The const qualifier on con is removed, making the source connection mutable so its owned resources can be transferred.
When the array is full, realloc_connection is invoked; a failure returns -1 immediately, and index is then taken from num_accepted_connections.

Fix tf.raw_ops.ImageProjectiveTransformV2 vulnerability with large output_shape.

We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 8faa6ea692985dbe6ce10e1a3168e0bd60a723ba. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.11. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.10.1, 2.9.3, and TensorFlow 2.8.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.
