description: The ICMPv6 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-icmp6.c.

code_evidence: In the NI_QTYPE_FQDN reply branch, cp is set to (ni6 + 1) + 4 and only cp[0] is checked with ND_TCHECK; the comparison cp[0] == ep - cp - 1 and the loop while (cp < ep) rely on ep being the true packet end, but the branch is entered after only ND_TCHECK2(*dp, sizeof(*ni6)) at line 119, so the FQDN bytes may extend beyond the captured buffer.

In the NI_QTYPE_NODEADDR branch, the loop condition i < siz uses siz = ep - bp, but each iteration reads ip6addr_string(ndo, bp + i) and EXTRACT_32BITS(bp + i) after checking only against siz; if ep lies beyond the actual captured data, these reads overrun the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads packet data past the end of the intended buffer without a bounds check. It is an out-of-bounds read, not an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) or an uninitialized read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser trusts the packet-derived length siz = ep - bp and the node-info structure fields without confirming that the referenced bytes are within the captured buffer. A truncated ICMPv6 node-info reply causes ip6addr_string, EXTRACT_32BITS, or safeputchar to read past the end of the buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read (crash or memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
ext4: fix slab-use-after-free in ext4_es_insert_extent()

Yikebaer reported an issue:
==================================================================
BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in ext4_es_insert_extent+0xc68/0xcb0
fs/ext4/extents_status.c:894
Read of size 4 at addr ffff888112ecc1a4 by task syz-executor/8438

CPU: 1 PID: 8438 Comm: syz-executor Not tainted 6.5.0-rc5 #1
Call Trace:
 [...]
 kasan_report+0xba/0xf0 mm/kasan/report.c:588
 ext4_es_insert_extent+0xc68/0xcb0 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:894
 ext4_map_blocks+0x92a/0x16f0 fs/ext4/inode.c:680
 ext4_alloc_file_blocks.isra.0+0x2df/0xb70 fs/ext4/extents.c:4462
 ext4_zero_range fs/ext4/extents.c:4622 [inline]
 ext4_fallocate+0x251c/0x3ce0 fs/ext4/extents.c:4721
 [...]

Allocated by task 8438:
 [...]
 kmem_cache_zalloc include/linux/slab.h:693 [inline]
 __es_alloc_extent fs/ext4/extents_status.c:469 [inline]
 ext4_es_insert_extent+0x672/0xcb0 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:873
 ext4_map_blocks+0x92a/0x16f0 fs/ext4/inode.c:680
 ext4_alloc_file_blocks.isra.0+0x2df/0xb70 fs/ext4/extents.c:4462
 ext4_zero_range fs/ext4/extents.c:4622 [inline]
 ext4_fallocate+0x251c/0x3ce0 fs/ext4/extents.c:4721
 [...]

Freed by task 8438:
 [...]
 kmem_cache_free+0xec/0x490 mm/slub.c:3823
 ext4_es_try_to_merge_right fs/ext4/extents_status.c:593 [inline]
 __es_insert_extent+0x9f4/0x1440 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:802
 ext4_es_insert_extent+0x2ca/0xcb0 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:882
 ext4_map_blocks+0x92a/0x16f0 fs/ext4/inode.c:680
 ext4_alloc_file_blocks.isra.0+0x2df/0xb70 fs/ext4/extents.c:4462
 ext4_zero_range fs/ext4/extents.c:4622 [inline]
 ext4_fallocate+0x251c/0x3ce0 fs/ext4/extents.c:4721
 [...]
==================================================================

The flow of issue triggering is as follows:
1. remove es
      raw es               es  removed  es1
|-------------------| -> |----|.......|------|

2. insert es
  es   insert   es1      merge with es  es1     merge with es and free es1
|----|.......|------| -> |------------|------| -> |-------------------|

es merges with newes, then merges with es1, frees es1, then determines
if es1->es_len is 0 and triggers a UAF.

The code flow is as follows:
ext4_es_insert_extent
  es1 = __es_alloc_extent(true);
  es2 = __es_alloc_extent(true);
  __es_remove_extent(inode, lblk, end, NULL, es1)
    __es_insert_extent(inode, &newes, es1) ---> insert es1 to es tree
  __es_insert_extent(inode, &newes, es2)
    ext4_es_try_to_merge_right
      ext4_es_free_extent(inode, es1) --->  es1 is freed
  if (es1 && !es1->es_len)
    // Trigger UAF by determining if es1 is used.

We determine whether es1 or es2 is used immediately after calling
__es_remove_extent() or __es_insert_extent() to avoid triggering a
UAF if es1 or es2 is freed.

Reported-by: Yikebaer Aizezi <yikebaer61@gmail.com>
Closes: https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/CALcu4raD4h9coiyEBL4Bm0zjDwxC2CyPiTwsP3zFuhot6y9Beg@mail.gmail.com
Fixes: 2a69c450083d ("ext4: using nofail preallocation in ext4_es_insert_extent()")
Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Baokun Li <libaokun1@huawei.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230815070808.3377171-1-libaokun1@huawei.com
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\t/* es is pre-allocated but not used, free it. */', '\tif (es1 && !es1->es_len)', '\t\t__es_free_extent(es1);', '\tif (es2 && !es2->es_len)', '\t\t__es_free_extent(es2);'], 'added_lines': ["\t/* Free preallocated extent if it didn't get used. */", '\tif (es1) {', '\t\tif (!es1->es_len)', '\t\t\t__es_free_extent(es1);', '\t\tes1 = NULL;', '\t}', "\t/* Free preallocated extent if it didn't get used. */", '\tif (es2) {', '\t\tif (!es2->es_len)', '\t\t\t__es_free_extent(es2);', '\t\tes2 = NULL;', '\t}']}
description: The Linux kernel before 6.5.4 has an es1 use-after-free in fs/ext4/extents_status.c, related to ext4_es_insert_extent.

code_evidence: After __es_remove_extent(inode, lblk, lblk, NULL, es1) at line 24, es1 may have been merged into and freed by __es_insert_extent (ext4_es_try_to_merge_right). __es_insert_extent at line 27 can likewise free es2 via merging. The pre-patch code at lines 32-35 dereferences es1->es_len and es2->es_len to decide whether to free them, reading a freed extent_status object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits: the function references extent_status memory (es1->es_len, es2->es_len) after that memory was freed by the merge logic. This is a classic use-after-free, distinct from a mere null-pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: __es_remove_extent/__es_insert_extent merge the preallocated es1/es2 into the extent status tree and free them through ext4_es_try_to_merge_right. The caller then reads es1->es_len/es2->es_len after the free, causing a slab-use-after-free read. Trigger: fallocate/zero-range path through ext4_es_insert_extent merging. Supported consequence: KASAN slab-use-after-free read, potential crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Fix failed check in SparseTensorToCSRSparseMatrix

Security vulnerability fix. A `CHECK` fails if inputing either an empty `dense_shape`,
or a non-rank-2 `indices`. Added appropriate checks and tests.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 446053984
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(', '        ctx, TensorShapeUtils::IsVector(dense_shape.shape()),', '        errors::InvalidArgument("dense_shape must be rank 1 but got rank",', '                                dense_shape.shape().dims()));', '    OP_REQUIRES(ctx, TensorShapeUtils::IsMatrix(indices.shape()),', '                errors::InvalidArgument("indices must be rank 2 but got rank",', '                                        indices.shape().dims()));']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.SparseTensorToCSRSparseMatrix` does not fully validate the input arguments. This results in a `CHECK`-failure which can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. The code assumes `dense_shape` is a vector and `indices` is a matrix (as part of requirements for sparse tensors) but there is no validation for this. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: The function reads indices (input 0), values (input 1) and dense_shape (input 2) but only validates that dense_shape.NumElements() is 2 or 3; it never checks that dense_shape is rank 1 or that indices is rank 2.

After the weak rank check, dense_shape.vec<int64_t>() assumes dense_shape is a vector and indices.template matrix<int64_t>() assumes indices is a rank-2 matrix, so malformed shapes reach these typed accessors unvalidated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of input tensor properties (rank/shape) before processing them, matching CWE-20's improper input validation of required data properties. The consequence is an availability-impacting crash, not a separate memory-safety flaw, so the class-level CWE-20 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the op trusts that dense_shape is a vector and indices is a matrix without checking their ranks. Trigger: a caller supplies an empty/multi-dimensional dense_shape or a non-rank-2 indices tensor. The typed vec/matrix accessors then fail a CHECK, aborting the process and causing a denial of service rather than returning InvalidArgument.

description: The cdxl_decode_frame function in libavcodec/cdxl.c in FFmpeg 2.8.x before 2.8.12, 3.0.x before 3.0.8, 3.1.x before 3.1.8, 3.2.x before 3.2.5, and 3.3.x before 3.3.1 does not exclude the CHUNKY format, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted file.

When c->format == CHUNKY, aligned_width is set to avctx->width and the size check uses aligned_width * height * bpp / 8, which does not match the layout assumed by the palette/BGR24 path.
The encoding==1 && (bpp==6||bpp==8) branch selects AV_PIX_FMT_BGR24 without excluding CHUNKY; the fix adds && c->format != CHUNKY to this condition.

commit_msg:
Fix OCSP Status Request extension unbounded memory growth

A malicious client can send an excessively large OCSP Status Request
extension. If that client continually requests renegotiation,
sending a large OCSP Status Request extension each time, then there will
be unbounded memory growth on the server. This will eventually lead to a
Denial Of Service attack through memory exhaustion. Servers with a
default configuration are vulnerable even if they do not support OCSP.
Builds using the "no-ocsp" build time option are not affected.

I have also checked other extensions to see if they suffer from a similar
problem but I could not find any other issues.

CVE-2016-6304

Issue reported by Shi Lei.

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    }', '                    if (!s->tlsext_ocsp_ids', '                        && !(s->tlsext_ocsp_ids =', '                             sk_OCSP_RESPID_new_null())) {', '                        OCSP_RESPID_free(id);', '                        *al = SSL_AD_INTERNAL_ERROR;', '                        return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['', '                /*', '                 * We remove any OCSP_RESPIDs from a previous handshake', '                 * to prevent unbounded memory growth - CVE-2016-6304', '                 */', '                sk_OCSP_RESPID_pop_free(s->tlsext_ocsp_ids,', '                                        OCSP_RESPID_free);', '                if (dsize > 0) {', '                    s->tlsext_ocsp_ids = sk_OCSP_RESPID_new_null();', '                    if (s->tlsext_ocsp_ids == NULL) {', '                        *al = SSL_AD_INTERNAL_ERROR;', '                        return 0;', '                    }', '                } else {', '                    s->tlsext_ocsp_ids = NULL;', '                }', '']}
description: Multiple memory leaks in t1_lib.c in OpenSSL before 1.0.1u, 1.0.2 before 1.0.2i, and 1.1.0 before 1.1.0a allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via large OCSP Status Request extensions.

code_evidence: The OCSP status_request branch parses a client-supplied dsize and appends each decoded OCSP_RESPID into the session-persistent list s->tlsext_ocsp_ids (lines 262-269). The list is only created if it is NULL and never cleared before pushing new entries, so on each renegotiation the previously stored RESPIDs remain referenced and are never freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated OCSP_RESPID memory is retained and not released after its effective lifetime, leaving it unavailable for reuse. The excessive allocation is a symptom; the underlying weakness is the missing release of previously stored memory, not a single oversized allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser accumulates OCSP_RESPID objects in s->tlsext_ocsp_ids across handshakes without releasing the prior list. Trigger: a client repeatedly renegotiates while sending large OCSP status_request extensions. Consequence: the server's memory grows unbounded, leading to memory-exhaustion denial of service.

commit_msg:
Both add_slot_store() and remove_slot_store() try to fix up the
drc_name copied from the store buffer by placing a NUL terminator at
nbyte + 1 or in place of a '\n' if present. However, the static buffer
that we copy the drc_name data into is not zeroed and can contain
anything past the n-th byte.

This is problematic if a '\n' byte appears in that buffer after nbytes
and the string copied into the store buffer was not NUL terminated to
start with as the strchr() search for a '\n' byte will mark this
incorrectly as the end of the drc_name string resulting in a drc_name
string that contains garbage data after the n-th byte.

Additionally it will cause us to overwrite that '\n' byte on the stack
with NUL, potentially corrupting data on the stack.

The following debugging shows an example of the drmgr utility writing
"PHB 4543" to the add_slot sysfs attribute, but add_slot_store()
logging a corrupted string value.

  drmgr: drmgr: -c phb -a -s PHB 4543 -d 1
  add_slot_store: drc_name = PHB 4543°|<82>!, rc = -19

Fix this by using strscpy() instead of memcpy() to ensure the string
is NUL terminated when copied into the static drc_name buffer.
Further, since the string is now NUL terminated the code only needs to
change '\n' to '\0' when present.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Tyrel Datwyler <tyreld@linux.ibm.com>
[mpe: Reformat change log and add mention of possible stack corruption]
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210315214821.452959-1-tyreld@linux.ibm.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmemcpy(drc_name, buf, nbytes);', '\tif (!end)', '\t\tend = &drc_name[nbytes];', "\t*end = '\\0';"], 'added_lines': ['\tstrscpy(drc_name, buf, nbytes + 1);', '\tif (end)', "\t\t*end = '\\0';"]}
description: In drivers/pci/hotplug/rpadlpar_sysfs.c in the Linux kernel through 5.11.8, the RPA PCI Hotplug driver has a user-tolerable buffer overflow when writing a new device name to the driver from userspace, allowing userspace to write data to the kernel stack frame directly. This occurs because add_slot_store and remove_slot_store mishandle drc_name '\0' termination, aka CID-cc7a0bb058b8.

code_evidence: Line 8 only rejects nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN, so nbytes up to MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1 passes. Line 10 memcpy copies nbytes bytes into the uninitialized stack buffer drc_name without adding a NUL terminator. Line 11 strchr scans drc_name past the copied bytes into uninitialized stack data; if a '\n' is found there, lines 12-14 set *end='\0' at a location beyond the intended nbytes region, writing outside the logical string and potentially corrupting the stack.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the function performs a buffer copy (memcpy) of a user-supplied length into a fixed-size stack buffer without ensuring the input is bounded/terminated for the subsequent string operations, enabling out-of-bounds writes. The strchr-based fix-up is a consequence of the unchecked copy rather than a distinct weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism:
Root cause: memcpy copies a user-controlled length without NUL-terminating the destination, and the subsequent strchr/terminator fix-up assumes a '
' or nbytes boundary exists within initialized data. Trigger: a userspace write to the remove_slot sysfs attribute whose buffer lacks a NUL and where uninitialized stack bytes past nbytes contain '
'. Consequence: the '
' is overwritten with NUL, corrupting stack data and producing a garbage drc_name; the missing terminator also lets dlpar_remove_slot read past the copied data.

description: Use-after-free vulnerability in the disk_seqf_stop function in block/genhd.c in the Linux kernel before 4.7.1 allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging the execution of a certain stop operation even if the corresponding start operation had failed.

code_evidence: disk_seqf_stop loads seqf->private into iter, and when iter is non-NULL calls class_dev_iter_exit(iter) and kfree(iter). The function never clears seqf->private afterward, so the struct seq_file retains a dangling pointer to the freed iterator that persists beyond this stop call.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees an object while leaving a reference (seqf->private) that is later used, exactly matching CWE-416 use-after-free. It is not merely a double-free or NULL dereference: the flaw is continued use of freed memory via a stale pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: seqf->private is freed but not reset, leaving a stale pointer. Trigger: when start fails to allocate a new iterator, stop is still invoked with the old dangling pointer, which class_dev_iter_exit then dereferences. Consequence: use-after-free read/exit on freed memory, as reported by KASAN in klist_iter_exit, allowing crash or memory corruption.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    pixels=(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory(max_packets,', '      bytes_per_pixel*sizeof(*pixels));'], 'added_lines': ['    pixels=(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory(MagickMax(number_pixels,', '      max_packets),bytes_per_pixel*sizeof(*pixels));']}
description: The ReadVIFFImage function in coders/viff.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault) via a crafted VIFF file.

code_evidence: max_packets is derived from number_pixels*number_data_bands (non-bit) or from image dimensions (bit); pixels is allocated with AcquireQuantumMemory(max_packets, bytes_per_pixel).
The min/max scan initializes value from pixels[0] and iterates i < max_packets, indexing pixels[i] as short/int/float/double/byte according to data_storage_type.
The later conversion loop also iterates i < max_packets reading pixels[i] with the same type-cast indexing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the typed loops read pixels[i] past the allocated buffer end, an out-of-bounds read. This is not a write overflow (CWE-787) because the unsafe operation is a read used for min/max and pixel conversion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocation is sized in units of max_packets elements of bytes_per_pixel, but the read loops index pixels as an array of bytes_per_pixel-sized elements for i in [0,max_packets). When bytes_per_pixel is greater than 1 (e.g., 2/4/8-byte storage types), the typed reads access up to max_packets*bytes_per_pixel bytes, which matches the allocation only if the allocation count equals max_packets; the pre-patch allocation used max_packets as the count, so typed indexing beyond the first byte range reads out of bounds when the blob supplies fewer elements. The fix allocates MagickMax(number_pixels,max_packets) elements, indicating the buffer could be too small relative to the read extent.

description: In FreeRDP after 1.0 and before 2.0.0, there is an out-of-bound read in in update_read_bitmap_data that allows client memory to be read to an image buffer. The result displayed on screen as colour.

Trigger: a crafted bitmap update with BITMAP_COMPRESSION set, NO_BITMAP_COMPRESSION_HDR clear, and a stream ending before these fields. commit_msg:
net: rose: fix UAF bugs caused by timer handler

There are UAF bugs in rose_heartbeat_expiry(), rose_timer_expiry()
and rose_idletimer_expiry(). The root cause is that del_timer()
could not stop the timer handler that is running and the refcount
of sock is not managed properly.

One of the UAF bugs is shown below:

    (thread 1)          |        (thread 2)
                        |  rose_bind
                        |  rose_connect
                        |    rose_start_heartbeat
rose_release            |    (wait a time)
  case ROSE_STATE_0     |
  rose_destroy_socket   |  rose_heartbeat_expiry
    rose_stop_heartbeat |
    sock_put(sk)        |    ...
  sock_put(sk) // FREE  |
                        |    bh_lock_sock(sk) // USE

The sock is deallocated by sock_put() in rose_release() and
then used by bh_lock_sock() in rose_heartbeat_expiry().

Although rose_destroy_socket() calls rose_stop_heartbeat(),
it could not stop the timer that is running.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tdel_timer(&rose_sk(sk)->timer);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsk_stop_timer(sk, &rose_sk(sk)->timer);']}
description: There are use-after-free vulnerabilities caused by timer handler in net/rose/rose_timer.c of linux that allow attackers to crash linux kernel without any privileges.

code_evidence: rose_stop_timer() only calls del_timer() on the socket's timer and returns without any synchronization or refcount handling. del_timer() does not wait for or cancel a timer handler already executing on another CPU; it only removes a pending timer. The function takes sk as its argument and directly dereferences rose_sk(sk)->timer without acquiring a reference or verifying the socket is still alive.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the freed sock is subsequently referenced by the timer handler after its lifetime ended; the missing safe-stop/refcount is the cause, not the weakness itself. This is a use-after-free rather than a double-free, since the memory is reused after deallocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: stopping the timer via del_timer() cannot prevent an already-running rose_timer_expiry handler from concurrently using the same sk. Trigger: a concurrent release path frees the sock while the timer handler executes. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the sock memory, leading to crash or memory corruption.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    const int step = img.step;', '    int bufferstep;'], 'added_lines': ['    const size_t step = img.step;', '    size_t bufferstep;']}
description: OpenCV (Open Source Computer Vision Library) 3.3 has an out-of-bounds write error in the function FillColorRow1 in utils.cpp when reading an image file by using cv::imread. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-12597.

code_evidence: img.step (a size_t stride) is narrowed into an int step and then into int bufferstep; the heap buffers allocated at 41/47 use width*channels elements while the per-line loop at 75 writes width*channels entries per row.

The write loops cast buffer to unsigned*/half* and index buf[i] for i in [0,width*channels), so any truncation of step or bufferstep to int, or mismatch between allocated size and write count, results in writes past the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly performs buffer writes indexed by width*channels with a truncated int stride, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. A related integer-overflow label would describe the cause, but the supported consequence here is memory written past the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stride img.step and bufferstep are stored in int, so large image strides overflow/truncate. Trigger: an image whose step exceeds INT_MAX (or large width*channels). Consequence: the FrameBuffer/Slice stride is wrong and per-line writes at buf[i] advance past the allocated buffer, corrupting memory (out-of-bounds write).

commit_msg:
- Modified TileManager.cc to verify that malloc() has correctly allocated memory.
- Updated numerical types to std::size_t in RawTile.h, TileManager.cc, KakaduImage.cc, OpenJPEG.cc and Transforms.cc when allocating memory via new to avoid integer overflow - fixes remaining problems identified in https://github.com/ruven/iipsrv/issues/223.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int len = tw * th * ttt->channels * (ttt->bpc/8);'], 'added_lines': ['  unsigned int len = tw * th * ttt->channels * (ttt->bpc/8);', '', '  // Check whether we have successfully allocated memory via malloc', '  if( buffer == NULL ){', '    std::bad_alloc e;', '    throw e;', '  }']}
description: IIPImage High Resolution Streaming Image Server prior to commit 882925b295a80ec992063deffc2a3b0d803c3195 is affected by an integer overflow in iipsrv.fcgi through malformed HTTP query parameters.

code_evidence: Line 9 computes the allocation length as a signed int product of tw, th, ttt->channels and ttt->bpc/8; the result is passed directly to malloc at line 10 and reused as the memcpy length at line 11.
Line 20 recomputes the same product and stores it into ttt->dataLength, so any wrapped value propagates as the buffer's recorded length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root defect is an unchecked integer multiplication whose result determines an allocation size and a copy length, matching CWE-190. The buffer overflow is a downstream consequence of the wraparound, not the primary weakness, so CWE-190 rather than an out-of-bounds write label is the correct mapping.

evidence_lines.code:
len = ttt->width * ttt->height * ttt->channels * (ttt->bpc/8);
ttt->dataLength = len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The multiplication at line 9 is performed in signed int arithmetic without an upper-bound check on the operands, so a large tile dimension, channel count or byte depth can wrap to a small or negative value. The wrapped value is then used as the malloc size and memcpy length, so the copy at line 11 can write past the undersized buffer, and the wrapped length is also persisted into ttt->dataLength at line 21.

description: A flaw was found in the opj2_decompress program in openjpeg2 2.4.0 in the way it handles an input directory with a large number of files. When it fails to allocate a buffer to store the filenames of the input directory, it calls free() on an uninitialized pointer, leading to a segmentation fault and a denial of service.

If the filename_buf malloc fails, failed is set and control jumps to fin without ever assigning dirptr->filename.
At fin, the dirptr block unconditionally reads dirptr->filename to decide whether to free it; the pointer was never explicitly initialized by this code path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-665 fits because the resource (pointer members of the allocated dircnt_t) is not properly initialized before use in the error path, leading to unexpected state when freed. This is improper initialization of a resource, distinct from a plain unbounded write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cleanup path at fin dereferences dirptr->filename and filename_buf assuming they were initialized. Trigger: a large input directory makes the filename_buf malloc fail, causing a goto fin before those members are set. The cleanup then reads an indeterminate pointer and may call free() on it, producing a crash/denial of service.

commit_msg:
On some architectures (like ARM64), it can support CONT-PTE/PMD size
hugetlb, which means it can support not only PMD/PUD size hugetlb (2M and
1G), but also CONT-PTE/PMD size(64K and 32M) if a 4K page size specified.

So when looking up a CONT-PTE size hugetlb page by follow_page(), it will
use pte_offset_map_lock() to get the pte entry lock for the CONT-PTE size
hugetlb in follow_page_pte().  However this pte entry lock is incorrect
for the CONT-PTE size hugetlb, since we should use huge_pte_lock() to get
the correct lock, which is mm->page_table_lock.

That means the pte entry of the CONT-PTE size hugetlb under current pte
lock is unstable in follow_page_pte(), we can continue to migrate or
poison the pte entry of the CONT-PTE size hugetlb, which can cause some
potential race issues, even though they are under the 'pte lock'.

For example, suppose thread A is trying to look up a CONT-PTE size hugetlb
page by move_pages() syscall under the lock, however antoher thread B can
migrate the CONT-PTE hugetlb page at the same time, which will cause
thread A to get an incorrect page, if thread A also wants to do page
migration, then data inconsistency error occurs.

Moreover we have the same issue for CONT-PMD size hugetlb in
follow_huge_pmd().

To fix above issues, rename the follow_huge_pmd() as follow_huge_pmd_pte()
to handle PMD and PTE level size hugetlb, which uses huge_pte_lock() to
get the correct pte entry lock to make the pte entry stable.

Mike said:

Support for CONT_PMD/_PTE was added with bb9dd3df8ee9 ("arm64: hugetlb:
refactor find_num_contig()").  Patch series "Support for contiguous pte
hugepages", v4.  However, I do not believe these code paths were
executed until migration support was added with 5480280d3f2d ("arm64/mm:
enable HugeTLB migration for contiguous bit HugeTLB pages") I would go
with 5480280d3f2d for the Fixes: targe.

Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/635f43bdd85ac2615a58405da82b4d33c6e5eb05.1662017562.git.baolin.wang@linux.alibaba.com
Fixes: 5480280d3f2d ("arm64/mm: enable HugeTLB migration for contiguous bit HugeTLB pages")
Signed-off-by: Baolin Wang <baolin.wang@linux.alibaba.com>
Suggested-by: Mike Kravetz <mike.kravetz@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Kravetz <mike.kravetz@oracle.com>
Cc: David Hildenbrand <david@redhat.com>
Cc: Muchun Song <songmuchun@bytedance.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tpage = follow_huge_pmd(mm, address, pmd, flags);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tpage = follow_huge_pmd_pte(vma, address, flags);']}
description: A vulnerability was found in Linux Kernel. It has been declared as problematic. Affected by this vulnerability is the function follow_page_pte of the file mm/gup.c of the component BPF. The manipulation leads to race condition. The attack can be launched remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier VDB-211921 was assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: For a huge PMD mapping in a hugetlb VMA, the code calls follow_huge_pmd(mm, address, pmd, flags) and returns the resulting page without ever acquiring huge_pte_lock() (mm->page_table_lock). The only synchronization used elsewhere in this function is pmd_lock(), which is not the correct lock for CONT-PTE/CONT-PMD hugetlb entries on architectures such as arm64.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the shared hugetlb page-table entry is accessed without the exclusive lock required for that resource, allowing an interfering concurrent sequence to modify it during the lookup. The defect is improper synchronization of a shared resource, not a missing bounds check or memory-corruption primitive.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The hugetlb folio is read and returned under no page-table lock that excludes huge-page migration or poisoning. A concurrent thread can migrate or poison the same CONT-PTE/CONT-PMD hugetlb entry while follow_pmd_mask() is looking it up, so the returned page can be stale or inconsistent, leading to data inconsistency or a crash.

md_is_named_entity_contents: Fix buffer overflow.

Fixes #38.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if(off <= max_end  &&  ISALPHA_(text[off]))'], 'added_lines': ['    if(off < max_end  &&  ISALPHA_(text[off]))']}
description: md4c 0.2.5 has a heap-based buffer over-read because md_is_named_entity_contents has an off-by-one error.

code_evidence: Line 5 guards the first character check with `off <= max_end`, then line 6 reads `text[off]` via `ISALPHA_(text[off])`. When `off == max_end`, the index is exactly at/one past the valid end, so the read occurs outside the intended buffer bounds; the following lines only increment or return and do not re-validate the index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a memory read indexed at `max_end`, beyond the intended buffer boundary, which is the defining behavior of CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). The defect is a read overrun, not a write, so it is distinct from CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the off-by-one boundary check using `<=` instead of `<` before dereferencing `text[off]`. Trigger: a call where `beg == max_end` (or `max_end` equals the last valid index limit), causing `ISALPHA_` to read one element past the buffer; supported consequence is an out-of-bounds heap read, potentially disclosing memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
libsepol/cil: Destroy classperm list when resetting map perms

Map perms share the same struct as regular perms, but only the
map perms use the classperms field. This field is a pointer to a
list of classperms that is created and added to when resolving
classmapping rules, so the map permission doesn't own any of the
data in the list and this list should be destroyed when the AST is
reset.

When resetting a perm, destroy the classperms list without destroying
the data in the list.

Signed-off-by: James Carter <jwcart2@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcil_reset_classperms_list(perm->classperms);'], 'added_lines': ['\tcil_list_destroy(&perm->classperms, CIL_FALSE);']}
description: The CIL compiler in SELinux 3.2 has a use-after-free in __cil_verify_classperms (called from __verify_map_perm_classperms and hashtab_map).

code_evidence: cil_reset_perm calls cil_reset_classperms_list(perm->classperms), which walks and frees the classperm list nodes referenced by perm->classperms but leaves the dangling pointer in the perm struct; the patch replaces this with cil_list_destroy(&perm->classperms, CIL_FALSE) so the list is destroyed and the pointer cleared.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly causes the classperm list to be freed without invalidating the stored pointer, and subsequent use of perm->classperms dereferences freed memory. This matches CWE-416 (use after free). The patch's cil_list_destroy confirms the missing pointer-clearing step, distinguishing it from a simple double-free or memory leak.

evidence_lines.code: cil_reset_classperms_list(perm->classperms);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: resetting a perm frees the classperm list nodes while perm->classperms continues to point at freed memory. Trigger: a later verification pass (e.g., __cil_verify_classperms via __verify_map_perm_classperms) dereferences the stale list. Supported consequence: use-after-free, permitting reads or writes through the dangling pointer, potentially crashing or corrupting memory.

description: In libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c in Pillow before 7.1.0, there are multiple out-of-bounds reads via a crafted JP2 file.

code_evidence: tile_info.data_size comes from opj_read_tile_header (line 88) on attacker-controlled JP2 data. Line 125 compares tile_bytes > data_size and line 126 raises data_size to tile_bytes, so the buffer is allocated to tile_bytes (lines 128-136). opj_decode_tile_data then writes into state->buffer using tile_info.data_size (lines 138-142), and unpack reads/writes that buffer (line 147). The comment notes data_size can be less than numcomps*w*h, so the decode handler may read past what was actually written.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a read past the end of the decoded buffer during unpack, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not a write overflow because the buffer is sized to the larger tile_bytes; the defect is reading uninitialized/out-of-bounds data.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code trusts the container-reported data_size and only enlarges it, never verifying that the decoded tile actually fills tile_bytes. Trigger: a crafted JP2 whose tile data_size is smaller than numcomps*w*h; the decoder fills only part of the buffer, and unpack reads beyond the initialized region. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of heap memory, potentially leaking data or crashing.

commit_msg:
Check memory allocation in ISoundTriggerHwService

Add memory allocation check in ISoundTriggerHwService::listModules().

Bug: 19385640.
Change-Id: Iaf74b6f154c3437e1bfc9da78b773d64b16a7604
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            if (numModulesReq > MAX_ITEMS_PER_LIST) {', '                numModulesReq = MAX_ITEMS_PER_LIST;', '            }', '            if (modules == NULL) {', '                reply->writeInt32(NO_MEMORY);', '                reply->writeInt32(0);', '                return NO_ERROR;', '            }']}
description: Integer overflow in soundtrigger/ISoundTriggerHwService.cpp in Android allows attacks to cause a denial of service via unspecified vectors.

code_evidence: Line 7 reads an attacker-controlled 32-bit module count from the Parcel and stores it in numModulesReq without any upper bound.
Lines 9-11 pass numModulesReq as the calloc element count; the allocation size is computed as numModulesReq * sizeof(struct sound_trigger_module_descriptor), which can wrap for large counts.
Line 12 calls listModules with the unvalidated buffer and count, so a wrapped allocation yields a buffer smaller than the requested module count.
Lines 20-21 write numModulesReq * sizeof(...) bytes from modules, repeating the size multiplication on the same untrusted count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because an untrusted integer count feeds a multiplication used as an allocation and copy size, and wraparound of that product is the direct cause of the undersized buffer. This is distinct from a plain NULL-check issue: the missing constraint is the arithmetic bound on the size computation.

evidence_lines.code: unsigned int numModulesReq = data.readInt32();
status_t status = listModules(modules, &numModules);

reply->write(modules,
numModulesReq * sizeof(struct sound_trigger_module_descriptor));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the requested module count from the Parcel is used directly in the size multiplication for calloc and for the reply write with no overflow check. Trigger: a large numModulesReq makes the product wrap, producing an undersized buffer. Supported consequence: listModules or the reply write accesses beyond the small allocation, causing a crash or memory corruption (DoS).

commit_msg:
Improve behaviour on fatal errors

If we didn't walk the whole chain, then there may be any kind of errors in the
part of the chain we didn't check, so setting all flags looks like the safe
thing to do.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        return( MBEDTLS_ERR_X509_BAD_INPUT_DATA );', '', '    *flags = 0;', '            return( ret );', '                return( ret );', '                return( ret );'], 'added_lines': ['    *flags = 0;', '', '    {', '        ret = MBEDTLS_ERR_X509_BAD_INPUT_DATA;', '        goto exit;', '    }', '            goto exit;', '                goto exit;', '                goto exit;', '    }', '', 'exit:', '    if( ret != 0 )', '    {', '        *flags = (uint32_t) -1;', '        return( ret );']}
description: ARM mbed TLS before 1.3.21 and 2.x before 2.1.9, if optional authentication is configured, allows remote attackers to bypass peer authentication via an X.509 certificate chain with many intermediates. NOTE: although mbed TLS was formerly known as PolarSSL, the releases shipped with the PolarSSL name are not affected.

code_evidence: The function searches trust_ca for a parent and, if found, calls x509_crt_verify_top; on a nonzero ret it returns immediately, leaving *flags as whatever partial value verification had set.

When no trusted parent is found, it walks crt->next for a chain parent and calls x509_crt_verify_child or x509_crt_verify_top; again a nonzero ret returns early without marking the remaining chain as unverified.
Only when *flags is nonzero does it return MBEDTLS_ERR_X509_CERT_VERIFY_FAILED; otherwise it returns 0, so an early error return with *flags still 0 is treated as success.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The consequence is that a claimed certificate identity is accepted without successful proof of the chain, which is improper authentication (CWE-287). It is not merely a certificate-validation bug (CWE-295) because the observable effect is bypass of peer authentication through an inconsistent success/failure result.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on an error from the top/child verification of a chain with many intermediates, the function returns the error code directly instead of setting *flags to a failure value. A caller that inspects *flags (the documented verification result) sees zero and accepts the certificate, so peer authentication is bypassed when the chain is not fully walked.

commit_msg:
Fix encoding bug in i2c_ASN1_INTEGER

Fix bug where i2c_ASN1_INTEGER mishandles zero if it is marked as
negative.

Thanks to Huzaifa Sidhpurwala <huzaifas@redhat.com> and
Hanno Böck <hanno@hboeck.de> for reporting this issue.

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
(cherry picked from commit a0eed48d37a4b7beea0c966caf09ad46f4a92a44)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        while (!*n) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (ret == 1 && i == 0)', '            neg = 0;', '        while (!*n && i > 1) {']}
description: The ASN.1 implementation in OpenSSL before 1.0.1o and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2c allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (buffer underflow and memory corruption) via an ANY field in crafted serialized data, aka the "negative zero" issue.

code_evidence: neg is taken from a->type and the loop at [41-48] copies a negative INTEGER by walking n backward from a->data + a->length - 1, writing to p and decrementing n, p and i for each zero byte encountered.

When the negative value is a single zero byte (a->length == 1, a->data[0] == 0), the loop at [44] enters with i == 1; it writes *(p--) and decrements n and i, then continues testing *n on the byte before the buffer, so the loop does not stop at the start of a->data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads and writes memory locations before the start of a->data, i.e. outside the intended buffer boundary, which is the out-of-bounds memory operation described by CWE-119. The defect is a missing length bound in the loop, not a type or logic error alone.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the zero-skipping loop in the negative branch lacks a bound tied to the remaining length, so for a negative INTEGER encoding of zero it reads and writes past the start of the source buffer. Trigger: an ANY field carrying a negative-zero INTEGER (length 1, value 0) passed to i2c_ASN1_INTEGER. Consequence: buffer underflow, out-of-bounds reads/writes and memory corruption, potentially code execution or DoS.

PJSIP versions 2.12 and prior do not parse incoming RTCP feedback RPSI (Reference Picture Selection Indication) packet, but any app that directly uses pjmedia_rtcp_fb_parse_rpsi() will be affected. code_evidence: The function validates only that length covers a pjmedia_rtcp_common header, then reads hdr->length from the packet and computes cnt from it.
The length check is derived from the attacker-controlled 16-bit length field (cnt), but the count used for the loop is bounded by the caller's *nack_cnt, not by the validated packet size.

The loop copies 4 bytes per iteration from p at offset sizeof(*hdr)+i*4; the check at lines 16-17 validates (cnt+3)*4 but the loop may iterate up to *nack_cnt, which can exceed cnt when the caller passes a larger nack_cnt.

Trigger: a caller passing nack_cnt larger than the validated packet body, or a malformed length. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of pj_memcpy into nack[] and possible out-of-bounds write into the caller's nack array.

commit_msg:
sched/fair: Fix infinite loop in update_blocked_averages() by reverting a9e7f6544b9c

Zhipeng Xie, Xie XiuQi and Sargun Dhillon reported lockups in the
scheduler under high loads, starting at around the v4.18 time frame,
and Zhipeng Xie tracked it down to bugs in the rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
manipulation.

Do a (manual) revert of:

  a9e7f6544b9c ("sched/fair: Fix O(nr_cgroups) in load balance path")

It turns out that the list_del_leaf_cfs_rq() introduced by this commit
is a surprising property that was not considered in followup commits
such as:

  9c2791f936ef ("sched/fair: Fix hierarchical order in rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list")

As Vincent Guittot explains:

 "I think that there is a bigger problem with commit a9e7f6544b9c and
  cfs_rq throttling:

  Let take the example of the following topology TG2 --> TG1 --> root:

   1) The 1st time a task is enqueued, we will add TG2 cfs_rq then TG1
      cfs_rq to leaf_cfs_rq_list and we are sure to do the whole branch in
      one path because it has never been used and can't be throttled so
      tmp_alone_branch will point to leaf_cfs_rq_list at the end.

   2) Then TG1 is throttled

   3) and we add TG3 as a new child of TG1.

   4) The 1st enqueue of a task on TG3 will add TG3 cfs_rq just before TG1
      cfs_rq and tmp_alone_branch will stay  on rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.

  With commit a9e7f6544b9c, we can del a cfs_rq from rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.
  So if the load of TG1 cfs_rq becomes NULL before step 2) above, TG1
  cfs_rq is removed from the list.
  Then at step 4), TG3 cfs_rq is added at the beginning of rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
  but tmp_alone_branch still points to TG3 cfs_rq because its throttled
  parent can't be enqueued when the lock is released.
  tmp_alone_branch doesn't point to rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list whereas it should.

  So if TG3 cfs_rq is removed or destroyed before tmp_alone_branch
  points on another TG cfs_rq, the next TG cfs_rq that will be added,
  will be linked outside rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list - which is bad.

  In addition, we can break the ordering of the cfs_rq in
  rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list but this ordering is used to update and
  propagate the update from leaf down to root."

Instead of trying to work through all these cases and trying to reproduce
the very high loads that produced the lockup to begin with, simplify
the code temporarily by reverting a9e7f6544b9c - which change was clearly
not thought through completely.

This (hopefully) gives us a kernel that doesn't lock up so people
can continue to enjoy their holidays without worrying about regressions. ;-)

description: In the Linux kernel before 4.20.2, kernel/sched/fair.c mishandles leaf cfs_rq's, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop in update_blocked_averages) or possibly have unspecified other impact by inducing a high load.

code_evidence: The loop uses for_each_leaf_cfs_rq_safe with the saved iterator pos (line 4), and inside the body it calls list_del_leaf_cfs_rq(cfs_rq) when cfs_rq_is_decayed(cfs_rq) is true (lines 19-20), unlinking the current element from rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list during iteration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's loop over leaf cfs_rq entries can fail to reach its exit condition because the underlying list is mutated/corrupted by list_del_leaf_cfs_rq, matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. This is an infinite-iteration availability issue, not merely a memory-safety bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: deleting the current leaf cfs_rq from rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list during traversal, combined with throttled parents preventing re-addition and tmp_alone_branch no longer pointing at the list head, desynchronizes the list and iterator bookkeeping. Under high load with cgroup throttling, list_add_leaf_cfs_rq can link nodes outside the list, so the traversal never reaches its terminal condition, spinning in update_blocked_averages and consuming CPU (DoS).

commit_msg:
The ptrace PEEKUSR/POKEUSR (aka PEEKUSER/POKEUSER) API allows a process
to read/write registers of another process.

To get/set a register, the API takes an index into an imaginary address
space called the "USER area", where the registers of the process are
laid out in some fashion.

The kernel then maps that index to a particular register in its own data
structures and gets/sets the value.

The API only allows a single machine-word to be read/written at a time.
So 4 bytes on 32-bit kernels and 8 bytes on 64-bit kernels.

The way floating point registers (FPRs) are addressed is somewhat
complicated, because double precision float values are 64-bit even on
32-bit CPUs. That means on 32-bit kernels each FPR occupies two
word-sized locations in the USER area. On 64-bit kernels each FPR
occupies one word-sized location in the USER area.

Internally the kernel stores the FPRs in an array of u64s, or if VSX is
enabled, an array of pairs of u64s where one half of each pair stores
the FPR. Which half of the pair stores the FPR depends on the kernel's
endianness.

To handle the different layouts of the FPRs depending on VSX/no-VSX and
big/little endian, the TS_FPR() macro was introduced.

Unfortunately the TS_FPR() macro does not take into account the fact
that the addressing of each FPR differs between 32-bit and 64-bit
kernels. It just takes the index into the "USER area" passed from
userspace and indexes into the fp_state.fpr array.

On 32-bit there are 64 indexes that address FPRs, but only 32 entries in
the fp_state.fpr array, meaning the user can read/write 256 bytes past
the end of the array. Because the fp_state sits in the middle of the
thread_struct there are various fields than can be overwritten,
including some pointers. As such it may be exploitable.

It has also been observed to cause systems to hang or otherwise
misbehave when using gdbserver, and is probably the root cause of this
report which could not be easily reproduced:
  https://lore.kernel.org/linuxppc-dev/dc38afe9-6b78-f3f5-666b-986939e40fc6@keymile.com/

Rather than trying to make the TS_FPR() macro even more complicated to
fix the bug, or add more macros, instead add a special-case for 32-bit
kernels. This is more obvious and hopefully avoids a similar bug
happening again in future.

Note that because 32-bit kernels never have VSX enabled the code doesn't
need to consider TS_FPRWIDTH/OFFSET at all. Add a BUILD_BUG_ON() to
ensure that 32-bit && VSX is never enabled.

Fixes: 87fec0514f61 ("powerpc: PTRACE_PEEKUSR/PTRACE_POKEUSER of FPR registers in little endian builds")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v3.13+
Reported-by: Ariel Miculas <ariel.miculas@belden.com>
Tested-by: Christophe Leroy <christophe.leroy@csgroup.eu>
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220609133245.573565-1-mpe@ellerman.id.au
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t// ptrace_get/put_fpr() rely on PPC32 and VSX being incompatible', '\tBUILD_BUG_ON(IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_PPC32) && IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_VSX));']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.18.3 on powerpc 32-bit platforms. There is a buffer overflow in ptrace PEEKUSER and POKEUSER (aka PEEKUSR and POKEUSR) when accessing floating point registers.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The provided function contains only compile-time BUILD_BUG_ON and CHECK_REG assertions verifying struct layout; it performs no buffer copy or input-dependent operation, so it cannot directly support CWE-120.

Fix integer overflow in BMP decoder by making the checks in DecodeBmp
more stringent.  Add fuzzer to improve the robustness of the decoder
in the future.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    const int last_pixel_offset =', '        header_size + (abs(height) - 1) * row_size + (width - 1) * channels_;', '    const int expected_file_size = last_pixel_offset + channels_;', '                     0, TensorShape({abs(height), width, channels_}), &output));', '           abs(height), channels_, top_down);'], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(context, width > 0 && header_size >= 0,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("Width must be positive"));', '    OP_REQUIRES(context, header_size >= 0,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("header size must be nonnegative"));', '', '    // The real requirement is < 2^31 minus some headers and channel data,', "    // so rounding down to something that's still ridiculously big.", '    OP_REQUIRES(', '        context,', '        (static_cast<int64>(width) * std::abs(static_cast<int64>(height))) <', '            static_cast<int64>(std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::max() / 8),', '        errors::InvalidArgument(', '            "Total possible pixel bytes must be less than 2^30"));', '', '    const int32 abs_height = abs(height);', '', '    const int64 last_pixel_offset = static_cast<int64>(header_size) +', '                                    (abs_height - 1) * row_size +', '                                    (width - 1) * channels_;', '    const int64 expected_file_size = last_pixel_offset + channels_;', '                     0, TensorShape({abs_height, width, channels_}), &output));', '           abs_height, channels_, top_down);']}
description: TensorFlow before 1.7.0 has an integer overflow that causes an out-of-bounds read, possibly causing disclosure of the contents of process memory. This occurs in the DecodeBmp feature of the BMP decoder in core/kernels/decode_bmp_op.cc.

code_evidence: row_size, last_pixel_offset and expected_file_size are computed with 32-bit int arithmetic from attacker-controlled width, height and header_size read from the BMP header (lines 13-21).
The bound check only compares expected_file_size <= input.size(); an overflowing computation can wrap to a small or negative value and pass.
bmp_pixels is offset by header_size and Decode reads width*abs(height)*channels_ bytes, so wrapped bounds let it read past the input buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unchecked size arithmetic lets Decode access pixels beyond the validated input buffer, directly matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. Integer overflow is the enabling cause, but the supported consequence is reading memory outside the intended buffer.

errors::InvalidArgument("Incomplete bmp content, requires at least ",

Trigger: a crafted BMP with large dimensions makes the size check accept a truncated buffer. Consequence: Decode reads past the input, disclosing process memory (out-of-bounds read).

commit_msg:
dm: Reset virtio device before release

With virtio polling mode enabled, a timer is running in the virtio
backend service. And the timer will also be triggered if its frondend
driver didn't do the device reset in shutdown. A freed virtio device
will be accessed in the polling timer handler.

Do the virtio reset() callback specifically to clear the polling timer
before the free.

Tracked-On: #6147
Signed-off-by: Shuo A Liu <shuo.a.liu@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Yonghua Huang <yonghua.huang@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tvirtio_reset_dev(&net->base);']}
description: The polling timer handler in ACRN before 2.5 has a use-after-free for a freed virtio device, related to devicemodel/hw/pci/virtio/*.c.

code_evidence: virtio_net_teardown frees the virtio_net object with free(net) without first resetting the virtio device; no virtio_reset_dev call appears before the release.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees memory that remains reachable by the polling timer's device pointer, so subsequent timer access reads or writes freed memory, matching CWE-416. This is a lifetime/ordering defect rather than a mere null-pointer or double-free issue.

evidence_lines.code: free(net);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The teardown path releases the net object while the virtio backend polling timer may still be active. That timer handler can later dereference the device embedded in the freed net allocation, producing a use-after-free with possible memory corruption or crash; the missing reset before free is the root cause, and the timer firing after release is the trigger.

net/mlx5: fix memory leak in mlx5_fw_fatal_reporter_dump

In mlx5_fw_fatal_reporter_dump if mlx5_crdump_collect fails the
allocated memory for cr_data must be released otherwise there will be
memory leak. To fix this, this commit changes the return instruction
into goto error handling.

description: A memory leak in the mlx5_fw_fatal_reporter_dump() function in drivers/net/ethernet/mellanox/mlx5/core/health.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering mlx5_crdump_collect() failures, aka CID-c7ed6d0183d5.

Add error logging on invalid cmap - DO NOT MERGE

This patch logs instances of fonts with invalid cmap tables.

description: The Minikin library in Android 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-04-01 does not properly consider negative size values in font data, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory corruption and reboot loop) via a crafted font, aka internal bug 26413177.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function receives untrusted font data and fails to validate derived size and range properties before using them. The missing checks are input-validation failures, not merely a downstream memory-safety symptom.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is insufficient validation of attacker-controlled font metadata: segCount-derived arithmetic in the size check can overflow, and segment end values are not constrained against the buffer or against overflow. A crafted cmap can therefore drive addRange with invalid ranges, leading to memory corruption and a crash/reboot loop rather than a clean rejection.

commit_msg:
x86: limit linear page table use to a single level

That's the only way that they're meant to be used. Without such a
restriction arbitrarily long chains of same-level page tables can be
built, tearing down of which may then cause arbitrarily deep recursion,
causing a stack overflow. To facilitate this restriction, a counter is
being introduced to track both the number of same-level entries in a
page table as well as the number of uses of a page table in another
same-level one (counting into positive and negative direction
respectively, utilizing the fact that both counts can't be non-zero at
the same time).

Note that the added accounting introduces a restriction on the number
of times a page can be used in other same-level page tables - more than
32k of such uses are no longer possible.

Note also that some put_page_and_type[_preemptible]() calls are
replaced with open-coded equivalents.  This seemed preferrable to
adding "parent_table" to the matrix of functions.

Note further that cross-domain same-level page table references are no
longer permitted (they probably never should have been).

This is XSA-240.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                    current->arch.old_guest_ptpg = NULL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service (unbounded recursion, stack consumption, and hypervisor crash) or possibly gain privileges via crafted page-table stacking.

code_evidence: On a failed get_page_from_l4e() call (rc<0), the function records the page in current->arch.old_guest_table for later teardown; when one is already pending it only increments page->nr_validated_ptes. The patch adds a reset of current->arch.old_guest_ptpg to NULL alongside this bookkeeping, tying the tracked old table to a single level.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is failure to bound a consumable resource (stack/recursion depth and table chaining) driven by guest-controlled input, matching CWE-400's uncontrolled resource consumption. It is not a simple memory-safety bug; the missing limit on stacking is the resource-control defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the validation/teardown bookkeeping for L4 tables does not constrain same-level page-table stacking, so a PV guest can build arbitrarily long chains of same-level tables. Trigger: crafted page-table entries cause nested same-level references; teardown then recurses without bound. Supported consequence: unbounded recursion and stack consumption, crashing the hypervisor (DoS).

commit_msg:
VMA with VM_GROWSDOWN or VM_GROWSUP flag set can change their size under
mmap_read_lock().  It can lead to race with __do_munmap():

	Thread A			Thread B
__do_munmap()
  detach_vmas_to_be_unmapped()
  mmap_write_downgrade()
				expand_downwards()
				  vma->vm_start = address;
				  // The VMA now overlaps with
				  // VMAs detached by the Thread A
				// page fault populates expanded part
				// of the VMA
  unmap_region()
    // Zaps pagetables partly
    // populated by Thread B

Similar race exists for expand_upwards().

The fix is to avoid downgrading mmap_lock in __do_munmap() if detached
VMAs are next to VM_GROWSDOWN or VM_GROWSUP VMA.

[akpm@linux-foundation.org: s/mmap_sem/mmap_lock/ in comment]

Fixes: dd2283f2605e ("mm: mmap: zap pages with read mmap_sem in munmap")
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Kirill A. Shutemov <kirill.shutemov@linux.intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Reviewed-by: Yang Shi <yang.shi@linux.alibaba.com>
Acked-by: Vlastimil Babka <vbabka@suse.cz>
Cc: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: Matthew Wilcox <willy@infradead.org>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>	[4.20+]
Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20200709105309.42495-1-kirill.shutemov@linux.intel.com
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void'], 'added_lines': ['static bool', '', '\t/*', '\t * Do not downgrade mmap_lock if we are next to VM_GROWSDOWN or', '\t * VM_GROWSUP VMA. Such VMAs can change their size under', '\t * down_read(mmap_lock) and collide with the VMA we are about to unmap.', '\t */', '\tif (vma && (vma->vm_flags & VM_GROWSDOWN))', '\t\treturn false;', '\tif (prev && (prev->vm_flags & VM_GROWSUP))', '\t\treturn false;', '\treturn true;']}
description: An issue was discovered in mm/mmap.c in the Linux kernel before 5.7.11. There is a race condition between certain expand functions (expand_downwards and expand_upwards) and page-table free operations from an munmap call, aka CID-246c320a8cfe.

code_evidence: The loop detaches VMAs from the shared mm->mm_rb tree and map_count while holding only the caller's mmap_lock, without any check of neighboring growable VMAs.

After detaching, the function rewires the insertion point and vm_prev/vm_next links and updates gaps; it returns void, so the caller cannot learn that a VM_GROWSDOWN/VM_GROWSUP neighbor exists and may downgrade the lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is part of a concurrent sequence that requires exclusive access to mm VMA structures, but it permits an interfering expand path to modify adjacent VMAs once the lock is downgraded, matching CWE-362's exclusivity/atomicity violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: detach_vmas_to_be_unmapped() tears VMAs out of the shared mm structures without accounting for adjacent growable VMAs that expand under mmap_read_lock(). Trigger: after the caller downgrades mmap_lock, expand_downwards()/expand_upwards() modify vm_start over the detached range while unmap_region() zaps page tables. Supported consequence: concurrent modification of shared VMA state, causing memory/page-table corruption or crash.

commit_msg: X3F property table list fix
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\t\t\t\tfor (i = 0; i < PL->property_table.size; i++) {', '\t\t\t\t\tFREE(PL->property_table.element[i].name_utf8);', '\t\t\t\t\tFREE(PL->property_table.element[i].value_utf8);', '\t\t\t\t}'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in LibRaw 0.18.9. There is an out-of-bounds read affecting the X3F property table list implementation in libraw_x3f.cpp and libraw_cxx.cpp.

code_evidence: The loop iterates i from 0 to PL->property_table.size and dereferences PL->property_table.element[i], freeing element[i].name_utf8 and element[i].value_utf8. The bounds depend on the attacker-influenced property_table.size, and the element pointer/array may be smaller or inconsistent, so indexing can read past the allocated property_table.element buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe operation is an out-of-bounds read of element[i] (and its name_utf8/value_utf8 fields) driven by an unvalidated size. This is a read-past-bounds defect; the patch removes this loop, consistent with eliminating the OOB read rather than a write-based weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cleanup loop trusts property_table.size to bound indexing into property_table.element without validating that the element array actually contains that many entries. When a malformed X3F property list yields an inconsistent size, the loop reads element[i] past the end of the intended buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read (and possibly invalid free) during deletion.

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Handle the Intel-specific MSR_MISC_ENABLE correctly

This MSR doesn't exist on AMD hardware, and switching away from the safe
functions in the common MSR path was an erroneous change.

Partially revert the change.

This is XSA-333.

Fixes: 4fdc932b3cc ("x86/Intel: drop another 32-bit leftover")
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        rdmsrl(reg, temp);'], 'added_lines': ['        if ( rdmsr_safe(reg, temp) )', '            break;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. An x86 PV guest can trigger a host OS crash when handling guest access to MSR_MISC_ENABLE. When a guest accesses certain Model Specific Registers, Xen first reads the value from hardware to use as the basis for auditing the guest access. For the MISC_ENABLE MSR, which is an Intel specific MSR, this MSR read is performed without error handling for a #GP fault, which is the consequence of trying to read this MSR on non-Intel hardware. A buggy or malicious PV guest administrator can crash Xen, resulting in a host Denial of Service. Only x86 systems are vulnerable. ARM systems are not vulnerable. Only Xen versions 4.11 and onwards are vulnerable. 4.10 and earlier are not vulnerable. Only x86 systems that do not implement the MISC_ENABLE MSR (0x1a0) are vulnerable. AMD and Hygon systems do not implement this MSR and are vulnerable. Intel systems do implement this MSR and are not vulnerable. Other manufacturers have not been checked. Only x86 PV guests can exploit the vulnerability. x86 HVM/PVH guests cannot exploit the vulnerability.

code_evidence: In the MSR_IA32_MISC_ENABLE case, the function reads the hardware MSR via rdmsrl(reg, temp) at line 88 with no return value checked and no error path. On hardware that does not implement MSR_MISC_ENABLE (AMD/Hygon), this read raises a #GP fault that is not handled here; the code proceeds directly to compare val against guest_misc_enable(temp) at line 89.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to handle the exceptional #GP condition raised by the MSR read, matching CWE-755's improper handling of exceptional conditions. Unlike a memory-safety flaw, the defect is the missing error check and recovery path for a faulting hardware access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the MSR read is performed with an unchecked, faulting accessor instead of an error-returning safe read. Trigger: an x86 PV guest administrator issues a WRMSR to MSR_IA32_MISC_ENABLE on a host whose CPU lacks that MSR, causing a #GP during the read. Consequence: the unhandled fault crashes Xen, yielding host denial of service.

An attacker with CAP_BPF can arbitrarily read memory from anywhere on the system. We recommend upgrading past commit 86f44fcec22c

commit_msg:
Currently the header size calculations are using an assignment
operator instead of a += operator when accumulating the header
size leading to incorrect sizes.  Fix this by using the correct
operator.

Addresses-Coverity: ("Unused value")
Fixes: 302d3deb2068 ("xprtrdma: Prevent inline overflow")
Signed-off-by: Colin Ian King <colin.king@canonical.com>
Reviewed-by: Chuck Lever <chuck.lever@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Anna Schumaker <Anna.Schumaker@Netapp.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsize = maxsegs * rpcrdma_readchunk_maxsz * sizeof(__be32);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsize += maxsegs * rpcrdma_readchunk_maxsz * sizeof(__be32);']}
description: An information leak flaw was found in NFS over RDMA in the net/sunrpc/xprtrdma/rpc_rdma.c in the Linux Kernel. This flaw allows an attacker with normal user privileges to leak kernel information.

code_evidence: Line 4 initializes size to RPCRDMA_HDRLEN_MIN, but line 5 overwrites it with an assignment instead of accumulating via '+='. Lines 6-8 then add only the minimal read-chunk, segment, and count overheads, so the returned header size omits the maximum read-chunk list contribution.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The incorrect size accumulation leads to an undersized header bound, enabling kernel data exposure to an unprivileged actor, which matches CWE-200. The defect is an arithmetic/logic sizing error rather than an explicit read of sensitive data, so CWE-200 is the appropriate impact-level target here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the '=' operator on line 5 discards the base header length and the maximum read-list size is never accumulated, yielding an undersized call header size. This undersized value feeds inline/header sizing decisions, permitting request data to be placed where it exceeds the intended inline region; the supported consequence per the commit context is kernel information disclosure to a normal user.

Fix bug #78256 (heap-buffer-overflow on exif_process_user_comment)

(cherry picked from commit aeb6d13185a2ea4f1496ede2697469faed98ce05)

description: When PHP EXIF extension is parsing EXIF information from an image, e.g. via exif_read_data() function, in PHP versions 7.1.x below 7.1.31, 7.2.x below 7.2.21 and 7.3.x below 7.3.8 it is possible to supply it with data what will cause it to read past the allocated buffer. This may lead to information disclosure or crash.

code_evidence: After subtracting 8 for the 'UNICODE\0' prefix, ByteCount can be 0 or 1, yet lines 13 and 17 call memcmp(szValuePtr, ..., 2) without verifying at least 2 bytes remain. The BOM checks read two bytes from szValuePtr before any length guard.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the missing ByteCount>=2 guard before the two-byte memcmp BOM probes. When a user comment is exactly 8 or 9 bytes of 'UNICODE\0' data, the read at lines 13/17 accesses past the allocated buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read that can disclose memory or crash.

commit_msg: fix #60 : invalid state(CCS_VALUE) in parse_char_class()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  *state = CCS_VALUE;'], 'added_lines': ['  if (*state != CCS_START)', '    *state = CCS_VALUE;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in Oniguruma 6.2.0, as used in Oniguruma-mod in Ruby through 2.4.1 and mbstring in PHP through 7.1.5. A heap out-of-bounds write occurs in bitset_set_range() during regular expression compilation due to an uninitialized variable from an incorrect state transition. An incorrect state transition in parse_char_class() could create an execution path that leaves a critical local variable uninitialized until it's used as an index, resulting in an out-of-bounds write memory corruption.

code_evidence: When *state is CCS_VALUE and *type is CCV_SB, line 10 writes to cc->bs at index (*vs) without validating *vs against the bitset bounds. Line 16 unconditionally sets *state = CCS_VALUE, so a caller can reach this branch with a value that was never validated as a codepoint.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because line 10 writes past the end of the cc->bs bitset when *vs exceeds its capacity, and the missing bound check is the direct cause. This is a write beyond the intended buffer, not merely an uninitialized-value read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unconditional state assignment on line 16 permits an invalid CCS_VALUE state, and BITSET_SET_BIT on line 10 uses *vs as an index without a range check. Trigger: a char-class parse path that supplies an out-of-range *vs while *type is CCV_SB. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write into the bitset buffer, causing heap memory corruption.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void iax2_add_ts_fields(packet_info *pinfo, proto_tree *iax2_tree, iax_packet_data *iax_packet, guint16 shortts)', '  guint32     longts =shortts;', '    /* deal with short timestamps by assuming that packets are never more than', '     * 16 seconds late */', '    while(abs_secs < pinfo->fd->abs_ts.secs - 16) {', '      longts += 32768;', '      abs_secs = start_secs + longts/1000;', '    item = proto_tree_add_time(iax2_tree, hf_iax2_absts, NULL, 0, 0, &iax_packet->abstime);', '    item = proto_tree_add_time(iax2_tree, hf_iax2_lateness, NULL, 0, 0, &ts);'], 'added_lines': ['static void iax2_add_ts_fields(packet_info *pinfo, proto_tree *iax2_tree, tvbuff_t *tvb, iax_packet_data *iax_packet, guint16 shortts)', '  guint       longts =shortts;', '    if (pinfo->abs_ts.secs - abs_secs > MAX_SECS_DIFF) {', '      proto_tree_add_expert(iax2_tree, pinfo, &ei_iax_invalid_ts, tvb, 0, 0);', '    } else {', '      /* deal with short timestamps by assuming that packets are never more than', '       * 16 seconds late */', '      while(abs_secs < pinfo->fd->abs_ts.secs - 16) {', '        longts += 32768;', '        abs_secs = start_secs + longts/1000;', '      }', '    item = proto_tree_add_time(iax2_tree, hf_iax2_absts, tvb, 0, 0, &iax_packet->abstime);', '    item = proto_tree_add_time(iax2_tree, hf_iax2_lateness, tvb, 0, 0, &ts);']}
description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.4 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.10, there is an IAX2 infinite loop, triggered by packet injection or a malformed capture file. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-iax2.c by constraining packet lateness.

code_evidence: start_secs and abs_secs derive from the untrusted IAX2 short timestamp (shortts/longts). The while-loop at [12] increments longts by 32768 each iteration and recomputes abs_secs, but its exit condition compares abs_secs against pinfo->fd->abs_ts.secs - 16. If the captured packet timestamp is far ahead of the call start time (e.g., malformed capture or injected packet), the loop must iterate an unbounded number of times, and longts (guint32) can wrap before abs_secs ever reaches the target.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The while-loop at [12] has an exit condition that cannot be reached for sufficiently large timestamp gaps, matching CWE-835's infinite-loop definition. It is not merely an integer-overflow issue: the loop termination itself is unreachable, causing resource-exhaustion denial of service.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop's exit condition depends on a packet-derived timestamp with no bound on the difference between pinfo abs_ts and the call start time. Trigger: a packet whose abs_ts.secs is more than the reachable range ahead of start_secs, or longts wraparound. Consequence: the dissector spins, consuming CPU and hanging Wireshark (DoS).

description: tcprewrite in Tcpreplay 4.4.1 has a heap-based buffer over-read in get_l2len_protocol in common/get.c.

code_evidence: eth_hdr is derived from pktdata + *l2offset and ether_type is read via eth_hdr->ether_type at line 63, but the datalen <= l2_net_off bounds check occurs only afterward at line 64. The read of the Ethernet header therefore precedes validation that the buffer actually contains sizeof(*eth_hdr) bytes.

description: An AddPortMapping Denial Of Service vulnerability in MiniUPnP MiniUPnPd through 2.1 exists due to a NULL pointer dereference in upnpredirect.c.

commit_msg:
Bug 700938: Fix stack overflow in numtostr as used by Number#toFixed().

32 is not enough to fit sprintf("%.20f", 1e20).
We need at least 43 bytes to fit that format.
Bump the static buffer size.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar buf[32], *e;'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* buf needs to fit printf("%.20f", 1e20) */', '\tchar buf[50], *e;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Artifex MuJS 1.0.5. The Number#toFixed() and numtostr implementations in jsnumber.c have a stack-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: A fixed-size stack buffer buf[32] is declared and passed directly as the destination of sprintf(buf, fmt, w, n), with no check that the formatted output fits within 32 bytes. The format and width arrive via fmt and w, and the numeric value n is caller-controlled, so a large value with a wide format (e.g. "%.20f" on 1e20) produces a much longer string than the buffer can hold.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes formatted data beyond the bounds of an intended fixed-size buffer, which is precisely CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely an off-by-one or a read overrun; the unbounded sprintf directly overflows the destination buffer on the stack.

evidence_lines.code:
char buf[32], *e;
sprintf(buf, fmt, w, n);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination buffer is sized independently of the formatted output length, and sprintf performs no bounds checking. Trigger: calling numtostr with a width/format and value whose formatted representation exceeds 32 bytes. Consequence: sprintf writes past the end of the stack buffer, corrupting adjacent stack memory and potentially enabling a crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
Timing vulnerability in DSA signature generation (CVE-2018-0734).

Avoid a timing attack that leaks information via a side channel that
triggers when a BN is resized.  Increasing the size of the BNs
prior to doing anything with them suppresses the attack.

Thanks due to Samuel Weiser for finding and locating this.

Reviewed-by: Bernd Edlinger <bernd.edlinger@hotmail.de>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/7486)

(cherry picked from commit a9cfb8c2aa7254a4aa6a1716909e3f8cb78049b6)

More', '     * specificly refer to the discussion starting with:', '     *     https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/7486#discussion_r228323705', "     * The fix is to rework BN so these gymnastics aren't required.", '        || !BN_add(k, l, dsa->q))', '', '    BN_consttime_swap(BN_is_bit_set(l, q_bits), k, l, q_words + 2);', "    /* Compute part of 's = inv(k) (m + xr) mod q' */"]}
