description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions due to incomplete validation in `tf.raw_ops.QuantizeV2`, an attacker can trigger undefined behavior via binding a reference to a null pointer or can access data outside the bounds of heap allocated arrays. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/84d053187cb80d975ef2b9684d4b61981bca0c41/tensorflow/core/kernels/quantize_op.cc#L59) has some validation but does not check that `min_range` and `max_range` both have the same non-zero number of elements. If `axis` is provided (i.e., not `-1`), then validation should check that it is a value in range for the rank of `input` tensor and then the lengths of `min_range` and `max_range` inputs match the `axis` dimension of the `input` tensor. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 6da6620efad397c85493b8f8667b821403516708. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: When axis_ > -1, num_slices is set directly from input.dim_size(axis_) with no check that axis_ is a valid index into input's dimensions.
When num_slices == 1, min_range and max_range are read at flat<float>()(0) without verifying the tensors are non-empty.
The slice loop indexes min_ranges(i) and max_ranges(i) for i in [0, num_slices) without confirming min_range/max_range element counts equal num_slices.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing/incorrect validation of input tensor metadata (axis index, range lengths) before it is used, matching CWE-20's improper input validation of indexes and sizes. It is not a transformation/filtering flaw, so a lower-level transform CWE does not apply.

evidence_lines.code:
if (axis_ > -1) {
num_slices = input.dim_size(axis_);

const float min_range = input_min_range.template flat<float>()(0);
const float max_range = input_max_range.template flat<float>()(0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the kernel trusts caller-supplied axis value and min_range/max_range tensor sizes without validating them against input rank or the axis dimension. Trigger: a crafted QuantizeV2 call with an out-of-range axis or mismatched/empty range tensors. Consequence: out-of-bounds dim_size access, null-pointer binding, or heap out-of-bounds reads.

description:
Versions of the package raysan5/raylib before 4.5.0 are vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting (XSS) such that the SetClipboardText API does not properly escape the ' character, allowing attacker-controlled input to break out of the string and execute arbitrary JavaScript via emscripten_run_script function.

**Note:** This vulnerability is present only when compiling raylib for PLATFORM_WEB. All the other Desktop/Mobile/Embedded platforms are not affected.

code_evidence: Lines 3-7 only reject input containing a single quote via strchr and merely log a warning; no neutralization of the url string is performed.
Line 24 passes url directly into TextFormat("window.open('%s', '_blank')", url), embedding attacker-controlled input inside a JavaScript string literal executed by emscripten_run_script.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-79 fits because user-controllable input is placed into generated web/script output without proper neutralization, allowing script injection. The single-character blocklist is an incorrect neutralization rather than a complete encoding of the value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the url argument is interpolated into a JavaScript string literal without escaping. The strchr check blocks only the ' character but is a partial filter and does not neutralize other breakout vectors. Trigger: an attacker-controlled url reaching OpenURL on PLATFORM_WEB. Consequence: the injected content executes as JavaScript in the page context, enabling script execution.

commit_msg:
rds_rm_zerocopy_callback() uses list_entry() on the head of a list
causing a type confusion.
Use list_first_entry() to actually access the first element of the
rs_zcookie_queue list.

Fixes: 9426bbc6de99 ("rds: use list structure to track information for zerocopy completion notification")
Reviewed-by: Willem de Bruijn <willemb@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Pietro Borrello <borrello@diag.uniroma1.it>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230202-rds-zerocopy-v3-1-83b0df974f9a@diag.uniroma1.it
Signed-off-by: Paolo Abeni <pabeni@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tinfo = list_entry(head, struct rds_msg_zcopy_info,', '\t\t\t\t  rs_zcookie_next);', '\t\tif (info && rds_zcookie_add(info, cookie)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tinfo = list_first_entry(head, struct rds_msg_zcopy_info,', '\t\t\t\t\trs_zcookie_next);', '\t\tif (rds_zcookie_add(info, cookie)) {']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux Kernel in RDS (Reliable Datagram Sockets) protocol. The rds_rm_zerocopy_callback() uses list_entry() on the head of a list causing a type confusion. Local user can trigger this with rds_message_put(). Type confusion leads to `struct rds_msg_zcopy_info *info` actually points to something else that is potentially controlled by local user. It is known how to trigger this, which causes an out of bounds access, and a lock corruption.

code_evidence: After checking !list_empty(head), the code passes head (the list head itself) to list_entry() instead of the first element. list_entry() casts head to struct rds_msg_zcopy_info via container_of, so info points at the embedded list_head inside the queue struct, not a real rds_msg_zcopy_info. info is then passed to rds_zcookie_add() at line 17.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The pointer is derived by casting a list_head to an incompatible struct type (container_of on the wrong object), and that mis-typed pointer is then used as rds_msg_zcopy_info. This is exactly access of a resource using an incompatible type; the fix uses list_first_entry() to obtain the correctly typed first element.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: list_entry() applied to the list head treats the queue's list_head as if it were the rs_zcookie_next member of rds_msg_zcopy_info, producing a mis-typed pointer. Trigger: any zerocopy completion where the zcookie list is non-empty. Consequence: rds_zcookie_add() dereferences fields at wrong offsets, giving out-of-bounds access and lock corruption, as the callback acts on a struct that is not the intended type.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.2110: [security]: overflow in ex address parsing

Problem:  [security]: overflow in ex address parsing
Solution: Verify that lnum is positive, before substracting from
          LONG_MAX

[security]: overflow in ex address parsing

When parsing relative ex addresses one may unintentionally cause an
overflow (because LONG_MAX - lnum will overflow for negative addresses).

So verify that lnum is actually positive before doing the overflow
check.

Signed-off-by: Christian Brabandt <cb@256bit.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t    if (n >= LONG_MAX - lnum)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t    if (lnum >= 0 && n >= LONG_MAX - lnum)']}
description:
Vim is an open source command line text editor. When parsing relative ex addresses one may unintentionally cause an
overflow. Ironically this happens in the existing overflow check, because the line number becomes negative and LONG_MAX - lnum will cause the overflow. Impact is low, user interaction is required and a crash may not even happen in all situations. This issue has been addressed in commit `060623e` which has been included in release version 9.0.2110. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: When the parsed relative address uses '-', lnum is decremented by n (line 299) with no check that lnum stays nonnegative, so lnum can become negative.
The '+' branch's overflow guard computes LONG_MAX - lnum (line 302) before adding n (line 307); with a negative lnum this subtraction itself overflows, defeating the intended bound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The signed integer arithmetic (LONG_MAX - lnum and lnum += n) can overflow/wrap because the code assumes lnum is nonnegative; the fix adds lnum >= 0, confirming the missing guard caused the overflow. This matches CWE-190 rather than a mere bounds check, since the check itself overflows.

evidence_lines.code:
if (i == '-')
lnum -= n;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard n >= LONG_MAX - lnum assumes lnum is nonnegative, but the '-' branch can leave lnum negative. Trigger: an ex address with repeated relative offsets, e.g. a large negative adjustment followed by a '+'. The wrapped comparison then passes, and lnum += n can wrap to an incorrect line number, leading to out-of-range state and a possible crash.

description: The perf_cpu_time_max_percent_handler function in kernel/events/core.c in the Linux kernel before 4.11 allows local users to cause a denial of service (integer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a large value, as demonstrated by an incorrect sample-rate calculation.

code_evidence: The handler parses the user-supplied sysctl value with proc_dointvec, which accepts any integer without lower or upper bounds; the value is stored into sysctl_perf_cpu_time_max_percent before the function proceeds to use it. No range check constrains the input before it feeds later arithmetic in the perf sample-rate calculation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the accepted large value causes a calculation whose result wraps rather than growing, exactly the integer overflow/wraparound pattern. The unbounded input is the enabling condition; the overflow in the derived sample-rate value is the weakness, distinct from a mere missing-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unvalidated, unbounded user-controlled integer from proc_dointvec is accepted and used in downstream sample-rate arithmetic. Trigger: a local user writes a very large value; the subsequent calculation wraps, yielding an incorrect (small/negative) sample rate. Supported consequence: denial of service via integer overflow and erroneous throttling behavior.

commit_msg:
The functions XGetFontPath, XListExtensions, and XListFonts are
vulnerable to an off-by-one override on malicious server responses.

The server replies consist of chunks consisting of a length byte
followed by actual string, which is not NUL-terminated.

While parsing the response, the length byte is overridden with '\0',
thus the memory area can be used as storage of C strings later on. To
be able to NUL-terminate the last string, the buffer is reserved with
an additional byte of space.

For a boundary check, the variable chend (end of ch) was introduced,
pointing at the end of the buffer which ch initially points to.
Unfortunately there is a difference in handling "the end of ch".

While chend points at the first byte that must not be written to,
the for-loop uses chend as the last byte that can be written to.

Therefore, an off-by-one can occur.

I have refactored the code so chend actually points to the last byte
that can be written to without an out of boundary access. As it is not
possible to achieve "ch + length < chend" and "ch + length + 1 > chend"
with the corrected chend meaning, I removed the inner if-check.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    chend = ch + (rlen + 1);', '\t\t    if (ch <= chend) {', '\t\t\tlength = *ch;', "\t\t\t*ch = '\\0'; /* and replace with null-termination */", '\t\t\tcount++;', '\t\t    } else {', '\t\t\tlist[i] = NULL;', '\t\t    }'], 'added_lines': ['\t    chend = ch + rlen;', '\t\t    length = *ch;', "\t\t    *ch = '\\0'; /* and replace with null-termination */", '\t\t    count++;']}
description: An issue was discovered in libX11 through 1.6.5. The function XListExtensions in ListExt.c is vulnerable to an off-by-one error caused by malicious server responses, leading to DoS or possibly unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: chend is set to ch + (rlen + 1), one past the allocated rlen+1 buffer's last writable byte, then the loop treats chend as writable: the inner check 'ch <= chend' permits dereferencing and writing *ch = '\0' at the chend position, which is past the allocated region.

ch is allocated with rlen + 1 bytes and filled via _XReadPad with rlen bytes of server-controlled data; rep.length and the length bytes come from the untrusted server reply, so the off-by-one index is attacker-influenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The boundary is off by exactly one: the buffer end is computed as rlen+1 while the writable check includes that extra position. This is a classic off-by-one maximum-value miscalculation, matching CWE-193 rather than a general buffer overflow.

evidence_lines.code:
ch = Xmalloc (rlen + 1);
_XReadPad (dpy, ch, rlen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is a mismatched boundary definition: chend marks one-past-the-end but the loop and inner check allow writing at chend. A malicious server reply with crafted length bytes drives ch to the boundary, and the NUL-termination write at *ch touches memory one byte beyond the buffer, causing out-of-bounds write and potential crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
evtchn: address races with evtchn_reset()

Neither d->evtchn_port_ops nor max_evtchns(d) may be used in an entirely
lock-less manner, as both may change by a racing evtchn_reset(). In the
common case, at least one of the domain's event lock or the per-channel
lock needs to be held. In the specific case of the inter-domain sending
by evtchn_send() and notify_via_xen_event_channel() holding the other
side's per-channel lock is sufficient, as the channel can't change state
without both per-channel locks held. Without such a channel changing
state, evtchn_reset() can't complete successfully.

Lock-free accesses continue to be permitted for the shim (calling some
otherwise internal event channel functions), as this happens while the
domain is in effectively single-threaded mode. Special care also needs
taking for the shim's marking of in-use ports as ECS_RESERVED (allowing
use of such ports in the shim case is okay because switching into and
hence also out of FIFO mode is impossihble there).

As a side effect, certain operations on Xen bound event channels which
were mistakenly permitted so far (e.g. unmask or poll) will be refused
now.

This is part of XSA-343.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['               evtchn_port_is_pending(d, port),', '               evtchn_port_is_masked(d, port));'], 'added_lines': ['               evtchn_is_pending(d, chn),', '               evtchn_is_masked(d, chn));']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The function takes d->event_lock at line 8 and iterates ports while holding it, calling port_is_valid(d, port) at line 9 and evtchn_from_port(d, port) at line 13 to fetch chn. It reads chn->state at line 14 and uses that chn pointer for evtchn_port_is_pending/evtchn_port_is_masked and evtchn_port_print_state at lines 18-20; the lock is released only at line 49. The patch replaces port-index-based helpers with chn-based helpers, indicating the port-to-channel mapping can change concurrently.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 matches: concurrent evtchn_reset() interferes with the dump's non-exclusive access to shared event-channel state, violating atomicity of the check-then-use sequence. The patch's switch to chn-based helpers addresses that race; this is not merely a missing lock, since the lock is held but the mapping can still change.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dump relies on port_is_valid/evtchn_from_port and then reads channel fields, while a racing evtchn_reset() can change d->max_evtchns or the port-to-channel mapping. Because the loop and subsequent reads assume the mapping is stable, a reset between the validity check and the channel access can yield an invalid or stale chn, leading to out-of-bounds access or bug checks rather than a simple stale print.

commit_msg:
x86/hap: do not switch on log dirty for VRAM tracking

XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram possibly calls into paging_log_dirty_enable
when using HAP mode, and it can interact badly with other ongoing
paging domctls, as XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram is not holding the domctl
lock.

This was detected as a result of the following assert triggering when
doing repeated migrations of a HAP HVM domain with a stubdom:

Assertion 'd->arch.paging.log_dirty.allocs == 0' failed at paging.c:198
----[ Xen-4.17-unstable  x86_64  debug=y  Not tainted ]----
CPU:    34
RIP:    e008:[<ffff82d040314b3b>] arch/x86/mm/paging.c#paging_free_log_dirty_bitmap+0x606/0x6
RFLAGS: 0000000000010206   CONTEXT: hypervisor (d0v23)
[...]
Xen call trace:
   [<ffff82d040314b3b>] R arch/x86/mm/paging.c#paging_free_log_dirty_bitmap+0x606/0x63a
   [<ffff82d040279f96>] S xsm/flask/hooks.c#domain_has_perm+0x5a/0x67
   [<ffff82d04031577f>] F paging_domctl+0x251/0xd41
   [<ffff82d04031640c>] F paging_domctl_continuation+0x19d/0x202
   [<ffff82d0403202fa>] F pv_hypercall+0x150/0x2a7
   [<ffff82d0403a729d>] F lstar_enter+0x12d/0x140

Such assert triggered because the stubdom used
XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram while dom0 was in the middle of executing
XEN_DOMCTL_SHADOW_OP_OFF, and so log dirty become enabled while
retiring the old structures, thus leading to new entries being
populated in already clear slots.

Fix this by not enabling log dirty for VRAM tracking, similar to what
is done when using shadow instead of HAP. Call
p2m_enable_hardware_log_dirty when enabling VRAM tracking in order to
get some hardware assistance if available. As a side effect the memory
pressure on the p2m pool should go down if only VRAM tracking is
enabled, as the dirty bitmap is no longer allocated.

Note that paging_log_dirty_range (used to get the dirty bitmap for
VRAM tracking) doesn't use the log dirty bitmap, and instead relies on
checking whether each gfn on the range has been switched from
p2m_ram_logdirty to p2m_ram_rw in order to account for dirty pages.

This is CVE-2022-26356 / XSA-397.

Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

+++ func_after
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-int paging_log_dirty_enable(struct domain *d, bool log_global)
+static int paging_log_dirty_enable(struct domain *d, bool log_global)
 {
     int ret;
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int paging_log_dirty_enable(struct domain *d, bool log_global)'], 'added_lines': ['static int paging_log_dirty_enable(struct domain *d, bool log_global)']}
description: Racy interactions between dirty vram tracking and paging log dirty hypercalls Activation of log dirty mode done by XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram (was named HVMOP_track_dirty_vram before Xen 4.9) is racy with ongoing log dirty hypercalls. A suitably timed call to XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram can enable log dirty while another CPU is still in the process of tearing down the structures related to a previously enabled log dirty mode (XEN_DOMCTL_SHADOW_OP_OFF). This is due to lack of mutually exclusive locking between both operations and can lead to entries being added in already freed slots, resulting in a memory leak.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only checks state and pauses the domain before calling the log_dirty enable op; it contains no lock acquisition/release or concurrent-operation synchronization, so the CWE-667 race with XEN_DOMCTL_SHADOW_OP_OFF is not evidenced in this code.

commit_msg:
Fixed bug: 'luaD_callnoyield' called twice in a row

In luaD_callnoyield, when there is a possible stack overflow, it
zeros the number of CallInfos to force a check when calling the
function. However, if the "function" is not a function, the code will
raise an error before checking the stack. Then, the error handling calls
luaD_callnoyield again and nCcalls is decremented again, crossing the
stack redzone without raising an error. (This loop can only happens
once, because the error handler must be a function.  But once is enough
to cross the redzone.)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (getCcalls(L) <= CSTACKERR)  /* possible stack overflow? */', '    luaE_freeCI(L);'], 'added_lines': ['  if (getCcalls(L) <= CSTACKERR) {  /* possible C stack overflow? */', '    luaE_exitCcall(L);  /* to compensate decrement in next call */', '    luaE_enterCcall(L);  /* check properly */', '  }']}
description: Lua through 5.4.0 allows a stack redzone cross in luaO_pushvfstring because a protection mechanism wrongly calls luaD_callnoyield twice in a row.

code_evidence: incXCcalls(L) increments the C-call counter at entry, and decXCcalls(L) decrements it after luaD_call. When getCcalls(L) <= CSTACKERR, the code only calls luaE_freeCI(L) to force a later check, without restoring the counter before the nested luaD_call. If func is not a function, luaD_call raises an error before the stack check; the error handler re-enters luaD_callnoyield, decrementing nCcalls again.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The double decrement lets the C-stack counter fall below the intended redzone boundary, so subsequent stack operations proceed outside the buffer's intended limits, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The underlying counter-mismatch is the cause; the out-of-bounds stack access is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the redzone guard frees CallInfos but does not compensate the counter increment, so a re-entrant call decrements nCcalls twice. Trigger: a non-function argument causes an error before the stack check, invoking error handling that calls luaD_callnoyield again. Consequence: nCcalls crosses the stack redzone without raising an error, permitting out-of-bounds stack handling.

commit_msg:
Resolve image enumerator ownership on error

Bug #697596 "Use-After-Free in i_free_object()"

There is confusion over ownership of 'penum' between gx_begin_image1(),
gx_begin_image4() and gx_image_enum_begin() which is called from these
two functions (and only from these two functions).

The enumerator is allocated in gx_begin_image?() and freed there if
gx_image_enum_begin() returns an error. However, gx_image_enum_begin()
also frees the enumerator on an error; except that it doesn't always do
so. Its a large function and there are at least 9 ways to exit it, only
4 of which free the enumerator.

This commit removes the 'free' instances from gx_image_enum_begin()
leaving the cleanup as the responsibility of the calling code, which
performed the allocation.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        gs_free_object(mem, penum, "gx_default_begin_image");', '            gs_free_object(mem, penum, "gx_default_begin_image");', '            gs_free_object(mem, penum, "gx_default_begin_image");', '        gs_free_object(mem, penum, "gx_default_begin_image");'], 'added_lines': []}
description: Multiple use-after-free vulnerabilities in the gx_image_enum_begin function in base/gxipixel.c in Ghostscript before ecceafe3abba2714ef9b432035fe0739d9b1a283 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PostScript document.

code_evidence: On matrix-compute failure, gs_free_object(mem, penum) is called and then the error code is returned; the caller gx_begin_image?() also frees the same penum it allocated, producing a double free.
The masked-rangecheck path frees penum and returns gs_error_rangecheck; the caller again frees the same pointer.
The negative-color-component path frees penum and returns gs_error_rangecheck, duplicating the caller's cleanup.
The buffer-allocation-failure path frees penum and returns gs_error_VMerror, again duplicating the caller's free.
The render-class failure path calls gx_default_end_image on penum and returns gs_error_rangecheck, after which the caller frees penum as well.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because penum is freed inside this function while ownership remains with the caller, which frees it again; the pointer is subsequently reused after release. This is a double-free leading to use-after-free, not merely a memory leak or missing free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: gx_image_enum_begin frees the caller-allocated enumerator on several error exits, but the calling gx_begin_image1/4 functions also free penum on error. The enumerator is thus freed twice, and the second free (or any later use of the dangling pointer) operates on already-released memory. Triggering any of these error paths with a crafted image causes heap corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
xen/rwlock: Add missing memory barrier in the unlock path of rwlock

The rwlock unlock paths are using atomic_sub() to release the lock.
However the implementation of atomic_sub() rightfully doesn't contain a
memory barrier. On Arm, this means a processor is allowed to re-order
the memory access with the preceeding access.

In other words, the unlock may be seen by another processor before all
the memory accesses within the "critical" section.

The rwlock paths already contains barrier indirectly, but they are not
very useful without the counterpart in the unlock paths.

The memory barriers are not necessary on x86 because loads/stores are
not re-ordered with lock instructions.

So add arch_lock_release_barrier() in the unlock paths that will only
add memory barrier on Arm.

Take the opportunity to document each lock paths explaining why a
barrier is not necessary.

This is XSA-314.

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.13.x, allowing guest OS users to cause a denial of service or possibly gain privileges because of missing memory barriers in read-write unlock paths. The read-write unlock paths don't contain a memory barrier. On Arm, this means a processor is allowed to re-order the memory access with the preceding ones. In other words, the unlock may be seen by another processor before all the memory accesses within the "critical" section. As a consequence, it may be possible to have a writer executing a critical section at the same time as readers or another writer. In other words, many of the assumptions (e.g., a variable cannot be modified after a check) in the critical sections are not safe anymore. The read-write locks are used in hypercalls (such as grant-table ones), so a malicious guest could exploit the race. For instance, there is a small window where Xen can leak memory if XENMAPSPACE_grant_table is used concurrently. A malicious guest may be able to leak memory, or cause a hypervisor crash resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leak and privilege escalation cannot be excluded.

code_evidence: _write_unlock() clears the write-lock bits with atomic_and() without any release barrier before the store. ASSERT at line 3 only checks ownership; lines 4-5 perform the unlock and preempt_enable() with no arch_lock_release_barrier(), so on weakly ordered architectures (Arm) the lock release can be reordered before prior critical-section memory accesses.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the missing release barrier creates a timing window in which another concurrent code sequence can access the shared resource (the protected data) without proper synchronization, breaking the exclusivity the rwlock is meant to guarantee. It is a synchronization-race weakness rather than a pure atomicity bug in a single operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unlock path lacks a release memory barrier, allowing the lock release to become visible before preceding writes inside the protected critical section. Trigger: a concurrent reader/writer on another processor observes the unlocked state and enters the critical section while the first writer's accesses are still pending, violating exclusivity/atomicity. Supported consequence: concurrent access to shared hypervisor state, enabling memory leak, crash/DoS, and potentially privilege escalation.

description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

code_evidence: Lines 14-16 shut down the received stream's read side whenever a stream object exists, without any accounting of how many RST_STREAM frames are being processed over time.
Lines 21-25 close the stream and return only on fatal errors; the non-fatal path falls through to the return at line 26, which unconditionally returns 0 with no throttling or rate-limit check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 covers failure to control consumption of a limited resource. Here the missing constraint is throttling of stream-reset processing, allowing excessive resource consumption; the fix's added rate-limit call confirms the intended control is absent in this function's return path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the RST_STREAM handler performs per-frame stream shutdown/close work but imposes no limit on how rapidly many streams can be reset. Trigger: a peer sends many RST_STREAM frames in quick succession, causing repeated stream teardown work (and associated session bookkeeping) per request. Supported consequence: unbounded CPU/processing consumption by the server, i.e., denial of service, since the handler does not throttle the reset rate before returning success.

commit_msg:
Bug 699661: Avoid sharing pointers between pdf14 compositors

If a copdevice is triggered when the pdf14 compositor is the device, we make
a copy of the device, then throw an error because, by default we're only allowed
to copy the device prototype - then freeing it calls the finalize, which frees
several pointers shared with the parent.

Make a pdf14 specific finish_copydevice() which NULLs the relevant pointers,
before, possibly, throwing the same error as the default method.

This also highlighted a problem with reopening the X11 devices, where a custom
error handler could be replaced with itself, meaning it also called itself,
and infifite recursion resulted.

Keep a note of if the handler replacement has been done, and don't do it a
second time.

description: In Artifex Ghostscript before 9.24, attackers able to supply crafted PostScript files to the builtin PDF14 converter could use a use-after-free in copydevice handling to crash the interpreter or possibly have unspecified other impact.

commit_msg:
p2m: Check return value of p2m_set_entry() when decreasing reservation

If the entire range specified to p2m_pod_decrease_reservation() is marked
populate-on-demand, then it will make a single p2m_set_entry() call,
reducing its PoD entry count.

Unfortunately, in the right circumstances, this p2m_set_entry() call
may fail.  It that case, repeated calls to decrease_reservation() may
cause p2m->pod.entry_count to fall below zero, potentially tripping
over BUG_ON()s to the contrary.

Instead, check to see if the entry succeeded, and return false if not.
The caller will then call guest_remove_page() on the gfns, which will
return -EINVAL upon finding no valid memory there to return.

Unfortunately if the order > 0, the entry may have partially changed.
A domain_crash() is probably the safest thing in that case.

Other p2m_set_entry() calls in the same function should be fine,
because they are writing the entry at its current order.  Nonetheless,
check the return value and crash if our assumption turns otu to be
wrong.

This is part of XSA-247.

Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing HVM guest OS users to gain privileges on the host OS, obtain sensitive information, or cause a denial of service (BUG and host OS crash) by leveraging the mishandling of Populate on Demand (PoD) Physical-to-Machine (P2M) errors.

description: ImageMagick 7.0.8-34 has a "use of uninitialized value" vulnerability in the WriteJP2Image function in coders/jp2.c.

code_evidence: RectangleInfo geometry is declared uninitialized inside the image_info->extract branch, then ParseAbsoluteGeometry fills only the fields flagged by its return value. geometry.width is read unconditionally at lines 64-65, and geometry.height/x/y are read only when the corresponding flag is set; any field not parsed retains indeterminate stack data that is copied into parameters.cp_tdx/cp_tdy (and cp_tx0/cp_ty0) and later passed to the encoder.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper initialization of a resource (the geometry variable) whose unset fields are subsequently accessed and used, matching CWE-665. It is not an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the access stays within the struct; the defect is the missing initialization before partial parsing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: local geometry is not initialized before ParseAbsoluteGeometry, which populates only the components present in the extract string. Trigger: a partial extract geometry (e.g. missing width/height/offset) makes the code read uninitialized RectangleInfo fields and propagate them into opj_cparameters_t. Consequence: indeterminate tile-size/offset values are used during JP2 encoding, matching the reported use of uninitialized value.

commit_msg:
gif: Fix LZW decoder accepting invalid LZW code.

The code value after a reset wasn't being validated, which means we would
accept invalid codes. This could cause an infinite loop in the decoder.

Fixes CVE-2020-29385

Fixes https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gdk-pixbuf/-/issues/164

description: GNOME gdk-pixbuf (aka GdkPixbuf) before 2.42.2 allows a denial of service (infinite loop) in lzw.c in the function write_indexes. if c->self_code equals 10, self->code_table[10].extends will assign the value 11 to c. The next execution in the loop will assign self->code_table[11].extends to c, which will give the value of 10. This will make the loop run infinitely. This bug can, for example, be triggered by calling this function with a GIF image with LZW compression that is crafted in a special way.

code_evidence: Lines 33-44 validate the decoded code only inside the branch where last_code != clear_code and code_table_size < MAX_CODES; when the table is full or just after a clear code, self->code is not range-checked before use.
Line 45 then calls write_indexes with the unvalidated code, which can drive the extends chain (e.g., 10 -> 11 -> 10) without termination.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the unvalidated code causes an iteration whose exit condition cannot be reached (cyclic extends chain). This is an unbounded-loop availability issue, not merely out-of-bounds memory access.

evidence_lines.code: n_written += write_indexes (self, output + n_written, output_length - n_written);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The decoder accepts an out-of-range LZW code because the invalid-code guard is nested inside the code_table_size < MAX_CODES condition. A crafted GIF emitting such a code after reset or when the table is full reaches write_indexes, whose extends traversal can cycle between entries indefinitely, consuming CPU (infinite loop / DoS). The root cause is the missing unconditional range check; the infinite loop is the consequence.

Return null if no charset matches

Fixes a segmentation fault if no charset matches. According to http://icu-project.org/apiref/icu4c/ucsdet_8h.html#aff2633b5055d472cff4108d94f97cf7d, ucsdet_detect() may return NULL if no charset matches.

Fixes: #15
Co-authored-by: chenzhip <letme2010@gmail.com>

description: detect-character-encoding is an open source character encoding inspection library. In detect-character-encoding v0.6.0 and earlier, data matching no charset causes the Node.js process to crash. The problem has been patched in [detect-character-encoding v0.7.0](https://github.com/sonicdoe/detect-character-encoding/releases/tag/v0.7.0). No workaround are available and all users should update to resolve this issue.

commit_msg:
tjLoadImage: Fix issues w/loading 16-bit PPMs/PGMs

- The PPM reader now throws an error rather than segfaulting (due to a
  buffer overrun) if an application attempts to load a 16-bit PPM file
  into a grayscale uncompressed image buffer.  No known applications
  allowed that (not even the test applications in libjpeg-turbo),
  because that mode of operation was never expected to work and did not
  work under any circumstances.  (In fact, it was necessary to modify
  TJBench in order to reproduce the issue outside of a fuzzing
  environment.)  This was purely a matter of making the library bow out
  gracefully rather than crash if an application tries to do something
  really stupid.

- The PPM reader now throws an error rather than generating incorrect
  pixels if an application attempts to load a 16-bit PGM file into an
  RGB uncompressed image buffer.

- The PPM reader now correctly loads 16-bit PPM files into extended
  RGB uncompressed image buffers.  (Previously it generated incorrect
  pixels unless the input colorspace was JCS_RGB or JCS_EXT_RGB.)

The only way that users could have potentially encountered these issues
was through the tjLoadImage() function.  cjpeg and TJBench were
unaffected.

commit_msg:
While a stack of states is a good way to maintain graphics contexts, if
the command stream you are interpreting is untrusted, we must place
appropriate guards to be sure that, not only do we not pop past the end
of the stack, but we do not pop past the stack as it was when we began
rendering.

description: poppler before 0.16.3 has malformed commands that may cause corruption of the internal stack.

code_evidence: Gfx::go() parses an untrusted content stream via parser->getObj() in a loop and dispatches each command object to execOp().

Arguments are accumulated in args[] up to maxArgs; on overflow the code logs an error and discards the object (lines 53-64) but continues parsing, so the command stream is only partially validated before execution.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits because externally influenced command tokens are passed to a downstream interpreter (execOp) without neutralizing special elements that alter stack/execution behavior. This is command injection into the graphics interpreter rather than a memory-safety issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function feeds externally supplied content-stream tokens directly into command execution (execOp) and state-stack operations. Malformed command sequences can pop the graphics state stack beyond its starting depth because the parser loop does not enforce stack-depth constraints. The added pushStateGuard/popStateGuard in the patch confirms the missing bound; the consequence is corruption of the internal state stack when untrusted commands are interpreted.

commit_msg:
Fixed String.prototype.trimEnd() with unicode string.

Previously, when the method was invoked with a string consisting of space
characters and at least one of them was a Unicode space separator (code
point above 127) it returned invalid string value with non-zero size
but zero length.

The fix is to update the size of the resulting string appropriately.

This closes #569 issue on Github.

code_evidence: In the non-ASCII TRIM_END branch, prev is initialized to end and the loop breaks when start == prev without updating end. When the string consists entirely of Unicode whitespace, every iteration continues and the loop exits with end still at the original buffer end while start has advanced, leaving end pointing past the trimmed region.

After the loop, start != end is possible only if the trimming stopped early, but in the all-whitespace case the un-updated end causes the subsequent size computation string->size = end - start to be wrong or the empty-string check at line 76 to be skipped, so string->start/size may reference an inconsistent range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the inconsistent start/size descriptor causes downstream code to read beyond the intended buffer, matching an out-of-bounds read. It is not merely an incorrect result; the incorrect size enables reading past the buffer boundary.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the non-ASCII trim-end loop fails to set end = prev when the loop terminates because start == prev, so end is not synchronized with the trimmed start. Trigger: trimEnd on a string composed of whitespace characters including a Unicode space separator. Consequence: the resulting string descriptor keeps a non-zero size with zero length, and later consumers can read past the intended buffer (segmentation violation via njs_utf8_next).

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions an attacker can trigger a denial of service via a segmentation fault in `tf.raw_ops.MaxPoolGrad` caused by missing validation. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/core/kernels/maxpooling_op.cc) misses some validation for the `orig_input` and `orig_output` tensors. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 21 reads depth_window from the user-supplied ksize tensor. Lines 25-26 only require depth_window == 1 or window_rows/window_cols == 1, so a depth_window of 0 passes this check and reaches the else branch. There, lines 50-53 check depth % depth_window == 0, which divides by the unvalidated quantity before any positivity check, and line 65 computes depth / depth_window.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the depth-window quantity from ksize is never constrained to be positive before being used as a divisor. Trigger: a caller supplies a depth_window of 0 with depth_window != 1, causing integer division/modulo by zero. Supported consequence: a crash (segmentation fault/DoS), consistent with the missing validation fix.

Ignore return value from mysql_stmt_close() and also its error message
because it points to freed memory after mysql_stmt_close() was called.

description: The DBD::mysql module through 4.043 for Perl allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering (1) certain error responses from a MySQL server or (2) a loss of a network connection to a MySQL server. Supported consequence: use-after-free read that can crash the application or, if the freed memory is reused, lead to further memory corruption.

The fuzzed image contains an AGF with an obviously garbage
agf_refcount_level value of 32, and a dirty log with a buffer log item
for that AGF.  The ondisk AGF has a higher LSN than the recovered log
item.  xlog_recover_buf_commit_pass2 reads the buffer, compares the
LSNs, and decides to skip replay because the ondisk buffer appears to be
newer.

Unfortunately, the ondisk buffer is corrupt, but recovery just read the
buffer with no buffer ops specified:

	error = xfs_buf_read(mp->m_ddev_targp, buf_f->blf_blkno,
			buf_f->blf_len, buf_flags, &bp, NULL);

Skipping the buffer leaves its contents in memory unverified.  This sets
us up for a kernel crash because xfs_refcount_recover_cow_leftovers
reads the buffer (which is still around in XBF_DONE state, so no read
verification) and creates a refcountbt cursor of height 32.  This is
impossible so we run off the end of the cursor object and crash.

Fix this by invoking the verifier on all skipped buffers and aborting
log recovery if the ondisk buffer is corrupt.  It might be smarter to
force replay the log item atop the buffer and then see if it'll pass the
write verifier (like ext4 does) but for now let's go with the
conservative option where we stop immediately.

Link: https://syzkaller.appspot.com/bug?extid=7e9494b8b399902e994e
Signed-off-by: Darrick J. Wong <djwong@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Dave Chinner <dchinner@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Chinner <david@fromorbit.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t/*', "\t\t * We're skipping replay of this buffer log item due to the log", '\t\t * item LSN being behind the ondisk buffer.  Verify the buffer', "\t\t * contents since we aren't going to run the write verifier.", '\t\t */', '\t\tif (bp->b_ops) {', '\t\t\tbp->b_ops->verify_read(bp);', '\t\t\terror = bp->b_error;', '\t\t}']}
description: An out-of-bounds memory access flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s XFS file system in how a user restores an XFS image after failure (with a dirty log journal). This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: The buffer is read with a NULL buffer-ops argument, so xfs_buf_read performs no read verification and the on-disk contents remain unvalidated.
When the recovered LSN is behind current_lsn, the code skips replay and jumps to out_release without invoking any verifier on the skipped buffer; the unverified buffer stays cached in XBF_DONE state.
out_release only releases the buffer reference and returns the unmodified error value, so the corrupt buffer content propagates to later users.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The target CWE-787 describes writing past a buffer's bounds, but the commit and call trace show a slab-out-of-bounds read in xfs_btree_lookup_get_block. The function's flaw is missing verification leading to invalid metadata, not a write past an allocated buffer, so the supplied target does not fit the demonstrated behavior.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: skipped log-replay buffers are accepted without verification, leaving corrupt on-disk metadata (e.g., a garbage refcount btree level) in memory. Trigger: mounting a crafted XFS image whose dirty-log buffer has an older LSN than the corrupt on-disk buffer. Consequence: later refcount recovery builds an oversized cursor and reads out of bounds; the crash here is a read, not a write, so out-of-bounds write is not directly demonstrated.

commit_msg:
The syzbot fuzzer found a bug in the p54 USB wireless driver.  The
issue involves a race between disconnect and the firmware-loader
callback routine, and it has several aspects.

One big problem is that when the firmware can't be loaded, the
callback routine tries to unbind the driver from the USB _device_ (by
calling device_release_driver) instead of from the USB _interface_ to
which it is actually bound (by calling usb_driver_release_interface).

The race involves access to the private data structure.  The driver's
disconnect handler waits for a completion that is signalled by the
firmware-loader callback routine.  As soon as the completion is
signalled, you have to assume that the private data structure may have
been deallocated by the disconnect handler -- even if the firmware was
loaded without errors.  However, the callback routine does access the
private data several times after that point.

Another problem is that, in order to ensure that the USB device
structure hasn't been freed when the callback routine runs, the driver
takes a reference to it.  This isn't good enough any more, because now
that the callback routine calls usb_driver_release_interface, it has
to ensure that the interface structure hasn't been freed.

Finally, the driver takes an unnecessary reference to the USB device
structure in the probe function and drops the reference in the
disconnect handler.  This extra reference doesn't accomplish anything,
because the USB core already guarantees that a device structure won't
be deallocated while a driver is still bound to any of its interfaces.

To fix these problems, this patch makes the following changes:

	Call usb_driver_release_interface() rather than
	device_release_driver().

	Don't signal the completion until after the important
	information has been copied out of the private data structure,
	and don't refer to the private data at all thereafter.

	Lock udev (the interface's parent) before unbinding the driver
	instead of locking udev->parent.

	During the firmware loading process, take a reference to the
	USB interface instead of the USB device.

	Don't take an unnecessary reference to the device during probe
	(and then don't drop it during disconnect).

Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+200d4bb11b23d929335f@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Acked-by: Christian Lamparter <chunkeey@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tusb_put_dev(interface_to_usbdev(intf));'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.1. There is a use-after-free caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/net/wireless/intersil/p54/p54usb.c driver.

code_evidence: p54u_disconnect waits for the firmware-loader completion (line 8), then unregisters and frees the common device state (lines 9, 12). The callback that signals fw_wait_load may still access priv after the completion is signaled, while this handler proceeds to p54_free_common(dev), which frees that private data. The deleted usb_put_dev line (10) also reflects the driver's flawed reference management around the device/interface lifetime.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees the shared private structure after waiting on a completion that does not guarantee the callback has stopped using it, so subsequent callback accesses reference freed memory. This is a lifetime/ordering flaw, not merely a double free or null dereference, matching CWE-416.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the completion is signaled by the firmware-loader callback before it finishes referencing priv, so disconnect can free the private structure while the callback still uses it. Trigger: firmware load completion racing with USB disconnect. Consequence: use-after-free of the p54u private data, leading to memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
gnttab: split maptrack lock to make it fulfill its purpose again

The way the lock is currently being used in get_maptrack_handle(), it
protects only the maptrack limit: The function acts on current's list
only, so races on list accesses are impossible even without the lock.

Otoh list access races are possible between __get_maptrack_handle() and
put_maptrack_handle(), due to the invocation of the former for other
than current from steal_maptrack_handle(). Introduce a per-vCPU lock
for list accesses to become race free again. This lock will be
uncontended except when it becomes necessary to take the steal path,
i.e. in the common case there should be no meaningful performance
impact.

When in get_maptrack_handle adds a stolen entry to a fresh, empty,
freelist, we think that there is probably no concurrency.  However,
this is not a fast path and adding the locking there makes the code
clearly correct.

Also, while we are here: the stolen maptrack_entry's tail pointer was
not properly set.  Set it.

This is CVE-2017-12136 / XSA-228.

Reported-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <Ian.Jackson@eu.citrix.com>

description: Race condition in the grant table code in Xen 4.6.x through 4.9.x allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (free list corruption and host crash) or gain privileges on the host via vectors involving maptrack free list handling.

code_evidence: The fast path calls __get_maptrack_handle() and returns without ever taking the per-vCPU freelist lock, so list accesses are unsynchronized against concurrent put_maptrack_handle()/steal_maptrack_handle().

The steal path reads curr->maptrack_tail and writes curr->maptrack_head without holding a per-vCPU lock; the maptrack_lock only guards the frame limit and is dropped at line 15, leaving the freelist head/tail updates exposed to concurrent modification.

The CAS loop updating curr->maptrack_head is performed under lgt->maptrack_lock, not a per-vCPU freelist lock, so another vCPU operating on the same stolen entry can interleave and corrupt the free list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic concurrent access to a shared resource (the maptrack free list) with improper synchronization: the required exclusive access is not enforced, allowing an interfering code sequence to modify the list mid-update. CWE-362 directly matches this race-condition pattern; list corruption and crash follow as consequences.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The maptrack free list (head/tail and entry refs) is shared across vCPUs via steal_maptrack_handle(), but the code protects it with the global maptrack_lock only around the frame limit and does not serialize list mutations in the fast and steal paths. Concurrent access can corrupt the free list, leading to host crash (DoS) or privilege escalation.

TFLite: Error out when the graph has a recurion.

Recursion is currently unsupported.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 371708957

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context,', '                 op_data->cond_subgraph_index != op_data->body_subgraph_index);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. TFlite graphs must not have loops between nodes. However, this condition was not checked and an attacker could craft models that would result in infinite loop during evaluation. In certain cases, the infinite loop would be replaced by stack overflow due to too many recursive calls. For example, the `While` implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/106d8f4fb89335a2c52d7c895b7a7485465ca8d9/tensorflow/lite/kernels/while.cc) could be tricked into a scneario where both the body and the loop subgraphs are the same. Evaluating one of the subgraphs means calling the `Eval` function for the other and this quickly exhaust all stack space. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range. Please consult our security guide(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/master/SECURITY.md) for more information regarding the security model and how to contact us with issues and questions.

code_evidence: Prepare validates that both subgraph indices are within bounds (lines 7-8), then the deleted guard on lines 9-10 would have rejected the case where cond_subgraph_index equals body_subgraph_index. In the patched function this equality check is gone, so a model whose While condition and body reference the same subgraph passes preparation and proceeds to allocate/evaluate that subgraph.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the function fails to reject a self-referential subgraph configuration, allowing uncontrolled recursion during evaluation. This is not merely a bounds issue (CWE-125/787); the indices are bounded, but the equality constraint that prevents recursive re-entry is absent.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the missing constraint that the cond and body subgraph indices must differ. Trigger: a crafted TFLite model sets both indices to the same subgraph. Consequence: evaluating the While op re-enters the same subgraph, producing unbounded recursion that exhausts the stack (DoS), as described in the commit.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-sccp.c had an infinite loop that was addressed by using a correct integer data type.

code_evidence: The offset parameter is declared as guint16 (line 3), an unsigned 16-bit type. It is passed directly to tvb_new_subset_length(tvb, offset, parameter_length) (line 23), which uses it as a signed byte offset. A 16-bit value above 32767 is interpreted as negative when the callee treats the offset as signed, so the subset offset becomes invalid and offset-advancing loops in the caller cannot progress.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit and description attribute the flaw to an incorrect integer type causing an infinite loop; the unsigned offset propagates into offset calculations that never reach an exit condition, matching CWE-835. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a 16-bit unsigned field is used as an offset without sign/range validation. Trigger: crafted SCCP packet with a large 16-bit offset value. Supported consequence: the offset is treated as negative downstream, causing iteration that cannot terminate (DoS resource consumption).

commit_msg:
index: convert `read_entry` to return entry size via an out-param

The function `read_entry` does not conform to our usual coding style of
returning stuff via the out parameter and to use the return value for
reporting errors. Due to most of our code conforming to that pattern, it
has become quite natural for us to actually return `-1` in case there is
any error, which has also slipped in with commit 5625d86b9 (index:
support index v4, 2016-05-17). As the function returns an `size_t` only,
though, the return value is wrapped around, causing the caller of
`read_tree` to continue with an invalid index entry. Ultimately, this
can lead to a double-free.

Improve code and fix the bug by converting the function to return the
index entry size via an out parameter and only using the return value to
indicate errors.

Reported-by: Krishna Ram Prakash R <krp@gtux.in>
Reported-by: Vivek Parikh <viv0411.parikh@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tsize_t entry_size = read_entry(&entry, index, buffer, buffer_size, last);', '\t\t/* 0 bytes read means an object corruption */', '\t\tif (entry_size == 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tsize_t entry_size;', '\t\tif ((error = read_entry(&entry, &entry_size, index, buffer, buffer_size, last)) < 0) {']}
description: Incorrect returning of an error code in the index.c:read_entry() function leads to a double free in libgit2 before v0.26.2, which allows an attacker to cause a denial of service via a crafted repository index file.

code_evidence: read_entry returns a size_t; an internal error is signaled as -1, which wraps to SIZE_MAX, so the entry_size == 0 corruption check does not fire.
entry is then inserted into index->entries at line 37; if that insert fails, index_entry_free(entry) is called and control jumps to done.
After a failed INSERT_IN_MAP, index_entry_free(entry) is called again, but the entry was already inserted into the vector, leaving a dangling pointer that is freed a second time.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the function frees the same heap entry twice: once in the git_vector_insert failure path and again in the INSERT_IN_MAP failure path. The missing error check is the cause, but the directly supported weakness is the double free, not merely improper input validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: read_entry encodes errors in a size_t return value, so the -1 error is wrapped and the invalid-entry guard at line 33 is bypassed. Trigger: a crafted index file makes read_entry fail while entry remains non-NULL; the wrapped size passes the check, and a subsequent insert or map-insert failure frees the entry. Consequence: the entry is freed twice, enabling a double-free denial of service.

commit_msg:
dccp/tcp: fix routing redirect race

As Eric Dumazet pointed out this also needs to be fixed in IPv6.
v2: Contains the IPv6 tcp/Ipv6 dccp patches as well.

We have seen a few incidents lately where a dst_enty has been freed
with a dangling TCP socket reference (sk->sk_dst_cache) pointing to that
dst_entry. If the conditions/timings are right a crash then ensues when the
freed dst_entry is referenced later on. A Common crashing back trace is:

 #8 [] page_fault at ffffffff8163e648
    [exception RIP: __tcp_ack_snd_check+74]
.
.
 #9 [] tcp_rcv_established at ffffffff81580b64
#10 [] tcp_v4_do_rcv at ffffffff8158b54a
#11 [] tcp_v4_rcv at ffffffff8158cd02
#12 [] ip_local_deliver_finish at ffffffff815668f4
#13 [] ip_local_deliver at ffffffff81566bd9
#14 [] ip_rcv_finish at ffffffff8156656d
#15 [] ip_rcv at ffffffff81566f06
#16 [] __netif_receive_skb_core at ffffffff8152b3a2
#17 [] __netif_receive_skb at ffffffff8152b608
#18 [] netif_receive_skb at ffffffff8152b690
#19 [] vmxnet3_rq_rx_complete at ffffffffa015eeaf [vmxnet3]
#20 [] vmxnet3_poll_rx_only at ffffffffa015f32a [vmxnet3]
#21 [] net_rx_action at ffffffff8152bac2
#22 [] __do_softirq at ffffffff81084b4f
#23 [] call_softirq at ffffffff8164845c
#24 [] do_softirq at ffffffff81016fc5
#25 [] irq_exit at ffffffff81084ee5
#26 [] do_IRQ at ffffffff81648ff8

Of course it may happen with other NIC drivers as well.

It's found the freed dst_entry here:

 224 static bool tcp_in_quickack_mode(struct sock *sk)↩
 225 {↩
 226 ▹       const struct inet_connection_sock *icsk = inet_csk(sk);↩
 227 ▹       const struct dst_entry *dst = __sk_dst_get(sk);↩
 228 ↩
 229 ▹       return (dst && dst_metric(dst, RTAX_QUICKACK)) ||↩
 230 ▹       ▹       (icsk->icsk_ack.quick && !icsk->icsk_ack.pingpong);↩
 231 }↩

But there are other backtraces attributed to the same freed dst_entry in
netfilter code as well.

All the vmcores showed 2 significant clues:

- Remote hosts behind the default gateway had always been redirected to a
different gateway. A rtable/dst_entry will be added for that host. Making
more dst_entrys with lower reference counts. Making this more probable.

- All vmcores showed a postitive LockDroppedIcmps value, e.g:

LockDroppedIcmps                  267

A closer look at the tcp_v4_err() handler revealed that do_redirect() will run
regardless of whether user space has the socket locked. This can result in a
race condition where the same dst_entry cached in sk->sk_dst_entry can be
decremented twice for the same socket via:

do_redirect()->__sk_dst_check()-> dst_release().

Which leads to the dst_entry being prematurely freed with another socket
pointing to it via sk->sk_dst_cache and a subsequent crash.

To fix this skip do_redirect() if usespace has the socket locked. Instead let
the redirect take place later when user space does not have the socket
locked.

The dccp/IPv6 code is very similar in this respect, so fixing it there too.

As Eric Garver pointed out the following commit now invalidates routes. Which
can set the dst->obsolete flag so that ipv4_dst_check() returns null and
triggers the dst_release().

Fixes: ceb3320610d6 ("ipv4: Kill routes during PMTU/redirect updates.")
Cc: Eric Garver <egarver@redhat.com>
Cc: Hannes Sowa <hsowa@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Jon Maxwell <jmaxwell37@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tdo_redirect(icmp_skb, sk);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!sock_owned_by_user(sk))', '\t\t\tdo_redirect(icmp_skb, sk);']}
description: Race condition in the audit_log_single_execve_arg function in kernel/auditsc.c in the Linux kernel through 4.7 allows local users to bypass intended character-set restrictions or disrupt system-call auditing by changing a certain string, aka a "double fetch" vulnerability.

code_evidence: The socket is locked with bh_lock_sock(sk) at line 36, and lines 37-40 only record a LINUX_MIB_LOCKDROPPEDICMPS counter when sock_owned_by_user(sk) is true; they do not prevent further handling. The ICMP_REDIRECT case at lines 56-59 then unconditionally calls do_redirect(icmp_skb, sk) even while user space owns the socket, so the redirect path releases/replaces the cached sk_dst_cache without exclusive access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent-access race: a shared resource (sk->sk_dst_cache) is modified by the redirect path while another code sequence holds the socket, violating exclusivity. The missing sock_owned_by_user guard is the synchronization defect, fitting CWE-362 rather than a memory-safety weakness, which is only the downstream consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: do_redirect() manipulates the socket's cached dst_entry without checking whether user space holds the socket lock. Trigger: an ICMP redirect arriving while the socket is owned by user space runs concurrently with user-space operations on the same sk_dst_cache, causing a double dst_release(). Supported consequence: the dst_entry is freed prematurely, leaving a dangling reference that later causes a crash (DoS).

evidence_lines.code:
}
while (*hdr == ' ' || *hdr == '\t');

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser splits headers on '\n' and treats leading-space lines as continuations but does not validate the header content for embedded CR/LF. commit_msg: [http2] delay processing requests upon observing suspicious behavior
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    config->http2.dos_delay = 100; /* 100ms processing delay when observing suspicious behavior */']}
description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

code_evidence: The init function sets HTTP/2 latency-optimization parameters, including min_rtt and max_additional_delay, but the function contains no throttling of request-cancellation/stream-reset processing; the diff only adds a dos_delay default for suspicious behavior.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the weakness is uncontrolled consumption of a limited resource (server processing capacity) via many rapidly cancelled HTTP/2 streams. This is a resource-consumption weakness, not merely an availability impact, and the patch targets that behavior by adding a processing delay.
