commit_msg:
Correctly handle bogusly large chunk sizes

This fixes a denial of service attack vector where bogusly large chunk
sizes in requests could be used to force restarts of the Varnish
server.

This is Varnish Security Vulnerability VSV00001

For more information visit: https://varnish-cache.org/security/VSV00001

Fixes: #2379
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif ((uintmax_t)cl != cll)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (cl < 0 || (uintmax_t)cl != cll)']}
description: An issue was discovered in Varnish HTTP Cache 4.0.1 through 4.0.4, 4.1.0 through 4.1.7, 5.0.0, and 5.1.0 through 5.1.2. A wrong if statement in the varnishd source code means that particular invalid requests from the client can trigger an assert, related to an Integer Overflow. This causes the varnishd worker process to abort and restart, losing the cached contents in the process. An attacker can therefore crash the varnishd worker process on demand and effectively keep it from serving content - a Denial-of-Service attack. The specific source-code filename containing the incorrect statement varies across releases.

code_evidence: strtoumax parses the chunk size into uintmax_t cll (line 46); the syntax check at 47-48 does not bound magnitude. Line 49 casts cll to signed ssize_t cl, and the only guard at 50 compares (uintmax_t)cl != cll, which catches truncation but not a value exceeding SSIZE_MAX that wraps to a negative ssize_t.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits: the unchecked narrowing conversion of an attacker-controlled integer yields a wrapped negative value that violates the function's invariant and crashes the process. The missing cl < 0 constraint is the integer-overflow/wraparound condition; this is distinct from a mere parsing error, which the surrounding checks already handle.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a chunk size larger than SSIZE_MAX is cast from uintmax_t to ssize_t, producing a negative value that still round-trips through the (uintmax_t)cl != cll check. The negative cl is stored in vfe->priv2 (line 52); the later AZ(vfe->priv2) invariant then fires, aborting the worker. Trigger is a client-supplied oversized chunked header; consequence is worker crash/restart, a DoS.

commit_msg:
Avoid dangling ptrs in header and data params for PEM_read_bio_ex

In the event of a failure in PEM_read_bio_ex() we free the buffers we
allocated for the header and data buffers. However we were not clearing
the ptrs stored in *header and *data. Since, on success, the caller is
responsible for freeing these ptrs this can potentially lead to a double
free if the caller frees them even on failure.

Thanks to Dawei Wang for reporting this issue.

Based on a proposed patch by Kurt Roeckx.

CVE-2022-4450

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Hugo Landau <hlandau@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        *header = NULL;', '        *data = NULL;']}
description:
The function PEM_read_bio_ex() reads a PEM file from a BIO and parses and
decodes the "name" (e.g. "CERTIFICATE"), any header data and the payload data.
If the function succeeds then the "name_out", "header" and "data" arguments are
populated with pointers to buffers containing the relevant decoded data. The
caller is responsible for freeing those buffers. It is possible to construct a
PEM file that results in 0 bytes of payload data. In this case PEM_read_bio_ex()
will return a failure code but will populate the header argument with a pointer
to a buffer that has already been freed. If the caller also frees this buffer
then a double free will occur. This will most likely lead to a crash. This
could be exploited by an attacker who has the ability to supply malicious PEM
files for parsing to achieve a denial of service attack.

The functions PEM_read_bio() and PEM_read() are simple wrappers around
PEM_read_bio_ex() and therefore these functions are also directly affected.

These functions are also called indirectly by a number of other OpenSSL
functions including PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() and
SSL_CTX_use_serverinfo_file() which are also vulnerable. Some OpenSSL internal
uses of these functions are not vulnerable because the caller does not free the
header argument if PEM_read_bio_ex() returns a failure code. These locations
include the PEM_read_bio_TYPE() functions as well as the decoders introduced in
OpenSSL 3.0.

The OpenSSL asn1parse command line application is also impacted by this issue.

code_evidence: After allocating *header and *data, the error branch at line 50 frees both buffers via pem_free without resetting the caller-visible pointers *header and *data. The function then goes to 'end' and returns failure with the freed addresses still stored in the out-parameters.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The freed memory addresses remain exposed to the caller, which can free them a second time, matching CWE-415. This is distinct from a simple memory leak: the same allocation is released twice rather than lost.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on allocation failure the code frees *header/*data but leaves the dangling pointers in the caller's out-parameters. Trigger: a PEM input where one of the two pem_malloc calls fails (e.g. 0-byte payload path). Consequence: the caller, which owns these buffers on success and may free them on failure, calls free() again on the same address, causing a double free and likely crash (DoS).

Thanks to Fakhri Zulkifli for reporting it.

The fix switched to dynamic allocation, copying the final prompt in the
static buffer only at the end.

description: Buffer overflow in redis-cli of Redis before 4.0.10 and 5.x before 5.0 RC3 allows an attacker to achieve code execution and escalate to higher privileges via a crafted command line. NOTE: It is unclear whether there are any common situations in which redis-cli is used with, for example, a -h (aka hostname) argument from an untrusted source.

code_evidence: len is set from snprintf/anetFormatAddr return values, which report the length the full formatted host/socket string would require, not the amount actually stored in the fixed config.prompt buffer.
When config.hostsocket is NULL, anetFormatAddr writes into config.prompt and returns the untruncated length; the truncated buffer contents are then treated as if len bytes were valid.

The subsequent snprintf calls at config.prompt+len with sizeof(config.prompt)-len compute a negative or underflowed size when len exceeds sizeof(config.prompt), producing an out-of-bounds write past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes outside the intended boundaries of the fixed config.prompt memory buffer via miscalculated offsets and sizes, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The underlying arithmetic error could also be described as an integer issue, but the supported consequence here is the out-of-bounds buffer write.

evidence_lines.code:
len = anetFormatAddr(config.prompt, sizeof(config.prompt),
config.hostip, config.hostport);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is trusting the return length of a truncating snprintf/anetFormatAddr as the number of bytes written into the fixed-size config.prompt. A crafted long hostname or hostsocket makes len exceed the buffer size, so the pointer arithmetic config.prompt+len and size subtraction sizeof(config.prompt)-len go out of bounds, causing memory corruption that can lead to code execution.

commit_msg:
Handle overflow errors in malformed zchunk files

Thanks to Agostino Sarubbo of Gentoo for the heads up!

Signed-off-by: Jonathan Dieter <jdieter@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if((comp->data_size > comp->data_size + src_size) ||', '       (src_size > comp->data_size + src_size)) {', '        zck_log(ZCK_LOG_ERROR, "Integer overflow when reading data");', '        return false;', '    }']}
description: zchunk before 1.3.2 has multiple integer overflows via malformed zchunk files to lib/comp/comp.c, lib/comp/zstd/zstd.c, lib/dl/multipart.c, or lib/header.c.

code_evidence: Line 6 computes comp->data_size + src_size and passes it directly to zrealloc as the new allocation size, with no prior check that the addition fits in size_t.

Lines 13-15 use the same unchecked sum: memcpy writes src_size bytes at comp->data + comp->data_size, then data_size and data_loc are incremented by src_size. The patch adds the overflow guard before line 6, confirming the sum was previously unvalidated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked size_t addition in the allocation and copy path is exactly CWE-190: the code assumes data_size + src_size is larger than its operands. The overflow then enables out-of-bounds memory modification, which is the downstream consequence rather than the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: comp->data_size + src_size is evaluated in size_t without a wraparound check. Trigger: a malformed zchunk file drives data_size or src_size so the sum wraps to a small value. Consequence: zrealloc allocates a too-small buffer, then memcpy at line 13 writes src_size bytes past it (heap overflow), and the incremented sizes/locations become inconsistent.

commit_msg: Merge pull request from GHSA-8fmx-hqw7-6gmc
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tpj_mutex_unlock(codec_factory.mutex);']}
description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in the C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In various parts of PJSIP, when error/failure occurs, it is found that the function returns without releasing the currently held locks. This could result in a system deadlock, which cause a denial of service for the users. No release has yet been made which contains the linked fix commit. All versions up to an including 2.11.1 are affected. Users may need to manually apply the patch.

code_evidence: Line 12 acquires codec_factory.mutex before scanning codec_desc. When no matching enabled codec is found, lines 25-27 set *p_codec to NULL and return PJMEDIA_CODEC_EUNSUP without unlocking. The success path at line 38 does release the mutex, showing the missing unlock is specific to this early-return branch.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function acquires a mutex and fails to release it on an error path, which is the improper lock acquisition/release behavior described by CWE-667. This is not merely a missing lock; the lock is taken but not balanced on return.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the idx == -1 early return exits the function while codec_factory.mutex is still held. Trigger: a lookup for an encoding name/clock rate/channel count that matches no enabled codec_desc entry. Consequence: subsequent lock attempts on the same mutex block, causing deadlock and denial of service.

commit_msg:
hw/core/loader: Fix possible crash in rom_copy()

Both, "rom->addr" and "addr" are derived from the binary image
that can be loaded with the "-kernel" paramer. The code in
rom_copy() then calculates:

    d = dest + (rom->addr - addr);

and uses "d" as destination in a memcpy() some lines later. Now with
bad kernel images, it is possible that rom->addr is smaller than addr,
thus "rom->addr - addr" gets negative and the memcpy() then tries to
copy contents from the image to a bad memory location. This could
maybe be used to inject code from a kernel image into the QEMU binary,
so we better fix it with an additional sanity check here.

Cc: qemu-stable@nongnu.org
Reported-by: Guangming Liu
Buglink: https://bugs.launchpad.net/qemu/+bug/1844635
Message-Id: <20190925130331.27825-1-thuth@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Huth <thuth@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (rom->addr > end) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (rom->addr > end || rom->addr < addr) {']}
description: rom_copy() in hw/core/loader.c in QEMU 4.0 and 4.1.0 does not validate the relationship between two addresses, which allows attackers to trigger an invalid memory copy operation.

code_evidence: The loop skips ROMs wholly below addr at lines 14-16, but the upper bound check at line 17 only rejects rom->addr > end. When rom->addr < addr, the subtraction at line 20 yields a negative offset, so d = dest + (rom->addr - addr) points before dest. The bounds clamp at lines 23-24 computes l = dest - d, which is positive when d < dest, so the memcpy at line 27 writes l bytes to a location before the destination buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-influenced image data to a pointer computed before the intended destination buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an integer underflow, because the underflowed offset is used directly as a memory write destination.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the missing lower-bound check rom->addr < addr allows a negative offset in the destination pointer computation. Trigger: a loaded kernel image whose ROM address falls below the requested addr. Consequence: memcpy writes before dest, corrupting adjacent memory, potentially enabling code injection or a crash.

Add dissection recursion checks.

Enforce a maximum layer limit in call_dissector_work and
dissector_try_heuristic.

Petri-Dish: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Dario Lombardo <lomato@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
(cherry picked from commit be9bdfda02a2498c6f65122d80e3a8b4235dc7f5)
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/33310
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tDISSECTOR_ASSERT(saved_layers_len < PINFO_LAYER_MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH);']}
description: In Wireshark 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.6.0 to 2.6.8, and 2.4.0 to 2.4.14, the dissection engine could crash. This was addressed in epan/packet.c by restricting the number of layers and consequently limiting recursion.

code_evidence: Line 16 counts current layer depth and lines 17-18 decrement can_desegment but impose no recursion-depth bound before invoking the dissector.
Lines 19-26 push another protocol onto pinfo->layers and increment curr_layer_num on every nested call, so each recursive dissection grows the layer list.
Lines 30-36 call the handle and only unwind layers when len==0; there is no cap on nesting depth, so a self-referential or maliciously nested packet can recurse without limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs recursive dissector invocation without a depth constraint, matching CWE-674's uncontrolled recursion consuming stack/memory. The added assertion in the patch confirms the missing depth limit was the intended fix; this is not merely resource cleanup (CWE-400) but specifically recursion depth.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: call_dissector_work recursively invokes dissectors while only tracking layer count for cleanup, never enforcing a maximum depth. Trigger: a crafted packet whose protocol dissector re-enters call_dissector_work (directly or via sub-dissectors). Consequence: unbounded stack recursion and layer-list growth, leading to resource exhaustion and a crash of the dissection engine.

commit_msg:
s390/mm: four page table levels vs. fork

The fork of a process with four page table levels is broken since
git commit 6252d702c5311ce9 "[S390] dynamic page tables."

All new mm contexts are created with three page table levels and
an asce limit of 4TB. If the parent has four levels dup_mmap will
add vmas to the new context which are outside of the asce limit.
The subsequent call to copy_page_range will walk the three level
page table structure of the new process with non-zero pgd and pud
indexes. This leads to memory clobbers as the pgd_index *and* the
pud_index is added to the mm->pgd pointer without a pgd_deref
in between.

The init_new_context() function is selecting the number of page
table levels for a new context. The function is used by mm_init()
which in turn is called by dup_mm() and mm_alloc(). These two are
used by fork() and exec(). The init_new_context() function can
distinguish the two cases by looking at mm->context.asce_limit,
for fork() the mm struct has been copied and the number of page
table levels may not change. For exec() the mm_alloc() function
set the new mm structure to zero, in this case a three-level page
table is created as the temporary stack space is located at
STACK_TOP_MAX = 4TB.

This fixes CVE-2016-2143.

Reported-by: Marcin Kościelnicki <koriakin@0x04.net>
Reviewed-by: Heiko Carstens <heiko.carstens@de.ibm.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Martin Schwidefsky <schwidefsky@de.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tspin_lock_init(&mm->context.list_lock);', '\tINIT_LIST_HEAD(&mm->context.pgtable_list);', '\tINIT_LIST_HEAD(&mm->context.gmap_list);', '\treturn (pgd_t *) crst_table_alloc(mm);'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned long *table = crst_table_alloc(mm);', '', '\tif (!table)', '\t\treturn NULL;', '\tif (mm->context.asce_limit == (1UL << 31)) {', '\t\t/* Forking a compat process with 2 page table levels */', '\t\tif (!pgtable_pmd_page_ctor(virt_to_page(table))) {', '\t\t\tcrst_table_free(mm, table);', '\t\t\treturn NULL;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '\treturn (pgd_t *) table;']}
description: The fork implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.5 on s390 platforms mishandles the case of four page-table levels, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted application, related to arch/s390/include/asm/mmu_context.h and arch/s390/include/asm/pgalloc.h.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown pgd_alloc function only initializes context lists and allocates a page table; it contains no input validation of page-table level or asce_limit, so it does not directly support CWE-20.

commit_msg:
Add boundary check for 802.11 decryption

Fixed stack-based buffer overflow when the frame length exceeds 8KB.

Bug: 11790
Change-Id: I20db8901765a7660e587057e955d4fb5a8645574
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/12237
Petri-Dish: Anders Broman <a.broman58@gmail.com>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot <buildbot-no-reply@wireshark.org>
Reviewed-by: Peter Wu <peter@lekensteyn.nl>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    }', '', '    /* Assume that the decrypt_data field is at least this size. */', '    if (tot_len > AIRPDCAP_MAX_CAPLEN) {', '        AIRPDCAP_DEBUG_PRINT_LINE("AirPDcapPacketProcess", "length too large", AIRPDCAP_DEBUG_LEVEL_3);', '        return AIRPDCAP_RET_UNSUCCESS;']}
description: The AirPDcapPacketProcess function in epan/crypt/airpdcap.c in the 802.11 dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.9 and 2.0.x before 2.0.1 does not validate the relationship between the total length and the capture length, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer overflow and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: tmp_data is a fixed stack buffer of AIRPDCAP_MAX_CAPLEN (line 13). When no caller buffer is supplied, decrypt_data is redirected to tmp_data (lines 66-69), and *decrypt_len is set to the attacker-controlled tot_len (line 71) before memcpy copies that many bytes into decrypt_data (line 72).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts external packet length metadata (tot_len) and uses it to size a copy without validating it against the destination capacity, which is improper input validation of a derived size property. The validated minimum-length check (line 34) shows only one bound is enforced; the maximum bound is absent, so CWE-20 fits as the class-level input-validation weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: tot_len is trusted as the copy size without any upper-bound check against the size of the destination buffer. When decrypt_data is NULL, the destination is the 8KB stack array tmp_data, so a crafted 802.11 data frame whose tot_len exceeds AIRPDCAP_MAX_CAPLEN makes memcpy write past the array, corrupting stack memory and crashing the application. The missing constraint is the relationship between the total length and the capacity of the decrypt buffer.

description: A null pointer dereference vulnerability exists in gpac 1.1.0-DEV in the gf_node_get_tag function, which causes a segmentation fault and application crash.

code_evidence: In case GF_SG_VRML_SFSCRIPT the function passes the possibly NULL node parameter directly to SFScript_Parse at line 159; no NULL check guards this call, unlike other cases such as line 120 which returns GF_BAD_PARAM when node is NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because a pointer expected to be valid (node) is passed to a callee that dereferences it without a NULL check, leading to a crash. This is a direct NULL dereference rather than an out-of-bounds or type-confusion issue.

SFScript_Parse is invoked with that NULL node and dereferences it internally, causing a segmentation fault and application crash. The root cause is the missing NULL guard before the call; the consequence is a denial-of-service crash.

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

Fixes: 52feb444a903 ("NFC: Extend netlink interface for LTO, RW, and MIUX parameters support")
Fixes: c7aa12252f51 ("NFC: Take a reference on the LLCP local pointer when creating a socket")
Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Reviewed-by: Simon Horman <simon.horman@corigine.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: nfc_llcp_find_local(dev) returns local without acquiring a reference; the NULL check only guards a missing entry, not lifetime.
On alloc_skb failure the function returns -ENOMEM directly, so a local obtained at line 6 is never released on this error path.

The success path passes local to nfc_data_exchange and returns without nfc_llcp_local_put(local), leaving the reference/lifetime balance to the callee while local is still dereferenced via local->target_idx.

nfc_llcp_recv, local);

commit_msg:
floppy_revalidate() doesn't perform any error handling on lock_fdc()
result. lock_fdc() might actually be interrupted by a signal (it waits for
fdc becoming non-busy interruptibly). In such case, floppy_revalidate()
proceeds as if it had claimed the lock, but it fact it doesn't.

In case of multiple threads trying to open("/dev/fdX"), this leads to
serious corruptions all over the place, because all of a sudden there is
no critical section protection (that'd otherwise be guaranteed by locked
fd) whatsoever.

While at this, fix the fact that the 'interruptible' parameter to
lock_fdc() doesn't make any sense whatsoever, because we always wait
interruptibly anyway.

Most of the lock_fdc() callsites do properly handle error (and propagate
EINTR), but floppy_revalidate() and floppy_check_events() don't. Fix this.

Spotted by 'syzkaller' tool.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive, true))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive, true))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive, true))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive, true))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive, true))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive, true))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive, true))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive))', '\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive))']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernels implementation of the floppy disk drive controller driver software. The impact of this issue is lessened by the fact that the default permissions on the floppy device (/dev/fd0) are restricted to root. If the permissions on the device have changed the impact changes greatly. In the default configuration root (or equivalent) permissions are required to attack this flaw.

code_evidence: FDEJECT calls lock_fdc(drive, true); on failure it returns -EINTR before fd_eject, so this path does check the lock result.
FDCLRPRM likewise returns -EINTR when lock_fdc fails, guarding the subsequent current_type/floppy_sizes updates.
FDPOLLDRVSTAT checks lock_fdc and poll_drive but falls through into FDGETDRVSTAT, which sets outparam = UDRS and later copies it out without any lock held.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because a shared resource (UDRS) is read in fd_copyout without holding the lock that other code sequences use, violating exclusivity. This is improper synchronization, not a lock-result oversight: the FDEJECT/FDCLRPRM branches do check lock_fdc, so the race arises from the unlocked FDGETDRVSTAT read path rather than from ignoring the lock return value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The ioctl handler releases the FDC lock (process_fd_request) or never holds it on the FDGETDRVSTAT fall-through path, yet FDGETDRVSTAT reads UDRS and fd_copyout copies that shared drive-status structure to user space. A concurrent open()/revalidate or another thread mutating UDRS can interleave with this read, so the copyout observes a torn or stale structure; the root cause is missing exclusive access around the shared UDRS read, and the consequence is a data race that can corrupt state or leak inconsistent data.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/519
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      profile=BlobToStringInfo((const unsigned char *) NULL,cin.file.user_length);'], 'added_lines': ['      if (cin.file.user_length > GetBlobSize(image))', '        ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"ImproperImageHeader");', '      profile=BlobToStringInfo((const unsigned char *) NULL,', '        cin.file.user_length);']}
description: The ReadCINImage function in coders/cin.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.9-0 and 7.x before 7.0.6-1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 60 reads cin.file.user_length from the file header without validating it. At line 294 this attacker-controlled length is passed directly to BlobToStringInfo, which allocates a StringInfo of that size; lines 297-299 then read that many bytes into it. The only check is for a NULL return at line 295, which does not bound the requested size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the function allocates a resource (a buffer via BlobToStringInfo) on behalf of an untrusted file without imposing any limit or throttle on its size, enabling memory-consumption DoS. This is distinct from a buffer overflow (CWE-787): the issue is unbounded allocation, not an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unvalidated file-header field (user_length) drives an allocation sized by attacker input with no upper bound. Trigger: a crafted CIN whose user_length is enormous causes BlobToStringInfo to attempt a huge allocation, consuming memory; consequence is memory exhaustion/DoS. The NULL check only handles allocation failure, not excessive size.

commit_msg:
Bug: finalizers can be called with an invalid stack

The call to 'checkstackGC' can run finalizers, which will find an
inconsistent CallInfo, as 'ci' is half updated at the point of call.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      checkstackGC(L, fsize);'], 'added_lines': ['      checkstackGCp(L, fsize - delta, func);']}
description: In Lua 5.4.3, an erroneous finalizer called during a tail call leads to a heap-based buffer over-read.

code_evidence: ci->func is decremented by delta and the function/arguments are moved down into the new frame via setobjs2s. checkstackGC is then called while ci remains only partially updated (ci->top and savedpc not yet set), so any finalizer run by GC observes an inconsistent CallInfo and can over-read the stack.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale half-updated CallInfo causes out-of-bounds memory access during finalizer execution; the observable impact is a heap buffer over-read. The fix moves checkstackGCp before the frame mutation so finalizers see a consistent state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: checkstackGC may trigger finalizers at a point where 'ci' is half-updated (func moved, top/pc stale). Trigger: an erroneous finalizer executed during a tail call. Consequence: heap-based buffer over-read from the inconsistent frame state.

commit_msg:
PR25823, Use after free in bfd_hash_lookup

	PR 25823
	* peXXigen.c (_bfd_XXi_swap_sym_in <C_SECTION>): Don't use a
	pointer into strings that may be freed for section name, always
	allocate a new string.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t  if (name == namebuf)', '\t      name = (const char *) bfd_alloc (abfd, strlen (namebuf) + 1);', '\t      if (name == NULL)', '\t\t{', '\t\t  _bfd_error_handler (_("%pB: out of memory creating name for empty section"),', '\t\t\t\t      abfd);', '\t\t  return;', '\t\t}', '\t      strcpy ((char *) name, namebuf);', '\t  sec = bfd_make_section_anyway_with_flags (abfd, name, flags);'], 'added_lines': ['\t  size_t name_len;', '\t  char *sec_name;', '\t  name_len = strlen (name) + 1;', '\t  sec_name = bfd_alloc (abfd, name_len);', '\t  if (sec_name == NULL)', '\t      _bfd_error_handler (_("%pB: out of memory creating name "', '\t\t\t\t    "for empty section"), abfd);', '\t      return;', '\t  memcpy (sec_name, name, name_len);', '\t  sec = bfd_make_section_anyway_with_flags (abfd, sec_name, flags);']}
description: A use after free issue exists in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd) in GNU Binutils 2.34 in bfd_hash_lookup, as demonstrated in nm-new, that can cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 30 obtains name from _bfd_coff_internal_syment_name, which may return a pointer into a string table. Line 38 uses name for lookup. Line 50 checks name == namebuf; only in that case (line 52) is a fresh allocation copied via strcpy (line 59). Otherwise name still points into the string table and is passed to bfd_make_section_anyway_with_flags (line 62), which may store or free it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reuses a pointer to memory that may already have been freed, matching CWE-416. Unlike a simple dangling read, this pointer is retained and dereferenced in a later section-creation path, so use-after-free is the appropriate label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: when name is not namebuf, the function passes a pointer into a possibly freed string-table region to bfd_make_section_anyway_with_flags. Trigger: crafted symbol with C_SECTION whose name comes from the string table; the referenced buffer is freed, then reused. Consequence: use-after-free leading to crash/DoS in bfd_hash_lookup.

KVM: x86: Avoid theoretical NULL pointer dereference in kvm_irq_delivery_to_apic_fast()

When kvm_irq_delivery_to_apic_fast() is called with APIC_DEST_SELF
shorthand, 'src' must not be NULL. Crash the VM with KVM_BUG_ON()
instead of crashing the host.

Signed-off-by: Vitaly Kuznetsov <vkuznets@redhat.com>
Message-Id: <20220325132140.25650-3-vkuznets@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>

description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s KVM when attempting to set a SynIC IRQ. This issue makes it possible for a misbehaving VMM to write to SYNIC/STIMER MSRs, causing a NULL pointer dereference. This flaw allows an unprivileged local attacker on the host to issue specific ioctl calls, causing a kernel oops condition that results in a denial of service.

code_evidence: In the APIC_DEST_SELF branch, line 11 dereferences 'src' via src->vcpu without any prior check that 'src' is non-NULL; line 12 then returns.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the code dereferences a pointer it expects to be valid but which can be NULL. This is a direct NULL dereference rather than an uninitialized-pointer or buffer issue, matching the target weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function assumes 'src' is valid whenever shorthand equals APIC_DEST_SELF, but callers can pass a NULL 'src' (e.g., a misbehaving VMM triggering SynIC IRQ handling). Dereferencing src->vcpu then causes a NULL pointer dereference, crashing the host kernel and yielding denial of service. The root cause is the missing validity check on 'src'; the crash is the consequence.

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow in TFLite concat

PiperOrigin-RevId: 371013841
Change-Id: I6a4782ce7ca753e23ff31e7fb6aeb7f9d412cd29
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        // Avoid integer overflow in sum_axis below', '        TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, t->dims->data[axis] >= 0);', '        TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, t->dims->data[axis] <=', '                                    std::numeric_limits<int>::max() - sum_axis);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The TFLite implementation of concatenation is vulnerable to an integer overflow issue(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/7b7352a724b690b11bfaae2cd54bc3907daf6285/tensorflow/lite/kernels/concatenation.cc#L70-L76). An attacker can craft a model such that the dimensions of one of the concatenation input overflow the values of `int`. TFLite uses `int` to represent tensor dimensions, whereas TF uses `int64`. Hence, valid TF models can trigger an integer overflow when converted to TFLite format. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: sum_axis is initialized from t0->dims->data[axis] and accumulates each input's axis dimension via sum_axis += t->dims->data[axis] in a loop over all num_inputs.
The accumulated sum_axis is written directly into output_size->data[d] for the concatenation axis and used to create/resize the output tensor.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits: the accumulation sum_axis += t->dims->data[axis] can exceed int range and wrap, and the wrapped result is used as a size for tensor allocation, matching integer overflow affecting allocation/size. It is not merely a bounds check issue; the calculation itself overflows.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sum_axis is an int and each per-input axis dimension is added without any bound check. With many inputs or large dimension values (valid in int64 TF models), the sum wraps to a small or negative value. The wrapped sum_axis then becomes the output dimension, causing an undersized allocation while later concatenation writes the true larger data, leading to memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

Signed-off-by: Jeff King <peff@peff.net>
Signed-off-by: Junio C Hamano <gitster@pobox.com>

We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.6.1, TensorFlow 2.5.2, and TensorFlow 2.4.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

errors::InvalidArgument("scale must be 1-dimensional",

Trigger: a caller supplies a one-dimensional per-channel tensor shorter than the channel dimension. commit_msg:
Fix the race condition between the following two flows that run in
parallel:

1. l2cap_reassemble_sdu -> chan->ops->recv (l2cap_sock_recv_cb) ->
   __sock_queue_rcv_skb.

2. bt_sock_recvmsg -> skb_recv_datagram, skb_free_datagram.

An SKB can be queued by the first flow and immediately dequeued and
freed by the second flow, therefore the callers of l2cap_reassemble_sdu
can't use the SKB after that function returns. However, some places
continue accessing struct l2cap_ctrl that resides in the SKB's CB for a
short time after l2cap_reassemble_sdu returns, leading to a
use-after-free condition (the stack trace is below, line numbers for
kernel 5.19.8).

Fix it by keeping a local copy of struct l2cap_ctrl.

description: A vulnerability classified as critical was found in Linux Kernel. Affected by this vulnerability is the function l2cap_reassemble_sdu of the file net/bluetooth/l2cap_core.c of the component Bluetooth. The manipulation leads to use after free. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The associated identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211087.

code_evidence: l2cap_stream_rx reads control->txseq in the classify call at line 6 and again after l2cap_reassemble_sdu at lines 25-26. l2cap_reassemble_sdu (line 12) can queue the skb, and a concurrent bt_sock_recvmsg can dequeue and free it, invalidating the control pointer that resides in the skb CB before the later reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function assumes exclusive access to the skb/control shared with the concurrent receive path, so a timing window lets another sequence free and modify the shared resource. This is improper synchronization on a shared resource (CWE-362); the use-after-free is the downstream consequence, not the root weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: control points into the skb CB, but the function re-reads control->txseq after a call that can hand the skb to another thread that frees it. Trigger: concurrent recvmsg path dequeues and frees the skb between the reassemble call and the later reads; the stale read yields a use-after-free. Consequence: freed memory is read (and seq state written from stale data).

commit_msg:
XRA: Fix an infinite loop

C compilers don't care what size a value was on the wire. Use
naturally-sized ints, including in dissect_message_channel_mb where we
would otherwise overflow and loop infinitely.

Fixes #19100
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  guint32 tlv_index =0;'], 'added_lines': ['  unsigned tlv_index = 0;']}
description: XRA dissector infinite loop in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.5 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.13 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: tlv_index is a 32-bit guint32 loop counter compared against the guint16 tlv_length in the while condition, and at line 30 it is incremented by the attacker-controlled length byte; the counter can wrap around 2^32 and the exit condition tlv_index < tlv_length is then never reached.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The while loop's exit condition cannot be reached once the unsigned counter wraps, which is exactly CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. This is a loop-termination flaw, not merely an integer overflow; the overflow is the cause and the infinite loop is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop index type (guint32) is narrower than the arithmetic needed, so tlv_index += length can overflow and wrap below tlv_length. Trigger: a crafted packet where accumulated increments push tlv_index past UINT32_MAX. The while condition remains true, so the dissector loops indefinitely, consuming CPU and causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
commit b86dab054059b970111b5516ae548efaae5b3aae upstream.

When k_ascii is invoked several times in a row there is a potential for
signed integer overflow:

UBSAN: Undefined behaviour in drivers/tty/vt/keyboard.c:888:19 signed integer overflow:
10 * 1111111111 cannot be represented in type 'int'
CPU: 0 PID: 0 Comm: swapper/0 Not tainted 5.6.11 #1
Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (i440FX + PIIX, 1996), BIOS Bochs 01/01/2011
Call Trace:
 <IRQ>
 __dump_stack lib/dump_stack.c:77 [inline]
 dump_stack+0xce/0x128 lib/dump_stack.c:118
 ubsan_epilogue+0xe/0x30 lib/ubsan.c:154
 handle_overflow+0xdc/0xf0 lib/ubsan.c:184
 __ubsan_handle_mul_overflow+0x2a/0x40 lib/ubsan.c:205
 k_ascii+0xbf/0xd0 drivers/tty/vt/keyboard.c:888
 kbd_keycode drivers/tty/vt/keyboard.c:1477 [inline]
 kbd_event+0x888/0x3be0 drivers/tty/vt/keyboard.c:1495

While it can be worked around by using check_mul_overflow()/
check_add_overflow(), it is better to introduce a separate flag to
signal that number pad is being used to compose a symbol, and
change type of the accumulator from signed to unsigned, thus
avoiding undefined behavior when it overflows.

Reported-by: Kyungtae Kim <kt0755@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Dmitry Torokhov <dmitry.torokhov@gmail.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (up_flag && shift_state != old_state && npadch != -1) {', '\t\t\tto_utf8(vc, npadch);', '\t\t\tput_queue(vc, npadch & 0xff);', '\t\tnpadch = -1;'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (up_flag && shift_state != old_state && npadch_active) {', '\t\t\tto_utf8(vc, npadch_value);', '\t\t\tput_queue(vc, npadch_value & 0xff);', '\t\tnpadch_active = false;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel 4.4 through 5.7.1. drivers/tty/vt/keyboard.c has an integer overflow if k_ascii is called several times in a row, aka CID-b86dab054059. NOTE: Members in the community argue that the integer overflow does not lead to a security issue in this case.

code_evidence: The kludge block tests the signed accumulator npadch != -1 and, when a key-up changes shift_state, passes npadch to to_utf8() or masks it with put_queue(vc, npadch & 0xff), then resets npadch = -1. The accumulator is not bounded here; it is built by the caller k_ascii across repeated invocations, so this function consumes the possibly wrapped signed value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the weakness is a signed integer overflow/wraparound of the npadch accumulator that this function reads and flushes; the function's use of the wrapped value without validation is the downstream effect of the unchecked arithmetic. It is not CWE-191 (underflow) or a buffer overflow, since no array index or length derived from the value is shown here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the number-pad accumulator is a signed int whose value is multiplied/added by k_ascii on every keypress without a range check. Trigger: k_ascii is invoked repeatedly so the signed int overflows (undefined behavior, e.g. 10*1111111111). Here the accumulated value is flushed via to_utf8()/put_queue() and masked with 0xff, so the supported consequence is an incorrect/undefined character emitted and potential execution-logic instability, not a demonstrated memory-safety violation.

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Harden slave timer list handling

A slave timer instance might be still accessible in a racy way while
operating the master instance as it lacks of locking.  Since the
master operation is mostly protected with timer->lock, we should cope
with it while changing the slave instance, too.  Also, some linked
lists (active_list and ack_list) of slave instances aren't unlinked
immediately at stopping or closing, and this may lead to unexpected
accesses.

This patch tries to address these issues.  It adds spin lock of
timer->lock (either from master or slave, which is equivalent) in a
few places.  For avoiding a deadlock, we ensure that the global
slave_active_lock is always locked at first before each timer lock.

Also, ack and active_list of slave instances are properly unlinked at
snd_timer_stop() and snd_timer_close().

Last but not least, remove the superfluous call of _snd_timer_stop()
at removing slave links.  This is a noop, and calling it may confuse
readers wrt locking.  Further cleanup will follow in a later patch.

Actually we've got reports of use-after-free by syzkaller fuzzer, and
this hopefully fixes these issues.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tspin_lock(&master->timer->lock);', '\t\t\tspin_unlock(&master->timer->lock);']}
description: sound/core/timer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 employs a locking approach that does not consider slave timer instances, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (race condition, use-after-free, and system crash) via a crafted ioctl call.

code_evidence: The function links a slave timer instance into the master's slave_list_head and then, under only slave_active_lock, assigns slave->master and slave->timer and conditionally adds slave->active_list to master->slave_active_head. The master's timer->lock is not held while these fields and lists are mutated, so another thread operating the master timer can concurrently read or modify the same slave fields and active list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent sequence lacking proper synchronization on a shared resource (the slave timer instance and its lists), matching CWE-362. The added spin_lock(&master->timer->lock) in the patch confirms the missing exclusivity; it is not merely a logic error or plain memory bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the slave instance's master/timer pointers and active_list are updated without the master timer->lock, so the update is not exclusive against master-timer operations. Trigger: a crafted ioctl that races slave attach (snd_timer_check_master) with master timer start/stop/close. Consequence: inconsistent list state and use-after-free, leading to crash or DoS.

commit_msg:
iso9660: Fail when expected Rockridge extensions is missing

A corrupted or malicious ISO9660 image can cause read_CE() to loop
forever.

read_CE() calls parse_rockridge(), expecting a Rockridge extension
to be read. However, parse_rockridge() is structured as a while
loop starting with a sanity check, and if the sanity check fails
before the loop has run, the function returns ARCHIVE_OK without
advancing the position in the file. This causes read_CE() to retry
indefinitely.

Make parse_rockridge() return ARCHIVE_WARN if it didn't read an
extension. As someone with no real knowledge of the format, this
seems more apt than ARCHIVE_FATAL, but both the call-sites escalate
it to a fatal error immediately anyway.

Found with a combination of AFL, afl-rb (FairFuzz) and qsym.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn (ARCHIVE_OK);'], 'added_lines': ['\tint entry_seen = 0;', '\t\tentry_seen = 1;', '', '\tif (entry_seen)', '\t\treturn (ARCHIVE_OK);', '\telse {', '\t\tarchive_set_error(&a->archive, ARCHIVE_ERRNO_FILE_FORMAT,', '\t\t\t\t  "Tried to parse Rockridge extensions, but none found");', '\t\treturn (ARCHIVE_WARN);', '\t}']}
description: libarchive version commit 5a98dcf8a86364b3c2c469c85b93647dfb139961 onwards (version v2.8.0 onwards) contains a CWE-835: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop') vulnerability in ISO9660 parser, archive_read_support_format_iso9660.c, read_CE()/parse_rockridge() that can result in DoS by infinite loop. This attack appears to be exploitable via the victim opening a specially crafted ISO9660 file.

code_evidence: The while loop is guarded by a sanity check on p, p[0], p[1], p[2] and p[2] bounds; if any condition fails before the first iteration, the body (including the p += p[2] advance at line 120) never runs.
After the loop, the function unconditionally returns ARCHIVE_OK at line 122 without indicating that no Rockridge entry was parsed or that p was not advanced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a loop whose termination depends on parse_rockridge() advancing the position; when it does not advance yet reports success, the caller's retry loop has no reachable exit, matching CWE-835's infinite-loop with unreachable exit condition. This is a missing-progress/success-signaling flaw, not a buffer or bounds error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: parse_rockridge() returns ARCHIVE_OK even when the leading sanity check fails and no entry is consumed, leaving the caller's file position unchanged. Trigger: a crafted/corrupt ISO9660 image whose CE area lacks a valid Rockridge signature. Consequence: read_CE() retries parse_rockridge() indefinitely, causing CPU-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg:
tun: call dev_get_valid_name() before register_netdevice()

register_netdevice() could fail early when we have an invalid
dev name, in which case ->ndo_uninit() is not called. For tun
device, this is a problem because a timer etc. are already
initialized and it expects ->ndo_uninit() to clean them up.

We could move these initializations into a ->ndo_init() so
that register_netdevice() knows better, however this is still
complicated due to the logic in tun_detach().

Therefore, I choose to just call dev_get_valid_name() before
register_netdevice(), which is quicker and much easier to audit.
And for this specific case, it is already enough.

Fixes: 96442e42429e ("tuntap: choose the txq based on rxq")
Reported-by: Dmitry Alexeev <avekceeb@gmail.com>
Cc: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
Cc: "Michael S. Tsirkin" <mst@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\terr = dev_get_valid_name(net, dev, name);', '\t\tif (err)', '\t\t\tgoto err_free_dev;']}
description: In the tun subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.14, dev_get_valid_name is not called before register_netdevice. This allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and panic) via an ioctl(TUNSETIFF) call with a dev name containing a / character. This is similar to CVE-2013-4343.

code_evidence: The user-supplied ifr->ifr_name is passed as the device name to alloc_netdev_mqs() without prior validation (lines 53-57), and the resulting dev is only checked for allocation failure (lines 58-59). register_netdevice() at line 95 can then fail on an invalid name (e.g., containing '/'), and the error path at lines 96-97 jumps to err_detach without the initialization/cleanup symmetry needed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described consequence is a NULL pointer dereference causing a panic, matching CWE-476. The weakness is the missing name-validation constraint that lets register_netdevice() fail after partial initialization, rather than a plain input-validation flaw; the dereference of invalid state is the supported impact.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the device name from the ioctl is used to allocate the net_device and passed to register_netdevice() without dev_get_valid_name() validation. Trigger: a TUNSETIFF ioctl whose ifr_name contains an invalid character such as '/'. register_netdevice() fails early before ndo_uninit(), so the already-initialized timer/state is not cleaned up, leading to a NULL pointer dereference and kernel panic (DoS).

commit_msg:
sched/fair: Fix low cpu usage with high throttling by removing expiration of cpu-local slices

It has been observed, that highly-threaded, non-cpu-bound applications
running under cpu.cfs_quota_us constraints can hit a high percentage of
periods throttled while simultaneously not consuming the allocated
amount of quota. This use case is typical of user-interactive non-cpu
bound applications, such as those running in kubernetes or mesos when
run on multiple cpu cores.

This has been root caused to cpu-local run queue being allocated per cpu
bandwidth slices, and then not fully using that slice within the period.
At which point the slice and quota expires. This expiration of unused
slice results in applications not being able to utilize the quota for
which they are allocated.

The non-expiration of per-cpu slices was recently fixed by
'commit 512ac999d275 ("sched/fair: Fix bandwidth timer clock drift
condition")'. Prior to that it appears that this had been broken since
at least 'commit 51f2176d74ac ("sched/fair: Fix unlocked reads of some
cfs_b->quota/period")' which was introduced in v3.16-rc1 in 2014. That
added the following conditional which resulted in slices never being
expired.

if (cfs_rq->runtime_expires != cfs_b->runtime_expires) {
	/* extend local deadline, drift is bounded above by 2 ticks */
	cfs_rq->runtime_expires += TICK_NSEC;

Because this was broken for nearly 5 years, and has recently been fixed
and is now being noticed by many users running kubernetes
(https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/67577) it is my opinion
that the mechanisms around expiring runtime should be removed
altogether.

This allows quota already allocated to per-cpu run-queues to live longer
than the period boundary. This allows threads on runqueues that do not
use much CPU to continue to use their remaining slice over a longer
period of time than cpu.cfs_period_us. However, this helps prevent the
above condition of hitting throttling while also not fully utilizing
your cpu quota.

This theoretically allows a machine to use slightly more than its
allotted quota in some periods. This overflow would be bounded by the
remaining quota left on each per-cpu runqueueu. This is typically no
more than min_cfs_rq_runtime=1ms per cpu. For CPU bound tasks this will
change nothing, as they should theoretically fully utilize all of their
quota in each period. For user-interactive tasks as described above this
provides a much better user/application experience as their cpu
utilization will more closely match the amount they requested when they
hit throttling. This means that cpu limits no longer strictly apply per
period for non-cpu bound applications, but that they are still accurate
over longer timeframes.

This greatly improves performance of high-thread-count, non-cpu bound
applications with low cfs_quota_us allocation on high-core-count
machines. In the case of an artificial testcase (10ms/100ms of quota on
80 CPU machine), this commit resulted in almost 30x performance
improvement, while still maintaining correct cpu quota restrictions.
That testcase is available at https://github.com/indeedeng/fibtest.

description: kernel/sched/fair.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.9, when cpu.cfs_quota_us is used (e.g., with Kubernetes), allows attackers to cause a denial of service against non-cpu-bound applications by generating a workload that triggers unwanted slice expiration, aka CID-de53fd7aedb1. (In other words, although this slice expiration would typically be seen with benign workloads, it is possible that an attacker could calculate how many stray requests are required to force an entire Kubernetes cluster into a low-performance state caused by slice expiration, and ensure that a DDoS attack sent that number of stray requests. An attack does not affect the stability of the kernel; it only causes mismanagement of application execution.)

code_evidence: start_cfs_bandwidth advances the period timer by overrun periods and then extends the bandwidth runtime deadline by (overrun + 1) periods, incrementing expires_seq before restarting the hrtimer. This couples the per-CPU runqueue slice deadline to the global period boundary instead of letting unused per-CPU slices persist.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 covers failure to properly control maintenance of a limited resource. Here the scheduler's quota resource is mismanaged by expiring slices prematurely, causing resource-consumption/throttling effects. It is not a memory-safety flaw; the weakness is in resource lifetime management.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function forces the global runtime_expires/expires_seq to track each period transition, so per-CPU runqueue slices are invalidated at every period boundary rather than being carried over. Trigger: a high-thread, non-CPU-bound workload under cpu.cfs_quota_us causes runqueues to hold unused slices that expire at the period edge. Supported consequence: periods are throttled while allocated quota is unused, degrading application execution (availability/CPU throughput).

This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

commit_msg:
i2c: fix stack buffer overflow vulnerability in i2c md command

When running "i2c md 0 0 80000100", the function do_i2c_md parses the
length into an unsigned int variable named length. The value is then
moved to a signed variable:

    int nbytes = length;
    #define DISP_LINE_LEN 16
    int linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;
    ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);

On systems where integers are 32 bits wide, 0x80000100 is a negative
value to "nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN" is false and linebytes gets assigned
0x80000100 instead of 16.

The consequence is that the function which reads from the i2c device
(dm_i2c_read or i2c_read) is called with a 16-byte stack buffer to fill
but with a size parameter which is too large. In some cases, this could
trigger a crash. But with some i2c drivers, such as drivers/i2c/nx_i2c.c
(used with "nexell,s5pxx18-i2c" bus), the size is actually truncated to
a 16-bit integer. This is because function i2c_transfer expects an
unsigned short length. In such a case, an attacker who can control the
response of an i2c device can overwrite the return address of a function
and execute arbitrary code through Return-Oriented Programming.

Fix this issue by using unsigned integers types in do_i2c_md. While at
it, make also alen unsigned, as signed sizes can cause vulnerabilities
when people forgot to check that they can be negative.

Signed-off-by: Nicolas Iooss <nicolas.iooss+uboot@ledger.fr>
Reviewed-by: Heiko Schocher <hs@denx.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint alen;'], 'added_lines': ['\tuint\talen;']}
description: In Das U-Boot through 2022.07-rc5, an integer signedness error and resultant stack-based buffer overflow in the "i2c md" command enables the corruption of the return address pointer of the do_i2c_md function.

code_evidence: alen is declared as a signed int and later receives the result of get_alen [6,18].
The only validation checks alen > 3 [19,20], which does not reject a negative value such as -1; a negative alen then passes to the i2c write calls.
The loop at [42] and the i2c_write calls at [37,47] pass alen as the address length to the device write routines without any lower-bound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function forwards an unvalidated negative length into a write routine, enabling data to be written outside the intended buffer bounds, which matches CWE-787. It is distinct from a pure integer overflow because the core defect is the missing range check leading to an out-of-bounds write.

evidence_lines.code: int alen;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing non-negative constraint on the signed alen value: get_alen can return -1, and the check alen > 3 fails to catch it. This negative length reaches i2c_write/dm_i2c_write, where it can be interpreted as a large unsigned size, causing an out-of-bounds write beyond the intended buffer and potential memory corruption or code execution.

Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/22276
Reviewed-by: Pascal Quantin <pascal.quantin@gmail.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tguint8 xid_param_len = 0, byte1 = 0, byte2 = 0, item_len = 0, tmp = 0;', '\tguint16 info_len;'], 'added_lines': ['\tguint8 xid_param_len = 0, byte1 = 0, byte2 = 0, tmp = 0;', '\tguint16 info_len, item_len;']}
description: In Wireshark 2.0.0 to 2.0.13, the GPRS LLC dissector could go into a large loop. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-gprs-llc.c by using a different integer data type.

code_evidence: item_len is declared guint8 while info_len is guint16; item_len is computed from xid_param_len (max 255) plus 1 or 2, so larger sums truncate/wrap in the byte.
The loop condition location < info_len uses the 16-bit length, but location is advanced by the 8-bit item_len at line 63 and by per-byte increments at lines 97-105.
item_len = xid_param_len + 2 can wrap when xid_param_len is near 255, making the advance smaller than the consumed parameter.
If xid_param_len is nonzero and location does not progress past info_len, the outer while loop iterates many times, exhausting CPU.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits because the outer while loop is not adequately bounded when the integer truncation keeps location from reaching info_len; the excessive iteration is the weakness, and resource exhaustion is the consequence, not a memory-safety flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
guint8 xid_param_len = 0, byte1 = 0, byte2 = 0, item_len = 0, tmp = 0;
guint16 info_len;

while (location < info_len)
byte1 = tvb_get_guint8(tvb, location);
item_len = xid_param_len + 2;

for (loop_counter = 0; loop_counter < xid_param_len; loop_counter++)
}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: item_len is stored as guint8, so xid_param_len + 2 can wrap to a small value. Trigger: a crafted XID parameter with a large length makes location advance less than the actual parameter size, keeping location < info_len. Consequence: the while loop runs excessively, causing CPU consumption/DoS.

commit_msg:
Fix issue of listen before chmod on Unix sockets (CVE-2023-45145) (#12671)

Before this commit, Unix socket setup performed chmod(2) on the socket
file after calling listen(2). Depending on what umask is used, this
could leave the file with the wrong permissions for a short period of
time. As a result, another process could exploit this race condition and
establish a connection that would otherwise not be possible.

We now make sure the socket permissions are set up prior to calling
listen(2).

(cherry picked from commit 1119ecae6fd8796fa337df2212f09173ab6c7b0a)

Co-authored-by: Yossi Gottlieb <yossigo@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (anetListen(err,s,(struct sockaddr*)&sa,sizeof(sa),backlog) == ANET_ERR)', '    if (perm)', '        chmod(sa.sun_path, perm);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (anetListen(err,s,(struct sockaddr*)&sa,sizeof(sa),backlog,perm) == ANET_ERR)']}
description: Redis is an in-memory database that persists on disk. On startup, Redis begins listening on a Unix socket before adjusting its permissions to the user-provided configuration. If a permissive umask(2) is used, this creates a race condition that enables, during a short period of time, another process to establish an otherwise unauthorized connection. This problem has existed since Redis 2.6.0-RC1. This issue has been addressed in Redis versions 7.2.2, 7.0.14 and 6.2.14. Users are advised to upgrade. For users unable to upgrade, it is possible to work around the problem by disabling Unix sockets, starting Redis with a restrictive umask, or storing the Unix socket file in a protected directory.

code_evidence: anetListen() binds and listens on the Unix socket at sa.sun_path, after which the code conditionally applies chmod(sa.sun_path, perm) only if perm is nonzero. During the window between listen() and chmod(), the socket file retains permissions derived from the process umask rather than the intended perm.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The socket resource is exposed to parties outside the intended control sphere because access permissions are set after the resource becomes reachable. This is a resource-exposure/access-control weakness (CWE-668), not a memory-safety or input-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the socket is made connectable via listen() before its permissions are restricted, so the file exists under default/umask-derived permissions. Trigger: a permissive umask at startup and a nonzero perm; another local process connects during the brief pre-chmod window. Consequence: an otherwise unauthorized peer establishes a connection to the Redis Unix socket.

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

Fixes: c7aa12252f51 ("NFC: Take a reference on the LLCP local pointer when creating a socket")

Reviewed-by: Simon Horman <simon.horman@corigine.com>

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: Line 31 obtains local via nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); the NULL check at 32-35 does not hold any reference, so local can be freed by a concurrent unregister before use.
Lines 36-47 lock the device, but the lock is released at 42 and the rf_mode/target_idx reads at 43-44 use local without a reference, leaving a race window.
Line 48-49 assigns llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); the reference is acquired only after the earlier unlocked dereferences, so a freed local may already have been used.
The error path at 86-91 calls nfc_llcp_put_ssap and nfc_llcp_local_put on llcp_sock->local, which may be NULL or stale, and the reference handling is inconsistent with the object actually fetched.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer whose lifetime is not pinned by a reference, producing a classic use-after-free (CWE-416). A plain NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476) does not fit because the flaw is the stale, freed object rather than a missing NULL check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: nfc_llcp_find_local returns a pointer without taking a reference, and the device lock is dropped before the local object is dereferenced and before nfc_llcp_local_get runs. A racing nfc_llcp_unregister_device can free the local in that window, so subsequent reads of local->rf_mode or target_idx access freed memory.

description: Heap-based buffer overflow in coders/psd.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted PSD file.

code_evidence: CheckNumberCompactPixels macro returns only when packets==0, guarding compact_pixels consumption before incrementing it.

The literal-run branch increments length (line 77) and loops j<length reading *compact_pixels at lines 85-114 without consuming compact_pixels per iteration; compact_pixels advances only once at line 119.
The guard at line 118 runs after the inner loop has already dereferenced *compact_pixels, so the bounds check does not protect the reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads *compact_pixels beyond the supplied buffer due to a missing or misordered bounds check, which is precisely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a write overflow because the dereferences are reads, though the same missing constraint could enable other impacts.

evidence_lines.code:
#define CheckNumberCompactPixels \
if (packets == 0) \
return(i); \
packets--

CheckNumberCompactPixels;
compact_pixels++;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the compact-pixel exhaustion check is placed after the inner loop that dereferences *compact_pixels repeatedly, instead of before each read. Trigger: a crafted PSD with a compact-pixel run whose length exceeds available input causes the j-loop to dereference compact_pixels past the buffer end. Consequence: out-of-bounds read, leading to crash/DoS and potential disclosure.

commit_msg:
* src/pathx.c (parse_name): correctly handle trailing whitespace in names

When a name ended in whitespace, we incorrectly assumed it was always ok to
trim that whitespace. That is not true if that whitespace is escaped,
i.e. if the path expression is something like '/x\ '. In that case, the
name really needs to be literally 'x ', i.e., we can not trim that
whitespace.

The incorrect behavior led to turning '/x\ ' first into 'x\' and then,
because we assume that '\' is always followed by a character inside the
string, when we removed the escaping '\', we would read beyond the end of
the intermediate string result; if we were lucky, that would lead to a
crash, otherwise we'd continue with junk.

We now make sure that escaped whitespace at the end of a string does not
get stripped, avoiding all these headaches.

Fixes RHBZ https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1475621

In other words, we'll parse 'x frob", "         * y' as one name, but for 'x or y', we consider 'x' a name in its", '         * own right. */', '    /* Strip trailing white space. Make sure we respect escaped whitespace', '     * and don\'t strip it as in "x\\\\ " */', '        while (isspace(*state->pos) && state->pos > s', '               && !backslash_escaped(state->pos, s))']}
description: Augeas versions up to and including 1.8.0 are vulnerable to heap-based buffer overflow due to improper handling of escaped strings. Attacker could send crafted strings that would cause the application using augeas to copy past the end of a buffer, leading to a crash or possible code execution.

code_evidence: The trailing-whitespace trimming loop decrements state->pos while isspace(*state->pos) is true, using only the bound state->pos >= s; when the name ends in an escaped space such as 'x\ ', it strips that space, leaving the backslash as the last character.

The unescape loop then sees '\' at *t, advances t past it (t += 1) and copies *t to *p; if the backslash was the final character, t points at the terminating NUL and the loop's next *t check reads past the intended buffer content.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads beyond the intended boundary of the intermediate string buffer, which is a memory-buffer out-of-bounds operation fitting CWE-119. The root cause is the missing escaped-whitespace check, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read of the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the whitespace-stripping loop does not respect backslash-escaped trailing whitespace, so an escaped trailing space is removed and the escape backslash becomes the last character. Trigger: a crafted path name like '/x\ '. The unescape loop then skips past the backslash and reads beyond the end of the intermediate string, producing an out-of-bounds read (crash or junk data).

description: The gst_asf_demux_process_ext_content_desc function in gst/asfdemux/gstasfdemux.c in gst-plugins-ugly in GStreamer allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds heap read) via vectors involving extended content descriptors.

CVE-2017-13014/White Board: Do more bounds checks.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Yannick Formaggio.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).

While we're at it, print a truncation error if the packets are

description: The White Board protocol parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-wb.c:wb_prep(), several functions.

code_evidence: The header pointer is cast from the untrusted packet buffer and only validated by a length check against sizeof(*ph) and ND_TTEST(*ph) before sizeof(*ph) is subtracted from len.
The switch dispatches on ph->ph_type, and each case passes (ph + 1) plus the reduced len to a subtype parser such as wb_prep, trusting that parser to re-validate the remaining length.
wb_prep receives the post-header length; if it does not fully bound-check reads against len, it reads past the captured buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits: the weakness is reading beyond the intended buffer during packet parsing, matching the CVE description of a buffer over-read in wb_prep and several functions. It is not CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) because the parser only consumes data; the impact is out-of-bounds memory read, not corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the top-level wb_print validates only the fixed-size header and delegates the truncated remaining payload to wb_prep and peers without ensuring each subtype parser bounds its reads by the supplied len. Trigger: a captured White Board packet whose header is valid but whose payload is shorter than the subtype structure. Consequence: the subtype parser reads past the end of the captured buffer (out-of-bounds read), disclosed by the CVE and fixed by added bounds checks.

description: decode_frame in libavcodec/exr.c in FFmpeg 4.3.1 has an out-of-bounds write because of errors in calculations of when to perform memset zero operations.

code_evidence: For each plane, ptr is set to picture->data[i] and the loop writes out_line_size bytes via memset, advancing ptr by picture->linesize[i] on each of s->ymin iterations. s->ymin is header-derived and not bounded by the allocated frame height s->h, so the number of zeroing writes can exceed the buffer's row count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loop writes data beyond the intended buffer because the iteration count is not constrained by the buffer's valid height, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The patch adds FFMIN(s->ymin, s->h) to cap iterations, confirming the missing upper bound as the cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the zeroing loop bound uses s->ymin without clamping to the allocated height, so when ymin exceeds h the loop iterates beyond the frame rows. Trigger: a crafted EXR header with ymin larger than h. Consequence: memset writes past the end of the allocated picture buffer (out-of-bounds write).

commit_msg:
mm: get rid of vmacache_flush_all() entirely

Jann Horn points out that the vmacache_flush_all() function is not only
potentially expensive, it's buggy too.  It also happens to be entirely
unnecessary, because the sequence number overflow case can be avoided by
simply making the sequence number be 64-bit.  That doesn't even grow the
data structures in question, because the other adjacent fields are
already 64-bit.

So simplify the whole thing by just making the sequence number overflow
case go away entirely, which gets rid of all the complications and makes
the code faster too.  Win-win.

[ Oleg Nesterov points out that the VMACACHE_FULL_FLUSHES statistics
  also just goes away entirely with this ]

min_val reads UINT(data,pos+4) and max_val reads UINT(data,pos+8); with the guard permitting pos+8 == len, the max_val read at pos+8..pos+11 exceeds the buffer.

max_val = (ut32)(UINT (data, pos + 8));

commit_msg:
Stop devirtualizing interface calls in preexistence

Previously, it was possible for the JIT to devirtualize an interface
call, and for execution to reach the call (whether inlined or not) with
a receiver that is not an instance of the class expected by the
implementing method. The callee could then access fields of the receiver
as though it were of the expected type.

The conditionals added in this commit still allow (on their own) for an
interface call to be devirtualized when preexistence has already proven
that the receiver is an instance of some particular class that
implements the expected interface. However, preexistence currently fails
to devirtualize in that situation. It passes the class to
TR_PersistentCHTable::findSingleInterfaceImplementer(), which needs the
interface. This can be improved in the future by having preexistence
treat the call in the same way as a non-interface call, but with the
added requirement that the devirtualized callee must be public.
