commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow in StringUtil::implode

Reviewed By: ricklavoie

Differential Revision: D3623922

fbshipit-source-id: 136d124a850c07cc6c63535afc11d36499d576fc
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int len = 0;', '  int lenDelim = delim.size();'], 'added_lines': ['  size_t len = 0;', '  size_t lenDelim = delim.size();']}
description: Integer overflow in StringUtil::implode in Facebook HHVM before 3.15.0 allows attackers to have unspecified impact via unknown vectors.

code_evidence: `len` and `lenDelim` are declared as signed `int`, and `lenDelim` receives `delim.size()` which may exceed INT_MAX on truncation.
The loop accumulates `sitems.back().size() + lenDelim` into `len` with no overflow check; a large delimiter times many items can wrap `len` negative or small.
`len` is then used as the size for `String(len, ReserveString)` and as the memcpy target bound, so the wrapped value drives allocation and copying.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the function performs a size calculation (`len += ...`) assuming the result stays larger, but the `int` representation wraps. The wrapped length is then used for allocation and memcpy, matching integer-overflow-to-memory-corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the accumulated total length is stored in a signed `int` and incremented without bounds checking, so concatenating large or numerous strings makes `len` wrap to a small or negative value. Trigger: attacker-supplied items or delimiter whose combined size exceeds INT_MAX. Consequence: `String(len, ...)` allocates an undersized buffer while the copy loop writes the full data, causing heap memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
netlink: fix possible spoofing from non-root processes

Non-root user-space processes can send Netlink messages to other
processes that are well-known for being subscribed to Netlink
asynchronous notifications. This allows ilegitimate non-root
process to send forged messages to Netlink subscribers.

The userspace process usually verifies the legitimate origin in
two ways:

a) Socket credentials. If UID != 0, then the message comes from
   some ilegitimate process and the message needs to be dropped.

b) Netlink portID. In general, portID == 0 means that the origin
   of the messages comes from the kernel. Thus, discarding any
   message not coming from the kernel.

However, ctnetlink sets the portID in event messages that has
been triggered by some user-space process, eg. conntrack utility.
So other processes subscribed to ctnetlink events, eg. conntrackd,
know that the event was triggered by some user-space action.

Neither of the two ways to discard ilegitimate messages coming
from non-root processes can help for ctnetlink.

This patch adds capability validation in case that dst_pid is set
in netlink_sendmsg(). This approach is aggressive since existing
applications using any Netlink bus to deliver messages between
two user-space processes will break. Note that the exception is
NETLINK_USERSOCK, since it is reserved for netlink-to-netlink
userspace communication.

Still, if anyone wants that his Netlink bus allows netlink-to-netlink
userspace, then they can set NL_NONROOT_SEND. However, by default,
I don't think it makes sense to allow to use NETLINK_ROUTE to
communicate two processes that are sending no matter what information
that is not related to link/neighbouring/routing. They should be using
NETLINK_USERSOCK instead for that.

Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (dst_group && !netlink_capable(sock, NL_NONROOT_SEND))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif ((dst_group || dst_pid) &&', '\t\t    !netlink_capable(sock, NL_NONROOT_SEND))']}
description: The netlink_sendmsg function in net/netlink/af_netlink.c in the Linux kernel before 3.5.5 does not validate the dst_pid field, which allows local users to have an unspecified impact by spoofing Netlink messages.

code_evidence: When a destination address is supplied, dst_pid is taken from the user-controlled addr->nl_pid and dst_group from addr->nl_groups. The only authorization check gates on dst_group; a unicast send (dst_group == 0) with a nonzero dst_pid skips netlink_capable entirely and proceeds to netlink_unicast at line 62.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to restrict who may send to a given destination port, so a non-root actor reaches a resource (the peer socket) it should not. This is an access-control enforcement failure, fitting CWE-284. It is not merely a credential-check bug: the missing dst_pid constraint is the access restriction defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the capability check conditions authorization solely on dst_group, leaving dst_pid unvalidated. Trigger: an unprivileged local process sends a netlink message with a user-supplied nl_pid and no group. Consequence: the message is delivered to the targeted peer without the NL_NONROOT_SEND capability check, enabling spoofed netlink messages to subscribers.

description: An issue was discovered in drivers/mtd/ubi/cdev.c in the Linux kernel 6.2. There is a divide-by-zero error in do_div(sz,mtd->erasesize), used indirectly by ctrl_cdev_ioctl, when mtd->erasesize is 0.

code_evidence: Lines 23-28 validate mtd->type and flags but never check mtd->erasesize; the function proceeds to allocate ubi and set ubi->mtd = mtd.
Lines 61-62 and 69-70 call mtd_div_by_eb(ubi->mtd->size, ubi->mtd), which divides by mtd->erasesize; with a zero erasesize this is a divide-by-zero before any guard.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a division whose divisor (mtd->erasesize) can be zero due to an unchecked device property, directly matching CWE-369. This is not merely a missing validation; the concrete division with a zero divisor is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The attach path accepts an MTD device whose erasesize is zero because no constraint rejects it. When fastmap sizing computes mtd_div_by_eb(size, mtd), the divisor erasesize is zero, causing a divide-by-zero exception during ubi_attach_mtd_dev.

commit_msg:
Avoid integer overflows in parsing fonts

A malformed TTF can cause size calculations to overflow. This patch
checks the maximum reasonable value so that the total size fits in 32
bits. It also adds some explicit casting to avoid possible technical
undefined behavior when parsing sized unsigned values.

Bug: 25645298
Change-Id: Id4716132041a6f4f1fbb73ec4e445391cf7d9616
(cherry picked from commit 183c9ec2800baa2ce099ee260c6cbc6121cf1274)

description: Integer overflow in the getCoverageFormat12 function in CmapCoverage.cpp in the Minikin library in Android 5.x before 5.1.1 LMY49G and 6.x before 2016-02-01 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (continuous rebooting) via an application that triggers loading of a crafted TTF font, aka internal bug 25645298.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: Target CWE-19 is a prohibited Category, not a weakness; the function's actual issue is an integer overflow in size calculation (CWE-190), so CWE-19 cannot be directly supported.

description: In Exiv2 0.26 and previous versions, PngChunk::readRawProfile in pngchunk_int.cpp may cause a denial of service (application crash due to a heap-based buffer over-read) via a crafted PNG file.

code_evidence: The scan loops advance sp only while pointerPos < text.size_-1, then atol(sp) and the decode loop dereference *sp without a reliable end-of-buffer bound.
The nibble decode loop dereferences *sp in the while condition and in unhex[(int)*sp] before checking for '\0', so a crafted profile lacking enough hex digits reads past text.pData_.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads bytes beyond the intended text buffer via *sp and unhex[(int)*sp], which is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a write overflow, since the destination dp is sized by the declared length.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser trusts the declared length and walks the profile buffer using pointerPos comparisons that can stop short of the actual end, then dereferences *sp. Trigger: a crafted PNG raw profile whose length field exceeds the available hex data. Consequence: heap-based buffer over-read, causing a crash/DoS and potentially leaking adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
Fix multiple heap-based buffer overflows in CmtkLoader::load()

Changes in src/mtk.cpp for loading files:
* Fail early if the (decompressed) size is too small to hold
  mtkdata minus patterns. That avoids attempts to copy data
  from beyond allocated memory.
* In the data decompression section, there are multiple cases
  where the code actually has checks for available space before
  copying data, but the size of the copy is increased after
  the check, so a buffer overflow is still possible (issue #90).
  Fix that by moving the check after the size computation,
  and also check for a valid source offset where applicable.
* Also add several checks whether source data is exhausted
  during decompession, so
* When copying the patterns, don't copy more data than the
  "pattern" array can hold.

In src/mtk.h, method getinstrument(), check for valid instrument
number to avoid accessing the array with an invalid index.

This commit fixes CVE-2019-14734.

Fixes: https://github.com/adplug/adplug/issues/90

description: AdPlug 2.3.1 has multiple heap-based buffer overflows in CmtkLoader::load() in mtk.cpp.

code_evidence: Case 0 checks orgptr + cnt against header.size while cnt still holds the 4-bit value, then increments cnt by 3 before the memset, so the guard can pass but the memset writes up to 3 bytes past the allocated org buffer.
Case 1 similarly bounds-checks the small cnt, then adds (cmp[cmpptr] << 4) + 19 before memset, allowing a write of many bytes beyond header.size.
Case 2 checks the small cnt, then recomputes cnt = cmp[++cmpptr] + 16 after the check; the subsequent memcpy can also read from &org[orgptr - offs] where offs may exceed orgptr.
Default case checks orgptr + cmd > header.size, then performs memcpy with cmd bytes from &org[orgptr-offs], where offs derived from input may exceed orgptr, causing out-of-bounds read/write.
memcpy(patterns,data->patterns,header.size-6084) copies an attacker-derived length into the fixed patterns array without clamping to its size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of heap-allocated buffers (org and patterns) due to missing/ineffective size constraints, matching CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. The out-of-bounds read via the offset is secondary; the primary defect supported by the code is the unconstrained write.

evidence_lines.code: memcpy(patterns,data->patterns,header.size-6084);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bounds checks in the decompression switch are performed before the copy length is finalized, so the checked size differs from the actual write size; additionally header.size is used as a copy length into a fixed-size patterns array. Trigger: a crafted MTK file whose compressed stream selects these command cases with large count/offset nibbles. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds writes into org and patterns, enabling memory corruption, crash, or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
netfilter: nf_tables: bail out on mismatching dynset and set expressions

If dynset expressions provided by userspace is larger than the declared
set expressions, then bail out.

Fixes: 48b0ae046ee9 ("netfilter: nftables: netlink support for several set element expressions")
Reported-by: Xingyuan Mo <hdthky0@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (set->num_exprs &&', '\t\t\t    dynset_expr->ops != set->exprs[i]->ops) {', '\t\t\t\terr = -EOPNOTSUPP;', '\t\t\t\tgoto err_expr_free;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (set->num_exprs) {', '\t\t\t\tif (i >= set->num_exprs) {', '\t\t\t\t\terr = -EINVAL;', '\t\t\t\t\tgoto err_expr_free;', '\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t\tif (dynset_expr->ops != set->exprs[i]->ops) {', '\t\t\t\t\terr = -EOPNOTSUPP;', '\t\t\t\t\tgoto err_expr_free;', '\t\t\t\t}']}
description: A null pointer dereference vulnerability was found in nft_dynset_init() in net/netfilter/nft_dynset.c in nf_tables in the Linux kernel. This issue may allow a local attacker with CAP_NET_ADMIN user privilege to trigger a denial of service.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over user-supplied NFTA_DYNSET_EXPRESSIONS entries. At [95] each dynset_expr is allocated and stored; [102] then checks only that set->num_exprs is nonzero before [103] dereferences set->exprs[i]->ops. i is the user-controlled expression index, bounded only by NFT_SET_EXPR_MAX at [87], not by set->num_exprs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked index allows set->exprs[i] to be NULL, which is then dereferenced for ->ops; this is a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476). The added i >= set->num_exprs guard confirms the missing bound.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the expression count from userspace can exceed the set's declared num_exprs, so set->exprs[i] reads out of bounds and yields NULL for i >= set->num_exprs. Trigger: a local CAP_NET_ADMIN user supplies more dynset expressions than the set declares. Consequence: NULL dereference at [103], causing a kernel crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
libXpm uses unsigned int to store sizes, which fits size_t on 32 bit
systems, but leads to issues on 64 bit systems.

On 64 bit systems, it is possible to overflow 32 bit integers while
parsing XPM extensions in a file.

At first, it looks like a rather unimportant detail, because nobody
will seriously open a 4 GB file. But unfortunately XPM has support for
gzip compression out of the box. An attacker can therefore craft a
compressed file which is merely 4 MB in size, which makes an attack
much for feasable.

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void', '\tsize += strlen(ext->name) + 8;', '\tfor (y = 0, line = ext->lines; y < a; y++, line++)', '\t    size += strlen(*line) + 1;'], 'added_lines': ['static int', '    size_t len;', '\tif (ext->nlines == UINT_MAX || nlines > UINT_MAX - ext->nlines - 1)', '\t    return (1);', '\tlen = strlen(ext->name) + 8;', '\tif (len > UINT_MAX - size)', '\t    return (1);', '\tsize += len;', '\tfor (y = 0, line = ext->lines; y < a; y++, line++) {', '\t    len = strlen(*line) + 1;', '\t    if (len > UINT_MAX - size)', '\t\treturn (1);', '\t    size += len;', '\t}', '    if (size > UINT_MAX - 10 || nlines > UINT_MAX - 1)', '\treturn (1);', '    return (0);']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in libXpm before 3.5.12, when a program requests parsing XPM extensions on a 64-bit platform, allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write) or execute arbitrary code via (1) the number of extensions or (2) their concatenated length in a crafted XPM file, which triggers a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Line 8 declares size and nlines as 32-bit unsigned int. In the loop, line 13 accumulates nlines += ext->nlines + 1 and line 14 accumulates size += strlen(ext->name) + 8, while lines 16-17 add strlen(*line) + 1 per extension line. These additions are unchecked and can wrap when the total exceeds UINT_MAX. Lines 19-20 then compute *ext_size = size + 10 and *ext_nlines = nlines + 1 from the wrapped values, so the reported sizes are too small.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unchecked unsigned additions can wrap before the result is used as a size, matching CWE-190 integer overflow/wraparound. The subsequent out-of-bounds write is the consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled extension counts and string lengths are summed into unsigned int without overflow checks. Trigger: a crafted XPM (possibly gzip-compressed) with many extensions or long concatenated lines. Consequence: the wrapped size is passed to later allocation/copy logic, producing a heap out-of-bounds write (DoS or code execution).

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/547
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  clone_info=DestroyImageInfo(clone_info);'], 'added_lines': ['  if (clone_info)', '    clone_info=DestroyImageInfo(clone_info);']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.0.6-1, a missing NULL check vulnerability was found in the function ReadMATImage in coders/mat.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (assertion failure) in DestroyImageInfo in image.c.

code_evidence: clone_info is initialized to NULL at line 41. The V4 path at lines 46-50 jumps to END_OF_READING without ever assigning clone_info. The label at line 394 is followed by an unconditional call to DestroyImageInfo(clone_info) at line 395, which receives NULL in that path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The attacker-reachable NULL argument violates DestroyImageInfo's assertion, producing an assertion failure that terminates the process. This matches CWE-617 (reachable assertion DoS), not merely a generic NULL-pointer dereference, because the observed consequence is the assert-triggered exit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a control-flow path (V4 fallback via goto END_OF_READING) reaches the cleanup code with clone_info still NULL, and DestroyImageInfo is called without a NULL guard. Trigger: a crafted MAT file taking the V4 branch. Consequence: DestroyImageInfo asserts on NULL, aborting the process (denial of service).

commit_msg: Fix #6829 oob write because of using wrong struct
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tstruct reloc_struct_t *got_table = calloc (1, n_got * sizeof (ut32));'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tstruct reloc_struct_t *got_table = calloc (', '\t\t\t\t1, n_got * sizeof (struct reloc_struct_t));']}
description: The relocs function in libr/bin/p/bin_bflt.c in radare2 1.2.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted binary file.

code_evidence: Line 12 computes amount as n_got * sizeof(ut32) (4 bytes), but line 16 allocates got_table as calloc(1, n_got * sizeof(ut32)), i.e. only 4 bytes per entry for a struct reloc_struct_t array.
The loop at line 19 iterates i < n_got and writes got_table[i].addr_to_patch and .data_offset at lines 30-31, requiring sizeof(struct reloc_struct_t) per element, exceeding the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to memory locations beyond the allocated got_table buffer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The underlying allocation-size error (CWE-131) manifests here as an improper-bounds write, but the observed unsafe operation is the OOB write itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the GOT table is allocated using the size of ut32 instead of the size of struct reloc_struct_t, so the heap buffer is roughly 4x too small. Trigger: a crafted bflt file with a GOTPIC flag and n_got>0 causes the loop to write struct fields past the allocation, producing a heap-based out-of-bounds write and likely crash or memory corruption.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. In versions of PJSIP prior to 2.13 the PJSIP parser, PJMEDIA RTP decoder, and PJMEDIA SDP parser are affeced by a buffer overflow vulnerability. Users connecting to untrusted clients are at risk. This issue has been patched and is available as commit c4d3498 in the master branch and will be included in releases 2.13 and later. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: parse_origin dereferences scanner->curptr+1 without first ensuring that position lies before scanner->end; when the scanner is at or near the end of input, this reads past the buffer boundary.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a missing size/bound check on scanner input before accessing the next byte, allowing an out-of-bounds access. evidence_lines.code: if (*(scanner->curptr+1) != '=') {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unchecked out-of-bounds read of the byte following the current scanner position. Trigger: malformed or truncated SDP input reaching parse_origin, where curptr+1 is at or beyond end. The patch adds the missing curptr+1 >= end bound check; consequence is an out-of-bounds memory access on attacker-supplied input.

commit_msg:
adb: use asocket's close function when closing.

close_all_sockets was assuming that all registered local sockets used
local_socket_close as their close function. However, this is not true
for JDWP sockets.

Bug: http://b/28347842
Change-Id: I40a1174845cd33f15f30ce70828a7081cd5a087e
(cherry picked from commit 53eb31d87cb84a4212f4850bf745646e1fb12814)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            local_socket_close(s);'], 'added_lines': ['            s->close(s);']}
description: The Java Debug Wire Protocol (JDWP) implementation in adb/sockets.cpp in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-09-01 mishandles socket close operations, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka internal bug 28347842.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over every registered local socket and, when a socket's transport or its peer's transport matches t, unconditionally invokes local_socket_close(s) rather than the socket's own close callback. JDWP sockets registered with a different close routine are therefore closed through the wrong function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The bug concerns improper management of socket teardown for a debug transport, allowing privilege gain, which fits the CWE-264 permissions/privileges category. It is not a memory-safety flaw; the defect is wrong close dispatch affecting access-control-related behavior.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: close_all_sockets hardcodes local_socket_close for all socket types instead of dispatching through s->close, so sockets whose close semantics differ (JDWP) are mishandled. Trigger: closing a transport that owns or peers with such a socket. Consequence: incorrect teardown of JDWP sockets, enabling privilege escalation per the advisory.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13690/IKEv2: Fix some bounds checks.

Use a pointer of the correct type in ND_TCHECK(), or use ND_TCHECK2()
and provide the correct length.

While we're at it, remove the blank line between some checks and the
UNALIGNED_MEMCPY()s they protect.

Also, note the places where we print the entire payload.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tND_TCHECK(*ext);'], 'added_lines': ['\tND_TCHECK2(*ext, sizeof(a));']}
description: The IKEv2 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isakmp.c, several functions.

code_evidence: Line 13 uses ND_TCHECK(*ext), which only verifies a single byte is present, then line 14 copies sizeof(a) bytes from ext into the local struct ikev2_auth, allowing a read past the captured buffer.

Line 16 derives len from the copied header; lines 17-19 and 22 use len to print and rawprint len - sizeof(a) bytes from authdata, and line 30 advances by len without validating it against the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the intended packet buffer, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. This is a read-only over-read rather than an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), consistent with the reported buffer over-read.

evidence_lines.code:
ND_TCHECK(*ext);
UNALIGNED_MEMCPY(&a, ext, sizeof(a));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is an insufficient bounds check: ND_TCHECK(*ext) checks only one byte before a multi-byte UNALIGNED_MEMCPY, and the length field len is used to read authdata payload bytes without confirming they lie within the capture. Triggered by a truncated IKEv2 auth payload, this yields an out-of-bounds read of captured/adjacent memory.

commit_msg: Fix #10498 - Fix crash in fuzzed java files (#10511)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (linenum_len > sz) {', '\t\tfree (attr);', '\t\treturn NULL;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t}', '\t\t// wtf it works', '\t\tif (offset - 2 > sz) {']}
description: The r_bin_java_annotation_new function in shlr/java/class.c in radare2 2.7.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted .class file because of missing input validation in r_bin_java_line_number_table_attr_new.

code_evidence: The length is read from the buffer at offset 6 [11] and offset becomes 8 [12]. The size check at [16] compares the entry count linenum_len to the total attribute size sz, not to the remaining bytes after offset, so the loop at [20] can iterate past the buffer. Each iteration reads two ushorts at buffer[offset] and buffer[offset+2] [26,28] while offset advances by 4 [27,29] with no per-iteration bound against sz; attr->size is then set from the final offset [34]. A crafted .class file with a large line_number_table_length relative to the remaining input drives reads beyond the supplied buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads buffer data beyond the supplied size bound, which is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a write overflow because no out-of-bounds write occurs; the impact is read memory and crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the only guard compares entry count to total size instead of bounding offset+4 against sz inside the loop. commit_msg:
On x86_64 we must disable preemption before we enable interrupts
for stack faults, int3 and debugging, because the current task is using
a per CPU debug stack defined by the IST. If we schedule out, another task
can come in and use the same stack and cause the stack to be corrupted
and crash the kernel on return.

When CONFIG_PREEMPT_RT_FULL is enabled, spin_locks become mutexes, and
one of these is the spin lock used in signal handling.

Some of the debug code (int3) causes do_trap() to send a signal.
This function calls a spin lock that has been converted to a mutex
and has the possibility to sleep. If this happens, the above issues with
the corrupted stack is possible.

Instead of calling the signal right away, for PREEMPT_RT and x86_64,
the signal information is stored on the stacks task_struct and
TIF_NOTIFY_RESUME is set. Then on exit of the trap, the signal resume
code will send the signal when preemption is enabled.

[ rostedt: Switched from #ifdef CONFIG_PREEMPT_RT_FULL to
  ARCH_RT_DELAYS_SIGNAL_SEND and added comments to the code. ]

Cc: stable-rt@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Steven Rostedt <rostedt@goodmis.org>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can cause a heap buffer overflow in `QuantizedMul` by passing in invalid thresholds for the quantization. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/87cf4d3ea9949051e50ca3f071fc909538a51cd0/tensorflow/core/kernels/quantized_mul_op.cc#L287-L290) assumes that the 4 arguments are always valid scalars and tries to access the numeric value directly. However, if any of these tensors is empty, then `.flat<T>()` is an empty buffer and accessing the element at position 0 results in overflow. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The four quantization threshold inputs (2–5) are accessed via context->input(n).flat<float>()(0) without any shape check. flat<float>() on an empty tensor yields an empty buffer, so indexing element 0 reads/writes outside the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked flat<float>()(0) on a possibly empty tensor performs an out-of-bounds memory access beyond the buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write/access). The fix adds IsScalar checks, confirming the missing bound constraint is the defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing scalar/shape validation before dereferencing the flat buffer of each threshold tensor. Trigger: a caller supplies an empty tensor for any of inputs 2–5. Consequence: the unchecked element-0 access overflows the buffer, producing the reported heap buffer overflow (memory corruption/out-of-bounds access).

commit_msg:
Prevent `CHECK`-fail when decoding resource handles from proto

In certain scenarios, the proto might contain tensors that have too many elements (overflow). This is a `CHECK`-fail in general, but we should prevent this, given how many CVEs caused by that we have received this year (a large fraction of 200).

PiperOrigin-RevId: 408049766
Change-Id: I2ac20b247aa8ed9110846fbdb7a0a9401f2c168c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  FromProto(proto);'], 'added_lines': ['  TF_CHECK_OK(FromProto(proto));']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. When decoding a resource handle tensor from protobuf, a TensorFlow process can encounter cases where a `CHECK` assertion is invalidated based on user controlled arguments. This allows attackers to cause denial of services in TensorFlow processes. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The constructor takes an attacker-influenced ResourceHandleProto and calls FromProto(proto) at line 2 without validating the decoded element count. The proto may encode tensors with too many elements (overflow), which FromProto detects and reports via a CHECK-style assertion rather than returning a recoverable error.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because an attacker-supplied proto can reach an internal assertion that terminates the process. This is a reachable-assertion availability failure, distinct from a plain input-validation or memory-corruption weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: user-controlled proto data reaches an assertion in the decode path because the constructor does not constrain the element count before calling FromProto. Trigger: a crafted ResourceHandleProto with overflowing tensor dimensions. Consequence: the CHECK assertion aborts the TensorFlow process, causing a denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overrun in zlib decompression

After updating next_in (to remove the gzip header), avail_in must also
be updated. Failing to do makes zlib read past the input buffer. In
theory this would resukt in a buffer overrun of at most double the input
length, in practice zlib returns as soon as the compression fails (after
reading a few bytes).

Bug: 11548
Change-Id: If71691a2846338f46d866964a77cc4e74a9b61dd
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/12038
Petri-Dish: Peter Wu <peter@lekensteyn.nl>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot <buildbot-no-reply@wireshark.org>
Reviewed-by: Peter Wu <peter@lekensteyn.nl>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tinflateReset(strm);', '\t\t\tnext = c;', '\t\t\tstrm->next_in = next;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t/* Drop gzip header */', '\t\t\tnext = c;', '', '\t\t\tinflateReset(strm);', '\t\t\tstrm->next_in   = next;', '\t\t\tstrm->avail_in  = comprlen;']}
description: Buffer overflow in the tvb_uncompress function in epan/tvbuff_zlib.c in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.9 and 2.0.x before 2.0.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted packet with zlib compression.

code_evidence: After parsing the gzip header, the code resets the stream and sets strm->next_in to the adjusted pointer c, but does not update strm->avail_in to the remaining length; the length check at 127 happens after next_in is already assigned, and comprlen is only reduced at 134.
In the fallback branch, next_in and avail_in are set from stale next/comprlen values without recomputing remaining input after header parsing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to correctly derive/validate the remaining input length (metadata about the buffer) after consuming header bytes, then passes inconsistent pointer/length data to inflate. This is improper input validation of derived size metadata, matching CWE-20.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the gzip-header skip updates the input pointer but leaves avail_in at the original length, so zlib believes more bytes are available than actually remain after the header. Trigger: a crafted zlib/gzip packet whose header is consumed. Consequence: inflate reads past the end of the allocated input buffer, causing a buffer overrun and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
evtchn: relax port_is_valid()

To avoid ports potentially becoming invalid behind the back of certain
other functions (due to ->max_evtchn shrinking) because of
- a guest invoking evtchn_reset() and from a 2nd vCPU opening new
  channels in parallel (see also XSA-343),
- alloc_unbound_xen_event_channel() produced channels living above the
  2-level range (see also XSA-342),
drop the max_evtchns check from port_is_valid(). For a port for which
the function once returned "true", the returned value may not turn into
"false" later on. The function's result may only depend on bounds which
can only ever grow (which is the case for d->valid_evtchns).

This also eliminates a false sense of safety, utilized by some of the
users (see again XSA-343): Without a suitable lock held, d->max_evtchns
may change at any time, and hence deducing that certain other operations
are safe when port_is_valid() returned true is not legitimate. The
opportunities to abuse this may get widened by the change here
(depending on guest and host configuration), but will be taken care of
by the other XSA.

This is XSA-338.

Fixes: 48974e6ce52e ("evtchn: use a per-domain variable for the max number of event channels")
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( p >= d->max_evtchns )', '        return 0;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There is mishandling of the constraint that once-valid event channels may not turn invalid. Logic in the handling of event channel operations in Xen assumes that an event channel, once valid, will not become invalid over the life time of a guest. However, operations like the resetting of all event channels may involve decreasing one of the bounds checked when determining validity. This may lead to bug checks triggering, crashing the host. An unprivileged guest may be able to crash Xen, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) for the entire system. All Xen versions from 4.4 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.3 and earlier are not vulnerable. Only systems with untrusted guests permitted to create more than the default number of event channels are vulnerable. This number depends on the architecture and type of guest. For 32-bit x86 PV guests, this is 1023; for 64-bit x86 PV guests, and for all ARM guests, this number is 4095. Systems where untrusted guests are limited to fewer than this number are not vulnerable. Note that xl and libxl limit max_event_channels to 1023 by default, so systems using exclusively xl, libvirt+libxl, or their own toolstack based on libxl, and not explicitly setting max_event_channels, are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: Lines 3-4 reject a port when p >= d->max_evtchns, using a bound that can shrink at runtime (e.g., evtchn_reset() or parallel channel allocation).
Line 5 then tests p < read_atomic(&d->valid_evtchns); this second bound is monotonic, but the earlier max_evtchns check can flip a previously valid port to invalid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function mishandles the exceptional condition where a previously valid port becomes invalid: the shrinking max_evtchns bound is checked without accounting for that state change, violating the once-valid-never-invalid constraint. This maps to CWE-755 rather than a pure bounds-error CWE.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( p >= d->max_evtchns )
return 0;
return p < read_atomic(&d->valid_evtchns);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: port_is_valid() depends on d->max_evtchns, which is mutable and may decrease, so a port that once returned true can later return false. Trigger: a guest resets event channels or opens new channels in parallel, shrinking max_evtchns. Consequence: callers relying on earlier validity results hit bug checks, crashing the host (DoS).

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.1367: divide by zero in zero-width window

Problem:    Divide by zero in zero-width window.
Solution:   Check the width is positive.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (col > width2)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (col > width2 && width2 > 0)']}
description: Divide By Zero in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.1367.

code_evidence: Lines 12-13 derive width2 from curwin->w_width minus col_off plus col_off2; for a zero-width window width2 can evaluate to 0 (or non-positive).
Line 135 guards only 'col > width2' before lines 137-138 divide and take modulo by width2.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs division and modulo by width2 when it can be zero, directly matching CWE-369. The fix adds 'width2 > 0', confirming the divisor was unchecked; this is a missing zero check, not a bounds or overflow issue.

evidence_lines.code:
width1 = curwin->w_width - curwin_col_off();
width2 = width1 + curwin_col_off2();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: width2 is computed from window width without ensuring it is positive, and the branch at line 135 does not exclude width2 == 0. Trigger: a zero-width window with do_sms and cursor on topline makes col exceed width2, reaching 'col / width2' and 'col % width2'. Consequence: integer divide-by-zero crash (DoS).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  lTar.ReadHeaders();'], 'added_lines': ['  if (lTar.ReadHeaders() == 1) {', '    this->EndModal(wxID_CANCEL);', '    return;', '  }', '', '  if (wxDirExists(destdir + wxFileName::GetPathSeparator() + lTar.getInstalledDmodDirectory())) {', '    wxString question;', '    question.Printf(_("Directory \'%s\' already exists. Continue?"), lTar.getInstalledDmodDirectory());', '    int lResult = wxMessageBox(question, _("DFArc - Installing"),', '\t\t\t       wxYES_NO | wxICON_WARNING, this);', '    if (lResult == wxNO)', '      return;', '  }', '']}
description: Directory traversal issues in the D-Mod extractor in DFArc and DFArc2 (as well as in RTsoft's Dink Smallwood HD / ProtonSDK version) before 3.14 allow an attacker to overwrite arbitrary files on the user's system.

code_evidence: destdir is chosen from configuration (lines 6-8) and passed unvalidated into lTar.Extract at line 11. The archive headers are read at line 10 without any check that entry names are confined to destdir, and the extraction result is only used to report success/failure, not to reject traversal.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-22 fits because external archive-controlled pathnames are combined with a restricted destination directory without neutralizing traversal elements, so extraction escapes the intended location. This is path traversal rather than a mere missing-existence check; the added directory-existence prompt in the patch does not constrain entry paths.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function delegates archive extraction to Tar::Extract with a caller-supplied destdir while never validating that the archive's entry paths (e.g., containing ../ or absolute paths) stay within destdir. Trigger: a crafted .dmod archive whose headers name paths outside the destination. Supported consequence: files are written outside the intended directory, allowing arbitrary file overwrite on the user's system.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.1376: accessing invalid memory with put in Visual block mode

Problem:    Accessing invalid memory with put in Visual block mode.
Solution:   Adjust the cursor column if needed.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif ((j < count - 1 || !shortline) && spaces)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif ((j < count - 1 || !shortline) && spaces > 0)', '    // Make sure the cursor is not after the NUL.', '    int len = (int)STRLEN(ml_get_curline());', '    if (curwin->w_cursor.col > len)', '    {', '\tif (cur_ve_flags == VE_ALL)', '\t    curwin->w_cursor.coladd = curwin->w_cursor.col - len;', '\tcurwin->w_cursor.col = len;', '    }', '']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.1376.

code_evidence: totlen is computed at line 307 as count*(yanklen+spaces)+startspaces+endspaces and newp is allocated with totlen+oldlen+1 at line 308; the per-iteration writes at 312-328 (memmove of yanklen bytes, memset of startspaces/spaces/endspaces) depend on this size. The guard at line 320 uses the truthiness of spaces rather than spaces > 0, so when spaces is negative the condition still passes, memset writes (size_t)spaces bytes (huge) past the heap buffer, and totlen is not reduced by the else at line 326.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The buffer newp is heap-allocated via alloc() and subsequently over-written past its bounds by a size derived from a negative signed value, matching CWE-122 heap-based buffer overflow. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the defect causes writes beyond the allocated region.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy loop tests `spaces` as a boolean instead of requiring a positive value, while the allocation size uses the signed arithmetic result. Trigger: a Visual block put where y_width+1 minus tab-expanded width of the yanked text yields a negative spaces value. Consequence: vim_memset with a negative value cast to size_t writes beyond the heap-allocated newp buffer, corrupting heap memory (crash or potential code execution).

commit_msg:
There is a current use after free possible on a gatt server if a client
disconnects while a WriteValue call is being processed with dbus.

This patch includes the addition of a pending disconnect callback to handle
cleanup better if a disconnect occurs during a write, an acquire write
or read operation using bt_att_register_disconnect with the cb.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tgatt_db_attribute_write_result(op->attrib, op->id, ecode);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Make sure that only reply if the device is connected */', '\tif (!bt_att_get_fd(op->att))', '\t\tgatt_db_attribute_write_result(op->attrib, op->id, ecode);']}
description: An issue was discovered in gatt-database.c in BlueZ 5.61. A use-after-free can occur when a client disconnects during D-Bus processing of a WriteValue call.

code_evidence: The callback only bails out when op->owner_queue is NULL; otherwise it proceeds to the done label and dereferences op->attrib, op->id and op->att at line 36.

Line 36 calls gatt_db_attribute_write_result(op->attrib, op->id, ecode) unconditionally, with no check that the pending operation or its ATT transport is still alive after the asynchronous D-Bus reply.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reuses freed pending-operation/ATT memory after disconnect, which matches CWE-416 (Use After Free). The missing liveness check before the reply is the direct cause; a mere null-pointer dereference (CWE-476) would not involve memory previously freed.

evidence_lines.code:
done:
gatt_db_attribute_write_result(op->attrib, op->id, ecode);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: write_reply_cb runs asynchronously after a D-Bus WriteValue reply. If the client disconnects while the write is pending, the pending_op and/or ATT connection can be freed, yet the callback still reaches done and dereferences op->attrib/op->att and replies on the freed transport. The owner_queue guard does not cover disconnect-driven teardown, so the stale pointer is used, giving a use-after-free with possible crash or memory corruption.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfloat *val = fz_hash_find(ctx, cc->hash, ss);', '\tint n = cc->base.ds->n * sizeof(float);', '\tif (val)', '\t\tmemcpy(ds, val, n);', '\t\treturn;', '', '\tcc->base.convert(ctx, &cc->base, ss, ds);', '', '\tval = Memento_label(fz_malloc_array(ctx, cc->base.ds->n, float), "cached_color_convert");', '\tmemcpy(val, ds, n);', '\tfz_try(ctx)', '\t\tfz_hash_insert(ctx, cc->hash, ss, val);', '\tfz_catch(ctx)', '\t\tfz_free(ctx, val);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (cc->hash)', '\t{', '\t\tfloat *val = fz_hash_find(ctx, cc->hash, ss);', '\t\tint n = cc->base.ds->n * sizeof(float);', '\t\tif (val)', '\t\t{', '\t\t\tmemcpy(ds, val, n);', '\t\t\treturn;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\tcc->base.convert(ctx, &cc->base, ss, ds);', '', '\t\tval = Memento_label(fz_malloc_array(ctx, cc->base.ds->n, float), "cached_color_convert");', '\t\tmemcpy(val, ds, n);', '\t\tfz_try(ctx)', '\t\t\tfz_hash_insert(ctx, cc->hash, ss, val);', '\t\tfz_catch(ctx)', '\t\t\tfz_free(ctx, val);', '\t}', '\telse', '\t\tcc->base.convert(ctx, &cc->base, ss, ds);']}
description: MuPDF through 1.18.1 has an out-of-bounds write because the cached color converter does not properly consider the maximum key size of a hash table. This can, for example, be seen with crafted "mutool draw" input.

code_evidence: The hash key is the caller-supplied color array ss, passed to fz_hash_find(ctx, cc->hash, ss) without any check that its size fits the hash table's maximum key size.
After conversion, a heap buffer val of cc->base.ds->n floats is allocated and filled by memcpy(val, ds, n); fz_hash_insert then stores this value under the same unchecked ss key.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is a missing bound on key size before a hash-table insertion that copies the key into fixed-size storage, producing a write past the intended buffer. This directly matches CWE-787; it is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the unsafe operation is the key insertion write.

evidence_lines.code:
float *val = fz_hash_find(ctx, cc->hash, ss);
int n = cc->base.ds->n * sizeof(float);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The cached converter uses ss as a hash-table key without constraining its length to the table's maximum key size. When a crafted color space yields a key larger than the table supports, fz_hash_insert writes the oversized key into the fixed key storage, overflowing the heap buffer. The consequence is an out-of-bounds write, potentially memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix security issue in _prolog_error().

Fix security issue caused by insecure file path handling triggered by
the failure of a Prolog script. To exploit this a user needs to
anticipate or cause the Prolog to fail for their job.

(This commit is slightly different from the fix to the 15.08 branch.)

CVE-2016-10030.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\tif ((fd = open(path_name, (O_CREAT|O_APPEND|O_WRONLY), 0644)) == -1) {', '\t\terror("Unable to open %s: %s", path_name,', '\t\t      slurm_strerror(errno));'], 'added_lines': ['\tif ((fd = _open_as_other(path_name, req)) == -1) {', '\t\terror("Unable to open %s: Permission denied", path_name);']}
description: The _prolog_error function in slurmd/req.c in Slurm before 15.08.13, 16.x before 16.05.7, and 17.x before 17.02.0-pre4 has a vulnerability in how the slurmd daemon informs users of a Prolog failure on a compute node. That vulnerability could allow a user to assume control of an arbitrary file on the system. Any exploitation of this is dependent on the user being able to cause or anticipate the failure (non-zero return code) of a Prolog script that their job would run on. This issue affects all Slurm versions from 0.6.0 (September 2005) to present. Workarounds to prevent exploitation of this are to either disable your Prolog script, or modify it such that it always returns 0 ("success") and adjust it to set the node as down using scontrol instead of relying on the slurmd to handle that automatically. If you do not have a Prolog set you are unaffected by this issue.

code_evidence: path_name is built from user-influenced err_name (req->std_err/std_out) or work_dir, and an absolute err_name is copied verbatim; no check confines it to a directory the job user owns.
The file is opened with O_CREAT|O_APPEND|O_WRONLY and mode 0644 without validating ownership/path, so slurmd can create or append to an arbitrary path.
fchown then changes the opened file's owner to req->uid/req->gid, letting the user take ownership of a file the daemon opened.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is that access to the file resource is not restricted to an authorized actor/scope: slurmd acts with its privileges on a user-chosen path and hands ownership to the user. This is improper access control (CWE-284); it is not merely a path-traversal parsing flaw, since the missing constraint is on who may cause privileged access to an arbitrary file.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the daemon opens an attacker-influenced path and then chowns it to the job user without restricting where the file may reside. Trigger: a user causes/anticipates a Prolog failure and sets std_err/std_out or work_dir to a target absolute path. Consequence: slurmd creates/appends to and transfers ownership of an arbitrary file to the user, i.e. unauthorized access/control over a resource.

commit_msg:
Prevent another division by zero.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 369338598
Change-Id: I55471d363e401fdcf8d259670ad4eef672b731e2
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (filter_shape.dim_size(num_dims - 2) <= 0) {', '    return errors ::InvalidArgument(', '        label, ": filter depth must be strictly greated than zero");', '  }']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a division by 0 in `tf.raw_ops.Conv2DBackpropFilter`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/496c2630e51c1a478f095b084329acedb253db6b/tensorflow/core/kernels/conv_grad_shape_utils.cc#L130) does a modulus operation where the divisor is controlled by the caller. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function computes dims->in_depth from the caller-supplied input shape and takes a modulus by filter_shape.dim_size(num_dims - 2), which is the caller-controlled filter depth. On line 33 that dimension is used as the divisor without any prior check that it is nonzero, so a filter shape with depth 0 reaches the modulus.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 applies because the function performs a modulus (division) where the divisor, filter depth, is controlled by the caller and can be zero. The missing constraint is the cause; the crash is the consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the filter-depth value read from the caller-supplied filter_shape is used as the divisor in the modulus at line 33, and no guard rejects a zero value before that point. Trigger: a caller passes a filter tensor whose depth dimension is 0 to Conv2DBackpropFilter. Consequence: the modulo-by-zero operation causes a crash (denial of service).

commit_msg:
passthrough: quarantine PCI devices

When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for
that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The
IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that
the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However,
when the guest domain is torn down the device is assigned back to dom0,
thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data.

This patch introduces a 'quarantine' for PCI devices using dom_io. When
the toolstack makes a device assignable (by binding it to pciback), it
will now also assign it to DOMID_IO and the device will only be assigned
back to dom0 when the device is made unassignable again. Whilst device is
assignable it will only ever transfer between dom_io and guest domains.
dom_io is actually only used as a sentinel domain for quarantining purposes;
it is not configured with any IOMMU mappings. Assignment to dom_io simply
means that the device's initiator (requestor) identifier is not present in
the IOMMU's device table and thus any DMA transactions issued will be
terminated with a fault condition.

In addition, a fix to assignment handling is made for VT-d.  Failure
during the assignment step should not lead to a device still being
associated with its prior owner. Hand the device to DomIO temporarily,
until the assignment step has completed successfully.  Remove the PI
hooks from the source domain then earlier as well.

Failure of the recovery reassign_device_ownership() may not go silent:
There e.g. may still be left over RMRR mappings in the domain assignment
to which has failed, and hence we can't allow that domain to continue
executing.

NOTE: This patch also includes one printk() cleanup; the
      "XEN_DOMCTL_assign_device: " tag is dropped in iommu_do_pci_domctl(),
      since similar printk()-s elsewhere also don't log such a tag.

This is XSA-302.

Signed-off-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    /* dom_io is used as a sentinel for quarantined devices */', '    if ( domain == dom_io )', '        return;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing attackers to gain host OS privileges via DMA in a situation where an untrusted domain has access to a physical device. This occurs because passed through PCI devices may corrupt host memory after deassignment. When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However, when the guest domain is torn down, or the device is deassigned, the device is assigned back to dom0, thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data. An untrusted domain with access to a physical device can DMA into host memory, leading to privilege escalation. Only systems where guests are given direct access to physical devices capable of DMA (PCI pass-through) are vulnerable. Systems which do not use PCI pass-through are not vulnerable.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs AMD IOMMU device-table setup and DMA requestor-ID mapping; it contains no OS command construction or execution, so it cannot support CWE-78.

commit_msg: Validate the length in the DIO prefix info option.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '        if(dio.prefix_info.length > sizeof(uip_ipaddr_t) * 8) {', '          LOG_WARN("Invalid DAG prefix info, len %u > %u\\n",', '                   dio.prefix_info.length, (unsigned)(sizeof(uip_ipaddr_t) * 8));', '          RPL_STAT(rpl_stats.malformed_msgs++);', '          goto discard;', '        }', '']}
description: Contiki-NG is an open-source, cross-platform operating system for IoT devices. In the RPL-Classic routing protocol implementation in the Contiki-NG operating system, an incoming DODAG Information Option (DIO) control message can contain a prefix information option with a length parameter. The value of the length parameter is not validated, however, and it is possible to cause a buffer overflow when copying the prefix in the set_ip_from_prefix function. This vulnerability affects anyone running a Contiki-NG version prior to 4.7 that can receive RPL DIO messages from external parties. To obtain a patched version, users should upgrade to Contiki-NG 4.7 or later. There are no workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The RPL_OPTION_PREFIX_INFO branch validates the option's total length (len != 32) but stores the attacker-controlled prefix length byte buffer[i+2] into dio.prefix_info.length at line 134 without any bound check. It then unconditionally copies a fixed 16 bytes into dio.prefix_info.prefix at line 138; the stored length later drives the prefix-to-address copy in set_ip_from_prefix.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because an input-derived length governs a buffer copy without verifying it against the destination size, yielding a classic buffer overflow. The related CWE-20 input-validation angle is the underlying flaw, but the direct unsafe copy without size checking is the supported weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dio.prefix_info.length is taken from the DIO prefix option and never constrained to the address size before being used to copy the prefix into a uip_ipaddr_t. Trigger: an external RPL DIO message carrying a prefix-info option with a length larger than sizeof(uip_ipaddr_t)*8. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write past the destination address buffer, enabling memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg: Moved EOF check.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if (EOFBlob(image) != MagickFalse)', '        {', '          ThrowFileException(exception,CorruptImageError,"UnexpectedEndOfFile",', '            image->filename);', '          return(MagickFalse);', '        }'], 'added_lines': ['  if (EOFBlob(image) != MagickFalse)', '    {', '      ThrowFileException(exception,CorruptImageError,"UnexpectedEndOfFile",', '        image->filename);', '      return(MagickFalse);', '    }']}
description: coders/dds.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted DDS file.

code_evidence: The function checks the crafted DDS header fields ddscaps1/ddscaps2 for mipmap/texture/cubemap flags, then validates the blob for EOF before proceeding.

After the EOF check, it derives w and h from dds_info->width/height and loops over dds_info->mipmapcount, seeking offset = w*h*pixel_size per iteration without validating that mipmapcount or the derived sizes are consistent with the actual file contents.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is missing validation of input-derived metadata (mipmapcount and dimensions) before it is used to compute offsets, matching CWE-20's improper validation of input properties. This is not a transformation/encoding issue; the crafted header values are consumed as-is, so CWE-20 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The DDS header's mipmapcount, width and height are attacker-controlled metadata that are used to compute seek offsets without validating them against the remaining blob data. A crafted file with a large mipmapcount or dimensions drives repeated SeekBlob calls past the end of the data, causing a denial of service (crash) in ImageMagick.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflows when parsing style records

Closes #124, #126.

According to https://download.microsoft.com/download/5/0/1/501ED102-E53F-4CE0-AA6B-B0F93629DDC6/Office/Excel97-2007BinaryFileFormat(xls)Specification.pdf
a "STYLE: Style Information (293h)" record might be 4 or 3+ bytes
long, depending on the first word.

We need to check that we've read enough bytes for the whole
record, so
- first we check that we have a word at least,
- then we check the subtype of the record.
- If it is a built-in style, then it has 4 bytes, so we check that.
- Otherwise the length of the name is in byte 3, so the whole record
  is 3 + buf[3] bytes long. So we need at least three bytes before we
  check the length in byte 3. Then we check if we have 3 + buf[3]
  bytes.

commit_msg: Suspend exception processing if there are too many exceptions
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (CheckMemoryOverflow(count,quantum) != MagickFalse)'], 'added_lines': ['  if (HeapOverflowSanityCheck(count,quantum) != MagickFalse)']}
description: magick/memory.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-5 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via vectors involving "too many exceptions," which trigger a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: The function guards the multiplication with CheckMemoryOverflow(count,quantum), returns NULL on overflow, then computes extent=count*quantum and passes it to AcquireMagickMemory. The patch replaces the overflow check with HeapOverflowSanityCheck, indicating the prior check was inadequate for detecting size overflow.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked multiplication leads to an allocation smaller than the intended buffer, so subsequent operations exceed the buffer's bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds read/write on a memory buffer. The root cause is an integer overflow, but the supported consequence is a buffer-bound violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an insufficient overflow check on count*quantum allows the multiplication to wrap, producing a small extent while the caller expects count*quantum bytes. Trigger: attacker-controlled count/quantum values near the size_t maximum. Consequence: a too-small buffer is allocated and later written beyond its boundary, causing out-of-bounds memory operations and a crash (DoS) as described.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs operations on the profile buffer using offsets and lengths that are not constrained to the buffer's intended boundary, yielding out-of-bounds memory access. The related CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) would be a narrower child, but the evidence here supports the buffer-boundary class weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the EXIF profile is written in fixed 65533-byte increments without validating the profile against the JPEG marker size limit; the loop and pointer arithmetic rely on the chunk length alone. Trigger: a crafted file carrying an oversized EXIF profile drives repeated marker writes and offset reads at profile+i. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read/write operations and an application crash (denial of service).

commit_msg:
(for 4.9.3) CVE-2018-14464/LMP: Add a missing bounds check

In lmp_print_data_link_subobjs().

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int hexdump;', '\t\tif (lmp_print_data_link_subobjs(ndo, obj_tptr, obj_tlen - 12, 12))', '\t\tif (lmp_print_data_link_subobjs(ndo, obj_tptr, obj_tlen - 36, 36))', '\t\tif (lmp_print_data_link_subobjs(ndo, obj_tptr, obj_tlen - 12, 12))'], 'added_lines': ['    int hexdump, ret;', '\t\tret = lmp_print_data_link_subobjs(ndo, obj_tptr, obj_tlen - 12, 12);', '\t\tif (ret == -1)', '\t\t    goto trunc;', '\t\tif (ret == TRUE)', '\t\tret = lmp_print_data_link_subobjs(ndo, obj_tptr, obj_tlen - 36, 36);', '\t\tif (ret == -1)', '\t\t    goto trunc;', '\t\tif (ret == TRUE)', '\t\tret = lmp_print_data_link_subobjs(ndo, obj_tptr, obj_tlen - 12, 12);', '\t\tif (ret == -1)', '\t\t    goto trunc;', '\t\tif (ret == TRUE)']}
description: The LMP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-lmp.c:lmp_print_data_link_subobjs().

code_evidence: For LMP_CTYPE_IPV4, obj_tlen is only checked against a lower bound (obj_tlen < 12) and then obj_tptr is dereferenced at offsets +4 and +8 via ipaddr_string/EXTRACT_32BITS; lmp_print_data_link_subobjs is called with obj_tlen-12 without validating the sub-object region against the captured buffer.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads packet data via ipaddr_string/EXTRACT_32BITS and delegates to lmp_print_data_link_subobjs without a sufficient bounds check, so the supported consequence is reading memory past the intended buffer—matching CWE-125. This is an over-read, not an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DATA_LINK branches pass the remaining length to the sub-object parser and dereference obj_tptr without ensuring the enclosing object/capture actually contains those bytes. Trigger: a crafted or truncated LMP packet whose object length passes the lower-bound check but whose actual captured data is shorter. Consequence: the sub-object parser and address extraction read beyond the buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
Do not dereference PKCS7 object data if not set

Fixes CVE-2023-0216

Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (p7->d.ptr == NULL)', '        return NULL;']}
description:
An invalid pointer dereference on read can be triggered when an
application tries to load malformed PKCS7 data with the
d2i_PKCS7(), d2i_PKCS7_bio() or d2i_PKCS7_fp() functions.

The result of the dereference is an application crash which could
lead to a denial of service attack. The TLS implementation in OpenSSL
does not call this function however third party applications might
call these functions on untrusted data.

code_evidence: PKCS7_type_is_signed(p7) is evaluated and, if true, p7->d.sign is dereferenced to return p7->d.sign->cert without first confirming p7->d.ptr is non-NULL.
The signedAndEnveloped branch similarly dereferences p7->d.signed_and_enveloped->cert based only on the type check, with no NULL guard on the union pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but possibly NULL, matching CWE-476 directly; the patch adds exactly the missing p7->d.ptr NULL check. This is distinct from a type-confusion issue because the failure is a NULL dereference, not use of a wrong-typed object.

evidence_lines.code:
if (PKCS7_type_is_signed(p7))
return p7->d.sign->cert;

if (PKCS7_type_is_signedAndEnveloped(p7))
return p7->d.signed_and_enveloped->cert;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function reads the p7->d union through type-specific members without verifying that p7->d.ptr was populated. When malformed PKCS7 data is parsed, the type field can indicate signed/signedAndEnveloped while the union pointer remains NULL, so the dereference of p7->d.sign or p7->d.signed_and_enveloped crashes the application (DoS).

commit_msg: - fixed buffer overflow bug (rxpacket size)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  uint8_t *rxpacket           = (uint8_t *)malloc(length + 11 + (length / 3));'], 'added_lines': ['  uint8_t *rxpacket           = (uint8_t *)malloc(RXPACKET_MAX_LEN);']}
description: ROBOTIS Dynamixel SDK through 3.7.11 has a buffer overflow via a large rxpacket.

code_evidence: readRx allocates rxpacket with size length + 11 + (length / 3), where length is a caller-supplied uint16_t; large length values drive the allocation size and the subsequent rxPacket read into that buffer.

The copy loop iterates s from 0 to length-1, reading rxpacket[PKT_PARAMETER0 + 1 + s]; the last index accessed is PKT_PARAMETER0 + length, which exceeds the intended parameter region within the allocated buffer when the incoming frame's actual payload is shorter than length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a read operation outside the intended bounds of the rxpacket memory buffer, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within a buffer's bounds. It is not merely an allocation-size error; the unchecked length-driven indexing is the direct out-of-bounds access.

evidence_lines.code:
uint8_t *rxpacket           = (uint8_t *)malloc(length + 11 + (length / 3));
result = rxPacket(port, rxpacket);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer size is computed from an untrusted length and the copy loop trusts that same length without validating the received packet's actual parameter size. Trigger: a large or mismatched rxpacket causes reads at PKT_PARAMETER0 + 1 + s beyond the intended buffer boundary. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds reads into adjacent heap memory copied into data, leaking memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
Bug 698830: Avoid recursion when loading object streams objects.

If there were indirect references in the object stream dictionary and
one of those indirect references referred to an object inside the object
stream itself, mupdf would previously enter recursion only bounded by the
exception stack. After this commit the object stream is checked if it is
marked immediately after being loaded. If it is marked then we terminate
the recursion at this point, if it is not marked then mark it and
attempt to load the desired object within. We also take care to unmark
the stream object when done or upon exception.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\tif (pdf_obj_marked(ctx, objstm))', '\t\t\tfz_throw(ctx, FZ_ERROR_GENERIC, "recursive object stream lookup");', '\t}', '\tfz_catch(ctx)', '\t{', '\t\tpdf_drop_obj(ctx, objstm);', '\t\tfz_rethrow(ctx);', '\t}', '', '\tfz_try(ctx)', '\t{', '\t\tpdf_mark_obj(ctx, objstm);', '\t\tpdf_unmark_obj(ctx, objstm);']}
description: pdf_load_obj_stm in pdf/pdf-xref.c in Artifex MuPDF 1.12.0 could reference the object stream recursively and therefore run out of error stack, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted PDF document.

code_evidence: pdf_load_object at line 20 loads the object stream; the dictionary values N and First are then read and used to drive the subsequent parsing loop.

The loop at lines 30-40 lexes count integer pairs from the stream, then lines 42-47 seek and parse each embedded object with pdf_parse_stm_obj, which can itself reference the enclosing object stream indirectly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because re-entrant loading of the same object stream is unbounded recursion not controlled by the function, and the supported impact is resource-consumption DoS. This is uncontrolled recursion, not merely a memory-corruption or input-validation flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function loads the object stream and parses its embedded objects without any marker or depth guard. A crafted PDF whose object-stream dictionary contains an indirect reference back to an object inside the same stream makes pdf_load_object re-enter pdf_load_obj_stm before the outer load completes. Each re-entry consumes stack until the error stack is exhausted, causing a denial of service. The cause is the missing recursion guard; the consequence is stack exhaustion DoS.

commit_msg:
fix a bunch of vsprintf -> vsnprintf

closes #1203
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tvsprintf(szMsg, format, args);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tvsnprintf(szMsg, 2048, format, args);']}
description: GPAC 0.7.1 has a buffer overflow issue in gf_import_message() in media_import.c.

code_evidence: A fixed 2048-byte stack buffer szMsg is declared at line 5 and filled by vsprintf at line 8, which writes the formatted variadic arguments into szMsg without any size bound. The format string and arguments originate from callers of svg_report and are not constrained here; va_start at line 7 only initializes the argument list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing past the end of the intended szMsg buffer is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is distinct from format-string issues (CWE-134) because the unsafe operation is the missing output-length bound, not misuse of the format specifiers.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: vsprintf performs an unbounded formatted write into the 2048-byte stack buffer szMsg. Trigger: a caller-supplied format/argument combination whose expansion exceeds 2048 bytes. Supported consequence: memory beyond szMsg is overwritten, corrupting adjacent stack data and potentially enabling a crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix security vulnerability in libstagefright

bug: 28175045
Change-Id: Icee6c7eb5b761da4aa3e412fb71825508d74d38f
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            CHECK(dstOffset + 4 <= (*buffer)->size());'], 'added_lines': ['            if (dstOffset > SIZE_MAX - 4 ||', '                dstOffset + 4 > SIZE_MAX - nalLength ||', '                dstOffset + 4 + nalLength > (*buffer)->size()) {', '                (*buffer)->release();', '                (*buffer) = NULL;', '                if (decryptedDrmBuffer.data) {', '                    delete [] decryptedDrmBuffer.data;', '                    decryptedDrmBuffer.data = NULL;', '                }', '                return ERROR_MALFORMED;', '            }']}
description: DRMExtractor.cpp in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-07-01 does not validate a certain offset value, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, aka internal bug 28175045.

code_evidence: Line 63 uses CHECK(dstOffset + 4 <= (*buffer)->size()) as the only bound check before writing the 4-byte NAL start code and then memcpy'ing nalLength bytes at line 68. The check accounts only for the 4-byte header, not for nalLength, so dstData writes at dstOffset+4..dstOffset+4+nalLength-1 can exceed the destination buffer. CHECK also aborts rather than returning a recoverable error.

Lines 52-59 validate the source-side end offset (srcOffset + nalLength against len), confirming nalLength is attacker-controlled from the media stream and can be large; this value feeds the unchecked destination write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to a memory buffer without restricting the operation to the buffer's intended boundary, fitting CWE-119. The more specific CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) is the underlying child weakness, but the target label CWE-119 correctly captures the out-of-bounds memory write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination bound check omits nalLength, so only the 4-byte header is validated. Trigger: a crafted AVC stream with a large NAL length passes the source check at lines 52-59 and the header-only check at line 63, then memcpy at line 68 writes past the end of (*buffer). Consequence: heap buffer overflow, enabling memory corruption and potentially arbitrary code execution or DoS.

commit_msg:
Fix oob memcpy in matrix_custom_frame methods

Adjust row_length if it exeeds the arguments array
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    const size_t start_arg_offset = 2;', '', '    if (row_length > sizeof(report.arguments) - start_arg_offset) {', '        printk(KERN_ALERT "razerchroma: RGB data too long\\n");', '        row_length = sizeof(report.arguments) - start_arg_offset;', '    }']}
description: A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the razerkbd driver of OpenRazer up to version v3.3.0 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) and possibly escalate their privileges via a crafted buffer sent to the matrix_custom_frame device.

Line 6 copies row_length bytes from rgb_data into &report.arguments[2] with no bound check against the remaining size of report.arguments.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code performs a buffer copy (memcpy) whose length is not checked against the destination size, matching CWE-120. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the write past report.arguments is the classic unchecked-copy overflow.

size_t row_length = (size_t) (((stop_col + 1) - start_col) * 3);
memcpy(&report.arguments[2], rgb_data, row_length);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: row_length derived from stop_col/start_col is used directly as the memcpy length without validating it against sizeof(report.arguments) minus the 2-byte offset. commit_msg: Fixed a problem with a null pointer dereference in the BMP decoder.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (numrows < 0 || numcols < 0) {', '\t\treturn 0;', '\t}']}
description: The bmp_getdata function in libjasper/bmp/bmp_dec.c in JasPer 1.900.5 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) by calling the imginfo command with a crafted BMP image. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2016-8690.

code_evidence: numrows and numcols are stored directly into matrix->numrows_, matrix->numcols_, maxrows_ and datasize_ without validating that they are non-negative.

Allocation and initialization are guarded only by > 0 checks: maxrows_ > 0 gates rows_ allocation, datasize_ > 0 gates data_ allocation, yet the loops at line 29 and line 32 iterate up to numrows and datasize_ unconditionally.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a dereference of a pointer that allocation guards left NULL, matching CWE-476's description of dereferencing a pointer expected to be valid but NULL. The weakness is the missing dimension validation, not an out-of-bounds write, so CWE-476 fits rather than a buffer-related CWE.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts caller-supplied dimensions and never rejects negative values, so datasize_ = numrows * numcols and maxrows_ can be negative. Trigger: a crafted BMP yielding negative dimensions reaches jas_matrix_create. The > 0 guards skip allocation, leaving rows_ or data_ NULL, while the subsequent loops dereference those NULL pointers, causing a crash (denial of service).

commit_msg: fixed #2061
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tu8 *res;', '\tres = gf_utf_get_utf8_string_from_bom((char *)probe_data, size, &dst);', '\tif (res) probe_data = res;'], 'added_lines': ['\tGF_Err e;', '\tchar *res=NULL;', '\te = gf_utf_get_utf8_string_from_bom(probe_data, size, &dst, &res);', '\tif (e) return NULL;']}

The subsequent parsing loops dereference probe_data (e.g. lines 12, 15, 39) and finally dst is freed at line 100; the previous API returned ownership ambiguously, so probe_data could alias freed or invalid memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because probe_data is rebound to memory returned by a conversion routine and then dereferenced after that memory's lifetime is not guaranteed, i.e. reuse of freed/released memory rather than a bounds error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the old API returned a pointer whose lifetime/ownership was not expressed, and the function adopted it as probe_data without tracking validity. After the BOM conversion buffer is freed (dst at exit), later dereferences of probe_data/res occur, yielding a use-after-free read/crash triggered by probe input with a UTF BOM header.
