commit_msg:
mt76: fix array overflow on receiving too many fragments for a packet

If the hardware receives an oversized packet with too many rx fragments,
skb_shinfo(skb)->frags can overflow and corrupt memory of adjacent pages.
This becomes especially visible if it corrupts the freelist pointer of
a slab page.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Felix Fietkau <nbd@nbd.name>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\toffset += q->buf_offset;', '\tskb_add_rx_frag(skb, skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags, page, offset, len,', '\t\t\tq->buf_size);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct skb_shared_info *shinfo = skb_shinfo(skb);', '\tif (shinfo->nr_frags < ARRAY_SIZE(shinfo->frags)) {', '\t\toffset += q->buf_offset;', '\t\tskb_add_rx_frag(skb, shinfo->nr_frags, page, offset, len,', '\t\t\t\tq->buf_size);', '\t}']}
description: An array overflow was discovered in mt76_add_fragment in drivers/net/wireless/mediatek/mt76/dma.c in the Linux kernel before 5.5.10, aka CID-b102f0c522cf. An oversized packet with too many rx fragments can corrupt memory of adjacent pages.

code_evidence: The function obtains the shared info from q->rx_head and passes skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags directly as the fragment index to skb_add_rx_frag, with no check that nr_frags is within the bounds of the frags array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a buffer copy with no size-of-input check: the fragment data is copied into an output buffer (frags) whose capacity is never compared against the incoming fragment count, producing an out-of-bounds write. CWE-120 applies because the copy proceeds without validating that the input fits the destination array.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: each received fragment is appended using the current nr_frags value as the destination index without verifying it stays below ARRAY_SIZE(shinfo->frags). Trigger: hardware delivers an oversized packet with more rx fragments than the frags array can hold, so nr_frags reaches the array limit and skb_add_rx_frag writes past the frags array into adjacent memory, corrupting adjacent pages.

commit_msg: TIFFReadDirectory(): avoid calling memcpy() with a null source pointer and size of zero (fixes #362)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                memcpy(new_sampleinfo, tif->tif_dir.td_sampleinfo, old_extrasamples * sizeof(uint16_t));'], 'added_lines': ['                if (old_extrasamples > 0)', '                    memcpy(new_sampleinfo, tif->tif_dir.td_sampleinfo, old_extrasamples * sizeof(uint16_t));']}
description: Null source pointer passed as an argument to memcpy() function within TIFFFetchStripThing() in tif_dirread.c in libtiff versions from 3.9.0 to 4.3.0 could lead to Denial of Service via crafted TIFF file. For users that compile libtiff from sources, the fix is available with commit eecb0712.

code_evidence: Line 458 enters the block when samplesperpixel minus extrasamples exceeds the color channels; line 464 saves td_extrasamples into old_extrasamples, which can be zero when the directory declares no ExtraSamples. Line 466 allocates new_sampleinfo based on the recomputed td_extrasamples, and line 474 then calls memcpy with source tif->tif_dir.td_sampleinfo and length old_extrasamples * sizeof(uint16_t). When old_extrasamples is 0, the source pointer may be NULL (no sampleinfo array was ever allocated), so memcpy receives a NULL source with zero length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a direct NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): the NULL td_sampleinfo pointer is passed as the memcpy source. It is not merely a buffer overflow, since the length is zero; the defect is the missing zero-count guard before dereferencing the potentially NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code copies old_extrasamples entries without guarding against old_extrasamples == 0, while td_sampleinfo is only populated when ExtraSamples exist. Trigger: a crafted TIFF whose SamplesPerPixel/Photometric combination forces the color-channel mismatch branch while declaring zero ExtraSamples. Consequence: memcpy with a NULL source, yielding undefined behavior and a denial-of-service crash.

commit_msg: fixed #1968
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif (!com->node) return GF_SG_UNKNOWN_NODE;']}
description: A Null Pointer Dereference vulnerability exists in gpac 1.1.0 in the gf_node_get_field function, which can cause a segmentation fault and application crash.

The added guard confirms the missing NULL constraint; it is not a different weakness such as a use-after-free.

Trigger: a delete command whose ref idref cannot be resolved while att_type>=0. Consequence: gf_node_get_field dereferences a NULL node, causing a segmentation fault and application crash (availability impact).

commit_msg: fix for stsc boxes with 0 entries (#1344)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (!ent) {', '\t\tstbl->SampleToChunk->ghostNumber = 0;', '\t\treturn;', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in gpac 0.8.0. The GetGhostNum function in stbl_read.c has a heap-based buffer overflow which can lead to a denial of service (DOS) via a crafted input.

Line 18 then reads nextEnt->firstChunk from that potentially out-of-range element.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked EntryIndex+1 access on the entries array is an out-of-bounds memory operation on a heap buffer, matching CWE-787's write-past-end pattern. Trigger: a crafted stsc box with zero entries (or a stale EntryIndex) reaches this function, so the unchecked index reads/writes outside the allocated entries array. The resulting out-of-bounds memory access corrupts heap metadata, producing a crash/DoS as reported.

commit_msg:

commit_msg:
cap_convert_nscap() does permission checking as well as conversion of the
xattr value conditionally based on fs's user-ns.

This is needed by overlayfs and probably other layered fs (ecryptfs) and is
what vfs_foo() is supposed to do anyway.

Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Acked-by: James Morris <jamorris@linux.microsoft.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tconst void  *orig_value = value;', '', '\tif (size && strcmp(name, XATTR_NAME_CAPS) == 0) {', '\t\terror = cap_convert_nscap(dentry, &value, size);', '\t\tif (error < 0)', '\t\t\treturn error;', '\t\tsize = error;', '\t}', '\tif (value != orig_value)', '\t\tkfree(value);', '']}
description: The overlayfs implementation in the linux kernel did not properly validate with respect to user namespaces the setting of file capabilities on files in an underlying file system. Due to the combination of unprivileged user namespaces along with a patch carried in the Ubuntu kernel to allow unprivileged overlay mounts, an attacker could use this to gain elevated privileges.

code_evidence: vfs_setxattr forwards the caller-supplied name, value and size directly to __vfs_setxattr_locked and returns its result after inode locking and delegation retry; the function itself contains no check on XATTR_NAME_CAPS or on whether the value is a namespaced capability relative to the caller's user namespace, so any authorization decision is deferred to the filesystem's setxattr handler.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an authorization check that is not correctly performed at the layer responsible for it: vfs_setxattr delegates without validating the capability value against the user namespace, matching CWE-863 rather than a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the VFS layer, the intended single point for generic xattr authorization, never validates capability xattr values against the caller's user namespace before dispatch. Trigger: an unprivileged user in a user namespace sets security.capability through a layered filesystem whose backing handler trusts the already-converted value. Consequence: an incorrect capability value is stored, allowing privilege gain on the underlying file.

commit_msg: Code Health (remove a compiler warning).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        assert(extra_group_size == 0 && extra_groups == NULL || extra_group_size);'], 'added_lines': ['        assert((extra_group_size == 0 && extra_groups == NULL) || extra_group_size);']}
description:
An issue was found in CPython 3.12.0 `subprocess` module on POSIX platforms. The issue was fixed in CPython 3.12.1 and does not affect other stable releases.

When using the `extra_groups=` parameter with an empty list as a value (ie `extra_groups=[]`) the logic regressed to not call `setgroups(0, NULL)` before calling `exec()`, thus not dropping the original processes' groups before starting the new process. There is no issue when the parameter isn't used or when any value is used besides an empty list.

This issue only impacts CPython processes run with sufficient privilege to make the `setgroups` system call (typically `root`).

code_evidence: The HAVE_SETGROUPS block calls setgroups(extra_group_size, extra_groups) only when extra_group_size >= 0. For an empty list, extra_group_size is 0 and extra_groups is NULL, so setgroups(0, NULL) is invoked to drop supplementary groups before exec. The changed assert merely adds parentheses to the precondition (size 0 with NULL groups, or nonzero size) and does not alter the call or its guard.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly manages child privilege state by dropping supplementary groups before exec, supporting CWE-269's improper privilege management scope. The assert edit is not itself a vulnerability, but the code path is the privilege-dropping control relevant to the commit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the privileged child_exec path relies on setgroups being reached for extra_group_size == 0 to clear inherited supplementary groups before exec. Trigger: a privileged parent passes extra_groups=[] so the guard is satisfied and setgroups(0, NULL) executes. Consequence: the spawned process loses the parent's supplementary groups, preventing unintended group-privilege retention. The assert change is only a compiler-warning fix and does not cause or remove this behavior.

commit_msg:
gnrc_sixlowpan_frag_rb: fix integer underflow in _6lo_frag_size()

(cherry picked from commit 9728f727e75d7d78dbfb5918e0de1b938b7b6d2c)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (pkt->size < sizeof(sixlowpan_frag_t)) {', '            return 0;', '        }', '        if (pkt->size < sizeof(sixlowpan_frag_n_t)) {', '            return 0;', '        }']}
description: RIOT-OS, an operating system that supports Internet of Things devices, contains a network stack with the ability to process 6LoWPAN frames. Prior to version 2022.10, an attacker can send a crafted frame to the device resulting in a large out of bounds write beyond the packet buffer. The write will create a hard fault exception after reaching the last page of RAM. The hard fault is not handled and the system will be stuck until reset, thus the impact is denial of service. Version 2022.10 fixes this issue. As a workaround, disable support for fragmented IP datagrams or apply the patches manually.

code_evidence: When offset == 0, frag_size is computed as pkt->size - sizeof(sixlowpan_frag_t) without checking that pkt->size is at least the header size; a small pkt->size underflows size_t to a huge value.
The else branch similarly subtracts sizeof(sixlowpan_frag_n_t) from pkt->size with no lower-bound check, again producing a huge frag_size on undersized packets.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing lower-bound check on pkt->size leads to an underflowed length that drives writes beyond the packet buffer, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. This is not merely an integer underflow (CWE-191); the supported security consequence is the memory write past the buffer end.

evidence_lines.code:
else {
frag_size = pkt->size - sizeof(sixlowpan_frag_n_t);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function derives a fragment payload size by subtracting a fixed header length from the attacker-controlled packet size without verifying pkt->size is large enough. An undersized 6LoWPAN fragment causes size_t underflow, returning a huge frag_size that callers use as a length for writing into the packet buffer, producing an out-of-bounds write and eventual hard fault (DoS). Root cause is the missing size check; the OOB write is the consequence.

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tprivate = t->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\tprivate = xt_table_get_private_protected(t);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: After local_bh_disable(), the function reads the table's private pointer directly from t->private into a local variable, then immediately dereferences private->number. This load is not protected by the sequence-count synchronization that xt_replace_table relies on to know the old rules are unused.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reuses a pointer to table information that can be freed concurrently, matching CWE-416. The root cause is the unsynchronized direct read of t->private rather than an access-control or integer issue; the missing constraint is ordering with the replacement/free sequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The replacement thread assigns new table information and relies on a write barrier plus an even per-CPU sequence count before freeing the old private data. Here the read of t->private can be reordered/observed before that assignment completes, so private may still reference the old table info. If a packet path is concurrently using it, xt_replace_table can free it, and the subsequent private->number access (and later iteration) is a use-after-free.

commit_msg:
Add missing checks when loading and playing .mkj files

Fix the following issues in src/mkj.cpp:
* Check number of channels before loading instruments data.
  This fixes a heap-based buffer overflow in CmkjPlayer::load()
  (issue #87).
* Check number of notes befor calculating size of song data
  to avoid interger overflows as well as out-of-bounds reads
  later in update(). (Size of song data vs. used data is really
  hilarious, but that's the way it is.)
* Fail loading if there was an error while reading file data.
* Also in update(), end the song if invalid data is encountered.
  That avoids integer overflows or out-of-range OPL writes.

This commit fixes CVE-2019-14692.

Fixes: https://github.com/adplug/adplug/issues/87

description: AdPlug 2.3.1 has a heap-based buffer overflow in CmkjPlayer::load() in mkj.cpp.

code_evidence: In case 255, songptr is advanced by maxchannel and songbuf[songptr] is read without validating the index against the buffer size; the value then drives pstat.
In case 254, songptr advances by maxchannel and songbuf[songptr] is stored into octave, an index-feeding field, with no range check before the write.
In case 252, songbuf[songptr] - 300 is written to the OPL register as waveform; c + (c+6) and c index register writes with attacker-controlled songptr.
Case 251 resets songptr for all channels and ends the song; the do-while loop at line 54 continues while pstat is unset, allowing repeated invalid reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because attacker-controlled indexing causes writes past the intended buffer: songbuf values select offsets and waveform/octave values that are written to OPL registers beyond valid ranges. This is an out-of-bounds write rather than only an out-of-bounds read, since the missing constraints let derived values reach write operations without bounds enforcement.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser trusts songptr derived from songbuf contents. In cases 255/254/252 it advances songptr by maxchannel and immediately reads songbuf[songptr] or writes derived values to OPL registers without checking bounds. A crafted .mkj file can drive songptr past the allocated song data, causing out-of-bounds reads that feed out-of-range OPL writes and corrupt memory/state.

commit_msg: Fix potential buffer overflow when writing a double (Issue #233)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t  sprintf(s, "%d", current->value.integer);', '\t  sprintf(s, "%f", current->value.real);'], 'added_lines': ['\t  snprintf(s, sizeof(s), "%d", current->value.integer);', '\t  snprintf(s, sizeof(s), "%f", current->value.real);']}
description: An issue has been found in Mini-XML (aka mxml) 2.12. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in mxml_write_node in mxml-file.c via vectors involving a double-precision floating point number and the '<order type="real">' substring, as demonstrated by testmxml.

code_evidence: Line 14 declares a fixed-size stack buffer `char s[255];` used for formatting numeric output.

In the MXML_REAL case, line 146 calls `sprintf(s, "%f", current->value.real)` with no bound on the number of characters written into `s`, then line 147 passes `s` to mxml_write_string and line 149 calls strlen on it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing formatted data past the end of the stack buffer `s` is an out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-787. The fix replaces sprintf with snprintf bounded by sizeof(s), confirming the missing length constraint; this is not merely a format-string issue (CWE-134) since the format is constant and the flaw is the absent bound.

evidence_lines.code: chars[255];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the unbounded sprintf writing a formatted double into the 255-byte stack buffer `s`. A crafted real value (e.g., a large-magnitude double whose %f expansion exceeds 255 characters) triggers the write past the end of `s`, corrupting adjacent stack memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
DNP3: fix reachable assertion and buffer over-read/overflow.

A DNP3 packet using a link layer header that specifies a zero length can
trigger an assertion failure if assertions are enabled.  Assertions are
enabled unless Bro is compiled with the NDEBUG preprocessor macro
defined.  The default configuration of Bro will define this macro and so
disables assertions, but using the --enable-debug option in the
configure script will enable assertions.  When assertions are disabled,
or also for certain length values, the DNP3 parser may attempt to pass a
negative value as the third argument to memcpy (number of bytes to copy)
and result in a buffer over-read or overflow.

Reported by Travis Emmert.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif ( ! AddToBuffer(endp, PSEUDO_APP_LAYER_INDEX, &data, &len) )', '\t\t\tassert(endp->pkt_length);', '\t\t\tif ( ! AddToBuffer(endp, n, &data, &len) )'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tint res = AddToBuffer(endp, PSEUDO_APP_LAYER_INDEX, &data, &len);', '', '\t\t\tif ( res == 0 )', '', '\t\t\tif ( res < 0 )', '\t\t\t\treturn false;', '\t\t\tif ( endp->pkt_length <= 0 )', '\t\t\t\t{', '\t\t\t\tanalyzer->Weird("dnp3_negative_or_zero_length_link_layer");', '\t\t\t\treturn false;', '\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tint res = AddToBuffer(endp, n, &data, &len);', '', '\t\t\tif ( res == 0 )', '', '\t\t\tif ( res < 0 )', '\t\t\t\treturn false;']}
description: analyzer/protocol/dnp3/DNP3.cc in Bro before 2.3.2 does not properly handle zero values of a packet length, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow or buffer over-read if NDEBUG; otherwise assertion failure) via a crafted DNP3 packet.

code_evidence: Line 29 sets endp->pkt_length from the attacker-controlled link-layer length byte; nothing constrains it to be non-zero. Line 37 only asserts pkt_length, which is compiled out when NDEBUG is defined. Lines 38-39 compute n = PSEUDO_APP_LAYER_INDEX + (pkt_length - 5) + ... using that unchecked value; a zero (or small) pkt_length makes the arithmetic negative. Line 40 passes n as the target buffer length to AddToBuffer, which then performs memory operations using this negative/short length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length flows into a buffer-size/copy computation and drives reads/writes outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The root arithmetic flaw could be described as integer underflow (CWE-191), but the supported consequence here is the out-of-bounds buffer access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the link-layer length byte is trusted without a lower-bound check before being used in the buffer-size computation. Trigger: a crafted DNP3 packet with a zero link-layer length reaches line 29, then lines 38-39 produce a negative n, and line 40 invokes AddToBuffer with it. Consequence: when assertions are disabled, the buffer copy uses a negative/short length, causing a buffer over-read or overflow (denial of service); with assertions enabled it aborts.

commit_msg:
Fix out of bound read in requantization_range_op.cc

PiperOrigin-RevId: 372129031
Change-Id: Ie684ab98a3840c5186ead3eafffc0e0ed0e8030d
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(ctx, ctx->input(1).NumElements() > 0,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("Input min must not be empty."));', '    OP_REQUIRES(ctx, ctx->input(2).NumElements() > 0,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("Input max must not be empty."));']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The implementation of `tf.raw_ops.MaxPoolGradWithArgmax` can cause reads outside of bounds of heap allocated data if attacker supplies specially crafted inputs. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/ac328eaa3870491ababc147822cd04e91a790643/tensorflow/core/kernels/requantization_range_op.cc#L49-L50) assumes that the `input_min` and `input_max` tensors have at least one element, as it accesses the first element in two arrays. If the tensors are empty, `.flat<T>()` is an empty object, backed by an empty array. Hence, accesing even the 0th element is a read outside the bounds. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Lines 3-4 read element 0 via flat<float>()(0) from ctx->input(1) and ctx->input(2) without checking that either tensor has at least one element; an empty tensor yields an empty flat buffer, so indexing 0 reads out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads the 0th element of an empty buffer, exactly the 'read past the end of the intended buffer' pattern of CWE-125. It is a read rather than a write, distinguishing it from CWE-787.

evidence_lines.code:
const float input_min_float = ctx->input(1).flat<float>()(0);
const float input_max_float = ctx->input(2).flat<float>()(0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the unchecked assumption that input_min and input_max each contain at least one float. When an attacker supplies empty tensors, flat<float>() is empty and the (0) access reads past the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds heap read (possible crash or information disclosure).

commit_msg:
x86: limit linear page table use to a single level

That's the only way that they're meant to be used. Without such a
restriction arbitrarily long chains of same-level page tables can be
built, tearing down of which may then cause arbitrarily deep recursion,
causing a stack overflow. To facilitate this restriction, a counter is
being introduced to track both the number of same-level entries in a
page table as well as the number of uses of a page table in another
same-level one (counting into positive and negative direction
respectively, utilizing the fact that both counts can't be non-zero at
the same time).

Note that the added accounting introduces a restriction on the number
of times a page can be used in other same-level page tables - more than
32k of such uses are no longer possible.

Note also that some put_page_and_type[_preemptible]() calls are
replaced with open-coded equivalents.  This seemed preferrable to
adding "parent_table" to the matrix of functions.

Note further that cross-domain same-level page table references are no
longer permitted (they probably never should have been).

This is XSA-240.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service (unbounded recursion, stack consumption, and hypervisor crash) or possibly gain privileges via crafted page-table stacking.

code_evidence: Line 3-4: the only guard is presence plus self-reference; no check on whether the referenced l2 entry forms a same-level page-table chain.
Lines 11-12: for non-PSE entries the function calls put_page_and_type on the referenced page without any depth/level accounting, so an arbitrarily stacked same-level reference is released here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the missing constraint permits uncontrolled growth of same-level page-table references, exhausting the finite hypervisor stack during recursive teardown. This is a resource-exhaustion weakness, not merely a memory-safety flaw; the trigger is crafted guest page-table stacking.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( !(l2e_get_flags(l2e) & _PAGE_PRESENT) || (l2e_get_pfn(l2e) == pfn) )
return 1;

} else
put_page_and_type(l2e_get_page(l2e));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function releases a referenced page table without limiting how many same-level references a table may hold or how deep such chains are. A PV guest can build long chains of same-level page tables; teardown then recurses through them, exhausting the stack and crashing the hypervisor. Root cause is missing depth/usage accounting; the consequence is unbounded recursion and resource exhaustion.

commit_msg:
Bug 699271: Fix eternal loop when skipping space before EOF.

Thanks to Michael J Gruber for providing this oneliner.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (c > 32 && c != EOF)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (c == EOF || c > 32)']}
description: In MuPDF 1.13.0, there is an infinite loop in the fz_skip_space function of the pdf/pdf-xref.c file. A remote adversary could leverage this vulnerability to cause a denial of service via a crafted pdf file.

code_evidence: The function is an unconditional do/while(1) loop that peeks a byte at line 6 and only returns when the guard at line 7 is true. The guard requires c > 32, so a byte value of EOF (negative) or any byte <= 32 fails the condition and falls through to fz_read_byte at line 9. For EOF specifically, fz_read_byte does not advance past end-of-stream, so the next iteration peeks the same EOF value again, and the loop never reaches its return.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loop's only exit path (the return at line 8) is guarded by a condition that is unreachable once EOF is encountered, matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. This is a loop-control defect rather than an out-of-bounds access or resource leak, so CWE-835 is the direct fit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the exit condition c > 32 && c != EOF treats EOF as a value to be consumed rather than a terminal state, and reading at EOF does not advance the stream. Trigger: a crafted PDF whose stream is exhausted while fz_skip_space is skipping whitespace. Consequence: the loop spins forever peeking the same EOF byte, consuming CPU and denying service.

commit_msg:
Detect invalid port in xp_socket parse ip address

For historical reasons, fsockopen() accepts the port and hostname
separately: fsockopen('127.0.0.1', 80)

However, with the introdcution of stream transports in PHP 4.3,
it became possible to include the port in the hostname specifier:

fsockopen('127.0.0.1:80')
Or more formally: fsockopen('tcp://127.0.0.1:80')

Confusing results when these two forms are combined, however.
fsockopen('127.0.0.1:80', 443) results in fsockopen() attempting
to connect to '127.0.0.1:80:443' which any reasonable stack would
consider invalid.

Unfortunately, PHP parses the address looking for the first colon
(with special handling for IPv6, don't worry) and calls atoi()
from there.  atoi() in turn, simply stops parsing at the first
non-numeric character and returns the value so far.

The end result is that the explicitly supplied port is treated
as ignored garbage, rather than producing an error.

This diff replaces atoi() with strtol() and inspects the
stop character.  If additional "garbage" of any kind is found,
it fails and returns an error.

description: PHP through 7.1.11 enables potential SSRF in applications that accept an fsockopen or pfsockopen hostname argument with an expectation that the port number is constrained. Because a :port syntax is recognized, fsockopen will use the port number that is specified in the hostname argument, instead of the port number in the second argument of the function.

code_evidence: Line 15 converts the substring after ':' in the IPv6 bracket form with atoi(), which stops at the first non-numeric character and silently accepts trailing garbage as the port.
Lines 24-26 take the first colon found by memchr (line 20) and again call atoi(colon + 1); a hostname like '127.0.0.1:80' yields port 80 while any trailing text is discarded without error.
Line 20 locates the first ':' in the input, so the port portion passed to atoi may contain arbitrary non-numeric characters.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function receives a hostname string and fails to validate that the embedded port token is well-formed, accepting malformed input as valid; this is improper input validation (CWE-20). It is not merely a transformation/filtering issue, since atoi() silently truncates rather than sanitizing the input.

evidence_lines.code: *portno = atoi(p + 2);

if (str_len) {
colon = memchr(str, ':', str_len - 1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the port field parsed from the hostname is converted with atoi(), which does not verify that the entire numeric token is valid. Trigger: attacker-controlled hostname containing ':port' followed by extra characters (e.g. '127.0.0.1:80:443'). Consequence: the parsed port is accepted rather than rejected, so the caller's intended port constraint is bypassed, enabling connections to an attacker-chosen port.

commit_msg:
There is a potential UAF between the unregistration routine and the NFC
netlink operations.

The race that cause that UAF can be shown as below:

 (FREE)                      |  (USE)
nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev   |  nfc_genl_dev_up
  nci_close_device           |
  nci_unregister_device      |    nfc_get_device
    nfc_unregister_device    |    nfc_dev_up
      rfkill_destory         |
      device_del             |      rfkill_blocked
  ...                        |    ...

The root cause for this race is concluded below:
1. The rfkill_blocked (USE) in nfc_dev_up is supposed to be placed after
the device_is_registered check.
2. Since the netlink operations are possible just after the device_add
in nfc_register_device, the nfc_dev_up() can happen anywhere during the
rfkill creation process, which leads to data race.

This patch reorder these actions to permit
1. Once device_del is finished, the nfc_dev_up cannot dereference the
rfkill object.
2. The rfkill_register need to be placed after the device_add of nfc_dev
because the parent device need to be created first. So this patch keeps
the order but inject device_lock to prevent the data race.

Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Fixes: be055b2f89b5 ("NFC: RFKILL support")

Reviewed-by: Krzysztof Kozlowski <krzysztof.kozlowski@canonical.com>

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nci_request in net/nfc/nci/core.c in NFC Controller Interface (NCI) in the Linux kernel. This flaw could allow a local attacker with user privileges to cause a data race problem while the device is getting removed, leading to a privilege escalation problem.

code_evidence: nfc_dev_up takes device_lock, then dereferences dev->rfkill via rfkill_blocked() before verifying the device is still registered with device_is_registered(). The registration check appears only afterward at line 10. The patch reorders these two checks so the registration test precedes the rfkill dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function accesses a shared resource (dev->rfkill) in a sequence that is not atomic with respect to concurrent unregistration, allowing an interfering code sequence to free it between the check and use. The flaw is improper synchronization/ordering rather than an absent bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the rfkill_blocked(dev->rfkill) read occurs before confirming the device is still registered, while unregistration can concurrently destroy the rfkill object. Trigger: an attacker invokes the NF netlink dev_up path during nfc_unregister_device/rfkill_destroy. Consequence: use-after-free dereference of dev->rfkill, supporting memory corruption or crash; the reordering under device_lock closes the window.

description: An issue was discovered in ssl.c in Axel before 2.17.8. The TLS implementation lacks hostname verification.

code_evidence: Verification is only configured when conf->insecure is false; the peer certificate is trusted via SSL_VERIFY_PEER and default verify paths, but nothing ties the certificate to the requested hostname.

After SSL_connect succeeds, the function returns the established ssl handle directly without calling SSL_get_verify_result, SSL_get_peer_certificate, or any hostname check against the hostname passed in and set via SNI.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-295 covers failing to validate a certificate for the intended peer; here hostname validation is entirely absent, so a certificate for another domain is accepted, matching improper certificate validation rather than a mere configuration issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function establishes a TLS session and returns it after only chain-based verification, never comparing the certificate's subject/SAN to hostname. Trigger: an attacker presenting any validly signed certificate for a different name. Consequence: the client accepts the connection, enabling man-in-the-middle interception.

commit_msg:
bpf: prevent out of bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic

Jann reported that the original commit back in b2157399cc98
("bpf: prevent out-of-bounds speculation") was not sufficient
to stop CPU from speculating out of bounds memory access:
While b2157399cc98 only focussed on masking array map access
for unprivileged users for tail calls and data access such
that the user provided index gets sanitized from BPF program
and syscall side, there is still a more generic form affected
from BPF programs that applies to most maps that hold user
data in relation to dynamic map access when dealing with
unknown scalars or "slow" known scalars as access offset, for
example:

  - Load a map value pointer into R6
  - Load an index into R7
  - Do a slow computation (e.g. with a memory dependency) that
    loads a limit into R8 (e.g. load the limit from a map for
    high latency, then mask it to make the verifier happy)
  - Exit if R7 >= R8 (mispredicted branch)
  - Load R0 = R6[R7]
  - Load R0 = R6[R0]

For unknown scalars there are two options in the BPF verifier
where we could derive knowledge from in order to guarantee
safe access to the memory: i) While </>/<=/>= variants won't
allow to derive any lower or upper bounds from the unknown
scalar where it would be safe to add it to the map value
pointer, it is possible through ==/!= test however. ii) another
option is to transform the unknown scalar into a known scalar,
for example, through ALU ops combination such as R &= <imm>
followed by R |= <imm> or any similar combination where the
original information from the unknown scalar would be destroyed
entirely leaving R with a constant. The initial slow load still
precedes the latter ALU ops on that register, so the CPU
executes speculatively from that point. Once we have the known
scalar, any compare operation would work then. A third option
only involving registers with known scalars could be crafted
as described in [0] where a CPU port (e.g. Slow Int unit)
would be filled with many dependent computations such that
the subsequent condition depending on its outcome has to wait
for evaluation on its execution port and thereby executing
speculatively if the speculated code can be scheduled on a
different execution port, or any other form of mistraining
as described in [1], for example. Given this is not limited
to only unknown scalars, not only map but also stack access
is affected since both is accessible for unprivileged users
and could potentially be used for out of bounds access under
speculation.

In order to prevent any of these cases, the verifier is now
sanitizing pointer arithmetic on the offset such that any
out of bounds speculation would be masked in a way where the
pointer arithmetic result in the destination register will
stay unchanged, meaning offset masked into zero similar as
in array_index_nospec() case. With regards to implementation,
there are three options that were considered: i) new insn
for sanitation, ii) push/pop insn and sanitation as inlined
BPF, iii) reuse of ax register and sanitation as inlined BPF.

Option i) has the downside that we end up using from reserved
bits in the opcode space, but also that we would require
each JIT to emit masking as native arch opcodes meaning
mitigation would have slow adoption till everyone implements
it eventually which is counter-productive. Option ii) and iii)
have both in common that a temporary register is needed in
order to implement the sanitation as inlined BPF since we
are not allowed to modify the source register. While a push /
pop insn in ii) would be useful to have in any case, it
requires once again that every JIT needs to implement it
first. While possible, amount of changes needed would also
be unsuitable for a -stable patch. Therefore, the path which
has fewer changes, less BPF instructions for the mitigation
and does not require anything to be changed in the JITs is
option iii) which this work is pursuing. The ax register is
already mapped to a register in all JITs (modulo arm32 where
it's mapped to stack as various other BPF registers there)
and used in constant blinding for JITs-only so far. It can
be reused for verifier rewrites under certain constraints.
The interpreter's tmp "register" has therefore been remapped
into extending the register set with hidden ax register and
reusing that for a number of instructions that needed the
prior temporary variable internally (e.g. div, mod). This
allows for zero increase in stack space usage in the interpreter,
and enables (restricted) generic use in rewrites otherwise as
long as such a patchlet does not make use of these instructions.
The sanitation mask is dynamic and relative to the offset the
map value or stack pointer currently holds.

There are various cases that need to be taken under consideration
for the masking, e.g. such operation could look as follows:
ptr += val or val += ptr or ptr -= val. Thus, the value to be
sanitized could reside either in source or in destination
register, and the limit is different depending on whether
the ALU op is addition or subtraction and depending on the
current known and bounded offset. The limit is derived as
follows: limit := max_value_size - (smin_value + off). For
subtraction: limit := umax_value + off. This holds because
we do not allow any pointer arithmetic that would
temporarily go out of bounds or would have an unknown
value with mixed signed bounds where it is unclear at
verification time whether the actual runtime value would
be either negative or positive. For example, we have a
derived map pointer value with constant offset and bounded
one, so limit based on smin_value works because the verifier
requires that statically analyzed arithmetic on the pointer
must be in bounds, and thus it checks if resulting
smin_value + off and umax_value + off is still within map
value bounds at time of arithmetic in addition to time of
access. Similarly, for the case of stack access we derive
the limit as follows: MAX_BPF_STACK + off for subtraction
and -off for the case of addition where off := ptr_reg->off +
ptr_reg->var_off.value. Subtraction is a special case for
the masking which can be in form of ptr += -val, ptr -= -val,
or ptr -= val. In the first two cases where we know that
the value is negative, we need to temporarily negate the
value in order to do the sanitation on a positive value
where we later swap the ALU op, and restore original source
register if the value was in source.

The sanitation of pointer arithmetic alone is still not fully
sufficient as is, since a scenario like the following could
happen ...

  PTR += 0x1000 (e.g. K-based imm)
  PTR -= BIG_NUMBER_WITH_SLOW_COMPARISON
  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= BIG_NUMBER_WITH_SLOW_COMPARISON
  [...]

... which under speculation could end up as ...

  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= 0 [ truncated by mitigation ]
  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= 0 [ truncated by mitigation ]
  [...]

... and therefore still access out of bounds. To prevent such
case, the verifier is also analyzing safety for potential out
of bounds access under speculative execution. Meaning, it is
also simulating pointer access under truncation. We therefore
"branch off" and push the current verification state after the
ALU operation with known 0 to the verification stack for later
analysis. Given the current path analysis succeeded it is
likely that the one under speculation can be pruned. In any
case, it is also subject to existing complexity limits and
therefore anything beyond this point will be rejected. In
terms of pruning, it needs to be ensured that the verification
state from speculative execution simulation must never prune
a non-speculative execution path, therefore, we mark verifier
state accordingly at the time of push_stack(). If verifier
detects out of bounds access under speculative execution from
one of the possible paths that includes a truncation, it will
reject such program.

Given we mask every reg-based pointer arithmetic for
unprivileged programs, we've been looking into how it could
affect real-world programs in terms of size increase. As the
majority of programs are targeted for privileged-only use
case, we've unconditionally enabled masking (with its alu
restrictions on top of it) for privileged programs for the
sake of testing in order to check i) whether they get rejected
in its current form, and ii) by how much the number of
instructions and size will increase. We've tested this by
using Katran, Cilium and test_l4lb from the kernel selftests.
For Katran we've evaluated balancer_kern.o, Cilium bpf_lxc.o
and an older test object bpf_lxc_opt_-DUNKNOWN.o and l4lb
we've used test_l4lb.o as well as test_l4lb_noinline.o. We
found that none of the programs got rejected by the verifier
with this change, and that impact is rather minimal to none.
balancer_kern.o had 13,904 bytes (1,738 insns) xlated and
7,797 bytes JITed before and after the change. Most complex
program in bpf_lxc.o had 30,544 bytes (3,817 insns) xlated
and 18,538 bytes JITed before and after and none of the other
tail call programs in bpf_lxc.o had any changes either. For
the older bpf_lxc_opt_-DUNKNOWN.o object we found a small
increase from 20,616 bytes (2,576 insns) and 12,536 bytes JITed
before to 20,664 bytes (2,582 insns) and 12,558 bytes JITed
after the change. Other programs from that object file had
similar small increase. Both test_l4lb.o had no change and
remained at 6,544 bytes (817 insns) xlated and 3,401 bytes
JITed and for test_l4lb_noinline.o constant at 5,080 bytes
(634 insns) xlated and 3,313 bytes JITed. This can be explained
in that LLVM typically optimizes stack based pointer arithmetic
by using K-based operations and that use of dynamic map access
is not overly frequent. However, in future we may decide to
optimize the algorithm further under known guarantees from
branch and value speculation. Latter seems also unclear in
terms of prediction heuristics that today's CPUs apply as well
as whether there could be collisions in e.g. the predictor's
Value History/Pattern Table for triggering out of bounds access,
thus masking is performed unconditionally at this point but could
be subject to relaxation later on. We were generally also
brainstorming various other approaches for mitigation, but the
blocker was always lack of available registers at runtime and/or
overhead for runtime tracking of limits belonging to a specific
pointer. Thus, we found this to be minimally intrusive under
given constraints.

With that in place, a simple example with sanitized access on
unprivileged load at post-verification time looks as follows:

  # bpftool prog dump xlated id 282
  [...]
  28: (79) r1 = *(u64 *)(r7 +0)
  29: (79) r2 = *(u64 *)(r7 +8)
  30: (57) r1 &= 15
  31: (79) r3 = *(u64 *)(r0 +4608)
  32: (57) r3 &= 1
  33: (47) r3 |= 1
  34: (2d) if r2 > r3 goto pc+19
  35: (b4) (u32) r11 = (u32) 20479  |
  36: (1f) r11 -= r2                | Dynamic sanitation for pointer
  37: (4f) r11 |= r2                | arithmetic with registers
  38: (87) r11 = -r11               | containing bounded or known
  39: (c7) r11 s>>= 63              | scalars in order to prevent
  40: (5f) r11 &= r2                | out of bounds speculation.
  41: (0f) r4 += r11                |
  42: (71) r4 = *(u8 *)(r4 +0)
  43: (6f) r4 <<= r1
  [...]

For the case where the scalar sits in the destination register
as opposed to the source register, the following code is emitted
for the above example:

  [...]
  16: (b4) (u32) r11 = (u32) 20479
  17: (1f) r11 -= r2
  18: (4f) r11 |= r2
  19: (87) r11 = -r11
  20: (c7) r11 s>>= 63
  21: (5f) r2 &= r11
  22: (0f) r2 += r0
  23: (61) r0 = *(u32 *)(r2 +0)
  [...]

JIT blinding example with non-conflicting use of r10:

  [...]
   d5:	je     0x0000000000000106    _
   d7:	mov    0x0(%rax),%edi       |
   da:	mov    $0xf153246,%r10d     | Index load from map value and
   e0:	xor    $0xf153259,%r10      | (const blinded) mask with 0x1f.
   e7:	and    %r10,%rdi            |_
   ea:	mov    $0x2f,%r10d          |
   f0:	sub    %rdi,%r10            | Sanitized addition. Both use r10
   f3:	or     %rdi,%r10            | but do not interfere with each
   f6:	neg    %r10                 | other. (Neither do these instructions
   f9:	sar    $0x3f,%r10           | interfere with the use of ax as temp
   fd:	and    %r10,%rdi            | in interpreter.)
  100:	add    %rax,%rdi            |_
  103:	mov    0x0(%rdi),%eax
 [...]

Tested that it fixes Jann's reproducer, and also checked that test_verifier
and test_progs suite with interpreter, JIT and JIT with hardening enabled
on x86-64 and arm64 runs successfully.

  [0] Speculose: Analyzing the Security Implications of Speculative
      Execution in CPUs, Giorgi Maisuradze and Christian Rossow,
      https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.04084.pdf

  [1] A Systematic Evaluation of Transient Execution Attacks and
      Defenses, Claudio Canella, Jo Van Bulck, Michael Schwarz,
      Moritz Lipp, Benjamin von Berg, Philipp Ortner, Frank Piessens,
      Dmitry Evtyushkin, Daniel Gruss,
      https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.05441.pdf

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    check_cursor_col();']}
description: vim is vulnerable to Heap-based Buffer Overflow

code_evidence: Line 9 sets curwin->w_cursor.lnum directly from eap->line2 without validating the cursor column; the following do_put call on lines 10-11 then operates with that cursor state. The patch inserts check_cursor_col() after line 9 to correct the column, indicating the pre-patch code could read a character past the end of the line.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-122 fits because the described defect is an out-of-bounds access on a heap-allocated line buffer, matching a heap-based buffer overflow variant. It is not merely a logic/off-by-one issue, since the consequence is memory access beyond the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cursor line is assigned from eap->line2 but the column is left unbounded/stale, so a line shorter than the current column is used. Trigger: ex_put with a line2 pointing to a short line while the cursor column exceeds that line's length. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read past the end of the line buffer, which the commit describes as a heap-based buffer overflow condition.

commit_msg:
dns: improve loop detection in label decompression

Previously the number of allowed pointers within a message is equal to
the data in a tvb (16575 in one example). This is still expensive, so
implement an alternative detection mechanism that looks for a direct
self-loop and limits the total pointers to about 256.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.6 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.12, the DNS dissector could go into an infinite loop. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-dns.c by trying to detect self-referencing pointers.

code_evidence: The 0xc0 case decodes a compression pointer into indir_offset and then unconditionally sets offset = indir_offset, so the for(;;) loop restarts at the pointer target. The only loop guard is chars_processed >= data_size, which counts characters seen rather than pointer hops; a pointer cycle can revisit characters while chars_processed stays below data_size, so the exit condition at line 112 is never reached.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the for(;;) loop's exit condition cannot be reached for cyclic pointer input, producing an infinite loop. A bounds/validation weakness (e.g., CWE-20) is not the target; the demonstrated consequence is an unreachable loop exit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop-exit check uses chars_processed against data_size, which does not bound the number of pointer redirections. Trigger: a DNS name containing a pointer cycle (direct or indirect) makes offset jump to an earlier location, re-entering the loop. commit_msg: Fix parser tmp-buffer overflow issue
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    } else if (pbuf.tmp_indx && '], 'added_lines': ['                    } else if (pbuf.tmp_indx &&', '                    p_buf_write_tmp(&pbuf, tmp_fd);', '                    p_buf_write_tmp(&pbuf, tmp_fd);']}
description: Buffer overflow vulnerability in function src_parser_trans_stage_1_2_3 trgil gilcc before commit 803969389ca9c06237075a7f8eeb1a19e6651759, allows attackers to cause a denial of service.

code_evidence: In P_STATE_CODE, case '\\' pushes a backslash into the temporary buffer via p_buf_push_tmp_char and immediately continues, so the accumulated tmp buffer is never flushed at that point.
The same pattern occurs in case '/': a slash is pushed with p_buf_push_tmp_char and the loop continues without writing the tmp buffer.
Once the switch falls through to the default path, p_buf_write_tmp and p_buf_write_f_char flush the tmp buffer, but the backslash/slash cases bypass this write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a copy into a destination buffer (tmp) without verifying that the input length is less than the destination capacity, matching CWE-120's 'buffer copy without checking size of input'. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the write past the tmp buffer is the core issue.

evidence_lines.code:
p_buf_write_tmp(&pbuf, tmp_fd);
p_buf_write_f_char(&pbuf, tmp_fd);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that escape/comment-prefix characters are appended to the fixed-size tmp buffer without a size check or flush, so repeated '\\' or '/' characters in the input grow pbuf.tmp_indx unbounded. The trigger is a source file containing long runs of these characters; the supported consequence is that p_buf_push_tmp_char writes past the tmp buffer, causing memory corruption or a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fixed bugs due to uninitialized data in the JP2 decoder.
Also, added some comments marking I/O stream interfaces that probably
need to be changed (in the long term) to fix integer overflow problems.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tbpcc->bpcs = 0;']}
description: The jp2_cdef_destroy function in jp2_cod.c in JasPer before 2.0.13 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via a crafted image.

code_evidence: bpcc->bpcs is allocated via jas_alloc2 and immediately overwritten; the allocation result is checked with 'if (!(bpcc->bpcs = ...))'. However, the diff adds 'bpcc->bpcs = 0;' before this, and the loop at lines 9-13 then writes to bpcc->bpcs[i]. No NULL guard exists between the failed allocation return and any later use of the pointer by callers (e.g., destruction/cleanup paths).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function manages a pointer (bpcc->bpcs) whose validity is not guaranteed before use; the added initialization and allocation-failure handling target a NULL dereference condition. This is distinct from integer overflow, which concerns size computation rather than dereferencing a NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bpcs pointer is left as the raw allocation result without a durable NULL-initialized state before allocation, so error/cleanup paths can operate on an uninitialized or NULL pointer. Trigger: a crafted JP2 box with a datalen causing allocation failure or a code path that reaches the pointer after a failed/absent initialization. Supported consequence: NULL pointer dereference leading to denial of service (crash).

description: A vulnerability in the Android media framework (libvpx) related to odd frame width. Product: Android. Versions: 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2, 8.0, 8.1. Android ID: A-64710201.

code_evidence: Lines 60-63 round d_w and d_h up to chroma-subsampling alignment, so the computed w/h (and derived stride s at lines 64-66) can exceed the caller-requested dimensions.

When img_data is supplied externally (line 75 skipped allocation), img->w/h are set to the aligned values at lines 86-87 while the external buffer was sized for the unaligned d_w/d_h; line 93 then sets the rect to d_w/d_h. For odd widths the aligned stride/dimensions exceed the external allocation, causing out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is failure to validate/account for the mismatch between the caller-supplied external buffer's implied size and the aligned dimensions the code computes, i.e., improper handling of input-derived size properties. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function derives storage dimensions by aligning d_w/d_h and applies them to both self-allocated and externally supplied buffers without checking whether an external buffer can accommodate the aligned size. commit_msg:
Fix redis-cli / redis-sential overflow on some platforms (CVE-2021-32762) (#9587)

The redis-cli command line tool and redis-sentinel service may be vulnerable
to integer overflow when parsing specially crafted large multi-bulk network
replies. This is a result of a vulnerability in the underlying hiredis
library which does not perform an overflow check before calling the calloc()
heap allocation function.

This issue only impacts systems with heap allocators that do not perform their
own overflow checks. Most modern systems do and are therefore not likely to
be affected. Furthermore, by default redis-sentinel uses the jemalloc allocator
which is also not vulnerable.

Co-authored-by: Yossi Gottlieb <yossigo@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ["        if (SIZE_MAX / sizeof(redisReply*) < elements) return NULL;  /* Don't overflow */"]}
description: Redis is an open source, in-memory database that persists on disk. The redis-cli command line tool and redis-sentinel service may be vulnerable to integer overflow when parsing specially crafted large multi-bulk network replies. This is a result of a vulnerability in the underlying hiredis library which does not perform an overflow check before calling the calloc() heap allocation function. This issue only impacts systems with heap allocators that do not perform their own overflow checks. Most modern systems do and are therefore not likely to be affected. Furthermore, by default redis-sentinel uses the jemalloc allocator which is also not vulnerable. The problem is fixed in Redis versions 6.2.6, 6.0.16 and 5.0.14.

code_evidence: Line 6 gates on elements > 0, then line 7 passes the attacker-controlled size_t elements directly to hi_calloc(elements, sizeof(redisReply*)) without any bounds check on the multiplication. The patched version inserts a SIZE_MAX / sizeof(redisReply*) < elements guard before this call.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer multiplication that can wrap before being used as an allocation size, exactly CWE-190's scope of size calculation in memory allocation. It is not merely an allocation-failure issue (CWE-789) because the defect is the arithmetic overflow, not unbounded but correctly sized allocation.

evidence_lines.code:
if (elements > 0) {
r->element = hi_calloc(elements,sizeof(redisReply*));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When elements is a large multi-bulk count, the allocator multiplies elements by the pointer size; on allocators without their own overflow checks this product wraps to a small value, yielding an undersized allocation. Subsequent writes to parent->element[task->idx] or element population can then overrun the heap, causing memory corruption or crash. Root cause is the unchecked size multiplication; trigger is a crafted large bulk reply count.

If the client connects to the server and sends a large radius packet, a buffer overflow vulnerability will be triggered.

commit_msg:
Prevent instability and crash due to message flood

This patch adds a rate limiting to selected patches. The underlying rate limiter
used is the Leaky-Bucket algorithm. It allows for a burst of messages, but
limits them after a specified amount of messages within a time frame.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tRATELIMIT(uSource);', '']}
description: murmur in Mumble through 1.2.19 before 2018-08-31 mishandles multiple concurrent requests that are persisted in the database, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (daemon hang or crash) via a message flood.

code_evidence: msgVersion processes a client-supplied MumbleProto::Version message and reads its fields (version, release, os, os_version) into ServerUser state, then logs them. The function performs no check on message frequency or size; the patch adds RATELIMIT(uSource) at entry, indicating the original code accepted an unbounded stream of these requests.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 covers failure to validate required input properties, explicitly including specified quantities such as frequency and rate. The function lacks any rate validation on client messages, matching that property. A related weakness like CWE-400 (resource consumption) describes the consequence; here the root cause is the unvalidated input rate, so CWE-20 fits the target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the handler accepts and processes every incoming Version message without any rate or frequency constraint on the client input. Trigger: a remote client floods Version messages; each invocation performs parsing, field assignment and logging, consuming resources. Supported consequence: resource exhaustion leading to daemon hang or crash. The missing constraint is on input rate, not on field values, so the cause is absent frequency validation rather than malformed data handling.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned long flags;', '\t/* protect against a concurrent page table upgrade */', '\tlocal_irq_save(flags);', '\tlocal_irq_restore(flags);']}
description: In the Linux kernel 4.19 through 5.6.7 on the s390 platform, code execution may occur because of a race condition, as demonstrated by code in enable_sacf_uaccess in arch/s390/lib/uaccess.c that fails to protect against a concurrent page table upgrade, aka CID-3f777e19d171. A crash could also occur.

code_evidence: The function reads current->thread.mm_segment, returns early if the secondary-address-mode bit is set, and otherwise sets that bit without any interrupt disabling or locking.
It then stores and conditionally reloads control register 1 and control register 7 based on S390_lowcore.kernel_asce/user_asce, mutating per-CPU control-register state and CPU flags.
The read-modify-write of mm_segment and the CR updates proceed without synchronization against a concurrent page-table upgrade (on_each_cpu IPI) that rewrites user_asce and CR1.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function implements a concurrent code sequence needing exclusive access to shared per-CPU/thread address-space state, but no synchronization prevents an interfering page-table-upgrade sequence from modifying it mid-sequence, matching CWE-362's exclusivity/atomicity violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: enable_sacf_uaccess updates thread.mm_segment and control registers non-atomically with interrupts enabled. Trigger: another CPU concurrently performs a page-table upgrade that delivers an IPI calling set_user_asce, changing CR1 while this thread runs in secondary space mode. Consequence: after interrupt return the CPU fetches kernel instructions through a stale/inconsistent address-space control, leading to crash or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Remove support for pre-authentication compression. Doing compression
early in the protocol probably seemed reasonable in the 1990s, but
today it's clearly a bad idea in terms of both cryptography (cf.
multiple compression oracle attacks in TLS) and attack surface.

Moreover, to support it across privilege-separation zlib needed
the assistance of a complex shared-memory manager that made the
required attack surface considerably larger.

Prompted by Guido Vranken pointing out a compiler-elided security
check in the shared memory manager found by Stack
(http://css.csail.mit.edu/stack/); ok deraadt@ markus@

NB. pre-auth authentication has been disabled by default in sshd
for >10 years.

description: Integer overflow vulnerability in Mat_VarReadNextInfo5 in mat5.c in tbeu matio (aka MAT File I/O Library) 1.5.17, allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service or possibly other unspecified impacts.

code_evidence: At [117] len is read from the file-supplied uncomp_buf[1] as mat_uint32_t; [118-119] rounds it up by adding 8-(len%8) without any overflow check, so a len near UINT32_MAX wraps to a small value that is then used as the allocation size at [120] and subtracted from nbytes at [121].
In the uncompressed branch, name_len is int-typed at [181], assigned from buf[1] at [241], rounded up unchecked at [242-243], and used to decrement nBytes [244] and seek [245].

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the alignment rounding len = len + (8 - len%8) is performed on an attacker-controlled 32-bit length without verifying that the addition cannot exceed UINT32_MAX. Trigger: a crafted MAT file whose name-field length is within 8 of UINT32_MAX. Consequence: len wraps to a tiny value, so malloc(len+1) under-allocates while nbytes accounting and subsequent reads assume the larger size, leading to memory corruption/DoS.

description: An integer overflow exists in pywin32 prior to version b301 when adding an access control entry (ACE) to an access control list (ACL) that would cause the size to be greater than 65535 bytes. An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could crash the vulnerable process.

code_evidence: Line 18 computes the new ACL size into an unsigned short: pdacl->AclSize + sizeof(ACCESS_ALLOWED_ACE) + (unsigned short)GetLengthSid(psid). The sum is truncated to 16 bits, so it can wrap to a small value when the ACL approaches 65535 bytes.

Lines 19-24 use that wrapped value for malloc, ZeroMemory and memcpy, then store it into pdacl_padded->AclSize, so the allocated buffer and recorded size are both too small relative to the data the subsequent addfunc call writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size calculation that wraps in a fixed-width integer and uses the wrapped result as an allocation and copy length, which is exactly CWE-190. The missing upper-bound check on required_size before malloc is the specific flaw; a mere out-of-bounds write would be CWE-787, but here the wraparound arithmetic is the root cause.

evidence_lines.code: unsigned short required_size = pdacl->AclSize + sizeof(ACCESS_ALLOWED_ACE) + (unsigned short)GetLengthSid(psid);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the required ACL size is stored in a 16-bit unsigned short, so adding an ACE to a large ACL wraps the computed size. Trigger: an ACL whose size plus the ACE and SID lengths exceeds USHRT_MAX. Consequence: an undersized allocation followed by addfunc writing the ACE into it, causing a crash (DoS) or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only computes a hash-length offset for flow_keys and contains no random value generation or secret handling; the CWE-330 issue described in the commit (jhash/hashrnd in flow_dissector) is not located in this function.

commit_msg: Address DSA/ECDSA side channel
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['ECDSA_PrivateKey::create_signature_op(RandomNumberGenerator& /*rng*/,', '      return std::unique_ptr<PK_Ops::Signature>(new ECDSA_Signature_Operation(*this, params));'], 'added_lines': ['ECDSA_PrivateKey::create_signature_op(RandomNumberGenerator& rng,', '      return std::unique_ptr<PK_Ops::Signature>(new ECDSA_Signature_Operation(*this, params, rng));']}
description: Botan 2.5.0 through 2.6.0 before 2.7.0 allows a memory-cache side-channel attack on ECDSA signatures, aka the Return Of the Hidden Number Problem or ROHNP, related to dsa/dsa.cpp, ec_group/ec_group.cpp, and ecdsa/ecdsa.cpp. To discover an ECDSA key, the attacker needs access to either the local machine or a different virtual machine on the same physical host.

code_evidence: create_signature_op ignores the RandomNumberGenerator parameter (declared unnamed at line 2) and constructs ECDSA_Signature_Operation without passing any RNG (line 35). The ECDSA_Signature_Operation therefore falls back to its default randomness handling rather than the caller-supplied RNG, which is the operation that produces ECDSA signatures for this private key.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch routes the RNG into ECDSA_Signature_Operation, indicating the prior construction exposed sensitive private-key-derived state through an observable side channel, i.e. unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information. CWE-200 fits as the confidentiality exposure; the underlying cache side channel is the enabling mechanism rather than a separate label here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signing operation is instantiated without the caller's RNG, so ECDSA nonce generation is not tied to the supplied randomness source. Trigger: an attacker able to observe cache/timing behavior on the host (or a co-resident VM) during ECDSA signing. Supported consequence: nonce-dependent secret information leaks through the side channel, enabling recovery of the private key.

commit_msg:
cryp: prevent direct calls to update and final functions

With inconsistent or malformed data it has been possible to call
"update" and "final" crypto functions directly. Using a fuzzer tool [1]
we have seen that this results in asserts, i.e., a crash that
potentially could leak sensitive information.

By setting the state (initialized) in the crypto context (i.e., the
tee_cryp_state) at the end of all syscall_*_init functions and then add
a check of the state at the beginning of all update and final functions,
  we prevent direct entrance to the "update" and "final" functions.

[1] https://github.com/MartijnB/optee_fuzzer

Fixes: OP-TEE-2019-0021

commit_msg:
Prevent unitialized variable use in grappler.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 399702928
Change-Id: Id7e75451fbff297692dfb687f60ea04b25c96b24
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  const NodeDef* dequeue_node;'], 'added_lines': ['  const NodeDef* dequeue_node = nullptr;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions TensorFlow's Grappler optimizer has a use of unitialized variable. If the `train_nodes` vector (obtained from the saved model that gets optimized) does not contain a `Dequeue` node, then `dequeue_node` is left unitialized. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.7.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.6.1, TensorFlow 2.5.2, and TensorFlow 2.4.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 70 declares `const NodeDef* dequeue_node;` with no initializer. The loop at 71-76 assigns it only if a train node satisfies `IsDequeueOp`; otherwise it remains uninitialized.
Line 78 then tests `if (dequeue_node)` and, when true, dereferences `dequeue_node->name()` at 79-80. With no Dequeue node present, the branch condition reads the uninitialized pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 covers use of a resource that has not been initialized. Here the uninitialized pointer is read in the condition and potentially dereferenced, matching that weakness; this is not merely a null dereference, since the value is indeterminate rather than deliberately null.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pointer is declared without initialization and only conditionally assigned inside the loop. Trigger: a saved model whose transitive fanin train_nodes contains no Dequeue op, leaving dequeue_node indeterminate. The subsequent `if (dequeue_node)` test reads the uninitialized value, so the guard may spuriously pass and lead to invalid pointer dereference, undefined behavior or a crash. The fix initializes it to nullptr, making the guard safe.

commit_msg:
nfsd: check permissions when setting ACLs

Use set_posix_acl, which includes proper permission checks, instead of
calling ->set_acl directly.  Without this anyone may be able to grant
themselves permissions to a file by setting the ACL.

Lock the inode to make the new checks atomic with respect to set_acl.
(Also, nfsd was the only caller of set_acl not locking the inode, so I
suspect this may fix other races.)

This also simplifies the code, and ensures our ACLs are checked by
posix_acl_valid.

The permission checks and the inode locking were lost with commit
4ac7249e, which changed nfsd to use the set_acl inode operation directly
instead of going through xattr handlers.

Reported-by: David Sinquin <david@sinquin.eu>
[agreunba@redhat.com: use set_posix_acl]
Fixes: 4ac7249e
Cc: Christoph Hellwig <hch@infradead.org>
Cc: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: J. Bruce Fields <bfields@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!IS_POSIXACL(inode) || !inode->i_op->set_acl) {', '\t\terror = -EOPNOTSUPP;', '\t\tgoto out_errno;', '\t}', '\terror = inode->i_op->set_acl(inode, argp->acl_access, ACL_TYPE_ACCESS);', '\t\tgoto out_drop_write;', '\terror = inode->i_op->set_acl(inode, argp->acl_default,', '\t\t\t\t     ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT);', '\t\tgoto out_drop_write;', 'out_drop_write:'], 'added_lines': ['\tfh_lock(fh);', '', '\terror = set_posix_acl(inode, ACL_TYPE_ACCESS, argp->acl_access);', '\t\tgoto out_drop_lock;', '\terror = set_posix_acl(inode, ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT, argp->acl_default);', '\t\tgoto out_drop_lock;', '', '\tfh_unlock(fh);', 'out_drop_lock:', '\tfh_unlock(fh);']}
description: nfsd in the Linux kernel through 4.6.3 allows local users to bypass intended file-permission restrictions by setting a POSIX ACL, related to nfs2acl.c, nfs3acl.c, and nfs4acl.c.

code_evidence: fh_verify is called with NFSD_MAY_SATTR, which only checks attribute-set permission on the file handle; it does not perform the ownership/permission checks required to modify a file's ACL.

The inode is derived from the verified dentry, and the only guard is IS_POSIXACL plus the presence of i_op->set_acl; no check that the caller owns the file or is otherwise authorized to change its ACL is performed.
The access ACL is applied through the inode operation directly, bypassing set_posix_acl and its permission checks.
The default ACL is likewise applied directly via i_op->set_acl, again without an authorization check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to enforce the access-control policy governing who may modify a file's ACL, allowing an unauthorized actor to change permissions and thereby gain access to a resource. This is improper access control (CWE-284); it is an enforcement failure of the authorization mechanism rather than a mere validation error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: SETACL handling calls inode->i_op->set_acl directly after only an NFSD_MAY_SATTR fh_verify, so the kernel ACL permission checks (and posix_acl_valid) are skipped. Trigger: a local user issues an NFS SETACL request for a file they do not own. Consequence: the caller can grant themselves access to the file by writing a permissive ACL.

commit_msg:
After commit cbfecb927f42 ("fs: record I_DIRTY_TIME even if inode
already has I_DIRTY_INODE") writeback_single_inode can push inode with
I_DIRTY_TIME set to b_dirty_time list. In case of freeing inode with
I_DIRTY_TIME set this can happen after deletion of inode from i_io_list
at evict. Stack trace is following.

evict
fat_evict_inode
fat_truncate_blocks
fat_flush_inodes
writeback_inode
sync_inode_metadata(inode, sync=0)
writeback_single_inode(inode, wbc) <- wbc->sync_mode == WB_SYNC_NONE

This will lead to use after free in flusher thread.

Similar issue can be triggered if writeback_single_inode in the
stack trace update inode->i_io_list. Add explicit check to avoid it.

Fixes: cbfecb927f42 ("fs: record I_DIRTY_TIME even if inode already has I_DIRTY_INODE")
Reported-by: syzbot+6ba92bd00d5093f7e371@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Reviewed-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Signed-off-by: Svyatoslav Feldsherov <feldsherov@google.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20221115202001.324188-1-feldsherov@google.com
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
