Otherwise the flusher threads are', '\t * responsible for the writeback lists.', '\tif (!(inode->i_state & I_DIRTY_ALL))', '\t\tinode_cgwb_move_to_attached(inode, wb);', '\telse if (!(inode->i_state & I_SYNC_QUEUED)) {', '\t\tif ((inode->i_state & I_DIRTY))', '\t\t\tredirty_tail_locked(inode, wb);', '\t\telse if (inode->i_state & I_DIRTY_TIME) {', '\t\t\tinode->dirtied_when = jiffies;', '\t\t\tinode_io_list_move_locked(inode, wb, &wb->b_dirty_time);'], 'added_lines': ["\t * If the inode is freeing, its i_io_list shoudn't be updated", '\t * as it can be finally deleted at this moment.', '\tif (!(inode->i_state & I_FREEING)) {', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * If the inode is now fully clean, then it can be safely', '\t\t * removed from its writeback list (if any). Otherwise the', '\t\t * flusher threads are responsible for the writeback lists.', '\t\t */', '\t\tif (!(inode->i_state & I_DIRTY_ALL))', '\t\t\tinode_cgwb_move_to_attached(inode, wb);', '\t\telse if (!(inode->i_state & I_SYNC_QUEUED)) {', '\t\t\tif ((inode->i_state & I_DIRTY))', '\t\t\t\tredirty_tail_locked(inode, wb);', '\t\t\telse if (inode->i_state & I_DIRTY_TIME) {', '\t\t\t\tinode->dirtied_when = jiffies;', '\t\t\t\tinode_io_list_move_locked(inode,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t\t  wb,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t\t  &wb->b_dirty_time);', '\t\t\t}']}
description: In the Linux kernel 6.0.8, there is a use-after-free in inode_cgwb_move_to_attached in fs/fs-writeback.c, related to __list_del_entry_valid.

code_evidence: After __writeback_single_inode, the function re-acquires wb->list_lock and inode->i_lock, then unconditionally touches the inode's writeback list state based only on I_DIRTY_ALL/I_SYNC_QUEUED/I_DIRTY/I_DIRTY_TIME. There is no I_FREEING check, so inode_cgwb_move_to_attached or inode_io_list_move_locked may manipulate i_io_list of an inode being evicted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe list operation on an inode whose i_io_list was freed at eviction is a use-after-free (CWE-416), matching the reported crash in inode_cgwb_move_to_attached. A missing synchronization/lock is not the target here; the defect is acting on freed inode state, so CWE-416 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: writeback_single_inode updates the inode's writeback list without verifying the inode is not freeing. Trigger: evict path calls sync_inode_metadata with WB_SYNC_NONE on an inode carrying I_DIRTY_TIME; concurrently the flusher thread updates a list entry already deleted at evict. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the inode/list memory in the flusher thread (crash or memory corruption).

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.3902: Vim9: double free with nested :def function

Problem:    Vim9: double free with nested :def function.
Solution:   Pass "line_to_free" from compile_def_function() and make sure
            cmdlinep is valid.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    vim_free(*line_to_free);', '\t\t\tif (*line_to_free != NULL)'], 'added_lines': ['\t    if (*eap->cmdlinep == *line_to_free)', '\t\t*eap->cmdlinep = theline;', '\t    vim_free(*line_to_free);', '\t\t\tif (*line_to_free != NULL', '\t\t\t\t\t    && *eap->cmdlinep != *line_to_free)']}
description: vim is vulnerable to Use After Free

code_evidence: In the getline branch, *line_to_free is freed at line 65 before a new line is read, but eap->cmdlinep may still point to that same buffer; it is only reassigned via *line_to_free after the free, so cmdlinep can dangle.

At the :enddef/:endfunction exit, if *line_to_free is non-NULL, *eap->cmdlinep is freed and then set to *line_to_free; because cmdlinep may already alias the freed buffer, this frees the same allocation again (double free), leaving a dangling pointer for later command processing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because freed memory remains referenced through eap->cmdlinep and is used/freed again after the original free; the aliasing between cmdlinep and line_to_free is the missing constraint. This is memory reuse after free rather than an out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code frees *line_to_free without first checking whether eap->cmdlinep aliases the same buffer, and later frees *eap->cmdlinep unconditionally. Trigger: a nested :def function where cmdlinep and line_to_free reference the same allocation. Consequence: double free and a dangling cmdlinep pointer, later reused as a use-after-free.

commit_msg:
If beacon protection is active but the beacon cannot be
decrypted or is otherwise malformed, we call the cfg80211
API to report this to userspace, but that uses a netdev
pointer, which isn't present for P2P-Device. Fix this to
call it only conditionally to ensure cfg80211 won't crash
in the case of P2P-Device.

This fixes CVE-2022-42722.

Reported-by: Sönke Huster <shuster@seemoo.tu-darmstadt.de>
Fixes: 9eaf183af741 ("mac80211: Report beacon protection failures to user space")
Signed-off-by: Johannes Berg <johannes.berg@intel.com>

description: In the Linux kernel 5.8 through 5.19.x before 5.19.16, local attackers able to inject WLAN frames into the mac80211 stack could cause a NULL pointer dereference denial-of-service attack against the beacon protection of P2P devices.

code_evidence: At the unexpected-BIP-keyidx branch, cfg80211_rx_unprot_mlme_mgmt() is called with rx->sdata->dev as the netdev argument without any NULL check, even though for P2P-Device sdata->dev is absent.
After the cipher switch, when the frame is a beacon and decryption yielded RX_DROP_UNUSABLE, cfg80211_rx_unprot_mlme_mgmt() is again invoked unconditionally with rx->sdata->dev.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function supplies a possibly-NULL pointer (rx->sdata->dev) to an API that dereferences it, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. The missing guard, not the malformed frame itself, is the defect; this is a direct NULL dereference rather than a general input-validation flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: both malformed-beacon paths pass rx->sdata->dev to cfg80211_rx_unprot_mlme_mgmt() without verifying the netdev exists. Trigger: a locally injected WLAN beacon that is protected/malformed and reaches either branch on a P2P-Device interface where sdata->dev is NULL. commit_msg:
x86/speculation: Allow enabling STIBP with legacy IBRS

When plain IBRS is enabled (not enhanced IBRS), the logic in
spectre_v2_user_select_mitigation() determines that STIBP is not needed.

The IBRS bit implicitly protects against cross-thread branch target
injection. However, with legacy IBRS, the IBRS bit is cleared on
returning to userspace for performance reasons which leaves userspace
threads vulnerable to cross-thread branch target injection against which
STIBP protects.

Exclude IBRS from the spectre_v2_in_ibrs_mode() check to allow for
enabling STIBP (through seccomp/prctl() by default or always-on, if
selected by spectre_v2_user kernel cmdline parameter).

commit_msg:
vfio/pci: Fix integer overflows, bitmask check

The VFIO_DEVICE_SET_IRQS ioctl did not sufficiently sanitize
user-supplied integers, potentially allowing memory corruption. This
patch adds appropriate integer overflow checks, checks the range bounds
for VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_NONE, and also verifies that only single element
in the VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_TYPE_MASK bitmask is set.
VFIO_IRQ_SET_ACTION_TYPE_MASK is already correctly checked later in
vfio_pci_set_irqs_ioctl().

Furthermore, a kzalloc is changed to a kcalloc because the use of a
kzalloc with an integer multiplication allowed an integer overflow
condition to be reached without this patch. kcalloc checks for overflow
and should prevent a similar occurrence.

Signed-off-by: Vlad Tsyrklevich <vlad@tsyrklevich.net>
Signed-off-by: Alex Williamson <alex.williamson@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tvdev->ctx = kzalloc(nvec * sizeof(struct vfio_pci_irq_ctx), GFP_KERNEL);'], 'added_lines': ['\tvdev->ctx = kcalloc(nvec, sizeof(struct vfio_pci_irq_ctx), GFP_KERNEL);']}
description: drivers/vfio/pci/vfio_pci.c in the Linux kernel through 4.8.11 allows local users to bypass integer overflow checks, and cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or have unspecified other impact, by leveraging access to a vfio PCI device file for a VFIO_DEVICE_SET_IRQS ioctl call, aka a "state machine confusion bug."

code_evidence: Line 8 allocates vdev->ctx using kzalloc(nvec * sizeof(struct vfio_pci_irq_ctx)). The multiplication nvec * sizeof(...) is computed in int arithmetic before reaching kzalloc, so a large nvec can wrap to a small size. Lines 11-12 then request nvec IRQ vectors and, on success, vdev->num_ctx is set to nvec at line 18, so later code indexing vdev->ctx over nvec entries operates on a buffer sized for a wrapped, smaller count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The allocation does not restrict the buffer to the intended nvec elements because of the integer overflow, and later indexed accesses can fall outside the allocated memory region. This is an out-of-bounds memory operation, matching CWE-119, though the underlying arithmetic flaw could be described more narrowly as an integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size expression nvec * sizeof(...) can overflow, yielding an undersized allocation for the number of contexts actually used. Trigger: a user-supplied nvec large enough to wrap the multiplication passes the is_irq_none check. Consequence: subsequent accesses to vdev->ctx entries beyond the allocated buffer corrupt memory, consistent with the description's memory corruption/DoS impact.

commit_msg:
rtl8xxxu: prevent leaking urb

In rtl8xxxu_submit_int_urb if usb_submit_urb fails the allocated urb
should be released.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Chris Chiu <chiu@endlessm.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tusb_free_urb(urb);']}
description: A memory leak in the rtl8xxxu_submit_int_urb() function in drivers/net/wireless/realtek/rtl8xxxu/rtl8xxxu_core.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering usb_submit_urb() failures, aka CID-a2cdd07488e6.

code_evidence: Line 7 allocates a URB via usb_alloc_urb and lines 8-9 return -ENOMEM if allocation fails; the urb is only released on the success path implicitly.
Lines 14-18: when usb_submit_urb fails, the error branch only calls usb_unanchor_urb and jumps to error, so the allocated urb is never freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory (urb) and fails to release it on an error path, matching CWE-401's missing release of memory after its effective lifetime. This is a leak, not a use-after-free or double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch for a failed usb_submit_urb releases the anchor but not the urb allocated at line 7. Trigger: repeated usb_submit_urb failures. Consequence: each failure leaks one urb, causing memory consumption and potential denial of service.

commit_msg:
PR22205, .debug_line file table NULL filename

The PR22200 fuzzer testcase found one way to put NULLs into .debug_line
file tables.  PR22205 finds another.  This patch gives up on trying to
prevent NULL files in the file table and instead just copes with them.
Arguably, this is better than giving up and showing no info from
.debug_line.  I've also fixed a case where the fairly recent DWARF5
support in handling broken DWARG could result in uninitialized memory
reads, and made a small tidy.

	PR 22205
	* dwarf2.c (concat_filename): Return "<unknown>" on NULL filename.
	(read_formatted_entries): Init "fe".
	(decode_line_info <DW_LNE_define_file>): Use line_info_add_file_name.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (filename == NULL)', '    return strdup ("<unknown>");']}
description: dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, mishandles NULL files in a .debug_line file table, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a crafted ELF file, related to concat_filename. NOTE: this issue is caused by an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-15023.

code_evidence: Line 12 reads filename from table->files[file-1].name, which can be NULL because the file table may contain NULL entries. Line 13 passes filename directly to IS_ABSOLUTE_PATH, and lines 31, 32, 38, 44 and 48 use it in strlen, sprintf and strdup without any NULL check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences a pointer it expects to be valid but which attacker-controlled debug data can set to NULL. This is a direct NULL dereference, not merely a malformed-input parsing error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that concat_filename assumes the file-table name pointer is non-NULL. A crafted ELF .debug_line file table with a NULL filename triggers a NULL pointer dereference at IS_ABSOLUTE_PATH or the subsequent string operations, causing a crash (denial of service).

I discovered that PostSRSd could be tricked into consuming a lot of CPU
time with an SRS address that has an excessively long time stamp tag,
e.g.

SRS0=HHHH=TTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTT=0@example.com

description: srs2.c in PostSRSd before 1.10 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) via a long timestamp tag in an SRS address.

code_evidence: The loop at line 10 iterates over the attacker-supplied stamp string until its NUL terminator, with no bound on the number of characters consumed. Each iteration performs toupper/strchr and accumulates bits into then at line 15.

The line-10 loop's trip count is directly controlled by the length of the supplied stamp, matching excessive iteration; the missing length check in the before version is the relevant constraint.

commit_msg:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

Signed-off-by: Junio C Hamano <gitster@pobox.com>

description: Google V8 before 5.2.361.32, as used in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.82, does not properly process left-trimmed objects, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted JavaScript code.

code_evidence: The function takes an Object** p, checks only IsHeapObject, then casts to HeapObject and immediately calls PurgeLeftTrimmedObject(p), which may rewrite *p to a forwarding/left-trimmed address and return true to stop.
When PurgeLeftTrimmedObject does not return true, the code proceeds to read object->map() and Marking::MarkBitFrom(object) and to SetMark/IterateBody using the original object pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is an out-of-bounds memory access on a stale/left-trimmed heap object during marking, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds buffer operation. The root cause is failure to properly process left-trimmed objects before dereferencing, not a mere null check or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A pointer slot may reference a left-trimmed object whose stored pointer no longer denotes the intended object base. If the purge path fails to identify or correct the slot, the marking visitor dereferences the stale object pointer to obtain map and mark bits and to iterate its body, reading/writing outside the intended object boundary. Trigger is crafted JavaScript that produces left-trimmed objects during GC marking; the supported consequence is memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
ip: fix IP_CHECKSUM handling

The skbs processed by ip_cmsg_recv() are not guaranteed to
be linear e.g. when sending UDP packets over loopback with
MSGMORE.
Using csum_partial() on [potentially] the whole skb len
is dangerous; instead be on the safe side and use skb_checksum().

Thanks to syzkaller team to detect the issue and provide the
reproducer.

v1 -> v2:
 - move the variable declaration in a tighter scope

Fixes: ad6f939ab193 ("ip: Add offset parameter to ip_cmsg_recv")
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Abeni <pabeni@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (offset != 0)', '\t\tcsum = csum_sub(csum,', '\t\t\t\tcsum_partial(skb_transport_header(skb) + tlen,', '\t\t\t\t\t     offset, 0));'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (offset != 0) {', '\t\tint tend_off = skb_transport_offset(skb) + tlen;', '\t\tcsum = csum_sub(csum, skb_checksum(skb, tend_off, offset, 0));', '\t}']}
description: The ip_cmsg_recv_checksum function in net/ipv4/ip_sockglue.c in the Linux kernel before 4.10.1 has incorrect expectations about skb data layout, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (buffer over-read) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls, as demonstrated by use of the MSG_MORE flag in conjunction with loopback UDP transmission.

code_evidence: csum is derived from skb->csum and only used when ip_summed is CHECKSUM_COMPLETE (lines 4-6). When offset != 0, line 9 computes skb_transport_header(skb) + tlen and line 10 passes offset to csum_partial(), which reads offset bytes directly from that pointer without validating the skb's linear layout or total length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits: the function reads past the intended buffer boundary because it treats a possibly non-linear skb as a flat buffer and uses an unchecked length. The fix uses skb_checksum() with a bounded offset, confirming the read was out of bounds rather than a mere checksum error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: csum_partial() is called on a raw pointer into the skb with an offset-length derived from cmsg data, assuming linear contiguous data. Trigger: a non-linear skb (e.g., loopback UDP with MSG_MORE) where the transport header plus tlen plus offset extends beyond the linear area. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of skb memory, causing a crash/DoS.

  [  208.068329] x3 : 000000000008647a x2 : 19868179b1484500
  [  208.073632] x1 : 0000000000000000 x0 : ffff000009578c08
  [  208.078938] Process test_verifier (pid: 2256, stack limit = 0x0000000049ca7974)
  [  208.086235] Call trace:
  [  208.088672]  bpf_skb_load_helper_8_no_cache+0x34/0xc0
  [  208.093713]  0xffff000000bdb754
  [  208.096845]  bpf_test_run+0x78/0xf8
  [  208.100324]  bpf_prog_test_run_skb+0x148/0x230
  [  208.104758]  sys_bpf+0x314/0x1198

  [  208.111632] Code: 91302260 f9400001 f9001fa1 d2800001 (29500680)
  [  208.117717] ---[ end trace 263cb8a59b5bf29f ]---

The program itself which caused this had a long jump over the whole
instruction sequence where all of the inner instructions required
heavy expansions into multiple BPF instructions. Additionally, I also
had BPF hardening enabled which requires once more rewrites of all
constant values in order to blind them. Each time we rewrite insns,
bpf_adj_branches() would need to potentially adjust branch targets
which cross the patchlet boundary to accommodate for the additional
delta. Eventually that lead to the case where the target offset could
not fit into insn->off's upper 0x7fff limit anymore where then offset
wraps around becoming negative (in s16 universe), or vice versa
depending on the jump direction.

Therefore it becomes necessary to detect and reject any such occasions
in a generic way for native eBPF and cBPF to eBPF migrations. For
the latter we can simply check bounds in the bpf_convert_filter()'s
BPF_EMIT_JMP helper macro and bail out once we surpass limits. The
bpf_patch_insn_single() for native eBPF (and cBPF to eBPF in case
of subsequent hardening) is a bit more complex in that we need to
detect such truncations before hitting the bpf_prog_realloc(). Thus
the latter is split into an extra pass to probe problematic offsets
on the original program in order to fail early. With that in place
and carefully tested I no longer hit the panic and the rewrites are
rejected properly. The above example panic I've seen on bpf-next,
though the issue itself is generic in that a guard against this issue
in bpf seems more appropriate in this case.

Acked-by: Martin KaFai Lau <kafai@fb.com>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>

commit_msg:
Fix a potential buffer overflow issue in reference kernel of the CONV_3D_TRANSPOSE

PiperOrigin-RevId: 479074072
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    const int num_channels = input_shape.Dims(4);', '      data_ptr += num_channels;'], 'added_lines': ['      data_ptr += output_num_channels;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. The reference kernel of the `CONV_3D_TRANSPOSE` TensorFlow Lite operator wrongly increments the data_ptr when adding the bias to the result. Instead of `data_ptr += num_channels;` it should be `data_ptr += output_num_channels;` as if the number of input channels is different than the number of output channels, the wrong result will be returned and a buffer overflow will occur if num_channels > output_num_channels. An attacker can craft a model with a specific number of input channels. It is then possible to write specific values through the bias of the layer outside the bounds of the buffer. This attack only works if the reference kernel resolver is used in the interpreter. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 72c0bdcb25305b0b36842d746cc61d72658d2941. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.11. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.10.1, 2.9.3, and TensorFlow 2.8.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: data_ptr is initialized to output_data and advanced by num_channels = input_shape.Dims(4) after each outer iteration, while the inner loop writes bias_data[c] and activation into data_ptr[c] for c < output_num_channels. When input_num_channels exceeds output_num_channels, each advance skips past output_num_channels elements, so later iterations write beyond the allocated output buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to a buffer using a stride inconsistent with the buffer's actual row width, copying/writing past the end without a size check, matching CWE-120's out-of-bounds write during a copy-like operation. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), since the flaw permits writing beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pointer stride uses the input channel count instead of the output channel count, mismatching the per-row write extent. Trigger: a crafted model where num_channels > output_num_channels with bias_data present. Consequence: out-of-bounds writes of bias-derived values into adjacent memory, enabling memory corruption.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.6-1, a memory exhaustion vulnerability was found in the function ReadSUNImage in coders/sun.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service.

code_evidence: sun_info.maplength is read directly from the file as an unsigned int [76] with no bound check against the blob size. When depth < 24, image->colors is set to sun_info.maplength [99], then for RMT_NONE overwritten by one<<depth [102] or for RMT_EQUAL_RGB divided by 3 [104], and AcquireImageColormap allocates a colormap of that size [105].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because a reusable resource (colormap memory) is allocated based on an unconstrained attacker-supplied length, enabling resource-consumption DoS. This is allocation without limits rather than a buffer overflow, since the size is used directly for allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the attacker-controlled maplength is used to size a colormap allocation without validating it against the actual file size. Trigger: a crafted SUN header with a huge maplength and maptype RMT_EQUAL_RGB (so colors=maplength/3). Consequence: AcquireImageColormap attempts a massive allocation, exhausting memory and causing denial of service.

Fix null deref in the ne parser ##crash

* Reported by @hmsec via huntr.dev
* Reproducer: nepoc00
* BountyID: bfeb8fb8-644d-4587-80d4-cb704c404013
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\twhile (true) {'], 'added_lines': ['\twhile (entries) {']}
description: NULL Pointer Dereference in r_bin_ne_get_entrypoints function in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.6.8. This vulnerability allows attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash).

code_evidence: Line 8 obtains entries from r_bin_ne_get_entrypoints, which may return NULL. Line 10 loops unconditionally with while (true), never checking entries. Line 43 passes entries to r_list_get_n; r_list_get_n dereferences the list pointer, so a NULL entries causes a NULL dereference. The else branch at 46-47 only guards a missing entry element, not a NULL list.

Line 56 iterates entries via r_list_foreach without a NULL guard; the macro dereferences the list, so a NULL entries is also dereferenced there. Line 57 then uses the found list and line 63 reads en->paddr.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a list pointer expected to be valid but that can be NULL, matching CWE-476. This is a missing NULL check rather than an out-of-bounds or use-after-free issue; the impact is availability loss via crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of r_bin_ne_get_entrypoints is used as a valid RList without a NULL check. Trigger: a crafted NE binary whose entrypoint extraction fails so the function returns NULL. Consequence: r_list_get_n (line 43) or r_list_foreach (line 56) dereferences NULL, causing a crash/DoS.

If io_setup is called successful in try_smi_init() but try_smi_init()
goes out_err before calling ipmi_register_smi(), so ipmi_unregister_smi()
will not be called while removing module. It leads to the resource that
allocated in io_setup() can not be freed, but the name(DEVICE_NAME) of
resource is freed while removing the module. It causes use-after-free
when cat /proc/ioports.

and don't call io_cleanup() until io_setup() returns successful to avoid
warning prints.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\tio->io_cleanup = mem_cleanup;'], 'added_lines': ['', '\tio->io_cleanup = mem_cleanup;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. There is a use-after-free upon attempted read access to /proc/ioports after the ipmi_si module is removed, related to drivers/char/ipmi/ipmi_si_intf.c, drivers/char/ipmi/ipmi_si_mem_io.c, and drivers/char/ipmi/ipmi_si_port_io.c.

code_evidence: Line 7 assigns io->io_cleanup = mem_cleanup unconditionally before the register-size validation and before any memory regions are requested.
The loop at lines 32-37 requests memory regions and returns -EIO on failure, but the cleanup callback is already installed.
Lines 42-45 return -EIO when ioremap fails, again leaving io->io_cleanup set even though setup failed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function leaves a cleanup callback referencing resource state that is freed during module removal, and subsequent /proc/ioports access reuses that freed name. This is a dangling-reference lifetime bug, not merely an invalid register size or allocation failure.

evidence_lines.code: io->io_cleanup = mem_cleanup;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: io_cleanup is registered before setup can fail, so error paths return with the cleanup handler installed but without the corresponding setup completing. Trigger: a later teardown invokes the registered cleanup against resources that were never fully acquired, and the DEVICE_NAME-backed region name is freed while still referenced. Supported consequence: a stale resource name is dereferenced when /proc/ioports is read, causing a use-after-free read and kernel crash.

commit_msg: Allocate enough dynamic memory to store .alt file prior to reading
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tchar str[1024];', '\t\t\t} else str[i++] = c; // FIXME: potential segfault here'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t// Seek to end of regular, non-binary, file', '\t\toff_t alt_file_size;', '\t\tif (fseeko(fp, 0, SEEK_END) != 0) {', '\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\t// Get file size', '\t\talt_file_size = ftello(fp);', '\t\tif (alt_file_size == -1) {', '\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\t// Allocate adequate memory to store .alt file', '\t\tchar *str = (char*)calloc(alt_file_size, sizeof(char));', '\t\tif (str == NULL) {', '\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t\t}', '\t\t// Seek back to beginning of file to be read', '\t\tfseeko(fp, 0, SEEK_SET);', '', '\t\t\t} else str[i++] = c;', '\t\tfree(str);']}
description: BWA (aka Burrow-Wheeler Aligner) before 2019-01-23 has a stack-based buffer overflow in the bns_restore function in bntseq.c via a long sequence name in a .alt file.

code_evidence: Line 11 declares a fixed 1024-byte stack buffer str for .alt file content. The loop at lines 21-31 reads one character at a time from the file and appends each non-delimiter character via str[i++] (line 31) without ever checking i against the buffer size. Line 23 writes a NUL terminator at str[i] on each delimiter, which can also land past the array once i reaches 1024.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes data beyond the bounds of the intended buffer str, matching CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. Unlike a pure read overflow (CWE-125), the defect is the write via str[i++], and unlike CWE-121's naming, the core weakness is the missing length constraint on the write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the read loop accumulates an unbounded number of characters from the attacker-controlled .alt file into a fixed-size stack buffer. Trigger: a long sequence name (or any long line) exceeding 1024 bytes before a tab/newline/CR/EOF. Consequence: out-of-bounds writes past str, corrupting stack memory and potentially enabling control-flow hijack or crash.

Check index before writing to result->chars

Fixes #595
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tresult->chars[out++] = (widechar)ch;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tresult->chars[out++] = (widechar)ch;']}
description: Liblouis 3.6.0 has a stack-based Buffer Overflow in the function parseChars in compileTranslationTable.c, a different vulnerability than CVE-2018-11440.

code_evidence: Line 79 writes result->chars[out++] before the MAXSTRING bounds check on lines 80-83; the post-increment means the check tests the already-incremented index, so a write at index MAXSTRING-1 passes the check and the next iteration can write at MAXSTRING.
The loop bound on line 11 uses token->length, and line 12 copies each token character into result, so an input token longer than MAXSTRING drives out past the fixed result buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes past the end of the fixed result->chars buffer due to the misplaced/off-by-one bounds check; this is a direct out-of-bounds write, not merely a read overrun or integer issue.

evidence_lines.code:
while (in < token->length) {
ch = token->chars[in++] & 0xff;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the store to result->chars occurs before validating out against MAXSTRING, and the check uses the post-incremented value, so the guard is off by one and late. Trigger: a token whose decoded length reaches or exceeds MAXSTRING. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write past result->chars, corrupting adjacent stack memory and potentially crashing or enabling code execution.

Solution:   Check for an empty word tree.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['     * in the trie.'], 'added_lines': ['     * in the trie.  Bail out if the tree is empty.', '    if (byts == NULL || idxs == NULL)', '\treturn FAIL;']}
description: NULL Pointer Dereference in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0240.

code_evidence: byts and idxs are loaded from slang->sl_fbyts/sl_fidxs without any NULL check. The while loop then indexes byts[arridx[depth]] at line 27 and byts[n] at line 39, and line 60 reads idxs[n]; an empty word tree leaves these pointers NULL, so the first iteration dereferences NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly dereferences pointers that may be NULL without a guard, matching CWE-476. This is not an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the pointer itself is NULL, not merely an invalid index into valid memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sug_filltree assumes the case-folded word tree is non-empty and never validates sl_fbyts/sl_fidxs before use. Trigger: running :mkspell on an empty .dic file produces NULL tree pointers, and the loop indexes them. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash (DoS).

description: In the Linux kernel before 5.0, a memory leak exists in sit_init_net() in net/ipv6/sit.c when register_netdev() fails to register sitn->fb_tunnel_dev, which may cause denial of service, aka CID-07f12b26e21a.

code_evidence: Line 22 registers the netdev allocated at line 12; on failure, lines 23-24 branch to err_reg_dev.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because an allocated object is not released after its effective lifetime on an error/exceptional path. This is distinct from a use-after-free (CWE-416), since the memory remains allocated but unreachable rather than being reused.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path for a failed register_netdev() releases tunnel-private data but omits free_netdev() on the netdev allocated by alloc_netdev(). description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-s7comm.c had an infinite loop that was addressed by correcting off-by-one errors.

code_evidence: Loop at line 14 iterates with `i = 1; i <= item_count`, so it processes item_count+1 iterations instead of item_count, an off-by-one upper-bound error over the guint8 item_count.
Line 33 tests `(i < item_count)` to decide whether the current item is the last, but with the 1-based loop this is wrong for the final iteration, so len2 handling is misapplied.

Lines 45-52 advance offset by head_len and len (plus fill byte when len != len2) each iteration; the extra iteration driven by the off-by-one continues reading and advancing offset past the declared items.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-193 fits because the loop uses an incorrect maximum value (item_count+1 iterations) and the last-element check is off by one. This is a boundary-calculation error, not merely a missing tvb length check.

evidence_lines.code: for (i = 1; i <= item_count; i++) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop index starts at 1 but is bounded by `i <= item_count`, causing one extra iteration (and a wrong last-element test at line 33). Trigger: a packet whose item_count field is small, especially 255, so the guint8 i wraps and the loop never terminates while offset keeps advancing. Supported consequence: infinite loop / CPU resource consumption (DoS).

bluetooth: Validate socket address length in sco_sock_bind().

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '', '\tif (addr_len < sizeof(struct sockaddr_sco))']}
description: The sco_sock_bind function in net/bluetooth/sco.c in the Linux kernel before 4.3.4 does not verify an address length, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory and bypass the KASLR protection mechanism via a crafted application.

code_evidence: Line 4 casts the user-controlled addr to struct sockaddr_sco without validating that addr_len covers that structure.
Line 7 dereferences sa->sco_bdaddr in BT_DBG before any length check, reading past the supplied buffer when addr_len is short.
Lines 8-9 only check addr non-null and sa_family, not the address length.
Line 19 copies sa->sco_bdaddr into the socket's source address, again reading beyond the caller buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing length constraint causes out-of-bounds kernel memory reads whose content becomes observable to the caller, i.e., exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor, matching CWE-200. The underlying read error is the cause; the confidentiality loss is the supported consequence.

evidence_lines.code: struct sockaddr_sco *sa = (struct sockaddr_sco *) addr;
BT_DBG("sk %p %pMR", sk, &sa->sco_bdaddr);

if (!addr || addr->sa_family != AF_BLUETOOTH)
return -EINVAL;
bacpy(&sco_pi(sk)->src, &sa->sco_bdaddr);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sco_sock_bind accepts a sockaddr_sco pointer without confirming addr_len >= sizeof(struct sockaddr_sco). Trigger: a local user passes a short address buffer, causing out-of-bounds reads of adjacent kernel stack memory. Supported consequence: the over-read data is stored as the bound address and can be retrieved, exposing kernel memory and aiding KASLR bypass.

Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/25787
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    proto_item *ti;', '    proto_tree_add_item(prop_tree, hf_openflow_v6_tablemod_prop_length, tvb, offset, 2, ENC_BIG_ENDIAN);'], 'added_lines': ['    proto_item *ti, *prop_item;', '    prop_item = proto_tree_add_item(prop_tree, hf_openflow_v6_tablemod_prop_length, tvb, offset, 2, ENC_BIG_ENDIAN);', '        if (prop_length <= 12) {', '            expert_add_info(pinfo, prop_item, &ei_openflow_v6_length_too_short);', '            offset = length;', '            break;', '        }', '        if (prop_length <= 4) {', '            expert_add_info(pinfo, prop_item, &ei_openflow_v6_length_too_short);', '            offset = length;', '            break;', '        }']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-openflow_v6.c had an infinite loop that was addressed by validating property lengths.

code_evidence: prop_length is read directly from the packet at line 9 and used as the subtree length at line 10 without any lower-bound validation.

In the OFPTMPT_EXPERIMENTER case, the code unconditionally consumes 8 bytes (lines 35-38) and then computes prop_length - 12 (lines 40-41); if prop_length < 12, this underflows the unsigned subtraction and adds a huge length.
In the default case, prop_length - 4 (line 45) and offset += prop_length - 4 (line 46) underflow when prop_length < 4.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the unchecked length causes an underflowed offset/length that prevents the caller's property-iteration loop from terminating normally, matching the commit's stated purpose of validating property lengths to fix an infinite loop. This is a loop-termination/availability weakness rather than a simple out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
prop_length = tvb_get_ntohs(tvb, offset + 2);
prop_tree = proto_tree_add_subtree(tree, tvb, offset, prop_length, ett_openflow_v6_tablemod_prop, NULL, "Tablemod property");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dissector trusts the attacker-controlled prop_length without checking it against the minimum sizes required by each property type. Trigger: a crafted OpenFlow 1.5 tablemod property with prop_length smaller than 12 (experimenter) or 4 (default). The unsigned subtraction underflows, producing a huge length passed to proto_tree_add_expert_format and a huge offset increment, which can drive the caller's dissection loop into an unreachable exit condition and cause CPU exhaustion.

commit_msg:
Correctly load/initialize classes when using ConstantPool

- do not load classes in the "ifLoaded" calls
- never intitialize classes in the natives
- do not update the constant pool when querying from the natives

Fixes: #12016

[ci skip]

Signed-off-by: Graham Chapman <graham_chapman@ca.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn getMethodAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_RUNTIME_RESOLVE | J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL);'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn getMethodAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, 0);']}
description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: getMethodAt0 forwards the caller's cpIndex and resolve flags directly to getMethodAt; the before version passed J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_RUNTIME_RESOLVE, which triggers class resolution/initialization during the ConstantPool lookup. The after version passes 0, removing the resolve flag so the native no longer forces class initialization as a side effect of reading the method entry.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Passing J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_RUNTIME_RESOLVE causes the class to be resolved/initialized as a side effect of the lookup, so the resource (class state) is used before proper initialization. Removing the flag (passing 0) prevents the premature initialization, matching CWE-909's missing-initialization pattern rather than a bounds/index weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ConstantPool native performs a runtime resolve that can load/initialize classes while merely querying a method entry, so static members become reachable before the class initializer runs. Trigger: a caller uses getMethodAt0 on a cpIndex whose class is not yet initialized. Consequence: static methods/members can be invoked or read without class initialization, exposing uninitialized values (CWE-909).

commit_msg:
To avoid a race between rmap walk and mremap, mremap does
take_rmap_locks().  The lock was taken to ensure that rmap walk don't miss
a page table entry due to PTE moves via move_pagetables().  The kernel
does further optimization of this lock such that if we are going to find
the newly added vma after the old vma, the rmap lock is not taken.  This
is because rmap walk would find the vmas in the same order and if we don't
find the page table attached to older vma we would find it with the new
vma which we would iterate later.

As explained in commit eb66ae030829 ("mremap: properly flush TLB before
releasing the page") mremap is special in that it doesn't take ownership
of the page.  The optimized version for PUD/PMD aligned mremap also
doesn't hold the ptl lock.  This can result in stale TLB entries as show
below.

This patch updates the rmap locking requirement in mremap to handle the race condition
explained below with optimized mremap::

Optmized PMD move

    CPU 1                           CPU 2                                   CPU 3

    mremap(old_addr, new_addr)      page_shrinker/try_to_unmap_one

    mmap_write_lock_killable()

                                    addr = old_addr
                                    lock(pte_ptl)
    lock(pmd_ptl)
    pmd = *old_pmd
    pmd_clear(old_pmd)
    flush_tlb_range(old_addr)

    *new_pmd = pmd
                                                                            *new_addr = 10; and fills
                                                                            TLB with new addr
                                                                            and old pfn

    unlock(pmd_ptl)
                                    ptep_clear_flush()
                                    old pfn is free.
                                                                            Stale TLB entry

Optimized PUD move also suffers from a similar race.  Both the above race
condition can be fixed if we force mremap path to take rmap lock.

Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20210616045239.370802-7-aneesh.kumar@linux.ibm.com
Fixes: 2c91bd4a4e2e ("mm: speed up mremap by 20x on large regions")
Fixes: c49dd3401802 ("mm: speedup mremap on 1GB or larger regions")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/CAHk-=wgXVR04eBNtxQfevontWnP6FDm+oj5vauQXP3S-huwbPw@mail.gmail.com

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\t   old_pud, new_pud, need_rmap_locks))', '\t\t\t\t\t   old_pmd, new_pmd, need_rmap_locks))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\t   old_pud, new_pud, true))', '\t\t\t\t\t   old_pmd, new_pmd, true))']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s mm/mremap memory address space accounting source code. This issue occurs due to a race condition between rmap walk and mremap, allowing a local user to crash the system or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: In the PUD-aligned branch, move_pgt_entry for NORMAL_PUD is called with the caller-supplied need_rmap_locks flag; when false, the page-table move proceeds without taking the rmap lock.
Similarly, the PMD-aligned branch passes need_rmap_locks into move_pgt_entry for NORMAL_PMD, so an optimized move can relocate the page table without the rmap lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the race lets an rmap walker or stale TLB entry reference a page after it has been freed and possibly reallocated. This is use-after-free, not merely a missing lock, since the freed page can be reused while still referenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the optimized PUD/PMD move path can skip the rmap lock, so a concurrent rmap walk may observe a cleared old entry without the lock serializing the PTE move. Trigger: mremap with a caller that sets need_rmap_locks false races with try_to_unmap_one, which frees the old page while a stale TLB entry or walker still references it. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the freed page, enabling crash or potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
A security advisory (TALOS-2019-0857/CVE-2019-5068) found that
creating shared memory regions with permission mode 0777 could allow
any user to access that memory.  Several Mesa drivers use shared-
memory XImages to implement back buffers for improved performance.

This path changes the shmget() calls to use 0600 (user r/w).

Tested with legacy Xlib driver and llvmpipe.

Cc: mesa-stable@lists.freedesktop.org
Reviewed-by: Kristian H. Kristensen <hoegsberg@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['   dri_sw_dt->shmid = shmget(IPC_PRIVATE, size, IPC_CREAT|0777);'], 'added_lines': ['   /* 0600 = user read+write */', '   dri_sw_dt->shmid = shmget(IPC_PRIVATE, size, IPC_CREAT | 0600);']}
description: An exploitable shared memory permissions vulnerability exists in the functionality of X11 Mesa 3D Graphics Library 19.1.2. An attacker can access the shared memory without any specific permissions to trigger this vulnerability.

code_evidence: alloc_shm creates a System V shared memory segment via shmget() with IPC_CREAT and permission bits 0777, granting read/write/execute to owner, group and all other users before any data is placed in it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-732 covers assigning permissions to a security-critical resource that allow unintended actors access. The 0777 mode on the shared memory segment is exactly such an over-permissive assignment, affecting confidentiality and integrity of the buffer; this is a permissions-assignment flaw, not merely a missing authorization check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shared-memory segment backing the XImage back buffer is created world-accessible (0777) instead of restricted to the creating user. Trigger: any local user on a multi-user host can attach to the predictable IPC_PRIVATE segment while it exists and read or modify the rendered buffer contents. Consequence: exposure and tampering of graphics data shared across users.

commit_msg:
Fix #171 (#175)

(slicen + 1) should not run after the array boundary;
to avoid possible overflow, we now check in 2 steps,
chained with short-circuit-and.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if (slicen < mp4config.frame.nsclices)', '            {'], 'added_lines': ['            if (slicen < mp4config.frame.nsclices &&', '                (slicen + 1) < mp4config.frame.nsclices) {']}
description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability infaad2 v.2.10.1 allows a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code and cause a denial of service via the stcoin function in mp4read.c.

code_evidence: The guard only checks slicen < mp4config.frame.nsclices, then reads mp4config.frame.map[slicen + 1].firstchunk at line 25; when slicen equals nsclices-1, the index slicen+1 equals nsclices, one past the valid map range.
Line 28 then indexes mp4config.frame.map[slicen] to read samplesperchunk, so the advanced slicen value is consumed as a map index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing upper-bound constraint permits an array access at slicen+1 beyond the intended map buffer, an out-of-bounds write/read of memory. It is not merely an integer overflow, since the unchecked index directly targets the map buffer.

evidence_lines.code: samplesleft = mp4config.frame.map[slicen].samplesperchunk;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check fails to account for the slicen+1 access, so the read at line 25 can occur at index nsclices. Trigger: an stcoin table where chunkn reaches map[slicen+1].firstchunk while slicen is the last valid slice. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds access to the map array, corrupting/altering memory state used for subsequent sample offsets.

commit_msg: Json library: fix a number of potential buffer overflows
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static char', '    return JSON_TYPE_ERROR;', '  return state->stack[state->depth];'], 'added_lines': ['static bool', '    return false;', '  return true;']}
description: Contiki-NG before 4.2 has a stack-based buffer overflow in the push function in os/lib/json/jsonparse.c that allows an out-of-bounds write of an '{' or '[' character.

code_evidence: pop() decrements state->depth after only checking depth != 0, then reads state->stack[state->depth] into state->vtype and returns it; no bound is placed on the index before the write to vtype or the stack access. The function itself performs indexed stack reads governed by depth.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the stack index derived from depth can point past the intended buffer, producing an out-of-bounds write. This is not merely an underflow/over-read: the same unvalidated depth also permits writing beyond the stack array, matching CWE-787 rather than a pure CWE-125 read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the depth counter being trusted to stay within the stack array bounds; if depth exceeds the allocated stack size (e.g., via repeated push of '{' or '['), the index state->stack[state->depth] is out of range. The trigger is unbalanced nesting that drives depth beyond capacity, and the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds memory access/write affecting state->vtype and stack contents.

description: A vulnerability, which was classified as problematic, was found in Linux Kernel. This affects the function tcp_getsockopt/tcp_setsockopt of the component TCP Handler. The manipulation leads to race condition. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier VDB-211089 was assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: When level != SOL_TCP, the function dereferences icsk->icsk_af_ops and immediately invokes its setsockopt callback without any READ_ONCE() or synchronization. icsk_af_ops is a shared field that tcp_v6_connect() and do_ipv6_setsockopt() overwrite under lock_sock(), so this lockless load of the pointer can race with that concurrent store.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a shared resource (icsk_af_ops) is accessed by concurrent code sequences without exclusive/atomic access, violating atomicity. The fix adds READ_ONCE() to pair with WRITE_ONCE(), confirming a race-condition root cause rather than a distinct weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shared icsk->icsk_af_ops pointer is read locklessly and used as an indirect-call target while another path writes it under lock_sock(). Trigger: two threads call tcp_setsockopt() and tcp_v6_connect() concurrently, producing a torn/inconsistent pointer load; the consequence is a data race that can lead to a crash or instability rather than a controlled memory-safety violation.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '      if (fd >= nFDs)', '\tcontinue;']}
description: The FoFiType1C::convertToType0 function in FoFiType1C.cc in Poppler 0.59.0 has a heap-based buffer over-read vulnerability if an out-of-bounds font dictionary index is encountered, which allows an attacker to launch a denial of service attack.

code_evidence: The loop at line 44 iterates over nCIDs in 256-blocks, initializes fd to 0 (line 45), and when fdSelect is present assigns fd = fdSelect[cidMap[i+j]] (line 49) without bounding fd against the number of private dictionaries. Line 61 then indexes privateDicts[fd] using this unbounded value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe indexed access privateDicts[fd] with an unchecked fd reads memory past the intended privateDicts buffer, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). The added guard fd >= nFDs confirms the missing upper-bound constraint; this is a read, not a write, so it is not CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fd derived from attacker-controlled fdSelect array is used to index privateDicts without a bounds check. Trigger: a crafted Type1C font with an out-of-range font dictionary index in fdSelect. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of privateDicts[fd], leading to a crash/DoS (and potentially info disclosure).

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4214: illegal memory access with large 'tabstop' in Ex mode

Problem:    Illegal memory access with large 'tabstop' in Ex mode.
Solution:   Allocate enough memory.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    alloc_cmdbuff(exmode_active ? 250 : indent + 1);'], 'added_lines': ['    alloc_cmdbuff(indent + 50);']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.

code_evidence: Line 7 allocates the command-line buffer via alloc_cmdbuff, sized from the indent argument (or a fixed 250 in Ex mode) rather than validating indent against a bound.
Lines 15-19 fill the buffer with ' ' for indent bytes and write ccline.cmdbuff[indent] = NUL, plus set cmdpos/cmdspos/cmdlen to indent, so subsequent editing assumes indent bytes are available.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a heap buffer and then writes indent bytes plus a NUL into it without ensuring the allocation covers that length, matching CWE-122 (heap-based buffer overflow). A simple out-of-bounds read would be CWE-125, but here the writes at lines 15-16 corrupt heap memory.

evidence_lines.code: alloc_cmdbuff(exmode_active ? 250 : indent + 1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the heap buffer is sized from an attacker-influenced indent value that can exceed the actual allocation (large 'tabstop' in Ex mode), while the memset and terminator write use the full indent. Trigger: opening Ex mode command-line with an oversized indent, causing writes past the heap allocation. Consequence: heap-based buffer overflow with potential crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
dlt_common: Fix buffer overflow in dlt_filter_load

A buffer overflow in the dlt_filter_load function in dlt_common.c in dlt-daemon allows arbitrary code execution via an unsafe usage of fscanf, because it does not limit the number of characters to be read in a format argument.

Fixed: #274

Signed-off-by: GwanYeong Kim <gy741.kim@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (fscanf(handle, "%s", str1) != 1)', '        if (fscanf(handle, "%s", str1) != 1)'], 'added_lines': ['        if (fscanf(handle, "%254s", str1) != 1)', '        if (fscanf(handle, "%254s", str1) != 1)']}
description: A buffer overflow in the dlt_filter_load function in dlt_common.c from dlt-daemon through 2.18.5 (GENIVI Diagnostic Log and Trace) allows arbitrary code execution because fscanf is misused (no limit on the number of characters to be read in the format argument).

code_evidence: Line 6 declares a fixed-size stack buffer str1 of DLT_COMMON_BUFFER_LENGTH; line 17 reads an unbounded token into it with fscanf using "%s", which has no field-width limit.
Line 26 resets str1[0] and line 27 performs the same unbounded fscanf("%s") read into the same fixed buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The reads write beyond the bounds of the intended fixed-size buffer str1, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The unbounded copy is the cause; the out-of-bounds write and resulting memory corruption are the weakness, distinct from a mere input-validation issue.

evidence_lines.code:
char str1[DLT_COMMON_BUFFER_LENGTH];
if (fscanf(handle, "%s", str1) != 1)

str1[0] = 0;
if (fscanf(handle, "%s", str1) != 1)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fscanf with "%s" copies an arbitrary-length token from the filter file into the fixed-size stack buffer str1 without a width limit. Trigger: a filter file containing a token longer than DLT_COMMON_BUFFER_LENGTH causes bytes to be written past str1's end. Supported consequence: stack memory corruption, potentially crashing the process or enabling code execution depending on the overwritten data.

commit_msg:
ipv6: check sk sk_type and protocol early in ip_mroute_set/getsockopt

Commit 5e1859fbcc3c ("ipv4: ipmr: various fixes and cleanups") fixed
the issue for ipv4 ipmr:

  ip_mroute_setsockopt() & ip_mroute_getsockopt() should not
  access/set raw_sk(sk)->ipmr_table before making sure the socket
  is a raw socket, and protocol is IGMP

The same fix should be done for ipv6 ipmr as well.

This patch can fix the panic caused by overwriting the same offset
as ipmr_table as in raw_sk(sk) when accessing other type's socket
by ip_mroute_setsockopt().

Signed-off-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (sk->sk_type != SOCK_RAW ||', '\t    inet_sk(sk)->inet_num != IPPROTO_ICMPV6)', '\t\treturn -EOPNOTSUPP;']}
description: An issue was discovered in net/ipv6/ip6mr.c in the Linux kernel before 4.11. By setting a specific socket option, an attacker can control a pointer in kernel land and cause an inet_csk_listen_stop general protection fault, or potentially execute arbitrary code under certain circumstances. The issue can be triggered as root (e.g., inside a default LXC container or with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability) or after namespace unsharing. This occurs because sk_type and protocol are not checked in the appropriate part of the ip6_mroute_* functions. NOTE: this affects Linux distributions that use 4.9.x longterm kernels before 4.9.187.

code_evidence: The function dereferences raw6_sk(sk)->ip6mr_table immediately after obtaining net, before any check that the socket is a raw ICMPv6 socket, so a socket of a different type/protocol reaches this access.
The switch then reads mrt fields (mroute_do_pim, mroute_do_assert) derived from that table for MRT6_PIM/MRT6_ASSERT options.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes socket metadata (sk_type, inet_num) without validating that it meets the required raw/ICMPv6 precondition before using it to select a table. This missing input-validation constraint on the socket type/protocol is the defect fixed by the added check, matching CWE-20.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the socket's sk_type and protocol are not validated before raw6_sk(sk) is treated as a raw-socket context. Trigger: an attacker with CAP_NET_ADMIN or after namespace unsharing invokes getsockopt with an MRT6 option on a non-raw or non-ICMPv6 socket. The unchecked raw6_sk cast interprets unrelated socket memory as ip6mr_table, yielding an invalid table pointer whose dereference can crash the kernel (general protection fault) or, per the report, enable further memory corruption.

commit_msg:
asymcute: don't make the assumption that req->arg is non-NULL

This fixes a denial of service where an attacker would be able to cause
a NULL pointer dereference by sending a spoofed packet. This attack only
requires knowledge about pending message ids.

description: RIOT 2019.07 contains a NULL pointer dereference in the MQTT-SN implementation (asymcute), potentially allowing an attacker to crash a network node running RIOT. This requires spoofing an MQTT server response. To do so, the attacker needs to know the MQTT MsgID of a pending MQTT protocol message and the ephemeral port used by RIOT's MQTT implementation. Additionally, the server IP address is required for spoofing the packet.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function expects req->arg to be a valid pointer but dereferences it without validating non-NULL, matching a classic NULL pointer dereference. It is not a type-confusion or use-after-free issue; the pointer is simply NULL.

sub->topic = NULL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: req->arg can be NULL when a spoofed MQTT-SN response (e.g., a suback) is matched to a pending request whose arg was never set. The unchecked cast propagates NULL, and the write to sub->topic dereferences it, crashing the node (DoS). Cause is the missing NULL check; consequence is a NULL-pointer write/crash.

commit_msg:
XRA: Fix an infinite loop

C compilers don't care what size a value was on the wire. Use
naturally-sized ints, including in dissect_message_channel_mb where we
would otherwise overflow and loop infinitely.

Fixes #19100
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  guint packet_start_pointer;', '    guint16 docsis_start = 3 + packet_start_pointer;', '      guint16 docsis_length = 256*tvb_get_guint8(tvb,docsis_start + 2) + tvb_get_guint8(tvb,docsis_start + 3);'], 'added_lines': ['  unsigned packet_start_pointer;', '    unsigned docsis_start = 3 + packet_start_pointer;', '      unsigned docsis_length = 256*tvb_get_guint8(tvb,docsis_start + 2) + tvb_get_guint8(tvb,docsis_start + 3);']}
description: XRA dissector infinite loop in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.5 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.13 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: packet_start_pointer is declared as guint (32-bit) and receives the 16-bit pointer value at line 8.
docsis_start is a guint16 initialized as 3 + packet_start_pointer, so the addition is truncated to 16 bits.
The while loop at line 10 uses docsis_start + 6 < remaining_length as its exit condition, but docsis_start is 16-bit.
docsis_length is also guint16, and line 26 advances docsis_start by 6 + docsis_length, which is truncated in 16-bit arithmetic.
Because docsis_start wraps, the loop condition can remain true indefinitely; the fix widens these variables to unsigned.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's loop exit condition (docsis_start + 6 < remaining_length) cannot be reached when 16-bit arithmetic causes docsis_start to wrap, matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. This is a loop-termination defect, not merely an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code: guint packet_start_pointer;
guint16 docsis_start = 3 + packet_start_pointer;
while (docsis_start + 6 < remaining_length) {
guint16 docsis_length = 256*tvb_get_guint8(tvb,docsis_start + 2) + tvb_get_guint8(tvb,docsis_start + 3);
docsis_start += 6 + docsis_length;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop index docsis_start and step docsis_length are 16-bit, so 3 + packet_start_pointer and docsis_start += 6 + docsis_length overflow and wrap. Trigger: a crafted packet with a large packet_start_pointer or docsis_length makes docsis_start wrap before satisfying the exit condition. Consequence: the while loop never terminates, causing CPU exhaustion (denial of service).

commit_msg:
crypto: algif_skcipher - Require setkey before accept(2)

Some cipher implementations will crash if you try to use them
without calling setkey first.  This patch adds a check so that
the accept(2) call will fail with -ENOKEY if setkey hasn't been
done on the socket yet.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>

description: crypto/algif_skcipher.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.2 does not verify that a setkey operation has been performed on an AF_ALG socket before an accept system call is processed, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash) via a crafted application that does not supply a key, related to the lrw_crypt function in crypto/lrw.c.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function is only a release/destructor that frees a skcipher and its wrapper; it contains no accept path, setkey check, or dereference of an unset key, so it does not itself support CWE-476.

commit_msg:
Fix division by zero

Fix uclouvain/openjpeg#733
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif ((((OPJ_UINT32)-1) / l_data_size) < (OPJ_UINT32)(l_tilec->y1 - l_tilec->y0)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* issue 733, l_data_size == 0U, probably something wrong should be checked before getting here */', '\t\tif ((l_data_size > 0U) && ((((OPJ_UINT32)-1) / l_data_size) < (OPJ_UINT32)(l_tilec->y1 - l_tilec->y0))) {']}
description: Divide-by-zero vulnerability in the opj_tcd_init_tile function in tcd.c in OpenJPEG before 2.1.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted jp2 file. NOTE: this issue exists because of an incorrect fix for CVE-2014-7947.

code_evidence: Line 53 computes l_data_size as the horizontal component width (x1 - x0). Line 54 then uses l_data_size as the divisor in ((OPJ_UINT32)-1) / l_data_size to perform an overflow check against the vertical component size before computing the allocation size on line 58. No guard ensures l_data_size is nonzero before the division.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 (Divide By Zero) directly matches: an unsigned integer divisor derived from image dimensions is used without a nonzero constraint, and a crafted JP2 can drive it to zero. This is a direct division-by-zero rather than a related integer-overflow weakness, which would concern the multiply on line 58.

Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>

description: sound/usb/mixer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (snd_usb_mixer_interrupt use-after-free and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted USB device.

code_evidence: snd_usb_mixer_disconnect unconditionally calls usb_kill_urb on mixer->urb and mixer->rc_urb without checking whether the URB pointers were initialized or whether the mixer is already being torn down; on the probe error path the URB submitted earlier can outlive the mixer struct that its completion/interrupt handler references.

usb_kill_urb(mixer->rc_urb);

commit_msg:
x86/cpu-policy: Hide CLWB by default on SKX/CLX/CPX

The August 2023 microcode for GDS has an impact on the CLWB instruction.  See
code comments for full details.

This is part of XSA-435 / CVE-2022-40982

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>

 	    c == &boot_cpu_data )

+
+	/*
+	 * The Gather Data Sampling microcode mitigation (August 2023) has an
+	 * adverse performance impact on the CLWB instruction on SKX/CLX/CPX.
+	 *
+	 * On this model, CLWB has equivalent behaviour to CLFLUSHOPT but the

commit_msg:
Prevent division by 0

PiperOrigin-RevId: 370998952
Change-Id: I6b1d49079624ee1447d2d9b53a8976fb356cc8f5
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, num_splits != 0);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The implementation of the `Split` TFLite operator is vulnerable to a division by zero error(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/e2752089ef7ce9bcf3db0ec618ebd23ea119d0c7/tensorflow/lite/kernels/split.cc#L63-L65). An attacker can craft a model such that `num_splits` would be 0. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: input_size is computed from the input tensor dimension at axis_value, then used in the modulo check input_size % num_splits and the integer division input_size / num_splits. num_splits is a function parameter derived from the model's split configuration and is not validated against zero before these operations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 directly describes dividing a value by zero; the code performs input_size % num_splits and input_size / num_splits with an unvalidated num_splits. This is the divide-by-zero weakness itself, not a separate bounds or type issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: num_splits is used as a divisor without a nonzero check. Trigger: a crafted model supplies num_splits == 0, so the modulo and division at lines 11-13 execute with a zero divisor. Supported consequence: division-by-zero crash, affecting availability of the TFLite interpreter.

description: The string_scan_range() function in radare2 2.5.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based out-of-bounds read and application crash) via a crafted binary file.

code_evidence: At [20] r_utf8_decode reads buf+needle-from for to-needle bytes; rc is the decoded length. At [26,28] w = buf+needle+rc-from, then w[0..4] are dereferenced when (to-needle)>5, but the bound check does not account for rc, so needle+rc+4 can exceed to and read past buf.

The decode loop [43-65] advances needle by rc each iteration; for WIDE32 rc is forced to 4 [47,48] and for WIDE rc may become 2 [52,53], so needle can reach to-1 while the wide32/wide checks still access w[0..4] beyond the allocated to-from buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code reads past the end of the calloc'd buf via w[0..4] without a correct length constraint, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. It is not a write (CWE-787) since only reads occur; the missing rc-aware bound is the direct cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the wide32/wide detection bound (to-needle)>5 ignores the already-consumed rc bytes, so w points rc bytes ahead but five bytes are still read. Trigger: a crafted binary whose final bytes at the range end form a partial wide marker. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds read and crash/DoS (CWE-125).

commit_msg:
Update unsquash-4.c

There seems to be a stack overflow in read_fragment_table_4 at via what seems to be an integer overflow. Still looking into this problem, it seems like two or three different problems combined.

The first problem overflows the bytes variable, so that the allocation is enormous.
```c
int bytes = SQUASHFS_FRAGMENT_BYTES(sBlk.s.fragments);
```

If we fix this by making the variable size_t, we run into an unrelated problem in which the stack VLA allocation of fragment_table_index can easily exceed RLIMIT_STACK.
```c
long long fragment_table_index[indexes];
```

In the case of my system, the RLIMIT_STACK is 8388608, and VLA is asking for 15728648. Plus the stack probably already has a bunch of other things. This is what I believe ultimately leads to the stack overflow.

Afterwards, the heap allocation seems to succeed, and the disastrous call to read_fs_bytes is made, which initiates transfer from the squashfs image to the stack. At this stage, a stack overflow appears to be in full effect.

```c
 res = read_fs_bytes(fd, sBlk.s.fragment_table_start,
         SQUASHFS_FRAGMENT_INDEX_BYTES(sBlk.s.fragments),
         fragment_table_index);
```
This problem is also present in other read_fragment_table_N functions, and in in the original squashfs-tools.

```
Parallel unsquashfs: Using 8 processors
ASAN:SIGSEGV
=================================================================
==8221==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-overflow on address 0x7ffef3ae9608 (pc 0x000000559011 bp 0x7ffef49e9670 sp 0x7ffef3ae9610 T0)
    #0 0x559010 in read_fragment_table_4 /home/septimus/vr/squashfs-vr/squashfs-tools/unsquash-4.c:40:9
    #1 0x525073 in main /home/septimus/vr/squashfs-vr/squashfs-tools/unsquashfs.c:2763:5
    #2 0x7fb56c533a3f in __libc_start_main (/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6+0x20a3f)
    #3 0x418468 in _start (/home/septimus/vr/squashfs-vr/squashfs-tools/unsquashfs+0x418468)
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: stack-overflow /home/septimus/vr/squashfs-vr/squashfs-tools/unsquash-4.c:40:9 in read_fragment_table_4
==8221==ABORTING
```

Perhaps we should avoid using VLA altogether, and allocate fragment_table_index to the heap?
This pull request is an example implementation of the fix for unsquash-4, but I don't have enough test vectors to verify it will not break anything.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint bytes = SQUASHFS_FRAGMENT_BYTES(sBlk.s.fragments);', '\tint  indexes = SQUASHFS_FRAGMENT_INDEXES(sBlk.s.fragments);', '\tlong long fragment_table_index[indexes];'], 'added_lines': ['\tsize_t bytes = SQUASHFS_FRAGMENT_BYTES(sBlk.s.fragments);', '\tsize_t indexes = SQUASHFS_FRAGMENT_INDEXES(sBlk.s.fragments);', '\tlong long *fragment_table_index;', '', '\tfragment_table_index = malloc(indexes*sizeof(long long));', '\tif(fragment_table_index == NULL)', '\t\tEXIT_UNSQUASH("read_fragment_table: failed to allocate "', '\t\t\t"fragment table index\\n");']}
description: Integer overflow in the read_fragment_table_4 function in unsquash-4.c in Squashfs and sasquatch allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted input, which triggers a stack-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Lines 4-5 compute bytes and indexes as signed int from the on-disk sBlk.s.fragments field; line 6 then uses indexes as a VLA dimension, so the size is derived from attacker-controlled metadata without bounds checking.
Line 14 allocates fragment_table with the possibly-wrapped int bytes. Lines 18-20 call read_fs_bytes into fragment_table_index using the index-byte count, transferring image data onto the stack VLA.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer wraparound in the size computation from untrusted fragment count, which then corrupts allocation/copy sizing; that matches CWE-190. The stack overflow is the downstream consequence, not the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sBlk.s.fragments is attacker-controlled and the derived byte/index counts are stored in int, so the multiplication can wrap, yielding a small or negative size. The wrapped bytes value feeds malloc at line 14, while indexes sizes the stack VLA at line 6 and the read at lines 18-20, so malformed input produces a mismatched allocation and an oversized/underflowed stack copy, crashing the process.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the RELRO segment's start/end range may not overlap any PT_LOAD segment, leaving lm NULL, yet the code immediately accesses lm->count and lm->sections. Trigger: a crafted ELF file with a PT_GNU_RELRO lacking a matching PT_LOAD processed by objcopy. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and application crash (denial of service).

commit_msg:
Events should only be added to a groups rb tree if they have not been
removed from their context by list_del_event(). Since remove_on_exec
made it possible to call list_del_event() on individual events before
they are detached from their group, perf_group_detach() should check each
sibling's attach_state before calling add_event_to_groups() on it.

Fixes: 2e498d0a74e5 ("perf: Add support for event removal on exec")
Signed-off-by: Budimir Markovic <markovicbudimir@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/ZBFzvQV9tEqoHEtH@gentoo
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!RB_EMPTY_NODE(&event->group_node)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (sibling->attach_state & PERF_ATTACH_CONTEXT) {']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux Kernel Performance Events system can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

The perf_group_detach function did not check the event's siblings' attach_state before calling add_event_to_groups(), but remove_on_exec made it possible to call list_del_event() on before detaching from their group, making it possible to use a dangling pointer causing a use-after-free vulnerability.

We recommend upgrading past commit fd0815f632c24878e325821943edccc7fde947a2.

code_evidence: The guard at line 22 tests RB_EMPTY_NODE(&event->group_node) on the leader event rather than on the sibling being processed; line 23 then calls add_event_to_groups(sibling, event->ctx) and lines 24-25 insert the sibling into the active list, even when the sibling was already removed from its context via list_del_event() during remove_on_exec.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reinserting a sibling whose context linkage was already torn down causes later operations to dereference freed/reused memory, matching CWE-416. This is a stale-reference lifetime bug, not merely a logic error, because the consequence is access through an invalid pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the detach path decides whether to re-add a sibling to the groups rb-tree based on the wrong object's node state, so a sibling already unlinked from its context is reinserted. Trigger: remove_on_exec removes an individual event before its group is detached, then perf_group_detach() iterates that sibling. Consequence: a dangling event reference is placed back into the rb-tree, yielding a use-after-free reachable for local privilege escalation.

description: C-blosc2 before 2.9.3 was discovered to contain a NULL pointer dereference in ndlz/ndlz8x8.c via a NULL pointer to memset.

code_evidence: Line 5-7: ip, ip_limit, and op are derived from the caller-supplied input and output pointers without any prior NULL check.

Line 29-32: after the length guard passes, memset(op, ...) dereferences the output pointer; if output is NULL this is a NULL dereference. The same missing check applies to input, which is read via *ip at line 17.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a write/read through a pointer that may be NULL, which is exactly CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). It is not a buffer overflow: the bug is the absent NULL validation, not an out-of-bounds index.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function never validates that input and output are non-NULL before building pointers from them and writing through op. Trigger: a caller passes a NULL output (or input) pointer with a length that passes the guards. Consequence: memset/read at a NULL address causes a crash (DoS); the patch adds BLOSC_ERROR_NULL checks to reject such calls.
