description: abrt-dbus in Automatic Bug Reporting Tool (ABRT) allows local users to delete or change the ownership of arbitrary files via the problem directory argument to the (1) ChownProblemDir, (2) DeleteElement, or (3) DeleteProblem method.

code_evidence: ChownProblemDir obtains problem_dir from the D-Bus parameter (line 66) and only applies allowed_problem_dir() before use.
The path is then passed to dump_dir_stat_for_uid() (line 73) and later to dd_opendir() (line 101); the check and the open are separate operations on the same name-based path.
The caller-controlled problem_dir is used across multiple path-based operations with no binding between the validated object and the object later opened.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 does not fit: the weakness is a check-then-use race on a pathname (TOCTOU), not missing validation of the input's required properties. allowed_problem_dir is present; the failure is that the validated input is not the object operated on.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the method validates a caller-supplied path string and later re-resolves that same string for stat and open, so the validated identity is not tied to the object eventually used. A local user can swap the directory between allowed_problem_dir/stat and dd_opendir, causing chown or deletion of an unintended file. The consequence is unauthorized modification of arbitrary files, not merely improper syntactic validation.

commit_msg:
Don't allow unhandled POSTs to write to the filesystem by default

If there's no registered handler for a POST request, the default behaviour
is to write it to the filesystem. Several million deployed devices appear
to have this behaviour, making it possible to (at least) store arbitrary
data on them. Add a configure option that enables this behaviour, and change
the default to just drop POSTs that aren't directly handled.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#ifdef UPNP_ENABLE_POST_WRITE', '#else', '\t\treturn HTTP_NOT_FOUND;', '#endif']}
description: Portable UPnP SDK (aka libupnp) before 1.6.21 allows remote attackers to write to arbitrary files in the webroot via a POST request without a registered handler.

code_evidence: When Instr is absent or not a virtual file, the else branch unconditionally opens the request-derived filename with fopen(filename, "wb") and only fails on I/O error; there is no check that a POST handler authorized this write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-284 fits because the code fails to restrict access to a filesystem resource: it performs a write without enforcing any authorization or handler-registration check. This is an access-control failure, not a buffer or injection weakness; the write itself is the unauthorized resource access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the default non-virtual-file path treats any POST as a file write, deriving the destination from the request filename without verifying an authorized handler. Trigger: a remote POST with no registered handler reaches this branch. Consequence: arbitrary data is written under the webroot, enabling file creation/overwrite by an unauthenticated actor.

commit_msg:
in_mqtt: fix memory corruption on dropping packet (#1135)

This patch adds an extra verification to the buffer counters to
avoid corruption when memmove() an extra byte.

In addition this patch implement a linked list for the active
connections so when closing Fluent Bit we have a clean exit.

Signed-off-by: Eduardo Silva <eduardo@treasure-data.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (conn->buf_pos == conn->buf_len) {', '        conn->buf_frame_end = 0;', '        conn->buf_len = 0;', '        conn->buf_pos = 0;', '        return 0;', '    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in the MQTT input plugin in Fluent Bit through 1.0.4. When this plugin acts as an MQTT broker (server), it mishandles incoming network messages. After processing a crafted packet, the plugin's mqtt_packet_drop function (in /plugins/in_mqtt/mqtt_prot.c) executes the memmove() function with a negative size parameter. That leads to a crash of the whole Fluent Bit server via a SIGSEGV signal.

code_evidence: move_bytes is computed as conn->buf_pos + 1 and then passed as the size argument (conn->buf_len - move_bytes) to memmove; both operands are signed int and the subtraction can go negative when buf_pos+1 exceeds buf_len, so the size argument becomes a negative int that is converted to size_t for memmove.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-681 fits because the negative signed int size is converted to size_t for memmove, producing an unexpected huge value used in a sensitive context. It is distinct from a plain out-of-bounds write, since the defect is the numeric conversion of the negative size.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer counters are not validated before the subtraction, so conn->buf_len - move_bytes can be negative and the signed int is implicitly converted to the size_t parameter of memmove. Trigger: a crafted MQTT packet leaves buf_pos+1 greater than buf_len. Consequence: memmove receives a huge unsigned size, causing out-of-bounds memory access and a SIGSEGV crash.

commit_msg:
Since commit 9e2369c06c8a18 ("xen: add helpers to allocate unpopulated
memory") foreign mappings are using guest physical addresses allocated
via ZONE_DEVICE functionality.

This will result in problems for the case of no balloon memory hotplug
being configured, as the p2m list will only cover the initial memory
size of the domain. Any ZONE_DEVICE allocated address will be outside
the p2m range and thus a mapping can't be established with that memory
address.

Fix that by extending the p2m size for that case. At the same time add
a check for a to be created mapping to be within the p2m limits in
order to detect errors early.

While changing a comment, remove some 32-bit leftovers.

This is XSA-369.

Fixes: 9e2369c06c8a18 ("xen: add helpers to allocate unpopulated memory")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # 5.9
Reported-by: Marek Marczykowski-Górecki <marmarek@invisiblethingslab.com>
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!p2m_limit && IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_XEN_UNPOPULATED_ALLOC))', '\t\tp2m_limit = xen_start_info->nr_pages * XEN_EXTRA_MEM_RATIO;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel 5.9.x through 5.11.3, as used with Xen. In some less-common configurations, an x86 PV guest OS user can crash a Dom0 or driver domain via a large amount of I/O activity. The issue relates to misuse of guest physical addresses when a configuration has CONFIG_XEN_UNPOPULATED_ALLOC but not CONFIG_XEN_BALLOON_MEMORY_HOTPLUG.

code_evidence: p2m_limit is computed from P2M_LIMIT at line 6; without the added guard it can be zero when no balloon hotplug is configured. vm.size (line 8) is derived from max(xen_max_p2m_pfn, p2m_limit) and then xen_max_p2m_pfn/xen_p2m_size (lines 12,15) are set from that same value, so the p2m array sizing depends on the computed limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an incorrect calculation of the buffer size (the p2m tree extent) that fails to cover addresses later used, matching CWE-131's incorrect size computation leading to out-of-bounds access. It is not merely a missing bounds check; the sizing itself is wrong, which the patch corrects by extending p2m_limit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the p2m size limit is calculated without accounting for ZONE_DEVICE-allocated guest physical addresses, so the p2m list covers only initial memory. Trigger: CONFIG_XEN_UNPOPULATED_ALLOC without CONFIG_XEN_BALLOON_MEMORY_HOTPLUG. Consequence: foreign mappings use addresses beyond the p2m range, causing a Dom0/driver-domain crash under heavy I/O.

commit_msg: Fix #8685 - Crash in ELF version parsing

description: The store_versioninfo_gnu_verdef function in libr/bin/format/elf/elf.c in radare2 2.0.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (r_read_le16 invalid write and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: Loop condition only bounds the start offset i against end before dereferencing verdef; it does not validate the size of the Verdef record read.
vstart points into the calloc'd defs buffer at offset i, then READ16/READ32 macros populate verdef fields from dfs; the record size is trusted implicitly.
vstart is advanced by attacker-controlled vd_aux and only checked afterward against end, so the aux reads at [60,61] occur after a bounded check but the outer iteration bound remains offset-only.
i is incremented by verdef->vd_next; when vd_next is zero or negative (signed), i can stay or move backward, causing repeated/out-of-range processing of the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs read/write operations on the defs buffer using offsets derived from untrusted ELF fields and fails to keep those accesses within the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The added vd_next check confirms the missing bound on the advancing offset.

evidence_lines.code: for (cnt = 0, i = 0; cnt < shdr->sh_info && ((char *)defs + i < end); ++cnt) {

vstart += verdef->vd_aux;
if (vstart > end || vstart + sizeof (Elf_(Verdaux)) > end) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop trusts the on-disk vd_next and vd_aux values without ensuring forward progress or record-size bounds. A crafted ELF with a zero/negative vd_next keeps i unchanged or decreasing, so the offset bound can be bypassed or the loop spins, and the READ16/READ32 parsing operates on memory outside the intended Verdef record, producing invalid reads/writes and a crash.

commit_msg:
x86/traps: Fix handling of #DB exceptions in hypervisor context

The WARN_ON() can be triggered by guest activities, and emits a full stack
trace without rate limiting.  Swap it out for a ratelimited printk with just
enough information to work out what is going on.

Not all #DB exceptions are traps, so blindly continuing is not a safe action
to take.  We don't let PV guests select these settings in the real %dr7 to
begin with, but for added safety against unexpected situations, detect the
fault cases and crash in an obvious manner.

This is part of XSA-260 / CVE-2018-8897

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        else', '            /*', '             * We ignore watchpoints when they trigger within Xen. This may', '             * happen when a buffer is passed to us which previously had a', '             * watchpoint set on it. No need to bump EIP; the only faulting', "             * trap is an instruction breakpoint, which can't happen to us.", '             */', '            WARN_ON(!search_exception_table(regs));'], 'added_lines': ['', '        /*', '         * Check for fault conditions.  General Detect, and instruction', '         * breakpoints are faults rather than traps, at which point attempting', '         * to ignore and continue will result in a livelock.', '         */', '        if ( dr6 & DR_GENERAL_DETECT )', '            printk(XENLOG_ERR "Hit General Detect in Xen context\\n");', '            fatal_trap(regs, 0);', '', '        if ( dr6 & (DR_TRAP3 | DR_TRAP2 | DR_TRAP1 | DR_TRAP0) )', '        {', '            unsigned int bp, dr7 = read_debugreg(7) >> DR_CONTROL_SHIFT;', '', '            for ( bp = 0; bp < 4; ++bp )', '            {', '                if ( (dr6 & (1u << bp)) && /* Breakpoint triggered? */', '                     ((dr7 & (3u << (bp * DR_CONTROL_SIZE))) == 0) /* Insn? */ )', '                {', '                    printk(XENLOG_ERR', '                           "Hit instruction breakpoint in Xen context\\n");', '                    fatal_trap(regs, 0);', '                }', '            }', '        }', '', '        /*', '         * Whatever caused this #DB should be a trap.  Note it and continue.', '         * Guests can trigger this in certain corner cases, so ensure the', '         * message is ratelimited.', '         */', '        gprintk(XENLOG_WARNING,', '                "Hit #DB in Xen context: %04x:%p [%ps], stk %04x:%p, dr6 %lx\\n",', '                regs->cs, _p(regs->rip), _p(regs->rip),', '                regs->ss, _p(regs->rsp), dr6);', '']}
description: A statement in the System Programming Guide of the Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual (SDM) was mishandled in the development of some or all operating-system kernels, resulting in unexpected behavior for #DB exceptions that are deferred by MOV SS or POP SS, as demonstrated by (for example) privilege escalation in Windows, macOS, some Xen configurations, or FreeBSD, or a Linux kernel crash. The MOV to SS and POP SS instructions inhibit interrupts (including NMIs), data breakpoints, and single step trap exceptions until the instruction boundary following the next instruction (SDM Vol. 3A; section 6.8.3). (The inhibited data breakpoints are those on memory accessed by the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction itself.) Note that debug exceptions are not inhibited by the interrupt enable (EFLAGS.IF) system flag (SDM Vol. 3A; section 2.3). If the instruction following the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction is an instruction like SYSCALL, SYSENTER, INT 3, etc. that transfers control to the operating system at CPL < 3, the debug exception is delivered after the transfer to CPL < 3 is complete. OS kernels may not expect this order of events and may therefore experience unexpected behavior when it occurs.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function handles a #DB exception in hypervisor context and adds fault detection for General Detect and instruction breakpoints; it contains no concurrent code sequence, shared-resource access, or synchronization window, so CWE-362 is not supported.

commit_msg:
_asn1_extract_der_octet: properly account the bytes read through indefinite encodings

This prevents infinite recursions in the function loop.
Reported by Pascal Cuoq.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t int der_len, unsigned flags)', '\t\t\t\t     der_len, flags);', '\t  len2 = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t int der_len, unsigned flags, int *bytes)', '\t\t\t\t     der_len, flags, &len2);', '', '\t  DECR_LEN(der_len, len2);', '', '  if (bytes)', '    *bytes = counter;']}
description: The _asn1_extract_der_octet function in lib/decoding.c in GNU Libtasn1 before 4.8, when used without the ASN1_DECODE_FLAG_STRICT_DER flag, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite recursion) via a crafted certificate.

code_evidence: The else branch for indefinite-length encodings recursively calls _asn1_extract_der_octet on der + counter + len3, then resets len2 = 0. Because len2 is zeroed, the subsequent counter += len2 + len3 + 1 advances only by len3 + 1, so the bytes consumed inside the recursive call are never accounted for in the parent's counter.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to manage its recursion/iteration resource, allowing unbounded recursion driven by attacker input; this is a resource management error matching CWE-399. It is not a memory-safety bug (e.g., CWE-119), since the flaw is improper accounting of consumed bytes causing infinite recursion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursive call's consumed length is discarded (len2 = 0) instead of being added to the parent's position. Trigger: a crafted certificate using indefinite-length DER octet encodings without strict DER flag. Consequence: the parent loop repeatedly re-processes the same region and recurses indefinitely, exhausting the stack/CPU (denial of service).

commit_msg:
PR25070, SEGV in function _bfd_dwarf2_find_nearest_line

Evil testcase with two debug info sections, with sizes of 2aaaabac4ec1
and ffffd5555453b140 result in a total size of 1.  Reading the first
section of course overflows the buffer and tramples on other memory.

	PR 25070
	* dwarf2.c (_bfd_dwarf2_slurp_debug_info): Catch overflow of
	total_size calculation.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttotal_size += msec->size;'], 'added_lines': ['\t{', '\t  /* Catch PR25070 testcase overflowing size calculation here.  */', '\t  if (total_size + msec->size < total_size', '\t      || total_size + msec->size < msec->size)', '\t    {', '\t      bfd_set_error (bfd_error_no_memory);', '\t      return FALSE;', '\t    }', '\t  total_size += msec->size;', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.32. It is an integer overflow leading to a SEGV in _bfd_dwarf2_find_nearest_line in dwarf2.c, as demonstrated by nm.

code_evidence: The loop accumulates section sizes into total_size with total_size += msec->size, with no overflow check, so total_size can wrap to a small value.
stash->info_ptr_memory is allocated with bfd_malloc(total_size) using the wrapped size, producing a buffer smaller than the actual debug data.
The second loop copies each section into stash->info_ptr_memory + total_size via bfd_simple_get_relocated_section_contents, writing past the undersized allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the size accumulation wraps to a smaller value that is then used as an allocation size, leading to buffer overflow and memory corruption. This is integer overflow driving a size calculation, not merely an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!(bfd_simple_get_relocated_section_contents
(debug_bfd, msec, stash->info_ptr_memory + total_size,
symbols)))
return FALSE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sum of debug-section sizes is computed without an overflow guard, so a crafted file with large section sizes wraps total_size to a tiny value. Trigger: parsing such a file. Consequence: bfd_malloc allocates a small buffer, and the subsequent section copy overflows it, corrupting memory and causing a crash (SEGV).

commit_msg:
ssl sigalg extension: fix NULL pointer dereference

As the variable peer_sigalgslen is not cleared on ssl rehandshake, it's
possible to crash an openssl tls secured server remotely by sending a
manipulated hello message in a rehandshake.

On such a manipulated rehandshake, tls1_set_shared_sigalgs() calls
tls12_shared_sigalgs() with the peer_sigalgslen of the previous
handshake, while the peer_sigalgs has been freed.
As a result tls12_shared_sigalgs() walks over the available
peer_sigalgs and tries to access data of a NULL pointer.

This issue was introduced by c589c34e61 (Add support for the TLS 1.3
signature_algorithms_cert extension, 2018-01-11).

Signed-off-by: Peter Kästle <peter.kaestle@nokia.com>
Signed-off-by: Samuel Sapalski <samuel.sapalski@nokia.com>
CVE-2021-3449

CLA: trivial

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    s->s3->tmp.peer_sigalgslen = 0;']}
description: An OpenSSL TLS server may crash if sent a maliciously crafted renegotiation ClientHello message from a client. If a TLSv1.2 renegotiation ClientHello omits the signature_algorithms extension (where it was present in the initial ClientHello), but includes a signature_algorithms_cert extension then a NULL pointer dereference will result, leading to a crash and a denial of service attack. A server is only vulnerable if it has TLSv1.2 and renegotiation enabled (which is the default configuration). OpenSSL TLS clients are not impacted by this issue. All OpenSSL 1.1.1 versions are affected by this issue. Users of these versions should upgrade to OpenSSL 1.1.1k. OpenSSL 1.0.2 is not impacted by this issue. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1k (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1j).

code_evidence: init_sig_algs frees s->s3->tmp.peer_sigalgs and sets the pointer to NULL, but returns without resetting the associated length field s->s3->tmp.peer_sigalgslen. The freed/NULL pointer and stale length are left in an inconsistent state for the next handshake.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function leaves a NULL pointer paired with a stale nonzero length, and downstream code dereferences that NULL pointer, matching CWE-476. The defect is the inconsistent reset state, not merely an out-of-bounds read, because the pointer itself is NULL.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the peer_sigalgs buffer is freed and NULLed while its length is not cleared, so a later rehandshake retains a nonzero peer_sigalgslen with a NULL peer_sigalgs. Trigger: a TLSv1.2 renegotiation ClientHello that omits signature_algorithms but includes signature_algorithms_cert causes tls12_shared_sigalgs to iterate using the stale length over the NULL pointer, producing a NULL pointer dereference and server crash (DoS).

description: An information leak flaw was found due to uninitialized memory in the Linux kernel's TIPC protocol subsystem, in the way a user sends a TIPC datagram to one or more destinations. This flaw allows a local user to read some kernel memory. This issue is limited to no more than 7 bytes, and the user cannot control what is read. This flaw affects the Linux kernel versions prior to 5.17-rc1.

code_evidence: Local struct tipc_socket_addr skaddr is declared at line 12 without initialization. It is fully assigned only on the TIPC_SOCKET_ADDR path (skaddr = ua->sk, line 58). On the TIPC_SERVICE_ADDR path only skaddr.node is set (line 53) and tipc_nametbl_lookup_anycast fills the remaining fields; skaddr.ref may remain uninitialized before msg_set_destport(hdr, skaddr.ref) at line 67 copies it into the message header, later reaching user space via getname.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function declares a resource (skaddr) and uses it without ensuring initialization on all paths, matching CWE-909 Missing Initialization of Resource. The added memset confirms the missing initialization; the information disclosure is the consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a stack-allocated destination address structure is used without being zero-initialized, so the ref field can carry uninitialized data. Trigger: a user sends a TIPC datagram to a service address; the uninitialized ref is stored into the message header and later copied to user space, leaking kernel stack bytes (CWE-909 leading to infoleak).

commit_msg:
CamelGpgContext: Enclose email addresses in brackets.

The recipient list for encrypting can be specified by either key ID or
email address.  Enclose email addresses in brackets to ensure an exact
match, as per the gpg man page:

HOW TO SPECIFY A USER ID

       ...

       By exact match on an email address.
              This is indicated by enclosing the email address in the
              usual way with left and right angles.

         <heinrichh@uni-duesseldorf.de>

Without the brackets gpg uses a substring match, which risks selecting
the wrong recipient.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tg_ptr_array_add (gpg->recipients, g_strdup (keyid));'], 'added_lines': ['\tgchar *safe_keyid;', '', '\tg_return_if_fail (keyid != NULL);', '', '\t/* If the recipient looks like an email address,', '\t * enclose it in brackets to ensure an exact match. */', "\tif (strchr (keyid, '@') != NULL) {", '\t\tsafe_keyid = g_strdup_printf ("<%s>", keyid);', '\t} else {', '\t\tsafe_keyid = g_strdup (keyid);', '\t}', '', '\tg_ptr_array_add (gpg->recipients, safe_keyid);']}
description: The gpg_ctx_add_recipient function in camel/camel-gpg-context.c in GNOME Evolution 3.8.4 and earlier and Evolution Data Server 3.9.5 and earlier does not properly select the GPG key to use for email encryption, which might cause the email to be encrypted with the wrong key and allow remote attackers to obtain sensitive information.

code_evidence: The function stores the caller-supplied recipient identifier verbatim into gpg->recipients via g_strdup(keyid) and g_ptr_array_add, with no validation of whether the string is a key ID or an email address and no exact-match bracketing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unvalidated recipient string leads to encryption under the wrong key, disclosing message contents to an unauthorized actor, which is the confidentiality exposure described by CWE-200. The defect is the missing exact-match constraint on recipient selection, not memory corruption or injection.

evidence_lines.code:
gpg->recipients = g_ptr_array_new ();
g_ptr_array_add (gpg->recipients, g_strdup (keyid));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: recipient identifiers are passed to gpg unchanged, so an email address is interpreted by gpg as a substring match rather than an exact user-ID match. Trigger: encrypting to an email address that is a substring of another key's user ID. Consequence: gpg may select the wrong recipient key, causing the message to be encrypted to an unintended party and exposing its contents.

commit_msg:
xen: Make coherent PV IOMMU discipline

In order for a PV domain to set up DMA from a passed-through device to
one of its pages, the page must be mapped in the IOMMU.  On the other
hand, before a PV page may be used as a "special" page type (such as a
pagetable or descriptor table), it _must not_ be writable in the IOMMU
(otherwise a malicious guest could DMA arbitrary page tables into the
memory, bypassing Xen's safety checks); and Xen's current rule is to
have such pages not in the IOMMU at all.

At the moment, in order to accomplish this, the code borrows HVM
domain's "physmap" concept: When a page is assigned to a guest,
guess_physmap_add_entry() is called, which for PV guests, will create
a writable IOMMU mapping; and when a page is removed,
guest_physmap_remove_entry() is called, which will remove the mapping.

Additionally, when a page gains the PGT_writable page type, the page
will be added into the IOMMU; and when the page changes away from a
PGT_writable type, the page will be removed from the IOMMU.

Unfortunately, borrowing the "physmap" concept from HVM domains is
problematic.  HVM domains have a lock on their p2m tables, ensuring
synchronization between modifications to the p2m; and all hypercall
parameters must first be translated through the p2m before being used.

Trying to mix this locked-and-gated approach with PV's lock-free
approach leads to several races and inconsistencies:

* A race between a page being assigned and it being put into the
  physmap; for example:
  - P1: call populate_physmap() { A = allocate_domheap_pages() }
  - P2: Guess page A's mfn, and call decrease_reservation(A).  A is owned by the domain,
        and so Xen will clear the PGC_allocated bit and free the page
  - P1: finishes populate_physmap() { guest_physmap_add_entry() }

  Now the domain has a writable IOMMU mapping to a page it no longer owns.

* Pages start out as type PGT_none, but with a writable IOMMU mapping.
  If a guest uses a page as a page table without ever having created a
  writable mapping, the IOMMU mapping will not be removed; the guest
  will have a writable IOMMU mapping to a page it is currently using
  as a page table.

* A newly-allocated page can be DMA'd into with no special actions on
  the part of the guest; However, if a page is promoted to a
  non-writable type, the page must be mapped with a writable type before
  DMA'ing to it again, or the transaction will fail.

To fix this, do away with the "PV physmap" concept entirely, and
replace it with the following IOMMU discipline for PV guests:
 - (type == PGT_writable) <=> in iommu (even if type_count == 0)
 - Upon a final put_page(), check to see if type is PGT_writable; if so,
   iommu_unmap.

In order to achieve that:

- Remove PV IOMMU related code from guest_physmap_*

- Repurpose cleanup_page_cacheattr() into a general
  cleanup_page_mappings() function, which will both fix up Xen
  mappings for pages with special cache attributes, and also check for
  a PGT_writable type and remove pages if appropriate.

- For compatibility with current guests, grab-and-release a
  PGT_writable_page type for PV guests in guest_physmap_add_entry().
  This will cause most "normal" guest pages to start out life with
  PGT_writable_page type (and thus an IOMMU mapping), but no type
  count (so that they can be used as special cases at will).

Also, note that there is one exception to to the "PGT_writable => in
iommu" rule: xenheap pages shared with guests may be given a
PGT_writable type with one type reference.  This reference prevents
the type from changing, which in turn prevents page from gaining an
IOMMU mapping in get_page_type().  It's not clear whether this was
intentional or not, but it's not something to change in a security
update.

This is XSA-288.

Reported-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        return (need_iommu_pt_sync(d) && t == p2m_ram_rw) ?', '            iommu_legacy_map(d, _dfn(mfn_x(mfn)), mfn, page_order,', '                             IOMMUF_readable | IOMMUF_writable) : 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    /* IOMMU for PV guests is handled in get_page_type() and put_page(). */', '    {', '        struct page_info *page = mfn_to_page(mfn);', '', '        /*', "         * Our interface for PV guests wrt IOMMU entries hasn't been very", '         * clear; but historically, pages have started out with IOMMU mappings,', '         * and only lose them when changed to a different page type.', '         *', '         * Retain this property by grabbing a writable type ref and then', '         * dropping it immediately.  The result will be pages that have a', '         * writable type (and an IOMMU entry), but a count of 0 (such that', '         * any guest-requested type changes succeed and remove the IOMMU', '         * entry).', '         */', '        if ( !need_iommu_pt_sync(d) || t != p2m_ram_rw )', '            return 0;', '', '        for ( i = 0; i < (1UL << page_order); ++i, ++page )', '        {', '            if ( get_page_and_type(page, d, PGT_writable_page) )', '                put_page_and_type(page);', '            else', '                return -EINVAL;', '        }', '', '        return 0;', '    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges by leveraging incorrect use of the HVM physmap concept for PV domains.

code_evidence: For non-translated (PV) domains, the function returns after performing iommu_legacy_map without taking p2m_lock(p2m), which is only acquired at line 19 for the translated path.
The PV path bypasses the p2m_lock synchronization that the HVM path relies on, so IOMMU mapping and p2m state updates are not serialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 fits because the lock protecting the p2m/IOMMU resource is not acquired on the PV path, creating unsynchronized shared-state modification. This is distinct from a mere missing bounds check; the core defect is improper locking discipline.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The PV early-return path performs IOMMU mapping without the p2m lock, so a guest can race page assignment against page freeing/type changes; the page may be freed or repurposed while a writable IOMMU mapping remains, allowing DMA to a page no longer owned or now used as a page table.

commit_msg:
Release "3.0.6": Fix crashes in Array for "integer overflow #10"

FossilOrigin-Name: 50642d64b8f0a4e62df68e59fcb2ef0923c3dbec8fc8a15d38b1ddbe655c38d6
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int i = Jsi_ObjGetLength(interp, _this->d.obj);'], 'added_lines': ['    int i = jsi_SizeOfArray(interp, _this->d.obj);']}
description: Integer overflow vulnerability in function Jsi_ObjSetLength in jsish before 3.0.6, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: Line 4 retrieves the array length via Jsi_ObjGetLength into a signed int i without any range validation; line 5 then passes i to Jsi_ValueMakeNumber, propagating the raw length value into a numeric result.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function stores a potentially unbounded length in a fixed-width signed int and uses it without a bounds check, which is exactly the integer-overflow/wraparound pattern in CWE-190. It is not merely a type-confusion or bounds issue, because the defect is the unvalidated narrowing conversion of a length value.

evidence_lines.code:
int i = Jsi_ObjGetLength(interp, _this->d.obj);
Jsi_ValueMakeNumber(interp, ret, i);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the array length is read into a signed int with no overflow check, so a length exceeding INT_MAX is truncated or wrapped to a small/negative value. Trigger: an array whose length is large enough to exceed int range. Supported consequence: the returned size is wrong, corrupting size-dependent logic (the commit replaces this with jsi_SizeOfArray to avoid the overflow).

commit_msg:
fix a bunch of vsprintf -> vsnprintf

closes #1203
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tvsprintf(msg, fmt, vl);'], 'added_lines': ['\tvsnprintf(msg, 1024, fmt, vl);']}
description: GPAC 0.7.1 has a buffer overflow issue in gf_import_message() in media_import.c.

code_evidence: msg is a fixed 1024-byte stack buffer. The only length check is assert(strlen(fmt) < 200), which constrains the format string, not the expanded output. vsprintf then formats fmt with the va_list arguments into msg with no destination size limit, so argument-driven expansion can exceed 1024 bytes and write past msg.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because vsprintf writes formatted data past the end of the intended msg buffer; the missing bound is on the write operation itself. It is an out-of-bounds write rather than merely a format-string issue, since fmt is not attacker-controlled for interpretation but the output size is unchecked.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unbounded vsprintf into a fixed-size stack buffer whose only guard checks the format string length, not the formatted result. Trigger: a caller-supplied format with large or long varargs expands beyond 1024 bytes. Consequence: out-of-bounds stack write, potentially corrupting adjacent memory or enabling code execution/crash.

commit_msg:
mmu_gather: Force tlb-flush VM_PFNMAP vmas

Jann reported a race between munmap() and unmap_mapping_range(), where
unmap_mapping_range() will no-op once unmap_vmas() has unlinked the
VMA; however munmap() will not yet have invalidated the TLBs.

Therefore unmap_mapping_range() will complete while there are still
(stale) TLB entries for the specified range.

Mitigate this by force flushing TLBs for VM_PFNMAP ranges.

Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Acked-by: Will Deacon <will@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\ttlb->vma_pfn  = !!(vma->vm_flags & (VM_PFNMAP|VM_MIXEDMAP));']}
description: An issue was discovered in include/asm-generic/tlb.h in the Linux kernel before 5.19. Because of a race condition (unmap_mapping_range versus munmap), a device driver can free a page while it still has stale TLB entries. This only occurs in situations with VM_PFNMAP VMAs.

code_evidence: The function only records vma_huge and vma_exec flags; it never records whether the VMA is VM_PFNMAP/VM_MIXEDMAP, so later TLB flushing logic cannot distinguish PFNMAP ranges.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a timing window where concurrent unmap paths act on a shared VMA/TLB state without the needed exclusive invalidation, matching CWE-362. It is not merely a missing bounds check; the concurrent interleaving is central.

evidence_lines.code:
tlb->vma_huge = is_vm_hugetlb_page(vma);
tlb->vma_exec = !!(vma->vm_flags & VM_EXEC);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is missing state needed to force TLB invalidation for VM_PFNMAP VMAs. During a race between munmap() and unmap_mapping_range(), unmap_mapping_range() can no-op after the VMA is unlinked while stale TLB entries remain; a driver can then free a page still reachable through those entries.

commit_msg:
avformat/mxfdec: Fix Sign error in mxf_read_primer_pack()

Fixes: 20170829B.mxf

Co-Author: 张洪亮(望初)" <wangchu.zhl@alibaba-inc.com>
Found-by: Xiaohei and Wangchu from Alibaba Security Team
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (item_num > 65536) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (item_num > 65536 || item_num < 0) {']}
description: In the mxf_read_primer_pack function in libavformat/mxfdec.c in FFmpeg 3.3.3 -> 2.4, an integer signedness error might occur when a crafted file, which claims a large "item_num" field such as 0xffffffff, is provided. As a result, the variable "item_num" turns negative, bypassing the check for a large value.

code_evidence: Line 4 reads a 32-bit unsigned value from the file into a signed int item_num, so 0xffffffff becomes -1. Line 10 only rejects values greater than 65536; a negative item_num passes this check and reaches line 18's av_calloc(item_num, item_len) and line 22's avio_read with item_num*item_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an attacker-controlled item_num from file data and fails to validate that it is non-negative before use, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The missing lower-bound constraint is the core validation gap; the consequence arises from using the unvalidated count in allocation and read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The signedness mismatch in the read into item_num, combined with a bound check that only tests the upper limit, lets a crafted primer-pack header with a large unsigned item count become negative and bypass validation. Subsequent allocation and read use the negative count, leading to invalid size computation and unsafe memory handling (e.g., undersized allocation with negative/overflowed product) and potential crash or out-of-bounds access.

commit_msg:
There is a Division by Zero in function OptimizeLayerFrames (#2743)

in file MagickCore/layer.c. cur->ticks_per_seconds can be zero
with a crafted input argument *image. This is similar to
CVE-2019-13454.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        time += curr->delay*1000/curr->ticks_per_second;', '      time += curr->delay*1000/curr->ticks_per_second;'], 'added_lines': ['        time +=(size_t) (curr->delay*1000*', '          PerceptibleReciprocal((double) curr->ticks_per_second));', '      time += (size_t)(curr->delay*1000*', '        PerceptibleReciprocal((double) curr->ticks_per_second));']}
description: ImageMagick 7.0.10-34 allows Division by Zero in OptimizeLayerFrames in MagickCore/layer.c, which may cause a denial of service.

code_evidence: In the DelDispose branch, the loop accumulates frame time as time += curr->delay*1000/curr->ticks_per_second at line 344, and after the loop line 348 again divides by curr->ticks_per_second. Neither line checks that curr->ticks_per_second is nonzero before using it as a divisor; curr is taken from the image list and its ticks_per_second field comes from the crafted input image.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 (Divide By Zero) fits because the function performs division where the divisor, curr->ticks_per_second, can be zero from attacker-controlled input, with no guard. This is a direct divide-by-zero, not a generic input-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the arithmetic divides by curr->ticks_per_second without validating it is nonzero. Trigger: a crafted image whose frame has ticks_per_second == 0 and whose disposal is DelDispose reaches the loop or the post-loop addition. Consequence: integer division by zero causes a crash/denial of service (availability impact).

commit_msg:
It is possible to trigger heap overflows due to an integer overflow
while parsing images.

The integer overflow occurs because the chosen limit 0x10000 for
dimensions is too large for 32 bit systems, because each pixel takes
4 bytes. Properly chosen values allow an overflow which in turn will
lead to less allocated memory than needed for subsequent reads.

See also: https://cgit.freedesktop.org/xorg/lib/libXcursor/commit/?id=4794b5dd34688158fb51a2943032569d3780c4b8
Fixes: https://bugs.freedesktop.org/show_bug.cgi?id=103961

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
[Pekka: add link to the corresponding libXcursor commit]
Signed-off-by: Pekka Paalanen <pekka.paalanen@collabora.co.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (head.width >= 0x10000 || head.height > 0x10000)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (head.width > XCURSOR_IMAGE_MAX_SIZE  ||', '\thead.height > XCURSOR_IMAGE_MAX_SIZE)']}
description: libXcursor before 1.1.15 has various integer overflows that could lead to heap buffer overflows when processing malicious cursors, e.g., with programs like GIMP. It is also possible that an attack vector exists against the related code in cursor/xcursor.c in Wayland through 1.14.0.

code_evidence: Lines 25-26 only reject width >= 0x10000 or height > 0x10000; with 4-byte pixels, a width up to 0xFFFF combined with a height up to 0x10000 passes the check while width*height*4 can exceed 32-bit range.

Line 31 calls XcursorImageCreate with attacker-controlled width/height; line 40 computes n = width*height as an int, and lines 42-44 read that many pixels into the buffer, so a wrapped product under-reads relative to the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is integer overflow in the width*height size calculation driven by insufficient dimension constraints, matching CWE-190. The heap overflow is the downstream consequence; the weakness itself is the unchecked integer arithmetic feeding allocation/read sizing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The dimension sanity check permits values whose pixel-count product overflows 32-bit int arithmetic. A crafted cursor supplies large width/height, the multiplication at line 40 wraps to a small count, and the subsequent read loop consumes fewer pixels than the allocation implied, enabling heap overflow via mismatched size assumptions.

commit_msg:
By validating length fields from server responses, out of boundary
accesses and endless loops can be mitigated.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>

description: Multiple integer overflows in X.org libXi before 1.7.7 allow remote X servers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds memory access or infinite loop) via vectors involving length fields.

code_evidence: At [27-29], the code validates rep.length against (INT_MAX >> 2) and then computes nbytes = (unsigned long) rep.length << 2; the shift is performed after an unsigned cast, so the multiply-by-4 length conversion avoids signed overflow here.

At [43-46], num_valuators is bounded below INT_MAX/(3*sizeof(int)) before val_size = 3*sizeof(int)*num_valuators and the size check sizeof(xDeviceResolutionState)+val_size > nbytes, keeping the arithmetic within range.

The patched bounds checks constrain both the byte-count shift and the num_valuators multiplication so the size computations cannot wrap, preventing the prior out-of-bounds access/infinite loop consequence.

commit_msg:
Check for errors in BN_bn2dec()

If an oversize BIGNUM is presented to BN_bn2dec() it can cause
BN_div_word() to fail and not reduce the value of 't' resulting
in OOB writes to the bn_data buffer and eventually crashing.

Fix by checking return value of BN_div_word() and checking writes
don't overflow buffer.

Thanks to Shi Lei for reporting this bug.

CVE-2016-2182

Reviewed-by: Tim Hudson <tjh@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    bn_data = OPENSSL_malloc((num / BN_DEC_NUM + 1) * sizeof(BN_ULONG));'], 'added_lines': ['    int bn_data_num;', '    bn_data_num = num / BN_DEC_NUM + 1;', '    bn_data = OPENSSL_malloc(bn_data_num * sizeof(BN_ULONG));', '            if (*lp == (BN_ULONG)-1)', '                goto err;', '            if (lp - bn_data >= bn_data_num)', '                goto err;']}
description: The BN_bn2dec function in crypto/bn/bn_print.c in OpenSSL before 1.1.0 does not properly validate division results, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via unknown vectors.

code_evidence: Line 10 allocates bn_data with a size derived from BN_num_bits(a), an upper-bound estimate.
Line 20 sets lp = bn_data, the write cursor into that allocation.

The loop at lines 28-31 writes *lp = BN_div_word(t, BN_DEC_CONV) then increments lp without any bounds check; if BN_div_word fails to reduce t (returning -1), the loop keeps writing past the allocated bn_data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Line 29 writes through lp into the bn_data buffer and line 30 advances the pointer with no capacity limit, so the function writes past the end of the allocated buffer — the defining behavior of CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write). The division failure is the trigger, not the weakness itself; the missing bound on lp is the direct cause.

evidence_lines.code: bn_data = OPENSSL_malloc((num / BN_DEC_NUM + 1) * sizeof(BN_ULONG));
lp = bn_data;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write loop advances lp unconditionally while relying on BN_div_word to shrink t, and the allocation is only an estimate. Trigger: an oversized BIGNUM for which BN_div_word(t, BN_DEC_CONV) fails, so t never reaches zero; lp keeps incrementing beyond bn_data_num entries. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds writes to the bn_data heap buffer, leading to memory corruption and application crash.

commit_msg:
Trying to fix some invalid left shift operations

Fixes issue #16
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn (b[0]<<24) | (b[1]<<16) | (b[2]<<8) | b[3];'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn ((unsigned int)b[0]<<24) | ((unsigned int)b[1]<<16) |', '\t\t((unsigned int)b[2]<<8) | (unsigned int)b[3];']}
description: libimageworsener.a in ImageWorsener before 1.3.1 has "left shift cannot be represented in type int" undefined behavior issues, which might allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted image, related to imagew-bmp.c and imagew-util.c.

code_evidence: Line 3 shifts each signed byte b[0], b[1], b[2] left by 24, 16 and 8 bits without first widening to unsigned int. Because iw_byte is a signed byte, a value with the high bit set (e.g. 0xFF) becomes negative, and shifting it left produces a result that cannot be represented in int, i.e. undefined behavior. The subsequent OR combines these shifts with b[3], so the computed 32-bit value may be incorrect.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-682 fits because the shift expression performs a calculation that can yield an unintended result (and undefined behavior) rather than the intended unsigned big-endian value. This is an incorrect calculation; the missing unsigned cast is the specific defect, not a separate memory-safety weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: signed integer promotion of byte operands before the left shift, with no cast to unsigned. Trigger: a crafted image supplies a byte >= 0x80 in positions b[0]–b[2]. Consequence: undefined behavior and an incorrect decoded 32-bit value, potentially crashing the application or corrupting size/offset values used later.

commit_msg:
Fix jpeg_skip_scanlines() segfault w/merged upsamp

The additional segfault mentioned in #244 was due to the fact that
the merged upsamplers use a different private structure than the
non-merged upsamplers.  jpeg_skip_scanlines() was assuming the latter, so
when merged upsampling was enabled, jpeg_skip_scanlines() clobbered one
of the IDCT method pointers in the merged upsampler's private structure.

For reasons unknown, the test image in #441 did not encounter this
segfault (too small?), but it encountered an issue similar to the one
fixed in 5bc43c7821df982f65aa1c738f67fbf7cba8bd69, whereby it was
necessary to set up a dummy postprocessing function in
read_and_discard_scanlines() when merged upsampling was enabled.
Failing to do so caused either a segfault in merged_2v_upsample() (due
to a NULL pointer being passed to jcopy_sample_rows()) or an error
("Corrupt JPEG data: premature end of data segment"), depending on the
number of scanlines skipped and whether the first scanline skipped was
an odd- or even-numbered row.

Fixes #441
Fixes #244 (for real this time)

description: A crafted input file could cause a null pointer dereference in jcopy_sample_rows() when processed by libjpeg-turbo.

code_evidence: Line 8 casts cinfo->upsample to my_upsample_ptr, but the merged upsampler actually owns a my_merged_upsample_ptr private struct. Lines 15-18 then read Cr_r_tab, Cb_b_tab, Cr_g_tab and Cb_g_tab through the wrong-typed pointer, so these fields are fetched from the wrong offsets in the merged upsampler's private structure rather than its real tables.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the wrong-typed struct pointer causes table pointers to be read from the wrong layout and later dereferenced while NULL/invalid, yielding a crash. A type-confusion label would describe the cause, but the concrete supported weakness here is the NULL pointer dereference the description reports.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a type-confused pointer: the merged-upsample routine interprets cinfo->upsample as the non-merged private struct. Accessing the color-conversion table fields at lines 15-18 then yields invalid or NULL pointers, and the later Crrtab[cr]/Cbgtab[cb] lookups (lines 33-35) dereference them. This produces the NULL-pointer crash in the color path and can clobber adjacent method pointers, matching the reported segfault/null dereference when merged upsampling is enabled.

commit_msg:
kvm:vmx: more complete state update on APICv on/off

The function to update APICv on/off state (in particular, to deactivate
it when enabling Hyper-V SynIC) is incomplete: it doesn't adjust
APICv-related fields among secondary processor-based VM-execution
controls.  As a result, Windows 2012 guests get stuck when SynIC-based
auto-EOI interrupt intersected with e.g. an IPI in the guest.

In addition, the MSR intercept bitmap isn't updated every time "virtualize
x2APIC mode" is toggled.  This path can only be triggered by a malicious
guest, because Windows didn't use x2APIC but rather their own synthetic
APIC access MSRs; however a guest running in a SynIC-enabled VM could
switch to x2APIC and thus obtain direct access to host APIC MSRs
(CVE-2016-4440).

The patch fixes those omissions.

Signed-off-by: Roman Kagan <rkagan@virtuozzo.com>
Reported-by: Steve Rutherford <srutherford@google.com>
Reported-by: Yang Zhang <yang.zhang.wz@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (cpu_has_secondary_exec_ctrls()) {', '\t\tif (kvm_vcpu_apicv_active(vcpu))', '\t\t\tvmcs_set_bits(SECONDARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL,', '\t\t\t\t      SECONDARY_EXEC_APIC_REGISTER_VIRT |', '\t\t\t\t      SECONDARY_EXEC_VIRTUAL_INTR_DELIVERY);', '\t\telse', '\t\t\tvmcs_clear_bits(SECONDARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL,', '\t\t\t\t\tSECONDARY_EXEC_APIC_REGISTER_VIRT |', '\t\t\t\t\tSECONDARY_EXEC_VIRTUAL_INTR_DELIVERY);', '\t}', '', '\tif (cpu_has_vmx_msr_bitmap())', '\t\tvmx_set_msr_bitmap(vcpu);']}
description: arch/x86/kvm/vmx.c in the Linux kernel through 4.6.3 mishandles the APICv on/off state, which allows guest OS users to obtain direct APIC MSR access on the host OS, and consequently cause a denial of service (host OS crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code on the host OS, via x2APIC mode.

code_evidence: The function only rewrites PIN_BASED_VM_EXEC_CONTROL via vmcs_write32; it never updates SECONDARY_VM_EXEC_CONTROL bits (APIC_REGISTER_VIRT, VIRTUAL_INTR_DELIVERY) nor refreshes the MSR intercept bitmap when APICv/x2APIC state toggles.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers improper management of access-control features; here VM-execution controls and MSR intercept permissions are not updated, granting the guest unauthorized access to host APIC MSRs. This is a permission/privilege management failure rather than a memory-safety flaw.

evidence_lines.code: vmcs_write32(PIN_BASED_VM_EXEC_CONTROL, vmx_pin_based_exec_ctrl(vmx));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When APICv is deactivated (e.g., enabling Hyper-V SynIC) or x2APIC is toggled, the secondary execution controls and MSR bitmap remain stale, so a guest retains direct host APIC MSR access. Trigger: guest switches to x2APIC in a SynIC-enabled VM; consequence: host APIC MSR access leading to host crash or possible code execution.

description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An out-of-bounds read was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The out-of-bounds read is triggered when Exiv2 is used to read the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

commit_msg:
smart_pkt: treat empty packet lines as error

The Git protocol does not specify what should happen in the case
of an empty packet line (that is a packet line "0004"). We
currently indicate success, but do not return a packet in the
case where we hit an empty line. The smart protocol was not
prepared to handle such packets in all cases, though, resulting
in a `NULL` pointer dereference.

Fix the issue by returning an error instead. As such kind of
packets is not even specified by upstream, this is the right
thing to do.

commit_msg:
Protect array_list_del_idx against size_t overflow.

If the assignment of stop overflows due to idx and count being
larger than SIZE_T_MAX in sum, out of boundary access could happen.

It takes invalid usage of this function for this to happen, but
I decided to add this check so array_list_del_idx is as safe against
bad usage as the other arraylist functions.

description: json-c through 0.14 has an integer overflow and out-of-bounds write via a large JSON file, as demonstrated by printbuf_memappend.

code_evidence: Line 3 declares size_t stop; line 4 computes stop = idx + count without any pre-check that idx and count cannot wrap. Only afterward, line 5 compares stop > arr->length, but a wrapped stop is small and can pass this bound check, allowing the loop and memmove to operate with a corrupted stop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is an integer addition whose result is used as an index/bound, exactly CWE-190. The missing constraint is that idx <= SIZE_T_MAX - count before summing; adding it in the patch confirms the overflow. This is not merely an off-by-one or bounds-check bug, since the wrap itself defeats the bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unsigned addition idx + count can wrap when the sum exceeds SIZE_T_MAX, so stop becomes a small value. Trigger: caller passes large idx/count; the post-addition check on line 5 no longer reflects the true intended end. Consequence: the memmove and loop use the wrapped stop, permitting out-of-bounds access/write and length corruption instead of rejecting the invalid range.

commit_msg: Fixed Login Exploit
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    uid = sessionMap[sessionId];'], 'added_lines': ['    auto sessionIt = sessionMap.find(sessionId);', '    if(sessionIt != sessionMap.end())', '      uid = sessionIt->second;']}
description: A vulnerability, which was classified as critical, was found in holdennb CollabCal. Affected is the function handleGet of the file calenderServer.cpp. The manipulation leads to improper authentication. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. The patch is identified as b80f6d1893607c99e5113967592417d0fe310ce6. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-217614 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: When a Cookie header is present, the code extracts the substring after '=' and parses it as a session id via stoll at line 9. Line 10 then does uid = sessionMap[sessionId]; operator[] on a std::map default-inserts a zero-initialized entry for any unknown key, so an attacker-supplied, nonexistent session id yields uid = 0 instead of an unauthenticated sentinel. The resulting uid gates later branches (e.g., createGroup/addToGroup/createEvent at lines 51, 66, 86).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to prove the claimed session identity: an unauthenticated caller can present a forged session id and pass the uid != -1 authentication checks, which is improper authentication (CWE-287). It is distinguished from authorization flaws because the defect is in verifying the identity claim itself, not in checking permissions after identity is established.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: session lookup via map operator[] fabricates a valid-looking uid (0) for any unknown/forged session id, and stoll accepts arbitrary numeric cookie values. Trigger: a remote request with a Cookie header whose value is not a real issued session id. Consequence: the request is treated as authenticated as uid 0, enabling actions (group/event creation, edits) without a valid login.

g->nimg++;

commit_msg:
Check for a NULL symbol pointer when reading relocs from a COFF based file.

	PR 22509
	* coffcode.h (coff_slurp_reloc_table): Check for a NULL symbol
	pointer when processing relocs.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if (dst.r_symndx != -1)'], 'added_lines': ['      if (dst.r_symndx != -1 && symbols != NULL)']}
description: The coff_slurp_reloc_table function in coffcode.h in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29.1, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a crafted COFF based file.

code_evidence: coff_slurp_symbol_table is checked but the caller-supplied symbols parameter is never validated; when dst.r_symndx != -1 the code enters the block and computes cache_ptr->sym_ptr_ptr = (symbols + obj_convert(abfd)[dst.r_symndx]) and dereferences it via ptr = *(cache_ptr->sym_ptr_ptr), then passes ptr to CALC_ADDEND. If symbols is NULL, pointer arithmetic and the dereference at line 52 occur on NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (symbols) expected to be valid but NULL, matching CWE-476; the fix adds the missing 'symbols != NULL' guard. This is a NULL dereference, not an out-of-bounds index issue, since the index range is already validated at line 40.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing NULL check on the symbols argument before using it in reloc processing. Trigger: a crafted COFF file with relocations whose r_symndx is valid (not -1) while symbols is NULL. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing application crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
I#226 - CVE-2020-14928: Response Injection via STARTTLS in SMTP and POP3

Closes https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/evolution-data-server/-/issues/226
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* Truncate any left cached input from the insecure part of the session */', '\t\tcamel_stream_buffer_truncate (transport->istream);']}
description: evolution-data-server (eds) through 3.36.3 has a STARTTLS buffering issue that affects SMTP and POP3. When a server sends a "begin TLS" response, eds reads additional data and evaluates it in a TLS context, aka "response injection."

code_evidence: After STARTTLS, the code reads the 220 response via camel_stream_buffer_read_line on the buffered istream (lines 115-116), which may have cached additional bytes from the insecure session. It then obtains base_stream and calls camel_network_service_starttls (lines 117-119), and on success swaps the stream's base stream to tls_stream (lines 121-123) without discarding buffered plaintext data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is that externally-influenced data (server responses) contains special elements that cross the plaintext/TLS trust boundary and alter interpretation by the downstream SMTP logic, matching CWE-74 injection. It is not a mere buffer overflow; the issue is unneutralized injected content evaluated in the wrong security context.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: buffered input read from the insecure pre-TLS stream is retained and later consumed in the TLS context after the base stream is replaced. Trigger: a malicious server sends extra data after the STARTTLS 220 response. Consequence: injected data is evaluated as if it came from the encrypted session, enabling response injection.

commit_msg:
Input: add safety guards to input_set_keycode()

If we happen to have a garbage in input device's keycode table with values
too big we'll end up doing clear_bit() with offset way outside of our
bitmaps, damaging other objects within an input device or even outside of
it. Let's add sanity checks to the returned old keycodes.

Reported-by: syzbot+c769968809f9359b07aa@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Reported-by: syzbot+76f3a30e88d256644c78@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20191207212757.GA245964@dtor-ws
Signed-off-by: Dmitry Torokhov <dmitry.torokhov@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t__clear_bit(*old_keycode, dev->keybit);', '\t__set_bit(ke->keycode, dev->keybit);', '', '\tfor (i = 0; i < dev->keycodemax; i++) {', '\t\tif (input_fetch_keycode(dev, i) == *old_keycode) {', '\t\t\t__set_bit(*old_keycode, dev->keybit);', '\t\t\tbreak; /* Setting the bit twice is useless, so break */'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (*old_keycode <= KEY_MAX) {', '\t\t__clear_bit(*old_keycode, dev->keybit);', '\t\tfor (i = 0; i < dev->keycodemax; i++) {', '\t\t\tif (input_fetch_keycode(dev, i) == *old_keycode) {', '\t\t\t\t__set_bit(*old_keycode, dev->keybit);', '\t\t\t\t/* Setting the bit twice is useless, so break */', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t}', '\t__set_bit(ke->keycode, dev->keybit);']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.4.12, drivers/input/input.c has out-of-bounds writes via a crafted keycode table, as demonstrated by input_set_keycode, aka CID-cb222aed03d7.

code_evidence: The keycode table is read and written at index without any bound check on the stored keycode value: *old_keycode = k[index] then k[index] = ke->keycode; index is bounded by keycodemax, but the keycode value itself is not constrained to KEY_MAX.

The fetched *old_keycode is passed directly to __clear_bit/__set_bit with no upper bound, so a garbage keycode value from the table becomes a bit offset into dev->keybit, which is a fixed-size bitmap.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unbounded keycode value causes a bit-set/clear write beyond the intended dev->keybit buffer. It is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the bitmap is modified.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the old keycode read from the table is used as a bit index in dev->keybit without validating it against KEY_MAX. Trigger: a crafted/garbage keycode table entry whose value exceeds the bitmap size. Consequence: __clear_bit/__set_bit operate at an offset past dev->keybit, causing an out-of-bounds write that corrupts other objects in or around the input device.

commit_msg:
vhost-vsock: detach the virqueue element in case of error

In vhost_vsock_common_send_transport_reset(), if an element popped from
the virtqueue is invalid, we should call virtqueue_detach_element() to
detach it from the virtqueue before freeing its memory.

Fixes: fc0b9b0e1c ("vhost-vsock: add virtio sockets device")
Fixes: CVE-2022-26354
Cc: qemu-stable@nongnu.org
Reported-by: VictorV <vv474172261@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefano Garzarella <sgarzare@redhat.com>
Message-Id: <20220228095058.27899-1-sgarzare@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        goto out;', '        goto out;', 'out:'], 'added_lines': ['        goto err;', '        goto err;', '    g_free(elem);', '    return;', '', 'err:', '    virtqueue_detach_element(vq, elem, 0);']}
description: A flaw was found in the vhost-vsock device of QEMU. In case of error, an invalid element was not detached from the virtqueue before freeing its memory, leading to memory leakage and other unexpected results. Affected QEMU versions <= 6.2.0.

code_evidence: On the invalid-element path (elem->out_num set), the function reports an error and jumps to the out label; no virtqueue_detach_element call occurs.
Similarly, when iov_from_buf fails (element too short), control jumps to out without detaching the element.
The shared out label only calls g_free(elem), releasing the buffer memory while the popped element remains attached to the virtqueue; the success path also frees elem after virtqueue_push.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The element is not released from the virtqueue after its effective lifetime, leaving a stale resource attached; this is a missing release of a resource (CWE-772). It is distinct from plain memory leak (CWE-401) because the buffer is freed but the virtqueue's element reference is not released.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: error paths free the popped VirtQueueElement without detaching it from the virtqueue. Trigger: a malformed event virtqueue element (out buffers present or too short buffer). Consequence: the virtqueue retains a reference to freed memory, causing use-after-free and resource inconsistency (CVE-2022-26354).

description: In ImageMagick 7.x before 7.0.8-42 and 6.x before 6.9.10-42, there is a use after free vulnerability in the UnmapBlob function that allows an attacker to cause a denial of service by sending a crafted file.

Trigger: any path that detaches a mapped blob and subsequently reads or dereferences blob_info->data. Supported consequence: use-after-free, enabling memory corruption or a crash/denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix off-by-one bounds check on CHM PMGI/PMGL chunk numbers and
reject empty filenames. Thanks to Hanno Böck for reporting
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (chm->index_root != 0xFFFFFFFF && chm->index_root > chm->num_chunks) {'], 'added_lines': ['  if (chm->index_root != 0xFFFFFFFF && chm->index_root >= chm->num_chunks) {', '      /* consider blank filenames to be an error */', '      if (name_len == 0) goto chunk_end;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in mspack/chmd.c in libmspack before 0.7alpha. There is an off-by-one error in the CHM PMGI/PMGL chunk number validity checks, which could lead to denial of service (uninitialized data dereference and application crash).

code_evidence: The index_root validity check uses a strict greater-than comparison against num_chunks: index_root > num_chunks is rejected, but index_root == num_chunks is accepted even though valid chunk indices run 0..num_chunks-1. The fix changes this to >=.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-193 fits because the maximum permitted chunk index is calculated one too high (index_root == num_chunks accepted rather than rejected), the classic off-by-one bounds error. It is a boundary-value mistake, not a missing length check or an integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the upper bound for index_root is off by one, allowing an index equal to num_chunks to pass validation. Trigger: a crafted CHM header sets index_root to num_chunks. The accepted out-of-range chunk number can then be used to locate a PMGI chunk, leading to an invalid/uninitialized data dereference and application crash (DoS).

commit_msg: Check types to avoid invalid reads/writes.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tassert(a->type == szMAPI_STRING);', '\t\tassert((a->type == szMAPI_BINARY) || (a->type == szMAPI_OBJECT));', '\t\tassert(a->type == szMAPI_STRING);', '                    assert(a->type == szMAPI_STRING);']}
description: An issue was discovered in tnef before 1.4.13. Two type confusions have been identified in the parse_file() function. These might lead to invalid read and write operations, controlled by an attacker.

code_evidence: Copies a->values[0].data.buf into file->data using file->len taken from a->values[0].len without validating that the buffer actually holds len bytes or matches the expected binary/object type.
Allocates file->mime_type with a->values[0].len then memmove copies that same len from a->values[0].data.buf, trusting the attribute's declared length and buffer type.
Allocates file->content_id with a->values[0].len and memmoves a->values[0].len bytes from a->values[0].data.buf, again relying on attacker-influenced length/type.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length/type on attacker-controlled attribute data drives memory copy operations, allowing reads/writes outside intended buffers, which matches CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. The strdup path is more a read/type-confusion issue, but the memmove paths write len bytes into fixed allocations, directly supporting out-of-bounds write.

evidence_lines.code:
file->mime_type = CHECKED_XMALLOC (char, a->values[0].len);
memmove (file->mime_type, a->values[0].data.buf, a->values[0].len);

file->content_id = CHECKED_XMALLOC (char, a->values[0].len);
memmove (file->content_id, a->values[0].data.buf, a->values[0].len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function trusts the MAPI attribute's declared type and value length. When an attacker supplies a mismatched type or a length larger than the actual data buffer, the memmove/strdup operations read beyond the source buffer and write len bytes into a destination sized by that same len, producing out-of-bounds memory access.

parsettf.c: Fix buffer overrun condition

Closes #3090
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tfor ( j=0; j<cnt; ++j )'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tfor ( j=0; j<cnt && i<len; ++j )']}
description: FontForge 20161012 is vulnerable to a heap-based buffer overflow in readcffset (parsettf.c) resulting in DoS or code execution via a crafted otf file.

code_evidence: The format==1 loop at [85,86,87,88,89,90] reads a glyph index via getushort into charset[i++] and a run count cnt via getc(ttf). The inner loop [88,89] then writes cnt entries into dict->charset[i++], but the loop condition only checks j<cnt; it never checks i<len. Since cnt comes from the crafted font file and charset was allocated with len*sizeof(uint16) at line 77, i can exceed len and the write at charset[i++] runs past the heap buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to dict->charset outside the allocated buffer's intended boundary, directly matching CWE-119. The missing i<len constraint (the patched condition) is the specific bounds-check failure; this is not merely a read overrun but an out-of-bounds write, so the general buffer-bounds class applies.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the format==1 range-expansion loop lacks a bound on the destination index i, so the attacker-controlled run count cnt drives writes past the len-element heap allocation. Trigger: a crafted OTF whose CFF charset uses format 1 with a run count exceeding the remaining glyph slots. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, giving memory corruption and possible DoS or code execution.

commit_msg:
cmd/snap-confine: chown private /tmp parent to root.root

When snap-confine creates a private /tmp directory for a given snap it
first creates a temporary directory in /tmp/ named after the snap, along
with a random name. Inside that directory it creates a /tmp directory
with permissions appropriate for a future /tmp, namely 1777.

Up until recently the that directory was owned by the user who first
invoked snap-confine. Since the directory is reused by all the users on
the system this logic makes no sense.

This patch changes the related logic so that the private /tmp directory
is owned by root, just like the real one.

Signed-off-by: Zygmunt Krynicki <zygmunt.krynicki@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tuid_t uid = getuid();', '\tgid_t gid = getgid();', '\tif (chown("/tmp/", uid, gid) < 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (chown("/tmp/", 0, 0) < 0) {']}
description: snap-confine in snapd before 2.38 incorrectly set the ownership of a snap application to the uid and gid of the first calling user. Consequently, that user had unintended access to a private /tmp directory.

code_evidence: The function captures the caller's uid/gid via getuid()/getgid() and then, after bind-mounting the private tmpdir onto /tmp, calls chown("/tmp/", uid, gid) to give ownership of the mounted /tmp to the first invoking user.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 applies to link/path resolution issues; here the path /tmp/ is operated on after a bind mount, and the chown targets the resolved mount point rather than a controlled target, but the core defect is ownership assignment, not link following. The evidence supports an ownership/permissions weakness rather than improper link resolution, so CWE-59 is not directly supported.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ownership of the shared private /tmp is set to the first caller's uid/gid rather than root. Trigger: a user invokes snap-confine first, ownering the private /tmp; subsequent users share that directory. Consequence: the first user retains unintended access to the private /tmp used by other users' snap applications, enabling cross-user file access/modification.

description: Zydis is an x86/x86-64 disassembler library. Users of Zydis versions v3.2.0 and older that use the string functions provided in `zycore` in order to append untrusted user data to the formatter buffer within their custom formatter hooks can run into heap buffer overflows. Older versions of Zydis failed to properly initialize the string object within the formatter buffer, forgetting to initialize a few fields, leaving their value to chance. This could then in turn cause zycore functions like `ZyanStringAppend` to make incorrect calculations for the new target size, resulting in heap memory corruption. This does not affect the regular uncustomized Zydis formatter, because Zydis internally doesn't use the string functions in zycore that act upon these fields. However, because the zycore string functions are the intended way to work with the formatter buffer for users of the library that wish to extend the formatter, we still consider this to be a vulnerability in Zydis. This bug is patched starting in version 3.2.1. As a workaround, users may refrain from using zycore string functions in their formatter hooks until updating to a patched version.

code_evidence: This initializer sets buffer fields and the embedded string vector's allocator, element_size, size, capacity and data, then writes the NUL terminator, but it leaves other vector fields (growth_factor, shrink_threshold, destructor) and buffer->capacity unset, so they retain indeterminate values. The buffer is handed to callers/custom formatter hooks that may pass it to zycore string functions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses/accesses a resource (the formatter buffer and its string vector) whose members are not fully initialized before being exposed, matching CWE-908. The heap overflow is a downstream consequence of reading the uninitialized fields, not the root weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the formatter buffer's string vector and capacity are only partially initialized, leaving fields whose values are indeterminate. Trigger: a custom formatter hook uses zycore string functions such as ZyanStringAppend on this buffer, which reads the uninitialized fields to compute the new target size. Supported consequence: incorrect size calculations leading to heap buffer overflow/memory corruption.

description: mediaserver in Android 6.x before 2016-03-01 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, related to decoder/ih264d_parse_islice.c and decoder/ih264d_parse_pslice.c, aka internal bug 25928803.

code_evidence: The macroblock index u1_num_mbs is used to index ps_nmb_info, ps_deblk_mbn and ps_mv_cur before the per-MB increment; u1_num_mbs is reset to 0 only when u1_tfr_n_mb is set, so the index is the transfer-group offset.
Incrementing u1_num_mbs per MB without advancing u2_total_mbs_coded here means the total-coded counter falls behind the actual number of parsed macroblocks within a group.

The transfer path uses u1_num_mbs (and u1_end_of_row / u1_tfr_n_mb) to advance ps_nmb_info and decode groups; the total-coded count is the value used to bound the remaining macroblock processing of the picture.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The counter mis-tracking causes indexed access into macroblock/deblock/motion buffers (ps_nmb_info, ps_deblk_mbn, ps_mv_cur) beyond intended bounds, matching CWE-119. This is a buffer-boundary violation rather than a pure integer overflow, though the stale count drives the out-of-bounds access.

evidence_lines.code:
u1_num_mbs++;
ps_dec->u2_total_mbs_coded++;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the total-macroblocks-coded counter is incremented once per MB while the group index u1_num_mbs grows, and the counter is only corrected at transfer points. Trigger: a crafted slice whose macroblock group transfer boundary or end-of-row condition leaves the counter inconsistent with the number of parsed MBs. Consequence: subsequent parsing/reconstruction indexes picture buffers using a stale count, producing out-of-bounds reads/writes and memory corruption.
