commit_msg:
evtchn: avoid NULL derefs

Commit fbbd5009e6 ("evtchn: refactor low-level event channel port ops")
added a de-reference of the struct evtchn pointer for a port without
first making sure the bucket pointer is non-NULL. This de-reference is
actually entirely unnecessary, as all relevant callers (beyond the
problematic do_poll()) already hold the port number in their hands, and
the actual leaf functions need nothing else.

For FIFO event channels there's a second problem in that the ordering
of reads and updates to ->num_evtchns and ->event_array[] was so far
undefined (the read side isn't always holding the domain's event lock).
Add respective barriers.

This is XSA-221.

Reported-by: Ankur Arora <ankur.a.arora@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['               !!evtchn_port_is_pending(d, chn),', '               !!evtchn_port_is_masked(d, chn));'], 'added_lines': ['               evtchn_port_is_pending(d, port),', '               evtchn_port_is_masked(d, port));']}
description: Xen through 4.8.x does not validate the port numbers of polled event channel ports, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and host OS crash) or possibly obtain sensitive information, aka XSA-221.

code_evidence: The loop skips ports failing port_is_valid but then obtains chn = evtchn_from_port(d, port); the validity check does not guarantee chn is non-NULL for FIFO channels.
The dump then passes chn to evtchn_port_is_pending and evtchn_port_is_masked, which dereference the struct evtchn pointer without a NULL check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (chn) that may be NULL, matching CWE-476. This is not merely an invalid port number issue; the direct cause is unchecked NULL dereference.

evidence_lines.code:
printk("    %4u [%d/%d/",
port,
!!evtchn_port_is_pending(d, chn),
!!evtchn_port_is_masked(d, chn));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: evtchn_from_port(d, port) can return a NULL bucket pointer for a port, and the code dereferences it through evtchn_port_is_pending/is_masked. Trigger: dumping event-channel info for a domain with such a port. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a host crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
As reported by Jann, ihold() does not in fact guarantee inode
persistence. And instead of making it so, replace the usage of inode
pointers with a per boot, machine wide, unique inode identifier.

This sequence number is global, but shared (file backed) futexes are
rare enough that this should not become a performance issue.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tget_futex_key_refs(key); /* implies smp_mb(); (B) */', '', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * Take a reference unless it is about to be freed. Previously', '\t\t * this reference was taken by ihold under the page lock', '\t\t * pinning the inode in place so i_lock was unnecessary. The', '\t\t * only way for this check to fail is if the inode was', '\t\t * truncated in parallel which is almost certainly an', '\t\t * application bug. In such a case, just retry.', '\t\t *', '\t\t * We are not calling into get_futex_key_refs() in file-backed', '\t\t * cases, therefore a successful atomic_inc return below will', '\t\t * guarantee that get_futex_key() will still imply smp_mb(); (B).', '\t\t */', '\t\tif (!atomic_inc_not_zero(&inode->i_count)) {', '\t\t\trcu_read_unlock();', '\t\t\tput_page(page);', '', '\t\t\tgoto again;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\t/* Should be impossible but lets be paranoid for now */', '\t\tif (WARN_ON_ONCE(inode->i_mapping != mapping)) {', '\t\t\terr = -EFAULT;', '\t\t\trcu_read_unlock();', '\t\t\tiput(inode);', '', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\tkey->shared.inode = inode;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tkey->shared.i_seq = get_inode_sequence_number(inode);', '', '\tget_futex_key_refs(key); /* implies smp_mb(); (B) */']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s futex implementation. This flaw allows a local attacker to corrupt system memory or escalate their privileges when creating a futex on a filesystem that is about to be unmounted. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to confidentiality, integrity, as well as system availability.

code_evidence: The function holds an inode reference only via atomic_inc_not_zero on inode->i_count while under rcu_read_lock, then stores the raw inode pointer in key->shared.inode after releasing the reference via rcu_read_unlock.

The stored inode pointer is used later as the futex key identity, but ihold/atomic_inc_not_zero does not guarantee the inode remains valid once the page lock and RCU section end, so the inode can be freed while key->shared.inode still references it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function stores and later uses an inode pointer after its backing object can be freed; the patch replaces it with a sequence number, confirming use-after-free as the addressed weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the futex key retains a raw struct inode pointer whose lifetime is only weakly pinned by an i_count increment that does not prevent the inode from being freed (e.g., during unmount). Trigger: a file-backed futex is created on a filesystem being unmounted, freeing the inode. Consequence: later key comparisons/use dereference freed inode memory, enabling memory corruption, privilege escalation, or crash.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.4+
Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (key_is_instantiated(key))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (key_is_positive(key))']}

description: binutils version 2.32 and earlier contains a Integer Overflow vulnerability in objdump, bfd_get_dynamic_reloc_upper_bound,bfd_canonicalize_dynamic_reloc that can result in Integer overflow trigger heap overflow. Successful exploitation allows execution of arbitrary code.. This attack appear to be exploitable via Local. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in after commit 3a551c7a1b80fca579461774860574eabfd7f18f.

code_evidence: ret is a signed long initialized to sizeof(arelent*) at line 11. The loop at lines 12-17 accumulates into ret: for each section with matching sh_link and type SHT_REL/SHT_RELA, it adds (s->size / sh_entsize) * sizeof(arelent*). The section size and entry count come from the parsed ELF file, so an attacker-controlled input with many large reloc sections can drive ret past LONG_MAX; no overflow check exists before return at line 18.

This is a classic integer overflow used as an allocation size, not merely an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unchecked signed accumulation of per-section relocation counts times pointer size into a long. Trigger: a crafted ELF with many or large SHT_REL/SHT_RELA sections linked to the dynamic symtab makes s->size/sh_entsize large, so the addition overflows to a small or negative value. Consequence: the returned upper bound is wrong, so later allocation/canonicalization uses an undersized buffer, enabling heap overflow and possible code execution.

commit_msg:
netlink: limit recursion depth in policy validation

Now that we have nested policies, we can theoretically
recurse forever parsing attributes if a (sub-)policy
refers back to a higher level one. This is a situation
that has happened in nl80211, and we've avoided it there
by not linking it.

Add some code to netlink parsing to limit recursion depth.

Signed-off-by: Johannes Berg <johannes.berg@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tstruct nlattr **tb)', '\t\t\t\t\t       validate, extack);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tstruct nlattr **tb, unsigned int depth)', '', '\tif (depth >= MAX_POLICY_RECURSION_DEPTH) {', '\t\tNL_SET_ERR_MSG(extack,', '\t\t\t       "allowed policy recursion depth exceeded");', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '\t\t\t\t\t       validate, extack, depth);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.8. lib/nlattr.c allows attackers to cause a denial of service (unbounded recursion) via a nested Netlink policy with a back reference.

code_evidence: The function signature at line 5 accepts only policy, validate, extack and tb; it carries no recursion-depth parameter or counter, so nested policy validation cannot be bounded.

Lines 21-26 call validate_nla for each attribute passing policy, validate and extack. Because no depth value is propagated, a nested policy that references back to a higher-level policy can re-enter validation indefinitely.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allows recursive policy validation with no depth cap, matching CWE-674 (uncontrolled recursion) whose impact is resource-consumption DoS. It is not merely unbounded iteration; the recursion arises from re-validating nested policies along the call chain.

evidence_lines.code: struct nlattr **tb)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: __nla_validate_parse performs attribute validation through validate_nla without tracking or limiting nesting depth. A crafted nested Netlink policy containing a back reference triggers repeated re-entry into validation, exhausting the stack and causing a denial of service.

commit_msg:
Add support for different number of page table levels dependent
on the highest address used for a process. This will cause a 31 bit
process to use a two level page table instead of the four level page
table that is the default after the pud has been introduced. Likewise
a normal 64 bit process will use three levels instead of four. Only
if a process runs out of the 4 tera bytes which can be addressed with
a three level page table the fourth level is dynamically added. Then
the process can use up to 8 peta byte.

Signed-off-by: Martin Schwidefsky <schwidefsky@de.ibm.com>

commit_msg:
Fix a check fail

PiperOrigin-RevId: 372011072
Change-Id: I1062cfaed0aa16884e9a16312483794d188db76f
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(', '        context, ckpt_path_t->NumElements() == 1,', '        errors::InvalidArgument("The `ckpt_path` tensor must have exactly one "', '                                "element, got tensor of shape ",', '                                ckpt_path_t->shape().DebugString()));']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can cause a denial of service by exploiting a `CHECK`-failure coming from `tf.raw_ops.LoadAndRemapMatrix`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/d94227d43aa125ad8b54115c03cece54f6a1977b/tensorflow/core/kernels/ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op.cc#L219-L222) assumes that the `ckpt_path` is always a valid scalar. However, an attacker can send any other tensor as the first argument of `LoadAndRemapMatrix`. This would cause the rank `CHECK` in `scalar<T>()()` to trigger and terminate the process. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 44 retrieves the attacker-supplied `ckpt_path` input tensor without validating its rank or element count. Line 45 immediately calls `ckpt_path_t->scalar<tstring>()()`, which assumes the tensor is a scalar; `scalar<T>()` performs a rank CHECK and terminates the process if the tensor has any other rank.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reaches a CHECK assertion (TensorFlow's equivalent of assert) that is controlled by untrusted input, and the failure terminates the whole process rather than returning an error. This is a reachable assertion leading to DoS, matching CWE-617. It is not merely missing input validation (CWE-20) because the supported impact is the assertion-triggered abort itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: absence of a rank/element-count check on the `ckpt_path` input before dereferencing it as a scalar. Trigger: an attacker passes a non-scalar tensor (e.g., a vector or matrix) as `ckpt_path` to `LoadAndRemapMatrix`. Consequence: the internal CHECK in `scalar<T>()` fails and aborts the process, causing a denial of service. The patch adds an `OP_REQUIRES` element-count check to reject such inputs gracefully instead of aborting.

commit_msg:
[CSP] Don't check the path component of the URL when the response was fetched via ServiceWorker.

In ResourceFetcher::didReceiveResponse() we check the response URL when the response is fetched via ServiceWorker.
But the match algorithm should ignore the path component of the URL.

BUG=542060

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1454003003

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#360733}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ResourceRequestBlockedReason reason = canRequestInternal(type, resourceRequest, url, options, forPreload, originRestriction);'], 'added_lines': ['    // As of CSP2, for requests that are the results of redirects, the match', '    // algorithm should ignore the path component of the URL.', '    ContentSecurityPolicy::RedirectStatus redirectStatus = resourceRequest.followedRedirect() ? ContentSecurityPolicy::DidRedirect : ContentSecurityPolicy::DidNotRedirect;', '', '    ResourceRequestBlockedReason reason = canRequestInternal(type, resourceRequest, url, options, forPreload, originRestriction, redirectStatus);']}
description: The Content Security Policy (CSP) implementation in Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 49.0.2623.75, does not ignore a URL's path component in the case of a ServiceWorker fetch, which allows remote attackers to obtain sensitive information about visited web pages by reading CSP violation reports, related to FrameFetchContext.cpp and ResourceFetcher.cpp.

code_evidence: canRequest calls canRequestInternal with the request URL, options and origin restriction but provides no RedirectStatus derived from resourceRequest.followedRedirect().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's failure to pass redirect status causes CSP matching to over-match on URL paths, leaking visited-page path information through CSP violation reports to an unauthorized actor, which fits CWE-200's exposure of sensitive information. A path-handling or redirect weakness is the underlying error, but the supported consequence here is confidentiality exposure.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The CSP check has no way to know whether the request followed a redirect, so the CSP2 match algorithm cannot ignore the URL path for ServiceWorker-fetched responses. A remote attacker can trigger a ServiceWorker fetch and read CSP violation reports that reveal path components of visited page URLs, exposing sensitive browsing information. The missing redirect constraint is the cause; the information leak is the consequence.

commit_msg:
The bounds checking in avc_ca_pmt() is not strict enough.  It should
be checking "read_pos + 4" because it's reading 5 bytes.  If the
"es_info_length" is non-zero then it reads a 6th byte so there needs to
be an additional check for that.

I also added checks for the "write_pos".  I don't think these are
required because "read_pos" and "write_pos" are tied together so
checking one ought to be enough.  But they make the code easier to
understand for me.  The check on write_pos is:

	if (write_pos + 4 >= sizeof(c->operand) - 4) {

The first "+ 4" is because we're writing 5 bytes and the last " - 4"
is to leave space for the CRC.

The other problem is that "length" can be invalid.  It comes from
"data_length" in fdtv_ca_pmt().

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Luo Likang <luolikang@nsfocus.com>
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab+huawei@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\twhile (read_pos < length) {', '\t\t\tif (es_info_length > sizeof(c->operand) - 4 -', '\t\t\t\t\t     write_pos) {'], 'added_lines': ['\twhile (read_pos + 4 < length) {', '\t\tif (write_pos + 4 >= sizeof(c->operand) - 4) {', '\t\t\tret = -EINVAL;', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t\t}', '\t\t\tif (read_pos >= length) {', '\t\t\t\tret = -EINVAL;', '\t\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tif (es_info_length > sizeof(c->operand) - 4 - write_pos ||', '\t\t\t    es_info_length > length - read_pos) {']}
description: The firewire subsystem in the Linux kernel through 5.14.13 has a buffer overflow related to drivers/media/firewire/firedtv-avc.c and drivers/media/firewire/firedtv-ci.c, because avc_ca_pmt mishandles bounds checking.

code_evidence: The while loop condition [64] only requires read_pos < length, yet the body unconditionally reads five bytes (three via [65,66,67] and two more via [68,69]) and, when es_info_length is non-zero, a sixth at [76]. With length at or near the buffer end, msg[read_pos] and msg[read_pos + 1] read past msg.

The loop also appends to c->operand via write_pos++ at [65,66,67,73,74] without verifying write_pos stays within sizeof(c->operand); the only guard [80,81] covers the es_info_length memcpy [85,86], not the per-iteration operand writes.
After the loop, write_pos += 4 [91] and the CRC writes at [97,98,99,100] index c->operand[write_pos - 4..1] based on the unchecked write_pos, allowing a write past the operand buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes attacker-influenced data past the end of the intended c->operand buffer through unchecked write_pos increments and CRC indexing, a direct out-of-bounds write rather than a mere read overrun.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: loop and write bounds checks are too weak (read_pos < length instead of read_pos + 4 < length, and no write_pos guard before operand appends). Trigger: a crafted CA PMT message with a length/es_info_length that leaves fewer than 5-6 bytes in msg or drives write_pos near the operand size. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads of msg and out-of-bounds writes into c->operand, corrupting adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
passthrough: quarantine PCI devices

When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for
that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The
IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that
the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However,
when the guest domain is torn down the device is assigned back to dom0,
thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data.

This patch introduces a 'quarantine' for PCI devices using dom_io. When
the toolstack makes a device assignable (by binding it to pciback), it
will now also assign it to DOMID_IO and the device will only be assigned
back to dom0 when the device is made unassignable again. Whilst device is
assignable it will only ever transfer between dom_io and guest domains.
dom_io is actually only used as a sentinel domain for quarantining purposes;
it is not configured with any IOMMU mappings. Assignment to dom_io simply
means that the device's initiator (requestor) identifier is not present in
the IOMMU's device table and thus any DMA transactions issued will be
terminated with a fault condition.

In addition, a fix to assignment handling is made for VT-d.  Failure
during the assignment step should not lead to a device still being
associated with its prior owner. Hand the device to DomIO temporarily,
until the assignment step has completed successfully.  Remove the PI
hooks from the source domain then earlier as well.

Failure of the recovery reassign_device_ownership() may not go silent:
There e.g. may still be left over RMRR mappings in the domain assignment
to which has failed, and hence we can't allow that domain to continue
executing.

NOTE: This patch also includes one printk() cleanup; the
      "XEN_DOMCTL_assign_device: " tag is dropped in iommu_do_pci_domctl(),
      since similar printk()-s elsewhere also don't log such a tag.

This is XSA-302.

Signed-off-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if ( d == dom_io )', '            return -EINVAL;', '', '        if ( d == dom_io )', '            return -EINVAL;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing attackers to gain host OS privileges via DMA in a situation where an untrusted domain has access to a physical device. This occurs because passed through PCI devices may corrupt host memory after deassignment. When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However, when the guest domain is torn down, or the device is deassigned, the device is assigned back to dom0, thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data. An untrusted domain with access to a physical device can DMA into host memory, leading to privilege escalation. Only systems where guests are given direct access to physical devices capable of DMA (PCI pass-through) are vulnerable. Systems which do not use PCI pass-through are not vulnerable.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs Xen device-assignment IOMMU operations and contains no OS command construction or execution, so it cannot support CWE-78.

commit_msg:
babeld: fix #10487 by adding a check on packet length

The body length of a packet should satisfy the condition:
packetlen >= bodylen + 4. Otherwise, heap overflows may happen.

Signed-off-by: whichbug <whichbug@github.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    unsigned i = 0, bodylen;'], 'added_lines': ['    int i = 0, bodylen;', '    if(bodylen + 4 > packetlen) {', '        debugf(BABEL_DEBUG_COMMON, "Received truncated packet (%d + 4 > %d).",', '                 bodylen, packetlen);', '        return 1;', '    }']}
description: A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in FRRouting through 8.1.0 due to missing a check on the input packet length in the babel_packet_examin function in babeld/message.c.

code_evidence: Lines 7-9 only reject packets shorter than the 4-byte header and then parse bodylen from packet bytes 2-3 without comparing bodylen against packetlen.
Line 10 loops while i < bodylen and line 11 computes message = packet + 4 + i, so bodylen controls both iteration and pointer offsets beyond the validated header.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an input-specified quantity (bodylen) and fails to validate that it is consistent with the actual packet size before using it to control iteration and buffer offsets, matching CWE-1284. This is the missing length-consistency constraint, distinct from the downstream memory-safety consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The 16-bit body length read from the packet is trusted without checking that bodylen + 4 fits within packetlen; a crafted packet declaring a large bodylen drives the loop and message pointer past the received buffer, causing out-of-bounds heap reads (and potential overflow consequences) instead of being rejected as truncated.

commit_msg:
Fix bug #72860: wddx_deserialize use-after-free

(cherry picked from commit ee552853ff4d72f626102025133e2cd1575043ee)

Conflicts:
	ext/wddx/wddx.c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tzval_ptr_dtor(&((st_entry *)stack->elements[i])->data);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (Z_TYPE(((st_entry *)stack->elements[i])->data) != IS_UNDEF', '\t\t\t\t\t&& ((st_entry *)stack->elements[i])->type != ST_FIELD)\t{', '\t\t\t\tzval_ptr_dtor(&((st_entry *)stack->elements[i])->data);', '\t\t\t}']}
description: Use-after-free vulnerability in the wddx_stack_destroy function in ext/wddx/wddx.c in PHP before 5.6.26 and 7.x before 7.0.11 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via a wddxPacket XML document that lacks an end-tag for a recordset field element, leading to mishandling in a wddx_deserialize call.

Because the destructor runs without checking whether the entry's zval is still defined or is a field entry, an entry whose data was already destroyed (or never initialized) is destroyed again, and the entry memory is then freed while the stack still references it for later cleanup.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the destructor reuses a zval that may already have been freed, then operates on the freed memory. The patch confirms this by guarding zval_ptr_dtor with an IS_UNDEF and ST_FIELD check, preventing the invalid reuse.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: wddx_stack_destroy frees each element's data via zval_ptr_dtor without verifying the zval is still defined or excluding ST_FIELD entries, so a partially parsed packet (missing recordset end-tag) leaves stack entries whose data has already been freed. Trigger: wddx_deserialize on a crafted wddxPacket lacking a recordset field end-tag. Consequence: double free/dangling pointer dereference during stack teardown, causing DoS or potential memory corruption.

[core] Fixed sender list to reallocate on insert
if required

description: Secure Reliable Transport (SRT) through 1.3.4 has a CSndUList array overflow if there are many SRT connections.

commit_msg:
Fix invalid memory write on lua stack overflow {CVE-2021-32626}

When LUA call our C code, by default, the LUA stack has room for 20
elements. In most cases, this is more than enough but sometimes it's not
and the caller must verify the LUA stack size before he pushes elements.

On 3 places in the code, there was no verification of the LUA stack size.
On specific inputs this missing verification could have lead to invalid
memory write:
1. On 'luaReplyToRedisReply', one might return a nested reply that will
   explode the LUA stack.
2. On 'redisProtocolToLuaType', the Redis reply might be deep enough
   to explode the LUA stack (notice that currently there is no such
   command in Redis that returns such a nested reply, but modules might
   do it)
3. On 'ldbRedis', one might give a command with enough arguments to
   explode the LUA stack (all the arguments will be pushed to the LUA
   stack)

This commit is solving all those 3 issues by calling 'lua_checkstack' and
verify that there is enough room in the LUA stack to push elements. In
case 'lua_checkstack' returns an error (there is not enough room in the
LUA stack and it's not possible to increase the stack), we will do the
following:
1. On 'luaReplyToRedisReply', we will return an error to the user.
2. On 'redisProtocolToLuaType' we will exit with panic (we assume this
   scenario is rare because it can only happen with a module).
3. On 'ldbRedis', we return an error.

description: Redis is an open source, in-memory database that persists on disk. In affected versions specially crafted Lua scripts executing in Redis can cause the heap-based Lua stack to be overflowed, due to incomplete checks for this condition. This can result with heap corruption and potentially remote code execution. This problem exists in all versions of Redis with Lua scripting support, starting from 2.6. The problem is fixed in versions 6.2.6, 6.0.16 and 5.0.14. For users unable to update an additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent users from executing Lua scripts. This can be done using ACL to restrict EVAL and EVALSHA commands.

code_evidence: luaReplyToRedisReply recurses into nested tables: lines 18-19 push and fetch the 'map' key, then line 58 iterates with lua_next while lines 59-61 push values and recursively call luaReplyToRedisReply. Each recursion pushes elements onto the Lua stack without any lua_checkstack guard, so a deeply nested reply exhausts the fixed stack.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked stack pushes cause writes beyond the intended Lua stack buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds Write). A stack-exhaustion CWE would describe resource depletion, but here the demonstrated effect is an out-of-bounds memory write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursive conversion of nested Lua tables pushes onto the Lua stack without verifying available capacity. Trigger: a crafted nested table reply drives recursion deep enough that lua_pushvalue/lua_pushstring/lua_pushnil write past the allocated stack. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, memory corruption and possible code execution.

description: Cherokee 0.4.27 to 1.2.104 is affected by a denial of service due to a NULL pointer dereferences. A remote unauthenticated attacker can crash the server by sending an HTTP request to protected resources using a malformed Authorization header that is mishandled during a cherokee_buffer_add call within cherokee_validator_parse_basic or cherokee_validator_parse_digest.

code_evidence: The prefix checks only set pre_len when ptr begins with "Basic " or "Digest "; otherwise pre_len stays 0 and req_auth_type is left unset, with no rejection of the malformed header.
ptr_len is reduced by the header length to the CR/LF and then by pre_len, but no lower-bound or emptiness check precedes the parse calls, so ptr_len can become zero or negative.
The resulting ptr/ptr_len are passed directly to cherokee_validator_parse_basic or cherokee_validator_parse_digest, which mishandle the empty/oversized buffer and dereference a NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function forwards an unvalidated, effectively empty authentication buffer to downstream parsers that dereference NULL, directly matching CWE-476 NULL Pointer Dereference. The missing ptr_len==0 guard is the specific constraint whose absence enables the crash; this is a NULL dereference rather than a generic buffer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: get_authorization computes ptr/ptr_len for the credentials without validating that the remaining authentication string is non-empty. Trigger: a malformed Authorization header lacking a valid scheme or with no credential bytes after the scheme causes ptr_len to be zero or negative before the parse calls. Consequence: the validator parse functions dereference a NULL pointer, crashing the server (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/MSI-X: restrict reading of table/PBA bases from BARs

When assigned to less trusted or un-trusted guests, devices may change
state behind our backs (they may e.g. get reset by means we may not know
about). Therefore we should avoid reading BARs from hardware once a
device is no longer owned by Dom0. Furthermore when we can't read a BAR,
or when we read zero, we shouldn't instead use the caller provided
address unless that caller can be trusted.

Re-arrange the logic in msix_capability_init() such that only Dom0 (and
only if the device isn't DomU-owned yet) or calls through
PHYSDEVOP_prepare_msix will actually result in the reading of the
respective BAR register(s). Additionally do so only as long as in-use
table entries are known (note that invocation of PHYSDEVOP_prepare_msix
counts as a "pseudo" entry). In all other uses the value already
recorded will get used instead.

Clear the recorded values in _pci_cleanup_msix() as well as on the one
affected error path. (Adjust this error path to also avoid blindly
disabling MSI-X when it was enabled on entry to the function.)

While moving around variable declarations (in many cases to reduce their
scopes), also adjust some of their types.

This is part of XSA-337.

Reviewed-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. The PCI passthrough code improperly uses register data. Code paths in Xen's MSI handling have been identified that act on unsanitized values read back from device hardware registers. While devices strictly compliant with PCI specifications shouldn't be able to affect these registers, experience shows that it's very common for devices to have out-of-spec "backdoor" operations that can affect the result of these reads. A not fully trusted guest may be able to crash Xen, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) for the entire system. Privilege escalation and information leaks cannot be excluded. All versions of Xen supporting PCI passthrough are affected. Only x86 systems are vulnerable. Arm systems are not vulnerable. Only guests with passed through PCI devices may be able to leverage the vulnerability. Only systems passing through devices with out-of-spec ("backdoor") functionality can cause issues. Experience shows that such out-of-spec functionality is common; unless you have reason to believe that your device does not have such functionality, it's better to assume that it does.

code_evidence: The function unconditionally reads the MSI-X table offset and BIR from the device's config space, resolves the physical BAR via read_pci_mem_bar(), and uses the result as table_paddr, with no check of caller privilege or device ownership before trusting hardware-returned registers.

When !msix->used_entries the computed table_paddr (and PBA base) are committed into msix->table/pba and the MSI-X fixmap without verifying that the caller is Dom0/PHYSDEVOP_prepare_msix, so a less-trusted domain controlling the device's backdoor register values can redirect the table base.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is improper privilege management: untrusted callers are allowed to influence privileged address-space state (MSI-X table base) that should be reserved for Dom0/prepare_msix, giving them an unintended sphere of control. This is distinct from a mere integer or bounds bug because the missing constraint is authorization/ownership.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: msix_capability_init() reads BAR/table-base registers from hardware and adopts the returned address regardless of whether the current domain is authorized to own or configure the device. Trigger: a guest with a passed-through device whose out-of-spec backdoor alters those register reads. Consequence: Xen maps attacker-influenced addresses into its MSI-X table/PBA ranges, enabling crash (DoS) and potentially privilege escalation or information leaks.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.5 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.13, the ADB dissector could crash with a heap-based buffer overflow. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-adb.c by checking for a length inconsistency.

code_evidence: save_command records data_length from the message header into command_data->data_length (line 87) and allocates reassemble_data with wmem_alloc of exactly command_data->data_length bytes (line 93). The buffer size is thus derived solely from the header-declared length, with no validation that it matches the actual payload length that will later be copied into this buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The allocation at line 93 uses a length that can be smaller than the data subsequently written, producing a write past the end of the intended heap buffer, which is exactly CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write). This is a write overflow rather than a read, distinguishing it from CWE-125.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reassembly buffer is sized from the header-declared data_length without checking it against the real payload length. Trigger: a message whose header length is smaller than its actual payload causes a later write of the payload into the undersized heap buffer. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds write (buffer overflow), enabling memory corruption or crash.

description: Use After Free vulnerability in nfc sockets in the Linux Kernel before 5.12.4 allows local attackers to elevate their privileges. In typical configurations, the issue can only be triggered by a privileged local user with the CAP_NET_RAW capability.

code_evidence: Line 34 stores a referenced local in llcp_sock->local via nfc_llcp_local_get. On the service_name allocation failure path, line 43 drops the reference with nfc_llcp_local_put but the error path branches to put_dev without clearing llcp_sock->local, leaving a dangling pointer.

Similarly, line 47 obtains the ssap; when it equals LLCP_SAP_MAX, line 49 drops the local reference but the field is not reset before goto put_dev, so llcp_sock->local still references freed/put memory on a later use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The retained llcp_sock->local pointer is used after the referenced object's refcount is released, matching CWE-416 use-after-free. This is not merely a refcount leak; the missing NULL assignment enables later dereference of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: error paths call nfc_llcp_local_put on llcp_sock->local without assigning NULL, so the socket retains a stale pointer after the reference is dropped. Trigger: a bind that fails service_name allocation or ssap assignment, followed by reuse of the socket (e.g., close or another bind), causing access to freed local memory and possible privilege escalation.

Add a check for pad width to be a positive value.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 413275853

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `StringNGrams` can be used to trigger a denial of service attack by causing an out of memory condition after an integer overflow. We are missing a validation on `pad_witdh` and that result in computing a negative value for `ngram_width` which is later used to allocate parts of the output. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: In the preserve_short_ branch, when no ngrams were produced, the code computes `int ngram_width = data_length + 2 * pad_width_` (line 80) without validating pad_width_. The added guard in the patch checks pad_width_ >= 0, but the function's arithmetic still relies on pad_width_ being non-negative; a negative pad_width_ makes ngram_width negative, and that value is passed to CreateNgrams (line 83).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer arithmetic computation whose result can become negative/invalid and is then used as a size, matching CWE-190 (integer wraparound/overflow leading to a bad size). The missing pad_width_ >= 0 constraint is the specific cause; this is not merely a bounds check but an arithmetic-derived size error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pad_width_ is used in an integer computation `data_length + 2 * pad_width_` without a prior non-negativity constraint, so a negative pad_width_ yields a negative ngram_width. Trigger: preserve_short_ is true, ngram_widths_ is empty/non-matching, and a nonzero data_length reaches this branch. Consequence: the negative width propagates to CreateNgrams output sizing, enabling out-of-memory/denial of service consistent with the commit description.

description: The abst_box_size function in GPAC 1.0.1 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via a crafted file in the MP4Box command.

commit_msg:
x86/hvm: Fix the handling of non-present segments

In 32bit, the data segments may be NULL to indicate that the segment is
ineligible for use.  In both 32bit and 64bit, the LDT selector may be NULL to
indicate that the entire LDT is ineligible for use.  However, nothing in Xen
actually checks for this condition when performing other segmentation
checks.  (Note however that limit and writeability checks are correctly
performed).

Neither Intel nor AMD specify the exact behaviour of loading a NULL segment.
Experimentally, AMD zeroes all attributes but leaves the base and limit
unmodified.  Intel zeroes the base, sets the limit to 0xfffffff and resets the
attributes to just .G and .D/B.

The use of the segment information in the VMCB/VMCS is equivalent to a native
pipeline interacting with the segment cache.  The present bit can therefore
have a subtly different meaning, and it is now cooked to uniformly indicate
whether the segment is usable or not.

GDTR and IDTR don't have access rights like the other segments, but for
consistency, they are treated as being present so no special casing is needed
elsewhere in the segmentation logic.

AMD hardware does not consider the present bit for %cs and %tr, and will
function as if they were present.  They are therefore unconditionally set to
present when reading information from the VMCB, to maintain the new meaning of
usability.

Intel hardware has a separate unusable bit in the VMCS segment attributes.
This bit is inverted and stored in the present field, so the hvm code can work
with architecturally-common state.

This is CVE-2016-9386 / XSA-191.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    reg->attr.bytes = (attr & 0xff) | ((attr >> 4) & 0xf00);', '    /* Unusable flag is folded into Present flag. */', '    if ( attr & (1u<<16) )', '        reg->attr.fields.p = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    /*', "     * Fold VT-x representation into Xen's representation.  The Present bit is", '     * unconditionally set to the inverse of unusable.', '     */', '    reg->attr.bytes =', '        (!(attr & (1u << 16)) << 7) | (attr & 0x7f) | ((attr >> 4) & 0xf00);']}
description: The x86 emulator in Xen does not properly treat x86 NULL segments as unusable when accessing memory, which might allow local HVM guest users to gain privileges via vectors involving "unexpected" base/limit values.

code_evidence: After reading VMCS segment attributes, the code copies attr into reg->attr.bytes and then only clears the Present bit (reg->attr.fields.p = 0) when the VT-x unusable bit (attr & (1u<<16)) is set; otherwise the present bit from attr is left as-is, so segment usability is not uniformly encoded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper enforcement of segment usability in permission/access-control checks, matching CWE-264's permissions/privileges category. It is not a plain memory-safety bug; the flaw is failure to correctly gate access based on segment state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Present/unusable mapping is not normalized, so a NULL (unusable) segment can still be reported as present and usable by the segmentation logic. Trigger: a guest loads an unexpected segment base/limit with attributes lacking the unusable bit; downstream access checks then treat the segment as usable. Consequence: guest memory accesses use attacker-influenced base/limit, potentially allowing privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
getcwd: Set errno to ERANGE for size == 1 (CVE-2021-3999)

No valid path returned by getcwd would fit into 1 byte, so reject the
size early and return NULL with errno set to ERANGE.  This change is
prompted by CVE-2021-3999, which describes a single byte buffer
underflow and overflow when all of the following conditions are met:

- The buffer size (i.e. the second argument of getcwd) is 1 byte
- The current working directory is too long
- '/' is also mounted on the current working directory

Sequence of events:

- In sysdeps/unix/sysv/linux/getcwd.c, the syscall returns ENAMETOOLONG
  because the linux kernel checks for name length before it checks
  buffer size

- The code falls back to the generic getcwd in sysdeps/posix

- In the generic func, the buf[0] is set to '\0' on line 250

- this while loop on line 262 is bypassed:

    while (!(thisdev == rootdev && thisino == rootino))

  since the rootfs (/) is bind mounted onto the directory and the flow
  goes on to line 449, where it puts a '/' in the byte before the
  buffer.

- Finally on line 458, it moves 2 bytes (the underflowed byte and the
  '\0') to the buf[0] and buf[1], resulting in a 1 byte buffer overflow.

- buf is returned on line 469 and errno is not set.

This resolves BZ #28769.

Reviewed-by: Andreas Schwab <schwab@linux-m68k.org>
Reviewed-by: Adhemerval Zanella  <adhemerval.zanella@linaro.org>
Signed-off-by: Qualys Security Advisory <qsa@qualys.com>
Signed-off-by: Siddhesh Poyarekar <siddhesh@sourceware.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  /* A size of 1 byte is never useful.  */', '  if (allocated == 1)', '    {', '      __set_errno (ERANGE);', '      return NULL;', '    }']}
description: A flaw was found in glibc. An off-by-one buffer overflow and underflow in getcwd() may lead to memory corruption when the size of the buffer is exactly 1. A local attacker who can control the input buffer and size passed to getcwd() in a setuid program could use this flaw to potentially execute arbitrary code and escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: allocated is set to size without rejecting size == 1; for buf != NULL, dirp = dir + allocated and *--dirp = '\0' places the terminator at buf[0], leaving no room for a component or leading '/'.

When the loop is bypassed (root bind-mounted), dirp == &dir[allocated - 1] causes *--dirp = '/' to write one byte before the buffer at buf[-1]; used then counts this underflowed byte plus '\0' and memmove copies 2 bytes into the 1-byte buffer, overflowing buf[1].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a boundary calculation that is off by one: the code writes at buf[-1] and copies two bytes into a one-byte buffer. CWE-193 (Off-by-one Error) directly names this incorrect minimum-size handling; the buffer overflow is the consequence, not the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size==1 case is not rejected, so the start/end pointer arithmetic and the leading-slash adjustment assume at least one byte of headroom that does not exist. Trigger: caller passes a 1-byte buffer and the current directory resolves to the root mount. Consequence: one-byte underflow and overflow, memory corruption, with errno not set on return.

commit_msg:
kvm:vmx: more complete state update on APICv on/off

The function to update APICv on/off state (in particular, to deactivate
it when enabling Hyper-V SynIC) is incomplete: it doesn't adjust
APICv-related fields among secondary processor-based VM-execution
controls.  As a result, Windows 2012 guests get stuck when SynIC-based
auto-EOI interrupt intersected with e.g. an IPI in the guest.

In addition, the MSR intercept bitmap isn't updated every time "virtualize
x2APIC mode" is toggled.  This path can only be triggered by a malicious
guest, because Windows didn't use x2APIC but rather their own synthetic
APIC access MSRs; however a guest running in a SynIC-enabled VM could
switch to x2APIC and thus obtain direct access to host APIC MSRs
(CVE-2016-4440).

The patch fixes those omissions.

Signed-off-by: Roman Kagan <rkagan@virtuozzo.com>
Reported-by: Steve Rutherford <srutherford@google.com>
Reported-by: Yang Zhang <yang.zhang.wz@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>

description: arch/x86/kvm/vmx.c in the Linux kernel through 4.6.3 mishandles the APICv on/off state, which allows guest OS users to obtain direct APIC MSR access on the host OS, and consequently cause a denial of service (host OS crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code on the host OS, via x2APIC mode.

code_evidence: The MSR bitmap selection is driven by the guest-controlled vcpu->arch.apic_base X2APIC_ENABLE bit, not by whether the SECONDARY_EXEC_VIRTUALIZE_X2APIC_MODE control is actually active in the VMCS. When x2APIC is enabled in the guest APIC base but the secondary execution control is off, this branch selects the x2APIC MSR bitmap and writes it to MSR_BITMAP at line 17, granting the guest interception-free access to host APIC MSRs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers permission/access-control management flaws. Here the MSR interception policy (an access-control mechanism) is misconfigured, allowing a guest to bypass host-imposed MSR restrictions and gain unauthorized host APIC MSR access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bitmap choice depends on a guest-modifiable APIC state bit rather than the actual virtualization control. Trigger: a malicious guest enables x2APIC (e.g., in a SynIC VM) while virtualize-x2APIC is disabled. Consequence: the guest gains direct host APIC MSR access, enabling host crash or possible host code execution.

commit_msg:
Fixed Array.prototype.concat() when "this" is a slow array.

Previously, when the current appended element is fast array the "this"
array was expected to always be a fast array also.  This may not be the
case when the previous appended element was not fast thus converting
the "this" array to a slow form.

Previous fix introduced in 2c1382bab643 (0.7.2) was not complete, the
correct fix is to never assume "this" is fast, whereas njs_array_add()
may only be called with fast arrays.

This closes #471 issue in Github.

description: nginx njs 0.7.2 is vulnerable to Buffer Overflow. Type confused in Array.prototype.concat() when a slow array appended element is fast array.

code_evidence: Free-space arithmetic derives free_before/free_after from array->start, array->length and array->size, then takes the fast path and returns NJS_OK without reallocating when the computed capacities appear sufficient.

The resize path computes size from prepend, length and append, guards only against size > UINT32_MAX/sizeof(njs_value_t), allocates, sets array->size = size, then memcpy's array->length elements from array->start into the new start at offset prepend.

This is a copy-size validation failure, not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function assumes the array is fast and that its length/start/size metadata are mutually consistent, so the memcpy at line 32 trusts array->length as the copy size and the free-space checks at lines 8-10 as capacity. When a slow/type-confused array is passed (per commit, concat converts this to slow form), the metadata no longer matches allocated storage, so the copy can exceed the allocated region. commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow leading to divide by zero error in Unravel index kernel when dimensions product exceeds max int value.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 413250052
Change-Id: I9450b6e8acecd2e881a64b882e2b7c70e8e9289a
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    double prod = 1;', '    uint64_t limit;', '    if (dtidx_ == DataType::DT_INT64) {', '      limit = kint64max;', '    } else {', '      limit = kint32max;', '    }', '', '      OP_REQUIRES(ctx, dims(i) > 0,', '                  errors::InvalidArgument(', '                      "Input dims cannot be negative. Got dim = ", dims(i),', '                      " at index ", i));', '      // Check interger overflow', '      OP_REQUIRES(', '          ctx, prod <= limit / dims(i),', '          errors::InvalidArgument("Input dims product is causing integer "', '                                  "overflow: (",', '                                  dims, ")"));', '      prod = (prod * dims(i));']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `UnravelIndex` is vulnerable to a division by zero caused by an integer overflow bug. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function multiplies all entries of dims via Eigen's dims.prod() at line 22, storing the result in Tidx dims_prod. The only pre-check loop (lines 15-21) rejects zero dims but never bounds the product against the Tidx maximum; large dims therefore overflow dims_prod, which then flows into the index bound check at line 27 and the stride computations at lines 37-47.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked multiplication of dims is an integer overflow/wraparound that violates the assumed monotonic growth of the product, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a divide-by-zero (CWE-369), since the division fault is a downstream consequence of the wrapped product; the fix would need an explicit overflow constraint on the product.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the product of dims is computed in the narrow Tidx type without an overflow guard. Trigger: caller supplies dims whose product exceeds the Tidx range, so dims_prod wraps to a small or negative value. Consequence: the bounds check at line 27 is defeated and downstream stride/modulo computations (lines 56, 75-77) operate on corrupted values, including a possible divide-by-zero when a shifted stride becomes zero.

commit_msg:
When parsing texture instruction, it doesn't stop if the
'cur' is ',', the loop variable 'i' will also be increased
and be used to index the 'inst.TexOffsets' array. This can lead
an oob access issue. This patch avoid this.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liq3ea@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Airlie <airlied@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["   for (i = 0; inst.Instruction.Texture && *cur == ','; i++) {"], 'added_lines': ["   for (i = 0; inst.Instruction.Texture && *cur == ',' && i < TGSI_FULL_MAX_TEX_OFFSETS; i++) {"]}
description: The parse_instruction function in gallium/auxiliary/tgsi/tgsi_text.c in virglrenderer before 0.6.0 allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds array access and process crash) via a crafted texture instruction.

code_evidence: The texture-offset loop at line 106 iterates while the instruction is a texture and the next character is a comma, incrementing i each iteration. It advances cur and calls parse_texoffset_operand with &inst.TexOffsets[i] at line 110. No bound on i is present before indexing the fixed-size TexOffsets array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function indexes inst.TexOffsets[i] without validating i against the buffer length, so it writes outside the intended array boundary. This is a direct out-of-bounds memory operation on a fixed-size buffer, matching CWE-119; the missing bounds check distinguishes it from unrelated parsing errors.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop condition only checks instruction type and the comma character, never the offset count against TGSI_FULL_MAX_TEX_OFFSETS. A crafted texture instruction with many comma-separated offset operands makes i exceed the array size; line 110 then writes past inst.TexOffsets, causing an out-of-bounds access that can crash the process (DoS).

Temporary over-allocation until Glenn applies a proper fix:
  https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/538
  https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/540
  https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/541

description: The mng_get_long function in coders/png.c in ImageMagick 7.0.6-0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted MNG image.

code_evidence: Lines 93-108 allocate a buffer of exactly 'length' bytes from the attacker-controlled chunk length and fill it by reading blob bytes until 'length' is reached or EOF. If EOF occurs early, the loop breaks with fewer bytes written, but 'length' is unchanged and 'p' still points at the short buffer.

Lines 110-153: when the chunk type is mng_JHDR and length==16, the code reads p[0]..p[15] unconditionally. A crafted MNG/JNG declaring a JHDR length of 16 but truncating the chunk data leaves the buffer partially filled, so the p[8]..p[15] reads (and p[0]..p[7]) access bytes past the written/valid region, causing the heap buffer over-read and crash.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads p[0]..p[15] beyond the validly populated portion of the heap buffer allocated for the chunk. The defect is an out-of-bounds read, not a write; the added MagickPathExtent overallocation only masks the over-read temporarily rather than validating the read length.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the JHDR parser trusts the declared length==16 and reads 16 header bytes from 'p' without confirming that all 16 bytes were actually read into the allocation. Trigger: a crafted JNG where the JHDR chunk declares length 16 but the blob ends early, so ReadBlobByte returns EOF and the fill loop breaks short. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap read of uninitialized/adjacent memory, resulting in a denial-of-service crash.

commit_msg:
CVE-2023-0286: Fix GENERAL_NAME_cmp for x400Address (3.0)

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        result = ASN1_TYPE_cmp(a->d.x400Address, b->d.x400Address);'], 'added_lines': ['        result = ASN1_STRING_cmp(a->d.x400Address, b->d.x400Address);']}
description:
There is a type confusion vulnerability relating to X.400 address processing
inside an X.509 GeneralName. X.400 addresses were parsed as an ASN1_STRING but
the public structure definition for GENERAL_NAME incorrectly specified the type
of the x400Address field as ASN1_TYPE. This field is subsequently interpreted by
the OpenSSL function GENERAL_NAME_cmp as an ASN1_TYPE rather than an
ASN1_STRING.

When CRL checking is enabled (i.e. the application sets the
X509_V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK flag), this vulnerability may allow an attacker to pass
arbitrary pointers to a memcmp call, enabling them to read memory contents or
enact a denial of service. In most cases, the attack requires the attacker to
provide both the certificate chain and CRL, neither of which need to have a
valid signature. If the attacker only controls one of these inputs, the other
input must already contain an X.400 address as a CRL distribution point, which
is uncommon. As such, this vulnerability is most likely to only affect
applications which have implemented their own functionality for retrieving CRLs
over a network.

code_evidence: In the GEN_X400 case, a->d.x400Address and b->d.x400Address are passed to ASN1_TYPE_cmp, which treats the pointer as an ASN1_TYPE. The x400Address field is actually parsed and stored as an ASN1_STRING, so the comparison reads the object through an incompatible type layout.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses a resource initialized as ASN1_STRING using the incompatible ASN1_TYPE abstraction, matching CWE-843 type confusion. This differs from a simple null or bounds bug because the defect is the mismatched type interpretation that corrupts the comparison logic.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the comparison routine interprets the x400Address union member as ASN1_TYPE although the field holds an ASN1_STRING. Trigger: comparing two GENERAL_NAME values with type GEN_X400, reachable during CRL checking. Consequence: ASN1_TYPE_cmp reads fields at the wrong offsets and may follow attacker-influenced pointers into memcmp, enabling out-of-bounds reads or a crash.

commit_msg:
Fix STARTTLS response injection attack.

Thanks again to Damian Poddebniak and Fabian Ising from the Münster
University of Applied Sciences for reporting this issue.  Their
summary in ticket 248 states the issue clearly:

  We found another STARTTLS-related issue in Mutt. Unfortunately, it
  affects SMTP, POP3 and IMAP.

  When the server responds with its "let's do TLS now message", e.g. A
  OK begin TLS\r\n in IMAP or +OK begin TLS\r\n in POP3, Mutt will
  also read any data after the \r\n and save it into some internal
  buffer for later processing. This is problematic, because a MITM
  attacker can inject arbitrary responses.

  There is a nice blogpost by Wietse Venema about a "command
  injection" in postfix (http://www.postfix.org/CVE-2011-0411.html).
  What we have here is the problem in reverse, i.e. not a command
  injection, but a "response injection."

This commit fixes the issue by clearing the CONNECTION input buffer in
mutt_ssl_starttls().

To make backporting this fix easier, the new functions only clear the
top-level CONNECTION buffer; they don't handle nested buffering in
mutt_zstrm.c or mutt_sasl.c.  However both of those wrap the
connection *after* STARTTLS, so this is currently okay.  mutt_tunnel.c
occurs before connecting, but it does not perform any nesting.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (mutt_socket_has_buffered_input (conn))', '  {', '    /* L10N:', '       The server is not supposed to send data immediately after', '       confirming STARTTLS.  This warns the user that something', '       weird is going on.', '    */', '    mutt_error _("Warning: clearing unexpected buffered data before STARTTLS");', '    mutt_sleep (0);', '    mutt_socket_clear_buffered_input (conn);', '  }', '']}
description: Mutt before 1.14.4 and NeoMutt before 2020-06-19 have a STARTTLS buffering issue that affects IMAP, SMTP, and POP3. When a server sends a "begin TLS" response, the client reads additional data (e.g., from a man-in-the-middle attacker) and evaluates it in a TLS context, aka "response injection."

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function contains no buffered-input handling or externally-influenced data parsing; the STARTTLS response injection fix (clearing conn input buffer) is absent from the provided function body, so the function does not directly support CWE-74.

commit_msg: Fixed memory leak reported in #459.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"CorruptImage");', '              ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"CorruptImage");'], 'added_lines': ['            {', '              one_row=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(one_row);', '              if (compressionType == PALM_COMPRESSION_SCANLINE)', '                lastrow=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(lastrow);', '              ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"CorruptImage");', '            }', '              {', '                one_row=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(one_row);', '                if (compressionType == PALM_COMPRESSION_SCANLINE)', '                  lastrow=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(lastrow);', '                ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"CorruptImage");', '              }']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.0.5-5, the ReadPALMImage function in palm.c allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory leak) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: one_row is allocated via AcquireQuantumMemory and is not freed on the allocation-failure path only (lastrow not yet allocated here).
lastrow is separately allocated for scanline compression; both buffers become owned resources that must be released on every exit path.
On the 16-bit path, when image->columns > 2*bytes_per_row, ThrowReaderException longjmps out before the normal release at line 287, leaking one_row (and lastrow if scanline).
On the non-16-bit path, the bounds check at line 253 also throws before the release, likewise leaking the row buffers.
The only normal release of one_row/lastrow occurs at lines 287-289; error exits bypass it, confirming the missing-release condition.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The row buffers are allocated and their effective lifetime ends on the exception exit, yet no release occurs, matching CWE-772's missing release of a resource after its lifetime. This is a resource-lifetime defect rather than out-of-bounds access; the corruption checks themselves are the leak trigger, not the weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (image->columns > (2*bytes_per_row))
ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"CorruptImage");

if ((size_t) (ptr-one_row) >= bytes_per_row)
ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"CorruptImage");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error paths at lines 236 and 254 raise an exception (longjmp) before the shared cleanup at lines 287-289, so one_row and, for scanline compression, lastrow are never relinquished. Trigger: a crafted PALM file whose columns exceed 2*bytes_per_row or whose row pointer overruns bytes_per_row. Consequence: per-read memory leak enabling denial of service; the patch adds RelinquishMagickMemory calls at those exits.

commit_msg:
rpmsg: virtio: Fix possible double free in rpmsg_virtio_add_ctrl_dev()

vch will be free in virtio_rpmsg_release_device() when
rpmsg_ctrldev_register_device() fails. There is no need to call
kfree() again.

Fixes: c486682ae1e2 ("rpmsg: virtio: Register the rpmsg_char device")
Signed-off-by: Hangyu Hua <hbh25y@gmail.com>
Tested-by: Arnaud Pouliquen <arnaud.pouliquen@foss.st.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220426060536.15594-3-hbh25y@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Mathieu Poirier <mathieu.poirier@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tkfree(vch);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* vch will be free in virtio_rpmsg_release_device() */']}
description: rpmsg_virtio_add_ctrl_dev in drivers/rpmsg/virtio_rpmsg_bus.c in the Linux kernel before 5.18.4 has a double free.

code_evidence: Line 14 sets rpdev_ctrl->dev.release = virtio_rpmsg_release_device, establishing the release callback for the device embedded in vch. Line 16 registers the ctrl device; on failure the error path at lines 17-19 calls kfree(vch) directly and returns ERR_PTR(err).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees the same vch allocation twice on the registration-failure path: once indirectly through the release callback and once explicitly with kfree. This is a direct instance of CWE-415 (Double Free), distinct from a use-after-free since no dereference of freed memory occurs here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the error path frees vch while the device core already owns it via the release callback set at line 14. When rpmsg_ctrldev_register_device() fails, the put_device path invokes virtio_rpmsg_release_device(), which frees vch, and the subsequent kfree(vch) at line 18 frees the same allocation again, causing a double free and potential memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
RTMPT: Fix infinite loop

The RTMPT dissector when over TCP reuses the TCP sequence numbers, so
it needs to consider wraparound, which can occur both with the
tcp.relative_sequence_numbers preference set to FALSE, or in some
unusual cases (such as a SYN packet with a bogus sequence number so
that later packets overlap its sequence number.)

Change a sequence number comparison to use the wrap around aware
macros from packet-tcp.h Fix #17745.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                while (tp && tp->lastseq >= seq) {'], 'added_lines': ["                /* XXX: If there's bogus sequence numbers and the", "                 * tcp.analyze_sequence_numbers pref is TRUE, we can't actually", '                 * assume that we processed this frame the first time around,', '                 * since the TCP dissector might not have given it to us.', '                 */', '                while (tp && GE_SEQ(tp->lastseq, seq)) {', '                        /* Sequence numbers can wrap around (especially with', '                         * tcp.relative_sequence_numbers FALSE), so use the', '                         * wrap around aware comparison from packet-tcp.h', '                         */', '                                /* XXX: Assuming tcp.relative_sequence_numbers', '                                 * is TRUE, that is, since on TCP we just', '                                 * reuse the sequence numbers from tcpinfo.', '                                 */']}
description: Infinite loop in the RTMPT dissector in Wireshark 3.6.0 and 3.4.0 to 3.4.10 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: The visited-frame branch walks back through previously seen RTMP packets via wmem_tree_lookup32_le, starting at seq+remain-1 and looping while tp->lastseq >= seq, pushing each packet and stepping to tp->seq-1. The plain >= comparison ignores 32-bit sequence wraparound, so when tp->lastseq wraps below the starting seq, the loop condition stays true or the lookup keeps returning overlapping packets, and the only in-loop exit is tp->seq == 0, which need not occur.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a loop whose exit condition relies on a sequence-number ordering that wraparound can make unreachable, directly matching CWE-835 (Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition). The fix replaces the comparison with the wrap-aware GE_SEQ macro, confirming the loop-termination defect rather than a mere logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a non-wrap-aware comparison (tp->lastseq >= seq) in the reverse packet-walk loop. Trigger: crafted/injected TCP sequence numbers that wrap around (relative seq numbers disabled or bogus SYN sequence), so the exit condition is never satisfied. Consequence: the dissector spins indefinitely, consuming CPU and causing denial of service (CWE-835).

commit_msg:
Fix #78943: mail() may release string with refcount==1 twice

Since we need `headers_lc` as well as `headers_trim` in the following,
we do not release the former even if they are the same string, to avoid
complicating the release logic even more.

A new test case is not necessary, since we already have
mail_basic_alt2-win32.phpt and others.

(cherry picked from commit 518a160b65fe1c535dc7e78972ba7428c2a4e197)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (headers_lc == headers_trim) {', '\t\t\tzend_string_release_ex(headers_lc, 0);', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': []}
description: In PHP versions 7.3.x below 7.3.13 and 7.4.0 on Windows, when supplying custom headers to mail() function, due to mistake introduced in commit 78f4b4a2dcf92ddbccea1bb95f8390a18ac3342e, if the header is supplied in lowercase, this can result in double-freeing certain memory locations.

code_evidence: headers_lc is created by zend_string_tolower(headers_trim); when the input is already lowercase, tolower returns the same string, so headers_lc == headers_trim and headers_lc is released here, while headers_trim still holds the same reference.
Later, when no From: header is found, both headers_trim and headers_lc are released, freeing the shared string a second time.
On the success/connect-error paths the same pair of releases (headers_trim and headers_lc) is performed, again double-freeing when they alias.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 is the direct fit: the same memory address (the shared zend_string) is passed to zend_string_release twice. It is not merely a use-after-free, since the defect is the duplicate release itself; the aliasing causes the double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code conditionally releases headers_lc when it aliases headers_trim, but does not clear or account for that alias, so the later unconditional release of both pointers frees the same zend_string twice. Trigger: supplying custom mail() headers already in lowercase, causing zend_string_tolower to return the same string. Supported consequence: double free, leading to memory corruption and potential code execution.

Thanks go to Pavel Cheremushkin of Kaspersky for reporting.

if (rfbWriteExact(cl, (char *)&sct,

description: libavcodec/hevcdec.c in FFmpeg 3.4 and 4.1.2 mishandles detection of duplicate first slices, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and out-of-array access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted HEVC data.

commit_msg:
candump: check for a too-long frame length.

If the frame length is longer than the maximum, report an error in the
file.

Fixes #19062, preventing the overflow on a buffer on the stack (assuming
your compiler doesn't call a bounds-checknig version of memcpy() if the
size of the target space is known).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    candump_write_packet(rec, buf, &msg);', '', '    return TRUE;'], 'added_lines': ['    return candump_write_packet(rec, buf, &msg, err, err_info);']}
description: Candump log parser crash in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.5 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.13 allows denial of service via crafted capture file

code_evidence: candump_seek_read calls candump_parse to populate a stack msg_t, then unconditionally calls candump_write_packet(rec, buf, &msg) and returns TRUE. The return value of candump_parse is checked, but the frame length carried in msg is never validated against the destination buffer size before candump_write_packet writes into buf; the pre-patch code ignored any error from candump_write_packet entirely.

Trigger is a malicious capture file; consequence is a stack buffer overflow leading to crash (DoS) and potential memory corruption.
