commit_msg:
xfs: don't BUG() on mixed direct and mapped I/O

We've had reports of generic/095 causing XFS to BUG() in
__xfs_get_blocks() due to the existence of delalloc blocks on a
direct I/O read. generic/095 issues a mix of various types of I/O,
including direct and memory mapped I/O to a single file. This is
clearly not supported behavior and is known to lead to such
problems. E.g., the lack of exclusion between the direct I/O and
write fault paths means that a write fault can allocate delalloc
blocks in a region of a file that was previously a hole after the
direct read has attempted to flush/inval the file range, but before
it actually reads the block mapping. In turn, the direct read
discovers a delalloc extent and cannot proceed.

While the appropriate solution here is to not mix direct and memory
mapped I/O to the same regions of the same file, the current
BUG_ON() behavior is probably overkill as it can crash the entire
system.  Instead, localize the failure to the I/O in question by
returning an error for a direct I/O that cannot be handled safely
due to delalloc blocks. Be careful to allow the case of a direct
write to post-eof delalloc blocks. This can occur due to speculative
preallocation and is safe as post-eof blocks are not accompanied by
dirty pages in pagecache (conversely, preallocation within eof must
have been zeroed, and thus dirtied, before the inode size could have
been increased beyond said blocks).

Finally, provide an additional warning if a direct I/O write occurs
while the file is memory mapped. This may not catch all problematic
scenarios, but provides a hint that some known-to-be-problematic I/O
methods are in use.

Signed-off-by: Brian Foster <bfoster@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Dave Chinner <dchinner@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Chinner <david@fromorbit.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tBUG_ON(direct && imap.br_startblock == DELAYSTARTBLOCK);', ''], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/*', '\t * The only time we can ever safely find delalloc blocks on direct I/O', '\t * is a dio write to post-eof speculative preallocation. All other', '\t * scenarios are indicative of a problem or misuse (such as mixing', '\t * direct and mapped I/O).', '\t *', '\t * The file may be unmapped by the time we get here so we cannot', '\t * reliably fail the I/O based on mapping. Instead, fail the I/O if this', '\t * is a read or a write within eof. Otherwise, carry on but warn as a', '\t * precuation if the file happens to be mapped.', '\t */', '\tif (direct && imap.br_startblock == DELAYSTARTBLOCK) {', '\t\tif (!create || offset < i_size_read(VFS_I(ip))) {', '\t\t\tWARN_ON_ONCE(1);', '\t\t\terror = -EIO;', '\t\t\tgoto out_unlock;', '\t\t}', '\t\tWARN_ON_ONCE(mapping_mapped(VFS_I(ip)->i_mapping));', '\t}']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 4.9.3, fs/xfs/xfs_aops.c allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) because there is a race condition between direct and memory-mapped I/O (associated with a hole) that is handled with BUG_ON instead of an I/O failure.

code_evidence: The block mapping is read via xfs_bmapi_read at lines 40-41 and stored in imap, then checked at lines 42-49. The deleted statement at line 107, BUG_ON(direct && imap.br_startblock == DELAYSTARTBLOCK), fired on a shared mapping state observed after the read.
The mapping can change between the read at lines 40-41 and the check at line 107 because the inode lock is only shared here and the write-fault path can allocate delalloc blocks concurrently.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the failure depends on a timing window between the mapping read (lines 40-41) and the assertion (line 107), during which an interfering write-fault sequence modifies the shared inode mapping and violates exclusivity. The crash is the consequence of that race, not an independent memory-safety flaw.

evidence_lines.code: BUG_ON(direct && imap.br_startblock == DELAYSTARTBLOCK);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the direct-I/O path reads the extent map under a shared inode lock and later assumes the observed mapping is stable, but a concurrent write fault can install delalloc blocks in the same file range. Trigger: mixing direct and memory-mapped I/O to the same region, as in generic/095. Consequence: the stale mapping reaches the BUG_ON at line 107, crashing the whole system (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix - memory leak when deleting client from client list

Signed-off-by: Rob White <rob@blue-wave.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t} else {', '\t\tclient->cpi_query = "none";'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in the captive portal in OpenNDS before version 10.1.3. It has multiple memory leaks due to not freeing up allocated memory. This may lead to a Denial-of-Service condition due to the consumption of all available memory.

code_evidence: When the requested URL is "/login", client->cpi_query is assigned a heap buffer from safe_strdup(originurl); the else branch instead assigns the string literal "none", so the field may or may not own heap memory.
The function frees originurl_raw, originurl, query and querystr before returning, but never releases client->cpi_query or clears it when the client is removed from the list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because an allocated buffer referenced by client->cpi_query is not released after its effective lifetime when the client is deleted. The leak stems from missing release/tracking of owned memory, not from an invalid pointer use such as CWE-416.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ownership of client->cpi_query is ambiguous—sometimes a safe_strdup allocation, sometimes a static literal—and the client-teardown path does not free it. Trigger: a client accesses /login, causing an allocation that persists for the client's lifetime; repeated client creation/removal without releasing cpi_query accumulates unreclaimed heap. Supported consequence: memory exhaustion leading to DoS.

commit_msg:
Bug 698908: Resize object use and renumbering lists after repair.

Previously repair might end up increasing xref_len, but the lists
were not correspodingly expanded, leading to ASAN complaints.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\texpand_lists(ctx, opts, xref_len + 3);'], 'added_lines': ['\texpand_lists(ctx, opts, xref_len);']}
description: In Artifex MuPDF 1.12.0, there is a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the do_pdf_save_document function in the pdf/pdf-write.c file. Remote attackers could leverage the vulnerability to cause a denial of service via a crafted pdf file.

code_evidence: Line 3 captures the current xref length into xref_len. Line 24 calls expand_lists with xref_len + 3, allocating list buffers sized to the inflated value rather than the actual xref count. The patch context shows the call was changed to expand_lists(ctx, opts, xref_len), indicating the +3 offset caused the lists to be sized inconsistently with xref_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The added +3 inflates the allocation size assumption relative to the real xref count, causing later indexed writes to fall outside the allocated list buffers; this is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an integer overflow, as the defect is the mismatched list sizing leading directly to writes beyond buffer bounds.

int xref_len = pdf_xref_len(ctx, doc);
expand_lists(ctx, opts, xref_len + 3);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: expand_lists is invoked with xref_len + 3, so the use/offset/generation lists are sized for a count that does not match the document's actual xref length. When later repair or renumbering expands xref_len to a value larger than the allocated list capacity, subsequent writes index past the allocated buffers, producing a heap-based out-of-bounds write and crash (DoS).

commit_msg: util-lib: use MODE_INVALID as invalid value for mode_t everywhere
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (mode > 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (mode != MODE_INVALID) {']}
description: A flaw in systemd v228 in /src/basic/fs-util.c caused world writable suid files to be created when using the systemd timers features, allowing local attackers to escalate their privileges to root. This is fixed in v229.

code_evidence: Line 7 passes `mode` directly to `open(...)` as the creation mode when `mode > 0`, otherwise falls back to 0644.

Lines 10-14 apply `fchmod(fd, mode)` only when `mode > 0`; the sentinel value MODE_INVALID (typically (mode_t)-1, i.e. all bits set) is greater than 0, so the fchmod branch executes and applies the invalid mode.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function mismanages permission bits on a created file, applying an unintended mode that grants excessive access and privilege bits. This is a permissions/access-control management weakness, matching CWE-264 (Permissions, Privileges, and Access Controls) rather than a generic input-validation issue.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard `mode > 0` treats the sentinel MODE_INVALID (a large unsigned mode_t) as a valid requested mode. Trigger: a caller passes MODE_INVALID to signal 'no mode change'; the condition is true, so fchmod applies the sentinel's permission bits, yielding world-writable and setuid/setgid bits. The supported consequence is creation of files with overly permissive and privilege-elevating modes, allowing local privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fix heap overflows in the various rectangle fill functions

Altough rfbproto.c does check whether the overall FramebufferUpdate rectangle is
too large, some of the individual encoding decoders do not, which allows a
malicious server to overwrite parts of the heap.

commit_msg:
ptrace: Check PTRACE_O_SUSPEND_SECCOMP permission on PTRACE_SEIZE

Setting PTRACE_O_SUSPEND_SECCOMP is supposed to be a highly privileged
operation because it allows the tracee to completely bypass all seccomp
filters on kernels with CONFIG_CHECKPOINT_RESTORE=y. It is only supposed to
be settable by a process with global CAP_SYS_ADMIN, and only if that
process is not subject to any seccomp filters at all.

However, while these permission checks were done on the PTRACE_SETOPTIONS
path, they were missing on the PTRACE_SEIZE path, which also sets
user-specified ptrace flags.

Move the permissions checks out into a helper function and let both
ptrace_attach() and ptrace_setoptions() call it.

Cc: stable@kernel.org
Fixes: 13c4a90119d2 ("seccomp: add ptrace options for suspend/resume")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20220319010838.1386861-1-jannh@google.com
Signed-off-by: Eric W. Biederman <ebiederm@xmission.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/*', '\t\t * This duplicates the check in check_ptrace_options() because', '\t\t * ptrace_attach() and ptrace_setoptions() have historically', '\t\t * used different error codes for unknown ptrace options.', '\t\t */', '\t\tretval = check_ptrace_options(flags);', '\t\tif (retval)', '\t\t\treturn retval;']}
description: The Linux kernel before 5.17.2 mishandles seccomp permissions. The PTRACE_SEIZE code path allows attackers to bypass intended restrictions on setting the PT_SUSPEND_SECCOMP flag.

code_evidence: In the seize path, ptrace_attach accepts caller-supplied ptrace flags and only rejects addr != 0 and bits outside PTRACE_O_MASK; it never calls check_ptrace_options(), so PTRACE_O_SUSPEND_SECCOMP is accepted without the CAP_SYS_ADMIN/seccomp checks that ptrace_setoptions() performs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes a privileged ptrace action to callers lacking the required capability because the authorization check is absent on this path, matching CWE-862 Missing Authorization rather than a validation flaw: the bitmask check exists but the permission check does not.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the PTRACE_SEIZE branch validates the option bitmask but omits the privileged-option authorization check. Trigger: an unprivileged tracer passes PTRACE_O_SUSPEND_SECCOMP in flags to PTRACE_SEIZE. Consequence: the tracee's seccomp filters can be suspended, bypassing a protection mechanism that should require global CAP_SYS_ADMIN and an unfiltered caller.

commit_msg:
Prevent `CHECK`-fail when decoding resource handles from proto

In certain scenarios, the proto might contain tensors that have too many elements (overflow). This is a `CHECK`-fail in general, but we should prevent this, given how many CVEs caused by that we have received this year (a large fraction of 200).

PiperOrigin-RevId: 408049766
Change-Id: I2ac20b247aa8ed9110846fbdb7a0a9401f2c168c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  const bool status = proto.ParseFromString(s);', '  if (status) FromProto(proto);', '  return status;'], 'added_lines': ['  return proto.ParseFromString(s) && FromProto(proto).ok();']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. When decoding a resource handle tensor from protobuf, a TensorFlow process can encounter cases where a `CHECK` assertion is invalidated based on user controlled arguments. This allows attackers to cause denial of services in TensorFlow processes. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 3 parses attacker-supplied serialized bytes into a ResourceHandleProto. When parsing succeeds, line 4 calls FromProto(proto) but discards its return value, and line 5 returns only the parse status. Any error condition inside FromProto—such as the CHECK-fail on oversized element counts noted in the commit—is not propagated or handled here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits a user-controlled input path to reach an internal assertion whose failure terminates the process, matching CWE-617's reachable assertion leading to a DoS. Contrasting CWE-20 (input validation) is less precise because the core defect is the unhandled fatal assertion, not merely missing validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: FromProto is invoked on user-controlled proto contents and its result is ignored, so an internal CHECK assertion triggered by overflowing tensor element counts is reachable. Trigger: a crafted serialized resource handle that parses successfully but contains too many elements. Consequence: process abort, causing denial of service.

Lines 21-22 and 29-30 depend on s->ps.pps/s->ps.sps being consistent; a duplicate first slice re-triggers SPS/PPS switching and reference clearing, corrupting decoder state that later dereferences assume valid.

if ((IS_IDR(s) || IS_BLA(s)) && sh->first_slice_in_pic_flag) {

Trigger: crafted HEVC data with duplicate first slices causes state reset/reference clearing mid-frame. Syzkaller reports a memory leak as follows:

unreferenced object 0xffff88810d81ac00 (size 240):

  hex dump (first 32 bytes):
    00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  ................
    00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  ................
  backtrace:
    [<ffffffff838733d9>] __alloc_skb+0x1f9/0x270 net/core/skbuff.c:418
    [<ffffffff833f742f>] alloc_skb include/linux/skbuff.h:1257 [inline]
    [<ffffffff833f742f>] bt_skb_alloc include/net/bluetooth/bluetooth.h:469 [inline]
    [<ffffffff833f742f>] vhci_get_user drivers/bluetooth/hci_vhci.c:391 [inline]
    [<ffffffff833f742f>] vhci_write+0x5f/0x230 drivers/bluetooth/hci_vhci.c:511
    [<ffffffff815e398d>] call_write_iter include/linux/fs.h:2192 [inline]
    [<ffffffff815e398d>] new_sync_write fs/read_write.c:491 [inline]
    [<ffffffff815e398d>] vfs_write+0x42d/0x540 fs/read_write.c:578
    [<ffffffff815e3cdd>] ksys_write+0x9d/0x160 fs/read_write.c:631
    [<ffffffff845e0645>] do_syscall_x64 arch/x86/entry/common.c:50 [inline]
    [<ffffffff845e0645>] do_syscall_64+0x35/0xb0 arch/x86/entry/common.c:80
    [<ffffffff84600087>] entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x63/0xcd
====================================

HCI core will uses hci_rx_work() to process frame, which is queued to
the hdev->rx_q tail in hci_recv_frame() by HCI driver.

Yet the problem is that, HCI core may not free the skb after handling
ACL data packets. To be more specific, when start fragment does not
contain the L2CAP length, HCI core just copies skb into conn->rx_skb and
finishes frame process in l2cap_recv_acldata(), without freeing the skb,
which triggers the above memory leak.

This patch solves it by releasing the relative skb, after processing
the above case in l2cap_recv_acldata().

Fixes: 4d7ea8ee90e4 ("Bluetooth: L2CAP: Fix handling fragmented length")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/all/0000000000000d0b1905e6aaef64@google.com/
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+8f819e36e01022991cfa@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Hawkins Jiawei <yin31149@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Luiz Augusto von Dentz <luiz.von.dentz@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (l2cap_recv_frag(conn, skb, conn->mtu) < 0)', '\t\t\t\tgoto drop;', '\t\t\treturn;', '\t\t\t\treturn;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tl2cap_recv_frag(conn, skb, conn->mtu);', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t\tbreak;']}
description: A vulnerability has been found in Linux Kernel and classified as problematic. This vulnerability affects the function l2cap_recv_acldata of the file net/bluetooth/l2cap_core.c of the component Bluetooth. The manipulation leads to memory leak. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-211918 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: When the start fragment is shorter than L2CAP_LEN_SIZE, l2cap_recv_frag() stores the skb into conn->rx_skb (via l2cap_recv_frag) and the function returns at line 24 without freeing skb; the drop label's kfree_skb(skb) at line 72 is bypassed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates/receives an skb and fails to release it after use on an exceptional path, matching CWE-401 (missing release of memory after effective lifetime). It is not a use-after-free (CWE-416) or double-free, since the defect is omission of kfree_skb, not misuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the early return on the short-start-fragment path skips the drop label, so the skb copied into conn->rx_skb is never released. Trigger: a start ACL frame with skb->len < L2CAP_LEN_SIZE (malformed/truncated length). Consequence: the skb allocation (bt_skb_alloc) leaks, causing memory exhaustion/DoS as reported by syzkaller.

commit_msg:
PR29495, rewrite_elf_program_header looping

This patch, in order of significance:
1) Replaces some macros with inline functions.
2) Those inline functions catch and avoid arithmetic overflows when
   comparing addresses.
3) When assigning sections to segments (IS_SECTION_IN_INPUT_SEGMENT)
   use bed->want_p_paddr_set_to_zero to decide whether lma vs p_paddr
   or vma vs p_vaddr should be tested.  When remapping, use the same
   test, and use is_note rather than the more restrictive
   IS_COREFILE_NOTE.

It's important that the later tests not be more restrictive.  If they
are it can lead to the situation triggered by the testcases, where a
section seemingly didn't fit and thus needed a new mapping.  It didn't
fit the new mapping either, and this repeated until memory exhausted.

	* elf.c (SEGMENT_END, SECTION_SIZE, IS_CONTAINED_BY_VMA): Delete.
	(IS_CONTAINED_BY_LMA, IS_NOTE, IS_COREFILE_NOTE): Delete.
	(segment_size, segment_end, section_size): New inline function.
	(is_contained_by, is_note): Likewise.
	(rewrite_elf_program_header): Use new functions.

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: make the internal memory data base the default

Having a file backed data base has the only advantage of being capable
to dump the contents of it while Xenstore is running, and potentially
using less swap space in case the data base can't be kept in memory.

It has the major disadvantage of a huge performance overhead: switching
to keep the data base in memory only speeds up live update of xenstored
with 120000 nodes from 20 minutes to 11 seconds. A complete tree walk
of this configuration will be reduced from 7 seconds to 280 msecs
(measured by "xenstore-control check").

So make the internal memory data base the default and enhance the
"--internal-db" command line parameter to take an optional parameter
allowing to switch the internal data base back to the file based one.

This is part of XSA-419.

Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>

description: mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-05-01 does not initialize certain data structures, which allows attackers to obtain sensitive information via a crafted application, related to IGraphicBufferConsumer.cpp and IGraphicBufferProducer.cpp, aka internal bug 27556038.

code_evidence: At line 61, `uint64_t slotMask;` is declared without initialization. Line 62 calls `getReleasedBuffers(&slotMask)`, which may return without writing the mask on error paths. Line 63 then unconditionally writes `static_cast<int64_t>(slotMask)` into the reply Parcel, so an uninitialized stack value is returned to the remote caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly transfers an uninitialized stack value into an externally visible reply, exposing internal memory contents to an unauthorized caller, which fits CWE-200 information exposure. The underlying defect is uninitialized use; the supported impact is confidentiality loss via the reply Parcel.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an uninitialized local `slotMask` is serialized into the Binder reply when `getReleasedBuffers` does not set it. Trigger: a crafted application invokes GET_RELEASED_BUFFERS such that the callee fails or skips writing the out-parameter. Consequence: uninitialized stack memory contents are disclosed to the caller, leaking potentially sensitive process state.

description: Xen 4.6.x, 4.5.x, 4.4.x, 4.3.x, and earlier do not initialize x86 FPU stack and XMM registers when XSAVE/XRSTOR are not used to manage guest extended register state, which allows local guest domains to obtain sensitive information from other domains via unspecified vectors.

code_evidence: The else branch allocates the FPU context with _xzalloc but, when allocation succeeds, returns without initializing the FPU control word (fcw) or MXCSR. The prior code only set rc on allocation failure, so a successfully allocated fpu_ctxt retains zeroed/default register state that is later exposed to the guest.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to initialize sensitive register state before it becomes accessible to a guest, directly enabling disclosure of information to an unauthorized actor. This fits CWE-200's information exposure to an unauthorized party rather than a memory-safety defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocated FPU/SSE save area is never initialized with FCW_DEFAULT and MXCSR_DEFAULT, so stale or zeroed register contents persist. Trigger: a guest domain first using this FPU context reads its register state. Consequence: the guest can obtain residual register values, a confidentiality exposure across domains.

description: A local privilege escalation vulnerability was found on polkit's pkexec utility. The pkexec application is a setuid tool designed to allow unprivileged users to run commands as privileged users according predefined policies. The current version of pkexec doesn't handle the calling parameters count correctly and ends trying to execute environment variables as commands. An attacker can leverage this by crafting environment variables in such a way it'll induce pkexec to execute arbitrary code. When successfully executed the attack can cause a local privilege escalation given unprivileged users administrative rights on the target machine.

code_evidence: At line 136 the code asserts argv[argc]==NULL and then reads argv[n] at line 137 where n is the index at which option parsing broke (or argc when all args were options). When argv[argc] is the NULL terminator, path becomes NULL and the shell branch runs.

Lines 153-162: when path is not absolute, g_find_program_in_path is called and the result s is written back via argv[n]=path=s. If n equals argc (all arguments parsed as options), this writes at argv[argc], overwriting the NULL terminator of the argv array rather than an element inside it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an out-of-bounds write: argv[n] is assigned when n==argc, writing past the last valid element of the argv buffer and clobbering its NULL terminator. This matches CWE-787's write-past-end description, distinct from a mere NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476) because the write target is valid memory just outside the intended array bound.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes the argument list always contains a program after the options, so n < argc, and writes argv[n] without bounding n against argc. Trigger: invoke the setuid pkexec with only option arguments (e.g. --user) so n reaches argc; the write at argv[argc] overwrites the terminating NULL. The corrupted argv is later passed to execv (line 415), so environment-variable-derived strings can be treated as commands, yielding local privilege escalation.

description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. commit_msg:
userfaultfd: non-cooperative: fix fork use after free

When reading the event from the uffd, we put it on a temporary
fork_event list to detect if we can still access it after releasing and
retaking the event_wqh.lock.

If fork aborts and removes the event from the fork_event all is fine as
long as we're still in the userfault read context and fork_event head is
still alive.

We've to put the event allocated in the fork kernel stack, back from
fork_event list-head to the event_wqh head, before returning from
userfaultfd_ctx_read, because the fork_event head lifetime is limited to
the userfaultfd_ctx_read stack lifetime.

Forgetting to move the event back to its event_wqh place then results in
__remove_wait_queue(&ctx->event_wqh, &ewq->wq); in
userfaultfd_event_wait_completion to remove it from a head that has been
already freed from the reader stack.

This could only happen if resolve_userfault_fork failed (for example if
there are no file descriptors available to allocate the fork uffd).  If
it succeeded it was put back correctly.

Furthermore, after find_userfault_evt receives a fork event, the forked
userfault context in fork_nctx and uwq->msg.arg.reserved.reserved1 can
be released by the fork thread as soon as the event_wqh.lock is
released.  Taking a reference on the fork_nctx before dropping the lock
prevents an use after free in resolve_userfault_fork().

If the fork side aborted and it already released everything, we still
try to succeed resolve_userfault_fork(), if possible.

Fixes: 893e26e61d04eac9 ("userfaultfd: non-cooperative: Add fork() event")

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in fs/userfaultfd.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.6. The issue is related to the handling of fork failure when dealing with event messages. Failure to fork correctly can lead to a situation where a fork event will be removed from an already freed list of events with userfaultfd_ctx_put().

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function manipulates wait-queue list entries and reference counts; the described flaw is a use-after-free of a freed list head/context (CWE-416), not an operation outside a memory buffer's intended boundary, so CWE-119 is not directly supported.

code_evidence: Line 7 dereferences ctrl_sock->sk and treats the resulting l2cap_pi(ctrl_sock->sk)->chan as a valid l2cap_chan before any validation. description: An issue was discovered in Pure-FTPd 1.0.49. An out-of-bounds (OOB) read has been detected in the pure_strcmp function in utils.c.

code_evidence: pure_strcmp calls pure_memcmp with a length of strlen(s1)+1U, so the comparison length is derived solely from s1 and ignores the actual length of s2.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads beyond the end of the s2 buffer rather than writing out of bounds. The missing length check on s2 is the direct cause of the over-read.

evidence_lines.code: return pure_memcmp(s1, s2, strlen(s1) + 1U);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the comparison length is computed from s1 only, so if s2 is shorter than s1, pure_memcmp reads strlen(s1)+1 bytes from s2 past its terminating NUL. Trigger: a caller passes a short s2. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read of s2 memory, potentially leaking adjacent bytes or crashing.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                !DoReadFile (infile, &ds64_chunk, chunk_header.ckSize, &bcount) ||', '                bcount != chunk_header.ckSize) {', '                !WavpackAddWrapper (wpc, &ds64_chunk, chunk_header.ckSize)) {'], 'added_lines': ['                !DoReadFile (infile, &ds64_chunk, sizeof (DS64Chunk), &bcount) ||', '                bcount != sizeof (DS64Chunk)) {', '                !WavpackAddWrapper (wpc, &ds64_chunk, sizeof (DS64Chunk))) {']}
description: A stack-based buffer over-read in the ParseRiffHeaderConfig function of cli/riff.c file of WavPack 5.1.0 allows a remote attacker to cause a denial-of-service attack or possibly have unspecified other impact via a maliciously crafted RF64 file.

code_evidence: The ds64 branch accepts any chunk_header.ckSize >= sizeof(DS64Chunk) and then calls DoReadFile with that attacker-controlled chunk_header.ckSize as the read length into the fixed stack buffer ds64_chunk.
The same oversized chunk_header.ckSize is passed to WavpackAddWrapper, which reads that many bytes from the fixed-size ds64_chunk buffer.
Only later does the code compare ds64_chunk.tableLength * sizeof(CS64Chunk) against chunk_header.ckSize - sizeof(DS64Chunk), so the over-read already occurs before any size consistency check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads a fixed stack buffer using an unbounded, attacker-controlled length, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). This is not a write overflow, since the excess data is read from, not written into, ds64_chunk.

evidence_lines.code:
else if (!(config->qmode & QMODE_NO_STORE_WRAPPER) &&
!WavpackAddWrapper (wpc, &ds64_chunk, chunk_header.ckSize)) {
if (ds64_chunk.tableLength * sizeof (CS64Chunk) != chunk_header.ckSize - sizeof (DS64Chunk)) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ds64 read length is taken from the untrusted chunk_header.ckSize rather than bounded to sizeof(DS64Chunk), although the destination is a fixed stack buffer. Trigger: a crafted RF64 file with a ds64 chunk whose ckSize exceeds sizeof(DS64Chunk). Consequence: DoReadFile and WavpackAddWrapper read past the end of ds64_chunk, causing an out-of-bounds read and potential crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
Security: more cmsgpack fixes by @soloestoy.

@soloestoy sent me this additional fixes, after searching for similar
problems to the one reported in mp_pack(). I'm committing the changes
because it was not possible during to make a public PR to protect Redis
users and give Redis providers some time to patch their systems.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    luaL_checkstack(L, 1, "in function mp_decode_to_lua_array");']}
description: Memory Corruption was discovered in the cmsgpack library in the Lua subsystem in Redis before 3.2.12, 4.x before 4.0.10, and 5.x before 5.0 RC2 because of stack-based buffer overflows.

code_evidence: The function decodes a msgpack array of length len into a Lua table. After creating the table, the while loop pushes two values per iteration (lua_pushnumber and mp_decode_to_lua_type) while only calling lua_settable to pop them; the loop runs len times with no stack-depth check before the added luaL_checkstack line.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The added luaL_checkstack guards the loop's pushes, and its absence directly permits writing past the Lua stack buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely an unchecked length (CWE-1284); the concrete defect is the resulting out-of-bounds stack write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decode loop grows the Lua stack by up to two slots per iteration without ensuring the stack has room for the requested len. Trigger: a crafted msgpack array with a large declared length causes unbounded pushes, overflowing the fixed Lua stack buffer. Consequence: stack-based buffer overflow, memory corruption and possible code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
ALSA: seq: Fix use-after-free at creating a port

There is a potential race window opened at creating and deleting a
port via ioctl, as spotted by fuzzing.  snd_seq_create_port() creates
a port object and returns its pointer, but it doesn't take the
refcount, thus it can be deleted immediately by another thread.
Meanwhile, snd_seq_ioctl_create_port() still calls the function
snd_seq_system_client_ev_port_start() with the created port object
that is being deleted, and this triggers use-after-free like:

 BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in snd_seq_ioctl_create_port+0x504/0x630 [snd_seq] at addr ffff8801f2241cb1

 	___slab_alloc+0x425/0x460

  	kmem_cache_alloc_trace+0x150/0x190
	snd_seq_create_port+0x94/0x9b0 [snd_seq]

  [<ffffffff81b03781>] dump_stack+0x63/0x82
  [<ffffffff81531b3b>] print_trailer+0xfb/0x160
  [<ffffffff81536db4>] object_err+0x34/0x40
  [<ffffffff815392d3>] kasan_report.part.2+0x223/0x520
  [<ffffffffa07aadf4>] ? snd_seq_ioctl_create_port+0x504/0x630 [snd_seq]
  [<ffffffff815395fe>] __asan_report_load1_noabort+0x2e/0x30
  [<ffffffffa07aadf4>] snd_seq_ioctl_create_port+0x504/0x630 [snd_seq]

  [<ffffffffa07abd10>] snd_seq_ioctl+0x40/0x80 [snd_seq]

We may fix this in a few different ways, and in this patch, it's fixed
simply by taking the refcount properly at snd_seq_create_port() and
letting the caller unref the object after use.  Also, there is another
potential use-after-free by sprintf() call in snd_seq_create_port(),
and this is moved inside the lock.

This fix covers CVE-2017-15265.

Reported-and-tested-by: Michael23 Yu <ycqzsy@gmail.com>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsprintf(new_port->name, "port-%d", num);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsnd_use_lock_use(&new_port->use_lock);', '\tsprintf(new_port->name, "port-%d", num);']}
description: Race condition in the ALSA subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (use-after-free) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted /dev/snd/seq ioctl calls, related to sound/core/seq/seq_clientmgr.c and sound/core/seq/seq_ports.c.

code_evidence: The newly allocated port is initialized and linked into client->ports_list_head at [32] while holding ports_lock, but the sprintf at [37] writing new_port->name occurs after write_unlock_irqrestore and mutex_unlock at [35,36].

The refcount is only initialized via snd_use_lock_init at [20]; the function returns new_port at [38] without taking a reference, so a concurrent delete path can free the object before the caller uses it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes a shared resource (the port object) to concurrent deletion without exclusive access or a refcount, so an interfering code sequence can free it while the creating sequence still accesses it. This improper synchronization window is exactly CWE-362; the use-after-free is the downstream consequence, not the root weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
new_port = kzalloc(sizeof(*new_port), GFP_KERNEL);
snd_use_lock_init(&new_port->use_lock);

list_add_tail(&new_port->list, &p->list);
sprintf(new_port->name, "port-%d", num);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the port is published to the shared list under lock but the name write at [37] and the returned pointer are not protected by a held reference. Trigger: a concurrent ioctl deletes the port immediately after it is linked, while the creating thread still writes new_port->name or the caller dereferences the returned pointer. Consequence: use-after-free, leading to KASAN crash/DoS and potentially other impact.

commit_msg: Fix for #4866: Added additional length checks
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (Stream_GetPosition(channel->dvc_data) + dataSize > (UINT32) Stream_Capacity(', '\t\t        channel->dvc_data))', '\t\tStream_Write(channel->dvc_data, Stream_Pointer(data), dataSize);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (Stream_GetPosition(channel->dvc_data) + dataSize > Stream_Capacity(channel->dvc_data))', '\t\tStream_Copy(data, channel->dvc_data, dataSize);']}
description: FreeRDP FreeRDP 2.0.0-rc3 released version before commit 205c612820dac644d665b5bb1cdf437dc5ca01e3 contains a Other/Unknown vulnerability in channels/drdynvc/client/drdynvc_main.c, drdynvc_process_capability_request that can result in The RDP server can read the client's memory.. This attack appear to be exploitable via RDPClient must connect the rdp server with echo option. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in after commit 205c612820dac644d665b5bb1cdf437dc5ca01e3.

code_evidence: dataSize is derived from the remaining length of the attacker-controlled network stream, so it is not a trusted bound.

When fragmented data exists, the check compares the current position plus dataSize against Stream_Capacity of the destination buffer; if it exceeds capacity the buffer is released and ERROR_INVALID_DATA is returned.
Stream_Write copies dataSize bytes from the source stream pointer into the destination buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is reading source data without ensuring dataSize is bounded by the source stream's valid remaining length, causing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The capacity check only constrains the destination, so it does not prevent reading beyond the source buffer; this is a read overrun rather than a write overflow.

evidence_lines.code: size_t dataSize = Stream_GetRemainingLength(data);
Stream_Write(channel->dvc_data, Stream_Pointer(data), dataSize);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The destination capacity check is present, but the source read length (dataSize) is computed from the input stream's remaining length. If the check passes but the source stream pointer has fewer valid bytes than dataSize, Stream_Write reads past the end of the source stream buffer. The trigger is a fragmented channel-data message whose declared/remaining size exceeds the actual valid source data, leading to an out-of-bounds read of client memory.

commit_msg: Fixed #5645: realloc return handling
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\ttmp = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\t\t\ttmp = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\t\t\ttmp = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\t\t\ttmp = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\t\t\ttmp = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\t\t\ttmp = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));'], 'added_lines': ['\tLPSTR tmp2 = NULL;', '\t{', '\t\ttmp2 = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\tif (!tmp2)', '\t\t\tfree(tmp);', '\t\ttmp = tmp2;', '\t}', '\t\t\t\ttmp2 = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\t\t\tif (!tmp2)', '\t\t\t\t\tfree(tmp);', '\t\t\t\ttmp = tmp2;', '\t\t\t\ttmp2 = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\t\t\tif (!tmp2)', '\t\t\t\t\tfree(tmp);', '\t\t\t\ttmp = tmp2;', '\t\t\t\ttmp2 = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\t\t\tif (!tmp2)', '\t\t\t\t\tfree(tmp);', '\t\t\t\ttmp = tmp2;', '\t\t\t\ttmp2 = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\t\t\tif (!tmp2)', '\t\t\t\t\tfree(tmp);', '\t\t\t\ttmp = tmp2;', '\t\t\t\ttmp2 = (LPSTR)realloc(tmp, ds * sizeof(CHAR));', '\t\t\t\tif (!tmp2)', '\t\t\t\t\tfree(tmp);', '\t\t\t\ttmp = tmp2;']}
description: libfreerdp/codec/region.c in FreeRDP through 1.1.x and 2.x through 2.0.0-rc4 has memory leaks because a supplied realloc pointer (i.e., the first argument to realloc) is also used for a realloc return value.

code_evidence: realloc return is assigned directly to tmp; if realloc fails it returns NULL, so tmp is overwritten and the original buffer pointer is lost. The NULL check at line 14 then exits, but the prior allocation can no longer be freed.
Same pattern at line 27: the realloc result replaces tmp, and on failure the original block is leaked before the exit(-3) check.
Same pattern at line 56 for the apostrophe case: tmp is overwritten by the realloc return and the original allocation is leaked when realloc returns NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-252 fits because the return value of realloc is not properly checked before the pointer is overwritten; the failure condition is detected only after the original pointer is lost. The commit fixes this by using a separate tmp2 and freeing tmp on failure, confirming the unchecked/improperly handled return value as the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function stores realloc's return value into the same pointer that holds the existing allocation. On allocation failure realloc returns NULL, the only reference to the original block is overwritten, and the subsequent NULL check exits without freeing it, leaking the previously allocated buffer. Trigger is a realloc failure (e.g., allocation-size exhaustion) during escaping.

commit_msg:
USB: serial: omninet: fix reference leaks at open

This driver needlessly took another reference to the tty on open, a
reference which was then never released on close. This lead to not just
a leak of the tty, but also a driver reference leak that prevented the
driver from being unloaded after a port had once been opened.

Fixes: 4a90f09b20f4 ("tty: usb-serial krefs")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>	# 2.6.28
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct usb_serial\t*serial = port->serial;', '\tstruct usb_serial_port\t*wport;', '', '\twport = serial->port[1];', '\ttty_port_tty_set(&wport->port, tty);', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: The omninet_open function in drivers/usb/serial/omninet.c in the Linux kernel before 4.10.4 allows local users to cause a denial of service (tty exhaustion) by leveraging reference count mishandling.

code_evidence: omninet_open resolves the second port via serial->port[1] and calls tty_port_tty_set(&wport->port, tty) on open, associating the caller's tty with wport without any corresponding release on close; the function then returns via usb_serial_generic_open.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 fits because a resource (tty reference) is acquired on open but never properly released, causing resource exhaustion. This is improper release rather than a simple null dereference or type confusion, since the defect is the unbalanced lifetime of the reference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the open path takes a tty reference for the companion port without a matching put in the close path, so the resource is never released. Trigger: repeatedly opening the device. Consequence: tty and driver reference exhaustion, leading to denial of service and preventing driver unload.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/601
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if ((image != image2) && (image2 != (Image *) NULL))', '          image2=DestroyImage(image2);', '        if (clone_info)', '          clone_info=DestroyImageInfo(clone_info);']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.0.6-2, a memory leak vulnerability was found in the function ReadMATImage in coders/mat.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service.

code_evidence: In the CellType switch, the default branch calls ThrowReaderException at line 223 without first releasing image2 (which may be a decompressed clone distinct from image) or clone_info (allocated at line 93), so the exception path leaks both resources.

Within the frame loop, clone_info is cloned at line 93 and image2 may be reassigned to a decompressed image at line 98; these are only conditionally freed in later blocks, leaving the default-case exception path with no cleanup.
The function later shows the intended cleanup pattern at lines 433-434, confirming that image2 must be destroyed when distinct from image, which the default branch omits.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 covers failing to release a resource after its effective lifetime, which is exactly the missing DestroyImageInfo/DestroyImage cleanup on the exception path; the impact is memory-consumption DoS, matching the target weakness rather than a memory-safety corruption.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((image != image2) && (image2 != (Image *) NULL))
image2=DestroyImage(image2);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the default case throws a reader exception before releasing clone_info and a distinct image2. Trigger: a crafted MAT file with an unsupported CellType reaches line 222. The un-freed ImageInfo and/or Image buffer accumulates across repeated reads, producing a memory leak that can exhaust memory and cause denial of service.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.6 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.12, the Bluetooth L2CAP dissector could divide by zero. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-btl2cap.c by validating an interval value.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function is protocol/field registration code; the only change is a display label string, and it contains no division or interval validation, so it does not support CWE-369.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        static XRefEntry dummy;', '        dummy.offset = 0;', '        dummy.gen = -1;', '        dummy.type = xrefEntryNone;', '        dummy.flags = 0;', '        return &dummy;'], 'added_lines': ['      if (unlikely(i >= capacity)) {', '\terror(errInternal, -1, "Request for out-of-bounds XRef entry [{0:d}]", i);', '\treturn &dummyXRefEntry;', '      }', '', '\treturn &dummyXRefEntry;']}
description: XRef::getEntry in XRef.cc in Poppler 0.72.0 mishandles unallocated XRef entries, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via a crafted PDF document, when XRefEntry::setFlag in XRef.h is called from Parser::makeStream in Parser.cc.

code_evidence: When the requested index is out of range or unallocated, the code enters the branch and, with a non-stream xref and a main offset, calls parseEntry directly on &entries[i] without first confirming i is within capacity.
The bounds check at line 10 only covers the reconstructed-xref path and returns a dummy; the direct parseEntry path has no such guard, so entries[i] can be accessed out of bounds.
The function unconditionally returns &entries[i], propagating a pointer derived from an out-of-range index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is dereferencing an invalid/NULL entry pointer obtained from getEntry, matching CWE-476. It is not primarily an out-of-bounds write, since the defect manifests as use of an invalid pointer that callers dereference.

evidence_lines.code: return &entries[i];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the direct parseEntry path lacks an index/capacity check for entries[i], so a crafted PDF that drives an out-of-range or unallocated XRef index causes access to an invalid entry. The caller later uses the returned entry (e.g., setFlag), leading to a NULL/invalid pointer dereference and a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix ANSI Escape Sequence Injection vulns via DWARF ##vuln

* Reported by @solid-snail via huntrdev
* BountyID: 583133af-7ae6-4a21-beef-a4b0182cf82e
* Reproducer: dwarf_test_func_patched
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tr_str_ansi_strip (o);']}
description: Failure to Sanitize Special Elements into a Different Plane (Special Element Injection) in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.8.2.

code_evidence: Line 6 copies caller-supplied string s into o; lines 10-11 strip only CR and TAB, and the new line 12 creates the list without any ANSI/escape-sequence removal. The loop at 19-31 then splits on newlines and appends each non-comment line via strdup (23) to the list consumed by r_cons_hud_line (32).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits because untrusted input is used to build records (HUD lines) without neutralizing special elements that a downstream component (the terminal/HUD renderer) interprets. The patch adding r_str_ansi_strip confirms the missing neutralization of escape elements; this is special-element injection rather than a memory-safety defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: externally influenced DWARF/input text is copied and only CR/TAB are neutralized, so embedded ANSI escape sequences survive into the HUD entries. Trigger: a crafted string containing terminal control sequences is passed in; the resulting lines are rendered by the HUD downstream, allowing the sequences to alter terminal interpretation. Supported consequence is injection into a downstream terminal consumer (display/execution-logic manipulation), not memory corruption.

commit_msg:
crypto: hmac - require that the underlying hash algorithm is unkeyed

Because the HMAC template didn't check that its underlying hash
algorithm is unkeyed, trying to use "hmac(hmac(sha3-512-generic))"
through AF_ALG or through KEYCTL_DH_COMPUTE resulted in the inner HMAC
being used without having been keyed, resulting in sha3_update() being
called without sha3_init(), causing a stack buffer overflow.

This is a very old bug, but it seems to have only started causing real
problems when SHA-3 support was added (requires CONFIG_CRYPTO_SHA3)
because the innermost hash's state is ->import()ed from a zeroed buffer,
and it just so happens that other hash algorithms are fine with that,
but SHA-3 is not.  However, there could be arch or hardware-dependent
hash algorithms also affected; I couldn't test everything.

Fix the bug by introducing a function crypto_shash_alg_has_setkey()
which tests whether a shash algorithm is keyed.  Then update the HMAC
template to require that its underlying hash algorithm is unkeyed.

Here is a reproducer:

    #include <linux/if_alg.h>
    #include <sys/socket.h>

    int main()
    {
        int algfd;
        struct sockaddr_alg addr = {
            .salg_type = "hash",
            .salg_name = "hmac(hmac(sha3-512-generic))",
        };
        char key[4096] = { 0 };

        algfd = socket(AF_ALG, SOCK_SEQPACKET, 0);
        bind(algfd, (const struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof(addr));
        setsockopt(algfd, SOL_ALG, ALG_SET_KEY, key, sizeof(key));
    }

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\talg = &salg->base;'], 'added_lines': ['\talg = &salg->base;', '', '\t/* The underlying hash algorithm must be unkeyed */', '\tif (crypto_shash_alg_has_setkey(salg))', '\t\tgoto out_put_alg;', '']}
description: The HMAC implementation (crypto/hmac.c) in the Linux kernel before 4.14.8 does not validate that the underlying cryptographic hash algorithm is unkeyed, allowing a local attacker able to use the AF_ALG-based hash interface (CONFIG_CRYPTO_USER_API_HASH) and the SHA-3 hash algorithm (CONFIG_CRYPTO_SHA3) to cause a kernel stack buffer overflow by executing a crafted sequence of system calls that encounter a missing SHA-3 initialization.

code_evidence: hmac_setkey derives the inner hash from ctx->hash and, when keylen > bs, calls crypto_shash_digest(shash, inkey, keylen, ipad) writing the digest into the ipad buffer; otherwise it memcpy's inkey into ipad.
The final chain initializes, updates with the ipad/opad blocks, and exports state into ipad/opad, assuming the underlying shash was properly initialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the supported consequence is a write beyond the intended buffer (KASAN stack-out-of-bounds in sha3_update) triggered through hmac_setkey's use of an unkeyed inner hash. The root cause is the missing keyed-algorithm check in the template creation, not a mere integrity/DoS condition.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: hmac_setkey assumes the spawned inner hash is a keyed-capable but properly initialized shash. When the inner algorithm is itself HMAC over an uninitialized SHA-3 state, crypto_shash_update processes data without sha3_init having been called, and sha3_update writes past the buffer. The missing constraint is that the underlying hash must be unkeyed, allowing a nested hmac(hmac(sha3-512)) to reach sha3_update with a zeroed state, causing a stack out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/120
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                      ldblk,sizeof(*BImgBuff));'], 'added_lines': ['                      ldblk+1,sizeof(*BImgBuff));']}
description: The ReadWPGImage function in coders/wpg.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted WPG file.

code_evidence: At [407], ldblk is computed as (bpp*columns+7)/8, the packed byte count per row. The buffer is allocated with exactly ldblk bytes at [408,409].

At [414], ReadBlob reads ldblk bytes into BImgBuff; InsertRow at [415] then interprets that buffer. Because the allocation equals the read length, any read that requires one extra byte beyond the packed row (e.g., padding/terminator access) reads past the allocated block.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The allocation at [408,409] is one byte short of what the subsequent ldblk-byte read and InsertRow processing require, so memory past the intended buffer is read — directly matching CWE-125. It is not a write overflow (CWE-787): the fault is reading beyond the allocated row buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the row buffer is sized to ldblk, the exact packed row length, with no extra byte for downstream row-processing code. Trigger: a crafted WPG file whose dimensions/bit depth drive a packed row length that InsertRow or blob reading overruns. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of heap memory, leading to crash/DoS and potential disclosure; the fix allocates ldblk+1.

commit_msg:
libelf: fix stack memory leak when loading 32 bit symbol tables

The 32 bit Elf structs are smaller than the 64 bit ones, which means that
when loading them there's some padding left uninitialized at the end of each
struct (because the size indicated in e_ehsize and e_shentsize is
smaller than the size of elf_ehdr and elf_shdr).

Fix this by introducing a new helper that is used to set
[caller_]xdest_{base/size} and that takes care of performing the appropriate
memset of the region. This newly introduced helper is then used to set and
unset xdest_{base/size} in elf_load_bsdsyms. Now that the full struct
is zeroed, there's no need to specifically zero the undefined section.

This is CVE-2016-9384 / XSA-164.

Suggested-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>

Also remove the open coded (and redundant with the earlier
elf_memset_unchecked()) use of caller_xdest_* from elf_init().

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <Ian.Jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( elf_ptrval_in_range(ptrval, size,', '                             elf->caller_xdest_base, elf->caller_xdest_size) )'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( elf_ptrval_in_range(ptrval, size, elf->xdest_base, elf->xdest_size) )']}
description: Buffer overflow in hw/pt-msi.c in Xen 4.6.x and earlier, when using the qemu-xen-traditional (aka qemu-dm) device model, allows local x86 HVM guest administrators to gain privileges by leveraging a system with access to a passed-through MSI-X capable physical PCI device and MSI-X table entries, related to a "write path."

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only performs range checks against image/dest/xdest regions and returns a boolean; the diff merely renames caller_xdest_* fields to xdest_*, and no out-of-bounds read/write operation on a memory buffer is present in this function.

commit_msg: Fix potential out-of-buffer read while parsing corrupt file, closes #35, #36
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    for (int i = 1; i < 33; i++) {'], 'added_lines': ['    for (int i = 1; i < HUFF_CODETABLE_SIZE; i++) {']}
description: libmobi is vulnerable to Out-of-bounds Read

code_evidence: Lines 27-31 validate that data2 has at least 64*4 bytes available before the loop, but the loop in lines 34-38 reads 32 pairs (64 uint32 reads) while the bound check only guarantees 64*4 bytes—matching only if the loop runs exactly 32 iterations.
Line 34 uses a hardcoded literal 33 instead of HUFF_CODETABLE_SIZE; if the table size differs, the loop can read beyond the validated region and write past mincode_table/maxcode_table.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs buffer reads/writes whose bounds are not consistently restricted, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The commit fixes this by replacing the literal 33 with HUFF_CODETABLE_SIZE, confirming the loop bound was the out-of-bounds source.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The buffer-length check at line 27 is computed with a fixed 64*4 size, but the loop bound at line 34 is a separate hardcoded literal (33). When these disagree with the actual table size, mobi_buffer_get32 reads past the validated data2 region, and the indexed writes to mincode_table/maxcode_table at lines 37-38 can exceed the arrays. The trigger is a corrupt or crafted HUFF record reaching this parse path.

commit_msg: iasecc: fixed unbound recursion
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (lpath.len >= 2 && lpath.value[0] == 0x3F && lpath.value[1] == 0x00)   {', '\t\tif (lpath.len >= 2 && lpath.value[0] == 0x3F && lpath.value[1] == 0x00)\t   {', '\t\t\tmemmove(&lpath.value[0], &lpath.value[2], lpath.len - 2);', '\t\t\tlpath.len -=  2;', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (path->type != SC_PATH_TYPE_DF_NAME', '\t\t\t&& lpath.len >= 2', '\t\t\t&& lpath.value[0] == 0x3F && lpath.value[1] == 0x00)   {', '\t\tmemmove(&lpath.value[0], &lpath.value[2], lpath.len - 2);', '\t\tlpath.len -=  2;']}
description: Endless recursion when handling responses from an IAS-ECC card in iasecc_select_file in libopensc/card-iasecc.c in OpenSC before 0.19.0-rc1 could be used by attackers able to supply crafted smartcards to hang or crash the opensc library using programs.

code_evidence: When lpath begins with 3F00, the code calls iasecc_select_mf and then strips those two bytes from lpath only if the same prefix test still holds; the inner guard is redundant but the outer block is entered based on path content alone, without checking path->type.
If lpath.aid.len is set, a new ppath is built from the AID with type SC_PATH_TYPE_DF_NAME and iasecc_select_file is recursively invoked on it.

On SC_ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND with a cached DF, the function invalidates the cache and recursively calls iasecc_select_file(card, path, file_out) with the original path, which can re-enter the same state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the weakness is unbounded self-recursion in iasecc_select_file driven by card-supplied responses, causing resource exhaustion. The missing constraint is a termination/progress check on recursive re-entry; the consequence is stack consumption/DoS rather than a memory-safety corruption such as CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function recurses on AID paths and, on file-not-found with a cached DF, re-invokes itself with the unchanged original path. A crafted smartcard response that keeps producing file-not-found while the cache/DF state is reapplied can drive repeated self-calls without a recursion-depth or progress bound, exhausting the stack and hanging or crashing the library.

commit_msg: Fix crash when mapping a big memory and calling uc_close
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    QLIST_REMOVE(block, next);'], 'added_lines': ['    QLIST_REMOVE_RCU(block, next);']}
description: Unicorn Engine v2.0.0-rc7 and below was discovered to contain a NULL pointer dereference via qemu_ram_free.

code_evidence: Lines 3-5 guard only the incoming block pointer, returning early when it is NULL.
Line 6 performs QLIST_REMOVE(block, next), which manipulates block's list linkage; line 7 sets uc->ram_list.mru_block to NULL and line 8 reclaims the block.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the confirmed impact is a NULL pointer dereference causing a crash in qemu_ram_free, consistent with the commit message and description. The root cause is insufficient validation/RCU-safe removal of the RAMBlock list rather than a general use-after-free classification.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function checks block for NULL but does not validate the list linkage or the concurrent removal path; QLIST_REMOVE is a non-RCU-safe list unlink, so when a big memory mapping is freed and uc_close races, the linkage/mru_block state can lead to dereferencing an invalid or NULL pointer in qemu_ram_free. The supported consequence is a crash (DoS) from NULL pointer dereference.

commit_msg:
drm/nouveau/mmu: add more general vmm free/node handling functions

Aside from being a nice cleanup, these will to allow the upcoming direct
page mapping interfaces to play nicely with normal mappings.

Signed-off-by: Ben Skeggs <bskeggs@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct nvkm_vma *next;', '\tif (vma->part) {', '\t\tstruct nvkm_vma *prev = node(vma, prev);', '\t\tif (!prev->memory) {', '\t\t\tprev->size += vma->size;', '\t\t\trb_erase(&vma->tree, &vmm->root);', '\t\t\tlist_del(&vma->head);', '\t\t\tkfree(vma);', '\t\t\tvma = prev;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '', '\tnext = node(vma, next);', '\tif (next && next->part) {', '\t\tif (!next->memory) {', '\t\t\tvma->size += next->size;', '\t\t\trb_erase(&next->tree, &vmm->root);', '\t\t\tlist_del(&next->head);', '\t\t\tkfree(next);', '\t\t}', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct nvkm_vma *next = node(vma, next);', '\tstruct nvkm_vma *prev = NULL;', '\tif (!vma->part || ((prev = node(vma, prev)), prev->memory))', '\t\tprev = NULL;', '\tif (!next->part || next->memory)', '\t\tnext = NULL;', '\tnvkm_vmm_node_merge(vmm, prev, vma, next, vma->size);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s nouveau driver in how a user triggers a memory overflow that causes the nvkm_vma_tail function to fail. This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: When vma->part is set and the previous node has no memory, lines 10-13 merge sizes, erase the node and free vma, then line 14 reassigns vma to prev.

After that free, line 17 computes next = node(vma, next) on the reassigned prev, and lines 18-23 may read next->part, next->memory and next->size, then free next; the freed original vma is not used again.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Although kfree(vma) at line 13 and kfree(next) at line 23 free nodes, subsequent uses go through the updated vma or a freshly computed next, not the freed pointer. This does not demonstrate reuse of freed memory, so CWE-416 is not directly supported by this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function frees a merged VMA and reassigns the local pointer to the retained predecessor before continuing, so the freed object is not dereferenced afterward. The described nvkm_vma_tail overflow is not represented in this function; no read, write or free through a stale pointer is shown here.

description: In the Linux kernel before 5.0.3, a memory leak exits in hsr_dev_finalize() in net/hsr/hsr_device.c if hsr_add_port fails to add a port, which may cause denial of service, aka CID-6caabe7f197d.

code_evidence: hsr_create_self_node() allocates a self node and links it into hsr->self_node_db; its return value is checked but the node is not released on any later failure path.
hsr_add_port(hsr, hsr_dev, HSR_PT_MASTER) failure returns res directly at line 27, bypassing the fail cleanup that only deletes ports via hsr_for_each_port/hsr_del_port.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The self node allocated by hsr_create_self_node() is only released on the success path; the early return when hsr_add_port() fails skips all cleanup. Repeated device creation failures leak the node and its list linkage, causing unbounded memory consumption and potential denial of service.

commit_msg:
x86/spec-ctrl: Enumerations for Speculative Return Stack Overflow

AMD have specified new CPUID bits relating to SRSO.

 * SRSO_NO indicates that hardware is no longer vulnerable to SRSO.
 * IBPB_BRTYPE indicates that IBPB flushes branch type information too.
 * SBPB indicates support for a relaxed form of IBPB that does not flush
   branch type information.

Current CPUs (Zen4 and older) are not expected to enumerate these bits.
Native software is expected to synthesise them for guests using model and
microcode revision checks.

Two are just status bits, and SBPB is trivial to support for guests by
tweaking the reserved bit calculation in guest_wrmsr() and feature
dependencies.  Expose all by default to guests, so they start showing up when
Xen synthesises them.

While adding feature dependenies for IBPB, fix up an overlooked issue from
XSA-422.  It's inappropriate to advertise that IBPB flushes RET predictions if
IBPB is unavailable itself.

This is part of XSA-434 / CVE-2023-20569

commit_msg:
mp4: limit the recursion depth for boxes

Although the dissection of each box header consumes a couple of bytes,
it turned out that it's still possible to crash wireshark with a sample
file that contains a large number of nested boxes. The stack will fill
up before we reach the end of the data bytes.

Keep track of the recursion depth as we walk through the hierarchy of
boxes. Abort if we reach the (locally defined) upper limit.

commit_msg:
ARM: 7735/2: Preserve the user r/w register TPIDRURW on context switch and fork

Since commit 6a1c53124aa1 the user writeable TLS register was zeroed to
prevent it from being used as a covert channel between two tasks.

There are more and more applications coming to Windows RT,
Wine could support them, but mostly they expect to have
the thread environment block (TEB) in TPIDRURW.

This patch preserves that register per thread instead of clearing it.
Unlike the TPIDRURO, which is already switched, the TPIDRURW
can be updated from userspace so needs careful treatment in the case that we
modify TPIDRURW and call fork(). To avoid this we must always read
TPIDRURW in copy_thread.

Signed-off-by: André Hentschel <nerv@dawncrow.de>
Signed-off-by: Will Deacon <will.deacon@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Jonathan Austin <jonathan.austin@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Russell King <rmk+kernel@arm.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tregs->uregs[reg] = current_thread_info()->tp_value;'], 'added_lines': ['\tregs->uregs[reg] = current_thread_info()->tp_value[0];']}
description: The Linux kernel before 3.11 on ARM platforms, as used in Android before 2016-08-05 on Nexus 5 and 7 (2013) devices, does not properly consider user-space access to the TPIDRURW register, which allows local users to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka Android internal bug 28749743 and Qualcomm internal bug CR561044.

code_evidence: get_tp_trap decodes a register index from the trapped instruction and, unless it is 15, writes current_thread_info()->tp_value into regs->uregs[reg]. This emulates user-space reads of the TPIDRURW thread register from the saved thread context. The value written is the per-thread tp_value, so the access path exposes that stored register content to the user process.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission and privilege management. Here the handler permits user-space access to a privileged thread register, a permission-boundary failure. The specific result (privilege escalation) is a consequence, not the root cause; the missing access restriction is what fits this permissions category.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the trap handler returns the thread's TPIDRURW value through the emulated register without restricting user-space access to this register. Trigger: a crafted application executes a TPIDRURW read that traps into this handler. Supported consequence: user space can observe a register value that should be isolated, enabling privilege-relevant abuse as described for this ARM context-switch handling.

description: In CollectValuesOrEntriesImpl of elements.cc, there is possible remote code execution due to type confusion. This could lead to remote escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation. Product: Android. Versions: Android-7.0 Android-7.1.1 Android-7.1.2 Android-8.0 Android-8.1 Android-9.0 Android ID: A-111274046

code_evidence: The function casts object->elements() directly to FixedArray and keeps a raw parameter_map handle, assuming the elements kind stays fixed during iteration.
element_k is fetched via Subclass::GetImpl from the cached parameter_map at an index computed by GetEntryForIndexImpl, tying the value type to the cached backing store.

When the element is an AccessorPair, an accessor is invoked; a user getter can mutate the object's elements, so the cached parameter_map no longer matches the object's current elements, and subsequent GetImpl reads through a stale, possibly wrong-kind FixedArray.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-704 fits because the code reuses a FixedArray cast/handle after the underlying object's type (elements kind) changed, treating data as the wrong type. This is a stale-reference type confusion rather than a simple bounds error.

evidence_lines.code:
Handle<FixedArray> parameter_map(FixedArray::cast(object->elements()),
isolate);

Handle<Object> element_k =
Subclass::GetImpl(isolate, *parameter_map, entry);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop caches parameter_map and only detects map changes after an accessor call, but the accessor can replace the elements backing store, so the cached FixedArray is reused for a different elements kind. Trigger: an accessor getter that mutates the object's elements during iteration. Consequence: type confusion when reading elements through the stale backing store.

description: The rs_filter_graph function in librawstudio/rs-filter.c in rawstudio might allow local users to truncate arbitrary files via a symlink attack on (1) /tmp/rs-filter-graph.png or (2) /tmp/rs-filter-graph.

code_evidence: g_file_set_contents writes attacker-predictable path /tmp/rs-filter-graph; a pre-existing symlink at that location is followed, truncating/overwriting the link target.
system() invokes dot with redirection to /tmp/rs-filter-graph.png and reads from /tmp/rs-filter-graph, so the output symlink is followed and the attacker-chosen target is truncated.
system() runs gnome-open on /tmp/rs-filter-graph.png, following any symlink at that predictable path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses files by predictable names and fails to prevent those names from resolving through symlinks to unintended resources, matching CWE-59 link following. This is not merely a predictable-name race; the core defect is following a link before file access.

evidence_lines.code: g_file_set_contents("/tmp/rs-filter-graph", str->str, str->len, NULL);
if (0 != system("dot -Tpng >/tmp/rs-filter-graph.png </tmp/rs-filter-graph"))
if (0 != system("gnome-open /tmp/rs-filter-graph.png"))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fixed, world-writable /tmp filenames are accessed without O_EXCL or symlink checks, so the paths are not guaranteed to name regular files. Trigger: a local attacker pre-creates /tmp/rs-filter-graph.png (or the dot file) as a symlink; the shell redirection and g_file_set_contents follow it. Consequence: truncation/modification of arbitrary files writable by the victim (integrity/availability impact).

description: The ReadOneLayer function in coders/xcf.c in ImageMagick 7.0.6-6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a crafted file.

tile_image->columns*tile_image->rows),sizeof(*xcfdata));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocation size is driven by the untrusted file's data_length (line 30-31) with no upper bound check, so a crafted XCF file can request a very large buffer. commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: remove nodes owned by destroyed domain

In case a domain is removed from Xenstore, remove all nodes owned by
it per default.

This tackles the problem that nodes might be created by a domain
outside its home path in Xenstore, leading to Xenstore hogging more
and more memory. Domain quota don't work in this case if the guest is
rebooting in between.

Since XSA-322 ownership of such stale nodes is transferred to dom0,
which is helping against unintended access, but not against OOM of
Xenstore.

As a fallback for weird cases add a Xenstore start parameter for
keeping today's way to handle stale nodes, adding the risk of Xenstore
hitting an OOM situation.

This is part of XSA-419 / CVE-2022-42322.

Fixes: 496306324d8d ("tools/xenstore: revoke access rights for removed domains")
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>

description: Xenstore: Cooperating guests can create arbitrary numbers of nodes T[his CNA information record relates to multiple CVEs; the text explains which aspects/vulnerabilities correspond to which CVE.] Since the fix of XSA-322 any Xenstore node owned by a removed domain will be modified to be owned by Dom0. This will allow two malicious guests working together to create an arbitrary number of Xenstore nodes. This is possible by domain A letting domain B write into domain A's local Xenstore tree. Domain B can then create many nodes and reboot. The nodes created by domain B will now be owned by Dom0. By repeating this process over and over again an arbitrary number of nodes can be created, as Dom0's number of nodes isn't limited by Xenstore quota.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only increments per-domain node entry counters; it contains no memory allocation or release, so it cannot demonstrate a missing-release memory leak (CWE-401).

commit_msg: Add an HTTP/2 related rate limiting
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (Http2::max_priority_frames_per_minute != 0 &&', '      cstate.get_received_priority_frame_count() > Http2::max_priority_frames_per_minute) {'], 'added_lines': ['  if (cstate.configured_max_priority_frames_per_minute != 0 &&', '      cstate.get_received_priority_frame_count() > cstate.configured_max_priority_frames_per_minute) {']}
description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

code_evidence: After each PRIORITY frame the connection counter is incremented (line 32), then the code compares it against the rate limit and returns an ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM connection error when exceeded (lines 33-40). The patch changes the limit source from the global Http2::max_priority_frames_per_minute to cstate.configured_max_priority_frames_per_minute, so throttling is now driven by per-connection configured state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function implements a throttle for the number of PRIORITY frames processed per minute; when that limit is absent or misconfigured, the product fails to restrict a limited resource, matching CWE-400's lack of throttling for allocated resources. This is about resource consumption rather than improper input validation (CWE-20) or memory corruption, so CWE-400 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: PRIORITY frames are accepted and counted per connection, and the only bound on their frequency is the configured max_priority_frames_per_minute value. Trigger: a peer sends many PRIORITY frames; if the configured limit is 0 (disabled) or otherwise too permissive, the counter grows without an effective cap. Consequence: unbounded processing and dependency-tree work per connection, i.e. resource consumption/DoS. The change makes the limit configurable per connection rather than a fixed global, which is the rate-limiting mechanism being adjusted.

commit_msg:
x86: limit GFNs to 32 bits for shadowed superpages.

Superpage shadows store the shadowed GFN in the backpointer field,
which for non-BIGMEM builds is 32 bits wide.  Shadowing a superpage
mapping of a guest-physical address above 2^44 would lead to the GFN
being truncated there, and a crash when we come to remove the shadow
from the hash table.

Track the valid width of a GFN for each guest, including reporting it
through CPUID, and enforce it in the shadow pagetables.  Set the
maximum witth to 32 for guests where this truncation could occur.

This is XSA-173.

Reported-by: Ling Liu <liuling-it@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( !p2m_is_valid(p2mt) && !p2m_is_grant(p2mt) )'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( (!p2m_is_valid(p2mt) && !p2m_is_grant(p2mt))', '         || gfn_x(target_gfn) >> d->arch.paging.gfn_bits )']}
description: Integer overflow in the x86 shadow pagetable code in Xen allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host crash) or possibly gain privileges by shadowing a superpage mapping.

code_evidence: Line 14 extracts target_gfn from the guest-supplied page-table entry. Lines 19-23 check only p2m validity/grant before inserting a shadow entry; the patch adds a gfn_bits bound test so oversized GFNs are rejected rather than truncated in the 32-bit backpointer field.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission/privilege management enabling a guest to exceed its intended access boundary; here missing GFN-range enforcement lets guest-controlled input corrupt host shadow state, supporting DoS or privilege gain. It is not merely a validation bug but a failure to constrain guest privileges over host pagetable structures.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shadow propagation path accepts a guest GFN without constraining it to the width of the backpointer storage, so a superpage mapping above the representable range is truncated. Trigger: a local guest shadows such a mapping; the truncated GFN later mismatches during hash-table removal, causing a host crash or memory corruption that may yield privilege escalation.

Resource requests from Save-Page-As should go through CanRequestURL checks.

This CL:

- Added checks to ResourceDispatcherHostImpl::BeginSaveFile to verify if
  the renderer process is authorized to access a given resource.

- Removed separate code path for file: URIs that used to be implemented
  in SaveFileManager::SaveLocalFile.  Avoiding a separate code path
  helps consolidate all authorization checks in one place.
