Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2075273002
Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#408235}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  SaveFileCreateInfo::SaveFileSource save_source =', '      url.SchemeIsFile() ? SaveFileCreateInfo::SAVE_FILE_FROM_FILE', '                         : SaveFileCreateInfo::SAVE_FILE_FROM_NET;', '      referrer, save_source);'], 'added_lines': ['      referrer, SaveFileCreateInfo::SAVE_FILE_FROM_NET);']}
description: The download implementation in Google Chrome before 53.0.2785.89 on Windows and OS X and before 53.0.2785.92 on Linux does not properly restrict saving a file:// URL that is referenced by an http:// URL, which makes it easier for user-assisted remote attackers to discover NetNTLM hashes and conduct SMB relay attacks via a crafted web page that is accessed with the "Save page as" menu choice.

code_evidence: EnqueueSavableResource derives save_source from url.SchemeIsFile() and passes it to CreatePendingSaveItemDeduplicatingByUrl without any CanRequestURL/authorization check on the renderer-supplied url. A file:// URL reaching this path is tagged SAVE_FILE_FROM_FILE and enqueued for saving, so the local file is read and written into the saved-page output.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing authorization check lets an unprivileged renderer cause sensitive local file data to be read and included in saved output, which is an exposure of information to an unauthorized actor. The weakness is the absent access-control decision on the URL, matching CWE-200's confidentiality-exposure scope rather than a memory-safety or injection error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the renderer-supplied URL and distinguishes file: scheme only to set a source flag, with no check that the requesting process may access that resource. Trigger: a crafted http:// page references a file:// URL and the user chooses Save page as. Consequence: the local file contents are fetched and saved, exposing local data and enabling NetNTLM hash disclosure/SMB relay.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar  strbuf[256];', '\tfor (line = 0; !error && gf_fgets(strbuf, sizeof(strbuf), file); line++)'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar  strbuf[257];', '\tfor (line = 0; !error && gf_fgets(strbuf, 256, file); line++)', '\t\t//make sure we are null-terminated - cf #2520', '\t\tstrbuf[256]=0;']}
description: Out-of-bounds Read in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.2.2.

code_evidence: strbuf is a 256-byte stack buffer. gf_fgets is called with size sizeof(strbuf)=256, so it may fill up to 255 bytes plus a terminator; strtrim then operates on strbuf. If the read line is long or the terminator handling is incomplete, strtrim can scan past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading beyond the intended strbuf bounds is an out-of-bounds read, matching CWE-125. The fix enlarges the buffer to 257 and forces strbuf[256]=0, confirming the missing NUL termination was the defect rather than a write overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the input buffer is sized 256 while the read path does not guarantee a NUL within the buffer before strtrim scans it. A crafted .idx line of sufficient length triggers strtrim to read past strbuf[255], producing an out-of-bounds read (crash/DoS or memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
Prevent crash when histogram is called with NaN values.

Fixes #45770

PiperOrigin-RevId: 443149951
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    // We cannot handle NANs in the algorithm below (due to the case to int32)', '    const Eigen::Tensor<int32, 1, 1> nans_tensor =', '        values.isnan().template cast<int32>();', '    const Eigen::Tensor<int32, 0, 1> reduced_tensor = nans_tensor.sum();', '    const int num_nans = reduced_tensor(0);', '    if (num_nans > 0) {', '      return errors::InvalidArgument("Histogram values must not contain NaN");', '    }']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.histogram_fixed_width` is vulnerable to a crash when the values array contain `Not a Number` (`NaN`) elements. The implementation assumes that all floating point operations are defined and then converts a floating point result to an integer index. If `values` contains `NaN` then the result of the division is still `NaN` and the cast to `int32` would result in a crash. This only occurs on the CPU implementation. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: The function computes a bin index by dividing each input value by `step` and casting the result to `int32` at lines 14-19.
The divisor `step` is derived from `value_range` and `nbins` at lines 11-13, with no check on the input `values`.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an input array without checking that its elements are valid numbers before arithmetic and a narrowing cast, which is a failure to validate input properties required for safe processing. This matches CWE-20. A related weakness such as numeric conversion error could describe the crash, but the underlying defect is absent input validation.

evidence_lines.code:
index_to_bin.device(d) =
((values.cwiseMax(value_range(0)) - values.constant(value_range(0)))
.template cast<double>() /
step)
.cwiseMin(nbins_minus_1)
.template cast<int32>();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The input tensor `values` is not validated for NaN. When a value is NaN, the arithmetic in lines 15-17 yields NaN, and the `.template cast<int32>()` at line 19 converts NaN to an integer, causing a crash. The root cause is missing validation of the `values` input; the consequence is a denial-of-service crash.

commit_msg:
Disable sub frame loads more reliably in frame detach.

Previously, guarding against attaching a new frame in frame detach
was done by inspecting LoadEventProgress. There are certain
operations, such as document.open(), that can cause LoadEventProgress
to never advance, causing the guard to get skipped.

BUG=577105

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1659013003

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#373581}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (owner.document().unloadStarted())', '            return false;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The DOM implementation in Google Chrome before 48.0.2564.109 does not properly restrict frame-attach operations from occurring during or after frame-detach operations, which allows remote attackers to bypass the Same Origin Policy via a crafted web site, related to FrameLoader.cpp, HTMLFrameOwnerElement.h, LocalFrame.cpp, and WebLocalFrameImpl.cpp.

code_evidence: Line 3 checks owner.document().unloadStarted() and returns false, preventing frame loads once the owner document has begun unloading.
Lines 5-7 only reject loads when an ancestor is in disabledSubtreeRoots(); they do not re-check detach/unload state for the owner document.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function governs whether a frame may be loaded/attached, i.e., a security-relevant restriction on frame operations; failing to enforce the unload/detach restriction lets an attacker bypass origin isolation. This fits CWE-264's permissions/access-control category rather than a memory-safety weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (owner.document().unloadStarted())
return false;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the only guard against loading a frame during or after document unload is the unloadStarted() check, which is bypassable when unload state never advances (e.g., document.open()). Trigger: a crafted page detaches a frame while load progress stalls, so canLoadFrame() returns true and permits re-attaching the frame. Consequence: a frame can be attached across a detach boundary, enabling Same Origin Policy bypass.

commit_msg:
Allow fuse device clones to refer to be distinguished.  This patch just
adds the infrastructure by associating a separate "struct fuse_dev" with
each clone.

Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@suse.cz>
Reviewed-by: Ashish Samant <ashish.samant@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tfuse_conn_put(&cc->fc);', '\tfile->private_data = &cc->fc;\t/* channel owns base reference to cc */'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct fuse_dev *fud;', '\tfud = fuse_dev_alloc(&cc->fc);', '\tif (!fud) {', '\t\tkfree(cc);', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\t}', '', '\t\tfuse_dev_free(fud);', '\tfile->private_data = fud;']}
description: Memory leak in the cuse_channel_release function in fs/fuse/cuse.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by opening /dev/cuse many times.

code_evidence: Allocates cuse_conn with kzalloc and initializes the fuse connection; the channel is the sole owner of the base reference to cc->fc.
On successful cuse_send_init, stores &cc->fc in file->private_data; on failure, calls fuse_conn_put and returns, but no per-clone fuse_dev is associated with the file.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources; the leaked fuse connection and repeated opens directly match this category, with CWE-772 as the specific descendant.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The channel's base reference to the fuse connection is stored only in file->private_data and never released on the release path, so each open of /dev/cuse that succeeds leaks the connection and its associated resources. Repeated opens accumulate memory, leading to resource exhaustion/denial of service; the root cause is the unmanaged lifetime of the channel-owned reference.

commit_msg:
Release "3.0.8": Address Array alloc sizing issues from issue "integer overflow and buffer overflow #5".

FossilOrigin-Name: 8c46a1d465b358110dcfb271721d35fe843a1b52f2fa24ccc10094eb8aaf6fe4
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (key >= 0 && key < interp->maxArrayList) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (key >= 0 && (uint)key < interp->maxArrayList) {']}
description: Integer overflow vulnerability in function Jsi_ObjArraySizer in jsish before 3.0.8, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: The function checks a signed int key against the signed maxArrayList bound with key < interp->maxArrayList before using key as an array index in Jsi_ObjArraySet. No unsigned/size conversion is applied to key, so a negative or large value is only screened by the signed comparison; the same commit changed this to (uint)key, indicating the signed comparison failed to constrain the value used for array sizing/indexing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the missing unsigned conversion lets the key/size arithmetic wrap, bypassing the intended bound check; this is an integer overflow/wraparound in a size/index computation, distinct from a plain missing bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the array-list key is validated with a signed comparison against maxArrayList without converting it to an unsigned size type. Trigger: a caller supplies a key whose signed/unsigned interpretation differs, causing the check to pass while the index or size calculation wraps. Consequence: out-of-bounds array access or undersized allocation, enabling memory corruption and potentially code execution.

description: The xps_select_font_encoding function in xps/xpsfont.c in Artifex Ghostscript GhostXPS 9.21 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted document, related to the xps_encode_font_char_imp function.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.2107: [security]: FPE in adjust_plines_for_skipcol

Problem:  [security]: FPE in adjust_plines_for_skipcol
Solution: don't divide by zero, return zero

Prevent a floating point exception when calculating w_skipcol (which can
happen with a small window when the number option is set and cpo+=n).

Add a test to verify

Signed-off-by: Christian Brabandt <cb@256bit.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (wp->w_skipcol >= width)', '\treturn (wp->w_skipcol - width) / (width + win_col_off2(wp)) + 1;'], 'added_lines': ['    int w2 = width + win_col_off2(wp);', '    if (wp->w_skipcol >= width && w2 > 0)', '\treturn (wp->w_skipcol - width) / w2 + 1;']}
description: Vim is an open source command line text editor. A floating point exception may occur when calculating the line offset for overlong lines and smooth scrolling is enabled and the cpo-settings include the 'n' flag. This may happen when a window border is present and when the wrapped line continues on the next physical line directly in the window border because the 'cpo' setting includes the 'n' flag. Only users with non-default settings are affected and the exception should only result in a crash. This issue has been addressed in commit `cb0b99f0` which has been included in release version 9.0.2107. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: Line 6 computes width as w_width minus win_col_off(wp); with a small window and border the resulting width can be zero or negative. Line 7 only checks w_skipcol >= width, and line 8 divides by (width + win_col_off2(wp)) without verifying the divisor is nonzero, so a zero divisor raises a floating point exception (FPE) and crashes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to handle the exceptional zero-divisor condition, letting a floating point exception escape as a crash. CWE-755 fits because the flaw is improper handling of an exceptional condition; the specific arithmetic trigger is incidental to this class-level weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the division on line 8 lacks a nonzero-divisor guard. Trigger: smooth scrolling with 'cpo+=n' and a small bordered window makes width + win_col_off2(wp) equal zero while w_skipcol >= width. Consequence: FPE crash rather than a handled/graceful return.

commit_msg:
Unfortunately, we ended up merging an old version of the patch "fix info
leak with DMA_FROM_DEVICE" instead of merging the latest one. Christoph
(the swiotlb maintainer), he asked me to create an incremental fix
(after I have pointed this out the mix up, and asked him for guidance).
So here we go.

The main differences between what we got and what was agreed are:
* swiotlb_sync_single_for_device is also required to do an extra bounce
* We decided not to introduce DMA_ATTR_OVERWRITE until we have exploiters
* The implantation of DMA_ATTR_OVERWRITE is flawed: DMA_ATTR_OVERWRITE
  must take precedence over DMA_ATTR_SKIP_CPU_SYNC

Thus this patch removes DMA_ATTR_OVERWRITE, and makes
swiotlb_sync_single_for_device() bounce unconditionally (that is, also
when dir == DMA_TO_DEVICE) in order do avoid synchronising back stale
data from the swiotlb buffer.

Let me note, that if the size used with dma_sync_* API is less than the
size used with dma_[un]map_*, under certain circumstances we may still
end up with swiotlb not being transparent. In that sense, this is no
perfect fix either.

To get this bullet proof, we would have to bounce the entire
mapping/bounce buffer. For that we would have to figure out the starting
address, and the size of the mapping in
swiotlb_sync_single_for_device(). While this does seem possible, there
seems to be no firm consensus on how things are supposed to work.

Signed-off-by: Halil Pasic <pasic@linux.ibm.com>
Fixes: ddbd89deb7d3 ("swiotlb: fix info leak with DMA_FROM_DEVICE")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reviewed-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

description: A memory leak flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s DMA subsystem, in the way a user calls DMA_FROM_DEVICE. This flaw allows a local user to read random memory from the kernel space.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only performs swiotlb bounce/sync logic; it contains no allocation, tracking, or release of memory, so it does not support CWE-401.

commit_msg:
KEYS: fix keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring() to not leak thread keyrings

This fixes CVE-2017-7472.

Running the following program as an unprivileged user exhausts kernel
memory by leaking thread keyrings:

	#include <keyutils.h>

	int main()
	{
		for (;;)
			keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring(KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING);
	}

Fix it by only creating a new thread keyring if there wasn't one before.
To make things more consistent, make install_thread_keyring_to_cred()
and install_process_keyring_to_cred() both return 0 if the corresponding
keyring is already present.

Fixes: d84f4f992cbd ("CRED: Inaugurate COW credentials")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 2.6.29+
Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tBUG_ON(new->thread_keyring);', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.10.13 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a series of KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring calls.

code_evidence: install_thread_keyring() unconditionally calls prepare_creds() to allocate a new cred, then install_thread_keyring_to_cred() creates/installs a thread keyring; commit_creds() commits the new cred. The removed BUG_ON(new->thread_keyring) shows the path previously assumed no existing thread keyring, and there is no check that a thread keyring already exists before allocating and installing another one on each repeated call.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function creates a resource (thread keyring via prepare_creds/install_thread_keyring_to_cred) on every call and never releases or reuses the previously installed one, matching CWE-404's improper resource release leading to resource-consumption DoS. It is not merely a null-dereference or bounds issue; the defect is repeated unreleased resource creation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: each invocation allocates a fresh cred and installs a new thread keyring without checking whether the current cred already holds one, so repeated keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring(KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING) calls keep creating keyrings. Trigger: an unprivileged user looping the keyctl call. Consequence: thread keyrings accumulate and exhaust kernel memory, causing a denial of service. The missing constraint is the prior-existence check, not the allocation itself.

commit_msg:
Fix typo in preprocessor macro in archive_read_format_zip_cleanup()

Frees lzma_stream on cleanup()

Fixes #1165
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['#if HAVA_LZMA_H && HAVE_LIBLZMA'], 'added_lines': ['#if HAVE_LZMA_H && HAVE_LIBLZMA']}
description: A memory leak in archive_read_format_zip_cleanup in archive_read_support_format_zip.c in libarchive 3.3.4-dev allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted ZIP file because of a HAVE_LZMA_H typo. NOTE: this only affects users who downloaded the development code from GitHub. Users of the product's official releases are unaffected.

code_evidence: The LZMA cleanup block is guarded by a misspelled macro 'HAVA_LZMA_H' instead of 'HAVE_LZMA_H', so the preprocessor condition is never true and the lzma_end call is compiled out. The zipx_lzma_valid flag and lzma_end(&zip->zipx_lzma_stream) release logic exist but are unreachable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated memory tied to the LZMA stream is not released after its effective lifetime due to the disabled cleanup branch, matching missing release of memory. This is a leak, not a double free or use-after-free, since no release occurs at all.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a typo in the preprocessor guard prevents the lzma_end release from being compiled into cleanup. Trigger: opening a ZIP using LZMA/zipx decompression sets zipx_lzma_valid and allocates LZMA stream resources; on archive cleanup the guard fails, so the stream is never ended. Consequence: the LZMA stream memory is not released, leaking memory per crafted ZIP and enabling resource-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg:
A race condition may occur if the user physically removes the
USB device while calling open() for this device node.

This is a race condition between the ufx_ops_open() function and
the ufx_usb_disconnect() function, which may eventually result in UAF.

So, add a mutex to the ufx_ops_open() and ufx_usb_disconnect() functions
to avoid race contidion of krefs.

Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Helge Deller <deller@gmx.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tmutex_lock(&disconnect_mutex);', '', '\tmutex_unlock(&disconnect_mutex);']}
description: drivers/video/fbdev/smscufx.c in the Linux kernel through 5.19.12 has a race condition and resultant use-after-free if a physically proximate attacker removes a USB device while calling open(), aka a race condition between ufx_ops_open and ufx_usb_disconnect.

code_evidence: ufx_usb_disconnect reads the interface's private data via usb_get_intfdata(interface) at line 4 without any synchronization, then immediately mutates shared state: sets dev->virtualized = true (line 6), atomically clears dev->usb_active (line 7), and detaches the interface data (line 8). It then schedules framebuffer work (line 10) and drops the device reference with kref_put(&dev->kref, ufx_free) at line 11, which may free dev. Because this disconnect path and ufx_ops_open both operate on the same dev/kref without a common lock, the sequence is not atomic with respect to open().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a non-atomic sequence (get intfdata, mutate flags, kref_put) on a shared resource that another code path (ufx_ops_open) can concurrently access, which is exactly a race condition with improper synchronization (CWE-362); the UAF is the downstream consequence rather than the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: disconnect and open concurrently access and mutate the shared ufx_data structure and its kref with no mutual exclusion. Trigger: a physically proximate attacker removes the USB device while open() is executing, so kref_put in disconnect can free dev while open still uses it. Supported consequence: use-after-free and potential crash/instability.

commit_msg:
avoid read-heap-buffer-overflow (#332)

Fix invalid read in ares_parse_soa_reply.c found during fuzzing

Fixes Bug: #333 
Fix By: lutianxiong (@ltx2018)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  if (alen <= len + HFIXEDSZ + 1)', '    goto failed;']}
description: Buffer overflow vulnerability in c-ares before 1_16_1 thru 1_17_0 via function ares_parse_soa_reply in ares_parse_soa_reply.c.

code_evidence: ares__expand_name_for_response() advances aptr by the decoded name length len (line 23); the code then reads qclass = DNS_QUESTION_TYPE(aptr) at line 24 before any bound check, so aptr may already point at or past abuf+alen.
The only guard, aptr + QFIXEDSZ > abuf + alen at line 25, runs after the read at line 24, so it cannot prevent the out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the intended packet buffer, which is precisely CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). It is not a write overflow because only a read occurs; the missing length check before the read is the defining flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
if (aptr + QFIXEDSZ > abuf + alen)
goto failed;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the response buffer is read at aptr (DNS_QUESTION_TYPE) immediately after aptr += len without first verifying that len + HFIXEDSZ + 1 bytes remain. Trigger: a crafted DNS response whose expanded question name consumes nearly the whole buffer, leaving fewer than the header/fixed fields. Consequence: a heap out-of-bounds read of the qclass field, as reported by the fuzzer.

commit_msg:
BLIP: Fix decompression buffer bug

Until now, mistakenly, the buffer for decompressing compressed BLIP messages
has been statically allocated as 16 Kb, but that is not valid behavior.
16 Kb is the maximum size of a _compressed_ frame.  In theory, due to the
ability to zipbomb, there is virtually no upper bound on what the maximum
size of an uncompressed frame could be.  However, to keep sanity, it has
been made into a preference with a reasonable default that is not likely to
be exceeded (64 Kb).  The behavior before for this was that wireshark would
crash because the dissector would return NULL for a decompressed buffer due
to error and then try to deference it later.  A null check has been added,
so that the behavior is now that the packet will show
'<Error decompressing message>' instead, and log why it couldn't handle the
compressed message.  Closes #16866.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\ttvb_to_use = decompress(pinfo, tvb, offset, tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset) - BLIP_BODY_CHECKSUM_SIZE);', '\t\t\tproto_tree_add_string(blip_tree, hf_blip_message_body, tvb, offset, tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset), "<Error decompressing message>");', '\t\tproto_tree_add_string(blip_tree, hf_blip_message_body, tvb, offset, tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset), "<decompression support is not available>");'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\ttvb_to_use = decompress(pinfo, blip_tree, tvb, offset, tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset) - BLIP_BODY_CHECKSUM_SIZE);', '\t\tproto_tree_add_string(tree, hf_blip_message_body, tvb, offset, tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset), "<decompression support is not available>");']}
description: In Wireshark 3.2.0 to 3.2.6 and 3.0.0 to 3.0.13, the BLIP protocol dissector has a NULL pointer dereference because a buffer was sized for compressed (not uncompressed) messages. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-blip.c by allowing reasonable compression ratios and rejecting ZIP bombs.

code_evidence: decompress() is called on attacker-controlled compressed data; its return value tvb_to_use is only checked by the if(!tvb_to_use) guard, which returns early on failure.
After decompression, tvb_to_use is used in tvb_get_varint() and tvb_get_string_enc() at lines 61-68; these rely on tvb_to_use being non-NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences tvb_to_use, which can be NULL when decompression fails, matching CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). The root cause is the unchecked decompression result; the consequence is a dissector crash (DoS), not a memory-safety write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The buffer for decompressed BLIP data is sized for compressed frames, so a zipbomb (high compression ratio) causes decompress() to fail and return NULL. Without a NULL check before dereferencing tvb_to_use in the property parsing path, the dissector crashes. The fix adds the NULL guard that returns the error string instead of proceeding.

`eexec' doesn't exceed `limit'.

code_evidence: At line 60, `c = cur[0]` dereferences the cursor before any bound check; the `cur + 9 < limit` guard at line 61 is only evaluated after the read, and the loop advances `cur++` (line 69) with the limit check at line 70 occurring after the dereference, so `cur[0]` can be read at or past `limit`.

In the second scan (lines 82-85), `*cur` is read and `ft_strncmp((char*)cur, "eexec", 5)` compares up to 5 bytes whenever `*cur == 'e'`, with no check that `cur + 5 < limit`; near the buffer end this reads beyond `parser->base_dict`.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the `eexec` detection loops dereference `cur[0]` and run `ft_strncmp` over 5 bytes without first ensuring enough bytes remain before `limit`. Trigger: a base_dict whose length places the scan cursor near or at the end, or a trailing 'e' byte. Consequence: reads past the allocated buffer (heap over-read), yielding disclosure or a crash.

commit_msg:
Out-of-bounds read in multiple decode functions

These were reported as:
- Out-of-bounds read in ntlm_decode_oem_str (GHSL-2023-019)
- Out-of-bounds read in ntlm_decode_u16l_str_hdr (GHSL-2023-020)
- Out-of-bounds read in ntlm_decode_field (GHSL-2023-021)

These are lall basically the same identical error replicated in 3
separate functions.

Fixes defects GHSL-2023-019, GHSL-2023-020, GHSL-2023-021 found by
the GitHub Security Lab team via oss-fuzz.

A 32-bit integer overflow condition can lead to incorrect checks of
consistency of length of internal buffers. This leads to a DoS
as the service may end up reading from unmapped memory and crashing.

Although most applications will error out before accepting a singe input
buffer of 4GB in lenght this could theoretically happen, and therefore
we fix it.

Fixes CVE-2023-25563

Signed-off-by: Simo Sorce <simo@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        (UINT32_MAX - str_offs < str_len) ||']}
description: GSS-NTLMSSP is a mechglue plugin for the GSSAPI library that implements NTLM authentication. Prior to version 1.2.0, multiple out-of-bounds reads when decoding NTLM fields can trigger a denial of service. A 32-bit integer overflow condition can lead to incorrect checks of consistency of length of internal buffers. Although most applications will error out before accepting a singe input buffer of 4GB in length this could theoretically happen. This vulnerability can be triggered via the main `gss_accept_sec_context` entry point if the application allows tokens greater than 4GB in length. This can lead to a large, up to 65KB, out-of-bounds read which could cause a denial-of-service if it reads from unmapped memory. Version 1.2.0 contains a patch for the out-of-bounds reads.

code_evidence: str_offs (uint32_t) is combined with str_len (uint16_t) in the check at line 13; without an overflow guard, str_offs + str_len can wrap modulo 2^32 and pass the bound check. Line 16 then reads str_len bytes from buffer->data[str_offs], which may lie past buffer->length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads buffer->data beyond the intended buffer boundary. The overflow is the enabling defect, but the resulting unsafe operation is an out-of-bounds read, not merely an integer overflow (CWE-190).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length/offset consistency check uses unchecked 32-bit addition, so str_offs + str_len can overflow and bypass the buffer->length comparison. Trigger: a crafted NTLM token with a large offset near UINT32_MAX and nonzero length. Consequence: strndup reads past the buffer end, an out-of-bounds read that can crash the service (DoS) or leak memory.

commit_msg:
It is possible to trigger heap overflows due to an integer overflow
while parsing images.

The integer overflow occurs because the chosen limit 0x10000 for
dimensions is too large for 32 bit systems, because each pixel takes
4 bytes. Properly chosen values allow an overflow which in turn will
lead to less allocated memory than needed for subsequent reads.

description: libXcursor before 1.1.15 has various integer overflows that could lead to heap buffer overflows when processing malicious cursors, e.g., with programs like GIMP. It is also possible that an attack vector exists against the related code in cursor/xcursor.c in Wayland through 1.14.0.

description: An issue was discovered in systemd 253. An attacker can modify the contents of past events in a sealed log file and then adjust the file such that checking the integrity shows no error, despite modifications. NOTE: the vendor reportedly sent "a reply denying that any of the finding was a security vulnerability."

code_evidence: Tracks max_entry_realtime and min_entry_realtime from entry objects, gated by min_entry_realtime_set; bounds only update when an entry is seen.
Compares entry_realtime against rt + f->fss_interval_usec using non-overflow-checked addition; rejects out-of-sync tag/entry realtime.
Compares max_entry_realtime against rt + f->fss_interval_usec; this bound is the only check that max entries fall before the tag window end.
Compares min_entry_realtime against rt only when min_entry_realtime_set; resets the flag afterward, so the lower bound is per-tag.
Final HMAC comparison of o->tag.tag against gcry_md_read; this is the integrity check value whose validation depends on correct realtime bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-354 fits because the function validates integrity check values (HMAC tags) but the validation is incomplete: the realtime range constraints that gate tag acceptance can be bypassed, so a modified sealed journal still reports integrity success. This is improper validation of an integrity check value, not merely a timestamp-ordering issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The integrity verification relies on realtime bounds (min/max entry realtime) checked against each tag's expected window before the HMAC tag is validated. Because min/max tracking is conditional and the window-end computation uses unchecked addition, an attacker able to craft a sealed journal file can place entries whose realtime values evade the bounds, allowing modified past events to pass tag verification without detection. Root cause is incomplete validation of the integrity-relevant range checks; consequence is undetected modification of sealed log contents.

commit_msg:
Fix TensorKey hash function.

The original hash function only used total estimated `AllocatedBytes()`, which (a) is an estimate per tensor, and (b) is a very poor hash function for constants (e.g. `int32_t`).
It also tried to access individual tensor bytes through `tensor.data()` of size `AllocatedBytes()`.  This led to ASAN failures because the `AllocatedBytes()` is an estimate of total bytes allocated by a tensor, including any pointed-to constructs (e.g. strings), and does not refer to contiguous bytes in the `.data()` buffer.  We couldn't use this byte vector anyways, since types like `tstring` include pointers, whereas we need to hash the string values themselves.

Modified the hash function to more closely mirror the `==` operator.  This correctly handles `tstring` and any numeric types that do have contiguous storage.  Other types are currently left as unimplemented.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 446265413
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    }', '    if (t1.dtype() == DT_STRING) {'], 'added_lines': ['    } else if (t1.dtype() == DT_STRING) {', '    } else {', '      DCHECK(false) << "Unimplemented dtype " << DataTypeString(t1.dtype())', '                    << std::endl;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In version 2.8.0, the `TensorKey` hash function used total estimated `AllocatedBytes()`, which (a) is an estimate per tensor, and (b) is a very poor hash function for constants (e.g. `int32_t`). It also tried to access individual tensor bytes through `tensor.data()` of size `AllocatedBytes()`. This led to ASAN failures because the `AllocatedBytes()` is an estimate of total bytes allocated by a tensor, including any pointed-to constructs (e.g. strings), and does not refer to contiguous bytes in the `.data()` buffer. The discoverers could not use this byte vector anyway because types such as `tstring` include pointers, whereas they needed to hash the string values themselves. This issue is patched in Tensorflow versions 2.9.0 and 2.8.1.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown operator== only compares dtypes, shapes, memcpy-eligible tensor data, and string elements; it performs no buffer write, so it does not support CWE-787 out-of-bounds write.

Previously, guarding against attaching a new frame in frame detach
was done by inspecting LoadEventProgress. There are certain
operations, such as document.open(), that can cause LoadEventProgress

commit_msg:
Fix KDC null deref on bad encrypted challenge

The function ec_verify() in src/kdc/kdc_preauth_ec.c contains a check
to avoid further processing if the armor key is NULL.  However, this
check is bypassed by a call to k5memdup0() which overwrites retval
with 0 if the allocation succeeds.  If the armor key is NULL, a call
to krb5_c_fx_cf2_simple() will then dereference it, resulting in a
crash.  Add a check before the k5memdup0() call to avoid overwriting
retval.

CVE-2021-36222:

In MIT krb5 releases 1.16 and later, an unauthenticated attacker can
cause a null dereference in the KDC by sending a request containing a
PA-ENCRYPTED-CHALLENGE padata element without using FAST.

[ghudson@mit.edu: trimmed patch; added test case; edited commit
message]

ticket: 9007 (new)
tags: pullup
target_version: 1.19-next
target_version: 1.18-next
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    realmstr = k5memdup0(realm.data, realm.length, &retval);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (retval == 0)', '        realmstr = k5memdup0(realm.data, realm.length, &retval);']}
description: ec_verify in kdc/kdc_preauth_ec.c in the Key Distribution Center (KDC) in MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) before 1.18.4 and 1.19.x before 1.19.2 allows remote attackers to cause a NULL pointer dereference and daemon crash. This occurs because a return value is not properly managed in a certain situation.

code_evidence: When armor_key is NULL, retval is set to ENOENT and an error message is recorded, but the function continues executing rather than returning.
The unconditional k5memdup0 call overwrites retval with 0 on successful allocation, clearing the ENOENT error previously set for the missing FAST armor key.
With retval reset to 0, the loop invokes krb5_c_fx_cf2_simple passing armor_key, which is still NULL, as an input keyblock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function passes a NULL pointer (armor_key) into a crypto routine that dereferences it, matching CWE-476. The defect is improper control flow that fails to halt on the NULL condition, not an out-of-bounds or type issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the armor_key==NULL guard only sets retval instead of returning, and the subsequent k5memdup0 call resets retval to 0, erasing the error state. Trigger: an unauthenticated PA-ENCRYPTED-CHALLENGE request without FAST. This lets execution reach krb5_c_fx_cf2_simple with a NULL armor_key, causing a NULL dereference and KDC crash.

commit_msg:
fscrypto: add authorization check for setting encryption policy

On an ext4 or f2fs filesystem with file encryption supported, a user
could set an encryption policy on any empty directory(*) to which they
had readonly access.  This is obviously problematic, since such a
directory might be owned by another user and the new encryption policy
would prevent that other user from creating files in their own directory
(for example).

Fix this by requiring inode_owner_or_capable() permission to set an
encryption policy.  This means that either the caller must own the file,
or the caller must have the capability CAP_FOWNER.

(*) Or also on any regular file, for f2fs v4.6 and later and ext4
    v4.8-rc1 and later; a separate bug fix is coming for that.

Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 4.1+; check fs/{ext4,f2fs}
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!inode_owner_or_capable(inode))', '\t\treturn -EACCES;', '']}
description: A missing authorization check in the fscrypt_process_policy function in fs/crypto/policy.c in the ext4 and f2fs filesystem encryption support in the Linux kernel before 4.7.4 allows a user to assign an encryption policy to a directory owned by a different user, potentially creating a denial of service.

code_evidence: fscrypt_process_policy takes an inode and policy, then proceeds to validate policy->version and check for an existing encryption context without ever verifying that the caller owns the inode or holds CAP_FOWNER. When no context exists and the directory is empty, it calls create_encryption_context_from_policy(inode, policy) at line 11, mutating the inode's encryption state for any caller that reaches this function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing ownership/capability check is an access-control weakness in the management of permissions, matching CWE-264's category of permission and privilege management flaws. It is not a memory-safety issue; the defect is purely missing authorization prior to a state-changing operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function lacks an inode_owner_or_capable(inode) authorization check before applying or inspecting a policy. Trigger: a user with only readonly access to an empty directory owned by another user invokes the policy-set path. Consequence: the attacker assigns an encryption policy to the victim's directory, preventing the owner from creating files there (denial of service).

Function calls to GetPixelIndex() could result in values outside the range of representable for the 'unsigned char'. When ImageMagick processes a crafted pdf file, this could lead to an undefined behaviour or a crash.

code_evidence: Line 23 casts GetPixelIndex(image,p) directly to unsigned char before masking with 0x01; the pixel value is narrowed without first normalizing to a signed range.
Line 68 likewise narrows the index to unsigned char before extracting the low nibble at line 69.
Line 89 passes the narrowed unsigned char index to PopCharPixel, so an out-of-range index value is truncated rather than validated.

*q=((pixel & 0x01) << 7);

for (x=0; x < (ssize_t) number_pixels; x++)
q=PopCharPixel((unsigned char) GetPixelIndex(image,p),q);

commit_msg:
parse: Check for non-empty command/rspfile/rspfile_content

This matches ninja behavior and prevents the possibility of a rule
with an empty (NULL) command string.

Fixes #68.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!val)', '\t\t\tcontinue;']}
description: samurai 1.2 has a NULL pointer dereference in printstatus() function in build.c via a crafted build file.

code_evidence: parselet(s, &val) may leave val NULL for an empty value; the result is passed directly to ruleaddvar(r, var, val) without a NULL check.
The subsequent strcmp checks only set hascommand/hasrspfile/hasrspcontent flags; they do not validate that the command's value is non-NULL, so an empty command is accepted as present.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits a NULL command value to be recorded and treated as valid, enabling a later NULL dereference. This directly matches CWE-476; it is not merely a missing-input-validation issue because the supported consequence is dereferencing the NULL pointer.

evidence_lines.code:
parselet(s, &val);
ruleaddvar(r, var, val);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser stores a possibly NULL evalstring for a rule variable and only verifies the variable name 'command' exists, not that its value is non-NULL. Trigger: a crafted build file declaring an empty command (or rspfile) value. Consequence: a rule with a NULL command string reaches later processing, causing a NULL pointer dereference and crash in printstatus().

commit_msg:

In babel_print_v2() the non-verbose branch for an Update TLV compared
the TLV Length against 1 instead of 10 (probably a typo), put it right.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Henri Salo from Nixu
Corporation.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).

description: The Babel parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-babel.c:babel_print_v2().

code_evidence: In the non-verbose MESSAGE_UPDATE branch, after len = message[1] is read, the code checks only if(len < 1). With len == 1 the else branch executes and reads message[3] at lines 131-133, although the TLV body only extends to message[2]; the correct minimum length is 10.

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Don't have %cr4.fsgsbase active behind a guest kernels back

Currently, a 64bit PV guest can appear to set and clear FSGSBASE in %cr4, but
the bit remains set in hardware.  Therefore, the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE are usable
even when the guest kernel believes that they are disabled.

The FSGSBASE feature isn't currently supported in Linux, and its context
switch path has some optimisations which rely on userspace being unable to use
the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions.  Xen's current behaviour undermines this
expectation.

In 64bit PV guest context, always load the guest kernels setting of FSGSBASE
into %cr4.  This requires adjusting how Xen uses the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE
instructions.

 * Delete the cpu_has_fsgsbase helper.  It is no longer safe, as users need to
   check %cr4 directly.
 * The raw __rd{fs,gs}base() helpers are only safe to use when %cr4.fsgsbase
   is set.  Comment this property.
 * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}{base,shadow}() and read_msr() helpers are updated to use
   the current %cr4 value to determine which mechanism to use.
 * toggle_guest_mode() and save_segments() are update to avoid reading
   fs/gsbase if the values in hardware cannot be stale WRT struct vcpu.  A
   consequence of this is that the write_cr() path needs to cache the current
   bases, as subsequent context switches will skip saving the values.
 * write_cr4() is updated to ensure that the shadow %cr4.fsgsbase value is
   observed in a safe way WRT the hardware setting, if an interrupt happens to
   hit in the middle.
 * load_segments() is updated to use the VMLOAD optimisation if FSGSBASE is
   unavailable, even if only gs_shadow needs updating.  As a minor perf
   improvement, check cpu_has_svm first to short circuit a context-dependent
   conditional on Intel hardware.
 * pv_make_cr4() is updated for 64bit PV guests to use the guest kernels
   choice of FSGSBASE.

This is part of XSA-293.

Reported-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@
 static inline void wrfsbase(unsigned long base)
 {
-    if ( cpu_has_fsgsbase )
+    if ( read_cr4() & X86_CR4_FSGSBASE )
 #ifdef HAVE_AS_FSGSBASE
         asm volatile ( "wrfsbase %0" :: "r" (base) );
 #else
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( cpu_has_fsgsbase )'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( read_cr4() & X86_CR4_FSGSBASE )']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges because a guest can manipulate its virtualised %cr4 in a way that is incompatible with Linux (and possibly other guest kernels).

code_evidence: wrfsbase() chooses between the WRFSBASE instruction and the WRMSR fallback based only on the global cpu_has_fsgsbase flag, which reflects hardware capability rather than the currently active %cr4.FSGSBASE bit. The caller-supplied base value is written to the FS base MSR/register without checking whether FSGSBASE is actually enabled in the guest's virtualised CR4.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate the effective hardware/CR4 state before selecting the write mechanism, allowing guest-controlled state to bypass the guest kernel's expected constraint. This is improper validation of the operational input/state governing the write, matching CWE-20; it is not merely a filtering or encoding issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the helper trusts a stale capability flag instead of the effective CR4 state, so it performs the WRFSBASE path even when the guest kernel believes FSGSBASE is disabled. Trigger: a 64-bit PV guest clearing CR4.FSGSBASE and then invoking a path that calls wrfsbase(). Consequence: the FS base is silently changed behind the guest kernel, undermining its context-switch assumptions and enabling privilege escalation or DoS.

commit_msg: Fix #8743 - Crash in ELF version parser on 32bit systems
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tvstart += verdef->vd_aux;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tint vdaux = verdef->vd_aux;', '\t\tif (vdaux < 1) {', '\t\t\tsdb_free (sdb_verdef);', '\t\t\tgoto out_error;', '\t\t}', '\t\tvstart += vdaux;']}
description: In radare2 2.0.1, an integer exception (negative number leading to an invalid memory access) exists in store_versioninfo_gnu_verdef() in libr/bin/format/elf/elf.c via crafted ELF files when parsing the ELF version on 32bit systems.

code_evidence: verdef->vd_aux is read from the file and added to vstart without checking for negative values; on 32-bit systems a large 32-bit value can wrap the pointer arithmetic, and the subsequent bounds check at line 55 is the only guard before vstart is dereferenced at lines 60-61.

Inside the parent loop, isum and vstart are advanced by aux.vda_next, another attacker-controlled 32-bit field, before the bounds check at line 78; integer overflow in these additions can produce a vstart that passes the check but points outside the defs buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads Elf_(Verdaux) fields through a vstart pointer that can be driven outside the intended defs buffer by overflowed offsets, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. The consequence is a memory read past the buffer, not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is unchecked 32-bit pointer/offset arithmetic on attacker-controlled vd_aux and vda_next fields. On 32-bit systems the addition wraps, so the end-of-buffer comparisons can be bypassed and READ32 at lines 60/61 or 84/85 dereferences memory outside the allocated defs buffer, causing an invalid read and crash.

commit_msg: Fix for OOB Read in DecodeJpeg2k
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    /* csiz*h*w + offset = tileinfo.datasize */']}
description: In libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c in Pillow before 7.1.0, there are multiple out-of-bounds reads via a crafted JP2 file.

code_evidence: w and h are derived from tileinfo bounds without verifying they match the actual tiledata buffer length.
csiz is computed from component precision and remapped from 3 to 4, selecting the element width used to index tiledata.
Case 1 indexes tiledata[y*w] and reads w bytes per row via *data++.
Case 2 casts tiledata[2*y*w] to UINT16 and reads w elements per row.
Case 4 casts tiledata[4*y*w] to UINT32 and reads w elements per row.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the tiledata buffer, matching CWE-125. This is a read overrun, not a write (CWE-787) or integer overflow per se, since the missing length constraint directly permits reads beyond the allocated tile data.

evidence_lines.code:
const UINT8 *data = &tiledata[y * w];
*row++ = j2ku_shift(offset + *data++, shift);

const UINT16 *data = (const UINT16 *)&tiledata[2 * y * w];
*row++ = j2ku_shift(offset + *data++, shift);

const UINT32 *data = (const UINT32 *)&tiledata[4 * y * w];
*row++ = j2ku_shift(offset + *data++, shift);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loops trust tile width/height and the precision-derived element size to bound reads of tiledata; no check ties csiz*h*w to the actual tile data size. A crafted JP2 with mismatched tileinfo dimensions or precision causes the pointer arithmetic to advance beyond tiledata, yielding out-of-bounds reads.

commit_msg:
(uid_t) -1 is still used as placeholder to mean "unset". This is OK, since
there should be no users with such number, see
https://systemd.io/UIDS-GIDS#special-linux-uids.

(uid_t) -1 is used as the default value in class initialization.

When a user or group above INT32_MAX is created, the numeric uid or
gid wraps around to negative when the value is assigned to gint, and
polkit gets confused. Let's accept such gids, except for -1.

A nicer fix would be to change the underlying type to e.g. uint32 to
not have negative values. But this cannot be done without breaking the
API, so likely new functions will have to be added (a
polkit_unix_user_new variant that takes a unsigned, and the same for
_group_new, _set_uid, _get_uid, _set_gid, _get_gid, etc.). This will
require a bigger patch.

Fixes https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/polkit/polkit/issues/74.

description: A flaw was found in PolicyKit (aka polkit) 0.115 that allows a user with a uid greater than INT_MAX to successfully execute any systemctl command.

code_evidence: The 'uid' GObject property is declared with g_param_spec_int, an int-typed spec whose minimum is -1 and default is -1. The class init thus constrains UID input to the signed int range with -1 as the sentinel, so any uid above INT_MAX is not representable and wraps negative, colliding with the -1 'unset' placeholder.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The property spec fails to correctly validate the uid's required range and reserved value, allowing a valid high uid to be accepted as a negative/sentinel value; this is improper input validation (CWE-20). joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the uid input is modeled and range-checked as a signed gint with -1 reserved as unset. commit_msg:
cac1: Correctly handle the buffer limits

Found by oss-fuzz

https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=18618
and others
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsize_t val_len;'], 'added_lines': ['\tsize_t val_len = 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in OpenSC through 0.19.0 and 0.20.x through 0.20.0-rc3. libopensc/card-cac1.c mishandles buffer limits for CAC certificates.

code_evidence: val_len is declared uninitialized at line 8; it is only assigned by cac_cac1_get_certificate at line 29, so a path leaving val_len unset would make the cert_len = val_len - 1 computation at line 38 and the subsequent buffer sizing unreliable.

The cached branch bounds idx against cache_buf_len at lines 16-18 and computes len = MIN(count, cache_buf_len-idx) at line 19 before memcpy at line 20, so it relies on cache_buf_len being a valid, initialized length.

After the decompression/malloc paths, line 59 computes len = MIN(count, priv->cache_buf_len-idx) and line 61 copies from &priv->cache_buf[idx]; this depends on cache_buf_len having been set to a correct size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs memcpy on cache_buf using lengths derived from potentially invalid buffer-limit state, which can result in out-of-bounds memory operations. The fix initializing val_len addresses the malformed bound feeding these copies.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that val_len (and thus derived cert_len and cache_buf_len) may be used without a guaranteed initialized/valid value, so the length checks and MIN computations can be based on stale or uninitialized bounds. The memcpy calls at lines 20 and 61 then operate with an incorrect length/offset against cache_buf, allowing reads or writes outside the intended buffer boundary.

commit_msg:
Prevent division by 0 in common shape functions.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 387712197
Change-Id: Id25c7460e35b68aeeeac23b9a88e455b443ee149
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (filter_input_depth_value == 0)', '      return errors::InvalidArgument("Depth of filter must not be 0");', '        if (num_groups == 0)', '          return errors::InvalidArgument("Number of groups must not be 0");']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions most implementations of convolution operators in TensorFlow are affected by a division by 0 vulnerability where an attacker can trigger a denial of service via a crash. The shape inference [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/core/framework/common_shape_fns.cc#L577) is missing several validations before doing divisions and modulo operations. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 8a793b5d7f59e37ac7f3cd0954a750a2fe76bad4. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: When both input depth and filter input depth are known, the code takes filter_input_depth_value from the filter shape and immediately computes input_depth_value % filter_input_depth_value without checking that the divisor is nonzero.

If input depth differs from filter input depth, num_groups = input_depth_value / filter_input_depth_value is computed, and later output_depth_value % num_groups is evaluated without verifying num_groups is nonzero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 applies because the function directly divides/modulos by attacker-influenced dimension values that can be zero, and the patch adds the missing zero checks. This is a divide-by-zero availability weakness, not merely an invalid-argument validation gap.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shape-inference function performs modulo and division using filter_input_depth_value and the derived num_groups as divisors without validating they are nonzero. Trigger: a crafted Conv2D filter shape with zero input depth (or a value yielding zero groups) reaches these operations. Consequence: a division-by-zero crash, i.e., denial of service during shape inference.

commit_msg:
arm: crash the guest when it traps on external abort

If we spot a data or prefetch abort bearing the ESR_EL2.EA bit set, we
know that this is an external abort, and that should crash the guest.

This is part of XSA-201.

Signed-off-by: Wei Chen <Wei.Chen@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Steve Capper <steve.capper@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <Julien.Grall@arm.com>

+++ func_after
@@ -6,6 +6,15 @@
     mmio_info_t info;
     uint8_t fsc = hsr.dabt.dfsc & ~FSC_LL_MASK;
     mfn_t mfn;
+
+    /*
+     * If this bit has been set, it means that this data abort is caused
+     * by a guest external abort. Currently we crash the guest to protect the
+     * hypervisor. In future one can better handle this by injecting a virtual
+     * abort to the guest.
+     */
+    if ( dabt.eat )
+        domain_crash_synchronous();
 
     info.dabt = dabt;
 #ifdef CONFIG_ARM_32

Currently we crash the guest to protect the', '     * hypervisor. In future one can better handle this by injecting a virtual', '     * abort to the guest.', '     */', '    if ( dabt.eat )', '        domain_crash_synchronous();']}

commit_msg:
Drop unreliable segments with weird offset/size.

And be more deliberate about limits of unreliable message/segment sizes.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tAssert( cbSegmentSize > 0 ); // !TEST! Bogus assert, zero byte messages are OK.  Remove after testing', '', '\t\t\t// Receive the segment', '\t\t\tbool bLastSegmentInMessage = ( nFrameType & 0x20 ) != 0;', '\t\t\tSNP_ReceiveUnreliableSegment( nCurMsgNum, nOffset, pSegmentData, cbSegmentSize, bLastSegmentInMessage, usecNow );'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t\t// Check if offset+size indicates a message larger than what we support.  (Also,', '\t\t\t// protect against malicious sender sending *extremely* large offset causing overflow.)', '\t\t\tif ( (int64)nOffset + cbSegmentSize > k_cbMaxUnreliableMsgSizeRecv || cbSegmentSize > k_cbMaxUnreliableSegmentSizeRecv )', '\t\t\t{', '', '\t\t\t\t// Since this is unreliable data, we can just ignore the segment.', '\t\t\t\tSpewWarningRateLimited( usecNow, "[%s] Ignoring unreliable segment with invalid offset %u size %d\\n",', '\t\t\t\t\tGetDescription(), nOffset, cbSegmentSize );', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\telse', '\t\t\t{', '', '\t\t\t\t// Receive the segment', '\t\t\t\tbool bLastSegmentInMessage = ( nFrameType & 0x20 ) != 0;', '\t\t\t\tSNP_ReceiveUnreliableSegment( nCurMsgNum, nOffset, pSegmentData, cbSegmentSize, bLastSegmentInMessage, usecNow );', '\t\t\t}']}
description: Valve's Game Networking Sockets prior to version v1.2.0 improperly handles unreliable segments with negative offsets in function SNP_ReceiveUnreliableSegment(), leading to a Heap-Based Buffer Underflow and a free() of memory not from the heap, resulting in a memory corruption and probably even a remote code execution.

code_evidence: nOffset is decoded as an attacker-controlled uint32 from the packet (line 117) and passed straight into SNP_ReceiveUnreliableSegment with no validation (line 121).
cbSegmentSize is derived from the frame type and length bytes (line 118); the preceding Assert at line 119 is not an enforcement and does not constrain nOffset or the offset+size relationship.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked offset/size leads to writing outside the intended buffer. The patch confirms this by rejecting segments where (int64)nOffset + cbSegmentSize exceeds k_cbMaxUnreliableMsgSizeRecv; the missing bound is the root cause, with the underflow write as the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The decoder trusts the attacker-supplied segment offset and size and forwards them to SNP_ReceiveUnreliableSegment without checking that offset+size stays within the supported message buffer. A malicious peer can send a huge offset or offset/size combination that makes the receive path compute a position before the buffer start, producing an out-of-bounds write (heap underflow) and memory corruption.

commit_msg:
ALSA: pcm : Call kill_fasync() in stream lock

Currently kill_fasync() is called outside the stream lock in
snd_pcm_period_elapsed().  This is potentially racy, since the stream
may get released even during the irq handler is running.  Although
snd_pcm_release_substream() calls snd_pcm_drop(), this doesn't
guarantee that the irq handler finishes, thus the kill_fasync() call
outside the stream spin lock may be invoked after the substream is
detached, as recently reported by KASAN.

As a quick workaround, move kill_fasync() call inside the stream
lock.  The fasync is rarely used interface, so this shouldn't have a
big impact from the performance POV.

Ideally, we should implement some sync mechanism for the proper finish
of stream and irq handler.  But this oneliner should suffice for most
cases, so far.

Reported-by: Baozeng Ding <sploving1@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tkill_fasync(&runtime->fasync, SIGIO, POLL_IN);'], 'added_lines': ['\tkill_fasync(&runtime->fasync, SIGIO, POLL_IN);']}
description: Race condition in the snd_pcm_period_elapsed function in sound/core/pcm_lib.c in the ALSA subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.7 allows local users to cause a denial of service (use-after-free) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted SNDRV_PCM_TRIGGER_START command.

code_evidence: Line 8 acquires the stream lock via snd_pcm_stream_lock_irqsave, protecting the running/hw_ptr update and timer interrupt path.
Line 17 releases the stream lock, and line 18 calls kill_fasync on runtime->fasync only after the lock has been dropped, so the fasync access occurs outside the exclusive critical section.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function's critical section fails to provide exclusivity/atomicity over the shared runtime->fasync resource; an interfering release sequence can modify the resource before the fasync access completes, yielding a race.

evidence_lines.code: snd_pcm_stream_lock_irqsave(substream, flags);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: kill_fasync() accesses runtime->fasync after snd_pcm_stream_unlock_irqrestore() has released the stream lock. Trigger: a concurrent release path can drop/detach the substream after the unlock but before line 18 executes, since the irq handler is not guaranteed to finish. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the runtime/substream, reported by KASAN, causing denial of service.

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

commit_msg:
mm: remove gup_flags FOLL_WRITE games from __get_user_pages()

This is an ancient bug that was actually attempted to be fixed once
(badly) by me eleven years ago in commit 4ceb5db9757a ("Fix
get_user_pages() race for write access") but that was then undone due to
problems on s390 by commit f33ea7f404e5 ("fix get_user_pages bug").

In the meantime, the s390 situation has long been fixed, and we can now
fix it by checking the pte_dirty() bit properly (and do it better).  The
s390 dirty bit was implemented in abf09bed3cce ("s390/mm: implement
software dirty bits") which made it into v3.9.  Earlier kernels will
have to look at the page state itself.

Also, the VM has become more scalable, and what used a purely
theoretical race back then has become easier to trigger.

To fix it, we introduce a new internal FOLL_COW flag to mark the "yes,
we already did a COW" rather than play racy games with FOLL_WRITE that
is very fundamental, and then use the pte dirty flag to validate that
the FOLL_COW flag is still valid.

Reported-and-tested-by: Phil "not Paul" Oester <kernel@linuxace.com>
Acked-by: Hugh Dickins <hughd@google.com>

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

description: Race condition in mm/gup.c in the Linux kernel 2.x through 4.x before 4.8.3 allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging incorrect handling of a copy-on-write (COW) feature to write to a read-only memory mapping, as exploited in the wild in October 2016, aka "Dirty COW."

code_evidence: Lines 12-14 take the pte lock and read the PTE into a local copy. Line 29 then decides whether a writable follow is permitted using only pte_write(pte) on that snapshot; if the check fails it unlocks and returns NULL. The decision is made from a stale copy rather than re-validating the PTE under the lock against the dirty state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the flaw is a timing window in a concurrent code sequence accessing shared page-table state without exclusivity: the check on the cached PTE can be invalidated by another sequence before use. This is a race on shared resource state, not merely a missing permission check, which is why the target CWE applies.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the writability decision for FOLL_WRITE relies on a racy PTE snapshot: pte_write(pte) is checked on a value read earlier, and there is no atomic validation that the mapping is still the private COW page rather than a read-only file mapping. A concurrent COW/update can change the PTE between the read and the check, so the caller obtains a writable reference to a page that should be read-only, enabling modification of a read-only mapping (privilege gain).

  [  208.073632] x1 : 0000000000000000 x0 : ffff000009578c08
  [  208.078938] Process test_verifier (pid: 2256, stack limit = 0x0000000049ca7974)
  [  208.086235] Call trace:
  [  208.088672]  bpf_skb_load_helper_8_no_cache+0x34/0xc0
  [  208.093713]  0xffff000000bdb754
  [  208.096845]  bpf_test_run+0x78/0xf8
  [  208.100324]  bpf_prog_test_run_skb+0x148/0x230
  [  208.104758]  sys_bpf+0x314/0x1198

The program itself which caused this had a long jump over the whole
instruction sequence where all of the inner instructions required
heavy expansions into multiple BPF instructions. Additionally, I also
had BPF hardening enabled which requires once more rewrites of all
constant values in order to blind them. Each time we rewrite insns,
bpf_adj_branches() would need to potentially adjust branch targets
which cross the patchlet boundary to accommodate for the additional
delta. Eventually that lead to the case where the target offset could
not fit into insn->off's upper 0x7fff limit anymore where then offset
wraps around becoming negative (in s16 universe), or vice versa
depending on the jump direction.

Therefore it becomes necessary to detect and reject any such occasions
in a generic way for native eBPF and cBPF to eBPF migrations. For
the latter we can simply check bounds in the bpf_convert_filter()'s
BPF_EMIT_JMP helper macro and bail out once we surpass limits. The
bpf_patch_insn_single() for native eBPF (and cBPF to eBPF in case
of subsequent hardening) is a bit more complex in that we need to
detect such truncations before hitting the bpf_prog_realloc(). Thus
the latter is split into an extra pass to probe problematic offsets
on the original program in order to fail early. With that in place
and carefully tested I no longer hit the panic and the rewrites are
rejected properly. The above example panic I've seen on bpf-next,
though the issue itself is generic in that a guard against this issue
in bpf seems more appropriate in this case.

Acked-by: Martin KaFai Lau <kafai@fb.com>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>

When an accessor is hidden behind an INTERCEPTOR, the compatibility check is not reached, so the IC may cache a handler for an incompatible receiver. Fix a null pointer exception in SVDF

Also fix a potential null pointer exception in `GetVariableInput`.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the implementation of SVDF in TFLite is [vulnerable to a null pointer error](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/svdf.cc#L300-L313). The [`GetVariableInput` function](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/kernel_util.cc#L115-L119) can return a null pointer but `GetTensorData` assumes that the argument is always a valid tensor. Furthermore, because `GetVariableInput` calls [`GetMutableInput`](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/kernel_util.cc#L82-L90) which might return `nullptr`, the `tensor->is_variable` expression can also trigger a null pointer exception. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 5b048e87e4e55990dae6b547add4dae59f4e1c76. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 3 stores the result of GetMutableInput into tensor without any null check; GetMutableInput can return nullptr. Line 4 unconditionally dereferences tensor via tensor->is_variable, so a null tensor triggers a null pointer dereference.

return tensor->is_variable ? tensor : nullptr;

When the input at the given index is absent or invalid, GetMutableInput returns nullptr and the subsequent tensor->is_variable access dereferences NULL, causing a crash (availability impact) in the TFLite SVDF path that calls this helper.

The chunk loop reads type and csize from the heap buffer and skips csize bytes without checking csize against gf_bs_available(bs), so a declared chunk size can exceed remaining data.

Trigger: a crafted WAVE header with an oversized chunk size makes the bitstream position/wav_hdr_size inconsistent with the allocated probe_data. Consequence: the subsequent arithmetic and memcpy from data can read past the heap allocation, producing a heap-based out-of-bounds access.

commit_msg:
Issue 547:  problems with compress bidder

The code previously was not very careful about verifying the
compression parameters.  This led to cases where it failed to
reject invalid compressed data at the beginning.  The invalid
left shift was one symptom of this.

The code is now more careful:  It verifies that the compression
parameter byte exists and verifies that the maximum code size
is <= 16 bits.

This also includes some new tests to verify that truncated or
otherwise invalid compressed data is rejected.

description: The compress_bidder_init function in archive_read_support_filter_compress.c in libarchive before 3.2.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a crafted tar file, which triggers an invalid left shift.

code_evidence: The bidder requests only 2 bytes via __archive_read_filter_ahead(filter, 2, &avail) at line 9, so buffer covers just the two magic bytes. Lines 13-14 check only buffer[0] and buffer[1] against 0x1F/0x9D, and line 15 credits 16 bits; the compression-parameter byte (the third byte of a compress stream) is never fetched or examined.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts input data without validating required structural properties (presence and reserved bits of the parameter byte), which is the core of CWE-20 improper input validation. It is not a transformation/filtering flaw; the missing constraint is the defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the format identification validates only the 2-byte magic and never inspects the mandatory third compression-parameter byte, so truncated or malformed headers are accepted as valid compress streams. Trigger: crafted or truncated input whose first two bytes match 0x1F 0x9D. Consequence: the bidder misidentifies the stream and later decompression consumes an invalid parameter byte, leading to the crash described (invalid left shift).

commit_msg:
There is a slab-out-of-bounds Write bug in hid-bigbenff driver.
The problem is the driver assumes the device must have an input but
some malicious devices violate this assumption.

Fix this by checking hid_device's input is non-empty before its usage.

Reported-by: syzkaller <syzkaller@googlegroups.com>
Signed-off-by: Dongliang Mu <mudongliangabcd@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (list_empty(&hid->inputs)) {', '\t\thid_err(hid, "no inputs found\\n");', '\t\terror = -ENODEV;', '\t\tgoto error_hw_stop;', '\t}']}
description: An out-of-bounds memory write flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s Kid-friendly Wired Controller driver. This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system. It is in bigben_probe of drivers/hid/hid-bigbenff.c. The reason is incorrect assumption - bigben devices all have inputs. However, malicious devices can break this assumption, leaking to out-of-bound write.

code_evidence: Line 30 unconditionally takes the first entry of hid->inputs via list_first_entry without verifying the list is non-empty.
Line 31 then dereferences hidinput->input->ffbit and writes a bit, and lines 33-34 pass hidinput->input to input_ff_create_memless.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through a pointer derived from an empty list, producing a memory write past the intended object boundary, matching CWE-787. A null-pointer dereference alone would not explain the write; here the unchecked list traversal yields a bogus hidinput whose input is then written to.

evidence_lines.code:
hidinput = list_first_entry(&hid->inputs, struct hid_input, list);
set_bit(FF_RUMBLE, hidinput->input->ffbit);

error = input_ff_create_memless(hidinput->input, NULL,
hid_bigben_play_effect);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A malicious HID device can enumerate with no input reports, leaving hid->inputs empty. list_first_entry on an empty list yields an invalid container pointer, so the subsequent set_bit write to hidinput->input->ffbit and the FF registration operate on out-of-bounds memory. Root cause is the missing emptiness check on hid->inputs; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds memory write that can crash or potentially escalate privileges.

commit_msg:
As reported by Jann, ihold() does not in fact guarantee inode
persistence. And instead of making it so, replace the usage of inode
pointers with a per boot, machine wide, unique inode identifier.

This sequence number is global, but shared (file backed) futexes are
rare enough that this should not become a performance issue.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>

--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -15,7 +15,7 @@
 
 	switch (key->both.offset & (FUT_OFF_INODE|FUT_OFF_MMSHARED)) {
 	case FUT_OFF_INODE:
-		ihold(key->shared.inode); /* implies smp_mb(); (B) */
+		smp_mb();		/* explicit smp_mb(); (B) */
 		break;
 	case FUT_OFF_MMSHARED:
 		futex_get_mm(key); /* implies smp_mb(); (B) */
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tihold(key->shared.inode); /* implies smp_mb(); (B) */'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tsmp_mb();\t\t/* explicit smp_mb(); (B) */']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s futex implementation. This flaw allows a local attacker to corrupt system memory or escalate their privileges when creating a futex on a filesystem that is about to be unmounted. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to confidentiality, integrity, as well as system availability.

code_evidence: In the FUT_OFF_INODE case, get_futex_key_refs takes a reference with ihold(key->shared.inode) on the inode pointer stored in the futex key. The commit message states ihold() does not actually guarantee inode persistence, so this reference does not prevent the inode from being torn down while the key still holds a pointer to it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is dereferencing/referencing inode memory whose lifetime is not guaranteed, matching CWE-416 (use after free). It is not merely a missing reference count; the defect is that the object can be freed while still referenced by the key.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the futex key retains a raw inode pointer and relies on ihold() for lifetime, but ihold() does not guarantee persistence after the inode is freed (e.g., during unmount). Trigger: a futex is created on a file-backed mapping whose filesystem is concurrently unmounted. Consequence: later use of the stale inode pointer is a use-after-free, enabling memory corruption or privilege escalation.
