Fix 'potential memory leak' compiler warning.

This CL fixes the following compiler warning:

frameworks/av/media/libstagefright/SampleTable.cpp:569:9: warning:
 Memory allocated by 'new[]' should be deallocated by 'delete[]', not
 'delete'.

Bug: 33137046
Test: Compiled with change; no warning generated.

Change-Id: I29abd90e02bf482fa840d1f7206ebbdacf7dfa37
(cherry picked from commit 158c197b668ad684f92829db6a31bee3aec794ba)
(cherry picked from commit 37c428cd521351837fccb6864f509f996820b234)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        delete mSyncSamples;'], 'added_lines': ['        delete[] mSyncSamples;']}
description: A denial of service vulnerability in the Android media framework (libstagefright). Product: Android. Versions: 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2. Android ID: A-36531046.

code_evidence: Line 33 allocates mSyncSamples as an array via new uint32_t[numSyncSamples]. Lines 39-40 read data into that array; on a short read, line 41 releases it with scalar delete instead of delete[], which is undefined behavior for array allocations and fails to correctly destroy/release the array resource before returning ERROR_IO.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the allocated array resource is not correctly released after its effective lifetime ends on the ERROR_IO path; the mismatched delete means the resource is not properly deallocated. This is distinct from a buffer overflow, since the defect is resource release, not out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path frees an array allocated with new[] using scalar delete, mismatching the allocation form. Trigger: mDataSource->readAt returns fewer bytes than allocSize. Consequence: the array's lifetime ends incorrectly, leaving the resource improperly released (undefined behavior), which the commit addresses as a potential memory leak affecting availability.

commit_msg:
powerpc/perf: Fix crash in perf_instruction_pointer() when ppmu is not set

On systems without any specific PMU driver support registered, running
perf record causes Oops.

The relevant portion from call trace:

  BUG: Kernel NULL pointer dereference on read at 0x00000040
  Faulting instruction address: 0xc0021f0c
  Oops: Kernel access of bad area, sig: 11 [#1]
  BE PAGE_SIZE=4K PREEMPT CMPCPRO
  SAF3000 DIE NOTIFICATION
  CPU: 0 PID: 442 Comm: null_syscall Not tainted 5.13.0-rc6-s3k-dev-01645-g7649ee3d2957 #5164
  NIP:  c0021f0c LR: c00e8ad8 CTR: c00d8a5c
  NIP perf_instruction_pointer+0x10/0x60
  LR  perf_prepare_sample+0x344/0x674
  Call Trace:
    perf_prepare_sample+0x7c/0x674 (unreliable)
    perf_event_output_forward+0x3c/0x94
    __perf_event_overflow+0x74/0x14c
    perf_swevent_hrtimer+0xf8/0x170
    __hrtimer_run_queues.constprop.0+0x160/0x318
    hrtimer_interrupt+0x148/0x3b0
    timer_interrupt+0xc4/0x22c
    Decrementer_virt+0xb8/0xbc

During perf record session, perf_instruction_pointer() is called to
capture the sample IP. This function in core-book3s accesses
ppmu->flags. If a platform specific PMU driver is not registered, ppmu
is set to NULL and accessing its members results in a crash. Fix this
crash by checking if ppmu is set.

Fixes: 2ca13a4cc56c ("powerpc/perf: Use regs->nip when SIAR is zero")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v5.11+
Reported-by: Christophe Leroy <christophe.leroy@csgroup.eu>
Signed-off-by: Athira Rajeev <atrajeev@linux.vnet.ibm.com>
Tested-by: Christophe Leroy <christophe.leroy@csgroup.eu>
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/1623952506-1431-1-git-send-email-atrajeev@linux.vnet.ibm.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (ppmu->flags & PPMU_P10_DD1) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (ppmu && (ppmu->flags & PPMU_P10_DD1)) {']}
description: arch/powerpc/perf/core-book3s.c in the Linux kernel before 5.12.13, on systems with perf_event_paranoid=-1 and no specific PMU driver support registered, allows local users to cause a denial of service (perf_instruction_pointer NULL pointer dereference and OOPS) via a "perf record" command.

code_evidence: perf_instruction_pointer() reads ppmu->flags at line 5 without first verifying that the global ppmu pointer is non-NULL; ppmu is only populated when a platform-specific PMU driver registers, so on systems lacking one it remains NULL. The dereference occurs before any of the fallback branches (lines 6-14) that would otherwise return siar, regs->nip or 0.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but actually NULL, and the observed impact is a kernel crash (availability DoS). It is distinct from an out-of-bounds read: the invalid value is the pointer itself, not an index or offset.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function unconditionally dereferences the optional ppmu pointer to test PPMU_P10_DD1. Trigger: a perf sample (e.g. perf record with perf_event_paranoid=-1) reaches perf_instruction_pointer() on a platform with no registered PMU driver, leaving ppmu NULL. The NULL read faults in kernel context, producing an Oops and denial of service. The consequence is the crash; the cause is the missing NULL guard on ppmu, not the subsequent flag logic.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.0101: invalid memory access in diff mode with "dp" and undo

Problem:    Invalid memory access in diff mode with "dp" and undo.
Solution:   Make sure the line number does not go below one.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t    dp->df_lnum[i] -= off;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t    if (dp->df_lnum[i] > off)', '\t\t\t\tdp->df_lnum[i] -= off;', '\t\t\t    else', '\t\t\t\tdp->df_lnum[i] = 1;']}
description: Out-of-bounds Write to API in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0100.

code_evidence: Inside the deleted-range branch, for each other diff buffer the code unconditionally subtracts 'off' from dp->df_lnum[i]. 'off' is derived earlier from dp->df_lnum[idx] - lnum_deleted (line 99) or zero, without checking that df_lnum[i] exceeds 'off'. When 'off' is larger than the other buffer's line number, the subtraction underflows the line number below one.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked arithmetic lets a stored line number underflow below the valid minimum, and that corrupted index is subsequently used to address memory, matching CWE-787 (write/access before the beginning of the intended buffer). The fix constrains the value to a valid lower bound rather than addressing a different weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a missing lower-bound check before subtracting 'off' from df_lnum[i]. Trigger: editing/deleting lines in diff mode (e.g. 'dp' with undo) so that 'off' exceeds another buffer's df_lnum[i]. Consequence: df_lnum[i] becomes zero or negative, producing an invalid line number that later causes out-of-bounds memory access. The patch adds a guard and clamps to 1.

commit_msg: jpeg loader: do not scan more than output_height lines
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tint                            scanned_lines;', '\tscanned_lines = 0;', '\t\t\t\tif (scanned_lines + n_lines > output_height)', '\t\t\t\t\tn_lines = output_height - scanned_lines;', '\t\t\t\t\tscanned_lines += 1;', '\t\t\t\tif (scanned_lines + n_lines > output_height)', '\t\t\t\t\tn_lines = output_height - scanned_lines;', '\t\t\t\t\tscanned_lines += 1;', '\t\t\t\tif (scanned_lines + n_lines > output_height)', '\t\t\t\t\tn_lines = output_height - scanned_lines;', '\t\t\t\t\tscanned_lines += 1;', '\t\t\t\tif (scanned_lines + n_lines > output_height)', '\t\t\t\t\tn_lines = output_height - scanned_lines;', '\t\t\t\t\tscanned_lines += 1;', '\t\t\t\tif (scanned_lines + n_lines > output_height)', '\t\t\t\t\tn_lines = output_height - scanned_lines;', '\t\t\t\t\tscanned_lines += 1;']}
description: A heap-based buffer overflow in _cairo_image_surface_create_from_jpeg() in extensions/cairo_io/cairo-image-surface-jpeg.c in GNOME gThumb before 3.8.3 and Linux Mint Pix before 2.4.5 allows attackers to cause a crash and potentially execute arbitrary code via a crafted JPEG file.

code_evidence: output_height is clamped to CAIRO_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE (line 110) and the destination surface is allocated from destination_width/destination_height derived from that clamped height (lines 111-128); surface_row starts at surface_data + line_start (line 137).

In each color-space loop, jpeg_read_scanlines is called with rec_outbuf_height and returns n_lines without bounding against the remaining destination rows (lines 145-148). The inner loop advances surface_row by line_step per line (lines 150-177), writing pixels via memcpy past the allocated surface when more lines than output_height are produced.

The RGB branch shows the same unbounded pattern: the while condition checks srcinfo.output_scanline < output_height (line 210), but n_lines from jpeg_read_scanlines (line 213) may overrun the last rows, and surface_row += line_step (line 229) walks beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes pixel data past the end of the allocated surface buffer; the missing output_height bound on n_lines is the direct cause of the out-of-bounds write, not merely a read or integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the scanline count returned by jpeg_read_scanlines is used directly to drive surface_row advancement and memcpy writes, without limiting the number of lines written to the remaining destination rows. Trigger: a crafted JPEG whose decompressor emits more scanlines than the clamped output_height. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds writes past the cairo image surface, causing crash and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
dd: harden functions against directory traversal issues

Test correctness of all accessed dump dir files in all dd* functions.
Before this commit, the callers were allowed to pass strings like
"../../etc/shadow" in the filename argument of all dd* functions.

Related: #1214457

Signed-off-by: Jakub Filak <jfilak@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (!str_is_correct_filename(path))', '        error_msg_and_die("Cannot test existence. \'%s\' is not a valid file name", path);', '']}
description: Directory traversal vulnerability in abrt-dbus in Automatic Bug Reporting Tool (ABRT) allows local users to read, write to, or change ownership of arbitrary files via unspecified vectors to the (1) NewProblem, (2) GetInfo, (3) SetElement, or (4) DeleteElement method.

code_evidence: The function passes the caller-supplied path directly to concat_path_file(dd->dd_dirname, path), joining it under the dump directory without validating that path is a single safe filename; exist_file_dir then resolves the combined path, so a value containing '../' or an absolute path escapes dd->dd_dirname.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-22 fits because external input builds a pathname meant to stay under dd->dd_dirname but is not neutralized, allowing '../' or absolute paths to resolve outside it. This is path traversal, not mere input validation, since the security-relevant effect is escaping the restricted parent directory.

evidence_lines.code:
char *full_path = concat_path_file(dd->dd_dirname, path);
int ret = exist_file_dir(full_path);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the path argument is concatenated into a filesystem path with no check for traversal elements or absolute components. Trigger: a caller (e.g., a D-Bus method) supplies a value like '../../etc/shadow'. Consequence: exist_file_dir probes a location outside the restricted dump directory, disclosing file existence and enabling broader read/write/ownership operations in sibling dd* functions.

commit_msg: Reject cpio symlinks that exceed 1MB
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (cpio->entry_bytes_remaining > 1024 * 1024) {', '\t\t\tarchive_set_error(&a->archive, ENOMEM,', '\t\t\t    "Rejecting malformed cpio archive: symlink contents exceed 1 megabyte");', '\t\t\treturn (ARCHIVE_FATAL);', '\t\t}']}
description: The archive_read_format_cpio_read_header function in archive_read_support_format_cpio.c in libarchive before 3.2.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a CPIO archive with a large symlink.

code_evidence: For a symlink entry, the code passes cpio->entry_bytes_remaining (an archive-controlled field) directly as the size argument to __archive_read_ahead, without any upper bound check on that length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an attacker-supplied size field and processes it without checking it satisfies the required property (bounded length), which is improper input validation of metadata; the added guard confirms this missing constraint. A more specific resource-exhaustion CWE could also apply, but the target CWE-20 fits the missing validation of the length field.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the symlink-content length from the CPIO header is trusted without validating it against a sane maximum. Trigger: a crafted CPIO archive declaring a symlink with a very large entry_bytes_remaining causes __archive_read_ahead to attempt a correspondingly large read/allocation. Supported consequence: resource exhaustion leading to application crash (DoS), as reflected by the ENOMEM path used in the fix.

commit_msg:
dnn_backend_native: Add overflow check for length calculation.

We should not silently allocate an incorrect sized buffer.
Fixes trac issue #8718.

Signed-off-by: Reimar Döffinger <Reimar.Doeffinger@gmx.de>
Reviewed-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
Reviewed-by: Guo, Yejun <yejun.guo@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (oprd->length <= 0)', '        return DNN_ERROR;']}
description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability in FFMpeg 4.2.3 in dnn_execute_layer_pad in libavfilter/dnn/dnn_backend_native_layer_pad.c due to a call to memcpy without length checks, which could let a remote malicious user execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: The function frees the operand data, then computes oprd->length via calculate_operand_data_length(oprd) from attacker-influenced dims[1..3] (input->height/width/channels set at lines 19-21), and passes that length directly to av_malloc without validating it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a size-calculation/under-allocation issue rather than a classic buffer copy without input size checking; the missing check on the computed length leads to an incorrectly sized buffer that later receives data. CWE-120 is supported to the extent that the unchecked length permits a buffer overflow, though the proximate defect is size validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length derived from input dimensions is used unchecked as the allocation size. A trigger is dimensions causing calculate_operand_data_length to return a negative or overflowing value; the allocation then succeeds with an incorrect small/zero size, so subsequent writes into input->data (line 27) overflow the buffer. Consequence is memory corruption potentially leading to code execution.

commit_msg:
evtchn: address races with evtchn_reset()

Neither d->evtchn_port_ops nor max_evtchns(d) may be used in an entirely
lock-less manner, as both may change by a racing evtchn_reset(). In the
common case, at least one of the domain's event lock or the per-channel
lock needs to be held. In the specific case of the inter-domain sending
by evtchn_send() and notify_via_xen_event_channel() holding the other
side's per-channel lock is sufficient, as the channel can't change state
without both per-channel locks held. Without such a channel changing
state, evtchn_reset() can't complete successfully.

Lock-free accesses continue to be permitted for the shim (calling some
otherwise internal event channel functions), as this happens while the
domain is in effectively single-threaded mode. Special care also needs
taking for the shim's marking of in-use ports as ECS_RESERVED (allowing
use of such ports in the shim case is okay because switching into and
hence also out of FIFO mode is impossihble there).

As a side effect, certain operations on Xen bound event channels which
were mistakenly permitted so far (e.g. unmask or poll) will be refused
now.

This is part of XSA-343.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned long flags;', '    spin_lock_irqsave(&evtchn->lock, flags);', '    spin_unlock_irqrestore(&evtchn->lock, flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The function validates the port, obtains the evtchn pointer via evtchn_from_port(d, port), and calls evtchn_port_unmask(d, evtchn) without holding evtchn->lock. The patch adds spin_lock_irqsave/spin_unlock_irqrestore around the unmask call, confirming the pre-patch code performed the unmask on a shared channel with no synchronization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the unmask operates on a shared resource without exclusive access, allowing an interfering concurrent code sequence (evtchn_reset) to modify channel state mid-operation. This is a synchronization/race weakness, distinct from a simple missing bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: evtchn_port_unmask() mutates the shared evtchn state while a concurrent evtchn_reset() can change the channel state, since neither the domain event lock nor the per-channel lock is held. Trigger: a racing reset (e.g., EVTCHNOP_reset) interleaves with this unmask. Consequence: violation of internal assumptions, potentially out-of-bounds accesses, bug checks, DoS, or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
driver core: platform: fix race condition with driver_override

The driver_override implementation is susceptible to race condition when
different threads are reading vs storing a different driver override.
Add locking to avoid race condition.

Fixes: 3d713e0e382e ("driver core: platform: add device binding path 'driver_override'")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Adrian Salido <salidoa@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar *driver_override, *old = pdev->driver_override, *cp;'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar *driver_override, *old, *cp;', '\tdevice_lock(dev);', '\told = pdev->driver_override;', '\tdevice_unlock(dev);']}
description: The driver_override implementation in drivers/base/platform.c in the Linux kernel before 4.12.1 allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging a race condition between a read operation and a store operation that involve different overrides.

code_evidence: Line 6 reads pdev->driver_override into 'old' without holding device_lock, and lines 15-20 overwrite pdev->driver_override under the same unlocked region; line 21 then frees the previously captured pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent access to the shared pdev->driver_override resource lacking exclusive access, matching CWE-362. It is not merely a missing check; the read-modify-free sequence is non-atomic across threads.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The store path reads, replaces and frees pdev->driver_override without synchronization against concurrent readers or other stores. Two racing stores can both capture the same 'old' pointer and one frees it after the other has already replaced or freed it, yielding a use-after-free/double-free that can escalate to privilege gain.

commit_msg:
Issue 4817 - BUG - locked crypt accounts on import may allow all passwords

Bug Description: Due to mishanding of short dbpwd hashes, the
crypt_r algorithm was misused and was only comparing salts
in some cases, rather than checking the actual content
of the password.

Fix Description: Stricter checks on dbpwd lengths to ensure
that content passed to crypt_r has at least 2 salt bytes and
1 hash byte, as well as stricter checks on ct_memcmp to ensure
that compared values are the same length, rather than potentially
allowing overruns/short comparisons.

fixes: https://github.com/389ds/389-ds-base/issues/4817

Author: William Brown <william@blackhats.net.au>

Review by: ???
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int rc;', '    char *cp;', '    /* we use salt (first 2 chars) of encoded password in call to crypt_r() */', '    cp = crypt_r(userpwd, dbpwd, &data);', '    if (cp) {', '        rc = slapi_ct_memcmp(dbpwd, cp, strlen(dbpwd));'], 'added_lines': ['    int rc = -1;', '    char *cp = NULL;', '    size_t dbpwd_len = strlen(dbpwd);', '    /*', '     * there MUST be at least 2 chars of salt and some pw bytes, else this is INVALID and will', '     * allow any password to bind as we then only compare SALTS.', '     */', '    if (dbpwd_len >= 3) {', '        /* we use salt (first 2 chars) of encoded password in call to crypt_r() */', '        cp = crypt_r(userpwd, dbpwd, &data);', '    }', '    /* If these are not the same length, we can not proceed safely with memcmp. */', '    if (cp && dbpwd_len == strlen(cp)) {', '        rc = slapi_ct_memcmp(dbpwd, cp, dbpwd_len);']}
description: A flaw was found in 389-ds-base. If an asterisk is imported as password hashes, either accidentally or maliciously, then instead of being inactive, any password will successfully match during authentication. This flaw allows an attacker to successfully authenticate as a user whose password was disabled.

code_evidence: crypt_r is called with dbpwd as salt without verifying dbpwd has enough bytes; if dbpwd is a short hash (e.g. '*'), crypt_r uses only the salt bytes and returns a value. slapi_ct_memcmp then compares dbpwd against cp using strlen(dbpwd), which for a short dbpwd compares only the salt portion, not the actual password content.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the password verification routine; its flawed length handling lets arbitrary credentials satisfy the check, directly constituting improper authentication (CWE-287). The related CWE-697 comparison issue is the mechanism, but the security outcome is failed identity proof.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the comparison length is derived from the untrusted stored hash (strlen(dbpwd)) and no minimum-length check is performed before calling crypt_r. Trigger: a stored hash with fewer than 3 bytes (e.g. '*') is imported. Consequence: the comparison reduces to a salt-only match, so any user password authenticates as that account, bypassing authentication.

commit_msg: Fix integer overflow for multiframe gifs.

Prior to versions 2.12.0 and 2.11.1, integer overflow occurs when `2^31 <= num_frames * height * width * channels < 2^32`, for example Full HD screencast of at least 346 frames. A fix is included in TensorFlow version 2.12.0 and version 2.11.1.

code_evidence: target_num_frames (from gif_file->ImageCount), width, height and channel=3 are ints; allocate_output is called with these ints [29,39,40,41,43,44] and the allocation size num_frames*width*height*channels is computed inside the allocator.

description: Multiple stack-based buffer underflows in decoder/ih264d_parse_cavlc.c in mediaserver in Android 6.x before 2016-04-01 allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, aka internal bug 26399350.

If u4_trailing_ones exceeds u4_total_coeff, i goes negative and the writes at lines 27 and 58 index below the array.

commit_msg:
a/ulaw: fix multiple buffer overflows

i2ulaw_array() and i2alaw_array() fail to handle ptr [count] = INT_MIN
properly, leading to buffer underflow. INT_MIN is a special value
since - INT_MIN cannot be represented as int.

In this case round - INT_MIN to INT_MAX and proceed as usual.

f2ulaw_array() and f2alaw_array() fail to handle ptr [count] = NaN
properly, leading to null pointer dereference.

In this case, arbitrarily set the buffer value to 0.

This commit fixes #429 (CVE-2018-19661 and CVE-2018-19662) and
fixes #344 (CVE-2017-17456 and CVE-2017-17457).

--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -1,7 +1,9 @@
 static inline void
 i2ulaw_array (const int *ptr, int count, unsigned char *buffer)
 {	while (--count >= 0)
-	{	if (ptr [count] >= 0)
+	{	if (ptr [count] == INT_MIN)
+			buffer [count] = ulaw_encode [INT_MAX >> (16 + 2)] ;
+		else if (ptr [count] >= 0)
 			buffer [count] = ulaw_encode [ptr [count] >> (16 + 2)] ;

code_evidence: The loop indexes ptr[count] and writes buffer[count] using count derived from the caller. When ptr[count] is negative, line 7 negates it (-ptr[count]) and shifts the result to index ulaw_encode. For ptr[count] == INT_MIN, -INT_MIN overflows, producing an undefined/out-of-range index into the ulaw_encode lookup table, so the table read occurs outside its bounds.

Trigger: a buffer element equal to INT_MIN. Consequence: the computed shift index falls outside ulaw_encode, causing an out-of-bounds table read (crash/DoS, possible memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121

commit_msg:
Fix invalid memory accesses and add missing checks in src/dtm.cpp

There are several issues when loading .dtm files which can lead
to invalid memory accesses. This patch fixes the following:

* In CdtmLoader::load(), ensure that title and author strings
  are properly terminated to avoid out-of-bounds reads.
* Check that the number of instruments is valid. This avoids a
  heap-based buffer overflow (see issue #86).
* Reading the description string could overflow a stack buffer
  by 1 byte and write past the end of the array into an adjacent
  class member (which is only initialized later). Get rid of the
  stack buffer and truncate the description if necessary.
* Fail loading when an error is detected while trying to read
  data from the file or while decoding RLE data.
* Check the argument of CdtmLoader::getinstrument() to avoid
  out-of-bound accesses.

This fixes CVE-2019-14691.

Fixes: https://github.com/adplug/adplug/issues/86

The stack allocated color map buffers were not zeroed before usage, and
so undefined palette indexes could cause information leakage.

description: The GIF decoding function gdImageCreateFromGifCtx in gd_gif_in.c in the GD Graphics Library (aka libgd), as used in PHP before 5.6.31 and 7.x before 7.1.7, does not zero colorMap arrays before use. description: The ReadWPGImage function in coders/wpg.c in ImageMagick 7.0.7-9 does not properly validate the colormap index in a WPG palette, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (use of uninitialized data or invalid memory allocation) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a malformed WPG file.

description: EOSIO/eos eos version after commit f1545dd0ae2b77580c2236fdb70ae7138d2c7168 contains a stack overflow vulnerability in abi_serializer that can result in attack eos network node. This attack appear to be exploitable via network request. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in after commit cf7209e703e6d3f7a5413e0cb1fe88a4d8e4b38d .

code_evidence: The function receives recursion_depth and immediately enforces a bound: FC_ASSERT(++recursion_depth < abi_serializer::max_recursion_depth), so nested extraction is depth-limited.
When data is an object, the resolver supplies the ABI and the function converts the nested object via abi->variant_to_binary(type, data) without forwarding recursion_depth.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the function fails to propagate the recursion bound into the nested conversion, allowing uncontrolled recursive descent. The local assertion alone does not cover the recursive call path, so the missing depth argument is the supported weakness rather than a separate deserialization error.

evidence_lines.code:

FC_ASSERT( ++recursion_depth < abi_serializer::max_recursion_depth, "recursive definition, max_recursion_depth" );

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the depth counter is incremented and checked at entry, but the recursive conversion call at the object branch invokes variant_to_binary without passing recursion_depth, so the nested serialization path restarts or loses the accumulated depth. Trigger: a network-supplied action with object-typed data whose ABI type recursively references itself. Consequence: unbounded recursion consumes the program stack, causing a stack overflow and node denial of service.

commit_msg:
x86/vpt: fix race when migrating timers between vCPUs

The current vPT code will migrate the emulated timers between vCPUs
(change the pt->vcpu field) while just holding the destination lock,
either from create_periodic_time or pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target if
the global target is adjusted. Changing the periodic_timer vCPU field
in this way creates a race where a third party could grab the lock in
the unlocked region of pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target (or before
create_periodic_time performs the vcpu change) and then release the
lock from a different vCPU, creating a locking imbalance.

Introduce a per-domain rwlock in order to protect periodic_time
migration between vCPU lists. Taking the lock in read mode prevents
any timer from being migrated to a different vCPU, while taking it in
write mode allows performing migration of timers across vCPUs. The
per-vcpu locks are still used to protect all the other fields from the
periodic_timer struct.

Note that such migration shouldn't happen frequently, and hence
there's no performance drop as a result of such locking.

This is XSA-336.

Reported-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Tested-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    rwlock_init(&d->arch.hvm.pl_time->pt_migrate);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There is a race condition when migrating timers between x86 HVM vCPUs. When migrating timers of x86 HVM guests between its vCPUs, the locking model used allows for a second vCPU of the same guest (also operating on the timers) to release a lock that it didn't acquire. The most likely effect of the issue is a hang or crash of the hypervisor, i.e., a Denial of Service (DoS). All versions of Xen are affected. Only x86 systems are vulnerable. Arm systems are not vulnerable. Only x86 HVM guests can leverage the vulnerability. x86 PV and PVH cannot leverage the vulnerability. Only guests with more than one vCPU can exploit the vulnerability.

code_evidence: pl_time is allocated with xzalloc and only its domain field is set (line 39); no synchronization primitive protecting the periodic_timer migration state is initialized.
The added fix initializes pt_migrate here, showing the original function lacked this lock initialization entirely.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function leaves shared pl_time timer state without a synchronization mechanism, enabling a concurrent sequence to modify the shared resource during migration, matching CWE-362's improper synchronization race condition. The fix's rwlock_init confirms the missing exclusivity constraint.

evidence_lines.code:
d->arch.hvm.pl_time = xzalloc(struct pl_time);
d->arch.hvm.pl_time->domain = d;

d->arch.hvm.pl_time->domain = d;
if ( is_hardware_domain(d) )

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: hvm_domain_initialise sets up the per-domain pl_time structure without initializing any lock to serialize migration of periodic timers between vCPUs. Trigger: a multi-vCPU x86 HVM guest where one vCPU migrates a timer while another concurrently operates on the same timer list, since only per-vCPU locks guard other fields. Consequence: locking imbalance leading to hypervisor hang or crash (DoS).

this commit:

description: QEMU (aka Quick Emulator), when built with the e1000e NIC emulation support, allows local guest OS privileged users to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via vectors related to setting the initial receive / transmit descriptor head (TDH/RDH) outside the allocated descriptor buffer.

code_evidence: desc_size is clamped to rx_desc_buf_size at lines 25-27, so the amount advanced per iteration is bounded regardless of the descriptor head position.

The do-while at line 90 continues while desc_offset < total_size; desc_offset is only incremented at line 78 inside the ba[0] branch. If the DMA-read descriptor at base has ba[0]==0 (null descriptor, line 82), desc_offset is never advanced and the ring is advanced at line 88-89, so the loop condition cannot be satisfied for a head outside the buffer.

This is a loop-termination flaw, not a bounded-buffer overrun; the missing e1000e_ring_empty check is the fix that restores termination.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop's exit condition depends on desc_offset reaching total_size, but desc_offset only increases when a valid buffer is found; a null descriptor skips the increment. Trigger: guest sets RDH/TDH outside the allocated descriptor buffer so the descriptor read yields ba[0]==0. Consequence: the do-while spins indefinitely, causing CPU denial of service.

commit_msg:
netlink: Fix dump skb leak/double free

When we free cb->skb after a dump, we do it after releasing the
lock.  This means that a new dump could have started in the time
being and we'll end up freeing their skb instead of ours.

This patch saves the skb and module before we unlock so we free
the right memory.

Fixes: 16b304f3404f ("netlink: Eliminate kmalloc in netlink dump operation.")
Reported-by: Baozeng Ding <sploving1@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Acked-by: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmodule_put(cb->module);', '\tconsume_skb(cb->skb);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct module *module;', '\tmodule = cb->module;', '\tskb = cb->skb;', '\tmodule_put(module);', '\tconsume_skb(skb);']}
description: Race condition in the netlink_dump function in net/netlink/af_netlink.c in the Linux kernel before 4.6.3 allows local users to cause a denial of service (double free) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted application that makes sendmsg system calls, leading to a free operation associated with a new dump that started earlier than anticipated.

code_evidence: After setting cb_running=false and releasing cb_mutex at line 53, the function dereferences cb->module and cb->skb outside the lock at lines 54-55, so a concurrent dump can overwrite these fields before they are consumed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The shared netlink_callback is accessed outside the lock that protects it, violating exclusivity/atomicity; an interfering dump modifies cb->skb before consume_skb. This is a concurrency race, not merely a memory-management bug, so CWE-362 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: cb->skb and cb->module are read after mutex_unlock, so the unlocked window lets a new dump reinitialize the shared cb and replace its skb. Trigger: a local user issues sendmsg calls that start a new dump between unlock and consume_skb. Consequence: the wrong skb is freed, causing a double free or leak leading to DoS.

commit_msg:
Validate intermediate symlinks during installation, CVE-2021-35939

Whenever directory changes during unpacking, walk the entire tree from
starting from / and validate any symlinks crossed, fail the install
on invalid links.

This is the first of step of many towards securing our file operations
against local tamperers and besides plugging that one CVE, paves the way
for the next step by adding the necessary directory fd tracking.
This also bumps the rpm OS requirements to a whole new level by requiring
the *at() family of calls from POSIX-1.2008.

This necessarily does a whole lot of huffing and puffing we previously
did not do. It should be possible to cache secure (ie root-owned)
directory structures to avoid validating everything a million times
but for now, just keeping things simple.

description: It was found that the fix for CVE-2017-7500 and CVE-2017-7501 was incomplete: the check was only implemented for the parent directory of the file to be created. A local unprivileged user who owns another ancestor directory could potentially use this flaw to gain root privileges. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to data confidentiality and integrity as well as system availability.

code_evidence: The install loop iterates package files and stat/verifies each path via fsmStat/fsmVerify using fp->fpath, a name-based path, before creating regular files, directories, symlinks, fifos or device nodes.
Directory creation is performed through fsmMkdir(fp->fpath, mode) using the full pathname rather than a validated directory descriptor, so any ancestor symlink swapped by a local user is followed.
Symlink creation via fsmSymlink(rpmfiFLink(fi), fp->fpath) likewise targets a name-based path without verifying that intermediate components are not attacker-controlled links.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the code accesses files by name and fails to prevent intermediate path components from resolving through attacker-controlled links, the classic link-following weakness. It is not merely a race on the final file (CWE-367); the cause is improper link resolution of ancestor directories before access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function resolves file operations by full pathname without validating that each intermediate directory component is a real root-owned directory. A local unprivileged user who owns an ancestor directory can replace it with a symlink before the install reaches the file, causing fsmMkdir, fsmSymlink or fsmMkfile to operate on an unintended location. The supported consequence is creation/modification of files outside the intended tree, enabling privilege escalation when run by root.

commit_msg: Fix the Rijndael timing attack counter measure
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tword32 u = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\tvolatile word32 u = 0;']}
description: The timing attack protection in Rijndael::Enc::ProcessAndXorBlock and Rijndael::Dec::ProcessAndXorBlock in Crypto++ (aka cryptopp) before 5.6.4 may be optimized out by the compiler, which allows attackers to conduct timing attacks.

code_evidence: The countermeasure declares a plain word32 accumulator u initialized to zero for the cache-line touch loop.
The loop iterates over Td cache lines; on the non-unaligned path it walks i<1024 in cacheLineSize steps.
Each iteration ANDs u with a loaded table word and finally with Td[255], then ORs u into s0..s3; the result is only used to force the table lines into cache.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing volatile qualifier lets the compiler strip the timing countermeasure, so secret-dependent cache behavior leaks key information to an unauthorized observer. CWE-200 fits as exposure of sensitive information; the timing side channel is the leak vector, distinct from a generic confidentiality impact.

evidence_lines.code:
for (i=0; i<2048; i+=cacheLineSize)
for (i=0; i<1024; i+=cacheLineSize)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: u is a non-volatile local whose only purpose is the side effect of reading table cache lines; the compiler may prove u's value is unused and remove the loop. Trigger: any build where the compiler optimizes away the dead countermeasure. Consequence: the table-lookup timing profile again depends on secret-dependent indices, enabling timing attacks that recover key data.

commit_msg:
Avoid integer overflows in SETRANGE and SORT (CVE-2022-35977) (#11720)

Authenticated users issuing specially crafted SETRANGE and SORT(_RO)
commands can trigger an integer overflow, resulting with Redis attempting
to allocate impossible amounts of memory and abort with an OOM panic.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (checkStringLength(c,offset+sdslen(value)) != C_OK)', '        if (checkStringLength(c,offset+sdslen(value)) != C_OK)'], 'added_lines': ['        if (checkStringLength(c,offset,sdslen(value)) != C_OK)', '        if (checkStringLength(c,offset,sdslen(value)) != C_OK)']}
description: Redis is an in-memory database that persists on disk. Authenticated users issuing specially crafted `SETRANGE` and `SORT(_RO)` commands can trigger an integer overflow, resulting with Redis attempting to allocate impossible amounts of memory and abort with an out-of-memory (OOM) panic. The problem is fixed in Redis versions 7.0.8, 6.2.9 and 6.0.17. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: offset is parsed into a long and only checked for negativity; no upper bound is enforced before it is used in size computations.
In the new-key branch, offset+sdslen(value) is evaluated as an addition before checkStringLength, and the same sum is passed to sdsnewlen as the allocation size.
In the existing-key branch, the identical unchecked offset+sdslen(value) sum is passed to sdsgrowzero and then used as the memcpy destination offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is an integer addition whose result is assumed to exceed its operands but can wrap, and the wrapped value directly controls memory allocation and copy sizing, matching CWE-190. This is distinct from an off-by-one or plain length-limit bypass because the flaw is the arithmetic wraparound itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: offset is attacker-controlled and the expression offset+sdslen(value) is computed in signed long arithmetic without an overflow guard. Trigger: a large positive SETRANGE offset near LONG_MAX combined with a nonzero value length wraps the sum to a small or negative number, so checkStringLength validates the wrapped value. The wrapped result then reaches sdsnewlen/sdsgrowzero and memcpy, causing impossible allocation or out-of-bounds access rather than the intended length rejection.

Moonlight-common-c is vulnerable to buffer overflow starting in commit f57bd745b4cbed577ea654fad4701bea4d38b44c. A malicious game streaming server could exploit a buffer overflow vulnerability to crash a moonlight client. Achieving RCE is possible but unlikely, due to stack canaries in use by modern compiler toolchains. The published binaries for official clients Qt, Android, iOS/tvOS, and Embedded are built with stack canaries, but some unofficial clients may not use stack canaries. This vulnerability takes place after the pairing process, so it requires the client to be tricked into pairing to a malicious host. It is not possible to perform using a man-in-the-middle due to public key pinning that takes place during the pairing process. The bug was addressed in commit b2497a3918a6d79808d9fd0c04734786e70d5954.

code_evidence: getOptionContent returns the server-controlled Session option string; the only validation is a NULL check at line 107. Line 112 then copies that string into the fixed-size global sessionIdString with unchecked strcpy, so a Session value longer than the destination overflows it. No length comparison against sizeof(sessionIdString) occurs before the copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because this is a buffer-copy operation (strcpy) from an input buffer to an output buffer with no verification that the input is smaller than the destination. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the copy writes past sessionIdString.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the RTSP Session header value comes from the remote server and is copied by strcpy without a size check into a fixed buffer. Trigger: a malicious host replies to SETUP with an oversized Session option. Consequence: a stack/global buffer overflow, potentially crashing the client or corrupting memory (RCE is limited by stack canaries).

description: The xmlParseElementDecl function in parser.c in libxml2 before 2.9.4 allows context-dependent attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer underread and application crash) via a crafted file, involving xmlParseName.

code_evidence: The INCLUDE loop at [29,30] iterates while the raw input is nonzero and not at the closing ']]>' and the parser state is not EOF. The more specific underread is a consequence rooted in this missing halt; the target label is CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on malformed conditional-section input the parser detects a no-progress condition but only breaks the inner loop, leaving the parser in a bad state. description: When using the gdImageCreateFromXbm() function in the GD Graphics Library (aka LibGD) 2.2.5, as used in the PHP GD extension in PHP versions 7.1.x below 7.1.30, 7.2.x below 7.2.19 and 7.3.x below 7.3.6, it is possible to supply data that will cause the function to use the value of uninitialized variable. commit_msg:
The X protocol uses CARD16 values to represent the length so
this would overflow.

CVE-2021-31535

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (strlen(pattern) >= USHRT_MAX)', '        return NULL;']}
description: LookupCol.c in X.Org X through X11R7.7 and libX11 before 1.7.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The libX11 XLookupColor request (intended for server-side color lookup) contains a flaw allowing a client to send color-name requests with a name longer than the maximum size allowed by the protocol (and also longer than the maximum packet size for normal-sized packets). The user-controlled data exceeding the maximum size is then interpreted by the server as additional X protocol requests and executed, e.g., to disable X server authorization completely. For example, if the victim encounters malicious terminal control sequences for color codes, then the attacker may be able to take full control of the running graphical session.

code_evidence: Line 22 truncates the caller-controlled pattern length to CARD16 via a cast into req->nbytes, while nbytes retains the full strlen value; line 23 computes the wire length from the truncated value, and line 24 sends nbytes bytes of pattern to the server. No check bounds strlen(pattern) before these operations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies/sends an input buffer (pattern) whose length exceeds the size representable in the output protocol field without checking that size, matching CWE-120's buffer copy without input size checking. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the unchecked length causes data to overflow into adjacent protocol request space.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pattern string length is cast to CARD16 without validating it against the protocol's 16-bit length field, so an oversized pattern yields a small nbytes in the request header while _XSend transmits the untruncated buffer. Trigger: a client supplies a color/font pattern longer than USHRT_MAX. Consequence: the excess user data is interpreted by the X server as additional protocol requests, enabling arbitrary request execution such as disabling authorization.

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The estimator for the cost of some convolution operations can be made to execute a division by 0. commit_msg:
Preemption must be disabled before enabling interrupts in do_trap
on x86_64 because the stack in use for int3 and debug is a per CPU
stack set by th IST. But 32bit does not have an IST and the stack
still belongs to the current task and there is no problem in scheduling
out the task.

Keep preemption enabled on X86_32 when enabling interrupts for
do_trap().

The name of the function is changed from preempt_conditional_sti/cli()
to conditional_sti/cli_ist(), to annotate that this function is used
when the stack is on the IST.

Cc: stable-rt@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Steven Rostedt <rostedt@goodmis.org>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tpreempt_conditional_sti(regs);', '\tpreempt_conditional_cli(regs);'], 'added_lines': ['\tconditional_sti_ist(regs);', '\tconditional_cli_ist(regs);']}
description: The int3 handler in the Linux kernel before 3.3 relies on a per-CPU debug stack, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (stack corruption and panic) via a crafted application that triggers certain lock contention.

code_evidence: do_int3 enables interrupts via preempt_conditional_sti(regs) before calling do_trap, then disables them via preempt_conditional_cli(regs) afterward. On x86_64 the int3 handler runs on the per-CPU IST debug stack, so enabling interrupts while preemption remains enabled allows the current task to be scheduled out and another task to reuse/corrupt that per-CPU stack.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect permits unbounded concurrent reuse of a limited shared resource (the single per-CPU IST stack), exhausting/corrupting it and causing a crash; this matches CWE-400's resource-consumption-to-DoS scope rather than a pure memory-safety bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: interrupts are re-enabled without first disabling preemption while executing on a shared per-CPU IST stack. Trigger: a crafted local application causes int3 handling with lock contention leading to a reschedule. Consequence: the per-CPU debug stack is corrupted and the kernel panics, a denial of service.

commit_msg: Fix buffer overflow vulnerability.  Issue #4.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  char dir[150];', '  char filepath[150];'], 'added_lines': ['  char* dir;', '  char* filepath;']}
description: borg-reducer c6d5240 is affected by: Buffer Overflow. The impact is: Possible code execution and denial of service. The component is: Output parameter within the executable.

It is not merely a read overrun or integer issue; the missing length constraint causes memory to be written past the end of the buffers.

Trigger: supplying an `output` value longer than the remaining space in `dir` (or `filepath`). commit_msg:
Prevent segfault with incorrect form_int fid

Bug-Debian: https://github.com/tats/w3m/issues/15
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    else if (forms_size <= form_max) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (forms_size <= form_max) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Tatsuya Kinoshita w3m fork before 0.5.3-31. w3m allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault and crash) via a crafted HTML page.

code_evidence: When fid < 0, form_max and form_sp are incremented and fid is set to the new form_max; otherwise form_max is raised to fid and form_sp set to fid, so a crafted form_int can drive fid/form_sp beyond the allocated forms_size.

The buffer growth is guarded by 'else if (forms_size <= form_max)': because the first branch (forms_size == 0) allocates INITIAL_FORM_SIZE and skips this else-if, a large initial form_max leaves forms allocated at INITIAL_FORM_SIZE while form_max exceeds it, so the resize is not performed.
form_stack[form_sp] is written using the unchecked form_sp index into the possibly undersized form_stack allocation.
forms[fid] = newFormList(...) stores through the unchecked fid index into the undersized forms array; the resulting out-of-bounds access corrupts/reads invalid memory and can crash (segfault).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The crash arises from the faulty else-if control flow that skips necessary allocation, leading to out-of-bounds indexing rather than a direct NULL dereference; the root cause is missing size enforcement, not dereferencing a NULL pointer, so CWE-476 is only loosely supported by the observed consequence.

evidence_lines.code: form_stack[form_sp] = fid;
forms[fid] = newFormList(q, p, r, s, tg, n, NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The size-0 initialization branch prevents the subsequent 'else if' resize from running even when form_max already exceeds INITIAL_FORM_SIZE, so forms/form_stack remain too small. A crafted HTML form_int with a large or negative fid sets form_sp/fid past the allocation, and the unchecked indexing at form_stack[form_sp] and forms[fid] writes out of bounds, causing a segmentation fault.

description: An issue was discovered in PHP 5.x and 7.x, when the configuration uses apache2handler/mod_php or php-fpm with OpCache enabled. With 5.x after 5.6.28 or 7.x after 7.0.13, the issue is resolved in a non-default configuration with the opcache.validate_permission=1 setting. The vulnerability details are as follows. In PHP SAPIs where PHP interpreters share a common parent process, Zend OpCache creates a shared memory object owned by the common parent during initialization. Child PHP processes inherit the SHM descriptor, using it to cache and retrieve compiled script bytecode ("opcode" in PHP jargon). Cache keys vary depending on configuration, but filename is a central key component, and compiled opcode can generally be run if a script's filename is known or can be guessed. Many common shared-hosting configurations change EUID in child processes to enforce privilege separation among hosted users (for example using mod_ruid2 for the Apache HTTP Server, or php-fpm user settings). In these scenarios, the default Zend OpCache behavior defeats script file permissions by sharing a single SHM cache among all child PHP processes. PHP scripts often contain sensitive information: Think of CMS configurations where reading or running another user's script usually means gaining privileges to the CMS database.

code_evidence: The function looks up a cached persistent_script by key/opened_path and, when found, reuses it without checking whether the current process may still read the underlying file; the pre-patch path jumps straight from hash lookup to SHM_UNPROTECT and cache use. The added guard at lines 89+ only runs when validate_permission is enabled and file_handle->type == ZEND_HANDLE_FILENAME, so cached opcode can be loaded from shared memory based solely on filename/key despite the file's permissions being revoked for the current (privilege-separated) user.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper enforcement of file access permissions: cached opcode is reused without validating the caller's read permission, so access control intended by filesystem permissions is defeated. This fits CWE-264's permissions/privileges/access-control category; the added access(file_handle->filename, R_OK) check confirms the missing permission constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: cached bytecode is served from shared memory keyed by filename, with no access() check on the cached file before reuse. Trigger: a shared-hosting child process whose EUID no longer permits reading a script still finds the script in the shared OpCache hash and executes its cached opcode. Consequence: file-permission boundaries between hosted users are bypassed, exposing sensitive script contents/behavior.

commit_msg:
nfsd: stricter decoding of write-like NFSv2/v3 ops

The NFSv2/v3 code does not systematically check whether we decode past
the end of the buffer.  This generally appears to be harmless, but there
are a few places where we do arithmetic on the pointers involved and
don't account for the possibility that a length could be negative.  Add
checks to catch these.

Reported-by: Tuomas Haanpää <thaan@synopsys.com>
Reported-by: Ari Kauppi <ari@synopsys.com>
Reviewed-by: NeilBrown <neilb@suse.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: J. Bruce Fields <bfields@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (hdr > head->iov_len)', '\t\treturn 0;']}
description: The NFSv2 and NFSv3 server implementations in the Linux kernel through 4.10.13 lack certain checks for the end of a buffer, which allows remote attackers to trigger pointer-arithmetic errors or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted requests, related to fs/nfsd/nfs3xdr.c and fs/nfsd/nfsxdr.c.

code_evidence: hdr is computed from the decoded pointer p relative to head->iov_base without checking that p lies within head; dlen is then derived by subtracting hdr, and the guard only checks dlen < XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4.

rq_vec[0].iov_len = head->iov_len - hdr can underflow when hdr exceeds iov_len, making the length huge; the while loop then walks vectors using that oversized length and writes rq_vec[v].iov_len past PAGE_SIZE.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe arithmetic produces a length not bounded by the actual request buffer, and the resulting vector loop operates outside the intended buffer boundaries, matching CWE-119. It is not merely a negative-length logic error: the computed size directly drives out-of-bounds reads/writes in the iovec array.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The decoder does not verify that the decoded write header position is within the request buffer before computing lengths. A crafted NFSv2 write request can make hdr exceed head->iov_len, causing unsigned underflow in the iov_len subtraction; the subsequent loop then uses the inflated length to index and size rq_vec entries beyond the allocated vector, leading to out-of-bounds memory operations.

commit_msg:
Have a common routine for converting dates and times to strings.

Have a routine that takes a buffer, a strftime format, and a struct tm *
as arguments, and:

* checks whether the struct tm * is null and, if so, returns a string
indicating that the date and time couldn't be converted;

* otherwise, passes it to strftime(), along with the buffer and the
format argument and, if strftime() returns 0, meaning the string didn't
fit into the buffer and thus that the buffer's contents are undefined,
returns a string indicating that the date and time didn't fit into the
buffer;

* otherwise, returns a pointer to the buffer.

Call that routine instead of directly calling strftime() in printers;
that prevents printing a buffer with undefined data if the buffer isn't
big enough for the string.

Also, when generating file names using an strftime format, check the
return value of strftime() to make sure the buffer didn't overflow.

description: The SMB protocol decoder in tcpdump version 4.99.3 can perform an out-of-bounds write when decoding a crafted network packet.

code_evidence: Line 7 declares a fixed-size stack buffer buf of BUFSIZE bytes.

Line 12 calls strftime with the fixed format and checks only whether the return is 0; on success the formatted string is written into buf, but the format/field widths are not bounded to a size that guarantees fit, and the caller-supplied nanoseconds value is later appended via the %09u specifier at line 15.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes formatted time data into a fixed-size buffer without ensuring the total output (date/time string plus appended nanoseconds) fits, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely a format-string or integer-overflow issue; the defect is the unbounded write past the intended buffer end.

evidence_lines.code: char buf[BUFSIZE];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination buffer is a fixed-size array whose capacity is not derived from the maximum formatted output of the strftime format plus the appended fractional-seconds field. Trigger: a struct tm whose formatted date/time plus the 9-digit nanosecond suffix exceeds BUFSIZE, so strftime may write up to the buffer boundary and the subsequent ND_PRINT append can extend beyond it. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds write to stack memory corrupting adjacent data, potentially causing a crash or memory corruption.

description: Envoy is an open source edge and service proxy, designed for cloud-native applications. The default_validator.cc implementation used to implement the default certificate validation routines has a "type confusion" bug when processing subjectAltNames. This processing allows, for example, an rfc822Name or uniformResourceIndicator to be authenticated as a domain name. This confusion allows for the bypassing of nameConstraints, as processed by the underlying OpenSSL/BoringSSL implementation, exposing the possibility of impersonation of arbitrary servers. As a result Envoy will trust upstream certificates that should not be trusted.

code_evidence: Line 10 iterates every GENERAL_NAME in the subjectAltName extension and line 11 converts it to a string via Utility::generalNameAsString without regard to general_name->type. Line 12 then applies the configured string matcher to that string; only line 13's ternary inspects the type, and only to choose DNS-exact matching semantics, not to reject non-DNS SANs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code accesses a GENERAL_NAME resource by treating its value as a plain domain-name string regardless of the actual GeneralName type, which is exactly accessing a resource using an incompatible type. The type check at line 13 governs matching semantics only, so the confusion is not prevented; this is CWE-843 rather than merely improper certificate validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: all SAN entries are flattened to strings and matched against a configured name, so an rfc822Name or URI entry is compared as if it were a dNSName. Trigger: a certificate carrying the target name in a non-DNS GeneralName type. Consequence: the matcher returns true (line 18) for a name that should not satisfy the DNS constraint, allowing nameConstraints bypass and server impersonation.

description: GNU Tar through 1.30, when --sparse is used, mishandles file shrinkage during read access, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (infinite read loop in sparse_dump_region in sparse.c) by modifying a file that is supposed to be archived by a different user's process (e.g., a system backup running as root).

code_evidence: COPY_BUF's inner do-while advances src and only refills the block buffer when src == endp; it exits solely when a '\n' is copied into dst, so a buffer region lacking a newline drives repeated refills.
The macro is invoked at line 40 and again inside the sparse-map loop at lines 54 and 62 for each entry, so each invocation can iterate over block data until a newline is found.
The for loop at line 51 runs sparse_map_size times, each iteration consuming two newline-terminated numbers via COPY_BUF.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-835: the macro's iteration has an exit condition (newline) that cannot be reached for the supplied data, yielding an infinite/very long loop. It is not merely a buffer overread; the weakness is the unreachable loop termination.

evidence_lines.code:
#define COPY_BUF(b,buf,src) do                                     \
{                                                                 \
char *endp = b->buffer + BLOCKSIZE;                             \
char *dst = buf;                                                \
do                                                              \
{                                                             \
if (dst == buf + UINTMAX_STRSIZE_BOUND -1)                  \
{                                                         \
ERROR ((0, 0, _("%s: numeric overflow in sparse archive member"), \
file->stat_info->orig_file_name));               \
return false;                                           \
}                                                         \
if (src == endp)                                            \
{                                                         \
set_next_block_after (b);                               \
file->dumped_size += BLOCKSIZE;                         \
b = find_next_block ();                                 \
src = b->buffer;                                        \
endp = b->buffer + BLOCKSIZE;                           \
}                                                         \
*dst = *src++;                                              \
}                                                             \
while (*dst++ != '\n');                                         \
dst[-1] = 0;                                                    \
} while (0)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: COPY_BUF's exit condition depends on encountering a newline in the archive block stream; when the stream data is truncated or malformed (e.g., file shrinkage during read), no terminating newline is reachable and the macro keeps refilling blocks, producing an unbounded read loop. The trigger is attacker-influenced sparse archive data; the supported consequence is CPU/resource exhaustion (DoS).

description: In Libgcrypt 1.8.4, the C implementation of AES is vulnerable to a flush-and-reload side-channel attack because physical addresses are available to other processes. (The C implementation is used on platforms where an assembly-language implementation is unavailable.) NOTE: the vendor's position is that the issue report cannot be validated because there is no description of an attack

Consequence: key-dependent lookup patterns in the AES C implementation leak, supporting key recovery; the fix moves tables to .data/unshared pages rather than changing this function's access logic.

commit_msg:
Fix a null pointer exception caused by branching on uninitialized data.

This is due to not checking that the params for the quantization exists. If there is no quantization, we should not access the `.params` field.

Change-Id: I8fc476c4b274fdb21ba741caa0fbc6d1b8840663

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions all TFLite operations that use quantization can be made to use unitialized values. [For example](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/depthwise_conv.cc#L198-L200). The issue stems from the fact that `quantization.params` is only valid if `quantization.type` is different that `kTfLiteNoQuantization`. However, these checks are missing in large parts of the code. We have patched the issue in GitHub commits 537bc7c723439b9194a358f64d871dd326c18887, 4a91f2069f7145aab6ba2d8cfe41be8a110c18a5 and 8933b8a21280696ab119b63263babdb54c298538. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function casts filter->quantization.params to TfLiteAffineQuantization without verifying that quantization.type is not kTfLiteNoQuantization.

The resulting affine_quantization pointer is dereferenced via affine_quantization->scale->data in both the reference and optimized branches, so an absent quantization leaves params uninitialized and the scale access reads invalid data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the function uses a resource (quantization.params) that has not been initialized/validated before reinterpretation and dereference. The missing type check is the constraint whose absence permits the uninitialized use; this is not merely a null-pointer issue but use of an uninitialized resource.

evidence_lines.code:
const auto* affine_quantization =
reinterpret_cast<TfLiteAffineQuantization*>(filter->quantization.params);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes filter->quantization.params is a valid TfLiteAffineQuantization whenever this hybrid eval path runs, but params is only meaningful when quantization.type differs from kTfLiteNoQuantization. Trigger: a model whose filter tensor has no quantization reaches EvalHybridPerChannel. Consequence: the uninitialized/absent params are reinterpreted and dereferenced, causing invalid memory access or a crash rather than a controlled error.

commit_msg:
net: shell: dns: Properly manage lifetime of callback data

DNS callback needs "struct shell *shell" data structure to pass as
a parameter to shell print. How it was achieved previously is that
it was packaged together with cosmetic "bool first" param into
"struct net_shell_user_data" on the stack, and passed to the
callback. The problem was that the original command handler then
returned, so the "struct net_shell_user_data" on the stack was
overwritten, and the callback crashed on accessing it.

An obvious solution was to make that structure static, but that would
leave to issues still, as turns out we allow system shell to be run
as more than one concurrent instances.

Next solution was to keep this structure on the stack, but block the
command handler until callback is finished. However, that hit a
deadlock due to not well thought out use of a mutex in the shell
printing routines.

The solution presented here is due to @nordic-krch, who noticed that
"bool first" param is indeed cosmetic and not really required. Then
we have only "struct shell *shell" to pass to the callback, and can
do that in callback's pointer param directly, ditching
"struct net_shell_user_data" which needs to be stored on the stack.

Signed-off-by: Paul Sokolovsky <paul.sokolovsky@linaro.org>

description: Use After Free vulnerability in the Zephyr shell allows a serial or telnet connected user to cause denial of service, and possibly remote code execution. This issue affects: Zephyr shell versions prior to 1.14.0 on all.

code_evidence: The callback dereferences user_data as struct net_shell_user_data, extracting data->shell and data->user_data without any lifetime guarantee.
The boolean pointed to by data->user_data is written via *first = false.
The first flag is again written via *first = false inside the INPROGRESS branch.
The ALLDONE branch writes *first = false.
The FAIL branch writes *first = false.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function reuses a pointer to stack memory whose lifetime ended when the command handler returned, and the writes to *first and reads of data->shell operate on freed storage. This is a stale-pointer lifetime flaw, not merely a missing NULL check or a buffer overflow.

evidence_lines.code: *first = false;
*first = false;
*first = false;
*first = false;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The command handler stores struct net_shell_user_data on its stack and passes it to the DNS callback; when the handler returns, that stack memory is reclaimed. The asynchronous callback later dereferences the stale data pointer and writes through data->user_data, so the trigger is a DNS event arriving after the handler returned, causing a crash or memory corruption.

description: ImageMagick 7.0.6-6 has a memory exhaustion vulnerability in ReadWPGImage in coders/wpg.c via a crafted wpg image file.

code_evidence: When image->colors is 0 and bpp is not 24, the code computes image->colors=one << bpp and calls AcquireImageColormap with that count.
bpp is taken directly from the file (BitmapHeader1.Depth at 162 or BitmapHeader2.Depth at 217), so a crafted image can force a huge color count and allocation.
UnpackWPGRaster is then invoked with the attacker-controlled bpp for raster processing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to bound an attacker-controlled resource request (colormap size) before allocation, allowing uncontrolled memory consumption that degrades availability, matching CWE-400. It is not primarily an integer-overflow or out-of-bounds flaw, but a missing throttle on resource allocation.

evidence_lines.code: if(UnpackWPGRaster(image,bpp) < 0)

bpp=BitmapHeader1.Depth;
bpp=BitmapHeader2.Depth;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the depth field from the WPG bitmap header is used unchecked to size the colormap via one << bpp. Trigger: a crafted WPG file with an excessive depth value reaches this branch before any bound is enforced. Consequence: AcquireImageColormap attempts an enormous allocation, exhausting memory (the NoMemory path throws a resource-limit error), causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
sctp: Prevent soft lockup when sctp_accept() is called during a timeout event

A case can occur when sctp_accept() is called by the user during
a heartbeat timeout event after the 4-way handshake.  Since
sctp_assoc_migrate() changes both assoc->base.sk and assoc->ep, the
bh_sock_lock in sctp_generate_heartbeat_event() will be taken with
the listening socket but released with the new association socket.
The result is a deadlock on any future attempts to take the listening
socket lock.

Note that this race can occur with other SCTP timeouts that take
the bh_lock_sock() in the event sctp_accept() is called.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct net *net = sock_net(asoc->base.sk);', '\tbh_lock_sock(asoc->base.sk);', '\tif (sock_owned_by_user(asoc->base.sk)) {', '\t\tasoc->base.sk->sk_err = -error;', '\tbh_unlock_sock(asoc->base.sk);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct sock *sk = asoc->base.sk;', '\tstruct net *net = sock_net(sk);', '\tbh_lock_sock(sk);', '\tif (sock_owned_by_user(sk)) {', '\t\tsk->sk_err = -error;', '\tbh_unlock_sock(sk);']}
description: net/sctp/sm_sideeffect.c in the Linux kernel before 4.3 does not properly manage the relationship between a lock and a socket, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock) via a crafted sctp_accept call.

code_evidence: The socket pointer is read from asoc->base.sk at line 6 and locked at line 7; the same expression is re-evaluated at line 8 for sock_owned_by_user and again at line 22 and line 24.

Because asoc->base.sk is re-read after the lock is acquired, a concurrent sctp_accept()/sctp_assoc_migrate() can change asoc->base.sk between the lock and unlock, so the socket released at line 24 may differ from the socket locked at line 7.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362 because concurrent timeout and accept sequences access the shared asoc->base.sk without preserving exclusivity between lock and unlock. The weakness is improper synchronization of a shared resource, not a memory-safety bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the locked socket is not saved, so lock and unlock use a mutable association field rather than the same sock object. Trigger: a heartbeat/T3 timeout event races with sctp_accept() migrating the association to a new endpoint socket. Consequence: the listening socket's lock is taken but never released, causing a deadlock/soft lockup (DoS).

commit_msg: fixed #1970
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tgf_bifs_dec_name(parser->bs, name);'], 'added_lines': ['\tgf_bifs_dec_name(parser->bs, name, 1000);']}
description: A stack overflow vulnerability exists in gpac 1.1.0 via the gf_bifs_dec_proto_list function, which causes a segmentation fault and application crash.

code_evidence: Line 3 allocates a fixed 1000-byte stack buffer 'name'. Line 5 calls gf_bifs_dec_name(parser->bs, name) with only the destination pointer and no length argument, so the callee has no bound on how many bytes it writes into 'name'. The patched call adds 1000 as the size, confirming the missing bound is the defect.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Target CWE-787 fits because the unchecked write past the end of the 'name' buffer is an out-of-bounds write. A CWE-121 stack-based overflow framing names the location, but the underlying defect is the out-of-bounds write supported here.

evidence_lines.code:
char name[1000];
gf_bifs_dec_name(parser->bs, name);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a fixed-size stack buffer is passed to a name decoder without conveying its capacity, so attacker-controlled name data drives the write length. Trigger: parsing a BIFS proto list whose name exceeds 1000 bytes. Consequence: the decoder writes past 'name' on the stack, causing stack corruption and a segmentation fault/crash, with possible code execution impact.

commit_msg: Fix #6816 - null deref in r_read_*
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!src) {', '\t\treturn UT16_MAX;', '\t}']}
description: The r_read_* functions in libr/include/r_endian.h in radare2 1.2.1 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a crafted binary file, as demonstrated by the r_read_le32 function.

code_evidence: src is added to offset without any NULL check before pointer arithmetic, so a NULL src is dereferenced when the resulting pointer is read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer it assumes is valid but may be NULL, matching CWE-476 exactly. This is a NULL dereference, not a general invalid-pointer or buffer issue.

evidence_lines.code: const ut8 *s = (const ut8*)src + offset;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: r_read_at_le16 accepts src and computes (const ut8*)src + offset without validating src. Trigger: a caller passes NULL (e.g., parsed from a crafted binary). Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash/DoS; the fix adds an explicit !src guard returning UT16_MAX.

Fixed CVE-2022-40761

Signed-off-by: Taras Drozdovskyi <t.drozdovsky@samsung.com>
