commit_msg: fix streams where SPS image size changes without refreshing PPS (#299)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  // Remove the all PPS that referenced the old SPS because parameters may have changed and we do not want to', '  // get the SPS and PPS parameters (e.g. image size) out of sync.', '  ', '  for (auto& p : pps) {', '    if (p && p->seq_parameter_set_id == new_sps->seq_parameter_set_id) {', '      p = nullptr;', '    }', '  }', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in libde265 v1.0.8.There is a Heap-use-after-free in intrapred.h when decoding file using dec265.

code_evidence: Line 12 overwrites sps[new_sps->seq_parameter_set_id] with a freshly allocated shared_ptr, releasing the previous seq_parameter_set object if it was the last reference. No cleanup of PPS entries that still point to the old SPS occurs in this function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the root cause is reuse of a freed SPS object through stale PPS references. It is not merely a stale-state or logic bug; the freed allocation is later accessed, matching use-after-free rather than a simple out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code: sps[ new_sps->seq_parameter_set_id ] = new_sps;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The old SPS is replaced and freed while PPS objects retain a seq_parameter_set_id referencing it, so later decoding can dereference freed SPS state (e.g. image size) during intrapred processing, yielding the reported heap-use-after-free. The trigger is an SPS redefinition with a changed image size without refreshing dependent PPS.

commit_msg:
Fix a possible security issue
- script output might have been stored to paths elsewhere
- Thanks to G.C. for reporting
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tQFileInfo outputInfo(outputFile);', '\tQDir dir=outputInfo.dir(); // will hold complete dirname', '\tQFileInfo newFileNameInfo(name);', '\tbool okToSaveToAbsolutePath=StelApp::getInstance().getSettings()->value("scripts/flag_script_allow_write_absolute_path", false).toBool();', '\tif (!okToSaveToAbsolutePath && (newFileNameInfo.isAbsolute()))', '\t\tqWarning() << "SCRIPTING CONFIGURATION ISSUE: You are trying to save to an absolute pathname.";'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst QFileInfo outputInfo(outputFile);', '\tconst QDir dir=outputInfo.dir(); // will hold complete dirname', '\tconst QFileInfo newFileNameInfo(name);', '\tconst bool okToSaveToAbsolutePath=StelApp::getInstance().getSettings()->value("scripts/flag_script_allow_write_absolute_path", false).toBool();', '\tif (!okToSaveToAbsolutePath && ((newFileNameInfo.isAbsolute() || (name.contains(".."))))) // The last condition may include dangerous/malicious paths', '\t\tqWarning() << "SCRIPTING CONFIGURATION ISSUE: You are trying to save to an absolute pathname or move up in directories.";']}
description: In Stellarium through 1.2, attackers can write to files that are typically unintended, such as ones with absolute pathnames or .. directory traversal.

code_evidence: The guard only rejects absolute names when the setting is false; a relative name containing ".." passes this branch and is not sanitized.
When the flag is enabled and the name is absolute, the raw name is used directly as the file path.
The default branch concatenates dir.absolutePath() with the raw name, so an embedded "../" sequence escapes the intended directory.
The resulting path is opened WriteOnly|Truncate and outputText is written, so traversal reaches an actual file write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-22: external input constructs a pathname meant to stay under a restricted directory, but ".." elements are not neutralized, so the path resolves outside it. It differs from CWE-36 (absolute path) because the bypass here is relative traversal.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!asFile.open(QIODevice::WriteOnly | QIODevice::Truncate | QIODevice::Text | QIODevice::Unbuffered))
asFile.write(qPrintable(outputText), outputText.size());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that name is used to build the output path without neutralizing ".." components; the check only considers isAbsolute. A script supplying a relative name like "../../target" reaches the open/write, letting it truncate or overwrite files outside the intended directory.

commit_msg:
Generating strings for XKB data used a single shared static buffer,
which offered several opportunities for errors. Use a ring of
resizable buffers instead, to avoid problems when strings end up
longer than anticipated.

Reviewed-by: Michal Srb <msrb@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Keith Packard <keithp@keithp.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Cristau <jcristau@debian.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (len > BUFFER_SIZE)', '            len = BUFFER_SIZE - 2;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: In X.Org Server (aka xserver and xorg-server) before 1.19.4, a local attacker authenticated to the X server could overflow a global buffer, causing crashes of the X server or potentially other problems by injecting large or malformed XKB related atoms and accessing them via xkbcomp.

code_evidence: len is derived from strlen(atmstr)+1 of an atom name; the clamp keeps len within BUFFER_SIZE before tbGetBuffer(len) and strlcpy. Without the clamp, an oversized atom string yields a length beyond the intended buffer bound, and strlcpy copies up to len bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a string copy whose length is not restricted to the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119 improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer. A more specific out-of-bounds write CWE could apply, but the target class-level CWE-119 is supported by the unbounded length flowing into the copy.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the removed bounds check allowed the computed atom-string length to exceed the intended global buffer size. Trigger: a local attacker injects large or malformed XKB atoms, so NameForAtom returns a long string. Consequence: the copy into the shared buffer can write past its intended boundary, causing X server crashes or other memory corruption.

commit_msg: dns: fix crash issue
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint target_len = strnlen(target, DNS_MAX_CNAME_LEN) + 1;'], 'added_lines': ['\tint target_len = 0;', '\tif (target == NULL) {', '\t\ttarget = "";', '\t}', '', '\ttarget_len = strnlen(target, DNS_MAX_CNAME_LEN) + 1;']}
description: SmartDNS through 41 before 56d0332 allows an out-of-bounds write because of a stack-based buffer overflow in the _dns_encode_domain function in the dns.c file, via a crafted DNS request.

code_evidence: Line 8 computes target_len via strnlen(target, DNS_MAX_CNAME_LEN)+1, but this is the only length bound; the following check at lines 9-11 only verifies the context has room for 2+target_len bytes, not that the write stays within the destination buffer.

Lines 12-14 write the priority short, then safe_strncpy copies target into context.ptr for target_len bytes and advances ptr by target_len, with no validation that the destination region actually has target_len bytes available.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes target_len bytes through safe_strncpy and advances the pointer without a matching destination-bound check, producing an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is a write past the intended buffer, not merely an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer-length check compares remaining context length against 2+target_len but the subsequent copy advances past the context without ensuring the destination can hold target_len bytes; a crafted DNS request with a long target drives the write beyond the context boundary. Consequence is an out-of-bounds write, enabling memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg: Fixed SEGV reported in https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/130
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ((p > (datum+length-count)) || (count > (ssize_t) length))'], 'added_lines': ['    if ((count < 0) || (p > (datum+length-count)) ||', '        (count > (ssize_t) length))']}
description: magick/profile.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault) via a crafted profile.

code_evidence: The length field value is read from the attacker-controlled 8BIM profile via ReadResourceLong and cast to ssize_t count; the pre-fix guard only checks p > (datum+length-count) and count > (ssize_t) length, so a value with the high bit set yields a negative count.
With count negative, the extent computation (datum+length)-(p+count) and the subsequent CopyMagickMemory calls at lines 83/89-90 use an out-of-range count, driving memory operations beyond bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate a required property (non-negativity) of an input-derived length before processing it, matching CWE-20 improper input validation. This is distinct from a pure integer overflow since the defect is the missing validation of the incoming length value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the profile's length field is accepted without rejecting negative values, so the signed count can be negative. Trigger: a crafted 8bim profile whose resource length has the sign bit set. Consequence: the bounds check passes and later extent/copy arithmetic uses the invalid count, causing a segmentation fault (DoS).

commit_msg:
Currently CONFIG_TIMER_STATS exposes process information across namespaces:

kernel/time/timer_list.c print_timer():

        SEQ_printf(m, ", %s/%d", tmp, timer->start_pid);

/proc/timer_list:

 #11: <0000000000000000>, hrtimer_wakeup, S:01, do_nanosleep, cron/2570

description: The time subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.9.9, when CONFIG_TIMER_STATS is enabled, allows local users to discover real PID values (as distinguished from PID values inside a PID namespace) by reading the /proc/timer_list file, related to the print_timer function in kernel/time/timer_list.c and the __timer_stats_timer_set_start_info function in kernel/time/timer.c.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function del_timer only removes a timer and clears its stats start info; it performs no output or access control, so it does not itself expose PID data. commit_msg:
Use relative paths in the handler_server_info page

Issue #1227 describes a XSS vulnerability on the about page of cherokee-admin.
While the report by LogicalTrust only describes a JavaScript variant, a CSS method could also be probed via logo.gif.

The root cause is the request being verbatim copied in to the HTML template. The request could be escaped, but leads to the question: Why are we presenting a full path, instead of a
relative path to the page? This change removes the full path, and makes it relative. No URL is being printed in the template, and the XSS is avoided and therefore it should also be
faster.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcherokee_buffer_replace_string (buffer, "{request}", 9,', '\t                                HANDLER_CONN(hdl)->request.buf,', '\t                                HANDLER_CONN(hdl)->request.len);', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: An XSS issue was discovered in handler_server_info.c in Cherokee through 1.2.104. The requested URL is improperly displayed on the About page in the default configuration of the web server and its administrator panel. The XSS in the administrator panel can be used to reconfigure the server and execute arbitrary commands.

code_evidence: Lines 10-12 call cherokee_buffer_replace_string to substitute the literal placeholder "{request}" in the generated HTML buffer with HANDLER_CONN(hdl)->request.buf, the raw request data, using the request length. No escaping or encoding is applied before insertion.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is improper neutralization of user-controllable input during web page generation, matching CWE-79: the request value reaches HTML output without encoding. It is not merely reflected data exposure; the missing output constraint enables script execution in a victim's browser.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The raw, attacker-influenced request string is copied verbatim into the HTML page template. When a crafted request causes the server-info/About page to be rendered, the unneutralized content is emitted as markup, allowing script or CSS injection in the admin panel context.

commit_msg: changed a check
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t// drop packet to dummy client', '\tif(0 <= ClientID && ClientID < MAX_CLIENTS && GameServer()->IsClientBot(ClientID))'], 'added_lines': ['\t// drop invalid packet', '\tif(ClientID != -1 && (ClientID < 0 || ClientID >= MAX_CLIENTS || m_aClients[ClientID].m_State == CClient::STATE_EMPTY || m_aClients[ClientID].m_Quitting))']}
description: CServer::SendMsg in engine/server/server.cpp in Teeworlds 0.7.x before 0.7.5 allows remote attackers to shut down the server.

code_evidence: Only pMsg is null-checked; ClientID is used without validating it against the valid client range before constructing the packet.
Packet.m_ClientID is set directly from the caller-supplied ClientID and the packet is populated without bounds or state validation.
In the send path, ClientID == -1 broadcasts to in-game clients, but any other value is passed to m_NetServer.Send without confirming the client index is valid or connected.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function accepts caller-supplied input (ClientID) and processes it without validating required properties (range and client state) before use. This is improper validation of an index/identifier, not a separate memory-safety flaw in the shown code.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: SendMsg trusts the ClientID argument without verifying it identifies a valid, active client. Trigger: a remote attacker causes a message to be sent with an out-of-range or empty/quitting client index. Consequence: the server can process or send to an invalid client slot, leading to the reported remote server shutdown (availability impact).

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Fix missing queue indices reset at SNDRV_TIMER_IOCTL_SELECT

snd_timer_user_tselect() reallocates the queue buffer dynamically, but
it forgot to reset its indices.  Since the read may happen
concurrently with ioctl and snd_timer_user_tselect() allocates the
buffer via kmalloc(), this may lead to the leak of uninitialized
kernel-space data, as spotted via KMSAN:

  BUG: KMSAN: use of unitialized memory in snd_timer_user_read+0x6c4/0xa10
  CPU: 0 PID: 1037 Comm: probe Not tainted 4.11.0-rc5+ #2739
  Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (i440FX + PIIX, 1996), BIOS Bochs 01/01/2011
  Call Trace:
   __dump_stack lib/dump_stack.c:16
   dump_stack+0x143/0x1b0 lib/dump_stack.c:52
   kmsan_report+0x12a/0x180 mm/kmsan/kmsan.c:1007
   kmsan_check_memory+0xc2/0x140 mm/kmsan/kmsan.c:1086
   copy_to_user ./arch/x86/include/asm/uaccess.h:725
   snd_timer_user_read+0x6c4/0xa10 sound/core/timer.c:2004
   do_loop_readv_writev fs/read_write.c:716
   __do_readv_writev+0x94c/0x1380 fs/read_write.c:864
   do_readv_writev fs/read_write.c:894
   vfs_readv fs/read_write.c:908
   do_readv+0x52a/0x5d0 fs/read_write.c:934
   SYSC_readv+0xb6/0xd0 fs/read_write.c:1021
   SyS_readv+0x87/0xb0 fs/read_write.c:1018

This patch adds the missing reset of queue indices.  Together with the
previous fix for the ioctl/read race, we cover the whole problem.

Reported-by: Alexander Potapenko <glider@google.com>
Tested-by: Alexander Potapenko <glider@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\ttu->qhead = tu->qtail = tu->qused = 0;']}
description: sound/core/timer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.11.5 is vulnerable to a data race in the ALSA /dev/snd/timer driver resulting in local users being able to read information belonging to other users, i.e., uninitialized memory contents may be disclosed when a read and an ioctl happen at the same time.

code_evidence: On select, the function frees tu->queue and tu->tqueue and sets them to NULL, then reallocates a fresh buffer via kmalloc() based on tu->queue_size; the queue head/tail/used indices are not reset here.

The freshly kmalloc'd buffer is uninitialized kernel memory; the ring-buffer indices (qhead/qtail/qused) retain stale values from the previous selection, so subsequent reads can copy uninitialized contents to user space.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The consequence is disclosure of uninitialized kernel-space data to an unauthorized local user, which is exactly an information exposure. The stale-index/uninitialized-buffer defect is the cause; the leaked memory is the supported confidentiality impact matching CWE-200.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: snd_timer_user_tselect() reallocates the queue buffer without resetting qhead/qtail/qused, so stale indices point into uninitialized kmalloc memory. Trigger: a concurrent read (snd_timer_user_read) after reallocation copies this uninitialized kernel data to a user buffer, disclosing kernel memory.

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  const uint32_t total =', '      current_header_field_.size() + current_header_value_.size() + current_header_map_->byteSize();'], 'added_lines': ['  // Verify that the cached value in byte size exists.', '  ASSERT(current_header_map_->byteSize().has_value());', '  const uint32_t total = current_header_field_.size() + current_header_value_.size() +', '                         current_header_map_->byteSize().value();']}
description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

code_evidence: onHeaderValue appends each incoming header value fragment to current_header_value_ and then recomputes total as current_header_field_.size() + current_header_value_.size() + current_header_map_->byteSize(). The byteSize() call iterates existing headers to sum key/value sizes, so this check is performed on every value fragment. The only bound is the comparison against max_request_headers_kb_ * 1024; there is no cap on the number of header entries or on the number of value fragments processed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the code fails to control consumption of a limited resource (CPU) while enforcing a size limit, allowing an attacker to drive quadratic work. This is resource exhaustion from missing throttling of per-header processing, not a memory-safety flaw such as CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-fragment size validation invokes a full O(n) byteSize() iteration over the accumulated header map, making header processing O(n^2) in the number of small headers. Trigger: a remote peer sends many thousands of tiny headers that collectively stay below the size limit, causing repeated full-map scans. Supported consequence: CPU exhaustion and denial of service for HTTP/1.x connections.

commit_msg:
Fix error in logic.

Signed-off-by: alex-z <blackslayer4@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            certs->append(error.certificate());', '            return false;', '    return true;'], 'added_lines': ['    bool allTrusted = true;', '', '            allTrusted = false;', '        certs->append(error.certificate());', '    return allTrusted;']}
description: Nextcloud also ships a CLI utility called nextcloudcmd which is sometimes used for automated scripting and headless servers. Versions of nextcloudcmd prior to 3.6.1 would incorrectly trust invalid TLS certificates, which may enable a Man-in-the-middle attack that exposes sensitive data or credentials to a network attacker. This affects the CLI only. It does not affect the standard GUI desktop Nextcloud clients, and it does not affect the Nextcloud server.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over TLS errors and only checks whether each error certificate is in account->approvedCerts(); when an unapproved certificate is found it appends it and immediately returns false. If the first error is approved but a later error is unapproved, the loop returns false only at that later point, so the function does not return true while an unapproved certificate exists—however the unapproved certificate is still appended to certs before returning false, and approved errors are also appended. The function returns true only after all errors pass the approvedCerts check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-295 covers incorrect certificate validation; here the check is a strict approvedCerts membership test that fails closed for unapproved certificates. The diff context shows the fix aggregates trust across all errors, but the shown function itself does not demonstrate trusting an invalid certificate, so evidence for CWE-295 as the introduced weakness is weak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: certificate acceptance is decided solely by membership in approvedCerts(), and the function's return value aggregates the check; any certificate not in the approved list yields false. Trigger: a TLS error whose certificate is not pre-approved. Supported consequence: the caller is told validation failed, so this code path rejects rather than trusts the invalid certificate, limiting MITM exposure.

If io_setup is called successful in try_smi_init() but try_smi_init()

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. There is a use-after-free upon attempted read access to /proc/ioports after the ipmi_si module is removed, related to drivers/char/ipmi/ipmi_si_intf.c, drivers/char/ipmi/ipmi_si_mem_io.c, and drivers/char/ipmi/ipmi_si_port_io.c.

code_evidence: Line 48 calls new_smi->io.io_setup(&new_smi->io); on success the resource (and its name such as DEVICE_NAME) is allocated and registered.
Lines 49-52 handle io_setup failure by jumping to out_err; later error paths (e.g., lines 53-58 on detect failure) also goto out_err after io_setup succeeded.
The original out_err block (lines 119-121) only frees init_name and returns rv; it never invokes io_cleanup, so an allocated resource name remains referenced after the module is removed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a missing cleanup causing a dangling reference to freed memory (the resource name) that is later read, which is exactly CWE-416 Use After Free. It is not a double-free because the cleanup is absent rather than duplicated.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: try_smi_init() can fail after io_setup() succeeds, but the out_err path does not release the I/O resource. The resource name allocated by io_setup() is freed during module removal while the resource entry persists; a later read of /proc/ioports dereferences the stale name pointer, causing the use-after-free crash shown in the report.

Line 7 then reads PathLength from the stream, and lines 8-9 pass Stream_Pointer with PathLength/2 WCHARs to ConvertFromUnicode without confirming PathLength bytes remain, so an attacker-controlled length or truncated input drives a read past the stream buffer.

commit_msg:
gsocketclient: Fix criticals

This ensures the parent GTask is kept alive as long as an enumeration
is running and trying to connect.

Closes #1646
Closes #1649
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      enumerator_next_async (data);'], 'added_lines': ['      enumerator_next_async (data, FALSE);']}
description: gio/gsocketclient.c in GNOME GLib 2.59.2 does not ensure that a parent GTask remains alive during the execution of a connection-attempting enumeration, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (g_socket_client_connected_callback mishandling and application crash) via a crafted web site, as demonstrated by GNOME Web (aka Epiphany).

code_evidence: The callback retrieves data from user_data and unconditionally unrefs data->connection, then calls g_proxy_connect_finish and stores the result in data->connection.
On proxy-connect failure (data->connection is NULL), the else branch calls enumerator_next_async(data) and returns, passing the enumeration data onward without any reference held on the parent GTask.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-754 fits because the error/exceptional proxy-negotiation path is handled without checking the lifetime precondition of the parent GTask, producing an availability-impacting crash. This is a missing check on an unusual condition rather than a memory-safety primitive like use-after-free itself.

evidence_lines.code:
enumerator_next_async (data);
return;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failure path forwards the async-connect data to enumerator_next_async without retaining the parent GTask, so the enumeration continues after the callback returns while the GTask can be finalized. Trigger: a failed proxy connection (crafted site causing proxy negotiation failure). Consequence: g_socket_client_connected_callback operates on freed data, crashing the application (DoS).

commit_msg:
Bug 701792: Avoid going beyond buffer in GetNumSameData() and GetNumWrongData().

GetNumSameData() compared buffer contents before checking that we are still
within bounds of buffer, which caused the bug.

Have made similar fix to GetNumWrongData() because it has similar error.

Fixes address sanitizer error in:
    ./sanbin/gs -sOutputFile=tmp -sDEVICE=lips4v ../bug-701792.pdf
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    while (*curPtr == *(curPtr + count) && maxnum > count) {'], 'added_lines': ['    while (maxnum > count && *curPtr == *(curPtr + count)) {']}
description: A buffer overflow vulnerability in GetNumWrongData() in contrib/lips4/gdevlips.c of Artifex Software GhostScript v9.50 allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via a crafted PDF file. This is fixed in v9.51.

code_evidence: The while condition dereferences *(curPtr + count) before evaluating maxnum > count. Due to left-to-right short-circuit evaluation, the bounds check is performed only after the out-of-bounds read, so count can reach maxnum and the dereference accesses past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 covers out-of-bounds memory access caused by missing effective bounds enforcement. Here the guard exists but is evaluated after the dereference, so the intended limit does not constrain the access; this is the direct buffer-overrun defect fixed by reordering the condition.

evidence_lines.code:
while (*curPtr == *(curPtr + count) && maxnum > count) {
count++;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the misordered conjunction: the buffer dereference precedes the maxnum > count guard, so the read is not protected by the bounds check. Trigger is a crafted PDF whose same-data run length reaches maxnum; the loop then reads one element beyond the buffer, and count increments accordingly, yielding an out-of-bounds access (address-sanitizer error, DoS).

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4979: accessing freed memory when line is flushed

Problem:    Accessing freed memory when line is flushed.
Solution:   Make a copy of the pattern to search for.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t// Make a copy, if the line was changed it will be freed.', '\t\tptr = vim_strnsave(ptr, len);', '\t\tif (ptr == NULL)', '\t\t    break;', '', '\t\tvim_free(ptr);']}
description: Use After Free in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.4979.

code_evidence: find_ident_under_cursor returns a pointer ptr into the current line buffer, then find_pattern_in_path is called with that pointer. If the line is flushed/changed during that call, the underlying buffer is freed while ptr still references it; the pointer is then used (curwin->w_set_curswant) after the call. The patch copies ptr via vim_strnsave before the call and frees the copy afterward, confirming the original pointer was used after free.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the code references memory (ptr) after the owning line buffer has been freed. Contrast with CWE-415: this is not a double free but reuse of a freed pointer, matching Use After Free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ptr aliases line-buffer memory that find_pattern_in_path may release when it flushes/changes the line. Trigger: invoking the 'i'/'d' window command on an identifier while the search flushes the line. Consequence: the stale ptr is dereferenced, causing a use-after-free that can crash or corrupt memory.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.20.15. The nfc_llcp_build_tlv function in net/nfc/llcp_commands.c may return NULL. If the caller does not check for this, it will trigger a NULL pointer dereference. This will cause denial of service. This affects nfc_llcp_build_gb in net/nfc/llcp_core.c.

code_evidence: nfc_llcp_build_tlv is called for the service-name TLV and its return value is assigned to service_name_tlv; the length is added to size without checking whether the returned pointer is NULL.
miux_tlv is assigned from nfc_llcp_build_tlv and its length added to size, again with no NULL check on the returned pointer.
rw_tlv is likewise assigned from nfc_llcp_build_tlv and its length added, with no NULL check.
The unchecked TLV pointers are later passed to llcp_add_tlv, which dereferences them when building the CONNECT PDU.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses a pointer expected to be valid but returned as NULL on allocation failure, and dereferences it without a check. This is a direct NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476), not a general out-of-bounds or use-after-free issue.

evidence_lines.code:
rw_tlv = nfc_llcp_build_tlv(LLCP_TLV_RW, &rw, 0, &rw_tlv_length);
size += rw_tlv_length;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nfc_llcp_send_connect does not validate the pointers returned by nfc_llcp_build_tlv before using them. When allocation inside the builder fails, the builder returns NULL; the caller still adds the length and later passes the NULL pointer to llcp_add_tlv, which dereferences it, causing a kernel NULL-pointer dereference and denial of service.

description: The sock_setsockopt function in net/core/sock.c in the Linux kernel before 3.5 mishandles negative values of sk_sndbuf and sk_rcvbuf, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory corruption and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability for a crafted setsockopt system call with the (1) SO_SNDBUF or (2) SO_RCVBUF option.

code_evidence: get_user() loads a signed int val from the caller; SO_SNDBUF only clamps val above sysctl_wmem_max, so a negative val survives and is multiplied by 2 at line 44/47, producing a negative sk_sndbuf.
SO_RCVBUF mirrors the same flaw: only val > sysctl_rmem_max is clamped, so negative val reaches val * 2 and assigns a negative sk_rcvbuf.
SO_SNDBUFFORCE and SO_RCVBUFFORCE (CAP_NET_ADMIN only) goto the same set_sndbuf/set_rcvbuf labels, bypassing even the upper-bound clamp and reaching the same negative multiplication.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing constraint lets a negative value become a buffer size used in subsequent memory operations, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds read/write within a buffer's intended boundary. It is not merely an integer overflow: the unchecked signed input directly produces an invalid buffer length.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is missing lower-bound validation of the signed user-supplied val before it is doubled and stored as sk_sndbuf/sk_rcvbuf. A crafted setsockopt with a negative SO_SNDBUF/SO_RCVBUF value yields a negative buffer size, which later buffer-size arithmetic treats as huge, corrupting memory and crashing the system.

description: FFmpeg before commit cced03dd667a5df6df8fd40d8de0bff477ee02e8 contains multiple out of array access vulnerabilities in the mms protocol that can result in attackers accessing out of bound data. This attack appear to be exploitable via network connectivity. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in cced03dd667a5df6df8fd40d8de0bff477ee02e8 and later.

code_evidence: For an ff_asf_stream_header chunk, flags is read via AV_RL16 at p + sizeof(ff_asf_guid)*3 + 24 with no check that those bytes lie before end; only the loop guard end - p >= sizeof(ff_asf_guid) + 8 is enforced.
For ff_asf_head1_guid, chunksize is forced to 46, then p += chunksize advances the cursor; if fewer than 46 bytes remain, the next iteration's memcmp/AV_RL64 at lines 18-20 reads past end.

commit_msg:
xen/arm: Always trap AMU system registers

The Activity Monitors Unit (AMU) has been introduced by ARMv8.4. It is
considered to be unsafe to be expose to guests as they might expose
information about code executed by other guests or the host.

Arm provided a way to trap all the AMU system registers by setting
CPTR_EL2.TAM to 1.

Unfortunately, on older revision of the specification, the bit 30 (now
CPTR_EL1.TAM) was RES0. Because of that, Xen is setting it to 0 and
therefore the system registers would be exposed to the guest when it is
run on processors with AMU.

As the bit is mark as UNKNOWN at boot in Armv8.4, the only safe solution
for us is to always set CPTR_EL1.TAM to 1.

Guest trying to access the AMU system registers will now receive an
undefined instruction. Unfortunately, this means that even well-behaved
guest may fail to boot because we don't sanitize the ID registers.

This is a known issues with other Armv8.0+ features (e.g. SVE, Pointer
Auth). This will taken care separately.

This is part of XSA-351 (or XSA-93 re-born).

Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Reviewed-by: Andre Przywara <andre.przywara@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Bertrand Marquis <bertrand.marquis@arm.com>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -21,7 +21,8 @@
      * On ARM64 the TCPx bits which we set here (0..9,12,13) are all
      * RES1, i.e. they would trap whether we did this write or not.
      */
-    WRITE_SYSREG((HCPTR_CP_MASK & ~(HCPTR_CP(10) | HCPTR_CP(11))) | HCPTR_TTA,
+    WRITE_SYSREG((HCPTR_CP_MASK & ~(HCPTR_CP(10) | HCPTR_CP(11))) |
+                 HCPTR_TTA | HCPTR_TAM,
                  CPTR_EL2);
 
     /*
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    WRITE_SYSREG((HCPTR_CP_MASK & ~(HCPTR_CP(10) | HCPTR_CP(11))) | HCPTR_TTA,'], 'added_lines': ['    WRITE_SYSREG((HCPTR_CP_MASK & ~(HCPTR_CP(10) | HCPTR_CP(11))) |', '                 HCPTR_TTA | HCPTR_TAM,']}
description: Xen through 4.14.x allows guest OS administrators to obtain sensitive information (such as AES keys from outside the guest) via a side-channel attack on a power/energy monitoring interface, aka a "Platypus" attack. NOTE: there is only one logically independent fix: to change the access control for each such interface in Xen.

code_evidence: init_traps programs CPTR_EL2 without HCPTR_TAM, so the AMU system-register trap bit is not set; only HCPTR_TTA and the CP10/CP11 mask handling are written.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the hypervisor omits the authorization/trap check for guest access to AMU registers, leaving a protected resource reachable without the required control. This is a missing access-control decision, not a memory-safety flaw; the confidentiality impact follows from the absent trap.

evidence_lines.code:
WRITE_SYSREG((HCPTR_CP_MASK & ~(HCPTR_CP(10) | HCPTR_CP(11))) | HCPTR_TTA,
CPTR_EL2);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the EL2 trap register is configured without enabling the AMU trap, so guest access to AMU system registers is not intercepted. Trigger: a guest executing AMU register reads reaches the hardware monitor state directly. Consequence: guest-visible power/energy monitoring data can leak information about host or other guest execution, supporting the Platypus side channel.

description: dwarf1.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, mishandles pointers, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted ELF file, related to parse_die and parse_line_table, as demonstrated by a parse_die heap-based buffer over-read.

code_evidence: bfd_get_32 reads four bytes at xptr immediately after entry, with no check that four bytes remain before aDiePtrEnd.
bfd_get_16 reads the tag at xptr without verifying two bytes are within the section limit.
The attribute loop reads attr via bfd_get_16 at xptr, then advances xptr by two, again without a per-read bounds check.
FORM_DATA4/FORM_REF reads bfd_get_32 at xptr for sibling/stmt_list when attr matches, with no check that four bytes remain.
FORM_BLOCK2/FORM_BLOCK4 read a length via bfd_get_16/bfd_get_32 at xptr and advance xptr by that length, trusting attacker-controlled values.
FORM_STRING calls strlen on xptr with no bounded limit, scanning past the buffer end.

evidence_lines.code:

xptr += 4;

aDieInfo->tag = bfd_get_16 (abfd, (bfd_byte *) xptr);
xptr += 2;

attr = bfd_get_16 (abfd, (bfd_byte *) xptr);
xptr += 2;

aDieInfo->sibling = bfd_get_32 (abfd, (bfd_byte *) xptr);
xptr += 4;

xptr += 2 + bfd_get_16 (abfd, (bfd_byte *) xptr);
xptr += 4 + bfd_get_32 (abfd, (bfd_byte *) xptr);
xptr += strlen ((char *) xptr) + 1;

A short or malformed DIE causes bfd_get_* or strlen to read beyond the section buffer, producing a heap-based out-of-bounds read and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
PR26574, heap buffer overflow in _bfd_elf_slurp_secondary_reloc_section

A horribly fuzzed object with section headers inside the ELF header.
Disallow that, and crazy reloc sizes.

	PR 26574
	* elfcode.h (elf_object_p): Sanity check section header offset.
	* elf.c (_bfd_elf_slurp_secondary_reloc_section): Sanity check
	sh_entsize.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (i_ehdrp->e_shoff == 0 && i_ehdrp->e_type == ET_REL)', '  if (i_ehdrp->e_shoff == 0 && i_ehdrp->e_shnum != 0)', '  if (i_ehdrp->e_shoff != 0)', '  if (i_ehdrp->e_shstrndx != 0 && i_ehdrp->e_shoff != 0)'], 'added_lines': ['  if (i_ehdrp->e_shoff < sizeof (x_ehdr) && i_ehdrp->e_type == ET_REL)', '  if (i_ehdrp->e_shoff < sizeof (x_ehdr) && i_ehdrp->e_shnum != 0)', '  if (i_ehdrp->e_shoff >= sizeof (x_ehdr))', '  if (i_ehdrp->e_shstrndx != 0 && i_ehdrp->e_shoff >= sizeof (x_ehdr))']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.35.1. A heap-based buffer over-read can occur in bfd_getl_signed_32 in libbfd.c because sh_entsize is not validated in _bfd_elf_slurp_secondary_reloc_section in elf.c.

code_evidence: The pre-patch check only rejects e_shoff == 0 for ET_REL; a nonzero e_shoff smaller than the ELF header size (e.g. pointing inside the header) passes.
Similarly, e_shoff == 0 && e_shnum != 0 is the only cross-check, so a small nonzero e_shoff with a section count is accepted.
When e_shoff != 0, the code seeks to that attacker-controlled offset and reads sizeof(x_shdr) bytes into x_shdr, then swaps and uses the section header.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits: the missing lower-bound check on e_shoff allows reading section-header data from an offset before the intended buffer region, an out-of-bounds read. It is not a write (CWE-787); the added >= sizeof(x_ehdr) guard confirms the offset constraint is the fix.

evidence_lines.code:
if (i_ehdrp->e_shoff == 0 && i_ehdrp->e_type == ET_REL)
goto got_wrong_format_error;

if (i_ehdrp->e_shoff == 0 && i_ehdrp->e_shnum != 0)
goto got_wrong_format_error;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: e_shoff is validated only against zero, not against the minimum valid offset (sizeof(x_ehdr)). A crafted ELF header sets e_shoff to a small nonzero value pointing inside/overlapping the ELF header, so the section-header read at lines 81-86 consumes bytes outside the intended section-header table, producing an out-of-bounds read of the file buffer.

Prevent possible double-free in ares_getaddrinfo() if ares_destroy() is called

In the event that ares_destroy() is called prior to ares_getaddrinfo() completing,
it would result in an invalid read and double-free due to calling end_hquery() twice.

Reported By: Jann Horn @ Google Project Zero

description: A possible use-after-free and double-free in c-ares lib version 1.16.0 if ares_destroy() is called prior to ares_getaddrinfo() completing. This flaw possibly allows an attacker to crash the service that uses c-ares lib. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to this service availability.

code_evidence: When status == ARES_EDESTRUCTION, the callback calls end_hquery(hquery, status) at line 14 but does not return, so execution continues into the remaining-count block below.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: end_hquery releases the hquery allocation; the missing return allows a second end_hquery on the same pointer, which is a double free (CWE-415). The use-after-free read is a secondary effect, but the core defect is the duplicate free of the same address.

If hquery->remaining is zero, the subsequent block calls end_hquery again, freeing the same query structure twice (and reading freed memory). Trigger: ares_destroy() during an outstanding ares_getaddrinfo(). Consequence: double-free/use-after-free leading to crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Preemption must be disabled before enabling interrupts in do_trap
on x86_64 because the stack in use for int3 and debug is a per CPU
stack set by th IST. But 32bit does not have an IST and the stack
still belongs to the current task and there is no problem in scheduling
out the task.

Keep preemption enabled on X86_32 when enabling interrupts for
do_trap().

The name of the function is changed from preempt_conditional_sti/cli()
to conditional_sti/cli_ist(), to annotate that this function is used
when the stack is on the IST.

Cc: stable-rt@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Steven Rostedt <rostedt@goodmis.org>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>

description: An issue was discovered in Schism Tracker through 20190722. There is a heap-based buffer overflow via a large number of song patterns in fmt_mtm_load_song in fmt/mtm.c, a different vulnerability than CVE-2019-14465.

code_evidence: The pattern loop iterates pat from 0 through npat inclusive, where npat is attacker-controlled via slurp_getc (line 20). Each iteration indexes song->patterns[pat] and writes pattern_size[pat]/pattern_alloc_size[pat] without any upper bound check against MAX_PATTERNS.

<https://github.com/LibVNC/libvncserver/issues/273>

commit_msg:
x86/mm: Add barriers and document switch_mm()-vs-flush synchronization

When switch_mm() activates a new PGD, it also sets a bit that
tells other CPUs that the PGD is in use so that TLB flush IPIs
will be sent.  In order for that to work correctly, the bit
needs to be visible prior to loading the PGD and therefore
starting to fill the local TLB.

Document all the barriers that make this work correctly and add
a couple that were missing.

Signed-off-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Cc: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Andy Lutomirski <luto@amacapital.net>
Cc: Borislav Petkov <bp@alien8.de>
Cc: Brian Gerst <brgerst@gmail.com>
Cc: Dave Hansen <dave.hansen@linux.intel.com>
Cc: Denys Vlasenko <dvlasenk@redhat.com>
Cc: H. Peter Anvin <hpa@zytor.com>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Rik van Riel <riel@redhat.com>
Cc: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: linux-mm@kvack.org
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Ingo Molnar <mingo@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (current->mm)', '\t\telse'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (current->mm) {', '\t\t\t/*', '\t\t\t * Implicit full barrier (INVLPG) that synchronizes', '\t\t\t * with switch_mm.', '\t\t\t */', '\t\t} else {', '', '\t\t\t/* Synchronize with switch_mm. */', '\t\t\tsmp_mb();', '\t\t}']}
description: Race condition in arch/x86/mm/tlb.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 allows local users to gain privileges by triggering access to a paging structure by a different CPU.

code_evidence: flush_tlb_page() checks current->active_mm == mm and, when current->mm is NULL, calls leave_mm() without any barrier ordering that operation against the concurrent switch_mm() that sets the mm's active bit; the non-NULL branch relies on INVLPG's implicit full barrier, but the leave_mm() path has none.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function executes a shared-resource (mm/TLB) sequence whose correctness depends on synchronization with a concurrent switch_mm(); the missing barrier creates a timing window in which the interfering code sequence is not excluded, matching CWE-362's exclusivity/atomicity violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mm_cpumask bit set by switch_mm() must be visible before the CPU loads the PGD and begins filling TLB entries, but the leave_mm() branch performs no ordering operation. A concurrent switch_mm() on another CPU can therefore observe stale/incomplete state, letting a TLB flush IPI miss this CPU and leaving stale TLB entries that allow access to paging structures, supporting the described privilege escalation.

surviving just because the results of calculations with s->tracks are

commit_msg:
Trap for overly large input to XmlRPCPP which could cause problems with int <-> size_t conversions.

 - In XmlRpcClient, XmlRpcServerConnection and XmlRpcSocket, recognize when incoming or outgoing data is too large, generate an error and discard the data when practical.
 - Use the safe strtol() rather than atoi() to decode an incoming content-length header, and generate an error if the length is invalid or too large.
 - In XmlRpcUtil, prevent attempts to parse overly large XML input.
 - Add tests where they can reasonably be inserted into existing test routines.

Although this fix could be cleaner the update is written to make the update ABI compatible.

This fix addresses CVE-2020-16124 / Integer overflow in ros_comm.

Signed-off-by: Sid Faber <sid.faber@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    // Avoid an overly large response', '    if (_response.length() > size_t(__INT_MAX__)) {', '      XmlRpcUtil::error("XmlRpcClient::readResponse: response length (%u) exceeds the maximum allowed size (%u).",', '                        _response.length(), __INT_MAX__);', '      _response.clear();', '      close();', '      return false;', '    }']}
description: Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability in the XML RPC library of OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages allows unauthenticated network traffic to cause unexpected behavior. This issue affects: OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages Noetic and prior versions. Fixed in https://github.com/ros/ros_comm/pull/2065.

code_evidence: Line 4 casts _response.length() (size_t) to int for comparison with _contentLength; after appending attacker-controlled data to _response on line 11, line 12 repeats the int cast, so a response longer than INT_MAX wraps to a negative value and the length check is bypassed.
Lines 21-22 pass the size_t _response.length() to a %d format specifier, a further size mismatch on the same length value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an integer conversion/wraparound of a length value used as a size check, which matches CWE-190. A plain unbounded-read weakness (CWE-400) would describe the consequence, but the specific flaw here is the int/size_t truncation enabling the bypass.

evidence_lines.code:
XmlRpcUtil::log(3, "XmlRpcClient::readResponse (read %d bytes)", _response.length());
XmlRpcUtil::log(5, "response:\n%s", _response.c_str());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the narrowing conversion of the accumulated response length from size_t to int in the loop condition. An unauthenticated peer controls how much data is sent; once _response exceeds INT_MAX the cast yields a negative int, so the comparison against _contentLength no longer bounds accumulation, leading to unbounded memory growth or other unexpected behavior.

commit_msg:
Bug 697985: bounds check the array allocations methods

The clump allocator has four allocation functions that use 'number of elements'
and 'size of elements' parameters (rather than a simple 'number of bytes').

Those need specific bounds checking.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '    obj = alloc_obj(imem,', '                    (ulong) num_elements * pstype->ssize,', '                    pstype, ALLOC_DIRECT, cname);'], 'added_lines': ['    ulong lsize;', '    if (alloc_array_check_size(num_elements, pstype->ssize, &lsize) == false)', '        return NULL;', '    obj = alloc_obj(imem, lsize, pstype, ALLOC_DIRECT, cname);']}
description: The gs_alloc_ref_array function in psi/ialloc.c in Artifex Ghostscript 9.21 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PostScript document. This is related to a lack of an integer overflow check in base/gsalloc.c.

code_evidence: The allocation size is computed as (ulong) num_elements * pstype->ssize and passed directly to alloc_obj. num_elements is caller-supplied (uint) and pstype->ssize comes from the structure type; neither is checked for multiplication overflow before the product is used as the byte count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an unchecked integer multiplication whose wrapped result is used as an allocation size, matching CWE-190. This is not merely a buffer overflow (CWE-119); the overflow of the size computation is the root cause enabling the undersized allocation.

commit_msg: Fixed memory leak when creating nested exceptions in Magick++.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['              nestedException=createException(p);', '                q=createException(p);', '                nestedException->nested(q);', '                nestedException=q;'], 'added_lines': ['              {', '                nestedException=createException(p);', '                q=nestedException;', '              }', '                Exception', '                  *r;', '', '                r=createException(p);', '                q->nested(r);', '                q=r;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Magick++ in ImageMagick 6.9.7. A specially crafted file creating a nested exception could lead to a memory leak (thus, a DoS).

code_evidence: In the loop, the first matching exception is stored in nestedException via createException(p) [30,31]. For each subsequent match, a new Exception is allocated with createException(p) and assigned to q [34], then linked with nestedException->nested(q) and the head pointer is overwritten with nestedException=q [35,36]. Because the head pointer is advanced, no reference to the earlier first-created exception is retained except through the nested chain.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the function creates Exception resources whose effective lifetime ends after chaining but does not release them, matching missing release of a resource after effective lifetime. This is a resource-lifetime flaw rather than an out-of-bounds or use-after-free issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the exception-list traversal replaces the tracked head pointer with each newly created nested exception, so previously created Exception objects are not reachable for release in this function. Trigger: a crafted file producing multiple distinct nested exceptions causes repeated allocation. Supported consequence: accumulated heap memory is not freed, enabling memory-consumption DoS; the defect is the missing release, not the allocation itself.

commit_msg:
iwlwifi: pcie: fix memory leaks in iwl_pcie_ctxt_info_gen3_init

In iwl_pcie_ctxt_info_gen3_init there are cases that the allocated dma
memory is leaked in case of error.

DMA memories prph_scratch, prph_info, and ctxt_info_gen3 are allocated
and initialized to be later assigned to trans_pcie. But in any error case
before such assignment the allocated memories should be released.

First of such error cases happens when iwl_pcie_init_fw_sec fails.
Current implementation correctly releases prph_scratch. But in two
sunsequent error cases where dma_alloc_coherent may fail, such
releases are missing.

This commit adds release for prph_scratch when allocation for
prph_info fails, and adds releases for prph_scratch and prph_info when
allocation for ctxt_info_gen3 fails.

Fixes: 2ee824026288 ("iwlwifi: pcie: support context information for 22560 devices")
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Luca Coelho <luciano.coelho@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (ret) {', '\t\tdma_free_coherent(trans->dev,', '\t\t\t\t  sizeof(*prph_scratch),', '\t\t\t\t  prph_scratch,', '\t\t\t\t  trans_pcie->prph_scratch_dma_addr);', '\t\treturn ret;', '\t}', '\tif (!prph_info)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\tif (!ctxt_info_gen3)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (ret)', '\t\tgoto err_free_prph_scratch;', '', '\tif (!prph_info) {', '\t\tret = -ENOMEM;', '\t\tgoto err_free_prph_scratch;', '\t}', '\tif (!ctxt_info_gen3) {', '\t\tret = -ENOMEM;', '\t\tgoto err_free_prph_info;', '\t}', '', 'err_free_prph_info:', '\tdma_free_coherent(trans->dev,', '\t\t\t  sizeof(*prph_info),', '\t\t\tprph_info,', '\t\t\ttrans_pcie->prph_info_dma_addr);', '', 'err_free_prph_scratch:', '\tdma_free_coherent(trans->dev,', '\t\t\t  sizeof(*prph_scratch),', '\t\t\tprph_scratch,', '\t\t\ttrans_pcie->prph_scratch_dma_addr);', '\treturn ret;', '']}
description: Multiple memory leaks in the iwl_pcie_ctxt_info_gen3_init() function in drivers/net/wireless/intel/iwlwifi/pcie/ctxt-info-gen3.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allow attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering iwl_pcie_init_fw_sec() or dma_alloc_coherent() failures, aka CID-0f4f199443fa.

code_evidence: After iwl_pcie_init_fw_sec fails, prph_scratch is freed and the function returns, so this path is handled.
prph_info is allocated via dma_alloc_coherent; on failure the code returns -ENOMEM without freeing the already-allocated prph_scratch, leaking it.
ctxt_info_gen3 is allocated; on failure the code returns -ENOMEM without freeing prph_scratch or prph_info, leaking both DMA allocations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory and fails to release it on error paths, matching CWE-401's missing release of memory after its effective lifetime. The leak depends on allocation-failure triggers rather than a size miscalculation or double free, so it is a leak rather than a related memory-safety weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the early error returns after the prph_info and ctxt_info_gen3 allocations skip dma_free_coherent for previously allocated DMA buffers. Trigger: a dma_alloc_coherent failure (e.g., under memory pressure), which returns NULL and takes the -ENOMEM return path. Consequence: the prph_scratch and/or prph_info DMA memory is never released, causing memory consumption (DoS).

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions TFLite's [`GatherNd` implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/149562d49faa709ea80df1d99fc41d005b81082a/tensorflow/lite/kernels/gather_nd.cc#L124) does not support negative indices but there are no checks for this situation. Hence, an attacker can read arbitrary data from the heap by carefully crafting a model with negative values in `indices`. Similar issue exists in [`Gather` implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/149562d49faa709ea80df1d99fc41d005b81082a/tensorflow/lite/kernels/gather.cc). We have patched the issue in GitHub commits bb6a0383ed553c286f87ca88c207f6774d5c4a8f and eb921122119a6b6e470ee98b89e65d721663179d. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Eval dispatches to Gather<float, int32_t>(*params, input, positions, output) for int32 positions without any validation of positions values before the call.
The same unchecked dispatch occurs for int64 positions via Gather<float, int64_t>(*params, input, positions, output); the caller passes attacker-controlled positions straight to the gather kernel.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing index validation permits reads before the start of the intended buffer, matching out-of-bounds read. It is not a write issue (CWE-787) since the operation only reads memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The Eval function routes the positions tensor directly into the Gather kernel with no check that index values are non-negative or within bounds. A crafted model supplying negative indices causes the kernel to compute an out-of-range offset, leading to a heap out-of-bounds read of arbitrary data.

commit_msg:
Security: fix Lua struct package offset handling.

After the first fix to the struct package I found another similar
problem, which is fixed by this patch. It could be reproduced easily by
running the following script:

    return struct.unpack('f', "xxxxxxxxxxxxx",-3)

The above will access bytes before the 'data' pointer.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  size_t pos = luaL_optinteger(L, 3, 1) - 1;', '    luaL_argcheck(L, pos+size <= ld, 2, "data string too short");'], 'added_lines': ['  size_t pos = luaL_optinteger(L, 3, 1);', '  luaL_argcheck(L, pos > 0, 3, "offset must be 1 or greater");', '  pos--; /* Lua indexes are 1-based, but here we want 0-based for C', '          * pointer math. */', '    luaL_argcheck(L, size <= ld && pos <= ld - size,', '                   2, "data string too short");']}
description: An Integer Overflow issue was discovered in the struct library in the Lua subsystem in Redis before 3.2.12, 4.x before 4.0.10, and 5.x before 5.0 RC2, leading to a failure of bounds checking.

code_evidence: Line 6 converts the user-supplied Lua offset (luaL_optinteger) into size_t after subtracting 1; a value of 0 wraps to SIZE_MAX because the subtraction occurs in unsigned arithmetic.
Line 13 checks pos+size <= ld, but pos+size itself can wrap around in size_t, so an out-of-bounds pos passes the bounds check.
Lines 19 and 28 then use data+pos and memcpy(&f, data+pos, size) with the unchecked position, reading before the data buffer.
Line 53 computes ld - pos for memchr; when pos exceeds ld, this underflows.
Line 62 advances pos by size without validating it stays within ld.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The bounds check is defeated by integer wraparound in unsigned size_t arithmetic (both pos-1 and pos+size), so the target CWE-190 integer overflow/wraparound directly describes the failure that leads to the out-of-bounds access.

evidence_lines.code: size_t pos = luaL_optinteger(L, 3, 1) - 1;
luaL_argcheck(L, pos+size <= ld, 2, "data string too short");

lua_Number res = getinteger(data+pos, h.endian, issigned, size);
memcpy(&f, data+pos, size);
const char *e = (const char *)memchr(data+pos, '\0', ld - pos);
pos += size;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the offset is cast to unsigned size_t and decremented without a lower-bound check, and the upper-bound test pos+size <= ld is itself subject to wraparound. Trigger: a negative or zero offset (e.g. struct.unpack('f', "xxxxxxxxxxxxx", -3)) produces a huge size_t pos or a wrapped pos+size that passes the check. Consequence: data+pos and memcpy read outside the data string, yielding out-of-bounds memory disclosure or crash.

description: In smp_proc_master_id of smp_act.cc, there is a possible out of bounds read due to a missing bounds check. This could lead to remote information disclosure over Bluetooth with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation. Product: Android Versions: Android-7.0 Android-7.1.1 Android-7.1.2 Android-8.0 Android-8.1 Android-9.0 Android ID: A-111937027

A short remote packet causes STREAM_TO_ARRAY to read past the end of the buffer, disclosing adjacent memory (or crashing) over Bluetooth without user interaction.

commit_msg:
Like other vectors already patched, this one here allows the root
user to load ACPI tables, which enables arbitrary physical address
writes, which in turn makes it possible to disable lockdown.

Prevents this by checking the lockdown status before allowing a new
ACPI table to be installed. The link in the trailer shows a PoC of
how this might be used.

Link: https://git.zx2c4.com/american-unsigned-language/tree/american-unsigned-language-2.sh
Cc: 5.4+ <stable@vger.kernel.org> # 5.4+
Signed-off-by: Jason A. Donenfeld <Jason@zx2c4.com>
Signed-off-by: Rafael J. Wysocki <rafael.j.wysocki@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint ret;'], 'added_lines': ['\tint ret = security_locked_down(LOCKDOWN_ACPI_TABLES);', '', '\tif (ret)', '\t\treturn ret;']}
description: An issue was discovered in drivers/acpi/acpi_configfs.c in the Linux kernel before 5.7.7. Injection of malicious ACPI tables via configfs could be used by attackers to bypass lockdown and secure boot restrictions, aka CID-75b0cea7bf30.

code_evidence: The write handler begins by binding the caller-supplied data pointer as an ACPI table header and the config item as an acpi_table, with no authorization check on the calling process.
It only rejects an already-loaded table (-EBUSY) and otherwise proceeds; length and signature checks appear later in the function.
The supplied header is copied via kmemdup and passed to acpi_load_table, installing attacker-controlled ACPI tables.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the handler omits an authorization decision before a security-sensitive action (loading ACPI tables), letting an unprivileged actor perform a privileged operation. This is missing authorization, not merely missing input validation: the length/signature checks do not constrain who may act.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write path performs no privilege/authorization check (e.g., lockdown or capability) before installing a caller-supplied ACPI table. Trigger: a process able to write the configfs attribute supplies a crafted header; the function validates length/signature but not actor authorization, then calls acpi_load_table. Consequence: unauthorized installation of ACPI tables, enabling arbitrary physical memory writes and bypass of lockdown/secure boot protections.

description: Rizin is a UNIX-like reverse engineering framework and command-line toolset. In versions up to and including 0.3.1 there is a heap-based out of bounds write in parse_die() when reversing an AMD64 ELF binary with DWARF debug info. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds write while zeroing/parsing attribute values, leading to crash or potential code execution.

description: RIOT-OS, an operating system for Internet of Things (IoT) devices, contains a network stack with the ability to process 6LoWPAN frames. In versions 2023.01 and prior, an attacker can send multiple crafted frames to the device to trigger a race condition. The race condition invalidates assumptions about the program state and leads to an invalid memory access resulting in denial of service. This issue is patched in pull request 19679. There are no known workarounds.

code_evidence: Line 9 clears the timer message content pointer (msg.content.ptr = NULL) without any locking, directly manipulating the shared ARQ timeout event state that a concurrent scheduler/timer may read.

Lines 4 and 18-22 capture fbuf->sfr.window.next into frag_desc/head and then walk the window list with frag_desc = frag_desc->super.super.next in a do-while loop until frag_desc != head, reading and advancing over shared fragment descriptors with no synchronization against concurrent modification of the window.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function accesses shared resources (the timeout event and fragment window) in a concurrent code sequence without synchronization, allowing an interfering sequence to violate atomicity/exclusivity. The stale-pointer invalid access is the resulting consequence, not a separate memory-safety CWE.

evidence_lines.code: fbuf->sfr.arq_timeout_event.msg.content.ptr = NULL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ARQ timeout handler mutates and traverses shared scheduler state (the timeout event's msg.content.ptr and the sfr.window fragment list) without exclusive access. Trigger: crafted frames cause the ARQ timer and fragment-processing code to run concurrently, so the window list or event pointer changes mid-sequence. Consequence: the list traversal reads a stale/invalid next pointer or the cleared event pointer, yielding an invalid memory access and denial of service.

commit_msg:
evtchn: convert per-channel lock to be IRQ-safe

... in order for send_guest_{global,vcpu}_virq() to be able to make use
of it.

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    double_evtchn_lock(lchn, rchn);', '    double_evtchn_unlock(lchn, rchn);'], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned long  flags;', '    flags = double_evtchn_lock(lchn, rchn);', '    double_evtchn_unlock(lchn, rchn, flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: After the XSM check succeeds, the function takes the per-channel locks via double_evtchn_lock(lchn, rchn) and then mutates both channels' interdomain fields and state, calls evtchn_port_init and evtchn_port_set_pending, and finally releases with double_evtchn_unlock. The patch changes these calls to acquire and restore IRQ flags, indicating the lock is taken in a context where an interrupt handler could attempt the same lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The bind sequence requires exclusive access to both event channels, but a timing window exists where an interfering interrupt-context sequence can access the same shared resource, matching CWE-362. The fix makes the critical section IRQ-safe, confirming improper synchronization rather than a missing bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-channel event lock protecting the lchn/rchn state transition is acquired without disabling interrupts, so an interrupt-context code sequence can re-enter and violate exclusivity/atomicity of the bind. Trigger: an interrupt arriving between double_evtchn_lock and double_evtchn_unlock while the channel state is half-updated. Consequence: corrupted channel state leading to internal assumption violations, out-of-bounds accesses or bug checks (DoS, potential privilege escalation).

commit_msg:
Currently, locking of ->session is very inconsistent; most places
protect it using the legacy tty mutex, but disassociate_ctty(),
__do_SAK(), tiocspgrp() and tiocgsid() don't.
Two of the writers hold the ctrl_lock (because they already need it for
->pgrp), but __proc_set_tty() doesn't do that yet.

On a PREEMPT=y system, an unprivileged user can theoretically abuse
this broken locking to read 4 bytes of freed memory via TIOCGSID if
tiocgsid() is preempted long enough at the right point. (Other things
might also go wrong, especially if root-only ioctls are involved; I'm
not sure about that.)

Change the locking on ->session such that:

 - tty_lock() is held by all writers: By making disassociate_ctty()
   hold it. This should be fine because the same lock can already be
   taken through the call to tty_vhangup_session().
   The tricky part is that we need to shorten the area covered by
   siglock to be able to take tty_lock() without ugly retry logic; as
   far as I can tell, this should be fine, since nothing in the
   signal_struct is touched in the `if (tty)` branch.
 - ctrl_lock is held by all writers: By changing __proc_set_tty() to
   hold the lock a little longer.
 - All readers that aren't holding tty_lock() hold ctrl_lock: By
   adding locking to tiocgsid() and __do_SAK(), and expanding the area
   covered by ctrl_lock in tiocspgrp().

Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Jiri Slaby <jirislaby@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!current->signal->tty ||', '\t    (current->signal->tty != real_tty) ||', '\t    (real_tty->session != task_session(current)))', '\t\treturn -ENOTTY;', '\tspin_lock_irq(&real_tty->ctrl_lock);', '\tspin_unlock_irq(&real_tty->ctrl_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['', '', '\tspin_lock_irq(&real_tty->ctrl_lock);', '\tif (!current->signal->tty ||', '\t    (current->signal->tty != real_tty) ||', '\t    (real_tty->session != task_session(current))) {', '\t\tretval = -ENOTTY;', '\t\tgoto out_unlock_ctrl;', '\t}', 'out_unlock_ctrl:', '\tspin_unlock_irq(&real_tty->ctrl_lock);']}
description: A locking inconsistency issue was discovered in the tty subsystem of the Linux kernel through 5.9.13. drivers/tty/tty_io.c and drivers/tty/tty_jobctrl.c may allow a read-after-free attack against TIOCGSID, aka CID-c8bcd9c5be24.

code_evidence: Lines 10-13 read current->signal->tty and real_tty->session for validation without holding real_tty->ctrl_lock, so these fields can be concurrently modified by writers holding ctrl_lock.
Lines 27-30 modify real_tty->pgrp under ctrl_lock, but the earlier session/tty checks were performed outside that lock, so the validated state may change before use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is inconsistent lock coverage: readers of shared tty/session state do not hold ctrl_lock while writers do, matching CWE-667 improper locking rather than a pure race or use-after-free.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!current->signal->tty ||
(current->signal->tty != real_tty) ||
(real_tty->session != task_session(current)))
return -ENOTTY;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function checks session and tty ownership outside ctrl_lock, while other paths update ->session under that lock. Under preemption, the checked state can change between validation and the locked pgrp update, leading to inconsistent state and a possible read-after-free of tty/session data.

commit_msg:
Continue to back away from the LEFT JOIN optimization of check-in [41c27bc0ff1d3135]
by disallowing query flattening if the outer query is DISTINCT.  Without this fix,
if an index scan is run on the table within the view on the right-hand side of the
LEFT JOIN, stale result registers might be accessed yielding incorrect results,
and/or an OP_IfNullRow opcode might be invoked on the un-opened table, resulting
in a NULL-pointer dereference.  This problem was found by the Yongheng and Rui fuzzer.

FossilOrigin-Name: 862974312edf00e9d1068115d1a39b7235b7db68b6d86b81d38a12f025a4748e
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if( pSubSrc->nSrc>1 || isAgg || IsVirtual(pSubSrc->a[0].pTab) ){', '      /*  (3a)             (3c)     (3b) */'], 'added_lines': ['    if( pSubSrc->nSrc>1                   /* (3a) */', '     || isAgg                             /* (3b) */', '     || IsVirtual(pSubSrc->a[0].pTab)     /* (3c) */', '     || (p->selFlags & SF_Distinct)!=0    /* (3d) */', '    ){']}
description: flattenSubquery in select.c in SQLite 3.30.1 mishandles certain uses of SELECT DISTINCT involving a LEFT JOIN in which the right-hand side is a view. This can cause a NULL pointer dereference (or incorrect results).

code_evidence: The LEFT JOIN guard at [55,56,57,58,59,60] sets isLeftJoin=1 and rejects flattening only for multi-source subqueries, aggregates, or virtual tables; it does not reject an outer query with SF_Distinct.

At [185,186,187,188], when isLeftJoin>0, the subquery WHERE is rewritten with sqlite3SetJoinExpr using iNewParent, and the parent WHERE is combined, allowing the subquery to be flattened into a LEFT JOIN context.
Line [198,199] merges SF_Compound flags and asserts the subquery lacks SF_Distinct, but nothing prevents an outer DISTINCT from being combined with this LEFT JOIN flattening.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's missing DISTINCT guard leads to an OP_IfNullRow dereference of a NULL table pointer, matching CWE-476. It is not merely an incorrect-result logic bug: the supported consequence includes a NULL pointer dereference during query execution.

evidence_lines.code:
pParent->selFlags |= pSub->selFlags & SF_Compound;
assert( (pSub->selFlags & SF_Distinct)==0 );

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: flattenSubquery permits flattening a LEFT JOIN whose right side is a view even when the outer query is DISTINCT, so the join rewriting at [185,186,187,188] produces a query plan where the right-hand table may be un-opened or stale result registers are read. Trigger: a DISTINCT outer query with a LEFT JOIN to a view, with an index scan on the view's table. Consequence: an OP_IfNullRow opcode runs on the un-opened table causing a NULL-pointer dereference, or stale registers yield incorrect results.

commit_msg:
Clean up handling of counted blobs of bytes.

Don't treat the count+blob as itself a blob of bytes; use FT_NONE.
Create it with an unknown length (-1, meaning "to end of packet, for
now"), and set its length once we've finished dissecting it.  Dissect
the raw bytes of a prefixed-bytes item regardless of whether we're
building a protocol tree or not.

This means we do a better job of handling a too-large length; instead of
overflowing the offset, we throw an exception and stop dissecting, so we
don't run the risk of looping infinitely.
