commit_msg:
Out-of-bounds read in multiple decode functions

These were reported as:
- Out-of-bounds read in ntlm_decode_oem_str (GHSL-2023-019)
- Out-of-bounds read in ntlm_decode_u16l_str_hdr (GHSL-2023-020)
- Out-of-bounds read in ntlm_decode_field (GHSL-2023-021)

These are lall basically the same identical error replicated in 3
separate functions.

Fixes defects GHSL-2023-019, GHSL-2023-020, GHSL-2023-021 found by
the GitHub Security Lab team via oss-fuzz.

A 32-bit integer overflow condition can lead to incorrect checks of
consistency of length of internal buffers. This leads to a DoS
as the service may end up reading from unmapped memory and crashing.

Although most applications will error out before accepting a singe input
buffer of 4GB in lenght this could theoretically happen, and therefore
we fix it.

Fixes CVE-2023-25563

Signed-off-by: Simo Sorce <simo@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        (UINT32_MAX - offs < len) ||']}
description: GSS-NTLMSSP is a mechglue plugin for the GSSAPI library that implements NTLM authentication. Prior to version 1.2.0, multiple out-of-bounds reads when decoding NTLM fields can trigger a denial of service. A 32-bit integer overflow condition can lead to incorrect checks of consistency of length of internal buffers. Although most applications will error out before accepting a singe input buffer of 4GB in length this could theoretically happen. This vulnerability can be triggered via the main `gss_accept_sec_context` entry point if the application allows tokens greater than 4GB in length. This can lead to a large, up to 65KB, out-of-bounds read which could cause a denial-of-service if it reads from unmapped memory. Version 1.2.0 contains a patch for the out-of-bounds reads.

code_evidence: The offset check compares offs against buffer->length and validates offs + len > buffer->length, but offs is uint32_t and len is uint16_t, so offs + len is computed in 32-bit and can wrap when offs is near UINT32_MAX.
After the check, malloc(len) allocates b.length and memcpy reads b.length bytes from &buffer->data[offs]; if the wrapped sum passed the check, the copy reads past buffer->length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe operation is a memcpy read past buffer->data[buffer->length], caused by an insufficient length/offset constraint rather than a write. The missing overflow guard (added in the patch) directly permits reading memory outside the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check relies on a 32-bit addition that can overflow, so a large attacker-controlled offset combined with len bypasses validation. Trigger: a crafted NTLM field header with an offset near UINT32_MAX. Consequence: memcpy reads beyond the intended buffer, an out-of-bounds read that can crash the service.

commit_msg:
xen/arm: p2m: Avoid off-by-one check on p2m->max_mapped_gfn

The code base is using inconsistently the field p2m->max_mapped_gfn.
Some of the useres expect that p2m->max_guest_gfn contain the highest
mapped GFN while others expect highest + 1.

p2m->max_guest_gfn is set as highest + 1, because of that the sanity
check on the GFN in p2m_resolved_translation_fault() and
p2m_get_entry() can be bypassed when GFN == p2m->max_guest_gfn.

p2m_get_root_pointer(p2m->max_guest_gfn) may return NULL if it is
outside of address range supported and therefore the BUG_ON() could be
hit.

The current value hold in p2m->max_mapped_gfn is inconsistent with the
expectation of the common code (see domain_get_maximum_gpfn()) and also
the documentation of the field.

Rather than changing the check in p2m_translation_fault() and
p2m_get_entry(), p2m->max_mapped_gfn is now containing the highest
mapped GFN and the callers assuming "highest + 1" are now adjusted.

Take the opportunity to use 1UL rather than 1 as page_order could
theoritically big enough to overflow a 32-bit integer.

Lastly, the documentation of the field max_guest_gfn to reflect how it
is computed.

This is part of XSA-301.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <Julien.Grall@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    end = p2m->max_mapped_gfn;'], 'added_lines': ['    end = gfn_add(p2m->max_mapped_gfn, 1);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing ARM guest OS users to cause a denial of service via a XENMEM_add_to_physmap hypercall. p2m->max_mapped_gfn is used by the functions p2m_resolve_translation_fault() and p2m_get_entry() to sanity check guest physical frame. The rest of the code in the two functions will assume that there is a valid root table and check that with BUG_ON(). The function p2m_get_root_pointer() will ignore the unused top bits of a guest physical frame. This means that the function p2m_set_entry() will alias the frame. However, p2m->max_mapped_gfn will be updated using the original frame. It would be possible to set p2m->max_mapped_gfn high enough to cover a frame that would lead p2m_get_root_pointer() to return NULL in p2m_get_entry() and p2m_resolve_translation_fault(). Additionally, the sanity check on p2m->max_mapped_gfn is off-by-one allowing "highest mapped + 1" to be considered valid. However, p2m_get_root_pointer() will return NULL. The problem could be triggered with a specially crafted hypercall XENMEM_add_to_physmap{, _batch} followed by an access to an address (via hypercall or direct access) that passes the sanity check but cause p2m_get_root_pointer() to return NULL. A malicious guest administrator may cause a hypervisor crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS). Xen version 4.8 and newer are vulnerable. Only Arm systems are vulnerable. x86 systems are not affected.

code_evidence: The loop bounds are derived from p2m->max_mapped_gfn, which the patch changes to hold the highest mapped GFN rather than highest+1. Before the fix, end = p2m->max_mapped_gfn made the loop condition gfn_x(start) < gfn_x(end) stop one GFN too early, so the highest mapped GFN was never processed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-193 fits because the bound uses a value one less than the correct exclusive limit, causing an iteration to omit exactly one element. This is a classic off-by-one boundary error rather than an integer overflow or an out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is an off-by-one in the loop's upper bound: max_mapped_gfn is the highest GFN, but the loop treats it as an exclusive end, excluding the last mapped GFN. Triggered during p2m teardown, the final mapping is skipped and never invalidated, leaving a stale entry. The supported consequence is incomplete cleanup of the p2m, not the hypervisor crash described elsewhere in the commit.

fixes #25

description: ngiflib commit 5e7292 was discovered to contain an infinite loop via the function DecodeGifImg at ngiflib.c.

code_evidence: The main loop at line 134 reads codes via GetGifWord and only exits on eof (line 136) or when npix==0 (line 142); otherwise it continues indefinitely.

In the else branch, npix is decremented by (stack_top - stackp) at line 189 regardless of how many pixels were actually written; when npix is smaller than the stack size, only npix pixels are written (line 187) but the full stack size is subtracted, driving npix negative so the npix==0 exit can no longer be reached.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the for(;;) loop's intended exit condition (npix==0) becomes unreachable due to incorrect npix accounting, producing an infinite/very long iteration. It is not a buffer overflow since writes are bounded by the npix checks; the defect is the loop termination condition.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop's termination depends on npix reaching exactly 0. When a decoded code's stack length exceeds remaining npix, the write is truncated to npix but npix is still reduced by the full stack length, making it negative; the npix==0 check never fires again, so the loop keeps consuming codes until eof or input exhaustion. This can cause the decoder to spin/consume resources, a denial of service.

commit_msg: Suspend exception processing if there are too many exceptions
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (CheckMemoryOverflow((image->columns+7UL) >> 3UL,image->rows) != MagickFalse)', '        if (CheckMemoryOverflow(number_pixels,viff_info.number_data_bands) != MagickFalse)'], 'added_lines': ['        if (HeapOverflowSanityCheck((image->columns+7UL) >> 3UL,image->rows) != MagickFalse)', '        if (HeapOverflowSanityCheck(number_pixels,viff_info.number_data_bands) != MagickFalse)']}
description: magick/memory.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-5 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via vectors involving "too many exceptions," which trigger a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: For the bit-storage branch, the computed row byte count `(image->columns+7)>>3` is multiplied by `image->rows` to form `max_packets`, guarded by the overflow check on line 315.

For the non-bit branch, `number_pixels*number_data_bands` forms `max_packets`; the buffer is then allocated with `AcquireQuantumMemory(MagickMax(number_pixels,max_packets),bytes_per_pixel)` and `ReadBlob` writes `bytes_per_pixel*max_packets` bytes into it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an out-of-bounds write on a heap buffer during image decoding, matching CWE-119's scope of operations outside a buffer's intended boundary. A more specific child such as CWE-787 could apply, but the target CWE-119 correctly captures the buffer-boundary violation shown here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocation size (`MagickMax(number_pixels,max_packets)`) and the read size (`bytes_per_pixel*max_packets`) are derived from separate products. If `max_packets` exceeds `number_pixels` and the multiplication or size computation is inconsistent, `ReadBlob` can write past the allocated buffer. Attacker-controlled header fields (rows, columns, number_data_bands) drive these values, so a crafted VIFF file can trigger an out-of-bounds write, causing a crash or memory corruption.

Correct declaration of ‘filesize’ shadows a previous local.

description: An out-of-memory flaw was found in libtiff. Passing a crafted tiff file to TIFFOpen() API may allow a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via a craft input with size smaller than 379 KB.

code_evidence: Line 10 obtains the file size and line 11 computes the allocation size from the attacker-controlled strip count td_nstrips; lines 12-20 reject the request only when that allocation exceeds the file size.

Lines 50-52 compute per-entry data size from tdir_count with an overflow guard, and lines 63-70 accumulate these sizes into space, capping space at filesize before it is used to fill the strip byte counts.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the root cause is insufficient control over resource consumption driven by untrusted file metadata, leading to a memory-exhaustion DoS. The added filesize comparisons are the attempted constraint; the weakness is that resource use is still tied to attacker-influenced counts.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function derives resource sizes (StripByteCounts allocation and strip data sizes) from attacker-controlled TIFF fields such as td_nstrips and tdir_count. The size checks compare these values against the file size, but a small crafted file can still drive large derived allocations or loop counts before the comparison limits them, allowing a remote attacker to provoke excessive memory consumption and denial of service when TIFFOpen reads the file.

commit_msg:
smart_pkt: treat empty packet lines as error

The Git protocol does not specify what should happen in the case
of an empty packet line (that is a packet line "0004"). We
currently indicate success, but do not return a packet in the
case where we hit an empty line. The smart protocol was not
prepared to handle such packets in all cases, though, resulting
in a `NULL` pointer dereference.

Fix the issue by returning an error instead. As such kind of
packets is not even specified by upstream, this is the right
thing to do.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t/* When a valid packet with no content has been', '\t\t * read, git_pkt_parse_line does not report an', '\t\t * error, but the pkt pointer has not been set.', '\t\t * Handle this by skipping over empty packets.', '\t\t */', '\t\tif (pkt == NULL)', '\t\t\tcontinue;', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: The Git Smart Protocol support in libgit2 before 0.24.6 and 0.25.x before 0.25.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via an empty packet line.

code_evidence: git_pkt_parse_line can succeed (return 0) while leaving pkt unset for an empty packet line; only GIT_EBUFS and negative errors are handled, so pkt remains NULL and the check at line 29 is what prevents it from reaching add_push_report_pkt(push, pkt) at line 31.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is a missing NULL check on a pointer the code assumes is valid, leading to dereference of NULL. This matches CWE-476; it is not merely an input-validation issue since the crash stems from the unchecked NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: An empty packet line ("0004") causes git_pkt_parse_line to return success without setting pkt. Without the NULL guard, the NULL pkt is passed to add_push_report_pkt, which dereferences it, crashing the process; a remote attacker triggers this via the smart protocol, causing denial of service.

description: An issue was discovered in Janus through 0.9.1. plugins/janus_voicemail.c in the VoiceMail plugin has a race condition that could cause a server crash.

code_evidence: Line 9 clears session->started with a plain non-atomic store, while other paths in the plugin test or set this shared flag via g_atomic_int_get/set; the same function already uses atomic accessors for destroyed and hangingup at lines 10 and 12.

The trigger is simultaneous hangup/media operations on one session, and the supported consequence is a race that can cause a server crash or resource instability.

commit_msg: Fix for #4866: Added additional length checks

description: FreeRDP FreeRDP 2.0.0-rc3 released version before commit 205c612820dac644d665b5bb1cdf437dc5ca01e3 contains a Other/Unknown vulnerability in channels/drdynvc/client/drdynvc_main.c, drdynvc_process_capability_request that can result in The RDP server can read the client's memory.. This attack appear to be exploitable via RDPClient must connect the rdp server with echo option. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in after commit 205c612820dac644d665b5bb1cdf437dc5ca01e3.

code_evidence: dataLength is a UINT32 supplied by the RDP peer via the virtual channel data callback.
The stream is sized from totalLength via Stream_New(NULL, totalLength).

Stream_EnsureRemainingCapacity is called with (int) dataLength; the cast converts an attacker-controlled UINT32 to signed int, so a value above INT_MAX becomes negative and cannot correctly bound the following write.
Stream_Write then copies dataLength bytes into data_in using the mis-validated capacity, allowing the stream to be overrun.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked/incorrectly cast length permits writing/reading beyond the stream's intended buffer, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read (with the described consequence of server reading client memory). It is distinct from an integer overflow alone because the observable weakness is the resulting out-of-bounds buffer access.

drdynvc->data_in = Stream_New(NULL, totalLength);
Stream_Write(data_in, pData, dataLength);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the capacity check narrows the peer-controlled UINT32 dataLength to signed int before Stream_EnsureRemainingCapacity, so oversized lengths bypass or corrupt the remaining-capacity validation. Trigger: an RDP server sends channel data with a large dataLength; the subsequent Stream_Write writes beyond the allocated stream buffer, enabling out-of-bounds memory access/read of client memory.

commit_msg:
Ensure that EXFLAG_INVALID_POLICY is checked even in leaf certs

Even though we check the leaf cert to confirm it is valid, we
later ignored the invalid flag and did not notice that the leaf
cert was bad.

Fixes: CVE-2023-0465
Reviewed-by: Hugo Landau <hlandau@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20587)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        int i;', '        for (i = 1; i < sk_X509_num(ctx->chain); i++) {'], 'added_lines': ['        int i, cbcalled = 0;', '        for (i = 0; i < sk_X509_num(ctx->chain); i++) {', '            if ((x->ex_flags & EXFLAG_INVALID_POLICY) != 0)', '                cbcalled = 1;', '        if (!cbcalled) {', '            /* Should not be able to get here */', '            ERR_raise(ERR_LIB_X509, ERR_R_INTERNAL_ERROR);', '            return 0;', '        }', '        /* The callback ignored the error so we return success */']}
description:
Applications that use a non-default option when verifying certificates may be
vulnerable to an attack from a malicious CA to circumvent certain checks.

Invalid certificate policies in leaf certificates are silently ignored by
OpenSSL and other certificate policy checks are skipped for that certificate.
A malicious CA could use this to deliberately assert invalid certificate policies
in order to circumvent policy checking on the certificate altogether.

Policy processing is disabled by default but can be enabled by passing
the `-policy' argument to the command line utilities or by calling the
`X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_policies()' function.

code_evidence: When X509_policy_check returns X509_PCY_TREE_INVALID, the loop starts at i = 1, skipping the leaf certificate at index 0. CB_FAIL_IF checks EXFLAG_INVALID_POLICY only for chain[i] with i >= 1, so an invalid-policy flag on the leaf is never reported to the verify callback. The function then unconditionally returns 1, treating the chain as valid despite the bad leaf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs certificate validation (policy checking) but incorrectly validates the leaf by skipping it, silently accepting a certificate with invalid policy extensions. This is improper certificate validation, matching CWE-295, rather than a memory-safety or parsing flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error-notification loop begins at index 1 and omits the leaf, so EXFLAG_INVALID_POLICY on the leaf is never surfaced. Trigger: a malicious CA asserts invalid certificate policies in a leaf certificate while policy processing is enabled. Consequence: the invalid flag is silently ignored and policy checking is bypassed, so a certificate that should be rejected is accepted.

commit_msg:
Disallow namespace nodes in XPointer ranges

Namespace nodes must be copied to avoid use-after-free errors.
But they don't necessarily have a physical representation in a
document, so simply disallow them in XPointer ranges.

Found with afl-fuzz.

Fixes CVE-2016-4658.

As per title

relocations applied to a section, the linker applies those with

checking that the relocation is within the section bounds.  The same
thing now happens when reading debug sections since commit
a4cd947aca23, the PR23425 fix.

	PR 23770
	PR 23425

	"buf" and "off".  Bounds check "off".  Return status.
	* cofflink.c (_bfd_coff_generic_relocate_section): Update
	_bfd_clear_contents call.
	* elf-bfd.h (RELOC_AGAINST_DISCARDED_SECTION): Likewise.
	* elf32-arc.c (elf_arc_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-i386.c (elf_i386_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-metag.c (metag_final_link_relocate): Likewise.

	* elf32-visium.c (visium_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf64-ppc.c (ppc64_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.

description: An issue was discovered in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.31. An invalid memory address dereference was discovered in read_reloc in reloc.c. The vulnerability causes a segmentation fault and application crash, which leads to denial of service, as demonstrated by objdump, because of missing _bfd_clear_contents bounds checking.

code_evidence: When a relocation's symbol is in a discarded section, or an undefined symbol in a SEC_DEBUGGING section during non-relocatable linking, the code computes p = data + (*parent)->address * bfd_octets_per_byte(input_bfd) and passes p to _bfd_clear_contents without checking that the relocation address is within input_section's buffer. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the relocation offset is used to form a pointer into the section data buffer without a bounds check before _bfd_clear_contents writes/clears relocation bytes. Trigger: a crafted relocation with an address beyond the section size whose symbol is in a discarded section (or undefined in a debug section). Consequence: out-of-bounds memory access, causing a segfault/crash (denial of service) as seen with objdump.

commit_msg:
When going through execve(), zero out the NUMA fault statistics instead of
freeing them.

During execve, the task is reachable through procfs and the scheduler. A
concurrent /proc/*/sched reader can read data from a freed ->numa_faults
allocation (confirmed by KASAN) and write it back to userspace.
I believe that it would also be possible for a use-after-free read to occur
through a race between a NUMA fault and execve(): task_numa_fault() can
lead to task_numa_compare(), which invokes task_weight() on the currently
running task of a different CPU.

Another way to fix this would be to make ->numa_faults RCU-managed or add
extra locking, but it seems easier to wipe the NUMA fault statistics on
execve.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.6. On NUMA systems, the Linux fair scheduler has a use-after-free in show_numa_stats() because NUMA fault statistics are inappropriately freed, aka CID-16d51a590a8c.

code_evidence: __put_task_struct() calls task_numa_free(tsk) to release the task's NUMA fault statistics during task teardown, after which the tsk->numa_faults pointers are left dangling for concurrently reachable readers, such as /proc/*/sched via show_numa_stats().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees ->numa_faults via task_numa_free() without ensuring no later access occurs, so subsequent reads through the stale pointer constitute referencing memory after it has been freed, matching CWE-416. The weakness is the dangling-pointer reuse, not merely a memory leak or missing lock.

evidence_lines.code: task_numa_free(tsk);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the NUMA fault statistics are freed while the task_struct remains reachable through procfs and the scheduler. Trigger: a concurrent /proc/*/sched reader or NUMA fault path dereferences ->numa_faults after task_numa_free() releases it. Supported consequence: use-after-free read (confirmed by KASAN), potentially leaking freed memory contents to userspace.

commit_msg:
CVE-2020-1898

Don't allow for unlimited nesting in FBUnserialize or fb_compact_unserialize
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['inline typename V::MapType FBUnserializer<V>::unserializeMap() {', '          auto value = unserializeThing();', '          auto value = unserializeThing();'], 'added_lines': ['inline typename V::MapType FBUnserializer<V>::unserializeMap(size_t depth) {', '          auto value = unserializeThing(depth + 1);', '          auto value = unserializeThing(depth + 1);']}
description: The fb_unserialize function did not impose a depth limit for nested deserialization. That meant a maliciously constructed string could cause deserialization to recurse, leading to stack exhaustion. This issue affected HHVM prior to v4.32.3, between versions 4.33.0 and 4.56.0, 4.57.0, 4.58.0, 4.58.1, 4.59.0, 4.60.0, 4.61.0, 4.62.0.

code_evidence: unserializeMap() takes no depth parameter, so it has no way to bound how deep nested map deserialization may go.
For string keys, the map value is produced by unserializeThing() with no depth argument, allowing a nested map value to re-enter unserializeMap() at the same unbounded level.
The default integer-key branch likewise calls unserializeThing() without any depth tracking, so each nested map/collection recurses without a limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly embodies CWE-674: recursion depth is uncontrolled because no depth counter or limit is propagated into nested unserializeThing() calls. This is uncontrolled recursion leading to resource exhaustion, not merely a memory-size issue.

evidence_lines.code: inline typename V::MapType FBUnserializer<V>::unserializeMap() {
auto value = unserializeThing();
auto value = unserializeThing();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the deserializer recurses through unserializeThing() into unserializeMap() without tracking or limiting nesting depth. Trigger: a maliciously constructed serialized string containing deeply nested map/collection structures drives unbounded recursive calls; the supported consequence is stack exhaustion and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Defend against bad PT_DYNAMIC

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/391
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
	modified:   p_lx_elf.h
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            invert_pt_dynamic(dynseg);'], 'added_lines': ['            invert_pt_dynamic(dynseg, get_te64(&phdr->p_filesz));']}
description: A heap-based buffer over-read was discovered in the acc_ua_get_be32 function in miniacc.h in UPX 4.0.0 via a crafted Mach-O file.

code_evidence: The PT_DYNAMIC loop computes dynseg via check_pt_dynamic(phdr)+file_image, then calls invert_pt_dynamic(dynseg) without passing the segment's p_filesz; the patched version adds get_te64(&phdr->p_filesz) as a bound. The dynamic segment is iterated/read based only on its contents, not on the declared segment size, so a crafted PT_DYNAMIC with a small p_filesz but non-null-terminated entries lets the reader walk past the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing p_filesz bound causes reads past the intended dynamic-segment buffer, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is a read, not a write, so not CWE-787; the flaw is the absent length constraint rather than an integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: invert_pt_dynamic traverses the dynamic array without a size limit; trigger: a crafted ELF with PT_DYNAMIC whose p_filesz is smaller than the array scanned; consequence: out-of-bounds read of memory beyond the dynamic segment, potentially crashing or disclosing adjacent data.

commit_msg:
The maximum name and file sizes in the "new" header format are 32-bit
unsigned values.  However, the I/O functions mostly use long for sizes
and offsets, so that sizes >= 2^31 are handled wrongly on 32-bit
systems.

The current GNU cpio code doesn't seem to have this problem, but the
divergence between this version and that is large enough that I can't
simply cherry-pick a fix for it.

As a short-term fix, in read_in_new_ascii(), fail if c_namesize or
c_filesize is > LONG_MAX.

CVE-2021-31872

Signed-off-by: Ben Hutchings <ben@decadent.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* Sizes > LONG_MAX can currently result in integer overflow', '\t   in various places.  Fail if name is too large. */', '\tif (file_hdr->c_namesize > LONG_MAX) {', '\t\tfprintf(stderr, "%s: name size out of range\\n",', '\t\t\tprogname);', '\t\texit(1);', '\t}', '', '', '\t/* Fail if file is too large.  We could check this earlier', "\t   but it's helpful to report the name. */", '\tif (file_hdr->c_filesize > LONG_MAX) {', '\t\tfprintf(stderr, "%s: %s: file size out of range\\n",', '\t\t\tprogname, file_hdr->c_name);', '\t\texit(1);', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in klibc before 2.0.9. Multiple possible integer overflows in the cpio command on 32-bit systems may result in a buffer overflow or other security impact.

code_evidence: c_hdr entries (including c_namesize and c_filesize) are parsed from the 32-bit ASCII header via strtoul and stored without any range check against LONG_MAX.

c_namesize is passed directly to xmalloc and to tape_buffered_read cast to (long), and c_namesize + 110 is used in tape_skip_padding; on 32-bit systems a value above LONG_MAX becomes negative/truncated, so the size used for allocation and read diverges.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an arithmetic conversion/overflow of size values used for allocation and copying, matching CWE-190. It is the root cause; the buffer overflow is a downstream consequence, not a separate primary label.

evidence_lines.code: file_hdr->c_hdr[i] = strtoul(hexbuf, NULL, 16);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: header size fields are 32-bit unsigned but consumed as signed long with no upper-bound validation. Trigger: a crafted cpio header with c_namesize or c_filesize > LONG_MAX. Supported consequence: the truncated/negative long feeds allocation, read length and padding arithmetic, yielding integer overflow/wraparound that can cause buffer overflow or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
[lite] Add validation check for dilation height/width to be positive integers.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 416429178
Change-Id: If7cdcddca54486434d9b2f06e7e2b401d7c3ee25
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, params->dilation_height_factor > 0);', '  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, params->dilation_width_factor > 0);']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. ### Impact An attacker can craft a TFLite model that would trigger a division by zero in the implementation of depthwise convolutions. The parameters of the convolution can be user controlled and are also used within a division operation to determine the size of the padding that needs to be added before applying the convolution. There is no check before this division that the divisor is strictly positive. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Prepare calls ComputePaddingHeightWidth, passing the user-controlled params->dilation_height_factor and params->dilation_width_factor from node->builtin_data. This function has no prior check that these dilation factors are strictly positive, so zero values reach the padding computation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a division by zero (CWE-369): an unchecked user-supplied divisor flows into the padding calculation. The missing positivity constraint on the dilation factors is the direct cause, matching the divide-by-zero weakness rather than a generic input-validation issue.

evidence_lines.code:
data->padding = ComputePaddingHeightWidth(
params->stride_height, params->stride_width,
params->dilation_height_factor, params->dilation_width_factor, height,
width, filter_height, filter_width, padding, &out_height, &out_width);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dilation height/width factors are taken from attacker-controlled model parameters and passed into the padding-size computation without a positivity check. Trigger: a crafted TFLite depthwise-convolution model sets a dilation factor to 0. Consequence: the padding computation divides by the dilation factor and triggers a division by zero, crashing the process (DoS).

commit_msg:
Make DH_check_pub_key() and DH_generate_key() safer yet

We already check for an excessively large P in DH_generate_key(), but not in
DH_check_pub_key(), and none of them check for an excessively large Q.

This change adds all the missing excessive size checks of P and Q.

It's to be noted that behaviours surrounding excessively sized P and Q
differ.  DH_check() raises an error on the excessively sized P, but only
sets a flag for the excessively sized Q.  This behaviour is mimicked in
DH_check_pub_key().

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Hugo Landau <hlandau@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22518)

(cherry picked from commit ddeb4b6c6d527e54ce9a99cba785c0f7776e54b6)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        goto err;', '    }', '', '    if (dh->params.q != NULL', '        && BN_num_bits(dh->params.q) > OPENSSL_DH_MAX_MODULUS_BITS) {', '        ERR_raise(ERR_LIB_DH, DH_R_Q_TOO_LARGE);']}
description:
Issue summary: Generating excessively long X9.42 DH keys or checking
excessively long X9.42 DH keys or parameters may be very slow.

Impact summary: Applications that use the functions DH_generate_key() to
generate an X9.42 DH key may experience long delays.  Likewise, applications
that use DH_check_pub_key(), DH_check_pub_key_ex() or EVP_PKEY_public_check()
to check an X9.42 DH key or X9.42 DH parameters may experience long delays.
Where the key or parameters that are being checked have been obtained from
an untrusted source this may lead to a Denial of Service.

While DH_check() performs all the necessary checks (as of CVE-2023-3817),
DH_check_pub_key() doesn't make any of these checks, and is therefore
vulnerable for excessively large P and Q parameters.

Likewise, while DH_generate_key() performs a check for an excessively large
P, it doesn't check for an excessively large Q.

An application that calls DH_generate_key() or DH_check_pub_key() and
supplies a key or parameters obtained from an untrusted source could be
vulnerable to a Denial of Service attack.

DH_generate_key() and DH_check_pub_key() are also called by a number of
other OpenSSL functions.  An application calling any of those other
functions may similarly be affected.  The other functions affected by this
are DH_check_pub_key_ex(), EVP_PKEY_public_check(), and EVP_PKEY_generate().

Also vulnerable are the OpenSSL pkey command line application when using the
"-pubcheck" option, as well as the OpenSSL genpkey command line application.

The OpenSSL SSL/TLS implementation is not affected by this issue.

The OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.1 FIPS providers are not affected by this issue.

code_evidence: The function validates only the modulus p against OPENSSL_DH_MAX_MODULUS_BITS; an oversized p raises an error and jumps to cleanup.

A lower-bound check on p's bit length exists, but there is no analogous upper-bound check on the subgroup order q (dh->params.q), so oversized q values are not rejected before the modular exponentiation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-754 fits because the function fails to check an unusual/extreme parameter condition (oversized q) that attackers can deliberately trigger, violating the assumption that such values need not be bounded. This is a missing exceptional-condition check rather than a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function omits an excessive-size check for the DH parameter q, assuming only p needs bounding. Trigger: an attacker supplies DH parameters with an extremely large q from an untrusted source. The missing constraint allows the subsequent bn_mod_exp operation to process the oversized value, causing long delays and a denial of service.

commit_msg: [cudapoa] replace size_t with int64_t
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    offset_d_ += cudautils::align<size_t, 8>(sizeof(int16_t) * max_graph_dimension_ * max_poas_);', '    offset_d_ += cudautils::align<size_t, 8>(sizeof(int16_t) * max_graph_dimension_ * max_poas_);'], 'added_lines': ['    offset_d_ += cudautils::align<int64_t, 8>(sizeof(int16_t) * max_graph_dimension_ * max_poas_);', '    offset_d_ += cudautils::align<int64_t, 8>(sizeof(int16_t) * max_graph_dimension_ * max_poas_);']}
description: Clara Genomics Analysis before 0.2.0 has an integer overflow for cudapoa memory management in allocate_block.cpp.

code_evidence: Lines 7 and 9 compute sizeof(int16_t) * max_graph_dimension_ * max_poas_ and cast the result through cudautils::align<size_t, 8> before adding it to offset_d_. The multiplication is performed before any widening, so the product is bounded by the operand types rather than by size_t.
Line 10 derives scorebuf_alloc_size as total_d_ - offset_d_, and line 11 bases the scores pointer on offset_d_, so an incorrect offset flows directly into the score-buffer region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because an integer multiplication used to compute a memory offset wraps before it is widened, and that wrapped value determines buffer layout. This is integer overflow feeding memory management, not a bounds-check omission (CWE-125/787).

evidence_lines.code:
offset_d_ += cudautils::align<size_t, 8>(sizeof(int16_t) * max_graph_dimension_ * max_poas_);
offset_d_ += cudautils::align<size_t, 8>(sizeof(int16_t) * max_graph_dimension_ * max_poas_);

alignment_details_d->scorebuf_alloc_size = total_d_ - offset_d_;
alignment_details_d->scores              = reinterpret_cast<int16_t*>(&block_data_d_[offset_d_]);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the element-count product sizeof(int16_t) * max_graph_dimension_ * max_poas_ is evaluated in a narrow type and the alignment/cast to size_t does not prevent wraparound. With large dimensions the product wraps to a small value, offset_d_ advances too little, and subsequent pointers and scorebuf_alloc_size are computed from a wrong offset, producing undersized/overlapping buffer regions.

commit_msg:
Pass origin clean flag of ImageBitmap when structure clone

In this CL, we pass the origin clean flag of an ImageBitmap when this
ImageBitmap is being structure cloned, so that the receive of the
ImageBitmap is aware of this flag.

BUG=623406

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2097393002
Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#402204}

description: Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.116, does not ensure that a taint property is preserved after a structure-clone operation on an ImageBitmap object derived from a cross-origin image, which allows remote attackers to bypass the Same Origin Policy via crafted JavaScript code.

code_evidence: On the non-transferred path, the function serializes an ImageBitmap by copying pixel data and calling m_writer.writeImageBitmap with only width, height, pixelData and byte length. The originClean() taint property is not passed, so the receiving side has no indication whether the bitmap derived from a cross-origin image.

Trigger: structured-clone of an ImageBitmap created from a cross-origin image. commit_msg:
mp4: limit the recursion depth for boxes

Although the dissection of each box header consumes a couple of bytes,
it turned out that it's still possible to crash wireshark with a sample
file that contains a large number of nested boxes. The stack will fill
up before we reach the end of the data bytes.

Keep track of the recursion depth as we walk through the hierarchy of
boxes. Abort if we reach the (locally defined) upper limit.

Bug: 13777
Change-Id: I0f67245a5c74131f10d0f9d99b39ad31711b9775
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/26167
Reviewed-by: Martin Kaiser <wireshark@kaiser.cx>
Petri-Dish: Martin Kaiser <wireshark@kaiser.cx>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Anders Broman <a.broman58@gmail.com>
(cherry picked from commit 620f69a74b18908e3424920c7bb01cb5e4cbd8b1)
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/26204
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        packet_info *pinfo, proto_tree *tree)', '        ret = dissect_mp4_box(BOX_TYPE_STSD, tvb, offset, pinfo, tree);'], 'added_lines': ['        packet_info *pinfo, guint depth, proto_tree *tree)', '        ret = dissect_mp4_box(BOX_TYPE_STSD, depth, tvb, offset, pinfo, tree);']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.5 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.13, the MP4 dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/file-mp4.c by restricting the box recursion depth.

code_evidence: entry_cnt is read directly from the file via tvb_get_ntohl with no bound, and the loop iterates i<entry_cnt, calling dissect_mp4_box on each nested box entry. The function itself performs no depth or count validation on the attacker-controlled entry count or on the recursion the box dissection triggers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the dissector accepts file-controlled structural metadata (entry count and box nesting) without validating it against a safe recursion limit before processing. The crash stems from unvalidated input driving unsafe recursion, not from an arithmetic overflow (CWE-190) or buffer bounds error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The number of sample entries and the nesting of boxes are taken straight from the file without validating a recursion or count limit; a crafted MP4 with deeply nested boxes drives unbounded recursion in dissect_mp4_box until the stack is exhausted, crashing the dissector. Root cause is missing input validation on the file-supplied structure; the consequence is a stack-exhaustion DoS.

commit_msg:
Implemented measures to prevent memory leaks in sn_coap_parser_options_parse().

Added a helper uint16_t addition function with overflow detection. The function is used when calculating the extended length and option delta. The overlow detection is needed to avoid wrap-around of option number or length.
Additional checks in options using sn_coap_parser_options_parse_multiple_options() have been implemented to avoid overwriting of pointers pointing to previously allocated memory.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        option_number += previous_option_number;'], 'added_lines': ['        if(sn_coap_parser_add_u16_limit(option_number, previous_option_number, &option_number) != 0)', '        {', '            return -1;', '        }', '                if (dst_coap_msg_ptr->options_list_ptr->etag_ptr)', '                {', '                    tr_error("sn_coap_parser_options_parse - COAP_OPTION_ETAG exists!");', '                    return -1;', '                }', '                if (dst_coap_msg_ptr->options_list_ptr->location_query_ptr)', '                {', '                    tr_error("sn_coap_parser_options_parse - COAP_OPTION_LOCATION_QUERY exists!");', '                    return -1;', '                }', '                if (dst_coap_msg_ptr->uri_path_ptr)', '                {', '                    tr_error("sn_coap_parser_options_parse - COAP_OPTION_URI_PATH exists!");', '                    return -1;', '                }']}
description: Memory leaks were discovered in the CoAP library in Arm Mbed OS 5.15.3 when using the Arm mbed-coap library 5.1.5. The CoAP parser is responsible for parsing received CoAP packets. The function sn_coap_parser_options_parse() parses the CoAP option number field of all options present in the input packet. Each option number is calculated as a sum of the previous option number and a delta of the current option. The delta and the previous option number are expressed as unsigned 16-bit integers. Due to lack of overflow detection, it is possible to craft a packet that wraps the option number around and results in the same option number being processed again in a single packet. Certain options allocate memory by calling a memory allocation function. In the cases of COAP_OPTION_URI_QUERY, COAP_OPTION_URI_PATH, COAP_OPTION_LOCATION_QUERY, and COAP_OPTION_ETAG, there is no check on whether memory has already been allocated, which in conjunction with the option number integer overflow may lead to multiple assignments of allocated memory to a single pointer. This has been demonstrated to lead to memory leak by buffer orphaning. As a result, the memory is never freed.

code_evidence: Line 44 accumulates option_number by adding the attacker-influenced delta (from parse_ext_option at lines 36-40) to previous_option_number as an unsigned 16-bit value with no overflow check, so the option number can wrap around and a prior option number recurs in the same packet.
For COAP_OPTION_ETAG, lines 107-112 call sn_coap_parser_options_parse_multiple_options passing &etag_ptr with no check that etag_ptr is already non-NULL, unlike e.g. proxy_uri_ptr at line 95.
For COAP_OPTION_LOCATION_QUERY, lines 151-158 pass &location_query_ptr to the multiple-options parser without a prior non-NULL check.
For COAP_OPTION_URI_PATH, lines 160-167 pass &uri_path_ptr without a prior non-NULL check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the pointer reassignment for ETAG/LOCATION_QUERY/URI_PATH overwrites the only reference to allocated memory, so it cannot be released. This is a missing-release weakness, not a buffer overflow: the allocation succeeds but its lifetime is not tracked.

evidence_lines.code: option_number += previous_option_number;

case COAP_OPTION_ETAG:
ret_status = sn_coap_parser_options_parse_multiple_options(handle, packet_data_pptr,
message_left,
&dst_coap_msg_ptr->options_list_ptr->etag_ptr,
(uint16_t *)&dst_coap_msg_ptr->options_list_ptr->etag_len,
COAP_OPTION_ETAG, option_len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: option_number += previous_option_number (line 44) lacks 16-bit overflow detection, letting a crafted packet wrap the option number so the same option is parsed twice. Trigger: a repeated ETAG, LOCATION_QUERY or URI_PATH option reaches the parse_multiple_options calls, which reassign the pointer without checking it is already set, orphaning the earlier allocation. Consequence: the previously allocated buffer is never freed, leaking memory.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  ZFP_ERROR_NULL(cparams->schunk);']}
description: C-blosc2 before 2.9.3 was discovered to contain a NULL pointer dereference via the function zfp_prec_decompress at zfp/blosc2-zfp.c.

code_evidence: Line 6 validates only the cparams pointer itself, not its schunk member; line 13 passes cparams->schunk into blosc2_meta_get without any prior NULL check on that field.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences/forwards a pointer it assumes valid (cparams->schunk) without verifying non-NULL, and the upstream fix adds exactly that guard. This is distinct from a general missing-initialization or integer issue; the weakness is the unchecked NULL pointer.

evidence_lines.code:
ZFP_ERROR_NULL(cparams);
if (blosc2_meta_get(cparams->schunk, "b2nd", &smeta, &smeta_len) < 0) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: cparams is checked for NULL but cparams->schunk is not, so a caller supplying a cparams with a NULL schunk reaches blosc2_meta_get with a NULL pointer argument. commit_msg:
rtmpt: limit the number of iterations in rtmpt_get_amf_length().

This prevents a infinite-loop caused by crafted packets.

Fix: #17813.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['rtmpt_get_amf_txid(tvbuff_t *tvb, gint offset)', '                guint32 itemlen = rtmpt_get_amf_length(tvb, offset);', '                if (remain<itemlen)'], 'added_lines': ['rtmpt_get_amf_txid(tvbuff_t *tvb, gint offset, proto_item* pi)', '                guint32 itemlen = rtmpt_get_amf_length(tvb, offset, pi);', '                if (itemlen == 0 || remain < itemlen)']}
description: Infinite loop in RTMPT protocol dissector in Wireshark 3.6.0 to 3.6.1 and 3.4.0 to 3.4.11 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: remain is the reported length remaining at offset; when remain > 0 the code calls rtmpt_get_amf_length and only rejects the item when remain < itemlen. There is no check that itemlen is nonzero, so a crafted packet yielding itemlen == 0 passes the guard, offset is advanced by zero, and remain is unchanged, leaving the caller's iteration state unable to progress.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the missing nonzero-length constraint lets a zero-length item prevent loop progress, producing an unreachable exit condition. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read: the defect is non-terminating iteration driven by attacker-controlled length, not memory access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard only compares remain against itemlen and never requires a positive item length. Trigger: a crafted RTMPT/AMF packet for which rtmpt_get_amf_length returns 0 while remain > 0. Consequence: offset and remain do not advance, so the surrounding parsing loop can iterate without reaching an exit condition, consuming CPU until the dissector is aborted (DoS).

commit_msg:
gnrc_sixlowpan_iphc: fix packet type confusion in _iphc_encode()

(cherry picked from commit 4a081f86616cb5c9dd0b5d7b286da03285d1652a)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (ptr->type == GNRC_NETTYPE_UNDEF) {', '            /* most likely UDP for now so use that (XXX: extend if extension', '             * headers make problems) */', '            dispatch_size += sizeof(udp_hdr_t);', '            break;  /* nothing special after UDP so quit even if more UNDEF', '                     * come */', '        }', '        else {', '            dispatch_size += ptr->size;', '        }'], 'added_lines': ['        dispatch_size += ptr->size;']}
description: RIOT-OS, an operating system that supports Internet of Things devices, contains a network stack with the ability to process 6LoWPAN frames. Prior to version 2022.10, an attacker can send a crafted frame to the device resulting in a type confusion between IPv6 extension headers and a UDP header. This occurs while encoding a 6LoWPAN IPHC header. The type confusion manifests in an out of bounds write in the packet buffer. The overflow can be used to corrupt other packets and the allocator metadata. Corrupting a pointer will easily lead to denial of service. While carefully manipulating the allocator metadata gives an attacker the possibility to write data to arbitrary locations and thus execute arbitrary code. Version 2022.10 fixes this issue. As a workaround, apply the patches manually.

code_evidence: _iphc_encode() walks the packet snip chain; for any snip whose type is GNRC_NETTYPE_UNDEF it unconditionally assumes the payload is a UDP header and adds sizeof(udp_hdr_t) to dispatch_size, then breaks, instead of using ptr->size.
dispatch_size (plus one) is passed to gnrc_pktbuf_add() to allocate the IPHC dispatch buffer, so the size computed from the assumed UDP type determines the buffer length.

Later, nh is read from the IPv6 header and the next-header loop dispatches on nh; a PROTNUM_UDP value reaches _nhc_udp_encode_snip(), which writes into iphc_hdr[inline_pos] within the allocated dispatch buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function interprets a packet snip of one type (UNDEF, actual size/type unknown) as a udp_hdr_t for sizing, then accesses the same buffer as UDP during encoding, which is exactly the incompatible-type access described by CWE-843. The size mismatch from this type confusion is the cause; the out-of-bounds write is the consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
dispatch = gnrc_pktbuf_add(NULL, NULL, dispatch_size + 1,
GNRC_NETTYPE_SIXLOWPAN);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an UNDEF-typed snip is treated as a UDP header based on GNRC_NETTYPE_UNDEF rather than its actual next-header type. Trigger: a crafted 6LoWPAN frame whose UNDEF snip is not UDP but whose IPv6 nh indicates UDP (or vice versa) makes the allocated dispatch_size inconsistent with the bytes later written by the NHC encoder. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write in the packet buffer, corrupting adjacent packets and allocator metadata, leading to DoS or potentially arbitrary code execution.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/550
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"CorruptImage");'], 'added_lines': ['      {', '        if (color_image != (Image *) NULL)', '          color_image=DestroyImage(color_image);', '        if (color_image_info != (Image *) NULL)', '          color_image_info=DestroyImageInfo(color_image_info);', '        ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"CorruptImage");', '      }']}
description: ImageMagick 7.0.6-1 has a memory leak vulnerability in ReadOneJNGImage in coders\png.c.

code_evidence: Line 89-90: when length exceeds PNG_UINT_31_MAX or the 4-byte chunk type read returns count 0, the code throws a reader exception immediately without releasing resources.

Lines 165-171: color_image_info and color_image are allocated (AcquireMagickMemory/AcquireImage) earlier in the loop; on later iterations a corrupt chunk triggering the line 89-90 throw exits while these handles remain owned by the function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function acquires heap resources whose lifetime ends when the loop aborts, but the abort path omits DestroyImage/DestroyImageInfo, matching CWE-772's missing release of a resource after its effective lifetime. It is not a use-after-free or double-free; the defect is simply unreleased ownership on an error exit.

evidence_lines.code:
if (length > PNG_UINT_31_MAX || count == 0)
ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"CorruptImage");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the early ThrowReaderException path at lines 89-90 unwinds ReadOneJNGImage without destroying color_image or color_image_info that were acquired in prior iterations (lines 165-171). Trigger: a JNG stream containing a valid JDAT/JDAT-derived chunk that allocates the color resources, followed by a chunk whose length exceeds PNG_UINT_31_MAX or whose type read returns count 0. Consequence: the Image and ImageInfo allocations are leaked on each malformed input, enabling memory-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix heap-buffer-overflow in getString

getString is allocating a 4-bytes buffer to store an 'R' and an
8-bit number.

t=malloc(4); /* Rdd */
sprintf(t,"R%d", act->p.RegisterNumber );
return t;

Since up to three digits can be required to store the 8-bit
number, the buffer has to be 5 bytes long.

In this commit we also fix the PUSH_DOUBLE case by dynamically
computing the required buffer size.

This commit fixes #116 (CVE-2018-7867).
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -26,7 +26,7 @@
 		}
 #if 0
 	  case 4: /* REGISTER */
-                t=malloc(4); /* Rdd */
+		t=malloc(5); /* Rddd */
   		sprintf(t,"R%d", act->p.RegisterNumber );
   		return t;
 #endif
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                t=malloc(4); /* Rdd */'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tt=malloc(5); /* Rddd */']}
description: There is a heap-based buffer overflow in the getString function of util/decompile.c in libming 0.4.8 during a RegisterNumber sprintf. A Crafted input will lead to a denial of service attack.

code_evidence: The case 4 branch allocates a fixed 4-byte heap buffer via t=malloc(4) and then writes the formatted string "R%d" into it with sprintf, which performs no bounds checking on the destination.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) fits because sprintf writes beyond the end of the malloc'd buffer. This is a classic heap-buffer-overflow write caused by an undersized allocation, not a read overrun (CWE-125) or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a fixed 4-byte allocation is used for sprintf output whose length depends on act->p.RegisterNumber. When RegisterNumber requires three digits, "R" plus three digits plus the terminating NUL needs 5 bytes, so sprintf writes one byte past the heap allocation, corrupting adjacent heap metadata and enabling a crash/DoS or potentially memory corruption.

commit_msg:
ctx->crypto_send.info is not protected by lock_sock in
do_tls_getsockopt_conf(). A race condition between do_tls_getsockopt_conf()
and error paths of do_tls_setsockopt_conf() may lead to a use-after-free
or null-deref.

More discussion:  https://lore.kernel.org/all/Y/ht6gQL+u6fj3dG@hog/

Fixes: 3c4d7559159b ("tls: kernel TLS support")
Signed-off-by: Hangyu Hua <hbh25y@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230228023344.9623-1-hbh25y@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tlock_sock(sk);', '\t\trelease_sock(sk);', '\t\tlock_sock(sk);', '\t\trelease_sock(sk);', '\t\tlock_sock(sk);', '\t\trelease_sock(sk);', '\t\tlock_sock(sk);', '\t\trelease_sock(sk);', '\t\tlock_sock(sk);', '\t\trelease_sock(sk);', '\t\tlock_sock(sk);', '\t\trelease_sock(sk);', '\t\tlock_sock(sk);', '\t\trelease_sock(sk);', '\t\tlock_sock(sk);', '\t\trelease_sock(sk);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: do_tls_getsockopt in net/tls/tls_main.c in the Linux kernel through 6.2.6 lacks a lock_sock call, leading to a race condition (with a resultant use-after-free or NULL pointer dereference).

code_evidence: do_tls_getsockopt_conf() selects crypto_info/cctx from ctx->crypto_send.info and ctx->tx (or recv/rx) at [20,21,23,24], checks TLS_CRYPTO_INFO_READY(crypto_info) at [26] and returns -EBUSY otherwise.

After that check, each cipher branch copies from cctx->iv and cctx->rec_seq into the user buffer object, e.g. [47,48,49,50,51] for AES-GCM-128 and [70,74] for AES-GCM-256, while holding lock_sock(sk) only around the memcpy at [46,52] and [69,75].
No lock is held between the TLS_CRYPTO_INFO_READY check and the switch on crypto_info->cipher_type (line 35), nor during the container_of derivation at [38,39,40,41].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The observable failure mode supported by the unlocked read of cctx after the readiness check is dereferencing a pointer that may have become NULL or invalid, matching CWE-476. The race is the trigger; the direct weakness is unchecked/unserialized pointer dereference, distinct from a pure missing-lock weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The readiness check on ctx->crypto_send.info and the subsequent switch/container_of/pointer use are not serialized against do_tls_setsockopt_conf() error paths that tear down the context. A concurrent setsockopt failure can free or clear the context after the check, so the memcpy from cctx->iv/cctx->rec_seq dereferences a stale or NULL pointer. Consequence is a kernel crash (NULL deref) or, with a freed object, use-after-free read.

commit_msg:
register_snap_client may return NULL, all the callers
check it, but only print a warning. This will result in
NULL pointer dereference in unregister_snap_client and other
places.

It has always been used like this since v2.6

Reported-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: YueHaibing <yuehaibing@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void __init aarp_proto_init(void)', '\tif (!aarp_dl)', '\tregister_netdevice_notifier(&aarp_notifier);'], 'added_lines': ['int __init aarp_proto_init(void)', '\tint rc;', '', '\tif (!aarp_dl) {', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\t}', '\trc = register_netdevice_notifier(&aarp_notifier);', '\tif (rc) {', '\t\tdel_timer_sync(&aarp_timer);', '\t\tunregister_snap_client(aarp_dl);', '\t}', '\treturn rc;']}
description: In the AppleTalk subsystem in the Linux kernel before 5.1, there is a potential NULL pointer dereference because register_snap_client may return NULL. This will lead to denial of service in net/appletalk/aarp.c and net/appletalk/ddp.c, as demonstrated by unregister_snap_client, aka CID-9804501fa122.

code_evidence: register_snap_client's return value is stored in aarp_dl and checked only by a printk warning; execution continues regardless of the NULL result.
Without an early return, the timer is set up and register_netdevice_notifier is called; the failed aarp_dl value persists for later callers such as unregister_snap_client.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because a checked-but-not-handled NULL pointer is retained and later dereferenced. The printk-only check is the missing constraint; the crash is the consequence, not the cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the NULL return of register_snap_client is not treated as a fatal error, so aarp_proto_init proceeds with aarp_dl unset. Trigger: register_snap_client fails and returns NULL. Consequence: later use of the NULL aarp_dl causes a NULL pointer dereference and denial of service.

commit_msg:
coolkey: Make sure the object ID is unique when filling list

Thanks to oss-fuzz

https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=19208
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* The object ID needs to be unique */', '\tif (coolkey_find_object_by_id(&priv->objects_list, object_id) != NULL) {', '\t\treturn SC_ERROR_INTERNAL;', '\t}']}
description: OpenSC before 0.20.0 has a double free in coolkey_free_private_data because coolkey_add_object in libopensc/card-coolkey.c lacks a uniqueness check.

code_evidence: Line 10 assigns object_id to new_object.id and line 11 sets its length; no check ensures this ID is unique before the object is inserted. Line 23 calls coolkey_add_object_to_list with &new_object; on failure lines 25-26 free new_object.data and null it. Because object_data may be NULL, new_object.data can be uninitialized/unallocated, and duplicate IDs allow the list to hold multiple entries sharing the same data pointer, so the cleanup free at line 25 can release memory already freed for another entry.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the supported consequence is a double free of the same memory address caused by duplicate-ID entries sharing data. This is a distinct double-free issue, not merely a memory leak or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: coolkey_add_object lacks a uniqueness check on object_id, so a duplicate ID can be added to priv->objects_list. Trigger: calling with an already-present object_id and object_data. Consequence: two list entries can reference the same allocated data; freeing one and then the other (or the error-path free at line 25) frees the same address twice, corrupting the heap.

commit_msg:
listdir(): reuse a single buffer to store every file name to display

Allocating a new buffer for each entry is useless.

And as these buffers are allocated on the stack, on systems with a
small stack size, with many entries, the limit can easily be reached,
causing a stack exhaustion and aborting the user session.

Reported by Antonio Morales from the GitHub Security Lab team, thanks!
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            char *alloca_subdir;', '            const size_t sizeof_subdir = PATH_MAX + 1U;', '', '            if ((alloca_subdir = ALLOCA(sizeof_subdir)) == NULL) {', '                goto toomany;', '            }', '            ALLOCA_FREE(alloca_subdir);'], 'added_lines': ['    char *alloca_subdir;', '    size_t sizeof_subdir;', '    sizeof_subdir = PATH_MAX + 1U;', '    if ((alloca_subdir = ALLOCA(sizeof_subdir)) == NULL) {', '        goto toomany;', '    }', '', '    ALLOCA_FREE(alloca_subdir);']}
description: In Pure-FTPd 1.0.49, a stack exhaustion issue was discovered in the listdir function in ls.c.

code_evidence: In the recursive descent loop, each directory entry that satisfies opt_R triggers an ALLOCA(sizeof_subdir) allocation on the stack, where sizeof_subdir is PATH_MAX+1U. The buffer is freed only after the recursive listdir call returns, so stack usage grows with recursion depth and the number of entries processed before unwinding.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function fails to control consumption of the limited stack resource, allocating a buffer per entry without bounding total usage. This is resource exhaustion due to lack of throttling, not a buffer overflow (CWE-121) or memory leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a fresh stack buffer is allocated per recursive entry rather than reused, so stack consumption accumulates across the recursion and directory iteration. Trigger: an attacker-controlled directory tree with many entries, or small stack limits, drives deep recursion. Consequence: stack exhaustion, leading to a crash or aborted user session (availability DoS).

commit_msg:
blk-mq: fix race between timeout and freeing request

Inside timeout handler, blk_mq_tag_to_rq() is called
to retrieve the request from one tag. This way is obviously
wrong because the request can be freed any time and some
fiedds of the request can't be trusted, then kernel oops
might be triggered[1].

Currently wrt. blk_mq_tag_to_rq(), the only special case is
that the flush request can share same tag with the request
cloned from, and the two requests can't be active at the same
time, so this patch fixes the above issue by updating tags->rqs[tag]
with the active request(either flush rq or the request cloned
from) of the tag.

Also blk_mq_tag_to_rq() gets much simplified with this patch.

Given blk_mq_tag_to_rq() is mainly for drivers and the caller must
make sure the request can't be freed, so in bt_for_each() this
helper is replaced with tags->rqs[tag].

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct request *rq = tags->rqs[tag];', '\t/* mq_ctx of flush rq is always cloned from the corresponding req */', '\tstruct blk_flush_queue *fq = blk_get_flush_queue(rq->q, rq->mq_ctx);', '', '\tif (!is_flush_request(rq, fq, tag))', '\t\treturn rq;', '', '\treturn fq->flush_rq;'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn tags->rqs[tag];']}
description: In blk_mq_tag_to_rq in blk-mq.c in the upstream kernel, there is a possible use after free due to a race condition when a request has been previously freed by blk_mq_complete_request. This could lead to local escalation of privilege. Product: Android. Versions: Android kernel. Android ID: A-63083046.

code_evidence: blk_mq_tag_to_rq() reads tags->rqs[tag] into rq without any lock or reference count protecting that slot. It then immediately dereferences rq->q and rq->mq_ctx to obtain the flush queue and calls is_flush_request() on the same rq pointer. Nothing prevents another context (e.g. a completion path freeing the request) from invalidating tags->rqs[tag] between the load and the dereferences.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an unsynchronized read of a shared resource (the tag's request slot) that a concurrent code sequence can modify or free, exactly the improper-synchronization race described by CWE-362. The use-after-free is the consequence of this race, not a separate missing-check weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the tag-to-request lookup trusts the shared tags->rqs[tag] slot while the request can be freed concurrently, so no exclusive access or lifetime guarantee exists. Trigger: a timeout handler calls this function on a tag whose request is being freed by blk_mq_complete_request; the subsequent rq->q / rq->mq_ctx dereference and is_flush_request() operate on freed memory, causing a kernel oops or worse.

commit_msg:
There are two sites that calls queue_work() after the
destroy_workqueue() and lead to possible UAF.

The first site is nci_send_cmd(), which can happen after the
nci_close_device as below

nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev   |  nfc_genl_dev_up
  nci_close_device           |
    flush_workqueue          |
    del_timer_sync           |
  nci_unregister_device      |    nfc_get_device
    destroy_workqueue        |    nfc_dev_up
    nfc_unregister_device    |      nci_dev_up
      device_del             |        nci_open_device
                             |          __nci_request
                             |            nci_send_cmd
                             |              queue_work !!!

Another site is nci_cmd_timer, awaked by the nci_cmd_work from the
nci_send_cmd.

  ...                        |  ...
  nci_unregister_device      |  queue_work
    destroy_workqueue        |
    nfc_unregister_device    |  ...
      device_del             |  nci_cmd_work
                             |  mod_timer
                             |  ...
                             |  nci_cmd_timer
                             |    queue_work !!!

For the above two UAF, the root cause is that the nfc_dev_up can race
between the nci_unregister_device routine. Therefore, this patch
introduce NCI_UNREG flag to easily eliminate the possible race. In
addition, the mutex_lock in nci_close_device can act as a barrier.

Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Fixes: 6a2968aaf50c ("NFC: basic NCI protocol implementation")
Reviewed-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Krzysztof Kozlowski <krzysztof.kozlowski@canonical.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20211116152732.19238-1-linma@zju.edu.cn
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (test_bit(NCI_UNREG, &ndev->flags)) {', '\t\trc = -ENODEV;', '\t\tgoto done;', '\t}']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nci_request in net/nfc/nci/core.c in NFC Controller Interface (NCI) in the Linux kernel. This flaw could allow a local attacker with user privileges to cause a data race problem while the device is getting removed, leading to a privilege escalation problem.

code_evidence: nci_open_device acquires req_lock and checks only NCI_UP; it does not check whether the device is being unregistered, so an open can proceed concurrently with nci_unregister_device's destroy_workqueue.

After the open/init requests, the function sets NCI_UP and runs __nci_request paths (nci_reset_req, nci_init_req, nci_init_complete_req) that ultimately call nci_send_cmd and queue_work, so this sequence can enqueue work after the workqueue is destroyed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent execution over shared ndev state with insufficient synchronization between open and unregister, matching CWE-362. The missing NCI_UNREG guard is the constraint that would prevent the interfering unregister sequence; the UAF is the downstream consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The shared ndev state is protected by req_lock, but nci_unregister_device does not serialize against this open path, so nfc_dev_up can race with device removal. The trigger is a concurrent open during unregister; the consequence is queue_work on a destroyed workqueue, leading to use-after-free of the workqueue/work structures.

commit_msg:
esp: Fix possible buffer overflow in ESP transformation

The maximum message size that can be send is bigger than
the  maximum site that skb_page_frag_refill can allocate.
So it is possible to write beyond the allocated buffer.

Fix this by doing a fallback to COW in that case.

v2:

Avoid get get_order() costs as suggested by Linus Torvalds.

Fixes: cac2661c53f3 ("esp4: Avoid skb_cow_data whenever possible")
Fixes: 03e2a30f6a27 ("esp6: Avoid skb_cow_data whenever possible")
Reported-by: valis <sec@valis.email>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned int allocsz;', '', '\tallocsz = ALIGN(skb->data_len + tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES);', '\tif (allocsz > ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE)', '\t\tgoto cow;']}
description: A heap buffer overflow flaw was found in IPsec ESP transformation code in net/ipv4/esp4.c and net/ipv6/esp6.c. This flaw allows a local attacker with a normal user privilege to overwrite kernel heap objects and may cause a local privilege escalation threat.

code_evidence: When the cloned/tailroom path is not taken and nr_frags is available, allocsize is computed from tailen alone (line 26), then skb_page_frag_refill(allocsize, ...) allocates a page fragment sized for that value. The trailer is written at page_address(page) + pfrag->offset (line 34) and the descriptor records tailen (line 38); pfrag->offset advances by allocsize (line 40). Nothing constrains the requested allocation against the maximum fragment size skb_page_frag_refill can serve.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes trailer data (esp_output_fill_trailer at line 35) into a page fragment sized by an unchecked allocation, allowing the write to exceed the intended buffer. This matches CWE-787; it is a direct out-of-bounds write rather than merely an integer overflow, since the write length and target address are misaligned with the allocated object.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation request is derived from tailen without bounding it to ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE, so skb_page_frag_refill may return a smaller fragment than requested. Trigger: a message whose trailer size exceeds the allocatable fragment size reaches this branch, and esp_output_fill_trailer writes tailen bytes at the fragment offset. Consequence: a heap out-of-bounds write beyond the allocated page fragment, enabling memory corruption and potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg: Add checking to make sure key is present in all cases. Explicitly set `validSigAlgo` to zero with comment to clarify the default assumption.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            int validSigAlgo = 0;', '                validSigAlgo = ssl->peerEd25519KeyPresent;', '                validSigAlgo = ssl->peerEd448KeyPresent;', '                validSigAlgo = ssl->peerEccDsaKeyPresent;', '                validSigAlgo = ssl->peerFalconKeyPresent;', '                validSigAlgo = ssl->peerFalconKeyPresent;', '            }', '        #endif', '', '                ret = SIG_VERIFY_E;', '                goto exit_dcv;'], 'added_lines': ['            int validSigAlgo;', '            /* Assume invalid unless signature algo matches the key provided */', '            validSigAlgo = 0;', '                validSigAlgo = (ssl->peerEd25519Key != NULL) &&', '                                                     ssl->peerEd25519KeyPresent;', '                validSigAlgo = (ssl->peerEd448Key != NULL) &&', '                                                       ssl->peerEd448KeyPresent;', '                validSigAlgo = (ssl->peerEccDsaKey != NULL) &&', '                                                      ssl->peerEccDsaKeyPresent;', '                validSigAlgo = (ssl->peerFalconKey != NULL) &&', '                                                      ssl->peerFalconKeyPresent;', '                validSigAlgo = (ssl->peerFalconKey != NULL) &&', '                                                      ssl->peerFalconKeyPresent;', '            }', '        #endif', '                ERROR_OUT(SIG_VERIFY_E, exit_dcv);']}
description: In wolfSSL before 5.2.0, certificate validation may be bypassed during attempted authentication by a TLS 1.3 client to a TLS 1.3 server. This occurs when the sig_algo field differs between the certificate_verify message and the certificate message.

code_evidence: validSigAlgo is initialized to 0, then set only by comparing the decoded args->sigAlgo against a specific algorithm constant; the certificate-verify message's sig_algo is the sole selector.

For ECC, validSigAlgo is assigned merely from ssl->peerEccDsaKeyPresent when args->sigAlgo equals ecc_dsa_sa_algo, without checking that the algorithm matches the key type actually established in the certificate message.

The guard rejects only when no branch matched or the key-present flag was clear, so a sig_algo that differs from the certificate's key type can still leave the flow proceeding to signature verification.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function implements the TLS 1.3 certificate_verify validation step, and its sig_algo check does not correctly validate the certificate's key algorithm, matching CWE-295. It is not merely a signature-verification failure; the weakness is in the certificate/algorithm validation logic itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the certificate_verify signature algorithm is validated against a per-algorithm key-present flag rather than against the algorithm of the peer key from the certificate message. Trigger: a TLS 1.3 client sends a sig_algo different from the certificate's key algorithm. Consequence: the algorithm-mismatch check can be bypassed, allowing certificate validation to be skipped during authentication.

commit_msg: fix inconsistent identation
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t  exit(EXIT_FAILURE);'], 'added_lines': ['    exit(EXIT_FAILURE);']}
description: Divide By Zero error in tiffcrop in libtiff 4.4.0 allows attackers to cause a denial-of-service via a crafted tiff file. For users that compile libtiff from sources, the fix is available with commit f3a5e010.

code_evidence: Lines 102-103 compute owidth and olength via TIFFhowmany(iwidth, page->cols) and TIFFhowmany(ilength, page->rows), dividing by user-supplied page->cols and page->rows with no prior check that they are nonzero in this branch.
Lines 122-126 only guard against owidth or olength being zero after the division; they do not prevent a zero divisor, and they call exit(EXIT_FAILURE) instead of returning an error.

Lines 131-132 and 143-146 further divide iwidth and ilength by owidth and olength in TIFFhowmany calls; if owidth or olength were zero these would also divide by zero, but the earlier exit prevents reaching them.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a division whose divisor is an unvalidated user-influenced value, directly matching CWE-369 (divide by zero). The zero-result check at lines 122-126 addresses a different condition (zero quotient) and does not constrain the divisor, so it does not mitigate this weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
owidth  = TIFFhowmany(iwidth, page->cols);
olength = TIFFhowmany(ilength, page->rows);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: page->cols or page->rows, read from attacker-controlled TIFF/page settings, can be zero, and TIFFhowmany divides by them without a zero check in the PAGE_MODE_ROWSCOLS branch. Trigger: a crafted input selects rows/cols mode with a zero divisor. Supported consequence: division by zero and process termination, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
hci_chan can be created in 2 places: hci_loglink_complete_evt() if
it is an AMP hci_chan, or l2cap_conn_add() otherwise. In theory,
Only AMP hci_chan should be removed by a call to
hci_disconn_loglink_complete_evt(). However, the controller might mess
up, call that function, and destroy an hci_chan which is not initiated
by hci_loglink_complete_evt().

This patch adds a verification that the destroyed hci_chan must have
been init'd by hci_loglink_complete_evt().
