diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\thchan->amp = true;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.12.4, net/bluetooth/hci_event.c has a use-after-free when destroying an hci_chan, aka CID-5c4c8c954409. This leads to writing an arbitrary value.

code_evidence: hci_loglink_complete_evt() creates an hci_chan via hci_chan_create(hcon) at line 13 and stores it in hchan; line 16 sets only its handle. The function never marks the channel as AMP-originated (the patch adds hchan->amp = true). The channel is handed to l2cap_logical_cfm() at line 23 and the connection is held at line 24, so the hchan remains reachable by l2cap/AMP teardown paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function creates and publishes an hci_chan that can be freed by a later disconnection event while still referenced by l2cap/ACL send paths, so the code supports CWE-416 (use after free). The missing type marker is the constraint that allows the wrong teardown; this is not merely a NULL-pointer or type-confusion issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the logical-link-complete event creates a non-AMP-typed hci_chan that later event processing can free through hci_disconn_loglink_complete_evt(), while other paths (l2cap_send_cmd/hci_send_acl) keep using the same hchan. Trigger: a controller/protocol sequence that delivers a disconnection for a channel not created by the loglink path. Consequence: use-after-free of the hci_chan, leading to KASAN bad access and arbitrary-value write.

commit_msg:
Fixed possible NULL pointer dereference.

Thanks to Jinsheng Ba <bajinsheng@u.nus.edu> for the report and patch.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            OFStandard::strlcpy(s, aString, bufsize);'], 'added_lines': ['            if (ec == EC_Normal)', '                OFStandard::strlcpy(s, aString, bufsize);']}
description: DCMTK through 3.6.6 does not handle string copy properly. Sending specific requests to the dcmqrdb program, it would query its database and copy the result even if the result is null, which can incur a head-based overflow. An attacker can use it to launch a DoS attack.

code_evidence: ec is set by obj->search(t, stack); stack.top() is then unconditionally cast and assigned to elem before any validity check.
In the else branch, elem->getString(aString) may fail and leave aString unset/NULL, yet strlcpy(s, aString, bufsize) is called unconditionally without checking the returned condition.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked failure path passes a possibly NULL source pointer into strlcpy, which dereferences it; this matches CWE-476. The separate elem NULL guard at line 10 shows the code handles one pointer but not the string pointer, distinguishing this from an out-of-bounds copy.

evidence_lines.code:
ec =  elem->getString(aString);
OFStandard::strlcpy(s, aString, bufsize);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of getString is ignored, so when it fails aString may be NULL and is passed to strlcpy as the source. Trigger: a request whose element is present but getString returns an error. The supported consequence is a NULL source dereference during string copy, causing a crash/DoS.

commit_msg: Bug 699659: Don't just assume an object is a t_(a)struct
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if (op[-1].value.pstruct != 0x00) {'], 'added_lines': ['            if ((r_has_type(&op[-1], t_struct) || r_has_type(&op[-1], t_astruct)) && op[-1].value.pstruct != 0x00) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in Artifex Ghostscript before 9.24. A type confusion in "ztype" could be used by remote attackers able to supply crafted PostScript to crash the interpreter or possibly have unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: check_op(2) only verifies two stack operands exist, then line 12 reads op[-1].value.pstruct without confirming the operand's type. The union field value.pstruct is only meaningful for t_struct/t_astruct; for other ref types this reinterprets unrelated union storage. That pointer is then passed to gs_object_type/gs_struct_type_name_string at lines 14-15.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading a union member appropriate only for t_struct/t_astruct from an unverified ref is incorrect type conversion/interpretation, matching CWE-704; the missing r_has_type guard is the direct defect, distinct from a mere null check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code treats op[-1] as a structure without a type check, reading value.pstruct from an arbitrary ref. Trigger: crafted PostScript supplies a non-struct operand where a struct name is expected. Consequence: type confusion feeds an invalid pointer to gs_object_type, risking interpreter crash or unspecified impact.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12894/In lookup_bytestring(), take the length of the byte string into account.

Otherwise, if, in our search of the hash table, we come across a byte
string that's shorter than the string we're looking for, we'll search
past the end of the string in the hash table.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Forcepoint's security
researchers Otto Airamo & Antti Levomäki.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).

commit_msg:
fix autofs/afs/etc. magic mountpoint breakage

We end up trying to kfree() nd.last.name on open("/mnt/tmp", O_CREAT)
if /mnt/tmp is an autofs direct mount.  The reason is that nd.last_type
is bogus here; we want LAST_BIND for everything of that kind and we
get LAST_NORM left over from finding parent directory.

So make sure that it *is* set properly; set to LAST_BIND before
doing ->follow_link() - for normal symlinks it will be changed
by __vfs_follow_link() and everything else needs it set that way.

Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tnd->last_type = LAST_BIND;']}
description: The __do_follow_link function in fs/namei.c in the Linux kernel before 2.6.33 does not properly handle the last pathname component during use of certain filesystems, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (incorrect free operations and system crash) via an open system call.

code_evidence: __do_follow_link invokes the filesystem's follow_link at line 13, then reads the resulting link via nd_get_link at line 16. When the link is NULL and nd->last_type equals LAST_BIND, it calls force_reval_path and path_put at lines 20-23. The function relies on nd->last_type being correctly established before follow_link; nothing in this function resets it, so stale LAST_NORM from parent lookup is trusted here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is an erroneous free followed by later use of the affected nameidata state, matching CWE-416's use-after-free: the crash stems from freeing/reusing memory that remains referenced. It is not merely a type-confusion or null-dereference issue, since the defect manifests as an invalid free/use sequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the last pathname component type is not normalized to LAST_BIND before follow_link, so a stale LAST_NORM persists for autofs/afs magic mountpoints. Trigger: open("/mnt/tmp", O_CREAT) on such a mountpoint makes the follow_link path see the wrong type and take the wrong branch, leading to incorrect free operations on nd.last.name and a kernel crash (DoS).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsize_t read_pos = consumed * subbuf_size + buf->bytes_consumed;'], 'added_lines': ['\tsize_t read_pos = (consumed * subbuf_size + buf->bytes_consumed)', '\t\t\t% (n_subbufs * subbuf_size);']}
description: An out of bounds (OOB) memory access flaw was found in the Linux kernel in relay_file_read_start_pos in kernel/relay.c in the relayfs. This flaw could allow a local attacker to crash the system or leak kernel internal information.

code_evidence: Line 6 reduces consumed modulo n_subbufs, but line 7 computes read_pos from consumed*subbuf_size + bytes_consumed without bounding it to the ring size. read_subbuf = read_pos / subbuf_size (line 8) can therefore index buf->padding beyond the allocated array on line 9, and the returned read_pos later drives copy_to_user from buf->start + read_start.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function derives an index and read offset that can exceed the intended buffer, then reads buf->padding and exposes the offset to a later copy from buf->start. This is a read past the end of an intended buffer, matching CWE-125; the missing modulo is the cause, not merely an integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: read_pos is not reduced modulo the total buffer size, so when bytes_consumed pushes the offset past the last subbuf, read_subbuf exceeds the valid subbuf range. Trigger: a concurrent softirq writer advances bytes_consumed while relay_file_read_avail computes the position. Consequence: buf->padding is read out of bounds and the returned offset yields an out-of-bounds read from buf->start during copy_to_user, crashing the system or leaking kernel memory.

description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0044.

code_evidence: When 'infercase' and 'ignorecase' are active, the function computes char_len by walking str_arg with MB_PTR_ADV until NUL; str may point to a caller-owned buffer rather than a heap allocation sized for the transform.

The resulting str is passed directly to ins_compl_add without any allocated buffer or bounds check, so an inconsistency between the multibyte-derived lengths and the actual buffer size can lead to an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is an out-of-bounds write into a heap-allocated completion buffer driven by unvalidated multibyte length calculations, which matches CWE-122 (heap-based buffer overflow). evidence_lines.code: return ins_compl_add(str, len, fname, NULL, NULL, dir, flags, FALSE);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: multibyte character counts (char_len/compl_char_len) are derived by scanning and passed to ins_compl_infercase_gettext, which uses them to write into a buffer whose size is not validated against those counts. commit_msg:
Trap for overly large input to XmlRPCPP which could cause problems with int <-> size_t conversions.

 - In XmlRpcClient, XmlRpcServerConnection and XmlRpcSocket, recognize when incoming or outgoing data is too large, generate an error and discard the data when practical.
 - Use the safe strtol() rather than atoi() to decode an incoming content-length header, and generate an error if the length is invalid or too large.
 - In XmlRpcUtil, prevent attempts to parse overly large XML input.
 - Add tests where they can reasonably be inserted into existing test routines.

Although this fix could be cleaner the update is written to make the update ABI compatible.

This fix addresses CVE-2020-16124 / Integer overflow in ros_comm.

Signed-off-by: Sid Faber <sid.faber@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (xml.length() > size_t(__INT_MAX__)) return std::string();']}
description: Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability in the XML RPC library of OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages allows unauthenticated network traffic to cause unexpected behavior. This issue affects: OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages Noetic and prior versions. Fixed in https://github.com/ros/ros_comm/pull/2065.

code_evidence: Line 4 compares *offset (int) against int(xml.length()), casting the size_t length to a signed int; when xml.length() exceeds INT_MAX the cast wraps to a negative value, so the bounds check can pass incorrectly.
The loop increments size_t pos while appending to s (lines 15-16), then line 17 stores pos back into *offset as int(pos), truncating/wrapping the offset when the scanned position exceeds INT_MAX.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe size_t-to-int conversions on lines 4 and 17 are integer overflow/wraparound operations whose results feed index and offset logic, matching CWE-190. A pure out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) would be the consequence, not the root cause fixed here.

evidence_lines.code:
if (*offset >= int(xml.length())) return std::string();
size_t pos = *offset;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: signed int is used for the offset and for a cast of the string length, so size_t-to-int conversions overflow for large XML input. Trigger: an unauthenticated peer supplies XML whose length or parsed tag position exceeds INT_MAX. Consequence: the bounds check is bypassed and *offset wraps negative, corrupting subsequent parsing logic and enabling out-of-range or resource-exhausting reads.

code_evidence: res.clear() empties the String; the loop over in.elements_obj() only appends when an element exists. If in is empty, res remains empty, yet line 15 calls res.back() to test for ':' before any size check. The patch adds !res.empty() before back().

commit_msg: KaxBlockInternal: check EBML lace sizes against available buffer space
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            if (!FrameSize || (static_cast<uint32>(FrameSize + SizeRead) > LastBufferSize))', '              throw SafeReadIOCallback::EndOfStreamX(SizeRead);', '              if (!FrameSize || (static_cast<uint32>(FrameSize + SizeRead) > LastBufferSize))', '                throw SafeReadIOCallback::EndOfStreamX(SizeRead);']}
description: The KaxInternalBlock::ReadData function in libMatroska before 1.4.4 allows context-dependent attackers to obtain sensitive information from process heap memory via crafted EBML lacing, which triggers an invalid memory access.

code_evidence: In LACING_EBML, FrameSize is decoded from attacker-controlled EBML data via ReadCodedSizeValue without checking it against LastBufferSize; LastBufferSize is then decremented by FrameSize + SizeRead.
The per-frame loop accumulates FrameSize with ReadCodedSizeSignedValue and likewise subtracts from LastBufferSize with no bound check, so SizeList entries can exceed the actual buffer.
The subsequent loop allocates DataBuffer(BufferStart + Mem.GetPosition(), SizeList[Index]) and calls Mem.Skip(SizeList[Index]) using these unchecked sizes, reading beyond the block buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The decoded lace sizes drive DataBuffer construction and Skip operations outside the intended block buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The added checks in the patch confirm the missing bound constraint; the weakness is the unchecked size leading to out-of-bounds reads.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: EBML lace sizes are trusted without verifying FrameSize + SizeRead against the remaining buffer space. A crafted lace size makes SizeList entries exceed the buffer, and the frame-construction loop then reads past the allocated block data, exposing heap memory or causing an invalid access.

description: An error in the lha_read_file_header_1() function (archive_read_support_format_lha.c) in libarchive 3.2.2 allows remote attackers to trigger an out-of-bounds read memory access and subsequently cause a crash via a specially crafted archive.

description: A vulnerability was found in GNOME gvdb. It has been classified as critical. This affects the function gvdb_table_write_contents_async of the file gvdb-builder.c. The manipulation leads to use after free. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The name of the patch is d83587b2a364eb9a9a53be7e6a708074e252de14. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier VDB-216789 was assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: Line 21 creates a GString str; line 22 passes it to g_string_free_to_bytes, which frees the GString and returns a GBytes retaining the underlying buffer. Line 29 then dereferences str->str and str->len after str has been freed.
The GBytes bytes from line 25 is the valid owner of the serialized data and is held in WriteContentsData; line 33 unrefs it after the async call, showing bytes is the intended live source, not str.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function dereferences a pointer to memory freed earlier in the same function, and the freed data is then passed to an asynchronous operation. This is a genuine use-after-free rather than a double-free or uninitialized read: the object is freed at line 22 and reused at line 29.

evidence_lines.code:
data = write_contents_data_new (bytes, file);
g_bytes_unref (bytes);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code reads str->str and str->len after g_string_free_to_bytes(str) has freed the GString. Trigger: any call to gvdb_table_write_contents_async reaches line 29, dereferencing the freed str to obtain a data pointer and length passed to g_file_replace_contents_async. Consequence: use-after-free of the GString header, yielding stale or invalid data (the saved file is empty) and potential memory-safety impact.

commit_msg:
Handling zero byte characters inside RegExp pattern strings.

Fixed heap-buffer-overflow in RegExp.prototype.source.
This closes #168 issue on Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    size_t      brackets;', '    if (!brackets) {', '    text->length = text->length + brackets;'], 'added_lines': ['    size_t      brackets, zeros;', '    zeros = 0;', '', "            if (p == end || *p != '\\0') {", '                break;', '            }', '', '            /* Fall through. */', '', "        case '\\0':", '            zeros++;', '            break;', '    if (!brackets && !zeros) {', '    text->length = text->length + brackets + zeros * nxt_length("\\\\u0000");', '', "            if (*p != '\\0') {", '                break;', '            }', '', '            /* Fall through. */', '', "        case '\\0':", '            dst = nxt_cpymem(dst, "\\\\u0000", 6);', '            continue;']}
description: njs through 0.3.1, used in NGINX, has a heap-based buffer over-read in nxt_utf8_decode in nxt/nxt_utf8.c.

code_evidence: In the first scan, case '\\' increments p without checking whether p has reached end; if the backslash is the last byte, p becomes end and the loop exits with no bounds violation yet, but the escape is not accounted for.
The escape decision uses only brackets: if no unbalanced ']' is found, the function returns NXT_OK without allocating or rewriting, so a trailing backslash is never validated.

The second scan writes into the allocated buffer; case '\\' copies *p and advances p, then checks p == end and goto done. Because the backslash case bypasses the bounds guard that the loop condition provides, p++ can move past end before *dst++ = *p is executed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences p after incrementing it beyond end in the backslash branch, which is a read past the intended buffer (CWE-125). This is an out-of-bounds read, not an out-of-bounds write, because the offending operation is the dereference of *p for copying.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When the pattern ends with an unescaped backslash, the first pass increments p past end and the escape count omits any extra space. If brackets is nonzero, allocation is sized without accounting for the trailing escape, and the second pass reads *p after p was advanced to end, dereferencing one byte past the input buffer.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['unsigned int GetU32LE (int nPos, bool *pbSuccess)', '            if ( nPos < 0 || nPos + 3 >= m_nLen )'], 'added_lines': ['unsigned int GetU32LE (const unsigned int& nPos, bool *pbSuccess)', '            if ( m_nLen < 4 || nPos > (m_nLen - 4) )']}
description: Onlyoffice Document Server v6.0.0 and below and Core 6.1.0.26 and below were discovered to contain a heap overflow via the component DesktopEditor/fontengine/fontconverter/FontFileBase.h.

code_evidence: Bounds check uses signed nPos and the condition nPos + 3 >= m_nLen, which permits nPos == m_nLen - 4 only when no overflow occurs; with a large positive nPos the addition nPos + 3 can wrap, bypassing the check.
The check is followed by four unchecked reads m_sFile[nPos+3], [nPos+2], [nPos+1], [nPos+0]; if the check is bypassed these index past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs out-of-bounds memory access due to a faulty length check, but the operations are reads (indexing m_sFile), not writes past the buffer. CWE-787 specifically requires writing past the end; the evidence here supports an out-of-bounds read, so the target CWE is not directly supported.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an insufficient bounds check that relies on signed arithmetic and can overflow when nPos is large, allowing the subsequent reads to access m_sFile beyond m_nLen. The supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read of heap memory, not a write.

commit_msg:
Fix a bug in the verifier's scalar32_min_max_*() functions which leads to
incorrect tracking of 32 bit bounds for the simulation of and/or/xor bitops.
When both the src & dst subreg is a known constant, then the assumption is
that scalar_min_max_*() will take care to update bounds correctly. However,
this is not the case, for example, consider a register R2 which has a tnum
of 0xffffffff00000000, meaning, lower 32 bits are known constant and in this
case of value 0x00000001. R2 is then and'ed with a register R3 which is a
64 bit known constant, here, 0x100000002.

What can be seen in line '10:' is that 32 bit bounds reach an invalid state
where {u,s}32_min_value > {u,s}32_max_value. The reason is scalar32_min_max_*()
delegates 32 bit bounds updates to scalar_min_max_*(), however, that really
only takes place when both the 64 bit src & dst register is a known constant.
Given scalar32_min_max_*() is intended to be designed as closely as possible
to scalar_min_max_*(), update the 32 bit bounds in this situation through
__mark_reg32_known() which will set all {u,s}32_{min,max}_value to the correct
constant, which is 0x00000000 after the fix (given 0x00000001 & 0x00000002 in
32 bit space). This is possible given var32_off already holds the final value
as dst_reg->var_off is updated before calling scalar32_min_max_*().

Before fix, invalid tracking of R2:

  [...]

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* Assuming scalar64_min_max_and will be called so its safe', '\t * to skip updating register for known 32-bit case.', '\t */', '\tif (src_known && dst_known)', ''], 'added_lines': ['\tif (src_known && dst_known) {', '\t\t__mark_reg32_known(dst_reg, var32_off.value);', '\t}']}
description: The eBPF ALU32 bounds tracking for bitwise ops (AND, OR and XOR) in the Linux kernel did not properly update 32-bit bounds, which could be turned into out of bounds reads and writes in the Linux kernel and therefore, arbitrary code execution. This issue was fixed via commit 049c4e13714e ("bpf: Fix alu32 const subreg bound tracking on bitwise operations") (v5.13-rc4) and backported to the stable kernels in v5.12.4, v5.11.21, and v5.10.37. The AND/OR issues were introduced by commit 3f50f132d840 ("bpf: Verifier, do explicit ALU32 bounds tracking") (5.7-rc1) and the XOR variant was introduced by 2921c90d4718 ("bpf:Fix a verifier failure with xor") ( 5.10-rc1).

code_evidence: Lines 4-6 derive src_known/dst_known from tnum_subreg_is_const and capture var32_off from the destination subregister.
Lines 9-10 return early when both subregisters are known constants, skipping any update of the 32-bit bounds.
Lines 11-12, the normal path, set u32_min/max from var32_off and min(); this path is bypassed by the early return.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale 32-bit bounds cause the verifier to misjudge register ranges, enabling subsequent memory accesses outside the intended buffer, i.e., an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The root cause is missing bound update, but the supported consequence is memory corruption via accepted OOB writes, matching the target.

evidence_lines.code:
if (src_known && dst_known)
return;

dst_reg->u32_min_value = var32_off.value;
dst_reg->u32_max_value = min(dst_reg->u32_max_value, umax_val);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When both subregisters are known constants, the early return leaves dst_reg's {u,s}32_min/max_value stale instead of matching the actual 32-bit constant. The verifier then tracks inconsistent 32-bit bounds (min > max), so later operations may accept a range wider than the true value. This incorrect bound tracking can let the verifier approve out-of-bounds memory accesses in JITed eBPF programs.

commit_msg:
Use correct origin when prompting for proxy authentication.

Since M49, Chrome has been prompting for proxy authentication
credentials using the target origin instead of the origin of the proxy
server. Even if the proxy origin was displayed correctly, a mischievous
network operator could still spoof the proxy server origin. To mitigate
these problems, this CL:

* Fixes the origin used in the proxy authentication login prompt to use
  the origin of the proxy server.

* Indicate if the proxy server connection is insecure.

* Always throw up an interstitial and clear the omnibox when showing a
  proxy auth prompt.

* Use the correct origin when saving proxy authentication credentials.

commit_msg:
Masking direction as indicated via mask_to_left is considered to be
calculated once and then used to derive pointer limits. Thus, this
needs to be placed into bpf_sanitize_info instead so we can pass it
to sanitize_ptr_alu() call after the pointer move. Piotr noticed a
corner case where the off reg causes masking direction change which
then results in an incorrect final aux->alu_limit.

Fixes: 7fedb63a8307 ("bpf: Tighten speculative pointer arithmetic mask")
Reported-by: Piotr Krysiuk <piotras@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Reviewed-by: Piotr Krysiuk <piotras@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\terr = retrieve_ptr_limit(ptr_reg, off_reg, &alu_limit, opcode);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!commit_window) {', '\t\tif (!tnum_is_const(off_reg->var_off) &&', '\t\t    (off_reg->smin_value < 0) != (off_reg->smax_value < 0))', '\t\t\treturn REASON_BOUNDS;', '', '\t\tinfo->mask_to_left = (opcode == BPF_ADD &&  off_is_neg) ||', '\t\t\t\t     (opcode == BPF_SUB && !off_is_neg);', '\t}', '', '\terr = retrieve_ptr_limit(ptr_reg, &alu_limit, info->mask_to_left);']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 5.12.7 enforces incorrect limits for pointer arithmetic operations, aka CID-bb01a1bba579. This can be abused to perform out-of-bounds reads and writes in kernel memory, leading to local privilege escalation to root. In particular, there is a corner case where the off reg causes a masking direction change, which then results in an incorrect final aux->alu_limit.

code_evidence: The function derives off_is_imm and off_is_neg from off_reg, and opcode from the instruction, but before the fix these values were passed directly to retrieve_ptr_limit without first fixing the masking direction; the direction could change depending on the offset register.
In the speculative path the code jumps to do_sim, and retrieve_ptr_limit computes alu_limit from ptr_reg, off_reg and opcode. An incorrect limit therefore flows into the ALU sanitation state.

The corrected logic records mask_to_left in info and reuses info->aux.alu_limit, showing that the limit used for masking must be stable across the pointer move. If it is not, the sanitization mask can be wrong, and the masked pointer arithmetic can reach beyond the intended object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the incorrect pointer-arithmetic limit lets the sanitized pointer address memory outside the intended buffer, and the stated impact is out-of-bounds reads/writes. The defect is a missing constraint on the masking direction, not merely a stack or logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the masking direction, and hence the pointer limit, was recomputed from the offset register and opcode, so a non-constant offset whose sign range spans zero could flip the direction and produce an incorrect alu_limit. Trigger: a BPF program performing pointer arithmetic with such an offset register. Consequence: insufficient masking leaves the pointer beyond bounds, enabling out-of-bounds reads/writes in kernel memory.

commit_msg:
Bug 701118: Limit size of begin layer nodes in display list.

The size of the begin layer node depends on the size of the layer
name. That name may be a string from the page's property resources,
and is only bounded by memory when parsed by lex_string(). The
layer name may cause a display node to be larger than the maximum
size allowed. This condition is now checked for.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tint max = SIZE_IN_NODES(MAX_NODE_SIZE) - size;', '\t\tif (SIZE_IN_NODES(private_data_len) > max)', '\t\t\tfz_throw(ctx, FZ_ERROR_GENERIC, "Private data too large to pack into display list node");']}
description: Artifex MuPDF 1.15.0 has a heap-based buffer overflow in fz_append_display_node located at fitz/list-device.c, allowing remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted PDF file. This occurs with a large BDC property name that overflows the allocated size of a display list node.

code_evidence: When private_data is non-NULL, private_off is set to the current size and size is increased by SIZE_IN_NODES(private_data_len) with no bound check against MAX_NODE_SIZE.
node.size stores the unbounded size, then node_ptr[path_off] and fz_pack_path use path_size derived from the same size, so an oversized private_data_len yields an oversized node.
The memcpy at line 449 copies private_data_len bytes into out_private, which is located at node_ptr[private_off] within the fixed-size fz_display_node, writing past the node's intended buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function performs a memcpy into a fixed-size node buffer at an offset computed from an unchecked length, writing past the buffer. This is a direct out-of-bounds write, not merely an integer overflow or a read past bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: private_data_len (a layer/BDC property name length) is added to size without enforcing MAX_NODE_SIZE, so the packed node exceeds its fixed allocation. Trigger: a crafted PDF with a large BDC property name reaches fz_append_display_node with a large private_data_len. Consequence: the memcpy of private_data into node_ptr[private_off] writes beyond the allocated display node, a heap-based out-of-bounds write.

   smb3_get_tree+0x1d5/0x300
   vfs_get_tree+0x41/0xf0
   path_mount+0x9b3/0xdd0
   __x64_sys_mount+0x190/0x1d0
   do_syscall_64+0x35/0x80
   entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x46/0xb0

The UAF is because:

 mount(pid: 921)               | cifsd(pid: 923)
-------------------------------|-------------------------------
                               | cifs_demultiplex_thread
SMB2_negotiate                 |
 cifs_send_recv                |
  compound_send_recv           |
   smb_send_rqst               |
    wait_for_response          |
     wait_event_state      [1] |
                               |  standard_receive3
                               |   cifs_handle_standard
                               |    handle_mid
                               |     mid->resp_buf = buf;  [2]
                               |     dequeue_mid           [3]
     KILL the process      [4] |
    resp_iov[i].iov_base = buf |
 free_rsp_buf              [5] |
                               |   is_network_name_deleted [6]
                               |   callback

1. After send request to server, wait the response until
    mid->mid_state != SUBMITTED;
2. Receive response from server, and set it to mid;
3. Set the mid state to RECEIVED;
4. Kill the process, the mid state already RECEIVED, get 0;
5. Handle and release the negotiate response;
6. UAF.

It can be easily reproduce with add some delay in [3] - [6].

Only sync call has the problem since async call's callback is
executed in cifsd process.

Add an extra state to mark the mid state to READY before wakeup the
waitter, then it can get the resp safely.

Fixes: ec637e3ffb6b ("[CIFS] Avoid extra large buffer allocation (and memcpy) in cifs_readpages")
Reviewed-by: Paulo Alcantara (SUSE) <pc@manguebit.com>
Signed-off-by: Zhang Xiaoxu <zhangxiaoxu5@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Steve French <stfrench@microsoft.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t(!(midQ->mid_state == MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED)) ||', '\t\t(midQ->mid_state == MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED) &&', '\t\t\tif (midQ->mid_state == MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED) {', '\tif (out_buf == NULL || midQ->mid_state != MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t(!(midQ->mid_state == MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED ||', '\t\t   midQ->mid_state == MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED)) ||', '\t\t(midQ->mid_state == MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED ||', '\t\t midQ->mid_state == MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED) &&', '\t\t\tif (midQ->mid_state == MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED ||', '\t\t\t    midQ->mid_state == MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED) {', '\tif (out_buf == NULL || midQ->mid_state != MID_RESPONSE_READY) {']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in smb2_is_status_io_timeout() in CIFS in the Linux Kernel. After CIFS transfers response data to a system call, there are still local variable points to the memory region, and if the system call frees it faster than CIFS uses it, CIFS will access a free memory region, leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: wait_event_interruptible wakes when mid_state is no longer MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED, which includes the transient MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED state set once the demultiplex thread stores resp_buf but before the response is fully ready.
The -ERESTARTSYS branch only treats MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED as cancelable, so a signal arriving while mid_state is MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED skips send_cancel and falls through.

wait_for_response's cancellation path likewise only checks MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED, so the mid callback is not redirected to release_mid for MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED, leaving the response buffer lifecycle tied to the racing waiter.
cifs_sync_mid_result then proceeds and the check accepts MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED, after which resp_buf is read; if the interrupted caller frees the buffer first, this is a use-after-free.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function reads midQ->resp_buf after the buffer may have been freed by the interrupted caller; the missing READY-state gate is the flawed lifetime synchronization enabling the dangling reference.

evidence_lines.code:
rc = wait_event_interruptible(server->response_q,
(!(midQ->mid_state == MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED)) ||
((server->tcpStatus != CifsGood) &&
(server->tcpStatus != CifsNew)));

if ((rc == -ERESTARTSYS) &&
(midQ->mid_state == MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED) &&
((server->tcpStatus == CifsGood) ||
(server->tcpStatus == CifsNew))) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the waiter treats MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED as a completed reply and the cancellation checks do not recognize that state, so the interrupt path can return while the demultiplex thread still owns/uses the mid response. Trigger: a signal interrupts the blocking send/receive after the response is stored but before it is marked ready; the caller frees the buffer and the receive path later dereferences resp_buf. Consequence: use-after-free read, leading to crash/DoS and potential memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Fix missing sparse matrix crash.

Calling a sparse matrix op with no matrix currently causes a crash.  Here we check and
return a non-ok status.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 476379116
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (!TensorShapeUtils::IsScalar(input_t.shape())) {', '    return errors::InvalidArgument(', '        "Invalid input matrix: Shape must be rank 0 but is rank ",', '        input_t.dims());', '  }']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. An input `sparse_matrix` that is not a matrix with a shape with rank 0 will trigger a `CHECK` fail in `tf.raw_ops.SparseMatrixNNZ`. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit f856d02e5322821aad155dad9b3acab1e9f5d693. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.11. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.10.1, 2.9.3, and TensorFlow 2.8.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: ExtractVariantFromInput obtains the input tensor and immediately calls input_t.scalar<Variant>() without verifying the tensor's rank; scalar<T>() requires a rank-0 (scalar) tensor and otherwise triggers a CHECK/assert failure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reaches an internal assertion (CHECK) through attacker-controlled input shape, matching CWE-617's reachable assertion leading to crash/exit. A related out-of-bounds read weakness is not the mechanism here; the failure is the rank precondition enforced by assertion, not a memory access violation.

evidence_lines.code:
const Tensor& input_t = ctx->input(index);
const Variant& input_variant = input_t.scalar<Variant>()();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no rank check before invoking scalar<Variant>() on the input tensor. Trigger: an input sparse_matrix whose tensor is not rank 0. Consequence: the scalar accessor's internal CHECK fails, aborting the process rather than returning an error status, giving a reachable assertion crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
timerfd: Protect the might cancel mechanism proper

The handling of the might_cancel queueing is not properly protected, so
parallel operations on the file descriptor can race with each other and
lead to list corruptions or use after free.

Protect the context for these operations with a seperate lock.

The wait queue lock cannot be reused for this because that would create a
lock inversion scenario vs. the cancel lock. Replacing might_cancel with an
atomic (atomic_t or atomic bit) does not help either because it still can
race vs. the actual list operation.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: "linux-fsdevel@vger.kernel.org"
Cc: syzkaller <syzkaller@googlegroups.com>
Cc: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Cc: linux-fsdevel@vger.kernel.org
Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.DEB.2.20.1701311521430.3457@nanos
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t} else if (ctx->might_cancel) {', '\t\ttimerfd_remove_cancel(ctx);'], 'added_lines': ['\tspin_lock(&ctx->cancel_lock);', '\t} else {', '\t\t__timerfd_remove_cancel(ctx);', '\tspin_unlock(&ctx->cancel_lock);']}
description: Race condition in fs/timerfd.c in the Linux kernel before 4.10.15 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (list corruption or use-after-free) via simultaneous file-descriptor operations that leverage improper might_cancel queueing.

code_evidence: The check of ctx->might_cancel at line 6 and the subsequent assignment and list_add_rcu at lines 7-9 are not serialized against the removal path. The else-branch at lines 12-13 calls timerfd_remove_cancel(ctx) based on the same ctx->might_cancel flag without holding a lock shared with the add path, so concurrent timerfd_setup_cancel calls can interleave list_add_rcu and removal on ctx->clist.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the race on might_cancel/clist allows the context's list node to be removed and freed while another path still operates on it, yielding a use-after-free. This is a concurrency-induced lifetime bug rather than a pure double-free or missing-lock-only issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the might_cancel flag and the clist list insertion/removal are read and mutated without a common lock, so parallel file-descriptor operations race. Trigger: simultaneous setup calls where one thread adds ctx->clist to cancel_list while another removes it. Supported consequence: list corruption and use-after-free of the timerfd context as the list operations act on freed or inconsistently linked memory.

commit_msg:
Do not use "/bin/sh" to run external commands.

Picocom no longer uses /bin/sh to run external commands for
file-transfer operations. Parsing the command line and spliting it into
arguments is now performed internally by picocom, using quoting rules
very similar to those of the Unix shell. Hopefully, this makes it
impossible to inject shell-commands when supplying filenames or
extra arguments to the send- and receive-file commands.

The shell-specific invocation also aligns with OS command injection (CWE-78), but the target CWE-77 correctly captures the improper neutralization of command syntax.

Prevent a crash due to heap OOB write in grappler.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 408318417
Change-Id: If095feb8c001e3a8ac4a85b7387b81e8309df47d
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      return errors::InvalidArgument("Missing context");'], 'added_lines': ['      return errors::InvalidArgument("SetUnknownShape: Missing context");', '    }', '    if (output_port < 0 || output_port >= ctx->num_outputs()) {', '      return errors::InvalidArgument(', '          "SetUnknownShape: output_port must be in [0, ", ctx->num_outputs(),', '          ") but was ", output_port);']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. TensorFlow is vulnerable to a heap OOB write in `Grappler`. The `set_output` function writes to an array at the specified index. Hence, this gives a malicious user a write primitive. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: SetUnknownShape takes an externally supplied int output_port and passes it directly, without any range check, to ctx->set_output(output_port, shape) at line 8. The function only guards against a null ctx (lines 5-7); output_port is never validated against ctx->num_outputs() before being used as the write index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked index is used for a write into the context's output storage, allowing writes before or past the buffer bounds. The null-context check addresses a different issue and does not constrain the index.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing bounds validation on output_port before it indexes the inference context's output array. Trigger: a malicious or malformed graph supplies a negative or out-of-range output_port. Consequence: set_output writes at an out-of-bounds index, producing a heap out-of-bounds write that can crash or corrupt memory.

commit_msg:
Add offset_ and size_ safely in LoaderExifJpeg::LoaderExifJpeg

offset_ can become arbitrarily large and overflows once its added to size_,
this causes all kinds of problems further in the code when offset_ is used
again.
=> Use Safe::add() to catch potential overflows
This fixes #365.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (offset_ + size_ > static_cast<uint32_t>(image_.io().size())) return;'], 'added_lines': ['        if (Safe::add(offset_, size_) > static_cast<uint32_t>(image_.io().size()))', '            return;']}
description: Exiv2 0.26 has an integer overflow in the LoaderExifJpeg class in preview.cpp, leading to an out-of-bounds read in Exiv2::MemIo::read in basicio.cpp.

code_evidence: offset_ is set from an Exif offsetKey_ value (line 8) and size_ from a sizeKey_ value (line 13); offset_ is further incremented by a baseOffsetKey_ value (line 19). Line 22 bounds-checks with offset_ + size_ before setting valid_ = true, so an attacker-controlled large offset_ can wrap the sum.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the flawed check relies on an addition that can wrap, so the size validation is bypassed when the sum overflows. The weakness is the unchecked integer arithmetic, not an out-of-bounds read itself; the OOB read is the downstream consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check computes offset_ + size_ in fixed-width unsigned arithmetic without overflow protection. Trigger: EXIF data supplies a large offset_ (directly or via baseOffsetKey_) such that offset_ + size_ wraps to a small value. Consequence: the check passes, valid_ becomes true, and downstream MemIo::read uses the oversized offset for an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
fix strncpy call to avoid ASAN violation

Ensure we're only reading to the size of the smallest buffer, since
they're both on the stack and could potentially overlap. Overlapping is
defined as ... undefined behavior. I've looked through all available
implementations of strncpy and they still only copy from the first \0
found.

We'll also never read past the end of sun_path since we _supply_
sun_path with a proper null terminator.

Since buf and', '            // sun_path here are both on the stack they could even overlap,', '            // which is "undefined". In all OSS versions of strncpy I could', "            // find this has no effect; it'll still only copy until the first null", "            // terminator is found. Thus it's possible to get the OS to", "            // examine past the end of sun_path but it's unclear to me if this", '            // can cause any actual problem.', '            //', "            // We need a safe_strncpy util function but I'll punt on figuring", '            // that out for now.', '            pathlen = sizeof(((struct sockaddr_un *)sock_addr)->sun_path);', '            if (MAXPATHLEN <= pathlen) {', '                pathlen = MAXPATHLEN - 1;', '            }', '                    pathlen);', "            addr_text[pathlen] = '\\0';"]}
description: memcached 1.5.16, when UNIX sockets are used, has a stack-based buffer over-read in conn_to_str in memcached.c.

code_evidence: addr_text is a fixed stack buffer of MAXPATHLEN; the AF_UNIX branch copies from sock_addr->sun_path into it with strncpy bounded by sizeof(addr_text)-1, then forces a terminator at the last byte. strncpy scans the source until a NUL, so the read bound is the source buffer, not the destination size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe operation reads beyond the intended source buffer (sun_path) rather than writing out of bounds; the destination bound and forced terminator prevent overflow, isolating the defect to an over-read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the strncpy length limit constrains the destination, not the source, so strncpy still reads past the end of sun_path if the kernel-supplied UNIX socket address lacks a NUL within the source object. Trigger: an AF_UNIX connection whose sun_path is not NUL-terminated within its declared size. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of stack memory, detectable by AddressSanitizer and potentially leaking adjacent stack bytes into the address string.

This zero value is stored into the cluster entry and later used in duration/sample calculations, leading to a divide-by-zero and crash (DoS). The patch adds a check rejecting samples_in_chunk < 1 before the value propagates.

description: In Wireshark 3.2.0 to 3.2.1, 3.0.0 to 3.0.8, and 2.6.0 to 2.6.14, the LTE RRC dissector could leak memory. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-lte-rrc.c by adjusting certain append operations.

code_evidence: A composite tvbuff gsm_rlcmac_dl_tvb is created, and a one-byte heap buffer pd is allocated from the pinfo pool and wrapped with tvb_new_real_data(pd, 1, 1), then appended to the composite. The composite is finalized and registered as a new data source, then passed to the gsm_rlcmac_dl dissector. The real-data tvb owns pd only if it is freed via tvb_free; appending it to a composite transfers that responsibility to the composite, whose lifetime is the data source.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the allocated pd buffer is not reliably released after its effective lifetime; the fix switches to tvb_new_child_real_data so the child tvb is owned by the parent and freed with it. This is a missing-release memory leak, not a use-after-free or out-of-bounds issue.

The composite holds the sub-tvb, but the allocation lifetime is not tied to the parent tvb's pool/chain. If the composite is not freed or is recreated on repeated dissection, pd can be orphaned and never released, leaking one byte per invocation. The trigger is dissection of a GERAN targetRAT container with a non-0x06 first byte and a registered gsm_rlcmac_dl handler.

commit_msg:
Fix conv2d crash when input size is empty.

If the input is empty (so convolution is only applied to padding), and if
the filter and padding sizes are still valid, then the output will be
all-zeros.  This previously caused a division-by-zero crash in multiple
kernels.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 463179650

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. If `Conv2D` is given empty `input` and the `filter` and `padding` sizes are valid, the output is all-zeros. This causes division-by-zero floating point exceptions that can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 611d80db29dd7b0cfb755772c69d60ae5bca05f9. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: Line 23 only guards the case where the output shape has zero elements and returns early; it does not guard an empty input tensor when the computed output shape is non-empty (all-padding convolution).

With input.NumElements()==0, execution reaches the kernel launchers starting at line 39 and the generic launcher_ call at line 50; the commit shows these kernels previously performed division-by-zero on the empty input, now avoided by an inserted early return.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because the empty-input path reaches kernel code that divides by zero, and the supported consequence is availability loss via crash. It is not a generic bounds issue; the defect is an unguarded zero divisor derived from empty input dimensions.

LaunchDeepConvOp<Device, T>::Run(

Fix null-pointer dereference issue in stackswap.

Avoid processing stackswap when stack only contains one element. In this
case, print a warning if debug mode is enabled, and return cleanly.

This commit fixes CVE-2017-11733 (fixes #78).

commit_msg:
It turns out that the combination of `(pid, start time)` is not
enough to be unique.  For temporary authorizations, we can avoid
separate users racing on pid reuse by simply comparing the uid.

https://bugs.chromium.org/p/project-zero/issues/detail?id=1692

And the above original email report is included in full in a new comment.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>

Closes: https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/polkit/polkit/issues/75
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        polkit_subject_equal (subject_to_use, authorization->subject))'], 'added_lines': ['        subject_equal_for_authz (subject_to_use, authorization->subject))']}
description: In PolicyKit (aka polkit) 0.115, the "start time" protection mechanism can be bypassed because fork() is not atomic, and therefore authorization decisions are improperly cached. This is related to lack of uid checking in polkitbackend/polkitbackendinteractiveauthority.c.

code_evidence: When the subject is a system bus name, the code resolves it to a process object via polkit_system_bus_name_get_process_sync before the comparison loop, so the resolved subject is a snapshot captured at one point in time.

The authorization lookup iterates cached entries and matches on action_id plus polkit_subject_equal(subject_to_use, authorization->subject); it relies on the resolved subject identity being stable for the decision.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a timing/atomicity gap in which the resolved subject used for cache lookup can be interfered with by a concurrent fork sequence, matching CWE-362's concurrent shared-resource access with improper synchronization. The fix switches to a uid-aware comparison to close the identity race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the authorization cache key is the resolved process identity, which is derived from (pid, start time) and can be reused or raced via fork() so the resolved subject no longer uniquely identifies the original requester. Trigger: an attacker races a process whose pid/start-time matches a cached temporary authorization, causing the lookup to match another user's cached authorization. Consequence: authorization decisions are improperly reused across users, bypassing the protection mechanism.

commit_msg: gnrc_tcp: Fix memory leak
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        gnrc_pktbuf_release(pkt);']}
description: RIOT through 2019.07 contains a memory leak in the TCP implementation (gnrc_tcp), allowing an attacker to consume all memory available for network packets and thus effectively stopping all network threads from working. This is related to _receive in sys/net/gnrc/transport_layer/tcp/gnrc_tcp_eventloop.c upon receiving an ACK before a SYN.

code_evidence: When no TCB matches the received packet, the else branch at lines 89-95 optionally builds and sends a reset, then returns -ENOTCONN at line 95 without releasing pkt. Every other error path (lines 15, 23, 30, 40, 48, 55) and the success path (line 97) call gnrc_pktbuf_release(pkt); only this branch omits it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates/holds pkt from the packet buffer and fails to release it on this return path, matching CWE-401 missing release of memory after its effective lifetime. It is not a double-free or use-after-free; ownership is simply abandoned on one early return.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the no-matching-TCB error branch returns -ENOTCONN while dropping the only reference to the packet buffer pkt. Trigger: an attacker sends a TCP packet (e.g., an ACK before any SYN) whose ports/addresses match no TCB. Each such packet leaks its pktbuf entry, exhausting the shared packet buffer and stalling network threads (DoS).

DO NOT MERGE: defensive parsing of mp3 album art information

several points in stagefrights mp3 album art code
used strlen() to parse user-supplied strings that may be
unterminated, resulting in reading beyond the end of a buffer.

This changes the code to use strnlen() for 8-bit encodings and
strengthens the parsing of 16-bit encodings similarly. It also
reworks how we watch for the end-of-buffer to avoid all over-reads.

Bug: 32377688
Test: crafted mp3's w/ good/bad cover art. See what showed in play music

(cherry picked from commit fa0806b594e98f1aed3ebcfc6a801b4c0056f9eb)

This issue is rated as Moderate because it could be used to access sensitive data without permission. Product: Android. Versions: 4.4.4, 5.0.2, 5.1.1, 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1. Android ID: A-32377688.

USB HID: Avoid allocating a huge amount of memory (second try).

10204490d7 / MR 80 ensured that we didn't grow field.usages due to an
underflow, but it neglected to check for a sane array size. Add another
check to make sure we don't wmem_array_grow() too much. Fixes #17165 and
fixes #16809 more completely.

description: Crash in USB HID dissector in Wireshark 3.4.0 to 3.4.2 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: usage_min and usage_max are attacker-controlled via hid_unpack_value at lines 106 and 112. The only prior guard is usage_min > usage_max (113-115), which does not bound the range width. Line 116 then calls wmem_array_grow(field.usages, usage_max - usage_min + 1), and the loop at 117-119 appends one element per value in that range, so a crafted descriptor with a very wide min/max span triggers a huge allocation and long loop.

[set] Make all operators null-safe again

Changed my mind.

Also for hb_map_clear().

Part of https://github.com/harfbuzz/harfbuzz/pull/3162
func:
[set]

0001 | void set (const hb_bit_set_invertible_t &other) { s.set (other.s); inverted = other.inverted; }
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void set (const hb_bit_set_invertible_t &other) { s.set (other.s); inverted = other.inverted; }'], 'added_lines': ['void set (const hb_bit_set_invertible_t &other)', '  {', '    s.set (other.s);', '    if (likely (s.successful))', '      inverted = other.inverted;', '  }']}
description: HarfBuzz 2.9.0 has an out-of-bounds write in hb_bit_set_invertible_t::set (called from hb_sparseset_t<hb_bit_set_invertible_t>::set and hb_set_copy).

code_evidence: The whole function is a single line: s.set(other.s) copies the source bit set into the destination, then inverted = other.inverted is assigned unconditionally. There is no success check after s.set, so the inverted flag is updated even if the underlying set copy failed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unsynchronized inverted flag leads to incorrect index computation and an out-of-bounds write in the set implementation (hb_bit_set_invertible_t::set), as described. The missing success guard is the cause; the OOB write is the supported consequence rather than a mere null dereference.

evidence_lines.code: void set (const hb_bit_set_invertible_t &other) { s.set (other.s); inverted = other.inverted; }

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination bit set's copy operation s.set(other.s) can fail (e.g., allocation failure) and leave s unsuccessful, yet the function still overwrites inverted from other. Trigger: calling set with a source whose copy cannot be completed. Consequence: the destination's inverted flag becomes inconsistent with its bit content, and later operations on this inconsistent state can compute wrong indices and write out of bounds.

Uninitialized Kernel memory can leak to USB devices.

Fix this by using kzalloc() instead of kmalloc().

commit_msg:
The location of the system.data extended attribute can change whenever
xattr_sem is not taken.  So we need to recalculate the i_inline_off
field since it mgiht have changed between ext4_write_begin() and
ext4_write_end().

This means that caching i_inline_off is probably not helpful, so in
the long run we should probably get rid of it and shrink the in-memory
ext4 inode slightly, but let's fix the race the simple way for now.

Cc: stable@kernel.org
Fixes: f19d5870cbf72 ("ext4: add normal write support for inline data")
Reported-by: syzbot+13146364637c7363a7de@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/*', '\t * ei->i_inline_off may have changed since ext4_write_begin()', '\t * called ext4_try_to_write_inline_data()', '\t */', '\t(void) ext4_find_inline_data_nolock(inode);', '']}
description: A race condition was discovered in ext4_write_inline_data_end in fs/ext4/inline.c in the ext4 subsystem in the Linux kernel through 5.13.13.

code_evidence: The function takes the xattr lock at line 19 and then writes inline data using the cached iloc and inode inline metadata at line 22. The commit notes the inode's i_inline_off can change whenever xattr_sem is not held, so the location used here may be stale relative to the write-begin phase.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits: a shared inode resource is accessed under a lock, but a timing window exists in which another concurrent sequence modifies the shared inline-data location before this sequence completes, violating exclusivity/atomicity of the write sequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the inline-data location (i_inline_off) is cached/reused across the window between ext4_write_begin and ext4_write_end without being revalidated under the xattr lock. An interfering code sequence can relocate the inline data during that window, so the write at line 22 operates on stale location metadata, producing incorrect inline-data updates.

Optimize CGI.escapeHTML by reducing buffer extension

and switch-case branches.

Buffer allocation optimization using `ALLOCA_N` would be the main
benefit of patch. It eliminates the O(N) buffer extensions.

It also reduces the number of branches using escape table like
https://mattn.kaoriya.net/software/lang/c/20160817011915.htm.

Closes: https://github.com/ruby/ruby/pull/2226

Co-authored-by: Nobuyoshi Nakada <nobu@ruby-lang.org>
Co-authored-by: Yasuhiro MATSUMOTO <mattn.jp@gmail.com>

code_evidence: len is a long derived from RSTRING_LEN(str) (line 7) and drives the loop bound (line 9). description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.6.1. drivers/media/usb/gspca/ov519.c allows NULL pointer dereferences in ov511_mode_init_regs and ov518_mode_init_regs when there are zero endpoints, aka CID-998912346c0d.

commit_msg:
Bluetooth: bnep: bnep_add_connection() should verify that it's dealing with l2cap socket

same story as cmtp

Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (!l2cap_is_socket(sock))', '\t\treturn -EBADFD;']}
description: The bnep_add_connection function in net/bluetooth/bnep/core.c in the Linux kernel before 3.19 does not ensure that an l2cap socket is available, which allows local users to gain privileges via a crafted application.

code_evidence: The function dereferences the caller-supplied socket through l2cap_pi(sock->sk)->chan without first confirming that sock is actually an L2CAP socket; both baswap calls read chan->dst and chan->src from that unchecked structure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function processes an input (the socket type) whose required property—being an L2CAP socket—is never validated before unsafe dereference. The missing l2cap_is_socket check is the absent validation; this is improper input validation rather than a bounds or memory-safety defect per se.

evidence_lines.code:
baswap((void *) dst, &l2cap_pi(sock->sk)->chan->dst);
baswap((void *) src, &l2cap_pi(sock->sk)->chan->src);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bnep_add_connection accepts an arbitrary struct socket and assumes its sk is an L2CAP socket, so no type check constrains the input before l2cap_pi(sock->sk)->chan is dereferenced. Trigger: a local caller passes a non-L2CAP socket to the ioctl path. The unchecked cast yields invalid pointer reads, which can crash the kernel or, as described, be leveraged for privilege escalation.

description: HarfBuzz 2.9.0 has an out-of-bounds write in hb_bit_set_invertible_t::set (called from hb_sparseset_t<hb_bit_set_invertible_t>::set and hb_set_copy).

code_evidence: intersect branches on inverted==other.inverted and, when both are inverted, calls process(hb_bitwise_or, other); otherwise it selects hb_bitwise_lt or hb_bitwise_gt. These process calls mutate the underlying set without checking whether the operation succeeded, so the branch choice alone does not constrain later memory writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function drives the bitwise set operation whose failure leads to an out-of-bounds write in hb_bit_set_invertible_t::set, matching CWE-787. The weakness is the unchecked write path, not merely a logic-state inconsistency.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the intersect operation relies on process() to perform in-place bitwise set mutation without validating success before the inverted flag is updated. When a call derived from hb_set_copy reaches this path with inconsistent invertible state, the subsequent bitwise operation can write past the intended set storage, producing memory corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
[gsm] Delay the creation of the GsmXSMPClient until it really exists

We used to create the GsmXSMPClient before the XSMP connection is really
accepted. This can lead to some issues, though. An example is:
https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=598211#c19. Quoting:

 "What is happening is that a new client (probably metacity in your
 case) is opening an ICE connection in the GSM_MANAGER_PHASE_END_SESSION
 phase, which causes a new GsmXSMPClient to be added to the client
 store. The GSM_MANAGER_PHASE_EXIT phase then begins before the client
 has had a chance to establish a xsmp connection, which means that
 client->priv->conn will not be initialized at the point that xsmp_stop
 is called on the new unregistered client."

The fix is to create the GsmXSMPClient object when there's a real XSMP
connection. This implies moving the timeout that makes sure we don't
have an empty client to the XSMP server.

https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=598211
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '        if (client->priv->protocol_timeout) {', '                g_source_remove (client->priv->protocol_timeout);', '                client->priv->protocol_timeout = 0;', '        }'], 'added_lines': []}
description: Bad reference counting in the context of accept_ice_connection() in gsm-xsmp-server.c in old versions of gnome-session up until version 2.29.92 allows a local attacker to establish ICE connections to gnome-session with invalid authentication data (an invalid magic cookie). Each failed authentication attempt will leak a file descriptor in gnome-session. When the maximum number of file descriptors is exhausted in the gnome-session process, it will enter an infinite loop trying to communicate without success, consuming 100% of the CPU. The graphical session associated with the gnome-session process will stop working correctly, because communication with gnome-session is no longer possible.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no loop or iteration; it only stores the connection, removes a timeout source, and registers XSMP callbacks, so it does not support an unreachable-exit-condition infinite loop.

commit_msg:
dm: Reset virtio device before release

With virtio polling mode enabled, a timer is running in the virtio
backend service. And the timer will also be triggered if its frondend
driver didn't do the device reset in shutdown. A freed virtio device
will be accessed in the polling timer handler.

Do the virtio reset() callback specifically to clear the polling timer
before the free.

Tracked-On: #6147
Signed-off-by: Shuo A Liu <shuo.a.liu@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Yonghua Huang <yonghua.huang@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (dev->arg)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (dev->arg) {', '\t\tvirtio_hyper_dmabuf_reset(dev->arg);', '\t}']}
description: The polling timer handler in ACRN before 2.5 has a use-after-free for a freed virtio device, related to devicemodel/hw/pci/virtio/*.c.

code_evidence: The deinit function frees dev->arg with free() but performs no device reset before releasing it. When polling mode is active, a backend timer still references the virtio device; the freed memory can then be accessed by the timer handler.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: free() on dev->arg leaves a dangling reference reachable by the polling timer, matching CWE-416 (referencing memory after it is freed). This is a use-after-free lifetime bug, not merely a double-free or leak.

evidence_lines.code:
if (dev->arg)
free((struct virtio_hyper_dmabuf *)dev->arg);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dev->arg is freed in deinit without first stopping/quiescing the virtio polling timer that retains a pointer to the device. Trigger: shutdown deinit while polling mode timer is running. Consequence: the timer handler dereferences freed memory (use-after-free), potentially reading/modifying reused memory or crashing.

description: The d_walk function in fs/dcache.c in the Linux kernel through 3.17.2 does not properly maintain the semantics of rename_lock, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock and system hang) via a crafted application.

code_evidence: The walk iterates child entries, locking each dentry with spin_lock_nested and later descending into subdirectories; the child lock is released when ascending [56-61] but the killed-child check is folded into the retry path [62-67].

On detecting DCACHE_DENTRY_KILLED or a rename seqretry, the code unlocks the parent and RCU and jumps to rename_retry [62-67], which restarts the entire walk via again with seq=1 [83-87], re-locking and re-traversing from the root.
Because retry is only cleared by D_WALK_NORETRY, a killed sibling encountered during ascent forces a full restart of the walk instead of skipping the dead entry.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function's retry logic allows unbounded, attacker-triggered re-execution of the walk, exhausting CPU/lock resources and causing a DoS hang. It is uncontrolled consumption of a limited resource (processing/lock availability), not memory corruption, so CWE-400 is the appropriate class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ascent path treats a concurrently killed dentry (DCACHE_DENTRY_KILLED) as a reason to abort and restart the whole d_walk, rather than skipping it. A local attacker racing rename/unlink against lookups repeatedly triggers restarts, each reacquiring locks and re-traversing the dentry tree, consuming CPU and holding lock cycles. The supported consequence is a deadlock/system hang (denial of service).

commit_msg:
dccp: fix freeing skb too early for IPV6_RECVPKTINFO

In the current DCCP implementation an skb for a DCCP_PKT_REQUEST packet
is forcibly freed via __kfree_skb in dccp_rcv_state_process if
dccp_v6_conn_request successfully returns.

However, if IPV6_RECVPKTINFO is set on a socket, the address of the skb
is saved to ireq->pktopts and the ref count for skb is incremented in
dccp_v6_conn_request, so skb is still in use. Nevertheless, it gets freed
in dccp_rcv_state_process.

Fix by calling consume_skb instead of doing goto discard and therefore
calling __kfree_skb.

Similar fixes for TCP:

fb7e2399ec17f1004c0e0ccfd17439f8759ede01 [TCP]: skb is unexpectedly freed.
0aea76d35c9651d55bbaf746e7914e5f9ae5a25d tcp: SYN packets are now
simply consumed

Signed-off-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Acked-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tgoto discard;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tconsume_skb(skb);', '\t\t\treturn 0;']}
description: The dccp_rcv_state_process function in net/dccp/input.c in the Linux kernel through 4.9.11 mishandles DCCP_PKT_REQUEST packet data structures in the LISTEN state, which allows local users to obtain root privileges or cause a denial of service (double free) via an application that makes an IPV6_RECVPKTINFO setsockopt system call.

code_evidence: In LISTEN state, a DCCP_PKT_REQUEST is passed to icsk_af_ops->conn_request; on success the code falls through to `goto discard`.

The discard label at line 75 unconditionally calls __kfree_skb(skb), freeing the skb after conn_request has already taken a reference (dccp_v6_conn_request saves it to ireq->pktopts and increments the refcount when IPV6_RECVPKTINFO is set).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the same skb is released twice: once by __kfree_skb at the discard label and again through the reference retained in ireq->pktopts. The fix replaces the goto with consume_skb and an early return, avoiding the second free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the LISTEN/REQUEST path frees the skb via __kfree_skb after conn_request has stored and refcounted it in ireq->pktopts. Trigger: a local socket with IPV6_RECVPKTINFO set sends a DCCP_PKT_REQUEST while the server is listening. Consequence: the skb is freed while still referenced, leading to a double free when the stored reference is later released, enabling memory corruption/privilege escalation or denial of service.

commit_msg:
- Modified TileManager.cc to verify that malloc() has correctly allocated memory.
- Updated numerical types to std::size_t in RawTile.h, TileManager.cc, KakaduImage.cc, OpenJPEG.cc and Transforms.cc when allocating memory via new to avoid integer overflow - fixes remaining problems identified in https://github.com/ruven/iipsrv/issues/223.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  in.dataLength = resampled_width * resampled_height * channels * (in.bpc/8);'], 'added_lines': ['  in.dataLength = (size_t)resampled_width * (size_t)resampled_height * (size_t)channels * (size_t)(in.bpc/8);']}
description: IIPImage High Resolution Streaming Image Server prior to commit 882925b295a80ec992063deffc2a3b0d803c3195 is affected by an integer overflow in iipsrv.fcgi through malformed HTTP query parameters.

code_evidence: Line 3 reads in.channels into an int, and lines 4-5 take in.width and in.height as unsigned int. Line 29 computes in.dataLength as resampled_width * resampled_height * channels * (in.bpc/8) in the operands' unsigned int/int type, so the product is evaluated before any widening and can wrap.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because a size calculation is performed with types that cannot hold the full product, producing wraparound; the patch casts each operand to size_t precisely to avoid this. It is distinct from a simple out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) because the defect is the overflowing arithmetic feeding the size field.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the length calculation on line 29 is performed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so a large resampled_width/resampled_height (attacker-influenced via malformed HTTP query parameters) multiplied by channels and bytes-per-channel wraps to a small value. The wrapped in.dataLength then misrepresents the buffer size, so downstream code that trusts it can under-allocate or over-read, leading to memory corruption or a crash.

For debugging purposes this behavior can be disabled with the command line flag --unsafe-pac-url.

BUG=593759
R=mmenke@chromium.org

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1996773002 .

description: net/proxy/proxy_service.cc in the Proxy Auto-Config (PAC) feature in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.82 does not ensure that URL information is restricted to a scheme, host, and port, which allows remote attackers to discover credentials by operating a server with a PAC script, a related issue to CVE-2016-3763.

It never configures the URL sanitization policy that governs what URL data is passed to PAC scripts; the added switch handling that would set SanitizeUrlPolicy::UNSAFE is absent from this function body, so the default sanitization behavior is what the returned service uses.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-200 fits because the weakness is explicit failure to sanitize sensitive URL information before it is made accessible to a remote PAC script, directly exposing credentials to an unauthorized party. It is an information-exposure mistake, not a memory-safety or access-control flaw.

proxy_service->set_quick_check_enabled(quick_check_enabled);
return proxy_service;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the factory does not enforce or even expose a restriction on URL information sent to PAC scripts, leaving the service to pass more than scheme/host/port (e.g., credentials) to a remote PAC script. commit_msg:
BUG/MAJOR: http/htx: prevent unbounded loop in http_manage_server_side_cookies

Ensure calls to http_find_header() terminate. If a "Set-Cookie2"
header is found then the while(1) loop in
http_manage_server_side_cookies() will never terminate, resulting in
the watchdog firing and the process terminating via SIGABRT.

The while(1) loop becomes unbounded because an unmatched call to
http_find_header("Set-Cookie") will leave ctx->blk=NULL. Subsequent
calls to check for "Set-Cookie2" will now enumerate from the beginning
of all the blocks and will once again match on subsequent
passes (assuming a match first time around), hence the loop becoming
unbounded.

This issue was introduced with HTX and this fix should be backported
to all versions supporting HTX.

Many thanks to Grant Spence (gspence@redhat.com) for working through
this issue with me.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!http_find_header(htx, ist("Set-Cookie"), &ctx, 1)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (is_cookie2 || !http_find_header(htx, ist("Set-Cookie"), &ctx, 1)) {']}
description: A flaw was found in the way HAProxy processed HTTP responses containing the "Set-Cookie2" header. This flaw could allow an attacker to send crafted HTTP response packets which lead to an infinite loop, eventually resulting in a denial of service condition. The highest threat from this vulnerability is availability.

code_evidence: ctx.blk is initialized to NULL and the while(1) loop at line 13 has its only exit at line 17. Each iteration calls http_find_header("Set-Cookie") with the shared ctx; when that call fails, ctx.blk is left NULL, so the fallback call for "Set-Cookie2" restarts enumeration from the beginning of all blocks. If a Set-Cookie2 header exists, that fallback matches again on every pass, is_cookie2 is set, and the loop never breaks.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a loop whose exit condition at line 17 cannot be reached once a Set-Cookie2 header is present, matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. It is not merely a resource-exhaustion weakness; the defect is the non-terminating iteration itself, with DoS as the resulting impact.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop exit depends on http_find_header("Set-Cookie2") failing, but a failed Set-Cookie lookup resets ctx.blk to NULL, so a present Set-Cookie2 header is re-found indefinitely. Trigger: a crafted response containing Set-Cookie2. Consequence: the server-side cookie loop spins forever, consuming CPU until the watchdog aborts the process (availability loss).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (buf_alloc<=fsize) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (buf_alloc <= fsize+2) {']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.2.2.

code_evidence: Lines 32-34: the reallocation guard only ensures buf_alloc > fsize, so a buffer of exactly fsize+3 is reused when fsize+3 <= buf_alloc, but the old condition buf_alloc<=fsize allowed reuse when buf_alloc==fsize+1 or fsize+2, which is too small for the writes that follow.
Line 36 reads fsize bytes into _buf+1, then lines 37-38 write terminators at _buf[fsize+1] and _buf[fsize+2], requiring fsize+3 bytes.
Line 39 sets buf = _buf+1, so subsequent tag parsing operates on the same undersized heap block.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a heap buffer overflow (CWE-122): a heap block sized via gf_realloc is written past its end due to an insufficient size check. It is not a stack overflow because _buf is heap-allocated and the out-of-bounds writes target that allocation.

evidence_lines.code: buf = _buf+1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a frame's fsize is such that buf_alloc (from a prior frame) satisfies buf_alloc<=fsize but is less than fsize+3, the guard skips reallocation. gf_bs_read_data then writes fsize bytes at _buf+1 and the two NUL writes at _buf[fsize+1]/_buf[fsize+2] exceed the heap allocation, causing a heap-based buffer overflow.

description: An issue was discovered in OpenEXR before v2.5.2. Invalid chunkCount attributes could cause a heap buffer overflow in getChunkOffsetTableSize() in IlmImf/ImfMisc.cpp.
