commit_msg:
cJSON: fix memory leak on object parsing error

Issue discovered during OpenSIPS Security Audit 2021/2022,
by Alfred Farrugia & Sandro Gauci (Enable Security)

https://github.com/OpenSIPS/opensips/security/advisories/GHSA-2mg2-g46r-j4qr
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        cJSON_Delete(child);'], 'added_lines': ['        cJSON_Delete(item->child);']}
description:
OpenSIPS, a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) server implementation, has a memory leak starting in the 2.3 branch and priot to versions 3.1.8 and 3.2.5. The memory leak was detected in the function `parse_mi_request` while performing coverage-guided fuzzing. This issue can be reproduced by sending multiple requests of the form `{"jsonrpc": "2.0","method": "log_le`. This malformed message was tested against an instance of OpenSIPS via FIFO transport layer and was found to increase the memory consumption over time.

To abuse this memory leak, attackers need to reach the management interface (MI) which typically should only be exposed on trusted interfaces. In cases where the MI is exposed to the internet without authentication, abuse of this issue will lead to memory exhaustion which may affect the underlying system’s availability. No authentication is typically required to reproduce this issue. On the other hand, memory leaks may occur in other areas of OpenSIPS where the cJSON library is used for parsing JSON objects.

The issue has been fixed in versions 3.1.8 and 3.2.5.

code_evidence: At line 15 a new child item is allocated and stored in item->child (line 16); on allocation failure the code jumps to fail (line 19).
In the loop each iteration allocates new_item (line 41) and links it into the child list (lines 45-47); failures at lines 43 and later goto fail.
The fail block checks item->child (line 72) but calls cJSON_Delete(child) (line 74), which frees only the current tail node, not the head item->child and thus not the preceding nodes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates heap nodes and fails to release them on an error path, matching CWE-401 (missing release of memory after effective lifetime). This is not a use-after-free: the nodes remain allocated and unreachable, not freed then reused.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path frees the wrong pointer (the current child instead of the list head item->child), so earlier allocated nodes in the linked list are not released. Trigger: malformed JSON object input that causes a goto fail after one or more children are linked (e.g., missing ':' or a failed parse_value). Consequence: leaked cJSON nodes accumulate per malformed request, enabling memory exhaustion/DoS.

Fixed bug #71527 Buffer over-write in finfo_open with malformed magic file

The actual fix is applying the upstream patch from

description: The file_check_mem function in funcs.c in file before 5.23, as used in the Fileinfo component in PHP before 5.5.34, 5.6.x before 5.6.20, and 7.x before 7.0.5, mishandles continuation-level jumps, which allows context-dependent attackers to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted magic file.

code_evidence: When level >= ms->c.len, the buffer is enlarged by a fixed increment of 20 entries and reallocated, so ms->c.len is set to old_len+20 regardless of the requested level.

After the conditional resize, the code unconditionally indexes ms->c.li[level] (and also level_info fields) without verifying that level < ms->c.len, so a level jump beyond the just-added increment writes past the allocated array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through an index (level) beyond the bounds of the heap buffer it just allocated, which is a classic out-of-bounds memory write within CWE-119. It is not merely a NULL-dereference or integer overflow at the allocation site; the missing level-vs-capacity check is the direct cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the growth amount (+20) is not tied to the attacker-controlled continuation level, so a crafted magic file with a large level jump produces an allocation smaller than the index used. Trigger: level >= ms->c.len with a jump larger than the new capacity. Consequence: out-of-bounds write to ms->c.li[level], causing memory corruption, crash, or possible code execution.

commit_msg:
tiffcrop: disable incompatibility of -Z, -X, -Y, -z options with any PAGE_MODE_x option (fixes #411 and #413)

tiffcrop does not support –Z, -z, -X and –Y options together with any other PAGE_MODE_x options like  -H, -V, -P, -J, -K or –S.

Code analysis:

With the options –Z, -z, the crop.selections are set to a value > 0. Within main(), this triggers the call of processCropSelections(), which copies the sections from the read_buff into seg_buffs[].
In the following code in main(), the only supported step, where that seg_buffs are further handled are within an if-clause with  if (page.mode == PAGE_MODE_NONE) .

Execution of the else-clause often leads to buffer-overflows.

Therefore, the above option combination is not supported and will be disabled to prevent those buffer-overflows.

The MR solves issues #411 and #413.

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: remove nodes owned by destroyed domain

In case a domain is removed from Xenstore, remove all nodes owned by
it per default.

This tackles the problem that nodes might be created by a domain
outside its home path in Xenstore, leading to Xenstore hogging more
and more memory. Domain quota don't work in this case if the guest is
rebooting in between.

Since XSA-322 ownership of such stale nodes is transferred to dom0,
which is helping against unintended access, but not against OOM of
Xenstore.

As a fallback for weird cases add a Xenstore start parameter for
keeping today's way to handle stale nodes, adding the risk of Xenstore
hitting an OOM situation.

This is part of XSA-419 / CVE-2022-42322.

Fixes: 496306324d8d ("tools/xenstore: revoke access rights for removed domains")
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tdomain_tree_remove(domain);']}
description: Xenstore: Cooperating guests can create arbitrary numbers of nodes T[his CNA information record relates to multiple CVEs; the text explains which aspects/vulnerabilities correspond to which CVE.] Since the fix of XSA-322 any Xenstore node owned by a removed domain will be modified to be owned by Dom0. This will allow two malicious guests working together to create an arbitrary number of Xenstore nodes. This is possible by domain A letting domain B write into domain A's local Xenstore tree. Domain B can then create many nodes and reboot. The nodes created by domain B will now be owned by Dom0. By repeating this process over and over again an arbitrary number of nodes can be created, as Dom0's number of nodes isn't limited by Xenstore quota.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Reported-by: syzbot+f427adf9324b92652ccc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tmake_bad_inode(inode);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tfuse_make_bad(inode);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the FUSE filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.10.6, aka CID-5d069dbe8aaf. fuse_do_getattr() calls make_bad_inode() in inappropriate situations, causing a system crash. NOTE: the original fix for this vulnerability was incomplete, and its incompleteness is tracked as CVE-2021-28950.

code_evidence: When fuse_simple_request succeeds but the server returns inconsistent attributes (fuse_invalid_attr or a file-type mismatch via S_IFMT), the code calls make_bad_inode(inode) on the live inode, which resets i_mode to S_IFREG without tearing down existing dnotify/inode watcher structures.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-459 fits because the code fails to properly tear down/clean up supporting inode-watcher state before invalidating the inode, leaving residual structures. This is incomplete cleanup of associated resources, not merely a type-confusion or improper-input-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: make_bad_inode() is invoked on a live, already-registered inode, mutating its mode while attached dnotify structures remain. Trigger: a FUSE server returns invalid or type-mismatched attributes for a directory that has a dnotify mark. Consequence: stale dnotify state persists and later accesses cause a crash (DoS).

nl80211: fix memory leak in nl80211_get_ftm_responder_stats

In nl80211_get_ftm_responder_stats, a new skb is created via nlmsg_new
named msg. If nl80211hdr_put() fails, then msg should be released. The
return statement should be replace by goto to error handling code.

Fixes: 81e54d08d9d8 ("cfg80211: support FTM responder configuration/statistics")
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20191004194220.19412-1-navid.emamdoost@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Johannes Berg <johannes.berg@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\treturn -ENOBUFS;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tgoto nla_put_failure;']}
description: A memory leak in the nl80211_get_ftm_responder_stats() function in net/wireless/nl80211.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering nl80211hdr_put() failures, aka CID-1399c59fa929. NOTE: third parties dispute the relevance of this because it occurs on a code path where a successful allocation has already occurred

code_evidence: msg is allocated by nlmsg_new() and its ownership is held locally; after nl80211hdr_put() at line 22 returns NULL, line 25 returns -ENOBUFS directly, bypassing the nla_put_failure path at lines 55-57 that calls nlmsg_free(msg).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a missing release of allocated memory on an error path, matching CWE-401. It is not a use-after-free or double-free, since msg is never freed on this branch; the defect is the omitted nlmsg_free() before returning.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch for a failed nl80211hdr_put() returns without freeing the already-allocated skb msg. Trigger: nl80211hdr_put() returns NULL after nlmsg_new() succeeded; the direct return leaks msg. Consequence: repeated triggering consumes kernel memory, supporting a resource-consumption DoS.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in the C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In various parts of PJSIP, when error/failure occurs, it is found that the function returns without releasing the currently held locks. This could result in a system deadlock, which cause a denial of service for the users. No release has yet been made which contains the linked fix commit. All versions up to an including 2.11.1 are affected. Users may need to manually apply the patch.

The apply_fmt failure branch returns status at line 71 while the mutex taken at line 18 remains held.
PJ_ASSERT_RETURN for listener_slots returns PJ_ENOMEM at line 86 without releasing vid_conf->mutex.
PJ_ASSERT_RETURN for transmitter_slots returns PJ_ENOMEM at line 91 leaving the lock held.
PJ_ASSERT_RETURN for render_states returns PJ_ENOMEM at line 96 leaving the lock held.
PJ_ASSERT_RETURN for render_pool returns PJ_ENOMEM at line 101 leaving the lock held.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 covers improper lock acquisition/release. Here the mutex is acquired but not released on multiple error returns, matching the improper-release pattern that leads to deadlock.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function locks vid_conf->mutex at line 18 but several error paths (lines 62, 71, 86, 91, 96, 101) return directly without unlocking. Trigger: an invalid format, apply_fmt failure, or pool allocation failure. Consequence: the mutex stays held, so subsequent callers block and the video conference bridge deadlocks, causing denial of service.

CBOR: Add a recursion check

Fixes #19144
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (!dissect_cbor_byte_string(tvb, pinfo, subtree, offset, eof_type & 0x1f)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tunsigned recursion_depth = p_get_proto_depth(pinfo, proto_cbor);', '\t\t\tif (++recursion_depth >= CBOR_MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH) {', '\t\t\t\tproto_tree_add_expert(subtree, pinfo, &ei_cbor_max_recursion_depth_reached, tvb, 0, 0);', '\t\t\t\treturn FALSE;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tp_set_proto_depth(pinfo, proto_cbor, recursion_depth);', '', '\t\t\tgboolean recursed = dissect_cbor_byte_string(tvb, pinfo, subtree, offset, eof_type & 0x1f);', '\t\t\tp_set_proto_depth(pinfo, proto_cbor, recursion_depth - 1);', '', '\t\t\tif (!recursed) {']}
description: CBOR dissector crash in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.6 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: The indefinite-length byte-string branch loops with while(1), reads the next element type with tvb_get_guint8, and on a nested byte string (type 0x1f) calls dissect_cbor_byte_string recursively at line 51 without any depth counter or recursion bound. The only termination conditions are an 0xff break marker (lines 41-45) or a non-byte-string element (lines 46-50); a crafted input of nested indefinite byte strings keeps re-entering the function, so the recursion depth is attacker-controlled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly recurses on attacker-controlled nesting with no recursion constraint, matching CWE-674 (Uncontrolled Recursion). This is not merely an integer-overflow or length-validation issue: those checks at lines 65-68 bound a single length, but they do not limit the recursive nesting depth that causes the crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursive call at line 51 in the indefinite-length loop has no depth limit, so nested CBOR byte-string headers drive unbounded stack recursion. Trigger: a crafted packet or capture containing many nested indefinite-length byte strings. Consequence: stack exhaustion and a dissector crash, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
HID: hiddev: validate num_values for HIDIOCGUSAGES, HIDIOCSUSAGES commands

This patch validates the num_values parameter from userland during the
HIDIOCGUSAGES and HIDIOCSUSAGES commands. Previously, if the report id was set
to HID_REPORT_ID_UNKNOWN, we would fail to validate the num_values parameter
leading to a heap overflow.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Scott Bauer <sbauer@plzdonthack.me>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\telse if ((cmd == HIDIOCGUSAGES || cmd == HIDIOCSUSAGES) &&', '\t\t\t\t (uref_multi->num_values > HID_MAX_MULTI_USAGES ||', '\t\t\t\t  uref->usage_index + uref_multi->num_values > field->report_count))', '\t\t\t\tgoto inval;', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t}', '\t\tif ((cmd == HIDIOCGUSAGES || cmd == HIDIOCSUSAGES) &&', '\t\t    (uref_multi->num_values > HID_MAX_MULTI_USAGES ||', '\t\t     uref->usage_index + uref_multi->num_values > field->report_count))', '\t\t\tgoto inval;']}
description: Multiple heap-based buffer overflows in the hiddev_ioctl_usage function in drivers/hid/usbhid/hiddev.c in the Linux kernel through 4.6.3 allow local users to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted (1) HIDIOCGUSAGES or (2) HIDIOCSUSAGES ioctl call.

code_evidence: When report_id is HID_REPORT_ID_UNKNOWN, field is resolved via hiddev_lookup_usage and control jumps past the else block that contains the num_values bounds check.
The num_values validation (HID_MAX_MULTI_USAGES and usage_index + num_values vs report_count) sits only in the else branch, so the unknown-report-id path skips it entirely.
HIDIOCGUSAGES loops i < uref_multi->num_values reading field->value[uref->usage_index + i] with no bound on num_values.
HIDIOCSUSAGES loops i < uref_multi->num_values writing field->value[uref->usage_index + i] with no bound on num_values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loops perform read/write operations on field->value at indices derived from unvalidated num_values, exceeding the buffer's intended boundary, which is exactly CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The missing bound check is the proximate cause; the out-of-bounds access is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the num_values bound check is nested in the else branch, so the HID_REPORT_ID_UNKNOWN path reaches the usage loops without validating num_values. Trigger: a local user issues HIDIOCGUSAGES/HIDIOCSUSAGES with report_id HID_REPORT_ID_UNKNOWN and an oversized num_values. The loops then index field->value beyond its report_count-sized buffer, causing out-of-bounds reads/writes (heap overflow).

commit_msg: Fix 698540: Check name, comment and meta size field signs.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (namesize < 0 || metasize < 0 || commentsize < 0)', '\t\t\tfz_throw(ctx, FZ_ERROR_GENERIC, "invalid size in zip entry");', '']}
description: Artifex MuPDF 1.11 allows attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service via a crafted .xps file, related to a "User Mode Write AV near NULL starting at wow64!Wow64NotifyDebugger+0x000000000000001d" on Windows. This occurs because read_zip_dir_imp in fitz/unzip.c does not check whether size fields in a ZIP entry are negative numbers.

code_evidence: namesize, metasize and commentsize are read from the ZIP central directory as signed 16-bit integers via fz_read_int16_le, without any sign check before use.

namesize is passed to fz_malloc(ctx, namesize + 1) and then to fz_read as a length; the subsequent check n < (size_t)namesize compares against the cast value, so a negative namesize yields a huge size_t and the guard does not catch the short read.
The metasize loop uses size from the file and decrements metasize -= 4 + size, so a negative metasize skips the loop while a large size can drive the seek/counter out of the intended entry bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked negative size leads to allocation and read operations using a size_t value that does not match the intended buffer size, causing reads/writes outside the allocated buffer, which is exactly CWE-119. The missing sign check is the enabling defect; the resulting out-of-bounds memory operation is the weakness class described.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: signed size fields from an untrusted ZIP entry are used as allocation, read and seek lengths without validating their sign. Trigger: a crafted .xps/ZIP file with negative namesize, metasize or commentsize. Consequence: the negative namesize is converted to a huge size_t in fz_malloc/fz_read, leading to out-of-bounds memory access (write/read near NULL or beyond the buffer), supporting code execution or DoS.

Prevent division by 0

PiperOrigin-RevId: 370984990
Change-Id: Ib324955bbeb1cbd97c82fd5d61a00a2697c9a2de
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, block_shape[dim] != 0);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The implementation of the `SpaceToBatchNd` TFLite operator is [vulnerable to a division by zero error](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/412c7d9bb8f8a762c5b266c9e73bfa165f29aac8/tensorflow/lite/kernels/space_to_batch_nd.cc#L82-L83). An attacker can craft a model such that one dimension of the `block` input is 0. Hence, the corresponding value in `block_shape` is 0. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: block_shape is read from attacker-controlled tensor data at line 4. In the loop at line 16, block_shape[dim] is used as a divisor in the modulo at line 19 and the division at line 20, and as a multiplier at line 21, without any prior check that it is nonzero. If a crafted model supplies block_shape[dim] == 0, the modulo/division executes with a zero divisor.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 directly matches: the function performs division (and modulo) using a value derived from input tensor data that can be zero, with no guard. This is a divide-by-zero weakness, not merely an input-validation issue, because the concrete unsafe operation is the division by an unvalidated zero value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop divides final_dim_size by block_shape[dim] (and takes it modulo) without validating that block_shape[dim] is nonzero. Trigger: an attacker-crafted model whose block_shape tensor contains a 0 for some spatial dimension. Supported consequence: an integer division/modulo by zero, causing a crash or undefined behavior (DoS). The missing constraint is the cause; the crash is the consequence.

commit_msg:
qcow2: Fix L1 allocation size in qcow2_snapshot_load_tmp() (CVE-2014-0145)

For the L1 table to loaded for an internal snapshot, the code allocated
only enough memory to hold the currently active L1 table. If the
snapshot's L1 table is actually larger than the current one, this leads
to a buffer overflow.

Signed-off-by: Kevin Wolf <kwolf@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Max Reitz <mreitz@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    new_l1_bytes = s->l1_size * sizeof(uint64_t);'], 'added_lines': ['    new_l1_bytes = sn->l1_size * sizeof(uint64_t);']}
description: Multiple buffer overflows in QEMU before 1.7.2 and 2.x before 2.0.0, allow local users to cause a denial of service (crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a large (1) L1 table in the qcow2_snapshot_load_tmp in the QCOW 2 block driver (block/qcow2-snapshot.c) or (2) uncompressed chunk, (3) chunk length, or (4) number of sectors in the DMG block driver (block/dmg.c).

code_evidence: Allocation size for the new L1 table is derived from the active table's s->l1_size, not the snapshot's sn->l1_size.
bdrv_pread then reads new_l1_bytes into that buffer, and later s->l1_size is set to sn->l1_size and the loop indexes s->l1_table[i] up to the snapshot's size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a buffer sized by one value and then reads/writes it using a larger snapshot-controlled size, performing operations outside the buffer's intended boundary. This is a classic out-of-bounds buffer operation, matching CWE-119 rather than a mere integer or resource issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer is sized from the current active L1 table (s->l1_size) while the snapshot's L1 table (sn->l1_size) may be larger. Trigger: loading an internal snapshot whose L1 table exceeds the active one; bdrv_pread and the subsequent be64_to_cpus loop access beyond the allocated buffer. Supported consequence: heap buffer overflow, enabling crash or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
x86/mm: PV superpage handling lacks sanity checks

MMUEXT_{,UN}MARK_SUPER fail to check the input MFN for validity before
dereferencing pointers into the superpage frame table.

Reported-by: Qinghao Tang <luodalongde@gmail.com>

get_superpage() has a similar issue.

This is CVE-2016-1570 / XSA-167.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Ian Campbell <ian.campbell@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if ( unlikely(d != pg_owner) )', '                rc = -EPERM;', '            else if ( mfn & (L1_PAGETABLE_ENTRIES-1) )', '            {', '                MEM_LOG("Unaligned superpage reference mfn %lx", mfn);', '                rc = -EINVAL;', '            }', '            else if ( !opt_allow_superpage )', '            else', '            break;', '        }', '', '        case MMUEXT_UNMARK_SUPER:', '        {', '            unsigned long mfn = op.arg1.mfn;', '', '            if ( unlikely(d != pg_owner) )', '                rc = -EPERM;', '            else if ( mfn & (L1_PAGETABLE_ENTRIES-1) )', '            {', '                MEM_LOG("Unaligned superpage reference mfn %lx", mfn);', '                rc = -EINVAL;', '            }', '            else if ( !opt_allow_superpage )', '            {', '                MEM_LOG("Superpages disallowed");', '                rc = -ENOSYS;', '            }'], 'added_lines': ['        case MMUEXT_UNMARK_SUPER:', '            if ( !opt_allow_superpage )', '            else if ( unlikely(d != pg_owner) )', '                rc = -EPERM;', '            else if ( mfn & (L1_PAGETABLE_ENTRIES - 1) )', '            {', '                MEM_LOG("Unaligned superpage reference mfn %lx", mfn);', '                rc = -EINVAL;', '            }', '            else if ( !mfn_valid(mfn | (L1_PAGETABLE_ENTRIES - 1)) )', '                rc = -EINVAL;', '            else if ( op.cmd == MMUEXT_MARK_SUPER )']}
description: The PV superpage functionality in arch/x86/mm.c in Xen 3.4.0, 3.4.1, and 4.1.x through 4.6.x allows local PV guests to obtain sensitive information, cause a denial of service, gain privileges, or have unspecified other impact via a crafted page identifier (MFN) to the (1) MMUEXT_MARK_SUPER or (2) MMUEXT_UNMARK_SUPER sub-op in the HYPERVISOR_mmuext_op hypercall or (3) unknown vectors related to page table updates.

code_evidence: MMUEXT_MARK_SUPER handler reads guest-controlled mfn from op.arg1.mfn, then only checks d==pg_owner, alignment (mfn & L1_PAGETABLE_ENTRIES-1), and opt_allow_superpage before calling mark_superpage(mfn_to_spage(mfn), d). No mfn_valid bounds check exists, so an out-of-range MFN is converted and dereferenced.

MMUEXT_UNMARK_SUPER handler mirrors the same path: mfn from op.arg1.mfn is only checked for ownership, alignment and the superpage option, then passed to unmark_superpage(mfn_to_spage(mfn)) without validating that the MFN is within valid frame range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of the properties (valid frame range) of an untrusted input MFN before it is used, which matches CWE-20 improper input validation. The alignment and ownership checks do not establish that the MFN is a valid frame, so the required constraint is absent.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: guest-supplied MFN in the mmuext_op hypercall is not range-validated before mfn_to_spage converts it and mark_superpage/unmark_superpage dereference superpage frame-table pointers. Trigger: a local PV guest issues MMUEXT_MARK_SUPER or MMUEXT_UNMARK_SUPER with an aligned but invalid/out-of-range MFN. Consequence: out-of-bounds frame-table access, yielding information disclosure, DoS, or privilege impact on the hypervisor.

commit_msg:
In sunxi_divs_clk_setup(), 'derived_name' is allocated by kstrndup().
It returns NULL when fails. 'derived_name' should be checked.

description: An issue was discovered in sunxi_divs_clk_setup in drivers/clk/sunxi/clk-sunxi.c in the Linux kernel through 5.1.5. There is an unchecked kstrndup of derived_name, which might allow an attacker to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash). NOTE: This id is disputed as not being an issue because “The memory allocation that was not checked is part of a code that only runs at boot time, before user processes are started. Therefore, there is no possibility for an unprivileged user to control it, and no denial of service.”

code_evidence: strchr() may return non-NULL endp, and kstrndup() at lines 33-34 can return NULL on allocation failure; the result is stored directly in derived_name and assigned to factors.name at line 35 without any NULL check.
factors.name (possibly NULL) is passed to sunxi_factors_clk_setup() at line 40; the unchecked NULL propagates into the clock setup path.

Consequence: a NULL name propagates to sunxi_factors_clk_setup(), potentially causing a NULL pointer dereference and crash (availability impact).

commit_msg:
Bug 697985: bounds check the array allocations methods

The clump allocator has four allocation functions that use 'number of elements'
and 'size of elements' parameters (rather than a simple 'number of bytes').

Those need specific bounds checking.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '', '    obj = alloc_obj(imem, (ulong) num_elements * elt_size,'], 'added_lines': ['    ulong lsize;', '    if (alloc_array_check_size(num_elements, elt_size, &lsize) == false)', '        return NULL;', '    obj = alloc_obj(imem, lsize,']}
description: The gs_alloc_ref_array function in psi/ialloc.c in Artifex Ghostscript 9.21 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PostScript document. This is related to a lack of an integer overflow check in base/gsalloc.c.

code_evidence: alloc_obj is called with the byte size computed as (ulong) num_elements * elt_size, with no check that the product fits in ulong or that num_elements*elt_size stays consistent with the allocation semantics. num_elements and elt_size are caller-supplied uint values, so a large product can wrap around.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits: the size calculation for array allocation can wrap before being passed as the allocation length, and the result is used as a memory size. This is an integer overflow feeding an undersized allocation, not merely a missing array-bound check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The multiplication of two uint operands is widened to ulong only after the product is formed within 32-bit arithmetic; a crafted num_elements/elt_size pair overflows, yielding a small byte count passed to alloc_obj. The allocator then reserves too little memory while the caller treats it as an array of num_elements elements, enabling a heap-based buffer overflow and crash.

Fix #196 and #199: Out of bound reads security issues

Check args before calling memmove() and memset() in remap_struct()
function to avoid out of bound reads which would possibly lead to
unknown code execution and/or sadf command crash.

Signed-off-by: Sebastien GODARD <sysstat@users.noreply.github.com>

memcpy(record_hdr, buffer, RECORD_HEADER_SIZE);

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflows.

The data structures linkhash and printbuf are limited to 2 GB in size
due to a signed integer being used to track their current size.

If too much data is added, then size variable can overflow, which is
an undefined behaviour in C programming language.

Assuming that a signed int overflow just leads to a negative value,
like it happens on many sytems (Linux i686/amd64 with gcc), then
printbuf is vulnerable to an out of boundary write on 64 bit systems.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (t->count >= t->size * LH_LOAD_FACTOR)', '\t\tif (lh_table_resize(t, t->size * 2) != 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (t->count >= t->size * LH_LOAD_FACTOR) {', '\t\t/* Avoid signed integer overflow with large tables. */', '\t\tint new_size = INT_MAX / 2 < t->size ? t->size * 2 : INT_MAX;', '\t\tif (t->size == INT_MAX || lh_table_resize(t, new_size) != 0)', '\t}']}
description: json-c through 0.14 has an integer overflow and out-of-bounds write via a large JSON file, as demonstrated by printbuf_memappend.

code_evidence: Line 5 computes t->size * LH_LOAD_FACTOR and compares against t->count; line 6 then passes t->size * 2 to lh_table_resize. Both multiplications operate on a signed int size field, so a sufficiently large table makes the products overflow (undefined behavior) before any resize guard is applied.

Line 8 uses t->size as the modulus, and lines 13-14 increment n and compare (int)++n == t->size. If the size value was corrupted/negative from the overflow path, the modulus and wrap-around comparison no longer bound n to a valid bucket, so t->table[n] at lines 16-18 can index outside the allocated table.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits directly: the function performs signed integer multiplications on t->size that can wrap, and the resulting value is then used as a size/offset for table access. This is a size-computation overflow, not merely a bounds-check omission (CWE-119) or a null-dereference issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signed int t->size is multiplied by LH_LOAD_FACTOR and by 2 without an upper-bound check before resize. Trigger: inserting enough entries that t->size approaches INT_MAX causes the multiplication to overflow to a small or negative value. Consequence: the resize decision and subsequent modulo/bucket indexing use an inconsistent size, enabling an out-of-bounds write to t->table[n].

commit_msg:
Similarly as b02709587ea3 ("bpf: Fix propagation of 32-bit signed bounds
from 64-bit bounds."), we also need to fix the propagation of 32 bit
unsigned bounds from 64 bit counterparts. That is, really only set the
u32_{min,max}_value when /both/ {umin,umax}_value safely fit in 32 bit
space. For example, the register with a umin_value == 1 does /not/ imply
that u32_min_value is also equal to 1, since umax_value could be much
larger than 32 bit subregister can hold, and thus u32_min_value is in
the interval [0,1] instead.

Before fix, invalid tracking result of R2_w=inv1:

  [...]
  5: R0_w=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv(id=0) R10=fp0
  5: (35) if r2 >= 0x1 goto pc+1
  [...] // goto path
  7: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2=inv(id=0,umin_value=1) R10=fp0
  7: (b6) if w2 <= 0x1 goto pc+1
  [...] // goto path
  9: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2=inv(id=0,smin_value=-9223372036854775807,smax_value=9223372032559808513,umin_value=1,umax_value=18446744069414584321,var_off=(0x1; 0xffffffff00000000),s32_min_value=1,s32_max_value=1,u32_max_value=1) R10=fp0
  9: (bc) w2 = w2
  10: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv1 R10=fp0
  [...]

After fix, correct tracking result of R2_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=1,var_off=(0x0; 0x1)):

  [...]
  5: R0_w=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv(id=0) R10=fp0
  5: (35) if r2 >= 0x1 goto pc+1
  [...] // goto path
  7: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2=inv(id=0,umin_value=1) R10=fp0
  7: (b6) if w2 <= 0x1 goto pc+1
  [...] // goto path
  9: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2=inv(id=0,smax_value=9223372032559808513,umax_value=18446744069414584321,var_off=(0x0; 0xffffffff00000001),s32_min_value=0,s32_max_value=1,u32_max_value=1) R10=fp0
  9: (bc) w2 = w2
  10: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=1,var_off=(0x0; 0x1)) R10=fp0
  [...]

Thus, same issue as in b02709587ea3 holds for unsigned subregister tracking.
Also, align __reg64_bound_u32() similarly to __reg64_bound_s32() as done in
b02709587ea3 to make them uniform again.

Fixes: 3f50f132d840 ("bpf: Verifier, do explicit ALU32 bounds tracking")
Reported-by: Manfred Paul (@_manfp)
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Reviewed-by: John Fastabend <john.fastabend@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (__reg64_bound_u32(reg->umin_value))', '\tif (__reg64_bound_u32(reg->umax_value))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (__reg64_bound_u32(reg->umin_value) && __reg64_bound_u32(reg->umax_value)) {', '\t}']}
description: This vulnerability allows local attackers to escalate privileges on affected installations of Linux Kernel 5.11.15. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability. The specific flaw exists within the handling of eBPF programs. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied eBPF programs prior to executing them. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the kernel. Was ZDI-CAN-13661.

code_evidence: Each 32-bit unsigned bound is propagated independently: u32_min_value is set from umin_value whenever umin_value fits in 32 bits, and u32_max_value is set from umax_value whenever umax_value fits, without requiring the other 64-bit bound to also fit.
__reg_deduce_bounds, __reg_bound_offset and __update_reg_bounds then consume these independently-derived u32 bounds to refine register state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a bound-conversion calculation that produces an incorrect u32 interval, and that wrong result feeds security-critical verifier decisions, matching CWE-682 Incorrect Calculation. It is a computation error rather than merely a missing check, so the target fits better than a generic validation weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (__reg64_bound_u32(reg->umin_value))
reg->u32_min_value = (u32)reg->umin_value;

if (__reg64_bound_u32(reg->umax_value))
reg->u32_max_value = (u32)reg->umax_value;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the u32 bounds are computed from umin_value and umax_value under separate conditions, so a umin_value fitting in 32 bits yields a u32_min_value even when umax_value does not fit, producing an interval that is narrower than the true 32-bit range. A verifier-tracked register whose real u32 range is [0,1] is instead recorded as a single value, so later ALU32 checks accept a path they should reject, enabling incorrect verifier conclusions on attacker-supplied eBPF programs and potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
A repeatable crash can be triggered by the perf_fuzzer on some Haswell
system.
https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/7170d3b-c17f-1ded-52aa-cc6d9ae999f4@maine.edu/

For some old CPUs (HSW and earlier), the PEBS status in a PEBS record
may be mistakenly set to 0. To minimize the impact of the defect, the
commit was introduced to try to avoid dropping the PEBS record for some
cases. It adds a check in the intel_pmu_drain_pebs_nhm(), and updates
the local pebs_status accordingly. However, it doesn't correct the PEBS
status in the PEBS record, which may trigger the crash, especially for
the large PEBS.

It's possible that all the PEBS records in a large PEBS have the PEBS
status 0. If so, the first get_next_pebs_record_by_bit() in the
__intel_pmu_pebs_event() returns NULL. The at = NULL. Since it's a large
PEBS, the 'count' parameter must > 1. The second
get_next_pebs_record_by_bit() will crash.

Besides the local pebs_status, correct the PEBS status in the PEBS
record as well.

Fixes: 01330d7288e0 ("perf/x86: Allow zero PEBS status with only single active event")
Reported-by: Vince Weaver <vincent.weaver@maine.edu>
Suggested-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Signed-off-by: Kan Liang <kan.liang@linux.intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/1615555298-140216-1-git-send-email-kan.liang@linux.intel.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tpebs_status = cpuc->pebs_enabled;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tpebs_status = p->status = cpuc->pebs_enabled;']}
description: In intel_pmu_drain_pebs_nhm in arch/x86/events/intel/ds.c in the Linux kernel through 5.11.8 on some Haswell CPUs, userspace applications (such as perf-fuzzer) can cause a system crash because the PEBS status in a PEBS record is mishandled, aka CID-d88d05a9e0b6.

code_evidence: Line 29 reads p->status and masks it; when the hardware reports a zero PEBS status, pebs_status becomes zero. Lines 36-38 special-case this by substituting cpuc->pebs_enabled into the local pebs_status only, leaving p->status uncorrected.
Lines 39-42 then call find_first_bit on the substituted status; the record itself still carries the anomalous zero status for later consumers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is improper handling of an exceptional condition: the zero-status defect is partially corrected locally (lines 36-38) but the record is left inconsistent, so the exceptional state is not fully handled and later processing faults. The fix stores the corrected value into p->status, confirming the mishandled exception.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the exceptional zero-PEBS-status condition is worked around only in the local variable, not in the PEBS record, so the anomalous status persists in the buffer. Trigger: on Haswell and earlier CPUs, a large PEBS where all records report status 0. The downstream drain path can then fail to locate a record and dereference a NULL pointer, crashing the system.

commit_msg:
avcodec/mpeg4videodec: Clear interlaced_dct for studio profile

Fixes: Out of array access
Fixes: 13090/clusterfuzz-testcase-minimized-ffmpeg_AV_CODEC_ID_MPEG4_fuzzer-5408668986638336

Found-by: continuous fuzzing process https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz/tree/master/projects/ffmpeg
Reviewed-by: Kieran Kunhya <kierank@obe.tv>
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    s->interlaced_dct = 0;']}
description: The studio profile decoder in libavcodec/mpeg4videodec.c in FFmpeg 4.0 before 4.0.4 and 4.1 before 4.1.2 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-array access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted MPEG-4 video data.

code_evidence: The function initializes s->partitioned_frame and s->decode_mb but, before the patch, leaves s->interlaced_dct at its previously decoded value.
s->progressive_frame is derived from a single bit and may be set, but interlaced_dct is not reset here for the studio profile.
s->alternate_scan and frame_pred_frame_dct come from bitstream bits and feed scan-table selection, so a stale interlaced_dct can steer later decoding down an inconsistent path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit explicitly fixes an out-of-array access by clearing interlaced_dct, and the description confirms an out-of-bounds read via crafted MPEG-4 data. CWE-125 fits the read past the intended buffer; it is not a write overflow (CWE-787) because the reported consequence is an out-of-array read.

evidence_lines.code:
s->partitioned_frame = 0;
s->decode_mb = mpeg4_decode_studio_mb;
s->progressive_frame = get_bits1(gb) ^ 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the studio VOP header parser does not reset s->interlaced_dct, so state from a prior frame persists while other DCT/scan state is reinitialized from the current bitstream. Trigger: crafted MPEG-4 studio-profile data that leaves interlaced_dct set while the current frame's scan/decoding parameters differ. This inconsistent state leads later macroblock decoding to access a scan table or buffer out of bounds, causing an out-of-array read (DoS or unspecified impact).

commit_msg:
x86/vpt: fix race when migrating timers between vCPUs

The current vPT code will migrate the emulated timers between vCPUs
(change the pt->vcpu field) while just holding the destination lock,
either from create_periodic_time or pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target if
the global target is adjusted. Changing the periodic_timer vCPU field
in this way creates a race where a third party could grab the lock in
the unlocked region of pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target (or before
create_periodic_time performs the vcpu change) and then release the
lock from a different vCPU, creating a locking imbalance.

Introduce a per-domain rwlock in order to protect periodic_time
migration between vCPU lists. Taking the lock in read mode prevents
any timer from being migrated to a different vCPU, while taking it in
write mode allows performing migration of timers across vCPUs. The
per-vcpu locks are still used to protect all the other fields from the
periodic_timer struct.

Note that such migration shouldn't happen frequently, and hence
there's no performance drop as a result of such locking.

This is XSA-336.

Reported-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Tested-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    spin_unlock(&pt->vcpu->arch.hvm.tm_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    pt_vcpu_unlock(pt->vcpu);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There is a race condition when migrating timers between x86 HVM vCPUs. When migrating timers of x86 HVM guests between its vCPUs, the locking model used allows for a second vCPU of the same guest (also operating on the timers) to release a lock that it didn't acquire. The most likely effect of the issue is a hang or crash of the hypervisor, i.e., a Denial of Service (DoS). All versions of Xen are affected. Only x86 systems are vulnerable. Arm systems are not vulnerable. Only x86 HVM guests can leverage the vulnerability. x86 PV and PVH cannot leverage the vulnerability. Only guests with more than one vCPU can exploit the vulnerability.

code_evidence: pt_unlock releases pt->vcpu->arch.hvm.tm_lock by dereferencing pt->vcpu at unlock time, rather than releasing the vCPU lock that was acquired when pt_lock was called.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The acquire/release pair is not atomic with respect to migration of the shared periodic_time's vCPU target, so an interfering sequence can alter which lock is released. This is a concurrent shared-resource synchronization flaw matching CWE-362, distinct from a mere deadlock.

evidence_lines.code: spin_unlock(&pt->vcpu->arch.hvm.tm_lock);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The lock is identified through the mutable pt->vcpu field, which can be migrated to another vCPU between acquisition and release. If another code path changes pt->vcpu while the destination lock is held, pt_unlock releases a lock belonging to a different vCPU than the one that acquired it, creating a locking imbalance. The supported consequence is hypervisor instability (hang or crash), i.e., denial of service.

description: Heap-based buffer overflow in libavformat/http.c in FFmpeg before 2.8.10, 3.0.x before 3.0.5, 3.1.x before 3.1.6, and 3.2.x before 3.2.2 allows remote web servers to execute arbitrary code via a negative chunk size in an HTTP response.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tmemset(&n->entries[tcount], 0, sizeof(MnoteFujiEntry));']}
description: An issue was discovered in libexif before 0.6.22. Use of uninitialized memory in EXIF Makernote handling could lead to crashes and potential use-after-free conditions.

code_evidence: n->entries is allocated for c MnoteFujiEntry records at line 29, but no per-entry initialization is performed before the loop. The loop writes tag, format, components and order at lines 42-45, then computes size s at line 56 and stores it at line 57. commit_msg:
perf: Tighten (and fix) the grouping condition

The fix from 9fc81d87420d ("perf: Fix events installation during
moving group") was incomplete in that it failed to recognise that
creating a group with events for different CPUs is semantically
broken -- they cannot be co-scheduled.

Furthermore, it leads to real breakage where, when we create an event
for CPU Y and then migrate it to form a group on CPU X, the code gets
confused where the counter is programmed -- triggered in practice
as well by me via the perf fuzzer.

Fix this by tightening the rules for creating groups. Only allow
grouping of counters that can be co-scheduled in the same context.
This means for the same task and/or the same cpu.

Fixes: 9fc81d87420d ("perf: Fix events installation during moving group")
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Arnaldo Carvalho de Melo <acme@kernel.org>
Cc: Jiri Olsa <jolsa@redhat.com>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20150123125834.090683288@infradead.org
Signed-off-by: Ingo Molnar <mingo@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tcpuctx->ctx.type = cpu_context;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: kernel/events/core.c in the Linux kernel before 3.19 mishandles counter grouping, which allows local users to gain privileges via a crafted application, related to the perf_pmu_register and perf_event_open functions.

code_evidence: The function resolves a shared per-PMU CPU context via find_pmu_context() and reuses it when found (lines 27-29), otherwise allocates per-CPU contexts and initializes each cpuctx->ctx (lines 34-45).

In the changed function the removed assignment cpuctx->ctx.type = cpu_context (line 40 in func_before) is absent; the context type is no longer forced here, so the type of a reused/reinitialized context is not constrained by this registration path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in managing permissions/privileges used for access control. Here a missing context-type constraint on PMU registration lets a crafted perf_event_open group misprogram counters and escalate privileges, matching that category. It is broader than a pure numeric/type-confusion defect because the consequence is an access-control/privilege violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The registration path no longer pins each per-CPU context to the cpu_context type. A PMU whose context is shared or reused can leave the context type unset or inconsistent, so later grouping logic in perf_event_open cannot reliably distinguish CPU-bound from task-bound contexts. The commit message states this leads to counters being programmed in the wrong context, enabling a local user to craft an event group that crosses contexts and gain privileges.

commit_msg: dns: fix crash issue
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (_dns_left_len(context) < 2) {', '\t\t\t\treturn -1;', '\t\t\t}', '', '\tif (_dns_left_len(context) < 1) {', '\t\treturn -1;', '\t}', '']}
description: SmartDNS through 41 before 56d0332 allows an out-of-bounds write because of a stack-based buffer overflow in the _dns_encode_domain function in the dns.c file, via a crafted DNS request.

code_evidence: When a prior domain suffix is found, the code writes a two-byte compression pointer via _dns_write_short(&ptr_num, offset) and advances context->ptr without first verifying that two bytes remain available in the output buffer.

After the label loop, *ptr_num = num writes the length byte and the terminator is written at context->ptr, but the remaining-space check occurs only after these writes, so the bounds check is too late to prevent the write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is missing bounds checks before writing DNS encoding bytes, producing a write beyond the destination buffer, which directly matches CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. This is not merely a read overrun; the defect is an unchecked write past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function emits DNS label length bytes, label data and compression pointers through context->ptr without confirming sufficient remaining buffer space before each write. A crafted domain requiring more output than the remaining buffer causes writes past the end of the destination buffer, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially crashing or enabling code execution.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/719
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (ignore == (TIFFFieldInfo *) NULL)', '    return;']}
description: ImageMagick 7.0.7-0 has a NULL Pointer Dereference in TIFFIgnoreTags in coders/tiff.c.

code_evidence: Line 40 allocates 'ignore' via AcquireQuantumMemory(count,...) but the return value is not checked against NULL before use.
Line 41 passes the possibly-NULL 'ignore' to ResetMagickMemory, and lines 42-52 subsequently write ignore[i].field_tag and pass 'ignore' to TIFFMergeFieldInfo without any NULL guard.

ResetMagickMemory(ignore,0,count*sizeof(*ignore));

The trigger is an allocation failure (e.g., large count from the tiff:ignore-tags artifact); the subsequent ResetMagickMemory and field writes dereference NULL, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Merge pull request from GHSA-8hcp-hm38-mfph

* Check hostname during TLS transport selection

* revision based on feedback

* remove the code in create_request that has been moved
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tpj_strdup(tdata->pool, &tdata->dest_info.name, ', '\t\t  &res_addr->dst_host.addr.host);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!tdata->dest_info.name.slen) {', '\t    pj_strdup(tdata->pool, &tdata->dest_info.name, ', '\t\t      &res_addr->dst_host.addr.host);', '\t}']}
description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In version 2.10 and earlier, PJSIP transport can be reused if they have the same IP address + port + protocol. However, this is insufficient for secure transport since it lacks remote hostname authentication. Suppose we have created a TLS connection to `sip.foo.com`, which has an IP address `100.1.1.1`. If we want to create a TLS connection to another hostname, say `sip.bar.com`, which has the same IP address, then it will reuse that existing connection, even though `100.1.1.1` does not have certificate to authenticate as `sip.bar.com`. The vulnerability allows for an insecure interaction without user awareness. It affects users who need access to connections to different destinations that translate to the same address, and allows man-in-the-middle attack if attacker can route a connection to another destination such as in the case of DNS spoofing.

code_evidence: In the no-explicit-transport branch, the function unconditionally copies res_addr->dst_host.addr.host into tdata->dest_info.name and then resolves/sends via pjsip_endpt_resolve; it does not verify that this destination hostname matches the hostname already bound to any reused TLS transport. The diff adds a guard preserving an existing dest_info.name, but the function itself still lacks any hostname/certificate comparison before transport selection.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-295 fits because the code fails to validate that the certificate/identity of the reused secure transport matches the requested destination hostname; the weakness is improper certificate/hostname validation for TLS, not merely a generic address-reuse bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The destination hostname is recorded and used for resolution without checking it against the identity authenticated by an existing TLS transport. When two distinct hostnames resolve to the same IP/port/protocol, a connection established for one hostname can be reused for the other, so the peer certificate is not validated for the requested name, enabling a man-in-the-middle/identity confusion.

commit_msg: Fix rare race condition when claiming sessions
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif(session != NULL && !g_atomic_int_get(&session->destroyed) && session->source != NULL && session->source->transport != NULL) {', '\t\t/* Send this to the transport client */', '\t\tJANUS_LOG(LOG_HUGE, "Sending event to %s (%p)\\n", session->source->transport->get_package(), session->source->instance);', '\t\tsession->source->transport->send_message(session->source->instance, NULL, FALSE, event);', '\t\t/* No transport, free the event */'], 'added_lines': ['\tif(session != NULL && !g_atomic_int_get(&session->destroyed)) {', '\t\tjanus_mutex_lock(&session->mutex);', '\t\tif(session->source != NULL && session->source->transport != NULL) {', '\t\t\t/* Send this to the transport client */', '\t\t\tJANUS_LOG(LOG_HUGE, "Sending event to %s (%p)\\n", session->source->transport->get_package(), session->source->instance);', '\t\t\tsession->source->transport->send_message(session->source->instance, NULL, FALSE, event);', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t\t/* No transport, free the event */', '\t\t\tjson_decref(event);', '\t\t}', '\t\tjanus_mutex_unlock(&session->mutex);', '\t\t/* No session, free the event */']}
description: An issue was discovered in Janus through 0.9.1. janus.c has multiple concurrent threads that misuse the source property of a session, leading to a race condition when claiming sessions.

code_evidence: The function reads session->source and session->source->transport in the condition and then dereferences them in the log call and send_message without any synchronization. Since the commit notes multiple concurrent threads misuse session->source, another thread can reassign or clear session->source between the check and the dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because concurrent threads access the shared session->source resource without exclusive synchronization, creating a timing window between validation and use. This is a race condition rather than a simple missing NULL check, since the pointer is valid at check time but can change concurrently.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the check-then-use of the shared session->source pointer is not atomic or protected by a lock. Trigger: a concurrent thread changes session->source after the NULL checks in line 2 but before the dereferences on lines 3-4. Supported consequence: the send_message call may operate on a stale or freed source, causing a crash or use-after-free; the fix adds session->mutex around the access.

description: In FreeRDP before version 2.1.2, there is an out of bounds read in TrioParse. Logging might bypass string length checks due to an integer overflow. This is fixed in version 2.1.2.

Trigger: caller passes a negative precision; the resulting length causes the read loop to overrun the string buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read (memory disclosure/crash).

commit_msg:
PR22201, DW_AT_name with out of bounds reference

DW_AT_name ought to always have a string value.

	PR 22201
	* dwarf2.c (scan_unit_for_symbols): Ignore DW_AT_name unless it
	has string form.
	(parse_comp_unit): Likewise.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t  var->name = attr.u.str;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t  if (is_str_attr (attr.form))', '\t\t    var->name = attr.u.str;']}
description: dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, does not validate the DW_AT_name data type, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (bfd_hash_hash NULL pointer dereference, or out-of-bounds access, and application crash) via a crafted ELF file, related to scan_unit_for_symbols and parse_comp_unit.

code_evidence: In the variable branch, the DW_AT_name case assigns var->name = attr.u.str unconditionally, without checking is_str_attr (attr.form). For a non-string form, attr.u.str is not a valid string pointer (the union holds other data, e.g. a block pointer or value), so var->name later receives a bogus pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked DW_AT_name assignment stores a pointer that may be NULL/invalid and is later dereferenced, matching CWE-476 NULL Pointer Dereference. This is not merely a type-confusion issue; the supported consequence is dereferencing an invalid pointer derived from the union.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: read_attribute populates attr.u based on the DWARF form; a crafted ELF can supply DW_AT_name with a non-string form, making attr.u.str an invalid/NULL pointer. The unchecked assignment stores it into var->name; downstream hashing/name use dereferences it, causing a crash or out-of-bounds access (the same fix adds is_str_attr checks at the func branch and parse_comp_unit).

commit_msg:
Fix tf.raw_ops. QuantizedMatMul vulnerability from non scalar min/max a/b arguments.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 465364257
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(context, TensorShapeUtils::IsScalar(context->input(2).shape()),', '                errors::InvalidArgument("min_a must be a scalar, but got shape",', '                                        context->input(2).shape()));', '    OP_REQUIRES(context, context->input(3).NumElements() == 1,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("max_a must be a scalar, but got shape",', '                                        context->input(3).shape()));', '    OP_REQUIRES(context, context->input(4).NumElements() == 1,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("min_b must be a scalar, but got shape",', '                                        context->input(4).shape()));', '    OP_REQUIRES(context, context->input(5).NumElements() == 1,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("max_b must be a scalar, but got shape",', '                                        context->input(5).shape()));']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. If `QuantizedMatMul` is given nonscalar input for: `min_a`, `max_a`, `min_b`, or `max_b` It gives a segfault that can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit aca766ac7693bf29ed0df55ad6bfcc78f35e7f48. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The function reads min_a, max_a, min_b and max_b directly via context->input(2..5).flat<float>()(0) without first verifying that each input tensor is a scalar. flat<float>()(0) assumes at least one element and scalar semantics, so a non-scalar or empty tensor is dereferenced without a shape/element-count check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is exactly improper input validation (CWE-20): the code consumes externally supplied tensors without checking their required shape/size property. The missing scalar constraint on inputs 2-5 is the unsafe operation; the segfault is only the downstream consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation of the expected scalar property of the four quantization-range inputs before indexing element 0. Trigger: a caller supplies a non-scalar (or empty) tensor for min_a/max_a/min_b/max_b. Consequence: out-of-bounds element access leading to a segfault, i.e. a denial of service. The later max_a > min_a checks do not establish scalar shape and occur after the unsafe reads.

commit_msg:
Don't try to be smart about probing the min/max tim_t values.
Just assume that a signed time_t is really a 64-bit or 32-bit integer.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tconst uintmax_t max_unsigned_time_t = (uintmax_t)(~(time_t)0);', '\t\tconst uintmax_t max_signed_time_t = max_unsigned_time_t >> 1;', '\t\treturn (time_t)max_signed_time_t;'], 'added_lines': ["\t\t/* Assume it's the same as int64_t or int32_t */", '\t\tif (sizeof(time_t) == sizeof(int64_t)) {', '\t\t\treturn (time_t)INT64_MAX;', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t\treturn (time_t)INT32_MAX;', '\t\t}']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the (1) get_time_t_max and (2) get_time_t_min functions in archive_read_support_format_mtree.c in libarchive before 3.2.0 allow remote attackers to have unspecified impact via a crafted mtree file, which triggers undefined behavior.

code_evidence: When time_t is signed, the function derives the maximum signed value by casting ~(time_t)0 to uintmax_t, shifting right by one, and casting the result back to time_t. The intermediate arithmetic is done in uintmax_t while the return type is the narrower signed time_t.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is an integer calculation whose result is assumed to fit the signed time_t representation but may overflow/wrap on narrowing conversion, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a signedness or truncation issue because the computed boundary value itself is wrong, not just misinterpreted.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the max signed time_t is computed via unsigned arithmetic and an unchecked narrowing conversion back to time_t, so the value can exceed the signed time_t range and become implementation-defined or trigger undefined behavior. Trigger: this branch is taken whenever TIME_T_MAX is undefined and time_t is signed; the resulting boundary value is then used as a min/max limit for parsed mtree timestamps. Consequence: integer overflow/wraparound in time-bound checks, leading to unspecified impact on crafted-file parsing.

commit_msg:
dccp/tcp: fix routing redirect race

As Eric Dumazet pointed out this also needs to be fixed in IPv6.
v2: Contains the IPv6 tcp/Ipv6 dccp patches as well.

We have seen a few incidents lately where a dst_enty has been freed
with a dangling TCP socket reference (sk->sk_dst_cache) pointing to that
dst_entry. If the conditions/timings are right a crash then ensues when the
freed dst_entry is referenced later on. A Common crashing back trace is:

 #8 [] page_fault at ffffffff8163e648
    [exception RIP: __tcp_ack_snd_check+74]
.
.
 #9 [] tcp_rcv_established at ffffffff81580b64
#10 [] tcp_v4_do_rcv at ffffffff8158b54a
#11 [] tcp_v4_rcv at ffffffff8158cd02
#12 [] ip_local_deliver_finish at ffffffff815668f4
#13 [] ip_local_deliver at ffffffff81566bd9
#14 [] ip_rcv_finish at ffffffff8156656d
#15 [] ip_rcv at ffffffff81566f06
#16 [] __netif_receive_skb_core at ffffffff8152b3a2
#17 [] __netif_receive_skb at ffffffff8152b608
#18 [] netif_receive_skb at ffffffff8152b690
#19 [] vmxnet3_rq_rx_complete at ffffffffa015eeaf [vmxnet3]
#20 [] vmxnet3_poll_rx_only at ffffffffa015f32a [vmxnet3]
#21 [] net_rx_action at ffffffff8152bac2
#22 [] __do_softirq at ffffffff81084b4f
#23 [] call_softirq at ffffffff8164845c
#24 [] do_softirq at ffffffff81016fc5
#25 [] irq_exit at ffffffff81084ee5
#26 [] do_IRQ at ffffffff81648ff8

Of course it may happen with other NIC drivers as well.

It's found the freed dst_entry here:

 224 static bool tcp_in_quickack_mode(struct sock *sk)↩
 225 {↩
 226 ▹       const struct inet_connection_sock *icsk = inet_csk(sk);↩
 227 ▹       const struct dst_entry *dst = __sk_dst_get(sk);↩
 228 ↩
 229 ▹       return (dst && dst_metric(dst, RTAX_QUICKACK)) ||↩
 230 ▹       ▹       (icsk->icsk_ack.quick && !icsk->icsk_ack.pingpong);↩
 231 }↩

But there are other backtraces attributed to the same freed dst_entry in
netfilter code as well.

All the vmcores showed 2 significant clues:

- Remote hosts behind the default gateway had always been redirected to a
different gateway. A rtable/dst_entry will be added for that host. Making
more dst_entrys with lower reference counts. Making this more probable.

- All vmcores showed a postitive LockDroppedIcmps value, e.g:

LockDroppedIcmps                  267

A closer look at the tcp_v4_err() handler revealed that do_redirect() will run
regardless of whether user space has the socket locked. This can result in a
race condition where the same dst_entry cached in sk->sk_dst_entry can be
decremented twice for the same socket via:

do_redirect()->__sk_dst_check()-> dst_release().

Which leads to the dst_entry being prematurely freed with another socket
pointing to it via sk->sk_dst_cache and a subsequent crash.

To fix this skip do_redirect() if usespace has the socket locked. Instead let
the redirect take place later when user space does not have the socket
locked.

The dccp/IPv6 code is very similar in this respect, so fixing it there too.

As Eric Garver pointed out the following commit now invalidates routes. Which
can set the dst->obsolete flag so that ipv4_dst_check() returns null and
triggers the dst_release().

Fixes: ceb3320610d6 ("ipv4: Kill routes during PMTU/redirect updates.")
Cc: Eric Garver <egarver@redhat.com>
Cc: Hannes Sowa <hsowa@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Jon Maxwell <jmaxwell37@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tstruct dst_entry *dst = __sk_dst_check(sk, np->dst_cookie);', '\t\tif (dst)', '\t\t\tdst->ops->redirect(dst, sk, skb);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!sock_owned_by_user(sk)) {', '\t\t\tstruct dst_entry *dst = __sk_dst_check(sk, np->dst_cookie);', '\t\t\tif (dst)', '\t\t\t\tdst->ops->redirect(dst, sk, skb);', '\t\t}']}
description: Race condition in the audit_log_single_execve_arg function in kernel/auditsc.c in the Linux kernel through 4.7 allows local users to bypass intended character-set restrictions or disrupt system-call auditing by changing a certain string, aka a "double fetch" vulnerability.

code_evidence: Line 31 acquires the socket lock with bh_lock_sock, and lines 32-33 merely count a dropped ICMP when sock_owned_by_user(sk) is true, then continue processing.

For NDISC_REDIRECT (lines 49-53), the code calls __sk_dst_check and dst->ops->redirect on the cached dst_entry without checking whether user space already owns the socket, so this path runs even while the socket is locked by another context.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent access to a shared resource (the cached dst_entry) lacking proper synchronization, matching CWE-362. The fix adds a sock_owned_by_user guard so redirect is deferred while the socket is locked, confirming the race rather than a simple use-after-free caused by a missing reference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The redirect handling mutates the shared sk->sk_dst_cache without respecting ownership of the socket lock. When user space holds the lock, an incoming ICMPv6 redirect concurrently invokes __sk_dst_check, which can release the cached dst_entry; a second release/free leaves sk->sk_dst_cache dangling, and later use causes a crash.

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Don't have %cr4.fsgsbase active behind a guest kernels back

Currently, a 64bit PV guest can appear to set and clear FSGSBASE in %cr4, but
the bit remains set in hardware.  Therefore, the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE are usable
even when the guest kernel believes that they are disabled.

The FSGSBASE feature isn't currently supported in Linux, and its context
switch path has some optimisations which rely on userspace being unable to use
the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions.  Xen's current behaviour undermines this
expectation.

In 64bit PV guest context, always load the guest kernels setting of FSGSBASE
into %cr4.  This requires adjusting how Xen uses the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE
instructions.

 * Delete the cpu_has_fsgsbase helper.  It is no longer safe, as users need to
   check %cr4 directly.
 * The raw __rd{fs,gs}base() helpers are only safe to use when %cr4.fsgsbase
   is set.  Comment this property.
 * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}{base,shadow}() and read_msr() helpers are updated to use
   the current %cr4 value to determine which mechanism to use.
 * toggle_guest_mode() and save_segments() are update to avoid reading
   fs/gsbase if the values in hardware cannot be stale WRT struct vcpu.  A
   consequence of this is that the write_cr() path needs to cache the current
   bases, as subsequent context switches will skip saving the values.
 * write_cr4() is updated to ensure that the shadow %cr4.fsgsbase value is
   observed in a safe way WRT the hardware setting, if an interrupt happens to
   hit in the middle.
 * load_segments() is updated to use the VMLOAD optimisation if FSGSBASE is
   unavailable, even if only gs_shadow needs updating.  As a minor perf
   improvement, check cpu_has_svm first to short circuit a context-dependent
   conditional on Intel hardware.
 * pv_make_cr4() is updated for 64bit PV guests to use the guest kernels
   choice of FSGSBASE.

This is part of XSA-293.

Reported-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        /*', "         * If this write will disable FSGSBASE, refresh Xen's idea of the", '         * guest bases now that they can no longer change.', '         */', '        if ( (curr->arch.pv.ctrlreg[4] & X86_CR4_FSGSBASE) &&', '             !(val & X86_CR4_FSGSBASE) )', '        {', '            curr->arch.pv.fs_base = __rdfsbase();', '            curr->arch.pv.gs_base_kernel = __rdgsbase();', '        }', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges because a guest can manipulate its virtualised %cr4 in a way that is incompatible with Linux (and possibly other guest kernels).

code_evidence: Case 4 handles a guest write to CR4: the guest-supplied val is passed to pv_fixup_guest_cr4 and then pv_make_cr4 before write_cr4, with no check that the resulting FSGSBASE state is consistent with the hardware bit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is that the guest-supplied CR4 input is not validated for the required property (FSGSBASE consistency with hardware), which is improper input validation (CWE-20).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The guest controls the CR4 value written via write_cr, and the function accepts it without ensuring the FSGSBASE bit actually takes effect in hardware. The guest kernel may believe FSGSBASE is disabled while hardware retains it, letting the guest use WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions, undermining the guest kernel's context-switch assumptions and enabling privilege escalation or DoS.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>

description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

commit_msg:
Fixed bug in 'lua_upvaluejoin'

Bug-fix: joining an upvalue with itself could cause a use-after-free
crash.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      return *getupvalref(L, fidx, n, NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['      return *getupvalref(L, fidx, n);']}
description: Lua 5.3.5 has a use-after-free in lua_upvaluejoin in lapi.c. For example, a crash outcome might be achieved by an attacker who is able to trigger a debug.upvaluejoin call in which the arguments have certain relationships.

code_evidence: lua_upvalueid resolves fidx to a stack slot, and for a Lua closure returns the upvalue's value via getupvalref(L, fidx, n, NULL), passing NULL for the owner reference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Returning a pointer into an upvalue whose ownership is not captured enables a later reference to memory that has been freed, matching CWE-416 use-after-free; the fix changes the call so the owner is tracked, preventing the invalid referencing path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The call passes NULL as the upvalue-owner output. When the target upvalue belongs to the same closure being joined (debug.upvaluejoin with related arguments), the missing owner tracking lets the join create a self-referential upvalue whose storage is then freed, and later upvalue access dereferences that freed memory, causing a use-after-free crash.

commit_msg:
When creating a raw AF_ISDN socket, CAP_NET_RAW needs to be checked
first.

Signed-off-by: Ori Nimron <orinimron123@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!capable(CAP_NET_RAW))', '\t\treturn -EPERM;']}
description: base_sock_create in drivers/isdn/mISDN/socket.c in the AF_ISDN network module in the Linux kernel through 5.3.2 does not enforce CAP_NET_RAW, which means that unprivileged users can create a raw socket, aka CID-b91ee4aa2a21.

code_evidence: The function only validates the socket type (SOCK_RAW) and returns -ESOCKTNOSUPPORT otherwise; there is no privilege/capability check before proceeding.

After the type check, the code allocates and initializes a raw ISDN socket (sk_alloc, sock_init_data, sock->ops = &base_sock_ops) and links it into base_sockets, returning success without verifying the caller holds CAP_NET_RAW.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an action (creating a privileged raw socket) without any authorization check, matching CWE-862 Missing Authorization. It is not merely improper input validation; the missing security control is the capability/authorization gate.

evidence_lines.code:
if (sock->type != SOCK_RAW)
return -ESOCKTNOSUPPORT;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: base_sock_create lacks an authorization check on the caller's capabilities before creating a raw AF_ISDN socket. Trigger: an unprivileged user calls socket(AF_ISDN, SOCK_RAW, ...). Consequence: the raw socket is allocated and registered, letting unprivileged users obtain raw socket access that should require CAP_NET_RAW.

Sanity check the total_length to make sure it doesn't go negative.
