Change-Id: I87e38f6c792fa81184e4c412d6433fbbf2060f28
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/25744
Reviewed-by: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
Petri-Dish: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Anders Broman <a.broman58@gmail.com>
(cherry picked from commit ba3cfb403a403647241062b933ff82808ac62a59)
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/25753
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (total_length < 0)', '        return length;']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-wccp.c had a large loop that was addressed by ensuring that a calculated length was monotonically increasing.

code_evidence: The loop iterates number_of_elements times, a value read from the packet via tvb_get_ntohl at line 19. Inside the loop, dissect_wccp2_web_cache_value_element returns new_length, and total_length accumulates length - new_length without any check that progress is being made or that total_length stays non-negative. The patch adds a total_length < 0 guard immediately after this accumulation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 (Excessive Iteration) fits because the function performs a loop whose iteration count is not sufficiently limited relative to available data, allowing an attacker-influenced excessive iteration. This is a resource-consumption DoS, not an out-of-bounds read/write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound number_of_elements is attacker-controlled and the per-iteration length accounting can make total_length go negative, so the loop can run far longer than the actual packet data supports. Trigger: a crafted WCCP packet with a large element count and value elements that return lengths causing negative accumulation. Consequence: a very long loop consuming CPU, causing a DoS (the commit title and description identify a large loop bug).

commit_msg:
Add checks that supplied samples are bounded within bits-per-sample

Credit: Oss-Fuzz
Issue: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=19758
Issue: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=31727
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tuint32_t i, j = 0, channel;'], 'added_lines': ['\tuint32_t i, j = 0, k = 0, channel;', '\tconst FLAC__int32 sample_max = INT32_MAX >> (32 - encoder->protected_->bits_per_sample);', '\tconst FLAC__int32 sample_min = INT32_MIN >> (32 - encoder->protected_->bits_per_sample);', '\t\t\tfor(i = encoder->private_->current_sample_number, k = j; i <= blocksize && k < samples; i++, k++) {', '\t\t\t\tif(buffer[channel][k] < sample_min || buffer[channel][k] > sample_max){', '\t\t\t\t\tencoder->protected_->state = FLAC__STREAM_ENCODER_CLIENT_ERROR;', '\t\t\t\t\treturn false;', '\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t}']}
description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability in function bitwriter_grow_ in flac before 1.4.0 allows remote attackers to run arbitrary code via crafted input to the encoder.

code_evidence: Loop iterates channels and copies n samples from caller buffer[channel]+j into integer_signal[channel] at current_sample_number using memcpy with size sizeof(int32)*n. The only guard checks buffer[channel]==NULL; there is no validation that samples fit the destination blocksize or that channel data stays within the bits-per-sample range before the copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the function performs a buffer copy (memcpy) into an output buffer without verifying the input size against the destination capacity. This is a classic buffer copy overflow, not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) or an integer size-calculation error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the memcpy at line 17 copies n elements into integer_signal without ensuring n is bounded by the remaining destination capacity derived from blocksize and current_sample_number. Trigger: crafted samples/block parameters cause n to exceed available space. Consequence: out-of-bounds write into the encoder's signal buffer, enabling memory corruption and potential code execution.

commit_msg: Fixed oob read in irp_write and similar
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void nego_process_negotiation_request(rdpNego* nego, wStream* s)'], 'added_lines': ['BOOL nego_process_negotiation_request(rdpNego* nego, wStream* s)', '', '\tif (Stream_GetRemainingLength(s) < 7)', '\t\treturn FALSE;', '\treturn TRUE;']}
description: In FreeRDP before 2.1.0, there is an out-of-bound read in irp functions (parallel_process_irp_create, serial_process_irp_create, drive_process_irp_write, printer_process_irp_write, rdpei_recv_pdu, serial_process_irp_write). This has been fixed in 2.1.0.

code_evidence: The function reads a BYTE, UINT16 and UINT32 sequentially from stream s via Stream_Read_UINT8/16/32 without first checking Stream_GetRemainingLength(s). No length or bounds validation precedes the three reads, so the stream cursor can advance beyond the available buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the reads access memory beyond the intended buffer end. This is a read overflow, not a write (CWE-787) and not an integer issue; the missing precondition is a buffer-length constraint on the stream.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the absence of a remaining-length check before consuming 7 bytes (1+2+4) from the input stream. Trigger: a negotiation request whose stream buffer holds fewer than 7 bytes. Consequence: Stream_Read_* dereferences past the end of the buffer, an out-of-bounds read affecting confidentiality/availability.

commit_msg:
virtio_console: Assure used length from device is limited

The buf->len might come from an untrusted device. This
ensures the value would not exceed the size of the buffer
to avoid data corruption or loss.

Signed-off-by: Xie Yongji <xieyongji@bytedance.com>
Acked-by: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210525125622.1203-1-xieyongji@bytedance.com
Signed-off-by: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tbuf->len = len;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tbuf->len = min_t(size_t, len, buf->size);']}
description: In drivers/char/virtio_console.c in the Linux kernel before 5.13.4, data corruption or loss can be triggered by an untrusted device that supplies a buf->len value exceeding the buffer size. NOTE: the vendor indicates that the cited data corruption is not a vulnerability in any existing use case; the length validation was added solely for robustness in the face of anomalous host OS behavior

code_evidence: virtqueue_get_buf(port->in_vq, &len) returns a device-supplied length into the unsigned len; the code then assigns buf->len = len without comparing len against buf->size, and also accumulates len into port->stats.bytes_received.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an input length and records it as a buffer length without checking it against the destination buffer size, matching CWE-120's unchecked-size condition; the missing min(len, buf->size) bound is the required constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the untrusted device-reported length is stored as the in-buffer length with no upper bound. Trigger: a malicious or anomalous host returns len larger than buf->size. Consequence: downstream consumers trust buf->len and can read/write past the allocated buffer, causing data corruption or loss.

commit_msg:
When an ULP-enabled socket enters the LISTEN status, the listener ULP data
pointer is copied inside the child/accepted sockets by sk_clone_lock().

The relevant ULP can take care of de-duplicating the context pointer via
the clone() operation, but only MPTCP and SMC implement such op.

Other ULPs may end-up with a double-free at socket disposal time.

We can't simply clear the ULP data at clone time, as TLS replaces the
socket ops with custom ones assuming a valid TLS ULP context is
available.

Instead completely prevent clone-less ULP sockets from entering the
LISTEN status.

Fixes: 734942cc4ea6 ("tcp: ULP infrastructure")
Reported-by: slipper <slipper.alive@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Abeni <pabeni@redhat.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/4b80c3d1dbe3d0ab072f80450c202d9bc88b4b03.1672740602.git.pabeni@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\terr = inet_ulp_can_listen(sk);', '\tif (unlikely(err))', '\t\treturn err;']}
description:
There is a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux Kernel which can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation. To reach the vulnerability kernel configuration flag CONFIG_TLS or CONFIG_XFRM_ESPINTCP has to be configured, but the operation does not require any privilege.

There is a use-after-free bug of icsk_ulp_data of a struct inet_connection_sock.

When CONFIG_TLS is enabled, user can install a tls context (struct tls_context) on a connected tcp socket. The context is not cleared if this socket is disconnected and reused as a listener. If a new socket is created from the listener, the context is inherited and vulnerable.

The setsockopt TCP_ULP operation does not require any privilege.

We recommend upgrading past commit 2c02d41d71f90a5168391b6a5f2954112ba2307c

code_evidence: The function declares err and proceeds directly to allocate the accept queue and enter TCP_LISTEN without validating the socket's ULP context; the added inet_ulp_can_listen() guard is absent from this version.

After the state is set to TCP_LISTEN and the port is bound/hashed, the function returns success; child sockets created via sk_clone_lock() inherit icsk_ulp_data, so a clone-less ULP context (e.g., TLS) is shared with accepted sockets.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The inherited icsk_ulp_data pointer is freed by one socket and later referenced/freed again by another, which is a use-after-free/double-free of the same memory. CWE-416 fits because memory is accessed after being freed; the missing listen-time constraint is the cause, the UAF is the consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
int err;
reqsk_queue_alloc(&icsk->icsk_accept_queue);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the listener path does not reject ULPs that lack a clone/dedup operation, so the listener's icsk_ulp_data pointer is copied into accepted children. Trigger: a user installs a TLS ULP context via setsockopt TCP_ULP, then listens; accepted sockets inherit the same context pointer. When both parent and child are disposed, the shared context is freed twice, producing a use-after-free.

description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging improper use of pointers in place of scalars.

code_evidence: In regsafe, when rold is SCALAR_VALUE but rcur is a pointer type, the else branch accepts the states as safe if the old scalar was fully unbounded (umin 0, umax U64_MAX, smin S64_MIN, smax S64_MAX, unknown tnum). This treats an unbounded scalar as equivalent to a pointer during verifier state pruning.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Improper verifier state equivalence allows a pointer to be treated as an unbounded scalar, enabling subsequent out-of-bounds reads/writes on BPF map-value buffers, matching CWE-119. The root cause is the flawed state comparison, not merely a type-confusion label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The verifier's state-pruning comparison considers an unbounded scalar old state safe against a current pointer state. Later paths may then reuse pruned state where a scalar replaced a pointer, so the verifier loses track of the pointer's provenance and permits unsafe pointer/scalar arithmetic on map values, leading to out-of-bounds memory access (memory corruption or DoS).

commit_msg: Safer std::vector indexing.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (idx == 1 && p[0] == \'\\\\\' && p[1] == \'\\\\\') return ""; // For Windows paths'], 'added_lines': ['        if (idx == 1 && p.at(0) == \'\\\\\' && p.at(1) == \'\\\\\') return ""; // For Windows paths']}
description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An out-of-bounds read was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The out-of-bounds read is triggered when Exiv2 is used to read the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: Line 10 indexes p[0] and p[1] with operator[] after only checking idx == 1; operator[] performs no bounds checking, so if p is shorter than 2 characters while idx still equals 1, the reads access memory before/outside the string buffer. The patch replaces these with p.at(), confirming the unsafe indexing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the valid bounds of the string buffer via unchecked indexing, matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). The consequence is a memory read beyond intended bounds, not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.

evidence_lines.code: if (idx == 1 && p[0] == '\\' && p[1] == '\\') return "";         if (idx != std::string::npos) p = p.substr(idx+1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is unchecked std::string operator[] access on p[0] and p[1] guarded only by idx == 1 rather than a length check. Triggered by a crafted path reaching this branch with insufficient length, causing an out-of-bounds read and potential denial of service.

commit_msg:
Prevent division by 0 in common shape functions.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 387712197
Change-Id: Id25c7460e35b68aeeeac23b9a88e455b443ee149
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (filter_input_depth_value == 0)', '      return errors::InvalidArgument("Depth of filter must not be 0");', '        if (num_groups == 0)', '          return errors::InvalidArgument("Number of groups must not be 0");']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions most implementations of convolution operators in TensorFlow are affected by a division by 0 vulnerability where an attacker can trigger a denial of service via a crash. The shape inference [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/core/framework/common_shape_fns.cc#L577) is missing several validations before doing divisions and modulo operations. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 8a793b5d7f59e37ac7f3cd0954a750a2fe76bad4. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: When both input depth and filter input depth dimensions are known, their values are read and then used as the divisor in the modulo expression at line 57 without verifying that filter_input_depth_value is nonzero.

When input depth differs from filter input depth, line 63 computes num_groups by dividing input_depth_value by filter_input_depth_value; line 66 then uses num_groups as the divisor in a modulo without checking whether it is zero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs division and modulo on values that can be zero, exactly matching CWE-369 (divide by zero). The consequence is an availability-impacting crash, consistent with the weakness scope; this is not merely an out-of-range or invalid-shape error because the unguarded arithmetic itself is the fault.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is missing zero checks on divisor values derived from input/filter shape dimensions before modulo and division operations. An attacker supplying a filter shape with input depth 0 (or a configuration yielding zero groups) triggers a division/modulo by zero during shape inference, causing a crash and denial of service.

commit_msg:
The current code performs the cancel of a delayed work at the late
stage of disconnection procedure, which may lead to the access to the
already cleared state.

This patch assures to call cancel_delayed_work_sync() at the beginning
of the disconnection procedure for avoiding that race.  The delayed
work object is now assigned in the common line6 object instead of its
derivative, so that we can call cancel_delayed_work_sync().

Along with the change, the startup function is called via the new
callback instead.  This will make it easier to port other LINE6
drivers to use the delayed work for startup in later patches.

Reported-by: syzbot+5255458d5e0a2b10bbb9@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Fixes: 7f84ff68be05 ("ALSA: line6: toneport: Fix broken usage of timer for delayed execution")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tschedule_delayed_work(&toneport->pcm_work,'], 'added_lines': ['\tschedule_delayed_work(&toneport->line6.startup_work,']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.1.8. There is a NULL pointer dereference caused by a malicious USB device in the sound/usb/line6/driver.c driver.

code_evidence: toneport_setup schedules delayed work on toneport->pcm_work without any check that this work object or its backing state is still valid; the object is only cancelled later in the disconnect path, so scheduling here can race with teardown that frees the toneport/line6 state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a dereference of invalidated (NULL) state reached through the race, matching CWE-476. It is not merely a use-after-free label because the demonstrated failure is the NULL dereference of cleared state during the delayed-work race.

evidence_lines.code:
schedule_delayed_work(&toneport->pcm_work,
msecs_to_jiffies(TONEPORT_PCM_DELAY * 1000));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the delayed work is armed in toneport_setup but cancelled only at the late stage of disconnection, so a concurrent disconnect can clear the toneport state while the work remains queued. Trigger: a malicious/hot-unplugged USB device causing setup and disconnect to race. Consequence: the delayed work runs against freed/cleared state, yielding a NULL pointer dereference and crash (DoS).

description: A use-after-free vulnerability exists in NanoMQ 0.17.2. The vulnerability can be triggered by calling the function nni_mqtt_msg_get_publish_property() in the file mqtt_msg.c. This vulnerability is caused by improper data tracing, and an attacker could exploit it to cause a denial of service attack.

code_evidence: In the END state, when a will flag is present, nano_pubmsg_composer() is called and its result is assigned to work->msg; the else branch frees work->msg and sets it NULL, then conn_param_free(work->cparam) is called at line 400. The composer consumes conn_param_get_will_msg/topic from work->cparam, so freeing the connection parameters while the composed message may still reference will-message data leaves work->msg pointing into freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function frees work->cparam while a still-referenced message (work->msg) may point into that freed allocation, and later operations on the message reuse that memory. This is a use-after-free rather than a double free, since the issue is continued use of freed memory, not repeated deallocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: conn_param_free(work->cparam) is executed unconditionally at line 400 after the will-message path, releasing the connection parameters that hold the will message/topic used to build work->msg. Trigger: a client with a will set disconnects, entering END; if the composed will message retains references to the freed conn_param data, subsequent publish handling via handle_pub reads freed memory. Consequence: use-after-free leading to crash/DoS or memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
We selectively grab the ctx->uring_lock for poll update/removal, but
we really should grab it from the start to fully synchronize with
linked timeouts. Normally this is indeed the case, but if requests
are forced async by the application, we don't fully cover removal
and timer disarm within the uring_lock.

Make this simpler by having consistent locking state for poll removal.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 6.1+
Reported-by: Querijn Voet <querijnqyn@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct io_tw_state ts = {};', '\tio_ring_submit_lock(ctx, issue_flags);', '\tio_ring_submit_unlock(ctx, issue_flags);', '\t\tret2 = io_poll_add(preq, issue_flags);', '\tts.locked = !(issue_flags & IO_URING_F_UNLOCKED);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct io_tw_state ts = { .locked = true };', '\tio_ring_submit_lock(ctx, issue_flags);', '\t\tret2 = io_poll_add(preq, issue_flags & ~IO_URING_F_UNLOCKED);', '\tio_ring_submit_unlock(ctx, issue_flags);']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux Kernel io_uring subsystem can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

Racing a io_uring cancel poll request with a linked timeout can cause a UAF in a hrtimer.

We recommend upgrading past commit ef7dfac51d8ed961b742218f526bd589f3900a59 (4716c73b188566865bdd79c3a6709696a224ac04 for 5.10 stable and 0e388fce7aec40992eadee654193cad345d62663 for 5.15 stable).

code_evidence: io_poll_find/io_poll_disarm are invoked on the unlocked cancel_table before any io_ring_submit_lock, so the found preq and its timer state are not synchronized with concurrent removal/disarm.

The locked pass acquires io_ring_submit_lock only for cancel_table_locked and immediately releases it at line 25 before the found: handling at 30-51, so later mutation of preq is again unsynchronized.
io_poll_add(preq, issue_flags) at 44 re-arms the found poll request while no uring_lock is held (unless caller lock semantics happen to apply), allowing a linked timeout to race.

io_req_task_complete(preq, &ts) at 51 is reached after the lock was dropped, and ts.locked is derived from issue_flags rather than the actual held lock, so completion can run against a preq whose timer was concurrently freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function continues to operate on preq (io_poll_add, io_req_task_complete) after concurrent removal/timer disarm can free it. This is a use-after-free rather than merely a race condition, since the supported consequence is reuse of freed memory.

evidence_lines.code:
ts.locked = !(issue_flags & IO_URING_F_UNLOCKED);
io_req_task_complete(preq, &ts);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is inconsistent locking: the poll request is located, disarmed, re-armed and completed without holding uring_lock across the whole sequence. A racing linked timeout or cancel can free the poll request/hrtimer while this path still references preq, producing the reported use-after-free and possible local privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fix heap buffer overflow in decompileCALLFUNCTION

Make sure that n > 0 before checking for the previous action in the
actions array, otherwise an overflow may occur.

This commit fixes CVE-2017-11734 (fixes #83).
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -4,7 +4,7 @@
 	struct SWF_ACTIONPUSHPARAM *meth, *nparam;
 
 	SanityCheck(SWF_CALLMETHOD,
-		actions[n-1].SWF_ACTIONRECORD.ActionCode == SWFACTION_PUSH,
+		n > 0 && actions[n-1].SWF_ACTIONRECORD.ActionCode == SWFACTION_PUSH,
 		"CALLMETHOD not preceeded by PUSH")
 
 	meth=pop();
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tactions[n-1].SWF_ACTIONRECORD.ActionCode == SWFACTION_PUSH,'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tn > 0 && actions[n-1].SWF_ACTIONRECORD.ActionCode == SWFACTION_PUSH,']}
description: A heap-based buffer over-read was found in the function decompileCALLFUNCTION in util/decompile.c in Ming 0.4.8, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: SanityCheck evaluates actions[n-1].SWF_ACTIONRECORD.ActionCode before verifying that n is positive; when n equals 0 the index becomes -1, reading one element before the actions buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads memory before the start of the intended buffer due to the unchecked negative index, matching the out-of-bounds read definition. It is not a write overflow (CWE-787) since the faulty access is a read in the sanity-check condition.

evidence_lines.code:
SanityCheck(SWF_CALLMETHOD,
actions[n-1].SWF_ACTIONRECORD.ActionCode == SWFACTION_PUSH,
"CALLMETHOD not preceeded by PUSH")

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check on the action count n is missing before indexing actions[n-1]. Trigger: decompileCALLFUNCTION is invoked with n=0, so the sanity-check expression reads actions[-1]. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds read that can crash the decoder (denial of service).

commit_msg:
fix: Do not use the "/tmp" directory

https://github.com/linuxdeepin/deepin-clone/issues/16
https://bugzilla.opensuse.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1130388
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        const QStringList &tmp_paths = QStandardPaths::standardLocations(QStandardPaths::TempLocation);', '        const QString tmp_dir = (tmp_paths.isEmpty() ? "/tmp" : tmp_paths.first()) + "/.deepin-clone";'], 'added_lines': ['        const QString tmp_dir = "/var/cache/deepin-clone";']}
description: deepin-clone before 1.1.3 uses a predictable path /tmp/.deepin-clone/mount/<block-dev-basename> in the Helper::temporaryMountDevice() function to temporarily mount a file system as root. An unprivileged user can prepare a symlink at this location to have the file system mounted in an arbitrary location. By winning a race condition, the attacker can also enter the mount point, thereby preventing a subsequent unmount of the file system.

code_evidence: The temp directory comes from QStandardPaths::standardLocations(TempLocation), falling back to /tmp, then appends /.deepin-clone and repo.iso; the path is predictable and in a world-writable location. The code later checks existence and copies into this path without exclusive creation.

The mount_root from Helper::temporaryMountDevice is used to build repo_mount_point and mount targets, and bind mounts are performed into mount_root; the predictable temp path and mount point are shared resources another process can pre-create or enter.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function relies on temporary exclusive access to a shared, predictable filesystem location while concurrent untrusted code can modify it between creation and use, which is exactly a race condition (CWE-362). The symlink/temp-path aspect is the vehicle; the core flaw is improper synchronization of the shared resource, not merely a fixed path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a predictable /tmp/.deepin-clone path and mount point are created and used as root without atomic, exclusive creation (mkpath followed by exists/copy, and mount into a path an attacker can pre-populate). Trigger: an unprivileged user pre-creates a symlink or directory, or enters the mount point before unmount. Consequence: filesystem mounted at an attacker-chosen location or unmount prevented, violating exclusivity/atomicity of the shared temp resource.

commit_msg:
Fix another division by 0 in TFLite

PiperOrigin-RevId: 370800181
Change-Id: I924809166a6131f5075e6d45c455106538d755f9
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  // Prevent divisions by 0', '  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, params->stride_height > 0);', '  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, params->stride_width > 0);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The optimized implementation of the `TransposeConv` TFLite operator is [vulnerable to a division by zero error](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/0d45ea1ca641b21b73bcf9c00e0179cda284e7e7/tensorflow/lite/kernels/internal/optimized/optimized_ops.h#L5221-L5222). An attacker can craft a model such that `stride_{h,w}` values are 0. Code calling this function must validate these arguments. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function reads TransposeConv parameters from node->builtin_data into params without validating stride values.
params->stride_height and params->stride_width are passed directly into ComputePaddingHeightWidth, which performs division using these stride values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a divide-by-zero: unvalidated stride values reach a division operation in ComputePaddingHeightWidth. This matches CWE-369 directly, distinct from an out-of-bounds issue, since the consequence is a crash from division by zero rather than memory corruption.

evidence_lines.code:
data->padding = ComputePaddingHeightWidth(
params->stride_height, params->stride_width, 1, 1, height, width,
filter_height, filter_width, params->padding, &unused_output_height,
&unused_output_width);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: Eval consumes attacker-controlled stride_height/stride_width from the model's builtin data and forwards them to ComputePaddingHeightWidth without any positivity check. A crafted model with a zero stride triggers a division by zero during padding computation, causing a crash (DoS). The patch adds TF_LITE_ENSURE guards requiring both strides to be greater than zero before use.

commit_msg:
Fix multiple buffer overflows in CradLoader::load()

This patches several memory issues while loading .rad files
in src/rad.cpp:
* Simplify the code reading the descrition and ensure not
  to write past the end of "desc".
* Add several checks for errors reading the file and fail
  loading in that case.
* Check instument number before using it as index to the
  "inst" array to avoid an out-of bounds write.
* Check order length before writing data to the array. Fixes
  a heap-based buffer overflow (issue #89).
* Check channel and row numbers before using them as indices
  for writing track data. Fixes another buffer overflow
  (issue #89).

This fixes CVE-2019-14733.

Fixes: https://github.com/adplug/adplug/issues/89
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  char bufstr[2] = "\\0";', '    memset(desc,0,80*22);', '    while((buf = f->readInt(1)))', '      if(buf == 1)', '\tstrcat(desc,"\\n");', '\tif(buf >= 2 && buf <= 0x1f)', '\t  for(i=0;i<buf;i++)', '\t    strcat(desc," ");', '\telse {', '\t  *bufstr = buf;', '\t  strcat(desc,bufstr);', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['  i = 0;', '    while ((buf = f->readInt(1)) && !f->error()) {', '      if (i >= 80 * 22 - 1)', '        continue;', '      if (buf == 1)', "\tdesc[i++] = '\\n';", '      else if (buf >= 2 && buf <= 0x1f)', '        while (buf-- && i < 80 * 22 - 1)', "          desc[i++] = ' ';", '        desc[i++] = buf;', '    }', '  desc[i] = 0;', '', '    if (buf > 250 || f->error()) {', '      fp.close(f); return false;', '    }', '', '  if (length > 128) {', '    fp.close(f); return false;', '  }', '  if (f->error()) {', '    fp.close(f); return false;', '  }', '', '          if (c >= 9 || b >= 64) {', '            fp.close(f); return false;', '          }', '      if (f->error()) {', '        fp.close(f); return false;', '      }']}
description: AdPlug 2.3.1 has multiple heap-based buffer overflows in CradLoader::load() in rad.cpp.

code_evidence: The instrument loop reads a byte into buf, decrements it, and uses it directly as index into inst[] without validating that buf is within the array bounds; a crafted file byte (e.g. 255) yields an out-of-range write to inst[buf].data[...].
length is read from the file and used as the loop bound for order[i] with no check against the order array size, so an oversized length writes past order[].
In the pattern loop, b = buf & 127 and c = ch & 127 are used to index tracks[i*9+c][b] with no bound check, so crafted pattern bytes write beyond the track array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to arrays using unvalidated attacker-controlled indices and lengths, directly producing out-of-bounds writes, which is CWE-787. This is a write past the intended buffer rather than a read, so it is not CWE-125.

evidence_lines.code:
length = f->readInt(1);
for(i = 0; i < length; i++) order[i] = f->readInt(1);  for(i = 0; i < 32; i++) patofs[i] = f->readInt(2);  init_trackord();  for(i=0;i<32;i++)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is missing bounds validation on file-controlled indices and lengths before array writes. A malicious .rad file supplies out-of-range instrument numbers, an oversized order length, or large channel/row values, causing heap writes past inst[], order[], and tracks[][]; this can corrupt memory or crash.

commit_msg:
rgw:  make init env methods return an error

Since web frontends may signal an error when requests are malformed or so, let
us double check this and raise errors early. The current user of this is
civetweb frontend; which can potentially return null from `parse_http_headers`
when a HTTP header without a ":" is supplied at which point headers.value is
null which can lead to undefined behaviour later in RGW.

Fixes: http://tracker.ceph.com/issues/23039
Signed-off-by: Abhishek Lekshmanan <abhishek@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void RGWFCGX::init_env(CephContext* const cct)'], 'added_lines': ['int RGWFCGX::init_env(CephContext* const cct)', '  return 0;']}
description: In Ceph before 12.2.3 and 13.x through 13.0.1, the rgw_civetweb.cc RGWCivetWeb::init_env function in radosgw doesn't handle malformed HTTP headers properly, allowing for denial of service.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown RGWFCGX::init_env function only initializes env and returns 0; it contains no pointer dereference or NULL check, and the NULL-header issue described belongs to the civetweb frontend's parse_http_headers, not this function.

commit_msg: Fix #6816 - null deref in r_read_*
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!src) {', '\t\treturn UT8_MAX;', '\t}']}
description: The r_read_* functions in libr/include/r_endian.h in radare2 1.2.1 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a crafted binary file, as demonstrated by the r_read_le32 function.

code_evidence: The function r_read_le8 accepts a const void *src and immediately passes it to r_read_ble8 without any NULL check. No validation or guard exists on src before the dereference occurs inside the helper.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the code dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but which can be NULL, leading to a crash. This is a direct NULL pointer dereference, not a general bounds or type confusion issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: src is dereferenced without a NULL check. Trigger: a caller passes NULL, e.g., from parsing a crafted binary file. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing an application crash (DoS); the fix adds a guard returning UT8_MAX.

commit_msg:
Fix segmentation fault when closing an element

Reported in issue #19. The error happened when the node passed to elm_close
wasn't an element as it was supposed to.

In the example files reported with the issue, the node causing the crash
was a comment.

Now, elm_close will exit with an error if the node it receives isn't
an element. Some calls that could potentially call it with something else
check the node type before calling it.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    for (p=actual_element; p != nodo; p=p->padre) elm_close(p);'], 'added_lines': ['    for (p=actual_element; p != nodo; p=p->padre)', '      if (p->tipo == Node_element) {', '        elm_close(p);', '      }']}
description: html2xhtml v1.3 was discovered to contain an Out-Of-Bounds read in the function static void elm_close(tree_node_t *nodo) at procesador.c. This vulnerability allows attackers to access sensitive files or cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via a crafted html file.

code_evidence: Line 20 iterates from actual_element up through parent pointers, calling elm_close(p) on every node until reaching nodo, without verifying each node's type.
Line 21 unconditionally calls elm_close(nodo) on the matched node, again without a type check.
Line 23 then dereferences nodo->padre to update actual_element after closing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the root cause is reading memory past the intended buffer/structure when elm_close and the later nodo->padre access operate on a node that is not an element. The fix adds a Node_element type check before calling elm_close, confirming a type-confusion-driven out-of-bounds read rather than an unrelated logic error.

evidence_lines.code: for (p=actual_element; p != nodo; p=p->padre) elm_close(p);
elm_close(nodo);
actual_element= nodo->padre;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop in line 20 and the call in line 21 pass nodes such as comments to elm_close, which assumes an element and reads element-specific fields (e.g., the parent pointer at line 23). A crafted HTML file that closes a non-element node triggers reads outside the intended element structure, causing an out-of-bounds read and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
ieee802154: atusb: do not use the stack for buffers to make them DMA able

From 4.9 we should really avoid using the stack here as this will not be DMA
able on various platforms. This changes the buffers already being present in
time of 4.9 being released. This should go into stable as well.

Reported-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Stefan Schmidt <stefan@osg.samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar build[ATUSB_BUILD_SIZE + 1];'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar *build;', '', '\tbuild = kmalloc(ATUSB_BUILD_SIZE + 1, GFP_KERNEL);', '\tif (!build)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\tkfree(build);']}
description: drivers/net/ieee802154/atusb.c in the Linux kernel 4.9.x before 4.9.6 interacts incorrectly with the CONFIG_VMAP_STACK option, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash or memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging use of more than one virtual page for a DMA scatterlist.

code_evidence: A fixed-size stack buffer build[ATUSB_BUILD_SIZE + 1] is declared and its address is passed to atusb_control_msg as the receive buffer with length ATUSB_BUILD_SIZE.
When the control transfer returns non-negative ret, build[ret] = 0 writes a terminator at index ret, and build is then passed to dev_info as a %s string.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a write (build[ret] = 0) and a subsequent string read on a buffer without validating that ret stays within the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The DMA-on-stack issue is a related platform-specific concern, but the unbounded index write directly supports the target weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The stack buffer is handed to a USB control transfer for DMA. On platforms with CONFIG_VMAP_STACK the stack may span multiple virtual pages, so DMA scatter-gather over the stack buffer can corrupt adjacent memory or crash. Additionally the terminator write at build[ret] uses the transfer return value without bounding ret to ATUSB_BUILD_SIZE, allowing an out-of-bounds write if the device reports more bytes than requested.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/574
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        ThrowBinaryException(ResourceLimitError,"MemoryAllocationFailed",', '          image->filename);'], 'added_lines': ['        {', '          colormap_index=(ssize_t *) RelinquishMagickMemory(colormap_index);', '          ThrowBinaryException(ResourceLimitError,"MemoryAllocationFailed",', '            image->filename);', '        }']}
description: ImageMagick 7.0.6-2 has a memory leak vulnerability in WritePALMImage in coders/palm.c.

code_evidence: colormap_index is allocated via AcquireQuantumMemory and the NULL check at lines 22-24 throws without freeing (acceptable, nothing yet to leak).

At line 29 AcquireImageColormap can return MagickFalse; the ThrowBinaryException at lines 30-31 exits while colormap_index (allocated at line 20) is still live, so it is never released on this error path.
The only release of colormap_index is the RelinquishMagickMemory at line 136 on the normal path; the error path bypasses it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because a resource (colormap_index) is not released after its effective lifetime ends on an early-exit path. It is a resource-release omission rather than a use-after-free or double-free; the normal path at line 136 correctly frees it.

evidence_lines.code: colormap_index=(ssize_t *) RelinquishMagickMemory(colormap_index);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failure branch for AcquireImageColormap throws before reaching the single RelinquishMagickMemory at line 136, orphaning the earlier colormap_index allocation. Trigger: a resource-allocation failure inside AcquireImageColormap when the image is not PseudoClass. Consequence: the heap block is leaked, enabling memory-consumption denial of service on repeated failures.

commit_msg:
Protect against size_t overflows in pb_dec_bytes/pb_dec_string.

Possible consequences of bug:
1) Denial of service by causing a crash
   Possible when all of the following apply:
      - Untrusted data is passed to pb_decode()
      - The top-level message contains a static string field as the first field.
   Causes a single write of '0' byte to 1 byte before the message struct.

2) Remote code execution
   Possible when all of the following apply:
      - 64-bit platform
      - The message or a submessage contains a static/pointer string field.
      - Decoding directly from a custom pb_istream_t
      - bytes_left on the stream is set to larger than 4 GB
   Causes a write of up to 4 GB of data past the string field.

3) Possible heap corruption or remote code execution
   Possible when all of the following apply:
      - less than 64-bit platform
      - The message or a submessage contains a pointer-type bytes field.
   Causes a write of sizeof(pb_size_t) bytes of data past a 0-byte long
   malloc()ed buffer. On many malloc() implementations, this causes at
   most a crash. However, remote code execution through a controlled jump
   cannot be ruled out.

--

Detailed analysis follows

In the following consideration, I define "platform bitness" as equal to
number of bits in size_t datatype. Therefore most 8-bit platforms are
regarded as 16-bit for the purposes of this discussion.

1. The overflow in pb_dec_string

The overflow happens in this computation:

uint32_t size;
size_t alloc_size;
alloc_size = size + 1;

There are two ways in which the overflow can occur: In the uint32_t
addition, or in the cast to size_t. This depends on the platform
bitness.

On 32- and 64-bit platforms, the size has to be UINT32_MAX for the
overflow to occur. In that case alloc_size will be 0.

On 16-bit platforms, overflow will happen whenever size is more than
UINT16_MAX, and resulting alloc_size is attacker controlled.

For static fields, the alloc_size value is just checked against the
field data size. For pointer fields, the alloc_size value is passed to
malloc(). End result in both cases is the same, the storage is 0 or
just a few bytes in length.

On 16-bit platforms, another overflow occurs in the call to pb_read(),
when passing the original size. An attacker will want the passed value
to be larger than the alloc_size, therefore the only reasonable choice
is to have size = UINT16_MAX and alloc_size = 0. Any larger multiple
will truncate to the same values.

At this point we have read atleast the tag and the string length of the
message, i.e. atleast 3 bytes. The maximum initial value for stream
bytes_left is SIZE_MAX, thus at this point at most SIZE_MAX-3 bytes are
remaining.

On 32-bit and 16-bit platforms this means that the size passed to
pb_read() is always larger than the number of remaining bytes. This
causes pb_read() to fail immediately, before reading any bytes.

On 64-bit platforms, it is possible for the bytes_left value to be set
to a value larger than UINT32_MAX, which is the wraparound point in
size calculation. In this case pb_read() will succeed and write up to 4
GB of attacker controlled data over the RAM that comes after the string
field.

On all platforms, there is an unconditional write of a terminating null
byte. Because the size of size_t typically reflects the size of the
processor address space, a write at UINT16_MAX or UINT32_MAX bytes
after the string field actually wraps back to before the string field.
Consequently, on 32-bit and 16-bit platforms, the bug causes a single
write of '0' byte at one byte before the string field.

If the string field is in the middle of a message, this will just
corrupt other data in the message struct. Because the message contents
is attacker controlled anyway, this is a non-issue. However, if the
string field is the first field in the top-level message, it can
corrupt other data on the stack/heap before it. Typically a single '0'
write at a location not controlled by attacker is enough only for a
denial-of-service attack.

When using pointer fields and malloc(), the attacker controlled
alloc_size will cause a 0-size allocation to happen. By the same logic
as before, on 32-bit and 16-bit platforms this causes a '0' byte write
only. On 64-bit platforms, however, it will again allow up to 4 GB of
malicious data to be written over memory, if the stream length allows
the read.

2. The overflow in pb_dec_bytes

This overflow happens in the PB_BYTES_ARRAY_T_ALLOCSIZE macro:

The computation is done in size_t data type this time. This means that
an overflow is possible only when n is larger than SIZE_MAX -
offsetof(..). The offsetof value in this case is equal to
sizeof(pb_size_t) bytes.

Because the incoming size value is limited to 32 bits, no overflow can
happen here on 64-bit platforms.

The size will be passed to pb_read(). Like before, on 32-bit and 16-bit
platforms the read will always fail before writing anything.

This leaves only the write of bdest->size as exploitable. On statically
allocated fields, the size field will always be allocated, regardless
of alloc_size. In this case, no buffer overflow is possible here, but
user code could possibly use the attacker controlled size value and
read past a buffer.

If the field is allocated through malloc(), this will allow a write of
sizeof(pb_size_t) attacker controlled bytes to past a 0-byte long
buffer. In typical malloc implementations, this will either fit in
unused alignment padding area, or cause a heap corruption and a crash.
Under very exceptional situation it could allow attacker to influence
the behaviour of malloc(), possibly jumping into an attacker-controlled
location and thus leading to remote code execution.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    ', '    if (alloc_size < size)', '        PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "size too large");']}
description: Nanopb before 0.3.1 allows size_t overflows in pb_dec_bytes and pb_dec_string.

code_evidence: size is an attacker-controlled uint32_t from pb_decode_varint32, while alloc_size is size_t; alloc_size = size + 1 can wrap to 0 when size is UINT32_MAX (or truncate on 16-bit size_t).
For pointer fields, the wrapped alloc_size is passed to allocate_field, yielding a zero or undersized allocation; dest is then reassigned to the allocated buffer.
For static fields, the check alloc_size > field->data_size uses the wrapped value, so it passes despite size being huge.
pb_read copies size (unwrapped) bytes into the undersized dest, and the terminating null write at dest + size also lands out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-influenced data past the end of an undersized buffer, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. The integer overflow is the root-cause mechanism; the supported weakness demonstrated in this function is the resulting out-of-bounds write, not merely the arithmetic error.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!allocate_field(stream, dest, alloc_size, 1))
dest = *(void**)dest;

if (alloc_size > field->data_size)
PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "string overflow");

status = pb_read(stream, (uint8_t*)dest, size);
*((uint8_t*)dest + size) = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The addition size + 1 is performed before any bound check, so an oversized length wraps alloc_size to a small value. The buffer is then sized from the wrapped value but filled using the original size, causing pb_read and the null terminator to write beyond the allocated buffer. Consequence is memory corruption, crash, or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
cryp: prevent direct calls to update and final functions

With inconsistent or malformed data it has been possible to call
"update" and "final" crypto functions directly. Using a fuzzer tool [1]
we have seen that this results in asserts, i.e., a crash that
potentially could leak sensitive information.

By setting the state (initialized) in the crypto context (i.e., the
tee_cryp_state) at the end of all syscall_*_init functions and then add
a check of the state at the beginning of all update and final functions,
  we prevent direct entrance to the "update" and "final" functions.

[1] https://github.com/MartijnB/optee_fuzzer

Fixes: OP-TEE-2019-0021

Signed-off-by: Joakim Bech <joakim.bech@linaro.org>
Reported-by: Martijn Bogaard <bogaard@riscure.com>
Acked-by: Jerome Forissier <jerome.forissier@linaro.org>
Reviewed-by: Jens Wiklander <jens.wiklander@linaro.org>

commit_msg:
staging/android/ion : fix a race condition in the ion driver

There is a use-after-free problem in the ion driver.
This is caused by a race condition in the ion_ioctl()
function.

A handle has ref count of 1 and two tasks on different
cpus calls ION_IOC_FREE simultaneously.

cpu 0                                   cpu 1
-------------------------------------------------------
ion_handle_get_by_id()
(ref == 2)
                            ion_handle_get_by_id()
                            (ref == 3)

ion_free()
(ref == 2)

ion_handle_put()
(ref == 1)

                            ion_free()
                            (ref == 0 so ion_handle_destroy() is
                            called
                            and the handle is freed.)

                            ion_handle_put() is called and it
                            decreases the slub's next free pointer

The problem is detected as an unaligned access in the
spin lock functions since it uses load exclusive
 instruction. In some cases it corrupts the slub's
free pointer which causes a mis-aligned access to the
next free pointer.(kmalloc returns a pointer like
ffffc0745b4580aa). And it causes lots of other
hard-to-debug problems.

This symptom is caused since the first member in the
ion_handle structure is the reference count and the
ion driver decrements the reference after it has been
freed.

To fix this problem client->lock mutex is extended
to protect all the codes that uses the handle.

Signed-off-by: Eun Taik Lee <eun.taik.lee@samsung.com>
Reviewed-by: Laura Abbott <labbott@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int ion_handle_put(struct ion_handle *handle)', '\tret = kref_put(&handle->ref, ion_handle_destroy);'], 'added_lines': ['int ion_handle_put(struct ion_handle *handle)', '\tret = ion_handle_put_nolock(handle);']}
description: Race condition in the ion_ioctl function in drivers/staging/android/ion/ion.c in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) by calling ION_IOC_FREE on two CPUs at the same time.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only wraps kref_put with the client mutex; it contains no permission, privilege, or access-control check, and the described race/use-after-free is a concurrency weakness rather than CWE-264.

description: The Array.prototype.concat implementation in builtins.cc in Google V8, as used in Google Chrome before 49.0.2623.108, does not properly consider element data types, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted JavaScript code.

PR22361 readelf buffer overflow on fuzzed archive header

	PR 22361
	* readelf.c (process_archive_index_and_symbols): Ensure ar_size
	field is zero terminated for strtoul.
	(setup_archive, get_archive_member_name): Likewise.

description: elfcomm.c in readelf in GNU Binutils 2.29 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive memory allocation) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted ELF file that triggers a "buffer overflow on fuzzed archive header," related to an uninitialized variable, an improper conditional jump, and the get_archive_member_name, process_archive_index_and_symbols, and setup_archive functions.

code_evidence: setup_archive reads a fixed-size archive header into arch->arhdr with fread and only validates the total byte count, not field termination.
The ar_size field is passed directly to strtoul; strtoul may scan beyond the field boundary since ar_size is not guaranteed NUL-terminated. The patch adds temporary NUL termination at ar_fmag[0].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe strtoul call operates on a non-terminated buffer and can read outside the ar_size field's intended boundary, which is an out-of-bounds memory operation under CWE-119. This is a read beyond a fixed buffer rather than an integer conversion error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ar_size array field is not NUL-terminated before strtoul, so strtoul can read past the ar_size buffer into adjacent struct memory. Trigger: a crafted archive header whose ar_size field fills its bytes without a terminator. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of memory within/beyond the header struct, matching the reported buffer overflow.

description: OpenCV (Open Source Computer Vision Library) 3.3 has an out-of-bounds write error in the function FillColorRow1 in utils.cpp when reading an image file by using cv::imread. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-12597.

code_evidence: Row stride and step variables are stored as 32-bit int; ystep is assigned from step and used in Slice address arithmetic (buffer - min.x*12 - min.y*ystep) and in step/xstep divisors passed to UpSample and ChromaToBGR, and out advances by step at line 171.

When native depth is disabled or a color image is read as a non-color target, a copy_buffer of sizeof(float)*m_width*3 is allocated and filled row-by-row; loop writes out[x] for x < m_width*3 and advances out += step, so the destination stride must match the buffer size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs writes (out[x], UpSample, ChromaToBGR) into a buffer whose size and stride derive from integer-typed dimensions without an overflow check, producing a write beyond the intended buffer, which is CWE-787. The patch changing step/xstep/ystep to size_t confirms the arithmetic width as the root cause rather than a pure read overrun.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The 32-bit step/ystep and the m_width*3 loop bound are derived from image/decoder-controlled dimensions. commit_msg:
When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via
/home/fred/keepalived.data.

There doesn't appear to be a way around this backward incompatibility,
since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

Signed-off-by: Quentin Armitage <quentin@armitage.org.uk>

commit_msg: postpone stream shutdown by H3 frame parsers
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                             const char **err_desc)', '            shutdown_stream(stream, H2O_HTTP3_ERROR_EARLY_RESPONSE, H2O_HTTP3_ERROR_GENERAL_PROTOCOL, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['                             int in_generator, const char **err_desc)', '            shutdown_stream(stream, H2O_HTTP3_ERROR_EARLY_RESPONSE, H2O_HTTP3_ERROR_GENERAL_PROTOCOL, in_generator);']}
description: h2o is an open source http server. In code prior to the `8c0eca3` commit h2o may attempt to access uninitialized memory. When receiving QUIC frames in certain order, HTTP/3 server-side implementation of h2o can be misguided to treat uninitialized memory as HTTP/3 frames that have been received. When h2o is used as a reverse proxy, an attacker can abuse this vulnerability to send internal state of h2o to backend servers controlled by the attacker or third party. Also, if there is an HTTP endpoint that reflects the traffic sent from the client, an attacker can use that reflector to obtain internal state of h2o. This internal state includes traffic of other connections in unencrypted form and TLS session tickets. This vulnerability exists in h2o server with HTTP/3 support, between commit 93af138 and d1f0f65. None of the released versions of h2o are affected by this vulnerability. There are no known workarounds. Users of unreleased versions of h2o using HTTP/3 are advised to upgrade immediately.

code_evidence: On a DATA frame, the code compares the remaining content length against frame.length and calls shutdown_stream(..., 0) when the declared body is exceeded. The literal 0 is passed as the in_generator/generator argument, and the function returns 0, so the caller continues processing the receive buffer as if the stream were still active.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fix replaces the literal 0 with an in_generator parameter, confirming that the parser was operating on uninitialized resource state after an incorrect shutdown. CWE-908 fits because the root cause is use of a resource (stream/generator state) that was not initialized/valid at that point, enabling reads of uninitialized memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The shutdown is performed with a hard-coded 0 instead of the caller's actual generator state, so the stream shutdown is not properly deferred when invoked from a frame parser. The caller then resumes parsing the buffer, reading memory that has not been initialized as if it contained HTTP/3 frames, leading to disclosure of internal state (or crash).

commit_msg:
[turbofan] Bailout if LoadBuffer typing assumption doesn't hold.

The LoadBuffer operator that is used for asm.js heap access claims to
return only the appropriate typed array type, but out of bounds access
could make it return undefined. So far we tried to "repair" the graph
later if we see that our assumption was wrong, and for various reasons
that worked for some time. But now that wrong type information that is
propagated earlier is picked up appropriately and thus we generate wrong
code, i.e. we in the repro case we feed NaN into ChangeFloat64Uint32 and
thus get 2147483648 instead of 0 (with proper JS truncation).

This was always considered a temporary hack until we have a proper
asm.js pipeline, but since we still run asm.js through the generic
JavaScript pipeline, we have to address this now. Quickfix is to just
bailout from the pipeline when we see that the LoadBuffer type was
wrong, i.e. the result of LoadBuffer is not properly truncated and thus
undefined or NaN would be observable.

commit_msg:
nfc: replace improper check device_is_registered() in netlink related functions

The device_is_registered() in nfc core is used to check whether
nfc device is registered in netlink related functions such as
nfc_fw_download(), nfc_dev_up() and so on. Although device_is_registered()
is protected by device_lock, there is still a race condition between
device_del() and device_is_registered(). The root cause is that
kobject_del() in device_del() is not protected by device_lock.

   (cleanup task)         |     (netlink task)
                          |
nfc_unregister_device     | nfc_fw_download
 device_del               |  device_lock
  ...                     |   if (!device_is_registered)//(1)
  kobject_del//(2)        |   ...
 ...                      |  device_unlock

The device_is_registered() returns the value of state_in_sysfs and
the state_in_sysfs is set to zero in kobject_del(). If we pass check in
position (1), then set zero in position (2). As a result, the check
in position (1) is useless.

This patch uses bool variable instead of device_is_registered() to judge
whether the nfc device is registered, which is well synchronized.

Fixes: 3e256b8f8dfa ("NFC: add nfc subsystem core")
Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel's NFC core functionality due to a race condition between kobject creation and delete. This vulnerability allows a local attacker with CAP_NET_ADMIN privilege to leak kernel information.

code_evidence: The function takes device_lock, then checks device_is_registered(&dev->dev) and bails out with -ENODEV if false.
After the check passes, it dereferences dev->ops and calls stop_poll, and writes dev->polling and dev->rf_mode without re-validating registration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic TOCTOU: the check of device_is_registered is separated from the subsequent use of dev, and the resource state can change between them via an unsynchronized path. The weakness is the racy check, not merely a missing lock; the same race class affects the sibling netlink functions fixed together.

A concurrent unregister can therefore invalidate the check after it passes, so nfc_stop_poll proceeds to use and mutate a device being torn down, producing a use-after-free/race.

commit_msg:
avcodec/mpeg4videodec: Clear bits_per_raw_sample if it has originated from a previous instance

Fixes: assertion failure
Fixes: ffmpeg_crash_5.avi

Found-by: Thuan Pham <thuanpv@comp.nus.edu.sg>, Marcel Böhme, Andrew Santosa and Alexandru Razvan Caciulescu with AFLSmart
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    // If we have not switched to studio profile than we also did not switch bps', '    // that means something else (like a previous instance) outside set bps which', '    // would be inconsistant with the currect state, thus reset it', '    if (!s->studio_profile && s->avctx->bits_per_raw_sample != 8)', '        s->avctx->bits_per_raw_sample = 0;']}
description: An inconsistent bits-per-sample value in the ff_mpeg4_decode_picture_header function in libavcodec/mpeg4videodec.c in FFmpeg 4.0 may trigger an assertion violation while converting a crafted AVI file to MPEG4, leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: The function begins parsing immediately after align_get_bits without checking that any parser state carried over from a prior decode instance is consistent; the patch adds a reset of bits_per_raw_sample only when not in studio_profile.
The studio-profile state is set from attacker-controlled VOS/profile/level fields, and decode_studiovisualobject is then dispatched based on s->studio_profile.
At the end, if studio_profile is set, the code requires bits_per_raw_sample to be nonzero and otherwise returns AVERROR_INVALIDDATA; this is the assertion-relevant state that the patch addresses.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function processes header/state data without validating that derived properties are consistent with the current parsing context, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The missing constraint is on the consistency of bits_per_raw_sample versus studio_profile, not a buffer or arithmetic flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder trusts parser state (studio_profile and bits_per_raw_sample) that may be inconsistent with the current input, because a previous instance can leave bits_per_raw_sample set. Trigger: a crafted AVI drives the profile/level path so studio_profile is set while bits_per_raw_sample is inconsistent, reaching the end-of-header check. Supported consequence: an assertion violation / denial of service rather than safe rejection of the malformed input.

commit_msg:
Currently, locking of ->session is very inconsistent; most places
protect it using the legacy tty mutex, but disassociate_ctty(),
__do_SAK(), tiocspgrp() and tiocgsid() don't.
Two of the writers hold the ctrl_lock (because they already need it for
->pgrp), but __proc_set_tty() doesn't do that yet.

On a PREEMPT=y system, an unprivileged user can theoretically abuse
this broken locking to read 4 bytes of freed memory via TIOCGSID if
tiocgsid() is preempted long enough at the right point. (Other things
might also go wrong, especially if root-only ioctls are involved; I'm
not sure about that.)

Change the locking on ->session such that:

 - tty_lock() is held by all writers: By making disassociate_ctty()
   hold it. This should be fine because the same lock can already be
   taken through the call to tty_vhangup_session().
   The tricky part is that we need to shorten the area covered by
   siglock to be able to take tty_lock() without ugly retry logic; as
   far as I can tell, this should be fine, since nothing in the
   signal_struct is touched in the `if (tty)` branch.
 - ctrl_lock is held by all writers: By changing __proc_set_tty() to
   hold the lock a little longer.
 - All readers that aren't holding tty_lock() hold ctrl_lock: By
   adding locking to tiocgsid() and __do_SAK(), and expanding the area
   covered by ctrl_lock in tiocspgrp().

Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Jiri Slaby <jirislaby@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttty = tty_kref_get(current->signal->tty);', '\tspin_unlock_irq(&current->sighand->siglock);'], 'added_lines': ['\ttty = tty_kref_get(current->signal->tty);', '\tspin_unlock_irq(&current->sighand->siglock);', '', '\t\ttty_lock(tty);', '\t\ttty_unlock(tty);']}
description: A locking inconsistency issue was discovered in the tty subsystem of the Linux kernel through 5.9.13. drivers/tty/tty_io.c and drivers/tty/tty_jobctrl.c may allow a read-after-free attack against TIOCGSID, aka CID-c8bcd9c5be24.

code_evidence: disassociate_ctty() takes current->sighand->siglock and, while holding it, reads current->signal->tty and mutates tty->session and tty->pgrp under tty->ctrl_lock only. Writers of ->session such as __proc_set_tty() and tiocspgrp() do not take siglock, and the function never takes tty_lock() before touching the tty; the tty_lock()/ctrl_lock pairing added elsewhere is absent here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 covers improper acquisition of a lock on a shared resource. Here the shared ->session field is written without the tty_lock() that the established protocol requires, so the lock acquisition is incomplete, matching improper locking rather than a simple race-free design choice.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ->session writer path is protected by siglock plus ctrl_lock but not by the tty_lock() that other writers/readers use, so the locking protocol is inconsistent. Trigger: a concurrent TIOCGSID or tiocspgrp path can race with this writer. Consequence: the reader observes a stale/freed tty->session value, enabling the read-after-free described in the commit.

commit_msg:
IxVeriWave: Adjust signature timestamp checking.

Move the signature timestamp bounds checks inside get_signature_ts. Fix
what appears to be an off-by-one error.

Manually backported from 5dbc1d8d1c.

Bug: 14297
Change-Id: I6455162d12fd0854ffe6daaf624eeaf94f6e32b0
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/25246
Petri-Dish: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['guint64 get_signature_ts(const guint8 *m_ptr,int sig_off)'], 'added_lines': ['guint64 get_signature_ts(const guint8 *m_ptr,int sig_off, int sig_max)', '', '    if (sig_off + 15 >= sig_max)', '        return 0;']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.3 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.11, the IxVeriWave file parser could crash. This was addressed in wiretap/vwr.c by correcting the signature timestamp bounds checks.

code_evidence: get_signature_ts takes only m_ptr and sig_off; no buffer length or upper bound is passed, so the function has no information about the size of the buffer m_ptr points to.

The function indexes m_ptr[sig_off + 15] and then reads a 32-bit value via pletoh32(&m_ptr[sig_off + ts_offset]), where ts_offset is 5 or 8. With no bound check, a sig_off near or past the end of the buffer reads beyond the intended boundary.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs reads on a memory buffer at offsets not restricted to the buffer's intended boundary, which is an out-of-bounds read within CWE-119. The missing upper-bound check in this function directly supports that weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dereferences m_ptr at offsets derived from caller-controlled sig_off without any length constraint. Trigger: a crafted IxVeriWave file places a signature offset such that sig_off+15 or sig_off+ts_offset exceeds the buffer. Consequence: out-of-bounds read, potentially a parser crash (DoS) or disclosure of adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
txmempool: have CompareDepthAndScore sort missing txs first

We use CompareDepthAndScore to choose an order of txs to inv. Rather
than sorting txs that have been evicted from the mempool at the end
of the list, sort them at the beginning so they are removed from
the queue immediately.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (i == mapTx.end()) return false;', '    indexed_transaction_set::const_iterator j = wtxid ? get_iter_from_wtxid(hashb) : mapTx.find(hashb);', '    if (j == mapTx.end()) return true;'], 'added_lines': ['    /* Return `true` if hasha should be considered sooner than hashb. Namely when:', '     *   a is not in the mempool, but b is', '     *   both are in the mempool and a has fewer ancestors than b', '     *   both are in the mempool and a has a higher score than b', '     */', '    indexed_transaction_set::const_iterator j = wtxid ? get_iter_from_wtxid(hashb) : mapTx.find(hashb);', '    if (j == mapTx.end()) return false;', '    if (i == mapTx.end()) return true;']}
description: Bitcoin Core before 24.1, when debug mode is not used, allows attackers to cause a denial of service (e.g., CPU consumption) because draining the inventory-to-send queue is inefficient, as exploited in the wild in May 2023.

code_evidence: The comparison looks up hasha before hashb; if hasha is absent it returns false (line 5), and if hashb is absent it returns true (line 7). This ordering places transactions evicted from the mempool at the end of the inventory-to-send queue rather than the front.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The inefficiency repeatedly consumes CPU during queue draining, which is uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400). The defect is the ordering logic, not memory corruption or an access-control bypass.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the comparator's handling of missing mempool entries sends evicted transactions to the tail of the queue. Trigger: attackers cause transactions to be evicted while they remain queued for inventory relay. Consequence: draining the inventory-to-send queue becomes inefficient, consuming CPU and enabling denial of service.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (CheckMemoryOverflow(count,quantum) != MagickFalse)'], 'added_lines': ['  if (HeapOverflowSanityCheck(count,quantum) != MagickFalse)']}
description: Buffer overflow in the ReadVIFFImage function in coders/viff.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-5 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 11 guards multiplication with CheckMemoryOverflow(count,quantum) and returns NULL on overflow; line 15 then computes size=count*quantum.
Lines 16-18 compute extent=AlignedExtent(size,alignment) and return NULL if size==0, alignment<sizeof(void*), or extent<size, covering the aligned-size wraparound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 requires a copy lacking an input-size check; this function performs no buffer copy, only allocation sizing with explicit overflow checks, so the classic buffer-copy pattern is not directly present. The related integer-overflow sizing concern is mitigated here, so the function does not support CWE-120.

evidence_lines.code:
if (CheckMemoryOverflow(count,quantum) != MagickFalse)
return((void *) NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function multiplies attacker-influenced count and quantum to size an allocation, so an unchecked multiplication overflow could yield a small buffer for a large requested extent and later overflow when the caller writes into it. Here the overflow guard at line 11 and the extent<size check at line 17 reject such inputs before allocation, so the unsafe size computation is constrained rather than exploitable in this function.

commit_msg:
On 64-bit systems, struct bcm_msg_head has an added padding of 4 bytes between
struct members count and ival1. Even though all struct members are initialized,
the 4-byte hole will contain data from the kernel stack. This patch zeroes out
struct bcm_msg_head before usage, preventing infoleaks to userspace.

Fixes: ffd980f976e7 ("[CAN]: Add broadcast manager (bcm) protocol")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/trinity-7c1b2e82-e34f-4885-8060-2cd7a13769ce-1623532166177@3c-app-gmx-bs52
Cc: linux-stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Norbert Slusarek <nslusarek@gmx.net>
Acked-by: Oliver Hartkopp <socketcan@hartkopp.net>
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tmemset(&msg_head, 0, sizeof(msg_head));']}
description: net/can/bcm.c in the Linux kernel through 5.12.10 allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel stack memory because parts of a data structure are uninitialized.

code_evidence: A stack-allocated struct bcm_msg_head msg_head is declared at line 4 but never initialized. Only individual fields (opcode, flags, count, ival1, ival2, can_id, nframes) are assigned at lines 8-14; any padding bytes within the struct are left uninitialized. The struct is then passed to bcm_send_to_user at line 15, which copies it to userspace.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-909 covers missing initialization of a resource; here the resource is the stack struct msg_head, whose padding is never initialized before being read and sent to userspace. This is the direct cause of the infoleak, not a separate weakness like buffer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the local struct msg_head is not zeroed before use, so padding bytes (4 bytes between count and ival1 on 64-bit) retain kernel stack contents. Trigger: a local user configures a TX counter event (TX_COUNTEVT) so the timer expires and this branch sends the notification. Consequence: uninitialized stack memory is copied to userspace, leaking sensitive kernel data.

commit_msg:
The Xv query functions for adaptors and encodings suffer from out of
boundary accesses if a hostile X server sends a maliciously crafted
response.

A previous fix already checks the received length against fixed values
but ignores additional length specifications which are stored inside
the received data.

These lengths are accessed in a for-loop. The easiest way to guarantee
a correct processing is by validating all lengths against the
remaining size left before accessing referenced memory.

This makes the previously applied check obsolete, therefore I removed
it.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["        /* If there's no adaptors, there's nothing more to do. */", '    if (size < (rep.num_adaptors * sz_xvAdaptorInfo)) {', "        /* If there's not enough data for the number of adaptors,", '           then we have a problem. */', '        status = XvBadReply;', '        goto out;', '    }', '    u.buffer = buffer;'], 'added_lines': ['    char *end;', "        /* If there are no adaptors, there's nothing more to do. */", '    u.buffer = buffer;', '    end = buffer + size;', '        if (u.buffer + sz_xvAdaptorInfo > end) {', '            status = XvBadReply;', '            goto out;', '        }', '        if (u.buffer + size > end) {', '            status = XvBadReply;', '            goto out;', '        }', '            if (u.buffer + sz_xvFormat > end) {', '                Xfree(pfs);', '                status = XvBadReply;', '                goto out;', '            }']}
description: The (1) XvQueryAdaptors and (2) XvQueryEncodings functions in X.org libXv before 1.0.11 allow remote X servers to trigger out-of-bounds memory access operations via vectors involving length specifications in received data.

code_evidence: The loop over rep.num_adaptors dereferences u.pa (e.g., u.pa->type, u.pa->name_size) and advances u.buffer by pad_to_int32(sz_xvAdaptorInfo) and pad_to_int32(size) without ever validating those offsets against the allocated buffer of size rep.length<<2; name_size from the server drives strncpy from u.string.
The inner loop over pa->num_formats, also server-supplied, reads u.pf->depth and u.pf->visual and advances u.buffer by sz_xvFormat with no remaining-length check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is reading from memory locations beyond the intended buffer boundary due to unchecked server-controlled lengths, which is exactly CWE-119's out-of-bounds buffer access. It is not merely an integer overflow: the lengths are used directly as offsets with no validation against the remaining size.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function trusts length fields embedded in the server reply (name_size, num_formats, num_adaptors) and walks u.buffer accordingly, but the only bound check (size < num_adaptors * sz_xvAdaptorInfo) covers just the fixed header array, not the variable-length name and format data. A hostile X server can make these counts exceed the actual reply size, so u.pa/u.pf reads and the strncpy read past the Xmalloc'd buffer, causing out-of-bounds reads (crash or memory disclosure).
