commit_msg:
libblkid: care about unsafe chars in cache

The high-level libblkid API uses /run/blkid/blkid.tab cache to
store probing results. The cache format is

   <device NAME="value" ...>devname</device>

and unfortunately the cache code does not escape quotation marks:

   # mkfs.ext4 -L 'AAA"BBB'

   # cat /run/blkid/blkid.tab
   ...
   <device ... LABEL="AAA"BBB" ...>/dev/sdb1</device>

such string is later incorrectly parsed and blkid(8) returns
nonsenses. And for use-cases like

   # eval $(blkid -o export /dev/sdb1)

it's also insecure.

Note that mount, udevd and blkid -p are based on low-level libblkid
API, it bypass the cache and directly read data from the devices.

The current udevd upstream does not depend on blkid(8) output at all,
it's directly linked with the library and all unsafe chars are encoded by
\x<hex> notation.

   # mkfs.ext4 -L 'X"`/tmp/foo` "' /dev/sdb1
   # udevadm info --export-db | grep LABEL
   ...
   E: ID_FS_LABEL=X__/tmp/foo___
   E: ID_FS_LABEL_ENC=X\x22\x60\x2ftmp\x2ffoo\x60\x20\x22

Signed-off-by: Karel Zak <kzak@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tend = strchr(*value + 1, \'"\');', '\t\tif (!end) {', '\t\tend++;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tchar *p = end = *value + 1;', '', '\t\t/* convert \'foo\\"bar\'  to \'foo"bar\' */', '\t\twhile (*p) {', "\t\t\tif (*p == '\\\\') {", '\t\t\t\tp++;', '\t\t\t\t*end = *p;', '\t\t\t} else {', '\t\t\t\t*end = *p;', '\t\t\t\tif (*p == \'"\')', '\t\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tp++;', '\t\t\tend++;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\tif (*end != \'"\') {', '\t\tend = ++p;']}
description: Blkid in util-linux before 2.26rc-1 allows local users to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: When the cache value starts with a quote, the code finds the closing quote via strchr(*value + 1, '"') and treats everything up to it as the value, with no handling of backslash-escaped quotes. A value like 'AAA"BBB' therefore terminates early at the embedded quote, leaving the remainder of the attacker-controlled label to be parsed as further cache syntax.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The injected special elements (quotes/shell metacharacters) survive into command strings that downstream consumers execute, matching CWE-77's improper neutralization of special elements used in a command. The parser failure is the root cause enabling command execution, not merely a parsing bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cache parser does not neutralize or escape quote/backslash characters inside quoted values, so an attacker-controlled device label can break out of the quoted field. Trigger: a filesystem label containing '"' is written to blkid.tab and later read by blkid. Consequence: the malformed cache is misparsed and, when blkid output is eval'd, the injected metacharacters are executed by the shell.

commit_msg:
Userland: Fix tar/unzip directory traversal vulnerability

This change validates the filenames within a tar/zip archive during
extraction. If the filename within a the archive is outside of the
current working directory the file will be skipped and not extracted
onto the host system.

Closes #3991
Closes #3992

description: SerenityOS before commit 3844e8569689dd476064a0759d704bc64fb3ca2c contains a directory traversal vulnerability in tar/unzip that may lead to command execution or privilege escalation.

code_evidence: The archive-controlled file name is read into a fixed buffer and null-terminated; its content is fully attacker-controlled from the zip's local file header.
That raw file_name is passed directly to mkdir() and to Core::File::construct()/open() without any validation of '..' components or absolute paths, so the write target is unconstrained.

The fix added later confirms the missing constraint; this is path traversal, not merely a generic file-write issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the extracted file name from the archive is used directly as a filesystem path with no neutralization of parent-directory or absolute-path elements. Trigger: an archive entry named like '../../etc/x' or '/abs/path'. Consequence: files are created or overwritten outside the intended extraction directory, enabling code execution or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
ucount:  Make get_ucount a safe get_user replacement

When the ucount code was refactored to create get_ucount it was missed
that some of the contexts in which a rlimit is kept elevated can be
the only reference to the user/ucount in the system.

Ordinary ucount references exist in places that also have a reference
to the user namspace, but in POSIX message queues, the SysV shm code,
and the SIGPENDING code there is no independent user namespace
reference.

Inspection of the the user_namespace show no instance of circular
references between struct ucounts and the user_namespace.  So
hold a reference from struct ucount to i's user_namespace to
resolve this problem.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/YZV7Z+yXbsx9p3JN@fixkernel.com/
Reported-by: Qian Cai <quic_qiancai@quicinc.com>
Reported-by: Mathias Krause <minipli@grsecurity.net>
Tested-by: Mathias Krause <minipli@grsecurity.net>
Reviewed-by: Mathias Krause <minipli@grsecurity.net>
Reviewed-by: Alexey Gladkov <legion@kernel.org>
Fixes: d64696905554 ("Reimplement RLIMIT_SIGPENDING on top of ucounts")
Fixes: 6e52a9f0532f ("Reimplement RLIMIT_MSGQUEUE on top of ucounts")
Fixes: d7c9e99aee48 ("Reimplement RLIMIT_MEMLOCK on top of ucounts")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tput_user_ns(ucounts->ns);']}
description: kernel/ucount.c in the Linux kernel 5.14 through 5.16.4, when unprivileged user namespaces are enabled, allows a use-after-free and privilege escalation because a ucounts object can outlive its namespace.

code_evidence: When the last reference is dropped, atomic_dec_and_lock_irqsave succeeds, the node is unlinked, the lock released, and ucounts is freed via kfree(ucounts) without releasing the user_namespace reference held by ucounts->ns. The freed ucounts therefore does not drop its reference on the namespace, so the namespace can be freed while ucounts-dependent objects still reference it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing put_user_ns leaves the namespace reachable after its memory is freed; subsequent uses of the dangling namespace reference constitute CWE-416 use-after-free. This is not merely a reference-count leak, since the freed namespace is later dereferenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: put_ucounts frees the ucounts object without calling put_user_ns(ucounts->ns), so the reference count on the user_namespace is not decremented. Trigger: the final put_ucounts on a ucounts that is the sole holder of its namespace (e.g., POSIX mqueue, SysV shm, SIGPENDING contexts). Consequence: the user_namespace is freed prematurely, later accesses to it are use-after-free, enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
floppy_revalidate() doesn't perform any error handling on lock_fdc()
result. lock_fdc() might actually be interrupted by a signal (it waits for
fdc becoming non-busy interruptibly). In such case, floppy_revalidate()
proceeds as if it had claimed the lock, but it fact it doesn't.

In case of multiple threads trying to open("/dev/fdX"), this leads to
serious corruptions all over the place, because all of a sudden there is
no critical section protection (that'd otherwise be guaranteed by locked
fd) whatsoever.

While at this, fix the fact that the 'interruptible' parameter to
lock_fdc() doesn't make any sense whatsoever, because we always wait
interruptibly anyway.

Most of the lock_fdc() callsites do properly handle error (and propagate
EINTR), but floppy_revalidate() and floppy_check_events() don't. Fix this.

Spotted by 'syzkaller' tool.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tlock_fdc(drive, false);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive))', '\t\t\treturn -EINTR;']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernels implementation of the floppy disk drive controller driver software. The impact of this issue is lessened by the fact that the default permissions on the floppy device (/dev/fd0) are restricted to root. If the permissions on the device have changed the impact changes greatly. In the default configuration root (or equivalent) permissions are required to attack this flaw.

code_evidence: At line 9 the return value of lock_fdc(drive, false) is ignored; lock_fdc waits interruptibly for the FDC to become non-busy and can fail with -EINTR when interrupted. Execution then unconditionally proceeds to poll_drive and process_fd_request at lines 10-11 without holding the FDC lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code sequence requires exclusive access to the shared FDC resource, but ignoring lock_fdc()'s failure breaks exclusivity, letting an interfering concurrent sequence modify shared state in the timing window; this matches CWE-362's race-condition definition rather than a simple missing check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a failed (signal-interrupted) lock acquisition is not detected, so the critical section is entered without exclusive access to the FDC. Trigger: concurrent open()/event-check threads on /dev/fdX where one is interrupted while waiting for the lock. Consequence: another thread mutates shared driver state concurrently, corrupting state due to loss of critical-section protection.

commit_msg:
evtchn: evtchn_reset() shouldn't succeed with still-open ports

While the function closes all ports, it does so without holding any
lock, and hence racing requests may be issued causing new ports to get
opened. This would have been problematic in particular if such a newly
opened port had a port number above the new implementation limit (i.e.
when switching from FIFO to 2-level) after the reset, as prior to
"evtchn: relax port_is_valid()" this could have led to e.g.
evtchn_close()'s "BUG_ON(!port_is_valid(d2, port2))" to trigger.

Introduce a counter of active ports and check that it's (still) no
larger then the number of Xen internally used ones after obtaining the
necessary lock in evtchn_reset().

As to the access model of the new {active,xen}_evtchns fields - while
all writes get done using write_atomic(), reads ought to use
read_atomic() only when outside of a suitably locked region.

Note that as of now evtchn_bind_virq() and evtchn_bind_ipi() don't have
a need to call check_free_port().

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    check_free_port(ld, lport);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: get_free_port(ld) reserves a local port while holding ld->event_lock, then the port's channel is populated and its state set to ECS_INTERDOMAIN under double_evtchn_lock.
The out path unlocks ld->event_lock and, when ld != rd, also unlocks rd->event_lock; the patch adds check_free_port(ld, lport) before these unlocks to account for the reserved port.
Without updating the active-port counter here, evtchn_reset() racing on another CPU could observe a stale count and succeed while this newly bound port remains open.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a shared resource (the event-channel port table and its active-port count) is accessed by concurrent sequences (bind and reset) without a common exclusive lock covering the whole reset, creating a timing window. The added check_free_port call closes the accounting gap rather than addressing a different weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The bind path allocates a port and transitions it to ECS_INTERDOMAIN, but the reset path's accounting of active ports is not synchronized with this allocation. A concurrent EVTCHNOP_reset can therefore complete while a port opened by this racing bind remains valid, violating the reset's precondition and leaving state inconsistent.

Fix a NPE issue in invalid Exit op. Now it will report an error instead of crash.

Change-Id: Ia6ec55445ea70ad045a4d339d354959ad0618f2a
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      if (!parent) {', '        return errors::InvalidArgument(', '            "Invalid Exit op: Cannot find a corresponding Enter op.");', '      }']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the process of building the control flow graph for a TensorFlow model is vulnerable to a null pointer exception when nodes that should be paired are not. This occurs because the code assumes that the first node in the pairing (e.g., an `Enter` node) always exists when encountering the second node (e.g., an `Exit` node). When this is not the case, `parent` is `nullptr` so dereferencing it causes a crash. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.7.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.6.1, TensorFlow 2.5.2, and TensorFlow 2.4.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: For an Exit node, parent is loaded from parent_nodes[curr_id] at line 28 without checking whether it was ever set. Line 29 immediately dereferences parent->id() to index cf_info->frame_names. The diff adds a null check after line 28, confirming that parent can be nullptr when no corresponding Enter node populated parent_nodes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences parent at line 29 while it may legitimately be nullptr, which is exactly CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read: the defect is the missing null constraint, not an invalid index, so the null-dereference label fits directly.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Exit branch assumes a paired Enter node has already assigned parent_nodes[curr_id], but an invalid graph can contain an Exit without a matching Enter, leaving parent null. description:
Apptainer is an open source container platform for Linux. There is an ext4 use-after-free flaw that is exploitable through versions of Apptainer < 1.1.0 and installations that include apptainer-suid < 1.1.8 on older operating systems where that CVE has not been patched. That includes Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7, Debian 10 buster (unless the linux-5.10 package is installed), Ubuntu 18.04 bionic and Ubuntu 20.04 focal. Use-after-free flaws in the kernel can be used to attack the kernel for denial of service and potentially for privilege escalation.

Apptainer 1.1.8 includes a patch that by default disables mounting of extfs filesystem types in setuid-root mode, while continuing to allow mounting of extfs filesystems in non-setuid "rootless" mode using fuse2fs.

Some workarounds are possible. Either do not install apptainer-suid (for versions 1.1.0 through 1.1.7) or set `allow setuid = no` in apptainer.conf.  This requires having unprivileged user namespaces enabled and except for apptainer 1.1.x versions will disallow mounting of sif files, extfs files, and squashfs files in addition to other, less significant impacts.  (Encrypted sif files are also not supported unprivileged in apptainer 1.1.x.). Alternatively, use the `limit containers` options in apptainer.conf/singularity.conf to limit sif files to trusted users, groups, and/or paths, and set `allow container extfs = no` to disallow mounting of extfs overlay files.  The latter option by itself does not disallow mounting of extfs overlay partitions inside SIF files, so that's why the former options are also needed.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs checksum computation over a group descriptor with a size bound check; the evidence shows an out-of-bounds read concern (CWE-125-style), not reuse of freed memory, so it does not directly support CWE-416.

commit_msg:
Fix #73280: Stack Buffer Overflow in GD dynamicGetbuf

We make sure to never pass a negative `rlen` as size to memcpy().

Cf. <https://github.com/libgd/libgd/commit/53110871>.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (remain == 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (remain <= 0) {']}
description: Integer signedness error in the dynamicGetbuf function in gd_io_dp.c in the GD Graphics Library (aka libgd) through 2.2.3, as used in PHP before 5.6.28 and 7.x before 7.0.13, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted imagecreatefromstring call.

code_evidence: Line 8 computes remain = logicalSize - pos; if pos exceeds logicalSize, remain is negative. The else branch at line 11 only guards remain == 0 (line 12), so a negative remain bypasses the EOF return and is assigned to rlen at line 15. Line 17 then passes that negative rlen to memcpy as the size, which is converted to a huge size_t, writing far beyond buf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The negative size flows into memcpy, causing a write outside the bounds of buf, exactly the out-of-bounds memory operation CWE-119 describes. The underlying signedness error is the cause; the supported weakness is the resulting out-of-bounds buffer write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing check for negative remain, an integer signedness flaw: the equality test at line 12 fails to reject negative values. When pos is advanced past logicalSize via a crafted image stream, rlen becomes negative and memcpy at line 17 receives it as a large unsigned count, overflowing the caller's stack buffer. Consequence is a stack-based buffer overflow enabling DoS or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
x86/mm: PV superpage handling lacks sanity checks

MMUEXT_{,UN}MARK_SUPER fail to check the input MFN for validity before
dereferencing pointers into the superpage frame table.

Reported-by: Qinghao Tang <luodalongde@gmail.com>

get_superpage() has a similar issue.

This is CVE-2016-1570 / XSA-167.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Ian Campbell <ian.campbell@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if ( !mfn_valid(mfn | (L1_PAGETABLE_ENTRIES - 1)) )', '        return -EINVAL;']}
description: The PV superpage functionality in arch/x86/mm.c in Xen 3.4.0, 3.4.1, and 4.1.x through 4.6.x allows local PV guests to obtain sensitive information, cause a denial of service, gain privileges, or have unspecified other impact via a crafted page identifier (MFN) to the (1) MMUEXT_MARK_SUPER or (2) MMUEXT_UNMARK_SUPER sub-op in the HYPERVISOR_mmuext_op hypercall or (3) unknown vectors related to page table updates.

code_evidence: The only constraint on the caller-supplied MFN is ASSERT(opt_allow_superpage); the MFN itself is never validated. Line 7 immediately converts it with mfn_to_spage(mfn) and line 8 dereferences the resulting spage->type_info, so an out-of-range MFN yields a pointer outside the superpage frame table.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an externally supplied page identifier and processes it without confirming it is a valid MFN before use, which is exactly missing input validation (CWE-20). The added mfn_valid(mfn | (L1_PAGETABLE_ENTRIES - 1)) check in the patch confirms the missing constraint; the weakness is absent validation, not an arithmetic or indexing bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the MFN input is used to index the superpage frame table without a validity check on the MFN or its range. Trigger: a guest passes a crafted MFN through the superpage path; the unchecked index produces an invalid spage pointer that is dereferenced and then updated via cmpxchg. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read/write on the frame table, enabling information disclosure, corruption or denial of service.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. A buffer overflow vulnerability in versions 2.12 and prior affects applications that use PJSIP DNS resolution. It doesn't affect PJSIP users who utilize an external resolver. This vulnerability is related to CVE-2023-27585. The difference is that this issue is in parsing the query record `parse_rr()`, while the issue in CVE-2023-27585 is in `parse_query()`. A patch is available in the `master` branch of the `pjsip/pjproject` GitHub repository. A workaround is to disable DNS resolution in PJSIP config (by setting `nameserver_count` to zero) or use an external resolver instead.

code_evidence: After get_name computes name_part_len, p is set to start+name_part_len [16]. The code immediately copies 2 bytes into q->type [17] and another 2 bytes into q->dnsclass [20] via pj_memcpy, advancing p to start+name_part_len+4 [19,22]. No check verifies that p+4 stays within max before these copies, and parsed_len is computed from the advanced pointer [23].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing size check before copying into the parsed structure supports an unchecked buffer-copy style overflow (CWE-120). This is a buffer copy without input-size validation rather than a pure read, though the resulting read past max is the observable defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the query record's type/dnsclass fields are read with pj_memcpy without verifying that the four bytes following the name lie within the packet's max bound. Trigger: a malformed DNS query whose name extends to or near the end of the packet. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of packet memory (and later misparsing), matching the commit's heap buffer overflow fix.

description: The Mobile Identity parser in (1) epan/dissectors/packet-ansi_a.c in the ANSI A dissector and (2) epan/dissectors/packet-gsm_a_common.c in the GSM A dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.9 and 2.0.x before 2.0.1 improperly uses the tvb_bcd_dig_to_wmem_packet_str function, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow and application crash) via a crafted packet.

commit_msg:
pk7_doit.c: Check return of BIO_set_md() calls

These calls invoke EVP_DigestInit() which can fail for digests
with implicit fetches. Subsequent EVP_DigestUpdate() from BIO_write()
or EVP_DigestFinal() from BIO_read() will segfault on NULL
dereference. This can be triggered by an attacker providing
PKCS7 data digested with MD4 for example if the legacy provider
is not loaded.

If BIO_set_md() fails the md BIO cannot be used.

CVE-2023-0401

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Dmitry Belyavskiy <beldmit@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    BIO_set_md(btmp, md);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (BIO_set_md(btmp, md) <= 0) {', '        ERR_raise(ERR_LIB_PKCS7, ERR_R_BIO_LIB);', '        EVP_MD_free(fetched);', '        goto err;', '    }']}
description:
A NULL pointer can be dereferenced when signatures are being
verified on PKCS7 signed or signedAndEnveloped data. In case the hash
algorithm used for the signature is known to the OpenSSL library but
the implementation of the hash algorithm is not available the digest
initialization will fail. There is a missing check for the return
value from the initialization function which later leads to invalid
usage of the digest API most likely leading to a crash.

The unavailability of an algorithm can be caused by using FIPS
enabled configuration of providers or more commonly by not loading
the legacy provider.

PKCS7 data is processed by the SMIME library calls and also by the
time stamp (TS) library calls. The TLS implementation in OpenSSL does
not call these functions however third party applications would be
affected if they call these functions to verify signatures on untrusted
data.

code_evidence: The digest is resolved via EVP_MD_fetch and falls back to EVP_get_digestbyname; md may be non-NULL while its implementation cannot be initialized. BIO_set_md(btmp, md) is called at line 26 with its return value ignored, and the function proceeds to return success.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The ignored initialization failure leads to a NULL pointer being dereferenced in subsequent digest API calls, matching CWE-476. This is not merely a missing error check (CWE-252); the supported consequence is a NULL dereference crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unchecked return of BIO_set_md (which invokes EVP_DigestInit) leaves the md BIO without an initialized digest context. Trigger: attacker-supplied PKCS7 data specifying a known but unavailable digest (e.g. MD4 without the legacy provider). Later BIO_write/BIO_read operations dereference the NULL digest state, causing a crash.

commit_msg:
The memory for filter names is reserved right after receiving the reply.
After that, filters are iterated and each individual filter name is
stored in that reserved memory.

The individual name lengths are not checked for validity, which means
that a malicious server can reserve less memory than it will write to
during each iteration.

description: The XRenderQueryFilters function in X.org libXrender before 0.9.10 allows remote X servers to trigger out-of-bounds write operations via vectors involving filter name lengths.

code_evidence: nbytesName is derived from the reply length minus alias bytes and used to size a single heap allocation that holds the filter-name buffer; name points to the start of that region.

The loop reads a one-byte length len, computes l = len & 0xff, then writes l bytes plus a NUL terminator at name without checking that l+1 bytes remain in the reserved nbytesName region; name advances by l+1 each iteration.

commit_msg:
Pass the ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS flag to libarchive

There are archive types which allow to first create a symlink and then
later on dereference it. If the symlink points outside of the archive,
this results in writing outside of the destination directory.

With the ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS option set, libarchive avoids
this situation by verifying that none of the target path components are
symlinks before writing.

Remove the commented out code in the method, which would actually
misbehave if enabled again.

Signed-off-by: Fabian Vogt <fabian@ritter-vogt.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int result = ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME;', '    result |= ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NODOTDOT;', '', "    // TODO: Don't use arksettings here", '    /*if ( ArkSettings::preservePerms() )', '    {', '        result &= ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM;', '    }', '', '    if ( !ArkSettings::extractOverwrite() )', '    {', '        result &= ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_NO_OVERWRITE;', '    }*/', '', '    return result;'], 'added_lines': ['    return ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME', '           | ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NODOTDOT', '           | ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS;']}
description: In KDE Ark before 20.08.1, a crafted TAR archive with symlinks can install files outside the extraction directory, as demonstrated by a write operation to a user's home directory.

code_evidence: extractionFlags() builds the libarchive extraction flag set from ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME and ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NODOTDOT, then returns it. It does not include ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS, so the returned flags permit archive entries to traverse symlinks during extraction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because file access follows a link that resolves to an unintended resource; the missing SECURE_SYMLINKS flag is the specific cause. This is not merely path traversal (CWE-22) via '..' because SECURE_NODOTDOT is already set; the residual weakness is link following.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the extraction flags omit symlink protection, so libarchive does not verify that path components are not symlinks before writing. Trigger: a crafted archive first creates a symlink pointing outside the destination, then writes through that link. Consequence: files are written outside the extraction directory, e.g., into a user's home directory.

commit_msg:
netfilter: nfnetlink: correctly validate length of batch messages

If nlh->nlmsg_len is zero then an infinite loop is triggered because
'skb_pull(skb, msglen);' pulls zero bytes.

The calculation in nlmsg_len() underflows if 'nlh->nlmsg_len <
NLMSG_HDRLEN' which bypasses the length validation and will later
trigger an out-of-bound read.

If the length validation does fail then the malformed batch message is
copied back to userspace. However, we cannot do this because the
nlh->nlmsg_len can be invalid. This leads to an out-of-bounds read in

                                            ^^ start of batch nlmsg with
                                               nlmsg_len=4294967280
    ...
    [   41.456431] Memory state around the buggy address:
    [   41.456431]  ffff880119e79400: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00

commit_msg:
Issue #148: Check for overflow when reading floating point exponent.

GCC with -O2 optimizes away the if(exp<-maxExponent) branch completely,
so we don't end up with the expected '512' value for overflowing
exponents. Limit the exponent parsing to MAX_INT instead to prevent
signed overflow from tripping up over-eager optimizing compilers.
description: Buffer-overflow in jsdtoa.c in Artifex MuJS in versions 1.0.1 to 1.1.1. An integer overflow happens when js_strtod() reads in floating point exponent, which leads to a buffer overflow in the pointer *d.

code_evidence: Lines 93-96 accumulate the exponent digits with exp = exp * 10 + (*p - '0') while the loop condition only checks that *p is a digit; no bound is placed on exp, so a long digit run in the input string overflows the signed int exp.
Lines 98-102 then combine this attacker-controlled exp with fracExp via exp = fracExp - exp or exp = fracExp + exp, propagating the wrapped value.

Lines 103-110 attempt to clamp exp against maxExponent, but this check runs after the overflow already occurred; the commit notes that -O2 optimization removes the exp < -maxExponent branch, so a wrapped negative/positive exp survives.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits directly: the arithmetic exp = exp * 10 + (*p - '0') can exceed INT_MAX and wrap, and the later maxExponent clamp is applied too late to prevent it. This is integer overflow leading to pointer misuse, not merely a buffer copy error (CWE-120).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the exponent parsing loop multiplies and adds into signed int exp without an upper bound, so a floating-point literal with a very long exponent causes signed integer overflow/wraparound. The wrapped exp is then used to index powersOf10 in the loop at line 118 and drives the pointer *d, leading to out-of-bounds reads and the reported buffer overflow.

description: GPAC MP4box 2.1-DEV-rev593-g007bf61a0 is vulnerable to Buffer Overflow in eac3_update_channels function of media_tools/av_parsers.c:9113

code_evidence: substreamid is read as a 3-bit field (line 66) and used as an index into main_substreams bitmask; the loop can re-enter next_block and process repeated main substreams, so nb_blocks_main can exceed 6 and the ==6 guard fails to trigger the early return, letting parsing continue.

hdr->streams[substreamid] is written (lines 139-143) and hdr->nb_streams++ at line 145 without bounding substreamid to the streams array size; substreamid can reach up to 7 while hdr->streams is a fixed array, so the increment and indexed writes overflow.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an indexed write into a fixed-size buffer (hdr->streams) driven by unchecked input, writing beyond its bounds — a classic buffer overflow from missing size validation, matching CWE-120. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) since the unsafe operation is a write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser indexes and increments hdr->streams using attacker-controlled substreamid without a bounds check, and the nb_blocks_main==6 equality check misses values >6, allowing repeated processing. Trigger: crafted E-AC3 frames with repeated/large substream IDs. Consequence: out-of-bounds write past the streams array (memory corruption/crash).

commit_msg:
Bug 700937: Limit recursion in regexp matcher.

Also handle negative return code as an error in the JS bindings.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!js_regexec(re->prog, text, &m, 0))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!js_doregexec(J, re->prog, text, &m, 0))']}
description: An issue was discovered in Artifex MuJS 1.0.5. It has unlimited recursion because the match function in regexp.c lacks a depth check.

code_evidence: Sp_search invokes the regexp matcher via js_regexec(re->prog, text, &m, 0) with no depth or recursion-limit argument; the only argument controlling execution is the flag 0, and the return value is checked solely for success/failure before pushing a match index or -1.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the function delegates to a matcher lacking recursion control, and the commit replaces js_regexec with js_doregexec to add a depth check. This is uncontrolled recursion, not merely a generic resource leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the search entry point calls the matcher without any recursion-depth bound, so a crafted pattern/text can drive unbounded recursive matching. Trigger: a user-supplied regexp is compiled at lines 7-12 and then executed at line 14. Consequence: excessive stack consumption leading to denial of service (crash/stack exhaustion).

The non-GD2PART branch likewise parses the filename with "s", again permitting NUL bytes.
The parsed file is passed directly to php_stream_open_wrapper without any check that file_len matches strlen(file) or that no NUL precedes the terminator.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The absence of a NUL-byte check on the path lets crafted input defeat intended file-access restrictions, so a reader can access files outside the permitted set; this is an exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor. The unsafe operation is the unvalidated path open at [25] following the "s" parsing, matching CWE-200.

stream = php_stream_open_wrapper(file, "rb", REPORT_ERRORS|IGNORE_PATH|IGNORE_URL_WIN, NULL);

Trigger: a caller supplies a crafted path such as "filename\0.xml". Because the C string terminates at the NUL, php_stream_open_wrapper opens the truncated path, bypassing an application-level restriction intended to limit reads to .xml files, exposing arbitrary file contents.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t  char filename[dirent.namelen + 1];'], 'added_lines': ['\t  char filename[MAX_NAMELEN + 1];']}
description: The grub_ext2_read_block function in fs/ext2.c in GNU GRUB before 2013-11-12, as used in shlr/grub/fs/ext2.c in radare2 1.5.0, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive stack use and application crash) via a crafted binary file, related to use of a variable-size stack array.

code_evidence: Line 22 gates the block only on dirent.inode and dirent.namelen being nonzero, with no upper bound check on namelen.
Line 24 declares a variable-length stack array sized from the attacker-controlled dirent.namelen field read from the ext2 directory entry.
Lines 27-28 copy dirent.namelen bytes from the crafted file into that array, and line 36 writes the terminator at filename[dirent.namelen], all bounded by the same unchecked value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a buffer write whose size derives from untrusted input without validating it against the buffer's intended bound, so it writes outside the allocated buffer boundary, matching CWE-119. The stack-array sizing makes the out-of-bounds region stack memory rather than heap, but the defect remains an operation beyond a memory buffer's boundary.

evidence_lines.code:
grub_ext2_read_file (diro, 0, 0, fpos + sizeof (struct ext2_dirent),
dirent.namelen, filename);
filename[dirent.namelen] = '\0';

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is an unchecked on-disk namelen used as the size of a stack array and as the copy length. A crafted ext2 directory entry with a large namelen triggers excessive stack allocation, exhausting or overflowing the stack and crashing GRUB; the write to filename[namelen] follows the same unchecked bound.

commit_msg:
x86/msi: get rid of read_msi_msg

It's safer and faster to just use the cached last written
(untranslated) MSI message stored in msi_desc for the single user that
calls read_msi_msg.

This also prevents relying on the data read from the device MSI
registers in order to figure out the index into the IOMMU interrupt
remapping table, which is not safe.

This is part of XSA-337.

Reported-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Requested-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    memset(&msg, 0, sizeof(msg));', '    if ( !read_msi_msg(msi_desc, &msg) )', '        return;', ''], 'added_lines': ['    msg = msi_desc->msg;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. The PCI passthrough code improperly uses register data. Code paths in Xen's MSI handling have been identified that act on unsanitized values read back from device hardware registers. While devices strictly compliant with PCI specifications shouldn't be able to affect these registers, experience shows that it's very common for devices to have out-of-spec "backdoor" operations that can affect the result of these reads. A not fully trusted guest may be able to crash Xen, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) for the entire system. Privilege escalation and information leaks cannot be excluded. All versions of Xen supporting PCI passthrough are affected. Only x86 systems are vulnerable. Arm systems are not vulnerable. Only guests with passed through PCI devices may be able to leverage the vulnerability. Only systems passing through devices with out-of-spec ("backdoor") functionality can cause issues. Experience shows that such out-of-spec functionality is common; unless you have reason to believe that your device does not have such functionality, it's better to assume that it does.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function uses unsanitized register data read via read_msi_msg to compute MSI message fields and the IOMMU remap index, which is an improper-trust/input-neutralization issue (e.g., CWE-20/CWE-345 family), not improper privilege management; no privilege assignment, tracking, or access-control logic is present to support CWE-269.

commit_msg:
Fix undefined behavior in CollectiveReduceV2 and others

We should not call done after it's moved.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 400838185
Change-Id: Ifc979740054b8f8c6f4d50acc89472fe60c4fdb1
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                         done);'], 'added_lines': ['                         done_with_cleanup);']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the async implementation of `CollectiveReduceV2` suffers from a memory leak and a use after free. This occurs due to the asynchronous computation and the fact that objects that have been `std::move()`d from are still accessed. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.7.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.6.1, as this version is the only one that is also affected.

code_evidence: The lambda done_with_cleanup captures done by move and dereferences col_params via Unref after calling done().
The LookupResource failure path passes the moved-from done directly to OP_REQUIRES_OK_ASYNC, invoking it without the cleanup lambda.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the code accesses a moved-from object whose resources have been transferred, effectively referencing invalid memory state. This is a use-after-free variant rather than an unrelated logic bug.

evidence_lines.code:
OP_REQUIRES_OK_ASYNC(c, LookupResource(c, HandleFromInput(c, 1), &resource),
done);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Because done is moved into done_with_cleanup, the original done object is in a moved-from state; passing it directly to OP_REQUIRES_OK_ASYNC on the lookup failure path invokes a moved-from callback, leading to undefined behavior and potential use-after-free. The trigger is a failed resource lookup, and the consequence is memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
mwifiex: Fix possible buffer overflows in mwifiex_cmd_append_vsie_tlv()

mwifiex_cmd_append_vsie_tlv() calls memcpy() without checking
the destination size may trigger a buffer overflower,
which a local user could use to cause denial of service
or the execution of arbitrary code.
Fix it by putting the length check before calling memcpy().

Signed-off-by: Qing Xu <m1s5p6688@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (le16_to_cpu(vs_param_set->header.len) >', '\t\t\t\tMWIFIEX_MAX_VSIE_LEN) {', '\t\t\t\tmwifiex_dbg(priv->adapter, ERROR,', '\t\t\t\t\t    "Invalid param length!\\n");', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t}', '']}
description: An issue was found in Linux kernel before 5.5.4. The mwifiex_cmd_append_vsie_tlv() function in drivers/net/wireless/marvell/mwifiex/scan.c allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service because of an incorrect memcpy and buffer overflow, aka CID-b70261a288ea.

code_evidence: The TLV length is derived from the attacker-influenced IE byte priv->vs_ie[id].ie[1] (masked to 8 bits) plus 2, and stored in vs_param_set->header.len without any upper-bound check against the destination capacity.
memcpy copies exactly le16_to_cpu(vs_param_set->header.len) bytes from priv->vs_ie[id].ie into vs_param_set->ie, the fixed-size buffer inside the TLV structure at *buffer.
The same unchecked length is then used to advance *buffer and accumulate ret_len, so the write and the reported size are both driven by the unvalidated value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a memcpy into a fixed-size destination using a length derived from input without a bound check, which is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The fix adds a MWIFIEX_MAX_VSIE_LEN check before the copy, confirming the missing constraint was the root cause rather than a read-side over-read.

evidence_lines.code:
memcpy(vs_param_set->ie, priv->vs_ie[id].ie,
le16_to_cpu(vs_param_set->header.len));

*buffer += le16_to_cpu(vs_param_set->header.len) +
sizeof(struct mwifiex_ie_types_header);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length copied into the destination TLV is computed from IE data and never validated against the size of vs_param_set->ie or the remaining command buffer. Trigger: a vs_ie entry whose ie[1] value yields a length exceeding the destination capacity. Consequence: memcpy writes past the intended buffer, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially enabling DoS or code execution.

After fetching a length from the packet ensure those bytes exist to
avoid integer overflows by callers (while avoiding having to ensure

(field = tvb_get_guint8(tvb, offset++)) != MM_CTYPE_HDR)
{
switch (field)

commit_msg:
This issue is conceptually identical to the one fixed in 29f077d07051
("io_uring: always use original task when preparing req identity"), so
rather than reinvent the wheel, I'm shamelessly quoting the commit
message from that patch - thanks Jens:

 "If the ring is setup with IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL and we have more than
  one task doing submissions on a ring, we can up in a situation where
  we assign the context from the current task rather than the request
  originator.

  Always use req->task rather than assume it's the same as current.

  No upstream patch exists for this issue, as only older kernels with
  the non-native workers have this problem."

Cc: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
Cc: Pavel Begunkov <asml.silence@gmail.com>
Cc: Alexander Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Cc: io-uring@vger.kernel.org
Cc: linux-fsdevel@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: 5c3462cfd123b ("io_uring: store io_identity in io_uring_task")
Signed-off-by: Lee Jones <lee@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct io_uring_task *tctx = current->io_uring;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct io_uring_task *tctx = req->task->io_uring;']}
description: In io_identity_cow of io_uring.c, there is a possible way to corrupt memory due to a use after free. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with System execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.Product: AndroidVersions: Android kernelAndroid ID: A-238177383References: Upstream kernel

code_evidence: Line 3 derives tctx from current->io_uring rather than req->task->io_uring, so with IOPOLL and multiple submitting tasks the wrong task's io_uring_task context is selected. Lines 17-19 read tctx->identity and free it via kfree(tctx->identity) when the refcount drops, while lines 20-24 then use and reassign req->work.identity and tctx->identity, mixing identities from different tasks.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees an io_identity through refcount_dec_and_test/kfree and subsequently references/reassigns identity pointers, matching CWE-416's reuse of freed memory. This is use-after-free, not merely a missing reference increment.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: using current instead of the request originator's task yields a tctx whose identity may be freed or replaced by another task's submission. Trigger: concurrent submissions on an IOPOLL ring. Consequence: the freed io_identity is reused, giving the described use-after-free and potential memory corruption.

commit_msg:
f2fs: fix a dead loop in f2fs_fiemap()

A dead loop can be triggered in f2fs_fiemap() using the test case
as below:

	...
	fd = open();
	fallocate(fd, 0, 0, 4294967296);
	ioctl(fd, FS_IOC_FIEMAP, fiemap_buf);
	...

It's caused by an overflow in __get_data_block():
	...
	bh->b_size = map.m_len << inode->i_blkbits;
	...
map.m_len is an unsigned int, and bh->b_size is a size_t which is 64 bits
on 64 bits archtecture, type conversion from an unsigned int to a size_t
will result in an overflow.

In the above-mentioned case, bh->b_size will be zero, and f2fs_fiemap()
will call get_data_block() at block 0 again an again.

Fix this by adding a force conversion before left shift.

Signed-off-by: Wei Fang <fangwei1@huawei.com>
Acked-by: Chao Yu <yuchao0@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Jaegeuk Kim <jaegeuk@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tbh->b_size = map.m_len << inode->i_blkbits;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tbh->b_size = (u64)map.m_len << inode->i_blkbits;']}
description: The __get_data_block function in fs/f2fs/data.c in the Linux kernel before 4.11 allows local users to cause a denial of service (integer overflow and loop) via crafted use of the open and fallocate system calls with an FS_IOC_FIEMAP ioctl.

code_evidence: Line 8 derives map.m_len (unsigned int) from bh->b_size >> inode->i_blkbits, so the block count comes from caller-controlled buffer size. Line 10 fills map via f2fs_map_blocks. Line 14 shifts map.m_len left by inode->i_blkbits and assigns to bh->b_size (size_t). Because the shift is performed in unsigned int width before widening, a large m_len wraps, yielding zero or a small bh->b_size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The shift produces an integer wraparound where the result is smaller than the mathematical value, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a type-confusion or logic error; the missing u64 cast before shifting is the integer overflow that drives the loop.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the left shift at line 14 is evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so a large map.m_len overflowes and truncates when stored into the 64-bit bh->b_size. Trigger: a local user calls fallocate with a large length then FS_IOC_FIEMAP, producing a huge m_len. Consequence: bh->b_size becomes zero, so fiemap re-requests block 0 indefinitely, causing a CPU-consuming dead loop (DoS).

commit_msg:
xenoprof: limit consumption of shared buffer data

Since a shared buffer can be written to by the guest, we may only read
the head and tail pointers from there (all other fields should only ever
be written to). Furthermore, for any particular operation the two values
must be read exactly once, with both checks and consumption happening
with the thus read values. (The backtrace related xenoprof_buf_space()
use in xenoprof_log_event() is an exception: The values used there get
re-checked by every subsequent xenoprof_add_sample().)

Since that code needed touching, also fix the double increment of the
lost samples count in case the backtrace related xenoprof_add_sample()
invocation in xenoprof_log_event() fails.

Where code is being touched anyway, add const as appropriate, but take
the opportunity to entirely drop the now unused domain parameter of
xenoprof_buf_space().

This is part of XSA-313.

Reported-by: Ilja Van Sprundel <ivansprundel@ioactive.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    xenoprof_buf_t *buf = d->xenoprof->vcpu[vcpu->vcpu_id].buffer;', '    return xenoprof_add_sample(d, buf, pc, mode, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['    return xenoprof_add_sample(d, &d->xenoprof->vcpu[vcpu->vcpu_id],', '                               pc, mode, 0);']}
description: An issue was discovered in xenoprof in Xen through 4.13.x, allowing guest OS users (without active profiling) to obtain sensitive information about other guests. Unprivileged guests can request to map xenoprof buffers, even if profiling has not been enabled for those guests. These buffers were not scrubbed.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only reads pc, forwards the vcpu buffer pointer and mode to xenoprof_add_sample, and rejects the escape code; it contains no resource initialization logic, so it does not directly demonstrate missing initialization of a critical resource.

commit_msg:
Re-sync with internal repository (#772)

Co-authored-by: Facebook Community Bot <6422482+facebook-github-bot@users.noreply.github.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  // Ensure we can fit the new capacity in 32 bits.', '  if (MinCapacity > UINT32_MAX)', '', '  size_t NewCapacity = 2 * capacity() + 1; // Always grow.', '  NewCapacity =', '      std::min(std::max(NewCapacity, MinCapacity), size_t(UINT32_MAX));'], 'added_lines': ['  constexpr size_t MinGrowth = 1;', '  size_t NewCapacity = 2 * capacity() + MinGrowth; // Always grow.', '  NewCapacity = static_cast<unsigned>(std::max(NewCapacity, MinCapacity));', '', '  // Ensure that NewCapacity did not overflow an unsigned int,', '  // and that the capacity in bytes will not overflow a size_t.', '  if (NewCapacity <= this->capacity() ||', '      NewCapacity < MinCapacity ||', '      NewCapacity > size_t(-1) / TSize)']}
description: An out of bounds write in hermes, while handling large arrays, prior to commit 06eaec767e376bfdb883d912cb15e987ddf2bda1 allows attackers to potentially execute arbitrary code via crafted JavaScript. Note that this is only exploitable if the application using Hermes permits evaluation of untrusted JavaScript. Hence, most React Native applications are not affected.

code_evidence: NewCapacity is computed as 2*capacity()+1 and then clamped with std::min(..., size_t(UINT32_MAX)); the prior guard only rejects MinCapacity > UINT32_MAX, so the doubling of an already-large capacity can wrap or exceed the 32-bit bound before clamping.

The allocation size NewCapacity * TSize is passed to safe_malloc/safe_realloc without checking multiplication overflow, so a wrapped or truncated NewCapacity yields a smaller-than-required buffer. memcpy then copies size() * TSize bytes into that buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a buffer based on an unchecked multiplication and then writes element data into it, so the write extends past the allocated region. This is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the integer overflow is the enabling condition, not the primary weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
size_t NewCapacity = 2 * capacity() + 1;   NewCapacity =
std::min(std::max(NewCapacity, MinCapacity), size_t(UINT32_MAX));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: capacity growth and byte-size computation lack overflow checks, so NewCapacity * TSize can wrap. Trigger: an attacker grows a SmallVector to large capacity via crafted JavaScript. Consequence: the allocation is undersized while memcpy writes the full element bytes, producing an out-of-bounds heap write.

commit_msg:
bpf: 32-bit RSH verification must truncate input before the ALU op

When I wrote commit 468f6eafa6c4 ("bpf: fix 32-bit ALU op verification"), I
assumed that, in order to emulate 64-bit arithmetic with 32-bit logic, it
is sufficient to just truncate the output to 32 bits; and so I just moved
the register size coercion that used to be at the start of the function to
the end of the function.

That assumption is true for almost every op, but not for 32-bit right
shifts, because those can propagate information towards the least
significant bit. Fix it by always truncating inputs for 32-bit ops to 32
bits.

Also get rid of the coerce_reg_to_size() after the ALU op, since that has
no effect.

Fixes: 468f6eafa6c4 ("bpf: fix 32-bit ALU op verification")
Acked-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tcoerce_reg_to_size(&src_reg, 4);'], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (insn_bitness == 32) {', '\t\t/* Relevant for 32-bit RSH: Information can propagate towards', "\t\t * LSB, so it isn't sufficient to only truncate the output to", '\t\t * 32 bits.', '\t\t */', '\t\tcoerce_reg_to_size(dst_reg, 4);', '\t\tcoerce_reg_to_size(&src_reg, 4);', '\t}']}
description: In the Linux kernel 4.14.x, 4.15.x, 4.16.x, 4.17.x, and 4.18.x before 4.18.13, faulty computation of numeric bounds in the BPF verifier permits out-of-bounds memory accesses because adjust_scalar_min_max_vals in kernel/bpf/verifier.c mishandles 32-bit right shifts.

code_evidence: Line 11 sets insn_bitness to 32 for non-ALU64 ops, so 32-bit RSH enters the BPF_RSH case. Lines 142-153 handle RSH: only umax_val >= insn_bitness is rejected, then bounds are shifted right without first truncating dst_reg/src_reg to 32 bits. The input registers may still carry 64-bit range metadata.
Lines 170-173 truncate dst_reg and src_reg to 4 bytes only after the ALU operation. For a 32-bit RSH, this post-op coercion does not repair bounds already computed from untruncated inputs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The faulty numeric-bound computation causes the verifier to permit an access outside the intended buffer, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. The weakness is the incorrect range tracking, not an integer overflow itself; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: 32-bit RSH computes shifted bounds from 64-bit register ranges because truncation occurs only after the switch. A right shift propagates high-bit information toward the LSB, so the resulting umin/umax and var_off can be too permissive. The verifier then accepts a later access whose range check is based on these wrong bounds, allowing an out-of-bounds memory read.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

code_evidence: When netal == 0, the code passes snpa (pointer to the SNPA field) to etheraddr_string, which unconditionally reads 6 bytes for a MAC address regardless of the actual snpal length. The SNPA length was validated only against snpal via ND_TCHECK2(*pptr, snpal) at line 87, so a zero-length or short SNPA causes a read beyond the captured buffer.

Trigger: a crafted ES-IS redirect PDU with a short SNPA. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of up to 6 bytes past the SNPA buffer, potentially past the capture boundary.

commit_msg:
The X protocol uses CARD16 values to represent the length so
this would overflow.

CVE-2021-31535

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (strlen(pattern) >= USHRT_MAX)', '        return NULL;']}
description: LookupCol.c in X.Org X through X11R7.7 and libX11 before 1.7.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The libX11 XLookupColor request (intended for server-side color lookup) contains a flaw allowing a client to send color-name requests with a name longer than the maximum size allowed by the protocol (and also longer than the maximum packet size for normal-sized packets). The user-controlled data exceeding the maximum size is then interpreted by the server as additional X protocol requests and executed, e.g., to disable X server authorization completely. For example, if the victim encounters malicious terminal control sequences for color codes, then the attacker may be able to take full control of the running graphical session.

code_evidence: strlen(pattern) is truncated to CARD16 via an unchecked cast into req->nbytes, so lengths >= 65536 wrap; the truncated nbytes then drives req->length and _XSend, sending fewer bytes than the actual pattern length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This fits CWE-120: user input (pattern) is copied into the fixed-width CARD16 protocol field and transmitted without verifying that the input size fits the destination, producing a size-derived overflow that lets excess data flow past the intended request boundary.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller-supplied pattern length is cast to CARD16 without a maximum-size check, so oversized names wrap the protocol length field. Trigger: a client passes a pattern longer than USHRT_MAX. Consequence: the server receives a length inconsistent with the request, and the excess user data is parsed as additional X protocol requests, enabling arbitrary request execution.

commit_msg:
guest_physmap_remove_page() needs its return value checked

Callers, namely such subsequently freeing the page, must not blindly
assume success - the function may namely fail when needing to shatter a
super page, but there not being memory available for the then needed
intermediate page table.

As it happens, guest_remove_page() callers now also all check the
return value.

Furthermore a missed put_gfn() on an error path in gnttab_transfer() is
also being taken care of.

This is part of XSA-222.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        guest_physmap_remove_page(d, _gfn(gop.mfn), _mfn(mfn), 0);', '            put_gfn(d, gop.mfn);', '            page->count_info &= ~(PGC_count_mask|PGC_allocated);', '            free_domheap_page(page);', '            goto copyback;', '            put_gfn(d, gop.mfn);', '            rcu_unlock_domain(e);', '            put_gfn(d, gop.mfn);', '            page->count_info &= ~(PGC_count_mask|PGC_allocated);', '            free_domheap_page(page);', '            goto copyback;', '            rcu_unlock_domain(e);', '', '            put_gfn(d, gop.mfn);', '            page->count_info &= ~(PGC_count_mask|PGC_allocated);', '            free_domheap_page(page);', '            goto copyback;'], 'added_lines': ['        int rc;', '        rc = guest_physmap_remove_page(d, _gfn(gop.mfn), _mfn(mfn), 0);', '        if ( rc )', '        {', '            gdprintk(XENLOG_INFO,', '                     "gnttab_transfer: can\'t remove GFN %"PRI_xen_pfn" (MFN %lx)\\n",', '                     gop.mfn, mfn);', '            gop.status = GNTST_general_error;', '            goto put_gfn_and_copyback;', '        }', '            goto put_gfn_and_copyback;', '        put_gfn_and_copyback:', '            put_gfn(d, gop.mfn);', '            goto unlock_and_copyback;', '            goto unlock_and_copyback;']}
description: Xen through 4.8.x does not validate memory allocations during certain P2M operations, which allows guest OS users to obtain privileged host OS access, aka XSA-222.

code_evidence: At line 57 the return value of guest_physmap_remove_page() is discarded, so a failure to shatter a super page (allocation failure) goes unnoticed and gnttab_flush_tlb() runs regardless.

The subsequent error paths at lines 59-68 (and similarly later paths) assume the P2M removal succeeded and proceed to free the page / transfer it, without checking whether the removal actually happened.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits: the function fails to validate the outcome of a critical operation and proceeds as if the required precondition (successful removal) held, processing data without confirming required properties. This is improper validation of a derived result rather than a separate memory-safety class.

evidence_lines.code:
guest_physmap_remove_page(d, _gfn(gop.mfn), _mfn(mfn), 0);
gnttab_flush_tlb(d);

if ( unlikely((e = rcu_lock_domain_by_id(gop.domid)) == NULL) )
}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unchecked return of guest_physmap_remove_page() means a failed P2M removal (e.g., memory exhaustion preventing super-page shatter) is treated as success. Trigger: a guest issues a grant transfer causing P2M removal to fail. Consequence: the page is freed/transferred while still mapped in the source domain's P2M, allowing stale/inconsistent mappings and potential privileged host access.

commit_msg: Fix CVE-2019-13225: problem in converting if-then-else pattern to bytecode.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        len += SIZE_OP_JUMP;'], 'added_lines': ['      len += SIZE_OP_JUMP + SIZE_OP_ATOMIC_END;', '']}
description: A NULL Pointer Dereference in match_at() in regexec.c in Oniguruma 6.9.2 allows attackers to potentially cause denial of service by providing a crafted regular expression. Oniguruma issues often affect Ruby, as well as common optional libraries for PHP and Rust.

code_evidence: In the BAG_IF_ELSE case, the Else branch adds SIZE_OP_JUMP before compiling the Else body, but the emitted bytecode for the if-then-else pattern also requires an ATOMIC_END after the jump; the length computation undercounts the emitted instruction size when Else is present, so the allocated bytecode buffer is shorter than what the compiler later writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a memory-safety failure (buffer overrun from an incorrect length) that manifests as a crash/NULL dereference in match_at, matching CWE-476's availability impact. The cause is the length miscalculation, not a standalone NULL check; the target CWE is the observed crash class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: compile_length_bag_node under-reports the bytecode length for an if-then-else with an Else branch by omitting SIZE_OP_ATOMIC_END. Trigger: a crafted regular expression containing an if-then-else with an Else clause. Consequence: the later bytecode emission writes past the sized buffer, corrupting memory and leading to a crash/NULL-pointer dereference during matching.

parsettf.c: Fix out of bounds read condition on buffer

Closes #3093

description: FontForge 20161012 is vulnerable to a heap-based buffer over-read in readttfcopyrights (parsettf.c) resulting in DoS or code execution via a crafted otf file.

code_evidence: Line 46 copies the substring after the 8-byte "Version " prefix into a new heap buffer temp. Line 47 then evaluates temp[strlen(temp)-1] without first checking that temp is non-empty; when the version string is exactly "Version " (or otherwise yields an empty remainder), strlen(temp) is 0 and the index -1 reads one byte before the allocated buffer. It is distinguished from a write-based CWE by the primary defect being the unchecked read at index -1; the potential write on the next line is secondary.

commit_msg:
cap_convert_nscap() does permission checking as well as conversion of the
xattr value conditionally based on fs's user-ns.

This is needed by overlayfs and probably other layered fs (ecryptfs) and is
what vfs_foo() is supposed to do anyway.

Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Acked-by: James Morris <jamorris@linux.microsoft.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int cap_convert_nscap(struct dentry *dentry, void **ivalue, size_t size)', '\tkvfree(*ivalue);'], 'added_lines': ['int cap_convert_nscap(struct dentry *dentry, const void **ivalue, size_t size)']}
description: The overlayfs implementation in the linux kernel did not properly validate with respect to user namespaces the setting of file capabilities on files in an underlying file system. Due to the combination of unprivileged user namespaces along with a patch carried in the Ubuntu kernel to allow unprivileged overlay mounts, an attacker could use this to gain elevated privileges.

code_evidence: Line 16-17 gates conversion on capable_wrt_inode_uidgid(inode, CAP_SETFCAP), i.e., authority over the inode's user namespace, not the filesystem's user namespace.
Lines 18-20 short-circuit and return the original size when the caller is ns_capable in the fs user-ns, skipping rootid translation entirely.
Lines 24-26 translate rootid into fs_ns and reject only -1; the check does not verify the caller may set caps in the fs namespace.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-863 fits because an authorization check is performed but bound to the wrong namespace, letting an actor bypass the intended CAP_SETFCAP constraint over the fs user-ns; this is an incorrect authorization check, not merely a missing one.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!capable_wrt_inode_uidgid(inode, CAP_SETFCAP))
return -EPERM;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function authorizes capability-xattr conversion against the inode's user namespace rather than the filesystem's user namespace, and the early-return path at line 19 bypasses translation. A caller privileged in an unprivileged user namespace (e.g., via overlayfs on an underlying fs) can therefore have foreign-namespace capabilities written, escalating privileges on the backing filesystem.

commit_msg:
cryp: prevent direct calls to update and final functions

With inconsistent or malformed data it has been possible to call
"update" and "final" crypto functions directly. Using a fuzzer tool [1]
we have seen that this results in asserts, i.e., a crash that
potentially could leak sensitive information.

By setting the state (initialized) in the crypto context (i.e., the
tee_cryp_state) at the end of all syscall_*_init functions and then add
a check of the state at the beginning of all update and final functions,
  we prevent direct entrance to the "update" and "final" functions.

[1] https://github.com/MartijnB/optee_fuzzer

Fixes: OP-TEE-2019-0021

Signed-off-by: Joakim Bech <joakim.bech@linaro.org>
Reported-by: Martijn Bogaard <bogaard@riscure.com>
Acked-by: Jerome Forissier <jerome.forissier@linaro.org>
Reviewed-by: Jens Wiklander <jens.wiklander@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcs->state = CRYP_STATE_UNINITIALIZED;']}

commit_msg:
CVE-2023-0286: Fix GENERAL_NAME_cmp for x400Address (1.1.1)

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        result = ASN1_TYPE_cmp(a->d.x400Address, b->d.x400Address);'], 'added_lines': ['        result = ASN1_STRING_cmp(a->d.x400Address, b->d.x400Address);']}
description:
There is a type confusion vulnerability relating to X.400 address processing
inside an X.509 GeneralName. X.400 addresses were parsed as an ASN1_STRING but
the public structure definition for GENERAL_NAME incorrectly specified the type
of the x400Address field as ASN1_TYPE. This field is subsequently interpreted by
the OpenSSL function GENERAL_NAME_cmp as an ASN1_TYPE rather than an
ASN1_STRING.

When CRL checking is enabled (i.e. the application sets the
X509_V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK flag), this vulnerability may allow an attacker to pass
arbitrary pointers to a memcmp call, enabling them to read memory contents or
enact a denial of service. In most cases, the attack requires the attacker to
provide both the certificate chain and CRL, neither of which need to have a
valid signature. If the attacker only controls one of these inputs, the other
input must already contain an X.400 address as a CRL distribution point, which
is uncommon. As such, this vulnerability is most likely to only affect
applications which have implemented their own functionality for retrieving CRLs
over a network.

code_evidence: In the GEN_X400 case, GENERAL_NAME_cmp passes a->d.x400Address and b->d.x400Address to ASN1_TYPE_cmp. The x400Address field is defined (per the description) as the ASN1_TYPE union member, while the value stored there was parsed as an ASN1_STRING. ASN1_TYPE_cmp then interprets those pointers as ASN1_TYPE, reading type/union fields that were never initialized as such.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The same memory resource is created as ASN1_STRING but accessed through ASN1_TYPE in ASN1_TYPE_cmp, matching CWE-843's incompatible-type access. This is a type confusion rather than a simple NULL-pointer dereference or buffer overflow, because the defect is the mismatched interpretation of the object's type.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the comparison helper treats an ASN1_STRING object as an ASN1_TYPE, so field offsets and the embedded union pointer are read from the wrong layout. Trigger: CRL checking with an X.400 address in a GeneralName reaches this switch branch. Consequence: ASN1_TYPE_cmp dereferences attacker-controlled/garbage pointers, leading to out-of-bounds reads in memcmp or a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix a security issue using `:quote` with `:escape_html`

Reported by @johan-smits.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbufput(ob, text->data, text->size);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct html_renderopt *options = opaque;', '', '', '\tif (options->flags & HTML_ESCAPE)', '\t\tescape_html(ob, text->data, text->size);', '\telse', '\t\tbufput(ob, text->data, text->size);', '']}
description: Redcarpet is a Ruby library for Markdown processing. In Redcarpet before version 3.5.1, there is an injection vulnerability which can enable a cross-site scripting attack. In affected versions no HTML escaping was being performed when processing quotes. This applies even when the `:escape_html` option was being used. This is fixed in version 3.5.1 by the referenced commit.

code_evidence: rndr_quote receives attacker-influenced quote text in `text`; after the null/empty check it emits the literal `<q>` and then copies `text->data` verbatim into the output buffer via `bufput(ob, text->data, text->size)` before closing `</q>`. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: user-controlled quote content is written directly into generated HTML without neutralization. description: main.c in Tinyproxy 1.8.4 and earlier creates a /run/tinyproxy/tinyproxy.pid file after dropping privileges to a non-root account, which might allow local users to kill arbitrary processes by leveraging access to this non-root account for tinyproxy.pid modification before a root script executes a "kill `cat /run/tinyproxy/tinyproxy.pid`" command.

code_evidence: Lines 37-41: privileges are dropped by calling change_user() when running as root, after which the process runs as a non-root account.
Lines 42-51: after setup_logging(), the PID file is created via pidfile_create(config.pidpath) only when config.pidpath is set, with failures exiting EX_OSERR.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-269 fits because the function manages the privilege transition incorrectly: it relinquishes root before performing a security-relevant file operation, giving the unprivileged actor control over the PID file. This is improper privilege assignment/ordering rather than merely an impact description.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The PID file is created after change_user() has already dropped root privileges, so the file is owned by the non-root account. That account can rewrite tinyproxy.pid; a root script later reading it with `kill $(cat ...)` may signal an arbitrary process. The root cause is the ordering of privilege drop relative to privileged file creation, not the pidfile_create call itself.

commit_msg:
When an error occurs while rewriting the parser tree for window functions
in the sqlite3WindowRewrite() routine, make sure that pParse->nErr is set,
and make sure that this shuts down any subsequent code generation that might
depend on the transformations that were implemented.  This fixes a problem
discovered by the Yongheng and Rui fuzzer.

FossilOrigin-Name: e2bddcd4c55ba3cbe0130332679ff4b048630d0ced9a8899982edb5a3569ba7f
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if( pParse->nErr ) return 0;']}
description: SQLite 3.30.1 mishandles certain parser-tree rewriting, related to expr.c, vdbeaux.c, and window.c. This is caused by incorrect sqlite3WindowRewrite() error handling.

code_evidence: codeCompare dereferences pParse to obtain comparison collations and then emits a VDBE comparison instruction via sqlite3VdbeAddOp4 and sqlite3VdbeChangeP5, with no check of pParse->nErr before proceeding.
The patch inserts an early return on pParse->nErr, showing the original code continued code generation after an already-recorded parse error.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to handle an exceptional parse-error condition, which is the core of CWE-755. This is improper error-state handling rather than a memory-safety flaw; the missing nErr check is the exceptional-condition handling defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: codeCompare does not honor an outstanding parse error and unconditionally builds VDBE comparison opcodes. Trigger: an error recorded earlier (e.g., during window-function parser-tree rewriting) leaves pParse->nErr set while code generation continues. Supported consequence: subsequent code generation proceeds on inconsistent state, allowing malformed or unexpected VDBE programs.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.8-36 Q16, there is a memory leak in the function SVGKeyValuePairs of coders/svg.c, which allows an attacker to cause a denial of service via a crafted image file.

Otherwise the loop at 240-248 iterates over the tokens, using keyword/value pointers, but never releases any token string or the tokens array itself. The 'style' branch simply breaks at 249, leaving the SVGKeyValuePairs allocation live.

Trigger: a crafted SVG image containing style elements, each causing SVGEndElement to enter this branch. Consequence: unbounded memory consumption, producing a denial of service as memory grows unavailable for reuse.

commit_msg:
x86/shadow: Don't create self-linear shadow mappings for 4-level translated guests

When initially creating a monitor table for 4-level translated guests, don't
install a shadow-linear mapping.  This mapping is actually self-linear, and
trips up the writeable heuristic logic into following Xen's mappings, not the
guests' shadows it was expecting to follow.

A consequence of this is that sh_guess_wrmap() needs to cope with there being
no shadow-linear mapping present, which in practice occurs once each time a
vcpu switches to 4-level paging from a different paging mode.

An appropriate shadow-linear slot will be inserted into the monitor table
either while constructing lower level monitor tables, or by sh_update_cr3().

While fixing this, clarify the safety of the other mappings.  Despite
appearing unsafe, it is correct to create a guest-linear mapping for
translated domains; this is self-linear and doesn't point into the translated
domain.  Drop a dead clause for translate != external guests.

This is XSA-243.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Acked-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 HVM guest OS users to cause a denial of service (hypervisor crash) or possibly gain privileges because self-linear shadow mappings are mishandled for translated guests.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only validates shadow page-table entries and returns 0 when the shadow-linear mapping is absent; it contains no operation that exposes a resource across a control sphere, so CWE-668 is not supported.

Add stack limit check to proxy operations

Fixes #3785.

JerryScript-DCO-1.0-Signed-off-by: Dániel Bátyai dbatyai@inf.u-szeged.hu
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  ECMA_CHECK_STACK_USAGE ();']}
description: JerryScript 2.2.0 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (stack consumption) via a proxy operation.

code_evidence: The function asserts the object is a proxy, then extracts handler and target and calls ecma_validate_proxy_object. If no trap is defined, it recurses into ecma_op_object_put_with_receiver on the target [19]; if a trap exists, it calls ecma_op_function_call with the handler [24]. Trigger: an attacker constructs deeply nested proxies or recursive set traps so each ecma_proxy_object_set call invokes another put/function call, growing the call stack. Supported consequence: unbounded stack consumption leading to a crash or stack-overflow denial of service.

commit_msg:
This change has the following effects, in order of descreasing importance:

1) Prevent a stack buffer overflow

2) Do not append an unnecessary NULL to an anyway binary buffer, which
   is writing one byte past client_digest when caller is:
   chap_string_to_hex(client_digest, chap_r, strlen(chap_r));

The latter was found by KASAN (see below) when input value hes expected size
(32 hex chars), and further analysis revealed a stack buffer overflow can
happen when network-received value is longer, allowing an unauthenticated
remote attacker to smash up to 17 bytes after destination buffer (16 bytes
attacker-controlled and one null).  As switching to hex2bin requires
specifying destination buffer length, and does not internally append any null,
it solves both issues.

This addresses CVE-2018-14633.

- Validate received value length and check hex2bin accepted the input, to log
  this rejection reason instead of just failing authentication.

- Only log received CHAP_R and CHAP_C values once they passed sanity checks.
