description: A security flaw was found in the chap_server_compute_md5() function in the ISCSI target code in the Linux kernel in a way an authentication request from an ISCSI initiator is processed. An unauthenticated remote attacker can cause a stack buffer overflow and smash up to 17 bytes of the stack. The attack requires the iSCSI target to be enabled on the victim host. Depending on how the target's code was built (i.e. depending on a compiler, compile flags and hardware architecture) an attack may lead to a system crash and thus to a denial-of-service or possibly to a non-authorized access to data exported by an iSCSI target. Due to the nature of the flaw, privilege escalation cannot be fully ruled out, although we believe it is highly unlikely. Kernel versions 4.18.x, 4.14.x and 3.10.x are believed to be vulnerable.

code_evidence: client_digest is a fixed 16-byte stack array (line 14). chap_r is filled from the network via extract_param with MAX_RESPONSE_LENGTH (line 54) and only checked for HEX type (line 59); its strlen is then passed to chap_string_to_hex writing into client_digest (line 64). No check restricts chap_r to 32 hex characters, so an oversized CHAP_R drives the conversion past the 16-byte stack buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The overwritten object is a local stack array (client_digest), and the overflow arises from unbounded copying of network-controlled input, matching CWE-121 stack-based buffer overflow. It is distinct from a heap overflow since the destination is a stack local, not allocated memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length of the attacker-supplied CHAP_R string is never bounded before chap_string_to_hex writes decoded bytes into the fixed-size stack buffer client_digest. Trigger: an unauthenticated initiator sends a CHAP_R longer than 32 hex characters. Consequence: a stack-based buffer overflow that can smash adjacent stack memory, causing crash/DoS and potentially further corruption.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE(xXFixesCopyRegionReq);'], 'added_lines': ['    REQUEST_SIZE_MATCH(xXFixesCopyRegionReq);']}
description: xorg-x11-server before 1.19.5 was missing length validation in XFIXES extension allowing malicious X client to cause X server to crash or possibly execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: REQUEST(xXFixesCopyRegionReq) casts the client-supplied request buffer to the fixed struct, then swaps length and reads source/destination fields. REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE only ensures the buffer is at least that large, so a length greater than the fixed struct size passes this check while the request is still dispatched via ProcXFixesVector.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts attacker-controlled request metadata (length) and fails to validate that it matches the required size before processing, which is improper input validation per CWE-20. The fix replaces the permissive size check with REQUEST_SIZE_MATCH, confirming the missing constraint is exactly the size validation weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the swapped length field is validated with an at-least-size check rather than an exact match, so a client can send an oversized xXFixesCopyRegionReq. Trigger: a malicious X client sends a request whose length exceeds the expected fixed size. The handler proceeds to read the fields and dispatch to the XFixes procedure, allowing the mismatch to be processed as if valid, with consequences including server crash or potential memory corruption.

Don't allow for unlimited nesting in FBUnserialize or fb_compact_unserialize

description: The fb_unserialize function did not impose a depth limit for nested deserialization. That meant a maliciously constructed string could cause deserialization to recurse, leading to stack exhaustion. This issue affected HHVM prior to v4.32.3, between versions 4.33.0 and 4.56.0, 4.57.0, 4.58.0, 4.58.1, 4.59.0, 4.60.0, 4.61.0, 4.62.0.

No depth counter is passed or checked at the recursive call site, so nesting depth is bounded only by the input string.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly performs unbounded recursive deserialization with no depth constraint, matching CWE-674's uncontrolled recursion consuming stack resources.

evidence_lines.code: V::setAppend(ret, unserializeThing());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the set deserializer recurses into unserializeThing without tracking or limiting nesting depth. Trigger: a maliciously crafted serialized string containing deeply nested set structures. Consequence: unbounded recursion consumes the program stack, leading to stack exhaustion and denial of service.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.7-29 and earlier, a memory leak in the formatIPTCfromBuffer function in coders/meta.c was found.

code_evidence: A buffer is allocated via AcquireQuantumMemory sized from the attacker-controlled taglen; only a NULL allocation result is handled, and the pointer str is stored in a local variable.
On EOF during tag reading, the code relinquishes str and returns -1, which is the one path that correctly frees the buffer.
The normal path calls formatString(ofile, str, taglen) and then relinquishes str; the buffer is not passed out, so its lifetime ends at this point.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the allocated str buffer's effective lifetime ends when formatIPTC returns, yet not all exit paths release it. This is a missing-release resource leak, distinct from an out-of-bounds write; the allocation is valid, but its cleanup is incomplete.

evidence_lines.code:
formatString( ofile, (char *)str, taglen );
str=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(str);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer allocated at lines 72-73 is not released on every exit path. Trigger: an input stream that causes an early return after allocation, such as the tag-length/EOF conditions, or a path that bypasses the relinquish call, leaves str allocated while the function returns. Consequence: repeated processing of crafted IPTC data accumulates unreleased memory, supporting memory-consumption denial of service.

CVE-2017-12898/NFS: Fix bounds checking.

Fix the bounds checking for the NFSv3 WRITE procedure to check whether the
length of the opaque data being written is present in the captured data,
not just whether the byte count is present in the captured data.
furthest forward in the packet, not the item before it.  (This also lets
us eliminate the check for the "stable" argument being present in the
captured data; rewrite the code to print that to make it a bit clearer.)

Check that the entire ar_stat field is present in the capture.

Note that parse_wcc_attr() is called after we've already checked whether
the wcc_data is present.

Check before fetching the "access" part of the NFSv3 ACCESS results.
This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kamil Frankowicz.

Include a test for the "check before fetching the "access" part..." fix,
using the capture supplied by the reporter(s).

description: The NFS parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-nfs.c:interp_reply().

code_evidence: In the NFSPROC_WRITE v3 branch, the code validates only dp[2] via ND_TCHECK at line 101, then dereferences dp[4] at line 103 (EXTRACT_32BITS(&dp[4])) and dp[0] at line 105. When ndo_vflag is set, lines 107-111 advance dp by 3 and read EXTRACT_32BITS(dp) at line 111, which corresponds to the original dp[3] without a preceding check of that position.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences packet fields (dp[4] at line 103, dp[3] at line 111) that were never verified as present in the captured data, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not an out-of-bounds write, since only extraction/printing occurs, and not a null-dereference, since the issue is insufficient bounds validation before reading.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the presence check at line 101 covers dp[2] but the subsequent EXTRACT_32BITS(&dp[4]) at line 103 and the vflag read at line 111 access bytes beyond the validated element. Trigger: a captured NFSv3 WRITE request whose opaque data length field is present but whose following four-byte fields are truncated. Consequence: the parser reads past the captured buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read (buffer over-read).

commit_msg:
netfilter: ipv6: nf_defrag: drop mangled skb on ream error

Dmitry Vyukov reported GPF in network stack that Andrey traced down to
negative nh offset in nf_ct_frag6_queue().

Problem is that all network headers before fragment header are pulled.
Normal ipv6 reassembly will drop the skb when errors occur further down
the line.

netfilter doesn't do this, and instead passed the original fragment
along.  That was also fine back when netfilter ipv6 defrag worked with
cloned fragments, as the original, pristine fragment was passed on.

So we either have to undo the pull op, or discard such fragments.
Since they're malformed after all (e.g. overlapping fragment) it seems
preferrable to just drop them.

Same for temporary errors -- it doesn't make sense to accept (and
perhaps forward!) only some fragments of same datagram.

Fixes: 029f7f3b8701cc7ac ("netfilter: ipv6: nf_defrag: avoid/free clone operations")
Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Debugged-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Diagnosed-by: Eric Dumazet <Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Acked-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn NF_ACCEPT;'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn err == 0 ? NF_ACCEPT : NF_DROP;']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.9 mishandles IPv6 reassembly, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (integer overflow, out-of-bounds write, and GPF) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted application that makes socket, connect, and writev system calls, related to net/ipv6/netfilter/nf_conntrack_reasm.c and net/ipv6/netfilter/nf_defrag_ipv6_hooks.c.

code_evidence: ipv6_defrag() calls nf_ct_frag6_gather() and stores its result in err. The only error handling is the -EINPROGRESS special case returning NF_STOLEN; all other errors, including the negative-offset failure that nf_ct_frag6_gather() can report, fall through to an unconditional NF_ACCEPT. The patch replaces line 14 with a conditional NF_DROP for nonzero err, confirming the pre-patch path forwarded a mangled skb after a failed gather.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a write past the end of a buffer arising from forwarding a malformed, header-pulled skb after reassembly failure, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. The defect is the missing error-to-drop mapping, not an integer overflow per se; CWE-787 fits the resulting memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a nonzero error from nf_ct_frag6_gather() is discarded, so the original skb whose network headers were already pulled is accepted and passed up the stack. Trigger: a crafted IPv6 fragment causing reassembly to fail (e.g. overlapping fragment, negative nh offset). Consequence: downstream code trusts the now-inconsistent header state, leading to out-of-bounds write and a general protection fault (DoS).

description: An issue was discovered in Exempi before 2.4.3. The VPXChunk class in XMPFiles/source/FormatSupport/WEBP_Support.cpp does not ensure nonzero widths and heights, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (assertion failure and application exit) via a crafted .webp file.

code_evidence: Line 3 stores the caller-supplied height via PutLE24(&this->data[7], val - 1) without checking that val is nonzero; a val of 0 underflows during the subtraction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function takes external file-derived input and fails to validate a required property (nonzero height) before processing, matching CWE-20's improper input validation. The patch adds the missing val > 0 constraint, confirming the validation gap rather than a separate encoding or filtering defect.

evidence_lines.code: PutLE24(&this->data[7], val - 1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the height setter accepts an attacker-controlled val and derives the stored value as val - 1 without validating that val is nonzero. A crafted .webp yielding height 0 triggers the underflow, which propagates into the encoded chunk and can lead to an assertion failure and application exit (DoS).

description: h2o is an open source http server. In code prior to the `8c0eca3` commit h2o may attempt to access uninitialized memory. When receiving QUIC frames in certain order, HTTP/3 server-side implementation of h2o can be misguided to treat uninitialized memory as HTTP/3 frames that have been received. When h2o is used as a reverse proxy, an attacker can abuse this vulnerability to send internal state of h2o to backend servers controlled by the attacker or third party. Also, if there is an HTTP endpoint that reflects the traffic sent from the client, an attacker can use that reflector to obtain internal state of h2o. This internal state includes traffic of other connections in unencrypted form and TLS session tickets. This vulnerability exists in h2o server with HTTP/3 support, between commit 93af138 and d1f0f65. None of the released versions of h2o are affected by this vulnerability. There are no known workarounds. Users of unreleased versions of h2o using HTTP/3 are advised to upgrade immediately.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only reads and validates an already-parsed frame and returns an error for unexpected frame types; it performs no operation that accesses or uses uninitialized memory, and the added in_generator parameter is unused in this fragment.

commit_msg:
CVE-2020-1898

Don't allow for unlimited nesting in FBUnserialize or fb_compact_unserialize
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  Variant& out, const char* buf, int n, int& p) {', '        int err = fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer(value, buf, n, p);', '          int err = fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer(value, buf, n, p);', '        int err = fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer(key, buf, n, p);', '        err = fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer(value, buf, n, p);'], 'added_lines': ['    Variant& out, const char* buf, int n, int& p, size_t depth) {', '  if (UNLIKELY(depth > 1024)) {', '    return FB_UNSERIALIZE_MAX_DEPTH_EXCEEDED;', '  }', '        int err =', '          fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer(value, buf, n, p, depth + 1);', '          int err =', '            fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer(value, buf, n, p, depth + 1);', '        int err = fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer(key, buf, n, p, depth + 1);', '        err = fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer(value, buf, n, p, depth + 1);']}
description: The fb_unserialize function did not impose a depth limit for nested deserialization. That meant a maliciously constructed string could cause deserialization to recurse, leading to stack exhaustion. This issue affected HHVM prior to v4.32.3, between versions 4.33.0 and 4.56.0, 4.57.0, 4.58.0, 4.58.1, 4.59.0, 4.60.0, 4.61.0, 4.62.0.

code_evidence: In the FB_CS_VECTOR case, the while loop reads container elements and recursively calls fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer(value, buf, n, p) for each nested element with no depth counter, so nesting depth is bounded only by the input buffer length.
The FB_CS_LIST_MAP case likewise recurses on each non-skip element via fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer(value, buf, n, p) without tracking nesting depth.
The FB_CS_MAP case recurses twice per entry, for key and value, again passing no depth argument, so each nested container adds a new stack frame.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 covers uncontrolled recursion consuming the program stack. The recursive self-calls at lines 62, 83, 100/105 with no depth bound directly match this class; the consequence is stack exhaustion rather than, e.g., unbounded allocation (CWE-770) or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursive parser has no depth limit, so a crafted buffer of deeply nested FB_CS_VECTOR/LIST_MAP/MAP codes drives one recursion per nesting level. Trigger: attacker-supplied serialized string passed to fb_compact_unserialize_from_buffer. Consequence: stack exhaustion/crash (DoS), since stack growth is proportional to nesting depth.

commit_msg:
[tls] Treat invalid block padding as zero length padding

Harden against padding oracle attacks by treating invalid block
padding as zero length padding, thereby deferring the failure until
after computing the (incorrect) MAC.

Signed-off-by: Michael Brown <mcb30@ipxe.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\trc = pad_len;', '\t\t\treturn rc;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t/* Assume zero padding length to avoid timing attacks */', '\t\t\tpad_len = 0;']}
description: A vulnerability was found in iPXE. It has been declared as problematic. This vulnerability affects the function tls_new_ciphertext of the file src/net/tls.c of the component TLS. The manipulation of the argument pad_len leads to information exposure through discrepancy. The name of the patch is 186306d6199096b7a7c4b4574d4be8cdb8426729. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-214054 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: When a block cipher is used, tls_verify_padding returns a negative value on invalid padding; the code stores it in rc and returns immediately at lines 49-50, before the MAC is computed and verified. Valid padding instead proceeds through iob_unput, MAC extraction and the memcmp at line 73, producing a distinct response path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-203 fits because the function returns observably different results (early padding error versus MAC verification failure) for different attacker-controlled inputs, leaking padding state. This is an observable discrepancy exploited as an oracle, not merely a generic crypto failure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: invalid padding is rejected early with -EINVAL before MAC computation, so the error path differs from the MAC-failure path. Trigger: an attacker submits crafted TLS records with malformed padding. Supported consequence: the distinct response/timing reveals padding validity, enabling a padding-oracle attack and information exposure.

code_evidence: When FLAG_REF is set, a placeholder pyc_object is appended to the global refs list and ref_idx points to the new list node.
In the TYPE_UNKNOWN branch, r_list_pop(refs) removes (and frees) that list node, then free_object(ret) runs and NULL is returned.

The ref_idx iterator was captured before the branch but is not used on the NULL-return path, so the dangling node is not dereferenced here; the UAF occurs through the freed refs node being reused by later parsing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function frees a list node (r_list_pop) whose allocation remains reachable via the refs list/iterator and can be used afterward. This is not a simple NULL-deref or double-free: the defect is continued reference to freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the TYPE_UNKNOWN error path pops the just-appended refs entry, freeing the RListIter node while the global refs list state and any retained iterator can still reference that freed allocation. Trigger: a pyc stream whose reference-flagged object has an unimplemented type byte reaches line 110. Consequence: subsequent list operations on refs or the stale ref_idx touch freed memory, yielding a crash/UAF (the reported fix simply comments out the pop).

commit_msg:
libmpa: Implement Montgomery ladder

The mpa_exp_mod() function implements a LtoR algorithm. The LtoR
algorithm is sensitive to timing attacks since it leaks information
about the exponent since it's doing a different amount of work in each
loop when doing the modular exponentiation. It will always do a square
in each loop, but it will also do an additional multiply when the
exponent bit k=1.

This patch implements the Montgomery ladder (and thereby replaces the
old LtoR implementation), which always does the same amount of
operations in each loop and thereby make it more robust to timing
attacks.

Fixes: OP-TEE-2016-0002 which was reported by Applus+ Laboratories.

Tested-by: Jerome Forissier <jerome.forissier@linaro.org> (HiKey, GP)
Tested-by: Etienne Carriere <etienne.carriere@linaro.org> (b2260, GP)

commit_msg:
Have a common routine for converting dates and times to strings.

Have a routine that takes a buffer, a strftime format, and a struct tm *
as arguments, and:

* checks whether the struct tm * is null and, if so, returns a string
indicating that the date and time couldn't be converted;

* otherwise, passes it to strftime(), along with the buffer and the
format argument and, if strftime() returns 0, meaning the string didn't
fit into the buffer and thus that the buffer's contents are undefined,
returns a string indicating that the date and time didn't fit into the
buffer;

* otherwise, returns a pointer to the buffer.

Call that routine instead of directly calling strftime() in printers;
that prevents printing a buffer with undefined data if the buffer isn't
big enough for the string.

Also, when generating file names using an strftime format, check the
return value of strftime() to make sure the buffer didn't overflow.

commit_msg:
hw/net/xgmac: Fix buffer overflow in xgmac_enet_send()

A buffer overflow issue was reported by Mr. Ziming Zhang, CC'd here. It
occurs while sending an Ethernet frame due to missing break statements
and improper checking of the buffer size.

Reported-by: Ziming Zhang <ezrakiez@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Matteo Cascella <mcascell@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Peter Maydell <peter.maydell@linaro.org>
Signed-off-by: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (len >= sizeof(frame)) {', '                        "buffer\\n" , __func__, len, sizeof(frame));'], 'added_lines': ['        /*', '         * FIXME: these cases of malformed tx descriptors (bad sizes)', '         * should probably be reported back to the guest somehow', '         * rather than simply silently stopping processing, but we', "         * don't know what the hardware does in this situation.", '         * This will only happen for buggy guests anyway.', '         */', '            break;', '            break;', '        if (frame_size + len >= sizeof(frame)) {', '                        "buffer\\n" , __func__, frame_size + len, sizeof(frame));', '            break;']}
description: hw/net/xgmac.c in the XGMAC Ethernet controller in QEMU before 07-20-2020 has a buffer overflow. This occurs during packet transmission and affects the highbank and midway emulated machines. A guest user or process could use this flaw to crash the QEMU process on the host, resulting in a denial of service or potential privileged code execution. This was fixed in commit 5519724a13664b43e225ca05351c60b4468e4555.

code_evidence: Line 15 computes len from guest-controlled descriptor sizes. Lines 16-25 only log oversized buffer1 or nonzero buffer2 sizes without breaking. Line 26 checks len against sizeof(frame) but only logs and does not stop. Line 32 then reads len bytes into ptr within the 8192-byte frame, and lines 33-34 advance ptr and accumulate frame_size without re-checking remaining capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked cumulative length causes cpu_physical_memory_read to write beyond the fixed frame buffer, which is the out-of-bounds write described by CWE-787. The missing break statements and the len-only size check are the root cause; the host memory corruption is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Guest-supplied TX descriptor sizes are not constrained: the size checks merely emit debug output and fall through, and the overflow check compares only the current len, not the cumulative frame_size. A guest can supply descriptors whose combined length exceeds the 8192-byte frame, so cpu_physical_memory_read writes past frame, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially crashing or executing code in the QEMU process.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13013/ARP: Fix printing of ARP protocol addresses.

If the protocol type isn't ETHERTYPE_IP or ETHERTYPE_TRAIL, or if the
protocol address length isn't 4, don't print the address as an IPv4 address.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s), modified
so the capture file won't be rejected as an invalid capture.

Update another test file's tcpdump output to reflect this change.

code_evidence: The guard checks pro against ETHERTYPE_IP/ETHERTYPE_TRAIL and both ATMSPROTO_LEN and ATMTPROTO_LEN against 4; only when all hold (and no verbose flag) does execution fall through to the print statements below.
In ARPOP_REQUEST, ipaddr_string(ndo, ATMTPA(ap)) and ipaddr_string(ndo, ATMSPA(ap)) are called unconditionally, treating the protocol address as a 4-byte IPv4 address.
ARPOP_REPLY, ARPOP_INVREPLY, and ARPOP_NAK likewise pass ATMSPA(ap) to ipaddr_string as if it were 4 bytes.
The only bounds check before these prints is ND_TTEST2 on aar_tpa(ap) with ATMTPROTO_LEN(ap); no check of the source protocol address length precedes the ATMSPA reads.

ATMSPROTO_LEN(ap) != 4 ||
ATMTPROTO_LEN(ap) != 4 ||
ndo->ndo_vflag) {

ND_PRINT((ndo, "tell %s", ipaddr_string(ndo, ATMSPA(ap))));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the switch arms call ipaddr_string on ATMTPA/ATMSPA assuming a 4-byte IPv4 address, but the earlier guard merely skips the verbose header when lengths differ and does not stop the switch. A crafted ARP packet with a short or non-IP protocol address length therefore causes ipaddr_string to read past the captured buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read (over-read) rather than a write.

commit_msg:
Avoid infinite recursion in the ALTER TABLE code when a view contains an unused CTE that references, directly or indirectly, the view itself.

FossilOrigin-Name: 1d2e53a39b87e364685e21de137655b6eee725e4c6d27fc90865072d7c5892b5
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      sqlite3SelectPrep(&sParse, sParse.pNewTable->pSelect, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['      pSelect->selFlags &= ~SF_View;', '      sqlite3SelectPrep(&sParse, pSelect, 0);']}
description: alter.c in SQLite through 3.30.1 allows attackers to trigger infinite recursion via certain types of self-referential views in conjunction with ALTER TABLE statements.

code_evidence: For a view (sParse.pNewTable->pSelect non-null), the function calls sqlite3SelectPrep on the view's SELECT without clearing the SF_View flag before preparation, then walks the same select. The prep step can re-enter view resolution on the self-referential view.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the missing guard (clearing SF_View before sqlite3SelectPrep) allows preparation to recurse without a terminating condition. This is uncontrolled recursion causing resource exhaustion, not a memory-corruption or injection weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the view's select is prepared while still marked SF_View, so resolving a CTE that references the view re-enters view preparation on the same select. Trigger: ALTER TABLE rename on a view whose unused CTE directly or indirectly references the view. Supported consequence: unbounded recursion exhausting the stack (DoS).

commit_msg:
sctp: deny peeloff operation on asocs with threads sleeping on it

commit 2dcab5984841 ("sctp: avoid BUG_ON on sctp_wait_for_sndbuf")
attempted to avoid a BUG_ON call when the association being used for a
sendmsg() is blocked waiting for more sndbuf and another thread did a
peeloff operation on such asoc, moving it to another socket.

As Ben Hutchings noticed, then in such case it would return without
locking back the socket and would cause two unlocks in a row.

Further analysis also revealed that it could allow a double free if the
application managed to peeloff the asoc that is created during the
sendmsg call, because then sctp_sendmsg() would try to free the asoc
that was created only for that call.

This patch takes another approach. It will deny the peeloff operation
if there is a thread sleeping on the asoc, so this situation doesn't
exist anymore. This avoids the issues described above and also honors
the syscalls that are already being handled (it can be multiple sendmsg
calls).

Joint work with Xin Long.

Fixes: 2dcab5984841 ("sctp: avoid BUG_ON on sctp_wait_for_sndbuf")
Cc: Alexander Popov <alex.popov@linux.com>
Cc: Ben Hutchings <ben@decadent.org.uk>
Signed-off-by: Marcelo Ricardo Leitner <marcelo.leitner@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: net/sctp/socket.c in the Linux kernel through 4.10.1 does not properly restrict association peel-off operations during certain wait states, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (invalid unlock and double free) via a multithreaded application.  NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incorrect fix for CVE-2017-5986.

code_evidence: The loop releases the socket lock, sleeps in schedule_timeout, and then checks whether the association still belongs to the original socket before re-locking. If a concurrent peeloff moves the association to another socket during the sleep, the check detects the change and jumps to do_error without re-acquiring the lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described supported consequence is a double free of the association created for the sendmsg call when peeloff races with the sleeping sender, matching CWE-415's repeated free of the same address. The invalid unlock is a related locking consequence, not the mapping target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the wait path assumes the association's socket cannot change while the lock is dropped during schedule_timeout. A multithreaded application triggers the race by peeling off the association while a sendmsg thread sleeps; the thread then returns an error without re-locking the original socket, and the subsequent cleanup path can unlock an already-unlocked socket or free an association owned by the peeloff, yielding an invalid unlock and possible double free.

commit_msg:
tcp: make challenge acks less predictable

Yue Cao claims that current host rate limiting of challenge ACKS
(RFC 5961) could leak enough information to allow a patient attacker
to hijack TCP sessions. He will soon provide details in an academic
paper.

This patch increases the default limit from 100 to 1000, and adds
some randomization so that the attacker can no longer hijack
sessions without spending a considerable amount of probes.

Based on initial analysis and patch from Linus.

Note that we also have per socket rate limiting, so it is tempting
to remove the host limit in the future.

v2: randomize the count of challenge acks per second, not the period.

Fixes: 282f23c6ee34 ("tcp: implement RFC 5961 3.2")

Cc: Yuchung Cheng <ycheng@google.com>

Acked-by: Yuchung Cheng <ycheng@google.com>

description: net/ipv4/tcp_input.c in the Linux kernel before 4.7 does not properly determine the rate of challenge ACK segments, which makes it easier for remote attackers to hijack TCP sessions via a blind in-window attack.

code_evidence: The rate limiter resets challenge_count to 0 at the start of each second (lines 11-15) and then allows one challenge ACK per increment up to the fixed sysctl_tcp_challenge_ack_limit (line 16), sending an ACK each time (lines 17-18). The count is deterministic and the limit is a fixed value, so the number of challenge ACKs emitted per second is predictable to an observer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes internal connection state (sequence-number validity) through a predictable, observable side channel, i.e., indirect information leakage to an unauthorized remote actor, matching CWE-200. The weakness is the deterministic rate that leaks state, not a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the global challenge-ACK budget is reset to a fixed value each second and decremented deterministically, so the per-second ACK count is a fixed, predictable quantity. Trigger: a remote attacker sends blind in-window probes and observes whether challenge ACKs are emitted; the predictable rate lets the attacker infer sequence-number state across probes. Supported consequence: disclosure of internal TCP state enables session hijacking.

commit_msg:
platform/chrome: cros_ec_dev - double fetch bug in ioctl

We verify "u_cmd.outsize" and "u_cmd.insize" but we need to make sure
that those values have not changed between the two copy_from_user()
calls.  Otherwise it could lead to a buffer overflow.

Additionally, cros_ec_cmd_xfer() can set s_cmd->insize to a lower value.
We should use the new smaller value so we don't copy too much data to
the user.

Reported-by: Pengfei Wang <wpengfeinudt@gmail.com>
Fixes: a841178445bb ('mfd: cros_ec: Use a zero-length array for command data')
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
Tested-by: Gwendal Grignou <gwendal@chromium.org>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v4.2+
Signed-off-by: Olof Johansson <olof@lixom.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (copy_to_user(arg, s_cmd, sizeof(*s_cmd) + u_cmd.insize))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (u_cmd.outsize != s_cmd->outsize ||', '\t    u_cmd.insize != s_cmd->insize) {', '\t\tret = -EINVAL;', '\t\tgoto exit;', '\t}', '', '\tif (copy_to_user(arg, s_cmd, sizeof(*s_cmd) + s_cmd->insize))']}
description: Race condition in the ec_device_ioctl_xcmd function in drivers/platform/chrome/cros_ec_dev.c in the Linux kernel before 4.7 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds array access) by changing a certain size value, aka a "double fetch" vulnerability.

code_evidence: The size fields are first read from user memory into u_cmd and validated against EC_MAX_MSG_BYTES.
A second copy_from_user at line 15 re-reads the same user buffer into s_cmd, so u_cmd.outsize/insize may differ from the values actually copied.
copy_to_user at line 23 uses the stale u_cmd.insize rather than the size accepted by cros_ec_cmd_xfer, so the copy length is not bound to the validated data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is a non-atomic check-then-use over a shared user buffer, matching CWE-362's timing window where an interfering sequence modifies the resource after validation. The double fetch violates exclusivity of the validated size values; the OOB access is the resulting consequence, not the primary weakness.

evidence_lines.code: if (copy_to_user(arg, s_cmd, sizeof(*s_cmd) + u_cmd.insize))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The user-controlled arg buffer is fetched twice: once for validation and once for the actual command. A racing thread can change outsize/insize between these fetches, so the validated bounds no longer match the copied data. The stale u_cmd.insize then drives copy_to_user, causing an out-of-bounds read/copy and potential DoS.

commit_msg:
Logical error fixed: node zeroing before call remove callback.

This closes #175  issue on Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        node->prev = NULL;', '    } else if(node->parent)', '    ', '    node->parent = NULL;', '    ', '    if(node->next)', '        node->next = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['        ', '    } else if(node->parent) {', '    }', '    node->next = NULL;', '    node->prev = NULL;', '    node->parent = NULL;', '    ']}
description: MyHTML through 4.0.5 has a NULL pointer dereference in myhtml_tree_node_remove in tree.c.

code_evidence: Line 9 nulls node->prev and line 12 nulls node->parent before the callback on line 15. The callback receives the node after its linkage fields are cleared, so any callback path that reads prev/parent/next sees NULL and may dereference it; the fix defers zeroing until after the callback.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function clears pointer fields to NULL and then passes the node into a callback that can dereference them, matching CWE-476's dereference of a pointer expected to be valid. The weakness is use of a NULLed pointer, not merely a logical ordering error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function mutates node->prev, node->parent and node->next to NULL before invoking myhtml_tree_node_callback_remove, so the callback operates on a partially zeroed node. Trigger: a remove callback that dereferences the node's linkage pointers. Supported consequence: NULL pointer dereference, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
resolved: pin stream while calling callbacks for it

These callbacks might unref the stream, but we still have to access it,
let's hence ref it explicitly.

Maybe fixes: #10725
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        DnsStream *s = userdata;'], 'added_lines': ['        _cleanup_(dns_stream_unrefp) DnsStream *s = dns_stream_ref(userdata); /* Protect stream while we process it */']}
description: A use-after-free vulnerability was found in systemd. This issue occurs due to the on_stream_io() function and dns_stream_complete() function in 'resolved-dns-stream.c' not incrementing the reference counting for the DnsStream object. Therefore, other functions and callbacks called can dereference the DNSStream object, causing the use-after-free when the reference is still used later.

code_evidence: Line 2 stores the raw userdata pointer as DnsStream *s without taking a reference. At lines 101-105, s->on_packet(s) invokes a callback that may unref and free the stream; after it returns, the same s is still dereferenced by dns_stream_update_io(s) and dns_stream_complete(s, ...) at lines 106-108 and 112-114.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses a DnsStream object after a callback may have freed it, matching CWE-416's reuse of memory after it has been freed. This is a lifetime/reference-counting defect, distinct from an out-of-bounds access, since the pointer is valid at acquisition but not after the callback.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on_stream_io() holds only a borrowed reference to the DnsStream and does not pin it across the on_packet callback. Trigger: the packet callback releases the last reference (e.g., unrefs the stream), freeing the object. The subsequent update/complete calls dereference the freed s, giving a use-after-free that can corrupt memory or crash.

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

Reviewed-by: Simon Horman <simon.horman@corigine.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tgoto exit;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tgoto put_local;', '', 'put_local:', '\tnfc_llcp_local_put(local);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: nfc_llcp_find_local(dev) returns a local pointer without taking a reference; on failure the code jumps to exit, which only unlocks the device and releases dev, never putting local.
If nlmsg_new fails, rc=-ENOMEM and control jumps to exit, again skipping any release of the local reference obtained at line 16.

After nfc_genl_send_params is called, control falls into exit; no nfc_llcp_local_put(local) exists, so the reference is leaked/never dropped, and the local object can be freed by the unregister path while still referenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is a missing reference/lifetime constraint allowing the local object to be freed while still used, which is exactly CWE-416 use-after-free. It is not merely a memory leak, since the freed object is later dereferenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function obtains a local LLCP object via nfc_llcp_find_local without holding a reference across its use, and its error/exit paths (lines 19, 24, 27) do not call nfc_llcp_local_put. Concurrent nfc_unregister_device can free the object; subsequent use of local (e.g. line 26) dereferences freed memory.

commit_msg:
Fix small OOB reads.

In ssl3_get_client_certificate, ssl3_get_server_certificate and
ssl3_get_certificate_request check we have enough room
before reading a length.

Thanks to Shi Lei (Gear Team, Qihoo 360 Inc.) for reporting these bugs.

CVE-2016-6306

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
(cherry picked from commit ff553f837172ecb2b5c8eca257ec3c5619a4b299)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (nc + 2 > llen) {', '            ssl3_send_alert(s, SSL3_AL_FATAL, SSL_AD_DECODE_ERROR);', '            SSLerr(SSL_F_SSL3_GET_CERTIFICATE_REQUEST, SSL_R_CA_DN_TOO_LONG);', '            goto err;', '        }']}
description: The certificate parser in OpenSSL before 1.0.1u and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2i might allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via crafted certificate operations, related to s3_clnt.c and s3_srvr.c.

code_evidence: The loop condition only checks nc < llen before calling n2s(p, l) at line 80, which reads two bytes from p without first verifying that two bytes remain within llen. The subsequent bounds check at line 81 occurs after the two-byte read, so when nc == llen-1 (or llen), n2s reads past the certificate-request buffer. The added guard in the patch confirms the missing pre-read length check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: n2s dereferences p beyond the validated message region, which is precisely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a write or an integer-overflow-only issue; the defect is reading data past the intended buffer, matching the target weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the two-byte length field is read by n2s before confirming that nc+2 <= llen. Trigger: a crafted CertificateRequest whose CA-name list length leaves only one trailing byte, so the loop iterates and n2s reads beyond the message. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read, causing a crash/denial of service and potential memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
Detect bogus DT_SYMENT.

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/331
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (sz_sym < sizeof(Elf32_Sym)) {', '            char msg[50]; snprintf(msg, sizeof(msg),', '                "bad DT_SYMENT %x", sz_sym);', '            throwCantPack(msg);', '        }', '        }', '        if (symnum_end < 1) {', '            throwCantPack("bad DT_SYMTAB");']}
description: A floating point exception issue was discovered in UPX in PackLinuxElf64::invert_pt_dynamic() function of p_lx_elf.cpp file. An attacker with a crafted input file could trigger this issue that could cause a crash leading to a denial of service. The highest impact is to Availability.

code_evidence: Lines 43-45 read DT_SYMENT into sz_sym, defaulting to sizeof(Elf32_Sym) only when z_sym is zero; a nonzero DT_SYMENT entry yields an attacker-controlled size value.
Lines 46-47 check v_sym < v_str and then compute symnum_end = (v_str - v_sym) / sz_sym, dividing by sz_sym without verifying it is nonzero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code performs an integer division where the divisor comes from untrusted file metadata and lacks a zero check, exactly matching CWE-369 (Divide By Zero). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the fault is division by zero leading to a crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sz_sym is derived from the attacker-supplied DT_SYMENT dynamic entry and is never constrained to be nonzero before use as a divisor. Trigger: a crafted ELF providing DT_SYMTAB, DT_STRTAB and a DT_SYMENT value of 0 (with v_sym < v_str) makes the division on line 47 divide by zero. Consequence: floating point exception/signal causing crash, a denial of service.

description: Buffer overflow in the calc_coeff function in libass/ass_blur.c in libass before 0.13.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via unspecified vectors.

commit_msg:
net: sctp: fix panic on duplicate ASCONF chunks

When receiving a e.g. semi-good formed connection scan in the
form of ...

  -------------- INIT[ASCONF; ASCONF_ACK] ------------->
  <----------- INIT-ACK[ASCONF; ASCONF_ACK] ------------
  -------------------- COOKIE-ECHO -------------------->
  <-------------------- COOKIE-ACK ---------------------
  ---------------- ASCONF_a; ASCONF_b ----------------->

... where ASCONF_a equals ASCONF_b chunk (at least both serials
need to be equal), we panic an SCTP server!

The problem is that good-formed ASCONF chunks that we reply with
ASCONF_ACK chunks are cached per serial. Thus, when we receive a
same ASCONF chunk twice (e.g. through a lost ASCONF_ACK), we do
not need to process them again on the server side (that was the
idea, also proposed in the RFC). Instead, we know it was cached
and we just resend the cached chunk instead. So far, so good.

Where things get nasty is in SCTP's side effect interpreter, that
is, sctp_cmd_interpreter():

While incoming ASCONF_a (chunk = event_arg) is being marked
!end_of_packet and !singleton, and we have an association context,
we do not flush the outqueue the first time after processing the
ASCONF_ACK singleton chunk via SCTP_CMD_REPLY. Instead, we keep it
queued up, although we set local_cork to 1. Commit 2e3216cd54b1
changed the precedence, so that as long as we get bundled, incoming
chunks we try possible bundling on outgoing queue as well. Before
this commit, we would just flush the output queue.

Now, while ASCONF_a's ASCONF_ACK sits in the corked outq, we
continue to process the same ASCONF_b chunk from the packet. As
we have cached the previous ASCONF_ACK, we find it, grab it and
do another SCTP_CMD_REPLY command on it. So, effectively, we rip
the chunk->list pointers and requeue the same ASCONF_ACK chunk
another time. Since we process ASCONF_b, it's correctly marked
with end_of_packet and we enforce an uncork, and thus flush, thus
crashing the kernel.

Fix it by testing if the ASCONF_ACK is currently pending and if
that is the case, do not requeue it. When flushing the output
queue we may relink the chunk for preparing an outgoing packet,
but eventually unlink it when it's copied into the skb right
before transmission.

Joint work with Vlad Yasevich.

Fixes: 2e3216cd54b1 ("sctp: Follow security requirement of responding with 1 packet")
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <dborkman@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Vlad Yasevich <vyasevich@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (sctp_chunk_pending(ack))', '\t\t\tcontinue;']}
description: The sctp_assoc_lookup_asconf_ack function in net/sctp/associola.c in the SCTP implementation in the Linux kernel through 3.17.2 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (panic) via duplicate ASCONF chunks that trigger an incorrect uncork within the side-effect interpreter.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only performs a serial-number lookup in asconf_ack_list; the diff adds a pending-chunk skip, but the resource-consumption/panic arises from duplicate ASCONF handling and requeueing in sctp_cmd_interpreter, not from this lookup, so CWE-400 is not directly supported here.

commit_msg:
Validate that `DataFormat*` attributes form a permutation.

The `src_format` and `dst_format` attributes for the `DataFormatDimMap` and `DataFormatVecPermute` raw ops are supposed to determine a permutation. However, this was not validated and could result in unitialized memory accesses as well as writes outside of bounds and potential crashes.

While here, we also test that the format attributes have the needed length, add tests for all validation failure cases, remove unnecessary calls to `strings::StrCat`, and fix a few grammar errors.

This will be cherry-picked on the supported release branches.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 346135579
Change-Id: I1c76392382c89ad8f072d5bc93d70669851eb404
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                errors::InvalidArgument(strings::StrCat(', '                    "Source format must of length 4 or 5, received "', '                    src_format)));', '        context, dst_format.size() == 4 || dst_format.size() == 5,', '        errors::InvalidArgument(strings::StrCat(', '            "Destination format must of length 4 or 5, received dst_format = ",', '            dst_format)));'], 'added_lines': ['                errors::InvalidArgument(', '                    "Source format must be of length 4 or 5, received "', '                    src_format));', '    OP_REQUIRES(context, dst_format.size() == 4 || dst_format.size() == 5,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("Destination format must be of length "', '                                        "4 or 5, received dst_format = ",', '                                        dst_format));', '        context, IsValidPermutation(src_format, dst_format),', '        errors::InvalidArgument(', '            "Destination and source format must determine a permutation, got ",', '            src_format, " and ", dst_format));']}
description: In affected versions of TensorFlow the tf.raw_ops.DataFormatVecPermute API does not validate the src_format and dst_format attributes. The code assumes that these two arguments define a permutation of NHWC. This can result in uninitialized memory accesses, read outside of bounds and even crashes. This is fixed in versions 1.15.5, 2.0.4, 2.1.3, 2.2.2, 2.3.2, and 2.4.0.

code_evidence: Only length 4/5 of src_format is checked; its characters are never validated to be a permutation of a known format.
dst_format length is checked but its characters are likewise not validated against src_format.

The dst_idx_ tensor is sized by src_format.size(), then filled by matching dst_format[j] == src_format[i]; if a src_format character is absent from dst_format, the inner loop completes without assignment, leaving dst_idx_ entry uninitialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing permutation validation leaves index values uninitialized, and downstream use of those indices reads memory outside the intended buffer. This is an out-of-bounds read rather than only a write issue; the unchecked indices drive the offending access.

evidence_lines.code:
OP_REQUIRES(context, src_format.size() == 4 || src_format.size() == 5,
errors::InvalidArgument(strings::StrCat(
"Source format must of length 4 or 5, received "
"src_format = ",
src_format)));

OP_REQUIRES(
context, dst_format.size() == 4 || dst_format.size() == 5,
errors::InvalidArgument(strings::StrCat(
"Destination format must of length 4 or 5, received dst_format = ",
dst_format)));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constructor accepts arbitrary src_format/dst_format character sets as long as lengths are 4 or 5, without verifying a permutation. Trigger: a non-permutation pair where some src_format character has no match in dst_format. Consequence: the break is never reached, so dst_idx_ elements remain uninitialized and later used as offsets, yielding uninitialized reads and possible out-of-bounds memory access.

commit_msg:
media: tw5864: Fix possible NULL pointer dereference in tw5864_handle_frame

'vb' null check should be done before dereferencing it in
tw5864_handle_frame, otherwise a NULL pointer dereference
may occur.

Fixes: 34d1324edd31 ("[media] pci: Add tw5864 driver")

Signed-off-by: YueHaibing <yuehaibing@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab+samsung@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tv4l2_buf = to_vb2_v4l2_buffer(&vb->vb.vb2_buf);', ''], 'added_lines': ['', '\tv4l2_buf = to_vb2_v4l2_buffer(&vb->vb.vb2_buf);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2. There is a NULL pointer dereference in tw5864_handle_frame() in drivers/media/pci/tw5864/tw5864-video.c, which may cause denial of service, aka CID-2e7682ebfc75.

code_evidence: input->vb is copied into vb and then set to NULL under the spinlock; vb may be NULL when no buffer is queued. Line 27 dereferences vb via &vb->vb.vb2_buf before the null check at line 28, so the guard is too late to protect the dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes a pointer from vb without validating it, then checks vb for NULL afterward; the unchecked dereference directly matches CWE-476. This is not merely an unchecked return value, since the null value originates from input->vb being cleared and the dereference occurs before the guard.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: vb is dereferenced in to_vb2_v4l2_buffer before the !vb check. Trigger: a frame arrives while input->vb is NULL (buffer gone because of disabling). Consequence: NULL pointer dereference, causing a kernel crash/denial of service, as the later guard cannot prevent the earlier dereference.

commit_msg:
nfc: replace improper check device_is_registered() in netlink related functions

The device_is_registered() in nfc core is used to check whether
nfc device is registered in netlink related functions such as
nfc_fw_download(), nfc_dev_up() and so on. Although device_is_registered()
is protected by device_lock, there is still a race condition between
device_del() and device_is_registered(). The root cause is that
kobject_del() in device_del() is not protected by device_lock.

   (cleanup task)         |     (netlink task)
                          |
nfc_unregister_device     | nfc_fw_download
 device_del               |  device_lock
  ...                     |   if (!device_is_registered)//(1)
  kobject_del//(2)        |   ...
 ...                      |  device_unlock

The device_is_registered() returns the value of state_in_sysfs and
the state_in_sysfs is set to zero in kobject_del(). If we pass check in
position (1), then set zero in position (2). As a result, the check
in position (1) is useless.

This patch uses bool variable instead of device_is_registered() to judge
whether the nfc device is registered, which is well synchronized.

Fixes: 3e256b8f8dfa ("NFC: add nfc subsystem core")
Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tdevice_lock(&dev->dev);', '\t\tdev->shutting_down = true;', '\t\tdevice_unlock(&dev->dev);'], 'added_lines': ['\tdev->shutting_down = true;']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel's NFC core functionality due to a race condition between kobject creation and delete. This vulnerability allows a local attacker with CAP_NET_ADMIN privilege to leak kernel information.

code_evidence: The function takes device_lock, inspects dev->rfkill under the lock, and releases the lock at line 14; the rfkill teardown is thus serialized against other locked users.
For check_presence devices, shutting_down is set under device_lock in a separate critical section, after the earlier unlock, and before del_timer_sync/cancel_work_sync run outside any lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-367 fits because the function's registration/shutdown state is checked by concurrent netlink paths while cleanup changes that state; the patch closes the window by setting shutting_down under the same device_lock that guards the check, aligning check and use.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The patch moves the dev->shutting_down assignment inside the existing device_lock critical section instead of a separate lock/unlock block. Before the fix, the state flag was set in its own critical section, leaving a gap in which concurrent netlink operations could observe inconsistent device state relative to teardown. The trigger is a cleanup task (nfc_unregister_device) racing a netlink task (e.g., nfc_fw_download) that checks registration state; the supported consequence is unexpected state/execution logic and potential use-after-free of the NFC device.

commit_msg:
Heap buffer overflow in tokenadd() (fix #105)

This was an off-by one: the NUL terminator byte was not allocated on
resize.  This was triggered by JSON-encoded numbers longer than 256
bytes.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (p->tokenpos == p->tokenlen) {'], 'added_lines': ['  if (p->tokenpos >= (p->tokenlen - 1)) {']}
description: Off-by-one error in the tokenadd function in jv_parse.c in jq allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a long JSON-encoded number, which triggers a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Line 3 only grows the buffer when tokenpos equals tokenlen, leaving no room for the NUL terminator; the write at line 8 stores c at tokenbuf[tokenpos++], which can reach the last allocated byte without reserving space for termination, so a later terminator write overruns the heap buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes outside the allocated token buffer's intended boundary, directly matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation; the root cause is the off-by-one resize condition rather than an unrelated defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The resize condition fails to reserve space for the NUL terminator, so after a token fills the buffer to tokenlen-1 the next append places a byte at the boundary and the terminator write goes one past the allocation. Triggered by a JSON-encoded number longer than the initial 256-byte token buffer, this causes an out-of-bounds heap write and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
s390/mm: four page table levels vs. fork

The fork of a process with four page table levels is broken since
git commit 6252d702c5311ce9 "[S390] dynamic page tables."

All new mm contexts are created with three page table levels and
an asce limit of 4TB. If the parent has four levels dup_mmap will
add vmas to the new context which are outside of the asce limit.
The subsequent call to copy_page_range will walk the three level
page table structure of the new process with non-zero pgd and pud
indexes. This leads to memory clobbers as the pgd_index *and* the
pud_index is added to the mm->pgd pointer without a pgd_deref
in between.

The init_new_context() function is selecting the number of page
table levels for a new context. The function is used by mm_init()
which in turn is called by dup_mm() and mm_alloc(). These two are
used by fork() and exec(). The init_new_context() function can
distinguish the two cases by looking at mm->context.asce_limit,
for fork() the mm struct has been copied and the number of page
table levels may not change. For exec() the mm_alloc() function
set the new mm structure to zero, in this case a three-level page
table is created as the temporary stack space is located at
STACK_TOP_MAX = 4TB.

This fixes CVE-2016-2143.

Reported-by: Marcin Kościelnicki <koriakin@0x04.net>
Reviewed-by: Heiko Carstens <heiko.carstens@de.ibm.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Martin Schwidefsky <schwidefsky@de.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmm->context.asce_bits = _ASCE_TABLE_LENGTH | _ASCE_USER_BITS;', '\tmm->context.asce_bits |= _ASCE_TYPE_REGION3;', '\tmm->context.asce_limit = STACK_TOP_MAX;'], 'added_lines': ['\tspin_lock_init(&mm->context.list_lock);', '\tINIT_LIST_HEAD(&mm->context.pgtable_list);', '\tINIT_LIST_HEAD(&mm->context.gmap_list);', '\tif (mm->context.asce_limit == 0) {', '\t\t/* context created by exec, set asce limit to 4TB */', '\t\tmm->context.asce_bits = _ASCE_TABLE_LENGTH |', '\t\t\t_ASCE_USER_BITS | _ASCE_TYPE_REGION3;', '\t\tmm->context.asce_limit = STACK_TOP_MAX;', '\t} else if (mm->context.asce_limit == (1UL << 31)) {', '\t\tmm_inc_nr_pmds(mm);', '\t}']}
description: The fork implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.5 on s390 platforms mishandles the case of four page-table levels, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted application, related to arch/s390/include/asm/mmu_context.h and arch/s390/include/asm/pgalloc.h.

code_evidence: init_new_context unconditionally overwrites mm->context.asce_bits and mm->context.asce_limit with a fixed three-level (REGION3) configuration and STACK_TOP_MAX, without inspecting the inherited asce_limit of a copied mm struct.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code accepts the mm context state without validating whether the existing asce_limit requires preserving four levels, so an unvalidated precondition drives unsafe page-table processing. This matches CWE-20's improper validation of input properties required for safe processing. It is not a simple bounds check but a missing consistency validation between inherited context state and the chosen table geometry.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function does not validate the incoming mm->context.asce_limit (state copied from the parent during fork) before reconfiguring the page-table geometry. Trigger: fork of a process whose parent uses four page-table levels; the new context is forced to three levels and a 4TB limit while dup_mmap adds VMAs beyond that limit. Consequence: copy_page_range walks a mismatched page-table structure, causing memory clobbers and a system crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
There are a couple bugs here:
1) If opt[1] is zero then this results in a forever loop.  If the value
   is less than 2 then it is invalid.
2) It assumes that "len" is more than sizeof(valid_accm) or 6 which can
   result in memory corruption.

In the case of LCP_OPTION_ACCM, then  we should check "opt[1]" instead
of "len" because, if "opt[1]" is less than sizeof(valid_accm) then
"nak_len" gets out of sync and it can lead to memory corruption in the
next iterations through the loop.  In case of LCP_OPTION_MAGIC, the
only valid value for opt[1] is 6, but the code is trying to log invalid
data so we should only discard the data when "len" is less than 6
because that leads to a read overflow.

Reported-by: ChenNan Of Chaitin Security Research Lab  <whutchennan@gmail.com>
Fixes: e022c2f07ae5 ("WAN: new synchronous PPP implementation for generic HDLC.")
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (len < 2 || len < opt[1]) {', '\t\t\tdev->stats.rx_errors++;', '\t\t\tkfree(out);', '\t\t\treturn; /* bad packet, drop silently */', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (len < 2 || opt[1] < 2 || len < opt[1])', '\t\t\tgoto err_out;', '\t\t\t\tif (opt[1] < sizeof(valid_accm))', '\t\t\t\t\tgoto err_out;', '\t\t\t\tif (len < 6)', '\t\t\t\t\tgoto err_out;', '\treturn;', '', 'err_out:', '\tdev->stats.rx_errors++;', '\tkfree(out);']}
description: A flaw was found in the HDLC_PPP module of the Linux kernel in versions before 5.9-rc7. Memory corruption and a read overflow is caused by improper input validation in the ppp_cp_parse_cr function which can cause the system to crash or cause a denial of service. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to data confidentiality and integrity as well as system availability.

code_evidence: The loop trusts the option length byte opt[1] for both the iteration step (len -= opt[1], opt += opt[1]) and the bounds check; it only rejects len < 2 or len < opt[1], never requiring opt[1] >= 2, so opt[1]==0 leaves len unchanged and loops forever.

For LCP_OPTION_ACCM the code compares and copies sizeof(valid_accm)=6 bytes without first checking opt[1] >= 6, so a shorter option causes memcmp/memcpy to read past the option and nak_len to advance out of sync.
For LCP_OPTION_MAGIC the code reads opt[2]..opt[5] after only validating opt[1]==6, without first checking that len >= 6, so a truncated option triggers an out-of-bounds read.
memcpy(out + rej_len, opt, opt[1]) and rej_len += opt[1] use the unchecked option length to write into out, which was sized only to req_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function processes attacker-supplied option data without enforcing the required length properties (opt[1]>=2, ACCM>=6, MAGIC len>=6), which is improper input validation of metadata that then drives unsafe memory operations.

evidence_lines.code:
memcpy(out + rej_len, opt, opt[1]);
rej_len += opt[1];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the option-length byte opt[1] and remaining len are not validated against the minimum sizes required by each option type. Trigger: a crafted LCP Configure-Request with opt[1]==0 (infinite loop), a short ACCM option (<6 bytes), or a truncated MAGIC option (len<6). Consequence: denial of service via hang, and out-of-bounds read/memory corruption from memcmp/memcpy and the nak_len/rej_len accounting.

description: A vulnerbility was found in OpenSC. This security flaw cause a buffer overrun vulnerability in pkcs15 cardos_have_verifyrc_package. The attacker can supply a smart card package with malformed ASN1 context. The cardos_have_verifyrc_package function scans the ASN1 buffer for 2 tags, where remaining length is wrongly caculated due to moved starting pointer. This leads to possible heap-based buffer oob read. In cases where ASAN is enabled while compiling this causes a crash. Further info leak or more damage is possible.

code_evidence: p starts at rbuf and is reassigned to the tag pointer returned by sc_asn1_find_tag; the loop then advances with p += tlen and len -= tlen + 2, but p and len are no longer anchored to the same buffer offset, so the remaining-length computation is inconsistent with the moved starting pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a read past the end of the response buffer because the length passed to the ASN.1 parser exceeds the actual remaining data; this is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), not an out-of-bounds write, since no data is written beyond bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop reuses p both as the scan cursor and as the tag result, so after sc_asn1_find_tag moves p past the 0xe1 tag header, len is still decremented as if scanning from the original position. Trigger: a malformed ASN.1 package from the smart card that makes tlen inconsistent with the actual consumed bytes. The resulting wrong remaining length lets subsequent sc_asn1_find_tag calls read past the end of rbuf, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read (crash under ASAN, possible info leak).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int          GetS16BE (int nPos, bool *pbSuccess)', '            if ( nPos < 0 || nPos + 1 >= m_nLen )'], 'added_lines': ['int          GetS16BE (const unsigned int& nPos, bool *pbSuccess)', '            if ( m_nLen < 2 || nPos > (m_nLen - 2) )']}
description: Onlyoffice Document Server v6.0.0 and below and Core 6.1.0.26 and below were discovered to contain a heap overflow via the component DesktopEditor/fontengine/fontconverter/FontFileBase.h.

code_evidence: GetS16BE takes a signed int nPos and validates it with `nPos < 0 || nPos + 1 >= m_nLen`; the addition `nPos + 1` can overflow for nPos near INT_MAX, and the signed comparison is the only bound check before indexing.
After the check, the function reads `m_sFile[nPos]` and `m_sFile[nPos + 1]` directly with no further bounds enforcement, so the validation is the sole guard on the two-element access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked index reaches `m_sFile[nPos + 1]`, an out-of-bounds write/read of the intended buffer. The overflowed bound check is the enabling cause rather than the weakness itself; the memory access past the buffer is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check uses signed arithmetic `nPos + 1`, which can wrap to a negative value and bypass the `>= m_nLen` test. Trigger: a caller supplies a large positive nPos. The subsequent reads at `m_sFile[nPos]` and `m_sFile[nPos + 1]` then index outside the buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds access; the patch replaces this with an unsigned parameter and `m_nLen < 2 || nPos > (m_nLen - 2)` to avoid overflow.

resip/stack: SdpContents: Avoid out-of-memory condition (CVE-2017-11521)

Adding too many media connections may lead to memory
exhaustion.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['         if (num > 255)', '         {', '            pb.fail(__FILE__, __LINE__, "Too many connection addresses");', '         }', '']}
description: The SdpContents::Session::Medium::parse function in resip/stack/SdpContents.cxx in reSIProcate 1.10.2 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering many media connections.

code_evidence: The while loop at 39-46 repeatedly parses 'c' connection lines, each appending a Connection via addConnection(Connection()) and reading an unbounded count num from pb.integer() after the slash.
For IPv4 addresses (56-63), the loop runs i from 1 to num-1, calling addConnection(con) each iteration, so num directly dictates how many Connection objects are allocated.
The IPv6 branch (66-76) has the same pattern: for (i=1; i<num; i++) calls addConnection(con) and writes mConnections.back(), with num taken directly from attacker-controlled input and no upper bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function fails to throttle or bound the number of Connection resources allocated in response to attacker-controlled input, exhausting a limited resource (memory). This is a missing upper-bound constraint on allocation, not a buffer overflow or injection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: num parsed from the SDP connection line is used as an unbounded loop count when expanding address ranges, and the outer loop also allows arbitrarily many connection lines. Trigger: a crafted SDP message with a large num value (or many 'c' lines) causes addConnection to allocate one Connection per iteration. Consequence: memory consumption grows without limit, leading to denial of service via memory exhaustion.

description: An issue was discovered in json-c from 20200420 (post 0.14 unreleased code) through 0.15-20200726. A stack-buffer-overflow exists in the auxiliary sample program json_parse which is located in the function parseit.

code_evidence: Line 31 forms aterr as &buf[start_pos + parse_end] with no check that start_pos + parse_end stays within the 32768-byte stack buffer buf declared at line 4. Line 35 then dereferences aterr[0] in the error fprintf, reading the byte at that computed offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The computed aterr points outside the intended stack buffer and is then dereferenced, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds access past the end of the buffer. The patch's bounds check on start_pos + parse_end < sizeof(buf) confirms the missing constraint; the flaw is an out-of-bounds access rather than a mere incorrect offset, so CWE-787 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path trusts json_tokener_get_parse_end(tok) to keep start_pos + parse_end within buf, but parse_end can point at or past the end of the consumed region, so aterr[0] at line 35 reads past buf. Trigger: malformed input that makes json_tokener_parse_ex fail with a parse_end placing start_pos + parse_end at sizeof(buf) or beyond. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds stack access (stack-buffer-overflow) on the error path.

commit_msg:
Q.931: fix use-after-free (write) of "q931_pi"

The dissect_q931_number_ie (and indirectly dissect_q931_cause_ie_unsafe)
write to the "q931_pi" structure which seems private to the q931
dissector, but can in fact be called through other dissectors (isup) as
well. Normally this structure is initialized in "dissect_q931_pdu" and
invalidated at the end of the function, but a malformed packet can
prevent the cleanup. In the next packet, a different dissector can thus
trigger a use-after-free via "dissect_q931_number_ie".

Rename "dissect_q931_cause_ie_unsafe" since "unsafe" meant that external
dissectors could not call it directly (see commit a83a87e9ca).

Based on commit 197ceddab109, it seems that the intended purpose of the
structure is to provide information to the VoIP Calls dialog, but it
would only be used when called through dissect_q931_pdu. Dissectors like
isup have their own routines to provide call information, but as a
side-effect of code sharing the problematic code path was reached.

An out-of-bounds read was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.3 and earlier. The out-of-bounds read is triggered when Exiv2 is used to write metadata into a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service by crashing Exiv2, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. Note that this bug is only triggered when writing the metadata, which is a less frequently used Exiv2 operation than reading the metadata. For example, to trigger the bug in the Exiv2 command-line application, you need to add an extra command-line argument such as `insert`. The bug is fixed in version v0.27.4.

Reported-by: Hulk Robot <hulkci@huawei.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!fm10k_workqueue)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.11. fm10k_init_module in drivers/net/ethernet/intel/fm10k/fm10k_main.c has a NULL pointer dereference because there is no -ENOMEM upon an alloc_workqueue failure.

code_evidence: fm10k_workqueue is assigned the result of alloc_workqueue without any check for a NULL return.

The unchecked handle is then used indirectly: fm10k_dbg_init() and fm10k_register_pci_driver() proceed unconditionally, and the workqueue is later consumed during driver unload (drain_workqueue/destroy_workqueue), where the NULL value is dereferenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function stores a possibly-NULL allocation result and propagates it into later workqueue use without a validity check, which is the direct cause of the NULL pointer dereference. The added -ENOMEM check confirms the missing constraint; this is not a use-after-free or uninitialized value issue.

evidence_lines.code:
fm10k_workqueue = alloc_workqueue("%s", WQ_MEM_RECLAIM, 0,
fm10k_driver_name);

fm10k_dbg_init();
return fm10k_register_pci_driver();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: alloc_workqueue can fail and return NULL, but fm10k_init_module does not test fm10k_workqueue before continuing initialization. Trigger: memory pressure or allocation failure makes alloc_workqueue return NULL; the driver still loads and later unloads, reaching workqueue teardown. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash/DoS during module unload, as shown in the reported general protection fault.

commit_msg:
Cast to size_t before multiplication

Need to cast to size_t before multiplication otherwise overflow check is useless.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tl_current_pi->include = (OPJ_INT16*) opj_calloc((l_tcp->numlayers +1) * l_step_l, sizeof(OPJ_INT16));'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tl_current_pi->include = (OPJ_INT16*) opj_calloc((size_t)(l_tcp->numlayers + 1U) * l_step_l, sizeof(OPJ_INT16));']}
description: Integer overflow in the opj_pi_create_decode function in pi.c in OpenJPEG allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted JP2 file, which triggers an out-of-bounds read or write.

code_evidence: Line 64 guards the calloc size with l_step_l <= SIZE_MAX / (l_tcp->numlayers + 1U). Line 66 multiplies (l_tcp->numlayers + 1) * l_step_l. If both operands are 32-bit OPJ_UINT32, the product is computed in 32-bit before being passed as the size_t count, so the division-based guard does not protect the actual multiplication.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the size computation (numlayers+1)*l_step_l can wrap before allocation, and the guard fails to prevent it. This is an integer overflow used as an allocation size, distinct from a simple missing bounds check.

evidence_lines.code:
if (l_step_l <= (SIZE_MAX / (l_tcp->numlayers + 1U)))
l_current_pi->include = (OPJ_INT16*) opj_calloc((l_tcp->numlayers +1) * l_step_l, sizeof(OPJ_INT16));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the overflow check assumes the multiplication is performed at size_t width, but the operands are OPJ_UINT32, so the product wraps in 32-bit arithmetic. Trigger: a crafted JP2 with attacker-controlled numlayers and resolution/precision-derived l_step_l such that the 32-bit product overflows. The wrapped small value is passed to opj_calloc, allocating a buffer smaller than the logical index space subsequently used via include, leading to out-of-bounds access.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Palash Oswal <oswalpalash@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Sudip Mukherjee <sudipm.mukherjee@gmail.com>
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+9671693590ef5aad8953@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
