diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tiov_iter_reexpand(iter, iter->count + iter->truncated);']}
description: An out-of-bounds read flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s io_uring module in the way a user triggers the io_read() function with some special parameters. This flaw allows a local user to read some memory out of bounds.

code_evidence: Line 17 snapshots io_size = iov_iter_count(iter) before the write attempt; line 18 stores it in req->result. At the copy_iov label (57), line 58 calls iov_iter_revert(iter, io_size - iov_iter_count(iter)), computing the revert amount from the initial size while the iterator may have been truncated and not reexpanded by call_write_iter/loop_rw_iter.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe revert causes the iterator to be positioned outside its valid buffer range, and subsequent access reads memory out of bounds, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. The flaw is not a write past the buffer (CWE-787); the reported consequence is a read, consistent with the target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the revert length is derived from the stale initial io_size rather than the iterator's current/truncated state, and no reexpansion occurs before reverting. Trigger: a nonblocking write path (lines 23-27 or 49-53) reaching copy_iov after the iterator was truncated. Consequence: iov_iter_revert miscalculates iterator bounds, yielding an out-of-bounds read, as reported by KASAN in the commit trace.

commit_msg:
pack: fix type confusion bugs. Amongst other OSS-Fuzz 5136174263566336

Signed-off-by: davkor <david@adalogics.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (root.type != MSGPACK_OBJECT_ARRAY) {', '            continue;', '        }', '        if (map.type != MSGPACK_OBJECT_MAP) {', '            continue;', '        }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Treasure Data Fluent Bit 1.7.1, erroneous parsing in flb_pack_msgpack_to_json_format leads to type confusion bug that interprets whatever is on the stack as msgpack maps and arrays, leading to use-after-free. This can be used by an attacker to craft a specially craft file and trick the victim opening it using the affect software, triggering use-after-free and execute arbitrary code on the target system.

code_evidence: After msgpack_unpack_next, root is assigned result.data and then accessed as root.via.array.size and root.via.array.ptr[1] without verifying the object type; flb_time_pop_from_msgpack and the array access assume an array.
map is taken from root.via.array.ptr[1] and then accessed as map.via.map.size and map.via.map.ptr[i] in the loop, assuming a map without a type check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function interprets a msgpack_object union using array and map types that may be incompatible with the actual unpacked type, which is precisely CWE-843: accessing a resource using an incompatible type. This is not merely a length check; the weakness is the missing type discrimination before union member access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unpacked msgpack object's runtime type is never validated before the union members via.array and via.map are read. A crafted input whose top-level object is not a two-element array, or whose second element is not a map, makes the code reinterpret the union as array/map members, so map_size and pointer reads are derived from unrelated data. Consequence: type confusion leading to invalid pointer dereference/out-of-bounds read, use-after-free and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overrun in EUC-KR conversion module (bz #24973)

The byte 0xfe as input to the EUC-KR conversion denotes a user-defined
area and is not allowed.  The from_euc_kr function used to skip two bytes
when told to skip over the unknown designation, potentially running over
the buffer end.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '  if (avail < 2)', '    return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['  if (avail < 2)', '    return 0;', '']}
description: The iconv feature in the GNU C Library (aka glibc or libc6) through 2.32, when processing invalid multi-byte input sequences in the EUC-KR encoding, may have a buffer over-read.

code_evidence: The length check 'if (avail < 2) return 0;' occurs after dereferencing and reading the first byte via '**s' at function entry, and it guards the read of the second byte '(*s)[1]'. If avail is less than 2 but the pointer is dereferenced, the second-byte access at line 11 reads past the available buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 matches because the function reads (*s)[1] beyond the intended buffer when the length check fails to prevent the access. This is a read-side bounds violation, not a write overflow (CWE-787).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the availability constraint for the two-byte EUC-KR sequence is not enforced before the second byte is read. Trigger: a multi-byte sequence where only one byte remains (avail < 2). Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of (*s)[1], potentially exposing adjacent memory or crashing the process.

commit_msg: Add carbons from check
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    Jid *my_jid = jid_create(connection_get_fulljid());'], 'added_lines': ['    Jid *my_jid = jid_create(connection_get_fulljid());', '    const char *const stanza_from = xmpp_stanza_get_from(stanza);', '    Jid *msg_jid = jid_create(stanza_from);', '    if (g_strcmp0(my_jid->barejid, msg_jid->barejid) != 0) {', '        log_warning("Invalid carbon received, from: %s", stanza_from);', '        return TRUE;', '    }', '']}
description: An incorrect implementation of "XEP-0280: Message Carbons" in multiple XMPP clients allows a remote attacker to impersonate any user, including contacts, in the vulnerable application's display. This allows for various kinds of social engineering attacks. This CVE is for profanity (0.4.7 - 0.5.0).

code_evidence: The function extracts the forwarded message's 'to' and 'from' attributes with xmpp_stanza_get_to/get_from, defaulting 'to' to 'from' when absent, without checking that these attributes correspond to the authenticated account.
It creates jid_from, jid_to and my_jid. my_jid is the local full JID; jid_to is derived solely from attacker-controlled stanza data.

The comparison g_strcmp0(my_jid->barejid, jid_to->barejid) decides whether the carbon is dispatched as incoming (using jid_from) or outgoing (using jid_to), so the display path is chosen by unvalidated input.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts stanza-supplied JID metadata and routes it based on that data without validating its authenticity or consistency with the local account, which is improper input validation (CWE-20) leading to spoofed message display.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the carbon's forwarded 'to'/'from' attributes are trusted without verifying the sender matches the authenticated user's bare JID. Trigger: a remote attacker sends a crafted carbon whose forwarded message spoofs a contact's JID; the missing check lets it be rendered as an incoming message from that contact, enabling impersonation in the display.

commit_msg:
9pfs: adjust the order of resource cleanup in device unrealize

Unrealize should undo things that were set during realize in
reverse order. So should do in the error path in realize.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liq3ea@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Greg Kurz <groug@kaod.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kurz <groug@kaod.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        g_free(s->tag);'], 'added_lines': ['        g_free(s->tag);']}
description: Memory leak in the v9fs_device_unrealize_common function in hw/9pfs/9p.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) allows local privileged guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host memory consumption and possibly QEMU process crash) via vectors involving the order of resource cleanup.

code_evidence: The error path at label out frees allocations made during realize: s->ctx.fs_root (allocated at line 30) and s->tag (allocated at line 38), then frees the local path. The cleanup executes only when rc is nonzero, which is the default value and remains set on every goto out failure branch (e.g., lines 22, 27, 36, 46, 51, 55, 58).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the function's error handling fails to sufficiently release memory allocated during realize, leaving allocations unavailable for reuse. This is a lifetime/release defect, distinct from a double free or use-after-free, which would involve reuse of freed memory rather than missing release.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the realize error path releases resources in an order that can leave an allocation unreleased when cleanup is interrupted or misordered, so on failure paths the host leaks memory. Trigger: a failed device realize (e.g., missing fsdev, missing tag, oversized tag, driver init failure, or invalid share path). Supported consequence: host memory consumption and possible QEMU process crash, a denial of service.

commit_msg: Fix corruption if Function.replaceWith called manually on something not a function (fix #1684)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (!jsvIsFunction(newFunc)) {', '    jsExceptionHere(JSET_TYPEERROR, "First argument of replaceWith should be a function - ignoring");'], 'added_lines': ['  if ((!jsvIsFunction(oldFunc)) || (!jsvIsFunction(newFunc))) {', '    jsExceptionHere(JSET_TYPEERROR, "Argument should be a function");']}
description: An issue found in Espruino Espruino 6ea4c0a allows an attacker to execute arbitrrary code via oldFunc parameter of the jswrap_object.c:jswrap_function_replacewith endpoint.

code_evidence: The guard validates only newFunc with jsvIsFunction; oldFunc is never type-checked before use.
oldFunc->flags is read and written directly (JSV_NATIVE / JSV_VARTYPEMASK), assuming oldFunc is a valid function JsVar with the expected layout.
jsvFindChildFromString and jsvRemoveAllChildren are invoked on oldFunc, again assuming a function object; a non-function oldFunc yields an invalid object for these operations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked oldFunc is treated as a function object and its fields are written without bounds/type validation, producing an out-of-bounds write. This is distinct from a mere type-confusion or logic error; the concrete impact is memory corruption via an invalid write target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: jswrap_function_replaceWith assumes oldFunc is a function and dereferences/mutates its flags and child list without validating its type. Trigger: calling Function.replaceWith with a non-function oldFunc (e.g., a plain object or primitive wrapper) passes the guard since only newFunc is checked. Consequence: out-of-bounds/mis-typed memory access on the invalid JsVar, leading to memory corruption and possible arbitrary code execution.

commit_msg:
gnttab: fix pin count / page reference race

Dropping page references before decrementing pin counts is a bad idea
if assumptions are being made that a non-zero pin count implies a valid
page. Fix the order of operations in gnttab_copy_release_buf(), but at
the same time also remove the assertion that was found to trigger:
map_grant_ref() also has the potential of causing a race here, and
changing the order of operations there would likely be quite a bit more
involved.

This is CVE-2017-15597 / XSA-236.

Reported-by: Pawel Wieczorkiewicz <wipawel@amazon.de>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['         * non-zero refcount and hence a valid owner.', '         */', '        ASSERT(td);'], 'added_lines': ['         * non-zero refcount and hence a valid owner (matching the one on', '         * record), with one exception: If the owning domain is dying we', '         * had better not make implications from pin count (map_grant_ref()', '         * updates pin counts before obtaining page references, for', '         * example).', '         */', '        if ( td != rd || rd->is_dying )', '        {', '            if ( td )', '                put_page(*page);', '            *page = NULL;', '            rc = GNTST_bad_domain;', '            goto unlock_out_clear;', '        }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x. Grant copying code made an implication that any grant pin would be accompanied by a suitable page reference. Other portions of code, however, did not match up with that assumption. When such a grant copy operation is being done on a grant of a dying domain, the assumption turns out wrong. A malicious guest administrator can cause hypervisor memory corruption, most likely resulting in host crash and a Denial of Service. Privilege escalation and information leaks cannot be ruled out.

code_evidence: When a grant is already pinned (the else branch), the code derives a page from the cached act->frame via mfn_valid and mfn_to_page, then calls page_get_owner_and_reference(*page) and asserts the returned owner is non-NULL. The cached frame/pin state is trusted without validating that the pin still corresponds to a live page reference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Using a stale cached frame/page after its reference was dropped means memory operations act on a location whose intended validity/boundary is no longer guaranteed, matching out-of-bounds/improper memory buffer operation (CWE-119). The missing check on td/rd and is_dying is the cause; the resulting corruption is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes a non-zero act->pin guarantees a valid page reference and owner, but map_grant_ref() increments pin counts before obtaining page references, so a dying domain can leave a pin without a matching reference. Trigger: a grant copy against a dying domain's grant whose page reference has been dropped. Consequence: the cached frame is used after the underlying page reference is gone, and the ASSERT(td) fires or stale memory is operated on, leading to hypervisor memory corruption and host crash (DoS).

fix a bunch of vsprintf -> vsnprintf

closes #1203

description: GPAC 0.7.1 has a buffer overflow issue in gf_import_message() in media_import.c.

code_evidence: The sscanf at line 8 parses an arbitrary-length decimal into the u32 ID; line 10 then writes that value as a decimal string into the fixed 20-byte stack buffer szURL via sprintf, with no bound check on the formatted length.

commit_msg:
bgpd: Check the length of the rcv software version

Make sure we don't exceed the maximum of BGP_MAX_SOFT_VERSION.

The Capability Length SHOULD be no greater than 64.

Reported-by: Iggy Frankovic <iggyfran@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Donatas Abraitis <donatas@opensourcerouting.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tstream_get(str, s, len);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (len > BGP_MAX_SOFT_VERSION) {', '\t\tflog_warn(EC_BGP_CAPABILITY_INVALID_LENGTH,', '\t\t\t  "%s: Received Software Version, but the length is too big, truncating, from peer %s",', '\t\t\t  __func__, peer->host);', '\t\tstream_get(str, s, BGP_MAX_SOFT_VERSION);', '\t\tstream_forward_getp(s, len - BGP_MAX_SOFT_VERSION);', '\t\tlen = BGP_MAX_SOFT_VERSION;', '\t} else if (len) {', '\t\tstream_get(str, s, len);', '\t}', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in FRRouting FRR 9.0. bgpd/bgp_open.c does not check for an overly large length of the rcv software version.

code_evidence: The destination buffer is fixed at BGP_MAX_SOFT_VERSION + 1 bytes, while len is an attacker-controlled 8-bit value read from the capability stream.
The only guard checks that len fits within the capability end, but never compares len against the destination buffer size before stream_get copies len bytes and str[len] is written.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic buffer copy without checking input size: an input-derived length is copied into a smaller fixed output buffer with no size comparison. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the copy and null termination write beyond str.

evidence_lines.code:
char str[BGP_MAX_SOFT_VERSION + 1];
uint8_t len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the received software-version length is trusted without bounding it to the fixed str buffer. Trigger: a peer sends a capability whose length byte exceeds BGP_MAX_SOFT_VERSION but still fits inside hdr->length. Consequence: stream_get overflows str and the subsequent str[len]='\0' writes out of bounds, corrupting stack memory.

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

In order to fail safe in the supported case, re-implement all the VT-x
instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int nvmx_handle_vmresume(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)'], 'added_lines': ['static int nvmx_handle_vmresume(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.9.x through 4.11.x, on Intel x86 platforms, allowing x86 HVM and PVH guests to cause a host OS denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) or possibly have unspecified other impact because nested VT-x is not properly restricted.

code_evidence: Line 4 obtains the current vcpu and line 5 derives nvmx = &vcpu_2_nvmx(v) from it; the privilege check on line 7 is invoked with vmxop_check=0, which skips the CR4.VMXE gate, so execution proceeds without confirming nested-virt state was initialised.
Line 21-22 uses nvmx->launched_list via vvmcs_launched, and line 28 calls nvmx_vmresume(v,regs), both consuming the nvmx structure that is only initialised when nested virt is enabled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The handler dereferences nvmx-derived state that can be NULL/uninitialised because the missing nested-virt restriction lets the operation proceed, matching CWE-476. This is a NULL dereference rather than merely a missing privilege check, since the concrete supported consequence is a host crash from dereferencing uninitialised nestedvmx state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nvmx_handle_vmresume trusts that the nestedvmx state reachable through vcpu_2_nvmx is valid, but nvmx_vcpu_initialise is dead code until nested virt is enabled, leaving the structure zeroed. A guest issuing VMRESUME when nested virt is disabled passes the weakened privilege check and reaches vvmcs_launched/nvmx_vmresume on uninitialised nvmx state, causing a host NULL-pointer dereference and denial of service.

commit_msg:
net: phy: mdio-bcm-unimac: fix potential NULL dereference in unimac_mdio_probe()

platform_get_resource() may fail and return NULL, so we should
better check it's return value to avoid a NULL pointer dereference
a bit later in the code.

This is detected by Coccinelle semantic patch.

@@
expression pdev, res, n, t, e, e1, e2;
@@

res = platform_get_resource(pdev, t, n);
+ if (!res)
+   return -EINVAL;
... when != res == NULL
e = devm_ioremap(e1, res->start, e2);

Signed-off-by: Wei Yongjun <weiyongjun1@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: The unimac_mdio_probe function in drivers/net/phy/mdio-bcm-unimac.c in the Linux kernel through 4.15.8 does not validate certain resource availability, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference).

code_evidence: platform_get_resource() is called and its return value stored in r without any NULL check; r is then immediately dereferenced via r->start and resource_size(r) in the devm_ioremap() call.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (r) that may be NULL because resource availability is not validated, which is exactly CWE-476. This is distinct from a general resource-handling flaw: the concrete weakness is the NULL dereference at line 14.

priv->base = devm_ioremap(&pdev->dev, r->start, resource_size(r));

commit_msg:
gnttab: deal with status frame mapping race

Once gnttab_map_frame() drops the grant table lock, the MFN it reports
back to its caller is free to other manipulation. In particular
gnttab_unpopulate_status_frames() might free it, by a racing request on
another CPU, thus resulting in a reference to a deallocated page getting
added to a domain's P2M.

Obtain a page reference in gnttab_map_frame() to prevent freeing of the
page until xenmem_add_to_physmap_one() has actually completed its acting
on the page. Do so uniformly, even if only strictly required for v2
status pages, to avoid extra conditionals (which then would all need to
be kept in sync going forward).

This is CVE-2021-28701 / XSA-384.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        gnttab_set_frame_gfn(gt, status, idx, gfn);'], 'added_lines': ['    {', '        /*', "         * Make sure gnttab_unpopulate_status_frames() won't (successfully)", '         * free the page until our caller has completed its operation.', '         */', '        if ( get_page(mfn_to_page(*mfn), d) )', '            gnttab_set_frame_gfn(gt, status, idx, gfn);', '        else', '            rc = -EBUSY;', '    }']}
description: Another race in XENMAPSPACE_grant_table handling Guests are permitted access to certain Xen-owned pages of memory. The majority of such pages remain allocated / associated with a guest for its entire lifetime. Grant table v2 status pages, however, are de-allocated when a guest switches (back) from v2 to v1. Freeing such pages requires that the hypervisor enforce that no parallel request can result in the addition of a mapping of such a page to a guest. That enforcement was missing, allowing guests to retain access to pages that were freed and perhaps re-used for other purposes. Unfortunately, when XSA-379 was being prepared, this similar issue was not noticed.

code_evidence: gnttab_map_frame() acquires grant_write_lock(gt) at line 6 and resolves the status frame MFN via gnttab_get_status_frame_mfn() at line 11 for v2 status pages. It then records the mapping with gnttab_set_frame_gfn() at line 22 before releasing the lock at line 23, without taking a page reference on the returned MFN.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a concurrency race: the shared status page is not kept exclusively owned across the lock-drop boundary, violating atomicity of the map-then-use sequence. CWE-362 fits because an interfering code sequence (status-frame teardown) can modify the shared resource during the window.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The MFN obtained at line 11 is only protected by the grant table lock, but after gnttab_map_frame() returns, gnttab_unpopulate_status_frames() can free that page on another CPU while xenmem_add_to_physmap_one() is still acting on it. The unprotected window allows a reference to a deallocated page to be added to the domain's P2M, letting the guest retain access to freed/reused memory.

portal: Convert --env in extra-args into --env-fd

This hides overridden variables from the command-line, which means
processes running under other uids can't see them in /proc/*/cmdline,
which might be important if they contain secrets.

Signed-off-by: Simon McVittie <smcv@collabora.com>
Part-of: https://github.com/flatpak/flatpak/security/advisories/GHSA-4ppf-fxf6-vxg2

description: Flatpak is a system for building, distributing, and running sandboxed desktop applications on Linux. A bug was discovered in the `flatpak-portal` service that can allow sandboxed applications to execute arbitrary code on the host system (a sandbox escape). This sandbox-escape bug is present in versions from 0.11.4 and before fixed versions 1.8.5 and 1.10.0. The Flatpak portal D-Bus service (`flatpak-portal`, also known by its D-Bus service name `org.freedesktop.portal.Flatpak`) allows apps in a Flatpak sandbox to launch their own subprocesses in a new sandbox instance, either with the same security settings as the caller or with more restrictive security settings. For example, this is used in Flatpak-packaged web browsers such as Chromium to launch subprocesses that will process untrusted web content, and give those subprocesses a more restrictive sandbox than the browser itself. In vulnerable versions, the Flatpak portal service passes caller-specified environment variables to non-sandboxed processes on the host system, and in particular to the `flatpak run` command that is used to launch the new sandbox instance. A malicious or compromised Flatpak app could set environment variables that are trusted by the `flatpak run` command, and use them to execute arbitrary code that is not in a sandbox. As a workaround, this vulnerability can be mitigated by preventing the `flatpak-portal` service from starting, but that mitigation will prevent many Flatpak apps from working correctly. This is fixed in versions 1.8.5 and 1.10.0.

commit_msg:
netfilter: add back stackpointer size checks

The rationale for removing the check is only correct for rulesets
generated by ip(6)tables.

In iptables, a jump can only occur to a user-defined chain, i.e.
because we size the stack based on number of user-defined chains we
cannot exceed stack size.

However, the underlying binary format has no such restriction,
and the validation step only ensures that the jump target is a
valid rule start point.

IOW, its possible to build a rule blob that has no user-defined
chains but does contain a jump.

If this happens, no jump stack gets allocated and crash occurs
because no jumpstack was allocated.

Fixes: 7814b6ec6d0d6 ("netfilter: xtables: don't save/restore jumpstack offset")
Reported-by: syzbot+e783f671527912cd9403@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif (unlikely(stackidx >= private->stacksize)) {', '\t\t\t\t\tverdict = NF_DROP;', '\t\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t\t}']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.15.7 mishandles the case of a rule blob that contains a jump but lacks a user-defined chain, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) by leveraging the CAP_NET_RAW or CAP_NET_ADMIN capability, related to arpt_do_table in net/ipv4/netfilter/arp_tables.c, ipt_do_table in net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c, and ip6t_do_table in net/ipv6/netfilter/ip6_tables.c.

code_evidence: Line 25 loads jumpstack from private->jumpstack[cpu]; if no user-defined chains exist, this array was never allocated and is NULL. Line 57-58 detects a jump whose target is not the next entry, then line 59 writes jumpstack[stackidx++] = e without checking stackidx against private->stacksize. Line 61 then follows the jump target.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences the jumpstack pointer on line 59 while it may be NULL due to absent allocation, matching CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). This is distinct from a plain out-of-bounds write, since the immediate fault is dereferencing a NULL pointer rather than exceeding a valid buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing stack-pointer bounds check before pushing onto jumpstack. A crafted rule blob with a jump but no user-defined chains yields a NULL jumpstack; the jump branch writes through it, causing a NULL pointer dereference and kernel crash (DoS). The added check prevents the push when stackidx >= stacksize.

commit_msg:
kvm: fix excessive pages un-pinning in kvm_iommu_map error path.

The third parameter of kvm_unpin_pages() when called from
kvm_iommu_map_pages() is wrong, it should be the number of pages to un-pin
and not the page size.

This error was facilitated with an inconsistent API: kvm_pin_pages() takes
a size, but kvn_unpin_pages() takes a number of pages, so fix the problem
by matching the two.

This was introduced by commit 350b8bd ("kvm: iommu: fix the third parameter
of kvm_iommu_put_pages (CVE-2014-3601)"), which fixes the lack of
un-pinning for pages intended to be un-pinned (i.e. memory leak) but
unfortunately potentially aggravated the number of pages we un-pin that
should have stayed pinned. As far as I understand though, the same
practical mitigations apply.

This issue was found during review of Red Hat 6.6 patches to prepare
Ksplice rebootless updates.

Thanks to Vegard for his time on a late Friday evening to help me in
understanding this code.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121

description: A flaw was found in GLib. GVariant deserialization is vulnerable to an exponential blowup issue where a crafted GVariant can cause excessive processing, leading to denial of service.

code_evidence: g_variant_fill_gvs receives a GVariant value via data, locks it, ensures its size, and then stores its serialised form into the caller-supplied serialised->data buffer via g_variant_store(). The function trusts value->type_info, value->size and value->depth and only asserts internal consistency; it performs no validation of the untrusted serialised content before serialising it out.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function participates in handling data derived from deserialised untrusted input without ensuring the resulting structure is valid, matching CWE-502's deserialization of untrusted data. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), since the weakness is the missing validity guarantee on deserialised data, not a single buffer access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the serialisation path trusts the in-memory GVariant's size/depth metadata and copies it out without validating frame offsets or element ordering. Trigger: a crafted, non-normal-form GVariant deserialised from untrusted input. Consequence: overlapping array elements can normalise to a much larger type, causing excessive processing (resource-consumption DoS) and unexpected state.

description: coffgen.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29.1, does not validate the symbol count, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (integer overflow and application crash, or excessive memory allocation) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PE file.

commit_msg:
gnttab: split maptrack lock to make it fulfill its purpose again

The way the lock is currently being used in get_maptrack_handle(), it
protects only the maptrack limit: The function acts on current's list
only, so races on list accesses are impossible even without the lock.

Otoh list access races are possible between __get_maptrack_handle() and
put_maptrack_handle(), due to the invocation of the former for other
than current from steal_maptrack_handle(). Introduce a per-vCPU lock
for list accesses to become race free again. This lock will be
uncontended except when it becomes necessary to take the steal path,
i.e. in the common case there should be no meaningful performance
impact.

When in get_maptrack_handle adds a stolen entry to a fresh, empty,
freelist, we think that there is probably no concurrency.  However,
this is not a fast path and adding the locking there makes the code
clearly correct.

Also, while we are here: the stolen maptrack_entry's tail pointer was
not properly set.  Set it.

This is CVE-2017-12136 / XSA-228.

Reported-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <Ian.Jackson@eu.citrix.com>

description: Use-after-free vulnerability in the xmlSAX2AttributeNs function in libxml2 before 2.9.4, as used in Apple iOS before 9.3.2 and OS X before 10.11.5, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted XML document.

The skip_default_ns path frees attvalue when alloc != 0 (line 106) but does not set attvalue to NULL, so a stale pointer can persist.
The skip_ns path similarly frees attvalue (line 177) without nulling it.
After SKIP_BLANKS, the loop re-checks base/inputNr and may goto base_changed (lines 186-188).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale attvalue is used to access memory outside the valid buffer after the base changed, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The commit explicitly fixes this by adding base-change checks and nulling attvalue after free, confirming the buffer-boundary violation; the use-after-free is the resultant mechanism rather than the target class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attvalue points into ctxt->input->base; when the input buffer is reallocated (base changes) or an entity boundary is crossed, the freed/relocated buffer leaves attvalue dangling, and the skip_default_ns/skip_ns paths free it without nulling. Trigger: a crafted XML start tag whose attribute parsing causes the input base to change between iterations. Consequence: use-after-free/double-free reads and writes of freed memory, enabling DoS and potentially memory corruption.

description: An issue was discovered in Erlang/OTP 18.x. Erlang's generation of compiled regular expressions is vulnerable to a heap overflow. Regular expressions using a malformed extpattern can indirectly specify an offset that is used as an array index. This ordinal permits arbitrary regions within the erts_alloc arena to be both read and written to.

code_evidence: The OP_RECURSE case resolves cs/ce from the pattern's back-reference offset GET(cc,1) and only rejects direct self-recursion when cc > cs && cc < ce; it then recurses into find_fixedlength(cs + IMM2_SIZE, ...) with no tracking of previously visited groups.
The OP_ASSERT family skips alternatives via GET(cc,1) then advances with cc += PRIV(OP_lengths)[*cc], indexing the opcode-length table by the byte at the computed position.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked recursion and opcode-table indexing operate on memory outside the intended code-buffer boundaries, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds read/write class. The patch's mutual-recursion guard confirms the missing bound on traversal rather than a mere logic error.

evidence_lines.code:
do cc += GET(cc, 1); while (*cc == OP_ALT);
cc += PRIV(OP_lengths)[*cc];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: recursion into referenced subpatterns lacks a visited-group check for mutual recursion, so a malformed extpattern can drive repeated/indirect recursion and misaligned cc advancement. The trigger is a crafted regex using OP_RECURSE/OP_ASSERT structures; the consequence is reads/writes or table indexing at attacker-influenced offsets beyond the intended pattern buffer.

commit_msg:
USB: uas: fix bug in handling of alternate settings

The uas driver has a subtle bug in the way it handles alternate
settings.  The uas_find_uas_alt_setting() routine returns an
altsetting value (the bAlternateSetting number in the descriptor), but
uas_use_uas_driver() then treats that value as an index to the
intf->altsetting array, which it isn't.

Normally this doesn't cause any problems because the various
alternate settings have bAlternateSetting values 0, 1, 2, ..., so the
value is equal to the index in the array.  But this is not guaranteed,
and Andrey Konovalov used the syzkaller fuzzer with KASAN to get a
slab-out-of-bounds error by violating this assumption.

This patch fixes the bug by making uas_find_uas_alt_setting() return a
pointer to the altsetting entry rather than either the value or the
index.  Pointers are less subject to misinterpretation.

Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Tested-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
CC: Oliver Neukum <oneukum@suse.com>
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int uas_find_uas_alt_setting(struct usb_interface *intf)', '\t\t\treturn alt->desc.bAlternateSetting;', '\treturn -ENODEV;'], 'added_lines': ['static struct usb_host_interface *uas_find_uas_alt_setting(', '\t\tstruct usb_interface *intf)', '\t\t\treturn alt;', '\treturn NULL;']}
description: The uas driver in the Linux kernel before 4.13.6 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted USB device, related to drivers/usb/storage/uas-detect.h and drivers/usb/storage/uas.c.

code_evidence: Loop indexes intf->altsetting[i] for i in [0, intf->num_altsetting), but returns alt->desc.bAlternateSetting, the descriptor's bAlternateSetting value rather than the array index.
Caller uas_use_uas_driver treats the returned int as an index into intf->altsetting, so a crafted bAlternateSetting outside the array bounds yields an out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is reading memory outside the intended altsetting array, matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). It is not merely integer misuse; the misused value directly drives an out-of-range array access.

evidence_lines.code: return alt->desc.bAlternateSetting;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function returns a descriptor field value that is semantically an index, violating the caller's assumed invariant that altsetting indices equal bAlternateSetting values. A crafted USB device with a non-sequential bAlternateSetting triggers indexing past intf->altsetting, causing a slab out-of-bounds read and system crash.

xt_compat_match/target_from_user doesn't check that zeroing the area
to start of next rule won't write past end of allocated ruleset blob.

Remove this code and zero the entire blob beforehand.

Reported-by: syzbot+cfc0247ac173f597aaaa@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Reported-by: Andy Nguyen <theflow@google.com>
Fixes: 9fa492cdc160c ("[NETFILTER]: x_tables: simplify compat API")
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>

description: A heap out-of-bounds write affecting Linux since v2.6.19-rc1 was discovered in net/netfilter/x_tables.c. This allows an attacker to gain privileges or cause a DoS (via heap memory corruption) through user name space

code_evidence: xt_alloc_table_info(size) allocates newinfo->entries of the caller-derived size [34-36]. The entries are not zeroed after allocation. entry1/pos are then set to newinfo->entries [42,43], size is reset to compatr->size [44], and compat_copy_entry_from_user walks the user-supplied compat entries copying into pos [45-47]. Because the destination region is uninitialized and its size is derived from the same user value, the copy can extend to the end of the allocated blob.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a write into newinfo->entries whose extent is not bounded by the allocated buffer size, matching CWE-787 (write past the end of the intended buffer). It is not merely an uninitialized read; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the newly allocated ruleset blob is not zeroed and compat_copy_entry_from_user can write padding/zeroing up to the start of the next rule based on user-controlled entry sizes. Trigger: a crafted compat arpt_replace with entry sizes that cause the copy/zeroing to run past the allocated size. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, leading to memory corruption, privilege escalation or DoS.

description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An out-of-bounds read was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The out-of-bounds read is triggered when Exiv2 is used to read the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: Line 21 checks *n > pvList.size(), so a value equal to pvList.size() passes the guard. Line 26 then indexes pvList[*n - 1], which equals pvList[pvList.size()], one past the last valid element. The fix changes the check to num >= pvList.size() after decrementing, preventing this off-by-one index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads a std::vector element past its end due to an off-by-one guard, which is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not CWE-129 alone because the actual weakness is the resulting out-of-bounds memory read; the flawed index check is the cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check rejects only values strictly greater than size, allowing *n == size through. Trigger: a user-supplied preview number equal to the preview list size (nonzero). Consequence: pvList[size] is read out of bounds, an out-of-bounds read that can crash (DoS) when getPreviewImage consumes the invalid entry.

description: Memory Corruption was discovered in the cmsgpack library in the Lua subsystem in Redis before 3.2.12, 4.x before 4.0.10, and 5.x before 5.0 RC2 because of stack-based buffer overflows.

It is distinct from a simple integer overflow because the core issue is absent limit enforcement on resource-controlling configuration.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function accepts caller-supplied option values and writes them directly into session limit fields without checking bounds. A caller passing an oversized max_send_header_block_length, max_outbound_ack, or max_settings causes the session to allocate or retain resources proportional to that value; subsequent buffering/queue operations consume memory or CPU without throttling, enabling resource exhaustion.

commit_msg:
MBIM: stop pre sizing wmem arrays

In case of malformed packet, this can lead to an insane amount of
memory.
Instead let's use the automatic growth mecanism. This way the malformed
packet is caught by the dissection engine.

Bug: 14056
Change-Id: I7bf5b80a516210b341356f5d495f08d1dba05805
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/23537
Reviewed-by: Pascal Quantin <pascal.quantin@gmail.com>

Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot <buildbot-no-reply@wireshark.org>
Reviewed-by: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.1 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.9, the MBIM dissector could crash or exhaust system memory. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-mbim.c by changing the memory-allocation approach.

code_evidence: Line 10 reads elem_count directly from the packet via proto_tree_add_item_ret_uint without validating it against the remaining tvb length. Line 12 gates allocation on elem_count being nonzero, and line 13 calls wmem_array_sized_new with that attacker-controlled elem_count, pre-allocating elem_count * sizeof(struct mbim_pair_list) bytes before any per-element data is parsed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function allocates a limited resource (memory) based on an unthrottled, packet-controlled count, enabling resource exhaustion. The fix removes the pre-sizing so growth is bounded by actual parsed data, confirming the allocation sizing was the flaw rather than, e.g., an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unvalidated 32-bit element count from the packet drives a pre-sized wmem array allocation. Trigger: a malformed MBIM packet declaring a huge elem_count causes the dissector to allocate a correspondingly huge buffer up front. Supported consequence: excessive memory consumption (or allocation failure/crash) before the loop can detect that the packet is truncated, a DoS condition.

commit_msg:
Add support for different number of page table levels dependent
on the highest address used for a process. This will cause a 31 bit
process to use a two level page table instead of the four level page
table that is the default after the pud has been introduced. Likewise
a normal 64 bit process will use three levels instead of four. Only
if a process runs out of the 4 tera bytes which can be addressed with
a three level page table the fourth level is dynamically added. Then
the process can use up to 8 peta byte.

TROVE-2017-004: Fix assertion failure in relay_send_end_cell_from_edge_

This fixes an assertion failure in relay_send_end_cell_from_edge_() when an
origin circuit and a cpath_layer = NULL were passed.

A service rendezvous circuit could do such a thing when a malformed BEGIN cell
is received but shouldn't in the first place because the service needs to send
an END cell on the circuit for which it can not do without a cpath_layer.

Fixes #22493

Reported-by: Roger Dingledine <arma@torproject.org>
Signed-off-by: David Goulet <dgoulet@torproject.org>

description: The hidden-service feature in Tor before 0.3.0.8 allows a denial of service (assertion failure and daemon exit) in the relay_send_end_cell_from_edge_ function via a malformed BEGIN cell.

code_evidence: When the circuit is not an origin circuit, only or_circ is set; origin_circ remains NULL and no cpath_layer is derived.
The rendezvous branch is entered based solely on circ->purpose == CIRCUIT_PURPOSE_S_REND_JOINED and unconditionally converts circ to an origin circuit.

or_circ = TO_OR_CIRCUIT(circ);

commit_msg:
xen/events: avoid removing an event channel while handling it

Today it can happen that an event channel is being removed from the
system while the event handling loop is active. This can lead to a
race resulting in crashes or WARN() splats when trying to access the
irq_info structure related to the event channel.

Fix this problem by using a rwlock taken as reader in the event
handling loop and as writer when deallocating the irq_info structure.

As the observed problem was a NULL dereference in evtchn_from_irq()
make this function more robust against races by testing the irq_info
pointer to be not NULL before dereferencing it.

And finally make all accesses to evtchn_to_irq[row][col] atomic ones
in order to avoid seeing partial updates of an array element in irq
handling. Note that irq handling can be entered only for event channels
which have been valid before, so any not populated row isn't a problem
in this regard, as rows are only ever added and never removed.

This is XSA-331.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Marek Marczykowski-Górecki <marmarek@invisiblethingslab.com>
Reported-by: Jinoh Kang <luke1337@theori.io>
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tevtchn_to_irq[row][col] = irq;'], 'added_lines': ['\tWRITE_ONCE(evtchn_to_irq[row][col], irq);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.9.1, as used with Xen through 4.14.x. drivers/xen/events/events_base.c allows event-channel removal during the event-handling loop (a race condition). This can cause a use-after-free or NULL pointer dereference, as demonstrated by a dom0 crash via events for an in-reconfiguration paravirtualized device, aka CID-073d0552ead5.

code_evidence: The row is lazily allocated: evtchn_to_irq[row] is checked for NULL and, when unset, a zeroed page is installed via a plain pointer assignment, with a separate clear_evtchn_to_irq_row(row) call afterward.
The slot write evtchn_to_irq[row][col] = irq is a plain, non-atomic store into an array element that the event-handling path concurrently reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function mutates shared event-channel state that is read concurrently by the handling loop, with no synchronization ensuring exclusive, atomic publication; this is exactly a race condition on a shared resource (CWE-362). The NULL/use-after-free crash is the consequence, not the root cause.

evidence_lines.code: evtchn_to_irq[row][col] = irq;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The irq_info pointer and the per-channel slot are published through ordinary stores without exclusive access or atomic publication. A concurrent event-handling loop can observe a partially initialized row or a torn/stale slot value, leading to a NULL or invalid irq_info dereference and a crash or WARN() splat.

commit_msg:
The VT_DISALLOCATE ioctl can free a virtual console while tty_release()
is still running, causing a use-after-free in con_shutdown().  This
occurs because VT_DISALLOCATE considers a virtual console's
'struct vc_data' to be unused as soon as the corresponding tty's
refcount hits 0.  But actually it may be still being closed.

Fix this by making vc_data be reference-counted via the embedded
'struct tty_port'.  A newly allocated virtual console has refcount 1.
Opening it for the first time increments the refcount to 2.  Closing it
for the last time decrements the refcount (in tty_operations::cleanup()
so that it happens late enough), as does VT_DISALLOCATE.

Reproducer:
	#include <fcntl.h>
	#include <linux/vt.h>
	#include <sys/ioctl.h>
	#include <unistd.h>

	int main()
	{
		if (fork()) {
			for (;;)
				close(open("/dev/tty5", O_RDWR));
		} else {
			int fd = open("/dev/tty10", O_RDWR);

			for (;;)
				ioctl(fd, VT_DISALLOCATE, 5);
		}
	}

description: A race condition in the Linux kernel before 5.6.2 between the VT_DISALLOCATE ioctl and closing/opening of ttys could lead to a use-after-free.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: vc_data is considered unused as soon as the tty refcount reaches zero, so VT_DISALLOCATE can free it while tty_release() is still closing the tty. commit_msg:
When doing a string comparison for a symbol name from the string table,
we should make sure we do a bounded comparison, otherwise a non-NUL
terminated string might make the code read out-of-bounds.

Warned-by: coverity
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t    strcmp(name, p->n_un.n_name+1) == 0)', '\t\t\t\t    || strcmp(name, p->n_un.n_name) == 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tElf_Word size;', '\t\t\tsize = symstrsize - s->st_name;', '\t\t\t\t     strncmp(name, p->n_un.n_name+1, size) == 0) ||', '\t\t\t\t    strncmp(name, p->n_un.n_name, size) == 0) {']}
description: nlist.c in libbsd before 0.10.0 has an out-of-bounds read during a comparison for a symbol name from the string table (strtab).

code_evidence: Line 79 computes name = strtab + s->st_name using the attacker-controlled symbol table name offset; nothing validates that s->st_name lies within the symstrsize-byte strtab buffer, and line 80 dereferences name[0] directly.

Lines 84-85 pass name into strcmp, which scans until a NUL terminator; a st_name near or beyond the strtab end yields a non-terminated string, so strcmp reads past the buffer. The pre-patch code has no bounded length for this comparison.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 directly fits: the function reads memory past the end of the intended strtab buffer during a string comparison. This is a read overrun, not a write (CWE-787) or an integer issue, so Out-of-bounds Read is the precise weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the symbol name pointer derived from s->st_name is never bounded against symstrsize, and strcmp requires NUL termination. Trigger: a crafted ELF symbol table entry whose st_name points at or near the end of the string table without a terminator. Consequence: strcmp reads beyond the allocated strtab buffer (out-of-bounds read), potentially leaking memory or crashing.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    str=(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory((size_t) count,sizeof(*str));'], 'added_lines': ['    str=(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory((size_t) count+1,sizeof(*str));']}
description: An off-by-one read vulnerability was discovered in ImageMagick before version 7.0.7-28 in the formatIPTCfromBuffer function in coders/meta.c. A local attacker may use this flaw to read beyond the end of the buffer or to crash the program.

code_evidence: count is read from the blob and validated only as non-negative and not exceeding blob size, then AcquireQuantumMemory allocates exactly count bytes for str.
The loop fills str[0..count-1] with count bytes read from the stream; no NUL terminator is written because the buffer holds exactly count elements.
str is passed to formatIPTCfromBuffer (and formatString) as a C string, which expects a NUL-terminated buffer and will read past the allocation when the data lacks an embedded terminator.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-193 fits because the maximum allocated size is one less than required: the buffer should hold count+1 bytes to include the terminator. The patch confirms this by changing the allocation to count+1. This is an off-by-one size error rather than an integer overflow or a general buffer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocation uses the exact count as the element maximum, but downstream string processing assumes one extra byte for a terminator. When the IPTC/string data fills the buffer without an embedded NUL, readers scan one byte beyond the allocated region, causing an out-of-bounds read and possible crash. Root cause is the missing +1 in the allocation; the over-read is the consequence.

commit_msg:
SSL Interception: Injection into default ssl error page via untrusted certificate

The error page allows injecting snippets using the distinguished name of
untrusted certificates via the %D template parameter.
This patch quote information retrieved from  remote certificates using the
%ssl_subject, %ssl_ca_name and %ssl_cn error details formating codes.

Thanks to Nikolas Lohmann [eBlocker] for identifying the problem.

This is a Measurement Factory project
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (tmpStr.size())', '            return tmpStr.termedBuf();'], 'added_lines': ['        if (tmpStr.size()) {', '            // quote to avoid possible html code injection through', '            // certificate subject', '            return html_quote(tmpStr.termedBuf());', '        }']}
description: Squid before 4.4 has XSS via a crafted X.509 certificate during HTTP(S) error page generation for certificate errors.

code_evidence: matchX509CommonNames copies the certificate's common name into tmpStr, and line 7 returns that raw buffer via termedBuf() without any HTML encoding. The certificate subject is attacker-controlled (untrusted cert), so the returned value flows into the generated error page unescaped.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-79 fits because untrusted certificate-derived input is placed into web page output without neutralization, matching improper neutralization during web page generation. This is not merely information exposure; the missing encoding enables script execution in the victim's browser.

Trigger: a crafted X.509 certificate whose CN contains markup is presented during an SSL error, causing the browser to render injected script. Add bounds check in SoftAACEncoder2::onQueueFilled()

Original code blindly copied some header information into the
user-supplied buffer without checking for sufficient space.
The code does check when it gets to filling the data -- it's
just the header copies that weren't checked.

Bug: 34617444
Test: ran POC before/after
Change-Id: I6e80ec90616f6cd02bb8316cd2d6e309b7e4729d
(cherry picked from commit 6231243626b8b9c57593b1f0ee417f2c4af4c0aa)

description: An elevation of privilege vulnerability in codecs/aacenc/SoftAACEncoder2.cpp in libstagefright in Mediaserver could enable a local malicious application to execute arbitrary code within the context of a privileged process. This issue is rated as High because it could be used to gain local access to elevated capabilities, which are not normally accessible to a third-party application. Product: Android. Versions: 4.4.4, 5.0.2, 5.1.1, 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2. Android ID: A-34617444.

code_evidence: The first-time codec-config path takes the output buffer header from the queue (lines 28-29), sets nFilledLen to encInfo.confSize (line 30), computes the destination as pBuffer + nOffset (line 32), and memcpy's encInfo.confSize bytes from encInfo.confBuf into it (line 33) without any check that nOffset + confSize fits within nAllocLen.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a buffer-copy operation where the copy size (encInfo.confSize) is not validated against the destination size before memcpy, matching CWE-120's definition of copying without checking input size. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the encoder-supplied configuration blob (encInfo.confSize/confBuf) is copied into the client output buffer with no comparison of confSize against the buffer's remaining capacity (nAllocLen - nOffset). Trigger: a crafted/first encode where confSize exceeds the available space in the caller-provided output buffer. commit_msg:
Fix the RC4-MD5 cipher

A copy&paste error meant that the RC4-MD5 cipher (used in TLS) used the TLS
AAD data as the MAC key.

CVE-2022-1434

Fixes #18112

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    p = OSSL_PARAM_locate_const(params, OSSL_CIPHER_PARAM_AEAD_TLS1_AAD);'], 'added_lines': ['    p = OSSL_PARAM_locate_const(params, OSSL_CIPHER_PARAM_AEAD_MAC_KEY);']}
description: The OpenSSL 3.0 implementation of the RC4-MD5 ciphersuite incorrectly uses the AAD data as the MAC key. This makes the MAC key trivially predictable. An attacker could exploit this issue by performing a man-in-the-middle attack to modify data being sent from one endpoint to an OpenSSL 3.0 recipient such that the modified data would still pass the MAC integrity check. Note that data sent from an OpenSSL 3.0 endpoint to a non-OpenSSL 3.0 endpoint will always be rejected by the recipient and the connection will fail at that point. Many application protocols require data to be sent from the client to the server first. Therefore, in such a case, only an OpenSSL 3.0 server would be impacted when talking to a non-OpenSSL 3.0 client. If both endpoints are OpenSSL 3.0 then the attacker could modify data being sent in both directions. In this case both clients and servers could be affected, regardless of the application protocol. Note that in the absence of an attacker this bug means that an OpenSSL 3.0 endpoint communicating with a non-OpenSSL 3.0 endpoint will fail to complete the handshake when using this ciphersuite. The confidentiality of data is not impacted by this issue, i.e. an attacker cannot decrypt data that has been encrypted using this ciphersuite - they can only modify it. In order for this attack to work both endpoints must legitimately negotiate the RC4-MD5 ciphersuite. This ciphersuite is not compiled by default in OpenSSL 3.0, and is not available within the default provider or the default ciphersuite list. This ciphersuite will never be used if TLSv1.3 has been negotiated. In order for an OpenSSL 3.0 endpoint to use this ciphersuite the following must have occurred: 1) OpenSSL must have been compiled with the (non-default) compile time option enable-weak-ssl-ciphers 2) OpenSSL must have had the legacy provider explicitly loaded (either through application code or via configuration) 3) The ciphersuite must have been explicitly added to the ciphersuite list 4) The libssl security level must have been set to 0 (default is 1) 5) A version of SSL/TLS below TLSv1.3 must have been negotiated 6) Both endpoints must negotiate the RC4-MD5 ciphersuite in preference to any others that both endpoints have in common Fixed in OpenSSL 3.0.3 (Affected 3.0.0,3.0.1,3.0.2).

code_evidence: Lines 43-50 locate OSSL_CIPHER_PARAM_AEAD_TLS1_AAD a second time and pass its p->data and p->data_size directly to GET_HW(ctx)->init_mackey as the MAC key, rather than the intended MAC-key parameter.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function configures the RC4-MD5 TLS ciphersuite with a MAC key that is not secret, undermining the integrity guarantee of a cryptographic construction; this is use of a risky/broken cryptographic scheme (RC4-MD5 with a predictable key), matching CWE-327 rather than a generic key-management issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a copy-paste error makes the MAC key derive from the TLS AAD (header data) instead of the negotiated MAC secret, so the key is trivially predictable. When RC4-MD5 is negotiated, an attacker able to modify traffic can forge a valid MAC that passes the integrity check, enabling undetected data modification.

as close() needs the lock. This is safe to do by dropping the
mutex as intfdata is already set to NULL, so open() will fail.

The else branch calls iowarrior_delete(dev), confirming dev is freed while disconnect still holds references used afterward.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: iowarrior_disconnect dereferences dev (mutex_lock, dev->present) after usb_deregister_dev() can trigger close() and free the structure. Trigger: a disconnect racing with an open/close path that frees dev. Consequence: use-after-free, leading to memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Signed-off-by: Vincent Pelletier <plr.vincent@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Christie <mchristi@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchap_binaryhex_to_asciihex(response, server_digest, MD5_SIGNATURE_SIZE);', '\tchap_binaryhex_to_asciihex(response, digest, MD5_SIGNATURE_SIZE);'], 'added_lines': ['\tbin2hex(response, server_digest, MD5_SIGNATURE_SIZE);', '\tbin2hex(response, digest, MD5_SIGNATURE_SIZE);']}
description: A security flaw was found in the chap_server_compute_md5() function in the ISCSI target code in the Linux kernel in a way an authentication request from an ISCSI initiator is processed. An unauthenticated remote attacker can cause a stack buffer overflow and smash up to 17 bytes of the stack. The attack requires the iSCSI target to be enabled on the victim host. Depending on how the target's code was built (i.e. depending on a compiler, compile flags and hardware architecture) an attack may lead to a system crash and thus to a denial-of-service or possibly to a non-authorized access to data exported by an iSCSI target. Due to the nature of the flaw, privilege escalation cannot be fully ruled out, although we believe it is highly unlikely. Kernel versions 4.18.x, 4.14.x and 3.10.x are believed to be vulnerable.

code_evidence: response is a stack buffer sized MD5_SIGNATURE_SIZE * 2 + 2, while digest and server_digest are MD5_SIGNATURE_SIZE stack arrays.

Line 107 passes server_digest and MD5_SIGNATURE_SIZE to chap_binaryhex_to_asciihex, which writes 2*MD5_SIGNATURE_SIZE hex chars plus a NUL into response; the old helper's output size handling is the unsafe conversion replaced by bin2hex.
Line 191 performs the same conversion of digest into response before line 192 appends 'CHAP_R=0x%s' via sprintf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The overflowed destination, response, is a local stack array, matching CWE-121 (stack-based buffer overflow). A heap overflow would require the destination to be heap-allocated, which it is not here.

evidence_lines.code:
chap_binaryhex_to_asciihex(response, server_digest, MD5_SIGNATURE_SIZE);
pr_debug("[server] MD5 Server Digest: %s\n", response);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the replaced chap_binaryhex_to_asciihex conversion does not bound its output to the destination response buffer when converting MD5_SIGNATURE_SIZE bytes. Trigger: an unauthenticated remote iSCSI initiator drives the CHAP authentication path so the server computes a digest and the conversion writes more than the stack-allocated response can hold. Supported consequence: stack memory adjacent to response is overwritten, enabling crash/DoS and potentially code execution.

commit_msg:
The bounds checking in avc_ca_pmt() is not strict enough.  It should
be checking "read_pos + 4" because it's reading 5 bytes.  If the
"es_info_length" is non-zero then it reads a 6th byte so there needs to
be an additional check for that.

I also added checks for the "write_pos".  I don't think these are
required because "read_pos" and "write_pos" are tied together so
checking one ought to be enough.  But they make the code easier to
understand for me.  The check on write_pos is:

	if (write_pos + 4 >= sizeof(c->operand) - 4) {

The first "+ 4" is because we're writing 5 bytes and the last " - 4"
is to leave space for the CRC.

The other problem is that "length" can be invalid.  It comes from
"data_length" in fdtv_ca_pmt().

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Luo Likang <luolikang@nsfocus.com>
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab+huawei@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (data_length > sizeof(msg->msg) - data_pos)', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;']}
description: The firewire subsystem in the Linux kernel through 5.14.13 has a buffer overflow related to drivers/media/firewire/firedtv-avc.c and drivers/media/firewire/firedtv-ci.c, because avc_ca_pmt mishandles bounds checking.

code_evidence: data_pos is initialized to 4 and advanced while parsing msg->msg[3] & 0x7f length bytes, so data_length is attacker-controlled and can exceed the remaining buffer. The function then calls avc_ca_pmt with &msg->msg[data_pos] and that unchecked data_length. The added patch guard (data_length > sizeof(msg->msg) - data_pos) is absent in this function, leaving the length passed downstream unbounded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked, oversized data_length flows into avc_ca_pmt, which writes operand data beyond the intended buffer bounds. This is a write-past-end, not merely a read overrun (CWE-125), since the downstream path copies the parsed data into a fixed buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: data_length derived from msg->msg[3] is not validated against the size of msg->msg or the remaining space after data_pos. Trigger: a crafted ca_msg with a large length field. Consequence: avc_ca_pmt reads and writes past the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds write (and read) in the firewire CI handling.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In version 2.10 and earlier, PJSIP transport can be reused if they have the same IP address + port + protocol. However, this is insufficient for secure transport since it lacks remote hostname authentication. Suppose we have created a TLS connection to `sip.foo.com`, which has an IP address `100.1.1.1`. If we want to create a TLS connection to another hostname, say `sip.bar.com`, which has the same IP address, then it will reuse that existing connection, even though `100.1.1.1` does not have certificate to authenticate as `sip.bar.com`. The vulnerability allows for an insecure interaction without user awareness. It affects users who need access to connections to different destinations that translate to the same address, and allows man-in-the-middle attack if attacker can route a connection to another destination such as in the case of DNS spoofing.

code_evidence: Lines 94-95 set dlg->secure only from transport security and SIPS URI scheme, with no hostname/certificate identity check against the remote host.
Lines 57-59 clone the From header into dlg->remote.info; this is the identity used for the dialog, not authenticated against the transport's certificate host.
Lines 91-92 bind the dialog to rdata->msg_info.cseq and remote contact URI without verifying the transport's remote_name host matches the claimed destination.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-295 fits because the function establishes secure dialog state without validating the certificate's hostname binding to the remote identity, an improper certificate validation. It is not merely a transport reuse issue; the missing hostname check on the certificate is the core weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
dlg->secure = PJSIP_TRANSPORT_IS_SECURE(rdata->tp_info.transport) &&
PJSIP_URI_SCHEME_IS_SIPS(rdata->msg_info.msg->line.req.uri);

dlg->remote.cseq = dlg->remote.first_cseq = rdata->msg_info.cseq->cseq;
dlg->target = dlg->remote.contact->uri;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dialog creation accepts an existing secure transport and marks the dialog secure based solely on transport security flags and SIPS scheme, without validating that the transport's certificate hostname matches the dialog's remote identity. Trigger: a TLS transport reused for a different hostname resolving to the same IP. Consequence: the dialog proceeds as authenticated, enabling MITM/identity confusion.

hyperstart: fix several mem leak

Signed-off-by: y00316549 <yangshukui@huawei.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tint i;', '\t\tif (num > 1) {', '\t\t\tfor (i = 0; i < num; i++) {', '\t\t\t\tfree(list[i]);', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tfree(list);', '\t\t}']}
description: hyperstart 1.0.0 in HyperHQ Hyper has memory leaks in the container_setup_modules and hyper_rescan_scsi functions in container.c, related to runV 1.0.0 for Docker.

code_evidence: scandir allocates an array of dirent pointers (and the entries) into list; when num > 2 the function prints and returns 0 without freeing list or its entries, so the allocation is leaked on that path. The patch adds frees for num > 1, confirming the missing release.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because a heap resource obtained from scandir is never released on the early-return path; the added free loop in the patch confirms the omission. This is a missing release, not a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the early return at [21] abandons the scandir-allocated list after its effective lifetime. Trigger: dst already contains more than two entries so num > 2. Consequence: repeated calls consume memory without release, a memory-exhaustion DoS.

commit_msg: Changes for issues #863 and #862
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif (p_image->comps[compno].data == NULL) return OPJ_FALSE;', '']}
description: An out-of-bounds read vulnerability was found in OpenJPEG 2.1.2, in the j2k_to_image tool. Converting a specially crafted JPEG2000 file to another format could cause the application to crash or, potentially, disclose some data from the heap.

Trigger: a crafted JPEG2000 file causes a component's decoded data pointer to be NULL; the loop at lines 59-64 stores it into the returned image. commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow in num_images

Includes the fix for CVE-2021-29338
Credit to @kaniini based on #1346
Fixes #1338
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        dirptr->filename_buf = (char*)malloc((size_t)num_images * OPJ_PATH_LEN * sizeof(', '                char)); /* Stores at max 10 image file names*/', '        dirptr->filename = (char**) malloc((size_t)num_images * sizeof(char*));'], 'added_lines': ['        /* Stores at max 10 image file names*/', '        dirptr->filename_buf = (char*) calloc((size_t) num_images,', '                                              OPJ_PATH_LEN * sizeof(char));', '        dirptr->filename = (char**) calloc((size_t) num_images, sizeof(char*));']}
description: Integer Overflow in OpenJPEG v2.4.0 allows remote attackers to crash the application, causing a Denial of Service (DoS). This occurs when the attacker uses the command line option "-ImgDir" on a directory that contains 1048576 files.

code_evidence: num_images comes from get_num_images(img_fol.imgdirpath), i.e. the count of files in an attacker-controlled directory. The allocation size is computed as (size_t)num_images * OPJ_PATH_LEN * sizeof(char) with no upper bound on num_images, so the multiplication can wrap for large counts.

A second allocation computes (size_t)num_images * sizeof(char*) without a bound, and the loop then indexes filename[it_image] up to num_images-1 and offsets filename_buf by it_image * OPJ_PATH_LEN. If either product wrapped, the allocated buffers are smaller than the indices used.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the weakness is an unchecked integer multiplication used as an allocation size, which wraps to a small value. The subsequent out-of-bounds writes are the consequence, not a separate CWE; the root cause is the missing overflow constraint on the size computation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the file count num_images is used directly in size multiplications for malloc without checking that num_images * OPJ_PATH_LEN and num_images * sizeof(char*) fit in size_t. Trigger: a directory containing enough files (e.g. 1048576) makes the products wrap, producing a small allocation. Consequence: the loop at lines 39-40 and later load_images/get_next_file write past the undersized buffers, causing heap corruption and a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
In theory, IO scheduler belongs to request queue, and the request pool
of sched tags belongs to the request queue too.

However, the current tags allocation interfaces are re-used for both
driver tags and sched tags, and driver tags is definitely host wide,
and doesn't belong to any request queue, same with its request pool.
So we need tagset instance for freeing request of sched tags.

Meantime, blk_mq_free_tag_set() often follows blk_cleanup_queue() in case
of non-BLK_MQ_F_TAG_SHARED, this way requires that request pool of sched
tags to be freed before calling blk_mq_free_tag_set().

Commit 47cdee29ef9d94e ("block: move blk_exit_queue into __blk_release_queue")
moves blk_exit_queue into __blk_release_queue for simplying the fast
path in generic_make_request(), then causes oops during freeing requests
of sched tags in __blk_release_queue().

Fix the above issue by move freeing request pool of sched tags into
blk_cleanup_queue(), this way is safe becasue queue has been frozen and no any
in-queue requests at that time. Freeing sched tags has to be kept in queue's
release handler becasue there might be un-completed dispatch activity
which might refer to sched tags.

Cc: Bart Van Assche <bvanassche@acm.org>
Cc: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Fixes: 47cdee29ef9d94e485eb08f962c74943023a5271 ("block: move blk_exit_queue into __blk_release_queue")
Tested-by: Yi Zhang <yi.zhang@redhat.com>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <rong.a.chen@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Ming Lei <ming.lei@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\televator_exit(q, q->elevator);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t__elevator_exit(q, q->elevator);']}
description: The block subsystem in the Linux kernel before 5.2 has a use-after-free that can lead to arbitrary code execution in the kernel context and privilege escalation, aka CID-c3e2219216c9. This is related to blk_mq_free_rqs and blk_cleanup_queue.

code_evidence: blk_exit_queue runs while q->elevator is still set: it clears the queue's I/O contexts via ioc_clear_queue(q) and then calls elevator_exit(q, q->elevator), which frees the scheduler and its sched-tags request pool, before setting q->elevator = NULL. The function retains no reference to the freed scheduler afterward, but the freed request pool may still be referenced by dispatch activity or by the later blk_mq_free_tag_set() path described in the commit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the defect is reuse of freed memory: the scheduler and its request pool are released by elevator_exit while later code paths may still dereference them. This is a lifetime/ordering flaw, not a separate weakness such as a double free or NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sched-tags request pool is freed inside blk_exit_queue, which is invoked from the queue's release handler after blk_cleanup_queue, so the pool can be freed while pending dispatch activity or tag-set teardown still refers to it. Trigger: queue release with a scheduler installed. Consequence: use-after-free of the freed scheduler/request pool, leading to kernel oops or memory corruption.

context-idr, that was previously guarded by struct_mutex. This allows us
to reduce the coverage of struct_mutex, with a view to removing the last
bits coordinating GEM context later. (In the short term, we avoid taking
struct_mutex while using the extended constructor functions, preventing
some nasty recursion.)

v2: s/context_lock/context_idr_lock/

Signed-off-by: Chris Wilson <chris@chris-wilson.co.uk>
Cc: Tvrtko Ursulin <tvrtko.ursulin@intel.com>
Reviewed-by: Tvrtko Ursulin <tvrtko.ursulin@intel.com>
Link: https://patchwork.freedesktop.org/patch/msgid/20190321140711.11190-2-chris@chris-wilson.co.uk
