description: In the Linux kernel 4.14 longterm through 4.14.165 and 4.19 longterm through 4.19.96 (and 5.x before 5.2), there is a use-after-free (write) in the i915_ppgtt_close function in drivers/gpu/drm/i915/i915_gem_gtt.c, aka CID-7dc40713618c. This is related to i915_gem_context_destroy_ioctl in drivers/gpu/drm/i915/i915_gem_context.c.

code_evidence: Line 12 obtains ctx via i915_gem_context_lookup, which returns a referenced context. Lines 15-17 take struct_mutex and jump to the out label if interrupted. Lines 18-19 remove the idr entry and call context_close(ctx), which drops the context reference and can free it; line 22 then calls i915_gem_context_put(ctx) on the same pointer, releasing it a second time after it may already be freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because ctx is freed by context_close and then dereferenced again by i915_gem_context_put at line 22, reusing freed memory. This is a use-after-free rather than a plain double-free label, since the second operation writes through the stale pointer after deallocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: context_close() consumes the caller's reference to ctx, potentially freeing the object. The error path at line 22 and the normal path both additionally call i915_gem_context_put(ctx), a second release of an already-freed context. Triggering the ioctl with a valid ctx_id reaches this double release; the supported consequence is a use-after-free write during the extra put, corrupting freed memory.

commit_msg:
Bug 699927: don't include operator arrays in execstack output

When we transfer the contents of the execution stack into the array, take the
extra step of replacing any operator arrays on the stack with the operator
that reference them.

This prevents the contents of Postscript defined, internal only operators (those
created with .makeoperator) being exposed via execstack (and thus, via error
handling).

This necessitates a change in the resource remapping 'resource', which contains
a procedure which relies on the contents of the operators arrays being present.
As we already had internal-only variants of countexecstack and execstack
(.countexecstack and .execstack) - using those, and leaving thier operation
including the operator arrays means the procedure continues to work correctly.

Both .countexecstack and .execstack are undefined after initialization.

Also, when we store the execstack (or part thereof) for an execstackoverflow
error, make the same oparray/operator substitution as above for execstack.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    return do_execstack(i_ctx_p, false, op);'], 'added_lines': ['    return do_execstack(i_ctx_p, false, false, op);']}
description: Artifex Ghostscript allows attackers to bypass a sandbox protection mechanism by leveraging exposure of system operators in the saved execution stack in an error object.

code_evidence: execstack_continue takes the operand stack pointer from the global osp and passes it directly to do_execstack with the 'include operator arrays' flag false (the third argument). It does not itself scrub or filter operator arrays; the substitution behavior is delegated to do_execstack.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The change makes execstack stop exposing internal operator array contents to callers, directly addressing disclosure of sensitive internal state (CWE-200). It is not a memory-safety bug; the weakness is explicit exposure of protected information through a user-visible operation.

evidence_lines.code:
os_ptr op = osp;
return do_execstack(i_ctx_p, false, op);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the execstack operation copies execution-stack contents, including internal operator arrays created via .makeoperator, into a user-accessible result. Trigger: a PostScript program invokes execstack (or error handling exposes the saved stack). Consequence: internal-only operator arrays are disclosed, enabling sandbox bypass. In this function, the added false argument is the caller-side control that suppresses operator arrays in the output.

commit_msg: Prevent arithmetic overflow on bounds check
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if( end != p + sig_len )'], 'added_lines': ['        if( p != end - sig_len )']}
description: ARM mbed TLS before 2.1.11, before 2.7.2, and before 2.8.0 has a buffer over-read in ssl_parse_server_key_exchange() that could cause a crash on invalid input.

code_evidence: sig_len is read as an attacker-controlled 16-bit big-endian length from the server key exchange message and p is advanced past the two length bytes. The bounds check compares end against p + sig_len; with a large sig_len, p + sig_len can wrap past the buffer, making the equality test behave unexpectedly and allowing processing to continue.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect lets an attacker-controlled length bypass the buffer-end check, so later code reads beyond the intended message buffer, which is exactly CWE-125. It is not an out-of-bounds write because the length is used for reading/verification data.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length check uses pointer addition (p + sig_len) instead of a subtraction that cannot overflow, so a large declared signature length defeats the end-of-buffer validation. Trigger: a crafted TLS server key exchange with an oversized sig_len. Consequence: subsequent reads of p for sig_len bytes can run past the received record, causing an out-of-bounds read and possible crash.

description: Sonivox in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-04-01 does not check for a negative number of samples, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, related to arm-wt-22k/lib_src/eas_wtengine.c and arm-wt-22k/lib_src/eas_wtsynth.c, aka internal bug 26366256.

commit_msg:
The functions that were used in the emulation of fxrstor, fxsave, sgdt and
sidt were originally meant for task switching, and as such they did not
check privilege levels.  This is very bad when the same functions are used
in the emulation of unprivileged instructions.  This is CVE-2018-10853.

The obvious fix is to add a new argument to ops->read_std and ops->write_std,
which decides whether the access is a "system" access or should use the
processor's CPL.

Fixes: 129a72a0d3c8 ("KVM: x86: Introduce segmented_write_std", 2017-01-12)
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn ctxt->ops->read_std(ctxt, linear, data, size, &ctxt->exception);'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn ctxt->ops->read_std(ctxt, linear, data, size, &ctxt->exception, false);']}
description: A flaw was found in the way Linux kernel KVM hypervisor before 4.18 emulated instructions such as sgdt/sidt/fxsave/fxrstor. It did not check current privilege(CPL) level while emulating unprivileged instructions. An unprivileged guest user/process could use this flaw to potentially escalate privileges inside guest.

code_evidence: segmented_read_std linearizes the segmented address and then delegates the actual read to ctxt->ops->read_std, passing only ctxt, linear, data, size and the exception pointer; no privilege level (CPL) is supplied or checked before the read is performed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function omits a privilege/CPL constraint when performing an operation reused for unprivileged instruction emulation, which is improper privilege management rather than a memory-safety flaw. The missing privilege check is the root cause; guest privilege escalation is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the read path performs a standard segmented memory access without conveying whether the access is a system access or must honor the processor's CPL. Trigger: emulation of unprivileged instructions such as sgdt/sidt/fxsave uses this helper, so a low-privilege guest can cause reads that task-switching code intended only for privileged/system contexts. Consequence: privilege boundary within the guest is not enforced, enabling privilege escalation inside the guest.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4151: reading beyond the end of a line

Problem:    Reading beyond the end of a line.
Solution:   For block insert only use the offset for correcting the length.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t{', '\t    int off;', '\t    // Avoid starting halfway a multi-byte character.', '\t    if (b_insert)', '\t    {', '\t\toff = (*mb_head_off)(oldp, oldp + offset + spaces);', '\t\tspaces -= off;', '\t\tcount -= off;', '\t    }', '\t    else', '\t    {', "\t\t// spaces fill the gap, the character that's at the edge moves", '\t\t// right', '\t\toff = (*mb_head_off)(oldp, oldp + offset);', '\t\toffset -= off;', '\t    }', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t    // avoid copying part of a multi-byte character', '\t    offset -= (*mb_head_off)(oldp, oldp + offset);']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in vim/vim prior to 8.2.

code_evidence: The multi-byte adjustment computes `off = (*mb_head_off)(oldp, oldp + offset + spaces)` for the b_insert case; `offset + spaces` can point beyond the end of the line buffer returned by `ml_get(lnum)`, and the resulting `spaces`/`count` feed allocation sizing.

Buffer size is `STRLEN(oldp) + spaces + ... + count + 1`, then `mch_memmove`/`vim_memset`/`STRMOVE` write at `offset`, `startcol` and `offset + count`; a miscomputed `spaces`/`offset` makes these writes exceed `newp`.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of the heap-allocated `newp` buffer due to unvalidated length computation, directly matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write; the read beyond the line is the cause, not the labeled weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the head-offset probe reads at `oldp + offset + spaces` without bounding against the line length, and the derived `spaces`/`count` are trusted for allocation and copy offsets. Trigger: block insert over a line ending in a multi-byte character. Consequence: heap buffer overflow when writing into `newp`.

commit_msg:
Add support for different number of page table levels dependent
on the highest address used for a process. This will cause a 31 bit
process to use a two level page table instead of the four level page
table that is the default after the pud has been introduced. Likewise
a normal 64 bit process will use three levels instead of four. Only
if a process runs out of the 4 tera bytes which can be addressed with
a three level page table the fourth level is dynamically added. Then
the process can use up to 8 peta byte.

Signed-off-by: Martin Schwidefsky <schwidefsky@de.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (tlb->mm->context.asce_limit <= (1UL << 42))', '\t\treturn;']}
description: The fork implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.5 on s390 platforms mishandles the case of four page-table levels, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted application, related to arch/s390/include/asm/mmu_context.h and arch/s390/include/asm/pgalloc.h.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. The 9p filesystem did not protect i_size_write() properly, which causes an i_size_read() infinite loop and denial of service on SMP systems.

code_evidence: iget5_locked returns a new inode (I_NEW set) that is then initialized via v9fs_init_inode; on success v9fs_stat2inode(st, inode, sb) is called to copy attributes into the inode without any inode->i_lock held. This call is the only place i_size is written in the function, and it is invoked before unlock_new_inode, so concurrent getattr readers can observe a partially updated i_size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The observable defect is a loop (read_seqcount_begin retry) whose exit condition is never reached under the unsynchronized write, matching CWE-835. The missing lock is the cause; the infinite loop and DoS are the supported consequence, not a separate race label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: i_size_write() in v9fs_stat2inode is performed without holding inode->i_lock, so on 32-bit SMP the seqcount-protected i_size update can be interleaved. Trigger: concurrent v9fs_vfs_getattr()/getattr_dotl() callers invoke i_size_read(), whose read_seqcount_begin() retries indefinitely. Supported consequence: soft lockup and CPU-denial of service.

commit_msg: codegen.c: fix a argument generation bug in array assignment.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if (n < 14) {'], 'added_lines': ['      if (n < 15) {', '        if (n == 15) {', '          pop_n(14);', '          genop_2(s, OP_ARRAY, cursp(), 15);', '        }']}
description: Out-of-bounds Read in GitHub repository mruby/mruby prior to 3.2.

code_evidence: The argument-count bookkeeping for the call/assign node tracks n and, when n reaches the boundary, executes pop()/genop_2(OP_ARYPUSH) to compact the stack. Before the fix the threshold was n < 14, so the compaction branch was entered at n == 14; the corrected code uses n < 15 and handles the n == 15 boundary with pop_n(14) plus OP_ARRAY.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the faulty boundary handling causes the bytecode generator to read stack slots beyond the intended argument region; the defect is a read past the intended buffer, not a write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is an off-by-one in the stack-slot counter n: the boundary condition n < 14 allowed the else branch to pop/compact at a count where the stack layout did not match, so the subsequent genop_3(OP_SEND ... n) and stack adjustment operated on a mismatched stack depth. The trigger is a call/assignment with exactly the threshold number of arguments, and the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read of the value stack during code generation.

commit_msg:
x86: limit linear page table use to a single level

That's the only way that they're meant to be used. Without such a
restriction arbitrarily long chains of same-level page tables can be
built, tearing down of which may then cause arbitrarily deep recursion,
causing a stack overflow. To facilitate this restriction, a counter is
being introduced to track both the number of same-level entries in a
page table as well as the number of uses of a page table in another
same-level one (counting into positive and negative direction
respectively, utilizing the fact that both counts can't be non-zero at
the same time).

Note that the added accounting introduces a restriction on the number
of times a page can be used in other same-level page tables - more than
32k of such uses are no longer possible.

Note also that some put_page_and_type[_preemptible]() calls are
replaced with open-coded equivalents.  This seemed preferrable to
adding "parent_table" to the matrix of functions.

Note further that cross-domain same-level page table references are no
longer permitted (they probably never should have been).

This is XSA-240.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>

commit_msg:
Fix heap overflow (reported by Jurriaan Bremer)

When setting a new array item with yr_object_array_set_item() the array size is doubled if the index for the new item is larger than the already allocated ones. No further checks were made to ensure that the index fits into the array after doubling its capacity. If the array capacity was for example 64, and a new object is assigned to an index larger than 128 the overflow occurs. As yr_object_array_set_item() is usually invoked with indexes that increase monotonically by one, this bug never triggered before. But the new "dotnet" module has the potential to allow the exploitation of this bug by scanning a specially crafted .NET binary.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    count = yr_max(64, (index + 1) * 2);'], 'added_lines': ['    count = 64;', '', '    while (count <= index)', '      count *= 2;', '', '    while (count <= index)', '      count *= 2;', '']}
description: Heap buffer overflow in the yr_object_array_set_item() function in object.c in YARA 3.x allows a denial-of-service attack by scanning a crafted .NET file.

code_evidence: On the initial allocation path, count is set to yr_max(64, (index + 1) * 2) and used to size the malloc at [15,16] and the memset at [19]; the count is then recorded as the array capacity at [20].

On the grow path, count is set to array->items->count * 2 at [24] and used to size the realloc at [25,27] and the initialization loop at [30,31]; the capacity is stored at [32]. The item is then written at [35] using the caller-supplied index without any check that index < count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to array->items->objects[index] without ensuring index is within the allocated buffer, so it performs an out-of-bounds write on a heap buffer, matching CWE-119. The root cause is the insufficient capacity-growth constraint (fixed upstream by growing while count <= index), not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The doubling heuristic does not guarantee that the new capacity exceeds the supplied index: a count of 64 doubled to 128 cannot hold index 128 or above. When index >= count after growth, the write at [35] lands past the allocated objects buffer, corrupting heap memory. Triggered by a crafted .NET binary that supplies a large array index; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds heap write leading to denial of service and possible memory corruption.

std::string translatedKeyText is likewise constructed from a raw pointer at keysize+3+languageTextSize+1 with no bound check; a crafted chunk can place this pointer beyond the buffer or with no terminator, causing an over-read.

commit_msg:
prefer memcpy to strcpy

When we already know the length of a string (e.g., because
we just malloc'd to fit it), it's nicer to use memcpy than
strcpy, as it makes it more obvious that we are not going to
overflow the buffer (because the size we pass matches the
size in the allocation).

This also eliminates calls to strcpy, which make auditing
the code base harder.

commit_msg:
pipe: limit the per-user amount of pages allocated in pipes

On no-so-small systems, it is possible for a single process to cause an
OOM condition by filling large pipes with data that are never read. A
typical process filling 4000 pipes with 1 MB of data will use 4 GB of
memory. On small systems it may be tricky to set the pipe max size to
prevent this from happening.

This patch makes it possible to enforce a per-user soft limit above
which new pipes will be limited to a single page, effectively limiting
them to 4 kB each, as well as a hard limit above which no new pipes may
be created for this user. This has the effect of protecting the system
against memory abuse without hurting other users, and still allowing
pipes to work correctly though with less data at once.

The limit are controlled by two new sysctls : pipe-user-pages-soft, and
pipe-user-pages-hard. Both may be disabled by setting them to zero. The
default soft limit allows the default number of FDs per process (1024)
to create pipes of the default size (64kB), thus reaching a limit of 64MB
before starting to create only smaller pipes. With 256 processes limited
to 1024 FDs each, this results in 1024*64kB + (256*1024 - 1024) * 4kB =
1084 MB of memory allocated for a user. The hard limit is disabled by
default to avoid breaking existing applications that make intensive use
of pipes (eg: for splicing).

Reported-by: socketpair@gmail.com
Reported-by: Tetsuo Handa <penguin-kernel@I-love.SAKURA.ne.jp>
Mitigates: CVE-2013-4312 (Linux 2.0+)
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t} else if ((too_many_pipe_buffers_hard(pipe->user) ||', '\t\t\t    too_many_pipe_buffers_soft(pipe->user)) &&', '\t\t           !capable(CAP_SYS_RESOURCE) && !capable(CAP_SYS_ADMIN)) {', '\t\t\tret = -EPERM;', '\t\t\tgoto out;']}
description: fs/pipe.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5 does not limit the amount of unread data in pipes, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by creating many pipes with non-default sizes.

code_evidence: F_SETPIPE_SZ takes a user-controlled arg, rounds it to size, converts to nr_pages, and calls pipe_set_size(pipe, nr_pages) after only checking CAP_SYS_RESOURCE against pipe_max_size. No check limits per-user buffer consumption before the resize, so a local user can repeatedly enlarge pipe buffers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources; the function fails to bound per-user pipe buffer allocation, enabling memory exhaustion. This is a resource-consumption DoS rather than a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pipe resizing lacks a per-user cap on total allocated pipe pages. Trigger: an unprivileged local user opens many pipes and issues F_SETPIPE_SZ with large sizes that stay under pipe_max_size. Consequence: unbounded kernel memory consumption, leading to OOM and denial of service. The patch's added too_many_pipe_buffers_{hard,soft} checks are absent here, confirming the missing constraint.

commit_msg:
Out-of-bounds read in multiple decode functions

These were reported as:
- Out-of-bounds read in ntlm_decode_oem_str (GHSL-2023-019)
- Out-of-bounds read in ntlm_decode_u16l_str_hdr (GHSL-2023-020)
- Out-of-bounds read in ntlm_decode_field (GHSL-2023-021)

These are lall basically the same identical error replicated in 3
separate functions.

Fixes defects GHSL-2023-019, GHSL-2023-020, GHSL-2023-021 found by
the GitHub Security Lab team via oss-fuzz.

A 32-bit integer overflow condition can lead to incorrect checks of
consistency of length of internal buffers. This leads to a DoS
as the service may end up reading from unmapped memory and crashing.

Although most applications will error out before accepting a singe input
buffer of 4GB in lenght this could theoretically happen, and therefore
we fix it.

Fixes CVE-2023-25563

Signed-off-by: Simo Sorce <simo@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        (UINT32_MAX - str_offs < str_len) ||']}
description: GSS-NTLMSSP is a mechglue plugin for the GSSAPI library that implements NTLM authentication. Prior to version 1.2.0, multiple out-of-bounds reads when decoding NTLM fields can trigger a denial of service. A 32-bit integer overflow condition can lead to incorrect checks of consistency of length of internal buffers. Although most applications will error out before accepting a singe input buffer of 4GB in length this could theoretically happen. This vulnerability can be triggered via the main `gss_accept_sec_context` entry point if the application allows tokens greater than 4GB in length. This can lead to a large, up to 65KB, out-of-bounds read which could cause a denial-of-service if it reads from unmapped memory. Version 1.2.0 contains a patch for the out-of-bounds reads.

code_evidence: str_len is a uint16_t read from the wire header (line 11) and str_offs is a uint32_t offset (line 13). The bounds check at lines 14-16 validates str_offs against payload_offs and buffer->length, and checks str_offs + str_len > buffer->length. Because the addition is performed in 32-bit arithmetic, str_offs near UINT32_MAX can wrap so the sum passes the check, after which line 19 computes &buffer->data[str_offs] and the subsequent conversion reads str_len bytes out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits: the function reads buffer->data beyond the intended buffer extent due to an insufficient (overflow-prone) bounds check. This is an out-of-bounds read, not an out-of-bounds write; the integer overflow is the enabler rather than the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length-consistency check uses unchecked 32-bit addition (str_offs + str_len), which can overflow when str_offs is close to UINT32_MAX. Trigger: a crafted NTLM field header with a large offset and nonzero length passes the check, then line 19 and the conversion read past the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and possible crash (DoS).

description: DOS / potential heap overwrite in mkv demuxing using zlib decompression. Integer overflow in matroskademux element in gst_matroska_decompress_data function which causes a segfault, or could cause a heap overwrite, depending on libc and OS. Depending on the libc used, and the underlying OS capabilities, it could be just a segfault or a heap overwrite. If the libc uses mmap for large chunks, and the OS supports mmap, then it is just a segfault (because the realloc before the integer overflow will use mremap to reduce the size of the chunk, and it will start to write to unmapped memory). However, if using a libc implementation that does not use mmap, or if the OS does not support mmap while using libc, then this could result in a heap overwrite.

code_evidence: After each inflate() call that returns Z_OK, *length is incremented by 4096 and the buffer is reallocated to the new *length. z.next_out is set to buffer + z.total_out, and z.avail_out is increased by a fixed 4096 rather than by the actual free space (new *length - z.total_out). Because *length is a guint with no overflow check, a large decompressed stream can wrap *length, shrinking the allocation while zlib continues writing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked size arithmetic and incorrect avail_out accounting let decompressed output be written beyond the allocated heap buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The integer overflow is the enabling cause, but the supported consequence is writing past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the output buffer size *length is grown by unchecked 4096 additions and z.avail_out is incremented by a constant instead of the real remaining capacity. Trigger: a crafted compressed MKV sample that inflates beyond the allocated capacity, especially once *length wraps past G_MAXUINT. Consequence: zlib writes past the reallocated buffer, causing a heap overwrite or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix segmentation fault when closing an element

Reported in issue #19. The error happened when the node passed to elm_close
wasn't an element as it was supposed to.

In the example files reported with the issue, the node causing the crash
was a comment.

Now, elm_close will exit with an error if the node it receives isn't
an element. Some calls that could potentially call it with something else
check the node type before calling it.

description: html2xhtml v1.3 was discovered to contain an Out-Of-Bounds read in the function static void elm_close(tree_node_t *nodo) at procesador.c. This vulnerability allows attackers to access sensitive files or cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via a crafted html file.

commit_msg:
Fix an invalid address vulnerability in `tf.raw_ops.RaggedBincount`.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 368293153
Change-Id: I4b4e493d3fd05e7dc55a55de3a041a80a4f275c3
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    OP_REQUIRES(ctx, splits(0) == 0,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("Splits must start with 0, not with ",', '                                        splits(0)));', '', '    OP_REQUIRES(ctx, splits(num_rows) == num_values,', '                errors::InvalidArgument(', '                    "Splits must end with the number of values, got ",', '                    splits(num_rows), " instead of ", num_values));']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. If the `splits` argument of `RaggedBincount` does not specify a valid `SparseTensor`(https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/sparse/SparseTensor), then an attacker can trigger a heap buffer overflow. This will cause a read from outside the bounds of the `splits` tensor buffer in the implementation of the `RaggedBincount` op(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/8b677d79167799f71c42fd3fa074476e0295413a/tensorflow/core/kernels/bincount_op.cc#L430-L433). Before the `for` loop, `batch_idx` is set to 0. The user controls the `splits` array, making it contain only one element, 0. Thus, the code in the `while` loop would increment `batch_idx` and then try to read `splits(1)`, which is outside of bounds. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2 and TensorFlow 2.3.3, as these are also affected.

code_evidence: num_rows is derived as splits.size()-1 and batch_idx starts at 0 without validating that splits is a well-formed SparseTensor (first element 0, last equal to num_values).

The while loop increments batch_idx while idx >= splits(batch_idx); with a malformed splits array (e.g., single element 0), batch_idx can advance beyond num_rows and read splits(batch_idx) out of bounds.
The resulting batch_idx is then used as out(batch_idx - 1, bin) to write into the allocated [num_rows, size] output, so an out-of-range batch_idx writes past the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked batch_idx leads to writes at out(batch_idx - 1, bin) beyond the allocated [num_rows, size] output, matching CWE-787 (write past the end of the intended buffer). The earlier splits read is a related out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), but the supported consequence here is an out-of-bounds write.

evidence_lines.code:
out(batch_idx - 1, bin) = T(1);
out(batch_idx - 1, bin) += value;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the kernel trusts the user-supplied splits tensor without checking its boundaries, so batch_idx can exceed num_rows. Trigger: a splits tensor whose entries do not bracket values correctly. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads of splits and, via batch_idx-1 indexing, out-of-bounds writes to the output matrix.

commit_msg:
ANDROID: incremental fs: Evict inodes before freeing mount data

Since evicting inodes triggers writes to the backing file, which uses
the mi_owner field from the mount_info struct, make sure inodes are
evicted before we free the mount_info data

Test: incfs_test
Bug: 270117845
Change-Id: I673b2e0e04b5adc3998caf6f22443598a30338af
Signed-off-by: Paul Lawrence <paullawrence@google.com>
(cherry picked from commit 7899985277527b29c47929a6d6a89c5c89b406ad)

description: In incfs_kill_sb of fs/incfs/vfs.c, there is a possible memory corruption due to a use after free. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with System execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: incfs_free_mount_info(mi) frees the mount_info structure and sb->s_fs_info is cleared, but kill_anon_super(sb) is invoked only afterward at line 20; inode eviction during super teardown still references mi fields (mi_owner) that were just freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees mi and then performs kill_anon_super, whose inode eviction path dereferences the freed mi; this is a direct use-after-free (CWE-416). It is not merely a double free or NULL dereference, since the memory is reused after release via the stale mount_info reference.

commit_msg:
Blink-in-JS should not run micro tasks

If Blink-in-JS runs micro tasks, there's a risk of causing a UXSS bug
(see 645211 for concrete steps).

This CL makes Blink-in-JS use callInternalFunction (instead of callFunction)
to avoid running micro tasks after Blink-in-JS' callbacks.

BUG=645211

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2330843002
Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#417874}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!V8ScriptRunner::callFunction(v8::Local<v8::Function>::Cast(setter), scriptState->getExecutionContext(), holder, WTF_ARRAY_LENGTH(argv), argv, isolate).ToLocal(&result)) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (!V8ScriptRunner::callInternalFunction(v8::Local<v8::Function>::Cast(setter), holder, WTF_ARRAY_LENGTH(argv), argv, isolate).ToLocal(&result)) {']}
description: Blink in Google Chrome prior to 54.0.2840.59 for Windows, Mac, and Linux; 54.0.2840.85 for Android permitted execution of v8 microtasks while the DOM was in an inconsistent state, which allowed a remote attacker to inject arbitrary scripts or HTML (UXSS) via crafted HTML pages.

code_evidence: runDOMAttributeSetter builds a one-element argv from the caller-supplied v8Value and invokes the private-script attribute setter through V8ScriptRunner::callFunction, which permits V8 microtasks to run after the setter returns. The TryCatch only handles exceptions; it does not prevent microtask execution while the DOM is in an inconsistent state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw permits attacker-influenced script execution in a victim's browsing context through improper handling of the setter invocation, matching CWE-79's neutralization failure that enables script injection. It is not merely an exception-handling bug, since the supported consequence is cross-site script execution.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the setter is dispatched via callFunction, which drains microtasks after the Blink-in-JS callback completes, so attacker-controlled microtasks execute while DOM state is inconsistent. Trigger: crafted HTML causes a DOM attribute setter to run and queues a microtask. Consequence: script/HTML injection leading to UXSS.

commit_msg:
netfilter: nf_tables: fix null deref due to zeroed list head

In nf_tables_updtable, if nf_tables_table_enable returns an error,
nft_trans_destroy is called to free the transaction object.

nft_trans_destroy() calls list_del(), but the transaction was never
placed on a list -- the list head is all zeroes, this results in
a null dereference:

BUG: KASAN: null-ptr-deref in nft_trans_destroy+0x26/0x59
Call Trace:
 nft_trans_destroy+0x26/0x59
 nf_tables_newtable+0x4bc/0x9bc
 [..]

Its sane to assume that nft_trans_destroy() can be called
on the transaction object returned by nft_trans_alloc(), so
make sure the list head is initialised.

Fixes: 55dd6f93076b ("netfilter: nf_tables: use new transaction infrastructure to handle table")
Reported-by: mingi cho <mgcho.minic@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tINIT_LIST_HEAD(&trans->list);']}
description: In nf_tables_updtable, if nf_tables_table_enable returns an error, nft_trans_destroy is called to free the transaction object. nft_trans_destroy() calls list_del(), but the transaction was never placed on a list -- the list head is all zeroes, this results in a NULL pointer dereference.

code_evidence: nft_trans_alloc_gfp allocates a transaction with kzalloc, so all fields including the embedded list head are zero-initialized; it only sets msg_type and ctx before returning. The list head is left as a zeroed (NULL) pointer rather than a valid self-linked list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because a pointer expected to be valid (the list head) is NULL and is dereferenced by list_del downstream, crashing the kernel. The defect is a missing initialization constraint, not a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocated transaction's list head is never initialized (zeroed by kzalloc). Trigger: on an error path such as nf_tables_table_enable failing, nft_trans_destroy is called on this transaction and invokes list_del() on the zeroed list head, dereferencing NULL. Consequence: kernel NULL pointer dereference/crash (DoS).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      for (i=0; i < (ssize_t) GetPixelChannels(Cr_image); i++)'], 'added_lines': ['', '  size_t', '    number_channels;', '  number_channels=MagickMin(MagickMin(MagickMin(', '    Ar_image->number_channels,Ai_image->number_channels),MagickMin(', '    Br_image->number_channels,Bi_image->number_channels)),MagickMin(', '    Cr_image->number_channels,Ci_image->number_channels));', '      for (i=0; i < (ssize_t) number_channels; i++)']}
description: ImageMagick 7.0.8-50 Q16 has a heap-based buffer over-read in MagickCore/fourier.c in ComplexImages.

code_evidence: The inner loop iterates i from 0 to GetPixelChannels(Cr_image), but the pixel buffers Ar, Ai, Br, Bi, Cr and Ci are advanced per row using each image's own GetPixelChannels(...) stride.
Inside the loop, Cr[i]=Ar[i]+Br[i] and Ci[i]=Ai[i]+Bi[i] (and analogous reads for other operators) index every buffer with the same i bound derived from Cr_image's channel count.

The stride increments at lines 173-178 use per-image channel counts, so when operand images have fewer channels than Cr_image, indexing i up to Cr_image->number_channels reads past the end of the smaller buffers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code reads past the end of intended pixel buffers, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). The patch confirms this by introducing number_channels as the minimum across all operand images to bound the loop, showing the prior GetPixelChannels(Cr_image) bound exceeded the smaller source buffers.

evidence_lines.code:
Cr[i]=Ar[i]+Br[i];
Ci[i]=Ai[i]+Bi[i];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound is taken solely from Cr_image's channel count while the source pixel buffers belong to images that may have fewer channels. Trigger: supply input images with differing channel counts so a source image has fewer channels than the output; the loop then reads Ar[i]/Ai[i]/Br[i]/Bi[i] beyond their allocated row buffers. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

Detect duplicate DT_*.
Detect out-of-bounds hashtab and gashtab.
Detect missing DT_REL, DT_RELA.

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/317

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    unsigned const v_hsh = elf_unsigned_dynamic(Elf64_Dyn::DT_HASH);', '        hashtab = (unsigned const *)elf_find_dynamic(Elf64_Dyn::DT_HASH);'], 'added_lines': ['            if (dt_table[d_tag]', '            &&    get_te32(&dynp->d_val)', '               != get_te32(&dynp0[-1+ dt_table[d_tag]].d_val)) {', '                char msg[50]; snprintf(msg, sizeof(msg),', '                    "duplicate DT_%#x: [%#x] [%#x]",', '                    d_tag, -1+ dt_table[d_tag], -1+ ndx);', '                throwCantPack(msg);', '            }', '    unsigned const v_hsh = elf_unsigned_dynamic(Elf32_Dyn::DT_HASH);', '        hashtab = (unsigned const *)elf_find_dynamic(Elf32_Dyn::DT_HASH);', '        if (!hashtab) {', '            char msg[40]; snprintf(msg, sizeof(msg),', '               "bad DT_HASH %#x", v_hsh);', '            throwCantPack(msg);', '        }', '        if (!gashtab) {', '            char msg[40]; snprintf(msg, sizeof(msg),', '               "bad DT_GNU_HASH %#x", v_gsh);', '            throwCantPack(msg);', '        }']}
description: p_lx_elf.cpp in UPX before 3.96 has an integer overflow during unpacking via crafted values in a PT_DYNAMIC segment.

code_evidence: The DT_HASH block derives nbucket from attacker-controlled hashtab[0]; buckets is &hashtab[2] and chains is &buckets[nbucket], and the guard computes 2*nbucket plus sizeof(*buckets)*nbucket and sizeof(*chains)*nbucket in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic.

The DT_GNU_HASH block derives n_bucket and n_bitmask from gashtab, then computes buckets = &bitmask[n_bitmask] and hasharr = &buckets[n_bucket]; its guard evaluates n_bitmask + 2*n_bucket and sizeof(*bitmask)*n_bitmask plus sizeof(*buckets)*n_bucket plus sizeof(*hasharr)*n_bucket, all in unsigned arithmetic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is arithmetic wraparound in the length/offset calculations (2*nbucket, n_bitmask + 2*n_bucket, sizeof*count products) that the logic assumes stay larger than their operands, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a missing-bounds check (CWE-125/787); the defect is that the computed sizes can wrap before being compared.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: size expressions for the hash tables are computed in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic without overflow checks, so crafted large nbucket/n_bucket/n_bitmask values wrap the products and sums. Trigger: a PT_DYNAMIC segment carrying inflated DT_HASH/DT_GNU_HASH metadata. Consequence: the bounds comparison passes and subsequent pointer/index computations exceed the mapped hashtab, yielding out-of-bounds reads or memory corruption during unpacking.

commit_msg:
Fix DTLS replay protection

The DTLS implementation provides some protection against replay attacks
in accordance with RFC6347 section 4.1.2.6.

A sliding "window" of valid record sequence numbers is maintained with
the "right" hand edge of the window set to the highest sequence number we
have received so far. Records that arrive that are off the "left" hand
edge of the window are rejected. Records within the window are checked
against a list of records received so far. If we already received it then
we also reject the new record.

If we have not already received the record, or the sequence number is off
the right hand edge of the window then we verify the MAC of the record.
If MAC verification fails then we discard the record. Otherwise we mark
the record as received. If the sequence number was off the right hand edge
of the window, then we slide the window along so that the right hand edge
is in line with the newly received sequence number.

Records may arrive for future epochs, i.e. a record from after a CCS being
sent, can arrive before the CCS does if the packets get re-ordered. As we
have not yet received the CCS we are not yet in a position to decrypt or
validate the MAC of those records. OpenSSL places those records on an
unprocessed records queue. It additionally updates the window immediately,
even though we have not yet verified the MAC. This will only occur if
currently in a handshake/renegotiation.

This could be exploited by an attacker by sending a record for the next
epoch (which does not have to decrypt or have a valid MAC), with a very
large sequence number. This means the right hand edge of the window is
moved very far to the right, and all subsequent legitimate packets are
dropped causing a denial of service.

A similar effect can be achieved during the initial handshake. In this
case there is no MAC key negotiated yet. Therefore an attacker can send a
message for the current epoch with a very large sequence number. The code
will process the record as normal. If the hanshake message sequence number
(as opposed to the record sequence number that we have been talking about
so far) is in the future then the injected message is bufferred to be
handled later, but the window is still updated. Therefore all subsequent
legitimate handshake records are dropped. This aspect is not considered a
security issue because there are many ways for an attacker to disrupt the
initial handshake and prevent it from completing successfully (e.g.
injection of a handshake message will cause the Finished MAC to fail and
the handshake to be aborted). This issue comes about as a result of trying
to do replay protection, but having no integrity mechanism in place yet.
Does it even make sense to have replay protection in epoch 0? That
issue isn't addressed here though.

This addressed an OCAP Audit issue.

CVE-2016-2181

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int dtls1_process_record(SSL *s)'], 'added_lines': ['int dtls1_process_record(SSL *s, DTLS1_BITMAP *bitmap)', '', '    /* Mark receipt of record. */', '    dtls1_record_bitmap_update(s, bitmap);', '']}
description: The Anti-Replay feature in the DTLS implementation in OpenSSL before 1.1.0 mishandles early use of a new epoch number in conjunction with a large sequence number, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (false-positive packet drops) via spoofed DTLS records, related to rec_layer_d1.c and ssl3_record.c.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no numeric calculation or conversion flaw; the diff adds a bitmap update call, and the described replay-window issue (CVE-2016-2181) is a logic flaw in sequence-number handling, not a CWE-189 numeric error supported by lines in this function.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.11.11. synic_get in arch/x86/kvm/hyperv.c has a NULL pointer dereference for certain accesses to the SynIC Hyper-V context, aka CID-919f4ebc5987.

code_evidence: synic_get resolves a vCPU via get_vcpu_by_vpidx and only checks the vCPU pointer for NULL on line 6. It then calls to_hv_synic(vcpu) and dereferences synic->active on line 9 without verifying that the Hyper-V context (to_hv_vcpu) was allocated or that to_hv_synic returned a valid pointer. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard only validates the vCPU, not the lazily-allocated Hyper-V/SynIC context. Trigger: irq routing is set directly without enabling SynIC, so the context is unallocated and to_hv_synic yields a NULL-derived synic. commit_msg:
Have a common routine for converting dates and times to strings.

Have a routine that takes a buffer, a strftime format, and a struct tm *
as arguments, and:

* checks whether the struct tm * is null and, if so, returns a string
indicating that the date and time couldn't be converted;

* otherwise, passes it to strftime(), along with the buffer and the
format argument and, if strftime() returns 0, meaning the string didn't
fit into the buffer and thus that the buffer's contents are undefined,
returns a string indicating that the date and time didn't fit into the
buffer;

* otherwise, returns a pointer to the buffer.

Call that routine instead of directly calling strftime() in printers;
that prevents printing a buffer with undefined data if the buffer isn't
big enough for the string.

Also, when generating file names using an strftime format, check the
return value of strftime() to make sure the buffer didn't overflow.

description: The SMB protocol decoder in tcpdump version 4.99.3 can perform an out-of-bounds write when decoding a crafted network packet.

code_evidence: A 32-byte stack buffer timestr is declared at line 7. Lines 20-23 call strftime() with that buffer and format strings, but the return value is not checked; strftime() returns 0 when the formatted result does not fit, leaving buffer contents undefined. Line 24 then prints timestr as a string via ND_PRINT, so an undersized/undefined buffer is consumed as if valid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked strftime() failure means the fixed-size buffer may not hold the produced output, and subsequent use can write/read past its intended bounds, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. This is distinct from a mere null-pointer dereference (CWE-476) because the buffer-capacity constraint is the missing check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the strftime() return value is ignored, so a formatting failure (0) leaves timestr without a valid NUL-terminated string. Trigger: a time/format combination that does not fit the 32-byte buffer. Consequence: ND_PRINT reads undefined buffer contents, supporting out-of-bounds read/write behavior during printing.

commit_msg:
[CVE-2017-0152] MSFT: 10592731 : Issue with Function name capturing in param scope

In a function expression with name, where the name is captured in one
of the param scope functions, if there is a function or var declaration
with the same name as the function expression name we were marking the
function expression name as shadowed. In non-eval case this causes
issue because the name symbol won't get added to the body. This change is to
fix it in such a way if the name is captured in the param scope then we
split the param and body scope such that the name symbol is added to the
param scope not body scope.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                else if (varSym && varSym->GetSymbolType() == STVariable && (varSym->IsInSlot(funcInfo) || varSym->GetLocation() != Js::Constants::NoRegister))'], 'added_lines': ['            Symbol* funcSym = funcInfo->root->sxFnc.GetFuncSymbol();', '                else if ((funcSym == nullptr || funcSym != param)    // Do not copy the symbol over to body as the function expression symbol', '                                                                     // is expected to stay inside the function expression scope', '                    && (varSym && varSym->GetSymbolType() == STVariable && (varSym->IsInSlot(funcInfo) || varSym->GetLocation() != Js::Constants::NoRegister)))']}
description: A remote code execution vulnerability exists in the way affected Microsoft scripting engine render when handling objects in memory in Microsoft browsers. The vulnerability could corrupt memory in such a way that an attacker could execute arbitrary code in the context of the current user. An attacker who successfully exploited the vulnerability could gain the same user rights as the current user, aka "Scripting Engine Memory Corruption Vulnerability."

code_evidence: The param-scope copy loop iterates every param symbol, finds a body-scope symbol by name, and when varSym is a variable with a slot, loads the param slot and stores it into varSym via EmitPropStore. The fix adds funcSym = GetFuncSymbol() and skips the copy when funcSym == param, because the function-expression name symbol belongs in the param scope, not the body scope.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is an out-of-bounds or mismatched memory write during bytecode emission (EmitPropStore into a symbol whose body binding was not properly established), which is an operation outside the buffer's intended boundary; CWE-119 is the appropriate class for this memory-corruption consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop copies a function-expression name symbol from param scope into a body binding, but that symbol is not intended to live in the body scope. Trigger: a named function expression whose name is captured in a param-scope function, with a same-named var/function declaration. The copy then writes through a mismatched/absent body binding, corrupting memory rather than a clean type error.

commit_msg:
The block number in the quota tree on disk should be smaller than the
v2_disk_dqinfo.dqi_blocks. If the quota file was corrupted, we may be
allocating an 'allocated' block and that would lead to a loop in a tree,
which will probably trigger oops later. This patch adds a check for the
block number in the quota tree to prevent such potential issue.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20211008093821.1001186-2-yi.zhang@huawei.com
Signed-off-by: Zhang Yi <yi.zhang@huawei.com>
Cc: stable@kernel.org

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. When `RangeSize` receives values that do not fit into an `int64_t`, it crashes. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 37e64539cd29fcfb814c4451152a60f5d107b0f0. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: Computes size as (abs(limit-start) + abs(delta) - 1) / abs(delta) for integral T; the addition abs(limit-start)+abs(delta) can exceed the range of T and wrap before division.
The overflow check compares the already-wrapped size against int64_t max, so wrapped small/negative values pass and do not trigger InvalidArgument.
The unvalidated size is cast to int64_t and used to construct the output vector shape, feeding a corrupted dimension into allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the arithmetic abs(limit-start)+abs(delta) can exceed the integer representation and wrap, and the resulting value is used for allocation sizing. This is a calculation overflow rather than merely a bounds-check omission; the missing constraint is on the operands before addition, not on the post-hoc comparison.

evidence_lines.code:
auto size = (std::is_integral<T>::value
? ((Eigen::numext::abs(limit - start) +
Eigen::numext::abs(delta) - T(1)) /
Eigen::numext::abs(delta))
: (Eigen::numext::ceil(
Eigen::numext::abs((limit - start) / delta))));
c->set_output(0, c->Vector(static_cast<int64_t>(size)));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the integral branch performs abs(limit-start)+abs(delta)-1 in type T without overflow protection, so large range endpoints wrap the computed size. The guard at line 23 inspects the wrapped result rather than operands, so it cannot detect the overflow. Trigger: RangeSize receives integral start/limit/delta whose span plus delta exceeds T's range; the wrapped size then reaches Vector construction, causing a crash or bad allocation as described.

commit_msg:
Restrict PixelBuffer dimensions to safe values

We do a lot of calculations based on pixel coordinates and we need
to make sure they do not overflow. Restrict the maximum dimensions
we support rather than try to switch over all calculations to use
64 bit integers.

This prevents attackers from from injecting code by specifying a
huge framebuffer size and relying on the values overflowing to
access invalid areas of the heap.

This primarily affects the client which gets both the screen
dimensions and the pixel contents from the remote side. But the
server might also be affected as a client can adjust the screen
dimensions, as can applications inside the session.

Issue found by Pavel Cheremushkin from Kaspersky Lab.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if ((width < 0) || (width > maxPixelBufferWidth))', '    throw rfb::Exception("Invalid PixelBuffer width of %d pixels requested", width);', '  if ((height < 0) || (height > maxPixelBufferHeight))', '    throw rfb::Exception("Invalid PixelBuffer height of %d pixels requested", height);', '']}
description: TigerVNC version prior to 1.10.1 is vulnerable to heap buffer overflow. Vulnerability could be triggered from CopyRectDecoder due to incorrect value checks. Exploitation of this vulnerability could potentially result into remote code execution. This attack appear to be exploitable via network connectivity.

code_evidence: PixelBuffer::setSize accepts arbitrary int width and height and stores them directly into width_ and height_ with no validation on line 3 and line 4. Negative or extremely large values are therefore accepted and become the buffer's declared geometry, which later size calculations use to allocate or index pixel storage.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Unvalidated dimensions that drive later pixel-coordinate arithmetic lead to writes outside the allocated buffer, which is exactly CWE-787. Integer overflow is the enabling condition, but the demonstrated impact is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an incorrect value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the setter performs no range or sign check before assigning attacker-influenced dimensions to width_/height_. Trigger: a remote peer or client supplies a huge or negative framebuffer size; downstream coordinate arithmetic overflows or underflows, and the resulting allocation/index mismatch lets pixel writes land outside the intended buffer. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds heap write, potentially memory corruption and code execution.

commit_msg:
asn1_find_node: added safety check on asn1_find_node()

This prevents a stack overflow in asn1_find_node() which
is triggered by too long variable names in the definitions
files. That means that applications have to deliberately
pass a too long 'name' constant to asn1_write_value()
and friends.  Reported by Jakub Jirasek.

Signed-off-by: Nikos Mavrogiannopoulos <nmav@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t  if (nsize >= sizeof(n))', '\t\treturn NULL;', '', '\t  if (nsize >= sizeof(n))', '\t\treturn NULL;', '']}
description: Two errors in the "asn1_find_node()" function (lib/parser_aux.c) within GnuTLS libtasn1 version 4.10 can be exploited to cause a stacked-based buffer overflow by tricking a user into processing a specially crafted assignments file via the e.g. asn1Coding utility.

code_evidence: n is a fixed stack buffer of ASN1_MAX_NAME_SIZE+1 bytes. In the first branch, nsize is computed as n_end - n_start from the attacker-influenced name string; memcpy then copies nsize bytes into n and n[nsize]=0 writes one more, with no bound check before the copy.
The second loop repeats the same pattern: nsize derived from strchr on n_start, then memcpy into the same fixed n followed by n[nsize]=0, again without comparing nsize to sizeof(n).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe memcpy and the n[nsize]=0 terminator write past the end of the intended stack buffer n, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely a read overrun or integer issue; the unbounded length directly causes the write beyond n's bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length of a dot-delimited name component is trusted and used as the memcpy size into the fixed-size stack array n, with no check that nsize < sizeof(n). Trigger: a name (or assignments-file-derived name) whose component before '.' exceeds ASN1_MAX_NAME_SIZE. Consequence: out-of-bounds stack write, stack corruption/overflow, potentially crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
delta: fix out-of-bounds read of delta

When computing the offset and length of the delta base, we repeatedly
increment the `delta` pointer without checking whether we have advanced
past its end already, which can thus result in an out-of-bounds read.
Fix this by repeatedly checking whether we have reached the end. Add a
test which would cause Valgrind to produce an error.

Reported-by: Riccardo Schirone <rschiron@redhat.com>
Test-provided-by: Riccardo Schirone <rschiron@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x01) off = *delta++;', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x02) off |= *delta++ << 8UL;', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x04) off |= *delta++ << 16UL;', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x08) off |= ((unsigned) *delta++ << 24UL);', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x10) len = *delta++;', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x20) len |= *delta++ << 8UL;', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x40) len |= *delta++ << 16UL;'], 'added_lines': ['#define ADD_DELTA(o, shift) { if (delta < delta_end) (o) |= ((unsigned) *delta++ << shift); else goto fail; }', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x01) ADD_DELTA(off, 0UL);', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x02) ADD_DELTA(off, 8UL);', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x04) ADD_DELTA(off, 16UL);', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x08) ADD_DELTA(off, 24UL);', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x10) ADD_DELTA(len, 0UL);', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x20) ADD_DELTA(len, 8UL);', '\t\t\tif (cmd & 0x40) ADD_DELTA(len, 16UL);', '#undef ADD_DELTA']}
description: A flaw was found in libgit2 before version 0.27.3. A missing check in git_delta_apply function in delta.c file, may lead to an out-of-bound read while reading a binary delta file. An attacker may use this flaw to cause a Denial of Service.

code_evidence: The loop is bounded by `delta < delta_end` at line 28, but only for the command byte at line 29. When the high bit is set, lines 32–38 increment `delta` and dereference it for off/len bytes without re-checking against `delta_end`, so a truncated delta can read past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory past the end of the `delta` buffer, matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). The later check at line 40 only validates base/res bounds, not delta consumption, so it does not prevent the over-read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy-instruction path advances and dereferences `delta` for each optional offset/length byte without a bounds check against `delta_end`. Trigger: a malicious binary delta whose command byte requests additional operand bytes that are absent. Consequence: out-of-bounds read, potentially crashing (DoS) and reading adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
Don't try to be smart about probing the min/max tim_t values.
Just assume that a signed time_t is really a 64-bit or 32-bit integer.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tconst uintmax_t max_unsigned_time_t = (uintmax_t)(~(time_t)0);', '\t\tconst uintmax_t max_signed_time_t = max_unsigned_time_t >> 1;', '\t\tconst intmax_t min_signed_time_t = (intmax_t)~max_signed_time_t;', '\t\treturn (time_t)min_signed_time_t;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (sizeof(time_t) == sizeof(int64_t)) {', '\t\t\treturn (time_t)INT64_MIN;', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t\treturn (time_t)INT32_MIN;', '\t\t}']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the (1) get_time_t_max and (2) get_time_t_min functions in archive_read_support_format_mtree.c in libarchive before 3.2.0 allow remote attackers to have unspecified impact via a crafted mtree file, which triggers undefined behavior.

code_evidence: Computes the minimum signed time_t by bitwise complement and shift on uintmax_t: max_unsigned_time_t = (uintmax_t)(~(time_t)0); max_signed_time_t = max_unsigned_time_t >> 1; min_signed_time_t = (intmax_t)~max_signed_time_t; then casts back to time_t.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the function performs arithmetic whose result is assumed to be a valid minimum value but can overflow/wrap due to representation and width assumptions; the fix replaces it with fixed INT64_MIN/INT32_MIN constants.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The code derives the signed time_t range via complement/shift/cast arithmetic instead of using the type's actual limits. The bitwise complement and cast depend on the width of time_t and intmax_t; when those assumptions do not hold, the computed value can wrap or be implementation-defined, yielding an incorrect bound. That bad bound is then used as a time limit when parsing crafted mtree timestamps, causing undefined behavior.

description: In LibRaw, there is a memory corruption vulnerability within the "crxFreeSubbandData()" function (libraw\src\decoders\crx.cpp) when processing cr3 files.

code_evidence: The loop sums bandSize (width * sizeof(int32_t)) over toSubbands = 3*img->levels+1 entries into compDataSize, with no upper bound check on levels or subband widths before accumulation.
The levels branch further enlarges compDataSize using encLevels and per-level transform widths, again without validating img->levels or tile dimensions against a maximum.
malloc(compDataSize) allocates directly from this attacker-influenced size; only the NULL result is checked, not whether the requested size is reasonable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the function allocates a buffer sized by untrusted input without limiting the amount or size of the allocation. It is allocation-without-throttling rather than an integer overflow or out-of-bounds write, since the size arithmetic is not shown to wrap and no bounds on the requested resource exist.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: compDataSize is derived from CR3 header fields (img->levels, subband widths, tile width) with no cap, and the resulting size is passed straight to malloc. A crafted file can drive a very large allocation, exhausting memory; the NULL check only converts failure to an error return rather than preventing the resource consumption.

description: FreeRDP prior to version 2.0.0-rc4 contains a Heap-Based Buffer Overflow in function zgfx_decompress() that results in a memory corruption and probably even a remote code execution.

code_evidence: 'extra' is declared as signed int (line 5) and incremented in the back-reference length loop (lines 68-74); 'count' doubles each iteration (line 72) and is then summed with the extra bits (line 76-77). The resulting 'count' is passed to zgfx_history_buffer_ring_read/write and used to advance OutputCount (lines 79-81) without bounds checking against OutputBuffer capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-derived data past the end of the intended OutputBuffer/history buffer, which directly matches CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. This is not merely an integer overflow (CWE-190); the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds memory write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: 'extra' is a signed int and the loop can make 'count' grow unbounded while 'extra' increments; the attacker-controlled token stream drives the doubling. The derived 'count' is then used to write into zgfx->OutputBuffer and history buffer without validating remaining capacity, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds write that can corrupt memory and potentially enable code execution.

callers of tegra_xusb_find_port_node() function only do NULL checking for
the return value. return NULL instead of ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM) to keep
consistent.

Acked-by: Thierry Reding <treding@nvidia.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20211213020507.1458-1-linmq006@gmail.com

description: In the Linux kernel before 5.17, drivers/phy/tegra/xusb.c mishandles the tegra_xusb_find_port_node return value. Callers expect NULL in the error case, but an error pointer is used.

code_evidence: On allocation failure of name via kasprintf, the function returns ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM) instead of NULL; callers only perform NULL checks on the returned pointer, so the error pointer passes the check and is later dereferenced as a valid device_node.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the error pointer is treated as a valid pointer and dereferenced by callers, producing a NULL/invalid pointer dereference consequence. The fix returning NULL aligns the contract with caller expectations.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the inconsistent error-return contract: an error pointer is returned where callers expect NULL. Import patch from mainline to fix an address violation when parsing a corrupt PE binary.

	PR binutils/22113
	* peXXigen.c (pe_print_idata): Extend check for HintName vector
	entries.

description: The pe_print_idata function in peXXigen.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, mishandles HintName vector entries, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted PE file, related to the bfd_getl16 function.

code_evidence: In the PEx64 branch, amt = member - adj (line 194) is derived from the attacker-controlled member read from the crafted PE. The guard at line 199 only checks amt + 2 >= datasize; if amt underflows (member < adj), amt becomes a huge unsigned value, wrapping amt + 2 to a small number and passing the check. bfd_get_16 at line 205 then reads past data.

The non-PEx64 branch has the same pattern: amt = member - adj (line 225), guard amt + 2 >= datasize (line 229), then bfd_get_16 (abfd, data + amt) at line 235 and member_name = data + amt + 2 at line 236. No lower-bound check constrains amt.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe bfd_get_16 dereference at data + amt (and the following member_name pointer) reads memory beyond the intended section buffer due to the missing lower-bound check on amt. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write, so CWE-125 rather than CWE-787 applies.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: amt is computed as member - adj without validating that member >= adj, so a corrupt HintName entry causes unsigned underflow; the subsequent amt + 2 >= datasize comparison can wrap and fail to reject the entry. Trigger: a crafted PE import table with a HintName member below adj. Consequence: bfd_getl16/bfd_get_16 reads outside the allocated section buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read and application crash.

description: An issue was discovered in PHP 5.x and 7.x, when the configuration uses apache2handler/mod_php or php-fpm with OpCache enabled. With 5.x after 5.6.28 or 7.x after 7.0.13, the issue is resolved in a non-default configuration with the opcache.validate_permission=1 setting. The vulnerability details are as follows. In PHP SAPIs where PHP interpreters share a common parent process, Zend OpCache creates a shared memory object owned by the common parent during initialization. Child PHP processes inherit the SHM descriptor, using it to cache and retrieve compiled script bytecode ("opcode" in PHP jargon). Cache keys vary depending on configuration, but filename is a central key component, and compiled opcode can generally be run if a script's filename is known or can be guessed. Many common shared-hosting configurations change EUID in child processes to enforce privilege separation among hosted users (for example using mod_ruid2 for the Apache HTTP Server, or php-fpm user settings). In these scenarios, the default Zend OpCache behavior defeats script file permissions by sharing a single SHM cache among all child PHP processes. PHP scripts often contain sensitive information: Think of CMS configurations where reading or running another user's script usually means gaining privileges to the CMS database.

code_evidence: accel_activate runs for each request and only returns early when opcache is disabled or startup failed; otherwise it proceeds to SHM_UNPROTECT and cache handling without computing any per-user/root identity. The patch's root_hash/stat("/") computation is absent here, so the function performs no permission or privilege check before the shared opcode cache is used.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission/privilege management. Here the missing identity constraint lets cached opcode cross user boundaries, directly undermining file-permission enforcement. It is not merely a cache-key collision; the security-relevant defect is the failure to validate that the requesting user may access the cached script.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the activation path has no user/root identity check, so a shared opcode cache created by a common parent is used by child processes running under different EUIDs. Trigger: a shared-hosting SAPI (mod_ruid2/php-fpm) with OpCache enabled serves a request whose script filename matches a cached entry owned by another user. Consequence: the child can execute another user's compiled bytecode, defeating script file permissions and potentially exposing sensitive CMS data.

commit_msg:
Trap for overly large input to XmlRPCPP which could cause problems with int <-> size_t conversions.

 - In XmlRpcClient, XmlRpcServerConnection and XmlRpcSocket, recognize when incoming or outgoing data is too large, generate an error and discard the data when practical.
 - Use the safe strtol() rather than atoi() to decode an incoming content-length header, and generate an error if the length is invalid or too large.
 - In XmlRpcUtil, prevent attempts to parse overly large XML input.
 - Add tests where they can reasonably be inserted into existing test routines.

Although this fix could be cleaner the update is written to make the update ABI compatible.

This fix addresses CVE-2020-16124 / Integer overflow in ros_comm.

Signed-off-by: Sid Faber <sid.faber@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (xml.length() > size_t(__INT_MAX__)) return false;']}
description: Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability in the XML RPC library of OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages allows unauthenticated network traffic to cause unexpected behavior. This issue affects: OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages Noetic and prior versions. Fixed in https://github.com/ros/ros_comm/pull/2065.

code_evidence: Line 4 converts xml.length() (size_t) to int for comparison with *offset; line 5 passes the int *offset to find(), and line 8 assigns int(istart + strlen(tag)) back to *offset. A string larger than INT_MAX makes the int conversion wrap, so the offset arithmetic and the stored offset no longer match the real string position.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the size_t-to-int conversion and the offset assignment produce a wraparound that the code then relies on as a valid offset. This is a narrow integer conversion error rather than a general out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function treats a size_t string length and find() result as int offsets without bounding the string size. Trigger: an oversized XML document (> INT_MAX bytes) reaches findTag. The int conversion wraps, so the offset comparison and the stored offset are wrong, leading to mis-parsing or out-of-range offset arithmetic; the fix adds a length check before the conversions.

description: An issue was discovered in Artifex MuJS 1.0.5. It has unlimited recursion because the match function in regexp.c lacks a depth check.

code_evidence: match() takes no depth/recursion counter, so each call has no bound on nesting.
I_SPLIT saves scratch and recursively calls match(pc->x, ...) with no limit before falling through to pc->y.
I_PLA recursively calls match(pc->x, ...) unconditionally; a pattern with nested groups/alternations can recurse per input position.
I_NLA also recurses into match(pc->x, ...) without any depth guard.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits: recursion in match() is unbounded and directly triggers stack exhaustion on crafted regex input. It is not merely a bad bounds check (CWE-125/787); the weakness is uncontrolled recursion depth itself.

evidence_lines.code: static int match(Reinst *pc, const char *sp, const char *bol, int flags, Resub *out)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The recursive matcher has no depth counter or limit, so attacker-controlled regular expressions with nested groups/alternations (and long inputs) drive recursion proportional to pattern/input depth. This exhausts the C stack, causing stack overflow/crash (DoS). The missing constraint is the cause; resource exhaustion is the consequence.

Fix abort caused by allocating a too large vector.

We need to make sure that the number of dimensions in a shape is within limits.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 408997911
Change-Id: If59e1c23f2ec9c2d4ff4d8632fd62b2a7773a4eb

Hence, just prevent doing a `reserve`', '    // with a very large argument.', '    const int64_t max_dimensions = 1 << 20;', '    if (num_dims >= max_dimensions) {', '      return errors::Internal(', '          "Cannot create a tensor with ", num_dims,', '          " dimensions, as these would be more than maximum of ",', '          max_dimensions);', '    }']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. During shape inference, TensorFlow can allocate a large vector based on a value from a tensor controlled by the user. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Dim(tensor_shape, 0) retrieves a DimensionHandle from the user-influenced shape, and Value(shape_dim) yields num_dims when the dimension is known. num_dims then flows directly into dims.reserve(num_dims) and the loop bound for pushing UnknownDim() entries, with no upper-bound check on the quantity before it controls allocation and iteration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function receives a specified quantity (number of dimensions) expected to size a vector but fails to validate that it is within required limits, matching CWE-1284. This is not a plain integer overflow; the defect is missing validation of the quantity before allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dimension count taken from the shape is trusted as a resource-control quantity without validating an upper bound. Trigger: a tensor/shape where the known dimension value is extremely large. Consequence: reserve() attempts a huge allocation, causing an abort/DoS rather than a clean error; the loop would also iterate that many times.

description: In Expat (aka libexpat) before 2.4.3, a left shift by 29 (or more) places in the storeAtts function in xmlparse.c can lead to realloc misbehavior (e.g., allocating too few bytes, or only freeing memory).

When m_nsAttsPower reaches or exceeds the int width, the left shift is undefined/overflowing, so nsAttsSize becomes incorrect. That value is then multiplied by sizeof(NS_ATT) and passed to REALLOC at 174-175.

Trigger: an XML document with enough namespace-prefixed attributes to drive m_nsAttsPower past 31. commit_msg:
xen/events: avoid removing an event channel while handling it

Today it can happen that an event channel is being removed from the
system while the event handling loop is active. This can lead to a
race resulting in crashes or WARN() splats when trying to access the
irq_info structure related to the event channel.

Fix this problem by using a rwlock taken as reader in the event
handling loop and as writer when deallocating the irq_info structure.

As the observed problem was a NULL dereference in evtchn_from_irq()
make this function more robust against races by testing the irq_info
pointer to be not NULL before dereferencing it.

And finally make all accesses to evtchn_to_irq[row][col] atomic ones
in order to avoid seeing partial updates of an array element in irq
handling. Note that irq handling can be entered only for event channels
which have been valid before, so any not populated row isn't a problem
in this regard, as rows are only ever added and never removed.

This is XSA-331.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Marek Marczykowski-Górecki <marmarek@invisiblethingslab.com>
Reported-by: Jinoh Kang <luke1337@theori.io>
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn evtchn_to_irq[EVTCHN_ROW(evtchn)][EVTCHN_COL(evtchn)];'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn READ_ONCE(evtchn_to_irq[EVTCHN_ROW(evtchn)][EVTCHN_COL(evtchn)]);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.9.1, as used with Xen through 4.14.x. drivers/xen/events/events_base.c allows event-channel removal during the event-handling loop (a race condition). This can cause a use-after-free or NULL pointer dereference, as demonstrated by a dom0 crash via events for an in-reconfiguration paravirtualized device, aka CID-073d0552ead5.

code_evidence: get_evtchn_to_irq bounds-checks evtchn, checks that the row pointer evtchn_to_irq[EVTCHN_ROW(evtchn)] is non-NULL, then returns the column element. The row and column index the shared global evtchn_to_irq array, which the commit states can be modified concurrently while event handling runs; the plain read of the column element can observe a partial/torn update.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because concurrent code sequences access the shared evtchn_to_irq table without proper synchronization/atomicity. The patch's READ_ONCE addresses the torn-read aspect. This is a race on shared state, not merely a missing NULL check (CWE-476), which is a separate hardening change.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function reads the shared evtchn_to_irq[row][col] element without atomic access while deallocation/handling can run concurrently. Trigger: an event channel is removed or its irq_info freed during the event-handling loop. Supported consequence: the reader may observe an inconsistent value, leading to crashes, WARN splats, or NULL dereference in the irq_info path.
