commit_msg:
CVE-2016-0798: avoid memory leak in SRP

The SRP user database lookup method SRP_VBASE_get_by_user had confusing
memory management semantics; the returned pointer was sometimes newly
allocated, and sometimes owned by the callee. The calling code has no
way of distinguishing these two cases.

Specifically, SRP servers that configure a secret seed to hide valid
login information are vulnerable to a memory leak: an attacker
connecting with an invalid username can cause a memory leak of around
300 bytes per connection.

Servers that do not configure SRP, or configure SRP but do not configure
a seed are not vulnerable.

In Apache, the seed directive is known as SSLSRPUnknownUserSeed.

To mitigate the memory leak, the seed handling in SRP_VBASE_get_by_user
is now disabled even if the user has configured a seed.

Applications are advised to migrate to SRP_VBASE_get1_by_user. However,
note that OpenSSL makes no strong guarantees about the
indistinguishability of valid and invalid logins. In particular,
computations are currently not carried out in constant time.

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        return SSL3_AL_FATAL;', '        return SSL3_AL_FATAL;', '    /* need to check whether there are memory leaks */', '    return SSL_ERROR_NONE;'], 'added_lines': ['    int ret = SSL3_AL_FATAL;', '', '        goto err;', '', '        goto err;', '    ret = SSL_ERROR_NONE;', '', 'err:', '    SRP_user_pwd_free(p->user);', '    return ret;']}
description: Memory leak in the SRP_VBASE_get_by_user implementation in OpenSSL 1.0.1 before 1.0.1s and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2g allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by providing an invalid username in a connection attempt, related to apps/s_server.c and crypto/srp/srp_vfy.c.

code_evidence: When the SRP lookup leaves p->user NULL (unknown/invalid username), the callback returns SSL3_AL_FATAL at line 11 without releasing any resource associated with the failed lookup path.
The SSL_set_srp_server_param error branch at lines 16-17 similarly returns SSL3_AL_FATAL early, skipping the p->user = NULL / p->login = NULL reset at lines 22-23.
The only cleanup is the unconditional reset at lines 22-23, which is reached solely on the success path; the two early returns bypass it entirely.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources such as memory. The early returns at lines 11 and 17 leave lookup-associated state unreleased on every invalid-username connection, directly matching this category rather than an unrelated weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the callback has multiple early-return paths that skip the resource resetting code at the end, so per-connection state tied to the failed SRP lookup is not released. Trigger: a remote client repeatedly connects with an invalid username, driving the line 9-11 branch on each attempt. Consequence: the leaked per-connection allocation accumulates, enabling memory exhaustion and denial of service.

commit_msg:
fix TLS Certificate CommonName NULL Byte Vulnerability

CVE-2020-7043 TLS Certificate CommonName NULL Byte Vulnerability is fixed
with this commit

with #8 hostname validation for the certificate was introduced
but unfortunately strncasecmp() was used to compare the byte array
against the expected hostname. This does not correctly treat a CN
which contains a NULL byte. In order to fix this vulnerability
the reference implementation from iSECPartners has been included
into the code.
diff_func:

char common_name[FIELD_SIZE + 1];

&& X509_NAME_get_text_by_NID(subj, NID_commonName, common_name,
FIELD_SIZE) > 0

description: A vulnerability has been found in FFmpeg 2.0 and classified as problematic. This vulnerability affects the function decode_hextile of the file libavcodec/vmnc.c. The manipulation leads to memory corruption. The attack can be initiated remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

code_evidence: Lines 45-46 read attacker-controlled sub-rectangle origin (xy) and size (wh) bytes from the VMNC stream without validating them against the remaining tile dimensions. Line 47-48 pass xy>>4, xy&0xF, (wh>>4)+1, (wh&0xF)+1 directly to paint_rect, which writes into dst2 using stride, so the rectangle can extend beyond the current tile/picture.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked rectangle leads paint_rect to write outside the intended destination buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). This is a write past the end of the buffer rather than merely an out-of-bounds read, so CWE-787 fits over CWE-125.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: decode_hextile trusts the encoded rectangle coordinates and dimensions and paints them without checking that they stay within the current tile (bw/bh) or picture (w/h). Trigger: a crafted VMNC stream supplies xy/wh values whose derived rectangle exceeds the tile, causing paint_rect to write past the destination buffer. Consequence: out-of-bounds write, memory corruption, and potential code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix DTLS buffered message DoS attack

DTLS can handle out of order record delivery. Additionally since
handshake messages can be bigger than will fit into a single packet, the
messages can be fragmented across multiple records (as with normal TLS).
That means that the messages can arrive mixed up, and we have to
reassemble them. We keep a queue of buffered messages that are "from the
future", i.e. messages we're not ready to deal with yet but have arrived
early. The messages held there may not be full yet - they could be one
or more fragments that are still in the process of being reassembled.

The code assumes that we will eventually complete the reassembly and
when that occurs the complete message is removed from the queue at the
point that we need to use it.

However, DTLS is also tolerant of packet loss. To get around that DTLS
messages can be retransmitted. If we receive a full (non-fragmented)
message from the peer after previously having received a fragment of
that message, then we ignore the message in the queue and just use the
non-fragmented version. At that point the queued message will never get
removed.

Additionally the peer could send "future" messages that we never get to
in order to complete the handshake. Each message has a sequence number
(starting from 0). We will accept a message fragment for the current
message sequence number, or for any sequence up to 10 into the future.
However if the Finished message has a sequence number of 2, anything
greater than that in the queue is just left there.

So, in those two ways we can end up with "orphaned" data in the queue
that will never get removed - except when the connection is closed. At
that point all the queues are flushed.

An attacker could seek to exploit this by filling up the queues with
lots of large messages that are never going to be used in order to
attempt a DoS by memory exhaustion.

I will assume that we are only concerned with servers here. It does not
seem reasonable to be concerned about a memory exhaustion attack on a
client. They are unlikely to process enough connections for this to be
an issue.

A "long" handshake with many messages might be 5 messages long (in the
incoming direction), e.g. ClientHello, Certificate, ClientKeyExchange,
CertificateVerify, Finished. So this would be message sequence numbers 0
to 4. Additionally we can buffer up to 10 messages in the future.
Therefore the maximum number of messages that an attacker could send
that could get orphaned would typically be 15.

The maximum size that a DTLS message is allowed to be is defined by
max_cert_list, which by default is 100k. Therefore the maximum amount of
"orphaned" memory per connection is 1500k.

Message sequence numbers get reset after the Finished message, so
renegotiation will not extend the maximum number of messages that can be
orphaned per connection.

As noted above, the queues do get cleared when the connection is closed.
Therefore in order to mount an effective attack, an attacker would have
to open many simultaneous connections.

Issue reported by Quan Luo.

CVE-2016-2179

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    pitem *item = NULL;', '    hm_fragment *frag = NULL;', '', '    while ((item = pqueue_pop(s->d1->buffered_messages)) != NULL) {', '        frag = (hm_fragment *)item->data;', '        dtls1_hm_fragment_free(frag);', '        pitem_free(item);', '    }', '', '    while ((item = pqueue_pop(s->d1->sent_messages)) != NULL) {', '        frag = (hm_fragment *)item->data;', '        dtls1_hm_fragment_free(frag);', '        pitem_free(item);', '    }'], 'added_lines': ['    dtls1_clear_received_buffer(s);', '    dtls1_clear_sent_buffer(s);']}
description: The DTLS implementation in OpenSSL before 1.1.0 does not properly restrict the lifetime of queue entries associated with unused out-of-order messages, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by maintaining many crafted DTLS sessions simultaneously, related to d1_lib.c, statem_dtls.c, statem_lib.c, and statem_srvr.c.

code_evidence: The function drains s->d1->buffered_messages via pqueue_pop, freeing each hm_fragment and pitem; the queue is only emptied here.
It similarly drains s->d1->sent_messages, freeing each fragment and pitem; this is the sole cleanup path shown.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is improper management of a system resource (memory) via unbounded queue retention, matching the CWE-399 resource-management category. It is not a single buffer overflow; the supported consequence is resource consumption through orphaned queue entries.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: buffered out-of-order DTLS messages are retained until this clear routine runs, with no per-entry lifetime limit. Trigger: a peer sends fragments or future-sequence messages that are never completed or consumed, so entries accumulate. Consequence: unbounded memory retention per connection, enabling memory-exhaustion DoS when many sessions are held open.

commit_msg:
Avoid integer overflows in parsing fonts

checks the maximum reasonable value so that the total size fits in 32
bits. It also adds some explicit casting to avoid possible technical
undefined behavior when parsing sized unsigned values.

commit_msg:
When doing option parsing for standard type values of 1, 2 or 4 octets,
the value is converted directly into a variable instead of a pointer. To
avoid being tricked into being a pointer, check that for these option
types that sizes actually match. In L2CAP every option is fixed size and
thus it is prudent anyway to ensure that the remote side sends us the
right option size along with option paramters.

If the option size is not matching the option type, then that option is
silently ignored. It is a protocol violation and instead of trying to
give the remote attacker any further hints just pretend that option is
not present and proceed with the default values. Implementation
following the specification and its qualification procedures will always
use the correct size and thus not being impacted here.

To keep the code readable and consistent accross all options, a few
cosmetic changes were also required.

Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hedberg <johan.hedberg@intel.com>

description: A heap data infoleak in multiple locations including L2CAP_PARSE_CONF_RSP was found in the Linux kernel before 5.1-rc1.

code_evidence: l2cap_get_conf_opt fills type/olen/val from the remote response, but the MTU case uses val and echoes chan->imtu without requiring olen==2, so a short option leaves val partially populated and the response is built from it.
The RFC case copies only when olen==sizeof(rfc); on mismatch it skips the memcpy yet still calls l2cap_add_conf_opt with sizeof(rfc) and &rfc, emitting the stack-initialized rfc struct.
The EFS case similarly guards memcpy by olen==sizeof(efs) but the surrounding block still forwards sizeof(efs) bytes from an uninitialized efs when the size does not match.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes remote-supplied option metadata (olen) without validating that it matches the required size, which is improper input validation of a length property. CWE-20 fits; the leak is the downstream consequence rather than the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the option length olen from the remote L2CAP response is not validated against each option type's fixed size before val/rfc/efs are used. Trigger: a crafted response with a mismatched option size. Consequence: partially filled or uninitialized stack data is copied into the outgoing configuration request, leaking heap/stack contents (infoleak).

commit_msg: Fix denial-of-service attack when reading corrupt PDF files.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      PDFIO_DEBUG("load_xref: Got trailer dict.\\n");', '']}
description: PDFio is a C library for reading and writing PDF files. In versions prior to 1.1.0 a denial of service (DOS) vulnerability exists in the pdfio parser. Crafted pdf files can cause the program to run at 100% utilization and never terminate. The pdf which causes this crash found in testing is about 28kb in size and was discovered via fuzzing. Anyone who uses this library either as a standalone binary or as a library can be DOSed when attempting to parse this type of file. Web servers or other automated processes which rely on this code to turn pdf submissions into plaintext can be DOSed when an attacker uploads the pdf. Please see the linked GHSA for an example pdf. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: The outer loop `while (!done)` is only terminated by `done = true` when the `Prev` trailer entry is <= 0 (line 281-282). A crafted PDF whose trailer `Prev` points back to a valid xref offset (positive value) keeps `done` false, so the parser repeatedly re-seeks to `xref_offset` and reprocesses the same xref/trailer without any progress or iteration bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a loop whose exit condition (`done`) is never reached because `Prev` stays positive, i.e., an unreachable exit condition producing an infinite loop (CWE-835). It is not merely a resource-exhaustion bug; the defect is the missing termination guarantee in the `while (!done)` iteration.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the outer `while (!done)` loop has no bound on the number of xref sections followed; termination depends solely on the attacker-controlled `Prev` value being non-positive. Trigger: a corrupt PDF whose trailer `Prev` forms a positive self-referential chain. Consequence: the parser loops indefinitely, consuming CPU (DoS), matching the reported 100% utilization/non-termination.

description: The mod_http2 module in the Apache HTTP Server 2.4.17 through 2.4.23, when the Protocols configuration includes h2 or h2c, does not restrict request-header length, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via crafted CONTINUATION frames in an HTTP/2 request.

code_evidence: Header fields are only length-checked while !stream->has_response; once a response exists, the limits are bypassed and processing falls through to add_trailer (line 36).
The field-count limit is applied only when name[0] != ':' and only compares against limit_req_fields, so pseudo-header and continuation header additions are not bounded before the value is stored.
add_trailer receives the attacker-supplied name/value with no additional length or count validation, so unbounded header data accumulates.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts request header input without consistently validating its size or frequency, matching CWE-20's improper input validation. The guard bypass and missing count cap are the validation gap; memory exhaustion is the resulting consequence, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code:
if (h2_stream_is_scheduled(stream)) {
return add_trailer(stream, name, nlen, value, vlen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: header length and count limits are conditionally applied (guarded by !has_response and name[0] != ':') and are not enforced on trailer/continuation additions. Trigger: an HTTP/2 peer sends endless CONTINUATION frames, each adding a header via add_trailer. Consequence: unbounded memory consumption leading to denial of service.

commit_msg: Fix CVE-2019-13224: don't allow different encodings for onig_new_deluxe()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    r = conv_encoding(ci->pattern_enc, ci->target_enc, pattern, pattern_end,', '                      &cpat, &cpat_end);', '    if (r != 0) return r;'], 'added_lines': ['    return ONIGERR_NOT_SUPPORTED_ENCODING_COMBINATION;']}
description: A use-after-free in onig_new_deluxe() in regext.c in Oniguruma 6.9.2 allows attackers to potentially cause information disclosure, denial of service, or possibly code execution by providing a crafted regular expression. The attacker provides a pair of a regex pattern and a string, with a multi-byte encoding that gets handled by onig_new_deluxe(). Oniguruma issues often affect Ruby, as well as common optional libraries for PHP and Rust.

code_evidence: When pattern_enc differs from target_enc, the original code calls conv_encoding() to allocate a converted copy cpat and returns early on failure, leaving cpat ownership to this function.
After successful conversion, cpat is freed at line 32 only if cpat != pattern, so the converted buffer's lifetime is tied to the compile path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described consequence and patch are specifically about a use-after-free in onig_new_deluxe() when encoding conversion is performed. CWE-416 fits because the weakness is reuse of freed memory, not merely an invalid encoding combination; the fix rejects the combination to avoid the freeing/reuse path entirely.

evidence_lines.code:
if (cpat != pattern) xfree(cpat);
return r;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the function accepts mismatched pattern/target encodings and routes the pattern through conv_encoding(), creating a separate converted buffer whose lifetime and error handling interact with the subsequent compile path. With a crafted multi-byte pattern, the converted memory can be freed while still referenced downstream, causing a use-after-free that may disclose information, crash, or enable code execution.

code_evidence: Line 71 stores sc_pkcs15_get_objects' return in rv and line 72 tests rv != SC_SUCCESS, so a negative error value (e.g. -1) is not treated as failure; line 78 then loops ii < rv, never iterating for negative rv, leaving pin_obj NULL and taking the SC_ERROR_SECURITY_STATUS_NOT_SATISFIED path at lines 87-89.

This is not merely a missing return-value check (CWE-252): the consequence is post-free reuse of the output buffer.

A caller trusting *out_len may read the freed/NULL buffer (or, if the length is used with the dangling allocation elsewhere, dereference freed memory). description: The IEEE 802.11 dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.11 and 2.0.x before 2.0.3 does not properly restrict element lists, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (deep recursion and application crash) via a crafted packet, related to epan/dissectors/packet-capwap.c and epan/dissectors/packet-ieee80211.c.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over tagged parameters while tagged_parameters_len > 0, calling add_tagged_field with the caller's ftype and no restriction on which element IDs are permitted.

The only bound check is after the call: if next_len exceeds tagged_parameters_len it is clamped, and offset/remaining length are advanced by next_len; there is no validation of the element IDs or nesting depth before parsing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts packet input and fails to validate that element IDs conform to an allowed list, which directly matches improper input validation (CWE-20). The recursion consequence stems from this missing constraint, not from length arithmetic alone.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function forwards attacker-controlled 802.11 element data to add_tagged_field without restricting the set of valid sub-element IDs or recursion depth. A crafted packet containing self-referential or deeply nested elements triggers deep recursion, causing a stack-exhaustion crash (DoS). The clamp on next_len limits length accounting but does not constrain element identity or nesting.

commit_msg:
tiff2pdf.c: properly calculate datasize when saving to JPEG YCbCr

fixes #220
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tk = checkMultiply64(TIFFScanlineSize(input), t2p->tiff_length, t2p);', '\tif(t2p->tiff_planar==PLANARCONFIG_SEPARATE){', '\t\tk = checkMultiply64(k, t2p->tiff_samplesperpixel, t2p);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif(t2p->pdf_compression == T2P_COMPRESS_JPEG', '\t   && t2p->tiff_photometric == PHOTOMETRIC_YCBCR) {', '\t\tk = checkMultiply64(TIFFNumberOfStrips(input), TIFFStripSize(input), t2p);', '\t} else {', '\t\tk = checkMultiply64(TIFFScanlineSize(input), t2p->tiff_length, t2p);', '\t\tif(t2p->tiff_planar==PLANARCONFIG_SEPARATE){', '\t\t\tk = checkMultiply64(k, t2p->tiff_samplesperpixel, t2p);', '\t\t}']}
description: A heap-based buffer overflow flaw was found in libtiff in the handling of TIFF images in libtiff's TIFF2PDF tool. A specially crafted TIFF file can lead to arbitrary code execution. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to confidentiality, integrity, as well as system availability.

code_evidence: The pre-patch fallback computes tiff_datasize as checkMultiply64(TIFFScanlineSize(input), t2p->tiff_length) and, for PLANARCONFIG_SEPARATE, multiplies again by tiff_samplesperpixel. For JPEG YCbCr data, the stored strip layout differs from scanline_size*length, so this product under/over-estimates the real buffer size, and the resulting tiff_datasize drives later allocation/copy in tiff2pdf. The checkMultiply64 overflow guard and the k==0 error path only reject arithmetic overflow, not a layout mismatch.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The size mismatch causes a write past the end of an allocated buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely an integer overflow: the arithmetic guard passes, and the defect is the incorrect size calculation that leads to the overflow write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: datasize for JPEG YCbCr is derived from scanline size times image length rather than actual strip byte sizes, so the size used for allocation/copy does not match the decoded data. Trigger: a crafted TIFF with JPEG compression and YCbCr photometric. Consequence: tiff_datasize is too small, and subsequent writing of decoded strip data overruns the heap buffer, enabling memory corruption or code execution.

commit_msg: Fix arbitrary heap exposure problem
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        state->space = strdup(RSTRING_PTR(space));'], 'added_lines': ['        state->space = fstrndup(RSTRING_PTR(space), len);']}
description: Ruby through 2.2.7, 2.3.x through 2.3.4, and 2.4.x through 2.4.1 can expose arbitrary memory during a JSON.generate call. The issues lies in using strdup in ext/json/ext/generator/generator.c, which will stop after encountering a '\0' byte, returning a pointer to a string of length zero, which is not the length stored in space_len.

code_evidence: len is computed from RSTRING_LEN(space) at line 6, which counts embedded NUL bytes. In the non-empty branch, line 15 uses strdup(RSTRING_PTR(space)), which copies only up to the first '\0' byte, while line 16 records the full len in state->space_len. The allocated buffer can therefore be shorter than the length stored alongside it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The mismatch between the allocated buffer length and the recorded length causes subsequent operations to read outside the buffer's intended boundary, which is CWE-119. The underlying strdup truncation could be framed as a length/termination issue, but the supported consequence here is out-of-bounds memory access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: strdup truncates at an embedded NUL instead of honoring the computed len. Trigger: setting the JSON generator space to a string containing a '\0' byte. The stored space_len overstates the buffer size, so later JSON.generate operations that use space_len to read or emit the space buffer access memory beyond the allocated string, exposing arbitrary heap contents.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.4 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.10, there is a K12 file parser crash, triggered by a malformed capture file. This was addressed in wiretap/k12.c by validating the relationships between lengths and offsets.

In the before version, the return value of process_packet_data() is ignored and the function unconditionally returns TRUE.

process_packet_data() is called with the file-derived len and its success/failure status is discarded; the seek-read path reports success regardless of whether the record's internal length/offset relationships were valid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing/mcorrect validation of input data (record length and offset relationships) from an untrusted capture file before processing, matching CWE-20. The crash is the consequence of failing to validate the input, not the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
process_packet_data(phdr, buf, buffer, len, k12);
return TRUE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts a file-supplied record length after only a minimal bound check and does not propagate the validation result of process_packet_data(). Trigger: a malformed K12 capture file whose record length is inconsistent with internal offsets. Consequence: the unchecked length reaches packet processing, causing a crash (DoS) rather than a controlled read error.

commit_msg:
A race condition was found in isotp_setsockopt() which allows to
change socket options after the socket was bound.
For the specific case of SF_BROADCAST support, this might lead to possible
use-after-free because can_rx_unregister() is not called.

Checking for the flag under the socket lock in isotp_bind() and taking
the lock in isotp_setsockopt() fixes the issue.

Fixes: 921ca574cd38 ("can: isotp: add SF_BROADCAST support for functional addressing")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/trinity-e6ae9efa-9afb-4326-84c0-f3609b9b8168-1620773528307@3c-app-gmx-bs06
Reported-by: Norbert Slusarek <nslusarek@gmx.net>
Signed-off-by: Thadeu Lima de Souza Cascardo <cascardo@canonical.com>
Signed-off-by: Norbert Slusarek <nslusarek@gmx.net>
Acked-by: Oliver Hartkopp <socketcan@hartkopp.net>
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* do not register frame reception for functional addressing */', '\tif (so->opt.flags & CAN_ISOTP_SF_BROADCAST)', '\t\tdo_rx_reg = 0;', '', '\t/* do not validate rx address for functional addressing */', '\tif (do_rx_reg) {', '\t\tif (addr->can_addr.tp.rx_id == addr->can_addr.tp.tx_id)', '\t\t\treturn -EADDRNOTAVAIL;', '', '\t\tif (addr->can_addr.tp.rx_id & (CAN_ERR_FLAG | CAN_RTR_FLAG))', '\t\t\treturn -EADDRNOTAVAIL;', '\t}', ''], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* do not register frame reception for functional addressing */', '\tif (so->opt.flags & CAN_ISOTP_SF_BROADCAST)', '\t\tdo_rx_reg = 0;', '', '\t/* do not validate rx address for functional addressing */', '\tif (do_rx_reg) {', '\t\tif (addr->can_addr.tp.rx_id == addr->can_addr.tp.tx_id) {', '\t\t\terr = -EADDRNOTAVAIL;', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\tif (addr->can_addr.tp.rx_id & (CAN_ERR_FLAG | CAN_RTR_FLAG)) {', '\t\t\terr = -EADDRNOTAVAIL;', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t\t}', '\t}']}
description: In the Linux kernel 5.11 through 5.12.2, isotp_setsockopt in net/can/isotp.c allows privilege escalation to root by leveraging a use-after-free. (This does not affect earlier versions that lack CAN ISOTP SF_BROADCAST support.)

code_evidence: The SF_BROADCAST flag and rx/tx validation are read at lines 14-21, before lock_sock(sk) at line 26, so the decision to skip reception registration is made without the socket lock and can race with isotp_setsockopt changing the flag.

Registration is conditional on the stale do_rx_reg at lines 49-52; the unregister branch at lines 54-61 only runs when so->bound && do_rx_reg, so a flag change after binding can leave a registration without a matching can_rx_unregister.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsynchronized flag read causes a missing can_rx_unregister, leaving a dangling receiver reference to freed socket memory later accessed via isotp_rcv; that reuse-after-free is CWE-416. The race is the trigger, not the weakness itself, so a race CWE would not capture the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the broadcast flag and do_rx_reg are evaluated outside the socket lock, so isotp_setsockopt can change CAN_ISOTP_SF_BROADCAST concurrently with isotp_bind. Trigger: setting the flag after the socket is bound makes the unregister path at lines 54-61 skip can_rx_unregister while the earlier registration remains. Consequence: the registered callback keeps a reference to the socket, and later teardown frees the socket, producing a use-after-free.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-thrift.c had a large loop that was addressed by not proceeding with dissection after encountering an unexpected type.

code_evidence: Line 12 reads an attacker-controlled 32-bit list_len from the packet. Line 14 loops i from 0 to (int)list_len, and line 15 calls dissect_thrift_type with the same list element type on each iteration without any bound on list_len or check on the callee's return value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits because the number of loop iterations is driven by unvalidated packet data and is not limited, allowing attacker-influenced resource consumption. The ignored return value is the trigger that lets an unexpected type fail to advance, rather than a separate weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop count comes directly from the wire (list_len) and is never capped, and the per-iteration dissect_thrift_type return is ignored, so an element type that cannot advance the offset keeps the loop running. A crafted Thrift packet declaring a huge list_len, or an unexpected element type that stalls offset, triggers excessive iteration and consumes CPU until the capture is exhausted.

This attack appear to be exploitable via network request. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in after commit cf7209e703e6d3f7a5413e0cb1fe88a4d8e4b38d .

commit_msg:
[IMAPx] 'STARTTLS not supported' error ignored

When a user has setup the STARTTLS encryption method, but the server doesn't
support it, then an error should be shown to the user, instead of using
unsecure connection. There had been two bugs in the existing code which
prevented this error from being used and the failure properly reported.

This had been filled at:
https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1334842
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tGError *local_error = NULL;', '\t\t\t\t&local_error, CAMEL_ERROR,'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tGError *local_error = NULL;', '\t\t\t\terror, CAMEL_ERROR,', '\t\t\tsuccess = FALSE;']}
description: camel/providers/imapx/camel-imapx-server.c in the IMAPx component in GNOME evolution-data-server before 3.21.2 proceeds with cleartext data containing a password if the client wishes to use STARTTLS but the server will not use STARTTLS, which makes it easier for remote attackers to obtain sensitive information by sniffing the network. The server code was intended to report an error and not proceed, but the code was written incorrectly.

code_evidence: When the security method is STARTTLS but the server lacks the STARTTLS capability, the error is written to the local_error variable rather than the caller's error pointer, and success is not set to FALSE before goto exit.
success is initialized to TRUE and only the exit block checks it to decide whether to tear down the connection.
At exit, because success remains TRUE, the connection and streams are not cleared, and the function returns success despite the STARTTLS failure, leaving the cleartext connection usable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The bug directly causes sensitive data (the password) to be transmitted over an unencrypted channel to an unauthorized network observer, which matches CWE-200 exposure of sensitive information. It is not merely a generic logic error because the concrete consequence is disclosure of credentials to a sniffer.

evidence_lines.code: gboolean success = TRUE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the STARTTLS-not-supported branch sets the wrong error target and omits success = FALSE, so the failure is never propagated. Trigger: client configured for STARTTLS connects to a server lacking STARTTLS. Consequence: the function returns success with a live cleartext connection, allowing subsequent credentials/password to be sent unencrypted and sniffed.

commit_msg:
The "ev->traffic_class" and "reply->ac" variables come from the network
and they're used as an offset into the wmi->stream_exist_for_ac[] array.
Those variables are u8 so they can be 0-255 but the stream_exist_for_ac[]
array only has WMM_NUM_AC (4) elements.  We need to add a couple bounds
checks to prevent array overflows.

I also modified one existing check from "if (traffic_class > 3) {" to
"if (traffic_class >= WMM_NUM_AC) {" just to make them all consistent.

Fixes: bdcd81707973 (" Add ath6kl cleaned up driver")
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (traffic_class > 3) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (traffic_class >= WMM_NUM_AC) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.3. Out of bounds access exists in the functions ath6kl_wmi_pstream_timeout_event_rx and ath6kl_wmi_cac_event_rx in the file drivers/net/wireless/ath/ath6kl/wmi.c.

code_evidence: The parameter traffic_class is a u8 (0-255) and is only rejected when greater than 3, so values 0-3 pass the check while values 4-255 are rejected; the guard does constrain the index used below.
After taking wmi->lock, the code indexes wmi->stream_exist_for_ac[traffic_class] and reads the value into active_tsids; this array has only WMM_NUM_AC (4) elements.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 requires an actual out-of-bounds read. This function's guard rejects traffic_class > 3 before the array access, so the read at line 19 is bounded; the patch merely normalizes the comparison to WMM_NUM_AC. The described OOB reads occur in ath6kl_wmi_pstream_timeout_event_rx and ath6kl_wmi_cac_event_rx, not in this delete_pstream_cmd function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the bounds check on the network-derived u8 traffic_class is not aligned with the actual array size, but in this function the check `traffic_class > 3` does reject all values >= 4, so the read at line 19 stays within the 4-element array. The trigger would require traffic_class to reach the index without passing the guard; the supplied code does not demonstrate that, so no out-of-bounds read is shown here.

Diameter: check IPv6 prefix length before copying it in e_in6_addr structure

Bug: 11792

Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/12248

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tproto_tree_add_item(tree, hf_framed_ipv6_prefix_length, tvb, 1, 1, ENC_BIG_ENDIAN);', '\t} else {'], 'added_lines': ['\tproto_item *pi;', '\tpi = proto_tree_add_item(tree, hf_framed_ipv6_prefix_length, tvb, 1, 1, ENC_BIG_ENDIAN);', '\tif (prefix_len > 128) {', '\t\texpert_add_info(pinfo, pi, &ei_diameter_invalid_ipv6_prefix_len);', '\t}', '\t} else if (prefix_len_bytes < 16) {']}
description: The dissect_diameter_base_framed_ipv6_prefix function in epan/dissectors/packet-diameter.c in the DIAMETER dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.9 and 2.0.x before 2.0.1 does not validate the IPv6 prefix length, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer overflow and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: Line 8 reads prefix_len directly from the packet byte as an unvalidated guint8; lines 9-11 derive prefix_len_bytes via division and rounding without any upper bound check, so prefix_len can be up to 255 and prefix_len_bytes up to 32.

Line 12 and line 19 then use prefix_len_bytes as a length: tvb_memcpy copies prefix_len_bytes into value.bytes, a 16-byte e_in6_addr, and line 20 indexes value.bytes[prefix_len_bytes]; the else branch at line 15 is entered for any prefix_len_bytes != 16, including values >16.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts a length field from the packet and processes it without validating that it is within the required range (<=128), which is precisely improper input validation of a metadata quantity leading to unsafe use; CWE-20 captures this missing constraint, while the buffer overflow is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the attacker-controlled IPv6 prefix length is never checked against 128 before being converted to a byte count and used as a copy size into a fixed 16-byte stack buffer. Trigger: a crafted DIAMETER packet with prefix_len >128 (e.g. 255) makes prefix_len_bytes exceed 16, so tvb_memcpy at line 19 and the index at line 20 overflow value.bytes, causing a stack-based buffer overflow and application crash.

In versions prior to 1.22.1 if Envoy attempts to send an internal redirect of an HTTP request consisting of more than HTTP headers, there’s a lifetime bug which can be triggered. If while replaying the request Envoy sends a local reply when the redirect headers are processed, the downstream state indicates that the downstream stream is not complete. On sending the local reply, Envoy will attempt to reset the upstream stream, but as it is actually complete, and deleted, this result in a use-after-free. Users are advised to upgrade. Users unable to upgrade are advised to disable internal redirects if crashes are observed.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function is only a State constructor initializing boolean flags; it contains no pointer/memory reuse or free operation, and the described use-after-free of the upstream stream is not visible in these lines.

commit_msg:
arm64: perf: reject groups spanning multiple HW PMUs

The perf core implicitly rejects events spanning multiple HW PMUs, as in
these cases the event->ctx will differ. However this validation is
performed after pmu::event_init() is called in perf_init_event(), and
thus pmu::event_init() may be called with a group leader from a
different HW PMU.

The ARM64 PMU driver does not take this fact into account, and when
validating groups assumes that it can call to_arm_pmu(event->pmu) for
any HW event. When the event in question is from another HW PMU this is
wrong, and results in dereferencing garbage.

This patch updates the ARM64 PMU driver to first test for and reject
events from other PMUs, moving the to_arm_pmu and related logic after
this test. Fixes a crash triggered by perf_fuzzer on Linux-4.0-rc2, with
a CCI PMU present:

Bad mode in Synchronous Abort handler detected, code 0x86000006 -- IABT (current EL)
CPU: 0 PID: 1371 Comm: perf_fuzzer Not tainted 3.19.0+ #249
Hardware name: V2F-1XV7 Cortex-A53x2 SMM (DT)
task: ffffffc07c73a280 ti: ffffffc07b0a0000 task.ti: ffffffc07b0a0000
PC is at 0x0
LR is at validate_event+0x90/0xa8
pc : [<0000000000000000>] lr : [<ffffffc000090228>] pstate: 00000145
sp : ffffffc07b0a3ba0

[<          (null)>]           (null)
[<ffffffc0000907d8>] armpmu_event_init+0x174/0x3cc
[<ffffffc00015d870>] perf_try_init_event+0x34/0x70
[<ffffffc000164094>] perf_init_event+0xe0/0x10c
[<ffffffc000164348>] perf_event_alloc+0x288/0x358
[<ffffffc000164c5c>] SyS_perf_event_open+0x464/0x98c
Code: bad PC value

Also cleans up the code to use the arm_pmu only when we know
that we are dealing with an arm pmu event.

Cc: Will Deacon <will.deacon@arm.com>
Acked-by: Mark Rutland <mark.rutland@arm.com>
Acked-by: Peter Ziljstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Signed-off-by: Suzuki K. Poulose <suzuki.poulose@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Will Deacon <will.deacon@arm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['validate_event(struct pmu_hw_events *hw_events,', '\t       struct perf_event *event)', '\tstruct arm_pmu *armpmu = to_arm_pmu(event->pmu);'], 'added_lines': ['validate_event(struct pmu *pmu, struct pmu_hw_events *hw_events,', '\t\t\t\tstruct perf_event *event)', '\tstruct arm_pmu *armpmu;', '', '\t/*', '\t * Reject groups spanning multiple HW PMUs (e.g. CPU + CCI). The', "\t * core perf code won't check that the pmu->ctx == leader->ctx", '\t * until after pmu->event_init(event).', '\t */', '\tif (event->pmu != pmu)', '\t\treturn 0;', '\tarmpmu = to_arm_pmu(event->pmu);']}
description: arch/arm64/kernel/perf_event.c in the Linux kernel before 4.1 on arm64 platforms allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (invalid pointer dereference) via vectors involving events that are mishandled during a span of multiple HW PMUs.

code_evidence: Line 5 unconditionally converts event->pmu to arm_pmu before any check that the event belongs to this PMU. Lines 8-9 only exempt software events. Lines 10-13 validate the group leader but never reject an event whose pmu differs from the driver's pmu, so armpmu on line 5 may be derived from a foreign PMU and dereferenced at line 14 via get_event_idx.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing PMU-ownership check lets a local user supply cross-PMU events that bypass intended access control over the driver's PMU, matching CWE-264's permissions/privileges management category. It is not merely a NULL check; the absent constraint on event->pmu is the security-relevant flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: validate_event trusts event->pmu to be an ARM PMU and calls to_arm_pmu on it before verifying ownership. Trigger: perf_event_open with a group leader/event from a different HW PMU (e.g., CPU + CCI), reaching event_init before core ctx checks. Consequence: invalid pointer dereference during get_event_idx, causing crash (privilege or DoS per description).

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: fix unconditional helper

Ben Hawkes says:

 In the mark_source_chains function (net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c) it
 is possible for a user-supplied ipt_entry structure to have a large
 next_offset field. This field is not bounds checked prior to writing a
 counter value at the supplied offset.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (s->target_offset == sizeof(struct ip6t_entry) &&', '\t\t    t->verdict < 0 &&', '\t\t    unconditional(&s->ipv6)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (unconditional(s) &&', '\t\t    t->verdict < 0) {']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

commit_msg:
Remove support for pre-authentication compression. Doing compression
early in the protocol probably seemed reasonable in the 1990s, but
today it's clearly a bad idea in terms of both cryptography (cf.
multiple compression oracle attacks in TLS) and attack surface.

Moreover, to support it across privilege-separation zlib needed
the assistance of a complex shared-memory manager that made the
required attack surface considerably larger.

Prompted by Guido Vranken pointing out a compiler-elided security
check in the shared memory manager found by Stack
(http://css.csail.mit.edu/stack/); ok deraadt@ markus@

NB. pre-auth authentication has been disabled by default in sshd
for >10 years.

commit_msg:
The 'blit_ctx->initialised' is not setted to true.
Every time init blit context, it will create a new
'blit_ctx->gl_context' thus causing a memory leak.
This patch avoid this.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liq3ea@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Airlie <airlied@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['   blit_ctx->initialised = true;']}
description: Memory leak in the vrend_renderer_init_blit_ctx function in vrend_blitter.c in virglrenderer before 0.6.0 allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host memory consumption) via a large number of VIRGL_CCMD_BLIT commands.

code_evidence: The guard checks blit_ctx->initialised and, when true, reuses the existing gl_context via make_current then returns.
No assignment sets blit_ctx->initialised to true after the context is created at line 12; the function ends without updating the flag.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to release/reuse a resource whose lifetime should be tracked by the initialised flag, matching CWE-772's missing release of resource after effective lifetime. It is not a use-after-free or null dereference; the defect is the leaked, repeatedly allocated context.

evidence_lines.code:
blit_ctx->gl_context = vrend_clicbs->create_gl_context(0, &ctx_params);
vrend_clicbs->make_current(0, blit_ctx->gl_context);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the initialized flag is never set, so every call bypasses the early-return path and allocates a fresh GL context at line 12. Trigger: repeated calls (e.g., many VIRGL_CCMD_BLIT commands) each create a new context that is never released, causing host memory consumption and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  }', '', '  ASSERT(connection_manager_.config_.maxRequestHeadersKb() > 0);', '  if (request_headers_->byteSize() > (connection_manager_.config_.maxRequestHeadersKb() * 1024)) {', '    sendLocalReply(Grpc::Common::hasGrpcContentType(*request_headers_),', '                   Code::RequestHeaderFieldsTooLarge, "", nullptr, is_head_request_, absl::nullopt,', '                   StreamInfo::ResponseCodeDetails::get().RequestHeadersTooLarge);', '    return;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

code_evidence: After host validation the function enforces the header-size cap by iterating request_headers_->byteSize() against maxRequestHeadersKb()*1024; exceeding it sends RequestHeaderFieldsTooLarge and returns. This per-header decode path calls byteSize() for every header set, and the commit description attributes the O(n^2) cost to recomputing total size over existing headers on each incoming request header.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the resource-limiting control for request headers, and its quadratic accounting lets a remote request consume disproportionate CPU without exceeding the configured size cap, matching CWE-400 uncontrolled resource consumption. A pure length-validation weakness would describe accepting oversized headers, which is not the issue here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the size check being recomputed by summing all header key/value sizes on each header decode, so cost grows quadratically with the number of small headers. Trigger is a request with many small headers kept under the maximum size limit; the supported consequence is excessive CPU consumption leading to denial of service.

patch 8.2.5013: after text formatting cursor may be in an invalid position

Problem:    After text formatting the cursor may be in an invalid position.
Solution:   Correct the cursor position after formatting.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t// formatting may have made the cursor position invalid', '\tcheck_cursor();']}
description: Out-of-bounds Read in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.

code_evidence: format_lines() at line 17 reformats text and can shrink the buffer; lines 18-20 then adjust and clamp the cursor but do not guarantee it stays within the new buffer.
Lines 25-29 restore the previously saved cursor position unconditionally when keep_cursor is set, without validating it against the post-format line count.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Text formatting can reduce the number of lines while a saved or adjusted cursor line number is restored without revalidation. Subsequent cursor-dependent operations may then index lines beyond the buffer end, yielding an out-of-bounds read; the missing check_cursor() after restoring the saved position is the root cause.

commit_msg: Fixed bug #71906: AddressSanitizer: negative-size-param (-1) in mbfl_strcut
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (from + length >= string->len) {', '\t\t\tif (from + length >= string->len) {', '\t\t\tif (from + length >= string->len) {', '\t\t\tif ((start - string->val) + length >= (int)string->len) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (length >= string->len - from) {', '\t\t\tif (length >= string->len - from) {', '\t\t\tif (length >= string->len - from) {', '\t\t\tif (length >= (int)string->len - (start - string->val)) {']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the mbfl_strcut function in ext/mbstring/libmbfl/mbfl/mbfilter.c in PHP before 5.5.34, 5.6.x before 5.6.20, and 7.x before 7.0.5 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted mb_strcut call.

code_evidence: In the WCS2 branch, `from + length` is computed as a signed int; a large attacker-supplied `length` can overflow, so the clamp to `string->len - from` is skipped and `length` stays huge.
The WCS4 branch repeats the same `from + length >= string->len` check, allowing the same signed overflow to bypass clamping.
The SBCS branch again uses `from + length`, so overflow leaves `length` unclamped before `end = start + length`.

The mblen_table branch adds `(start - string->val) + length`, which can overflow and skip the `end = string->val + string->len` clamp, so the later loop and `sz = end - start` operate on an oversized range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes buffer boundaries with an overflowable sum and then copies `sz = end - start` bytes, producing out-of-bounds memory access. This is an improper restriction of operations within a buffer boundary, matching CWE-119; the underlying integer overflow is the cause, not the labeled weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((start - string->val) + length >= (int)string->len) {
end = string->val + string->len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bounds checks add `length` to an offset in signed int arithmetic, so a crafted large `length` overflows and the clamp to the string length is not applied. Trigger: an `mb_strcut` call with a huge length and a multibyte or SBCS encoding. Consequence: `end` points beyond the buffer, and the subsequent `memcpy(w, start, sz)` reads out of bounds (negative or oversized `sz`), causing a crash and possible memory disclosure/corruption.

There are UAF bugs in rose_heartbeat_expiry(), rose_timer_expiry()
and rose_idletimer_expiry(). The root cause is that del_timer()
could not stop the timer handler that is running and the refcount
of sock is not managed properly.

One of the UAF bugs is shown below:

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the timer is started using raw del_timer/add_timer, so no sock reference is retained while the timer is pending. commit_msg:
Add support for mount options to restrict access to /proc/PID/
directories.  The default backward-compatible "relaxed" behaviour is left
untouched.

The first mount option is called "hidepid" and its value defines how much
info about processes we want to be available for non-owners:

hidepid=0 (default) means the old behavior - anybody may read all
world-readable /proc/PID/* files.

hidepid=1 means users may not access any /proc/<pid>/ directories, but
their own.  Sensitive files like cmdline, sched*, status are now protected
against other users.  As permission checking done in proc_pid_permission()
and files' permissions are left untouched, programs expecting specific
files' modes are not confused.

hidepid=2 means hidepid=1 plus all /proc/PID/ will be invisible to other
users.  It doesn't mean that it hides whether a process exists (it can be
learned by other means, e.g.  by kill -0 $PID), but it hides process' euid
and egid.  It compicates intruder's task of gathering info about running
processes, whether some daemon runs with elevated privileges, whether
another user runs some sensitive program, whether other users run any
program at all, etc.

gid=XXX defines a group that will be able to gather all processes' info
(as in hidepid=0 mode).  This group should be used instead of putting
nonroot user in sudoers file or something.  However, untrusted users (like
daemons, etc.) which are not supposed to monitor the tasks in the whole
system should not be added to the group.

hidepid=1 or higher is designed to restrict access to procfs files, which
might reveal some sensitive private information like precise keystrokes
timings:

http://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2011/11/05/3

hidepid=1/2 doesn't break monitoring userspace tools.  ps, top, pgrep, and
conky gracefully handle EPERM/ENOENT and behave as if the current user is
the only user running processes.  pstree shows the process subtree which
contains "pstree" process.

Note: the patch doesn't deal with setuid/setgid issues of keeping
preopened descriptors of procfs files (like
https://lkml.org/lkml/2011/2/7/368).  We rely on that the leaked
information like the scheduling counters of setuid apps doesn't threaten
anybody's privacy - only the user started the setuid program may read the
counters.

Signed-off-by: Vasiliy Kulikov <segoon@openwall.com>
Cc: Alexey Dobriyan <adobriyan@gmail.com>

Cc: James Morris <jmorris@namei.org>
Cc: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: Hugh Dickins <hughd@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct pid_namespace *pid = dentry->d_sb->s_fs_info;', '\t\tif (!has_pid_permissions(pid, task, 2)) {', '\t\t\trcu_read_unlock();', '\t\t\t/*', "\t\t\t * This doesn't prevent learning whether PID exists,", '\t\t\t * it only makes getattr() consistent with readdir().', '\t\t\t */', '\t\t\treturn -ENOENT;', '\t\t}']}
description: fs/proc/base.c in the Linux kernel through 3.1 allows local users to obtain sensitive keystroke information via access to /proc/interrupts.

code_evidence: pid_getattr fills stat->uid/gid with the target task's euid/egid whenever the inode mode matches S_IFDIR|S_IRUGO|S_IXUGO or task_dumpable() is true; there is no caller-credential check against the task owner before exposing these attributes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is explicit disclosure of sensitive process metadata to unauthorized local actors, matching CWE-200's scope of confidentiality exposure through intentional information management. It is not a memory-safety flaw; the defect is missing authorization on attribute disclosure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pid_getattr discloses process ownership metadata (euid/egid) derived from __task_cred without verifying that the requesting user is the task owner or otherwise authorized. Trigger: any local user performing stat() on /proc/<pid>/ for another user's process. Consequence: exposure of another process's effective uid/gid, aiding information gathering about privileged daemons or sensitive programs.

commit_msg:
nbd/server: get rid of nbd_negotiate_read and friends

Functions nbd_negotiate_{read,write,drop_sync} were introduced in
1a6245a5b, when nbd_rwv (was nbd_wr_sync) was working through
qemu_co_sendv_recvv (the path is nbd_wr_sync -> qemu_co_{recv/send} ->

watchers are redundant in nbd_negotiate_{read,write,drop_sync}, then,

this patch. This will be fixed later.

commit_msg:
A recent fix addressing a deadlock on disconnect introduced a new bug
by moving the present flag out of the critical section protected by the
driver-data mutex. This could lead to a racing release() freeing the
driver data before disconnect() is done with it.

Due to insufficient locking a related use-after-free could be triggered
also before the above mentioned commit. Specifically, the driver needs
to hold the driver-data mutex also while checking the opened flag at
disconnect().

Fixes: c468a8aa790e ("usb: iowarrior: fix deadlock on disconnect")
Fixes: 946b960d13c1 ("USB: add driver for iowarrior devices.")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>	# 2.6.21
Reported-by: syzbot+0761012cebf7bdb38137@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20191009104846.5925-2-johan@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* prevent device read, write and ioctl */', '\tdev->present = 0;', '', '\tmutex_unlock(&dev->mutex);'], 'added_lines': ['\tdev->present = 0;', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&dev->mutex);', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&dev->mutex);']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.3.7, there is a use-after-free bug that can be caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/usb/misc/iowarrior.c driver, aka CID-edc4746f253d.

code_evidence: In this version the present flag is cleared at line 8 while only iowarrior_open_disc_lock is held; dev->mutex is not held, so a concurrent release() is not serialized against this write and can observe/act on present independently.

After usb_deregister_dev, the code locks dev->mutex at line 12 but immediately unlocks at line 13, then reads dev->opened at line 14 outside the lock; the else branch at lines 18-19 calls iowarrior_delete(dev) without holding dev->mutex, so a racing release() can free dev while disconnect still uses it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing locking permits iowarrior_delete() to free dev before disconnect() finishes referencing it, so subsequent accesses use freed memory, directly matching CWE-416. The defect is the unsynchronized lifetime check/free, not merely a data race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: disconnect() checks dev->opened and frees the driver data without holding dev->mutex, and clears present outside the mutex, so it is not serialized against release(). Trigger: a malicious USB device disconnect racing with a process closing its file descriptor makes release() free dev while disconnect() continues to dereference it. Consequence: use-after-free of the iowarrior structure, enabling memory corruption or crash.

description: The Fiddle::Handle implementation in ext/fiddle/handle.c in Ruby before 2.0.0-p648, 2.1 before 2.1.8, and 2.2 before 2.2.4, as distributed in Apple OS X before 10.11.4 and other products, mishandles tainting, which allows context-dependent attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted string, related to the DL module and the libffi library. commit_msg:
When trying to mount a file system which does not contain a journal,
but which does have a orphan list containing an inode which needs to
be truncated, the mount call with hang forever in
ext4_orphan_cleanup() because ext4_orphan_del() will return
immediately without removing the inode from the orphan list, leading
to an uninterruptible loop in kernel code which will busy out one of
the CPU's on the system.

This can be trivially reproduced by trying to mount the file system
found in tests/f_orphan_extents_inode/image.gz from the e2fsprogs
source tree.  If a malicious user were to put this on a USB stick, and
mount it on a Linux desktop which has automatic mounts enabled, this
could be considered a potential denial of service attack.  (Not a big
deal in practice, but professional paranoids worry about such things,
and have even been known to allocate CVE numbers for such problems.)

Signed-off-by: "Theodore Ts'o" <tytso@mit.edu>
Reviewed-by: Zheng Liu <wenqing.lz@taobao.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!EXT4_SB(inode->i_sb)->s_journal)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif ((!EXT4_SB(inode->i_sb)->s_journal) &&', '\t    !(EXT4_SB(inode->i_sb)->s_mount_state & EXT4_ORPHAN_FS))']}
description: fs/ext4/namei.c in the Linux kernel before 3.7 allows physically proximate attackers to cause a denial of service (system crash) via a crafted no-journal filesystem, a related issue to CVE-2013-2015.

code_evidence: When the superblock has no journal, ext4_orphan_del returns 0 immediately without taking s_orphan_lock or removing the inode from ei->i_orphan.
Because the call returns success without clearing the orphan list entry, the caller's cleanup loop cannot make progress; the list_del_init and NEXT_ORPHAN reset at lines 18 and 46 are never reached.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to release/clear the orphan-list resource, producing an unbounded loop that consumes CPU. This is improper management of a system resource leading to denial of service, matching the CWE-399 resource-management category; the defect is the missing state check, not memory corruption.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!EXT4_SB(inode->i_sb)->s_journal)
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the no-journal early return skips orphan-list removal even when a mounted filesystem carries an orphan list (EXT4_ORPHAN_FS state). Trigger: mounting a crafted no-journal image with an orphan inode needing truncation. Consequence: ext4_orphan_cleanup loops indefinitely, busy-waiting a CPU (denial of service).

commit_msg:
demux: mp4: fix buffer overflow in parsing of string boxes.

We ensure that pbox->i_size is never smaller than 8 to avoid an
integer underflow in the third argument of the subsequent call to
memcpy. We also make sure no truncation occurs when passing values
derived from the 64 bit integer p_box->i_size to arguments of malloc
and memcpy that may be 32 bit integers on 32 bit platforms.

Signed-off-by: Jean-Baptiste Kempf <jb@videolan.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if( p_box->i_size < 8 || p_box->i_size > SIZE_MAX )', '        MP4_READBOX_EXIT( 0 );']}
description: Integer underflow in the MP4_ReadBox_String function in modules/demux/mp4/libmp4.c in VideoLAN VLC media player before 2.1.6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via a box size less than 7.

code_evidence: Line 4 computes the malloc size as p_box->i_size + 1 - 8, and lines 7-8 use p_box->i_size - 8 as a memcpy length and array index. p_box->i_size derives from the box header and is attacker-controlled; when it is less than 8, these unsigned expressions underflow to a huge value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The underflow arises from implicit conversion of the box size into unsigned arithmetic used as allocation/copy sizes, an incorrect type/size interpretation. This fits CWE-704; CWE-191 describes the underflow symptom but the target class is the conversion weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the box size is used in unsigned arithmetic without checking that it is at least 8, so the subtraction underflows. Trigger: a crafted MP4 box with size < 8. Consequence: oversized allocation/copy length and out-of-bounds write, causing denial of service or possible code execution.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

Reviewed-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Fam Zheng <famz@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Daniel P. Berrange <berrange@redhat.com>
Message-id: 20170213135235.12274-8-pbonzini@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    nbd_coroutine_end(client, &request);'], 'added_lines': ['    nbd_coroutine_end(bs, &request);']}
description: An assertion-failure flaw was found in Qemu before 2.10.1, in the Network Block Device (NBD) server's initial connection negotiation, where the I/O coroutine was undefined. This could crash the qemu-nbd server if a client sent unexpected data during connection negotiation. A remote user or process could use this flaw to crash the qemu-nbd server resulting in denial of service.

code_evidence: Lines 15-17: if the caller passes BDRV_REQ_FUA, the function asserts that the negotiated NBD flags include NBD_FLAG_SEND_FUA; otherwise the process aborts.

Lines 22-29: the request is started with nbd_coroutine_start, sent and replied to, but the function does not verify that the server negotiated write-zeroes support beyond the flag check at line 12; the coroutine state is only cleaned up at line 29.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because an attacker-influenced negotiation value controls a reachable assert() that terminates the process rather than returning an error, which is an availability-only impact. A missing-validation weakness would be relevant only if the assertion were removed, but the abort behavior itself is the supported weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the assert at line 16 depends on client->nbdflags, which is set during connection negotiation with the remote NBD server. Trigger: a server that does not advertise NBD_FLAG_SEND_FUA, combined with a caller request carrying BDRV_REQ_FUA, reaches the assert and aborts the process. Consequence: the qemu-nbd process exits, causing denial of service for all connections handled by that process.

commit_msg:
decompile: introduce new method Offset

The getString method in decompile.c is vulnerable to a buffer
overflow which can be triggered using a crafted SWF file.

This vulnerability is the consequence of unchecked accesses to the
actions array when getting the offset of SWF_ACTIONRECORD objects.

This pattern is present a bit everywhere in the source code, leading
to a large number of potential flaws similar to this one. In this
commit we introduce a new Offset method similar to the OpCode method
which handles bound checking when retrieving the offset of
SWF_ACTIONRECORD objects.

This commit also modifies getString to use this newly introduced
method and address the previously explained bug.

Usage of the newly introduced Offset method will be generalized in a
future commit.

Please, note that this commit won't be sufficient to fix #144
(CVE-2018-11226) since another issue is triggered by the same sample.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (actions[i+1].SWF_ACTIONRECORD.Offset==off1end)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (Offset(actions, i+1, maxn) == off1end)']}
description: The getString function in decompile.c in libming through 0.4.8 mishandles cases where the header indicates a file size greater than the actual size, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (Segmentation fault and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: The loop iterates i from 0 while i < n_firstactions (initialized to maxn), then indexes actions[i+1] and actions[i] without any upper-bound check against maxn. When i reaches n_firstactions-1 == maxn-1, actions[i+1] reads actions[maxn], one element past the allocated actions array. OpCode(actions, i, maxn) is called on the same potentially out-of-range index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory at actions[i+1] outside the intended actions buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory access. The specific descendant is an off-by-one out-of-bounds read, but the supplied target is CWE-119, which this directly supports.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound n_firstactions=maxn allows i+1 to equal maxn, so the SWF_ACTIONRECORD.Offset read at actions[i+1] and the OpCode access at actions[i] reach beyond the buffer. Trigger: a crafted SWF whose action list makes the loop run to its last iteration. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of adjacent memory, leading to a segfault/DoS or unintended control decisions from attacker-influenced data.

commit_msg:
The dvb-core tries to sync the releases of opened files at
dvb_dmxdev_release() with two refcounts: dvbdev->users and
dvr_dvbdev->users.  A problem is present in those two syncs: when yet
another dvb_demux_open() is called during those sync waits,
dvb_demux_open() continues to process even if the device is being
closed.  This includes the increment of the former refcount, resulting
in the leftover refcount after the sync of the latter refcount at
dvb_dmxdev_release().  It ends up with use-after-free, since the
function believes that all usages were gone and releases the
resources.

This patch addresses the problem by adding the check of dmxdev->exit
flag at dvb_demux_open(), just like dvb_dvr_open() already does.  With
the exit flag check, the second call of dvb_demux_open() fails, hence
the further corruption can be avoided.

Also for avoiding the races of the dmxdev->exit flag reference, this
patch serializes the dmxdev->exit set up and the sync waits with the
dmxdev->mutex lock at dvb_dmxdev_release().  Without the mutex lock,
dvb_demux_open() (or dvb_dvr_open()) may run concurrently with
dvb_dmxdev_release(), which allows to skip the exit flag check and
continue the open process that is being closed.

CVE-2022-41218 is assigned to those bugs above.

Reported-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/20220908132754.30532-1-tiwai@suse.de
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (dmxdev->exit) {', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&dmxdev->mutex);', '\t\treturn -ENODEV;', '\t}']}
description: In drivers/media/dvb-core/dmxdev.c in the Linux kernel through 5.19.10, there is a use-after-free caused by refcount races, affecting dvb_demux_open and dvb_dmxdev_release.

code_evidence: The function locks dmxdev->mutex but, in the pre-patch version, proceeds directly to allocate a filter without checking whether dmxdev is being torn down.
It scans for a free filter, initializes it, stores it in file->private_data, and increments dvbdev->users before unlocking.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing exit-flag check under the mutex permits the open path to outlive the release and reference freed dmxdev/filter resources, which is CWE-416. This is a lifetime/race issue, not a mere missing lock (CWE-362), since the supported consequence is use of freed memory.

evidence_lines.code:
if (mutex_lock_interruptible(&dmxdev->mutex))
return -ERESTARTSYS;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: dvb_demux_open can run concurrently with dvb_dmxdev_release's teardown because it never re-checks dmxdev->exit after acquiring the mutex. The open then allocates a filter and increments dvbdev->users on a device already being released, leaving a stale reference so the release frees shared resources while the newly opened file still uses them, yielding use-after-free.

commit_msg:
The length value is interpreted as signed char on many systems
(depending on default signedness of char), which can lead to an out of
boundary write up to 128 bytes in front of the allocated storage, but
limited to NUL byte(s).

Casting the length value to unsigned char fixes the problem and allows
string values with up to 255 characters.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    length = *ch;', '\t\t    length = *ch;'], 'added_lines': ['\t    length = *(unsigned char *)ch;', '\t\t    length = *(unsigned char *)ch;']}
description: An issue was discovered in libX11 through 1.6.5. The function XListExtensions in ListExt.c interprets a variable as signed instead of unsigned, resulting in an out-of-bounds write (of up to 128 bytes), leading to DoS or remote code execution.

code_evidence: length is declared int and loaded from *ch, a plain char; on signed-char platforms a byte >=0x80 yields a negative length.
The bounds check ch + length < chend uses that negative value, and ch += length + 1 moves ch backwards, before the buffer start; *ch = '\0' then writes one NUL byte before the allocation.

Trigger: a length byte >=0x80 makes length negative, so the check passes while ch is decremented below the allocation start; the subsequent NUL store writes out of bounds. commit_msg:
Fixed arrays expansion.

There were two problems with njs_array_expand():

 1. It checked that the requred size with the appended elements wasn't bigger
    then the array size and then did nothing.  If there were elements removed
    from the beggining (by shift() operation), then "size <= array->size" can
    be true even if there wasn't enought free space after the array.

 2. After allocating more space to prepend elements, it set array->size without
    counting those elements.

Probably, the original idea was to decrement array->size while removing
elements from the beginning, but it wasn't done right.  Even if so, the
new version of the function looks cleaner.

This closes #152 and closes #153 issues on Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    size = (uint64_t) append + array->length;', '    if (nxt_fast_path(size <= array->size && prepend == 0)) {', '    if (nxt_slow_path((prepend + size) > NJS_ARRAY_MAX_LENGTH)) {', '                         (prepend + size) * sizeof(njs_value_t));'], 'added_lines': ['    uint32_t     free_before, free_after;', '    free_before = array->start - array->data;', '    free_after = array->size - array->length - free_before;', '    if (nxt_fast_path(free_before >= prepend && free_after >= append)) {', '', '    size = (uint64_t) prepend + array->length + append;', '    if (nxt_slow_path(size > NJS_ARRAY_MAX_LENGTH)) {', '                         size * sizeof(njs_value_t));']}
description: njs through 0.3.1, used in NGINX, has a heap-based buffer overflow in Array.prototype.splice after a resize, related to njs_array_prototype_splice in njs/njs_array.c, because of njs_array_expand size mishandling.

code_evidence: The fast path returns NXT_OK when size (append + length) <= array->size and prepend == 0; it ignores free space shifted by prior shift() operations, so insufficient tail capacity can pass the check.

After allocation, array->size = size is set without accounting for prepend, while start is advanced by prepend and memcpy copies array->length elements into start; the recorded size then understates the region actually used.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes buffer capacity and placement for array data; its incorrect size check and size assignment permit writes beyond the allocated region, directly matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write rather than a mere integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the capacity check compares requested length against array->size without accounting for elements removed from the beginning, and the new size omits the prepended count. Trigger: splice/shift sequences shrink the logical start so the fast path or size bookkeeping approves a buffer with insufficient tail space. Consequence: subsequent element writes go past the allocated buffer, a heap out-of-bounds write.

description: The NetKVM Windows Virtio driver allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (guest crash) via a crafted length value in an IP packet, as demonstrated by a value that does not account for the size of the IP options.

code_evidence: QueryL4HeaderOffset passes GetDataLength() as the packet length to ParaNdis_ReviewIPPacket along with a pointer offset by IpHeaderOffset; the diff adds a FALSE flag (read-only) but leaves the length unvalidated.

The returned ppr.ipHeaderSize is added to IpHeaderOffset and cast to USHORT to form the L4 offset, with no check that the reported header size (including IP options) fits within the supplied data length.

This is improper validation of input properties (CWE-20), not a transformation/filtering error; the unsupported consequence is the out-of-bounds read/crash.

GetDataLength(), __FUNCTION__);

if (ppr.ipStatus != ppresNotIP)
Res = static_cast<USHORT>(IpHeaderOffset + ppr.ipHeaderSize);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller supplies the packet length but the review does not ensure it accounts for the IP header size including options. Trigger: a crafted IP packet whose length value is too small for the declared IP options. Consequence: the computed L4 header offset exceeds the actual buffer, leading to out-of-bounds access and a guest crash (DoS).
