description: epan/dissectors/packet-wbxml.c in the WBXML dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.12 mishandles offsets, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (integer overflow and infinite loop) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: off is initialized from offset and the loop reads tvb_get_guint8(tvb, off) while off < tvb_len, so bounds depend on off advancing correctly.
tvb_get_guintvar returns len used in off += 1+len; a large len can wrap the guint32 off past tvb_len.
LITERAL case: idx from tvb_get_guintvar, then tvb_strsize(tvb, str_tbl+idx) and tvb_format_text with str_tbl+idx, str_len-1; str_tbl+idx can exceed buffer.
EXT_T case passes idx and str_tbl to extension callbacks and uses 1+len for off, same overflow exposure.
STR_T case computes tvb_strsize(tvb, str_tbl+idx) and formats str_tbl+idx, str_len-1, reading outside the tvb buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs buffer reads at str_tbl+idx and at wrapped off values without restricting them to the intended tvb boundary, reading memory outside the buffer. The specific impact is out-of-bounds read rather than a write; the arithmetic wrap is the mechanism enabling the out-of-bounds access.

off += 1+len;

idx = tvb_get_guintvar (tvb, off+1, &len);
off += 1+len;

idx = tvb_get_guintvar (tvb, off+1, &len);
off += 1+len;

commit_msg:
v2: FontNames.c  return a NULL list whenever a single
length field from the server is incohent.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (rep.length < (INT_MAX >> 2)) {', '\t\tlength = *(unsigned char *)ch;', "\t\t*ch = '\\0';  /* and replace with null-termination */", '\t\tcount++;', '\t    } else', '\t\tflist[i] = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (rep.length > 0 && rep.length < (INT_MAX >> 2)) {', '\t\tif (ch <= chend) {', '\t\t    length = *(unsigned char *)ch;', "\t\t    *ch = '\\0';  /* and replace with null-termination */", '\t\t    count++;', '\t\t} else {', '                    Xfree(flist);', '                    flist = NULL;', '                    count = 0;', '                    break;', '\t\t}', '\t    } else {', '                Xfree(flist);', '                flist = NULL;', '                count = 0;', '                break;', '            }']}
description: The XListFonts function in X.org libX11 before 1.6.4 might allow remote X servers to gain privileges via vectors involving length fields, which trigger out-of-bounds write operations.

code_evidence: rep.length comes from the server reply; the guard only checks an upper bound, so a zero/negative length leaves rlen=0 and ch unallocated or the buffer too small relative to chend computed as ch + (rlen + 1).
After _XReadPad fills ch, chend is set to ch + (rlen + 1) and the first length byte is read and overwritten at ch without verifying the buffer actually holds data.

The loop trusts the per-name length byte: it checks ch + length < chend, then advances ch by length+1 and unconditionally reads and writes *ch = '\0' at the new position, which can point at or past chend when the server-supplied length is inconsistent with the reply size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a memory write through a pointer derived from unchecked server lengths, landing outside the allocated buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the null-termination store modifies memory beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: server-controlled rep.length and per-name length fields are used to compute buffer bounds and pointer advances without validating that ch stays within the allocated rlen+1 region. Trigger: a malicious X server returns a reply whose length or name-length bytes are inconsistent. Consequence: the write *ch = '\0' (and the read on the following line) occurs past the end of the allocated buffer, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg:
ASAN SFTP Fixes
When decoding SFTP messages, fix the size checks so they don't wrap. (ZD12766)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (sz + idx > maxSz) {', '    if (sz + idx > maxSz) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (sz > maxSz - idx) {', '    if (sz > maxSz - idx) {']}
description: WolfSSH v1.4.7 was discovered to contain an integer overflow via the function wolfSSH_SFTP_RecvRMDIR.

code_evidence: A 32-bit size sz is read from the request and idx is advanced by UINT32_SZ; the bound check computes sz + idx, which can wrap before comparison with maxSz, letting an oversized sz pass validation.
The accepted sz is used to allocate sz + 1 and copy sz bytes from data + idx; a wrapped/oversized value leads to undersized allocation or out-of-bounds copy.
The second filename repeats the same pattern: ato32 reads sz, idx advances, and sz + idx > maxSz can wrap, bypassing the length check.
The second allocation WMALLOC(sz + 1) and WMEMCPY(nw, data + idx, sz) consume the unchecked sz, enabling memory corruption or crash.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an addition on a 32-bit size derived from untrusted input and assumes the sum will not wrap before validating it against maxSz. That integer overflow directly defeats the bounds check, matching CWE-190 rather than a pure out-of-bounds read/write, because the wrap in the size computation is the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
old = (char*)WMALLOC(sz + 1, ssh->ctx->heap, DYNTYPE_BUFFER);
WMEMCPY(old, data + idx, sz); idx += sz;

nw = (char*)WMALLOC(sz + 1, ssh->ctx->heap, DYNTYPE_BUFFER);
WMEMCPY(nw, data + idx, sz);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the validation expression sz + idx is computed in word32 and can wrap when sz is near UINT32_MAX, so the comparison fails to reject an out-of-range length. Trigger: an attacker sends an SFTP rename request with a crafted 32-bit filename length. Consequence: the check is bypassed, an incorrect allocation size may result, and WMEMCPY copies attacker-influenced length, causing memory corruption or denial of service.

commit_msg:
The X protocol uses CARD16 values to represent the length so
this would overflow.

CVE-2021-31535

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\tn = (int) strlen (spec);'], 'added_lines': ['\tn = (int) strlen (spec);', '\tif (n >= USHRT_MAX)', '            return 0;']}
description: LookupCol.c in X.Org X through X11R7.7 and libX11 before 1.7.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The libX11 XLookupColor request (intended for server-side color lookup) contains a flaw allowing a client to send color-name requests with a name longer than the maximum size allowed by the protocol (and also longer than the maximum packet size for normal-sized packets). The user-controlled data exceeding the maximum size is then interpreted by the server as additional X protocol requests and executed, e.g., to disable X server authorization completely. For example, if the victim encounters malicious terminal control sequences for color codes, then the attacker may be able to take full control of the running graphical session.

code_evidence: Line 31 computes n as the strlen of the user-controlled spec without any length check before use. Line 35 stores n into req->nbytes, and line 36 adds (n+3)>>2 to req->length, which is a CARD16 protocol field. Line 37 then copies n bytes of spec into the request via Data, so an oversized name is transmitted and the length field wraps.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because Data copies the input buffer (spec) into the request buffer without checking the input size against the destination's size constraints, producing an out-of-bounds-style overwrite of adjacent protocol data. The missing length check on line 31 is the root cause; the consequence is protocol-request injection, not merely a read overrun (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function copies the input string into the X protocol request without verifying that its length fits the protocol's 16-bit length representation. A spec longer than USHRT_MAX causes req->length to overflow; the server then interprets the excess copied data as additional protocol requests, enabling arbitrary request injection in the victim's session.

description: The Broadcom brcmfmac WiFi driver prior to commit a4176ec356c73a46c07c181c6d04039fafa34a9f is vulnerable to a frame validation bypass. If the brcmfmac driver receives a firmware event frame from a remote source, the is_wlc_event_frame function will cause this frame to be discarded and unprocessed. If the driver receives the firmware event frame from the host, the appropriate handler is called. This frame validation can be bypassed if the bus used is USB (for instance by a wifi dongle). This can allow firmware event frames from a remote source to be processed. In the worst case scenario, by sending specially-crafted WiFi packets, a remote, unauthenticated attacker may be able to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable system. More typically, this vulnerability will result in denial-of-service conditions.

code_evidence: The function casts skb_mac_header to struct brcmf_event and checks only the BRCM OUI via memcmp; no check constrains the event subtype to a firmware-event value.

After the OUI check the function reads usr_subtype and compares it to BCMILCP_BCM_SUBTYPE_EVENT; frames with other subtypes fall through and are dispatched to brcmf_fweh_process_event without verifying the frame's origin or event subtype.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of the event subtype metadata before dispatching input to the event handler, matching CWE-20 improper input validation. It is not a mere OUI/format filter bypass; the required subtype constraint is absent, so unsafe data reaches processing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates only the OUI and usr_subtype, not the actual event subtype, so on USB buses a mock event frame from a remote source can pass validation. Trigger: an attacker sends a crafted link-control frame with the expected OUI/subtype. Consequence: the remote frame is processed as a firmware event, potentially enabling DoS or arbitrary code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix protocol parsing on 'ldbReplParseCommand' (CVE-2021-32672)

The protocol parsing on 'ldbReplParseCommand' (LUA debugging)
Assumed protocol correctness. This means that if the following
is given:
*1
$100
test
The parser will try to read additional 94 unallocated bytes after
the client buffer.
This commit fixes this issue by validating that there are actually enough
bytes to read. It also limits the amount of data that can be sent by
the debugger client to 1M so the client will not be able to explode
the memory.

When using the Redis Lua Debugger, users can send malformed requests that cause the debugger’s protocol parser to read data beyond the actual buffer. This issue affects all versions of Redis with Lua debugging support (3.2 or newer). The problem is fixed in versions 6.2.6, 6.0.16 and 5.0.14.

commit_msg:
Don't follow symlinks on file creation (CVE-2017-7501)

Open newly created files with O_EXCL to prevent symlink tricks.
When reopening hardlinks for writing the actual content, use append
mode instead. This is compatible with the write-only permissions but
is not destructive in case we got redirected to somebody elses file,
verify the target before actually writing anything.

As these are files with the temporary suffix, errors mean a local
user with sufficient privileges to break the installation of the package
anyway is trying to goof us on purpose, don't bother trying to mend it
(we couldn't fix the hardlink case anyhow) but just bail out.

Based on a patch by Florian Festi.

An attacker with ability to write in a directory where files will be installed could create symbolic links to an arbitrary location and modify content, and possibly permissions to arbitrary files, which could be used for denial of service or possibly privilege escalation.

For a single-link file, expandRegular is invoked again with the default (non-exclusive) creation behavior, so a pre-existing symlink at dest would be followed.
For a hardlinked file with content, expandRegular is called with the same non-exclusive behavior, allowing a symlink planted at the predictable dest path to redirect the write.

Trigger: an attacker with write access to the install directory pre-creates a symlink at dest. Consequence: content and possibly permissions are written to an unintended file, enabling modification of arbitrary files (DoS or privilege escalation).

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow (CVE-2021-21309). (#8522)

On 32-bit systems, setting the proto-max-bulk-len config parameter to a high value may result with integer overflow and a subsequent heap overflow when parsing an input bulk (CVE-2021-21309).

This fix has two parts:

Set a reasonable limit to the config parameter.
Add additional checks to prevent the problem in other potential but unknown code paths.

description: Redis is an open-source, in-memory database that persists on disk. In affected versions of Redis an integer overflow bug in 32-bit Redis version 4.0 or newer could be exploited to corrupt the heap and potentially result with remote code execution. Redis 4.0 or newer uses a configurable limit for the maximum supported bulk input size. By default, it is 512MB which is a safe value for all platforms. If the limit is significantly increased, receiving a large request from a client may trigger several integer overflow scenarios, which would result with buffer overflow and heap corruption. We believe this could in certain conditions be exploited for remote code execution. By default, authenticated Redis users have access to all configuration parameters and can therefore use the “CONFIG SET proto-max-bulk-len” to change the safe default, making the system vulnerable. **This problem only affects 32-bit Redis (on a 32-bit system, or as a 32-bit executable running on a 64-bit system).** The problem is fixed in version 6.2, and the fix is back ported to 6.0.11 and 5.0.11. Make sure you use one of these versions if you are running 32-bit Redis. An additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent clients from directly executing `CONFIG SET`: Using Redis 6.0 or newer, ACL configuration can be used to block the command. Using older versions, the `rename-command` configuration directive can be used to rename the command to a random string unknown to users, rendering it inaccessible. Please note that this workaround may have an additional impact on users or operational systems that expect `CONFIG SET` to behave in certain ways.

code_evidence: mallocx is called with size+PREFIX_SIZE, an addition of a caller-controlled size_t. If size is near SIZE_MAX, PREFIX_SIZE addition wraps to a small value, so a small allocation is returned for a much larger requested size while callers treat the pointer as holding size bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the function performs an arithmetic size computation that can wrap before being used for memory allocation. The patch's ASSERT_NO_SIZE_OVERFLOW(size) confirms the missing constraint; this is integer overflow feeding a buffer overflow (CWE-122), not merely a generic out-of-bounds write.

evidence_lines.code: void *ptr = mallocx(size+PREFIX_SIZE, MALLOCX_TCACHE_NONE);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unchecked addition size+PREFIX_SIZE in the allocation size calculation. Trigger: a large size value (e.g., from bulk length parsing) close to the size_t maximum. Consequence: wraparound yields an undersized heap allocation, and subsequent writes based on the intended size corrupt the heap, supporting memory corruption and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Prevent array write out-of-bounds.

If user passes an invalid axis, then we copy one too many dimensions to the output in the loop below these checks. Even if we didn't do that, there will be further issues with an invalid axis, so we check for that right now.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 371023299
Change-Id: I9eca37ffc2b29e8e48710f500701270ef0790224
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, axis_value >= 0);', '  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, axis_value < NumDimensions(input));', '']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. A specially crafted TFLite model could trigger an OOB write on heap in the TFLite implementation of `ArgMin`/`ArgMax`(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/102b211d892f3abc14f845a72047809b39cc65ab/tensorflow/lite/kernels/arg_min_max.cc#L52-L59). If `axis_value` is not a value between 0 and `NumDimensions(input)`, then the condition in the `if` is never true, so code writes past the last valid element of `output_dims->data`. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: axis_value is read from the axis tensor and only adjusted when negative; no check enforces it lies within [0, NumDimensions(input)).

output_dims is allocated with NumDimensions(input)-1 slots, but the loop writes output_dims->data[j] for every dimension i where i != axis_value; an out-of-range axis_value makes the condition always true, so j reaches NumDimensions(input) and writes one element past the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes one element beyond an allocated buffer's intended bound, matching CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. It is a write past the end, not merely an out-of-bounds read, so CWE-787 fits rather than CWE-125.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing bounds validation on the user-controlled axis_value after negative-index normalization. Trigger: a crafted model supplies axis outside [0, NumDimensions(input)). Consequence: the copy loop writes past the end of the heap-allocated output_dims->data buffer (OOB write).

commit_msg:
prefer memcpy to strcpy

When we already know the length of a string (e.g., because
we just malloc'd to fit it), it's nicer to use memcpy than
strcpy, as it makes it more obvious that we are not going to
overflow the buffer (because the size we pass matches the
size in the allocation).

This also eliminates calls to strcpy, which make auditing
the code base harder.

Signed-off-by: Jeff King <peff@peff.net>
Signed-off-by: Junio C Hamano <gitster@pobox.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstrcpy(m, name);'], 'added_lines': ['\tmemcpy(m, name, nlen + 1);']}
description: revision.c in git before 2.7.4 uses an incorrect integer data type, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a (1) long filename or (2) many nested trees, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: nlen and len are computed as int from strlen(name), so the total buffer size calculation uses a signed integer type.
The loop accumulates elem_len into len without checking for integer overflow; a long name or many nested trees can wrap len.
xmalloc(len) allocates using the possibly wrapped len, then m is positioned at n + len - (nlen + 1).
strcpy(m, name) then copies the full name without a bound, and the following loop writes p->elem_len bytes plus a '/' into m.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function writes beyond the intended heap buffer boundary due to the flawed size computation. It is the class-level buffer-bounds weakness; the integer overflow is the underlying trigger rather than a separate mapped label.

evidence_lines.code:
int nlen = strlen(name);
int len = nlen + 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the signed int size arithmetic (len/nlen) that can overflow when accumulating long filenames or many nested trees. The wrapped value sizes the heap allocation, but strcpy and the subsequent memcpy writes use the true string lengths, so writes land outside the allocated buffer, giving a heap-based buffer overflow that can lead to code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix EC_GROUP_new_from_ecparameters to check the base length

Check that there's at least one byte in params->base before trying to
read it.

CVE-2021-3712

Reviewed-by: Viktor Dukhovni <viktor@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!params->order || !params->base || !params->base->data) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (params->order == NULL', '            || params->base == NULL', '            || params->base->data == NULL', '            || params->base->length == 0) {']}
description: ASN.1 strings are represented internally within OpenSSL as an ASN1_STRING structure which contains a buffer holding the string data and a field holding the buffer length. This contrasts with normal C strings which are repesented as a buffer for the string data which is terminated with a NUL (0) byte. Although not a strict requirement, ASN.1 strings that are parsed using OpenSSL's own "d2i" functions (and other similar parsing functions) as well as any string whose value has been set with the ASN1_STRING_set() function will additionally NUL terminate the byte array in the ASN1_STRING structure. However, it is possible for applications to directly construct valid ASN1_STRING structures which do not NUL terminate the byte array by directly setting the "data" and "length" fields in the ASN1_STRING array. This can also happen by using the ASN1_STRING_set0() function. Numerous OpenSSL functions that print ASN.1 data have been found to assume that the ASN1_STRING byte array will be NUL terminated, even though this is not guaranteed for strings that have been directly constructed. Where an application requests an ASN.1 structure to be printed, and where that ASN.1 structure contains ASN1_STRINGs that have been directly constructed by the application without NUL terminating the "data" field, then a read buffer overrun can occur. The same thing can also occur during name constraints processing of certificates (for example if a certificate has been directly constructed by the application instead of loading it via the OpenSSL parsing functions, and the certificate contains non NUL terminated ASN1_STRING structures). It can also occur in the X509_get1_email(), X509_REQ_get1_email() and X509_get1_ocsp() functions. If a malicious actor can cause an application to directly construct an ASN1_STRING and then process it through one of the affected OpenSSL functions then this issue could be hit. This might result in a crash (causing a Denial of Service attack). It could also result in the disclosure of private memory contents (such as private keys, or sensitive plaintext). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1l (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1k). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.0.2za (Affected 1.0.2-1.0.2y).

code_evidence: Before the fix, the guard only verifies params->base and params->base->data are non-NULL, but does not check params->base->length is nonzero.
Line 149 reads params->base->data[0] to set the point conversion form without any length check, assuming at least one byte exists.
Line 150-151 then passes params->base->data and params->base->length to EC_POINT_oct2point, which also processes the base buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads params->base->data[0] without confirming the buffer has at least one byte, i.e., an out-of-bounds read past the intended buffer. This is a read overrun rather than a NULL-pointer dereference, since the pointer check alone does not constrain the length.

evidence_lines.code:
EC_GROUP_set_point_conversion_form(ret, (point_conversion_form_t)
(params->base->data[0] & ~0x01));

if (!EC_POINT_oct2point(ret, point, params->base->data,
params->base->length, NULL)) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is a missing lower-bound length constraint: params->base->data is validated for non-NULL but a zero-length ASN1_STRING buffer is accepted. When such a params structure is supplied, line 149 dereferences data[0] on an empty buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read. The trigger is an EC parameters structure whose base has length 0; the supported consequence is reading before/at the end of the intended buffer, potentially a crash or memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
Bug 699661: Avoid sharing pointers between pdf14 compositors

If a copdevice is triggered when the pdf14 compositor is the device, we make
a copy of the device, then throw an error because, by default we're only allowed
to copy the device prototype - then freeing it calls the finalize, which frees
several pointers shared with the parent.

Make a pdf14 specific finish_copydevice() which NULLs the relevant pointers,
before, possibly, throwing the same error as the default method.

This also highlighted a problem with reopening the X11 devices, where a custom
error handler could be replaced with itself, meaning it also called itself,
and infifite recursion resulted.

Keep a note of if the handler replacement has been done, and don't do it a
second time.

commit_msg:
Make --nofilesystem=host/home remove access to subdirs of those

Previously --nofilesystem=host only removed specifically access to the
`host` permissions, and not necessarily other filesystems (like `home`
or `/some/path`). This isn't very useful to limit access because you
don't know what other filesystems the app may have access too.

We change this to mean that `--nofilesystem=host` removes *all* filesystem
access from the parent layer, and `--nofilesystem=home` removes all
file access to the homedir and paths inside it.

The available layers are, in order:

 * app permissions
 * overrides
 * commandline args

This allows you to start from scratch with the filesystem permissions
in the overrides or the commandline. This is a small change in
behaviour, but not a lot of things use --nofilesystem, and the ones
that do probably expects this behaviour.

description: Flatpak is a Linux application sandboxing and distribution framework. A path traversal vulnerability affects versions of Flatpak prior to 1.12.3 and 1.10.6. flatpak-builder applies `finish-args` last in the build. At this point the build directory will have the full access that is specified in the manifest, so running `flatpak build` against it will gain those permissions. Normally this will not be done, so this is not problem. However, if `--mirror-screenshots-url` is specified, then flatpak-builder will launch `flatpak build --nofilesystem=host appstream-utils mirror-screenshots` after finalization, which can lead to issues even with the `--nofilesystem=host` protection. However, a malicious application could replace the `appstream-util` binary and potentially do something more hostile. This has been resolved in Flatpak 1.12.3 and 1.10.6 by changing the behaviour of `--nofilesystem=home` and `--nofilesystem=host`.

description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's netfilter: nf_tables component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

On an error when building a nftables rule, deactivating immediate expressions in nft_immediate_deactivate() can lead unbinding the chain and objects be deactivated but later used.

We recommend upgrading past commit 0a771f7b266b02d262900c75f1e175c7fe76fec2.

code_evidence: The chain referenced by the verdict is taken from data->verdict.chain and only processed when nft_chain_binding(chain) is true.
The bound chain's rules are walked and their expressions deactivated using a chain_ctx pointing at that chain.
On NFT_TRANS_PREPARE_ERROR the chain is unbound via nf_tables_unbind_chain, but the code falls through to the PREPARE case and calls nft_deactivate_next, deactivating the chain during an error path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fallthrough causes a chain/objects to be deactivated and freed while still referenced by the transaction records, matching use of memory after free (CWE-416). This is a lifetime/ordering flaw rather than a mere logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the PREPARE_ERROR path unbinds the chain yet still falls through, deactivating a chain that should remain active for the aborted transaction. Trigger: building an immediate expression rule fails, invoking deactivation with phase NFT_TRANS_PREPARE_ERROR. The wrongly deactivated chain and its objects can later be used, giving use-after-free (crash or memory corruption).

description: In avrc_pars_browsing_cmd of avrc_pars_tg.cc, there is a possible use-after-free due to improper locking. This could lead to remote escalation of privilege in the Bluetooth service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation. Product: Android Versions: Android-8.0 Android-8.1 Android ID: A-109699112

code_evidence: On BTA_AV_META_MSG_EVT, the function frees av->meta_msg.p_data (line 5) and, for AVRC_OP_VENDOR, frees vendor.p_vendor_data (line 8). It then frees and resets the meta message struct itself via osi_free_and_reset on av->meta_msg.p_msg (line 10). The browse.p_browse_data member is never freed here, leaving that allocation unreleased when the message is destroyed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the code frees the message structure while leaving the browse data pointer unmanaged, enabling later reuse of freed memory. A plain memory leak (CWE-401) would only cover the missing free, not the subsequent stale-pointer use.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the deep-copy/free path does not account for the browse payload, so browse.p_browse_data is not freed alongside the message struct. Trigger: an AVRC_OP_BROWSE meta message reaches this free routine. Consequence: the browse buffer is leaked or later accessed through a stale pointer after the owning structure is freed, supporting a use-after-free condition described in the commit/description.

commit_msg: Fix issue with miscalculation of block overflow size (#8)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                size_t size = num_blocks * 64 * sizeof(*c->blocks) + OK_JPG_BLOCK_EXTRA_SPACE;'], 'added_lines': ['                size_t size = (num_blocks * 64 + OK_JPG_BLOCK_EXTRA_SPACE) * sizeof(*c->blocks);']}
description: A heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the function ok_jpg_decode_block_progressive() at ok_jpg.c:1054 of ok-file-formats through 2020-06-26 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DOS) via a crafted jpeg file.

code_evidence: num_blocks is computed from attacker-influenced data_units_x/data_units_y and component sampling factors c->H/c->V (lines 111-112). The allocation size at line 113 computes num_blocks * 64 * sizeof(*c->blocks) + OK_JPG_BLOCK_EXTRA_SPACE; because the extra space is added as a byte count after the multiplication, the arithmetic can overflow size_t for large num_blocks, yielding a smaller-than-required allocation. c->blocks is then allocated with this undersized value at line 114.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the undersized allocation leads to writes past the end of the intended heap buffer. The integer overflow is the root cause enabling the out-of-bounds write, so CWE-787 is the supported consequence rather than a separate integer-overflow label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the block-buffer size is computed with an arithmetic expression whose intermediate product (num_blocks * 64 * sizeof) can wrap around size_t before adding the extra space, so the allocated size is too small. Trigger: a crafted JPEG whose sampling factors and dimensions make num_blocks large enough to overflow. Consequence: later block writes exceed the undersized heap buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds write/DoS.

commit_msg:
Bug 698908: Resize object use and renumbering lists after repair.

Previously repair might end up increasing xref_len, but the lists
were not correspodingly expanded, leading to ASAN complaints.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tnum++;'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* objects are numbered 0..num and maybe two additional objects for linearization */', '\tnum += 3;']}
description: In Artifex MuPDF 1.12.0, there is a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the do_pdf_save_document function in the pdf/pdf-write.c file. Remote attackers could leverage the vulnerability to cause a denial of service via a crafted pdf file.

code_evidence: The function computes the new capacity as num++ and immediately resizes all five parallel arrays to exactly that many elements.

The initialization loop indexes from the old list_len up to num-1, writing use_list[i], ofs_list[i], gen_list[i], renumber_map[i] and rev_renumber_map[i]; these writes are only in bounds if num matches the allocated element count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-787 because the loop writes beyond the buffer allocated by fz_resize_array when the array length is under-sized relative to the index range used. The defect is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an integer overflow or a read; the insufficient capacity increment is the root cause enabling the past-the-end writes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The capacity passed to fz_resize_array is derived solely from num, but callers may increase the document xref length by more than this increment (e.g., repair adding objects plus linearization objects). When a later iteration expects a larger index than the allocated length, the loop writes past the end of the resized heap arrays, corrupting memory and causing a crash/DoS.

Trying to fix some invalid left shift operations

Fixes issue #16

description: libimageworsener.a in ImageWorsener before 1.3.1 has "left shift cannot be represented in type int" undefined behavior issues, which might allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted image, related to imagew-bmp.c and imagew-util.c.

code_evidence: Line 3 computes a 32-bit little-endian value by shifting each byte: b[1]<<8, b[2]<<16, b[3]<<24. b is iw_byte (unsigned char), which undergoes integer promotion to signed int before the shift. Shifting a set high bit into or beyond the sign bit of int is undefined behavior, so the composed result may be wrong.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an integer calculation whose result is unintended due to undefined shift behavior, matching CWE-682 (Incorrect Calculation). The weakness is the incorrect computation itself; the crash is its consequence, not a separate memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bytes are promoted to signed int and shifted without conversion to unsigned, so b[3]<<24 can overflow int and is undefined. Trigger: a crafted image supplies b[3] >= 0x80 (or other high-set bytes). Consequence: the computed 32-bit value is incorrect or the program crashes, supporting DoS as described in the commit.

commit_msg:
GHSL-2023-010: Memory leak when parsing usernames

Memory leak when parsing usernames (GHSL-2023-010)

Fixes defect GHSL-2023-010 found by the GitHub Security Lab team via
oss-fuzz.

The domain portion may be overridden causing an allocated memory area
the size of the domain name to be lost. This could be used to mount a
DoS by depleeting the server memory.

Signed-off-by: Simo Sorce <simo@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        bool domain_handled = false;', '            /* leading domain, copy if domain name is not empty */', '            domain_handled = true;', '', '                if (domain_handled) {', '            } else if (!domain_handled) {'], 'added_lines': ['                if (*domain) {', '            } else if (!*domain) {']}
description: GSS-NTLMSSP is a mechglue plugin for the GSSAPI library that implements NTLM authentication. Prior to version 1.2.0, a memory leak can be triggered when parsing usernames which can trigger a denial-of-service. The domain portion of a username may be overridden causing an allocated memory area the size of the domain name to be leaked. An attacker can leak memory via the main `gss_accept_sec_context` entry point, potentially causing a denial-of-service. This issue is fixed in version 1.2.0.

code_evidence: When a backslash separator is present, the leading domain is split and strdup'd into *domain (line 34), making *domain non-NULL.

The later loop over '@' previously guarded allocation with the local boolean domain_handled; the '@' branch at line 51-53 conditionally overwrites *domain with a new strdup without releasing the existing allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because an allocated domain buffer is overwritten without free, so its lifetime ends but the memory is never released, matching missing release of memory after effective lifetime. It is not a dangling-pointer/UAF issue since the old pointer is simply lost, not freed then reused.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decision whether *domain already holds an allocation is tracked by a local flag (domain_handled) rather than the actual pointer state, so the '@' handling path can strdup over a non-NULL *domain. Trigger: a username containing both a backslash-split leading domain and an unescaped '@' (e.g. DOM\foo@bar) reaches line 51-53, replacing the earlier allocation. Consequence: the original domain buffer is leaked, and repeated invocation depletes server memory leading to DoS.

commit_msg: fix #289
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        } else {', '            break;']}
description: In Bento4 v1.5.1-624, AP4_File::ParseStream in Ap4File.cpp allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via a crafted MP4 file.

code_evidence: The for loop at line 12 iterates i from 0 to entry_count, an attacker-controlled value read from the stream at line 9. Inside, CreateAtomFromStream is called; only on success (line 16) is an atom added to m_Children. If CreateAtomFromStream fails, the loop body does nothing and i still increments, so the loop continues consuming iterations without progress. The fix adds an else { break; } to exit on failure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the loop's effective exit condition (successful atom creation) is unreachable when parsing fails, producing an infinite/attacker-lengthened loop. This is a loop-termination flaw, not merely a resource-size issue like CWE-400.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop's progress depends on a stream read that can fail, but failure is silently ignored and iteration continues. Trigger: a crafted MP4 with a large entry_count and a malformed/truncated sample-description entry makes CreateAtomFromStream fail repeatedly. Consequence: the loop keeps spinning over entry_count iterations, consuming CPU (DoS).

commit_msg:
libceph: harden msgr2.1 frame segment length checks

ceph_frame_desc::fd_lens is an int array.  decode_preamble() thus
effectively casts u32 -> int but the checks for segment lengths are
written as if on unsigned values.  While reading in HELLO or one of the
AUTH frames (before authentication is completed), arithmetic in
head_onwire_len() can get duped by negative ctrl_len and produce
head_len which is less than CEPH_PREAMBLE_LEN but still positive.
This would lead to a buffer overrun in prepare_read_control() as the
preamble gets copied to the newly allocated buffer of size head_len.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: cd1a677cad99 ("libceph, ceph: implement msgr2.1 protocol (crc and secure modes)")
Reported-by: Thelford Williams <thelford@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Ilya Dryomov <idryomov@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Xiubo Li <xiubli@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tpr_err("last segment empty\\n");', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '', '\tif (desc->fd_lens[0] > CEPH_MSG_MAX_CONTROL_LEN) {', '\t\tpr_err("control segment too big %d\\n", desc->fd_lens[0]);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '\tif (desc->fd_lens[1] > CEPH_MSG_MAX_FRONT_LEN) {', '\t\tpr_err("front segment too big %d\\n", desc->fd_lens[1]);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '\tif (desc->fd_lens[2] > CEPH_MSG_MAX_MIDDLE_LEN) {', '\t\tpr_err("middle segment too big %d\\n", desc->fd_lens[2]);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '\tif (desc->fd_lens[3] > CEPH_MSG_MAX_DATA_LEN) {', '\t\tpr_err("data segment too big %d\\n", desc->fd_lens[3]);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (desc->fd_lens[0] < 0 ||', '\t    desc->fd_lens[0] > CEPH_MSG_MAX_CONTROL_LEN) {', '\t\tpr_err("bad control segment length %d\\n", desc->fd_lens[0]);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '\tif (desc->fd_lens[1] < 0 ||', '\t    desc->fd_lens[1] > CEPH_MSG_MAX_FRONT_LEN) {', '\t\tpr_err("bad front segment length %d\\n", desc->fd_lens[1]);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '\tif (desc->fd_lens[2] < 0 ||', '\t    desc->fd_lens[2] > CEPH_MSG_MAX_MIDDLE_LEN) {', '\t\tpr_err("bad middle segment length %d\\n", desc->fd_lens[2]);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '\tif (desc->fd_lens[3] < 0 ||', '\t    desc->fd_lens[3] > CEPH_MSG_MAX_DATA_LEN) {', '\t\tpr_err("bad data segment length %d\\n", desc->fd_lens[3]);', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '', '\t\tpr_err("last segment empty, segment count %d\\n",', '\t\t       desc->fd_seg_cnt);']}
description: An issue was discovered in net/ceph/messenger_v2.c in the Linux kernel before 6.4.5. There is an integer signedness error, leading to a buffer overflow and remote code execution via HELLO or one of the AUTH frames. This occurs because of an untrusted length taken from a TCP packet in ceph_decode_32.

code_evidence: Untrusted preamble fields are decoded from the network buffer: fd_seg_cnt is read via ceph_decode_8 and each fd_lens[i] via ceph_decode_32, which returns a u32 stored into the int fd_lens array.
The only length guard checks the last segment for zero; there is no per-segment upper bound and no signedness check.
The subsequent checks compare fd_lens[i] > CEPH_MSG_MAX_*_LEN, but fd_lens is int. A decoded u32 >= 0x80000000 becomes negative, so these unsigned-style comparisons pass.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate the size of the input before the preamble is copied into a buffer sized from the unvalidated length, producing a classic buffer overflow write. The missing signedness/negative check is the root cause enabling the unchecked copy, matching CWE-120 rather than a pure integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a u32 segment length is stored into int fd_lens and validated only with '>' against maximums, so values with the high bit set become negative and evade the bound checks. Trigger: an attacker sends a HELLO or AUTH preamble with such a control length before authentication. Downstream head_onwire_len() computes a small positive head_len, and prepare_read_control() copies the full preamble into a buffer of that size, causing an out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
sys/base64: Use void pointer for buffers in API

This is a non-breaking change, as `unsigned char *` can implicitly be converted
to `void *`.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int getcode(char symbol)'], 'added_lines': ['static uint8_t getcode(char symbol)']}
description: RIOT 2020.04 has a buffer overflow in the base64 decoder. The decoding function base64_decode() uses an output buffer estimation function to compute the required buffer capacity and validate against the provided buffer size. The base64_estimate_decode_size() function calculates the expected decoded size with an arithmetic round-off error and does not take into account possible padding bytes. Due to this underestimation, it may be possible to craft base64 input that causes a buffer overflow.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The getcode function only maps individual characters to base64 values and returns constants/arithmetic results; it performs no buffer indexing or memory access, so it does not directly support a buffer-bounds weakness. The described overflow arises in base64_estimate_decode_size/base64_decode, not in this function.

commit_msg:
Fix TensorKey hash function.

The original hash function only used total estimated `AllocatedBytes()`, which (a) is an estimate per tensor, and (b) is a very poor hash function for constants (e.g. `int32_t`).
It also tried to access individual tensor bytes through `tensor.data()` of size `AllocatedBytes()`.  This led to ASAN failures because the `AllocatedBytes()` is an estimate of total bytes allocated by a tensor, including any pointed-to constructs (e.g. strings), and does not refer to contiguous bytes in the `.data()` buffer.  We couldn't use this byte vector anyways, since types like `tstring` include pointers, whereas we need to hash the string values themselves.

Modified the hash function to more closely mirror the `==` operator.  This correctly handles `tstring` and any numeric types that do have contiguous storage.  Other types are currently left as unimplemented.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 446265413
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    const uint8* d = static_cast<uint8*>(k.data());', '    size_t s = k.AllocatedBytes();', '    std::vector<uint8> vec;', '    vec.reserve(s);', '    for (int i = 0; i < s; i++) {', '      vec.push_back(d[i]);', '    return H::combine(std::move(h), s);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (DataTypeCanUseMemcpy(k.dtype())) {', '      return H::combine(std::move(h), k.tensor_data());', '    } else if (k.dtype() == DT_STRING) {', '      const auto strs = k.unaligned_flat<tstring>();', '      for (int64_t i = 0, n = k.NumElements(); i < n; ++i) {', '        h = H::combine(std::move(h), strs(i));', '      }', '      return h;', '    } else {', '      DCHECK(false) << "Unimplemented dtype " << DataTypeString(k.dtype())', '                    << std::endl;', '    return h;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In version 2.8.0, the `TensorKey` hash function used total estimated `AllocatedBytes()`, which (a) is an estimate per tensor, and (b) is a very poor hash function for constants (e.g. `int32_t`). It also tried to access individual tensor bytes through `tensor.data()` of size `AllocatedBytes()`. This led to ASAN failures because the `AllocatedBytes()` is an estimate of total bytes allocated by a tensor, including any pointed-to constructs (e.g. strings), and does not refer to contiguous bytes in the `.data()` buffer. The discoverers could not use this byte vector anyway because types such as `tstring` include pointers, whereas they needed to hash the string values themselves. This issue is patched in Tensorflow versions 2.9.0 and 2.8.1.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only reads bytes from tensor.data() into a vector and hashes the size; it performs no write past a buffer boundary, and the described ASAN failure stems from reading an overestimated AllocatedBytes() region, which is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), not an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

commit_msg:
sched: Fix information leak in sys_sched_getattr()

We're copying the on-stack structure to userspace, but forgot to give
the right number of bytes to copy. This allows the calling process to
obtain up to PAGE_SIZE bytes from the stack (and possibly adjacent
kernel memory).

This fix copies only as much as we actually have on the stack
(attr->size defaults to the size of the struct) and leaves the rest of
the userspace-provided buffer untouched.

Found using kmemcheck + trinity.

Fixes: d50dde5a10f30 ("sched: Add new scheduler syscalls to support an extended scheduling parameters ABI")
Cc: Dario Faggioli <raistlin@linux.it>
Cc: Juri Lelli <juri.lelli@gmail.com>
Cc: Ingo Molnar <mingo@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Vegard Nossum <vegard.nossum@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/1392585857-10725-1-git-send-email-vegard.nossum@oracle.com
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tret = copy_to_user(uattr, attr, usize);'], 'added_lines': ['\tret = copy_to_user(uattr, attr, attr->size);']}
description: The sched_read_attr function in kernel/sched/core.c in the Linux kernel 3.14-rc before 3.14-rc4 uses an incorrect size, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel stack memory via a crafted sched_getattr system call.

code_evidence: After validating only usize bytes against uattr via access_ok and checking the tail of the struct, the function copies usize bytes to user space. usize is caller-controlled and may exceed sizeof(*attr), so the copy reads beyond the on-stack sched_attr object and exposes adjacent kernel stack memory to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The direct consequence is disclosure of sensitive kernel stack contents to an unprivileged local caller, matching CWE-200's exposure of information to an unauthorized actor. The underlying over-read is the mechanism; the observable, supported impact here is confidentiality loss of kernel memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy length uses the user-supplied usize instead of the actual initialized struct size (attr->size). Trigger: a sched_getattr call with usize larger than sizeof(struct sched_attr) passes the access_ok check and the tail check, then copy_to_user reads past the stack struct. Consequence: up to PAGE_SIZE bytes of kernel stack memory are disclosed to a local user.

commit_msg:
The passthrough structure is declared off of the stack, so it needs to be
set to zero before copied back to userspace to prevent any unintentional
data leakage.  Switch things to be statically allocated which will fill the
unused fields with 0 automatically.

description: drivers/scsi/stex.c in the Linux kernel through 5.19.9 allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory because stex_queuecommand_lck lacks a memset for the PASSTHRU_CMD case.

code_evidence: A stack-local struct st_drvver ver is declared at line 68 and never zero-initialized; only the seven named fields (major, minor, oem, build, signature[0], console_id, host_no) are assigned at lines 70-76. Any remaining bytes of the struct, including the tail of the signature array, stay uninitialized. Line 77 then copies the whole sizeof(ver) buffer back toward userspace via scsi_sg_copy_from_buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 covers use/access of a resource not initialized; here the uninitialized st_drvver bytes are read and copied to userspace. This is a use of uninitialized resource, not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the buffer is valid but its contents were never set.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: partial field assignment leaves padding/unassigned struct bytes uninitialized. Trigger: a local user issues a PASSTHRU_CMD with cmnd[1] == PASSTHRU_GET_DRVVER, causing the full struct to be copied out. Consequence: uninitialized kernel stack memory is disclosed to userspace (information leak).

commit_msg: fixed #2576
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!ctx->fps.num) ctx->fps.num = ctx->fps.den = 1000;']}
description: Divide By Zero in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.3-DEV.

code_evidence: When ctx->use_file_fps is set, AVI_frame_rate() is read and passed to gf_media_get_video_timing(), which fills ctx->fps.num and ctx->fps.den; the pre-patch code has no check that the resulting numerator is non-zero.
The very next statements use ctx->fps.num as a denominator: dur.den = ctx->fps.num, and dur is later published as a fraction property. A zero numerator from the file timing makes dur.den zero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because an externally derived value (ctx->fps.num) is used as a divisor with no zero check, and the patch adds exactly that zero check. This is a divide-by-zero rather than a generic input-validation issue; the consequence is a crash/DoS.

evidence_lines.code:
dur.den = ctx->fps.num;
dur.num = (u64) (ctx->fps.den * AVI_video_frames(ctx->avi));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the frame-rate timing returned for the input AVI is trusted without validating that the numerator is non-zero. Trigger: a crafted file whose frame rate yields fps.num == 0. Consequence: dur.den becomes zero, so the fraction is invalid and later division by dur.den (or fraction handling) crashes the demuxer, giving a denial of service. The added guard resetting num/den to 1000 confirms this missing constraint.

commit_msg: fix integer overflow in Resample.c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    // check for overflow', '    if (kmax > 0 && xsize > SIZE_MAX / kmax)', '        return (Imaging) ImagingError_MemoryError();', '', '    // sizeof(float) should be greater than 0', '    if (xsize * kmax > SIZE_MAX / sizeof(float))', '        return (Imaging) ImagingError_MemoryError();', '', '        return (Imaging) ImagingError_MemoryError();', '', '    // sizeof(int) should be greater than 0 as well', '    if (xsize > SIZE_MAX / (2 * sizeof(int)))']}
description: Integer overflow in the ImagingResampleHorizontal function in libImaging/Resample.c in Pillow before 3.1.1 allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via negative values of the new size, which triggers a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: kmax is derived from ceil(support)*2+1 and multiplied by xsize before allocation; no overflow check exists before this malloc, so a large/negative xsize can wrap the size computation and yield an undersized kk buffer.
xbounds is allocated as xsize*2*sizeof(int) with no overflow guard; a wrapped size produces a small buffer.
The loop indexes kk and xbounds using xx*kmax and xx*2 offsets for xx in [0,xsize), writing past the undersized allocations when the size product wrapped.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through kk and xbounds beyond their allocated boundaries, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds buffer operations. The integer overflow is the root cause, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write within a heap buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: xsize is multiplied by kmax and by 2 without validating that the products fit size_t, so the allocation size wraps to a small value while the loops still iterate xsize times. Trigger: an attacker supplies a large or negative new size. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds writes to kk and xbounds, corrupting adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
The syzkaller USB fuzzer found a general-protection-fault bug in the
smsusb part of the Siano DVB driver.  The fault occurs during probe
because the driver assumes without checking that the device has both
IN and OUT endpoints and the IN endpoint is ep1.

By slightly rearranging the driver's initialization code, we can make
the appropriate checks early on and thus avoid the problem.  If the
expected endpoints aren't present, the new code safely returns -ENODEV
from the probe routine.

Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+53f029db71c19a47325a@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tdev->response_alignment =', '\t\t    le16_to_cpu(dev->udev->ep_in[1]->desc.wMaxPacketSize) -', '\t\t    sizeof(struct sms_msg_hdr);', '', '\tfor (i = 0; i < intf->cur_altsetting->desc.bNumEndpoints; i++) {', '\t\tif (intf->cur_altsetting->endpoint[i].desc. bEndpointAddress & USB_DIR_IN)', '\t\t\tdev->in_ep = intf->cur_altsetting->endpoint[i].desc.bEndpointAddress;', '\t\telse', '\t\t\tdev->out_ep = intf->cur_altsetting->endpoint[i].desc.bEndpointAddress;', '\t}', '', '\tpr_debug("in_ep = %02x, out_ep = %02x\\n",', '\t\tdev->in_ep, dev->out_ep);'], 'added_lines': ['\tint in_maxp;', '', '\tfor (i = 0; i < intf->cur_altsetting->desc.bNumEndpoints; i++) {', '\t\tstruct usb_endpoint_descriptor *desc =', '\t\t\t\t&intf->cur_altsetting->endpoint[i].desc;', '', '\t\tif (desc->bEndpointAddress & USB_DIR_IN) {', '\t\t\tdev->in_ep = desc->bEndpointAddress;', '\t\t\tin_maxp = usb_endpoint_maxp(desc);', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t\tdev->out_ep = desc->bEndpointAddress;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '', '\tpr_debug("in_ep = %02x, out_ep = %02x\\n", dev->in_ep, dev->out_ep);', '\tif (!dev->in_ep || !dev->out_ep) {\t/* Missing endpoints? */', '\t\tsmsusb_term_device(intf);', '\t\treturn -ENODEV;', '\t}', '\t\tdev->response_alignment = in_maxp - sizeof(struct sms_msg_hdr);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.1.8. There is a NULL pointer dereference caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/media/usb/siano/smsusb.c driver.

code_evidence: In the default/USB2 branch, response_alignment is computed by dereferencing dev->udev->ep_in[1]->desc.wMaxPacketSize without verifying that ep_in[1] exists.
The endpoint scan that populates dev->in_ep/out_ep occurs only after this dereference, so no endpoint validation precedes the access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (udev->ep_in[1]) that is not guaranteed non-NULL, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. The missing endpoint check, not an out-of-bounds index per se, is the direct cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the driver assumes the USB device exposes an IN endpoint at index 1 and dereferences udev->ep_in[1] unconditionally during probe. Trigger: a malicious or malformed USB device lacking that endpoint presents ep_in[1] as NULL. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference, causing a general-protection fault/crash (DoS) in the probe path.

commit_msg:
xfs: fix two memory leaks in xfs_attr_list.c error paths

This plugs 2 trivial leaks in xfs_attr_shortform_list and
xfs_attr3_leaf_list_int.

Signed-off-by: Mateusz Guzik <mguzik@redhat.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Eric Sandeen <sandeen@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Chinner <david@fromorbit.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif (retval)', '\t\t\t\t\treturn retval;', '\t\t\t\tretval = context->put_listent(context,', '\t\t\t\t\t\tentry->flags,', '\t\t\t\t\t\tname_rmt->name,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t(int)name_rmt->namelen,', '\t\t\t\t\t\tvaluelen,', '\t\t\t\t\t\targs.value);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif (!retval)', '\t\t\t\t\tretval = context->put_listent(context,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t\tentry->flags,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t\tname_rmt->name,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t\t(int)name_rmt->namelen,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t\tvaluelen,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t\targs.value);']}
description: Multiple memory leaks in error paths in fs/xfs/xfs_attr_list.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5.1 allow local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via crafted XFS filesystem operations.

code_evidence: Line 75 allocates args.value with kmem_alloc; line 79 calls xfs_attr_rmtval_get, and the original error check at lines 80-81 returns retval immediately without freeing args.value.
The subsequent put_listent and kmem_free at line 88 are bypassed on that early return, so the allocation leaks on this error path.

evidence_lines.code: kmem_free(args.value);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch after xfs_attr_rmtval_get returns before the paired kmem_free. Trigger: a crafted XFS attribute whose remote value read fails causes xfs_attr_rmtval_get to return nonzero. Consequence: each failed list operation leaks a valuelen-sized kernel buffer, enabling memory exhaustion/DoS.

commit_msg:
patch 8.1.0881: can execute shell commands in rvim through interfaces

Problem:    Can execute shell commands in rvim through interfaces.
Solution:   Disable using interfaces in restricted mode. Allow for writing
            file with writefile(), histadd() and a few others.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (check_restricted() || check_secure())', '\treturn;', '']}
description: In Vim before 8.1.0881, users can circumvent the rvim restricted mode and execute arbitrary OS commands via scripting interfaces (e.g., Python, Ruby, or Lua).

code_evidence: f_pyxeval() dispatches to f_pyeval()/f_py3eval() based on build flags and p_pyx, with no restricted-mode or secure-mode check anywhere in the function body; the guard is absent from the shown source. The function therefore exposes the Python evaluation interface unconditionally to whatever caller invokes it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing restriction check lets attacker-supplied scripting input reach an interpreter that constructs and runs OS commands, matching CWE-78's improper neutralization of special elements used in an OS command. The weakness is the absent policy gate rather than, e.g., a plain access-control check, because the downstream effect is command execution.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the interface function performs no check_restricted()/check_secure() gate before forwarding to the Python evaluator. Trigger: in restricted (rvim) mode a user calls pyxeval(), which reaches the Python interpreter and can run OS commands. Consequence: the restricted-mode boundary is bypassed, allowing execution of arbitrary OS commands with the process's privileges.

description: Rizin is a UNIX-like reverse engineering framework and command-line toolset. Versions 0.4.0 and prior are vulnerable to an out-of-bounds write when getting data from Luac files. A user opening a malicious Luac file could be affected by this vulnerability, allowing an attacker to execute code on the user's machine. Commits 07b43bc8aa1ffebd9b68d60624c9610cf7e460c7 and 05bbd147caccc60162d6fba9baaaf24befa281cd contain fixes for the issue.

code_evidence: upvalue_names is allocated with RZ_NEWS0(char *, real_upvalue_cnt), where real_upvalue_cnt is the length of proto->upvalue_entries, not of proto->dbg_upvalue_entries.

The following rz_list_foreach iterates over proto->dbg_upvalue_entries, a different, attacker-controlled list, writing upvalue_names[i] = debug_upv_entry->upvalue_name for each entry without any bound check against real_upvalue_cnt and without incrementing i.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through upvalue_names[i] past the end of a heap buffer sized from a mismatched list count, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). A plain buffer overflow is not the fit here; the defect is a write beyond the intended bounds caused by an unchecked list-length mismatch.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer size is derived from upvalue_entries while the write loop iterates dbg_upvalue_entries, and the index i is never incremented in the loop, so every iteration writes to upvalue_names[0] while the loop can run more times than the allocation. Trigger: a crafted Luac file whose dbg_upvalue_entries list is longer than upvalue_entries. description: The broker in Eclipse Mosquitto 1.3.2 through 2.x before 2.0.16 has a memory leak that can be abused remotely when a client sends many QoS 2 messages with duplicate message IDs, and fails to respond to PUBREC commands. This occurs because of mishandling of EAGAIN from the libc send function.

code_evidence: After a QoS>0 PUBLISH, db__message_store_find is used to locate an existing incoming message for source_mid; if found and identical, the new msg is freed at [247] and dup is set to 1 at [249], but the existing stored message is not released here.

For QoS 2, when dup!=0 the code skips db__message_insert at [270-271] (res=0) and still sends PUBREC at [274]; repeated duplicate PUBLISH packets with the same mid take this branch without adding or removing stored state, so the incoming message record persists while the client never completes PUBREL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the function fails to release or bound allocated message storage for duplicate QoS 2 flows, leaving memory unavailable for reuse. This is a missing-release/resource-retention flaw, not a single out-of-bounds or use-after-free issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: duplicate QoS 2 PUBLISH handling treats a repeated message as already stored, sends PUBREC again, and never frees or progresses the stored incoming message when the peer does not respond to PUBREC. Trigger: a remote client sends many QoS 2 PUBLISH packets reusing the same message ID and ignores PUBREC. Consequence: stored message records and associated memory accumulate, causing memory exhaustion/DoS.

description: The scp client in OpenSSH 8.2 incorrectly sends duplicate responses to the server upon a utimes system call failure, which allows a malicious unprivileged user on the remote server to overwrite arbitrary files in the client's download directory by creating a crafted subdirectory anywhere on the remote server. The victim must use the command scp -rp to download a file hierarchy containing, anywhere inside, this crafted subdirectory. NOTE: the vendor points out that "this attack can achieve no more than a hostile peer is already able to achieve within the scp protocol" and "utimes does not fail under normal circumstances.

code_evidence: The filename token cp is checked for NUL, '/', '.', '..' and pattern match ([132-143]), but the 'D' directory record branch ([162-189]) recurses via sink(1, vect, src) and calls utimes/chmod on vect[0] without any per-record error accounting; a utimes() failure there invokes run_err() ([182-184]), which emits an error reply to the peer.

After the file body, the code sends a single success reply only when wrerr == NO ([290-292]); but the earlier utimes failure in the directory branch already sent a reply via run_err, so the stream's reply accounting is not consistently tracked per control record, letting the peer desynchronize replies from records.

The write/truncate/chmod/close/utimes error paths ([243-295]) use run_err() (which sends a reply) and then the switch still sends another reply for the NO case, so multiple responses can be emitted for one file record when an error occurs; the peer's response consumption is not bounded to one reply per record.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because sink() accepts peer-supplied protocol records and filenames without validating the invariant that exactly one reply corresponds to each record; the missing consistency check on the reply/record state is the improper validation of received input. This is not merely a path-traversal filtering issue (CWE-22), since the filename checks exist; the flaw is failure to validate protocol-state consistency.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sink() protocol handler does not validate/account for the correspondence between received control records and replies it emits; error paths in the directory branch and file branch can each send a run_err() reply while the normal path also sends a success byte. Trigger: a malicious peer sends a crafted hierarchy (e.g., a directory whose utimes fails) causing an extra error reply. Consequence: source()/sink() reply streams desynchronize, and the peer can cause the client to write a subsequent file over an unintended path within the download directory.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13035/Properly handle IS-IS IDs shorter than a system ID (MAC address).

Some of them are variable-length, with a field giving the total length,
and therefore they can be shorter than 6 octets.  If one is, don't run
past the end.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s), modified
so the capture file won't be rejected as an invalid capture.

commit_msg:
[tflite] Ensure input tensors don't have `nullptr` buffers.

A crafted TFLite model can force a node to have as input a tensor backed by a `nullptr` buffer. That is, by carefully changing the buffer index in the flatbuffer serialization, we can force the TFLite interpreter to consider a read-only tensor to be a read-write one and assume that there is an operator that has this tensor as output, writing to it and allocating memory before the tensor is used as input. If this does not happen, we get memory corruption.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 332524692
Change-Id: I57ef175152a29020af9ab041dc959e5631dce40f
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      if (tensor->data.raw == nullptr && tensor->bytes > 0) {', '        if (registration.builtin_code == kTfLiteBuiltinReshape && i == 1) {', '          // In general, having a tensor here with no buffer will be an error.', '          // However, for the reshape operator, the second input tensor is only', '          // used for the shape, not for the data. Thus, null buffer is ok.', '          continue;', '        } else {', '          // In all other cases, we need to return an error as otherwise we will', '          // trigger a null pointer dereference (likely).', '          ReportError("Input tensor %d lacks data", tensor_index);', '          return kTfLiteError;', '        }', '      }']}
description: In tensorflow-lite before versions 1.15.4, 2.0.3, 2.1.2, 2.2.1 and 2.3.1, a crafted TFLite model can force a node to have as input a tensor backed by a `nullptr` buffer. This can be achieved by changing a buffer index in the flatbuffer serialization to convert a read-only tensor to a read-write one. The runtime assumes that these buffers are written to before a possible read, hence they are initialized with `nullptr`. However, by changing the buffer index for a tensor and implicitly converting that tensor to be a read-write one, as there is nothing in the model that writes to it, we get a null pointer dereference. The issue is patched in commit 0b5662bc, and is released in TensorFlow versions 1.15.4, 2.0.3, 2.1.2, 2.2.1, or 2.3.1.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over node inputs, resolves each tensor_index into a TfLiteTensor pointer, and only checks delegate staleness before proceeding. There is no check that tensor->data.raw is non-null when the tensor is used as an input, so a tensor backed by a nullptr buffer reaches OpInvoke.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the unchecked null input buffer is later dereferenced by the operator. This is a null pointer dereference, not merely a missing validation error, since the consequence is dereferencing a NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: input tensors are not validated for a null data buffer before operator invocation. Trigger: a crafted model changes a buffer index so a read-only tensor becomes read-write with no writer, leaving data.raw as nullptr. Consequence: the operator dereferences the null buffer, causing a null pointer dereference and crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg: Fix access violation problem on high color mode (#116), Thanks to SuhwanSong
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (dirty && mod_y == 5) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (dirty && (mod_y == 5 || y >= height)) {', '            if (y >= orig_height) {', '              goto end;', '            }', '']}
description: Libsixel 1.8.3 contains a heap-based buffer overflow in the sixel_encode_highcolor function in tosixel.c.

code_evidence: When y reaches height, the loop only breaks out via goto end if not dirty; if dirty it sets mod_y=5 and continues the outer while(1) loop.

The dirty && mod_y==5 branch then encodes a body using height=y, rewinds pixels by 6*width*3, and computes height = orig_height - height + 6, then jumps to next, reinitializing y=0 and re-reading pixel data.
The inner loop advances pixels += 3 per column and calls sixel_apply_15bpp_dither using y, width, height, so the rewound pointer and recomputed height determine subsequent reads/writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect permits writes/reads beyond the allocated pixel and paletted buffers due to missing bounds termination, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The patch adds y >= height and y >= orig_height checks to stop processing at the buffer boundary, confirming the boundary-check root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the high-color encoder does not guard against re-entering the row loop after y has already reached the image height when dirty pixels remain, allowing pixels to be rewound and height recomputed beyond the original buffer. Trigger: a high-color image whose final rows still produce a dirty palette. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds memory access/write past paletted_pixels or pixels, matching the reported heap-based buffer overflow.

commit_msg:
invalidate startline and bottom_startline when hidden

this was overlooked when adding hidden line support. if the lines are
removed, Irssi has to update the startline. It does that by "scrolling"
the lines to the proper place. The scroll function was adjusted to
calculate 0 for hidden lines, thus it would miss them.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\tif (view->startline == line) {', '\t\t\tview->startline = line->next;', '\t\t\tview->subline = 0;', '\t\t}', '\t\t}', '', '\t\tif (view->bottom_startline == line) {', '\t\t\tview->bottom_startline = view->bottom_startline->next;', '\t\t\tview->bottom_subline = 0;']}
description: Irssi 1.1.x before 1.1.2 has a use after free when hidden lines are expired from the scroll buffer.

code_evidence: When the removed line is the buffer's first_line and equals view->startline, view_scroll is called to advance startline; if the line was the last (next==NULL), startline is set to NULL, otherwise startline is left pointing at a LINE_REC that is being removed.

In the else branch, view_scroll is only invoked when the removed line exists after bottom_startline; hidden lines are skipped by view_scroll, so bottom_startline can remain pointing at the removed line without being advanced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function leaves view->startline/bottom_startline referencing a LINE_REC that is subsequently freed, and later code reuses those pointers; this matches CWE-416 (use after free). It is not merely a NULL dereference or integer issue, since the defect is reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: view_remove_line fails to invalidate view->startline and view->bottom_startline when the removed line is hidden, because the scroll logic computes zero movement for hidden lines and the equality check is skipped. After the LINE_REC is freed, these pointers dangle; later scrolling or rendering dereferences freed memory, causing a use-after-free (crash or memory corruption).

description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0742.

code_evidence: At line 17 the code tests *var_start == '@' and, without validating the character following '@', sets var_end = var_start + 2 at line 18. might just mean "no more strings") and running out of captured data
(which means "truncated").

researchers Otto Airamo & Antti Levomäki.

code_evidence: PARSE_STRING expands to a call to parse_field that advances parse and decreases parselen; the returned pointer s is only null-checked, so a non-null string near the packet end can be consumed without validating a terminating NUL within bounds.

PARSE_FIELD_INT uses strtol(s,0,16) on the parse_field result, and PARSE_FIELD_STR stores s; later strncmp/strcmp calls on z.version, z.class, z.opcode and others read until a NUL, which may lie past the captured data.
z.version is checked with strncmp(z.version,"ZEPH",4) right after parsing; if fewer than 4 bytes were captured, this reads beyond the packet buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs string comparisons and printing on data whose bounds were never validated, directly reading beyond the intended capture buffer, which is CWE-125. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write (CWE-787) or an integer overflow.

evidence_lines.code:
PARSE_FIELD_STR(z.version);
if (lose) return;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: parse_field's returned string is trusted without confirming the field terminator lies within the captured packet. Trigger: a truncated or crafted Zephyr payload whose string field ends at the capture boundary. Consequence: strncmp/strcmp and ND_PRINT str_to_lower calls read past the buffer, leaking memory or crashing.

description: An out-of-bounds (OOB) memory write flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s watch_queue event notification subsystem. This flaw can overwrite parts of the kernel state, potentially allowing a local user to gain privileged access or cause a denial of service on the system.

code_evidence: nr_notes is bounded to 1..512 and nr_pages is derived by ceil division, so the page array and note count are sized from nr_notes.
pipe_resize_ring is called with nr_notes rather than a power-of-two ring size; the ring size may not match the number of notes later posted.

wqueue->nr_notes is set to nr_pages * WATCH_QUEUE_NOTES_PER_PAGE, which can exceed the nr_notes value used for the bitmap allocation when nr_notes is not a multiple of WATCH_QUEUE_NOTES_PER_PAGE.

evidence_lines.code: wqueue->nr_notes = nr_pages * WATCH_QUEUE_NOTES_PER_PAGE;

commit_msg:
drm/amd/display: memory leak

In dcn*_clock_source_create when dcn20_clk_src_construct fails allocated
clk_src needs release.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Alex Deucher <alexander.deucher@amd.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tkfree(clk_src);']}
description: Memory leaks in *clock_source_create() functions under drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc in the Linux kernel before 5.3.8 allow attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption). This affects the dce112_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce112/dce112_resource.c, the dce100_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce100/dce100_resource.c, the dcn10_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dcn10/dcn10_resource.c, the dcn20_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dcn20/dcn20_resource.c, the dce120_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce120/dce120_resource.c, the dce110_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce110/dce110_resource.c, and the dce80_clock_source_create() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce80/dce80_resource.c, aka CID-055e547478a1.

code_evidence: clk_src is allocated with kzalloc and checked for NULL; on allocation failure the function returns without any further resource to release.
If dce112_clk_src_construct succeeds, the base pointer is returned and ownership transfers to the caller, so no free is needed here.
When construct fails, control falls through to BREAK_TO_DEBUGGER and returns NULL without releasing the previously allocated clk_src; the patch adds kfree(clk_src) before this return.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The allocation is never released on the construct-failure path, matching CWE-401's missing release of allocated memory after its effective lifetime. This is a leak on an exceptional path, not a use-after-free or double-free, since the pointer is simply discarded without further use.

evidence_lines.code:
BREAK_TO_DEBUGGER();
return NULL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path after a failed dce112_clk_src_construct returns NULL without freeing the kzalloc'd clk_src. Trigger: repeated construct failures (e.g., invalid clock source configuration) call this create function and abandon each allocation. Consequence: cumulative unreleased kernel memory leading to resource consumption and possible denial of service.
