commit_msg:
Simplify the timerqueue code by using cached rbtrees and rely on the tree
leftmost node semantics to get the timer with earliest expiration time.
This is a drop in conversion, and therefore semantics remain untouched.

The runtime overhead of cached rbtrees is be pretty much the same as the
current head->next method, noting that when removing the leftmost node,
a common operation for the timerqueue, the rb_next(leftmost) is O(1) as
well, so the next timer will either be the right node or its parent.
Therefore no extra pointer chasing. Finally, the size of the struct
timerqueue_head remains the same.

Passes several hours of rcutorture.

Signed-off-by: Davidlohr Bueso <dbueso@suse.de>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190724152323.bojciei3muvfxalm@linux-r8p5
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct rb_node **p = &head->head.rb_node;', '\tstruct timerqueue_node  *ptr;', '\t\tif (node->expires < ptr->expires)', '\t\telse', '\trb_insert_color(&node->node, &head->head);', '\tif (!head->next || node->expires < head->next->expires) {', '\t\thead->next = node;', '\t\treturn true;', '\t}', '\treturn false;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct rb_node **p = &head->rb_root.rb_root.rb_node;', '\tstruct timerqueue_node *ptr;', '\tbool leftmost = true;', '\t\tif (node->expires < ptr->expires) {', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t\tleftmost = false;', '\t\t}', '\trb_insert_color_cached(&node->node, &head->rb_root, leftmost);', '\treturn leftmost;']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. A corrupted timer tree caused the task wakeup to be missing in the timerqueue_add function in lib/timerqueue.c. This flaw allows a local attacker with special user privileges to cause a denial of service, slowing and eventually stopping the system while running OSP.

code_evidence: Local search state is set up: p points at the tree root, parent is NULL, and ptr is declared but not yet assigned.
The traversal loop dereferences and compares node->expires against ptr->expires while descending left or right to locate the insertion point.

After rb_link_node and rb_insert_color, head->next is conditionally updated only when the new node's expiry is earlier than the cached next node; otherwise the cached earliest pointer is left unchanged.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-665 fits because the cached earliest-node state in head->next is not properly (re)initialized or reconciled on every insertion, leaving the resource in an unexpected state when later accessed. This is distinct from a bounds or type error: the weakness is improper initialization of the cached tree state, not a memory-safety violation per se.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function maintains head->next as the cached earliest-expiration node, but the update at lines 17-21 only replaces it when the inserted node is strictly earlier. If the tree's cached earliest state is corrupted or inconsistent, insertion does not re-derive it; the stale head->next persists. Triggered by a corrupted timer tree, later timerqueue reads consume this inconsistent cached state, and the described consequence is a missing task wakeup leading to DoS.

commit_msg:
Eric Dumazet says:

====================
Juha-Matti Tilli reported that malicious peers could inject tiny
packets in out_of_order_queue, forcing very expensive calls
to tcp_collapse_ofo_queue() and tcp_prune_ofo_queue() for
every incoming packet.

With tcp_rmem[2] default of 6MB, the ooo queue could
contain ~7000 nodes.

This patch series makes sure we cut cpu cycles enough to
render the attack not critical.

We might in the future go further, like disconnecting
or black-holing proven malicious flows.
====================

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tsk_mem_reclaim(sk);', '\t\tif (atomic_read(&sk->sk_rmem_alloc) <= sk->sk_rcvbuf &&', '\t\t    !tcp_under_memory_pressure(sk))', '\t\t\tbreak;'], 'added_lines': ['\tint goal;', '\tgoal = sk->sk_rcvbuf >> 3;', '\t\tgoal -= rb_to_skb(node)->truesize;', '\t\tif (!prev || goal <= 0) {', '\t\t\tsk_mem_reclaim(sk);', '\t\t\tif (atomic_read(&sk->sk_rmem_alloc) <= sk->sk_rcvbuf &&', '\t\t\t    !tcp_under_memory_pressure(sk))', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\tgoal = sk->sk_rcvbuf >> 3;', '\t\t}']}
description: Linux kernel versions 4.9+ can be forced to make very expensive calls to tcp_collapse_ofo_queue() and tcp_prune_ofo_queue() for every incoming packet which can lead to a denial of service.

code_evidence: The loop walks the out-of-order queue from ooo_last_skb backwards, erasing and dropping one skb per iteration. Each iteration calls sk_mem_reclaim(sk) and then re-evaluates atomic_read(&sk->sk_rmem_alloc) <= sk->sk_rcvbuf and !tcp_under_memory_pressure(sk) before deciding to break; otherwise it continues to prev. There is no bound on iterations per call other than the queue contents, so a large queue (up to ~7000 nodes per the commit message) forces the full reclaim/check sequence for every node.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 applies because the function fails to bound/throttle the per-call resource (CPU) consumption while draining a queue whose size is attacker-influenced. The missing constraint is the lack of a per-iteration work budget, matching uncontrolled consumption rather than an out-of-bounds or memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pruning loop performs an expensive sk_mem_reclaim and memory-pressure check on every removed node without throttling the work per call. Trigger: an attacker injects many tiny out-of-order packets, inflating the ooo queue; each subsequent packet invokes this traversal. Consequence: excessive CPU consumption, a denial of service, as reported in the commit message.

avcodec/tiff: Check subsample & rps values more completely

Fixes out of array access
Fixes: 83aedfb29af669c4d6e10f1bfad974d2/asan_heap-oob_1ab42fe_4984_9f6ec14462f8d8a00ea24b320572a963.tif

Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        for (i = 0; i < count; i++)'], 'added_lines': ['        for (i = 0; i < count; i++) {', '            if (s->subsampling[i] <= 0) {', '                av_log(s->avctx, AV_LOG_ERROR, "subsampling %d is invalid\\n", s->subsampling[i]);', '                return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;', '            }', '        }']}
description: libavcodec/tiff.c in FFmpeg before 2.8.6 does not properly validate RowsPerStrip values and YCbCr chrominance subsampling factors, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds array access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted TIFF file, related to the tiff_decode_tag and decode_frame functions.

code_evidence: The TIFF_YCBCR_SUBSAMPLING case validates only that count == 2, then loops i < count reading two values from the bitstream into s->subsampling[i] without checking that each value is positive. The fix adds a check that s->subsampling[i] <= 0 returns AVERROR_INVALIDDATA, showing the pre-fix code accepted zero or negative subsampling factors that are later used as dimensions/divisors.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an improperly bounded memory operation: unvalidated subsampling values lead to reads/writes outside the intended buffer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory access. The missing input validation is the root cause, but the direct supported consequence is out-of-bounds buffer access, so CWE-119 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation of YCbCr subsampling factors read from the TIFF tag. A crafted TIFF supplies a subsampling value of zero or negative; downstream decode_frame uses these factors to compute buffer sizes and offsets, producing out-of-bounds array access. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds read/write leading to denial of service or possibly code execution.

commit_msg:
misc: sgi-gru: fix use-after-free error in gru_set_context_option, gru_fault and gru_handle_user_call_os

In some bad situation, the gts may be freed gru_check_chiplet_assignment.
The call chain can be gru_unload_context->gru_free_gru_context->gts_drop
and kfree finally. However, the caller didn't know if the gts is freed
or not and use it afterwards. This will trigger a Use after Free bug.

Fix it by introducing a return value to see if it's in error path or not.
Free the gts in caller if gru_check_chiplet_assignment check failed.

Fixes: 55484c45dbec ("gru: allow users to specify gru chiplet 2")
Signed-off-by: Zheng Wang <zyytlz.wz@163.com>
Acked-by: Dimitri Sivanich <sivanich@hpe.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20221110035033.19498-1-zyytlz.wz@163.com
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tgru_check_context_placement(gts);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (gru_check_context_placement(gts)) {', '\t\tpreempt_enable();', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&gts->ts_ctxlock);', '\t\tgru_unload_context(gts, 1);', '\t\treturn VM_FAULT_NOPAGE;', '\t}']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s SGI GRU driver in the way the first gru_file_unlocked_ioctl function is called by the user, where a fail pass occurs in the gru_check_chiplet_assignment function. This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: After locking gts->ts_ctxlock and disabling preemption, the code calls gru_check_context_placement(gts) but ignores any failure indication, then immediately dereferences gts->ts_gru at line 18.

The retry path at 'again' reuses gts after gru_assign_gru_context fails: it unlocks, sleeps, calls gru_steal_context(gts), and jumps back to 'again', re-reading gts->ts_ctxlock and gts->ts_gru without revalidating that gts still exists.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function retains and reuses a gts pointer after an error path may have freed it, with no null/validity recheck. This is a stale-pointer reuse, not merely a missing error return or double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that a failed placement/assignment check can free the gts (via gru_unload_context/gts_drop), yet the caller continues to dereference or re-lock the same stale gts pointer. Trigger is the check failing and the retry loop reusing gts; the supported consequence is use-after-free of freed gru_thread_state memory, leading to crash or potential memory corruption.

commit_msg:
x86,kvm,vmx: Preserve CR4 across VM entry

CR4 isn't constant; at least the TSD and PCE bits can vary.

TBH, treating CR0 and CR3 as constant scares me a bit, too, but it looks
like it's correct.

This adds a branch and a read from cr4 to each vm entry.  Because it is
extremely likely that consecutive entries into the same vcpu will have
the same host cr4 value, this fixes up the vmcs instead of restoring cr4
after the fact.  A subsequent patch will add a kernel-wide cr4 shadow,
reducing the overhead in the common case to just two memory reads and a
branch.

Signed-off-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@amacapital.net>
Acked-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Cc: Petr Matousek <pmatouse@redhat.com>
Cc: Gleb Natapov <gleb@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tvmcs_writel(HOST_CR4, read_cr4());  /* 22.2.3, 22.2.5 */'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned long cr4;', '', "\t/* Save the most likely value for this task's CR4 in the VMCS. */", '\tcr4 = read_cr4();', '\tvmcs_writel(HOST_CR4, cr4);\t\t\t/* 22.2.3, 22.2.5 */', '\tvmx->host_state.vmcs_host_cr4 = cr4;']}
description: arch/x86/kvm/vmx.c in the KVM subsystem in the Linux kernel before 3.17.2 on Intel processors does not ensure that the value in the CR4 control register remains the same after a VM entry, which allows host OS users to kill arbitrary processes or cause a denial of service (system disruption) by leveraging /dev/kvm access, as demonstrated by PR_SET_TSC prctl calls within a modified copy of QEMU.

code_evidence: The function writes the host's current CR4 into the VMCS via vmcs_writel(HOST_CR4, read_cr4()) only once during this 'constant' setup, alongside HOST_CR0 and HOST_CR3. Because CR4 is not actually constant (e.g., TSD/PCE bits can change per task), the VMCS retains a stale host CR4 value across VM entries.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is failure to properly maintain a shared/limited host resource (control-register state) across VM entries, enabling attacker-triggered system disruption; this is the resource-maintenance/availability impact captured by CWE-400, though the immediate mechanism is state corruption rather than allocation throttling.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function caches read_cr4() as a constant host-state value in the VMCS instead of preserving/restoring it per VM entry. Trigger: a userspace process with /dev/kvm access alters its CR4 (e.g., via PR_SET_TSC) before/around VM entry, so the stale cached CR4 is loaded on VM exit. Consequence: host CR4 state corruption causing system disruption/DoS (arbitrary process kill).

commit_msg:
This code calls fd_install() which gives the userspace access to the fd.
Then if copy_info_records_to_user() fails it calls put_unused_fd(fd) but
that will not release it and leads to a stale entry in the file
descriptor table.

Generally you can't trust the fd after a call to fd_install().  The fix
is to delay the fd_install() until everything else has succeeded.

Fortunately it requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN to reach this code so the security
impact is less.

Fixes: f644bc449b37 ("fanotify: fix copy_event_to_user() fid error clean up")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220128195656.GA26981@kili
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Mathias Krause <minipli@grsecurity.net>
Signed-off-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (f)', '\t\tfd_install(fd, f);', ''], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (f)', '\t\tfd_install(fd, f);']}
description: A use after free in the Linux kernel File System notify functionality was found in the way user triggers copy_info_records_to_user() call to fail in copy_event_to_user(). A local user could use this flaw to crash the system or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: Line 50 installs the file into the fd table with fd_install(fd, f), making the descriptor visible to userspace before the copy at lines 52-53 can fail.
If copy_info_records_to_user() returns negative, line 55 jumps to out_close_fd, where lines 59-61 call put_unused_fd(fd) and fput(f) on an fd that was already installed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale fd entry references a file whose fput() cleanup releases it while userspace can still access the descriptor, matching CWE-416 use after free. A mere resource leak would not free the object; here the file is freed while still reachable through the fd table.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fd_install() is performed before all remaining operations succeed. Trigger: copy_info_records_to_user() fails after the fd is installed. The cleanup path then treats the installed fd as unused and frees the file via fput(), leaving a stale descriptor table entry that can be reused, producing a use-after-free.

description: Moonlight-common-c contains the core GameStream client code shared between Moonlight clients. Moonlight-common-c is vulnerable to buffer overflow starting in commit f57bd745b4cbed577ea654fad4701bea4d38b44c. A malicious game streaming server could exploit a buffer overflow vulnerability to crash a moonlight client. Achieving RCE is possible but unlikely, due to stack canaries in use by modern compiler toolchains. The published binaries for official clients Qt, Android, iOS/tvOS, and Embedded are built with stack canaries, but some unofficial clients may not use stack canaries. This vulnerability takes place after the pairing process, so it requires the client to be tricked into pairing to a malicious host. It is not possible to perform using a man-in-the-middle due to public key pinning that takes place during the pairing process. The bug was addressed in commit b2497a3918a6d79808d9fd0c04734786e70d5954.

code_evidence: Line 11 derives currentPos.length from the attacker-controlled packet length minus the header size. At lines 73-76, when firstPacket is set and the version check passes, the code unconditionally adds 8 to currentPos.offset and subtracts 8 from currentPos.length without verifying that length is at least 8. The resulting length can underflow or become inconsistent with the actual buffer, and the adjusted descriptor is then passed to processRtpPayloadSlow/Fast for parsing and copying.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the unchecked length adjustment lets subsequent copy/parse operations write or read past the output buffer based on an unvalidated input size. It is a size-checking failure on a copy path rather than a pure out-of-bounds read, so CWE-120 is preferred over CWE-125.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the frame-header skip adjusts the buffer descriptor (offset += 8, length -= 8) without checking that the packet actually contains the 8-byte header. Trigger: a malicious server sends a first packet whose declared length is small (e.g., <= sizeof(*videoPacket)+8) and version qualifies. Consequence: currentPos.length underflows to a huge or negative value, so downstream parsing/copying reads or writes beyond the packet buffer, causing crash or memory corruption (RCE unlikely due to canaries).

commit_msg:
When setting up a device, we can krealloc the config->socks array to add
new sockets to the configuration.  However if we happen to get a IO
request in at this point even though we aren't setup we could hit a UAF,
as we deref config->socks without any locking, assuming that the
configuration was setup already and that ->socks is safe to access it as
we have a reference on the configuration.

But there's nothing really preventing IO from occurring at this point of
the device setup, we don't want to incur the overhead of a lock to
access ->socks when it will never change while the device is running.
To fix this UAF scenario simply freeze the queue if we are adding
sockets.  This will protect us from this particular case without adding
any additional overhead for the normal running case.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Josef Bacik <josef@toxicpanda.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/*', "\t * We need to make sure we don't get any errant requests while we're", '\t * reallocating the ->socks array.', '\t */', '\tblk_mq_freeze_queue(nbd->disk->queue);', '\tblk_mq_unfreeze_queue(nbd->disk->queue);', '\tblk_mq_unfreeze_queue(nbd->disk->queue);']}
description: nbd_add_socket in drivers/block/nbd.c in the Linux kernel through 5.10.12 has an ndb_queue_rq use-after-free that could be triggered by local attackers (with access to the nbd device) via an I/O request at a certain point during device setup, aka CID-b98e762e3d71.

code_evidence: nbd_add_socket grows config->socks with krealloc and reassigns config->socks, then writes socks[config->num_connections++] and increments live_connections with no synchronization against request processing.
The function performs no queue freeze or lock around the krealloc/reassign and array write, so an I/O request can dereference config->socks concurrently during setup.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because a shared resource (config->socks) is modified in a code sequence that lacks exclusive access, allowing an interfering concurrent request path to observe the stale or freed array. The weakness is the missing synchronization window, not merely an invalid pointer.

evidence_lines.code:
socks[config->num_connections++] = nsock;
atomic_inc(&config->live_connections);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: config->socks is reallocated and reassigned without excluding concurrent ndb_queue_rq execution. Trigger: a local attacker with nbd device access issues an I/O request while another task is adding a socket, so the queue path dereferences config->socks during or after krealloc. Supported consequence: use-after-free and kernel crash/instability (DoS).

commit_msg:
xen: Make coherent PV IOMMU discipline

In order for a PV domain to set up DMA from a passed-through device to
one of its pages, the page must be mapped in the IOMMU.  On the other
hand, before a PV page may be used as a "special" page type (such as a
pagetable or descriptor table), it _must not_ be writable in the IOMMU
(otherwise a malicious guest could DMA arbitrary page tables into the
memory, bypassing Xen's safety checks); and Xen's current rule is to
have such pages not in the IOMMU at all.

At the moment, in order to accomplish this, the code borrows HVM
domain's "physmap" concept: When a page is assigned to a guest,
guess_physmap_add_entry() is called, which for PV guests, will create
a writable IOMMU mapping; and when a page is removed,
guest_physmap_remove_entry() is called, which will remove the mapping.

Additionally, when a page gains the PGT_writable page type, the page
will be added into the IOMMU; and when the page changes away from a
PGT_writable type, the page will be removed from the IOMMU.

Unfortunately, borrowing the "physmap" concept from HVM domains is
problematic.  HVM domains have a lock on their p2m tables, ensuring
synchronization between modifications to the p2m; and all hypercall
parameters must first be translated through the p2m before being used.

Trying to mix this locked-and-gated approach with PV's lock-free
approach leads to several races and inconsistencies:

* A race between a page being assigned and it being put into the
  physmap; for example:
  - P1: call populate_physmap() { A = allocate_domheap_pages() }
  - P2: Guess page A's mfn, and call decrease_reservation(A).  A is owned by the domain,
        and so Xen will clear the PGC_allocated bit and free the page
  - P1: finishes populate_physmap() { guest_physmap_add_entry() }

  Now the domain has a writable IOMMU mapping to a page it no longer owns.

* Pages start out as type PGT_none, but with a writable IOMMU mapping.
  If a guest uses a page as a page table without ever having created a
  writable mapping, the IOMMU mapping will not be removed; the guest
  will have a writable IOMMU mapping to a page it is currently using
  as a page table.

* A newly-allocated page can be DMA'd into with no special actions on
  the part of the guest; However, if a page is promoted to a
  non-writable type, the page must be mapped with a writable type before
  DMA'ing to it again, or the transaction will fail.

To fix this, do away with the "PV physmap" concept entirely, and
replace it with the following IOMMU discipline for PV guests:
 - (type == PGT_writable) <=> in iommu (even if type_count == 0)
 - Upon a final put_page(), check to see if type is PGT_writable; if so,
   iommu_unmap.

In order to achieve that:

- Remove PV IOMMU related code from guest_physmap_*

- Repurpose cleanup_page_cacheattr() into a general
  cleanup_page_mappings() function, which will both fix up Xen
  mappings for pages with special cache attributes, and also check for
  a PGT_writable type and remove pages if appropriate.

- For compatibility with current guests, grab-and-release a
  PGT_writable_page type for PV guests in guest_physmap_add_entry().
  This will cause most "normal" guest pages to start out life with
  PGT_writable_page type (and thus an IOMMU mapping), but no type
  count (so that they can be used as special cases at will).

Also, note that there is one exception to to the "PGT_writable => in
iommu" rule: xenheap pages shared with guests may be given a
PGT_writable type with one type reference.  This reference prevents
the type from changing, which in turn prevents page from gaining an
IOMMU mapping in get_page_type().  It's not clear whether this was
intentional or not, but it's not something to change in a security
update.

This is XSA-288.

Reported-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges by leveraging incorrect use of the HVM physmap concept for PV domains.

code_evidence: The page's count_info is updated with a cmpxchg loop that clears PGC_count_mask|PGC_allocated without holding d->page_alloc_lock; the lock is only taken later at line 27.

commit_msg:
dccp/tcp: do not inherit mc_list from parent

syzkaller found a way to trigger double frees from ip_mc_drop_socket()

It turns out that leave a copy of parent mc_list at accept() time,
which is very bad.

Very similar to commit 8b485ce69876 ("tcp: do not inherit
fastopen_req from parent")

Initial report from Pray3r, completed by Andrey one.
Thanks a lot to them !

Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Pray3r <pray3r.z@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Tested-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tinet_sk(newsk)->mc_list = NULL;', '']}
description: The inet_csk_clone_lock function in net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c in the Linux kernel through 4.10.15 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (double free) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging use of the accept system call.

code_evidence: sk_clone_lock(sk, priority) copies the listener socket into newsk, so the child inherits the parent's inet_sk mc_list pointer.
The child is only marked with sock_reset_flag(newsk, SOCK_RCU_FREE); no per-socket multicast list is cleared or reset.
The cloned child retains shared pointer fields (e.g., sk_mark, sk_cookie are then copied from the request) but the inherited mc_list pointer is never detached from the parent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit and description state that ip_mc_drop_socket() frees the inherited mc_list twice because parent and child share the same pointer, which is exactly CWE-415. It is not merely a use-after-free: the same memory is freed on two separate drop paths.

evidence_lines.code:
struct sock *newsk = sk_clone_lock(sk, priority);
if (newsk) {
sock_reset_flag(newsk, SOCK_RCU_FREE);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Because mc_list is inherited by reference from the listener at accept() time, the child and parent reference the same multicast membership list. Dropping the socket on either side frees the shared list; a subsequent drop frees it again. The root cause is missing detachment of the inherited pointer, and the trigger is accept() followed by socket teardown, yielding a double free (DoS).

description: The base64decode function in base64.c in libimobiledevice libplist through 1.12 allows attackers to obtain sensitive information from process memory or cause a denial of service (buffer over-read) via split encoded Apple Property List data.

code_evidence: The loop calls strspn(ptr, ...) to skip whitespace, then dereferences *ptr in the check at line 12. strspn stops at the first non-whitespace byte, but if the input has no terminating byte within buf+len (e.g., len is caller-supplied and the buffer is not NUL-terminated), *ptr reads at or beyond buf+len.

strcspn(ptr, ...) at line 15 similarly scans until a whitespace or NUL, potentially reading past buf+len. The guard ptr+l <= buf+len at line 16 is evaluated only after strcspn has already scanned the memory, so it does not prevent the over-read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the intended buf+len region, which is exactly CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). It is not an out-of-bounds write because the reads occur in strspn/strcspn and the *ptr dereference, not in the output buffer writes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: whitespace-scanning functions (strspn/strcspn) and the *ptr check operate on a buffer whose length is given by len but which need not be NUL-terminated, and the bounds guard runs after the scan. Trigger: split encoded input lacking a terminator within len. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of process memory, leaking data or crashing (DoS).

commit_msg: flac: Fix improper buffer reusing

description: An out-of-bounds read flaw was found in libsndfile's FLAC codec functionality. Protect against bad crafted input.

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/128
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (0==e_phnum) throwCantUnpack("0==e_phnum");', '    if ((unsigned long)file_size < (e_phoff + e_phnum * sizeof(Elf64_Phdr))) {', '        throwCantUnpack("bad e_phoff");', '    }', '    if ((unsigned long)file_size < (e_shoff + e_shnum * sizeof(Elf64_Shdr))) {', '        throwCantUnpack("bad e_shoff");', '    }']}
description: p_lx_elf.cpp in UPX 3.94 mishandles ELF headers, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted binary file, as demonstrated by an Invalid Pointer Read in PackLinuxElf64::unpack().

code_evidence: e_phoff and e_shoff are read directly from the crafted ELF header, then sz_phdrs = e_phnum * e_phentsize; the non-ET_DYN path allocates len = sz_phdrs + e_phoff, reads len bytes, and sets phdri = e_phoff + file_image without validating e_phoff against file_size.

The ET_DYN path allocates file_size bytes, reads them, and sets phdri/shdri from e_phoff/e_shoff; the loop then dereferences each phdr->p_type without checking that e_phoff + e_phnum*sizeof(Elf64_Phdr) lies within the allocated image.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing file_size bounds check lets header offsets produce an out-of-range pointer that is then dereferenced, the invalid-pointer-read crash described in the advisory. This is CWE-476 rather than CWE-125 because the defect is the unchecked offset arithmetic yielding an invalid pointer before dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Untrusted e_phoff/e_shoff/e_phnum from the ELF header are used to compute buffer offsets and the phdr iteration range without bounds checks. A crafted binary makes phdri or shdri point outside the file_image allocation, and subsequent reads of phdr->p_type or the section data dereference an invalid pointer, crashing the unpacker (invalid pointer read).

commit_msg:
drm/ttm: fix start page for huge page check in ttm_put_pages()

The first page entry is always the same with itself.

Signed-off-by: Christian König <christian.koenig@amd.com>
Reviewed-by: Michel Dänzer <michel.daenzer@amd.com>
Reviewed-by: Junwei Zhang <Jerry.Zhang@amd.com>
Reviewed-by: Huang Rui <ray.huang@amd.com>
Signed-off-by: Alex Deucher <alexander.deucher@amd.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tfor (j = 0; j < HPAGE_PMD_NR; ++j)', '\t\t\tfor (j = 0; j < HPAGE_PMD_NR; ++j)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tfor (j = 1; j < HPAGE_PMD_NR; ++j)', '\t\t\tfor (j = 1; j < HPAGE_PMD_NR; ++j)']}
description: In the Linux kernel 5.0.0-rc7 (as distributed in ubuntu/linux.git on kernel.ubuntu.com), mounting a crafted f2fs filesystem image and performing some operations can lead to slab-out-of-bounds read access in ttm_put_pages in drivers/gpu/drm/ttm/ttm_page_alloc.c. This is related to the vmwgfx or ttm module.

code_evidence: In the pool==NULL path, p is initialized to pages[i] at line 14, then the huge-page loop at 24-26 compares p++ against pages[i+j] for j=0..HPAGE_PMD_NR-1, so the first comparison is pages[i] against itself and the last reads pages[i+HPAGE_PMD_NR-1].
In the huge-pool path, p=pages[i] at line 48 and the loop at 52-54 similarly indexes pages[i+j] starting at j=0, reading up to pages[i+HPAGE_PMD_NR-1].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The off-by-one loop bound causes a read past the end of the pages array, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not merely a logic error because the extra iteration dereferences an out-of-range element; the self-comparison at j=0 is the root cause of the shifted access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The huge-page detection loop starts its index at 0 while p already holds pages[i], so the loop performs one extra iteration and indexes pages[i+HPAGE_PMD_NR-1]. When npages-i is exactly HPAGE_PMD_NR the bound is satisfied but the shifted indexing still reads one element beyond the intended contiguous run; the fix starts j at 1. The trigger is a crafted page array with a huge-page-sized run, and the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read of the pages array.

commit_msg:
The ALSA proc helper manages the child nodes in a linked list, but its
addition and deletion is done without any lock.  This leads to a
corruption if they are operated concurrently.  Usually this isn't a
problem because the proc entries are added sequentially in the driver
probe procedure itself.  But the card registrations are done often
asynchronously, and the crash could be actually reproduced with
syzkaller.

This patch papers over it by protecting the link addition and deletion
with the parent's mutex.  There is "access" mutex that is used for the
file access, and this can be reused for this purpose as well.

Reported-by: syzbot+48df349490c36f9f54ab@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (parent)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (parent) {', '\t\tmutex_lock(&parent->access);', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&parent->access);', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10. There is a use-after-free in the sound subsystem because card disconnection causes certain data structures to be deleted too early. This is related to sound/core/init.c and sound/core/info.c.

code_evidence: snd_info_create_entry allocates a new entry with kzalloc [6] and, when a parent is supplied [21], links it into parent->children via list_add_tail [22] without any synchronization. The entry becomes reachable through the parent's child list while the parent may be concurrently torn down, so the list operation can touch a freed parent/children list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unlocked insertion into a parent list that may be freed concurrently is a use-after-free pattern, matching CWE-416. It is not merely a missing-lock issue because the supported consequence is access to freed memory, not just a data race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the unsynchronized list_add_tail on parent->children while parent deletion can run concurrently. Trigger is a card registration/disconnection race where the child entry is added after the parent's list is freed; the list operation then dereferences freed memory, causing corruption or crash (use-after-free).

Fixed OOB Read in license_read_new_or_upgrade_license_packet

CVE-2020-11099 thanks to @antonio-morales for finding this.

Stream_Seek(cbScope) then Stream_Read_UINT32(cbCompanyName) at lines 39-40 reads 4 bytes with no remaining-length check before the read; the check at line 41 applies to the company-name payload, not the length field.
Stream_Seek(cbProductId) then Stream_Read_UINT32(cbProductId) at lines 47-48 likewise reads a 4-byte length field without a preceding remaining-length guard.
Stream_Seek(cbLicenseInfo) then Stream_Read_UINT32(cbLicenseInfo) at lines 55-56 reads the license-info length field with no prior bounds check.

commit_msg:
Seth found that the CPU-entry-area; the piece of per-cpu data that is
mapped into the userspace page-tables for kPTI is not subject to any
randomization -- irrespective of kASLR settings.

On x86_64 a whole P4D (512 GB) of virtual address space is reserved for
this structure, which is plenty large enough to randomize things a
little.

As such, use a straight forward randomization scheme that avoids
duplicates to spread the existing CPUs over the available space.

  [ bp: Fix le build. ]

Reviewed-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>

Signed-off-by: Borislav Petkov <bp@suse.de>

commit_msg:
net: rose: fix UAF bugs caused by timer handler

There are UAF bugs in rose_heartbeat_expiry(), rose_timer_expiry()
and rose_idletimer_expiry(). The root cause is that del_timer()
could not stop the timer handler that is running and the refcount
of sock is not managed properly.

One of the UAF bugs is shown below:

    (thread 1)          |        (thread 2)
                        |  rose_bind
                        |  rose_connect
                        |    rose_start_heartbeat
rose_release            |    (wait a time)
  case ROSE_STATE_0     |
  rose_destroy_socket   |  rose_heartbeat_expiry
    rose_stop_heartbeat |
    sock_put(sk)        |    ...
  sock_put(sk) // FREE  |
                        |    bh_lock_sock(sk) // USE

The sock is deallocated by sock_put() in rose_release() and
then used by bh_lock_sock() in rose_heartbeat_expiry().

Although rose_destroy_socket() calls rose_stop_heartbeat(),
it could not stop the timer that is running.

description: There are use-after-free vulnerabilities caused by timer handler in net/rose/rose_timer.c of linux that allow attackers to crash linux kernel without any privileges.

code_evidence: The timer callback derives sk from the timer (from_timer) and immediately dereferences it via bh_lock_sock(sk), with no reference held on the socket.

In the ROSE_STATE_0 branch, rose_destroy_socket(sk) is invoked and the function returns; the callback continues to use sk without any refcount protection, and the release path can free it concurrently.
The normal path calls rose_start_heartbeat(sk) and bh_unlock_sock(sk) on sk, so the timer handler keeps operating on the socket object after it may have been deallocated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The callback dereferences and locks a struct sock that a concurrent release path can free, matching CWE-416's use of memory after deallocation. This is a lifetime/refcount flaw, not a simple null dereference or double free.

evidence_lines.code:
struct sock *sk = from_timer(sk, t, sk_timer);
bh_lock_sock(sk);

rose_start_heartbeat(sk);
bh_unlock_sock(sk);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The socket is not reference-counted across the timer handler's lifetime. del_timer() in rose_stop_heartbeat() cannot stop a handler already running, so rose_release()/sock_put() can free sk while rose_heartbeat_expiry() still locks or otherwise accesses it, causing a use-after-free crash (potential memory corruption).

commit_msg:
Don't crash if user specified invalid encoding.

This is CVE-2019-9917
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (pSock->GetEncoding().empty()) {', '            pSock->SetEncoding("UTF-8");', '        }'], 'added_lines': ['        pSock->SetEncoding(FixupEncoding(pSock->GetEncoding()));']}
description: ZNC before 1.7.3-rc1 allows an existing remote user to cause a Denial of Service (crash) via invalid encoding.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over every socket and, when GetEncoding() returns an empty string, replaces it with "UTF-8"; otherwise the user-supplied encoding value is passed through unchanged to SetEncoding without any validation or sanitization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function handles an externally supplied encoding string but fails to validate its properties (well-formedness/validity) before use, matching CWE-20 Improper Input Validation. The empty-check is a partial validation that misses invalid non-empty encodings; the fix routes values through FixupEncoding, confirming the missing validation is the root cause rather than output encoding (CWE-116).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-socket encoding taken from the remote user is accepted without validating that it is a valid/known encoding, and only the empty case is handled. Trigger: an existing remote user specifies an invalid encoding value. Consequence: the invalid encoding reaches downstream ICU conversion, causing a crash/denial of service (CVE-2019-9917).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    ok_jpg_decode_restart_if_needed(decoder);', '                    ok_jpg_decode_restart_if_needed(decoder);', '                ok_jpg_decode_restart_if_needed(decoder);'], 'added_lines': ['                    if (!ok_jpg_decode_restart_if_needed(decoder)) {', '                        return false;', '                    }', '                    if (!ok_jpg_decode_restart_if_needed(decoder)) {', '                        return false;', '                    }', '                if (!ok_jpg_decode_restart_if_needed(decoder)) {', '                    return false;', '                }']}
description: David Brackeen ok-file-formats 97f78ca is vulnerable to Buffer Overflow. When the function of the ok-file-formats project is used, a heap-buffer-overflow occurs in function ok_jpg_convert_YCbCr_to_RGB() in "/ok_jpg.c:513" .

code_evidence: Loop decodes blocks into c->blocks via decode_function without checking the restart helper's return value; only eof/huffman_error are checked after the inner loop.
Multi-component path similarly invokes decode_function writing to c->blocks + block_index*64, and block_index advances per component without validating restart success.
Non-progressive path decodes into c->output via idct at offset_x+offset_y and calls ok_jpg_convert_data_unit before any restart-failure check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Ignoring the restart failure lets subsequent decode writes exceed the intended block/output buffer bounds, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The root cause is the unchecked failure, not merely a read overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The restart handler can fail (e.g., truncated input) but its return value is ignored, so decoding continues with stale/invalid restart state and writes proceed to block/output buffers. The trigger is a malformed JPEG restart segment; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write during block/IDCT/YCbCr conversion.

commit_msg: gnrc_sixlowpan_frag_sfr: fix ARQ scheduler race-condition
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            fbuf->sfr.arq_timeout_event.msg.content.ptr = NULL;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: RIOT-OS, an operating system for Internet of Things (IoT) devices, contains a network stack with the ability to process 6LoWPAN frames. In versions 2023.01 and prior, an attacker can send multiple crafted frames to the device to trigger a race condition. The race condition invalidates assumptions about the program state and leads to an invalid memory access resulting in denial of service. This issue is patched in pull request 19679. There are no known workarounds.

code_evidence: _handle_ack looks up the fragmentation buffer by tag, then cancels the ARQ evtimer and clears msg.content.ptr on the shared fbuf->sfr.arq_timeout_event. The event callback can run concurrently with this acknowledgment handling, so the timer state and pointer are accessed without exclusive synchronization between the ACK path and the timeout path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function mutates shared timer/event state (evtimer_del and msg.content.ptr) without exclusive access relative to the concurrently running ARQ timeout sequence, matching CWE-362's non-atomic shared-resource access. The invalid memory access is the downstream effect, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ARQ timeout event and the ACK handler race on the same fragmentation buffer state; the ACK path deletes the timer and nulls the message pointer while the timeout callback may still be executing or pending. Trigger: crafted ACK frames arriving as the ARQ timer fires. Consequence: stale/invalid fbuf access and invalid memory access, leading to denial of service.

commit_msg: Added range check on XRsiz and YRsiz fields of SIZ marker segment.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (siz->comps[i].hsamp == 0 || siz->comps[i].hsamp > 255) {', '\t\t\tjas_eprintf("invalid XRsiz value %d\\n", siz->comps[i].hsamp);', '\t\t\tjas_free(siz->comps);', '\t\t\treturn -1;', '\t\t}', '\t\tif (siz->comps[i].vsamp == 0 || siz->comps[i].vsamp > 255) {', '\t\t\tjas_eprintf("invalid YRsiz value %d\\n", siz->comps[i].vsamp);', '\t\t\tjas_free(siz->comps);', '\t\t\treturn -1;', '\t\t}']}
description: The jpc_dec_process_siz function in libjasper/jpc/jpc_dec.c in JasPer before 1.900.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero error and application crash) via a crafted XRsiz value in a BMP image to the imginfo command.

code_evidence: The loop reads attacker-controlled XRsiz (hsamp) and YRsiz (vsamp) bytes from the input stream via jpc_getuint8 and stores them without any lower-bound check.
These values are retained in siz->comps[i].hsamp/vsamp and later used as sampling factors; nothing in this function rejects a zero value before the component parameters are accepted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because an unvalidated zero sampling factor reaches a division operation. This is distinct from a generic input-validation weakness: the specific supported consequence is division by zero leading to DoS.

evidence_lines.code:
siz->comps[i].sgnd = (tmp >> 7) & 1;
siz->comps[i].prec = (tmp & 0x7f) + 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: hsamp/vsamp are parsed from untrusted input and accepted even when zero, since only the read failure is checked. Trigger: a crafted SIZ marker sets XRsiz to 0. Downstream sampling-factor arithmetic then divides by this value, producing a divide-by-zero crash (availability impact).

commit_msg: TLS 1.3: ensure key for signature in CertificateVerify
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                WOLFSSL_MSG("Oops, peer sent ED25519 key but not in verify");', '                WOLFSSL_MSG("Oops, peer sent ED448 key but not in verify");', '                WOLFSSL_MSG("Oops, peer sent ECC key but not in verify");', '                WOLFSSL_MSG("Oops, peer sent PKCS#1.5 signature");', '                WOLFSSL_MSG("Oops, peer sent RSA key but not in verify");'], 'added_lines': ['                WOLFSSL_MSG("Peer sent ED22519 sig but not ED22519 cert");', '                ret = SIG_VERIFY_E;', '                goto exit_dcv;', '                WOLFSSL_MSG("Peer sent ED448 sig but not ED448 cert");', '                ret = SIG_VERIFY_E;', '                goto exit_dcv;', '                WOLFSSL_MSG("Peer sent ECC sig but not ECC cert");', '                ret = SIG_VERIFY_E;', '                goto exit_dcv;', '                WOLFSSL_MSG("Peer sent PKCS#1.5 algo but not in certificate");', '                WOLFSSL_MSG("Peer sent RSA sig but not RSA cert");', '                ret = SIG_VERIFY_E;', '                goto exit_dcv;']}
description: DoTls13CertificateVerify in tls13.c in wolfSSL before 4.7.0 does not cease processing for certain anomalous peer behavior (sending an ED22519, ED448, ECC, or RSA signature without the corresponding certificate). The client side is affected because man-in-the-middle attackers can impersonate TLS 1.3 servers.

code_evidence: For ED25519, when the peer's sigAlgo is ed25519_sa_algo but peerEd25519KeyPresent is false, the branch only logs a message and falls through without setting an error or jumping to exit_dcv.
For ED448, the analogous check logs and falls through with no error return when peerEd448KeyPresent is false.
For ECC, the ecc_dsa_sa_algo check with !peerEccDsaKeyPresent likewise only logs and continues.
For RSA-PSS, when peerRsaKey is NULL or peerRsaKeyPresent is false, the code only logs and proceeds instead of aborting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to enforce the certificate/key correspondence required to validate the peer's CertificateVerify, so the peer's certificate is not properly validated. That is improper certificate validation (CWE-295), distinct from e.g. a signature-verification bug, because the missing check is on certificate key presence before accepting the handshake.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the CertificateVerify handler detects that the peer sent a signature algorithm without the corresponding certificate key present, but the ED25519/ED448/ECC/RSA-PSS branches merely log and continue rather than aborting. Trigger: a man-in-the-middle sends a TLS 1.3 CertificateVerify using one of these algorithms without the matching certificate. Because processing does not cease, the handshake is not rejected on this basis, letting the attacker impersonate a server.

commit_msg:
ieee802154: atusb: do not use the stack for buffers to make them DMA able

From 4.9 we should really avoid using the stack here as this will not be DMA
able on various platforms. This changes the buffers already being present in
time of 4.9 being released. This should go into stable as well.

Reported-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Stefan Schmidt <stefan@osg.samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned char buffer[3];'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned char *buffer;', '', '\tbuffer = kmalloc(3, GFP_KERNEL);', '\tif (!buffer)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\tkfree(buffer);']}
description: drivers/net/ieee802154/atusb.c in the Linux kernel 4.9.x before 4.9.6 interacts incorrectly with the CONFIG_VMAP_STACK option, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash or memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging use of more than one virtual page for a DMA scatterlist.

code_evidence: The function declares a 3-byte stack array buffer[3] and passes it to atusb_control_msg (a USB control transfer) which writes received device data into it. The buffer is stack-allocated, so it resides in the kernel stack region that may span more than one virtual page under CONFIG_VMAP_STACK.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The transfer writes device-supplied bytes into a buffer whose intended bounds and storage assumptions are violated by DMA scatter-gather across non-contiguous stack pages, producing out-of-bounds memory access/corruption within the buffer's memory region, matching CWE-119. This is not a plain length-check overflow but a buffer-storage/placement error that results in operations outside intended boundaries.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a stack-allocated buffer is handed to a USB/DMA-capable transfer routine that assumes a physically contiguous, DMA-able buffer. Trigger: performing the control transfer on a kernel built with CONFIG_VMAP_STACK, where the stack is not DMA-able and may cross virtual page boundaries. Consequence: DMA scatterlist operates across multiple virtual pages, leading to system crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Bug 697169: Be rigorous with SAFER permissions

Once we've opened our input file from the command line, enforce the SAFER
rules.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (i_ctx_p && starting_arg_file)', '        i_ctx_p->starting_arg_file = false;']}
description: Ghostscript before 9.21 might allow remote attackers to bypass the SAFER mode protection mechanism and consequently read arbitrary files via the use of the .libfile operator in a crafted postscript document.

code_evidence: Line 5 captures starting_arg_file from i_ctx_p and it drives search behavior; for relative names, lines 18-19 set search_with_no_combine to starting_arg_file and enable combined search.
Lines 21-32 branch on minst->search_here_first and pass starting_arg_file into the open helpers, so the SAFER-relevant starting-arg status is propagated into path resolution for the requested fname.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The bypass exposes file contents the operator should not be allowed to read, which is an unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information (CWE-200). The root cause is stale permission-relevant state in lib_file_open rather than a memory-safety bug, so CWE-200 is the appropriate target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function derives the starting-arg-file flag from interpreter state and uses it to select path search behavior for every subsequent lib_file_open call. If that flag remains set after the command-line input is opened, later operations such as .libfile are treated as starting-arg files and get relaxed SAFER path handling. Trigger: a crafted PostScript document invoking file-opening operators after startup. Consequence: SAFER restrictions are bypassed, enabling reads of arbitrary files.

commit_msg:
Remove support for pre-authentication compression. Doing compression
early in the protocol probably seemed reasonable in the 1990s, but
today it's clearly a bad idea in terms of both cryptography (cf.
multiple compression oracle attacks in TLS) and attack surface.

Moreover, to support it across privilege-separation zlib needed
the assistance of a complex shared-memory manager that made the
required attack surface considerably larger.

Prompted by Guido Vranken pointing out a compiler-elided security
check in the shared memory manager found by Stack
(http://css.csail.mit.edu/stack/); ok deraadt@ markus@

NB. pre-auth authentication has been disabled by default in sshd
for >10 years.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\t\t/* Sync memory */', '\t\tmonitor_sync(pmonitor);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The shared memory manager (associated with pre-authentication compression) in sshd in OpenSSH before 7.4 does not ensure that a bounds check is enforced by all compilers, which might allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging access to a sandboxed privilege-separation process, related to the m_zback and m_zlib data structures.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only manages privilege-separation fork/monitor lifecycle and does not itself perform any buffer operation or bounds check; the described out-of-bounds weakness lies in the shared-memory manager (m_zback/m_zlib), not in this code.

description: In BlueZ before 5.55, a double free was found in the gatttool disconnect_cb() routine from shared/att.c. A remote attacker could potentially cause a denial of service or code execution, during service discovery, due to a redundant disconnect MGMT event.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bt_att_cancel only searches chan, req_queue, ind_queue and write_queue, but during disconnect pending discovery operations are notified through a separate discovery queue. commit_msg:
xen/mm: make sure node is less than MAX_NUMNODES

The output of MEMF_get_node(memflags) can be as large as nodeid_t can
hold (currently 255).  This is then used as an index to arrays of size
MAX_NUMNODE, which is 64 on x86 and 1 on ARM, can be passed in by an
untrusted guest (via memory_exchange and increase_reservation) and is
not currently bounds-checked.

Check the value in page_alloc.c before using it, and also check the
value in the hypercall call sites and return -EINVAL if appropriate.
Don't permit domains other than the hardware or control domain to
allocate node-constrained memory.

This is CVE-2017-14316 / XSA-231.

Reported-by: Matthew Daley <mattd@bugfuzz.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    memflags |= MEMF_node(XENMEMF_get_node(exch.out.mem_flags));'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( unlikely(!propagate_node(exch.out.mem_flags, &memflags)) )', '    {', '        rc = -EINVAL;', '        goto fail_early;', '    }', '']}
description: A parameter verification issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x. The function `alloc_heap_pages` allows callers to specify the first NUMA node that should be used for allocations through the `memflags` parameter; the node is extracted using the `MEMF_get_node` macro. While the function checks to see if the special constant `NUMA_NO_NODE` is specified, it otherwise does not handle the case where `node >= MAX_NUMNODES`. This allows an out-of-bounds access to an internal array.

code_evidence: memflags is built from the guest-supplied exch.out.mem_flags; XENMEMF_get_node(exch.out.mem_flags) is placed into MEMF_node without any check that the node index is below MAX_NUMNODES (only the address-bits value is clamped at [73,76]).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked node index is used as an array index into node tables, reading past the array bounds, which matches CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. It is not merely an integer overflow, since the defect is the missing bounds check on the index before use.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a guest-controlled NUMA node index is packed into memflags and propagated to page allocation without bounds validation. Trigger: a guest issues XENMEM_exchange with an out-of-range node. Consequence: allocation code indexes node-sized arrays with this value, causing an out-of-bounds read (and possible crash); the patch adds propagate_node validation returning -EINVAL.

commit_msg:
Packet sockets may switch ring versions. Avoid misinterpreting state
between versions, whose fields share a union. rx_owner_map is only
allocated with a packet ring (pg_vec) and both are swapped together.
If pg_vec is NULL, meaning no packet ring was allocated, then neither
was rx_owner_map. And the field may be old state from a tpacket_v3.

Fixes: 61fad6816fc1 ("net/packet: tpacket_rcv: avoid a producer race condition")
Reported-by: Syzbot <syzbot+1ac0994a0a0c55151121@syzkaller.appspotmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Willem de Bruijn <willemb@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20211215143937.106178-1-willemdebruijn.kernel@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbitmap_free(rx_owner_map);', '\tif (pg_vec)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (pg_vec) {', '\t\tbitmap_free(rx_owner_map);', '\t}']}
description: A double free bug in packet_set_ring() in net/packet/af_packet.c can be exploited by a local user through crafted syscalls to escalate privileges or deny service. We recommend upgrading kernel past the effected versions or rebuilding past ec6af094ea28f0f2dda1a6a33b14cd57e36a9755

code_evidence: At [109,110], rx_owner_map is swapped with rb->rx_owner_map only when po->tp_version <= TPACKET_V2, so it holds prior ring state and may alias an already-freed pointer when pg_vec is NULL.
At [136,137,138,139], out_free_pg_vec unconditionally calls bitmap_free(rx_owner_map) before checking pg_vec, so a non-NULL stale rx_owner_map is freed even though no new ring was allocated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Freeing rx_owner_map on a path where it was already released by a prior ring setup is a second free of the same address, matching CWE-415. This is distinct from a use-after-free, since the defect is the duplicate release itself.

evidence_lines.code:
if (po->tp_version <= TPACKET_V2)
swap(rb->rx_owner_map, rx_owner_map);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cleanup path frees rx_owner_map without requiring pg_vec, while the field can retain old union state from a prior tpacket_v3 ring. Trigger: a packet_set_ring call that reaches out_free_pg_vec with pg_vec NULL but rx_owner_map non-NULL. Consequence: the same address is freed twice, enabling memory corruption, denial of service, or potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg: fix issues 1368:exist a issues of freeing uninitialized pointer in src/bin/jp2/opj_decompress.c，that will cause a segfault
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '        memset(dirptr, 0, sizeof(dircnt_t));', '']}
description: A flaw was found in the opj2_decompress program in openjpeg2 2.4.0 in the way it handles an input directory with a large number of files. When it fails to allocate a buffer to store the filenames of the input directory, it calls free() on an uninitialized pointer, leading to a segmentation fault and a denial of service.

code_evidence: Line 24 allocates a dircnt_t with malloc but does not zero it; only filename_buf/filename are assigned later. If the buffer allocation at line 29-30 fails, the code jumps to fin at line 33 with dirptr->filename and dirptr->filename_buf still holding unspecified heap contents.
At fin, lines 379-386 test dirptr->filename and dirptr->filename_buf and free() them based on those uninitialized values, causing invalid frees.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a resource (struct) not properly initialized before its fields are read on an error path, matching CWE-665 Improper Initialization. The uninitialized pointer values are then used by free(), which is the concrete manifestation; the fix memset's the struct.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dircnt_t struct is malloc'd without initialization, so its pointer fields contain indeterminate values. Trigger: num_images is large enough that the filename_buf malloc fails, taking the error path to fin before the fields are set. The consequence is free() on garbage pointers, producing a crash/segmentation fault (DoS).

description: In SkSampler::Fill of SkSampler.cpp, there is a possible out of bounds write due to an integer overflow. This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation. Product: Android Versions: Android-7.0 Android-7.1.1 Android-7.1.2 Android-8.0 Android-8.1 Android ID: A-78354855

code_evidence: reset() takes a user-controlled size_t count and, when count exceeds kCount, computes the allocation size as count * sizeof(T) in an unchecked multiplication before passing it to sk_malloc_throw.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the multiplication of two size values can wrap before being used as an allocation size, and the wrapped result is not validated. The consequence is a too-small allocation rather than a mere denial of service; the missing check on the multiplication result is the specific integer-overflow weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (count > kCount) {
fPtr = (T*)sk_malloc_throw(count * sizeof(T));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the unchecked multiplication count * sizeof(T) at line 6: a large count can wrap to a small size_t. commit_msg:
Fix stack buffer overflows when parsing corrupt ihex files.

	PR binutils/18750
	* ihex.c (ihex_scan): Fixes incorrect escape sequence in error message
	and stack overflow when char is signed and \200-\376 was in place of hex
	digit; also fixes \377 was handled as EOF instead of "incorrect character".
	(ihex_read_section): Changed for consistency.
	(ihex_bad_byte): Prevent (now impossible to trigger) stack
	overflow and incorrect escape sequence handling.
	* srec.c (srec_bad_byte): Likewise.

	* readelf.c (process_mips_specific): Fix incorrect escape
	sequence handling.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsprintf (buf, "\\\\%03o", (unsigned int) c);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsprintf (buf, "\\\\%03o", (unsigned int) c & 0xff);']}
description: ihex.c in GNU Binutils before 2.26 contains a stack buffer overflow when printing bad bytes in Intel Hex objects.

code_evidence: A fixed 10-byte stack buffer `buf` is declared, and the non-printable branch formats the byte `c` into it with `sprintf (buf, "\\%03o", (unsigned int) c)` without masking to 8 bits.
For printable input the branch writes only `buf[0]` and `buf[1]`, so the overflow is confined to the `sprintf` path; the resulting `buf` is then passed to the error handler.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe `sprintf` writes past the declared bounds of the stack buffer `buf`, which is a memory-buffer write outside its intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The fix masks with `& 0xff` to bound the formatted output.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: `c` is an `int` that may carry a negative or sign-extended value, and `(unsigned int) c` converts it to a large unsigned value, so `%03o` can emit many octal digits into the 10-byte `buf`. Trigger: a corrupt Intel Hex file supplying a byte such as \200-\376 when `char` is signed. Consequence: a stack buffer overflow with memory corruption when the bad byte is reported.

commit_msg:
Reject fonts with invalid ranges in cmap

A corrupt or malicious font may have a negative size in its cmap
range, which in turn could lead to memory corruption. This patch
detects the case and rejects the font, and also includes an assertion
in the sparse bit set implementation if we missed any such case.

External issue:
https://code.google.com/p/android/issues/detail?id=192618

Bug: 26413177
Change-Id: Icc0c80e4ef389abba0964495b89aa0fae3e9f4b2
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        int end = readU16(data, kEndCountOffset + 2 * i);', '        int start = readU16(data, kHeaderSize + 2 * (segCount + i));', '        int rangeOffset = readU16(data, kHeaderSize + 2 * (3 * segCount + i));', '            int delta = readU16(data, kHeaderSize + 2 * (2 * segCount + i));', '                for (int j = start; j < end + 1; j++) {', '            for (int j = start; j < end + 1; j++) {', '                int glyphId = readU16(data, actualRangeOffset);'], 'added_lines': ['        uint32_t end = readU16(data, kEndCountOffset + 2 * i);', '        uint32_t start = readU16(data, kHeaderSize + 2 * (segCount + i));', '        if (end < start) {', '            // invalid segment range: size must be positive', '            return false;', '        }', '        uint32_t rangeOffset = readU16(data, kHeaderSize + 2 * (3 * segCount + i));', '            uint32_t delta = readU16(data, kHeaderSize + 2 * (2 * segCount + i));', '                for (uint32_t j = start; j < end + 1; j++) {', '            for (uint32_t j = start; j < end + 1; j++) {', '                uint32_t glyphId = readU16(data, actualRangeOffset);']}
description: The Minikin library in Android 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-04-01 does not properly consider negative size values in font data, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory corruption and reboot loop) via a crafted font, aka internal bug 26413177.

code_evidence: end, start and rangeOffset are read directly from attacker-controlled font cmap data with no check that end >= start; the segment size derived from end - start can therefore be negative.

When rangeOffset is nonzero, the loop bounds and actualRangeOffset are computed from start/end and j; a negative or inconsistent range drives offset arithmetic and glyphId reads at unintended positions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts untrusted font metadata and fails to validate a required property (end >= start) before using it in size and offset computations, matching improper input validation. The missing constraint is the cause; memory corruption is the downstream consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cmap format 4 segment fields are parsed without validating that end is not less than start, so the implied segment size becomes negative. Trigger: a crafted font with an inverted segment range. Consequence: incorrect range/offset computation and out-of-bounds handling leading to memory corruption (DoS/reboot loop).

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Reviewed-by: Simon Horman <simon.horman@corigine.com>

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: The function obtains a pointer to the LLCP local object via nfc_llcp_find_local(dev) and only checks it for NULL; it does not acquire a reference on the returned object before continuing.

It then dereferences that pointer by writing local->remote_miu and local->remote_lto and passes it to nfc_llcp_socket_release(local, true, 0); the patch adds nfc_llcp_local_put(local) after this use, confirming the function previously used the object without owning a reference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences and passes along a pointer whose lifetime is not protected by a reference, allowing the object to be freed and then reused. This is memory reuse after free, matching CWE-416 rather than a mere NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nfc_llcp_find_local returns the list entry without taking a reference, so a concurrent nfc_llcp_unregister_device/local_release can free the local object while this function holds the raw pointer. Trigger: unregistration racing with this MAC-down handler. Consequence: the writes and socket-release call operate on freed memory, yielding a use-after-free.

description: The broker in Eclipse Mosquitto 1.3.2 through 2.x before 2.0.16 has a memory leak that can be abused remotely when a client sends many QoS 2 messages with duplicate message IDs, and fails to respond to PUBREC commands. This occurs because of mishandling of EAGAIN from the libc send function.

code_evidence: The function releases the single current_out_packet and then walks the out_packet linked list, calling packet__cleanup and mosquitto__free on each node before resetting out_packet_count.

The patch introduces context__cleanup_out_packets(context) to replace this inline cleanup; the before/after diff shows the same free logic extracted into a shared helper so that all callers release queued output packets.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the weakness is failure to release allocated memory (packet structures) after its effective lifetime, causing a leak. The fix centralizes freeing of current_out_packet and the out_packet list, directly addressing missing release rather than, e.g., a use-after-free.

Trigger: if cleanup is skipped or a caller does not invoke the shared helper, the current_out_packet and out_packet chain remain allocated. Supported consequence: unbounded memory growth, leading to resource exhaustion/DoS.

I got the below warning when do fuzzing test:

 process_one_work+0x49c/0xbdc
 worker_thread+0x124/0x880
 kthread+0x210/0x260
 ret_from_fork+0x10/0x18

This is because the value of rec_seq of tls_crypto_info configured by the
user program is too large, for example, 0xffffffffffffff. In addition, TLS
is asynchronously accelerated. When tls_do_encryption() returns
-EINPROGRESS and sk->sk_err is set to EBADMSG due to rec_seq overflow,
skmsg is released before the asynchronous encryption process ends. As a
result, the UAF problem occurs during the asynchronous processing of the
encryption module.

If the operation is asynchronous and the encryption module returns
EINPROGRESS, do not free the record information.

Fixes: 635d93981786 ("net/tls: free record only on encryption error")
Signed-off-by: Liu Jian <liujian56@huawei.com>
Reviewed-by: Sabrina Dubroca <sd@queasysnail.net>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230909081434.2324940-1-liujian56@huawei.com
Signed-off-by: Paolo Abeni <pabeni@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (err && sk->sk_err == EBADMSG) {', '\t\tif (err && sk->sk_err == EBADMSG) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (err && err != -EINPROGRESS && sk->sk_err == EBADMSG) {', '\t\tif (err && err != -EINPROGRESS && sk->sk_err == EBADMSG) {']}
description: A null pointer dereference flaw was found in the Linux kernel API for the cryptographic algorithm scatterwalk functionality. This issue occurs when a user constructs a malicious packet with specific socket configuration, which could allow a local user to crash the system or escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: After tls_push_record() returns, the error path tests only sk->sk_err == EBADMSG without excluding -EINPROGRESS; on the asynchronous path err is -EINPROGRESS while sk->sk_err was already set to EBADMSG, so the block runs.
The block frees the message and open record (sk_msg_free, tls_free_open_rec) and overwrites err with -sk->sk_err, releasing record state while the async crypto operation still references it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The observed crash is a NULL pointer dereference in the crypto scatterwalk path, matching CWE-476, but the function's defect is premature freeing of asynchronously used state (a use-after-free condition). The NULL dereference is the downstream symptom; the missing -EINPROGRESS constraint is the cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch conflates the asynchronous return -EINPROGRESS with a real EBADMSG failure because it checks only sk->sk_err. Trigger: a user sets an oversized rec_seq so the async encryption sets sk->sk_err=EBADMSG while returning -EINPROGRESS. Consequence: the record and skmsg are freed before async processing completes, leading to a use-after-free that surfaces as a NULL pointer dereference (read at addr 0x8) in scatterwalk_copychunks.

description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: When the CHECK_CLINIT flag is set and the resolved method's class initializeStatus equals vmStruct, the function returns -1. Otherwise, without the new NO_CP_UPDATE guard, it writes the resolved method into staticSplitMethodTable, caching a method whose class may not have run its class initializer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-909 fits because a critical resource—the class's static state—is used before the class initialization method runs. The missing NO_CP_UPDATE constraint lets the uninitialized resource be cached and consumed; this is a missing-initialization issue rather than a simple race or memory-safety defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constant-pool update path caches a resolved static-split method even when class initialization has not completed. Trigger: resolving a static method reference with the class-init check while the class is uninitialized; the method is stored in the split table. Consequence: later callers observe a pre-resolved entry and can invoke static methods or read static members before initialization, exposing uninitialized values.

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tprivate = t->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\tprivate = xt_table_get_private_protected(t);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: After local_bh_disable, the function reads the table private pointer directly from t->private into private, then immediately dereferences private->number without any ordering barrier or protective accessor. Concurrent table replacement can free the old xt_table_info while this dereference or the later xt_entry_foreach over private->entries is still pending.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a table-info pointer that can be freed concurrently, matching CWE-416 (Use After Free). The patch replaces the raw t->private read with xt_table_get_private_protected, confirming the access is the unsafe operation rather than a mere data race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unprotected load of t->private is not ordered against the replacement path's free, so a concurrent rules replacement may release the old table info while this thread still uses it. Trigger: do_add_counters racing with xt_replace_table. Supported consequence: use-after-free read/crash in the counter update path.
