Later, m_SttsAtom is dereferenced via GetDts, again with no NULL check.
When m_CttsAtom is non-NULL, m_CttsAtom is dereferenced via GetCtsOffset; only the m_CttsAtom NULL case itself is handled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function calls methods through pointers it does not verify are non-NULL, directly matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. The missing constraint on m_StscAtom before GetChunkForSample is the clearest instance; this is a null-check omission, not an out-of-bounds access.

evidence_lines.code: result = m_StscAtom->GetChunkForSample(index, chunk, skip, desc);
result = m_SttsAtom->GetDts(index, dts, &duration);
result = m_CttsAtom->GetCtsOffset(index, cts_offset);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dereferences member pointers (m_StscAtom, m_SttsAtom, m_CttsAtom) that malformed MP4 input can leave NULL, since only the stco/co64 atoms are validated. Trigger: a crafted file lacking the stsc (or stts/ctts) atom reaches GetSample. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing an application crash (DoS).

Move onAuthenticated XAUTHORITY generation to the helper

This avoids it being created as root and then chown'd.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '            // redirect standard error to a file', '            m_app->session()->setStandardErrorFile(QString("%1/.xsession-errors").arg(pw->pw_dir));'], 'added_lines': []}
description: Simple Desktop Display Manager (SDDM) before 0.10.0 allows local users to gain root privileges because code running as root performs write operations within a user home directory, and this user may have created links in advance (exploitation requires the user to win a race condition in the ~/.Xauthority chown case, but not other cases).

code_evidence: Line 3 resolves the target user's passwd entry, and the block at [4] runs privileged helper code using pw->pw_dir. Lines [11,12] build a path inside that user-controlled home directory (XAUTHORITY), and line [14] opens/writes ~/.xsession-errors as root via setStandardErrorFile without verifying the path is not a pre-created symlink or hardlink.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission and privilege management; here root privileges are applied to operations on user-controlled paths, allowing the user to redirect privileged writes. The race variant (chown of ~/.Xauthority) is a narrower related issue, but the unsanitized path use as root is the direct supported weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: privileged code performs file creation/redirection inside a directory writable by the unprivileged target user, without checking for existing links. Trigger: the user pre-creates a symlink at ~/.xsession-errors (or ~/.Xauthority) pointing to a root-owned file; the root helper then opens the path. Consequence: arbitrary file write as root, enabling privilege escalation.

description: An issue was discovered in tcpreplay tcpprep v4.3.3. There is a heap buffer overflow vulnerability in get_l2len() that can make tcpprep crash and cause a denial of service.

code_evidence: Only caplen < TCPR_IPV6_H is rejected; smaller IPv4 packets or Ethernet frames with a short L2 header pass this check.

ether_type is read at packet+l2_len and the VLAN loop advances l2_len by 4 per iteration without ever comparing l2_len against pkthdr->caplen, so a crafted/truncated frame can drive l2_len past the capture buffer.
ip_hdr is then formed at packet+l2_len with no per-header bounds check before ip_src/ip_dst are read.
Similarly ip6_hdr at packet+l2_len is dereferenced without verifying caplen covers an IPv6 header.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes an offset from packet data and dereferences it past the allocated capture buffer without a length check, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write/access. The later switch writes ip_hdr->ip_src/ip_dst, so the out-of-range pointer is used for writes, not merely reads.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: l2_len derived from attacker-controlled packet bytes and VLAN iteration is never constrained by pkthdr->caplen. Trigger: a truncated or crafted capture with a short L2 header or repeated VLAN tags. Consequence: reads/writes at packet+l2_len fall outside the heap packet buffer, causing out-of-bounds access and tcpprep crash (DoS).

For configuration protocol options, use ND_TCHECK() and
ND_TCHECK_nBITS() macros, passing them the appropriate pointer argument.
This fixes one case where the ND_TCHECK2() call they replace was not
checking enough bytes.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s), modified
so the capture file won't be rejected as an invalid capture.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tND_TCHECK2(*(p + 2), 2);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tND_TCHECK_16BITS(p+2);']}
description: The PPP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-ppp.c:print_ccp_config_options().

code_evidence: For the IPCPOPT_IPCOMP case, the code only verifies len >= 4 at lines 37-40, then the pre-patch ND_TCHECK2(*(p + 2), 2) at line 41 checked a dereferenced byte value as the buffer pointer (and too few bytes), so it did not reliably validate the 2 bytes read by EXTRACT_16BITS(p+2) at line 42.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads two bytes via EXTRACT_16BITS(p+2) without a correct bounds check, reading past the end of the intended buffer. This is exactly CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read); it is an insufficient validation of a read, not a write or an integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check at line 41 was miswritten, passing a dereferenced value rather than the address p+2 and checking an inadequate length, so the subsequent 16-bit read at line 42 could exceed the captured/allocated buffer when the option length is small. Trigger: a truncated IPCOMP option with len >= 4 but insufficient captured bytes. Consequence: out-of-bounds read (buffer over-read).

commit_msg:
Fix stack buffer overflows when parsing corrupt ihex files.

	PR binutils/18750
	* ihex.c (ihex_scan): Fixes incorrect escape sequence in error message
	and stack overflow when char is signed and \200-\376 was in place of hex
	digit; also fixes \377 was handled as EOF instead of "incorrect character".
	(ihex_read_section): Changed for consistency.
	(ihex_bad_byte): Prevent (now impossible to trigger) stack
	overflow and incorrect escape sequence handling.
	* srec.c (srec_bad_byte): Likewise.

	* readelf.c (process_mips_specific): Fix incorrect escape
	sequence handling.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t  char hdr[8];'], 'added_lines': ['\t  unsigned char hdr[8];']}
description: ihex.c in GNU Binutils before 2.26 contains a stack buffer overflow when printing bad bytes in Intel Hex objects.

code_evidence: Line 38 declares a fixed 8-byte stack buffer 'char hdr[8]' whose element type is signed char.
Line 46 reads exactly 8 bytes from the corrupt ihex file into hdr, then line 48 loops over all 8 indices and line 50 tests each hdr[i] with ISHEX; on failure line 52 passes hdr[i] to ihex_bad_byte.
Line 21 supplies attacker-controlled bytes via ihex_get_byte, so hdr holds file data that can be any byte value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a write beyond the intended bounds of a stack memory buffer, which is exactly CWE-119's out-of-bounds buffer operation. Changing the buffer to unsigned char removes the negative-value path; the root cause is the signed element type interacting with the bad-byte printing routine, not merely an information leak.

evidence_lines.code: char hdr[8];
while ((c = ihex_get_byte (abfd, &error)) != EOF)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a corrupt ihex file places bytes in the range \200-\376 where hex digits are expected, each hdr[i] is a negative signed char. Passing that negative value into ihex_bad_byte's formatting path causes an out-of-bounds stack write (stack buffer overflow) while printing the bad byte, corrupting adjacent stack memory. The trigger is a malformed record; the consequence is memory corruption potentially leading to code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.9. There is a use-after-free in atalk_proc_exit, related to net/appletalk/atalk_proc.c, net/appletalk/ddp.c, and net/appletalk/sysctl_net_atalk.c.

code_evidence: atalk_register_sysctl() stores the return of register_net_sysctl() into the global atalk_table_header without checking it; when registration fails, atalk_table_header is left NULL (or invalid) while the function still returns success to its caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The reported KASAN trace shows a read of freed proc_dir_entry memory (pde_subdir_find) reached through the unchecked-failure cleanup path this function participates in; that is a use-after-free (CWE-416). The unchecked return here is the missing-constraint cause rather than a separate NULL-dereference weakness, since the observable consequence is reuse of freed memory.

evidence_lines.code:
void atalk_register_sysctl(void)
atalk_table_header = register_net_sysctl(&init_net, "net/appletalk", atalk_table);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the registration helper provides no failure signal and no NULL check on register_net_sysctl(). Trigger: atalk_init proceeds as if sysctl registration succeeded even when it failed, so later teardown paths (atalk_proc_exit/atalk_exit) operate on inconsistent proc/sysctl state and reference freed proc_dir_entry memory, as reported in pde_subdir_find. Supported consequence: use-after-free read on the freed proc_dir_entry slab object, leading to crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
Bug 698883: Reset cmap splay tree pointer, handling resized tree.

Without this change a resized cmap splay tree leads to using stale pointers.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\ttree = cmap->tree;']}
description: In MuPDF 1.12.0 and earlier, a stack buffer overflow in function pdf_lookup_cmap_full in pdf/pdf-cmap.c could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code via a crafted file.

code_evidence: tree is cached from cmap->tree at line 11; the recursive add_range call at line 42 can resize cmap->tree via line 98, reallocating it and freeing the old buffer, yet the outer frame continues using its stale local tree pointer at lines 44-52.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer to memory freed by reallocation, which is exactly CWE-416 use after free. The commit fix resets tree = cmap->tree after the recursive call, confirming the stale-pointer root cause. It is not a simple out-of-bounds write because the buffer was reallocated, not merely indexed past its end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a local tree pointer is cached before a recursive call that may reallocate cmap->tree, invalidating the cache. Trigger: a range that strictly encloses an existing node (line 38) recurses, and the recursive call grows the splay array via fz_resize_array. The stale pointer is then dereferenced for tree[current], reading freed memory and potentially corrupting the new allocation.

in heap allocated buffers. Reported as MSVR 35094. Discovered by

Mitigations team.
* libtiff/tif_write.c: fix issue in error code path of TIFFFlushData1()
that didn't reset the tif_rawcc and tif_rawcp members. I'm not
completely sure if that could happen in practice outside of the odd
behaviour of t2p_seekproc() of tiff2pdf). The report points that a
better fix could be to check the return value of TIFFFlushData1() in
places where it isn't done currently, but it seems this patch is enough.
Reported as MSVR 35095. Discovered by Axel Souchet & Vishal Chauhan &

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        {', "            /* We update those variables even in case of error since there's */", "            /* code that doesn't really check the return code of this */", '            /* function */', '            tif->tif_rawcc = 0;', '            tif->tif_rawcp = tif->tif_rawdata;', '        }']}
description: tif_pixarlog.c in libtiff 4.0.6 has out-of-bounds write vulnerabilities in heap allocated buffers. Reported as MSVR 35094, aka "PixarLog horizontalDifference heap-buffer-overflow."

code_evidence: TIFFAppendToStrip is called with tif->tif_rawdata and tif->tif_rawcc; on failure the function returns 0 without resetting tif_rawcc.
The buffer state tif_rawcc/tif_rawcp is only cleared after a successful append (lines 13-14), so an error leaves rawcc pointing at stale data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale length/cursor state feeds subsequent writes beyond the allocated raw buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not simply a missing return-value check (CWE-252); the missing check is the trigger, while the out-of-bounds write is the supported weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
tif->tif_rawcc = 0;
tif->tif_rawcp = tif->tif_rawdata;

description: rudp v0.6 was discovered to contain a memory leak in the component main.c.

code_evidence: rudp_delete releases the nested heap members (send_queue.head, recv_queue.head, send_history.head, free_list, outpackage contents, and send_again.a) but never frees the top-level struct rudp *U itself, so the allocation backing U is left unreleased.

commit_msg:
Forget to reset ctx->password to NULL will lead to bug like double free

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Reviewed-by: Namjae Jeon <linkinjeon@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Quang Le <quanglex97@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Steve French <stfrench@microsoft.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tctx->password = NULL;']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's fs/smb/client component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

In case of an error in smb3_fs_context_parse_param, ctx->password was freed but the field was not set to NULL which could lead to double free.

We recommend upgrading past commit e6e43b8aa7cd3c3af686caf0c2e11819a886d705.

code_evidence: Opt_pass frees ctx->password with kfree_sensitive and sets it to NULL before reallocating via kstrdup; if kstrdup fails, it jumps to cifs_parse_mount_err.
The error label frees ctx->password again with kfree_sensitive but does not reset it to NULL, leaving a dangling pointer in ctx.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The dangling ctx->password is a stale pointer into freed memory that is later used for another free/access, matching CWE-416 use-after-free. The double free is the concrete manifestation of reusing the freed allocation rather than a distinct weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path at cifs_parse_mount_err frees ctx->password without clearing the field. Trigger: an Opt_pass allocation failure (or any parse error after a password was stored) jumps to the label. Consequence: ctx->password remains dangling, so later cleanup/context teardown frees it again (double free) or references freed memory, supporting use-after-free/double-free behavior.

commit_msg:
Hunk extracted from commit 70aacfe66136809d7f080f89c492c278298719f4
upstream.

If the sqpoll thread has died, the out condition doesn't remove the
waiting task from the waitqueue. The goto and check are not needed, just
make it a break condition after setting the error value. That ensures
that we always remove ourselves from sqo_sq_wait waitqueue.

Reported-by: Xingyuan Mo <hdthky0@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tgoto out;', 'out:'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tbreak;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel 5.10.x before 5.10.155. A use-after-free in io_sqpoll_wait_sq in fs/io_uring.c allows an attacker to crash the kernel, resulting in denial of service. finish_wait can be skipped. An attack can occur in some situations by forking a process and then quickly terminating it. NOTE: later kernel versions, such as the 5.15 longterm series, substantially changed the implementation of io_sqpoll_wait_sq.

code_evidence: prepare_to_wait enqueues the task on ctx->sqo_sq_wait, then if ctx->sqo_dead is set the error path takes goto out, jumping over the finish_wait call.
The out label sits after finish_wait, so this early exit returns without removing the wait entry from the waitqueue.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function leaves a stack wait object reachable from ctx->sqo_sq_wait after its lifetime ends; subsequent waitqueue access references freed stack memory, matching CWE-416. The defect is a skipped cleanup that yields a dangling reference, not merely a missing wakeup or logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sqo_dead branch jumps over finish_wait, leaving a waitqueue entry linked to a stack-local wait object after the function returns. Trigger: an attacker forks a process and terminates it quickly, so the sqpoll thread dies and sqo_dead becomes set while a waiter is enqueued. Consequence: the stale waitqueue entry is later traversed and dereferenced, causing a use-after-free that crashes the kernel (DoS).

commit_msg:
io_get_file_fixed will access io_uring's context. Lock it if it is
invoked unlocked (eg via io-wq) to avoid a race condition with fixed
files getting unregistered.

No single upstream patch exists for this issue, it was fixed as part
of the file assignment changes that went into the 5.18 cycle.

Signed-off-by: Jheng, Bing-Jhong Billy <billy@starlabs.sg>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\t(sqe_flags & IOSQE_FIXED_FILE));'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\t(sqe_flags & IOSQE_FIXED_FILE), 0);']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux Kernel io_uring system can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

The io_file_get_fixed function lacks the presence of ctx->uring_lock which can lead to a Use-After-Free vulnerability due a race condition with fixed files getting unregistered.

We recommend upgrading past commit da24142b1ef9fd5d36b76e36bab328a5b27523e8.

code_evidence: io_init_req is annotated __must_hold(&ctx->uring_lock), so its callers are expected to hold the uring_lock. At [40,41] it calls io_file_get with the fixed-file flag derived from the SQE, retrieving a fixed file reference while relying on that lock to serialize against fixed-file unregistration. The return is only null-checked at [42,43]; no additional reference/lifetime guard or lock is acquired here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the fixed-file lookup can race with unregistration, leaving req->file referencing memory that has been freed and later reused. The weakness is the missing lock protecting the lookup lifetime, not merely an improper reference count (CWE-911) or unchecked error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fixed-file lookup in io_file_get is performed without acquiring ctx->uring_lock on paths that may invoke it unlocked (e.g. via io-wq), so it can race with concurrent unregistration of fixed files. Trigger: submit an operation using IOSQE_FIXED_FILE while another thread unregisters the fixed file set. The lookup may return a file pointer whose reference is being torn down, and later access to req->file uses freed memory, supporting UAF consequences such as memory corruption or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Bug 697762: Fix scan converter SEGVs.

The SEGVs are caused by the scan converter allowing less room
in the table than is actually required. This happens due to
the mark_curve subdivision overflowing.

For example, if we have a curve such as:

 0 0x80000000 moveto
 0 0x80000000 0 0x80000000 0 0x80000000 curveto

Then the current subdivision logic does:

 fixed ay = (sy + c1y)>>1

For sy = c1y = 0x80000000 this gives ay = 0, when clearly
the average should be 0x80000000.

An alternative formulation of the splitting code:

 fixed ay = (sy>>1) + (c1y>>1)

gives the required result, at the expense of dropping accuracy at
the low end.

This commit therefore has 2 formulations of the splitting code, one
for 'big' values (values that might overflow), and ones for normal
values (values that won't).

We select between the two pieces of code by comparing the top 2
bits of each value; if they differ, then we use the big variant.

Also, when calculating the size of the table required, we were
incorrectly closing the curve more often than we needed to. This
had no ill effect other than inflating the amount of memory we
needed.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    mark_curve_tr(sx, sy, pcur->p1.x, pcur->p1.y, pcur->p2.x, pcur->p2.y, ex, ey, ibox.p.y, scanlines, table, index, &id, k);'], 'added_lines': ['                    mark_curve_top_tr(sx, sy, pcur->p1.x, pcur->p1.y, pcur->p2.x, pcur->p2.y, ex, ey, ibox.p.y, scanlines, table, index, &id, k);']}
description: Integer overflow in the mark_curve function in Artifex Ghostscript 9.21 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PostScript document.

code_evidence: For each s_curve segment the function computes a sample count k via gx_curve_log2_samples and passes the curve endpoints and control points to mark_curve_tr (line 49), which performs the fixed-point midpoint subdivision (sy + c1y)>>1. With large coordinates such as 0x80000000 this addition overflows, so the subdivision and the resulting table size derived from k disagree; the caller supplies the table/index from make_table_tr at line 24.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an arithmetic wraparound in fixed-point addition that the code assumes cannot overflow, matching CWE-190. It is not a simple bounds-check omission (CWE-787); the out-of-bounds write is the downstream consequence of the integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mark_curve_tr averages fixed-point control coordinates by adding them before shifting, so large values wrap to a small or negative midpoint. Trigger: a crafted PostScript curve whose control-point coordinates are near the fixed-point limit. Consequence: the scan converter writes more entries than the allocated table holds, causing an out-of-bounds write and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
CVE-2018-6340 Fix buffer overread

Summary:
snprintf() returns the number of would be written bytes if the buffer had
enough size, letting the original code to construct output string from
arbitrary data on the stack.

Fix this by properly assembling the String without trying to arbitrarily
limiting the length to 30 bytes.

Reviewed By: ottoni

Differential Revision: D13509547

fbshipit-source-id: aa401b83d356f5b261433c4b16d777948ba7f9b4
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    char stats_key[30] = {0};', '    size_t key_len;', '', '    key_len = snprintf(stats_key, sizeof(stats_key), "%s:%d", hostname, port);', '', '    return_val.set(String(stats_key, key_len, CopyString), server_stats);'], 'added_lines': ['    auto const port_str = folly::to<std::string>(port);', '    auto const key_len = strlen(hostname) + 1 + port_str.length();', '    auto key = String(key_len, ReserveString);', '    key += hostname;', '    key += ":";', '    key += port_str;', '    return_val.set(key, server_stats);']}
description: The Memcache::getextendedstats function can be used to trigger an out-of-bounds read. Exploiting this issue requires control over memcached server hostnames and/or ports. This affects all supported versions of HHVM (3.30 and 3.27.4 and below).

code_evidence: The function declares a fixed-size stack buffer stats_key[30] at line 15 and key_len at line 16; the formatted hostname:port string is written into this 30-byte buffer.

At line 26 snprintf writes the formatted hostname and port into the buffer, but its return value key_len represents the number of characters that would have been written if the buffer were sufficiently large, not the number of characters actually stored. When the formatted string exceeds the buffer capacity, key_len can exceed the number of valid bytes in stats_key. At line 27 String(stats_key, key_len, CopyString) uses this oversized length to copy data from the 30-byte stack buffer, reading beyond its boundary.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read) applies because the program uses an unchecked length returned by snprintf as the number of bytes to read from a fixed-size stack buffer. When the formatted string exceeds the buffer capacity, the constructor reads beyond the valid bounds of stats_key. The vulnerability is the subsequent out-of-bounds memory read, rather than merely the truncation of the formatted string.

size_t key_len;

key_len = snprintf(stats_key, sizeof(stats_key), "%s:%d", hostname, port);
return_val.set(String(stats_key, key_len, CopyString), server_stats);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: snprintf returns the length required for the complete formatted string, even when the output is truncated to fit the 30-byte stats_key buffer. Trigger: an attacker controls a memcached server hostname and/or port such that the formatted hostname:port string exceeds the buffer capacity. The oversized key_len is subsequently passed to String(stats_key, key_len, CopyString), causing the constructor to read beyond the stack-allocated stats_key array. Consequence: out-of-bounds stack memory disclosure, potentially exposing unintended data from the HHVM process.

commit_msg:
scsi: sg: fixup infoleak when using SG_GET_REQUEST_TABLE

When calling SG_GET_REQUEST_TABLE ioctl only a half-filled table is
returned; the remaining part will then contain stale kernel memory
information.  This patch zeroes out the entire table to avoid this
issue.

Signed-off-by: Hannes Reinecke <hare@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Bart Van Assche <bart.vanassche@wdc.com>
Reviewed-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Reviewed-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tmemset(&rinfo[val], 0, SZ_SG_REQ_INFO);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The sg_ioctl function in drivers/scsi/sg.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.4 allows local users to obtain sensitive information from uninitialized kernel heap-memory locations via an SG_GET_REQUEST_TABLE ioctl call for /dev/sg0.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over sfp->rq_list and writes only the fields req_state, problem, duration, orphan, sg_io_owned, pack_id and usr_ptr into rinfo[val]; the memset at line 11 clears each entry but its removal would leave the remaining bytes of each sg_req_info_t uninitialized.
The done branch sets duration from srp->header.duration; the else branch computes it from jiffies; all other fields are copied from srp, but no code zeroes padding or unused bytes of the structure.
val increments per list entry, so entries beyond the current request count, and unused bytes within each filled entry, are never initialized by this function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function transfers an under-initialized kernel structure to a user-accessible ioctl result, directly exposing sensitive kernel memory to an unauthorized actor, which matches CWE-200 exposure of sensitive information. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the defect is failure to cleanse/initialize the returned data.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sg_fill_request_table does not initialize the full sg_req_info_t array, leaving stale kernel heap bytes in the request table returned to userspace. Trigger: a local user invokes SG_GET_REQUEST_TABLE on /dev/sg0; the partially filled table carries uninitialized memory. Consequence: kernel heap contents are exposed, a confidentiality loss.

commit_msg:
Fix usage of custom EVP_CIPHER objects

If a custom EVP_CIPHER object has been passed to EVP_CipherInit() then it
should be used in preference to a fetched cipher.

We also fix a possible NULL pointer deref in the same code for digests.

If the custom cipher passed to EVP_CipherInit() happens to use NID_undef
(which should be a discouraged practice), then in the previous
implementation this could result in the NULL cipher being fetched and
hence NULL encryption being unexpectedly used.

CVE-2022-3358

Fixes #18970

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/19300)

(cherry picked from commit 25d47cccf203c3b71171e78865e48ea061a039a8)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            || impl != NULL) {', ''], 'added_lines': ['            || impl != NULL', '            || (cipher != NULL && cipher->origin == EVP_ORIG_METH)', '            || (cipher == NULL && ctx->cipher != NULL', '                               && ctx->cipher->origin == EVP_ORIG_METH)) {']}
description: OpenSSL supports creating a custom cipher via the legacy EVP_CIPHER_meth_new() function and associated function calls. This function was deprecated in OpenSSL 3.0 and application authors are instead encouraged to use the new provider mechanism in order to implement custom ciphers. OpenSSL versions 3.0.0 to 3.0.5 incorrectly handle legacy custom ciphers passed to the EVP_EncryptInit_ex2(), EVP_DecryptInit_ex2() and EVP_CipherInit_ex2() functions (as well as other similarly named encryption and decryption initialisation functions). Instead of using the custom cipher directly it incorrectly tries to fetch an equivalent cipher from the available providers. An equivalent cipher is found based on the NID passed to EVP_CIPHER_meth_new(). This NID is supposed to represent the unique NID for a given cipher. However it is possible for an application to incorrectly pass NID_undef as this value in the call to EVP_CIPHER_meth_new(). When NID_undef is used in this way the OpenSSL encryption/decryption initialisation function will match the NULL cipher as being equivalent and will fetch this from the available providers. This will succeed if the default provider has been loaded (or if a third party provider has been loaded that offers this cipher). Using the NULL cipher means that the plaintext is emitted as the ciphertext. Applications are only affected by this issue if they call EVP_CIPHER_meth_new() using NID_undef and subsequently use it in a call to an encryption/decryption initialisation function. Applications that only use SSL/TLS are not impacted by this issue. Fixed in OpenSSL 3.0.6 (Affected 3.0.0-3.0.5).

code_evidence: Guard only rejects when both cipher and ctx->cipher are NULL; a custom cipher with prov==NULL and NID_undef proceeds.

With cipher->prov==NULL, code fetches a provider cipher using "NULL" when nid==NID_undef; if fetch succeeds, cipher is replaced by the fetched NULL cipher (no deref of NULL here, but wrong cipher selected).
The legacy path dereferences ctx->cipher without checking it is non-NULL (e.g., ctx->cipher->ctx_size, ctx->cipher->init), so a NULL ctx->cipher after fetch failure or reset leads to a NULL deref.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences ctx->cipher (e.g., ctx->cipher->ctx_size, init) without ensuring it is non-NULL. The related wrong-cipher selection is a distinct weakness; the supported dereference is the NULL pointer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the initialization path does not require a valid custom cipher and can replace a NID_undef custom cipher with a fetched NULL cipher, or leave ctx->cipher NULL. Trigger: caller passes a custom EVP_CIPHER created with NID_undef; the code fetches the NULL cipher or fails, then later dereferences ctx->cipher in the legacy block. Supported consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing crash (availability impact); the wrong NULL cipher also defeats confidentiality.

By validating length fields from server responses, out of boundary
accesses and endless loops can be mitigated.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>

commit_msg:
Fix Integer overflow issue with intsets (CVE-2021-32687)

The vulnerability involves changing the default set-max-intset-entries
configuration parameter to a very large value and constructing specially
crafted commands to manipulate sets
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    uint32_t size = len*intrev32ifbe(is->encoding);'], 'added_lines': ['    uint64_t size = (uint64_t)len*intrev32ifbe(is->encoding);', '    assert(size <= SIZE_MAX - sizeof(intset));']}
description: Redis is an open source, in-memory database that persists on disk. An integer overflow bug affecting all versions of Redis can be exploited to corrupt the heap and potentially be used to leak arbitrary contents of the heap or trigger remote code execution. The vulnerability involves changing the default set-max-intset-entries configuration parameter to a very large value and constructing specially crafted commands to manipulate sets. The problem is fixed in Redis versions 6.2.6, 6.0.16 and 5.0.14. An additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent users from modifying the set-max-intset-entries configuration parameter. This can be done using ACL to restrict unprivileged users from using the CONFIG SET command.

code_evidence: Line 2 computes the allocation payload size as a 32-bit uint32_t product of the requested element count len and the intset encoding width (intrev32ifbe(is->encoding)), so the multiplication wraps when len is large. Line 3 passes sizeof(intset)+size to zrealloc, using the wrapped value as the heap allocation size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the code multiplies two integers in a fixed-width type whose result can wrap, and the wrapped value is used directly as a memory allocation size, exactly the size-determination scenario the CWE describes. The fix widens the computation to uint64_t and asserts size <= SIZE_MAX - sizeof(intset), confirming an overflow in the size calculation.

evidence_lines.code:
uint32_t size = len*intrev32ifbe(is->encoding);
is = zrealloc(is,sizeof(intset)+size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size calculation len*encoding is performed in uint32_t, so a large len produces a truncated (wrapped) size. Trigger: a caller supplies a large element count (reachable via crafted set commands with a very large set-max-intset-entries). Consequence: zrealloc allocates a buffer far smaller than the logical intset capacity, and subsequent element writes corrupt the heap.

commit_msg:
tcp: initialize rcv_mss to TCP_MIN_MSS instead of 0

When tcp_disconnect() is called, inet_csk_delack_init() sets
icsk->icsk_ack.rcv_mss to 0.
This could potentially cause tcp_recvmsg() => tcp_cleanup_rbuf() =>
__tcp_select_window() call path to have division by 0 issue.
So this patch initializes rcv_mss to TCP_MIN_MSS instead of 0.

Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov  <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Wei Wang <weiwan@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Neal Cardwell <ncardwell@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Yuchung Cheng <ycheng@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Initialize rcv_mss to TCP_MIN_MSS to avoid division by 0', '\t * issue in __tcp_select_window()', '\t */', '\ticsk->icsk_ack.rcv_mss = TCP_MIN_MSS;']}
description: The tcp_disconnect function in net/ipv4/tcp.c in the Linux kernel before 4.12 allows local users to cause a denial of service (__tcp_select_window divide-by-zero error and system crash) by triggering a disconnect within a certain tcp_recvmsg code path.

code_evidence: inet_csk_delack_init(sk) resets the ACK state, leaving icsk->icsk_ack.rcv_mss at 0; the following line proceeds without restoring a nonzero rcv_mss, so the connection's receive MSS remains zero after disconnect.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a divisor reaching zero through a missing initialization constraint, matching CWE-369 (Divide By Zero). It is not merely an uninitialized-value bug; the concrete consequence is division by zero in __tcp_select_window().

evidence_lines.code:
inet_csk_delack_init(sk);
tcp_init_send_head(sk);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: tcp_disconnect() reinitializes the ACK parameters via inet_csk_delack_init(), which zeroes rcv_mss, and does not set a valid minimum. A later tcp_recvmsg() -> tcp_cleanup_rbuf() -> __tcp_select_window() path uses rcv_mss as a divisor, so the zero value triggers a divide-by-zero and crashes the system (availability DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/shadow: correct an inverted conditional in dirty VRAM tracking

This originally was "mfn_x(mfn) == INVALID_MFN". Make it like this
again, taking the opportunity to also drop the unnecessary nearby
braces.

This is XSA-319.

Fixes: 246a5a3377c2 ("xen: Use a typesafe to define INVALID_MFN")
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if ( !mfn_eq(mfn, INVALID_MFN) )', '            {', '            }'], 'added_lines': ['            if ( mfn_eq(mfn, INVALID_MFN) )']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.13.x, allowing x86 HVM guest OS users to cause a hypervisor crash. An inverted conditional in x86 HVM guests' dirty video RAM tracking code allows such guests to make Xen de-reference a pointer guaranteed to point at unmapped space. A malicious or buggy HVM guest may cause the hypervisor to crash, resulting in Denial of Service (DoS) affecting the entire host. Xen versions from 4.8 onwards are affected. Xen versions 4.7 and earlier are not affected. Only x86 systems are affected. Arm systems are not affected. Only x86 HVM guests using shadow paging can leverage the vulnerability. In addition, there needs to be an entity actively monitoring a guest's video frame buffer (typically for display purposes) in order for such a guest to be able to leverage the vulnerability. x86 PV guests, as well as x86 HVM guests using hardware assisted paging (HAP), cannot leverage the vulnerability.

code_evidence: At line 63 get_gfn_query_unlocked may return INVALID_MFN for an unpopulated guest frame. The condition at line 67 tests !mfn_eq(mfn, INVALID_MFN), so the valid-MFN branch only sets dirty=1, while the else branch (lines 71-73) runs mfn_to_page(mfn) on an invalid MFN.

mfn_to_page on INVALID_MFN yields a pointer into unmapped space; the subsequent page->u.inuse.type_info read at line 74 dereferences it. The later sl1ma-derived map_domain_page/sl1e access at lines 93-97 is reached through this already-corrupted path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer derived from an invalid MFN, performing a memory access outside any valid buffer/page structure, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The root cause is a logic error, but the supported consequence is an invalid memory read leading to crash; final_cwe stays the target CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the inverted validity test: the invalid-MFN case is routed into the page-dereference branch instead of being treated as dirty. A malicious HVM guest with shadow paging and an active framebuffer monitor can cause get_gfn_query_unlocked to return INVALID_MFN, triggering mfn_to_page on unmapped memory and a hypervisor crash (host-wide DoS).

commit_msg:
ovl: fix dentry reference leak

In ovl_copy_up_locked(), newdentry is leaked if the function exits through
out_cleanup as this just to out after calling ovl_cleanup() - which doesn't
actually release the ref on newdentry.

The out_cleanup segment should instead exit through out2 as certainly
newdentry leaks - and possibly upper does also, though this isn't caught
given the catch of newdentry.

Without this fix, something like the following is seen:

	BUG: Dentry ffff880023e9eb20{i=f861,n=#ffff880023e82d90} still in use (1) [unmount of tmpfs tmpfs]
	BUG: Dentry ffff880023ece640{i=0,n=bigfile}  still in use (1) [unmount of tmpfs tmpfs]

when unmounting the upper layer after an error occurred in copyup.

An error can be induced by creating a big file in a lower layer with
something like:

	dd if=/dev/zero of=/lower/a/bigfile bs=65536 count=1 seek=$((0xf000))

to create a large file (4.1G).  Overlay an upper layer that is too small
(on tmpfs might do) and then induce a copy up by opening it writably.

Reported-by: Ulrich Obergfell <uobergfe@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <miklos@szeredi.hu>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v3.18+
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tgoto out;'], 'added_lines': ['\tgoto out2;']}
description: fs/overlayfs/copy_up.c in the Linux kernel before 4.2.6 uses an incorrect cleanup code path, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (dentry reference leak) via filesystem operations on a large file in a lower overlayfs layer.

code_evidence: The out_cleanup block calls ovl_cleanup(wdir, newdentry) and then jumps directly to out, skipping the dput(newdentry) release at out1. newdentry was obtained from ovl_lookup_temp at line 12 and still holds a reference; only out1 releases it, so this error path leaks the dentry reference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources; the leaked dentry reference is an unreleased resource on an error path, matching this category. The defect is a missing reference release, not an out-of-bounds or injection issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cleanup error path bypasses the reference-release label. Trigger: any failure after newdentry is created that jumps to out_cleanup (ovl_copy_up_data, ovl_copy_xattr, ovl_set_attr/notify_change, or ovl_do_rename errors). Consequence: the newdentry reference is never dropped, leaking a dentry and causing a denial of service (unmount reports 'still in use').

commit_msg:
KEYS: add missing permission check for request_key() destination

When the request_key() syscall is not passed a destination keyring, it
links the requested key (if constructed) into the "default" request-key
keyring.  This should require Write permission to the keyring.  However,
there is actually no permission check.

This can be abused to add keys to any keyring to which only Search
permission is granted.  This is because Search permission allows joining
the keyring.  keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring(KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_SESSION_KEYRING)
then will set the default request-key keyring to the session keyring.
Then, request_key() can be used to add keys to the keyring.

Both negatively and positively instantiated keys can be added using this
method.  Adding negative keys is trivial.  Adding a positive key is a
bit trickier.  It requires that either /sbin/request-key positively
instantiates the key, or that another thread adds the key to the process
keyring at just the right time, such that request_key() misses it
initially but then finds it in construct_alloc_key().

Fix this bug by checking for Write permission to the keyring in
construct_get_dest_keyring() when the default keyring is being used.

We don't do the permission check for non-default keyrings because that
was already done by the earlier call to lookup_user_key().  Also,
request_key_and_link() is currently passed a 'struct key *' rather than
a key_ref_t, so the "possessed" bit is unavailable.

We also don't do the permission check for the "requestor keyring", to
continue to support the use case described by commit 8bbf4976b59f
("KEYS: Alter use of key instantiation link-to-keyring argument") where
/sbin/request-key recursively calls request_key() to add keys to the
original requestor's destination keyring.  (I don't know of any users
who actually do that, though...)

Fixes: 3e30148c3d52 ("[PATCH] Keys: Make request-key create an authorisation key")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>	# v2.6.13+
Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!user)', '\t\treturn ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM);', '', '\tconstruct_get_dest_keyring(&dest_keyring);', '\t\tgoto couldnt_alloc_key;', 'couldnt_alloc_key:'], 'added_lines': ['\tret = construct_get_dest_keyring(&dest_keyring);', '\tif (ret)', '\t\tgoto error;', '', '\tif (!user) {', '\t\tret = -ENOMEM;', '\t\tgoto error_put_dest_keyring;', '\t}', '\t\tgoto error_put_dest_keyring;', 'error_put_dest_keyring:', 'error:']}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.14.6 omitted an access-control check when adding a key to the current task's "default request-key keyring" via the request_key() system call, allowing a local user to use a sequence of crafted system calls to add keys to a keyring with only Search permission (not Write permission) to that keyring, related to construct_get_dest_keyring() in security/keys/request_key.c.

code_evidence: construct_get_dest_keyring(&dest_keyring) is called at line 17 and the resulting dest_keyring is passed to construct_alloc_key at line 18, then used to link/construct the key. No return value from construct_get_dest_keyring is checked, so any permission failure inside it is ignored and the key is still allocated/linked into dest_keyring. The dest_keyring is only released via key_put at line 32 or the error label.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the function proceeds to add a key to a destination keyring without performing the required authorization check on that keyring; the missing Write-permission enforcement is a missing authorization control, not a memory-safety or input-validation flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller never inspects the authorization result from construct_get_dest_keyring, so when the default request-key keyring is selected without Write permission, the missing check is not enforced and the key is added anyway. Trigger: request_key() with a default destination keyring to which the caller has only Search permission. Consequence: unauthorized addition of keys to that keyring (integrity/access-control bypass).

commit_msg:
[tf.data] Set limit on number of threads used in threadpool_dataset.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 410922677
Change-Id: Ib25814a99043ab10805b5d2d7088ae0e0b7b04fd
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(', '        ctx, num_threads_ > 0,', '        errors::InvalidArgument("`num_threads` must be greater than zero."));'], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES_OK(ctx, ValidateNumThreads(num_threads_));']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `ThreadPoolHandle` can be used to trigger a denial of service attack by allocating too much memory. This is because the `num_threads` argument is only checked to not be negative, but there is no upper bound on its value. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The constructor reads the user-supplied `num_threads` attribute into `num_threads_` without any upper-bound check.
The only validation constrains `num_threads_ > 0`; there is no maximum, so an arbitrarily large value is accepted and later used to size the thread pool.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits: a reusable resource (threads) is allocated on behalf of an actor without throttling the number or size. It is not merely improper input validation (CWE-20) because the specific defect and impact are unbounded resource allocation leading to DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the `num_threads` attribute is trusted with only a lower-bound check and no upper bound. Trigger: an actor supplies an extremely large `num_threads` value to `ThreadPoolHandle`. Consequence: the pool allocates excessive threads/memory, exhausting resources and causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
mm: fix prctl_set_vma_anon_name

prctl_set_vma_anon_name could attempt to set the name across
two vmas at the same time due to a typo, which might corrupt
the vma list.  Fix it to use tmp instead of end to limit
the name setting to a single vma at a time.

Change-Id: Ie32d8ddb0fd547efbeedd6528acdab5ca5b308b4
Reported-by: Jed Davis <jld@mozilla.com>
Signed-off-by: Colin Cross <ccross@android.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\terror = prctl_update_vma_anon_name(vma, &prev, start, end,'], 'added_lines': ['\t\terror = prctl_update_vma_anon_name(vma, &prev, start, tmp,']}
description: The prctl_set_vma_anon_name function in kernel/sys.c in Android before 5.1.1 LMY49F and 6.0 before 2016-01-01 does not ensure that only one vma is accessed in a certain update action, which allows attackers to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (vma list corruption) via a crafted application, aka internal bug 20017123.

code_evidence: tmp is clamped to min(vma->vm_end, end) at lines 21-23, correctly bounding the current vma. However, the update call at lines 24-25 passes end instead of tmp, so the requested range can extend past the current vma's vm_end into an adjacent vma.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is a missing boundary constraint on the range passed to a privileged operation, letting a caller affect memory-management state beyond the intended single vma; this is a permissions/access-control management weakness consistent with CWE-264. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the cross-vma update corrupts list state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop intends to process one vma per iteration, but prctl_update_vma_anon_name receives end rather than the clamped tmp. A crafted application supplying a start/end spanning two adjacent vmas causes the update to operate across both simultaneously, corrupting the vma list and enabling privilege escalation or denial of service.

commit_msg:
RDMA/hfi1: Prevent memory leak in sdma_init

In sdma_init if rhashtable_init fails the allocated memory for
tmp_sdma_rht should be released.

Fixes: 5a52a7acf7e2 ("IB/hfi1: NULL pointer dereference when freeing rhashtable")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20190925144543.10141-1-navid.emamdoost@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Dennis Dalessandro <dennis.dalessandro@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@mellanox.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (ret < 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (ret < 0) {', '\t\tkfree(tmp_sdma_rht);', '\t}', '']}
description: A memory leak in the sdma_init() function in drivers/infiniband/hw/hfi1/sdma.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.9 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering rhashtable_init() failures, aka CID-34b3be18a04e. NOTE: This has been disputed as not a vulnerability because "rhashtable_init() can only fail if it is passed invalid values in the second parameter's struct, but when invoked from sdma_init() that is a pointer to a static const struct, so an attacker could only trigger failure if they could corrupt kernel memory (in which case a small memory leak is not a significant problem).

code_evidence: tmp_sdma_rht is allocated with kzalloc at [128]; if allocation fails, the code jumps to bail. At [133] rhashtable_init is called on the allocated table; when it returns negative, [134,135] jump directly to bail without freeing tmp_sdma_rht, so the allocation from [128] is leaked on this error path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because memory allocated at [128] is not released when the subsequent initialization at [133] fails, leaving it unreachable. This is a missing-release-on-error-path leak, distinct from a NULL-pointer dereference, which would involve invalid access rather than unreleased memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch for a failed rhashtable_init does not release the kzalloc'd tmp_sdma_rht before jumping to bail, and bail calls sdma_clean, which has no reference to this local pointer. Trigger: rhashtable_init returns a negative value. Consequence: the allocated rhashtable memory becomes unreachable and unavailable for reuse, supporting resource-consumption DoS.

commit_msg:
cryp: prevent direct calls to update and final functions

With inconsistent or malformed data it has been possible to call
"update" and "final" crypto functions directly. Using a fuzzer tool [1]
we have seen that this results in asserts, i.e., a crash that
potentially could leak sensitive information.

By setting the state (initialized) in the crypto context (i.e., the
tee_cryp_state) at the end of all syscall_*_init functions and then add
a check of the state at the beginning of all update and final functions,
  we prevent direct entrance to the "update" and "final" functions.

[1] https://github.com/MartijnB/optee_fuzzer

Fixes: OP-TEE-2019-0021

Signed-off-by: Joakim Bech <joakim.bech@linaro.org>
Reported-by: Martijn Bogaard <bogaard@riscure.com>
Acked-by: Jerome Forissier <jerome.forissier@linaro.org>
Reviewed-by: Jens Wiklander <jens.wiklander@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcs->state = CRYP_STATE_INITIALIZED;', '']}
description: In Linaro OP-TEE before 3.7.0, by using inconsistent or malformed data, it is possible to call update and final cryptographic functions directly, causing a crash that could leak sensitive information.

commit_msg:
security fix: scrub headers on `OIDCUnAuthAction pass`; closes #222

On accessing paths protected with `OIDCUnAuthAction pass` no headers
would be scrubbed when a user is not authenticated so malicious
software/users could set OIDC_CLAIM_ and OIDCAuthNHeader headers that
applications would interpret as set by mod_auth_openidc. Thanks
@wouterhund.

Signed-off-by: Hans Zandbelt <hans.zandbelt@zmartzone.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t\t/*', "\t\t\t * we're not going to pass information about an authenticated user to the application,", '\t\t\t * but we do need to scrub the headers that mod_auth_openidc would set for security reasons', '\t\t\t */', '\t\t\toidc_scrub_headers(r);', '']}
description: The "OpenID Connect Relying Party and OAuth 2.0 Resource Server" (aka mod_auth_openidc) module before 2.1.5 for the Apache HTTP Server does not skip OIDC_CLAIM_ and OIDCAuthNHeader headers in an "OIDCUnAuthAction pass" configuration, which allows remote attackers to bypass authentication via crafted HTTP traffic.

code_evidence: In the OIDC_UNAUTH_PASS branch, the function sets r->user = "" and returns OK, passing the request to the application without removing client-supplied OIDC_CLAIM_/OIDCAuthNHeader headers. The patched version adds oidc_scrub_headers(r) before return OK; the pre-patch code has no such scrubbing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to prove the claimed identity because it passes attacker-set identity headers to the application as if they came from the module, which is improper authentication (CWE-287). This is not merely header injection: the missing scrub lets untrusted input masquerade as an authenticated identity.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unauthenticated pass path forwards the request without stripping headers that mod_auth_openidc reserves for authenticated identity. Trigger: a remote client sends crafted OIDC_CLAIM_ or OIDCAuthNHeader headers on a path configured with OIDCUnAuthAction pass. Consequence: the backend interprets attacker-controlled values as authenticated claims, enabling authentication bypass/identity assumption.

commit_msg:
USB: core: fix out-of-bounds access bug in usb_get_bos_descriptor()

Andrey used the syzkaller fuzzer to find an out-of-bounds memory
access in usb_get_bos_descriptor().  The code wasn't checking that the
next usb_dev_cap_header structure could fit into the remaining buffer
space.

This patch fixes the error and also reduces the bNumDeviceCaps field
in the header to match the actual number of capabilities found, in
cases where there are fewer than expected.

Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Tested-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\t\tif (total_len < length)', '\t\t\tbreak;'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\tif (total_len < sizeof(*cap) || total_len < cap->bLength) {', '\t\t\tdev->bos->desc->bNumDeviceCaps = i;', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t}']}
description: The usb_get_bos_descriptor function in drivers/usb/core/config.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.10 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted USB device.

code_evidence: The loop advances buffer by length and casts the new position to cap, then reads cap->bLength before any bounds check. The check total_len < length only compares the declared length, not the size of the cap header itself, so reading cap->bLength can occur past the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads past the end of the kzalloc(total_len) buffer before validating the remaining space. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write, and the missing length constraint is the direct cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code dereferences cap->bLength at line 46 without first verifying that sizeof(*cap) fits in the remaining total_len. Trigger: a crafted USB device supplies a BOS descriptor set whose capability count and lengths cause buffer to reach the end of the allocation. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of cap fields, leading to crash/DoS or unspecified impact.

commit_msg:
x86: limit linear page table use to a single level

That's the only way that they're meant to be used. Without such a
restriction arbitrarily long chains of same-level page tables can be
built, tearing down of which may then cause arbitrarily deep recursion,
causing a stack overflow. To facilitate this restriction, a counter is
being introduced to track both the number of same-level entries in a
page table as well as the number of uses of a page table in another
same-level one (counting into positive and negative direction
respectively, utilizing the fact that both counts can't be non-zero at
the same time).

Note that the added accounting introduces a restriction on the number
of times a page can be used in other same-level page tables - more than
32k of such uses are no longer possible.

Note also that some put_page_and_type[_preemptible]() calls are
replaced with open-coded equivalents.  This seemed preferrable to
adding "parent_table" to the matrix of functions.

Note further that cross-domain same-level page table references are no
longer permitted (they probably never should have been).

This is XSA-240.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

commit_msg:
Go into the error state if a fatal alert is sent or received

If an application calls SSL_shutdown after a fatal alert has occured and
then behaves different based on error codes from that function then the
application may be vulnerable to a padding oracle.

CVE-2019-1559

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* If a fatal one, remove from cache */', '    if ((level == 2) && (s->session != NULL))', '        SSL_CTX_remove_session(s->session_ctx, s->session);'], 'added_lines': ['    /* If a fatal one, remove from cache and go into the error state */', '    if (level == SSL3_AL_FATAL) {', '        if (s->session != NULL)', '            SSL_CTX_remove_session(s->session_ctx, s->session);', '        s->state = SSL_ST_ERR;', '    }']}
description: If an application encounters a fatal protocol error and then calls SSL_shutdown() twice (once to send a close_notify, and once to receive one) then OpenSSL can respond differently to the calling application if a 0 byte record is received with invalid padding compared to if a 0 byte record is received with an invalid MAC. If the application then behaves differently based on that in a way that is detectable to the remote peer, then this amounts to a padding oracle that could be used to decrypt data. In order for this to be exploitable "non-stitched" ciphersuites must be in use. Stitched ciphersuites are optimised implementations of certain commonly used ciphersuites. Also the application must call SSL_shutdown() twice even if a protocol error has occurred (applications should not do this but some do anyway). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.0.2r (Affected 1.0.2-1.0.2q).

code_evidence: On a fatal alert (level == 2), the function only removes the session from the cache and returns; it does not transition s->state to an error state. The alert is still queued via s->s3->alert_dispatch and send_alert, so the connection state remains usable and a subsequent SSL_shutdown() proceeds rather than short-circuiting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-203 fits because the missing error-state transition lets the library respond differently under distinct internal conditions (invalid padding vs invalid MAC) in a way observable to a remote peer. The cause is the absent state change; the padding oracle is the downstream consequence, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((level == 2) && (s->session != NULL))
SSL_CTX_remove_session(s->session_ctx, s->session);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a fatal alert does not force the SSL object into SSL_ST_ERR, so later operations such as SSL_shutdown() continue and produce responses that differ depending on whether a received record failed padding versus MAC validation. Trigger: an application calls SSL_shutdown() after a fatal protocol error. Supported consequence: an observable discrepancy that can form a padding oracle and leak plaintext.

commit_msg:
tiffcrop: disable incompatibility of -Z, -X, -Y, -z options with any PAGE_MODE_x option (fixes #411 and #413)

tiffcrop does not support –Z, -z, -X and –Y options together with any other PAGE_MODE_x options like  -H, -V, -P, -J, -K or –S.

Code analysis:

With the options –Z, -z, the crop.selections are set to a value > 0. Within main(), this triggers the call of processCropSelections(), which copies the sections from the read_buff into seg_buffs[].
In the following code in main(), the only supported step, where that seg_buffs are further handled are within an if-clause with  if (page.mode == PAGE_MODE_NONE) .

Execution of the else-clause often leads to buffer-overflows.

Therefore, the above option combination is not supported and will be disabled to prevent those buffer-overflows.

The MR solves issues #411 and #413.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      /* Crop input image and copy zones and regions from input image into seg_buffs or crop_buff. */', '      /* Format and write selected image parts to output file(s). */']}
description: LibTIFF 4.4.0 has an out-of-bounds write in _TIFFmemset in libtiff/tif_unix.c:340 when called from processCropSelections, tools/tiffcrop.c:7619, allowing attackers to cause a denial-of-service via a crafted tiff file. For users that compile libtiff from sources, the fix is available with commit 236b7191.

code_evidence: When crop.selections > 0, processCropSelections copies input sections into seg_buffs[].
The only path that consumes seg_buffs[] is guarded by page.mode == PAGE_MODE_NONE; writeSelections is called there.
When page.mode != PAGE_MODE_NONE, the else branch instead chooses sect_src from crop_buff or read_buff and calls writeImageSections, ignoring the populated seg_buffs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit documents that this mismatched branch leads to buffer overflows, i.e., writes past intended buffer boundaries, matching CWE-787. The function itself only routes data; the actual out-of-bounds write occurs downstream, so the evidence is the unsafe option/branch combination rather than a direct write statement.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the option combination sets crop.selections > 0 (populating seg_buffs) while page.mode is a PAGE_MODE_x other than NONE, so the page-mode branch processes sect_src rather than the crop selections. Trigger: crafted TIFF plus incompatible -Z/-z/-X/-Y and PAGE_MODE options. Supported consequence: downstream section handling writes out of bounds (as reported in processCropSelections/_TIFFmemset), causing memory corruption or DoS.

commit_msg:
sbr_fbt: sbr->M should not exceed MAX_M

sbr->M is set by derived_frequency_table() from user-passed input
without checking for > MAX_M.

This leads to out-of-bounds accesses later, crashes and potential
security relevant issues. It should be considered a fatal error for
the SBR block.

return error code if sbr->M > MAX_M.

also, in some cases sbr_extension_data() ignores the return value of
calc_sbr_tables, probably assuming that sbr is always valid. It should
almost certainly not do that.

fixes #19 (CVE-2018-20196).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (sbr->M > MAX_M)', '        return 1;']}
description: There is a stack-based buffer overflow in the third instance of the calculate_gain function in libfaad/sbr_hfadj.c in Freeware Advanced Audio Decoder 2 (FAAD2) 2.8.8. A crafted input will lead to a denial of service or possibly unspecified other impact because the S_M array is mishandled.

code_evidence: Line 16 computes sbr->M from the difference of user-derived frequency table entries without any upper bound check against MAX_M.
Lines 12-14 fill f_table_res[HI_RES] from sbr->f_master for k up to N_high; the resulting M value is derived from attacker-influenced table data.
Lines 20-21 only bound kx+M against 64, not M itself against MAX_M, so the constraint protecting later array indexing is missing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing MAX_M constraint allows sbr->M to exceed the buffer dimension used by later SBR processing, producing out-of-bounds writes (CWE-787). This is distinct from a mere out-of-bounds read: the oversized M drives writes into fixed-size arrays, matching the target weakness.

evidence_lines.code: sbr->M = sbr->f_table_res[HI_RES][sbr->N_high] - sbr->f_table_res[HI_RES][0];

if (sbr->kx + sbr->M > 64)
return 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: derived_frequency_table computes sbr->M from user-controlled frequency-table values but never enforces sbr->M <= MAX_M. Trigger: crafted SBR input yields a large M that passes the kx+M>64 check in some configurations. Consequence: downstream code indexes arrays such as S_M with M-sized ranges, writing past buffer bounds, causing crashes or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Avoid infinite recursion in the ALTER TABLE code when a view contains an unused CTE that references, directly or indirectly, the view itself.

FossilOrigin-Name: 1d2e53a39b87e364685e21de137655b6eee725e4c6d27fc90865072d7c5892b5
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            Select *pSelect = pTab->pSelect;', '            assert( pSelect->selFlags & SF_View );', '            pSelect->selFlags &= ~SF_View;']}
description: alter.c in SQLite through 3.30.1 allows attackers to trigger infinite recursion via certain types of self-referential views in conjunction with ALTER TABLE statements.

code_evidence: At [36,37] the view branch runs sqlite3SelectPrep on pTab->pSelect while the SF_View flag is still set; sqlite3SelectPrep then resolves the view by recursively expanding/parsing it. At [43] sqlite3WalkSelect walks the same select again. Because the self-referential view is not marked as already being processed, resolution re-enters the same view.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the code performs recursive view resolution without a proper conditional guard against cycles, causing uncontrolled recursion. This is distinct from CWE-20 input validation: the flaw is the missing recursion-termination control, not bad input parsing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the view's SF_View flag is not cleared before sqlite3SelectPrep, so a self-referential view is re-resolved recursively with no termination guard. Trigger: ALTER TABLE (rename) on a view whose unused CTE references the view directly or indirectly. Supported consequence: unbounded recursion during select preparation, exhausting the stack/CPU (DoS).

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ["  // Validate that the completed HeaderMap's cached byte size exists and is correct.", '  // This assert iterates over the HeaderMap.', '  ASSERT(current_header_map_->byteSize().has_value() &&', '         current_header_map_->byteSize() == current_header_map_->byteSizeInternal());']}
description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only adds a debug ASSERT validating a cached header byte size; it contains no resource-consumption or throttling logic that directly supports CWE-400, and the O(n^2) header-iteration behavior described in the commit is not implemented here.

commit_msg:
ASAN SFTP Fixes
When decoding SFTP messages, fix the size checks so they don't wrap. (ZD12766)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (sz + idx > maxSz) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (sz > maxSz - idx) {']}
description: WolfSSH v1.4.7 was discovered to contain an integer overflow via the function wolfSSH_SFTP_RecvRMDIR.

code_evidence: ato32 reads attacker-controlled sz from the SFTP message; idx is incremented by UINT32_SZ. The size check computes sz + idx in word32, so a large sz wraps to a small value and passes the maxSz test.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the vulnerability is an integer wraparound in the sz + idx bounds calculation that defeats the length validation. The downstream memory corruption is the consequence, not a separate weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check adds sz and idx without guarding against word32 wraparound. Trigger: a crafted LSTAT request with a large sz field. Consequence: the check is bypassed, and the wrapped sz then flows into WMALLOC(sz + 1) and WMEMCPY(name, data + idx, sz), enabling undersized allocation and out-of-bounds copy.

commit_msg:
(uid_t) -1 is still used as placeholder to mean "unset". This is OK, since
there should be no users with such number, see
https://systemd.io/UIDS-GIDS#special-linux-uids.

(uid_t) -1 is used as the default value in class initialization.

When a user or group above INT32_MAX is created, the numeric uid or
gid wraps around to negative when the value is assigned to gint, and
polkit gets confused. Let's accept such gids, except for -1.

A nicer fix would be to change the underlying type to e.g. uint32 to
not have negative values. But this cannot be done without breaking the
API, so likely new functions will have to be added (a
polkit_unix_user_new variant that takes a unsigned, and the same for
_group_new, _set_uid, _get_uid, _set_gid, _get_gid, etc.). This will
require a bigger patch.

Fixes https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/polkit/polkit/issues/74.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    case PROP_UID:', '      polkit_unix_process_set_uid (unix_process, g_value_get_int (value));'], 'added_lines': ['    case PROP_UID: {', '      gint val;', '', '      val = g_value_get_int (value);', '      g_return_if_fail (val != -1);', '      polkit_unix_process_set_uid (unix_process, val);', '    }']}
description: A flaw was found in PolicyKit (aka polkit) 0.115 that allows a user with a uid greater than INT_MAX to successfully execute any systemctl command.

code_evidence: In the PROP_UID case, the GValue is read with g_value_get_int and passed directly to polkit_unix_process_set_uid without checking the resulting gint; a gid/uid above INT32_MAX wraps to a negative value here.
The PROP_START_TIME case is unrelated to the UID flow and does not constrain the PROP_UID value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate the UID input's sign/range before processing it, matching CWE-20 improper input validation. This is not merely a type-conversion bug: the missing constraint on the received value is what lets the wrapped negative UID reach polkit_unix_process_set_uid.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the setter accepts any gint from the property GValue and never rejects the sentinel or wrapped negative values. Trigger: a caller sets the UID property with a value that was stored as an unsigned uid above INT32_MAX, which g_value_get_int converts to a negative gint. Consequence: the process identity is set to an invalid/wrapped UID, which downstream authorization logic misinterprets (the described polkit flaw: a high-UID user can execute privileged systemctl commands).

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Don't have %cr4.fsgsbase active behind a guest kernels back

Currently, a 64bit PV guest can appear to set and clear FSGSBASE in %cr4, but
the bit remains set in hardware.  Therefore, the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE are usable
even when the guest kernel believes that they are disabled.

The FSGSBASE feature isn't currently supported in Linux, and its context
switch path has some optimisations which rely on userspace being unable to use
the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions.  Xen's current behaviour undermines this
expectation.

In 64bit PV guest context, always load the guest kernels setting of FSGSBASE
into %cr4.  This requires adjusting how Xen uses the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE
instructions.

 * Delete the cpu_has_fsgsbase helper.  It is no longer safe, as users need to
   check %cr4 directly.
 * The raw __rd{fs,gs}base() helpers are only safe to use when %cr4.fsgsbase
   is set.  Comment this property.
 * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}{base,shadow}() and read_msr() helpers are updated to use
   the current %cr4 value to determine which mechanism to use.
 * toggle_guest_mode() and save_segments() are update to avoid reading
   fs/gsbase if the values in hardware cannot be stale WRT struct vcpu.  A
   consequence of this is that the write_cr() path needs to cache the current
   bases, as subsequent context switches will skip saving the values.
 * write_cr4() is updated to ensure that the shadow %cr4.fsgsbase value is
   observed in a safe way WRT the hardware setting, if an interrupt happens to
   hit in the middle.
 * load_segments() is updated to use the VMLOAD optimisation if FSGSBASE is
   unavailable, even if only gs_shadow needs updating.  As a minor perf
   improvement, check cpu_has_svm first to short circuit a context-dependent
   conditional on Intel hardware.
 * pv_make_cr4() is updated for 64bit PV guests to use the guest kernels
   choice of FSGSBASE.

This is part of XSA-293.

Reported-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if ( !cpu_has_fsgsbase )', '            per_cpu(host_vmcb_va, cpu) = __map_domain_page_global(pg);'], 'added_lines': ['        per_cpu(host_vmcb_va, cpu) = __map_domain_page_global(pg);']}

commit_msg:
(for 4.9.3) CVE-2018-14882/ICMP6 RPL: Add a missing bounds check

Moreover:
Add and use *_tstr[] strings.
Update four tests outputs accordingly.
Fix a space.

Wang Junjie of 360 ESG Codesafe Team had independently identified this
vulnerability in 2018 by means of fuzzing and provided the packet capture
file for the test.

description: The ICMPv6 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-icmp6.c.

code_evidence: Case ND_RPL_MESSAGE dispatches to rpl_print with a length computed as length-sizeof(struct icmp6_hdr)+4 without a bounds check ensuring the packet actually contains the RPL body.
The ICMP6_DST_UNREACH path reads oip->ip6_dst via ND_TCHECK(oip->ip6_dst) and prints it, showing the parser dereferences embedded IPv6 header fields whose presence depends on the supplied length.

Trigger is a malformed/truncated ICMPv6 RPL message; consequence is an out-of-bounds read (crash or memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
Bug 698825: Do not drop borrowed colorspaces.

Previously the borrowed colorspace was dropped when updating annotation
appearances, leading to use after free warnings from valgrind/ASAN.

description: Artifex Mupdf version 1.12.0 contains a Use After Free vulnerability in fz_keep_key_storable that can result in DOS / Possible code execution. This attack appear to be exploitable via Victim opens a specially crafted PDF.

code_evidence: Line 9 declares cs as a function-scope pointer initialized to NULL and line 21 registers it with fz_var, so it is a tracked variable across fz_try/fz_always. Line 39 assigns cs = fz_device_rgb(ctx), a borrowed reference, and lines 44-46 replace it with other borrowed device colorspaces. Lines 50 and 61 pass cs to fz_fill_text; the fz_always block (line 77) drops other objects but never drops cs, and cs is no longer declared inside the try scope.

Bug 701799: avoid out-of-range array access in mj_color_correct().

Code is obscure, so this fix merely avoids out-of-range access in the simplest
