Force flush TLBs for such ranges to avoid munmap() vs', '\t * unmap_mapping_range() races.', '\tif (tlb->vma_pfn || !IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MMU_GATHER_MERGE_VMAS)) {', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * Do a TLB flush and reset the range at VMA boundaries; this avoids', '\t\t * the ranges growing with the unused space between consecutive VMAs.', '\t\t */', '\t\ttlb_flush_mmu_tlbonly(tlb);', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in include/asm-generic/tlb.h in the Linux kernel before 5.19. Because of a race condition (unmap_mapping_range versus munmap), a device driver can free a page while it still has stale TLB entries. This only occurs in situations with VM_PFNMAP VMAs.

code_evidence: tlb_end_vma returns early when tlb->fullmm or CONFIG_MMU_GATHER_MERGE_VMAS is enabled, and otherwise calls tlb_flush_mmu_tlbonly(tlb) only at the end of the VMA. Because the flush is deferred to the VMA boundary, the TLB invalidation for a VM_PFNMAP range happens later than the VMA teardown, leaving a window in which stale TLB entries remain. The function has no check of tlb->vma_pfn and no forced flush for PFNMAP ranges.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function participates in a concurrent teardown sequence whose lack of a forced flush for VM_PFNMAP ranges leaves a timing window for an interfering unmap_mapping_range() call, matching CWE-362's concurrent shared-resource race. It is not a simple missing-lock issue but a deferred-synchronization window between munmap and unmap_mapping_range.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: TLB invalidation is deferred until tlb_end_vma for merged VMAs, so a VM_PFNMAP VMA can be unlinked by munmap() before its TLB entries are flushed. Trigger: concurrent unmap_mapping_range() observes the VMA already unlinked and no-ops while stale TLB entries persist. Consequence: a device driver can free a PFN page still referenced by stale TLB entries, corrupting memory or causing a crash.

Fix one division by zero

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a division by 0 in `tf.raw_ops.QuantizedMul`. Calling TF operations with tensors of non-numeric types when the operations expect numeric tensors result in null pointer dereferences. commit_msg:
(for 4.9.3) CVE-2018-14466/Rx: fix an over-read bug

In rx_cache_insert() and rx_cache_find() properly read the serviceId
field of the rx_header structure as a 16-bit integer. When those
functions tried to read 32 bits the extra 16 bits could be outside of
the bounds checked in rx_print() for the rx_header structure, as
serviceId is the last field in that structure.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\trxent->serviceId = EXTRACT_32BITS(&rxh->serviceId);'], 'added_lines': ['\trxent->serviceId = EXTRACT_16BITS(&rxh->serviceId);']}

code_evidence: Line 7 bounds-checks only sizeof(struct rx_header) + sizeof(int32_t) against the captured data, then line 16 reads serviceId with EXTRACT_32BITS. Since serviceId is the last field of rx_header, reading 32 bits extends 16 bits beyond the validated header region and can exceed ndo_snapend.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads beyond the intended/validated buffer extent, which is the definition of CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. The fix's switch to EXTRACT_16BITS confirms the over-wide read; this is not a write error or integer overflow.

Trigger: a truncated Rx packet where less than 32 bits of serviceId remain in the capture. Consequence: out-of-bounds read past the captured buffer, leaking adjacent memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4040: keeping track of allocated lines is too complicated

Problem:    Keeping track of allocated lines in user functions is too
            complicated.
Solution:   Instead of freeing individual lines keep them all until the end.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    char_u\t*line_to_free = NULL;', '    if (get_function_body(&eap, &newlines, NULL, &line_to_free) == FAIL)', '    {', '\tif (cmdline != line_to_free)', '\t    vim_free(cmdline);', '    }', '\t    if (cmdline == line_to_free)', '\t\tline_to_free = NULL;', '    vim_free(line_to_free);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (get_function_body(&eap, &newlines, NULL,', '\t\t\t\t\t     &evalarg->eval_tofree_ga) == FAIL)']}
description: vim is vulnerable to Use After Free

code_evidence: get_function_body stores an allocated line into line_to_free; on failure, cmdline is freed unless it aliases line_to_free, then control jumps to erret.

When eap.nextcmd is set, cmdline is appended to eval_tofree_ga and the alias is nulled only if cmdline == line_to_free, so cmdline may be stored in the tofree array while line_to_free still points to it.

The erret label unconditionally calls vim_free(line_to_free) and then ga_clear_strings(&newlines); if line_to_free aliases a line also retained in a tofree array, the later cleanup can free memory that remains referenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code can free a line at erret while an alias remains in a tofree array, exactly matching CWE-416 (reuse/reference of freed memory). This is not merely a double free: the retained pointer is used later, so the use-after-free classification fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ownership of cmdline/line_to_free is tracked by aliasing comparisons rather than a single owning container. Trigger: a code path where cmdline is added to eval_tofree_ga while line_to_free remains non-NULL, followed by the erret cleanup. Consequence: the same allocation is freed while still reachable, enabling use-after-free on later access.

commit_msg:
Don't change the state of the ETM flags until CCS processing

Changing the ciphersuite during a renegotiation can result in a crash
leading to a DoS attack. ETM has not been implemented in 1.1.0 for DTLS
so this is TLS only.

The problem is caused by changing the flag indicating whether to use ETM
or not immediately on negotiation of ETM, rather than at CCS. Therefore,
during a renegotiation, if the ETM state is changing (usually due to a
change of ciphersuite), then an error/crash will occur.

Due to the fact that there are separate CCS messages for read and write
we actually now need two flags to determine whether to use ETM or not.

CVE-2017-3733

commit_msg:
udf_write_fi() uses lengthOfImpUse of the entry it is writing to.
However this field has not yet been initialized so it either contains
completely bogus value or value from last directory entry at that place.
In either case this is wrong and can lead to filesystem corruption or
kernel crashes.

Reported-by: butt3rflyh4ck <butterflyhuangxx@gmail.com>
CC: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: 979a6e28dd96 ("udf: Get rid of 0-length arrays in struct fileIdentDesc")

description: A flaw out of bounds memory write in the Linux kernel UDF file system functionality was found in the way user triggers some file operation which triggers udf_write_fi(). A local user could use this flaw to crash the system or potentially

code_evidence: Line 8 reads liu from cfi->lengthOfImpUse, and lines 10-11 derive padlen from liu and lfi; these drive the destination offsets.

When fileident is set, the adinicb/negative-offset branch at lines 29-30 copies lfi bytes to udf_get_fi_ident(sfi), which computes the identifier location from the current sfi->lengthOfImpUse rather than the cfi value being written.
Lines 39-41 and 45 then use offset (advanced by liu and lfi) to memset padding relative to the same udf_get_fi_ident(sfi) base.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs memcpy and memset writes whose destination offset depends on an unvalidated, uninitialized length field, allowing writes beyond the intended buffer boundary. This is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the root cause is the stale lengthOfImpUse rather than a mere read overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The destination for the file identifier and padding is computed by udf_get_fi_ident(sfi), which uses sfi->lengthOfImpUse; this field has not been initialized from the incoming cfi and holds a stale or bogus value. The write offsets therefore diverge from the actual descriptor layout, so memcpy/memset can write outside the intended buffer, corrupting the UDF filesystem or crashing the kernel.

commit_msg:
dentry name snapshots

take_dentry_name_snapshot() takes a safe snapshot of dentry name;
if the name is a short one, it gets copied into caller-supplied
structure, otherwise an extra reference to external name is grabbed
(those are never modified).  In either case the pointer to stable
string is stored into the same structure.

dentry must be held by the caller of take_dentry_name_snapshot(),
but may be freely dropped afterwards - the snapshot will stay
until destroyed by release_dentry_name_snapshot().

Intended use:
	struct name_snapshot s;

	take_dentry_name_snapshot(&s, dentry);
	...
	access s.name
	...
	release_dentry_name_snapshot(&s);

Replaces fsnotify_oldname_...(), gets used in fsnotify to obtain the name
to pass down with event.

Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t       dentry->d_name.name, 0);', '\t\t\t\t       dentry->d_name.name, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tstruct name_snapshot name;', '', '\t\ttake_dentry_name_snapshot(&name, dentry);', '\t\t\t\t       name.name, 0);', '\t\t\t\t       name.name, 0);', '\t\trelease_dentry_name_snapshot(&name);']}
description: Race condition in the fsnotify implementation in the Linux kernel through 4.12.4 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted application that leverages simultaneous execution of the inotify_handle_event and vfs_rename functions.

code_evidence: Both fsnotify() calls pass dentry->d_name.name, a pointer into the dentry's name storage, rather than a stable copy.
The name pointer is read and handed to fsnotify while the dentry is only pinned by the caller; no snapshot or reference to the external name is taken before use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads a shared, concurrently mutable resource (the dentry name) without exclusive access, matching CWE-362's timing-window/exclusivity violation. This is a race on name lifetime rather than a simple missing bounds check, so CWE-362 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the event name is passed as a raw pointer into dentry->d_name.name without taking a stable snapshot, so a concurrent vfs_rename can modify or free the external name storage while fsnotify_handle_event consumes it. Trigger: simultaneous execution of __fsnotify_parent/fsnotify_handle_event and vfs_rename on the same dentry. Supported consequence: use-after-free/memory corruption leading to privilege escalation or denial of service.

description: libfreerdp/codec/region.c in FreeRDP through 1.1.x and 2.x through 2.0.0-rc4 has memory leaks because a supplied realloc pointer (i.e., the first argument to realloc) is also used for a realloc return value.

code_evidence: The realloc result is assigned directly to dst->data on line 114, overwriting the only pointer to newItems. The null check on line 115 then tests dst->data, not the original allocation. If realloc fails, dst->data becomes NULL and line 117 frees newItems, which is still the original valid block, so the failure path actually frees correctly here. The unchecked-return concern is that realloc's failure is only detected via the overwritten pointer, and the code relies on free(newItems) after the assignment rather than preserving the original pointer before realloc.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-252 applies to unchecked return values, but here the realloc result is checked on line 115 via dst->data after assignment. The weakness is that the check occurs after the pointer is overwritten rather than before, so the return is effectively used without preserving the original allocation state. This is a return-value handling flaw rather than a pure unchecked-return case.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of realloc is stored directly into dst->data instead of a temporary, so the original allocation pointer is lost before the null check. Trigger: realloc returning NULL on allocation failure. Consequence: the code tests the overwritten field and frees newItems, which is the original block; the failure is handled, but the pattern is fragile because the original pointer is no longer available through dst->data, and any later use of dst->data before reassignment would dereference NULL.

commit_msg:
Fix possible infinite loop in BN_mod_sqrt()

The calculation in some cases does not finish for non-prime p.

This fixes CVE-2022-0778.

Based on patch by David Benjamin <davidben@google.com>.

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [' * Theory", algorithm 1.5.1). \'p\' must be prime!', '        /* find smallest  i  such that  b^(2^i) = 1 */', '        i = 1;', '        if (!BN_mod_sqr(t, b, p, ctx))', '            goto end;', '        while (!BN_is_one(t)) {', '            i++;', '            if (i == e) {', '                BNerr(BN_F_BN_MOD_SQRT, BN_R_NOT_A_SQUARE);', '                goto end;', '            if (!BN_mod_mul(t, t, t, p, ctx))', '                goto end;'], 'added_lines': [' * Theory", algorithm 1.5.1). \'p\' must be prime, otherwise an error or', ' * an incorrect "result" will be returned.', '        /* Find the smallest i, 0 < i < e, such that b^(2^i) = 1. */', '        for (i = 1; i < e; i++) {', '            if (i == 1) {', '                if (!BN_mod_sqr(t, b, p, ctx))', '                    goto end;', '', '            } else {', '                if (!BN_mod_mul(t, t, t, p, ctx))', '                    goto end;', '            if (BN_is_one(t))', '                break;', '        }', '        /* If not found, a is not a square or p is not prime. */', '        if (i >= e) {', '            BNerr(BN_F_BN_MOD_SQRT, BN_R_NOT_A_SQUARE);', '            goto end;']}
description: The BN_mod_sqrt() function, which computes a modular square root, contains a bug that can cause it to loop forever for non-prime moduli. Internally this function is used when parsing certificates that contain elliptic curve public keys in compressed form or explicit elliptic curve parameters with a base point encoded in compressed form. It is possible to trigger the infinite loop by crafting a certificate that has invalid explicit curve parameters. Since certificate parsing happens prior to verification of the certificate signature, any process that parses an externally supplied certificate may thus be subject to a denial of service attack. The infinite loop can also be reached when parsing crafted private keys as they can contain explicit elliptic curve parameters. Thus vulnerable situations include: - TLS clients consuming server certificates - TLS servers consuming client certificates - Hosting providers taking certificates or private keys from customers - Certificate authorities parsing certification requests from subscribers - Anything else which parses ASN.1 elliptic curve parameters Also any other applications that use the BN_mod_sqrt() where the attacker can control the parameter values are vulnerable to this DoS issue. In the OpenSSL 1.0.2 version the public key is not parsed during initial parsing of the certificate which makes it slightly harder to trigger the infinite loop. However any operation which requires the public key from the certificate will trigger the infinite loop. In particular the attacker can use a self-signed certificate to trigger the loop during verification of the certificate signature. This issue affects OpenSSL versions 1.0.2, 1.1.1 and 3.0. It was addressed in the releases of 1.1.1n and 3.0.2 on the 15th March 2022. Fixed in OpenSSL 3.0.2 (Affected 3.0.0,3.0.1). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1n (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1m). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.0.2zd (Affected 1.0.2-1.0.2zc).

code_evidence: The outer while(1) loop at line 156 continues until b == 1 (line 157). Inside, i is reset to 1 (line 163), t is set to b^2 (line 164), and the inner loop at line 166 increments i while t is not one, exiting only when i == e (line 168) or t becomes one. After the inner loop, e is reassigned to i (line 187), and the outer loop repeats; if the inner loop never reaches a state where t becomes one and i never equals e for non-prime p, the outer loop can iterate without terminating.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains an iteration whose exit conditions cannot be reached for certain inputs, matching CWE-835's infinite loop with availability impact. It is not merely an incorrect result; the loop fails to terminate, which is the defining characteristic of CWE-835.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the inner search for i such that b^(2^i)=1 has no bound that is guaranteed reachable when p is non-prime; the exit condition i == e depends on the modulus structure. Trigger: attacker-supplied non-prime modulus via crafted EC parameters. Consequence: the outer while(1) loop spins indefinitely, consuming CPU (DoS).

description: The XWD image (X Window System window dumping file) parsing component in ImageMagick 7.0.8-41 Q16 allows attackers to cause a denial-of-service (application crash resulting from an out-of-bounds Read) in ReadXWDImage in coders/xwd.c by crafting a corrupted XWD image file, a different vulnerability than CVE-2019-11472.

code_evidence: The header is read from the blob, but header.header_size is only checked to be at least sz_XWDheader; length is computed as header_size-sz_XWDheader and used to allocate and read the comment buffer, so a header_size inconsistent with the actual blob length drives a read sized by the file header.

ximage->bytes_per_line and height are taken from the header and multiplied into length; the overflow check only validates the multiplication, not that length bytes exist in the blob. ReadBlob then reads length bytes into ximage->data, and a short read is detected only after the read attempt.

The pixel-decoding loops call XGetPixel on the buffer filled by ReadBlob; when the blob is shorter than the computed length, XGetPixel indexes beyond the allocated/read data, producing an out-of-bounds read and crash.

Trigger: a crafted XWD file whose header_size, bytes_per_line and height imply more data than the blob contains. Consequence: XGetPixel reads past the buffer end, causing an out-of-bounds read and denial of service.

code_evidence: Line 2 overwrites the member displayProfile with displayProfileA without releasing or closing any previously stored profile, and the subsequent block (lines 3-18) creates a transform and XYZProfile from the new profile. Each call therefore abandons the prior profile reference held by the member, while line 18 only closes the locally created XYZProfile.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the function fails to release a resource (the previous display color profile) after its effective lifetime ends when the member is reassigned. This is a missing-release weakness, not a use-after-free or null dereference: the defect is the absent cleanup on overwrite.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: setDisplayProfile unconditionally assigns displayProfileA to the member, discarding any prior profile without a matching cmsCloseProfile. Trigger: repeated calls to setDisplayProfile, as exercised by pdftocairo rendering. Consequence: the overwritten profile resources accumulate, producing a memory leak and potential resource-consumption DoS.

Bug 701819: fixed ordering in if expression to avoid out-of-bounds access.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (data != *from || from == end) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (from >= end || data != *from) {']}
description: A buffer overflow vulnerability in pcx_write_rle() in contrib/japanese/gdev10v.c of Artifex Software GhostScript v9.50 allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via a crafted PDF file. This is fixed in v9.51.

code_evidence: Line 7 reads *from while from < end. Line 8 advances from += step. Line 9 then evaluates data != *from before checking from == end, so when the increment moves from to end (or past it), *from dereferences one element beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an out-of-bounds memory access at the buffer end caused by dereferencing past end; the fix guards the pointer bound before the dereference. CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) is the target, and the same boundary-ordering flaw underlies the access; the evidence directly shows the missing end check preceding the dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop advances the pointer before the bound check, and the pre-fix condition dereferences *from prior to testing from == end, so the short-circuit ordering permits an out-of-bounds read at the buffer boundary. Trigger: a crafted input whose run reaches end exactly at the increment. Supported consequence is an out-of-bounds access at the end of the buffer, which the fix addresses by reordering the from >= end guard first.

description: Sonivox in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-04-01 does not check for a negative number of samples, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, related to arm-wt-22k/lib_src/eas_wtengine.c and arm-wt-22k/lib_src/eas_wtsynth.c, aka internal bug 26366256.

code_evidence: Line 14 reads numSamples from the frame; lines 15-18 reject only non-positive values and otherwise continue, so a positive but oversized count is not bounded against the input/mix buffers.
Line 29 loops numSamples times, and line 30 reads *pInputBuffer++ without verifying that the pAudioBuffer (line 20) holds that many samples.
Lines 36-45 read and write *pMixBuffer++ twice per iteration without checking the pMixBuffer (line 19) capacity, so the loop advances both pointers past their intended bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loop performs reads and writes on pInputBuffer and pMixBuffer at offsets beyond their allocated bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operations. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts numSamples from pWTIntFrame and only guards against values <= 0, without validating it against the size of pAudioBuffer or pMixBuffer. Trigger: a crafted media file that yields a positive but too-large sample count. Consequence: the while loop at line 29 reads and writes past the input and mix buffers, causing memory corruption that may lead to code execution or a crash.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In versions up to and including 2.11.1 when in a dialog set (or forking) scenario, a hash key shared by multiple UAC dialogs can potentially be prematurely freed when one of the dialogs is destroyed . The issue may cause a dialog set to be registered in the hash table multiple times (with different hash keys) leading to undefined behavior such as dialog list collision which eventually leading to endless loop. A patch is available in commit db3235953baa56d2fb0e276ca510fefca751643f which will be included in the next release. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The function locates the target dialog by walking dlg_set->dlg_list and erases it with pj_list_erase(dlg) at line 19, but the freed dlg is still referenced afterward.

When the list becomes empty, the hash key is taken from dlg->local.info->tag.ptr/slen and dlg->local.tag_hval (lines 21-23) after the dialog has been removed, so a stale dialog pointer is dereferenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function dereferences a dialog structure after it has been removed from its list (freed/unlinked), using that stale pointer to access tag fields and the hash value. This is a use-after-free rather than a simple null-dereference or double-free, since the stale object is read for key computation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: after pj_list_erase(dlg) the code continues to read dlg->local.info->tag and dlg->local.tag_hval to compute the hash key. Trigger: unregistering a dialog whose removal empties its dialog set. Consequence: use-after-free reads of the erased dialog, potentially freeing or re-keying the wrong hash entry, causing hash table corruption and undefined behavior such as list collision or endless loop.

description: The ReadPCXImage function in coders/pcx.c in ImageMagick 7.0.4.9 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (attempted large memory allocation and application crash) via a crafted file. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2016-8862 and CVE-2016-8866.

code_evidence: map_length is read from the file (line 76) and only checked against the old bound of 32 before being shifted (lines 77-80), so large shift results are permitted.
colormap allocation multiplies number_colormaps by 3*map_length (lines 108-109) and the read loop iterates map_length times (lines 113-115); a large map_length drives the oversized allocation.
Later, for number_colormaps > 1, the loop reads *p, *(p+map_length), and *(p+map_length*2) for each of image->colors entries (lines 358-365), indexing beyond the allocated colormap buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads from a memory location outside the intended colormap buffer (lines 358-365), which is an out-of-bounds read within a memory buffer, matching CWE-119. The oversized allocation is the trigger, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds memory access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the insufficient upper bound on map_length combined with shift, producing an oversized colormap allocation and later out-of-bounds reads of the colormap buffer. A crafted RLE file with a large map_length triggers the oversized allocation and subsequent out-of-bounds access, causing memory exhaustion or a crash.

description: drivers/input/serio/i8042.c in the Linux kernel before 4.12.4 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact because the port->exists value can change after it is validated.

code_evidence: Line 50 sets serio to NULL when port->exists is false. Line 55 passes serio to i8042_filter, and line 56 releases i8042_lock. After the unlock, line 57 re-reads port->exists as the guard for line 58, which calls serio_interrupt(serio,...) using the serio value captured earlier.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The target CWE-476 fits because the function can pass a NULL serio pointer into serio_interrupt, which dereferences it, matching a NULL pointer dereference caused by a stale validation check. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the value of port->exists (and thus port->serio) can change between the assignment at line 50 and the use at line 57, so the guard no longer matches the captured serio pointer. Trigger: an interrupt path where port->exists becomes false after serio was set non-NULL, or vice versa, while the lock is released. joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only shows a missing cleanup of Info->ReturnObject on failure, which is a memory-leak root cause; the stack-dump/information exposure occurs elsewhere and is not evidenced by lines in this function.

commit_msg:
Change pairing_cb to assume temporary pairing by default

When pairing takes place, the pairing_cb.is_temp flag indicates whether
a pairing is temporary or permanent. Link keys are not stored for
temporary pairings. Since this is a "positive" flag, resetting the
pairing_cb control block (ex. memset to 0), it will assume persistent
pairing by default. Under certain circumstances, this can lead to a link
key being stored for temporarily secured connection.

This patch reverses the flag to be a "negative" flag. Renamed to
"persistent_bond", the default 0 meaning is now used to indicate a
temporary bond. If the lag is not properly set now, it will default to a
temporary bond and will not save the link key erronously.

This fix is for CVE-2014-7914

Bug: 18345373
Change-Id: I6e821595877ff30d64dc6e33602ac049cab3dd1e
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        pairing_cb.is_temp = TRUE;', '        pairing_cb.is_temp = FALSE;'], 'added_lines': ['        pairing_cb.bond_type = BOND_TYPE_TEMPORARY;', '        pairing_cb.bond_type = BOND_TYPE_PERSISTENT;']}
description: btif/src/btif_dm.c in Android before 5.1 does not properly enforce the temporary nature of a Bluetooth pairing, which allows user-assisted remote attackers to bypass intended access restrictions via crafted Bluetooth packets after the tapping of a crafted NFC tag.

code_evidence: The branch derives pairing_cb.is_temp from attacker-influenced SSP confirmation fields: just_works, loc_auth_req/rmt_auth_req BTM_AUTH_BONDS bits, and the remote device class via check_cod. When the conditions are not all met, line 18 sets is_temp = FALSE, marking the bond as permanent even for a just-works/temporary pairing, so the decision that governs whether a link key is stored is made here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs the authorization-relevant check that decides bond persistence (temporary vs permanent) and incorrectly classifies the pairing, allowing the temporary-bond restriction to be bypassed. This is incorrect authorization (CWE-863), not merely missing input validation, because the flawed check grants persistent access it should deny.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the temporary/permanent bond classification is computed from pairing-request fields without a safe default, so any unexpected or crafted combination falls into the permanent branch. Trigger: crafted Bluetooth packets after NFC-tag-assisted pairing that fail the just_works/BTM_AUTH_BONDS/COD conditions. Consequence: a link key is stored for a connection that should be temporary, bypassing the intended restriction.

commit_msg: Fix memleak in tcp server by wiping priority queues on deletion

description: The TCP Server module in toxcore before 0.2.8 doesn't free the TCP priority queue under certain conditions, which allows a remote attacker to exhaust the system's memory, causing a denial of service (DoS).

code_evidence: Line 12 zeroes the connection struct in place but does not release resources it owns (e.g., the priority queues); line 15 calls realloc_connection(tcp_server, 0) to shrink the accepted-connection array when the count reaches zero, which likewise does not free the per-connection priority queues.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 fits because the function fails to release a resource (priority queues) before the connection slot is invalidated and reused. This is improper resource release, not a bounds error; the memory exhaustion is the consequence, not the cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: deletion of an accepted connection only memzeros the struct and reallocs the array, without freeing the connection's priority queues. Trigger: repeated accept/delete cycles (remote connections) cause those queues to leak; supported consequence is unbounded memory growth leading to DoS.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-wccp.c had a large loop that was addressed by ensuring that a calculated length was monotonically increasing.

code_evidence: The loop at lines 11-16 is bounded only by the unchanged local `length` parameter. Inside the body, line 14 computes `new_length` from the value-set-list dissector, but line 15's macro consumes that value without updating `offset` or `length`. Because neither the loop variable nor the offset advances, the loop condition `length > 4` remains true for the same iteration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 covers loops whose iteration count is not sufficiently limited. Here the loop lacks a working advance of the offset/length, so attacker-controlled packet data can cause excessive iteration and resource consumption, matching the target weakness rather than a simple length miscalculation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop counter/length is never advanced by the value returned from the nested dissector. Trigger: a crafted packet whose alternate mask assignment data element has a value-set list that returns without moving the offset. Consequence: the loop repeats indefinitely, consuming CPU and stalling the dissector (DoS). The fix renames the macro to CHECK_LENGTH_ADVANCE_OFFSET to enforce offset advancement.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/131
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    quantum_info=DestroyQuantumInfo(quantum_info);']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the CalcMinMax function in coders/mat.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and application crash) via a crafted mat file.

code_evidence: BImgBuff is allocated with AcquireQuantumMemory(ldblk, sizeof(double)), i.e. ldblk*8 bytes, where ldblk is derived from attacker-controlled MATLAB_HDR.SizeX (e.g. 4*SizeX for miSINGLE, 8*SizeX for miDOUBLE).

CalcMinMax is called with MATLAB_HDR.SizeX, MATLAB_HDR.SizeY, CellType, ldblk and BImgBuff, passing quantum_info->minimum/maximum; the buffer size and dimensions come directly from file header fields.

The row loop reads ldblk bytes into BImgBuff via ReadBlob and then imports them; the allocation sizing versus the read/processing size is the relevant boundary. The patch adds DestroyQuantumInfo at the loop exit, but the read bound is governed by header-derived SizeX/SizeY.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the weakness is reading memory beyond the intended buffer during CalcMinMax over header-controlled dimensions, matching the out-of-bounds read description; it is not a write overflow (CWE-787) since the fault is a read past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: buffer sizing and dimensions for CalcMinMax/BImgBuff are derived from untrusted MAT header fields (SizeX, SizeY, CellType) without validating that the allocated ldblk*8 buffer covers the dimensions CalcMinMax traverses. Trigger: a crafted .mat file with mismatched SizeX/SizeY causes CalcMinMax to index past the BImgBuff allocation, producing an out-of-bounds read and crash (DoS).

description: Jsish v3.5.0 was discovered to contain a heap-use-after-free via /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libasan.so.4+0x79732. This vulnerability can lead to a Denial of Service (DoS).

commit_msg:
Add support for different number of page table levels dependent
on the highest address used for a process. This will cause a 31 bit
process to use a two level page table instead of the four level page
table that is the default after the pud has been introduced. Likewise
a normal 64 bit process will use three levels instead of four. Only
if a process runs out of the 4 tera bytes which can be addressed with
a three level page table the fourth level is dynamically added. Then
the process can use up to 8 peta byte.

Signed-off-by: Martin Schwidefsky <schwidefsky@de.ibm.com>

commit_msg: Fix bug #71498: Out-of-Bound Read in phar_parse_zipfile()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!memcmp(p + 1, "K\\5\\6", 3)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif ((p - buf) + sizeof(locator) <= size && !memcmp(p + 1, "K\\5\\6", 3)) {']}
description: The phar_parse_zipfile function in zip.c in the PHAR extension in PHP before 5.5.33 and 5.6.x before 5.6.19 allows remote attackers to obtain sensitive information from process memory or cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and application crash) by placing a PK\x05\x06 signature at an invalid location.

code_evidence: Line 31 locates a 'P' byte within buf using memchr, then line 32 performs memcmp(p + 1, "K\5\6", 3) to test the ZIP end-of-central-directory signature. p may point to the final byte of buf, so p+1 can be one past the end of the buffer; the 3-byte memcmp then reads out of bounds. Line 33's memcpy of sizeof(locator) from p similarly assumes a full locator is present, but the signature check guards the branch and lacks any size check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function reads past the intended buf boundary during memcmp/memcpy without validating that enough bytes remain. This is a direct out-of-bounds memory buffer operation, distinct from a pure integer overflow since the size arithmetic itself is not the defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signature probe and locator copy are not bounded by the remaining buffer size. Trigger: an attacker places a 'P' (or PK\x05\x06) near the end of the archive data so p+1 or p+sizeof(locator) exceeds buf. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of process memory, leading to information disclosure or a crash (CVE-2016-3141-style).

babeld: fix #10502 #10503 by repairing the checks on length

This patch repairs the checking conditions on length in four functions:
babel_packet_examin, parse_hello_subtlv, parse_ihu_subtlv, and parse_update_subtlv

commit_msg:
svc: check for allocation overflow in crypto calls

Without checking for overflow there is a risk of allocating a buffer
with size smaller than anticipated and as a consequence of that it might
lead to a heap based overflow with attacker controlled data written
outside the boundaries of the buffer.

Fixes: OP-TEE-2018-0010: "Integer overflow in crypto system calls (x2)"

Signed-off-by: Joakim Bech <joakim.bech@linaro.org>
Tested-by: Joakim Bech <joakim.bech@linaro.org> (QEMU v7, v8)
Reviewed-by: Jens Wiklander <jens.wiklander@linaro.org>
Reported-by: Riscure <inforequest@riscure.com>
Reported-by: Alyssa Milburn <a.a.milburn@vu.nl>
Acked-by: Etienne Carriere <etienne.carriere@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tparams = malloc(sizeof(TEE_Attribute) * param_count);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsize_t alloc_size = 0;', '', '\tif (MUL_OVERFLOW(sizeof(TEE_Attribute), param_count, &alloc_size))', '\t\treturn TEE_ERROR_OVERFLOW;', '', '\tparams = malloc(alloc_size);']}
description: Linaro/OP-TEE OP-TEE 3.3.0 and earlier is affected by: Buffer Overflow. The impact is: Execution of code in TEE core (kernel) context. The component is: optee_os. The fixed version is: 3.4.0 and later.

code_evidence: Line 32 computes the allocation size as sizeof(TEE_Attribute) * param_count, where param_count is an unsigned long supplied by the caller, without any overflow check. The product is passed directly to malloc, so a large param_count can wrap the multiplication to a small value, and the following NULL check at lines 33-34 does not detect the undersized allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size calculation assumed to be larger than its operands, but the arithmetic can wrap to a small value; this directly matches CWE-190. The undersized allocation and copy are the downstream consequence, not the root cause, so the integer overflow is the appropriate label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unchecked multiplication of a fixed element size by an attacker-controlled param_count before malloc. Trigger: pass a param_count large enough that sizeof(TEE_Attribute) * param_count wraps. Consequence: a small buffer is allocated, and the subsequent copy_in_attrs (line 35) writes param_count attributes into it, producing a heap-based out-of-bounds write that can lead to code execution in TEE core context.

commit_msg: Added missing calls to destroy methods (#2889).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['          return(StreamUsage());'], 'added_lines': ['          {', '            DestroyStream();', '            return(StreamUsage());', '          }']}
description: A memory leak in ImageMagick 7.0.10-45 and 6.9.11-22 allows remote attackers to perform a denial of service via the "identify -help" command.

code_evidence: The help branch returns StreamUsage() directly when option matches help/-help, without invoking DestroyStream().
DestroyStream() is the cleanup macro that releases stream_info, the image stack, and argv strings; it must be called before returning.
stream_info is acquired at line 74 via AcquireStreamInfo and OpenStream, so the help return path abandons that allocated state.
The patched code adds DestroyStream() before return(StreamUsage()) so the help path releases the acquired resources.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated memory (stream_info and related structures) is not released after its effective lifetime on the early-return help path. This is a missing-release memory leak affecting availability, not an out-of-bounds or use-after-free issue.

evidence_lines.code:
#define DestroyStream() \
{ \
DestroyImageStack(); \
stream_info=DestroyStreamInfo(stream_info); \
for (i=0; i < (ssize_t) argc; i++) \
argv[i]=DestroyString(argv[i]); \
argv=(char **) RelinquishMagickMemory(argv); \
}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the help/-help option path returns immediately after StreamUsage() without invoking DestroyStream(), leaving the stream_info and associated allocations unreleased. Trigger: running the command with a help option (e.g., "identify -help"). Supported consequence: repeated invocations leak memory, leading to resource consumption and potential denial of service.

commit_msg:
We need to drop skb references taken in j1939_session_skb_queue() when
destroying a session in j1939_session_destroy(). Otherwise those skbs
would be lost.

Link to Syzkaller info and repro: https://forge.ispras.ru/issues/11743.

Found by Linux Verification Center (linuxtesting.org) with Syzkaller.

V1: https://lore.kernel.org/all/20220708175949.539064-1-pchelkin@ispras.ru

Fixes: 9d71dd0c7009 ("can: add support of SAE J1939 protocol")
Suggested-by: Oleksij Rempel <o.rempel@pengutronix.de>
Signed-off-by: Fedor Pchelkin <pchelkin@ispras.ru>
Signed-off-by: Alexey Khoroshilov <khoroshilov@ispras.ru>
Acked-by: Oleksij Rempel <o.rempel@pengutronix.de>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/all/20220805150216.66313-1-pchelkin@ispras.ru
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tskb_queue_purge(&session->skb_queue);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct sk_buff *skb;', '', '\twhile ((skb = skb_dequeue(&session->skb_queue)) != NULL) {', '\t\t/* drop ref taken in j1939_session_skb_queue() */', '\t\tskb_unref(skb);', '\t\tkfree_skb(skb);', '\t}']}
description: A vulnerability classified as problematic has been found in Linux Kernel. Affected is the function j1939_session_destroy of the file net/can/j1939/transport.c. The manipulation leads to memory leak. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211932.

code_evidence: Line 14 purges session->skb_queue with skb_queue_purge(), which frees the skbs but does not drop the extra reference taken when they were queued via j1939_session_skb_queue(). The session and its queue are then torn down by __j1939_session_drop(), j1939_priv_put() and kfree(session) without any skb_unref() calls, so the queued skbs' reference counts are never decremented.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is responsible for releasing memory owned by the session but omits the skb_unref() needed to drop queued skb references before freeing the session, leaving allocated memory unreachable and unreleased. This is a missing release of memory after its effective lifetime, matching CWE-401.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: destruction of a J1939 session releases the skbs in skb_queue but fails to drop the reference acquired at enqueue time, so the skb memory (and its associated data) remains allocated after the session is freed. Trigger: any session teardown path that reaches j1939_session_destroy() with non-empty skb_queue. Consequence: leaked sk_buff memory, exhausting kernel memory over repeated session lifecycles (DoS/resource consumption).

description: async.c and dict.c in libhiredis.a in hiredis through 0.14.0 allow a NULL pointer dereference because malloc return values are unchecked.

code_evidence: Line 6 assigns the result of hiredis_safe_malloc(sizeof(*entry)) to entry with no NULL check. Lines 7 and 8 immediately dereference entry (entry->next and ht->table[index] = entry), so a NULL return from the allocator is used as a valid pointer.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation result in entry is never validated before use. Trigger: the allocator returns NULL (e.g., on allocation failure). Consequence: the unconditional dereferences at lines 7-8 cause a NULL pointer dereference, crashing the process and supporting a denial-of-service impact.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13005/NFS: Add two bounds checks before fetching data

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kamil Frankowicz.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!ND_TTEST(rp->rm_call.cb_proc))', '\t\treturn (0);', '\tif (!ND_TTEST(rp->rm_call.cb_vers))', '\t\treturn (0);']}
description: The NFS parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-nfs.c:xid_map_enter().

code_evidence: The function reads 32-bit fields via EXTRACT_32BITS(&rp->rm_call.cb_proc) and EXTRACT_32BITS(&rp->rm_call.cb_vers) without checking that these bytes lie within the captured packet buffer. The only prior check at line 8 tests cb_vers but the reads at 34-35 still dereference rm_call.cb_proc/cb_vers on rp, and no ND_TTEST guard precedes the cb_proc extraction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe operation is reading memory beyond the intended buffer boundary, matching the reported buffer over-read in xid_map_enter. The missing ND_TTEST bounds checks before the EXTRACT_32BITS reads directly enable the out-of-bounds read; this is a read, not a write.

xmep->proc = EXTRACT_32BITS(&rp->rm_call.cb_proc);
xmep->vers = EXTRACT_32BITS(&rp->rm_call.cb_vers);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unchecked extraction of rm_call.cb_proc and cb_vers from a packet whose capture length may be shorter than the RPC call structure. Trigger: a truncated NFS/RPC packet reaches xid_map_enter, so EXTRACT_32BITS dereferences past the captured data. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of packet buffer memory.

commit_msg:
tls_is_tx_ready() checks that list_first_entry() does not return NULL.
This condition can never happen. For empty lists, list_first_entry()
returns the list_entry() of the head, which is a type confusion.
Use list_first_entry_or_null() which returns NULL in case of empty
lists.

Fixes: a42055e8d2c3 ("net/tls: Add support for async encryption of records for performance")
Signed-off-by: Pietro Borrello <borrello@diag.uniroma1.it>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230128-list-entry-null-check-tls-v1-1-525bbfe6f0d0@diag.uniroma1.it
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\trec = list_first_entry(&ctx->tx_list, struct tls_rec, list);'], 'added_lines': ['\trec = list_first_entry_or_null(&ctx->tx_list, struct tls_rec, list);']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux Kernel. The tls_is_tx_ready() incorrectly checks for list emptiness, potentially accessing a type confused entry to the list_head, leaking the last byte of the confused field that overlaps with rec->tx_ready.

code_evidence: list_first_entry() is used on ctx->tx_list and its result is only checked with if (!rec); for an empty list list_first_entry() returns list_entry() of the list head, not NULL, so the guard is ineffective. rec is then treated as struct tls_rec and rec->tx_ready is read at line 7.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code accesses memory as struct tls_rec when it actually points to a list_head, matching CWE-843's incompatible-type access. This is not a generic NULL dereference; the missing emptiness handling causes the wrong object type to be interpreted.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: list_first_entry() on an empty tx_list yields the container_of the list_head itself, a pointer that does not refer to a struct tls_rec. Because the !rec check never triggers, READ_ONCE(rec->tx_ready) reads a field at the head's offset, producing a type-confused access and leaking/using data from the list_head memory.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/644
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if ((image != image2) && (image2 != (Image *) NULL))', '          image2=DestroyImage(image2);']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.0.6-5, a memory leak vulnerability was found in the function ReadMATImage in coders/mat.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: At [259-264] SetImageExtent failure returns DestroyImageList(image) without releasing image2, even though image2 may be a separate decompressed image allocated at [96-101].
[96-102] shows image2 can be reassigned by decompress_block, distinct from image, so the early return leaks that allocation.
[365-368] confirms image2 is normally freed via DeleteImageFromList only on the normal path, not on this error return.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates image2 via decompress_block and omits its release on the SetImageExtent error path, matching CWE-772's missing resource release after effective lifetime. The fix adds DestroyImage(image2), confirming the missing release rather than a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When SetImageExtent fails on a crafted MAT file, the function returns DestroyImageList(image) but image2 (a decompressed image from decompress_block) is not destroyed, leaking its memory. Repeated processing of crafted files can exhaust memory, causing denial of service.

commit_msg: tiffcrop: Correct simple copy paste error. Fix #488.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                prev_cropsize = seg_buffs[0].size;'], 'added_lines': ['                prev_cropsize = seg_buffs[i].size;']}
description: processCropSelections in tools/tiffcrop.c in LibTIFF through 4.5.0 has a heap-based buffer overflow (e.g., "WRITE of size 307203") via a crafted TIFF image.

code_evidence: Inside the per-selection loop, cropsize is set from crop->bufftotal and crop_buff is taken from seg_buffs[i].buffer, but the size comparison uses seg_buffs[0].size instead of seg_buffs[i].size.
After the allocation/realloc decision, the code stores seg_buffs[i].buffer = crop_buff and seg_buffs[i].size = cropsize, then calls extractSeparateRegion on crop_buff.
In the rotate branch, seg_buffs[i].size is reassigned from regionlist[i] dimensions, so buffer size and actual content length can diverge from bufftotal.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a write into a heap buffer whose size was validated against the wrong element, allowing data past the end of the i-th buffer. That is a direct out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-787 rather than an out-of-bounds read or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The wrong index in the size check means a later selection's buffer is compared against selection 0's size. If seg_buffs[0].size is larger than the current cropsize, realloc is skipped even though the i-th buffer is smaller, so extractSeparateRegion (and later rotate/mirror/invert operations) writes up to cropsize bytes into an undersized buffer. The root cause is reading the wrong array element; the consequence is a heap-based out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg: fixed potential crash in adts reframer with broken streams - cf #1723
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (ctx->hdr.frame_size < ctx->hdr.hdr_size) {', '\t\t\tGF_LOG(GF_LOG_WARNING, GF_LOG_PARSER, ("[ADTSDmx] Corrupted ADTS frame header, resyncing\\n"));', '\t\t\tctx->nb_frames = 0;', '\t\t\tgoto drop_byte;', '\t\t}', '']}
description: In the adts_dmx_process function in filters/reframe_adts.c in GPAC 1.0.1, a crafted file may cause ctx->hdr.frame_size to be smaller than ctx->hdr.hdr_size, resulting in size to be a negative number and a heap overflow in the memcpy.

code_evidence: Header fields frame_size (13 bits, line 124) and hdr_size (7 plus CRC/block skip, lines 127-134, 161) are read from the stream without any ordering constraint; frame_size is only checked for zero and for the next sync at offset frame_size.

size is computed as frame_size - hdr_size (line 185) and further reduced by 2 (line 188) when a two-block CRC frame is parsed, so a crafted header with frame_size < hdr_size yields a negative u32 that wraps.

size feeds gf_filter_pck_new_alloc (line 201) and the memcpy(output, sync + offset, size) at line 203; offset=hdr_size (line 186) can also exceed the buffer. bytes_to_drop=frame_size at line 195 is independent of size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe subtraction and unchecked size lead directly to a memcpy that writes beyond the allocated output buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The integer underflow is the cause; the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds write, not merely an integer error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no validation that frame_size >= hdr_size before the unsigned subtraction. A crafted ADTS header (e.g., large CRC/multi-block header with small frame_size) makes size a huge wrapped u32, so the allocation at line 201 is undersized relative to the copy length and memcpy at line 203 writes past the destination buffer, causing heap corruption/crash.

used only if registered at init time (httpd.conf).

Calling ap_method_register() in children processes is not the right scope
since it won't be shared for all requests.


git-svn-id: https://svn.apache.org/repos/asf/httpd/httpd/trunk@1807655 13f79535-47bb-0310-9956-ffa450edef68

description: Apache httpd allows remote attackers to read secret data from process memory if the Limit directive can be set in a user's .htaccess file, or if httpd.conf has certain misconfigurations, aka Optionsbleed. This affects the Apache HTTP Server through 2.2.34 and 2.4.x through 2.4.27. The attacker sends an unauthenticated OPTIONS HTTP request when attempting to read secret data. This is a use-after-free issue and thus secret data is not always sent, and the specific data depends on many factors including configuration. commit_msg: Fix bug #80672 - Null Dereference in SoapClient
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tsoap_error1(E_ERROR, "Parsing WSDL: Unexpected WSDL element <%s>", trav->name);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tsoap_error1(E_ERROR, "Parsing WSDL: Unexpected WSDL element <%s>",  SAFE_STR(trav->name));']}
description: In PHP versions 7.3.x below 7.3.27, 7.4.x below 7.4.15 and 8.0.x below 8.0.2, when using SOAP extension to connect to a SOAP server, a malicious SOAP server could return malformed XML data as a response that would cause PHP to access a null pointer and thus cause a crash.

code_evidence: In the loop over node children, the else-if branch detects an unexpected WSDL element and passes trav->name directly to soap_error1 as a %s argument. If a malformed response yields a node whose name field is NULL, the formatting of the error message dereferences that NULL pointer.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path formats trav->name without validating that the node name is non-NULL. Trigger: a malicious SOAP server returns malformed XML/WSDL producing an unexpected element with a NULL name. Consequence: a null pointer dereference during error formatting, crashing PHP (DoS).

commit_msg: Reject qname's wirelength > 255, `chopOff()` handle dot inside labels
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["  string::size_type fdot=domain.find('.');", '  if(fdot==string::npos) ', '    domain="";', '  else {', '    string::size_type remain = domain.length() - (fdot + 1);', '    char tmp[remain];', '    memcpy(tmp, domain.c_str()+fdot+1, remain);', "    domain.assign(tmp, remain); // don't dare to do this w/o tmp holder :-)"], 'added_lines': ['  bool escaped = false;', '  const string::size_type domainLen = domain.length();', '  for (size_t fdot = 0; fdot < domainLen; fdot++)', '  {', "    if (domain[fdot] == '.' && !escaped) {", '      string::size_type remain = domainLen - (fdot + 1);', '      char tmp[remain];', '      memcpy(tmp, domain.c_str()+fdot+1, remain);', "      domain.assign(tmp, remain); // don't dare to do this w/o tmp holder :-)", '      return true;', '    }', "    else if (domain[fdot] == '\\\\' && !escaped) {", '      escaped = true;', '    }', '    else {', '      escaped = false;', '    }', '', '  domain = "";']}
description: PowerDNS (aka pdns) Authoritative Server before 3.4.10 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (backend CPU consumption) via a long qname.

code_evidence: The function operates on the caller's qname via domain.find('.'), then allocates a variable-length stack buffer char tmp[remain] sized directly from the untrusted domain length and memcpy's the remainder into it. No bound on domain length exists before this stack allocation and copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources; the unchecked length-derived stack allocation and copy from an attacker-controlled qname is a resource-consumption management failure. The commit's stated fix (reject qnames with wirelength > 255) confirms the missing length constraint is the resource-management root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the qname length is never constrained before computing remain = domain.length() - (fdot + 1) and allocating char tmp[remain] on the stack. Trigger: a caller passes an arbitrarily long qname, making remain huge; the subsequent memcpy copies the full remainder. Supported consequence: unbounded stack allocation/copy per qname drives excessive CPU and memory consumption (the described backend CPU-consumption DoS).

commit_msg: fix stack overflow vulnerability
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            strcpy(CP,ClientPortPtr);'], 'added_lines': ['    int Length;', '', '            Length = strlen(ClientPortPtr);', '            if (Length > 128)', '            {', '                Length = 128;', '            }', '            strncpy(CP,ClientPortPtr, Length);']}
description: Tasmota before commit 066878da4d4762a9b6cb169fdf353e804d735cfd was discovered to contain a stack overflow via the ClientPortPtr parameter at lib/libesp32/rtsp/CRtspSession.cpp.

code_evidence: CP is a fixed 128-byte stack buffer, and strcpy(CP,ClientPortPtr) copies the attacker-controlled client_port substring into it with no size limit.
TmpPtr = strstr(ClientPortPtr,"\r\n") locates the request line terminator, and TmpPtr[0]=0x00 truncates there; the resulting string length is still fully attacker-controlled via the RTSP request.
A second unbounded strcpy(CP,pCP) copies the remainder after '=' back into the same 128-byte buffer, compounding the overflow.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-controlled data past the end of the intended 128-byte stack buffer, which is precisely an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), not merely a length miscalculation; the write itself is the defect.

evidence_lines.code:
char CP[128];     char * pCP;
strcpy(CP,ClientPortPtr);

pCP = strstr(CP,"=");
strcpy(CP,pCP);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unbounded strcpy into the fixed-size stack buffer CP. Trigger: an RTSP request whose client_port value exceeds 128 bytes (before the CRLF terminator). Consequence: stack memory past CP is overwritten, enabling crash/DoS and potentially controlled memory corruption or code execution.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        int nBufLen = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['        unsigned int nBufLen = 0;']}
description: Onlyoffice Document Server v6.0.0 and below and Core 6.1.0.26 and below were discovered to contain a heap overflow via the component DesktopEditor/fontengine/fontconverter/FontFileBase.h.

code_evidence: nBufLen is declared as a signed int and accumulates block lengths read from the input via ReadU32LE.

On the first block sBuffer is allocated with nBlockLen; on subsequent blocks MemUtilsRealloc uses nBufLen + nBlockLen, and Read writes nBlockLen bytes at sBuffer + nBufLen before nBufLen is incremented.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes read data beyond the bounds of the resized heap buffer due to uncontrolled length accumulation, directly matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely an integer overflow; the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds write itself.

evidence_lines.code: int nBufLen = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: nBufLen is a signed int while nBlockLen comes from attacker-controlled ReadU32LE. Repeated large blocks can overflow the int arithmetic in nBufLen + nBlockLen, making the realloc size smaller than the offset plus write length; Read then writes past the allocated buffer, causing a heap overflow and possible code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
The user can control the size of the next command passed along, but the
value passed to the ioctl isn't checked against the usable max command
size.

Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Peter Chang <dpf@google.com>
Acked-by: Douglas Gilbert <dgilbert@interlog.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (val > SG_MAX_CDB_SIZE)', '\t\t\treturn -ENOMEM;']}
description: The sg_ioctl function in drivers/scsi/sg.c in the Linux kernel through 4.10.4 allows local users to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a large command size in an SG_NEXT_CMD_LEN ioctl call, leading to out-of-bounds write access in the sg_write function.

code_evidence: In the SG_NEXT_CMD_LEN case, a user-supplied int is read via get_user into val and stored directly into sfp->next_cmd_len with only a lower clamp ((val > 0) ? val : 0); there is no upper bound check against SG_MAX_CDB_SIZE before the value is retained for later command handling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length flows into later buffer operations that exceed intended boundaries, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer; the ioctl itself is the origin of the unconstrained length rather than a separate weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ioctl accepts an arbitrarily large next_cmd_len from user space without validating it against the maximum command size. Trigger: a local user issues SG_NEXT_CMD_LEN with a large value, which is persisted in sfp and later consumed by the write path. Consequence: subsequent command handling performs out-of-bounds memory access, enabling a stack-based buffer overflow/out-of-bounds write and denial of service.

commit_msg:
ucount: Remove the atomicity from ucount->count

Always increment/decrement ucount->count under the ucounts_lock.  The
increments are there already and moving the decrements there means the
locking logic of the code is simpler.  This simplification in the
locking logic fixes a race between put_ucounts and get_ucounts that
could result in a use-after-free because the count could go zero then
be found by get_ucounts and then be freed by put_ucounts.

A bug presumably this one was found by a combination of syzkaller and
KASAN.  JongWhan Kim reported the syzkaller failure and Dmitry Vyukov
spotted the race in the code.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: f6b2db1a3e8d ("userns: Make the count of user namespaces per user")
Reported-by: JongHwan Kim <zzoru007@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrei Vagin <avagin@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tatomic_set(&new->count, 0);', '\tif (!atomic_add_unless(&ucounts->count, 1, INT_MAX))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tnew->count = 0;', '\tif (ucounts->count == INT_MAX)', '\telse', '\t\tucounts->count += 1;']}
description: Race condition in kernel/ucount.c in the Linux kernel through 4.10.2 allows local users to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls that leverage certain decrement behavior that causes incorrect interaction between put_ucounts and get_ucounts.

code_evidence: get_ucounts reads the shared ucounts count under ucounts_lock, but the increment at line 24 uses atomic_add_unless on ucounts->count; the lock is released at line 8 while allocating new and reacquired at line 15, and the count is initialized with atomic_set at line 14. The vulnerable path is the atomic increment at line 24 while a concurrent put_ucounts decrements without the lock, allowing the count to reach zero between the check and the increment.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because get_ucounts performs a check-and-increment on a shared reference count that a concurrent put_ucounts can modify without the same exclusive synchronization, violating atomicity and allowing a use-after-free. It is a race condition rather than a simple integer overflow, since the flaw is the unsynchronized timing window on the shared resource.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reference count on ucounts is modified by atomic operations outside ucounts_lock, so the check-and-increment at line 24 is not atomic with respect to put_ucounts. Trigger: concurrent get_ucounts and put_ucounts on the same ucounts entry can let the count drop to zero, be observed by get_ucounts, and then be freed by put_ucounts. Consequence: use-after-free and system crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
On unpacking key blob output buffer size should be fixed

Related: CVE-2022-29242
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!key) {', '        *key_len = 32;', '        return 1;', '    }', '  '], 'added_lines': ['', '    *key_len = 32;']}
description: GOST engine is a reference implementation of the Russian GOST crypto algorithms for OpenSSL. TLS clients using GOST engine when ciphersuite `TLS_GOSTR341112_256_WITH_KUZNYECHIK_CTR_OMAC` is agreed and the server uses 512 bit GOST secret keys are vulnerable to buffer overflow. GOST engine version 3.0.1 contains a patch for this issue. Disabling ciphersuite `TLS_GOSTR341112_256_WITH_KUZNYECHIK_CTR_OMAC` is a possible workaround.

code_evidence: expkeys is a fixed 64-byte stack buffer; gost_keg writes 32 bytes into it and gost_kimp15 is invoked with expkeys+32 and expkeys+0 as inputs, then writes unpacked key material into caller-supplied key with no length check against *key_len.

The early return when key==NULL sets *key_len=32 and skips unpacking; the patch removes this branch so *key_len=32 is set only later at line 86, meaning the caller's buffer-size query path no longer short-circuits before gost_kimp15 writes output.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a buffer write (unpacked key) whose size depends on parsed key transport data and is not checked against the destination size, matching CWE-120's buffer-copy-without-size-check pattern rather than an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: gost_kimp15 writes decrypted key material into the output pointer key without validating that the caller-provided buffer (sized by the pre-call *key_len) is large enough; the removed key==NULL branch previously prevented any write during size queries. Trigger: a TLS peer using the GOST ciphersuite with 512-bit keys causes larger unpacked output than the 32-byte expectation, so the copy overruns the caller's buffer, corrupting memory.

_bfd_clear_contents bounds checking

This PR shows a fuzzed binary triggering a segfault via a bad
relocation in .debug_line.  It turns out that unlike normal
relocations applied to a section, the linker applies those with
symbols from discarded sections via _bfd_clear_contents without
checking that the relocation is within the section bounds.  The same
thing now happens when reading debug sections since commit
a4cd947aca23, the PR23425 fix.

	PR 23770
	PR 23425
	* reloc.c (_bfd_clear_contents): Replace "location" param with
	"buf" and "off".  Bounds check "off".  Return status.
	* cofflink.c (_bfd_coff_generic_relocate_section): Update
	_bfd_clear_contents call.
	* elf-bfd.h (RELOC_AGAINST_DISCARDED_SECTION): Likewise.
	* elf32-arc.c (elf_arc_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-i386.c (elf_i386_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-metag.c (metag_final_link_relocate): Likewise.
	* elf32-nds32.c (nds32_elf_get_relocated_section_contents): Likewise.
	* elf32-ppc.c (ppc_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf32-visium.c (visium_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf64-ppc.c (ppc64_elf_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* elf64-x86-64.c *(elf_x86_64_relocate_section): Likewise.
	* libbfd-in.h (_bfd_clear_contents): Update prototype.
	* libbfd.h: Regenerate.

description: An issue was discovered in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.31. An invalid memory address dereference was discovered in read_reloc in reloc.c. The vulnerability causes a segmentation fault and application crash, which leads to denial of service, as demonstrated by objdump, because of missing _bfd_clear_contents bounds checking.

code_evidence: When the relocation's symbol belongs to a discarded section, the code computes p = data + (*parent)->address * bfd_octets_per_byte (input_bfd) and passes p to _bfd_clear_contents, which writes to that location. The relocation address comes from the input file and is never checked against the size of data/input_section before the pointer arithmetic and write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through a computed pointer without bounding the offset to the buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds memory operation on an intended buffer, matching CWE-119. The specific missing bounds check is the cause; the crash is only the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the relocation offset is trusted without validating that it lies within the section buffer. Trigger: a crafted relocation with a discarded-section symbol and an out-of-range address; the resulting p points outside data, and _bfd_clear_contents writes there. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write causing an invalid memory dereference and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Fix incorrectly assigned timer instance

The clean up commit 41672c0c24a6 ("ALSA: timer: Simplify error path in
snd_timer_open()") unified the error handling code paths with the
standard goto, but it introduced a subtle bug: the timer instance is
stored in snd_timer_open() incorrectly even if it returns an error.
This may eventually lead to UAF, as spotted by fuzzer.

The culprit is the snd_timer_open() code checks the
SNDRV_TIMER_IFLG_EXCLUSIVE flag with the common variable timeri.
This variable is supposed to be the newly created instance, but we
(ab-)used it for a temporary check before the actual creation of a
timer instance.  After that point, there is another check for the max
number of instances, and it bails out if over the threshold.  Before
the refactoring above, it worked fine because the code returned
directly from that point.  After the refactoring, however, it jumps to
the unified error path that stores the timeri variable in return --
even if it returns an error.  Unfortunately this stored value is kept
in the caller side (snd_timer_user_tselect()) in tu->timeri.  This
causes inconsistency later, as if the timer was successfully
assigned.

In this patch, we fix it by not re-using timeri variable but a
temporary variable for testing the exclusive connection, so timeri
remains NULL at that point.

Fixes: 41672c0c24a6 ("ALSA: timer: Simplify error path in snd_timer_open()")
Reported-and-tested-by: Tristan Madani <tristmd@gmail.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20191106165547.23518-1-tiwai@suse.de
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\ttimeri = list_entry(timer->open_list_head.next,', '\t\tif (timeri->flags & SNDRV_TIMER_IFLG_EXCLUSIVE) {', '\t\t\ttimeri = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tstruct snd_timer_instance *t =', '\t\t\tlist_entry(timer->open_list_head.next,', '\t\tif (t->flags & SNDRV_TIMER_IFLG_EXCLUSIVE) {']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.3.11, sound/core/timer.c has a use-after-free caused by erroneous code refactoring, aka CID-e7af6307a8a5. This is related to snd_timer_open and snd_timer_close_locked. The timeri variable was originally intended to be for a newly created timer instance, but was used for a different purpose after refactoring.

code_evidence: The exclusive-flag check loads the existing instance from timer->open_list_head into the shared variable timeri, then clears timeri only on the EBUSY branch.
When the instance-count limit is exceeded, the code jumps to unlock without resetting timeri, so the stale pointer to the pre-existing instance survives.
At unlock the function unconditionally stores timeri through *ti = timeri even on the error return, handing the caller a reference to an instance it never created.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the defect yields a dangling/incorrectly owned reference to a timer instance that may be freed by its real owner while the caller still treats it as valid; the flaw is the erroneous reference retained after an error return, not merely a resource leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the temporary list_entry result is stored in timeri, the variable later returned to the caller, and the max_instances error path does not clear it. Trigger: open a timer whose open_list is non-empty and whose num_instances reaches max_instances, so snd_timer_open returns -EBUSY while *ti still points to an existing instance. The caller keeps that pointer as its own timer instance, producing inconsistent ownership that can later lead to use-after-free of the instance.

commit_msg:
Add missing checks when loading and playing .mkj files

Fix the following issues in src/mkj.cpp:
* Check number of channels before loading instruments data.
  This fixes a heap-based buffer overflow in CmkjPlayer::load()
  (issue #87).
* Check number of notes befor calculating size of song data
  to avoid interger overflows as well as out-of-bounds reads
  later in update(). (Size of song data vs. used data is really
  hilarious, but that's the way it is.)
* Fail loading if there was an error while reading file data.
* Also in update(), end the song if invalid data is encountered.
  That avoids integer overflows or out-of-range OPL writes.

This commit fixes CVE-2019-14692.

Fixes: https://github.com/adplug/adplug/issues/87

code_evidence: The file-controlled 16-bit maxchannel is read at line 11 and used directly as the loop bound writing inst[i].value[j] for i < maxchannel, so a value above the inst array capacity writes out of bounds.

The file-controlled maxnotes at line 17 is multiplied with (maxchannel+1) to size songbuf at line 18, and the same product bounds the write loop at lines 20-21; no range or overflow check constrains these values.

The integer overflow is the sizing root cause; the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds write, not merely a read.

A large maxchannel overflows the fixed inst array in the load loop, and large maxnotes can make the allocation size computation overflow, so the subsequent songbuf writes exceed the intended buffer, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg: fs: Don't try to delete the file when copying. It could cause a security issue if the file exists and doesn't allow other's to read/write. delete could allow someone to create the file and have access to the data.

description: mstdlib (aka the M Standard Library for C) 1.2.0 has incorrect file access control in situations where M_fs_perms_can_access attempts to delete an existing file (that lacks public read/write access) during a copy operation, related to fs/m_fs.c and fs/m_fs_path.c. An attacker could create the file and then would have access to the data.

code_evidence: On any copy failure without M_FS_FILE_MODE_OVERWRITE, the function calls M_fs_delete(path_new, M_TRUE, NULL, ...) unconditionally. This deletes the destination path (recursively, per the M_TRUE flag) even though the failure may stem from permissions or other errors, not from a file the copy itself created.

It is not merely a missing authorization check (CWE-285) because the defect is the resulting exposure via the attacker-controlled file permissions.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path deletes path_new without verifying that the copy created it or that the caller owns it. Trigger: an attacker pre-creates path_new with restrictive read/write permissions so the copy fails; the cleanup then removes that file, letting the attacker recreate it with looser permissions and read data placed there. Consequence: unintended actors gain read/write access to the copied data, i.e. permission/access-control exposure of a critical resource.

commit_msg:
RAR5 reader: reject files that declare invalid header flags

One of the fields in RAR5's base block structure is the size of the
header. Some invalid files declare a 0 header size setting, which can
confuse the unpacker. Minimum header size for RAR5 base blocks is 7
bytes (4 bytes for CRC, and 3 bytes for the rest), so block size of 0
bytes should be rejected at header parsing stage.

The fix adds an error condition if header size of 0 bytes is detected.
In this case, the unpacker will not attempt to unpack the file, as the
header is corrupted.

The commit also adds OSSFuzz #20459 sample to test further regressions
in this area.

commit_msg: Detect extra data after SMTP STARTTLS response and return error
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  // Detect if the server send extra data after the STARTTLS response.', '  // This *may* be a "response injection attack".', '  if (session->stream->read_buffer_len != 0) {', '    // Since it is also protocol violation, exit.', '    // There is no general error type for STARTTLS errors in SMTP', '    return MAILSMTP_ERROR_SSL;', '  }']}
description: LibEtPan through 1.9.4, as used in MailCore 2 through 0.6.3 and other products, has a STARTTLS buffering issue that affects IMAP, SMTP, and POP3. When a server sends a "begin TLS" response, the client reads additional data (e.g., from a meddler-in-the-middle attacker) and evaluates it in a TLS context, aka "response injection."

code_evidence: After read_response(session) at line 9, the code immediately switches on the returned status and returns success on 220, or an error otherwise. It is not a memory-safety or authentication flaw; the defect is failure to constrain special elements crossing into a downstream parser.
