See https://crbug.com/585267.', '                m_integrityFailure = true;', '            } else if (disposition == ScriptIntegrityDisposition::NotChecked && resource->resourceBuffer()) {', '                scriptResource->setIntegrityDisposition(m_integrityFailure ? ScriptIntegrityDisposition::Failed : ScriptIntegrityDisposition::Passed);']}
description: The PendingScript::notifyFinished function in WebKit/Source/core/dom/PendingScript.cpp in Google Chrome before 49.0.2623.75 relies on memory-cache information about integrity-check occurrences instead of integrity-check successes, which allows remote attackers to bypass the Subresource Integrity (aka SRI) protection mechanism by triggering two loads of the same resource.

code_evidence: When the integrity attribute and metadata are non-empty, line 8 gates the actual SRI verification on integrityAlreadyChecked() being false; line 9 then marks the check as done before line 10 computes m_integrityFailure. On a second load of the same resource, integrityAlreadyChecked() is true, so line 10 never runs and m_integrityFailure retains its default (success) value, even if the first check failed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function mismanages a security-check state, causing a security feature (SRI enforcement) to be skipped on reload; this is a permissions/security-feature enforcement failure consistent with CWE-264's category. It is not a memory-safety or injection flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cache records only that an integrity check occurred, not its outcome, so the guard at line 8 suppresses re-evaluation. Trigger: loading the same resource twice in the same origin. Consequence: the second load is treated as integrity-passed, bypassing Subresource Integrity protection and allowing a tampered resource to execute.

Zero-initialize memory for new map's value in function nsim_bpf_map_alloc
since it may cause a potential kernel information leak issue, as follows:

commit_msg:
[sipmsgops] fix codec_delete_XX() parsing

Issue discovered during OpenSIPS Security Audit 2021,
        by Alfred Farrugia & Sandro Gauci (Enable Security)

https://github.com/OpenSIPS/opensips/security/advisories/GHSA-xj5x-g52f-548h
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int delete_sdp_line( struct sip_msg * msg, char * s)', "\twhile(*start != '\\n')", "\twhile(*end != '\\n')"], 'added_lines': ['int delete_sdp_line( struct sip_msg * msg, char * s, struct sdp_stream_cell *stream)', "\twhile(*start != '\\n' && start > stream->body.s)", "\twhile(*end != '\\n' && end < (stream->body.s+stream->body.len) )"]}
description:
OpenSIPS is a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) server implementation. Prior to versions 3.1.7 and 3.2.4, OpenSIPS crashes when a malformed SDP body is received and is processed by the `delete_sdp_line` function in the sipmsgops module. This issue can be reproduced by calling the function with an SDP body that does not terminate by a line feed (i.e. `\n`).

The vulnerability was found while performing black-box fuzzing against an OpenSIPS server running a configuration that made use of the functions `codec_delete_except_re` and `codec_delete_re`. The same issue was also discovered while performing coverage guided fuzzing on the function `codec_delete_except_re`. The crash happens because the function `delete_sdp_line` expects that an SDP line is terminated by a line feed (`\n`):

By abusing this vulnerability, an attacker is able to crash the server. It affects configurations containing functions that rely on the affected code, such as the function `codec_delete_except_re`. Due to the sanity check that is performed in the `del_lump` function, exploitation of this issue will generate an `abort` in the lumps processing function, resulting in a Denial of Service. This issue has been fixed in versions 3.1.7 and 3.2.4.

code_evidence: start and end are initialized to the caller-supplied pointer s; the backward scan `while(*start != '\n') start--;` has no lower bound, so a body lacking a preceding line feed walks before the SDP buffer.
The forward scan `while(*end != '\n') end++;` has no upper bound, so a body not terminated by a line feed walks past the buffer end.
The derived offsets `start - msg->buf` and length `end - start` are passed to del_lump without confirming the scans stayed within the SDP body.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes attacker-controlled SDP data without validating the required well-formedness property (newline termination) or derived buffer bounds before using offsets. That is improper input validation (CWE-20); the crash is the consequence, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code: if( del_lump(msg, start - msg->buf, end - start,0) == NULL )

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function assumes every SDP line is newline-terminated and never validates that assumption or constrains the pointer scans. Trigger: an SDP body with no line feed (or a line lacking a preceding '\n') processed via codec_delete_except_re/codec_delete_re. The unbounded scans read outside the body buffer, and the resulting out-of-range start/end values cause del_lump's sanity check to abort, crashing the server (DoS).

commit_msg:
libsepol/cil: Check for statements not allowed in optional blocks

While there are some checks for invalid statements in an optional
block when resolving the AST, there are no checks when building the
AST.

OSS-Fuzz found the following policy which caused a null dereference
in cil_tree_get_next_path().
  (blockinherit b3)
  (sid SID)
  (sidorder(SID))
  (optional o
    (ibpkeycon :(1 0)s)
    (block b3
      (filecon""block())
      (filecon""block())))

The problem is that the blockinherit copies block b3 before
the optional block is disabled. When the optional is disabled,
block b3 is deleted along with everything else in the optional.
Later, when filecon statements with the same path are found an
error message is produced and in trying to find out where the block
was copied from, the reference to the deleted block is used. The
error handling code assumes (rightly) that if something was copied
from a block then that block should still exist.

It is clear that in-statements, blocks, and macros cannot be in an
optional, because that allows nodes to be copied from the optional
block to somewhere outside even though the optional could be disabled
later. When optionals are disabled the AST is reset and the
resolution is restarted at the point of resolving macro calls, so
anything resolved before macro calls will never be re-resolved.
This includes tunableifs, in-statements, blockinherits,
blockabstracts, and macro definitions. Tunable declarations also
cannot be in an optional block because they are needed to resolve
tunableifs. It should be fine to allow blockinherit statements in
an optional, because that is copying nodes from outside the optional
to the optional and if the optional is later disabled, everything
will be deleted anyway.

Check and quit with an error if a tunable declaration, in-statement,
block, blockabstract, or macro definition is found within an
optional when either building or resolving the AST.

Signed-off-by: James Carter <jwcart2@gmail.com>

Fix heap OOB read/write due to incorrect indexing.

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. There is a typo in TensorFlow's `SpecializeType` which results in heap OOB read/write. Due to a typo, `arg` is initialized to the `i`th mutable argument in a loop where the loop index is `j`. Hence it is possible to assign to `arg` from outside the vector of arguments. Since this is a mutable proto value, it allows both read and write to outside of bounds data. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, and TensorFlow 2.6.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The loop iterates j over t->args_size(), but the mutable accessor is called with i (the outer output_arg index) instead of j, so arg does not correspond to the current j element.
arg is then mutated: set_type_id at line 19, map_dtype_to_tensor/add_args at lines 21/24, and clear_s at line 30, all through the mismatched index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to a mutable argument selected by an index outside the vector's valid range, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. The read of arg->type_id()/s() is incidental; the supported consequence is the memory write through the mismatched index.

evidence_lines.code:
for (int j = 0; j < t->args_size(); j++) {
auto* arg = t->mutable_args(i);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the wrong index i used in t->mutable_args(i) inside a loop bounded by t->args_size(). When i exceeds the size of t's args vector, mutable_args(i) yields an out-of-bounds mutable proto element; subsequent set_type_id/add_args/clear_s write past the buffer. Trigger is an op whose output full type has fewer args than the output_arg index, causing heap OOB read/write.

commit_msg: fixed theoretical stack overflow identified in #195)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        memset(addr1,0,sizeof(addr1)); memcpy(addr1,addr,(depth+7)/8); setbit(addr1,depth);'], 'added_lines': ['        memset(addr1,0,sizeof(addr1)); memcpy(addr1,addr,(depth+7)/8);', '        setbit(addr1,sizeof(addr1),depth);']}
description: A stack-based buffer over-read exists in setbit() at iptree.h of TCPFLOW 1.5.0, due to received incorrect values causing incorrect computation, leading to denial of service during an address_histogram call or a get_histogram call.

code_evidence: addr1 is a fixed ADDRBYTES buffer; memcpy copies (depth+7)/8 bytes into it, and setbit(addr1,depth) then indexes addr1 based on the attacker-influenced depth value without passing the buffer size, so a large depth makes setbit read (and write) past addr1.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function indexes and reads the stack array addr1 at an offset beyond its ADDRBYTES bound, which is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The fix passes sizeof(addr1) so setbit bounds the index; this is an OOB read rather than merely an integer issue.

evidence_lines.code:
memset(addr0,0,sizeof(addr0)); memcpy(addr0,addr,(depth+7)/8);
memset(addr1,0,sizeof(addr1)); memcpy(addr1,addr,(depth+7)/8); setbit(addr1,depth);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that setbit derives its byte/bit offset from depth while addr1 is only ADDRBYTES long and the copy length (depth+7)/8 can exceed that size. A caller passing an incorrect/large depth (e.g. via address_histogram/get_histogram) triggers out-of-bounds access on the stack buffer, causing a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

description: Buffer overflow in MagickCore/enhance.c in ImageMagick before 7.0.2-7 allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via vectors related to pixel cache morphology.

code_evidence: The equalize_map, histogram and map buffers are sized by GetPixelChannels(image) at allocation time (lines 29-34).

Trigger: an image whose cache was built with a different channel layout than the current GetPixelChannels value. description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.6 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.12, the DICOM dissector has an infinite loop. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-dcm.c by validating a length value.

This is a reachability/termination failure, not merely an out-of-bounds read, so CWE-835 is the appropriate label.

Because the bounds test at [19] computes pdv_len + 4 without overflow protection, a value near UINT32_MAX wraps the sum, so the 'too large' branch at [20,21] is skipped. diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['_PyMemoTable_ResizeTable(PyMemoTable *self, Py_ssize_t min_size)', '    Py_ssize_t new_size = MT_MINSIZE;', '    Py_ssize_t to_process;', '    /* Find the smallest valid table size >= min_size. */', '    while (new_size < min_size && new_size > 0)', '        new_size <<= 1;', '    if (new_size <= 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['_PyMemoTable_ResizeTable(PyMemoTable *self, size_t min_size)', '    size_t new_size = MT_MINSIZE;', '    size_t to_process;', '    if (min_size > PY_SSIZE_T_MAX) {', '    }', '', '    /* Find the smallest valid table size >= min_size. */', '    while (new_size < min_size) {', '        new_size <<= 1;']}
description: Modules/_pickle.c in Python before 3.7.1 has an integer overflow via a large LONG_BINPUT value that is mishandled during a "resize to twice the size" attempt. This issue might cause memory exhaustion, but is only relevant if the pickle format is used for serializing tens or hundreds of gigabytes of data. This issue is fixed in: v3.4.10, v3.4.10rc1; v3.5.10, v3.5.10rc1, v3.5.7, v3.5.7rc1, v3.5.8, v3.5.8rc1, v3.5.8rc2, v3.5.9; v3.6.10, v3.6.10rc1, v3.6.11, v3.6.11rc1, v3.6.12, v3.6.7, v3.6.7rc1, v3.6.7rc2, v3.6.8, v3.6.8rc1, v3.6.9, v3.6.9rc1; v3.7.1, v3.7.1rc1, v3.7.1rc2, v3.7.2, v3.7.2rc1, v3.7.3, v3.7.3rc1, v3.7.4, v3.7.4rc1, v3.7.4rc2, v3.7.5, v3.7.5rc1, v3.7.6, v3.7.6rc1, v3.7.7, v3.7.7rc1, v3.7.8, v3.7.8rc1, v3.7.9.

code_evidence: new_size is a signed Py_ssize_t initialized to MT_MINSIZE and doubled in the loop at lines 9-10. The loop guard only checks new_size < min_size && new_size > 0, so a sufficiently large min_size drives repeated left shifts of a signed value, which is undefined on signed overflow and can yield a negative or zero result. The post-loop check at line 11 only catches new_size <= 0 after the overflow may already have occurred. new_size is then used directly as the allocation count at line 17, stored in mt_allocated (line 23), and used to compute mt_mask = new_size - 1 (line 24).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size calculation (repeated left shift of a signed integer) whose result is assumed to grow but can overflow/wrap, and the wrapped value is used for allocation and indexing. This is the classic integer-overflow-or-wraparound pattern, matching CWE-190; it is not merely an out-of-bounds read/write, since the defect is the unchecked arithmetic producing the size.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the table-size computation doubles a signed Py_ssize_t without bounding the shift, so a large min_size can overflow the signed type before the <= 0 check runs. Trigger: an attacker-supplied large LONG_BINPUT value reaches resize with a huge min_size. Consequence: the wrapped/small new_size propagates into allocation, mt_allocated and mt_mask, leading to incorrect sizing and memory exhaustion or memory-safety issues rather than a correctly sized table.

description: Contiki-NG is an open-source, cross-platform operating system for IoT devices. Because of insufficient validation of IPv6 neighbor discovery options in Contiki-NG, attackers can send neighbor solicitation packets that trigger an out-of-bounds read. The problem exists in the module os/net/ipv6/uip-nd6.c, where memory read operations from the main packet buffer, uip_buf, are not checked if they go out of bounds. In particular, this problem can occur when attempting to read the 2-byte option header and the Source Link-Layer Address Option (SLLAO). This attack requires ipv6 be enabled for the network. The problem has been patched in the develop branch of Contiki-NG. The upcoming 4.8 release of Contiki-NG will include the patch.Users unable to upgrade may apply the patch in Contiki-NG PR #1654.

code_evidence: Line 3 only checks that nd6_opt_llao is non-NULL, not that the option header and data fit within the received packet buffer. Line 4 then reads UIP_LLADDR_LEN bytes starting at nd6_opt_llao[UIP_ND6_OPT_DATA_OFFSET] without any length or bounds validation against uip_buf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an unchecked read past the end of the packet buffer, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. A NULL-pointer check alone does not constrain the read length relative to the buffer, so the weakness is the absent bounds validation, not a NULL dereference.

evidence_lines.code:
if(dest != NULL && nd6_opt_llao != NULL) {
memcpy(dest, &nd6_opt_llao[UIP_ND6_OPT_DATA_OFFSET], UIP_LLADDR_LEN);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the missing bound check on the ND6 option pointer before the memcpy from the packet buffer. A truncated neighbor solicitation whose SLLAO option lies near the buffer end causes line 4 to read past the intended buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read (information disclosure or crash).

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in the C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In various parts of PJSIP, when error/failure occurs, it is found that the function returns without releasing the currently held locks. This could result in a system deadlock, which cause a denial of service for the users. No release has yet been made which contains the linked fix commit. All versions up to an including 2.11.1 are affected. Users may need to manually apply the patch.

code_evidence: Line 12 acquires ipp_factory.mutex. When the codec lookup fails, the idx == -1 branch at lines 25-28 sets *p_codec to NULL and returns PJMEDIA_CODEC_EFAILED without calling pj_mutex_unlock, unlike the success path at line 61 and the error paths at lines 43 and 55.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 covers improper lock acquisition/release. Here the function acquires a lock but fails to release it on one return path, producing the availability impact the weakness describes; this is a lock-release defect rather than a distinct race condition.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The mutex is acquired at line 12 but the early failure return on the not-found path (lines 25-28) omits pj_mutex_unlock. Any caller requesting an unsupported codec triggers this path, leaving the mutex permanently held; subsequent lock attempts block, causing deadlock and denial of service.

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tsfbhash = jhash_1word(salt, q->bins[slot].perturbation);', '\t\tsfbhash = skb_get_hash_perturb(skb, q->bins[slot].perturbation);', '\t\t\t    q->bins[slot].perturbation);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tsfbhash = siphash_1u32(salt, &q->bins[slot].perturbation);', '\t\tsfbhash = skb_get_hash_perturb(skb, &q->bins[slot].perturbation);', '\t\t\t    &q->bins[slot].perturbation);']}
description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: When a classifier is present, salt is obtained from sfb_classify and combined with the per-bin perturbation via jhash_1word to produce sfbhash, which is then used to select buckets ([33],[41-42]).
When no classifier is present, sfbhash comes from skb_get_hash_perturb using the per-bin perturbation ([35]), which in this version is a 32-bit jhash-based value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because a security-relevant value (the flow hash/perturbation) relies on insufficiently random/unpredictable derivation (jhash over known fields), enabling inference. The patch replacing jhash_1word/skb_get_hash_perturb with siphash confirms the weakness is insufficient randomness, not a memory-safety bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The flow hash used for bucket selection is derived from a 32-bit perturbation secret combined via jhash, a non-cryptographic hash over attacker-observable packet fields. An attacker can infer the perturbation and thereby predict bucket placement, allowing tracking of flows/devices; the root cause is the weak, non-cryptographic hash rather than the bucket logic itself.

commit_msg:
hw/scsi/scsi-disk: Disallow block sizes smaller than 512 [CVE-2023-42467]

We are doing things like

    nb_sectors /= (s->qdev.blocksize / BDRV_SECTOR_SIZE);

in the code here (e.g. in scsi_disk_emulate_mode_sense()), so if
the blocksize is smaller than BDRV_SECTOR_SIZE (=512), this crashes
with a division by 0 exception. Thus disallow block sizes of 256
bytes to avoid this situation.

Resolves: https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/issues/1813
CVE: 2023-42467
Signed-off-by: Thomas Huth <thuth@redhat.com>
Message-ID: <20230925091854.49198-1-thuth@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['         * a subsequent SCSI command will be the same', '        if (bs && !(bs & ~0xff00) && bs != s->qdev.blocksize) {'], 'added_lines': ['         * a subsequent SCSI command will be the same. Also disallow a block', '         * size of 256 since we cannot handle anything below BDRV_SECTOR_SIZE.', '        if (bs && !(bs & ~0xfe00) && bs != s->qdev.blocksize) {']}
description: QEMU through 8.0.0 could trigger a division by zero in scsi_disk_reset in hw/scsi/scsi-disk.c because scsi_disk_emulate_mode_select does not prevent s->qdev.blocksize from being 256. This stops QEMU and the guest immediately.

code_evidence: Line 29 derives bs from the mode-select block descriptor bytes p[5..7]. Line 30 validates it with only `!(bs & ~0xff00)`, which permits bs=256 (0x100) and other values below 512; the accepted value is then stored into s->qdev.blocksize on line 31.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stored undersized blocksize becomes a zero divisor in later division, which is exactly CWE-369 (divide by zero). The weakness is the missing lower-bound constraint on bs, not an out-of-bounds access or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the block-size validation accepts 256-byte sectors, so s->qdev.blocksize can become smaller than BDRV_SECTOR_SIZE (512). Trigger: a guest issues MODE SELECT with a block descriptor setting bs=256. Later code (e.g. scsi_disk_emulate_mode_sense) divides nb_sectors by (blocksize/512), yielding a zero divisor and crashing QEMU, an availability DoS.

commit_msg:
Add error checking to ImmutableConst OP that strings are not yet supported.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 401065359
Change-Id: I9dd2bd2a2c36f22f4a05153daf6ebdc4613469d2

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the `ImmutableConst` operation in TensorFlow can be tricked into reading arbitrary memory contents. This is because the `tstring` TensorFlow string class has a special case for memory mapped strings but the operation itself does not offer any support for this datatype. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.7.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.6.1, TensorFlow 2.5.2, and TensorFlow 2.4.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function initializes a MemmappedTensorAllocator from a region and immediately constructs a tensor with the caller-supplied dtype_ and shape_ at line 6, without validating that dtype_ is a supported type. The patch adds a DT_STRING rejection check before this tensor creation, showing the original code accepted DT_STRING and passed it into the memory-mapped tensor path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing dtype constraint lets the memory-mapped string path read past the intended buffer, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. It is not merely a type-confusion issue because the supported consequence is reading arbitrary memory beyond the mapped buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the operation builds a tensor over a memory-mapped region for any dtype_, including DT_STRING, whose tstring representation has a special memory-mapped-string case unsupported by ImmutableConst. Trigger: supplying dtype_=DT_STRING causes tensor construction to interpret mapped memory as string data incorrectly, reading beyond the intended region. Consequence: arbitrary memory contents can be read (information disclosure).

description: The ReadDPXImage function in coders\dpx.c in ImageMagick 7.0.6-0 has a large loop vulnerability that can cause CPU exhaustion via a crafted DPX file, related to lack of an EOF check.

code_evidence: Loop advances offset one byte per iteration until offset reaches dpx.file.image_offset, calling ReadBlobByte each time with no EOF check in the loop condition.
dpx.file.image_offset is a 32-bit value read directly from the file header, so an attacker controls the loop bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits because the iteration count is controlled by untrusted input and not sufficiently limited, yielding resource exhaustion; the missing EOF check is the implementation detail enabling the excessive iteration, not a separate weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
for ( ; offset < (MagickOffsetType) dpx.file.image_offset; offset++)
(void) ReadBlobByte(image);

dpx.file.image_offset=ReadBlobLong(image);
offset+=4;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the header-supplied image_offset is used as an unbounded loop bound while ReadBlobByte is called once per iteration without checking for EOF. Trigger: a crafted DPX file declaring a very large image_offset. Consequence: the loop iterates up to the declared offset, consuming CPU even after the blob is exhausted.

commit_msg: misc oom and possible memory leak fix
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    for (p = s1; (p = strchr(p, *s2)) != NULL; p = strchr(p + 1, *s2)) {'], 'added_lines': ['    for (p = s1; (p = strchr(p, *s2)) != NULL; p++) {']}
description: Boa through 0.94.14rc21 allows remote attackers to trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) condition because malloc is mishandled.

Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds read past the s1 buffer, potentially disclosing adjacent memory or crashing.

payload area.  A negatively instantiated key may be then be positively
instantiated by updating it with valid data.  However, the ->update key
type method must be aware that the error code may be there.

The following may be used to trigger the bug in the user key type:

    keyctl request2 user user "" @u
    keyctl add user user "a" @u

commit_msg:
Make extensions use a correct same-origin check.

GURL::GetOrigin does not do the right thing for all types of URLs.

BUG=573317

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1658913002

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#373381}

description: The Extensions subsystem in Google Chrome before 50.0.2661.75 incorrectly relies on GetOrigin method calls for origin comparisons, which allows remote attackers to bypass the Same Origin Policy and obtain sensitive information via a crafted extension.

code_evidence: Line 2 only asserts that origin equals its GetOrigin() result; the release build performs no enforcement, and GetOrigin() is the very method known to misbehave for some URL types.
Lines 4-6 parse origin.GetOrigin().spec() into the pattern, so the stored origin pattern derives from GetOrigin() rather than the actual origin.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-284 fits because the incorrect origin derivation causes the access-control check to fail to restrict access to the intended origin, letting unauthorized actors cross the origin boundary. A specific descendant (e.g., improper same-origin enforcement) would be more precise, but the target CWE-284 is supported.

evidence_lines.code: DCHECK_EQ(origin.GetOrigin(), origin);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the origin pattern is built from GURL::GetOrigin(), which does not correctly normalize all URL schemes, so distinct or crafted origins can collapse to a matching origin. Trigger: a crafted extension URL whose GetOrigin() result differs from its true origin. Consequence: the pattern matches origins it should not, enabling Same Origin Policy bypass and disclosure of sensitive data.

commit_msg:
Calculate the reply payload length in a local variable.

Using the same variable for the remaining request length and the reply
length is confusing at best and can cause errors at worst (if the
request had extra stuff at the end, so that the variable is non-zero).

This addresses Include Security issue I8: [libpcap] Remote Packet
Capture Daemon Parameter Reuse.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t// checks the number of interfaces and it computes the total length of the payload', '\t\t\tplen+= strlen(d->description);', '\t\t\tplen+= strlen(d->name);', '', '\t\tplen+= sizeof(struct rpcap_findalldevs_if);', '\t\t\t\tplen+= (sizeof(struct rpcap_sockaddr) * 4);', '\t    RPCAP_MSG_FINDALLIF_REPLY, nif, plen);'], 'added_lines': ['\tuint32 replylen;\t\t\t// length of reply payload', '\t// This checks the number of interfaces and computes the total', '\t// length of the payload.', '\treplylen = 0;', '\t\t\treplylen += strlen(d->description);', '\t\t\treplylen += strlen(d->name);', '', '\t\treplylen += sizeof(struct rpcap_findalldevs_if);', '\t\t\t\treplylen += (sizeof(struct rpcap_sockaddr) * 4);', '\t    RPCAP_MSG_FINDALLIF_REPLY, nif, replylen);']}
description: rpcapd/daemon.c in libpcap before 1.9.1 mishandles certain length values because of reuse of a variable. This may open up an attack vector involving extra data at the end of a request.

code_evidence: The function receives a request length plen as a parameter, and line 5 discards exactly plen bytes of request payload before building the reply.

The reply-length computation at lines 23-45 accumulates interface, name, description and address sizes into plen, the same variable that held the request length, rather than into a fresh reply-length accumulator.

The header at lines 46-51 is created with that accumulated plen as the reply payload length, so the value placed in the RPCAP_MSG_FINDALLIF_REPLY header is the request remainder plus the computed reply size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-131 covers incorrect calculation of a buffer/size value; here the reply payload size written into the protocol header is computed incorrectly because the request length contaminates the accumulator, which is exactly a size-calculation error rather than a separate validation or pointer flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the incoming request length (plen) is reused as the accumulator for the outgoing reply payload length. Trigger: a request with extra trailing data makes plen non-zero after line 5, so the reply header advertises a length larger than the payload actually serialized. Consequence: the client receives an inflated reply length, causing a length/state mismatch in the RPCAP protocol handling that may lead to incorrect parsing or buffer misuse on the receiving side.

commit_msg:
gnttab: deal with status frame mapping race

Once gnttab_map_frame() drops the grant table lock, the MFN it reports
back to its caller is free to other manipulation. In particular
gnttab_unpopulate_status_frames() might free it, by a racing request on
another CPU, thus resulting in a reference to a deallocated page getting
added to a domain's P2M.

Obtain a page reference in gnttab_map_frame() to prevent freeing of the
page until xenmem_add_to_physmap_one() has actually completed its acting
on the page. Do so uniformly, even if only strictly required for v2
status pages, to avoid extra conditionals (which then would all need to
be kept in sync going forward).

This is CVE-2021-28701 / XSA-384.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* If we fail to add the mapping, we need to drop the reference we', '     * took earlier on foreign pages */', '    if ( rc && space == XENMAPSPACE_gmfn_foreign )'], 'added_lines': ['        /* Need to take care of the reference obtained in gnttab_map_frame(). */', '        page = mfn_to_page(mfn);', '    /*', '     * For XENMAPSPACE_gmfn_foreign if we failed to add the mapping, we need', '     * to drop the reference we took earlier. In all other cases we need to', '     * drop any reference we took earlier (perhaps indirectly).', '     */', '    if ( space == XENMAPSPACE_gmfn_foreign ? rc : page != NULL )']}
description: Another race in XENMAPSPACE_grant_table handling Guests are permitted access to certain Xen-owned pages of memory. The majority of such pages remain allocated / associated with a guest for its entire lifetime. Grant table v2 status pages, however, are de-allocated when a guest switches (back) from v2 to v1. Freeing such pages requires that the hypervisor enforce that no parallel request can result in the addition of a mapping of such a page to a guest. That enforcement was missing, allowing guests to retain access to pages that were freed and perhaps re-used for other purposes. Unfortunately, when XSA-379 was being prepared, this similar issue was not noticed.

code_evidence: For XENMAPSPACE_grant_table the function calls gnttab_map_frame() to obtain an MFN; gnttab_map_frame() drops the grant table lock before returning, so the returned MFN is no longer protected against concurrent manipulation.

The function then passes that MFN to guest_physmap_add_entry() and only conditionally calls put_page() when rc && space == XENMAPSPACE_gmfn_foreign; no reference is held for the grant-table MFN, so a racing gnttab_unpopulate_status_frames() can free the page before the mapping is added.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a timing window in which a shared resource (the grant-table status page) is modified by a concurrent code sequence after exclusivity is dropped, matching CWE-362. It is not merely a missing bounds check; the defect is improper synchronization across a lock-release window.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the grant-table MFN is used after gnttab_map_frame() releases the lock without the caller holding a page reference, so the page can be freed concurrently. Trigger: a guest maps a v2 status frame while another CPU frees it via gnttab_unpopulate_status_frames(). Consequence: a deallocated page is added to the domain's P2M, letting the guest retain access to reused memory.

commit_msg:
Avoid needless resource usage when processing a corrupt DWARF directory or file name table.

	PR 22210
	* dwarf2.c (read_formatted_entries): Fail early if we know that
	the loop parsing data entries will overflow the end of the
	section.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      bfd_set_error (bfd_error_bad_value);', '      return FALSE;', '    }', '', "  /* PR 22210.  Paranoia check.  Don't bother running the loop", '     if we know that we are going to run out of buffer.  */', '  if (data_count > (bfd_vma) (buf_end - buf))', '    {', '      _bfd_error_handler (_("Dwarf Error: data count (%Lx) larger than buffer size."),', '\t\t\t  data_count);']}
description: read_formatted_entries in dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: data_count is read via _bfd_safe_read_leb128 at line 26 and, absent a buffer-size check, drives the outer loop at line 34. The only guard before the patch is format_count==0 && data_count!=0 at line 28.

The inner loop consumes format entries from format_header_data (lines 45-47, 71-73) and reads per-entry data advancing buf (lines 77-86), but no comparison of data_count against remaining buffer (buf_end - buf) bounds the outer iteration count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the outer data-entry loop's termination depends on an attacker-controlled data_count that is not constrained by the actual buffer size, so the exit condition is effectively unreachable within valid data, yielding resource-exhaustion DoS. The missing bound check is the cause; the loop behavior is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parsed data_count is trusted as a loop bound without verifying it fits the section buffer. Trigger: a crafted ELF with a DWARF directory/file-name table whose data_count exceeds the available buffer. Consequence: the outer loop at line 34 iterates far beyond the buffer, causing excessive resource consumption/denial of service as reads continually fail or return without terminating the loop usefully.

commit_msg: Merge pull request from GHSA-8fmx-hqw7-6gmc
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tpj_mutex_unlock (opus_data->mutex);', '\tpj_mutex_unlock (opus_data->mutex);']}
description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in the C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In various parts of PJSIP, when error/failure occurs, it is found that the function returns without releasing the currently held locks. This could result in a system deadlock, which cause a denial of service for the users. No release has yet been made which contains the linked fix commit. All versions up to an including 2.11.1 are affected. Users may need to manually apply the patch.

code_evidence: The function acquires opus_data->mutex at line 8 before any error path. When opus_encoder_init fails, the branch at lines 75-78 logs and returns PJMEDIA_CODEC_EFAILED without unlocking the held mutex.
Similarly, when opus_decoder_init fails, the branch at lines 107-110 returns PJMEDIA_CODEC_EFAILED while the mutex acquired at line 8 remains held.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a lock acquired but not released on an error path, matching CWE-667 improper locking. The consequence is deadlock/DoS rather than data corruption, distinguishing it from a race condition on shared data.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The mutex is locked at entry, but the encoder-init and decoder-init failure paths return early without releasing it. Triggering these failures (e.g., invalid codec parameters causing OPUS init errors) leaves the mutex permanently locked, so later codec operations block and the system deadlocks, denying service.

commit_msg:
ecryptfs: forbid opening files without mmap handler

This prevents users from triggering a stack overflow through a recursive
invocation of pagefault handling that involves mapping procfs files into
virtual memory.

Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Tyler Hicks <tyhicks@canonical.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tgoto out;', '\tif (IS_ERR(*lower_file))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tgoto have_file;', '\tif (IS_ERR(*lower_file)) {', '\t\tgoto out;', '\t}', 'have_file:', '\tif ((*lower_file)->f_op->mmap == NULL) {', '\t\tfput(*lower_file);', '\t\t*lower_file = NULL;', '\t\trc = -EMEDIUMTYPE;', '\t}']}
description: The ecryptfs_privileged_open function in fs/ecryptfs/kthread.c in the Linux kernel before 4.6.3 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (stack memory consumption) via vectors involving crafted mmap calls for /proc pathnames, leading to recursive pagefault handling.

code_evidence: The function opens the lower file via dentry_open and, on success, jumps to out/returns without inspecting the file's f_op->mmap handler.
After the kthread completes the open, only IS_ERR is checked; a successfully opened file lacking an mmap handler is returned to the caller unchanged.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing mmap-handler check permits recursive pagefault handling that drives stack memory past its intended bound, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The missing validation is the cause; the stack overflow is the resultant out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ecryptfs_privileged_open does not verify that the opened lower file provides an mmap handler before returning it. Trigger: a user maps a procfs path through ecryptfs, so recursive pagefault handling occurs on a file whose f_op->mmap is NULL. Supported consequence: unbounded stack consumption/overflow leading to denial of service or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
bpf: Fix leakage of uninitialized bpf stack under speculation

The current implemented mechanisms to mitigate data disclosure under
speculation mainly address stack and map value oob access from the
speculative domain. However, Piotr discovered that uninitialized BPF
stack is not protected yet, and thus old data from the kernel stack,
potentially including addresses of kernel structures, could still be
extracted from that 512 bytes large window. The BPF stack is special
compared to map values since it's not zero initialized for every
program invocation, whereas map values /are/ zero initialized upon
their initial allocation and thus cannot leak any prior data in either
domain. In the non-speculative domain, the verifier ensures that every
stack slot read must have a prior stack slot write by the BPF program
to avoid such data leaking issue.

However, this is not enough: for example, when the pointer arithmetic
operation moves the stack pointer from the last valid stack offset to
the first valid offset, the sanitation logic allows for any intermediate
offsets during speculative execution, which could then be used to
extract any restricted stack content via side-channel.

Given for unprivileged stack pointer arithmetic the use of unknown
but bounded scalars is generally forbidden, we can simply turn the
register-based arithmetic operation into an immediate-based arithmetic
operation without the need for masking. This also gives the benefit
of reducing the needed instructions for the operation. Given after
the work in 7fedb63a8307 ("bpf: Tighten speculative pointer arithmetic
mask"), the aux->alu_limit already holds the final immediate value for
the offset register with the known scalar. Thus, a simple mov of the
immediate to AX register with using AX as the source for the original
instruction is sufficient and possible now in this case.

Reported-by: Piotr Krysiuk <piotras@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>

commit_msg:
In da9150_charger_probe, &charger->otg_work is bound with
da9150_charger_otg_work. da9150_charger_otg_ncb may be
called to start the work.

If we remove the module which will call da9150_charger_remove
to make cleanup, there may be a unfinished work. The possible
sequence is as follows:

Fix it by canceling the work before cleanup in the da9150_charger_remove

CPU0                  CPUc1

                    |da9150_charger_otg_work
da9150_charger_remove      |
power_supply_unregister  |
device_unregister   |
power_supply_dev_release|
kfree(psy)          |
                    |
                    | 	power_supply_changed(charger->usb);
                    |   //use

Fixes: c1a281e34dae ("power: Add support for DA9150 Charger")
Signed-off-by: Zheng Wang <zyytlz.wz@163.com>
Signed-off-by: Sebastian Reichel <sebastian.reichel@collabora.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcancel_work_sync(&charger->otg_work);']}
description: The Linux kernel before 6.2.9 has a race condition and resultant use-after-free in drivers/power/supply/da9150-charger.c if a physically proximate attacker unplugs a device.

code_evidence: Lines 13-14 unregister the USB notifier but do not cancel the pending charger->otg_work before teardown.
Lines 15-16 unregister the battery and USB power supplies, freeing their resources while the async otg_work may still run and call power_supply_changed() on charger->usb.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's teardown frees the power supply object while a still-schedulable work item retains a pointer to it and later uses it, which is exactly CWE-416. This is a lifetime/race issue rather than merely a missing cancel; the freed-memory reuse is the supported weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!IS_ERR_OR_NULL(charger->usb_phy))
usb_unregister_notifier(charger->usb_phy, &charger->otg_nb);

power_supply_unregister(charger->battery);
power_supply_unregister(charger->usb);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: da9150_charger_remove never synchronizes with the queued otg_work, so the work can execute concurrently with power_supply_unregister. Trigger: module removal or device unbind while otg_work is pending. Consequence: the work dereferences charger->usb after it was freed, producing a use-after-free (crash or memory corruption). The fix adds cancel_work_sync before unregistering the supplies.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflow in ModifiablePixelBuffer::fillRect.

It can be triggered by RRE message with subrectangle out of framebuffer
boundaries. It may prevent the same kind of issue caused by evil message
from another encoding too.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  w = r.width();', '  h = r.height();', '  buf = getBufferRW(r, &stride);', '  commitBufferRW(r);'], 'added_lines': ['  Rect drect;', '  drect = r;', '  if (!drect.enclosed_by(getRect())) {', '    vlog.error("Destination rect %dx%d at %d,%d exceeds framebuffer %dx%d",', '               drect.width(), drect.height(), drect.tl.x, drect.tl.y, width_, height_);', '    drect = drect.intersect(getRect());', '  }', '', '  if (drect.is_empty())', '    return;', '', '  w = drect.width();', '  h = drect.height();', '  buf = getBufferRW(drect, &stride);', '  commitBufferRW(drect);']}
description: Buffer overflow in the ModifiablePixelBuffer::fillRect function in TigerVNC before 1.7.1 allows remote servers to execute arbitrary code via an RRE message with subrectangle outside framebuffer boundaries.

code_evidence: The function derives w and h directly from the caller-supplied rect r without validating it against the framebuffer bounds. getBufferRW(r, &stride) returns a buffer for r, then the loops write w bytes per row for h rows (memset at line 14, memcpy at lines 23/29) and advance by stride*b, so an oversized or out-of-bounds r drives writes past the allocated buffer; commitBufferRW(r) finalizes it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked rectangle leads directly to out-of-bounds memory writes in fillRect, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within buffer bounds. This is a concrete buffer overflow rather than a mere integer issue, so the target class fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: r is trusted as a destination rect without clipping to getRect(). Trigger: an RRE message (or other encoding) supplies a subrectangle extending beyond framebuffer boundaries, producing a buffer smaller than w*h*b. Consequence: memset/memcpy write outside the buffer, allowing memory corruption and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
misc: sgi-gru: fix use-after-free error in gru_set_context_option, gru_fault and gru_handle_user_call_os

In some bad situation, the gts may be freed gru_check_chiplet_assignment.
The call chain can be gru_unload_context->gru_free_gru_context->gts_drop
and kfree finally. However, the caller didn't know if the gts is freed
or not and use it afterwards. This will trigger a Use after Free bug.

Fix it by introducing a return value to see if it's in error path or not.
Free the gts in caller if gru_check_chiplet_assignment check failed.

Fixes: 55484c45dbec ("gru: allow users to specify gru chiplet 2")
Signed-off-by: Zheng Wang <zyytlz.wz@163.com>
Acked-by: Dimitri Sivanich <sivanich@hpe.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20221110035033.19498-1-zyytlz.wz@163.com
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s SGI GRU driver in the way the first gru_file_unlocked_ioctl function is called by the user, where a fail pass occurs in the gru_check_chiplet_assignment function. This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

gru_check_context_placement(gts) is called without checking a return value; the subsequent lines dereference gts->ts_gru and gts->ts_force_cch_reload, then pass gts to gru_update_cch, thread_cbr_number and gru_user_dropin before gru_unlock_gts. commit_msg:
The functions that were used in the emulation of fxrstor, fxsave, sgdt and
sidt were originally meant for task switching, and as such they did not
check privilege levels.  This is very bad when the same functions are used
in the emulation of unprivileged instructions.  This is CVE-2018-10853.

The obvious fix is to add a new argument to ops->read_std and ops->write_std,
which decides whether the access is a "system" access or should use the
processor's CPL.

Fixes: 129a72a0d3c8 ("KVM: x86: Introduce segmented_write_std", 2017-01-12)
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn ctxt->ops->read_std(ctxt, linear, data, size, &ctxt->exception);'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn ctxt->ops->read_std(ctxt, linear, data, size, &ctxt->exception, true);']}
description: A flaw was found in the way Linux kernel KVM hypervisor before 4.18 emulated instructions such as sgdt/sidt/fxsave/fxrstor. It did not check current privilege(CPL) level while emulating unprivileged instructions. An unprivileged guest user/process could use this flaw to potentially escalate privileges inside guest.

code_evidence: linear_read_system wraps the emulator's read_std operation to perform a linear-memory read, but the call at line 4 passes only ctxt, linear, data, size and &ctxt->exception; it supplies no indication of whether the access is a privileged system access or one that must honor the guest's CPL. The function name and commit context indicate this helper is intended for system-level reads used by instructions such as sgdt/sidt/fxsave/fxrstor, yet the wrapper cannot distinguish or enforce privilege for those emulated instructions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-269 fits because the code fails to track or check the privilege level for an emulated memory access, creating an unintended sphere of control for an unprivileged guest actor. The missing privilege argument on the read_std call is the implementation-level cause; the resulting escalation is only the impact, not the labeled weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the wrapper performs the memory read through read_std without conveying any privilege/CPL requirement, so emulation of unprivileged instructions can reuse a path meant for privileged task-switching accesses. Trigger: an unprivileged guest process executes an emulated instruction whose handling reaches this read helper. Consequence: the guest CPU privilege check is bypassed, allowing access to privileged state and potential guest privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
i2c: fix stack buffer overflow vulnerability in i2c md command

When running "i2c md 0 0 80000100", the function do_i2c_md parses the
length into an unsigned int variable named length. The value is then
moved to a signed variable:

    int nbytes = length;
    #define DISP_LINE_LEN 16
    int linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;
    ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);

On systems where integers are 32 bits wide, 0x80000100 is a negative
value to "nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN" is false and linebytes gets assigned
0x80000100 instead of 16.

The consequence is that the function which reads from the i2c device
(dm_i2c_read or i2c_read) is called with a 16-byte stack buffer to fill
but with a size parameter which is too large. In some cases, this could
trigger a crash. But with some i2c drivers, such as drivers/i2c/nx_i2c.c
(used with "nexell,s5pxx18-i2c" bus), the size is actually truncated to
a 16-bit integer. This is because function i2c_transfer expects an
unsigned short length. In such a case, an attacker who can control the
response of an i2c device can overwrite the return address of a function
and execute arbitrary code through Return-Oriented Programming.

Fix this issue by using unsigned integers types in do_i2c_md. While at
it, make also alen unsigned, as signed sizes can cause vulnerabilities
when people forgot to check that they can be negative.

Signed-off-by: Nicolas Iooss <nicolas.iooss+uboot@ledger.fr>
Reviewed-by: Heiko Schocher <hs@denx.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint alen;', '\tint\tj, nbytes, linebytes;'], 'added_lines': ['\tuint\talen;', '\tuint\tj, nbytes, linebytes;']}
description: In Das U-Boot through 2022.07-rc5, an integer signedness error and resultant stack-based buffer overflow in the "i2c md" command enables the corruption of the return address pointer of the do_i2c_md function.

code_evidence: Signed int variables alen and nbytes/linebytes are declared.
length is parsed with hextoul from argv[3] into an unsigned uint, so values like 0x80000100 are accepted.
nbytes = length assigns the unsigned length to signed int nbytes, converting 0x80000100 to a negative value.
linebuf is a fixed 16-byte stack buffer (DISP_LINE_LEN); linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes yields the negative nbytes when the comparison is false.
linebytes is passed as the size argument to dm_i2c_read/i2c_read, which writes device data into linebuf.
The loop update nbytes -= linebytes relies on the same signed value, sustaining the flawed size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function passes an unvalidated, wrongly converted size to a device read that writes into a fixed 16-byte stack buffer, producing a write past the buffer's end. This is CWE-787; the signedness error is the cause, not a separate integer weakness label.

evidence_lines.code:
int alen;
intj, nbytes, linebytes;
length = hextoul(argv[3], NULL);
nbytes = length;

unsigned charlinebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN];
linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;

ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);
ret = i2c_read(chip, addr, alen, linebuf, linebytes);
nbytes -= linebytes;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unsigned length is converted to a signed int, so a large value becomes negative and bypasses the DISP_LINE_LEN clamp. Trigger: i2c md with a length such as 0x80000100 makes linebytes negative/large and dm_i2c_read or i2c_read fills the 16-byte stack linebuf with that size. Consequence: stack out-of-bounds write that can corrupt the return address and enable code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
mm: enforce min addr even if capable() in expand_downwards()

security_mmap_addr() does a capability check with current_cred(), but
we can reach this code from contexts like a VFS write handler where
current_cred() must not be used.

This can be abused on systems without SMAP to make NULL pointer
dereferences exploitable again.

Fixes: 8869477a49c3 ("security: protect from stack expansion into low vm addresses")
Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint error;', '\terror = security_mmap_addr(address);', '\tif (error)', '\t\treturn error;'], 'added_lines': ['\tint error = 0;', '\tif (address < mmap_min_addr)', '\t\treturn -EPERM;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 4.20.14, expand_downwards in mm/mmap.c lacks a check for the mmap minimum address, which makes it easier for attackers to exploit kernel NULL pointer dereferences on non-SMAP platforms. This is related to a capability check for the wrong task.

code_evidence: Line 7 masks the requested address, then lines 8-10 gate the expansion through security_mmap_addr(address), a capability check evaluated against current_cred().
Lines 20-33 show that when address < vma->vm_start the VMA is grown downward and vma->vm_start is set to the (possibly very low) address; no comparison against mmap_min_addr constrains this path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the missing min-address constraint allows a NULL (low) address to be backed by an attacker-controlled mapping, turning a kernel NULL pointer dereference into an exploitable condition. The capability check is merely the flawed guard; the supported weakness is the dereference of a pointer expected valid but NULL.

evidence_lines.code:
if (address < vma->vm_start) {
vma->vm_start = address;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the only low-address guard is a current_cred()-based capability check rather than an unconditional mmap_min_addr comparison. In contexts such as VFS write handlers where current_cred() is not meaningful, the check can pass and the stack VMA is expanded down to page zero, so a later kernel NULL-pointer dereference at a low address becomes mappable and attacker-controllable, enabling privilege escalation on non-SMAP systems.

commit_msg:
objstack: assert that the alloc size will fit within a chunk
to prevent a buffer overflow

Bug found using OSS-Fuze.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (top < bottom) {new_chunk(); goto loop;}'], 'added_lines': ['    if (top < bottom) {check_size(size); new_chunk(); goto loop;}']}
description: objstack in GNU Aspell 0.60.8 has a heap-based buffer overflow in acommon::ObjStack::dup_top (called from acommon::StringMap::add and acommon::Config::lookup_list).

code_evidence: alloc_top subtracts the caller-supplied size from top before any bound check (line 3), then aligns the pointer (line 4). Only after the pointer may already be below bottom does line 5 test top < bottom and allocate a new chunk, so an oversized size is never rejected before the pointer arithmetic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unvalidated size produces a pointer beyond the intended buffer, enabling an out-of-bounds write. This is the size-validation cause of the overflow, not merely an integer underflow or a null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the requested allocation size is not validated against the chunk capacity before top is decremented. Trigger: a caller passes a size larger than the remaining chunk space, so top moves past bottom and the returned pointer addresses memory outside the chunk. Consequence: subsequent writes through that pointer overflow the heap buffer, matching the dup_top/StringMap path in the description.

commit_msg:
Fixed type confusion bug while resolving promises.

Previously, the internal function njs_promise_perform_then() which
implements PerformPromiseThen() expects its first argument to always be
a promise instance.  This assertion might be invalid because the
functions corresponding to Promise.prototype.then() and
Promise.resolve() incorrectly verified their arguments.

Specifically, the functions recognized their first argument as promise
if it was an object which was an Promise or had Promise object in its
prototype chain.  The later condition is not correct because internal
slots are not inherited according to the spec.

This closes #447 issue in Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    njs_object_t              *object;', '    if (njs_slow_path(!njs_is_object(promise))) {', '        goto failed;', '    }', '', '    object = njs_object_proto_lookup(njs_object(promise), NJS_PROMISE,', '                                     njs_object_t);', '    if (njs_slow_path(object == NULL)) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (njs_slow_path(!njs_is_promise(promise))) {']}
description: njs through 0.7.1, used in NGINX, was discovered to contain a control flow hijack caused by a Type Confusion vulnerability in njs_promise_perform_then().

code_evidence: The first argument is read into promise and accepted if it is merely an object; the check does not require an own internal promise slot.
The code then looks up NJS_PROMISE along the prototype chain, so an object that merely inherits from a Promise (or has Promise in its chain) passes validation despite lacking its own internal slots.
The validated promise is forwarded to njs_promise_perform_then(), which treats it as a genuine promise instance.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts a resource of one type (a plain object with an inherited promise prototype) and passes it to code that accesses it as a promise instance, exactly matching CWE-843. This is not merely a missing validation; the mismatch of type interpretation is the operative flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the argument is validated by object-ness plus prototype-chain lookup rather than by an own promise internal slot, so a non-promise object that inherits from a Promise is accepted. Trigger: calling then()/resolve() with such an object. Consequence: njs_promise_perform_then() reads promise-internal state from an incompatible object, yielding type confusion and potentially control-flow hijack.

commit_msg:
usbip_host updates device status without holding lock from stub probe,
disconnect and rebind code paths. When multiple requests to import a
device are received, these unprotected code paths step all over each
other and drive fails with NULL-ptr deref and use-after-free errors.

The driver uses a table lock to protect the busid array for adding and
deleting busids to the table. However, the probe, disconnect and rebind
paths get the busid table entry and update the status without holding
the busid table lock. Add a new finer grain lock to protect the busid
entry. This new lock will be held to search and update the busid entry
fields from get_busid_idx(), add_match_busid() and del_match_busid().

match_busid_show() does the same to access the busid entry fields.

get_busid_priv() changed to return the pointer to the busid entry holding
the busid lock. stub_probe(), stub_disconnect() and stub_device_rebind()
call put_busid_priv() to release the busid lock before returning. This
changes fixes the unprotected code paths eliminating the race conditions
in updating the busid entries.

Reported-by: Jakub Jirasek
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan (Samsung OSG) <shuah@kernel.org>
Cc: stable <stable@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\treturn;', '\t\treturn;', '\t\treturn;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tgoto call_put_busid_priv;', '\t\tgoto call_put_busid_priv;', '\t\tgoto call_put_busid_priv;', '', 'call_put_busid_priv:', '\tput_busid_priv(busid_priv);']}
description: In the Linux Kernel before version 4.16.11, 4.14.43, 4.9.102, and 4.4.133, multiple race condition errors when handling probe, disconnect, and rebind operations can be exploited to trigger a use-after-free condition or a NULL pointer dereference by sending multiple USB over IP packets.

code_evidence: get_busid_priv() acquires the busid entry/lock; the !busid_priv path BUGs and returns without releasing it, and the normal path proceeds to mutate the entry.
When dev_get_drvdata() returns NULL the function returns without releasing the busid lock acquired at line 8.
On usb_hub_release_port() failure the function returns early, again without releasing the busid lock.
When running in the event handler, the function returns before shutdown_busid() and without releasing the lock.
Only the normal path reaches shutdown_busid(), clears busid_priv->sdev, frees sdev and updates status; these entry-field updates are the shared resource being protected.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is a concurrent code sequence that accesses the shared busid entry but fails to preserve exclusive access on all paths, matching CWE-362; the missing lock release is the synchronization defect, and the crash/UAF is its consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
if (usbip_in_eh(current))
return;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: stub_disconnect() obtains a pointer/lock to the shared busid entry via get_busid_priv(), but several early-return paths skip releasing it. Concurrent probe/disconnect/rebind operations then update busid_priv->sdev and status without mutual exclusion, causing NULL-pointer dereference and use-after-free.

avformat/nutdec: Add check for avformat_new_stream

Check for failure of avformat_new_stream() and propagate
the error code.

description: A null pointer dereference issue was discovered in 'FFmpeg' in decode_main_header() function of libavformat/nutdec.c file. The flaw occurs because the function lacks check of the return value of avformat_new_stream() and triggers the null pointer dereference error, causing an application to crash.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Propagate trust when getting a child of a serialised variant

If a variant is trusted, that means all its children are trusted, so
ensure that their checked offsets are set as such.

This allows a lot of the offset table checks to be avoided when getting
children from trusted serialised tuples, which speeds things up.

No unit test is included because this is just a performance fix. If
there are other slownesses, or regressions, in serialised `GVariant`
performance, the fuzzing setup will catch them like it did this one.

This change does reduce the time to run the oss-fuzz reproducer from 80s
to about 0.7s on my machine.

Signed-off-by: Philip Withnall <pwithnall@endlessos.org>

Fixes: #2841
oss-fuzz#54314

commit_msg:
Fixed heap-use-after-free in JSON.stringify().

njs_json_stringify_iterator() assumed, while stringifying flat arrays, that a
flat array will always remain flat.  This is not the case for flat arrays with
values with custom getters which may modify the enclosing array upon
invocation.

This closes #322 issue on GitHub.

description: njs through 0.4.3, used in NGINX, has an out-of-bounds read in njs_json_stringify_iterator in njs_json.c.

code_evidence: Line 97 bounds the loop using njs_array_len(&state->value), but line 110 bypasses property access and directly indexes the fast-array backing store with njs_array_start(&state->value)[state->index++]. A custom getter invoked during stringification (e.g., via njs_json_stringify_to_json/replacer on earlier elements) can modify the enclosing array, changing its length/backing store so state->index no longer matches the live array, yielding an out-of-bounds read at line 110.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because line 110 reads memory past the intended array buffer. It is distinct from a pure UAF in that the direct indexed read of the backing store exceeds valid bounds after mutation; the fix switches to njs_value_property_i64 to respect current state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes a flat array stays flat and reads its backing store by index without revalidating against the array's current length or representation. Trigger: a value with a custom getter mutates the enclosing array during stringify. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of the array backing store (heap-use-after-free/read).

commit_msg:
Since the tee subsystem does not keep a strong reference to its idle
shared memory buffers, it races with other threads that try to destroy a
shared memory through a close of its dma-buf fd or by unmapping the
memory.

In tee_shm_get_from_id() when a lookup in teedev->idr has been
successful, it is possible that the tee_shm is in the dma-buf teardown
path, but that path is blocked by the teedev mutex. Since we don't have
an API to tell if the tee_shm is in the dma-buf teardown path or not we
must find another way of detecting this condition.

Fix this by doing the reference counting directly on the tee_shm using a
new refcount_t refcount field. dma-buf is replaced by using
anon_inode_getfd() instead, this separates the life-cycle of the
underlying file from the tee_shm. tee_shm_put() is updated to hold the
mutex when decreasing the refcount to 0 and then remove the tee_shm from
teedev->idr before releasing the mutex. This means that the tee_shm can
never be found unless it has a refcount larger than 0.

Fixes: 967c9cca2cc5 ("tee: generic TEE subsystem")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reviewed-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Reviewed-by: Lars Persson <larper@axis.com>
Reviewed-by: Sumit Garg <sumit.garg@linaro.org>
Reported-by: Patrik Lantz <patrik.lantz@axis.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Wiklander <jens.wiklander@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\telse if (shm->flags & TEE_SHM_DMA_BUF)', '\t\tget_dma_buf(shm->dmabuf);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/*', '\t * If the tee_shm was found in the IDR it must have a refcount', '\t * larger than 0 due to the guarantee in tee_shm_put() below. So', "\t * it's safe to use refcount_inc().", '\t */', '\telse', '\t\trefcount_inc(&shm->refcount);']}
description: A use-after-free exists in drivers/tee/tee_shm.c in the TEE subsystem in the Linux kernel through 5.15.11. This occurs because of a race condition in tee_shm_get_from_id during an attempt to free a shared memory object.

code_evidence: Under teedev->mutex the function looks up the shared buffer in teedev->idr, then takes a lifetime reference only through get_dma_buf(shm->dmabuf) when the TEE_SHM_DMA_BUF flag is set; the tee_shm object itself is not reference-counted here. The mutex protects the IDR lookup but not the tee_shm lifetime, so a concurrent close of the dma-buf fd or unmap can enter the teardown path for the same object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a concurrent access race: teedev->mutex serializes the IDR lookup but does not prevent an interfering teardown sequence from modifying the shared tee_shm before the reference is held, violating exclusivity/atomicity. This matches CWE-362 rather than a simple missing-lock issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: lookup and reference acquisition are not atomic with respect to tee_shm teardown, and the reference is taken on the dma-buf rather than on the tee_shm. Trigger: another thread concurrently closes or unmaps the shared memory while this thread finds it in the IDR. Consequence: the returned pointer can refer to freed memory, yielding a use-after-free.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.4+
Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>

commit_msg:
Don't change the state of the ETM flags until CCS processing

Changing the ciphersuite during a renegotiation can result in a crash
leading to a DoS attack. ETM has not been implemented in 1.1.0 for DTLS
so this is TLS only.

The problem is caused by changing the flag indicating whether to use ETM
or not immediately on negotiation of ETM, rather than at CCS. Therefore,
during a renegotiation, if the ETM state is changing (usually due to a
change of ciphersuite), then an error/crash will occur.

Due to the fact that there are separate CCS messages for read and write
we actually now need two flags to determine whether to use ETM or not.

CVE-2017-3733

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!send && !SSL_USE_ETM(ssl) &&', '        if (!send && !SSL_USE_ETM(ssl) && FIPS_mode())'], 'added_lines': ['    if (!send && !SSL_READ_ETM(ssl) &&', '        if (!send && !SSL_READ_ETM(ssl) && FIPS_mode())']}
description: During a renegotiation handshake if the Encrypt-Then-Mac extension is negotiated where it was not in the original handshake (or vice-versa) then this can cause OpenSSL 1.1.0 before 1.1.0e to crash (dependent on ciphersuite). Both clients and servers are affected.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function selects MAC handling based on the ETM flag; the root cause is stale ETM state during renegotiation, not improper validation of input data, so CWE-20 is not directly supported.

description: NetScaler file parser crash in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.5 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.13 allows denial of service via crafted capture file

Trigger: a crafted capture whose record offset leaves fewer than sizeof(nspr_pktracefull_v10_t) bytes remaining. Consequence: out-of-bounds read/write on the heap buffer, causing a crash (DoS) and possible memory corruption.

commit_msg:
As kzalloc() may return null pointer, it should be better to
check the return value and return error if fails in order
to avoid dereference of null pointer.
Moreover, the return value of rtw_alloc_hwxmits() should also
be dealt with.

Fixes: 15865124feed ("staging: r8188eu: introduce new core dir for RTL8188eu driver")
Reviewed-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiasheng Jiang <jiasheng@iscas.ac.cn>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220518075957.514603-1-jiasheng@iscas.ac.cn
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void rtw_alloc_hwxmits(struct adapter *padapter)'], 'added_lines': ['int rtw_alloc_hwxmits(struct adapter *padapter)', '\tif (!pxmitpriv->hwxmits)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '', '\treturn 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.16-rc6. _rtw_init_xmit_priv in drivers/staging/r8188eu/core/rtw_xmit.c lacks check of the return value of rtw_alloc_hwxmits() and will cause the null pointer dereference.

code_evidence: Line 6 assigns the result of kzalloc() to pxmitpriv->hwxmits without checking it; line 7 copies that possibly-NULL pointer into hwxmits.
The if/else branches at lines 8-18 dereference hwxmits[...] (e.g., hwxmits[0].sta_queue = ...) unconditionally whenever hwxmit_entry is 5 or 4.
No NULL guard exists before these writes, so under allocation failure the dereference occurs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid without a NULL check, matching CWE-476. This is distinct from a general memory leak or unchecked error code, since the direct consequence is dereferencing the NULL hwxmits pointer.

evidence_lines.code:
pxmitpriv->hwxmits = kzalloc(sizeof(struct hw_xmit) * pxmitpriv->hwxmit_entry, GFP_KERNEL);
hwxmits = pxmitpriv->hwxmits;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: kzalloc() can return NULL on allocation failure, but rtw_alloc_hwxmits() stores it and immediately writes through the pointer via hwxmits[n].sta_queue. Trigger: memory pressure makes kzalloc fail while hwxmit_entry is 5 or 4. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference, causing a kernel crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13039/IKEv1: Do more bounds checking.

Have ikev1_attrmap_print() and ikev1_attr_print() do full bounds
checking, and return null on a bounds overflow.  Have their callers
check for a null return.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s), modified
so the capture file won't be rejected as an invalid capture.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (map && nmap) {', '\t\t\tcp = ikev1_attrmap_print(ndo, cp, (ep < ep2) ? ep : ep2,', '\t\t\t\tmap, nmap);', '\t\t} else', '\t\t\tcp = ikev1_attr_print(ndo, cp, (ep < ep2) ? ep : ep2);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (map && nmap)', '\t\t\tcp = ikev1_attrmap_print(ndo, cp, ep2, map, nmap);', '\t\telse', '\t\t\tcp = ikev1_attr_print(ndo, cp, ep2);', '\t\tif (cp == NULL)', '\t\t\tgoto trunc;']}
description: The ISAKMP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isakmp.c, several functions.

code_evidence: cp starts after the header and ep2 is computed as p + item_len without validating item_len against the actual captured buffer ep.
The loop passes (ep < ep2) ? ep : ep2 as the end bound to ikev1_attrmap_print/ikev1_attr_print; the return value cp is not checked, and the loop can continue with an unchecked/advanced cp.
If ep < ep2 the code prints "..." but still returns cp, so callers receive a pointer that may exceed the captured data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reading memory beyond the intended buffer, matching CWE-125. It is not CWE-787 because the defect is an over-read from missing bounds validation, not an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: item_len is taken from attacker-controlled ISAKMP payload data and ep2 is derived from it without a bound check against the real buffer end ep. The attribute-printing helpers can advance cp past the captured data, and the unchecked return lets subsequent iterations or callers dereference beyond the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read.
