commit_msg:
char: serial: check divider value against baud base

16550A UART device uses an oscillator to generate frequencies
(baud base), which decide communication speed. This speed could
be changed by dividing it by a divider. If the divider is
greater than the baud base, speed is set to zero, leading to a
divide by zero error. Add check to avoid it.

Reported-by: Huawei PSIRT <psirt@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Message-Id: <1476251888-20238-1-git-send-email-ppandit@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (s->divider == 0)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (s->divider == 0 || s->divider > s->baudbase) {', '    }']}
description: The serial_update_parameters function in hw/char/serial.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero error and QEMU process crash) via vectors involving a value of divider greater than baud base.

code_evidence: The only guard before the division is [5,6], which rejects s->divider == 0 but does not bound the upper side; a divider larger than baudbase passes this check.
Line [23] then computes speed = s->baudbase / s->divider with the unvalidated divider, and line 28 divides NANOSECONDS_PER_SECOND by the resulting speed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because the function performs a division whose divisor (speed) can be driven to zero by an unchecked input value, and the commit adds the missing divider > baudbase check. This is a divide-by-zero availability issue, not merely an incorrect baud rate calculation.

evidence_lines.code:
if (s->divider == 0)
return;
speed = s->baudbase / s->divider;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates only that divider is nonzero, not that divider <= baudbase, so an attacker-controlled divider greater than baudbase is accepted. Trigger: a guest sets a divider exceeding baudbase; the integer division at line 23 yields speed 0, and line 28 divides by that zero speed, causing a divide-by-zero crash of the QEMU process (DoS).

commit_msg:
(uid_t) -1 is still used as placeholder to mean "unset". This is OK, since
there should be no users with such number, see
https://systemd.io/UIDS-GIDS#special-linux-uids.

(uid_t) -1 is used as the default value in class initialization.

When a user or group above INT32_MAX is created, the numeric uid or
gid wraps around to negative when the value is assigned to gint, and
polkit gets confused. Let's accept such gids, except for -1.

A nicer fix would be to change the underlying type to e.g. uint32 to
not have negative values. But this cannot be done without breaking the
API, so likely new functions will have to be added (a
polkit_unix_user_new variant that takes a unsigned, and the same for
_group_new, _set_uid, _get_uid, _set_gid, _get_gid, etc.). This will
require a bigger patch.

Fixes https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/polkit/polkit/issues/74.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  g_return_val_if_fail (uid != -1, NULL);', '']}
description: A flaw was found in PolicyKit (aka polkit) 0.115 that allows a user with a uid greater than INT_MAX to successfully execute any systemctl command.

code_evidence: polkit_unix_user_new accepts a signed gint uid and passes it directly to g_object_new as the "uid" property without any range or sentinel check. The only constraint is the parameter type gint; there is no rejection of the (uid_t)-1 placeholder value or other negative values before the identity object is constructed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function receives an input value (uid) and fails to validate that it has the required property (not the reserved -1/negative sentinel) before processing it, which is exactly improper input validation. The missing check, not a transformation error, is the defect, so CWE-20 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constructor trusts the caller-supplied uid and performs no validation of its value before storing it in the identity object. Trigger: a caller supplies a uid that wraps to a negative gint (e.g. -1 from (uid_t)-1). Consequence: the unvalidated value propagates into the identity, letting the sentinel/negative uid be treated as a valid identity and enabling the authorization bypass described in the commit.

commit_msg:
Always revoke certificate on CRL

RFC5280 does not state that the `revocationDate` should be checked.

In addition, when no time source is available (i.e., when MBEDTLS_HAVE_TIME_DATE is not defined), `mbedtls_x509_time_is_past` always returns 0. This results in the CRL not being checked at all.

https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5280
Signed-off-by: Raoul Strackx <raoul.strackx@fortanix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if( mbedtls_x509_time_is_past( &cur->revocation_date ) )', '                return( 1 );'], 'added_lines': ['            return( 1 );']}
description: An issue was discovered in Arm Mbed TLS before 2.24.0. It incorrectly uses a revocationDate check when deciding whether to honor certificate revocation via a CRL. In some situations, an attacker can exploit this by changing the local clock.

code_evidence: On a serial-number match between the certificate and a CRL entry (lines 6-7), the code returns revoked status (line 10) only if mbedtls_x509_time_is_past(&cur->revocation_date) is true (line 9). If the time check returns 0 — e.g., no time source or a manipulated local clock — the matching entry is skipped and the loop continues, so a revoked certificate is treated as valid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function incorrectly validates certificate revocation data, causing a revoked certificate to be accepted — improper certificate validation (CWE-295). Contrast with CWE-299 (improper check for certificate revocation), which is narrower; the target's broader certificate-validation framing fits the observed bypass.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: certificate revocation status is gated on a local-clock-dependent revocationDate comparison rather than honoring the CRL entry unconditionally. Trigger: an attacker alters the local clock or runs without a time source so the date is not 'past'. Consequence: a revoked certificate passes validation, bypassing revocation enforcement.

commit_msg:
Budimir noted that perf_event_validate_size() only checks the size of
the newly added event, even though the sizes of all existing events
can also change due to not all events having the same read_format.

When we attach the new event, perf_group_attach(), we do re-compute
the size for all events.

Fixes: a723968c0ed3 ("perf: Fix u16 overflows")
Reported-by: Budimir Markovic <markovicbudimir@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void __perf_event_read_size(struct perf_event *event, int nr_siblings)', '\tif (event->attr.read_format & PERF_FORMAT_TOTAL_TIME_ENABLED)', '\tif (event->attr.read_format & PERF_FORMAT_TOTAL_TIME_RUNNING)', '\tif (event->attr.read_format & PERF_FORMAT_ID)', '\tif (event->attr.read_format & PERF_FORMAT_LOST)', '\tif (event->attr.read_format & PERF_FORMAT_GROUP) {', '\tsize += entry * nr;', '\tevent->read_size = size;'], 'added_lines': ['static int __perf_event_read_size(u64 read_format, int nr_siblings)', '\tif (read_format & PERF_FORMAT_TOTAL_TIME_ENABLED)', '\tif (read_format & PERF_FORMAT_TOTAL_TIME_RUNNING)', '\tif (read_format & PERF_FORMAT_ID)', '\tif (read_format & PERF_FORMAT_LOST)', '\tif (read_format & PERF_FORMAT_GROUP) {', '\t/*', '\t * Since perf_event_validate_size() limits this to 16k and inhibits', '\t * adding more siblings, this will never overflow.', '\t */', '\treturn size + nr * entry;']}
description:
A heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Linux kernel's Performance Events system component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

A perf_event's read_size can overflow, leading to an heap out-of-bounds increment or write in perf_read_group().

We recommend upgrading past commit 382c27f4ed28f803b1f1473ac2d8db0afc795a1b.

code_evidence: When PERF_FORMAT_GROUP is set, nr becomes 1 + nr_siblings (line 15) and size gains sizeof(u64) (line 16). Line 18 computes size += entry * nr as a 32-bit int product, and line 19 stores the result into event->read_size without any overflow check. entry is 8, 16, or 24 bytes depending on the PERF_FORMAT_ID/LOST flags (lines 10-13), so a large nr_siblings makes entry * nr wrap.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the faulty size calculation directly enables writes past the end of the heap buffer in perf_read_group(); the overflow is the cause, not the memory-write weakness itself. A pure integer-overflow label (CWE-190) would describe the arithmetic but not the supported out-of-bounds write consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the read_size computation uses unchecked 32-bit int arithmetic, so a group with many siblings overflows entry * nr and produces a small, wrapped read_size. Trigger: attaching a perf event with PERF_FORMAT_GROUP and enough siblings so the product exceeds INT_MAX. Consequence: perf_read_group() later uses this undersized read_size for heap output, causing an out-of-bounds increment/write.

commit_msg: Fix issue #198: AESNI breaks with messages shorter than 16 bytes
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    for (;data_len>0; data_len-=16, in+=16, out+=16) {'], 'added_lines': ['    for (;data_len>=BLOCK_SIZE; data_len-=BLOCK_SIZE, in+=BLOCK_SIZE, out+=BLOCK_SIZE) {']}
description: PyCryptodome before 3.6.6 has an integer overflow in the data_len variable in AESNI.c, related to the AESNI_encrypt and AESNI_decrypt functions, leading to the mishandling of messages shorter than 16 bytes.

code_evidence: Line 72 loops while data_len>0, decrementing by 16 and advancing in/out by 16 each iteration. Line 75 unconditionally loads a full 16-byte block from in, and line 85 stores a full block to out. When data_len is between 1 and 15, the loop still executes once: data_len-16 wraps to a huge size_t value, so the condition remains true and the loop continues, reading and writing 16-byte blocks past the caller's buffer. Line 87's final check never sees the wrapped value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The size_t data_len is decremented below zero and wraps to a huge value, so the loop bound is computed incorrectly and iteration continues beyond valid data. This integer wraparound directly drives the unsafe memory access, matching CWE-190 rather than a pure out-of-bounds defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop condition data_len>0 permits processing a partial trailing block, and subtracting 16 from a size_t smaller than 16 wraps to a very large value. Trigger: a message whose length is not a multiple of 16 (e.g., 1-15 bytes). Consequence: out-of-bounds reads/writes via the 16-byte load/store, causing memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
net: usb: lan78xx: reorder cleanup operations to avoid UAF bugs

The timer dev->stat_monitor can schedule the delayed work dev->wq and
the delayed work dev->wq can also arm the dev->stat_monitor timer.

When the device is detaching, the net_device will be deallocated. but
the net_device private data could still be dereferenced in delayed work
or timer handler. As a result, the UAF bugs will happen.

One racy situation is shown below:

      (Thread 1)                 |      (Thread 2)
lan78xx_stat_monitor()           |
 ...                             |  lan78xx_disconnect()
 lan78xx_defer_kevent()          |    ...
  ...                            |    cancel_delayed_work_sync(&dev->wq);
  schedule_delayed_work()        |    ...
  (wait some time)               |    free_netdev(net); //free net_device
  lan78xx_delayedwork()          |
  //use net_device private data  |
  dev-> //use                    |

Although we use cancel_delayed_work_sync() to cancel the delayed work
in lan78xx_disconnect(), it could still be scheduled in timer handler
lan78xx_stat_monitor().

Another racy situation is shown below:

      (Thread 1)                |      (Thread 2)
lan78xx_delayedwork             |
 mod_timer()                    |  lan78xx_disconnect()
                                |   cancel_delayed_work_sync()
 (wait some time)               |   if (timer_pending(&dev->stat_monitor))
             	                |       del_timer_sync(&dev->stat_monitor);
 lan78xx_stat_monitor()         |   ...
  lan78xx_defer_kevent()        |   free_netdev(net); //free
   //use net_device private data|
   dev-> //use                  |

Although we use del_timer_sync() to delete the timer, the function
timer_pending() returns 0 when the timer is activated. As a result,
the del_timer_sync() will not be executed and the timer could be
re-armed.

In order to mitigate this bug, We use timer_shutdown_sync() to shutdown
the timer and then use cancel_delayed_work_sync() to cancel the delayed
work. As a result, the net_device could be deallocated safely.

What's more, the dev->flags is set to EVENT_DEV_DISCONNECT in
lan78xx_disconnect(). But it could still be set to EVENT_STAT_UPDATE
in lan78xx_stat_monitor(). So this patch put the set_bit() behind
timer_shutdown_sync().

Fixes: 77dfff5bb7e2 ("lan78xx: Fix race condition in disconnect handling")
Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tset_bit(EVENT_DEV_DISCONNECT, &dev->flags);', '', '\tif (timer_pending(&dev->stat_monitor))', '\t\tdel_timer_sync(&dev->stat_monitor);', ''], 'added_lines': ['\ttimer_shutdown_sync(&dev->stat_monitor);', '\tset_bit(EVENT_DEV_DISCONNECT, &dev->flags);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in lan78xx_disconnect in drivers/net/usb/lan78xx.c in the network sub-component, net/usb/lan78xx in the Linux Kernel. This flaw allows a local attacker to crash the system when the LAN78XX USB device detaches.

code_evidence: unregister_netdev(net) is called, then cancel_delayed_work_sync(&dev->wq) cancels the delayed work, but the timer dev->stat_monitor can still re-arm dev->wq after this cancel, so dev->wq may run later.

The timer cleanup is guarded by timer_pending(&dev->stat_monitor) and only then calls del_timer_sync; timer_pending returns 0 when the timer is activated, so the timer is not deleted and can re-arm the delayed work.
free_netdev(net) frees the net_device (and its private data) while the delayed work or timer handler may still dereference dev, producing a use-after-free.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees the net_device via free_netdev while a timer/delayed-work path can still access dev, which is reference-after-free; CWE-416 applies. The root cause is incomplete timer shutdown ordering, not a race on a live object.

evidence_lines.code:
unregister_netdev(net);
cancel_delayed_work_sync(&dev->wq);
free_netdev(net);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The disconnect path cancels the delayed work before shutting down the timer, and the timer_pending guard skips del_timer_sync when the timer is active. The timer can therefore re-arm dev->wq after cancellation, and free_netdev then frees the private data while the work or timer handler still dereferences dev, causing a use-after-free crash.

commit_msg:
Check that ecall [user_check] pointers and ocall_malloc result pointer are outside enclave (#67)

This should reduce the enclave's attack surface by preventing an attacker from invoking ecalls on or triggering unexpected writes to arbitrary enclave memory, which could potentially leak information about that memory or lead to incorrect results.

Fixes #36. Fixes #66.

description: An issue was discovered in UC Berkeley RISE Opaque before 2018-12-01. There is no boundary check on ocall_malloc. The return value could be a pointer to enclave memory. It could cause an arbitrary enclave memory write.

code_evidence: The ecall receives caller-supplied pointers such as input_rows, first_row, last_group and last_row plus their lengths, with no boundary validation in the function body.
These unvalidated pointers and lengths are passed directly to non_oblivious_aggregate_step1, which uses them as output/input buffers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked output pointers are used as buffers by the callee, so writes can land outside the intended caller buffer, matching CWE-787. This is out-of-bounds write rather than merely an access-control or pointer-validation issue because the supported impact is memory modification beyond buffer bounds.

evidence_lines.code:
uint8_t *input_rows, size_t input_rows_length,
uint8_t **first_row, size_t *first_row_length,
uint8_t **last_group, size_t *last_group_length,
uint8_t **last_row, size_t *last_row_length) {

non_oblivious_aggregate_step1(
agg_op, agg_op_length,
input_rows, input_rows_length,
first_row, first_row_length,
last_group, last_group_length,
last_row, last_row_length);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ecall copies caller-provided pointer/length pairs into internal processing without checking they lie outside the enclave. Trigger: an attacker invokes the ecall with pointers targeting enclave memory. Consequence: the downstream step writes results through those pointers, enabling arbitrary enclave memory writes; the missing check is the cause, the out-of-bounds write the consequence.

commit_msg:
Fix packet length handling.

Treat the packet length as unsigned - it shouldn't be negative in the
file.  If it is, that'll probably cause the sscanf to fail, so we'll
report the file as bad.

Check it against WTAP_MAX_PACKET_SIZE to make sure we don't try to
allocate a huge amount of memory, just as we do in other file readers.

Use the now-validated packet size as the length in
ws_buffer_assure_space(), so we are certain to have enough space, and
don't allocate too much space.

Merge the header and packet data parsing routines while we're at it.

commit_msg:
There are multiple similar bugs implicitly introduced by the
commit c0cfa2d8a788fcf4 ("vsock: add multi-transports support") and
commit 6a2c0962105ae8ce ("vsock: prevent transport modules unloading").

The bug pattern:
 [1] vsock_sock.transport pointer is copied to a local variable,
 [2] lock_sock() is called,
 [3] the local variable is used.
VSOCK multi-transport support introduced the race condition:
vsock_sock.transport value may change between [1] and [2].

Let's copy vsock_sock.transport pointer to local variables after
the lock_sock() call.

Fixes: c0cfa2d8a788fcf4 ("vsock: add multi-transports support")
Signed-off-by: Alexander Popov <alex.popov@linux.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Garzarella <sgarzare@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Jorgen Hansen <jhansen@vmware.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210201084719.2257066-1-alex.popov@linux.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttransport = vsk->transport;'], 'added_lines': ['', '\ttransport = vsk->transport;']}
description: A local privilege escalation was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.10.13. Multiple race conditions in the AF_VSOCK implementation are caused by wrong locking in net/vmw_vsock/af_vsock.c. The race conditions were implicitly introduced in the commits that added VSOCK multi-transport support.

code_evidence: Line 28 reads vsk->transport into the local transport before lock_sock(sk) is called on line 29.
The cached transport is then passed to vsock_update_buffer_size on lines 33, 38 and 43 after the lock is acquired, so the value used is not the one protected by the lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 fits because the function acquires the socket lock but reads the shared vsk->transport field outside that critical section, violating the required locking discipline. This is improper lock scope/ordering rather than a missing null check or type confusion.

evidence_lines.code:
transport = vsk->transport;
lock_sock(sk);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The transport pointer is snapshotted before the socket lock is taken, so a concurrent transport change can occur between the read and lock_sock(). The stale local transport is then used inside the locked region, causing the operation to act on a transport that no longer matches the socket state; the commit describes this as enabling a race condition.

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

In order to fail safe in the supported case, re-implement all the VT-x
instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int nvmx_handle_invept(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)'], 'added_lines': ['static int nvmx_handle_invept(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.9.x through 4.11.x, on Intel x86 platforms, allowing x86 HVM and PVH guests to cause a host OS denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) or possibly have unspecified other impact because nested VT-x is not properly restricted.

code_evidence: decode_vmx_inst() validates/decodes the INVEPT instruction and returns early with ret on failure, but this function performs no check that nested VMX is enabled or that the nvmx state is initialised before acting.

For INVEPT_SINGLE_CONTEXT the decoded eptp is passed to np2m_flush_base(current, eptp), which walks the nested p2m structures; these depend on nvmx state that may be uninitialised (zeroed) when nested virt was never enabled.
For INVEPT_ALL_CONTEXT, p2m_flush_nestedp2m(current->domain) is invoked on the nested p2m, again without confirming the nvmx/nested-p2m structures were initialised.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The reachable consequence is dereferencing a pointer expected to be valid but actually NULL due to uninitialised nested-virt state, matching CWE-476. It is distinct from a pure logic/privilege flaw because the supported impact is the host crash from the invalid dereference.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( (ret = decode_vmx_inst(regs, &decode, &eptp, 0)) != X86EMUL_OKAY )
return ret;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a missing precondition: the handler runs whenever the guest executes INVEPT, without verifying nested VMX is enabled or the nvmx/nested-p2m state was initialised. The zeroed vcpu memory makes the structures appear valid, so np2m_flush_base/p2m_flush_nestedp2m dereference uninitialised pointers, causing a host NULL pointer dereference and denial of service.

commit_msg:

(cherry picked from commit 497df00f741dd4fc89292aaef2db7368aee45d0d)

description: FreeRDP is a free remote desktop protocol library and clients. Affected versions of FreeRDP are missing input length validation in the `urbdrc` channel. A malicious server can trick a FreeRDP based client to read out of bound data and send it back to the server. This issue has been addressed in version 2.9.0 and all users are advised to upgrade. The pointer returned at line 29 (Stream_Pointer(s)) is passed to isoch_transfer as the output payload for USBD_TRANSFER_DIRECTION_OUT transfers, so the transfer consumes OutputBufferSize bytes from an unvalidated position.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a missing bounds check before consuming a length-controlled buffer, causing reads beyond the intended input buffer, matching CWE-125. It is not CWE-190/787 primarily because the consequence is an out-of-bounds read of stream data rather than an arithmetic wrap leading to a write.

return pdev->isoch_transfer(
pdev, callback, MessageId, RequestId, EndpointAddress, TransferFlags, StartFrame,
ErrorCount, noAck, packetDescriptorData, NumberOfPackets, OutputBufferSize,

For an OUT transfer, the output buffer pointer is taken directly from the stream without verifying that OutputBufferSize bytes are available, so the transfer reads past the received buffer; the read data may then be sent back to the malicious server, exposing out-of-bounds memory.

commit_msg:
Prevent `CHECK`-fail when building reference tensor.

The tensor constructor does not allow reference dtypes, as these should not show up explicitly. However, when passed these invalid types instead of building an invalid object the constructor crashes via a `CHECK`-fail. We have a static builder that properly handles this case but is not applicable given current usage.

Instead, before calling the constructor, we can check that the dtype is not a reference type and return an error otherwise, given that the dtype is user controlled so malicious users can trigger denial of service.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 409662503
Change-Id: I5892f831fde7f276cd7ab34519cf6b8061c71a59
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (IsRefType(raw_val.dtype())) {', '      return errors::InvalidArgument(', '          "Not allowed to construct a tensor with reference dtype, got ",', '          DataTypeString(raw_val.dtype()));', '    }']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. A malicious user can cause a denial of service by altering a `SavedModel` such that Grappler optimizer would attempt to build a tensor using a reference `dtype`. This would result in a crash due to a `CHECK`-fail in the `Tensor` constructor as reference types are not allowed. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: EvaluateOneFoldable reads raw_val from the user-supplied input node's 'value' TensorProto (line 196). It only rejects DT_INVALID (lines 197-203), then directly constructs 'new Tensor(raw_val.dtype(), raw_val.tensor_shape())' at line 204 without excluding reference dtypes. The patch adds an IsRefType check immediately before this constructor call, confirming the dtype is attacker-controlled and reaches the Tensor constructor.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The pre-patch code lets attacker-controlled input reach a CHECK-fail assertion in the Tensor constructor, causing abrupt process termination rather than a graceful error. This is a reachable assertion leading to DoS, matching CWE-617, distinct from a mere invalid-argument handling bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dtype of the input tensor proto is user-controlled (from a crafted SavedModel) and is passed to the Tensor constructor after only a DT_INVALID check. Trigger: a reference dtype such as DT_FLOAT_REF passes validation and reaches the constructor, which CHECK-fails on reference types. Consequence: process abort, i.e., denial of service during Grappler constant folding.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.7. The KVM subsystem allows out-of-range access to memslots after a deletion, aka CID-0774a964ef56. This affects arch/s390/kvm/kvm-s390.c, include/linux/kvm_host.h, and virt/kvm/kvm_main.c.

code_evidence: Line 5 caches slots = kvm_memslots(kvm), and lines 7-8 immediately dereference it via kvm_s390_next_dirty_cmma and gfn_to_memslot without checking whether any slots are in use.
Line 14 reads slots->memslots[0].base_gfn and .npages unconditionally, so an empty memslot array yields an out-of-range read.
Lines 32-34 re-fetch ms via gfn_to_memslot as cur_gfn advances past ms->npages, but a stale slot iteration can return an invalid pointer that is then dereferenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences memslot pointers/array entries that can refer to freed or invalid memory after deletion, matching CWE-416. It is not merely an integer overflow; the core defect is use of a stale/freed slot reference.

evidence_lines.code: mem_end = slots->memslots[0].base_gfn + slots->memslots[0].npages;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: After a memslot deletion the LRU slot array may contain no used slots, yet kvm_s390_get_cmma still iterates and indexes slots->memslots[0] and follows gfn_to_memslot results. The trigger is calling this path when used_slots is zero, causing an out-of-range/stale memslot access whose consequence is a use-after-free or out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
bplist: Disallow key nodes with non-string node types

As reported in #86, the binary plist parser would force the type of the
key node to be of type PLIST_KEY while the node might be of a different
i.e. non-string type. A following plist_free() might then call free() on
an invalid pointer; e.g. if the node is of type integer, its value would
be considered a pointer, and free() would cause an error.
We prevent this issue by disallowing non-string key nodes during parsing.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '        if (plist_get_data(key)->type != PLIST_STRING) {', '            fprintf(stderr, "ERROR: Malformed binary plist dict, invalid node type for key!\\n");', '            plist_free(node);', '            return NULL;', '        }', '']}
description: The plist_free_data function in plist.c in libplist allows attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via vectors involving an integer node that is treated as a PLIST_KEY and then triggers an invalid free.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function forces a key node's type to PLIST_KEY without validating it, which can lead to a type-confusion invalid free in plist_free; the code does not itself call free() twice on the same address, so CWE-415 is not directly supported.

commit_msg:
ipv6: Prevent overrun when parsing v6 header options

The KASAN warning repoted below was discovered with a syzkaller
program.  The reproducer is basically:
  int s = socket(AF_INET6, SOCK_RAW, NEXTHDR_HOP);
  send(s, &one_byte_of_data, 1, MSG_MORE);
  send(s, &more_than_mtu_bytes_data, 2000, 0);

The socket() call sets the nexthdr field of the v6 header to
NEXTHDR_HOP, the first send call primes the payload with a non zero
byte of data, and the second send call triggers the fragmentation path.

The fragmentation code tries to parse the header options in order
to figure out where to insert the fragment option.  Since nexthdr points
to an invalid option, the calculation of the size of the network header
can made to be much larger than the linear section of the skb and data
is read outside of it.

This fix makes ip6_find_1stfrag return an error if it detects
running out-of-bounds.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (unfrag_ip6hlen < 0)', '\t\t\t\treturn ERR_PTR(unfrag_ip6hlen);']}
description: The IPv6 fragmentation implementation in the Linux kernel through 4.11.1 does not consider that the nexthdr field may be associated with an invalid option, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and BUG) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted socket and send system calls.

code_evidence: ip6_find_1stfragopt() returns a header-length value that is stored in unfrag_ip6hlen and used directly as an offset into the skb linear data; the code computes fptr = ipv6h + unfrag_ip6hlen and then writes fptr->frag_off without validating that the offset stays within the buffer. An attacker-controlled nexthdr (e.g. NEXTHDR_HOP) can make the parsed option length exceed the linear skb, so the offset points past the intended data and the subsequent access reads out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses an unvalidated parsed length as a buffer offset and accesses memory past the intended skb data, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. This is not merely an integer overflow; the direct defect is the missing bounds check on the computed header offset.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of ip6_find_1stfragopt is not checked for a negative error or bounded against skb length before being used as an offset. Trigger: a raw IPv6 socket with nexthdr set to an invalid option plus a send that enters fragmentation. Consequence: out-of-bounds read/write beyond the skb linear region, causing KASAN slab-out-of-bounds and potential DoS.

commit_msg:
Bug 697762: Fix scan converter SEGVs.

The SEGVs are caused by the scan converter allowing less room
in the table than is actually required. This happens due to
the mark_curve subdivision overflowing.

For example, if we have a curve such as:

 0 0x80000000 moveto
 0 0x80000000 0 0x80000000 0 0x80000000 curveto

Then the current subdivision logic does:

 fixed ay = (sy + c1y)>>1

For sy = c1y = 0x80000000 this gives ay = 0, when clearly
the average should be 0x80000000.

An alternative formulation of the splitting code:

 fixed ay = (sy>>1) + (c1y>>1)

gives the required result, at the expense of dropping accuracy at
the low end.

This commit therefore has 2 formulations of the splitting code, one
for 'big' values (values that might overflow), and ones for normal
values (values that won't).

We select between the two pieces of code by comparing the top 2
bits of each value; if they differ, then we use the big variant.

Also, when calculating the size of the table required, we were
incorrectly closing the curve more often than we needed to. This
had no ill effect other than inflating the amount of memory we
needed.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    mark_curve(sx, sy, pcur->p1.x, pcur->p1.y, pcur->p2.x, pcur->p2.y, ex, ey, ibox.p.y, scanlines, table, index, k);'], 'added_lines': ['                    mark_curve_top(sx, sy, pcur->p1.x, pcur->p1.y, pcur->p2.x, pcur->p2.y, ex, ey, ibox.p.y, scanlines, table, index, k);']}
description: Integer overflow in the mark_curve function in Artifex Ghostscript 9.21 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PostScript document.

code_evidence: The s_curve branch computes subdivision depth k via gx_curve_log2_samples from the curve's fixed-point control points, then passes the raw curve coordinates into mark_curve at line 48. The overflow fixed by the patch occurs inside mark_curve's midpoint averaging of large fixed coordinates; this caller supplies those coordinates directly and allocates table/index earlier via make_table, so the curve geometry determines both the subdivision count and the memory written.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits: the defect is a signed fixed-point addition whose result wraps, defeating the size/space assumption used for the table and leading to out-of-bounds writes. It is not merely a bounds error; the missing overflow constraint is the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mark_curve averages fixed-point control-point coordinates (sy + c1y)>>1, which overflows for large values such as 0x80000000, yielding a wrong midpoint and an underestimated required table size. Trigger: a crafted PostScript curve with large coordinates. Consequence: mark_curve writes beyond the allocated table, causing an out-of-bounds write, crash, or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
mm: remove gup_flags FOLL_WRITE games from __get_user_pages()

This is an ancient bug that was actually attempted to be fixed once
(badly) by me eleven years ago in commit 4ceb5db9757a ("Fix
get_user_pages() race for write access") but that was then undone due to
problems on s390 by commit f33ea7f404e5 ("fix get_user_pages bug").

In the meantime, the s390 situation has long been fixed, and we can now
fix it by checking the pte_dirty() bit properly (and do it better).  The
s390 dirty bit was implemented in abf09bed3cce ("s390/mm: implement
software dirty bits") which made it into v3.9.  Earlier kernels will
have to look at the page state itself.

Also, the VM has become more scalable, and what used a purely
theoretical race back then has become easier to trigger.

To fix it, we introduce a new internal FOLL_COW flag to mark the "yes,
we already did a COW" rather than play racy games with FOLL_WRITE that
is very fundamental, and then use the pte dirty flag to validate that
the FOLL_COW flag is still valid.

Reported-and-tested-by: Phil "not Paul" Oester <kernel@linuxace.com>
Acked-by: Hugh Dickins <hughd@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>
Cc: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Cc: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
Cc: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: Nick Piggin <npiggin@gmail.com>
Cc: Greg Thelen <gthelen@google.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t*flags &= ~FOLL_WRITE;'], 'added_lines': ['\t        *flags |= FOLL_COW;']}
description: Race condition in mm/gup.c in the Linux kernel 2.x through 4.x before 4.8.3 allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging incorrect handling of a copy-on-write (COW) feature to write to a read-only memory mapping, as exploited in the wild in October 2016, aka "Dirty COW."

code_evidence: fault_flags derives FAULT_FLAG_WRITE from *flags; handle_mm_fault() then resolves the fault under that flag, so the write intent is baked into the fault handling call before any later check.
After the fault, if VM_FAULT_WRITE is set and the VMA lacks VM_WRITE, the code clears FOLL_WRITE from *flags, mutating shared caller state based on the fault outcome.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits: a shared resource (the VMA/PTE and *flags) is accessed without exclusive synchronization, and the check-then-modify at [45,46] races with concurrent fault handling. The defect is the non-atomic sequence, not a missing bounds check (CWE-125) or pointer misuse.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((ret & VM_FAULT_WRITE) && !(vma->vm_flags & VM_WRITE))
*flags &= ~FOLL_WRITE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write intent (FOLL_WRITE) is derived once at [12,13] and passed to handle_mm_fault() at [24], while the post-fault adjustment at [45,46] clears it only afterward. Between the fault and the clearing, another thread can modify the shared mapping/PTE, so the cleared FOLL_WRITE no longer reflects the page state; the caller then proceeds with a stale, racy view. Trigger: concurrent writes to a read-only private mapping (COW). Consequence: writes reach read-only memory, enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Server: Fix two issues identified by ASan

1. If the TLSPlain and X509Plain security types were both disabled, then
   rfbOptPamAuth() would overflow the name field in the secTypes
   structure when testing the "none" security type, since the name of
   that security type has less than five characters.  This issue was
   innocuous, since the overflow was fully contained within the secTypes
   structure, but the ASan error caused Xvnc to abort, which made it
   difficult to detect other errors.

2. If an ill-behaved RFB client sent the TurboVNC Server a fence
   message with more than 64 bytes, then the TurboVNC Server would
   try to read that message and subsequently overflow the stack before
   it detected that the payload was too large.  This could never have
   occurred with any of the VNC viewers that currently support the RFB
   flow control extensions (TigerVNC and TurboVNC, namely.)  This issue
   was also innocuous, since the stack overflow affected two variables
   (newScreens and errMsg) that were never accessed before the function
   returned.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['         !strcmp(&s->name[strlen(s->name) - 5], "plain")) && s->enabled)'], 'added_lines': ['         strstr(s->name, "plain")) && s->enabled)']}
description: TurboVNC server code contains stack buffer overflow vulnerability in commit prior to cea98166008301e614e0d36776bf9435a536136e. This could possibly result into remote code execution, since stack frame is not protected with stack canary. This attack appear to be exploitable via network connectivity. To exploit this vulnerability authorization on server is required. These issues have been fixed in commit cea98166008301e614e0d36776bf9435a536136e.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over secTypes entries and, for each name, evaluates strlen(s->name) - 5 to index into the name. No check ensures the name is at least 5 characters before the subtraction and pointer offset are formed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 covers writes past/ before a buffer; here the analogous out-of-bounds access is a read caused by an unchecked length subtraction. The missing lower-bound constraint on the index directly enables the out-of-bounds access, matching the target weakness class of an out-of-bounds operation on a buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code computes &s->name[strlen(s->name) - 5] without verifying the name length, so a security type name shorter than five characters (e.g. the "none" type) produces a negative offset. Trigger: rfbOptPamAuth() runs with such an entry present and enabled. Consequence: the strcmp reads before the start of the name buffer, an out-of-bounds access that ASan reports and that can abort the process.

commit_msg:
Eric Dumazet says:

====================
Juha-Matti Tilli reported that malicious peers could inject tiny
packets in out_of_order_queue, forcing very expensive calls
to tcp_collapse_ofo_queue() and tcp_prune_ofo_queue() for
every incoming packet.

With tcp_rmem[2] default of 6MB, the ooo queue could
contain ~7000 nodes.

This patch series makes sure we cut cpu cycles enough to
render the attack not critical.

We might in the future go further, like disconnecting
or black-holing proven malicious flows.
====================

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (tcp_try_coalesce(sk, tp->ooo_last_skb,', '\t\t\t     skb, &fragstolen)) {', '\t\t\t\t__kfree_skb(skb);', '\t\t\t\t__kfree_skb(skb1);', '\t\t} else if (tcp_try_coalesce(sk, skb1,', '\t\t\t\t\t    skb, &fragstolen)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (tcp_ooo_try_coalesce(sk, tp->ooo_last_skb,', '\t\t\t\t skb, &fragstolen)) {', '\t\t\t\ttcp_drop(sk, skb);', '\t\t\t\ttcp_drop(sk, skb1);', '\t\t} else if (tcp_ooo_try_coalesce(sk, skb1,', '\t\t\t\t\t\tskb, &fragstolen)) {']}
description: Linux kernel versions 4.9+ can be forced to make very expensive calls to tcp_collapse_ofo_queue() and tcp_prune_ofo_queue() for every incoming packet which can lead to a denial of service.

code_evidence: Lines 33-39 attempt coalescing an incoming out-of-order skb with tp->ooo_last_skb; if it succeeds the skb is freed and the function returns via add_sack, otherwise the skb is inserted into the out_of_order_queue rbtree.

Lines 47-81 walk the rbtree to locate the insert/merge position, performing per-node comparisons and possibly tcp_try_coalesce (lines 76-78). The number of nodes traversed and the cost of merge/coalesce work scale with the existing out_of_order_queue size, which is bounded only by rmem scheduling at lines 9-13, not by a per-packet work cap.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's per-packet processing cost is not bounded or throttled relative to attacker-controlled queue growth, matching CWE-400's uncontrolled consumption of a limited resource (CPU). This is resource-consumption weakness, not a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: each incoming out-of-order packet triggers rbtree traversal and coalesce/merge work proportional to the out_of_order_queue size, with no throttle limiting per-packet work. Trigger: a peer sends many tiny out-of-order segments that fill the queue (up to rmem[2] worth of nodes). Consequence: repeated expensive tcp_collapse/prune-style processing per packet consumes CPU, enabling denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix dtype bug in draw bounding boxes.

Boxes always needs to be type `float`.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 461800676
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      const auto tboxes = boxes.tensor<T, 3>();'], 'added_lines': ['      const auto tboxes = boxes.tensor<float, 3>();']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. When `DrawBoundingBoxes` receives an input `boxes` that is not of dtype `float`, it gives a `CHECK` fail that can trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit da0d65cdc1270038e72157ba35bf74b85d9bda11. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The function fetches boxes from context->input(1) and validates only its rank and third-dimension size; it never checks the element dtype of boxes.
Line 58 accesses boxes.tensor<T, 3>(), which requires the tensor's actual element type to match template parameter T; a mismatched dtype triggers a TensorFlow CHECK failure.

commit_msg:
portal: Do not use caller-supplied variables in environment

If the caller specifies a variable that can be used to inject arbitrary
code into processes, we must not allow it to enter the environment
block used to run `flatpak run`, which runs unsandboxed.

This change requires the previous commit "context: Add --env-fd option",
which adds infrastructure used here.

To be secure, this change also requires the previous commit
"run: Convert all environment variables into bwrap arguments", which
protects a non-setuid bwrap(1) from the same attack.

Signed-off-by: Simon McVittie <smcv@collabora.com>
Part-of: https://github.com/flatpak/flatpak/security/advisories/GHSA-4ppf-fxf6-vxg2
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      env = g_environ_setenv (env, var, val, TRUE);'], 'added_lines': ['  /* Let the environment variables given by the caller override the ones', "   * from extra_args. Don't add them to @env, because they are controlled", '   * by our caller, which might be trying to use them to inject code into', '   * flatpak(1); add them to the environment block instead.', '   *', "   * We don't use --env= here, so that if the values are something that", '   * should not be exposed to other uids, they can remain confidential. */', "      if (var[0] == '\\0')", '        {', '          g_dbus_method_invocation_return_error (invocation, G_DBUS_ERROR,', '                                                 G_DBUS_ERROR_INVALID_ARGS,', '                                                 "Environment variable cannot have empty name");', '          return G_DBUS_METHOD_INVOCATION_HANDLED;', '        }', '', "      if (strchr (var, '=') != NULL)", '        {', '          g_dbus_method_invocation_return_error (invocation, G_DBUS_ERROR,', '                                                 G_DBUS_ERROR_INVALID_ARGS,', '                                                 "Environment variable name cannot contain \'=\'");', '          return G_DBUS_METHOD_INVOCATION_HANDLED;', '        }', '', '      g_string_append (env_string, var);', "      g_string_append_c (env_string, '=');", '      g_string_append (env_string, val);', "      g_string_append_c (env_string, '\\0');"]}
description: Flatpak is a system for building, distributing, and running sandboxed desktop applications on Linux. A bug was discovered in the `flatpak-portal` service that can allow sandboxed applications to execute arbitrary code on the host system (a sandbox escape). This sandbox-escape bug is present in versions from 0.11.4 and before fixed versions 1.8.5 and 1.10.0. The Flatpak portal D-Bus service (`flatpak-portal`, also known by its D-Bus service name `org.freedesktop.portal.Flatpak`) allows apps in a Flatpak sandbox to launch their own subprocesses in a new sandbox instance, either with the same security settings as the caller or with more restrictive security settings. For example, this is used in Flatpak-packaged web browsers such as Chromium to launch subprocesses that will process untrusted web content, and give those subprocesses a more restrictive sandbox than the browser itself. In vulnerable versions, the Flatpak portal service passes caller-specified environment variables to non-sandboxed processes on the host system, and in particular to the `flatpak run` command that is used to launch the new sandbox instance. A malicious or compromised Flatpak app could set environment variables that are trusted by the `flatpak run` command, and use them to execute arbitrary code that is not in a sandbox. As a workaround, this vulnerability can be mitigated by preventing the `flatpak-portal` service from starting, but that mitigation will prevent many Flatpak apps from working correctly. This is fixed in versions 1.8.5 and 1.10.0.

code_evidence: The loop reads caller-supplied environment variable names and values from arg_envs via g_variant_get_child and passes them unvalidated into g_environ_setenv, which builds the environment block used by the spawned process.
The env_string (built from caller-controlled var/val) is written into a memfd/tmpfile and passed to flatpak via --env-fd, so caller-supplied variables reach the unsandboxed flatpak run command.
g_spawn_async_with_pipes launches flatpak_argv with env as the environment block, allowing the caller-influenced variables to affect how flatpak run is interpreted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits because externally influenced input is incorporated into a structure (the environment) that a downstream component (flatpak run) interprets, without proper neutralization of special elements. The consequence is injection into the downstream command's execution logic, matching the target weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!g_spawn_async_with_pipes (NULL,
(char **) flatpak_argv->pdata,
env,
G_SPAWN_SEARCH_PATH | G_SPAWN_DO_NOT_REAP_CHILD | G_SPAWN_LEAVE_DESCRIPTORS_OPEN,
child_setup_func, &child_setup_data,
&pid,
NULL,
NULL,
NULL,
&error))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The portal accepts environment variable names/values from the sandboxed caller and places them into the environment used to execute flatpak run without neutralizing variables that affect flatpak's behavior. A malicious app can set such variables to alter how the downstream flatpak command is parsed/executed, yielding host code execution (sandbox escape).

commit_msg:
drbg: ensure fork-safety without using a pthread_atfork handler

When the new OpenSSL CSPRNG was introduced in version 1.1.1,
it was announced in the release notes that it would be fork-safe,
which the old CSPRNG hadn't been.

The fork-safety was implemented using a fork count, which was
incremented by a pthread_atfork handler. Initially, this handler
was enabled by default. Unfortunately, the default behaviour
had to be changed for other reasons in commit b5319bdbd095, so
the new OpenSSL CSPRNG failed to keep its promise.

This commit restores the fork-safety using a different approach.
It replaces the fork count by a fork id, which coincides with
the process id on UNIX-like operating systems and is zero on other
operating systems. It is used to detect when an automatic reseed
after a fork is necessary.

To prevent a future regression, it also adds a test to verify that
the child reseeds after fork.

CVE-2019-1549

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <paul.dale@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/9802)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    rand_fork();'], 'added_lines': []}
description: OpenSSL 1.1.1 introduced a rewritten random number generator (RNG). This was intended to include protection in the event of a fork() system call in order to ensure that the parent and child processes did not share the same RNG state. However this protection was not being used in the default case. A partial mitigation for this issue is that the output from a high precision timer is mixed into the RNG state so the likelihood of a parent and child process sharing state is significantly reduced. If an application already calls OPENSSL_init_crypto() explicitly using OPENSSL_INIT_ATFORK then this problem does not occur at all. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1d (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1c).

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only clears the fork hook by calling rand_fork() and contains no random-number generation or state reuse logic; it does not itself demonstrate insufficient randomness.

Fix jpeg_skip_scanlines() segfault w/merged upsamp

The additional segfault mentioned in #244 was due to the fact that
the merged upsamplers use a different private structure than the
non-merged upsamplers.  jpeg_skip_scanlines() was assuming the latter, so
when merged upsampling was enabled, jpeg_skip_scanlines() clobbered one

necessary to set up a dummy postprocessing function in

to a NULL pointer being passed to jcopy_sample_rows()) or an error
("Corrupt JPEG data: premature end of data segment"), depending on the
number of scanlines skipped and whether the first scanline skipped was
an odd- or even-numbered row.

Fixes #441
Fixes #244 (for real this time)

commit_msg:
evtchn: address races with evtchn_reset()

Neither d->evtchn_port_ops nor max_evtchns(d) may be used in an entirely
lock-less manner, as both may change by a racing evtchn_reset(). In the
common case, at least one of the domain's event lock or the per-channel
lock needs to be held. In the specific case of the inter-domain sending
by evtchn_send() and notify_via_xen_event_channel() holding the other
side's per-channel lock is sufficient, as the channel can't change state
without both per-channel locks held. Without such a channel changing
state, evtchn_reset() can't complete successfully.

Lock-free accesses continue to be permitted for the shim (calling some
otherwise internal event channel functions), as this happens while the
domain is in effectively single-threaded mode. Special care also needs
taking for the shim's marking of in-use ports as ECS_RESERVED (allowing
use of such ports in the shim case is okay because switching into and
hence also out of FIFO mode is impossihble there).

As a side effect, certain operations on Xen bound event channels which
were mistakenly permitted so far (e.g. unmask or poll) will be refused
now.

This is part of XSA-343.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static bool evtchn_2l_is_masked(const struct domain *d, evtchn_port_t port)'], 'added_lines': ['static bool evtchn_2l_is_masked(const struct domain *d,', '                                const struct evtchn *evtchn)', '    evtchn_port_t port = evtchn->port;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The function computes max_ports from BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d), which reads the domain's max_evtchns, then uses the caller-supplied port to test the shared evtchn_mask bit. No event lock or per-channel lock is taken, so the port bound and mask word can be observed while a concurrent evtchn_reset() changes the domain's event-channel configuration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent read of shared event-channel state with no synchronization, matching CWE-362's improper synchronization race on a shared resource. It is not merely an off-by-one bound error: the bound itself changes concurrently, so the missing lock is the core weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the is_masked check reads max_ports and the shared evtchn_mask without holding the domain event lock or per-channel lock. Trigger: a racing evtchn_reset() alters max_evtchns/port state between the ASSERT/bound check and the mask test. Supported consequence: the port bound assumption is violated, leading to out-of-bounds mask access or triggering bug checks.

description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

code_evidence: The function processes each received RST_STREAM frame by locating the stream and calling stream->change_state, then initiating stream close at lines 37-38; the diff adds a per-minute RST_STREAM frame counter check that returns HTTP2_ERROR_ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM once the configured limit is exceeded. Unbounded, rapid RST_STREAM frames therefore force repeated stream resets and connection teardown work without throttling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the weakness is lack of throttling of a resource-consuming operation (stream resets), allowing resource exhaustion. It is distinct from a memory-safety bug; the harm is availability via uncontrolled consumption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the frame handler accepts and acts on RST_STREAM frames for streams without bounding how many resets a peer may trigger in a time window. Trigger: a client rapidly sends RST_STREAM frames to cancel many streams. Consequence: server CPU and connection-state resources are consumed by repeated stream teardown, enabling denial of service; the added counter check is the mitigation.

Reviewed by: William Brown, Viktor Ashirov, Mark Reynolds (thank you all)

Platforms tested:  F31
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        slapi_pblock_get(pb, SLAPI_PB_RESULT_TEXT, &pbtext);'], 'added_lines': ['        slapi_pblock_get(pb, SLAPI_RESULT_TEXT, &pbtext);']}
description: When binding against a DN during authentication, the reply from 389-ds-base will be different whether the DN exists or not. This can be used by an unauthenticated attacker to check the existence of an entry in the LDAP database.

code_evidence: When no explicit text is supplied, the function retrieves a result message from the pblock into pbtext using SLAPI_PB_RESULT_TEXT; this value is later emitted to the client via ber_printf with pbtext ? pbtext : "".
The retrieved diagnostic string is included in the LDAP result sent to the requester, so its content depends on server-side lookup state rather than on client-supplied data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function produces observably different LDAP responses depending on whether the target entry exists, matching CWE-203's observable discrepancy that leaks information to an unauthorized actor. The fix changes the retrieved key so no entry-existence detail is returned; this is an information-disclosure discrepancy rather than an authentication bypass.

evidence_lines.code:
rc = ber_printf(ber, "{it{ess", operation->o_msgid, tag, err,
matched ? matched : "", pbtext ? pbtext : "");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bind result path attaches a pblock-derived diagnostic message (SLAPI_PB_RESULT_TEXT) that reveals whether the target entry exists. Trigger: an unauthenticated bind against a non-existent DN; the response text differs from the response for an existing DN. Consequence: an attacker can distinguish entry existence, disclosing directory information.

commit_msg:
timerfd: Protect the might cancel mechanism proper

The handling of the might_cancel queueing is not properly protected, so
parallel operations on the file descriptor can race with each other and
lead to list corruptions or use after free.

Protect the context for these operations with a seperate lock.

The wait queue lock cannot be reused for this because that would create a
lock inversion scenario vs. the cancel lock. Replacing might_cancel with an
atomic (atomic_t or atomic bit) does not help either because it still can
race vs. the actual list operation.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: "linux-fsdevel@vger.kernel.org"
Cc: syzkaller <syzkaller@googlegroups.com>
Cc: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Cc: linux-fsdevel@vger.kernel.org
Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.DEB.2.20.1701311521430.3457@nanos
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (ctx->might_cancel) {', '\t\tctx->might_cancel = false;', '\t\tspin_lock(&cancel_lock);', '\t\tlist_del_rcu(&ctx->clist);', '\t\tspin_unlock(&cancel_lock);', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tspin_lock(&ctx->cancel_lock);', '\t__timerfd_remove_cancel(ctx);', '\tspin_unlock(&ctx->cancel_lock);']}
description: Race condition in fs/timerfd.c in the Linux kernel before 4.10.15 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (list corruption or use-after-free) via simultaneous file-descriptor operations that leverage improper might_cancel queueing.

code_evidence: timerfd_remove_cancel tests ctx->might_cancel and clears it (line 4) outside any lock protecting list membership; the list_del_rcu on ctx->clist (line 6) is only serialized by the global cancel_lock, while the check/clear on might_cancel is not. A concurrent path can therefore observe might_cancel and act on ctx->clist after it was already removed/freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the race lets a path operate on ctx/clist after the context has been freed, matching reuse of freed memory. It is a race-condition enabler, but the supported impact is use-after-free, not merely a generic race (CWE-362).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the might_cancel flag and the clist removal are not protected by a common lock, so the check-then-clear-then-list_del sequence is non-atomic. Trigger: simultaneous file-descriptor operations (e.g., cancel and release) race; one path frees or detaches ctx while another still performs list_del_rcu on ctx->clist, causing list corruption or a use-after-free of the timerfd context.

commit_msg:
security fix: scrub headers on `OIDCUnAuthAction pass`; closes #222

On accessing paths protected with `OIDCUnAuthAction pass` no headers
would be scrubbed when a user is not authenticated so malicious
software/users could set OIDC_CLAIM_ and OIDCAuthNHeader headers that
applications would interpret as set by mod_auth_openidc. Thanks
@wouterhund.

Signed-off-by: Hans Zandbelt <hans.zandbelt@zmartzone.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (cfg->scrub_request_headers != 0) {', '', '\t\t/* scrub all headers starting with OIDC_ first */', '\t\toidc_scrub_request_headers(r, OIDC_DEFAULT_HEADER_PREFIX,', '\t\t\t\toidc_cfg_dir_authn_header(r));', '', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * then see if the claim headers need to be removed on top of that', '\t\t * (i.e. the prefix does not start with the default OIDC_)', '\t\t */', '\t\tif ((strstr(cfg->claim_prefix, OIDC_DEFAULT_HEADER_PREFIX)', '\t\t\t\t!= cfg->claim_prefix)) {', '\t\t\toidc_scrub_request_headers(r, cfg->claim_prefix, NULL);', '\t\t}', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\toidc_scrub_headers(r);']}
description: The "OpenID Connect Relying Party and OAuth 2.0 Resource Server" (aka mod_auth_openidc) module before 2.1.5 for the Apache HTTP Server does not skip OIDC_CLAIM_ and OIDCAuthNHeader headers in an "OIDCUnAuthAction pass" configuration, which allows remote attackers to bypass authentication via crafted HTTP traffic.

code_evidence: The header-scrubbing block is gated on cfg->scrub_request_headers != 0, so when that option is disabled, client-supplied OIDC_CLAIM_/OIDCAuthNHeader headers are left untouched before the code proceeds.
Line 22-23 then sets the authentication header (authn_header) from r->user, but only when r->user is non-NULL; the scrubbing of attacker-controlled claim headers is the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the missing header scrubbing lets an unauthenticated actor's self-asserted identity headers be accepted as a valid authentication claim, directly defeating identity verification. This is improper authentication rather than mere header injection because the consequence is assuming an authenticated identity.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((r->user != NULL) && (authn_header != NULL))
oidc_util_set_header(r, authn_header, r->user);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: scrubbing of security-relevant OIDC_CLAIM_ and OIDCAuthNHeader headers is conditional and skipped when scrub_request_headers is off, so spoofed identity headers survive into the request. Trigger: a remote client sends crafted OIDC_CLAIM_/authn headers in an OIDCUnAuthAction pass configuration; the backend application trusts them as authenticated identity, enabling authentication bypass.

commit_msg:
scsi: libsas: fix a race condition when smp task timeout

When the lldd is processing the complete sas task in interrupt and set the
task stat as SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE, the smp timeout timer is able to be
triggered at the same time. And smp_task_timedout() will complete the task
wheter the SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE is set or not. Then the sas task may freed
before lldd end the interrupt process. Thus a use-after-free will happen.

Fix this by calling the complete() only when SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE is not
set. And remove the check of the return value of the del_timer(). Once the
LLDD sets DONE, it must call task->done(), which will call
smp_task_done()->complete() and the task will be completed and freed
correctly.

Reported-by: chenxiang <chenxiang66@hisilicon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Yan <yanaijie@huawei.com>
CC: John Garry <john.garry@huawei.com>
CC: Johannes Thumshirn <jthumshirn@suse.de>
CC: Ewan Milne <emilne@redhat.com>
CC: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
CC: Tomas Henzl <thenzl@redhat.com>
CC: Dan Williams <dan.j.williams@intel.com>
CC: Hannes Reinecke <hare@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Hannes Reinecke <hare@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: John Garry <john.garry@huawei.com>
Reviewed-by: Johannes Thumshirn <jthumshirn@suse.de>
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!(task->task_state_flags & SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE))', '', '\tcomplete(&task->slow_task->completion);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!(task->task_state_flags & SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE)) {', '\t\tcomplete(&task->slow_task->completion);', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.20. There is a race condition in smp_task_timedout() and smp_task_done() in drivers/scsi/libsas/sas_expander.c, leading to a use-after-free.

code_evidence: The timeout callback takes task_state_lock and checks SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE, but complete() at line 10 is invoked unconditionally after the lock is dropped. Concurrent smp_task_done() can set DONE and complete/free the task between the check and the complete() call, so the timeout path signals completion of a task already being torn down.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent execution using a shared task-state resource with improper synchronization: a timing window between the state check and the completion action allows an interfering code sequence. The defect is the race window itself, not merely the resulting memory error, so CWE-362 fits as the root weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DONE-state check and the completion signal are not performed under one exclusive sequence; the check is inside the lock but complete() is outside. Trigger: the LLDD's interrupt handler sets SAS_TASK_STATE_DONE and calls task->done() while the timeout timer fires concurrently. Consequence: smp_task_timedout() completes a task that is being freed, producing a use-after-free and potential crash/instability.

description: ARM mbed TLS before 1.3.21 and 2.x before 2.1.9, if optional authentication is configured, allows remote attackers to bypass peer authentication via an X.509 certificate chain with many intermediates. NOTE: although mbed TLS was formerly known as PolarSSL, the releases shipped with the PolarSSL name are not affected.

code_evidence: The chain-depth check rejects certificates once 1 + path_cnt exceeds MBEDTLS_X509_MAX_INTERMEDIATE_CA, but it only sets MBEDTLS_X509_BADCERT_NOT_TRUSTED and returns MBEDTLS_ERR_X509_CERT_VERIFY_FAILED rather than a fatal error. The recursion into x509_crt_verify_child at lines 81-83 depends on this guard to bound intermediate-CA traversal.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the depth-limit handling fails to decisively prove the peer's claimed identity when the chain is excessive; the fix returns a fatal error. This is improper authentication, not merely a resource-exhaustion issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: exceeding the intermediate-CA limit is treated as an ordinary verification failure that callers may tolerate rather than an unconditional rejection. Trigger: a peer presents an X.509 chain containing many intermediates under optional authentication. Consequence: the depth limit does not reliably abort verification, so peer authentication can be bypassed.

commit_msg: Fix unmatched array length in core_java.c (issue #16304) (#16313)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfor (; i < END_CMDS; i++) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tfor (; i < END_CMDS - 1; i++) {']}
description: An off-by-one overflow flaw was found in radare2 due to mismatched array length in core_java.c. This could allow an attacker to cause a crash, and perform a denail of service attack.

code_evidence: The loop condition uses `i < END_CMDS`, so iteration reaches index `END_CMDS - 1`. At that index, `JAVA_CMDS[i].name`, `.name_len` and `.handler` are dereferenced (lines 12-14 and 19). If `END_CMDS` is the array length rather than the last valid index, the final iteration accesses one element past the end of `JAVA_CMDS`.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-193 fits because the loop uses a maximum index one greater than the correct value, an off-by-one error in the array bound. The weakness is the incorrect boundary (CWE-193), not the generic out-of-bounds read itself, which is the resulting effect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound permits `i` to equal `END_CMDS - 1` while the table's valid indices end at `END_CMDS - 2`, producing an out-of-bounds read of `JAVA_CMDS[i]`. Trigger: input starting with "java " that reaches the loop and matches no earlier command. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read/possible crash (DoS), consistent with the commit fixing the bound to `END_CMDS - 1`.

commit_msg:
KEYS: fix keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring() to not leak thread keyrings

This fixes CVE-2017-7472.

Running the following program as an unprivileged user exhausts kernel
memory by leaking thread keyrings:

	#include <keyutils.h>

	int main()
	{
		for (;;)
			keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring(KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING);
	}

Fix it by only creating a new thread keyring if there wasn't one before.
To make things more consistent, make install_thread_keyring_to_cred()
and install_process_keyring_to_cred() both return 0 if the corresponding
keyring is already present.

Fixes: d84f4f992cbd ("CRED: Inaugurate COW credentials")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 2.6.29+
Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\treturn ret != -EEXIST ? ret : 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn ret;']}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.10.13 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a series of KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring calls.

code_evidence: install_process_keyring() allocates new credentials via prepare_creds() at line 5, then calls install_process_keyring_to_cred(new) at line 8. When that call returns -EEXIST (keyring already present), the code aborts the new cred and returns 0, treating the existing keyring as success. The caller then proceeds as though a fresh keyring was installed, so the prior keyring object is neither released nor accounted for on this path, and repeated calls re-enter the same path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers failure to properly release or account for a resource across all paths. Here the early-return path treats an existing keyring as success while leaving the resource unreleased, matching CWE-404 rather than a mere logic error; the DoS is the consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the -EEXIST branch returns success without releasing or reconciling the already-present keyring/cred resource, so each call leaves resource state unaccounted for. Trigger: repeated install_process_keyring() calls where the keyring already exists. Supported consequence: unbounded resource accumulation leading to denial of service (memory consumption).

https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/663

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (SyncImagePixelCache(image,exception) == MagickFalse)', '    return(MagickFalse);']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in enhance.c in ImageMagick before 7.0.6-6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Three heap buffers (equalize_map, histogram, map) are allocated with size (MaxMap+1)*GetPixelChannels(image)*sizeof(double), so their valid index range is bounded by GetPixelChannels(image)*MaxMap plus the channel offset.
The histogram is incremented at index GetPixelChannels(image)*ScaleQuantumToMap(intensity)+i; the map and equalize_map are likewise indexed by GetPixelChannels(image)*j+i where j runs to MaxMap.
The per-pixel write q[j]=ClampToQuantum(equalize_map[...]) reads the map using the same scaling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The indexing arithmetic writes past the end of the heap-allocated histogram/map arrays sized by (MaxMap+1)*GetPixelChannels(image), which is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The added SyncImagePixelCache guard confirms the missing cache synchronization is the root cause; this is distinct from a mere out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code: histogram[GetPixelChannels(image)*ScaleQuantumToMap(intensity)+i]++;

q[j]=ClampToQuantum(equalize_map[GetPixelChannels(image)*
ScaleQuantumToMap(q[j])+j]);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The buffers are sized from GetPixelChannels(image) at allocation time, but the function does not synchronize the pixel cache before computing channel counts and indexing. If the channel count or pixel cache state used for indexing diverges from the allocation size, ScaleQuantumToMap(intensity) can reach MaxMap while the channel offset pushes the computed index past the (MaxMap+1)*channels allocation, producing a heap-based out-of-bounds write into histogram/equalize_map and corrupting adjacent heap memory, leading to a crash or DoS.

commit_msg:
Userland: Fix tar/unzip directory traversal vulnerability

This change validates the filenames within a tar/zip archive during
extraction. If the filename within a the archive is outside of the
current working directory the file will be skipped and not extracted
onto the host system.

Closes #3991
Closes #3992
