commit_msg:
gtTileContig(): check Tile width for overflow

fixes #211
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    y = h - 1;', '\t    toskew = -(int32)(tw + w);', '\t    y = 0;', '\t    toskew = -(int32)(tw - w);'], 'added_lines': ['        if ((tw + w) > INT_MAX) {', '            TIFFErrorExt(tif->tif_clientdata, TIFFFileName(tif), "%s", "unsupported tile size (too wide)");', '            return (0);', '        }', '        y = h - 1;', '        toskew = -(int32)(tw + w);', '        if (tw > (INT_MAX + w)) {', '            TIFFErrorExt(tif->tif_clientdata, TIFFFileName(tif), "%s", "unsupported tile size (too wide)");', '            return (0);', '        }', '        y = 0;', '        toskew = -(int32)(tw - w);']}
description: An integer overflow flaw was found in libtiff that exists in the tif_getimage.c file. This flaw allows an attacker to inject and execute arbitrary code when a user opens a crafted TIFF file. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to confidentiality, integrity, as well as system availability.

code_evidence: Tile width tw and length th are read from the TIFF via TIFFGetField without validating their magnitude relative to the raster width w.
In the vertical-flip branch, tw + w is computed in uint32 arithmetic and then cast to int32 for toskew; no overflow check guards this sum.
In the else branch, tw - w is computed in uint32 and cast to int32; when w > tw the subtraction wraps to a huge uint32 before the cast.
The derived toskew/leftmost_toskew values are passed as this_toskew into put, which uses them as raster stride offsets in raster+y*w+tocol.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the weakness is an unchecked integer calculation (tw+w, tw-w) that can overflow or wrap before being narrowed to int32 and used as an offset. The fix adds explicit INT_MAX bounds checks on those sums, confirming the arithmetic overflow is the root cause rather than a separate out-of-bounds write defect.

evidence_lines.code:
TIFFGetField(tif, TIFFTAG_TILEWIDTH, &tw);
TIFFGetField(tif, TIFFTAG_TILELENGTH, &th);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled tile width tw and raster width w are combined in unsigned arithmetic (tw+w, tw-w) and narrowed to int32 without overflow/underflow checks. Trigger: a crafted TIFF whose tile width is large or exceeds the raster width causes the sum or difference to wrap. Consequence: the resulting skewed stride is used by the put routine to index the raster, leading to out-of-bounds memory access and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
evtchn: evtchn_reset() shouldn't succeed with still-open ports

While the function closes all ports, it does so without holding any
lock, and hence racing requests may be issued causing new ports to get
opened. This would have been problematic in particular if such a newly
opened port had a port number above the new implementation limit (i.e.
when switching from FIFO to 2-level) after the reset, as prior to
"evtchn: relax port_is_valid()" this could have led to e.g.
evtchn_close()'s "BUG_ON(!port_is_valid(d2, port2))" to trigger.

Introduce a counter of active ports and check that it's (still) no
larger then the number of Xen internally used ones after obtaining the
necessary lock in evtchn_reset().

As to the access model of the new {active,xen}_evtchns fields - while
all writes get done using write_atomic(), reads ought to use
read_atomic() only when outside of a suitably locked region.

Note that as of now evtchn_bind_virq() and evtchn_bind_ipi() don't have
a need to call check_free_port().

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int            port, pirq = bind->pirq;'], 'added_lines': ['    int            port = 0, pirq = bind->pirq;', '    check_free_port(d, port);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function evtchn_bind_pirq only adds a check_free_port() call under d->event_lock; it does not contain the evtchn_reset() race described, and no unsynchronized shared-resource access is shown.

commit_msg:
arm64: dma-mapping: always clear allocated buffers

Buffers allocated by dma_alloc_coherent() are always zeroed on Alpha,
ARM (32bit), MIPS, PowerPC, x86/x86_64 and probably other architectures.
It turned out that some drivers rely on this 'feature'. Allocated buffer
might be also exposed to userspace with dma_mmap() call, so clearing it
is desired from security point of view to avoid exposing random memory
to userspace. This patch unifies dma_alloc_coherent() behavior on ARM64
architecture with other implementations by unconditionally zeroing
allocated buffer.

Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v3.14+
Signed-off-by: Marek Szyprowski <m.szyprowski@samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Will Deacon <will.deacon@arm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (flags & __GFP_ZERO)', '\t\t\tmemset(ptr, 0, size);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tmemset(ptr, 0, size);']}
description: arch/arm64/mm/dma-mapping.c in the Linux kernel before 4.0.3, as used in the ION subsystem in Android and other products, does not initialize certain data structures, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory by triggering a dma_mmap call.

code_evidence: When gen_pool_alloc succeeds (val nonzero), the function records the page and returns ptr = (void *)val. The newly allocated pool buffer is cleared only when flags contains __GFP_ZERO; otherwise the buffer contents are left uninitialized and returned to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing unconditional initialization lets uninitialized memory reach a userspace mapping, which is a confidentiality exposure consistent with CWE-200. The flaw is the failure to sanitize the buffer before exposure, not an out-of-bounds access or permission error, so CWE-200 fits the target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the memset of the freshly allocated coherent-pool buffer is conditional on __GFP_ZERO, so callers that do not pass that flag receive uninitialized pool memory. When such a buffer is later exposed to userspace via dma_mmap, stale kernel memory contents can be read, disclosing sensitive information.

commit_msg: gnrc_sixlowpan_frag_sfr: fix ARQ scheduler race-condition
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    fbuf->sfr.arq_timeout_event.event.next = NULL;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: RIOT-OS, an operating system for Internet of Things (IoT) devices, contains a network stack with the ability to process 6LoWPAN frames. In versions 2023.01 and prior, an attacker can send multiple crafted frames to the device to trigger a race condition. The race condition invalidates assumptions about the program state and leads to an invalid memory access resulting in denial of service. This issue is patched in pull request 19679. There are no known workarounds.

code_evidence: The function resets the ARQ timeout event state: it clears msg.content.ptr, calls evtimer_del() on the shared _arq_timer, and then directly writes event.next = NULL. This manual list-pointer write occurs outside evtimer_del()'s synchronization, so it can interleave with the timer scheduler touching the same event node.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because a shared resource (the _arq_timer event list node) is modified without exclusive access, creating a timing window where concurrent scheduler code interferes. The patch removes the unsynchronized assignment, confirming the race; this is improper synchronization rather than a plain null-pointer bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code mutates the evtimer event's list linkage (event.next) directly instead of letting the timer subsystem manage it atomically. Trigger: an ARQ timeout fires or the scheduler processes the event concurrently with _clean_slate_datagram(). The intervening sequence can observe or overwrite next, corrupting the timer list and causing an invalid memory access and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Remove access to the root FS from lua

On linux / is mounted to /rootfs in RageFile, which allows access to the
_whole_ filesystem from lua. This means themes and mod files can
re-write user data and extract files via USB profiles.

/rootfs was only added for internal use by the alsa, oss and memory card
drivers, so it can be easily replaced with direct fstream file access.

-	if( !IsADirectory("/rootfs/proc/asound/") )
+	struct stat st;
+	if (stat("/proc/asound/", &st) == -1 || !(st.st_mode & S_IFDIR))
 		return "/proc/asound/ does not exist";

code_evidence: LoadALSA gates ALSA loading on IsADirectory("/rootfs/proc/asound/"); the /rootfs prefix is a RageFile virtual mount exposing the entire host filesystem, so this check references a path that grants broad filesystem reachability rather than the real /proc/asound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function participates in exposing a critical resource (the whole root filesystem) through an overly broad mount/permission path, matching CWE-732's incorrect permission assignment allowing unintended actors access. It is not merely a missing authorization check, since the exposure stems from the /rootfs permission mapping.

return "/proc/asound/ does not exist";

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function depends on the /rootfs virtual root that maps the whole filesystem, giving Lua/themes/mod files access to arbitrary paths. Trigger: any caller reaching this path resolution can traverse beyond intended data. Supported consequence: unintended read/modify of user data; the patch replaces it with a direct stat("/proc/asound/") to remove that exposure.

commit_msg: Fixed issue where an index in qs_parse is incorrectly incremented beyond the maximum possible value
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["        if ( substr_ptr[j] == '\\0' ) {  break;  }", "    i++;  // x &'s -> means x iterations of this loop -> means *x+1* k/v pairs"], 'added_lines': ["        if ( substr_ptr[j] == '\\0' ) { i++; break;  } // x &'s -> means x iterations of this loop -> means *x+1* k/v pairs"]}
description: Crow before 1.0+4 has a heap-based buffer overflow via the function qs_parse in query_string.h. On successful exploitation this vulnerability allows attackers to remotely execute arbitrary code in the context of the vulnerable service.

code_evidence: The loop at [14] iterates while i<qs_kv_size, storing qs_kv[i] and advancing substr_ptr. At [18] the break occurs when the last token has no '&', leaving i at the current index. The unconditional i++ at [22] then increments i beyond the number of valid entries, so the decode loop at [23] reads qs_kv[i] one past the last populated slot (which may be NULL or out of the intended range).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes an index/count that is one greater than the correct maximum (the number of parsed key/value pairs), exactly matching CWE-193 (Off-by-one Error). The incorrect bound then drives an out-of-bounds read/write, distinguishing it from a generic buffer overflow whose root cause is a missing size check rather than an off-by-one miscalculation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the off-by-one increment at [22] makes i one larger than the count of stored key/value pointers. Trigger: a query string whose final token lacks a trailing '&' causes the early break at [18]. Consequence: the decode loop at [23] dereferences qs_kv[j] for the extra index, leading to out-of-bounds access and potential memory corruption (heap-based buffer overflow).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (!n_bucket || (1u<<31) <= n_bucket  /* fie on fuzzers */', '        || (void const *)&file_image[file_size] <= (void const *)hasharr) {', '            char msg[80]; snprintf(msg, sizeof(msg),', '                "bad n_bucket %#x\\n", n_bucket);', '            throwCantPack(msg);', '        }']}

commit_msg:
MDEV-26556 An improper locking bug(s) due to unreleased lock.

Get rid of the global big_buffer.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  flogger_mutex_init(key_LOCK_operations, &lock_bigbuffer, MY_MUTEX_INIT_FAST);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: MariaDB Server before 10.7 is vulnerable to Denial of Service. While executing the plugin/server_audit/server_audit.c method log_statement_ex, the held lock lock_bigbuffer is not released correctly, which allows local users to trigger a denial of service due to the deadlock.

code_evidence: server_audit_init initializes mutexes lock_operations, lock_atomic and lock_bigbuffer via flogger_mutex_init; the patch removes the lock_bigbuffer initialization at line 47, showing this function is where the shared big-buffer lock is set up. This function initializes the relevant mutex but contains no acquire/release logic, so it does not itself demonstrate improper locking; the evidence for the weakness lies in log_statement_ex, not here.

The deadlock described in the commit arises in a different function (log_statement_ex), where lock_bigbuffer is held without release. commit_msg:
Kafka: Be more strict when dissecting varints.

The Kafka dissector uses the return value of tvb_get_varint to advance
the packet offset in many places. If tvb_get_varint fails it returns 0,
which means our offset isn't guaranteed to advance. Stop dissection
whenever that happens. Fixes #17811.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["        //This will probably lead to a malformed packet, but it's better than not incrementing the offset", '        len = FT_VARINT_MAX_LEN;'], 'added_lines': ['        return tvb_captured_length(tvb);']}
description: Large loop in the Kafka dissector in Wireshark 3.6.0 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: Line 9 calls tvb_get_varint and stores the returned length in len; when the varint is malformed tvb_get_varint returns 0. Lines 14-16 detect len == 0, but instead of stopping, line 15 forces len = FT_VARINT_MAX_LEN and line 18 returns offset+len, so the caller's offset advances by a fixed amount even though no valid varint was consumed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits because the unsafe return value feeds a caller-controlled dissection loop that is not bounded when decoding fails, yielding unbounded iteration. The fix returns tvb_captured_length(tvb) to stop dissection; this is a loop-termination/iteration-limit issue, not merely an out-of-bounds read or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a failed varint decode (len == 0) is masked by substituting FT_VARINT_MAX_LEN, so the function always reports forward progress and the caller cannot detect the malformed length field. Trigger: an injected or crafted Kafka capture containing a truncated/invalid varint. Supported consequence: the outer dissector loop keeps advancing without terminating, causing excessive iteration and denial of service (CPU consumption).

commit_msg:
Add security vulnerability test for raw_ops.Conv2DBackpropInput

PiperOrigin-RevId: 463395218
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(', '        context, out_backprop.dims() == 4,', '        errors::InvalidArgument("input_sizes must be 4-dimensional, got: ",', '                                out_backprop.dims()));']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. The implementation of `Conv2DBackpropInput` requires `input_sizes` to be 4-dimensional. Otherwise, it gives a `CHECK` failure which can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 50156d547b9a1da0144d7babe665cf690305b33c. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The function reads input_sizes (input 0), filter (input 1) and out_backprop (input 2) directly from the op context without validating their ranks before passing their shapes into Conv2DBackpropComputeInputShape at [7,8,9]. This helper is where the 4-dimensional requirement on input_sizes is enforced via a CHECK-style assertion, so a caller-supplied non-4D input_sizes reaches the assertion unguarded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because an attacker-controlled tensor shape reaches a CHECK/assertion that terminates the process rather than producing a recoverable error. The missing graceful validation (OP_REQUIRES) is the cause; the reachable assertion crash is the impact, matching the Reachable Assertion description.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the op accepts an arbitrary-rank input_sizes tensor and forwards it to Conv2DBackpropComputeInputShape without an OP_REQUIRES rank check. Trigger: a user invokes Conv2DBackpropInput with an input_sizes tensor that is not 4-dimensional. Consequence: the downstream helper's CHECK fails, aborting the process (denial of service) instead of returning an InvalidArgument error.

commit_msg:
IOMMU: always call teardown callback

There is a possible scenario when (d)->need_iommu remains unset
during guest domain execution. For example, when no devices
were assigned to it. Taking into account that teardown callback
is not called when (d)->need_iommu is unset we might have unreleased
resourses after destroying domain.

So, always call teardown callback to roll back actions
that were performed in init callback.

This is XSA-207.

Signed-off-by: Oleksandr Tyshchenko <olekstysh@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Tested-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Tested-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( need_iommu(d) )', '        iommu_teardown(d);'], 'added_lines': ['    iommu_teardown(d);']}
description: Memory leak in Xen 3.3 through 4.8.x allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (ARM or x86 AMD host OS memory consumption) by continually rebooting, because certain cleanup is skipped if no pass-through device was ever assigned, aka XSA-207.

code_evidence: The destroy path only invokes iommu_teardown(d) when need_iommu(d) is true; when no pass-through device was ever assigned, need_iommu(d) is false and the teardown call is skipped entirely.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the function fails to release a resource after its effective lifetime (domain destruction) has ended, due solely to the need_iommu guard. This is a missing-release weakness, not a double-free or use-after-free; the consequence is resource-consumption DoS.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( need_iommu(d) )
iommu_teardown(d);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: cleanup of IOMMU resources is conditionally gated on need_iommu(d), but resources may have been allocated in the init callback even when that flag remains unset. Trigger: a guest domain is destroyed without ever having a device assigned. Consequence: iommu_teardown is never called, so resources allocated during domain initialization are not released, causing host memory consumption and DoS across repeated reboots.

Lines 221-223 locate the module Value= string and call sscanf with an unbounded %[^"] conversion that writes the entire matched text into io_data_object->moduleNameStr, with no width limit or capacity check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unbounded sscanf copy into an undersized heap buffer writes data past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. A related CWE-120 buffer overflow is the same mechanism at a different abstraction; the target's out-of-bounds write framing fits the write-past-end consequence directly.

evidence_lines.code: io_data_object->moduleNameStr = wmem_strdup(wmem_file_scope(), "Unknown");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: moduleNameStr is allocated far smaller than the GSDML-sourced module name that sscanf copies into it, and the conversion lacks a field width. Trigger: a parsed GSDML file whose module Name Value= attribute exceeds the small allocation causes sscanf to write past the buffer. Consequence: an out-of-bounds heap write, leading to memory corruption or a dissector crash.

commit_msg:
vhost: fix queue number check when setting inflight FD

In function vhost_user_set_inflight_fd, queue number in inflight
message is used to access virtqueue. However, queue number could
be larger than VHOST_MAX_VRING and cause write OOB as this number
will be used to write inflight info in virtqueue structure. This
patch checks the queue number to avoid the issue and also make
sure virtqueues are allocated before setting inflight information.

Fixes: ad0a4ae491fe ("vhost: checkout resubmit inflight information")
Cc: stable@dpdk.org

Reported-by: Wenxiang Qian <leonwxqian@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Chenbo Xia <chenbo.xia@intel.com>
Reviewed-by: Maxime Coquelin <maxime.coquelin@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcase VHOST_USER_SET_INFLIGHT_FD:', '\t\tvring_idx = ctx->msg.payload.inflight.num_queues - 1;', '\t\tbreak;']}
description: A flaw was found in the vhost library in DPDK. Function vhost_user_set_inflight_fd() does not validate `msg->payload.inflight.num_queues`, possibly causing out-of-bounds memory read/write. Any software using DPDK vhost library may crash as a result of this vulnerability.

code_evidence: vring_idx is declared uninitialized (line 5) and only assigned within switch cases; the default case returns before use. The added SET_INFLIGHT_FD case derives vring_idx from ctx->msg.payload.inflight.num_queues - 1, but this function's shown switch does not include that case, so it falls to default and returns 0. The bounds check vring_idx >= VHOST_MAX_VRING guards the index before alloc_vring_queue(dev, vring_idx), and dev->virtqueue[vring_idx] is indexed only after that check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 requires a write past a buffer boundary; the visible code enforces an upper bound before indexing, and the inflight queue number is not even handled in this switch. The function therefore does not directly support the out-of-bounds write weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The shown function validates vring_idx against VHOST_MAX_VRING and returns -1 on violation before using it to index dev->virtqueue or allocate a queue. No unvalidated attacker-controlled queue number reaches an array write in this function, so the described out-of-bounds write occurs in the inflight handling path, not here.

Fix security vulnerability with LRNGradOp

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. If `LRNGrad` is given an `output_image` input tensor that is not 4-D, it results in a `CHECK` fail that can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit bd90b3efab4ec958b228cd7cfe9125be1c0cf255. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: Only in_grads and in_image are required to be 4-D; out_image is not checked for rank before its dimensions are compared.
The OP_REQUIRES shape check accesses out_image.dim_size(0..3) but does not constrain out_image.dims() to 4, so a lower-rank out_image makes dim_size calls on missing dimensions fail.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits attacker-controlled input to reach a reachable CHECK/assertion that terminates the process, matching CWE-617's reachable assertion leading to DoS. The fix adds out_image.dims() == 4 to the guarded condition, confirming the missing rank constraint as the trigger.

OP_REQUIRES(context, in_grads.dims() == 4 && in_image.dims() == 4,
errors::InvalidArgument("inputs must be 4-dimensional"));

OP_REQUIRES(
context,
in_image.dim_size(0) == batch && in_image.dim_size(1) == rows &&
in_image.dim_size(2) == cols && in_image.dim_size(3) == depth &&
out_image.dim_size(0) == batch && out_image.dim_size(1) == rows &&
out_image.dim_size(2) == cols && out_image.dim_size(3) == depth,
errors::InvalidArgument(
"input_grads, input_image, and out_image should have the same "
"shape"));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the rank of out_image is unconstrained while its dimensions are queried. An attacker supplying a non-4-D output_image reaches a TensorFlow CHECK failure in dim_size rather than a graceful InvalidArgument, aborting the process and causing denial of service.

commit_msg: Bug 697193: status operator honour SAFER option
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                code = (*pname.iodev->procs.file_status)(pname.iodev,'], 'added_lines': ['                if ((code = check_file_permissions(i_ctx_p, pname.fname, pname.len,', '                                       "PermitFileReading")) >= 0) {', '                    code = (*pname.iodev->procs.file_status)(pname.iodev,', '                }']}
description: psi/zfile.c in Artifex Ghostscript before 9.21rc1 permits the status command even if -dSAFER is used, which might allow remote attackers to determine the existence and size of arbitrary files, a similar issue to CVE-2016-7977.

code_evidence: The t_string branch parses an arbitrary filename supplied by the PostScript operand op and, when parsing succeeds, proceeds to query the file.
After terminating the name, the code calls the device's file_status directly on pname.fname; there is no permission check gating this call before it occurs.
On code 0 the function pushes stat_blocks, st_size, st_mtime and st_ctime into the operand stack, exposing file metadata to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function discloses file metadata (existence, size, timestamps) to a caller not authorized to read that path, an explicit information-exposure behavior matching CWE-200. It is not merely a generic confidentiality impact of another flaw; the missing permission constraint on the status query is the direct cause of the exposure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the status operator invokes file_status on an attacker-chosen path without enforcing the PermitFileReading permission (SAFER). Trigger: a PostScript string operand naming an arbitrary file. When the file exists, the returned fstat data (size, timestamps, blocks) is pushed to the operand stack, letting an unauthorized actor infer existence and size of files outside the permitted set.

commit_msg:
Validate work in `QuantizedAdd`, ensure at least one element.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 370127996
Change-Id: I57c6f3e01afdeada84737820a131590137463855
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      OP_REQUIRES(context, vector_num_elements > 0,', '                  errors::InvalidArgument("Must have some elements to add"));']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can cause a runtime division by zero error and denial of service in `tf.raw_ops.QuantizedBatchNormWithGlobalNormalization`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/6f26b3f3418201479c264f2a02000880d8df151c/tensorflow/core/kernels/quantized_add_op.cc#L289-L295) computes a modulo operation without validating that the divisor is not zero. Since `vector_num_elements` is determined based on input shapes(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/6f26b3f3418201479c264f2a02000880d8df151c/tensorflow/core/kernels/quantized_add_op.cc#L522-L544), a user can trigger scenarios where this quantity is 0. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: In the ndims == 2 branch, vector_num_elements is assigned from x.NumElements() or y.NumElements() (lines 56-74) and passed directly to VectorTensorAddition (lines 75-78) without any check that it is greater than zero; the commit adds an OP_REQUIRES guard for vector_num_elements > 0 in the patched function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 (Divide By Zero) fits because the missing vector_num_elements > 0 constraint allows a zero divisor to flow into the addition helper, producing a runtime division-by-zero. This is a missing input-validation cause leading to an availability consequence, not a memory-safety issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the two-dimensional broadcast path derives vector_num_elements from user-controlled input shapes but never validates it is nonzero before invoking VectorTensorAddition. Trigger: an input whose vector-side tensor has zero elements (e.g., a dimension of 0) reaches this branch. Consequence: the downstream helper performs a modulo/division by vector_num_elements, causing a divide-by-zero crash and denial of service.

commit_msg: Fix crash when mapping a big memory and calling uc_close
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    uc->invalid_addr = UC_ERR_OK;', '', '    if (uc->invalid_error != UC_ERR_OK) {', '        g_free(new_block);', '        return NULL;', '    }']}
description: Unicorn Engine v2.0.0-rc7 and below was discovered to contain a NULL pointer dereference via qemu_ram_free.

code_evidence: new_block is allocated with g_malloc0 and checked for NULL, returning early, so the allocation path itself handles failure.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function returns a pointer whose validity is not guaranteed after ram_block_add, enabling a NULL/invalid pointer to reach later dereferences, consistent with CWE-476. This is a missing error-propagation issue rather than a direct in-function NULL dereference; the fix adds the missing check.

return new_block;

commit_msg:
Preserve GSS context on init/accept failure

After gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() has created a
context, don't delete the mechglue context on failures from subsequent
calls, even if the mechanism deletes the mech-specific context (which
is allowed by RFC 2744 but not preferred).  Check for union contexts
with no mechanism context in each GSS function which accepts a
gss_ctx_id_t.

CVE-2017-11462:

RFC 2744 permits a GSS-API implementation to delete an existing
security context on a second or subsequent call to
gss_init_sec_context() or gss_accept_sec_context() if the call results
in an error.  This API behavior has been found to be dangerous,
leading to the possibility of memory errors in some callers.  For
safety, GSS-API implementations should instead preserve existing
security contexts on error until the caller deletes them.

All versions of MIT krb5 prior to this change may delete acceptor
contexts on error.  Versions 1.13.4 through 1.13.7, 1.14.1 through
1.14.5, and 1.15 through 1.15.1 may also delete initiator contexts on
error.

commit_msg: Bug 703791: Stay within hash table max key size in cached color converter.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tassert(keylen <= MAX_KEY_LEN);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (keylen > FZ_HASH_TABLE_KEY_LENGTH)', '\t\tfz_throw(ctx, FZ_ERROR_GENERIC, "hash table key length too large");']}
description: MuPDF through 1.18.1 has an out-of-bounds write because the cached color converter does not properly consider the maximum key size of a hash table. This can, for example, be seen with crafted "mutool draw" input.

code_evidence: Line 5 constrains keylen only with assert(keylen <= MAX_KEY_LEN); assert is compiled out under NDEBUG, so no runtime check remains. Line 7 stores the caller-supplied keylen into table->keylen, which later governs key copying/hashing in the table.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked keylen propagates into hash-table operations that write past the intended fixed-size key buffer, matching CWE-787 (writing past the end of a buffer). It is not merely an assertion/logic issue because the supported consequence is memory corruption via out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the only guard on keylen is a debug-only assert, so in release builds an oversized key length from crafted input is accepted. Trigger: a caller passes keylen exceeding the hash table's fixed key field; table->keylen is then set to that value, and subsequent key storage/hashing writes beyond the fixed-size key buffer, an out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg: Bug 704834: Fix division by zero for zero width pages in muraster.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treps = (int)(max_band_memory / min_band_mem);', '\tif (reps < 1)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (min_band_mem > 0)', '\t\treps = (int)(max_band_memory / min_band_mem);', '\tif (min_band_mem == 0 || reps < 1)']}
description: A Floating point exception (division-by-zero) flaw was found in Mupdf for zero width pages in muraster.c. It is fixed in Mupdf-1.20.0-rc1 upstream.

code_evidence: Line 39 computes page width as x1-x0; for a zero-width page this is 0. Line 40 multiplies bpp*w*min_band_height, yielding min_band_mem == 0. Skip reordering dq-q patterns when the new quantization dimension is unknown.

It also adds the canonicalization patterns to remove redundant TF reshape ops
to infer the quantization dimension from the user ops (e.g, conv2d, depthwise
conv2d) over those redundant TF reshape ops.

Only if the new quantization dimension can', '    // be inferred, it is safe to reset the per-axis quantized type.', '    if (axis == -1) return {};']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. When converting transposed convolutions using per-channel weight quantization the converter segfaults and crashes the Python process. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit aa0b852a4588cea4d36b74feb05d93055540b450. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: When the source element type is a UniformQuantizedPerAxisType, the function calls ResetAxisAndBroadcast using the caller-supplied axis value without first confirming that axis is a valid, known quantization dimension; the patch adds an axis == -1 guard before this call.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an axis input that must satisfy a precondition (a known, valid dimension) but processes it without checking for the sentinel invalid value, matching CWE-20 improper input validation. The added axis == -1 guard confirms the missing validation; this is not a mere transformation error but a missing precondition check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the axis parameter (unknown quantization dimension, represented as -1 for pass-through ops) is passed into ResetAxisAndBroadcast without validation. Trigger: a per-axis quantized source whose new quantization dimension cannot be inferred. Consequence: the axis is used to reset axis/broadcast metadata, leading to invalid per-axis type computation and a downstream crash (segfault).

description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: canRunJavaCode/throwException gate resolution; when JIT compile-time or redefinition flags are set, line 15-16 returns NULL without resolving, so the handle is never produced.

MH_REF_INVOKESTATIC calls resolveStaticMethodRef with the caller's resolveFlags; if those flags suppress class initialization, the static method's class initializer is not run before the method handle is built.

sendResolveMethodHandle constructs the method handle from definingClass and nameAndSig after resolution; if initialization was skipped, the handle can target an uninitialized class, exposing default/uninitialized static values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-909 fits because the class-initialization step, a required initialization of the class resource, is skipped before the static method handle is usable. This is missing initialization of a critical resource rather than a simple NULL dereference; the defect is the absent <clinit> constraint, not the resulting exception.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: resolution paths pass through resolveFlags that suppress class initialization, and the handle is created without verifying the target class was initialized. Trigger: a caller using resolveFlags such as JIT-compile-time or no-init flags on an INVOKESTATIC method handle reference. Consequence: invoking the handle reaches static members before <clinit> runs, exposing uninitialized values or causing inconsistent state.

commit_msg:
The syzkaller USB fuzzer found a general-protection-fault bug in the
yurex driver.  The fault occurs when a device has been unplugged; the
driver's interrupt-URB handler logs an error message referring to the
device by name, after the device has been unregistered and its name
deallocated.

This problem is caused by the fact that the interrupt URB isn't
cancelled until the driver's private data structure is released, which
can happen long after the device is gone.  The cure is to make sure
that the interrupt URB is killed before yurex_disconnect() returns;
this is exactly the sort of thing that usb_poison_urb() was meant for.

Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+2eb9121678bdb36e6d57@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tusb_poison_urb(dev->urb);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.14. There is a NULL pointer dereference caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/usb/misc/yurex.c driver.

code_evidence: disconnect takes dev from interface data and clears the interface pointer under io_mutex, but does not cancel dev->urb before returning.

The interrupt URB remains active; its completion handler can still run and dereference dev/interface state after disconnect, leading to a NULL dereference. The fix adds usb_poison_urb(dev->urb) to stop the URB before teardown.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unsafe teardown leaves an active URB that can dereference cleared pointers, matching CWE-476. The added usb_poison_urb confirms the missing cancellation constraint.

evidence_lines.code: kref_put(&dev->kref, yurex_delete);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the interrupt URB is not killed in yurex_disconnect, so the URB completion handler can execute after the device is unregistered and interface/name data is cleared. Trigger: unplugging a malicious USB device while the URB is in flight. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and possible crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
MS-MMS: Use format_text_string()

The length of a string transcoded from UTF-16 to UTF-8 can be
shorter (or longer) than the original length in bytes in the packet.
Use the new string length, not the original length.

Use format_text_string, which is a convenience function that
calls strlen.

Fix #19086

description: Due to failure in validating the length provided by an attacker-crafted MSMMS packet, Wireshark version 4.0.5 and prior, in an unusual configuration, is susceptible to a heap-based buffer overflow, and possibly code execution in the context of the process running Wireshark

code_evidence: Line 16 transcodes length_remaining-20 bytes of UTF-16 into a newly allocated UTF-8 string transport_info, whose actual byte length can differ from the input byte count. Lines 20-21 then call format_text with the original length_remaining-20 as the length, telling it to read that many bytes from transport_info even though the transcoded buffer may be shorter.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a length mismatch between the allocated transcoded buffer and the length used to access it, an out-of-bounds memory access rooted in using a stale, packet-derived length. The patch replaces it with format_text_string, which derives length via strlen, directly confirming the length-validation flaw that CWE-787 captures for out-of-bounds memory operations.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code passes the packet-derived input length (length_remaining-20) to format_text instead of the length of the transcoded UTF-8 string. Trigger: a crafted MSMMS packet whose UTF-16 payload shrinks when transcoded to UTF-8, so the actual buffer is smaller than the claimed length. commit_msg:
infiniband: fix a possible use-after-free bug

ucma_process_join() will free the new allocated "mc" struct,
if there is any error after that, especially the copy_to_user().

But in parallel, ucma_leave_multicast() could find this "mc"
through idr_find() before ucma_process_join() frees it, since it
is already published.

So "mc" could be used in ucma_leave_multicast() after it is been
allocated and freed in ucma_process_join(), since we don't refcnt
it.

Fix this by separating "publish" from ID allocation, so that we
can get an ID first and publish it later after copy_to_user().

Fixes: c8f6a362bf3e ("RDMA/cma: Add multicast communication support")
Reported-by: Noam Rathaus <noamr@beyondsecurity.com>
Signed-off-by: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@mellanox.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmc->id = idr_alloc(&multicast_idr, mc, 0, 0, GFP_KERNEL);'], 'added_lines': ['\tmc->id = idr_alloc(&multicast_idr, NULL, 0, 0, GFP_KERNEL);']}
description: drivers/infiniband/core/ucma.c in the Linux kernel through 4.17.11 allows ucma_leave_multicast to access a certain data structure after a cleanup step in ucma_process_join, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free).

code_evidence: ucma_alloc_multicast allocates mc with kzalloc (line 4) and immediately publishes it into the global multicast_idr via idr_alloc(&multicast_idr, mc, ...) under mutex (lines 7-9). After publication, the function returns mc (line 14) or, on idr_alloc failure, jumps to error: and kfree(mc) (lines 15-17). Because the object is reachable through idr_find before the caller finishes its own error handling (e.g., copy_to_user in ucma_process_join), a concurrent ucma_leave_multicast can obtain and use mc while or after it is freed; no refcount protects the published object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function publishes a heap object into a shared lookup table and later frees it without ensuring no other thread holds a reference, so another path can dereference freed memory. This is a direct instance of CWE-416 (Use After Free), not merely a memory leak or double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mc object is inserted into the shared idr before the caller's later operations can fail, and there is no reference counting to keep it alive. Trigger: a concurrent lookup via ucma_leave_multicast races with allocation failure or the caller's error path that frees mc. Supported consequence: use-after-free of mc, leading to memory corruption or denial of service.

commit_msg:
x86/mm: alloc/free_lN_table: Retain partial_flags on -EINTR

When validating or de-validating pages (in alloc_lN_table and
free_lN_table respectively), the `partial_flags` local variable is
used to keep track of whether the "current" PTE started the entire
operation in a "may be partial" state.

One of the patches in XSA-299 addressed the fact that it is possible
for a previously-partially-validated entry to subsequently be found to
have invalid entries (indicated by returning -EINVAL); in which case
page->partial_flags needs to be set to indicate that the current PTE
may have the partial bit set (and thus _put_page_type() should be
called with PTF_partial_set).

Unfortunately, the patches in XSA-299 assumed that once
put_page_from_lNe() returned -ERESTART on a page, it was not possible
for it to return -EINTR.  This turns out to be true for
alloc_lN_table() and free_lN_table, but not for _get_page_type() and
_put_page_type(): both can return -EINTR when called on pages with
PGT_partial set.  In these cases, the pages PGT_partial will still be
set; failing to set partial_flags appropriately may allow an attacker
to do a privilege escalation similar to those described in XSA-299.

Fix this by always copying the local partial_flags variable into
page->partial_flags when exiting early.

NB that on the "get" side, no adjustment to nr_validated_entries is
needed: whether pte[i] is partially validated or entirely
un-validated, we want nr_validated_entries = i.  On the "put" side,
however, we need to adjust nr_validated_entries appropriately: if
pte[i] is entirely validated, we want nr_validated_entries = i + 1; if
pte[i] is partially validated, we want nr_validated_entries = i.

This is part of XSA-310.

Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        page->nr_validated_ptes = i + 1;', '        page->partial_flags = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['        page->nr_validated_ptes = i + !(partial_flags & PTF_partial_set);', '        page->partial_flags = partial_flags;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to gain host OS privileges by leveraging race conditions in pagetable promotion and demotion operations, because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2019-18421. XSA-299 addressed several critical issues in restartable PV type change operations. Despite extensive testing and auditing, some corner cases were missed. A malicious PV guest administrator may be able to escalate their privilege to that of the host. All security-supported versions of Xen are vulnerable. Only x86 systems are affected. Arm systems are not affected. Only x86 PV guests can leverage the vulnerability. x86 HVM and PVH guests cannot leverage the vulnerability. Note that these attacks require very precise timing, which may be difficult to exploit in practice.

code_evidence: The -EINTR early-exit branch at lines 32-36 resets page->partial_flags to 0 and sets nr_validated_ptes to i+1, discarding the local partial_flags captured at line 7.

The loop at lines 12-15 calls put_page_from_l3e with partial_flags and clears it after the first iteration, so the retained state matters when the hypercall is preempted at line 22 with a partially validated PTE.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's failure to preserve shared page state across a preemption window lets an interfering concurrent pagetable operation observe inconsistent partial/nr_validated state, matching CWE-362's non-atomic shared-resource update. The defect is an incomplete synchronization/state-retention fix rather than a pure logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that on a preemptible -EINTR return the function unconditionally clears page->partial_flags and advances nr_validated_ptes, losing the PGT_partial state of the current PTE. A later resumption or concurrent pagetable operation then operates on a PTE whose partial state no longer matches, allowing type-change bookkeeping to be desynchronized and enabling privilege escalation as in XSA-299/XSA-310.

Bug 763071: heap-buffer-overflow in xmlStrncat <https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=763071>

* xmlstring.c:
(xmlStrncat): Return NULL if xmlStrlen returns a negative length.
(xmlStrncatNew): Ditto.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (len < 0)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (len < 0) {', '        if (len < 0)', '            return(NULL);', '    }', '    if (size < 0)', '        return(NULL);']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the xmlStrncat function in libxml2 before 2.9.4, as used in Apple iOS before 9.3.2, OS X before 10.11.5, tvOS before 9.2.1, and watchOS before 2.2.1, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted XML document.

code_evidence: When len is negative, it is replaced by xmlStrlen(str2) without checking whether that result is negative; the fixed code adds a check returning NULL here.
size = xmlStrlen(str1) is used directly as the left-copy length; the fixed code adds a size < 0 guard before allocation.

The allocation size (size + len + 1) and the subsequent memcpy calls of size and len bytes rely on non-negative lengths; a negative size or len makes the size arithmetic and copies inconsistent with the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs memcpy writes into an allocated buffer using lengths that can be negative, so it writes outside the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The defect is specifically an out-of-bounds write rather than an integer-only or NULL-dereference issue.

evidence_lines.code:
if (len < 0)
len = xmlStrlen(str2);

size = xmlStrlen(str1);
ret = (xmlChar *) xmlMalloc((size + len + 1) * sizeof(xmlChar));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: xmlStrlen can return a negative value, and the function uses that value as a length in size+len+1 allocation arithmetic and in memcpy bounds. Trigger: a crafted XML string reaching xmlStrncatNew with a negative computed length. Consequence: the allocated buffer is smaller than the copied region, producing a heap-buffer-overflow write that can corrupt memory and enable code execution or crash.

description: singlevar in lparser.c in Lua from (including) 5.4.0 up to (excluding) 5.4.4 lacks a certain luaK_exp2anyregup call, leading to a heap-based buffer over-read that might affect a system that compiles untrusted Lua code.

code_evidence: singlevaraux resolves the _ENV variable into var, and the code only asserts var->k != VVOID before passing var directly to luaK_indexed. There is no luaK_exp2anyregup call to force a constant _ENV (e.g. <const>) into a register, so var may still be a constant-kind expression when luaK_indexed treats it as an indexable register-based value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing register conversion lets luaK_indexed operate on a constant expression and read past the intended buffer during code generation. This is an out-of-bounds read, not merely incorrect code emission; the wrong code is the observable symptom of the out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the resolved environment expression is not converted to a register (missing luaK_exp2anyregup), so a constant _ENV reaches luaK_indexed. Trigger: compiling untrusted Lua code where _ENV is declared <const>. Consequence: downstream register/constant handling reads beyond the intended buffer (heap-based out-of-bounds read), affecting the compiling system.

In order to avoid it, let's set the cached value of the firmware
name to NULL after freeing it. While here, return an error if

Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@osg.samsung.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\trc = -ENOMEM;'], 'added_lines': ['\tpriv->ctrl.fname = NULL;', '\t\t\treturn -ENOMEM;']}
description: The xc2028_set_config function in drivers/media/tuners/tuner-xc2028.c in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) via vectors involving omission of the firmware name from a certain data structure.

code_evidence: Line 8 frees priv->ctrl.fname but does not clear the pointer. Line 9 then overwrites priv->ctrl with memcpy from p. If p->fname is NULL, the block at lines 10-14 is skipped, so priv->ctrl.fname retains the stale freed pointer from the memcpy, and later code (e.g., line 22 priv->fname = priv->ctrl.fname, and line 16 strcmp against priv->fname) references freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function retains and later dereferences a pointer to memory freed at line 8. Contrast with CWE-476 (NULL pointer dereference): here the pointer is non-NULL but dangling, so use-after-free is the precise weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the freed fname pointer is copied into priv->ctrl without being reset, and when the caller supplies no firmware name the pointer is left dangling. Trigger: xc2028_config passed with p->fname == NULL. Consequence: subsequent strcmp/firmware use dereferences freed memory, producing a use-after-free (KASAN strcmp report), enabling DoS or potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
protect dwg_obj_block_control_get_block_headers

from empty ctrl->block_headers. Fixes [GH #32]
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      if (ctrl->num_entries && !ctrl->block_headers)', '        {', '          *error = 1;', '          LOG_ERROR("%s: null block_headers", __FUNCTION__);', '          return NULL;', '        }']}
description: dwg_obj_block_control_get_block_headers in dwg_api.c in GNU LibreDWG 0.5.1048 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and SEGV) via a crafted dwg file.

code_evidence: The function allocates ptx based on ctrl->num_entries but never checks whether ctrl->block_headers is non-NULL before the loop.
Inside the loop, each iteration reads ctrl->block_headers[i]; when block_headers is NULL while num_entries is nonzero, this dereferences a NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the loop directly reads through ctrl->block_headers[i] without a NULL check, and the patch adds exactly that guard. This is a direct NULL dereference, not an out-of-bounds read or unchecked malloc failure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing validation that ctrl->block_headers is non-NULL while ctrl->num_entries is positive. A crafted dwg file yielding a control object with entries but no block_headers array triggers the loop, causing a NULL pointer dereference and crash (SEGV), a denial of service.

commit_msg:
misc: fastrpc: prevent memory leak in fastrpc_dma_buf_attach

In fastrpc_dma_buf_attach if dma_get_sgtable fails the allocated memory
for a should be released.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20190925152742.16258-1-navid.emamdoost@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tkfree(a);']}
description: A memory leak in the fastrpc_dma_buf_attach() function in drivers/misc/fastrpc.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.9 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering dma_get_sgtable() failures, aka CID-fc739a058d99.

code_evidence: Line 7 allocates a heap object with kzalloc and stores the only pointer in local variable a; lines 8-9 return early only when allocation failed.
Lines 10-11 call dma_get_sgtable using a->sgt; when ret < 0, lines 12-14 log the error and return -EINVAL without freeing a, losing the sole reference to the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits: allocated memory is not released after its effective lifetime on an error path, and the pointer is lost. This is a memory leak, not a use-after-free (CWE-416), since the object is never accessed again after the failed return.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: On the error path where dma_get_sgtable fails, the kzalloc'd attachment object a is never released before returning, so the allocation becomes unreachable. Repeated triggering of this failure leaks memory, leading to resource consumption/DoS as described; the cause is the missing free, not the DMA failure itself.

commit_msg:
Avoid a double-free when a window size of 0 is specified

new_size can be 0 with a malicious or corrupted RAR archive.

realloc(area, 0) is equivalent to free(area), so the region would
be free()d here and the free()d again in the cleanup function.

Found with a setup running AFL, afl-rb, and qsym.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (new_size == 0) {', '      archive_set_error(&a->archive, ARCHIVE_ERRNO_FILE_FORMAT,', '                        "Zero window size is invalid.");', '      return (ARCHIVE_FATAL);', '    }']}
description: libarchive version commit 416694915449219d505531b1096384f3237dd6cc onwards (release v3.1.0 onwards) contains a CWE-415: Double Free vulnerability in RAR decoder - libarchive/archive_read_support_format_rar.c, parse_codes(), realloc(rar->lzss.window, new_size) with new_size = 0 that can result in Crash/DoS. This attack appear to be exploitable via the victim must open a specially crafted RAR archive.

code_evidence: free_codes(a) is called at the start of parse_codes, releasing rar->lzss.window and related state. Later, when the dictionary is absent, new_size is derived from rar->unp_size; for a malicious archive with unp_size 0, rar_fls(0) << 1 yields 0, and realloc(rar->lzss.window, 0) is passed as new_window. On success the result is stored back into rar->lzss.window, and the cleanup path later frees it again.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits the same allocation to be freed twice: realloc(area, 0) frees the region, and the region is later freed in cleanup. This directly matches CWE-415 (Double Free), distinct from a simple use-after-free or memory leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code does not reject new_size == 0 before calling realloc, which frees the existing window and returns a value that may be treated as a valid allocation. Trigger: a crafted RAR archive causing rar->unp_size to be 0. Consequence: the same region is freed again during cleanup, producing a double free and crash/DoS, with potential memory corruption.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: make sure e->next_offset covers remaining blob size

Otherwise this function may read data beyond the ruleset blob.

Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    (unsigned char *)e + sizeof(struct compat_arpt_entry) >= limit) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t    (unsigned char *)e + sizeof(struct compat_arpt_entry) >= limit ||', '\t    (unsigned char *)e + e->next_offset > limit) {']}
description: The IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt implementation in the netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) or possibly obtain sensitive information from kernel heap memory by leveraging in-container root access to provide a crafted offset value that leads to crossing a ruleset blob boundary.

code_evidence: The bounds check only validates that the fixed-size compat_arpt_entry header (e + sizeof(struct compat_arpt_entry)) stays below limit; it never validates that the variable-length entry described by e->next_offset stays within limit.
The next_offset sanity check only enforces a minimum size; it does not ensure e + e->next_offset <= limit, so an attacker-controlled next_offset can point past the ruleset blob.
compat_arpt_get_target(e) then dereferences the target located via the unchecked entry extent, and xt_request_find_target reads t->u.user.name/revision beyond the blob.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory outside the intended ruleset-blob buffer boundary because the offset constraint is missing, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. This is a missing upper-bound check leading to OOB read, not merely an integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the entry-size validation omits an upper bound on e->next_offset relative to limit. Trigger: a local root supplies a crafted compat ruleset via IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE where next_offset extends past the blob. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads of kernel heap memory when the target name/revision are accessed, causing DoS or information disclosure.

commit_msg:
[bug] Fix integer overflow

Fixes issue #510.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '        if (hdrSize > (uint64_t)1 << 61)', '            break;']}
description: An integer overflow in DTSStreamReader::findFrame() of tsMuxer git-2678966 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 7 computes hdrSize from an untrusted 64-bit field plus 16, which can wrap to a small value; the subsequent checks at lines 12-13 and 17-19 compare this wrapped value against the remaining buffer and then advance buff by it, so a crafted DTS file can steer pointer arithmetic with an inconsistent size.
The added guard at lines 7/12/17 constrains hdrSize before use, confirming the pre-patch absence of a bound check on the attacker-controlled length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer overflow in a size calculation feeding pointer offset logic, matching CWE-190. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); the overflowed size is the root cause that defeats the length validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: hdrSize = my_ntohll(ptr[1]) + 16 can overflow for a crafted header size, producing a small value. Trigger: a malicious DTS file with a near-maximum size field. Consequence: the buffer-bound checks pass against the wrapped value and buff advances incorrectly, enabling out-of-bounds access and a denial of service (crash).

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow vulnerability in util/read.c.

This vulnerability is caused by a regression introduced in
d468907.

In this commit we cast the result of readUInt8(f) before left
shifting by 24 in order to avoid out of range shift.

This commit fixes CVE-2018-5251 (fixes #98).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  result |= readUInt8(f) << 24;'], 'added_lines': ['  result |= (long) readUInt8(f) << 24;']}
description: In libming 0.4.8, there is an integer overflow (caused by an out-of-range left shift) in the readUInt32 function (util/read.c). Remote attackers could leverage this vulnerability to cause a denial-of-service via a crafted swf file.

code_evidence: readSInt32 builds a 32-bit value in a long accumulator by OR-ing bytes shifted left by 0, 8, 16 and 24. At line 7 the byte from readUInt8(f) is shifted left by 24 without a prior widening cast, so the shift is performed on the byte's (int) type.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an arithmetic calculation whose intermediate result exceeds the range of the operand type, matching CWE-190 integer overflow/wraparound. The patch's cast to long before shifting confirms the missing widening constraint; this is not a buffer issue or mere truncation of the final value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the left shift by 24 is applied to a value that is not widened before shifting, so the high byte can produce an out-of-range shift/overflow instead of contributing correctly to the 32-bit result. Trigger: a crafted SWF file whose fourth byte has the high bit or otherwise large value reaches readSInt32 via readUInt8. Consequence: incorrect or undefined signed value, leading to denial of service in libming.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.6 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.12, the Bluetooth L2CAP dissector could divide by zero. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-btl2cap.c by validating an interval value.

commit_msg:
Restrict following symlinks to directories by ownership (CVE-2017-7500)

Only follow directory symlinks owned by target directory owner or root.
This prevents privilege escalation from user-writable directories via
directory symlinks to privileged directories on package upgrade, while
still allowing admin to arrange disk usage with symlinks.

The rationale is that if you can create symlinks owned by user X you *are*
user X (or root), and if you also own directory Y you can do whatever with
it already, including change permissions. So when you create a symlink to
that directory, the link ownership acts as a simple stamp of authority that
you indeed want rpm to treat this symlink as it were the directory that
you own. Such a permission can only be given by you or root, which
is just the way we want it. Plus it's almost ridiculously simple as far
as rules go, compared to trying to calculate something from the
source vs destination directory permissions etc.

In the normal case, the user arranging diskspace with symlinks is indeed
root so nothing changes, the only real change here is to links created by
non-privileged users which should be few and far between in practise.
Unfortunately our test-suite runs as a regular user via fakechroot and
thus the testcase for this fails under the new rules. Adjust the testcase
to get the ownership straight and add a second case for the illegal
behavior, basically the same as the old one but with different expectations.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\trc = fsmVerify(fpath, fi);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\trc = fsmVerify(fpath, fi, &sb);']}
description: It was found that rpm did not properly handle RPM installations when a destination path was a symbolic link to a directory, possibly changing ownership and permissions of an arbitrary directory, and RPM files being placed in an arbitrary destination. An attacker, with write access to a directory in which a subdirectory will be installed, could redirect that directory to an arbitrary location and gain root privilege.

code_evidence: When the entry is a directory (suffix NULL), the code computes fpath from the archive entry and calls fsmVerify(fpath, fi) to check the existing path before deciding whether to create or modify it.
The action and path are derived from rpmfiStat metadata and fsmFsPath, without verifying whether fpath resolves through a symlink to a directory owned by an untrusted user.
On success, fsmSetmeta(fpath, fi, ...) applies ownership and mode to the resolved path, so a pre-existing directory symlink redirects these operations to an attacker-chosen location.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses files by pathname without preventing a directory symlink from resolving to an unintended resource, matching CWE-59's improper link resolution before file access. The fix passes the stat buffer to fsmVerify to enforce ownership checks, confirming the weakness is link following rather than a generic permission bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fsmVerify and the subsequent metadata application operate on a path whose directory component may be a symlink, and ownership of that symlink is not checked against the target directory owner. Trigger: an attacker with write access to a parent directory places a directory symlink at an install destination. Consequence: RPM follows the link and changes ownership/permissions or writes files in a privileged directory, enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fixed Error() instance dumping when "name" prop is not primitive.

Previously, njs_error_to_string2() might be invoked with error argument
pointing to vm->retval.  When "name" prop was not primitive vm->retval
might be overwritten.  As a result error pointer might be referencing a
primitive value.  In turn the second call of njs_object_property()
received an invalid object pointer because it expects only object value
types.

The fix is to ensure that error object pointer is never overwritten.

This closes #615 issue on Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (njs_is_object(&args[0])) {', '        ret = njs_object_property(vm, &args[0], &lhq, &value);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (njs_is_object(njs_argument(args, 0))) {', '        ret = njs_object_property(vm, njs_object(njs_argument(args, 0)), &lhq,', '                                  &value);']}
description: Nginx NJS v0.7.10 was discovered to contain a segmentation violation via the function njs_lvlhsh_find at src/njs_lvlhsh.c.

code_evidence: The function checks njs_is_object(&args[0]) and then passes &args[0] directly to njs_object_property(). The value is not unwrapped via njs_argument()/njs_object(), so if the argument is a non-primitive object whose property resolution overwrites vm->retval, the args pointer may reference a primitive value; the subsequent njs_object_property() then treats it as an object and reads past the intended value buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the invalid object pointer causes reads beyond the intended buffer during hash lookup, matching out-of-bounds read. This is not merely a null dereference or type confusion; the observable impact is reading past a buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the object pointer passed to njs_object_property() is not stabilized against overwriting of vm->retval, so a later property lookup receives an invalid object pointer. Trigger: calling toJSON on an object with a non-primitive 'name' property that mutates retval. Consequence: out-of-bounds read (segmentation violation in njs_lvlhsh_find).

commit_msg:
Check that a secondary auth manager is set before dereferencing.

Summary: CVE-2018-6343

Reviewed By: mingtaoy

Differential Revision: D12994423

fbshipit-source-id: 9229ec11da8085f1fa153595e8e5353e19d06fb7
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  if (!secondAuthManager_) {', '    return;', '  }']}
description: Proxygen fails to validate that a secondary auth manager is set before dereferencing it. That can cause a denial of service issue when parsing a Certificate/CertificateRequest HTTP2 Frame over a fizz (TLS 1.3) transport. This issue affects Proxygen releases starting from v2018.10.29.00 until the fix in v2018.11.19.00.

code_evidence: After obtaining fizzBase, the function calls secondAuthManager_->validateAuthenticator(...) on both the upstream branch (line 9) and downstream branch (line 15) without first checking that secondAuthManager_ is non-null. The authenticator input from the peer is only processed inside the fizzBase branch, so the dereference is reached whenever a Certificate frame is handled over a fizz transport.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts peer-supplied Certificate frame data and processes it without validating the required precondition (a configured auth manager) before use, matching CWE-20's improper validation of input/precondition leading to availability impact. The fix adds the missing guard, confirming the absent validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes a secondary auth manager is configured and dereferences secondAuthManager_ unconditionally. Trigger: an attacker sends a Certificate/CertificateRequest HTTP2 frame over a fizz (TLS 1.3) transport while no secondary auth manager is set. The null dereference crashes the process, causing a denial of service.

commit_msg:
x86/grant: disallow misaligned PTEs

Pagetable entries must be aligned to function correctly.  Disallow attempts
from the guest to have a grant PTE created at a misaligned address, which
would result in corruption of the L1 table with largely-guest-controlled
values.

This is CVE-2017-12137 / XSA-227.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    /*', "     * addr comes from Xen's active_entry tracking so isn't guest controlled,", '     * but it had still better be PTE-aligned.', '     */', '    if ( !IS_ALIGNED(addr, sizeof(ol1e)) )', '    {', '        ASSERT_UNREACHABLE();', '        return GNTST_general_error;', '    }']}
description: arch/x86/mm.c in Xen allows local PV guest OS users to gain host OS privileges via vectors related to map_grant_ref.

code_evidence: addr is shifted to a gfn and mapped, then offset by addr & ~PAGE_MASK to form va (lines 9,10,18). The PTE is read at line 30 and rewritten via UPDATE_ENTRY at lines 40-41 using that va. Without alignment, va may not point to a valid PTE slot, so the write targets an out-of-bounds location within the mapped L1 page.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the PTE update writes to a destination computed from addr without checking that the destination has room for a full l1_pgentry_t, yielding an out-of-bounds write. This is a size/alignment check omission leading to a buffer overwrite, not merely an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the PTE write address derived from addr is not validated for alignment, so a misaligned addr produces a va that is not PTE-aligned. Trigger: a guest-controlled grant PTE address that is not sizeof(l1_pgentry_t)-aligned. Consequence: UPDATE_ENTRY writes a largely guest-controlled value past the intended PTE slot, corrupting the L1 page table and enabling host privilege escalation.

commit_msg: Fix #9727 - Null terminate mach0 classes to avoid this oobread
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\ttype[left - 1] = 0;']}
description: In radare2 2.4.0, there is a heap-based buffer over-read in the get_ivar_list_t function of mach0_classes.c. Remote attackers could leverage this vulnerability to cause a denial of service via a crafted Mach-O file.

code_evidence: Lines 145-146 allocate a buffer of exactly `left` bytes via calloc and read `left` attacker-controlled bytes into it from the Mach-O file (r_buf_read_at), with no guarantee the data contains a NUL terminator.
Line 148 then passes the non-terminated `type` buffer to strdup, which scans for a NUL byte; if none exists within `left` bytes it reads past the end of the heap allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe operation is a read past the end of an intended buffer: strdup's unbounded NUL scan overruns the `left`-sized allocation. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.

evidence_lines.code: field->type = strdup (type);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the type string is copied with a length-bounded read into a buffer sized exactly to `left`, but is then treated as a C string. Trigger: a crafted Mach-O ivar type field containing no NUL byte. Consequence: strdup reads beyond the allocated heap block, causing an out-of-bounds read (DoS/crash and potential info exposure).

commit_msg:
polkit: when authorizing via PK let's re-resolve callback/userdata instead of caching it

Previously, when doing an async PK query we'd store the original
callback/userdata pair and call it again after the PK request is
complete. This is problematic, since PK queries might be slow and in the
meantime the userdata might be released and re-acquired. Let's avoid
this by always traversing through the message handlers so that we always
re-resolve the callback and userdata pair and thus can be sure it's
up-to-date and properly valid.

description: A heap use-after-free vulnerability was found in systemd before version v245-rc1, where asynchronous Polkit queries are performed while handling dbus messages. A local unprivileged attacker can abuse this flaw to crash systemd services or potentially execute code and elevate their privileges, by sending specially crafted dbus messages.

code_evidence: After the asynchronous Polkit reply arrives, the stored q->callback and q->userdata are invoked directly: r = q->callback(q->request, q->userdata, ...). The callback pointer and userdata were captured earlier and cached in the AsyncPolkitQuery q; they are not re-resolved through the message handlers. Since Polkit queries can be slow, the original userdata may have been released and re-acquired by the time this runs, so the cached pair can reference freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function dereferences q->userdata (and invokes q->callback) after the referenced data may already have been freed during the asynchronous wait. This is a temporal memory-safety flaw, not merely a stale-logic or NULL-dereference issue; the fix re-enqueues the message to re-resolve the callback/userdata rather than reusing the cached pointers.

evidence_lines.code:
r = q->callback(q->request, q->userdata, &error_buffer);
r = bus_maybe_reply_error(q->request, r, &error_buffer);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the async query caches the callback/userdata pair and reuses it after a slow Polkit round-trip instead of re-resolving it. Trigger: a local attacker sends crafted D-Bus messages that cause the userdata to be released while the Polkit query is outstanding. Consequence: q->callback dereferences the stale userdata, yielding a use-after-free that can crash systemd services or potentially enable code execution and privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
x86/spec-ctrl: Add spec-ctrl=unpriv-mmio

Per Xen's support statement, PCI passthrough should be to trusted domains
because the overall system security depends on factors outside of Xen's
control.

As such, Xen, in a supported configuration, is not vulnerable to DRPW/SBDR.

However, users who have risk assessed their configuration may be happy with
the risk of DoS, but unhappy with the risk of cross-domain data leakage.  Such
users should enable this option.

On CPUs vulnerable to MDS, the existing mitigations are the best we can do to
mitigate MMIO cross-domain data leakage.

On CPUs fixed to MDS but vulnerable MMIO stale data leakage, this option:

 * On CPUs susceptible to FBSDP, mitigates cross-domain fill buffer leakage
   using FB_CLEAR.
 * On CPUs susceptible to SBDR, mitigates RNG data recovery by engaging the
   srb-lock, previously used to mitigate SRBDS.

Both mitigations require microcode from IPU 2022.1, May 2022.

This is part of XSA-404.

Reviewed-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>

description: An issue was discovered in tnef before 1.4.13. Several Integer Overflows, which can lead to Heap Overflows, have been identified in the functions that wrap memory allocation.

code_evidence: Line 4 computes num*size inside alloc_limit_assert without any overflow check; line 5 then passes the same num and size to xcalloc, so the guard's product and the allocation are decoupled from any validated size.

return xcalloc (num, size);
