Trigger: caller supplies large num and size whose product exceeds SIZE_MAX. Supported consequence: the limit guard is bypassed, permitting excessive or inconsistent allocation behavior that the wrapper was meant to prevent.

commit_msg:
When huang uses sched_switch tracepoint, the tracepoint
does only one thing in the mounted ebpf program, which
deletes the fixed elements in sockhash ([0])

It seems that elements in sockhash are rarely actively
deleted by users or ebpf program. Therefore, we do not
pay much attention to their deletion. Compared with hash
maps, sockhash only provides spin_lock_bh protection.
This causes it to appear to have self-locking behavior
in the interrupt context.

  [0]:https://lore.kernel.org/all/CABcoxUayum5oOqFMMqAeWuS8+EzojquSOSyDA3J_2omY=2EeAg@mail.gmail.com/

Reported-by: Hsin-Wei Hung <hsinweih@uci.edu>
Fixes: 604326b41a6f ("bpf, sockmap: convert to generic sk_msg interface")
Signed-off-by: Xin Liu <liuxin350@huawei.com>
Acked-by: John Fastabend <john.fastabend@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230406122622.109978-1-liuxin350@huawei.com
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\traw_spin_lock_bh(&stab->lock);', '\traw_spin_unlock_bh(&stab->lock);'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned long flags;', '\traw_spin_lock_irqsave(&stab->lock, flags);', '\traw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&stab->lock, flags);']}
description: A deadlock flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s BPF subsystem. This flaw allows a local user to potentially crash the system.

code_evidence: The function protects sockhash element deletion with raw_spin_lock_bh(&stab->lock), which disables only bottom halves.
The matching raw_spin_unlock_bh(&stab->lock) releases the same lock with the same BH-only discipline.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 covers improper lock acquisition that leaves a shared resource in an unpredictable state; here the BH-only locking discipline is insufficient for interrupt-context callers, so the lock is not safely acquired. This is a locking-discipline flaw rather than a generic race, since the defect is the wrong lock primitive for the context.

evidence_lines.code: raw_spin_lock_bh(&stab->lock);
raw_spin_unlock_bh(&stab->lock);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The deletion path acquires stab->lock using raw_spin_lock_bh, so an interrupt-context invocation that already holds the same lock cannot be excluded, producing self-deadlock when the lock is re-acquired. The trigger is a tracepoint/eBPF program calling this deletion path from interrupt context; the supported consequence is a hung CPU and system DoS.

commit_msg:
passthrough: quarantine PCI devices

When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for
that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The
IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that
the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However,
when the guest domain is torn down the device is assigned back to dom0,
thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data.

This patch introduces a 'quarantine' for PCI devices using dom_io. When
the toolstack makes a device assignable (by binding it to pciback), it
will now also assign it to DOMID_IO and the device will only be assigned
back to dom0 when the device is made unassignable again. Whilst device is
assignable it will only ever transfer between dom_io and guest domains.
dom_io is actually only used as a sentinel domain for quarantining purposes;
it is not configured with any IOMMU mappings. Assignment to dom_io simply
means that the device's initiator (requestor) identifier is not present in
the IOMMU's device table and thus any DMA transactions issued will be
terminated with a fault condition.

In addition, a fix to assignment handling is made for VT-d.  Failure
during the assignment step should not lead to a device still being
associated with its prior owner. Hand the device to DomIO temporarily,
until the assignment step has completed successfully.  Remove the PI
hooks from the source domain then earlier as well.

Failure of the recovery reassign_device_ownership() may not go silent:
There e.g. may still be left over RMRR mappings in the domain assignment
to which has failed, and hence we can't allow that domain to continue
executing.

NOTE: This patch also includes one printk() cleanup; the
      "XEN_DOMCTL_assign_device: " tag is dropped in iommu_do_pci_domctl(),
      since similar printk()-s elsewhere also don't log such a tag.

This is XSA-302.

Signed-off-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    libxl_ctx *ctx = libxl__gc_owner(gc);', '', '    /* De-quarantine */', '    rc = xc_deassign_device(ctx->xch, DOMID_IO, pcidev_encode_bdf(pcidev));', '    if ( rc < 0 ) {', '        LOG(ERROR, "failed to de-quarantine "PCI_BDF, pcidev->domain, pcidev->bus,', '            pcidev->dev, pcidev->func);', '        return ERROR_FAIL;', '    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing attackers to gain host OS privileges via DMA in a situation where an untrusted domain has access to a physical device. This occurs because passed through PCI devices may corrupt host memory after deassignment. When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However, when the guest domain is torn down, or the device is deassigned, the device is assigned back to dom0, thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data. An untrusted domain with access to a physical device can DMA into host memory, leading to privilege escalation. Only systems where guests are given direct access to physical devices capable of DMA (PCI pass-through) are vulnerable. Systems which do not use PCI pass-through are not vulnerable.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs PCI device de-assignment and sysfs bind operations via helper functions; it contains no OS command construction or execution, so it does not support CWE-78.

commit_msg:
Fix stack-based bufferoverflow

Fix: #81
Fix: #82
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar device_address_str[20];'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar device_address_str[20 + 1];', '', '\t// Force a null-terminated character', "\tdevice_address_str[20] = '\\0';"]}
description: GattLib 0.2 has a stack-based buffer over-read in gattlib_connect in dbus/gattlib.c because strncpy is misused.

code_evidence: device_address_str is a 20-byte stack buffer; strncpy copies up to sizeof(device_address_str) bytes from dst without guaranteeing a terminating NUL when dst is 20 or more characters.
The loop calls strlen on the possibly unterminated buffer, reading past its end, and snprintf later consumes device_address_str as a %s argument, again reading past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a read past the end of the intended buffer (strlen/snprintf on a non-terminated array), matching CWE-125. It is not CWE-121 (stack write overflow) because no out-of-bounds write occurs here.

evidence_lines.code: snprintf(object_path, sizeof(object_path), "/org/bluez/%s/dev_%s", adapter_name, device_address_str);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: strncpy with sizeof(buffer) never appends a NUL terminator when the source fills the buffer. Trigger: a dst address string of at least 20 bytes. Consequence: strlen and snprintf read beyond the 20-byte stack array, an out-of-bounds read that may leak stack data or crash.

commit_msg:
ipv4: keep skb->dst around in presence of IP options

Andrey Konovalov got crashes in __ip_options_echo() when a NULL skb->dst
is accessed.

ipv4_pktinfo_prepare() should not drop the dst if (evil) IP options
are present.

We could refine the test to the presence of ts_needtime or srr,
but IP options are not often used, so let's be conservative.

Thanks to syzkaller team for finding this bug.

Fixes: d826eb14ecef ("ipv4: PKTINFO doesnt need dst reference")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tskb_dst_drop(skb);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* We need to keep the dst for __ip_options_echo()', '\t * We could restrict the test to opt.ts_needtime || opt.srr,', '\t * but the following is good enough as IP options are not often used.', '\t */', '\tif (unlikely(IPCB(skb)->opt.optlen))', '\t\tskb_dst_force(skb);', '\telse', '\t\tskb_dst_drop(skb);']}
description: The ipv4_pktinfo_prepare function in net/ipv4/ip_sockglue.c in the Linux kernel through 4.9.9 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (system crash) via (1) an application that makes crafted system calls or possibly (2) IPv4 traffic with invalid IP options.

code_evidence: The prepare branch populates pktinfo only when prepare && skb_rtable(skb); otherwise lines 11-12 zero the fields. Regardless of branch, line 14 unconditionally calls skb_dst_drop(skb), discarding the skb's dst reference even when IP options are present and later code may need it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an unconditional dst drop that leaves a NULL skb->dst to be dereferenced downstream, matching CWE-476 NULL Pointer Dereference; it is not merely a lifetime/refcount issue, since the crash stems from dereferencing the absent pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function drops skb->dst unconditionally, so when the skb carries IP options, __ip_options_echo() later dereferences a NULL skb->dst. Trigger: crafted system calls or IPv4 traffic with IP options reaching this path. Consequence: kernel NULL pointer dereference and system crash (DoS).

commit_msg: fixes #2633 - 3 segv + memleak
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (!ptr || !ptr->lsr_config || !ptr->lsr_config->hdr_size)', '\t\t\t\treturn GF_ISOM_INVALID_MEDIA;']}

commit_msg:
USB: serial: io_ti: fix div-by-zero in set_termios

Fix a division-by-zero in set_termios when debugging is enabled and a
high-enough speed has been requested so that the divisor value becomes
zero.

Instead of just fixing the offending debug statement, cap the baud rate
at the base as a zero divisor value also appears to crash the firmware.

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>     # 2.6.12
Reviewed-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t} else'], 'added_lines': ['\t} else {', '\t\t/* Avoid a zero divisor. */', '\t\tbaud = min(baud, 461550);', '\t}']}
description: In change_port_settings in drivers/usb/serial/io_ti.c in the Linux kernel before 4.11.3, local users could cause a denial of service by division-by-zero in the serial device layer by trying to set very high baud rates.

code_evidence: Line 83 reads the user-requested baud rate via tty_get_baud_rate(tty); only a zero value is replaced with 9600 (lines 84-85). Any nonzero high rate flows through to line 89, where config->wBaudRate is computed as (461550L + baud/2) / baud.

For a baud rate above 461550, the numerator stays below the divisor's magnitude while the integer division truncates the result to zero; line 91 then divides 461550L by that zero wBaudRate, and line 89's own division is also affected for extreme values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs integer division whose divisor (baud on line 89, config->wBaudRate on line 91) can become zero from unvalidated user input, matching CWE-369. The missing upper bound is the root cause; the crash is the consequence, distinguishing it from mere input validation issues.

evidence_lines.code:
dev_dbg(dev, "%s - baud rate = %d, wBaudRate = %d\n", __func__, baud, config->wBaudRate);
dev_dbg(dev, "wBaudRate:   %d\n", (int)(461550L / config->wBaudRate));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the baud value from the tty termios is not capped, so a high user-requested rate yields a zero divisor in the baud-rate computation. Trigger: a local user sets a very high baud rate. Consequence: integer division by zero in the serial layer causes a kernel crash (DoS).

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/131
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    BImgBuff = (unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory((size_t) (ldblk),sizeof(unsigned char));    /* Ldblk was set in the check phase */'], 'added_lines': ['    BImgBuff = (unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory((size_t) (ldblk),sizeof(double));    /* Ldblk was set in the check phase */']}
description: coders/mat.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and application crash) via a crafted mat file.

code_evidence: BImgBuff is allocated with ldblk bytes of unsigned char (236), but for miDOUBLE/miSINGLE data CalcMinMax is invoked with that buffer (241-243).

The same undersized buffer is passed to ReadBlob (257), ImportQuantumPixels (276), and the complex branches cast it to double*/float* for ReadBlobDoublesXXX/ReadBlobFloatsXXX (302,308), which write/read 8- or 4-byte elements.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an allocation size mismatch that leaves the buffer too small for the element type later accessed, producing reads beyond the intended buffer boundary — exactly CWE-125. This is not a write overflow or integer overflow; the allocation itself succeeds but is undersized relative to access width.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: For miDOUBLE/miSINGLE cell types, ldblk = 8*SizeX or 4*SizeX bytes, but BImgBuff is allocated with sizeof(unsigned char) instead of sizeof(double). Downstream double/float readers and complex-row handlers access the buffer as 8- or 4-byte elements, reading past the allocated region. A crafted .mat file selecting these cell types triggers the out-of-bounds access and can crash the process.

commit_msg:
gnrc_sixlowpan_frag_rb: fix integer underflow in _6lo_frag_size()

(cherry picked from commit 9728f727e75d7d78dbfb5918e0de1b938b7b6d2c)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (frag_size == 0) {', '            DEBUG("6lo rbuf: integer underflow detected.\\n");', '            gnrc_pktbuf_release(pkt);', '            return RBUF_ADD_ERROR;', '        }']}
description: RIOT-OS, an operating system that supports Internet of Things devices, contains a network stack with the ability to process 6LoWPAN frames. Prior to version 2022.10, an attacker can send a crafted frame to the device resulting in a large out of bounds write beyond the packet buffer. The write will create a hard fault exception after reaching the last page of RAM. The hard fault is not handled and the system will be stuck until reset, thus the impact is denial of service. Version 2022.10 fixes this issue. As a workaround, disable support for fragmented IP datagrams or apply the patches manually.

code_evidence: Line 19 computes frag_size via _6lo_frag_size() without validating it; the fix adds a zero/underflow check after this call.
Lines 80-86 only guard (offset + frag_size) > datagram_size; if frag_size underflows to a huge size_t, the addition wraps and this bound check can pass.
Line 159-160 memcpy writes frag_size bytes to entry.rbuf->pkt->data + offset, so an invalid frag_size drives the out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe memcpy with an underflowed length writes past the intended packet buffer, which is exactly CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The integer underflow is the root-cause enabler, but the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds memory write, not merely an integer error.

evidence_lines.code:
frag_size = _6lo_frag_size(pkt, offset, data);
datagram_size = sixlowpan_frag_datagram_size(pkt->data);

memcpy(((uint8_t *)entry.rbuf->pkt->data) + offset, data,
frag_size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: _6lo_frag_size() can underflow, yielding a huge size_t frag_size that is not validated. Trigger: a crafted 6LoWPAN fragment where the computed payload size wraps. The wrap can bypass the size check at line 80 and cause memcpy at line 159 to write far beyond the reassembly buffer, producing the described out-of-bounds write and hard-fault DoS.

Added control character check

Added control character check, returning -1 (to "err") if control characters are present.

Although it is not possible to exploit this directly (e.g., adding a new user fails because \n is in the block list), it is possible to misrepresent the /etc/passwd file when viewed. commit_msg:
x86/hap: do not switch on log dirty for VRAM tracking

XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram possibly calls into paging_log_dirty_enable
when using HAP mode, and it can interact badly with other ongoing
paging domctls, as XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram is not holding the domctl
lock.

This was detected as a result of the following assert triggering when
doing repeated migrations of a HAP HVM domain with a stubdom:

Assertion 'd->arch.paging.log_dirty.allocs == 0' failed at paging.c:198
----[ Xen-4.17-unstable  x86_64  debug=y  Not tainted ]----
CPU:    34
RIP:    e008:[<ffff82d040314b3b>] arch/x86/mm/paging.c#paging_free_log_dirty_bitmap+0x606/0x6
RFLAGS: 0000000000010206   CONTEXT: hypervisor (d0v23)
[...]
Xen call trace:
   [<ffff82d040314b3b>] R arch/x86/mm/paging.c#paging_free_log_dirty_bitmap+0x606/0x63a
   [<ffff82d040279f96>] S xsm/flask/hooks.c#domain_has_perm+0x5a/0x67
   [<ffff82d04031577f>] F paging_domctl+0x251/0xd41
   [<ffff82d04031640c>] F paging_domctl_continuation+0x19d/0x202
   [<ffff82d0403202fa>] F pv_hypercall+0x150/0x2a7
   [<ffff82d0403a729d>] F lstar_enter+0x12d/0x140

Such assert triggered because the stubdom used
XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram while dom0 was in the middle of executing
XEN_DOMCTL_SHADOW_OP_OFF, and so log dirty become enabled while
retiring the old structures, thus leading to new entries being
populated in already clear slots.

Fix this by not enabling log dirty for VRAM tracking, similar to what
is done when using shadow instead of HAP. Call
p2m_enable_hardware_log_dirty when enabling VRAM tracking in order to
get some hardware assistance if available. As a side effect the memory
pressure on the p2m pool should go down if only VRAM tracking is
enabled, as the dirty bitmap is no longer allocated.

Note that paging_log_dirty_range (used to get the dirty bitmap for
VRAM tracking) doesn't use the log dirty bitmap, and instead relies on
checking whether each gfn on the range has been switched from
p2m_ram_logdirty to p2m_ram_rw in order to account for dirty pages.

This is CVE-2022-26356 / XSA-397.

Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '        if ( !paging_mode_log_dirty(d) )', '        {', '            rc = paging_log_dirty_enable(d, false);', '            if ( rc )', '                goto out;', '        }'], 'added_lines': ['', '            domain_pause(d);', '            p2m_enable_hardware_log_dirty(d);', '            domain_unpause(d);']}
description: Racy interactions between dirty vram tracking and paging log dirty hypercalls Activation of log dirty mode done by XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram (was named HVMOP_track_dirty_vram before Xen 4.9) is racy with ongoing log dirty hypercalls. A suitably timed call to XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram can enable log dirty while another CPU is still in the process of tearing down the structures related to a previously enabled log dirty mode (XEN_DOMCTL_SHADOW_OP_OFF). This is due to lack of mutually exclusive locking between both operations and can lead to entries being added in already freed slots, resulting in a memory leak.

code_evidence: When log dirty is not already active, hap_track_dirty_vram calls paging_log_dirty_enable(d, false) outside paging_lock(d); the lock is only taken later at line 22.

The function then acquires paging_lock, mutates dirty_vram and releases the lock at line 41 before calling p2m_change_type_range to switch pages to p2m_ram_logdirty, so enabling log dirty and manipulating the p2m are not serialized with a concurrent XEN_DOMCTL_SHADOW_OP_OFF teardown.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 fits because the function performs shared paging state changes (paging_log_dirty_enable, p2m type changes) without the mutually exclusive locking required against other paging domctls; the race, not just a single missing check, produces the inconsistent state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: enabling log dirty and reconfiguring the p2m range are performed without holding the lock that serializes paging domctls, so a concurrent shadow-off teardown can free/clear log-dirty slots while this path repopulates them. Trigger: a timed XEN_DMOP_track_dirty_vram call racing XEN_DOMCTL_SHADOW_OP_OFF. Supported consequence: entries written into already-freed structures, causing a memory leak and tripping the allocs assert.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/1542
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  status=MagickTrue;', '  group4_image=CloneImage(inject_image,0,0,MagickTrue,exception);', '  if (group4_image == (Image *) NULL)', '    return(MagickFalse);', '  write_info=DestroyImageInfo(write_info);'], 'added_lines': ['  group4_image=CloneImage(inject_image,0,0,MagickTrue,exception);', '  if (group4_image == (Image *) NULL)', '    return(MagickFalse);', '  write_info=DestroyImageInfo(write_info);', '  status=MagickTrue;']}
description: ImageMagick 7.0.8-40 has a memory leak in Huffman2DEncodeImage in coders/ps2.c.

code_evidence: write_info is allocated by CloneImageInfo at line 15, and group4_image is allocated by CloneImage at line 18. If CloneImage returns NULL, line 20 returns without destroying write_info, leaking that ImageInfo. If ImageToBlob returns NULL, line 25 returns without destroying write_info (line 26 is only reached on the success path), leaking the ImageInfo as well.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because heap memory allocated by CloneImageInfo remains unreleased when error conditions cause early return; the missing release after effective lifetime is the direct weakness, distinct from a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocated write_info is released only on the successful path, so the two early error returns at lines 20 and 25 bypass DestroyImageInfo. Trigger: CloneImage or ImageToBlob fails (e.g., under memory pressure). Consequence: the ImageInfo allocation is never freed, causing a memory leak and possible resource-consumption DoS across repeated failures.

commit_msg:
evtchn: avoid NULL derefs

Commit fbbd5009e6 ("evtchn: refactor low-level event channel port ops")
added a de-reference of the struct evtchn pointer for a port without
first making sure the bucket pointer is non-NULL. This de-reference is
actually entirely unnecessary, as all relevant callers (beyond the
problematic do_poll()) already hold the port number in their hands, and
the actual leaf functions need nothing else.

For FIFO event channels there's a second problem in that the ordering
of reads and updates to ->num_evtchns and ->event_array[] was so far
undefined (the read side isn't always holding the domain's event lock).
Add respective barriers.

This is XSA-221.

Reported-by: Ankur Arora <ankur.a.arora@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static bool_t evtchn_2l_is_pending(struct domain *d,', '                                   const struct evtchn *evtchn)', '    return test_bit(evtchn->port, &shared_info(d, evtchn_pending));'], 'added_lines': ['static bool_t evtchn_2l_is_pending(struct domain *d, evtchn_port_t port)', '    unsigned int max_ports = BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d) * BITS_PER_EVTCHN_WORD(d);', '', '    ASSERT(port < max_ports);', '    return port < max_ports && test_bit(port, &shared_info(d, evtchn_pending));']}
description: Xen through 4.8.x does not validate the port numbers of polled event channel ports, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and host OS crash) or possibly obtain sensitive information, aka XSA-221.

code_evidence: evtchn_2l_is_pending takes a const struct evtchn *evtchn and, without any NULL check, dereferences it as evtchn->port inside the test_bit call on line 4. The port value used to index the pending bitmap therefore comes from a pointer the function assumes is non-NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function reads evtchn->port from a pointer it expects to be valid but that may be NULL, matching the target weakness directly; the fix removes the dereference rather than adding a check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the function dereferences the evtchn pointer unconditionally; the caller path (do_poll) can supply a NULL pointer for a port without a valid bucket. The trigger is polling such a port, and the consequence is a NULL pointer dereference causing a host crash (DoS).

commit_msg: Bug 701176: Handle TIFFs with alpha that have more than 8 bits per sample.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t*dst++ = a << (8 - tiff->bitspersample);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif (tiff->bitspersample <= 8)', '\t\t\t\t\t*dst++ = a << (8 - tiff->bitspersample);', '\t\t\t\telse', '\t\t\t\t\t*dst++ = a >> (tiff->bitspersample - 8);']}
description: Artifex MuPDF before 1.18.0 has a heap based buffer over-write in tiff_expand_colormap() function when parsing TIFF files allowing attackers to cause a denial of service.

code_evidence: maxval is computed as 1 << bitspersample, so a 16-bit sample yields maxval 65536.
The validation accepts bitspersample == 16, permitting 16-bit palette samples.
The output buffer is allocated as stride * imagelength bytes, where stride = imagewidth * (samplesperpixel + 2).
The loops iterate over imagelength rows and imagewidth columns, with dst advancing per pixel.
Each pixel reads two 16-bit components (color index c and alpha a) via tiff_getcomp.
The alpha byte is written as a << (8 - bitspersample); with bitspersample 16 this is a left shift by -8, an undefined/oversized shift producing an out-of-range value written to *dst.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes an out-of-range byte through *dst into a heap buffer sized by stride, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write; the root cause is the missing bitspersample > 8 handling, not merely a bad arithmetic value.

evidence_lines.code: int maxval = 1 << tiff->bitspersample;

if (tiff->bitspersample != 1 && tiff->bitspersample != 2 && tiff->bitspersample != 4 && tiff->bitspersample != 8 && tiff->bitspersample != 16)
fz_throw(ctx, FZ_ERROR_GENERIC, "invalid number of bits for RGBPal");
samples = fz_malloc(ctx, stride * tiff->imagelength);

int c = tiff_getcomp(src, x * 2, tiff->bitspersample);
int a = tiff_getcomp(src, x * 2 + 1, tiff->bitspersample);
*dst++ = a << (8 - tiff->bitspersample);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: For 16-bit RGBA palette TIFFs, the shift amount 8 - bitspersample becomes negative, so the computed alpha byte is not a valid 0-255 value and writing it to *dst corrupts memory; the per-pixel dst pointer advances within a buffer sized for imagewidth*(samplesperpixel+2), so the malformed write can overrun the heap allocation.

commit_msg: fixed #1970
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tgf_bifs_dec_name(parser->bs, name);'], 'added_lines': ['\tgf_bifs_dec_name(parser->bs, name, 1000);']}

commit_msg:
x86: limit linear page table use to a single level

That's the only way that they're meant to be used. Without such a
restriction arbitrarily long chains of same-level page tables can be
built, tearing down of which may then cause arbitrarily deep recursion,
causing a stack overflow. To facilitate this restriction, a counter is
being introduced to track both the number of same-level entries in a
page table as well as the number of uses of a page table in another
same-level one (counting into positive and negative direction
respectively, utilizing the fact that both counts can't be non-zero at
the same time).

Note that the added accounting introduces a restriction on the number
of times a page can be used in other same-level page tables - more than
32k of such uses are no longer possible.

Note also that some put_page_and_type[_preemptible]() calls are
replaced with open-coded equivalents.  This seemed preferrable to
adding "parent_table" to the matrix of functions.

Note further that cross-domain same-level page table references are no
longer permitted (they probably never should have been).

This is XSA-240.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                    {', '                        curr->arch.old_guest_ptpg = NULL;', '                    }', '                curr->arch.old_guest_ptpg = NULL;', '                    curr->arch.old_guest_ptpg = NULL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service (unbounded recursion, stack consumption, and hypervisor crash) or possibly gain privileges via crafted page-table stacking.

code_evidence: Guest-controlled mmuext_op commands reach pin_page, which validates the level via op.cmd and then obtains the page and page type (get_page_type_preemptible) without any check on existing same-level page-table chaining.
On failure/drop, non-L1 pages are stashed in curr->arch.old_guest_table instead of being fully released, so a page-table reference is retained across the hypercall.
MMUEXT_UNPIN_TABLE similarly stores the page in old_guest_table on -EINTR/-ERESTART, deferring the put and keeping the reference alive.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is missing accounting/limiting of a bounded resource (same-level page-table references), allowing a guest to consume it without bound and cause a DoS crash, matching CWE-400's uncontrolled resource consumption. It is not merely a memory-safety bug; the weakness is the absent resource cap.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A PV guest can repeatedly issue pin/unpin operations on page-table pages; the function defers put_page_and_type via old_guest_table and imposes no limit on same-level page-table references. This lets the guest build arbitrarily long same-level page-table chains, whose teardown recurses deeply and exhausts the hypervisor stack, crashing it.

commit_msg: Add a bounds check to ByteArray::Get().
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (index < 0 || index >= Length())', '    return -1;']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the ByteArray::Get method in data/byte_array.cc in Google sfntly before 2016-06-10, as used in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.82, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted SFNT font.

code_evidence: ByteArray::Get takes an externally supplied int32_t index and passes it directly to InternalGet(index) with no validation of index against the array length. The result is masked with 0xff and returned, so an out-of-range index reaches InternalGet unmodified.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a buffer access at a location outside the intended boundary because the index constraint is missing; this matches CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The added bounds check in the patch confirms the missing restriction, rather than an integer-overflow or format-string weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the index parameter is not constrained to [0, Length()) before InternalGet dereferences the underlying buffer. Trigger: a crafted SFNT font drives Get with a negative or oversized index, causing InternalGet to read memory outside the intended ByteArray buffer; the masked value is then returned or later used, yielding out-of-bounds memory read and possible crash or unspecified impact.

description: KernelSU is a Kernel based root solution for Android. Starting in version 0.6.1 and prior to version 0.7.0, if a KernelSU installed device is infected with a malware whose app signing block specially constructed, it can take over root privileges on the device. The vulnerable verification logic actually obtains the signature of the last block with an id of `0x7109871a`, while the verification logic during Android installation is to obtain the first one. In addition to the actual signature upgrade that has been fixed (KSU thought it was V2 but was actually V3), there is also the problem of actual signature downgrading (KSU thought it was V2 but was actually V1). Find a condition in the signature verification logic that will cause the signature not to be found error, and KernelSU does not implement the same conditions, so KSU thinks there is a V2 signature, but the APK signature verification actually uses the V1 signature. This issue is fixed in version 0.7.0. As workarounds, keep the KernelSU manager installed and avoid installing unknown apps.

code_evidence: The only authorization gate before granting manager privileges is a check that the caller's real parent has uid 0; no binding to the expected manager package is enforced here.
The package name is located via strstr(cwd, pkg) anywhere in the APK path, so an attacker-controlled package string can match a substring rather than the exact package directory.
The only additional constraint is that the character after the match is '-', which is a weak delimiter check and does not verify the full package identity.
Once is_manager_apk(cwd) passes, the current uid is unconditionally promoted to manager via ksu_set_manager_uid, so the weak package matching directly gates a privilege grant.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-863 fits because the function performs an authorization decision (who may become manager) but the check is incorrectly performed, allowing privilege gain. It is an authorization-flaw issue, not merely improper input validation, since the defective check directly gates ksu_set_manager_uid.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the privilege-granting path authorizes on a substring package match and a parent-uid check rather than an exact, trusted package identity, and the new compile-time package check is only present under KSU_MANAGER_PACKAGE. Trigger: a crafted app path/package string that satisfies the substring and '-' checks while is_manager_apk succeeds. Consequence: an unintended app's uid is recorded as manager, granting root-equivalent access.

commit_msg:
We recently had an oops reported on a 4.14 kernel in
xfs_reclaim_inodes_count() where sb->s_fs_info pointed to garbage
and so the m_perag_tree lookup walked into lala land.

Essentially, the machine was under memory pressure when the mount
was being run, xfs_fs_fill_super() failed after allocating the
xfs_mount and attaching it to sb->s_fs_info. It then cleaned up and
freed the xfs_mount, but the sb->s_fs_info field still pointed to
the freed memory. Hence when the superblock shrinker then ran
it fell off the bad pointer.

With the superblock shrinker problem fixed at teh VFS level, this
stale s_fs_info pointer is still a problem - we use it
unconditionally in ->put_super when the superblock is being torn
down, and hence we can still trip over it after a ->fill_super
call failure. Hence we need to clear s_fs_info if
xfs-fs_fill_super() fails, and we need to check if it's valid in
the places it can potentially be dereferenced after a ->fill_super
failure.

Signed-Off-By: Dave Chinner <dchinner@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Paranoia: catch incorrect calls during mount setup or teardown */', '\tif (WARN_ON_ONCE(!sb->s_fs_info))', '\t\treturn 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in fs/xfs/xfs_super.c in the Linux kernel before 4.18. A use after free exists, related to xfs_fs_fill_super failure.

code_evidence: Line 6 unconditionally dereferences the superblock's filesystem-private pointer via XFS_M(sb), which expands to sb->s_fs_info, and passes it to xfs_reclaim_inodes_count() without any validity check. Per the commit, xfs_fs_fill_super() can fail after allocating and attaching the xfs_mount, then free it while leaving sb->s_fs_info stale.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function operates on an xfs_mount pointer after that object was freed during failed mount cleanup, and the dereference through the stale s_fs_info is exactly a use-after-free. A plain NULL-pointer dereference would not capture the freed-object lifetime issue described in the commit.

evidence_lines.code: return xfs_reclaim_inodes_count(XFS_M(sb));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts sb->s_fs_info and dereferences it with no NULL/staleness guard. Trigger: a mount failure path frees the xfs_mount but leaves the dangling pointer in s_fs_info; the superblock shrinker then invokes this callback. Consequence: xfs_reclaim_inodes_count() walks the m_perag_tree through freed memory, causing an invalid read and kernel crash/oops. The missing check is the cause; the crash is the consequence.

commit_msg:
USB: check usb_get_extra_descriptor for proper size

When reading an extra descriptor, we need to properly check the minimum
and maximum size allowed, to prevent from invalid data being sent by a
device.

Reported-by: Hui Peng <benquike@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Mathias Payer <mathias.payer@nebelwelt.net>
Co-developed-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Hui Peng <benquike@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Mathias Payer <mathias.payer@nebelwelt.net>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: stable <stable@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tUSB_DT_SECURITY, (void **) &secd);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tUSB_DT_SECURITY, (void **) &secd, sizeof(*secd));']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.19.9. The USB subsystem mishandles size checks during the reading of an extra descriptor, related to __usb_get_extra_descriptor in drivers/usb/core/usb.c.

code_evidence: __usb_get_extra_descriptor is called with the device-supplied raw descriptor buffer and its wTotalLength, but the size argument for the security descriptor is omitted, so the lookup does not validate that the returned descriptor is at least sizeof(*secd) before secd is used.

The encryption-descriptor loop trusts etd->bLength to advance itr, checking only that bLength >= sizeof(*etd); a zero or otherwise non-advancing bLength leaves itr unchanged, so the loop condition itr < top never terminates.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing constraint on the descriptor size and the unbounded, non-advancing parse loop let untrusted device data drive the kernel into an effectively infinite loop, exhausting CPU. This is a resource-consumption DoS, matching CWE-400; it is not a memory-corruption issue such as an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A malicious USB device supplies a security descriptor whose extra-descriptor lookup succeeds without a minimum-size check, and encryption descriptors whose bLength does not advance the iterator. The non-advancing loop spins indefinitely over device-controlled data, consuming CPU and hanging the host while parsing descriptors, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
packet: fix race condition in packet_set_ring

When packet_set_ring creates a ring buffer it will initialize a
struct timer_list if the packet version is TPACKET_V3. This value
can then be raced by a different thread calling setsockopt to
set the version to TPACKET_V1 before packet_set_ring has finished.

This leads to a use-after-free on a function pointer in the
struct timer_list when the socket is closed as the previously
initialized timer will not be deleted.

The bug is fixed by taking lock_sock(sk) in packet_setsockopt when
changing the packet version while also taking the lock at the start
of packet_set_ring.

Fixes: f6fb8f100b80 ("af-packet: TPACKET_V3 flexible buffer implementation.")
Signed-off-by: Philip Pettersson <philip.pettersson@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tlock_sock(sk);', '\trelease_sock(sk);'], 'added_lines': ['\tlock_sock(sk);', '\trelease_sock(sk);']}
description: Race condition in net/packet/af_packet.c in the Linux kernel through 4.8.12 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) by leveraging the CAP_NET_RAW capability to change a socket version, related to the packet_set_ring and packet_setsockopt functions.

code_evidence: lock_sock(sk) is taken only at line 79, after ring allocation and TPACKET_V3 timer initialization (init_prb_bdqc at line 68); the ring/version state is read and mutated before the socket lock is held.
The TPACKET_V3 branch initializes the block timer via init_prb_bdqc while no socket lock protects po->tp_version, so a concurrent setsockopt version change can interleave.

Timer teardown at lines 116-118 is conditional on po->tp_version > TPACKET_V2; if another thread downgrades the version before this point, the previously initialized timer is not deleted, leaving a stale timer_list function pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a concurrent code sequence requiring exclusive access to shared socket/ring state (po->tp_version, timer) but lacks synchronization, allowing an interfering setsockopt to modify the resource mid-sequence, matching CWE-362. The use-after-free is a downstream consequence of the race, not a separate labeling target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: packet_set_ring reads and acts on po->tp_version for timer initialization and teardown without holding the socket lock across that sequence. Trigger: a concurrent setsockopt changes the packet version to TPACKET_V1 while packet_set_ring is mid-execution. Consequence: the initialized timer is not shut down, and closing the socket later invokes a stale timer function pointer (use-after-free).

description: An issue was discovered in function _libssh2_packet_add in libssh2 1.10.0 allows attackers to access out of bounds memory.

p->payload is then used as the write destination for memcpy(p->wptr, &block[5], blocksize - 5) at line 116 and memcpy(p->wptr, &p->buf[p->readidx], numbytes) at line 161, writing packet data into the zero-length allocation.

commit_msg:
Fix jpeg_skip_scanlines() segfault w/merged upsamp

The additional segfault mentioned in #244 was due to the fact that
the merged upsamplers use a different private structure than the
non-merged upsamplers.  jpeg_skip_scanlines() was assuming the latter, so
when merged upsampling was enabled, jpeg_skip_scanlines() clobbered one
of the IDCT method pointers in the merged upsampler's private structure.

For reasons unknown, the test image in #441 did not encounter this
segfault (too small?), but it encountered an issue similar to the one
fixed in 5bc43c7821df982f65aa1c738f67fbf7cba8bd69, whereby it was
necessary to set up a dummy postprocessing function in
read_and_discard_scanlines() when merged upsampling was enabled.
Failing to do so caused either a segfault in merged_2v_upsample() (due
to a NULL pointer being passed to jcopy_sample_rows()) or an error
("Corrupt JPEG data: premature end of data segment"), depending on the
number of scanlines skipped and whether the first scanline skipped was
an odd- or even-numbered row.

Fixes #441
Fixes #244 (for real this time)

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.1969: [security] buffer-overflow in trunc_string()

Problem:  buffer-overflow in trunc_string()
Solution: Add NULL at end of buffer

Currently trunc_string() assumes that when the string is too long,
buf[e-1] will always be writeable. But that assumption may not always be
true. The condition currently looks like this

    else if (e + 3 < buflen)
    [...]
    else
    {
	// can't fit in the "...", just truncate it
	buf[e - 1] = NUL;
    }

but this means, we may run into the last else clause with e still being
larger than buflen. So a buffer overflow occurs.

So instead of using `buf[e - 1]`, let's just always
truncate at `buf[buflen - 1]` which should always be writable.

Signed-off-by: Christian Brabandt <cb@256bit.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbuf[e - 1] = NUL;'], 'added_lines': ['\tbuf[buflen - 1] = NUL;']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.1969.

code_evidence: Line 73 enters the truncation branch when i <= e + 3. Line 87 only appends "..." when e + 3 < buflen; otherwise control reaches the final else at lines 96-99. There, buf[e - 1] = NUL is written without checking e against buflen, so e - 1 may be at or beyond buflen - 1. Line 79 shows buflen is the caller-supplied size used to clamp other copies, confirming the buffer bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked write buf[e - 1] can exceed the heap buffer sized by buflen, directly matching a heap-based buffer overflow. This is an out-of-bounds write rather than an under-read or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the final else writes buf[e - 1] although the earlier loop can leave e equal to or larger than buflen. Trigger: a long input string with a small caller-supplied buflen reaching the truncation path. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write past the heap-allocated buffer, enabling memory corruption and possible code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix segfault when attempting to convert string to float16.

To make sure this gets fixed, add test for converting string to any numeric type.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 286650886
Change-Id: I81f770ec2bbd33a863e8057ce198c679912fa8e0
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      RETURN_STRING_AS_STATUS(NumpyHalfConverter::Convert(obj, &state, ret));'], 'added_lines': ['      if (NumpyHalfConverter::Convert(obj, &state, ret) == nullptr)', '        return Status::OK();', '      break;']}
description: In TensorFlow before 1.15.2 and 2.0.1, converting a string (from Python) to a tf.float16 value results in a segmentation fault in eager mode as the format checks for this use case are only in the graph mode. This issue can lead to denial of service in inference/training where a malicious attacker can send a data point which contains a string instead of a tf.float16 value. Similar effects can be obtained by manipulating saved models and checkpoints whereby replacing a scalar tf.float16 value with a scalar string will trigger this issue due to automatic conversions. This can be easily reproduced by tf.constant("hello", tf.float16), if eager execution is enabled. This issue is patched in TensorFlow 1.15.1 and 2.0.1 with this vulnerability patched. TensorFlow 2.1.0 was released after we fixed the issue, thus it is not affected. Users are encouraged to switch to TensorFlow 1.15.1, 2.0.1 or 2.1.0.

code_evidence: In the requested_dtype switch, case DT_HALF calls NumpyHalfConverter::Convert and passes its result directly to RETURN_STRING_AS_STATUS without checking for nullptr.

The same unchecked RETURN_STRING_AS_STATUS(NumpyHalfConverter::Convert(...)) pattern recurs in the inferred_dtype switch for DT_HALF, so a string input inferred as DT_HALF also reaches the converter's null return path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts a Python object whose actual type (string) is inconsistent with the requested/inferred DT_HALF type, and the half branches fail to validate that mismatch before processing, matching CWE-20's improper input validation of derived type. The flaw is missing validation in the DT_HALF paths, not a transform of otherwise-valid input.

evidence_lines.code:
case DT_HALF:
RETURN_STRING_AS_STATUS(NumpyHalfConverter::Convert(obj, &state, ret));

case DT_HALF:
RETURN_STRING_AS_STATUS(NumpyHalfConverter::Convert(obj, &state, ret));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DT_HALF branches do not validate the converter result before dereferencing/using it, unlike sibling cases that test Convert(...) == nullptr. Trigger: a Python string supplied as a tf.float16 value (e.g., tf.constant("hello", tf.float16)) in eager mode makes NumpyHalfConverter::Convert return null for the type mismatch. The unchecked null is then consumed, producing a segmentation fault and denial of service.

description: ClamAV version version 0.99.3 contains a Out of bounds heap memory read vulnerability in XAR parser, function xar_hash_check() that can result in Leaking of memory, may help in developing exploit chains.. This attack appear to be exploitable via The victim must scan a crafted XAR file. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in after commit d96a6b8bcc7439fa7e3876207aa0a8e79c8451b6.

code_evidence: at is computed from attacker-controlled offset in the TOC (line 114) and used as the fmap_need_off_once offset; the read size bytes is derived from length without clamping to map->len - at, so a crafted XAR can request a read past the mapping.

LZMA branch sets in_remaining = length (line 189) and reads CLI_LZMA_HDR_SIZE at 'at' (line 199) without checking at+header against map->len; later loop reads MIN(CLI_LZMA_IBUF_SIZE, in_remaining) bytes at 'at' (lines 230-231) where in_remaining is not bounded by remaining mapping.

The ANY/BZ/XZ branch reads length bytes at 'at' via fmap_need_off_once (line 291) and passes length to xar_hash_update (line 300) without bounding length to map->len - at, so an oversized TOC length causes an out-of-bounds heap read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads data beyond the intended buffer boundary because the read length is not validated against the remaining mapped region, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. This is a read overrun, not a write overrun (CWE-787), since only read/hash operations consume the excess bytes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: length/offset values parsed from the untrusted XAR TOC are used as fmap read sizes and hash-update lengths without clamping to the remaining mapped file (map->len - at). Trigger: a crafted XAR file whose TOC declares a length exceeding the actual data. Consequence: fmap_need_off_once / hash update read past the mapped heap buffer, leaking memory or crashing.

commit_msg: fix #147: Stack Exhaustion Problem caused by some parsing functions in regcomp.c making recursive calls to themselves.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int r, len, group = 0;', ''], 'added_lines': ['  int r, len, group;', '  unsigned int parse_depth;', '', '  group = 0;', '', '  parse_depth = env->parse_depth;', '      parse_depth++;', '      if (parse_depth > ParseDepthLimit)', '        return ONIGERR_PARSE_DEPTH_LIMIT_OVER;', '']}
description: Oniguruma before 6.9.3 allows Stack Exhaustion in regcomp.c because of recursion in regparse.c.

code_evidence: In TK_SUBEXP_OPEN, parse_exp calls parse_bag (line 20), and the nested r==2 branch calls parse_subexp (line 41), which re-enters parse_exp on nested group content; this recursion carries no depth counter.

The repeat block at lines 278-331 loops via goto re_entry, but the only guard before constructing a quantifier is is_invalid_quantifier_target; nothing limits how deeply nested constructs are recursed through parse_bag/parse_subexp.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 covers uncontrolled recursion consuming the program stack. The missing depth bound on the parse_exp -> parse_bag/parse_subexp cycle directly matches this, whereas a plain memory-limit or input-validation weakness would not describe the recursive stack growth.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: parse_exp recurses into parse_bag/parse_subexp for each nested group without tracking recursion depth. Trigger: an attacker-supplied regular expression with deeply nested parentheses forces unbounded recursive parse_exp invocations. Consequence: stack exhaustion/crash, a denial of service during regex compilation.

commit_msg:
Fix heap overflows in the various rectangle fill functions

Altough rfbproto.c does check whether the overall FramebufferUpdate rectangle is
too large, some of the individual encoding decoders do not, which allows a
malicious server to overwrite parts of the heap.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  }', '', '  if (!CheckRect(client, x, y, w, h)) {', '    rfbClientLog("Rect out of bounds: %dx%d at (%d, %d)\\n", x, y, w, h);', '    return;']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in rfbproto.c in LibVNCClient in LibVNCServer before 0.9.11 allows remote servers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted FramebufferUpdate message containing a subrectangle outside of the client drawing area.

code_evidence: CopyRectangle takes attacker-influenced x, y, w, h from a FramebufferUpdate subrectangle and, after only a null-frameBuffer check, proceeds to the copy macro with no bounds validation.

COPY_RECT computes rs = w*BPP/8 and rs2 = client->width*BPP/8, then loops j from (x*(BPP/8)+y*rs2) to (y+h)*rs2, calling memcpy(client->frameBuffer + j, buffer, rs) each iteration. If x, y, w, or h place the subrectangle outside the framebuffer, j and rs index/write beyond frameBuffer's allocated size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs memcpy into a memory buffer using computed offsets without restricting them to the buffer's intended boundary, directly matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. It is a heap write overflow rather than an integer-only issue, since the unchecked coordinates/lengths drive the out-of-bounds memcpy.

evidence_lines.code:
int rs = w * BPP / 8, rs2 = client->width * BPP / 8; \
for (j = ((x * (BPP / 8)) + (y * rs2)); j < (y + h) * rs2; j += rs2) { \
memcpy(client->frameBuffer + j, buffer, rs); \
buffer += rs; \
} \

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation that the subrectangle lies within the client drawing area before computing offsets and copy lengths. Trigger: a crafted FramebufferUpdate subrectangle with out-of-range x/y/w/h. Consequence: memcpy writes past the heap framebuffer, causing heap corruption, crash, or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
delay bailout for invalid authenticating user until after the packet
containing the request has been fully parsed. Reported by Dariusz Tytko
and Michał Sajdak; ok deraadt
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\tif (!authctxt->valid || authctxt->user == NULL)', '\t\treturn (0);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!authctxt->valid || authctxt->user == NULL) {', '\t\tdebug2("%s: disabled because of invalid user", __func__);', '\t\tfree(doid);', '\t\treturn (0);', '\t}', '']}
description: OpenSSH through 7.7 is prone to a user enumeration vulnerability due to not delaying bailout for an invalid authenticating user until after the packet containing the request has been fully parsed, related to auth2-gss.c, auth2-hostbased.c, and auth2-pubkey.c.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only moves an invalid-user check after packet parsing to delay bailout; it contains no concurrent code sequence or shared-resource synchronization window, so it does not support CWE-362.

commit_msg:
set_fat(): Fix off-by-2 error leading to corruption in FAT12

In FAT12 two 12 bit entries are combined to a 24 bit value (three
bytes). Therefore, when an even numbered FAT entry is set in FAT12, it
must be be combined with the following entry. To prevent accessing
beyond the end of the FAT array, it must be checked that the cluster is
not the last one.

Previously, the check tested that the requested cluster was equal to
fs->clusters - 1. However, fs->clusters is the number of data clusters
not including the two reserved FAT entries at the start so the test
triggered two clusters early.

If the third to last entry was written on a FAT12 filesystem with an
odd number of clusters, the second to last entry would be corrupted.
This corruption may also lead to invalid memory accesses when the
corrupted entry becomes out of bounds and is used later.

Change the test to fs->clusters + 1 to fix.

Reported-by: Hanno Böck
Signed-off-by: Andreas Bombe <aeb@debian.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    if (cluster != fs->clusters - 1)'], 'added_lines': ['\t    if (cluster != fs->clusters + 1)']}
description: The set_fat function in fat.c in dosfstools before 4.0 might allow attackers to corrupt a FAT12 filesystem or cause a denial of service (invalid memory read and crash) by writing an odd number of clusters to the third to last entry on a FAT12 filesystem, which triggers an "off-by-two error."

code_evidence: Line 12/13 compute the FAT12 byte offset from cluster; line 21's guard compares cluster to fs->clusters - 1, but fs->clusters excludes the two reserved entries, so the boundary is two clusters early. When the guard is false, line 22 reads get_fat(cluster + 1), and line 26 merges that subsequent entry's low byte into data[1].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is an off-by-two error in the cluster-boundary numeric comparison, a miscalculation of the valid entry limit, matching the Numeric Errors category (CWE-189). The defect is the incorrect bound arithmetic, not a separate memory-safety weakness; the out-of-bounds read is a downstream consequence of the wrong number.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The guard at line 21 uses the wrong upper bound (fs->clusters - 1 instead of the correct +1), so for a FAT12 filesystem with an odd cluster count the third-to-last even entry is treated as the last. Its write at lines 25-26 then combines with the following entry read at line 22, corrupting the second-to-last entry; the corrupted value can later be used as an out-of-bounds index, causing invalid memory access or crash.

commit_msg:
_asn1_extract_der_octet: catch invalid input cases early

That is, check the calculated lengths for validity prior
to entering a loop. This avoids an infinite recursion.
Reported by Pascal Cuoq.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    counter_end = der_len - 2;'], 'added_lines': ['    {', '      if (der_len < 2)', '        return ASN1_DER_ERROR;', '      counter_end = der_len - 2;', '    }', '', '  if (counter_end < counter)', '    return ASN1_DER_ERROR;']}
description: The _asn1_extract_der_octet function in lib/decoding.c in GNU Libtasn1 before 4.8, when used without the ASN1_DECODE_FLAG_STRICT_DER flag, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite recursion) via a crafted certificate.

code_evidence: When len2 is -1 (indefinite length), counter_end is set to der_len - 2 with no check that der_len is at least 2, so the subtraction can underflow or produce a value below counter.

The while loop recurses via _asn1_extract_der_octet on the nested content (lines 34-36) and advances counter by len2 + len3 + 1; with a malformed counter_end the loop bound can fail to progress toward termination.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 covers improper resource management errors; here the missing length validation leads to exhausted call-stack resources via infinite recursion. The weakness is the unconstrained loop/recursion bound, distinct from a simple buffer overread.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound counter_end is computed from attacker-controlled lengths without validating that it is reachable from counter. Trigger: a crafted DER certificate with an indefinite-length octet string where der_len < 2 or counter_end < counter. Consequence: the loop and its recursive call do not terminate, causing unbounded recursion and a denial of service.

code_evidence: Line 4 casts face->var (a generic void pointer) to FT_Service_MetricsVariations, then line 5 invokes var->metrics_adjust through that cast pointer without validating the actual pointed-to object type.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The cast at line 4 treats a resource as an incompatible type and line 5 dereferences it, matching CWE-843. This is not merely a missing NULL check; the weakness is the type mismatch enabling invalid function-pointer dispatch.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the generic face->var slot is reinterpreted as FT_Service_MetricsVariations and its function pointer is called. Trigger: a face where face->var holds a different object (e.g. a TrueType variation service rather than the CFF metrics service). Consequence: the wrong function pointer is dispatched, leading to type confusion and possible arbitrary code execution.

patch 9.0.0579: using freed memory when 'tagfunc' wipes out buffer

Problem:    Using freed memory when 'tagfunc' wipes out buffer that holds
            'complete'.
Solution:   Make a copy of the option.  Make sure cursor position is valid.

--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -5,7 +5,8 @@
 
     if (flag == 'w')		// just windows
     {
-	if (buf == curbuf || wp == NULL)  // first call for this flag/expansion
+	if (buf == curbuf || !win_valid(wp))
+	    // first call for this flag/expansion or window was closed
 	    wp = curwin;
 	while ((wp = (wp->w_next != NULL ? wp->w_next : firstwin)) != curwin
 		&& wp->w_buffer->b_scanned)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (buf == curbuf || wp == NULL)  // first call for this flag/expansion'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (buf == curbuf || !win_valid(wp))', '\t    // first call for this flag/expansion or window was closed']}
description: Use After Free in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0579.

code_evidence: The static pointer wp persists across calls. Line 6 only checks wp == NULL before reuse; a stored wp pointing to a window that was closed (and freed) by the 'tagfunc' callback still passes this check. Lines 7-10 then dereference wp->w_next and wp->w_buffer on the freed window.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function reads wp->w_next and wp->w_buffer from a window that may already be freed, exactly the reuse of freed memory. The missing win_valid() check is the constraint gap; the resulting access, not just a NULL check, is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cached static window pointer wp is validated only for NULL, not for liveness, so a window freed during the 'tagfunc' callback is reused. Trigger: completion traversal calls ins_compl_next_buf after 'tagfunc' wipes out the buffer/window. Consequence: dereference of freed memory leads to use-after-free read/crash or memory corruption.
