diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (vorbis_update_metadata(s, idx) >= 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (vorbis_update_metadata(s, idx) >= 0 && priv->len[1] > 10) {']}
description: A vulnerability classified as problematic has been found in FFmpeg 2.0. Affected is the function vorbis_header of the file libavformat/oggparsevorbis.c. The manipulation leads to memory corruption. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

code_evidence: At line 61, new_len is computed from AV_RL32(priv->packet[1] + 7) without first ensuring packet[1] contains at least 11 bytes (read at offset 7); the fix adds priv->len[1] > 10 to the guard at line 60. If vorbis_update_metadata succeeds while len[1] <= 10, the 4-byte read at packet[1]+7 extends past the allocation made at line 23 (size os->psize). Subsequent writes at lines 63-64 are bounded by new_len < os->psize, so the primary defect is the unchecked read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 covers writing past buffer bounds; here the same missing size constraint exposes an out-of-bounds access on packet[1], and new_len derived from the OOB read can drive later in-buffer writes. The direct supported defect is the unchecked length leading to out-of-bounds memory access, consistent with the out-of-bounds memory-corruption class targeted.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the metadata branch trusts priv->packet[1] to hold a Vorbis comment header and reads a 32-bit length at offset 7 without verifying len[1] exceeds 10. Trigger: a crafted Ogg packet with pkt_type 3 arriving when packet[1] is short (or absent) while vorbis_update_metadata returns >=0. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of the heap buffer, leading to memory corruption/crash as reported.

commit_msg:
Bug 698592: Mark variable fz_var(), avoiding optimization.

The change in 2707fa9e8e6d17d794330e719dec1b08161fb045
in build_filter_chain() allows for the variable chain
to reside in a register, which means that the bug is
likely to only be visible if built under optimization.

First the chain variable is transferred to chain2, then
set to NULL, then when an exception occurs in build_filter()
the filter chain will be freed by build_filter(). Next
the expectation is that execution proceeds to fz_catch()
where fz_drop_stream() would be called with chain == NULL.

However due to the chain variable residing in a register,
its value is not NULL as expected, but was reset to its
original value upon the exception (since they use setjmp()),
hence fz_drop_stream() is called with a non-NULL value.

Marking the chain variable with fz_var() prevents the
compiler from allowing the chain variable to reside in
a register and hence its value will remain NULL and
never be reset.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tfz_var(chain);']}
description: The build_filter_chain function in pdf/pdf-stream.c in Artifex MuPDF before 2017-09-25 mishandles a certain case where a variable may reside in a register, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (Fitz fz_drop_imp use-after-free and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PDF document.

code_evidence: The loop copies chain into chain2, sets chain to NULL, then assigns the result of build_filter() back to chain; if build_filter() throws, chain is expected to remain NULL.

In fz_catch(), fz_drop_stream(ctx, chain) is called on chain; due to setjmp/longjmp and register allocation, chain may be restored to its pre-try value (the already-consumed chain2), so fz_drop_stream() operates on a stream that build_filter() already freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because fz_drop_stream() dereferences/releases a stream object after build_filter() freed it, matching reuse of freed memory. This is a stale-pointer lifetime defect, not merely a NULL-pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: chain is not marked fz_var(), so it may live in a register and its NULL assignment at line 16 is lost when fz_catch() resumes after an exception. Trigger: build_filter() throws during filter-chain construction. Consequence: fz_drop_stream() at line 22 receives a stale non-NULL pointer to a stream already freed by build_filter(), causing use-after-free and application crash.

commit_msg:
userfaultfd: hugetlbfs: prevent UFFDIO_COPY to fill beyond the end of i_size

This oops:

  kernel BUG at fs/hugetlbfs/inode.c:484!
  RIP: remove_inode_hugepages+0x3d0/0x410
  Call Trace:
    hugetlbfs_setattr+0xd9/0x130
    notify_change+0x292/0x410
    do_truncate+0x65/0xa0
    do_sys_ftruncate.constprop.3+0x11a/0x180
    SyS_ftruncate+0xe/0x10
    tracesys+0xd9/0xde

was caused by the lack of i_size check in hugetlb_mcopy_atomic_pte.

mmap() can still succeed beyond the end of the i_size after vmtruncate
zapped vmas in those ranges, but the faults must not succeed, and that
includes UFFDIO_COPY.

We could differentiate the retval to userland to represent a SIGBUS like
a page fault would do (vs SIGSEGV), but it doesn't seem very useful and
we'd need to pick a random retval as there's no meaningful syscall
retval that would differentiate from SIGSEGV and SIGBUS, there's just
-EFAULT.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20171016223914.2421-2-aarcange@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Kravetz <mike.kravetz@oracle.com>
Cc: Mike Rapoport <rppt@linux.vnet.ibm.com>
Cc: "Dr. David Alan Gilbert" <dgilbert@redhat.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tstruct address_space *mapping = dst_vma->vm_file->f_mapping;', '\t\tpgoff_t idx = vma_hugecache_offset(h, dst_vma, dst_addr);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct address_space *mapping;', '\tpgoff_t idx;', '\tunsigned long size;', '\tmapping = dst_vma->vm_file->f_mapping;', '\tidx = vma_hugecache_offset(h, dst_vma, dst_addr);', '', '\t\tsize = i_size_read(mapping->host) >> huge_page_shift(h);', '\t\tret = -EFAULT;', '\t\tif (idx >= size)', '\t\t\tgoto out_release_nounlock;', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * Serialization between remove_inode_hugepages() and', '\t\t * huge_add_to_page_cache() below happens through the', '\t\t * hugetlb_fault_mutex_table that here must be hold by', '\t\t * the caller.', '\t\t */', '', '\t/*', '\t * Recheck the i_size after holding PT lock to make sure not', '\t * to leave any page mapped (as page_mapped()) beyond the end', '\t * of the i_size (remove_inode_hugepages() is strict about', "\t * enforcing that). If we bail out here, we'll also leave a", '\t * page in the radix tree in the vm_shared case beyond the end', '\t * of the i_size, but remove_inode_hugepages() will take care', '\t * of it as soon as we drop the hugetlb_fault_mutex_table.', '\t */', '\tsize = i_size_read(mapping->host) >> huge_page_shift(h);', '\tret = -EFAULT;', '\tif (idx >= size)', '\t\tgoto out_release_unlock;']}
description: A flaw was found in the hugetlb_mcopy_atomic_pte function in mm/hugetlb.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.12. A lack of size check could cause a denial of service (BUG).

code_evidence: In the shared case the page is inserted into the page cache at idx derived from dst_addr without any comparison against the file's i_size, so a UFFDIO_COPY beyond EOF adds a page past the intended inode boundary.
After taking the PTE lock, the function maps the page into the destination without rechecking i_size; the page can be mapped beyond the end of the file.
The mapping, rmap and PTE installation proceed unconditionally for the in-range-checked offset, leaving a page_mapped page beyond i_size that remove_inode_hugepages later trips over.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits an operation on a memory region (the hugetlbfs page cache/PTE range) outside the intended i_size boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation class. The missing bound check is the direct cause; the crash is the resultant consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: hugetlb_mcopy_atomic_pte never verifies that the target offset is below i_size before adding the page to the page cache and installing the huge PTE. Trigger: a user issues UFFDIO_COPY for an address beyond EOF after truncation zapped the VMA range. Consequence: a page exists and is mapped past the inode size, causing remove_inode_hugepages to hit its BUG and crash the kernel (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix a dangerous integer overflow and a malloc of negative size.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 371254154
Change-Id: I250a98a3df26328770167025670235a963a72da0
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  TfLiteIntArray* ret =', '      (TfLiteIntArray*)malloc(TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(size));'], 'added_lines': ['  int alloc_size = TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(size);', '  if (alloc_size <= 0) return NULL;', '  TfLiteIntArray* ret = (TfLiteIntArray*)malloc(alloc_size);', '  if (!ret) return ret;']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The TFLite code for allocating `TFLiteIntArray`s is vulnerable to an integer overflow issue(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/4ceffae632721e52bf3501b736e4fe9d1221cdfa/tensorflow/lite/c/common.c#L24-L27). An attacker can craft a model such that the `size` multiplier is so large that the return value overflows the `int` datatype and becomes negative. In turn, this results in invalid value being given to `malloc`(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/4ceffae632721e52bf3501b736e4fe9d1221cdfa/tensorflow/lite/c/common.c#L47-L52). In this case, `ret->size` would dereference an invalid pointer. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The allocation size is computed by TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(size) and passed directly to malloc; the int-typed size multiplier can overflow, yielding a negative or small value that is used as the allocation size.
The returned pointer from malloc is dereferenced via ret->size without a NULL or negative-size check, so an overflowed allocation size propagates into an invalid pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's allocation-size calculation can wrap to a negative value in the int type before use in malloc, which is the integer overflow described by CWE-190. The NULL dereference is a downstream consequence, not a separate root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
TfLiteIntArray* ret =
(TfLiteIntArray*)malloc(TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(size));
ret->size = size;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size computation is performed in int and its result is used as a malloc argument without validating that it is positive. Trigger: an attacker-controlled large size multiplier causes the byte count to overflow to a negative value, malloc returns NULL (or an undersized block), and ret->size dereferences the invalid pointer. Consequence: crash/DoS and potential memory corruption.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    return "ASCII";', "      t = strchr (s, '@');", '      return ++s;', '  else if (STREQ (locale, "UTF-8"))', '    return "UTF-8";', '  else', '    return "ASCII";'], 'added_lines': ['    {', '      strcpy (charsetbuf, "ASCII");', '      return charsetbuf;', '    }', '      strcpy (charsetbuf, s+1);', "      t = strchr (charsetbuf, '@');", '      return charsetbuf;', '  strcpy (charsetbuf, locale);', '  return charsetbuf;']}
description: A heap-based buffer overflow exists in GNU Bash before 4.3 when wide characters, not supported by the current locale set in the LC_CTYPE environment variable, are printed through the echo built-in function. A local attacker, who can provide data to print through the "echo -e" built-in function, may use this flaw to crash a script or execute code with the privileges of the bash process. This occurs because ansicstr() in lib/sh/strtrans.c mishandles u32cconv().

code_evidence: Line 4 declares a fixed-size buffer (charsetbuf) used as the return storage. Line 8 locates the '.' in the LC_CTYPE locale string; lines 10-14 copy the charset suffix starting at s+1 into charsetbuf with strcpy and no destination length check, so a long locale suffix overflows charsetbuf and the returned pointer exposes the corrupted buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: strcpy writing an unbounded locale-derived string into a fixed buffer is an out-of-bounds write, directly matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer's bounds. A related CWE-120 (buffer copy without size check) is the more specific descendant, but the supplied target is CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an attacker-influenced LC_CTYPE value with an overlong charset suffix is copied by strcpy into the fixed charsetbuf without bounds validation, writing past the buffer's end. Trigger: a crafted locale reaching stub_charset; consequence: heap/static buffer overflow corrupting adjacent memory, enabling crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
media: stv06xx: add missing descriptor sanity checks

Make sure to check that we have two alternate settings and at least one
endpoint before accessing the second altsetting structure and
dereferencing the endpoint arrays.

This specifically avoids dereferencing NULL-pointers or corrupting
memory when a device does not have the expected descriptors.

Note that the sanity checks in stv06xx_start() and pb0100_start() are
not redundant as the driver is mixing looking up altsettings by index
and by number, which may not coincide.

Fixes: 8668d504d72c ("V4L/DVB (12082): gspca_stv06xx: Add support for st6422 bridge and sensor")
Fixes: c0b33bdc5b8d ("[media] gspca-stv06xx: support bandwidth changing")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>     # 2.6.31
Cc: Hans de Goede <hdegoede@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab+huawei@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/*', '\t * Existence of altsetting and endpoint was verified in', '\t * stv06xx_isoc_init()', '\t */']}
description: An issue was discovered in the stv06xx subsystem in the Linux kernel before 5.6.1. drivers/media/usb/gspca/stv06xx/stv06xx.c and drivers/media/usb/gspca/stv06xx/stv06xx_pb0100.c mishandle invalid descriptors, as demonstrated by a NULL pointer dereference, aka CID-485b06aadb93.

code_evidence: The function indexes intf_cache[0]->altsetting[1] and immediately dereferences alt->endpoint[0].desc.wMaxPacketSize without checking that a second altsetting or any endpoint descriptor exists.
The same alt->endpoint[0] is later written via cpu_to_le16, so a missing endpoint yields a NULL dereference on both read and write paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences altsetting[1] and endpoint[0] without validating descriptor existence, so a malformed device descriptor produces a NULL pointer dereference, matching CWE-476. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read, since the failure is a NULL/invalid pointer dereference from missing descriptors.

evidence_lines.code:
alt = &gspca_dev->dev->actconfig->intf_cache[0]->altsetting[1];
packet_size = le16_to_cpu(alt->endpoint[0].desc.wMaxPacketSize);
alt->endpoint[0].desc.wMaxPacketSize = cpu_to_le16(packet_size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: descriptor arrays (altsetting[1], endpoint[0]) are assumed present. Trigger: a device exposing fewer than two alternate settings or zero endpoints. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference in stv06xx_isoc_nego, crashing the kernel; the write path could also corrupt memory if the pointer is invalid.

commit_msg:
floppy_revalidate() doesn't perform any error handling on lock_fdc()
result. lock_fdc() might actually be interrupted by a signal (it waits for
fdc becoming non-busy interruptibly). In such case, floppy_revalidate()
proceeds as if it had claimed the lock, but it fact it doesn't.

In case of multiple threads trying to open("/dev/fdX"), this leads to
serious corruptions all over the place, because all of a sudden there is
no critical section protection (that'd otherwise be guaranteed by locked
fd) whatsoever.

While at this, fix the fact that the 'interruptible' parameter to
lock_fdc() doesn't make any sense whatsoever, because we always wait
interruptibly anyway.

Most of the lock_fdc() callsites do properly handle error (and propagate
EINTR), but floppy_revalidate() and floppy_check_events() don't. Fix this.

Spotted by 'syzkaller' tool.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive, false))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (lock_fdc(drive))']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernels implementation of the floppy disk drive controller driver software. The impact of this issue is lessened by the fact that the default permissions on the floppy device (/dev/fd0) are restricted to root. If the permissions on the device have changed the impact changes greatly. In the default configuration root (or equivalent) permissions are required to attack this flaw.

code_evidence: get_floppy_geometry calls lock_fdc(drive, false) and, on a nonzero result, returns -EINTR without touching the controller.
When lock_fdc succeeds, the function calls poll_drive, process_fd_request and dereferences current_type[drive]; these operations assume the fdc/drive lock is held.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the floppy driver relies on lock_fdc to provide exclusive access to the shared controller and drive state; an interruptible lock wait that fails without enforcing exclusivity allows concurrent code sequences to modify that shared resource. This function itself propagates the error, so the weakness is the lock primitive's non-atomic acquisition semantics, not a missing return-value check here.

evidence_lines.code:
if (lock_fdc(drive, false))
return -EINTR;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of lock_fdc is checked, but the locking primitive is interruptible, so a signal can abort the wait and the caller must not proceed. In this function, a failed lock returns early, so the critical section is not entered unlocked; the described corruption arises in callers such as floppy_revalidate that ignore the lock_fdc result. Trigger: a signal interrupting lock_fdc while another thread operates on the same drive. Consequence: absent mutual exclusion, concurrent access to the floppy controller and current_type state can corrupt driver state.

commit_msg:
Fixed aggregation methods of Promise ctor with array-like object.

Previously, while iterating over an array-like object the methods may be
resolved with INVALID values. INVALID value is a special internal type which
should never be visible by ordinary functions.

The fix is to ensure that absent elements are represented by undefined value.

The following methods were fixed Promise.all(), Promise.allSettled(),
    Promise.any(), Promise.race().

This closes #483 issue on Github.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-wccp.c had a large loop that was addressed by ensuring that a calculated length was monotonically increasing.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over n_routers, a 32-bit value read directly from the packet at line 31. Inside the loop, length is only checked against 12; when it is smaller, the function returns, but the return value is a negative offset adjustment rather than a bound on iterations. Each iteration calls dissect_wccp2_router_assignment_element and EAT(12), which advances offset by 12. The patch's CHECK_LENGTH_ADVANCE_OFFSET on new_length at line 30 is intended to ensure the offset monotonically increases, but the loop itself still uses the attacker-controlled n_routers without any cap.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 (Excessive Iteration) fits because the loop count is derived from untrusted input without a sufficient upper bound, allowing resource-exhausting iteration. This is a loop-bound weakness, not merely a length-calculation error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound n_routers comes from the packet and is never validated against the available data before iteration. Trigger: a crafted WCCP packet with a large n_routers value. Consequence: excessive iterations consume CPU, causing a DoS; the offset-advance check mitigates one path but does not limit the loop count.

description: In HTMLDOC 1.9.14, an infinite loop in the gif_read_lzw function can lead to a pointer arbitrarily pointing to heap memory and resulting in a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: The while loop at [82] walks the LZW prefix chain via table[0][code] at [87]. It only exits when code < clear_code or when code == table[0][code] at [85]. If the table entries form a cycle that never reaches a code below clear_code and never self-references, the condition at [85] is never satisfied and the loop never terminates.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a loop whose exit condition depends on data-derived table links that can form a cycle, making termination unreachable; this is exactly CWE-835. It is distinguished from a buffer overflow: the defect here is non-termination, not an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the prefix-chain traversal has no bound on iteration count and relies on table[0] entries eventually dropping below clear_code. A crafted GIF whose decoded table entries form a non-self cycle keeps code >= clear_code indefinitely, so the loop spins forever. The supported consequence is CPU resource consumption (denial of service); the arbitrary pointer/buffer overflow described in the advisory is not demonstrated by these lines.

The "data->block[0]" variable comes from the user and is a number
between 0-255.  It needs to be capped to prevent writing beyond the end
of dma_buffer[].

Fixes: 5e9a97b1f449 ("i2c: ismt: Adding support for I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL")
Reported-and-tested-by: Zheyu Ma <zheyuma97@gmail.com>

Reviewed-by: Mika Westerberg <mika.westerberg@linux.intel.com>

description: A buffer overflow vulnerability was found in the Linux kernel Intel’s iSMT SMBus host controller driver in the way it handled the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL case (via the ioctl I2C_SMBUS) with malicious input data. This flaw could allow a local user to crash the system.

code_evidence: In the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL case, data->block[0] is an attacker-controlled length (0-255) taken directly from the user-supplied i2c_smbus_data. Line 109 uses it as wr_len_cmd, and line 114 passes it as the copy size to memcpy(&dma_buffer[1], &data->block[1], data->block[0]) without any upper-bound check against I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX or the size of dma_buffer (priv->buffer). dma_size is fixed to I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX at line 107, so the copy length is not constrained by the buffer capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 applies because the function copies an input buffer to an output buffer via memcpy without verifying that the input size fits the destination. A related out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) is not the issue here; the unchecked length causes a write past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the block length data->block[0] is used unchecked as the memcpy size into the fixed-size dma_buffer. Trigger: a local user issues an I2C_SMBUS ioctl with I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL and block[0] greater than I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write past dma_buffer, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially crashing the system or enabling code execution.

commit_msg: fix #55 : Byte value expressed in octal must be smaller than 256
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (num < 0) return ONIGERR_TOO_BIG_NUMBER;'], 'added_lines': ['        if (num < 0 || num >= 256) return ONIGERR_TOO_BIG_NUMBER;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Oniguruma 6.2.0, as used in Oniguruma-mod in Ruby through 2.4.1 and mbstring in PHP through 7.1.5. A heap out-of-bounds write or read occurs in next_state_val() during regular expression compilation. Octal numbers larger than 0xff are not handled correctly in fetch_token() and fetch_token_in_cc(). A malformed regular expression containing an octal number in the form of '\700' would produce an invalid code point value larger than 0xff in next_state_val(), resulting in an out-of-bounds write memory corruption.

code_evidence: In the octal escape case, scan_unsigned_octal_number(&p, end, 3, enc) parses up to three octal digits and the result is stored in int num. The only guard is 'if (num < 0)', so a value like '\700' (octal 0700 = 448) passes validation. num is then assigned directly to tok->u.c with tok->base = 8 and tok->type = TK_RAW_BYTE without narrowing to a byte.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing upper-bound check lets an invalid code point flow into a byte-sized consumer, writing past the intended buffer in next_state_val(). CWE-787 matches the resulting out-of-bounds write; it is not merely an integer/numeric error because the supported consequence is memory corruption from the write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the octal token parser accepts values up to 0o777 but the token is treated as a raw byte, so values >= 256 exceed the byte domain expected downstream. Trigger: a malformed pattern containing an octal escape such as '\700' in a character class. Consequence: the oversized token propagates to next_state_val() and causes an out-of-bounds write (memory corruption).

commit_msg: MC: check that image chroma format matches the SPS chroma format (#339)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  if (sps->chroma_format_idc != img->get_chroma_format()) {', '    img->integrity = INTEGRITY_DECODING_ERRORS;', '    ctx->add_warning(DE265_WARNING_CHROMA_OF_CURRENT_IMAGE_DOES_NOT_MATCH_SPS, false);', '    return;', '  }']}
description: Libde265 v1.0.8 was discovered to contain a heap-buffer-overflow vulnerability via ff_hevc_put_weighted_pred_avg_8_sse in sse-motion.cc. This vulnerability allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via a crafted video file.

code_evidence: sps and its SubWidthC/SubHeightC are taken from the PPS/SPS with no check that they match the actual decoded image's chroma format.

pixels[1] and pixels[2] are computed at xP/SubWidthC, yP/SubHeightC using SPS-derived subsampling, while strides come from the image; if the image chroma format differs, these pointers/strides are inconsistent with the real plane layout.
put_weighted_pred writes nPbW/SubWidthC by nPbH/SubHeightC chroma samples into pixels[1]/pixels[2] using the mismatched stride.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing chroma-format consistency check lets put_weighted_pred write chroma samples beyond the intended image plane buffer. It is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the prediction samples are stored into pixels[1]/pixels[2] with mismatched dimensions/stride.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SPS chroma subsampling used to locate chroma planes and size the write is not validated against the current image's chroma format. A crafted bitstream with mismatched SPS/image chroma makes SubWidthC/SubHeightC disagree with the plane layout, so the weighted-prediction write at [124-129] indexes past the allocated chroma buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds write (DoS/crash).

commit_msg:
libXpm uses unsigned int to store sizes, which fits size_t on 32 bit
systems, but leads to issues on 64 bit systems.

On 64 bit systems, it is possible to overflow 32 bit integers while
parsing XPM extensions in a file.

At first, it looks like a rather unimportant detail, because nobody
will seriously open a 4 GB file. But unfortunately XPM has support for
gzip compression out of the box. An attacker can therefore craft a
compressed file which is merely 4 MB in size, which makes an attack
much for feasable.

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tCountExtensions(info->extensions, info->nextensions,', '\t\t\t&ext_size, &ext_nlines);', '    if( (image->height + ext_nlines) >= UINT_MAX / sizeof(char *))', '    if( (header_size + ext_size) >= (UINT_MAX - data_size) )'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (CountExtensions(info->extensions, info->nextensions,', '\t\t\t&ext_size, &ext_nlines))', '\t    return(XpmNoMemory);', '    if (image->height > UINT_MAX - ext_nlines ||', '\timage->height + ext_nlines >= UINT_MAX / sizeof(char *))', '    if (header_size > UINT_MAX - ext_size ||', '\theader_size + ext_size >= (UINT_MAX - data_size) )']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in libXpm before 3.5.12, when a program requests parsing XPM extensions on a 64-bit platform, allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write) or execute arbitrary code via (1) the number of extensions or (2) their concatenated length in a crafted XPM file, which triggers a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Sizes are held in unsigned int (32-bit): header_size, data_size, ext_size, ext_nlines, offset.
data_size = (image->height + ext_nlines) * sizeof(char *); the addition of image->height and ext_nlines can wrap in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic before being used as allocation size.

if( (header_size + ext_size) >= (UINT_MAX - data_size) ) RETURN(XpmNoMemory); then data_size += header_size + ext_size; the sum header_size + ext_size is computed first and can wrap, defeating the guard before the allocation at XpmMalloc(data_size).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs arithmetic on size values without pre-checking that operands exceed UINT_MAX minus the other operand, allowing integer wraparound that produces an undersized allocation and out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a logic flaw; the unchecked wrap directly precedes allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: size computations in unsigned int wrap when attacker-controlled extension counts/lengths and image dimensions are added or multiplied. Trigger: a crafted XPM with extensions yields ext_nlines/ext_size such that image->height + ext_nlines or header_size + ext_size exceeds UINT_MAX. The wrapped small value passes the bounds check, so XpmMalloc allocates too little, and subsequent writes (CreatePixels/CreateExtensions/strcpy) overflow the heap.

description: A vulnerability was found in FFmpeg 2.0. It has been declared as problematic. Affected by this vulnerability is the function truemotion1_decode_header of the component Truemotion1 Handler. The manipulation leads to memory corruption. The attack can be launched remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

code_evidence: header_size is derived from s->buf[0] via rotation/mask (line 9); the check at lines 10-14 only rejects buf[0] < 0x10, so header_size can be up to 0x7f while the input buffer s->size may be smaller.
The loop at lines 15-16 reads s->buf[i] and s->buf[i+1] for i up to header_size-1, i.e. up to s->buf[header_size], with no validation that header_size+1 <= s->size.

Later, s->mb_change_bits = s->buf + header.header_size (line 98) and index_stream/index_stream_size are computed relative to s->size (lines 99-105), so an oversized header_size also yields a negative index_stream_size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked header_size lets the code index s->buf[header_size] (line 16) beyond the allocated input buffer, writing/reading outside the intended buffer bounds. The patch adds exactly this missing size constraint (header.header_size + 1 > s->size), confirming the out-of-bounds access is the targeted weakness rather than a mere logic error.

evidence_lines.code:
for (i = 1; i < header.header_size; i++)
header_buffer[i - 1] = s->buf[i] ^ s->buf[i + 1];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the header-size check only enforces a minimum (buf[0] >= 0x10) and never verifies header.header_size + 1 <= s->size before the loop dereferences s->buf[i+1]. Trigger: a crafted packet whose first byte encodes a header_size larger than the actual packet. Consequence: the loop at lines 15-16 reads past the input buffer, and the derived index_stream_size becomes negative, leading to invalid reads/out-of-bounds access and memory corruption.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['#ifndef _MSC_VER', '\t  char filename[dirent.namelen + 1]; ', '#else', '#endif', '\t  if (grub_errno)', '\t  if (! fdiro)', '\t      if (grub_errno)', '\t\t{', '\t  if (hook (filename, type, fdiro, closure))'], 'added_lines': ['if (!filename) {', 'break;', '}', '\t  if (grub_errno) {', '            free (filename);', '\t  }', '\t  if (! fdiro) {', '            free (filename);', '          }', '\t      if (grub_errno) {', '                  free (filename);', '\t  if (hook (filename, type, fdiro, closure)) {', '            free (filename);', '          }', '          free (filename);']}
description: The grub_memmove function in shlr/grub/kern/misc.c in radare2 1.5.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer underflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted binary file, possibly related to a buffer underflow in fs/ext2.c in GNU GRUB 2.02.

code_evidence: On non-MSVC builds, filename is a fixed-size stack array sized from the on-disk dirent.namelen field (lines 29-33), with no validation that namelen is bounded.
grub_ext2_read_file copies dirent.namelen bytes from the crafted filesystem image into that buffer (lines 36-38).
The terminator write filename[dirent.namelen] = '\0' (line 46) further indexes using the attacker-controlled length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-influenced data beyond the bounds of the stack-allocated filename buffer, which is the defining pattern of CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the copy and the terminating store both place bytes outside the intended array.

evidence_lines.code: filename[dirent.namelen] = '\0';

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stack buffer is allocated using an unvalidated 8-bit namelen from the untrusted ext2 directory entry, and the same length drives the subsequent read and null-termination. Trigger: a crafted ext2 image with an oversized namelen causes grub_ext2_read_file to write more bytes than the array holds, and the terminating store at index namelen also falls outside it. Supported consequence: stack memory corruption, potentially leading to crash or code execution.

description: Squid before 4.4, when SNMP is enabled, allows a denial of service (Memory Leak) via an SNMP packet.

Defend against bad PT_DYNAMIC

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/391
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
	modified:   p_lx_elf.h

description: A heap-based buffer over-read was discovered in the acc_ua_get_be32 function in miniacc.h in UPX 4.0.0 via a crafted Mach-O file.

The dynamic table is later indexed at [186,188] via dynseg[-1+ z_rel] and dynseg[-1+ z_rsz] using values dt_table from DT_REL/DT_RELSZ, with no bound against the PT_DYNAMIC region before dereferencing.

commit_msg:
Fix check-fail when bincount ops are passed invalid values.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 415063028
Change-Id: I20f8dc09933ddca1111c4efbf9a3a1e863215d02
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(ctx, size_t.dims() == 0,', '                errors::InvalidArgument("Shape must be rank 0 but is rank ",', '                                        size_t.dims()));']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `*Bincount` operations allows malicious users to cause denial of service by passing in arguments which would trigger a `CHECK`-fail. There are several conditions that the input arguments must satisfy. Some are not caught during shape inference and others are not caught during kernel implementation. This results in `CHECK` failures later when the output tensors get allocated. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Input 2 (size_t) is fetched as a Tensor at line 4, but its rank is never validated before size_t.scalar<Tidx>() is invoked at line 7. The only check on size (lines 8-10) tests the extracted value's sign, not the tensor's shape, so a non-rank-0 size_t reaches scalar<>().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code fails to check an unusual input condition (non-scalar size tensor) that the programmer assumed could not occur, leading to a CHECK-fail crash rather than a handled InvalidArgument error. This is exactly CWE-754: improper checking of exceptional conditions enabling DoS; it is not a memory-safety issue like CWE-125.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the kernel assumes size_t is rank 0 and dereferences it via scalar<Tidx>() without verifying dims()==0. Trigger: a malicious caller supplies a size tensor with rank > 0 (or otherwise malformed), which is not caught by shape inference, causing scalar() to fail a CHECK and abort the process. Supported consequence: denial of service via crash, matching the commit's reported CHECK-fail.

commit_msg:
storage_driver: Unlock object on ACL fail in storagePoolLookupByTargetPath

'virStoragePoolObjListSearch' returns a locked and refed object, thus we
must release it on ACL permission failure.

Fixes: 7aa0e8c0cb8
Resolves: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1984318
Signed-off-by: Peter Krempa <pkrempa@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Michal Privoznik <mprivozn@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (virStoragePoolLookupByTargetPathEnsureACL(conn, def) < 0)'], 'added_lines': ['        if (virStoragePoolLookupByTargetPathEnsureACL(conn, def) < 0) {', '            virStoragePoolObjEndAPI(&obj);', '        }']}
description: An improper locking issue was found in the virStoragePoolLookupByTargetPath API of libvirt. It occurs in the storagePoolLookupByTargetPath function where a locked virStoragePoolObj object is not properly released on ACL permission failure. Clients connecting to the read-write socket with limited ACL permissions could use this flaw to acquire the lock and prevent other users from accessing storage pool/volume APIs, resulting in a denial of service condition. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

code_evidence: virStoragePoolObjListSearch returns a locked and refed obj; on ACL failure at line 16 the function returns NULL at line 17 without calling virStoragePoolObjEndAPI, leaving the lock held on the early-return path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 fits because the function acquires a lock via virStoragePoolObjListSearch but fails to release it on the ACL failure path, an improper lock release. This is a lock-lifecycle defect rather than missing synchronization generally; the paired unlock on the success path confirms the intended contract.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the early ACL-denial return bypasses the virStoragePoolObjEndAPI(&obj) unlock/release that the normal path performs at line 19. Trigger: a client with insufficient ACL permissions calls the API and virStoragePoolLookupByTargetPathEnsureACL returns <0. Consequence: the storage pool object lock remains held, blocking other users' storage pool/volume operations and causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
Have a common routine for converting dates and times to strings.

Have a routine that takes a buffer, a strftime format, and a struct tm *
as arguments, and:

* checks whether the struct tm * is null and, if so, returns a string
indicating that the date and time couldn't be converted;

* otherwise, passes it to strftime(), along with the buffer and the
format argument and, if strftime() returns 0, meaning the string didn't
fit into the buffer and thus that the buffer's contents are undefined,
returns a string indicating that the date and time didn't fit into the
buffer;

* otherwise, returns a pointer to the buffer.

Call that routine instead of directly calling strftime() in printers;
that prevents printing a buffer with undefined data if the buffer isn't
big enough for the string.

Also, when generating file names using an strftime format, check the
return value of strftime() to make sure the buffer didn't overflow.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    struct tm *tm;', '\t\tND_PRINT(" (unrepresentable)");', '\t\ttm = gmtime(&seconds);', '\t\tif (tm == NULL) {', '\t\t    /*', "\t\t     * gmtime() can't handle it.", '\t\t     * (Yes, that might happen with some version of', "\t\t     * Microsoft's C library.)", '\t\t     */', '\t\t    ND_PRINT(" (unrepresentable)");', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t    /* use ISO 8601 (RFC3339) format */', '\t\t    strftime(time_buf, sizeof (time_buf), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tm);', '\t\t    ND_PRINT(" (%s)", time_buf);', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t    const char *time_string;', '\t\ttime_string = "[Time is too large to fit into a time_t]";', '\t\t/* use ISO 8601 (RFC3339) format */', '\t\ttime_string = nd_format_time(time_buf, sizeof (time_buf),', '\t\t  "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", gmtime(&seconds));', '\t    ND_PRINT(" (%s)", time_string);']}
description: The SMB protocol decoder in tcpdump version 4.99.3 can perform an out-of-bounds write when decoding a crafted network packet.

code_evidence: time_buf is a 128-byte stack buffer [21]. The result of strftime is discarded [30], so the code cannot detect when the formatted ISO 8601 string did not fit; in that case strftime leaves the buffer contents undefined, and the code then prints it with ND_PRINT(" (%s)", time_buf) [31]. The prior gmtime NULL check [27-28] only guards the tm pointer, not the buffer size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 applies because the unchecked strftime result allows the buffer to remain undefined and then be consumed by ND_PRINT, which is the memory-safety defect the commit fixes by routing through nd_format_time. A pure format-string weakness (CWE-134) does not fit: the format is a constant, and the defect is the missing buffer-overflow check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of strftime is ignored, so a failed conversion leaves time_buf with undefined contents that are still passed to ND_PRINT. The trigger is a strftime result of 0 (output exceeding the 128-byte buffer), which the code treats as success; the supported consequence is use of undefined buffer data and possible out-of-bounds read/write during printing, not a direct write past time_buf by this function.

commit_msg:
ohci: allocate timer only once.

Allocate timer once, at init time, instead of allocating/freeing
it all the time when starting/stopping the bus.  Simplifies the
code, also fixes bugs (memory leak) due to missing checks whenever
the time is already allocated or not.

Cc: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Reported-by: Zuozhi Fzz <zuozhi.fzz@alibaba-inc.com>
Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    ohci->eof_timer = timer_new_ns(QEMU_CLOCK_VIRTUAL,', '                                   ohci_frame_boundary, ohci);']}
description: The ohci_bus_start function in the USB OHCI emulation support (hw/usb/hcd-ohci.c) in QEMU allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and QEMU process crash) via vectors related to multiple eof_timers.

code_evidence: usb_ohci_init initializes the OHCIState fields but never allocates ohci->eof_timer; the patch adds timer_new_ns at the end of this function. Without that allocation, ohci->eof_timer remains NULL for callers of ohci_bus_start, which then use the timer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is use of a NULL timer pointer, matching CWE-476. Contrasted with a memory leak (CWE-401), which is the other symptom noted, but the crash arises from dereferencing the NULL eof_timer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: eof_timer is only allocated at bus start and freed at stop, so repeated start/stop cycles leave it NULL or dangling; starting the bus again uses the timer without a validity check. Trigger: a guest administrator repeatedly starts/stops the OHCI bus. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and QEMU process crash (DoS).

commit_msg: fixed #2238
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (parser->codec->LastError) return;']}
description: Uncontrolled Recursion in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.1.0-DEV.

code_evidence: Line 5 reads a bit and returns early only when it is zero; the added line 3 guard checks LastError only before SFS_Expression, not before the recursive call. Line 6 appends a comma and line 7 calls SFS_CompoundExpression(parser) again with no recursion-depth counter or bound.

Trigger: a crafted stream keeps the read bit nonzero, so each frame recurses without the LastError guard being re-checked before line 7, exhausting the stack and causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
ARM: 7735/2: Preserve the user r/w register TPIDRURW on context switch and fork

Since commit 6a1c53124aa1 the user writeable TLS register was zeroed to
prevent it from being used as a covert channel between two tasks.

There are more and more applications coming to Windows RT,
Wine could support them, but mostly they expect to have
the thread environment block (TEB) in TPIDRURW.

This patch preserves that register per thread instead of clearing it.
Unlike the TPIDRURO, which is already switched, the TPIDRURW
can be updated from userspace so needs careful treatment in the case that we
modify TPIDRURW and call fork(). To avoid this we must always read
TPIDRURW in copy_thread.

Signed-off-by: André Hentschel <nerv@dawncrow.de>
Signed-off-by: Will Deacon <will.deacon@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Jonathan Austin <jonathan.austin@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Russell King <rmk+kernel@arm.linux.org.uk>

+++ func_after
@@ -52,7 +52,7 @@
 #endif
 
 		case PTRACE_GET_THREAD_AREA:
-			ret = put_user(task_thread_info(child)->tp_value,
+			ret = put_user(task_thread_info(child)->tp_value[0],
 				       datap);

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tret = put_user(task_thread_info(child)->tp_value,'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tret = put_user(task_thread_info(child)->tp_value[0],']}
description: The Linux kernel before 3.11 on ARM platforms, as used in Android before 2016-08-05 on Nexus 5 and 7 (2013) devices, does not properly consider user-space access to the TPIDRURW register, which allows local users to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka Android internal bug 28749743 and Qualcomm internal bug CR561044.

code_evidence: In the PTRACE_GET_THREAD_AREA case, arch_ptrace reads task_thread_info(child)->tp_value and copies it to the caller-supplied user pointer datap via put_user. The ptrace caller's privilege over the child task is not re-validated here; the value exposed is the child's thread-area register state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers improper management of permissions/privileges around access control. Here the ptrace path discloses task register state without a permission constraint, matching that category; the weakness is the missing access check, not memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The handler exposes per-task thread-pointer state (tp_value) to whoever issues PTRACE_GET_THREAD_AREA on the child, without any access-control check in this function. A local process that can ptrace the target task (or a task with insufficient privilege separation) triggers the read and obtains the register value, enabling observation of security-relevant per-thread state and privilege escalation as described.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.1 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.7, the AllJoyn dissector could crash with a buffer over-read, triggered by network traffic or a capture file. commit_msg:
[CVE-2022-40304] Fix dict corruption caused by entity reference cycles

When an entity reference cycle is detected, the entity content is
cleared by setting its first byte to zero. But the entity content might
be allocated from a dict. In this case, the dict entry becomes corrupted
leading to all kinds of logic errors, including memory errors like
double-frees.

Stop storing entity content, orig, ExternalID and SystemID in a dict.
These values are unlikely to occur multiple times in a document, so they
shouldn't have been stored in a dict in the first place.

Thanks to Ned Williamson and Nathan Wachholz working with Google Project
Zero for the report!
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (ExternalID != NULL)', '\t    ret->ExternalID = xmlDictLookup(dict, ExternalID, -1);', '\tif (SystemID != NULL)', '\t    ret->SystemID = xmlDictLookup(dict, SystemID, -1);', '\tif ((dict != NULL) && (ret->length < 5))', '\t    ret->content = (xmlChar *)', '\t                   xmlDictLookup(dict, content, ret->length);', '\telse', '\t    ret->content = xmlStrndup(content, ret->length);'], 'added_lines': ['\tret->ExternalID = xmlStrdup(ExternalID);', '\tret->SystemID = xmlStrdup(SystemID);', '\tret->content = xmlStrndup(content, ret->length);']}
description: An issue was discovered in libxml2 before 2.10.3. Certain invalid XML entity definitions can corrupt a hash table key, potentially leading to subsequent logic errors. In one case, a double-free can be provoked.

code_evidence: When a dict is supplied, ExternalID and SystemID are interned into the dict via xmlDictLookup, so ret->ExternalID and ret->SystemID alias dict-owned storage rather than independent allocations.
Short entity content (length < 5) with a non-NULL dict is also interned via xmlDictLookup, making ret->content point into the dict's string pool instead of a separate xmlStrndup allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is aliasing of dict-owned memory that is later mutated/freed through the entity, producing a double-free as the supported consequence. This directly matches CWE-415 (calling free twice on the same address); the dict-key corruption is the mechanism, not a separate weakness label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Entity fields (ExternalID, SystemID, and short content) are stored as pointers into the shared dict. If an entity reference cycle is later detected, the entity content is cleared by writing a zero byte to ret->content, which actually mutates the dict key, corrupting the hash table; subsequent logic errors can lead to a double-free.

commit_msg:
ipsec: Fix aborted xfrm policy dump crash

An independent security researcher, Mohamed Ghannam, has reported
this vulnerability to Beyond Security's SecuriTeam Secure Disclosure
program.

The xfrm_dump_policy_done function expects xfrm_dump_policy to
have been called at least once or it will crash.  This can be
triggered if a dump fails because the target socket's receive
buffer is full.

This patch fixes it by using the cb->start mechanism to ensure that
the initialisation is always done regardless of the buffer situation.

description: The XFRM dump policy implementation in net/xfrm/xfrm_user.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.11 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) via a crafted SO_RCVBUF setsockopt system call in conjunction with XFRM_MSG_GETPOLICY Netlink messages.

code_evidence: Line 3 casts the netlink callback argument area (&cb->args[1]) to a struct xfrm_policy_walk pointer without verifying that xfrm_dump_policy initialized that walk state; line 5 then passes this pointer to xfrm_policy_walk_done, which walks and frees entries reached through it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The crash stems from dereferencing and freeing policy entries via a walk structure whose lifetime/initialization was never established, so memory is accessed after being freed. This matches CWE-416 (Use After Free) rather than a simple null dereference, since stale pointers are traversed and released.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The done handler assumes xfrm_dump_policy ran and populated the walk structure at &cb->args[1]. When the dump aborts early (e.g., receive buffer full), that state was never initialized, yet xfrm_policy_walk_done traverses the uninitialized walk and frees/references policy entries through stale pointers. The supported consequence is use-after-free, leading to memory corruption, denial of service, or privilege escalation.

commit_msg: Issue #161: Don't fclose a FILE that is NULL.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tfclose(f);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (f) fclose(f);']}
description: In Artifex MuJS through 1.2.0, jsP_dumpsyntax in jsdump.c has a NULL pointer dereference, as demonstrated by mujs-pp.

code_evidence: f is initialized to NULL at line 3 and only assigned by fopen at line 11. The js_try error handler at lines 6-10 runs fclose(f) at line 8 before any successful fopen; if js_malloc or an earlier checked call throws while f is still NULL, the handler passes NULL to fclose, which dereferences it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function passes a pointer expected to be a valid FILE to fclose while it is provably NULL, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. This is a missing NULL guard, not a use-after-free or double-free, since the pointer was never assigned.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cleanup handler unconditionally calls fclose on a FILE* that may still be NULL when an exception is raised before fopen succeeds. Trigger: any throwing operation during that window (e.g., js_malloc failure). Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
blk-mq: fix race between timeout and freeing request

Inside timeout handler, blk_mq_tag_to_rq() is called
to retrieve the request from one tag. This way is obviously
wrong because the request can be freed any time and some
fiedds of the request can't be trusted, then kernel oops
might be triggered[1].

Currently wrt. blk_mq_tag_to_rq(), the only special case is
that the flush request can share same tag with the request
cloned from, and the two requests can't be active at the same
time, so this patch fixes the above issue by updating tags->rqs[tag]
with the active request(either flush rq or the request cloned
from) of the tag.

Also blk_mq_tag_to_rq() gets much simplified with this patch.

Given blk_mq_tag_to_rq() is mainly for drivers and the caller must
make sure the request can't be freed, so in bt_for_each() this
helper is replaced with tags->rqs[tag].

description: In blk_mq_tag_to_rq in blk-mq.c in the upstream kernel, there is a possible use after free due to a race condition when a request has been previously freed by blk_mq_complete_request. This could lead to local escalation of privilege. Product: Android. Versions: Android kernel. Android ID: A-63083046.

code_evidence: In the multi-queue path, blk_kick_flush copies first_rq->mq_ctx and first_rq->tag into the shared flush_rq but never publishes flush_rq as the owner of that tag in the driver's tag map; the tag continues to resolve to first_rq.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is improper synchronization over the shared tag slot: two code sequences (flush setup and timeout lookup) can act on the same tag without exclusivity, matching CWE-362. It is a race rather than a plain lifetime bug because the stale mapping only becomes dangerous when the concurrent timeout interleaves with request freeing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the flush request borrows another request's tag without taking exclusive ownership, so the tag-to-request mapping still points at the original request. A concurrent timeout path resolving that tag can retrieve a request that is being completed/freed, yielding a use-after-free; the supported consequence is a kernel oops or local privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Bluetooth: hci_qca: Fix NULL vs IS_ERR_OR_NULL check in qca_serdev_probe

The function devm_gpiod_get_index() return error pointers on error.
Thus devm_gpiod_get_index_optional() could return NULL and error pointers.
The same as devm_gpiod_get_optional() function. Using IS_ERR_OR_NULL()
check to catch error pointers.

Fixes: 77131dfe ("Bluetooth: hci_qca: Replace devm_gpiod_get() with devm_gpiod_get_optional()")
Signed-off-by: Miaoqian Lin <linmq006@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!qcadev->bt_en && data->soc_type == QCA_WCN6750) {', '\t\tif (!qcadev->sw_ctrl && data->soc_type == QCA_WCN6750)', '\t\tif (!qcadev->bt_en) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (IS_ERR_OR_NULL(qcadev->bt_en) && data->soc_type == QCA_WCN6750) {', '\t\tif (IS_ERR_OR_NULL(qcadev->sw_ctrl) && data->soc_type == QCA_WCN6750)', '\t\tif (IS_ERR_OR_NULL(qcadev->bt_en)) {']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.16.3, drivers/bluetooth/hci_qca.c misinterprets the devm_gpiod_get_index_optional return value (expects it to be NULL in the error case, whereas it is actually an error pointer).

code_evidence: qcadev->bt_en is assigned from devm_gpiod_get_optional(), which returns an ERR_PTR on error; the check `!qcadev->bt_en` is false for error pointers, so the error path is skipped and the failure is not recorded (power_ctrl_enabled stays true).
qcadev->sw_ctrl likewise receives an optional GPIO result, but the `!qcadev->sw_ctrl` test misses ERR_PTR values, so no warning is emitted and the invalid pointer persists.
In the else branch, bt_en is fetched the same way and only tested with `!qcadev->bt_en`; an error pointer passes the check, leaving power_ctrl_enabled true.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an incomplete NULL/error-pointer validation that allows an invalid pointer to flow into later use, matching CWE-476's expectation of a valid pointer where an error pointer is actually present. It is a pointer-validation flaw rather than a general logic bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: optional GPIO getters return ERR_PTR on failure, but the code tests only for NULL. Trigger: a GPIO lookup failure (e.g. bad DT mapping) yields an error pointer. Consequence: the error is silently ignored, power_ctrl_enabled remains true, and later qca_power_off/hdev shutdown paths may use the invalid GPIO pointer, risking a crash or unexpected power handling.

description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. A null pointer dereference in bond_ipsec_add_sa() may lead to local denial of service.

commit_msg:
9pfs: fix memory leak in v9fs_write

If an error occurs when marshalling the transfer length to the guest, the
v9fs_write() function doesn't free an IO vector, thus leading to a memory
leak. This patch fixes the issue.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liqiang6-s@360.cn>
Reviewed-by: Greg Kurz <groug@kaod.org>
[groug, rephrased the changelog]
Signed-off-by: Greg Kurz <groug@kaod.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        goto out;'], 'added_lines': ['        goto out_qiov;']}
description: Memory leak in the v9fs_write function in hw/9pfs/9p.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by leveraging failure to free an IO vector.

code_evidence: Line 41 initializes the local QEMUIOVector qiov via qemu_iovec_init. After the write loop, line 61 marshals the total length; if pdu_marshal fails (err < 0), line 63 jumps to the out label, skipping the out_qiov block at lines 67-68 that calls qemu_iovec_destroy(&qiov). The qiov's allocated iovec array is therefore never released on this error path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 covers failure to release a resource after its effective lifetime. The qiov is allocated at line 41 and its lifetime ends at function exit, but the err<0 path at line 63 skips qemu_iovec_destroy, matching missing resource release. This is distinct from a use-after-free or double-free since the resource is simply never freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch after pdu_marshal bypasses the out_qiov cleanup label, so the initialized qiov is not destroyed. Trigger: a guest-driven 9p write where marshalling the transfer length fails. Consequence: repeated failures leak memory in the QEMU process, enabling guest-admin-induced resource-consumption DoS.

commit_msg:
Seth found that the CPU-entry-area; the piece of per-cpu data that is
mapped into the userspace page-tables for kPTI is not subject to any
randomization -- irrespective of kASLR settings.

On x86_64 a whole P4D (512 GB) of virtual address space is reserved for
this structure, which is plenty large enough to randomize things a
little.

As such, use a straight forward randomization scheme that avoids
duplicates to spread the existing CPUs over the available space.

  [ bp: Fix le build. ]

Reported-by: Seth Jenkins <sethjenkins@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Signed-off-by: Dave Hansen <dave.hansen@linux.intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Borislav Petkov <bp@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tinit_cea_offsets();']}
description: A flaw possibility of memory leak in the Linux kernel cpu_entry_area mapping of X86 CPU data to memory was found in the way user can guess location of exception stack(s) or other important data. A local user could use this flaw to get access to some important data with expected location in memory.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only initializes CPU entry area page tables and never allocates or releases heap memory, so it does not support CWE-401 (missing release of memory).

commit_msg:
In function ip6_ra_control(), the pointer new_ra is allocated a memory
space via kmalloc(). And it is used in the following codes. However,
when there is a memory allocation error, kmalloc() fails. Thus null
pointer dereference may happen. And it will cause the kernel to crash.
Therefore, we should check the return value and handle the error.

Signed-off-by: Gen Zhang <blackgod016574@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (sel >= 0 && !new_ra)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;']}
description: An issue was discovered in ip6_ra_control in net/ipv6/ipv6_sockglue.c in the Linux kernel through 5.1.5. There is an unchecked kmalloc of new_ra, which might allow an attacker to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash). NOTE: This has been disputed as not an issue

code_evidence: Line 6 allocates new_ra with kmalloc when sel >= 0 but does not check the result; the pointer may be NULL. Lines 7-10 enter the locked loop and may dereference ra, but new_ra is not used there. Line 22 checks !new_ra only after the loop, and line 26 dereferences new_ra->sk without a prior NULL check when sel >= 0, so a failed allocation reaches a NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences a pointer (new_ra) that it expects to be valid but that can be NULL after a failed allocation. This is a NULL pointer dereference, not a use-after-free or buffer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the kmalloc result in line 6 is used unconditionally at line 26 for the sel >= 0 path. Trigger: kmalloc fails and returns NULL. Consequence: new_ra->sk dereferences NULL, causing a kernel crash (denial of service). The line 22 check is too late to prevent this dereference.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: fix unconditional helper

Ben Hawkes says:

 In the mark_source_chains function (net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c) it
 is possible for a user-supplied ipt_entry structure to have a large
 next_offset field. This field is not bounds checked prior to writing a
 counter value at the supplied offset.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!unconditional(&e->arp))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!unconditional(e))']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

code_evidence: Line 5 gates the function on unconditional(&e->arp), which only inspects the arp header's address-match flags, not the presence of matches/targets. Lines 7-9 then accept the entry's target only if it is XT_STANDARD_TARGET, and lines 10-12 derive the verdict from that target. Because the gate is weaker than the caller's notion of 'unconditional', an entry with matches but wildcard addresses passes here, so malformed user-supplied entries reach later chain-walking code that trusts next_offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write beyond the intended buffer based on an unchecked offset, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The flaw here is the insufficient validation enabling that write; the write itself is the direct manifestation of the buffer-bounds violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the underflow check uses a narrower 'unconditional' predicate (address-only) than the caller's, so entries containing matches are misclassified as unconditional absolute verdicts. Trigger: a local user supplies an ipt_entry with wildcard addresses plus matches and a large next_offset via IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE. Consequence: the rule is accepted and later code writes a counter at the attacker-controlled offset, causing out-of-bounds heap write (memory corruption/privilege escalation).

commit_msg:
x86/hvm: Fix the handling of non-present segments

In 32bit, the data segments may be NULL to indicate that the segment is
ineligible for use.  In both 32bit and 64bit, the LDT selector may be NULL to
indicate that the entire LDT is ineligible for use.  However, nothing in Xen
actually checks for this condition when performing other segmentation
checks.  (Note however that limit and writeability checks are correctly
performed).

Neither Intel nor AMD specify the exact behaviour of loading a NULL segment.
Experimentally, AMD zeroes all attributes but leaves the base and limit
unmodified.  Intel zeroes the base, sets the limit to 0xfffffff and resets the
attributes to just .G and .D/B.

The use of the segment information in the VMCB/VMCS is equivalent to a native
pipeline interacting with the segment cache.  The present bit can therefore
have a subtly different meaning, and it is now cooked to uniformly indicate
whether the segment is usable or not.

GDTR and IDTR don't have access rights like the other segments, but for
consistency, they are treated as being present so no special casing is needed
elsewhere in the segmentation logic.

AMD hardware does not consider the present bit for %cs and %tr, and will
function as if they were present.  They are therefore unconditionally set to
present when reading information from the VMCB, to maintain the new meaning of
usability.

Intel hardware has a separate unusable bit in the VMCS segment attributes.
This bit is inverted and stored in the present field, so the hvm code can work
with architecturally-common state.

This is CVE-2016-9386 / XSA-191.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    /* Segment not valid for use (cooked meaning of .p)? */', '    if ( !desctab.attr.fields.p )', '        goto raise_exn;']}
description: The x86 emulator in Xen does not properly treat x86 NULL segments as unusable when accessing memory, which might allow local HVM guest users to gain privileges via vectors involving "unexpected" base/limit values.

code_evidence: The function reads the GDT/LDT descriptor table and then the target descriptor, but after reading the descriptor it never validates the segment's present (P) bit before using the descriptor attributes to build the segment register.
The descriptor-table limit check is performed, but no check of desc.b bit 15 (present) occurs prior to the type/DPL checks and final sreg assignment at lines 108-116.

The present-bit check at lines 95-98 is only reached for later validation and raises an exception, but the missing early present check means a non-present (NULL) segment descriptor's base/limit/attributes are still consumed and loaded into sreg.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers permission/access-control management weaknesses; failing to enforce segment usability (present bit) lets a guest bypass segmentation access constraints and reach privileged state, matching improper access control.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( ((sel & 0xfff8) + 7) > desctab.limit )
goto raise_exn;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the emulator loads segment descriptors without verifying the present bit, so a NULL/non-present segment is treated as usable. Trigger: an HVM guest loads a NULL data/LDT segment selector; the descriptor's stale base/limit are copied into the segment register. Consequence: subsequent memory accesses use attacker-influenced base/limit, enabling privilege escalation from the guest.

description: A flaw was found in the way signature calculation was handled by cephx authentication protocol. An attacker having access to ceph cluster network who is able to alter the message payload was able to bypass signature checks done by cephx protocol. Ceph branches master, mimic, luminous and jewel are believed to be vulnerable.

code_evidence: The signature block is built only from header.crc, footer.front_crc, footer.middle_crc and footer.data_crc, plus a fixed magic/version; no message payload bytes are included.
That fixed-size block is encrypted with key.encrypt and the first 8 output bytes become the signature, so the computed signature is independent of the actual front/middle/data payload.
The resulting signature is written to *psig and returned for authentication.

Trigger: an attacker on the cluster network alters the message payload while leaving the CRCs consistent (or with the same computed signature). Consequence: the signature check passes for tampered data, letting the attacker bypass cephx authentication of message integrity.

commit_msg:
Fix null pointer dereference when parsing a corrupt ELF binary.

	PR 21957
	* elf.c (setup_group): Check for an empty or very small group
	section.
	* po/bfd.pot: Regenerate.

description: The setup_group function in elf.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a group section that is too small.

code_evidence: Line 121 declares n_elt as unsigned int and line 125 derives it from shdr->sh_size / 4; line 124 casts shdr->contents to idx without verifying contents is non-NULL or that sh_size is at least 4.
Line 126 decrements n_elt in the loop condition and line 127 dereferences (++idx)->shdr, assuming idx points to valid group entries.
Lines 130-133 reset idx from shdr->contents and again dereference (++idx)->shdr->bfd_section inside the nested loop, repeating the unvalidated pointer access.

This is a missing-validity check rather than an out-of-bounds read, since the unsafe access is to a NULL pointer.

while (--n_elt != 0)
if ((++idx)->shdr == hdr)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop trusts that a group-section header has non-NULL contents and a size large enough for at least one 4-byte entry. Trigger: a corrupt ELF with a group section whose contents are NULL or sh_size < 4. Consequence: dereferencing idx (or idx->shdr) yields a NULL pointer dereference and application crash, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
x86/insn-eval: Fix use-after-free access to LDT entry

get_desc() computes a pointer into the LDT while holding a lock that
protects the LDT from being freed, but then drops the lock and returns the
(now potentially dangling) pointer to its caller.

Fix it by giving the caller a copy of the LDT entry instead.

Fixes: 670f928ba09b ("x86/insn-eval: Add utility function to get segment descriptor")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct desc_struct *desc;', '\tdesc = get_desc(sel);', '\tif (!desc)', '\tif (!(desc->type & BIT(3)))', '\tswitch ((desc->l << 1) | desc->d) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct desc_struct desc;', '\tif (!get_desc(&desc, sel))', '\tif (!(desc.type & BIT(3)))', '\tswitch ((desc.l << 1) | desc.d) {']}
description: In arch/x86/lib/insn-eval.c in the Linux kernel before 5.1.9, there is a use-after-free for access to an LDT entry because of a race condition between modify_ldt() and a #BR exception for an MPX bounds violation.

code_evidence: The function declares a pointer desc and assigns it from get_desc(sel); get_desc acquires the LDT lock, computes a pointer into the LDT, then releases the lock before returning that pointer. The pointer is checked for NULL but not copied.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the LDT is a shared resource whose exclusive access is not preserved across the lock boundary; the interfering modify_ldt() sequence races the dereference. The fix passes a stack copy, confirming the missing atomicity rather than a simple NULL-check bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: get_desc returns a pointer into the LDT after dropping the lock that protects the LDT from being freed. Trigger: a concurrent modify_ldt() frees or replaces the LDT entry in the window between get_desc releasing the lock and the caller dereferencing desc->type and desc->l/desc->d. Consequence: use-after-free read of freed LDT memory, supporting a crash or potential information disclosure.

commit_msg:
Fix handling of invalid union data in table-based serializer

Summary:
Fix handling of invalid union data in the table-based serializer. Previously if the input contained duplicate union data, previous active member of the union was overwritten without calling the destructor of the old object, potentially causing a memory leak. In addition to that, if the second piece of data was incomplete the wrong destructor would be called during stack unwinding causing a segfault, data corruption or other undesirable effects.

Fix the issue by clearing the union if there is an active member.

Also fix the type of the data member that holds the active field id (it's `int`, not `FieldID`).

Reviewed By: yfeldblum

Differential Revision: D26440248

fbshipit-source-id: fae9ab96566cf07e14dabe9663b2beb680a01bb4
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    const auto& unionId =', '        activeUnionMemberId(object, structInfo.unionExt->unionTypeOffset);', '        unionId,', '    if (found < end && found->id == unionId) {'], 'added_lines': ['    const auto& activeId = getActiveId(object, structInfo);', '        activeId,', '    if (found < end && found->id == activeId) {']}
description: An invalid free in Thrift's table-based serialization can cause the application to crash or potentially result in code execution or other undesirable effects. This issue affects Facebook Thrift prior to v2021.02.22.00.

code_evidence: The union branch reads the active member id via activeUnionMemberId using structInfo.unionExt->unionTypeOffset, then locates the matching FieldInfo by lower_bound over fieldInfos using that id and compares found->id == unionId.

When a match is found, getValue(*found->typeInfo, object) retrieves the value according to the located type and writes it; the type-specific accessor depends on the id resolving to the correct active member.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-763 fits because the wrong release path can be selected for the union's active object: mismatched member type information leads to an incorrect destructor being called on storage that does not hold that type, matching release of an invalid pointer/reference rather than a simple leak or bounds error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The serializer derives the active union member id from a raw offset and indexes the field table by that id. If the id is stale or the union payload is invalid/incomplete, the located FieldInfo may not correspond to the actually active member, so getValue applies the wrong member type to the storage. This yields a type-confused read/write, and on unwinding a mismatched destructor may be invoked on the union storage, releasing an invalid pointer or reference (crash, corruption, possible code execution).

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.7. The KVM subsystem allows out-of-range access to memslots after a deletion, aka CID-0774a964ef56. This affects arch/s390/kvm/kvm-s390.c, include/linux/kvm_host.h, and virt/kvm/kvm_main.c.
