commit_msg:
Don't try to be smart about probing the min/max tim_t values.
Just assume that a signed time_t is really a 64-bit or 32-bit integer.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tlong ns;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tlong ns = 0;']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the (1) get_time_t_max and (2) get_time_t_min functions in archive_read_support_format_mtree.c in libarchive before 3.2.0 allow remote attackers to have unspecified impact via a crafted mtree file, which triggers undefined behavior.

code_evidence: Local m, my_time_t_max and my_time_t_min are declared int64_t; ns is a long left uninitialized before the branch.
m is parsed from attacker-controlled val via mtree_atol10; if val begins with '.', ns is cast from a parsed long, otherwise ns is set to 0.
The parsed m is clamped to the bounds returned by get_time_t_max()/get_time_t_min() and passed with ns to archive_entry_set_mtime.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the root cause is integer overflow/wraparound in computing signed time_t min/max values consumed here; the parse_keyword change merely initializes ns, but the overflow originates in the bound calculation feeding lines 132-133.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The commit fixes the min/max time_t probe (get_time_t_max/min) that computed signed time_t bounds by shifting, producing overflow/undefined behavior; that flawed bound then flows into this clamping logic as my_time_t_max/my_time_t_min. The trigger is a crafted mtree 'time' value, and the supported consequence is undefined-behavior-driven incorrect bounds handling rather than memory corruption in this function itself.

commit_msg:
Don't change the state of the ETM flags until CCS processing

Changing the ciphersuite during a renegotiation can result in a crash
leading to a DoS attack. ETM has not been implemented in 1.1.0 for DTLS
so this is TLS only.

The problem is caused by changing the flag indicating whether to use ETM
or not immediately on negotiation of ETM, rather than at CCS. Therefore,
during a renegotiation, if the ETM state is changing (usually due to a
change of ciphersuite), then an error/crash will occur.

Due to the fact that there are separate CCS messages for read and write
we actually now need two flags to determine whether to use ETM or not.

CVE-2017-3733

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (SSL_USE_ETM(s) && s->read_hash) {', '        (EVP_MD_CTX_md(s->read_hash) != NULL) && !SSL_USE_ETM(s)) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (SSL_READ_ETM(s) && s->read_hash) {', '        (!SSL_READ_ETM(s) && EVP_MD_CTX_md(s->read_hash) != NULL)) {']}
description: During a renegotiation handshake if the Encrypt-Then-Mac extension is negotiated where it was not in the original handshake (or vice-versa) then this can cause OpenSSL 1.1.0 before 1.1.0e to crash (dependent on ciphersuite). Both clients and servers are affected.

code_evidence: When SSL_USE_ETM(s) is set, the code derives mac_size from s->read_hash, requires rr[j].length >= mac_size, subtracts it, and verifies the MAC via s->method->ssl3_enc->mac and CRYPTO_memcmp.
The non-ETM branch likewise computes mac_size and checks orig_len against mac_size (plus one for CBC), then subtracts and compares the MAC.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function processes attacker-controlled record data whose structure must match the negotiated ETM/ciphersuite configuration, but the shared ETM flag is not a validated per-direction state, so the record is parsed under an inconsistent assumption. This is improper validation of input/state consistency (CWE-20); the fix introduces separate read/write ETM flags rather than a generic memory-safety fix.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The read-side ETM decision is taken from a single shared SSL_USE_ETM flag that changes during renegotiation, so the record parsing path can select the ETM MAC layout while the negotiated ciphersuite expects the non-ETM layout. A crafted renegotiation that flips ETM state causes inconsistent MAC size/length handling and a crash, yielding DoS.

commit_msg:
Bug 703366: Fix double free of object during linearization.

This appears to happen because we parse an illegal object from
a broken file and assign it to object 0, which is defined to
be free.

Here, we fix the parsing code so this can't happen.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (num == 0)', '\t\t\tfz_throw(ctx, FZ_ERROR_GENERIC, "Trailer object number cannot be 0\\n");']}
description: A flaw was found in mupdf 1.18.0. Double free of object during linearization may lead to memory corruption and other potential consequences.

code_evidence: pdf_parse_ind_obj writes the parsed object number into num; when a broken file yields num==0, no check rejects it before the parse succeeds and trailer is retained.

The catch block drops trailer and rethrows; later code uses num as the xref entry index: pdf_get_populating_xref_entry(ctx, doc, num) with num==0 selects the free entry, then pdf_drop_obj(ctx, entry->obj) and entry->obj = pdf_keep_obj(ctx, trailer) overwrite that entry's object with trailer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is the absent num==0 guard, and the resulting supported consequence is the same object being freed twice via the overwritten free xref entry, which matches CWE-415. It is not merely an invalid index or out-of-bounds access, because the duplicate release of one object is the specific weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Missing validation that the parsed trailer object number is nonzero allows num=0 to index the xref entry defined as free. The trailer object is then stored into that entry after dropping the entry's prior object, so the same object can be released again through the free-entry handling, causing a double free and memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Use new libostree APIs to reject world-writable/suid content

This uses the new libostree APIs that landed recently to ensure
that we reject any files with mode outside of `0775` for system
helper pulls, and we also mask directory modes during checkout.

However, this does *not* fix up any already downloaded content.
For that, one could uninstall/reinstall; or a future patch could
do a one-time fixup pass.

Note that I am not aware of a way for flatpak applications to escalate their
privileges directly with this flaw; the bubblewrap `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` turns
of setuid. However, in combination with code execution on the host via another
mechanism (e.g. unsandboxed app), a setuid app injected could be used to gain
full host privileges.

At this time we're not aware of any flatpak content exploiting this issue.

Closes: https://github.com/flatpak/flatpak/issues/845
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  /* We always want this on for every type of pull */', '  flags |= OSTREE_REPO_PULL_FLAGS_BAREUSERONLY_FILES;']}
description: In Flatpak before 0.8.7, a third-party app repository could include malicious apps that contain files with inappropriate permissions, for example setuid or world-writable. The files are deployed with those permissions, which would let a local attacker run the setuid executable or write to the world-writable location. In the case of the "system helper" component, files deployed as part of the app are owned by root, so in the worst case they could be setuid root.

code_evidence: The pull options built at [35,36] embed the caller-supplied `flags` value into the "flags" variant, which is later passed to `ostree_repo_pull_with_options` at [58,59,60].
Before the patch, no constraint forces the bareuser-only flag, so content with unsafe modes (setuid/world-writable) is accepted and deployed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function governs which file modes are accepted during pull, and the missing permission constraint lets a critical resource (deployed app files) receive permissions broader than intended, matching CWE-732. This is a permission-assignment flaw, not an authorization check on an actor.

evidence_lines.code:
g_variant_builder_add (&builder, "{s@v}", "flags",
g_variant_new_variant (g_variant_new_int32 (flags)));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pull request does not require the repository to reject files whose permission bits exceed `0775`, so a malicious third-party repository can include setuid or world-writable files that are checked out as-is. Trigger: pulling from such a repository; consequence: root-owned setuid or world-writable files are deployed, enabling privilege escalation or modification by unintended actors.

commit_msg:
usbip_host updates device status without holding lock from stub probe,
disconnect and rebind code paths. When multiple requests to import a
device are received, these unprotected code paths step all over each
other and drive fails with NULL-ptr deref and use-after-free errors.

The driver uses a table lock to protect the busid array for adding and
deleting busids to the table. However, the probe, disconnect and rebind
paths get the busid table entry and update the status without holding
the busid table lock. Add a new finer grain lock to protect the busid
entry. This new lock will be held to search and update the busid entry
fields from get_busid_idx(), add_match_busid() and del_match_busid().

match_busid_show() does the same to access the busid entry fields.

get_busid_priv() changed to return the pointer to the busid entry holding
the busid lock. stub_probe(), stub_disconnect() and stub_device_rebind()
call put_busid_priv() to release the busid lock before returning. This
changes fixes the unprotected code paths eliminating the race conditions
in updating the busid entries.

Reported-by: Jakub Jirasek
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan (Samsung OSG) <shuah@kernel.org>
Cc: stable <stable@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tspin_lock(&busid_table[idx].busid_lock);', '', '\tspin_unlock(&busid_table[idx].busid_lock);']}
description: In the Linux Kernel before version 4.16.11, 4.14.43, 4.9.102, and 4.4.133, multiple race condition errors when handling probe, disconnect, and rebind operations can be exploited to trigger a use-after-free condition or a NULL pointer dereference by sending multiple USB over IP packets.

code_evidence: del_match_busid holds only busid_table_lock (line 5) while get_busid_idx searches the table (line 6). After locating idx, it reads busid_table[idx].status (line 10) and may memset name (line 11) or overwrite status to STUB_BUSID_REMOV (lines 12-14) without any per-entry lock; only the global table lock is released at line 16. The patched version adds spin_lock/spin_unlock on busid_table[idx].busid_lock around lines 10-14, confirming these field accesses were previously unsynchronized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits an interfering sequence to modify the shared busid_table[idx] entry between the lookup and status/name updates, violating exclusivity/atomicity of the shared resource. This matches CWE-362; it is a synchronization race, not merely a missing bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: per-entry busid status/name fields are modified under only the coarse table lock, while probe/disconnect/rebind paths access the same entry without that lock. Trigger: concurrent USB/IP import requests racing get_busid_idx/add/del paths. Consequence: unsynchronized read-modify-write of status/name yields NULL-ptr deref or use-after-free/DoS.

commit_msg: Safer std::vector indexing.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        char        C = c[0];'], 'added_lines': ['        char        C = c.at(0);']}
description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An out-of-bounds read was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The out-of-bounds read is triggered when Exiv2 is used to read the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: The loop is guarded by in.length(), so in is non-empty; line 9 builds c from the first character via in.substr(0,1), yielding a one-character string, and line 10 then reads c[0] with unchecked operator[].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading c[0] via unchecked operator[] on a string whose size is not verified at that point is an out-of-bounds read, matching CWE-125. This is a read past the buffer end, not a write (CWE-787) or integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The guard checks the length of in, but the read is performed on the derived string c using operator[], which does not bounds-check. If c were empty, c[0] would read past the end of the string's buffer. The patch replaces this with c.at(0), adding a bounds check, confirming the unsafe indexing is the root cause; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read (DoS/crash) on crafted input.

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        subtractSize(i->key().size() + i->value().size());']}
description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only erases matching headers and does not itself track, limit, or fail to limit resource consumption; the added subtractSize call maintains a cached size and does not establish an uncontrolled-resource weakness within this function.

commit_msg:
Bug #484 CVE-2018-17582 Check for corrupt PCAP files

* Check for packets that are larger than 262144 bytes
* Check for capture lengths that are greater than packet length

Example of a corrupt PCAP file ...

sudo src/tcpreplay -i ens33 --unique-ip -t --loop 4 get_next_paket_01
safe_pcap_next ERROR: Invalid packet length in send_packets.c:get_next_packet() line 1054: 8388670 is greater than maximum 262144
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    while ((pktconst = pcap_next(pin, pkthdr_ptr)) != NULL) {'], 'added_lines': ['    while ((pktconst = safe_pcap_next(pin, pkthdr_ptr)) != NULL) {']}
description: Tcpreplay v4.3.0 beta1 contains a heap-based buffer over-read. The get_next_packet() function in the send_packets.c file uses the memcpy() function unsafely to copy sequences from the source buffer pktdata to the destination (*prev_packet)->pktdata. This will result in a Denial of Service (DoS) and potentially Information Exposure when the application attempts to process a file.

code_evidence: Line 21 obtains a packet pointer and header via pcap_next without validating that the capture length is consistent with the actual packet data. Line 24 only checks caplen > MAXPACKET, but a corrupt PCAP can report a caplen larger than the real buffer while still <= MAXPACKET. Line 26 then memcpy's pkthdr.caplen bytes from pktconst into *pktdata, reading past the end of the source packet buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe memcpy at line 26 reads past the end of the intended source buffer. This is specifically an out-of-bounds read, not a write or an integer overflow; the missing caplen-vs-actual-length constraint is the direct cause of the over-read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop trusts the attacker-controlled caplen from the PCAP header and only bounds it against MAXPACKET, not against the actual captured data length. Trigger: a crafted/corrupt PCAP whose caplen exceeds the real packet bytes but stays within MAXPACKET. Consequence: memcpy reads beyond the source buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read (DoS/crash and possible information exposure).

commit_msg:
nsenter: clone /proc/self/exe to avoid exposing host binary to container

There are quite a few circumstances where /proc/self/exe pointing to a
pretty important container binary is a _bad_ thing, so to avoid this we
have to make a copy (preferably doing self-clean-up and not being
writeable).

We require memfd_create(2) -- though there is an O_TMPFILE fallback --
but we can always extend this to use a scratch MNT_DETACH overlayfs or
tmpfs. The main downside to this approach is no page-cache sharing for
the runc binary (which overlayfs would give us) but this is far less
complicated.

This is only done during nsenter so that it happens transparently to the
Go code, and any libcontainer users benefit from it. This also makes
ExtraFiles and --preserve-fds handling trivial (because we don't need to
worry about it).

Fixes: CVE-2019-5736
Co-developed-by: Christian Brauner <christian.brauner@ubuntu.com>
Signed-off-by: Aleksa Sarai <asarai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/*', '\t * We need to re-exec if we are not in a cloned binary. This is necessary', "\t * to ensure that containers won't be able to access the host binary", '\t * through /proc/self/exe. See CVE-2019-5736.', '\t */', '\tif (ensure_cloned_binary() < 0)', '\t\tbail("could not ensure we are a cloned binary");']}
description: runc through 1.0-rc6, as used in Docker before 18.09.2 and other products, allows attackers to overwrite the host runc binary (and consequently obtain host root access) by leveraging the ability to execute a command as root within one of these types of containers: (1) a new container with an attacker-controlled image, or (2) an existing container, to which the attacker previously had write access, that can be attached with docker exec. This occurs because of file-descriptor mishandling, related to /proc/self/exe.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no construction or execution of an OS command from externally-influenced input; the changed lines only add a call to ensure_cloned_binary(), which does not support CWE-78.

commit_msg:
coredump: fix race condition between mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and core dumping

The core dumping code has always run without holding the mmap_sem for
writing, despite that is the only way to ensure that the entire vma
layout will not change from under it.  Only using some signal
serialization on the processes belonging to the mm is not nearly enough.
This was pointed out earlier.  For example in Hugh's post from Jul 2017:

  https://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.LSU.2.11.1707191716030.2055@eggly.anvils

  "Not strictly relevant here, but a related note: I was very surprised
   to discover, only quite recently, how handle_mm_fault() may be called
   without down_read(mmap_sem) - when core dumping. That seems a
   misguided optimization to me, which would also be nice to correct"

In particular because the growsdown and growsup can move the
vm_start/vm_end the various loops the core dump does around the vma will
not be consistent if page faults can happen concurrently.

Pretty much all users calling mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and then
taking the mmap_sem had the potential to introduce unexpected side
effects in the core dumping code.

Adding mmap_sem for writing around the ->core_dump invocation is a
viable long term fix, but it requires removing all copy user and page
faults and to replace them with get_dump_page() for all binary formats
which is not suitable as a short term fix.

For the time being this solution manually covers the places that can
confuse the core dump either by altering the vma layout or the vma flags
while it runs.  Once ->core_dump runs under mmap_sem for writing the
function mmget_still_valid() can be dropped.

Allowing mmap_sem protected sections to run in parallel with the
coredump provides some minor parallelism advantage to the swapoff code
(which seems to be safe enough by never mangling any vma field and can
keep doing swapins in parallel to the core dumping) and to some other
corner case.

In order to facilitate the backporting I added "Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6"
however the side effect of this same race condition in /proc/pid/mem
should be reproducible since before 2.6.12-rc2 so I couldn't add any
other "Fixes:" because there's no hash beyond the git genesis commit.

Because find_extend_vma() is the only location outside of the process
context that could modify the "mm" structures under mmap_sem for
reading, by adding the mmget_still_valid() check to it, all other cases
that take the mmap_sem for reading don't need the new check after
mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm().  The expand_stack() in page fault
context also doesn't need the new check, because all tasks under core
dumping are frozen.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190325224949.11068-1-aarcange@redhat.com
Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6 ("userfaultfd: add new syscall to provide memory externalization")
Signed-off-by: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Peter Xu <peterx@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Rapoport <rppt@linux.ibm.com>
Reviewed-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@mellanox.com>
Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t/*', '\t\t\t\t * Avoid to modify vma->vm_flags', '\t\t\t\t * without locked ops while the', '\t\t\t\t * coredump reads the vm_flags.', '\t\t\t\t */', '\t\t\t\tif (!mmget_still_valid(mm)) {', '\t\t\t\t\t/*', '\t\t\t\t\t * Silently return "count"', '\t\t\t\t\t * like if get_task_mm()', '\t\t\t\t\t * failed. FIXME: should this', '\t\t\t\t\t * function have returned', '\t\t\t\t\t * -ESRCH if get_task_mm()', '\t\t\t\t\t * failed like if', '\t\t\t\t\t * get_proc_task() fails?', '\t\t\t\t\t */', '\t\t\t\t\tup_write(&mm->mmap_sem);', '\t\t\t\t\tgoto out_mm;', '\t\t\t\t}']}
description: The coredump implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10 does not use locking or other mechanisms to prevent vma layout or vma flags changes while it runs, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information, cause a denial of service, or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a race condition with mmget_not_zero or get_task_mm calls. This is related to fs/userfaultfd.c, mm/mmap.c, fs/proc/task_mmu.c, and drivers/infiniband/core/uverbs_main.c.

code_evidence: The CLEAR_REFS_SOFT_DIRTY branch takes mmap_sem for read at line 47, then releases it at line 53 and re-acquires it for write at line 54 before mutating vma->vm_flags at lines 58-61. The write lock is held while the vma list is walked and vm_flags/vma_set_page_prot are modified, then downgraded at line 62.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 fits because the weakness is improper lock acquisition/coordination on the shared vma structure: the clear_refs path locks mmap_sem while the coredump path does not, so the resource is not consistently protected. This is a locking-consistency issue rather than a generic race (CWE-362) or missing-check issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function modifies vma->vm_flags under mmap_sem, but the concurrent core-dump path reads vm_flags without that lock, so the locking discipline is not shared across the two code paths. Trigger: a coredump racing with clear_refs_write on the same mm. Consequence: inconsistent vma flag/page-prot state visible to the coredump, enabling the described race-related impact.

commit_msg:
Fix integer underflow vulnerability in L3 decode.

Marcin 'Icewall' Noga of Cisco TALOS discovered that the level 3 header
decoding routines were vulnerable to an integer underflow, if the 32-bit
header length was less than the base level 3 header length. This could
lead to an exploitable heap corruption condition.

Thanks go to Marcin Noga and Regina Wilson of Cisco TALOS for reporting
this vulnerability.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (header_len > LEVEL_3_MAX_HEADER_LEN) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (header_len > LEVEL_3_MAX_HEADER_LEN', '\t || header_len < RAW_DATA_LEN(header)) {']}
description: Integer underflow in the decode_level3_header function in lib/lha_file_header.c in Lhasa before 0.3.1 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted archive.

code_evidence: Line 11 reads an attacker-controlled 32-bit header_len from the archive. Line 12 only rejects header_len greater than LEVEL_3_MAX_HEADER_LEN, so a header_len smaller than RAW_DATA_LEN(header) passes the check. Line 16 then computes header_len - RAW_DATA_LEN(header) as an unsigned subtraction, which wraps to a huge value and is passed to extend_raw_data as an allocation/growth length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 covers integer wraparound where a subtraction produces a value larger than expected; here the missing lower-bound check lets header_len - RAW_DATA_LEN(header) wrap to a huge unsigned value used as a size. This is integer underflow/wraparound, not merely an out-of-bounds read, because the wrapped size drives extend_raw_data.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the upper-bound check at line 12 lacks a lower-bound constraint, so an attacker-supplied header_len below the current raw-data length causes unsigned integer underflow/wraparound at line 16. Trigger: a crafted L3 archive with a small 32-bit header length. Consequence: an enormous size reaches extend_raw_data, leading to heap corruption or a crash rather than a controlled allocation.

commit_msg:
Fix BZ 22786: integer addition overflow may cause stack buffer overflow
when realpath() input length is close to SSIZE_MAX.

2018-05-09  Paul Pluzhnikov  <ppluzhnikov@google.com>

	[BZ #22786]
	* stdlib/canonicalize.c (__realpath): Fix overflow in path length
	computation.
	* stdlib/Makefile (test-bz22786): New test.
	* stdlib/test-bz22786.c: New test.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t      if ((long int) (n + len) >= path_max)'], 'added_lines': ['\t      if (path_max - n <= len)']}
description: stdlib/canonicalize.c in the GNU C Library (aka glibc or libc6) 2.27 and earlier, when processing very long pathname arguments to the realpath function, could encounter an integer overflow on 32-bit architectures, leading to a stack-based buffer overflow and, potentially, arbitrary code execution.

code_evidence: n is the int return of __readlink (line 107), len is size_t from strlen(end) (line 113). The bound check casts n+len to long int and compares against path_max (line 114); on 32-bit, n+len can wrap before the cast, so the guard passes. memmove then writes len+1 bytes into extra_buf at offset n (line 119).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The guarding arithmetic n+len can wrap, defeating the length check that protects the subsequent memory copy. This is precisely an integer overflow leading to an out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a missing length check: the check exists but is bypassed by wraparound.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size check n+len >= path_max is performed on a value that can overflow, so an oversized len is not rejected. Trigger: a symlink target and trailing path whose combined length approaches the integer limit. Consequence: memmove copies beyond the fixed path_max alloca buffer, a stack-based buffer overflow.

commit_msg:
Add a failsafe on the maximum number of Canon MakerNote subtags.

A malicious file could be crafted to cause extremely large values in some
tags without tripping any buffer range checks.  This is bad with the libexif
representation of Canon MakerNotes because some arrays are turned into
individual tags that the application must loop around.

The largest value I've seen for failsafe_size in a (very small) sample of valid
Canon files is <5000.  The limit is set two orders of magnitude larger to avoid
tripping up falsely in case some models use much larger values.

Patch from Google.

CVE-2020-13114
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tlong failsafe_size = 0;', '\t\t/* Track the size of decoded tag data. A malicious file could', '\t\t * be crafted to cause extremely large values here without', '\t\t * tripping any buffer range checks.  This is especially bad', '\t\t * with the libexif representation of Canon MakerNotes because', '\t\t * some arrays are turned into individual tags that the', '\t\t * application must loop around. */', '\t\tfailsafe_size += mnote_canon_entry_count_values(&n->entries[tcount]);', '', '\t\tif (failsafe_size > FAILSAFE_SIZE_MAX) {', '\t\t\t/* Abort if the total size of the data in the tags extraordinarily large, */', '\t\t\texif_mem_free (ne->mem, n->entries[tcount].data);', '\t\t\texif_log (ne->log, EXIF_LOG_CODE_CORRUPT_DATA,', '\t\t\t\t\t  "ExifMnoteCanon", "Failsafe tag size overflow (%lu > %ld)",', '\t\t\t\t\t  failsafe_size, FAILSAFE_SIZE_MAX);', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t}', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in libexif before 0.6.22. An unrestricted size in handling Canon EXIF MakerNote data could lead to consumption of large amounts of compute time for decoding EXIF data.

code_evidence: The loop reads tag, format and components from the buffer; components is attacker-controlled and only bounded against buf_size, so a single tag may declare a very large count.

The format-size check compares buf_size against components, but this constrains bytes in the buffer, not the number of logical values the application must iterate over when arrays are expanded into individual tags.

The decoded size s is computed and the data block is allocated and memcpy'd; the loop then advances tcount without any cumulative bound on total decoded values, so many tags can each carry large component counts.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because resource allocation (memory for tag data and the derived per-value tag expansion) proceeds without any intended cap on size or count. The weakness is the missing aggregate limit, not a buffer overflow, which the existing CHECKOVERFLOW checks already address.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loader accepts attacker-controlled component counts and allocates/copies per-tag data without limiting the aggregate number of decoded MakerNote values. Trigger: a crafted Canon MakerNote with large component counts across tags passes the per-tag range checks. Consequence: the application must loop over an unbounded number of expanded tags, consuming excessive CPU time (DoS).

commit_msg:
Prevent heap OOB error in `MaxPoolGrad`

PiperOrigin-RevId: 372424854
Change-Id: Idac0f23867ad8b0601cafbaaa52d5e64269e63a7
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        input_backprop_flat(input_backprop_index) += out_backprop_flat(index);'], 'added_lines': ['        if (index < out_backprop.NumElements()) {', '          input_backprop_flat(input_backprop_index) += out_backprop_flat(index);', '        }']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The implementation of `tf.raw_ops.MaxPoolGrad` is vulnerable to a heap buffer overflow. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/ab1e644b48c82cb71493f4362b4dd38f4577a1cf/tensorflow/core/kernels/maxpooling_op.cc#L194-L203) fails to validate that indices used to access elements of input/output arrays are valid. Whereas accesses to `input_backprop_flat` are guarded by `FastBoundsCheck`, the indexing in `out_backprop_flat` can result in OOB access. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Loop iterates index from out_start to out_end over out_backprop_flat and uses out_arg_max_flat(index) as input_backprop_index. FastBoundsCheck guards input_backprop_flat indexing, but out_backprop_flat(index) at line 109 is read without any bounds check against out_backprop.NumElements().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked indexing writes to memory outside the intended out_backprop_flat buffer; the patch adds an explicit index < out_backprop.NumElements() guard, confirming an out-of-bounds write/access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound out_end is derived from output dimensions (out_height*out_width*depth) while out_backprop_flat has its own element count; the argmax-derived index is bounds-checked but the out_backprop_flat access is not. Trigger: a crafted out_backprop tensor whose size is smaller than the computed output size causes index >= NumElements(), producing a heap out-of-bounds read/write on the flat buffer.

commit_msg:
tcp: avoid infinite loop in tcp_splice_read()

Splicing from TCP socket is vulnerable when a packet with URG flag is
received and stored into receive queue.

__tcp_splice_read() returns 0, and sk_wait_data() immediately
returns since there is the problematic skb in queue.

This is a nice way to burn cpu (aka infinite loop) and trigger
soft lockups.

Again, this gem was found by syzkaller tool.

Fixes: 9c55e01c0cc8 ("[TCP]: Splice receive support.")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov  <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t/* if __tcp_splice_read() got nothing while we have', '\t\t\t * an skb in receive queue, we do not want to loop.', '\t\t\t * This might happen with URG data.', '\t\t\t */', '\t\t\tif (!skb_queue_empty(&sk->sk_receive_queue))', '\t\t\t\tbreak;']}
description: The tcp_splice_read function in net/ipv4/tcp.c in the Linux kernel before 4.9.11 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop and soft lockup) via vectors involving a TCP packet with the URG flag.

code_evidence: The while (tss.len) loop calls __tcp_splice_read at line 21. When it returns 0 and no prior data was spliced, the code only breaks on SOCK_DONE, sk_err, RCV_SHUTDOWN, TCP_CLOSE, or exhausted timeo; otherwise it calls sk_wait_data and continues. A queued URG skb makes __tcp_splice_read return 0 while sk_wait_data returns immediately, so none of the exit conditions are met and the loop repeats.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loop's exit conditions cannot be satisfied when a URG skb is queued and __tcp_splice_read returns 0, matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. The availability impact from CPU consumption is the consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the zero-return path in the while loop lacks a check for a non-empty receive queue. Trigger: a remote TCP packet with the URG flag is stored in sk_receive_queue, causing __tcp_splice_read to return 0 and sk_wait_data to return immediately. Consequence: the loop never exits, consuming CPU and causing a soft lockup (denial of service).

commit_msg:
Fix DTLS replay protection

The DTLS implementation provides some protection against replay attacks
in accordance with RFC6347 section 4.1.2.6.

A sliding "window" of valid record sequence numbers is maintained with
the "right" hand edge of the window set to the highest sequence number we
have received so far. Records that arrive that are off the "left" hand
edge of the window are rejected. Records within the window are checked
against a list of records received so far. If we already received it then
we also reject the new record.

If we have not already received the record, or the sequence number is off
the right hand edge of the window then we verify the MAC of the record.
If MAC verification fails then we discard the record. Otherwise we mark
the record as received. If the sequence number was off the right hand edge
of the window, then we slide the window along so that the right hand edge
is in line with the newly received sequence number.

Records may arrive for future epochs, i.e. a record from after a CCS being
sent, can arrive before the CCS does if the packets get re-ordered. As we
have not yet received the CCS we are not yet in a position to decrypt or
validate the MAC of those records. OpenSSL places those records on an
unprocessed records queue. It additionally updates the window immediately,
even though we have not yet verified the MAC. This will only occur if
currently in a handshake/renegotiation.

This could be exploited by an attacker by sending a record for the next
epoch (which does not have to decrypt or have a valid MAC), with a very
large sequence number. This means the right hand edge of the window is
moved very far to the right, and all subsequent legitimate packets are
dropped causing a denial of service.

A similar effect can be achieved during the initial handshake. In this
case there is no MAC key negotiated yet. Therefore an attacker can send a
message for the current epoch with a very large sequence number. The code
will process the record as normal. If the hanshake message sequence number
(as opposed to the record sequence number that we have been talking about
so far) is in the future then the injected message is bufferred to be
handled later, but the window is still updated. Therefore all subsequent
legitimate handshake records are dropped. This aspect is not considered a
security issue because there are many ways for an attacker to disrupt the
initial handshake and prevent it from completing successfully (e.g.
injection of a handshake message will cause the Finished MAC to fail and
the handshake to be aborted). This issue comes about as a result of trying
to do replay protection, but having no integrity mechanism in place yet.
Does it even make sense to have replay protection in epoch 0? That
issue isn't addressed here though.

This addressed an OCAP Audit issue.

CVE-2016-2181

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>

commit_msg: MQTT parse_publish_vhdr: added missing initialization of topic_pos
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    conn->in_packet.topic_pos = 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the MQTT server in Contiki-NG before 4.2. The function parse_publish_vhdr() that parses MQTT PUBLISH messages with a variable length header uses memcpy to input data into a fixed size buffer. The allocated buffer can fit only MQTT_MAX_TOPIC_LENGTH (default 64) bytes, and a length check is missing. This could lead to Remote Code Execution via a stack-smashing attack (overwriting the function return address). Contiki-NG does not separate the MQTT server from other servers and the OS modules, so access to all memory regions is possible.

code_evidence: When topic_len_received==1 and topic_received==0, copy_bytes is computed as MIN(topic_len - topic_pos, input_data_len - *pos) [21,22] and used to memcpy into conn->in_publish_msg.topic at offset topic_pos [25,26,27]. The only bound is the wire-provided topic_len; nothing constrains it to the destination topic buffer size. After copying, topic_pos advances [30] and a NUL is written at topic[topic_pos] [34].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a memcpy and terminator store into a memory buffer without validating the length against the buffer's intended boundary, directly matching CWE-119. This is a buffer-bounds violation rather than an integer or pointer-arithmetic flaw; the missing length check against the fixed topic buffer is the operative weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination topic buffer is fixed-size but copy_bytes derives solely from the attacker-controlled MQTT topic_len field. Trigger: a PUBLISH variable header whose topic_len exceeds the buffer capacity, causing memcpy to write past conn->in_publish_msg.topic and the terminator write at [34] to land out of bounds. Consequence: stack/heap memory corruption enabling crash or return-address overwrite.

commit_msg:
Add check for string length in getCachedUTFString()

Signed-off-by: Peter Shipton <Peter_Shipton@ca.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tJ9UTF8* temputf = (J9UTF8*)&temp;', '\tchar* tempstr = (char*)J9UTF8_DATA(temputf);', '\tstrncpy(tempstr, local, J9UTF8_LENGTH(temputf));', ''], 'added_lines': ['\tJ9UTF8* temputf = (J9UTF8*)temp;', '\tPORT_ACCESS_FROM_VMC(currentThread);', '\tif (localLen > J9SH_MAXPATH) {', '\t\ttemputf = (J9UTF8 *)j9mem_allocate_memory(localLen + sizeof(J9UTF8), J9MEM_CATEGORY_CLASSES);', '\t\tif (NULL == temputf) {', '\t\t\tTrc_SHR_CM_getCachedUTFString_exit4(currentThread);', '\t\t\treturn NULL;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '', '\tmemcpy(J9UTF8_DATA(temputf), local, localLen);', '\t\t\t\t\tif ((J9UTF8 *)temp != temputf) {', '\t\t\t\t\t\tj9mem_free_memory(temputf);', '\t\t\t\t\t}', '\tif ((J9UTF8 *)temp != temputf) {', '\t\tj9mem_free_memory(temputf);', '\t}']}
description: In Eclipse Openj9 before version 0.38.0, in the implementation of the shared cache (which is enabled by default in OpenJ9 builds) the size of a string is not properly checked against the size of the buffer.

code_evidence: A fixed-size stack buffer temp of J9SH_MAXPATH + sizeof(J9UTF8) bytes is used, and temputf/tempstr are derived from it without any check of localLen against the buffer capacity.

J9UTF8_SET_LENGTH stores the caller-supplied localLen into the header, then strncpy copies J9UTF8_LENGTH(temputf) bytes (i.e., localLen) into tempstr, which points just past the header inside the fixed stack buffer.
findScopeForUTF then consumes temputf, whose declared length now exceeds the actual data written, so the cache reads beyond the initialized region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length leads to reading memory beyond the intended buffer when the oversized J9UTF8 is subsequently processed, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. The overflow write is a contributing cause, but the supported consequence here is an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
J9UTF8_SET_LENGTH(temputf, localLen);
strncpy(tempstr, local, J9UTF8_LENGTH(temputf));
pathUTF = localSCM->findScopeForUTF(currentThread, temputf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the string length localLen is trusted and written into the J9UTF8 header before being bounded by the stack buffer size. Trigger: a caller passes a local string longer than J9SH_MAXPATH. Consequence: the copy overruns temp and later lookups read past the buffer end, exposing adjacent stack memory or crashing.

NOTE: the vendor says "In my opinion this issue should not have a CVE, since the GD and GD2 formats are documented to be 'obsolete, and should only be used for development and testing purposes.'

description: Directory traversal vulnerability in the ZipArchive::extractTo function in ext/zip/php_zip.c in PHP before 5.4.45, 5.5.x before 5.5.29, and 5.6.x before 5.6.13 and ext/zip/ext_zip.cpp in HHVM before 3.12.1 allows remote attackers to create arbitrary empty directories via a crafted ZIP archive.

snprintf(fullpath, MAXPATHLEN, "%s%c%s", path, DEFAULT_SLASH, namelist[i]);

description: Insufficient checks in the USB packet handling of the ShapeShift KeepKey hardware wallet before firmware 6.2.2 allow out-of-bounds writes in the .bss segment via crafted messages. The vulnerability could allow code execution or other forms of impact. It can be triggered by unauthenticated attackers and the interface is reachable via WebUSB.

msgSize is reconstructed from attacker-controlled bytes buf[8]..buf[5]; the only check is msgSize > 64 - 9, which bounds the declared length against the 64-byte buffer but not against the real received len.
tiny_dispatch(entry, buf + 9, msgSize) passes the payload pointer and the unvalidated msgSize into the dispatcher, which performs the actual write using that length.

memcpy(buf, msg, sizeof(buf));

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            out[j++] = (accum >> 16);', ''], 'added_lines': ['            if (j < outLen) { out[j++] = (accum >> 16); }']}
description: A remote code execution vulnerability in the Android media framework (libstagefright). Product: Android. Versions: 4.4.4, 5.0.2, 5.1.1, 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2, 8.0. Android ID: A-62673128.

code_evidence: outLen is computed from input length and padding, and out points to a buffer of that size; j is initialized to 0 as the write index.

Each 4-character group writes up to three bytes. The second and third stores are guarded by j < outLen, but the first store out[j++] = (accum >> 16) is unconditional, so j can reach outLen and this store writes one byte past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to a memory location beyond the intended buffer boundary, which is an out-of-bounds write supporting CWE-119. The root cause is the missing j < outLen constraint on the first store, not a read past the buffer or an integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The first output write in each quantum lacks the bounds check applied to the other two writes. When the decoded group count makes j equal outLen at the start of a group (e.g. due to padding handling), out[j++] writes outside the allocated ABuffer, corrupting adjacent heap memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
dvb_register_device() dynamically allocates fops with kmemdup()
to set the fops->owner.
And these fops are registered in 'file->f_ops' using replace_fops()
in the dvb_device_open() process, and kfree()d in dvb_free_device().

However, it is not common to use dynamically allocated fops instead
of 'static const' fops as an argument of replace_fops(),
and UAF may occur.
These UAFs can occur on any dvb type using dvb_register_device(),
such as dvb_dvr, dvb_demux, dvb_frontend, dvb_net, etc.

So, instead of kfree() the fops dynamically allocated in
dvb_register_device() in dvb_free_device() called during the
.disconnect() process, kfree() it collectively in exit_dvbdev()
called when the dvbdev.c module is removed.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-media/20221117045925.14297-4-imv4bel@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Reported-by: Dan Carpenter <error27@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tkfree (dvbdev->fops);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 6.0.9. drivers/media/dvb-core/dvbdev.c has a use-after-free, related to dvb_register_device dynamically allocating fops.

code_evidence: dvb_free_device() frees dvbdev->fops via kfree() and then frees dvbdev itself, with no synchronization guarding these frees against concurrent readers of the device.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a timing window in which a shared resource (the fops pointer) is freed by one execution sequence while another can still access it, i.e., improper synchronization of concurrent execution. This fits CWE-362; the use-after-free is the resulting consequence rather than the target class itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The dynamically allocated fops is freed when the device reference count drops to zero, but the same fops was installed into file->f_ops via replace_fops() during open. If a concurrent open/read path still references that fops while release/disconnect frees it, a use-after-free occurs; the missing mutual exclusion between the free sequence and the concurrent access is the root cause.

description: The ICMPv6 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-icmp6.c.

code_evidence: The loop count n is derived from the packet field match->rpm_len as (rpm_len - 3)/4 at lines 72-75, with no bounds check against the remaining captured length ep.

The while loop at lines 76-79 casts cp to rr_pco_use and dereferences use->rpu_prefix via ND_TCHECK, walking cp forward by sizeof(struct rr_pco_use) each iteration regardless of ep, so cp can exceed the buffer end.
The trunc label at lines 116-117 is the only bail-out, reached via goto trunc when n % 4 is nonzero, not when the walk overruns the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads struct fields from memory beyond the intended packet buffer, matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). It is not a write overflow (CWE-787) because only reads occur; the missing ep bound check is the read-side weakness.

ND_PRINT((ndo,"[|icmp6]"));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the number of rr_pco_use records is computed solely from the attacker-controlled rpm_len field without validating that the remaining captured bytes (ep - cp) can hold that many records. Trigger: a crafted ICMPv6 router-renumbering packet with an inflated rpm_len. Consequence: the loop dereferences use->rpu_prefix past the end of the captured buffer, an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
libdw: Check end of attributes list consistently.

dwarf_child (__libdw_find_attr), dwarf_getabbrevattr[_data] and
dwarf_getattrs all assume the end of the attribute list is when
both the name (code) and form of the attribute are zero.

dwarf_getabbrev (__libdw_getabbrev) and dwarf_hasattr assume the
end of the attribute list is when either the name (code) or the
form of the attribute is zero.

The DWARF spec says: "The series of attribute specifications ends
with an entry containing 0 for the name and 0 for the form." So
the first check is correct.

Make sure dwarf_getabbrev and dwarf_hasattr use the same check.
This is important since all other functions expect dwarf_getabbrev
(__libdw_getabbrev) to have done a data sanity check of the attribute.
So if the ending condition is different it could cause a crash.

https://sourceware.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=23529

Signed-off-by: Mark Wielaard <mark@klomp.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      /* We can stop if we found the attribute with value zero.  */', '      if (attr_name == 0 || attr_form == 0)'], 'added_lines': ['      /* We can stop if we found the end of the attribute list.  */', '      if (attr_name == 0 && attr_form == 0)']}
description: libdw in elfutils 0.173 checks the end of the attributes list incorrectly in dwarf_getabbrev in dwarf_getabbrev.c and dwarf_hasattr in dwarf_hasattr.c, leading to a heap-based buffer over-read and an application crash.

code_evidence: The loop reads attr_name and attr_form with get_uleb128_unchecked, which performs no bounds check on attrp. It terminates only when attr_name == 0 || attr_form == 0; a legitimate attribute with form 0 but nonzero name (or vice versa) causes early return instead of continuing to the true end-of-list marker (0,0), leaving the caller's assumption about a fully validated list unmet.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the incorrect termination check lets later code read beyond the intended attribute buffer, matching out-of-bounds read. It is not merely improper input validation; the supported consequence is a read past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the end-of-attributes test uses OR rather than AND, so the scan can stop before reaching the (0,0) terminator and does not validate the remainder of the abbreviation list. Trigger: a malformed or truncated abbreviation where a name/form is zero before the real terminator. Consequence: subsequent attribute processing trusts the list and reads past the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and crash.

description: Use-after-free vulnerability in the wddx_stack_destroy function in ext/wddx/wddx.c in PHP before 5.6.26 and 7.x before 7.0.11 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via a wddxPacket XML document that lacks an end-tag for a recordset field element, leading to mishandling in a wddx_deserialize call.

commit_msg:
As report by Wenqing Liu in bugzilla:

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=215231

- Overview
kernel NULL pointer dereference triggered  in folio_mark_dirty() when mount and operate on a crafted f2fs image

- Reproduce
tested on kernel 5.16-rc3, 5.15.X under root

1. mkdir mnt
2. mount -t f2fs tmp1.img mnt
3. touch tmp
4. cp tmp mnt

F2FS-fs (loop0): sanity_check_inode: inode (ino=49) extent info [5942, 4294180864, 4] is incorrect, run fsck to fix
F2FS-fs (loop0): f2fs_check_nid_range: out-of-range nid=31340049, run fsck to fix.
BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000000
 folio_mark_dirty+0x33/0x50
 move_data_page+0x2dd/0x460 [f2fs]
 do_garbage_collect+0xc18/0x16a0 [f2fs]
 f2fs_gc+0x1d3/0xd90 [f2fs]
 f2fs_balance_fs+0x13a/0x570 [f2fs]
 f2fs_create+0x285/0x840 [f2fs]
 path_openat+0xe6d/0x1040
 do_filp_open+0xc5/0x140
 do_sys_openat2+0x23a/0x310
 do_sys_open+0x57/0x80

The root cause is for special file: e.g. character, block, fifo or socket file,
f2fs doesn't assign address space operations pointer array for mapping->a_ops field,
so, in a fuzzed image, SSA table indicates a data block belong to special file, when
f2fs tries to migrate that block, it causes NULL pointer access once move_data_page()
calls a_ops->set_dirty_page().

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Wenqing Liu <wenqingliu0120@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Chao Yu <chao@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Jaegeuk Kim <jaegeuk@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (IS_ERR(inode) || is_bad_inode(inode))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (IS_ERR(inode) || is_bad_inode(inode) ||', '\t\t\t\t\tspecial_file(inode->i_mode))']}
description: In gc_data_segment in fs/f2fs/gc.c in the Linux kernel before 5.16.3, special files are not considered, leading to a move_data_page NULL pointer dereference.

code_evidence: In phase 3, gc_data_segment obtains an inode with f2fs_iget() and only rejects it when IS_ERR(inode) or is_bad_inode(inode) is true. A crafted image can make the SSA table point a data block at a special file (char, block, fifo, socket), and such inodes pass this check because they are valid, non-error inodes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function admits a special-file inode that lacks address-space operations, and the later dirty-page path dereferences a NULL function pointer/address space operation, matching CWE-476. The missing special_file() check is the direct cause; the NULL dereference is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the phase-3 validation does not exclude special files, whose mapping->a_ops is not initialized. Trigger: a crafted f2fs image makes SSA reference a data block belonging to a special file, so the inode is added to gc_list and later processed. Consequence: move_data_page() calls a NULL a_ops->set_dirty_page, causing a NULL pointer dereference (DoS crash).

description: An issue was discovered in Oniguruma 6.2.0, as used in Oniguruma-mod in Ruby through 2.4.1 and mbstring in PHP through 7.1.5. commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.4+
Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>

description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.10 does not correctly synchronize the actions of updating versus finding a key in the "negative" state to avoid a race condition, which allows local users to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls.

commit_msg:
There is a current use after free possible on a gatt server if a client
disconnects while a WriteValue call is being processed with dbus.

This patch includes the addition of a pending disconnect callback to handle
cleanup better if a disconnect occurs during a write, an acquire write
or read operation using bt_att_register_disconnect with the cb.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static struct pending_op *pending_write_new(struct btd_device *device,', '\t\t\t\t\tuint16_t offset, uint8_t link_type,', '\top->device = device;', '\top->link_type = link_type;'], 'added_lines': ['static struct pending_op *pending_write_new(struct bt_att *att,', '\t\t\t\t\tuint16_t offset,', '\top->att = bt_att_ref(att);', '\top->link_type = bt_att_get_link_type(att);', '\tbt_att_register_disconnect(att,', '\t\t\t    pending_disconnect_cb,', '\t\t\t    op, NULL);', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in gatt-database.c in BlueZ 5.61. A use-after-free can occur when a client disconnects during D-Bus processing of a WriteValue call.

code_evidence: pending_write_new allocates op, stores the raw value pointer and the device pointer, then pushes op onto owner_queue. The function returns op, so callers retain and later dereference this object while it remains queued.
No disconnect callback is registered before returning op, so a client disconnect during D-Bus processing is not tied to cleanup of this pending operation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the queued, returned op is used after connection teardown frees associated memory. This is a lifetime/ownership flaw, not merely an unchecked input or null dereference.

evidence_lines.code: return op;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pending write operation is queued and returned without any lifetime link to the underlying bt_att connection. Trigger: a client disconnects while a WriteValue is being processed, causing connection teardown to free related state while the queued op still references it. Consequence: later use of the stale op/device/value is a use-after-free (crash or memory corruption).

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.4 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.10, there is an LDSS dissector crash, triggered by packet injection or a malformed capture file. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-ldss.c by ensuring that memory is allocated for a certain data structure.

code_evidence: The dissector reads fixed offsets (messageID at 0, size at 40, offset at 48, port at 64, rate at 66) and calls tvb_memdup for DIGEST_LEN bytes at offset 8 without first checking that the captured length is at least 72 bytes.
The properties item is added using tvb_captured_length(tvb) - 72 when reported length exceeds 72, so a short captured buffer combined with a large reported length yields an underflowed length.
The processing branch is gated only by messageDetail and frame-visit state; no length validation guards the allocation of ldss_broadcast_t and related structures.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is that input properties (actual captured length and consistency with reported length) are not validated before the data is processed, matching CWE-20's improper input validation. Trigger: a malformed capture or injected packet with a short captured length (or reported length > captured length). Consequence: out-of-bounds reads and an underflowed length passed to proto_tree_add_item, leading to a dissector crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
vc2enc_dwt: pad the temporary buffer by the slice size

Since non-Haar wavelets need to look into pixels outside the frame, we
need to pad the buffer. The old factor of two seemed to be a workaround
that fact and only padded to the left and bottom. This correctly pads
by the slice size and as such reduces memory usage and potential
exploits.
Reported by Liu Bingchang.

Ideally, there should be no temporary buffer but the encoder is designed
to deinterleave the coefficients into the classical wavelet structure
with the lower frequency values in the top left corner.

Signed-off-by: Rostislav Pehlivanov <atomnuker@gmail.com>
(cherry picked from commit 3228ac730c11eca49d5680d5550128e397061c85)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['av_cold int ff_vc2enc_init_transforms(VC2TransformContext *s, int p_width, int p_height)', '    s->buffer = av_malloc(2*p_width*p_height*sizeof(dwtcoef));'], 'added_lines': ['av_cold int ff_vc2enc_init_transforms(VC2TransformContext *s, int p_stride,', '                                      int p_height, int slice_w, int slice_h)', '    /* Pad by the slice size, only matters for non-Haar wavelets */', '    s->buffer = av_calloc((p_stride + slice_w)*(p_height + slice_h), sizeof(dwtcoef));', '    s->padding = (slice_h >> 1)*p_stride + (slice_w >> 1);', '    s->buffer += s->padding;', '']}
description: The VC-2 Video Compression encoder in FFmpeg 3.0 and 3.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) because of incorrect buffer padding for non-Haar wavelets, related to libavcodec/vc2enc.c and libavcodec/vc2enc_dwt.c.

code_evidence: The function allocates the temporary DWT buffer as av_malloc(2*p_width*p_height*sizeof(dwtcoef)) using only the plane width and height, with no allowance for the slice dimensions or the additional rows/columns that non-Haar (9/7 and 5/3) wavelets inspect outside the nominal frame.

The allocation size is computed solely from p_width and p_height; a failed allocation returns 1, otherwise the function returns 0 with the buffer sized to the un-padded plane, and later transform code indexes beyond that allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The allocation omits the padding required by the filter footprint, so subsequent reads go past the end of the intended buffer, which is exactly CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. It is not CWE-787 (write) because the supported impact is reading memory outside the buffer bounds.

evidence_lines.code:
av_cold int ff_vc2enc_init_transforms(VC2TransformContext *s, int p_width, int p_height)
s->buffer = av_malloc(2*p_width*p_height*sizeof(dwtcoef));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the temporary buffer is sized to 2*p_width*p_height without padding for the slice size that non-Haar wavelet filters read beyond the frame. Trigger: encoding with a non-Haar wavelet causes the DWT routines to access coefficients outside the allocated region. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds read, leading to a crash/denial of service (and potentially information disclosure).

This occurs because of a race condition involving a failed delayed load and other worker threads.

code_evidence: The load->real check and creation at [6-8] are not synchronized; another thread can enter the same branch concurrently.
class->load() and vips_image_pio_input() results are checked at [15-17], but a failure just returns NULL without recording that the load failed.

commit_msg:
log: fix potential overflow with long log messages (#490)

qb_vsnprintf_serialize was called with 'max_size' as the
limiting number for the length of the formatted log
message. But the buffer also needs to contain the
log header (given by 'actual_size'), so we now pass
't->max_line_length' as the maximum length of the
formatted log message to limit space to the actual 
bytes left

Also added error checks to the blackbox calls at
the end of the test, as these now provide a proper
test that the BB is functioning. Before they were
masking failures.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmsg_len = qb_vsnprintf_serialize(chunk, max_size, cs->format, ap);', '\tif (msg_len >= max_size) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tmsg_len = qb_vsnprintf_serialize(chunk, t->max_line_length, cs->format, ap);', '\tif (msg_len >= t->max_line_length) {']}
description: log_blackbox.c in libqb before 2.0.8 allows a buffer overflow via long log messages because the header size is not considered.

code_evidence: actual_size reserves the fixed header (4 uint32_t, uint8_t, function name, timespec) and max_size adds t->max_line_length on top; chunk is allocated for max_size bytes.

chunk is advanced past the header and a uint32_t length slot, then qb_vsnprintf_serialize is called with max_size rather than the remaining space (t->max_line_length), so the formatted message may write up to max_size bytes into the smaller tail region, and the msg_len >= max_size check compares against the wrong bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies a formatted input (the log message) into a destination chunk without checking it against the destination's remaining capacity, matching CWE-120's buffer copy without size checking. The defect is a wrong size bound for the copy, not merely an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the formatted log message is serialized with the full allocation size max_size as its limit instead of the space actually left after the header. Trigger: a long log message whose formatted length exceeds t->max_line_length but stays under max_size. Consequence: qb_vsnprintf_serialize writes past the message region, corrupting the blackbox ring buffer and potentially the log header.

Fix #196 and #199: Out of bound reads security issues

Check args before calling memmove() and memset() in remap_struct()
function to avoid out of bound reads which would possibly lead to
unknown code execution and/or sadf command crash.

Signed-off-by: Sebastien GODARD <sysstat@users.noreply.github.com>

description: An issue was discovered in sysstat 12.1.1. The remap_struct function in sa_common.c has an out-of-bounds read during a memmove call, as demonstrated by sadf.

code_evidence: The header size from the file (file_magic->header_size) is validated only against MIN/MAX bounds at lines 11-12, then used to allocate and read buffer at lines 19-20; remap_struct is called at lines 21-22 without the buffer length, so it can memmove past the buffer end.

For each activity, file_hdr->act_size is allocated at line 42 and read into buffer at line 47; remap_struct at lines 48-49 likewise receives no buffer capacity, allowing a memmove read beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a read beyond an allocated buffer during memmove, matching CWE-125. This is a read-overrun, not an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), since the affected copies are reads from buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: remap_struct copies based on attacker-controlled structure sizes without a buffer-bound argument, so its memmove can read past the allocated buffer. Trigger: a crafted sysstat file whose size fields are within the coarse MIN/MAX checks but inconsistent with the actual buffer contents. Consequence: out-of-bounds read that may crash sadf or leak/execute using adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
display-store: Pass the display object rather than the id in the removed signal

By the time GdmDisplayStore emits the "display-removed" signal, the display
is no longer in the store and gdm_display_store_lookup will not work in
signal handlers.

Change the "display-removed" parameter from the display id to the GdmDisplay
object, so that signal handers can perform any cleanup they need to do

CVE-2018-14424

Closes: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gdm/issues/401
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    const char             *id,', '        GdmDisplay *display;', '', '        display = gdm_display_store_lookup (display_store, id);', '', '        if (display != NULL) {', '                g_signal_handlers_disconnect_by_func (display, G_CALLBACK (on_display_status_changed), factory);', '                g_object_weak_unref (G_OBJECT (display), (GWeakNotify)on_display_disposed, factory);', '', '        }'], 'added_lines': ['                    GdmDisplay             *display,', '        g_signal_handlers_disconnect_by_func (display, G_CALLBACK (on_display_status_changed), factory);', '        g_object_weak_unref (G_OBJECT (display), (GWeakNotify)on_display_disposed, factory);']}
description: The daemon in GDM through 3.29.1 does not properly unexport display objects from its D-Bus interface when they are destroyed, which allows a local attacker to trigger a use-after-free via a specially crafted sequence of D-Bus method calls, resulting in a denial of service or potential code execution.

code_evidence: on_display_removed looks up the display by id via gdm_display_store_lookup, then only if non-NULL disconnects the status-changed handler and removes the weak reference. Because the display-removed signal is emitted after the display has already been removed from the store, the lookup returns NULL, so the cleanup of the handler and weak reference is skipped for the destroyed display.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's skipped cleanup leaves a dangling reference to a freed GdmDisplay that is later accessed, which is exactly CWE-416 use after free. A mere NULL-pointer dereference is not at issue, since the code guards against NULL; the flaw is the missing cleanup of the freed object's handlers.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: cleanup of signal handlers and the weak reference is gated on a lookup that cannot succeed once the store no longer owns the display. Trigger: a display is destroyed and the display-removed signal fires; the handler is left attached and the weak reference remains. Consequence: later signal emission or disposal touches the freed display, yielding a use-after-free (DoS or potential code execution).

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.8-3 Q16, ReadBMPImage and WriteBMPImage in coders/bmp.c allow attackers to cause an out of bounds write via a crafted file.

code_evidence: bmp_info.image_size is computed as bytes_per_line*image->rows and truncated to unsigned int at [213]; the buffer is then allocated with that value at [234,235] and zeroed with the same size at [239].

bytes_per_line is derived from image->columns*bmp_info.bits_per_pixel at [177], while each row write starts at q=pixels+(image->rows-y-1)*bytes_per_line and advances q per pixel, e.g. at [254,341,366,427,454].
Padding loops advance q up to bytes_per_line per row, e.g. [275,276,277], [321,322,323], [347,348], [408,409], [435,436], so the total bytes written is rows*bytes_per_line.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a buffer whose size can be smaller than the number of bytes the subsequent row/padding loops write, producing a write past the end of the intended buffer, which is exactly CWE-787. This is not merely an integer overflow (CWE-190); the overflow is the cause, but the demonstrated weakness is the out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocation size at [234,235] uses the 32-bit-truncated bmp_info.image_size, but the row loops write up to bytes_per_line per row for image->rows rows. When bytes_per_line*image->rows exceeds UINT_MAX, the truncated allocation is smaller than the actual write span, so q writes past the allocated pixels buffer, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg:
Eric Dumazet says:

====================
Juha-Matti Tilli reported that malicious peers could inject tiny
packets in out_of_order_queue, forcing very expensive calls
to tcp_collapse_ofo_queue() and tcp_prune_ofo_queue() for
every incoming packet.

With tcp_rmem[2] default of 6MB, the ooo queue could
contain ~7000 nodes.

This patch series makes sure we cut cpu cycles enough to
render the attack not critical.

We might in the future go further, like disconnecting
or black-holing proven malicious flows.
====================

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (atomic_read(&sk->sk_rmem_alloc) <= sk->sk_rcvbuf)', '\t\treturn 0;']}
description: Linux kernel versions 4.9+ can be forced to make very expensive calls to tcp_collapse_ofo_queue() and tcp_prune_ofo_queue() for every incoming packet which can lead to a denial of service.

code_evidence: tcp_prune_queue is invoked per incoming packet; the rmem threshold check at line 6 only clamps the window, then the function unconditionally calls tcp_collapse_ofo_queue() (line 10) and later tcp_prune_ofo_queue() (line 19) regardless of whether the out-of-order queue needs pruning.

The early returns at lines 17-18 and 20-21 only short-circuit after the expensive collapse/prune work has already been performed, so the queue-walk cost is paid on every call rather than only when memory is actually over budget.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to throttle costly per-packet processing relative to a bounded resource (rmem), enabling CPU exhaustion via attacker-controlled traffic; this is the resource-consumption mistake CWE-400 targets, distinct from a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: tcp_prune_queue performs expensive ofo-queue collapse/prune work unconditionally instead of first checking whether sk_rmem_alloc is at/over sk_rcvbuf. Trigger: a malicious peer injects tiny out-of-order packets, causing tcp_prune_queue to run per packet and walk an ooo queue of up to ~7000 nodes. Supported consequence: high CPU consumption per packet, degrading availability (denial of service).

commit_msg:
Remove support for pre-authentication compression. Doing compression
early in the protocol probably seemed reasonable in the 1990s, but
today it's clearly a bad idea in terms of both cryptography (cf.
multiple compression oracle attacks in TLS) and attack surface.

Moreover, to support it across privilege-separation zlib needed
the assistance of a complex shared-memory manager that made the
required attack surface considerably larger.

Prompted by Guido Vranken pointing out a compiler-elided security
check in the shared memory manager found by Stack
(http://css.csail.mit.edu/stack/); ok deraadt@ markus@

NB. pre-auth authentication has been disabled by default in sshd
for >10 years.

description: Buffer overflow in the xmlrpc_char_encode function in modules/transport/xmlrpc/xmlrpclib.c in Atheme before 7.2.7 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via vectors related to XMLRPC response encoding.

code_evidence: The loop at [13-41] expands each input character into an entity (e.g. '&' is 5 bytes, '&#%d;' up to 7 bytes) and appends it to the dynamically grown string s, so s->str can be far longer than the input. diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (CheckMemoryOverflow(count,quantum) != MagickFalse)'], 'added_lines': ['  if (HeapOverflowSanityCheck(count,quantum) != MagickFalse)']}
description: magick/memory.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-5 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via vectors involving "too many exceptions," which trigger a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: AcquireVirtualMemory checks count and quantum with CheckMemoryOverflow and returns NULL on overflow, but this guard only covers the count*quantum product used later.
extent=count*quantum is computed after the guard, so the product is bounded, yet the per-element allocation path below still trusts extent as the buffer length.
AcquireAlignedMemory(1,extent) allocates a buffer of extent bytes; if extent is inconsistent with the size actually written by callers, writes can exceed the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs memory allocation and returns a buffer whose intended boundary is extent, and the weakness concerns operations outside that boundary. The overflow check addresses integer overflow (CWE-190) but does not by itself prevent out-of-bounds access; the supported consequence is a buffer-boundary violation leading to DoS/crash.

evidence_lines.code:
if (CheckMemoryOverflow(count,quantum) != MagickFalse)
return((MemoryInfo *) NULL);

extent=count*quantum;
memory_info->length=extent;
memory_info->blob=AcquireAlignedMemory(1,extent);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function's root cause is reliance on a single overflow check on count*quantum while the resulting extent is used as the authoritative buffer length for AcquireAlignedMemory without validating that allocated size against later writes. A trigger occurs when callers pass values whose product passes the check but whose subsequent use writes beyond the extent-sized buffer, producing out-of-bounds memory operations and a crash or memory corruption.

description: PDFio is a C library for reading and writing PDF files. In versions 1.1.0 and prior, a denial of service vulnerability exists in the pdfio parser. Crafted pdf files can cause the program to run at 100% utilization and never terminate. This is different from CVE-2023-24808. A patch for this issue is available in version 1.1.1.

code_evidence: Bounded while loops drive inflate() until avail_out reaches 0; the only normal exit is status == Z_STREAM_END.

The loop condition st->flate.avail_out > 0 remains true, so the loop re-invokes inflate() indefinitely on crafted flate data, consuming CPU at 100% and never terminating.
