commit_msg:
Check rest initializer existence after pattern finalization

Since the scanner info is not present for invalid destructuring patterns we can only ensure the existence of the rest element after the pattern is finalized.
This patch fixes #4928.

JerryScript-DCO-1.0-Signed-off-by: Robert Fancsik robert.fancsik@h-lab.eu
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      /* Checked at the end because there might be syntax errors before. */', '      JERRY_ASSERT (flags & PARSER_PATTERN_HAS_REST_ELEMENT);'], 'added_lines': ['', '#ifndef JERRY_NDEBUG', '  bool rest_found = false;', '#endif /* !defined(JERRY_NDEBUG) */', '#ifndef JERRY_NDEBUG', '      rest_found = true;', '#endif /* !defined(JERRY_NDEBUG) */', '', '#ifndef JERRY_NDEBUG', '  /* Checked at the end because there might be syntax errors before. */', '  JERRY_ASSERT (!!(flags & PARSER_PATTERN_HAS_REST_ELEMENT) == rest_found);', '#endif /* !defined(JERRY_NDEBUG) */']}
description: There is an Assertion 'flags & PARSER_PATTERN_HAS_REST_ELEMENT' failed at /jerry-core/parser/js/js-parser-expr.c in JerryScript 3.0.0.

code_evidence: When LEXER_THREE_DOTS is seen, the code sets PARSER_PATTERN_REST_ELEMENT (line 33) and then asserts flags & PARSER_PATTERN_HAS_REST_ELEMENT (line 46) before breaking; the HAS_REST_ELEMENT bit is set elsewhere by parser_pattern_process_assignment, so a malformed destructuring pattern that reaches this assert without that bit set aborts the parser.

At the end, the rest-element stack adjustment and finalization (lines 111-117) run; the original assert here fired for invalid patterns because scanner info was absent, which the patch replaces with a deferred rest_found check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a JERRY_ASSERT reachable from untrusted input parsing, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion). The patch confirms the assert was reachable for invalid patterns; this is not a memory-safety issue but an availability-impacting abort.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a JERRY_ASSERT on PARSER_PATTERN_HAS_REST_ELEMENT is reachable during parsing of a malformed object destructuring pattern where the rest marker is present but the flag was never set. Trigger: attacker-supplied source with an invalid destructuring pattern. Consequence: assertion failure aborts the process (DoS) rather than reporting a syntax error.

commit_msg:
su: properly clear child PID

Reported-by: Tobias Stöckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Signed-off-by: Karel Zak <kzak@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (caught_signal)', '      sleep (2);', '      kill (child, SIGKILL);', '      fprintf (stderr, _(" ...killed.\\n"));'], 'added_lines': ['', "\t  /* child is gone, don't use the PID anymore */", '\t  child = (pid_t) -1;', '  if (caught_signal && child != (pid_t)-1)', '      if (child != (pid_t)-1)', '\t{', '\t  sleep (2);', '\t  kill (child, SIGKILL);', '\t  fprintf (stderr, _(" ...killed.\\n"));', '\t}']}
description: A race condition was found in util-linux before 2.32.1 in the way su handled the management of child processes. A local authenticated attacker could use this flaw to kill other processes with root privileges under specific conditions.

code_evidence: The waitpid loop reaps the child and the code proceeds to the signal-handling block without invalidating the stored child PID; after waitpid returns the dead child's PID (line 69) and status is computed, child still holds that PID.
When caught_signal is set, the handler sends kill(child, SIGTERM) using the stale PID (line 99) even though the child may already have been reaped.
After a two-second sleep, kill(child, SIGKILL) is again issued against the stale PID (line 105); between reap and these calls the PID can be recycled by another process.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale child PID is a shared resource accessed without synchronization between reaping and signaling, allowing an interfering process to acquire the same PID concurrently; this is the timing/atomicity violation described by CWE-362. It is not merely improper resource release, since the exploitable effect is killing an unrelated privileged process.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reaped child's PID is never cleared, so the signal-termination path treats a dead PID as live. Trigger: a caught signal arrives while or after waitpid has reaped the child; during the sleep window the kernel may assign that PID to an unrelated process. Consequence: kill() with SIGTERM/SIGKILL is delivered to the recycled PID, letting a local user terminate other processes running with su's (root) privileges.

commit_msg: Add appheader tests; fix buffer overflow in main_get_appheader
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      char *parsed[4];', "      while ((slash = strchr (start, '/')) != NULL)"], 'added_lines': ['      const int kMaxArgs = 4;', '      char *parsed[kMaxArgs];', "      while ((slash = strchr (start, '/')) != NULL && place < (kMaxArgs-1))"]}
description: Buffer overflow in the main_get_appheader function in xdelta3-main.h in xdelta3 before 3.0.9 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted input file.

code_evidence: A fixed array parsed[4] is declared at line 16 and zeroed; the loop at line 18 iterates once per '/' delimiter with no bound on place, storing start into parsed[place++] at line 21.

After the loop, line 24 unconditionally writes parsed[place++] = start, and lines 25-31 read parsed[0..3] based on place; if apphead contains four or more slashes, place exceeds 3 and the write/read escapes the four-element array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to and later reads from a fixed-size stack buffer outside its intended boundary, which is exactly the memory-buffer boundary violation described by CWE-119. The missing bound on place is the underlying implementation error producing the out-of-bounds operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the delimiter-scanning loop lacks an index bound before incrementing place, so attacker-controlled appheader content with many '/' characters drives parsed[place++] past the array's end. Trigger: a crafted input file whose appheader contains four or more slashes. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds stack write at line 24 (and subsequent out-of-bounds reads at lines 25-31), potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg: Add bound check in datafile.cpp anywhere m_ppDataPtrs is accessed as an array. Should fix #2073
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif(Index < 0 || Index >= m_pDataFile->m_Header.m_NumRawData)', '\t\treturn;', '']}
description: In Teeworlds 0.7.2, there is a failed bounds check in CDataFileReader::GetData() and CDataFileReader::ReplaceData() and related functions in engine/shared/datafile.cpp that can lead to an arbitrary free and out-of-bounds pointer write, possibly resulting in remote code execution.

code_evidence: ReplaceData takes an int Index from the caller and uses it directly to index m_pDataFile->m_ppDataPtrs without any range check before the write on line 5. GetDataImpl and UnloadData on lines 3-4 also receive the unchecked Index, but the write on line 5 is the definite out-of-bounds store.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked Index causes a store past the bounds of m_ppDataPtrs, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The arbitrary-free aspect is a separate consequence, but the direct code-level defect here is the missing bound on the array write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: Index is never validated against m_Header.m_NumRawData. A negative or oversized Index passes through GetDataImpl/UnloadData and then m_ppDataPtrs[Index] = pData writes a caller-controlled pointer outside the array, corrupting memory; the patch adds the missing lower/upper bound check.

commit_msg:

The subsystem.su_mutex is required while accessing the item->ci_parent,
otherwise, NULL pointer dereference to the item->ci_parent will be
triggered in the following situation:

add node                     delete node
sys_write
 vfs_write
  configfs_write_file
   o2nm_node_store
    o2nm_node_local_write
                             do_rmdir
                              vfs_rmdir
                               configfs_rmdir
                                mutex_lock(&subsys->su_mutex);
                                unlink_obj
                                 item->ci_group = NULL;
                                 item->ci_parent = NULL;
	 to_o2nm_cluster_from_node
	  node->nd_item.ci_parent->ci_parent
	  BUG since of NULL pointer dereference to nd_item.ci_parent

Moreover, the o2nm_cluster also should be protected by the
subsystem.su_mutex.

commit_msg: lib: Detect and prevent integer overflow in XML_GetBuffer (CVE-2022-23852)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    /* Detect and prevent integer overflow */', '    if (keep > INT_MAX - neededSize) {', '      parser->m_errorCode = XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY;', '      return NULL;', '    }']}
description: Expat (aka libexpat) before 2.4.4 has a signed integer overflow in XML_GetBuffer, for configurations with a nonzero XML_CONTEXT_BYTES.

code_evidence: neededSize is computed as (int) of the sum of len and the buffer tail, then neededSize += keep adds the context bytes without any overflow check before the value is used.

bufferSize is cast to int and repeatedly doubled; the loop's only guard is bufferSize > 0, so an overflowed negative value is caught but a positive wraparound-derived size is not validated against neededSize.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs signed integer addition and doubling on sizes used for allocation without ensuring the result stays representable, which is exactly CWE-190; the patch's keep > INT_MAX - neededSize guard confirms the intended pre-add overflow constraint. This is not merely a length-validation issue, since the arithmetic itself wraps.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signed int neededSize accumulates len, the used buffer length, and keep (XML_CONTEXT_BYTES) without a bound check, so the addition can wrap to a small or negative value. Trigger: a large len near INT_MAX combined with a nonzero context. The wrapped size then drives the buffer-growth decision and MALLOC size, yielding an undersized allocation that later memory copies can overrun.

commit_msg:
PR23804, buffer overflow in sec_merge_hash_lookup

	PR 23804
	* merge.c (_bfd_add_merge_section): Don't attempt to merge
	sections where size is not a multiple of entsize.
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -15,6 +15,9 @@
   if (sec->size == 0
       || (sec->flags & SEC_EXCLUDE) != 0
       || sec->entsize == 0)
+    return TRUE;
+
+  if (sec->size % sec->entsize != 0)
     return TRUE;
 
   if ((sec->flags & SEC_RELOC) != 0)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    return TRUE;', '', '  if (sec->size % sec->entsize != 0)']}
description: A heap-based buffer over-read issue was discovered in the function sec_merge_hash_lookup in merge.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.31, because _bfd_add_merge_section mishandles section merges when size is not a multiple of entsize. A specially crafted ELF allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service, as demonstrated by ld.

code_evidence: Lines 13-16 only reject zero-size, excluded, or zero-entsize sections; there is no check that sec->size is a multiple of sec->entsize before merging.
Line 50 sizes the allocation from sec->size, and lines 51-52 add only one entsize when SEC_STRINGS is set, so the buffer ends at a partial element boundary.
Line 71 memsets one entsize at offset sec->size, and line 73 reads the section contents into this undersized buffer; later merge lookups walk element-sized strides over the truncated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits reads beyond the intended allocated contents buffer while processing malformed section sizes, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. It is not an out-of-bounds write, since the defect is reading past the buffer during merge lookup.

evidence_lines.code:
if (sec->size == 0
|| (sec->flags & SEC_EXCLUDE) != 0
|| sec->entsize == 0)
return TRUE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing size % entsize validation lets a section whose size is not a multiple of its element size be merged. Trigger: a crafted ELF section with a partial trailing element causes the merge table to stride by entsize past the allocated contents buffer, producing a heap out-of-bounds read and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
In parse_identifier, it doesn't stop copying '*pcur'
untill encounter the NULL. As the 'ret' has a
fixed-size buffer, if the '*pcur' has a long string,
there will be a buffer overflow. This patch avoid this.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liq3ea@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Marc-André Lureau <marcandre.lureau@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Airlie <airlied@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['   if (!parse_identifier( &ctx->cur, id )) {'], 'added_lines': ['   if (!parse_identifier( &ctx->cur, id, sizeof(id) )) {']}
description: Stack-based buffer overflow in the parse_identifier function in tgsi_text.c in the TGSI auxiliary module in the Gallium driver in virglrenderer before 0.6.0 allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds array access and QEMU process crash) via vectors related to parsing properties.

code_evidence: Line 7 declares a fixed-size stack buffer `char id[64]` that receives the parsed property identifier.
Line 12 calls `parse_identifier( &ctx->cur, id )` without conveying the destination capacity, so the callee has no bound on how many characters it copies into `id`.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a write beyond the intended boundary of the `id` memory buffer, which matches CWE-119's scope of reading/writing outside a buffer's intended boundary. This is the buffer-overflow class; the more specific stack-based overflow is a child weakness, but the target label CWE-119 is directly supported by the unbounded copy into `id`.

evidence_lines.code: char id[64];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the identifier copy into the fixed 64-byte stack buffer `id` is performed without any length limit because the buffer size is not passed at the call site. Trigger: a property name token longer than the buffer supplied by the parsed input causes `parse_identifier` to keep writing past `id`. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds stack write, leading to memory corruption and a crash (DoS) of the QEMU process.

commit_msg:
Bug #520 Fix heap overflow on zero or 0xFFFF packet length

Add check for packets that report zero packet length. Example
of fix:

    src/tcpprep --auto=bridge --pcap=poc16-get_l2len-heapoverflow --cachefile=/dev/null
    Warning: poc16-get_l2len-heapoverflow was captured using a snaplen of 17 bytes.  This may mean you have truncated packets.
    safe_pcap_next ERROR: Invalid packet length in tcpprep.c:process_raw_packets() line 334: packet length=0 capture length=0
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (pkthdr->len < pkthdr->caplen) {', '            fprintf(stderr, "safe_pcap_next ERROR: Invalid packet length in %s:%s() line %d: packet length %u is less than capture length %u\\n",'], 'added_lines': ['        if (!pkthdr->len || pkthdr->len < pkthdr->caplen) {', '            fprintf(stderr, "safe_pcap_next ERROR: Invalid packet length in %s:%s() line %d: packet length=%u capture length=%u\\n",']}
description: Tcpreplay before 4.3.1 has a heap-based buffer over-read in packet2tree in tree.c.

code_evidence: Line 4 obtains packet data and fills pkthdr via pcap_next; the returned pktdata is subsequently used by callers, so pkthdr->len and pkthdr->caplen constrain how much data is considered valid.
Lines 6 and 11 validate only len > MAXPACKET and len < caplen. A packet with len == 0 (and caplen == 0) passes both checks, so the function returns pktdata without rejecting a zero-length packet.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing zero-length check allows later code to read past the end of the packet buffer. This is an input-validation gap whose supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read, not an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), which would require a store past the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard at line 11 omits the zero-length case, so a packet reporting len == 0 is accepted and returned. Downstream parsing code that assumes a positive captured length then reads beyond the available buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read; the trigger is a crafted pcap record with zero packet length.

commit_msg: Fix #15545 - Fix NULL derefs after r_file_slurp() fails
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!lines) {', '\t\t\teprintf ("Failed to load \'%s\'.\\n", file);', '\t\t\tR_FREE (path);', '\t\t\treturn NULL;', '\t\t}']}
description: radare2 through 4.0.0 lacks validation of the content variable in the function r_asm_pseudo_incbin at libr/asm/asm.c, ultimately leading to an arbitrary write. This allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted input.

code_evidence: Line 11 assigns the result of r_file_slurp() to lines, which may be NULL when the file cannot be read. Line 12 immediately passes lines to r_str_split() without any NULL check, so a failed slurp flows directly into the split routine.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (lines) it expects to be valid but which can be NULL on slurp failure, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. This is a missing-validation NULL dereference rather than an out-of-bounds or use-after-free issue.

nlines = r_str_split (lines, '\n');

commit_msg:
sbr_hfadj: sanitize frequency band borders

user passed f_table_lim contains frequency band borders. Frequency
bands are groups of consecutive QMF channels. This means that their
bounds, as provided by f_table_lim, should never exceed MAX_M (maximum
number of QMF channels). c.f. ISO/IEC 14496-3:2001

FAAD2 does not verify this, leading to security issues when
processing files defining f_table_lim with values > MAX_M.

This patch sanitizes the values of f_table_lim so that they can be safely
used as index for Q_M_lim and G_lim arrays.

Fixes #21 (CVE-2018-20194).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            if (ml1 > MAX_M)', '                ml1 = MAX_M;', '', '            if (ml2 > MAX_M)', '                ml2 = MAX_M;', '']}
description: A NULL pointer dereference was discovered in ifilter_bank of libfaad/filtbank.c in Freeware Advanced Audio Decoder 2 (FAAD2) 2.8.8. The vulnerability causes a segmentation fault and application crash because adding to windowed output is mishandled in the EIGHT_SHORT_SEQUENCE case.

code_evidence: Lines 33-34 load ml1/ml2 from sbr->f_table_lim without bounding them to MAX_M; the loop at 35 then iterates m over that range.
The loops at 51 and 126 iterate m from ml1 to ml2 and write Q_M_lim[m], G_lim[m], S_M[m], and adj->G_lim_boost[l][m]/Q_M_lim_boost[l][m]/S_M_boost[l][m] using m as index.
These arrays are fixed size MAX_M (lines 7-10), so an unvalidated f_table_lim value greater than MAX_M causes writes past the end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of fixed-size buffers (Q_M_lim, G_lim, S_M, G_lim_boost, etc.) because the index bound is unvalidated. This is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), not merely an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: f_table_lim borders are used as loop bounds and array indices without clamping to MAX_M. When a crafted file supplies values above MAX_M, the m loops run beyond the fixed-size MAX_M arrays, writing out of bounds and corrupting memory (crash or potential code execution).

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/575

description: ImageMagick 7.0.6-2 has a memory leak vulnerability in WritePCXImage in coders/pcx.c.

code_evidence: Lines 110-113 allocate pcx_colormap via AcquireQuantumMemory and throw a ResourceLimitError if allocation fails, without freeing anything.
Lines 131-133 allocate pixel_info via AcquireVirtualMemory; on failure the function throws a writer exception while pcx_colormap from line 110 is still live.
Lines 265-266 show the normal cleanup path that relinquishes pixel_info and pcx_colormap, confirming both are owned resources.

This is a missing release, not a use-after-free or double-free.

pcx_colormap=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(pcx_colormap);

Trigger: AcquireVirtualMemory returning NULL after a successful pcx_colormap allocation. Consequence: a leaked heap buffer on each failed write, enabling memory exhaustion/DoS.

key = val + len + 1 and the do/while condition then allow further reads past the allocated region.

pcm_read(&reader->io, buf, chunk_size);

key = val + len + 1;
} while (key < end && val < end);

Trigger: a CAF chunk whose remaining bytes contain no NUL, making strlen(key) or strlen(val) scan beyond the malloc'd block. commit_msg:
Do not set the b_modified flag in block's journal head should not
until after we're sure that jbd2_journal_dirty_metadat() will not
abort with an error due to there not being enough space reserved in
the jbd2 handle.

Otherwise, future attempts to modify the buffer may lead a large
number of spurious errors and warnings.

This addresses CVE-2018-10883.

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=200071

Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tjh->b_modified = 1;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (jh->b_transaction == transaction &&', '\t\t\t    jh->b_jlist != BJ_Metadata)', '\t\t\t\tpr_err("JBD2: assertion failure: h_type=%u "', '\t\t\t\t       "h_line_no=%u block_no=%llu jlist=%u\\n",', '\t\t\t\t       handle->h_type, handle->h_line_no,', '\t\t\t\t       (unsigned long long) bh->b_blocknr,', '\t\t\t\t       jh->b_jlist);', '\t\tjh->b_modified = 1;']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's ext4 filesystem. A local user can cause an out-of-bounds write in jbd2_journal_dirty_metadata(), a denial of service, and a system crash by mounting and operating on a crafted ext4 filesystem image.

code_evidence: When jh->b_modified == 0, the function sets jh->b_modified = 1 at line 36 before checking handle->h_buffer_credits <= 0. If no credits remain, it returns -ENOSPC via out_unlock_bh with the modified flag already set, so the buffer is left marked modified without a reserved journal credit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The inconsistent modified state corrupts journal bookkeeping rather than writing past a buffer bound; the described out-of-bounds write is a downstream consequence, not an operation performed in this function. The direct defect is a state-ordering flaw (CWE-787 does not fit the code shown).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: b_modified is committed before the handle-reservation check, so an ENOSPC abort leaves the journal head marked modified while no credit backs it. A crafted ext4 image can drive subsequent dirty_metadata calls down the b_modified==1 fast path, producing inconsistent journal state and spurious assertion failures that can crash the system.

commit_msg:
calloc() multiplies its 2 arguments together and passes the result to
malloc().  Since the factors and product both have type size_t, this
can result in an integer overflow and subsequent buffer overflow.
Check for this and fail if it happens.

CVE-2021-31870

Signed-off-by: Ben Hutchings <ben@decadent.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn zalloc(nmemb * size);'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned long prod;', '', '\tif (__builtin_umull_overflow(nmemb, size, &prod)) {', '\t\terrno = ENOMEM;', '\t\treturn NULL;', '\t}', '\treturn zalloc(prod);']}
description: An issue was discovered in klibc before 2.0.9. Multiplication in the calloc() function may result in an integer overflow and a subsequent heap buffer overflow.

code_evidence: calloc multiplies the two size_t parameters nmemb * size in a single expression and passes the product directly to zalloc, with no check that the multiplication stays within size_t range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is the arithmetic wraparound of a size computation used for memory allocation, matching CWE-190's integer overflow in a size context. The heap overflow is the downstream consequence, not the root weakness.

evidence_lines.code: return zalloc(nmemb * size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unchecked multiplication of attacker-influenced nmemb and size, both size_t, can wrap to a small value. Trigger: large allocation arguments. The wrapped product is then used as the allocation size, so zalloc reserves a much smaller heap buffer than the caller expects, enabling a subsequent heap buffer overflow when the caller writes nmemb*size bytes.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Reported-by: syzbot+f427adf9324b92652ccc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (is_bad_inode(inode))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (fuse_is_bad(inode))']}
description: An issue was discovered in the FUSE filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.10.6, aka CID-5d069dbe8aaf. fuse_do_getattr() calls make_bad_inode() in inappropriate situations, causing a system crash. NOTE: the original fix for this vulnerability was incomplete, and its incompleteness is tracked as CVE-2021-28950.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The readdir function only gates on inode validity; the incomplete-cleanup flaw (make_bad_inode leaving dnotify structures) lies in fuse_do_getattr, not in this function.

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: remove nodes owned by destroyed domain

In case a domain is removed from Xenstore, remove all nodes owned by
it per default.

This tackles the problem that nodes might be created by a domain
outside its home path in Xenstore, leading to Xenstore hogging more
and more memory. Domain quota don't work in this case if the guest is
rebooting in between.

Since XSA-322 ownership of such stale nodes is transferred to dom0,
which is helping against unintended access, but not against OOM of
Xenstore.

As a fallback for weird cases add a Xenstore start parameter for
keeping today's way to handle stale nodes, adding the risk of Xenstore
hitting an OOM situation.

This is part of XSA-419 / CVE-2022-42322.

Fixes: 496306324d8d ("tools/xenstore: revoke access rights for removed domains")

Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>

commit_msg:
Fix crash from integer overflow in SMsgReader::readClientCutText

The length sent by client is U32, but is converted into int. If it was bigger than 0x7fffffff the resulting int is negative, it passes the check against maxCutText and later throws std::bad_alloc from CharArray which takes down the whole server.

All the Streaming API deals with lengths in ints, so we can't tell it to skip that big amount of data. And it is not realistic to expect more than 2GB of clipboard data anyway. So lets just throw rdr::Exception that will disconnect this client and keep the server alive.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (len < 0) {', '    throw Exception("Cut text too long.");', '  }']}
description: In TigerVNC 1.7.1 (SMsgReader.cxx SMsgReader::readClientCutText), by causing an integer overflow, an authenticated client can crash the server.

code_evidence: Line 4 reads a U32 length into a signed int, so values above 0x7fffffff become negative. Line 5 checks only len > maxCutText, which a negative len passes; lines 6-8 are skipped. Line 10 then allocates CharArray(len+1) with the negative-derived size, leading to a huge allocation or bad_alloc.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe conversion of a U32 into int and the resulting negative value used as an allocation size is an integer overflow/wraparound (CWE-190). The missing len < 0 guard is the specific defect; this is not merely an excessive-length check because the value is reinterpreted as negative and used downstream.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unsigned 32-bit client length is truncated into a signed int without a lower-bound check, and the only guard is an upper-bound comparison. A client sending a length greater than 0x7fffffff produces a negative len that bypasses the maxCutText check, so the allocation at line 10 uses a wrapped size and throws std::bad_alloc, crashing the server.

commit_msg:
cryp: prevent direct calls to update and final functions

With inconsistent or malformed data it has been possible to call
"update" and "final" crypto functions directly. Using a fuzzer tool [1]
we have seen that this results in asserts, i.e., a crash that
potentially could leak sensitive information.

By setting the state (initialized) in the crypto context (i.e., the
tee_cryp_state) at the end of all syscall_*_init functions and then add
a check of the state at the beginning of all update and final functions,
  we prevent direct entrance to the "update" and "final" functions.

[1] https://github.com/MartijnB/optee_fuzzer

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow (CVE-2021-21309). (#8522)

On 32-bit systems, setting the proto-max-bulk-len config parameter to a high value may result with integer overflow and a subsequent heap overflow when parsing an input bulk (CVE-2021-21309).

This fix has two parts:

Set a reasonable limit to the config parameter.
Add additional checks to prevent the problem in other potential but unknown code paths.

(cherry picked from commit d32f2e9999ce003bad0bd2c3bca29f64dcce4433)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    ASSERT_NO_SIZE_OVERFLOW(size);']}
description: Redis is an open-source, in-memory database that persists on disk. In affected versions of Redis an integer overflow bug in 32-bit Redis version 4.0 or newer could be exploited to corrupt the heap and potentially result with remote code execution. Redis 4.0 or newer uses a configurable limit for the maximum supported bulk input size. By default, it is 512MB which is a safe value for all platforms. If the limit is significantly increased, receiving a large request from a client may trigger several integer overflow scenarios, which would result with buffer overflow and heap corruption. We believe this could in certain conditions be exploited for remote code execution. By default, authenticated Redis users have access to all configuration parameters and can therefore use the “CONFIG SET proto-max-bulk-len” to change the safe default, making the system vulnerable. **This problem only affects 32-bit Redis (on a 32-bit system, or as a 32-bit executable running on a 64-bit system).** The problem is fixed in version 6.2, and the fix is back ported to 6.0.11 and 5.0.11. Make sure you use one of these versions if you are running 32-bit Redis. An additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent clients from directly executing `CONFIG SET`: Using Redis 6.0 or newer, ACL configuration can be used to block the command. Using older versions, the `rename-command` configuration directive can be used to rename the command to a random string unknown to users, rendering it inaccessible. Please note that this workaround may have an additional impact on users or operational systems that expect `CONFIG SET` to behave in certain ways.

code_evidence: zmalloc computes malloc(size+PREFIX_SIZE) without checking that adding PREFIX_SIZE to the caller-supplied size_t size wraps around.

In the non-HAVE_MALLOC_SIZE path, the same size+PREFIX_SIZE expression is stored as the allocation header and passed to update_zmalloc_stat_alloc, so the wrapped small value is used as the recorded allocation size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the function performs an integer addition whose result can wrap and then uses the wrapped value for memory allocation and size bookkeeping. This is not merely a resource-exhaustion issue; the wrapped size directly undermines the allocation-size invariant, matching integer overflow leading to heap corruption.

evidence_lines.code:
void *zmalloc(size_t size) {
void *ptr = malloc(size+PREFIX_SIZE);

*((size_t*)ptr) = size;
update_zmalloc_stat_alloc(size+PREFIX_SIZE);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unchecked size+PREFIX_SIZE addition on a size_t parameter that can wrap when size is near SIZE_MAX, e.g. when a large proto-max-bulk-len drives a bulk allocation on 32-bit Redis. The wrapped small value is used as the malloc argument and as the size header, so the buffer is under-allocated while callers believe the original large size was allocated, enabling heap overflow and corruption.

commit_msg:
Fix a bug in the verifier's scalar32_min_max_*() functions which leads to
incorrect tracking of 32 bit bounds for the simulation of and/or/xor bitops.
When both the src & dst subreg is a known constant, then the assumption is
that scalar_min_max_*() will take care to update bounds correctly. However,
this is not the case, for example, consider a register R2 which has a tnum
of 0xffffffff00000000, meaning, lower 32 bits are known constant and in this
case of value 0x00000001. R2 is then and'ed with a register R3 which is a
64 bit known constant, here, 0x100000002.

What can be seen in line '10:' is that 32 bit bounds reach an invalid state
where {u,s}32_min_value > {u,s}32_max_value. The reason is scalar32_min_max_*()
delegates 32 bit bounds updates to scalar_min_max_*(), however, that really
only takes place when both the 64 bit src & dst register is a known constant.
Given scalar32_min_max_*() is intended to be designed as closely as possible
to scalar_min_max_*(), update the 32 bit bounds in this situation through
__mark_reg32_known() which will set all {u,s}32_{min,max}_value to the correct
constant, which is 0x00000000 after the fix (given 0x00000001 & 0x00000002 in
32 bit space). This is possible given var32_off already holds the final value
as dst_reg->var_off is updated before calling scalar32_min_max_*().

Before fix, invalid tracking of R2:

  [...]
  9: R0_w=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv(id=0,smin_value=-9223372036854775807 (0x8000000000000001),smax_value=9223372032559808513 (0x7fffffff00000001),umin_value=1,umax_value=0xffffffff00000001,var_off=(0x1; 0xffffffff00000000),s32_min_value=1,s32_max_value=1,u32_min_value=1,u32_max_value=1) R3_w=inv4294967298 R10=fp0
  9: (5f) r2 &= r3
  10: R0_w=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv(id=0,smin_value=0,smax_value=4294967296 (0x100000000),umin_value=0,umax_value=0x100000000,var_off=(0x0; 0x100000000),s32_min_value=1,s32_max_value=0,u32_min_value=1,u32_max_value=0) R3_w=inv4294967298 R10=fp0
  [...]

After fix, correct tracking of R2:

  [...]
  9: R0_w=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv(id=0,smin_value=-9223372036854775807 (0x8000000000000001),smax_value=9223372032559808513 (0x7fffffff00000001),umin_value=1,umax_value=0xffffffff00000001,var_off=(0x1; 0xffffffff00000000),s32_min_value=1,s32_max_value=1,u32_min_value=1,u32_max_value=1) R3_w=inv4294967298 R10=fp0
  9: (5f) r2 &= r3
  10: R0_w=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv(id=0,smin_value=0,smax_value=4294967296 (0x100000000),umin_value=0,umax_value=0x100000000,var_off=(0x0; 0x100000000),s32_min_value=0,s32_max_value=0,u32_min_value=0,u32_max_value=0) R3_w=inv4294967298 R10=fp0
  [...]

Fixes: 3f50f132d840 ("bpf: Verifier, do explicit ALU32 bounds tracking")
Fixes: 2921c90d4718 ("bpf: Fix a verifier failure with xor")
Reported-by: Manfred Paul (@_manfp)
Reported-by: Thadeu Lima de Souza Cascardo <cascardo@canonical.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Reviewed-by: John Fastabend <john.fastabend@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* Assuming scalar64_min_max_xor will be called so it is safe', '\t * to skip updating register for known case.', '\t */', '\tif (src_known && dst_known)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (src_known && dst_known) {', '\t\t__mark_reg32_known(dst_reg, var32_off.value);', '\t}']}
description: The eBPF ALU32 bounds tracking for bitwise ops (AND, OR and XOR) in the Linux kernel did not properly update 32-bit bounds, which could be turned into out of bounds reads and writes in the Linux kernel and therefore, arbitrary code execution. This issue was fixed via commit 049c4e13714e ("bpf: Fix alu32 const subreg bound tracking on bitwise operations") (v5.13-rc4) and backported to the stable kernels in v5.12.4, v5.11.21, and v5.10.37. The AND/OR issues were introduced by commit 3f50f132d840 ("bpf: Verifier, do explicit ALU32 bounds tracking") (5.7-rc1) and the XOR variant was introduced by 2921c90d4718 ("bpf:Fix a verifier failure with xor") ( 5.10-rc1).

code_evidence: When both the source and destination 32-bit subregisters are known constants (src_known && dst_known), the function returns at line 9 without updating dst_reg->u32_min_value, u32_max_value, s32_min_value, or s32_max_value. The comment in the pre-fix code assumed scalar64_min_max_xor would handle this, but that only occurs when the full 64-bit registers are known constants.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale 32-bit bounds let the verifier accept memory accesses beyond the intended buffer, directly enabling out-of-bounds writes (CWE-787). The incorrect bound tracking is the cause; the out-of-bounds write is the supported consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
if (src_known && dst_known)
return;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the known-constant branch skips updating the 32-bit bounds, leaving stale {u,s}32_min/max values that can become inconsistent (e.g., min > max). Trigger: an AND/OR/XOR with a 64-bit constant where only the 32-bit subregs are known. Consequence: the BPF verifier tracks incorrect bounds, permitting out-of-bounds reads/writes and potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fix Integer overflow issue with intsets (CVE-2021-32687)

The vulnerability involves changing the default set-max-intset-entries
configuration parameter to a very large value and constructing specially
crafted commands to manipulate sets
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                if (intsetLen(subject->ptr) > server.set_max_intset_entries)'], 'added_lines': ['                size_t max_entries = server.set_max_intset_entries;', '                /* limit to 1G entries due to intset internals. */', '                if (max_entries >= 1<<30) max_entries = 1<<30;', '                if (intsetLen(subject->ptr) > max_entries)']}
description: Redis is an open source, in-memory database that persists on disk. An integer overflow bug affecting all versions of Redis can be exploited to corrupt the heap and potentially be used to leak arbitrary contents of the heap or trigger remote code execution. The vulnerability involves changing the default set-max-intset-entries configuration parameter to a very large value and constructing specially crafted commands to manipulate sets. The problem is fixed in Redis versions 6.2.6, 6.0.16 and 5.0.14. An additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent users from modifying the set-max-intset-entries configuration parameter. This can be done using ACL to restrict unprivileged users from using the CONFIG SET command.

code_evidence: The intset branch validates value as a long long and calls intsetAdd, storing the result in subject->ptr. On success, the entry count is compared against server.set_max_intset_entries, a configurable value, to decide whether to convert to a hash table. The pre-patch comparison at line 16 uses the raw configuration value without bounding it, so an oversized configured limit lets the intset grow beyond what its internal integer size fields can represent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the weakness is integer overflow/wraparound in internal size arithmetic, reached when the configured entry limit is not bounded. The missing cap is the root cause; the heap corruption is its consequence, distinguishing it from a mere logic or resource-limit issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the entry-count check uses an unbounded, user-configurable set_max_intset_entries. Trigger: setting that parameter to a very large value and issuing crafted set commands that add many integer entries. Consequence: intset internal length/size arithmetic overflows or wraps, corrupting heap memory, which can leak heap data or enable code execution; the patch caps the effective limit at 1<<30 to prevent this.

commit_msg:
ipf: release unhandled packets from the batch

Since 640d4db788ed ("ipf: Fix a use-after-free error, ...") the ipf
framework unconditionally allocates a new dp_packet to track
individual fragments.  This prevents a use-after-free.  However, an
additional issue was present - even when the packet buffer is cloned,
if the ip fragment handling code keeps it, the original buffer is
leaked during the refill loop.  Even in the original processing code,
the hardcoded dnsteal branches would always leak a packet buffer from
the refill loop.

This can be confirmed with valgrind:

==717566== 16,672 (4,480 direct, 12,192 indirect) bytes in 8 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 390 of 390
==717566==    at 0x484086F: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:380)
==717566==    by 0x537BFD: xmalloc__ (util.c:137)
==717566==    by 0x537BFD: xmalloc (util.c:172)
==717566==    by 0x46DDD4: dp_packet_new (dp-packet.c:153)
==717566==    by 0x46DDD4: dp_packet_new_with_headroom (dp-packet.c:163)
==717566==    by 0x550AA6: netdev_linux_batch_rxq_recv_sock.constprop.0 (netdev-linux.c:1262)
==717566==    by 0x5512AF: netdev_linux_rxq_recv (netdev-linux.c:1511)
==717566==    by 0x4AB7E0: netdev_rxq_recv (netdev.c:727)
==717566==    by 0x47F00D: dp_netdev_process_rxq_port (dpif-netdev.c:4699)
==717566==    by 0x47FD13: dpif_netdev_run (dpif-netdev.c:5957)
==717566==    by 0x4331D2: type_run (ofproto-dpif.c:370)
==717566==    by 0x41DFD8: ofproto_type_run (ofproto.c:1768)
==717566==    by 0x40A7FB: bridge_run__ (bridge.c:3245)
==717566==    by 0x411269: bridge_run (bridge.c:3310)
==717566==    by 0x406E6C: main (ovs-vswitchd.c:127)

The fix is to delete the original packet when it isn't able to be
reinserted into the packet batch.  Subsequent valgrind runs show that
the packets are not leaked from the batch any longer.

Fixes: 640d4db788ed ("ipf: Fix a use-after-free error, and remove the 'do_not_steal' flag.")
Fixes: 4ea96698f667 ("Userspace datapath: Add fragmentation handling.")
Reported-by: Wan Junjie <wanjunjie@bytedance.com>
Reported-at: https://github.com/openvswitch/ovs-issues/issues/226
Signed-off-by: Aaron Conole <aconole@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: David Marchand <david.marchand@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Wan Junjie <wanjunjie@bytedance.com>
Signed-off-by: Alin-Gabriel Serdean <aserdean@ovn.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            } else {', '                dp_packet_delete(pkt);']}
description: A memory leak was found in Open vSwitch (OVS) during userspace IP fragmentation processing. An attacker could use this flaw to potentially exhaust available memory by keeping sending packet fragments.

code_evidence: Under ipf->ipf_lock, ipf_handle_frag() is called with pkt. If it returns false, the packet is reinserted via dp_packet_batch_refill(pb, pkt, pb_idx) at line 17. When it returns true (the fragment-handling code retains the packet), no else branch releases pkt; the loop iteration ends and the batch refill no longer holds a reference to the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated memory is not released after its effective lifetime; the packet buffer is neither refilled into the batch nor freed on the true branch. This is a leak, not a use-after-free, since no stale reference is later dereferenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the retained-packet path of ipf_handle_frag() returns true without any dp_packet_delete(pkt) call, so the allocated dp_packet buffer is dropped from the batch without being freed. Trigger: a valid IPv4/IPv6 fragment that ipf_handle_frag() keeps. Consequence: repeated fragments leak memory, exhausting available memory (DoS).

commit_msg:
Q.931: fix use-after-free (write) of "q931_pi"

The dissect_q931_number_ie (and indirectly dissect_q931_cause_ie_unsafe)
write to the "q931_pi" structure which seems private to the q931
dissector, but can in fact be called through other dissectors (isup) as
well. Normally this structure is initialized in "dissect_q931_pdu" and
invalidated at the end of the function, but a malformed packet can
prevent the cleanup. In the next packet, a different dissector can thus
trigger a use-after-free via "dissect_q931_number_ie".

Rename "dissect_q931_cause_ie_unsafe" since "unsafe" meant that external
dissectors could not call it directly (see commit a83a87e9ca).

Based on commit 197ceddab109, it seems that the intended purpose of the
structure is to provide information to the VoIP Calls dialog, but it
would only be used when called through dissect_q931_pdu. Dissectors like
isup have their own routines to provide call information, but as a
side-effect of code sharing the problematic code path was reached.

Change-Id: I871525db560f24690ade9a0b944c6d0e655ed34b
Link: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=6711

Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot

(cherry picked from commit d08a53a7b9ebf723816f224897c68aa652589050)

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    have_valid_q931_pi=TRUE;', '    if(have_valid_q931_pi && q931_pi) {', '        q931_pi->message_type = message_type;', '    }', '        dissect_q931_IEs(tvb, pinfo, tree, q931_tree, is_over_ip, offset, 0);', '        dissect_q931_IEs(tvb, pinfo, tree, q931_tree, is_over_ip, offset, 0);', '        dissect_q931_IEs(next_tvb, pinfo, tree, q931_tree, is_over_ip, 0, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['    q931_packet_info *q931_pi = NULL;', '    q931_pi->message_type = message_type;', '        dissect_q931_IEs(tvb, pinfo, tree, q931_tree, is_over_ip, offset, 0, q931_pi);', '        dissect_q931_IEs(tvb, pinfo, tree, q931_tree, is_over_ip, offset, 0, q931_pi);', '        dissect_q931_IEs(next_tvb, pinfo, tree, q931_tree, is_over_ip, 0, 0, q931_pi);']}
description: In Wireshark 2.6.0, 2.4.0 to 2.4.6, and 2.2.0 to 2.2.14, the Q.931 dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-q931.c by avoiding a use-after-free after a malformed packet prevented certain cleanup.

code_evidence: The function allocates q931_pi in packet scope, resets it, and sets the global have_valid_q931_pi flag to TRUE, marking the structure valid for later use.
The guarded write only updates q931_pi->message_type when have_valid_q931_pi is set; the global flag and pointer are not cleared on the early return paths.
An early return after dissect_q931_IEs leaves the global q931_pi pointer and have_valid_q931_pi flag intact instead of invalidating them.
The reassembly path passes the same q931_pi into dissect_q931_IEs via the final call, so callers can still reach the stale global structure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function leaves a global pointer to packet-scope memory valid across packets and later writes through it, which is a use-after-free (CWE-416) rather than a simple NULL dereference or out-of-bounds access.

evidence_lines.code: dissect_q931_IEs(tvb, pinfo, tree, q931_tree, is_over_ip, offset, 0);

if (next_tvb)
dissect_q931_IEs(next_tvb, pinfo, tree, q931_tree, is_over_ip, 0, 0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the global q931_pi pointer and have_valid_q931_pi flag are set but never invalidated when the function returns early after a malformed packet. Trigger: a subsequent packet or external dissector calls dissect_q931_number_ie, which writes through the stale global pointer whose memory may have been freed/reused. Consequence: use-after-free write, causing crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
KVM: x86: Forbid VMM to set SYNIC/STIMER MSRs when SynIC wasn't activated

Setting non-zero values to SYNIC/STIMER MSRs activates certain features,
this should not happen when KVM_CAP_HYPERV_SYNIC{,2} was not activated.

Note, it would've been better to forbid writing anything to SYNIC/STIMER
MSRs, including zeroes, however, at least QEMU tries clearing
HV_X64_MSR_STIMER0_CONFIG without SynIC. HV_X64_MSR_EOM MSR is somewhat
'special' as writing zero there triggers an action, this also should not
happen when SynIC wasn't activated.

Signed-off-by: Vitaly Kuznetsov <vkuznets@redhat.com>
Message-Id: <20220325132140.25650-4-vkuznets@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!synic->active && !host)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!synic->active && (!host || count))']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s KVM when attempting to set a SynIC IRQ. This issue makes it possible for a misbehaving VMM to write to SYNIC/STIMER MSRs, causing a NULL pointer dereference. This flaw allows an unprivileged local attacker on the host to issue specific ioctl calls, causing a kernel oops condition that results in a denial of service.

code_evidence: The guard only rejects the call when synic is inactive AND the write does not come from the host (!synic->active && !host). A host-originated write with non-zero count bypasses this check and proceeds to stimer_cleanup/stimer_mark_pending on a SynIC that was never activated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw ultimately yields a NULL pointer dereference from operating on an inactive SynIC; the code fails to enforce the activation precondition before touching timer state, matching CWE-476 rather than a mere logic/validation error.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!synic->active && !host)
return 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the missing count condition lets a VMM set a non-zero STIMER count while SynIC is inactive, so timer machinery runs against an uninitialized/inactive SynIC state. Trigger: a host-side set of the STIMER count MSR with count != 0 when SynIC was not activated. Supported consequence: subsequent dereference of a NULL SynIC-related pointer, causing a kernel oops/DoS.

commit_msg: Fix buffer overflow in Gorilla codec
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void decompressDataForType(const char * source, UInt32 source_size, char * dest)'], 'added_lines': ['void decompressDataForType(const char * source, UInt32 source_size, char * dest, UInt32 dest_size)', '    const char * const dest_end = dest + dest_size;', '', '    if (dest + items_count * sizeof(T) > dest_end)', '        throw Exception(ErrorCodes::CANNOT_DECOMPRESS, "Cannot decompress Gorilla-encoded data: corrupted input data.");']}
description: ClickHouse is an open-source column-oriented database management system that allows generating analytical data reports in real-time. A heap buffer overflow issue was discovered in ClickHouse server. An attacker could send a specially crafted payload to the native interface exposed by default on port 9000/tcp, triggering a bug in the decompression logic of Gorilla codec that crashes the ClickHouse server process. This attack does not require authentication. This issue has been addressed in ClickHouse Cloud version 23.9.2.47551 and ClickHouse versions 23.10.5.20, 23.3.18.15, 23.8.8.20, and 23.9.6.20.

code_evidence: The function receives only source/source_size and a raw dest pointer; no destination capacity is passed, so dest_end cannot be computed or checked. items_count is attacker-controlled from the payload (line 6) and bounds only the source. After writing the first item at line 12, the loop at line 19 iterates up to items_count, and each iteration writes T at line 42 and advances dest at line 43 with no check against the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing T values at line 42 and advancing dest at line 43 past the allocated buffer is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the source is bounds-checked while the destination is not.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decompressor writes items_count decoded values into dest without knowing the destination size. Trigger: a crafted native-interface payload whose item count exceeds the allocated output buffer. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds writes past dest_end, corrupting memory and crashing the server (DoS, potential code execution).

commit_msg:
packet: Don't write vnet header beyond end of buffer

... which may happen with certain values of tp_reserve and maclen.

Fixes: 58d19b19cd99 ("packet: vnet_hdr support for tpacket_rcv")
Signed-off-by: Benjamin Poirier <bpoirier@suse.com>
Cc: Willem de Bruijn <willemb@google.com>
Acked-by: Willem de Bruijn <willemb@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (po->has_vnet_hdr)', '\t\t\tif ((int)snaplen < 0)', '\tif (po->has_vnet_hdr) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tbool do_vnet = false;', '\t\tif (po->has_vnet_hdr) {', '\t\t\tdo_vnet = true;', '\t\t}', '\t\t\tif ((int)snaplen < 0) {', '\t\t\t\tdo_vnet = false;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tdo_vnet = false;', '\tif (do_vnet) {']}
description: The tpacket_rcv function in net/packet/af_packet.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13 mishandles vnet headers, which might allow local users to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow, and disk and memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls.

code_evidence: When has_vnet_hdr is set, netoff is enlarged by sizeof(struct virtio_net_hdr), shifting macoff accordingly; macoff is the write offset into the ring frame.
If the frame-size clamp yields snaplen < 0, snaplen is forced to 0 but the unpatched code still proceeds; macoff remains potentially larger than the frame, so no room exists for the vnet header.
With has_vnet_hdr true, virtio_net_hdr_from_skb writes to h.raw + macoff - sizeof(struct virtio_net_hdr); when macoff is below sizeof(struct virtio_net_hdr) this address precedes the frame buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a write through h.raw + macoff - sizeof(struct virtio_net_hdr) without a lower-bound check, resulting in an out-of-bounds memory write, which is the buffer-boundary violation described by CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the vnet-header write offset is derived from macoff without verifying that the clamped frame still has room for the header. Trigger: crafted tp_reserve/maclen values make macoff small (or snaplen clamped to 0) while has_vnet_hdr is enabled. Consequence: virtio_net_hdr_from_skb writes before/outside the ring buffer, corrupting adjacent memory or causing DoS.

commit_msg:
Zero and sanity check all dynamic allocs.

This addresses the memory issues in Issue #6 expressed in
calloc_some.pdf and malloc_some.pdf
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    new_fname = malloc(strlen(fname) + strlen(dirname) + 16);'], 'added_lines': ['    new_fname = safe_calloc(strlen(fname) + strlen(dirname) + 16);']}
description: An issue was discovered in PDFResurrect before 0.18. pdf_load_pages_kids in pdf.c doesn't validate a certain size value, which leads to a malloc failure and out-of-bounds write.

code_evidence: Line 13 allocates new_fname with malloc(strlen(fname) + strlen(dirname) + 16) and does not check the return value for NULL; on allocation failure new_fname is NULL. Line 14 then passes that same size expression to snprintf as the buffer bound, and line 15 writes the formatted dirname/fname/version string into new_fname. Because the allocation result is unchecked, a failed malloc leaves a NULL pointer that snprintf subsequently writes through.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked allocation leads snprintf to write past the end of (or through an absent) intended buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is distinct from a pure NULL-pointer dereference because the write operation targets memory outside the intended buffer boundary.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dynamic allocation size is not validated and malloc's return is not checked. Trigger: an allocation failure (e.g., oversized size value causing malloc to fail), leaving new_fname NULL. description: A write-what-where condition in hermes caused by an integer overflow, prior to commit 5b6255ae049fa4641791e47fad994e8e8c4da374 allows attackers to potentially execute arbitrary code via crafted JavaScript. Note that this is only exploitable if the application using Hermes permits evaluation of untrusted JavaScript. Hence, most React Native applications are not affected.

The new capacity is passed directly to CompactTable(newCapacity, ...) and then used to size and index the table during rehashing (loop bound oldIdx < tmpTable.size(), set(idx, oldVal)), tying the raw capacity value to memory layout.

tmpTable.swap(table_);
table_.set(idx, oldVal);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the new capacity is derived by arithmetic that can wrap to a small value, and the function accepts it without a runtime check (assert only). Trigger: creating enough identifiers that the capacity computation overflows. Consequence: a too-small table is allocated while rehash indexing proceeds, yielding out-of-bounds writes (write-what-where) that can lead to arbitrary code execution.

commit_msg:
Timing vulnerability in DSA signature generation (CVE-2018-0734).

Avoid a timing attack that leaks information via a side channel that
triggers when a BN is resized.  Increasing the size of the BNs
prior to doing anything with them suppresses the attack.

Thanks due to Samuel Weiser for finding and locating this.

Reviewed-by: Bernd Edlinger <bernd.edlinger@hotmail.de>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/7486)

description: FreeRDP is a free remote desktop protocol library and clients. Affected versions of FreeRDP are missing input validation in `urbdrc` channel. A malicious server can trick a FreeRDP based client to crash with division by zero. This issue has been addressed in version 2.9.0. All users are advised to upgrade. Users unable to upgrade should not use the `/usb` redirection switch.

code_evidence: Line 26 divides BufferSize by the attacker-controlled NumberOfPackets without first ensuring it is nonzero; NumberOfPackets arrives as a function parameter from the server-side isochronous transfer request. Line 27 then passes the same unvalidated count to libusb_alloc_transfer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the defect is the absence of input validation on a quantity (NumberOfPackets) received from an untrusted peer; the zero value is not rejected before processing, leading to the crash. iso_transfer = libusb_alloc_transfer(NumberOfPackets);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the server-supplied NumberOfPackets without validating that it is greater than zero before using it as a divisor. Trigger: a malicious server sends an isochronous transfer request with NumberOfPackets == 0, causing BufferSize / NumberOfPackets to divide by zero. Supported consequence: the client crashes (denial of service).

commit_msg:
Always generate DH keys for ephemeral DH cipher suites

Modified version of the commit ffaef3f15 in the master branch by Stephen
Henson. This makes the SSL_OP_SINGLE_DH_USE option a no-op and always
generates a new DH key for every handshake regardless.

CVE-2016-0701 (fix part 2 or 2)

Issue reported by Antonio Sanso

Reviewed-by: Viktor Dukhovni <viktor@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            }', '            if (!(ctx->options & SSL_OP_SINGLE_DH_USE)) {', '                if (!DH_generate_key(new)) {', '                    SSLerr(SSL_F_SSL3_CTX_CTRL, ERR_R_DH_LIB);', '                    DH_free(new);', '                    return 0;', '                }'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The DH_check_pub_key function in crypto/dh/dh_check.c in OpenSSL 1.0.2 before 1.0.2f does not ensure that prime numbers are appropriate for Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange, which makes it easier for remote attackers to discover a private DH exponent by making multiple handshakes with a peer that chose an inappropriate number, as demonstrated by a number in an X9.42 file.

code_evidence: SSL_CTRL_SET_TMP_DH duplicates the supplied DH params into 'new' via DHparams_dup, then only calls DH_generate_key(new) when the SSL_OP_SINGLE_DH_USE option is not set. The supplied 'dh' (parg) is never validated with DH_check for appropriate primes before being installed as cert->dh_tmp at line 63.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported impact is disclosure of the private DH exponent/secret key material to an unauthorized observer, matching CWE-200's confidentiality scope. The function's missing DH_check constraint is the enabling mistake; the exposure of sensitive key data is the resultant weakness CWE-200 describes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accepts and stores caller-supplied DH parameters without validating that the prime is safe/appropriate for DH key exchange. Trigger: a peer supplies an inappropriate DH number (e.g., an X9.42 file value) and multiple handshakes reuse the resulting weak DH state. Consequence: an attacker observing handshakes can more easily recover the private DH exponent, exposing secret key material (confidentiality loss).

commit_msg:
Namespace: fix operand cache leak

I found some ACPI operand cache leaks in ACPI early abort cases.

Boot log of ACPI operand cache leak is as follows:
>[    0.174332] ACPI: Added _OSI(Module Device)
>[    0.175504] ACPI: Added _OSI(Processor Device)
>[    0.176010] ACPI: Added _OSI(3.0 _SCP Extensions)
>[    0.177032] ACPI: Added _OSI(Processor Aggregator Device)
>[    0.178284] ACPI: SCI (IRQ16705) allocation failed
>[    0.179352] ACPI Exception: AE_NOT_ACQUIRED, Unable to install
System Control Interrupt handler (20160930/evevent-131)
>[    0.180008] ACPI: Unable to start the ACPI Interpreter
>[    0.181125] ACPI Error: Could not remove SCI handler
(20160930/evmisc-281)
>[    0.184068] kmem_cache_destroy Acpi-Operand: Slab cache still has
objects
>[    0.185358] CPU: 0 PID: 1 Comm: swapper/0 Not tainted 4.10.0-rc3 #2
>[    0.186820] Hardware name: innotek GmbH VirtualBox/VirtualBox, BIOS
VirtualBox 12/01/2006
>[    0.188000] Call Trace:
>[    0.188000]  ? dump_stack+0x5c/0x7d
>[    0.188000]  ? kmem_cache_destroy+0x224/0x230
>[    0.188000]  ? acpi_sleep_proc_init+0x22/0x22
>[    0.188000]  ? acpi_os_delete_cache+0xa/0xd
>[    0.188000]  ? acpi_ut_delete_caches+0x3f/0x7b
>[    0.188000]  ? acpi_terminate+0x5/0xf
>[    0.188000]  ? acpi_init+0x288/0x32e
>[    0.188000]  ? __class_create+0x4c/0x80
>[    0.188000]  ? video_setup+0x7a/0x7a
>[    0.188000]  ? do_one_initcall+0x4e/0x1b0
>[    0.188000]  ? kernel_init_freeable+0x194/0x21a
>[    0.188000]  ? rest_init+0x80/0x80
>[    0.188000]  ? kernel_init+0xa/0x100
>[    0.188000]  ? ret_from_fork+0x25/0x30

When early abort is occurred due to invalid ACPI information, Linux kernel
terminates ACPI by calling AcpiTerminate() function. The function calls
AcpiNsTerminate() function to delete namespace data and ACPI operand cache
(AcpiGbl_ModuleCodeList).

But the deletion code in AcpiNsTerminate() function is wrapped in
ACPI_EXEC_APP definition, therefore the code is only executed when the
definition exists. If the define doesn't exist, ACPI operand cache
(AcpiGbl_ModuleCodeList) is leaked, and stack dump is shown in kernel log.

This causes a security threat because the old kernel (<= 4.9) shows memory
locations of kernel functions in stack dump, therefore kernel ASLR can be
neutralized.

To fix ACPI operand leak for enhancing security, I made a patch which
removes the ACPI_EXEC_APP define in AcpiNsTerminate() function for
executing the deletion code unconditionally.

Signed-off-by: Seunghun Han <kkamagui@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Lv Zheng <lv.zheng@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['#ifdef ACPI_EXEC_APP', '        ACPI_OPERAND_OBJECT     *Prev;', '        ACPI_OPERAND_OBJECT     *Next;', '', '        /* Delete any module-level code blocks */', '', '        Next = AcpiGbl_ModuleCodeList;', '        while (Next)', '        {', '            Prev = Next;', '            Next = Next->Method.Mutex;', '            Prev->Method.Mutex = NULL; /* Clear the Mutex (cheated) field */', '            AcpiUtRemoveReference (Prev);', '        }', '#endif'], 'added_lines': ['    ACPI_OPERAND_OBJECT     *Prev;', '    ACPI_OPERAND_OBJECT     *Next;', '    /* Delete any module-level code blocks */', '', '    Next = AcpiGbl_ModuleCodeList;', '    while (Next)', '        Prev = Next;', '        Next = Next->Method.Mutex;', '        Prev->Method.Mutex = NULL; /* Clear the Mutex (cheated) field */', '        AcpiUtRemoveReference (Prev);']}
description: The acpi_ns_terminate() function in drivers/acpi/acpica/nsutils.c in the Linux kernel before 4.12 does not flush the operand cache and causes a kernel stack dump, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory and bypass the KASLR protection mechanism (in the kernel through 4.9) via a crafted ACPI table.

code_evidence: The operand-cache cleanup loop that walks AcpiGbl_ModuleCodeList and calls AcpiUtRemoveReference is entirely enclosed in the #ifdef ACPI_EXEC_APP block; when that define is absent, the cleanup is compiled out and the module-level code objects remain allocated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-755 fits because the function fails to handle the early-abort/termination condition by skipping required resource cleanup, producing an improper exceptional-condition response. This is not a simple memory-safety bug at the cited lines; the defect is the conditional omission of cleanup on an error path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the exceptional early-termination path (AcpiTerminate during ACPI init abort) does not perform operand-cache cleanup because the deletion code is conditional on ACPI_EXEC_APP. Trigger: an invalid ACPI table causes early abort, invoking AcpiNsTerminate without the define. Consequence: AcpiGbl_ModuleCodeList objects leak, and the resulting stack dump exposes kernel addresses, defeating KASLR on older kernels.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: check for bogus target offset

We're currently asserting that targetoff + targetsize <= nextoff.

Extend it to also check that targetoff is >= sizeof(xt_entry).
Since this is generic code, add an argument pointing to the start of the
match/target, we can then derive the base structure size from the delta.

We also need the e->elems pointer in a followup change to validate matches.

Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tret = xt_compat_check_entry_offsets(e,'], 'added_lines': ['\tret = xt_compat_check_entry_offsets(e, e->elems,']}
description: The compat IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE and IP6T_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt implementations in the netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.6.3 allow local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) by leveraging in-container root access to provide a crafted offset value that triggers an unintended decrement.

code_evidence: Bounds checks at [18,19,20] validate alignment and that e plus next_offset stays within limit, and [24,25] enforce a minimum next_offset. [30,31] validate the IP header. The offset-validation call at [32,33,34,35] passes e, e->target_offset and e->next_offset to xt_compat_check_entry_offsets, but in the before state it does not supply the start of the match/target region, so the callee cannot verify that target_offset is at least the base structure size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permissions and access controls; here the compat setsockopt path is reachable with in-container root privileges, and the incomplete offset validation in this privileged path permits memory corruption that can escalate privileges. The defect is the missing offset constraint, not the privilege itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller does not provide e->elems to xt_compat_check_entry_offsets, so the helper cannot enforce a lower bound on target_offset relative to the start of the entries. Trigger: a local user with in-container root supplies a crafted compat iptables entry with a bogus target_offset. Consequence: the offset check is incomplete, enabling later unintended pointer arithmetic that causes memory corruption and potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
AutoarExtractor: Do not extract files outside the destination dir

Currently, a malicious archive can cause that the files are extracted
outside of the destination dir. This can happen if the archive contains
a file whose parent is a symbolic link, which points outside of the
destination dir. This is potentially a security threat similar to
CVE-2020-11736. Let's skip such problematic files when extracting.

Fixes: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gnome-autoar/-/issues/7
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  g_autofree char *sanitized_pathname;', '  valid_filename =', '    g_file_equal (extracted_filename, self->destination_dir) ||', '    g_file_has_prefix (extracted_filename, self->destination_dir);', '', '    g_autofree char *basename;', '', '    basename = g_file_get_basename (extracted_filename);', '    extracted_filename = g_file_get_child (self->destination_dir,', '                                           basename);'], 'added_lines': ['  g_autofree char *sanitized_pathname = NULL;', '  valid_filename = is_valid_filename (extracted_filename, self->destination_dir);', '    g_warning ("autoar_extractor_do_sanitize_pathname: %s is outside of the destination dir",', '                g_file_peek_path (extracted_filename));', '    return NULL;']}
description: autoar-extractor.c in GNOME gnome-autoar through 0.2.4, as used by GNOME Shell, Nautilus, and other software, allows Directory Traversal during extraction because it lacks a check of whether a file's parent is a symlink to a directory outside of the intended extraction location.

code_evidence: The pathname from the archive is joined to destination_dir to form extracted_filename.

The only containment check is a lexical g_file_equal/g_file_has_prefix comparison against destination_dir; it never resolves symlinks, so a path whose parent is a symlink outside the destination still passes.
When the lexical check fails, the code strips to the basename and rebuilds the path; it does not detect symlinked parents, so the returned GFile can resolve outside the destination.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the function accesses a file named by an untrusted path without preventing that path from resolving through a link to an unintended location. The lexical prefix check is insufficient link resolution, distinct from pure path traversal (CWE-22) because the bypass relies on a symlinked parent.

evidence_lines.code:
extracted_filename = g_file_get_child (self->destination_dir,
utf8_pathname ?  utf8_pathname : pathname_bytes);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sanitizer validates paths lexically without resolving symlinks in intermediate components. Trigger: an archive entry whose parent directory is a symlink pointing outside destination_dir. Consequence: the caller writes the extracted file through the symlink, modifying files outside the intended directory.

description: vim is vulnerable to Use After Free

code_evidence: At lines 155-162, when a next command follows the end marker, the code checks whether *line_to_free is non-NULL and differs from *eap->cmdlinep, then calls vim_free(*eap->cmdlinep) and reassigns *eap->cmdlinep = *line_to_free, setting *line_to_free = NULL. The freed pointer is the old cmdline buffer; the saved line pointer is then handed to eap->cmdlinep for later use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code explicitly calls vim_free on a pointer and then continues to use/reassign pointers derived from the same allocation, matching use-after-free semantics. It is not merely a double free because the stale pointer may be dereferenced after the free.
