Trigger: a user function whose end marker is followed by another command on the same line. Consequence: later access through the stale cmdline pointer reads freed memory (CWE-416).

commit_msg:
libndp: validate the IPv6 hop limit

None of the NDP messages should ever come from a non-local network; as
stated in RFC4861's 6.1.1 (RS), 6.1.2 (RA), 7.1.1 (NS), 7.1.2 (NA),
and 8.1. (redirect):

  - The IP Hop Limit field has a value of 255, i.e., the packet
    could not possibly have been forwarded by a router.

This fixes CVE-2016-3698.

Reported by: Julien BERNARD <julien.bernard@viagenie.ca>
Signed-off-by: Lubomir Rintel <lkundrak@v3.sk>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Pirko <jiri@mellanox.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t  &msg->addrto, &msg->ifindex);', '\tdbg(ndp, "rcvd from: %s, ifindex: %u",', '\t\t str_in6_addr(&msg->addrto), msg->ifindex);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t  &msg->addrto, &msg->ifindex, &msg->hoplimit);', '\tdbg(ndp, "rcvd from: %s, ifindex: %u, hoplimit: %d",', '\t\t str_in6_addr(&msg->addrto), msg->ifindex, msg->hoplimit);', '', '\tif (msg->hoplimit != 255) {', '\t\twarn(ndp, "ignoring packet with bad hop limit (%d)", msg->hoplimit);', '\t\terr = 0;', '\t\tgoto free_msg;', '\t}']}
description: libndp before 1.6, as used in NetworkManager, does not properly validate the origin of Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) messages, which allows remote attackers to conduct man-in-the-middle attacks or cause a denial of service (network connectivity disruption) by advertising a node as a router from a non-local network.

code_evidence: The receive call at [10,11,12] obtains the packet and remote address but passes no hop-limit information to myrecvfrom6; the returned msg carries no validated hop-limit restriction before dispatch.

After only a length check at [19,20,21,22,23], the function proceeds to type lookup, validity checks and ndp_call_handlers at line 42 without ever verifying that the packet's IPv6 Hop Limit was 255, so a forwarded (non-local) NDP message is accepted and processed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to enforce the access restriction that only local, non-forwarded NDP messages may be processed, allowing unauthorized off-link actors to influence node configuration; this is a missing enforcement of an intended security policy, fitting CWE-284. It is not merely a spoofing issue: the defect is the absent hop-limit gate on message admission.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the receive path never constrains the IPv6 Hop Limit of incoming NDP messages, so packets forwarded by an off-link router are treated as local. Trigger: a remote attacker sends an NDP RS/RA/NS/NA/redirect with a Hop Limit other than 255; the function accepts it and invokes handlers. Supported consequence: the node can be advertised as a router from a non-local network, enabling man-in-the-middle or network-connectivity denial of service.

commit_msg:
When doing option parsing for standard type values of 1, 2 or 4 octets,
the value is converted directly into a variable instead of a pointer. To
avoid being tricked into being a pointer, check that for these option
types that sizes actually match. In L2CAP every option is fixed size and
thus it is prudent anyway to ensure that the remote side sends us the
right option size along with option paramters.

If the option size is not matching the option type, then that option is
silently ignored. It is a protocol violation and instead of trying to
give the remote attacker any further hints just pretend that option is
not present and proceed with the default values. Implementation
following the specification and its qualification procedures will always
use the correct size and thus not being impacted here.

To keep the code readable and consistent accross all options, a few
cosmetic changes were also required.

Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hedberg <johan.hedberg@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (olen == sizeof(rfc))', '\t\t\t\tmemcpy(&rfc, (void *) val, olen);', '\t\t\tif (olen == sizeof(efs)) {', '\t\t\t\tremote_efs = 1;', '\t\t\t\tmemcpy(&efs, (void *) val, olen);', '\t\t\t}', '', ''], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (olen != 2)', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\tif (olen != 2)', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\tif (olen != sizeof(rfc))', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\tmemcpy(&rfc, (void *) val, olen);', '\t\t\tif (olen != 1)', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\tif (olen != sizeof(efs))', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\tremote_efs = 1;', '\t\t\tmemcpy(&efs, (void *) val, olen);', '\t\t\tif (olen != 2)', '\t\t\t\tbreak;']}
description: A heap data infoleak in multiple locations including L2CAP_PARSE_CONF_RSP was found in the Linux kernel before 5.1-rc1.

code_evidence: The option loop reads remote-supplied type/olen/val via l2cap_get_conf_opt, then dispatches on the masked type; for L2CAP_CONF_MTU it assigns mtu = val without checking that olen equals 2, so a short option leaves mtu partially uninitialized.
L2CAP_CONF_FLUSH_TO similarly stores val into chan->flush_to with no length check, accepting a 1- or 4-octet option as a full value.
L2CAP_CONF_RFC checks olen == sizeof(rfc) before memcpy, but on mismatch rfc keeps its zero-initialized/default contents and parsing continues as if a valid RFC was received.
L2CAP_CONF_FCS compares val to L2CAP_FCS_NONE without verifying olen == 1, so the option length is not validated against the expected fixed size.
L2CAP_CONF_EFS only copies when olen == sizeof(efs); otherwise remote_efs stays 0 and the option is treated as absent rather than rejected as malformed.
L2CAP_CONF_EWS sets flags and chan->remote_tx_win = val without confirming olen == 2.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes structured peer input and fails to validate a required metadata property—the option length—against the expected size before use, which is precisely improper input validation (CWE-20). The weakness is the missing size check on entry, not the downstream memory disclosure itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser dispatches on the option type but does not enforce that the option length (olen) matches the fixed size required by that type before converting the raw value into a typed variable or copying it. Trigger: a remote peer sends a configuration request whose option type is valid but whose length differs from the expected size. Consequence: typed fields (mtu, flush_to, rfc, efs, tx_win) are populated from malformed input or left at defaults while parsing proceeds, enabling the described heap data infoleak and protocol-state confusion.

commit_msg:
Zero and sanity check all dynamic allocs.

This addresses the memory issues in Issue #6 expressed in
calloc_some.pdf and malloc_some.pdf
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        dname = malloc(strlen(name) + 16);'], 'added_lines': ['        dname = safe_calloc(strlen(name) + 16);']}
description: An issue was discovered in PDFResurrect before 0.18. pdf_load_pages_kids in pdf.c doesn't validate a certain size value, which leads to a malloc failure and out-of-bounds write.

code_evidence: At line 67, dname is allocated with malloc(strlen(name) + 16) but the return value is never checked for NULL. Line 68 then unconditionally calls sprintf(dname, "%s-versions", name), writing strlen(name)+10 bytes into the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked NULL allocation leads sprintf to write past the end of (or to no) intended buffer. A related weakness is the missing NULL check, but the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds write itself.

evidence_lines.code:
dname = malloc(strlen(name) + 16);
sprintf(dname, "%s-versions", name);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unchecked allocation result. When malloc fails and returns NULL (e.g., under memory pressure or an oversized name), sprintf writes the formatted string to a NULL pointer, producing an out-of-bounds/NULL write rather than a safe failure. Trigger: do_write mode with a name whose allocation cannot succeed. Supported consequence: memory corruption or crash.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE(xXFixesSetCursorNameReq);'], 'added_lines': ['    REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE(xXFixesSetCursorNameReq, stuff->nbytes);']}
description: xorg-x11-server before 1.19.5 was missing length validation in XFIXES extension allowing malicious X client to cause X server to crash or possibly execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: Line 8 only enforces REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE for the fixed header, not the variable-length name payload. Line 10 derives tchar as &stuff[1], and line 11 passes stuff->nbytes to MakeAtom without confirming that many bytes actually follow the request header.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is missing validation of a client-supplied length field before it is used to process input, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). This is not merely a transformation or encoding issue; the required size property of the input is left unchecked.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The request's nbytes field is client-controlled metadata that is used as a length but never validated against the actual remaining request length. A malicious client can set nbytes larger than the supplied data, causing MakeAtom to read past the request buffer; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read leading to server crash or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
protocols: don't use assert on paths that can be reached

Malformed packets should not make lldpd crash. Ensure we can handle them
by not using assert() in this part.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tassert(proto != LLDP_MGMT_ADDR_NONE);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (proto == LLDP_MGMT_ADDR_NONE) continue;']}
description: lldpd before 0.8.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (assertion failure and daemon crash) via a malformed packet.

code_evidence: The management-address loop iterates over chassis->c_mgmt entries, maps each entry's m_family via lldpd_af_to_lldp_proto(mgmt->m_family) into proto, then asserts proto != LLDP_MGMT_ADDR_NONE. If a management entry carries a family for which the mapping returns LLDP_MGMT_ADDR_NONE, the assert fires instead of skipping the entry, terminating the process rather than continuing packet construction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a reachable assert() whose failure condition can be induced by malformed input, causing an unnecessary process exit. This matches CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion) with availability impact. It is not a memory-safety issue such as an out-of-bounds write; the weakness is the assertion-triggered crash itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an assert() guards a condition that depends on data reachable from parsed/attacker-influenced management-address entries, so a malformed packet can yield an unmappable family. Trigger: processing such an entry makes lldpd_af_to_lldp_proto return LLDP_MGMT_ADDR_NONE, firing the assertion. Consequence: the daemon aborts, causing a denial of service; the patch replaces the assert with a continue to handle the case gracefully.

commit_msg: fix crash because of unaligned accesses in hybiReadAndDecode()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  uint32_t *data32;', '  data32= (uint32_t *)data;', '    data32[i] ^= wsctx->header.mask.u;'], 'added_lines': ['    uint32_t tmp;', '    memcpy(&tmp, data + i * sizeof(tmp), sizeof(tmp));', '    tmp ^= wsctx->header.mask.u;', '    memcpy(data + i * sizeof(tmp), &tmp, sizeof(tmp));']}
description: An issue was discovered in LibVNCServer before 0.9.13. libvncserver/ws_decode.c can lead to a crash because of unaligned accesses in hybiReadAndDecode.

code_evidence: data is derived from the write pointer minus toDecode, then cast to uint32_t* at line 52. The loop at 53-54 writes data32[i] for i < (toDecode >> 2), i.e. 4-byte stores through a uint32_t pointer with no alignment guarantee on data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 is not supported: the loop bound (toDecode >> 2) keeps writes within the toDecode-byte region, so no out-of-bounds write occurs. The defect is an improper alignment assumption (CWE-704/CWE-188 style), not writing past the buffer end; the observed consequence is a crash from unaligned access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the unchecked cast of an arbitrary unsigned char* to uint32_t* and 4-byte XOR stores through it. When data is not 4-byte aligned, the store causes an unaligned access fault, crashing the process. This is an alignment/memory-access defect rather than a length overflow of the intended buffer.

commit_msg:
Fixed type confusion bug while resolving promises.

Previously, the internal function njs_promise_perform_then() which
implements PerformPromiseThen() expects its first argument to always be
a promise instance.  This assertion might be invalid because the
functions corresponding to Promise.prototype.then() and
Promise.resolve() incorrectly verified their arguments.

Specifically, the functions recognized their first argument as promise
if it was an object which was an Promise or had Promise object in its
prototype chain.  The later condition is not correct because internal
slots are not inherited according to the spec.

This closes #447 issue in Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    njs_object_t              *object;', '    if (njs_is_object(x)) {', '        object = njs_object_proto_lookup(njs_object(x), NJS_PROMISE,', '                                         njs_object_t);', '        if (object != NULL) {', '            ret = njs_value_property(vm, x, njs_value_arg(&string_constructor),', '                                     &value);', '            if (njs_slow_path(ret == NJS_ERROR)) {', '                return NULL;', '            }', '', '            if (njs_values_same(&value, constructor)) {', '                return njs_promise(x);', '            }'], 'added_lines': ['    if (njs_is_promise(x)) {', '        ret = njs_value_property(vm, x, njs_value_arg(&string_constructor),', '                                 &value);', '        if (njs_slow_path(ret == NJS_ERROR)) {', '            return NULL;', '        }', '        if (njs_values_same(&value, constructor)) {', '            return njs_promise(x);']}
description: njs through 0.7.1, used in NGINX, was discovered to contain a control flow hijack caused by a Type Confusion vulnerability in njs_promise_perform_then().

code_evidence: The check uses njs_is_object(x) and then njs_object_proto_lookup(...) to decide whether x is a promise, so any object inheriting NJS_PROMISE in its prototype chain is accepted. On that basis line 19 returns njs_promise(x), a cast of x to a promise pointer even though x may not itself carry the promise internal slots.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function treats an object of an incompatible type as a promise and accesses it through njs_promise(x), matching CWE-843. It is not mere argument validation: the defect is the mismatched type interpretation of a resource.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: promise identity is inferred from prototype-chain lookup rather than from the object's own type, so a non-promise object passing the check is cast to njs_promise_t and later consumed by promise-internal operations. Trigger: Promise.resolve/then receives an object whose prototype chain contains a promise. Consequence: type confusion, potentially control-flow hijack in njs_promise_perform_then().

commit_msg:
Fix 4 byte oobread in msp430 disassembler ##crash

* Only crashes with asan builds
* Add missing =SN register
* Reported by cnitlrt via huntrdev
* BountyID: 1c22055b-b015-47a8-a57b-4982978751d0
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tR_LOG_ERROR ("Cannot allocate memory (Check Elf_(Verdef))");'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tR_LOG_DEBUG ("Cannot allocate memory (Check Elf_(Verdef))");']}
description: Out-of-bounds Read in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.7.0. The bug causes the program reads data past the end of the intented buffer. Typically, this can allow attackers to read sensitive information from other memory locations or cause a crash.

code_evidence: The loop reads a Verdef record into the fixed dfs buffer via r_buf_read_at at shdr->sh_offset + i, then parses fields from dfs; the loop condition only checks i < shdr->sh_size, not that the file actually contains sizeof(Verdef) bytes at that offset, so a truncated section yields a short read leaving dfs partially stale/uninitialized.

After advancing vstart by vdaux, the bounds check at line 82 compares vstart against end but then reads READ32(vstart) for vda_name/vda_next at lines 87-88; the check uses shdr->sh_size - sizeof(Verdaux) < vstart_off, but vstart may point near end while the 8-byte read crosses the allocated defs buffer boundary.
aux.vda_name is checked against dynstr_size with > rather than >=, and then used to index bin->dynstr at line 98; an equal value reads one byte past the dynstr buffer.

The nested parent loop similarly advances vstart by aux.vda_next and reads READ32 at lines 117-118 after a bounds check that can still permit an 8-byte read past end, and the same off-by-one dynstr check at 119 precedes indexing at 126.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads data past the end of the intended defs and dynstr buffers, matching the out-of-bounds read description; the weakness is an unchecked read boundary, not a write overflow (CWE-787).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is insufficient validation that the Verdef/Verdaux structures and the dynstr name offset fit within their buffers before dereferencing: short reads into dfs and vstart advancing near end allow READ32 to read past the allocated defs buffer, and the > vs >= check lets aux.vda_name equal dynstr_size index one byte past dynstr. Trigger is a crafted ELF with a truncated/oversized verdef section or a name offset equal to dynstr_size; consequence is an out-of-bounds read (crash under ASan, potential info leak).

commit_msg:
Avoid using short exponents with ElGamal

Some off-brand PGP implementation generates keys where p - 1 is
smooth, as a result short exponents can leak enough information about
k to allow decryption.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['   const size_t k_bits = m_group.exponent_bits();', '   const BigInt k(rng, k_bits);'], 'added_lines': ['   /*', '   Some ElGamal implementations foolishly use prime fields where p - 1 is', '   smooth, as a result it is unsafe to use short exponents.', '   */', '   const size_t k_bits = m_group.p_bits() - 1;', '   const BigInt k(rng, k_bits, false);']}
description: The ElGamal implementation in Botan through 2.18.1, as used in Thunderbird and other products, allows plaintext recovery because, during interaction between two cryptographic libraries, a certain dangerous combination of the prime defined by the receiver's public key, the generator defined by the receiver's public key, and the sender's ephemeral exponents can lead to a cross-configuration attack against OpenPGP.

code_evidence: The ephemeral exponent k is sized from m_group.exponent_bits() and generated via BigInt(rng, k_bits), which can produce a short exponent relative to the group prime p.
k is then used in power_g_p and monty_execute to compute a and b; the exponent length directly controls the cryptographic computation, so its weakness propagates to the ciphertext.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Using short exponents with ElGamal is a risky cryptographic construction that weakens the algorithm and enables plaintext recovery, matching CWE-327's broken/risky cryptographic algorithm class; the defect is in the cryptographic scheme's parameter choice, not mere key management.

evidence_lines.code:
const size_t k_bits = m_group.exponent_bits();
const BigInt k(rng, k_bits);

const BigInt a = m_group.power_g_p(k, k_bits);
const BigInt b = m_group.multiply_mod_p(m, monty_execute(*m_monty_y_p, k, k_bits));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the encryption operation derives the ephemeral secret exponent length from exponent_bits() rather than the prime size, allowing short exponents. Trigger: when the receiver's ElGamal group has p-1 smooth, short exponents leak enough information about k. Consequence: plaintext recovery through a cross-configuration attack, compromising confidentiality.

Rather han checking everywhere that the RLC and MAC info are present in pinfo,
allocate a temporary structure that will be dropped once packet dissection is
over.

description: epan/dissectors/packet-umts_fp.c in the UMTS FP dissector in Wireshark 2.x before 2.0.6 does not ensure that memory is allocated for certain data structures, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (invalid write access and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: macinf is fetched from proto data at line 140 but no NULL check is added before use.
Inside the MAC-d PDU loop, macinf->content[macd_idx] and macinf->lchid[macd_idx] are written without verifying macinf is non-NULL.
rlcinf->mode/urnti/rbid/li_size/ciphered/deciphered[macd_idx] are written unconditionally; the patch removed the earlier rlcinf NULL guard at the DDI site, so rlcinf may also be NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing through an unvalidated pointer into macinf/rlcinf buffers is an out-of-bounds/invalid write (CWE-787), matching the described invalid write access. It is not a mere NULL dereference read; the faulting operation is a memory write.

evidence_lines.code:
macinf = (umts_mac_info *)p_get_proto_data(wmem_file_scope(), pinfo, proto_umts_mac, 0);
subframe_ti = proto_tree_add_string_format(tree, hf_fp_edch_subframe, tvb, offset, 0,

rlcinf->ciphered[macd_idx] = FALSE;
rlcinf->deciphered[macd_idx] = FALSE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The dissector obtains umts_mac_info via p_get_proto_data but dereferences it (and rlcinf) without a NULL check before indexed writes. A crafted packet whose dissection path leaves these structures unallocated triggers a write through a NULL/garbage pointer, causing an invalid write access and crash.

commit_msg:
Remove access to the root FS from lua

On linux / is mounted to /rootfs in RageFile, which allows access to the
_whole_ filesystem from lua. This means themes and mod files can
re-write user data and extract files via USB profiles.

/rootfs was only added for internal use by the alsa, oss and memory card
drivers, so it can be easily replaced with direct fstream file access.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif( DoesFileExist("/rootfs/proc/asound/version") )', '\t\tRString sVersion;', '\t\tGetFileContents( "/rootfs/proc/asound/version", sVersion, true );', '\t\tLOG->Info( "ALSA: %s", sVersion.c_str() );'], 'added_lines': ['\tstd::ifstream f("/proc/asound/version");', '\tif (f.good())', '\t\tstd::string version;', '\t\tstd::getline(f, version);', '\t\tLOG->Info( "ALSA: %s", version.c_str() );']}
description: The component /rootfs in RageFile of Stepmania v5.1b2 and below allows attackers access to the entire file system.

code_evidence: The function probes an ALSA version file through RageFile's virtual filesystem using the hard-coded path "/rootfs/proc/asound/version" (lines 7,10), where the "/rootfs" prefix maps to the host root filesystem. Because RageFile resolves paths against this mount, the same prefix lets any caller (themes, mods, Lua) reach arbitrary files outside the intended sandbox. The existence check and GetFileContents call treat this host-root-relative path as an ordinary readable resource without restricting who may supply or resolve such paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-732 fits because the function assigns a permission/mount such that a critical resource (the whole filesystem) is reachable by actors who should not have it; the fix removes the broad "/rootfs" access in favor of direct fstream access. This is not a missing authorization check (CWE-285) but an overly permissive resource-access assignment.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function authorizes access to a security-critical resource (the entire host filesystem) by routing reads through the "/rootfs" RageFile mount, which is exposed to untrusted content. Trigger: code paths like this one that resolve paths under "/rootfs" enable themes/mods to read and rewrite user data and extract files. Consequence: unintended actors gain read/write access to files beyond the intended scope.

In versions older than 1.0.0, however, the MXNet framework will listen on 0.0.0.0 rather than user specified DMLC_PS_ROOT_URI once a scheduler node is initialized. Lines 9-10 concatenate the wildcard address with the port and pass it to zmq_bind, making the service reachable on every network interface rather than the intended one.

int local = GetEnv("DMLC_LOCAL", 0);
std::string addr = local ? "ipc:    int port = node.port;

auto address = addr + std::to_string(port);
if (zmq_bind(receiver_, address.c_str()) == 0) break;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bind address uses the wildcard '*:' instead of the configured node hostname, so the ROUTER socket listens on all interfaces. Trigger: a clustered scheduler is started with a hostname intended to restrict access (e.g., 127.0.0.1). description: epan/dissectors/packet-alljoyn.c in the AllJoyn dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.9 does not check for empty arguments, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: parse_arg reads a 32-bit length from the packet (line 43) and computes a starting offset; it rejects negative/oversized lengths (line 46) but does not reject a zero-length array.

The array loop condition (offset - starting_offset) < length combined with the recursive call (lines 57-74) can leave offset unchanged when the supplied argument consumes no bytes, so the loop never progresses.
The generic clamp at lines 319-321 only bounds offset to the reported length; it does not detect that offset did not advance relative to the input offset, so no guard stops the non-progressing loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of an input property (argument size) before processing, matching CWE-20 improper input validation; the zero-length input is accepted and drives unsafe loop behavior. The infinite loop is the resulting consequence, not the validation defect itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dissector accepts a crafted argument with null/zero size and never validates that parsing consumed at least one byte, so the caller's while loop (or the array loop) re-invokes parse_arg with the same offset. Trigger: a crafted packet whose argument length is zero. Consequence: infinite loop, causing a denial of service (CPU consumption/hang) in Wireshark.

commit_msg: Fix possible integer overflow
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '   if (size < 0) {', '      return MP_VAL;', '   }']}
description: Integer Overflow vulnerability in mp_grow in libtom libtommath before commit beba892bc0d4e4ded4d667ab1d2a94f4d75109a9, allows attackers to execute arbitrary code and cause a denial of service (DoS).

code_evidence: mp_grow compares the signed int parameter size against a->alloc and, when allocation is needed, computes the reallocation byte count as (size_t)size * sizeof(mp_digit) at line 8. The parameter size is never validated as non-negative before this multiplication; the fix in the diff adds a size < 0 check above the a->alloc < size test, confirming the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the size arithmetic at line 8 can wrap when size is negative or large, and the code assumes the resulting allocation length is valid. This is an integer wraparound in size computation, not merely a missing NULL check (CWE-476).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a caller-supplied signed int size is used directly as an allocation size multiplier without a lower-bound check. Trigger: a negative size reaches mp_grow, whose cast to size_t produces a huge value that wraps in the multiplication, so MP_REALLOC receives a small or mismatched length. Supported consequence: undersized allocation followed by the zeroing at line 15, leading to out-of-bounds memory writes and possible code execution or DoS.

commit_msg:
saslserv/main: Track EID we're pending login to

The existing model does not remember that we've sent a SVSLOGIN for a
given SASL session, and simply assumes that if a client is introduced
with a SASL session open, that session must have succeeded. The security
of this approach requires ircd to implicitly abort SASL sessions on
client registration.

This also means that if a client successfully authenticates and then
does something else its pending login is forgotten about, even though a
SVSLOGIN has been sent for it, and the ircd is going to think it's
logged in.

This change removes the dependency on ircd's state machine by keeping
explicit track of the pending login, i.e. the one we've most recently
sent a SVSLOGIN for. The next commit will ensure that a client abort
(even an implicit one) doesn't blow that information away.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t(void) mowgli_strlcpy(p->pendingeid, p->authzeid, sizeof p->pendingeid);', '']}
description: Atheme IRC Services before 7.2.12, when used in conjunction with InspIRCd, allows authentication bypass by ending an IRC handshake at a certain point during a challenge-response login sequence.

code_evidence: On ASASL_MRESULT_SUCCESS, the code looks up the user and calls sasl_user_can_login(p); if that returns NULL it only sends a cancellation notice and returns false without aborting or invalidating the SASL session state. The authentication decision is thus tied to the session object rather than to a verified, tracked pending login, so the success path can proceed to sasl_session_success based on prior session state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's success branch accepts the claimed identity through SASL/session state without proving the claim corresponds to a completed, tracked login, which is improper authentication (CWE-287). It is not merely a state-machine bug in ircd; the authentication proof is insufficient here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function does not record which EID it has sent an SVSLOGIN for, so a session's success is inferred from the continued existence of an open SASL session. Trigger: a client ends the IRC handshake at a particular point in the challenge-response sequence. Consequence: the ircd treats the session as authenticated, yielding authentication bypass.

commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>

description:
A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions

of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service

commit_msg: libarchive: Handle a `calloc` returning NULL (fixes #1754)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (f == NULL)', '\t\treturn (NULL);', '']}
description: In libarchive before 3.6.2, the software does not check for an error after calling calloc function that can return with a NULL pointer if the function fails, which leads to a resultant NULL pointer dereference. NOTE: the discoverer cites this CWE-476 remark but third parties dispute the code-execution impact: "In rare circumstances, when NULL is equivalent to the 0x0 memory address and privileged code can access it, then writing or reading memory is possible, which may lead to code execution."

code_evidence: calloc(1, sizeof(*f)) can return NULL on allocation failure, yet line 7 immediately dereferences f via f->archive = _a without any NULL check; line 8 similarly dereferences f->state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (f) that can be NULL because its allocation result is not validated, matching CWE-476's definition of dereferencing a pointer expected to be valid but NULL. The patch's added NULL check confirms the missing constraint; this is not a separate weakness such as an integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the unchecked return value of calloc, so a failed allocation yields a NULL f that is then dereferenced at f->archive and f->state. Trigger is memory-allocation failure; the supported consequence is a NULL pointer dereference, typically crashing the process (availability impact).

description: The time subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.9.9, when CONFIG_TIMER_STATS is enabled, allows local users to discover real PID values (as distinguished from PID values inside a PID namespace) by reading the /proc/timer_list file, related to the print_timer function in kernel/time/timer_list.c and the __timer_stats_timer_set_start_info function in kernel/time/timer.c.

commit_msg:
kexec/uefi: copy secure_boot flag in boot params across kexec reboot

Kexec reboot in case secure boot being enabled does not keep the secure
boot mode in new kernel, so later one can load unsigned kernel via legacy
kexec_load.  In this state, the system is missing the protections provided
by secure boot. Adding a patch to fix this by retain the secure_boot flag
in original kernel.

secure_boot flag in boot_params is set in EFI stub, but kexec bypasses the
stub. Fixing this issue by copying secure_boot flag across kexec reboot.

Signed-off-by: Dave Young <dyoung@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tparams->secure_boot = boot_params.secure_boot;']}
description: The Linux kernel, as used in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7, kernel-rt, and Enterprise MRG 2 and when booted with UEFI Secure Boot enabled, allows local users to bypass intended securelevel/secureboot restrictions by leveraging improper handling of secure_boot flag across kexec reboot.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only copies EFI info fields and does not itself handle the secure_boot flag; the diff shows the secure_boot copy was added, so the before-state function lacks the operation that would demonstrate the weakness.

description: An issue was discovered in Exempi before 2.4.3. The VPXChunk class in XMPFiles/source/FormatSupport/WEBP_Support.cpp does not ensure nonzero widths and heights, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (assertion failure and application exit) via a crafted .webp file.

code_evidence: VP8XChunk::width() stores an externally supplied width value into the chunk data without checking that val is nonzero: it unconditionally computes val - 1 and writes the result via PutLE24. A caller passing 0 causes unsigned underflow to 0xFFFFFF.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts input data (width) without validating a required property — nonzero value — before processing it, which matches CWE-20 improper input validation. The fix adds exactly this missing constraint (val > 0 ? val - 1 : 0), confirming validation of input properties was absent.

evidence_lines.code: PutLE24(&this->data[4], val - 1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the setter trusts the caller-provided width and performs no validation of the zero case before the decrement. Trigger: a crafted .webp file yields a zero width that reaches this setter, producing a huge wrapped value in the stored field. Supported consequence: later code relying on a valid nonzero width fails an assertion, terminating the application (DoS).

commit_msg:
cifs: Fix use-after-free in SMB2_read

There is a KASAN use-after-free:
BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in SMB2_read+0x1136/0x1190
Read of size 8 at addr ffff8880b4e45e50 by task ln/1009

Should not release the 'req' because it will use in the trace.

Fixes: eccb4422cf97 ("smb3: Add ftrace tracepoints for improved SMB3 debugging")

Signed-off-by: ZhangXiaoxu <zhangxiaoxu5@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Steve French <stfrench@microsoft.com>
CC: Stable <stable@vger.kernel.org> 4.18+
Reviewed-by: Pavel Shilovsky <pshilov@microsoft.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcifs_small_buf_release(req);', ''], 'added_lines': ['', '\tcifs_small_buf_release(req);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10. SMB2_read in fs/cifs/smb2pdu.c has a use-after-free. NOTE: this was not fixed correctly in 5.0.10; see the 5.0.11 ChangeLog, which documents a memory leak.

code_evidence: Line 25 sends the request, then line 26 immediately releases the request buffer via cifs_small_buf_release(req).
After the release, the error path dereferences req->PersistentFileId in trace_smb3_read_err at lines 32-35.
The -ENODATA branch also reads req->PersistentFileId in trace_smb3_read_done at lines 37-39.
The success path likewise reads req->PersistentFileId in trace_smb3_read_done at lines 43-45, all after the free.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function releases req then reads req->PersistentFileId through the trace macros, which is exactly the reuse of freed memory defined by CWE-416. This is not merely a memory leak or double free; the stale pointer is dereferenced after cifs_small_buf_release.

evidence_lines.code:
rc = cifs_send_recv(xid, ses, &rqst, &resp_buftype, flags, &rsp_iov);
cifs_small_buf_release(req);

trace_smb3_read_err(xid, req->PersistentFileId,
io_parms->tcon->tid, ses->Suid,
io_parms->offset, io_parms->length,
rc);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: req is freed at line 26 before the tracepoint calls that dereference req->PersistentFileId. Trigger: any completed cifs_send_recv, since every subsequent path (error, -ENODATA, or success) reads the freed req. Supported consequence: a use-after-free read of the freed request buffer, matching the reported KASAN read of size 8.

commit_msg:
The functions XGetFontPath, XListExtensions, and XListFonts are
vulnerable to an off-by-one override on malicious server responses.

The server replies consist of chunks consisting of a length byte
followed by actual string, which is not NUL-terminated.

While parsing the response, the length byte is overridden with '\0',
thus the memory area can be used as storage of C strings later on. To
be able to NUL-terminate the last string, the buffer is reserved with
an additional byte of space.

For a boundary check, the variable chend (end of ch) was introduced,
pointing at the end of the buffer which ch initially points to.
Unfortunately there is a difference in handling "the end of ch".

While chend points at the first byte that must not be written to,
the for-loop uses chend as the last byte that can be written to.

Therefore, an off-by-one can occur.

I have refactored the code so chend actually points to the last byte
that can be written to without an out of boundary access. As it is not
possible to achieve "ch + length < chend" and "ch + length + 1 > chend"
with the corrected chend meaning, I removed the inner if-check.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchend = ch + (rlen + 1);', '\t\tif (ch <= chend) {', '\t\t    length = *(unsigned char *)ch;', "\t\t    *ch = '\\0';  /* and replace with null-termination */", '\t\t    count++;', '\t\t} else {', '                    Xfree(chstart);', '                    Xfree(flist);', '                    flist = NULL;', '                    count = 0;', '                    break;', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tchend = ch + rlen;', '\t\tlength = *(unsigned char *)ch;', "\t\t*ch = '\\0';  /* and replace with null-termination */", '\t\tcount++;']}
description: An issue was discovered in libX11 through 1.6.5. The function XListExtensions in ListExt.c is vulnerable to an off-by-one error caused by malicious server responses, leading to DoS or possibly unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: Line 35 allocates rlen+1 bytes, so the last writable byte is ch+rlen. Line 48 sets chend = ch + (rlen + 1), one past that last writable byte. Line 52's guard ch + length < chend admits ch+length == rlen (valid last byte), but line 55's check ch <= chend also admits ch == chend == ch+rlen+1, where lines 56-57 read and then overwrite the byte with '\0'.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code uses an incorrect maximum boundary value, chend = ch+(rlen+1) instead of ch+rlen, producing a write exactly one byte beyond the buffer. That is the defining off-by-one miscalculation of CWE-193; the resulting out-of-bounds write is the consequence, not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: chend is computed as ch+(rlen+1) yet used as the last writable byte, so the boundary is off by one. A malicious server response whose length bytes walk ch exactly onto chend passes the ch<=chend test, and line 57 writes '\0' one byte past the allocated buffer. This heap out-of-bounds write can crash the client (DoS) or corrupt adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
regulator: core: Fix regualtor_ena_gpio_free not to access pin after freeing

After freeing pin from regulator_ena_gpio_free, loop can access
the pin. So this patch fixes not to access pin after freeing.

Signed-off-by: Seung-Woo Kim <sw0312.kim@samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Mark Brown <broonie@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\trdev->ena_pin = NULL;', '\t\t\t\treturn;']}
description: The regulator_ena_gpio_free function in drivers/regulator/core.c in the Linux kernel before 3.19 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) via a crafted application.

code_evidence: The loop at [6] iterates over regulator_ena_gpio_list using list_for_each_entry_safe, which caches the next entry n. When a matching pin has request_count <= 1, [10,11,12] release the GPIO, unlink the node, and kfree(pin). The loop then continues its traversal from the saved n pointer at [6] without returning, so the freed node's list linkage may be read during continuation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because memory is freed at [12] and subsequently referenced by the ongoing traversal at [6] and comparison at [7]. This is a use-after-free, not merely a double free or leak; the defect is reuse of freed memory rather than missing deallocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: after kfree(pin) at [12], the function does not terminate the loop iteration or clear rdev->ena_pin, so the list traversal and later comparisons may touch freed memory. Trigger: rdev->ena_pin matches a pin whose request_count is <= 1. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the freed regulator_enable_gpio node, potentially enabling memory corruption or crash under attacker-controlled enable/disable sequences.

commit_msg:
As part of CVE-2013-4288, the D-Bus clients were allowed (and
encouraged) to submit the UID of the subject of authorization checks
to avoid races against UID changes (notably using executables
set-UID to root).

However, that also allowed any client to submit an arbitrary UID, and
that could be used to bypass "can only ask about / affect the same UID"
checks in CheckAuthorization / RegisterAuthenticationAgent /
UnregisterAuthenticationAgent.  This allowed an attacker:

- With CheckAuthorization, to cause the registered authentication
  agent in victim's session to pop up a dialog, or to determine whether
  the victim currently has a temporary authorization to perform an
  operation.

  (In principle, the attacker can also determine whether JavaScript
  rules allow the victim process to perform an operation; however,
  usually rules base their decisions on information determined from
  the supplied UID, so the attacker usually won't learn anything new.)

- With RegisterAuthenticationAgent, to prevent the victim's
  authentication agent to work (for a specific victim process),
  or to learn about which operations requiring authorization
  the victim is attempting.

To fix this, expose internal _polkit_unix_process_get_owner() /
obsolete polkit_unix_process_get_owner() as a private
polkit_unix_process_get_racy_uid__() (being more explicit about the
dangers on relying on it), and use it in
polkit_backend_session_monitor_get_user_for_subject() to return
a boolean indicating whether the subject UID may be caller-chosen.

Then, in the permission checks that require the subject to be
equal to the caller, fail on caller-chosen UIDs (and continue
through the pre-existing code paths which allow root, or root-designated
server processes, to ask about arbitrary subjects.)

Signed-off-by: Miloslav Trmač <mitr@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  gchar *group;', '  guint32 uid;', '      uid = polkit_unix_process_get_uid (POLKIT_UNIX_PROCESS (subject));', '      if ((gint) uid == -1)', '      ret = polkit_unix_user_new (uid);'], 'added_lines': ['                                                     gboolean                     *result_matches,', '  gboolean matches;', '  matches = FALSE;', '      gint subject_uid, current_uid;', '', '      subject_uid = polkit_unix_process_get_uid (POLKIT_UNIX_PROCESS (subject));', '      if (subject_uid == -1)', '      local_error = NULL;', '      current_uid = polkit_unix_process_get_racy_uid__ (POLKIT_UNIX_PROCESS (subject), &local_error);', '      if (local_error != NULL)', '\t{', '\t  g_propagate_error (error, local_error);', '\t  goto out;', '\t}', '      ret = polkit_unix_user_new (subject_uid);', '      matches = (subject_uid == current_uid);', '      matches = TRUE;', '      gint uid;', '      gchar *group;', '', '      matches = TRUE;', '  if (result_matches != NULL)', '    {', '      *result_matches = matches;', '    }']}
description: A flaw was found in polkit before version 0.116. The implementation of the polkit_backend_interactive_authority_check_authorization function in polkitd allows to test for authentication and trigger authentication of unrelated processes owned by other users. This may result in a local DoS and information disclosure.

code_evidence: When the subject is a PolkitUnixProcess, the function reads the caller-supplied UID via polkit_unix_process_get_uid() and returns polkit_unix_user_new(uid) without verifying that this UID matches the actual owner of the process. The only check is that the UID is not -1; no comparison against the process's real/racy UID or the caller is performed before the identity is returned to the authorization path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the function omits the authorization-relevant constraint that the subject UID must equal the process's real owner; it returns an identity for an arbitrary supplied UID. This missing check, not just a race, is what lets callers act on unrelated subjects.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the process-subject branch trusts an attacker-controlled UID field and performs no ownership validation. Trigger: a caller submits a PolkitUnixProcess subject whose UID belongs to another user. Consequence: downstream CheckAuthorization/RegisterAuthenticationAgent checks operate on that arbitrary UID, enabling information disclosure and DoS against unrelated users' authentication agents.

commit_msg:
Fix integer underflow vulnerability in L3 decode.

Marcin 'Icewall' Noga of Cisco TALOS discovered that the level 3 header
decoding routines were vulnerable to an integer underflow, if the 32-bit
header length was less than the base level 3 header length. This could
lead to an exploitable heap corruption condition.

Thanks go to Marcin Noga and Regina Wilson of Cisco TALOS for reporting
this vulnerability.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (nbytes > LEVEL_3_MAX_HEADER_LEN) {', '\t\treturn NULL;', '\t}']}
description: Integer underflow in the decode_level3_header function in lib/lha_file_header.c in Lhasa before 0.3.1 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted archive.

code_evidence: Line 8 computes new_raw_len = RAW_DATA_LEN(header) + nbytes without any bound on nbytes; the added guard in the patched version is absent here. Line 9 passes sizeof(LHAFileHeader) + new_raw_len to realloc, and lines 14-15 derive raw_data/result from that allocation, so a wrapped new_raw_len yields a too-small buffer. Line 19 stores the wrapped length as raw_data_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because a size calculation used for memory allocation wraps to a small value, and the unchecked result is then used as an allocation size and write offset. This is an integer wraparound in memory sizing, not merely a length-validation flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size_t addition RAW_DATA_LEN(header) + nbytes can wrap when nbytes is attacker-controlled and large, so realloc allocates a buffer smaller than the data later written. Trigger: a crafted archive whose level-3 header length drives nbytes. Consequence: lha_input_stream_read writes past the allocation, causing heap corruption potentially leading to code execution.

commit_msg: [core] CSndUList initial size is reduced to 512 elements
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      insert_norealloc(1, u);'], 'added_lines': ['      insert_norealloc_(1, u);']}
description: Secure Reliable Transport (SRT) through 1.3.4 has a CSndUList array overflow if there are many SRT connections.

code_evidence: On reschedule with an existing heap location greater than zero, update() calls remove_(u) then insert_norealloc(1, u), re-inserting the node at index 1 via a no-reallocation path that assumes the array already has capacity for that slot.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses an array index (1) in a no-realloc insertion without ensuring the index references a valid position in the allocated array, matching CWE-129. It is not merely a buffer-capacity/CWE-120 issue because the weakness is the unvalidated index into the list structure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: insert_norealloc writes at a fixed index without validating that the underlying CSndUList array has sufficient capacity for the current number of SRT connections. Trigger: many concurrent connections cause the initial fixed-size list to be exceeded; the no-realloc insert then indexes beyond the allocated array. Consequence: out-of-bounds write, memory corruption and potential crash (DoS).

commit_msg: Fix a crash bug with bogus text (Issue #426)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["\t  if (t->data[strlen((char *)t->data) - 1] == '\\n')"], 'added_lines': ["\t  if (t->data[0] && t->data[strlen((char *)t->data) - 1] == '\\n')"]}
description: HTMLDoc v1.9.15 was discovered to contain a heap overflow via (write_header) /htmldoc/htmldoc/html.cxx:273.

code_evidence: At line 17 t->data is only checked for NULL; when non-NULL but the string is empty, strlen returns 0. Line 23 then indexes t->data[strlen(t->data)-1], i.e. t->data[-1], an out-of-bounds read before the buffer. The loop at line 21 iterates zero times for empty data, so the preformatted branch reaches line 23 with an empty string.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code indexes one element before the beginning of the intended buffer, which matches CWE-787's out-of-bounds write/access scope at the boundary. The missing nonempty length check is the direct cause; this is a boundary/length error rather than a use-after-free or NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length used to index the last character is not validated to be nonzero, so an empty t->data yields index -1. Trigger: a preformatted node whose data is an empty string. Consequence: an out-of-bounds access before the allocated buffer, causing the crash described; the patch adds a t->data[0] guard.

commit_msg:
Disallow @@ and @@u usage in desktop files

Fixes #4146.

(cherry picked from commit 652a28ffab67cb6cd7d12dc3a93979bcd3731c7f)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['              else if (strcmp (arg, "@@") == 0 || strcmp (arg, "@@u") == 0)', '                g_print (_("Skipping invalid Exec argument %s\\n"), arg);']}
description: Flatpak is a system for building, distributing, and running sandboxed desktop applications on Linux. In Flatpack since version 0.9.4 and before version 1.10.2 has a vulnerability in the "file forwarding" feature which can be used by an attacker to gain access to files that would not ordinarily be allowed by the app's permissions. By putting the special tokens `@@` and/or `@@u` in the Exec field of a Flatpak app's .desktop file, a malicious app publisher can trick flatpak into behaving as though the user had chosen to open a target file with their Flatpak app, which automatically makes that file available to the Flatpak app. This is fixed in version 1.10.2. A minimal solution is the first commit "`Disallow @@ and @@U usage in desktop files`". The follow-up commits "`dir: Reserve the whole @@ prefix`" and "`dir: Refuse to export .desktop files with suspicious uses of @@ tokens`" are recommended, but not strictly required. As a workaround, avoid installing Flatpak apps from untrusted sources, or check the contents of the exported `.desktop` files in `exports/share/applications/*.desktop` (typically `~/.local/share/flatpak/exports/share/applications/*.desktop` and `/var/lib/flatpak/exports/share/applications/*.desktop`) to make sure that literal filenames do not follow `@@` or `@@u`.

code_evidence: The Exec arguments from the attacker-controlled .desktop file are parsed into old_argv at line 122 and each argument is quoted at line 140. Literal @@ and @@u tokens are not recognized as special; they fall through to the generic else at lines 145-146 and are appended verbatim into new_exec, which is written back as the exported Exec line at line 154.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Untrusted input (the .desktop Exec field) is incorporated into an output command line without neutralizing special elements that a downstream interpreter (flatpak file-forwarding) parses, matching CWE-74 injection. The fix adds a dedicated branch rejecting these tokens, confirming they are the injected special elements rather than plain arguments.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the export loop neutralizes %f/%u placeholders but never treats literal @@/@@u tokens specially, so an untrusted .desktop author can embed them in Exec. Trigger: a crafted Exec argument equal to @@ or @@u is copied into the rewritten Exec line; downstream file-forwarding parses these tokens as forwarding delimiters, granting the app access to target files outside its permissions.

commit_msg:
Fix for handling streams which resulted in negative num_mbs_left

Bug: 26070014
Change-Id: Id9f063a2c72a802d991b92abaf00ec687db5bb0f
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            if (1 == ps_dec->i4_num_cores && 0 == ps_dec->u2_num_mbs_left)', '            {', '                i4_continue_decode = 0;', '                android_errorWriteLog(0x534e4554, "26070014");', '            }', '']}
description: decoder/impeg2d_dec_hdr.c in mediaserver in Android 6.x before 2016-04-01 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file that triggers a certain negative value, aka internal bug 26070014.

code_evidence: The loop reads the next start code and computes i4_continue_decode from the bitstream value; when a valid slice header for the current row is found, it sets i4_dequeue_job=0 and breaks to continue decoding without re-dequeueing a job.

u2_num_mbs_left is assigned from the dequeued job's row range at [37], then impeg2d_dec_slice consumes macroblocks at [52]; the loop condition at [63] does not check whether the MB budget has been exhausted before continuing the slice decode.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the missing budget check lets a buffer operation proceed outside its intended boundary, matching improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer. The added zero-MB guard confirms the bounded-resource violation is the fixed root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decode loop continues processing a slice while u2_num_mbs_left may be zero or negative, so impeg2d_dec_slice operates past the intended macroblock buffer budget. Trigger: a crafted media file with slice/start-code values that keep i4_continue_decode true after the macroblock count is exhausted. Consequence: out-of-bounds memory access leading to memory corruption, potential code execution or DoS.

commit_msg:
In theory, IO scheduler belongs to request queue, and the request pool
of sched tags belongs to the request queue too.

However, the current tags allocation interfaces are re-used for both
driver tags and sched tags, and driver tags is definitely host wide,
and doesn't belong to any request queue, same with its request pool.
So we need tagset instance for freeing request of sched tags.

Meantime, blk_mq_free_tag_set() often follows blk_cleanup_queue() in case
of non-BLK_MQ_F_TAG_SHARED, this way requires that request pool of sched
tags to be freed before calling blk_mq_free_tag_set().

Commit 47cdee29ef9d94e ("block: move blk_exit_queue into __blk_release_queue")
moves blk_exit_queue into __blk_release_queue for simplying the fast
path in generic_make_request(), then causes oops during freeing requests
of sched tags in __blk_release_queue().

Fix the above issue by move freeing request pool of sched tags into
blk_cleanup_queue(), this way is safe becasue queue has been frozen and no any
in-queue requests at that time. Freeing sched tags has to be kept in queue's
release handler becasue there might be un-completed dispatch activity
which might refer to sched tags.

Cc: Bart Van Assche <bvanassche@acm.org>
Cc: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Fixes: 47cdee29ef9d94e485eb08f962c74943023a5271 ("block: move blk_exit_queue into __blk_release_queue")
Tested-by: Yi Zhang <yi.zhang@redhat.com>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <rong.a.chen@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Ming Lei <ming.lei@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/*', '\t * In theory, request pool of sched_tags belongs to request queue.', '\t * However, the current implementation requires tag_set for freeing', '\t * requests, so free the pool now.', '\t *', "\t * Queue has become frozen, there can't be any in-queue requests, so", '\t * it is safe to free requests now.', '\t */', '\tmutex_lock(&q->sysfs_lock);', '\tif (q->elevator)', '\t\tblk_mq_sched_free_requests(q);', '\tmutex_unlock(&q->sysfs_lock);', '']}
description: The block subsystem in the Linux kernel before 5.2 has a use-after-free that can lead to arbitrary code execution in the kernel context and privilege escalation, aka CID-c3e2219216c9. This is related to blk_mq_free_rqs and blk_cleanup_queue.

code_evidence: blk_freeze_queue(q) at line 9 drains in-flight requests, then line 15-16 call blk_mq_exit_queue(q) for MQ queues, which tears down the tag set. Line 17 then exits q_usage_counter.
Line 18 calls blk_put_queue(q), dropping the queue reference; the sched-tag request pool was not freed before this teardown, so freeing requests can occur after the tag set/queue structures are gone.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's ordering frees the tag set before the dependent sched-tag request pool, so subsequent request-freeing dereferences freed memory; this matches CWE-416 rather than a mere resource leak.

evidence_lines.code: blk_put_queue(q);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The queue is exited and its MQ tag set released without first freeing the sched_tags request pool. Later release-path handling of sched-tag requests references freed tag-set/queue memory, causing a use-after-free that can crash or execute code.

  7: R0_w=inv2 R1_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=4294967295,var_off=(0x0; 0xffffffff)) R2_w=inv4294967295 R10=fp0
  7: (95) exit
  7: R0=inv1 R1=inv(id=0,umin_value=4294967295,umax_value=4294967295,var_off=(0x0; 0xffffffff)) R2=inv4294967295 R10=fp0
  7: (95) exit

However, as a runtime result, we get 2 instead of 1, meaning the dst
register does not contain (u32)-1 in this case. The reason is fairly
straight forward given the 0 test leaves the dst register as-is:

  # ./bpftool p d x i 23
   0: (b7) r0 = 0
   1: (b7) r1 = -1
   2: (b4) w2 = -1
   3: (16) if w0 == 0x0 goto pc+1
   4: (9c) w1 %= w0
   5: (b7) r0 = 1
   6: (1d) if r1 == r2 goto pc+1
   7: (b7) r0 = 2
   8: (95) exit

This was originally not an issue given the dst register was marked as
completely unknown (aka 64 bit unknown). However, after 468f6eafa6c4
("bpf: fix 32-bit ALU op verification") the verifier casts the register
output to 32 bit, and hence it becomes 32 bit unknown. Note that for
the case where the src register is unknown, the dst register is marked
64 bit unknown. After the fix, the register is truncated by the runtime
and the test passes:

  # ./bpftool p d x i 23
   0: (b7) r0 = 0
   1: (b7) r1 = -1
   2: (b4) w2 = -1
   3: (16) if w0 == 0x0 goto pc+2
   4: (9c) w1 %= w0
   5: (05) goto pc+1
   6: (bc) w1 = w1
   7: (b7) r0 = 1
   8: (1d) if r1 == r2 goto pc+1
   9: (b7) r0 = 2
  10: (95) exit

Semantics also match with {R,W}x mod{64,32} 0 -> {R,W}x. Invalid div
has always been {R,W}x div{64,32} 0 -> 0. Rewrites are as follows:

  mod32:                            mod64:

  (16) if w0 == 0x0 goto pc+2       (15) if r0 == 0x0 goto pc+1
  (9c) w1 %= w0                     (9f) r1 %= r0
  (05) goto pc+1
  (bc) w1 = w1

Fixes: 468f6eafa6c4 ("bpf: fix 32-bit ALU op verification")
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Reviewed-by: John Fastabend <john.fastabend@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t/* Rx div 0 -> 0 */', '\t\t\t\t/* Rx mod 0 -> Rx */', '\t\t\t\t\t     0, 1, 0),', '\t\t\t\t      ARRAY_SIZE(chk_and_mod);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t/* [R,W]x div 0 -> 0 */', '\t\t\t\t/* [R,W]x mod 0 -> [R,W]x */', '\t\t\t\t\t     0, 1 + (is64 ? 0 : 1), 0),', '\t\t\t\tBPF_JMP_IMM(BPF_JA, 0, 0, 1),', '\t\t\t\tBPF_MOV32_REG(insn->dst_reg, insn->dst_reg),', '\t\t\t\t      ARRAY_SIZE(chk_and_mod) - (is64 ? 2 : 0);']}
description: The bpf verifier in the Linux kernel did not properly handle mod32 destination register truncation when the source register was known to be 0. A local attacker with the ability to load bpf programs could use this gain out-of-bounds reads in kernel memory leading to information disclosure (kernel memory), and possibly out-of-bounds writes that could potentially lead to code execution. This issue was addressed in the upstream kernel in commit 9b00f1b78809 ("bpf: Fix truncation handling for mod32 dst reg wrt zero") and in Linux stable kernels 5.11.2, 5.10.19, and 5.4.101.

code_evidence: Lines 15-21 detect 32/64-bit MOD/DIV register operations and derive is64/isdiv flags used to choose a rewrite.

Lines 30-35 build the mod-0 rewrite: a conditional jump over the original instruction, but for a 32-bit MOD the destination register is never truncated, so the verifier's modeled 32-bit result differs from runtime.
Lines 36-38 select the patchlet and count; the mod patchlet lacks the 32-bit truncation of the destination, permitting a mismatch between verified and actual register width.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-681 fits because truncating a 64-bit value to 32-bit is a numeric type conversion; failing to perform that conversion for the mod-0 destination produces an unexpected value used in a sensitive verifier context.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mod-0 rewrite leaves a 32-bit destination register untruncated, so the verifier models a 32-bit value while runtime retains the full value. Trigger: a BPF program performs Wx %= 0 with a known-zero source and branches on the result. Consequence: verifier/runtime divergence enables out-of-bounds memory access and possible kernel memory disclosure or writes.

description: FFmpeg before 2017-01-24 has an out-of-bounds write caused by a heap-based buffer overflow related to the ipvideo_decode_block_opcode_0xA function in libavcodec/interplayvideo.c and the avcodec_align_dimensions2 function in libavcodec/utils.c.

code_evidence: For PAL8/BGR8/RGB8 formats, alignment is raised to 8x8 only when codec_id is AV_CODEC_ID_JV; INTERPLAY_VIDEO is not included, so w_align/h_align stay at 1 (or chroma-derived) for that codec.
The computed alignment is then applied via FFALIGN to *width and *height, so the caller's buffer dimensions are padded by too small an amount.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is a missing constraint (insufficient alignment) that leads to writing beyond the intended buffer, which is CWE-787. It is not merely an integer issue: the concrete consequence is an out-of-bounds write enabled by the undersized allocation.

evidence_lines.code:
*width  = FFALIGN(*width, w_align);
*height = FFALIGN(*height, h_align);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The alignment function under-aligns dimensions for INTERPLAY_VIDEO, producing a buffer smaller than the decoder's block-write granularity. When the decoder later writes blocks at 8-pixel alignment, it can write past the allocated end, yielding an out-of-bounds heap write.

commit_msg: Fix memleak in tcp server by wiping priority queues on deletion
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        memcpy(conn_new, conn_old, sizeof(TCP_Secure_Connection));', '        crypto_memzero(conn_old, sizeof(TCP_Secure_Connection));'], 'added_lines': ['        move_secure_connection(conn_new, conn_old);']}
description: The TCP Server module in toxcore before 0.2.8 doesn't free the TCP priority queue under certain conditions, which allows a remote attacker to exhaust the system's memory, causing a denial of service (DoS).

code_evidence: Line 16 overwrites conn_new with a raw memcpy of the entire TCP_Secure_Connection struct, and line 17 zeroes conn_old. When conn_new->status is set (line 13), kill_TCP_secure_connection(conn_new) is called at line 14, but the struct copy still discards whatever resource-bearing state conn_new held afterward, since only status is checked before the overwrite.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 fits because the function fails to properly shut down/release the destination connection's resource before reusing the slot. It is not merely a memory-safety bug; the weakness is improper resource release along a reuse path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the struct is copied over conn_new after the conditional cleanup, so internal resources associated with the destination slot (notably its priority queue) can be replaced without being released. Trigger: an incoming connection completes the handshake (ret==1) while the target unconfirmed slot already holds allocated state. Consequence: unreleased memory accumulates, enabling remote memory exhaustion (DoS).

description: A Denial of Service vulnerability exists in FFmpeg 4.2 due to a memory leak in the av_dict_set function in dict.c.

commit_msg: Json library: fix a number of potential buffer overflows
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int', '  state->stack[state->depth] = c;', '  state->depth++;', '  state->vtype = 0;', '  return state->depth < JSONPARSE_MAX_DEPTH;'], 'added_lines': ['static bool', '  if(state->depth < JSONPARSE_MAX_DEPTH) {', '    state->stack[state->depth] = c;', '    state->depth++;', '    state->vtype = 0;', '    return true;', '  } else {', '    return false;', '  }']}
description: Contiki-NG before 4.2 has a stack-based buffer overflow in the push function in os/lib/json/jsonparse.c that allows an out-of-bounds write of an '{' or '[' character.

code_evidence: push writes state->stack[state->depth] = c and then increments state->depth without first checking that depth is within JSONPARSE_MAX_DEPTH; the return value only reports depth < JSONPARSE_MAX_DEPTH after the write has already occurred.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes data past the end of the intended buffer; the missing pre-write depth constraint is the direct cause of the out-of-bounds store, not merely a misreported return value.

evidence_lines.code:
state->stack[state->depth] = c;
state->depth++;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check is performed after the store instead of before it, so state->stack is indexed at state->depth even when depth has reached or exceeded JSONPARSE_MAX_DEPTH. Trigger: repeated push calls (e.g., nested '{' or '[' characters) drive depth to the maximum. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write past the end of the stack buffer, corrupting adjacent memory.

if (h->avctx->debug & FF_DEBUG_PICT_INFO) {

This vulnerability allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via supplying a crafted XML file. commit_msg: Prevent buffer overflow in BMP & SGI coders (bug report from pwchen&rayzhong of tencent)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      image->depth=(size_t) MagickMin((size_t) 8*', '        iris_info.bytes_per_pixel,MAGICKCORE_QUANTUM_DEPTH);'], 'added_lines': ['      image->depth=(size_t) MagickMin((size_t) 8*iris_info.bytes_per_pixel,', '        MAGICKCORE_QUANTUM_DEPTH);', '    if (EOFBlob(image) != MagickFalse)', '      ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"ImproperImageHeader");']}
description: The SGI coder in ImageMagick before 7.0.2-10 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a large row value in an sgi file.

code_evidence: image->depth is derived from iris_info.bytes_per_pixel and depth without validating that the declared rows/columns produce a pixel buffer large enough for the subsequent per-row reads.

number_pixels is computed as columns*rows and used for the allocation size, but the later pixel loop indexes p using a row stride of 8*image->columns (bytes_per_pixel==2) or 4*image->columns, so the stride/layout is not tied to the validated allocation size.

The DirectClass 2-byte loop computes p=pixels+(image->rows-y-1)*8*image->columns and reads *(p+6),*(p+7) per pixel; a large row value can make this offset exceed the allocated pixels buffer, reading out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe pointer arithmetic in the pixel loop reads data beyond the intended pixels buffer. It is not merely an integer overflow (CWE-190); the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reader trusts the SGI row/column values and derives a row stride (8*columns) that is not reconciled with the allocated buffer size or the actual decoded data length. Trigger: a crafted SGI file with a large row value causes the pointer arithmetic in the pixel conversion loop to walk past the end of the pixels allocation. Consequence: out-of-bounds read, leading to denial of service (crash) and potential memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
By validating length fields from server responses, out of boundary
accesses and endless loops can be mitigated.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (rep.length <= (sizeof(mapping) >> 2)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (rep.length <= (sizeof(mapping) >> 2) &&', '\t    rep.nElts <= (rep.length << 2)) {']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in X.org libXi before 1.7.7 allow remote X servers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds memory access or infinite loop) via vectors involving length fields.

code_evidence: Line 22 bounds rep.length (server-supplied) to sizeof(mapping)>>2 and computes nbytes = rep.length << 2 before reading that many bytes into the fixed 256-byte mapping buffer at line 24.
Lines 25-27 copy MIN((int)rep.nElts, nmap) bytes from mapping into the caller's map and return rep.nElts as status, all derived from the server-controlled length fields.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer arithmetic/size calculation on the length field (rep.length << 2) used as a copy size with insufficient validation, matching CWE-190's integer overflow/wraparound in size computations. The patch adds rep.nElts <= (rep.length << 2), confirming that the missing constraint on the shifted length is the defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is trusting the server reply's length fields: rep.length is shifted left by 2 (line 23) and rep.nElts is used as a copy count and return status without cross-checking them against each other. A malicious X server can supply inconsistent length/nElts values that pass the single rep.length bound, causing out-of-bounds reads from mapping or an oversized reported length, leading to memory disclosure or denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix use-after-free with `xmllint --html --push`

Call htmlCtxtUseOptions to make sure that names aren't stored in
dictionaries.

Note that this issue only affects xmllint using the HTML push parser.

Fixes #230.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                xmlCtxtUseOptions(ctxt, options);'], 'added_lines': ['                htmlCtxtUseOptions(ctxt, options);']}
description: There's a flaw in libxml2's xmllint in versions before 2.9.11. An attacker who is able to submit a crafted file to be processed by xmllint could trigger a use-after-free. The greatest impact of this flaw is to confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

code_evidence: In the HTML push-parser branch, htmlCreatePushParserCtxt creates an HTML parser context (line 40-41), then xmlCtxtUseOptions is called on that context (line 42). The context is subsequently fed via htmlParseChunk (line 44, 46), its document is taken as doc = ctxt->myDoc (line 47), and the context is freed with htmlFreeParserCtxt (line 48).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's flow creates a context, parses into it, extracts ctxt->myDoc, then frees the context; the misapplied option call causes retained references into freed memory, matching CWE-416. This is a lifetime/reference error, distinct from a simple null dereference or resource leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: applying the generic XML option handling (xmlCtxtUseOptions) to an HTML push context leaves HTML internals configured inconsistently, so names may be stored in dictionaries that are freed with the context. Trigger: a crafted file processed by xmllint --html --push. Consequence: the document/context still references freed memory, leading to a use-after-free with possible crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
blkcg: fix double free of new_blkg in blkcg_init_queue

If blkg_create fails, new_blkg passed as an argument will
be freed by blkg_create, so there is no need to free it again.

Signed-off-by: Hou Tao <houtao1@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@fb.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (IS_ERR(blkg)) {', '\t\tblkg_free(new_blkg);', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (IS_ERR(blkg))']}
description: The blkcg_init_queue function in block/blk-cgroup.c in the Linux kernel before 4.11 allows local users to cause a denial of service (double free) or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a creation failure.

code_evidence: blkg_create() is called with new_blkg at line 12; on creation failure it returns an ERR_PTR, and blkg_create itself frees the passed new_blkg. The error branch at lines 17-19 then calls blkg_free(new_blkg) on the same pointer before returning PTR_ERR(blkg).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the same heap pointer new_blkg is freed by blkg_create on failure and then explicitly freed again at line 18. This is a double free, not merely a use-after-free or memory leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ownership of new_blkg is transferred to blkg_create, but the error path retains a stale reference and frees it again. Trigger: a local user causes blkg_create to fail (e.g., allocation failure), entering the IS_ERR(blkg) branch. Consequence: double free of new_blkg, supporting denial of service or possibly memory corruption/arbitrary code execution.

description: An out of bounds write in hermes, while handling large arrays, prior to commit 06eaec767e376bfdb883d912cb15e987ddf2bda1 allows attackers to potentially execute arbitrary code via crafted JavaScript. Note that this is only exploitable if the application using Hermes permits evaluation of untrusted JavaScript. Hence, most React Native applications are not affected.

code_evidence: The capacity computation adds a growth increment to this->capacity(), rounds it up via NextPowerOf2, then clamps with std::min(..., UINT32_MAX). If this->capacity() + 2 overflows size_t or NextPowerOf2 overflows, the resulting NewCapacity can be smaller than MinSize, yet only MinSize > UINT32_MAX is rejected.

The buffer is allocated with NewCapacity*sizeof(T) and Capacity is later stored as NewCapacity, so an under-sized allocation combined with a caller expecting MinSize elements permits writes past the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes and stores an insufficient capacity, leading to writes beyond the allocated buffer, which directly matches CWE-787. It is a capacity/arithmetic flaw enabling the out-of-bounds write rather than a pure integer-overflow label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the overflow check only compares MinSize to UINT32_MAX and never validates that the computed NewCapacity actually covers MinSize or that byte sizing does not overflow. Trigger: a large array growth where the capacity arithmetic wraps or clamps to a value below the requested size. Consequence: allocation smaller than needed and subsequent out-of-bounds writes to the SmallVector storage.

commit_msg:
In commit 6a53b7593233 ("xfrm: check id proto in validate_tmpl()")
I introduced a check for xfrm protocol, but according to Herbert
IPSEC_PROTO_ANY should only be used as a wildcard for lookup, so
it should be removed from validate_tmpl().

And, IPSEC_PROTO_ANY is expected to only match 3 IPSec-specific
protocols, this is why xfrm_state_flush() could still miss
IPPROTO_ROUTING, which leads that those entries are left in
net->xfrm.state_all before exit net. Fix this by replacing
IPSEC_PROTO_ANY with zero.

This patch also extracts the check from validate_tmpl() to
xfrm_id_proto_valid() and uses it in parse_ipsecrequest().
With this, no other protocols should be added into xfrm.

Fixes: 6a53b7593233 ("xfrm: check id proto in validate_tmpl()")

Cc: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>

Acked-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
