description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.19. The XFRM subsystem has a use-after-free, related to an xfrm_state_fini panic, aka CID-dbb2483b2a46.

code_evidence: xfrm_state_flush is called with IPSEC_PROTO_ANY as the protocol filter, so the flush may not remove all states, notably those with IPPROTO_ROUTING.
The WARN_ON only checks state_all emptiness; it does not prevent later teardown.
The hash tables state_byspi, state_bysrc and state_bydst are freed unconditionally even if states were not flushed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function frees hash table memory while xfrm states that were not removed may still reference that memory. The defect is the incomplete flush combined with unconditional free, not merely a missing warning.

evidence_lines.code: xfrm_state_flush(net, IPSEC_PROTO_ANY, false, true);
WARN_ON(!list_empty(&net->xfrm.state_all));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the wildcard protocol filter leaves some xfrm states in the per-net lists while their hash tables are freed. Trigger: net namespace exit calls xfrm_state_fini, the incomplete flush leaves states, and the hash structures are freed. Supported consequence: remaining state references point to freed hash memory, leading to use-after-free and the reported xfrm_state_fini panic.

description: plugins/preauth/pkinit/pkinit_crypto_openssl.c in MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) through 1.15.2 mishandles Distinguished Name (DN) fields, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (buffer overflow and application crash) in situations involving untrusted X.509 data, related to the get_matching_data and X509_NAME_oneline_ex functions. NOTE: this has security relevance only in use cases outside of the MIT Kerberos distribution, e.g., the use of get_matching_data in KDC certauth plugin code that is specific to Red Hat.

code_evidence: A fixed stack buffer buf[DN_BUF_LEN] is declared with bufsize set to its size; this buffer receives the DN string.
X509_NAME_oneline_ex writes the subject DN into buf using the bufsize parameter; the return value is not checked, so truncation or overflow indication is ignored.
The possibly untruncated/overflowed buf is copied via strdup into md->subject_dn, propagating any out-of-bounds data.
The same fixed buf and bufsize are reused for the issuer DN, with the return value again unchecked before strdup.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a write into a fixed stack buffer based on attacker-influenced DN length without enforcing the buffer's intended boundary, which is an out-of-bounds memory operation within CWE-119. The unchecked return is the missing constraint that permits the boundary violation.

evidence_lines.code:
char buf[DN_BUF_LEN];
unsigned int bufsize = sizeof(buf);

X509_NAME_oneline_ex(X509_get_subject_name(cert), buf, &bufsize,
XN_FLAG_SEP_COMMA_PLUS);

Kafka: Limit our decompression size.

Don't assume that the Internet has our best interests at heart when it
gives us the size of our decompression buffer. Assign an arbitrary limit
of 50 MB.

This fixes #16739 in that it takes care of

** (process:17681): WARNING **: 20:03:07.440: Dissector bug, protocol Kafka, in packet 31: ../epan/proto.c:7043: failed assertion "end >= fi->start"

which is different from the original error output. It looks like *that*
might have taken care of in one of the other recent Kafka bug fixes.

The decompression routines return a success or failure status. Use
gbooleans instead of ints for that.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int', '    int ret = 0;', '    ret = 1;'], 'added_lines': ['static gboolean', '    gboolean ret = FALSE;', '    ret = TRUE;']}
description: Memory leak in Kafka protocol dissector in Wireshark 3.4.0 and 3.2.0 to 3.2.8 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file.

code_evidence: ret is initialized to 0 and only set to 1 after the decompression loop completes; any early failure path leaves it 0.

Inside the do/while loop, decompressed_buffer is allocated with wmem_alloc and immediately wrapped by tvb_new_child_real_data into composite_tvb. The failure exits at lines 50-51 (src_size==0), 56-57 (LZ4F_isError) and 59-60 (dst_size==0) jump to end before appending the current buffer, so that allocation is never attached to composite_tvb.

At end, composite_tvb is finalized and the context freed, but when ret==0 the else branch only appends a column string; nothing frees the buffer allocated in the current iteration that was not appended.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because memory allocated for decompression is not released when the error/zero-size path is taken; the ownership is lost rather than merely misused. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds write, which the function does not exhibit.

evidence_lines.code:
int ret = 0;
guint8 *data = (guint8*)tvb_memdup(wmem_packet_scope(), tvb, offset, length);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: each loop iteration allocates decompressed_buffer, but the zero-size and LZ4 error exits jump to end before the buffer is appended to composite_tvb, and the failure path performs no free. Trigger: a crafted LZ4 frame whose decompression yields a zero dst_size or an error causes repeated aborts. Consequence: the allocated packet-scope memory is left unreleased, supporting resource consumption/DoS consistent with CWE-401.

Fix OOB error when op input sizes do not match.

In cases where op input sizes are specified as in
```
REGISTER_OP("DynamicStitch")
    .Input("indices: N * int32")
    .Input("data: N * T")
    .Output("merged: T")
    .Attr("N : int >= 1")
    .Attr("T : type")
    .SetShapeFn(DynamicStitchShapeFunction);
```
if differing number of inputs are provided (e.g. 3 for `indices` and 4 for `data`)
we can get a crash in the executor when parsing the inputs, even before the kernel
called.  Here we avoid this by checking the return code for the argument id and
exit early.

commit_msg:
Avoid some undefined pointer arithmetic

A common idiom in the codebase is:

if (p + len > limit)
{
    return; /* Too long */
}

Where "p" points to some malloc'd data of SIZE bytes and
limit == p + SIZE

"len" here could be from some externally supplied data (e.g. from a TLS
message).

The rules of C pointer arithmetic are such that "p + len" is only well
defined where len <= SIZE. Therefore the above idiom is actually
undefined behaviour.

For example this could cause problems if some malloc implementation
provides an address for "p" such that "p + len" actually overflows for
values of len that are too big and therefore p + len < limit!

Issue reported by Guido Vranken.

CVE-2016-2177

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>

commit_msg:
Check basic auth result against != NGX_OK rather than == NGX_DECLINED

This corrects the error handling case when ngx_http_auth_spnego_basic is called with a bad configuration or bad username. These cases return NGX_ERROR, which allowed basic auth to proceed.

Thanks to Prakapovich Pavel aka Flyguy.by for pointing this out.

description: In the SPNEGO HTTP Authentication Module for nginx (spnego-http-auth-nginx-module) before version 1.1.1 basic Authentication can be bypassed using a malformed username. This affects users of spnego-http-auth-nginx-module that have enabled basic authentication. This is fixed in version 1.1.1 of spnego-http-auth-nginx-module. As a workaround, one may disable basic authentication.

code_evidence: Line 38 enters the basic-auth path only when ngx_http_auth_basic_user returned NGX_OK, meaning credentials were supplied. Line 40 checks ngx_http_auth_spnego_basic only for NGX_DECLINED, so an NGX_ERROR result (bad config or bad username) skips the failure block (41-47) and reaches the principal check at 48; if that check passes, line 53 returns NGX_OK, authenticating the request.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the handler fails to properly verify the claimed identity before granting access: an error result is treated as non-failure and the request is marked authenticated. This is an authentication-check flaw, distinct from a pure authorization error, since the credential verification outcome is mishandled.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of ngx_http_auth_spnego_basic is compared against a single error code (NGX_DECLINED) instead of requiring NGX_OK. Trigger: a malformed username or bad configuration makes the helper return NGX_ERROR. Because NGX_ERROR is not NGX_DECLINED, execution falls through to the success path and returns NGX_OK, letting the request proceed as authenticated. Consequence: authentication is bypassed for basic-auth users.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflows in TGA and troff exports (addresses #53, #54)

These were all caused by sprintf() appending a null char that was not actually used.
Fixes CVE-2021-30498 and CVE-2021-30499.

commit_msg:
cryp: prevent direct calls to update and final functions

With inconsistent or malformed data it has been possible to call
"update" and "final" crypto functions directly. Using a fuzzer tool [1]
we have seen that this results in asserts, i.e., a crash that
potentially could leak sensitive information.

By setting the state (initialized) in the crypto context (i.e., the
tee_cryp_state) at the end of all syscall_*_init functions and then add
a check of the state at the beginning of all update and final functions,
  we prevent direct entrance to the "update" and "final" functions.

[1] https://github.com/MartijnB/optee_fuzzer

Fixes: OP-TEE-2019-0021

Signed-off-by: Joakim Bech <joakim.bech@linaro.org>
Reported-by: Martijn Bogaard <bogaard@riscure.com>
Acked-by: Jerome Forissier <jerome.forissier@linaro.org>
Reviewed-by: Jens Wiklander <jens.wiklander@linaro.org>

commit_msg:
Fix various overflows in util/ (CVE-2017-11704)

* Add a check in decompileIF to avoid overflows.

    Avoid processing block when sact->numActions is 0, as
    sact->numActions - 1 may be used as index when accessing
    sact->Actions array.

* Fix overflow in readUInt32.

    o Fix declaration of readUInt32 and readSInt32 in util/read.h:
      return types should be unsigned long and long.
    o readUInt32: Avoid calling all readUInt8(f) in one line, order of
      evaluation is not guaranteed in the C standard.
    o readUInt32: Cast result of readUInt8(f) before << 24 to avoid
      overflow.

* Fix overflow in readMovie.

    length has int type but according to the specification it should be able
    to store unsigned 32bit numbers. Instead of changing the type of
    length, which would be a major refactoring, we verify that the value
    returned by readUInt32 is smaller than INT_MAX and update length if
    it's the case. Otherwise we print a warning and ignore the block.

This commit fixes CVE-2017-11704.

fixed some data-races around sk->sk_prot but it was not enough.

Some functions in inet6_(stream|dgram)_ops still access sk->sk_prot
without lock_sock() or rtnl_lock(), so they need READ_ONCE() to avoid
load tearing.

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")

Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>

description: A vulnerability has been found in Linux Kernel and classified as problematic. This vulnerability affects the function inet6_stream_ops/inet6_dgram_ops of the component IPv6 Handler. The manipulation leads to race condition. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-211090 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: Line 4 caches sk from sock, but each operation re-reads sk->sk_prot directly at lines 9, 11 and 17 without holding lock_sock() or rtnl_lock(). The commit notes IPV6_ADDRFORM can change sk->sk_prot concurrently, so these pointer dereferences are unsynchronized reads of shared state.

Trigger: a concurrent IPV6_ADDRFORM changes the protocol while connect/autobind executes. This can cause load tearing or dispatch to an inconsistent proto, yielding a crash or memory-safety issue rather than a clean single read.

commit_msg:
Fix cwise dimension overflow issue again.

If resulting dimensions overflow an int32, we were seeing an overflow and
crash due to size mismatch during broadcast assignment.  The cause is a simple
dimension type mismatch.

Note that actual tests for this are currently impractical, since successful
operations require more than 2^32 elements and OOM on most machines.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 479336566
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['inline Eigen::IndexList<Eigen::type2index<1>, int> OneByM(int m) {', '    Eigen::IndexList<Eigen::type2index<1>, int> ret;'], 'added_lines': ['inline Eigen::IndexList<Eigen::type2index<1>, Eigen::DenseIndex> OneByM(', '      Eigen::DenseIndex m) {', '    Eigen::IndexList<Eigen::type2index<1>, Eigen::DenseIndex> ret;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. `tf.keras.losses.poisson` receives a `y_pred` and `y_true` that are passed through `functor::mul` in `BinaryOp`. If the resulting dimensions overflow an `int32`, TensorFlow will crash due to a size mismatch during broadcast assignment. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit c5b30379ba87cbe774b08ac50c1f6d36df4ebb7c. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.11. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.10.1 and 2.9.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range. However, we will not cherrypick this commit into TensorFlow 2.8.x, as it depends on Eigen behavior that changed between 2.8 and 2.9.

code_evidence: OneByM takes an int m and stores it into an IndexList whose second entry is declared int; the dimension size is computed and carried in a 32-bit int type. The set(1, m) call assigns the caller-supplied dimension directly into this int-typed index without any wider type or overflow check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-131 fits because the dimension/size computation uses an int type that cannot represent the true size, producing an incorrect size value later used in allocation/assignment. It is a size-calculation error, not merely an out-of-bounds access, so the incorrect-size root cause is the appropriate mapping.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dimension index is typed as int, so a product of dimensions exceeding 2^31-1 overflows when stored/combined. Trigger: callers pass a large m (e.g., resulting broadcast dimensions over int32). Consequence: the wrapped/negative size yields a size mismatch during broadcast assignment and a crash, matching the reported overflow.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the include-directory array entry is assumed non-NULL and formatted as a string. Trigger: a corrupted DWARF5 line-table header yields a NULL directory entry. Consequence: the formatting routine receives NULL, causing a NULL pointer dereference and application crash (availability impact).

commit_msg:
Q.931: fix use-after-free (write) of "q931_pi"

The dissect_q931_number_ie (and indirectly dissect_q931_cause_ie_unsafe)
write to the "q931_pi" structure which seems private to the q931
dissector, but can in fact be called through other dissectors (isup) as
well. Normally this structure is initialized in "dissect_q931_pdu" and
invalidated at the end of the function, but a malformed packet can
prevent the cleanup. In the next packet, a different dissector can thus
trigger a use-after-free via "dissect_q931_number_ie".

Rename "dissect_q931_cause_ie_unsafe" since "unsafe" meant that external
dissectors could not call it directly (see commit a83a87e9ca).

Based on commit 197ceddab109, it seems that the intended purpose of the
structure is to provide information to the VoIP Calls dialog, but it
would only be used when called through dissect_q931_pdu. Dissectors like
isup have their own routines to provide call information, but as a
side-effect of code sharing the problematic code path was reached.

description: In Wireshark 2.6.0, 2.4.0 to 2.4.6, and 2.2.0 to 2.2.14, the Q.931 dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-q931.c by avoiding a use-after-free after a malformed packet prevented certain cleanup.

commit_msg:
vasnprintf: Fix heap memory overrun bug.

Reported by Ben Pfaff <blp@cs.stanford.edu> in
<https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/bug-gnulib/2018-09/msg00107.html>.

* lib/vasnprintf.c (convert_to_decimal): Allocate one more byte of
memory.
* tests/test-vasnprintf.c (test_function): Add another test.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  char *c_ptr = (char *) malloc (xsum (c_len, extra_zeroes));'], 'added_lines': ['  /* We need extra_zeroes bytes for zeroes, followed by c_len bytes for the', '     digits of a, followed by 1 byte for the terminating NUL.  */', '  char *c_ptr = (char *) malloc (xsum (xsum (extra_zeroes, c_len), 1));']}
description: The convert_to_decimal function in vasnprintf.c in Gnulib before 2018-09-23 has a heap-based buffer overflow because memory is not allocated for a trailing '\0' character during %f processing.

code_evidence: Line 7 allocates only c_len + extra_zeroes bytes, with no space reserved for a terminating NUL byte.

Lines 33-36 trim trailing zeros and, if all digits were removed, write a single '0' at c_ptr; line 37 then unconditionally writes '\0' at *d_ptr. When the digit buffer and zero padding exactly fill the allocation, this final write lands one byte past the allocated region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes a NUL byte past the end of the malloc'd buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the root cause is the off-by-one allocation size rather than an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code: char *c_ptr = (char *) malloc (xsum (c_len, extra_zeroes));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The malloc size omits the terminating NUL, so the mandatory write of '\0' after the digit-emission/trimming loop can occur one byte beyond the heap allocation. Triggered by %f conversion with a value whose digit count fills c_len plus extra_zeroes, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and potential corruption or crash.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-openflow_v6.c had an infinite loop that was addressed by validating property lengths.

code_evidence: prop_length is read from the packet at line 8 and used to size the subtree at line 9; prop_type is read at line 7 and drives the switch at line 14.

In the default branch, length - 4 and prop_length - 4 are computed from the packet-supplied length; if prop_length is small (e.g., 0-3), offset += prop_length - 4 is negative, moving offset backward instead of advancing.
The OFPMP_EXPERIMENTER branch similarly does offset += prop_length - 12; with prop_length < 12 this subtracts and rewinds offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a loop whose exit condition cannot be reached because the offset used to terminate iteration is never advanced (or moves backward) for malformed lengths; this matches CWE-835's infinite-loop definition. It is distinct from a plain out-of-bounds read, since the demonstrated effect is non-terminating iteration.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the property length read from the packet is not validated against the minimum header size before computing offset advancement. Trigger: a queue stats property with a small or zero prop_length makes offset += prop_length - 4 (or -12) non-positive, so the caller's iteration over properties does not advance and re-parses the same bytes. Supported consequence: the dissector loops indefinitely, causing CPU exhaustion/DoS.

description: An improper link resolution flaw can occur while extracting an archive leading to changing modes, times, access control lists, and flags of a file outside of the archive. An attacker may provide a malicious archive to a victim user, who would trigger this flaw when trying to extract the archive. A local attacker may use this flaw to gain more privileges in a system.

code_evidence: When TODO_MODE_BASE is set, the code applies mode changes: it uses fchmod(fd) only if fd >= 0, otherwise falls back to chmod(p->name, p->mode), which follows symbolic links and changes the mode of the link's target.
The descriptor is opened with O_NOFOLLOW, so if p->name is a symlink the open fails and fd stays -1, forcing the chmod() fallback on the symlink path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the function accesses a file by name (chmod(p->name,...)) without preventing the name from resolving through a symbolic link to an unintended resource; the O_NOFOLLOW open does not protect the pathname-based chmod fallback.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mode fixup is applied by pathname via chmod() when no O_NOFOLLOW descriptor is available, so a symlink in the extracted archive resolves to a file outside the archive. Trigger: a malicious archive containing a symlink whose fixup entry requests a mode change. Consequence: the mode of the link target outside the extraction directory is modified, enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg: fixed #2425
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (bs->position>bs->size) {', '\t\t\t\tbs->position = bs->size;', '\t\t\t\tbs->overflow_state = 1;', '\t\t\t}']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.4.0.

code_evidence: In the GF_BITSTREAM_READ branch (no emulation-prevention byte), the code does bs->position += nbBytes with no check against bs->size, so a caller-controlled skip length can advance the position past the buffer end.

The FILE_READ branch shows the intended bound: after advancing position it clamps to bs->size (line 22). The READ branch lacks this clamp, and the patch adds the missing size check and overflow_state assignment to that branch.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-122 fits because the unvalidated position advance can drive accesses beyond a heap-allocated buffer, matching a heap-based buffer overflow. It is not merely an integer issue: the missing size constraint on the offset is the core defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: gf_bs_skip_bytes advances bs->position by an unbounded nbBytes in the memory-read path without constraining it to bs->size. Trigger: a caller passes a skip length larger than the remaining heap buffer. Consequence: subsequent reads/writes operate at an out-of-bounds position on the heap-allocated bitstream buffer, enabling heap corruption/overflow.

commit_msg:
Avoid negative integer overflow when `iccOffset > chunkLength`.

This fixes #790.

(cherry picked from commit 6fa2e31206127bd8bcac0269311f3775a8d6ea21)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                    enforce(iccOffset <= chunkLength, Exiv2::kerCorruptedMetadata);']}
description: An integer overflow in Exiv2 through 0.27.1 allows an attacker to cause a denial of service (SIGSEGV) via a crafted PNG image file, because PngImage::readMetadata mishandles a chunkLength - iccOffset subtraction.

code_evidence: iccOffset is a uint32_t starting at 0 and advanced by the iCCP profile-name scan, which stops at 80 or chunkLength. After the scan, profileName_ is built with length iccOffset - 1, then ++iccOffset is applied unconditionally. If the scan ends without finding a NUL byte, iccOffset equals chunkLength (or 80) and the increment makes iccOffset greater than chunkLength. The subtraction chunkLength - iccOffset at line 54 then wraps to a huge unsigned value and is passed as the compressed length to zlibToDataBuf with pointer chunkData.pData_ + iccOffset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an unsigned subtraction wraparound that yields a huge length instead of a negative value, exactly the integer overflow/wraparound pattern of CWE-190. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the missing iccOffset <= chunkLength constraint is the cause, and the resulting oversized length drives the memory access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes iccOffset stays below chunkLength after the unconditional increment, but a crafted iCCP chunk whose name lacks a NUL terminator drives iccOffset to chunkLength. The subtraction chunkLength - iccOffset then wraps to a very large uint32_t, so zlibToDataBuf reads beyond the chunk buffer, causing out-of-bounds access and a SIGSEGV denial of service.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a division by 0 in `tf.raw_ops.Conv2DBackpropInput`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/b40060c9f697b044e3107917c797ba052f4506ab/tensorflow/core/kernels/conv_grad_input_ops.h#L625-L655) does a division by a quantity that is controlled by the caller. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: work_unit_size is computed from caller-controlled tensor dimensions (size_A, size_B, size_C); it can be zero when the tensors have zero elements.
shard_size is computed as (target_working_set_size + work_unit_size - 1) / work_unit_size, dividing by work_unit_size in the non-parallel branch.
Shard(...) is then called with work_unit_size, which may be zero, propagating a zero divisor into the sharding logic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an unchecked division by a caller-controlled quantity that can be zero, matching CWE-369. The patch adds OP_REQUIRES(work_unit_size > 0) before this division, confirming the missing zero constraint rather than a separate out-of-bounds issue.

evidence_lines.code: const size_t work_unit_size = size_A + size_B + size_C;

Shard(worker_threads.num_threads, worker_threads.workers, shard_limit,
work_unit_size, shard);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: work_unit_size derived from attacker-influenced shapes may be zero, and the non-parallel path divides by it to compute shard_size. Trigger: supplying empty input, filter, or out_backprop tensors makes work_unit_size 0, causing division by zero. Supported consequence: crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
ALSA: hrtimer: Fix stall by hrtimer_cancel()

hrtimer_cancel() waits for the completion from the callback, thus it
must not be called inside the callback itself.  This was already a
problem in the past with ALSA hrtimer driver, and the early commit
[fcfdebe70759: ALSA: hrtimer - Fix lock-up] tried to address it.

However, the previous fix is still insufficient: it may still cause a
lockup when the ALSA timer instance reprograms itself in its callback.
Then it invokes the start function even in snd_timer_interrupt() that
is called in hrtimer callback itself, results in a CPU stall.  This is
no hypothetical problem but actually triggered by syzkaller fuzzer.

This patch tries to fix the issue again.  Now we call
hrtimer_try_to_cancel() at both start and stop functions so that it
won't fall into a deadlock, yet giving some chance to cancel the queue
if the functions have been called outside the callback.  The proper
hrtimer_cancel() is called in anyway at closing, so this should be
enough.

Reported-and-tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\thrtimer_try_to_cancel(&stime->hrt);']}
description: sound/core/hrtimer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 does not prevent recursive callback access, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock) via a crafted ioctl call.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only clears a running flag and returns; the patch adds hrtimer_try_to_cancel, addressing recursive callback/deadlock behavior rather than any input validation, so there is no code-grounded support for CWE-20.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (info->value.bufferInfo.length < (offset + size))', '\t\t\tif (info->value.bufferInfo.length < (offset + size))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\ttxInteger end = offset + size;', '\t\tif ((info->value.bufferInfo.length < end) || (end < offset))', '\t\t\ttxInteger end = offset + size;', '\t\t\tif ((info->value.bufferInfo.length < end) || (end < offset))']}
description: Moddable commit before 135aa9a4a6a9b49b60aa730ebc3bcc6247d75c45 was discovered to contain an out-of-bounds read via the function fxUint8Getter at /moddable/xs/sources/xsDataView.c.

code_evidence: At line 24 the attacker-controlled byteLength is parsed, and line 26 checks only `bufferInfo.length < (offset + size)` without guarding against integer overflow of `offset + size`.
The same unchecked `offset + size` comparison recurs at line 46 when the buffer info is re-read for the view.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing overflow guard lets the byteLength/byteOffset validation be bypassed, permitting reads past the intended buffer bounds, which matches CWE-125. This is an out-of-bounds read rather than an out-of-bounds write, since the DataView is used for reads.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the range check computes `offset + size` in a signed integer without verifying that the sum did not overflow, so a large size can wrap to a small or negative value that passes the length comparison. Trigger: constructing a DataView with a crafted byteOffset and byteLength. Consequence: subsequent reads via the DataView accessors can access memory outside the backing buffer, i.e., an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
Fix check for VCF record size

The check for excessive record size in vcf_parse_format() only
looked at individual fields.  It was therefore possible to
exceed the limit and overflow fmt_aux_t::offset by having
multiple fields with a combined size that went over INT_MAX.
Fix by including the amount of memory used so far in the check.

Credit to OSS-Fuzz
Fixes oss-fuzz 24097
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        f->offset = mem->l;', '        if (v->n_sample * (uint64_t)f->size > INT_MAX) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if ((uint64_t) mem->l + v->n_sample * (uint64_t)f->size > INT_MAX) {', '', '        f->offset = mem->l;']}
description: HTSlib through 1.10.2 allows out-of-bounds write access in vcf_parse_format (called from vcf_parse and vcf_read).

code_evidence: The per-field limit check at [132] compares only v->n_sample * f->size against INT_MAX, ignoring mem->l (memory already consumed by earlier fields). f->offset is set to mem->l at [131] before the check, so a row with many fields can push the cumulative offset past INT_MAX.
After the loop, [145] computes each field buffer pointer as mem->s + fmt[j].offset using these offsets.
Later, [296]/[298]/[301] write z->size * v->n_sample bytes from z->buf, so an overflowed offset produces a write beyond the allocated mem->s buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the insufficient cumulative limit leads directly to writes past the end of the allocated format buffer, modifying memory beyond its bounds.

evidence_lines.code:
for (j = 0; j < v->n_fmt; ++j)
fmt[j].buf = (uint8_t*)mem->s + fmt[j].offset;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size guard omits the running memory total mem->l, so multiple FORMAT fields whose combined size exceeds INT_MAX pass the check while each field's individual size is small. Trigger: a crafted VCF with many/large FORMAT fields. Consequence: f->offset overflows, field buffer pointers computed at [145] point outside mem->s, and writes at [296]/[298]/[301] corrupt memory out of bounds.

commit_msg:
ALSA: seq: Fix race at timer setup and close

ALSA sequencer code has an open race between the timer setup ioctl and
the close of the client.  This was triggered by syzkaller fuzzer, and
a use-after-free was caught there as a result.

This patch papers over it by adding a proper queue->timer_mutex lock
around the timer-related calls in the relevant code path.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_lock(&q->timer_mutex);', '\tmutex_unlock(&q->timer_mutex);']}
description: Race condition in the queue_delete function in sound/core/seq/seq_queue.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 allows local users to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and system crash) by making an ioctl call at a certain time.

code_evidence: queue_delete stops and closes q->timer at [3,4] without holding q->timer_mutex, then waits on q->use_lock at [5] before releasing the queue.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function executes a shared-resource teardown sequence that lacks exclusive synchronization against an interfering concurrent code sequence, matching CWE-362's race-condition definition. The missing timer_mutex lock, not the subsequent free alone, is the weakness; the use-after-free is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: timer teardown in queue_delete is not serialized against the timer-setup ioctl path, so a concurrent caller can access the timer while it is being stopped/closed. Trigger: a local user issues the timer-setup ioctl concurrently with client close. Supported consequence: use-after-free and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/spec-ctrl: Make VERW flushing runtime conditional

Currently, VERW flushing to mitigate MDS is boot time conditional per domain
type.  However, to provide mitigations for DRPW (CVE-2022-21166), we need to
conditionally use VERW based on the trustworthiness of the guest, and the
devices passed through.

Remove the PV/HVM alternatives and instead issue a VERW on the return-to-guest
path depending on the SCF_verw bit in cpuinfo spec_ctrl_flags.

Introduce spec_ctrl_init_domain() and d->arch.verw to calculate the VERW
disposition at domain creation time, and context switch the SCF_verw bit.

For now, VERW flushing is used and controlled exactly as before, but later
patches will add per-domain cases too.

No change in behaviour.

This is part of XSA-404.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>

description: Out-of-bounds write vulnerability in CX-Programmer v9.76.1 and earlier which is a part of CX-One (v4.60) suite allows an attacker to cause information disclosure and/or arbitrary code execution by having a user to open a specially crafted CXP file. This vulnerability is different from CVE-2022-25234.

commit_msg:
Both add_slot_store() and remove_slot_store() try to fix up the
drc_name copied from the store buffer by placing a NUL terminator at
nbyte + 1 or in place of a '\n' if present. However, the static buffer
that we copy the drc_name data into is not zeroed and can contain
anything past the n-th byte.

This is problematic if a '\n' byte appears in that buffer after nbytes
and the string copied into the store buffer was not NUL terminated to
start with as the strchr() search for a '\n' byte will mark this
incorrectly as the end of the drc_name string resulting in a drc_name
string that contains garbage data after the n-th byte.

Additionally it will cause us to overwrite that '\n' byte on the stack
with NUL, potentially corrupting data on the stack.

The following debugging shows an example of the drmgr utility writing
"PHB 4543" to the add_slot sysfs attribute, but add_slot_store()
logging a corrupted string value.

  drmgr: drmgr: -c phb -a -s PHB 4543 -d 1
  add_slot_store: drc_name = PHB 4543°|<82>!, rc = -19

Fix this by using strscpy() instead of memcpy() to ensure the string
is NUL terminated when copied into the static drc_name buffer.
Further, since the string is now NUL terminated the code only needs to
change '\n' to '\0' when present.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Tyrel Datwyler <tyreld@linux.ibm.com>
[mpe: Reformat change log and add mention of possible stack corruption]
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210315214821.452959-1-tyreld@linux.ibm.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmemcpy(drc_name, buf, nbytes);', '\tif (!end)', '\t\tend = &drc_name[nbytes];', "\t*end = '\\0';"], 'added_lines': ['\tstrscpy(drc_name, buf, nbytes + 1);', '\tif (end)', "\t\t*end = '\\0';"]}
description: In drivers/pci/hotplug/rpadlpar_sysfs.c in the Linux kernel through 5.11.8, the RPA PCI Hotplug driver has a user-tolerable buffer overflow when writing a new device name to the driver from userspace, allowing userspace to write data to the kernel stack frame directly. This occurs because add_slot_store and remove_slot_store mishandle drc_name '\0' termination, aka CID-cc7a0bb058b8.

code_evidence: Line 7 rejects only nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN, allowing nbytes up to MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1, so memcpy at line 9 copies nbytes bytes into the stack buffer leaving no guaranteed NUL terminator.

After the copy, strchr at line 10 scans the non-terminated drc_name; if no newline is found, line 12 sets end to drc_name[nbytes] and line 13 writes NUL there, potentially past the initialized region and into uninitialized stack data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a buffer-copy operation (memcpy) into a fixed stack buffer where input size is not checked against the destination's usable capacity including terminator, matching CWE-120. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the unsafe copy and NUL write modify memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the user-supplied buffer is copied with memcpy without NUL-terminating the stack buffer, and the subsequent strchr/termination logic can write NUL at drc_name[nbytes]. Trigger: a write to add_slot whose data lacks a newline and fills the buffer. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds stack write and garbage data passed to dlpar_add_slot, i.e., stack memory corruption.

commit_msg:
xen/arm: p2m: Avoid off-by-one check on p2m->max_mapped_gfn

The code base is using inconsistently the field p2m->max_mapped_gfn.
Some of the useres expect that p2m->max_guest_gfn contain the highest
mapped GFN while others expect highest + 1.

p2m->max_guest_gfn is set as highest + 1, because of that the sanity
check on the GFN in p2m_resolved_translation_fault() and
p2m_get_entry() can be bypassed when GFN == p2m->max_guest_gfn.

p2m_get_root_pointer(p2m->max_guest_gfn) may return NULL if it is
outside of address range supported and therefore the BUG_ON() could be
hit.

The current value hold in p2m->max_mapped_gfn is inconsistent with the
expectation of the common code (see domain_get_maximum_gpfn()) and also
the documentation of the field.

Rather than changing the check in p2m_translation_fault() and
p2m_get_entry(), p2m->max_mapped_gfn is now containing the highest
mapped GFN and the callers assuming "highest + 1" are now adjusted.

Take the opportunity to use 1UL rather than 1 as page_order could
theoritically big enough to overflow a 32-bit integer.

Lastly, the documentation of the field max_guest_gfn to reflect how it
is computed.

This is part of XSA-301.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <Julien.Grall@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                                      gfn_add(sgfn, 1 << page_order));'], 'added_lines': ['                                      gfn_add(sgfn, (1UL << page_order) - 1));']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing ARM guest OS users to cause a denial of service via a XENMEM_add_to_physmap hypercall. p2m->max_mapped_gfn is used by the functions p2m_resolve_translation_fault() and p2m_get_entry() to sanity check guest physical frame. The rest of the code in the two functions will assume that there is a valid root table and check that with BUG_ON(). The function p2m_get_root_pointer() will ignore the unused top bits of a guest physical frame. This means that the function p2m_set_entry() will alias the frame. However, p2m->max_mapped_gfn will be updated using the original frame. It would be possible to set p2m->max_mapped_gfn high enough to cover a frame that would lead p2m_get_root_pointer() to return NULL in p2m_get_entry() and p2m_resolve_translation_fault(). Additionally, the sanity check on p2m->max_mapped_gfn is off-by-one allowing "highest mapped + 1" to be considered valid. However, p2m_get_root_pointer() will return NULL. The problem could be triggered with a specially crafted hypercall XENMEM_add_to_physmap{, _batch} followed by an access to an address (via hypercall or direct access) that passes the sanity check but cause p2m_get_root_pointer() to return NULL. A malicious guest administrator may cause a hypervisor crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS). Xen version 4.8 and newer are vulnerable. Only Arm systems are vulnerable. x86 systems are not affected.

code_evidence: p2m->max_mapped_gfn is updated as gfn_max(p2m->max_mapped_gfn, gfn_add(sgfn, 1 << page_order)), i.e. the end boundary sgfn + 2^page_order rather than the highest mapped GFN sgfn + 2^page_order - 1. The 1 << page_order term also uses 32-bit int arithmetic, so a large page_order can overflow.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an incorrect maximum boundary computed one greater than the correct highest mapped GFN, exactly CWE-193's off-by-one. The consequence is a bypassed sanity check leading to a hypervisor crash, matching the availability impact; this is a boundary miscalculation, not a generic integer overflow alone.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: max_mapped_gfn is recorded as highest+1 instead of highest, making it inconsistent with callers that treat the field as the highest mapped GFN. A crafted XENMEM_add_to_physmap hypercall drives this value high; the off-by-one sanity check then admits GFN == max_mapped_gfn, p2m_get_root_pointer() returns NULL, and the subsequent BUG_ON crashes the hypervisor (DoS).

commit_msg:
Implement fLimitFree to CTxMemPool::accept()

Works around a potential DoS vulnerability (see Bitcoin commit
ce99358f4aa4182d6983fde3e33a8fdbe1dfe4c3).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (tx.AcceptToMemoryPool(txdb, true, &fMissingInputs))', '        {', '                    if (tx.AcceptToMemoryPool(txdb, true, &fMissingInputs2))', '                    {', '                    else if (!fMissingInputs2)', '                    {', '                        // invalid orphan', '                        printf("   removed invalid orphan tx %s\\n", inv.hash.ToString().substr(0,10).c_str());'], 'added_lines': ['        if(tx.AcceptToMemoryPool(txdb, true, true, &fMissingInputs)) {', '                    if(tx.AcceptToMemoryPool(txdb, true, true, &fMissingInputs2)) {', '                    else if(!fMissingInputs2) {', '                        /* Invalid or insufficient fee orphan */', '                        printf("   removed orphan tx %s\\n", inv.hash.ToString().substr(0,10).c_str());']}
description: A vulnerability was found in ghostlander Phoenixcoin. It has been classified as problematic. Affected is the function CTxMemPool::accept of the file src/main.cpp. The manipulation leads to denial of service. Upgrading to version 0.6.6.1-pxc is able to address this issue. The name of the patch is 987dd68f71a7d8276cef3b6c3d578fd4845b5699. It is recommended to upgrade the affected component. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-217068.

code_evidence: AcceptToMemoryPool is called without the third fee-limiting argument, so a tx with sufficient inputs but insufficient fee is admitted and its hash queued in vWorkQueue/vEraseQueue.

The orphan path re-checks each orphan with the same call lacking fee limit; orphans with missing inputs are retained while fee-deficient ones are only distinguished by the added comment, not by a fee constraint.
When fMissingInputs is true, AddOrphanTx stores the message and LimitOrphanTxSize evicts only by count, so an attacker can flood the orphan pool with fee-insufficient transactions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function admits attacker-supplied transactions into persistent pools without the fLimitFree constraint, so resources are held rather than released, matching CWE-404's improper resource release leading to availability impact. It is not a memory-safety issue but an unbounded resource retention weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing fee-limit enforcement in the mempool/orphan acceptance path, allowing an unauthenticated peer to submit many low- or zero-fee transactions. Trigger is repeated 'tx' messages whose inputs are absent; these are added to the orphan map and only count-bounded, so memory and processing resources are consumed without release. Supported consequence is a denial of service through resource exhaustion.

commit_msg:
ksmbd: fix memory leak in smb2_handle_negotiate

The allocated memory didn't free under an error
path in smb2_handle_negotiate().

Fixes: e2f34481b24d ("cifsd: add server-side procedures for SMB3")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com # ZDI-CAN-17815
Signed-off-by: Namjae Jeon <linkinjeon@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Hyunchul Lee <hyc.lee@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Steve French <stfrench@microsoft.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tkfree(conn->preauth_info);', '\t\t\tconn->preauth_info = NULL;', '\t\t\tkfree(conn->preauth_info);', '\t\t\tconn->preauth_info = NULL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in ksmbd in the Linux kernel 5.15 through 5.19 before 5.19.2. fs/ksmbd/smb2pdu.c omits a kfree call in certain smb2_handle_negotiate error conditions, aka a memory leak.

code_evidence: conn->preauth_info is allocated with kzalloc for the SMB311 dialect; if allocation fails the request aborts, otherwise the pointer is retained for error paths.
After allocation, deassemble_neg_contexts may return a non-success status; the code sets rc = -EINVAL and jumps to err_out without releasing the allocated preauth_info.
init_smb3_11_server can return a negative rc; this path likewise jumps to err_out, leaving conn->preauth_info allocated and still referenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because a heap allocation made with kzalloc is not released on error paths after its effective lifetime, matching missing release of memory. It is not a use-after-free (CWE-416) since the pointer is not dereferenced after release; the defect is the absent kfree on exceptional exits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SMB311 negotiate path allocates conn->preauth_info but the error branches at deassemble_neg_contexts failure and init_smb3_11_server failure exit via err_out without freeing it. Trigger: a client sends a negotiate request that causes either callee to fail. Consequence: the allocation is leaked, and repeated failed negotiations consume kernel memory (availability impact).

commit_msg:
If there is a directory entry pointing to a system inode (such as a
journal inode), complain and declare the file system to be corrupted.

Also, if the superblock's first inode number field is too small,
refuse to mount the file system.

This addresses CVE-2018-10882.

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=200069

Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!ext4_valid_inum(sb, inode->i_ino))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (inode->i_ino < EXT4_ROOT_INO ||', '\t    inode->i_ino > le32_to_cpu(EXT4_SB(sb)->s_es->s_inodes_count))']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's ext4 filesystem. A local user can cause an out-of-bound write in in fs/jbd2/transaction.c code, a denial of service, and a system crash by unmounting a crafted ext4 filesystem image.

code_evidence: Line 10 validates inode->i_ino with ext4_valid_inum before use; the fixed version instead bounds i_ino against EXT4_ROOT_INO and s_inodes_count.
i_ino drives block_group (line 12) and inode_offset (lines 17-18), which compute the inode table block and offset (lines 19-20) without further bounds checking on the group index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked inode number leads to writes past the intended buffer via the computed iloc->offset. It is an out-of-bounds write rather than merely an invalid index or corruption check failure.

if (!ext4_valid_inum(sb, inode->i_ino))
return -EFSCORRUPTED;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that inode->i_ino from a crafted filesystem image is used to compute block_group and inode_offset; an out-of-range inode number yields a group index or offset outside the valid inode table, so the read/write into the buffer at iloc->offset (lines 20-21 onward) can go out of bounds. Trigger is mounting/using a crafted ext4 image; consequence is memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
ensure fragment offset is less than total length

Summary:
when messages are received in fragments, we need to make sure the offset value is less than the length of all fragments to be received.

CVE-2023-28753

Reviewed By: kernelslacker

Differential Revision: D44277643

fbshipit-source-id: 8b4b163503a5574b05c0a185b615de61442a0309
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -63,6 +63,7 @@
 				goto einval;
 			if (!msg->text_len ||
 			    nf_len >= NCRX_LINE_MAX ||
+			    nf_off >= nf_len ||
 			    nf_off + msg->text_len > nf_len)
 				goto einval;
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t    nf_off >= nf_len ||']}
description: netconsd prior to v0.2 was vulnerable to an integer overflow in its parse_packet function. A malicious individual could leverage this overflow to create heap memory corruption with attacker controlled data.

code_evidence: sscanf parses attacker-controlled nf_off and nf_len from the ncfrag value; the pre-patch validation checks nf_len >= NCRX_LINE_MAX and nf_off + msg->text_len > nf_len but never rejects nf_off >= nf_len.

Since nf_off is unsigned, nf_off + msg->text_len can wrap when nf_off is near UINT_MAX, bypassing the sum check; the function then stores ncfrag_off, computes ncfrag_left = nf_len - ncfrag_len, and sets text_len = nf_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the accepted attacker-controlled fragment offset leads to writing data past the end of a heap buffer during reassembly. The overflow is the enabling cause; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an integer overflow (CWE-190).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing bound nf_off < nf_len allows an unsigned integer overflow in nf_off + msg->text_len. A malicious ncfrag header with a huge offset wraps the sum below nf_len, so validation passes and the fragment offset/length state is accepted. Downstream fragment reassembly using this offset writes attacker-controlled data outside the intended heap buffer, causing heap corruption.

commit_msg:
x86/entry/64: Don't use IST entry for #BP stack

There's nothing IST-worthy about #BP/int3.  We don't allow kprobes
in the small handful of places in the kernel that run at CPL0 with
an invalid stack, and 32-bit kernels have used normal interrupt
gates for #BP forever.

Furthermore, we don't allow kprobes in places that have usergs while
in kernel mode, so "paranoid" is also unnecessary.

Signed-off-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org

That's okay.", '\t */', '']}
description: A statement in the System Programming Guide of the Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual (SDM) was mishandled in the development of some or all operating-system kernels, resulting in unexpected behavior for #DB exceptions that are deferred by MOV SS or POP SS, as demonstrated by (for example) privilege escalation in Windows, macOS, some Xen configurations, or FreeBSD, or a Linux kernel crash. The MOV to SS and POP SS instructions inhibit interrupts (including NMIs), data breakpoints, and single step trap exceptions until the instruction boundary following the next instruction (SDM Vol. 3A; section 6.8.3). (The inhibited data breakpoints are those on memory accessed by the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction itself.) Note that debug exceptions are not inhibited by the interrupt enable (EFLAGS.IF) system flag (SDM Vol. 3A; section 2.3). If the instruction following the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction is an instruction like SYSCALL, SYSENTER, INT 3, etc. that transfers control to the operating system at CPL < 3, the debug exception is delivered after the transfer to CPL < 3 is complete. OS kernels may not expect this order of events and may therefore experience unexpected behavior when it occurs.

code_evidence: Line 10 calls ist_enter(regs) to establish entry context, and line 11 warns if RCU is not watching, indicating the handler may run during context-tracking state changes or from a kprobe in non-CONTEXT_KERNEL mode.
Lines 24-28 bracket do_trap with debug_stack_usage_inc/dec and cond_local_irq_enable/disable, so the handler mutates shared debug-stack usage state and enables interrupts around trap handling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's comment explicitly states it can be called from kprobes or during context tracking state changes, and it manipulates shared debug-stack usage and interrupt state around do_trap. That is a concurrent code sequence lacking guaranteed exclusive access to shared entry/debug state, matching CWE-362. It is not primarily an out-of-bounds or input-validation flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
ist_enter(regs);
RCU_LOCKDEP_WARN(!rcu_is_watching(), "entry code didn't wake RCU");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: do_int3 can be reached from a kprobe in non-CONTEXT_KERNEL kernel mode or during context tracking state changes, so the entry path and debug-stack usage accounting run in a context where another sequence can observe or modify shared state. The root cause is the assumption that #BP handling is exclusive/atomic with respect to these concurrent entry paths; the trigger is an int3 delivered in that window, and the supported consequence is unexpected kernel behavior such as crash/instability rather than a guaranteed privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Check for multiplication overflow in MSADPCM decodeSample

Check for multiplication overflow (using __builtin_mul_overflow
if available) in MSADPCM.cpp decodeSample and return an empty
decoded block if an error occurs.

This fixes the 00193-audiofile-signintoverflow-MSADPCM case of #41

description: Integer overflow in modules/MSADPCM.cpp in Audio File Library (aka audiofile) 0.3.6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: The loop bound is computed as (m_framesPerPacket - 2) * m_track->f.channelCount in plain int arithmetic; a crafted file with a large frames-per-packet value can overflow this product, yielding a small or negative samplesRemaining.

The decode loop then consumes encoded bytes and writes to decoded while samplesRemaining > 0; decodeSample is called without any overflow check on its internal arithmetic, and there is no validation that the encoded buffer holds the number of samples implied by samplesRemaining.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the flaw is an unchecked integer multiplication/wraparound in the decode path that the logic assumes stays in range. The commit's added __builtin_mul_overflow check on decodeSample confirms the overflow is the targeted root cause; the resulting memory corruption/crash is the consequence, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code: int samplesRemaining = (m_framesPerPacket - 2) * m_track->f.channelCount;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sample count and per-sample decode arithmetic assume the multiplication result fits in int/int16_t without validation. Trigger: a crafted MSADPCM file with attacker-controlled frames-per-packet or sample state drives decodeSample's multiply into overflow. Consequence: a wrapped value causes incorrect sample decoding and out-of-bounds reads/writes, leading to a crash (DoS) as described for the crafted-file case.

commit_msg:
Correctly load/initialize classes when using ConstantPool

- do not load classes in the "ifLoaded" calls
- never intitialize classes in the natives
- do not update the constant pool when querying from the natives

Fixes: #12016

[ci skip]

Signed-off-by: Graham Chapman <graham_chapman@ca.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\tif (ramCPEntry != NULL) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\tif ((NULL != ramCPEntry) && J9_ARE_NO_BITS_SET(resolveFlags, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE)) {']}
description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: The virtual-method resolution path writes the resolved vTable offset back into ramCPEntry->methodIndexAndArgCount unconditionally whenever ramCPEntry is non-NULL, without checking resolveFlags. The patched guard adds J9_ARE_NO_BITS_SET(resolveFlags, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE), so when callers request no constant-pool update (e.g. JCL ConstantPool queries), the entry is still mutated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-909 fits because the cached constant-pool entry is a critical resource that must be initialized by the proper class-initialization path; prematurely populating it bypasses that initialization, leaving the resource in an uninitialized/invalid state. This is distinct from a mere race or null dereference: the missing constraint (flag check) causes a resource to be used before its required initialization.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the resolution routine updates the shared constant-pool cache entry even when the caller explicitly forbids CP updates. Trigger: a JCL ConstantPool API call resolves a virtual method reference with J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE set, causing methodIndexAndArgCount to be pre-populated. Consequence: later use of the cached entry skips class initialization, allowing static access without running the initializer and observation of uninitialized values.

used is the Leaky-Bucket algorithm. It allows for a burst of messages, but
limits them after a specified amount of messages within a time frame.

Only _put_page_type() does the necessary cleanup, and hence not all
domain pages can be released during guest cleanup (leaving around
zombie domains) if we get this wrong.

This is XSA-242.

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service (memory leak) because reference counts are mishandled.

code_evidence: The loop reads type_info into x (line 5) and unconditionally subtracts 1 | PGT_locked (line 6), clearing the locked bit and decrementing the type count in one cmpxchg (line 7). No check prevents the count field from reaching zero, so page_unlock() can drop the last type reference without the cleanup that _put_page_type() performs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the reference-counted page resource is not released after its effective lifetime ends: the last reference is dropped via a path that skips required cleanup, causing a memory leak and DoS. This is a missing-release flaw, not merely a race, since the cmpxchg loop is atomic but permits an invalid zero-count transition.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: page_unlock() decrements the type reference count without ensuring a remaining reference exists, bypassing the cleanup path in _put_page_type(). Trigger: a caller invokes page_unlock() when the count is one, after which the page is neither properly freed nor cleaned up, leaving a zombie domain and leaking the page during guest cleanup.

commit_msg:
avcodec/utils: Check close before calling it

Fixes: NULL pointer dereference
Fixes: 15733/clusterfuzz-testcase-minimized-ffmpeg_AV_CODEC_ID_IDF_fuzzer-5658616977162240

Reviewed-by: Paul B Mahol <onemda@gmail.com>
Found-by: continuous fuzzing process https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz/tree/master/projects/ffmpeg
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -483,7 +483,7 @@
 
     return ret;
 free_and_end:
-    if (avctx->codec &&
+    if (avctx->codec && avctx->codec->close &&
         (codec_init_ok ||
          (avctx->codec->caps_internal & FF_CODEC_CAP_INIT_CLEANUP)))
         avctx->codec->close(avctx);
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (avctx->codec &&'], 'added_lines': ['    if (avctx->codec && avctx->codec->close &&']}
description: In FFmpeg before 4.2, avcodec_open2 in libavcodec/utils.c allows a NULL pointer dereference and possibly unspecified other impact when there is no valid close function pointer.

code_evidence: At the free_and_end cleanup label, the guard checks only avctx->codec and the init-ok/caps condition, then unconditionally calls avctx->codec->close(avctx). There is no check that the codec's close function pointer is non-NULL before it is invoked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly dereferences avctx->codec->close without verifying it is non-NULL, matching CWE-476's definition of calling through a pointer expected to be valid but NULL. This is a null-pointer call, not a missing-return-value or use-after-free issue.

evidence_lines.code:
free_and_end:
if (avctx->codec &&
(codec_init_ok ||
(avctx->codec->caps_internal & FF_CODEC_CAP_INIT_CLEANUP)))
avctx->codec->close(avctx);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cleanup path assumes every codec provides a close callback. When a codec lacks a close function pointer and initialization reaches free_and_end (e.g., via an init failure or cleanup-cap flag), the call dereferences a NULL function pointer. Trigger: codec without close plus an error path into free_and_end. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash (DoS).

description: An integer overflow issue was discovered in ImageMagick's ExportIndexQuantum() function in MagickCore/quantum-export.c. Function calls to GetPixelIndex() could result in values outside the range of representable for the 'unsigned char'. When ImageMagick processes a crafted pdf file, this could lead to an undefined behaviour or a crash.

code_evidence: Index values are read via *indexes++ and cast to unsigned char without a prior range check; the patch's added (ssize_t) casts indicate the value can exceed the unsigned char range.

GetPixelIndex(indexes+x) results are passed to PopCharPixel/PopShortPixel/PopLongPixel via narrowing casts to unsigned char, unsigned short, and unsigned int, again without validating the returned index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is a narrowing integer conversion where the value is assumed to fit the target type but may exceed it, producing wraparound/truncation—matching CWE-190 (Integer Overflow or Wraparound). It is distinct from an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the unsafe operation is the arithmetic/conversion, not the array access itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Index values from the colormap/index buffer are narrowed to fixed-width integer types (unsigned char, unsigned short, unsigned int) without bounds validation. When a crafted PDF produces index values outside the representable range, the conversion wraps/truncates, yielding an unexpected pixel value that can drive undefined behavior or a crash during export.

commit_msg:
af_key: add __GFP_ZERO flag for compose_sadb_supported in function pfkey_register

Add __GFP_ZERO flag for compose_sadb_supported in function pfkey_register
to initialize the buffer of supp_skb to fix a kernel-info-leak issue.
1) Function pfkey_register calls compose_sadb_supported to request
a sk_buff. 2) compose_sadb_supported calls alloc_sbk to allocate
a sk_buff, but it doesn't zero it. 3) If auth_len is greater 0, then
compose_sadb_supported treats the memory as a struct sadb_supported and
begins to initialize. But it just initializes the field sadb_supported_len
and field sadb_supported_exttype without field sadb_supported_reserved.

Reported-by: TCS Robot <tcs_robot@tencent.com>
Signed-off-by: Haimin Zhang <tcs_kernel@tencent.com>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsupp_skb = compose_sadb_supported(hdr, GFP_KERNEL);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsupp_skb = compose_sadb_supported(hdr, GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_ZERO);']}
description: A vulnerability was found in the pfkey_register function in net/key/af_key.c in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local, unprivileged user to gain access to kernel memory, leading to a system crash or a leak of internal kernel information.

code_evidence: Line 13 allocates supp_skb via compose_sadb_supported with GFP_KERNEL, so the buffer is not zeroed; the returned skb's data may contain uninitialized kernel heap memory. Lines 19-20 then broadcast this skb to registered pfkey sockets and the requesting socket, exposing the buffer contents to user space. The failure check at 14-18 only handles allocation failure, not initialization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly causes disclosure of uninitialized kernel memory to an unauthorized local user via the broadcast of supp_skb, which matches CWE-200's exposure of sensitive information. The underlying allocation flaw could also be framed as uninitialized-memory use, but the demonstrated impact here is information exposure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reply skb is allocated without zeroing and compose_sadb_supported leaves reserved padding bytes uninitialized. Trigger: a local unprivileged user sends a SADB_REGISTER message with a valid satype, causing pfkey_register to build and broadcast the partially initialized buffer. Consequence: uninitialized kernel heap contents are copied to user-accessible pfkey sockets, leaking kernel memory (CWE-200).

commit_msg:
make_mmu_pages_available() must be called with mmu_lock held for write.
However, if the TDP MMU is used, it will be called with mmu_lock held for
read.
This function does nothing unless shadow pages are used, so there is no
race unless nested TDP is used.
Since nested TDP uses shadow pages, old shadow pages may be zapped by this
function even when the TDP MMU is enabled.
Since shadow pages are never allocated by kvm_tdp_mmu_map(), a race
condition can be avoided by not calling make_mmu_pages_available() if the
TDP MMU is currently in use.

I encountered this when repeatedly starting and stopping nested VM.
It can be artificially caused by allocating a large number of nested TDP
SPTEs.

For example, the following BUG and general protection fault are caused in
the host kernel.

pte_list_remove: 00000000cd54fc10 many->many
------------[ cut here ]------------
kernel BUG at arch/x86/kvm/mmu/mmu.c:963!
invalid opcode: 0000 [#1] PREEMPT SMP NOPTI
RIP: 0010:pte_list_remove.cold+0x16/0x48 [kvm]
Call Trace:

CVE: CVE-2022-45869
Fixes: a2855afc7ee8 ("KVM: x86/mmu: Allow parallel page faults for the TDP MMU")
Signed-off-by: Kazuki Takiguchi <takiguchi.kazuki171@gmail.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tr = make_mmu_pages_available(vcpu);', '\tif (r)', '\t\tgoto out_unlock;', '', '\tif (is_tdp_mmu_fault)', '\telse'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (is_tdp_mmu_fault) {', '\t} else {', '\t\tr = make_mmu_pages_available(vcpu);', '\t\tif (r)', '\t\t\tgoto out_unlock;', '\t}']}
description: A race condition in the x86 KVM subsystem in the Linux kernel through 6.1-rc6 allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host OS crash or host OS memory corruption) when nested virtualisation and the TDP MMU are enabled.

code_evidence: When is_tdp_mmu_fault is true, mmu_lock is taken only via read_lock (line 26); the write_lock path (line 28) is used only for the non-TDP-MMU case.

make_mmu_pages_available() is invoked unconditionally at line 31, before the is_tdp_mmu_fault branch selects kvm_tdp_mmu_map() or __direct_map(). It can zap shadow pages, which requires exclusive write ownership of mmu_lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function executes a shared-resource mutation under an insufficient lock mode, allowing an interfering concurrent sequence to access the same state—exactly CWE-362. It is not merely an improper-lock-type defect in isolation; the supported consequence is a race yielding host DoS/memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is calling make_mmu_pages_available(), which mutates shared shadow-page structures, while the TDP MMU path holds mmu_lock only for read, so exclusivity/atomicity is not enforced. A concurrent page-fault path can modify the same page lists during the zap, producing the observed BUG and general-protection fault and a host crash; the trigger requires nested TDP with shadow pages present.
