commit_msg:
x86/shadow: account for log-dirty mode when pre-allocating

Pre-allocation is intended to ensure that in the course of constructing
or updating shadows there won't be any risk of just made shadows or
shadows being acted upon can disappear under our feet. The amount of
pages pre-allocated then, however, needs to account for all possible
subsequent allocations. While the use in sh_page_fault() accounts for
all shadows which may need making, so far it didn't account for
allocations coming from log-dirty tracking (which piggybacks onto the
P2M allocation functions).

Since shadow_prealloc() takes a count of shadows (or other data
structures) rather than a count of pages, putting the adjustment at the
call site of this function won't work very well: We simply can't express
the correct count that way in all cases. Instead take care of this in
the function itself, by "snooping" for L1 type requests. (While not
applicable right now, future new request sites of L1 tables would then
also be covered right away.)

It is relevant to note here that pre-allocations like the one done from
shadow_alloc_p2m_page() are benign when they fall in the "scope" of an
earlier pre-alloc which already included that count: The inner call will
simply find enough pages available then; it'll bail right away.

This is CVE-2022-42332 / XSA-427.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    BUILD_BUG_ON(paging_logdirty_levels() != 4);']}
description: x86 shadow plus log-dirty mode use-after-free In environments where host assisted address translation is necessary but Hardware Assisted Paging (HAP) is unavailable, Xen will run guests in so called shadow mode. Shadow mode maintains a pool of memory used for both shadow page tables as well as auxiliary data structures. To migrate or snapshot guests, Xen additionally runs them in so called log-dirty mode. The data structures needed by the log-dirty tracking are part of aformentioned auxiliary data. In order to keep error handling efforts within reasonable bounds, for operations which may require memory allocations shadow mode logic ensures up front that enough memory is available for the worst case requirements. Unfortunately, while page table memory is properly accounted for on the code path requiring the potential establishing of new shadows, demands by the log-dirty infrastructure were not taken into consideration. As a result, just established shadow page tables could be freed again immediately, while other code is still accessing them on the assumption that they would remain allocated.

code_evidence: paging_mark_pfn_dirty allocates log-dirty nodes via paging_new_log_dirty_node()/paging_new_log_dirty_leaf() at lines 19,26,33,40 and then maps and writes them (e.g. l4[i4], l3[i3], l2[i2], __test_and_set_bit). These allocations occur inside the shadow/log-dirty path and depend on pre-allocated pools; if insufficient pages were reserved by shadow_prealloc(), a just-created shadow table can be freed while still referenced. The added BUILD_BUG_ON itself is not a memory operation, but the surrounding allocation/mapping sequence is the site where the unaccounted log-dirty allocations occur.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described consequence is that shadow page tables are freed while other code still holds references to them and continues to use them, which is exactly CWE-416 use-after-free. The missing pre-allocation accounting is the cause; the stale reference to freed shadow memory is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: shadow_prealloc() did not account for pages needed by log-dirty allocations triggered during shadow construction, so the pre-allocated pool could be exhausted. Trigger: a shadow page fault that also marks PFNs dirty causes paging_mark_pfn_dirty to allocate nodes while shadows are live. Consequence: shadows just established can be freed and later referenced, yielding use-after-free (modify/read freed memory, crash).

description: A vulnerability, which was classified as problematic, was found in Linux Kernel. This affects the function tcp_getsockopt/tcp_setsockopt of the component TCP Handler. The manipulation leads to race condition. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier VDB-211089 was assigned to this vulnerability.

commit_msg:
nfsd: stricter decoding of write-like NFSv2/v3 ops

The NFSv2/v3 code does not systematically check whether we decode past
the end of the buffer.  This generally appears to be harmless, but there
are a few places where we do arithmetic on the pointers involved and
don't account for the possibility that a length could be negative.  Add
checks to catch these.

Reported-by: Tuomas Haanpää <thaan@synopsys.com>
Reported-by: Ari Kauppi <ari@synopsys.com>
Reviewed-by: NeilBrown <neilb@suse.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: J. Bruce Fields <bfields@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif ((void *)p > head->iov_base + head->iov_len)', '\t\treturn 0;']}
description: The NFSv2 and NFSv3 server implementations in the Linux kernel through 4.10.13 lack certain checks for the end of a buffer, which allows remote attackers to trigger pointer-arithmetic errors or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted requests, related to fs/nfsd/nfs3xdr.c and fs/nfsd/nfsxdr.c.

code_evidence: Line 15 stores the attacker-controlled XDR length in args->len and len, but the code does not first verify that the three preceding ntohl reads advanced p within head's buffer. Line 18 computes hdr as a pointer difference; if p has already advanced past head->iov_base + head->iov_len, hdr exceeds head->iov_len, so the dlen expression at line 19 underflows (unsigned) and the bounds check at line 20 passes. Line 27 then computes head->iov_len - hdr, which also underflows, producing an oversized rq_vec[0].iov_len used for subsequent buffer operations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs pointer arithmetic and buffer-length operations without ensuring decoded pointers remain within the buffer, leading to out-of-bounds memory access, which matches CWE-119. This is a buffer-bounds restriction failure rather than a mere integer overflow, though the underflow is the enabling mechanism.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing end-of-buffer validation after decoding the write header fields, so p may point beyond the received buffer. Trigger: a crafted short NFSv3 WRITE request whose decoded header overruns head. The unsigned subtraction then wraps, defeating the length check and yielding an out-of-bounds iov span, allowing reads/writes outside the intended buffer.

commit_msg:
When the inode is in extent format, it can't have more extents that
fit in the inode fork. We don't currenty check this, and so this
corruption goes unnoticed by the inode verifiers. This can lead to
crashes operating on invalid in-memory structures.

Attempts to access such a inode will now error out in the verifier
rather than allowing modification operations to proceed.

Reported-by: Wen Xu <wen.xu@gatech.edu>
Signed-off-by: Dave Chinner <dchinner@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>
[darrick: fix a typedef, add some braces and breaks to shut up compiler warnings]
Signed-off-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>

description: An issue was discovered in fs/xfs/libxfs/xfs_inode_buf.c in the Linux kernel through 4.17.3. A denial of service (memory corruption and BUG) can occur for a corrupted xfs image upon encountering an inode that is in extent format, but has more extents than fit in the inode fork.

code_evidence: The inode fork format switch for S_IFREG/S_IFLNK/S_IFDIR accepts XFS_DINODE_FMT_EXTENTS and XFS_DINODE_FMT_BTREE without checking that di_nextents fits within the inode fork (XFS_DFORK_DSIZE); only the LOCAL case bounds di_size and di_nextents.

The generic extent check compares di_nextents + di_anextents against di_nblocks, a block count, not against the fork capacity, so an extent-format inode with more extents than the fork can hold passes verification.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Accepting an extent count exceeding the fork's capacity lets downstream code index/write beyond the inode fork buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is distinct from a mere read overrun because subsequent modification operations write into the invalid structure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the verifier fails to constrain di_nextents against the inode fork size for extent/btree formats. Trigger: a corrupted xfs image whose extent-format inode declares more extents than fit in the fork. Consequence: later in-memory operations on the oversized extent array write past the fork buffer, causing memory corruption and a BUG/crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/vtx: Fix the checking for unknown/invalid MSR_DEBUGCTL bits

The VPMU_MODE_OFF early-exit in vpmu_do_wrmsr() introduced by c/s
11fe998e56 bypasses all reserved bit checking in the general case.  As a
result, a guest can enable BTS when it shouldn't be permitted to, and
lock up the entire host.

With vPMU active (not a security supported configuration, but useful for
debugging), the reserved bit checking in broken, caused by the original
BTS changeset 1a8aa75ed.

From a correctness standpoint, it is not possible to have two different
pieces of code responsible for different parts of value checking, if
there isn't an accumulation of bits which have been checked.  A
practical upshot of this is that a guest can set any value it
wishes (usually resulting in a vmentry failure for bad guest state).

Therefore, fix this by implementing all the reserved bit checking in the
main MSR_DEBUGCTL block, and removing all handling of DEBUGCTL from the
vPMU MSR logic.

This is XSA-269.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x. The DEBUGCTL MSR contains several debugging features, some of which virtualise cleanly, but some do not. In particular, Branch Trace Store is not virtualised by the processor, and software has to be careful to configure it suitably not to lock up the core. As a result, it must only be available to fully trusted guests. Unfortunately, in the case that vPMU is disabled, all value checking was skipped, allowing the guest to choose any MSR_DEBUGCTL setting it likes. A malicious or buggy guest administrator (on Intel x86 HVM or PVH) can lock up the entire host, causing a Denial of Service.

code_evidence: The MSR_IA32_DEBUGCTLMSR case builds a 'supported' mask of LBR|BTF (+RTM if host supports it). Only when msr_content contains bits outside this mask does it call vpmu_do_wrmsr(); if that helper returns nonzero it breaks out of the switch, otherwise execution falls through to __vmwrite(GUEST_IA32_DEBUGCTL, msr_content) at line 92, writing the unchecked value. Thus guest-chosen DEBUGCTL bits (e.g. BTS) are accepted when vPMU is off because the vpmu_do_wrmsr early-exit bypasses the reserved-bit rejection.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a privilege/feature gate check on guest MSR writes but does it incorrectly: the allowlist check is bypassed, granting the guest access to DEBUGCTL features it is not authorized to use. This is incorrect authorization of a restricted operation, matching CWE-863.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reserved-bit validation for MSR_IA32_DEBUGCTLMSR is delegated to vpmu_do_wrmsr() and skipped when vPMU is disabled, so the guest-controlled msr_content is written to GUEST_IA32_DEBUGCTL without a complete allowlist check. Trigger: a guest writes DEBUGCTL with bits such as BTS. Consequence: unvalidated debug state is accepted, enabling a host lockup (DoS).

commit_msg: Prevent HTTP pipelining which Crow doesn't support.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                  parser_.clear();']}
description: HTTP applications (servers) based on Crow through 1.0+4 may allow a Use-After-Free and code execution when HTTP pipelining is used. The HTTP parser supports HTTP pipelining, but the asynchronous Connection layer is unaware of HTTP pipelining. Specifically, the Connection layer is unaware that it has begun processing a later request before it has finished processing an earlier request.

code_evidence: The async_write completion handler captures the Connection object by reference (&) and, after the write completes, clears res and res_body_copy_ and only then checks ec; the handler retains and mutates this connection state without resetting parser state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the weakness is reuse of freed connection/parser state after a prior request completes; the fix adds parser_.clear() to reset that state. This is use-after-free rather than a simple race, since the stale state is dereferenced after release.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write completion path reuses connection/parser state across pipelined requests without clearing the parser, so a later request can be processed while the earlier request's state is still live. Trigger: HTTP pipelining on a Crow server. Consequence: the Connection layer can operate on state already released for a prior request, yielding a use-after-free that may allow code execution.

commit_msg:
BUG/CRITICAL: http_ana: Fix parsing of malformed cookies which start by a delimiter

When client-side or server-side cookies are parsed, HAProxy enters in an
infinite loop if a Cookie/Set-Cookie header value starts by a delimiter (a colon
or a semicolon). Depending on the operating system, the service may become
degraded, unresponsive, or may trigger haproxy's watchdog causing a service stop
or automatic restart.

To fix this bug, in the loop parsing the attributes, we must be sure to always
skip delimiters once the first attribute-value pair was parsed, empty or
not. The credit for the fix goes to Olivier.

CVE-2019-14241 was assigned to this bug. This patch fixes the Github issue #181.

This patch must be backported to 2.0 and 1.9. However, the patch will have to be
adapted.

description: HAProxy through 2.0.2 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (ha_panic) via vectors related to htx_manage_client_side_cookies in proto_htx.c.

code_evidence: The outer header loop calls http_find_header at line 12, and the inner for-loop at line 17 advances via 'prev = next' (line 191). att_beg starts at prev (line 18); line 19 increments it only when prev > hdr_beg, so for the first attribute att_beg stays at prev. Line 191 sets att_beg = next, but next comes from parsing at lines 24-41 and may remain equal to prev when the value starts with a delimiter, so prev does not advance.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the for-loop at line 17 cannot reach its exit condition when prev is not advanced, producing an unbounded iteration. This is a loop-progress defect, not merely a parsing error; the parsing flaw is the trigger that makes the loop exit unreachable.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop's progress depends on next advancing past prev, but when a Cookie value begins with a delimiter, the attribute scan sets next back to the same position, so 'prev = next' never moves forward. Trigger: a malformed Cookie/Set-Cookie header whose value starts with ':' or ';'. Consequence: infinite loop causing CPU exhaustion and potential ha_panic/watchdog restart (DoS).

commit_msg:
basic/user-util: always use base 10 for user/group numbers

We would parse numbers with base prefixes as user identifiers. For example,
"0x2b3bfa0" would be interpreted as UID==45334432 and "01750" would be
interpreted as UID==1000. This parsing was used also in cases where either a
user/group name or number may be specified. This means that names like
0x2b3bfa0 would be ambiguous: they are a valid user name according to our
documented relaxed rules, but they would also be parsed as numeric uids.

This behaviour is definitely not expected by users, since tools generally only
accept decimal numbers (e.g. id, getent passwd), while other tools only accept
user names and thus will interpret such strings as user names without even
attempting to convert them to numbers (su, ssh). So let's follow suit and only
accept numbers in decimal notation. Effectively this means that we will reject
such strings as a username/uid/groupname/gid where strict mode is used, and try
to look up a user/group with such a name in relaxed mode.

Since the function changed is fairly low-level and fairly widely used, this
affects multiple tools: loginctl show-user/enable-linger/disable-linger foo',
the third argument in sysusers.d, fourth and fifth arguments in tmpfiles.d,
etc.

Fixes #15985.

commit_msg:
kafka: lz4: free the composite tvb only once

Try to clean up the composite tvb handling during lz4 decompression.

If we detect an error straight away before doing any lz4 decompression, we
don't allocate a composite tvb at all. The comments in the tvb code say
explicitly that we must not call tvb_new_composite() without adding at
least one piece of data.

If we start decompressing and run into problems after creating the
composite tvb and linking it to the packet's main tvb, we must not free
the composite tvb manually. The epan library will do this for us when
dissection of the packet is finished.

While at it, make sure that we always finalize the composite tvb if we

description: In Wireshark 3.2.0 to 3.2.5, the Kafka protocol dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-kafka.c by avoiding a double free during LZ4 decompression.

code_evidence: Line 9 unconditionally creates a composite tvb; if an error occurs before any data is appended (lines 22-28, 43-44, 50-51), the goto end path reaches line 72-74 and frees the composite tvb with tvb_free_chain. On the success path, lines 65-68 finalize the composite, assign it to *decompressed_tvb (linking it to the packet's main tvb), and set composite_tvb to NULL so the end cleanup does not free it.

commit_msg:
Currently, if you bind the socket to something like:
        servaddr.sin6_family = AF_INET6;
        servaddr.sin6_port = htons(0);
        servaddr.sin6_scope_id = 0;
        inet_pton(AF_INET6, "::1", &servaddr.sin6_addr);

And then request a connect to:
        connaddr.sin6_family = AF_INET6;
        connaddr.sin6_port = htons(20000);
        connaddr.sin6_scope_id = if_nametoindex("lo");
        inet_pton(AF_INET6, "fe88::1", &connaddr.sin6_addr);

What the stack does is:
 - bind the socket
 - create a new asoc
 - to handle the connect
   - copy the addresses that can be used for the given scope
   - try to connect

But the copy returns 0 addresses, and the effect is that it ends up
trying to connect as if the socket wasn't bound, which is not the
desired behavior. This unexpected behavior also allows KASLR leaks
through SCTP diag interface.

The fix here then is, if when trying to copy the addresses that can
be used for the scope used in connect() it returns 0 addresses, bail
out. This is what TCP does with a similar reproducer.

Reported-by: Pietro Borrello <borrello@diag.uniroma1.it>
Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
Signed-off-by: Marcelo Ricardo Leitner <marcelo.leitner@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/9fcd182f1099f86c6661f3717f63712ddd1c676c.1674496737.git.marcelo.leitner@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* If somehow no addresses were found that can be used with this', "\t * scope, it's an error.", '\t */', '\tif (list_empty(&dest->address_list))', '\t\terror = -ENETUNREACH;', '']}
description: A memory leak flaw was found in the Linux kernel's Stream Control Transmission Protocol. This issue may occur when a user starts a malicious networking service and someone connects to this service. This could allow a local user to starve resources, causing a denial of service.

code_evidence: The loop copies each source address into dest via sctp_copy_one_addr, which may allocate entries in dest->address_list; on error it jumps to out.
If dest->address_list is empty after the first pass and scope is global, a second pass retries with SCTP_SCOPE_LINK, allocating more entries; on error it jumps to out.
At out, cleanup occurs only when error is nonzero, so a zero-address result is treated as success and dest may remain in an inconsistent state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fix adds an explicit empty-list check setting -ENETUNREACH so cleanup runs; the pre-fix function failed to recognize the unpopulated state and release/handle associated resources, matching missing memory release after effective lifetime.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When no source address matches the requested scope, the copy loops complete without error and dest->address_list stays empty, yet the function returns success. The caller proceeds to connect as if the socket were unbound, leaving state unaccounted for and enabling resource exhaustion/KASLR leak via the SCTP diag interface.

description: An issue was discovered in OpenCV before 4.1.1. There is a NULL pointer dereference in the function cv::XMLParser::parse at modules/core/src/persistence.cpp.

After the recursive call at line 46 or parseBase64/skipSpaces at lines 49-50, the returned pointer is passed directly to parseTag at line 52 with no validation, so a NULL return from skipSpaces or a parse helper flows into subsequent dereferences.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences pointers that may be NULL, directly matching CWE-476's definition of dereferencing a pointer expected to be valid but NULL. This is not an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) since the flaw is the missing NULL check rather than an index beyond allocation bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: parseValue assumes ptr and pointers returned by skipSpaces/parseBase64/parseTag are non-NULL and dereferences them (lines 9, 12, 16, 18). Trigger: malformed XML input causing skipSpaces or an inner parse to return NULL, or a NULL ptr passed in. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash (DoS), matching the known OpenCV persistence parse issue.

Add the check for the return value of kzalloc in order to avoid
NULL pointer dereference.

Fixes: 6e977eaa8280 ("nvmem: brcm_nvram: parse NVRAM content into NVMEM cells")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jiasheng Jiang <jiasheng@iscas.ac.cn>
Signed-off-by: Srinivas Kandagatla <srinivas.kandagatla@linaro.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230127104015.23839-2-srinivas.kandagatla@linaro.org
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!data)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel brcm_nvram_parse in drivers/nvmem/brcm_nvram.c. Lacks for the check of the return value of kzalloc() can cause the NULL Pointer Dereference.

code_evidence: kzalloc(len, GFP_KERNEL) returns a pointer assigned to data with no NULL check; the next statements immediately pass data to memcpy_fromio and write data[len - 1] = '\0'.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences an allocation pointer expected to be valid while it can be NULL, matching CWE-476 NULL Pointer Dereference. This is a missing-check cause, not a separate memory-corruption weakness; the unchecked NULL is the direct defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation result in data is used without validating it. Trigger: kzalloc fails (e.g., len is large or memory is exhausted), returning NULL. Consequence: memcpy_fromio and the subsequent write dereference NULL, causing a kernel crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
Fix vi_pci_read null vc_cfgread function pointer dereference (GHSL-2021-054)

This is backport of what is done in bhyve

Signed-off-by: Frederic Dalleau <frederic.dalleau@docker.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\terror = (*vc->vc_cfgread)(DEV_SOFTC(vs), ((int) newoff), size, &value);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (vc->vc_cfgread != NULL)', '\t\t\terror = (*vc->vc_cfgread)(DEV_SOFTC(vs), ((int) newoff), size, &value);', '\t\telse', '\t\t\terror = 0;']}
description: HyperKit is a toolkit for embedding hypervisor capabilities in an application. In versions 0.20210107 and prior of HyperKit, `virtio.c` has is a call to `vc_cfgread` that does not check for null which when called makes the host crash. This issue may lead to a guest crashing the host causing a denial of service. This issue is fixed in commit df0e46c7dbfd81a957d85e449ba41b52f6f7beb4.

code_evidence: When guest-supplied offset is at or beyond virtio_config_size, newoff is computed and bounds-checked against max, then vc->vc_cfgread is invoked unconditionally via (*vc->vc_cfgread)(...). No NULL check precedes this indirect call, so a virtio_consts whose vc_cfgread is NULL causes a null function-pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function invokes a function pointer expected to be valid but which may be NULL, and the patch adds a NULL guard. This is a NULL dereference rather than a type-confusion or out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes vc->vc_cfgread is always a valid callback and calls it without a NULL check. Trigger: a guest PCI config read with an offset in the device-specific config region on a virtio device whose vc_cfgread is unset. Consequence: the host dereferences NULL and crashes, causing denial of service.

Trigger: a caller supplies a format string and/or arguments whose expansion exceeds 2048 bytes. Consequence: the write runs past the end of szMsg, corrupting adjacent stack memory and potentially enabling crashes or code execution.

'hwname' is malloced in hwsim_new_radio_nl() and should be freed

description: Memory leak in the hwsim_new_radio_nl function in drivers/net/wireless/mac80211_hwsim.c in the Linux kernel through 4.15.9 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering an out-of-array error case.

commit_msg:
scsi/lsi53c895a: really fix use-after-free in lsi_do_msgout (CVE-2022-0216)

Set current_req to NULL, not current_req->req, to prevent reusing a free'd
buffer in case of repeated SCSI cancel requests.  Also apply the fix to
CLEAR QUEUE and BUS DEVICE RESET messages as well, since they also cancel
the request.

Thanks to Alexander Bulekov for providing a reproducer.

Fixes: CVE-2022-0216
Resolves: https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/issues/972
Signed-off-by: Mauro Matteo Cascella <mcascell@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Alexander Bulekov <alxndr@bu.edu>
Message-Id: <20220711123316.421279-1-mcascell@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                current_req->req = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['                current_req = NULL;', '                current_req = NULL;']}
description: A use-after-free vulnerability was found in the LSI53C895A SCSI Host Bus Adapter emulation of QEMU. The flaw occurs while processing repeated messages to cancel the current SCSI request via the lsi_do_msgout function. This flaw allows a malicious privileged user within the guest to crash the QEMU process on the host, resulting in a denial of service.

code_evidence: On the ABORT message path, current_req->req is cancelled and then only the req field is cleared, leaving current_req itself cached; a later message reuses this stale request object.
On the CLEAR QUEUE / BUS DEVICE RESET path, s->current->req is cancelled but current_req is not cleared, so the cached pointer remains usable after cancellation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function cancels a request and then continues to reference the cached request object through current_req, which is exactly reuse of freed memory (CWE-416). The fix sets current_req to NULL to invalidate the dangling pointer; a mere null-check omission would be a different weakness, but here the freed object is retained and reused.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: after scsi_req_cancel frees the underlying request, the cached current_req pointer is not invalidated (only current_req->req is set NULL, or nothing at all). Trigger: repeated SCSI cancel/abort, CLEAR QUEUE or BUS DEVICE RESET messages that re-enter the message loop with the stale current_req. Consequence: reuse of freed memory, causing host QEMU crash/denial of service.

commit_msg: Catch SGI buffer overruns
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int expandrow(UINT8* dest, UINT8* src, int n, int z)'], 'added_lines': ['static int expandrow(UINT8* dest, UINT8* src, int n, int z, int xsize)', '        if (count > xsize) {', '            return -1;', '        }']}
description: libImaging/SgiRleDecode.c in Pillow before 6.2.2 has an SGI buffer overflow.

code_evidence: count is derived from the RLE run-length byte (pixel & RLE_MAX_RUN) with no bound against the destination size; when RLE_COPY_FLAG is set, the loop writes *dest = *src++ and advances dest += z for each count, so a run longer than the row/destination can write past dest.
In the else branch a single pixel is expanded count times with *dest = pixel and dest += z, again with no check that count fits the destination buffer, producing the same unbounded write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the function copies/expands input data into dest without checking that the input run length is smaller than the destination, a classic unchecked buffer copy leading to out-of-bounds writes; it is a write overflow, not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoded run length count is used directly to drive writes into dest without verifying it against the destination/xsize bound. Trigger: a crafted SGI RLE stream whose run-length byte encodes a count exceeding the row width. Consequence: writes past the end of the destination buffer, causing memory corruption (and potential code execution or crash).

As the possible failure of the allocation, kmemdup() may return NULL
pointer.
Therefore, it should be better to check the 'props2' in order to prevent
the dereference of NULL pointer.

Fixes: 3a87177eb141 ("drm/amdkfd: Add topology support for dGPUs")
Signed-off-by: Jiasheng Jiang <jiasheng@iscas.ac.cn>
Reviewed-by: Felix Kuehling <Felix.Kuehling@amd.com>
Signed-off-by: Felix Kuehling <Felix.Kuehling@amd.com>

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.16-rc6. kfd_parse_subtype_iolink in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/amdkfd/kfd_crat.c lacks check of the return value of kmemdup().

code_evidence: Line 44 calls kmemdup(props, sizeof(*props2), GFP_KERNEL) and assigns the result to props2 without any NULL check. Lines 45-47 immediately dereference props2 to set node_from, node_to and kobj, and lines 48-50 use it in counters and list_add_tail. This is unchecked-return-value leading to a NULL dereference, distinct from a simple missing NULL check only in that the failure signal is the unchecked return.

commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20569)

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tprivate = READ_ONCE(table->private); /* Address dependency. */'], 'added_lines': ['\tprivate = rcu_access_pointer(table->private);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: The function disables bottom halves and enters the per-CPU sequence counter with xt_write_recseq_begin() at [22,23], then loads table->private into the local private pointer at [24]. The subsequent dereferences private->entries and private->jumpstack[cpu] at [26,27] use whatever pointer value was loaded; the source uses READ_ONCE, which only guarantees the load is not torn, not that it is ordered before the sequence-counter check performed by the concurrent replacement thread.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the packet path retains and dereferences private->entries/jumpstack after the replacement thread can free that table info; the weakness is use of freed memory, not merely a race. The change to rcu_access_pointer is the intended ordering fix, confirming the lifetime hazard.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the new table->private assignment in the replacement path and the sequence-counter check are not ordered, so the packet path can observe an old table while the replacement thread frees it. Trigger: concurrent iptables rule replacement with CAP_NET_ADMIN while packets traverse ip6t_do_table. Consequence: use-after-free of the table info, leading to a NULL-pointer dereference crash or memory corruption in packet processing.

commit_msg:
Fix empty resource handle vulnerability.

Some ops that attempt to extract a resource handle from user input
can lead to nullptr dereferences.  This returns an error in such
a case.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 445571938
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (tensor->NumElements() == 0) {', '      return errors::InvalidArgument("Empty resource handle");', '    }']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, multiple TensorFlow operations misbehave in eager mode when the resource handle provided to them is invalid. In graph mode, it would have been impossible to perform these API calls, but migration to TF 2.x eager mode opened up this vulnerability. If the resource handle is empty, then a reference is bound to a null pointer inside TensorFlow codebase (various codepaths). This is undefined behavior. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: For a LOCAL DT_RESOURCE handle, the code fetches the backing Tensor via tensor_handle->Tensor(&tensor) and immediately dereferences it at line 12 (tensor->flat<ResourceHandle>()(0)) without checking that the resource tensor actually contains an element.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes a caller-provided resource handle and fails to validate that it is non-empty before indexing it, which is improper validation of input properties (size) required for safe processing — matching CWE-20. The patch adds exactly this emptiness check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The resource handle is user-supplied input; an empty resource tensor yields NumElements()==0, so flat<ResourceHandle>()(0) indexes a zero-length buffer, binding a reference to a null/invalid pointer. Trigger is an eager-mode op given an empty resource handle; consequence is undefined behavior (nullptr dereference) rather than a clean error.

commit_msg:
usb: max-3421: Prevent corruption of freed memory

The MAX-3421 USB driver remembers the state of the USB toggles for a
device/endpoint. To save SPI writes, this was only done when a new
device/endpoint was being used. Unfortunately, if the old device was
removed, this would cause writes to freed memory.

To fix this, a simpler scheme is used. The toggles are read from
hardware when a URB is completed, and the toggles are always written to
hardware when any URB transaction is started. This will cause a few more
SPI transactions, but no causes kernel panics.

Fixes: 2d53139f3162 ("Add support for using a MAX3421E chip as a host driver.")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Mark Tomlinson <mark.tomlinson@alliedtelesis.co.nz>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210625031456.8632-1-mark.tomlinson@alliedtelesis.co.nz
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint epnum, force_toggles = 0;', '\t\t\tforce_toggles = 1;', '\tmax3421_set_address(hcd, urb->dev, epnum, force_toggles);'], 'added_lines': ['\tint epnum;', '\tmax3421_set_address(hcd, urb->dev, epnum);']}
description: drivers/usb/host/max3421-hcd.c in the Linux kernel before 5.13.6 allows physically proximate attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and panic) by removing a MAX-3421 USB device in certain situations.

code_evidence: Line 8 declares the stale-state flag force_toggles, which is set from a USB toggle cache rather than read from hardware.

After selecting curr_urb, lines 79-93 derive epnum from urb->ep, set toggles and force_toggles for control endpoints, drop the lock, then pass urb->dev and force_toggles into max3421_set_address, which writes the remembered toggle state to hardware.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly supports CWE-416: it reads and forwards cached device/toggle state (force_toggles, urb->dev) to hardware after the lock is dropped, without revalidating that the referenced device still exists. This is use-after-free rather than a plain null dereference or double free, since the freed object is referenced, not allocated or freed again.

evidence_lines.code: int epnum, force_toggles = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The driver caches per-device/endpoint toggle state and only refreshes it when a new endpoint is first used. If the old device is removed while its cached state is retained, the cached state points at freed device memory; the next URB start reuses it in max3421_set_address, causing a use-after-free and kernel panic. Root cause is reuse of a stale cached reference after device teardown; the trigger is device removal during active scheduling.

commit_msg:
net: vmxnet3: fix possible NULL pointer dereference in vmxnet3_rq_cleanup()

In vmxnet3_rq_create(), when dma_alloc_coherent() fails,
vmxnet3_rq_destroy() is called. It sets rq->rx_ring[i].base to NULL. Then
vmxnet3_rq_create() returns an error to its callers mxnet3_rq_create_all()
-> vmxnet3_change_mtu(). Then vmxnet3_change_mtu() calls
vmxnet3_force_close() -> dev_close() in error handling code. And the driver
calls vmxnet3_close() -> vmxnet3_quiesce_dev() -> vmxnet3_rq_cleanup_all()
-> vmxnet3_rq_cleanup(). In vmxnet3_rq_cleanup(),
rq->rx_ring[ring_idx].base is accessed, but this variable is NULL, causing
a NULL pointer dereference.

To fix this possible bug, an if statement is added to check whether
rq->rx_ring[0].base is NULL in vmxnet3_rq_cleanup() and exit early if so.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static bool ok_csv_circular_buffer_read(ok_csv_circular_buffer *buffer, uint8_t *dst,', '                                        size_t length) {', '        const size_t readable1 = ok_csv_circular_buffer_readable(buffer);', '        if (length <= readable1) {', '            memcpy(dst, buffer->data + buffer->start, length);', '        } else {', '            const size_t readable2 = buffer->length - readable1;', '            memcpy(dst, buffer->data + buffer->start, readable1);', '            memcpy(dst + readable1, buffer->data, readable2);', '        }', '        buffer->start = (buffer->start + length) % buffer->capacity;', '        buffer->length -= length;', '        return true;'], 'added_lines': ['static bool ok_csv_circular_buffer_read(ok_csv_circular_buffer *buffer, uint8_t *dst, size_t length) {', '    ok_assert(length <= buffer->length);', '    }', '    const size_t readable_length = ok_csv_circular_buffer_readable(buffer);', '    if (length <= readable_length) {', '        memcpy(dst, buffer->data + buffer->start, length);', '        memcpy(dst, buffer->data + buffer->start, readable_length);', '        memcpy(dst + readable_length, buffer->data, length - readable_length);', '    buffer->start = (buffer->start + length) % buffer->capacity;', '    buffer->length -= length;', '    return true;']}
description: ok-file-formats through 2021-04-29 has a heap-based buffer overflow in the ok_csv_circular_buffer_read function in ok_csv.c.

code_evidence: The guard only rejects length > buffer->length; otherwise execution proceeds and returns true after writing length bytes.

readable1 is the contiguous readable count from the current start; readable2 is computed as buffer->length - readable1, not buffer->capacity - readable1, so the second segment size is derived from the logical length rather than the ring capacity.

The two memcpy calls write readable1 bytes at dst and readable2 bytes at dst+readable1, totaling buffer->length bytes into a destination sized for length; when length < buffer->length the second write exceeds the caller-provided buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs memcpy into caller-supplied dst with a computed length that can exceed the requested length, writing past the end of the intended buffer; this is CWE-787 rather than a read overrun because the overflow occurs on the destination write.

evidence_lines.code:
memcpy(dst, buffer->data + buffer->start, readable1);
memcpy(dst + readable1, buffer->data, readable2);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the wrap-around branch sizes the second copy with buffer->length - readable1 instead of capacity - readable1, and the only length check permits length < buffer->length. Trigger: a read that crosses the ring boundary with length smaller than buffer->length. Consequence: memcpy writes past dst, a heap-based out-of-bounds write.

description: A vulnerability has been found in MZ Automation libiec61850 up to 1.4 and classified as critical. This vulnerability affects unknown code of the file src/mms/iso_mms/client/mms_client_files.c of the component MMS File Services. The manipulation of the argument filename leads to path traversal. Upgrading to version 1.5 is able to address this issue. The name of the patch is 10622ba36bb3910c151348f1569f039ecdd8786f. It is recommended to upgrade the affected component. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-213556.

code_evidence: The client-supplied filename is parsed from the PDU tag 0xa0 into the fixed buffer filename via mmsMsg_parseFileName at line 17, then hasFileName is set; no validation or normalization of the name is performed before use.

When hasFileName is true, the unvalidated filename is passed directly to mmsMsg_openFile with the filestore basepath at line 41, and the same name is echoed in mmsMsg_createFileOpenResponse at lines 47-48; the open result is stored in the read state machine.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-22 fits because external input constructs a pathname intended to be confined under a restricted parent directory, and special elements are not neutralized before the file operation. The weakness is the missing pathname constraint, not merely a malformed-PDU handling bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the filename parsed from the incoming MMS request is used to open a file relative to the filestore basepath without neutralizing path elements. Trigger: a client sends a file-open request whose filename contains '../' sequences or an absolute path. Consequence: the open resolves outside the intended filestore directory, allowing read/access of unintended files (confidentiality/integrity impact).

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `ThreadPoolHandle` can be used to trigger a denial of service attack by allocating too much memory. This is because the `num_threads` argument is only checked to not be negative, but there is no upper bound on its value. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

commit_msg:
Fix segfault when attempting to convert string to float16.

To make sure this gets fixed, add test for converting string to any numeric type.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 286650886
Change-Id: I81f770ec2bbd33a863e8057ce198c679912fa8e0
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    // NOTE(nareshmodi): Is there a way to convert to C double without the', '    // intermediate Python double? This will help with ConvertOneFloat as well.', '    Safe_PyObjectPtr as_float = make_safe(PyNumber_Float(v));', '    double v_double = PyFloat_AS_DOUBLE(as_float.get());', '    *out = Eigen::half(v_double);', '', '    return nullptr;'], 'added_lines': ['    return ConvertOneFloat<Eigen::half>(v, out);']}
description: In TensorFlow before 1.15.2 and 2.0.1, converting a string (from Python) to a tf.float16 value results in a segmentation fault in eager mode as the format checks for this use case are only in the graph mode. This issue can lead to denial of service in inference/training where a malicious attacker can send a data point which contains a string instead of a tf.float16 value. Similar effects can be obtained by manipulating saved models and checkpoints whereby replacing a scalar tf.float16 value with a scalar string will trigger this issue due to automatic conversions. This can be easily reproduced by tf.constant("hello", tf.float16), if eager execution is enabled. This issue is patched in TensorFlow 1.15.1 and 2.0.1 with this vulnerability patched. TensorFlow 2.1.0 was released after we fixed the issue, thus it is not affected. Users are encouraged to switch to TensorFlow 1.15.1, 2.0.1 or 2.1.0.

code_evidence: ConvertScalar passes the untrusted PyObject* v to PyNumber_Float without checking that v is actually a numeric/float-convertible type; PyNumber_Float can fail and return NULL. The result is wrapped in make_safe and then PyFloat_AS_DOUBLE is applied unconditionally to out, so a failed conversion yields a null/invalid pointer dereference leading to a segfault.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the code accepts external Python input without validating that it has the required numeric type before processing, and this missing type check leads to a crash. It is improper input validation rather than an encoding or filtering flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function assumes the incoming Python object is convertible to float and does not validate the type or the success of PyNumber_Float. Trigger: a string (e.g. tf.constant("hello", tf.float16)) reaches this path in eager mode; PyNumber_Float fails, yet PyFloat_AS_DOUBLE dereferences the failed result. Supported consequence: crash/denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix security vulnerability with DenseBincountOp

PiperOrigin-RevId: 460826735
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(ctx,', '                xla::ShapeUtil::CompatibleIgnoringElementType(weights_shape,', '                                                              input_shape) ||', '                    (weights_shape.dimensions_size() > 0 &&', '                     weights_shape.dimensions(0) == 0),', '                errors::InvalidArgument(', '                    "`weights` must be the same shape as `arr` or a length-0 "', '                    "`Tensor`, in which case it acts as all weights equal to "', '                    "1. Received ",', '                    weights_shape.DebugString()));', '']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. `DenseBincount` assumes its input tensor `weights` to either have the same shape as its input tensor `input` or to be length-0. A different `weights` shape will trigger a `CHECK` fail that can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit bf4c14353c2328636a18bfad1e151052c81d5f43. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The function reads the `weights` input at line 35 and obtains its shape at line 36-38. It then derives `weights_size` from `weights_shape.dimensions(0)` (line 39) and only checks whether that dimension is nonzero to set `has_weights` (lines 41-43). The weights tensor is later reshaped to `{input_shape.dimensions(0) * input_shape.dimensions(1)}` (lines 69-70) or assigned directly as updates (line 79) without verifying that the weights shape matches the input shape.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a missing shape constraint that lets attacker-controlled `weights` reach an internal assertion/CHECK, crashing the process. This is a reachable assertion leading to DoS (CWE-617), not merely an invalid-argument handling gap.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code never validates that `weights` has the same shape as `input` (or is length-0) before reshaping/using it as scatter updates. Trigger: a caller supplies a `weights` tensor whose shape differs from `input`. The incompatible shape flows into `xla::Reshape`/`Scatter`, causing a shape mismatch that fails a CHECK/assertion and aborts the process, yielding a denial of service.

XwdLoader: Fix buffer over-read and improve general robustness

This commit fixes a buffer over-read that could occur due to g_ntohl()
evaluating its argument more than once if at least one of the following
is true:

* Build target is not x86.
* __OPTIMIZE__ is not set during compilation (e.g. -O0 was used).

It also improves robustness more generally and fixes an issue where the
wrong field was being used to calculate the color map size, causing some
image files that were otherwise fine to be rejected.

commit_msg:
fuse: break infinite loop in fuse_fill_write_pages()

I got a report about unkillable task eating CPU. Further
investigation shows, that the problem is in the fuse_fill_write_pages()
function. If iov's first segment has zero length, we get an infinite
loop, because we never reach iov_iter_advance() call.

Fix this by calling iov_iter_advance() before repeating an attempt to
copy data from userspace.

A similar problem is described in 124d3b7041f ("fix writev regression:
pan hanging unkillable and un-straceable"). If zero-length segmend
is followed by segment with invalid address,
iov_iter_fault_in_readable() checks only first segment (zero-length),
iov_iter_copy_from_user_atomic() skips it, fails at second and
returns zero -> goto again without skipping zero-length segment.

Patch calls iov_iter_advance() before goto again: we'll skip zero-length
segment at second iteraction and iov_iter_fault_in_readable() will detect
invalid address.

Special thanks to Konstantin Khlebnikov, who helped a lot with the commit
description.

Cc: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Maxim Patlasov <mpatlasov@parallels.com>
Cc: Konstantin Khlebnikov <khlebnikov@yandex-team.ru>
Signed-off-by: Roman Gushchin <klamm@yandex-team.ru>
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <miklos@szeredi.hu>
Fixes: ea9b9907b82a ("fuse: implement perform_write")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tiov_iter_advance(ii, tmp);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tiov_iter_advance(ii, tmp);']}
description: The fuse_fill_write_pages function in fs/fuse/file.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows local users to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via a writev system call that triggers a zero length for the first segment of an iov.

code_evidence: The 'again:' label at line 18 is the re-entry point. iov_iter_copy_from_user_atomic at line 28 returns tmp; if tmp is zero (line 30), the page is released and control jumps back to 'again' at line 34 without advancing the iterator.

iov_iter_advance(ii, tmp) at line 40 is only reached after a successful nonzero copy, so a zero-length first iov segment is never skipped; the do-while condition at lines 48-49 is never reevaluated during the goto again path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the goto-again loop's exit condition cannot be reached when the iterator is not advanced on the zero-copy path, producing an infinite loop. This is an availability weakness (unreachable exit), not a memory-safety issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the retry path (goto again) does not advance the iterator, so a zero-length first iov segment makes iov_iter_copy_from_user_atomic return zero repeatedly. Trigger: a local writev where the first iov segment has zero length. Consequence: the loop never terminates, consuming CPU in an unkillable task (DoS).

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in smb2_is_status_io_timeout() in CIFS in the Linux Kernel. After CIFS transfers response data to a system call, there are still local variable points to the memory region, and if the system call frees it faster than CIFS uses it, CIFS will access a free memory region, leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: On wait failure, the code marks the MID cancelled and only assigns cifs_cancelled_callback when mid_state == MID_REQUEST_SUBMITTED; a MID already in MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED keeps its normal callback.
Later the response buffer is taken from midQ[i]->resp_buf and installed into resp_iov[i].iov_base, and the buffer is detached from the MID only when CIFS_NO_RSP_BUF is clear.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function retains and later dereferences midQ[i]->resp_buf after it may have been released during cancellation, which is exactly referencing memory after free (CWE-416). This is not merely a null-pointer or race on state; the consequence is access to freed buffer memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cancellation path does not neutralize a MID that has already received its response, so the received buffer is still referenced and handed to the caller. If the waiting process is killed and the response buffer is freed (e.g. by free_rsp_buf) while the MID's callback or the caller still uses resp_buf, the freed memory is accessed, causing a use-after-free and read of freed data (DoS/crash).

description: libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-06-01 does not validate OMX buffer sizes for the GSM and G711 codecs, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, as demonstrated by obtaining Signature or SignatureOrSystem access, aka internal bug 27793163.

code_evidence: The output BufferInfo/header is obtained from the output port queue but its nAllocLen is never compared against the size required by the decoder before decoding.
The input length is only checked for a maximum (kMaxNumSamplesPerFrame) and frame-size multiple; no constraint ties inHeader->nFilledLen to the capacity of outHeader->pBuffer.
DecodeGSM writes decoded samples into outHeader->pBuffer sized by the input length, without verifying the output allocation is large enough.
outHeader->nFilledLen is then set from the returned sample count, reflecting data written beyond the intended output buffer bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing decoded data past the end of the output buffer is an operation outside the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The missing size validation causes the out-of-bounds write; the consequence (corruption/privilege escalation) is distinct from the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
BufferInfo *outInfo = *outQueue.begin();
OMX_BUFFERHEADERTYPE *outHeader = outInfo->mHeader;
outHeader->nFilledLen = n * sizeof(int16_t);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder writes decoded output into outHeader->pBuffer based on the input frame count without ensuring outHeader->nAllocLen is large enough. Trigger: a crafted input buffer with a filled length exceeding the output allocation. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write past the output buffer, enabling memory corruption and potential privilege escalation in mediaserver.

description: The upnp_event_prepare function in upnpevents.c in MiniUPnP MiniUPnPd through 2.1 allows a remote attacker to leak information from the heap due to improper validation of an snprintf return value.

code_evidence: Line 52 fixes buffersize at 1024 and line 53 allocates exactly that many bytes. Lines 62-65 call snprintf into obj->buffer with obj->buffersize as the limit and store the result in obj->tosend, but no branch examines obj->tosend afterward. Execution falls directly to freeing xml and setting state ESending (lines 66-70), regardless of whether snprintf returned a negative error or a value >= buffersize indicating truncation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-252 directly matches: a function return value that signals error or truncation is ignored, so the caller cannot detect the unexpected state and continues with invalid data. This is distinct from a buffer overflow, since snprintf bounds the write; the weakness is the unchecked return leading to downstream information leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the return value of snprintf is assigned but never validated. If the formatted notification exceeds the 1024-byte buffer, snprintf truncates and returns the would-be length; if it fails, it returns a negative value. Because neither case is handled, the function proceeds to send a partially written or invalid buffer, and the negative return may later be interpreted as a length, exposing uninitialized heap contents.

commit_msg:
Fixed recursive async function calls.

Previously, PromiseCapability record was stored (function->context)
directly in function object during a function invocation.  This is
not correct, because PromiseCapability record should be linked to
current execution context.  As a result, function->context is
overwritten with consecutive recursive calls which results in
use-after-free.

This closes #451 issue on Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    njs_function_t      *function;', '', '    function = async->function;', '    function->context = ctx->capability;', '    function->await = ctx;', '', '    ret = njs_vmcode_interpreter(vm, ctx->pc);', '', '    function->context = NULL;', '    function->await = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['    ret = njs_vmcode_interpreter(vm, ctx->pc, ctx->capability, ctx);']}
description: njs through 0.7.0, used in NGINX, was discovered to contain a heap use-after-free in njs_await_fulfilled.

code_evidence: Line 11 reads the async context from vm->top_frame->function->context, and lines 16/19 derive async_frame and its function from that context.
Lines 33-34 store ctx->capability and ctx into the shared function object before the interpreter runs, then lines 36-37 clear them to NULL afterward.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reuses per-function state that is freed/overwritten by a nested invocation, exactly the reuse-after-free pattern of CWE-416. This is not merely a NULL-pointer issue: the outer call's context is invalidated by the inner call's cleanup.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The capability/await state is attached to the function object (function->context, function->await) rather than the execution context. A recursive async call re-enters this path and overwrites the same function fields; when the inner call returns it sets them to NULL, so the outer frame later reads a stale/NULL context (line 11) and dereferences freed async state, causing use-after-free.

commit_msg: Include the `havePeerCert` argument in the check.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (ssl->options.side == WOLFSSL_SERVER_END &&', '        if (!ssl->options.havePeerVerify && !ssl->options.resuming) {', '            ret = NO_PEER_CERT;'], 'added_lines': ['    if (ssl->options.side == WOLFSSL_SERVER_END && !ssl->options.resuming &&', '        if (!ssl->options.havePeerCert || !ssl->options.havePeerVerify) {', '            ret = NO_PEER_CERT; /* NO_PEER_VERIFY */', '            WOLFSSL_MSG("TLS v1.3 client did not present peer cert");']}
description: In wolfSSL before 5.2.0, a TLS 1.3 server cannot properly enforce a requirement for mutual authentication. A client can simply omit the certificate_verify message from the handshake, and never present a certificate.

code_evidence: On the TLS 1.3 server side, when mutualAuth or failNoCert is set, the check only tests !ssl->options.havePeerVerify (guarded by !resuming) and returns NO_PEER_CERT. It never inspects ssl->options.havePeerCert, so a client that omits certificate_verify and presents no certificate still satisfies this gate.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate that a peer certificate was actually received before accepting the client's Finished message, which is improper certificate validation (CWE-295) leading to authentication bypass. It is not merely missing a verification step (CWE-345); the certificate-presence constraint itself is absent.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mutual-authentication enforcement condition omits the havePeerCert flag, so absence of a client certificate is not detected. Trigger: a TLS 1.3 client skips certificate_verify and sends no certificate while the server requires mutual auth. Consequence: the handshake proceeds, bypassing the server's requirement to authenticate the client.

description: An issue was discovered in OpenSC through 0.19.0 and 0.20.x through 0.20.0-rc3. libopensc/card-cac1.c mishandles buffer limits for CAC certificates.

code_evidence: len is MIN(left,100) but next_len is computed from apdu.sw2; the loop's post-increment left -= len, out_ptr += len uses the old len while next_len can differ, so out_ptr and left can advance inconsistently with the actual response size.
On the sw1==0x63 path, left -= len then break, but out_ptr is not advanced and the returned r = size - left may exceed what was copied.
The caller-visible result r = size - left is used to malloc and memcpy from buf; inconsistent left accounting yields a length not matching valid data, enabling out-of-bounds read of buf.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop tracks two length variables (len and next_len) that diverge when apdu.sw2 differs from the prior chunk, and the sw1==0x63 branch decrements left by len without advancing out_ptr. Consequence: left and out_ptr no longer reflect bytes actually written, so r = size - left can exceed valid buffer content, causing an out-of-bounds read in memcpy.

commit_msg:
CVE-2016-0798: avoid memory leak in SRP

The SRP user database lookup method SRP_VBASE_get_by_user had confusing
memory management semantics; the returned pointer was sometimes newly
allocated, and sometimes owned by the callee. The calling code has no
way of distinguishing these two cases.

Specifically, SRP servers that configure a secret seed to hide valid
login information are vulnerable to a memory leak: an attacker
connecting with an invalid username can cause a memory leak of around
300 bytes per connection.

Servers that do not configure SRP, or configure SRP but do not configure
a seed are not vulnerable.

In Apache, the seed directive is known as SSLSRPUnknownUserSeed.

To mitigate the memory leak, the seed handling in SRP_VBASE_get_by_user
is now disabled even if the user has configured a seed.

Applications are advised to migrate to SRP_VBASE_get1_by_user. However,
note that OpenSSL makes no strong guarantees about the
indistinguishability of valid and invalid logins. In particular,
computations are currently not carried out in constant time.

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void SRP_user_pwd_free(SRP_user_pwd *user_pwd)'], 'added_lines': ['void SRP_user_pwd_free(SRP_user_pwd *user_pwd)']}
description: Memory leak in the SRP_VBASE_get_by_user implementation in OpenSSL 1.0.1 before 1.0.1s and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2g allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by providing an invalid username in a connection attempt, related to apps/s_server.c and crypto/srp/srp_vfy.c.

code_evidence: SRP_user_pwd_free is the deallocation routine: it guards against NULL, frees the BIGNUM fields s and v, frees the id and info strings, and finally frees the struct itself. The commit changes only its linkage from static to external so callers can release a returned pointer; the function body performs complete cleanup of an owned SRP_user_pwd.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) is the target category and covers improper resource management such as unfreed allocations leading to memory exhaustion. This function implements the correct free path whose inconsistent use by the caller causes the leak, supporting the resource-management error rather than a buffer or pointer-validity weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is in the lookup API's ownership semantics, not in this routine: SRP_VBASE_get_by_user sometimes returns a newly allocated record and sometimes a callee-owned one, so callers cannot know when to invoke this free routine. Trigger: a remote invalid username with a configured seed causes an allocation that is never released, consuming memory per connection; this function is the missing-cleanup mechanism, not the leak source itself.

description: Flatpak is a system for building, distributing, and running sandboxed desktop applications on Linux. A bug was discovered in the `flatpak-portal` service that can allow sandboxed applications to execute arbitrary code on the host system (a sandbox escape). This sandbox-escape bug is present in versions from 0.11.4 and before fixed versions 1.8.5 and 1.10.0. The Flatpak portal D-Bus service (`flatpak-portal`, also known by its D-Bus service name `org.freedesktop.portal.Flatpak`) allows apps in a Flatpak sandbox to launch their own subprocesses in a new sandbox instance, either with the same security settings as the caller or with more restrictive security settings. For example, this is used in Flatpak-packaged web browsers such as Chromium to launch subprocesses that will process untrusted web content, and give those subprocesses a more restrictive sandbox than the browser itself. In vulnerable versions, the Flatpak portal service passes caller-specified environment variables to non-sandboxed processes on the host system, and in particular to the `flatpak run` command that is used to launch the new sandbox instance. A malicious or compromised Flatpak app could set environment variables that are trusted by the `flatpak run` command, and use them to execute arbitrary code that is not in a sandbox. As a workaround, this vulnerability can be mitigated by preventing the `flatpak-portal` service from starting, but that mitigation will prevent many Flatpak apps from working correctly. This is fixed in versions 1.8.5 and 1.10.0.

code_evidence: The pre-patch code copies each caller-supplied extra_args[i] verbatim into flatpak_argv, which becomes the argv of the host-side `flatpak run` process.
Caller-controlled environment variables from arg_envs are merged into env via g_environ_setenv, and env is passed unchanged to g_spawn_async_with_pipes.

g_spawn_async_with_pipes launches `flatpak` with that argv and environment; no allowlist or neutralization of special elements (e.g. --env=, --command=, LD_*/loader variables) is applied before the downstream flatpak binary parses them.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits because externally influenced input is used to build a command/argument structure passed to a downstream component (flatpak run) without neutralizing special elements that change its parsing. It is not merely CWE-78 shell injection since no shell is used; the injection targets option/argv parsing of the downstream program.

evidence_lines.code:
for (i = 0; extra_args != NULL && extra_args[i] != NULL; i++)
g_ptr_array_add (flatpak_argv, g_strdup (extra_args[i]));

if (!g_spawn_async_with_pipes (NULL,
(char **) flatpak_argv->pdata,
env,
G_SPAWN_SEARCH_PATH | G_SPAWN_DO_NOT_REAP_CHILD | G_SPAWN_LEAVE_DESCRIPTORS_OPEN,
child_setup_func, &child_setup_data,
&pid,
NULL,
NULL,
NULL,
&error))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: untrusted sandbox-app input (extra_args and arg_envs) is concatenated into the command line and environment of the privileged `flatpak run` invocation without filtering. Trigger: a malicious app supplies options or environment variables that flatpak run interprets as trusted configuration. Consequence: those elements alter flatpak run's behavior, enabling host-side code execution (sandbox escape).

description: xbuf_format_converter, used as part of exif_read_data, was appending a terminating null character to the generated string, but was not using its standard append char function. As a result, if the buffer was full, it would result in an out-of-bounds write. This issue affects HHVM versions prior to 4.56.3, all versions between 4.57.0 and 4.80.1, all versions between 4.81.0 and 4.93.1, and versions 4.94.0, 4.95.0, 4.96.0, 4.97.0, 4.98.0.

code_evidence: paddedSalt is a fixed buffer of size maxSaltLength+1 (124). memcpy copies min(maxSaltLength, saltLen) bytes, but the null terminator is written at paddedSalt[saltLen] without clamping saltLen.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes a '\0' beyond the bounds of the fixed-size paddedSalt array, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The fix clamps the index with std::min, confirming the missing constraint is the root cause rather than a read overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the terminating null write uses raw saltLen rather than the clamped length. Trigger: a salt whose strlen exceeds maxSaltLength (123) enters the $2X$ branch (saltLen > 8). Consequence: paddedSalt[saltLen] writes past the 124-byte stack buffer, a stack out-of-bounds write.

description: A vulnerability was found in the Linux kernel, where accessing a deallocated instance in printer_ioctl() printer_ioctl() tries to access of a printer_dev instance. However, use-after-free arises because it had been freed by gprinter_free().

code_evidence: Line 11 allocates dev with kzalloc; line 16 increments opts->refcnt but no reference count is initialized on the device object itself, so the object's lifetime is not tracked.
Line 28 assigns gprinter_free as the function's free_func, meaning the device can be released through usb_put_function independent of other holders.

dev = kzalloc(sizeof(*dev), GFP_KERNEL);
++opts->refcnt;
dev->function.free_func = gprinter_free;

commit_msg:
Fixed Array.prototype.lastIndexOf() with unicode string as "this".

Previously, when lastIndexOf() was called with unicode string as "this"
argument and a negative "fromIndex" argument null-pointer dererence
might occur because njs_string_offset() was called with invalid index
value whereas njs_string_offset() should always be called with valid
index argument.

The fix is to verify that from index is valid.

This closes #482 issue on Github.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12989/RESP: Make sure resp_get_length() advances the pointer for invalid lengths.

Make sure that it always sends *endp before returning and that, for
invalid lengths where we don't like a character in the length string,
what it sets *endp to is past the character in question, so we don't
run the risk of infinitely looping (or doing something else random) if a
character in the length is invalid.

This fixes an infinite loop discovered by Forcepoint's security
researchers Otto Airamo & Antti Levomäki.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if (!saw_digit)', "    if (*bp != '\\r')", "    if (*bp != '\\n')"], 'added_lines': ['            if (!saw_digit) {', '                bp++;', '            }', "    if (*bp != '\\r') {", '        bp++;', '    }', "    if (*bp != '\\n') {", '        bp++;', '    }', '    *endp = bp;', '    *endp = bp;']}
description: The RESP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 could enter an infinite loop due to a bug in print-resp.c:resp_get_length().

code_evidence: On encountering a non-digit before any digit, the loop jumps to invalid without advancing bp.
When the byte after the digits is not '\r', control jumps to invalid without advancing bp.
Likewise a non-'\n' byte jumps to invalid without advancing bp.
The trunc and invalid labels return without setting *endp, so the caller's pointer is not advanced past the offending character.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the pointer not being advanced on the invalid paths lets the calling parse loop re-process the identical input indefinitely; the exit condition (consuming the bad character) is unreachable. This is distinct from a mere parsing error, since the defect is the non-terminating iteration.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser returns an invalid/trunc status without advancing the output pointer past the rejected character. If the caller retries parsing from the returned pointer, the same character is examined forever, so the loop's exit condition is never reached, causing CPU consumption.

commit_msg:
If the response query string is malformed, we might access memory
pass the end of "name" variable in parse_response().
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\ttype, class, ttl, &rdlen, &next, name);', '\t\t\t\t\tname, &name_len);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\ttype, class, ttl, &rdlen, &next, name,', '\t\t\tsizeof(name) - 1);', '\t\t\t\t\tname, sizeof(name) - 1, &name_len);']}
description: Stack-based buffer overflow in "dnsproxy.c" in connman 1.34 and earlier allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) or execute arbitrary code via a crafted response query string passed to the "name" variable.

code_evidence: A fixed-size stack buffer name[NS_MAXDNAME + 1] is declared and zeroed, but the calls that populate it do not bound the write.
parse_rr is called with name and no length argument, so it can write past the buffer end when a crafted response query string is long.
The get_name call likewise passes name without a size limit, allowing another unbounded write into the same stack buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing past the fixed stack buffer name[] is an out-of-bounds memory write, matching CWE-119's operations outside a buffer's intended boundary. A more specific child such as CWE-121 (stack-based buffer overflow) would also fit, but the target CWE-119 directly describes the out-of-bounds write observed here.

evidence_lines.code:
char name[NS_MAXDNAME + 1];
memset(name, 0, sizeof(name));

ret = parse_rr(buf, ptr, buf + buflen, rsp, &rsp_len,
type, class, ttl, &rdlen, &next, name);

ret = get_name(0, buf, next - rdlen, buf + buflen,
name, &name_len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the name buffer's capacity is never conveyed to parse_rr or get_name, so neither callee can enforce a bound. Trigger: a remote DNS response whose name/query string exceeds NS_MAXDNAME causes the callee to write beyond name[]. Consequence: stack corruption, leading to crash or possible code execution.
