commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12897/ISO CLNS: Use ND_TTEST() for the bounds checks in isoclns_print().

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kamil Frankowicz.

Don't pass the remaining caplen - that's too hard to get right, and we
were getting it wrong in at least one case; just use ND_TTEST().

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                isoclns_print(ndo, p, l2info.length, l2info.caplen);', '            isoclns_print(ndo, p + 1, l2info.length - 1, l2info.caplen - 1);', '            isoclns_print(ndo, p - 1, l2info.length + 1, l2info.caplen + 1);'], 'added_lines': ['                isoclns_print(ndo, p, l2info.length);', '            isoclns_print(ndo, p + 1, l2info.length - 1);', '            isoclns_print(ndo, p - 1, l2info.length + 1);']}
description: The ISO CLNS parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isoclns.c:isoclns_print().

code_evidence: In the JUNIPER_LSQ_L3_PROTO_ISO case, isoclns_print is called with l2info.length as the length but l2info.caplen as a separate caplen argument, so the callee must reconcile two lengths.

For the LLCSAP_ISONS protocol, isoclns_print is passed p + 1 with l2info.length - 1 and l2info.caplen - 1, again forwarding a caplen that can be inconsistent with the length and the actual captured buffer.

For the LLC_UI/NLPID cases, isoclns_print is called with p - 1 and l2info.length + 1 plus l2info.caplen + 1, adding to the caplen; passing a caplen that was already hard to compute correctly is the pattern the fix removes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The forwarded caplen can exceed the real captured data, so the downstream parser performs reads beyond the buffer end, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not merely an integer issue; the consequence is reading memory outside the intended buffer.

evidence_lines.code:
isoclns_print(ndo, p - 1, l2info.length + 1, l2info.caplen + 1);
break;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function forwards a separately computed caplen (l2info.caplen, with -1/+1 adjustments) to isoclns_print instead of deriving bounds from the actual captured data. Trigger: a crafted Juniper MFR packet whose length/caplen fields are inconsistent. This can cause the ISO CLNS parser to read past the end of the captured buffer, an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
schema tree BUGFIX freeing nodes with no module set

Context must be passed explicitly for these cases.
Fixes #1452
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    lys_node_free(retval, NULL, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['    lys_node_free(ctx, retval, NULL, 0);']}
description: In function lys_node_free() in libyang <= v1.0.225, it asserts that the value of node->module can't be NULL. But in some cases, node->module can be null, which triggers a reachable assertion (CWE-617).

code_evidence: The error path calls lys_node_free(retval, NULL, 0) with a NULL module/context argument before returning NULL. Per the commit, lys_node_free() asserts node->module is non-NULL; passing NULL here reaches that assertion when the error label is taken.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: A reachable assert() triggered by malformed input that terminates the application matches CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion). The fix passes ctx explicitly, confirming the NULL argument caused the assertion rather than a generic NULL-pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error cleanup invokes lys_node_free() with a NULL context/module argument. Trigger: any parse error in read_yin_case that jumps to the error label. Consequence: lys_node_free()'s assertion on node->module fires, aborting the process (DoS).

commit_msg:
PR22443, Global buffer overflow in _bfd_elf_get_symbol_version_string

Symbols like *ABS* defined in bfd/section.c:global_syms are not
elf_symbol_type.  They can appear on relocs and perhaps other places
in an ELF bfd, so a number of places in nm.c and objdump.c are wrong
to cast an asymbol based on the bfd being ELF.  I think we lose
nothing by excluding all section symbols, not just the global_syms.

	PR 22443
	* nm.c (sort_symbols_by_size): Don't attempt to access
	section symbol internal_elf_sym.
	(print_symbol): Likewise.  Don't call bfd_get_symbol_version_string
	for section symbols.
	* objdump.c (compare_symbols): Don't attempt to access
	section symbol internal_elf_sym.
	(objdump_print_symname): Don't call bfd_get_symbol_version_string
	for section symbols.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  /* Synthetic symbols do not have a full symbol type set of data available.  */', '  if ((sym->flags & BSF_SYNTHETIC) != 0)', '      if ((sym->flags & BSF_SYNTHETIC) == 0)'], 'added_lines': ['  /* Synthetic symbols do not have a full symbol type set of data available.', '     Nor do bfd/section.c:global_syms like *ABS*.  */', '  if ((sym->flags & (BSF_SECTION_SYM | BSF_SYNTHETIC)) != 0)', '      if ((sym->flags & (BSF_SECTION_SYM | BSF_SYNTHETIC)) == 0)']}
description: nm.c and objdump.c in GNU Binutils 2.29.1 mishandle certain global symbols, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (_bfd_elf_get_symbol_version_string buffer over-read and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: The guard only excludes BSF_SYNTHETIC symbols; section symbols such as global_syms (*ABS*) are not synthetic, so they fall into the else branch and elf_symbol_from(abfd, sym) is called on an asymbol that is not an elf_symbol_type.
Likewise, when with_symbol_versions is set, bfd_get_symbol_version_string is called for any non-synthetic symbol, including section symbols lacking the ELF internal symbol layout.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The consequence is reading memory beyond the intended symbol structure, matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). This is not merely a type confusion: the unsupported cast yields an over-read in _bfd_elf_get_symbol_version_string.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((sym->flags & BSF_SYNTHETIC) == 0)
version_string = bfd_get_symbol_version_string (abfd, sym, &hidden);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: print_symbol assumes every non-synthetic symbol for an ELF bfd has a valid elf_symbol_type, but section symbols (global_syms) do not. Trigger: a crafted ELF containing such symbols reaches elf_symbol_from or bfd_get_symbol_version_string, which reads fields based on the ELF layout past the actual object, causing an out-of-bounds read and crash.

commit_msg: Fixed possible memory leak reported in #1206
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      base_image=DestroyImage(base_image);', '      base_image=DestroyImage(base_image);', '      base_image=DestroyImage(base_image);']}
description: ImageMagick 7.0.8-6 has a memory leak vulnerability in the TIFFWritePhotoshopLayers function in coders/tiff.c.

code_evidence: base_image is allocated by CloneImage and becomes the sole owner of a cloned image resource.
When AcquireStringInfo fails, the error path destroys clone_info and throws but never releases base_image, leaking the cloned image.
When TIFFAcquireCustomStreamForWriting fails, the error path frees clone_info and layers but still leaves base_image allocated.
When CloneBlobInfo returns NULL, the error path frees clone_info, layers and custom_stream yet omits base_image, leaking it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because base_image is a resource whose effective lifetime ends on the error path, but the function fails to release it before throwing. This is a missing release of an allocated image resource, not a use-after-free or double-free; the added DestroyImage calls confirm the intended cleanup.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: each early error branch after base_image=CloneImage returns via ThrowBinaryException without destroying base_image. Trigger: any of the three allocation failures (layers, custom_stream, blob) during TIFF layer writing. The un-freed cloned image persists, causing a memory leak and possible resource-consumption DoS on repeated failures.

commit_msg:
vc2enc_dwt: pad the temporary buffer by the slice size

Since non-Haar wavelets need to look into pixels outside the frame, we
need to pad the buffer. The old factor of two seemed to be a workaround
that fact and only padded to the left and bottom. This correctly pads
by the slice size and as such reduces memory usage and potential
exploits.
Reported by Liu Bingchang.

Ideally, there should be no temporary buffer but the encoder is designed
to deinterleave the coefficients into the classical wavelet structure
with the lower frequency values in the top left corner.

Signed-off-by: Rostislav Pehlivanov <atomnuker@gmail.com>
(cherry picked from commit 3228ac730c11eca49d5680d5550128e397061c85)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    av_freep(&s->buffer);'], 'added_lines': ['    av_free(s->buffer - s->padding);', '    s->buffer = NULL;']}
description: The VC-2 Video Compression encoder in FFmpeg 3.0 and 3.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) because of incorrect buffer padding for non-Haar wavelets, related to libavcodec/vc2enc.c and libavcodec/vc2enc_dwt.c.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The only function shown is a cleanup routine that frees s->buffer; it contains no read operation, index computation, or wavelet padding logic, so it cannot directly demonstrate an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg: Fix #10498 - Fix crash in fuzzed java files (#10511)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t}', '\t\tif (offset + 10 > sz) {', '\t\t\teprintf ("oob");']}
description: The r_bin_java_annotation_new function in shlr/java/class.c in radare2 2.7.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted .class file because of missing input validation in r_bin_java_line_number_table_attr_new.

code_evidence: Line 10 reads a ushort from buffer at offset 6 with no check that sz is large enough; line 11 then advances offset to 8.
The loop at line 13 iterates table_length times; each iteration allocates lvattr and, if allocation fails, breaks (lines 16-19), but there is no bounds check against sz before reading.
Lines 20-29 perform five consecutive R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT reads at offset and advance by 2 each time, consuming 10 bytes per entry without verifying offset+10 <= sz.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs sequential reads beyond the supplied buffer size, which is exactly CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). The missing sz check is the cause; the crash is the consequence. This is not a write overflow (CWE-787) because no out-of-bounds write occurs.

evidence_lines.code:
attr->info.local_variable_type_table_attr.table_length = R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT (buffer, offset);
offset += 2;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function parses attacker-controlled table_length and entry fields from a .class file without validating that the buffer size sz covers the reads. Trigger: a crafted class file with a large table_length or truncated entry data causes lines 10 and 20-29 to read past the end of buffer. Supported consequence: heap-based buffer over-read, leading to a crash/DoS (and potentially information disclosure).

commit_msg:
[trunk] fixed a buffer overflow in opj_tcd_init_decode_tile

Update issue 431
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tl_tile->x0 = opj_int_max((OPJ_INT32)(l_cp->tx0 + p * l_cp->tdx), (OPJ_INT32)l_image->x0);', '\tl_tile->y0 = opj_int_max((OPJ_INT32)(l_cp->ty0 + q * l_cp->tdy), (OPJ_INT32)l_image->y0);', '\tl_tile->x1 = opj_int_min((OPJ_INT32)(l_cp->tx0 + (p + 1) * l_cp->tdx), (OPJ_INT32)l_image->x1);', '\tl_tile->y1 = opj_int_min((OPJ_INT32)(l_cp->ty0 + (q + 1) * l_cp->tdy), (OPJ_INT32)l_image->y1);'], 'added_lines': ['\tl_tile->x0 = (OPJ_INT32)opj_uint_max(l_cp->tx0 + p * l_cp->tdx, l_image->x0);', '\tl_tile->y0 = (OPJ_INT32)opj_uint_max(l_cp->ty0 + q * l_cp->tdy, l_image->y0);', '\tl_tile->x1 = (OPJ_INT32)opj_uint_min(l_cp->tx0 + (p + 1) * l_cp->tdx, l_image->x1);', '\tl_tile->y1 = (OPJ_INT32)opj_uint_min(l_cp->ty0 + (q + 1) * l_cp->tdy, l_image->y1);', '']}
description: An improper computation of p_tx0, p_tx1, p_ty0 and p_ty1 in the function opj_get_encoding_parameters in openjp2/pi.c in OpenJPEG through 2.3.0 can lead to an integer overflow.

code_evidence: Tile indices p and q are derived from p_tile_no (lines 34-35). Lines 36-39 compute tile bounds as (OPJ_INT32)(l_cp->tx0 + p * l_cp->tdx) and (p + 1) * l_cp->tdx, then cast the arithmetic result to signed OPJ_INT32 before opj_int_max/opj_int_min. The multiply/add is performed in the unsigned/attacker-influenced coordinate domain and only truncated at the cast, so a large tile offset or tile size wraps the computed bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an integer overflow/wraparound in the tile coordinate calculation, directly matching CWE-190's 'calculation that can produce an integer overflow or wraparound' used for size/offset computations. The patch switches to unsigned opj_uint_max/opj_uint_min, confirming the signed overflow was the flaw rather than a mere off-by-one or truncation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: tile boundary arithmetic (tx0 + p*tdx, tx0 + (p+1)*tdx, similarly for y) is evaluated and then narrowed to OPJ_INT32 without overflow checking. Trigger: crafted codestream/image parameters making these products/exceeds exceed the signed range. Consequence: wrapped tile x0/y0/x1/y1 values propagate into downstream size and allocation computations, enabling out-of-bounds access or buffer overflow (as noted in the commit).

commit_msg:
Remove support for pre-authentication compression. Doing compression
early in the protocol probably seemed reasonable in the 1990s, but
today it's clearly a bad idea in terms of both cryptography (cf.
multiple compression oracle attacks in TLS) and attack surface.

Moreover, to support it across privilege-separation zlib needed
the assistance of a complex shared-memory manager that made the
required attack surface considerably larger.

Prompted by Guido Vranken pointing out a compiler-elided security
check in the shared memory manager found by Stack
(http://css.csail.mit.edu/stack/); ok deraadt@ markus@

NB. pre-auth authentication has been disabled by default in sshd
for >10 years.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    (r = sshbuf_get_u32(b, (u_int *)&comp->enabled)) != 0 ||'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The shared memory manager (associated with pre-authentication compression) in sshd in OpenSSH before 7.4 does not ensure that a bounds check is enforced by all compilers, which might allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging access to a sandboxed privilege-separation process, related to the m_zback and m_zlib data structures.

code_evidence: Lines 44-47 parse comp->type, comp->enabled and comp->name from the peer-supplied blob b via sshbuf_get_u32/sshbuf_get_cstring, casting comp->enabled to u_int*.
Lines 53-56 check sshbuf_len(b) != 0 only after the compression fields were consumed, so the pre-auth compression parsing path is reachable with attacker-controlled values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits as the class-level weakness: the function feeds unvalidated peer data into structures (comp->enabled/type) that drive a compression buffer manager whose bounds check was not reliably enforced, permitting out-of-bounds memory operations. Note the true root cause is the missing/elided bounds check in the shm manager, not this parser alone.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((r = sshbuf_get_u32(b, &comp->type)) != 0 ||
(r = sshbuf_get_u32(b, (u_int *)&comp->enabled)) != 0 ||
(r = sshbuf_get_cstring(b, &comp->name, NULL)) != 0)
goto out;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parsing routine accepts peer-controlled compression metadata (type, enabled, name) without validating enabled/type combinations, leaving the pre-auth compression state machine reachable. The commit removed this field precisely because the shared-memory zlib manager behind it had a compiler-elided bounds check; the function itself does not enforce a boundary constraint over the parsed comp structure.

commit_msg:
Trap for overly large input to XmlRPCPP which could cause problems with int <-> size_t conversions.

 - In XmlRpcClient, XmlRpcServerConnection and XmlRpcSocket, recognize when incoming or outgoing data is too large, generate an error and discard the data when practical.
 - Use the safe strtol() rather than atoi() to decode an incoming content-length header, and generate an error if the length is invalid or too large.
 - In XmlRpcUtil, prevent attempts to parse overly large XML input.
 - Add tests where they can reasonably be inserted into existing test routines.

Although this fix could be cleaner the update is written to make the update ABI compatible.

This fix addresses CVE-2020-16124 / Integer overflow in ros_comm.

Signed-off-by: Sid Faber <sid.faber@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  // avoid attempting to parse overly long xml input', '  if (xml.length() > size_t(__INT_MAX__)) return std::string();']}
description: Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability in the XML RPC library of OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages allows unauthenticated network traffic to cause unexpected behavior. This issue affects: OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages Noetic and prior versions. Fixed in https://github.com/ros/ros_comm/pull/2065.

code_evidence: parseTag receives xml as a std::string whose length() is size_t; line 4 compares *offset (int) to int(xml.length()), narrowing the size_t length to int before the bounds check.
Line 12 stores the computed end position iend + etag.length() back into *offset via int(), another size_t-to-int narrowing conversion.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the function performs size_t-to-int conversions whose results can overflow/wrap when input length exceeds INT_MAX, and the logic assumes the converted value stays valid. This is an integer conversion overflow, not a mere out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), since the narrowing conversion is the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
XmlRpcUtil::parseTag(const char* tag, std::string const& xml, int* offset)
if (*offset >= int(xml.length())) return std::string();
*offset = int(iend + etag.length());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: size_t string lengths and positions are cast to int without validating that they fit, so oversized XML input makes int(xml.length()) and int(iend + etag.length()) wrap to negative or truncated values. Trigger: unauthenticated network traffic supplying XML exceeding INT_MAX. Consequence: the offset bounds check and subsequent parsing operate on corrupted offsets, yielding incorrect parsing behavior and potential out-of-bounds access.

commit_msg:
Fix heap overflow in the ultra.c decoder

The Ultra type tile decoder does not use the _safe variant of the LZO
decompress function, which allows a maliciuous server to overwrite parts of the
heap by sending a larger-than-specified LZO data stream.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  inflateResult = lzo1x_decompress('], 'added_lines': ['  inflateResult = lzo1x_decompress_safe(']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in rfbproto.c in LibVNCClient in LibVNCServer before 0.9.11 allows remote servers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted FramebufferUpdate message containing a subrectangle outside of the client drawing area.

code_evidence: The server-provided LZO stream in ultra_buffer of length toRead is passed to the unchecked lzo1x_decompress, with output capacity uncompressedBytes set to client->raw_buffer_size (line 38).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked decompression writes beyond the intended bounds of the heap-allocated raw_buffer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds write to a memory buffer. The root cause is the missing safe decompression bound, not merely the later rectangle parsing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The decoder trusts the attacker-supplied LZO stream and uses the non-safe LZO API, which does not strictly bound the decompressed output to the destination buffer size. A malicious server can send a stream whose decompressed data exceeds raw_buffer_size, causing a heap write past the raw_buffer allocation. This yields heap memory corruption, crash, or possible code execution.

description: tsMuxer v2.6.16 was discovered to contain a heap overflow via the function BitStreamWriter::flushBits() at /tsMuxer/bitStream.h.

code_evidence: Bounded per-row vectors are sized vps_max_layers (max 64) for ReferenceLayerIdx, OutputLayerIdx and NumRefLayers; all indexed by layer ids.

Single counter r is reused across the outer loop i instead of resetting per layer; r accumulates across all layers, so ReferenceLayerIdx[i][r++] writes past the row end once cumulative references exceed vps_max_layers.

Loop over l uses j (number of output layers) and reads OutputLayerIdx[i][l]; the same shared r index is later used to bound NumRefLayers[idx], driving out-of-range accesses in layerIncludedInOlsFlag[i][ReferenceLayerIdx[idx][k]].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code writes past the end of a fixed-size per-row vector buffer (ReferenceLayerIdx[i][r++]) and subsequently reads out of bounds, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the primary defect is the overflowing indexed write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reference-layer counter r is not reset for each layer i, so ReferenceLayerIdx[i][r++] and NumRefLayers[i]=r use a monotonically growing index that can exceed the per-row length vps_max_layers. With attacker-controlled VPS layer flags, the write crosses the vector row boundary, and the inflated NumRefLayers then steers out-of-bounds reads in the output-layer loop.

it all the time when starting/stopping the bus.  Simplifies the
code, also fixes bugs (memory leak) due to missing checks whenever
the time is already allocated or not.

Reported-by: Zuozhi Fzz <zuozhi.fzz@alibaba-inc.com>

This could lead to remote information disclosure in the Bluetooth service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation. The only guard (line 10) checks ea and length after these reads, and the length-- at lines 17/21/24 can underflow the unsigned uint16_t.

commit_msg:
copy: CVE-2022-0485: Fail nbdcopy if NBD read or write fails

nbdcopy has a nasty bug when performing multi-threaded copies using
asynchronous nbd calls - it was blindly treating the completion of an
asynchronous command as successful, rather than checking the *error
parameter.  This can result in the silent creation of a corrupted
image in two different ways: when a read fails, we blindly wrote
garbage to the destination; when a write fails, we did not flag that
the destination was not written.

Since nbdcopy already calls exit() on a synchronous read or write
failure to a file, doing the same for an asynchronous op to an NBD
server is the simplest solution.  A nicer solution, but more invasive
to code and thus not done here, might be to allow up to N retries of
the transaction (in case the read or write failure was transient), or
even having a mode where as much data is copied as possible (portions
of the copy that failed would be logged on stderr, and nbdcopy would
still fail with a non-zero exit status, but this would copy more than
just stopping at the first error, as can be done with rsync or
ddrescue).

Note that since we rely on auto-retiring and do NOT call
nbd_aio_command_completed, our completion callbacks must always return
1 (if they do not exit() first), even when acting on *error, so as not
leave the command allocated until nbd_close.  As such, there is no
sane way to return an error to a manual caller of the callback, and
therefore we can drop dead code that calls perror() and exit() if the
callback "failed".  It is also worth documenting the contract on when
we must manually call the callback during the asynch_zero callback, so
that we do not leak or double-free the command; thankfully, all the
existing code paths were correct.

The added testsuite script demonstrates several scenarios, some of
which fail without the rest of this patch in place, and others which
showcase ways in which sparse images can bypass errors.

Once backports are complete, a followup patch on the main branch will
edit docs/libnbd-security.pod with the mailing list announcement of
the stable branch commit ids and release versions that incorporate
this fix.

commit_msg:
Andrey Konovalov reported out of bound accesses in ip6gre_err()

If GRE flags contains GRE_KEY, the following expression
*(((__be32 *)p) + (grehlen / 4) - 1)

accesses data ~40 bytes after the expected point, since
grehlen includes the size of IPv6 headers.

Let's use a "struct gre_base_hdr *greh" pointer to make this
code more readable.

p[1] becomes greh->protocol.
grhlen is the GRE header length.

Fixes: c12b395a4664 ("gre: Support GRE over IPv6")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tu8 type, u8 code, int offset, __be32 info)', '\tconst struct ipv6hdr *ipv6h = (const struct ipv6hdr *)skb->data;', '\t__be16 *p = (__be16 *)(skb->data + offset);', '\tint grehlen = offset + 4;', '\tflags = p[0];', '\tif (flags&(GRE_CSUM|GRE_KEY|GRE_SEQ|GRE_ROUTING|GRE_VERSION)) {', '\t\tif (flags&(GRE_VERSION|GRE_ROUTING))', '\t\t\treturn;', '\t\tif (flags&GRE_KEY) {', '\t\t\tgrehlen += 4;', '\t\t\tif (flags&GRE_CSUM)', '\t\t\t\tgrehlen += 4;', '\t\t}', '\t/* If only 8 bytes returned, keyed message will be dropped here */', '\tif (!pskb_may_pull(skb, grehlen))', '\tp = (__be16 *)(skb->data + offset);', '\t\t\t\tflags & GRE_KEY ?', '\t\t\t\t*(((__be32 *)p) + (grehlen / 4) - 1) : 0,', '\t\t\t\tp[1]);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t       u8 type, u8 code, int offset, __be32 info)', '\tconst struct gre_base_hdr *greh;', '\tconst struct ipv6hdr *ipv6h;', '\tint grehlen = sizeof(*greh);', '\tint key_off = 0;', '\t__be32 key;', '\tif (!pskb_may_pull(skb, offset + grehlen))', '\t\treturn;', '\tgreh = (const struct gre_base_hdr *)(skb->data + offset);', '\tflags = greh->flags;', '\tif (flags & (GRE_VERSION | GRE_ROUTING))', '\t\treturn;', '\tif (flags & GRE_CSUM)', '\t\tgrehlen += 4;', '\tif (flags & GRE_KEY) {', '\t\tkey_off = grehlen + offset;', '\t\tgrehlen += 4;', '\tif (!pskb_may_pull(skb, offset + grehlen))', '\tgreh = (const struct gre_base_hdr *)(skb->data + offset);', '\tkey = key_off ? *(__be32 *)(skb->data + key_off) : 0;', '\t\t\t\t key, greh->protocol);']}
description: The ip6gre_err function in net/ipv6/ip6_gre.c in the Linux kernel allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via vectors involving GRE flags in an IPv6 packet, which trigger an out-of-bounds access.

code_evidence: grehlen is computed as offset+4, and flags are read from p[0] at skb->data+offset before any length validation of the GRE header.
When GRE_KEY is set, grehlen is incremented; the CSUM branch adds only inside the KEY branch, so the computed key offset does not track the actual header layout.
pskb_may_pull only ensures grehlen bytes are present, then p is re-derived at skb->data+offset.
The key is read as *(((__be32 *)p) + (grehlen/4) - 1), indexing relative to offset using grehlen, which includes offset, reaching past the validated region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory beyond the validated buffer boundary via a miscomputed pointer, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is a read, not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.

evidence_lines.code:
int grehlen = offset + 4;
flags = p[0];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the key access computes its pointer from grehlen, which already includes the IPv6 offset, and is validated against a length that does not account for the actual key position. Trigger: a remote IPv6 packet with GRE_KEY set in the GRE flags. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of roughly 40 bytes beyond the intended point, potentially reading adjacent memory.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. The 9p filesystem did not protect i_size_write() properly, which causes an i_size_read() infinite loop and denial of service on SMP systems.

code_evidence: The function takes inode->i_lock, snapshots inode->i_size into i_size, calls v9fs_stat2inode_dotl(st, inode), and then restores inode->i_size via a plain assignment under the lock. Because the size is written directly (inode->i_size = i_size) rather than through i_size_write(), the seqcount used by i_size_read() is not updated consistently, so concurrent readers in generic_fillattr() can spin in read_seqcount_begin().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The observable failure is a read_seqcount_begin() loop whose exit condition is never reached, matching CWE-835's unreachable-exit-condition infinite loop. It is not merely a race/data-integrity issue (CWE-362) because the demonstrated impact is the non-terminating loop and resulting lockup.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the inode size is mutated with a plain store while only i_lock is held, bypassing the i_size_write() seqcount protocol. Trigger: concurrent v9fs_vfs_getattr/v9fs_vfs_getattr_dotl calls on 32-bit SMP race with this refresh path, and a reader's seqcount retry loop never observes a stable value. Consequence: CPU-bound infinite loop and soft lockup (denial of service).

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.0552: crash when using NUL in buffer that uses :source

Problem:    Crash when using NUL in buffer that uses :source.
Solution:   Don't get a next line when skipping over NL.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    *getnext = TRUE;'], 'added_lines': ['\t    *getnext = *p != NL;']}
description: NULL Pointer Dereference in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0552.

code_evidence: When *p == NL, next is set from newline_skip_comments(p); otherwise from getline_peek_skip_comments or peek_next_line_from_context. The NULL check at line 20 guards only the return of skipwhite(next); the changed line 22 sets *getnext = TRUE unconditionally when next != NULL, signaling the caller to advance to a next line.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's incorrect *getnext flag causes a downstream NULL pointer dereference, matching CWE-476's expectation of a valid pointer that is actually NULL. The fix conditions the flag on *p != NL, confirming the flag/NULL-line mismatch is the defect, not merely a bounds check (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller is told a next line exists (*getnext = TRUE) even when the current pointer is at a NL and the peeked line is NULL, so the caller advances past the buffer end and dereferences a NULL line pointer. Trigger: a buffer using :source containing a NUL/NL boundary. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix race condition when creating/rotating keys (#123)

When we create/rotate keys using either the tangd-keygen and
tangd-rotate-keys helpers, there is a small window between the
keys being created and then the proper ownership permissions being
set. This also happens when there are no keys and tang creates a
pair of keys itself.

In certain situations, such as the keys directory having wide open
permissions, a user with local access could exploit this race
condition and read the keys before they are set to more restrictive
permissions.

To prevent this issue, we now set the default umask to 0337 before
creating the files, so that they are already created with restrictive
permissions; afterwards, we set the proper ownership as usual.

Issue reported by Brian McDermott of CENSUS labs.

Fixes CVE-2023-1672


Reviewed-by: Sergio Arroutbi <sarroutb@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Sergio Correia <scorreia@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    /* Set default umask for file creation. */', '    umask(0337);']}
description: A race condition exists in the Tang server functionality for key generation and key rotation. This flaw results in a small time window where Tang private keys become readable by other processes on the same host.

code_evidence: create_new_keys writes each private JWK to disk with json_dump_file(jwk, path, 0), creating the file with default process umask, and only afterwards calls chmod(path, S_IRUSR | S_IRGRP) to restrict permissions. Between these two operations the file exists with the process's default permissions, so a concurrent local process can open and read the key material within that window.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a race condition: an interfering code sequence accesses the shared resource (the key file) in a timing window before the original sequence completes its exclusive setup, violating atomicity. CWE-362 fits because the flaw is the non-atomic create-then-chmod sequence, not merely weak permissions.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the private key file is created and made readable before its restrictive permissions are applied, so creation and permission-setting are not atomic. Trigger: a local process opens the key path during the interval between json_dump_file and chmod, especially when the umask leaves the file group/world-readable. Supported consequence: disclosure of Tang private keys to an unauthorized local reader.

commit_msg:
libelf: fix stack memory leak when loading 32 bit symbol tables

The 32 bit Elf structs are smaller than the 64 bit ones, which means that
when loading them there's some padding left uninitialized at the end of each
struct (because the size indicated in e_ehsize and e_shentsize is
smaller than the size of elf_ehdr and elf_shdr).

Fix this by introducing a new helper that is used to set
[caller_]xdest_{base/size} and that takes care of performing the appropriate
memset of the region. This newly introduced helper is then used to set and
unset xdest_{base/size} in elf_load_bsdsyms. Now that the full struct
is zeroed, there's no need to specifically zero the undefined section.

This is CVE-2016-9384 / XSA-164.

Suggested-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>

Also remove the open coded (and redundant with the earlier
elf_memset_unchecked()) use of caller_xdest_* from elf_init().

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <Ian.Jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    elf->caller_xdest_base = NULL;', '    elf->caller_xdest_size = 0;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: Buffer overflow in hw/pt-msi.c in Xen 4.6.x and earlier, when using the qemu-xen-traditional (aka qemu-dm) device model, allows local x86 HVM guest administrators to gain privileges by leveraging a system with access to a passed-through MSI-X capable physical PCI device and MSI-X table entries, related to a "write path."

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only zeroes the struct and performs bounds-checked ELF header/section offset validation; the removed caller_xdest initialization is redundant with the earlier memset and no out-of-bounds buffer operation is present in this function.

commit_msg: fix some exploitable overflows (#994, #997)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (op->layer_count > ARRAY_LENGTH(op->layers_info))', '\t\t\treturn GF_NON_COMPLIANT_BITSTREAM;']}
description: GPAC MP4Box version 0.7.1 and earlier contains a Buffer Overflow vulnerability in src/isomedia/avc_ext.c lines 2417 to 2420 that can result in Heap chunks being modified, this could lead to RCE. This attack appear to be exploitable via an attacker supplied MP4 file that when run by the victim may result in RCE.

code_evidence: Line 27 reads an attacker-controlled layer_count (u8) from the bitstream and stores it without any bounds check. Line 28 uses that count as the loop bound, and lines 29-32 write into op->layers_info[j] for each iteration. If layer_count exceeds the fixed capacity of the layers_info array, the writes go past the array's end, corrupting adjacent heap memory within the allocated LHEVC_OperatingPoint.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs writes to a memory buffer (layers_info) beyond its intended boundary due to the missing bound check on layer_count. This is a buffer-bounds violation with integrity/availability impact, matching the CWE-119 class of operations outside buffer boundaries.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the untrusted layer_count value read at line 27 is used directly as the loop bound for indexing the fixed-size layers_info array. Trigger: a crafted MP4 bitstream supplies a layer_count larger than the array capacity. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap writes through op->layers_info[j], allowing heap chunk modification and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix jpeg_skip_scanlines() segfault w/merged upsamp

The additional segfault mentioned in #244 was due to the fact that
the merged upsamplers use a different private structure than the
non-merged upsamplers.  jpeg_skip_scanlines() was assuming the latter, so
when merged upsampling was enabled, jpeg_skip_scanlines() clobbered one
of the IDCT method pointers in the merged upsampler's private structure.

For reasons unknown, the test image in #441 did not encounter this
segfault (too small?), but it encountered an issue similar to the one
fixed in 5bc43c7821df982f65aa1c738f67fbf7cba8bd69, whereby it was
necessary to set up a dummy postprocessing function in
read_and_discard_scanlines() when merged upsampling was enabled.
Failing to do so caused either a segfault in merged_2v_upsample() (due
to a NULL pointer being passed to jcopy_sample_rows()) or an error
("Corrupt JPEG data: premature end of data segment"), depending on the
number of scanlines skipped and whether the first scanline skipped was
an odd- or even-numbered row.

Fixes #441
Fixes #244 (for real this time)

description: A crafted input file could cause a null pointer dereference in jcopy_sample_rows() when processed by libjpeg-turbo.

code_evidence: Line 8 casts cinfo->upsample to my_upsample_ptr and stores it in upsample; lines 15-18 then dereference upsample to fetch Cr_r_tab, Cb_b_tab, Cr_g_tab and Cb_g_tab.

Lines 23-26 read input_buf[0..2][in_row_group_ctr] and output_buf[0] into inptr0/1/2 and outptr, which are later dereferenced in the pixel loop; these buffers are populated by the upsampler's private structure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is a type-confused struct cast leading to invalid/NULL pointers that are subsequently dereferenced, matching CWE-476. It is not a mere out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); the reported failure is dereferencing a NULL pointer passed to jcopy_sample_rows().
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function assumes cinfo->upsample points to a my_upsample_struct, but merged upsampling uses a different private layout. Casting to the wrong type makes the tab pointers at lines 15-18 read fields from the wrong struct, so downstream buffer setup (lines 23-26) receives NULL or invalid pointers, and jcopy_sample_rows() dereferences NULL. Trigger: crafted input with merged upsampling and skipped scanlines. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Made some changes to the I/O stream library for memory streams.
There were a number of potential problems due to the possibility
of integer overflow.
Changed some integral types to the larger types size_t or ssize_t.
For example, the function mem_resize now takes the buffer size parameter
as a size_t.
Added a new function jas_stream_memopen2, which takes a
buffer size specified as a size_t instead of an int.
This can be used in jas_image_cmpt_create to avoid potential
overflow problems.

Added a new function jas_deprecated to warn about reliance on
deprecated library behavior.

commit_msg:
drm/ttm: fix out-of-bounds read in ttm_put_pages() v2

When ttm_put_pages() tries to figure out whether it's dealing with
transparent hugepages, it just reads past the bounds of the pages array
without a check.

v2: simplify the test if enough pages are left in the array (Christian).

Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Christian König <christian.koenig@amd.com>
Fixes: 5c42c64f7d54 ("drm/ttm: fix the fix for huge compound pages")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reviewed-by: Michel Dänzer <michel.daenzer@amd.com>
Reviewed-by: Junwei Zhang <Jerry.Zhang@amd.com>
Reviewed-by: Huang Rui <ray.huang@amd.com>
Signed-off-by: Alex Deucher <alexander.deucher@amd.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (!(flags & TTM_PAGE_FLAG_DMA32)) {', '\t\twhile (i < npages) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (!(flags & TTM_PAGE_FLAG_DMA32) &&', '\t\t\t    (npages - i) >= HPAGE_PMD_NR) {', '\t\twhile ((npages - i) >= HPAGE_PMD_NR) {']}
description: In the Linux kernel 5.0.0-rc7 (as distributed in ubuntu/linux.git on kernel.ubuntu.com), mounting a crafted f2fs filesystem image and performing some operations can lead to slab-out-of-bounds read access in ttm_put_pages in drivers/gpu/drm/ttm/ttm_page_alloc.c. This is related to the vmwgfx or ttm module.

code_evidence: At [22-25], when CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE is enabled and the DMA32 flag is clear, the loop iterates j from 0 to HPAGE_PMD_NR-1 and dereferences pages[i + j] without first ensuring that i + HPAGE_PMD_NR <= npages, so the read can extend past the end of the pages array.

At [46-53], the second loop is guarded only by i < npages; it reads pages[i] and then pages[i + j] for j < HPAGE_PMD_NR, so for a tail of fewer than HPAGE_PMD_NR pages the compound-page check reads beyond npages.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads pages[i + j] beyond the bounds of the supplied pages buffer; this is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), not a write or a null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the transparent-hugepage detection compares up to HPAGE_PMD_NR consecutive entries starting at index i but does not verify that i + HPAGE_PMD_NR is within npages. Trigger: ttm_put_pages receives a page count that is not a multiple of HPAGE_PMD_NR (or a short tail in the huge pool path), and the hugepage branch scans past the array end. Supported consequence: slab out-of-bounds read of adjacent memory, potentially leaking page data or crashing the kernel.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.19.3. crypto_report_one() and related functions in crypto/crypto_user.c (the crypto user configuration API) do not fully initialize structures that are copied to userspace, potentially leaking sensitive memory to user programs. commit_msg:
net: mpls: fix stale pointer if allocation fails during device rename

lianhui reports that when MPLS fails to register the sysctl table
under new location (during device rename) the old pointers won't
get overwritten and may be freed again (double free).

Handle this gracefully. The best option would be unregistering
the MPLS from the device completely on failure, but unfortunately
mpls_ifdown() can fail. So failing fully is also unreliable.

Another option is to register the new table first then only
remove old one if the new one succeeds. That requires more
code, changes order of notifications and two tables may be
visible at the same time.

sysctl point is not used in the rest of the code - set to NULL
on failures and skip unregister if already NULL.

Reported-by: lianhui tang <bluetlh@gmail.com>
Fixes: 0fae3bf018d9 ("mpls: handle device renames for per-device sysctls")
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tmdev->sysctl = NULL;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 6.1.13, there is a double free in net/mpls/af_mpls.c upon an allocation failure (for registering the sysctl table under a new location) during the renaming of a device.

code_evidence: Line 17 stores the result of register_net_sysctl in mdev->sysctl; when it returns NULL, line 18-19 jumps to free, which kfree()s table at line 23 but leaves mdev->sysctl unchanged.
The out path at lines 24-25 returns -ENOBUFS without clearing mdev->sysctl, so the stale pointer persists after the failed registration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale mdev->sysctl value causes the same sysctl table to be freed twice, matching CWE-415 (double free). This is not merely a NULL-pointer dereference; the core defect is repeated freeing of the same address.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on allocation/registration failure the function frees the table but does not reset mdev->sysctl, leaving a dangling pointer. When this runs during device rename, later cleanup can unregister/free the same stale sysctl table again, producing a double free. The fix sets mdev->sysctl = NULL on the failure path so subsequent unregister is skipped.

* libtiff/tif_next.c: fix potential out-of-bound write in NeXTDecode()
triggered by http://lcamtuf.coredump.cx/afl/vulns/libtiff5.tif

commit_msg:
i2c: fix stack buffer overflow vulnerability in i2c md command

When running "i2c md 0 0 80000100", the function do_i2c_md parses the
length into an unsigned int variable named length. The value is then
moved to a signed variable:

    int nbytes = length;
    #define DISP_LINE_LEN 16
    int linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;
    ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);

On systems where integers are 32 bits wide, 0x80000100 is a negative
value to "nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN" is false and linebytes gets assigned
0x80000100 instead of 16.

The consequence is that the function which reads from the i2c device
(dm_i2c_read or i2c_read) is called with a 16-byte stack buffer to fill
but with a size parameter which is too large. In some cases, this could
trigger a crash. But with some i2c drivers, such as drivers/i2c/nx_i2c.c
(used with "nexell,s5pxx18-i2c" bus), the size is actually truncated to
a 16-bit integer. This is because function i2c_transfer expects an
unsigned short length. In such a case, an attacker who can control the
response of an i2c device can overwrite the return address of a function
and execute arbitrary code through Return-Oriented Programming.

Fix this issue by using unsigned integers types in do_i2c_md. While at
it, make also alen unsigned, as signed sizes can cause vulnerabilities
when people forgot to check that they can be negative.

Signed-off-by: Nicolas Iooss <nicolas.iooss+uboot@ledger.fr>
Reviewed-by: Heiko Schocher <hs@denx.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint\talen;', '\tint\tcount;'], 'added_lines': ['\tuint\talen;', '\tuint\tcount;']}
description: In Das U-Boot through 2022.07-rc5, an integer signedness error and resultant stack-based buffer overflow in the "i2c md" command enables the corruption of the return address pointer of the do_i2c_md function.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The provided function is do_i2c_crc, which only reads one byte at a time into a single uchar; it contains no stack buffer write and no signed-size-to-read-length flow, so it does not support the target out-of-bounds write.

Fixes out of array accesses

commit_msg:
x86/vpt: fix race when migrating timers between vCPUs

The current vPT code will migrate the emulated timers between vCPUs
(change the pt->vcpu field) while just holding the destination lock,
either from create_periodic_time or pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target if
the global target is adjusted. Changing the periodic_timer vCPU field
in this way creates a race where a third party could grab the lock in
the unlocked region of pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target (or before
create_periodic_time performs the vcpu change) and then release the
lock from a different vCPU, creating a locking imbalance.

Introduce a per-domain rwlock in order to protect periodic_time
migration between vCPU lists. Taking the lock in read mode prevents
any timer from being migrated to a different vCPU, while taking it in
write mode allows performing migration of timers across vCPUs. The
per-vcpu locks are still used to protect all the other fields from the
periodic_timer struct.

Note that such migration shouldn't happen frequently, and hence
there's no performance drop as a result of such locking.

This is XSA-336.

Reported-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Tested-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    spin_lock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock);', '    spin_unlock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    write_lock(&v->domain->arch.hvm.pl_time->pt_migrate);', '    write_unlock(&v->domain->arch.hvm.pl_time->pt_migrate);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There is a race condition when migrating timers between x86 HVM vCPUs. When migrating timers of x86 HVM guests between its vCPUs, the locking model used allows for a second vCPU of the same guest (also operating on the timers) to release a lock that it didn't acquire. The most likely effect of the issue is a hang or crash of the hypervisor, i.e., a Denial of Service (DoS). All versions of Xen are affected. Only x86 systems are vulnerable. Arm systems are not vulnerable. Only x86 HVM guests can leverage the vulnerability. x86 PV and PVH cannot leverage the vulnerability. Only guests with more than one vCPU can exploit the vulnerability.

code_evidence: create_periodic_time acquires only the per-vCPU spin_lock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock) at line 15, then writes the timer's owning vCPU via pt->vcpu = v at line 27 and links the timer into that vCPU's tm_list at line 47 before releasing the same per-vCPU lock at line 50. The commit states the timer can be migrated between vCPUs (pt->vcpu changed) by create_periodic_time or pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target while only the destination lock is held, so a third party can acquire the lock in the unlocked region and later release it from a different vCPU.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function manipulates a shared resource (periodic_timer and its vCPU list membership) under insufficient synchronization, leaving a timing window where a concurrent code sequence violates exclusivity/atomicity, matching CWE-362. This is a race on lock ownership rather than merely missing a lock on one field.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: timer migration between vCPU lists is protected only by a per-vCPU lock, not a domain-wide lock, so the lock protecting pt->vcpu and tm_list membership is not exclusive against concurrent migration. Trigger: a second vCPU of the same HVM guest operates on the timers during migration, acquiring/releasing the lock inconsistently. Supported consequence: locking imbalance leading to hypervisor hang or crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
kvm: x86: Check memopp before dereference (CVE-2016-8630)

Commit 41061cdb98 ("KVM: emulate: do not initialize memopp") removes a
check for non-NULL under incorrect assumptions. An undefined instruction
with a ModR/M byte with Mod=0 and R/M-5 (e.g. 0xc7 0x15) will attempt
to dereference a null pointer here.

Fixes: 41061cdb98a0bec464278b4db8e894a3121671f5
Message-Id: <1477592752-126650-2-git-send-email-osh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Owen Hofmann <osh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (ctxt->rip_relative)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (ctxt->rip_relative && likely(ctxt->memopp))']}
description: The x86_decode_insn function in arch/x86/kvm/emulate.c in the Linux kernel before 4.8.7, when KVM is enabled, allows local users to cause a denial of service (host OS crash) via a certain use of a ModR/M byte in an undefined instruction.

code_evidence: Line 10 initializes ctxt->memopp to NULL. decode_operand at lines 200-206 may leave ctxt->memopp NULL for an undefined instruction whose ModR/M byte has Mod=0 and R/M=5, which sets ctxt->rip_relative without allocating a memory operand. Line 207 then tests only ctxt->rip_relative and line 208 unconditionally dereferences ctxt->memopp->addr.mem.ea, writing the masked effective address through the NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but left NULL, matching CWE-476. This is a NULL pointer dereference, not a general invalid-pointer or type-confusion issue, because the pointer is explicitly initialized to NULL and never reassigned on this path.

Trigger: an undefined instruction with ModR/M Mod=0, R/M=5 (e.g. 0xc7 0x15) sets rip_relative while memopp remains NULL. Supported consequence: a NULL write in the host kernel, crashing the host (DoS).

commit_msg:
The Xv query functions for adaptors and encodings suffer from out of
boundary accesses if a hostile X server sends a maliciously crafted
response.

A previous fix already checks the received length against fixed values
but ignores additional length specifications which are stored inside
the received data.

These lengths are accessed in a for-loop. The easiest way to guarantee
a correct processing is by validating all lengths against the
remaining size left before accessing referenced memory.

This makes the previously applied check obsolete, therefore I removed
it.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["        /* If there's no encodings, there's nothing more to do. */", '    if (size < (rep.num_encodings * sz_xvEncodingInfo)) {', "        /* If there's not enough data for the number of adaptors,", '           then we have a problem. */', '        status = XvBadReply;', '        goto out;', '    }', '    u.buffer = buffer;', ''], 'added_lines': ['    char *end;', "        /* If there are no encodings, there's nothing more to do. */", '    u.buffer = buffer;', '    end = buffer + size;', '        if (u.buffer + sz_xvEncodingInfo > end) {', '            status = XvBadReply;', '            goto out;', '        }', '        if (u.buffer + size > end) {', '            status = XvBadReply;', '            goto out;', '        }']}
description: The (1) XvQueryAdaptors and (2) XvQueryEncodings functions in X.org libXv before 1.0.11 allow remote X servers to trigger out-of-bounds memory access operations via vectors involving length specifications in received data.

code_evidence: The loop iterates rep.num_encodings times and dereferences u.pe fields (encoding, width, height, rate, name_size) without checking that u.buffer plus sz_xvEncodingInfo stays within the received reply of size bytes.

After reading name_size, u.buffer is advanced by pad_to_int32(sz_xvEncodingInfo) and strncpy copies name_size bytes from u.string without verifying that u.buffer plus size remains within the buffer; name_size comes from the hostile reply.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs reads outside the intended bounds of the received memory buffer due to missing length validation. This is a buffer bounds weakness rather than a pure integer issue, since the unchecked name_size directly drives out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the received reply length is trusted only against a fixed per-encoding size, while the variable name_size and loop count are not validated against remaining buffer space. Trigger: a malicious X server returns a short reply or oversized name_size. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads of the reply buffer during field access and strncpy, potentially crashing or leaking memory.

commit_msg:
coredump: fix race condition between mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and core dumping

The core dumping code has always run without holding the mmap_sem for
writing, despite that is the only way to ensure that the entire vma
layout will not change from under it.  Only using some signal
serialization on the processes belonging to the mm is not nearly enough.
This was pointed out earlier.  For example in Hugh's post from Jul 2017:

  https://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.LSU.2.11.1707191716030.2055@eggly.anvils

  "Not strictly relevant here, but a related note: I was very surprised
   to discover, only quite recently, how handle_mm_fault() may be called
   without down_read(mmap_sem) - when core dumping. That seems a
   misguided optimization to me, which would also be nice to correct"

In particular because the growsdown and growsup can move the
vm_start/vm_end the various loops the core dump does around the vma will
not be consistent if page faults can happen concurrently.

Pretty much all users calling mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and then
taking the mmap_sem had the potential to introduce unexpected side
effects in the core dumping code.

Adding mmap_sem for writing around the ->core_dump invocation is a
viable long term fix, but it requires removing all copy user and page
faults and to replace them with get_dump_page() for all binary formats
which is not suitable as a short term fix.

For the time being this solution manually covers the places that can
confuse the core dump either by altering the vma layout or the vma flags
while it runs.  Once ->core_dump runs under mmap_sem for writing the
function mmget_still_valid() can be dropped.

Allowing mmap_sem protected sections to run in parallel with the
coredump provides some minor parallelism advantage to the swapoff code
(which seems to be safe enough by never mangling any vma field and can
keep doing swapins in parallel to the core dumping) and to some other
corner case.

In order to facilitate the backporting I added "Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6"
however the side effect of this same race condition in /proc/pid/mem
should be reproducible since before 2.6.12-rc2 so I couldn't add any
other "Fixes:" because there's no hash beyond the git genesis commit.

Because find_extend_vma() is the only location outside of the process
context that could modify the "mm" structures under mmap_sem for
reading, by adding the mmget_still_valid() check to it, all other cases
that take the mmap_sem for reading don't need the new check after
mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm().  The expand_stack() in page fault
context also doesn't need the new check, because all tasks under core
dumping are frozen.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190325224949.11068-1-aarcange@redhat.com
Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6 ("userfaultfd: add new syscall to provide memory externalization")
Signed-off-by: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Peter Xu <peterx@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Rapoport <rppt@linux.ibm.com>
Reviewed-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@mellanox.com>
Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!prev || expand_stack(prev, addr))'], 'added_lines': ["\t/* don't alter vm_end if the coredump is running */", '\tif (!prev || !mmget_still_valid(mm) || expand_stack(prev, addr))']}
description: The coredump implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10 does not use locking or other mechanisms to prevent vma layout or vma flags changes while it runs, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information, cause a denial of service, or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a race condition with mmget_not_zero or get_task_mm calls. This is related to fs/userfaultfd.c, mm/mmap.c, fs/proc/task_mmu.c, and drivers/infiniband/core/uverbs_main.c.

code_evidence: find_extend_vma() looks up the VMA for addr and, when the address falls in a gap, calls expand_stack(prev, addr) to grow the previous VMA's vm_end. The checked-out version performs this modification with no validation that the mm is still valid for concurrent access; the added mmget_still_valid(mm) guard is absent, so expand_stack can alter the vma layout while a coredump is iterating it. The VM_LOCKED branch then populates the expanded range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is a missing lock/validity check around a shared resource (the mm's VMA layout), allowing unsynchronized state change during coredump, matching CWE-667 Improper Locking. It is not merely a stale-pointer issue; the defect is the absent synchronization guard on expand_stack.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the VMA layout is mutated by expand_stack without synchronizing against the core-dumping reader, which does not hold mmap_sem for writing. Trigger: a local user causes a page fault/grow-down in a VMA gap concurrently with a coredump of the same mm. Consequence: the coredump's vma traversal becomes inconsistent, supporting information disclosure or denial of service.

Input: ims-psu - check if CDC union descriptor is sane

Before trying to use CDC union descriptor, try to validate whether that it
is sane by checking that intf->altsetting->extra is big enough and that
descriptor bLength is not too big and not too small.

Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Dmitry Torokhov <dmitry.torokhov@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\twhile (buflen > 0) {', '\t\t\treturn union_desc;'], 'added_lines': ['\twhile (buflen >= sizeof(*union_desc)) {', '', '\t\tif (union_desc->bLength > buflen) {', '\t\t\tdev_err(&intf->dev, "Too large descriptor\\n");', '\t\t\treturn NULL;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\t\tif (union_desc->bLength >= sizeof(*union_desc))', '\t\t\t\treturn union_desc;', '', '\t\t\tdev_err(&intf->dev,', '\t\t\t\t"Union descriptor to short (%d vs %zd\\n)",', '\t\t\t\tunion_desc->bLength, sizeof(*union_desc));', '\t\t\treturn NULL;']}
description: The ims_pcu_get_cdc_union_desc function in drivers/input/misc/ims-pcu.c in the Linux kernel through 4.13.11 allows local users to cause a denial of service (ims_pcu_parse_cdc_data out-of-bounds read and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted USB device.

code_evidence: The loop condition only checks buflen > 0, so the buffer may hold fewer bytes than a full usb_cdc_union_desc before the cast and field reads occur.

The code dereferences union_desc->bDescriptorType and bDescriptorSubType without first verifying that the descriptor's bLength is at least sizeof(*union_desc) or that enough bytes remain in the buffer.

bLength is attacker-controlled and is subtracted from buflen and added to buf; a small or zero bLength can leave the loop reading fields from the buffer tail or looping without progress, and a large bLength can make buflen underflow.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe dereferences read memory beyond the intended descriptor buffer extent. This is a bounds-checking omission leading to an out-of-bounds read, not a write or integer-only issue.

evidence_lines.code:
while (buflen > 0) {
union_desc = (struct usb_cdc_union_desc *)buf;

buflen -= union_desc->bLength;
buf += union_desc->bLength;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser trusts the USB-provided bLength and reads descriptor fields without ensuring the remaining buffer is large enough. A crafted USB device's extra descriptor data triggers reads past the end of the altsetting->extra buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and a kernel crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
mlx4_en: Fix out of bounds array access

When searching for a free entry in either mlx4_register_vlan() or
mlx4_register_mac(), and there is no free entry, the loop terminates without
updating the local variable free thus causing out of array bounds access. Fix
this by adding a proper check outside the loop.

Signed-off-by: Eli Cohen <eli@mellanox.co.il>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t}', '', '\tif (free < 0) {', '\t\terr = -ENOMEM;', '\t\tgoto out;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 2.6.37, an out of bounds array access happened in drivers/net/mlx4/port.c. When searching for a free entry in either mlx4_register_vlan() or mlx4_register_mac(), and there is no free entry, the loop terminates without updating the local variable free thus causing out of array bounds access.

code_evidence: free is initialized to -1 and only updated inside the loop when an empty slot is found. If every entry from MLX4_VLAN_REGULAR to MLX4_MAX_VLAN_NUM is occupied, the loop ends without setting free. The total==max check is the only guard before indexing, and total may not reflect a full refs table (e.g., entries reserved or refs inconsistent), so table->refs[free] and table->entries[free] are written with index -1.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function indexes memory arrays with an unvalidated negative index, producing reads/writes outside the intended buffer, which is the core of CWE-119. A related weakness such as CWE-129 (improper validation of array index) describes the cause, but the supported operation-level defect is an out-of-bounds buffer access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the search loop can terminate with free still -1, and the subsequent bounds guard relies on table->total rather than free itself. Trigger: a lookup/registration where no free slot exists but total != max. Consequence: out-of-bounds write/read at index -1 on the refs/entries arrays, corrupting adjacent memory.

wr_buf = kcalloc(wr_buf_size, sizeof(char), GFP_KERNEL);

commit_msg:
tcp: fix use after free in tcp_xmit_retransmit_queue()

When tcp_sendmsg() allocates a fresh and empty skb, it puts it at the
tail of the write queue using tcp_add_write_queue_tail()

Then it attempts to copy user data into this fresh skb.

If the copy fails, we undo the work and remove the fresh skb.

Unfortunately, this undo lacks the change done to tp->highest_sack and
we can leave a dangling pointer (to a freed skb)

Later, tcp_xmit_retransmit_queue() can dereference this pointer and
access freed memory. For regular kernels where memory is not unmapped,
this might cause SACK bugs because tcp_highest_sack_seq() is buggy,
returning garbage instead of tp->snd_nxt, but with various debug
features like CONFIG_DEBUG_PAGEALLOC, this can crash the kernel.

This bug was found by Marco Grassi thanks to syzkaller.

Fixes: 6859d49475d4 ("[TCP]: Abstract tp->highest_sack accessing & point to next skb")
Reported-by: Marco Grassi <marco.gra@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>

commit_msg:
Q.931: fix use-after-free (write) of "q931_pi"

The dissect_q931_number_ie (and indirectly dissect_q931_cause_ie_unsafe)
write to the "q931_pi" structure which seems private to the q931
dissector, but can in fact be called through other dissectors (isup) as
well. Normally this structure is initialized in "dissect_q931_pdu" and
invalidated at the end of the function, but a malformed packet can
prevent the cleanup. In the next packet, a different dissector can thus
trigger a use-after-free via "dissect_q931_number_ie".

Rename "dissect_q931_cause_ie_unsafe" since "unsafe" meant that external
dissectors could not call it directly (see commit a83a87e9ca).

Based on commit 197ceddab109, it seems that the intended purpose of the
structure is to provide information to the VoIP Calls dialog, but it
would only be used when called through dissect_q931_pdu. Dissectors like
isup have their own routines to provide call information, but as a
side-effect of code sharing the problematic code path was reached.

description: In Wireshark 2.6.0, 2.4.0 to 2.4.6, and 2.2.0 to 2.2.14, the Q.931 dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-q931.c by avoiding a use-after-free after a malformed packet prevented certain cleanup.

code_evidence: The function writes to the file-scope q931_pi->calling_number and q931_pi->called_number whenever have_valid_q931_pi is set, without receiving q931_pi as a parameter or verifying the structure is still live; the diff replaces this global validity flag with a passed-in q931_pi pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits: the code writes to memory via q931_pi after it may have been freed, and the trigger is a malformed packet preventing invalidation. This is a use-after-free, not a mere null dereference, because the pointer still references freed memory rather than being absent.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dereferences the shared q931_pi pointer guarded only by have_valid_q931_pi, whose validity is established in dissect_q931_pdu and cleared at its end; a malformed packet can skip that cleanup, leaving the flag set while the structure is freed. A later packet from another dissector (e.g., isup) calls this function and writes through the dangling pointer, causing a use-after-free write that can crash or corrupt memory.

description: A remote code execution vulnerability in libavc in Mediaserver could enable an attacker using a specially crafted file to cause memory corruption during media file and data processing. This issue is rated as Critical due to the possibility of remote code execution within the context of the Mediaserver process. Product: Android. Versions: 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1.1. Android ID: A-34097866.

code_evidence: The removed guard `if(ps_dec->u1_first_slice_in_stream)` previously gated the block at lines 222-226. After the patch the block executes unconditionally, so lines 223-225 write `*ps_cur_pic` into `ps_init_dpb[0][0]` and `ps_init_dpb[0][MAX_REF_BUFS]` even when `u1_first_slice_in_stream` is false, i.e., for pictures after the first slice/stream.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unconditional copy into fixed DPB reference slots causes reference buffers to be overwritten outside their intended initialization condition, producing out-of-bounds memory operations on reference data. This matches CWE-119's out-of-bounds buffer access; the defect is not merely a null-pointer or type issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the conditional that limited default reference-buffer initialization to the first slice in the stream was deleted, so every picture overwrites the initial DPB reference entries. Trigger: a crafted H.264 stream with multiple pictures/slices reaches this block. Consequence: reference-picture structures are overwritten with the current picture, and later motion/reference access can read or write outside the intended reference buffer, enabling memory corruption and possible code execution in Mediaserver.

Added an extra check to MLU bounds

Thanks to Ibrahim el-sayed for spotting the bug
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if ((Offset + Len) > SizeOfTag + 8) goto Error;']}
description: The Type_MLU_Read function in cmstypes.c in Little CMS (aka lcms2) allows remote attackers to obtain sensitive information or cause a denial of service via an image with a crafted ICC profile, which triggers an out-of-bounds heap read.

code_evidence: Len and Offset are read from the untrusted ICC profile; the only guard requires Offset >= SizeOfHeader+8. BeginOfThisString and EndOfThisString=BeginOfThisString+Len are computed from these attacker-controlled values without checking that the string extent stays within the tag.
LargestPosition drives SizeOfTag, which sizes the heap Block; _cmsReadWCharArray then reads NumOfWchar elements into that buffer based on the unchecked extent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads profile data based on an unchecked computed extent, so it reads past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. It is not a write overflow because the weakness manifests in reading memory beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the tag-string length/offset fields are not bounded against the declared tag size, so EndOfThisString and LargestPosition can exceed the actual profile data. Trigger: a crafted ICC profile with an oversized Len or Offset. Consequence: the read of the string block overruns the intended buffer, exposing heap data or causing a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
The memory stream interface allows for a buffer size of zero.
The case of a zero-sized buffer was not handled correctly, as it could
lead to a double free.
This problem has now been fixed (hopefully).
One might ask whether a zero-sized buffer should be allowed at all,
but this is a question for another day.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tassert(m->buf_);', '\tif (!(buf = jas_realloc2(m->buf_, bufsize, sizeof(unsigned char)))) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t//assert(m->buf_);', '\tif (!(buf = jas_realloc2(m->buf_, bufsize, sizeof(unsigned char))) &&', '\t  bufsize) {']}
description: Double free vulnerability in the mem_close function in jas_stream.c in JasPer before 1.900.10 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted BMP image to the imginfo command.

code_evidence: The function asserts m->buf_ is non-null, then calls jas_realloc2(m->buf_, bufsize, ...). With bufsize==0, realloc may free the old buffer and return NULL; the code treats NULL as failure and returns -1 without updating m->buf_, leaving a dangling pointer that can later be freed again.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 matches because the same memory address can be freed twice: realloc frees it on zero size, and the stale m->buf_ is freed later. This is a double free, not merely a null-pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a zero-sized reallocation returning NULL is conflated with allocation failure, so m->buf_ is not cleared after the underlying buffer is freed. Trigger: mem_resize called with bufsize 0. Consequence: dangling m->buf_ leads to a double free, causing crash or possible code execution.

description: Integer overflow in the php_html_entities function in ext/standard/html.c in PHP before 5.5.36 and 5.6.x before 5.6.22 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a large output string from the htmlspecialchars function.

Trigger: input that expands to more than INT_MAX bytes during htmlspecialchars escaping. Consequence: the wrapped length is passed to the string constructor, producing an inconsistent buffer length that can cause memory corruption, crash or DoS.

commit_msg: Fix struct initialization in formatter
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    buffer->is_token_list              = ZYAN_TRUE;', '    buffer->capacity                   = length;', '    buffer->string.flags               = ZYAN_STRING_HAS_FIXED_CAPACITY;', '    buffer->string.vector.allocator    = ZYAN_NULL;', '    buffer->string.vector.element_size = sizeof(char);', '    buffer->string.vector.size         = 1;', '    buffer->string.vector.capacity     = length;', '    buffer->string.vector.data         = user_buffer;'], 'added_lines': ['    buffer->is_token_list                  = ZYAN_TRUE;', '    buffer->capacity                       = length;', '    buffer->string.flags                   = ZYAN_STRING_HAS_FIXED_CAPACITY;', '    buffer->string.vector.allocator        = ZYAN_NULL;', '    buffer->string.vector.growth_factor    = 1;', '    buffer->string.vector.shrink_threshold = 0;', '    buffer->string.vector.destructor       = ZYAN_NULL;', '    buffer->string.vector.element_size     = sizeof(char);', '    buffer->string.vector.size             = 1;', '    buffer->string.vector.capacity         = length;', '    buffer->string.vector.data             = user_buffer;', '']}
description: Zydis is an x86/x86-64 disassembler library. Users of Zydis versions v3.2.0 and older that use the string functions provided in `zycore` in order to append untrusted user data to the formatter buffer within their custom formatter hooks can run into heap buffer overflows. Older versions of Zydis failed to properly initialize the string object within the formatter buffer, forgetting to initialize a few fields, leaving their value to chance. This could then in turn cause zycore functions like `ZyanStringAppend` to make incorrect calculations for the new target size, resulting in heap memory corruption. This does not affect the regular uncustomized Zydis formatter, because Zydis internally doesn't use the string functions in zycore that act upon these fields. However, because the zycore string functions are the intended way to work with the formatter buffer for users of the library that wish to extend the formatter, we still consider this to be a vulnerability in Zydis. This bug is patched starting in version 3.2.1. As a workaround, users may refrain from using zycore string functions in their formatter hooks until updating to a patched version.

code_evidence: The function initializes the formatter buffer's embedded string/vector by assigning flags, allocator, element_size, size, capacity and data. It never sets the vector's growth_factor, shrink_threshold or destructor fields, so those members keep whatever values the caller's memory contained. The buffer is then handed to users as a usable string for custom formatter hooks.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the code uses/returns a resource whose fields were never initialized, and that uninitialized state is what the downstream string functions consume. This is not a simple out-of-bounds write in this function; the defect is the missing initialization of vector members.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the string vector inside the formatter buffer is only partially initialized; growth_factor, shrink_threshold and destructor are left uninitialized. Trigger: a user calls zycore string functions such as ZyanStringAppend on the formatter buffer. Those functions read the uninitialized fields and compute an incorrect target size, leading to heap buffer overflow and memory corruption.
