description: A stack buffer overflow exists in the ec_glob function of editorconfig-core-c before v0.12.6 which allowed an attacker to arbitrarily write to the stack and possibly allows remote code execution. editorconfig-core-c v0.12.6 resolved this vulnerability by bound checking all write operations over the p_pcre buffer.

code_evidence: Copies the escaped character and the following character into p_pcre via post-increment writes with no check against pcre_str_end.
Writes '[' into p_pcre with no bounds check.
Writes ']' into p_pcre with no bounds check.
Writes '-' into p_pcre with no bounds check.
Writes ')' into p_pcre with no bounds check.
Writes '|' into p_pcre with no bounds check.
Writes an escape backslash and the character into p_pcre with no bounds check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The writes lack any capacity constraint and can write beyond the intended pcre_str buffer, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. The consequence is stack memory corruption rather than merely a read overrun (CWE-125).

evidence_lines.code: *(p_pcre ++) = *c;
*(p_pcre ++) = *c;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: p_pcre advances through the fixed stack buffer pcre_str (2*PATTERN_MAX bytes) as the attacker-controlled pattern is expanded, and these raw post-increment writes never compare p_pcre to pcre_str_end. A long or heavily escaped pattern therefore drives p_pcre past the buffer end, corrupting adjacent stack memory.

commit_msg: fix upgrade check is not using TLS correctly
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        QNetworkRequest request(QUrl("https://check.shotcut.org/version.json"));', '        QSslConfiguration sslConfig = request.sslConfiguration();', '        sslConfig.setPeerVerifyMode(QSslSocket::VerifyNone);', '        request.setSslConfiguration(sslConfig);', '        m_network.get(request);', '        m_network.setStrictTransportSecurityEnabled(false);'], 'added_lines': ['        m_network.get(QNetworkRequest(QUrl("https://check.shotcut.org/version.json")));']}
description: In mainwindow.cpp in Shotcut before 20.09.13, the upgrade check misuses TLS because of setPeerVerifyMode(QSslSocket::VerifyNone). A man-in-the-middle attacker could offer a spoofed download resource.

code_evidence: Builds a QNetworkRequest for the HTTPS upgrade-check URL, extracts its QSslConfiguration, disables certificate verification with setPeerVerifyMode(QSslSocket::VerifyNone), applies it back to the request, and issues the GET via m_network.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-295 covers not validating or incorrectly validating a certificate; VerifyNone directly disables certificate validation on the TLS connection, matching the target. It is distinct from transport-security misconfiguration (e.g. HSTS) because the core defect is absent peer certificate verification.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SSL configuration explicitly sets peer verification to VerifyNone, so the TLS peer certificate is never validated. Trigger: any automatic upgrade check (Settings.checkUpgradeAutomatic() true) makes an HTTPS request to check.shotcut.org. Consequence: a man-in-the-middle can present an untrusted/spoofed certificate and serve a forged version.json, enabling a spoofed download resource.

The trigger is a short Oracle-port packet; the consequence is an out-of-bounds heap read, which can crash or leak adjacent memory.

description: An elevation of privilege vulnerability in the Android media framework (audio hal). Product: Android. Versions: 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2, 8.0. Android ID: A-62873231.

code_evidence: read_frames() writes frames into in->proc_buf_in at an offset computed from in->proc_buf_frames and src_frame_size; the buffer was only reallocated when in->proc_buf_size < frames_num (line 22), not when the byte count frames_num*src_channels*bytes_per_sample exceeds the allocation, so the offset can exceed the buffer.

The memcpy at lines 55-57 reads from in->proc_buf_in + in_buf.frameCount*src_channels*bytes_per_sample for in->proc_buf_frames*src_frame_size bytes, using an in_buf.frameCount supplied by preprocessors without validating that the source range stays within proc_buf_in.
When no preprocessing is active, frames_wr = read_frames(in, proc_buf_out, frames_num) can return a negative error code.
adjust_channels() is then called with frames_wr, which is cast to size_t, turning the negative value into a huge byte count that drives out-of-bounds reads of proc_buf_out.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads from buffers (proc_buf_in, proc_buf_out) at offsets/lengths that can exceed their allocated sizes, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The weakness is a read overrun rather than a write overrun (CWE-787), since the unsafe accesses are reads feeding audio processing/adjust_channels.

evidence_lines.code:
frames_rd = read_frames(in,
in->proc_buf_in +
in->proc_buf_frames * src_channels * bytes_per_sample,
frames_num - in->proc_buf_frames);

frames_wr = read_frames(in, proc_buf_out, frames_num);
ALOG_ASSERT(frames_wr <= frames_num, "read more frames than requested");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The size check compares in->proc_buf_size against frames_num rather than the byte size frames_num*src_frame_size, so reallocation can be skipped and subsequent reads at proc_buf_frames-based offsets exceed the allocated buffer. A preprocessor-reported frameCount can also make the memcpy source range too large. Additionally, a failed read returning negative frames_wr is passed to adjust_channels() as a size_t, causing an enormous out-of-bounds read. Trigger: crafted audio stream/effect metadata; consequence: out-of-bounds memory read.

description: An issue was discovered in OpenSSH before 8.9. If a client is using public-key authentication with agent forwarding but without -oLogLevel=verbose, and an attacker has silently modified the server to support the None authentication option, then the user cannot determine whether FIDO authentication is going to confirm that the user wishes to connect to that server, or that the user wishes to allow that server to connect to a different server on the user's behalf. NOTE: the vendor's position is "this is not an authentication bypass, since nothing is being bypassed.

code_evidence: The auth context is initialized with authctxt.method = authmethod_lookup("none"), selecting the 'none' authentication method as the initial method for the userauth exchange.

After ssh_dispatch_run_fatal completes, success is only checked via if (!authctxt.success); there is no verification of which method actually authenticated the user, and no constraint rejecting the trivial 'none' method before success is accepted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the function does not adequately prove the claimed identity before treating authentication as successful; the missing check on the authenticating method means the authentication claim is insufficiently verified. A related weakness such as improper restriction of authentication attempts is narrower and does not capture the absent proof of identity here.

evidence_lines.code: authctxt.method = authmethod_lookup("none");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accepts completion of the userauth exchange as proof of authentication without constraining the authenticating method, while initializing the context to the 'none' method. Trigger: a server that offers the None authentication option causes success to be set, and the function proceeds to 'Authentication succeeded' without confirming a non-trivial method was used. Consequence: the client cannot distinguish genuine authentication from trivial acceptance, enabling identity/authorization confusion (e.g., agent-forwarding misuse).

description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An out-of-bounds read was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The out-of-bounds read is triggered when Exiv2 is used to print the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. Note that this bug is only triggered when printing the image ICC profile, which is a less frequently used Exiv2 operation that requires an extra command line option (`-p C`). The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: A DataBuf is allocated for subBox.length - sizeof(box) bytes and filled from the input stream [52,53]. For a color-header subBox, the code reads a 4-byte iccLength from data.pData_ + pad without checking that data.size_ is at least pad+4 [61,62,67]. When bICC is set, it then writes iccLength bytes from data.pData_ + pad to the output, with no check that iccLength fits within the allocated buffer [71,72]. A crafted subBox length or attacker-controlled iccLength value drives the read past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unvalidated iccLength is used as the length of a read from a heap buffer, so the read extends past the end of the intended buffer. This is a read-side bounds error, not a write overflow (CWE-787), since the operation only copies data out of the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the color-header branch trusts both the fixed padding offset and the embedded iccLength field without validating them against the actual DataBuf size. Trigger: printing an ICC profile (-p C) on a crafted JP2 file whose color-header subBox is too short or whose iccLength exceeds the remaining buffer. Consequence: out.write reads beyond data.pData_, an out-of-bounds read that can crash Exiv2 (DoS) or leak adjacent memory.

The profile field is changed by code inside and outside the decoder,
its not a reliable indicator of the internal codec state.
Maintaining it consistency with studio_profile is messy.
Its easier to just avoid it and use only studio_profile

commit_msg:
In commit 6a53b7593233 ("xfrm: check id proto in validate_tmpl()")
I introduced a check for xfrm protocol, but according to Herbert
IPSEC_PROTO_ANY should only be used as a wildcard for lookup, so
it should be removed from validate_tmpl().

And, IPSEC_PROTO_ANY is expected to only match 3 IPSec-specific
protocols, this is why xfrm_state_flush() could still miss
IPPROTO_ROUTING, which leads that those entries are left in
net->xfrm.state_all before exit net. Fix this by replacing
IPSEC_PROTO_ANY with zero.

This patch also extracts the check from validate_tmpl() to
xfrm_id_proto_valid() and uses it in parse_ipsecrequest().
With this, no other protocols should be added into xfrm.

Fixes: 6a53b7593233 ("xfrm: check id proto in validate_tmpl()")
Reported-by: syzbot+0bf0519d6e0de15914fe@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Cc: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
Cc: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.19. The XFRM subsystem has a use-after-free, related to an xfrm_state_fini panic, aka CID-dbb2483b2a46.

code_evidence: The function copies the caller-controlled protocol field rq->sadb_x_ipsecrequest_proto directly into the template t->id.proto at line 11 without validating it; only the mode field is checked at line 9-10. No constraint on the protocol value exists before the template is stored and later used by the XFRM state machinery.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch adds xfrm_id_proto_valid() to prevent unvalidated protocols from entering xfrm; the described consequence is a use-after-free (dangling xfrm state references) at teardown, matching CWE-416. This is a missing-input-validation root cause whose supported impact is reuse of freed memory, not merely an invalid-value rejection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: parse_ipsecrequest accepts any protocol value from the userspace sadb_x_ipsecrequest message and stores it in xp->xfrm_vec. Trigger: a crafted PF_KEY message supplies an unexpected/zero protocol. The resulting template can create xfrm states whose protocol does not match the IPSec-specific set, so xfrm_state_flush() fails to remove them, leaving stale state and enabling a use-after-free/panic during xfrm_state_fini at net exit.

description: Envoy is an open source edge and service proxy, designed for cloud-native applications. The default_validator.cc implementation used to implement the default certificate validation routines has a "type confusion" bug when processing subjectAltNames. This processing allows, for example, an rfc822Name or uniformResourceIndicator to be authenticated as a domain name. This confusion allows for the bypassing of nameConstraints, as processed by the underlying OpenSSL/BoringSSL implementation, exposing the possibility of impersonation of arbitrary servers. As a result Envoy will trust upstream certificates that should not be trusted.

code_evidence: The constructor initializes subject_alt_name_matchers_ directly from config.match_subject_alt_names(), copying each configured matcher without assigning or checking a SAN type. No constraint ties the matcher to a specific GeneralName type (e.g., DNS), so the stored matcher list carries no type discrimination.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The resource (a SAN matcher) is initialized without a type and later interpreted as a domain-name matcher, exactly the incompatible-type access CWE-843 describes. This is distinct from a simple missing validation: the weakness is the absence of type tracking, not a failed check on a correctly typed value.

evidence_lines.code:
subject_alt_name_matchers_(config.match_subject_alt_names().begin(),
config.match_subject_alt_names().end()),

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: SAN matchers are built from configuration with no associated name-type, so a matcher intended for one GeneralName kind is later applied as if it were a domain-name matcher. Trigger: a certificate whose subjectAltName holds an rfc822Name or URI that matches the configured value. Consequence: the mismatched type is authenticated as a DNS name, bypassing nameConstraints and enabling impersonation of an arbitrary server.

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: dont unlink connection object twice

A connection object of a domain with associated stubdom has two
parents: the domain and the stubdom. When cleaning up the list of
active domains in domain_cleanup() make sure not to unlink the
connection twice from the same domain. This could happen when the
domain and its stubdom are being destroyed at the same time leading
to the domain loop being entered twice.

Additionally don't use talloc_free() in this case as it will remove
a random parent link, leading eventually to a memory leak. Use
talloc_unlink() instead specifying the context from which the
connection object should be removed.

This is CVE-2017-14317 / XSA-233.

Reported-by: Eric Chanudet <chanudete@ainfosec.com>
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct domain *domain, *tmp;', '\tlist_for_each_entry_safe(domain, tmp, &domains, list) {', '\t\ttalloc_free(domain->conn);', '\t\tnotify = 0; /* destroy_domain() fires the watch */'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct domain *domain;', ' again:', '\tlist_for_each_entry(domain, &domains, list) {', '\t\tif (domain->conn) {', '\t\t\ttalloc_unlink(talloc_autofree_context(), domain->conn);', '\t\t\tdomain->conn = NULL;', '\t\t\tnotify = 0; /* destroy_domain() fires the watch */', '\t\t\tgoto again;', '\t\t}']}
description: A domain cleanup issue was discovered in the C xenstore daemon (aka cxenstored) in Xen through 4.9.x. When shutting down a VM with a stubdomain, a race in cxenstored may cause a double-free. The xenstored daemon may crash, resulting in a DoS of any parts of the system relying on it (including domain creation / destruction, ballooning, device changes, etc.).

code_evidence: The loop iterates the shared global 'domains' list with list_for_each_entry_safe, holding a saved tmp pointer across the body; the body performs xc_domain_getinfo and may continue without unlinking.

The body unconditionally calls talloc_free(domain->conn) for any entry reaching this point, then resets notify; nothing marks the connection as already freed or guards against re-entering cleanup for the same domain/connection while domain destruction proceeds concurrently.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits: concurrent destruction sequences interfere with the shared 'domains' list and connection object, violating exclusivity/atomicity of the cleanup sequence and yielding a double-free crash. It is not merely a memory-management bug; the unsafe operation depends on concurrent modification of shared state.

evidence_lines.code: list_for_each_entry_safe(domain, tmp, &domains, list) {

talloc_free(domain->conn);
notify = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: domain_cleanup() frees domain->conn without a guard or exclusive state, and the safe-iterator's saved tmp pointer can become stale if the shared 'domains' list is modified concurrently by domain/stubdom destruction. Trigger: a VM with a stubdom is shut down so the domain and its stubdom are torn down at the same time, causing the cleanup loop to process the same connection twice. Consequence: double-free of the connection object, crashing cxenstored (DoS).

commit_msg: Fix out of buffer access in #1529
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if (box.length == 1)', '            {', '                // FIXME. Special case. the real box size is given in another place.'], 'added_lines': ['            if (box.length < 8)', '            {', '                // box is broken -> there is nothing we can do here', '                throw Error(kerCorruptedMetadata);']}
description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. A heap buffer overflow was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.3 and earlier. The heap overflow is triggered when Exiv2 is used to write metadata into a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to gain code execution, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. Note that this bug is only triggered when _writing_ the metadata, which is a less frequently used Exiv2 operation than _reading_ the metadata. For example, to trigger the bug in the Exiv2 command-line application, you need to add an extra command-line argument such as `insert`. The bug is fixed in version v0.27.4.

code_evidence: box.length is read directly from the attacker-controlled 8-byte box header via getLong. Only box.length==0 is normalized (line 34-40); the special case box.length==1 at line 42-44 is an empty block that leaves the length unchanged. Line 45 then allocates DataBuf boxBuf(box.length) and immediately does memcpy(boxBuf.pData_, bheaderBuf.pData_, 8) plus io_->read(boxBuf.pData_+8, box.length-8), so a small declared length such as 1 yields a heap buffer smaller than the 8 bytes copied and a negative/underflowed read size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The overflow targets a heap-allocated DataBuf (malloc-backed) and is caused by a missing lower-bound check on a size field, matching CWE-122. It is distinct from a stack overflow since the overwritten buffer is heap-allocated; the fix adds box.length < 8 rejection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the box length field is trusted without enforcing a minimum of 8 bytes (header size). Trigger: a crafted JP2 whose box length is 1 (or any value < 8) during metadata write. Consequence: heap buffer allocated with box.length is overflowed by the 8-byte memcpy and the length-8 read, corrupting heap memory and potentially enabling code execution.

description: If a TLS 1.3 client gets neither a PSK (pre shared key) extension nor a KSE (key share extension) when connecting to a malicious server, a default predictable buffer gets used for the IKM (Input Keying Material) value when generating the session master secret. Using a potentially known IKM value when generating the session master secret key compromises the key generated, allowing an eavesdropper to reconstruct it and potentially allowing access to or meddling with message contents in the session. This issue does not affect client validation of connected servers, nor expose private key information, but could result in an insecure TLS 1.3 session when not controlling both sides of the connection. wolfSSL recommends that TLS 1.3 client side users update the version of wolfSSL used.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function parses TLS key-share/hello-retry extensions and records the negotiated named group; it contains no certificate parsing or certificate validation logic, so it does not support CWE-295.

commit_msg: fixed #2238
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (parser->codec->LastError) return;']}
description: Uncontrolled Recursion in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.1.0-DEV.

code_evidence: The function checks parser->codec->LastError only before calling SFS_Expression (line 3-4), then unconditionally calls SFS_AddString and SFS_Identifier (lines 5-6) without re-checking the error state. The added guard in the patch confirms that SFS_Expression can set LastError, yet the pre-patch code continues parsing after that point.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the function participates in a recursive-descent parse chain (SFS_Expression -> SFS_ObjectMemberAccess) without a post-recursion guard to stop continued recursion; the added LastError check is the termination constraint whose absence enables uncontrolled recursion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing error/termination check after the recursive SFS_Expression call, so parsing continues on a failed or recursive expression path. Trigger: an expression that drives SFS_Expression into repeated object-member-access recursion. Consequence: unbounded recursion consumes stack, leading to resource exhaustion/DoS.

commit_msg:
Kafka: Limit our decompression size.

Don't assume that the Internet has our best interests at heart when it
gives us the size of our decompression buffer. Assign an arbitrary limit
of 50 MB.

This fixes #16739 in that it takes care of

** (process:17681): WARNING **: 20:03:07.440: Dissector bug, protocol Kafka, in packet 31: ../epan/proto.c:7043: failed assertion "end >= fi->start"

which is different from the original error output. It looks like *that*
might have taken care of in one of the other recent Kafka bug fixes.

The decompression routines return a success or failure status. Use
gbooleans instead of ints for that.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int', '            return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['static gboolean', '    if (length > MAX_DECOMPRESSION_SIZE) {', '        expert_add_info(pinfo, NULL, &ei_kafka_bad_decompression_length);', '        return FALSE;', '    }', '            return FALSE;']}
description: Memory leak in Kafka protocol dissector in Wireshark 3.4.0 and 3.2.0 to 3.2.8 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file.

code_evidence: decompress() forwards the caller-supplied guint32 length directly to decompress_snappy/lz4/zstd/gzip/none without any upper bound check; the switch at line 4 dispatches on codec and each case returns the codec routine's result, so an attacker-controlled decompression length reaches the allocation paths in those routines.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length drives allocation in the decompression routines without a bound, enabling resource-consumption/DoS consistent with CWE-401's availability impact; the fix caps length and returns FALSE. It is not a plain integer overflow, since the weakness is unbounded allocation rather than arithmetic wrapping.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the wire-provided decompression length and passes it unchecked to codec decompressors that allocate buffers sized from it. Trigger: a crafted Kafka packet declaring a very large compressed length. Consequence: excessive/attacker-driven allocation leading to memory exhaustion and denial of service; the commit adds a MAX_DECOMPRESSION_SIZE guard for exactly this.

description: GPAC 2.3-DEV-rev605-gfc9e29089-master contains a heap-buffer-overflow in gf_isom_use_compact_size gpac/src/isomedia/isom_write.c:3403:3 in gpac/MP4Box.

code_evidence: When stsz->sampleSize is nonzero, the code frees stsz->sizes and allocates sizeof(u32)*stsz->sampleCount bytes, then memset's the entire allocation using stsz->sampleSize as the fill byte. The allocation size is governed by sampleCount, while the write extent is governed by the byte count derived from sampleCount; the guard only tests sampleSize, not sampleCount, so a zero or inconsistent sampleCount drives the allocation/write size mismatch.

Trigger: a crafted STSZ box with sampleSize set and sampleCount zero (or inconsistent with sizes) reaches this branch. Consequence: gf_malloc(sizeof(u32)*0)/memset writes past the allocated buffer, producing the reported heap-buffer-overflow and potential crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
gsocketclient: Fix criticals

This ensures the parent GTask is kept alive as long as an enumeration
is running and trying to connect.

Closes #1646
Closes #1649
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['enumerator_next_async (GSocketClientAsyncConnectData *data)'], 'added_lines': ['enumerator_next_async (GSocketClientAsyncConnectData *data,', '                       gboolean                       add_task_ref)', '', '  /* Each enumeration takes a ref. This arg just avoids repeated unrefs when', '     an enumeration starts another enumeration */', '  if (add_task_ref)', '    g_object_ref (data->task);']}
description: gio/gsocketclient.c in GNOME GLib 2.59.2 does not ensure that a parent GTask remains alive during the execution of a connection-attempting enumeration, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (g_socket_client_connected_callback mishandling and application crash) via a crafted web site, as demonstrated by GNOME Web (aka Epiphany).

code_evidence: enumerator_next_async clears data->socket, data->proxy_addr and data->connection at the start of each enumeration but performs no reference on data->task before the function returns, so the task's lifetime depends solely on other holders.

The function then starts an asynchronous continuation via g_socket_address_enumerator_next_async, passing data and a cancellable obtained from data->task (g_task_get_cancellable (data->task)); if an enumeration starts another enumeration, the parent GTask may be finalized before the callback g_socket_client_enumerator_callback runs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code assumes the parent GTask remains alive during the asynchronous enumeration and omits the lifetime check/ref needed for this exceptional re-entrant condition, matching CWE-754's improper check for unusual conditions leading to crash; the fix adds g_object_ref when add_task_ref is set.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the enumeration path fails to keep the parent GTask alive across the asynchronous next_async call. Trigger: a connection-attempting enumeration that starts another enumeration, dropping the last reference to data->task. Consequence: the callback later operates on a freed task (g_socket_client_connected_callback mishandling), crashing the application (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow (CVE-2021-21309). (#8522)

On 32-bit systems, setting the proto-max-bulk-len config parameter to a high value may result with integer overflow and a subsequent heap overflow when parsing an input bulk (CVE-2021-21309).

This fix has two parts:

Set a reasonable limit to the config parameter.
Add additional checks to prevent the problem in other potential but unknown code paths.

(cherry picked from commit d32f2e9999ce003bad0bd2c3bca29f64dcce4433)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    assert(initlen + hdrlen + 1 > initlen); /* Catch size_t overflow */']}
description: Redis is an open-source, in-memory database that persists on disk. In affected versions of Redis an integer overflow bug in 32-bit Redis version 4.0 or newer could be exploited to corrupt the heap and potentially result with remote code execution. Redis 4.0 or newer uses a configurable limit for the maximum supported bulk input size. By default, it is 512MB which is a safe value for all platforms. If the limit is significantly increased, receiving a large request from a client may trigger several integer overflow scenarios, which would result with buffer overflow and heap corruption. We believe this could in certain conditions be exploited for remote code execution. By default, authenticated Redis users have access to all configuration parameters and can therefore use the “CONFIG SET proto-max-bulk-len” to change the safe default, making the system vulnerable. **This problem only affects 32-bit Redis (on a 32-bit system, or as a 32-bit executable running on a 64-bit system).** The problem is fixed in version 6.2, and the fix is back ported to 6.0.11 and 5.0.11. Make sure you use one of these versions if you are running 32-bit Redis. An additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent clients from directly executing `CONFIG SET`: Using Redis 6.0 or newer, ACL configuration can be used to block the command. Using older versions, the `rename-command` configuration directive can be used to rename the command to a random string unknown to users, rendering it inaccessible. Please note that this workaround may have an additional impact on users or operational systems that expect `CONFIG SET` to behave in certain ways.

code_evidence: Line 8 computes the allocation size as hdrlen+initlen+1 using size_t arithmetic and passes it directly to s_malloc without any overflow check; if initlen is near SIZE_MAX, the sum wraps to a small value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an addition whose result is assumed larger than its operands and used as an allocation size; wraparound of that size is exactly CWE-190. The heap overflow is the downstream consequence, not the root weakness.

evidence_lines.code: sh = s_malloc(hdrlen+initlen+1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size expression hdrlen+initlen+1 is computed in size_t with no prior bound check, so a large initlen (e.g., a high proto-max-bulk-len on 32-bit systems) wraps to a small allocation. Trigger: sdsnewlen called with a near-SIZE_MAX initlen. Consequence: a small buffer is allocated, then line 51 memcpy(s, init, initlen) and line 52 s[initlen]='\0' write out of bounds, corrupting the heap.

arguments were handled, two memory allocations were made but alas, only
the latter one of them was released. This happened because there was only
a single local variable to hold such a temporary allocation.

Fix this by adding separate variables to hold the pointers to the
temporary allocations.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.11.3 when a webcam device exists. video_usercopy in drivers/media/v4l2-core/v4l2-ioctl.c has a memory leak for large arguments, aka CID-fb18802a338b.

code_evidence: When ioc_size exceeds sizeof(sbuf), a temporary buffer is allocated into mbuf (line 20) and parg is redirected to it; this mbuf is later freed at out (line 82).
For array-argument ioctls, a second allocation overwrites the same local variable mbuf (line 35) and its pointer is stored in *kernel_ptr (line 49), so the earlier ioc_size buffer pointer is lost.
The array path ends with goto out_array_args (line 74), and the only out label frees mbuf (line 82), which now holds the array buffer, leaving the original ioc_size allocation unreleased.
The function returns after kvfree(mbuf) (lines 81-83); no separate pointer exists to release the overwritten allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the function allocates memory whose effective lifetime ends after the ioctl but is never released: the pointer is overwritten before any free. This is a missing release of an allocated buffer, not a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: one local variable mbuf is reused for two distinct kvmalloc allocations when an ioctl has both a large argument (ioc_size > 128) and array arguments. The second allocation at line 35 overwrites the pointer to the first, and the single kvfree at line 82 releases only the array buffer. Trigger: a user-supplied largish ioctl with array arguments, e.g. via a webcam device. Consequence: the ioc_size-sized kernel allocation leaks, allowing repeated calls to exhaust kernel memory (DoS).

commit_msg: Fix #9903 - oobread in RAnal.sh
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!data)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!data || len < 2) {', '\t}']}
description: The sh_op() function in radare2 2.5.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based out-of-bounds read and application crash) via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: The guard only checks for a null data pointer; it does not constrain len, so a buffer shorter than two bytes still reaches the decode path.
op->size is hard-coded to 2, and op_MSB/op_LSB unconditionally read data[0] and data[1]; with len < 2 these reads pass the end of the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads one byte beyond the supplied buffer when len < 2, which matches CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. It is not CWE-476 (null pointer dereference) because data is non-null yet the length constraint is missing.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!data)
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the entry check validates data but not the required minimum length, while the decoder assumes a 2-byte instruction. Trigger: a crafted ELF causes sh_op to be called with len of 0 or 1. Consequence: data[0]/data[1] read out of bounds, yielding a heap out-of-bounds read and possible crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
fixing string check

Signed-off-by: Daniel Wang <daniel.wang@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  char namebuf[128];', '      strcpy(namebuf, inet_ntoa(sin->sin_addr));'], 'added_lines': ['  char namebuf[128] = {};', '      strncpy(namebuf, inet_ntoa(sin->sin_addr), sizeof(namebuf)-1);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the ROS communications-related packages (aka ros_comm or ros-melodic-ros-comm) through 1.14.3. A buffer overflow allows attackers to cause a denial of service and possibly execute arbitrary code via an IP address with a long hostname.

code_evidence: namebuf is a fixed 128-byte stack buffer (line 9). On the AF_INET path, strcpy copies the string returned by inet_ntoa into namebuf without any length check (line 15), so the copy size is unbounded relative to the destination.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a buffer copy (strcpy) into a fixed destination without validating the input length, matching CWE-120's definition. The sibling AF_INET6 path uses inet_ntop with sizeof(namebuf), and the patch replaces strcpy with strncpy, confirming the missing size constraint rather than an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence_lines.code:
char namebuf[128];
strcpy(namebuf, inet_ntoa(sin->sin_addr));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unchecked strcpy into the fixed-size namebuf. Trigger: an AF_INET peer address whose textual form exceeds 127 bytes plus terminator, so strcpy writes past the stack buffer. Supported consequence: stack memory corruption, enabling crash/DoS and potentially code execution.

commit_msg:
Tidy reading data in read_formatted_entries

Using read_attribute_value accomplishes two things: It checks for
unexpected formats, and ensures the buffer pointer always increments.

	PR 22210
	* dwarf2.c (read_formatted_entries): Use read_attribute_value to
	read data.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t      *stringp = read_string (abfd, buf, buf_end, &bytes_read);', '\t      buf += bytes_read;', '\t      break;', '', '\t      *stringp = read_indirect_line_string (unit, buf, buf_end, &bytes_read);', '\t      buf += bytes_read;', '\t      *uintp = read_1_byte (abfd, buf, buf_end);', '\t      buf += 1;', '\t      break;', '', '\t      *uintp = read_2_bytes (abfd, buf, buf_end);', '\t      buf += 2;', '\t      break;', '', '\t      *uintp = read_4_bytes (abfd, buf, buf_end);', '\t      buf += 4;', '\t      break;', '', '\t      *uintp = read_8_bytes (abfd, buf, buf_end);', '\t      buf += 8;', '\t      break;', '', '\t      *uintp = _bfd_safe_read_leb128 (abfd, buf, &bytes_read, FALSE,', '\t\t\t\t\t      buf_end);', '\t      buf += bytes_read;', '\t      break;', '', '\t    case DW_FORM_block:', '\t      /* It is valid only for DW_LNCT_timestamp which is ignored by', '\t\t current GDB.  */'], 'added_lines': ['\t  struct attribute attr;', '', '\t  buf = read_attribute_value (&attr, form, 0, unit, buf, buf_end);', '\t  if (buf == NULL)', '\t    return FALSE;', '\t      *stringp = attr.u.str;', '\t      *uintp = attr.u.val;']}
description: read_formatted_entries in dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: The outer loop is bounded by data_count (line 41) and the inner loop by format_count (line 46). The inner loop reads form via _bfd_safe_read_leb128 from format and advances format by bytes_read (lines 78-80). The switch on form (line 81) has a DW_FORM_block case that does nothing (lines 112-113) and no default, so unknown forms also fall through; in both cases buf is never advanced and no error is raised.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The DW_FORM_block case with a bare break, plus the missing default, leaves the loop without a reachable exit/advance path, matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. This is a loop-progress flaw, distinct from an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: for an unrecognized DW_FORM_block or any form not matching a case, the loop body neither consumes data from buf nor aborts. Since the outer loop iterates data_count times and each iteration re-reads the same format stream without advancing buf, the function repeats reading identical values, never making progress toward termination, causing CPU resource exhaustion (DoS).

description: The get_relocs_64 function in libr/bin/format/mach0/mach0.c in radare2 1.3.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and application crash) via a crafted Mach0 file.

code_evidence: bin->dyld_info is allocated with malloc at [207]; if the size check at [208] fails, the pointer is freed at [210] and the function returns false at [211].
If r_buf_read_at fails at [213], [214] frees bin->dyld_info and [215] sets it to NULL; the success branch at [217,218] dereferences bin->dyld_info->cmd.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees bin->dyld_info and leaves it referencing freed memory, which matches CWE-416 use-after-free. This is distinct from a pure null dereference because the stale pointer, not a NULL value, is the defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocated dyld_info object is freed on the error path at [210] without being nulled before return, and on the read-failure path at [214] it is freed then nulled. The dangling/freed pointer state can be reused by later code that trusts bin->dyld_info, producing a use-after-free triggered by a crafted Mach0 LC_DYLD_INFO command.

commit_msg:
libxl: qemu_disk_scsi_drive_string: Break out common parts of disk config

The generated configurations are identical apart from, in some cases,
reordering of the id=%s element.  So, overall, no functional change.

This is part of XSA-266.

Reported-by: Andrew Reimers <andrew.reimers@orionvm.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <Ian.Jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        drive = GCSPRINTF("file=%s,if=none,id=%s,format=%s,cache=writeback",', '                          target_path, id, format);', '            "if=none,cache=writeback,driver=quorum,"', '            "id=%s,"', '            id, target_path, format);', '            "if=none,id=%s,cache=writeback,"', '            "driver=replication,"', '            id, active_disk, hidden_disk, exportname);'], 'added_lines': ['    char *common = GCSPRINTF("if=none,cache=writeback");', '        drive = GCSPRINTF("file=%s,id=%s,format=%s,%s",', '                          target_path, id, format, common);', '            "%s,id=%s,driver=quorum,"', '            common, id, target_path, format);', '            "%s,id=%s,driver=replication,"', '            common, id, active_disk, hidden_disk, exportname);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.7 through 4.10.x. libxl fails to pass the readonly flag to qemu when setting up a SCSI disk, due to what was probably an erroneous merge conflict resolution. Malicious guest administrators or (in some situations) users may be able to write to supposedly read-only disk images. Only emulated SCSI disks (specified as "sd" in the libxl disk configuration, or an equivalent) are affected. IDE disks ("hd") are not affected (because attempts to make them readonly are rejected). Additionally, CDROM devices (that is, devices specified to be presented to the guest as CDROMs, regardless of the nature of the backing storage on the host) are not affected; they are always read only. Only systems using qemu-xen (rather than qemu-xen-traditional) as the device model version are vulnerable. Only systems using libxl or libxl-based toolstacks are vulnerable. (This includes xl, and libvirt with the libxl driver.) The vulnerability is present in Xen versions 4.7 and later. (In earlier versions, provided that the patch for XSA-142 has been applied, attempts to create read only disks are rejected.) If the host and guest together usually support PVHVM, the issue is exploitable only if the malicious guest administrator has control of the guest kernel or guest kernel command line.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only builds QEMU drive option strings for SCSI disks and never handles a readonly flag or any sensitive information; the described write-to-readonly-disk flaw is a missing access-control/immutability constraint, not an exposure of sensitive information, so CWE-200 is not supported by the code.

commit_msg:
Use `PartialTensorShape` instead of `TensorShape`.

`TensorShape` constructor throws a CHECK-fail if shape is partial/overflows which the other doesn't. We are only determining the number of elements in the shape and partial shape should be used as it returns negative number when needed.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 409205384
Change-Id: Ia56542ff9ec758f2c9ffc7e4dcc9fa7eecd86e7b
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int64_t num_elems = TensorShape(t.tensor_shape()).num_elements();'], 'added_lines': ['  int64_t num_elems = PartialTensorShape(t.tensor_shape()).num_elements();']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. A malicious user can cause a denial of service by altering a `SavedModel` such that `TensorByteSize` would trigger `CHECK` failures. `TensorShape` constructor throws a `CHECK`-fail if shape is partial or has a number of elements that would overflow the size of an `int`. The `PartialTensorShape` constructor instead does not cause a `CHECK`-abort if the shape is partial, which is exactly what this function needs to be able to return `-1`. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 2 constructs TensorShape(t.tensor_shape()), whose constructor CHECK-fails on a partial shape or on a shape whose element count overflows int, aborting the process. Line 3's ternary intends to return -1 when num_elements() is negative, but the CHECK-fail in line 2 occurs before that guard can execute.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reaches an assertion/CHECK that an attacker can trigger via the TensorProto shape, causing an abort more severe than necessary—matching CWE-617 Reachable Assertion. The guard on line 3 handles negative counts but cannot prevent the constructor's CHECK, distinguishing this from a mere integer-overflow issue.

evidence_lines.code:
int64_t num_elems = TensorShape(t.tensor_shape()).num_elements();
return num_elems < 0 ? -1 : num_elems * DataTypeSize(t.dtype());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: TensorShape's constructor enforces a CHECK that aborts on partial/overflowing shapes from an attacker-controlled TensorProto. Trigger: a crafted SavedModel supplies a partial tensor shape; the CHECK-fail fires in line 2 before the negative-count guard. Consequence: process abort (availability loss), not a returned -1.

commit_msg:
hw/nvme: fix null pointer access in directive receive

nvme_directive_receive() does not check if an endurance group has been
configured (set) prior to testing if flexible data placement is enabled
or not.

Fix this.

Cc: qemu-stable@nongnu.org
Resolves: https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/issues/1815
Fixes: 73064edfb864 ("hw/nvme: flexible data placement emulation")
Reviewed-by: Jesper Wendel Devantier <j.devantier@samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Klaus Jensen <k.jensen@samsung.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if (ns->endgrp->fdp.enabled) {'], 'added_lines': ['            if (ns->endgrp && ns->endgrp->fdp.enabled) {']}
description: QEMU through 8.0.4 accesses a NULL pointer in nvme_directive_receive in hw/nvme/ctrl.c because there is no check for whether an endurance group is configured before checking whether Flexible Data Placement is enabled.

code_evidence: Lines 21-24 resolve the namespace via nvme_ns and reject only a missing namespace; nothing establishes that ns->endgrp is configured.
At line 29 the code dereferences ns->endgrp->fdp.enabled without first verifying ns->endgrp is non-NULL, so an unconfigured endurance group yields a NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly dereferences a pointer (ns->endgrp) that can legitimately be NULL, matching CWE-476's core definition of dereferencing a pointer expected to be valid but NULL. This is a missing NULL check, not an out-of-bounds or use-after-free issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the RETURN_PARAMS path assumes ns->endgrp is always set after the namespace lookup. Trigger: a DIRECTIVE RECEIVE command with dtype NVME_DIRECTIVE_IDENTIFY and doper NVME_DIRECTIVE_RETURN_PARAMS against a namespace whose endurance group was never configured. Supported consequence: a NULL pointer dereference, crashing the emulator (DoS).

Fix heap buffer overflow in dyldcache parser ##crash

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static cache_accel_t *read_cache_accel(RBuffer *cache_buf, cache_hdr_t *hdr, cache_map_t *maps) {', '', '\tut64 offset = va2pa (hdr->accelerateInfoAddr, hdr->mappingCount, maps, cache_buf, 0, NULL, NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['static cache_accel_t *read_cache_accel(RBuffer *cache_buf, cache_hdr_t *hdr, cache_map_t *maps, int n_maps) {', '\tsize_t mc = R_MIN (hdr->mappingCount, n_maps);', '\tut64 offset = va2pa (hdr->accelerateInfoAddr, mc, maps, cache_buf, 0, NULL, NULL);']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.6.4.

code_evidence: read_cache_accel computes an offset via va2pa using hdr->mappingCount as the map count, but the maps array is supplied by the caller and may hold fewer entries; the returned offset is only checked for nonzero before being used in r_buf_fread_at at line 14.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is an out-of-bounds access driven by an unchecked count; the patch caps mappingCount with R_MIN against n_maps, confirming the missing upper bound. CWE-787 fits because the unchecked count leads to writing/reading beyond the intended maps buffer; the fix is a bounds constraint, not a type or integer-overflow issue.

A crafted dyld cache with an inflated mappingCount causes va2pa to walk past the maps allocation and derive an invalid offset. commit_msg:
Seth found that the CPU-entry-area; the piece of per-cpu data that is
mapped into the userspace page-tables for kPTI is not subject to any
randomization -- irrespective of kASLR settings.

On x86_64 a whole P4D (512 GB) of virtual address space is reserved for
this structure, which is plenty large enough to randomize things a
little.

As such, use a straight forward randomization scheme that avoids
duplicates to spread the existing CPUs over the available space.

  [ bp: Fix le build. ]

Reported-by: Seth Jenkins <sethjenkins@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Signed-off-by: Dave Hansen <dave.hansen@linux.intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Borislav Petkov <bp@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned long va = CPU_ENTRY_AREA_PER_CPU + cpu * CPU_ENTRY_AREA_SIZE;'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned long va = CPU_ENTRY_AREA_PER_CPU + cea_offset(cpu) * CPU_ENTRY_AREA_SIZE;']}
description: A flaw possibility of memory leak in the Linux kernel cpu_entry_area mapping of X86 CPU data to memory was found in the way user can guess location of exception stack(s) or other important data. A local user could use this flaw to get access to some important data with expected location in memory.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: get_cpu_entry_area only computes a virtual address from cpu and CPU_ENTRY_AREA_SIZE; it performs no allocation or release, so it cannot support a missing-release (CWE-401) claim. The patch adds cea_offset(cpu) for address randomization, which relates to address-space predictability, not memory lifetime.

commit_msg:
tiffcrop correctly update buffersize after rotateImage() fix#520
rotateImage() set up a new buffer and calculates its size individually. Therefore, seg_buffs[] size needs to be updated accordingly. Before this fix, the seg_buffs buffer size was calculated with a different formula than within rotateImage().

Closes #520.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                       unsigned char **ibuff_ptr)'], 'added_lines': ['                       unsigned char **ibuff_ptr, size_t *rot_buf_size)', '    if (rot_buf_size != NULL)', '        *rot_buf_size = buffsize;']}
description: libtiff 4.5.0 is vulnerable to Buffer Overflow via /libtiff/tools/tiffcrop.c:8499. Incorrect updating of buffer size after rotateImage() in tiffcrop cause heap-buffer-overflow and SEGV.

code_evidence: Lines 22-25 compute buffsize using a heuristic max of (colsize+1)*width or (rowsize+1)*length, an estimate not derived from exact rotated output dimensions.
Lines 46-47 allocate rbuff of buffsize + NUM_BUFF_OVERSIZE_BYTES; the caller's seg_buffs size is not updated to this value, so downstream code assumes a different size.
Lines 61-71 copy bytes_per_pixel per pixel into rbuff at dst_offset based on rowsize; when buffsize underestimates the rotated layout, writes exceed the allocated region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies pixel data into rbuff without verifying that the destination buffer is large enough for the input-derived output, matching CWE-120's buffer copy without size check. The underlying size-calculation error could also suggest CWE-131, but the direct unsafe copy without adequate bound is the supported weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!(rbuff =
(unsigned char *)limitMalloc(buffsize + NUM_BUFF_OVERSIZE_BYTES)))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: rotateImage() allocates a rotation buffer using an estimated buffsize formula that can be smaller than the actual rotated data, and it never reports this size back to the caller. Trigger: a crafted TIFF whose width/length/spp/bps combination makes the formula underestimate the required size for 90/270-degree rotation. Consequence: heap-buffer-overflow writes past rbuff, leading to memory corruption or SEGV.

commit_msg:
Handle overflow errors in malformed zchunk files

Thanks to Agostino Sarubbo of Gentoo for the heads up!

Signed-off-by: Jonathan Dieter <jdieter@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', "    /* Verify that we're not going to overflow */", '    if(length > length + zck->hash_type.digest_size) {', '        zck_log(ZCK_LOG_ERROR, "Integer overflow when reading lead");', '        return false;', '    }']}
description: zchunk before 1.3.2 has multiple integer overflows via malformed zchunk files to lib/comp/comp.c, lib/comp/zstd/zstd.c, lib/dl/multipart.c, or lib/header.c.

code_evidence: length accumulates the parsed header offset; line 55 computes length + zck->hash_type.digest_size for zrealloc, and lines 61-62 compute the same sum for to_read, then read_data writes to header + lead.
Line 92-93 copies digest_size bytes at header + length and increments length by digest_size, again relying on the unvalidated sum.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an unchecked integer addition used for allocation and copy sizing, matching CWE-190. The missing overflow guard on length + digest_size is the integer wraparound; the out-of-bounds access is its consequence, not a separate primary weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
memcpy(zck->header_digest, header + length, zck->hash_type.digest_size);
length += zck->hash_type.digest_size;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The size calculations length + zck->hash_type.digest_size assume no wraparound; when length is near SIZE_MAX, the sum wraps small. The allocation and to_read become undersized while offset arithmetic and the memcpy at header + length then access memory out of bounds, yielding heap corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflow

In case the descriptor contains more endpoints than USBH_MAX_NUM_ENDPOINTS the Ep_Desc array and subsequent members of USBH_HandleTypeDef that contains function pointers are overwritten allowing arbitrary code execution.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if_descriptor->bNumEndpoints      = *(uint8_t *)(buf + 4);'], 'added_lines': ['  if_descriptor->bNumEndpoints      = MIN(*(uint8_t *)(buf + 4), USBH_MAX_NUM_ENDPOINTS);']}
description: A buffer overflow vulnerability in stm32_mw_usb_host of STMicroelectronics in versions before 3.5.1 allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code when the descriptor contains more endpoints than USBH_MAX_NUM_ENDPOINTS. The library is typically integrated when using a RTOS such as FreeRTOS on STM32 MCUs.

code_evidence: Line 8 copies the attacker-controlled byte at buf+4 directly into if_descriptor->bNumEndpoints with no bound check against USBH_MAX_NUM_ENDPOINTS. The fixed version clamps this value with MIN(), confirming the missing size constraint on the parsed endpoint count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because an input-derived length is stored without validating it against the destination buffer capacity, leading to a classic buffer overflow on later copy. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the unchecked count drives an over-write of a bounded array.

evidence_lines.code: if_descriptor->bNumEndpoints      = *(uint8_t *)(buf + 4);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The interface descriptor's bNumEndpoints field is taken verbatim from the device-supplied buffer. Downstream code uses this count to populate the fixed-size Ep_Desc array; an oversized value causes writes past the array into adjacent USBH_HandleTypeDef members, including function pointers. Trigger is a malicious USB descriptor; consequence is memory corruption enabling arbitrary code execution.

to implicitly unpin here: The caller should really unpin itself before
(or after, if they so wish) requesting the page to be removed.

This is XSA-252.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>

@@ -81,11 +81,6 @@
 
     rc = guest_physmap_remove_page(d, _gfn(gmfn), mfn, 0);
 
-#ifdef _PGT_pinned
-    if ( !rc && test_and_clear_bit(_PGT_pinned, &page->u.inuse.type_info) )
-        put_page_and_type(page);
-#endif
-

      * With the lack of an IOMMU on some platforms, domains with DMA-capable

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.10.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host OS CPU hang) via non-preemptable L3/L4 pagetable freeing.

code_evidence: After removing the page mapping at line 64, the pre-patch code implicitly cleared _PGT_pinned and called put_page_and_type, releasing the pin reference the caller was responsible for.
The remaining block at lines 69-72 still drops the mapped page and the get_page reference via put_page, but no longer releases the caller's pin.

With that implicit release removed, callers that relied on it leave the page pinned; a PV guest repeatedly triggering this path accumulates pinned page-table pages, and freeing L3/L4 pagetable chains stays non-preemptable, hanging host CPU.

commit_msg:
The boundary test for the fixed-offset parts of xfs_attr_sf_entry in
xfs_attr_shortform_verify is off by one, because the variable array
at the end is defined as nameval[1] not nameval[].
Hence we need to subtract 1 from the calculation.

This can be shown by:

# touch file
# setfattr -n root.a file

and verifications will fail when it's written to disk.

This only matters for a last attribute which has a single-byte name
and no value, otherwise the combination of namelen & valuelen will
push endp further out and this test won't fail.

Fixes: 1e1bbd8e7ee06 ("xfs: create structure verifier function for shortform xattrs")
Signed-off-by: Eric Sandeen <sandeen@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -30,8 +30,10 @@
 		 * struct xfs_attr_sf_entry has a variable length.
 		 * Check the fixed-offset parts of the structure are
 		 * within the data buffer.
+		 * xfs_attr_sf_entry is defined with a 1-byte variable
+		 * array at the end, so we must subtract that off.
 		 */
-		if (((char *)sfep + sizeof(*sfep)) >= endp)
+		if (((char *)sfep + sizeof(*sfep) - 1) >= endp)
 			return __this_address;
 
 		/* Don't allow names with known bad length. */
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (((char *)sfep + sizeof(*sfep)) >= endp)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t * xfs_attr_sf_entry is defined with a 1-byte variable', '\t\t * array at the end, so we must subtract that off.', '\t\tif (((char *)sfep + sizeof(*sfep) - 1) >= endp)']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel before 5.9-rc4. A failure of the file system metadata validator in XFS can cause an inode with a valid, user-creatable extended attribute to be flagged as corrupt. This can lead to the filesystem being shutdown, or otherwise rendered inaccessible until it is remounted, leading to a denial of service. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

code_evidence: endp is computed as the buffer end (sfp + size), and sfep starts at the first entry; the loop then checks whether the fixed-offset portion of each entry lies within the buffer.
The boundary test adds sizeof(*sfep) without accounting for the 1-byte variable array already included in the struct size, so the fixed-offset extent is over-counted by one byte.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The check derives a buffer extent from an incorrect size computation (sizeof includes the variable array), which is the core of CWE-131. The off-by-one rejects a valid entry rather than under-bounding, but the root cause is a miscalculated structure size boundary; this is distinct from a general out-of-bounds read/write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The size/boundary calculation for xfs_attr_sf_entry over-counts the fixed portion by one byte because the trailing nameval[1] array is already part of sizeof(*sfep). Trigger: a final shortform attribute with a single-byte name and no value makes the computed extent reach endp, so the check rejects a valid, user-creatable attribute. Consequence: the inode is flagged corrupt, causing filesystem shutdown or unavailability (availability impact).

commit_msg:
When allocating MMIO space for the MSI-X table, kvmtool rounds the
allocation to the host's page size to make it as easy as possible for the
guest to map the table to a page, if it wants to (and doesn't do BAR
reassignment, like the x86 architecture for example). However, the host's
page size can differ from the guest's on architectures which support
multiple page sizes. For example, arm64 supports three different page size,
and it is possible for the host to be using 4k pages, while the guest is
using 64k pages.

To make sure the allocation is always aligned to a guest's page size, round
it up to the maximum architectural page size. Do the same for the pending
bit array if it lives in its own BAR.

Signed-off-by: Alexandru Elisei <alexandru.elisei@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Andre Przywara <andre.przywara@arm.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20211012132510.42134-8-alexandru.elisei@arm.com
Signed-off-by: Will Deacon <will@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmap_size = ALIGN(info.size, PAGE_SIZE);', '\t\tmap_size = ALIGN(info.size, PAGE_SIZE);'], 'added_lines': ['\tmap_size = ALIGN(info.size, MAX_PAGE_SIZE);', '\t\tmap_size = ALIGN(info.size, MAX_PAGE_SIZE);']}
description: kvmtool through 39181fc allows an out-of-bounds write, related to virtio/balloon.c and virtio/pci.c. This allows a guest OS user to execute arbitrary code on the host machine.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only computes MMIO allocation sizes and guest physical addresses using ALIGN; it contains no buffer write or index into a bounded buffer, so it cannot establish an out-of-bounds write within this function.

For DT_GNU_HASH, n_bucket and n_bitmask are read from gashtab and used to derive buckets, hasharr, and bitmask indices without validating that these arrays lie within file_image; buckets[h % n_bucket] and hasharr[bucket - symbias] are then read.

Trigger: a crafted ELF with zero or oversized counts makes buckets[si], buckets[m], hasharr[bucket - symbias], or bitmask[...] point outside the mapped image; the get_le32/get_le64 reads then access out-of-bounds memory, causing a heap-based buffer overflow/crash during unpacking.

commit_msg:
Unsquashfs: additional write outside destination directory exploit fix

An issue on github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
showed how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and '..') can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

Since then it has been shown that specially crafted Squashfs filesystems
that contain a symbolic link pointing outside of the destination directory,
coupled with an identically named file within the same directory, can
cause Unsquashfs to write files outside of the destination directory.

Specifically the symbolic link produces a pathname pointing outside
of the destination directory, which is then followed when writing the
duplicate identically named file within the directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by explictly checking for duplicate
filenames within a directory.  As directories in v2.1, v3.x, and v4.0
filesystems are sorted, this is achieved by checking for consecutively
identical filenames.  Additionally directories are checked to
ensure they are sorted, to avoid attempts to evade the duplicate
check.

Version 1.x and 2.0 filesystems (where the directories were unsorted)
are sorted and then the above duplicate filename check is applied.

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* check directory for duplicate names and sorting */', '\tif(check_directory(dir) == FALSE) {', '\t\tERROR("File system corrupted: directory has duplicate names or is unsorted\\n");', '\t\tgoto corrupted;', '\t}', '']}
description: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-2.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 allows Directory Traversal, a different vulnerability than CVE-2021-40153. A squashfs filesystem that has been crafted to include a symbolic link and then contents under the same filename in a filesystem can cause unsquashfs to first create the symbolic link pointing outside the expected directory, and then the subsequent write operation will cause the unsquashfs process to write through the symbolic link elsewhere in the filesystem.

code_evidence: check_name validates only each entry's characters; it does not compare the entry against a previously stored entry with the same name.

The directory entries are appended to dir->dirs with ent->name = strdup(dire->name) and no duplicate-name detection, so a crafted filesystem can contain two entries with the same name, e.g. a symlink and a regular file.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the unsafe behavior is following a link resolved from a directory entry to an unintended resource during file access. The missing duplicate-name constraint permits the symlink/file name collision that causes the write to follow the link; this is link resolution, not merely path traversal.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: squashfs_opendir builds the directory list without rejecting duplicate filenames, so a crafted image can supply a symlink and an identically named file in one directory. Trigger: extraction creates the symlink first, then writes the duplicate file through that link. Consequence: files are written outside the destination directory (link following, directory traversal).

commit_msg:
We recently had an oops reported on a 4.14 kernel in
xfs_reclaim_inodes_count() where sb->s_fs_info pointed to garbage
and so the m_perag_tree lookup walked into lala land.

Essentially, the machine was under memory pressure when the mount
was being run, xfs_fs_fill_super() failed after allocating the
xfs_mount and attaching it to sb->s_fs_info. It then cleaned up and
freed the xfs_mount, but the sb->s_fs_info field still pointed to
the freed memory. Hence when the superblock shrinker then ran
it fell off the bad pointer.

With the superblock shrinker problem fixed at teh VFS level, this
stale s_fs_info pointer is still a problem - we use it
unconditionally in ->put_super when the superblock is being torn
down, and hence we can still trip over it after a ->fill_super
call failure. Hence we need to clear s_fs_info if
xfs-fs_fill_super() fails, and we need to check if it's valid in
the places it can potentially be dereferenced after a ->fill_super
failure.

Signed-Off-By: Dave Chinner <dchinner@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* if ->fill_super failed, we have no mount to tear down */', '\tif (!sb->s_fs_info)', '\t\treturn;', '', '\tsb->s_fs_info = NULL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in fs/xfs/xfs_super.c in the Linux kernel before 4.18. A use after free exists, related to xfs_fs_fill_super failure.

code_evidence: Line 5 unconditionally derives mp from XFS_M(sb), i.e. from sb->s_fs_info, without checking that it is non-NULL; the patch adds an early return guarding exactly this dereference.

Lines 6-15 then use mp in xfs_notice, xfs_filestream_unmount, xfs_unmountfs, xfs_freesb, free_percpu(mp->m_stats.xs_stats), workqueue teardown, device close and finally kfree(mp), all operating on the same possibly-stale pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reuses a pointer to memory that was already freed during failed mount cleanup, which is the definition of CWE-416; the crash from walking the freed mount is its consequence, not the root cause.

evidence_lines.code: struct xfs_mount*mp = XFS_M(sb);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When xfs_fs_fill_super fails it frees the xfs_mount but leaves sb->s_fs_info pointing at the freed memory. A later ->put_super call therefore obtains a dangling mp and dereferences and frees it again, causing the reported use after free. The patch guards the NULL case and clears s_fs_info after teardown.

commit_msg:
Add a container structure struct bpf_sanitize_info which holds
the current aux info, and update call-sites to sanitize_ptr_alu()
to pass it in. This is needed for passing in additional state
later on.

Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Reviewed-by: Piotr Krysiuk <piotras@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t    struct bpf_insn_aux_data *tmp_aux,', '\tstruct bpf_insn_aux_data *aux = commit_window ? cur_aux(env) : tmp_aux;', '\t\talu_state = tmp_aux->alu_state;', '\t\talu_limit = abs(tmp_aux->alu_limit - alu_limit);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t    struct bpf_sanitize_info *info,', '\tstruct bpf_insn_aux_data *aux = commit_window ? cur_aux(env) : &info->aux;', '\t\talu_state = info->aux.alu_state;', '\t\talu_limit = abs(info->aux.alu_limit - alu_limit);']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 5.12.7 enforces incorrect limits for pointer arithmetic operations, aka CID-bb01a1bba579. This can be abused to perform out-of-bounds reads and writes in kernel memory, leading to local privilege escalation to root. In particular, there is a corner case where the off reg causes a masking direction change, which then results in an incorrect final aux->alu_limit.

code_evidence: Line 9 selects the aux record: cur_aux(env) during commit, otherwise the caller-supplied tmp_aux, so the sanitization limit is stored per instruction.

Lines 26-34 compute alu_state from off_is_neg/off_is_imm and, in commit phase, derive alu_limit from the prior aux record via abs(tmp_aux->alu_limit - alu_limit); the masking direction is encoded only by off_is_neg.
Line 35 passes alu_state and alu_limit to update_alu_sanitation_state, which enforces the pointer-arithmetic window.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the flawed limit computation lets verified BPF pointer arithmetic write past the intended buffer in kernel memory; the root cause is the incorrect sanitization limit, and the out-of-bounds write is the supported consequence.

evidence_lines.code: struct bpf_insn_aux_data *aux = commit_window ? cur_aux(env) : tmp_aux;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The sanitizer derives the masking window from off_is_neg and the stored aux->alu_limit, but the corner case where the offset register flips the masking direction yields an incorrect final aux->alu_limit. The verifier then accepts pointer arithmetic beyond the intended bounds, allowing out-of-bounds kernel reads/writes and local privilege escalation.

Both btrfs_find_device() and find_device() does the same thing except
that the latter does not take the seed device onto account in the device
scanning context. We can merge them.

Signed-off-by: Anand Jain <anand.jain@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: David Sterba <dsterba@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: David Sterba <dsterba@suse.com>

description: fs/btrfs/volumes.c in the Linux kernel before 5.1 allows a btrfs_verify_dev_extents NULL pointer dereference via a crafted btrfs image because fs_devices->devices is mishandled within find_device, aka CID-09ba3bc9dd15.

code_evidence: The function walks the seed chain with `while (fs_devices)` and, for each entry, calls `find_device(fs_devices, devid, uuid)`. It returns the found device or falls through to `fs_devices = fs_devices->seed`. The loop guards only the outer `fs_devices` pointer; it does not verify that `fs_devices->devices` (used inside `find_device`) is initialized before dereferencing it.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a caller supplies fs_devices whose device list is not populated (e.g., a crafted btrfs image where fs_devices->devices is mishandled), find_device iterates over an uninitialized/NULL list head, causing a NULL pointer dereference. The trigger is reaching btrfs_find_device with such an fs_devices; the consequence is a crash (denial of service).

commit_msg:
io_get_file_fixed will access io_uring's context. Lock it if it is
invoked unlocked (eg via io-wq) to avoid a race condition with fixed
files getting unregistered.

No single upstream patch exists for this issue, it was fixed as part
of the file assignment changes that went into the 5.18 cycle.

Signed-off-by: Jheng, Bing-Jhong Billy <billy@starlabs.sg>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t  (sp->flags & SPLICE_F_FD_IN_FIXED));'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t (sp->flags & SPLICE_F_FD_IN_FIXED), issue_flags);']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux Kernel io_uring system can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

The io_file_get_fixed function lacks the presence of ctx->uring_lock which can lead to a Use-After-Free vulnerability due a race condition with fixed files getting unregistered.

We recommend upgrading past commit da24142b1ef9fd5d36b76e36bab328a5b27523e8.

code_evidence: io_tee resolves the input file via io_file_get using sp->splice_fd_in and the SPLICE_F_FD_IN_FIXED flag, but the call passes no issue_flags/lock context.
The fixed-file path returns a file reference that is later used by do_tee (line 17) and conditionally released at lines 18-19.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing lock allows a race between fixed-file resolution and unregistration, so a pointer to freed file state is subsequently dereferenced. This matches CWE-416 (use after free) rather than a pure race condition, because the supported consequence is reuse of freed memory.

evidence_lines.code:
in = io_file_get(req->ctx, req, sp->splice_fd_in,
(sp->flags & SPLICE_F_FD_IN_FIXED));

if (!(sp->flags & SPLICE_F_FD_IN_FIXED))
io_put_file(in);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: io_tee can resolve a fixed file without holding ctx->uring_lock (e.g., when invoked via io-wq), so fixed-file unregistration can race with the lookup. Trigger: concurrent unregister of the fixed file while io_tee calls io_file_get. Consequence: the returned file pointer may reference freed memory used later in do_tee, yielding a use-after-free.

commit_msg:
irc: fix crash when a new message 005 is received with longer nick prefixes

Thanks to Stuart Nevans Locke for reporting the issue.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int i, length_modes, length_chars;'], 'added_lines': ['    int i, old_length_chars, length_modes, length_chars;', '', '    old_length_chars = (server->prefix_chars) ?', '        strlen (server->prefix_chars) : 0;', '', '    length_chars = (server->prefix_chars) ? strlen (server->prefix_chars) : 0;', '    if (server->prefix_chars && (length_chars != old_length_chars))', '        irc_nick_realloc_prefixes (server, old_length_chars, length_chars);']}
description: An issue was discovered in WeeChat before 2.7.1 (0.3.4 to 2.7 are affected). When a new IRC message 005 is received with longer nick prefixes, a buffer overflow and possibly a crash can happen when a new mode is set for a nick.

code_evidence: length_modes is derived from the modes string and length_chars from the trailing characters after ')'. server->prefix_chars is allocated with length_modes + 1 bytes, and the loop writes exactly length_modes characters using pos[i] when i < length_chars, then terminates at index length_modes. The allocation is sized to the modes count, not the chars count, so the copy length is bounded by length_modes rather than the actual length of the source pos.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 requires a buffer copy lacking an input-size check that writes past the destination. Here the copy is bounded by length_modes and the terminator is placed at length_modes, so the shown code does not itself overflow the allocated buffer; the weakness is a size relationship mismatch affecting later prefix handling, which is not directly demonstrated as a classic buffer copy overflow in this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination prefix_chars buffer is sized from the number of mode characters, while the loop copies from the separate chars string without ensuring the destination accommodates the source length. Trigger: an IRC 005 PREFIX value whose chars portion is longer than the modes portion. The loop writes only up to length_modes, so the supported consequence is truncation/padding of prefix_chars rather than an out-of-bounds write; the later fix reallocates nick prefixes when the chars length changes, indicating a downstream size mismatch.

commit_msg: Fix #6816 - null deref in r_read_*
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tint types_list_size = r_read_le32(p);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tint types_list_size = r_read_le32 (p);']}
description: The r_read_* functions in libr/include/r_endian.h in radare2 1.2.1 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a crafted binary file, as demonstrated by the r_read_le32 function.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but which can be NULL, matching CWE-476 exactly. The unchecked r_buf_get_at return is the specific missing constraint; the crash from r_read_le32 is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the result of r_buf_get_at is used without a NULL check. Trigger: a crafted binary whose interfaces_offset causes r_buf_get_at to return NULL (e.g., offset at/after buffer end) while still satisfying the bounds condition at lines 43-46. Consequence: r_read_le32 dereferences NULL, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg: Fix #7723 - crash in ext2 GRUB code because of variable size array in stack
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['#ifndef _MSC_VER', '\tchar fpath[grub_strlen (currpath) + 1];', '#else', '#endif', '\t  if (grub_errno)'], 'added_lines': ['free (fpath);', 'free (fpath);', '\t  if (grub_errno) {', 'free (fpath);', '}', 'free (fpath);', 'free (fpath);', 'free (fpath);', 'free (fpath);', 'free (fpath);']}
description: The grub_ext2_read_block function in fs/ext2.c in GNU GRUB before 2013-11-12, as used in shlr/grub/fs/ext2.c in radare2 1.5.0, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive stack use and application crash) via a crafted binary file, related to use of a variable-size stack array.

code_evidence: The function declares fpath as a variable-length stack array sized at runtime from grub_strlen(currpath)+1 (lines 6-10), so the buffer size is attacker-influenced via the supplied path.
Line 17 copies currpath into fpath with grub_strncpy using grub_strlen(currpath)+1 as the count, relying entirely on the VLA allocation to match the source length; no independent bound is enforced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The operation writes into a stack buffer whose bounds are set by untrusted input size, so memory handling exceeds safe bounds and exhausts the stack; this is an out-of-bounds/memory-buffer restriction failure matching CWE-119. It is not merely a resource leak (the patch adds frees), which is secondary.
