commit_msg:
Fix a null pointer exception caused by branching on uninitialized data.

This is due to not checking that the params for the quantization exists. If there is no quantization, we should not access the `.params` field.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 385168337
Change-Id: I28661e4f12ba1c92cfeae23d22a3fb2df2a2c6a4
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context,', '                 intermediate->quantization.type != kTfLiteNoQuantization);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions all TFLite operations that use quantization can be made to use unitialized values. [For example](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/depthwise_conv.cc#L198-L200). The issue stems from the fact that `quantization.params` is only valid if `quantization.type` is different that `kTfLiteNoQuantization`. However, these checks are missing in large parts of the code. We have patched the issue in GitHub commits 537bc7c723439b9194a358f64d871dd326c18887, 4a91f2069f7145aab6ba2d8cfe41be8a110c18a5 and 8933b8a21280696ab119b63263babdb54c298538. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The intermediate tensor is fetched from node->intermediates, then its quantization.params is cast to TfLiteAffineQuantization* and dereferenced via params->zero_point->data[0] without verifying that quantization.type is not kTfLiteNoQuantization; when no quantization exists, params is not a valid initialized pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the function uses a quantization resource (params) that was never initialized for the kTfLiteNoQuantization case; the added TF_LITE_ENSURE check confirms the missing initialization guard. It is a use-of-uninitialized-resource issue rather than merely a null check, since the params field may be absent entirely.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code reads intermediate->quantization.params unconditionally, although that field is only valid when quantization.type differs from kTfLiteNoQuantization. Trigger: an LSTM op whose intermediate tensor has no quantization. Consequence: dereferencing an uninitialized/invalid params pointer, causing invalid memory read or a null-pointer crash.

commit_msg: fixed #2138
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (j+4>=outSize)', '\t\t\treturn 0;']}
description: GPAC 2.0 allows a heap-based buffer overflow in gf_base64_encode. It can be triggered via MP4Box.

code_evidence: Line 8 checks outSize against inSize*4/3, but this integer expression truncates and does not account for the final 4-byte output group written when the input length is not a multiple of 3.
Lines 12-15 write four bytes out[j]..out[j+3] for the padding==2 branch.
Lines 22-25 write four bytes out[j]..out[j+3] for the full three-byte branch.
Lines 27-28 advance i by 3 and j by 4 without any per-iteration bound check on j against outSize.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of the caller's output buffer because the capacity constraint is insufficient, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an off-by-one read or integer overflow in isolation; the supported consequence is memory corruption via writes beyond the intended buffer.

evidence_lines.code: if (outSize < (inSize * 4 / 3)) return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The only size guard is the truncated check at line 8, so for certain inSize/outSize combinations the loop writes a full 4-byte group at out[j..j+3] while j+4 exceeds outSize. The trigger is a caller-supplied output buffer sized per the flawed check; the consequence is a heap out-of-bounds write, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially enabling code execution.

commit_msg: Fix dereferencing null pointer when running wavm with WebAssembly main function that takes command-line arguments but no Emscripten memory to write them to
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tMemoryInstance* defaultMemory = Runtime::getDefaultMemory(moduleInstance);', '\t\t\tif(!defaultMemory)', '\t\t\tstd::vector<const char*> argStrings;', '\t\t\targStrings.push_back(options.filename);', '\t\t\tchar** args = options.args;', '\t\t\twhile(*args) { argStrings.push_back(*args++); };', '', '\t\t\tEmscripten::injectCommandArgs(emscriptenInstance, argStrings, invokeArgs);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif(!emscriptenInstance)', '\t\t\telse', '\t\t\t{', '\t\t\t\tstd::vector<const char*> argStrings;', '\t\t\t\targStrings.push_back(options.filename);', '\t\t\t\tchar** args = options.args;', '\t\t\t\twhile(*args) { argStrings.push_back(*args++); };', '\t\t\t\twavmAssert(emscriptenInstance);', '\t\t\t\tEmscripten::injectCommandArgs(emscriptenInstance, argStrings, invokeArgs);', '\t\t\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in WAVM before 2018-09-16. The run function in Programs/wavm/wavm.cpp does not check whether there is Emscripten memory to store the command-line arguments passed by the input WebAssembly file's main function, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash by NULL pointer dereference) or possibly have unspecified other impact by crafting certain WebAssembly files.

code_evidence: When the exported main takes two parameters, the code obtains defaultMemory via Runtime::getDefaultMemory and only checks that memory is non-null; it then calls Emscripten::injectCommandArgs(emscriptenInstance, ...) at line 111 without verifying emscriptenInstance is non-null. emscriptenInstance is initialized to nullptr at line 32 and only set when options.enableEmscripten is true, so a two-parameter main with Emscripten disabled passes a null instance into injectCommandArgs.

The check on defaultMemory is a related null guard, but it does not protect the actual dereferenced instance, so the weakness is specifically a NULL pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the two-argument path guards defaultMemory but not emscriptenInstance, which is null when Emscripten is not enabled. Trigger: a crafted WebAssembly main with two params processed without Emscripten support. Consequence: injectCommandArgs dereferences the null instance, crashing the process (DoS).

commit_msg: sock_dns: remove out-of-place puts() call
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            puts("a");'], 'added_lines': []}
description: RIOT RIOT-OS version after commit 7af03ab624db0412c727eed9ab7630a5282e2fd3 contains a Buffer Overflow vulnerability in sock_dns, an implementation of the DNS protocol utilizing the RIOT sock API that can result in Remote code executing. This attack appears to be exploitable via network connectivity.

code_evidence: Two fixed-size stack buffers are declared: buf[SOCK_DNS_QUERYBUF_LEN] and reply_buf[512].

buf is reinterpreted as sock_dns_hdr_t and bufpos advances through buf while encoding the domain name (_enc_domain_name) and writing shorts (AAAA/A type, class, compression pointer) without any check that bufpos stays within SOCK_DNS_QUERYBUF_LEN.
The accumulated length (bufpos-buf) is passed to sock_udp_send, so an oversized encoded query would already have been written past buf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The core defect is writing beyond the end of the intended buffer (buf) during query construction, which is exactly CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. It is not merely a read overflow or integer issue; the unchecked pointer advancement directly produces writes past the allocated array.

evidence_lines.code:
uint8_t buf[SOCK_DNS_QUERYBUF_LEN];
uint8_t reply_buf[512];
res = sock_udp_send(&sock_dns, buf, (bufpos-buf), NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The query buffer size is fixed but the encoder appends the encoded domain name plus multiple short fields using pointer arithmetic with no bound check against SOCK_DNS_QUERYBUF_LEN. A long or crafted domain_name (within the strlen limit but larger when encoded, or combined with AF_UNSPEC adding a second record) drives bufpos past the buffer end, causing an out-of-bounds stack write before the send call; this corrupts adjacent stack memory and can lead to memory modification or code execution.

commit_msg: fix use-after-free crash in RT #97625
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    do_error(dbh, mysql_errno(imp_dbh->pmysql),', '            mysql_error(imp_dbh->pmysql) ,mysql_sqlstate(imp_dbh->pmysql));'], 'added_lines': ['    if(imp_dbh->pmysql)', '        do_error(dbh, mysql_errno(imp_dbh->pmysql),', '                mysql_error(imp_dbh->pmysql) ,mysql_sqlstate(imp_dbh->pmysql));']}
description: Use-after-free vulnerability in DBD::mysql before 4.029 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (program crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via vectors related to a lost server connection.

code_evidence: my_login returns false on a lost server connection; the failure branch then passes imp_dbh->pmysql to mysql_errno, mysql_error and mysql_sqlstate without first checking that the pointer is non-NULL, so the error-reporting calls dereference a stale handle.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Dereferencing imp_dbh->pmysql after the connection has been lost and its handle freed is a use-after-free (CWE-416); the fix guards the dereference with a NULL check. This is not merely a NULL-pointer dereference, since the handle may have been freed rather than never allocated.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failure path unconditionally dereferences imp_dbh->pmysql after my_login fails, even though a lost connection can leave that pointer freed/NULL. Trigger: a failed login caused by a lost server connection. Consequence: use-after-free read leading to a program crash (DoS) or potentially arbitrary code execution.

commit_msg:
extractor: Do not allow symlink in parents

Currently, it is still possible that some files are extracted outside of
the destination dir in case of malicious archives. The checks from commit
adb067e6 can be still bypassed in certain cases. See GNOME/file-roller#108
for more details. After some investigation, I am convinced that it would be
best to	simply disallow symlinks in parents. For example, `tar` fails to
extract such files with the `ENOTDIR` error. Let's do the same here.

Fixes: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gnome-autoar/-/issues/12
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    gboolean file_conflict;', '    file_conflict = autoar_extractor_check_file_conflict (extracted_filename,', '      file_conflict = autoar_extractor_check_file_conflict (extracted_filename,'], 'added_lines': ['    g_autoptr (GFile) file_conflict = NULL;', '    file_conflict = autoar_extractor_check_file_conflict (self,', '                                                          extracted_filename,', '', '      /* Do not try to solve any conflicts in parents for now. Especially', '       * symlinks in parents are dangerous as it can easily happen that files', '       * are written outside of the destination. The tar cmd fails to extract', "       * such archives with ENOTDIR. Let's do the same here. This is most", '       * probably malicious, or corrupted archive if the conflict was caused', '       * only by files from the archive...', '       */', '      if (!g_file_equal (file_conflict, extracted_filename)) {', '        self->error = g_error_new (G_IO_ERROR,', '                                   G_IO_ERROR_NOT_DIRECTORY,', '                                   "The file is not a directory");', '        archive_read_free (a);', '        return;', '      }', '      g_clear_object (&file_conflict);', '      file_conflict = autoar_extractor_check_file_conflict (self,', '                                                            extracted_filename,']}
description: autoar-extractor.c in GNOME gnome-autoar before 0.3.1, as used by GNOME Shell, Nautilus, and other software, allows Directory Traversal during extraction because it lacks a check of whether a file's parent is a symlink in certain complex situations. NOTE: this issue exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2020-36241.

code_evidence: The conflict check is invoked on extracted_filename and its result drives the while loop that resolves conflicts.

The loop only exits without re-checking when the action is not AUTOAR_CONFLICT_CHANGE_DESTINATION; otherwise it calls autoar_extractor_check_file_conflict again. In the pre-patch version this check does not detect that a parent of the path is a symlink, so a sanitized pathname whose parent resolves through a symlink to a location outside the destination is not treated as a conflict.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses a filesystem path based on archive-controlled filename components without preventing a parent symlink from redirecting the access to an unintended resource, matching CWE-59 link following. It is not merely path traversal (CWE-22) because the bypass relies on link resolution in parents rather than raw '..' sequences already sanitized.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the conflict check does not verify that parents are real directories, only that the leaf path collides. Trigger: a malicious archive entry whose parent component is a symlink resolving outside the destination. Consequence: the entry is written via autoar_extractor_do_write_entry through the symlinked parent, escaping the destination directory (directory traversal / arbitrary file write).

description: WavPack 5.1 and earlier is affected by: CWE 369: Divide by Zero. The impact is: Divide by zero can lead to sudden crash of a software/service that tries to parse a .wav file. The component is: ParseDsdiffHeaderConfig (dsdiff.c:282). The attack vector is: Maliciously crafted .wav file. The fixed version is: After commit https://github.com/dbry/WavPack/commit/4c0faba32fddbd0745cbfaf1e1aeb3da5d35b9fc.

code_evidence: When a DSD chunk is encountered, total_samples is computed as dff_chunk_header.ckDataSize / config->num_channels. config->num_channels is only assigned from numChannels inside the PROP/SND branch (line 158); if no valid PROP/SND chunk set it, it remains zero, so the division at line 168 divides by zero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a division whose divisor, config->num_channels, can be zero for malformed input, exactly matching CWE-369 (Divide By Zero). The added guard preventing a zero channel count confirms the missing constraint; this is a direct division flaw, not merely a missing validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DSD branch divides by config->num_channels without verifying it is nonzero, and parsing can reach this branch with the field unset. Trigger: a crafted .DFF file whose DSD chunk appears without a prior valid PROP/SND channel definition. Consequence: integer divide-by-zero, crashing the parser (DoS).

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.2068: [security] overflow in :history

Problem:  [security] overflow in :history
Solution: Check that value fits into int

The get_list_range() function, used to parse numbers for the :history
and :clist command internally uses long variables to store the numbers.
However function arguments are integer pointers, which can then
overflow.

Check that the return value from the vim_str2nr() function is not larger
than INT_MAX and if yes, bail out with an error. I guess nobody uses a
cmdline/clist history that needs so many entries... (famous last words).

It is only a moderate vulnerability, so impact should be low.

Github Advisory:
https://github.com/vim/vim/security/advisories/GHSA-q22m-h7m2-9mgm

Signed-off-by: Christian Brabandt <cb@256bit.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsemsg(_(e_trailing_characters_str), end);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (*end != NUL)', '\t    semsg(_(e_trailing_characters_str), end);', '\telse', '\t    semsg(_(e_val_too_large), arg);']}
description: Vim is an improved version of the good old UNIX editor Vi. Heap-use-after-free in memory allocated in the function `ga_grow_inner` in in the file `src/alloc.c` at line 748, which is freed in the file `src/ex_docmd.c` in the function `do_cmdline` at line 1010 and then used again in `src/cmdhist.c` at line 759. When using the `:history` command, it's possible that the provided argument overflows the accepted value. Causing an Integer Overflow and potentially later an use-after-free. This vulnerability has been patched in version 9.0.2068.

code_evidence: ex_history passes &hisidx1/&hisidx2 (int pointers) to get_list_range, then only checks the boolean result and *end != NUL; when the parsed numbers overflow the int destinations, *end is NUL so the error path does not fire and execution continues with wrapped indices.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an unbounded numeric range that is converted into fixed-width ints, producing wraparound before the value is used for indexing—matching CWE-190's integer overflow/wraparound. It is not merely a trailing-character parse error (CWE-20-style validation) because the value is accepted and then used in its wrapped form.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: get_list_range stores parsed values into int variables, so a large :history argument wraps to a small or negative index. The guard at line 47 treats a successful parse with *end == NUL as valid, so wrapped hisidx1/hisidx2 flow into the history indexing loop (lines 59-64, 71), where negative offsets are only partially normalized, leading to out-of-range access; the commit notes this can later become a use-after-free. Root cause is the missing INT_MAX bound on the parsed value; the trigger is an oversized numeric argument to :history.

description: The DGifDecompressLine function in dgif_lib.c in GIFLIB (possibly version 3.0.x), as later shipped in cgif.c in sam2p 0.49.4, has a heap-based buffer overflow because a certain CrntCode array index is not checked. This will lead to a denial of service or possibly unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: curimg[0] is allocated with row stride for 2-bit pixels (new Indexed(wd, ht, 2, 1)); toend is computed as to+((wdcpp+7)>>3), rounding the byte count up, so the while loop writes one byte per iteration past the allocated row when wd is not a multiple of 8. After the loop, line 30 adjusts p by p+=(wdcpp&7)-8, a negative offset when the remainder is nonzero, moving the source pointer backwards.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of the allocated row buffer due to an unchecked/incorrectly rounded length, directly matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read: the write occurs via *to++=i into the undersized destination.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination row length is rounded up with (wdcpp+7)>>3 while the packed 2-bit buffer only has wdcpp>>3 bytes, so the loop's final write goes past the row end. Trigger: a width not divisible by 8. Consequence: a heap out-of-bounds write of one byte per row, corrupting adjacent heap memory and enabling crash or possible code execution.

commit_msg:
Patch series "Fix several device private page reference counting issues",
v2

This series aims to fix a number of page reference counting issues in
drivers dealing with device private ZONE_DEVICE pages.  These result in
use-after-free type bugs, either from accessing a struct page which no
longer exists because it has been removed or accessing fields within the
struct page which are no longer valid because the page has been freed.

During normal usage it is unlikely these will cause any problems.  However
without these fixes it is possible to crash the kernel from userspace. 
These crashes can be triggered either by unloading the kernel module or
unbinding the device from the driver prior to a userspace task exiting. 
In modules such as Nouveau it is also possible to trigger some of these
issues by explicitly closing the device file-descriptor prior to the task
exiting and then accessing device private memory.

This involves some minor changes to both PowerPC and AMD GPU code. 
Unfortunately I lack hardware to test either of those so any help there
would be appreciated.  The changes mimic what is done in for both Nouveau
and hmm-tests though so I doubt they will cause problems.


This patch (of 8):

When the CPU tries to access a device private page the migrate_to_ram()
callback associated with the pgmap for the page is called.  However no
reference is taken on the faulting page.  Therefore a concurrent migration
of the device private page can free the page and possibly the underlying
pgmap.  This results in a race which can crash the kernel due to the
migrate_to_ram() function pointer becoming invalid.  It also means drivers
can't reliably read the zone_device_data field because the page may have
been freed with memunmap_pages().

Close the race by getting a reference on the page while holding the ptl to
ensure it has not been freed.  Unfortunately the elevated reference count
will cause the migration required to handle the fault to fail.  To avoid
this failure pass the faulting page into the migrate_vma functions so that
if an elevated reference count is found it can be checked to see if it's
expected or not.

description: A vulnerability was found in Linux Kernel. It has been classified as problematic. Affected is an unknown function of the file mm/memory.c of the component Driver Handler. The manipulation leads to use after free. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211020.

code_evidence: migrate is zero-initialized at line 16 and fault_page is never assigned into it; the function relies solely on migrate_vma_setup at line 37 to collect pages. When cpages is zero (line 44), the code takes the unsuccessful-pages path at lines 47-48 without ever pinning or holding a reference on the faulting page.

The collected migrate state is passed to svm_migrate_copy_to_ram and finalized via migrate_vma_pages/migrate_vma_finalize at lines 57-62, but with no fault_page reference the page can be concurrently migrated and freed, so later accesses in this path operate on freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function continues to reference page state (migrate.src entries and associated pgmap) after a concurrent free, with no reference held to prevent deallocation. This is a use-after-free rather than a simple missing check; the missing page reference enables the freed-memory reuse.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: svm_migrate_vma_to_ram performs migration and page bookkeeping without acquiring a reference on the faulting device-private page. Trigger: a CPU fault races with a concurrent migration that frees the page/pgmap while cpages handling and copy/finalize run. Consequence: use-after-free of the struct page and possibly pgmap, leading to kernel crash or invalid reads.

description: Apache OpenOffice opens dBase/DBF documents and shows the contents as spreadsheets. DBF are database files with data organized in fields. When reading DBF data the size of certain fields is not checked: the data is just copied into local variables. A carefully crafted document could overflow the allocated space, leading to the execution of arbitrary code by altering the contents of the program stack. This issue affects Apache OpenOffice up to and including version 4.1.10

code_evidence: For TIMESTAMP, fixed memcpy of 4 bytes each into nDate/nTime from pData, whose length nLen is not validated before the copy.
For INTEGER, memcpy copies nLen bytes from pData into a 4-byte sal_Int32 nValue; nLen comes from field metadata (m_aRealFieldLengths or precision property) and was unchecked.
For DOUBLE, memcpy copies nLen bytes into an 8-byte sal_Int64 (currency branch) or double d; nLen is attacker-influenced field length with no bound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits: the function performs buffer copy operations (memcpy) from input pData into fixed-size stack buffers without checking that the input size is less than the destination, exactly the classic buffer copy weakness. The added nLen checks in the patch confirm the missing size validation was the defect.

evidence_lines.code:
sal_Int32 nValue = 0;
memcpy(&nValue, pData, nLen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: field length nLen derived from the DBF document is used directly as the memcpy count into fixed-size local variables without verifying nLen against the destination size. Trigger: a crafted DBF declaring an oversized field for INTEGER/DOUBLE/TIMESTAMP. Consequence: stack buffer overflow, corrupting adjacent stack memory and potentially enabling arbitrary code execution.

commit_msg:
packet: fix races in fanout_add()

Multiple threads can call fanout_add() at the same time.

We need to grab fanout_mutex earlier to avoid races that could
lead to one thread freeing po->rollover that was set by another thread.

Do the same in fanout_release(), for peace of mind, and to help us
finding lockdep issues earlier.

Fixes: dc99f600698d ("packet: Add fanout support.")
Fixes: 0648ab70afe6 ("packet: rollover prepare: per-socket state")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Cc: Willem de Bruijn <willemb@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t\treturn -EALREADY;', '\t\tpo->rollover = kzalloc(sizeof(*po->rollover), GFP_KERNEL);', '\t\tif (!po->rollover)', '\t\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\t\tatomic_long_set(&po->rollover->num, 0);', '\t\tatomic_long_set(&po->rollover->num_huge, 0);', '\t\tatomic_long_set(&po->rollover->num_failed, 0);', '\tmutex_lock(&fanout_mutex);', '\tmutex_unlock(&fanout_mutex);', '\tif (err) {', '\t\tkfree(po->rollover);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct packet_rollover *rollover = NULL;', '\tmutex_lock(&fanout_mutex);', '', '\terr = -EINVAL;', '\t\tgoto out;', '\terr = -EALREADY;', '\t\tgoto out;', '\t\terr = -ENOMEM;', '\t\trollover = kzalloc(sizeof(*rollover), GFP_KERNEL);', '\t\tif (!rollover)', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t\tatomic_long_set(&rollover->num, 0);', '\t\tatomic_long_set(&rollover->num_huge, 0);', '\t\tatomic_long_set(&rollover->num_failed, 0);', '\t\tpo->rollover = rollover;', '\tif (err && rollover) {', '\t\tkfree(rollover);', '\tmutex_unlock(&fanout_mutex);']}
description: Race condition in net/packet/af_packet.c in the Linux kernel before 4.9.13 allows local users to cause a denial of service (use-after-free) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a multithreaded application that makes PACKET_FANOUT setsockopt system calls.

code_evidence: The running/fanout checks and the allocation and assignment of po->rollover at lines 23-35 occur before mutex_lock(&fanout_mutex) at line 36, so concurrent fanout_add() calls can interleave on the shared po->rollover field.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a shared resource (po->rollover) is accessed without exclusive synchronization, violating atomicity of the check-and-store sequence. It is not merely a memory leak; the missing lock allows concurrent modification of shared state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: po->rollover is checked, allocated and stored outside fanout_mutex, so two threads can each allocate and overwrite po->rollover, and one thread's later failure path frees the pointer the other thread installed. Trigger: concurrent PACKET_FANOUT setsockopt calls on the same socket; supported consequence is a race leading to use-after-free/denial of service.

commit_msg:
'hostcmd' is alloced by kzalloc, should be freed before
leaving from the error handling cases, otherwise it will
cause mem leak.

Fixes: 3935ccc14d2c ("mwifiex: add cfg80211 testmode support")
Signed-off-by: YueHaibing <yuehaibing@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!skb)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tkfree(hostcmd);', '\t\tif (!skb) {', '\t\t\tkfree(hostcmd);', '\t\t}', '\t\t\tkfree(hostcmd);']}
description: mwifiex_tm_cmd in drivers/net/wireless/marvell/mwifiex/cfg80211.c in the Linux kernel before 5.1.6 has some error-handling cases that did not free allocated hostcmd memory, aka CID-003b686ace82. This will cause a memory leak and denial of service.

code_evidence: hostcmd is allocated with kzalloc and is the only owning pointer; the normal path frees it at line 41 after cfg80211_testmode_reply.
On mwifiex_send_cmd failure the function logs and returns -EFAULT at line 29 without releasing hostcmd.
If cfg80211_testmode_alloc_reply_skb returns NULL, the function returns -ENOMEM at line 33, abandoning hostcmd.
If nla_put fails, only skb is freed via kfree_skb at line 37 and the function returns -EMSGSIZE, leaving hostcmd allocated.
The final return passes err from cfg80211_testmode_reply after freeing hostcmd, confirming the intended release point that the error paths bypass.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because an allocated object loses its last reference on error returns without being released. This is a missing-release leak, not a use-after-free or double free, since the memory is simply abandoned rather than accessed or freed twice.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the hostcmd buffer allocated at line 21 is freed only on the success path at line 41, while three error branches return early without kfree. Trigger: a failed send, failed reply-skb allocation, or failed nla_put. Consequence: repeated calls leak kernel memory, supporting resource-exhaustion denial of service.

commit_msg: Fix conversion from GDB register profile to rizin profile
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar name[1024], region1[100], region2[100], perms[5];', '\t\tret = sscanf(ptr, "%s %s %" PFMT64x " %*s %*s %[^\\n]", &region1[2],', '\t\t\tperms, &offset, name);'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar name[PROC_NAME_SZ + 1], region1[PROC_REGION_SZ + 1], region2[PROC_REGION_SZ + 1], perms[PROC_PERM_SZ + 1];', '\t\tret = sscanf(ptr, "%" RZ_STR_DEF(PROC_REGION_LEFT_SZ) "s %" RZ_STR_DEF(PROC_PERM_SZ) "s %" PFMT64x " %*s %*s %" RZ_STR_DEF(PROC_NAME_SZ) "[^\\n]",', '\t\t\t&region1[2], perms, &offset, name);']}
description: Rizin is a UNIX-like reverse engineering framework and command-line toolset. In version 0.5.1 and prior, converting a GDB registers profile file into a Rizin register profile can result in a stack-based buffer overflow when the `name`, `type`, or `groups` fields have longer values than expected. Users opening untrusted GDB registers files (e.g. with the `drpg` or `arpg` commands) are affected by this flaw. Commit d6196703d89c84467b600ba2692534579dc25ed4 contains a patch for this issue. As a workaround, review the GDB register profiles before loading them with `drpg`/`arpg` commands.

code_evidence: Line 49 declares fixed-size stack buffers, notably name[1024] and perms[5], without bounds tied to the parsed input. Line 70-71 use sscanf with unbounded %s for region1[2] and perms and unbounded %[^\n] for name, copying attacker-controlled map-line fields directly into these stack buffers with no width limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a buffer copy (sscanf into fixed arrays) without checking input size, so writes can exceed the destination bounds, which is exactly CWE-120's classic buffer overflow. The patch confirms this by adding RZ_STR_DEF width limits and resizing buffers. A mere out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) is not the issue here since the overflow writes past the stack buffers.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sscanf conversion specifiers lack field widths, so tokens from the /proc/pid/maps content (or GDB-provided maps data) longer than the destination buffers are copied past their ends. Trigger: a crafted or malformed maps line with an overlong region, perms, or name field. Consequence: stack-based buffer overflow, corrupting adjacent stack memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
dtls client hello: fix zeroed random (fixes #960)

This broke with bcf4de03 "handshake: treat reply to HRR as a reply to
hello verify request", which failed to "De Morgan" properly.

Signed-off-by: Stefan Bühler <stbuehler@web.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t    !(IS_DTLS(session) && session->internals.dtls.hsk_hello_verify_requests == 0)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t    !(IS_DTLS(session) && session->internals.dtls.hsk_hello_verify_requests != 0)) {']}
description: GnuTLS 3.6.x before 3.6.13 uses incorrect cryptography for DTLS. The earliest affected version is 3.6.3 (2018-07-16) because of an error in a 2017-10-06 commit. The DTLS client always uses 32 '\0' bytes instead of a random value, and thus contributes no randomness to a DTLS negotiation. This breaks the security guarantees of the DTLS protocol.

code_evidence: The guard at [74,75] decides whether _gnutls_gen_client_random() is called. With the pre-fix condition, for DTLS a fresh client hello (hsk_hello_verify_requests == 0) evaluates the second clause to true, so the negated conjunction is false and random generation is skipped. Line [76] is then never executed on that path, leaving security_parameters.client_random at its zeroed value, which [82,83,84] append into the ClientHello.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because the function fails to produce a random value in a security-critical handshake field, sending a fixed all-zero value instead. The flaw is a missing/incorrect random generation step, not weak PRNG output quality (CWE-338) or mere predictability of a generated number.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an inverted DTLS comparison in the condition guarding random generation: generation is suppressed exactly when it is first required. Trigger is a DTLS client sending its initial ClientHello; the consequence is a ClientHello carrying 32 zero bytes instead of a random value, removing client randomness from the DTLS negotiation and breaking its security guarantees.

commit_msg:
net: avoid signed overflows for SO_{SND|RCV}BUFFORCE

CAP_NET_ADMIN users should not be allowed to set negative
sk_sndbuf or sk_rcvbuf values, as it can lead to various memory
corruptions, crashes, OOM...

Note that before commit 82981930125a ("net: cleanups in
sock_setsockopt()"), the bug was even more serious, since SO_SNDBUF
and SO_RCVBUF were vulnerable.

This needs to be backported to all known linux kernels.

Again, many thanks to syzkaller team for discovering this gem.

Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tsk->sk_sndbuf = max_t(u32, val * 2, SOCK_MIN_SNDBUF);', '\t\tsk->sk_rcvbuf = max_t(u32, val * 2, SOCK_MIN_RCVBUF);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tsk->sk_sndbuf = max_t(int, val * 2, SOCK_MIN_SNDBUF);', '\t\tsk->sk_rcvbuf = max_t(int, val * 2, SOCK_MIN_RCVBUF);']}
description: The sock_setsockopt function in net/core/sock.c in the Linux kernel before 4.8.14 mishandles negative values of sk_sndbuf and sk_rcvbuf, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory corruption and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability for a crafted setsockopt system call with the (1) SO_SNDBUFFORCE or (2) SO_RCVBUFFORCE option.

code_evidence: SO_SNDBUF clamps val with min_t(u32,...) at line 43, but the set_sndbuf label at line 44 is also reached from SO_SNDBUFFORCE via goto at line 54, bypassing that clamp. Line 46 then computes max_t(u32, val*2, ...) with a signed val, so a negative val is converted to unsigned and assigned to sk_sndbuf.
SO_SNDBUFFORCE (lines 49-54) only checks CAP_NET_ADMIN then jumps to set_sndbuf, so the negative val read at line 13 reaches line 46 unclamped.

SO_RCVBUF clamps at line 56, but set_rcvbuf at line 57 is also reached from SO_RCVBUFFORCE via goto at line 66. Line 59 computes max_t(u32, val*2,...) with signed val, producing a huge unsigned sk_rcvbuf.
SO_RCVBUFFORCE (lines 61-66) only checks CAP_NET_ADMIN then jumps to set_rcvbuf, so a negative val reaches line 59 unclamped.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The oversized sk_sndbuf/sk_rcvbuf values propagate into socket buffer allocation and queue accounting, causing reads/writes outside intended buffer boundaries and memory corruption—the out-of-bounds memory operation described by CWE-119. The defect is the missing signedness/negative-value constraint, but the supported impact is buffer-bound violation rather than merely a logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the u32-typed max_t in lines 46 and 59 reinterprets a negative signed val*2 as a huge unsigned buffer size, and the FORCE paths skip the min_t clamp. Trigger: a CAP_NET_ADMIN setsockopt with SO_SNDBUFFORCE/SO_RCVBUFFORCE and a negative integer. Consequence: sk_sndbuf/sk_rcvbuf become enormous, later driving out-of-bounds buffer operations, memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Don't go past the end of a page in a NetScaler file.

Records in a properly formatted NetScaler file shouldn't go past the end
of a page, but nothing guarantees that a NetScaler file will be properly
formatted.

NetScaler 3.x files allow record bodies to go past the end of a page,
but 1.x and 2.x files don't, so treat record headers that go past the
end of a page, and record bodies in 1.x and 2.x files that go past the
end of a page, as errors.

Clean up some stuff while we're at it.

Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/20326
Reviewed-by: Guy Harris <guy@alum.mit.edu>
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/20329

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.4 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.10, there is a NetScaler file parser crash, triggered by a malformed capture file. This was addressed in wiretap/netscaler.c by validating the relationship between pages and records.

code_evidence: Buffer offset/length are signed gint32 values at [6,7], so a malformed value could be negative and bypass the offset bound check.

At [19,20] the offset comparison uses <= NSPR_PAGESIZE_TRACE, permitting offset equal to page size; [22,23] memsets from bytes_read without validating bytes_read against page size, and the guard only checks bytes_read>0.

The while loop [25,26] indexes nstrace_buf[nstrace_buf_offset] and casts hdp at [28] without ensuring the record size from nspr_getv20recordsize stays within the page; offset advances by that unvalidated size at [54,66] and the read loop at [74] iterates without validating page/record relationship.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes attacker-controlled file metadata (record sizes/offsets) and fails to validate that derived positions conform to the page boundary before use, which is exactly improper input validation (CWE-20); the resulting out-of-bounds access is the consequence of the missing validation.

evidence_lines.code:
gint32 nstrace_buf_offset = nstrace->nstrace_buf_offset;
gint32 nstrace_buflen = nstrace->nstrace_buflen;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser trusts record header sizes and offsets from the malformed NetScaler file without confirming they stay within a page. A record body or header whose size pushes nstrace_buf_offset past NSPR_PAGESIZE_TRACE is still used to index nstrace_buf, producing an out-of-bounds read/memset and a crash.

commit_msg: Updated the adaptors to have a config.h preproc definition which, if enabled, compiles the adaptors without the ability to check for invalid URL characters.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#ifndef __PRESERVE_UNSAFE_URLS', '#endif']}
description: Project Wonder WebObjects 1.0 through 5.4.3 is vulnerable to Arbitrary HTTP Header injection and URL- or Header-based XSS reflection in all web-server adaptor interfaces.

code_evidence: The function builds url by concatenating environment-derived script_name and path_info [48-50], logs it [51], then validates it with WOValidateInitialURL before parsing [52-58]. The diff wraps this validation in #ifndef __PRESERVE_UNSAFE_URLS; when that macro is defined, the check of forbidden characters (0x0D/0x0A) is compiled out, so the raw URL proceeds to WOParseApplicationName [59] and later tr_handleRequest [126] unchecked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-79 fits because user-controllable URL input is no longer neutralized before being used in generated responses, permitting script/header reflection to victims. The removed check specifically guards against CR/LF injection that enables response splitting and XSS; this is improper output neutralization, not merely parsing failure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the URL validation that rejects CR/LF characters is conditionally removed, allowing attacker-controlled path_info/script_name to reach request handling with embedded control characters. Trigger: compiling with __PRESERVE_UNSAFE_URLS and sending a request whose URL contains 0x0D/0x0A. Supported consequence: injected header/URL content can be reflected into responses, enabling header injection and reflected XSS.

commit_msg:
This fixes CVE-2017-7482.

When a kerberos 5 ticket is being decoded so that it can be loaded into an
rxrpc-type key, there are several places in which the length of a
variable-length field is checked to make sure that it's not going to
overrun the available data - but the data is padded to the nearest
four-byte boundary and the code doesn't check for this extra.  This could
lead to the size-remaining variable wrapping and the data pointer going
over the end of the buffer.

Fix this by making the various variable-length data checks use the padded
length.

Reported-by: 石磊 <shilei-c@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Marc Dionne <marc.c.dionne@auristor.com>
Reviewed-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned int len, tmp, loop, ntoken, toklen, sec_ix;', '\ttmp = (len + 3) & ~3;', '\tif (tmp > datalen)', '\tif (len < tmp)', '\t\tfor (; loop < tmp; loop++)', '\t\t\tif (cp[loop])', '\t\t\t\tgoto not_xdr;', '\t       len, tmp, len, len, (const char *) xdr);', '\tdatalen -= tmp;', '\txdr += tmp >> 2;', '\t\tif (toklen < 20 || toklen > datalen)', '\t\tdatalen -= (toklen + 3) & ~3;', '\t\txdr += (toklen + 3) >> 2;'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned int len, paddedlen, loop, ntoken, toklen, sec_ix;', '\tpaddedlen = (len + 3) & ~3;', '\tif (paddedlen > datalen)', '\tfor (; loop < paddedlen; loop++)', '\t\tif (cp[loop])', '\t\t\tgoto not_xdr;', '\t       len, paddedlen, len, len, (const char *) xdr);', '\tdatalen -= paddedlen;', '\txdr += paddedlen >> 2;', '\t\tpaddedlen = (toklen + 3) & ~3;', '\t\tif (toklen < 20 || toklen > datalen || paddedlen > datalen)', '\t\tdatalen -= paddedlen;', '\t\txdr += paddedlen >> 2;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before version 4.12, Kerberos 5 tickets decoded when using the RXRPC keys incorrectly assumes the size of a field. This could lead to the size-remaining variable wrapping and the data pointer going over the end of the buffer. This could possibly lead to memory corruption and possible privilege escalation.

code_evidence: In the token loop, toklen is validated against datalen (line 53), but then datalen is decremented by the padded size (toklen + 3) & ~3 (line 55) and xdr advanced by (toklen + 3) >> 2 (line 56). The check compares unpadded toklen to datalen, so a toklen near datalen with padding can make datalen -= paddedlen wrap to a huge size_t, and xdr moves past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The subtraction datalen -= paddedlen can underflow/wrap because the guard does not ensure paddedlen <= datalen, matching CWE-190 integer wraparound used as a size/offset. It is distinct from a pure bounds-check omission because the arithmetic wrap is the enabling flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length check uses the unpadded toklen while the pointer/remaining-size update uses the padded length, so a padded length exceeding datalen is not rejected. Trigger: a crafted Kerberos ticket with a token length whose padded size is larger than the remaining data. Consequence: datalen wraps and xdr advances beyond the buffer, leading to out-of-bounds reads and possible memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Bug 700937: Limit recursion in regexp matcher.

Also handle negative return code as an error in the JS bindings.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn !match(prog->start, sp, sp, prog->flags | eflags, sub);'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn match(prog->start, sp, sp, prog->flags | eflags, sub, 0);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Artifex MuJS 1.0.5. It has unlimited recursion because the match function in regexp.c lacks a depth check.

code_evidence: regexec invokes match(prog->start, sp, sp, ...) with no recursion-depth argument or bound; the call is unconditional and recurses through the matcher without any depth check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the matcher recursion is uncontrolled with no depth constraint; the call site shows the missing bound rather than a different weakness such as an off-by-one or buffer overflow.

evidence_lines.code: return !match(prog->start, sp, sp, prog->flags | eflags, sub);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the entry point into the regexp matcher lacks a depth limit, so nested/recursive match invocations can grow unbounded. Trigger: a crafted pattern/input that forces deep recursion in match. Supported consequence: excessive stack consumption leading to resource exhaustion (DoS).

commit_msg: Checks if ordinal < exp->NumberOfFuntions before assigning value to an element in an array
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\toffsets_to_Names[ordinal] = entry_name_ofs;'], 'added_lines': ['', '        if (ordinal < exp->NumberOfFuntions) {', '            offsets_to_Names[ordinal] = entry_name_ofs;', '        }']}
description: A Buffer Overflow vulnerabilityexists in Pev 0.81 via the pe_exports function from exports.c.. The array offsets_to_Names is dynamically allocated on the stack using exp->NumberOfFunctions as its size. However, the loop uses exp->NumberOfNames to iterate over it and set its components value. Therefore, the loop code assumes that exp->NumberOfFunctions is greater than ordinal at each iteration. This can lead to arbitrary code execution.

code_evidence: Line 47 declares offsets_to_Names as a variable-length stack array sized by exp->NumberOfFunctions; line 48 zeroes it.

Line 49 iterates i up to exp->NumberOfNames, line 55 reads a 16-bit ordinal from the file-controlled AddressOfNameOrdinals table, and line 63 writes offsets_to_Names[ordinal] without any bound check on ordinal against NumberOfFunctions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a buffer write whose index is not validated against the destination size, matching CWE-120's unchecked-size copy into a fixed-size buffer. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the flaw is the unchecked store at line 63.

evidence_lines.code:
uint64_t offsets_to_Names[exp->NumberOfFunctions];
memset(offsets_to_Names, 0, sizeof(offsets_to_Names));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The stack array size derives from exp->NumberOfFunctions, but the write index ordinal comes from the untrusted AddressOfNameOrdinals table and the loop is controlled by NumberOfNames. A crafted PE with an ordinal >= NumberOfFunctions (or NumberOfNames exceeding NumberOfFunctions) makes line 63 write past the array, corrupting stack memory and supporting arbitrary code execution.

commit_msg:
Refs #16784. Fix issue.

Signed-off-by: Miguel Company <MiguelCompany@eprosima.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                ch.serializedPayload.data = nullptr;', '                ch.inline_qos.data = nullptr;', '                ch.serializedPayload.data = nullptr;', '                ch.inline_qos.data = nullptr;']}
description: Fast DDS is a C++ implementation of the DDS (Data Distribution Service) standard of the OMG (Object Management Group). In affected versions specific DATA submessages can be sent to a discovery locator which may trigger a free error. This can remotely crash any Fast-DDS process. The call to free() could potentially leave the pointer in the attackers control which could lead to a double free. This issue has been addressed in versions 2.12.0, 2.11.3, 2.10.3, and 2.6.7. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: On the dataFlag success path, ch.serializedPayload.data is set to &msg->buffer[msg->pos] with length/max_size = payload_size, and msg->pos advances. On the invalid-payload branch the function returns false without clearing ch.serializedPayload.data.
On the keyFlag path, an invalid payload_size (<=0) causes an early return false, again leaving ch.inline_qos.data pointing at inline QoS buffer memory set earlier at line 73.

At the normal end, process_data_message_function_ is invoked, then payload_pool->release_payload(ch) releases the payload; afterwards serializedPayload.data and inline_qos.data are nulled. The added nulls in the error branches show the fix nulls these pointers before returning.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a double free (CWE-415): the same buffer pointer may be freed twice because error returns leave dangling ownership pointers. This is distinct from a simple use-after-free since the supported consequence is repeated release of the same address.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: error paths return after partially populating ch.serializedPayload/inline_qos pointers without clearing them, so ownership state is ambiguous. Trigger: a crafted DATA submessage with an invalid payload size or too-short key payload reaches these branches. Consequence: the stale pointer can be released again by later cleanup, leading to a double free and remote crash.

commit_msg:
sctp_make_strreset_req() makes repeated calls to sctp_addto_chunk()
which will automatically account for padding on each call. inreq and
outreq are already 4 bytes aligned, but the payload is not and doing
SCTP_PAD4(a + b) (which _sctp_make_chunk() did implicitly here) is
different from SCTP_PAD4(a) + SCTP_PAD4(b) and not enough. It led to
possible attempt to use more buffer than it was allocated and triggered
a BUG_ON.

This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation. Each directory entry's size (line 39) and offset (line 40) are attacker-controlled 32-bit values stored into directoryEntries (lines 41-42) and later used directly.

At line 67 an embedded buffer is allocated with sk_malloc_flags(size,0) using the untrusted entry size, and line 72 reads exactly size bytes into it; the allocation sizing and subsequent read depend on the same unchecked value.

if (inputStream->read(buffer.get(), size) != size) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is unchecked arithmetic on file-derived integer fields: sizeof(Entry)*numImages and the per-entry size are used to size allocations without verifying the multiplication/size fits. commit_msg:
bplist: Fix data range check for string/data/dict/array nodes

Passing a size of 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF to parse_string_node() might result
in a memcpy with a size of -1, leading to undefined behavior.
This commit makes sure that the actual node data (which depends on the size)
is in the range start_of_object..start_of_object+size.

Credit to OSS-Fuzz
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (*object + size > bplist->offset_table) {', '        if (*object + size > bplist->offset_table) {', '        if (*object + size*2 > bplist->offset_table) {', '        if (*object + size > bplist->offset_table) {', '        if (*object + size > bplist->offset_table) {', '            PLIST_BIN_ERR("%s: BPLIST_REAL data bytes point outside of valid range\\n", __func__);'], 'added_lines': ['        if (*object + size < *object || *object + size > bplist->offset_table) {', '        if (*object + size < *object || *object + size > bplist->offset_table) {', '        if (*object + size*2 < *object || *object + size*2 > bplist->offset_table) {', '        if (*object + size < *object || *object + size > bplist->offset_table) {', '        if (*object + size < *object || *object + size > bplist->offset_table) {', '            PLIST_BIN_ERR("%s: BPLIST_DICT data bytes point outside of valid range\\n", __func__);']}
description: The parse_string_node function in bplist.c in libimobiledevice libplist 1.12 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory allocation error) via a crafted plist file.

code_evidence: size is attacker-controlled: low nibble at line 8, or a 64-bit value read via UINT_TO_HOST at line 30, and is used in arithmetic with *object without overflow checking.
For BPLIST_DATA, the bounds check computes *object + size; a huge size can wrap the pointer, bypass the check, and reach parse_data_node.
BPLIST_STRING check has the same missing wraparound check, allowing parse_string_node to receive an oversized size.
BPLIST_UNICODE guards size*2 overflow at line 98 but not *object + size*2 overflow at line 102, so the range check can be bypassed.
BPLIST_ARRAY/SET check lacks the wraparound guard, letting parse_array_node process an oversized size.
BPLIST_DICT check lacks the wraparound guard, letting parse_dict_node process an oversized size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing overflow guard on *object + size lets a wrapped range check admit an oversized node, and the size is subsequently used in a write path, matching CWE-787. A pure allocation failure would be CWE-789, but the primary defect here is the unchecked pointer arithmetic enabling out-of-bounds writes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is an unchecked addition of an attacker-controlled size to the object pointer, which wraps so the range check passes. The trigger is a crafted plist node whose encoded size is near UINT64_MAX; the downstream parse_*_node then uses this size for memory operations, producing an out-of-bounds write (or invalid allocation/DoS).

description: ngiflib.c in MiniUPnP ngiflib 0.4 has a stack-based buffer overflow in DecodeGifImg.

code_evidence: When act_code >= free, the decoder pushes casspecial onto the stack and rewinds act_code to old_code before the prefix walk.
The while loop indexes ab_suffx[act_code] and ab_prfx[act_code] using act_code, which is only bounded by clr from the earlier comparison, not by free or the 4096-entry array size.
stackp starts at ab_stack+4096 and is only decremented by *(--stackp); no check ensures stackp stays above ab_stack, so repeated pushes can write below the array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to ab_suffx/ab_prfx and ab_stack outside their intended bounds, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. The issue is a missing bound on the write index/pointer, not merely an out-of-bounds read or integer overflow.

evidence_lines.code:
stackp = stack_top = ab_stack + 4096;
*(--stackp) = casspecial;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder trusts the LZW code act_code without validating it against the current dictionary size or the 4096-element tables, and it pushes prefix-chain bytes onto ab_stack without a lower-bound check. A crafted GIF whose codes exceed free (or a long chain) drives act_code past the table bounds and/or decrements stackp below ab_stack, causing out-of-bounds writes that can corrupt memory and potentially execute code.

description: UnRAR 5.6.1.2 and 5.6.1.3 has a heap-based buffer overflow in Unpack::CopyString (called from Unpack::Unpack5 and CmdExtract::ExtractCurrentFile).

code_evidence: Line 14 resets the mbstate, then line 15 calls mbrtowc writing to Dest+DestPos without first checking that DestPos<DestSize-1; the loop only guarantees DestPos<DestSize, so a multibyte conversion can write up to MB_CUR_MAX wide chars at the final slot.

commit_msg:
xfrm: fix crash in XFRM_MSG_GETSA netlink handler

If we hit any of the error conditions inside xfrm_dump_sa(), then
xfrm_state_walk_init() never gets called. However, we still call
xfrm_state_walk_done() from xfrm_dump_sa_done(), which will crash
because the state walk was never initialized properly.

We can fix this by setting cb->args[0] only after we've processed the
first element and checking this before calling xfrm_state_walk_done().

Fixes: d3623099d3 ("ipsec: add support of limited SA dump")
Cc: Nicolas Dichtel <nicolas.dichtel@6wind.com>
Cc: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
Signed-off-by: Vegard Nossum <vegard.nossum@oracle.com>
Acked-by: Nicolas Dichtel <nicolas.dichtel@6wind.com>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\txfrm_state_walk_done(walk, net);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (cb->args[0])', '\t\txfrm_state_walk_done(walk, net);']}
description: A NULL pointer dereference vulnerability was found in netlink_dump. This issue can occur when the Netlink socket receives the message(sendmsg) for the XFRM_MSG_GETSA, XFRM_MSG_GETPOLICY type message, and the DUMP flag is set and can cause a denial of service or possibly another unspecified impact. Due to the nature of the flaw, privilege escalation cannot be fully ruled out, although it is unlikely.

code_evidence: Line 3 casts cb->args[1] into a struct xfrm_state_walk pointer, and line 6 unconditionally passes it to xfrm_state_walk_done(). If xfrm_dump_sa() hit an error before xfrm_state_walk_init(), that walk state was never initialized, so the done handler operates on invalid/NULL internal pointers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The handler dereferences a walk pointer expected to be valid but which may be NULL/uninitialized when the dump setup failed, matching CWE-476. The missing initialization guard is the cause, not merely a resource leak.

evidence_lines.code:
struct xfrm_state_walk *walk = (struct xfrm_state_walk *) &cb->args[1];
xfrm_state_walk_done(walk, net);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: xfrm_dump_sa_done() calls xfrm_state_walk_done() without checking whether the walk was actually initialized. Trigger: an XFRM_MSG_GETSA dump request that fails inside xfrm_dump_sa() before xfrm_state_walk_init() runs. Consequence: dereference of uninitialized/NULL walk pointer fields, causing a kernel crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
net: rose: fix UAF bugs caused by timer handler

There are UAF bugs in rose_heartbeat_expiry(), rose_timer_expiry()
and rose_idletimer_expiry(). The root cause is that del_timer()
could not stop the timer handler that is running and the refcount
of sock is not managed properly.

One of the UAF bugs is shown below:

    (thread 1)          |        (thread 2)
                        |  rose_bind
                        |  rose_connect
                        |    rose_start_heartbeat
rose_release            |    (wait a time)
  case ROSE_STATE_0     |
  rose_destroy_socket   |  rose_heartbeat_expiry
    rose_stop_heartbeat |
    sock_put(sk)        |    ...
  sock_put(sk) // FREE  |
                        |    bh_lock_sock(sk) // USE

The sock is deallocated by sock_put() in rose_release() and
then used by bh_lock_sock() in rose_heartbeat_expiry().

Although rose_destroy_socket() calls rose_stop_heartbeat(),
it could not stop the timer that is running.

description: There are use-after-free vulnerabilities caused by timer handler in net/rose/rose_timer.c of linux that allow attackers to crash linux kernel without any privileges.

code_evidence: The timer callback acquires the socket lock with bh_lock_sock(sk) at line 5 and releases it at line 24, but before the patch the function returned without dropping the reference that the timer start path held on sk; the added sock_put(sk) at line 25 releases that reference after the handler finishes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because sk is referenced after its last reference is dropped and the object is deallocated; the fix's added sock_put at line 25 balances the reference held for the timer so the handler's use of sk remains valid. This is a lifetime/refcount flaw, not merely a race in lock handling.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is unbalanced socket reference counting across the timer lifecycle: the handler uses sk (line 5 and the state cases) while a concurrent rose_release/rose_destroy_socket path can free sk via sock_put. The trigger is a running timer that del_timer cannot stop; the supported consequence is use-after-free of sk, leading to crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
The check_interval file in

  /sys/devices/system/machinecheck/machinecheck<cpu number>

directory is a global timer value for MCE polling. If it is changed by one
CPU, mce_restart() broadcasts the event to other CPUs to delete and restart
the MCE polling timer and __mcheck_cpu_init_timer() reinitializes the
mce_timer variable.

If more than one CPU writes a specific value to the check_interval file
concurrently, mce_timer is not protected from such concurrent accesses and
all kinds of explosions happen. Since only root can write to those sysfs
variables, the issue is not a big deal security-wise.

However, concurrent writes to these configuration variables is void of
reason so the proper thing to do is to serialize the access with a mutex.

Boris:

 - Make store_int_with_restart() use device_store_ulong() to filter out
   negative intervals
 - Limit min interval to 1 second
 - Correct locking
 - Massage commit message

Signed-off-by: Seunghun Han <kkamagui@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Borislav Petkov <bp@suse.de>

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20180302202706.9434-1-kkamagui@gmail.com

description: Race condition in the store_int_with_restart() function in arch/x86/kernel/cpu/mcheck/mce.c in the Linux kernel through 4.15.7 allows local users to cause a denial of service (panic) by leveraging root access to write to the check_interval file in a /sys/devices/system/machinecheck/machinecheck<cpu number> directory. NOTE: a third party has indicated that this report is not security relevant

code_evidence: set_ignore_ce reads and writes the shared mca_cfg.ignore_ce flag and manipulates per-CPU state via mce_timer_delete_all(), on_each_cpu(mce_disable_cmci), and on_each_cpu(mce_enable_ce) without any synchronization protecting these operations. The check-then-act on ignore_ce (line 8) and the subsequent toggling and CPU-wide callbacks form a non-atomic sequence that concurrent sysfs writers can interleave.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a concurrent code sequence requiring exclusive access to shared mca_cfg and per-CPU timer state, yet provides no serialization, so an interfering code sequence can modify the resource mid-operation. This directly matches CWE-362; it is not merely a missing-input-validation issue, since the flaw is the timing window on shared state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the unsynchronized check-then-act on the shared mca_cfg.ignore_ce state and the resulting per-CPU timer/CMCI manipulation. Concurrent writers to the ignore_ce sysfs attribute can interleave, causing inconsistent state and timer reinitialization races, leading to kernel instability or panic (availability impact).

commit_msg:
PR22443, Global buffer overflow in _bfd_elf_get_symbol_version_string

Symbols like *ABS* defined in bfd/section.c:global_syms are not
elf_symbol_type.  They can appear on relocs and perhaps other places
in an ELF bfd, so a number of places in nm.c and objdump.c are wrong
to cast an asymbol based on the bfd being ELF.  I think we lose
nothing by excluding all section symbols, not just the global_syms.

	PR 22443
	* nm.c (sort_symbols_by_size): Don't attempt to access
	section symbol internal_elf_sym.
	(print_symbol): Likewise.  Don't call bfd_get_symbol_version_string
	for section symbols.
	* objdump.c (compare_symbols): Don't attempt to access
	section symbol internal_elf_sym.
	(objdump_print_symname): Don't call bfd_get_symbol_version_string
	for section symbols.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if ((sym->flags & BSF_SYNTHETIC) == 0)'], 'added_lines': ['  if ((sym->flags & (BSF_SECTION_SYM | BSF_SYNTHETIC)) == 0)']}
description: nm.c and objdump.c in GNU Binutils 2.29.1 mishandle certain global symbols, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (_bfd_elf_get_symbol_version_string buffer over-read and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: Line 16 gates the call to bfd_get_symbol_version_string only on BSF_SYNTHETIC, so section symbols (BSF_SECTION_SYM) that are not synthetic still reach line 17. Line 17 passes such a symbol to bfd_get_symbol_version_string, which expects an ELF symbol and reads internal_elf_sym beyond the asymbol storage.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a read past the end of the symbol buffer, matching CWE-125. This is not CWE-787 (write) or a type-confusion label per se; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((sym->flags & BSF_SYNTHETIC) == 0)
version_string = bfd_get_symbol_version_string (abfd, sym, &hidden);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard admits section symbols (e.g. *ABS*) whose asymbol layout is not elf_symbol_type, so downstream version-string lookup reads past the intended object. Trigger: a crafted ELF reloc referencing a section symbol passed to objdump_print_symname. Consequence: out-of-bounds read, crash/DoS and possible information exposure.

commit_msg:
Restrict the size of OBJECT IDENTIFIERs that OBJ_obj2txt will translate

OBJ_obj2txt() would translate any size OBJECT IDENTIFIER to canonical
numeric text form.  For gigantic sub-identifiers, this would take a very
long time, the time complexity being O(n^2) where n is the size of that
sub-identifier.

To mitigate this, a restriction on the size that OBJ_obj2txt() will
translate to canonical numeric text form is added, based on RFC 2578
(STD 58), which says this:

> 3.5. OBJECT IDENTIFIER values
>
> An OBJECT IDENTIFIER value is an ordered list of non-negative numbers.
> For the SMIv2, each number in the list is referred to as a sub-identifier,
> there are at most 128 sub-identifiers in a value, and each sub-identifier
> has a maximum value of 2^32-1 (4294967295 decimal).

Fixes otc/security#96
Fixes CVE-2023-2650

Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>

description:
Issue summary: Processing some specially crafted ASN.1 object identifiers or
data containing them may be very slow.

Impact summary: Applications that use OBJ_obj2txt() directly, or use any of
the OpenSSL subsystems OCSP, PKCS7/SMIME, CMS, CMP/CRMF or TS with no message
size limit may experience notable to very long delays when processing those
messages, which may lead to a Denial of Service.

An OBJECT IDENTIFIER is composed of a series of numbers - sub-identifiers -
most of which have no size limit.  OBJ_obj2txt() may be used to translate
an ASN.1 OBJECT IDENTIFIER given in DER encoding form (using the OpenSSL
type ASN1_OBJECT) to its canonical numeric text form, which are the
sub-identifiers of the OBJECT IDENTIFIER in decimal form, separated by
periods.

When one of the sub-identifiers in the OBJECT IDENTIFIER is very large
(these are sizes that are seen as absurdly large, taking up tens or hundreds
of KiBs), the translation to a decimal number in text may take a very long
time.  The time complexity is O(n^2) with 'n' being the size of the
sub-identifiers in bytes (*).

With OpenSSL 3.0, support to fetch cryptographic algorithms using names /
identifiers in string form was introduced.  This includes using OBJECT
IDENTIFIERs in canonical numeric text form as identifiers for fetching
algorithms.

Such OBJECT IDENTIFIERs may be received through the ASN.1 structure
AlgorithmIdentifier, which is commonly used in multiple protocols to specify
what cryptographic algorithm should be used to sign or verify, encrypt or
decrypt, or digest passed data.

Applications that call OBJ_obj2txt() directly with untrusted data are
affected, with any version of OpenSSL.  If the use is for the mere purpose
of display, the severity is considered low.

In OpenSSL 3.0 and newer, this affects the subsystems OCSP, PKCS7/SMIME,
CMS, CMP/CRMF or TS.  It also impacts anything that processes X.509
certificates, including simple things like verifying its signature.

The impact on TLS is relatively low, because all versions of OpenSSL have a
100KiB limit on the peer's certificate chain.  Additionally, this only
impacts clients, or servers that have explicitly enabled client
authentication.

In OpenSSL 1.1.1 and 1.0.2, this only affects displaying diverse objects,
such as X.509 certificates.  This is assumed to not happen in such a way
that it would cause a Denial of Service, so these versions are considered
not affected by this issue in such a way that it would be cause for concern,
and the severity is therefore considered low.

code_evidence: len = a->length and p = a->data take the attacker-controlled OID encoding length directly, and the while loop processes it without any upper bound before the patch.
The inner loop reads continuation bytes (c = *p++) and only rejects a trailing 0x80 byte; a long run of 0x80 bytes drives the sub-identifier to arbitrary size.
Once l exceeds ULONG_MAX>>7, a BIGNUM is created and repeatedly shifted by 7 bits per byte, so the sub-identifier grows linearly in bytes with quadratic cost.
BN_bn2dec(bl) converts the large BIGNUM to decimal text, producing a huge string and consuming CPU proportional to the square of the sub-identifier size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the function performs an expensive resource-consuming computation (BIGNUM shifts and decimal conversion) on attacker-supplied input without throttling or size limits, leading to CPU exhaustion. The patch adds a length cap (len > 586) to bound the work, confirming the missing allocation/consumption limit as the cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: OBJ_obj2txt accepts an OBJECT IDENTIFIER of unbounded length and builds arbitrarily large BIGNUM sub-identifiers, then converts them to decimal text, with O(n^2) time. Trigger: untrusted DER containing a very large sub-identifier. Consequence: long CPU consumption in the calling process, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
nfc: replace improper check device_is_registered() in netlink related functions

The device_is_registered() in nfc core is used to check whether
nfc device is registered in netlink related functions such as
nfc_fw_download(), nfc_dev_up() and so on. Although device_is_registered()
is protected by device_lock, there is still a race condition between
device_del() and device_is_registered(). The root cause is that
kobject_del() in device_del() is not protected by device_lock.

   (cleanup task)         |     (netlink task)
                          |
nfc_unregister_device     | nfc_fw_download
 device_del               |  device_lock
  ...                     |   if (!device_is_registered)//(1)
  kobject_del//(2)        |   ...
 ...                      |  device_unlock

The device_is_registered() returns the value of state_in_sysfs and
the state_in_sysfs is set to zero in kobject_del(). If we pass check in
position (1), then set zero in position (2). As a result, the check
in position (1) is useless.

This patch uses bool variable instead of device_is_registered() to judge
whether the nfc device is registered, which is well synchronized.

Fixes: 3e256b8f8dfa ("NFC: add nfc subsystem core")
Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!device_is_registered(&dev->dev)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (dev->shutting_down) {']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel's NFC core functionality due to a race condition between kobject creation and delete. This vulnerability allows a local attacker with CAP_NET_ADMIN privilege to leak kernel information.

code_evidence: The function takes device_lock, then checks device_is_registered(&dev->dev) and returns -ENODEV if it fails, before using the device.

After the check, the code dereferences dev->ops and calls dev->ops->dep_link_down(dev), and on success accesses dev->dep_link_up, dev->active_target, dev->rf_mode, and calls nfc_llcp_mac_is_down(dev) and nfc_genl_dep_link_down_event(dev).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code checks whether the device is registered and then uses the device, while a concurrent unregister can invalidate the check between check and use. This is a TOCTOU race, so CWE-367 fits; it is not merely a missing lock, because the lock does not cover kobject_del().
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the registration check relies on device_is_registered(), whose state_in_sysfs is cleared by kobject_del() in device_del() without device_lock, so the check does not exclude a concurrent nfc_unregister_device. Trigger: a cleanup task calls nfc_unregister_device while a netlink task executes nfc_dep_link_down. Consequence: after the stale check passes, the function uses the device state and ops, leading to use-after-free and possible kernel information leak.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In version 2.10 and earlier, PJSIP transport can be reused if they have the same IP address + port + protocol. However, this is insufficient for secure transport since it lacks remote hostname authentication. Suppose we have created a TLS connection to `sip.foo.com`, which has an IP address `100.1.1.1`. If we want to create a TLS connection to another hostname, say `sip.bar.com`, which has the same IP address, then it will reuse that existing connection, even though `100.1.1.1` does not have certificate to authenticate as `sip.bar.com`. The vulnerability allows for an insecure interaction without user awareness. It affects users who need access to connections to different destinations that translate to the same address, and allows man-in-the-middle attack if attacker can route a connection to another destination such as in the case of DNS spoofing.

code_evidence: Transport lookup key is built from type plus the remote socket address (remote IP/port) only; the destination hostname is not part of the hash key, so connections to different hostnames resolving to the same address collide.

The reuse loop walks the hash bucket and, in the non-listener branch, accepts the first non-shutdown transport (tp_ref = tp_iter->tp; break) without comparing the transport's remote hostname to the requested destination hostname.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-295 fits because the function fails to verify that the reused TLS transport's identity (remote hostname) matches the destination the certificate must authenticate; the missing hostname constraint is the certificate-validation defect, distinct from generic connection reuse.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: secure-transport reuse is decided solely by IP address + port + protocol, with no hostname check against the existing transport's remote_name.host. Trigger: a TLS transport to sip.foo.com exists at 100.1.1.1 and a request targets sip.bar.com at the same address; the loop reuses the foo.com connection. Consequence: the certificate is never validated against the requested hostname, enabling MITM via DNS spoofing or routing.

commit_msg:
Fix/improve buffer overflow in MSG_ReadBits/MSG_WriteBits

Prevent reading past end of message in MSG_ReadBits. If read past
end of msg->data buffer (16348 bytes) the engine could SEGFAULT.
Make MSG_WriteBits use an exact buffer overflow check instead of
possibly failing with a few bytes left.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tHuff_offsetReceive (msgHuff.decompressor.tree, &get, msg->data, &msg->bit);'], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif ( msg->readcount > msg->cursize ) {', '\t\treturn 0;', '\t}', '\t\tif (msg->readcount + (bits>>3) > msg->cursize) {', '\t\t\tmsg->readcount = msg->cursize + 1;', '\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\t\tif (msg->bit + nbits > msg->cursize << 3) {', '\t\t\t\tmsg->readcount = msg->cursize + 1;', '\t\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t\tHuff_offsetReceive (msgHuff.decompressor.tree, &get, msg->data, &msg->bit, msg->cursize<<3);', '', '\t\t\t\tif (msg->bit > msg->cursize<<3) {', '\t\t\t\t\tmsg->readcount = msg->cursize + 1;', '\t\t\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t\t\t\t}']}
description: Buffer overflow in ioquake3 before 2017-08-02 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: In the out-of-band branch, msg->data[msg->readcount] is read directly and readcount is advanced with no comparison against msg->cursize, so a crafted packet can make the index exceed the 16348-byte buffer.
The 16-bit path copies two bytes from &msg->data[msg->readcount] via CopyLittleShort without a bounds check before advancing readcount by 2.
The 32-bit path copies four bytes with CopyLittleLong from the same unchecked offset, allowing a read past the end of msg->data.
In the non-oob path, Huff_getBit and Huff_offsetReceive consume msg->data using msg->bit with no limit against cursize<<3, so Huffman decoding can walk past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading msg->data at indices not validated against cursize is an out-of-bounds memory-buffer access, matching CWE-119. The root cause is the missing length check, not the later crash; CWE-125 is a narrower read-specific child, but the target label is CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function trusts msg->readcount and msg->bit as in-bounds offsets while decoding attacker-controlled network messages. A crafted packet drives these counters past msg->cursize, causing out-of-bounds reads of msg->data; the supported consequence is a crash (SEGFAULT/DoS), with possible unintended memory disclosure.
