commit_msg:
x86/hvm: Fix the handling of non-present segments

In 32bit, the data segments may be NULL to indicate that the segment is
ineligible for use.  In both 32bit and 64bit, the LDT selector may be NULL to
indicate that the entire LDT is ineligible for use.  However, nothing in Xen
actually checks for this condition when performing other segmentation
checks.  (Note however that limit and writeability checks are correctly
performed).

Neither Intel nor AMD specify the exact behaviour of loading a NULL segment.
Experimentally, AMD zeroes all attributes but leaves the base and limit
unmodified.  Intel zeroes the base, sets the limit to 0xfffffff and resets the
attributes to just .G and .D/B.

The use of the segment information in the VMCB/VMCS is equivalent to a native
pipeline interacting with the segment cache.  The present bit can therefore
have a subtly different meaning, and it is now cooked to uniformly indicate
whether the segment is usable or not.

GDTR and IDTR don't have access rights like the other segments, but for
consistency, they are treated as being present so no special casing is needed
elsewhere in the segmentation logic.

AMD hardware does not consider the present bit for %cs and %tr, and will
function as if they were present.  They are therefore unconditionally set to
present when reading information from the VMCB, to maintain the new meaning of
usability.

Intel hardware has a separate unusable bit in the VMCS segment attributes.
This bit is inverted and stored in the present field, so the hvm code can work
with architecturally-common state.

This is CVE-2016-9386 / XSA-191.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    /* Segment not valid for use (cooked meaning of .p)? */', '    if ( !desctab.attr.fields.p )', '        goto fail;']}
description: The x86 emulator in Xen does not properly treat x86 NULL segments as unusable when accessing memory, which might allow local HVM guest users to gain privileges via vectors involving "unexpected" base/limit values.

code_evidence: The function reads the descriptor-table register (GDTR/LDT) into desctab via hvm_get_segment_register before validating it.
Only the descriptor-table limit is checked ((sel & 0xfff8)+7 > desctab.limit); the table's present/usable attribute is never validated.
The entry is then dereferenced and copied from pdesc, and desc.b is used for segmentation checks without confirming the descriptor table itself is usable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 (Permissions, Privileges, and Access Controls) covers failures to enforce segmentation-based access-control state. Accepting non-present segments lets the guest bypass intended privilege checks, matching this category; the missing presence check is the specific access-control gap.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( ((sel & 0xfff8) + 7) > desctab.limit )
goto fail;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a NULL/non-present segment selector is accepted because the code validates the descriptor-table limit and the loaded entry's present bit, but never checks whether the descriptor table (desctab.attr.fields.p) is usable. Trigger: a guest supplies a selector referencing a non-present GDTR/LDT. The emulator proceeds with stale/zeroed base and limit, producing unexpected segment state that the guest can leverage to bypass segmentation protections, supporting privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fix CVE-2022-43995, potential heap overflow for passwords < 8 characters.
Starting with sudo 1.8.0 the plaintext password buffer is dynamically
sized so it is not safe to assume that it is at least 9 bytes in size.
Found by Hugo Lefeuvre (University of Manchester) with ConfFuzz.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    char sav, *epass;', "     * If this turns out not to be safe we will have to use OS #ifdef's (sigh).", '    sav = pass[8];', '    if (pw_len == DESLEN || HAS_AGEINFO(pw_epasswd, pw_len))', "\tpass[8] = '\\0';", '    pass[8] = sav;'], 'added_lines': ['    char des_pass[9], *epass;', '    if (pw_len == DESLEN || HAS_AGEINFO(pw_epasswd, pw_len)) {', '\tstrlcpy(des_pass, pass, sizeof(des_pass));', '\tpass = des_pass;', '    }']}
description: Sudo 1.8.0 through 1.9.12, with the crypt() password backend, contains a plugins/sudoers/auth/passwd.c array-out-of-bounds error that can result in a heap-based buffer over-read. This can be triggered by arbitrary local users with access to Sudo by entering a password of seven characters or fewer. The impact could vary depending on the system libraries, compiler, and processor architecture.

code_evidence: The function assumes the caller-provided pass buffer is at least 9 bytes: it reads pass[8] into sav at line 11 before any length check, later writes a NUL at pass[8] (line 14) when the stored hash is DESLEN or carries age info, then restores pass[8] from sav at line 16. When pass holds a plaintext password of seven characters or fewer, these accesses read and write beyond the end of the dynamically sized buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsupported pass[8] access reads past the end of the plaintext password buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not merely a write overflow: the primary documented impact is a heap-based buffer over-read, with the read of pass[8] occurring before any bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code hardcodes index 8 into pass without validating its allocated length, relying on an assumption that the buffer is at least 9 bytes. Trigger: a local user submits a password of seven characters or fewer while the crypt() backend handles a DES-length or age-info hash. This causes an out-of-bounds read (and paired write) of the heap buffer; the read can expose adjacent heap memory and may crash depending on allocator and architecture.

commit_msg:
Bug#24388746: PRIVILEGE ESCALATION AND RACE CONDITION USING CREATE TABLE

During REPAIR TABLE of a MyISAM table, a temporary data file (.TMD)
is created. When repair finishes, this file is renamed to the original
.MYD file. The problem was that during this rename, we copied the
stats from the old file to the new file with chmod/chown. If a user
managed to replace the temporary file before chmod/chown was executed,
it was possible to get an arbitrary file with the privileges of the
mysql user.

This patch fixes the problem by not copying stats from the old
file to the new file. This is not needed as the new file was
created with the correct stats. This fix only changes server
behavior - external utilities such as myisamchk still does
chmod/chown.

No test case provided since the problem involves synchronization
with file system operations.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (my_copystat(org_name,tmp_name,MyFlags) < 0)', '    goto end;'], 'added_lines': ['  if (!(MyFlags & MY_REDEL_NO_COPY_STAT))', '  {', '    if (my_copystat(org_name,tmp_name,MyFlags) < 0)', '      goto end;', '  }']}
description: Race condition in Oracle MySQL before 5.5.52, 5.6.x before 5.6.33, 5.7.x before 5.7.15, and 8.x before 8.0.1; MariaDB before 5.5.52, 10.0.x before 10.0.28, and 10.1.x before 10.1.18; Percona Server before 5.5.51-38.2, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-78-1, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-8; and Percona XtraDB Cluster before 5.5.41-37.0, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-25.17, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-26.17 allows local users with certain permissions to gain privileges by leveraging use of my_copystat by REPAIR TABLE to repair a MyISAM table.

code_evidence: my_redel first calls my_copystat(org_name,tmp_name,...) to copy ownership and permission metadata from the original .MYD onto the temporary .TMD file.
The temporary file is later renamed into place via my_rename(tmp_name,org_name,...); the stat-copy and rename are separate, non-atomic operations on the same path.
Failure of my_copystat jumps to end, but there is no lock or check tying the tmp_name identity at stat-copy time to the file that is renamed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic time-of-check/time-of-use race on a shared filesystem resource: an interfering sequence can modify tmp_name while the privileged sequence still assumes exclusive access to it. CWE-362 fits because the flaw is improper synchronization over a shared resource, not merely incorrect permission copying.

evidence_lines.code:
if (my_copystat(org_name,tmp_name,MyFlags) < 0)
goto end;

if (my_rename(tmp_name,org_name,MyFlags))
goto end;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the metadata-copy on tmp_name and the subsequent rename are not performed atomically, and nothing prevents another process from replacing tmp_name between them. Trigger: a local user with access to the temp file path swaps it before chmod/chown runs. Consequence: the attacker's file receives the mysql user's ownership/permissions, enabling privilege escalation.

description: Off-by-one error in the t2p_readwrite_pdf_image_tile function in tools/tiff2pdf.c in LibTIFF 4.0.7 allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via a crafted image.

code_evidence: JPEGTABLES count is read from the input TIFF; the guard at line 132 permits count==4, then line 134 copies count-2=2 bytes into buffer.

Line 136 reads buffer[bufferoffset-2] and line 137 buffer[bufferoffset-1] after bufferoffset=2, so indexes 0 and 1 are valid; the subsequent tile read and writes at buffer[xuint32-2]/[xuint32-1] operate with the same small offset.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The boundary check on the attacker-controlled JPEGTABLES count is off by one: accepting count==4 leaves only two bytes in buffer, and the code's table_end save/restore arithmetic assumes a larger table. The crafted image triggers an under-sized buffer state, supporting an out-of-bounds access (heap-based overflow per the fix).

description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An infinite loop was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The infinite loop is triggered when Exiv2 is used to print the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. Note that this bug is only triggered when printing the image ICC profile, which is a less frequently used Exiv2 operation that requires an extra command line option (`-p C`). The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: The do-while loop at lines 9-130 is driven by the file-controlled value `start`; the loop body reads a 2-byte directory length and continues while `start` remains nonzero.
The directory length `dirLength` is read from the crafted file (line 15) and only checked to be >0 and <=500; the inner loop iterates `i < dirLength` and reads 12-byte entries.

At lines 126-130, when `start` is nonzero, 4 bytes are read and `start` is reassigned from the file via `byteSwap4(dir,0,bSwap)`; if the crafted data keeps yielding a nonzero value, `while (start)` never terminates.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's `do { ... } while (start)` loop has an exit condition (`start == 0`) that attacker-controlled data can keep false indefinitely, matching CWE-835. This is distinct from a memory-corruption issue; the supported impact is resource-consumption DoS from a non-terminating loop.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop continuation condition `start` is derived directly from attacker-controlled file bytes, and the prior read did not guarantee progress or a terminating value. Trigger: a crafted image whose IFD chain keeps producing nonzero `start` (or a directory value that never resolves to zero) under `-p C` printing. Consequence: unbounded iteration and repeated I/O, consuming CPU (DoS).

commit_msg:
Made some changes to the I/O stream library for memory streams.
There were a number of potential problems due to the possibility
of integer overflow.
Changed some integral types to the larger types size_t or ssize_t.
For example, the function mem_resize now takes the buffer size parameter
as a size_t.
Added a new function jas_stream_memopen2, which takes a
buffer size specified as a size_t instead of an int.
This can be used in jas_image_cmpt_create to avoid potential
overflow problems.

Added a new function jas_deprecated to warn about reliance on
deprecated library behavior.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int mem_resize(jas_stream_memobj_t *m, int bufsize)', '\tassert(bufsize >= 0);', '\tJAS_DBGLOG(100, ("mem_resize(%p, %d)\\n", m, bufsize));'], 'added_lines': ['static int mem_resize(jas_stream_memobj_t *m, size_t bufsize)', '\t//assert(bufsize >= 0);', '\tJAS_DBGLOG(100, ("mem_resize(%p, %zu)\\n", m, bufsize));', '\tif (!bufsize) {', '\t\tjas_eprintf(', '\t\t  "mem_resize was not really designed to handle a buffer of size 0\\n"', '\t\t  "This may not work.\\n"', '\t\t);', '\t}', '']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the (1) jas_realloc function in base/jas_malloc.c and (2) mem_resize function in base/jas_stream.c in JasPer before 1.900.22 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted image, which triggers use after free vulnerabilities.

code_evidence: mem_resize accepts bufsize as a signed int, so the size parameter itself is constrained to int range and the only guard is assert(bufsize >= 0), which checks sign but not arithmetic overflow.

jas_realloc2(m->buf_, bufsize, sizeof(unsigned char)) computes the allocation size from bufsize; with a signed int bufsize a large value can wrap during the element-count multiplication inside the allocator.
m->bufsize_ = bufsize stores the unvalidated signed size into the memory object, so the recorded size may not match the actual allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer wraparound in a size calculation used for memory allocation, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a signedness or bounds issue: the missing constraint is that the computed allocation size can exceed the integer representation, which is exactly the wraparound condition.

evidence_lines.code:
static int mem_resize(jas_stream_memobj_t *m, int bufsize)
assert(bufsize >= 0);

if (!(buf = jas_realloc2(m->buf_, bufsize, sizeof(unsigned char))) &&
bufsize) {
m->bufsize_ = bufsize;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer size is carried as a signed int and passed to jas_realloc2 without any bound check on the multiplication, so a crafted image can drive bufsize to a value whose size computation wraps. The wrapped small allocation is then treated as if it were the larger size, leading to out-of-bounds access or use-after-free and a denial of service.

commit_msg:
prlimit: do_prlimit needs to have a speculation check

do_prlimit() adds the user-controlled resource value to a pointer that
will subsequently be dereferenced.  In order to help prevent this
codepath from being used as a spectre "gadget" a barrier needs to be
added after checking the range.

Reported-by: Jordy Zomer <jordyzomer@google.com>
Tested-by: Jordy Zomer <jordyzomer@google.com>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>

description: A speculative pointer dereference problem exists in the Linux Kernel on the do_prlimit() function. The resource argument value is controlled and is used in pointer arithmetic for the 'rlim' variable and can be used to leak the contents. We recommend upgrading past version 6.1.8 or commit 739790605705ddcf18f21782b9c99ad7d53a8c11

description: In coders/psd.c in ImageMagick 7.0.7-0 Q16, a DoS in ReadPSDLayersInternal() due to lack of an EOF (End of File) check might cause huge CPU consumption. When a crafted PSD file, which claims a large "length" field in the header but does not contain sufficient backing data, is provided, the loop over "length" would consume huge CPU resources, since there is no EOF check inside the loop.

code_evidence: Line 143 reads an attacker-controlled 'length' field from the PSD layer blending-ranges block, and line 177 reads the blending-range length again. Line 185 loops 'for (j=0; j < (ssize_t) length; j+=8)' over that length, with each iteration performing two ReadBlobLong calls (lines 187-188). The loop has no EOF check and no bound tying the iteration count to the actual remaining blob data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits because iteration is bounded only by an attacker-supplied length and not by available data, enabling resource exhaustion. This is excessive iteration rather than a simple out-of-bounds read, since the loop continues performing reads for the full declared count.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the blending-range loop count is taken directly from the file's 'length' field without verifying that the backing data exists. Trigger: a crafted PSD declaring a large length but truncated data. Consequence: the loop iterates on stale/EOF reads, consuming excessive CPU (DoS).

description: EOSIO/eos eos version after commit f1545dd0ae2b77580c2236fdb70ae7138d2c7168 contains a stack overflow vulnerability in abi_serializer that can result in attack eos network node. This attack appear to be exploitable via network request. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in after commit cf7209e703e6d3f7a5413e0cb1fe88a4d8e4b38d .

code_evidence: Constructor of abi_from_variant_visitor stores the variant_object reference, resolver, and reflector_verifier_visitor base, but accepts no recursion depth parameter and performs no depth check; it merely initializes members and an empty body.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 covers uncontrolled recursion consuming stack resources leading to DoS. This constructor lacks the depth-limiting parameter that the fix later adds, directly supporting the uncontrolled recursion weakness rather than a generic resource or input-validation issue.

evidence_lines.code:
abi_from_variant_visitor( const variant_object& _vo, T& v, Resolver _resolver )
: reflector_verifier_visitor<T>(v)
,_vo(_vo)
,_resolver(_resolver)
{}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The visitor is constructed without any bound on recursion depth, so recursive traversal of nested variant_object structures proceeds unchecked. A deeply nested ABI supplied over the network can drive recursion until the program stack is exhausted, causing a crash/DoS on the node. The constructor itself only wires members; the missing constraint (no depth counter) is the root cause enabling uncontrolled recursion in the traversal that uses this visitor.

commit_msg:
Curl_close: clear data->multi_easy on free to avoid use-after-free

Regression from b46cfbc068 (7.59.0)
CVE-2018-16840
Reported-by: Brian Carpenter (Geeknik Labs)

Bug: https://curl.haxx.se/docs/CVE-2018-16840.html
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if(data->multi_easy)'], 'added_lines': ['  if(data->multi_easy) {', '    data->multi_easy = NULL;', '  }']}
description: A heap use-after-free flaw was found in curl versions from 7.59.0 through 7.61.1 in the code related to closing an easy handle. When closing and cleaning up an 'easy' handle in the `Curl_close()` function, the library code first frees a struct (without nulling the pointer) and might then subsequently erroneously write to a struct field within that already freed struct.

code_evidence: Line 10 checks data->multi_easy and line 11 passes it to curl_multi_cleanup, which frees the associated multi handle but leaves data->multi_easy pointing at freed memory.
Line 46 frees the easy handle itself; the stale multi_easy pointer can be dereferenced during or after cleanup, and the patch adds data->multi_easy = NULL after cleanup to prevent reuse.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the code frees the object referenced by data->multi_easy and does not clear that pointer, enabling later reuse of freed memory. This is a use-after-free rather than a double-free, since the defect is referencing the stale pointer after cleanup.

evidence_lines.code:
if(data->multi_easy)
curl_multi_cleanup(data->multi_easy);
free(data);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: curl_multi_cleanup frees the multi_easy struct without nulling data->multi_easy. Trigger: closing an easy handle that used curl_easy_perform, where the stale pointer is subsequently referenced. Supported consequence: use-after-free leading to invalid memory access and potential crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Write protect anon page faults require an accurate mapcount to decide
if to break the COW or not. This is implemented in the THP path with
reuse_swap_page() ->
page_trans_huge_map_swapcount()/page_trans_huge_mapcount().

If the COW triggers while the other processes sharing the page are
under a huge pmd split, to do an accurate reading, we must ensure the
mapcount isn't computed while it's being transferred from the head
page to the tail pages.

reuse_swap_cache() already runs serialized by the page lock, so it's
enough to add the page lock around __split_huge_pmd_locked too, in
order to add the missing serialization.

Note: the commit in "Fixes" is just to facilitate the backporting,
because the code before such commit didn't try to do an accurate THP
mapcount calculation and it instead used the page_count() to decide if
to COW or not. Both the page_count and the pin_count are THP-wide
refcounts, so they're inaccurate if used in
reuse_swap_page(). Reverting such commit (besides the unrelated fix to
the local anon_vma assignment) would have also opened the window for
memory corruption side effects to certain workloads as documented in
such commit header.

Signed-off-by: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Suggested-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Kirill A. Shutemov <kirill.shutemov@linux.intel.com>
Fixes: 6d0a07edd17c ("mm: thp: calculate the mapcount correctly for THP pages during WP faults")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (page && page != pmd_page(*pmd))', '\t        goto out;', '\t\tpage = pmd_page(*pmd);'], 'added_lines': ['\tbool was_locked = false;', '\tpmd_t _pmd;', '\tif (page) {', '\t\tVM_WARN_ON_ONCE(!PageLocked(page));', '\t\twas_locked = true;', '\t\tif (page != pmd_page(*pmd))', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t}', 'repeat:', '\t\tif (!page) {', '\t\t\tpage = pmd_page(*pmd);', '\t\t\tif (unlikely(!trylock_page(page))) {', '\t\t\t\tget_page(page);', '\t\t\t\t_pmd = *pmd;', '\t\t\t\tspin_unlock(ptl);', '\t\t\t\tlock_page(page);', '\t\t\t\tspin_lock(ptl);', '\t\t\t\tif (unlikely(!pmd_same(*pmd, _pmd))) {', '\t\t\t\t\tunlock_page(page);', '\t\t\t\t\tput_page(page);', '\t\t\t\t\tpage = NULL;', '\t\t\t\t\tgoto repeat;', '\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t\tput_page(page);', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t}', '\tif (!was_locked && page)', '\t\tunlock_page(page);']}
description: An issue was discovered in __split_huge_pmd in mm/huge_memory.c in the Linux kernel before 5.7.5. The copy-on-write implementation can grant unintended write access because of a race condition in a THP mapcount check, aka CID-c444eb564fb1.

code_evidence: The function acquires ptl at line 10, but the pmd's page is read via pmd_page(*pmd) at line 12 and line 15 without holding the page lock, so the page mapping/mapcount can change concurrently with a THP split.
The check at line 12 compares the caller's page to the pmd page, and line 15 reassigns page from the pmd; neither read is serialized against other code sequences mutating the same pmd/page.
__split_huge_pmd_locked is invoked at line 20 while only ptl is held; the page lock is not taken, leaving the mapcount transfer during a split unserialized with reuse_swap_page.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a concurrent code sequence accessing the shared pmd/page without exclusive synchronization, a timing window in which another sequence modifies the shared resource, matching CWE-362. It is a race from missing locking, not a bounds or type error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pmd-to-page resolution and the subsequent split run without the page lock, so a concurrent THP split can transfer the mapcount while __split_huge_pmd observes or acts on it. Trigger: a write-protect fault races with a huge pmd split. Consequence: the COW decision uses an inaccurate mapcount, possibly granting unintended write access.

When SCTP makes INIT or INIT_ACK packet the total chunk length
can exceed SCTP_MAX_CHUNK_LEN which leads to kernel panic when
transmitting these packets, e.g. the crash on sending INIT_ACK:

...
[  597.976970] ------------[ cut here ]------------
[  598.033408] kernel BUG at net/core/skbuff.c:104!
[  600.314841] Call Trace:
[  600.345829]  <IRQ>
[  600.371639]  ? sctp_packet_transmit+0x2095/0x26d0 [sctp]
[  600.436934]  skb_put+0x16c/0x200

[  600.540630]  ? sctp_packet_config+0x890/0x890 [sctp]
[  600.601781]  ? __sctp_packet_append_chunk+0x3b4/0xd00 [sctp]

[  600.731482]  sctp_outq_flush+0x663/0x30d0 [sctp]
[  600.788565]  ? sctp_make_init+0xbf0/0xbf0 [sctp]
[  600.845555]  ? sctp_check_transmitted+0x18f0/0x18f0 [sctp]
[  600.912945]  ? sctp_outq_tail+0x631/0x9d0 [sctp]
[  600.969936]  sctp_cmd_interpreter.isra.22+0x3be1/0x5cb0 [sctp]
[  601.041593]  ? sctp_sf_do_5_1B_init+0x85f/0xc30 [sctp]
[  601.104837]  ? sctp_generate_t1_cookie_event+0x20/0x20 [sctp]
[  601.175436]  ? sctp_eat_data+0x1710/0x1710 [sctp]
[  601.233575]  sctp_do_sm+0x182/0x560 [sctp]

[  601.345586]  ? sctp_rcv+0xef4/0x32f0 [sctp]
[  601.397478]  ? sctp6_rcv+0xa/0x20 [sctp]
...

Here the chunk size for INIT_ACK packet becomes too big, mostly
because of the state cookie (INIT packet has large size with
many address parameters), plus additional server parameters.

Later this chunk causes the panic in skb_put_data():

      sctp_packet_pack()
          skb_put_data(nskb, chunk->skb->data, chunk->skb->len);

'nskb' (head skb) was previously allocated with packet->size
from u16 'chunk->chunk_hdr->length'.

As suggested by Marcelo we should check the chunk's length in
_sctp_make_chunk() before trying to allocate skb for it and
discard a chunk if its size bigger than SCTP_MAX_CHUNK_LEN.

description: In the Linux Kernel before version 4.15.8, 4.14.25, 4.9.87, 4.4.121, 4.1.51, and 3.2.102, an error in the "_sctp_make_chunk()" function (net/sctp/sm_make_chunk.c) when handling SCTP packets length can be exploited to cause a kernel crash.

code_evidence: The paylen parameter (line 2) is caller-controlled and is used directly in SCTP_PAD4(sizeof(*chunk_hdr) + paylen) to size the alloc_skb allocation (line 9). No check bounds the resulting chunk length against SCTP_MAX_CHUNK_LEN before allocation. The header length field is set to only sizeof(*chunk_hdr) (line 15), while the actual skb is sized from paylen, so the derived length can exceed the protocol maximum.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function accepts a length-derived input (paylen) without validating it against the required maximum. The missing constraint, not a transformation error, is the cause; the crash is the downstream consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the derived chunk length from paylen is never validated against SCTP_MAX_CHUNK_LEN before alloc_skb. Trigger: an SCTP INIT/INIT_ACK path passes a large paylen (e.g., large state cookie plus address parameters). Consequence: an oversized chunk is created and later transmitted, causing skb_over_panic and a kernel crash (DoS).

Fix integer issues leading to out of bounds access in fx_ge_text.cpp.

- Using |-skew| to get positive index, which doesn't work when skew is
  INT_MIN
- Incorrect logic when determining when to use |-skew| as an index.

R=tsepez@chromium.org,weili@chromium.org
BUG=chromium:601362

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1875673004
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      // skew is nonpositive so -skew is used as the index.', '      skew = -skew <= static_cast<int>(ANGLESKEW_ARRAY_SIZE)', '                 ? -58', '                 : -g_AngleSkew[-skew];'], 'added_lines': ['      // |skew| is nonpositive so |-skew| is used as the index. We need to make', '      // sure |skew| != INT_MIN since -INT_MIN is undefined.', '      if (skew <= 0 && skew != std::numeric_limits<int>::min() &&', '          static_cast<size_t>(-skew) < ANGLESKEW_ARRAY_SIZE) {', '        skew = -g_AngleSkew[-skew];', '      } else {', '        skew = -58;', '      }']}
description: core/fxge/ge/fx_ge_text.cpp in PDFium, as used in Google Chrome before 51.0.2704.63, miscalculates certain index values, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted PDF document.

code_evidence: When skew is nonzero, the code computes -skew and uses it directly as an index into g_AngleSkew without bounding it against the array size. The guard -skew <= ANGLESKEW_ARRAY_SIZE is inverted, so indices smaller than the array size are replaced by -58 while larger indices fall through to -g_AngleSkew[-skew], reading outside the array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function indexes a fixed-size array with an unchecked, attacker-influenced value, producing a read outside the buffer boundary, which is the out-of-bounds memory access described by CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: inverted bounds check plus an unguarded negation/index. Trigger: a substituted font with a large italic skew (from a crafted PDF) makes -skew exceed the array size; the condition is false, so the out-of-range index is used. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of g_AngleSkew, causing a crash/DoS and potentially disclosing adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
TFLite: Error out when the graph has a recurion.

Recursion is currently unsupported.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 371708957
Change-Id: I8dfad0d85cbfe08e39ae8ea7bad21254ddee5003
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  // Note `AllocateTensors` sometimes calls itself recursively above', '  // for delegates. Therefore only the logic below need to be guarded', '  // by `SubgraphGuard`.', '  SubgraphGuard guard(&context_, &is_subgraph_in_use_);', '  TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK(&context_, guard.status());', '']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. TFlite graphs must not have loops between nodes. However, this condition was not checked and an attacker could craft models that would result in infinite loop during evaluation. In certain cases, the infinite loop would be replaced by stack overflow due to too many recursive calls. For example, the `While` implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/106d8f4fb89335a2c52d7c895b7a7485465ca8d9/tensorflow/lite/kernels/while.cc) could be tricked into a scneario where both the body and the loop subgraphs are the same. Evaluating one of the subgraphs means calling the `Eval` function for the other and this quickly exhaust all stack space. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range. Please consult our security guide(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/master/SECURITY.md) for more information regarding the security model and how to contact us with issues and questions.

code_evidence: AllocateTensors() calls RedoAllDelegates() at line 7, which can re-enter AllocateTensors() recursively for delegates before the new guard is established.

The early-return path at lines 8-14 and the allocation/preparation path at lines 15-24 run without any per-subgraph reentrancy guard; the added SubgraphGuard only protects this lower portion, not the recursive RedoAllDelegates() call.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the function lacks a recursion-depth or reentrancy constraint on a self-calling path, allowing unbounded recursion that consumes stack resources. It is not merely an infinite loop bug; the recursive call chain is the resource-consuming mechanism.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the subgraph allocation path permits re-entry into AllocateTensors() via delegate redirection without bounding the recursion depth. A crafted model with self-referencing or cyclic subgraphs (e.g., While body/cond sharing a subgraph) triggers repeated recursive calls, exhausting the stack (stack overflow) or looping indefinitely, causing denial of service.

code_evidence: The teardown only frees socks_listening and accepted_connection_array (line 14-15) and then frees the server struct (line 16); the incoming_connection_queue and unconfirmed_connection_queue arrays are never wiped, and accepted connections are released via a bare free() rather than free_accepted_connection_array().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers failure to properly release resources on shutdown; here the kill function leaks queue-held connection resources instead of freeing them, matching improper resource release rather than a buffer or pointer defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destruction path omits releasing per-connection resources held in the priority/incoming queues and accepted connection array. Trigger: repeated TCP server creation/deletion (e.g., remote connection churn) leaves queue entries and their buffers allocated. commit_msg:
Merge pull request from GHSA-686w-5m7m-54vc

decNumberToString calls for a buffer that can hold a string of digits+14
characters, not a buffer of size digits+14.
We need to allocate an extra byte for the NUL byte.

-10E-1000010001, for example, will be stringified as -1.0E-1000010000
and decNumberToString will currently write an extra NUL byte after the
allocated buffer in the heap.

Originally reported by @SEU-SSL on GitHub.

Ref: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=64574

Fixes GHSA-686w-5m7m-54vc
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int len = jvp_dec_number_ptr(n)->digits + 14;'], 'added_lines': ['    int len = jvp_dec_number_ptr(n)->digits + 15 /* 14 + NUL */;']}
description: jq is a command-line JSON processor. Version 1.7 is vulnerable to heap-based buffer overflow. Version 1.7.1 contains a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: Line 12 computes the allocation size as digits + 14, then line 13 allocates exactly that many bytes via jv_mem_alloc. Line 14 passes this buffer to decNumberToString, which writes the stringified number plus a terminating NUL byte. The buffer is sized for digits + 14 characters but not for the trailing NUL, so the write at line 14 exceeds the allocation by one byte.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) fits because line 14 writes the terminating NUL byte beyond the end of the heap buffer allocated at line 13. This is a direct write past the intended buffer boundary, not merely a read overrun or an integer overflow; the cause is the undersized allocation expression at line 12.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the heap allocation is one byte short because the size expression omits the NUL terminator required by decNumberToString. Trigger: a number literal whose stringified form needs the full digits + 14 characters, such as -1.0E-1000010000, causes decNumberToString to write the extra NUL past the buffer. Consequence: a one-byte heap out-of-bounds write, corrupting adjacent heap metadata and potentially leading to a crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
Decoder: Fixed error handling for dangling fields

In case of dangling fields with gaps in frames enabled,
field pic in cur_slice was wrongly set to 0.

This would cause dangling field to be concealed as a frame, which would
result in a number of MB mismatch and hence a hang.

Bug: 34097672
Change-Id: Ia9b7f72c4676188c45790b2dfbb4fe2c2d2c01f8
(cherry picked from commit 1a13168ca3510ba91274d10fdee46b3642cc9554)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ps_cur_slice->u1_field_pic_flag = 0;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: A remote code execution vulnerability in libavc in Mediaserver could enable an attacker using a specially crafted file to cause memory corruption during media file and data processing. This issue is rated as Critical due to the possibility of remote code execution within the context of the Mediaserver process. Product: Android. Versions: 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2. Android ID: A-34097672.

code_evidence: Line 46 forces ps_cur_slice->u1_field_pic_flag to 0 before gap processing; the slice state is rewritten rather than preserved. Lines 49-60 index ai4_gaps_start_frm_num[i1_gap_idx] up to MAX_FRAMES, returning an error if all slots are occupied, so the gap array index is bounded.
Lines 62-65 store the gap range at i1_gap_idx and reset ai1_gaps_per_seq[i1_gap_idx] to 0, then the loop at 66-117 increments that counter per gap.

Line 99-105 insert each gap picture with u4_next_frm_num and increment pi1_gaps_per_seq[i1_gap_idx]; the counter is not re-checked against any bound within the while loop, so a long gap sequence can drive it past the per-entry capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs gap insertion and MMCO operations on DPB buffer structures using a counter that can exceed the intended per-sequence capacity, i.e., operations outside intended buffer boundaries, matching CWE-119. The field/frame flag reset is the trigger; the out-of-bounds buffer operation is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: clearing u1_field_pic_flag makes a dangling field be concealed as a frame, so the gap loop at 66-117 processes more entries than the field path would. The gaps counter ai1_gaps_per_seq[i1_gap_idx] is incremented per iteration (105) without a bound check, and downstream insert/MMCO operations consume the oversized gap count, producing buffer-bound violations and the reported memory corruption/hang.

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = t->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = xt_table_get_private_protected(t);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: get_entries obtains the table via xt_find_table_lock, then dereferences t->private directly at line 17 to read private->size and copy the entries to userspace. The patch replaces this direct read with xt_table_get_private_protected(t), indicating the raw t->private read races with concurrent ruleset replacement that frees the old table info.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the code accesses memory (private->size and copied entries) that may already have been freed by the concurrent replacement path. This is a use-after-free, not merely a race condition: the race is the trigger, the freed-memory access is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the private pointer is read without the protection needed against concurrent xt_replace_table, which frees the old table info after the per-CPU sequence check. Trigger: a user with CAP_NET_ADMIN replaces iptables rules while get_entries reads t->private. Consequence: dereferencing a freed xt_table_info in copy_entries_to_user, yielding use-after-free (crash/read of freed memory).

commit_msg:
rxrpc: Fix race between conn bundle lookup and bundle removal [ZDI-CAN-15975]

After rxrpc_unbundle_conn() has removed a connection from a bundle, it
checks to see if there are any conns with available channels and, if not,
removes and attempts to destroy the bundle.

Whilst it does check after grabbing client_bundles_lock that there are no
connections attached, this races with rxrpc_look_up_bundle() retrieving the
bundle, but not attaching a connection for the connection to be attached
later.

There is therefore a window in which the bundle can get destroyed before we
manage to attach a new connection to it.

Fix this by adding an "active" counter to struct rxrpc_bundle:

 (1) rxrpc_connect_call() obtains an active count by prepping/looking up a
     bundle and ditches it before returning.

 (2) If, during rxrpc_connect_call(), a connection is added to the bundle,
     this obtains an active count, which is held until the connection is
     discarded.

 (3) rxrpc_deactivate_bundle() is created to drop an active count on a
     bundle and destroy it when the active count reaches 0.  The active
     count is checked inside client_bundles_lock() to prevent a race with
     rxrpc_look_up_bundle().

 (4) rxrpc_unbundle_conn() then calls rxrpc_deactivate_bundle().

commit_msg:
posix-timers: Sanitize overrun handling

The posix timer overrun handling is broken because the forwarding functions
can return a huge number of overruns which does not fit in an int. As a
consequence timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun can turn into
random number generators.

The k_clock::timer_forward() callbacks return a 64 bit value now. Make
k_itimer::ti_overrun[_last] 64bit as well, so the kernel internal
accounting is correct. 3Remove the temporary (int) casts.

Add a helper function which clamps the overrun value returned to user space
via timer_getoverrun(2) or siginfo::si_overrun limited to a positive value
between 0 and INT_MAX. INT_MAX is an indicator for user space that the
overrun value has been clamped.

Reported-by: Team OWL337 <icytxw@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Acked-by: John Stultz <john.stultz@linaro.org>
Cc: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Michael Kerrisk <mtk.manpages@gmail.com>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20180626132705.018623573@linutronix.de
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\ttimr->it_overrun += (int)kc->timer_forward(timr, now);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\ttimr->it_overrun += kc->timer_forward(timr, now);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.17.3. An Integer Overflow in kernel/time/posix-timers.c in the POSIX timer code is caused by the way the overrun accounting works. Depending on interval and expiry time values, the overrun can be larger than INT_MAX, but the accounting is int based. This basically makes the accounting values, which are visible to user space via timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun, random. For example, a local user can cause a denial of service (signed integer overflow) via crafted mmap, futex, timer_create, and timer_settime system calls.

code_evidence: Line 17 gates the update only on a nonzero interval and pending/notify state; line 18 accumulates kc->timer_forward() into timr->it_overrun, whose type was int in the vulnerable version.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This matches CWE-190: the accumulation of a value too large for its int representation wraps, violating the assumption that the running total grows monotonically. It is not merely a truncation of one conversion; the wrapped result is then stored and reported as the overrun count.

evidence_lines.code:
if (iv && (timr->it_requeue_pending & REQUEUE_PENDING || sig_none))
timr->it_overrun += (int)kc->timer_forward(timr, now);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: timer_forward() can return a 64-bit overrun count, but it is cast to int and added into the int-typed ti_overrun, so a large overrun wraps to a negative or small value. Trigger: a local user creates an interval timer whose expiry/interval values make overruns exceed INT_MAX. The corrupted accounting is exposed via timer_getoverrun() and si_overrun, producing wrong values and signed-overflow instability (DoS).

description: The ntpd_driver component before 1.3.0 and 2.x before 2.2.0 for Robot Operating System (ROS) allows attackers, who control the source code of a different node in the same ROS application, to change a robot's behavior. This occurs because a topic name depends on the attacker-controlled time_ref_topic parameter.

code_evidence: Line 7 declares a global-ish string time_ref_topic that will hold the topic name.
Line 11 reads the topic name from the ROS parameter server via nh.param, defaulting to "time_ref"; any node in the same ROS application can set this parameter.
Line 17 subscribes to whatever name was supplied in time_ref_topic, so the subscription target is fully attacker-controlled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-668 fits because the node's time-reference resource (the subscribed topic) is exposed to the wrong control sphere: a parameter controlled by another application node determines which resource this component consumes. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the subscription topic name is taken from an externally settable ROS parameter rather than a fixed value. description: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in WebKit/Source/platform/v8_inspector/V8Debugger.cpp in Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 53.0.2785.89 on Windows and OS X and before 53.0.2785.92 on Linux, allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML into the Developer Tools (aka DevTools) subsystem via a crafted web site, aka "Universal XSS (UXSS)."

code_evidence: The function retrieves scopes via callDebuggerMethod and checks only that the result is an array; it then treats the returned scopesValue as an array and marks it internal within the debugger context.
The scopes array is not copied into the inspected context; it is marked as internal and its prototype is set to null in the debugger context before being returned to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-79 fits because the missing context boundary allows attacker-influenced debugger objects to be placed into the inspected web context without neutralization, enabling arbitrary script execution. It is not merely a generic isolation bug: the supported consequence is script injection into a served page context.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the debugger-context scope array is returned without being copied into the inspected page's context, so objects from the debugger context reach the inspected context. Trigger: a crafted page causes DevTools to invoke functionScopes and receive the non-copied array. Supported consequence: cross-context object exposure enables script injection into the DevTools/inspected context (UXSS).

Fix DoS in the minidump parser ##crash

* Reported by lazymio via huntr.dev
* Reproducer: mdmp-dos
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void read_module(RBuffer *b, ut64 addr, struct minidump_module *module) {', '\tr_buf_seek (b, addr, R_BUF_SET);'], 'added_lines': ['static struct minidump_module *read_module(RBuffer *b, ut64 addr) {', '\tif (r_buf_seek (b, addr, R_BUF_SET) == -1) {', '\t\treturn NULL;', '\t}', '\tstruct minidump_module *module = R_NEW0 (struct minidump_module);', '\tif (!module) {', '\t\treturn NULL;', '\t}', '\treturn module;']}
description: Denial of Service in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.6.4.

code_evidence: The original seek to the attacker-controlled `addr` is performed without checking the return value, so a failed or out-of-range seek is not detected before reads begin.
A long sequence of `r_buf_read_le64`/`r_buf_read_le32` calls then populates the caller-supplied module struct, parsing whatever buffer state results from the unchecked seek.
The buffer position is restored afterwards, but nothing constrains the seek target or validates that the parsed data is within bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked, attacker-influenced seek and subsequent unbounded parsing let a crafted file drive the parser into an invalid state that can crash it, exhausting availability — matching CWE-400's availability/DoS scope. This is a resource/availability failure rather than memory corruption such as CWE-125, since the demonstrated impact is crash/DoS.

evidence_lines.code:
st64 o_addr = r_buf_seek (b, 0, R_BUF_CUR);
r_buf_seek (b, addr, R_BUF_SET);
r_buf_seek (b, o_addr, R_BUF_SET);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the module offset `addr` from the minidump is used in `r_buf_seek` without validating success or bounds, so a crafted minidump drives parsing from an invalid position. Trigger: a malformed mdmp file supplying a bad module address; the parser then reads many fields from an uncontrolled buffer location. Supported consequence: crash/DoS during minidump parsing, consistent with the reported reproducer.

commit_msg:
Since commit 9e2369c06c8a18 ("xen: add helpers to allocate unpopulated
memory") foreign mappings are using guest physical addresses allocated
via ZONE_DEVICE functionality.

This will result in problems for the case of no balloon memory hotplug
being configured, as the p2m list will only cover the initial memory
size of the domain. Any ZONE_DEVICE allocated address will be outside
the p2m range and thus a mapping can't be established with that memory
address.

Fix that by extending the p2m size for that case. At the same time add
a check for a to be created mapping to be within the p2m limits in
order to detect errors early.

While changing a comment, remove some 32-bit leftovers.

This is XSA-369.

Fixes: 9e2369c06c8a18 ("xen: add helpers to allocate unpopulated memory")

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel 5.9.x through 5.11.3, as used with Xen. In some less-common configurations, an x86 PV guest OS user can crash a Dom0 or driver domain via a large amount of I/O activity. The issue relates to misuse of guest physical addresses when a configuration has CONFIG_XEN_UNPOPULATED_ALLOC but not CONFIG_XEN_BALLOON_MEMORY_HOTPLUG.

code_evidence: max_pages is derived from xen_get_max_pages() plus remap pages; when max_pages exceeds max_pfn, extra_pages is set to the difference and then clamped by min3 against max_pages - max_pfn. This computed extent determines how much additional memory is added via xen_add_extra_mem and how xen_max_p2m_pfn is set (lines 56-62).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-131 fits because the function incorrectly computes the size of the extra memory/p2m region (extra_pages and resulting pfn range) used to cover addresses, leaving the region undersized relative to addresses actually used.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the extra memory/p2m extent is sized from max_pages relative to max_pfn without accounting for ZONE_DEVICE addresses allocated outside the initial p2m range. Trigger: a configuration with CONFIG_XEN_UNPOPULATED_ALLOC but no CONFIG_XEN_BALLOON_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, where foreign mappings use guest physical addresses beyond the computed p2m size. Consequence: mappings cannot be established and a Dom0/driver domain can be crashed via heavy I/O activity.

commit_msg:
Bluetooth: L2CAP: Fix attempting to access uninitialized memory

On l2cap_parse_conf_req the variable efs is only initialized if
remote_efs has been set.

CVE: CVE-2022-42895
CC: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Tamás Koczka <poprdi@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Luiz Augusto von Dentz <luiz.von.dentz@intel.com>
Reviewed-by: Tedd Ho-Jeong An <tedd.an@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (test_bit(FLAG_EFS_ENABLE, &chan->flags)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (remote_efs &&', '\t\t\t    test_bit(FLAG_EFS_ENABLE, &chan->flags)) {']}
description:
There is an infoleak vulnerability in the Linux kernel's net/bluetooth/l2cap_core.c's l2cap_parse_conf_req function which can be used to leak kernel pointers remotely.
We recommend upgrading past commit  https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/b1a2cd50c0357f243b7435a732b4e62ba3157a2e https://www.google.com/url

code_evidence: efs is declared uninitialized at line 11 and remote_efs starts as 0; efs is only populated in the L2CAP_CONF_EFS case (lines 47-52) when olen matches sizeof(efs).
FLAG_EFS_ENABLE is only set when remote_efs is true (lines 81-86), so an attacker omitting the EFS option leaves efs uninitialized.
The FLAG_EFS_ENABLE block at lines 143-156 dereferences efs fields (id, stype, msdu, flush_to, acc_lat, sdu_itime) and copies efs into the response, reading uninitialized stack memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-824 fits because the function accesses the uninitialized efs structure, whose fields are used as values and copied to the peer. This is a use of uninitialized data rather than a null-pointer dereference or out-of-bounds access, matching the uninitialized-pointer/access weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the EFS-enabled branch reads the stack variable efs without verifying that the EFS configuration option was actually received and parsed. Trigger: a remote peer sends an L2CAP configuration request that enables EFS support without including the EFS option. Consequence: uninitialized stack contents are copied into the configuration response, leaking kernel memory (infoleak).

mwifiex: Fix three heap overflow at parsing element in cfg80211_ap_settings

mwifiex_update_vs_ie(),mwifiex_set_uap_rates() and
mwifiex_set_wmm_params() call memcpy() without checking
the destination size.Since the source is given from
user-space, this may trigger a heap buffer overflow.

Fix them by putting the length check before performing memcpy().

This fix addresses CVE-2019-14814,CVE-2019-14815,CVE-2019-14816.

Signed-off-by: Wen Huang <huangwenabc@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Ganapathi Bhat <gbhat@marvell.comg>

description: A vulnerability was found in Linux Kernel, where a Heap Overflow was found in mwifiex_set_wmm_params() function of Marvell Wifi Driver.

code_evidence: The vendor IE pointer comes from cfg80211_find_vendor_ie() over the caller-supplied ies/ies_len buffer, so vs_ie->len is attacker-influenced.

The memcpy() writes vs_ie->len + 2 bytes into ie->ie_buffer at offset le16_to_cpu(ie->ie_length) with no check that this destination index plus the copy length stays within the heap-allocated mwifiex_ie buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The destination buffer is heap-allocated via kzalloc, and the missing length check allows an out-of-bounds write past it, which is precisely a heap-based buffer overflow. This differs from a stack overflow because the overwritten region is the heap-allocated mwifiex_ie structure.

evidence_lines.code:
vendor_ie = cfg80211_find_vendor_ie(oui, oui_type, ies, ies_len);
if (vendor_ie) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unbounded memcpy into the fixed-size ie_buffer of a kzalloc'd mwifiex_ie, with both the offset (ie_length) and the copy length (vs_ie->len + 2) derived from user-supplied IE data. Trigger: a vendor IE whose length exceeds the remaining space in ie_buffer. Consequence: heap buffer overflow, corrupting adjacent heap memory, potentially leading to crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
Use a separate journal transaction if it turns out that we need to
convert an inline file to use an data block.  Otherwise we could end
up failing due to not having journal credits.

This addresses CVE-2018-10883.

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=200071

Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (error) {', '\t\tif (error == -ENOSPC &&', '\t\t    ext4_has_inline_data(inode)) {', '\t\t\terror = ext4_try_to_evict_inline_data(handle, inode,', '\t\t\t\t\tEXT4_XATTR_LEN(strlen(i->name) +', '\t\t\t\t\tEXT4_XATTR_SIZE(i->value_len)));', '\t\t\tif (error)', '\t\t\t\treturn error;', '\t\t\terror = ext4_xattr_ibody_find(inode, i, is);', '\t\t\tif (error)', '\t\t\t\treturn error;', '\t\t\terror = ext4_xattr_set_entry(i, s, handle, inode,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t     false /* is_block */);', '\t\t}', '\t\tif (error)', '\t\t\treturn error;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (error)', '\t\treturn error;']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's ext4 filesystem. A local user can cause an out-of-bounds write in jbd2_journal_dirty_metadata(), a denial of service, and a system crash by mounting and operating on a crafted ext4 filesystem image.

code_evidence: ext4_xattr_set_entry is called at line 10 with the caller's handle; on -ENOSPC with inline data, lines 14-16 call ext4_try_to_evict_inline_data to convert inline data into a block, then lines 22-23 retry ext4_xattr_set_entry using that same handle, and any error at 25-26 is returned to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a write beyond the intended journal/metadata buffer, matching CWE-787. The missing journal-credit constraint is the cause, not the write itself; CWE-787 fits the resulting out-of-bounds write rather than the resource-exhaustion root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the inline-to-block conversion path reuses the caller's journal handle. Converting inline data to an extent block requires additional journal credits; if the handle lacks them, the retried xattr set at lines 22-23 proceeds without sufficient transaction reservation. Trigger: a crafted ext4 image where setting an xattr on an inline-data inode hits -ENOSPC and forces conversion. Consequence: jbd2_journal_dirty_metadata performs an out-of-bounds write, crashing the system (CVE-2018-10883).

description: PHP before 5.4.42, 5.5.x before 5.5.26, and 5.6.x before 5.6.10 does not ensure that pathnames lack %00 sequences, which might allow remote attackers to read or write to arbitrary files via crafted input to an application that calls (1) a DOMDocument save method or (2) the GD imagepsloadfont function, as demonstrated by a filename\0.html attack that bypasses an intended configuration in which client users may write to only .html files.

code_evidence: The source path is parsed with "p|l" (line 12), which accepts a string but does not reject embedded NUL bytes; the only check before file parsing is a non-empty length test (lines 15-18). When mode is DOM_LOAD_FILE, source is passed directly to htmlCreateFileParserCtxt (line 20) without validating that the pathname lacks a NUL sequence.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts external input and fails to validate a required property (absence of NUL bytes) before using it as a file path, which is improper input validation. The later addition of CHECK_NULL_PATH confirms the missing constraint; this is a validation gap rather than a transformation or encoding flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates only that the path string is non-empty but never checks for embedded NUL bytes, so a crafted filename such as "name\0.html" reaches the file parser. Trigger: a caller invokes the DOM load method in file mode with an attacker-influenced path. Consequence: the path is truncated at the NUL, allowing reads or writes to arbitrary files outside the intended .html restriction.

description: A Buffer Overflow vulnerability exists in NumPy 1.9.x in the PyArray_NewFromDescr_int function of ctors.c when specifying arrays of large dimensions (over 32) from Python code, which could let a malicious user cause a Denial of Service. NOTE: The vendor does not agree this is a vulneraility; In (very limited) circumstances a user may be able provoke the buffer overflow, the user is most likely already privileged to at least provoke denial of service by exhausting memory. Triggering this further requires the use of uncommon API (complicated structured dtypes), which is very unlikely to be available to an unprivileged user

code_evidence: When descr->subarray is set, line 15 performs memcpy(newdims, dims, nd*sizeof(npy_intp)) into the fixed stack buffer newdims[2*NPY_MAXDIMS] (line 13), and lines 17-18 copy into newstrides = newdims + NPY_MAXDIMS, also bounded by NPY_MAXDIMS entries.
The nd > NPY_MAXDIMS guard is at line 29, after the subarray branch, so it does not protect these copies.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The copies at lines 15 and 18 are buffer copies whose size (nd) is not checked against the destination capacity before writing, matching CWE-120. The later check at line 29 is a validation gap rather than a calculation error, so CWE-131 is less fitting.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: For a structured dtype with a subarray field, the recursive subarray branch copies nd dimension entries into fixed-size stack arrays before any bound check on nd. A caller supplying more than NPY_MAXDIMS dimensions (reachable via the recursive _update_descr_and_dimensions path) overflows the stack buffers, causing memory corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
ax25: Fix NULL pointer dereferences in ax25 timers

The previous commit 7ec02f5ac8a5 ("ax25: fix NPD bug in ax25_disconnect")
move ax25_disconnect into lock_sock() in order to prevent NPD bugs. But
there are race conditions that may lead to null pointer dereferences in
ax25_heartbeat_expiry(), ax25_t1timer_expiry(), ax25_t2timer_expiry(),
ax25_t3timer_expiry() and ax25_idletimer_expiry(), when we use
ax25_kill_by_device() to detach the ax25 device.

One of the race conditions that cause null pointer dereferences can be
shown as below:

      (Thread 1)                    |      (Thread 2)
ax25_connect()                      |
 ax25_std_establish_data_link()     |
  ax25_start_t1timer()              |
   mod_timer(&ax25->t1timer,..)     |
                                    | ax25_kill_by_device()
   (wait a time)                    |  ...
                                    |  s->ax25_dev = NULL; //(1)
   ax25_t1timer_expiry()            |
    ax25->ax25_dev->values[..] //(2)|  ...
     ...                            |

We set null to ax25_cb->ax25_dev in position (1) and dereference
the null pointer in position (2).

The corresponding fail log is shown below:
===============================================================
BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000050
CPU: 1 PID: 0 Comm: swapper/1 Not tainted 5.17.0-rc6-00794-g45690b7d0
RIP: 0010:ax25_t1timer_expiry+0x12/0x40
...
Call Trace:
 call_timer_fn+0x21/0x120
 __run_timers.part.0+0x1ca/0x250
 run_timer_softirq+0x2c/0x60
 __do_softirq+0xef/0x2f3
 irq_exit_rcu+0xb6/0x100
 sysvec_apic_timer_interrupt+0xa2/0xd0
...

This patch moves ax25_disconnect() before s->ax25_dev = NULL
and uses del_timer_sync() to delete timers in ax25_disconnect().
If ax25_disconnect() is called by ax25_kill_by_device() or
ax25->ax25_dev is NULL, the reason in ax25_disconnect() will be
equal to ENETUNREACH, it will wait all timers to stop before we
set null to s->ax25_dev in ax25_kill_by_device().

Fixes: 7ec02f5ac8a5 ("ax25: fix NPD bug in ax25_disconnect")
Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tax25_disconnect(s, ENETUNREACH);', '\t\t\tax25_disconnect(s, ENETUNREACH);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tax25_disconnect(s, ENETUNREACH);', '\t\t\tax25_disconnect(s, ENETUNREACH);']}
description: A NULL pointer dereference flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s Amateur Radio AX.25 protocol functionality in the way a user connects with the protocol. This flaw allows a local user to crash the system.

code_evidence: In the no-socket path, s->ax25_dev is set to NULL before ax25_disconnect(s, ENETUNREACH) is invoked, so any timer or path reached through disconnect can observe a cleared device pointer.
In the socket path, s->ax25_dev = NULL occurs before ax25_disconnect(s, ENETUNREACH); the patch moves disconnect ahead of the assignment to close the race with the AX.25 timers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function clears ax25_dev and leaves timer paths that dereference it, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference; the patch ordering fixes the race. This is not a generic use-after-free because the dereferenced value is explicitly NULL.

evidence_lines.code:
s->ax25_dev = NULL;
ax25_disconnect(s, ENETUNREACH);

s->ax25_dev = NULL;
ax25_disconnect(s, ENETUNREACH);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the callback's device pointer is cleared while pending AX.25 timers may still run and dereference ax25_dev->values. Trigger: a user connects (arming t1timer) while ax25_kill_by_device detaches the device, so the timer expiry races the NULL assignment. Consequence: kernel NULL pointer dereference and system crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Check Shdr more

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/395
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (last_Phdr < e_phoff || (unsigned long)file_size < last_Phdr) {', '    if (last_Shdr < e_shoff || (unsigned long)file_size < last_Shdr) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (last_Phdr < e_phoff  // wrap-around', '    ||  e_phoff != sizeof(Elf32_Ehdr)  // must be contiguous', '    ||  (unsigned long)file_size < last_Phdr) {', '    if (last_Shdr < e_shoff  // wrap-around', '    ||  e_shoff < last_Phdr', '    ||  (unsigned long)file_size < last_Shdr) {']}
description: A heap-based buffer over-read was discovered in the get_le32 function in bele.h in UPX 4.0.0 via a crafted Mach-O file.

code_evidence: e_shoff and e_shnum come from the untrusted ELF header; last_Shdr = e_shoff + e_shnum * sizeof(Elf32_Shdr) can wrap, and the pre-patch check only rejects wrap or file_size < last_Shdr, so a section header table can be accepted that overlaps or precedes the program headers within file_size.
For ET_DYN the whole file is read into file_image and shdri is set to (Elf32_Shdr *)(e_shoff + file_image) without verifying e_shoff >= last_Phdr or that the table fits the loaded buffer.
elf_find_section_type walks shdri, and sec_dynstr = &shdri[t] indexes by sh_link; e_shnum <= t is the only bound, so a crafted sh_link or mispositioned table causes reads outside file_image.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory past the end or before the beginning of the intended file_image buffer through unchecked section-header indexing, which is exactly CWE-125. It is not a write (CWE-787) because shdri is only dereferenced for reads.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the section-header offset/count are trusted without a lower bound relative to the program-header region or a check that the table lies within the loaded image. Trigger: a crafted ELF32 ET_DYN file with a small or wrapped e_shoff (or large sh_link). Consequence: out-of-bounds reads of section headers and dynstr, matching the reported heap over-read via get_le32.

Here's what happens to hit that BUG_ON():

2) Another task is at ctree.c:balance_level() and we have eb X currently as
   the root of the tree, and we promote its single child, eb Y, as the new
   root.

   Then, at ctree.c:balance_level(), we call:

      tree_mod_log_insert_root(eb X, eb Y, 1);

3) At tree_mod_log_insert_root() we create tree mod log elements for each
   slot of eb X, of operation type MOD_LOG_KEY_REMOVE_WHILE_FREEING each
   with a ->logical pointing to ebX->start. These are placed in an array
   named tm_list.
   Lets assume there are N elements (N pointers in eb X);

4) Then, still at tree_mod_log_insert_root(), we create a tree mod log
   element of operation type MOD_LOG_ROOT_REPLACE, ->logical set to
   ebY->start, ->old_root.logical set to ebX->start, ->old_root.level set
   to the level of eb X and ->generation set to the generation of eb X;

5) Then tree_mod_log_insert_root() calls tree_mod_log_free_eb() with
   tm_list as argument. After that, tree_mod_log_free_eb() calls
   __tree_mod_log_insert() for each member of tm_list in reverse order,
   from highest slot in eb X, slot N - 1, to slot 0 of eb X;

6) __tree_mod_log_insert() sets the sequence number of each given tree mod

   fs_info->tree_mod_seq as the sequence number of the given tree mod log
   operation.

   the element corresponding to slot 0 of eb X has the highest sequence
   number (1 + N), and the element corresponding to the last slot has the
   lowest sequence number (2);

7) Then, after inserting tm_list's elements into the tree mod log rbtree,
   the MOD_LOG_ROOT_REPLACE element is inserted, which gets the highest
   sequence number, which is N + 2;

8) Back to ctree.c:balance_level(), we free eb X by calling
   btrfs_free_tree_block() on it. Because eb X was created in the current
   transaction, has no other references and writeback did not happen for
   it, we add it back to the free space cache/tree;

9) Later some other task T allocates the metadata extent from eb X, since
   it is marked as free space in the space cache/tree, and uses it as a
   node for some other btree;

10) The tree mod log user task calls btrfs_search_old_slot(), which calls
    get_old_root(), and finally that calls __tree_mod_log_oldest_root()
    with time_seq == 1 and eb_root == eb Y;

11) First iteration of the while loop finds the tree mod log element with
    sequence number N + 2, for the logical address of eb Y and of type
    MOD_LOG_ROOT_REPLACE;

12) Because the operation type is MOD_LOG_ROOT_REPLACE, we don't break out
    of the loop, and set root_logical to point to tm->old_root.logical
    which corresponds to the logical address of eb X;

13) On the next iteration of the while loop, the call to
    tree_mod_log_search_oldest() returns the smallest tree mod log element
    for the logical address of eb X, which has a sequence number of 2, an
    operation type of MOD_LOG_KEY_REMOVE_WHILE_FREEING and corresponds to
    the old slot N - 1 of eb X (eb X had N items in it before being freed);

14) We then break out of the while loop and return the tree mod log operation
    of type MOD_LOG_ROOT_REPLACE (eb Y), and not the one for slot N - 1 of
    eb X, to get_old_root();

15) At get_old_root(), we process the MOD_LOG_ROOT_REPLACE operation
    and set "logical" to the logical address of eb X, which was the old
    root. We then call tree_mod_log_search() passing it the logical
    address of eb X and time_seq == 1;

16) Then before calling tree_mod_log_search(), task T adds a key to eb X,
    which results in adding a tree mod log operation of type
    MOD_LOG_KEY_ADD to the tree mod log - this is done at
    ctree.c:insert_ptr() - but after adding the tree mod log operation
    and before updating the number of items in eb X from 0 to 1...

17) The task at get_old_root() calls tree_mod_log_search() and gets the
    tree mod log operation of type MOD_LOG_KEY_ADD just added by task T.
    Then it enters the following if branch:

    if (old_root && tm && tm->op != MOD_LOG_KEY_REMOVE_WHILE_FREEING) {
       (...)
    } (...)

    Calls read_tree_block() for eb X, which gets a reference on eb X but
    does not lock it - task T has it locked.
    Then it clones eb X while it has nritems set to 0 in its header, before
    task T sets nritems to 1 in eb X's header. From hereupon we use the
    clone of eb X which no other task has access to;

18) Then we call __tree_mod_log_rewind(), passing it the MOD_LOG_KEY_ADD
    mod log operation we just got from tree_mod_log_search() in the
    previous step and the cloned version of eb X;

19) At __tree_mod_log_rewind(), we set the local variable "n" to the number
    of items set in eb X's clone, which is 0. Then we enter the while loop,
    and in its first iteration we process the MOD_LOG_KEY_ADD operation,
    which just decrements "n" from 0 to (u32)-1, since "n" is declared with
    a type of u32. At the end of this iteration we call rb_next() to find the
    next tree mod log operation for eb X, that gives us the mod log operation
    of type MOD_LOG_KEY_REMOVE_WHILE_FREEING, for slot 0, with a sequence
    number of N + 1 (steps 3 to 6);

20) Then we go back to the top of the while loop and trigger the following
    BUG_ON():

        (...)
        switch (tm->op) {
        case MOD_LOG_KEY_REMOVE_WHILE_FREEING:
                 BUG_ON(tm->slot < n);
                 fallthrough;
        (...)

    Because "n" has a value of (u32)-1 (4294967295) and tm->slot is 0.

Fix this by taking a read lock on the extent buffer before cloning it at
ctree.c:get_old_root(). This should be done regardless of the extent
buffer having been freed and reused, as a concurrent task might be
modifying it (while holding a write lock on it).

Reported-by: Zygo Blaxell <ce3g8jdj@umail.furryterror.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-btrfs/20210227155037.GN28049@hungrycats.org/
Fixes: 834328a8493079 ("Btrfs: tree mod log's old roots could still be part of the tree")
CC: stable@vger.kernel.org # 4.4+

Signed-off-by: David Sterba <dsterba@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tbtrfs_tree_read_lock(old);', '\t\t\tbtrfs_tree_read_unlock(old);']}
description: A race condition was discovered in get_old_root in fs/btrfs/ctree.c in the Linux kernel through 5.11.8. It allows attackers to cause a denial of service (BUG) because of a lack of locking on an extent buffer before a cloning operation, aka CID-dbcc7d57bffc.

code_evidence: The code reads an extent buffer with read_tree_block(), which returns a referenced buffer without acquiring the tree lock, then immediately clones it with btrfs_clone_extent_buffer(old) at line 40 without holding any exclusive or read lock on the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing lock around the read-and-clone sequence allows a concurrent interfering code sequence to modify the shared extent buffer, violating exclusivity/atomicity of the clone, matching CWE-362. It is a race condition rather than a mere NULL dereference because the defect is the absent synchronization window.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the extent buffer 'old' is cloned while a concurrent task may hold the write lock and be modifying it (e.g., updating nritems in insert_ptr). Trigger: a tree mod log user races with another task modifying the same reused extent buffer. Consequence: the clone captures an inconsistent header (nritems 0), later leading to underflow and BUG_ON in __tree_mod_log_rewind, crashing the kernel (DoS).

commit_msg:
amd/iommu: fix flush checks

Flush checking for AMD IOMMU didn't check whether the previous entry
was present, or whether the flags (writable/readable) changed in order
to decide whether a flush should be executed.

Fix this by taking the writable/readable/next-level fields into account,
together with the present bit.

Along these lines the flushing in amd_iommu_map_page() must not be
omitted for PV domains. The comment there was simply wrong: Mappings may
very well change, both their addresses and their permissions. Ultimately
this should honor iommu_dont_flush_iotlb, but to achieve this
amd_iommu_ops first needs to gain an .iotlb_flush hook.

Also make clear_iommu_pte_present() static, to demonstrate there's no
caller omitting the (subsequent) flush.

This is part of XSA-275.
