description: An issue was discovered in the ROS communications-related packages (aka ros_comm or ros-melodic-ros-comm) through 1.14.3. A buffer overflow allows attackers to cause a denial of service and possibly execute arbitrary code via an IP address with a long hostname.

code_evidence: A fixed 128-byte stack buffer namebuf is declared at line 8. Line 10 copies the string returned by inet_ntoa(sin->sin_addr) into namebuf using strcpy, which performs no destination-size check. The source address comes from getpeername at line 6, so the copied string is derived from the peer connection. Line 11 then builds a std::string from the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic buffer copy without input-size validation: an unbounded strcpy writes untrusted-derived data into a fixed-size stack buffer. It is not an out-of-bounds read, so CWE-125 does not apply; the weakness is the missing size check before the copy, matching CWE-120.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: strcpy copies the inet_ntoa result into the fixed 128-byte namebuf without bounding the copy length. Trigger: a peer address whose textual form exceeds 127 bytes. Consequence: the copy writes past namebuf, corrupting adjacent stack memory and potentially enabling a crash (DoS) or code execution; the subsequent std::string construction may also read the overrun region.

commit_msg:
crypto: replace rwlocks with simple mutexes

It was pointed out by Zhou Ran that the Windows XP implementation of
uv_rwlock_rdlock() and friends may unlock the inner write mutex on a
different thread than the one that locked it, resulting in undefined
behavior.

The only place that uses rwlocks is the crypto module.  Make that use
normal (simple) mutexes instead.

OpenSSL's critical sections are generally very short, with exclusive
access outnumbering shared access by a factor of three or more, so
it's not as if using rwlocks gives a decisive performance advantage.

PR-URL: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/2723
Reviewed-By: Fedor Indutny <fedor@indutny.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  locks = new uv_rwlock_t[n];', '    if (uv_rwlock_init(locks + i))'], 'added_lines': ['  locks = new uv_mutex_t[n];', '    if (uv_mutex_init(locks + i))']}
description: The uv_rwlock_t fallback implementation for Windows XP and Server 2003 in libuv before 1.7.4 does not properly prevent threads from releasing the locks of other threads, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (deadlock) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging a race condition.

code_evidence: The function allocates an array of locks sized by CRYPTO_num_locks() and initializes each entry with uv_rwlock_init, the libuv reader-writer lock type whose Windows XP fallback may release the inner write mutex from a different thread.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the lock array is the shared resource meant to serialize concurrent crypto access, and the rwlock fallback permits an interfering thread to break exclusivity, producing a race. The consequence is a timing-dependent deadlock rather than a plain memory error, matching the race-condition class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shared crypto lock array is built from uv_rwlock_t, whose fallback implementation does not enforce that a lock is released by the locking thread. Trigger: concurrent crypto callers on Windows XP/Server 2003 contend on these rwlocks, so one thread can release another thread's lock. Supported consequence: loss of exclusivity leading to deadlock (DoS) or undefined behavior.

commit_msg:
ath9k: release allocated buffer if timed out

In ath9k_wmi_cmd, the allocated network buffer needs to be released
if timeout happens. Otherwise memory will be leaked.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tkfree_skb(skb);']}
description: A memory leak in the ath9k_wmi_cmd() function in drivers/net/wireless/ath/ath9k/wmi.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption), aka CID-728c1e2a05e4.

code_evidence: Line 15 allocates a network buffer with alloc_skb; on failure the function returns -ENOMEM without leaking, so ownership of skb passes to the remainder of the function.

Line 32 waits for completion; when the wait times out (line 33), lines 34-36 log and unlock the mutex, then line 37 returns -ETIMEDOUT without freeing skb. The normal out path at line 44 does call kfree_skb(skb), showing the timeout return bypasses release.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory and fails to release it on an exceptional timeout path, matching CWE-401 (missing release of memory after effective lifetime). This is not a use-after-free (CWE-416), since the buffer remains allocated but becomes unreachable.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the timeout branch returns early without releasing the skb allocated at line 15. Trigger: ath9k_wmi_cmd_issue succeeds but wait_for_completion_timeout returns zero (no response within the caller-supplied timeout). Consequence: each timed-out command leaks one skb buffer, allowing repeated timeouts to consume kernel memory and cause denial of service.

commit_msg:
bpf: fix integer overflows

There were various issues related to the limited size of integers used in
the verifier:
 - `off + size` overflow in __check_map_access()
 - `off + reg->off` overflow in check_mem_access()
 - `off + reg->var_off.value` overflow or 32-bit truncation of
   `reg->var_off.value` in check_mem_access()
 - 32-bit truncation in check_stack_boundary()

Make sure that any integer math cannot overflow by not allowing
pointer math with large values.

Also reduce the scope of "scalar op scalar" tracking.

Fixes: f1174f77b50c ("bpf/verifier: rework value tracking")
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!check_reg_sane_offset(env, off_reg, ptr_reg->type) ||', '\t    !check_reg_sane_offset(env, ptr_reg, ptr_reg->type))', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '', '\tif (!check_reg_sane_offset(env, dst_reg, ptr_reg->type))', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (integer overflow and memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging unrestricted integer values for pointer arithmetic.

code_evidence: In the BPF_ADD path, dst_reg->off is set to ptr_reg->off + smin_val after only a 32-bit truncation self-check (s64)(s32)(...); the addition itself is not guarded against s64 overflow.

Bounds are updated with signed_add_overflows and unsigned wraparound checks (umin_ptr + umin_val < umin_ptr), but the fixed offset stored in dst_reg->off bypasses these guards, so a large scalar can wrap the pointer offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an integer addition whose result is assumed not to wrap; CWE-190 covers this wraparound. The commit's added check_reg_sane_offset calls confirm the intended fix was constraining offset magnitude, distinguishing it from a pure bounds-check omission (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Unrestricted scalar values added to a pointer are combined into dst_reg->off without a bound on the magnitude of off_reg; the only check is a 32-bit truncation equality test. A crafted BPF program supplies a large offset, the s64 addition wraps to a small or negative value, and the verifier accepts an out-of-bounds pointer, enabling memory corruption or DoS.

code_evidence: The value-copy loop at [52,53,54,55] stops when length becomes 0, at the separator, or at '>'. After the loop, line 56 unconditionally reads *(data - 1) and *data without verifying that any byte was copied or that length remains. Trigger: malformed/corrupt markup causing the loop to terminate at the length boundary. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of adjacent memory, potentially crash or information disclosure.

commit_msg:
Don't crash if crypt() fails.

It can fail, so make sure it doesn't before comparing its result with
the password.

This addresses Include Security issue F12: [libpcap] Remote Packet
Capture Daemon Null Pointer Dereference Denial of Service.

description: Integer overflow in the php_html_entities function in ext/standard/html.c in PHP before 5.5.36 and 5.6.x before 5.6.22 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a large output string from the htmlspecialchars function.

replaced is allocated with emalloc(maxlen + 1) on line 45, so a wrapped maxlen yields an undersized buffer.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size calculation maxlen = 2 * oldlen can wrap for very large input lengths; the guard on line 40 is meant to catch this, but the fix commit targets length handling outside the int range. commit_msg:
Fix invalid memory accesses while loading .a2m files

Missing checks and wrong calculations in src/a2m.cpp cause
multiple heap-based buffer overflows and out-of-bounds reads
in heap, stack, and static data.

Bugs addressed in this commit:
* Check the number of patterns. Too big values can cause reads
  past the end of the len array.
* Reading a not packed data block with odd length will allocate
  a buffer which is one byte too small and write past the end
  of it (issue #88). Change the allocation/deallocation code
  to fix that in both places.
* Check that data blocks (afer unpacking if applicable) are big
  enough for the expected data before accessing the memory.
* Ensure that the length byte for author, song name, and instrument
  names doesn't exceed the maximum size available.
* Also change the accessor functions for these strings to call
  the proper std::string constructors for char arrays.
* Avoid reads past the end of convfx/newconvfx arrays while
  converting track data.

This commit fixes CVE-2019-14732.

Fixes: https://github.com/adplug/adplug/issues/88

commit_msg:
USB: gadget: f_midi: fixing a possible double-free in f_midi

It looks like there is a possibility of a double-free vulnerability on an
error path of the f_midi_set_alt function in the f_midi driver. If the
path is feasible then free_ep_req gets called twice:

         req->complete = f_midi_complete;
         err = usb_ep_queue(midi->out_ep, req, GFP_ATOMIC);
            => ...
             usb_gadget_giveback_request
               =>
                 f_midi_complete (CALLBACK)
                   (inside f_midi_complete, for various cases of status)
                   free_ep_req(ep, req); // first kfree
         if (err) {
                 ERROR(midi, "%s: couldn't enqueue request: %d\n",
                             midi->out_ep->name, err);
                 free_ep_req(midi->out_ep, req); // second kfree
                 return err;
         }

The double-free possibility was introduced with commit ad0d1a058eac
("usb: gadget: f_midi: fix leak on failed to enqueue out requests").

Found by MOXCAFE tool.

Signed-off-by: Tuba Yavuz <tuba@ece.ufl.edu>
Fixes: ad0d1a058eac ("usb: gadget: f_midi: fix leak on failed to enqueue out requests")
Acked-by: Felipe Balbi <felipe.balbi@linux.intel.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tWARN_ON(req->buf == NULL);', '\treq->buf = NULL;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 4.16.4, a double free vulnerability in the f_midi_set_alt function of drivers/usb/gadget/function/f_midi.c in the f_midi driver may allow attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: free_ep_req unconditionally calls kfree(req->buf) and then usb_ep_free_request(ep, req) with no guard or state reset; the same req/buf can be passed again from an error path after the completion callback already freed it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 is exactly the double invocation of free() on the same address, matching kfree(req->buf) being reachable twice for one request. A use-after-free (CWE-416) would require dereferencing freed memory, which is not shown here; the defect is the duplicate release.

evidence_lines.code:
kfree(req->buf);
usb_ep_free_request(ep, req);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the absence of any ownership marker: free_ep_req frees req->buf without nulling it, so a second invocation on the same request (e.g., from an error path after the completion callback freed it) calls kfree on an already-freed buffer. Trigger is re-entry with the same req; consequence is a double free enabling memory corruption or denial of service.

*src)', '          break;', '        src++;', '      }', '      dest->numchildren = 0;', '      dest->children = NULL;', '    } else {', '      unsigned int i;', '      int cn;', '      dest->name = NULL;', '      dest->numchildren = dtd->scaffold[src_node].childcnt;', '      dest->children = &dest[1];', '', '      /* Push children to the stack', '       * in a way where the first child ends up at the top of the', '       * (downwards growing) stack, in order to be processed first. */', '      stackTop -= dest->numchildren;', '      for (i = 0, cn = dtd->scaffold[src_node].firstchild;', '           i < dest->numchildren; i++, cn = dtd->scaffold[cn].nextsib) {', '        (stackTop + i)->numchildren = (unsigned int)cn;', '      }', '    }', '  }', '']}
description: In Expat (aka libexpat) before 2.4.5, an attacker can trigger stack exhaustion in build_model via a large nesting depth in the DTD element.

code_evidence: build_model declares cpos and str (lines 5-6) as traversal state passed into build_node.
The function allocates ret of size proportional to scaffCount and contentStringLen (lines 21-23), then initializes str and cpos (lines 24-25).
build_node(parser, 0, ret, &cpos, &str) is invoked once (line 26) and internally recurses per nested DTD content node, with depth driven by the input DTD nesting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 covers uncontrolled recursion consuming the program stack. Here recursion depth is attacker-controlled via DTD nesting and is not bounded, matching the target weakness; the fix replaces recursion with an iterative stack, confirming the cause.

evidence_lines.code:
XML_Content *cpos;
XML_Char *str;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: build_node is recursively called once per nested DTD content node, and the input controls nesting depth. A crafted DTD with deeply nested element content causes unbounded call-stack growth, exhausting the stack and crashing the parser (availability impact). Cause is uncontrolled recursion; consequence is stack exhaustion/DoS.

commit_msg: Fix r2_hbo_grub_memmove ext2 crash
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t  if (buf)'], 'added_lines': ['\t  if (buf) {', '\t    if (pos + real_offset + len >= size) {', '              // prevent read overflow', '              grub_errno = GRUB_ERR_BAD_FS;', '              return grub_errno;', '\t    }', '          }']}
description: The grub_memmove function in shlr/grub/kern/misc.c in radare2 1.5.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted binary file, possibly related to a read overflow in the grub_disk_read_small_real function in kern/disk.c in GNU GRUB 2.02.

code_evidence: len is computed as the cache buffer size minus pos and real_offset; the memcpy at line 35 copies len bytes from data+pos+real_offset without checking that pos+real_offset+len stays within the fetched cache block, so a crafted sector/offset/size can drive the source read past the cache buffer.

The cache-miss path reallocs tmp_buf to num sectors based on size+real_offset, then reads and copies size bytes at line 62; the read_hook loop at 63-77 and the sector/size arithmetic at 102-106 advance through buffers with the same unchecked offset arithmetic, allowing reads beyond the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs a memory read outside the intended buffer boundary; the missing bounds check on the source range before grub_memcpy is the direct cause. A narrower CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read) would also apply, but the target label CWE-119 is the specified parent class for this out-of-bounds memory operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: grub_disk_read computes len and copy offsets from attacker-influenced sector, offset and size values but never verifies pos+real_offset+len against the cache block or tmp_buf allocation before grub_memcpy. Trigger: a crafted binary that requests a read whose offset/len combination exceeds the fetched buffer. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read from the heap, leading to crash or disclosure of adjacent memory.

Fixes #36. Fixes #66.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\te = gf_rtp_builder_process(tkHint->rtp_p, ptr, size, (u8) !remain, samp->dataLength, duration, (u8) (descIndex + GF_RTP_TX3G_SIDX_OFFSET) );', '\t\t\t\tptr += size;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif (!size) {', '\t\t\t\t\tGF_LOG(GF_LOG_WARNING, GF_LOG_RTP, ("[rtp hinter] Broken AVC nalu encapsulation: NALU size is 0, ignoring it\\n", size));', '\t\t\t\t} else {', '\t\t\t\t\te = gf_rtp_builder_process(tkHint->rtp_p, ptr, size, (u8) !remain, samp->dataLength, duration, (u8) (descIndex + GF_RTP_TX3G_SIDX_OFFSET) );', '\t\t\t\t\tptr += size;', '\t\t\t\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in GPAC version 0.8.0 and 1.0.1. There is heap-based buffer overflow in the function gp_rtp_builder_do_avc() in ietf/rtp_pck_mpeg4.c.

code_evidence: The loop parses AVC NALU sizes: [55] initializes size=0, [61-67] read avc_nalu_size bytes from ptr accumulating into size, then [69-72] validate remain>=size and [73] subtract. [75] passes ptr and size to gf_rtp_builder_process and [76] advances ptr by size. A zero-length NALU (size==0) passes the remain<size check and is forwarded with size 0, then ptr is not advanced while remain is unchanged, so the loop iterates with no progress.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 requires a write beyond the intended buffer; the shown code guards remain<size before consuming and passes a bounded size to the builder, and the defect is a missing zero-size rejection, not an out-of-bounds write in this function. The evidence supports a logic/loop issue rather than CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size==0 case is not rejected, so gf_rtp_builder_process is invoked with a zero-length NALU and the loop makes no forward progress. Trigger: crafted AVC sample whose NALU length field is zero. Supported consequence: the builder receives an invalid zero-size unit and the parse loop can spin, leading to incorrect state/handling rather than a demonstrated write past the buffer.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.0225: using freed memory with multiple line breaks in expression

Problem:    Using freed memory with multiple line breaks in expression.
Solution:   Free eval_tofree later.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tvim_free(evalarg->eval_tofree);'], 'added_lines': ['\tfree_eval_tofree_later(evalarg);']}
description: Use After Free in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0225.

code_evidence: In the else-if branch, when the growable array cannot be grown, the code frees evalarg->eval_tofree and then stores the newly obtained line in that same field. The freed pointer is the previously stored line, and line is a separate allocation from eval_getline/next_line_from_context.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees memory still referenced through eval_tofree and continues using it in later evaluation steps, which is the defining pattern of CWE-416 Use After Free. This is a lifetime/ordering defect, not merely a double free or memory leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: evalarg->eval_tofree is freed immediately while the evaluation may still reference the earlier stored line across subsequent calls (e.g., multiple line breaks). Trigger: a multi-line expression where ga_grow fails so this branch executes repeatedly. Consequence: the earlier line buffer is freed while still reachable, leading to use-after-free reads or writes; the fix defers freeing via free_eval_tofree_later.

commit_msg:
Fix use-after-free in regexp source property access.

The underlying string of the "source" property of a regular expression
object can be freed if the regexp is garbage collected.

This could lead to a use-after-free, because the accessor incorrectly
assumed that the regexp source was an interned (thus never freed) string.
Fix this by calling js_pushstring instead of the faster but unsafe
js_pushliteral.

Many thanks to Connor Nelson for spotting this!
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tjs_pushliteral(J, obj->u.r.source);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tjs_pushstring(J, obj->u.r.source);']}
description: In MuJS before version 1.1.2, a use-after-free flaw in the regexp source property access may cause denial of service.

code_evidence: For a JS_CREGEXP object, the 'source' accessor reads obj->u.r.source and passes it to js_pushliteral, which assumes the string is interned and therefore never freed. The regexp's source string is not guaranteed to be interned, so this dereference can occur after the regexp has been garbage collected and its backing string freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the code references memory (obj->u.r.source) that may already have been freed, and the fix replaces js_pushliteral with js_pushstring to copy the string safely. This is a use-after-free rather than a mere type confusion or buffer overflow, since the stale pointer is dereferenced after release.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the accessor treats obj->u.r.source as an interned, immortal literal via js_pushliteral instead of copying it. Trigger: accessing the 'source' property of a regexp whose underlying source string was freed after garbage collection. Consequence: a use-after-free read that can crash (denial of service) or read freed memory.

commit_msg:
Fix a json_decode crash when depth==0

Summary:
Setting depth=0 is an error, and should result in NULL, but we weren't
checking for it, so in the case of a single, top-level string, we
would reading the -1th element of the stack.

Differential Revision: D19609959

fbshipit-source-id: 04ca1e0965e04b44df2d5c806a73c3da99ff66fb
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (depth <= 0) {', '    json->error_code = json_error_codes::JSON_ERROR_DEPTH;', '    return false;', '  }']}
description: Insufficient boundary checks when decoding JSON in JSON_parser allows read access to out of bounds memory, potentially leading to information leak and DOS. This issue affects HHVM 4.45.0, 4.44.0, 4.43.0, 4.42.0, 4.41.0, 4.40.0, 4.39.0, versions between 4.33.0 and 4.38.0 (inclusive), versions between 4.9.0 and 4.32.0 (inclusive), and versions prior to 4.8.7.

code_evidence: JSON_parser accepts an attacker-influenced depth parameter and immediately calls json->initSb(length) without validating depth. The added patch shows the missing guard: depth <= 0 must set JSON_ERROR_DEPTH and return false before any stack use; without it, a top-level string causes a read of the -1th stack element.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading the -1th stack element is an access before the beginning of the intended buffer, matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). The missing depth<=0 constraint is the direct cause of that out-of-bounds access, not merely a logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no lower-bound check on depth before parsing, so depth=0 (an invalid value) is processed. Trigger: decoding a single top-level string with depth=0 causes indexing of the -1th element of the parser stack. Consequence: out-of-bounds memory read, potentially leaking information or crashing the process (DoS).

commit_msg:
Jann Horn reported that SO_PEERCRED and SO_PEERGROUPS implementations
are racy, as af_unix can concurrently change sk_peer_pid and sk_peer_cred.

In order to fix this issue, this patch adds a new spinlock that needs
to be used whenever these fields are read or written.

Jann also pointed out that l2cap_sock_get_peer_pid_cb() is currently
reading sk->sk_peer_pid which makes no sense, as this field
is only possibly set by AF_UNIX sockets.
We will have to clean this in a separate patch.
This could be done by reverting b48596d1dc25 "Bluetooth: L2CAP: Add get_peer_pid callback"
or implementing what was truly expected.

Fixes: 109f6e39fa07 ("af_unix: Allow SO_PEERCRED to work across namespaces.")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Cc: Eric W. Biederman <ebiederm@xmission.com>
Cc: Luiz Augusto von Dentz <luiz.von.dentz@intel.com>
Cc: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (sk->sk_peer_cred)', '\t\tput_cred(sk->sk_peer_cred);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* We do not need to acquire sk->sk_peer_lock, we are the last user. */', '\tput_cred(sk->sk_peer_cred);', '']}
description: A use-after-free read flaw was found in sock_getsockopt() in net/core/sock.c due to SO_PEERCRED and SO_PEERGROUPS race with listen() (and connect()) in the Linux kernel. In this flaw, an attacker with a user privileges may crash the system or leak internal kernel information.

code_evidence: In the destructor, sk->sk_peer_cred is read and passed to put_cred(), and sk->sk_peer_pid is read and passed to put_pid(), with no sk_peer_lock held; the comment in the patch notes only that this is safe because the destructor is the last user.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent access to shared state lacking proper synchronization (a missing lock around reads/writes of sk_peer_cred and sk_peer_pid), matching CWE-362 rather than a plain memory-safety bug; the UAF is the consequence of the race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The shared fields sk_peer_cred and sk_peer_pid can be concurrently replaced by af_unix code (listen()/connect()) while sock_getsockopt() reads them, without the new sk_peer_lock; the unprotected read in the getsockopt path races with the write, so the read may observe a credential/pid that is freed, yielding a use-after-free read that can crash or leak kernel memory.

commit_msg: Defensive coding to avoid 0x80000000/0xFFFFFFFF FPE.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        ok_ = (value_.at(n).second != 0 && value_.at(n).first < LARGE_INT);'], 'added_lines': ['        ok_ = (value_.at(n).second > 0 && value_.at(n).first < LARGE_INT);']}
description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. A floating point exception (FPE) due to an integer divide by zero was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The FPE is triggered when Exiv2 is used to print the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. Note that this bug is only triggered when printing the interpreted (translated) data, which is a less frequently used Exiv2 operation that requires an extra command line option (`-p t` or `-P t`). The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: Line 3 sets ok_ only when value_.at(n).second != 0 and the numerator is below LARGE_INT; line 4 returns 0 only when that guard fails; line 5 otherwise performs value_.at(n).first / value_.at(n).second.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a division whose denominator is validated insufficiently, allowing a crafted value to reach a divide operation that faults, matching CWE-369 (Divide By Zero). The fix tightens the check to second > 0, confirming the missing constraint was the root cause rather than a generic arithmetic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The guard on line 3 checks only that the denominator is nonzero, so a negative denominator such as 0xFFFFFFFF (interpreted as -1 in the signed second component) passes the check. The division on line 5 then executes with that unexpected denominator, and the crafted value triggers an FPE/divide-by-zero, crashing Exiv2 during interpreted-data printing (DoS).

description: In radare2 2.4.0, there is a heap-based buffer over-read in the r_asm_disassemble function of asm.c. Remote attackers could leverage this vulnerability to cause a denial of service via a crafted dex file.

code_evidence: Line 72 copies oplen bytes from the caller-supplied buf into op->buf. oplen derives from op->size/op->bitsize (lines 41-55) and is only clamped to a minimum of 1, never to the actual input length len, so the copy can read beyond buf when the disassembler reports a size larger than the remaining input. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the number of bytes read from buf is bounded by R_ASM_BUFSIZE but not by the real input length len, so a crafted dex file that makes the disassembler report a larger oplen causes reads past the end of the heap-allocated input. Trigger: a short input whose decoded instruction size exceeds len. Consequence: out-of-bounds read, crash/DoS, or disclosure of adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
Fix `tf.raw_ops.SparseAdd ` invalid memory access failure.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 370568774
Change-Id: I5f73b31c865f2948a1c8dfb7ebd22b3cfb6405bf

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. Incomplete validation in `SparseAdd` results in allowing attackers to exploit undefined behavior (dereferencing null pointers) as well as write outside of bounds of heap allocated data. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/656e7673b14acd7835dc778867f84916c6d1cac2/tensorflow/core/kernels/sparse_add_op.cc) has a large set of validation for the two sparse tensor inputs (6 tensors in total), but does not validate that the tensors are not empty or that the second dimension of `*_indices` matches the size of corresponding `*_shape`. This allows attackers to send tensor triples that represent invalid sparse tensors to abuse code assumptions that are not protected by validation. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 63 derives num_dims from a_shape->dim_size(0) without checking it is nonzero; the added guard is absent here, so an empty shape vector yields num_dims = 0.
num_dims is passed to sparse::DimComparator::cmp and later used as the second dimension of the output allocation at lines 102-103, TensorShape({sum_nnz, num_dims}).
The loop at lines 108-112 writes each row via out_indices_mat.chip<0>(i) = a_indices_mat.chip<0>(idx), using indices whose width depends on the unvalidated num_dims.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes index rows into a heap-allocated output tensor whose dimensions are computed from unvalidated input, so writes can exceed the intended buffer. This is CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write), not merely an input-validation or null-dereference issue, because the supported consequence is memory written past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: num_dims is taken from an unvalidated input shape and can be zero or inconsistent with the *_indices second dimension. Trigger: a crafted sparse tensor triple with an empty or mismatched shape. Consequence: the output index matrix is allocated with a wrong width, and chip writes at lines 111-112 can write outside the heap buffer, causing out-of-bounds memory corruption.

without checking the size. If the size is less than 8 it would read
beyond the bounds of this heap buffer. This commit prevents that.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: fix unconditional helper

Ben Hawkes says:

 In the mark_source_chains function (net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c) it
 is possible for a user-supplied ipt_entry structure to have a large
 next_offset field. This field is not bounds checked prior to writing a
 counter value at the supplied offset.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif ((e->target_offset == sizeof(struct arpt_entry) &&', '\t\t\t     t->verdict < 0 && unconditional(&e->arp)) ||', '\t\t\t    visited) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif ((unconditional(e) &&', '\t\t\t     t->verdict < 0) || visited) {']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

code_evidence: The unconditional-rule test at [23-27] uses the weak condition e->target_offset == sizeof(struct arpt_entry) plus unconditional(&e->arp), which only checks wildcard address matching and ignores whether matches (-m) are present, unlike the unified unconditional(e) helper.

Because a rule with matches can be misclassified as an unconditional absolute verdict, the else branch at [52] is skipped and control enters the visited/absolute-verdict path; the loop at [44-51] then walks to entry0 + pos + size using e->next_offset without validating that offset against the table size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes a counter value through a pointer derived from an unchecked next_offset, performing a write outside the intended buffer boundary, which directly matches CWE-119. The root cause is the incorrect unconditional-rule validation, but the supported weakness is the unbounded buffer operation.

if ((e->target_offset == sizeof(struct arpt_entry) &&
(strcmp(t->target.u.user.name,
XT_STANDARD_TARGET) == 0) &&
t->verdict < 0 && unconditional(&e->arp)) ||

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the conditional()/unconditional logic fails to require absence of matches, so a crafted user-supplied ipt/arpt entry with matches is treated as an unconditional END rule. Trigger: an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE call supplies an entry whose next_offset is large; mark_source_chains proceeds to the next (non-existent) entry and computes entry0 + pos + size at [47-49], then writes e->counters.pcnt at [50] outside the intended buffer. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds heap write leading to memory corruption.

commit_msg:
fix crsf_rc: prevent potential buffer overflow for unknown packets

The length check for unknown packets did not include PACKET_SIZE_TYPE_SIZE
and CRC_SIZE, and hence working_index could overflow CRSF_MAX_PACKET_LEN,
triggering invalid memory access further down in QueueBuffer_PeekBuffer.

Also the working_segment_size was wrong for unknown packets.

Credits for finding this go to @Pwn9uin.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tworking_segment_size = packet_size + PACKET_SIZE_TYPE_SIZE;', '\t\t\t\tif (working_segment_size > CRSF_MAX_PACKET_LEN) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tworking_segment_size = packet_size - PACKET_SIZE_TYPE_SIZE;', '\t\t\t\tif (working_index + working_segment_size + CRC_SIZE > CRSF_MAX_PACKET_LEN) {']}
description: PX4 autopilot is a flight control solution for drones. In affected versions a global buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the CrsfParser_TryParseCrsfPacket function in /src/drivers/rc/crsf_rc/CrsfParser.cpp:298 due to the invalid size check. A malicious user may create an RC packet remotely and that packet goes into the device where the _rcs_buf reads. The global buffer overflow vulnerability will be triggered and the drone can behave unexpectedly. This issue has been addressed in version 1.14.0. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: For unknown packet types, working_segment_size is computed from the untrusted packet_size byte as packet_size + PACKET_SIZE_TYPE_SIZE, and the only bounds check compares working_segment_size alone against CRSF_MAX_PACKET_LEN, ignoring the current working_index and CRC_SIZE.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked, attacker-controlled size drives a copy into a fixed-size buffer, matching CWE-120's buffer copy without input size verification. The defect is a missing bound on the copied length, not merely a size-calculation error (CWE-131) or an isolated out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size check omits working_index and CRC_SIZE, so a crafted unknown packet can make working_index + CRC_SIZE exceed the process_buffer/CRSF_MAX_PACKET_LEN capacity. Trigger: a remotely supplied RC packet with a large size byte and unknown type reaches PARSER_STATE_CRC, where QueueBuffer_PeekBuffer copies working_index + CRC_SIZE bytes. Consequence: out-of-bounds write/read of process_buffer, corrupting memory and potentially crashing or miscontrolling the drone.

Consequence: privilege escalation within the guest or guest OS crash, as the hypervisor mishandles the segment state.

commit_msg:
ppp: take reference on channels netns

Let channels hold a reference on their network namespace.
Some channel types, like ppp_async and ppp_synctty, can have their
userspace controller running in a different namespace. Therefore they
can't rely on them to preclude their netns from being removed from
under them.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tpch->chan_net = net;'], 'added_lines': ['\tpch->chan_net = get_net(net);']}
description: Use-after-free vulnerability in drivers/net/ppp/ppp_generic.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5.2 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory corruption and system crash, or spinlock) or possibly have unspecified other impact by removing a network namespace, related to the ppp_register_net_channel and ppp_unregister_channel functions.

code_evidence: pch is allocated with kzalloc, then ppp_pernet(net) is called on the supplied net pointer [8]. The channel stores the raw pointer net in pch->chan_net without taking a namespace reference [11], and later links it into pn->new_channels [23].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stored chan_net pointer outlives the object it references, and later channel teardown accesses that freed namespace memory, which is precisely CWE-416. It is not merely a missing-reference error; the observable defect is use of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pch->chan_net retains a borrowed pointer to the ppp net namespace without incrementing its refcount. Trigger: a userspace controller in a different namespace closes the channel or removes the namespace, freeing the net_namespace while pch still references it. Consequence: ppp_unregister_channel dereferences freed ppp_pernet memory, producing a use-after-free read (KASAN report), memory corruption, or crash.

In version 2.11.1 and prior, there are various cases where it is possible that certain incoming RTP/RTCP packets can potentially cause out-of-bound read access. commit_msg:
At image reading, compare data size of some tags / data structures (StripByteCounts, StripOffsets, StripArray, TIFF directory) with file size to prevent provoked out-of-memory attacks.

See issue #614.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        /* Before allocating a huge amount of memory for corrupted files, check', '         * if size of requested memory is not greater than file size. */', '        uint64_t filesize = TIFFGetFileSize(tif);', '        uint64_t allocsize = (uint64_t)nstrips * sizeof(uint64_t);', '        if (allocsize > filesize)', '        {', '            TIFFWarningExtR(tif, module,', '                            "Requested memory size for StripArray of %" PRIu64', '                            " is greather than filesize %" PRIu64', '                            ". Memory not allocated",', '                            allocsize, filesize);', '            _TIFFfreeExt(tif, data);', '            return (0);', '        }']}
description: An out-of-memory flaw was found in libtiff. Passing a crafted tiff file to TIFFOpen() API may allow a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via a craft input with size smaller than 379 KB.

code_evidence: When the directory count is smaller than the requested strip count nstrips, the function resizes the array. nstrips is attacker-influenced via the TIFF strip count, and the subsequent _TIFFCheckMalloc allocates nstrips * sizeof(uint64_t) elements without any bound relating the requested allocation to the actual file size.
The only guard before allocation is the environment-controlled max_nstrips (default 1000000), which still permits large allocations relative to a tiny crafted file.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to throttle or bound an attacker-controlled allocation, directly matching CWE-400 Uncontrolled Resource Consumption. The fix in the same commit adds a filesize-versus-allocsize check, confirming the missing resource constraint; this is resource-exhaustion, not a memory-safety write issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the resize path allocates memory proportional to the attacker-supplied nstrips without verifying that the requested allocation is plausible for the input file size. Trigger: a crafted TIFF whose StripOffsets/StripByteCounts count is much smaller than nstrips forces the resize branch. Consequence: excessive memory consumption leading to out-of-memory denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix bug #78222 (heap-buffer-overflow on exif_scan_thumbnail)

(cherry picked from commit dea2989ab8ba87a6180af497b2efaf0527e985c5)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!data) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!data || ImageInfo->Thumbnail.size < 4) {']}
description: When PHP EXIF extension is parsing EXIF information from an image, e.g. via exif_read_data() function, in PHP versions 7.1.x below 7.1.31, 7.2.x below 7.2.21 and 7.3.x below 7.3.8 it is possible to supply it with data what will cause it to read past the allocated buffer. This may lead to information disclosure or crash.

code_evidence: The guard checks only data != NULL before use; it does not verify that ImageInfo->Thumbnail.size is at least the number of bytes read.
memcmp(data, "\xFF\xD8\xFF", 3) unconditionally reads 3 bytes from data, but a thumbnail buffer smaller than 3 bytes (or size 0) passes the null check.
The loop reads data[pos++] with a size comparison only after the increment, so the initial read at pos can occur before any bound check for very small sizes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 directly matches: the function reads memory past the end of the allocated thumbnail buffer due to a missing size check before the fixed-length memcmp. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write or a null-pointer dereference, so the target CWE fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the entry guard validates only non-null data, not the allocated Thumbnail.size, so the fixed 3-byte memcmp (and early loop reads) can access beyond a short buffer. Trigger: a crafted image producing a thumbnail with fewer than 3 bytes. Consequence: out-of-bounds read, potentially disclosing memory or crashing the process.

commit_msg:
[media] cx24116: fix a buffer overflow when checking userspace params

The maximum size for a DiSEqC command is 6, according to the
userspace API. However, the code allows to write up much more values:
	drivers/media/dvb-frontends/cx24116.c:983 cx24116_send_diseqc_msg() error: buffer overflow 'd->msg' 6 <= 23

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@osg.samsung.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\t/* Validate length */', '\tif (d->msg_len > (CX24116_ARGLEN - CX24116_DISEQC_MSGOFS))', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* Validate length */', '\tif (d->msg_len > sizeof(d->msg))', '                return -EINVAL;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 4.1.4, a buffer overflow occurs when checking userspace params in drivers/media/dvb-frontends/cx24116.c. The maximum size for a DiSEqC command is 6, according to the userspace API. However, the code allows larger values such as 23.

code_evidence: The length check compares d->msg_len against (CX24116_ARGLEN - CX24116_DISEQC_MSGOFS), which is larger than the fixed 6-byte d->msg array, so it fails to constrain msg_len to the source buffer size.
The loop then indexes d->msg[i] for i < d->msg_len, reading elements beyond the 6-byte userspace-supplied msg array when msg_len is between 7 and the larger limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the intended d->msg buffer during the copy loop, matching CWE-125. The write into args is bounded by the wider check, so the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read rather than the buffer overflow described in the commit message.

evidence_lines.code:
if (d->msg_len > (CX24116_ARGLEN - CX24116_DISEQC_MSGOFS))
return -EINVAL;

for (i = 0; i < d->msg_len; i++)
state->dsec_cmd.args[CX24116_DISEQC_MSGOFS + i] = d->msg[i];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a length validation against the destination command buffer bound rather than the source d->msg array size. A userspace caller supplying msg_len larger than 6 passes the check, and the copy loop reads d->msg[i] out of bounds, causing an out-of-bounds read of adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Fix race among timer ioctls

ALSA timer ioctls have an open race and this may lead to a
use-after-free of timer instance object.  A simplistic fix is to make
each ioctl exclusive.  We have already tread_sem for controlling the
tread, and extend this as a global mutex to be applied to each ioctl.

The downside is, of course, the worse concurrency.  But these ioctls
aren't to be parallel accessible, in anyway, so it should be fine to
serialize there.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tmutex_lock(&tu->ioctl_lock);', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&tu->ioctl_lock);']}
description: sound/core/timer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 uses an incorrect type of mutex, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (race condition, use-after-free, and system crash) via a crafted ioctl call.

code_evidence: Release path reads file->private_data, clears it, then conditionally calls snd_timer_close(tu->timeri) and frees tu->queue, tu->tqueue, and tu itself without any lock in the pre-patch function. The timeri pointer and tu object are shared with concurrent ioctl paths, which can access and modify them between the NULL assignment and the frees.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unsynchronized teardown of a shared resource concurrently reachable by ioctl sequences is exactly the concurrent-access-without-exclusivity pattern of CWE-362. The use-after-free is the downstream consequence, not a separate label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: snd_timer_user_release performs teardown of the shared snd_timer_user object without exclusive synchronization against timer ioctls. Trigger: a local user races an ioctl that operates on tu->timeri against file release. commit_msg:
fbdev: Fixing arbitrary kernel leak in case FBIOGETCMAP_SPARC in sbusfb_ioctl_helper().

Fixing arbitrary kernel leak in case FBIOGETCMAP_SPARC in
sbusfb_ioctl_helper().

'index' is defined as an int in sbusfb_ioctl_helper().
We retrieve this from the user:
if (get_user(index, &c->index) ||
    __get_user(count, &c->count) ||
    __get_user(ured, &c->red) ||
    __get_user(ugreen, &c->green) ||
    __get_user(ublue, &c->blue))
       return -EFAULT;

and then we use 'index' in the following way:
red = cmap->red[index + i] >> 8;
green = cmap->green[index + i] >> 8;
blue = cmap->blue[index + i] >> 8;

This is a classic information leak vulnerability. 'index' should be
an unsigned int, given its usage above.

This patch is straight-forward; it changes 'index' to unsigned int
in two switch-cases: FBIOGETCMAP_SPARC && FBIOPUTCMAP_SPARC.

This patch fixes CVE-2018-6412.

Signed-off-by: Peter Malone <peter.malone@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Mathieu Malaterre <malat@debian.org>
Signed-off-by: Bartlomiej Zolnierkiewicz <b.zolnierkie@samsung.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tint index, count, i;', '\t\tint index, count, i;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tunsigned int index, count, i;', '\t\tunsigned int index, count, i;']}
description: In the function sbusfb_ioctl_helper() in drivers/video/fbdev/sbuslib.c in the Linux kernel through 4.15, an integer signedness error allows arbitrary information leakage for the FBIOPUTCMAP_SPARC and FBIOGETCMAP_SPARC commands.

code_evidence: In FBIOPUTCMAP_SPARC, index and count are declared as signed int and read from user-controlled c->index/c->count; index + i at line 46 can overflow or be negative, so cmap.start derived from it is not a valid bounded offset when passed to fb_set_cmap.

In FBIOGETCMAP_SPARC, index and count are signed int from user; the check index + count > cmap->len at line 67 can be bypassed by signed overflow or a negative index, and cmap->red/green/blue[index + i] at lines 70-72 then reads outside the cmap arrays and copies kernel data to user via put_user.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies out-of-bounds kernel memory contents to a user buffer, exposing sensitive kernel information to an unauthorized actor, which is the confidentiality impact described by CWE-200. The signed-index error is the enabling defect, but the demonstrated consequence is direct information exposure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: user-controlled signed index/count are used in index + i and as array indices without signedness or overflow validation. A negative index or wrapped sum passes the length check, and the loop reads out-of-bounds kernel cmap memory that is returned to the caller, disclosing kernel data.

commit_msg:
Fix loop in blocking read on transport timeout

The loop was cased by an incorrect errno if the transport read in
mgs_transport_read() fails with an APR TIMEUP status, as happens when
mod_reqtimeout limits are exceeded. Setting the transport errno to
EGAIN meant that a blocking read would be retried endlessly, setting
ETIMEDOUT instead makes the read fail as it should.

The bug was introduced in commit 92cb0cca41af946055307e373b6ab6d76d34f356,
first release to include it was 0.9.0.

Many thanks to Félix Arreola Rodríguez for the detailed analysis [1]
on the Debian bug tracker!

[1] https://bugs.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?bug=942737#25
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            gnutls_transport_set_errno(ctxt->session, EAGAIN);'], 'added_lines': ['            gnutls_transport_set_errno(ctxt->session, ETIMEDOUT);']}
description: Mod_gnutls is a TLS module for Apache HTTPD based on GnuTLS. Versions from 0.9.0 to 0.12.0 (including) did not properly fail blocking read operations on TLS connections when the transport hit timeouts. Instead it entered an endless loop retrying the read operation, consuming CPU resources. This could be exploited for denial of service attacks. If trace level logging was enabled, it would also produce an excessive amount of log output during the loop, consuming disk space. The problem has been fixed in commit d7eec4e598158ab6a98bf505354e84352f9715ec, please update to version 0.12.1. There are no workarounds, users who cannot update should apply the errno fix detailed in the security advisory.

code_evidence: When a blocking read returns APR_STATUS_IS_TIMEUP with an empty brigade, the function sets the GnuTLS transport errno to EAGAIN (line 37) and returns -1. EAGAIN signals a retryable condition, so the caller's blocking read is retried instead of failing on the timeout.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The retry loop driven by the incorrect EAGAIN errno never reaches a terminating exit condition for persistent timeouts, matching CWE-835's unreachable-exit-condition infinite loop. Contrast with CWE-400: the loop is the specific defect, with resource exhaustion as its consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a transport timeout is reported to GnuTLS as EAGAIN rather than a terminal timeout error. Trigger: a blocking read under mod_reqtimeout where ap_get_brigade returns TIMEUP with an empty brigade repeatedly. Consequence: the blocking read is retried endlessly, consuming CPU (and excessive trace-log disk output), a denial of service.

commit_msg:
Avoid some undefined pointer arithmetic

A common idiom in the codebase is:

if (p + len > limit)
{
    return; /* Too long */
}

Where "p" points to some malloc'd data of SIZE bytes and
limit == p + SIZE

"len" here could be from some externally supplied data (e.g. from a TLS
message).

The rules of C pointer arithmetic are such that "p + len" is only well
defined where len <= SIZE. Therefore the above idiom is actually
undefined behaviour.

For example this could cause problems if some malloc implementation
provides an address for "p" such that "p + len" actually overflows for
values of len that are too big and therefore p + len < limit!

Issue reported by Guido Vranken.

CVE-2016-2177

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (data >= (limit - 2))', '    if (data > (limit - 4))', '    if (data + size > limit)', '        if (data + len1 + len2 != limit)', '        if (data + len != limit)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (limit - data <= 2)', '    if (limit - data < 4)', '    if (limit - data < size)', '        if (limit - data != (int)(len1 + len2))', '        if (limit - data != (int)(len))']}
description: OpenSSL through 1.0.2h incorrectly uses pointer arithmetic for heap-buffer boundary checks, which might allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (integer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging unexpected malloc behavior, related to s3_srvr.c, ssl_sess.c, and t1_lib.c.

code_evidence: Boundary check computes `data >= (limit - 2)` and then advances `data += 2`; the guard is expressed via arithmetic on the pointer rather than comparing remaining length.
After the first advance, `data > (limit - 4)` is checked before `n2s(data, type)` and `n2s(data, size)` read two bytes each from `data`.
The externally supplied `size` from the TLS message is used in `data + size > limit`; if `data + size` wraps, the comparison may pass and `data += size` moves past `limit`.
The equality check `data + len1 + len2 != limit` adds two `size_t` constants to the pointer, again relying on pointer arithmetic not overflowing.
The non-TLS1.2 branch uses `data + len != limit` for the same boundary decision.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the guard relies on integer/pointer addition whose result can wrap, so a length that should be rejected is accepted; the flaw is the unchecked arithmetic, not merely a missing bounds check (contrast CWE-125).

evidence_lines.code:
if (data + len1 + len2 != limit)
return;

if (data + len != limit)
return;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: heap-buffer boundary checks are performed by adding an externally influenced length (`size`) or fixed offsets to the `data` pointer instead of comparing against `limit - data`. Trigger: a crafted TLS ClientHello supplies a length such that `data + size` (or the offset additions) wraps past the allocated region. Consequence: the length check is bypassed, allowing out-of-bounds reads or subsequent memory access leading to crash/DoS.

commit_msg:

validated = Envoy::Ssl::ClientValidationStatus::Validated;

Consequence: the certificate is validated as a domain, bypassing nameConstraints and enabling server impersonation.

commit_msg:
It is possible to trigger heap overflows due to an integer overflow
while parsing images and a signedness issue while parsing comments.

The integer overflow occurs because the chosen limit 0x10000 for
dimensions is too large for 32 bit systems, because each pixel takes
4 bytes. Properly chosen values allow an overflow which in turn will
lead to less allocated memory than needed for subsequent reads.

The signedness bug is triggered by reading the length of a comment
as unsigned int, but casting it to int when calling the function
XcursorCommentCreate. Turning length into a negative value allows the
check against XCURSOR_COMMENT_MAX_LEN to pass, and the following
addition of sizeof (XcursorComment) + 1 makes it possible to allocate
less memory than needed for subsequent reads.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (head.width >= 0x10000 || head.height > 0x10000)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (head.width > XCURSOR_IMAGE_MAX_SIZE  ||', '\thead.height > XCURSOR_IMAGE_MAX_SIZE)', '    if (image == NULL)', '\treturn NULL;']}
description: libXcursor before 1.1.15 has various integer overflows that could lead to heap buffer overflows when processing malicious cursors, e.g., with programs like GIMP. It is also possible that an attack vector exists against the related code in cursor/xcursor.c in Wayland through 1.14.0.

code_evidence: The width/height sanity check caps dimensions below 0x10000, but each pixel is 4 bytes, so width*height*4 can exceed the 32-bit allocation size.
XcursorImageCreate(head.width, head.height) allocates based on that product; the return value is not checked for NULL before dereference at line 32.
n = image->width * image->height is computed; the loop then reads n pixels via _XcursorReadUInt into image->pixels.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the flaw is an integer overflow in the size calculation used for allocation, which then enables out-of-bounds writes. This is distinct from a mere missing NULL check; the arithmetic wraparound is the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
if (head.width >= 0x10000 || head.height > 0x10000)
return NULL;
image = XcursorImageCreate (head.width, head.height);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dimension limit does not account for 4-byte pixels, so width*height*4 wraps in the allocation computation on 32-bit systems, allocating less memory than the pixel count implies. Trigger: a malicious cursor with large dimensions passes the check. Consequence: the read loop writes past the undersized heap buffer, causing a heap buffer overflow.

commit_msg:
can: bcm: delay release of struct bcm_op after synchronize_rcu()

can_rx_register() callbacks may be called concurrently to the call to
can_rx_unregister(). The callbacks and callback data, though, are
protected by RCU and the struct sock reference count.

So the callback data is really attached to the life of sk, meaning
that it should be released on sk_destruct. However, bcm_remove_op()
calls tasklet_kill(), and RCU callbacks may be called under RCU
softirq, so that cannot be used on kernels before the introduction of
HRTIMER_MODE_SOFT.

However, bcm_rx_handler() is called under RCU protection, so after
calling can_rx_unregister(), we may call synchronize_rcu() in order to
wait for any RCU read-side critical sections to finish. That is,
bcm_rx_handler() won't be called anymore for those ops. So, we only
free them, after we do that synchronize_rcu().

Fixes: ffd980f976e7 ("[CAN]: Add broadcast manager (bcm) protocol")

description: .A flaw was found in the CAN BCM networking protocol in the Linux kernel, where a local attacker can abuse a flaw in the CAN subsystem to corrupt memory, crash the system or escalate privileges. This race condition in net/can/bcm.c in the Linux kernel allows for local privilege escalation to root.

code_evidence: The rx_ops loop unregisters the CAN receive handler via can_rx_unreg()/can_rx_unregister() and immediately frees each op with bcm_remove_op() in the same iteration. Because bcm_rx_handler() runs under RCU protection and can still be executing concurrently after unregistration, freeing op here leaves a window where the callback accesses freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function lacks the synchronization (synchronize_rcu()) needed to ensure exclusive access to the shared op before releasing it, allowing an interfering concurrent callback to access freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bcm_remove_op() frees the shared op while an RCU-protected bcm_rx_handler() callback may still be running against it. Trigger: a concurrent CAN frame invokes the handler while bcm_release() unregisters and frees the op. Consequence: use-after-free of op, enabling memory corruption, crash, or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
ppp: take reference on channels netns

Let channels hold a reference on their network namespace.
Some channel types, like ppp_async and ppp_synctty, can have their
userspace controller running in a different namespace. Therefore they
can't rely on them to preclude their netns from being removed from
under them.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tput_net(pch->chan_net);', '\tpch->chan_net = NULL;']}
description: Use-after-free vulnerability in drivers/net/ppp/ppp_generic.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5.2 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory corruption and system crash, or spinlock) or possibly have unspecified other impact by removing a network namespace, related to the ppp_register_net_channel and ppp_unregister_channel functions.

code_evidence: ppp_unregister_channel dereferences pch->chan_net at line 15 via ppp_pernet(pch->chan_net) to obtain the per-net ppp_net structure, then locks and modifies pn->all_channels_lock and pch->list at lines 16-18. The function holds no reference on that network namespace, so pch->chan_net can already point to freed net_namespace memory when this code runs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The core defect is use of freed memory: the net_namespace referenced by pch->chan_net is freed before ppp_unregister_channel reads it at line 15. This matches CWE-416 rather than a mere missing-lock issue, since the lock taken at line 16 does not protect against the namespace already being deallocated.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A channel's chan_net is stored without taking a net reference, so a userspace controller in another namespace can drop the namespace while the channel remains registered. When ppp_unregister_channel later executes, ppp_pernet(pch->chan_net) dereferences the freed net_namespace, causing a use-after-free read and subsequent lock/list operations on freed memory (memory corruption or crash).

commit_msg:
Always generate DH keys for ephemeral DH cipher suites

Modified version of the commit ffaef3f15 in the master branch by Stephen
Henson. This makes the SSL_OP_SINGLE_DH_USE option a no-op and always
generates a new DH key for every handshake regardless.

CVE-2016-0701 (fix part 2 or 2)

Issue reported by Antonio Sanso

Reviewed-by: Viktor Dukhovni <viktor@openssl.org>

description: The DH_check_pub_key function in crypto/dh/dh_check.c in OpenSSL 1.0.2 before 1.0.2f does not ensure that prime numbers are appropriate for Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange, which makes it easier for remote attackers to discover a private DH exponent by making multiple handshakes with a peer that chose an inappropriate number, as demonstrated by a number in an X9.42 file.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The changed function only sets a temporary DH parameter (SSL_CTRL_SET_TMP_DH) and duplicates/generates keys locally; it contains no operation that discloses sensitive information to an unauthorized actor, so CWE-200 is not directly supported by this code.

description: The DrawDashPolygon function in MagickCore/draw.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-0 and 7.x before 7.0.1-2 mishandles calculations of certain vertices integer data, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted file.

code_evidence: At line 162 the loop checks q against max_strokes-6*BezierQuantum-360; when the bound is reached, line 164 increments max_strokes by a fixed 6*BezierQuantum+360 and lines 165-168 resize path_p and path_q to the new size. The growth is unconditional and there is no overflow check on max_strokes, so a crafted file with many vertices can drive max_strokes past its size_t range, wrap, and shrink the allocation while q continues to advance through later writes at lines 182-183, 231-241 and 243.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe write outside the intended path_p/path_q bounds caused by unchecked size arithmetic is exactly an improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer, matching CWE-119. A related integer-overflow label would name the precursor, but the demonstrated consequence is the out-of-bounds memory operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size_t max_strokes growth at line 164 is not checked for integer overflow before ResizeQuantumMemory uses it. Trigger: a crafted drawing whose vertex count forces repeated growth. Consequence: after wraparound the buffers are under-allocated while q/p keep indexing, producing out-of-bounds writes and a crash (buffer overflow).

description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability in Michaelrsweet codedoc v.3.7 allows an attacker to cause a denial of service via the codedoc.c:1742 comppnent.

code_evidence: The loop copies each accepted character from text into the static buffer while advancing bufptr, gated by the bound check bufptr < (buffer + sizeof(buffer) - 1).
After the loop, *bufptr = '\0' writes the terminator at the current position, which is within bounds because bufptr never exceeds buffer+1023.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 requires copying input to an output buffer without verifying the input size fits. Here the loop explicitly checks the destination bound, so the classic buffer copy overflow is prevented; the patch addresses a NULL input, not a missing size check.

evidence_lines.code: *bufptr = '\0';

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a copy loop from the input text into a fixed 1024-byte static buffer; the trigger is a long input string. The bound check bufptr < (buffer + sizeof(buffer) - 1) stops copying before overflow, so the buffer is not overrun. The added NULL check prevents a NULL dereference, not a buffer copy overflow.

description: A race condition in the Linux kernel before 5.5.7 involving VT_RESIZEX could lead to a NULL pointer dereference and general protection fault.

code_evidence: The VT_RESIZEX loop checks vc_cons[i].d for NULL at line 374 before taking console_lock() at line 376, then dereferences vc_cons[i].d at lines 378, 380, 381 and 382 without re-checking it. Between the check and the lock, another thread can free or clear the console entry, so the dereference targets a NULL (or stale) pointer.

commit_msg:
ipsec: Fix aborted xfrm policy dump crash

An independent security researcher, Mohamed Ghannam, has reported
this vulnerability to Beyond Security's SecuriTeam Secure Disclosure
program.

The xfrm_dump_policy_done function expects xfrm_dump_policy to
have been called at least once or it will crash.  This can be
triggered if a dump fails because the target socket's receive
buffer is full.

This patch fixes it by using the cb->start mechanism to ensure that
the initialisation is always done regardless of the buffer situation.

Change-Id: Id41cdd41c4e43e0c3ac30c5d03c15b8046d70845
Fixes: 12a169e7d8f4 ("ipsec: Put dumpers on the dump list")
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t.start = link->start,']}
description: A vulnerability classified as problematic has been found in flar2 ElementalX up to 6.x on Nexus 9. Affected is the function xfrm_dump_policy_done of the file net/xfrm/xfrm_user.c of the component ipsec. The manipulation leads to denial of service. Upgrading to version 7.00 is able to address this issue. The name of the patch is 1df72c9f0f61304437f4f1037df03b5fb36d5a79. It is recommended to upgrade the affected component. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-217152.

code_evidence: The dump branch builds a netlink_dump_control c containing only .dump and .done, omitting .start; it then passes this control to netlink_dump_start at line 24. Without a start callback, the dump initialization that xfrm_dump_policy_done relies on is not guaranteed to run when the dump is aborted early.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers improper resource shutdown/release; here the dump's lifecycle is not properly initialized/closed on the abort path, leaving the done handler to act on an unprepared resource and crashing. This is a resource-lifecycle defect, not merely a null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dump control lacks the start callback, so initialization is deferred to the dump path and skipped when the receive buffer is full and the dump aborts. The done handler then operates on uninitialized state, causing a crash/denial of service.

commit_msg:
NFSv4: Handle case where the lookup of a directory fails

If the application sets the O_DIRECTORY flag, and tries to open a
regular file, nfs_atomic_open() will punt to doing a regular lookup.
If the server then returns a regular file, we will happily return a
file descriptor with uninitialised open state.

The fix is to return the expected ENOTDIR error in these cases.

Reported-by: Lyu Tao <tao.lyu@epfl.ch>
Fixes: 0dd2b474d0b6 ("nfs: implement i_op->atomic_open()")
Signed-off-by: Trond Myklebust <trond.myklebust@hammerspace.com>
Signed-off-by: Anna Schumaker <Anna.Schumaker@Netapp.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!res) {', '\t\tinode = d_inode(dentry);', '\t\tif ((lookup_flags & LOOKUP_DIRECTORY) && inode &&', '\t\t    !S_ISDIR(inode->i_mode))', '\t\t\tres = ERR_PTR(-ENOTDIR);', '\t} else if (!IS_ERR(res)) {', '\t\tinode = d_inode(res);', '\t\tif ((lookup_flags & LOOKUP_DIRECTORY) && inode &&', '\t\t    !S_ISDIR(inode->i_mode)) {', '\t\t\tdput(res);', '\t\t\tres = ERR_PTR(-ENOTDIR);', '\t\t}', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in fs/nfs/dir.c in the Linux kernel before 5.16.5. If an application sets the O_DIRECTORY flag, and tries to open a regular file, nfs_atomic_open() performs a regular lookup. If a regular file is found, ENOTDIR should occur, but the server instead returns uninitialized data in the file descriptor.

code_evidence: When O_DIRECTORY is set, the code sets lookup_flags = LOOKUP_OPEN|LOOKUP_DIRECTORY and jumps to no_open, which performs nfs_lookup and then finish_no_open without verifying the looked-up inode is a directory.
The no_open path returns finish_no_open(file, res) for any successful lookup result; it never rejects a regular file, so the open state tied to a non-directory is returned to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing directory-type constraint lets a successful non-directory lookup reach finish_no_open, producing a file descriptor whose open state was never initialized. That directly matches CWE-908 (use of an uninitialized resource); it is not merely a wrong error code, since the uninitialized open state is the exposed defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the O_DIRECTORY lookup path delegates to nfs_lookup and unconditionally passes the resulting dentry to finish_no_open without checking S_ISDIR. Trigger: an application opens a regular file with O_DIRECTORY and the server returns that regular file. Consequence: a file descriptor with uninitialized open state is returned instead of ENOTDIR.

commit_msg:
nbd/server: get rid of nbd_negotiate_read and friends

Functions nbd_negotiate_{read,write,drop_sync} were introduced in
1a6245a5b, when nbd_rwv (was nbd_wr_sync) was working through
qemu_co_sendv_recvv (the path is nbd_wr_sync -> qemu_co_{recv/send} ->
qemu_co_send_recv -> qemu_co_sendv_recvv), which just yields, without
setting any handlers. But starting from ff82911cd nbd_rwv (was
nbd_wr_syncv) works through qio_channel_yield() which sets handlers, so
watchers are redundant in nbd_negotiate_{read,write,drop_sync}, then,
let's just use nbd_{read,write,drop} functions.

Functions nbd_{read,write,drop} has errp parameter, which is unused in
this patch. This will be fixed later.

commit_msg:
Defend against bad PT_DYNAMIC

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/391
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
	modified:   p_lx_elf.h
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            invert_pt_dynamic(dynseg);'], 'added_lines': ['            invert_pt_dynamic(dynseg, get_te64(&phdr->p_filesz));']}
description: A heap-based buffer over-read was discovered in the acc_ua_get_be32 function in miniacc.h in UPX 4.0.0 via a crafted Mach-O file.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over e_phnum program headers and, for a PT_DYNAMIC entry, computes dynseg from check_pt_dynamic(phdr) plus file_image, then calls invert_pt_dynamic(dynseg) without passing the segment's p_filesz. The dynamic-segment walker therefore has no declared length bound for the region it reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a missing length constraint on a read loop over attacker-controlled segment data, causing reads beyond the intended buffer, which is CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. It is not merely integer overflow; the unchecked boundary is the segment size passed to the walker.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dynamic segment is traversed without a size limit derived from p_filesz, so the walker can advance past the intended dynamic array within the file image. Trigger: a crafted ELF with a PT_DYNAMIC program header whose contents are shorter than the walker expects or whose entries lack a terminating DT_NULL. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of heap memory (crash/DoS or disclosure), matching the issue's bad-PT_DYNAMIC report.

Greg Kroah-Hartman says:

====================
Raw socket cleanups

Ori Nimron pointed out that there are a number of places in the kernel
where you can create a raw socket, without having to have the
CAP_NET_RAW permission.

To resolve this, here's a short patch series to test these odd and old
protocols for this permission before allowing the creation to succeed

All patches are currently against the net tree.
====================

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!capable(CAP_NET_RAW))', '\t\treturn -EPERM;']}
description: ax25_create in net/ax25/af_ax25.c in the AF_AX25 network module in the Linux kernel 3.16 through 5.3.2 does not enforce CAP_NET_RAW, which means that unprivileged users can create a raw socket, aka CID-0614e2b73768.

code_evidence: base_sock_create accepts any socket whose type is SOCK_RAW and proceeds directly to sk_alloc and socket initialization; no capability or privilege check is performed before the socket is created and linked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function omits any authorization decision before granting access to a privileged resource (a raw socket), matching missing authorization. It is not merely a validation defect: the input is well-formed, but the required privilege check is absent.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the raw-socket creation path lacks an authorization check on the caller. Trigger: an unprivileged user requests a SOCK_RAW PF_ISDN socket. Consequence: the socket is allocated and registered, letting the caller bypass the intended privilege restriction on raw socket access.

description: GNU Tar through 1.30, when --sparse is used, mishandles file shrinkage during read access, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (infinite read loop in sparse_dump_region in sparse.c) by modifying a file that is supposed to be archived by a different user's process (e.g., a system backup running as root).

code_evidence: The while loop at line 6 advances beg by bytes_read at line 27. safe_read at line 11 returns 0 on EOF for a shrunk file; only SAFE_READ_ERROR (line 12) is handled, so a zero read is not rejected and zero_block_p on an empty buffer passes, leaving beg unchanged and looping forever.

code_evidence: zend_parse_method_parameters parses the schema source argument using the "Op" format specifier, which accepts the raw string including any embedded NUL bytes; source and source_len come directly from the caller.

In the DOM_LOAD_FILE case, source is passed to _dom_get_valid_file_path and used as a file path without checking for embedded NUL bytes; the added CHECK_NULL_PATH guard is absent in this version, so a pathname containing %00 can truncate the effective path and bypass intended filename restrictions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function fails to validate that the input pathname lacks NUL sequences before processing it as a file path. This is missing input validation of the source argument, distinct from an encoding/escaping flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accepts a caller-controlled schema source string and uses it as a filesystem path without rejecting embedded NUL bytes. Trigger: an application passes crafted input such as filename\0.html to DOMDocument schema validation. Supported consequence: the NUL truncates the path, allowing the attacker to read or write files outside the intended .html restriction.
