commit_msg:
x86/ioreq server: correctly handle bogus XEN_DMOP_{,un}map_io_range_to_ioreq_server arguments

Misbehaving device model can pass incorrect XEN_DMOP_map/
unmap_io_range_to_ioreq_server arguments, namely end < start when
specifying address range. When this happens we hit ASSERT(s <= e) in
rangeset_contains_range()/rangeset_overlaps_range() with debug builds.
Production builds will not trap right away but may misbehave later
while handling such bogus ranges.

This is XSA-238.

Signed-off-by: Vitaly Kuznetsov <vkuznets@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if ( start > end )', '        return -EINVAL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.5.x through 4.9.x allowing attackers (who control a stub domain kernel or tool stack) to cause a denial of service (host OS crash) because of a missing comparison (of range start to range end) within the DMOP map/unmap implementation.

code_evidence: hvm_unmap_io_range_from_ioreq_server accepts caller-supplied start and end addresses (lines 1-3) and proceeds directly to locking and range lookup without any comparison of start versus end.

The supplied range is passed unchecked into rangeset_contains_range(r, start, end) at line 33; only the result is used to break or continue, so an inverted range (end < start) reaches the rangeset code.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of an externally supplied input property (ordering of range bounds) before use, matching CWE-20's improper input validation. It is not a transformation or sanitization flaw; the code simply fails to reject an inconsistent start/end pair.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates that the range exists in the rangeset but never validates the basic input property that start <= end. Trigger: a misbehaving device model issues XEN_DMOP_unmap_io_range_to_ioreq_server with end < start. Consequence: the inverted range propagates into rangeset_contains_range/rangeset_remove_range, violating their start<=end assumption, which trips an assertion in debug builds and may cause host misbehavior or crash in production builds.

commit_msg:
ext4: add more paranoia checking in ext4_expand_extra_isize handling

It's possible to specify a non-zero s_want_extra_isize via debugging
option, and this can cause bad things(tm) to happen when using a file
system with an inode size of 128 bytes.

Add better checking when the file system is mounted, as well as when
we are actually doing the trying to do the inode expansion.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20191110121510.GH23325@mit.edu
Reported-by: syzbot+f8d6f8386ceacdbfff57@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Reported-by: syzbot+33d7ea72e47de3bdf4e1@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Reported-by: syzbot+44b6763edfc17144296f@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned int inode_size = EXT4_INODE_SIZE(inode->i_sb);', '\tstruct ext4_inode_info *ei = EXT4_I(inode);', '', '\t/* this was checked at iget time, but double check for good measure */', '\tif ((EXT4_GOOD_OLD_INODE_SIZE + ei->i_extra_isize > inode_size) ||', '\t    (ei->i_extra_isize & 3)) {', '\t\tEXT4_ERROR_INODE(inode, "bad extra_isize %u (inode size %u)",', '\t\t\t\t ei->i_extra_isize,', '\t\t\t\t EXT4_INODE_SIZE(inode->i_sb));', '\t\treturn -EFSCORRUPTED;', '\t}', '\tif ((new_extra_isize < ei->i_extra_isize) ||', '\t    (new_extra_isize < 4) ||', '\t    (new_extra_isize > inode_size - EXT4_GOOD_OLD_INODE_SIZE))', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;\t/* Should never happen */']}
description: The Linux kernel before 5.4.2 mishandles ext4_expand_extra_isize, as demonstrated by use-after-free errors in __ext4_expand_extra_isize and ext4_xattr_set_entry, related to fs/ext4/inode.c and fs/ext4/super.c, aka CID-4ea99936a163.

code_evidence: The function validates ext4_test_inode_state and header->h_magic before deciding whether inline xattr data exists; if either check fails it falls into the memset/state-update branch.

The memset at lines 13-15 computes the destination from EXT4_GOOD_OLD_INODE_SIZE + i_extra_isize and a length of new_extra_isize - i_extra_isize, then updates i_extra_isize without any bound check on new_extra_isize.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit's use-after-free reports arise because oversized extra_isize causes out-of-bounds writes into memory that may have been freed and reallocated, matching CWE-416's reuse of invalid memory. The missing bound check is the enabling defect, but the demonstrated consequence (write into freed/reused memory) fits the target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: new_extra_isize (and the current i_extra_isize) are used to compute a write offset and length without validating that they stay within the inode's allocated size. A malformed or attacker-influenced extra_isize can therefore drive the memset past the inode buffer, corrupting adjacent freed/reused slab memory; the corruption is the supported consequence, not a direct free in this function.

commit_msg:
Security: fix Lua cmsgpack library stack overflow.

During an auditing effort, the Apple Vulnerability Research team discovered
a critical Redis security issue affecting the Lua scripting part of Redis.

-- Description of the problem

Several years ago I merged a pull request including many small changes at
the Lua MsgPack library (that originally I authored myself). The Pull
Request entered Redis in commit 90b6337c1, in 2014.
Unfortunately one of the changes included a variadic Lua function that
lacked the check for the available Lua C stack. As a result, calling the
"pack" MsgPack library function with a large number of arguments, results
into pushing into the Lua C stack a number of new values proportional to
the number of arguments the function was called with. The pushed values,
moreover, are controlled by untrusted user input.

This in turn causes stack smashing which we believe to be exploitable,
while not very deterministic, but it is likely that an exploit could be
created targeting specific versions of Redis executables. However at its
minimum the issue results in a DoS, crashing the Redis server.

-- Versions affected

Versions greater or equal to Redis 2.8.18 are affected.

-- Reproducing

Reproduce with this (based on the original reproduction script by
Apple security team):

https://gist.github.com/antirez/82445fcbea6d9b19f97014cc6cc79f8a

-- Verification of the fix

The fix was tested in the following way:

1) I checked that the problem is no longer observable running the trigger.
2) The Lua code was analyzed to understand the stack semantics, and that
actually enough stack is allocated in all the cases of mp_pack() calls.
3) The mp_pack() function was modified in order to show exactly what items
in the stack were being set, to make sure that there is no silent overflow
even after the fix.

-- Credits

Thank you to the Apple team and to the other persons that helped me
checking the patch and coordinating this communication.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (!lua_checkstack(L, nargs))', '        return luaL_argerror(L, 0, "Too many arguments for MessagePack pack.");']}
description: Memory Corruption was discovered in the cmsgpack library in the Lua subsystem in Redis before 3.2.12, 4.x before 4.0.10, and 5.x before 5.0 RC2 because of stack-based buffer overflows.

code_evidence: nargs is derived from lua_gettop(L), i.e., the untrusted number of arguments passed to pack. The loop at lines 8-14 iterates over every argument and pushes values onto the Lua C stack via lua_pushvalue and mp_encode_lua_type, with no prior lua_checkstack(L, nargs) to reserve capacity. lua_concat(L, nargs) at line 16 then consumes nargs values from the same stack.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked argument count drives stack pushes beyond the intended buffer boundary, an out-of-bounds write. This is the memory-corruption consequence; the missing lua_checkstack is the root cause, not merely a resource-exhaustion issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the variadic function pushes a number of Lua stack values proportional to the caller-supplied argument count without reserving stack space. Trigger: calling pack with a very large number of arguments. Consequence: writes past the allocated Lua C stack, causing stack smashing, memory corruption and at minimum a server crash.

commit_msg:
avformat/hls: Check local file extensions

This reduces the attack surface of local file-system
information leaking.

It prevents the existing exploit leading to an information leak. As
well as similar hypothetical attacks.

Leaks of information from files and symlinks ending in common multimedia extensions
are still possible. But files with sensitive information like private keys and passwords
generally do not use common multimedia filename extensions.
It does not stop leaks via remote addresses in the LAN.

The existing exploit depends on a specific decoder as well.
It does appear though that the exploit should be possible with any decoder.
The problem is that as long as sensitive information gets into the decoder,
the output of the decoder becomes sensitive as well.
The only obvious solution is to prevent access to sensitive information. Or to
disable hls or possibly some of its feature. More complex solutions like
checking the path to limit access to only subdirectories of the hls path may
work as an alternative. But such solutions are fragile and tricky to implement
portably and would not stop every possible attack nor would they work with all
valid hls files.

Developers have expressed their dislike / objected to disabling hls by default as well
as disabling hls with local files. There also where objections against restricting
remote url file extensions. This here is a less robust but also lower
inconvenience solution.
It can be applied stand alone or together with other solutions.
limiting the check to local files was suggested by nevcairiel

This recommits the security fix without the author name joke which was
originally requested by Nicolas.

Found-by: Emil Lerner and Pavel Cheremushkin
Reported-by: Thierry Foucu <tfoucu@google.com>

Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!av_strstart(proto_name, "http", NULL) && !av_strstart(proto_name, "file", NULL))'], 'added_lines': ['    if (av_strstart(proto_name, "file", NULL)) {', '        if (strcmp(c->allowed_extensions, "ALL") && !av_match_ext(url, c->allowed_extensions)) {', '            av_log(s, AV_LOG_ERROR,', '                "Filename extension of \\\'%s\\\' is not a common multimedia extension, blocked for security reasons.\\n"', '                "If you wish to override this adjust allowed_extensions, you can set it to \\\'ALL\\\' to allow all\\n",', '                url);', '            return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;', '        }', '    } else if (av_strstart(proto_name, "http", NULL)) {', '        ;', '    } else', '']}
description: FFmpeg before 2.8.12, 3.0.x and 3.1.x before 3.1.9, 3.2.x before 3.2.6, and 3.3.x before 3.3.2 does not properly restrict HTTP Live Streaming filename extensions and demuxer names, which allows attackers to read arbitrary files via crafted playlist data.

code_evidence: proto_name is derived from the attacker-controlled url (including after a crypto prefix), so the scheme check operates on playlist-supplied data.
The only scheme restriction is http/file; any file: URL is accepted without validating the target path or extension, so arbitrary local paths reach the open call.
s->io_open is invoked with the unvalidated url, opening the attacker-chosen local file and feeding its contents into the demuxer/decoder pipeline.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly enables reading of arbitrary local files chosen by an unauthorized playlist author, disclosing sensitive information. That matches CWE-200's explicit exposure of sensitive information; the underlying path/extension restriction error is the means, while the supported impact is confidentiality loss.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!av_strstart(proto_name, "http", NULL) && !av_strstart(proto_name, "file", NULL))
return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: open_url permits file: URLs from crafted HLS playlist data and opens them without restricting the local path or extension. Trigger: a malicious playlist references a sensitive local file; the demuxer/decoder processes its contents. Consequence: local file contents can be exposed through parsed/decoded output, an information leak.

commit_msg: add sgpd constant_iv_size check (#1345)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tassert((ptr->constant_IV_size == 8) || (ptr->constant_IV_size == 16));'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif ((ptr->constant_IV_size != 8) && (ptr->constant_IV_size != 16)) {', '\t\t\t\tGF_LOG(GF_LOG_WARNING, GF_LOG_CONTAINER, ("[iso file] seig sample group have invalid constant_IV size\\n"));', '\t\t\t\tgf_free(ptr);', '\t\t\t\treturn NULL;', '\t\t\t}']}
description: Memory leak in the sgpd_parse_entry function in MP4Box in gpac 0.8.0 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (DoS) via a crafted input.

code_evidence: Line 60 allocates a GF_CENCSampleEncryptionGroupEntry via GF_SAFEALLOC; line 61 only returns NULL on allocation failure. In the SEIG branch, when IsProtected==1 and Per_Sample_IV_size is 0, line 69 reads an attacker-controlled constant_IV_size, and line 70 merely asserts it equals 8 or 16. Lines 71-72 then use that size for a read and byte accounting, and line 77 returns ptr without validating or releasing it on an invalid size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the allocated SEIG entry (line 60) is not released when the invalid constant_IV_size condition is detected, leaving memory unavailable for reuse. This is a missing-release path, distinct from an out-of-bounds read, which would be CWE-125.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the only constraint on constant_IV_size is an assert, which is compiled out in release builds, so malformed input with an invalid size proceeds past the check. Trigger: a crafted sgpd SEIG entry with IsProtected==1, Per_Sample_IV_size==0 and constant_IV_size other than 8/16. The allocated entry is not freed on the abnormal path, so repeated parsing leaks memory, supporting a denial of service.

commit_msg:
Replace most malloc uses with calloc

Closes #236.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    mmdb->metadata.languages.names = malloc(array_size * sizeof(char *));', '        // We assign this as we go so that if we fail a malloc and need to'], 'added_lines': ['    mmdb->metadata.languages.names = calloc(array_size, sizeof(char *));', '        // We assign this as we go so that if we fail a calloc and need to']}
description: libmaxminddb before 1.4.3 has a heap-based buffer over-read in dump_entry_data_list in maxminddb.c.

code_evidence: array_size is taken from member->entry_data.data_size and only checked for multiplication overflow before allocation.
The loop iterates i from 0 to array_size while advancing member = member->next without verifying that the linked list actually contains array_size elements.
mmdb_strndup reads member->entry_data.utf8_string for member->entry_data.data_size bytes, assuming the entry_data points to valid string data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads past the end of the intended buffer when consuming metadata-sized array elements and string lengths that are not validated against actual data. The malloc-to-calloc change addresses uninitialized memory, not this over-read, so it does not mitigate the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code trusts the declared array_size from the metadata but does not validate that the entry_data_list has that many members or that each member contains a UTF8 string of the stated length. Trigger: a crafted metadata database where data_size exceeds the actual list length or string payload, causing member->next to return a sentinel/NULL-like entry or utf8_string to point to insufficient bytes. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap read in MMDB_get_entry_data_list traversal or mmdb_strndup, matching the reported heap-based buffer over-read.

commit_msg:
USB: usbip: fix potential out-of-bounds write

Fix potential out-of-bounds write to urb->transfer_buffer
usbip handles network communication directly in the kernel. When receiving a
packet from its peer, usbip code parses headers according to protocol. As
part of this parsing urb->actual_length is filled. Since the input for
urb->actual_length comes from the network, it should be treated as untrusted.
Any entity controlling the network may put any value in the input and the
preallocated urb->transfer_buffer may not be large enough to hold the data.
Thus, the malicious entity is able to write arbitrary data to kernel memory.

Signed-off-by: Ignat Korchagin <ignat.korchagin@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (size > urb->transfer_buffer_length) {', '\t\t/* should not happen, probably malicious packet */', '\t\tif (ud->side == USBIP_STUB) {', '\t\t\tusbip_event_add(ud, SDEV_EVENT_ERROR_TCP);', '\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t\tusbip_event_add(ud, VDEV_EVENT_ERROR_TCP);', '\t\t\treturn -EPIPE;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '']}
description: The usbip_recv_xbuff function in drivers/usb/usbip/usbip_common.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5.3 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted length value in a USB/IP packet.

code_evidence: In the VDEV branch, size is taken directly from urb->actual_length, a value parsed from network input, without bounding it against urb->transfer_buffer_length.
The only check is !(size > 0); a positive size larger than the allocated transfer buffer is then passed as the length to usbip_recv, which writes into urb->transfer_buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a write into urb->transfer_buffer using an unchecked length, so the operation can exceed the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The missing size constraint is the cause; the out-of-bounds write is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the VDEV path trusts the network-supplied actual_length and uses it as the receive length without validating it against the buffer capacity. Trigger: a USB/IP peer sends a packet with a crafted length exceeding transfer_buffer_length. Consequence: usbip_recv writes past the intended transfer_buffer boundary, causing an out-of-bounds write in kernel memory.

x86/msr: Free msr_vcpu_policy during vcpu destruction

c/s 4187f79dc7 "x86/msr: introduce struct msr_vcpu_policy" introduced a
per-vcpu memory allocation, but failed to free it in the clean vcpu
destruction case.

This is XSA-253.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    xfree(v->arch.msr);', '    v->arch.msr = NULL;']}
description: In Xen 4.10, new infrastructure was introduced as part of an overhaul to how MSR emulation happens for guests. Unfortunately, one tracking structure isn't freed when a vcpu is destroyed. This allows guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (host OS memory consumption) by rebooting many times.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only frees an allocation; the described defect is a missing free causing memory-consumption DoS, which is not an out-of-bounds memory buffer operation required by CWE-119.

commit_msg:
bpf: fix sanitation of alu op with pointer / scalar type from different paths

While 979d63d50c0c ("bpf: prevent out of bounds speculation on pointer
arithmetic") took care of rejecting alu op on pointer when e.g. pointer
came from two different map values with different map properties such as
value size, Jann reported that a case was not covered yet when a given
alu op is used in both "ptr_reg += reg" and "numeric_reg += reg" from
different branches where we would incorrectly try to sanitize based
on the pointer's limit. Catch this corner case and reject the program
instead.

Fixes: 979d63d50c0c ("bpf: prevent out of bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic")
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (env->allow_ptr_leaks || BPF_SRC(insn->code) == BPF_K)', '', '\t/* If we arrived here from different branches with different', "\t * limits to sanitize, then this won't work.", '\t */', '\tif (aux->alu_state &&', '\t    (aux->alu_state != alu_state ||', '\t     aux->alu_limit != alu_limit))', '', '\t/* Corresponding fixup done in fixup_bpf_calls(). */', '\taux->alu_state = alu_state;', '\taux->alu_limit = alu_limit;', ''], 'added_lines': ['\tif (can_skip_alu_sanitation(env, insn))', '\tif (update_alu_sanitation_state(aux, alu_state, alu_limit))']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel before 4.20.6 performs undesirable out-of-bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic in various cases, including cases of different branches with different state or limits to sanitize, leading to side-channel attacks.

code_evidence: When an ALU operation on a pointer is reached, the verifier computes alu_state and alu_limit and stores them in aux. The guard only rejects if aux->alu_state is already nonzero and differs in state or limit; otherwise it overwrites aux->alu_state and aux->alu_limit with the current path's values. Because the same instruction may be reached from different branches where the register is a pointer in one and a scalar in the other, the first path's sanitation limit can be replaced, so the later fixup in fixup_bpf_calls() masks against the wrong bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an improper numeric calculation of the ALU sanitation limit/state and its associated mask, fitting CWE-189 Numeric Errors. It is not a generic logic flaw: the wrong bound is computed and then applied to pointer arithmetic.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-instruction sanitation state is overwritten instead of being checked for a pointer/scalar type mismatch across paths. Trigger: an ALU op is shared by a pointer-arithmetic branch and a numeric branch with different limits. Consequence: out-of-bounds speculative access with a mis-computed mask, enabling side-channel leakage.

commit_msg: imgcodecs: remove assert() usage

commit_msg:
Ban setting 'Object.prototype.__proto__' as Proxy to prevent circular referencing
in prototype chain.

This patch fixes #4941

JerryScript-DCO-1.0-Signed-off-by: Martin Negyokru negyokru@inf.u-szeged.hu
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      /**', "       * Prevent setting 'Object.prototype.__proto__'", '       * to avoid circular referencing in the prototype chain.', '       */', '      if (obj_p == ecma_builtin_get (ECMA_BUILTIN_ID_OBJECT_PROTOTYPE))', '      {', '        return ECMA_VALUE_FALSE;', '      }', '']}
description: There is an Assertion 'ECMA_STRING_IS_REF_EQUALS_TO_ONE (string_p)' failed at /jerry-core/ecma/base/ecma-literal-storage.c in JerryScript 3.0.0.

code_evidence: The prototype-chain walk in the while(true) loop breaks immediately when iter_p is a Proxy [34,35,36], without traversing the proxy's target/prototype, so the circularity check obj_p == iter_p [29,30,31] can be bypassed. ECMA_SET_POINTER then installs new_proto_p [41] even though the chain may be circular.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch prevents setting Object.prototype.__proto__ to a Proxy to avoid circular referencing, confirming that a reachable assertion can be triggered through this path. The assertion failure is the crash mechanism, matching CWE-617 rather than a generic logic flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop stops at a Proxy instead of resolving its prototype, so a proxy-mediated circular prototype chain is not detected. Trigger: setting a prototype whose chain reaches the object through a Proxy; the later assertion in literal storage fails, causing an abort. Consequence: reachable assertion leading to process crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
Fix failed check in Conv3DBackpropFilterV2.

Passing in a rank-0 `filter_size` causes a check fail and crash,
coming from a `filter_size.vec<>()` call.  Here we check the size
first.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 445517122
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      OP_REQUIRES(context, TensorShapeUtils::IsVector(filter_sizes.shape()),', '                  errors::InvalidArgument(', '                      "filter_sizes shape must be rank 1 but is rank ",', '                      filter_sizes.shape().dims()));']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.Conv3DBackpropFilterV2` does not fully validate the input arguments. This results in a `CHECK`-failure which can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. The code does not validate that the `filter_sizes` argument is a vector. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: The op reads the user-supplied `filter_sizes` tensor via `context->input(1)` and passes it directly to `tensor::MakeShape` without checking that it is a rank-1 vector; a rank-0 tensor therefore reaches the shape-conversion helper.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-1284 covers missing validation of an input that specifies a quantity (here a shape/size vector). The unchecked rank of `filter_sizes` is exactly such a specified-quantity validation gap; the crash is its consequence, not a separate memory-safety flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
const Tensor& filter_sizes = context->input(1);
OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, tensor::MakeShape(filter_sizes, &filter_shape));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the specified quantity `filter_sizes` is consumed without validating its rank. commit_msg: Handle image size overflow
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    data_ = new png_byte[info_.height * info_.rowbytes];', '        rowPtrs_[i] = data_ + i * info_.rowbytes;'], 'added_lines': ['    // Extend height and rowbytes from uint32_t to size_t to avoid multiplication overflow when size_t is larger', '    size_t h = info_.height;', '    size_t rb = info_.rowbytes;', '    // We need to make sure that info_.height * info_.rowbytes will not overflow size_t', "    // Unfotunately, there's no simple and portable way to do this in C++", '    // For integer division of positive numbers a * b > c <==> a > c / b holds', '    if (h > std::numeric_limits<size_t>::max() / rb) {', '        // TODO Propagate this exception to JS, and test it', '        throw std::runtime_error("Image is too large to allocate single buffer");', '    }', '    data_ = new png_byte[h * rb];', '        rowPtrs_[i] = data_ + i * rb;']}
description: An integer overflow in the PngImg::InitStorage_() function of png-img before 3.1.0 leads to an under-allocation of heap memory and subsequently an exploitable heap-based buffer overflow when loading a crafted PNG file.

code_evidence: Line 3 computes the allocation size as the product info_.height * info_.rowbytes and passes it directly to new png_byte[]; both operands come from the PNG header, so the product is attacker-influenced.
Lines 4-6 write rowPtrs_[i] = data_ + i * info_.rowbytes for each row i, indexing into the buffer using the same rowbytes-based stride, so row pointers are derived from the same arithmetic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an unchecked integer multiplication used to size a heap allocation, and the wrapped result under-allocates memory, which matches CWE-190's integer overflow/wraparound leading to memory corruption. It is the root cause; the heap overflow is a downstream consequence rather than a separate CWE.

evidence_lines.code: data_ = new png_byte[info_.height * info_.rowbytes];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the height-by-rowbytes multiplication is performed in the operand type without a pre-multiplication bound check, so a crafted PNG whose dimensions make the product wrap yields a small allocation. Trigger: loading such a PNG causes the loop to compute row offsets beyond the truncated buffer, producing a heap-based buffer overflow (out-of-bounds writes/reads).

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Reported-by: syzbot+f427adf9324b92652ccc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (fuse_is_bad(inode))', '\t\treturn -EIO;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in the FUSE filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.10.6, aka CID-5d069dbe8aaf. fuse_do_getattr() calls make_bad_inode() in inappropriate situations, causing a system crash. NOTE: the original fix for this vulnerability was incomplete, and its incompleteness is tracked as CVE-2021-28950.

code_evidence: fuse_xattr_get directly forwards to fuse_getxattr without checking whether the inode has been marked bad; the added guard (fuse_is_bad) is absent in this function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is incomplete cleanup of supporting state: the bad inode is not properly torn down and operations continue on it. CWE-459 fits because the function lacks the bad-inode check that prevents use of improperly cleaned-up inode state; this is distinct from a simple null-dereference.

evidence_lines.code: return fuse_getxattr(inode, name, value, size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function performs xattr retrieval on an inode that may have been marked bad via make_bad_inode, without verifying inode validity. Trigger: a FUSE inode whose attributes are inconsistent gets marked bad; subsequent xattr operations proceed on the live but invalid inode, allowing stale/inconsistent state to be used and contributing to dnotify structure confusion and a crash.

description: The iwmiffr_convert_row32 function in imagew-miff.c in libimageworsener.a in ImageWorsener 1.3.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read) via a crafted file.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: fix unconditional helper

Ben Hawkes says:

 In the mark_source_chains function (net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c) it
 is possible for a user-supplied ipt_entry structure to have a large
 next_offset field. This field is not bounds checked prior to writing a
 counter value at the supplied offset.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static inline bool unconditional(const struct ip6t_ip6 *ipv6)', '\treturn memcmp(ipv6, &uncond, sizeof(uncond)) == 0;'], 'added_lines': ['static inline bool unconditional(const struct ip6t_entry *e)', '\treturn e->target_offset == sizeof(struct ip6t_entry) &&', '\t       memcmp(&e->ipv6, &uncond, sizeof(uncond)) == 0;']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

code_evidence: unconditional() takes only the ip6t_ip6 sub-structure and compares it against a zeroed template with memcmp, returning true whenever the address fields are wildcarded. It performs no check of the enclosing ip6t_entry's target_offset or match layout, so a rule containing matches (e.g. -m args) but wildcard addresses is still classified as unconditional.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing constraint on target_offset/match presence lets downstream code compute an offset beyond the intended entry buffer and write outside its boundary, directly matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation; the defect is the inadequate validation in this helper, not merely an integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the helper's notion of 'unconditional' omits the requirement that the rule have no matches and a target_offset equal to sizeof(struct ip6t_entry). Trigger: a user-supplied IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE entry with wildcard addresses but a nonzero-match/target layout passes the unconditional test, so mark_source_chains proceeds to a non-existent next entry and writes a counter at an attacker-influenced next_offset. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap write (memory corruption, potential privilege escalation or DoS).

commit_msg: Fix 698920: Guard jsdtoa from integer overflow wreaking havoc.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (exp < 0) {', '\t}', '\tif (exp > maxExponent) {', '\t\texp = maxExponent;', '\t\terrno = ERANGE;'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (exp < -maxExponent) {', '\t\texp = maxExponent;', '\t\texpSign = TRUE;', '\t\terrno = ERANGE;', '\t} else if (exp > maxExponent) {', '\t\texp = maxExponent;', '\t\texpSign = FALSE;', '\t\terrno = ERANGE;', '\t} else if (exp < 0) {']}
description: The js_strtod function in jsdtoa.c in Artifex MuJS through 1.0.2 has an integer overflow because of incorrect exponent validation.

code_evidence: The exponent digits are accumulated without any bound: exp = exp * 10 + (*p - '0') inside the digit loop, so a long exponent string can wrap the signed int exp.
The wrapped value is then combined with fracExp: exp = fracExp - exp or exp = fracExp + exp, which can itself overflow or change sign.
Only after negation is the magnitude compared to maxExponent; the earlier accumulation and combination are unguarded, so the overflow has already occurred before the check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the defect is an integer wraparound in the exponent arithmetic (exp * 10 + digit and fracExp ± exp) that the later maxExponent clamp cannot prevent. This is not merely a missing range check on a parsed value; the calculation itself overflows before validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser builds the decimal exponent in a signed int with unchecked multiplication/addition and then adds fracExp before any range check. Trigger: a numeric string with an overlong exponent field. The wrapped exp then feeds the powersOf10 loop and fraction scaling, producing incorrect results and, per the commit, havoc in jsdtoa rather than a bounded ERANGE result.

description: In the Linux kernel before 3.1, an off by one in the drivers/target/loopback/tcm_loop.c tcm_loop_make_naa_tpg() function could result in at least memory corruption.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.3950: going beyond the end of the line with /\%V

Problem:    Going beyond the end of the line with /\%V.
Solution:   Check for valid column in getvcol().
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t// Special check for an empty line, which can happen on exit, when', '\t// ml_get_buf() always returns an empty string.', '\tif (*ptr == NUL)', '\t    pos->col = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\tcolnr_T i;', '', '\t// In a few cases the position can be beyond the end of the line.', '\tfor (i = 0; i < pos->col; ++i)', '\t    if (ptr[i] == NUL)', '\t    {', '\t\tpos->col = i;', '\t\tbreak;', '\t    }']}

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      bytes_per_line*sizeof(*sun_pixels));'], 'added_lines': ['      MagickMax(image->columns,bytes_per_line)*sizeof(*sun_pixels));', '    ResetMagickMemory(sun_pixels,0,height*MagickMax(image->columns,', '      bytes_per_line)*sizeof(*sun_pixels));']}
description: The ReadRLEImage function in coders/rle.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted file.

The per-pixel loops (e.g. lines 247-251 and 277-292) read *p for image->columns pixels per row, but the buffer holds only bytes_per_line bytes per row; when bytes_per_line < image->columns, reads pass the row end into adjacent rows or past the allocation.

commit_msg:
show_opcodes() is used both for dumping kernel instructions and for dumping
user instructions. If userspace causes #PF by jumping to a kernel address,
show_opcodes() can be reached with regs->ip controlled by the user,
pointing to kernel code. Make sure that userspace can't trick us into
dumping kernel memory into dmesg.

Fixes: 7cccf0725cf7 ("x86/dumpstack: Add a show_ip() function")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Reviewed-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
Reviewed-by: Borislav Petkov <bp@suse.de>
Cc: "H. Peter Anvin" <hpa@zytor.com>
Cc: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Cc: security@kernel.org
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20180828154901.112726-1-jannh@google.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tshow_opcodes((u8 *)regs->ip, loglvl);'], 'added_lines': ['\tshow_opcodes(regs, loglvl);']}
description: A missing address check in the callers of the show_opcodes() in the Linux kernel allows an attacker to dump the kernel memory at an arbitrary kernel address into the dmesg log.

code_evidence: show_ip takes a pt_regs pointer and uses regs->ip directly as the address dumped by show_opcodes at line 8; no check constrains regs->ip to a user or otherwise safe range.
Line 6 prints regs->ip via %pS, and line 8 passes the same unvalidated regs->ip as the opcode address to show_opcodes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function accepts regs->ip as input and fails to validate that it has the required property (a safe, non-kernel address range) before processing it as an opcode dump address. The disclosure is the consequence of that missing input constraint, not a separate weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
void show_ip(struct pt_regs *regs, const char *loglvl)
show_opcodes((u8 *)regs->ip, loglvl);

printk("%sRIP: %04x:%pS\n", loglvl, (int)regs->cs, (void *)regs->ip);
show_opcodes((u8 *)regs->ip, loglvl);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: regs->ip, which can be attacker-influenced when userspace faults at a kernel address, is passed to show_opcodes without validating that it is a permissible address. Trigger: a user-caused fault whose regs->ip points at kernel code. The supported consequence is disclosure of kernel memory bytes into dmesg.

This is distinct from a plain CWE-787 out-of-bounds write: the write is the consequence, while the wraparound calculation is the root cause the patch addresses by bounding the user-data count.

Inside that callee, size/index arithmetic on the payload length can wrap, so a crafted SEI payload causes an out-of-bounds write (remote code execution per the advisory) instead of a bounded copy. Root cause is the missing size/count constraint at the call site; the overflow and OOB write are the consequence.

description: In the Linux kernel before 4.12, Hisilicon Network Subsystem (HNS) does not consider the ETH_SS_PRIV_FLAGS case when retrieving sset_count data, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow and memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact, as demonstrated by incompatibility between hns_get_sset_count and ethtool_get_strings.

code_evidence: Line 4 passes Int_val(n) as the memmove byte count. Int_val truncates the OCaml value to a C int, while the string length is a long; a length above INT_MAX wraps to a small or negative count, so the length argument no longer matches the actual buffer size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the truncated length causes memmove to operate outside the intended bounds of s1/s2. This is a memory-buffer boundary violation; the underlying defect is the integer truncation, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds memory operation.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy length is converted with Int_val (int) instead of Long_val (long), truncating or sign-extending a large n. Trigger: a long string or large length passed to the copy/blit operation. Consequence: memmove uses a count inconsistent with the source/destination buffers, enabling out-of-bounds read or write (buffer overflow or information disclosure).

Add a function to check overflow when calculating metadata
data size.

description: camera/src/camera_metadata.c in the Camera service in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, 6.x before 2016-10-01, and 7.0 before 2016-10-01 allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka internal bug 30741779.

Line 6 then uses the wrapped data_bytes for the <=4 test and ALIGN_TO, producing an undersized allocation/offset that later metadata writes exceed.

size_t data_bytes = data_count *
camera_metadata_type_size[type];
return data_bytes <= 4 ? 0 : ALIGN_TO(data_bytes, DATA_ALIGNMENT);

avcodec/evc_ps: Check ref_pic_num and sps_max_dec_pic_buffering_minus1

Fixes: out of array write

Reviewed-by: James Almer <jamrial@gmail.com>

description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability in Ffmpeg before github commit 4565747056a11356210ed8edcecb920105e40b60 allows a remote attacker to achieve an out-of-array write, execute arbitrary code, and cause a denial of service (DoS) via the ref_pic_list_struct function in libavcodec/evc_ps.c

Line 5 only guards the lower path, and the loop at line 13 iterates i from 1 up to ref_pic_num, writing rpl->ref_pics[i] at line 17 for every iteration. The fixed-size ref_pics array is indexed by an unbounded count, so a large ref_pic_num writes far past the array end.

Consequence: the loop at lines 13-17 performs out-of-bounds writes into adjacent memory, corrupting state and potentially enabling code execution or a crash; the fix adds a check against sps_max_dec_pic_buffering_minus1.

commit_msg:
Fixed Error() instance dumping when "name" prop is not primitive.

Previously, njs_error_to_string2() might be invoked with error argument
pointing to vm->retval.  When "name" prop was not primitive vm->retval
might be overwritten.  As a result error pointer might be referencing a
primitive value.  In turn the second call of njs_object_property()
received an invalid object pointer because it expects only object value
types.

The fix is to ensure that error object pointer is never overwritten.

This closes #615 issue on Github.

commit_msg:
syzkaller found a reliable way to crash the host, hitting a BUG()
in __tcp_retransmit_skb()

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\ttcp_write_queue_purge(sk);']}
description: In the Linux kernel, a certain net/ipv4/tcp_output.c change, which was properly incorporated into 4.16.12, was incorrectly backported to the earlier longterm kernels, introducing a new vulnerability that was potentially more severe than the issue that was intended to be fixed by backporting. Specifically, by adding to a write queue between disconnection and re-connection, a local attacker can trigger multiple use-after-free conditions. This can result in a kernel crash, or potentially in privilege escalation. NOTE: this affects (for example) Linux distributions that use 4.9.x longterm kernels before 4.9.190 or 4.14.x longterm kernels before 4.14.139.

code_evidence: tcp_connect_init resets snd_una/snd_sml/snd_up/snd_nxt to write_seq without first purging the write queue; the fix inserts tcp_write_queue_purge(sk) just before this block. Stale skbs queued from a prior MSG_FASTOPEN connection remain when sequence state is reinitialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing purge leaves pointers to skbs/freed memory reachable through the write queue after connection state is reinitialized, so subsequent retransmit reuse references freed memory, matching CWE-416 rather than a mere logic/sequence error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on reconnect, sequence variables are reset to write_seq while the write queue still holds skbs whose sequence numbers and ownership belong to the previous connection state. Trigger: a malicious MSG_FASTOPEN path re-enters tcp_connect_init. The stale queue then conflicts with the reset sequence state, causing later retransmission paths (__tcp_retransmit_skb) to operate on freed or inconsistent skb memory, yielding use-after-free and a kernel crash.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstatic_key_enable(&sched_feat_keys[i]);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstatic_key_enable_cpuslocked(&sched_feat_keys[i]);']}
description: Race condition in the audit_log_single_execve_arg function in kernel/auditsc.c in the Linux kernel through 4.7 allows local users to bypass intended character-set restrictions or disrupt system-call auditing by changing a certain string, aka a "double fetch" vulnerability.

code_evidence: sched_feat_enable calls static_key_enable, which internally acquires cpu_hotplug_lock via cpus_read_lock while the caller may already hold the debugfs inode mutex (&sb->s_type->i_mutex_key) from sched_feat_write. The patch switches to static_key_enable_cpuslocked, assuming the CPU hotplug read lock is already held, reversing the lock order.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function participates in a lock-ordering inversion between concurrent code sequences over shared lock resources; the missing constraint is that cpu_hotplug_lock must already be held (cpuslocked variant), so CWE-362 concurrent execution with improper synchronization fits. The consequence is deadlock rather than a data race on memory, but the weakness class is the unsynchronized lock acquisition ordering.

evidence_lines.code: static_key_enable(&sched_feat_keys[i]);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: static_key_enable obtains the CPU hotplug read lock underneath the debugfs inode mutex held during sched_feat_write, creating the reverse ordering versus cpufreq registration (cpu_hotplug_lock then inode mutex). Trigger: a user writes to /sys/kernel/debug/sched_features while cpufreq_dt/OPP initialization takes the opposite order. Consequence: a circular locking dependency that lockdep flags as a possible deadlock, risking hang/instability.

containing the request has been fully parsed. Reported by Dariusz Tytko

description: OpenSSH through 7.7 is prone to a user enumeration vulnerability due to not delaying bailout for an invalid authenticating user until after the packet containing the request has been fully parsed, related to auth2-gss.c, auth2-hostbased.c, and auth2-pubkey.c.

commit_msg: libnsgif: fix oob in lzw_decode
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn LZW_BAD_CODE;', '', '\t} else if (code_new >= 1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) {', "\t\t/* Don't access out of bound */"]}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository hpjansson/chafa prior to 1.12.0.

code_evidence: Lines 20-22 validate code_new only against current_entry; the before version allowed code_new values up to current_entry without bounding them against the table size before use.
Line 44 indexes table[code_new].first_value and lines 46-51 walk code_out through table[code_out] without any check that code_new/code_out stay below the dictionary capacity (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX).
The added condition rejects code_new >= 1 << LZW_CODE_MAX, confirming that code_new can otherwise exceed the table bounds and cause out-of-bounds reads/writes on table entries.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing upper bound lets attacker-controlled codes index past the allocated dictionary, producing writes/reads outside the intended buffer, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. It is distinct from an out-of-bounds read alone because table entries are also written (lines 31-34) and traversed, corrupting adjacent memory.

evidence_lines.code:
ctx->previous_code_first = table[code_new].first_value;
ctx->previous_code = code_new;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: code_new from the LZW input stream is used to index the fixed dictionary table without enforcing an upper bound tied to table capacity, only compared to current_entry. Trigger: a crafted GIF/LZW stream yields a code at or above the table size. Consequence: out-of-bounds access to table entries, corrupting memory (heap-based buffer overflow) and enabling crash or code execution.

commit_msg: SA79000 advisory fix
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#ifdef LIBRAW_LIBRARY_BUILD', '  if(!image)', '    throw LIBRAW_EXCEPTION_IO_CORRUPT;', '#endif', '']}
description: An error within the "LibRaw::unpack()" function (src/libraw_cxx.cpp) in LibRaw versions prior to 0.18.7 can be exploited to trigger a NULL pointer dereference.

code_evidence: The function body begins with local declarations and performs no validation that the global image buffer is non-NULL before entering the decode loop.
The nested loops read pixel bytes and unconditionally write each decoded channel into image[row * width + col][c]; this dereferences the image pointer without any prior NULL check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (image) that may be NULL, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. This is not an out-of-bounds or uninitialized-memory issue; the defect is the missing NULL constraint before the store.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: kodak_c603_load_raw writes decoded samples through the global image pointer with no guard that image was allocated. Trigger: a corrupt or crafted file reaching this loader while image is NULL. Supported consequence: the dereference at the FORC3 store crashes the process (DoS).

commit_msg:
Bug 699927: don't include operator arrays in execstack output

When we transfer the contents of the execution stack into the array, take the
extra step of replacing any operator arrays on the stack with the operator
that reference them.

This prevents the contents of Postscript defined, internal only operators (those
created with .makeoperator) being exposed via execstack (and thus, via error
handling).

This necessitates a change in the resource remapping 'resource', which contains
a procedure which relies on the contents of the operators arrays being present.
As we already had internal-only variants of countexecstack and execstack
(.countexecstack and .execstack) - using those, and leaving thier operation
including the operator arrays means the procedure continues to work correctly.

Both .countexecstack and .execstack are undefined after initialization.

Also, when we store the execstack (or part thereof) for an execstackoverflow
error, make the same oparray/operator substitution as above for execstack.
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-static int
+int
 errorexec_find(i_ctx_t *i_ctx_p, ref *perror_object)
 {
     long i;
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int'], 'added_lines': ['int']}
description: Artifex Ghostscript allows attackers to bypass a sandbox protection mechanism by leveraging exposure of system operators in the saved execution stack in an error object.

code_evidence: The loop walks the execution stack via ref_stack_index. On an estack mark whose opproc is oparray_cleanup, it reads the operator index from ep[1] and, when nonzero, calls op_index_ref to place a reference to that operator object into perror_object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly places internal operator-array data into an error object that is later made accessible, which is an information-exposure/scrubbing mistake matching CWE-200 (sensitive info exposed to unauthorized actors). The commit's fix substitutes the operator for the array, confirming the array contents were the sensitive data being leaked.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: errorexec_find copies the operator array reference (oparray_cleanup mark) directly into the caller-supplied error object without substituting the operator. Trigger: an error unwinds an execution stack containing a .makeoperator-created internal operator, and the resulting error object is exposed (e.g., via error handling). Consequence: the internal operator array contents become readable, leaking system operators and enabling sandbox bypass, i.e., exposure of sensitive internal state.

description: An issue was discovered in drivers/scsi/qedi/qedi_dbg.c in the Linux kernel before 5.1.12. In the qedi_dbg_* family of functions, there is an out-of-bounds read.

code_evidence: Line 7 declares a 32-byte stack buffer nfunc; lines 8-9 zero it and then memcpy up to sizeof(nfunc)-1 (31) bytes from func regardless of func's actual length.

description: A debug function in the lua-resty-json package, up to commit id 3ef9492bd3a44d9e51301d6adc3cd1789c8f534a (merged in PR #14) contained an out of bounds access bug that could have allowed an attacker to launch a DoS if the function was used to parse untrusted input data. It is important to note that because this debug function was only used in tests and demos, it was not exploitable in a normal environment.

code_evidence: After handling a primitive type (lines 8-11), the code unconditionally casts obj to obj_composite_t* at line 12 and iterates cobj->reverse_nesting_order at line 13. For a primitive object, that field lies beyond the allocated primitive object, so the loop reads past the buffer.

Trigger: dump_obj is called with an object whose type is <= OT_LAST_PRIMITIVE. The loop dereferences reverse_nesting_order outside the primitive object's allocation, causing an out-of-bounds read that can crash the process (DoS).

commit_msg:
Security: CONFIG SET client-output-buffer-limit overflow fixed.

This commit fixes a vunlerability reported by Cory Duplantis
of Cisco Talos, see TALOS-2016-0206 for reference.

CONFIG SET client-output-buffer-limit accepts as client class "master"
which is actually only used to implement CLIENT KILL. The "master" class
has ID 3. What happens is that the global structure:

    server.client_obuf_limits[class]

Is accessed with class = 3. However it is a 3 elements array, so writing
the 4th element means to write up to 24 bytes of memory *after* the end
of the array, since the structure is defined as:

    typedef struct clientBufferLimitsConfig {
        unsigned long long hard_limit_bytes;
        unsigned long long soft_limit_bytes;
        time_t soft_limit_seconds;
    } clientBufferLimitsConfig;

EVALUATION OF IMPACT:

Checking what's past the boundaries of the array in the global
'server' structure, we find AOF state fields:

    clientBufferLimitsConfig client_obuf_limits[CLIENT_TYPE_OBUF_COUNT];
    /* AOF persistence */
    int aof_state;                  /* AOF_(ON|OFF|WAIT_REWRITE) */
    int aof_fsync;                  /* Kind of fsync() policy */
    char *aof_filename;             /* Name of the AOF file */
    int aof_no_fsync_on_rewrite;    /* Don't fsync if a rewrite is in prog. */
    int aof_rewrite_perc;           /* Rewrite AOF if % growth is > M and... */
    off_t aof_rewrite_min_size;     /* the AOF file is at least N bytes. */
    off_t aof_rewrite_base_size;    /* AOF size on latest startup or rewrite. */
    off_t aof_current_size;         /* AOF current size. */

Writing to most of these fields should be harmless and only cause problems in
Redis persistence that should not escalate to security problems.
However unfortunately writing to "aof_filename" could be potentially a
security issue depending on the access pattern.

Searching for "aof.filename" accesses in the source code returns many different
usages of the field, including using it as input for open(), logging to the
Redis log file or syslog, and calling the rename() syscall.

It looks possible that attacks could lead at least to informations
disclosure of the state and data inside Redis. However note that the
attacker must already have access to the server. But, worse than that,
it looks possible that being able to change the AOF filename can be used
to mount more powerful attacks: like overwriting random files with AOF
data (easily a potential security issue as demostrated here:
http://antirez.com/news/96), or even more subtle attacks where the
AOF filename is changed to a path were a malicious AOF file is loaded
in order to exploit other potential issues when the AOF parser is fed
with untrusted input (no known issue known currently).

The fix checks the places where the 'master' class is specifiedf in
order to access configuration data structures, and return an error in
this cases.

WHO IS AT RISK?

The "master" client class was introduced in Redis in Jul 28 2015.
Every Redis instance released past this date is not vulnerable
while all the releases after this date are. Notably:

    Redis 3.0.x is NOT vunlerable.
    Redis 3.2.x IS vulnerable.
    Redis unstable is vulnerable.

In order for the instance to be at risk, at least one of the following
conditions must be true:

    1. The attacker can access Redis remotely and is able to send
       the CONFIG SET command (often banned in managed Redis instances).

    2. The attacker is able to control the "redis.conf" file and
       can wait or trigger a server restart.

The problem was fixed 26th September 2016 in all the releases affected.

description: A buffer overflow in Redis 3.2.x prior to 3.2.4 causes arbitrary code execution when a crafted command is sent. An out of bounds write vulnerability exists in the handling of the client-output-buffer-limit option during the CONFIG SET command for the Redis data structure store. A crafted CONFIG SET command can lead to an out of bounds write potentially resulting in code execution.

code_evidence: getClientTypeByName(argv[1]) returns a client class index; only class == -1 is rejected, so the 'master' class (ID 3) passes validation.

The three writes index server.client_obuf_limits[class] with that unvalidated class; for class 3 the array has only CLIENT_TYPE_OBUF_COUNT (3) elements, so all three assignments write past the array end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function performs writes through an array index derived from attacker-influenced input without an upper-bound check, writing past the end of the intended buffer. This is a direct out-of-bounds write, not merely an integer or logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the class value from the configuration argument is not constrained to the valid buffer-limit class range before being used as an array index. Trigger: a config line (or CONFIG SET) specifying client-output-buffer-limit with class 'master' yields class 3, and the three field assignments at lines 433-435 write up to 24 bytes beyond server.client_obuf_limits, corrupting adjacent server state such as AOF fields. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds memory write, potentially modifying the AOF filename and enabling further attacks.

commit_msg:
Use copyDataProperties slow path for objects with accessors

Summary:
Fix a bug present in `hermesBuiltinCopyDataProperties`.
`hermesBuiltinCopyDataProperties` is meant to copy an object. It does
this by iterating over all the properties in the source object, and
then writing the key-value pair into a new object which is returned.The
iteration is done using `JSObject::forEachOwnPropertyWhile`, providing
a callback to process each property. It will take the property id, look
it up in the source object using `getNamedPropertyValue_RJS`, then take
that resulting value and write it into the target. However, that API
explicitly states the following:

> Obviously the callbacks shouldn't be  doing naughty things like modifying
the property map or creating new hidden classes (even implicitly)

But, `getNamedPropertyValue_RJS` can
perform arbitrary JS execution if it is a getter, including
adding/deleting new properties, which would modify the object's
HiddenClass, thus violating `JSObject::forEachOwnPropertyWhile`'s
precondition.Therefore, the fix is to use the correct, but slower path,
whenever there is an accessor on the object. This code path is more 1:1
to the spec. At the beginning, it will simply find all the properties
of the source object using `JSObject::getOwnPropertyKeys` and then
iterate on those, rather than use `JSObject::forEachOwnPropertyWhile`.
This way, we are allowed to manipulate the source object however we
wish, which is necessary in order to call `getNamedPropertyValue_RJS`.

Reviewed By: neildhar

Differential Revision: D41701871

description: An error in Hermes' algorithm for copying objects properties prior to commit a00d237346894c6067a594983be6634f4168c9ad could be used by a malicious attacker to execute arbitrary code via type confusion. Note that this is only exploitable in cases where Hermes is used to execute untrusted JavaScript. Hence, most React Native applications are not affected.

code_evidence: Function asserts the source is a Proxy and uses JSProxy accessors, so only proxy semantics are expected here.
It obtains a descriptor via JSProxy::getOwnProperty and, if enumerable, reads the value via JSProxy::getComputed, which invokes the getter and can execute arbitrary JS.
It then writes the value into target via JSObject::defineOwnComputed, asserting that CreateDataProperty succeeded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root issue is that accessor execution during property copying lets the source object change between descriptor lookup and value use, so later operations treat it as a type/shape it no longer has, matching CWE-843. It is not merely a logic bug; the mis-typed access is the confusion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The callback path reads a property value with JSProxy::getComputed while iterating/assuming proxy-only handling; a getter can mutate the source object during this access. The resulting value/descriptor assumptions are applied inconsistently to the object, allowing an object to be interpreted with an unexpected shape/type. Trigger is a malicious accessor on a copied object; supported consequence is type confusion potentially leading to arbitrary code execution.

description: Buffer Overflow in Tcpreplay v4.3.2 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service via the 'do_checksum' function in 'checksum.c'. It can be triggered by sending a crafted pcap file to the 'tcpreplay-edit' binary. This issue is different than CVE-2019-8381.

code_evidence: At [22] the IPv6 branch tests payload_len against sizeof(*ipv6) before [26] casts data to ipv6_hdr_t and dereferences it.

After the cast, [28] and [30] call get_ipv6_l4proto/get_layer4_v6 with payload_len + sizeof(ipv6_hdr_t), and [35] computes ip_hl as a pointer difference; [37] then subtracts (ip_hl - TCPR_IPV6_H) from payload_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function's insufficient bounds validation permits memory operations beyond the intended buffer boundary. The root cause is the inadequate length check and derived-length arithmetic, not merely a signed/unsigned comparison warning.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The length check at [22] validates only that the buffer holds a bare IPv6 header, but later parsing at [28]/[30] operates on payload_len + sizeof(ipv6_hdr_t) and derives ip_hl from the returned layer pointer. A crafted pcap with a truncated or inconsistent IPv6 packet can pass the check while the extended header/L4 parsing and the [37] length adjustment operate on data outside the intended buffer, yielding out-of-bounds reads and a crash (DoS).

description: GPAC version before commit 71460d72ec07df766dab0a4d52687529f3efcf0a (version v1.0.1 onwards) contains loop with unreachable exit condition ('infinite loop') vulnerability in ISOBMFF reader filter, isoffin_read.c. Function isoffin_process() can result in DoS by infinite loop. To exploit, the victim must open a specially crafted mp4 file.

code_evidence: The per-channel loop at 137 iterates while nb_pck is nonzero. nb_pck is only decremented at line 254 when ch->sample is set; otherwise the loop continues.

When ch->sample is NULL and ch->last_state is neither GF_EOS nor GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE, the else branch at 280 only sets read->force_fetch and breaks, so the exit condition is not advanced and the same channel state recurs on the next process call. The patch adds a GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE branch to terminate this path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the processing loop's termination depends on reaching a sample or an EOS/invalid-file exit that was unreachable for GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE; the added branch supplies the missing exit. This is not merely a null dereference; the defect is non-termination causing resource exhaustion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: for a channel whose last_state is GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE (not GF_EOS), no sample is produced and no EOS is signaled, so the channel is never marked ended. Trigger: opening a crafted MP4 that drives a channel into the invalid-file state. The reader repeatedly re-enters the same non-progressing path, consuming CPU indefinitely (DoS).

description: An issue was discovered in faad2 through 2.10.0. A heap-buffer-overflow exists in the function sbr_qmf_analysis_32 located in sbr_qmf.c. It allows an attacker to cause code Execution.

code_evidence: Fixed-size 1024-sample buffers spec_data1/spec_data2 are declared, so later spectral/SBR processing is bounded by 1024 elements per channel.
sbrDecodeInit is called with hDecoder->frameLength; the returned sbr[0] is used without validating frameLength against the 1024-element buffer size.

ALIGN int16_t spec_data1[1024] = {0};
ALIGN int16_t spec_data2[1024] = {0};
hDecoder->sbr[0]->ret = sbr_extension_data(&ld_sbr, hDecoder->sbr[0], count, hDecoder->postSeekResetFlag);

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. If `QuantizeDownAndShrinkRange` is given nonscalar inputs for `input_min` or `input_max`, it results in a segfault that can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 73ad1815ebcfeb7c051f9c2f7ab5024380ca8613. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. const float input_max_float = ctx->input(2).flat<float>()(0);

commit_msg:
write_wakeup can happen in parallel with close/hangup where tty->disc_data
is set to NULL and the netdevice is freed thus also freeing
disc_data. write_wakeup accesses disc_data so we must prevent close from
freeing the netdev while write_wakeup has a non-NULL view of
tty->disc_data.

We also need to make sure that accesses to disc_data are atomic. Which can
all be done with RCU.

This problem was found by Syzkaller on SLCAN, but the same issue is
reproducible with the SLIP line discipline using an LTP test based on the
Syzkaller reproducer.

A fix which didn't use RCU was posted by Hillf Danton.

Fixes: 661f7fda21b1 ("slip: Fix deadlock in write_wakeup")
Fixes: a8e83b17536a ("slcan: Port write_wakeup deadlock fix from slip")
Reported-by: syzbot+017e491ae13c0068598a@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Richard Palethorpe <rpalethorpe@suse.com>
Cc: Wolfgang Grandegger <wg@grandegger.com>

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: In the Linux kernel before 5.4.16, a race condition in tty->disc_data handling in the slip and slcan line discipline could lead to a use-after-free, aka CID-0ace17d56824. This affects drivers/net/slip/slip.c and drivers/net/can/slcan.c.

code_evidence: slip_write_wakeup reads tty->disc_data into sl and immediately dereferences it via schedule_work(&sl->tx_work) with no lock or synchronization protecting the disc_data pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses a shared resource (tty->disc_data) concurrently with another code sequence without exclusive/atomic access, which is the definition of a race condition (CWE-362); the resulting use-after-free is the consequence, not the root weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
struct slip *sl = tty->disc_data;
schedule_work(&sl->tx_work);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The pointer tty->disc_data is read without synchronization while a concurrent close/hangup path can set it to NULL and free the netdev (and thus disc_data). The unsynchronized read allows slip_write_wakeup to hold a stale, non-NULL view and dereference freed memory, giving a use-after-free race.

description: curl 7.61.0 through 7.76.1 suffers from exposure of data element to wrong session due to a mistake in the code for CURLOPT_SSL_CIPHER_LIST when libcurl is built to use the Schannel TLS library. The selected cipher set was stored in a single "static" variable in the library, which has the surprising side-effect that if an application sets up multiple concurrent transfers, the last one that sets the ciphers will accidentally control the set used by all transfers. In a worst-case scenario, this weakens transport security significantly.

code_evidence: Line 6 declares algIds as a function-local static array, so its contents persist and are shared across every call to set_ssl_ciphers rather than belonging to one transfer/session.

Lines 7,24,25 populate that shared static array from the caller-supplied cipher list and then assign it to schannel_cred->palgSupportedAlgs with count cSupportedAlgs, so one session's credential points at storage shared with other sessions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes a per-session security resource (the negotiated cipher set) to the wrong control sphere: data belonging to one transfer becomes visible/usable by another. This is CWE-668's resource-exposed-to-wrong-sphere pattern; it is not merely a memory-safety bug, since each write is in-bounds but crosses session boundaries.

evidence_lines.code: static ALG_ID algIds[45];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the selected cipher set is held in a static variable shared process-wide instead of per-connection storage. Trigger: an application runs multiple concurrent transfers and sets different CURLOPT_SSL_CIPHER_LIST values; a later call overwrites the shared array that earlier sessions still reference. Consequence: one transfer's credentials can use another transfer's cipher selection, weakening transport security for the wrong session.

commit_msg:
floppy: disable FDRAWCMD by default

Minh Yuan reported a concurrency use-after-free issue in the floppy code
between raw_cmd_ioctl and seek_interrupt.

[ It turns out this has been around, and that others have reported the
  KASAN splats over the years, but Minh Yuan had a reproducer for it and
  so gets primary credit for reporting it for this fix   - Linus ]

The problem is, this driver tends to break very easily and nowadays,
nobody is expected to use FDRAWCMD anyway since it was used to
manipulate non-standard formats.  The risk of breaking the driver is
higher than the risk presented by this race, and accessing the device
requires privileges anyway.

Let's just add a config option to completely disable this ioctl and
leave it disabled by default.  Distros shouldn't use it, and only those
running on antique hardware might need to enable it.

description: drivers/block/floppy.c in the Linux kernel before 5.17.6 is vulnerable to a denial of service, because of a concurrency use-after-free flaw after deallocating raw_cmd in the raw_cmd_ioctl function.

code_evidence: The FDRAWCMD case takes the user-supplied param, locks the floppy controller, calls set_floppy, then passes the raw user pointer to raw_cmd_ioctl. raw_cmd_ioctl builds a raw_cmd and submits it for asynchronous processing; the controller lock is released via process_fd_request before returning. The object referenced by the user-supplied param and any raw_cmd state can therefore outlive this call and be accessed later by interrupt/seek_interrupt context, with no lifetime or ownership constraint tying the request to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described defect is concurrent reuse of freed raw_cmd memory, which is exactly CWE-416 (Use After Free). It is not merely a race on shared state: the harmful operation is dereferencing memory after deallocation, matching the target weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that raw_cmd_ioctl hands a request to asynchronous controller/interrupt processing and returns after process_fd_request without ensuring the request's memory stays valid until completion. A concurrent call (e.g., a second ioctl or interrupt path such as seek_interrupt) can free or replace the raw_cmd while the interrupt handler still references it, producing a use-after-free and a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
Fix issue #27252896: Security Vulnerability -- weak binder

Sending transaction to freed BBinder through weak handle
can cause use of a (mostly) freed object.  We need to try to
safely promote to a strong reference first.

Change-Id: Ic9c6940fa824980472e94ed2dfeca52a6b0fd342
(cherry picked from commit c11146106f94e07016e8e26e4f8628f9a0c73199)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                sp<BBinder> b((BBinder*)tr.cookie);', '                error = b->transact(tr.code, buffer, &reply, tr.flags);'], 'added_lines': ['                // We only have a weak reference on the target object, so we must first try to', '                // safely acquire a strong reference before doing anything else with it.', '                if (reinterpret_cast<RefBase::weakref_type*>(', '                        tr.target.ptr)->attemptIncStrong(this)) {', '                    error = reinterpret_cast<BBinder*>(tr.cookie)->transact(tr.code, buffer,', '                            &reply, tr.flags);', '                    reinterpret_cast<BBinder*>(tr.cookie)->decStrong(this);', '                } else {', '                    error = UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION;', '                }']}
description: libs/binder/IPCThreadState.cpp in Binder in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-05-01 mishandles object references, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka internal bug 27252896.

code_evidence: At BR_TRANSACTION, tr.target.ptr is non-null, so the code constructs sp<BBinder> b from tr.cookie and immediately calls b->transact. This creates a strong reference via sp from a raw pointer without first verifying the target object is still alive; the comment in the patch confirms only a weak reference exists on the target.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper management of a security-relevant object reference (weak->strong promotion) that lets an attacker influence a privileged binder operation, fitting CWE-264's permissions/privileges management category rather than a pure memory-safety label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The target binder is held only by a weak reference, but the code promotes it to a strong reference implicitly through sp<BBinder> without an attemptIncStrong/decStrong safety check. A crafted application can cause the weak target to be freed, so transact operates on a freed BBinder, yielding use-after-free and potential privilege escalation.
