commit_msg:
Doing a "get_user_pages()" on a copy-on-write page for reading can be
ambiguous: the page can be COW'ed at any time afterwards, and the
direction of a COW event isn't defined.

Yes, whoever writes to it will generally do the COW, but if the thread
that did the get_user_pages() unmapped the page before the write (and
that could happen due to memory pressure in addition to any outright
action), the writer could also just take over the old page instead.

End result: the get_user_pages() call might result in a page pointer
that is no longer associated with the original VM, and is associated
with - and controlled by - another VM having taken it over instead.

So when doing a get_user_pages() on a COW mapping, the only really safe
thing to do would be to break the COW when getting the page, even when
only getting it for reading.

At the same time, some users simply don't even care.

For example, the perf code wants to look up the page not because it
cares about the page, but because the code simply wants to look up the
physical address of the access for informational purposes, and doesn't
really care about races when a page might be unmapped and remapped
elsewhere.

This adds logic to force a COW event by setting FOLL_WRITE on any
copy-on-write mapping when FOLL_GET (or FOLL_PIN) is used to get a page
pointer as a result.

The current semantics end up being:

 - __get_user_pages_fast(): no change. If you don't ask for a write,
   you won't break COW. You'd better know what you're doing.

 - get_user_pages_fast(): the fast-case "look it up in the page tables
   without anything getting mmap_sem" now refuses to follow a read-only
   page, since it might need COW breaking.  Which happens in the slow
   path - the fast path doesn't know if the memory might be COW or not.

 - get_user_pages() (including the slow-path fallback for gup_fast()):
   for a COW mapping, turn on FOLL_WRITE for FOLL_GET/FOLL_PIN, with
   very similar semantics to FOLL_FORCE.

If it turns out that we want finer granularity (ie "only break COW when
it might actually matter" - things like the zero page are special and
don't need to be broken) we might need to push these semantics deeper
into the lookup fault path.  So if people care enough, it's possible
that we might end up adding a new internal FOLL_BREAK_COW flag to go
with the internal FOLL_COW flag we already have for tracking "I had a
COW".

Alternatively, if it turns out that different callers might want to
explicitly control the forced COW break behavior, we might even want to
make such a flag visible to the users of get_user_pages() instead of
using the above default semantics.

But for now, this is mostly commentary on the issue (this commit message
being a lot bigger than the patch, and that patch in turn is almost all
comments), with that minimal "enable COW breaking early" logic using the
existing FOLL_WRITE behavior.

[ It might be worth noting that we've always had this ambiguity, and it
  could arguably be seen as a user-space issue.

  You only get private COW mappings that could break either way in
  situations where user space is doing cooperative things (ie fork()
  before an execve() etc), but it _is_ surprising and very subtle, and
  fork() is supposed to give you independent address spaces.

  So let's treat this as a kernel issue and make the semantics of
  get_user_pages() easier to understand. Note that obviously a true
  shared mapping will still get a page that can change under us, so this
  does _not_ mean that get_user_pages() somehow returns any "stable"
  page ]

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Tested-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Acked-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Kirill Shutemov <kirill@shutemov.name>

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.7.3, related to mm/gup.c and mm/huge_memory.c. The get_user_pages (aka gup) implementation, when used for a copy-on-write page, does not properly consider the semantics of read operations and therefore can grant unintended write access, aka CID-17839856fd58.

code_evidence: When mm == current->mm, kvmalloc_array allocates pvec and __get_user_pages_fast is called with write argument !i915_gem_object_is_readonly(obj), so a read-only object requests read-only page lookup (lines 17-26). The added comment just before line 22 warns that a read-only page may be COW-broken and give the wrong side of the COW. The function performs no locking or COW-breaking before/around this lookup.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a timing window on a shared COW page: the read-only GUP sequence lacks exclusive/atomic access, so an interfering concurrent write changes the page. This is improper synchronization over a shared resource (CWE-362). It is not merely an incorrect permission check; the defect is the concurrent COW race, as the commit describes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: read-only __get_user_pages_fast pins a copy-on-write page without breaking COW, so a concurrent writer (or unmapping/remapping under memory pressure) can take over the page after the lookup. Trigger: another thread writes or unmaps the COW page between the GUP lookup and later use. Supported consequence: the returned page is no longer associated with the original VM and is controlled by another VM, giving unintended write access/aliasing.

commit_msg:
Propagate allocation failure from ogg_sync_buffer.

Instead of segfault, report OP_EFAULT if ogg_sync_buffer returns
a null pointer. This allows more graceful recovery by the caller
in the unlikely event of a fallible ogg_malloc call.

We do check the return value elsewhere in the code, so the new
checks make the code more consistent.

Thanks to https://github.com/xiph/opusfile/issues/36 for reporting.

Signed-off-by: Timothy B. Terriberry <tterribe@xiph.org>
Signed-off-by: Mark Harris <mark.hsj@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if(OP_UNLIKELY(buffer==NULL))return OP_EFAULT;']}
description: A null pointer dereference issue was discovered in functions op_get_data and op_open1 in opusfile.c in xiph opusfile 0.9 thru 0.12 allows attackers to cause denial of service or other unspecified impacts.

code_evidence: When _initial_bytes>0, ogg_sync_buffer's return value is stored in buffer without a NULL check; line 18 immediately passes buffer to memcpy, which dereferences it. The patch adds a NULL check between lines 17 and 18, confirming the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because a pointer expected to be valid (buffer) is passed to memcpy while NULL, directly causing a NULL pointer dereference. This is a missing-check NULL dereference, not a use-after-free or out-of-bounds write, so CWE-476 is the precise Base weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the result of ogg_sync_buffer (a fallible allocation) is used without validating it against NULL. Trigger: _initial_bytes>0 and ogg_sync_buffer returns NULL on allocation failure. Consequence: memcpy dereferences the NULL buffer, causing a crash/denial of service rather than a graceful OP_EFAULT return.

commit_msg:
drm/nouveau/mmu: add more general vmm free/node handling functions

Aside from being a nice cleanup, these will to allow the upcoming direct
page mapping interfaces to play nicely with normal mappings.

Signed-off-by: Ben Skeggs <bskeggs@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\trb_erase(&vma->tree, &vmm->root);'], 'added_lines': ['\tnvkm_vmm_node_remove(vmm, vma);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s nouveau driver in how a user triggers a memory overflow that causes the nvkm_vma_tail function to fail. This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: Two do/while loops traverse sibling nodes via node(next,next) and node(vma,next), dereferencing next->part, next->memory, next->refd and next->size while accumulating size and unmapping regions.
After traversal, rb_erase removes vma from vmm->root and the code resets vma->page, refd, used and user before nvkm_vmm_put_region(vmm, vma), which returns the node to the free list.
The traversal and unmapping operate on nodes that may already have been freed and reused elsewhere in the tree, so the dereferences and the final rb_erase act on stale memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function references and erases VMA nodes after they may have been freed and reallocated, matching CWE-416 use-after-free; it is not merely an out-of-bounds or double-free because the stale pointer is dereferenced and used in tree operations.

evidence_lines.code:
while ((next = node(next, next)) && next->part &&
(next->memory != NULL) == map &&
(next->refd == refd))
size += next->size;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the free path traverses and mutates VMA nodes without verifying they are still allocated, and node()/rb_erase can touch memory already returned to the free list. Trigger: a local user frees or merges VMAs such that a traversal reaches a freed node; the subsequent dereferences or rb_erase of vma corrupt freed memory, causing a crash or potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
ipv6: Use result arg in fib_lookup_arg consistently

arg.result is sometimes used as fib6_result and sometimes used to
hold the rt6_info. Add rt6_info to fib6_result and make the use
of arg.result consistent through ipv6 rules.

The rt6 entry is filled in for lookups returning a dst_entry, but not
for direct fib_lookups that just want a fib6_info.

Fixes: effda4dd97e8 ("ipv6: Pass fib6_result to fib lookups")
Signed-off-by: David Ahern <dsahern@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (arg.result)', '\t\t\treturn arg.result;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tstruct fib6_result res = {};', '\t\t\t.result = &res,', '\t\tif (res.rt6)', '\t\t\treturn &res.rt6->dst;']}
description: A flaw was found in the IPv6 module of the Linux kernel. The arg.result was not used consistently in fib6_rule_lookup, sometimes holding rt6_info and other times fib6_info. This was not accounted for in other parts of the code where rt6_info was expected unconditionally, potentially leading to a kernel panic in fib6_rule_suppress.

code_evidence: The fib_lookup_arg is initialized without setting .result, so the union/pointer field holds its default value while lookup_ptr is invoked via fib_rules_lookup.

After fib_rules_lookup, the code checks arg.result and, if non-null, returns it directly as a struct dst_entry pointer, without distinguishing whether the lookup stored a fib6_info or an rt6_info in that field.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The same arg.result memory is interpreted as one type by the lookup and as a different, incompatible type (dst_entry/rt6_info) by the caller, matching CWE-843 type confusion. This is not a simple null dereference; the flaw is incompatible interpretation of the stored pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: arg.result is treated as a dst_entry pointer regardless of what the lookup callback actually stored. Trigger: a custom IPv6 rule lookup that fills result with a fib6_info (direct fib lookup) instead of an rt6_info. The caller then returns that pointer as a dst_entry, so downstream code such as fib6_rule_suppress accesses it using the wrong type, causing a kernel panic.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Reported-by: syzbot+f427adf9324b92652ccc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (is_bad_inode(inode))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (fuse_is_bad(inode))']}
description: An issue was discovered in the FUSE filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.10.6, aka CID-5d069dbe8aaf. fuse_do_getattr() calls make_bad_inode() in inappropriate situations, causing a system crash. NOTE: the original fix for this vulnerability was incomplete, and its incompleteness is tracked as CVE-2021-28950.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only replaces is_bad_inode with fuse_is_bad in a read-iteration guard; it contains no cleanup or resource-release logic, so the incomplete-cleanup weakness described in the commit (bad-inode handling in fuse_do_getattr) is not demonstrated here.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.3611: crash when using CTRL-W f without finding a file name

Problem:    Crash when using CTRL-W f without finding a file name.
Solution:   Bail out when the file name length is zero.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['# endif', '    if (len == 0)', '\treturn NULL;', '', '# if defined(FEAT_FIND_ID) && defined(FEAT_EVAL)']}
description: vim is vulnerable to Heap-based Buffer Overflow

code_evidence: When find_file_in_path fails and FNAME_MESS is set, the code writes a NUL terminator at ptr[len] and restores it afterward. len is the caller-supplied length of ptr; nothing here bounds it against the actual allocation of ptr, and the subsequent semsg reads ptr up to that NUL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an out-of-bounds write past the end of a heap-allocated string, matching CWE-122 (heap-based buffer overflow). It is not merely a NULL-pointer or logic error, since the write itself corrupts heap memory; the missing len==0 guard is a related symptom, but the overflowing index write is the core weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ptr[len] is written without validating that len lies within the buffer backing ptr (or that len is nonzero). Trigger: a caller passes a length at or past the allocated size, or zero, so the terminator write lands outside the heap buffer; the later restore of ptr[len] repeats the out-of-bounds access. Consequence: heap memory corruption, crash, or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Prevent invalid columnPos() call in formUpdateBuffer()

Bug-Debian: https://github.com/tats/w3m/issues/89
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t    if (l == NULL)', '\t\tbreak;']}
description: w3m through 0.5.3 is prone to a NULL pointer dereference flaw in formUpdateBuffer in form.c.

code_evidence: The loop advances l via l = l->next each iteration and, when rows > 1, immediately calls columnPos(l, col) and dereferences l->linenumber without checking l.
Later in the same iteration, l->len and COLPOS(l, ...) dereference l; the pre-patch code had no NULL guard at the loop head.

if (a->start.line != a->end.line || spos > epos || epos >= l->len ||
spos < 0 || epos < 0 || COLPOS(l, epos) < col)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop walks the line list for up to form->rows iterations but never verifies that l is non-NULL before dereferencing it. Trigger: a textarea whose line list is shorter than form->rows, so l becomes NULL after the last line. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference in columnPos()/l->linenumber, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Update utfcpp to v2.3.6

Fixes #2657

Incorporates the following utfcpp patches:

1. Sass addition of `retreat`.
   https://github.com/nemtrif/utfcpp/pull/20

2. Fix for `replace_invalid` throwing on incomplete sequence at the end
   of the input.
   https://github.com/nemtrif/utfcpp/pull/21
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    throw not_enough_room();'], 'added_lines': ['                    out = utf8::append (replacement, out);', '                    start = end;', '                    break;']}
description: In LibSass prior to 3.5.5, the function handle_error in sass_context.cpp allows attackers to cause a denial-of-service resulting from a heap-based buffer over-read via a crafted sass file.

code_evidence: validate_next(start, end) advances start based on the input sequence; the NOT_ENOUGH_ROOM case is reached when the remaining bytes at start cannot form a complete sequence relative to end.

The loop condition start != end only bounds start against end, and the trail-byte skip at line 22-23 relies on validate_next having already advanced start within [start, end]; the NOT_ENOUGH_ROOM path throws instead of consuming the incomplete tail.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: validate_next can report NOT_ENOUGH_ROOM while start has been moved to a position where the incomplete trailing sequence is not properly consumed. The while loop's only guard is start != end, so the incomplete sequence at end of input is not handled, and iteration/consumption can proceed past the intended end, yielding an out-of-bounds read (heap over-read) and DoS.

commit_msg:
CVE-2020-1900

Pre-reserve object dynamic properties when unserializing
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    obj->reserveDynProps(nProp);']}
description: When unserializing an object with dynamic properties HHVM needs to pre-reserve the full size of the dynamic property array before inserting anything into it. Otherwise the array might resize, invalidating previously stored references. This pre-reservation was not occurring in HHVM prior to v4.32.3, between versions 4.33.0 and 4.56.0, 4.57.0, 4.58.0, 4.58.1, 4.59.0, 4.60.0, 4.61.0, 4.62.0.

code_evidence: When the property is dynamic (slot invalid or inaccessible), the function stores a reference/lvalue t via obj->makeDynProp(realKey.get()) at line 12, and later writes the unserialized value through that same lvalue t at line 16. The patch adds obj->reserveDynProps(nProp) before makeDynProp to pre-size the dynamic property array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The captured lvalue is a reference into the dynamic property array; if the array resizes after the reference is taken, the reference points to freed storage and is reused at line 16, matching CWE-416 Use After Free. The pre-reservation is the missing constraint that prevents the invalidation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Without pre-reserving the dynamic property array to nProp, inserting each dynamic property can cause the underlying array to reallocate. Reallocation moves the storage, so the lvalue t captured at line 12 points to freed memory; the subsequent unserializePropertyValue write at line 16 then operates on a stale reference, yielding memory corruption/crash.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13055/IS-IS: fix an Extended IS Reachability sub-TLV

In isis_print_is_reach_subtlv() one of the case blocks did not check that
the sub-TLV "V" is actually present and could over-read the input buffer.
Add a length check to fix that and remove a useless boundary check from
a loop because the boundary is tested for the full length of "V" before
the switch block.

Update one of the prior test cases as it turns out it depended on this
previously incorrect code path to make it to its own malformed structure
further down the buffer, the bugfix has changed its output.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                ND_TCHECK2(*tptr, 4);'], 'added_lines': ['            if (subl == 0)', '                break;']}
description: The ISO IS-IS parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isoclns.c:isis_print_is_reach_subtlv().

code_evidence: The BW_CONSTRAINTS case dereferences *tptr at line 53 and advances tptr at line 55 without first checking that subl (the sub-TLV length) is nonzero, so a zero-length sub-TLV causes a read of one byte beyond the provided sub-TLV buffer.

The loop at line 56 computes (subl-1)/4 and reads EXTRACT_32BITS(tptr) at line 58; the guard ND_TCHECK2(*tptr,4) at line 57 only stops on truncation, but the missing subl==0 check lets the pre-loop *tptr read occur before any valid length is established.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads *tptr without ensuring the sub-TLV length covers that byte, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read; the missing subl==0 constraint is the direct cause of reading past the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the BW_CONSTRAINTS case lacks a length check before dereferencing and incrementing tptr. Trigger: a sub-TLV with subl==0 reaches this case. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of the buffer, as reflected by the fix adding an if (subl==0) break guard.

commit_msg:
can: kvaser_usb: kvaser_usb_leaf: Fix some info-leaks to USB devices

Uninitialized Kernel memory can leak to USB devices.

Fix this by using kzalloc() instead of kmalloc().

Signed-off-by: Xiaolong Huang <butterflyhuangxx@gmail.com>
Fixes: 7259124eac7d ("can: kvaser_usb: Split driver into kvaser_usb_core.c and kvaser_usb_leaf.c")
Cc: linux-stable <stable@vger.kernel.org> # >= v4.19
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcmd = kmalloc(sizeof(*cmd), GFP_KERNEL);'], 'added_lines': ['\tcmd = kzalloc(sizeof(*cmd), GFP_KERNEL);']}
description: In the Linux kernel through 5.4.6, there are information leaks of uninitialized memory to a USB device in the drivers/net/can/usb/kvaser_usb/kvaser_usb_leaf.c driver, aka CID-da2311a6385c.

code_evidence: cmd is allocated with kmalloc, which does not zero the buffer. Only id, len, tid, channel and ctrl_mode are assigned; the remaining bytes of struct kvaser_cmd (including any padding or unused union members) stay uninitialized. kvaser_usb_send_cmd then transmits cmd->len bytes, so those uninitialized bytes are sent to the USB device.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the function uses and transmits a resource (the cmd buffer) whose contents were never initialized. It is not a simple out-of-bounds read: the leak comes from uninitialized memory being passed to kvaser_usb_send_cmd.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an uninitialized heap buffer sent over USB: kmalloc returns stale memory and the code writes only some fields before sending the full cmd->len. Trigger is calling kvaser_usb_leaf_set_opt_mode, which reaches kvaser_usb_send_cmd with the partially initialized struct. Consequence is disclosure of kernel heap contents to the USB device (information leak).

commit_msg: Add check after call strtok_r
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ((*portmap = ports2PORT(substr)) == NULL) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (substr == NULL || (*portmap = ports2PORT(substr)) == NULL) {']}
description: An issue found in TCPprep v.4.4.3 allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via the macinstring function.

code_evidence: Line 6 asserts the caller-supplied pointer ourstr is non-NULL. Line 8 calls strtok_r(ourstrcpy, ",", &token); if the input contains no comma or is empty, strtok_r returns NULL. Line 9 passes that NULL substr into ports2PORT without any NULL check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because the function relies on the reachable assert(ourstr) at line 6 as its only guard, and the unvalidated strtok_r result at lines 8-9 exposes a reachable failure path from attacker input that terminates processing; the fix adds an explicit NULL check rather than a new assertion, confirming the abort/DoS nature of the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the result of strtok_r is used without validating it against NULL. Trigger: attacker-controlled input passed to parse_portmap that yields a NULL token from strtok_r. Supported consequence: a NULL pointer is propagated into ports2PORT, and the missing check (added in the patch) indicates a crash/abort condition reachable from remote input, i.e., denial of service.

commit_msg:
settings: Add support for defaults to keyfile backend

Stacked databases and locks are dconf features that allow
management software like Fleet Commander to set system-wide
defaults and overrides centrally for applications.

This patch adds minimal support for the same to the keyfile
backend. We look for a keyfile named 'defaults' and a
lock-list named 'locks'.

Suitable files can be produced from a dconf database with
dconf dump and dconf list-locks, respectively.

The default location for these files is /etc/glib-2.0/settings/.
For test purposes, this can be overwritten with the
GSETTINGS_DEFAULTS_DIR environment variable.

Writes always go to the per-user keyfile.

commit_msg:
Fix a null pointer exception caused by branching on uninitialized data.

This is due to not checking that the params for the quantization exists. If there is no quantization, we should not access the `.params` field.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 385173491
Change-Id: I8fc476c4b274fdb21ba741caa0fbc6d1b8840663
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, filter->quantization.type != kTfLiteNoQuantization);', '    TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, filter->quantization.type != kTfLiteNoQuantization);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions all TFLite operations that use quantization can be made to use unitialized values. [For example](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/depthwise_conv.cc#L198-L200). The issue stems from the fact that `quantization.params` is only valid if `quantization.type` is different that `kTfLiteNoQuantization`. However, these checks are missing in large parts of the code. We have patched the issue in GitHub commits 537bc7c723439b9194a358f64d871dd326c18887, 4a91f2069f7145aab6ba2d8cfe41be8a110c18a5 and 8933b8a21280696ab119b63263babdb54c298538. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: In the non-float branch, only quantization.type is compared to kTfLiteAffineQuantization before filter->quantization.params is reinterpret_cast and dereferenced via affine_quantization->scale.
In the hybrid branch, filter->quantization.params is reinterpret_cast directly with no check on quantization.type, then affine_quantization->scale is accessed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the function uses a resource (quantization.params) that was never initialized when quantization.type is kTfLiteNoQuantization. This is a use-of-uninitialized-resource defect, not merely a missing null check; the missing type guard is the constraint whose absence exposes the uninitialized field.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code reads filter->quantization.params without first ensuring the quantization type is not kTfLiteNoQuantization, so params may be uninitialized. Trigger: a TFLite model supplies a depthwise-conv filter tensor whose quantization.type is kTfLiteNoQuantization. Consequence: the cast pointer and subsequent scale access operate on uninitialized data, causing a crash or invalid read.

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e

commit_msg:
net: stellaris_enet: check packet length against receive buffer

When receiving packets over Stellaris ethernet controller, it
uses receive buffer of size 2048 bytes. In case the controller
accepts large(MTU) packets, it could lead to memory corruption.
Add check to avoid it.

Reported-by: Oleksandr Bazhaniuk <oleksandr.bazhaniuk@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Message-id: 1460095428-22698-1-git-send-email-ppandit@redhat.com
Reviewed-by: Peter Maydell <peter.maydell@linaro.org>
Signed-off-by: Peter Maydell <peter.maydell@linaro.org>

description: Buffer overflow in the stellaris_enet_receive function in hw/net/stellaris_enet.c in QEMU, when the Stellaris ethernet controller is configured to accept large packets, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (QEMU crash) via a large packet.

code_evidence: The packet length size is stored into s->rx[n].len and then used directly as the copy length for memcpy(p, buf, size) into s->rx[n].data, with no bound check on size against the destination buffer capacity.
After the copy, the code writes CRC bytes and padding at p (advanced by size), so an oversized size also pushes these trailing writes past the end of rx[n].data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the function performs a buffer copy (memcpy) of input buf of length size into a fixed destination without checking input size against the destination, producing an out-of-bounds write; this is a classic buffer-copy overflow, not merely an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled packet size is copied into the fixed-size receive buffer without validating that it fits. Trigger: a large packet accepted by the controller makes memcpy and the subsequent CRC/padding writes exceed rx[n].data, corrupting adjacent memory and causing a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
HID: cp2112: fix sleep-while-atomic

A recent commit fixing DMA-buffers on stack added a shared transfer
buffer protected by a spinlock. This is broken as the USB HID request
callbacks can sleep. Fix this up by replacing the spinlock with a mutex.

Fixes: 1ffb3c40ffb5 ("HID: cp2112: make transfer buffers DMA capable")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>	# 4.9
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Benjamin Tissoires <benjamin.tissoires@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned long flags;', '\tspin_lock_irqsave(&dev->lock, flags);', '\tspin_unlock_irqrestore(&dev->lock, flags);'], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_lock(&dev->lock);', '\tmutex_unlock(&dev->lock);']}
description: drivers/hid/hid-cp2112.c in the Linux kernel 4.9.x before 4.9.9 uses a spinlock without considering that sleeping is possible in a USB HID request callback, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock) via unspecified vectors.

code_evidence: Line 6 declares the flags used by the irqsave locking variant; line 8 acquires dev->lock with spin_lock_irqsave before touching the shared buffer. Line 12-14 calls hid_hw_raw_request, a USB HID request callback that can sleep, while the lock is still held. Line 17 releases the lock only after that call returns.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers improper resource shutdown/release; here the spinlock resource is held and not released before the sleeping callback makes it unavailable for re-use, producing a deadlock/DoS. This is about the lock not being released, not a simple race on the buffer, so CWE-404 fits the target over a generic locking race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a spinlock is held across hid_hw_raw_request, which may sleep in the USB HID callback. Trigger: any cp2112_gpio_set call reaching the raw request. Because the lock is never released while the task sleeps, the resource (the lock) is not properly released for re-use, so other users of dev->lock can deadlock, causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Sort out big_key initialisation

big_key has two separate initialisation functions, one that registers the
key type and one that registers the crypto.  If the key type fails to
register, there's no problem if the crypto registers successfully because
there's no way to reach the crypto except through the key type.

However, if the key type registers successfully but the crypto does not,
big_key_rng and big_key_blkcipher may end up set to NULL - but the code
neither checks for this nor unregisters the big key key type.

Furthermore, since the key type is registered before the crypto, it is
theoretically possible for the kernel to try adding a big_key before the
crypto is set up, leading to the same effect.

Fix this by merging big_key_crypto_init() and big_key_init() and calling
the resulting function late.  If they're going to be encrypted, we
shouldn't be creating big_keys before we have the facilities to do the
encryption available.  The key type registration is also moved after the
crypto initialisation.

The fix also includes message printing on failure.

If the big_key type isn't correctly set up, simply doing:

	dd if=/dev/zero bs=4096 count=1 | keyctl padd big_key a @s

ought to cause an oops.

Fixes: 13100a72f40f5748a04017e0ab3df4cf27c809ef ('Security: Keys: Big keys stored encrypted')
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
cc: Peter Hlavaty <zer0mem@yahoo.com>
cc: Kirill Marinushkin <k.marinushkin@gmail.com>
cc: Artem Savkov <asavkov@redhat.com>
cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: James Morris <james.l.morris@oracle.com>

description: security/keys/big_key.c in the Linux kernel before 4.8.7 mishandles unsuccessful crypto registration in conjunction with successful key-type registration, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and panic) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted application that uses the big_key data type.

code_evidence: The function body is only `return register_key_type(&key_type_big_key);`. It registers the big_key key type unconditionally and performs no crypto (RNG/skcipher) initialisation, and it does not verify that big_key_rng or big_key_skcipher are non-NULL before the key type becomes reachable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a NULL pointer dereference of the crypto objects, matching CWE-476. The missing constraint is the ordering/validation of crypto initialisation relative to key-type registration; this is not an integer or memory-corruption issue but a NULL-dereference availability flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: key-type registration is decoupled from crypto setup, so the big_key type can be registered while the RNG/cipher globals remain NULL. Trigger: a local user adds a big_key after key-type registration succeeds but crypto registration fails or has not yet run; the encryption path then dereferences the NULL big_key_rng/big_key_skcipher, causing an oops/panic (DoS).

commit_msg:
Preemption must be disabled before enabling interrupts in do_trap
on x86_64 because the stack in use for int3 and debug is a per CPU
stack set by th IST. But 32bit does not have an IST and the stack
still belongs to the current task and there is no problem in scheduling
out the task.

Keep preemption enabled on X86_32 when enabling interrupts for
do_trap().

The name of the function is changed from preempt_conditional_sti/cli()
to conditional_sti/cli_ist(), to annotate that this function is used
when the stack is on the IST.

Cc: stable-rt@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Steven Rostedt <rostedt@goodmis.org>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>

description: The int3 handler in the Linux kernel before 3.3 relies on a per-CPU debug stack, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (stack corruption and panic) via a crafted application that triggers certain lock contention.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            fMemArray = sk_malloc_throw(fAllocCount * sizeof(T));'], 'added_lines': ['            fMemArray = sk_malloc_throw(fAllocCount, sizeof(T));']}
description: In SkSampler::Fill of SkSampler.cpp, there is a possible out of bounds write due to an integer overflow. This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation. Product: Android Versions: Android-7.0 Android-7.1.1 Android-7.1.2 Android-8.0 Android-8.1 Android ID: A-78354855

code_evidence: init asserts count and reserveCount are nonnegative and stores count in fCount, but fAllocCount is set to SkTMax(count, SkTMax(kMinHeapAllocCount, reserveCount)). Line 12 then computes fAllocCount * sizeof(T) as the allocation size, multiplying two values without any overflow check before passing the result to sk_malloc_throw.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the allocation size is the product of an attacker-influenced element count and element size, and the code assumes the product is always larger than its operands. The patch replaces this with the two-argument sk_malloc_throw, which uses saturating multiplication to reject overflow, confirming the original multiplication was the weakness rather than a separate bounds-check bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the byte-size multiplication fAllocCount * sizeof(T) is performed in the caller with no saturation or overflow guard, so a large fAllocCount can wrap to a small size. Trigger: a large count/reserveCount reaching init. Consequence: sk_malloc_throw allocates a buffer smaller than fAllocCount elements, and subsequent element writes exceed the allocation, supporting an out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
oauth2: do not blindly accept requests with a token in the Authorization headera (781)

The logic was broken because it assumed an additional call would be
performed to the auth server, which isn't the case. Per the filter
documentation, a request is only considered subsequently authenticated
if there's valid cookie that was set after the access token was received
from the auth server:

https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/http/http_filters/oauth2_filter

More info about how to validate an access token (which we don't do, per
above):

https://www.oauth.com/oauth2-servers/token-introspection-endpoint/
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7662

Also fix the fact that ee shouldn't be calling continueDecoding() after
decoder_callbacks_->encodeHeaders().

Signed-off-by: Raul Gutierrez Segales <rgs@pinterest.com>
Signed-off-by: Matt Klein <mklein@lyft.com>
Signed-off-by: Pradeep Rao <pcrao@google.com>

Note this comes after HMAC validation, so technically this', '  // header is sanitized in a way, as the validation check forces the correct Bearer Cookie value.', '  access_token_ = extractAccessToken(headers);', '  if (!access_token_.empty()) {', '    found_bearer_token_ = true;', '    finishFlow();', '    return Http::FilterHeadersStatus::Continue;', '  }', '', "  // If no access token and this isn't the callback URI, redirect to acquire credentials."], 'added_lines': ['  // Sanitize the Authorization header, since we have no way to validate its content. description: Envoy is a cloud-native high-performance proxy. In versions prior to 1.22.1 the OAuth filter implementation does not include a mechanism for validating access tokens, so by design when the HMAC signed cookie is missing a full authentication flow should be triggered. However, the current implementation assumes that access tokens are always validated thus allowing access in the presence of any access token attached to the request. Users are advised to upgrade. There is no known workaround for this issue.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function handles OAuth bearer-token acceptance and header sanitization; it contains no memory free/reuse operations or pointer lifetime issues that support CWE-416.

copy of a sosreport file in abrt problem directories, and include

commit_msg:
Open bind mount sources from the host userns

The source of the bind mount might not be accessible in a different user
namespace because a component of the source path might not be traversed
under the users and groups mapped inside the user namespace. This caused
errors such as the following:

  # time="2020-06-22T13:48:26Z" level=error msg="container_linux.go:367:
  starting container process caused: process_linux.go:459:
  container init caused: rootfs_linux.go:58:
  mounting \"/tmp/busyboxtest/source-inaccessible/dir\"
  to rootfs at \"/tmp/inaccessible\" caused:
  stat /tmp/busyboxtest/source-inaccessible/dir: permission denied"

To solve this problem, this patch performs the following:

1. in nsexec.c, it opens the source path in the host userns (so we have
   the right permissions to open it) but in the container mntns (so the
   kernel cross mntns mount check let us mount it later:
   https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v5.8/fs/namespace.c#L2312).

2. in nsexec.c, it passes the file descriptors of the source to the
   child process with SCM_RIGHTS.

3. In runc-init in Golang, it finishes the mounts while inside the
   userns even without access to the some components of the source
   paths.

Passing the fds with SCM_RIGHTS is necessary because once the child
process is in the container mntns, it is already in the container userns
so it cannot temporarily join the host mntns.

This patch uses the existing mechanism with _LIBCONTAINER_* environment
variables to pass the file descriptors from runc to runc init.

This patch uses the existing mechanism with the Netlink-style bootstrap
to pass information about the list of source mounts to nsexec.c.

Rootless containers don't use this bind mount sources fdpassing
mechanism because we can't setns() to the target mntns in a rootless
container (we don't have the privileges when we are in the host userns).

This patch takes care of using O_CLOEXEC on mount fds, and close them
early.

Fixes: #2484.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Campos <rodrigo@kinvolk.io>
Co-authored-by: Rodrigo Campos <rodrigo@kinvolk.io>

description: runc is a CLI tool for spawning and running containers on Linux according to the OCI specification. In runc, netlink is used internally as a serialization system for specifying the relevant container configuration to the `C` portion of the code (responsible for the based namespace setup of containers). In all versions of runc prior to 1.0.3, the encoder did not handle the possibility of an integer overflow in the 16-bit length field for the byte array attribute type, meaning that a large enough malicious byte array attribute could result in the length overflowing and the attribute contents being parsed as netlink messages for container configuration. This vulnerability requires the attacker to have some control over the configuration of the container and would allow the attacker to bypass the namespace restrictions of the container by simply adding their own netlink payload which disables all namespaces. The main users impacted are those who allow untrusted images with untrusted configurations to run on their machines (such as with shared cloud infrastructure). runc version 1.0.3 contains a fix for this bug. As a workaround, one may try disallowing untrusted namespace paths from your container. It should be noted that untrusted namespace paths would allow the attacker to disable namespace protections entirely even in the absence of this bug.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains only synchronization and file-descriptor passing logic; no integer arithmetic, length calculation, or allocation is performed, so CWE-190 is not supported by this code.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10. SMB2_negotiate in fs/cifs/smb2pdu.c has an out-of-bounds read because data structures are incompletely updated after a change from smb30 to smb21.

code_evidence: When the default dialect is negotiated and the server returns SMB2.1, only ses->server->ops is updated to &smb21_operations; the matching ses->server->vals remains the default (smb30) value. The SMB3.1.1 branch likewise sets only ops, leaving vals inconsistent with the negotiated dialect.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale vals/ops mismatch makes a later length computed from the wrong dialect exceed the allocated buffer, and the send path reads beyond it. This is a read past the intended buffer, matching CWE-125; the root cause is incomplete state update rather than a write, so it is not an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: after negotiation the code updates the operations pointer but not the dialect values pointer, so ops and vals describe different dialects. A later lease-context construction allocates iov_base using the smb21 ops while iov_len is sized from the stale smb30 vals, causing the send path to read past the allocated buffer. Consequence is an out-of-bounds read (KASAN slab-out-of-bounds).

This will be required when', '    // u4_total_coeff is less than u4_trailing_ones', '    WORD16 ai2_level_arr[19];', '    WORD16 *i2_level_arr = &ai2_level_arr[3];']}
description: Multiple stack-based buffer underflows in decoder/ih264d_parse_cavlc.c in mediaserver in Android 6.x before 2016-04-01 allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, aka internal bug 26399350.

code_evidence: The 4x4 level buffer is declared with only 16 WORD16 entries, but the parser indexes it with a signed counter that can go negative.

i is initialized to u4_total_coeff - 1; when trailing-ones decoding runs, the loop while(u4_cnt--) writes i2_level_arr[i--] for each trailing one, so i can fall below 0 when u4_trailing_ones exceeds u4_total_coeff.
The later level-decode path guards only with if(i >= 0) and while(i >= 0), but the trailing-ones writes at line 28 are unguarded, so the negative index reaches the stack array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to a stack memory buffer at an index outside its 16-element intended boundary, which is exactly the out-of-bounds memory-buffer operation described by CWE-119. The missing constraint on u4_trailing_ones versus u4_total_coeff is the cause; the underflow write is the resultant memory-buffer violation.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the level array is sized for total_coeff entries and indexed by a decrementing counter without bounding trailing_ones to total_coeff. Trigger: a crafted CAVLC bitstream where u4_trailing_ones is greater than u4_total_coeff makes i start negative and line 28 writes below i2_level_arr. Supported consequence: stack-based out-of-bounds write, corrupting adjacent stack data and enabling memory corruption or code execution.

commit_msg:
Doing a "get_user_pages()" on a copy-on-write page for reading can be
ambiguous: the page can be COW'ed at any time afterwards, and the
direction of a COW event isn't defined.

Yes, whoever writes to it will generally do the COW, but if the thread
that did the get_user_pages() unmapped the page before the write (and
that could happen due to memory pressure in addition to any outright
action), the writer could also just take over the old page instead.

End result: the get_user_pages() call might result in a page pointer
that is no longer associated with the original VM, and is associated
with - and controlled by - another VM having taken it over instead.

So when doing a get_user_pages() on a COW mapping, the only really safe
thing to do would be to break the COW when getting the page, even when
only getting it for reading.

At the same time, some users simply don't even care.

For example, the perf code wants to look up the page not because it
cares about the page, but because the code simply wants to look up the
physical address of the access for informational purposes, and doesn't
really care about races when a page might be unmapped and remapped
elsewhere.

This adds logic to force a COW event by setting FOLL_WRITE on any
copy-on-write mapping when FOLL_GET (or FOLL_PIN) is used to get a page
pointer as a result.

The current semantics end up being:

 - __get_user_pages_fast(): no change. If you don't ask for a write,
   you won't break COW. You'd better know what you're doing.

 - get_user_pages_fast(): the fast-case "look it up in the page tables
   without anything getting mmap_sem" now refuses to follow a read-only
   page, since it might need COW breaking.  Which happens in the slow
   path - the fast path doesn't know if the memory might be COW or not.

 - get_user_pages() (including the slow-path fallback for gup_fast()):
   for a COW mapping, turn on FOLL_WRITE for FOLL_GET/FOLL_PIN, with
   very similar semantics to FOLL_FORCE.

If it turns out that we want finer granularity (ie "only break COW when
it might actually matter" - things like the zero page are special and
don't need to be broken) we might need to push these semantics deeper
into the lookup fault path.  So if people care enough, it's possible
that we might end up adding a new internal FOLL_BREAK_COW flag to go
with the internal FOLL_COW flag we already have for tracking "I had a
COW".

Alternatively, if it turns out that different callers might want to
explicitly control the forced COW break behavior, we might even want to
make such a flag visible to the users of get_user_pages() instead of
using the above default semantics.

But for now, this is mostly commentary on the issue (this commit message
being a lot bigger than the patch, and that patch in turn is almost all
comments), with that minimal "enable COW breaking early" logic using the
existing FOLL_WRITE behavior.

[ It might be worth noting that we've always had this ambiguity, and it
  could arguably be seen as a user-space issue.

  You only get private COW mappings that could break either way in
  situations where user space is doing cooperative things (ie fork()
  before an execve() etc), but it _is_ surprising and very subtle, and
  fork() is supposed to give you independent address spaces.

  So let's treat this as a kernel issue and make the semantics of
  get_user_pages() easier to understand. Note that obviously a true
  shared mapping will still get a page that can change under us, so this
  does _not_ mean that get_user_pages() somehow returns any "stable"
  page ]

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn pte_write(pte) ||', '\t\t((flags & FOLL_FORCE) && (flags & FOLL_COW) && pte_dirty(pte));'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn pte_write(pte) || ((flags & FOLL_COW) && pte_dirty(pte));']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.7.3, related to mm/gup.c and mm/huge_memory.c. The get_user_pages (aka gup) implementation, when used for a copy-on-write page, does not properly consider the semantics of read operations and therefore can grant unintended write access, aka CID-17839856fd58.

code_evidence: can_follow_write_pte decides whether a PTE may be followed for writing based on pte_write(pte) or the FOLL_FORCE/FOLL_COW/dirty combination. The function takes no lock and reads the PTE state without any synchronization, so the decision can be made against a stale mapping.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The check and the subsequent page use form a check-then-act sequence over shared page-table state without exclusive access, which is a concurrent race on a shared resource (CWE-362). The weakness is the improper synchronization window, not merely a missing permission check.

evidence_lines.code:
return pte_write(pte) ||
((flags & FOLL_FORCE) && (flags & FOLL_COW) && pte_dirty(pte));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: This predicate authorizes a write-follow decision from PTE flags alone, with no serialization against a concurrent COW or unmapping event. A racing thread that changes the mapping after this check can leave get_user_pages() holding a page no longer associated with the original VM, so the page can be taken over by another address space.

commit_msg:
LDSS: Fix a read overrun in dissect_ldss_transfer.

dissect_ldss_transfer had a trivial read overrun: "line" was not
NUL-terminated, and strtol/g_ascii_strtoull will keep reading and discarding
any leading whitespace, so a malformed LDSS packet (with only whitespace
characters following the tag on a "Size:"/"Start:"/"Compression:" line) could
trigger a read overrun.

Let's replace the tvb_memdup with tvb_get_string_enc, which does some checking
of the input characters (which, it seems, must always be ASCII), and produces a
neat NUL-terminated string.

Testing Done: On Linux x64, ran "valgrind tshark -r fuzz-2018-04-23-14422.pcap"
   without the fix (to reproduce the failure), and then with the fix, and
   observed that no errors were reported anymore after the fix. 60,000 iters of
   fuzz-test with ldss_filtered.pcap as input, plus 1,000 iters under valgrind.
   Launched wireshark and opened ldss_filtered.pcap, and examined the dissection
   of the "ldss and tcp" packets; All looks good.

description: In Wireshark 2.6.0, 2.4.0 to 2.4.6, and 2.2.0 to 2.2.14, the LDSS dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-ldss.c by avoiding a buffer over-read upon encountering a missing '\0' character.

code_evidence: tvb_find_line_end returns the line length excluding the terminator; tvb_memdup copies linelen+1 bytes into a buffer that is not guaranteed to be NUL-terminated.

The copied line is passed to g_ascii_strtoull and strtol at line+6, line+7 and line+13; these functions skip leading whitespace and continue reading past the intended line when the remainder is only whitespace.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory past the allocated line buffer through the string-to-integer helpers, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The consequence is a crash/DoS rather than an out-of-bounds write, distinguishing it from CWE-787.

evidence_lines.code:
linelen = tvb_find_line_end(tvb, offset, -1, &next_offset, FALSE);
line = (guint8 *)tvb_memdup(wmem_packet_scope(), tvb, offset, linelen+1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that the packet-derived line buffer from tvb_memdup lacks a guaranteed NUL terminator. A malformed LDSS transfer line such as "Size:" followed only by whitespace causes g_ascii_strtoull/strtol to keep scanning beyond the allocated buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read and a dissector crash.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ThrowWriterException(ResourceLimitError,"MemoryAllocationFailed");'], 'added_lines': ['    {', '      if (global_colormap != (unsigned char *) NULL)', '        global_colormap=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(', '          global_colormap);', '      if (colormap != (unsigned char *) NULL)', '        colormap=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(colormap);', '      ThrowWriterException(ResourceLimitError,"MemoryAllocationFailed");', '    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in ImageMagick 7.0.7. A memory leak vulnerability was found in the function WriteGIFImage in coders/gif.c, which allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Two heap buffers are acquired: global_colormap at [40,41] and colormap at [42]. The combined NULL check at [43,44] then invokes ThrowWriterException at [45] without releasing whichever allocation succeeded, so the successful allocation's lifetime ends at the error path but is never freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because a resource (heap memory) is not released after its effective lifetime ends on the error path. This is a missing-release defect rather than CWE-476 (NULL dereference) or CWE-401 (which is a narrower memory-specific variant); the fix confirms the intended cleanup by adding RelinquishMagickMemory calls before the throw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation-failure branch exits via ThrowWriterException (a goto-based macro) without relinquishing the non-NULL buffer. Trigger: AcquireQuantumMemory fails for one of the two 768-byte requests while the other succeeds. Consequence: the surviving allocation leaks, and repeated crafted writes can exhaust memory, causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

inotify_add_watch()") forgot to call fsnotify_put_mark() with
IN_MASK_CREATE after fsnotify_find_mark()

description: In the Linux kernel through 5.0.2, the function inotify_update_existing_watch() in fs/notify/inotify/inotify_user.c neglects to call fsnotify_put_mark() with IN_MASK_CREATE after fsnotify_find_mark(), which will cause a memory leak (aka refcount leak). Trigger: a caller invokes inotify_add_watch with IN_MASK_CREATE on an inode that already has a watch for the group, repeatedly. Consequence: each call leaks one mark reference, so the mark is never freed, causing a refcount/memory leak and eventual resource exhaustion (DoS).

description: vim is vulnerable to Heap-based Buffer Overflow

code_evidence: Line 14 reads the next character with PTR2CHAR(rex.line + col + len2) without first confirming that col + len2 is within the line's NUL terminator. Line 20 then advances len2 by MB_CHAR2LEN(c2), a fixed-width macro that can step past the end when c2 is an invalid or truncated UTF-8 byte. The commit message explicitly notes reading beyond the end of the line with invalid UTF-8, and the fixed advancement logic confirms the boundary violation rather than a mere logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is advancing the scan offset with MB_CHAR2LEN(c2), which assumes a well-formed multi-byte character, while rex.line may contain an invalid UTF-8 sequence near its end. The trigger is a match attempt at such a position; the offset then passes the terminating NUL and subsequent PTR2CHAR reads out of bounds, giving an out-of-bounds heap read (the patch replaces this with utf_ptr2len for UTF-8).

After the loop, the buffer is allocated using the computed l via fxNewChunk(fxAddChunkSizes(l,1)), then the second pass copies into s.
Case '&' copies length bytes via c_memcpy(s, match->value.string, l) and advances s by l, assuming the allocation accounted for this.
Case capture copies mxStringLength(capture->value.string) bytes into s, again relying on the first-pass length being correct.

The buffer is sized with the under-counted l, then the second pass memcpy's the actual match/capture content, writing past the allocated chunk. commit_msg:
x86/spec-ctrl: Make VERW flushing runtime conditional

Currently, VERW flushing to mitigate MDS is boot time conditional per domain
type.  However, to provide mitigations for DRPW (CVE-2022-21166), we need to
conditionally use VERW based on the trustworthiness of the guest, and the
devices passed through.

Remove the PV/HVM alternatives and instead issue a VERW on the return-to-guest
path depending on the SCF_verw bit in cpuinfo spec_ctrl_flags.

Introduce spec_ctrl_init_domain() and d->arch.verw to calculate the VERW
disposition at domain creation time, and context switch the SCF_verw bit.

For now, VERW flushing is used and controlled exactly as before, but later
patches will add per-domain cases too.

No change in behaviour.

This is part of XSA-404.

Envoy can perform various types of upstream health checking. One of them uses gRPC. Envoy also has a feature which can “hold” (prevent removal) upstream hosts obtained via service discovery until configured active health checking fails. If an attacker controls an upstream host and also controls service discovery of that host (via DNS, the EDS API, etc.), an attacker can crash Envoy by forcing removal of the host from service discovery, and then failing the gRPC health check request. This will crash Envoy via a null pointer dereference. Users are advised to upgrade to resolve this vulnerability. Users unable to upgrade may disable gRPC health checking and/or replace it with a different health checking type as a mitigation.

if (!parent_.reuse_connection_ || goaway) {
client_->close();

description: RIOT 2020.04 has a buffer overflow in the base64 decoder. The decoding function base64_decode() uses an output buffer estimation function to compute the required buffer capacity and validate against the provided buffer size. The base64_estimate_decode_size() function calculates the expected decoded size with an arithmetic round-off error and does not take into account possible padding bytes. Due to this underestimation, it may be possible to craft base64 input that causes a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: The output buffer size is validated only against required_size from base64_estimate_encode_size() at lines 14-17, which is not shown to account for padding.

The encoder writes symbols at line 40 and 44, then appends '=' padding in the loop at lines 45-47, so the actual bytes written can exceed required_size while the caller-supplied *base64_out_size check already passed.

Trigger: caller provides a buffer sized to the underestimated value; the padding loop then writes past the buffer end, causing an out-of-bounds write (CWE-119 consequence).

By validating length fields from server responses, out of boundary
accesses and endless loops can be mitigated.

Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>

Line 40 allocates wire->name_len + 1 bytes and line 41 copies wire->name_len bytes, then line 42 advances ptr by ((wire->name_len + 3)/4) * 4, all driven by an unbounded server-supplied length.

commit_msg:
A race condition may occur between the .disconnect function, which
is called when the device is disconnected, and the dvb_device_open()
function, which is called when the device node is open()ed.
This results in several types of UAFs.

The root cause of this is that you use the dvb_device_open() function,
which does not implement a conditional statement
that checks 'dvbnet->exit'.

So, add 'remove_mutex` to protect 'dvbnet->exit' and use
locked_dvb_net_open() function to check 'dvbnet->exit'.

[mchehab: fix a checkpatch warning]

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-media/20221117045925.14297-3-imv4bel@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tdvbnet->dvbdev->users==1);'], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_lock(&dvbnet->remove_mutex);', '\tmutex_unlock(&dvbnet->remove_mutex);', '', '\t\t\t\tdvbnet->dvbdev->users == 1);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 6.0.9. drivers/media/dvb-core/dvb_net.c has a .disconnect versus dvb_device_open race condition that leads to a use-after-free.

code_evidence: dvb_net_release sets dvbnet->exit = 1 without synchronization, then reads dvbnet->dvbdev->users and waits for users == 1 before calling dvb_unregister_device. The patch adds remove_mutex around the exit write, showing the unguarded write and the read/wait window are the shared-state access points.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unsynchronized write to shared dvbnet->exit concurrent with open constitutes a race condition on a shared resource (CWE-362). The UAF is the downstream consequence, not a separate memory-safety label here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dvbnet->exit and the dvbdev usage state are modified/read without exclusive synchronization, so dvb_device_open can run concurrently with release. Trigger: release sets exit and waits/checks users while open proceeds; the timing window allows the device to be unregistered/freed while open still uses it, yielding use-after-free.

commit_msg:
There are multiple similar bugs implicitly introduced by the
commit c0cfa2d8a788fcf4 ("vsock: add multi-transports support") and
commit 6a2c0962105ae8ce ("vsock: prevent transport modules unloading").

The bug pattern:
 [1] vsock_sock.transport pointer is copied to a local variable,
 [2] lock_sock() is called,
 [3] the local variable is used.
VSOCK multi-transport support introduced the race condition:
vsock_sock.transport value may change between [1] and [2].

Let's copy vsock_sock.transport pointer to local variables after
the lock_sock() call.

Fixes: c0cfa2d8a788fcf4 ("vsock: add multi-transports support")
Signed-off-by: Alexander Popov <alex.popov@linux.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Garzarella <sgarzare@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Jorgen Hansen <jhansen@vmware.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210201084719.2257066-1-alex.popov@linux.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttransport = vsk->transport;'], 'added_lines': ['', '\ttransport = vsk->transport;']}
description: A local privilege escalation was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.10.13. Multiple race conditions in the AF_VSOCK implementation are caused by wrong locking in net/vmw_vsock/af_vsock.c. The race conditions were implicitly introduced in the commits that added VSOCK multi-transport support.

code_evidence: The transport pointer is read from the shared vsk->transport at line 14 before lock_sock(sk) is called at line 15, so the snapshot is taken outside the socket lock.
The cached transport is later dereferenced at lines 23, 31, 40 and 45 (get_local_cid, dgram_allow, dgram_enqueue) after the lock is acquired, but the value may already be stale.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 covers improper lock acquisition ordering that lets a shared resource change unexpectedly. Here the shared transport pointer is read outside the critical section established by lock_sock(), exactly the improper-locking pattern the target describes; the fix moves the copy after lock_sock().
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: vsk->transport is copied to a local before lock_sock() serializes access to the vsock socket state. Trigger: a concurrent thread changes vsk->transport (multi-transport support) between the copy and the lock, so the local pointer no longer matches the locked socket. Supported consequence: the sendmsg path invokes transport operations on a stale/replaced transport, giving an inconsistent resource state that can be exploited for privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Add the sanity check of the 'nr_cbufs' to avoid stack
overflow.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liq3ea@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Airlie <airlied@redhat.com>

The only bound check at line 9 ties length to 2 + nr_cbufs but does not constrain nr_cbufs itself. The loop at lines 11-12 then writes surf_handle[i] for every i < nr_cbufs, so a value above 8 writes past the stack array.

commit_msg:
Add support for mount options to restrict access to /proc/PID/
directories.  The default backward-compatible "relaxed" behaviour is left
untouched.

The first mount option is called "hidepid" and its value defines how much
info about processes we want to be available for non-owners:

hidepid=0 (default) means the old behavior - anybody may read all
world-readable /proc/PID/* files.

hidepid=1 means users may not access any /proc/<pid>/ directories, but
their own.  Sensitive files like cmdline, sched*, status are now protected
against other users.  As permission checking done in proc_pid_permission()
and files' permissions are left untouched, programs expecting specific
files' modes are not confused.

hidepid=2 means hidepid=1 plus all /proc/PID/ will be invisible to other
users.  It doesn't mean that it hides whether a process exists (it can be
learned by other means, e.g.  by kill -0 $PID), but it hides process' euid
and egid.  It compicates intruder's task of gathering info about running
processes, whether some daemon runs with elevated privileges, whether
another user runs some sensitive program, whether other users run any
program at all, etc.

gid=XXX defines a group that will be able to gather all processes' info
(as in hidepid=0 mode).  This group should be used instead of putting
nonroot user in sudoers file or something.  However, untrusted users (like
daemons, etc.) which are not supposed to monitor the tasks in the whole
system should not be added to the group.

hidepid=1 or higher is designed to restrict access to procfs files, which
might reveal some sensitive private information like precise keystrokes
timings:

http://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2011/11/05/3

hidepid=1/2 doesn't break monitoring userspace tools.  ps, top, pgrep, and
conky gracefully handle EPERM/ENOENT and behave as if the current user is
the only user running processes.  pstree shows the process subtree which
contains "pstree" process.

Note: the patch doesn't deal with setuid/setgid issues of keeping
preopened descriptors of procfs files (like
https://lkml.org/lkml/2011/2/7/368).  We rely on that the leaked
information like the scheduling counters of setuid apps doesn't threaten
anybody's privacy - only the user started the setuid program may read the
counters.

commit_msg:
xen/arm: p2m: Avoid off-by-one check on p2m->max_mapped_gfn

The code base is using inconsistently the field p2m->max_mapped_gfn.
Some of the useres expect that p2m->max_guest_gfn contain the highest
mapped GFN while others expect highest + 1.

p2m->max_guest_gfn is set as highest + 1, because of that the sanity
check on the GFN in p2m_resolved_translation_fault() and
p2m_get_entry() can be bypassed when GFN == p2m->max_guest_gfn.

p2m_get_root_pointer(p2m->max_guest_gfn) may return NULL if it is
outside of address range supported and therefore the BUG_ON() could be
hit.

The current value hold in p2m->max_mapped_gfn is inconsistent with the
expectation of the common code (see domain_get_maximum_gpfn()) and also
the documentation of the field.

Rather than changing the check in p2m_translation_fault() and
p2m_get_entry(), p2m->max_mapped_gfn is now containing the highest
mapped GFN and the callers assuming "highest + 1" are now adjusted.

Take the opportunity to use 1UL rather than 1 as page_order could
theoritically big enough to overflow a 32-bit integer.

Lastly, the documentation of the field max_guest_gfn to reflect how it
is computed.

This is part of XSA-301.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <Julien.Grall@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    end = gfn_min(end, p2m->max_mapped_gfn);'], 'added_lines': ['    end = gfn_min(end, gfn_add(p2m->max_mapped_gfn, 1));']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing ARM guest OS users to cause a denial of service via a XENMEM_add_to_physmap hypercall. p2m->max_mapped_gfn is used by the functions p2m_resolve_translation_fault() and p2m_get_entry() to sanity check guest physical frame. The rest of the code in the two functions will assume that there is a valid root table and check that with BUG_ON(). The function p2m_get_root_pointer() will ignore the unused top bits of a guest physical frame. This means that the function p2m_set_entry() will alias the frame. However, p2m->max_mapped_gfn will be updated using the original frame. It would be possible to set p2m->max_mapped_gfn high enough to cover a frame that would lead p2m_get_root_pointer() to return NULL in p2m_get_entry() and p2m_resolve_translation_fault(). Additionally, the sanity check on p2m->max_mapped_gfn is off-by-one allowing "highest mapped + 1" to be considered valid. However, p2m_get_root_pointer() will return NULL. The problem could be triggered with a specially crafted hypercall XENMEM_add_to_physmap{, _batch} followed by an access to an address (via hypercall or direct access) that passes the sanity check but cause p2m_get_root_pointer() to return NULL. A malicious guest administrator may cause a hypervisor crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS). Xen version 4.8 and newer are vulnerable. Only Arm systems are vulnerable. x86 systems are not affected.

code_evidence: Line 13 clamps the flush range end to p2m->max_mapped_gfn, but the field holds the highest mapped GFN (highest+1 semantics expected by callers). Line 15 then iterates while gfn_x(start) < gfn_x(end), so a GFN equal to max_mapped_gfn is treated as in range and p2m_get_entry is called on it at line 29.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-193 fits: the maximum bound is used as an exclusive limit without the +1 adjustment, making the accepted range one element larger than correct. This is a boundary off-by-one, not a general integer overflow or a missing authorization check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the boundary comparison uses an inclusive maximum as an exclusive end without adding one, so the range check is off by one. Trigger: a caller passing an end at or beyond max_mapped_gfn. The loop then processes one frame past the valid mapped range; p2m_get_entry may compute a root pointer from an out-of-range GFN and hit BUG_ON, crashing the hypervisor (DoS).

commit_msg:
opt_go: Tolerate unplanned server death

While debugging some experimental nbdkit code that was triggering an
assertion failure in nbdkit, I noticed a secondary failure of nbdsh
also dying from an assertion:

libnbd: debug: nbdsh: nbd_opt_go: transition: NEWSTYLE.OPT_GO.SEND -> DEAD
libnbd: debug: nbdsh: nbd_opt_go: option queued, ignoring state machine failure
nbdsh: opt.c:86: nbd_unlocked_opt_go: Assertion `nbd_internal_is_state_negotiating (get_next_state (h))' failed.

Although my trigger was from non-production nbdkit code, libnbd should
never die from an assertion failure merely because a server
disappeared at the wrong moment during an incomplete reply to
NBD_OPT_GO or NBD_OPT_INFO.  If this is assigned a CVE, a followup
patch will add mention of it in docs/libnbd-security.pod.

Fixes: bbf1c51392 (api: Give aio_opt_go a completion callback)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    assert (nbd_internal_is_state_negotiating (get_next_state (h)));'], 'added_lines': ['    assert (nbd_internal_is_state_negotiating (get_next_state (h)) ||', '            nbd_internal_is_state_dead (get_next_state (h)));']}
description: A flaw was found in libnbd 1.7.3. An assertion failure in nbd_unlocked_opt_go in ilb/opt.c may lead to denial of service.

code_evidence: When wait_for_option returns 0 with err set, the code asserts that the next state is negotiating. If the server dies mid-reply, get_next_state(h) is DEAD, so the assert fails and aborts the process instead of returning the error.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because an attacker-influenced server state reaches an assert() that terminates the application rather than handling the error. The reachable assertion, not the disconnect itself, is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the assert assumes the next state is always negotiating after an error reply, but a server disconnect during an incomplete NBD_OPT_INFO reply yields a DEAD state. Trigger: an unplanned server death at that moment reaches the assert. Consequence: process abort, i.e., denial of service.

commit_msg:
patch 9.0.2010: [security] use-after-free from buf_contents_changed()

Problem:  [security] use-after-free from buf_contents_changed()
Solution: block autocommands

Signed-off-by: Christian Brabandt <cb@256bit.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ["    // We don't want to trigger autocommands now, they may have nasty", '    // side-effects like wiping buffers', '    block_autocmds();', '    unblock_autocmds();', '']}
description: Use After Free in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to v9.0.2010.

code_evidence: aucmd_prepbuf(&aco, newbuf) switches curbuf to the temporary buffer; the only guard is a NULL check, and on failure the code wipes newbuf and returns.
The readfile and ml_get_buf/ml_get loop operate on buf and curbuf under the switched buffer context; this region is where autocommands could fire and wipe newbuf, leaving curbuf dangling.
aucmd_restbuf(&aco) then restores the previous buffer, and the safety check wipes newbuf again, so subsequent references to the freed temporary buffer can occur.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the temporary buffer can be freed by an autocommand and then reused/referenced by the still-active curbuf or the trailing wipe_buffer call. This is a lifetime/ordering flaw, not merely a NULL dereference or integer issue.

evidence_lines.code:
aucmd_restbuf(&aco);
if (curbuf != newbuf)wipe_buffer(newbuf, FALSE);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function switches to a temporary buffer but does not suspend autocommands while reading file contents into it. Triggered autocommands (e.g., BufWipeout) can free newbuf, after which curbuf or the later wipe_buffer(newbuf) reference freed memory, causing use-after-free with crash or memory corruption.
