description: In the Linux kernel before 5.0.6, there is a NULL pointer dereference in drop_sysctl_table() in fs/proc/proc_sysctl.c, related to put_links, aka CID-23da9588037e.

code_evidence: Line 3 caches header->parent into parent, which may be NULL. Line 6 guards only put_links(header), but line 8 calls start_unregistering(header) unconditionally; that callee reaches erase_header() and accesses &header->parent->root, dereferencing the NULL parent. Line 11 re-checks parent before recursing, confirming the NULL case is expected.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the defect is a missing NULL check leading to dereference of header->parent inside the unregister path; the crash trace confirms the NULL-pointer access. It is not merely a logic error, since the directly supported consequence is a NULL dereference crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: start_unregistering() is invoked even when header->parent is NULL, so erase_header() follows the NULL parent pointer. Trigger: dropping a sysctl table whose header has no parent (e.g., failed module init during br_netfilter registration). Consequence: general protection fault / kernel crash, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
linux: handle glibc cpuset allocation failures

Closes #544
CVE-2022-47022

Signed-off-by: Brice Goglin <Brice.Goglin@inria.fr>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['     if (!plinux_set)', '       return -1;']}
description: An issue was discovered in open-mpi hwloc 2.1.0 allows attackers to cause a denial of service or other unspecified impacts via glibc-cpuset in topology-linux.c.

code_evidence: CPU_ALLOC(last+1) returns a cpu_set_t pointer that can be NULL on allocation failure; the unchanged code at line 29 passes plinux_set directly to pthread_getaffinity_np without a NULL check, and the error path at 31 only executes after the call has already used the pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer it expects to be valid but which may be NULL, matching CWE-476. The fix adds the missing NULL check; this is not a use-after-free or integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the result of CPU_ALLOC is not validated before use. Trigger: glibc cpuset allocation fails and returns NULL, then pthread_getaffinity_np dereferences the NULL pointer. Supported consequence: crash/denial of service, consistent with the CVE description.

commit_msg:
Fix NULL dereference triggered via dbus (#183)

Instead of crashing, print the following warning message and ignore it
when no current view exists.
dbus should not be called when there is no document open.

** (gobby-0.5:78328): WARNING **: 10:01:05.468: No current view exists.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tg_assert(m_current_view != NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!m_current_view) {', '\t\tg_warning("No current view exists.");', '\t\treturn;', '\t}']}
description: Gobby 0.4.11 allows a NULL pointer dereference in the D-Bus handler for certain set_language calls.

code_evidence: Line 3 asserts that m_current_view is non-NULL, but g_assert is a debug check that aborts on failure rather than preventing execution; in release builds where assertions are disabled, control continues to line 4.
Lines 4-10 dereference m_current_view repeatedly through get_text_buffer(), get_session(), get_active_user() and get_undo_grouping() without any prior NULL guard.
Lines 11-21 likewise dereference m_current_view via get_text_buffer() and scroll_to_cursor_position() with no validation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences the m_current_view pointer without a genuine NULL check, matching CWE-476. The fix replaces the assert with an explicit if (!m_current_view) return guard, confirming the missing NULL constraint was the defect rather than a logic or type error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on_undo assumes m_current_view is valid and only enforces this with g_assert, which does not stop execution when assertions are compiled out. Trigger: an undo action (e.g., D-Bus-driven) while no document/view is open. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference, causing a crash (DoS) and potential memory access issues.

commit_msg:
For USB there is no separate channel being used to pass events
from firmware to the host driver and as such are passed over the
data path. In order to detect mock event messages an additional
check is needed on event subtype. This check is added conditionally
using unlikely() keyword.

Reviewed-by: Hante Meuleman <hante.meuleman@broadcom.com>
Reviewed-by: Pieter-Paul Giesberts <pieter-paul.giesberts@broadcom.com>
Reviewed-by: Franky Lin <franky.lin@broadcom.com>
Signed-off-by: Arend van Spriel <arend.vanspriel@broadcom.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tbrcmf_fweh_process_skb(ifp->drvr, skb);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tbrcmf_fweh_process_skb(ifp->drvr, skb,', '\t\t\t\t\t       BCMILCP_SUBTYPE_VENDOR_LONG);']}
description: The Broadcom brcmfmac WiFi driver prior to commit a4176ec356c73a46c07c181c6d04039fafa34a9f is vulnerable to a frame validation bypass. If the brcmfmac driver receives a firmware event frame from a remote source, the is_wlc_event_frame function will cause this frame to be discarded and unprocessed. If the driver receives the firmware event frame from the host, the appropriate handler is called. This frame validation can be bypassed if the bus used is USB (for instance by a wifi dongle). This can allow firmware event frames from a remote source to be processed. In the worst case scenario, by sending specially-crafted WiFi packets, a remote, unauthenticated attacker may be able to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable system. More typically, this vulnerability will result in denial-of-service conditions.

code_evidence: When handle_event is set, the received skb is passed to brcmf_fweh_process_skb without any event-subtype argument; the pre-fix call validates only the frame type, so a USB-delivered frame that should be discarded as a non-host event is instead processed as a firmware event and also delivered via brcmf_netif_rx.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function processes received input (skb) without validating a required property (event subtype), which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The fix adds the missing BCMILCP_SUBTYPE_VENDOR_LONG check, confirming the validation gap.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the event-frame check lacks a subtype constraint for the USB data path, so frames from a remote source are not distinguished from host-originated firmware events. Trigger: a crafted frame arriving over USB with handle_event set. Consequence: remote event frames reach the firmware-event handler, enabling DoS or possibly code execution.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13010/BEEP: Do bounds checking when comparing strings.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Brian 'geeknik' Carpenter.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['l_strnstart(const char *tstr1, u_int tl1, const char *str2, u_int l2)', ''], 'added_lines': ['l_strnstart(netdissect_options *ndo, const char *tstr1, u_int tl1,', '    const char *str2, u_int l2)', '\tif (!ND_TTEST2(*str2, tl1)) {', '\t\t/*', "\t\t * We don't have tl1 bytes worth of captured data", "\t\t * for the string, so we can't check for this", '\t\t * string.', '\t\t */', '\t\treturn 0;', '\t}']}
description: The BEEP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-beep.c:l_strnstart().

code_evidence: The guard only compares lengths: if tl1 > l2 it returns 0, otherwise it calls strncmp(tstr1, str2, tl1). It never verifies that tl1 bytes are actually captured at str2, so strncmp may read beyond the captured buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function performs a bounded comparison without confirming the source buffer holds tl1 readable bytes, causing reads past the intended buffer. A length-mismatch issue (CWE-130) is not the flaw; the missing bounds check on captured data is.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length check constrains tl1 against l2 but not against the available captured data at str2. When str2 points near the end of a truncated capture and tl1 exceeds the remaining captured bytes, strncmp reads past the buffer. The supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read (buffer over-read), potentially disclosing memory or crashing.

commit_msg: Multiplayer API now respects allow_object_decoding

description: In Godot through 3.1, remote code execution is possible due to the deserialization policy not being applied correctly.

commit_msg:
xen/rwlock: Add missing memory barrier in the unlock path of rwlock

The rwlock unlock paths are using atomic_sub() to release the lock.
However the implementation of atomic_sub() rightfully doesn't contain a
memory barrier. On Arm, this means a processor is allowed to re-order
the memory access with the preceeding access.

In other words, the unlock may be seen by another processor before all
the memory accesses within the "critical" section.

The rwlock paths already contains barrier indirectly, but they are not
very useful without the counterpart in the unlock paths.

The memory barriers are not necessary on x86 because loads/stores are
not re-ordered with lock instructions.

So add arch_lock_release_barrier() in the unlock paths that will only
add memory barrier on Arm.

Take the opportunity to document each lock paths explaining why a
barrier is not necessary.

This is XSA-314.

Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Acked-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    /*', '     * atomic_add_return() is a full barrier so no need for an', '     * arch_lock_acquire_barrier().', '     */', '    /*', '     * queue_read_lock_slowpath() is using spinlock and therefore is a', '     * full barrier. So no need for an arch_lock_acquire_barrier().', '     */']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.13.x, allowing guest OS users to cause a denial of service or possibly gain privileges because of missing memory barriers in read-write unlock paths. The read-write unlock paths don't contain a memory barrier. On Arm, this means a processor is allowed to re-order the memory access with the preceding ones. In other words, the unlock may be seen by another processor before all the memory accesses within the "critical" section. As a consequence, it may be possible to have a writer executing a critical section at the same time as readers or another writer. In other words, many of the assumptions (e.g., a variable cannot be modified after a check) in the critical sections are not safe anymore. The read-write locks are used in hypercalls (such as grant-table ones), so a malicious guest could exploit the race. For instance, there is a small window where Xen can leak memory if XENMAPSPACE_grant_table is used concurrently. A malicious guest may be able to leak memory, or cause a hypervisor crash resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leak and privilege escalation cannot be excluded.

code_evidence: preempt_disable() then atomic_add_return(_QR_BIAS, &lock->cnts) increments the reader count; the acquisition ordering relies on atomic_add_return being a full barrier, as the added comments state.
The fast path returns when _can_read_lock(cnts) succeeds; otherwise queue_read_lock_slowpath() is called, which uses a spinlock and thus provides a full barrier.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the rwlock is meant to give exclusive access to shared resources, but missing release-side ordering permits an interfering code sequence to run concurrently with a critical section, violating exclusivity and atomicity.

evidence_lines.code:
preempt_disable();
cnts = atomic_add_return(_QR_BIAS, &lock->cnts);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The acquisition side depends on atomic_add_return and the slowpath spinlock for ordering. The commit fixes the counterpart unlock path, which used atomic_sub without arch_lock_release_barrier(); on Arm, the unlock can become visible before critical-section memory accesses. That allows a writer to enter while readers or another writer still execute, violating lock exclusivity and causing races such as memory leaks or hypervisor crashes.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tGF_ItemLocationEntry *location_entry = (GF_ItemLocationEntry *)gf_malloc(sizeof(GF_ItemLocationEntry));', '\t\t\tGF_ItemExtentEntry *extent_entry = (GF_ItemExtentEntry *)gf_malloc(sizeof(GF_ItemExtentEntry));'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tGF_ItemLocationEntry *location_entry;', '\t\tGF_SAFEALLOC(location_entry, GF_ItemLocationEntry);', '\t\t\tGF_ItemExtentEntry *extent_entry;', '\t\t\tGF_SAFEALLOC(extent_entry, GF_ItemExtentEntry);']}
description: The binary MP4Box in Gpac through 1.0.1 has a double-free vulnerability in the iloc_entry_del funciton in box_code_meta.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service.

code_evidence: For each item, a GF_ItemLocationEntry is allocated with gf_malloc and immediately added to ptr->location_entries before its fields are populated; on allocation failure the function returns GF_OUT_OF_MEM.
Within each item, a GF_ItemExtentEntry is allocated with gf_malloc, added to location_entry->extent_entries, then populated; failure returns GF_OUT_OF_MEM mid-loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described defect is releasing the same heap object more than once, which is exactly CWE-415. It is not merely a missing NULL check (CWE-476) or a use-after-free (CWE-416), because the supported failure is a second free of the same address via the list ownership.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: entries are linked into the box's lists before they are fully initialized, and error exits return without unwinding. If a later read or allocation fails, the partially built entries remain owned by the box; the cleanup path (iloc_entry_del) later frees them, and a subsequent free of the same entry yields a double free. Trigger: crafted iloc input causing an allocation failure or size-underflow error after an entry was added to a list. Supported consequence: memory corruption/denial of service.

Fix oobread in the macho parser ##crash

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (sym_num > bin->nsymtab) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (sym_num >= bin->nsymtab) {']}
description: Heap buffer overflow in libr/bin/format/mach0/mach0.c in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.8.6. If address sanitizer is disabled during the compiling, the program should executes into the `r_str_ncpy` function. Therefore I think it is very likely to be exploitable. For more general description of heap buffer overflow, see [CWE](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/122.html).

code_evidence: Line 24 reads r_symbolnum from the relocation entry into sym_num. Line 25 bounds-checks it with `sym_num > bin->nsymtab`, which permits sym_num == nsymtab. Line 28 then indexes bin->symtab[sym_num], reading the symtab array one element past its valid range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through r_str_ncpy into a fixed-size buffer using data derived from an out-of-bounds symtab access, matching out-of-bounds write. The root cause is the incorrect `>` comparison instead of `>=`, an off-by-one that fails to constrain the index, aligning with CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The off-by-one check accepts sym_num equal to nsymtab, so bin->symtab[sym_num] accesses an out-of-range element; the resulting n_strx is then used by get_name, whose derived pointer feeds r_str_ncpy writing into reloc->name. Crafted relocation entries in the Mach-O file trigger this, causing an out-of-bounds read/write and potential memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Remove support for pre-authentication compression. Doing compression
early in the protocol probably seemed reasonable in the 1990s, but
today it's clearly a bad idea in terms of both cryptography (cf.
multiple compression oracle attacks in TLS) and attack surface.

Moreover, to support it across privilege-separation zlib needed
the assistance of a complex shared-memory manager that made the
required attack surface considerably larger.

Prompted by Guido Vranken pointing out a compiler-elided security
check in the shared memory manager found by Stack
(http://css.csail.mit.edu/stack/); ok deraadt@ markus@

NB. pre-auth authentication has been disabled by default in sshd
for >10 years.

description: The shared memory manager (associated with pre-authentication compression) in sshd in OpenSSH before 7.4 does not ensure that a bounds check is enforced by all compilers, which might allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging access to a sandboxed privilege-separation process, related to the m_zback and m_zlib data structures.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only allocates a monitor, opens fds, and sets up zlib shared-memory hooks; it performs no buffer indexing or bounds-checked memory operation, so CWE-119 is not directly evidenced here.

commit_msg:
tunnels: Don't apply GRO to multiple layers of encapsulation.

When drivers express support for TSO of encapsulated packets, they
only mean that they can do it for one layer of encapsulation.
Supporting additional levels would mean updating, at a minimum,
more IP length fields and they are unaware of this.

No encapsulation device expresses support for handling offloaded
encapsulated packets, so we won't generate these types of frames
in the transmit path. However, GRO doesn't have a check for
multiple levels of encapsulation and will attempt to build them.

UDP tunnel GRO actually does prevent this situation but it only
handles multiple UDP tunnels stacked on top of each other. This
generalizes that solution to prevent any kind of tunnel stacking
that would cause problems.

Fixes: bf5a755f ("net-gre-gro: Add GRE support to the GRO stack")
Signed-off-by: Jesse Gross <jesse@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (NAPI_GRO_CB(skb)->encap_mark)', '\t\tgoto out;', '', '\tNAPI_GRO_CB(skb)->encap_mark = 1;']}
description: The IP stack in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack consumption and panic) or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering use of the GRO path for packets with tunnel stacking, as demonstrated by interleaved IPv4 headers and GRE headers, a related issue to CVE-2016-7039.

code_evidence: The function parses a GRE header at the current GRO offset and, when the header is valid, pulls that header and recursively invokes the next protocol's gro_receive callback on the same skb (lines 61-63).

No state is checked or set to record that this skb has already passed through a tunnel encapsulation layer before recursing, so a crafted packet with stacked GRE/IP headers drives repeated nested GRO processing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing encapsulation-depth constraint lets a remote peer force repeated resource-consuming processing (stack consumption) until the system crashes, matching CWE-400's uncontrolled resource consumption with DoS impact. The fix adds an encap_mark guard, confirming the defect is lack of throttling of nested GRO processing rather than a parsing memory-safety bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: gre_gro_receive lacks a per-skb marker preventing re-entry through another encapsulation layer, so attacker-supplied tunnel stacking causes recursion through the GRO path. Trigger: a remote packet carrying interleaved IPv4 and GRE headers. Consequence: unbounded stack consumption in the GRO path, leading to kernel panic/denial of service.

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  headers_.remove_if([&](const HeaderEntryImpl& entry) {'], 'added_lines': ['  headers_.remove_if([&prefix, this](const HeaderEntryImpl& entry) {', '          const uint32_t key_value_size = (*ref_lookup_response.entry_)->key().size() +', '                                          (*ref_lookup_response.entry_)->value().size();', '          subtractSize(key_value_size);', '      } else {', '        subtractSize(entry.key().size() + entry.value().size());']}
description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only removes headers matching a prefix and adjusts cached byte-size bookkeeping; it contains no header-size limit check or iteration pattern demonstrating uncontrolled resource consumption, so CWE-400 is not directly supported by this code.

Fixed a memory leak in the BMP decoder

Fixes issue #10
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ["\t\t// If we didn't call iw_set_input_image, 'img' still belongs to us,", '\t\t// so free its contents.', '\t\tiw_free(ctx, img.pixels);']}
description: The iw_read_bmp_file function in imagew-bmp.c in libimageworsener.a in ImageWorsener 1.3.0 allows remote attackers to consume an amount of available memory via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Local struct iw_image img is declared and zero-initialized; its pixels buffer is allocated during the header/bitfields/palette/bit-reading steps via rctx.img.

Any failure in iwbmp_read_file_header, iwbmp_read_info_header, iwbmp_read_bitfields, iwbmp_read_palette or iwbmp_read_bits jumps to done before iw_set_input_image transfers ownership; img.pixels may already be allocated at that point.
The done block only records an error and returns retval; no iw_free of img.pixels occurs on the failure path, so the allocated pixel buffer is leaked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the function fails to release an allocated resource (the pixel buffer) after its effective lifetime ends on the failure path. This is a missing-release defect, not a buffer overflow or use-after-free, since no further access to the buffer occurs.

evidence_lines.code:
struct iw_image img;
iw_zeromem(&img,sizeof(struct iw_image));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path at done omits releasing img.pixels, which is owned by this function until iw_set_input_image is called. Trigger: a crafted BMP causing any early read step to fail after pixels were allocated. Consequence: repeated parsing of such files consumes memory without release, supporting resource-exhaustion DoS.

commit_msg:
Various variables were of smaller types than needed and there were no
checks for any overflows when doing additions on the sizes. This is all
checked now.

In addition the size of the decompressed data is limited to 120MB now as
any larger sizes are likely pathological and we can avoid out of memory
situations in many cases like this.

Also fix a bug where the available output size on the next iteration in
the zlib/bz2 decompression code was provided too large and could
potentially lead to out of bound writes.

Thanks to Adam Doupe for analyzing and reporting the issue.

CVE: CVE-2022-1922, CVE-2022-1923, CVE-2022-1924, CVE-2022-1925

https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org/security/sa-2022-0002.html

Fixes https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/gstreamer/gstreamer/-/issues/1225

Part-of: <https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/gstreamer/gstreamer/-/merge_requests/2610>

description: DOS / potential heap overwrite in mkv demuxing using zlib decompression. Integer overflow in matroskademux element in gst_matroska_decompress_data function which causes a segfault, or could cause a heap overwrite, depending on libc and OS. Depending on the libc used, and the underlying OS capabilities, it could be just a segfault or a heap overwrite. If the libc uses mmap for large chunks, and the OS supports mmap, then it is just a segfault (because the realloc before the integer overflow will use mremap to reduce the size of the chunk, and it will start to write to unmapped memory). However, if using a libc implementation that does not use mmap, or if the OS does not support mmap while using libc, then this could result in a heap overwrite.

code_evidence: In the zlib branch, new_size is guint; each loop adds 4096 and reallocs, then sets zstream.next_out to new_data + zstream.total_out while incrementing avail_out by 4096. If new_size overflows, g_realloc gets a small size and next_out/avail_out point past the allocation, so inflate writes out of bounds.

The bzlib branch mirrors this: new_size += 4096 then g_realloc, and next_out = new_data + bzstream.total_out_lo32 with avail_out += 4096; overflow of new_size yields an undersized buffer that BZ2_bzDecompress writes past.
The LZO branch uses int new_size; new_size += 4096 then g_realloc while lzo1x_decode writes out_size bytes into new_data, so integer overflow makes the buffer too small for the decoder's output.
The HEADERSTRIP branch computes size + enc->comp_settings_length without an overflow check, mallocs that wrapped small size, then memcpy writes comp_settings_length and size bytes into it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes decoder output and memcpy data into buffers sized by overflowed integer arithmetic, so writes land past the intended allocation—directly the out-of-bounds write described by CWE-787. The integer overflow is the enabling cause, but the supported weakness is the resulting buffer overrun, not merely CWE-190.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: decompressed-size counters (guint/int) are incremented by 4096 and used for g_realloc without overflow checks, and headerstrip addition is unchecked. Trigger: attacker-supplied compressed Matroska data that forces many growth iterations or a large size plus comp_settings_length. Consequence: undersized heap allocation followed by decompressor/memcpy writes past the buffer, causing heap overwrite or crash.

commit_msg:
It's buggy:

On Fri, Nov 06, 2020 at 10:30:08PM +0800, Minh Yuan wrote:
> We recently discovered a slab-out-of-bounds read in fbcon in the latest
> kernel ( v5.10-rc2 for now ).  The root cause of this vulnerability is that
> "fbcon_do_set_font" did not handle "vc->vc_font.data" and
> "vc->vc_font.height" correctly, and the patch
> <https://lkml.org/lkml/2020/9/27/223> for VT_RESIZEX can't handle this
> issue.
>
> Specifically, we use KD_FONT_OP_SET to set a small font.data for tty6, and
> use  KD_FONT_OP_SET again to set a large font.height for tty1. After that,
> we use KD_FONT_OP_COPY to assign tty6's vc_font.data to tty1's vc_font.data
> in "fbcon_do_set_font", while tty1 retains the original larger
> height. Obviously, this will cause an out-of-bounds read, because we can
> access a smaller vc_font.data with a larger vc_font.height.

Further there was only one user ever.
- Android's loadfont, busybox and console-tools only ever use OP_GET
  and OP_SET
- fbset documentation only mentions the kernel cmdline font: option,
  not anything else.
- systemd used OP_COPY before release 232 published in Nov 2016

Now unfortunately the crucial report seems to have gone down with
gmane, and the commit message doesn't say much. But the pull request
hints at OP_COPY being broken

https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/3651

So in other words, this never worked, and the only project which
foolishly every tried to use it, realized that rather quickly too.

Instead of trying to fix security issues here on dead code by adding
missing checks, fix the entire thing by removing the functionality.

Note that systemd code using the OP_COPY function ignored the return
value, so it doesn't matter what we're doing here really - just in
case a lone server somewhere happens to be extremely unlucky and
running an affected old version of systemd. The relevant code from
font_copy_to_all_vcs() in systemd was:

	/* copy font from active VT, where the font was uploaded to */
	cfo.op = KD_FONT_OP_COPY;
	cfo.height = vcs.v_active-1; /* tty1 == index 0 */
	(void) ioctl(vcfd, KDFONTOP, &cfo);

Note this just disables the ioctl, garbage collecting the now unused
callbacks is left for -next.

description: A slab-out-of-bounds read in fbcon in the Linux kernel before 5.9.7 could be used by local attackers to read privileged information or potentially crash the kernel, aka CID-3c4e0dff2095. This occurs because KD_FONT_OP_COPY in drivers/tty/vt/vt.c can be used for manipulations such as font height.

code_evidence: con_font_op dispatches KD_FONT_OP_COPY directly to con_font_copy(vc, op) without validating that the incoming op->height and op->data are consistent with the current vc->vc_font state before copying.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): access uses a mismatched height over a smaller data buffer. The dispatch at lines 10-11 is the reachable path; the patch removes it. This is not an out-of-bounds write because the operation reads font data.

evidence_lines.code:
case KD_FONT_OP_COPY:
return con_font_copy(vc, op);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the KD_FONT_OP_COPY path copies font data between virtual consoles without constraining font.data size against font.height. Trigger: an attacker sets a small font.data on one tty and a large font.height on another, then issues KD_FONT_OP_COPY. Consequence: the larger height indexes past the smaller data buffer, causing a slab-out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg: [FIX] revisit CVE-2015-8080 vulnerability
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["    case 'c': return getnum(fmt, 1);", '      int sz = getnum(fmt, sizeof(int));'], 'added_lines': ["    case 'c': return getnum(L, fmt, 1);", '      int sz = getnum(L, fmt, sizeof(int));']}
description: An integer overflow in the getnum function in lua_struct.c in Redis before 6.0.3 allows context-dependent attackers with permission to run Lua code in a Redis session to cause a denial of service (memory corruption and application crash) or possibly bypass intended sandbox restrictions via a large number, which triggers a stack-based buffer overflow. NOTE: this issue exists because of a CVE-2015-8080 regression.

code_evidence: optsize returns getnum(fmt, 1) for the 'c' option without validating the parsed count against the remaining format or buffer size.
For 'i'/'I', getnum(fmt, sizeof(int)) produces sz, and only the upper bound MAXINTSIZE is checked before sz is returned as a size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The size calculation performed by getnum and returned through optsize can overflow or yield an invalid value that is then used as a length, matching CWE-190's integer-overflow-in-size-calculation pattern. The function itself parses and bounds-checks the size, so the weakness is directly supported here rather than a pure out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), which is the downstream consequence.

evidence_lines.code: case 'c': return getnum(fmt, 1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: getnum parses an attacker-controlled numeric field from the format string; the returned value is used as a size/count for struct packing or unpacking. Because optsize only enforces sz <= MAXINTSIZE and does not constrain the value against the actual data length, an oversized or wrapped size can drive subsequent buffer operations beyond their bounds. Root cause is missing validation of the computed size; trigger is a crafted format string; supported consequence is memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
gnttab: fix unmap pin accounting race

Once all {writable} mappings of a grant entry have been unmapped, the
hypervisor informs the guest that the grant entry has been released by
clearing the _GTF_{reading,writing} usage flags in the guest's grant
table as appropriate.

Unfortunately, at the moment, the code that updates the accounting
happens in a different critical section than the one which updates the
usage flags; this means that under the right circumstances, there may be
a window in time after the hypervisor reported the grant as being free
during which the grant referee still had access to the page.

Move the grant accounting code into the same critical section as the
reporting code to make sure this kind of race can't happen.

This is part of XSA-218.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['             * replace_grant_host_mapping() so nothing further to do'], 'added_lines': ['', '        ASSERT(act->pin & (GNTPIN_devw_mask | GNTPIN_devr_mask));', '        if ( op->flags & GNTMAP_readonly )', '            act->pin -= GNTPIN_devr_inc;', '        else', '            act->pin -= GNTPIN_devw_inc;', '             * replace_grant_host_mapping() or IOMMU handling, so nothing', '             * further to do (short of re-establishing the mapping in the', '             * latter case).', '', '        ASSERT(act->pin & (GNTPIN_hstw_mask | GNTPIN_hstr_mask));', '        if ( op->flags & GNTMAP_readonly )', '            act->pin -= GNTPIN_hstr_inc;', '        else', '            act->pin -= GNTPIN_hstw_inc;']}
description: The grant-table feature in Xen through 4.8.x provides false mapping information in certain cases of concurrent unmap calls, which allows backend attackers to obtain sensitive information or gain privileges, aka XSA-218 bug 1.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs grant-table reference/accounting updates and page-put operations; the evidence shows a race between accounting and flag reporting, not a double free() of the same address, so CWE-415 is unsupported.

mpi: Fix NULL ptr dereference in mpi_powm() [ver #3]

This fixes CVE-2016-8650.

If mpi_powm() is given a zero exponent, it wants to immediately return
either 1 or 0, depending on the modulus.  However, if the result was
initalised with zero limb space, no limbs space is allocated and a
NULL-pointer exception ensues.

Fix this by allocating a minimal amount of limb space for the result when
the 0-exponent case when the result is 1 and not touching the limb space
when the result is 0.

This affects the use of RSA keys and X.509 certificates that carry them.

description: In the Linux kernel before 5.3.11, there is a use-after-free bug that can be caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/net/can/usb/mcba_usb.c driver, aka CID-4d6636498c41.

code_evidence: Line 7 frees the netdev via free_candev(priv->netdev); line 8 then calls mcba_urb_unlink(priv), which must access the driver's private data/URBs associated with that netdev after it has been released. The fix reorders these calls so unlink runs before free.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/1554
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  while(!EOFBlob(image)) /* object parser loop */', '    if (filepos != (unsigned int) filepos)', '    if((MagickSizeType) (MATLAB_HDR.ObjectSize+filepos) > GetBlobSize(image))'], 'added_lines': ['  while(filepos < GetBlobSize(image) && !EOFBlob(image)) /* object parser loop */', '    if(filepos > GetBlobSize(image) || filepos < 0)', '    if((MagickSizeType) (MATLAB_HDR.ObjectSize+filepos) >= GetBlobSize(image))', '            ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"UnexpectedEndOfFile");']}
description: coders/mat.c in ImageMagick 7.0.8-43 Q16 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by crafting a Matlab image file that is mishandled in ReadImage in MagickCore/constitute.c.

code_evidence: The object parser loop at 87-92 only stops on EOFBlob or a failed SeekBlob; filepos is a MagickOffsetType advanced at 99 by untrusted ObjectSize, so the loop can iterate over crafted offsets rather than bounded blob positions.
Lines 97-99 reject only when ObjectSize+filepos exceeds blob size, then advance filepos; the weak bound permits revisiting/overlapping regions and multiple image2 lifetimes.

Lines 103-105 free the prior image2 and reassign it to image, while 451-454 and 483-485 DeleteImageFromList(&image2) without consistently clearing it; later iterations reuse image2 in reads at 123-134 and 407-425.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reuses a freed image2 pointer after DeleteImageFromList/DestroyImage, matching CWE-416's post-free reference. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read: the defect is lifetime management of a freed object, so CWE-416 fits the target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser loop lacks a strict filepos/blob-size bound and frees/reassigns image2 across iterations without reliably nulling it. A crafted MAT file drives repeated frames/objects so a stale image2 pointer is dereferenced by ReadBlobXXXLong or CalcMinMax after its list entry was deleted, producing use-after-free and crash.

commit_msg:
ipv4: Don't do expensive useless work during inetdev destroy.

When an inetdev is destroyed, every address assigned to the interface
is removed.  And in this scenerio we do two pointless things which can
be very expensive if the number of assigned interfaces is large:

1) Address promotion.  We are deleting all addresses, so there is no
   point in doing this.

2) A full nf conntrack table purge for every address.  We only need to
   do this once, as is already caught by the existing
   masq_dev_notifier so masq_inet_event() can skip this.

Reported-by: Solar Designer <solar@openwall.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
Tested-by: Cyrill Gorcunov <gorcunov@openvz.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct net_device *dev = ((struct in_ifaddr *)ptr)->ifa_dev->dev;', '\tnetdev_notifier_info_init(&info, dev);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct in_device *idev = ((struct in_ifaddr *)ptr)->ifa_dev;', '\t/* The masq_dev_notifier will catch the case of the device going', '\t * down.  So if the inetdev is dead and being destroyed we have', '\t * no work to do.  Otherwise this is an individual address removal', '\t * and we have to perform the flush.', '\t */', '\tif (idev->dead)', '\t\treturn NOTIFY_DONE;', '', '\tnetdev_notifier_info_init(&info, idev->dev);']}
description: The IPv4 implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.5.2 mishandles destruction of device objects, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host OS networking outage) by arranging for a large number of IP addresses.

code_evidence: masq_inet_event unconditionally dereferences the in_ifaddr's in_device and calls masq_device_event for every notifier event, with no check on idev->dead. During inetdev destruction the notifier fires for each assigned address, so the conntrack flush in masq_device_event runs once per address instead of once per device.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function lacks the idev->dead guard, so resource-consuming work scales with the number of addresses, exhausting host networking resources. This is improper management of system resources, matching CWE-399's resource-management category.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the handler performs per-address work (a full nf conntrack purge via masq_device_event) even when the inetdev is being destroyed and all addresses are removed anyway. Trigger: a guest arranges many IP addresses on an interface, then triggers device destruction. Consequence: unbounded repeated expensive work causes a host networking outage (denial of service).

commit_msg: Multiplayer API now respects allow_object_decoding
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tError err = encode_variant(*p_arg[0], NULL, len);', '\t\tencode_variant(*p_arg[0], &(packet_cache.write[ofs]), len);', '\t\t\tError err = encode_variant(*p_arg[i], NULL, len);', '\t\t\tencode_variant(*p_arg[i], &(packet_cache.write[ofs]), len);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tError err = encode_variant(*p_arg[0], NULL, len, !network_peer->is_object_decoding_allowed());', '\t\tencode_variant(*p_arg[0], &(packet_cache.write[ofs]), len, !network_peer->is_object_decoding_allowed());', '\t\t\tError err = encode_variant(*p_arg[i], NULL, len, !network_peer->is_object_decoding_allowed());', '\t\t\tencode_variant(*p_arg[i], &(packet_cache.write[ofs]), len, !network_peer->is_object_decoding_allowed());']}
description: In Godot through 3.1, remote code execution is possible due to the deserialization policy not being applied correctly.

code_evidence: The RSET branch calls encode_variant on *p_arg[0] without any allow_object_decoding flag argument, so the encoding policy is not applied when serializing the RSET value.
The RPC argument loop likewise calls encode_variant on each *p_arg[i] with only the Variant, buffer and length; the object-decoding restriction is absent from these serialization calls.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function produces serialized Variant data that is subsequently deserialized by peers, and it fails to apply the object-decoding restriction, directly supporting CWE-502's deserialization of untrusted data. This is the serialization-side omission; it is not merely a generic input-validation flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
Error err = encode_variant(*p_arg[0], NULL, len);
encode_variant(*p_arg[0], &(packet_cache.write[ofs]), len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the RPC/RSET serialization path encodes Variant arguments (including objects) without consulting the peer's object-decoding policy. Trigger: a caller sends RPC/RSET arguments containing object data while the policy should restrict decoding; the encoded packet then propagates object data to the remote end. Supported consequence: untrusted serialized object data reaches deserialization, enabling remote code execution or state manipulation.

commit_msg:
Eliminate `CHECK`-fails from `IsSimplifiableReshape` via `MakeShape(<invalid shape>)`

PiperOrigin-RevId: 409166738
Change-Id: I7f0a3590b8acae3f3e3e2fe636e1f5ef285693cf
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    TF_CHECK_OK(TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape(shp, &new_dims));', '    TF_CHECK_OK(TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape(shp, &new_dims));'], 'added_lines': ['    s = TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape(shp, &new_dims);', '    if (!s.ok()) return s;', '    s = TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape(shp, &new_dims);', '    if (!s.ok()) return s;']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The Grappler optimizer in TensorFlow can be used to cause a denial of service by altering a `SavedModel` such that `IsSimplifiableReshape` would trigger `CHECK` failures. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: For DT_INT32 output, the shape values from the evaluated constant input are collected into shp and passed to TensorShapeUtils::MakeShape via TF_CHECK_OK, which aborts if MakeShape returns an error (e.g., invalid/negative dims).
The else branch does the same for int64 shape values, again using TF_CHECK_OK on MakeShape, so an attacker-controlled constant shape can reach an assertion.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses TF_CHECK_OK (a reachable assertion/CHECK) on a status derived from attacker-influenced model data, causing an application exit instead of graceful error handling. This directly matches CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion); it is not merely a generic error-handling issue because the fatal CHECK is the crash mechanism.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The reshape target shape comes from a constant node evaluated at runtime (outputs[0]). When those dimensions are invalid, MakeShape returns a non-OK status, but TF_CHECK_OK turns it into a fatal CHECK failure, crashing the Grappler optimizer process. Trigger: a crafted SavedModel whose Reshape shape constant contains invalid dimensions; consequence: process termination (DoS).

code_evidence: Line 65 checks only hlen+1 bytes via ND_TCHECK2 before line 66 reads bp[hlen]; the individual flag tests at lines 68-74 read the same single byte, but the preceding length check is the only bound on the read.
Line 84 checks only ip6m_data8[0]; line 85 then reads mh->ip6m_data8[1] to test the K flag without a prior ND_TCHECK for that byte.
Line 99 checks hlen+16 bytes, then line 100 passes &bp[hlen] to ip6addr_string, which reads 16 bytes; the check is on *mh rather than the bp-based range the read uses.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads packet bytes beyond the validated portion of the captured buffer, which is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not CWE-787 (write) since only reads occur, and the flaw is a missing/insufficient bounds constraint rather than a length-field overflow.

evidence_lines.code:
ND_TCHECK2(*mh, hlen + 16);
ND_PRINT((ndo, " homeaddr %s", ip6addr_string(ndo, &bp[hlen])));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser derives hlen and mhlen from attacker-controlled IPv6 mobility header fields and performs ND_TCHECK bounds checks that are narrower than or offset from the subsequent EXTRACT_/byte reads. When a crafted packet is truncated at the boundary, checks like ip6m_data8[0] or hlen+1 pass while the following read of ip6m_data8[1] or bp[hlen] extends past the captured buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg: Fixed #6011: Bounds check in rdp_read_font_capability_set
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -1,10 +1,10 @@
 static BOOL rdp_read_font_capability_set(wStream* s, UINT16 length, rdpSettings* settings)
 {
 	WINPR_UNUSED(settings);
-	if (length > 4)
+	if (length > 5)
 		Stream_Seek_UINT16(s); /* fontSupportFlags (2 bytes) */
 
-	if (length > 6)
+	if (length > 7)
 		Stream_Seek_UINT16(s); /* pad2Octets (2 bytes) */
 
 	return TRUE;
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (length > 4)', '\tif (length > 6)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (length > 5)', '\tif (length > 7)']}
description: In FreeRDP after 1.1 and before 2.0.0, a stream out-of-bounds seek in rdp_read_font_capability_set could lead to a later out-of-bounds read. As a result, a manipulated client or server might force a disconnect due to an invalid data read. This has been fixed in 2.0.0.

code_evidence: The length parameter is compared against fixed thresholds before each Stream_Seek_UINT16. With the prior thresholds, a length of 5 or 6 allowed the first seek even though only part of the 2-byte fontSupportFlags field was present, and length 7 allowed the second seek prematurely.
These checks gate stream seeks based on the declared capability-set length, but the boundary comparison is off relative to the 2-byte fields being skipped.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an out-of-bounds memory access driven by an incorrect length constraint: operations on the stream buffer proceed past its intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The consequence is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write, consistent with the buffer-bounds class.

evidence_lines.code:
if (length > 4)
Stream_Seek_UINT16(s);

if (length > 6)
Stream_Seek_UINT16(s);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: length bounds are checked with thresholds that do not account for the full 2-byte field sizes, so the stream position can be advanced beyond the intended capability-set boundary. Trigger: a manipulated length value (5, 6 or 7) causes a partial/oversized seek; the subsequent stream read then accesses memory outside the buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read and possible disconnect.

commit_msg:
xenoprof: clear buffer intended to be shared with guests

alloc_xenheap_pages() making use of MEMF_no_scrub is fine for Xen
internally used allocations, but buffers allocated to be shared with
(unpriviliged) guests need to be zapped of their prior content.

This is part of XSA-313.

Reported-by: Ilja Van Sprundel <ivansprundel@ioactive.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    for ( i = 0; i < npages; ++i )', '        clear_page(d->xenoprof->rawbuf + i * PAGE_SIZE);', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in xenoprof in Xen through 4.13.x, allowing guest OS users (without active profiling) to obtain sensitive information about other guests. Unprivileged guests can request to map xenoprof buffers, even if profiling has not been enabled for those guests. These buffers were not scrubbed.

code_evidence: Line 43 allocates the guest-shareable xenoprof buffer via alloc_xenheap_pages() with no scrub flag, so the pages retain prior heap content.
After allocation, only bookkeeping fields and per-vcpu buffer metadata (lines 51-68) are written; the raw buffer body is never initialized before being exposed to the guest.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The allocated shared resource is not initialized before use by the guest, matching CWE-909 Missing Initialization of Resource. The leak is the consequence of missing initialization rather than a separate memory-safety flaw; the fix adds clear_page() over the pages.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the rawbuf pages are allocated without zeroing and the function never clears the buffer body, only setting size/metadata fields. Trigger: an unprivileged guest maps the xenoprof buffer even without profiling enabled. Consequence: the guest reads stale heap contents from other guests/domains, leaking sensitive information.

commit_msg:
x86/spec-ctrl: Enumerations for Speculative Return Stack Overflow

AMD have specified new CPUID bits relating to SRSO.

 * SRSO_NO indicates that hardware is no longer vulnerable to SRSO.
 * IBPB_BRTYPE indicates that IBPB flushes branch type information too.
 * SBPB indicates support for a relaxed form of IBPB that does not flush
   branch type information.

Current CPUs (Zen4 and older) are not expected to enumerate these bits.
Native software is expected to synthesise them for guests using model and
microcode revision checks.

Two are just status bits, and SBPB is trivial to support for guests by
tweaking the reserved bit calculation in guest_wrmsr() and feature
dependencies.  Expose all by default to guests, so they start showing up when
Xen synthesises them.

While adding feature dependenies for IBPB, fix up an overlooked issue from
XSA-422.  It's inappropriate to advertise that IBPB flushes RET predictions if
IBPB is unavailable itself.

This is part of XSA-434 / CVE-2023-20569

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -79,7 +79,10 @@
         if ( !cp->feat.ibrsb && !cp->extd.ibpb )
             goto gp_fault; /* MSR available? */
 
-        if ( val & ~PRED_CMD_IBPB )
+        rsvd = ~(PRED_CMD_IBPB |
+                 (cp->extd.sbpb ? PRED_CMD_SBPB : 0));
+
+        if ( val & rsvd )
             goto gp_fault; /* Rsvd bit set? */
 
         if ( v == curr )
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if ( val & ~PRED_CMD_IBPB )'], 'added_lines': ['        rsvd = ~(PRED_CMD_IBPB |', '                 (cp->extd.sbpb ? PRED_CMD_SBPB : 0));', '', '        if ( val & rsvd )']}
description: A side channel vulnerability on some of the AMD CPUs may allow an attacker to influence the return address prediction. This may result in speculative execution at an attacker-controlled address, potentially leading to information disclosure.

code_evidence: In the MSR_PRED_CMD case, the handler validates the guest-written value against a reserved-bit mask before performing wrmsrl(). The mask is computed as ~(PRED_CMD_IBPB | (cp->extd.sbpb ? PRED_CMD_SBPB : 0)), so acceptance of the SBPB bit depends on the guest-visible cp->extd.sbpb policy bit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-203 fits because the function's accept/reject behavior for the same MSR write varies with the sbpb policy bit, giving an unauthorized observer a distinguishable response. It is not CWE-200: the code does not directly read or return sensitive data here; the weakness is the observable behavioral difference itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The guest's write to MSR_PRED_CMD is accepted or rejected (GP fault) depending on whether the SBPB control bit is set in the CPU policy. This creates a guest-observable behavioral difference tied to a feature/policy bit; the patch merely widens the accepted reserved-bit mask. The consequence is an observable discrepancy in guest handling rather than a direct memory disclosure in this function.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

Reviewed-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Fam Zheng <famz@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Daniel P. Berrange <berrange@redhat.com>
Message-id: 20170213135235.12274-8-pbonzini@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    nbd_update_can_read(client);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An assertion-failure flaw was found in Qemu before 2.10.1, in the Network Block Device (NBD) server's initial connection negotiation, where the I/O coroutine was undefined. This could crash the qemu-nbd server if a client sent unexpected data during connection negotiation. A remote user or process could use this flaw to crash the qemu-nbd server resulting in denial of service.

code_evidence: nbd_request_get asserts client->nb_requests <= MAX_NBD_REQUESTS - 1, then increments nb_requests and calls nbd_update_can_read(client). The assertion is reachable from connection negotiation handling; if nb_requests already equals MAX_NBD_REQUESTS, the assert aborts the process.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because an attacker-reachable assert() causes process termination rather than graceful error handling. This is a reachable-assertion availability weakness, not memory corruption or input validation per se.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is an assert() guarding a request-count invariant that can be violated by client-driven request flow. A client sending unexpected data during negotiation can drive nb_requests to the limit and trigger the assertion, aborting the qemu-nbd server and dropping all connections (denial of service).

commit_msg:
Handle overflow errors in malformed zchunk files

Thanks to Agostino Sarubbo of Gentoo for the heads up!

Signed-off-by: Jonathan Dieter <jdieter@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if((comp->dc_data_size > comp->dc_data_size + src_size) ||', '       (src_size > comp->dc_data_size + src_size)) {', '        zck_log(ZCK_LOG_ERROR, "Integer overflow when reading decompressed data");', '        return false;', '    }']}
description: zchunk before 1.3.2 has multiple integer overflows via malformed zchunk files to lib/comp/comp.c, lib/comp/zstd/zstd.c, lib/dl/multipart.c, or lib/header.c.

code_evidence: Line 9 computes comp->dc_data_size + src_size for zrealloc without a prior bounds check in the original code; the size passed to allocation is the sum of an existing buffer size and attacker-influenced src_size. Line 14 then uses the same sum as the write offset in memcpy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unsafe addition is used directly for memory allocation and copying, the classic security-critical integer wraparound case. It is not merely a logic error; the wrapped size undermines allocation bounds and enables memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size addition comp->dc_data_size + src_size is performed without overflow checking before being used as an allocation size and memcpy offset. If both operands are large, the sum wraps to a small value, so zrealloc allocates a too-small buffer while memcpy copies src_size bytes at the wrapped offset, causing out-of-bounds writes. Trigger: malformed zchunk input reaching compress with large sizes; consequence: heap corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
amd/iommu: fix flush checks

Flush checking for AMD IOMMU didn't check whether the previous entry
was present, or whether the flags (writable/readable) changed in order
to decide whether a flush should be executed.

Fix this by taking the writable/readable/next-level fields into account,
together with the present bit.

Along these lines the flushing in amd_iommu_map_page() must not be
omitted for PV domains. The comment there was simply wrong: Mappings may
very well change, both their addresses and their permissions. Ultimately
this should honor iommu_dont_flush_iotlb, but to achieve this
amd_iommu_ops first needs to gain an .iotlb_flush hook.

Also make clear_iommu_pte_present() static, to demonstrate there's no
caller omitting the (subsequent) flush.

This is part of XSA-275.

commit_msg:
bpf: prevent out of bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic

Jann reported that the original commit back in b2157399cc98
("bpf: prevent out-of-bounds speculation") was not sufficient
to stop CPU from speculating out of bounds memory access:
While b2157399cc98 only focussed on masking array map access
for unprivileged users for tail calls and data access such
that the user provided index gets sanitized from BPF program
and syscall side, there is still a more generic form affected
from BPF programs that applies to most maps that hold user
data in relation to dynamic map access when dealing with
unknown scalars or "slow" known scalars as access offset, for
example:

  - Load a map value pointer into R6
  - Load an index into R7
  - Do a slow computation (e.g. with a memory dependency) that
    loads a limit into R8 (e.g. load the limit from a map for
    high latency, then mask it to make the verifier happy)
  - Exit if R7 >= R8 (mispredicted branch)
  - Load R0 = R6[R7]
  - Load R0 = R6[R0]

For unknown scalars there are two options in the BPF verifier
where we could derive knowledge from in order to guarantee
safe access to the memory: i) While </>/<=/>= variants won't
allow to derive any lower or upper bounds from the unknown
scalar where it would be safe to add it to the map value
pointer, it is possible through ==/!= test however. ii) another
option is to transform the unknown scalar into a known scalar,
for example, through ALU ops combination such as R &= <imm>
followed by R |= <imm> or any similar combination where the
original information from the unknown scalar would be destroyed
entirely leaving R with a constant. The initial slow load still
precedes the latter ALU ops on that register, so the CPU
executes speculatively from that point. Once we have the known
scalar, any compare operation would work then. A third option
only involving registers with known scalars could be crafted
as described in [0] where a CPU port (e.g. Slow Int unit)
would be filled with many dependent computations such that
the subsequent condition depending on its outcome has to wait
for evaluation on its execution port and thereby executing
speculatively if the speculated code can be scheduled on a
different execution port, or any other form of mistraining
as described in [1], for example. Given this is not limited
to only unknown scalars, not only map but also stack access
is affected since both is accessible for unprivileged users
and could potentially be used for out of bounds access under
speculation.

In order to prevent any of these cases, the verifier is now
sanitizing pointer arithmetic on the offset such that any
out of bounds speculation would be masked in a way where the
pointer arithmetic result in the destination register will
stay unchanged, meaning offset masked into zero similar as
in array_index_nospec() case. With regards to implementation,
there are three options that were considered: i) new insn
for sanitation, ii) push/pop insn and sanitation as inlined
BPF, iii) reuse of ax register and sanitation as inlined BPF.

Option i) has the downside that we end up using from reserved
bits in the opcode space, but also that we would require
each JIT to emit masking as native arch opcodes meaning
mitigation would have slow adoption till everyone implements
it eventually which is counter-productive. Option ii) and iii)
have both in common that a temporary register is needed in
order to implement the sanitation as inlined BPF since we
are not allowed to modify the source register. While a push /
pop insn in ii) would be useful to have in any case, it
requires once again that every JIT needs to implement it
first. While possible, amount of changes needed would also
be unsuitable for a -stable patch. Therefore, the path which
has fewer changes, less BPF instructions for the mitigation
and does not require anything to be changed in the JITs is
option iii) which this work is pursuing. The ax register is
already mapped to a register in all JITs (modulo arm32 where
it's mapped to stack as various other BPF registers there)
and used in constant blinding for JITs-only so far. It can
be reused for verifier rewrites under certain constraints.
The interpreter's tmp "register" has therefore been remapped
into extending the register set with hidden ax register and
reusing that for a number of instructions that needed the
prior temporary variable internally (e.g. div, mod). This
allows for zero increase in stack space usage in the interpreter,
and enables (restricted) generic use in rewrites otherwise as
long as such a patchlet does not make use of these instructions.
The sanitation mask is dynamic and relative to the offset the
map value or stack pointer currently holds.

There are various cases that need to be taken under consideration
for the masking, e.g. such operation could look as follows:
ptr += val or val += ptr or ptr -= val. Thus, the value to be
sanitized could reside either in source or in destination
register, and the limit is different depending on whether
the ALU op is addition or subtraction and depending on the
current known and bounded offset. The limit is derived as
follows: limit := max_value_size - (smin_value + off). For
subtraction: limit := umax_value + off. This holds because
we do not allow any pointer arithmetic that would
temporarily go out of bounds or would have an unknown
value with mixed signed bounds where it is unclear at
verification time whether the actual runtime value would
be either negative or positive. For example, we have a
derived map pointer value with constant offset and bounded
one, so limit based on smin_value works because the verifier
requires that statically analyzed arithmetic on the pointer
must be in bounds, and thus it checks if resulting
smin_value + off and umax_value + off is still within map
value bounds at time of arithmetic in addition to time of
access. Similarly, for the case of stack access we derive
the limit as follows: MAX_BPF_STACK + off for subtraction
and -off for the case of addition where off := ptr_reg->off +
ptr_reg->var_off.value. Subtraction is a special case for
the masking which can be in form of ptr += -val, ptr -= -val,
or ptr -= val. In the first two cases where we know that
the value is negative, we need to temporarily negate the
value in order to do the sanitation on a positive value
where we later swap the ALU op, and restore original source
register if the value was in source.

The sanitation of pointer arithmetic alone is still not fully
sufficient as is, since a scenario like the following could
happen ...

  PTR += 0x1000 (e.g. K-based imm)
  PTR -= BIG_NUMBER_WITH_SLOW_COMPARISON
  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= BIG_NUMBER_WITH_SLOW_COMPARISON
  [...]

... which under speculation could end up as ...

  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= 0 [ truncated by mitigation ]
  PTR += 0x1000
  PTR -= 0 [ truncated by mitigation ]
  [...]

... and therefore still access out of bounds. To prevent such
case, the verifier is also analyzing safety for potential out
of bounds access under speculative execution. Meaning, it is
also simulating pointer access under truncation. We therefore
"branch off" and push the current verification state after the
ALU operation with known 0 to the verification stack for later
analysis. Given the current path analysis succeeded it is
likely that the one under speculation can be pruned. In any
case, it is also subject to existing complexity limits and
therefore anything beyond this point will be rejected. In
terms of pruning, it needs to be ensured that the verification
state from speculative execution simulation must never prune
a non-speculative execution path, therefore, we mark verifier
state accordingly at the time of push_stack(). If verifier
detects out of bounds access under speculative execution from
one of the possible paths that includes a truncation, it will
reject such program.

Given we mask every reg-based pointer arithmetic for
unprivileged programs, we've been looking into how it could
affect real-world programs in terms of size increase. As the
majority of programs are targeted for privileged-only use
case, we've unconditionally enabled masking (with its alu
restrictions on top of it) for privileged programs for the
sake of testing in order to check i) whether they get rejected
in its current form, and ii) by how much the number of
instructions and size will increase. We've tested this by
using Katran, Cilium and test_l4lb from the kernel selftests.
For Katran we've evaluated balancer_kern.o, Cilium bpf_lxc.o
and an older test object bpf_lxc_opt_-DUNKNOWN.o and l4lb
we've used test_l4lb.o as well as test_l4lb_noinline.o. We
found that none of the programs got rejected by the verifier
with this change, and that impact is rather minimal to none.
balancer_kern.o had 13,904 bytes (1,738 insns) xlated and
7,797 bytes JITed before and after the change. Most complex
program in bpf_lxc.o had 30,544 bytes (3,817 insns) xlated
and 18,538 bytes JITed before and after and none of the other
tail call programs in bpf_lxc.o had any changes either. For
the older bpf_lxc_opt_-DUNKNOWN.o object we found a small
increase from 20,616 bytes (2,576 insns) and 12,536 bytes JITed
before to 20,664 bytes (2,582 insns) and 12,558 bytes JITed
after the change. Other programs from that object file had
similar small increase. Both test_l4lb.o had no change and
remained at 6,544 bytes (817 insns) xlated and 3,401 bytes
JITed and for test_l4lb_noinline.o constant at 5,080 bytes
(634 insns) xlated and 3,313 bytes JITed. This can be explained
in that LLVM typically optimizes stack based pointer arithmetic
by using K-based operations and that use of dynamic map access
is not overly frequent. However, in future we may decide to
optimize the algorithm further under known guarantees from
branch and value speculation. Latter seems also unclear in
terms of prediction heuristics that today's CPUs apply as well
as whether there could be collisions in e.g. the predictor's
Value History/Pattern Table for triggering out of bounds access,
thus masking is performed unconditionally at this point but could
be subject to relaxation later on. We were generally also
brainstorming various other approaches for mitigation, but the
blocker was always lack of available registers at runtime and/or
overhead for runtime tracking of limits belonging to a specific
pointer. Thus, we found this to be minimally intrusive under
given constraints.

With that in place, a simple example with sanitized access on
unprivileged load at post-verification time looks as follows:

  # bpftool prog dump xlated id 282
  [...]
  28: (79) r1 = *(u64 *)(r7 +0)
  29: (79) r2 = *(u64 *)(r7 +8)
  30: (57) r1 &= 15
  31: (79) r3 = *(u64 *)(r0 +4608)
  32: (57) r3 &= 1
  33: (47) r3 |= 1
  34: (2d) if r2 > r3 goto pc+19
  35: (b4) (u32) r11 = (u32) 20479  |
  36: (1f) r11 -= r2                | Dynamic sanitation for pointer
  37: (4f) r11 |= r2                | arithmetic with registers
  38: (87) r11 = -r11               | containing bounded or known
  39: (c7) r11 s>>= 63              | scalars in order to prevent
  40: (5f) r11 &= r2                | out of bounds speculation.
  41: (0f) r4 += r11                |
  42: (71) r4 = *(u8 *)(r4 +0)
  43: (6f) r4 <<= r1
  [...]

For the case where the scalar sits in the destination register
as opposed to the source register, the following code is emitted
for the above example:

  [...]
  16: (b4) (u32) r11 = (u32) 20479
  17: (1f) r11 -= r2
  18: (4f) r11 |= r2
  19: (87) r11 = -r11
  20: (c7) r11 s>>= 63
  21: (5f) r2 &= r11
  22: (0f) r2 += r0
  23: (61) r0 = *(u32 *)(r2 +0)
  [...]

JIT blinding example with non-conflicting use of r10:

  [...]
   d5:	je     0x0000000000000106    _
   d7:	mov    0x0(%rax),%edi       |
   da:	mov    $0xf153246,%r10d     | Index load from map value and
   e0:	xor    $0xf153259,%r10      | (const blinded) mask with 0x1f.
   e7:	and    %r10,%rdi            |_
   ea:	mov    $0x2f,%r10d          |
   f0:	sub    %rdi,%r10            | Sanitized addition. Both use r10
   f3:	or     %rdi,%r10            | but do not interfere with each
   f6:	neg    %r10                 | other. (Neither do these instructions
   f9:	sar    $0x3f,%r10           | interfere with the use of ax as temp
   fd:	and    %r10,%rdi            | in interpreter.)
  100:	add    %rax,%rdi            |_
  103:	mov    0x0(%rdi),%eax
 [...]

Tested that it fixes Jann's reproducer, and also checked that test_verifier
and test_progs suite with interpreter, JIT and JIT with hardening enabled
on x86-64 and arm64 runs successfully.

tools/libxl: report trusted backend status to frontends

Allow administrators to notify a frontend driver that it's backend
counterpart is not to be trusted, so the frontend can deploy whatever
mitigations required in order to secure itself.

Allow such option for disk and network frontends only, as those are
the only hardened ones currently supported.

This is part of XSA-403

Fix `tf.raw_ops.RaggedTensorToTensor` failing CHECK.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 368706628
Change-Id: I5c9ea4833f38835ee183ca50d63251dc89c9f3bc
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            row_partition_tensor, parent_output_index, output_index_multiplier,', '            output_size, result);', '        CalculateOutputIndexRowSplit(row_partition_tensor, parent_output_index,', '                                     output_index_multiplier, output_size,', '                                     result);'], 'added_lines': ['            context, row_partition_tensor, parent_output_index,', '            output_index_multiplier, output_size, result);', '        CalculateOutputIndexRowSplit(', '            context, row_partition_tensor, parent_output_index,', '            output_index_multiplier, output_size, result);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. Due to lack of validation in `tf.raw_ops.RaggedTensorToTensor`, an attacker can exploit an undefined behavior if input arguments are empty. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/656e7673b14acd7835dc778867f84916c6d1cac2/tensorflow/core/kernels/ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op.cc#L356-L360) only checks that one of the tensors is not empty, but does not check for the other ones. There are multiple `DCHECK` validations to prevent heap OOB, but these are no-op in release builds, hence they don't prevent anything. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick these commits on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: CalculateOutputIndex dispatches to CalculateOutputIndexValueRowID or CalculateOutputIndexRowSplit based solely on the partition type, passing row_partition_tensor and the caller-supplied output_size/output_index_multiplier without any size validation or bounds check before the callee computes output indices.
Both branches unconditionally return Status::OK() after the call, so no error from size/index computation is surfaced to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-131 fits because the unsafe index/size computation is performed without validating the partition tensor against output_size, so a buffer size derived from these values can be miscalculated. This is a size-calculation defect rather than a pure missing-check or integer-overflow issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function delegates index/size computation to helpers using an unvalidated row_partition_tensor and output_size, relying on downstream DCHECK-only assumptions. Trigger: malformed or empty row partition inputs reaching either helper. Consequence: incorrect computed sizes/indices can lead to heap out-of-bounds access when the results are used to size or index buffers.

util/genrand: don't ignore errors in random number generation

In this case it is probably better to crash out.

description: In Samba, GnuTLS gnutls_rnd() can fail and give predictable random values.

code_evidence: generate_nonce_buffer calls gnutls_rnd(GNUTLS_RND_NONCE, out, len) to fill a security nonce buffer, but the return value is discarded, so a failed RNG call leaves out unchanged or partially filled with predictable/zero bytes while the function still returns success.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 covers use of insufficiently random values in a security context; here the nonce buffer may be filled with predictable data because RNG failure is silently accepted. This is the insufficient-randomness consequence, not merely a generic error-handling flaw.

evidence_lines.code: gnutls_rnd(GNUTLS_RND_NONCE, out, len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return status of the RNG call is ignored, so there is no check that unpredictable bytes were produced. Trigger: gnutls_rnd returns an error (e.g., entropy exhaustion). Consequence: callers receive a nonce buffer that is not random and may be predictable, undermining security uses such as nonces and keys.

commit_msg:
wimax: i2400: Fix memory leak in i2400m_op_rfkill_sw_toggle

In the implementation of i2400m_op_rfkill_sw_toggle() the allocated
buffer for cmd should be released before returning. The
documentation for i2400m_msg_to_dev() says when it returns the buffer
can be reused. Meaning cmd should be released in either case. Move
kfree(cmd) before return to be reached by all execution paths.

Fixes: 2507e6ab7a9a ("wimax: i2400: fix memory leak")
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tkfree(cmd);'], 'added_lines': ['\tkfree(cmd);']}
description: A memory leak in the i2400m_op_rfkill_sw_toggle() function in drivers/net/wimax/i2400m/op-rfkill.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption), aka CID-6f3ef5c25cc7.

code_evidence: Line 15 allocates cmd via kzalloc; on success execution continues and cmd is only freed at the error_cmd label (line 57).

i2400m_msg_to_dev() at line 33 returns ack_skb; when IS_ERR(ack_skb) is true, line 38 jumps to error_msg_to_dev, which is below error_cmd, so kfree(cmd) at line 57 is skipped and the allocated cmd leaks.
The error_msg_to_dev/error_alloc labels and the return at line 63 are reached without freeing cmd on the error path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the function allocates memory and fails to release it on an error path, leaving the allocation unavailable for reuse; the root cause is the mismatched cleanup label placement, not a buffer overrun or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocated cmd buffer is only released at the error_cmd label, but the error path for a failed i2400m_msg_to_dev() call jumps past that label to error_msg_to_dev. Repeated triggers of the failure path leak the cmd allocation, causing unbounded memory consumption and eventual denial of service.

commit_msg:
mime-actions: use file metadata for trusting desktop files

Currently we only trust desktop files that have the executable bit
set, and don't replace the displayed icon or the displayed name until
it's trusted, which prevents for running random programs by a malicious
desktop file.

However, the executable permission is preserved if the desktop file
comes from a compressed file.

To prevent this, add a metadata::trusted metadata to the file once the
user acknowledges the file as trusted. This adds metadata to the file,
which cannot be added unless it has access to the computer.

Also remove the SHEBANG "trusted" content we were putting inside the
desktop file, since that doesn't add more security since it can come
with the file itself.

https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=777991

In other words, Nautilus provides no UI indication that a file actually has the potentially unsafe .desktop extension; instead, the UI only shows the .pdf extension. One (slightly) mitigating factor is that an attack requires the .desktop file to have execute permission. The solution is to ask the user to confirm that the file is supposed to be treated as a .desktop file, and then remember the user's answer in the metadata::trusted field.

Trigger: an attacker supplies a .desktop file with the executable bit set (e.g., inside a compressed archive). Because the trust decision never validates the confirmed-trust property, the launcher is treated as trusted and can display a spoofed name/icon and run its Exec command, enabling spoofing and code execution.

Prevent nullptr dereference in MLIR TFLite dialect/optimizer.
