description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions an attacker can craft a TFLite model that would trigger a null pointer dereference, which would result in a crash and denial of service. This is caused by the MLIR optimization of `L2NormalizeReduceAxis` operator. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/149562d49faa709ea80df1d99fc41d005b81082a/tensorflow/compiler/mlir/lite/transforms/optimize.cc#L67-L70) unconditionally dereferences a pointer to an iterator to a vector without checking that the vector has elements. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit d6b57f461b39fd1aa8c1b870f1b974aac3554955. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Lines 2-4 unconditionally call axis.getValues<int>().begin() and dereference the resulting iterator via *...begin() in the rank comparison and the == -1 check, without first verifying that the DenseElementsAttr axis contains any elements.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unconditional dereference of an iterator obtained from an empty value range is a NULL/invalid pointer dereference (CWE-476), with the crash/DoS impact matching that entry. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the missing constraint is on emptiness of the container before dereferencing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dereferences the begin() iterator of axis's value range before any emptiness check. Trigger: a crafted TFLite model supplies L2NormalizeReduceAxis with an empty axis attribute, so begin() equals end() and dereferencing it is invalid; the later size check at line 7 occurs after the dereference. Supported consequence: null/invalid iterator dereference leading to a crash and denial of service.

description: Rizin is a UNIX-like reverse engineering framework and command-line toolset. Versions 0.4.0 and prior are vulnerable to an out-of-bounds write when parsing Mach-O files. A user opening a malicious Mach-O file could be affected by this vulnerability, allowing an attacker to execute code on the user's machine. Commit number 7323e64d68ecccfb0ed3ee480f704384c38676b2 contains a patch.

code_evidence: page_count is derived from attacker-controlled Mach-O segment vmsize (line 67) and page_start is allocated with page_count ut16 elements (line 69), then zero-initialized over the same count (line 73).

The write index page_index = seg_off / ps (line 78) is compared against maxsize = page_count * sizeof(ut16) (line 79), i.e. a byte count, before writing page_start[page_index] (line 81), so the bound check is too permissive.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through page_start[page_index] past the allocated buffer because the size check uses a byte count instead of the element count; this is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), not merely an integer overflow, since the faulty comparison permits the write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard at line 80 mixes element count with byte count, so page_index up to page_count*2-1 passes even though page_start holds only page_count ut16 elements. Trigger: a crafted Mach-O bind opcode stream drives seg_off so page_index lands in [page_count, page_count*2), causing page_start[page_index] to write beyond the heap buffer. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, potentially code execution.

commit_msg: dirLength == 0 can cause an infinite loop.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            // Prevent infinite loops. (GHSA-m479-7frc-gqqg)', '            enforce(dirLength > 0, kerCorruptedMetadata);']}
description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An infinite loop was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The infinite loop is triggered when Exiv2 is used to print the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. Note that this bug is only triggered when printing the image ICC profile, which is a less frequently used Exiv2 operation that requires an extra command line option (`-p C`). The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: The outer do/while loop at line 9 continues while start is nonzero (line 129). dirLength is read from attacker-controlled file bytes (line 15) and only an upper bound of 500 is enforced (lines 16-17). The inner for loop at line 22 iterates i < dirLength; when dirLength is 0 the loop body never executes, so start is not updated inside it. start is then only reassigned at line 127 (start = tooBig ? 0 : byteSwap4(...)) when the original start was nonzero (line 125). With a crafted directory whose entry count is zero, the outer loop can repeat without progress.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the do/while exit condition (start == 0) cannot be reached when dirLength is 0 and start remains nonzero, yielding a loop with an unreachable exit condition. This is a resource-consumption DoS, not a memory-safety flaw such as an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dirLength is not constrained to be positive, so a zero entry count skips the inner loop that advances state, while the outer do/while retains a nonzero start and iterates again. Trigger: printing metadata (e.g., ICC profile with -p C) of a crafted TIFF/ICC file. Consequence: the process spins indefinitely, consuming CPU and causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
gnttab: fix unmap pin accounting race

Once all {writable} mappings of a grant entry have been unmapped, the
hypervisor informs the guest that the grant entry has been released by
clearing the _GTF_{reading,writing} usage flags in the guest's grant
table as appropriate.

Unfortunately, at the moment, the code that updates the accounting
happens in a different critical section than the one which updates the
usage flags; this means that under the right circumstances, there may be
a window in time after the hypervisor reported the grant as being free
during which the grant referee still had access to the page.

Move the grant accounting code into the same critical section as the
reporting code to make sure this kind of race can't happen.

This is part of XSA-218.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

description: The grant-table feature in Xen through 4.8.x provides false mapping information in certain cases of concurrent unmap calls, which allows backend attackers to obtain sensitive information or gain privileges, aka XSA-218 bug 1.

commit_msg:
Add recursion limit for ASN.1 indefinite lengths

The libkrb5 ASN.1 decoder supports BER indefinite lengths.  It
computes the tag length using recursion; the lack of a recursion limit
allows an attacker to overrun the stack and cause the process to
crash.  Reported by Demi Obenour.

CVE-2020-28196:

In MIT krb5 releases 1.11 and later, an unauthenticated attacker can
cause a denial of service for any client or server to which it can
send an ASN.1-encoded Kerberos message of sufficient length.

ticket: 8959 (new)
tags: pullup
target_version: 1.18-next
target_version: 1.17-next

description: MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) before 1.17.2 and 1.18.x before 1.18.3 allows unbounded recursion via an ASN.1-encoded Kerberos message because the lib/krb5/asn.1/asn1_encode.c support for BER indefinite lengths lacks a recursion limit.

code_evidence: decode_sequence iterates over seq->n_fields and calls get_tag on each encoded tag, passing the remaining buffer and length. The call at line 13 provides no recursion-depth argument, so any nested indefinite-length tag processed by get_tag can recurse without a bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the function's call into get_tag lacks a recursion-depth constraint, allowing attacker-controlled nesting to consume the stack. This is uncontrolled recursion causing resource exhaustion, not merely an input-length or buffer-overflow issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: get_tag is invoked without any recursion-depth limit, so nested BER indefinite-length tags drive unbounded recursion in the decoder. Trigger: an attacker sends an ASN.1/Kerberos message with deeply nested indefinite-length encodings. Consequence: stack exhaustion leading to a process crash (denial of service).

We have a policy that if API may end up talking to a guest agent
it should require RW connection. We don't obey the rule in
virDomainGetTime().

commit_msg:
Bug 699927: don't include operator arrays in execstack output

When we transfer the contents of the execution stack into the array, take the
extra step of replacing any operator arrays on the stack with the operator
that reference them.

This prevents the contents of Postscript defined, internal only operators (those
created with .makeoperator) being exposed via execstack (and thus, via error
handling).

This necessitates a change in the resource remapping 'resource', which contains
a procedure which relies on the contents of the operators arrays being present.
As we already had internal-only variants of countexecstack and execstack
(.countexecstack and .execstack) - using those, and leaving thier operation
including the operator arrays means the procedure continues to work correctly.

Both .countexecstack and .execstack are undefined after initialization.

Also, when we store the execstack (or part thereof) for an execstackoverflow
error, make the same oparray/operator substitution as above for execstack.

The result array is returned to the caller with its raw stack entries intact.

commit_msg:
Use req::strndup in php_mb_parse_encoding_list to prevent oob memory write.

Summary:
Fix out of bounds write access in mb_detect_encoding.  Using strndup in
php_mb_parse_encoding_list will cause strings with embedded nulls to be
unexpectedly shortened.  The expected length of the string is tracked in
value_length but since strndup may copy fewer characters when there are
mbedded null this can lead to oob writes into tmpstr.

I've found a couple other places in this file that use strndup and replaced
them with req::strndup as well.  The use of strndup in mb_send_mail also seemed
to be a leak.

This replaces uses of strndup with req::strndup which can handle embedded
nulls properly.

It looks like I also accidentally fixed t11337047 at the same time.  Adding it to the list of tasks.

Reviewed By: paulbiss

Differential Revision: D3360065

fbshipit-source-id: 99776cf9105e3789883380bf30240009eec52cec
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  char *encstr = strndup(encoded_string.data(), encoded_string.size());', '  free(encstr);'], 'added_lines': ['  char *encstr = req::strndup(encoded_string.data(), encoded_string.size());', '  req::free(encstr);']}
description: Out-of-bounds write in the (1) mb_detect_encoding, (2) mb_send_mail, and (3) mb_detect_order functions in Facebook HHVM before 3.15.0 allows attackers to have unspecified impact via unknown vectors.

code_evidence: Line 14 allocates encstr via strndup(encoded_string.data(), encoded_string.size()), which stops at the first embedded NUL and may return a buffer shorter than encoded_string.size(). The full length is not carried into the handler; line 17 passes encstr to _php_mb_encoding_handler_ex, which relies on the expected string length when parsing and writing into tmpstr, so a shorter allocation can be overrun.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's allocation-size mismatch leads downstream writes beyond the intended buffer, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. It is distinguished from a mere leak or improper free: the defect is the size/length inconsistency that produces writes past the end of tmpstr.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy length is derived from a NUL-terminated strndup instead of the tracked value_length, so embedded NULs shorten the allocated buffer while downstream code still assumes the full size. Trigger: user-supplied encoded_string containing embedded NULs. Consequence: writes past the end of the allocated buffer, corrupting memory and potentially enabling code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
video: uvesafb: Fix integer overflow in allocation

cmap->len can get close to INT_MAX/2, allowing for an integer overflow in
allocation. This uses kmalloc_array() instead to catch the condition.

Reported-by: Dr Silvio Cesare of InfoSect <silvio.cesare@gmail.com>
Fixes: 8bdb3a2d7df48 ("uvesafb: the driver core")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tentries = kmalloc(sizeof(*entries) * cmap->len, GFP_KERNEL);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tentries = kmalloc_array(cmap->len, sizeof(*entries),', '\t\t\t\t\tGFP_KERNEL);']}
description: An integer overflow in the uvesafb_setcmap function in drivers/video/fbdev/uvesafb.c in the Linux kernel before 4.17.4 could result in local attackers being able to crash the kernel or potentially elevate privileges because kmalloc_array is not used.

code_evidence: Line 10 computes the allocation size as sizeof(*entries) * cmap->len using plain multiplication in kmalloc; cmap->len is attacker-influenced via the framebuffer cmap and can approach INT_MAX/2, so the product can wrap to a small value. The subsequent write loop indexes entries[i] for i < cmap->len, exceeding the undersized buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the size calculation assumes the product is larger than cmap->len, but wraparound produces a small allocation later used for larger indexing, a classic integer-overflow-to-heap-overflow pattern.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unchecked multiplication of the element size by cmap->len in the kmalloc size argument can integer-overflow, yielding an undersized allocation. Trigger: a large cmap->len passing the start/len bounds check. Consequence: the loop at lines 13-17 writes past the allocation, causing memory corruption, kernel crash, or potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg: Fix handling of APNG with 0 delay_den (#313)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['          if (!delay_den) delay_den = 100;', '']}
description: libjxl v0.3.7 is affected by a Divide By Zero in issue in lib/extras/codec_apng.cc jxl::DecodeImageAPNG(). When encoding a malicous APNG file using cjxl, an attacker can trigger a denial of service.

code_evidence: Line 133 reads delay_den from the fcTL chunk via png_get_uint_16, so an attacker-controlled APNG can set it to 0. The bounds check at lines 136-138 validates w0/h0/x0/y0/dop/bop but never constrains delay_den, so zero passes through. Line 68 then computes bundle.duration = delay_num * 1000 / delay_den, dividing by the unvalidated value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 (Divide By Zero) fits because the vulnerable operation is a direct division by attacker-supplied delay_den lacking a zero check. It is not a generic input-validation issue but specifically a divide-by-zero leading to a crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder accepts a zero delay_den from the fcTL chunk and later uses it as a divisor without a nonzero check. Trigger: a malicious APNG whose fcTL frame-control chunk sets delay_den to 0. Consequence: integer division by zero in the duration computation, crashing the decoder (DoS). The commit's added guard confirms this path.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    STRCPY(p + len, _("[Help]"));', '\t    STRCPY(p + len, _("[Preview]"));', '\t    STRCPY(p + len, "[+]");', '\t    len += 3;', '\t    STRCPY(p + len, _("[RO]"));'], 'added_lines': ['\t    vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", _("[Help]"));', '\t    vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", _("[Preview]"));', '\t    vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", "[+]");', '\t    len += (int)STRLEN(p + len);', '\t    vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", _("[RO]"));']}
description: vim is vulnerable to Heap-based Buffer Overflow

code_evidence: get_trans_bufname fills the global NameBuff and p points to it; len is its current length, and a space is appended when a status flag is set, yielding p+len as the write offset.
STRCPY copies the unbounded translated "[Help]" string to p+len with no remaining-capacity check against MAXPATHL.
STRCPY copies the unbounded translated "[Preview]" string to p+len, again without a bounds check.
STRCPY writes the literal "[+]" to p+len and unconditionally advances len by 3, with no capacity check.
STRCPY copies the translated "[RO]" string to p+len with no remaining-capacity check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe STRCPY operations write beyond the fixed-size heap-allocated NameBuff, which is exactly a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122). It is not merely a stack overflow or off-by-one, since the target buffer is heap-allocated and the overflow is driven by unbounded string copying.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: NameBuff is a fixed MAXPATHL-sized heap buffer, and the buffer name from get_trans_bufname can already be near MAXPATHL; the code then appends status markers via STRCPY without verifying remaining space. Trigger: a buffer whose name is long enough that len plus the marker exceeds MAXPATHL. Consequence: writes past the heap allocation, i.e. heap-based buffer overflow with memory corruption/crash.

commit_msg:
powerpc/tm: Check for already reclaimed tasks

Currently we can hit a scenario where we'll tm_reclaim() twice.  This
results in a TM bad thing exception because the second reclaim occurs
when not in suspend mode.

The scenario in which this can happen is the following.  We attempt to
deliver a signal to userspace.  To do this we need obtain the stack
pointer to write the signal context.  To get this stack pointer we
must tm_reclaim() in case we need to use the checkpointed stack
pointer (see get_tm_stackpointer()).  Normally we'd then return
directly to userspace to deliver the signal without going through
__switch_to().

Unfortunatley, if at this point we get an error (such as a bad
userspace stack pointer), we need to exit the process.  The exit will
result in a __switch_to().  __switch_to() will attempt to save the
process state which results in another tm_reclaim().  This
tm_reclaim() now causes a TM Bad Thing exception as this state has
already been saved and the processor is no longer in TM suspend mode.
Whee!

This patch checks the state of the MSR to ensure we are TM suspended
before we attempt the tm_reclaim().  If we've already saved the state
away, we should no longer be in TM suspend mode.  This has the
additional advantage of checking for a potential TM Bad Thing
exception.

Found using syscall fuzzer.

Fixes: fb09692e71f1 ("powerpc: Add reclaim and recheckpoint functions for context switching transactional memory processes")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v3.9+
Signed-off-by: Michael Neuling <mikey@neuling.org>
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>

commit_msg:
In commit 73f156a6e8c1 ("inetpeer: get rid of ip_id_count")
I used a very small hash table that could be abused
by patient attackers to reveal sensitive information.

Switch to a dynamic sizing, depending on RAM size.

Typical big hosts will now use 128x more storage (2 MB)
to get a similar increase in security and reduction
of hash collisions.

As a bonus, use of alloc_large_system_hash() spreads
allocated memory among all NUMA nodes.

Fixes: 73f156a6e8c1 ("inetpeer: get rid of ip_id_count")

Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

commit_msg:
Bug#24388746: PRIVILEGE ESCALATION AND RACE CONDITION USING CREATE TABLE

During REPAIR TABLE of a MyISAM table, a temporary data file (.TMD)
is created. When repair finishes, this file is renamed to the original
.MYD file. The problem was that during this rename, we copied the
stats from the old file to the new file with chmod/chown. If a user
managed to replace the temporary file before chmod/chown was executed,
it was possible to get an arbitrary file with the privileges of the
mysql user.

This patch fixes the problem by not copying stats from the old
file to the new file. This is not needed as the new file was
created with the correct stats. This fix only changes server
behavior - external utilities such as myisamchk still does
chmod/chown.

No test case provided since the problem involves synchronization
with file system operations.

description: Race condition in Oracle MySQL before 5.5.52, 5.6.x before 5.6.33, 5.7.x before 5.7.15, and 8.x before 8.0.1; MariaDB before 5.5.52, 10.0.x before 10.0.28, and 10.1.x before 10.1.18; Percona Server before 5.5.51-38.2, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-78-1, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-8; and Percona XtraDB Cluster before 5.5.41-37.0, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-25.17, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-26.17 allows local users with certain permissions to gain privileges by leveraging use of my_copystat by REPAIR TABLE to repair a MyISAM table.

code_evidence: After repair succeeds, the code closes the temporary data file and calls change_to_newfile to rename the .TMD file onto the original .MYD name; the backup flag is passed via MY_REDEL_MAKE_BACKUP, and inside change_to_newfile the stats (chmod/chown) are copied from the old file to the new one. The rename and the subsequent stat copy are not atomic with respect to the temporary file's pathname, so another process can replace the temp file between the rename and the chmod/chown.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's rename-then-copystat sequence is a concurrent code sequence over a shared filesystem resource with a timing window in which another process can modify the resource, matching CWE-362. The privilege gain is the consequence of this race, not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: change_to_newfile renames the attacker-influenced temporary file and then copies ownership/permissions from the original file, without exclusive control of the temp path during that window. Trigger: a local user with write access to the temp directory swaps the .TMD file before chmod/chown runs. Consequence: the attacker-chosen file receives the mysql user's privileges, enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
x86/shadow: hold references for the duration of emulated writes

The (misnamed) emulate_gva_to_mfn() function translates a linear address to an
mfn, but releases its page reference before returning the mfn to its caller.

sh_emulate_map_dest() uses the results of one or two translations to construct
a virtual mapping to the underlying frames, completes an emulated
write/cmpxchg, then unmaps the virtual mappings.

The page references need holding until the mappings are unmapped, or the
frames can change ownership before the writes occurs.

This is XSA-219.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    put_page(mfn_to_page(sh_ctxt->mfn[0]));', '        put_page(mfn_to_page(sh_ctxt->mfn[1]));']}
description: The shadow-paging feature in Xen through 4.8.x mismanages page references and consequently introduces a race condition, which allows guest OS users to obtain Xen privileges, aka XSA-219.

code_evidence: The function marks mfn[0] and mfn[1] dirty and unmaps the virtual mappings, but only after the fix does it call put_page() to release the page references it acquired via emulate_gva_to_mfn().
Line 5 dereferences mfn_to_page(mfn[0])->shadow_flags, showing the code operates on page structures whose lifetime must remain pinned during the write/unmap sequence.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The exclusive access to the shared page resource spans translation through unmap, and the missing reference hold creates a timing window where an interfering sequence modifies the frame; this is a race condition (CWE-362), distinct from a simple use-after-free because the flaw is improper synchronization of the resource lifetime.

evidence_lines.code: shflags = mfn_to_page(sh_ctxt->mfn[0])->shadow_flags;

commit_msg:
[CVE-2022-23308] Use-after-free of ID and IDREF attributes

If a document is parsed with XML_PARSE_DTDVALID and without
XML_PARSE_NOENT, the value of ID attributes has to be normalized after
potentially expanding entities in xmlRemoveID. Otherwise, later calls
to xmlGetID can return a pointer to previously freed memory.

ID attributes which are empty or contain only whitespace after
entity expansion are affected in a similar way. This is fixed by
not storing such attributes in the ID table.

The test to detect streaming mode when validating against a DTD was
broken. In connection with the defects above, this could result in a
use-after-free when using the xmlReader interface with validation.
Fix detection of streaming mode to avoid similar issues. (This changes
the expected result of a test case. But as far as I can tell, using the
XML reader with XIncludes referencing the root document never worked
properly, anyway.)

All of these issues can result in denial of service. Using xmlReader
with validation could result in disclosure of memory via the error
channel, typically stderr. The security impact of xmlGetID returning
a pointer to freed memory depends on the application. The typical use
case of calling xmlGetID on an unmodified document is not affected.

The function duplicates value into ret->value and, when ctxt->vstateNr != 0, stores only ret->name, leaving ret->attr NULL because the streaming-mode attribute is expected to disappear.
xmlHashAddEntry(table, value, ret) stores this ID entry in the document's ID table keyed by value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a dangling reference to freed ID memory, matching CWE-416 Use After Free. The fix prevents storing empty values and corrects streaming detection, avoiding the stale entry rather than a simple NULL dereference (CWE-476).

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: xmlAddID stores ID entries whose value may later change (entity normalization) or be empty, and the streaming-mode detection via ctxt->vstateNr is unreliable. The stored value is not re-normalized, so xmlGetID can return a pointer to an ID entry whose value was freed. Consequence is use-after-free, potentially DoS or memory disclosure via error channel.

EVM: Use crypto_memneq() for digest comparisons

This patch fixes vulnerability CVE-2016-2085.  The problem exists
because the vm_verify_hmac() function includes a use of memcmp().
Unfortunately, this allows timing side channel attacks; specifically
a MAC forgery complexity drop from 2^128 to 2^12.  This patch changes
the memcmp() to the cryptographically safe crypto_memneq().

The implementation of the `OneHot` TFLite operator is vulnerable to a division by zero error(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/f61c57bd425878be108ec787f4d96390579fb83e/tensorflow/lite/kernels/one_hot.cc#L68-L72). commit_msg:
libelf: fix stack memory leak when loading 32 bit symbol tables

The 32 bit Elf structs are smaller than the 64 bit ones, which means that
when loading them there's some padding left uninitialized at the end of each
struct (because the size indicated in e_ehsize and e_shentsize is
smaller than the size of elf_ehdr and elf_shdr).

Fix this by introducing a new helper that is used to set
[caller_]xdest_{base/size} and that takes care of performing the appropriate
memset of the region. This newly introduced helper is then used to set and
unset xdest_{base/size} in elf_load_bsdsyms. Now that the full struct
is zeroed, there's no need to specifically zero the undefined section.

This is CVE-2016-9384 / XSA-164.

Suggested-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>

Also remove the open coded (and redundant with the earlier
elf_memset_unchecked()) use of caller_xdest_* from elf_init().

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <Ian.Jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* Allow elf_memcpy_safe to write to symbol_header. */', '    elf->caller_xdest_base = &header;', '    elf->caller_xdest_size = sizeof(header);', '    /* Zero the undefined section. */', '    section_handle = ELF_MAKE_HANDLE(elf_shdr,', '                     ELF_REALPTR2PTRVAL(&header.elf_header.section[SHN_UNDEF]));', '    elf_memset_safe(elf, ELF_HANDLE_PTRVAL(section_handle), 0, shdr_size);', '    elf->caller_xdest_base = NULL;', '    elf->caller_xdest_size = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    /* Allow elf_memcpy_safe to write to header. */', '    elf_set_xdest(elf, &header, sizeof(header));', '    elf_set_xdest(elf, NULL, 0);']}
description: Buffer overflow in hw/pt-msi.c in Xen 4.6.x and earlier, when using the qemu-xen-traditional (aka qemu-dm) device model, allows local x86 HVM guest administrators to gain privileges by leveraging a system with access to a passed-through MSI-X capable physical PCI device and MSI-X table entries, related to a "write path."

code_evidence: The caller_xdest_base/size window is set to the full local `header` before elf_memcpy_safe writes the ehdr into header.elf_header.header; the copy length is the guest-supplied e_ehsize, which for 32-bit ELF is smaller than the 64-bit elf_ehdr, leaving trailing padding uninitialized.

shdr_size is taken from the guest e_shentsize (smaller than elf_shdr for 32-bit) and used as the length for elf_memcpy_safe into section[SYMTAB_INDEX], again leaving padding bytes uninitialized rather than bounding the write to the destination element size.
The same shdr_size is reused for the STRTAB_INDEX copy at line 73-75, so the destination-bound mismatch is exercised again on the strtab section header.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs memory writes whose length is not restricted to the intended destination buffer/struct boundaries, allowing reads/writes outside the intended region. A narrower child such as CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) or CWE-125 could apply, but CWE-119 is the supplied target and the buffer-boundary violation is directly evidenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: copy lengths derived from guest-controlled e_ehsize/e_shentsize are used to write into fixed-size local Elf structs, and the caller_xdest window spans the whole `header` rather than being checked against each destination sub-object. Trigger: loading a 32-bit BSD symbol table where the guest sizes are smaller than the local struct sizes, leaving padding uninitialized. Consequence: uninitialized stack data is later copied into guest memory (information disclosure); the same pattern permits out-of-bounds writes if the guest sizes exceed the destination object.

fix PR#7003 and a few other bugs caused by misuse of Int_val

description: OCaml before 4.03.0 does not properly handle sign extensions, which allows remote attackers to conduct buffer overflow attacks or obtain sensitive information as demonstrated by a long string to the String.copy function.

code_evidence: Line 3 reads the OCaml value `size` with `Int_val`, which interprets only the low 32 bits and does not sign-extend a 64-bit boxed integer. The resulting `wosize` (mlsize_t) can therefore be a truncated or sign-extended-wrong value. Lines 4-5 use `wosize` directly as the element count passed to `caml_alloc`, with no bound or consistency check against the actual size of the source data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The incorrect size used to allocate a buffer causes later operations to read/write outside the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The sign-extension/truncation is the root cause; the buffer-boundary violation is the directly supported weakness.

commit_msg:
rxrpc: Fix race between conn bundle lookup and bundle removal [ZDI-CAN-15975]

After rxrpc_unbundle_conn() has removed a connection from a bundle, it
checks to see if there are any conns with available channels and, if not,
removes and attempts to destroy the bundle.

Whilst it does check after grabbing client_bundles_lock that there are no
connections attached, this races with rxrpc_look_up_bundle() retrieving the
bundle, but not attaching a connection for the connection to be attached
later.

There is therefore a window in which the bundle can get destroyed before we
manage to attach a new connection to it.

Fix this by adding an "active" counter to struct rxrpc_bundle:

 (1) rxrpc_connect_call() obtains an active count by prepping/looking up a
     bundle and ditches it before returning.

 (2) If, during rxrpc_connect_call(), a connection is added to the bundle,
     this obtains an active count, which is held until the connection is
     discarded.

 (3) rxrpc_deactivate_bundle() is created to drop an active count on a
     bundle and destroy it when the active count reaches 0.  The active
     count is checked inside client_bundles_lock() to prevent a race with
     rxrpc_look_up_bundle().

 (4) rxrpc_unbundle_conn() then calls rxrpc_deactivate_bundle().

Fixes: 245500d853e9 ("rxrpc: Rewrite the client connection manager")
Reported-by: zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com # ZDI-CAN-15975
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Tested-by: zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com
cc: Marc Dionne <marc.dionne@auristor.com>
cc: linux-afs@lists.infradead.org
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tatomic_set(&bundle->active, 1);']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernel's RxRPC network protocol, within the processing of RxRPC bundles. This issue results from the lack of proper locking when performing operations on an object. This may allow an attacker to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the kernel.

code_evidence: rxrpc_alloc_bundle() allocates a bundle with kzalloc and initializes its reference count, peer reference, channel lock and waiting_calls list, but the patch adds atomic_set(&bundle->active, 1) as the only lifetime/active-count initialization. The allocation path itself provides no synchronization against rxrpc_look_up_bundle()/rxrpc_unbundle_conn() concurrently finding or removing the same bundle; the added active counter is the mechanism that later guards destruction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a timing window on a shared bundle object whose exclusivity/atomicity is not ensured across concurrent lookup, attachment and removal, matching CWE-362. The added atomic active counter is the synchronization fix; the consequence is use-after-free/race, not a distinct weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The bundle is published and can be looked up while its lifetime is tracked only by the refcount and, after the fix, the active counter. Without that active count being set/held during lookup and connection attachment, an interfering sequence can remove and destroy the bundle in the window between lookup and attachment, so a connection later attaches to freed memory.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

commit_msg:
The functions that were used in the emulation of fxrstor, fxsave, sgdt and
sidt were originally meant for task switching, and as such they did not
check privilege levels.  This is very bad when the same functions are used
in the emulation of unprivileged instructions.  This is CVE-2018-10853.

The obvious fix is to add a new argument to ops->read_std and ops->write_std,
which decides whether the access is a "system" access or should use the
processor's CPL.

Fixes: 129a72a0d3c8 ("KVM: x86: Introduce segmented_write_std", 2017-01-12)
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn ctxt->ops->write_std(ctxt, linear, data, size, &ctxt->exception);'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn ctxt->ops->write_std(ctxt, linear, data, size, &ctxt->exception, false);']}
description: A flaw was found in the way Linux kernel KVM hypervisor before 4.18 emulated instructions such as sgdt/sidt/fxsave/fxrstor. It did not check current privilege(CPL) level while emulating unprivileged instructions. An unprivileged guest user/process could use this flaw to potentially escalate privileges inside guest.

code_evidence: segmented_write_std linearizes the segmented address and then unconditionally forwards the write to ctxt->ops->write_std with no privilege-level argument or CPL check; the patched call adds a false 'system access' flag, showing the original call performed a privileged write path regardless of the emulated context's CPL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function omits a privilege check when performing an operation on behalf of the emulated instruction, giving an unprivileged actor an unintended sphere of control; this is improper privilege management, not merely a bounds or memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the helper performs a standard-address write through a callback that was designed for task switching and does not verify the current privilege level. Trigger: an unprivileged guest process causes emulation of an instruction (e.g. sgdt/sidt) that reaches this write path. Consequence: the emulated write is performed with system privileges, allowing privilege escalation inside the guest.

description: FreeRDP is a free remote desktop protocol library and clients. Affected versions of FreeRDP are missing input length validation in the `urbdrc` channel. commit_msg:
libblkid: care about unsafe chars in cache

The high-level libblkid API uses /run/blkid/blkid.tab cache to
store probing results. The cache format is

   <device NAME="value" ...>devname</device>

and unfortunately the cache code does not escape quotation marks:

   # mkfs.ext4 -L 'AAA"BBB'

   # cat /run/blkid/blkid.tab
   ...
   <device ... LABEL="AAA"BBB" ...>/dev/sdb1</device>

such string is later incorrectly parsed and blkid(8) returns
nonsenses. And for use-cases like

   # eval $(blkid -o export /dev/sdb1)

it's also insecure.

Note that mount, udevd and blkid -p are based on low-level libblkid
API, it bypass the cache and directly read data from the devices.

The current udevd upstream does not depend on blkid(8) output at all,
it's directly linked with the library and all unsafe chars are encoded by
\x<hex> notation.

   # mkfs.ext4 -L 'X"`/tmp/foo` "' /dev/sdb1
   # udevadm info --export-db | grep LABEL
   ...
   E: ID_FS_LABEL=X__/tmp/foo___
   E: ID_FS_LABEL_ENC=X\x22\x60\x2ftmp\x2ffoo\x60\x20\x22

Signed-off-by: Karel Zak <kzak@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tfprintf(file, " %s=\\"%s\\"", tag->bit_name,tag->bit_val);'], 'added_lines': ['', '', "\t\tfputc(' ', file);\t\t\t/* space between tags */", '\t\tfputs(tag->bit_name, file);\t\t/* tag NAME */', "\t\tfputc('=', file);\t\t\t/* separator between NAME and VALUE */", '\t\tsave_quoted(tag->bit_val, file);\t/* tag "VALUE" */']}
description: Blkid in util-linux before 2.26rc-1 allows local users to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: The tag loop writes each tag value into the cache file with fprintf using the format " %s=\"%s\"", embedding tag->bit_val verbatim between double quotes without escaping. A value containing a double quote (e.g. a filesystem LABEL with '"') breaks out of the quoted attribute and injects additional text into the cache entry.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The cache line is a command-language record whose special elements (quotes) are not neutralized, so externally influenced input can alter the intended command when consumed by shell evaluation, matching CWE-77's non-OS-specific command injection. It is not CWE-78 because the injection is via the blkid cache syntax, not direct shell invocation in this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: tag->bit_val from device metadata is written to the blkid.tab cache without neutralizing quote characters. Trigger: a local user sets a filesystem label containing '"' and backticks/commands; the crafted cache line is later parsed and, for consumers like 'eval $(blkid -o export)', interpreted as shell syntax. Supported consequence: command execution in the context of the evaluating user.

description: A heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability exists in GPAC v1.0.1 in the gf_isom_dovi_config_get function in MP4Box, which causes a denial of service or execute arbitrary code via a crafted file.

Lines 12-24 switch on entry->type and cast entry to GF_MPEGAudioSampleEntryBox (line 18) or GF_MPEGVisualSampleEntryBox (line 22) based solely on the fourcc subtype, without verifying entry->internal_type matches the expected audio or video box layout before dereferencing cfg_3gpp.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing internal_type check allows an out-of-bounds write via the memcpy of config through a mis-cast pointer; this is an out-of-bounds write rather than a mere type-confusion read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the subtype switch trusts the box fourcc to imply a concrete sample-entry structure, so a crafted file declaring a 3GP audio/video subtype on a differently-sized sample entry leads to a wrongly-typed cast. The cast then reads cfg_3gpp at an offset beyond the actual allocation, and line 19/23 take the address of the embedded cfg used by the later memcpy at line 31, producing an out-of-bounds access. Trigger: crafted MP4 sample description. Consequence: heap memory corruption, denial of service, or code execution.

commit_msg:
NetKVM: BZ#1169718: Checking the length only on read

Signed-off-by: Joseph Hindin <yhindin@rehat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['tTcpIpPacketParsingResult ParaNdis_ReviewIPPacket(PVOID buffer, ULONG size, LPCSTR caller)', '    tTcpIpPacketParsingResult res = QualifyIpPacket((IPHeader *) buffer, size);'], 'added_lines': ['tTcpIpPacketParsingResult ParaNdis_ReviewIPPacket(PVOID buffer, ULONG size, BOOLEAN verifyLength, LPCSTR caller)', '    tTcpIpPacketParsingResult res = QualifyIpPacket((IPHeader *) buffer, size, verifyLength);']}
description: The NetKVM Windows Virtio driver allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (guest crash) via a crafted length value in an IP packet, as demonstrated by a value that does not account for the size of the IP options.

code_evidence: The wrapper accepts a packet buffer and a caller-supplied size and forwards them directly to QualifyIpPacket((IPHeader *) buffer, size) without any length or IP-option consistency check in this function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper validation of attacker-controlled length metadata before it is used to parse the packet, matching CWE-20. It is not merely a transformation or encoding issue; the missing size/consistency check is the core defect.

evidence_lines.code:
tTcpIpPacketParsingResult ParaNdis_ReviewIPPacket(PVOID buffer, ULONG size, LPCSTR caller)
tTcpIpPacketParsingResult res = QualifyIpPacket((IPHeader *) buffer, size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function passes the untrusted packet length to QualifyIpPacket without verifying that it accounts for IP header options, so a crafted length value reaches the parser unchecked. Trigger: a remote attacker sends an IP packet whose length field is inconsistent with the actual header/options size. Supported consequence: the guest driver crashes, i.e., denial of service.

commit_msg:
net: vmxnet3: check for device_active before write

Vmxnet3 device emulator does not check if the device is active,
before using it for write. It leads to a use after free issue,
if the vmxnet3_io_bar0_write routine is called after the device is
deactivated. Add check to avoid it.

Reported-by: Li Qiang <liqiang6-s@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Acked-by: Dmitry Fleytman <dmitry@daynix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (!s->device_active) {', '        return;', '    }']}
description: Use-after-free vulnerability in the vmxnet3_io_bar0_write function in hw/net/vmxnet3.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (QEMU instance crash) by leveraging failure to check if the device is active.

code_evidence: The function dereferences the device state pointer s (obtained from opaque) and passes it to vmxnet3_process_tx_queue without verifying that the device is still active.
Similarly, the interrupt-mask branch invokes vmxnet3_on_interrupt_mask_changed(s, l, val) using the same device state with no liveness check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing device_active guard allows the function to reference freed VMXNET3State memory, matching CWE-416 use after free. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds access, since the weakness is lifetime misuse of the device object rather than an index/range violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: vmxnet3_io_bar0_write operates on VMXNET3State without confirming s->device_active, so a BAR0 write issued after device deactivation accesses state that may already be freed. Trigger: a guest administrator writes to the BAR0 MMIO region following deactivation; the consequence is a use-after-free that can crash the QEMU instance.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overrun when parsing an ELF attribute string that is not NUL terminated.

	PR 22058
	* elf-attrs.c (_bfd_elf_parse_attributes): Ensure that the
	attribute buffer is NUL terminated.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  contents = (bfd_byte *) bfd_malloc (hdr->sh_size);'], 'added_lines': ['  contents = (bfd_byte *) bfd_malloc (hdr->sh_size + 1);', '  /* Ensure that the buffer is NUL terminated.  */', '  contents[hdr->sh_size] = 0;']}
description: The _bfd_elf_parse_attributes function in elf-attrs.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (_bfd_elf_attr_strdup heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: The section contents are allocated with exactly hdr->sh_size bytes via bfd_malloc(hdr->sh_size) and filled with hdr->sh_size bytes from the file; no extra byte is reserved and no NUL terminator is appended.

Parsed attribute names and string values are passed as C strings to strcmp and strlen (e.g., p += strlen((char *)p) + 1), which scan until a NUL byte. If the crafted ELF attribute data lacks a NUL within the buffer, these reads continue past contents[hdr->sh_size-1] into adjacent heap memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory beyond the allocated buffer boundary via unbounded string scans, which is precisely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The missing terminator is the cause; the read past the buffer end is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the attribute buffer is exactly section-sized and not NUL-terminated, while strcmp/strlen treat offsets within it as C strings. Trigger: a crafted ELF file whose attribute string reaches the end of the section without a terminating NUL. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read, potentially crashing the application (DoS).

commit_msg:
Avoid 0==nbucket

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/393

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        unsigned const m = elf_hash(name) % nbucket;'], 'added_lines': ['        unsigned const m = elf_hash(name) % nbucket;']}
description: An floating point exception was discovered in the elf_lookup function in p_lx_elf.cpp in UPX 4.0.0 via a crafted Mach-O file.

commit_msg:
mp4: limit the recursion depth for boxes

Although the dissection of each box header consumes a couple of bytes,
it turned out that it's still possible to crash wireshark with a sample
file that contains a large number of nested boxes. The stack will fill
up before we reach the end of the data bytes.

Keep track of the recursion depth as we walk through the hierarchy of
boxes. Abort if we reach the (locally defined) upper limit.

Bug: 13777
Change-Id: I0f67245a5c74131f10d0f9d99b39ad31711b9775
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/26167
Reviewed-by: Martin Kaiser <wireshark@kaiser.cx>
Petri-Dish: Martin Kaiser <wireshark@kaiser.cx>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Anders Broman <a.broman58@gmail.com>
(cherry picked from commit 620f69a74b18908e3424920c7bb01cb5e4cbd8b1)
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/26204
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        packet_info *pinfo, proto_tree *tree)'], 'added_lines': ['        packet_info *pinfo, guint depth _U_, proto_tree *tree)']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.5 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.13, the MP4 dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/file-mp4.c by restricting the box recursion depth.

code_evidence: The function signature now accepts a recursion depth parameter (guint depth _U_) but marks it _U_ (unused) and never reads or validates it.
The body reads box fields and computes time_len from an unvalidated version byte, advancing offset through the buffer without checking remaining length.
Offset arithmetic and tvb_get_ntohl at line 47 consume data with no bounds or depth check before returning offset-offset_start.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts structured input (box headers, depth) without validating required properties such as nesting depth, matching CWE-20 improper input validation. A related but distinct weakness would be CWE-674 uncontrolled recursion; here the missing depth constraint is the validation failure.

evidence_lines.code:
dissect_mp4_mvhd_body(tvbuff_t *tvb, gint offset, gint len _U_,
packet_info *pinfo, proto_tree *tree)

version = tvb_get_guint8(tvb, offset);
time_len = (version==0) ? 4 : 8;

next_tid = tvb_get_ntohl(tvb, offset);
return offset-offset_start;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dissector does not validate the recursion depth (or remaining buffer length) while walking nested MP4 box headers. Trigger: a crafted file with deeply nested boxes causes unbounded recursion. Supported consequence: stack exhaustion and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
button->xkb_acts is supposed to be an array sufficiently large for all
our buttons, not just a single XkbActions struct. Allocating
insufficient memory here means when we memcpy() later in
XkbSetDeviceInfo we write into memory that wasn't ours to begin with,
leading to the usual security ooopsiedaisies.

CVE-2023-6377, ZDI-CAN-22412, ZDI-CAN-22413

This vulnerability was discovered by:
Jan-Niklas Sohn working with Trend Micro Zero Day Initiative
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if (!to->button->xkb_acts) {', '                to->button->xkb_acts = calloc(1, sizeof(XkbAction));', '                if (!to->button->xkb_acts)', '                    FatalError("[Xi] not enough memory for xkb_acts.\\n");', '            }', '                   sizeof(XkbAction));'], 'added_lines': ['            size_t maxbuttons = max(to->button->numButtons, from->button->numButtons);', '            to->button->xkb_acts = xnfreallocarray(to->button->xkb_acts,', '                                                   maxbuttons,', '                                                   sizeof(XkbAction));', '            memset(to->button->xkb_acts, 0, maxbuttons * sizeof(XkbAction));', '                   from->button->numButtons * sizeof(XkbAction));']}
description: A flaw was found in xorg-server. Querying or changing XKB button actions such as moving from a touchpad to a mouse can result in out-of-bounds memory reads and writes. This may allow local privilege escalation or possible remote code execution in cases where X11 forwarding is involved.

code_evidence: When from->button->xkb_acts is set, the code allocates only one XkbAction (calloc(1, sizeof(XkbAction))) at line 65 if to->button->xkb_acts is absent, then memcpy's sizeof(XkbAction) at lines 69-70. The allocation is sized for a single element rather than the button count, so the source buffer is read using the wrong extent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The faulty single-element allocation makes the memcpy read beyond the intended buffer, which is precisely CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not merely an out-of-bounds write because the read of from->button->xkb_acts occurs against an undersized buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: xkb_acts is treated as a one-element array during allocation while the copy later assumes an array sized by numButtons. Trigger: a button class with xkb_acts whose numButtons exceeds one. The memcpy reads past the allocated source region, yielding an out-of-bounds read of adjacent heap memory.

commit_msg:
mnt: Honor MNT_LOCKED when detaching mounts

Modify umount(MNT_DETACH) to keep mounts in the hash table that are
locked to their parent mounts, when the parent is lazily unmounted.

In mntput_no_expire detach the children from the hash table, depending
on mnt_pin_kill in cleanup_mnt to decrement the mnt_count of the children.

In __detach_mounts if there are any mounts that have been unmounted
but still are on the list of mounts of a mountpoint, remove their
children from the mount hash table and those children to the unmounted
list so they won't linger potentially indefinitely waiting for their
final mntput, now that the mounts serve no purpose.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tpin_insert_group(&p->mnt_umount, &p->mnt_parent->mnt, &unmounted);', '\t\t\tumount_mnt(p);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tbool disconnect;', '\t\tdisconnect = !IS_MNT_LOCKED_AND_LAZY(p);', '', '\t\tpin_insert_group(&p->mnt_umount, &p->mnt_parent->mnt,', '\t\t\t\t disconnect ? &unmounted : NULL);', '\t\t\tif (!disconnect) {', "\t\t\t\t/* Don't forget about p */", '\t\t\t\tlist_add_tail(&p->mnt_child, &p->mnt_parent->mnt_mounts);', '\t\t\t} else {', '\t\t\t\tumount_mnt(p);', '\t\t\t}']}
description: fs/namespace.c in the Linux kernel before 4.0.2 processes MNT_DETACH umount2 system calls without verifying that the MNT_LOCKED flag is unset, which allows local users to bypass intended access restrictions and navigate to filesystem locations beneath a mount by calling umount2 within a user namespace.

code_evidence: umount_tree unconditionally detaches each mount p: it calls pin_insert_group with &unmounted and, when mnt_has_parent(p), decrements the parent count and calls umount_mnt(p). There is no check of the mount's MNT_LOCKED flag, so a locked mount is torn down like any other during a MNT_DETACH umount.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to enforce the MNT_LOCKED access restriction on mount detachment, so a protected mount can be removed contrary to the intended policy. This is an access-control enforcement failure (CWE-284); it is not a memory-safety flaw, so a descendant such as improper resource handling does not fit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the detach path lacks any constraint honoring MNT_LOCKED, which is meant to keep mounts locked to their parent. Trigger: a local user in a user namespace issues umount2 with MNT_DETACH on a mount whose submounts are locked. Consequence: the locked mount is removed and the restriction is bypassed, enabling navigation to filesystem locations beneath the mount.

commit_msg:
Fix encoding bug in i2c_ASN1_INTEGER

Fix bug where i2c_ASN1_INTEGER mishandles zero if it is marked as
negative.

Thanks to Huzaifa Sidhpurwala <huzaifas@redhat.com> and
Hanno Böck <hanno@hboeck.de> for reporting this issue.

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
(cherry picked from commit a0eed48d37a4b7beea0c966caf09ad46f4a92a44)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (BN_is_negative(bn))'], 'added_lines': ['    if (BN_is_negative(bn) && !BN_is_zero(bn))']}
description: The ASN.1 implementation in OpenSSL before 1.0.1o and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2c allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (buffer underflow and memory corruption) via an ANY field in crafted serialized data, aka the "negative zero" issue.

code_evidence: Line 13 sets the ASN.1 type to V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER solely from BN_is_negative(bn); negative zero is therefore encoded as a negative integer rather than plain zero.
Lines 17-18 compute len from BN_num_bits(bn), giving len 0 for zero; line 27 stores BN_bn2bin output, and lines 28-31 handle a zero-length encoding by writing data[0]=0 and setting length 1.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The mis-tagged negative zero causes consumers to perform reads outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The function itself mislabels the value rather than directly indexing out of bounds, but this inconsistency is the origin of the resultant out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: negative zero is tagged as a negative integer while the buffer length is derived from a zero bit count, producing a mismatch between the declared signed encoding and the single byte actually written. Downstream ASN.1 readers trusting the negative-integer tag can miscompute the content length, yielding a buffer underflow and out-of-bounds memory access.

commit_msg:
Prevent division by zero.

Under specific test cases, the application could crash with a
floating point exception.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  presult->value /= parg->value;'], 'added_lines': ['  if (parg->value != 0)', '  {', '    presult->value /= parg->value;', '  }']}
description: In crasm 1.8-3, invalid input validation, specific files passed to the command line application, can lead to a NULL pointer dereference in the function Xasc.

code_evidence: Line 5 validates the operand types via checktype but does not constrain parg->value; line 6 divides presult->value by parg->value unconditionally, so a zero divisor reaches the division.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs integer division where the divisor can be zero, directly matching CWE-369 (Divide By Zero). Type checks on lines 4-5 do not prevent a zero value, so the missing guard is the relevant constraint, not a type-confusion issue.

evidence_lines.code:
checktype(parg, L_ABSOLUTE);
presult->value /= parg->value;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the divisor parg->value is used in an integer division without any zero check. Trigger: a caller supplies an operand whose value is zero (reachable through command-line input). Consequence: the division raises a floating-point/divide exception and crashes the application, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
The comparison for devnr limits is off-by-one, the current check
allows 0 to AD5755_NUM_CHANNELS and the limit should be in fact
0 to AD5755_NUM_CHANNELS - 1.  This can lead to an out of bounds
write to pdata->dac[devnr]. Fix this by replacing > with >= on the
comparison.

Signed-off-by: Colin Ian King <colin.king@canonical.com>
Fixes: c947459979c6 ("iio: ad5755: add support for dt bindings")
Signed-off-by: Jonathan Cameron <jic23@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (devnr > AD5755_NUM_CHANNELS) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (devnr >= AD5755_NUM_CHANNELS) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in drivers/iio/dac/ad5755.c in the Linux kernel before 4.8.6. There is an out of bounds write in the function ad5755_parse_dt.

code_evidence: devnr starts at 0 and each device-tree child node increments it at line 93; the loop guard checks devnr > AD5755_NUM_CHANNELS, so devnr == AD5755_NUM_CHANNELS is accepted.
Inside the loop, pdata->dac[devnr] is indexed for mode, sense resistor, slew and other fields; with devnr equal to the array size, the write goes one element past pdata->dac.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through an index equal to the buffer's element count, a direct out-of-bounds write to pdata->dac. The fix changes > to >=, confirming the boundary error rather than a read overflow or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the off-by-one comparison (>) that permits devnr to reach AD5755_NUM_CHANNELS instead of stopping at NUM_CHANNELS-1. A device-tree node with enough child channels triggers writes such as pdata->dac[devnr].mode at the out-of-range index, corrupting memory beyond the dac array.

commit_msg:
Prevent segfault with incorrect form_int fid

Bug-Debian: https://github.com/tats/w3m/issues/15
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tforms[form_id]->next = forms[form_id - 1];'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (forms[form_id])', '\t    forms[form_id]->next = forms[form_id - 1];']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Tatsuya Kinoshita w3m fork before 0.5.3-31. w3m allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault and crash) via a crafted HTML page.

code_evidence: The loop iterates form_id from 1 to form_max and unconditionally dereferences forms[form_id] via forms[form_id]->next. The patch adds a NULL check, confirming forms[form_id] can be NULL when a crafted form_int fid produces a sparse form array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Dereferencing a possibly NULL forms[form_id] pointer without a guard is a direct NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476). The added if(forms[form_id]) guard confirms the missing validity check is the root cause, not an out-of-bounds index.

The loop dereferences each forms[form_id] without checking, so a crafted HTML page with an inconsistent form_int fid causes a NULL pointer dereference, crashing w3m (segmentation fault/DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix handling of symbolic link ACLs

On Linux ACLs on symbolic links are not supported.
We must avoid calling acl_set_file() on symbolic links as their
targets are modified instead.

While here, do not try to set default ACLs on non-directories.

Fixes #1565
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t}', '', '\tif (S_ISLNK(mode)) {', '\t\t/* Linux does not support RichACLs on symbolic links */', '\t\treturn (ARCHIVE_OK);']}
description: An improper link resolution flaw while extracting an archive can lead to changing the access control list (ACL) of the target of the link. An attacker may provide a malicious archive to a victim user, who would trigger this flaw when trying to extract the archive. A local attacker may use this flaw to change the ACL of a file on the system and gain more privileges.

code_evidence: After building the richacl, the function applies it by fd when fd>=0 (richacl_set_fd) or, in the else branch, by pathname via richacl_set_file(name, richacl) at line 0107. The pathname-based call resolves name without any check that name is not a symbolic link; the mode parameter is available but not consulted here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits: the product accesses a file by filename (richacl_set_file(name,...)) without preventing that filename from being a link resolving to an unintended resource, exactly the link-following pattern. Contrast with CWE-22 (path traversal), which concerns escaping a directory via path components rather than following a symlink to a different target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pathname branch (line 0107) calls richacl_set_file on name without rejecting a symlink, so the ACL is applied to the link target rather than the link itself. Trigger: an attacker-supplied archive entry whose name is a symbolic link to a victim file; on extraction the else branch runs and modifies the target's ACL, potentially granting more privileges. Consequence: unauthorized ACL modification of an unintended file (integrity/access-control impact). The fd branch is not affected because it operates on an already-opened descriptor.

commit_msg:
hv: validate input for dmar_free_irte function

 Malicious input 'index' may trigger buffer
 overflow on array 'irte_alloc_bitmap[]'.

 This patch validate that 'index' shall be
 less than 'CONFIG_MAX_IR_ENTRIES' and also
 remove unnecessary check on 'index' in
 'ptirq_free_irte()' function with this fix.

Tracked-On: #6132
Signed-off-by: Yonghua Huang <yonghua.huang@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (is_dmar_unit_valid(dmar_unit, sid)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (is_dmar_unit_valid(dmar_unit, sid) && (index < CONFIG_MAX_IR_ENTRIES)) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in ACRN before 2.5. dmar_free_irte in hypervisor/arch/x86/vtd.c allows an irte_alloc_bitmap buffer overflow.

code_evidence: The guard at line 11 only checks is_dmar_unit_valid(dmar_unit, sid); it does not bound the caller-supplied uint16_t index before the pointer arithmetic ir_table + index at line 13, and line 14 then writes ir_entry->bits.remap.present = 0x0UL through that out-of-range pointer.
Line 19 derives the bitmap word from the same unbounded index (index >> 6U) and clears a bit in dmar_unit->irte_alloc_bitmap, so an oversized index also reaches the bitmap array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an out-of-bounds write driven by an unchecked index, i.e. a write past the end of a buffer without validating the input size/offset — the classic buffer overflow pattern. CWE-120 fits this write-overflow; it is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), since the defect is the unchecked write.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!is_irte_reserved(dmar_unit, index)) {
bitmap_clear_nolock(index & 0x3FU, &dmar_unit->irte_alloc_bitmap[index >> 6U]);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dmar_free_irte trusts the index argument and computes ir_table + index without checking index against CONFIG_MAX_IR_ENTRIES. Trigger: a caller or malicious input supplies an index at or beyond the table size, so the present-bit write and the bitmap_clear_nolock operate outside their arrays. The supported consequence is memory modification beyond the intended IR entry/bitmap, as the commit describes for irte_alloc_bitmap; the patch adds the missing index < CONFIG_MAX_IR_ENTRIES check.

commit_msg: fixed #2138
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbuf64 = gf_malloc(size*2);', '\tsize64 = gf_base64_encode( buffer, size, buf64, size*2);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsize64 = size*2 + 3;', '\tbuf64 = gf_malloc(sizeof(char) * size64);', '\tsize64 = gf_base64_encode( buffer, size, buf64, size64);']}
description: GPAC 2.0 allows a heap-based buffer overflow in gf_base64_encode. It can be triggered via MP4Box.

code_evidence: Line 16 allocates only size*2 bytes for buf64, and line 17 passes size*2 as the output capacity to gf_base64_encode; base64 output for size input bytes is 4*ceil(size/3), which can exceed size*2. Line 18 then writes the terminator at buf64[size64], an additional byte beyond the returned encoded length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes encoded data and a NUL terminator beyond the malloc'd buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). A related integer issue is not the direct weakness here; the supported defect is the write past the end of the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer capacity is underestimated relative to base64 expansion plus a NUL terminator. description: The ReadPESImage function in coders\pes.c in ImageMagick 7.0.6-1 has an infinite loop vulnerability that can cause CPU exhaustion via a crafted PES file.

code_evidence: The parsing loop at line 92 continues while EOFBlob(image) != EOF. It reads two bytes at lines 94-95 and only breaks on the marker (0xff,0x00) at lines 96-97, or on the block marker at lines 98-105.

Each successful iteration appends a stitch and increments i (line 144); when the buffer fills, it doubles number_stitches and resizes (lines 145-152). If ReadBlobByte returns EOF, the loop condition is never re-evaluated as true and the marker check cannot terminate it.

CVE-2017-13012/ICMP: Add a missing bounds check.

Check before fetching the length from the included packet's IPv4 header.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s), modified
so the capture file won't be rejected as an invalid capture.

description: The ICMP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-icmp.c:icmp_print().

code_evidence: Line 21 casts the second packet pointer bp2 to a const struct ip * without validating that bp2 points to a complete IPv4 header.

Lines 218-224 enter the error-payload branch when ndo_vflag>=1 and the ICMP type is an error type; bp is advanced by 8 and cast to struct ip, then line 223 reads ip->ip_len via EXTRACT_16BITS without any prior bounds test against ndo->ndo_snapend.

commit_msg:
tcp: mark skbs with SCM_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS

SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS can be enabled and disabled
while packets are collected on the error queue.
So, checking SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS in sk->sk_tsflags
is not enough to safely assume that the skb contains
OPT_STATS data.

Add a bit in sock_exterr_skb to indicate whether the
skb contains opt_stats data.

Fixes: 1c885808e456 ("tcp: SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS option for SO_TIMESTAMPING")
Reported-by: JongHwan Kim <zzoru007@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Soheil Hassas Yeganeh <soheil@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Willem de Bruijn <willemb@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t    (sk->sk_tsflags & SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t    SKB_EXT_ERR(skb)->opt_stats)']}
description: The TCP stack in the Linux kernel through 4.10.6 mishandles the SCM_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS feature, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from the kernel's internal socket data structures or cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via crafted system calls, related to net/core/skbuff.c and net/socket.c.

code_evidence: The OPT_STATS cmsg is emitted based on the live socket flag sk->sk_tsflags rather than on whether the skb actually carries opt_stats data. skb->len and skb->data are then passed directly to put_cmsg, so the copied length derives from the skb payload while the flag can be toggled independently of the skb contents.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function performs a buffer read whose length is not validated against the actual data present, reading past the intended bounds. It is not simply an info-leak variant; the underlying operation is an out-of-bounds read driven by stale opt_stats assumption.

evidence_lines.code:
if (skb_is_err_queue(skb) && skb->len &&
(sk->sk_tsflags & SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS))
put_cmsg(msg, SOL_SOCKET, SCM_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS,
skb->len, skb->data);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decision to copy OPT_STATS data is gated on mutable socket state (sk->sk_tsflags), not on per-skb metadata. Trigger: OPT_STATS is enabled/disabled while error-queue packets are collected, so a skb lacking opt_stats data is treated as containing it. Consequence: put_cmsg copies skb->len bytes from skb->data, reading beyond the intended buffer, leaking kernel memory or causing an out-of-bounds read/DoS.

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Rewrite guest %cr4 handling from scratch

The PV cr4 logic is almost impossible to follow, and leaks bits into guest
context which definitely shouldn't be visible (in particular, VMXE).

The biggest problem however, and source of the complexity, is that it derives
new real and guest cr4 values from the current value in hardware - this is
context dependent and an inappropriate source of information.

Rewrite the cr4 logic to be invariant of the current value in hardware.

First of all, modify write_ptbase() to always use mmu_cr4_features for IDLE
and HVM contexts.  mmu_cr4_features *is* the correct value to use, and makes
the ASSERT() obviously redundant.

For PV guests, curr->arch.pv.ctrlreg[4] remains the guests view of cr4, but
all logic gets reworked in terms of this and mmu_cr4_features only.

Two masks are introduced; bits which the guest has control over, and bits
which are forwarded from Xen's settings.  One guest-visible change here is
that Xen's VMXE setting is no longer visible at all.

pv_make_cr4() follows fairly closely from pv_guest_cr4_to_real_cr4(), but
deliberately starts with mmu_cr4_features, and only alters the minimal subset
of bits.

The boot-time {compat_,}pv_cr4_mask variables are removed, as they are a
remnant of the pre-CPUID policy days.  pv_fixup_guest_cr4() gains a related
derivation from the policy.

Another guest visible change here is that a 32bit PV guest can now flip
FSGSBASE in its view of CR4.  While the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE instructions are
unusable outside of a 64bit code segment, the ability to modify FSGSBASE
matches real hardware behaviour, and avoids the need for any 32bit/64bit
differences in the logic.

Overall, this patch shouldn't have a practical change in guest behaviour.
VMXE will disappear from view, and an inquisitive 32bit kernel can now see
FSGSBASE changing, but this new logic is otherwise bug-compatible with before.

This is part of XSA-293.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    unsigned long cr4;', '    cr4 = v->arch.pv.ctrlreg[4];', '    v->arch.pv.ctrlreg[4] = cr4 ? pv_guest_cr4_fixup(v, cr4) :', '        real_cr4_to_pv_guest_cr4(mmu_cr4_features);'], 'added_lines': ['    v->arch.pv.ctrlreg[4] = pv_fixup_guest_cr4(v, v->arch.pv.ctrlreg[4]);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges because a guest can manipulate its virtualised %cr4 in a way that is incompatible with Linux (and possibly other guest kernels).

code_evidence: Line 133 copies all guest-supplied ctrlreg values, including ctrlreg[4] (%cr4), directly into v->arch.pv.ctrlreg from the guest context c(ctrlreg[i]). Lines 152-154 then take that guest-controlled cr4 value and only pass it through pv_guest_cr4_fixup(), or fall back to real_cr4_to_pv_guest_cr4(mmu_cr4_features) when zero; the guest value is never validated against a permitted set before being accepted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because untrusted guest input (%cr4) is processed without validating that its properties (allowed/forbidden bits) are safe and correct for the guest. This is improper input validation rather than a pure transformation flaw, since no check constrains the accepted value before use.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the guest's %cr4 is accepted from the hypercall-supplied context and merely masked/fixed up rather than validated against the set of bits Xen permits the guest to control. Trigger: a PV guest supplies a crafted ctrlreg[4] in its vcpu context. Consequence: the guest can manipulate virtualised %cr4 in a way incompatible with guest kernels, enabling DoS or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
x86/mm: properly flush TLB in switch_cr3_cr4()

The CR3 values used for contexts run with PCID enabled uniformly have
CR3.NOFLUSH set, resulting in the CR3 write itself to not cause any
flushing at all. When the second CR4 write is skipped or doesn't do any
flushing, there's nothing so far which would purge TLB entries which may
have accumulated again if the PCID doesn't change; the "just in case"
flush only affects the case where the PCID actually changes. (There may
be particularly many TLB entries re-accumulated in case of a watchdog
NMI kicking in during the critical time window.)

Suppress the no-flush behavior of the CR3 write in this particular case.

Similarly the second CR4 write may not cause any flushing of TLB entries
established again while the original PCID was still in use - it may get
performed because of unrelated bits changing. The flush of the old PCID
needs to happen nevertheless.

At the same time also eliminate a possible race with lazy context
switch: Just like for CR4, CR3 may change at any time while interrupts
are enabled, due to the __sync_local_execstate() invocation from the
flush IPI handler. It is for that reason that the CR3 read, just like
the CR4 one, must happen only after interrupts have been turned off.

This is XSA-292.

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Reported-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Tested-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
