description: A remote code execution vulnerability in id3/ID3.cpp in libstagefright in Mediaserver could enable an attacker using a specially crafted file to cause memory corruption during media file and data processing. This issue is rated as Critical due to the possibility of remote code execution within the context of the Mediaserver process. Product: Android. Versions: 4.4.4, 5.0.2, 5.1.1, 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2. Android ID: A-34618607.

code_evidence: The unsynchronization loop and the trailing memmove run without verifying that readOffset stays within the buffer. With flags&2 set, readOffset starts at offset+11 and can advance past oldSize (mSize) when dataSize is small, so the loop reads mData[readOffset] and memmove copies oldSize - readOffset bytes from &mData[readOffset] beyond the allocated mData buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs reads and a memmove on mData at offsets beyond the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The fix's readOffset <= oldSize guard confirms the missing bounds constraint; this is a buffer-boundary error rather than an integer-only weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unsynchronization block trusts dataSize and never bounds readOffset against oldSize/mSize before indexing and memmove. Trigger: a crafted ID3v2.4 tag with the unsynchronization flag and a small/truncated frame causes readOffset to exceed oldSize. Consequence: out-of-bounds read from mData and an oversized memmove length (oldSize - readOffset underflows), causing memory corruption and possible remote code execution in Mediaserver.

Allow fuse device clones to refer to be distinguished.  This patch just
adds the infrastructure by associating a separate "struct fuse_dev" with

Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@suse.cz>
Reviewed-by: Ashish Samant <ashish.samant@oracle.com>

description: Memory leak in the cuse_channel_release function in fs/fuse/cuse.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by opening /dev/cuse many times.

code_evidence: The release handler obtains the connection via fuse_get_conn(file) and only releases it with fuse_conn_put(fc) when fc is non-NULL. The reference is tied to the shared fuse_conn rather than a per-open fuse_dev, so each open of the device does not have an independently freed resource.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources; here the missing per-open resource release leads to resource exhaustion. It is a category, but the function's failure to free the per-open device state directly supports this resource-management weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The per-open device state is not separately tracked or freed; release only drops the shared connection reference. Repeatedly opening the device (e.g. /dev/cuse) accumulates resources that are never released per open, causing unbounded memory consumption and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Validate `proto.dtype()` before calling `set_dtype()`.

This prevents a `DCHECK`-fail when the proto contains an invalid dtype for a tensor shape with 0 elements or for an incomplete tensor shape.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 408369083
Change-Id: Ia21a3e3d62a90d642a4561f08f3b543e5ad00c46
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  } else {', '    // Handle the case of empty tensors (N = 0) or tensors with incomplete shape', '    // (N = -1). All other values of `shape.num_elements()` should be invalid by', '    // construction.', '    // Here, we just need to validate that the `proto.dtype()` value is valid.', '    bool dtype_error = false;', '    CASES_WITH_DEFAULT(proto.dtype(), break, dtype_error = true,', '                       dtype_error = true);', '    if (dtype_error) return false;']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. When decoding a tensor from protobuf, a TensorFlow process can encounter cases where a `CHECK` assertion is invalidated based on user controlled arguments, if the tensors have an invalid `dtype` and 0 elements or an invalid shape. This allows attackers to cause denial of services in TensorFlow processes. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 7 computes N from the attacker-supplied tensor_shape; line 8 gates the dtype validation block on N > 0, so when N is 0 or negative the entire dtype-checking branch (lines 8-19) is skipped.
With the guard bypassed, line 21 unconditionally calls set_dtype(proto.dtype()) with the unvalidated proto value, which reaches a DCHECK/CHECK on the invalid dtype.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits attacker-controlled proto fields to reach an assertion that terminates the process, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion). This is not merely improper input validation: the specific consequence is an assertion-triggered crash/exit from a reachable path.

evidence_lines.code:
shape_ = shape;
set_dtype(proto.dtype());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dtype validation is conditioned on N > 0, so empty (N=0) or incomplete (N=-1) shapes skip the CASES_WITH_DEFAULT check. Trigger: a crafted TensorProto with an invalid dtype and zero-element or incomplete shape. Consequence: set_dtype receives the unvalidated dtype and a reachable assertion aborts the process, causing denial of service.

description: In OpenCV 3.3.1, a heap-based buffer over-read exists in the function cv::HdrDecoder::checkSignature in modules/imgcodecs/src/grfmt_hdr.cpp.

code_evidence: The guard checks signature.size() against m_signature.size(), but the OR expression also calls memcmp with m_signature_alt.size() without verifying signature.size() >= m_signature_alt.size(). If the signature buffer is shorter than the alternate magic string, memcmp reads past the end of the signature buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads past the intended buffer boundary. It is not an out-of-bounds write, and the weakness is the missing per-comparison length constraint rather than a generic bounds error.

evidence_lines.code:
if(signature.size() >= m_signature.size() &&
(!memcmp(signature.c_str(), m_signature.c_str(), m_signature.size()) ||
!memcmp(signature.c_str(), m_signature_alt.c_str(), m_signature_alt.size())))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a single size check is applied to two different-length comparisons. Trigger: a candidate signature whose length satisfies the first check but is smaller than m_signature_alt.size(). Consequence: memcmp reads beyond the signature buffer (out-of-bounds read of heap memory).

Exit the max size loop when there's nothing left possible to find

exit too early.

description: libebml before 1.3.6, as used in the MKV module in VideoLAN VLC Media Player binaries before 3.0.3, has a heap-based buffer over-read in EbmlElement::FindNextElement.

code_evidence: The outer do-loop reads bytes into PossibleIdNSize[ReadIndex++] (line 34) and increments ReadSize, but the termination guard uses MaxDataSize <= ReadSize (line 32) rather than bounding the actual buffer index; ReadIndex is asserted <16 only before the read.

Inner size loop reads into PossibleIdNSize[SizeIdx++] (line 59) while PossibleSizeLength advances; loop breaks only on PossibleSizeLength >= 8 or MaxDataSize <= ReadSize, so buffer index growth depends on ReadSize accounting rather than the buffer bound.

After a failed element match, ReadIndex = SizeIdx - 1 and memmove (lines 83-84) shift the buffer, then the do-while condition (line 86) uses DataStream.getFilePointer() to decide continuation, which the commit notes is incorrect and may force early exit, leaving stale buffer state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads element ID/size bytes into a fixed 16-byte stack/heap-adjacent buffer whose index can exceed the intended bound, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. It is not merely an integer overflow; the observable defect is reading beyond the intended buffer extent.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: loop continuation and buffer-index advancement are governed by MaxDataSize/ReadSize and file-pointer arithmetic rather than the fixed 16-byte PossibleIdNSize buffer bound. Trigger: malformed EBML input where the size-value decoding loop keeps reading while ReadSize lags the index, causing PossibleIdNSize[SizeIdx++] to write/read past the array; the erroneous getFilePointer-based condition compounds stale state. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read of adjacent memory.

commit_msg: fix #345
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (cursor > payload_size) return NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['    if (cursor+1 > payload_size) return NULL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Bento4 1.5.1-627. There is a heap-based buffer over-read in AP4_AvccAtom::Create in Core/Ap4AvccAtom.cpp, as demonstrated by mp42hls.

code_evidence: After the sequence-parameter loop, bounds are checked only after reading payload[cursor++] at line 20; line 21's check (cursor > payload_size) occurs too late. The pre-read guard cursor+1 > payload_size (added by the patch) is missing here, so when cursor equals payload_size the read at line 20 accesses one byte past the buffer. The loop guards at 16 and 23 use cursor+2, but the single-byte read at 20 has no equivalent pre-check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads payload[cursor] beyond the allocated payload buffer's end before validating the index. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write (CWE-787) or integer overflow; the missing pre-read length constraint is the direct cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the single-byte read of num_pic_params at line 20 is not preceded by a cursor+1 bound check, only followed by a post-read check. Trigger: a crafted AVCC payload whose sequence-parameter parsing leaves cursor == payload_size. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read of one byte past payload_data, potentially disclosing or misusing adjacent memory and crashing.

description: logger.c in the logger plugin in WeeChat before 1.9.1 allows a crash via strftime date/time specifiers, because a buffer is not initialized.

code_evidence: length is computed from strlen(mask_decoded4)+256+1, then mask_decoded5 is malloc'd and only mask_decoded5[0] is set before strftime writes into it. If strftime encounters a date/time specifier producing output larger than the allocated buffer (the +256 slack is a heuristic, not a bound), it writes past mask_decoded5; the return value is ignored, so truncation/overflow is not detected.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a strftime write into a heap buffer whose intended boundary is not enforced against actual formatted output, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds write. The fix moves strftime earlier and checks its return value, confirming the sizing/strftime interaction as the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination buffer size is guessed from the input length plus a fixed 256 bytes rather than from the maximum expansion of the format string. Trigger: a mask containing strftime specifiers whose expansion exceeds strlen(mask_decoded4)+256. Consequence: strftime writes beyond the heap allocation, corrupting adjacent heap memory and potentially crashing.

description: ImageMagick 7.0.7-17 Q16 x86_64 has memory leaks in coders/msl.c, related to MSLPopImage and ProcessMSLScript, and associated with mishandling of MSLPushImage calls.

code_evidence: ProcessMSLScript allocates parallel arrays image_info, draw_info, image and attributes (and group_info) and initializes element 0; MSLPushImage can append further entries indexed by msl_info.n.

At cleanup only the element-0 objects are destroyed and the arrays are freed; entries 1..n created by MSLPushImage are never destroyed, leaking each pushed Image, ImageInfo, DrawInfo and attributes object. The leaked *msl_info.image is also assigned to *image without being tracked for release.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to release resources (the pushed image structures) after their effective lifetime ends, matching CWE-772. This is a missing-release defect, not a use-after-free or double-free, since the leaked entries are simply never destroyed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cleanup path assumes a single entry per array and destroys only index 0, while MSLPushImage grows the stacks to n entries. Trigger: any MSL document that pushes images via MSLPushImage. Consequence: the pushed Image/ImageInfo/DrawInfo/attributes objects are never released, leaking memory per processed script (DoS resource consumption).

commit_msg:
Trap for overly large input to XmlRPCPP which could cause problems with int <-> size_t conversions.

 - In XmlRpcClient, XmlRpcServerConnection and XmlRpcSocket, recognize when incoming or outgoing data is too large, generate an error and discard the data when practical.
 - Use the safe strtol() rather than atoi() to decode an incoming content-length header, and generate an error if the length is invalid or too large.
 - In XmlRpcUtil, prevent attempts to parse overly large XML input.
 - Add tests where they can reasonably be inserted into existing test routines.

Although this fix could be cleaner the update is written to make the update ABI compatible.

This fix addresses CVE-2020-16124 / Integer overflow in ros_comm.

Signed-off-by: Sid Faber <sid.faber@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  _response = header + body;', '  XmlRpcUtil::log(5, "XmlRpcServerConnection::generateResponse:\\n%s\\n", _response.c_str()); '], 'added_lines': ['  // Avoid an overly large response', '  if ((header.length() + body.length()) > size_t(__INT_MAX__)) {', '    XmlRpcUtil::error("XmlRpcServerConnection::generateResponse: response length (%u) exceeds the maximum allowed size (%u).",', '                      _response.length(), __INT_MAX__);', '    _response = "";', '  }', '  else {', '    _response = header + body;', '    XmlRpcUtil::log(5, "XmlRpcServerConnection::generateResponse:\\n%s\\n", _response.c_str());', '  }']}
description: Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability in the XML RPC library of OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages allows unauthenticated network traffic to cause unexpected behavior. This issue affects: OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages Noetic and prior versions. Fixed in https://github.com/ros/ros_comm/pull/2065.

code_evidence: Line 9 builds body by concatenating RESPONSE_1, resultXml and RESPONSE_2; header is generated from body at line 10. Line 11 concatenates header + body into _response with no length check on the combined result, and line 12 logs the full _response. The size of resultXml is attacker-influenced and unbounded here, so the concatenation can produce a response larger than the int/size_t range assumed elsewhere.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unsafe operation is an unchecked length computation over attacker-controlled data that can exceed the representable integer range used by the surrounding int/size_t logic. This is the integer-overflow/wraparound root cause, not merely a generic memory-exhaustion or unbounded-allocation weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the response string is assembled by unbounded concatenation of attacker-influenced resultXml with fixed wrappers and header, without validating the total length against the int/size_t limit. Trigger: an XML-RPC request producing a very large resultXml. Consequence: an oversized response whose length mismatches downstream int/size_t conversions, enabling the integer-overflow/wraparound behavior described in the CVE (availability/instability impact).

commit_msg:
pam_tacplus.c: Fallback to using PID as task ID

If there is a failure obtaining a random task ID for the session
accounting request then fallback to using the PID, as this is unique
for the lifetime of the PAM application and therefore session.

--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -3,9 +3,8 @@
                         const char **argv) {
 
 /* Task ID has no need to be cryptographically strong so we don't
- * check for failures of the RAND functions. If they fail then we are
- * as well sending the accounting request regardless of whether any value
- * was written to task_id.
+ * check for failures of the RAND functions. If we fail to get an ID we
+ * fallback to using our PID (in _pam_send_account).
  */
 #if defined(HAVE_OPENSSL_RAND_H) && defined(HAVE_LIBCRYPTO)
 # if defined(HAVE_RAND_BYTES)
@@ -17,5 +16,9 @@
 	task_id=(short int) magic();
 #endif
 
+	if (task_id == 0)
+		syslog(LOG_INFO, "%s: failed to generate random task ID, "
+				"falling back to PID", __FUNCTION__);
+
 	return _pam_account(pamh, argc, argv, TAC_PLUS_ACCT_FLAG_START, NULL);
 }

If we fail to get an ID we', ' * fallback to using our PID (in _pam_send_account).', '\tif (task_id == 0)', '\t\tsyslog(LOG_INFO, "%s: failed to generate random task ID, "', '\t\t\t\t"falling back to PID", __FUNCTION__);', '']}
description: libtac in pam_tacplus through 1.5.1 lacks a check for a failure of RAND_bytes()/RAND_pseudo_bytes(). This could lead to use of a non-random/predictable session_id.

code_evidence: RAND_bytes/RAND_pseudo_bytes write task_id but their return value is ignored, so a failed call leaves task_id unset or zero.
task_id is then passed implicitly into _pam_account for the accounting session request without any failure check or fallback.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is use of insufficiently random values: a security-relevant session identifier is derived from a RNG whose failure is unchecked. Contrast CWE-252 (unchecked return value) as the proximate cause; the supported weakness is the predictable/non-random identifier (CWE-330).

evidence_lines.code:
RAND_bytes((unsigned char *) &task_id, sizeof(task_id));
RAND_pseudo_bytes((unsigned char *) &task_id, sizeof(task_id));
return _pam_account(pamh, argc, argv, TAC_PLUS_ACCT_FLAG_START, NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The random-generation return status is discarded, so when RAND_bytes/RAND_pseudo_bytes fail the session task_id is not populated with unpredictable bytes. The resulting accounting session identifier can be zero or stale, letting an observer correlate, predict or forge session accounting records tied to that ID.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12988/TELNET: Add a missing bounds check.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Forcepoint's security
researchers Otto Airamo & Antti Levomäki.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tND_TCHECK(*p);']}
description: The telnet parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-telnet.c:telnet_parse().

code_evidence: The SB subnegotiation scan advances p up to the point where length > (p+1-sp) fails, then dereferences *p at line 51 without verifying p is within the captured buffer; ND_TCHECK2 only checks the two bytes read inside the loop, not the terminating byte after the loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Dereferencing p after a loop that only guarantees coverage of p[0..1] while p was advancing directly supports CWE-125: reading data past the end of the intended buffer. It is not a write overflow, since only a read of *p occurs.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The while loop stops when the remaining length no longer covers p+1, leaving p possibly at or beyond the end of captured data. The subsequent dereference *p reads one byte past the intended buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read of packet memory (crash or memory disclosure) triggered by a truncated SB subnegotiation.

description: A vulnerability, which was classified as problematic, was found in GPAC 2.1-DEV-rev490-g68064e101-master. Affected is the function lsr_translate_coords of the file laser/lsr_dec.c. The manipulation leads to integer overflow. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. The name of the patch is b3d821c4ae9ba62b3a194d9dcb5e99f17bd56908. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-214518 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: Line 3 tests the sign bit of val using lsr->coord_bits; when set, line 4 computes v = val - (1<<lsr->coord_bits). The shift is performed in int (1 is int), and the result is stored in a signed 32-bit s32. If coord_bits reaches 31 or more, 1<<coord_bits overflows the int shift; and the subtraction/multiplication in INT2FIX can overflow s32 for large val and coord_bits.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is improper numeric calculation/overflow in the coordinate translation, matching CWE-189 Numeric Errors. It is an integer overflow (CWE-190), a member of this category, rather than a format/string or memory-corruption weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sign-extension subtraction and INT2FIX conversion are performed in 32-bit signed arithmetic without range checks on lsr->coord_bits or val. Trigger: attacker-controlled coordinate bit width or value causing the shift or subtraction to exceed s32. Consequence: signed integer overflow yields a wrong Fixed coordinate (supported by the patch widening v to s64 and the shift to unsigned long).

commit_msg:
Fixed aggregation methods of Promise ctor with array-like object.

Previously, while iterating over an array-like object the methods may be
resolved with INVALID values. INVALID value is a special internal type which
should never be visible by ordinary functions.

The fix is to ensure that absent elements are represented by undefined value.

The following methods were fixed Promise.all(), Promise.allSettled(),
    Promise.any(), Promise.race().

This closes #483 issue on Github.

commit_msg:
copy: CVE-2022-0485: Fail nbdcopy if NBD read or write fails

nbdcopy has a nasty bug when performing multi-threaded copies using
asynchronous nbd calls - it was blindly treating the completion of an
asynchronous command as successful, rather than checking the *error
parameter.  This can result in the silent creation of a corrupted
image in two different ways: when a read fails, we blindly wrote
garbage to the destination; when a write fails, we did not flag that
the destination was not written.

Since nbdcopy already calls exit() on a synchronous read or write
failure to a file, doing the same for an asynchronous op to an NBD
server is the simplest solution.  A nicer solution, but more invasive
to code and thus not done here, might be to allow up to N retries of
the transaction (in case the read or write failure was transient), or
even having a mode where as much data is copied as possible (portions
of the copy that failed would be logged on stderr, and nbdcopy would
still fail with a non-zero exit status, but this would copy more than
just stopping at the first error, as can be done with rsync or
ddrescue).

Note that since we rely on auto-retiring and do NOT call
nbd_aio_command_completed, our completion callbacks must always return
1 (if they do not exit() first), even when acting on *error, so as not
leave the command allocated until nbd_close.  As such, there is no
sane way to return an error to a manual caller of the callback, and
therefore we can drop dead code that calls perror() and exit() if the
callback "failed".  It is also worth documenting the contract on when
we must manually call the callback during the asynch_zero callback, so
that we do not leak or double-free the command; thankfully, all the
existing code paths were correct.

The added testsuite script demonstrates several scenarios, some of
which fail without the rest of this patch in place, and others which
showcase ways in which sparse images can bypass errors.

Once backports are complete, a followup patch on the main branch will
edit docs/libnbd-security.pod with the mailing list announcement of
the stable branch commit ids and release versions that incorporate
this fix.

description: A flaw was found in the copying tool `nbdcopy` of libnbd. When performing multi-threaded copies using asynchronous nbd calls, nbdcopy was blindly treating the completion of an asynchronous command as successful, rather than checking the *error parameter. This could result in the silent creation of a corrupted destination image.

commit_msg:
bpf: fix incorrect tracking of register size truncation

Properly handle register truncation to a smaller size.

The old code first mirrors the clearing of the high 32 bits in the bitwise
tristate representation, which is correct. But then, it computes the new
arithmetic bounds as the intersection between the old arithmetic bounds and
the bounds resulting from the bitwise tristate representation. Therefore,
when coerce_reg_to_32() is called on a number with bounds
[0xffff'fff8, 0x1'0000'0007], the verifier computes
[0xffff'fff8, 0xffff'ffff] as bounds of the truncated number.
This is incorrect: The truncated number could also be in the range [0, 7],
and no meaningful arithmetic bounds can be computed in that case apart from
the obvious [0, 0xffff'ffff].

Starting with v4.14, this is exploitable by unprivileged users as long as
the unprivileged_bpf_disabled sysctl isn't set.

Debian assigned CVE-2017-16996 for this issue.

v2:
 - flip the mask during arithmetic bounds calculation (Ben Hutchings)
v3:
 - add CVE number (Ben Hutchings)

Fixes: b03c9f9fdc37 ("bpf/verifier: track signed and unsigned min/max values")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Edward Cree <ecree@solarflare.com>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t/* high 32 bits are known zero. */', '\t\t\t\tregs[insn->dst_reg].var_off = tnum_cast(', '\t\t\t\t\t\tregs[insn->dst_reg].var_off, 4);', '\t\t\t\t__update_reg_bounds(&regs[insn->dst_reg]);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tcoerce_reg_to_size(&regs[insn->dst_reg], 4);']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging register truncation mishandling.

code_evidence: For a 32-bit BPF_MOV X, the destination is marked unknown and its var_off is truncated via tnum_cast(var_off, 4); then __update_reg_bounds intersects the old arithmetic bounds with the truncated tristate bounds, yielding an incorrect (too narrow) range for the truncated register.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsound bounds tracking permits a program to bypass verifier range checks and perform memory accesses outside the intended buffer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operations. The root cause is incorrect truncation-bound computation rather than the memory access itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the verifier derives 32-bit truncation bounds by intersecting old bounds with the cast tristate, which is unsound when the value straddles the 32-bit boundary, so the tracked min/max can be narrower than the actual possible range. A user-supplied BPF program exploiting this lets later bounds checks pass, and out-of-range memory accesses or corruption can result (CVE-2017-16996).

CVE-2017-13690/IKEv2: Fix some bounds checks.

Use a pointer of the correct type in ND_TCHECK(), or use ND_TCHECK2()
and provide the correct length.

While we're at it, remove the blank line between some checks and the
UNALIGNED_MEMCPY()s they protect.

Also, note the places where we print the entire payload.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).

description: The IKEv2 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isakmp.c, several functions.

code_evidence: The loop casts cp to isakmp_gen, checks prop_length >= sizeof(*ext), then ND_TCHECK(*ext) and UNALIGNED_MEMCPY(&e, ext, sizeof(e)). item_len from e.len is then validated (item_len<=4 trunc, prop_length<item_len toolong) and ND_TCHECK2(*cp, item_len) bounds the payload before ikev2_t_print or cp += item_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described defect is a read beyond the captured buffer in the IKEv2 parser, matching CWE-125. It is not CWE-787, since no out-of-bounds write occurs.

commit_msg:
Add command line and configuration option to set umask

Issue #1048 identified that files created by keepalived are created
with mode 0666. This commit changes the default to 0644, and also
allows the umask to be specified in the configuration or as a command
line option.

Signed-off-by: Quentin Armitage <quentin@armitage.org.uk>

description: keepalived 2.0.8 used mode 0666 when creating new temporary files upon a call to PrintData or PrintStats, potentially leaking sensitive information.

code_evidence: Line 202 calls umask(0) immediately after the daemon fork, clearing the file creation mask so all subsequently created files use the process-requested mode (e.g. 0666) without restriction.

Line 88 allocates global_data, but the function never applies a restrictive mask before files such as temporary PrintData/PrintStats output are created; the default mask is only set later/elsewhere, not in this path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is that files holding sensitive data are created overly permissive due to umask(0), enabling unauthorized actors to read the contents. This is an information exposure through insecure file permissions; CWE-200 covers such resultant disclosure of sensitive information.

umask(0);
#ifdef _MEM_CHECK_

global_data = alloc_global_data();
read_config_file();

Trigger: a call to PrintData/PrintStats after startup creates such a file. Consequence: sensitive information written to those files is readable by unauthorized local users, an information exposure.

-				if (sactif->Actions[sactif->numActions-1].SWF_ACTIONRECORD.ActionCode==SWFACTION_JUMP

commit_msg:
In the event of a failure in tcf_change_indev(), u32_set_parms() will
immediately return without decrementing the recently incremented
reference counter.  If this happens enough times, the counter will
rollover and the reference freed, leading to a double free which can be
used to do 'bad things'.

In order to prevent this, move the point of possible failure above the
point where the reference counter is incremented.  Also save any
meaningful return values to be applied to the return data at the
appropriate point in time.

This issue was caught with KASAN.

Fixes: 705c7091262d ("net: sched: cls_u32: no need to call tcf_exts_change for newly allocated struct")
Suggested-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Lee Jones <lee@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Acked-by: Jamal Hadi Salim <jhs@mojatatu.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint err;', '\tif (tb[TCA_U32_INDEV]) {', '\t\tint ret;', '\t\tret = tcf_change_indev(net, tb[TCA_U32_INDEV], extack);', '\t\tif (ret < 0)', '\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t\tn->ifindex = ret;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tint err, ifindex = -1;', '', '\tif (tb[TCA_U32_INDEV]) {', '\t\tifindex = tcf_change_indev(net, tb[TCA_U32_INDEV], extack);', '\t\tif (ifindex < 0)', '\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t}', '\tif (ifindex >= 0)', '\t\tn->ifindex = ifindex;', '']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's net/sched: cls_u32 component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

If tcf_change_indev() fails, u32_set_parms() will immediately return an error after incrementing or decrementing the reference counter in tcf_bind_filter(). If an attacker can control the reference counter and set it to zero, they can cause the reference to be freed, leading to a use-after-free vulnerability.

We recommend upgrading past commit 04c55383fa5689357bcdd2c8036725a55ed632bc.

code_evidence: Lines 36-39 update n->res.classid and call tcf_bind_filter(), which adjusts reference counters on the bound filter/class; this state change is not undone if a later step fails.

Lines 40-45 call tcf_change_indev() after that binding; on ret < 0 the function returns -EINVAL at line 44, leaving the earlier reference increment in place while the caller's error path tears down the node.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsynchronized reference increment followed by an early error return causes premature freeing and subsequent access through a stale reference, matching CWE-416 (Use After Free). The flaw is an error-path refcount imbalance, not merely an integer overflow, though counter rollover is the trigger.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a failure return (tcf_change_indev() < 0) occurs after tcf_bind_filter() has already incremented a reference counter, with no rollback. Repeated failed u32_set_parms() calls accumulate increments; when the counter wraps, the referenced object is freed while still pointed to, and later use of that pointer is a use-after-free.

commit_msg:
perf: Fix race in swevent hash

There's a race on CPU unplug where we free the swevent hash array
while it can still have events on. This will result in a
use-after-free which is BAD.

Simply do not free the hash array on unplug. This leaves the thing
around and no use-after-free takes place.

When the last swevent dies, we do a for_each_possible_cpu() iteration
anyway to clean these up, at which time we'll free it, so no leakage
will occur.

Reported-by: Sasha Levin <sasha.levin@oracle.com>
Tested-by: Sasha Levin <sasha.levin@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Arnaldo Carvalho de Melo <acme@redhat.com>
Cc: Frederic Weisbecker <fweisbec@gmail.com>
Cc: Jiri Olsa <jolsa@redhat.com>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Stephane Eranian <eranian@google.com>
Cc: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: Vince Weaver <vincent.weaver@maine.edu>
Signed-off-by: Ingo Molnar <mingo@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tswhash->online = true;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: Race condition in kernel/events/core.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) by leveraging incorrect handling of an swevent data structure during a CPU unplug operation.

code_evidence: perf_event_init_cpu takes hlist_mutex, sets swhash->online = true, and only allocates/reassigns swhash->swevent_hlist under rcu_assign_pointer when hlist_refcount > 0. The online flag and hash pointer are shared per-CPU state modified here while other sequences (CPU unplug/teardown, swevent events) can access them. The diff removes the online assignment, indicating the flag/hash lifetime interplay is the synchronization concern.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because concurrent code sequences access the per-CPU swevent hash without sufficient exclusive synchronization, creating a timing window during unplug. This is a race enabling a use-after-free consequence; CWE-416 describes that consequence, but the underlying weakness here is the improper synchronization of the shared resource.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function mutates shared swevent hash state and the online flag under only hlist_mutex, without coordinating with the teardown path that frees the hash on CPU unplug. A concurrent unplug/event sequence can observe or use the hash after it is freed, yielding a use-after-free; root cause is the unsynchronized lifetime of the shared hash, not the allocation itself.

commit_msg:
assoc_array: Fix a buggy node-splitting case

This fixes CVE-2017-12193.

Fix a case in the assoc_array implementation in which a new leaf is
added that needs to go into a node that happens to be full, where the
existing leaves in that node cluster together at that level to the
exclusion of new leaf.

What needs to happen is that the existing leaves get moved out to a new
node, N1, at level + 1 and the existing node needs replacing with one,
N0, that has pointers to the new leaf and to N1.

The code that tries to do this gets this wrong in two ways:

 (1) The pointer that should've pointed from N0 to N1 is set to point
     recursively to N0 instead.

 (2) The backpointer from N0 needs to be set correctly in the case N0 is
     either the root node or reached through a shortcut.

commit_msg:
gh-112334: Restore subprocess's use of `vfork()` & fix `extra_groups=[]`.

Fixed a performance regression in 3.12's :mod:`subprocess` on Linux where it
would no longer use the fast-path ``vfork()`` system call when it could have
due to a logic bug, instead falling back to the safe but slower ``fork()``.

Also fixed a second 3.12.0 potential security bug.  If a value of
``extra_groups=[]`` was passed to :mod:`subprocess.Popen` or related APIs,
the underlying ``setgroups(0, NULL)`` system call to clear the groups list
would not be made in the child process prior to ``exec()``.

The security issue was identified via code inspection in the process of
fixing the first bug.  Thanks to @vain for the detailed report and
analysis in the initial bug on Github.

 * [ ] A regression test is desirable. I'm pondering a test that runs when
   `strace` is available and permitted which and confirms use of `vfork()`
   vs `clone()`...
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (extra_group_size > 0)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (extra_group_size >= 0) {', '        assert(extra_group_size == 0 && extra_groups == NULL || extra_group_size);', '    }']}
description:
An issue was found in CPython 3.12.0 `subprocess` module on POSIX platforms. The issue was fixed in CPython 3.12.1 and does not affect other stable releases.

When using the `extra_groups=` parameter with an empty list as a value (ie `extra_groups=[]`) the logic regressed to not call `setgroups(0, NULL)` before calling `exec()`, thus not dropping the original processes' groups before starting the new process. There is no issue when the parameter isn't used or when any value is used besides an empty list.

This issue only impacts CPython processes run with sufficient privilege to make the `setgroups` system call (typically `root`).

code_evidence: The guard `if (extra_group_size > 0)` only invokes `setgroups(extra_group_size, extra_groups)` when the group count is strictly positive. An empty list yields `extra_group_size == 0`, so the call is skipped and the child retains the parent's supplementary groups before `execve`/`execv` at lines 113-119.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-269 fits because the function fails to properly modify/drop privileges (supplementary groups) in the child before exec, leaving the child with the parent's group privileges. The defect is in privilege management logic, not merely a generic input-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the privilege-dropping constraint is expressed as `> 0` instead of `>= 0`, so the zero-size case is treated as 'no request' rather than 'clear groups'. Trigger: a privileged (typically root) parent calls Popen with `extra_groups=[]`. Consequence: the child is executed without `setgroups(0, NULL)`, so it inherits the parent's supplementary group memberships, granting an unintended sphere of control.

commit_msg:
bpf: fix branch pruning logic

when the verifier detects that register contains a runtime constant
and it's compared with another constant it will prune exploration
of the branch that is guaranteed not to be taken at runtime.
This is all correct, but malicious program may be constructed
in such a way that it always has a constant comparison and
the other branch is never taken under any conditions.
In this case such path through the program will not be explored
by the verifier. It won't be taken at run-time either, but since
all instructions are JITed the malicious program may cause JITs
to complain about using reserved fields, etc.
To fix the issue we have to track the instructions explored by
the verifier and sanitize instructions that are dead at run time
with NOPs. We cannot reject such dead code, since llvm generates
it for valid C code, since it doesn't do as much data flow
analysis as the verifier does.

Fixes: 17a5267067f3 ("bpf: verifier (add verifier core)")
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Acked-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tint i;', '\tfor (i = off; i < off + cnt - 1; i++)', '\t\tnew_data[i].seen = true;']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.8 ignores unreachable code, even though it would still be processed by JIT compilers. This behavior, also considered an improper branch-pruning logic issue, could possibly be used by local users for denial of service.

code_evidence: The function reallocates insn_aux_data and copies entries before and after the inserted range [off, off+cnt-1), but does not initialize the newly created entries in that gap.

The pre-fix code at lines 10-12 copies only the prefix and suffix; no validation or initialization constrains the inserted range. The new entries therefore retain vzalloc zero state and their 'seen' flag is not set.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate/initialize the properties of the inserted instruction range, so derived metadata (the seen flag) is incorrect for input-controlled offsets, matching CWE-20 improper input validation. It is not a bounds error; the range is valid but its state is not established.

evidence_lines.code:
env->insn_aux_data = new_data;
vfree(old_data);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the range of new auxiliary entries created for inserted instructions is left uninitialized (seen=false) because the function does not validate/initialize that derived range. Trigger: a malicious BPF program that makes the verifier prune runtime-constant branches, so inserted dead instructions are never marked seen. Consequence: dead instructions are not sanitized with NOPs and reach the JIT, which may complain about reserved fields, enabling a DoS.

commit_msg:
Bug 697762: Fix scan converter SEGVs.

The SEGVs are caused by the scan converter allowing less room
in the table than is actually required. This happens due to
the mark_curve subdivision overflowing.

For example, if we have a curve such as:

 0 0x80000000 moveto
 0 0x80000000 0 0x80000000 0 0x80000000 curveto

Then the current subdivision logic does:

 fixed ay = (sy + c1y)>>1

For sy = c1y = 0x80000000 this gives ay = 0, when clearly
the average should be 0x80000000.

An alternative formulation of the splitting code:

 fixed ay = (sy>>1) + (c1y>>1)

gives the required result, at the expense of dropping accuracy at
the low end.

This commit therefore has 2 formulations of the splitting code, one
for 'big' values (values that might overflow), and ones for normal
values (values that won't).

We select between the two pieces of code by comparing the top 2
bits of each value; if they differ, then we use the big variant.

Also, when calculating the size of the table required, we were
incorrectly closing the curve more often than we needed to. This
had no ill effect other than inflating the amount of memory we
needed.

description: Integer overflow in the mark_curve function in Artifex Ghostscript 9.21 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PostScript document.

code_evidence: For each s_curve segment, the code computes a subdivision level k via gx_curve_log2_samples and then calls mark_curve_app with the curve control points and endpoints [56-61]. The overflow arises inside the subdivision arithmetic of mark_curve_app (the (sy + c1y)>>1 averaging), which this call site drives with attacker-controlled fixed coordinates; the diff replaces this call with mark_curve_top_app to select the overflow-safe big-value formulation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an integer wraparound in the coordinate arithmetic that corrupts the computed table size, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a bounds-check omission; the missing constraint is on the arithmetic itself, and the patch selects an overflow-safe averaging formulation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mark_curve_app's midpoint computation (sy + c1y)>>1 can wrap when curve coordinates are large (e.g. 0x80000000), yielding a wrong average. Trigger: a crafted PostScript curveto with extreme fixed-point coordinates reaches this call. Consequence: the required table size is underestimated, producing an out-of-bounds write and crash (DoS).

Limit tvbparse recursion.

Add a recursion check to tvbparse so that we don't overflow our stack.

Bug: 14253

Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/25202

Petri-Dish: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        return -1;', '', '    if (++tt->recursion_depth > TVBPARSE_MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH)']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.3 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.11, the JSON, XML, NTP, XMPP, and GDB dissectors could crash. This was addressed in epan/tvbparse.c by limiting the recursion depth.

code_evidence: The function only guards the offset against tt->end_offset before recursing.
It then calls the nested key condition at the same offset, and independently calls a value condition at offset + key_len without any depth or bound check on those recursive calls.
The recursive condition calls re-enter cond_hash, so a pathological nested hash structure can drive unbounded recursion until the stack is exhausted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit limits recursion to prevent stack overflow, which is a resource-consumption/DoS issue, not a read or write outside a buffer's intended boundary. CWE-119 (improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer) does not describe unbounded recursion; a stack-exhaustion weakness such as CWE-674 would fit better.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( offset > tt->end_offset )
return -1;
key_len = wanted->control.hash.key->condition(tt, offset, wanted->control.hash.key,  &key_elem);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the absence of a recursion-depth limit: cond_hash recursively invokes wanted->control.hash.key->condition and other/value conditions, which can call back into cond_hash. Trigger is crafted input producing deeply nested hash conditions; the supported consequence is stack exhaustion and a crash (availability), not an out-of-bounds memory access.

commit_msg:
tiff: Handle failure from TIFFReadRGBAImageOriented

The TIFFReadRGBAImageOriented function returns zero if it was unable to
read the image. Return NULL in this case instead of displaying
uninitialized memory.

Fixes #1129

description: The tiff_document_render() and tiff_document_get_thumbnail() functions in the TIFF document backend in GNOME Evince through 3.32.0 did not handle errors from TIFFReadRGBAImageOriented(), leading to uninitialized memory use when processing certain TIFF image files.

code_evidence: Buffer allocated with g_try_malloc; only NULL is checked, contents remain uninitialized.
Return value of TIFFReadRGBAImageOriented is ignored, so a failed read leaves pixels untouched without any error path.
The while loop then reads every pixel via TIFFGetR/G/B/A and rewrites it, consuming the possibly uninitialized buffer contents.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the allocated pixel buffer is used without being initialized after a failed read; the missing error check is the mechanism, and use of an uninitialized resource is the supported weakness. It is not CWE-457 (uninitialized variable) since the resource is a heap buffer whose initialization depends on an unchecked external call.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return status of TIFFReadRGBAImageOriented is discarded, so a failed decode does not stop rendering. Trigger: a malformed TIFF for which libtiff returns zero. Consequence: the loop over pixels reads and converts uninitialized heap memory, producing garbage output and possibly leaking memory contents into the rendered surface.

commit_msg:
Move the buffer size check to decode_attr_security_label() before memcpy()
Only call memcpy() if the buffer is large enough

Fixes: aa9c2669626c ("NFS: Client implementation of Labeled-NFS")
Signed-off-by: Jeffrey Mitchell <jeffrey.mitchell@starlab.io>
[Trond: clean up duplicate test of label->len != 0]
Signed-off-by: Trond Myklebust <trond.myklebust@hammerspace.com>

description: A TOCTOU mismatch in the NFS client code in the Linux kernel before 5.8.3 could be used by local attackers to corrupt memory or possibly have unspecified other impact because a size check is in fs/nfs/nfs4proc.c instead of fs/nfs/nfs4xdr.c, aka CID-b4487b935452.

code_evidence: The decoded length len is validated only against NFS4_MAXLABELLEN at line 27, then memcpy(label->label, p, len) at line 29 copies into label->label without verifying the destination buffer label->label is at least len bytes. label->len, the destination capacity indicator, is only set afterward at line 30, so the copy precedes any destination-size constraint.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The check (len < NFS4_MAXLABELLEN) is performed before the use (memcpy) but does not validate the actual destination buffer state, so the resource state used at copy time is inconsistent with the validated constraint, matching CWE-367's check-then-use mismatch.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size check at line 27 constrains only the incoming XDR length, not the destination buffer capacity, and label->len is assigned after the copy. Trigger: a server-supplied security label whose len exceeds the caller-allocated label->label buffer. Consequence: out-of-bounds write corrupting kernel memory, because the destination check is bypassed relative to the use at memcpy.

description: Project Wonder WebObjects 1.0 through 5.4.3 is vulnerable to Arbitrary HTTP Header injection and URL- or Header-based XSS reflection in all web-server adaptor interfaces.

code_evidence: Line 7 gates processing on the configured alias prefix or handler, then line 12 passes the raw, client-controlled r->uri into WOParseApplicationName. Lines 13-16 only reject on parser errors or app-listing authorization; they do not inspect r->uri for CR (0x0D) or LF (0x0A) characters before the URI is later used to build output/response paths.

It is XSS rather than mere header injection because the reflected URI content becomes executable page output for other users.

Trigger: a crafted request whose r->uri contains CR/LF reaches the alias/parse branch. Consequence: injected characters can split or forge HTTP headers and reflect attacker-controlled content, enabling header injection and reflected XSS in the adaptor interface.

commit_msg:
PR22443, Global buffer overflow in _bfd_elf_get_symbol_version_string

Symbols like *ABS* defined in bfd/section.c:global_syms are not
elf_symbol_type.  They can appear on relocs and perhaps other places
in an ELF bfd, so a number of places in nm.c and objdump.c are wrong
to cast an asymbol based on the bfd being ELF.  I think we lose
nothing by excluding all section symbols, not just the global_syms.

	PR 22443
	* nm.c (sort_symbols_by_size): Don't attempt to access
	section symbol internal_elf_sym.
	(print_symbol): Likewise.  Don't call bfd_get_symbol_version_string
	for section symbols.
	* objdump.c (compare_symbols): Don't attempt to access
	section symbol internal_elf_sym.
	(objdump_print_symname): Don't call bfd_get_symbol_version_string
	for section symbols.

Ditto for", '\t bfd/section.c:global_syms like *ABS*.  */', '      if ((sym->flags & (BSF_SECTION_SYM | BSF_SYNTHETIC)) == 0', '\t  && bfd_get_flavour (abfd) == bfd_target_elf_flavour)', '      else if ((sym->flags & (BSF_SECTION_SYM | BSF_SYNTHETIC)) == 0', '\t       && bfd_is_com_section (sec))']}
description: nm.c and objdump.c in GNU Binutils 2.29.1 mishandle certain global symbols, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (_bfd_elf_get_symbol_version_string buffer over-read and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: sec = bfd_get_section (sym) retrieves the symbol's section. The guard only excludes synthetic symbols (BSF_SYNTHETIC) before casting sym to elf_symbol_type and reading internal_elf_sym.st_size at line 44. Section symbols such as *ABS* from bfd/section.c:global_syms are not elf_symbol_type, so the cast and field access read memory beyond the intended asymbol object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads past the end of an asymbol not of elf_symbol_type, an out-of-bounds memory read. A type-confusion label would describe the cast, but the supported consequence here is the out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the type check relies on BSF_SYNTHETIC but omits BSF_SECTION_SYM, so non-ELF section symbols are treated as elf_symbol_type. Trigger: a crafted ELF containing such symbols reaches sort_symbols_by_size. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of internal_elf_sym.st_size, supporting crash/denial of service.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int  fileSize = fileStep*height + headerSize;', '    strm.putDWord( fileSize ); // file size'], 'added_lines': ['    size_t fileSize = (size_t)fileStep*height + headerSize;', '    strm.putDWord( validateToInt(fileSize) ); // file size']}
description: OpenCV (Open Source Computer Vision Library) 3.3 has an out-of-bounds write error in the function FillColorRow1 in utils.cpp when reading an image file by using cv::imread. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-12597.

code_evidence: fileStep is computed as (width*channels + 3) & -4 and fileSize as fileStep*height + headerSize, both in signed int arithmetic; large width/height/channels can overflow, yielding a too-small or negative fileSize used by m_buf->reserve( alignSize(fileSize + 16, 256) ).

After width *= channels, the loop writes rows via strm.putBytes( img.ptr(y), width ) and pads fileStep - width bytes into the buffer the encoder opened, without rechecking the buffer's capacity against the actual row data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a write (putBytes for each row) into a buffer whose allocation was derived from an integer-overflow-prone size, so data is written past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. The integer overflow is the enabling cause, not the primary weakness label here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is unchecked signed 32-bit multiplication in fileStep/fileSize and the subsequent reserve sized by the overflowing value. With large image dimensions the computed size is smaller than the data actually written, so the row-writing loop in the opened stream writes past the allocated buffer, corrupting memory (CWE-787); the wrong fileSize is also serialized into the BMP header.

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The estimator for the cost of some convolution operations can be made to execute a division by 0. code_evidence: Line 22-23 calls OpDimensionsFromInputs to derive ConvolutionDimensions (including strides sx, sy) from the shape, but the returned dimensions are used without validating that the stride values are nonzero.
Line 25 compares dims.kx <= dims.sx and dims.ky <= dims.sy, and line 26 computes ops using dims.iz, dims.ix, dims.iy, dims.ox, dims.oy; the stride-derived dims feed downstream cost computation.

ConvolutionDimensions dims =
OpDimensionsFromInputs(x_shape, op_info, &found_unknown_shapes);

if (dims.kx <= dims.sx && dims.ky <= dims.sy) {
ops = dims.batch * dims.iz * (dims.ix * dims.iy + dims.ox * dims.oy);

When a stride of zero is supplied, downstream convolution cost arithmetic divides by the stride, triggering a division-by-zero that can crash the process (DoS).

Fixes: 7549ae3e81cc ("9p: Use the i_size_[read, write]() macros instead of using inode->i_size directly.")
Reported-by: Xing Gaopeng <xingaopeng@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Hou Tao <houtao1@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Dominique Martinet <dominique.martinet@cea.fr>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tv9fs_stat2inode(st, d_inode(dentry), dentry->d_sb);'], 'added_lines': ['\tv9fs_stat2inode(st, d_inode(dentry), dentry->d_sb, 0);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. The 9p filesystem did not protect i_size_write() properly, which causes an i_size_read() infinite loop and denial of service on SMP systems.

code_evidence: In the cached path (CACHE_LOOSE/CACHE_FSCACHE) the function calls generic_fillattr() directly on the inode without any i_lock protection around the inode size snapshot.

On the uncached path, v9fs_stat2inode() updates inode metadata (including i_size via i_size_write) and then generic_fillattr() reads it; the call here passes no locking flag, so the size write/read pair is not serialized against concurrent getattr callers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a retry loop (read_seqcount_begin) whose exit condition cannot be reached because of the unsynchronized size update, matching CWE-835's infinite loop with unreachable exit condition. The missing lock is the cause; the infinite loop is the weakness manifestation, not merely a generic race.

evidence_lines.code:
v9fs_stat2inode(st, d_inode(dentry), dentry->d_sb);
generic_fillattr(d_inode(dentry), stat);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: i_size_write() in v9fs_stat2inode() and i_size_read() in generic_fillattr() are not protected by inode->i_lock, so on 32-bit SMP a concurrent writer can leave the seqcount in a state that the reader's read_seqcount_begin() retry loop never exits. Trigger: multiple processes invoking v9fs_vfs_getattr()/v9fs_vfs_getattr_dotl() simultaneously. Consequence: soft lockup/CPU spin, i.e., denial of service.

commit_msg:
seq_buf: Fix overflow in seq_buf_putmem_hex()

There's two variables being increased in that loop (i and j), and i
follows the raw data, and j follows what is being written into the buffer.
We should compare 'i' to MAX_MEMHEX_BYTES or compare 'j' to HEX_CHARS.
Otherwise, if 'j' goes bigger than HEX_CHARS, it will overflow the
destination buffer.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/20210625122453.5e2fe304@oasis.local.home/
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20210626032156.47889-1-yun.zhou@windriver.com

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: 5e3ca0ec76fce ("ftrace: introduce the "hex" output method")
Signed-off-by: Yun Zhou <yun.zhou@windriver.com>
Signed-off-by: Steven Rostedt (VMware) <rostedt@goodmis.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tstart_len = min(len, HEX_CHARS - 1);'], 'added_lines': ['\tBUILD_BUG_ON(MAX_MEMHEX_BYTES * 2 >= HEX_CHARS);', '', '\t\tstart_len = min(len, MAX_MEMHEX_BYTES);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.13.3. lib/seq_buf.c has a seq_buf_putmem_hex buffer overflow.

code_evidence: hex is a fixed stack buffer of HEX_CHARS bytes, but start_len is derived from the caller-supplied len, so the loop bound is not tied to the destination capacity.
The inner loop writes two hex characters per data byte (hex[j++] twice) for each of start_len iterations, so j can reach 2*start_len.
Only after the loop does the code check j/2 > len; it never checks j against HEX_CHARS, and hex[j++] = ' ' appends a further byte before seq_buf_putmem copies j bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies caller-controlled data into a fixed-size destination without ensuring the input size fits, producing a write past the buffer; this is a classic buffer-copy overflow, matching CWE-120.

evidence_lines.code:
unsigned char hex[HEX_CHARS];
start_len = min(len, HEX_CHARS - 1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: start_len = min(len, HEX_CHARS - 1) bounds iterations by the character count HEX_CHARS rather than by the number of bytes that fit, while each byte emits two characters. Trigger: a caller passes len >= HEX_CHARS/2, making j exceed the HEX_CHARS-byte hex array. Consequence: out-of-bounds writes to the stack buffer before the copy to seq_buf, enabling memory corruption.

commit_msg: fix #349
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '            if (size <= 0xFFFFFFFF) {', '                size_32 = (AP4_UI32)size;', '            } else {', '                size_32 = 1; // signal a large atom', '            }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Bento4 1.5.1-627. There is an attempt at excessive memory allocation in the AP4_DataBuffer class when called from AP4_HvccAtom::Create in Core/Ap4HvccAtom.cpp.

code_evidence: When the 32-bit size field is 0, the code derives size from the entire stream length (stream_size - start) rather than a bounded atom size; this attacker-influenced 64-bit value is then used downstream.

The only guard rejects size > bytes_available, but bytes_available itself reflects the caller-supplied available length, so a large declared stream still permits an oversized allocation through CreateAtomFromStream.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function fails to restrict how much memory an atom can cause to be allocated, letting crafted input drive unbounded resource consumption. This is resource-exhaustion behavior, not a memory-safety corruption such as an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size==0 branch substitutes the remaining stream length as the atom size without an upper bound. Trigger: a crafted atom whose 32-bit size is 0 in a large stream makes size equal to the full remaining length. Supported consequence: the derived size flows to atom creation/allocation, enabling excessive memory allocation and denial of service.

commit_msg:
tcp: fix zero cwnd in tcp_cwnd_reduction

Patch 3759824da87b ("tcp: PRR uses CRB mode by default and SS mode
conditionally") introduced a bug that cwnd may become 0 when both
inflight and sndcnt are 0 (cwnd = inflight + sndcnt). This may lead
to a div-by-zero if the connection starts another cwnd reduction
phase by setting tp->prior_cwnd to the current cwnd (0) in
tcp_init_cwnd_reduction().

To prevent this we skip PRR operation when nothing is acked or
sacked. Then cwnd must be positive in all cases as long as ssthresh
is positive:

1) The proportional reduction mode
   inflight > ssthresh > 0

2) The reduction bound mode
  a) inflight == ssthresh > 0

  b) inflight < ssthresh
     sndcnt > 0 since newly_acked_sacked > 0 and inflight < ssthresh

Therefore in all cases inflight and sndcnt can not both be 0.
We check invalid tp->prior_cwnd to avoid potential div0 bugs.

In reality this bug is triggered only with a sequence of less common
events.  For example, the connection is terminating an ECN-triggered
cwnd reduction with an inflight 0, then it receives reordered/old
ACKs or DSACKs from prior transmission (which acks nothing). Or the
connection is in fast recovery stage that marks everything lost,
but fails to retransmit due to local issues, then receives data
packets from other end which acks nothing.

Fixes: 3759824da87b ("tcp: PRR uses CRB mode by default and SS mode conditionally")
Reported-by: Oleksandr Natalenko <oleksandr@natalenko.name>
Signed-off-by: Yuchung Cheng <ycheng@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Neal Cardwell <ncardwell@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (newly_acked_sacked <= 0 || WARN_ON_ONCE(!tp->prior_cwnd))', '\t\treturn;']}
description: The tcp_cwnd_reduction function in net/ipv4/tcp_input.c in the Linux kernel before 4.3.5 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero error and system crash) via crafted TCP traffic.

code_evidence: In the delta < 0 branch, the dividend is divided by tp->prior_cwnd via div_u64 without checking that tp->prior_cwnd is nonzero; the divisor is a field that can be zero (as the fix's new WARN_ON_ONCE(!tp->prior_cwnd) indicates).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-189 (Numeric Errors) covers improper numeric calculation; the missing zero-divisor check leads to a divide-by-zero (CWE-369), a member of this category. The unsafe division is directly in this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the PRR proportional-reduction path performs integer division using tp->prior_cwnd as divisor with no nonzero constraint. Trigger: a cwnd reduction where prior_cwnd was set to 0 (e.g., inflight and sndcnt both zero from a prior phase). Consequence: divide-by-zero in the kernel, crashing the system (remote DoS).

check to prevent writing beyond the end of the ->ssid[] array.

Fixes: a2c60d42d97c ("staging: r8188eu: Add files for new driver - part 16")
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/YEHymwsnHewzoam7@mwanda

description: rtw_wx_set_scan in drivers/staging/rtl8188eu/os_dep/ioctl_linux.c in the Linux kernel through 5.11.6 allows writing beyond the end of the ->ssid[] array. NOTE: from the perspective of kernel.org releases, CVE IDs are not normally used for drivers/staging/* (unfinished work); however, system integrators may have situations in which a drivers/staging issue is relevant to their own customer base.

code_evidence: sec_len is read from the attacker-controlled scan buffer at line 67 and only checked against remaining len (line 68), not against the destination ssid[].ssid size. Line 70 memcpy copies sec_len bytes into ssid[ssid_index].ssid, and line 71 increments ssid_index without any bound against RTW_SSID_SCAN_AMOUNT, so both the fixed-size ssid array and each element's ssid[] can be overrun.

description: Nginx NJS v0.7.2 was discovered to contain a heap-use-after-free bug caused by illegal memory copy in the function njs_json_parse_iterator_call at njs_json.c.

code_evidence: The reviver branch stores the reviver function and depth into a stack-local `njs_json_parse_t json_parse` object via `parse = &json_parse` (line 12), then passes `parse` to `njs_json_parse_iterator`. The iterator retains this pointer while invoking the user-supplied reviver; if the reviver re-enters JSON.parse, the same stack frame/object can be overwritten or the retained pointer becomes stale, and later iterator operations dereference it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the iterator continues to reference the parse structure after its lifetime/validity is compromised by reentrancy, matching use-after-free semantics. It is distinct from a simple type confusion since the core flaw is reuse of an invalidated reference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a pointer to a stack-allocated parse structure escapes into `njs_json_parse_iterator` and is used after the reviver callback may have reentered or unwound the frame. Trigger: a reviver function that causes reentrant invocation while the iterator still holds `parse`. Consequence: dereferencing the stale pointer yields a heap/stack use-after-free, corrupting memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
If FI_EXTRA_ATTR is set in inode by fuzzing, inode.i_addr[0] will be
parsed as inode.i_extra_isize, then in __recover_inline_status, inline
data address will beyond boundary of page, result in accessing invalid
memory.

So in this condition, during reading inode page, let's do sanity check
with EXTRA_ATTR feature of fs and extra_attr bit of inode, if they're
inconsistent, deny to load this inode.

- Overview
Out-of-bound access in f2fs_iget() when mounting a corrupted f2fs image

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!sanity_check_inode(inode)) {', '\t\tret = -EINVAL;', '\t\tgoto bad_inode;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in fs/f2fs/inode.c in the Linux kernel through 4.17.3. A denial of service (slab out-of-bounds read and BUG) can occur for a modified f2fs filesystem image in which FI_EXTRA_ATTR is set in an inode.

code_evidence: After do_read_inode() populates the inode from the on-disk image, the code calls sanity_check_inode(inode) and rejects the inode with -EINVAL on failure. This is the only validation of the loaded inode metadata before its fields drive later reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is reading memory past the intended page/buffer boundary, which matches CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. The missing sanity check is the cause; the read beyond the page is the weakness. It is not merely a logic error because the demonstrated impact is an out-of-bounds memory read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the inode loaded by do_read_inode() is not validated against the filesystem's EXTRA_ATTR feature and the inode's extra_attr bit, so a crafted image can set FI_EXTRA_ATTR while the feature is inconsistent. Trigger: mounting such an image parses i_addr[0] as i_extra_isize, and a subsequent inline-data lookup uses an address beyond the page. Consequence: out-of-bounds read (KASAN slab-out-of-bounds) leading to crash/DoS.

commit_msg: fixed #1766 (fuzz)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', "\t//we don't know what's a URN yet", '\tif (entry->type == GF_ISOM_BOX_TYPE_URN) return GF_NOT_SUPPORTED;'], 'added_lines': ['\t//we only support alias and URL boxes', '\tif ((entry->type != GF_ISOM_BOX_TYPE_URL) && (entry->type != GF_QT_BOX_TYPE_ALIS) )', '\t\treturn GF_NOT_SUPPORTED;', '']}
description: Heap buffer overflow in the URL_GetProtocolType function in MP4Box in GPAC 1.0.1 allows attackers to cause a denial of service or execute arbitrary code via a crafted file.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only validates box type and delegates to gf_isom_datamap_new; it contains no buffer write, and the heap overflow described in the commit belongs to URL_GetProtocolType, not this function.

commit_msg: sgpd box entry: disallow null grouping_type (#2389)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcase 0:', '\t\tGF_LOG(GF_LOG_WARNING, GF_LOG_CONTAINER, ("[iso file] sgpd entry null grouping_type is invalid\\n") );', '\t\treturn NULL;']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to V2.1.0-DEV.

code_evidence: When grouping_type is 0, no case matches and the switch falls to default; entry_size and null_size_ok are unchanged, so the guard at line 268 does not return. A GF_DefaultSampleGroupDescriptionEntry is allocated (272), and if entry_size is nonzero, def_ptr->length is set from the caller-supplied entry_size and a heap buffer of that length is allocated (275-276). gf_bs_read_data then reads def_ptr->length bytes from the bitstream into that buffer (281).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-122 fits because the unsafe write occurs into a heap buffer allocated via gf_malloc, with the size derived from the unvalidated sgpd entry_size, matching a heap-based buffer overflow. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the destination is a heap allocation written by gf_bs_read_data.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a null grouping_type leaves entry_size and null_size_ok at their defaults, bypassing the rejection at line 268, so the default entry path treats a caller-controlled entry_size as a valid length. Trigger: an sgpd box with grouping_type 0 and a nonzero entry_size. Consequence: gf_bs_read_data at line 281 reads entry_size bytes into a heap buffer allocated with the same length, so the overflow is driven by entry_size exceeding the actual data available; the fix adds a case 0 that logs and returns NULL.

commit_msg:
Fixed njs_object_property() with NJS_WHITEOUT properties.

Previosly, an error object dumping might result in invalid pointer
dereference when 'name' or 'message' property of accessor descriptor
type was added and removed before.

The fix is to properly handle NJS_WHITEOUT properties.

This fixes #617 issue on Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* GC: release value. */', '        njs_value_assign(removed, njs_prop_value(prop));', '    njs_set_invalid(njs_prop_value(prop));'], 'added_lines': ['        if (njs_is_valid(njs_prop_value(prop))) {', '            njs_value_assign(removed, njs_prop_value(prop));', '', '        } else {', '            njs_set_undefined(removed);', '        }']}
description: Nginx NJS v0.7.10 was discovered to contain a segmentation violation via the function njs_function_frame at src/njs_function.h.

code_evidence: When a property is deleted with a non-NULL removed output, the code reads njs_prop_value(prop) and assigns it to removed without checking whether the property value is valid. It then sets prop->type to NJS_WHITEOUT and marks the value invalid. For a previously removed/whiteout property, the stored value can be invalid, so the assignment reads an invalid value slot.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads a value slot (njs_prop_value(prop)) that is no longer valid for whiteout properties, leading to an out-of-bounds/invalid memory read and crash. The patch adds a validity check before reading, confirming the missing constraint is on the read side.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the delete path unconditionally reads njs_prop_value(prop) even when the property is already a whiteout with an invalid value. Trigger: deleting an accessor-type 'name' or 'message' property that was added and removed before, then dumping the error object. Consequence: invalid pointer dereference/segmentation fault, an out-of-bounds/invalid read of the value slot.

net: nfc: Fix use-after-free caused by nfc_llcp_find_local

This commit fixes several use-after-free that caused by function
nfc_llcp_find_local(). For example, one UAF can happen when below buggy
time window occurs.

// nfc_genl_llc_get_params   | // nfc_unregister_device
                             |
dev = nfc_get_device(idx);   | device_lock(...)
if (!dev)                    | dev->shutting_down = true;
    return -ENODEV;          | device_unlock(...);
                             |
device_lock(...);            |   // nfc_llcp_unregister_device
                             |   nfc_llcp_find_local()
nfc_llcp_find_local(...);    |
                             |   local_cleanup()
if (!local) {                |
    rc = -ENODEV;            |     // nfc_llcp_local_put
    goto exit;               |     kref_put(.., local_release)
}                            |
                             |       // local_release

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: nfc_llcp_find_local walks the global llcp_devices list under no lock and, on a matching local->dev, returns the raw local pointer without taking a reference (no nfc_llcp_local_get). The pointer is handed to callers that hold no ownership, so a concurrent release path (nfc_llcp_unregister_device/local_release) can free the object after it is returned but before the caller dereferences fields such as local->dev.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's missing reference acquisition permits a returned pointer to be dereferenced after the object is freed, which is exactly CWE-416. This is not merely a race condition: the defect is the dangling pointer usage, and the fix's key change (nfc_llcp_local_get under spin_lock) confirms the lifetime flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the lookup returns an unreferenced list entry, so the object's lifetime is not extended past the list traversal and no serialization guards against concurrent removal/free. Consequence: use-after-free read (and possible write) on freed memory, matching the reported KASAN slab-use-after-free in nfc_genl_llc_get_params.

description: PowerDNS (aka pdns) Authoritative Server before 3.4.10 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (backend CPU consumption) via a long qname.

code_evidence: getLabelFromContent reads qname labels from attacker-controlled content. The loop at [6] consumes bytes and recurses at [16] on compression pointers; the only bound on accumulated output is ret.length() > 1024 at [34], checked after each label is fully appended. No wirelength parameter constrains total name size, so a long or pointer-heavy qname drives repeated label processing and ret growth.
The inner loop at [21-32] appends every content byte (escaping '.', '\\' and space), so output can expand per input byte; recursion at [16] re-enters this expansion for each pointer target.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 covers improper resource management; here unbounded name-length processing consumes CPU, matching the DoS described. It is distinct from memory-safety issues because the consequence is resource exhaustion via repeated parsing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accumulates decompressed qname data into ret without limiting total wire length, only checking ret.length() > 1024 after each label. Trigger: a crafted long qname or pointer chain causes repeated label parsing and string appends. Consequence: high CPU consumption in the backend (denial of service), not memory corruption.
