commit_msg:
If the device node of dvb_frontend is open() and the device is
disconnected, many kinds of UAFs may occur when calling close()
on the device node.

The root cause of this is that wake_up() for dvbdev->wait_queue
is implemented in the dvb_frontend_release() function, but
wait_event() is not implemented in the dvb_frontend_stop() function.

So, implement wait_event() function in dvb_frontend_stop() and
add 'remove_mutex' which prevents race condition for 'fe->exit'.

[mchehab: fix a couple of checkpatch warnings and some mistakes at the error handling logic]

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-media/20221117045925.14297-2-imv4bel@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (fe->exit == DVB_FE_DEVICE_REMOVED)', '\t\treturn -ENODEV;', '\t\t\t\treturn -EBUSY;', '\t\t\t\t\tif (signal_pending(current))', '\t\t\t\t\t\treturn -EINTR;', '\t\t\t\t\treturn -EBUSY;'], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_lock(&fe->remove_mutex);', '', '\tif (fe->exit == DVB_FE_DEVICE_REMOVED) {', '\t\tret = -ENODEV;', '\t\tgoto err_remove_mutex;', '\t}', '\t\t\t\tret = -EBUSY;', '\t\t\t\tgoto err_remove_mutex;', '\t\t\t\t\tif (signal_pending(current)) {', '\t\t\t\t\t\tret = -EINTR;', '\t\t\t\t\t\tgoto err_remove_mutex;', '\t\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t\t\tret = -EBUSY;', '\t\t\t\t\tgoto err_remove_mutex;', '', '\tmutex_unlock(&fe->remove_mutex);', '', 'err_remove_mutex:', '\tmutex_unlock(&fe->remove_mutex);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 6.0.9. drivers/media/dvb-core/dvb_frontend.c has a race condition that can cause a use-after-free when a device is disconnected.

code_evidence: Checks fe->exit without holding fe->remove_mutex, then returns early on DVB_FE_DEVICE_REMOVED; the check is not synchronized with the disconnect path that sets fe->exit.
After taking adapter->mfe_lock, the shared mfe_dvbdev/writers state is inspected and on conflict the function unlocks mfe_lock and returns -EBUSY without any remove lock.
The retry loop reads mfedev->users and mfepriv->thread, drops mfe_lock, sleeps, and returns -EINTR on a pending signal, leaving no serialization against device removal.
Second check of mfedev->users/mfepriv->thread returns -EBUSY after unlocking mfe_lock; again no fe-level exclusion.
On success dvb_frontend_get(fe) is called and mfe_lock is released; the open path holds no lock serializing it with the disconnect/release path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs concurrent accesses to shared fe/adapter state (fe->exit, mfe_dvbdev, users, thread) with only mfe_lock and no atomic exclusion against removal, a timing window matching CWE-362. The use-after-free is the downstream consequence, not the labeled weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (fe->exit == DVB_FE_DEVICE_REMOVED)
return -ENODEV;

mutex_unlock(&adapter->mfe_lock);
return -EBUSY;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dvb_frontend_open reads fe->exit and shared adapter/frontend state without a lock shared with the disconnect path, so a concurrent removal can interleave between the exit check and dvb_frontend_get(fe). Trigger: open() racing with device disconnect. Consequence: the frontend may be freed while open continues, enabling use-after-free.

commit_msg:
* src/retr.c (fd_read_body): Stop processing on negative chunk size

Reported-by: Antti Levomäki, Christian Jalio, Joonas Pihlaja from Forcepoint
Reported-by: Juhani Eronen from Finnish National Cyber Security Centre
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '              if (remaining_chunk_size < 0)', '                {', '                  ret = -1;', '                  break;', '                }']}
description: The retr.c:fd_read_body() function is called when processing OK responses. When the response is sent chunked in wget before 1.19.2, the chunk parser uses strtol() to read each chunk's length, but doesn't check that the chunk length is a non-negative number. The code then tries to read the chunk in pieces of 8192 bytes by using the MIN() macro, but ends up passing the negative chunk length to retr.c:fd_read(). As fd_read() takes an int argument, the high 32 bits of the chunk length are discarded, leaving fd_read() with a completely attacker controlled length argument. The attacker can corrupt malloc metadata after the allocated buffer.

code_evidence: Line 93 parses the attacker-supplied chunk-size line with strtol() into the signed wgint remaining_chunk_size, and line 95 only checks equality to zero; no lower-bound check exists, so a negative value is accepted.

Line 110 computes rdsize = MIN(remaining_chunk_size, dlbufsize), which for a negative remaining_chunk_size yields the negative value; line 132 then passes this rdsize as the length argument to fd_read() on the fixed dlbuf buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked negative length causes a read into dlbuf that exceeds its intended bounds, an improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer, matching CWE-119. It is not merely a signedness parsing bug (CWE-190) because the supported consequence is a concrete out-of-bounds buffer write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the chunk length parsed from the network is never validated as non-negative before being used as a read size. Trigger: a chunked HTTP response with a negative chunk-size line makes rdsize negative; fd_read() truncates the high bits and reads a large attacker-controlled count into the fixed 8 KB dlbuf, overflowing it and corrupting adjacent heap/malloc metadata. Consequence: out-of-bounds write leading to memory corruption and potential code execution.

Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The per-channel lock protecting chn state is taken with plain spin_lock (line 15) and released with spin_unlock (line 20), while the outer event_lock is also held via spin_lock (line 7).

Between acquiring event_lock/get_free_port and taking chn->lock, the port is freed/validated (lines 8-14); the chn fields (lines 16-19) are then modified under a non-IRQ-safe lock, so an IRQ-context interfering sequence using the same per-channel lock can interleave.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function relies on a lock for exclusive access to shared chn state, but the non-IRQ-safe acquisition leaves a timing window in which an interfering IRQ-context sequence can modify the resource concurrently. The weakness is improper synchronization, not merely a missing bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-channel lock is acquired without disabling interrupts, so an interrupt handler or IRQ-context code path taking the same chn->lock can run concurrently with this sequence. Trigger: IRQ-context event-channel activity racing with this allocation/initialization. Consequence: interleaved modification of chn state, violating exclusivity and enabling internal-assumption violations, out-of-bounds accesses, bug checks, DoS, or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = table->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = xt_table_get_private_protected(table);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: Line 5 reads table->private directly into a local pointer without any synchronization or protection against concurrent replacement. Line 6 then dereferences private->number, and line 10 passes private to get_counters, which walks the table entries. Since the replacement path can free the old table info once the per-CPU sequence count appears even, these uses may operate on freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly dereferences and iterates a pointer to table state that another thread may have freed, which is exactly CWE-416. The fix replaces the unprotected read with xt_table_get_private_protected, confirming the missing protection; this is not merely a NULL dereference or race-condition label, since the supported consequence is reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the table private pointer is captured and consumed without ordering/synchronization against the concurrent iptables replacement that frees it. If a replacement frees the old table between the read of table->private and its dereference in get_counters, the function accesses freed memory, causing a use-after-free and potential crash or memory corruption in the packet/counter context.

commit_msg:
ZDI-CAN-19866/CVE-2023-1393

If a client explicitly destroys the compositor overlay window (aka COW),
we would leave a dangling pointer to that window in the CompScreen
structure, which will trigger a use-after-free later.

Make sure to clear the CompScreen pointer to the COW when the latter gets
destroyed explicitly by the client.

This vulnerability was discovered by:
Jan-Niklas Sohn working with Trend Micro Zero Day Initiative

Signed-off-by: Olivier Fourdan <ofourdan@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Adam Jackson <ajax@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    /* Did we just destroy the overlay window? */', '    if (pWin == cs->pOverlayWin)', '        cs->pOverlayWin = NULL;', '']}
description: A flaw was found in X.Org Server Overlay Window. A Use-After-Free may lead to local privilege escalation. If a client explicitly destroys the compositor overlay window (aka COW), the Xserver would leave a dangling pointer to that window in the CompScreen structure, which will trigger a use-after-free later.

code_evidence: Line 19 calls the underlying DestroyWindow, which frees the window object pointed to by pWin. The function then restores the screen hooks and returns without checking whether pWin was the compositor overlay window stored in cs->pOverlayWin, so that pointer is left dangling after the free.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a stale pointer to freed memory that is reused later, which is exactly CWE-416 (Use After Free). It is not merely a missing NULL check; the object is freed at line 19 and the surviving pointer is the reuse hazard.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: compDestroyWindow frees pWin via (*pScreen->DestroyWindow)(pWin) but never clears cs->pOverlayWin when the destroyed window is the overlay window. Trigger: a client explicitly destroys the COW. Consequence: cs->pOverlayWin retains a dangling pointer that is later dereferenced, yielding a use-after-free (potential memory corruption/privilege escalation).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tbuf2 = smb_fdata(ndo, buf, fmt, maxbuf, unicodestr);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* Not sure how this relates with the protocol specification,', '\t\t * but in order to avoid stack exhaustion recurse at most that', '\t\t * many levels.', '\t\t */', '\t\tif (depth == 10)', '\t\t\tND_PRINT((ndo, "(too many nested levels, not recursing)"));', '\t\telse', '\t\t\tbuf2 = smb_fdata(ndo, buf, fmt, maxbuf, unicodestr);']}
description: The SMB parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has stack exhaustion in smbutil.c:smb_fdata() via recursion.

code_evidence: The '*' format case loops over the buffer and, for each iteration, increments the static depth [15] then calls smb_fdata recursively [16] with the same fmt pointer. There is no bound on depth before the recursive call, so nested '*' formats drive unbounded recursion. depth is only decremented after return [17], so it tracks nesting but does not constrain it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the function's recursion depth is controlled only by input-driven format expansion with no cap, directly causing resource exhaustion of the stack. This is uncontrolled recursion, not merely a generic infinite loop, since each level consumes a stack frame.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursive call at [16] lacks any depth limit, and the static depth counter is incremented but never checked. Trigger: attacker-controlled SMB data whose format string contains repeated '*' expansions causes deep self-recursion. Consequence: stack exhaustion and process crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
A NULL pointer dereference was reported by Wei Chen:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000000
  RIP: 0010:__list_del_entry_valid+0x26/0x80
  Call Trace:
   <TASK>
   sctp_sched_dequeue_common+0x1c/0x90
   sctp_sched_prio_dequeue+0x67/0x80
   __sctp_outq_teardown+0x299/0x380
   sctp_outq_free+0x15/0x20
   sctp_association_free+0xc3/0x440
   sctp_do_sm+0x1ca7/0x2210
   sctp_assoc_bh_rcv+0x1f6/0x340

This happens when calling sctp_sendmsg without connecting to server first.
In this case, a data chunk already queues up in send queue of client side
when processing the INIT_ACK from server in sctp_process_init() where it
calls sctp_stream_init() to alloc stream_in. If it fails to alloc stream_in
all stream_out will be freed in sctp_stream_init's err path. Then in the
asoc freeing it will crash when dequeuing this data chunk as stream_out
is missing.

As we can't free stream out before dequeuing all data from send queue, and
this patch is to fix it by moving the err path stream_out/in freeing in
sctp_stream_init() to sctp_stream_free() which is eventually called when
freeing the asoc in sctp_association_free(). This fix also makes the code
in sctp_process_init() more clear.

Note that in sctp_association_init() when it fails in sctp_stream_init(),
sctp_association_free() will not be called, and in that case it should
go to 'stream_free' err path to free stream instead of 'fail_init'.

Fixes: 5bbbbe32a431 ("sctp: introduce stream scheduler foundations")
Reported-by: Wei Chen <harperchen1110@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/831a3dc100c4908ff76e5bcc363be97f2778bc0b.1658787066.git.lucien.xin@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tgoto out_err;', '\t\tgoto out;', '\tret = sctp_stream_alloc_in(stream, incnt, gfp);', '\tif (ret)', '\t\tgoto in_err;', '', '\tgoto out;', '', 'in_err:', '\tsched->free(stream);', '\tgenradix_free(&stream->in);', 'out_err:', '\tgenradix_free(&stream->out);', '\tstream->outcnt = 0;', 'out:', '\treturn ret;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn ret;', '\t\treturn 0;', '\treturn sctp_stream_alloc_in(stream, incnt, gfp);']}
description: A null pointer dereference issue was found in the sctp network protocol in net/sctp/stream_sched.c in Linux Kernel. If stream_in allocation is failed, stream_out is freed which would further be accessed. A local user could use this flaw to crash the system or potentially cause a denial of service.

code_evidence: On failure of sctp_stream_alloc_out, control jumps to out_err, which genradix_free(&stream->out) and sets stream->outcnt = 0.
On failure of sctp_stream_alloc_in, in_err frees scheduler state and stream->in, then falls through out_err to free stream->out and zero outcnt; both error paths tear down stream_out state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The freed/absent stream_out leads to a NULL pointer dereference (as in the __list_del_entry_valid crash), matching CWE-476. It is not merely a use-after-free because outcnt is zeroed and the pointer is accessed as invalid/NULL during dequeue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path frees stream_out (genradix_free and outcnt=0) while queued data chunks still reference stream_out via the scheduler. Trigger: sctp_sendmsg before connect leaves a chunk queued, then sctp_stream_init fails allocating stream_in and frees stream_out. Later association teardown dequeues the chunk, dereferencing missing stream_out and crashing (DoS).

description: OpenSIPS is a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) server implementation. Prior to versions 3.1.9 and 3.2.6, if `ds_is_in_list()` is used with an invalid IP address string (`NULL` is illegal input), OpenSIPS will attempt to print a string from a random address (stack garbage), which could lead to a crash.  All users of `ds_is_in_list()` without the `$si` variable as 1st parameter could be affected by this vulnerability to a larger, lesser or no extent at all, depending if the data passed to the function is a valid IPv4 or IPv6 address string or not. Fixes will are available starting with the 3.1.9 and 3.2.6 minor releases. There are no known workarounds.

code_evidence: Line 10 passes the caller-supplied str *_ip to str2ip/str2ip6; when both fail, the error branch at line 11 formats the message using val.rs.len and val.rs.s even though val is only zeroed later at line 23 and never populated from _ip, so uninitialized stack contents are read as a length/pointer pair.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an input string and, on failure of its syntactic validation (str2ip/str2ip6), mishandles that invalid input by printing unrelated stack data. This is improper handling of input that fails validation, matching CWE-20; the memory disclosure is the consequence, not a separate validation of buffer bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failure path of the IP-parsing check dereferences an uninitialized pv_value_t (val) instead of the validated input _ip. Trigger: any call to ds_is_in_list with a string that is not a valid IPv4/IPv6 address. Consequence: LM_ERR reads an attacker-influenced stack value as a length and pointer, producing an out-of-bounds read of stack memory and a possible crash (DoS); the valid-input path is unaffected.

code_evidence: Line 40 computes image->columns from metrics.width+stroke_width+0.5 using a plain C cast to size_t, without floor, while the sibling row computation on line 41 already uses floor.

image->columns=(size_t) (metrics.width+draw_info->stroke_width+0.5);
image->rows=(size_t) floor(metrics.height+draw_info->stroke_width+0.5);
status=SetImageExtent(image,image->columns,image->rows);

description: Contiki-NG is an open-source, cross-platform operating system for IoT devices. In affected versions it is possible to cause a buffer overflow when copying an IPv6 address prefix in the RPL-Classic implementation in Contiki-NG. In order to trigger the vulnerability, the Contiki-NG system must have joined an RPL DODAG. After that, an attacker can send a DAO packet with a Target option that contains a prefix length larger than 128 bits. The problem was fixed after the release of Contiki-NG 4.7. Users unable to upgrade may apply the patch in Contiki-NG PR #1615.

code_evidence: Line 53 reads attacker-controlled prefixlen from the DAO Target option (buffer[i+3]). Line 54 zeroes the 16-byte prefix, then line 55 copies (prefixlen + 7)/CHAR_BIT bytes from the packet into prefix without any bound on prefixlen or the source buffer length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe memcpy copies a variable-length input into a fixed-size destination without checking the input size, matching CWE-120's buffer copy without size validation. The missing prefixlen/buffer-length checks are the specific cause rather than a mere out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the RPL Target prefix length is copied into the fixed 16-byte prefix destination with no validation that prefixlen <= 128 or that the packet holds enough bytes. Trigger: a DAO with a Target option whose prefix length exceeds 128 bits makes the copy length exceed sizeof(prefix), writing past the stack buffer; an over-long length also reads beyond the packet. Supported consequence: stack buffer overflow, memory corruption and potential crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
btrfs: fix deadlock with concurrent chunk allocations involving system chunks

When a task attempting to allocate a new chunk verifies that there is not
currently enough free space in the system space_info and there is another
task that allocated a new system chunk but it did not finish yet the
creation of the respective block group, it waits for that other task to
finish creating the block group. This is to avoid exhaustion of the system
chunk array in the superblock, which is limited, when we have a thundering
herd of tasks allocating new chunks. This problem was described and fixed
by commit eafa4fd0ad0607 ("btrfs: fix exhaustion of the system chunk array
due to concurrent allocations").

However there are two very similar scenarios where this can lead to a
deadlock:

1) Task B allocated a new system chunk and task A is waiting on task B
   to finish creation of the respective system block group. However before
   task B ends its transaction handle and finishes the creation of the
   system block group, it attempts to allocate another chunk (like a data
   chunk for an fallocate operation for a very large range). Task B will
   be unable to progress and allocate the new chunk, because task A set
   space_info->chunk_alloc to 1 and therefore it loops at
   btrfs_chunk_alloc() waiting for task A to finish its chunk allocation
   and set space_info->chunk_alloc to 0, but task A is waiting on task B
   to finish creation of the new system block group, therefore resulting
   in a deadlock;

2) Task B allocated a new system chunk and task A is waiting on task B to
   finish creation of the respective system block group. By the time that
   task B enter the final phase of block group allocation, which happens
   at btrfs_create_pending_block_groups(), when it modifies the extent
   tree, the device tree or the chunk tree to insert the items for some
   new block group, it needs to allocate a new chunk, so it ends up at
   btrfs_chunk_alloc() and keeps looping there because task A has set
   space_info->chunk_alloc to 1, but task A is waiting for task B to
   finish creation of the new system block group and release the reserved
   system space, therefore resulting in a deadlock.

In short, the problem is if a task B needs to allocate a new chunk after
it previously allocated a new system chunk and if another task A is
currently waiting for task B to complete the allocation of the new system
chunk.

Unfortunately this deadlock scenario introduced by the previous fix for
the system chunk array exhaustion problem does not have a simple and short
fix, and requires a big change to rework the chunk allocation code so that
chunk btree updates are all made in the first phase of chunk allocation.
And since this deadlock regression is being frequently hit on zoned
filesystems and the system chunk array exhaustion problem is triggered
in more extreme cases (originally observed on PowerPC with a node size
of 64K when running the fallocate tests from stress-ng), revert the
changes from that commit. The next patch in the series, with a subject
of "btrfs: rework chunk allocation to avoid exhaustion of the system
chunk array" does the necessary changes to fix the system chunk array
exhaustion problem.

Reported-by: Naohiro Aota <naohiro.aota@wdc.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-btrfs/20210621015922.ewgbffxuawia7liz@naota-xeon/

commit_msg:
unix: correctly track in-flight fds in sending process user_struct

The commit referenced in the Fixes tag incorrectly accounted the number
of in-flight fds over a unix domain socket to the original opener
of the file-descriptor. This allows another process to arbitrary
deplete the original file-openers resource limit for the maximum of
open files. Instead the sending processes and its struct cred should
be credited.

To do so, we add a reference counted struct user_struct pointer to the
scm_fp_list and use it to account for the number of inflight unix fds.

Fixes: 712f4aad406bb1 ("unix: properly account for FDs passed over unix sockets")
Reported-by: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Hannes Frederic Sowa <hannes@stressinduktion.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tfree_uid(fpl->user);']}
description: The Linux kernel before 4.5 allows local users to bypass file-descriptor limits and cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by leveraging incorrect tracking of descriptor ownership and sending each descriptor over a UNIX socket before closing it. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incorrect fix for CVE-2013-4312.

code_evidence: When fpl is non-NULL, the function releases the files via fput() and frees the scm_fp_list with kfree(), but it never releases the user_struct reference that accounts for in-flight descriptors.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing resource-release step in cleanup matches CWE-399 Resource Management Errors: improper management of system resources during destruction of the scm_fp_list. The fix adds free_uid(fpl->user) to balance the reference, confirming the omission is the relevant resource-management defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that __scm_destroy tears down the in-flight fd list without decrementing/releasing the associated user accounting (free_uid), so the sending process's file-descriptor resource accounting is not corrected when the descriptors are destroyed. Repeatedly sending and closing descriptors can therefore leave accounting unbalanced, enabling resource exhaustion/DoS. The consequence is resource-accounting leakage, not the fput/kfree themselves.

commit_msg:
ASAN SFTP Fixes
When decoding SFTP messages, fix the size checks so they don't wrap. (ZD12766)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (sz + idx > maxSz) {', '    if (idx + sz > maxSz) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (sz > maxSz - idx) {', '    if (sz > maxSz - idx) {']}
description: WolfSSH v1.4.7 was discovered to contain an integer overflow via the function wolfSSH_SFTP_RecvRMDIR.

code_evidence: Line 18 reads attacker-controlled sz from the SFTP packet, then line 19 checks sz + idx > maxSz. Since both are word32, a large sz can wrap the sum to a small value and bypass the bound check, allowing dir allocation/copy beyond the buffer.
Lines 33-34 repeat the same pattern for the second length field: idx + sz is computed before comparison, so wraparound can pass the check and let line 44 read mode from an out-of-bounds offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an unchecked integer wraparound in a size/offset calculation used for buffer bounds and allocation, matching CWE-190. It is not a simple off-by-one or missing length check: the check exists but is defeated by arithmetic overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: length validation adds two word32 values (sz + idx / idx + sz) and compares the result to maxSz, so an oversized sz wraps to a small sum and defeats the check. Trigger: a crafted SFTP MKDIR request with a large length field. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads/copies relative to the received buffer, leading to memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/1552
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        gamma=1.0/count;'], 'added_lines': ['        gamma=PerceptibleReciprocal(count);']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.x before 7.0.8-41 and 6.x before 6.9.10-41, there is a divide-by-zero vulnerability in the MeanShiftImage function. It allows an attacker to cause a denial of service by sending a crafted file.

code_evidence: count is initialized to 0 and only incremented when a neighbor pixel passes the distance threshold; if no pixel satisfies distance <= color_distance*color_distance, count remains 0.
gamma is then computed as the reciprocal of count, dividing by zero when count is 0; the result is used to scale the summed location and pixel values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a direct division where the divisor, count, can be zero based on input-dependent loop conditions, matching CWE-369's divide-by-zero pattern and its availability impact. This is a zero-divisor arithmetic fault, not merely an uninitialized or out-of-bounds value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the normalization factor gamma is derived by dividing by count without verifying that at least one neighbor was accumulated. Trigger: a crafted image or parameter combination where the inner neighborhood loop never satisfies the color-distance condition leaves count at zero. Consequence: division by zero yields an undefined/infinite gamma, propagating into mean_location and mean_pixel computations and causing a crash or denial of service.

commit_msg:
Remove access to the root FS from lua

On linux / is mounted to /rootfs in RageFile, which allows access to the
_whole_ filesystem from lua. This means themes and mod files can
re-write user data and extract files via USB profiles.

/rootfs was only added for internal use by the alsa, oss and memory card
drivers, so it can be easily replaced with direct fstream file access.

description: The component /rootfs in RageFile of Stepmania v5.1b2 and below allows attackers access to the entire file system.

code_evidence: The function opens "/rootfs/etc/fstab" through RageFile, whose virtual root exposes the host filesystem under /rootfs; this grants the Lua-exposed file API access to a path outside the intended sandbox.
Lines read and parse that fstab content, extracting device and mount-point strings that would not normally be reachable through the sandboxed path.
The parsed mount point is trimmed and stored into usbd.sOsMountDir, propagating host filesystem layout into data exposed to callers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is that access to a critical resource is granted more broadly than intended: the /rootfs mount makes the entire filesystem accessible through a sandboxed interface, matching incorrect permission assignment for a critical resource rather than a mere missing authorization check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function references the /rootfs-prefixed path, which RageFile maps to the real root filesystem, so a security-critical resource (the whole FS) is reachable by lower-privileged actors (themes/mod Lua). Trigger: any caller of the Lua file API opening /rootfs/... . Consequence: unintended read/modify access to user data and filesystem extraction.

description: EOSIO/eos eos version after commit f1545dd0ae2b77580c2236fdb70ae7138d2c7168 contains a stack overflow vulnerability in abi_serializer that can result in attack eos network node. This attack appear to be exploitable via network request. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in after commit cf7209e703e6d3f7a5413e0cb1fe88a4d8e4b38d .

code_evidence: Constructor initializes _vo, _val, and _resolver but stores no recursion-depth counter or bound; nothing here constrains how deep a subsequent visitor traversal may recurse.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the constructor's state lacks any depth tracking, enabling uncontrolled recursion that consumes stack resources; contrast CWE-400 resource exhaustion, which is broader and less specific to recursion.

abi_to_variant_visitor( mutable_variant_object& _mvo, const T& _val, Resolver _resolver )
:_vo(_mvo)
,_val(_val)
,_resolver(_resolver)
{}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the visitor carries no recursion-depth state or limit, so nested ABI/variant structures can drive unbounded recursive visitation. Trigger: a crafted network-supplied ABI or value with deeply nested structure. Consequence: stack exhaustion leading to node crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
bpf: fix sanitation of alu op with pointer / scalar type from different paths

While 979d63d50c0c ("bpf: prevent out of bounds speculation on pointer
arithmetic") took care of rejecting alu op on pointer when e.g. pointer
came from two different map values with different map properties such as
value size, Jann reported that a case was not covered yet when a given
alu op is used in both "ptr_reg += reg" and "numeric_reg += reg" from
different branches where we would incorrectly try to sanitize based
on the pointer's limit. Catch this corner case and reject the program
instead.

Fixes: 979d63d50c0c ("bpf: prevent out of bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic")
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tu32 dst = insn->dst_reg;', '\tint ret;', '\t\tret = sanitize_val_alu(env, insn);', '\t\tif (ret < 0) {', '\t\t\tverbose(env, "R%d tried to add from different pointers or scalars\\n", dst);', '\t\t\treturn ret;', '\t\t}', '\t\tret = sanitize_val_alu(env, insn);', '\t\tif (ret < 0) {', '\t\t\tverbose(env, "R%d tried to sub from different pointers or scalars\\n", dst);', '\t\t\treturn ret;', '\t\t}']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel before 4.20.6 performs undesirable out-of-bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic in various cases, including cases of different branches with different state or limits to sanitize, leading to side-channel attacks.

code_evidence: In the BPF_ADD case, the verifier updates dst_reg's signed and unsigned bounds by adding smin_val/smax_val and umin_val/umax_val, resetting to S64_MIN/S64_MAX or 0/U64_MAX on overflow, then sets var_off via tnum_add.
The BPF_SUB case performs the analogous subtraction of the same src_reg-derived bounds, resetting on overflow and using tnum_sub.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper numeric calculation of register bounds (overflow handling and tnum arithmetic) that fails to account for mixed pointer/scalar inputs, fitting CWE-189's numeric-error category. It is not merely an access-control gap: the defect is in the bound computation itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bound arithmetic is applied without first checking whether the ALU op mixes pointer and scalar register types across different verifier paths. Trigger: a program uses the same add/sub instruction with a pointer-derived register on one branch and a numeric register on another, so the sanitization is computed from the pointer's limits. Consequence: incorrect register bounds allow out-of-bounds pointer speculation, a side-channel leak.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* RichEd20.DLL is needed for filter entries. */'], 'added_lines': ['    /* RichEd20.DLL is needed for native file dialog filter entries. */']}
description: Untrusted search path vulnerability in the WiresharkApplication class in ui/qt/wireshark_application.cpp in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.10 and 2.0.x before 2.0.2 on Windows allows local users to gain privileges via a Trojan horse riched20.dll.dll file in the current working directory, related to use of QLibrary.

code_evidence: Line 8 calls ws_init_dll_search_path() to establish the DLL search path, then line 13 loads the bare name "riched20.dll" via ws_load_library. The loaded module's resolved location depends on the configured search path and current working directory rather than an absolute path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission and privilege management; loading an attacker-controlled DLL grants the attacker the process's privileges via the search-path resolution, matching this permissions/privileges category. The search-path origin is the cause, the elevated execution is the consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
ws_init_dll_search_path();
ws_load_library("riched20.dll");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a DLL is loaded by relative name without pinning to a trusted absolute directory. Trigger: a local attacker places a malicious riched20.dll (or riched20.dll.dll under the prior QLibrary behavior) in a directory earlier on the search path, such as the current working directory. Consequence: the attacker's code is loaded into the Wireshark process, yielding privilege/access-control impact.

commit_msg: Issue #161: Cope with empty programs in mujs-pp.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (prog->type == AST_LIST)', '\t\tpstmlist(-1, prog);', '\telse {', '\t\tpstm(0, prog);', '\t\tnl();'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (prog) {', '\t\tif (prog->type == AST_LIST)', '\t\t\tpstmlist(-1, prog);', '\t\telse {', '\t\t\tpstm(0, prog);', '\t\t\tnl();', '\t\t}']}
description: In Artifex MuJS through 1.2.0, jsP_dumpsyntax in jsdump.c has a NULL pointer dereference, as demonstrated by mujs-pp.

code_evidence: Line 4 unconditionally reads prog->type without first verifying that prog is non-NULL.
Lines 5-9 then pass prog to pstmlist or pstm, which also dereference the AST node; the else branch is reached whenever prog->type is not AST_LIST.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a direct NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): the function reads prog->type without validating prog. It is not an out-of-bounds or use-after-free issue, since the defect is the missing NULL guard on a pointer the code expects to be valid.

evidence_lines.code: if (prog->type == AST_LIST)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: jsP_dumpsyntax dereferences the prog pointer (prog->type) before any NULL check, so a caller that passes a NULL program AST triggers a NULL pointer dereference. The trigger is an empty program passed by mujs-pp; the supported consequence is a crash/DoS, not memory corruption.

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \

    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: nfc_llcp_find_local() returns a local pointer that, without a matching reference, can be released concurrently by nfc_llcp_unregister_device().

Consequence: use-after-free read/integrity impact on the local structure.

commit_msg:
SPOOLSS: Try to avoid an infinite loop.

Use tvb_reported_length_remaining in dissect_spoolss_uint16uni. Make
sure our offset always increments in dissect_spoolss_keybuffer.

Change-Id: I7017c9685bb2fa27161d80a03b8fca4ef630e793
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/14687
Reviewed-by: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
Petri-Dish: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot <buildbot-no-reply@wireshark.org>
Reviewed-by: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tremaining = tvb_captured_length_remaining(tvb, offset);'], 'added_lines': ['\tremaining = tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset);']}
description: epan/dissectors/packet-dcerpc-spoolss.c in the SPOOLS component in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.12 and 2.x before 2.0.4 mishandles unexpected offsets, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: The remaining length is derived from tvb_captured_length_remaining at the given offset; if it is non-positive the function returns the current offset unchanged after optionally setting an empty string.
The string is decoded over the full remaining length, and the return value is offset + (len + 1) * 2, so the next offset depends on the decoded string length rather than the consumed buffer length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper management of loop/resource progression leading to a non-terminating dissection loop, which fits the resource-management error category CWE-399; the consequence is resource exhaustion via an infinite loop, not memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function computes the buffer remainder with captured length and advances the caller's offset from strlen of the decoded UTF-16 text instead of the actual reported buffer extent. A crafted packet whose reported length exceeds captured data, or whose decoded text does not consume the remaining buffer, can cause the returned offset to fail to advance past the data, so a caller looping over this function never progresses, producing an infinite loop and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Detect infinite recursion in parameter entities

When expanding a parameter entity in a DTD, infinite recursion could
lead to an infinite loop or memory exhaustion.

Thanks to Wei Lei for the first of many reports.

Fixes bug 759579.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (((ctxt->inputNr > 40) && ((ctxt->options & XML_PARSE_HUGE) == 0)) ||', '        (ctxt->inputNr > 1024)) {', '        xmlFatalErr(ctxt, XML_ERR_ENTITY_LOOP, NULL);', '        while (ctxt->inputNr > 1)', '            xmlFreeInputStream(inputPop(ctxt));', '\treturn(-1);', '    }']}
description: parser.c in libxml2 before 2.9.5 does not prevent infinite recursion in parameter entities.

code_evidence: xmlPushInput unconditionally calls inputPush(ctxt, input) to add a new parser input, with no check on ctxt->inputNr or recursion depth before pushing. The only post-push check tests ctxt->instate == XML_PARSER_EOF, which does not bound stack growth when parameter entities recursively push inputs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the input-pushing loop lacks a reachable exit condition on nesting depth, allowing unbounded iteration. Contrast with CWE-674 (uncontrolled recursion), which concerns recursion depth generally; here the observable defect is the unbounded push loop.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no depth limit or cycle detection before pushing each input. Trigger: a DTD with self-referential parameter entities causes inputPush to recurse/push indefinitely. Supported consequence: unbounded input stack growth leading to infinite loop or memory exhaustion (DoS).

description: The d_walk function in fs/dcache.c in the Linux kernel through 3.17.2 does not properly maintain the semantics of rename_lock, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock and system hang) via a crafted application.

code_evidence: The function walks inode->i_dentry under inode->i_lock and takes alias->d_lock for each alias, then iterates alias->d_subdirs taking child->d_lock with spin_lock_nested.
The outer inode->i_lock is held across the entire traversal, so lock ordering and nesting depth are fixed by this loop structure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 covers uncontrolled consumption of a limited resource; here the resource is the lock set, and the flaw is failure to constrain lock acquisition so a deadlock consumes execution indefinitely. This matches the described deadlock/hang DoS rather than a memory-corruption or access-control weakness.

spin_lock(&inode->i_lock);
spin_unlock(&inode->i_lock);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the lock-acquisition pattern in the dentry traversal: inode->i_lock is held while acquiring alias->d_lock and then child->d_lock. A concurrent path taking these locks in a conflicting order (the rename_lock semantics issue in the commit description) can deadlock, hanging the system. The supported consequence is a denial of service via system hang, not memory or CPU exhaustion.

commit_msg:
This works just like close(2), unsurprisingly. We remove the file
descriptor and post the completion inline, then offload the actual
(potential) last file put to async context.

Mark the async part of this work as uncancellable, as we really must
guarantee that the latter part of the close is run.

Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcase IORING_OP_CLOSE:', '\t\tif (sqe) {', '\t\t\tret = io_close_prep(req, sqe);', '\t\t\tif (ret)', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t}', '\t\tret = io_close(req, nxt, force_nonblock);', '\t\tbreak;']}
description: A time-of-check to time-of-use issue exists in io_uring subsystem's IORING_OP_CLOSE operation in the Linux kernel's versions 5.6 - 5.11 (inclusive), which allows a local user to elevate their privileges to root. Introduced in b5dba59e0cf7e2cc4d3b3b1ac5fe81ddf21959eb, patched in 9eac1904d3364254d622bf2c771c4f85cd435fc2, backported to stable in 788d0824269bef539fe31a785b1517882eafed93.

code_evidence: io_issue_sqe dispatches IORING_OP_CLOSE by first running io_close_prep(req, sqe) under the sqe branch, then unconditionally invoking io_close(req, nxt, force_nonblock) to perform the actual file-descriptor close. The prep step validates the requested fd, while io_close later uses that same fd; the two operations are separate and not atomic, so the descriptor table state consulted during prep can differ from the state at close time.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-367 fits because the function performs a state check (io_close_prep validation of the fd) followed by a non-atomic use (io_close), allowing the checked resource state to change between check and use. This is a TOCTOU race in the close operation, not merely a missing validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the close path checks the target file descriptor in io_close_prep and then acts on it later in io_close, with the descriptor table shared and mutable between the two steps. Trigger: a local user racing close/dup operations on the same fd, or concurrent io_uring submissions, causes the fd checked to differ from the fd actually closed. Consequence: an unintended descriptor is closed, enabling privilege escalation via descriptor confusion.

commit_msg:
delta: fix sign-extension of big left-shift

Our delta code was originally adapted from JGit, which itself adapted it
from git itself. Due to this heritage, we inherited a bug from git.git
in how we compute the delta offset, which was fixed upstream in
48fb7deb5 (Fix big left-shifts of unsigned char, 2009-06-17). As
explained by Linus:

    Shifting 'unsigned char' or 'unsigned short' left can result in sign
    extension errors, since the C integer promotion rules means that the
    unsigned char/short will get implicitly promoted to a signed 'int' due to
    the shift (or due to other operations).

    This normally doesn't matter, but if you shift things up sufficiently, it
    will now set the sign bit in 'int', and a subsequent cast to a bigger type
    (eg 'long' or 'unsigned long') will now sign-extend the value despite the
    original expression being unsigned.

    One example of this would be something like

            unsigned long size;
            unsigned char c;

            size += c << 24;

    where despite all the variables being unsigned, 'c << 24' ends up being a
    signed entity, and will get sign-extended when then doing the addition in
    an 'unsigned long' type.

    Since git uses 'unsigned char' pointers extensively, we actually have this
    bug in a couple of places.

In our delta code, we inherited such a bogus shift when computing the
offset at which the delta base is to be found. Due to the sign extension
we can end up with an offset where all the bits are set. This can allow
an arbitrary memory read, as the addition in `base_len < off + len` can
now overflow if `off` has all its bits set.

Fix the issue by casting the result of `*delta++ << 24UL` to an unsigned
integer again. Add a test with a crafted delta that would actually
succeed with an out-of-bounds read in case where the cast wouldn't
exist.

Reported-by: Riccardo Schirone <rschiron@redhat.com>
Test-provided-by: Riccardo Schirone <rschiron@redhat.com>

description: A flaw was found in libgit2 before version 0.27.3. It has been discovered that an unexpected sign extension in git_delta_apply function in delta.c file may lead to an integer overflow which in turn leads to an out of bound read, allowing to read before the base object. An attacker may use this flaw to leak memory addresses or cause a Denial of Service.

code_evidence: off is a size_t. Each delta byte is an unsigned char, but in expressions like *delta++ << 24UL it is integer-promoted to signed int before the shift. When the high bit becomes set, the signed int is then converted to size_t and sign-extended, filling the upper bits of off with ones. The bounds check base_len < off + len can overflow because off is near SIZE_MAX, so it passes, and memcpy(res_dp, base + off, len) reads out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-681 covers incorrect conversion between numeric types; here the promoted signed int is converted to size_t with sign extension, producing an unexpected huge offset. This is distinct from a plain arithmetic overflow, since the flawed conversion is what enables the later bounds-check overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: implicit integer promotion of unsigned char to signed int before a large left shift, followed by conversion to size_t, sign-extends the value. Trigger: a crafted delta copy instruction with the 0x08 bit and a byte whose high bit is set. Consequence: off becomes huge, the base_len < off + len check overflows, and memcpy performs an out-of-bounds read of the base object.

description: In function lys_node_free() in libyang <= v1.0.225, it asserts that the value of node->module can't be NULL. But in some cases, node->module can be null, which triggers a reachable assertion (CWE-617).

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a required context is not propagated to lys_node_free for children of an unresolved/not-applied augment. Trigger: freeing such nodes whose module is NULL reaches the assertion. Consequence: process abort (DoS).

commit_msg:
Bug 702253: Avoid a use-after-free in fz_drop_band_writer

A use-after-free would occur when a valid page was followed by
a page with invalid pixmap dimensions, causing bander --
a static -- to point to previously freed memory instead of a new
band_writer.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t{', '\t\t\t\t/* bander must be set to NULL to avoid use-after-frees. A use-after-free', '\t\t\t\t * would occur when a valid page was followed by a page with invalid', '\t\t\t\t * pixmap dimensions, causing bander -- a static -- to point to previously', '\t\t\t\t * freed memory instead of a new band_writer. */', '\t\t\t\tbander = NULL;', '\t\t\t}']}
description: A Use After Free vulnerability exists in Artifex Software, Inc. MuPDF library 1.17.0-rc1 and earlier when a valid page was followed by a page with invalid pixmap dimensions, causing bander - a static - to point to previously freed memory instead of a newband_writer.

code_evidence: In the fz_always cleanup block, bander is passed to fz_drop_band_writer when output_format != OUT_PCLM, but bander is not reset to NULL afterward.
During band output, if (bander) fz_write_band(ctx, bander, ...) dereferences bander; bander is a static assigned in the output setup block, so it persists across dodrawpage invocations.
bander is (re)assigned only inside the output setup branches (e.g., fz_new_*_band_writer), which are skipped when a later page has invalid pixmap dimensions and raises an error before reaching them.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code references freed memory via a stale pointer that is not nulled after fz_drop_band_writer, matching CWE-416. This is distinct from a double-free because the pointer is dereferenced/used after the free.

evidence_lines.code:
if (output_format != OUT_PCLM)
fz_drop_band_writer(ctx, bander);

if (bander)
fz_write_band(ctx, bander, bit ? bit->stride : pix->stride, drawheight, bit ? bit->samples : pix->samples);

bander = fz_new_pnm_band_writer(ctx, out);
if (bander)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cleanup frees bander but leaves the static pointer dangling. Trigger: a valid page creates and frees a bander, then a subsequent page with invalid pixmap dimensions errors before allocating a new bander. The stale bander is then reused by fz_write_band or freed again, yielding a use-after-free.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4563: "z=" in Visual mode may go beyond the end of the line

Problem:    "z=" in Visual mode may go beyond the end of the line.
Solution:   Adjust "badlen".

description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow occurs in vim in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.4563.

code_evidence: Visual-mode path computes badlen as the absolute column distance plus one (lines 36-41) and never bounds it against the current line length before end_visual_mode().

The resulting badlen is passed to spell_find_suggest along with line + curwin->w_cursor.col (lines 68-69), where line is a heap copy from vim_strsave (line 61); an oversized badlen makes spell_find_suggest treat bytes past the heap buffer as part of the bad word.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an unchecked length used against a heap-allocated line buffer (vim_strsave), matching CWE-122's heap-allocated buffer overwrite. It is not merely an off-by-one read: the attacker-controlled badlen can exceed the allocation, enabling memory corruption beyond the heap buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: badlen from the Visual selection is not clamped to the text remaining on the line. Trigger: a Visual selection ending at or beyond the line end (e.g. "z=") yields a length exceeding the heap-allocated line buffer; spell_find_suggest then reads/writes based on that length, producing a heap-based out-of-bounds access and possible crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
fix bug #71719 (Buffer overflow in HTTP url parsing functions)

The parser's offset was not reset when we softfail in scheme
parsing and continue to parse a path.
Thanks to hlt99 at blinkenshell dot org for the report.

description: Buffer overflow in the HTTP URL parsing functions in pecl_http before 3.0.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via non-printable characters in a URL.

code_evidence: maxlen is computed as 3 * len with no allowance for the additional null bytes written for each URL component; the allocation at line 4 is sizeof(*state) + maxlen and state->maxlen is set to this same value, so parsers later appending terminators have no headroom beyond the buffer size derived from the input length.

The weakness is the out-of-bounds write, not merely an integer overflow, so CWE-119 applies.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer-size calculation omits space for per-component null terminators, so the parser can write past the allocated state buffer when a URL is fully parsed. Trigger: a crafted URL whose length saturates the 3*len budget causes out-of-bounds writes during component parsing; the supported consequence is memory corruption potentially leading to code execution.

well:

 - verify that there are no locked children

Reported-by: Alois Wohlschlager <alois1@gmx-topmail.de>
Fixes: c771d683a62e ("vfs: introduce clone_private_mount()")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v3.18

commit_msg: Guard binary expressions from too much recursion.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tjs_Ast *a;', '\ta = conditional(J, notin);'], 'added_lines': ['\tjs_Ast *a = conditional(J, notin);']}
description: jsparse.c in Artifex MuJS through 1.0.2 does not properly maintain the AST depth for binary expressions, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive recursion) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: INCREC() increments the recursion counter before the recursive descent into conditional() and the chained assignment operators.

Each assignment operator branch recurses into assignment(J, notin) for the right-hand side; a crafted file with a long chain of assignment operators drives this recursion without a depth cap visible here.
DECREC() only decrements on the normal return path, so the depth guard is paired with the recursive calls rather than bounding the recursion depth.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs unbounded self-recursion driven by attacker-controlled input length, matching CWE-674 uncontrolled recursion. The concern is recursion depth, not a buffer overflow (CWE-121/122) or mere infinite loop, since recursion is bounded only by input size.

evidence_lines.code:
INCREC();
a = conditional(J, notin);
DECREC();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: assignment() recurses into itself for each assignment operator while only tracking recursion via INCREC/DECREC, without limiting the depth of nested assignment/binary expressions. Trigger: a crafted input containing a long chain of assignment operators causes repeated self-recursion. Supported consequence: excessive stack consumption leading to denial of service.

commit_msg:
Add negative bound check for row and column pooling_sequence in FractionalAvgPoolGrad op to avoid out of bound heap access

PiperOrigin-RevId: 413837346
Change-Id: I2b86034101df31bee161abcb781755e236c7bccd
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '        OP_REQUIRES(context, in_row_start >= 0 && in_row_end >= 0,', '                    errors::InvalidArgument(', '                        "Row sequence tensor values must not be negative, got ",', '                        row_seq_tensor_flat));', '', '          OP_REQUIRES(', '              context, in_col_start >= 0 && in_col_end >= 0,', '              errors::InvalidArgument(', '                  "Column sequence tensor values must not be negative, got ",', '                  col_seq_tensor_flat));']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `FractionalAvgPoolGrad` does not consider cases where the input tensors are invalid allowing an attacker to read from outside of bounds of heap. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: in_row_start is read directly from the user-supplied row_seq_tensor_flat(r) with no lower-bound check; in_row_end is derived from the next element and only clamped to in_max_row_index, so negative values pass through.
in_col_start and in_col_end are similarly taken from col_seq_tensor_flat(c) and col_seq_tensor_flat(c+1) with only an upper clamp, allowing negative column indices.

The loops iterate from in_row_start/in_col_start to in_row_end/in_col_end and compute in_index = (b*in_rows + in_r)*in_cols + in_c, then call in_backprop_tensor_temp_mat.coeffRef(d, in_index); negative in_r or in_c yields an out-of-range index.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked negative indices lead to reading (and writing) outside the allocated in_backprop_tensor_temp buffer, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. The patch adds OP_REQUIRES lower-bound checks confirming the missing constraint; the primary weakness is reading before the buffer, not an integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the row/column sequence tensors are not validated for non-negativity before being used as loop bounds. Trigger: a caller supplies negative entries in row_seq_tensor or col_seq_tensor. Consequence: in_index can become negative or otherwise outside the temp buffer, so the Eigen coeffRef read/write accesses memory before the buffer, an out-of-bounds access.

We will soon need to fetch part of the page state outside of invalid
PTE entries, so provide the input address to the get_page_state()
helper.

Signed-off-by: Quentin Perret <qperret@google.com>
Bug: 279739439
[willdeacon@: Dropped hunks modifying non-existent code]
Signed-off-by: Will Deacon <willdeacon@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstate = guest_get_page_state(pte);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstate = guest_get_page_state(pte, tx->initiator.addr);']}
description: In multiple functions of mem_protect.c, there is a possible way to access hypervisor memory due to a memory access check in the wrong place. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with System execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: The function fetches a leaf PTE for tx->initiator.addr via kvm_pgtable_get_leaf(), then derives page state with guest_get_page_state(pte) and later computes phys = kvm_pte_to_phys(pte). The address used for the page-table walk (tx->initiator.addr) is the initiator's address, while the descriptor's content is validated only through the PTE state/level checks and addr_is_allowed_memory(phys).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 covers operations on memory outside the intended boundary; here the page-table walk/PTE-derived access is performed for an address that is not properly constrained to the initiator's valid range, enabling access to memory outside the intended buffer/page region. The missing address validation is the root cause; the out-of-range memory access is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The page-table lookup and the subsequent state/phys checks are not bound to the same validated address context; the initiator address drives the PTE fetch, so a mismatch between the checked address and the accessed page can let the request operate on a PTE outside the intended initiator range. The consequence is a page-state transition on an unintended page (hypervisor memory), not a direct out-of-bounds array access in this function.

commit_msg:
evtchn: convert per-channel lock to be IRQ-safe

... in order for send_guest_{global,vcpu}_virq() to be able to make use
of it.

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    spin_lock(&chn->lock);', '    spin_unlock(&chn->lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned long  flags;', '    spin_lock_irqsave(&chn->lock, flags);', '    spin_unlock_irqrestore(&chn->lock, flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The channel is locked with plain spin_lock(&chn->lock) and unlocked with spin_unlock(&chn->lock) while holding d->event_lock; the same channel lock is converted to IRQ-safe variants in the patch because send_guest_{global,vcpu}_virq() may take it from IRQ context. Plain locking here leaves a window where an interrupt-context sequence can acquire or observe chn concurrently, so the ECS_IPI state, notify_vcpu_id and port initialization are not exclusively protected.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the code sequence requires exclusive access to the shared evtchn resource but improper synchronization (non-IRQ-safe locking) allows a concurrent interfering sequence to modify it. This is a synchronization/atomicity flaw, not merely a missing bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-channel lock protecting chn fields is acquired without disabling interrupts, so an interfering IRQ-context sequence using the same lock can run concurrently. Trigger: an IPI bind races with virq sending on the same port. Consequence: non-exclusive access to chn state, violating internal evtchn assumptions and enabling out-of-bounds access, bug checks, host/guest crash, or privilege escalation.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error manager's profile pointer and exception are mishandled across the JPEG error path. When GetCharacter hits EOF, the code destroys the profile and invokes ThrowMagickException using the cached exception, which can longjmp through libjpeg back to the caller. The image's profile state and error_manager->profile may then reference freed memory used later during cleanup, yielding a use-after-free.

commit_msg:
ahci: Update byte count after DMA completion

Currently, DMA read/write operations neglect to update
the byte count after a successful transfer like ATAPI
DMA read or PIO read/write operations do.

We correct this oversight by adding another callback into
the IDEDMAOps structure. The commit callback is called
whenever we are cleaning up a scatter-gather list.
AHCI can register this callback in order to update post-
transfer information such as byte count updates.

We use this callback in AHCI to consolidate where we delete
the SGlist as generated from the PRDT, as well as update the
byte count after the transfer is complete.

The QEMUSGList structure has an init flag added to it in order
to make qemu_sglist_destroy a nop if it is called when
there is no sglist, which simplifies cleanup and error paths.

This patch fixes several AHCI problems, notably Non-NCQ modes
of operation for Windows 7 as well as Hibernate support for Windows 7.

Signed-off-by: John Snow <jsnow@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>
Message-id: 1412204151-18117-3-git-send-email-jsnow@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* update number of transferred bytes */', '    ad->cur_cmd->status = cpu_to_le32(le32_to_cpu(ad->cur_cmd->status) + size);', '', '    if (has_sglist) {', '        qemu_sglist_destroy(&s->sg);', '    }'], 'added_lines': ['    /* Update number of transferred bytes, destroy sglist */', '    ahci_commit_buf(dma, size);']}
description: The ahci_commit_buf function in ide/ahci.c in QEMU allows attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL dereference) when the command header 'ad->cur_cmd' is null.

code_evidence: Line 6 unconditionally dereferences ad->cur_cmd to read opts without checking whether the command header pointer is NULL.
Line 27 dereferences ad->cur_cmd->status to update the transferred byte count, again with no NULL guard.
Line 35 dereferences ad->cur_cmd->status when writing the PIO FIS, reached after the out label and end_transfer_func.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is exactly a NULL pointer dereference: a pointer expected to be valid is used to read fields (opts, status) without validation, and the supported consequence is an availability-impacting crash. This is distinct from a bounds or use-after-free issue since the pointer is simply NULL.

evidence_lines.code: uint32_t opts = le32_to_cpu(ad->cur_cmd->opts);
ad->cur_cmd->status = cpu_to_le32(le32_to_cpu(ad->cur_cmd->status) + size);
ahci_write_fis_pio(ad, le32_to_cpu(ad->cur_cmd->status));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function assumes ad->cur_cmd is always a valid command header and dereferences it at entry and again after transfer completion. If the command header is unset or cleared (NULL), these dereferences crash the QEMU process, causing a denial of service. The root cause is the missing NULL check on the pointer before use, not the transfer logic itself.

commit_msg: Issue #539:  Try a different way to compute max/min time_t values.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstatic time_t t;', '\ttime_t a;', '\tif (t == 0) {', '\t\ta = 1;', '\t\twhile (a > t) {', '\t\t\tt = a;', '\t\t\ta = a * 2 + 1;', '\t\t}', '\treturn t;'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* ISO C allows time_t to be a floating-point type,', '\t   but POSIX requires an integer type.  The following', '\t   should work on any system that follows the POSIX', '\t   conventions. */', '\tif (((time_t)0) < ((time_t)-1)) {', '\t\t/* Time_t is unsigned */', '\t\treturn (~(time_t)0);', '\t} else {', '\t\t/* Time_t is signed. */', '\t\tconst uintmax_t max_unsigned_time_t = (uintmax_t)(~(time_t)0);', '\t\tconst uintmax_t max_signed_time_t = max_unsigned_time_t >> 1;', '\t\treturn (time_t)max_signed_time_t;']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the (1) get_time_t_max and (2) get_time_t_min functions in archive_read_support_format_mtree.c in libarchive before 3.2.0 allow remote attackers to have unspecified impact via a crafted mtree file, which triggers undefined behavior.

code_evidence: The loop computes a maximum time_t by repeatedly doubling: a starts at 1, and while a > t, t is set to a and a is recomputed as a * 2 + 1. On the final iteration, a * 2 + 1 exceeds the representable range of time_t, so the multiplication and addition wrap around. The wrapped value then fails the a > t comparison, terminating the loop with a maximum value that may be incorrect.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the arithmetic a * 2 + 1 can exceed the time_t representation and wrap before the comparison, which is exactly an integer overflow that the logic assumes cannot occur.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop doubles and increments a signed time_t without any bound check, so the final a * 2 + 1 step overflows. Trigger: calling get_time_t_max on platforms lacking TIME_T_MAX. Consequence: undefined behavior and a potentially wrong maximum time_t, which callers may use for size or time computations.

commit_msg:
power: supply: bq24190: Fix use after free bug in bq24190_remove due to race condition

In bq24190_probe, &bdi->input_current_limit_work is bound
with bq24190_input_current_limit_work. When external power
changed, it will call bq24190_charger_external_power_changed
 to start the work.

If we remove the module which will call bq24190_remove to make
cleanup, there may be a unfinished work. The possible
sequence is as follows:

CPU0                  CPUc1

                    |bq24190_input_current_limit_work
bq24190_remove      |
power_supply_unregister  |
device_unregister   |
power_supply_dev_release|
kfree(psy)          |
                    |
                    | power_supply_get_property_from_supplier
                    |   //use

Fix it by finishing the work before cleanup in the bq24190_remove

Fixes: 97774672573a ("power_supply: Initialize changed_work before calling device_add")
Signed-off-by: Zheng Wang <zyytlz.wz@163.com>
Signed-off-by: Sebastian Reichel <sebastian.reichel@collabora.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcancel_delayed_work_sync(&bdi->input_current_limit_work);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.2.9. A use-after-free was found in bq24190_remove in drivers/power/supply/bq24190_charger.c. It could allow a local attacker to crash the system due to a race condition.

code_evidence: bq24190_remove unregisters bdi->battery and bdi->charger via power_supply_unregister without first canceling the pending input_current_limit_work that was scheduled in probe. Once unregistration releases the power supply objects, the still-queued work can run bq24190_input_current_limit_work, which dereferences the freed bdi/psy memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees/releases objects (via power_supply_unregister) while an asynchronous work item still holds references to them, so the work later accesses freed memory. This is a lifetime/ordering flaw matching CWE-416, not merely a race without a use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the removal path does not synchronize with the delayed work bound to bdi->input_current_limit_work before freeing the power supply objects. Trigger: an external power change queues the work, then the driver is removed concurrently. Consequence: the work executes after unregistration/free, causing a use-after-free that can crash the kernel.

commit_msg: fixed #2364
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [''], 'added_lines': ['\tif (NbBits>32) return GF_NON_COMPLIANT_BITSTREAM;']}
description: Integer overflow vulnerability in function Q_DecCoordOnUnitSphere file bifs/unquantize.c in GPAC version 2.2-rev0-gab012bbfb-master.

code_evidence: Line 13 reads NbBits bits and computes (1 << (NbBits-1)); line 15 calls Q_InverseQuantize with NbBits-1. The function applies no bound on NbBits before these shifts/subtractions, so a large NbBits value drives the shift and exponent computations past the integer range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is an integer shift/arithmetic calculation whose result is assumed representable, matching CWE-190 integer overflow/wraparound. It is not a bounds/array-index issue (CWE-125/787), because the defect is the unchecked numeric computation itself.

evidence_lines.code:
value = gf_bs_read_int(bs, NbBits) - (1 << (NbBits-1) );
m_ft[i] = sign * Q_InverseQuantize(0, 1, NbBits-1, sign*value);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: NbBits is attacker-controlled and unvalidated, so the shift (1 << (NbBits-1)) and the NbBits-1 exponent used in inverse quantization can overflow/wrap. Trigger: a bitstream supplying NbBits greater than the bit width. Consequence: wrapped arithmetic yields incorrect or extreme values feeding later tangent/delta and index computation, causing instability (e.g., crash) rather than a bounded decode.
