commit_msg:
Issue 711:  Be more careful about verifying filename lengths when writing ISO9660 archives

* Don't cast size_t to int, since this can lead to overflow
  on machines where sizeof(int) < sizeof(size_t)
* Check a + b > limit by writing it as
    a > limit || b > limit || a + b > limit
  to avoid problems when a + b wraps around.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint ffmax, parent_len;', '\tr = idr_start(a, idr, isoent->children.cnt, ffmax, 6, 2, &rb_ops);', '\t\tif ((int)(l = np->file->basename_utf16.length) > ffmax)', '\t\tif ((int)np->file->basename_utf16.length > ffmax) {', '\t\tif (parent_len + np->mb_len > 240) {', '\t\tif ((int)l == ffmax)', '\t\telse if ((int)l == ffmax-2)', '\t\telse if ((int)l == ffmax-4)'], 'added_lines': ['\tsize_t ffmax, parent_len;', '\tr = idr_start(a, idr, isoent->children.cnt, (int)ffmax, 6, 2, &rb_ops);', '\t\tif ((l = np->file->basename_utf16.length) > ffmax)', '\t\tif (np->file->basename_utf16.length > ffmax) {', '\t\tif (parent_len > 240', '\t\t    || np->mb_len > 240', '\t\t    || parent_len + np->mb_len > 240) {', '\t\tif (l == ffmax)', '\t\telse if (l == ffmax-2)', '\t\telse if (l == ffmax-4)']}
description: Integer overflow in the ISO9660 writer in libarchive before 3.2.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or execute arbitrary code via vectors related to verifying filename lengths when writing an ISO9660 archive, which trigger a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: ffmax and parent_len are declared as int; parent_len is accumulated over the parent chain and passed to idr_start as an int length/count parameter.
parent_len is summed from mb_len values across parents without any bound, so it can grow large or wrap; the type is int rather than size_t.
The length check computes parent_len + np->mb_len > 240 in int arithmetic; if the sum wraps, the comparison can pass and the over-long pathname is accepted.
l is assigned from basename_utf16.length (size_t) and cast to int in the comparison; a large length truncates, so the clamp to ffmax is skipped and malloc((l+1)*2) uses the wrong size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer overflow/wraparound: signed int arithmetic produces a small or negative result that defeats length validation. This is CWE-190 rather than merely CWE-787, because the missing constraint is the integer calculation itself.

evidence_lines.code:
int ffmax, parent_len;
r = idr_start(a, idr, isoent->children.cnt, ffmax, 6, 2, &rb_ops);

parent_len = 1;
parent_len += np->mb_len + 1;

if (parent_len + np->mb_len > 240) {
}

if ((int)(l = np->file->basename_utf16.length) > ffmax)
p[l+1] = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: filename/path lengths are held in int and combined with int arithmetic. Trigger: a crafted ISO9660 entry with a very long UTF-16 basename or deep parent chain makes l or parent_len + mb_len exceed INT_MAX. The wrapped/truncated value bypasses the 240-byte and ffmax checks, leading to undersized allocation and out-of-bounds write, supporting crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
ffprobe: Fix null pointer dereference with color primaries

Found-by: AD-lab of venustech
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (frame->color_primaries != AVCOL_PRI_UNSPECIFIED)', '            print_str("color_primaries", av_color_primaries_name(frame->color_primaries));', '        else', '            print_str_opt("color_primaries", av_color_primaries_name(frame->color_primaries));'], 'added_lines': ['        print_primaries(w, frame->color_primaries);']}
description: The av_color_primaries_name function in libavutil/pixdesc.c in FFmpeg 3.3.3 may return a NULL pointer depending on a value contained in a file, but callers do not anticipate this, as demonstrated by the avcodec_string function in libavcodec/utils.c, leading to a NULL pointer dereference. (It is also conceivable that there is security relevance for a NULL pointer dereference in av_color_primaries_name calls within the ffprobe command-line program.)

code_evidence: Lines 55-58 call av_color_primaries_name(frame->color_primaries) and pass the returned const char* directly into print_str/print_str_opt without checking for NULL. The value of frame->color_primaries comes from decoded frame metadata, so a file-provided enum value that av_color_primaries_name does not recognize yields a NULL name pointer that is then handed to the printing routine.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a direct NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): a pointer expected valid is used without a NULL check. It is not a buffer overflow or uninitialized read; the specific weakness is the missing NULL guard on the name lookup result.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of av_color_primaries_name is assumed non-NULL, but it returns NULL for unrecognized color_primaries values. Trigger: a crafted media file sets frame->color_primaries to a value outside the known table. Consequence: the NULL name string is dereferenced/printed, causing a crash (DoS) in the ffprobe path.

commit_msg:
Limit the number of HTTP requests processed from a connection in I/O cycle

Signed-off-by: Yan Avlasov <yavlasov@google.com>

Signed-off-by: Ryan Northey <ryan@synca.io>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  filter_manager_.decodeHeaders(*request_headers_, end_stream);'], 'added_lines': ['  if (!connection_manager_.shouldDeferRequestProxyingToNextIoCycle()) {', '    filter_manager_.decodeHeaders(*request_headers_, end_stream);', '  } else {', '    state_.deferred_to_next_io_iteration_ = true;', '    state_.deferred_end_stream_ = end_stream;', '  }']}
description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

code_evidence: After tracing, decodeHeaders directly invokes filter_manager_.decodeHeaders for every parsed request. The patch replaces this unconditional proxy dispatch with a check of connection_manager_.shouldDeferRequestProxyingToNextIoCycle(), deferring the call and recording deferred_end_stream_ instead of processing immediately. The original unconditional path therefore processes all requests arriving in one I/O cycle without a per-cycle bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function lacks throttling of the number of requests processed per I/O cycle, allowing attacker-driven resource exhaustion. This is a missing throttling constraint, not an out-of-bounds or type error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: request proxying is dispatched immediately for each stream parsed in an I/O cycle, with no limit on how many are handled per cycle. Trigger: a peer rapidly cancels many HTTP/2 streams, causing many request-header completions in a single cycle. Consequence: unbounded CPU/processing consumption, enabling denial of service. The fix bounds work per cycle by deferring excess requests.

commit_msg:
Fix 4 byte oobread in msp430 disassembler ##crash

* Only crashes with asan builds
* Add missing =SN register
* Reported by cnitlrt via huntrdev
* BountyID: 1c22055b-b015-47a8-a57b-4982978751d0
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tR_LOG_ERROR ("read (magic)");', '\t\tR_LOG_ERROR ("read (ehdr)");'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tR_LOG_DEBUG ("read (magic)");', '\t\tR_LOG_DEBUG ("read (ehdr)");']}
description: Out-of-bounds Read in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.7.0. The bug causes the program reads data past the end of the intented buffer. Typically, this can allow attackers to read sensitive information from other memory locations or cause a crash.

code_evidence: ehdr is sized sizeof(Elf_(Ehdr)) and only zero-initialized; len = r_buf_read_at(bin->b, 0, ehdr, sizeof(ehdr)) records how many bytes were actually read, and the guard rejects only len < 32.
After that guard, i starts at 16 and READ16/READ32/READ64 macros sequentially consume bytes from ehdr up to offset 95 (e_shstrndx), regardless of the actual len returned.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because parsing reads data beyond the intended valid length of the buffer. The defect is insufficient validation of len against the bytes actually consumed, not a write overflow (CWE-787) or a type confusion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length check accepts any read of at least 32 bytes, but the subsequent header field parsing consumes up to 96 bytes of the ehdr buffer. Trigger: a truncated ELF file whose buffer read returns between 32 and 95 bytes. Consequence: the READ macros read past the initialized portion of ehdr, giving an out-of-bounds read that can crash or leak adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
journalctl: verify that old entries are not sealed with too recent key

When verifying seals produced with forward secure sealing, the verification
currently does not check that old entries are only sealed with the key for
their epoch and not a more recent one. This missing check allows an attacker
to remove seals, and create new ones with the currently available key, and
verify will claim everything is in order, although all entries could have
been modified.

This resolves CVE-2023-31439.

description: An issue was discovered in systemd 253. An attacker can modify the contents of past events in a sealed log file and then adjust the file such that checking the integrity shows no error, despite modifications. NOTE: the vendor reportedly sent "a reply denying that any of the finding was a security vulnerability."

code_evidence: At a tag, rt is computed from the tag epoch and the code checks only that the last entry_realtime is not later than rt + fss_interval_usec (line 275), then verifies the HMAC tag (line 308).
There is no check that entries preceding the tag were sealed with the key for their own epoch rather than a more recent key, so a rewritten file with re-created seals passes verification.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-354 fits because the integrity-check validation is incomplete: the tag/HMAC check is performed but the epoch-to-entry binding that makes the seal meaningful is not validated, so modification escapes detection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the integrity check of forward-secure seals only bounds the newest entry realtime against the tag interval and never confirms older entries belong to the tag's epoch. Trigger: an attacker removes seals, modifies old entries, and re-seals with the currently available key; verification accepts the file. Consequence: undetected modification of past sealed log entries.

commit_msg:
Release "3.0.8": Address Array alloc sizing issues from issue "integer overflow and buffer overflow #5".

FossilOrigin-Name: 8c46a1d465b358110dcfb271721d35fe843a1b52f2fa24ccc10094eb8aaf6fe4
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int nsiz = len + 1, mod = ALLOC_MOD_SIZE;', '    if (nsiz > MAX_ARRAY_LIST) {', '        Jsi_LogError("array size too large");'], 'added_lines': ['    uint nsiz = len + 1, mod = ALLOC_MOD_SIZE;', '    if (len >= interp->maxArrayList || nsiz > interp->maxArrayList) {', '        Jsi_LogError("array size too big: %u >= %u", len, interp->maxArrayList);']}
description: Integer overflow vulnerability in function Jsi_ObjArraySizer in jsish before 3.0.8, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: Line 3 computes nsiz = len + 1 in a signed int, so a large uint len can wrap to a negative or small value; line 6 then rounds nsiz up modulo ALLOC_MOD_SIZE, propagating the wrapped value.
Lines 7-10 only compare nsiz against the fixed MAX_ARRAY_LIST constant, so a wrapped/negative nsiz passes this check and returns 0 only on the fixed limit.
Lines 11-14 use nsiz as the realloc size (nsiz*sizeof(Jsi_Value*)) and as the memset length via oldsz = nsiz-obj->arrMaxSize, so the wrapped size drives allocation and memory initialization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size computation (len+1, rounding) that can overflow/wrap and then uses the result for allocation and memory writes, matching CWE-190. This is distinct from a pure out-of-bounds write because the unsafe size arithmetic is the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
int nsiz = len + 1, mod = ALLOC_MOD_SIZE;
nsiz = nsiz + ((mod-1) - (nsiz + mod - 1)%mod);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size calculation len+1 is stored in signed int and rounded without checking len against a maximum, so attacker-controlled len can wrap to a small or negative nsiz that still satisfies the MAX_ARRAY_LIST check. Trigger: a large array length passed to Jsi_ObjArraySizer. Consequence: undersized allocation and memset with a wrapped length, enabling heap buffer overflow and potential code execution.

If io_setup is called successful in try_smi_init() but try_smi_init()
goes out_err before calling ipmi_register_smi(), so ipmi_unregister_smi()

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. There is a use-after-free upon attempted read access to /proc/ioports after the ipmi_si module is removed, related to drivers/char/ipmi/ipmi_si_intf.c, drivers/char/ipmi/ipmi_si_mem_io.c, and drivers/char/ipmi/ipmi_si_port_io.c.

code_evidence: Line 7 assigns io->io_cleanup = port_cleanup before the register-size switch and before any request_region calls, so the cleanup callback is installed even when setup later fails.

Lines 26-35 loop over io_size calling request_region with DEVICE_NAME; on failure the while loop releases already-acquired regions and returns -EIO, but io->io_cleanup remains set. The patch moves the assignment to after the loop so cleanup is only registered on success.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the freed resource->name memory is later dereferenced by seq_printf in r_show when reading /proc/ioports, matching reuse-after-free. This is not merely a resource leak: the premature io_cleanup assignment enables freeing of a name still referenced by procfs.

evidence_lines.code: io->io_cleanup = port_cleanup;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: io_cleanup is registered (line 7) before request_region can fail. Trigger: request_region returns NULL mid-loop (lines 27-28) causing early return -EIO while io_cleanup still points to port_cleanup. If the error path then runs cleanup, or the module is removed without ipmi_unregister_smi, the resource name (DEVICE_NAME string) is freed while /proc/ioports still references it, yielding a use-after-free read.

Add missing returns

Reported by Behzad Najjarpour Jabbari, Secunia Research.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.6-0, a heap-based buffer over-read in the GetNextToken function in token.c allows remote attackers to obtain sensitive information from process memory or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted SVG document that is mishandled in the GetUserSpaceCoordinateValue function in coders/svg.c.

code_evidence: The quoted-token loop at 35-48 advances p until '\0', but at 37 evaluates *(p+1) when *p is a backslash; if the backslash is the final character before the terminator, the read at p+1 is the terminator itself and the loop continues, so a following iteration can read past the end of the string.

The default branch loop at 82-101 dereferences *p and *(p-1) at 85 and 98 while advancing p; the inner parenthesis loop at 94 has no bound relative to start, so a crafted unterminated token can drive p beyond the string's allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory beyond the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. The patch's added strlen-based length checks confirm the missing bound; this is a read overrun rather than a write (CWE-787) or an injection issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the tokenizer scans for delimiters and escape sequences without a length bound, relying only on '\0' or ')' to stop. A crafted SVG coordinate string lacking the expected terminator causes the pointer to advance past the allocated buffer, yielding a heap-based out-of-bounds read that can leak process memory.

description: The exif_convert_any_to_int function in ext/exif/exif.c in PHP before 5.6.30, 7.0.x before 7.0.15, and 7.1.x before 7.1.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via crafted EXIF data that triggers an attempt to divide the minimum representable negative integer by -1.

code_evidence: In the TAG_FMT_SRATIONAL case, s_den is read as a signed 32-bit value from attacker-controlled EXIF data and only checked against zero. The signed numerator php_ifd_get32s(value) is then divided by s_den; when the numerator is INT_MIN and s_den is -1, the signed division overflows.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-189 (Numeric Errors) covers improper numeric calculation such as this signed division overflow. The missing guard against INT_MIN/-1 directly supports the numeric-error category rather than a memory-safety weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an unchecked signed division of an attacker-supplied numerator by an attacker-supplied denominator. The zero check does not exclude the INT_MIN / -1 case, so crafted EXIF rational data triggers signed integer overflow, causing a floating-point exception and application crash (denial of service).

backport from 1.9 (rev #9980)
fixed temporary GRUU bug that lead to infinite loop
Credits to Tolga Tarhan

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tit=it->next;']}
description: A Denial of Service (infinite loop) exists in OpenSIPS before 1.10 in lookup.c.

code_evidence: The inner loop `while (it)` at [84] only breaks when a valid contact matches the sip_instance and has a newer last_modified [88,89]. The pointer `it` is initialized from `ptr->next` [83] but the loop body never advances `it`, so when the match conditions are false the loop re-tests the same node forever.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a loop whose exit condition is unreachable because the iterator is never advanced, which is the defining characteristic of CWE-835. The related missing-increment could also be framed as a general logic error, but the concrete availability impact of the non-terminating loop makes CWE-835 the direct fit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the traversal loop lacks an `it = it->next` increment, so the exit condition (break or `it` becoming NULL) can never be reached for a non-matching contact. Trigger: a lookup whose R-URI carries a GRUU sip_instance and call_id matching a contact that has subsequent contacts not satisfying the instance/last_modified test. Consequence: the process spins indefinitely, consuming CPU and denying service (CWE-835).

commit_msg:
passthrough: quarantine PCI devices

When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for
that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The
IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that
the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However,
when the guest domain is torn down the device is assigned back to dom0,
thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data.

This patch introduces a 'quarantine' for PCI devices using dom_io. When
the toolstack makes a device assignable (by binding it to pciback), it
will now also assign it to DOMID_IO and the device will only be assigned
back to dom0 when the device is made unassignable again. Whilst device is
assignable it will only ever transfer between dom_io and guest domains.
dom_io is actually only used as a sentinel domain for quarantining purposes;
it is not configured with any IOMMU mappings. Assignment to dom_io simply
means that the device's initiator (requestor) identifier is not present in
the IOMMU's device table and thus any DMA transactions issued will be
terminated with a fault condition.

In addition, a fix to assignment handling is made for VT-d.  Failure
during the assignment step should not lead to a device still being
associated with its prior owner. Hand the device to DomIO temporarily,
until the assignment step has completed successfully.  Remove the PI
hooks from the source domain then earlier as well.

Failure of the recovery reassign_device_ownership() may not go silent:
There e.g. may still be left over RMRR mappings in the domain assignment
to which has failed, and hence we can't allow that domain to continue
executing.

NOTE: This patch also includes one printk() cleanup; the
      "XEN_DOMCTL_assign_device: " tag is dropped in iommu_do_pci_domctl(),
      since similar printk()-s elsewhere also don't log such a tag.

This is XSA-302.

Signed-off-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>

+++ func_after
@@ -15,6 +15,7 @@
      * Initialise our DOMID_IO domain.
      * This domain owns I/O pages that are within the range of the page_info
      * array. Mappings occur at the priv of the caller.
+     * Quarantined PCI devices will be associated with this domain.
      */
     dom_io = domain_create(DOMID_IO, NULL, false);
     if ( IS_ERR(dom_io) )
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['     * Quarantined PCI devices will be associated with this domain.']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing attackers to gain host OS privileges via DMA in a situation where an untrusted domain has access to a physical device. This occurs because passed through PCI devices may corrupt host memory after deassignment. When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However, when the guest domain is torn down, or the device is deassigned, the device is assigned back to dom0, thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data. An untrusted domain with access to a physical device can DMA into host memory, leading to privilege escalation. Only systems where guests are given direct access to physical devices capable of DMA (PCI pass-through) are vulnerable. Systems which do not use PCI pass-through are not vulnerable.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only creates Xen system domains (DOMID_XEN, DOMID_IO, DOMID_COW) and panics on error; it contains no OS command construction or execution, so it cannot support CWE-78.

commit_msg:
conversation: Remove conversation from the correct table

In conversation_set_addr2, if the existing conversation has
a port2, remove it from the _no_addr2 hashtable, not the _no_port2
hashtable.

Fix #18766
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        conversation_remove_from_hashtable(conversation_hashtable_no_port2, conv);'], 'added_lines': ['        conversation_remove_from_hashtable(conversation_hashtable_no_addr2, conv);']}
description: Dissection engine bug in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.2 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.10 and allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: When NO_ADDR2 is set, the function removes conv from a hashtable. If NO_PORT2 is also set it removes from conversation_hashtable_no_addr2_or_port2; otherwise it removes from conversation_hashtable_no_port2. The removed entry is then re-inserted (line 30) under a new key.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers failing to properly release a resource before reuse. Here the conversation's stale hashtable entry is not removed from the correct table before the object is re-inserted, matching improper resource release. It is a bookkeeping/release defect rather than a memory-corruption issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the else branch removes the conversation from the wrong hashtable (no_port2 instead of no_addr2), so the stale entry in conversation_hashtable_no_addr2 is never released. Trigger: calling conversation_set_addr2 on a conversation lacking NO_PORT2. Consequence: the old hashtable entry persists, leaving an improperly released resource that can accumulate and contribute to denial of service.

commit_msg:
Add limits to the size of received {A,I}XFR, in megabytes

This prevents memory exhaustion in case the master is sending a
very large amount of data in an update.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  AXFRRetriever retriever(raddr, domain, tt, (laddr.sin4.sin_family == 0) ? NULL : &laddr);'], 'added_lines': ['  AXFRRetriever retriever(raddr, domain, tt, (laddr.sin4.sin_family == 0) ? NULL : &laddr, ((size_t) ::arg().asNum("xfr-max-received-mbytes")) * 1024 * 1024);']}
description: PowerDNS (aka pdns) Authoritative Server before 4.0.1 allows remote primary DNS servers to cause a denial of service (memory exhaustion and secondary DNS server crash) via a large (1) AXFR or (2) IXFR response.

code_evidence: Line 4 constructs AXFRRetriever without any size or byte limit parameter, so the transfer reader has no bound on how much data it will accept from the remote primary.

Line 9 loops on retriever.getChunk(recs) until the peer stops sending; each chunk's records are appended via rrs.push_back(rr) at line 33 and the full vector is returned at line 37, so accumulated records are retained for the whole transfer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to restrict the amount of a limited resource (memory) consumed during a transfer, matching CWE-400's lack of throttling for allocated resources. It is not a length-calculation overflow; the defect is the missing consumption bound itself.

evidence_lines.code: AXFRRetriever retriever(raddr, domain, tt, (laddr.sin4.sin_family == 0) ? NULL : &laddr);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the AXFR/IXFR retriever is created with no maximum received size, and doAxfr keeps consuming chunks and appending records to rrs for as long as the remote server sends data. Trigger: a malicious or compromised primary streams an extremely large transfer. Consequence: unbounded memory growth in the secondary, leading to memory exhaustion and crash.

commit_msg:
sunrpc: Avoid a KASAN slab-out-of-bounds bug in xdr_set_page_base()

This seems to happen fairly easily during READ_PLUS testing on NFS v4.2.
I found that we could end up accessing xdr->buf->pages[pgnr] with a pgnr
greater than the number of pages in the array. So let's just return
early if we're setting base to a point at the end of the page data and
let xdr_set_tail_base() handle setting up the buffer pointers instead.

Signed-off-by: Anna Schumaker <Anna.Schumaker@Netapp.com>
Fixes: 8d86e373b0ef ("SUNRPC: Clean up helpers xdr_set_iov() and xdr_set_page_base()")
Signed-off-by: Trond Myklebust <trond.myklebust@hammerspace.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (base >= maxlen) {', '\t\tbase = maxlen;', '\t\tmaxlen = 0;', '\t} else'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (base >= maxlen)', '\t\treturn 0;', '\telse']}
description: net/sunrpc/xdr.c in the Linux kernel before 5.13.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (xdr_set_page_base slab-out-of-bounds access) by performing many NFS 4.2 READ_PLUS operations.

code_evidence: maxlen is set from xdr->buf->page_len; when base >= maxlen the function clamps base to maxlen, sets maxlen to 0, and does not return early, so execution continues.
base is then incremented by xdr->buf->page_base and shifted (base >> PAGE_SHIFT) to compute pgnr, which indexes xdr->buf->pages[pgnr] without checking pgnr against the page array size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes an array index from attacker-influenced base without bounding it against the pages array, causing an out-of-bounds memory access. This directly matches CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within a buffer's bounds; the missing early-return guard is the specific cause.

evidence_lines.code:
pgnr = base >> PAGE_SHIFT;
xdr->page_ptr = &xdr->buf->pages[pgnr];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: when base reaches or exceeds page_len, base is clamped to page_len rather than causing an early return, so page_base addition and the shift can yield pgnr beyond the allocated pages array. Trigger: a caller passing base at/after the end of page data (e.g. NFSv4.2 READ_PLUS). Consequence: out-of-bounds access to xdr->buf->pages[pgnr], a slab-out-of-bounds read leading to a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
KVM: Don't accept obviously wrong gsi values via KVM_IRQFD

We cannot add routes for gsi values >= KVM_MAX_IRQ_ROUTES -- see
kvm_set_irq_routing(). Hence, there is no sense in accepting them
via KVM_IRQFD. Prevent them from entering the system in the first
place.

Signed-off-by: Jan H. Schönherr <jschoenh@amazon.de>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\tif (args->gsi >= KVM_MAX_IRQ_ROUTES)']}
description: The KVM subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.13.3 allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (assertion failure, and hypervisor hang or crash) via an out-of bounds guest_irq value, related to arch/x86/kvm/vmx.c and virt/kvm/eventfd.c.

code_evidence: The function checks only args->flags against the allowed flag mask; it does not validate the args->gsi field before dispatching.
Valid flags fall through to kvm_irqfd_deassign or kvm_irqfd_assign, which receive the unchecked gsi value from user-supplied args.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is missing validation of an input property (gsi range) before processing, which matches CWE-20's improper input validation. It is not a transformation or filtering flaw; the value is simply accepted unchecked.

evidence_lines.code:
if (args->flags & ~(KVM_IRQFD_FLAG_DEASSIGN | KVM_IRQFD_FLAG_RESAMPLE))
return -EINVAL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: kvm_irqfd accepts a user-controlled gsi without checking it against KVM_MAX_IRQ_ROUTES. Trigger: a caller passes a gsi >= KVM_MAX_IRQ_ROUTES through KVM_IRQFD, reaching assign/deassign paths that cannot handle such routes. Supported consequence: an assertion failure and hypervisor hang or crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Correctly calculate the length of SM2 plaintext given the ciphertext

Previously the length of the SM2 plaintext could be incorrectly calculated.
The plaintext length was calculated by taking the ciphertext length and
taking off an "overhead" value.

The overhead value was assumed to have a "fixed" element of 10 bytes.
This is incorrect since in some circumstances it can be more than 10 bytes.
Additionally the overhead included the length of two integers C1x and C1y,
which were assumed to be the same length as the field size (32 bytes for
the SM2 curve). However in some cases these integers can have an additional
padding byte when the msb is set, to disambiguate them from negative
integers. Additionally the integers can also be less than 32 bytes in
length in some cases.

If the calculated overhead is incorrect and larger than the actual value
this can result in the calculated plaintext length being too small.
Applications are likely to allocate buffer sizes based on this and therefore
a buffer overrun can occur.

CVE-2021-3711

Issue reported by John Ouyang.

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Nicola Tuveri <nic.tuv@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int sm2_plaintext_size(const EC_KEY *key, const EVP_MD *digest, size_t msg_len,', '                       size_t *pt_size)', '    const size_t field_size = ec_field_size(EC_KEY_get0_group(key));', '    const int md_size = EVP_MD_size(digest);', '    size_t overhead;', '    if (md_size < 0) {', '        SM2err(SM2_F_SM2_PLAINTEXT_SIZE, SM2_R_INVALID_DIGEST);', '        return 0;', '    }', '    if (field_size == 0) {', '        SM2err(SM2_F_SM2_PLAINTEXT_SIZE, SM2_R_INVALID_FIELD);', '        return 0;', '    }', '    overhead = 10 + 2 * field_size + (size_t)md_size;', '    if (msg_len <= overhead) {', '    *pt_size = msg_len - overhead;'], 'added_lines': ['int sm2_plaintext_size(const unsigned char *ct, size_t ct_size, size_t *pt_size)', '    struct SM2_Ciphertext_st *sm2_ctext = NULL;', '    sm2_ctext = d2i_SM2_Ciphertext(NULL, &ct, ct_size);', '    if (sm2_ctext == NULL) {', '    *pt_size = sm2_ctext->C2->length;', '    SM2_Ciphertext_free(sm2_ctext);', '']}
description: In order to decrypt SM2 encrypted data an application is expected to call the API function EVP_PKEY_decrypt(). Typically an application will call this function twice. The first time, on entry, the "out" parameter can be NULL and, on exit, the "outlen" parameter is populated with the buffer size required to hold the decrypted plaintext. The application can then allocate a sufficiently sized buffer and call EVP_PKEY_decrypt() again, but this time passing a non-NULL value for the "out" parameter. A bug in the implementation of the SM2 decryption code means that the calculation of the buffer size required to hold the plaintext returned by the first call to EVP_PKEY_decrypt() can be smaller than the actual size required by the second call. This can lead to a buffer overflow when EVP_PKEY_decrypt() is called by the application a second time with a buffer that is too small. A malicious attacker who is able present SM2 content for decryption to an application could cause attacker chosen data to overflow the buffer by up to a maximum of 62 bytes altering the contents of other data held after the buffer, possibly changing application behaviour or causing the application to crash. The location of the buffer is application dependent but is typically heap allocated. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1l (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1k).

code_evidence: field_size is derived from the key group and assumed to be the exact C1x/C1y integer length; overhead hardcodes a fixed 10-byte element plus 2*field_size and the digest size.

The only guard checks msg_len <= overhead and otherwise rejects, but overhead itself may be larger than the true ciphertext overhead when integers are shorter or padded, so the computed size is wrong rather than rejected.
*pt_size = msg_len - overhead stores an under-estimated plaintext length that the caller uses to allocate a buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The wrong size calculation causes a later unchecked copy of plaintext into an application-allocated buffer, whose size is derived from this function, resulting in a classic buffer overflow (CWE-120). A size-calculation error (CWE-131) is the mechanism, but the supported consequence is the unchecked buffer copy overflow.

evidence_lines.code:
const size_t field_size = ec_field_size(EC_KEY_get0_group(key));
overhead = 10 + 2 * field_size + (size_t)md_size;
*pt_size = msg_len - overhead;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the plaintext size is computed by subtracting an assumed fixed overhead, ignoring that the DER-encoded C1x/C1y integers vary in length. When the real overhead is smaller than the assumed one, the reported plaintext length is too small; the application then allocates that undersized buffer and the second EVP_PKEY_decrypt call writes the larger plaintext past its end.

commit_msg:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

Signed-off-by: Jeff King <peff@peff.net>
Signed-off-by: Junio C Hamano <gitster@pobox.com>

commit_msg:
Fix dangling pointer in xsltCopyText

xsltCopyText didn't reset ctxt->lasttext in some cases which could
lead to various memory errors in relation with CDATA sections in input
documents.

Found by OSS-Fuzz.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tctxt->lasttext = NULL;']}
description: In xsltCopyText in transform.c in libxslt 1.1.33, a pointer variable isn't reset under certain circumstances. If the relevant memory area happened to be freed and reused in a certain way, a bounds check could fail and memory outside a buffer could be written to, or uninitialized data could be disclosed.

code_evidence: In the CDATA-block branch, after xmlNewCDataBlock succeeds, ctxt->lasttext is set to copy->content and lasttsize/lasttuse to len, so the cached text pointer refers to the CDATA buffer.

In the final else branch, after xmlNewTextLen succeeds, ctxt->lasttext is again assigned copy->content with matching size fields; no path in this function clears lasttext once these cached values are set.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the function leaves a resource (the cached lasttext pointer state) uninitialized/stale for later use, and downstream reuse of that state causes memory errors. The weakness is improper initialization/reset of cached state rather than merely a dangling pointer, which is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function caches ctxt->lasttext (and lasttsize/lasttuse) pointing into a newly created text/CDATA block but never resets it when the block is later freed or the text handling context changes. Trigger: a subsequent CDATA section in the input causes code to reuse the stale lasttext pointer, which may have been freed and reused. Consequence: a bounds check based on stale size data can pass, leading to out-of-bounds write or disclosure of uninitialized/freed memory.

commit_msg:
Prevent undefined behavior

Fix #2068 in main branch.

Signed-off-by: Steven Bellock <sbellock@nvidia.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '    libspdm_sleep((2 << extend_error_data->rd_exponent));'], 'added_lines': ['', '        return LIBSPDM_STATUS_INVALID_MSG_FIELD;', '    }', '    if (extend_error_data->rd_exponent > LIBSPDM_MAX_RDT_EXPONENT) {', '    libspdm_sleep((uint64_t)1 << extend_error_data->rd_exponent);', '']}
description:
libspdm is a sample implementation that follows the DMTF SPDM specifications. Prior to versions 2.3.3 and 3.0, following a successful CAPABILITIES response, a libspdm Requester stores the Responder's CTExponent into its context without validation. If the Requester sends a request message that requires a cryptography operation by the Responder, such as CHALLENGE, libspdm will calculate the timeout value using the Responder's unvalidated CTExponent.

A patch is available in version 2.3.3. A workaround is also available. After completion of VCA, the Requester can check the value of the Responder's CTExponent. If it greater than or equal to 64, then the Requester can stop communication with the Responder.

code_evidence: The function only checks that the response is large enough to hold the not-ready error structure; it does not constrain the value of extend_error_data->rd_exponent before use.

After the rd_tm check, the responder-supplied rd_exponent is stored into context and then used directly in libspdm_sleep((2 << extend_error_data->rd_exponent)); no upper bound is applied to rd_exponent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the code accepts a Responder-supplied input field and uses it in a shift/timeout computation without validating that it is within the required range. The missing bound check on rd_exponent is the direct cause; the undefined shift and DoS are consequences.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Responder's rd_exponent field from the RESPONSE_NOT_READY error is trusted without validating it against LIBSPDM_MAX_RDT_EXPONENT. Trigger: a malicious Responder returns an error with an oversized rd_exponent. Consequence: the shift expression evaluates undefined behavior and the computed timeout is unbounded, causing a crash or excessive delay (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/shadow: Don't create self-linear shadow mappings for 4-level translated guests

When initially creating a monitor table for 4-level translated guests, don't
install a shadow-linear mapping.  This mapping is actually self-linear, and
trips up the writeable heuristic logic into following Xen's mappings, not the
guests' shadows it was expecting to follow.

A consequence of this is that sh_guess_wrmap() needs to cope with there being
no shadow-linear mapping present, which in practice occurs once each time a
vcpu switches to 4-level paging from a different paging mode.

An appropriate shadow-linear slot will be inserted into the monitor table
either while constructing lower level monitor tables, or by sh_update_cr3().

While fixing this, clarify the safety of the other mappings.  Despite
appearing unsafe, it is correct to create a guest-linear mapping for
translated domains; this is self-linear and doesn't point into the translated
domain.  Drop a dead clause for translate != external guests.

This is XSA-243.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Acked-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* Shadow linear mapping for 4-level shadows.  N.B. for 3-level', '     * shadows on 64-bit xen, this linear mapping is later replaced by the', '     * monitor pagetable structure, which is built in make_monitor_table', '     * and maintained by sh_update_linear_entries. */', '    sl4e[shadow_l4_table_offset(SH_LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START)] =', '        shadow_l4e_from_mfn(sl4mfn, __PAGE_HYPERVISOR_RW);', '    /* Self linear mapping.  */', '    if ( shadow_mode_translate(d) && !shadow_mode_external(d) )', '    {', '        // linear tables may not be used with translated PV guests', '        sl4e[shadow_l4_table_offset(LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START)] =', '        sl4e[shadow_l4_table_offset(LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START)] =', '            shadow_l4e_from_mfn(gl4mfn, __PAGE_HYPERVISOR_RW);'], 'added_lines': ['    /*', '     * Linear mapping slots:', '     *', '     * Calling this function with gl4mfn == sl4mfn is used to construct a', '     * monitor table for translated domains.  In this case, gl4mfn forms the', '     * self-linear mapping (i.e. not pointing into the translated domain), and', '     * the shadow-linear slot is skipped.  The shadow-linear slot is either', '     * filled when constructing lower level monitor tables, or via', '     * sh_update_cr3() for 4-level guests.', '     *', '     * Calling this function with gl4mfn != sl4mfn is used for non-translated', '     * guests, where the shadow-linear slot is actually self-linear, and the', '     * guest-linear slot points into the guests view of its pagetables.', '     */', '    if ( shadow_mode_translate(d) )', '    {', '        ASSERT(mfn_eq(gl4mfn, sl4mfn));', '        sl4e[shadow_l4_table_offset(SH_LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START)] =', '        ASSERT(!mfn_eq(gl4mfn, sl4mfn));', '', '        sl4e[shadow_l4_table_offset(SH_LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START)] =', '            shadow_l4e_from_mfn(sl4mfn, __PAGE_HYPERVISOR_RW);', '', '    sl4e[shadow_l4_table_offset(LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START)] =', '        shadow_l4e_from_mfn(gl4mfn, __PAGE_HYPERVISOR_RW);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 HVM guest OS users to cause a denial of service (hypervisor crash) or possibly gain privileges because self-linear shadow mappings are mishandled for translated guests.

code_evidence: The function installs a self-linear shadow mapping at SH_LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START pointing at sl4mfn unconditionally (lines 21-22). It then decides the LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START slot: for translated non-external domains it stores an empty entry (lines 23-27), otherwise it maps gl4mfn (lines 28-32). For translated guests, gl4mfn equals sl4mfn, so the guest-linear slot becomes a self-linear mapping into the shadow page tables rather than the guest's view.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The bug places a shadow-linear mapping into a slot that should expose only the guest's own linear view, so a control sphere intended to confine access to the translated guest's pagetables instead exposes Xen's own page tables to the wrong sphere. This matches CWE-668's exposure-of-resource-to-wrong-sphere abstraction better than a pure memory-safety class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START slot is populated from gl4mfn without distinguishing translated domains, where gl4mfn is actually sl4mfn. Trigger: a 4-level translated guest causes this slot to be self-linear, so writeable-heuristic logic follows Xen's mappings instead of the guest's shadows. Supported consequence: mishandled shadow mappings cause hypervisor crash (DoS) and potentially privilege gain.

commit_msg:
daemon: allow only root user to trigger the post-create

There is no reason to allow non-root users to trigger this
functionality. Regular users can create abrt problems only through
abrtd or abrt-dbus and both triggers the post-create.

Other hooks run under root user (CCpp, Koops, VMCore, Xorg).

Related: #1212861

Signed-off-by: Jakub Filak <jfilak@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    }', '    else if (!dump_dir_accessible_by_uid(dirname, client_uid))', '    {', '        if (errno == ENOTDIR)', '        {', '            error_msg("Path \'%s\' isn\'t problem directory", dirname);', '            return 404; /* Not Found */', '        }', '        error_msg("Problem directory \'%s\' can\'t be accessed by user with uid %ld", dirname, (long)client_uid);', '        return 403; /* Forbidden */'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The default event handling scripts in Automatic Bug Reporting Tool (ABRT) allow local users to gain privileges as demonstrated by a symlink attack on a var_log_messages file.

code_evidence: Checks that dirname is under the dump location and has correct permissions, but these checks operate on the path string, not a resolved file descriptor.
dir_has_correct_permissions validates ownership/mode of the path; a symlink can point to a directory that passes or bypasses these checks depending on resolution.
When privatereports is unset, the removed accessibility branch is gone; the function proceeds to spawn the post-create event handler on the supplied dirname.
spawn_event_handler_child runs the handler using dirname as the problem directory, so a symlinked dirname redirects privileged hook execution.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the access decision and subsequent privileged operation follow a filename that may be a link to an unintended resource; the checks are on the path rather than the resolved object. This is link following, not merely missing authorization.

int child_stdout_fd;
int child_pid = spawn_event_handler_child(dirname, "post-create", &child_stdout_fd);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts a caller-supplied path and performs path-based validity checks (location prefix, permissions) without resolving symlinks or using openat/O_NOFOLLOW, then launches the post-create hook on that path. Trigger: a local user supplies a symlink under the dump location pointing to an unintended directory. Consequence: the hook runs with elevated privileges against attacker-chosen content, enabling privilege escalation.

description: In BTM_BleVerifySignature of btm_ble.cc, there is a possible way to bypass signature validation due to side channel information disclosure. This could lead to remote escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: Line 19-20 computes the expected AES-CMAC into p_mac; line 21 compares it to the supplied p_comp with the ordinary memcmp over BTM_CMAC_TLEN_SIZE bytes. memcmp short-circuits at the first differing byte, so the number of compared bytes and execution time depend on how many leading bytes of p_comp match p_mac. On a match, lines 22-23 increment the sign counter and set verified=true.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-203 fits because the function's response timing differs based on secret MAC contents, leaking information to an unauthorized observer. This is a timing side channel in a comparison, distinct from a mere logic flaw in verification.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a non-constant-time memcmp is used to validate an attacker-supplied signature against a secret-derived MAC. Trigger: an attacker submits candidate p_comp values and observes response timing to learn matching prefix bytes, reconstructing a valid signature. Consequence: signature validation can be bypassed, enabling spoofed signed BLE traffic; the timing difference is the observable discrepancy.

commit_msg:
drm/nouveau/mmu: add more general vmm free/node handling functions

Aside from being a nice cleanup, these will to allow the upcoming direct
page mapping interfaces to play nicely with normal mappings.

Signed-off-by: Ben Skeggs <bskeggs@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\trb_erase(&prev->tree, &vmm->free);', '\t\tlist_del(&prev->head);', '\t\tkfree(prev);', '\t\trb_erase(&next->tree, &vmm->free);', '\t\tlist_del(&next->head);', '\t\tkfree(next);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tnvkm_vmm_free_delete(vmm, prev);', '\t\tnvkm_vmm_free_delete(vmm, next);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s nouveau driver in how a user triggers a memory overflow that causes the nvkm_vma_tail function to fail. This flaw allows a local user to crash or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: When the previous free node is unused, it is removed from the free tree/list and merged into vma, then prev is freed at line 10; the merged fields are copied before the free, so no direct reuse of prev occurs here.
The symmetric next branch removes next from the free structures and frees it at line 16 after merging its size into vma.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function frees an nvkm_vma object (kfree(prev)/kfree(next)) and subsequent tree/list operations on the merged region may reference that freed memory. This is a use-after-free rather than a double-free, since the flaw concerns later access to the freed node's memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that vma is merged with an adjacent free node and that node is kfree'd while vma is then reinserted into vmm->free as a combined region. If the merge/insert accounting is inconsistent, the freed node's memory can remain reachable through tree/list links and be referenced later. Trigger is freeing a region adjacent to an unused VMA; supported consequence is use-after-free of the freed nvkm_vma, leading to crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg: fixed #2575

description: NULL Pointer Dereference in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.3-DEV.

code_evidence: When MPEG12_ParseSeqHdr fails (return < 0), the code resets m_stream_id and m_fd but does not stop execution; control falls through to line 16 and computes 90000.0 / sptr->frame_rate. The parser may leave frame_rate at 0 on failure, making the division invalid and leaving ticks_per_frame undefined for downstream consumers that assume valid stream info.

Trigger: a malformed/truncated video frame causes MPEG12_ParseSeqHdr to fail. Consequence: division by a zero frame_rate yields an invalid ticks_per_frame that later dereference/use paths rely on, leading to a crash (DoS) rather than a clean abort.

commit_msg:
nla: invalidate sec handle after creation

If sec pointer isn't invalidated after creation it is not possible
to check if the upper and lower pointers are valid.

This fixes a segfault in the server part if the client disconnects before
the authentication was finished.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!handle)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!handle || !SecIsValidHandle(handle))']}
description: FreeRDP before 1.1.0-beta+2013071101 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) by disconnecting before authentication has finished.

code_evidence: The function only checks `if (!handle)` before dereferencing `handle->dwUpper` on line 6. It never validates that the SecHandle's internal upper/lower fields form a valid handle. When the client disconnects before authentication finishes, the handle can be non-NULL but uninitialized/invalid, so `handle->dwUpper` is dereferenced on a stale or null-backed structure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The dereference of `handle->dwUpper` on an invalid/NULL-backed handle is a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476). A mere missing NULL check on `handle` would be the same class, but here the missing validity check on the handle contents is what permits the NULL dereference; this still falls under CWE-476 rather than a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guard validates only the outer pointer, not the SecHandle contents, so an invalid handle passes the check and is dereferenced at line 6. Trigger: client disconnect before authentication completes leaves the sec handle invalid while non-NULL. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a server crash (DoS).

Avoid 0==nbucket

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/393
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp

description: An floating point exception was discovered in the elf_lookup function in p_lx_elf.cpp in UPX 4.0.0 via a crafted Mach-O file.

code_evidence: Line 4 reads nbucket from the untrusted ELF hash table header. Line 7 computes elf_hash(name) % nbucket before any validation. The guard at lines 8-14 checks !nbucket and table bounds only after the modulo, so a crafted file with nbucket==0 reaches the division first.

commit_msg:
pipe: limit the per-user amount of pages allocated in pipes

On no-so-small systems, it is possible for a single process to cause an
OOM condition by filling large pipes with data that are never read. A
typical process filling 4000 pipes with 1 MB of data will use 4 GB of
memory. On small systems it may be tricky to set the pipe max size to
prevent this from happening.

This patch makes it possible to enforce a per-user soft limit above
which new pipes will be limited to a single page, effectively limiting
them to 4 kB each, as well as a hard limit above which no new pipes may
be created for this user. This has the effect of protecting the system
against memory abuse without hurting other users, and still allowing
pipes to work correctly though with less data at once.

The limit are controlled by two new sysctls : pipe-user-pages-soft, and
pipe-user-pages-hard. Both may be disabled by setting them to zero. The
default soft limit allows the default number of FDs per process (1024)
to create pipes of the default size (64kB), thus reaching a limit of 64MB
before starting to create only smaller pipes. With 256 processes limited
to 1024 FDs each, this results in 1024*64kB + (256*1024 - 1024) * 4kB =
1084 MB of memory allocated for a user. The hard limit is disabled by
default to avoid breaking existing applications that make intensive use
of pipes (eg: for splicing).

Reported-by: socketpair@gmail.com
Reported-by: Tetsuo Handa <penguin-kernel@I-love.SAKURA.ne.jp>
Mitigates: CVE-2013-4312 (Linux 2.0+)
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\taccount_pipe_buffers(pipe, pipe->buffers, nr_pages);']}
description: fs/pipe.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5 does not limit the amount of unread data in pipes, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by creating many pipes with non-default sizes.

code_evidence: kcalloc allocates nr_pages pipe_buffer structures with no check against any per-user or global accounting limit before committing the memory.

After the copy, the old buffer array is freed and pipe->buffers is set to the caller-supplied nr_pages, so each call permanently enlarges the pipe's memory footprint; no accounting is performed against user resource limits.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly performs unaccounted resource allocation and retention (CWE-399 Resource Management Errors), matching the described unbounded pipe memory consumption. It is not a buffer overflow (CWE-119); the defect is missing resource accounting/limit, not memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pipe_set_size trusts nr_pages and allocates/frees buffers without tracking per-user page consumption, so a local user can repeatedly create large pipes whose unread buffers consume unbounded kernel memory. Trigger: many pipes with large non-default sizes; consequence is memory exhaustion and denial of service.

commit_msg:
* libtiff/tif_pixarlog.c: fix potential buffer write overrun in
PixarLogDecode() on corrupted/unexpected images (reported by Mathias Svensson)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn (0);', '\t}', '\t/* Check that we will not fill more than what was allocated */', '\tif (sp->stream.avail_out > sp->tbuf_size)', '\t{', '\t\tTIFFErrorExt(tif->tif_clientdata, module, "sp->stream.avail_out > sp->tbuf_size");']}
description: Buffer overflow in the PixarLogDecode function in tif_pixarlog.c in LibTIFF 4.0.6 and earlier allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted TIFF image, as demonstrated by overwriting the vgetparent function pointer with rgb2ycbcr.

code_evidence: sp->stream.next_out is set to sp->tbuf, then avail_out is derived from caller-supplied occ (nsamples*sizeof(uint16)); only the truncation to uInt is checked, not whether the requested output exceeds the allocated tbuf_size.
inflate() writes up to avail_out bytes into sp->tbuf; the loop and later up = sp->tbuf / horizontalAccumulate* consume llen-sized chunks, so a large occ makes zlib write past tbuf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The added bound check exists precisely because zlib writes avail_out bytes into tbuf, which can exceed the intended buffer; writing past tbuf is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). A mere integer truncation issue (CWE-197) is already handled by the uInt equality check; the overflow here is spatial, not arithmetic.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: PixarLogDecode trusts the requested output size (occ) to size the zlib output buffer without comparing it to the allocated sp->tbuf_size. Trigger: a crafted TIFF image yields a large nsamples, so sp->stream.avail_out exceeds tbuf_size; inflate() then writes beyond sp->tbuf. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap write corrupting adjacent memory (e.g., function pointers), leading to crash or possible code execution.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls

the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

commit_msg:
Coalesce handshake buffers

Summary:
It is possible that a peer might send us records in a manner such
that there is a 16KB record and only 1 byte of handshake message in
each record. Since we normally just trim the IOBuf, we would end up
holding 16K of data per actual byte of data. To prevent this we allocate a contiguous
buffer to copy over these bytes for handshake messages for now.

This is a partial fix for CVE-2019-11924

Reviewed By: ngoyal

Differential Revision: D16478044

fbshipit-source-id: 464bc68eaefda065d9a327818100427377293fbd
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        unparsedHandshakeData_.append(std::move(message->fragment));'], 'added_lines': ['        std::unique_ptr<folly::IOBuf> handshakeMessage =', '            unparsedHandshakeData_.move();', '        // It is possible that a peer might send us records in a manner such', '        // that there is a 16KB record and only 1 byte of handshake message in', '        // each record. Since we normally just trim the IOBuf, we would end up', '        // holding 16K of data. To prevent this we allocate a contiguous', '        // buffer to copy over these bytes. We supply kExtraAlloc bytes in', '        // order to avoid needing to re-allocate a lot of times if we receive', '        // a lot of small messages. There might be more optimal reallocation', '        // policies, but this should be fine.', '        message->fragment->coalesce();', '        constexpr size_t kExtraAlloc = 1024;', '        if (!handshakeMessage) {', '          handshakeMessage =', '              folly::IOBuf::create(message->fragment->length() + kExtraAlloc);', '        } else if (handshakeMessage->tailroom() < message->fragment->length()) {', '          handshakeMessage->reserve(', '              0, message->fragment->length() + kExtraAlloc);', '        }', '        memcpy(', '            handshakeMessage->writableTail(),', '            message->fragment->data(),', '            message->fragment->length());', '        handshakeMessage->append(message->fragment->length());', '        unparsedHandshakeData_.append(std::move(handshakeMessage));']}
description: A peer could send empty handshake fragments containing only padding which would be kept in memory until a full handshake was received, resulting in memory exhaustion. This issue affects versions v2019.01.28.00 and above of fizz, until v2019.08.05.00.

code_evidence: In the handshake case, the incoming record fragment is appended to unparsedHandshakeData_ without any size cap; a peer can send many tiny handshake fragments (each padded to a full record) so the queue grows while decodeHandshakeMessage fails and the loop continues.
The splice guard only checks that non-handshake records don't follow pending handshake data; it does not limit how much handshake data can accumulate.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the code allocates/stores a reusable resource (the handshake buffer) on behalf of a remote actor without throttling its size or number. This is resource exhaustion, not a single overflow or length miscalculation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unparsedHandshakeData_ accumulates attacker-supplied fragments with no limit on accumulated size or count. Trigger: a peer sends repeated minimal handshake records that fail to decode, causing each iteration to append and continue. Consequence: memory consumption grows unbounded, enabling memory-exhaustion DoS.

commit_msg:
x86: limit GFNs to 32 bits for shadowed superpages.

Superpage shadows store the shadowed GFN in the backpointer field,
which for non-BIGMEM builds is 32 bits wide.  Shadowing a superpage
mapping of a guest-physical address above 2^44 would lead to the GFN
being truncated there, and a crash when we come to remove the shadow
from the hash table.

Track the valid width of a GFN for each guest, including reporting it
through CPUID, and enforce it in the shadow pagetables.  Set the
maximum witth to 32 for guests where this truncation could occur.

This is XSA-173.

Reported-by: Ling Liu <liuling-it@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if ( gfn_x(gfn) >> p2m->domain->arch.paging.gfn_bits )', '    {', '        *rc = _PAGE_INVALID_BIT;', '        return NULL;', '    }']}
description: Integer overflow in the x86 shadow pagetable code in Xen allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host crash) or possibly gain privileges by shadowing a superpage mapping.

code_evidence: The function passes gfn_x(gfn) directly into get_page_from_gfn_p2m without validating that the guest-physical frame number fits the GFN width supported by the domain's shadow pagetable backpointer. The diff adds a gfn_bits range check before this call; the pre-patch function lacks any such bound, so an out-of-range GFN reaches the p2m translation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission and privilege management enabling a guest to exceed the access bounds its configuration permits. The missing GFN-width enforcement lets an unprivileged guest operate on out-of-range frames, so the target category fits; the concrete integer-truncation defect is a narrower weakness, but the access-control framing is what the target labels.

evidence_lines.code:
struct page_info *page;
page = get_page_from_gfn_p2m(p2m->domain, p2m, gfn_x(gfn), p2mt, NULL, q);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no constraint on the width of the GFN before it is translated and later stored in the 32-bit shadow backpointer. Trigger: a local guest shadows a superpage mapping whose GFN exceeds the representable width, causing truncation. Consequence: the shadow hash entry is keyed inconsistently, leading to a host crash when the shadow is removed; privilege gain is only speculative.
