commit_msg:
SampleTable.cpp: Fixed a regression caused by a fix for bug
28076789.

Detail: Before the original fix
(Id207f369ab7b27787d83f5d8fc48dc53ed9fcdc9) for 28076789, the
code allowed a time-to-sample table size to be 0. The change
made in that fix disallowed such situation, which in fact should
be allowed. This current patch allows it again while maintaining
the security of the previous fix.

Bug: 28288202
Bug: 28076789
Change-Id: I1c9a60c7f0cfcbd3d908f24998dde15d5136a295
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        && !mTimeToSample.empty();'], 'added_lines': ['        && mHasTimeToSample;']}
description: SampleTable.cpp in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-06-01 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (device hang or reboot) via a crafted file, aka internal bug 28076789.

code_evidence: isValid() gates table usability on the presence of time-to-sample data via !mTimeToSample.empty(). If the time-to-sample table is empty, the whole table is rejected regardless of whether the other offsets are valid. The commit notes the prior fix disallowed a zero-sized time-to-sample table, which should be permitted; this function encodes that over-restrictive input check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function performs an incorrect validation check on input-derived table state, treating a valid empty time-to-sample table as invalid. The defect is in the validation condition itself, not in a downstream transformation or filter.

evidence_lines.code:
return mChunkOffsetOffset >= 0
&& mSampleToChunkOffset >= 0
&& mSampleSizeOffset >= 0
&& !mTimeToSample.empty();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: validity is conditioned on a non-empty time-to-sample vector rather than on the correctness of the parsed table metadata. Trigger: a crafted media file that legitimately has a zero-length time-to-sample table. Consequence: the sample table is deemed invalid, leading to processing failure/hang or reboot (DoS) as described.

commit_msg:
Avoid integer overflows in SETRANGE and SORT (CVE-2022-35977) (#11720)

Authenticated users issuing specially crafted SETRANGE and SORT(_RO)
commands can trigger an integer overflow, resulting with Redis attempting
to allocate impossible amounts of memory and abort with an OOM panic.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int checkStringLength(client *c, long long size) {', '    if (!mustObeyClient(c) && size > server.proto_max_bulk_len) {'], 'added_lines': ['static int checkStringLength(client *c, long long size, long long append) {', '    if (mustObeyClient(c))', '        return C_OK;', "    /* 'uint64_t' cast is there just to prevent undefined behavior on overflow */", '    long long total = (uint64_t)size + append;', '    /* Test configured max-bulk-len represending a limit of the biggest string object,', '     * and also test for overflow. */', '    if (total > server.proto_max_bulk_len || total < size || total < append) {']}
description: Redis is an in-memory database that persists on disk. Authenticated users issuing specially crafted `SETRANGE` and `SORT(_RO)` commands can trigger an integer overflow, resulting with Redis attempting to allocate impossible amounts of memory and abort with an out-of-memory (OOM) panic. The problem is fixed in Redis versions 7.0.8, 6.2.9 and 6.0.17. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: The function takes a signed long long size and compares it directly against proto_max_bulk_len without any overflow check. A caller that computes size by adding an append length to an existing string length can pass a wrapped (negative or small) value that satisfies the size > proto_max_bulk_len test as false, so the length check passes and returns C_OK.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the guard assumes the computed size is trustworthy while an integer wraparound can make it appear within bounds, defeating the size limit. This is a missing overflow constraint, not merely an overly permissive maximum check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length validation only compares size against the configured maximum and does not detect wraparound in the size value itself. Trigger: an authenticated client issues SETRANGE/SORT with an offset/append combination whose sum overflows the signed length. Supported consequence: the check returns C_OK for an impossible length, and downstream allocation attempts consume unbounded memory, aborting the server (OOM panic).

commit_msg:
evtchn: avoid NULL derefs

Commit fbbd5009e6 ("evtchn: refactor low-level event channel port ops")
added a de-reference of the struct evtchn pointer for a port without
first making sure the bucket pointer is non-NULL. This de-reference is
actually entirely unnecessary, as all relevant callers (beyond the
problematic do_poll()) already hold the port number in their hands, and
the actual leaf functions need nothing else.

For FIFO event channels there's a second problem in that the ordering
of reads and updates to ->num_evtchns and ->event_array[] was so far
undefined (the read side isn't always holding the domain's event lock).
Add respective barriers.

This is XSA-221.

Reported-by: Ankur Arora <ankur.a.arora@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static bool_t evtchn_fifo_is_masked(struct domain *d,', '                                    const struct evtchn *evtchn)', '    word = evtchn_fifo_word_from_port(d, evtchn->port);'], 'added_lines': ['static bool_t evtchn_fifo_is_masked(struct domain *d, evtchn_port_t port)', '    word = evtchn_fifo_word_from_port(d, port);']}
description: Xen through 4.8.x does not validate the port numbers of polled event channel ports, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and host OS crash) or possibly obtain sensitive information, aka XSA-221.

code_evidence: The function now receives evtchn_port_t port and dereferences it via evtchn_fifo_word_from_port(d, port) to obtain word.
The NULL check on word occurs only after the port lookup; it does not guard against a NULL struct evtchn pointer, since the pointer parameter was removed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a direct dereference of a pointer expected to be non-NULL without a validity check, causing a crash; this fits CWE-476 rather than a bounds/validation weakness because the supported impact is NULL dereference DoS.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( unlikely(!word) )
return 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: callers such as do_poll() can pass a port for which no valid evtchn bucket/struct exists, and the earlier code dereferenced evtchn->port without validating the struct evtchn pointer. Trigger: a guest supplies an out-of-range polled event-channel port. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and host OS crash (DoS), matching XSA-221.

commit_msg:
Add dissection recursion checks.

Enforce a maximum layer limit in call_dissector_work and
dissector_try_heuristic.

Bug: 15778
Change-Id: I691868e980384b76a64f88de4db5bb7340a7c4aa
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/33301
Petri-Dish: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Dario Lombardo <lomato@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
(cherry picked from commit be9bdfda02a2498c6f65122d80e3a8b4235dc7f5)
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/33310
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tDISSECTOR_ASSERT(saved_layers_len < PINFO_LAYER_MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH);']}
description: In Wireshark 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.6.0 to 2.6.8, and 2.4.0 to 2.4.14, the dissection engine could crash. This was addressed in epan/packet.c by restricting the number of layers and consequently limiting recursion.

code_evidence: The function records the current layer count into saved_layers_len before iterating heuristic dissectors, establishing the recursion baseline.
Each enabled heuristic's proto_id is appended to pinfo->layers before invoking its dissector, deepening the layer stack.
On failure the code trims pinfo->layers back down to saved_layers_len, but the added assertion now guards against the layer count reaching PINFO_LAYER_MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the weakness is uncontrolled recursion depth in the dissection engine, limited only by the newly added PINFO_LAYER_MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH check. This is not a simple buffer overflow; the missing constraint is recursion depth, whose consequence is resource/stack exhaustion.

evidence_lines.code:
saved_layers_len = wmem_list_count(pinfo->layers);
*heur_dtbl_entry = NULL;

wmem_list_append(pinfo->layers, GINT_TO_POINTER(proto_id));
pinfo->heur_list_name = hdtbl_entry->list_name;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: heuristic dissectors can recursively re-enter dissection via dissector_try_heuristic without any bound on pinfo->layers depth, so a crafted packet triggers unbounded recursion. Trigger: a heuristic dissector that re-invokes dissection on the same tvb. Supported consequence: stack exhaustion and a crash (DoS). The patch adds a depth assertion to stop the recursion.

commit_msg:
smtp: use the upload buffer size for scratch buffer malloc

... not the read buffer size, as that can be set smaller and thus cause
a buffer overflow! CVE-2018-0500

Reported-by: Peter Wu
Bug: https://curl.haxx.se/docs/adv_2018-70a2.html
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    scratch = newscratch = malloc(2 * data->set.buffer_size);'], 'added_lines': ['    scratch = newscratch = malloc(2 * UPLOAD_BUFSIZE);', '  DEBUGASSERT(UPLOAD_BUFSIZE >= nread);']}
description: Curl_smtp_escape_eob in lib/smtp.c in curl 7.54.1 to and including curl 7.60.0 has a heap-based buffer overflow that might be exploitable by an attacker who can control the data that curl transmits over SMTP with certain settings (i.e., use of a nonstandard --limit-rate argument or CURLOPT_BUFFERSIZE value).

code_evidence: The scratch buffer is allocated with malloc(2 * data->set.buffer_size), sizing it from the user-controllable read buffer setting rather than the upload buffer size.
The loop iterates i < nread and writes into scratch at index si via scratch[si++] and memcpy(&scratch[si], ...); si can grow up to nread, so nread bytes must fit in the allocation.
On the si != nread path, scratch is retained as data->state.scratch and upload_fromhere, so an undersized allocation persists for later use rather than being freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes attacker-influenced upload bytes past the end of a heap allocation whose size is derived from a mismatched buffer-size setting. This is a direct out-of-bounds write, not merely an integer or use-after-free issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an allocation sized by data->set.buffer_size, which can be set smaller than the upload data length nread. When nread exceeds the allocation, writes at scratch[si] and memcpy into &scratch[si] run past the heap buffer, producing a heap-based out-of-bounds write and possible code execution or crash.

commit_msg: replace the magic number with a define
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (fileName == NULL || fileName[0] == 0 || strlen(fileName) >= 256) return;'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (fileName == NULL || fileName[0] == 0 || strlen(fileName) >= FILENAMESIZE) return;']}
description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability found in Liblouis v.3.24.0 allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via the compileTranslationTable.c and lou_setDataPath functions.

code_evidence: Line 7 only rejects fileName when strlen(fileName) >= 256, then line 8 copies fileName into the fixed-size global initialLogFileName via strcpy with no destination-size argument; the guard is a magic constant rather than the actual buffer size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because line 8 is a buffer copy (strcpy) whose only size check is a literal unrelated to the destination buffer. This is a copy-bound defect, not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) or a numeric error alone.

evidence_lines.code:
if (fileName == NULL || fileName[0] == 0 || strlen(fileName) >= 256) return;
if (initialLogFileName[0] == 0) strcpy(initialLogFileName, fileName);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The copy into initialLogFileName relies on a hard-coded 256 bound instead of the destination's declared size (FILENAMESIZE). If the guard and buffer size diverge, an over-long fileName passes the check and strcpy writes past the buffer, corrupting memory; the commit's replacement with FILENAMESIZE is the intended alignment of that bound.

commit_msg:
In theory, IO scheduler belongs to request queue, and the request pool
of sched tags belongs to the request queue too.

However, the current tags allocation interfaces are re-used for both
driver tags and sched tags, and driver tags is definitely host wide,
and doesn't belong to any request queue, same with its request pool.
So we need tagset instance for freeing request of sched tags.

Meantime, blk_mq_free_tag_set() often follows blk_cleanup_queue() in case
of non-BLK_MQ_F_TAG_SHARED, this way requires that request pool of sched
tags to be freed before calling blk_mq_free_tag_set().

Commit 47cdee29ef9d94e ("block: move blk_exit_queue into __blk_release_queue")
moves blk_exit_queue into __blk_release_queue for simplying the fast
path in generic_make_request(), then causes oops during freeing requests
of sched tags in __blk_release_queue().

Fix the above issue by move freeing request pool of sched tags into
blk_cleanup_queue(), this way is safe becasue queue has been frozen and no any
in-queue requests at that time. Freeing sched tags has to be kept in queue's
release handler becasue there might be un-completed dispatch activity
which might refer to sched tags.

Cc: Bart Van Assche <bvanassche@acm.org>
Cc: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Fixes: 47cdee29ef9d94e485eb08f962c74943023a5271 ("block: move blk_exit_queue into __blk_release_queue")
Tested-by: Yi Zhang <yi.zhang@redhat.com>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <rong.a.chen@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Ming Lei <ming.lei@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tblk_mq_sched_free_requests(q);', '\tblk_mq_sched_free_requests(q);']}
description: The block subsystem in the Linux kernel before 5.2 has a use-after-free that can lead to arbitrary code execution in the kernel context and privilege escalation, aka CID-c3e2219216c9. This is related to blk_mq_free_rqs and blk_cleanup_queue.

code_evidence: Per-hw-ctx sched tags are allocated in the queue_for_each_hw_ctx loop; on allocation failure the code jumps to err, which tears down sched tags and clears q->elevator.

In the second loop, if e->ops.init_hctx fails after some hw contexts were initialized, the function calls blk_mq_exit_sched and kobject_put on the elevator and returns without freeing the sched-tag request pool.
The err label similarly runs blk_mq_sched_tags_teardown and clears the elevator but does not free the sched-tag requests, leaving request-pool state that outlives the tagset teardown.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing blk_mq_sched_free_requests calls cause request objects of sched tags to be referenced after their backing tagset/request pool is freed, matching use-after-free. It is not merely a leak because the freed memory is subsequently accessed during queue teardown/dispatch.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error paths of blk_mq_init_sched tear down sched tags and the elevator without freeing the sched-tag request pool. Later blk_cleanup_queue/blk_mq_free_tag_set frees the tagset while stale sched-tag request references remain, so dispatch or request freeing touches freed memory.

commit_msg: Added missing calls to destroy methods (#2889).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['              return(ConjureUsage());'], 'added_lines': ['              {', '                DestroyConjure();', '                return(ConjureUsage());', '              }']}
description: A memory leak in ImageMagick 7.0.10-45 and 6.9.11-22 allows remote attackers to perform a denial of service via the "identify -help" command.

code_evidence: The DestroyConjure macro releases the image list, each argv string, and the argv array itself.
ConjureImageCommand allocates state before option parsing: image=NewImageList() and ExpandFilenames(&argc,&argv), which allocates argv.
The -help branch returns ConjureUsage() immediately when *option == '-', bypassing DestroyConjure() and abandoning the allocated image list and argv.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory (NewImageList, ExpandFilenames) and the early-return path skips the only release path (DestroyConjure), so memory is not released after its effective lifetime. This is a direct missing-release defect, matching CWE-401 rather than an out-of-bounds or use-after-free weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
#define DestroyConjure() \
{ \
image=DestroyImageList(image); \
for (i=0; i < (ssize_t) argc; i++) \
argv[i]=DestroyString(argv[i]); \
argv=(char **) RelinquishMagickMemory(argv); \
}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the early return on the '-help' option exits the command without invoking DestroyConjure(), so the image list created at line 44 and the argv array allocated by ExpandFilenames at line 48 are never released. Trigger: invoking the command with '-help'. Consequence: the allocations remain live, producing a memory leak that repeated invocations can exploit for denial of service via resource exhaustion.

commit_msg:
avcodec/tiff: Check subsample & rps values more completely

Fixes out of array access
Fixes: 83aedfb29af669c4d6e10f1bfad974d2/asan_heap-oob_1ab42fe_4984_9f6ec14462f8d8a00ea24b320572a963.tif

Found-by: Mateusz "j00ru" Jurczyk and Gynvael Coldwind
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (s->rps <= 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (s->rps <= 0 || s->rps % s->subsampling[1]) {']}
description: libavcodec/tiff.c in FFmpeg before 2.8.6 does not properly validate RowsPerStrip values and YCbCr chrominance subsampling factors, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds array access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted TIFF file, related to the tiff_decode_tag and decode_frame functions.

code_evidence: The rps validation at [75,76,77,78] rejects only rps <= 0 and does not check rps against the chrominance subsampling factor s->subsampling[1].
The strip loop at [80,81,82,83] iterates i over s->height in increments of s->rps and advances dst by s->rps * stride at [102], using the unvalidated rps as a row-step.
tiff_unpack_strip is called at [96,97] with FFMIN(s->rps, s->height - i) as the line count and the rps-based dst pointer, so a crafted RowsPerStrip value drives the destination offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unvalidated rps drives pointer arithmetic and strip unpacking past the intended frame buffer boundary, which is an out-of-bounds memory operation matching CWE-119. The missing constraint is the root cause; the out-of-bounds access is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: decode_frame accepts any positive RowsPerStrip (rps) without requiring it to be compatible with the YCbCr chrominance subsampling factor. Trigger: a crafted TIFF sets an rps that is not a multiple of subsampling[1]. The loop then advances dst by rps * stride and unpacks full strips, producing an out-of-bounds write on the frame buffer (out-of-array access, DoS or worse).

description: A NULL pointer dereference vulnerability exists in GPAC v1.1.0 via the function gf_sg_vrml_field_pointer_del () at scenegraph/vrml_tools.c. This vulnerability can lead to a Denial of Service (DoS).

code_evidence: The precondition field->field_pointer is only checked in the else-if at line 10; the regular-type branch at lines 7-9 calls gf_sg_vrml_field_pointer_del(field->field_pointer, ...) unconditionally for any non-node FieldType.

commit_msg:
ofp-actions: Avoid buffer overread in BUNDLE action decoding.

Reported-at: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=9052
Signed-off-by: Ben Pfaff <blp@ovn.org>
Acked-by: Justin Pettit <jpettit@ovn.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    }', '', '    for (i = 0; i < bundle->n_slaves; i++) {', '        ofp_port_t ofp_port = u16_to_ofp(ntohs(((ovs_be16 *)(nab + 1))[i]));', '        ofpbuf_put(ofpacts, &ofp_port, sizeof ofp_port);', '        bundle = ofpacts->header;'], 'added_lines': ['    } else {', '        for (i = 0; i < bundle->n_slaves; i++) {', '            ofp_port_t ofp_port', '                = u16_to_ofp(ntohs(((ovs_be16 *)(nab + 1))[i]));', '            ofpbuf_put(ofpacts, &ofp_port, sizeof ofp_port);', '            bundle = ofpacts->header;', '        }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Open vSwitch (OvS) 2.7.x through 2.7.6. The decode_bundle function inside lib/ofp-actions.c is affected by a buffer over-read issue during BUNDLE action decoding.

code_evidence: Line 54 computes slaves_size as nab->len minus the header size and compares it against bundle->n_slaves * sizeof(ovs_be16); on failure it sets error = OFPERR_OFPBAC_BAD_LEN at line 60. However, the loop at lines 62-66 executes unconditionally and indexes ((ovs_be16 *)(nab + 1))[i] for i up to bundle->n_slaves, reading slave ports beyond the actual action buffer whenever the length check failed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a read that can extend past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. It is not a write overflow (CWE-787) because ofpbuf_put writes into the separately allocated ofpacts buffer; the flaw is the unchecked read from the input action.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length validation at line 54 only sets an error code but does not guard the subsequent slave-decoding loop, so control flow continues into the read loop. Trigger: a BUNDLE action whose nab->len is smaller than n_slaves * sizeof(ovs_be16). Consequence: the loop reads ovs_be16 values past the end of the received action buffer, a heap over-read that can crash or disclose adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
Harden CMD_SUBMIT path to handle malicious input that could trigger
large memory allocations. Add checks to validate transfer_buffer_length
and number_of_packets to protect against bad input requesting for
unbounded memory allocations. Validate early in get_pipe() and return
failure.

Reported-by: Secunia Research <vuln@secunia.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan <shuahkh@osg.samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>

description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

} else if (value == TotalSize) {
return CelValue::CreateInt64(info_.bytesReceived() + headers_.value_->byteSize());

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function exposes a header-size value used by callers to enforce the maximum request header limit. If the underlying byteSize accounting is recomputed by iterating headers, evaluating this expression repeatedly over many small headers yields quadratic work. The trigger is a request with thousands of small headers; the supported consequence is CPU consumption leading to denial of service. The cause is the cost of size accounting, not this expression's arithmetic.

commit_msg: exit program when bmp file is oversize

description: A Null Pointer Dereference vulnerability exits in ffjpeg d5cfd49 (2021-12-06) in bmp_load(). When the size information in metadata of the bmp is out of range, it returns without assign memory buffer to `pb->pdata` and did not exit the program. So the program crashes when it tries to access the pb->data, in jfif_encode() at jfif.c:763. This is due to the incomplete patch for CVE-2020-13438.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function continues after a failed load and passes a BMP whose data pointer is NULL into jfif_encode, which dereferences it. This is a direct NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476), not merely an unchecked return value, because the unchecked failure leads to an actual NULL dereference.

bmp_load(&bmp, argv[2]);
jfif = jfif_encode(&bmp);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing check of bmp_load's failure return, so a failed load leaves the BMP buffer unassigned. Trigger: oversized BMP metadata causes bmp_load to return early. Consequence: jfif_encode dereferences the NULL buffer, crashing the program (DoS).

commit_msg:
use fixed authentication tag length of 16 octets in AES GCM decryption

see: https://github.com/cisco/cjose/issues/125

Signed-off-by: Hans Zandbelt <hans.zandbelt@openidc.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    {', '        CJOSE_ERROR(err, CJOSE_ERR_CRYPTO);', '        goto _cjose_jwe_decrypt_dat_aes_gcm_fail;', '    }', '', '    if (jwe->enc_auth_tag.raw_len != 16)']}
description: OpenIDC/cjose is a C library implementing the Javascript Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE). The AES GCM decryption routine incorrectly uses the Tag length from the actual Authentication Tag provided in the JWE. The spec  says that a fixed length of 16 octets must be applied. Therefore this bug allows an attacker to provide a truncated Authentication Tag and to modify the JWE accordingly. Users should upgrade to a version >= 0.6.2.2. Users unable to upgrade should avoid using AES GCM encryption and replace it with another encryption algorithm (e.g. AES CBC).

code_evidence: The GCM authentication tag is configured using the attacker-influenced length jwe->enc_auth_tag.raw_len rather than the spec-mandated fixed 16-octet tag length, so a truncated tag is accepted by the cipher context.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Using a non-standard, reduced-length authentication tag weakens the AES-GCM construction below the required 16-octet tag, matching CWE-327's risky cryptographic configuration. This is a misuse of a sound algorithm's parameters rather than a distinct algorithm choice, but it still renders the cryptographic protection broken as specified.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the tag length passed to CJOSE_EVP_CTRL_GCM_SET_TAG is taken from the JWE-supplied enc_auth_tag.raw_len instead of being fixed at 16 octets. Trigger: an attacker crafts a JWE with a shortened authentication tag. Consequence: GCM authentication is weakened, allowing forged/modified JWE content to pass decryption verification.

commit_msg:
Jonathan Looney reported that TCP can trigger the following crash
in tcp_shifted_skb() :

	BUG_ON(tcp_skb_pcount(skb) < pcount);

This can happen if the remote peer has advertized the smallest
MSS that linux TCP accepts : 48

An skb can hold 17 fragments, and each fragment can hold 32KB
on x86, or 64KB on PowerPC.

This means that the 16bit witdh of TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->tcp_gso_segs
can overflow.

Note that tcp_sendmsg() builds skbs with less than 64KB
of payload, so this problem needs SACK to be enabled.
SACK blocks allow TCP to coalesce multiple skbs in the retransmit
queue, thus filling the 17 fragments to maximal capacity.

CVE-2019-11477 -- u16 overflow of TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->tcp_gso_segs

Fixes: 832d11c5cd07 ("tcp: Try to restore large SKBs while SACK processing")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Looney <jtl@netflix.com>
Acked-by: Neal Cardwell <ncardwell@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Tyler Hicks <tyhicks@canonical.com>
Cc: Yuchung Cheng <ycheng@google.com>
Cc: Bruce Curtis <brucec@netflix.com>
Cc: Jonathan Lemon <jonathan.lemon@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tBUILD_BUG_ON(TCP_MIN_SND_MSS <= MAX_TCP_OPTION_SPACE);']}
description: Jonathan Looney discovered that the TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->tcp_gso_segs value was subject to an integer overflow in the Linux kernel when handling TCP Selective Acknowledgments (SACKs). A remote attacker could use this to cause a denial of service. This has been fixed in stable kernel releases 4.4.182, 4.9.182, 4.14.127, 4.19.52, 5.1.11, and is fixed in commit 3b4929f65b0d8249f19a50245cd88ed1a2f78cff.

code_evidence: tcp_init() only contains compile-time BUILD_BUG_ON checks and initialization; the patch adds BUILD_BUG_ON(TCP_MIN_SND_MSS <= MAX_TCP_OPTION_SPACE) alongside the existing struct-size check, but neither line performs or guards the runtime u16 tcp_gso_segs accumulation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The target CWE-190 describes a runtime integer wraparound, but the only relevant lines here are static BUILD_BUG_ON assertions evaluated at build time and unrelated to the gso_segs increment. The function neither contains the overflowing arithmetic nor a runtime constraint preventing it, so it does not directly support CWE-190.

evidence_lines.code:
BUILD_BUG_ON(sizeof(struct tcp_skb_cb) >
FIELD_SIZEOF(struct sk_buff, cb));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause of CVE-2019-11477 is a 16-bit tcp_gso_segs counter in tcp_shifted_skb() overflowing when SACK coalesces many fragments, not any calculation in this init function. The trigger is remote SACK processing with small MSS; the consequence is a BUG_ON crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fixed bugs of stack reallocation x GC

Macro 'checkstackGC' was doing a GC step after resizing the stack;
the GC could shrink the stack and undo the resize. Moreover, macro
'checkstackp' also does a GC step, which could remove the preallocated
CallInfo when calling a function. (Its name has been changed to
'checkstackGCp' to emphasize that it calls the GC.)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  checkstackGC(L, p->maxstacksize + 1);'], 'added_lines': ['  luaD_checkstack(L, p->maxstacksize + 1);']}
description: Lua through 5.4.0 mishandles the interaction between stack resizes and garbage collection, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow, heap-based buffer over-read, or use-after-free.

code_evidence: Line 7 uses checkstackGC, which performs a GC step after resizing the stack; the GC can shrink the stack and undo the resize. Lines 8-12 then write to L->top (setobjs2s/setnilvalue) relying on the space supposedly reserved by line 7, and lines 13-14 advance ci->func/ci->top by actual+1. If the GC shrunk the stack, these writes exceed the available stack buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes objects to L->top after the stack reservation can be undone by GC, producing writes beyond the intended stack buffer, matching CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. The fix replaces the GC-invoking macro with luaD_checkstack, showing the defect is the unsafe write after insufficient/rescinded allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: stack space is reserved with a macro that runs GC, and GC may shrink the stack, invalidating the reservation. Trigger: a vararg function call where the GC step shrinks the stack. Consequence: subsequent setobjs2s/setnilvalue writes past the stack end, i.e., heap-based out-of-bounds write (also enabling over-read or use-after-free).

commit_msg:
If sctp_destroy_sock is called without sock_net(sk)->sctp.addr_wq_lock
held and sp->do_auto_asconf is true, then an element is removed
from the auto_asconf_splist without any proper locking.

This can happen in the following functions:
1. In sctp_accept, if sctp_sock_migrate fails.
2. In inet_create or inet6_create, if there is a bpf program
   attached to BPF_CGROUP_INET_SOCK_CREATE which denies
   creation of the sctp socket.

The bug is fixed by acquiring addr_wq_lock in sctp_destroy_sock
instead of sctp_close.

This addresses CVE-2021-23133.

Reported-by: Or Cohen <orcohen@paloaltonetworks.com>
Reviewed-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Fixes: 610236587600 ("bpf: Add new cgroup attach type to enable sock modifications")
Signed-off-by: Or Cohen <orcohen@paloaltonetworks.com>
Acked-by: Marcelo Ricardo Leitner <marcelo.leitner@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t * Also, sctp_destroy_sock() needs to be called with addr_wq_lock', '\t * held and that should be grabbed before socket lock.', '\tspin_lock_bh(&net->sctp.addr_wq_lock);', '\tbh_lock_sock_nested(sk);', '\tspin_unlock_bh(&net->sctp.addr_wq_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['\tlocal_bh_disable();', '\tbh_lock_sock(sk);', '\tlocal_bh_enable();']}
description: A race condition in Linux kernel SCTP sockets (net/sctp/socket.c) before 5.12-rc8 can lead to kernel privilege escalation from the context of a network service or an unprivileged process. If sctp_destroy_sock is called without sock_net(sk)->sctp.addr_wq_lock then an element is removed from the auto_asconf_splist list without any proper locking. This can be exploited by an attacker with network service privileges to escalate to root or from the context of an unprivileged user directly if a BPF_CGROUP_INET_SOCK_CREATE is attached which denies creation of some SCTP socket.

code_evidence: sctp_close releases the socket lock at line 35, then reacquires addr_wq_lock and the socket lock before calling sk_common_release, which invokes sctp_destroy_sock. The commit notes sctp_destroy_sock removes an element from auto_asconf_splist and must hold addr_wq_lock; this function only takes that lock here, not on the other path where destroy runs without it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the weakness is improper synchronization around a shared list: concurrent sequences access auto_asconf_splist without exclusive access. This is a race condition, not a simple missing check or memory-safety bug; the supported consequence is list corruption exploitable for privilege escalation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sctp_destroy_sock can run without sock_net(sk)->sctp.addr_wq_lock while manipulating auto_asconf_splist. Trigger: an SCTP socket destroyed via paths such as failed sctp_sock_migrate in sctp_accept or a BPF cgroup denial during inet_create. The unlocked list removal races with concurrent list access, corrupting the list and enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
RDMA/hns: Fix init resp when alloc ucontext

The data in resp will be copied from kernel to userspace, thus it needs to
be initialized to zeros to avoid copying uninited stack memory.

Reported-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Fixes: e088a685eae9 ("RDMA/hns: Support rq record doorbell for the user space")
Signed-off-by: Yixian Liu <liuyixian@huawei.com>

Line 19 passes &resp and sizeof(resp) to ib_copy_to_udata, copying the entire structure, including uninitialized padding/fields, from the kernel stack to userspace.

resp.qp_tab_size = hr_dev->caps.num_qps;

Trigger: a userspace caller invokes the alloc-ucontext ioctl path, causing ib_copy_to_udata to copy the full structure size. Supported consequence: uninitialized kernel stack bytes are disclosed to userspace, leaking sensitive kernel memory.

description: In the Linux kernel through 6.3.1, a use-after-free in Netfilter nf_tables when processing batch requests can be abused to perform arbitrary read and write operations on kernel memory. Unprivileged local users can obtain root privileges. This occurs because anonymous sets are mishandled.

code_evidence: In the NFT_TRANS_PREPARE branch the function only decrements set->use and returns; it performs no state transition on the set itself, so an anonymous set bound in the same batch remains active and reachable for later operations.

The ABORT/RELEASE/default branches decrement use and then call nf_tables_unbind_set, which is the only path that unbinds the binding; the PREPARE path never reaches this unbind, leaving the binding intact.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing deactivation in nf_tables_deactivate_set allows an already-removed anonymous set to be referenced and modified, matching CWE-416 use-after-free. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the preparation phase does not mark a bound anonymous set inactive, so a set removed earlier in the same transaction can still be targeted by subsequent element updates. Trigger: a batch request that deletes an anonymous set and then acts on it causes stale references to be processed during commit, yielding a use-after-free. Supported consequence: wild-memory write/read on kernel memory, potentially privilege escalation.

commit_msg: Guard binary expressions from too much recursion.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (jsP_accept(J, TK_AND))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (jsP_accept(J, TK_AND)) {', '\t\tINCREC();', '\t\tDECREC();', '\t}']}
description: jsparse.c in Artifex MuJS through 1.0.2 does not properly maintain the AST depth for binary expressions, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive recursion) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: logand recursively calls itself for each TK_AND chain via logand(J, notin) with no depth counter or bound, so the recursion depth follows attacker-controlled input length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because recursion depth is unbounded and controlled by input, consuming the stack; this is uncontrolled recursion rather than a simple resource leak or infinite loop.

if (jsP_accept(J, TK_AND))
a = EXP2(LOGAND, a, logand(J, notin));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursive descent for binary '&&' expressions recurses once per accepted TK_AND without any recursion limit. Trigger: a crafted file containing a long chain of '&&' operators drives logand into deep recursion, exhausting the program stack and causing a denial of service.

description: curl 7.61.0 through 7.76.1 suffers from exposure of data element to wrong session due to a mistake in the code for CURLOPT_SSL_CIPHER_LIST when libcurl is built to use the Schannel TLS library. The selected cipher set was stored in a single "static" variable in the library, which has the surprising side-effect that if an application sets up multiple concurrent transfers, the last one that sets the ciphers will accidentally control the set used by all transfers. In a worst-case scenario, this weakens transport security significantly.

code_evidence: The function builds per-connection Schannel credentials from SSL_CONN_CONFIG(cipher_list), but the cipher selection is passed to set_ssl_ciphers without any per-backend identifier; the vulnerability description states that set_ssl_ciphers stored the selected cipher set in a single static variable shared by the whole library, so one connection's cipher list overwrites the cipher set used by every other concurrent transfer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The shared static causes a per-session security configuration resource to be exposed to the wrong control sphere: one transfer's settings leak into unrelated transfers. This matches CWE-668's exposure of a resource to the wrong party.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the selected cipher set is kept in a process-wide static rather than scoped to the connection's Schannel credentials. Trigger: an application runs concurrent transfers and sets different CURLOPT_SSL_CIPHER_LIST values. Consequence: the last-set cipher list controls all transfers, potentially weakening transport security for other sessions.

description: An issue was discovered in Janus through 0.9.1. plugins/janus_voicemail.c in the VoiceMail plugin has a race condition that could cause a server crash.

The patch's replacement with g_atomic_int_set confirms the intended fix for the concurrent shared-resource access.

A concurrent reader can observe inconsistent session state during setup, leading to the race that the commit describes as causing a server crash. commit_msg:
Affected are ProcRRChangeProviderProperty and ProcRRChangeOutputProperty.
See also xserver@8f454b79 where this same bug was fixed for the core
protocol and XI.

This fixes an OOB read and the resulting information disclosure.

Length calculation for the request was clipped to a 32-bit integer. With
the correct stuff->nUnits value the expected request size was
truncated, passing the REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE check.

The server then proceeded with reading at least stuff->num_items bytes
(depending on stuff->format) from the request and stuffing whatever it
finds into the property. In the process it would also allocate at least
stuff->nUnits bytes, i.e. 4GB.

CVE-2023-6478, ZDI-CAN-22561

This vulnerability was discovered by:
Jan-Niklas Sohn working with Trend Micro Zero Day Initiative
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int totalSize;'], 'added_lines': ['    uint64_t totalSize;']}
description: A flaw was found in xorg-server. A specially crafted request to RRChangeProviderProperty or RRChangeOutputProperty can trigger an integer overflow which may lead to a disclosure of sensitive information.

code_evidence: totalSize is declared int (line 9). len is taken from stuff->nUnits (line 24) and only bounded by a check against bytes_to_int32(0xffffffff - sizeof(xChangePropertyReq)) (line 25), which is a 32-bit byte limit. sizeInBytes is format>>3, i.e. 1/2/4 (line 27). totalSize = len * sizeInBytes (line 28) is a signed int multiplication where the product can exceed INT_MAX, truncating/wrapping. The wrapped totalSize then feeds REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE (line 29), so the length check passes even though the actual request payload is far larger.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits: an arithmetic size calculation wraps in the 32-bit totalSize, defeating the subsequent size validation. This is the integer-overflow root cause; the OOB read is its consequence, not a separate weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the request-length product len*sizeInBytes is computed in a 32-bit int, so a large nUnits with format 32 wraps to a small or negative totalSize. Trigger: a crafted RRChangeOutputProperty request with large nUnits. Consequence: REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE accepts the truncated size, after which the server reads/allocates based on len, causing OOB read and information disclosure.

commit_msg:
packet: hold bind lock when rebinding to fanout hook

Packet socket bind operations must hold the po->bind_lock. This keeps
po->running consistent with whether the socket is actually on a ptype
list to receive packets.

fanout_add unbinds a socket and its packet_rcv/tpacket_rcv call, then
binds the fanout object to receive through packet_rcv_fanout.

Make it hold the po->bind_lock when testing po->running and rebinding.
Else, it can race with other rebind operations, such as that in
packet_set_ring from packet_rcv to tpacket_rcv. Concurrent updates
can result in a socket being added to a fanout group twice, causing
use-after-free KASAN bug reports, among others.

Reported independently by both trinity and syzkaller.
Verified that the syzkaller reproducer passes after this patch.

Fixes: dc99f600698d ("packet: Add fanout support.")
Reported-by: nixioaming <nixiaoming@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Willem de Bruijn <willemb@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\terr = -EINVAL;', '\tif (!po->running)', '\t\tgoto out;', '\tif (match->type == type &&'], 'added_lines': ['', '\tspin_lock(&po->bind_lock);', '\tif (po->running &&', '\t    match->type == type &&', '\tspin_unlock(&po->bind_lock);', '', '\tif (err && !refcount_read(&match->sk_ref)) {', '\t\tlist_del(&match->list);', '\t\tkfree(match);', '\t}', '']}
description: net/packet/af_packet.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.6 allows local users to gain privileges via crafted system calls that trigger mishandling of packet_fanout data structures, because of a race condition (involving fanout_add and packet_do_bind) that leads to a use-after-free, a different vulnerability than CVE-2017-6346.

code_evidence: fanout_add only takes fanout_mutex; the po->running check and the subsequent rebind test/update of po->fanout and match->sk_ref are not protected by po->bind_lock, so a concurrent packet_set_ring rebind can interleave.
The match/sk_ref test and the __dev_remove_pack, po->fanout assignment and refcount increment form a non-atomic check-then-act sequence on shared fanout state.
The cleanup path frees rollover and unlocks fanout_mutex without having serialized against bind operations, leaving the shared socket binding state unprotected.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent code sequence lacking exclusive access to the shared po->running/po->fanout resource; the missing bind_lock permits an interfering rebind to violate atomicity, matching CWE-362. It is not merely a logic error, since the defect is the unsynchronized timing window.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fanout_add reads po->running and rebinds the socket without holding po->bind_lock, so it races with other rebind operations such as packet_set_ring. Trigger: concurrent bind/rebind calls from local users interleave between the check and the update. Consequence: the socket can be added to a fanout group twice, leading to a use-after-free (KASAN reports) and potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
ext4: zero out the unused memory region in the extent tree block

This commit zeroes out the unused memory region in the buffer_head
corresponding to the extent metablock after writing the extent header
and the corresponding extent node entries.

This is done to prevent random uninitialized data from getting into
the filesystem when the extent block is synced.

This fixes CVE-2019-11833.

Signed-off-by: Sriram Rajagopalan <sriramr@arista.com>
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmemmove(bh->b_data, EXT4_I(inode)->i_data,', '\t\tsizeof(EXT4_I(inode)->i_data));'], 'added_lines': ['\tsize_t ext_size = 0;', '\text_size = sizeof(EXT4_I(inode)->i_data);', '\tmemmove(bh->b_data, EXT4_I(inode)->i_data, ext_size);', '\t/* zero out unused area in the extent block */', '\tmemset(bh->b_data + ext_size, 0, inode->i_sb->s_blocksize - ext_size);']}
description: fs/ext4/extents.c in the Linux kernel through 5.1.2 does not zero out the unused memory region in the extent tree block, which might allow local users to obtain sensitive information by reading uninitialized data in the filesystem.

code_evidence: Only the inode's inline extent data (sizeof(EXT4_I(inode)->i_data)) is copied into the newly allocated metadata block via memmove at lines 29-30; the remainder of bh->b_data up to s_blocksize is never written.

The block header and extent entries are then set at lines 31-40 and the buffer is marked uptodate and dirtied, causing the partially initialized block to be written to disk. The unused tail retains whatever uninitialized contents the buffer had.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses/accesses a buffer resource (the extent metadata block) whose unused region was never initialized before being marked uptodate and written out, matching CWE-908's use of an uninitialized resource. The fix adds a memset zeroing the tail, confirming the missing initialization rather than, e.g., an out-of-bounds access.

evidence_lines.code:
memmove(bh->b_data, EXT4_I(inode)->i_data,
sizeof(EXT4_I(inode)->i_data));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the extent tree block is only partially initialized by the memmove of i_data, leaving the region beyond that size uninitialized. Trigger: growing the depth of an inode's extent tree allocates a new metadata block, then syncs it with the uninitialized tail intact. Supported consequence: uninitialized kernel memory is written into the filesystem and can later be read back, leaking sensitive data (CWE-908, confidentiality impact).

with length not multiple of 256.
(prefetch_enc, prefetch_dec): Modify pre- and post-table counters
to unshare look-up table pages between processes.
--

GnuPG-bug-id: 4541
Signed-off-by: Jussi Kivilinna <jussi.kivilinna@iki.fi>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t       &dec_tables);', '\t\t\t\t     &dec_tables);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t       dec_tables.T);', '\t\t\t\t     dec_tables.T);']}
description: In Libgcrypt 1.8.4, the C implementation of AES is vulnerable to a flush-and-reload side-channel attack because physical addresses are available to other processes. (The C implementation is used on platforms where an assembly-language implementation is unavailable.) NOTE: the vendor's position is that the issue report cannot be validated because there is no description of an attack

code_evidence: do_decrypt dispatches to assembly decrypt routines (_gcry_aes_amd64_decrypt_block or _gcry_aes_arm_decrypt_block) passing the decryption lookup table &dec_tables together with the round keys and round count. The table is a process-shared .data object whose physical pages are reachable/observable by other processes; the function simply hands that shared resource to the cipher implementation with no access restriction or page isolation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes the decryption lookup table resource to a control sphere beyond the calling process, matching CWE-668's exposure of a resource to unintended actors. A related weakness such as CWE-203 concerns the observable discrepancy itself, but here the code-grounded defect is the shared-table exposure in do_decrypt's dispatch.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the AES decryption table passed by do_decrypt resides in a shared .data section, so its cache/physical-page activity is visible across process boundaries. Trigger: a co-resident attacker monitors the table's memory accesses during decryption. Supported consequence: leakage of key-dependent table-index information enabling flush-and-reload style side-channel recovery of plaintext/keys. The cause is the shared resource exposure; the leak is the consequence.

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: remove nodes owned by destroyed domain

In case a domain is removed from Xenstore, remove all nodes owned by
it per default.

This tackles the problem that nodes might be created by a domain
outside its home path in Xenstore, leading to Xenstore hogging more
and more memory. Domain quota don't work in this case if the guest is
rebooting in between.

Since XSA-322 ownership of such stale nodes is transferred to dom0,
which is helping against unintended access, but not against OOM of
Xenstore.

As a fallback for weird cases add a Xenstore start parameter for
keeping today's way to handle stale nodes, adding the risk of Xenstore
hitting an OOM situation.

This is part of XSA-419 / CVE-2022-42322.

Fixes: 496306324d8d ("tools/xenstore: revoke access rights for removed domains")
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\twhile ((opt = getopt_long(argc, argv, "DE:F:HNPS:t:A:M:Q:q:T:RVW:w:U",'], 'added_lines': ['\twhile ((opt = getopt_long(argc, argv, "DE:F:HKNPS:t:A:M:Q:q:T:RVW:w:U",', '\t\t\tbreak;', "\t\tcase 'K':", '\t\t\tkeep_orphans = true;']}
description: Xenstore: Cooperating guests can create arbitrary numbers of nodes T[his CNA information record relates to multiple CVEs; the text explains which aspects/vulnerabilities correspond to which CVE.] Since the fix of XSA-322 any Xenstore node owned by a removed domain will be modified to be owned by Dom0. This will allow two malicious guests working together to create an arbitrary number of Xenstore nodes. This is possible by domain A letting domain B write into domain A's local Xenstore tree. Domain B can then create many nodes and reboot. The nodes created by domain B will now be owned by Dom0. By repeating this process over and over again an arbitrary number of nodes can be created, as Dom0's number of nodes isn't limited by Xenstore quota.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only parses command-line options and runs the daemon loop; it contains no memory allocation or release logic, and the diff merely adds a 'K' flag, so it does not demonstrate missing release of allocated memory (CWE-401).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  jsvGetString(name, &buf[1], JSLEX_MAX_TOKEN_LENGTH);'], 'added_lines': ['  size_t l = jsvGetString(name, &buf[1], JSLEX_MAX_TOKEN_LENGTH);', "  buf[l] = 0; // zero terminate since jsvGetString doesn't add one"]}
description: Espruino 2v11.251 was discovered to contain a stack buffer overflow via src/jsvar.c in jsvNewFromString.

code_evidence: A 1+JSLEX_MAX_TOKEN_LENGTH byte stack buffer 'buf' is declared, and buf[0] is set. jsvGetString copies up to JSLEX_MAX_TOKEN_LENGTH bytes into &buf[1] but, as the fix comment notes, does not append a NUL terminator. joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 concerns writing past buffer bounds. Here the missing terminator causes an out-of-bounds read by string consumers rather than a write, so this function better matches an out-of-bounds read weakness than CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: jsvGetString is called without ensuring the destination is NUL-terminated, so a name whose length reaches JSLEX_MAX_TOKEN_LENGTH leaves buf with no terminator. Trigger: a long function-parameter name. Consequence: jsvAddNamedChild reads past buf's end for a terminator, causing an out-of-bounds read; the missing terminator is the defect, not a write past the buffer.

commit_msg:
rgw:  make init env methods return an error

Since web frontends may signal an error when requests are malformed or so, let
us double check this and raise errors early. The current user of this is
civetweb frontend; which can potentially return null from `parse_http_headers`
when a HTTP header without a ":" is supplied at which point headers.value is
null which can lead to undefined behaviour later in RGW.

Fixes: http://tracker.ceph.com/issues/23039
Signed-off-by: Abhishek Lekshmanan <abhishek@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int ret = 0;', '', '  client_io->init(g_ceph_context);', '  RGWOp* op = NULL;', '    abort_early(s, NULL, init_error, NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['  int ret = client_io->init(g_ceph_context);', '  if (ret < 0) {', '    s->cio = client_io;', '    abort_early(s, nullptr, ret, nullptr);', '    return ret;', '  }', '', '  RGWOp* op = nullptr;', '    abort_early(s, nullptr, init_error, nullptr);']}
description: In Ceph before 12.2.3 and 13.x through 13.0.1, the rgw_civetweb.cc RGWCivetWeb::init_env function in radosgw doesn't handle malformed HTTP headers properly, allowing for denial of service.

code_evidence: Line 10 initializes ret to 0 and line 11 calls client_io->init(g_ceph_context) without capturing or checking its return value; the result is discarded, so any failure signaled by init goes unnoticed.

Line 16 obtains the environment via client_io->get_env() and line 18 constructs req_state from that RGWEnv; if init failed to build valid header state (e.g. a header lacking ':' yielding a null headers.value), the environment passed downstream is malformed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked init result lets execution continue with a null/invalid header value that is later dereferenced, matching CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). It is not merely improper input validation: the specific consequence is dereference of a pointer expected to be valid.

evidence_lines.code:
int ret = 0;
client_io->init(g_ceph_context);

RGWEnv& rgw_env = client_io->get_env();
struct req_state rstate(g_ceph_context, &rgw_env, &userinfo);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ignored return value of client_io->init allows a failed/partial initialization to proceed. Trigger: a malformed HTTP header causes the frontend's header parsing to produce a null value, leaving the environment inconsistent. Consequence: subsequent processing dereferences the invalid environment/header state, causing a crash or undefined behavior (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix format string vulnerability

Reported by Kapil Anand on ayttm-users:
https://sourceforge.net/p/ayttm/mailman/message/34397158/

This patch does the following two things:

1. Makes sure debug_print is only used in DEBUG mode and not in non-DEBUG mode
2. Since debug_print is basically printf, we don't really need to first
   snprintf into a buffer and then print the buffer.
3. We no longer need debug_buff

description: A vulnerability, which was classified as critical, was found in ayttm up to 0.5.0.89. This affects the function http_connect in the library libproxy/proxy.c. The manipulation leads to format string. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. The complexity of an attack is rather high. The exploitability is told to be difficult. The patch is named 40e04680018614a7d2b68566b261b061a0597046. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The associated identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-222267.

code_evidence: In the non-DEBUG build, cmd (built from host/port and proxy auth) is first formatted into debug_buff with snprintf, then passed directly as the format argument to debug_print(debug_buff).
The received proxy response line inputline is similarly passed as the sole format argument: debug_print(debug_buff) where debug_buff contains inputline.
Inside the receive loop, subsequent inputline values are again passed directly as the format string to debug_print.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-134 applies because the format string passed to debug_print originates from external input (proxy response) rather than a fixed literal; the patch's change to debug_print("<%s>\n", inputline) confirms the format string was externally controlled.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: debug_print is treated as printf, and the externally influenced buffer (server response line inputline, or host-derived cmd) is supplied as the format string rather than as an argument. Trigger: a proxy response or host value containing '%n'/'%s' specifiers reaches these non-DEBUG debug_print calls. Consequence: format-specifier interpretation can read memory and potentially write memory or crash the process.

description: An issue was discovered in PHP before 5.6.37, 7.0.x before 7.0.31, 7.1.x before 7.1.20, and 7.2.x before 7.2.8. An Integer Overflow leads to a heap-based buffer over-read in exif_thumbnail_extract of exif.c.

If the addition wraps, the sum is small and the check on line 16 succeeds, so the subsequent estrndup on line 20 copies from offset+offset with size bytes beyond the intended buffer, yielding a heap-based over-read. description: epan/dissectors/packet-pktc.c in the PKTC dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.11 and 2.0.x before 2.0.3 does not verify BER identifiers, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: The function builds a subset tvb from the remaining packet bytes and passes it directly to dissect_kerberos_main without inspecting the BER application tag; the second call reuses the offset returned by the first call and again dissects unconditionally. The Kerberos dissector's expected application value (and thus its private data layout) is never validated against the actual packet content.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing tag check leads to operations outside the intended buffer boundary (out-of-bounds write/read) in the called dissector, matching CWE-119. The defect is a missing validation constraint rather than an integer overflow or type confusion per se; CWE-119 captures the resultant out-of-bounds memory operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: untrusted PKTC payload bytes are handed to the Kerberos dissector regardless of the BER application tag, so the dissector interprets the buffer using the wrong application's private data structure. Trigger: a crafted packet whose tag differs from KRB_AP_REQ/REP or KRB_SAFE. This causes the dissector to operate on mismatched internal structures, producing out-of-bounds memory access and a crash.

Merge pull request from GHSA-q9cp-8wcq-7pfr

* Prevent heap buffer overflow when parsing DNS packet

* Fixed incorrect check in get_name*()

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. A buffer overflow vulnerability in versions 2.13 and prior affects applications that use PJSIP DNS resolver. It doesn't affect PJSIP users who do not utilise PJSIP DNS resolver. This vulnerability is related to CVE-2022-24793. The difference is that this issue is in parsing the query record `parse_query()`, while the issue in CVE-2022-24793 is in `parse_rr()`. A patch is available as commit `d1c5e4d` in the `master` branch. A workaround is to disable DNS resolution in PJSIP config (by setting `nameserver_count` to zero) or use an external resolver implementation instead.

code_evidence: The loop dereferences *p at line 12 and reads label_len = *p at line 30 before any bound check; the check at line 31 (p+1+label_len+1 > max) occurs only after the read and never validates that p itself is below max. The added guard is only at function entry after the diff, not present in this function body, so a start equal to or beyond max still enters the loop.

After advancing p by label_len+1 at line 33, the loop re-tests *p at line 12 and finally increments p and parsed_len at lines 40–41 without confirming p < max, permitting reads/writes past the packet buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function parses a copied DNS packet and computes lengths from unchecked label bytes, producing an out-of-bounds memory access consistent with the buffer overflow described. Note CWE-120 strictly concerns buffer copies; the read-before-bounds pattern here is closer to CWE-125, but within the supplied target the unsafe size handling is supported.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the name parser advances p through packet bytes based on attacker-controlled label lengths and dereferences *p without first checking that the current pointer is within [pkt, max). Trigger: a DNS name whose labels walk p to or past max. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of packet memory (and parsed_len/name_len accounting) leading to heap buffer overflow/crash as described in the advisory.

commit_msg:
scsi: pvscsi: limit loop to fetch SG list

In PVSCSI paravirtual SCSI bus, pvscsi_convert_sglist can take a very
long time or go into an infinite loop due to two different bugs:

1) the request descriptor data length is defined to be 64 bit. While
building SG list from a request descriptor, it gets truncated to 32bit
in routine 'pvscsi_convert_sglist'. This could lead to an infinite loop
situation large 'dataLen' values when data_length is cast to uint32_t and
chunk_size becomes always zero.  Fix this by removing the incorrect cast.

2) pvscsi_get_next_sg_elem can be called arbitrarily many times if the
element has a zero length.  Get out of the loop early when this happens,
by introducing an upper limit on the number of SG list elements.

Reported-by: Li Qiang <liqiang6-s@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Message-Id: <1473108643-12983-1-git-send-email-ppandit@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int chunk_size;', '    while (data_length) {', '        while (!sg.resid) {', '        assert(data_length > 0);', '        chunk_size = MIN((unsigned) data_length, sg.resid);'], 'added_lines': ['    uint32_t chunk_size, elmcnt = 0;', '    while (data_length && elmcnt < PVSCSI_MAX_SG_ELEM) {', '        while (!sg.resid && elmcnt++ < PVSCSI_MAX_SG_ELEM) {', '        chunk_size = MIN(data_length, sg.resid);']}
description: The pvscsi_convert_sglist function in hw/scsi/vmw_pvscsi.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (infinite loop and QEMU process crash) by leveraging an incorrect cast.

code_evidence: chunk_size is declared as a signed int while data_length is a 64-bit uint64_t.
MIN casts data_length to unsigned (32-bit), truncating the 64-bit length; the truncated chunk_size is then used to decrement data_length and sg.resid.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an incorrect narrowing conversion/cast of a 64-bit length to 32-bit, matching CWE-704 Incorrect Type Conversion or Cast. The infinite loop is the downstream consequence, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code:
int chunk_size;
uint64_t data_length = r->req.dataLen;

chunk_size = MIN((unsigned) data_length, sg.resid);
data_length -= chunk_size;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the 64-bit data_length is narrowed to a 32-bit unsigned value when computing chunk_size. Trigger: a request dataLen whose low 32 bits are zero yields chunk_size of 0, so data_length is never decremented and the while(data_length) loop never terminates. Supported consequence is a denial of service via infinite loop/hang.

commit_msg: Added check for out of bounds read (https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/108).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      break;', '    if ((id == 0x000003ed) && (PSDQuantum(count) < (ssize_t) (length-12)))', '        (void) CopyMagickMemory(q,q+PSDQuantum(count)+12,length-', '          (PSDQuantum(count)+12)-(q-datum));', '        SetStringInfoLength(bim_profile,length-(PSDQuantum(count)+12));'], 'added_lines': ['    ssize_t', '      cnt;', '', '      return;', '    cnt=PSDQuantum(count);', '    if (cnt < 0)', '      return;', '    if ((id == 0x000003ed) && (cnt < (ssize_t) (length-12)))', '        (void) CopyMagickMemory(q,q+cnt+12,length-(cnt+12)-(q-datum));', '        SetStringInfoLength(bim_profile,length-(cnt+12));']}
description: coders/psd.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted PSD file.

code_evidence: The 32-bit `count` read from the PSD resource block is converted via `PSDQuantum(count)` and only checked against the upper bound `length-12`; a negative/wrapped value is not rejected before the copy.
The pointer `p` is advanced by the raw `count` (`p+=count`) and optionally `p++`, with no check that `p` stays within `datum+length`, so the next loop iteration can read past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs buffer reads whose bounds depend on unchecked file-supplied `count`, so data is read past the end of the intended buffer, directly matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). This is distinct from an out-of-bounds write, since no out-of-range write is shown here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the resource-block length `count` is attacker-controlled and used to advance the read pointer and size the copy without validating that it keeps accesses within the profile buffer. Trigger: a crafted PSD file with an oversized or wrapping count makes `p+=count` move beyond `datum+length`, and the loop condition/`LocaleNCompare`/`Push*Pixel` then read out of bounds. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read causing a crash (DoS) or memory disclosure.

The profile field is changed by code inside and outside the decoder,
its not a reliable indicator of the internal codec state.
Maintaining it consistency with studio_profile is messy.
Its easier to just avoid it and use only studio_profile

description: In libavcodec in FFmpeg 4.0.1, improper maintenance of the consistency between the context profile field and studio_profile in libavcodec may trigger an assertion failure while converting a crafted AVI file to MPEG4, leading to a denial of service, related to error_resilience.c, h263dec.c, and mpeg4videodec.c.

code_evidence: At the end of header parsing, when s->studio_profile is set, the code asserts av_assert0(s->avctx->profile == FF_PROFILE_MPEG4_SIMPLE_STUDIO). The profile field and studio_profile are maintained separately (studio_profile set at lines 100-102, profile assigned at line 109), so a crafted stream can leave studio_profile set while avctx->profile differs, making the assertion reachable.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an assertion that ties two independently maintained fields (studio_profile and avctx->profile) together. Trigger: a crafted AVI/MPEG4 stream sets studio_profile while causing avctx->profile to hold a different value. Consequence: av_assert0 aborts the decoder process, a denial of service.

The UAF is because:

 mount(pid: 921)               | cifsd(pid: 923)
-------------------------------|-------------------------------
                               | cifs_demultiplex_thread
SMB2_negotiate                 |
 cifs_send_recv                |
  compound_send_recv           |
   smb_send_rqst               |
    wait_for_response          |
     wait_event_state      [1] |
                               |  standard_receive3
                               |   cifs_handle_standard
                               |    handle_mid
                               |     mid->resp_buf = buf;  [2]
                               |     dequeue_mid           [3]
     KILL the process      [4] |
    resp_iov[i].iov_base = buf |
 free_rsp_buf              [5] |

1. After send request to server, wait the response until
    mid->mid_state != SUBMITTED;
2. Receive response from server, and set it to mid;
3. Set the mid state to RECEIVED;
4. Kill the process, the mid state already RECEIVED, get 0;
5. Handle and release the negotiate response;

Fixes: ec637e3ffb6b ("[CIFS] Avoid extra large buffer allocation (and memcpy) in cifs_readpages")
Reviewed-by: Paulo Alcantara (SUSE) <pc@manguebit.com>
Signed-off-by: Zhang Xiaoxu <zhangxiaoxu5@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Steve French <stfrench@microsoft.com>

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in smb2_is_status_io_timeout() in CIFS in the Linux Kernel. After CIFS transfers response data to a system call, there are still local variable points to the memory region, and if the system call frees it faster than CIFS uses it, CIFS will access a free memory region, leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: cifs_compound_callback reads mid->server and mid->optype, and calls server->ops->get_credits(mid) to compute credits.value. The callback operates on the mid_q_entry without any state check, so it may run while the caller's response buffer is being released.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the callback uses mid-related memory after the response buffer that backs the operation has been released by the waiting thread. The added MID_RESPONSE_READY transition in the patch confirms the missing ownership/state constraint; this is a lifetime error, not a mere race on a valid object.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the callback dereferences mid and its server/optype fields without ensuring the response is still owned by the mid. Trigger: a synchronous caller receives the response, the mid state becomes RECEIVED, and the caller frees the response buffer while cifsd still invokes this callback. The freed buffer/mid data is accessed, giving a use-after-free read and possible DoS.

commit_msg:
Save stack space while handling errors

Because error handling (luaG_errormsg) uses slots from EXTRA_STACK,
and some errors can recur (e.g., string overflow while creating an
error message in 'luaG_runerror', or a C-stack overflow before calling
the message handler), the code should use stack slots with parsimony.

This commit fixes the bug "Lua-stack overflow when C stack overflows
while handling an error".
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (l_unlikely(l >= (MAX_SIZE/sizeof(char)) - tl))', "    L->top -= n-1;  /* popped 'n' strings and pushed one */"], 'added_lines': ['        if (l_unlikely(l >= (MAX_SIZE/sizeof(char)) - tl)) {', '          L->top = top - total;  /* pop strings to avoid wasting stack */', '        }', "    L->top = top - (n - 1);  /* popped 'n' strings and pushed one */"]}
description: An issue in the component luaG_runerror of Lua v5.4.4 and below leads to a heap-buffer overflow when a recursive error occurs.

code_evidence: The loop accumulates string lengths into tl while tostring may convert stack values; the guard l >= (MAX_SIZE/sizeof(char)) - tl triggers luaG_runerror without first restoring L->top to top - total. The error path thus leaves extra stack slots occupied, and recursive error handling re-enters this path, consuming EXTRA_STACK slots until the stack is exhausted and subsequent writes/uses exceed the allocated stack.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing L->top restoration before raising the error causes stack-pointer drift leading to writes past the intended stack buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the overflow error branch calls luaG_runerror without popping the strings it already pushed onto the stack, so repeated recursive errors deplete EXTRA_STACK and L->top advances past the allocated stack region; the resulting out-of-bounds stack access/write produces the heap-buffer overflow.

commit_msg:
[MJ2] To avoid divisions by zero / undefined behaviour on shift

Signed-off-by: Young_X <YangX92@hotmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '                    /* To avoid divisions by zero / undefined behaviour on shift */', '                    if (rpx >= 31 || ((comp->dx << rpx) >> rpx) != comp->dx ||', '                            rpy >= 31 || ((comp->dy << rpy) >> rpy) != comp->dy) {', '                        continue;', '                    }', '']}
description: Division-by-zero vulnerabilities in the functions pi_next_pcrl, pi_next_cprl, and pi_next_rpcl in openmj2/pi.c in OpenJPEG through 2.3.0 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash).

code_evidence: rpx and rpy are computed from res->pdx/pdy plus levelno, then used as shift amounts and in modulo denominators: (comp->dy << rpy), (1 << rpy), (comp->dx << rpx), (1 << rpx).
The x/y alignment checks divide by shifted component dimensions (comp->dx << rpx) and (1 << rpx); if these shifts yield zero, the modulo is a division by zero.
The prci/prcj computations use int_ceildiv(pi->x, comp->dx << levelno) and int_floordivpow2, which also depend on shifted values being nonzero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs modulo and division operations whose denominators depend on shifted component dimensions; when those become zero the code divides by zero, matching CWE-369. The added guard confirms the unsafe shift/divide path rather than a separate out-of-bounds or integer-overflow weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: shift amounts rpx/rpy derived from resolution pdx/pdy and levelno are not bounded before being used in shifts and modulo divisors. Trigger: crafted resolution parameters make the shifted component dimensions evaluate to zero or overflow, so the modulo/ceildiv denominators become zero. Consequence: division-by-zero causes an application crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix out of bounds copy in LoadBorders()

When processing groups out of order with an image where the last group
size  is smaller than the needed border it was possible to attempt to
load the right or bottom border from the next group when already
processing the rightmost or bottom group respectively. This situation
was causing an out-of-bounds copy on saved Image3F buffer in release
mode (or hitting a JXL_DASSERT in debug mode).

The order in which the groups are processed depends on many factors,
including the order in which the threads are scheduled when using
multiple threads, and potentially the order of the groups in the file
(not checked).

Added a test to force the out-of-order situation in a simulated parallel
runner that forces a random order on the tasks. The new test triggers
the assert in debug mode, which is now fixed.

Fixes #708.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      DivCeil(r.x0() + r.xsize() +', '                  (r.x0() + r.xsize() == frame_dim.xsize_padded ? 0 : borderx),', '      DivCeil(r.y0() + r.ysize() +', '                  (r.y0() + r.ysize() == frame_dim.ysize_padded ? 0 : bordery),'], 'added_lines': ['  // r may be such that r.x1 (namely x0() + xsize()) is within borderx of the', '  // right side of the image, so we use min() here.', '      DivCeil(std::min(r.x0() + r.xsize() + borderx, frame_dim.xsize_padded),', '  // Similar to x1, y1 might be closer than bordery from the bottom.', '      DivCeil(std::min(r.y0() + r.ysize() + bordery, frame_dim.ysize_padded),', '    JXL_DASSERT(gy > 0);', '    // When copying the bottom border we must not be on the bottom groups.', '    JXL_DASSERT(gy + 1 < frame_dim.ysize_groups);', '    JXL_DASSERT(gx > 0);', '    // When copying the right border we must not be on the rightmost groups.', '    JXL_DASSERT(gx + 1 < frame_dim.xsize_groups);']}
description: For certain valid JPEG XL images with a size slightly larger than an integer number of groups (256x256 pixels) when processing the groups out of order the decoder can perform an out of bounds copy of image pixels from an image buffer in the heap to another. This copy can occur when processing the right or bottom edges of the image, but only when groups are processed in certain order. Groups can be processed out of order in multi-threaded decoding environments with heavy thread load but also with images that contain the groups in an arbitrary order in the file. It is recommended to upgrade past 0.6.0 or patch with https://github.com/libjxl/libjxl/pull/775

code_evidence: x1src is computed as r.x0()+r.xsize()+borderx unless the right edge exactly equals frame_dim.xsize_padded; when r.x1 lies within borderx of the padded right edge but is not equal to it, x1src exceeds the image width.
y1src has the same defect on the bottom edge: bordery is added whenever r.y1 != frame_dim.ysize_padded, even if the remaining margin is smaller than bordery.
When y1src > y1, CopyImageTo reads a Rect of width x1src-x0src from border_storage_h; the oversized x1src makes this source rectangle extend past the border buffer.
When x1src > x1, CopyImageTo reads a Rect of height y1src-y0src from border_storage_v, so the oversized y1src causes an out-of-bounds read region to be copied.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch fixes an out-of-bounds memory access caused by an unclamped size computation feeding a copy into/out of an image buffer, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write/copy. The defect is a missing upper-bound constraint on x1src/y1src, not merely an integer overflow.
