commit_msg:
string_number_format: Correctly handles return value of snprintf

Summary: `snprintf` can return a value greater than the number of bytes copied. In case the first byte of the string is not a digit (could be '-'), size of `tmpstr` was being updated without checking `tmplen`. This resulted in either an assertion error or a heap overflow depending on whether the assertion is compiled or not.

Reviewed By: mofarrell, qianxuweiren

Differential Revision: D17327899

fbshipit-source-id: ee53875d21e02608c6d870388eecf1464de24ff1
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (tmpbuf == nullptr || !isdigit((int)tmpbuf[0])) {'], 'added_lines': ["  // This actually means 63 bytes for characters + 1 byte for '\\0'", '  // From the man page of snprintf, the return value is:', '  // The number of characters that would have been written if n had been', '  // sufficiently large, not counting the terminating null character.', '  if (tmplen < 64 && (tmpbuf == nullptr || !isdigit((int)tmpbuf[0]))) {']}
description: Insufficient boundary checks when formatting numbers in number_format allows read/write access to out-of-bounds memory, potentially leading to remote code execution. This issue affects HHVM versions prior to 3.30.10, all versions between 4.0.0 and 4.8.5, all versions between 4.9.0 and 4.18.2, and versions 4.19.0, 4.19.1, 4.20.0, 4.20.1, 4.20.2, 4.21.0, 4.22.0, 4.23.0.

code_evidence: A 63-byte String buffer is reserved and snprintf is called with size 64; snprintf returns the number of characters that would have been written, which can exceed the buffer.
The pre-patch guard only checks the first byte via isdigit; when the result starts with '-' the non-digit branch calls setSize(tmplen) with a tmplen that may be larger than the 63-byte allocation.
The tmplen >= 64 reallocation branch runs only after the first guard, so an oversized tmplen reaching line 22 grows the string beyond its buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing a size derived from snprintf's would-be length into a fixed 63-byte buffer causes operations outside the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The defect is a missing bounds check on tmplen before setSize, not merely a numeric conversion error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of snprintf (required length) is used as the string size without confirming it fits the allocated buffer. Trigger: formatting a value whose output begins with a non-digit such as '-' while the required length exceeds 63 bytes. Consequence: setSize(tmplen) sets a size larger than the allocation, leading to heap overflow or an assertion failure.

cdrom: information leak in cdrom_ioctl_media_changed()

This cast is wrong.  "cdi->capacity" is an int and "arg" is an unsigned
long.  The way the check is written now, if one of the high 32 bits is
set then we could read outside the info->slots[] array.

This bug is pretty old and it predates git.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>

description: The cdrom_ioctl_media_changed function in drivers/cdrom/cdrom.c in the Linux kernel before 4.16.6 allows local attackers to use a incorrect bounds check in the CDROM driver CDROM_MEDIA_CHANGED ioctl to read out kernel memory.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/879
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['              return((Image *) NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['              ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"ImproperImageHeader");']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.0.7-12 Q16, a memory leak vulnerability was found in the function ReadPICTImage in coders/pict.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted PICT image file.

code_evidence: CloneImage allocates a new tile_image (lines 264-265). When the clone fails and returns NULL, the function exits with a bare return((Image *) NULL) (lines 266-267) instead of a ThrowReaderException cleanup path. The patch replaces this bare return with ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"ImproperImageHeader").
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the defect is a failure to release an allocated resource after its effective lifetime has ended: the early bare return at line 267 skips the cleanup performed by the ThrowReaderException path. joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: On a crafted PICT image whose frame causes CloneImage to fail, the reader takes the early return at line 267 rather than the exception path. The bare return bypasses the normal reader-error teardown that releases resources (e.g., the image list and blob) associated with the reader, so those resources are not released after their effective lifetime ends. Repeated parsing of such crafted images can accumulate unreleased resources, supporting a memory-consumption denial of service.

description: ImageMagick 7.0.6-1 has a memory exhaustion vulnerability in ReadOneJNGImage in coders\png.c.

commit_msg:
ehci: apply limit to iTD/sidt descriptors

Commit "156a2e4 ehci: make idt processing more robust" tries to avoid a
DoS by the guest (create a circular iTD queue and let qemu ehci
emulation run in circles forever).  Unfortunately this has two problems:
First it misses the case of siTDs, and second it reportedly breaks
FreeBSD.

So lets go for a different approach: just count the number of iTDs and
siTDs we have seen per frame and apply a limit.  That should really
catch all cases now.

Reported-by: 杜少博 <dushaobo@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (again < 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['    int itd_count = 0;', '            itd_count++;', '            itd_count++;', '        if (again < 0 || itd_count > 16) {', '            /* TODO: notify guest (raise HSE irq?) */']}
description: The ehci_advance_state function in hw/usb/hcd-ehci.c in QEMU allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (infinite loop and CPU consumption) via a circular split isochronous transfer descriptor (siTD) list, a related issue to CVE-2015-8558.

code_evidence: The do/while loop at lines 5 and 72-73 repeatedly advances EHCI state while 'again' remains nonzero. Cases EST_FETCHITD (22-24) and EST_FETCHSITD (25-27) call fetchitd/fetchsitd and set 'again' from their return, but nothing bounds how many times these states can recur. The only escape at line 67 is 'if (again < 0)', so a guest-controlled circular siTD/iTD list that keeps returning a positive 'again' makes the loop spin indefinitely.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 covers failure to throttle consumption of a limited resource. Here the code lacks a limit on repeated descriptor processing, so unbounded iteration exhausts CPU. It is not CWE-835 (infinite loop) as the core defect is missing throttling of guest-controlled resource requests, matching CWE-400's 'lack of throttling for the number of allocated resources'.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the state machine loop has no per-frame bound on how many iTD/siTD descriptors it will process; the sole exit condition is a negative return. Trigger: a guest OS administrator supplies a circular split isochronous transfer descriptor list. Consequence: ehci_advance_state loops forever, consuming CPU (denial of service).

commit_msg:
Throw exception when IV is used with ECB or CTR

The IV parameter is currently ignored when initializing
a cipher in ECB or CTR mode.

For CTR mode, it is confusing: it takes some time to see
that a different parameter is needed (the counter).

For ECB mode, it is outright dangerous.

This patch forces an exception to be raised.

description: The Apache HTTP Server 2.4.18 through 2.4.20, when mod_http2 and mod_ssl are enabled, does not properly recognize the "SSLVerifyClient require" directive for HTTP/2 request authorization, which allows remote attackers to bypass intended access restrictions by leveraging the ability to send multiple requests over a single connection and aborting a renegotiation.

code_evidence: Lines 140-155 compute the requested client-verification mode from the per-directory and server auth configuration and apply it with SSL_set_verify; verify_old at line 142 preserves the prior mode.

Lines 157-168 detect a transition to a stricter verify mode and set renegotiate; on a slave connection (HTTP/2 request sharing the master SSL) the function notes 'ssl-renegotiate-forbidden' and returns HTTP_FORBIDDEN at line 168, aborting the renegotiation.

The added line 213 restores the prior verify mode via SSL_set_verify(ssl, verify_old, NULL) only in the virtual-host CA-mismatch branch; the earlier abort path at line 168 returns without restoring verify_old, leaving the stricter SSL_VERIFY_PEER_STRICT state on the shared SSL object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-284 covers failing to enforce an intended access-control policy. Here the intended policy is mandatory client certificate verification (SSLVerifyClient require), but the aborted-renegotiation path leaves verification state unrestored, so later requests can proceed without the required authorization check. This is an enforcement failure of access control rather than a certificate-validation logic flaw, matching CWE-284.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: when renegotiation is aborted for a slave connection, the function returns HTTP_FORBIDDEN without resetting the SSL verify mode it just changed. Trigger: a client sends multiple requests on one connection and aborts the renegotiation, so the SSL object retains the modified verification state. Consequence: subsequent requests on that connection are evaluated with inconsistent client-verification state, enabling the 'SSLVerifyClient require' directive to be bypassed for HTTP/2 requests, i.e., access restrictions are not enforced.

commit_msg:
evtchn: address races with evtchn_reset()

Neither d->evtchn_port_ops nor max_evtchns(d) may be used in an entirely
lock-less manner, as both may change by a racing evtchn_reset(). In the
common case, at least one of the domain's event lock or the per-channel
lock needs to be held. In the specific case of the inter-domain sending
by evtchn_send() and notify_via_xen_event_channel() holding the other
side's per-channel lock is sufficient, as the channel can't change state
without both per-channel locks held. Without such a channel changing
state, evtchn_reset() can't complete successfully.

Lock-free accesses continue to be permitted for the shim (calling some
otherwise internal event channel functions), as this happens while the
domain is in effectively single-threaded mode. Special care also needs
taking for the shim's marking of in-use ports as ECS_RESERVED (allowing
use of such ports in the shim case is okay because switching into and
hence also out of FIFO mode is impossihble there).

As a side effect, certain operations on Xen bound event channels which
were mistakenly permitted so far (e.g. unmask or poll) will be refused
now.

This is part of XSA-343.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static bool evtchn_fifo_is_pending(const struct domain *d, evtchn_port_t port)', '    const event_word_t *word = evtchn_fifo_word_from_port(d, port);'], 'added_lines': ['static bool evtchn_fifo_is_pending(const struct domain *d,', '                                   const struct evtchn *evtchn)', '    const event_word_t *word = evtchn_fifo_word_from_port(d, evtchn->port);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The function derives the FIFO event word directly from the port via evtchn_fifo_word_from_port(d, port) and then reads the pending bit with guest_test_bit, without holding the domain event lock or the per-channel lock. The port value and the resulting word pointer are used lock-lessly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses shared event-channel state concurrently without exclusive access, exactly the race window described by CWE-362; the patch changes the signature to pass the channel object, supporting the lock-holding caller. It is not merely a bounds issue, since the defect is the missing synchronization.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pending-bit read is performed without synchronization, so a concurrent evtchn_reset() can change port/channel state between the port lookup and the bit read. Trigger: an operation such as EVTCHNOP_reset or a poll/unmask on a Xen-bound channel races with this lock-less check. Consequence: the word may refer to stale or out-of-bounds state, violating internal assumptions and potentially causing memory-safety faults or bug checks.

which is the size of the layer field, however valid values are 0-255

needed to be sized to 256 entries. Update the size and add tests.

but earlier implementations returned 255:0xFFFF, dropping the middle
bits, this patch fixes that.

description: The function number_format is vulnerable to a heap overflow issue when its second argument ($dec_points) is excessively large. The internal implementation of the function will cause a string to be created with an invalid length, which can then interact poorly with other functions. This affects all supported versions of HHVM (3.30.1 and 3.27.5 and below).

code_evidence: snprintf returns the length the output would need, which for a huge dec can exceed 64; the code trusts tmplen to size tmpstr (line 25) and then snprintf writes tmplen+1 bytes into it (line 27), but the return value is not validated against the allocated buffer, so a negative or inconsistent tmplen propagates.

reslen is computed from integral/dec and used to allocate resstr (line 62); the backward copy starts at t = resbuf+reslen-1 and s = tmpbuf+tmplen-1, assuming reslen matches the actual digit count. When dec is excessively large, reslen can be smaller than the data actually copied, so *t-- and memcpy advance t before resbuf, writing out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The writes via *t-- and memcpy land outside the resstr allocation, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is not merely an integer overflow (CWE-190); the integer miscalculation is the cause, and the memory write beyond the buffer is the supported weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function derives buffer sizes from snprintf's return value and from arithmetic on dec without validating that the computed reslen bounds all subsequent writes. Trigger: passing an excessively large dec_points makes tmplen/reslen inconsistent with the real formatted length. Consequence: the backward copy and padding loops write past the beginning of resstr, causing heap corruption.

code_evidence: The loop calls dma_alloc_coherent and stores the result in in_data->sensor_virt_addr[i] without checking it for NULL before proceeding to use the sensor slot and later pass its DMA address to the sensor start path.
The allocated DMA address is copied into info.dma_address [60] and mp2_ops->start consumes that info [70], so a failed allocation leaves a NULL sensor buffer that is subsequently dereferenced/used.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function relies on a pointer expected to be valid but never checks it for NULL before use, matching CWE-476. This is a direct missing NULL check rather than a bounds or integer issue.

evidence_lines.code:
info.dma_address = cl_data->sensor_dma_addr[i];
mp2_ops->start(privdata, info);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of dma_alloc_coherent is not validated, so an allocation failure yields a NULL sensor_virt_addr entry. Trigger: memory pressure causes dma_alloc_coherent to return NULL during amd_sfh_hid_client_init. Consequence: the NULL buffer is used in the sensor start/response path, causing a NULL pointer dereference and local system crash (DoS).

commit_msg: Bug #703 safeguard against corrupt packet lengths in checksum functions
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['fix_ipv4_checksums(tcpedit_t *tcpedit, struct pcap_pkthdr *pkthdr, ipv4_hdr_t *ip_hdr)', '    if (pkthdr->caplen < sizeof(*ip_hdr)) {', '        ip_len = (int)ntohs(ip_hdr->ip_len);', '        ret1 = do_checksum(tcpedit, (u_char *) ip_hdr, ip_hdr->ip_p,', '                ip_len - (ip_hdr->ip_hl << 2));', '    ip_len = (int)ntohs(ip_hdr->ip_len);'], 'added_lines': ['fix_ipv4_checksums(tcpedit_t *tcpedit, struct pcap_pkthdr *pkthdr,', '                   ipv4_hdr_t *ip_hdr, const size_t l2len)', '    if (pkthdr->caplen < (sizeof(*ip_hdr) + l2len)) {', '    ip_len = (int)ntohs(ip_hdr->ip_len);', '        if (ip_len != (int)(pkthdr->caplen - l2len)) {', '            tcpedit_seterr(tcpedit,', '                           "caplen minus L2 length %u does IPv4 header length %u",', '                           pkthdr->caplen - l2len,', '                           ip_len);', '            return TCPEDIT_ERROR;', '        }', '        ret1 = do_checksum(tcpedit, (u_char*)ip_hdr, ip_hdr->ip_p,', '                           ip_len - (ip_hdr->ip_hl << 2));']}
description: Tcpreplay v4.4.1 has a heap-based buffer overflow in do_checksum_math at /tcpedit/checksum.c.

code_evidence: The guard only checks caplen against sizeof(*ip_hdr), not accounting for L2 header length, so the IPv4 header may be read at an offset beyond the captured buffer.

ip_len is derived from the untrusted packet header (ntohs(ip_hdr->ip_len)) and passed directly as the length to do_checksum for both the L4 and IP checksums, without verifying it against the actual captured packet length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked length drives an out-of-bounds write past the intended buffer in the checksum path; the missing length validation is the cause, the memory corruption the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the untrusted ip_hdr->ip_len field is used as a length argument to do_checksum without being bounded by the real packet/capture size, and the header guard ignores l2len. Trigger: a crafted packet with an inflated ip_len and/or truncated capture causes do_checksum to read/write beyond the allocated packet buffer, yielding a heap-based out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
Fix certauth built-in module returns

The PKINIT certauth eku module should never authoritatively authorize
a certificate, because an extended key usage does not establish a
relationship between the certificate and any specific user; it only
establishes that the certificate was created for PKINIT client
authentication.  Therefore, pkinit_eku_authorize() should return
KRB5_PLUGIN_NO_HANDLE on success, not 0.

The certauth san module should pass if it does not find any SANs of
the types it can match against; the presence of other types of SANs
should not cause it to explicitly deny a certificate.  Check for an
empty result from crypto_retrieve_cert_sans() in verify_client_san(),
instead of returning ENOENT from crypto_retrieve_cert_sans() when
there are no SANs at all.

ticket: 8561
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (retval == ENOENT) {', '        TRACE_PKINIT_SERVER_NO_SAN(context);', '        goto out;', '    } else if (retval) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (retval) {', '', '    if (princs == NULL && upns == NULL) {', '        TRACE_PKINIT_SERVER_NO_SAN(context);', '        retval = ENOENT;', '        goto out;', '    }', '']}
description: An authentication bypass flaw was found in the way krb5's certauth interface before 1.16.1 handled the validation of client certificates. A remote attacker able to communicate with the KDC could potentially use this flaw to impersonate arbitrary principals under rare and erroneous circumstances.

code_evidence: On ENOENT from crypto_retrieve_cert_sans(), the code jumps to out with retval still ENOENT and *valid_san left at 0, so the caller sees a non-authoritative 'no decision' rather than a name mismatch.

When SAN lists exist but no principal or UPN matches, the mismatch is set at line 90 but then unconditionally overwritten by retval = 0 at line 92, so verify_client_san returns success with *valid_san = 0.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Returning success after a failed SAN-to-principal comparison means the certificate's claimed identity is not actually proven against the requested principal, which is improper authentication (CWE-287). The defect is the missing/overwritten mismatch return, not a certificate-parsing error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function conflates 'no matching SAN found' with success. When matching fails, line 90 sets KRB5KDC_ERR_CLIENT_NAME_MISMATCH, but line 92 unconditionally resets retval to 0, so a certificate whose SANs do not match the requested client principal is reported as verified. Trigger: a PKINIT client certificate carrying SANs that do not match the target principal. Consequence: the certauth SAN module can accept the certificate, enabling impersonation of an arbitrary principal.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tu32 i;', '\tchar str[1024];', '\ti=0;', '\tstr[0]=0;', '\twhile (1) {', '\t\tstr[i] = gf_bs_read_u8(bs);', '\t\tif (!str[i]) break;', '\t\ti++;', '\t}', '\tISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(p, i);', '', '\tp->content_script_types = gf_strdup(str);'], 'added_lines': ['\tp->content_script_types = gf_malloc(sizeof(char) * (s->size+1));', '\tif (!p->content_script_types) return GF_OUT_OF_MEM;', '\tgf_bs_read_data(bs, p->content_script_types, s->size);', '\tp->content_script_types[s->size] = 0;']}
description: MP4Box is a component of GPAC-2.0.0, which is a widely-used third-party package on RPM Fusion. When MP4Box tries to parse a MP4 file, it calls the function `diST_box_read()` to read from video. In this function, it allocates a buffer `str` with fixed length. However, content read from `bs` is controllable by user, so is the length, which causes a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: A fixed 1024-byte stack buffer str is declared, and the loop writes each byte read from the bitstream at str[i] without any check that i remains below 1024; the loop only exits when a zero byte is read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unbounded index and missing length constraint cause reads/writes outside the 1024-byte buffer, with gf_strdup scanning beyond the intended bounds. A pure write-only overflow (CWE-787) is related, but the string duplication directly reads out of bounds, matching the target out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop's termination depends entirely on attacker-controlled bitstream content containing a NUL byte. If the input lacks a zero byte within the first 1024 bytes, the index increments past the buffer boundary, causing a stack buffer overflow write; subsequent gf_strdup reads the buffer as a C string, so the overflow also enables an out-of-bounds read past the intended buffer.

The actual tracing of this bug is shown below:

commit 8c71fe750215 ("io_uring: ensure fput() called correspondingly
when direct install fails") adds an additional fput() in
io_fixed_fd_install() when io_file_bitmap_get() returns error values. In
that case, the routine will never make it to io_install_fixed_file() due
to an early return.

static int io_fixed_fd_install(...)
{
  if (alloc_slot) {
    ...
    ret = io_file_bitmap_get(ctx);
    if (unlikely(ret < 0)) {
      io_ring_submit_unlock(ctx, issue_flags);
      fput(file);
      return ret;
    }
    ...
  }
  ...
  ret = io_install_fixed_file(req, file, issue_flags, file_slot);
  ...
}

In the above scenario, the reference is okay as io_fixed_fd_install()
ensures the fput() is called when something bad happens, either via
bitmap or via inner io_install_fixed_file().

However, the commit 61c1b44a21d7 ("io_uring: fix deadlock on iowq file
slot alloc") breaks the balance because it places fput() into the common
path for both io_file_bitmap_get() and io_install_fixed_file(). Since
io_install_fixed_file() handles the fput() itself, the reference
underflow come across then.

There are some extra commits make the current code into
io_fixed_fd_install() -> __io_fixed_fd_install() ->
io_install_fixed_file()

However, the fact that there is an extra fput() is called if
io_install_fixed_file() calls fput(). Traversing through the code, I
find that the existing two callers to __io_fixed_fd_install():
io_fixed_fd_install() and io_msg_send_fd() have fput() when handling
error return, this patch simply removes the fput() in
io_install_fixed_file() to fix the bug.

Fixes: 61c1b44a21d7 ("io_uring: fix deadlock on iowq file slot alloc")
Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/be4ba4b.5d44.184a0a406a4.Coremail.linma@zju.edu.cn
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>

description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux Kernel io_uring subsystem can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

Both io_install_fixed_file and its callers call fput in a file in case of an error, causing a reference underflow which leads to a use-after-free vulnerability.

We recommend upgrading past commit 9d94c04c0db024922e886c9fd429659f22f48ea4.

code_evidence: io_scm_file_account(ctx, file) is called at line 30; on failure ret is nonzero, and the err block at lines 39-40 executes fput(file). The error return at line 41 then propagates to callers that also fput the same file, underflowing the file reference count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The double fput frees a file object that callers still hold and later dereference, matching CWE-416 use-after-free. It is not merely a reference-count leak; the extra release enables premature free and subsequent invalid access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: io_install_fixed_file() releases the caller-owned file reference on error while its callers (io_fixed_fd_install/io_msg_send_fd) also fput on error, causing a reference underflow. Trigger: io_scm_file_account() fails (e.g., -ENOMEM), or an earlier goto err occurs. Consequence: the struct file is freed while still referenced, leading to use-after-free (KASAN in unix_get_socket during ring teardown).

commit_msg:
i2c: fix stack buffer overflow vulnerability in i2c md command

When running "i2c md 0 0 80000100", the function do_i2c_md parses the
length into an unsigned int variable named length. The value is then
moved to a signed variable:

    int nbytes = length;
    #define DISP_LINE_LEN 16
    int linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;
    ret = dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes);

On systems where integers are 32 bits wide, 0x80000100 is a negative
value to "nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN" is false and linebytes gets assigned
0x80000100 instead of 16.

The consequence is that the function which reads from the i2c device
(dm_i2c_read or i2c_read) is called with a 16-byte stack buffer to fill
but with a size parameter which is too large. In some cases, this could
trigger a crash. But with some i2c drivers, such as drivers/i2c/nx_i2c.c
(used with "nexell,s5pxx18-i2c" bus), the size is actually truncated to
a 16-bit integer. This is because function i2c_transfer expects an
unsigned short length. In such a case, an attacker who can control the
response of an i2c device can overwrite the return address of a function
and execute arbitrary code through Return-Oriented Programming.

Fix this issue by using unsigned integers types in do_i2c_md. While at
it, make also alen unsigned, as signed sizes can cause vulnerabilities
when people forgot to check that they can be negative.

Signed-off-by: Nicolas Iooss <nicolas.iooss+uboot@ledger.fr>
Reviewed-by: Heiko Schocher <hs@denx.de>

description: The AP4_AvccAtom and AP4_HvccAtom classes in Bento4 version 1.5.0-617 do not properly validate data sizes, leading to a heap-based buffer over-read and application crash in AP4_DataBuffer::SetData in Core/Ap4DataBuffer.cpp.

code_evidence: payload_size is derived as size-AP4_ATOM_HEADER_SIZE with no check that size is at least the header size, then m_RawBytes.SetData(payload, payload_size) copies that many bytes. The constructor immediately dereferences payload[0] through payload[12] and AP4_BytesToUInt32BE(&payload[6])/&payload[10] regardless of payload_size.

The sequence loop reads payload[22] for num_seq and starts cursor=23, then reads payload[cursor] for m_ArrayCompleteness/m_NaluType after only checking cursor+1 > payload_size, so a short payload is read past its end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads payload bytes beyond the actual supplied buffer length, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. This is a missing length check leading to over-read, not a write overflow (CWE-787) or integer wrap alone.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constructor trusts the atom size and reads fixed-offset fields and sequence bytes from payload without validating that payload_size covers them. Trigger: a crafted Hvcc atom whose declared size yields a payload smaller than the accessed offsets. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read (and crash) in SetData and the field decoders.

evtchn/x86: enforce correct upper limit for 32-bit guests

The recording of d->max_evtchns in evtchn_2l_init(), in particular with
the limited set of callers of the function, is insufficient. Neither for
PV nor for HVM guests the bitness is known at domain_create() time, yet
the upper bound in 2-level mode depends upon guest bitness. Recording
too high a limit "allows" x86 32-bit domains to open not properly usable
event channels, management of which (inside Xen) would then result in
corruption of the shared info and vCPU info structures.

Keep the upper limit dynamic for the 2-level case, introducing a helper
function to retrieve the effective limit. This helper is now supposed to
be private to the event channel code. The used in do_poll() and
domain_dump_evtchn_info() weren't consistent with port uses elsewhere
and hence get switched to port_is_valid().

Furthermore FIFO mode's setup_ports() gets adjusted to loop only up to
the prior ABI limit, rather than all the way up to the new one.

Finally a word on the change to do_poll(): Accessing ->max_evtchns
without holding a suitable lock was never safe, as it as well as
->evtchn_port_ops may change behind do_poll()'s back. Using
port_is_valid() instead widens some the window for potential abuse,
until we've dealt with the race altogether (see XSA-343).

This is XSA-342.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Fixes: 48974e6ce52e ("evtchn: use a per-domain variable for the max number of event channels")
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        d->max_evtchns = EVTCHN_FIFO_NR_CHANNELS;', '        setup_ports(d);'], 'added_lines': ['        /* Latch the value before it changes during setup_event_array(). */', '        unsigned int prev_evtchns = max_evtchns(d);', '        setup_ports(d, prev_evtchns);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. Out of bounds event channels are available to 32-bit x86 domains. The so called 2-level event channel model imposes different limits on the number of usable event channels for 32-bit x86 domains vs 64-bit or Arm (either bitness) ones. 32-bit x86 domains can use only 1023 channels, due to limited space in their shared (between guest and Xen) information structure, whereas all other domains can use up to 4095 in this model. The recording of the respective limit during domain initialization, however, has occurred at a time where domains are still deemed to be 64-bit ones, prior to actually honoring respective domain properties. At the point domains get recognized as 32-bit ones, the limit didn't get updated accordingly. Due to this misbehavior in Xen, 32-bit domains (including Domain 0) servicing other domains may observe event channel allocations to succeed when they should really fail. Subsequent use of such event channels would then possibly lead to corruption of other parts of the shared info structure. An unprivileged guest may cause another domain, in particular Domain 0, to misbehave. This may lead to a Denial of Service (DoS) for the entire system. All Xen versions from 4.4 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.3 and earlier are not vulnerable. Only x86 32-bit domains servicing other domains are vulnerable. Arm systems, as well as x86 64-bit domains, are not vulnerable.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only initializes FIFO event channel control blocks and latches the prior max_evtchns limit; it contains no buffer write past bounds, and the described corruption arises from a stale upper limit in other code, not from an out-of-bounds write in this function.

commit_msg:
guest_physmap_remove_page() needs its return value checked

Callers, namely such subsequently freeing the page, must not blindly
assume success - the function may namely fail when needing to shatter a
super page, but there not being memory available for the then needed
intermediate page table.

As it happens, guest_remove_page() callers now also all check the
return value.

Furthermore a missed put_gfn() on an error path in gnttab_transfer() is
also being taken care of.

This is part of XSA-222.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            guest_physmap_remove_page(d, _gfn(xrfp.gpfn),', '                                      _mfn(page_to_mfn(page)), 0);'], 'added_lines': ['            rc = guest_physmap_remove_page(d, _gfn(xrfp.gpfn),', '                                           _mfn(page_to_mfn(page)), 0);']}
description: Xen through 4.8.x does not validate memory allocations during certain P2M operations, which allows guest OS users to obtain privileged host OS access, aka XSA-222.

code_evidence: The XENMEM_remove_from_physmap handler obtains a page via get_page_from_gfn() and then calls guest_physmap_remove_page() without checking its return value; only put_page() follows. The operation's success/failure is discarded, so callers/continuations proceed as if the P2M removal succeeded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The failure arises from not validating/checking the result of a memory operation before proceeding, so an error condition is treated as success—matching improper validation of operation outcome (CWE-20). It is not an out-of-bounds index or integer issue, but unchecked operation status.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return status of guest_physmap_remove_page() is ignored, so a failed P2M removal (e.g., super-page shatter requiring memory that is unavailable) is not detected. Trigger: a guest issues XENMEM_remove_from_physmap while the operation fails. Consequence: the page is freed/reused while still mapped, enabling privileged host access as described in XSA-222.

commit_msg:
Fixes CVE-2023-3138: X servers could return values from XQueryExtension
that would cause Xlib to write entries out-of-bounds of the arrays to
store them, though this would only overwrite other parts of the Display
struct, not outside the bounds allocated for that structure.

Reported-by: Gregory James DUCK <gjduck@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Alan Coopersmith <alan.coopersmith@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (extension < FirstExtensionRequest ||', '\t    extension > LastExtensionRequest) {', '\t    fprintf(stderr, "Xlib: ignoring invalid extension opcode %d\\n",', '\t\t    extension);', '\t    return (CopyEventCookieType)_XUnknownCopyEventCookie;', '\t}']}
description: A vulnerability was found in libX11. The security flaw occurs because the functions in src/InitExt.c in libX11 do not check that the values provided for the Request, Event, or Error IDs are within the bounds of the arrays that those functions write to, using those IDs as array indexes. They trust that they were called with values provided by an Xserver adhering to the bounds specified in the X11 protocol, as all X servers provided by X.Org do. As the protocol only specifies a single byte for these values, an out-of-bounds value provided by a malicious server (or a malicious proxy-in-the-middle) can only overwrite other portions of the Display structure and not write outside the bounds of the Display structure itself, possibly causing the client to crash with this memory corruption.

code_evidence: Line 8 only replaces a NULL proc; it does not validate the extension argument. Lines 10 and 11 use extension & 0x7F directly as an index into dpy->generic_event_copy_vec, a fixed-size array, without any range check on extension.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the code performs an array write through an unchecked, attacker-influenced index (lines 10-11), producing an out-of-bounds write of a function pointer within the Display structure. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since line 11 stores proc at the unvalidated index.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the caller-supplied extension opcode and masks it with 0x7F before indexing the generic_event_copy_vec array, so no bounds constraint is enforced. Trigger: a malicious X server or proxy returns an out-of-range extension opcode that reaches this setter. Consequence: the masked index can address entries outside the intended array region, corrupting adjacent fields of the Display struct (as the CVE notes, confined to the Display allocation), which may cause the client to crash or behave unexpectedly.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/143
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  buffer=(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory(256,sizeof(*buffer));'], 'added_lines': ['  buffer=(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory(257,sizeof(*buffer));']}
description: MagickCore/memory.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds access) via a crafted PDB file.

code_evidence: Line 110 allocates buffer with only 256 bytes, while the encoding loop at lines 135-180 indexes buffer[literal+repeat] and buffer[literal+repeat+1] as literal and repeat grow; the RLE logic can push literal+repeat to 256, requiring a 257th byte.
Line 144 reads buffer[literal+repeat-1] and line 166 reads buffer[literal+repeat], and line 174 CopyMagickMemory reads from buffer+literal+repeat, all operating on the undersized buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the code reads past the end of the intended buffer at lines 144, 166 and 174 when literal+repeat equals the 256-byte allocation size; the missing 257th byte is precisely an out-of-bounds read. This is distinct from CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write), though a write also occurs.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The buffer is allocated with 256 elements but the run-length encoding loop can set literal+repeat to 256 (e.g., after a literal flush), so buffer[literal+repeat] and buffer[literal+repeat-1] access index 256, one past the allocation. The trigger is a crafted PDB image whose pixel pattern drives the encoder to fill the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read (and write at line 179) that can crash the process.

Fixes #423
Fixes #427
Fixes #430

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        for (; *curBuff == 0xFF && curBuff < nalEnd; curBuff++)', '        for (; *curBuff == 0xFF && curBuff < nalEnd; curBuff++)'], 'added_lines': ['        for (; curBuff < nalEnd && *curBuff == 0xFF; curBuff++)', '        for (; curBuff < nalEnd && *curBuff == 0xFF; curBuff++)']}
description: Heap based buffer overflow in tsMuxer 2.6.16 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by running the application with a crafted file.

code_evidence: In the payloadType loop, the condition tests *curBuff == 0xFF before checking curBuff < nalEnd, so when curBuff reaches nalEnd the dereference reads past the buffer before the bound is evaluated.
The payloadSize loop at line 23 has the identical ordering defect, again dereferencing *curBuff ahead of the nalEnd check.
The unbounded memcpy at line 42 copies payloadSize bytes into the fixed 4096-byte tmpBuffer, and tmpBufferLen is incremented by payloadSize without any capacity check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-influenced data past the end of tmpBuffer and m_nalBuffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The misordered loop condition is the enabling defect, but the supported consequence is the buffer overflow rather than a pure out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop guards dereference *curBuff before verifying curBuff < nalEnd, and payloadSize derived from the stream is copied into the fixed 4096-byte tmpBuffer without a bounds check. Trigger: a crafted SEI NAL whose last byte is 0xFF drives curBuff to nalEnd and produces an oversized payloadSize. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads and heap/stack writes corrupt memory, causing a crash or potential code execution.

Fix heap OOB / undefined behavior in `RaggedTensorToTensor`

PiperOrigin-RevId: 373244623
Change-Id: I2d6cbbc8c67b238a8815bf58097f7586d87c54f2
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void CalculateOutputIndexValueRowID(', '      OpKernelContext* context, const RowPartitionTensor& value_rowids,', '      return;', '    DCHECK_LT(current_value_rowid, parent_output_index.size());', '        DCHECK_LT(next_value_rowid, parent_output_index.size());', '    OP_REQUIRES(context, result->size() == value_rowids.size(),', '                errors::InvalidArgument("Invalid row ids."));'], 'added_lines': ['Status CalculateOutputIndexValueRowID(', '      const RowPartitionTensor& value_rowids,', '      return Status::OK();', '', '    if (current_value_rowid >= parent_output_index.size()) {', '      return errors::InvalidArgument(', '          "Got current_value_rowid=", current_value_rowid,', '          " which is not less than ", parent_output_index.size());', '    }', '', '', '        if (next_value_rowid >= parent_output_index.size()) {', '          return errors::InvalidArgument(', '              "Got next_value_rowid=", next_value_rowid,', '              " which is not less than ", parent_output_index.size());', '        }', '', '', '    if (result->size() != value_rowids.size()) {', '      return errors::InvalidArgument("Invalid row ids.");', '    }', '', '    return Status::OK();']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. Due to lack of validation in `tf.raw_ops.RaggedTensorToTensor`, an attacker can exploit an undefined behavior if input arguments are empty. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/656e7673b14acd7835dc778867f84916c6d1cac2/tensorflow/core/kernels/ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op.cc#L356-L360) only checks that one of the tensors is not empty, but does not check for the other ones. There are multiple `DCHECK` validations to prevent heap OOB, but these are no-op in release builds, hence they don't prevent anything. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick these commits on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: value_rowids(0) yields current_value_rowid, which is used to index parent_output_index at line 14; the only bound check is DCHECK_LT at line 13, a no-op in release builds.
In the else branch, next_value_rowid is similarly used to index parent_output_index at line 31, guarded only by DCHECK_LT at line 30.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-131 fits because the code indexes a buffer using an unvalidated index derived from value_rowids without correctly constraining it to the buffer's calculated size, causing an OOB access. This is a size/index validation defect rather than a class of unrelated memory-safety flaws.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size of parent_output_index is never validated against the row-id values before indexing, since DCHECK_LT is compiled out in release builds. Trigger: a caller supplies value_rowids entries exceeding parent_output_index.size(). Consequence: out-of-bounds read/write leading to heap OOB and undefined behavior.

commit_msg:
Fix xsltNumberFormatGetMultipleLevel

Namespace nodes are actually an xmlNs, not an xmlNode. They must be
special-cased in xsltNumberFormatGetMultipleLevel to avoid an
out-of-bounds heap access.

Move the test whether a node matches the "count" pattern to a separate
function to make the code more readable. As a side effect, we also
compare expanded names when walking up the ancestor axis, fixing an
insignificant bug.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (countPat == NULL) {', '\t    if ((node->type == cur->type) &&', '\t\t/* FIXME: must use expanded-name instead of local name */', '\t\txmlStrEqual(node->name, cur->name)) {', '\t\t    if ((node->ns == cur->ns) ||', '\t\t        ((node->ns != NULL) &&', '\t\t\t (cur->ns != NULL) &&', '\t\t         (xmlStrEqual(node->ns->href,', '\t\t             cur->ns->href) )))', '\t\t        cnt++;', '\t    }', '\t} else {', '\t    if (xsltTestCompMatchList(context, cur, countPat))', '\t\tcnt++;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (xsltTestCompMatchCount(context, cur, countPat, node))', '\t    cnt++;']}
description: numbers.c in libxslt before 1.1.29, as used in Google Chrome before 51.0.2704.63, mishandles namespace nodes, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds heap memory access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted document.

code_evidence: For an attribute node, cur is set to the attribute's parent element. In the countPat==NULL branch, the loop compares node->type and node->name against cur, and dereferences node->ns->href. The function never checks whether node is a namespace node (xmlNs) rather than an xmlNode before treating it as having node->name/node->ns fields.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe field accesses on a mis-typed namespace node read outside the object's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. It is a resultant memory-safety weakness rather than a name-comparison logic bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the count-matching path assumes node is an xmlNode and accesses xmlNode-specific fields (name, ns, type). Trigger: a crafted document makes the node a namespace node (xmlNs), whose layout differs, so node->name/node->ns are read at wrong offsets. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap read, causing a crash/DoS or other impact.

commit_msg:
ALSA: compress_core: integer overflow in snd_compr_allocate_buffer()

These are 32 bit values that come from the user, we need to check for
integer overflows or we could end up allocating a smaller buffer than
expected.

Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (params->buffer.fragment_size == 0 ||', '\t    params->buffer.fragments > SIZE_MAX / params->buffer.fragment_size)', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;']}
description: Integer overflow in the snd_compr_allocate_buffer function in sound/core/compress_offload.c in the ALSA subsystem in the Linux kernel before 3.6-rc6-next-20120917 allows local users to cause a denial of service (insufficient memory allocation) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted SNDRV_COMPRESS_SET_PARAMS ioctl call.

code_evidence: Line 6 multiplies two user-controlled unsigned int fields (fragment_size and fragments) with no pre-check, so the product can wrap around in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic.

The wrapped buffer_size is then passed to kmalloc at line 10, and the same unvalidated fragment_size/fragments values are stored into stream->runtime at lines 14,15,17, so a small allocation is paired with large logical fragment metadata.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the size calculation wraps before being used as an allocation size, which the description identifies as security-critical for memory allocation. The missing precondition check (fragment_size != 0 and fragments <= SIZE_MAX/fragment_size) is exactly the integer-overflow guard; this is not merely a bounds check on a single value.

evidence_lines.code:
buffer_size = params->buffer.fragment_size * params->buffer.fragments;
buffer = kmalloc(buffer_size, GFP_KERNEL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the unchecked multiplication of two user-supplied 32-bit values at line 6; a crafted SNDRV_COMPRESS_SET_PARAMS ioctl with large fragment_size and fragments makes buffer_size wrap to a small value. kmalloc then allocates a buffer smaller than the logical size recorded in stream->runtime, enabling insufficient allocation and possible out-of-bounds access or DoS.

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static inline const u32 *flow_keys_hash_start(const struct flow_keys *flow)', '\tconst void *p = flow;', '', '\tBUILD_BUG_ON(FLOW_KEYS_HASH_OFFSET % sizeof(u32));', '\treturn (const u32 *)(p + FLOW_KEYS_HASH_OFFSET);'], 'added_lines': ['static const void *flow_keys_hash_start(const struct flow_keys *flow)', '\tBUILD_BUG_ON(FLOW_KEYS_HASH_OFFSET % SIPHASH_ALIGNMENT);', '\treturn &flow->FLOW_KEYS_HASH_START_FIELD;']}
description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only computes an aligned pointer into flow_keys for hashing; it contains no random value, secret, or hash generation, so it does not itself exhibit insufficient randomness (the weak jhash secret is in other code).

description: A heap-based buffer over-read was found in the function OpCode (called from decompileSETMEMBER) in util/decompile.c in Ming 0.4.8, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: malloc allocates sizeof(char)*size bytes using the caller-supplied size without validating it; the loop then iterates i from 0 to size-1, reading one byte per iteration via readUInt8 and storing into buf[i].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory outside the intended buffer through the size-driven loop over buf, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read) rather than a write, since only reads produce the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: size is trusted for both allocation and loop bound, and no lower-bound check exists. If a caller passes a negative size, the malloc size computation and loop bound are inconsistent, so the loop reads past the allocated buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read (DoS per the description). commit_msg: Fix left shift of a negative value in SWFInput_readSBits. Check for number before before left-shifting by (number-1).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif ( num & (1<<(number-1)) )'], 'added_lines': ['\tif(number && num & (1<<(number-1)))']}
description: In Ming (aka libming) 0.4.8, there is an integer overflow (caused by an out-of-range left shift) in the SWFInput_readSBits function in blocks/input.c. Remote attackers could leverage this vulnerability to cause a denial-of-service via a crafted swf file.

code_evidence: Line 4 obtains `num` from `SWFInput_readBits(input, number)`, where `number` is a caller-supplied bit count with no visible bound check in this function. Line 5 computes `1<<(number-1)` and masks it against `num`; if `number` is 0 the shift count is -1, and if `number` is large the shift count or the shifted value exceeds the width of `int`. Line 6 likewise computes `1<<number` without a constraint on `number`.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe shift produces an out-of-range integer computation in which the assumed result width is not honored, matching CWE-190's integer overflow/wraparound calculation. It is not merely an out-of-bounds array access, since the defect is the unconstrained arithmetic shift itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shift amounts `number-1` and `number` are not constrained before being used in left-shift expressions, so an out-of-range shift count (negative when `number` is 0, or too large for `int`) produces undefined behavior. Trigger: a crafted SWF drives `number` to such a value. Supported consequence: undefined shift behavior can disrupt execution and cause a denial of service.

description: In the AppleTalk subsystem in the Linux kernel before 5.1, there is a potential NULL pointer dereference because register_snap_client may return NULL. This will lead to denial of service in net/appletalk/aarp.c and net/appletalk/ddp.c, as demonstrated by unregister_snap_client, aka CID-9804501fa122.

commit_msg:
Add recursion limit for ASN.1 indefinite lengths

The libkrb5 ASN.1 decoder supports BER indefinite lengths.  It
computes the tag length using recursion; the lack of a recursion limit
allows an attacker to overrun the stack and cause the process to
crash.  Reported by Demi Obenour.

CVE-2020-28196:

In MIT krb5 releases 1.11 and later, an unauthenticated attacker can
cause a denial of service for any client or server to which it can
send an ASN.1-encoded Kerberos message of sufficient length.

ticket: 8959 (new)
tags: pullup
target_version: 1.18-next
target_version: 1.17-next
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                  &clen, &remainder, &rlen);'], 'added_lines': ['                  &clen, &remainder, &rlen, 0);']}
description: MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) before 1.17.2 and 1.18.x before 1.18.3 allows unbounded recursion via an ASN.1-encoded Kerberos message because the lib/krb5/asn.1/asn1_encode.c support for BER indefinite lengths lacks a recursion limit.

code_evidence: k5_asn1_full_decode calls get_tag with the caller-supplied code->data and code->length. In the patched version the call passes a recursion depth argument of 0, indicating get_tag recurses on nested BER indefinite-length encodings and this entry point supplies the initial depth without any bound tied to the input.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function feeds attacker-controlled ASN.1 data into a recursive get_tag without a recursion cap, directly matching CWE-674 (Uncontrolled Recursion). This is not merely deep nesting of data structures but actual call-stack growth; the added depth argument is the missing constraint.

evidence_lines.code:
ret = get_tag((uint8_t *)code->data, code->length, &t, &contents,
&clen, &remainder, &rlen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: get_tag recurses for each nested indefinite-length ASN.1 tag, and the depth is driven by attacker-controlled message content with no limit. Trigger: an unauthenticated attacker sends a Kerberos message containing deeply nested indefinite-length encodings. Consequence: unbounded stack consumption leading to process crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
gh-112334: Restore subprocess's use of `vfork()` & fix `extra_groups=[]`.

Fixed a performance regression in 3.12's :mod:`subprocess` on Linux where it
would no longer use the fast-path ``vfork()`` system call when it could have
due to a logic bug, instead falling back to the safe but slower ``fork()``.

Also fixed a second 3.12.0 potential security bug.  If a value of
``extra_groups=[]`` was passed to :mod:`subprocess.Popen` or related APIs,
the underlying ``setgroups(0, NULL)`` system call to clear the groups list
would not be made in the child process prior to ``exec()``.

The security issue was identified via code inspection in the process of
fixing the first bug.  Thanks to @vain for the detailed report and
analysis in the initial bug on Github.

 * [ ] A regression test is desirable. I'm pondering a test that runs when
   `strace` is available and permitted which and confirms use of `vfork()`
   vs `clone()`...
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    Py_ssize_t extra_group_size = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['', '    // Special initial value meaning that subprocess API was called with', '    // extra_groups=None leading to _posixsubprocess.fork_exec(gids=None).', '    // We use this to differentiate between code desiring a setgroups(0, NULL)', '    // call vs no call at all.  The fast vfork() code path could be used when', '    // there is no setgroups call.', '    Py_ssize_t extra_group_size = -2;']}
description:
An issue was found in CPython 3.12.0 `subprocess` module on POSIX platforms. The issue was fixed in CPython 3.12.1 and does not affect other stable releases.

When using the `extra_groups=` parameter with an empty list as a value (ie `extra_groups=[]`) the logic regressed to not call `setgroups(0, NULL)` before calling `exec()`, thus not dropping the original processes' groups before starting the new process. There is no issue when the parameter isn't used or when any value is used besides an empty list.

This issue only impacts CPython processes run with sufficient privilege to make the `setgroups` system call (typically `root`).

code_evidence: extra_group_size is initialized to 0, so an empty extra_groups list leaves it at 0, which is indistinguishable from the no-groups-requested default.
The block only allocates and fills extra_groups when extra_group_size > 0; an empty list passes validation but produces no group array and size 0.
The vfork fast-path condition requires extra_group_size < 0, so size 0 disables vfork, but the child still receives extra_group_size=0 with extra_groups=NULL.
do_fork_exec receives extra_group_size and extra_groups, so the child's setgroups decision depends on this value; size 0 means setgroups(0, NULL) is skipped rather than clearing groups.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function mishandles privilege-relevant state: an explicit empty group list is treated as no privilege change, leaving the child with the parent's groups. This is improper assignment/tracking of privileges (CWE-269), not merely a performance bug; the vfork check is a symptom of the same sentinel confusion.

evidence_lines.code: Py_ssize_t extra_group_size = 0;

pid = do_fork_exec(exec_array, argv, envp, cwd,
p2cread, p2cwrite, c2pread, c2pwrite,
errread, errwrite, errpipe_read, errpipe_write,
close_fds, restore_signals, call_setsid, pgid_to_set,
gid, extra_group_size, extra_groups,
uid, child_umask, old_sigmask,
c_fds_to_keep, fds_to_keep_len,
preexec_fn, preexec_fn_args_tuple);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: extra_group_size=0 conflates 'extra_groups=[]' (clear groups) with 'no groups specified', so the child never calls setgroups(0,NULL). Trigger: a privileged process passes extra_groups=[] to Popen; the child retains the parent's supplementary groups across exec(). Consequence: the new process runs with unintended group privileges, an improper privilege management issue.

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tq->perturbation = prandom_u32();'], 'added_lines': ['\tget_random_bytes(&q->perturbation, sizeof(q->perturbation));']}
description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: Line 24 sets q->perturb_period = 0, and line 25 initializes the SFQ hash perturbation secret with prandom_u32(). This perturbation value seeds the per-flow hashing used by the SFQ scheduler to assign flows to slots, so its unpredictability is security-relevant.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because a security-relevant value (the SFQ perturbation secret) is produced by an insufficiently random source. This is a direct use of weak randomness for a value meant to be unpredictable; the fix switches to get_random_bytes(), confirming the seed's unpredictability requirement.

evidence_lines.code:
q->perturb_period = 0;
q->perturbation = prandom_u32();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the flow-hashing secret is generated with prandom_u32(), a non-cryptographic PRNG whose output is predictable/observable rather than a strong random value. An attacker who can observe or infer the perturbation can predict how flows map to SFQ slots, enabling traffic analysis or targeted flow collisions. The consequence is weakened unpredictability of the scheduler's hashing, not memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Merge pull request from GHSA-q9cp-8wcq-7pfr

* Prevent heap buffer overflow when parsing DNS packet

* Fixed incorrect check in get_name*()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (start >= max)', '        return PJLIB_UTIL_EDNSINNAMEPTR;']}
description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. A buffer overflow vulnerability in versions 2.13 and prior affects applications that use PJSIP DNS resolver. It doesn't affect PJSIP users who do not utilise PJSIP DNS resolver. This vulnerability is related to CVE-2022-24793. The difference is that this issue is in parsing the query record `parse_query()`, while the issue in CVE-2022-24793 is in `parse_rr()`. A patch is available as commit `d1c5e4d` in the `master` branch. A workaround is to disable DNS resolution in PJSIP config (by setting `nameserver_count` to zero) or use an external resolver implementation instead.

code_evidence: The label branch reads the label length from the packet (*p), bounds-checks the packet read (p+1+label_len+1 > max), then copies label_len bytes into name->ptr+name->slen via pj_memcpy without checking that name->slen+label_len stays within the destination name buffer.
The loop starts at p=start and only checks the packet-side bounds (offset >= max-pkt, and the label read bound); no destination capacity is enforced before the copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a copy of input-derived label data into an output buffer without verifying the input size fits the output size, matching CWE-120's buffer-copy definition. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the unchecked write past name->ptr is the unsafe operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination name buffer capacity is never validated before pj_memcpy, so accumulated label lengths (name->slen) from a crafted DNS packet can exceed the output buffer. Trigger: a DNS response with many/oversized labels reaching get_name; the packet read bound passes while the write overflows. Consequence: heap buffer overflow, memory corruption and potential crash or code execution.

commit_msg: Improve the client certificate checking logic. Make sure calling `wolfSSL_CTX_mutual_auth` is also checked.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '#if !defined(NO_CERTS) && !defined(WOLFSSL_NO_CLIENT_AUTH)', '    /* verify the client sent certificate if required */', '    if (ssl->options.side == WOLFSSL_SERVER_END &&', '            (ssl->options.mutualAuth || ssl->options.failNoCert)) {', '        if (!ssl->options.havePeerVerify && !ssl->options.resuming) {', '            ret = NO_PEER_CERT;', '            DoCertFatalAlert(ssl, ret);', '            return ret;', '        }', '    }', '#endif']}
description: In wolfSSL before 5.2.0, a TLS 1.3 server cannot properly enforce a requirement for mutual authentication. A client can simply omit the certificate_verify message from the handshake, and never present a certificate.

code_evidence: On the server side, after processing the Finished message, the function transitions handshake state to CLIENT_FINISHED_COMPLETE and HANDSHAKE_DONE without any check that the client actually presented a certificate_verify message when mutual authentication was configured. The added mutualAuth/failNoCert check is absent from this function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function finalizes the TLS 1.3 handshake without validating the required client certificate exchange, allowing authentication to be bypassed, which matches CWE-295 Improper Certificate Validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the server-side Finished handling completes the handshake without verifying that a peer certificate/certificate_verify was received when mutual authentication is required. Trigger: a client omitting the certificate_verify message. Consequence: the server accepts a handshake while the client never presented a certificate, bypassing the mutual-authentication requirement.

commit_msg:
When kmalloc memory for sd->sev_vmcbs failed, we forget to free the page
held by sd->save_area. Also get rid of the var r as '-ENOMEM' is actually
the only possible outcome here.

Reviewed-by: Liran Alon <liran.alon@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Vitaly Kuznetsov <vkuznets@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Miaohe Lin <linmiaohe@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint r;', '\tr = -ENOMEM;', '\t\tgoto err_1;', '\t\tr = -ENOMEM;', '\t\t\tgoto err_1;', 'err_1:', '\treturn r;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tgoto free_cpu_data;', '\t\t\tgoto free_save_area;', 'free_save_area:', '\t__free_page(sd->save_area);', 'free_cpu_data:', '\treturn -ENOMEM;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.6. svm_cpu_uninit in arch/x86/kvm/svm.c has a memory leak, aka CID-d80b64ff297e. NOTE: third parties dispute this issue because it's a one-time leak at the boot, the size is negligible, and it can't be triggered at will

code_evidence: alloc_page assigns sd->save_area; on failure the code jumps to err_1.
When SEV is enabled, kmalloc_array for sd->sev_vmcbs fails and control jumps to the same err_1 label.
err_1 only calls kfree(sd) and returns r; it never calls __free_page(sd->save_area).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because memory allocated by alloc_page remains unreleased when the later allocation fails; the error-handling path omits the required __free_page, leaving the page unavailable for reuse. This is a missing-release leak, not a use-after-free or double free, since the page is never freed at all on this path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shared error path err_1 frees only the struct sd but not the page stored in sd->save_area. Trigger: svm_sev_enabled() is true and the kmalloc_array for sev_vmcbs returns NULL at line 18, so the goto at line 19 reaches err_1 after save_area was successfully allocated. The consequence is that the allocated page is never released, leaking memory on this error path.

description: An issue was discovered in OpenCV 4.1.0. There is a divide-by-zero error in cv::HOGDescriptor::getDescriptorSize in modules/objdetect/src/hog.cpp.

code_evidence: numPartsWithin takes an integer stride and returns (size - part_size + stride) / stride, dividing by stride with no guard before the patch. The added CV_Assert(stride != 0) confirms stride could be zero when this helper is called from the HOG descriptor-size path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because the function performs a direct division by a parameter that can be zero and previously had no check. This is a pure arithmetic divide-by-zero, not an out-of-bounds access or null dereference, so the base weakness is CWE-369.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the division uses a caller-supplied stride without validating it is nonzero. Trigger: a HOG configuration or call path that yields stride == 0 reaches this helper. Supported consequence: integer divide-by-zero, causing a crash/DoS rather than memory corruption.

RLC: fix a stack overflow in rlc_decode_li function

The test to check whether the array was full or not was off by 1

Bug: 12664
Change-Id: If2057b71d92c7f03e05b0f4676abc62d5a03ae73
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/16640
Reviewed-by: Pascal Quantin <pascal.quantin@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (num_li > max_li) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (num_li >= max_li) {']}
description: Off-by-one error in epan/dissectors/packet-rlc.c in the RLC dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.13 and 2.x before 2.0.5 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer overflow and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: After writing li[num_li] and incrementing num_li (lines 96-97), the bounds check uses num_li > max_li (line 98); with num_li already incremented, the array is written at index max_li before the check fires, exceeding the li[max_li] buffer. The guard should reject when num_li >= max_li.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is an improper numeric calculation (off-by-one comparison) leading to out-of-bounds write, matching the Numeric Errors category CWE-189. It is distinct from a generic buffer overflow because the defect is the incorrect comparison boundary in the numeric check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an off-by-one bounds check: num_li is incremented before comparison, so the condition num_li > max_li allows one extra write past the array end. A crafted packet with many extension bits in the LI loop drives num_li up to max_li, causing a stack-based buffer overflow and crash.

commit_msg: Fixed #2582
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\toffset_table[0] = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (ft->nbGlyphs) offset_table[0] = 0;']}
description: Out-of-bounds Write in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.3-DEV.

code_evidence: count comes from the bitstream via swf_get_16; nbGlyphs = count/2 can be 0 while gf_malloc(0) may return NULL or a zero-size block, yet offset_table[0] is written unconditionally.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing offset_table[0] when the allocated buffer has zero elements is a write past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. It is not merely a NULL dereference, since the index is outside the allocated size regardless of the allocator's return value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no check that nbGlyphs is nonzero before indexing offset_table[0]. When count is 0 or 1, nbGlyphs is 0, so the allocation is zero-sized and the write at index 0 goes past the buffer. Trigger: a crafted SWF font record with a small glyph count; consequence is a heap out-of-bounds write (memory corruption/crash).
