commit_msg:
codegen.c: stack position may be wrong on assignments.

When `[]=` access includes keyword arguments.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            push();', '            pop();'], 'added_lines': ['          if (n == 14) {', '            pop_n(n);', '            genop_2(s, OP_ARRAY, cursp(), n);', '            push();', '            n = 15;', '          }', '            pop_n(2);', '          push();']}
description: Out-of-bounds Read in Homebrew mruby prior to 3.2.

code_evidence: gen_values caps the positional argument count at 14; when it overflows it returns a negative value, sets n = 15 and pushes one placeholder array, but the keyword-argument branch then operates on this state.

In the keyword branch, when n >= 14 the code pops one stack slot and emits OP_ARYPUSH; the stack accounting does not match the number of values actually pushed for the overflowed argument list, so the emitted stack pointer used for the call is inconsistent with the real operand layout.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a stack-position/accounting error that causes the VM to read past the end of the intended operand buffer, which matches CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). It is not a write past bounds, so CWE-787 does not apply.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stack position (cursp) is adjusted incorrectly when a call with both an overflowing positional argument list and keyword arguments is compiled. The [] = assignment path then emits OP_SETIDX/OP_SEND with a stack pointer that no longer corresponds to the pushed operands, so the VM reads an operand slot beyond the intended argument region. Trigger: a method call whose positional arguments exceed the 14-slot limit and that also carries keyword arguments. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read of the interpreter stack during execution.

commit_msg:
Trap for overly large input to XmlRPCPP which could cause problems with int <-> size_t conversions.

 - In XmlRpcClient, XmlRpcServerConnection and XmlRpcSocket, recognize when incoming or outgoing data is too large, generate an error and discard the data when practical.
 - Use the safe strtol() rather than atoi() to decode an incoming content-length header, and generate an error if the length is invalid or too large.
 - In XmlRpcUtil, prevent attempts to parse overly large XML input.
 - Add tests where they can reasonably be inserted into existing test routines.

Although this fix could be cleaner the update is written to make the update ABI compatible.

This fix addresses CVE-2020-16124 / Integer overflow in ros_comm.

Signed-off-by: Sid Faber <sid.faber@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (xml.length() > size_t(__INT_MAX__)) return false;']}
description: Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability in the XML RPC library of OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages allows unauthenticated network traffic to cause unexpected behavior. This issue affects: OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages Noetic and prior versions. Fixed in https://github.com/ros/ros_comm/pull/2065.

code_evidence: The cast int(xml.length()) converts a size_t length to int before comparing with *offset; for xml strings longer than INT_MAX this conversion wraps to a negative or small value, so the bounds check can pass incorrectly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The narrowing size_t-to-int conversion is an integer wraparound used as a bounds check, which matches CWE-190. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the wrap of the length value is the direct cause that defeats the offset guard.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unchecked narrowing conversion of xml.length() from size_t to int in the bounds comparison. Trigger: an attacker supplies XML input whose length exceeds INT_MAX. The wrapped negative value makes *offset >= int(...) evaluate false, so parsing proceeds and cp = xml.c_str() + *offset can point outside the buffer, leading to out-of-bounds reads and potential crash or memory disclosure.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (buf->offset < aoffset) {', '            debug_print("%s", "End of buffer\\n");'], 'added_lines': ['        if ( (buf->offset < aoffset) || (buf->offset + len > buf->maxlen) ) {', '            debug_print("%s", "Beyond start/end of buffer\\n");']}
description: libmobi is vulnerable to Out-of-bounds Write

code_evidence: In the negative-offset branch, the guard only checks buf->offset < aoffset, i.e., that source (buf->data + buf->offset - aoffset) does not go before buf->data. It never constrains the forward extent of the copied region.
After passing that guard, source -= aoffset is computed and memmove(buf->data + buf->offset, source, len) copies len bytes starting at the lowered source, then buf->offset += len advances the offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a memmove whose destination range can exceed the buffer's maxlen because the bound check is incomplete, directly producing a write past the end of the intended buffer, which is CWE-787. The missing upper-bound check is the cause; the out-of-bounds write is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the negative-offset path validates only the lower bound of the source pointer and omits any check that buf->offset + len stays within buf->maxlen. Trigger: callers supply a negative offset with a len large enough that the memmove destination buf->data + buf->offset plus len exceeds the allocated buffer. Consequence: memmove writes past the end of buf->data, corrupting adjacent heap memory or crashing.

doesn't need to be big enough to hold the entire on-the-network packet,

resolved: fix loop on packets with pseudo dns types

Reported by Karim Hossen & Thomas Imbert from Sogeti ESEC R&D.

https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/systemd/+bug/1725351
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                while (bitmask) {', '', '                        bit++;', '                        bitmask >>= 1;', '                }'], 'added_lines': ['                for (; bitmask; bit++, bitmask >>= 1)']}
description: In systemd 223 through 235, a remote DNS server can respond with a custom crafted DNS NSEC resource record to trigger an infinite loop in the dns_packet_read_type_window() function of the 'systemd-resolved' service and cause a DoS of the affected service.

code_evidence: The inner while loop iterates while bitmask is nonzero. When bitmap[i] & bitmask is set and the resulting type n is pseudo, line 40 executes continue, which jumps back to the while condition without executing the bit++ and bitmask >>= 1 updates at lines 45-46. The bitmask and bit values therefore never advance for that iteration.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the continue on the pseudo-type branch skips the loop's only state updates (bit++ and bitmask >>= 1), so the exit condition bitmask==0 can never be reached once a pseudo type bit is encountered. Trigger: a remote DNS server returns an NSEC type bitmap whose set bit maps to a pseudo type via dns_type_is_pseudo. Consequence: the while loop spins forever, consuming CPU and hanging systemd-resolved (DoS).

commit_msg:
PR29925, Memory leak in find_abstract_instance

The testcase in the PR had a variable with both DW_AT_decl_file and
DW_AT_specification, where the DW_AT_specification also specified
DW_AT_decl_file.  This leads to a memory leak as the file name is
malloced and duplicates are not expected.

I've also changed find_abstract_instance to not use a temp for "name",
because that can result in a change in behaviour from the usual last
of duplicate attributes wins.

	PR 29925
	* dwarf2.c (find_abstract_instance): Delete "name" variable.
	Free *filename_ptr before assigning new file name.
	(scan_unit_for_symbols): Similarly free func->file and
	var->file before assigning.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t    func->file = concat_filename (unit->line_table,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t  attr.u.val);', '\t\t    var->file = concat_filename (unit->line_table,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t attr.u.val);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t    {', '\t\t      free (func->file);', '\t\t      func->file = concat_filename (unit->line_table,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t    attr.u.val);', '\t\t    }', '\t\t    {', '\t\t      free (var->file);', '\t\t      var->file = concat_filename (unit->line_table,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t   attr.u.val);', '\t\t    }']}
description: GNU Binutils before 2.40 was discovered to contain a memory leak vulnerability var the function find_abstract_instance in dwarf2.c.

code_evidence: In the DW_AT_decl_file case, func->file is overwritten with a fresh concat_filename allocation without freeing the prior pointer; a duplicate DW_AT_decl_file attribute (e.g., via DW_AT_specification) leaks the earlier allocation.
The var branch does the same: var->file is reassigned by concat_filename with no free of the previous value, leaking on repeated attributes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated filename memory is not released after its effective lifetime when the pointer is reassigned. This is a missing-release leak, not a use-after-free or double-free, since the stale pointer is simply dropped.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DW_AT_decl_file handlers overwrite func->file/var->file with newly malloced filenames without releasing the existing allocation. Trigger: a DIE carrying duplicate decl_file attributes, such as through DW_AT_specification, causes concat_filename to run twice. Consequence: the first filename buffer becomes unreachable, leaking memory (availability impact).

commit_msg:
libsepol/cil: Check for statements not allowed in optional blocks

While there are some checks for invalid statements in an optional
block when resolving the AST, there are no checks when building the
AST.

OSS-Fuzz found the following policy which caused a null dereference
in cil_tree_get_next_path().
  (blockinherit b3)
  (sid SID)
  (sidorder(SID))
  (optional o
    (ibpkeycon :(1 0)s)
    (block b3
      (filecon""block())
      (filecon""block())))

The problem is that the blockinherit copies block b3 before
the optional block is disabled. When the optional is disabled,
block b3 is deleted along with everything else in the optional.
Later, when filecon statements with the same path are found an
error message is produced and in trying to find out where the block
was copied from, the reference to the deleted block is used. The
error handling code assumes (rightly) that if something was copied
from a block then that block should still exist.

It is clear that in-statements, blocks, and macros cannot be in an
optional, because that allows nodes to be copied from the optional
block to somewhere outside even though the optional could be disabled
later. When optionals are disabled the AST is reset and the
resolution is restarted at the point of resolving macro calls, so
anything resolved before macro calls will never be re-resolved.
This includes tunableifs, in-statements, blockinherits,
blockabstracts, and macro definitions. Tunable declarations also
cannot be in an optional block because they are needed to resolve
tunableifs. It should be fine to allow blockinherit statements in
an optional, because that is copying nodes from outside the optional
to the optional and if the optional is later disabled, everything
will be deleted anyway.

Check and quit with an error if a tunable declaration, in-statement,
block, blockabstract, or macro definition is found within an
optional when either building or resolving the AST.

Signed-off-by: James Carter <jwcart2@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (ast->flavor == CIL_OPTIONAL) {', '\t\tstruct cil_tree_node *n = ast->parent;', '\t\targs->optional = NULL;', '\t\t/* Optionals can be nested */', '\t\twhile (n && n->flavor != CIL_ROOT) {', '\t\t\tif (n->flavor == CIL_OPTIONAL) {', '\t\t\t\targs->optional = n;', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tn = n->parent;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '']}
description: The CIL compiler in SELinux 3.2 has a heap-based buffer over-read in ebitmap_match_any (called indirectly from cil_check_neverallow). This occurs because there is sometimes a lack of checks for invalid statements in an optional block.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only manages build-argument state (resetting tunif/in/macro/boolif pointers and destroying child nodes); it performs no buffer access, so it does not support an out-of-bounds read.

* Fix integer overflow in layer_resize in map_engine.c

There's a buffer overflow bug in the function layer_resize. It allocates
a buffer `tilemap` with size `x_size * y_size * sizeof(struct map_tile)`.
But it didn't check for integer overflow, so if x_size and y_size are
very large, it's possible that the buffer size is smaller than needed,
causing a buffer overflow later.

description: A heap-based buffer overflow was discovered in upx, during the generic pointer 'p' points to an inaccessible address in func get_le32(). The problem is essentially caused in PackLinuxElf32::elf_lookup() at p_lx_elf.cpp:5382.

code_evidence: nbucket is read from the hash table header and used to form buckets/chains and index buckets[m] without validating that the table contains nbucket entries, so the loop reads chains[si] from beyond the mapped table.

The GNU-hash path derives n_bitmask, n_bucket and symbias from gashtab, then indexes buckets[h % n_bucket] and hasharr[bucket - symbias]; the only guard checks n_bucket <= bucket, not whether these derived pointers lie within file_image, so hp is dereferenced past the table end in the do/while.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked size fields cause access past the intended hash-table buffer, i.e. an out-of-bounds access rooted in missing bounds constraints. The patch adds file_size checks, confirming the intended buffer boundary. This fits CWE-787's out-of-bounds write scope; it is not merely an integer overflow, since no arithmetic wrap is required to reach the bad access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: header-supplied table sizes (nbucket, n_bitmask, n_bucket, symbias) are used to compute pointers and indexes without bounding them against file_size. Trigger: a crafted ELF whose hash-table metadata is inconsistent with the actual table extent. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads/writes at attacker-influenced pointers, matching the reported heap overflow / inaccessible-address crash in get_le32().

commit_msg:
x86/speculation: Allow enabling STIBP with legacy IBRS

When plain IBRS is enabled (not enhanced IBRS), the logic in
spectre_v2_user_select_mitigation() determines that STIBP is not needed.

The IBRS bit implicitly protects against cross-thread branch target
injection. However, with legacy IBRS, the IBRS bit is cleared on
returning to userspace for performance reasons which leaves userspace
threads vulnerable to cross-thread branch target injection against which
STIBP protects.

Exclude IBRS from the spectre_v2_in_ibrs_mode() check to allow for
enabling STIBP (through seccomp/prctl() by default or always-on, if
selected by spectre_v2_user kernel cmdline parameter).

  [ bp: Massage. ]

Fixes: 7c693f54c873 ("x86/speculation: Add spectre_v2=ibrs option to support Kernel IBRS")
Reported-by: José Oliveira <joseloliveira11@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Rodrigo Branco <rodrigo@kernelhacking.com>
Signed-off-by: KP Singh <kpsingh@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Borislav Petkov (AMD) <bp@alien8.de>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230220120127.1975241-1-kpsingh@kernel.org
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230221184908.2349578-1-kpsingh@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (spectre_v2_in_ibrs_mode(spectre_v2_enabled))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (spectre_v2_in_eibrs_mode(spectre_v2_enabled))']}
description:
The Linux kernel allows userspace processes to enable mitigations by calling prctl with PR_SET_SPECULATION_CTRL which disables the speculation feature as well as by using seccomp. We had noticed that on VMs of at least one major cloud provider, the kernel still left the victim process exposed to attacks in some cases even after enabling the spectre-BTI mitigation with prctl. The same behavior can be observed on a bare-metal machine when forcing the mitigation to IBRS on boot command line.

This happened because when plain IBRS was enabled (not enhanced IBRS), the kernel had some logic that determined that STIBP was not needed. The IBRS bit implicitly protects against cross-thread branch target injection. However, with legacy IBRS, the IBRS bit was cleared on returning to userspace, due to performance reasons, which disabled the implicit STIBP and left userspace threads vulnerable to cross-thread branch target injection against which STIBP protects.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only formats a human-readable STIBP status string for reporting; it performs no security decision or observable behavioral difference exploitable by an unauthorized actor, so it does not support CWE-203.

commit_msg:
Improve the assertion.

Co-authored-by: Serhiy Storchaka <storchaka@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        assert((extra_group_size == 0 && extra_groups == NULL) || extra_group_size);'], 'added_lines': ['        assert((extra_group_size == 0) == (extra_groups == NULL));']}
description:
An issue was found in CPython 3.12.0 `subprocess` module on POSIX platforms. The issue was fixed in CPython 3.12.1 and does not affect other stable releases.

When using the `extra_groups=` parameter with an empty list as a value (ie `extra_groups=[]`) the logic regressed to not call `setgroups(0, NULL)` before calling `exec()`, thus not dropping the original processes' groups before starting the new process. There is no issue when the parameter isn't used or when any value is used besides an empty list.

This issue only impacts CPython processes run with sufficient privilege to make the `setgroups` system call (typically `root`).

code_evidence: The HAVE_SETGROUPS block only calls setgroups when extra_group_size >= 0, and the assertion at line 90 was the only guard tying an empty list (size 0) to a NULL pointer; the old assertion accepted the case extra_group_size == 0 with non-NULL extra_groups, so setgroups(0, extra_groups) is invoked instead of the required setgroups(0, NULL) for an empty list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-269 fits because the child process's effective group privileges are not properly dropped before exec, leaving the new process with an unintended sphere of control. This is a privilege-management flaw in the group-dropping step, not a generic privilege-escalation impact label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the precondition assertion did not enforce that an empty extra_groups list maps to a NULL pointer before setgroups is called, allowing the supplementary group set to remain un-cleared. Trigger: a privileged (typically root) process passing extra_groups=[] with extra_group_size==0. Consequence: the child retains the parent's original supplementary groups, an unintended privilege retention.

commit_msg:
Correctly load/initialize classes when using ConstantPool

- do not load classes in the "ifLoaded" calls
- never intitialize classes in the natives
- do not update the constant pool when querying from the natives

Fixes: #12016

[ci skip]

Signed-off-by: Graham Chapman <graham_chapman@ca.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn getMethodAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_JIT_COMPILE_TIME | J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL);'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn getMethodAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CLASS_LOAD);']}
description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: The JNI entry point getMethodAtIfLoaded0 forwards the caller-supplied cpIndex and resolve flags to getMethodAt. The original call passes J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_JIT_COMPILE_TIME | J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL, which permits resolution without a class-load/initialization restriction; the fix replaces it with J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CLASS_LOAD.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-909 fits because the missing step is class initialization of the referenced resource before its static members are exposed; the defect is a missing initialization constraint, not merely a stale lookup. The flag change directly enforces that constraint, distinguishing it from a pure access-control weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
Java_sun_reflect_ConstantPool_getMethodAtIfLoaded0(JNIEnv *env, jobject unusedObject, jobject constantPoolOop, jint cpIndex)
return getMethodAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_JIT_COMPILE_TIME | J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the resolve flags on line 4 allow getMethodAt to resolve and load the class referenced by the constant-pool entry while servicing an 'ifLoaded' query. Trigger: a user invokes the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API on an entry whose class has not been initialized. Consequence: the entry is pre-resolved without running class initialization, so static state may be observed uninitialized or invalid.

description: async.c and dict.c in libhiredis.a in hiredis through 0.14.0 allow a NULL pointer dereference because malloc return values are unchecked.

code_evidence: Line 3 assigns the result of hiredis_safe_malloc to dup and line 4 immediately passes it to memcpy without any NULL check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a possibly-NULL pointer returned by allocation without validation, matching CWE-476. This is not a buffer overflow; the defect is the missing NULL check before the dereference.

evidence_lines.code:
redisCallback *dup = hiredis_safe_malloc(sizeof(*dup));
memcpy(dup,src,sizeof(*dup));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation result is used unconditionally. If allocation fails and returns NULL, memcpy dereferences a NULL destination, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg: Replace sprintf with snprintf in RegenerateThumbnail
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    sprintf(ThumbnailGenCommand, "mogrify -thumbnail %dx%d -quality 80 \\"%s\\"",'], 'added_lines': ['    snprintf(ThumbnailGenCommand, sizeof(ThumbnailGenCommand),', '        "mogrify -thumbnail %dx%d -quality 80 \\"%s\\"",']}
description: Jhead 3.06.0.1 allows attackers to execute arbitrary OS commands by placing them in a JPEG filename and then using the regeneration -rgt50 option.

code_evidence: Line 7 builds an OS command string with sprintf, interpolating FileName into the mogrify command inside double quotes; line 9 passes the resulting ThumbnailGenCommand to system(). FileName is not validated or escaped before interpolation, so shell metacharacters in the filename (e.g. quotes, ;, $()) become part of the command executed by the shell.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-78 fits because externally influenced input is used to construct an OS command that is sent to a command interpreter without neutralizing special elements, allowing command injection. This is distinct from a pure buffer overflow (CWE-120), which the size-bounded snprintf addresses but the injection remains.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-influenced FileName is concatenated into a shell command without neutralization and then executed via system(). Trigger: a crafted JPEG filename containing shell metacharacters. Consequence: arbitrary OS commands run with the privileges of the jhead process; the sprintf-to-snprintf change only bounds buffer size and does not prevent injection.

commit_msg:
Avoid division by zero in opj_pi_next_rpcl, opj_pi_next_pcrl and opj_pi_next_cprl (#938)

Fixes issues with id:000026,sig:08,src:002419,op:int32,pos:60,val:+32 and
id:000019,sig:08,src:001098,op:flip1,pos:49
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '                    /* To avoid divisions by zero / undefined behaviour on shift */', '                    /* in below tests */', '                    /* Relates to id:000019,sig:08,src:001098,op:flip1,pos:49 */', '                    /* of https://github.com/uclouvain/openjpeg/issues/938 */', '                    if (rpx >= 31 || ((comp->dx << rpx) >> rpx) != comp->dx ||', '                            rpy >= 31 || ((comp->dy << rpy) >> rpy) != comp->dy) {', '                        continue;', '                    }', '', '                    /* See ISO-15441. B.12.1.4 Position-component-resolution level-layer progression */']}
description: Division-by-zero vulnerabilities in the functions opj_pi_next_cprl, opj_pi_next_pcrl, and opj_pi_next_rpcl in pi.c in OpenJPEG before 2.2.0 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via crafted j2k files.

code_evidence: rpx and rpy are computed from res->pdx/pdy plus levelno with no bound check, so they can reach or exceed 31.
The test at line 53 computes (OPJ_INT32)(comp->dy << rpy) and then pi->y % that divisor; when rpy >= 31 the shift is undefined and the divisor can become zero.
Line 57 performs the same modulo with (comp->dx << rpx), giving a second zero-divisor path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits: the code performs modulo (division) using a computed divisor that is not constrained to be nonzero. The missing guard against oversized shifts is the root cause; the divide-by-zero crash is the consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
rpx = res->pdx + levelno;
rpy = res->pdy + levelno;

if (!((pi->y % (OPJ_INT32)(comp->dy << rpy) == 0) || ((pi->y == pi->ty0) &&
((try0 << levelno) % (1 << rpy))))) {

if (!((pi->x % (OPJ_INT32)(comp->dx << rpx) == 0) || ((pi->x == pi->tx0) &&
((trx0 << levelno) % (1 << rpx))))) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Untrusted resolution/component parameters yield large rpx/rpy; shifting comp->dy or comp->dx by such amounts is undefined and can produce a zero divisor, so the modulo at lines 53 or 57 divides by zero. The reachable consequence is a crash (DoS) while iterating packets from a crafted j2k file.

commit_msg: Lock down search_path in SPI calls
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Lock down search_path */', '\trc = SPI_exec("SET LOCAL search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp", 0);', '\tif (rc < 0)', '\t\tereport(ERROR, (errcode(ERRCODE_INTERNAL_ERROR), (errmsg("could not set search_path"))));', '']}
description:
TimescaleDB, an open-source time-series SQL database, has a privilege escalation vulnerability in versions 2.8.0 through 2.9.2. During installation, TimescaleDB creates a telemetry job that is runs as the installation user. The queries run as part of the telemetry data collection were not run with a locked down `search_path`, allowing malicious users to create functions that would be executed by the telemetry job, leading to privilege escalation. In order to be able to take advantage of this vulnerability, a user would need to be able to create objects in a database and then get a superuser to install TimescaleDB into their database. When TimescaleDB is installed as trusted extension, non-superusers can install the extension without help from a superuser.

Version 2.9.3 fixes this issue. As a mitigation, the `search_path` of the user running the telemetry job can be locked down to not include schemas writable by other users. The vulnerability is not exploitable on instances in Timescale Cloud and Managed Service for TimescaleDB due to additional security provisions in place on those platforms.

code_evidence: The function opens an SPI connection and immediately invokes chunk_copy_cleanup(operation_id), which runs SQL using the caller's search_path; no locked-down search_path is established before the cleanup queries execute. SPI_connect_ext and SPI_finish bracket the untrusted-name-driven work without constraining schema resolution.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs privileged operations while delegating schema/object resolution to an actor-controlled search_path, an improper privilege-management flaw: the actor's sphere of control extends into the privileged job. The missing search_path constraint is the cause; escalation is the consequence, so CWE-269 fits the privilege-handling root cause rather than a mere impact label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: privileged SPI work runs under the caller's search_path, so object names in cleanup resolve against schemas a low-privileged user can write. Trigger: a user creates a function/object shadowing a name used by the telemetry cleanup, then the job executes it. Consequence: the job's privileges are assumed, yielding privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fix ANSI Escape Sequence Injection vulns via DWARF ##vuln

* Reported by @solid-snail via huntrdev
* BountyID: 583133af-7ae6-4a21-beef-a4b0182cf82e
* Reproducer: dwarf_test_func_patched
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tr_str_cpy (str + i + 1, str + i + chlen);', '\t\ti++;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tr_str_cpy (str + i, str + i + chlen);', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t\ti++;']}
description: Failure to Sanitize Special Elements into a Different Plane (Special Element Injection) in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.8.2.

code_evidence: Loop scans str and calls __str_ansi_length on str+i; when chlen>1 (an ANSI escape sequence is detected) it invokes r_str_cpy(str+i+1, str+i+chlen), copying the tail over the escape's first byte only, leaving the remaining escape bytes in place and shifting content by one, then i++ advances regardless.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is intended to neutralize ANSI escape sequences (special elements) before output to a downstream interpreter, but the off-by-one copy fails to remove them, matching CWE-74 improper neutralization of special elements used by a downstream component.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ANSI escape sequence is removed by shifting the tail to str+i+1 instead of str+i, so the sequence is only partially overwritten and residual bytes remain in the string. Trigger: any input containing an ANSI escape sequence passed to r_str_ansi_strip. Consequence: the malformed residual bytes persist in output that downstream consumers (e.g. terminal or DWARF name display) may interpret, enabling escape-sequence injection rather than proper sanitization.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Reported-by: syzbot+f427adf9324b92652ccc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (S_ISREG(inode->i_mode) && !is_bad_inode(inode)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (S_ISREG(inode->i_mode) && !fuse_is_bad(inode)) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in the FUSE filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.10.6, aka CID-5d069dbe8aaf. fuse_do_getattr() calls make_bad_inode() in inappropriate situations, causing a system crash. NOTE: the original fix for this vulnerability was incomplete, and its incompleteness is tracked as CVE-2021-28950.

code_evidence: fuse_evict_inode() is the cleanup path for a FUSE inode: it truncates pages, clears the inode, queues forget for nlookup, and asserts write_files/queued_writes are empty for regular inodes. The guard at line 16 uses is_bad_inode(inode), which relies on the inode mode being S_IFREG. When fuse_do_getattr() earlier calls make_bad_inode(), the live inode's i_mode is overwritten to S_IFREG, so this guard's S_ISREG check and the bad-inode check interact incorrectly, letting the cleanup proceed with inconsistent dnotify state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the inode teardown path and its bad-inode test fails to correctly gate cleanup after mode corruption, so supporting resources (dnotify marks) are left uncleaned, matching CWE-459 Incomplete Cleanup. It is not merely improper input validation; the defect manifests as incomplete resource teardown during eviction.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: make_bad_inode() mutates a live inode's i_mode to S_IFREG, corrupting the type used by the eviction cleanup checks. Trigger: a FUSE server returns inconsistent attributes causing make_bad_inode() on an open, dnotify-marked directory. Consequence: dnotify structures are not torn down properly, leading to a system crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Made some changes to the I/O stream library for memory streams.
There were a number of potential problems due to the possibility
of integer overflow.
Changed some integral types to the larger types size_t or ssize_t.
For example, the function mem_resize now takes the buffer size parameter
as a size_t.
Added a new function jas_stream_memopen2, which takes a
buffer size specified as a size_t instead of an int.
This can be used in jas_image_cmpt_create to avoid potential
overflow problems.

Added a new function jas_deprecated to warn about reliance on
deprecated library behavior.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcmpt->stream_ = (inmem) ? jas_stream_memopen(0, size) :'], 'added_lines': ['\tcmpt->stream_ = (inmem) ? jas_stream_memopen2(0, size) :']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the (1) jas_realloc function in base/jas_malloc.c and (2) mem_resize function in base/jas_stream.c in JasPer before 1.900.22 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted image, which triggers use after free vulnerabilities.

code_evidence: cmpt->cps_ is derived from depth as (depth+7)/8, and size is computed by multiplying width*height then by cps_ using jas_safe_size_mul; failure of either safe multiply jumps to error.
The stream is then opened with jas_stream_memopen(0, size), passing the computed size as an int-sized argument, so a size that does not fit the callee's int parameter is truncated before allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer overflow/wraparound at the size conversion boundary: a size_t product is narrowed into an int parameter, producing a small or negative value the logic assumes is still the full size. CWE-190 fits because the truncation/wraparound in size handling is the root cause; the subsequent memory error is its consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
cmpt->stream_ = (inmem) ? jas_stream_memopen(0, size) :
jas_stream_tmpfile();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size computed with safe size_t arithmetic is handed to jas_stream_memopen, whose buffer-size parameter is int, so a large but non-overflowing size_t value is truncated/wrapped when converted. Trigger: an attacker-supplied image with large width/height/depth reaching this branch with inmem set. Consequence: the buffer is allocated smaller than the seek/write target, enabling out-of-bounds access or a use-after-free/DoS in stream handling.

commit_msg:
kvm: initialize all of the kvm_debugregs structure before sending it to userspace

When calling the KVM_GET_DEBUGREGS ioctl, on some configurations, there
might be some unitialized portions of the kvm_debugregs structure that
could be copied to userspace.  Prevent this as is done in the other kvm
ioctls, by setting the whole structure to 0 before copying anything into
it.

Bonus is that this reduces the lines of code as the explicit flag
setting and reserved space zeroing out can be removed.

Cc: Sean Christopherson <seanjc@google.com>
Cc: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Cc: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: Ingo Molnar <mingo@redhat.com>
Cc: Borislav Petkov <bp@alien8.de>
Cc: Dave Hansen <dave.hansen@linux.intel.com>
Cc: <x86@kernel.org>
Cc: "H. Peter Anvin" <hpa@zytor.com>
Cc: stable <stable@kernel.org>
Reported-by: Xingyuan Mo <hdthky0@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Message-Id: <20230214103304.3689213-1-gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Tested-by: Xingyuan Mo <hdthky0@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tdbgregs->flags = 0;', '\tmemset(&dbgregs->reserved, 0, sizeof(dbgregs->reserved));'], 'added_lines': ['\tmemset(dbgregs, 0, sizeof(*dbgregs));']}
description: A flaw was found in KVM. When calling the KVM_GET_DEBUGREGS ioctl, on 32-bit systems, there might be some uninitialized portions of the kvm_debugregs structure that could be copied to userspace, causing an information leak.

code_evidence: The function fills only db, dr6, dr7, flags, and reserved of the caller-supplied kvm_debugregs structure; any other bytes of the structure remain uninitialized before it is returned to userspace via the KVM_GET_DEBUGREGS ioctl.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-665 (Improper Initialization) directly matches: the returned resource (kvm_debugregs) is incompletely initialized, leaving bytes in an unexpected state that are then read by userspace, consistent with the Confidentiality/Read Memory impact scope.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The output structure is not fully initialized before being populated: memcpy and assignments write selected fields, and while flags and reserved are zeroed, the whole structure is not cleared. On configurations where padding or other bytes are not covered, the ioctl copies uninitialized kernel stack memory to userspace, leaking information. Root cause is partial initialization of a structure returned across a trust boundary; the trigger is the KVM_GET_DEBUGREGS ioctl.

description: ssh-agent in OpenSSH before 8.5 has a double free that may be relevant in a few less-common scenarios, such as unconstrained agent-socket access on a legacy operating system, or the forwarding of an agent to an attacker-controlled host.

commit_msg:
bpf: Fix leakage under speculation on mispredicted branches

The verifier only enumerates valid control-flow paths and skips paths that
are unreachable in the non-speculative domain. And so it can miss issues
under speculative execution on mispredicted branches.

For example, a type confusion has been demonstrated with the following
crafted program:

  // r0 = pointer to a map array entry
  // r6 = pointer to readable stack slot
  // r9 = scalar controlled by attacker
  1: r0 = *(u64 *)(r0) // cache miss
  2: if r0 != 0x0 goto line 4
  3: r6 = r9
  4: if r0 != 0x1 goto line 6
  5: r9 = *(u8 *)(r6)
  6: // leak r9

Since line 3 runs iff r0 == 0 and line 5 runs iff r0 == 1, the verifier
concludes that the pointer dereference on line 5 is safe. But: if the
attacker trains both the branches to fall-through, such that the following
is speculatively executed ...

  r6 = r9
  r9 = *(u8 *)(r6)
  // leak r9

... then the program will dereference an attacker-controlled value and could
leak its content under speculative execution via side-channel. This requires
to mistrain the branch predictor, which can be rather tricky, because the
branches are mutually exclusive. However such training can be done at
congruent addresses in user space using different branches that are not
mutually exclusive. That is, by training branches in user space ...

  A:  if r0 != 0x0 goto line C
  B:  ...
  C:  if r0 != 0x0 goto line D
  D:  ...

... such that addresses A and C collide to the same CPU branch prediction
entries in the PHT (pattern history table) as those of the BPF program's
lines 2 and 4, respectively. A non-privileged attacker could simply brute
force such collisions in the PHT until observing the attack succeeding.

Alternative methods to mistrain the branch predictor are also possible that
avoid brute forcing the collisions in the PHT. A reliable attack has been
demonstrated, for example, using the following crafted program:

  // r0 = pointer to a [control] map array entry
  // r7 = *(u64 *)(r0 + 0), training/attack phase
  // r8 = *(u64 *)(r0 + 8), oob address
  // [...]
  // r0 = pointer to a [data] map array entry
  1: if r7 == 0x3 goto line 3
  2: r8 = r0
  // crafted sequence of conditional jumps to separate the conditional
  // branch in line 193 from the current execution flow
  3: if r0 != 0x0 goto line 5
  4: if r0 == 0x0 goto exit
  5: if r0 != 0x0 goto line 7
  6: if r0 == 0x0 goto exit
  [...]
  187: if r0 != 0x0 goto line 189
  188: if r0 == 0x0 goto exit
  // load any slowly-loaded value (due to cache miss in phase 3) ...
  189: r3 = *(u64 *)(r0 + 0x1200)
  // ... and turn it into known zero for verifier, while preserving slowly-
  // loaded dependency when executing:
  190: r3 &= 1
  191: r3 &= 2
  // speculatively bypassed phase dependency
  192: r7 += r3
  193: if r7 == 0x3 goto exit
  194: r4 = *(u8 *)(r8 + 0)
  // leak r4

As can be seen, in training phase (phase != 0x3), the condition in line 1
turns into false and therefore r8 with the oob address is overridden with
the valid map value address, which in line 194 we can read out without
issues. However, in attack phase, line 2 is skipped, and due to the cache
miss in line 189 where the map value is (zeroed and later) added to the
phase register, the condition in line 193 takes the fall-through path due
to prior branch predictor training, where under speculation, it'll load the
byte at oob address r8 (unknown scalar type at that point) which could then
be leaked via side-channel.

One way to mitigate these is to 'branch off' an unreachable path, meaning,
the current verification path keeps following the is_branch_taken() path
and we push the other branch to the verification stack. Given this is
unreachable from the non-speculative domain, this branch's vstate is
explicitly marked as speculative. This is needed for two reasons: i) if
this path is solely seen from speculative execution, then we later on still
want the dead code elimination to kick in in order to sanitize these
instructions with jmp-1s, and ii) to ensure that paths walked in the
non-speculative domain are not pruned from earlier walks of paths walked in
the speculative domain. Additionally, for robustness, we mark the registers
which have been part of the conditional as unknown in the speculative path
given there should be no assumptions made on their content.

The fix in here mitigates type confusion attacks described earlier due to
i) all code paths in the BPF program being explored and ii) existing
verifier logic already ensuring that given memory access instruction
references one specific data structure.

An alternative to this fix that has also been looked at in this scope was to
mark aux->alu_state at the jump instruction with a BPF_JMP_TAKEN state as
well as direction encoding (always-goto, always-fallthrough, unknown), such
that mixing of different always-* directions themselves as well as mixing of
always-* with unknown directions would cause a program rejection by the
verifier, e.g. programs with constructs like 'if ([...]) { x = 0; } else
{ x = 1; }' with subsequent 'if (x == 1) { [...] }'. For unprivileged, this
would result in only single direction always-* taken paths, and unknown taken
paths being allowed, such that the former could be patched from a conditional
jump to an unconditional jump (ja). Compared to this approach here, it would
have two downsides: i) valid programs that otherwise are not performing any
pointer arithmetic, etc, would potentially be rejected/broken, and ii) we are
required to turn off path pruning for unprivileged, where both can be avoided
in this work through pushing the invalid branch to the verification stack.

The issue was originally discovered by Adam and Ofek, and later independently
discovered and reported as a result of Benedict and Piotr's research work.

description: In kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel before 5.12.13, a branch can be mispredicted (e.g., because of type confusion) and consequently an unprivileged BPF program can read arbitrary memory locations via a side-channel attack, aka CID-9183671af6db.

code_evidence: When the current verifier state is speculative, the function jumps directly to the do_sim label, bypassing the non-speculative pointer-limit checks in lines 23-44.
In the do_sim block, commit_window and immediate offsets return early; otherwise the original destination register is saved and replaced with the pointer register.
The function then calls push_stack to fork the fall-through path, restoring the saved destination register only when the push succeeds, and returns REASON_STACK on failure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root issue is that a register value validated under one type (pointer) can be treated as a different type (scalar) along the speculative path, i.e., type confusion, and the resulting access can read arbitrary memory. This matches CWE-843 rather than a pure bounds-check weakness because the missing constraint is the resource's type across the speculative state.

evidence_lines.code:
if (vstate->speculative)
goto do_sim;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The verifier's speculative path simulation does not carry the type/pointer constraints established on the non-speculative path; a speculative state can reach the ALU sanitization with a register whose type was not validated, so the sanitized pointer arithmetic is applied to a value that may be an attacker-controlled scalar. This allows the speculative path to perform an out-of-bounds/typed access that the non-speculative verifier would reject, enabling side-channel leakage.

commit_msg:
For USB there is no separate channel being used to pass events
from firmware to the host driver and as such are passed over the
data path. In order to detect mock event messages an additional
check is needed on event subtype. This check is added conditionally
using unlikely() keyword.

Reviewed-by: Hante Meuleman <hante.meuleman@broadcom.com>
Reviewed-by: Pieter-Paul Giesberts <pieter-paul.giesberts@broadcom.com>
Reviewed-by: Franky Lin <franky.lin@broadcom.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbrcmf_fweh_process_skb(ifp->drvr, skb);'], 'added_lines': ['\tbrcmf_fweh_process_skb(ifp->drvr, skb, 0);']}
description: The Broadcom brcmfmac WiFi driver prior to commit a4176ec356c73a46c07c181c6d04039fafa34a9f is vulnerable to a frame validation bypass. If the brcmfmac driver receives a firmware event frame from a remote source, the is_wlc_event_frame function will cause this frame to be discarded and unprocessed. If the driver receives the firmware event frame from the host, the appropriate handler is called. This frame validation can be bypassed if the bus used is USB (for instance by a wifi dongle). This can allow firmware event frames from a remote source to be processed. In the worst case scenario, by sending specially-crafted WiFi packets, a remote, unauthenticated attacker may be able to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable system. More typically, this vulnerability will result in denial-of-service conditions.

code_evidence: Event buffer is cast to msgbuf_rx_event and the request_id and event_data_len fields are taken directly from the received data without validating the event subtype or source.

The skb length is trimmed to the attacker-influenced event_data_len, and the skb is then passed to brcmf_fweh_process_skb with no event-subtype argument (0), so the frame's provenance/subtype is never checked here.
eth_type_trans is applied and the skb is dispatched to the firmware-event handler based on unvalidated frame metadata.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is missing validation of input frame properties (event subtype/source) before processing, matching CWE-20 improper input validation; the missing check permits a frame-validation bypass rather than a length/type confusion issue.

evidence_lines.code:
skb_pull(skb, msgbuf->rx_dataoffset);
skb_trim(skb, buflen);

skb->protocol = eth_type_trans(skb, ifp->ndev);
brcmf_fweh_process_skb(ifp->drvr, skb);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function forwards an incoming frame to brcmf_fweh_process_skb without verifying that it is a legitimate firmware event frame (no event subtype/source check is supplied). A remote attacker able to inject a frame over the USB data path can therefore have it treated as a firmware event and processed, potentially leading to code execution or denial of service.

Validate that the IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_OPER_CHANNEL attribute contains
enough space for a 'struct struct wilc_attr_oper_ch'. If the attribute is
too small then it triggers an out-of-bounds write later in the function.

Signed-off-by: Phil Turnbull <philipturnbull@github.com>
Tested-by: Ajay Kathat <ajay.kathat@microchip.com>
Acked-by: Ajay Kathat <ajay.kathat@microchip.com>

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.0.11. Missing validation of IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_OPER_CHANNEL in drivers/net/wireless/microchip/wilc1000/cfg80211.c in the WILC1000 wireless driver can trigger an out-of-bounds write when parsing the channel list attribute from Wi-Fi management frames.

code_evidence: The loop records op_ch_idx whenever an attribute has attr_type IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_OPER_CHANNEL, without checking that the attribute is large enough to hold a struct wilc_attr_oper_ch.
Later, op_ch is cast from &buf[op_ch_idx] and its op_class and op_channel fields are written, assuming the full struct wilc_attr_oper_ch is present in the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing struct fields through a pointer into a buffer that was not validated to be large enough is a direct out-of-bounds write past the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the code actively stores to op_ch fields.

evidence_lines.code:
else if (e->attr_type == IEEE80211_P2P_ATTR_OPER_CHANNEL)
op_ch_idx = index;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser trusts the attacker-controlled attribute length/type and stores a pointer to a short OPER_CHANNEL attribute. Trigger: a management frame whose OPER_CHANNEL attribute is shorter than struct wilc_attr_oper_ch. The later writes to op_ch->op_class and op_ch->op_channel then extend past the parsed buffer, corrupting adjacent memory (integrity/DoS).

commit_msg:
evtchn: evtchn_reset() shouldn't succeed with still-open ports

While the function closes all ports, it does so without holding any
lock, and hence racing requests may be issued causing new ports to get
opened. This would have been problematic in particular if such a newly
opened port had a port number above the new implementation limit (i.e.
when switching from FIFO to 2-level) after the reset, as prior to
"evtchn: relax port_is_valid()" this could have led to e.g.
evtchn_close()'s "BUG_ON(!port_is_valid(d2, port2))" to trigger.

Introduce a counter of active ports and check that it's (still) no
larger then the number of Xen internally used ones after obtaining the
necessary lock in evtchn_reset().

As to the access model of the new {active,xen}_evtchns fields - while
all writes get done using write_atomic(), reads ought to use
read_atomic() only when outside of a suitably locked region.

Note that as of now evtchn_bind_virq() and evtchn_bind_ipi() don't have
a need to call check_free_port().

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if ( consumer_is_xen(chn) )', '        write_atomic(&d->xen_evtchns, d->xen_evtchns - 1);', '    write_atomic(&d->active_evtchns, d->active_evtchns - 1);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: evtchn_free() clears the pending state and resets chn->state, notify_vcpu_id, xen_consumer and the XSM post state without acquiring any lock protecting the event-channel array or the domain-wide port counters. The diff adds write_atomic() decrements of d->xen_evtchns and d->active_evtchns, but these are plain read-modify-write updates outside any serializing lock, so they are themselves non-atomic against concurrent binds/resets.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits: a shared resource (the event-channel array and d->active_evtchns/d->xen_evtchns) is modified by concurrent code sequences without exclusive access, violating atomicity. The write_atomic() calls are not synchronization and do not prevent the race; this is not merely a missing lock around a single field but a non-atomic multi-step close/reset sequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: port teardown and the new active/xen port counters are updated without holding the event-channel lock, so an interfering sequence (e.g. evtchn_reset() or a concurrent bind) can observe or produce inconsistent state. Trigger: a racing request opens or closes a port while evtchn_free() runs. Consequence: internal port-validity assumptions can be violated, leading to out-of-bounds access, BUG_ON crash, host/guest DoS, or privilege escalation for x86 PV guests.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflow in M_LoadDefaults

Too much data will most likely result in a crash or freeze, but you can overwrite the stack which can be used to do an arbitrary code execution. (https://twitter.com/notrevenant/status/1268654123903340544)

description: A buffer overflow in the M_LoadDefaults function in m_misc.c in id Tech 1 (aka Doom engine) allows arbitrary code execution via an unsafe usage of fscanf, because it does not limit the number of characters to be read in a format argument.

code_evidence: strparm is a fixed 100-byte stack buffer at line 7. Line 28 uses fscanf with the unbounded scanset %[^\n], so a config line longer than 99 characters writes past strparm. The read value then feeds strlen (33), malloc(len) (34) and strcpy (36), propagating the corrupted length and content.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because input is copied into a fixed-size output buffer (strparm) without checking that the input length is smaller than the buffer, causing a classic stack buffer overflow. The patch's addition of %99 confirms the missing size bound; this is a write overflow, not a mere out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fscanf's %[^\n] has no field-width limit, so attacker-controlled config-file data overflows the 100-byte strparm stack buffer. Trigger: a long default line in the loaded config file. Consequence: stack memory corruption, crash, and potential arbitrary code execution via overwritten return state.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.7 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.13, the AMQP dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-amqp.c by checking for successful list dissection.

commit_msg:
IB/security: Restrict use of the write() interface

The drivers/infiniband stack uses write() as a replacement for
bi-directional ioctl().  This is not safe. There are ways to
trigger write calls that result in the return structure that
is normally written to user space being shunted off to user
specified kernel memory instead.

For the immediate repair, detect and deny suspicious accesses to
the write API.

For long term, update the user space libraries and the kernel API
to something that doesn't present the same security vulnerabilities
(likely a structured ioctl() interface).

The impacted uAPI interfaces are generally only available if
hardware from drivers/infiniband is installed in the system.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jann@thejh.net>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgunthorpe@obsidianresearch.com>
[ Expanded check to all known write() entry points ]
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Doug Ledford <dledford@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (WARN_ON_ONCE(!ib_safe_file_access(filp)))', '\t\treturn -EACCES;']}
description: The InfiniBand (aka IB) stack in the Linux kernel before 4.5.3 incorrectly relies on the write system call, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (kernel memory write operation) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a uAPI interface.

code_evidence: ib_ucm_write trusts filp->private_data (line 4) and processes a user-supplied command header without any check that the write() caller is a legitimate IB uAPI user. It validates length (7-8), copies the header (9-10), bounds hdr.cmd (11-12) and hdr.in (13-14), then dispatches ucm_cmd_table[hdr.cmd] with hdr.in/hdr.out (15-16). The dispatch runs whichever command the user selects, and hdr.out lets the command direct its result buffer to user-specified memory; no file-access/permission gate exists before dispatch.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs privileged operations driven by unprivileged write() input while omitting the permission/access check that should gate them; the fix adds ib_safe_file_access() to deny suspicious callers. This fits CWE-264's permission/access-control category. It is not merely a bounds issue (CWE-119), since the header bounds checks at 11-14 are present; the missing control is caller authorization.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: write() is used as an ioctl replacement with no access-control check on the file before executing user-selected commands. Trigger: a local user issues a crafted write() with a chosen cmd and out value, reaching the dispatch at lines 15-16. Supported consequence: the command's return structure is written to attacker-chosen kernel memory, enabling a kernel memory write (DoS or worse).

commit_msg: Lock down search_path in SPI calls
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* SPI calls must be qualified otherwise they are unsafe */', '\tres = SPI_exec("SET search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp", 0);', '\tres = SPI_exec("RESET search_path", 0);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Lock down search_path */', '\tres = SPI_exec("SET LOCAL search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp", 0);']}
description:
TimescaleDB, an open-source time-series SQL database, has a privilege escalation vulnerability in versions 2.8.0 through 2.9.2. During installation, TimescaleDB creates a telemetry job that is runs as the installation user. The queries run as part of the telemetry data collection were not run with a locked down `search_path`, allowing malicious users to create functions that would be executed by the telemetry job, leading to privilege escalation. In order to be able to take advantage of this vulnerability, a user would need to be able to create objects in a database and then get a superuser to install TimescaleDB into their database. When TimescaleDB is installed as trusted extension, non-superusers can install the extension without help from a superuser.

Version 2.9.3 fixes this issue. As a mitigation, the `search_path` of the user running the telemetry job can be locked down to not include schemas writable by other users. The vulnerability is not exploitable on instances in Timescale Cloud and Managed Service for TimescaleDB due to additional security provisions in place on those platforms.

code_evidence: After SPI_connect, the function runs SET search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp via SPI_exec but does not use SET LOCAL, so the search_path change persists beyond this SPI session for the calling telemetry job's user.

The subsequent SPI_execute of command_string runs with that search_path, and the later RESET search_path is executed only after processing; the persistent SET combined with execution under the telemetry job's privileges is the relevant flow.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-269 fits because the function fails to properly constrain the privilege context (search_path) under which the telemetry job's queries run, allowing an attacker to gain the installation user's privileges. The weakness is improper privilege management in the query execution context, not merely a generic SQL injection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the search_path is modified with a session-level SET instead of SET LOCAL, so it is not scoped to the SPI call and is not locked down for the duration of the query execution. Trigger: a user who can create objects/schemas can influence name resolution for unqualified names used by the telemetry job. Consequence: functions chosen via the altered search_path execute with the telemetry job's (installation user's) privileges, enabling privilege escalation.

description: ext/spl/spl_array.c in PHP before 5.6.26 and 7.x before 7.0.11 proceeds with SplArray unserialization without validating a return value and data type, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted serialized data.

code_evidence: Line 6 obtains ht from spl_array_get_hash_table(intern) without checking the result. Lines 7-9 guard only against a NULL/UNDEF offset, so execution proceeds with a potentially NULL ht into the switch, where ht is dereferenced by zend_symtable_find/update and zend_hash_index_find/update (lines 22, 55, 76, 89).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is failure to validate a derived data property (the hash table pointer) before processing, matching CWE-20's improper validation of input-derived data. The consequence is a NULL-pointer dereference; it is not a type-confusion or bounds weakness, so CWE-20 is the fitting label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function trusts that the hash table returned for the SplArray is always valid and validates only the offset argument. Crafted serialized data yields an object whose hash table is absent, so ht stays NULL; the missing !ht check lets the subsequent hash-table lookups dereference NULL, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Currently ext4 directory handling code implicitly assumes that the
directory blocks are always within the i_size. In fact ext4_append()
will attempt to allocate next directory block based solely on i_size and
the i_size is then appropriately increased after a successful
allocation.

However, for this to work it requires i_size to be correct. If, for any
reason, the directory inode i_size is corrupted in a way that the
directory tree refers to a valid directory block past i_size, we could
end up corrupting parts of the directory tree structure by overwriting
already used directory blocks when modifying the directory.

Fix it by catching the corruption early in __ext4_read_dirblock().

Addresses Red-Hat-Bugzilla: #2070205
CVE: CVE-2022-1184
Signed-off-by: Lukas Czerner <lczerner@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reviewed-by: Andreas Dilger <adilger@dilger.ca>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220704142721.157985-1-lczerner@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (block >= inode->i_size) {', '\t\text4_error_inode(inode, func, line, block,', '\t\t       "Attempting to read directory block (%u) that is past i_size (%llu)",', '\t\t       block, inode->i_size);', '\t\treturn ERR_PTR(-EFSCORRUPTED);', '\t}']}
description:
Apptainer is an open source container platform for Linux. There is an ext4 use-after-free flaw that is exploitable through versions of Apptainer < 1.1.0 and installations that include apptainer-suid < 1.1.8 on older operating systems where that CVE has not been patched. That includes Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7, Debian 10 buster (unless the linux-5.10 package is installed), Ubuntu 18.04 bionic and Ubuntu 20.04 focal. Use-after-free flaws in the kernel can be used to attack the kernel for denial of service and potentially for privilege escalation.

Apptainer 1.1.8 includes a patch that by default disables mounting of extfs filesystem types in setuid-root mode, while continuing to allow mounting of extfs filesystems in non-setuid "rootless" mode using fuse2fs.

Some workarounds are possible. Either do not install apptainer-suid (for versions 1.1.0 through 1.1.7) or set `allow setuid = no` in apptainer.conf.  This requires having unprivileged user namespaces enabled and except for apptainer 1.1.x versions will disallow mounting of sif files, extfs files, and squashfs files in addition to other, less significant impacts.  (Encrypted sif files are also not supported unprivileged in apptainer 1.1.x.). Alternatively, use the `limit containers` options in apptainer.conf/singularity.conf to limit sif files to trusted users, groups, and/or paths, and set `allow container extfs = no` to disallow mounting of extfs overlay files.  The latter option by itself does not disallow mounting of extfs overlay partitions inside SIF files, so that's why the former options are also needed.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only reads a directory block and checks bounds against i_size; it contains no free or reuse of freed memory, so it does not support CWE-416.

commit_msg:
x86: limit linear page table use to a single level

That's the only way that they're meant to be used. Without such a
restriction arbitrarily long chains of same-level page tables can be
built, tearing down of which may then cause arbitrarily deep recursion,
causing a stack overflow. To facilitate this restriction, a counter is
being introduced to track both the number of same-level entries in a
page table as well as the number of uses of a page table in another
same-level one (counting into positive and negative direction
respectively, utilizing the fact that both counts can't be non-zero at
the same time).

Note that the added accounting introduces a restriction on the number
of times a page can be used in other same-level page tables - more than
32k of such uses are no longer possible.

Note also that some put_page_and_type[_preemptible]() calls are
replaced with open-coded equivalents.  This seemed preferrable to
adding "parent_table" to the matrix of functions.

Note further that cross-domain same-level page table references are no
longer permitted (they probably never should have been).

This is XSA-240.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        page->linear_pt_count = 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service (unbounded recursion, stack consumption, and hypervisor crash) or possibly gain privileges via crafted page-table stacking.

code_evidence: The loop increments the type count (nx = x + 1) and only rejects when PGT_count_mask wraps to zero, so a page can be referenced by many same-level page tables without any bound on linear page-table depth.

When the page is not yet validated and not partial, nr_validated_ptes and partial_pte are reset and alloc_page_type is invoked; the patch adds linear_pt_count = 0 in this block, showing accounting for same-level references was previously absent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function fails to track/restrict consumption of a bounded resource (stack depth via page-table references), enabling resource exhaustion. It is not merely memory corruption; the missing constraint is on the number of same-level uses, matching uncontrolled resource consumption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: __get_page_type permits arbitrarily many same-level page-table references because nothing limits linear page-table nesting; only the generic type count is checked. Trigger: a PV guest crafts chains of same-level page tables, each referencing the previous. Consequence: teardown recurses through the long chain, exhausting the hypervisor stack and crashing it (DoS), with possible privilege impact.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tret = key_validate(key);', '\tif (ret == 0) {', '\t\tret = -EOPNOTSUPP;', '\t\tif (key->type->read) {', '\t\t\t/* read the data with the semaphore held (since we', '\t\t\t * might sleep) */', '\t\t\tdown_read(&key->sem);', '\t\t\tup_read(&key->sem);', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tret = -EOPNOTSUPP;', '\tif (key->type->read) {', '\t\t/* Read the data with the semaphore held (since we might sleep)', '\t\t * to protect against the key being updated or revoked.', '\t\t */', '\t\tdown_read(&key->sem);', '\t\tret = key_validate(key);', '\t\tif (ret == 0)', '\t\tup_read(&key->sem);']}
description: The keyctl_read_key function in security/keys/keyctl.c in the Linux kernel before 4.3.4 does not properly use a semaphore, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted application that leverages a race condition between keyctl_revoke and keyctl_read calls.

code_evidence: key_validate(key) checks the key's validity at line 22 before any lock is taken; only afterward, at line 26, is down_read(&key->sem) acquired. The key's read method is then invoked at line 27 while holding the semaphore, but the validity check already happened outside the lock, so a concurrent revoke can occur between validation and the semaphore acquisition.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a shared resource (the key) is accessed without holding the semaphore across the check-and-use sequence, leaving a timing window where a concurrent revoke interferes. The missing constraint is that validation must occur under key->sem, not that a pointer is unchecked (a downstream NULL dereference consequence).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the key validity check (line 22) and the protected read (lines 26-27) are not atomic with respect to key revocation, because the semaphore is taken only after validation. Trigger: a second thread calls keyctl_revoke between line 22 and line 26. The read method then runs on a revoked key whose payload is NULL, causing a NULL pointer dereference and kernel crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix invalid memory accesses and add missing checks in src/dtm.cpp

There are several issues when loading .dtm files which can lead
to invalid memory accesses. This patch fixes the following:

* In CdtmLoader::load(), ensure that title and author strings
  are properly terminated to avoid out-of-bounds reads.
* Check that the number of instruments is valid. This avoids a
  heap-based buffer overflow (see issue #86).
* Reading the description string could overflow a stack buffer
  by 1 byte and write past the end of the array into an adjacent
  class member (which is only initialized later). Get rid of the
  stack buffer and truncate the description if necessary.
* Fail loading when an error is detected while trying to read
  data from the file or while decoding RLE data.
* Check the argument of CdtmLoader::getinstrument() to avoid
  out-of-bound accesses.

This fixes CVE-2019-14691.

Fixes: https://github.com/adplug/adplug/issues/86
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['          if (input_length == ilen)', '            return output_length; // truncated input']}
description: AdPlug 2.3.1 has a heap-based buffer overflow in CdtmLoader::load() in dtm.cpp.

code_evidence: Loop condition only checks input_length < ilen before reading a byte at line 10. When that byte signals an RLE run ((repeat_byte & 0xF0) == 0xD0), line 14 reads input[input_length++] again without verifying input_length < ilen, so a truncated input ending on a 0xD0 marker reads one byte past ibuf. The following for-loop at lines 18-21 writes repeat_counter bytes into output, but each write is guarded by output_length < olen, bounding the output buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's only unbounded memory access is the input read at line 14, which over-reads the source buffer; writes at lines 20-21 are guarded by output_length < olen. That is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), not a write past the intended buffer, so CWE-787 is not supported by this function's code.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the RLE repeat-byte fetch at line 14 consumes a second input byte without an ilen bound, so a crafted/truncated .dtm stream whose last byte has high nibble 0xD0 causes an out-of-bounds read past ibuf. The output copy loop is already length-checked, so the supported consequence is an invalid read rather than an out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
h264: reset data partitioning at the beginning of each decode call

Prevents using GetBitContexts with data from previous calls.

Fixes access to freed memory.

Found-by: Mateusz "j00ru" Jurczyk and Gynvael Coldwind
CC:libav-stable@libav.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                if (h->avctx->flags & CODEC_FLAG2_CHUNKS) {', '                    av_log(h->avctx, AV_LOG_ERROR,', '                           "Decoding in chunks is not supported for "', '                           "partitioned slices.\\n");', '                    return AVERROR(ENOSYS);', '                }', '']}
description: A vulnerability has been found in FFmpeg 2.0 and classified as critical. This vulnerability affects the function decode_update_thread_context. The manipulation leads to memory corruption. The attack can be initiated remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

code_evidence: At function entry, the reset of h->current_slice, h->cur_pic_ptr and SEI state (lines 13-16) is skipped when CODEC_FLAG2_CHUNKS is set, so per-call state persists across decode calls.

In the NAL_DPA case, init_get_bits(&hx->gb, ptr, bit_length) is invoked and slice-header decoding proceeds without rejecting chunked decoding, leaving GetBitContexts tied to data that may be freed between calls.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch adds an explicit rejection of chunked partitioned slices, indicating the unsafe path leads to memory corruption consistent with an out-of-bounds write through stale bit-reader state. This is an OOB write (CWE-787), not a pure use-after-free label, because the supported consequence is memory corruption from writes driven by stale context.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When chunked decoding is enabled, the entry guard skips resetting slice/picture state, and the NAL_DPA branch still initializes bit readers and decodes slice headers. Stale GetBitContexts referencing buffers from a previous call can then be consumed into freed memory, corrupting memory rather than merely failing cleanly.

commit_msg:
Fix stack corruption happening in aacDecoder_drcExtractAndMap()

In the aacDecoder_drcExtractAndMap() function, self->numThreads
  can be used after having exceeded its intended max value,
  MAX_DRC_THREADS, causing memory to be cleared after the
  threadBs[MAX_DRC_THREADS] array.
The crash is prevented by never using self->numThreads with
  a value equal to or greater than MAX_DRC_THREADS.
A proper fix will be required as there seems to be an issue as
  to which entry in the threadBs array is meant to be initialized
  and used.

Bug 26751339

Change-Id: I655cc40c35d4206ab72e83b2bdb751be2fe52b5a
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (self->numThreads >= MAX_DRC_THREADS) {', '      self->numThreads = MAX_DRC_THREADS - 1;', '  }', '', '', '  if (self->numThreads >= MAX_DRC_THREADS) {', '      self->numThreads = MAX_DRC_THREADS - 1;', '  }']}
description: libAACdec/src/aacdec_drc.cpp in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-05-01 does not properly limit the number of threads, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (stack memory corruption) via a crafted media file, aka internal bug 26751339.

code_evidence: Fixed-size arrays threadBs, validThreadBs, and numExcludedChns are sized MAX_DRC_THREADS; self->numThreads is used as their index.
The DVB branch unconditionally clears and writes threadBs[self->numThreads] before parsing, with no check that numThreads is below MAX_DRC_THREADS.
If parsing succeeds, numThreads is incremented without any upper bound, so it can reach or exceed MAX_DRC_THREADS.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to a fixed-size stack buffer using an unbounded index, producing an out-of-bounds write, which is the core of CWE-119. The patch's added clamp confirms the missing bound; this is a buffer-boundary violation rather than a pure integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: self->numThreads is incremented after a successful DVB payload parse without enforcing the MAX_DRC_THREADS limit, while it indexes the fixed-size threadBs array. Trigger: a crafted media file providing DVB ancillary data (and prior payloads) that drives numThreads to MAX_DRC_THREADS. Consequence: FDKmemclear and bandTop writes at threadBs[self->numThreads] occur past the array end, corrupting adjacent stack memory.

commit_msg:
x86/PV: check GDT/LDT limits during emulation

Accesses beyond the LDT limit originating from emulation would trigger
the ASSERT() in pv_map_ldt_shadow_page(). On production builds such
accesses would cause an attempt to promote the touched page (offset from
the present LDT base address) to a segment descriptor one. If this
happens to succeed, guest user mode would be able to elevate its
privileges to that of the guest kernel. This is particularly easy when
there's no LDT at all, in which case the LDT base stored internally to
Xen is simply zero.

Also adjust the ASSERT() that was triggering: It was off by one to
begin with, and for production builds we also better use
ASSERT_UNREACHABLE() instead with suitable recovery code afterwards.

This is XSA-298.

Reported-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
