description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing 32-bit PV guest OS users to gain guest OS privileges by installing and using descriptors. There is missing descriptor table limit checking in x86 PV emulation. When emulating certain PV guest operations, descriptor table accesses are performed by the emulating code. Such accesses should respect the guest specified limits, unless otherwise guaranteed to fail in such a case. Without this, emulation of 32-bit guest user mode calls through call gates would allow guest user mode to install and then use descriptors of their choice, as long as the guest kernel did not itself install an LDT. (Most OSes don't install any LDT by default). 32-bit PV guest user mode can elevate its privileges to that of the guest kernel. Xen versions from at least 3.2 onwards are affected. Only 32-bit PV guest user mode can leverage this vulnerability. HVM, PVH, as well as 64-bit PV guests cannot leverage this vulnerability. Arm systems are unaffected.

code_evidence: The function reads a segment descriptor for selector sel. The pre-patch guard only zeroes desc for sel < 4; for any sel >= 4 it calls __get_user(desc, gdt_ldt_desc_ptr(sel)) without verifying that an LDT selector's index is below v->arch.pv.ldt_ents. Thus emulation of a user-mode LDT access can fetch a descriptor from memory beyond the LDT, including when no LDT exists (base zero).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked descriptor-table access lets a low-privileged guest user-mode actor obtain and exercise kernel-level descriptor privileges, i.e. improper privilege management enabling unintended privilege escalation. The flaw is the missing limit constraint, not merely the resulting privilege gain.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing LDT limit check before dereferencing the descriptor table during PV emulation. Trigger: a 32-bit PV guest user-mode call through a call gate with an LDT selector whose index exceeds ldt_ents (or with no LDT installed). The out-of-bounds descriptor is returned and used, allowing user mode to install and use descriptors of its choice, escalating to guest-kernel privilege.

commit_msg: Fix to prevent SASL security vulnerability
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ["      if (*parv[1] == ':' || strchr(parv[1], ' '))", '\t\treturn exit_client(cptr, sptr, sptr, "Malformed AUTHENTICATE");', "      if (*parv[1] == ':' || strchr(parv[1], ' '))", '        return exit_client(cptr, sptr, sptr, "Malformed AUTHENTICATE");']}
description: The m_authenticate function in ircd/m_authenticate.c in nefarious2 allows remote attackers to spoof certificate fingerprints and consequently log in as another user via a crafted AUTHENTICATE parameter.

code_evidence: Function derives hoststr from the client socket host/IP and brackets it into realhost when it contains a colon.

In the first SASL exchange, parv[1] (the AUTHENTICATE payload) is sent to the SASL agent together with cli_sslclifp(cptr) as the SSL client fingerprint via sendcmdto_one format '%C %C!%u.%u S %s :%s'.
The same unvalidated parv[1] is forwarded to other servers in the non-agent branch via sendcmdto_serv_butone with the identical S/SSL-fingerprint format.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unvalidated parameter lets an attacker manipulate the data used in the SASL authentication exchange, undermining proof of identity and enabling impersonation, which is improper authentication (CWE-287). This is not merely input validation; the defect is that identity-proving data is not adequately verified.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the AUTHENTICATE parameter parv[1] is forwarded into the SASL protocol message without rejecting leading ':' or embedded spaces, so it can alter the field structure of the relayed SASL message. Trigger: a remote client sends a crafted first AUTHENTICATE value. Consequence: the SASL agent/other servers may parse a spoofed certificate fingerprint field, allowing an attacker to be authenticated as another user.

commit_msg:
Avoid bogus values in PT_DYNAMIC segment.

Detect duplicate DT_*.
Detect out-of-bounds hashtab and gashtab.
Detect missing DT_REL, DT_RELA.
Detect out-of-bounds d_val.
https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/317
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (t) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (t && t < file_size) {']}
description: p_lx_elf.cpp in UPX before 3.96 has an integer overflow during unpacking via crafted values in a PT_DYNAMIC segment.

code_evidence: Line 8 derives offset t from the untrusted DT_* d_val via elf_get_offset_from_address; line 9 only checks t != 0 before line 10 computes t + file_image and returns it as a pointer into the file image, with no upper bound on t.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe addition t + file_image in line 10 is performed without constraining t to file_size, so the sum can overflow the pointer/integer representation and produce a bogus location. That matches CWE-190's integer overflow/wraparound in offset computation; the missing bound check is the specific manifestation, not a separate weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DT entry's d_val is attacker-controlled and the resulting offset t is only tested for nonzero, not against file_size. A crafted PT_DYNAMIC value yields an offset near/at the address-space limit, so t + file_image wraps around; the returned pointer then points before the intended image, and subsequent reads/uses operate on bogus data. Trigger is a malicious ELF PT_DYNAMIC segment; consequence is out-of-bounds access driven by the wrapped offset.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  /* All offsets have now been checked. */', '  value.ordered_offsets_up_to = G_MAXSIZE;', '']}
description: A flaw was found in GLib. GVariant deserialization is vulnerable to an exponential blowup issue where a crafted GVariant can cause excessive processing, leading to denial of service.

code_evidence: The function obtains frame offsets from the untrusted serialized value and rejects the array only if offsets.is_normal is false, which relies on the offset table being self-consistent.
It reads each element end offset from the untrusted offsets.array and checks this_end < offset or this_end > offsets.data_size, bounding each child within the data region.
The alignment padding loop validates padding bytes; otherwise ordering/overlap between consecutive child elements is not checked here.
The final assert only verifies offset equals offsets.data_size, which holds for consistent frames but does not prevent overlapping child frames.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function validates deserialized untrusted GVariant data; its incomplete ordering/overlap constraint permits malformed serialized input to produce an inconsistent in-memory value, matching deserialization of untrusted data without sufficient validity checks. This is the missing-validation aspect of CWE-502 rather than an integer or memory-safety weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
g_assert (offset == offsets.data_size);
return TRUE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: this normality check trusts the frame offset table and does not detect child elements whose frames overlap each other. Trigger: crafted non-normal GVariant data whose offsets are individually in range but not monotonically ordered. Consequence: overlapping children can cause the deserialized value to normalize to a much larger type, leading to excessive processing and denial of service.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tjas_tvparser_destroy(tvp);'], 'added_lines': ['\tjas_tvparser_destroy(tvp);']}
description: Use-after-free vulnerability in the mif_process_cmpt function in libjasper/mif/mif_cod.c in the JasPer JPEG-2000 library before 1.900.2 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a crafted JPEG 2000 image file.

This is use-after-free rather than a mere double free, since the pointer is dereferenced by the destroy routine after its lifetime ended.

commit_msg:
Check whether there is enough space for ND6 option headers when processing
incoming packets.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  while(uip_l3_icmp_hdr_len + nd6_opt_offset < uip_len) {'], 'added_lines': ['  while(uip_l3_icmp_hdr_len + nd6_opt_offset + UIP_ND6_OPT_HDR_LEN < uip_len) {', '      if(uip_l3_icmp_hdr_len + nd6_opt_offset +', '         UIP_ND6_OPT_DATA_OFFSET + UIP_LLADDR_LEN > uip_len) {', '        LOG_ERR("Insufficient data for NS SLLAO option\\n");', '        goto discard;', '      }']}
description: Contiki-NG is an open-source, cross-platform operating system for IoT devices. Because of insufficient validation of IPv6 neighbor discovery options in Contiki-NG, attackers can send neighbor solicitation packets that trigger an out-of-bounds read. The problem exists in the module os/net/ipv6/uip-nd6.c, where memory read operations from the main packet buffer, uip_buf, are not checked if they go out of bounds. In particular, this problem can occur when attempting to read the 2-byte option header and the Source Link-Layer Address Option (SLLAO). This attack requires ipv6 be enabled for the network. The problem has been patched in the develop branch of Contiki-NG. The upcoming 4.8 release of Contiki-NG will include the patch.Users unable to upgrade may apply the patch in Contiki-NG PR #1654.

code_evidence: The option-walking loop guard [23] only ensures the offset is less than uip_len before dereferencing ND6_OPT_HDR_BUF(nd6_opt_offset)->len [25] and ->type [30], so the 2-byte option header may extend past the packet end.

On the SLLAO path [32] nd6_opt_llao points into uip_buf without checking that UIP_ND6_OPT_DATA_OFFSET + UIP_LLADDR_LEN bytes exist; extract_lladdr_from_llao_aligned [40] and memcmp over nd6_opt_llao[UIP_ND6_OPT_DATA_OFFSET] [50,51] then read past the buffer.
The offset advances by the attacker-controlled option length [72], letting crafted NS options position the read beyond uip_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe reads of option header fields and the SLLAO data beyond the packet buffer directly match CWE-125 (reading past the end of an intended buffer). It is not CWE-787 because no out-of-bounds write occurs.

evidence_lines.code: nd6_opt_offset += (ND6_OPT_HDR_BUF(nd6_opt_offset)->len << 3);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the NS option loop lacks bounds checks for the option header and SLLAO data, so attacker-supplied IPv6 neighbor solicitation options can make ND6_OPT_HDR_BUF and the SLLAO reads run past uip_buf. Trigger: a malformed NS packet with truncated options; consequence is an out-of-bounds read (memory disclosure or crash), not a write.

commit_msg: opj_j2k_write_sot(): fix potential write heap buffer overflow (#991)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (! opj_j2k_write_sot(p_j2k, p_data, &l_current_nb_bytes_written, p_stream,', '            if (! opj_j2k_write_sot(p_j2k, p_data, &l_current_nb_bytes_written, p_stream,'], 'added_lines': ['        if (! opj_j2k_write_sot(p_j2k, p_data,', '                                p_total_data_size,', '                                &l_current_nb_bytes_written,', '                                p_stream,', '            if (! opj_j2k_write_sot(p_j2k, p_data,', '                                    p_total_data_size,', '                                    &l_current_nb_bytes_written, p_stream,']}
description: A size-validation issue was discovered in opj_j2k_write_sot in lib/openjp2/j2k.c in OpenJPEG 2.2.0. The vulnerability causes an out-of-bounds write, which may lead to remote denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow affecting opj_write_bytes_LE in lib/openjp2/cio.c) or possibly remote code execution. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-14152.

code_evidence: The first tile-part loop calls opj_j2k_write_sot without passing p_total_data_size, so the SOT writer has no knowledge of the remaining buffer capacity.
After the SOT write, p_data is advanced by l_current_nb_bytes_written and p_total_data_size is decremented, but the write itself was not bounded against the available size.
The SOD write is passed p_total_data_size, yet p_data was already advanced past the SOT bytes; the remaining size and pointer are only tracked after the fact.
The POC loop repeats the same unbounded opj_j2k_write_sot call, again without the remaining-size argument.
p_data and p_total_data_size are updated after each write rather than used to constrain the preceding write.
The same pattern repeats after the SOD write: pointer and size are adjusted after the write, so no pre-write bound prevents writing beyond the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes SOT/SOD data through p_data without enforcing the remaining buffer capacity before the write, producing a write past the end of the heap buffer. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read, as the unsafe operation is a write into the output buffer.

evidence_lines.code:
p_data += l_current_nb_bytes_written;
p_total_data_size -= l_current_nb_bytes_written;

p_data += l_current_nb_bytes_written;
p_total_data_size -= l_current_nb_bytes_written;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: opj_j2k_write_sot is invoked without the remaining buffer size, so the SOT write can exceed the destination buffer. Trigger: multiple tile-parts or POCs cause repeated writes that consume more space than p_total_data_size allows. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds write, leading to denial of service or potential code execution.

description: An issue was discovered in CCN-lite 2.0.1. There is a heap-based buffer overflow in mkAddToRelayCacheRequest and in ccnl_populate_cache for an array lacking '\0' termination when reading a binary CCNx or NDN file. This is an out-of-bounds write rather than a read (CWE-125) because the missing terminator enables writing beyond the allocation.

Trigger: reading a binary CCNx/NDN file whose contents are later processed as a NUL-terminated string. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write past the heap allocation, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg:
checkout: fix bug that makes checkout follow symlinks in leading path

Before checking out a file, we have to confirm that all of its leading
components are real existing directories. And to reduce the number of
lstat() calls in this process, we cache the last leading path known to
contain only directories. However, when a path collision occurs (e.g.
when checking out case-sensitive files in case-insensitive file
systems), a cached path might have its file type changed on disk,
leaving the cache on an invalid state. Normally, this doesn't bring
any bad consequences as we usually check out files in index order, and
therefore, by the time the cached path becomes outdated, we no longer
need it anyway (because all files in that directory would have already
been written).

But, there are some users of the checkout machinery that do not always
follow the index order. In particular: checkout-index writes the paths
in the same order that they appear on the CLI (or stdin); and the
delayed checkout feature -- used when a long-running filter process
replies with "status=delayed" -- postpones the checkout of some entries,
thus modifying the checkout order.

When we have to check out an out-of-order entry and the lstat() cache is
invalid (due to a previous path collision), checkout_entry() may end up
using the invalid data and thrusting that the leading components are
real directories when, in reality, they are not. In the best case
scenario, where the directory was replaced by a regular file, the user
will get an error: "fatal: unable to create file 'foo/bar': Not a
directory". But if the directory was replaced by a symlink, checkout
could actually end up following the symlink and writing the file at a
wrong place, even outside the repository. Since delayed checkout is
affected by this bug, it could be used by an attacker to write
arbitrary files during the clone of a maliciously crafted repository.

Some candidate solutions considered were to disable the lstat() cache
during unordered checkouts or sort the entries before passing them to
the checkout machinery. But both ideas include some performance penalty
and they don't future-proof the code against new unordered use cases.

Instead, we now manually reset the lstat cache whenever we successfully
remove a directory. Note: We are not even checking whether the directory
was the same as the lstat cache points to because we might face a
scenario where the paths refer to the same location but differ due to
case folding, precomposed UTF-8 issues, or the presence of `..`
components in the path. Two regression tests, with case-collisions and
utf8-collisions, are also added for both checkout-index and delayed
checkout.

Note: to make the previously mentioned clone attack unfeasible, it would
be sufficient to reset the lstat cache only after the remove_subtree()
call inside checkout_entry(). This is the place where we would remove a
directory whose path collides with the path of another entry that we are
currently trying to check out (possibly a symlink). However, in the
interest of a thorough fix that does not leave Git open to
similar-but-not-identical attack vectors, we decided to intercept
all `rmdir()` calls in one fell swoop.

This addresses CVE-2021-21300.

Co-authored-by: Johannes Schindelin <johannes.schindelin@gmx.de>
Signed-off-by: Matheus Tavares <matheus.bernardino@usp.br>

description: Git is an open-source distributed revision control system. In affected versions of Git a specially crafted repository that contains symbolic links as well as files using a clean/smudge filter such as Git LFS, may cause just-checked out script to be executed while cloning onto a case-insensitive file system such as NTFS, HFS+ or APFS (i.e. the default file systems on Windows and macOS). Note that clean/smudge filters have to be configured for that. Git for Windows configures Git LFS by default, and is therefore vulnerable. The problem has been patched in the versions published on Tuesday, March 9th, 2021. As a workaound, if symbolic link support is disabled in Git (e.g. via `git config --global core.symlinks false`), the described attack won't work. Likewise, if no clean/smudge filters such as Git LFS are configured globally (i.e. _before_ cloning), the attack is foiled. As always, it is best to avoid cloning repositories from untrusted sources. The earliest impacted version is 2.14.2. The fix versions are: 2.30.1, 2.29.3, 2.28.1, 2.27.1, 2.26.3, 2.25.5, 2.24.4, 2.23.4, 2.22.5, 2.21.4, 2.20.5, 2.19.6, 2.18.5, 2.17.62.17.6.

code_evidence: The function performs directory removal via _wrmdir(wpathname) in two loops (lines 7 and 22) but never invalidates the lstat cache on success. The patch adds cache invalidation only after a successful removal, showing the pre-patch function leaves stale cache state. The retry logic checks EACCES, empty-directory status, and file-in-use errors, but none of these guards the identity of the path being removed or refreshes cached leading-path directory assumptions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's failure to reset the lstat cache after a successful rmdir allows a path component to resolve to a symlink that is subsequently followed during file access, which is exactly improper link resolution before file access. CWE-59 fits because the stale cached directory identity lets a symlink substitute for an intended directory during checkout.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mingw_rmdir removes a directory without invalidating the cached lstat leading-path state. Trigger: an out-of-order checkout (checkout-index or delayed checkout) where a cached path was replaced by a symlink. Consequence: later checkout_entry() trusts the stale cache, follows the symlink, and writes files outside the repository, enabling arbitrary file write/execution.

commit_msg:
Fix a possible heap-buffer-overflow in archive_string_append_from_wcs()

When we grow the archive_string buffer, we have to make sure it fits
at least one maximum-sized multibyte character in the current locale
and the null character.

Fixes #1298
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t    as->length + len * 2 + 1) == NULL)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t    as->length + max(len * 2,', '\t\t\t    (size_t)MB_CUR_MAX) + 1) == NULL)']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in archive_string_append_from_wcs() (archive_string.c) in libarchive-3.4.1dev allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write in heap memory resulting into a crash) via a crafted archive file. NOTE: this only affects users who downloaded the development code from GitHub. Users of the product's official releases are unaffected.

code_evidence: Line 21 sets the write bound end to buffer_length - MB_CUR_MAX - 1, reserving room for one maximum multibyte character. When p reaches end (line 24), the buffer is grown using only as->length + len * 2 + 1 (line 27), which may not reserve MB_CUR_MAX bytes plus the terminator. wcrtomb/wctomb (lines 40/42) can then write up to MB_CUR_MAX bytes at p, and p += n (line 46) advances past the allocated buffer; the trailing as->s[as->length]='\0' (line 49) can also fall out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes converted multibyte characters and a terminator past the end of a heap buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The root cause is an undersized allocation constraint rather than a read overrun or an integer overflow in the size computation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The growth request fails to guarantee space for a maximum-sized multibyte character and the null terminator. If len is small while the current locale's MB_CUR_MAX is large, the reallocated buffer is too short, so wcrtomb writes beyond it, causing a heap out-of-bounds write and possible crash.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a heap buffer overflow in Eigen implementation of `tf.raw_ops.BandedTriangularSolve`. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/eccb7ec454e6617738554a255d77f08e60ee0808/tensorflow/core/kernels/linalg/banded_triangular_solve_op.cc#L269-L278) calls `ValidateInputTensors` for input validation but fails to validate that the two tensors are not empty. Furthermore, since `OP_REQUIRES` macro only stops execution of current function after setting `ctx->status()` to a non-OK value, callers of helper functions that use `OP_REQUIRES` must check value of `ctx->status()` before continuing. This doesn't happen in this op's implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/eccb7ec454e6617738554a255d77f08e60ee0808/tensorflow/core/kernels/linalg/banded_triangular_solve_op.cc#L219), hence the validation that is present is also not effective. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function reads both inputs, calls ValidateInputTensors(ctx, in0, in1), which reports failures only via ctx->status(), and then proceeds to MatMulBCast using in0/in1 shapes without checking ctx->status().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing status check allows invalid tensor state to reach the Eigen kernel, which writes past the intended buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). This is distinct from merely missing input validation (CWE-20) because the supported consequence is a memory write violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value/status of input validation is ignored, so execution continues after a failed validation (e.g., empty tensors). Trigger: a caller supplies malformed/empty tensors such that ValidateInputTensors sets a non-OK status. Consequence: subsequent shape and launch logic runs on invalid tensors, leading to a heap buffer overflow in the Eigen banded triangular solve.

commit_msg:
wmem: Fix leak in block_fast when realloc'ing jumbo blocks

In block fast wmem_allocator is used, keep the double linked
list of jumbo blocks accurate by pointing the prev pointer of
the old head (if it exists) to the newly allocated jumbo block.

This prevents a leak if a jumbo block which is not the most
recently added jumbo block is realloc'ed. If the prev pointer
isn't set properly, then all the jumbo blocks added afterwards
will be lost from the list and leaked.

Fix #19259

description: BT SDP dissector memory leak in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.7 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.15 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: The jumbo block is linked into allocator->jumbo_list by setting block->next = allocator->jumbo_list and block->prev = NULL, then replacing the list head. The previously-head block's prev pointer is never updated to point to the new block.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing prev-pointer update leaves allocated jumbo blocks untracked and unreleasable, which is a missing release of memory after its effective lifetime (CWE-401). The root cause is list-linkage bookkeeping, and the supported consequence is memory leak leading to DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a jumbo block that is not the current head is realloc'ed, the new block's prev is set to NULL and the old head's prev still points to the replaced block. The doubly linked list is broken, so subsequent jumbo blocks become unreachable from the head and their memory is never released, causing a leak and resource-consumption DoS.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.4+
Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>

commit_msg:
Bug 697762: Fix scan converter SEGVs.

The SEGVs are caused by the scan converter allowing less room
in the table than is actually required. This happens due to
the mark_curve subdivision overflowing.

For example, if we have a curve such as:

 0 0x80000000 moveto
 0 0x80000000 0 0x80000000 0 0x80000000 curveto

Then the current subdivision logic does:

 fixed ay = (sy + c1y)>>1

For sy = c1y = 0x80000000 this gives ay = 0, when clearly
the average should be 0x80000000.

An alternative formulation of the splitting code:

 fixed ay = (sy>>1) + (c1y>>1)

gives the required result, at the expense of dropping accuracy at
the low end.

This commit therefore has 2 formulations of the splitting code, one
for 'big' values (values that might overflow), and ones for normal
values (values that won't).

We select between the two pieces of code by comparing the top 2
bits of each value; if they differ, then we use the big variant.

Also, when calculating the size of the table required, we were
incorrectly closing the curve more often than we needed to. This
had no ill effect other than inflating the amount of memory we
needed.

The call site here is the dispatch that invokes the vulnerable routine; the overflow itself is in the callee, so this function supports the label only as the caller path.

commit_msg:
copy: CVE-2022-0485: Fail nbdcopy if NBD read or write fails

nbdcopy has a nasty bug when performing multi-threaded copies using
asynchronous nbd calls - it was blindly treating the completion of an
asynchronous command as successful, rather than checking the *error
parameter.  This can result in the silent creation of a corrupted
image in two different ways: when a read fails, we blindly wrote
garbage to the destination; when a write fails, we did not flag that
the destination was not written.

Since nbdcopy already calls exit() on a synchronous read or write
failure to a file, doing the same for an asynchronous op to an NBD
server is the simplest solution.  A nicer solution, but more invasive
to code and thus not done here, might be to allow up to N retries of
the transaction (in case the read or write failure was transient), or
even having a mode where as much data is copied as possible (portions
of the copy that failed would be logged on stderr, and nbdcopy would
still fail with a non-zero exit status, but this would copy more than
just stopping at the first error, as can be done with rsync or
ddrescue).

Note that since we rely on auto-retiring and do NOT call
nbd_aio_command_completed, our completion callbacks must always return
1 (if they do not exit() first), even when acting on *error, so as not
leave the command allocated until nbd_close.  As such, there is no
sane way to return an error to a manual caller of the callback, and
therefore we can drop dead code that calls perror() and exit() if the
callback "failed".  It is also worth documenting the contract on when
we must manually call the callback during the asynch_zero callback, so
that we do not leak or double-free the command; thankfully, all the
existing code paths were correct.

The added testsuite script demonstrates several scenarios, some of
which fail without the rest of this patch in place, and others which
showcase ways in which sparse images can bypass errors.

Once backports are complete, a followup patch on the main branch will
edit docs/libnbd-security.pod with the mailing list announcement of
the stable branch commit ids and release versions that incorporate
this fix.

At [97-106] the loop then reads count bytes one at a time from the blob, so a large count drives both a large allocation and a long read loop.

Trigger: an 8BIM resource block whose length field is a very large non-negative value. Consequence: the allocation at [90] and the byte-by-byte loop at [97-106] consume memory and processing proportional to the attacker-chosen count, exhausting resources and causing denial of service.

When using AMI GetConfig, it was possible to access files outside of the
Asterisk configuration directory by using filenames with ".." and "./"
even while live_dangerously was not enabled. This change resolves the
full path and ensures we are still in the configuration directory before
attempting to access the file.

commit_msg:
WireGuard: fix null pointer crash

It was assumed that the WireGuard dissector is always called on the
first pass before the second pass. That might not be the case when the
heuristics dissector sets a conversation dissector later in the stream.
Be prepared to handle this case. Do not simply abort, the previous
packets may be valid data messages.

This is an integer overflow used as a size/offset, not merely a logic error.

evidence_lines.code: Jsi_ObjSetLength(interp, obj, curlen+argc);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sum curlen+argc is computed in signed int without an overflow guard, and the negative-curlen clamp does not constrain large values. Trigger: unshift on an array whose length plus argument count exceeds INT_MAX. The wrapped value can pass or distort the sizer check and drive memmove and arrCnt with an incorrect size/offset, causing memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg: Check for image list before we destroy the last image in XCF coder (patch sent privately by Андрей Черный)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  DestroyImage(RemoveFirstImageFromList(&image));'], 'added_lines': ['  if (GetNextImageInList(image) != (Image *) NULL)', '    DestroyImage(RemoveFirstImageFromList(&image));']}
description: An issue was discovered in ImageMagick 6.9.7. A specially crafted xcf file could lead to a NULL pointer dereference.

code_evidence: The layer loop appends each layer image onto the list via AppendImageToList(&image,layer_info[j].image); if number_layers is zero this loop body never executes, so the list is not extended.

After CloseBlob(image), the code unconditionally calls DestroyImage(RemoveFirstImageFromList(&image)); RemoveFirstImageFromList returns NULL when the list is empty, and DestroyImage then dereferences that NULL pointer. The subsequent image->type access at line 271 also relies on image being non-NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This directly matches CWE-476: a pointer expected to be valid is NULL and is dereferenced without a check. The fix adds a GetNextImageInList guard before destruction, confirming the missing constraint rather than a use-after-free or out-of-bounds issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the list-destruction call assumes at least one image remains in the list, but a crafted XCF with zero layers leaves the list empty. Trigger: reading such a file reaches line 269 with an empty list; RemoveFirstImageFromList returns NULL and DestroyImage dereferences it, causing a NULL pointer dereference and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
The bg_flags field in the block group descripts is only valid if the
uninit_bg or metadata_csum feature is enabled.  We were not
consistently looking at this field; fix this.

Also block group #0 must never have uninitialized allocation bitmaps,
or need to be zeroed, since that's where the root inode, and other
special inodes are set up.  Check for these conditions and mark the
file system as corrupted if they are detected.

This addresses CVE-2018-10876.

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=199403

Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org

description: A flaw was found in Linux kernel in the ext4 filesystem code. A use-after-free is possible in ext4_ext_remove_space() function when mounting and operating a crafted ext4 image.

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \

    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Reviewed-by: Simon Horman <simon.horman@corigine.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tllcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local);'], 'added_lines': ['\tllcp_sock->local = local;']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: nfc_llcp_find_local(dev) at line 28 returns a local pointer without holding a reference, and only at line 34 is nfc_llcp_local_get() called to acquire one. Between these two operations the local can be released by a concurrent nfc_llcp_unregister_device path, so the reference grabbed at line 34 may act on already-freed memory. The patch changes line 34 to 'llcp_sock->local = local;' because the lookup itself now returns a referenced object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the code retains and later uses a pointer to an object that can be freed before the reference is taken. This is a lifetime/race use-after-free, not merely a null-pointer or reference-count leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the local object is fetched from the list without a reference, then referenced later in a separate step, leaving a race window. Trigger: concurrent unregister/cleanup frees the local between lookup and get. Consequence: the socket stores a dangling local pointer, later dereferenced (e.g., in nfc_llcp_sock_link), causing use-after-free reads or corruption.

commit_msg:
vms: fix the search for the packet length field.

The packet length field is of the form

    Total Length = DDD = ^xXXX

where "DDD" is the length in decimal and "XXX" is the length in
hexadecimal.

Search for "length ". not just "Length", as we skip past "Length ", not
just "Length", so if we assume we found "Length " but only found
"Length", we'd skip past the end of the string.

While we're at it, fail if we don't find a length field, rather than
just blithely acting as if the packet length were zero.

Fixes #19083.

commit_msg:
mctp: defer the kfree of object mdev->addrs

The function mctp_unregister() reclaims the device's relevant resource
when a netcard detaches. However, a running routine may be unaware of
this and cause the use-after-free of the mdev->addrs object.

The race condition can be demonstrated below

 cleanup thread               another thread
                          |
unregister_netdev()       |  mctp_sendmsg()
...                       |    ...
  mctp_unregister()       |    rt = mctp_route_lookup()
    ...                   |    mctl_local_output()
    kfree(mdev->addrs)    |      ...
                          |      saddr = rt->dev->addrs[0];
                          |

description: A flaw was found in the MCTP protocol in the Linux kernel. The function mctp_unregister() reclaims the device's relevant resource when a netcard detaches. commit_msg:
nfsd: check permissions when setting ACLs

Use set_posix_acl, which includes proper permission checks, instead of
calling ->set_acl directly.  Without this anyone may be able to grant
themselves permissions to a file by setting the ACL.

Lock the inode to make the new checks atomic with respect to set_acl.
(Also, nfsd was the only caller of set_acl not locking the inode, so I
suspect this may fix other races.)

This also simplifies the code, and ensures our ACLs are checked by
posix_acl_valid.

The permission checks and the inode locking were lost with commit
4ac7249e, which changed nfsd to use the set_acl inode operation directly
instead of going through xattr handlers.

Reported-by: David Sinquin <david@sinquin.eu>
[agreunba@redhat.com: use set_posix_acl]
Fixes: 4ac7249e
Cc: Christoph Hellwig <hch@infradead.org>
Cc: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: J. Bruce Fields <bfields@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!IS_POSIXACL(inode) || !inode->i_op->set_acl) {', '\t\terror = -EOPNOTSUPP;', '\t\tgoto out_errno;', '\t}', '\terror = inode->i_op->set_acl(inode, argp->acl_access, ACL_TYPE_ACCESS);', '\t\tgoto out_drop_write;', '\terror = inode->i_op->set_acl(inode, argp->acl_default,', '\t\t\t\t     ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT);', 'out_drop_write:'], 'added_lines': ['\tfh_lock(fh);', '', '\terror = set_posix_acl(inode, ACL_TYPE_ACCESS, argp->acl_access);', '\t\tgoto out_drop_lock;', '\terror = set_posix_acl(inode, ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT, argp->acl_default);', 'out_drop_lock:', '\tfh_unlock(fh);']}
description: nfsd in the Linux kernel through 4.6.3 allows local users to bypass intended file-permission restrictions by setting a POSIX ACL, related to nfs2acl.c, nfs3acl.c, and nfs4acl.c.

code_evidence: fh_verify is called with NFSD_MAY_SATTR, so the caller is only checked for attribute-set permission, not for the ownership/permission constraints required to change an ACL.
The inode is derived from the verified filehandle, then fh_want_write is called; no check restricts who may modify the ACL beyond the SATTR permission.
The ACL is applied by invoking inode->i_op->set_acl directly, bypassing set_posix_acl and its permission checks (the inode is not locked here either).
The default ACL is likewise set through the raw inode operation with no additional authorization check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-284 fits because the function fails to enforce the access-control policy governing who may alter a file's ACL: it checks only SATTR and bypasses the ACL permission checks, allowing unauthorized actors to change permissions.

evidence_lines.code:
error = inode->i_op->set_acl(inode, argp->acl_default,
ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nfsd3_proc_setacl calls the inode's set_acl operation directly instead of the permission-checking set_posix_acl path. Trigger: a local user who passes the coarse NFSD_MAY_SATTR check submits an ACL granting themselves access. Consequence: the ACL is installed without ownership/permission validation, letting the user grant permissions they should not have.

commit_msg:
httplive: fix use-after-free

Implement a mutex to ensure secure multi-threaded
access to the KeyedVector in MetaDataBase.
Concurrent access by different threads can lead
to accessing the wrong memory location due to
potential changes in the vector

Bug: 298057702
Test: HTTP Live Streaming test
(cherry picked from https://partner-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:a2dfb31957a9d5358d0219a0eda7dcb5b0fff5fe)
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:90fb4ca425444429ada6ce0de1c13d35829bc196)
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:3c1d9613ef64e01d2e81c4aa44c90dcd8ca958b9)
Merged-In: I46b05c85d9c39f4ce549efc160c08a0646c9fd0a
Change-Id: I46b05c85d9c39f4ce549efc160c08a0646c9fd0a
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> guard(mInternalData->mLock);']}
description: In multiple functions of MetaDataBase.cpp, there is a possible UAF write due to a race condition. This could lead to remote escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: Line 3 reads mItems.size() and line 4 serializes that count into the parcel without holding any lock on mInternalData, so the size snapshot can diverge from the container state actually iterated.

Lines 8-10 iterate mItems using keyAt(i) and valueAt(i) with i bounded by the earlier numItems, then line 14 dereferences the returned typed_data reference; if another thread mutates or reallocates mItems concurrently, indices become stale and valueAt/keyAt can access freed or wrong memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a multi-step read of a shared resource with no exclusive-access guarantee, allowing an interfering concurrent sequence to change the resource mid-operation. This is exactly a race condition (CWE-362); the UAF is the downstream consequence, not the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
size_t numItems = mInternalData->mItems.size();
ret = parcel.writeUint32(uint32_t(numItems));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: writeToParcel accesses the shared KeyedVector mItems without synchronization, while other threads modify the same vector. Trigger: concurrent modification between the size() read and the indexed keyAt/valueAt accesses. Consequence: stale indices cause out-of-bounds or use-after-free access, yielding memory corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
Bug 697015: Avoid object references vanishing during repair.

A PDF repair can be triggered 'just in time', when we encounter
a problem in the file. The idea is that this can happen without
the enclosing code being aware of it.

Thus the enclosing code may be holding 'borrowed' references
(such as those returned by pdf_dict_get()) at the time when the
repair is triggered. We are therefore at pains to ensure that
the repair does not replace any objects that exist already, so
that the calling code will not have these references unexpectedly
invalidated.

The sole exception to this is when we replace the 'Length' fields
in stream dictionaries with the actual lengths. Bug 697015 shows
exactly this situation causing a reference to become invalid.

The solution implemented here is to add an 'orphan list' to the
document, where we put these (hopefully few, small) objects. These
orphans are kept around until the document is closed.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tpdf_dict_put(ctx, dict, PDF_NAME_Length, length);', '\t\t\t\tpdf_drop_obj(ctx, length);', ''], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tpdf_obj *old_obj = NULL;', '\t\t\t\tpdf_dict_get_put_drop(ctx, dict, PDF_NAME_Length, length, &old_obj);', '\t\t\t\tif (old_obj)', '\t\t\t\t\torphan_object(ctx, doc, old_obj);']}
description: The pdf_to_num function in pdf-object.c in MuPDF before 1.10 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: At [203]-[205], when a stream length is present and no encryption is active, the code loads the object dictionary via pdf_load_object, obtaining a borrowed reference. At [206]-[208], a new Length integer is created and inserted with pdf_dict_put, which replaces the existing Length value; the old value is not retained or orphaned before insertion, so any borrowed reference held by the enclosing repair code can be invalidated. The dict reference is dropped at [209], but that does not preserve the replaced child object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the replaced Length object can be freed while an outstanding borrowed reference still points to it, and later use of that reference accesses freed memory. This is not merely a memory leak; the defect is the invalidated reference, matching use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pdf_dict_put replaces the existing Length entry without preserving the old object, even though repair may be triggered just-in-time while callers hold borrowed references. Trigger: a crafted PDF whose stream dictionary Length is replaced during repair. Consequence: the borrowed reference is used after the underlying object is freed, causing a use-after-free and crash.

commit_msg: Fixed bug #69090 (check cached files permissions)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#ifndef ZEND_WIN32', '\thash_value ^= ZCG(root_hash);', '#endif']}
description: An issue was discovered in PHP 5.x and 7.x, when the configuration uses apache2handler/mod_php or php-fpm with OpCache enabled. With 5.x after 5.6.28 or 7.x after 7.0.13, the issue is resolved in a non-default configuration with the opcache.validate_permission=1 setting. The vulnerability details are as follows. In PHP SAPIs where PHP interpreters share a common parent process, Zend OpCache creates a shared memory object owned by the common parent during initialization. Child PHP processes inherit the SHM descriptor, using it to cache and retrieve compiled script bytecode ("opcode" in PHP jargon). Cache keys vary depending on configuration, but filename is a central key component, and compiled opcode can generally be run if a script's filename is known or can be guessed. Many common shared-hosting configurations change EUID in child processes to enforce privilege separation among hosted users (for example using mod_ruid2 for the Apache HTTP Server, or php-fpm user settings). In these scenarios, the default Zend OpCache behavior defeats script file permissions by sharing a single SHM cache among all child PHP processes. PHP scripts often contain sensitive information: Think of CMS configurations where reading or running another user's script usually means gaining privileges to the CMS database.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only computes a hash and unlinks a matching cache entry; it contains no permission or privilege checks, and the permission-related fix (hash_value ^= ZCG(root_hash)) appears only in the diff, not in the provided func lines.

commit_msg:
[CVE-2020-1911] Look up HostObject computed properties on the right object in the prototype chain.

Summary:
The change in the hermes repository fixes the security vulnerability
CVE-2020-1911.  This vulnerability only affects applications which
allow evaluation of uncontrolled, untrusted JavaScript code not
shipped with the app, so React Native apps will generally not be affected.

This revision includes a test for the bug.  The test is generic JSI
code, so it is included in the hermes and react-native repositories.

Changelog: [Internal]

Reviewed By: tmikov

Differential Revision: D23322992

fbshipit-source-id: 4e88c974afe1ad33a263f9cac03e9dc98d33649a
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    auto propRes = vmcast<HostObject>(selfHandle.get())->get(id);'], 'added_lines': ['    auto propRes = vmcast<HostObject>(propObj.get())->get(id);']}
description: A type confusion vulnerability when resolving properties of JavaScript objects with specially-crafted prototype chains in Facebook Hermes prior to commit fe52854cdf6725c2eaa9e125995da76e6ceb27da allows attackers to potentially execute arbitrary code via crafted JavaScript. Note that this is only exploitable if the application using Hermes permits evaluation of untrusted JavaScript. Hence, most React Native applications are not affected.

code_evidence: getComputedPrimitiveDescriptor resolves the property descriptor and stores the object that actually owns the host object in propObj, which may differ from selfHandle when the property is found up the prototype chain.
In the hostObject branch the code casts selfHandle.get() to HostObject and calls get(id) on it, ignoring propObj.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Casting selfHandle, which is not guaranteed to be a HostObject, and then invoking HostObject::get is accessing a resource using an incompatible type, matching CWE-843. The fix casts propObj, the object whose descriptor actually carries the hostObject flag, restoring type agreement.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the host-object accessor is invoked on the receiver-side object selfHandle instead of the descriptor-owning object propObj. Trigger: a host object property reached via a prototype chain where selfHandle is not itself a HostObject. The vmcast then reinterprets a non-HostObject JSObject as HostObject, and the virtual get() call reads through an incompatible layout, causing type confusion that can lead to memory corruption or arbitrary code execution.

Fix heap-buffer-overflow in color_esycc_to_rgb (#748)

When all components do not have the same dx/dy, components buffer are
read beyond their end.
Do not convert in this case.

Update uclouvain/openjpeg#725

Lines 8-9 size the loop from component 0's w and h, and line 12 computes max = w * h. Line 13 iterates i < max, and line 15 indexes image->comps[1].data[i] and image->comps[2].data[i] with that same i.

commit_msg:
Both bpf_ringbuf_submit() and bpf_ringbuf_discard() have ARG_PTR_TO_ALLOC_MEM
in their bpf_func_proto definition as their first argument. They both expect
the result from a prior bpf_ringbuf_reserve() call which has a return type of
RET_PTR_TO_ALLOC_MEM_OR_NULL.

Meaning, after a NULL check in the code, the verifier will promote the register
type in the non-NULL branch to a PTR_TO_MEM and in the NULL branch to a known
zero scalar. Generally, pointer arithmetic on PTR_TO_MEM is allowed, so the
latter could have an offset.

The ARG_PTR_TO_ALLOC_MEM expects a PTR_TO_MEM register type. However, the non-
zero result from bpf_ringbuf_reserve() must be fed into either bpf_ringbuf_submit()
or bpf_ringbuf_discard() but with the original offset given it will then read
out the struct bpf_ringbuf_hdr mapping.

The verifier missed to enforce a zero offset, so that out of bounds access
can be triggered which could be used to escalate privileges if unprivileged
BPF was enabled (disabled by default in kernel).

Fixes: 457f44363a88 ("bpf: Implement BPF ring buffer and verifier support for it")
Reported-by: <tr3e.wang@gmail.com> (SecCoder Security Lab)
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: John Fastabend <john.fastabend@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>

+++ func_after
@@ -59,9 +59,15 @@
 	case PTR_TO_BUF:
 	case PTR_TO_BUF | MEM_RDONLY:
 	case PTR_TO_STACK:
+		/* Some of the argument types nevertheless require a
+		 * zero register offset.
+		 */
+		if (arg_type == ARG_PTR_TO_ALLOC_MEM)
+			goto force_off_check;
 		break;
 	/* All the rest must be rejected: */
 	default:
+force_off_check:
 		err = __check_ptr_off_reg(env, reg, regno,
 					  type == PTR_TO_BTF_ID);
 		if (err < 0)

Therefore, it might be better to check it and return -ENOMEM.

Reviewed-by: Leon Romanovsky <leonro@nvidia.com>

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.16-rc6. uapi_finalize in drivers/infiniband/core/uverbs_uapi.c lacks check of kmalloc_array().

code_evidence: kmalloc_array() return value is stored in data without any NULL check; the allocation size depends on uapi->num_write + uapi->num_write_ex, which can be large enough for the allocation to fail.
The loop immediately writes data[i] = &uapi->notsupp_method for every index, and data is later stored and offset into uapi->write_methods/write_ex_methods, all assuming data is non-NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (data) it expects to be valid but which can be NULL from a failed allocation, matching CWE-476. This is not a buffer overflow (CWE-787) because the flaw is the missing NULL check, not an out-of-bounds index.

uapi->write_methods = data;
uapi->write_ex_methods = data + uapi->num_write;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unchecked return of kmalloc_array() may be NULL on allocation failure. Trigger: sufficiently large num_write + num_write_ex (or memory pressure) makes the allocation fail; the subsequent loop dereferences the NULL data pointer, causing a kernel NULL-pointer dereference and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Release "3.0.6": Fix crashes in Array for "integer overflow #10"

FossilOrigin-Name: 50642d64b8f0a4e62df68e59fcb2ef0923c3dbec8fc8a15d38b1ddbe655c38d6
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int len = Jsi_ObjGetLength(interp, v->d.obj);'], 'added_lines': ['    int len = jsi_SizeOfArray(interp, v->d.obj);']}
description: Integer overflow vulnerability in function Jsi_ObjSetLength in jsish before 3.0.6, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: Line 20 obtains the array length as an int via Jsi_ObjGetLength; no upper-bound or overflow check is performed before using it.
The loop at lines 27-29 iterates i from 1 to len, calling Jsi_ValueArrayIndex for each index, so len drives the number of iterations and indexing operations.
Line 34 computes len - 1 and passes it to Jsi_ObjSetLength as the new array length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs arithmetic on a length value (len - 1 and loop bounds) assuming the int result remains valid and positive; an oversized length causes wraparound, matching CWE-190. The later crash/memory effects are consequences of that integer wraparound, not a separate weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
int len = Jsi_ObjGetLength(interp, v->d.obj);
if (len <= 0) return;
Jsi_ObjSetLength(interp, v->d.obj, len - 1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the array length is read into a signed int and used directly in loop bounds and a length-1 computation without validating that it fits and is non-negative. Trigger: a very large array length that overflows or wraps the int value. Supported consequence: the wrapped length corrupts the loop bounds/indexing and the new length passed to Jsi_ObjSetLength, leading to out-of-bounds or inconsistent array state rather than the intended decrement.

commit_msg:
Add support for different number of page table levels dependent
on the highest address used for a process. This will cause a 31 bit
process to use a two level page table instead of the four level page
table that is the default after the pud has been introduced. Likewise
a normal 64 bit process will use three levels instead of four. Only
if a process runs out of the 4 tera bytes which can be addressed with
a three level page table the fourth level is dynamically added. Then
the process can use up to 8 peta byte.

Signed-off-by: Martin Schwidefsky <schwidefsky@de.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tset_fs(current->thread.mm_segment);']}
description: The fork implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.5 on s390 platforms mishandles the case of four page-table levels, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted application, related to arch/s390/include/asm/mmu_context.h and arch/s390/include/asm/pgalloc.h.

code_evidence: update_mm derives the address-space control element from mm->pgd and mm->context.asce_bits without checking the number of page-table levels, and only conditionally adjusts pgd for the shadow table based on mm->context.noexec.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of mm context/page-table-level properties before computing the control registers, matching CWE-20's improper validation of input-derived properties. The consequence is not a generic memory bug but a failure to check required properties.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function builds user_asce/user_exec_asce from mm context fields without validating that the page-table level count is consistent with the highest address, so a four-level configuration is mishandled. Trigger: a crafted local application forking with an mm whose context does not match the required page-table level. Supported consequence: system crash (DoS) and possibly unspecified impact, as described for the s390 fork path.

The bg_flags field in the block group descripts is only valid if the
uninit_bg or metadata_csum feature is enabled.  We were not
consistently looking at this field; fix this.

Also block group #0 must never have uninitialized allocation bitmaps,
or need to be zeroed, since that's where the root inode, and other
special inodes are set up.  Check for these conditions and mark the
file system as corrupted if they are detected.

description: Moonlight-common-c contains the core GameStream client code shared between Moonlight clients. Moonlight-common-c is vulnerable to buffer overflow starting in commit f57bd745b4cbed577ea654fad4701bea4d38b44c. A malicious game streaming server could exploit a buffer overflow vulnerability to crash a moonlight client. Achieving RCE is possible but unlikely, due to stack canaries in use by modern compiler toolchains. The published binaries for official clients Qt, Android, iOS/tvOS, and Embedded are built with stack canaries, but some unofficial clients may not use stack canaries. This vulnerability takes place after the pairing process, so it requires the client to be tricked into pairing to a malicious host. It is not possible to perform using a man-in-the-middle due to public key pinning that takes place during the pairing process. The bug was addressed in commit b2497a3918a6d79808d9fd0c04734786e70d5954.

code_evidence: payloadStr is a fixed 92-byte stack buffer written by sprintf with %d of several int fields and slicesPerFrame; no bound check precedes the writes.
ServerMajorVersion selects which sprintf/addAttributeString branches execute, but every path still formats into payloadStr before copying it into attribute strings.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the function copies formatted input into a fixed buffer without checking input size, causing a classic stack overflow. It is a write overflow, not an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), and no size-calculation error is shown.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: repeated sprintf into a fixed-size stack buffer with no length validation. Trigger: the formatted integer values (e.g., bitrate, width, height, slicesPerFrame) exceed the buffer capacity or the surrounding attribute handling writes past it. Consequence: stack buffer overflow, enabling crash and potentially memory corruption; RCE is limited by stack canaries.

commit_msg:
netfilter: nf_nat_snmp_basic: add missing length checks in ASN.1 cbs

The generic ASN.1 decoder infrastructure doesn't guarantee that callbacks
will get as much data as they expect; callbacks have to check the `datalen`
parameter before looking at `data`. Make sure that snmp_version() and
snmp_helper() don't read/write beyond the end of the packet data.

(Also move the assignment to `pdata` down below the check to make it clear
that it isn't necessarily a pointer we can use before the `datalen` check.)

Fixes: cc2d58634e0f ("netfilter: nf_nat_snmp_basic: use asn1 decoder library")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t__be32 *pdata = (__be32 *)data;'], 'added_lines': ['\t__be32 *pdata;', '\tif (datalen != 4)', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\tpdata = (__be32 *)data;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 4.20.12, net/ipv4/netfilter/nf_nat_snmp_basic_main.c in the SNMP NAT module has insufficient ASN.1 length checks (aka an array index error), making out-of-bounds read and write operations possible, leading to an OOPS or local privilege escalation. This affects snmp_version and snmp_helper.

code_evidence: Line 5 casts the callback's `data` pointer to `__be32 *` and line 6 immediately dereferences it with `*pdata` to compare against `ctx->from`, without any check that `datalen` is at least 4 bytes.
Line 11 writes `*pdata = ctx->to`, storing a 4-byte value through the same pointer that may point to less than 4 bytes of remaining ASN.1 data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function performs a 4-byte store through a pointer whose bounds are never validated against `datalen`, directly writing beyond the intended buffer. This is an out-of-bounds write rather than only an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), since line 11 modifies memory outside the supplied data region.

evidence_lines.code:
__be32 *pdata = (__be32 *)data;
if (*pdata == ctx->from) {
*pdata = ctx->to;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The ASN.1 decoder does not guarantee the callback receives a full 4-byte value, but snmp_helper() dereferences and stores through `(__be32 *)data` unconditionally. When a truncated SNMP value reaches this callback, line 11 writes four bytes past the end of the packet buffer, corrupting adjacent kernel memory; the read at line 6 is also out of bounds.

commit_msg: Check types to avoid invalid reads/writes.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbody[j] = XMALLOC(VarLenData, 1);', '\tbody[j]->len = a->values[j].len;', '\tbody[j]->data = CHECKED_XCALLOC(unsigned char, a->values[j].len);', '\tmemmove (body[j]->data, a->values[j].data.buf, body[j]->len);'], 'added_lines': ['        if (a->type == szMAPI_BINARY) {', ' \t    body[j] = XMALLOC(VarLenData, 1);', '\t    body[j]->len = a->values[j].len;', '\t    body[j]->data = CHECKED_XCALLOC(unsigned char, a->values[j].len);', '\t    memmove (body[j]->data, a->values[j].data.buf, body[j]->len);', '        }']}
description: An issue was discovered in tnef before 1.4.13. Two type confusions have been identified in the parse_file() function. These might lead to invalid read and write operations, controlled by an attacker.

code_evidence: For every index j up to a->num_values, the function allocates body[j]->data with CHECKED_XCALLOC sized by a->values[j].len, then copies a->values[j].len bytes from a->values[j].data.buf. No check confirms that the union member data.buf actually holds a len-sized buffer for this attribute type; the copy trusts len and buf regardless of a->type.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 requires writing past the intended buffer. Here the destination is allocated to a->values[j].len and the copy uses the same length, so the unsafe access is a source-side over-read (CWE-125), not a write beyond the destination. The type confusion is the root cause, but the evidence does not support an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy uses a->values[j].len as the source length and destination allocation size without verifying the attribute's type, so a non-binary value's len/data.buf fields are misinterpreted. Trigger: an attacker-controlled attribute whose type is not binary but whose len exceeds the actual buffer causes memmove to read past the real source buffer; the destination allocation matches len, so the write itself is bounded by that allocation. Consequence: out-of-bounds read and potential memory corruption/crash, not a demonstrated out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
win: fix unsavory rwlock fallback implementation

Before this patch an uv_mutex_t (backed by a critical section) could be
released by a tread different from the thread that acquired it, which is
not allowed. This is fixed by using a semaphore instead.

Note that the affected code paths were used on Windows XP and Windows
Server 2003 only.

Fixes: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/issues/515
PR-URL: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/pull/516
Reviewed-By: Ben Noordhuis <info@bnoordhuis.nl>
Reviewed-By: Saúl Ibarra Corretgé <saghul@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  return uv_mutex_trylock(&rwlock->fallback_.write_mutex_);'], 'added_lines': ['  DWORD r = WaitForSingleObject(rwlock->fallback_.write_lock_.sem, 0);', '  if (r == WAIT_OBJECT_0)', '    return 0;', '  else if (r == WAIT_TIMEOUT)', '    return UV_EAGAIN;', '  else if (r == WAIT_FAILED)', '    return uv_translate_sys_error(GetLastError());', '  else', '    return UV_EIO;']}
description: The uv_rwlock_t fallback implementation for Windows XP and Server 2003 in libuv before 1.7.4 does not properly prevent threads from releasing the locks of other threads, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (deadlock) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging a race condition.

code_evidence: The function implements trywrlock for the Windows fallback rwlock by delegating directly to uv_mutex_trylock on rwlock->fallback_.write_mutex_, a mutex backed by a critical section. A critical section is thread-owned, so only the acquiring thread may release it; nothing in this lock path enforces that ownership restriction or coordinates release with acquisition.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The lock is a shared synchronization resource whose exclusive ownership is not properly constrained across concurrent threads, allowing an interfering sequence (a different thread's release) to violate exclusivity—a race condition. CWE-362 fits; a deadlock-specific CWE would describe the consequence rather than the concurrent synchronization flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write lock is modeled with a critical-section-backed mutex, which cannot enforce that only the acquiring thread releases it. Trigger: one thread acquires the write lock and another thread later releases it (e.g., via the paired unlock path), which is permitted by this lock primitive. Consequence: the lock state can be corrupted or left held, enabling a deadlock/DoS under race conditions.

code_evidence: The sentinel check reads 16 bytes via memcmp at dat->chain[dat->byte]; the preceding bound check only guarantees dat->byte + 16 <= dat->size, so this read is guarded.
When the size check fails, endpos is set to address + size - 16 (or dat->byte + size) but the function only logs and continues; there is no early exit.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-sccp.c had an infinite loop that was addressed by using a correct integer data type.

off += 1+len;

idx = tvb_get_guintvar (tvb, off+1, &len);

if (tvb_get_guint8 (tvb, 0)) {

commit_msg:
Fixed bug: barriers cannot be active during sweep

Barriers cannot be active during sweep, even in generational mode.
(Although gen. mode is not incremental, it can hit a barrier when
deleting a thread and closing its upvalues.)  The colors of objects are
being changed during sweep and, therefore, cannot be trusted.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  g->gcstate = GCSswpallgc;']}
description: lgc.c in Lua 5.4.0 mishandles the interaction between barriers and the sweep phase, leading to a memory access violation involving collectgarbage.

code_evidence: atomic(L) performs the final marking/barrier work, then sweepgen is invoked on g->allgc and the returned pointer. The patch adds g->gcstate = GCSswpallgc before the sweep; without it, gcstate remains GCSpropagate during sweeping, so barriers can still fire and mutate object colors while sweepgen reads them.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function releases/advances memory objects via sweepgen using state that is incorrectly maintained (a wrong/invalid release precondition), matching CWE-763's 'release function used incorrectly' form. It is not CWE-416 (use-after-free), because the defect is the invalid state under which sweeping releases objects, not dereferencing freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sweepgen runs while gcstate still reports propagation, allowing a barrier (e.g. closing upvalues when deleting a thread) to change object colors mid-sweep. Trigger: collectgarbage reaching youngcollection with a concurrent barrier during sweep; sweepgen then trusts inconsistent color/pointer state, causing a memory access violation.

description: SmartDNS through 41 before 56d0332 allows an out-of-bounds write because of a stack-based buffer overflow in the _dns_encode_domain function in the dns.c file, via a crafted DNS request.

The loop iterates i from 0 to addr_num-1 and copies DNS_RR_A_LEN bytes from addr[i] into the nested rr buffer, with no check that addr[i] is a valid pointer or that the destination has sufficient space for each iteration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the loop writes past the intended buffer when addr_num exceeds the available addresses or destination capacity; the missing bounds check is the root cause, and memory corruption/crash is the supported consequence, distinct from a pure out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
kvm:vmx: more complete state update on APICv on/off

The function to update APICv on/off state (in particular, to deactivate
it when enabling Hyper-V SynIC) is incomplete: it doesn't adjust
APICv-related fields among secondary processor-based VM-execution
controls.  As a result, Windows 2012 guests get stuck when SynIC-based
auto-EOI interrupt intersected with e.g. an IPI in the guest.

In addition, the MSR intercept bitmap isn't updated every time "virtualize
x2APIC mode" is toggled.  This path can only be triggered by a malicious
guest, because Windows didn't use x2APIC but rather their own synthetic
APIC access MSRs; however a guest running in a SynIC-enabled VM could
switch to x2APIC and thus obtain direct access to host APIC MSRs
(CVE-2016-4440).

The patch fixes those omissions.

Signed-off-by: Roman Kagan <rkagan@virtuozzo.com>
Reported-by: Steve Rutherford <srutherford@google.com>
Reported-by: Yang Zhang <yang.zhang.wz@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>

Need to', '\t\t * intercept it */', '\t\tvmx_enable_intercept_msr_read_x2apic(0x802);', '\t\t/* TMCCT */', '\t\tvmx_enable_intercept_msr_read_x2apic(0x839);', '\t\t/* TPR */', '\t\tvmx_disable_intercept_msr_write_x2apic(0x808);', '\t\t/* EOI */', '\t\tvmx_disable_intercept_msr_write_x2apic(0x80b);', '\t\t/* SELF-IPI */', '\t\tvmx_disable_intercept_msr_write_x2apic(0x83f);', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tfor (msr = 0x800; msr <= 0x8ff; msr++)', '\t\tvmx_disable_intercept_msr_read_x2apic(msr);', '', '\t/* According SDM, in x2apic mode, the whole id reg is used.  But in', '\t * KVM, it only use the highest eight bits. Need to intercept it */', '\tvmx_enable_intercept_msr_read_x2apic(0x802);', '\t/* TMCCT */', '\tvmx_enable_intercept_msr_read_x2apic(0x839);', '\t/* TPR */', '\tvmx_disable_intercept_msr_write_x2apic(0x808);', '\t/* EOI */', '\tvmx_disable_intercept_msr_write_x2apic(0x80b);', '\t/* SELF-IPI */', '\tvmx_disable_intercept_msr_write_x2apic(0x83f);']}
description: arch/x86/kvm/vmx.c in the Linux kernel through 4.6.3 mishandles the APICv on/off state, which allows guest OS users to obtain direct APIC MSR access on the host OS, and consequently cause a denial of service (host OS crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code on the host OS, via x2APIC mode.

code_evidence: The x2APIC MSR intercept bitmap is only configured when enable_apicv is true; the entire block that disables read intercepts for MSRs 0x800-0x8ff and adjusts specific read/write intercepts is guarded by this single condition. Since the bitmap is memset to 0xff (lines 44-47), if APICv is disabled or later toggled off the x2APIC MSRs remain intercepted, and the APICv on/off state is not fully reconciled here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in management of permissions/access controls. Here the hypervisor's access-control configuration (MSR intercept bitmap) is incomplete, letting a guest obtain direct APIC MSR access it should be denied, fitting the target category.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: x2APIC MSR intercept configuration is conditioned on the APICv enable flag rather than unconditionally applied, so the intercept bitmap does not track APICv/x2APIC state transitions. Trigger: a guest in a SynIC-enabled VM switching to x2APIC mode. Consequence: direct host APIC MSR access, host crash or possible code execution.
