description: Moddable SDK v11.5.0 was discovered to contain a stack buffer overflow via the component __interceptor_strcat.

code_evidence: Line 8 declares a fixed-size stack buffer `char map[C_PATH_MAX]`.
Lines 20-22 derive `slash` from `path`, truncate `path` at the separator, then append `name` with `c_strcat` into the caller-provided `path` buffer without any length check.
Lines 30-32 repeat the same unchecked `c_strcat(path, name)` after a second `c_realpath`, again with no bounds validation on `path` or `name`.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs unbounded string concatenation into a fixed-size destination, directly producing a write past the end of an intended buffer, which is the definition of CWE-787. A related CWE-121 (stack-based buffer overflow) is a more specific variant, but the target CWE-787 accurately captures the out-of-bounds write behavior.

evidence_lines.code: char map[C_PATH_MAX];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: `c_strcat` appends the attacker-influenced `name` onto `path` without verifying remaining capacity, and the resulting string is then passed to `c_realpath` writing into the fixed stack buffer `map`. Trigger: a source-map or script name long enough that `path + name` exceeds the destination buffer. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds stack write, corrupting adjacent memory and enabling crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
usbip_host updates device status without holding lock from stub probe,
disconnect and rebind code paths. When multiple requests to import a
device are received, these unprotected code paths step all over each
other and drive fails with NULL-ptr deref and use-after-free errors.

The driver uses a table lock to protect the busid array for adding and
deleting busids to the table. However, the probe, disconnect and rebind
paths get the busid table entry and update the status without holding
the busid table lock. Add a new finer grain lock to protect the busid
entry. This new lock will be held to search and update the busid entry
fields from get_busid_idx(), add_match_busid() and del_match_busid().

match_busid_show() does the same to access the busid entry fields.

get_busid_priv() changed to return the pointer to the busid entry holding
the busid lock. stub_probe(), stub_disconnect() and stub_device_rebind()
call put_busid_priv() to release the busid lock before returning. This
changes fixes the unprotected code paths eliminating the race conditions
in updating the busid entries.

Reported-by: Jakub Jirasek
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan (Samsung OSG) <shuah@kernel.org>
Cc: stable <stable@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfor (i = 0; i < MAX_BUSID; i++)'], 'added_lines': ['\tfor (i = 0; i < MAX_BUSID; i++) {', '\t\tspin_lock(&busid_table[i].busid_lock);', '\t\t\t\tspin_unlock(&busid_table[i].busid_lock);', '\t\tspin_unlock(&busid_table[i].busid_lock);', '\t}']}
description: In the Linux Kernel before version 4.16.11, 4.14.43, 4.9.102, and 4.4.133, multiple race condition errors when handling probe, disconnect, and rebind operations can be exploited to trigger a use-after-free condition or a NULL pointer dereference by sending multiple USB over IP packets.

code_evidence: get_busid_idx() iterates over the shared busid_table array and reads each entry's name[0] (line 6) and compares name with strncmp (line 7) without acquiring any lock on the entry. The loop reads the shared busid_table fields directly, so a concurrent add_match_busid(), del_match_busid() or stub probe/disconnect path can modify or clear the same entry while it is being searched.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses a shared resource (busid_table entries) concurrently without synchronization, which is exactly a race condition (CWE-362). The missing lock is the cause; the resulting NULL deref / UAF is the consequence, not a separate weakness label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The lookup sequence reads busid_table[i].name and its contents without holding the per-entry busid_lock, so the read is neither exclusive nor atomic with respect to concurrent writers. A concurrent import/disconnect/rebind operation can modify or free the entry between the name[0] check and the strncmp, causing a race that leads to a NULL-pointer dereference or use-after-free.

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. An attacker can craft a TFLite model that would cause a write outside of bounds of an array in TFLite. In fact, the attacker can override the linked list used by the memory allocator. This can be leveraged for an arbitrary write primitive under certain conditions. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Sparse weight path takes filter->sparsity from the model and only checks SupportedSparsityFormat, with no validation that dim_metadata counts and dense_size values match the actual filter/input/output shapes before dispatch.
Random-sparse branch calls FullyConnectedSparseWeight with raw tensor shapes and data pointers, relying on sparsity metadata to bound indexing; malformed metadata can drive writes past output buffer.
Block-sparse 1x4 branch reads sparsity.dim_metadata[2].dense_size and dispatches FullyConnectedSparseWeight1x4 with unvalidated shapes.
Fallthrough logs unsupported format, but the preceding branches already trust attacker-controlled sparsity metadata.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked sparsity metadata leads to writes past the output tensor's bounds in FullyConnectedSparseWeight/1x4, matching CWE-787. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read because the vulnerable path writes computed activations into output memory.

evidence_lines.code:
if (sparsity.dim_metadata_size == kDimMetadataSizeRandomSparse) {
optimized_ops::FullyConnectedSparseWeight(
sparsity, op_params, GetTensorShape(input),
GetTensorData<float>(input), GetTensorShape(filter),
GetTensorData<float>(filter), GetTensorShape(bias),
GetTensorData<float>(bias), GetTensorShape(output),
GetTensorData<float>(output));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts attacker-supplied sparsity dim_metadata without cross-checking it against tensor dimensions. Trigger: a crafted TFLite model whose sparse filter metadata is inconsistent with input/filter/output shapes. Consequence: the sparse kernels compute indices from the metadata and write outside the output buffer, corrupting adjacent memory such as allocator linked lists.

commit_msg:
s390/sclp_ctl: fix potential information leak with /dev/sclp

The sclp_ctl_ioctl_sccb function uses two copy_from_user calls to
retrieve the sclp request from user space. The first copy_from_user
fetches the length of the request which is stored in the first two
bytes of the request. The second copy_from_user gets the complete
sclp request, but this copies the length field a second time.
A malicious user may have changed the length in the meantime.

Reported-by: Pengfei Wang <wpengfeinudt@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Michael Holzheu <holzheu@linux.vnet.ibm.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin Schwidefsky <schwidefsky@de.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (copy_from_user(sccb, u64_to_uptr(ctl_sccb.sccb), sizeof(*sccb))) {', '\tif (sccb->length > PAGE_SIZE || sccb->length < 8)', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\tif (copy_from_user(sccb, u64_to_uptr(ctl_sccb.sccb), sccb->length)) {', '\t\trc = -EFAULT;'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned long copied;', '\tcopied = PAGE_SIZE -', '\t\tcopy_from_user(sccb, u64_to_uptr(ctl_sccb.sccb), PAGE_SIZE);', '\tif (offsetof(struct sccb_header, length) +', '\t    sizeof(sccb->length) > copied || sccb->length > copied) {', '\tif (sccb->length < 8) {', '\t\trc = -EINVAL;']}
description: Race condition in the sclp_ctl_ioctl_sccb function in drivers/s390/char/sclp_ctl.c in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory by changing a certain length value, aka a "double fetch" vulnerability.

code_evidence: The function copies the sccb header from user memory at line 13, then validates sccb->length against PAGE_SIZE at line 17, and finally re-copies from the same user pointer using the previously validated length at line 19. The user-controlled length field is read twice from userspace without any synchronization, so the value validated at line 17 need not be the value used as the copy size at line 19.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the same shared user-memory resource is accessed non-atomically across two fetches, with an interfering user thread able to modify it between the validation and use. The double-fetch timing window is the race; the leak is its consequence rather than a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length field resides in user memory and is fetched twice (header copy then length-driven copy). Trigger: a local user thread changes the length between the two copy_from_user calls. Consequence: the second copy reads up to the attacker-chosen length, potentially exceeding the header validated earlier and leaking kernel memory via the subsequent copy_to_user at line 26.

description: DCMTK through 3.6.6 does not handle memory free properly. The program malloc a heap memory for parsing data, but does not free it when error in parsing. Sending specific requests to the dcmqrdb program incur the memory leak. An attacker can use it to launch a DoS attack.

code_evidence: Line 85 mallocs a PRV_PRESENTATIONCONTEXTITEM into context; line 89 returns on a bad parse condition without freeing context, leaving it unowned.
Line 93 enqueues the same context pointer into assoc->presentationContextList on success, so ownership transfers to that list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 requires the same address to be passed to free() twice, but no free() of context appears in this function and the enqueue path transfers ownership rather than releasing it. The observable defect is an unfreed allocation on the error return, which fits an improper-resource-release class, not double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: On a parsePresentationContext failure the heap block allocated at line 85 is abandoned and never freed, while on success it is handed to the list at line 93. The allocation is not tracked under a single consistent ownership rule, so error paths leak memory and later cleanup of the list can operate on inconsistently owned nodes; the supported consequence is resource exhaustion from repeated malformed associate PDUs.

The unchecked remainder allows the object to be accepted as a cholmod_factor, leading to invalid pointer use and a crash (DoS).

description: When using the gdImageCreateFromXbm() function in the GD Graphics Library (aka LibGD) 2.2.5, as used in the PHP GD extension in PHP versions 7.1.x below 7.1.30, 7.2.x below 7.2.19 and 7.3.x below 7.3.6, it is possible to supply data that will cause the function to use the value of uninitialized variable. This may lead to disclosing contents of the stack that has been left there by previous code.

code_evidence: b is declared as an uninitialized unsigned int at line 15. Bytes read from the XBM file are placed into h at lines 86,90,95,99, and h is NUL-terminated only at h[2] and h[4]. Line 101 calls sscanf(h, "%x", &b) without checking the return value; if the collected characters do not form a valid hex number, sscanf leaves b untouched. Line 103 then reads b in (b & bit) to set pixels, so the uninitialized stack value is consumed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly reads an uninitialized local variable (b) whose initialization depends on a successful sscanf conversion that is never verified. This matches CWE-908 (Use of Uninitialized Resource), where an uninitialized resource is accessed. It is not merely a missing return-value check; the concrete effect is consumption of uninitialized memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of sscanf is ignored, so a failed conversion leaves b uninitialized. Trigger: a crafted XBM whose data bytes after 'x' are not valid hex digits. Consequence: the pixel loop reads the stale stack contents of b, which can leak memory contents into the decoded image and may cause unexpected pixel data or behavior.

commit_msg:
Using tp_reserve to calculate netoff can overflow as
tp_reserve is unsigned int and netoff is unsigned short.

This may lead to macoff receving a smaller value then
sizeof(struct virtio_net_hdr), and if po->has_vnet_hdr
is set, an out-of-bounds write will occur when
calling virtio_net_hdr_from_skb.

The bug is fixed by converting netoff to unsigned int
and checking if it exceeds USHRT_MAX.

This addresses CVE-2020-14386

Fixes: 8913336a7e8d ("packet: add PACKET_RESERVE sockopt")
Signed-off-by: Or Cohen <orcohen@paloaltonetworks.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned short macoff, netoff, hdrlen;'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned short macoff, hdrlen;', '\tunsigned int netoff;', '\t}', '\tif (netoff > USHRT_MAX) {', '\t\tatomic_inc(&po->tp_drops);', '\t\tgoto drop_n_restore;']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel before 5.9-rc4. Memory corruption can be exploited to gain root privileges from unprivileged processes. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to data confidentiality and integrity.

code_evidence: netoff is declared unsigned short (line 12) yet is computed from TPACKET_ALIGN(po->tp_hdrlen + ...) plus the user-controlled unsigned int po->tp_reserve (lines 51-57) and sizeof(struct virtio_net_hdr) (line 59); the assignment truncates modulo 65536. macoff = netoff - maclen (line 62) then derives a too-small offset.

The truncated macoff feeds the frame-size checks and packet_current_rx_frame(..., macoff+snaplen) (lines 65,83-84,97-98); with do_vnet set, virtio_net_hdr_from_skb writes at h.raw + macoff - sizeof(struct virtio_net_hdr) (lines 107-109), and skb_copy_bits writes at h.raw + macoff (line 126), placing writes before/outside the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked arithmetic truncation causes writes past the intended ring-buffer slot, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The integer overflow is the enabling root cause, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write rather than a mere numeric error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: netoff is stored in an unsigned short, so adding a large unprivileged-controlled tp_reserve wraps the value. Trigger: a PACKET_RESERVE sockopt near USHRT_MAX with has_vnet_hdr yields a tiny macoff that passes the size checks. Consequence: virtio_net_hdr_from_skb and skb_copy_bits write outside the ring slot, causing memory corruption exploitable for privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
When a client has a USB device attached over IP, the vhci_hcd driver is
locally leaking a socket pointer address via the

/sys/devices/platform/vhci_hcd/status file (world-readable) and in debug

commit_msg:
Fix stack buffer overflows when parsing corrupt ihex files.

	PR binutils/18750
	* ihex.c (ihex_scan): Fixes incorrect escape sequence in error message
	and stack overflow when char is signed and \200-\376 was in place of hex
	digit; also fixes \377 was handled as EOF instead of "incorrect character".
	(ihex_read_section): Changed for consistency.
	(ihex_bad_byte): Prevent (now impossible to trigger) stack
	overflow and incorrect escape sequence handling.
	* srec.c (srec_bad_byte): Likewise.

	* readelf.c (process_mips_specific): Fix incorrect escape
	sequence handling.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      char hdr[8];'], 'added_lines': ['      unsigned char hdr[8];']}
description: ihex.c in GNU Binutils before 2.26 contains a stack buffer overflow when printing bad bytes in Intel Hex objects.

code_evidence: A fixed 8-byte stack buffer hdr is filled by bfd_bread at line 23; HEX2(hdr) and HEX2(hdr+6) then decode bytes from it.

The len field controls realloc size and the second bfd_bread, then the loop at 43-44 writes len decoded bytes into p without verifying that (p - contents) + len stays within section->size; the bounds check at line 45 occurs only after the writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code writes decoded data beyond the intended contents buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The fix's hdr type change addresses signed-char handling, but the write loop remains the direct overflow; this is not merely an integer issue but an actual out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled len from a corrupt ihex record is used to write HEX2-decoded bytes through p into the contents buffer before any capacity check. Trigger: a malformed record with a large len while the destination section is smaller. Consequence: heap/stack buffer overflow of the destination, corrupting adjacent memory.

description: An invalid memory access flaw is present in libyang before v1.0-r1 in the function resolve_feature_value() when an if-feature statement is used inside a list key node, and the feature used is not defined. Applications that use libyang to parse untrusted input yang files may crash.

The diff shows the pre-fix call omitted the new 'options' argument (added as 0), indicating the call signature/argument handling changed. The result snode is then dereferenced/used by _lyd_new at line 20 without any bounds or validity re-check beyond the !snode test.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described consequence is an invalid memory access (read/use of an out-of-bounds or invalid memory location) during schema resolution, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. It is not merely a logic error because the flaw culminates in operating on an unintended memory location, though a more specific descendant CWE could also apply.

evidence_lines.code:
if (lys_getnext_data(module, lys_parent(siblings), name, strlen(name), LYS_CONTAINER | LYS_LIST | LYS_NOTIF
| LYS_RPC | LYS_ACTION, &snode) || !snode) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The schema-resolution routine (lys_getnext_data) is invoked with flags and name data derived from the parsed YANG schema; when an if-feature sits inside a list key and the feature is undefined, resolution proceeds without properly checking features, yielding an invalid schema node. commit_msg:
Remove a `DCHECK`-fail, log an error instead.

`DCHECK` in debug mode results in crashes. TensorFlow has had multiple vulnerabilities due to this.

Outside of debug mode, `DCHECK` is a no-op.

A better alternative is to report an error to the log buffer and continue. This should happen both in debug mode and in prod mode.

Change-Id: Id5b3e19c73f3fbe0cc4bba26ca44ff9607bb6356

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. An attacker can trigger denial of service via assertion failure by altering a `SavedModel` on disk such that `AttrDef`s of some operation are duplicated. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over attacker-controlled AttrDef entries from a SavedModel and checks name uniqueness only via DCHECK, which aborts the process in debug builds when a duplicate name is found; the following unconditional insertion at line 9 does not block the duplicate.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains an assertion reachable through attacker-supplied model data that terminates the application, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion). The uniqueness check is a validation concern, but the supported weakness here is the assertion-driven crash rather than improper input validation itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a reachable DCHECK on duplicate AttrDef names, which is a no-op in release builds and a hard crash in debug builds. Trigger: a crafted SavedModel with duplicated AttrDefs of an operation. Consequence: process abort/denial of service in debug configurations.

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

    ..... \

    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.

even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

commit_msg:
virtio_console: Assure used length from device is limited

The buf->len might come from an untrusted device. This
ensures the value would not exceed the size of the buffer
to avoid data corruption or loss.

Signed-off-by: Xie Yongji <xieyongji@bytedance.com>
Acked-by: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210525125622.1203-1-xieyongji@bytedance.com
Signed-off-by: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tbuf->len = len;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tbuf->len = min_t(size_t, len, buf->size);']}
description: In drivers/char/virtio_console.c in the Linux kernel before 5.13.4, data corruption or loss can be triggered by an untrusted device that supplies a buf->len value exceeding the buffer size. NOTE: the vendor indicates that the cited data corruption is not a vulnerability in any existing use case; the length validation was added solely for robustness in the face of anomalous host OS behavior

code_evidence: virtqueue_get_buf writes the device-supplied used length into len at line 10; line 12 then assigns that untrusted value directly to buf->len without comparing it to buf->size, and line 14 passes the buffer to handle_control_message for consumption.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 applies because a device-supplied input length is accepted without verifying it is less than the destination/holding buffer size, and that unvalidated length drives subsequent buffer handling. The fix (min_t with buf->size) confirms the missing size check; this is a size-validation flaw rather than an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length reported by the untrusted virtio device is stored as the buffer's data length without any bound check against the allocated buffer size. Trigger: a device returning len greater than buf->size. Consequence: downstream control-message handling trusts buf->len, enabling out-of-bounds memory access/corruption or data loss within the buffer.

commit_msg:
x86/vpt: fix race when migrating timers between vCPUs

The current vPT code will migrate the emulated timers between vCPUs
(change the pt->vcpu field) while just holding the destination lock,
either from create_periodic_time or pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target if
the global target is adjusted. Changing the periodic_timer vCPU field
in this way creates a race where a third party could grab the lock in
the unlocked region of pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target (or before
create_periodic_time performs the vcpu change) and then release the
lock from a different vCPU, creating a locking imbalance.

Introduce a per-domain rwlock in order to protect periodic_time
migration between vCPU lists. Taking the lock in read mode prevents
any timer from being migrated to a different vCPU, while taking it in
write mode allows performing migration of timers across vCPUs. The
per-vcpu locks are still used to protect all the other fields from the
periodic_timer struct.

Note that such migration shouldn't happen frequently, and hence
there's no performance drop as a result of such locking.

This is XSA-336.

Reported-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Tested-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    spin_lock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock);', '    spin_unlock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    pt_vcpu_lock(v);', '    pt_vcpu_unlock(v);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There is a race condition when migrating timers between x86 HVM vCPUs. When migrating timers of x86 HVM guests between its vCPUs, the locking model used allows for a second vCPU of the same guest (also operating on the timers) to release a lock that it didn't acquire. The most likely effect of the issue is a hang or crash of the hypervisor, i.e., a Denial of Service (DoS). All versions of Xen are affected. Only x86 systems are vulnerable. Arm systems are not vulnerable. Only x86 HVM guests can leverage the vulnerability. x86 PV and PVH cannot leverage the vulnerability. Only guests with more than one vCPU can exploit the vulnerability.

code_evidence: pt_restore_timer holds only the per-vCPU tm_lock (line 5) while iterating the vCPU's tm_list and calling pt_process_missed_ticks/set_timer on each periodic_time (lines 6-13); it then calls pt_thaw_time and releases the same lock at line 15. The lock protects the list traversal but the periodic_time entries can be migrated between vCPU lists by pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target or create_periodic_time, which take only the destination lock, so the shared tm_list/pt->vcpu state is not exclusively held during this sequence.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function operates on a shared timer list under insufficient synchronization, allowing a concurrent migrating sequence to interfere with the traversal/lock release, matching CWE-362's exclusivity violation. The consequence is a locking imbalance leading to DoS, not a separate weakness such as use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: timer migration between vCPU lists is not serialized against this restore traversal, since only the per-vCPU lock is taken and migration holds just the destination lock. Trigger: a second vCPU concurrently migrates a timer while pt_restore_timer walks the list, allowing a lock to be released from a different vCPU and creating a locking imbalance. Supported consequence: hypervisor hang or crash (DoS).

The stack object “ci” has a total size of 8 bytes. Its last 3 bytes
are padding bytes which are not initialized and leaked to userland
via “copy_to_user”.

Signed-off-by: Kangjie Lu <kjlu@gatech.edu>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct usbdevfs_connectinfo ci = {', '\t\t.devnum = ps->dev->devnum,', '\t\t.slow = ps->dev->speed == USB_SPEED_LOW', '\t};'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct usbdevfs_connectinfo ci;', '', '\tmemset(&ci, 0, sizeof(ci));', '\tci.devnum = ps->dev->devnum;', '\tci.slow = ps->dev->speed == USB_SPEED_LOW;']}
description: The proc_connectinfo function in drivers/usb/core/devio.c in the Linux kernel through 4.6 does not initialize a certain data structure, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel stack memory via a crafted USBDEVFS_CONNECTINFO ioctl call.

code_evidence: The stack object ci is initialized with a designated initializer that sets only .devnum and .slow; the remaining bytes of struct usbdevfs_connectinfo are left uninitialized.
copy_to_user(arg, &ci, sizeof(ci)) copies the entire structure, including the uninitialized trailing padding bytes, to the caller-supplied user buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly copies uninitialized memory into a user-accessible buffer, exposing kernel data to an actor not authorized to see it, matching CWE-200. This is an explicit information-transfer error rather than a separate memory-safety flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
if (copy_to_user(arg, &ci, sizeof(ci)))
return -EFAULT;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: partial initialization of a stack structure followed by a full-size copy to userland. Trigger: any local caller of USBDEVFS_CONNECTINFO, which invokes proc_connectinfo and receives sizeof(ci) bytes. Consequence: residual kernel stack contents are disclosed to the unprivileged caller.

commit_msg:
gnttab: set page refcount for copy-on-grant-transfer

Commit 5cc77f9098 ("32-on-64: Fix domain address-size clamping,
implement"), which introduced this functionality, took care of clearing
the old page's PGC_allocated, but failed to set the bit (and install the
associated reference) on the newly allocated one. Furthermore the "mfn"
local variable was never updated, and hence the wrong MFN was passed to
guest_physmap_add_page() (and back to the destination domain) in this
case, leading to an IOMMU mapping into an unowned page.

Ideally the code would use assign_pages(), but the call to
gnttab_prepare_for_transfer() sits in the middle of the actions
mirroring that function.

This is XSA-284.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            page->count_info = PGC_allocated | 1;', '            mfn = page_to_mfn(page);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges because grant-table transfer requests are mishandled.

code_evidence: In the copy-on-transfer branch, a new page is allocated with alloc_domheap_page(e, ...) at [89,90]. The old page's PGC_allocated is cleared and it is freed at [97,98], but the new page assigned to 'page' at [99] never receives PGC_allocated or its associated reference, and 'mfn' is not updated to the new page's MFN.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing PGC_allocated/reference on the newly allocated page means the page's ownership and release bookkeeping is not established, so the allocated page is not correctly tracked for later release — matching CWE-401's failure to sufficiently track/release allocated memory. The stale MFN is a related but distinct correctness issue; the core supported weakness is the untracked allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: after replacing the transferred page with a freshly allocated one, the code frees the old page but fails to set PGC_allocated (and the reference) on the new page and leaves 'mfn' stale. Trigger: a transfer request whose MFN exceeds the transferee's clamped bitsize. Consequence: the new page is not properly owned/tracked, and the stale MFN is later used in guest_physmap_add_page(), mapping an unowned page (IOMMU mapping) and mishandling the page's lifetime.

commit_msg:
[MJ2] To avoid divisions by zero / undefined behaviour on shift

Signed-off-by: Young_X <YangX92@hotmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '                    /* To avoid divisions by zero / undefined behaviour on shift */', '                    if (rpx >= 31 || ((comp->dx << rpx) >> rpx) != comp->dx ||', '                            rpy >= 31 || ((comp->dy << rpy) >> rpy) != comp->dy) {', '                        continue;', '                    }', '']}
description: Division-by-zero vulnerabilities in the functions pi_next_pcrl, pi_next_cprl, and pi_next_rpcl in openmj2/pi.c in OpenJPEG through 2.3.0 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash).

code_evidence: rpx and rpy are computed from res->pdx/pdy plus levelno and then used as shift amounts: comp->dy << rpy and 1 << rpy (and dx << rpx) feed the modulo operations on lines 50-55. No check bounds rpx/rpy before these shifts, so oversized or negative values shift out of range and can yield zero divisors.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs modulo (division) by a value derived from an unvalidated shift count, allowing the divisor to become zero; this matches CWE-369 divide-by-zero. It is not merely an integer overflow: the overflow/shift defect is the cause, and the zero divisor is the directly reachable weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-influenced pdx/pdy and levelno produce unbounded rpx/rpy, and these are used directly as shift counts in the modulo divisors (comp->dy << rpy, 1 << rpy, comp->dx << rpx, 1 << rpx). Trigger: crafted image geometry makes a shift produce zero, so the modulo divisor becomes zero. Supported consequence: division-by-zero/undefined shift crashes the decoder (DoS).

commit_msg:
(for 4.9.3) CVE-2018-14464/LMP: Add a missing bounds check

In lmp_print_data_link_subobjs().

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t    ND_TCHECK_32BITS(obj_tptr + offset + 4);', 'trunc:', '    return -1;']}
description: The LMP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-lmp.c:lmp_print_data_link_subobjs().

code_evidence: At line 44 the code reads EXTRACT_32BITS(obj_tptr+offset+4) and at line 47 EXTRACT_32BITS(obj_tptr+offset+8) without any bounds check confirming that offset+4..offset+11 lie within the captured buffer; the patch adds ND_TCHECK_32BITS(obj_tptr + offset + 4) and a trunc label to catch this.

The loop guards at lines 20-31 only constrain subobj_len (>=4, multiple of 4, not exceeding total_subobj_len), which validates the subobject length field but not the actual captured bytes available at obj_tptr+offset, so a truncated capture passes these checks and reaches the 32-bit reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads data beyond the intended buffer via EXTRACT_32BITS on unverified offsets; the missing ND_TCHECK bounds check is the direct cause. This is a read overrun, not a write (CWE-787) or integer overflow, since the length arithmetic itself is not the flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the INT_SWITCHING_TYPE_SUBOBJ branch reads 32-bit fields at offset+4 and offset+8 while only subobj_len and total_subobj_len are validated, not the remaining captured buffer length. Trigger: a truncated LMP packet whose subobject declares a valid length reaches the EXTRACT_32BITS calls. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of up to several bytes past the captured buffer.

commit_msg:
Just allocate 20 bytes extra at the end of a section. Otherwise, we end
up with a whole lot of little checks for structures that the file says
are there but are unexpectedly cut off in fuzz tests
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        Data = (uchar *)malloc(itemlen);'], 'added_lines': ['        // Allocate an extra 20 bytes more than needed, because sometimes when reading structures,', '        // if the section erroneously ends before short structures that should be there, that can trip', '        // memory checkers in combination with fuzzers.', '        Data = (uchar *)malloc(itemlen+20);']}
description: JHEAD is a simple command line tool for displaying and some manipulation of EXIF header data embedded in Jpeg images from digital cameras. In affected versions there is a heap-buffer-overflow on jhead-3.04/jpgfile.c:285 ReadJpegSections. Crafted jpeg images can be provided to the user resulting in a program crash or potentially incorrect exif information retrieval. Users are advised to upgrade. There is no known workaround for this issue.

code_evidence: itemlen is derived from two file bytes (lh<<8|ll) and only rejected when <2; the buffer is malloc(itemlen) and stored in Sections[SectionsRead].Data, with Data[0],Data[1] and fread(Data+2,itemlen-2) filling exactly itemlen bytes.

Downstream consumers such as the M_JFIF branch validate only itemlen<16, then index Data[9]..Data[15] (e.g. Data[10]<<8|Data[11], Data[12],Data[13], Data[14]/Data[15]) without confirming the section actually contains those bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the code allocates a section buffer sized to attacker-controlled itemlen and later structure parsing accesses fixed offsets (Data[9]..Data[15]) beyond the allocated bytes, i.e., writing/reading outside the intended buffer. The fix adds 20 bytes of slack, confirming insufficient allocation relative to downstream fixed-offset accesses.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: section buffers are allocated exactly itemlen bytes while later section parsers read fixed offsets assuming a minimum structure size. Trigger: a crafted JPEG declaring a JFIF section with itemlen between 2 and 15 (past the <16 check? no—the check catches <16, but other paths/truncated structures or the short-structure reads noted in the commit occur). The supported consequence is a heap out-of-bounds read/write past the section buffer, detected by memory checkers/fuzzers, causing a crash.

commit_msg: Prevent buffer overflow in SIXEL, PDB, MAP, and CALS coders (bug report from Donghai Zhu)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (image->depth <= 8)', '      *q++=(unsigned char) image->colormap[i].red;', '      *q++=(unsigned char) image->colormap[i].green;', '      *q++=(unsigned char) image->colormap[i].blue;', '      *q++=(unsigned char) ((size_t) image->colormap[i].red >> 8);', '      *q++=(unsigned char) image->colormap[i].red;', '      *q++=(unsigned char) ((size_t) image->colormap[i].green >> 8);', '      *q++=(unsigned char) image->colormap[i].green;', '      *q++=(unsigned char) ((size_t) image->colormap[i].blue >> 8);', '      *q++=(unsigned char) image->colormap[i].blue;'], 'added_lines': ['  q=colormap;', '  if (image->colors <= 256)', '      *q++=(unsigned char) ScaleQuantumToChar(image->colormap[i].red);', '      *q++=(unsigned char) ScaleQuantumToChar(image->colormap[i].green);', '      *q++=(unsigned char) ScaleQuantumToChar(image->colormap[i].blue);', '      *q++=(unsigned char) (ScaleQuantumToShort(image->colormap[i].red) >> 8);', '      *q++=(unsigned char) (ScaleQuantumToShort(image->colormap[i].red) & 0xff);', '      *q++=(unsigned char) (ScaleQuantumToShort(image->colormap[i].green) >> 8);', '      *q++=(unsigned char) (ScaleQuantumToShort(image->colormap[i].green) & 0xff);;', '      *q++=(unsigned char) (ScaleQuantumToShort(image->colormap[i].blue) >> 8);', '      *q++=(unsigned char) (ScaleQuantumToShort(image->colormap[i].blue) & 0xff);']}
description: Buffer overflow in the WriteMAPImage function in coders/map.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.5-8 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or have other unspecified impact via a crafted file.

code_evidence: The colormap buffer is sized using packet_size, which is set to 6 bytes per color when image->colors > 256 and 3 bytes otherwise [38,39,40].

The write loop branches on image->depth <= 8 [45]: the 8-bit branch writes 3 bytes per color [48,49,50], while the else branch writes 6 bytes per color [55,56,57,58,59,60]. The branch condition does not match the allocation condition, so depth and colors are inconsistent.
The buffer is written out with packet_size*image->colors bytes [62], which can differ from the number of bytes actually written by the loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs buffer writes and reads whose length depends on inconsistent depth/colors values, exceeding the allocated colormap buffer bounds. This directly matches CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operations; the patch aligns the loop condition with the allocation condition to prevent the overflow.

evidence_lines.code: (void) WriteBlob(image,packet_size*image->colors,colormap);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Buffer allocation uses image->colors to choose 3 or 6 bytes per entry, but the fill loop uses image->depth to choose the same widths. When depth <= 8 with more than 256 colors, the loop writes only 3 bytes per color into a buffer allocated for 6, and the subsequent WriteBlob reads packet_size*colors bytes, reading past the initialized region. Conversely, a mismatch can cause the loop to write more bytes than allocated, producing an out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
KVM: x86: drop error recovery in em_jmp_far and em_ret_far

em_jmp_far and em_ret_far assumed that setting IP can only fail in 64
bit mode, but syzkaller proved otherwise (and SDM agrees).
Code segment was restored upon failure, but it was left uninitialized
outside of long mode, which could lead to a leak of host kernel stack.
We could have fixed that by always saving and restoring the CS, but we
take a simpler approach and just break any guest that manages to fail
as the error recovery is error-prone and modern CPUs don't need emulator

commit_msg:
Don't go past the end of a page in a NetScaler file.

Records in a properly formatted NetScaler file shouldn't go past the end
of a page, but nothing guarantees that a NetScaler file will be properly
formatted.

NetScaler 3.x files allow record bodies to go past the end of a page,
but 1.x and 2.x files don't, so treat record headers that go past the
end of a page, and record bodies in 1.x and 2.x files that go past the
end of a page, as errors.

Clean up some stuff while we're at it.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")

Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>

description: xbuf_format_converter, used as part of exif_read_data, was appending a terminating null character to the generated string, but was not using its standard append char function. As a result, if the buffer was full, it would result in an out-of-bounds write. This issue affects HHVM versions prior to 4.56.3, all versions between 4.57.0 and 4.80.1, all versions between 4.81.0 and 4.93.1, and versions 4.94.0, 4.95.0, 4.96.0, 4.97.0, 4.98.0.

code_evidence: Line 14 allocates a buffer of size 4*str.size()+1, assuming each input char expands to at most 4 output chars, and line 15 obtains a raw writable pointer.

The loop writes through q without bounds checks: quoted special chars write 2 bytes (lines 26-27), the NUL case writes 4 bytes (lines 30-33), and delimiter quoting may add an extra byte (lines 36-37). The terminating null at line 42 is written unconditionally.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing the terminating NUL past the allocated buffer is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the root cause is a missing capacity check on q before line 42, not a read overrun or use-after-free.

char* out_str = ret.mutableData();

When the input is crafted so expansions and the terminating NUL exhaust the allocated buffer, *q = '\0' writes one byte past the end, corrupting adjacent heap memory.

commit_msg:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

Signed-off-by: Jeff King <peff@peff.net>
Signed-off-by: Junio C Hamano <gitster@pobox.com>

description: revision.c in git before 2.7.4 uses an incorrect integer data type, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a (1) long filename or (2) many nested trees, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow.

After appending, it builds a tree descriptor from tree->buffer and iterates entries, recursing into subtrees/objects while base keeps growing with each path component.
strbuf_setlen(base, baselen) restores the length only after the loop completes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unbounded accumulation of path data in a strbuf, combined with the integer type flaw, leads to writes beyond the allocated buffer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operations. This is a buffer-bounds violation rather than merely a resource-exhaustion issue.

commit_msg:
This fixes CVE-2017-7482.

When a kerberos 5 ticket is being decoded so that it can be loaded into an
rxrpc-type key, there are several places in which the length of a
variable-length field is checked to make sure that it's not going to
overrun the available data - but the data is padded to the nearest
four-byte boundary and the code doesn't check for this extra.  This could
lead to the size-remaining variable wrapping and the data pointer going
over the end of the buffer.

Fix this by making the various variable-length data checks use the padded
length.

Reported-by: 石磊 <shilei-c@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Marc Dionne <marc.c.dionne@auristor.com>
Reviewed-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned int toklen = *_toklen, len;', '\t\tlen = (len + 3) & ~3;', '\t\ttoklen -= len;', '\t\txdr += len >> 2;'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned int toklen = *_toklen, len, paddedlen;', '\tpaddedlen = (len + 3) & ~3;', '\tif (paddedlen > toklen)', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t\ttoklen -= paddedlen;', '\t\txdr += paddedlen >> 2;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before version 4.12, Kerberos 5 tickets decoded when using the RXRPC keys incorrectly assumes the size of a field. This could lead to the size-remaining variable wrapping and the data pointer going over the end of the buffer. This could possibly lead to memory corruption and possible privilege escalation.

code_evidence: toklen is an unsigned int initialized from *_toklen; only a check toklen <= 4 guards the header, after which len is read from the buffer.
len is capped only by AFSTOKEN_K5_TIX_MAX and toklen is reduced by 4; no check relates len to the remaining toklen before the padded length is computed.
Inside the len > 0 branch, len is rounded up to a four-byte boundary (len = (len + 3) & ~3) and then subtracted from toklen without verifying that the padded length fits within the remaining buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an unchecked unsigned integer subtraction whose result wraps when the padded length exceeds the remaining data, matching CWE-190's integer wraparound. The missing paddedlen <= toklen constraint is the defect; the resulting out-of-bounds pointer is the consequence, not a separate weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The padded length is computed and subtracted from the unsigned toklen without confirming paddedlen <= toklen. When the padded ticket length exceeds the remaining token bytes, the unsigned subtraction wraps toklen to a huge value, and xdr is advanced past the end of the buffer; the wrapped size-remaining value is then propagated to the caller, enabling out-of-bounds pointer movement and subsequent memory corruption.

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

In order to fail safe in the supported case, re-implement all the VT-x
instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.9.x through 4.11.x, on Intel x86 platforms, allowing x86 HVM and PVH guests to cause a host OS denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) or possibly have unspecified other impact because nested VT-x is not properly restricted.

code_evidence: VT-x vmexit cases such as VMXOFF/VMXON dispatch unconditionally into nvmx_handle_* handlers without any prior check that nested virt is enabled or that the nvmx state is initialised.
Each VT-x case calls its nvmx handler and only guards the EIP update on X86EMUL_OKAY, so the handler runs regardless of guest configuration.
The only nested-virt gate is nestedhvm_vcpu_in_guestmode(v) at line 81, which routes to nvmx_n2_vmexit_handler; when false, execution falls through to the switch and reaches the VT-x cases.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a host NULL/uninitialised-pointer dereference reached by guest-controlled VT-x instructions, matching CWE-476. It is distinct from a mere missing privilege check (CWE-269); the crash stems from dereferencing an invalid pointer in the nvmx handler.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dispatches VT-x instruction vmexits to nvmx handlers without verifying nested virt is enabled or that the nvmx structure is initialised. Trigger: a guest executes a VT-x instruction (e.g. VMXON/VMCLEAR) while nested virt is disabled, so the zeroed vcpu state makes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() true but the nvmx structure is uninitialised. The handler then dereferences uninitialised/NULL nested state, crashing the host (DoS).

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads array elements past the valid bounds (empty array at index 0, and trun_index beyond ItemCount) and then dereferences the out-of-bounds value. This is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write or a generic null-pointer issue; the missing bounds constraint is the direct cause of the observed segmentation violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is unchecked indexing into the truns array: truns[0] is dereferenced even when the TRUN collection is empty, and truns[++trun_index] advances without a bounds check relative to the number of TRUN atoms. A crafted fragment lacking or under-provisioning TRUN atoms triggers an out-of-bounds read of the array element, leading to a dereference of invalid memory and a crash/segmentation violation.

commit_msg:
KEYS: fix keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring() to not leak thread keyrings

This fixes CVE-2017-7472.

Running the following program as an unprivileged user exhausts kernel
memory by leaking thread keyrings:

	#include <keyutils.h>

	int main()
	{
		for (;;)
			keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring(KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING);
	}

Fix it by only creating a new thread keyring if there wasn't one before.
To make things more consistent, make install_thread_keyring_to_cred()
and install_process_keyring_to_cred() both return 0 if the corresponding
keyring is already present.

Fixes: d84f4f992cbd ("CRED: Inaugurate COW credentials")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 2.6.29+
Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (ret < 0) {', '\t\t\tif (ret != -EEXIST)', '\t\t\t\tgoto error;', '\t\t\tret = 0;', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (ret < 0)', '\t\t\tgoto error;']}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.10.13 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a series of KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring calls.

code_evidence: In the KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING case, install_thread_keyring_to_cred(new) is called on freshly prepared credentials and the result is only checked for ret < 0; there is no handling of an already-present keyring, so a new thread keyring is installed each call.

The PROCESS_KEYRING case explicitly tolerates -EEXIST (lines 19-23), showing the pattern the thread case lacks; without it, repeated calls allocate a thread keyring that is never released as creds are committed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 fits because the allocated thread keyring resource is not properly released/reused across repeated calls, leading to resource consumption. The process-keyring branch's explicit -EEXIST handling shows the missing constraint is resource lifecycle management, not a credential check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the thread-keyring branch unconditionally installs a new keyring into new credentials without recognizing that one already exists, and success commits the credentials. Trigger: an unprivileged user repeatedly invokes keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring with KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING. Consequence: thread keyrings accumulate without being released, exhausting kernel memory (DoS).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct Qdisc *q = NULL;', '\tstruct tcf_chain *chain = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct Qdisc *q;', '\tstruct tcf_chain *chain;', '\tq = NULL;', '\tchain = NULL;']}
description: A use-after-free exists in the Linux Kernel in tc_new_tfilter that could allow a local attacker to gain privilege escalation. The exploit requires unprivileged user namespaces. We recommend upgrading past commit 04c2a47ffb13c29778e2a14e414ad4cb5a5db4b5

code_evidence: q and chain are function-scoped locals declared at [13,15] and only initialized once before the replay label; the replay path re-enters at [26] without reinitializing them.
After the replay, __tcf_qdisc_find, __tcf_qdisc_cl_find, __tcf_block_find and tcf_chain_get reassign q/chain at [50,64,67,80], overwriting the stale pointers from the prior iteration.

The error path at [166] releases the previous chain and block via tcf_block_release at [176], then when err == -EAGAIN [179] sets rtnl_held and jumps back to replay [181], leaving q/chain pointing to freed objects.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits: the function retains and dereferences a pointer to memory released earlier in the same call, exactly the reuse-after-free pattern. The fix moves q=NULL and chain=NULL to after the replay label, confirming the dangling-pointer defect rather than a mere null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: On the EAGAIN retry, the code loops to replay while q and chain still hold pointers to objects already released by tcf_block_release/tcf_chain_put; the subsequent iteration reuses those dangling pointers (e.g. q->ops and chain->filter_chain_lock) before reassignment. Root cause is failure to reset locals on retry; consequence is use-after-free, potentially privilege escalation from unprivileged user namespaces.

commit_msg:
app: fix #8120 GIMP 2.10.30 crashed when allocate large memory

GIMP could crash if the information regarding old path properties read
from XCF was incorrect. It did not check if xcf_old_path succeeded and
kept trying to load more paths even if the last one failed to load.

Instead we now stop loading paths as soon as that function fails.
In case we have a failure here we also try to skip to the next property
based on the size of the path property, in hopes that the only problem
was this property.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      g_printerr ("Unknown path type. Possibly corrupt XCF file");'], 'added_lines': ['      g_printerr ("Unknown path type (version: %u). Possibly corrupt XCF file.\\n", version);']}
description: GIMP 2.10.30 and 2.99.10 are vulnerable to Buffer Overflow. Through a crafted XCF file, the program will allocate for a huge amount of memory, resulting in insufficient memory or program crash.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no buffer copy operation; num_points drives a g_new0 allocation and per-element reads, not an unchecked copy into a fixed output buffer, so CWE-120 is not supported by this code.

commit_msg:
crypto: algif_skcipher - Require setkey before accept(2)

Some cipher implementations will crash if you try to use them
without calling setkey first.  This patch adds a check so that
the accept(2) call will fail with -ENOKEY if setkey hasn't been
done on the socket yet.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>

description: crypto/algif_skcipher.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.2 does not verify that a setkey operation has been performed on an AF_ALG socket before an accept system call is processed, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash) via a crafted application that does not supply a key, related to the lrw_crypt function in crypto/lrw.c.

commit_msg:
pegasus: Use heap buffers for all register access

Allocating USB buffers on the stack is not portable, and no longer
works on x86_64 (with VMAP_STACK enabled as per default).

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
References: https://bugs.debian.org/852556
Reported-by: Lisandro Damián Nicanor Pérez Meyer <lisandro@debian.org>
Tested-by: Lisandro Damián Nicanor Pérez Meyer <lisandro@debian.org>
Signed-off-by: Ben Hutchings <ben@decadent.org.uk>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t      indx, data, size, 1000);'], 'added_lines': ['\tu8 *buf;', '', '\tbuf = kmalloc(size, GFP_NOIO);', '\tif (!buf)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\t\t\t      indx, buf, size, 1000);', '\telse if (ret <= size)', '\t\tmemcpy(data, buf, ret);', '\tkfree(buf);']}
description: drivers/net/usb/pegasus.c in the Linux kernel 4.9.x before 4.9.11 interacts incorrectly with the CONFIG_VMAP_STACK option, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash or memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging use of more than one virtual page for a DMA scatterlist.

code_evidence: usb_control_msg writes up to size bytes received from the device directly into the caller-supplied data buffer, with no local bound check on size against that buffer. The USB read is the only bound on the write extent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a memory write operation (usb_control_msg filling data) whose extent (size) is not constrained to the destination buffer's bounds, so it writes outside the intended buffer, matching CWE-119. The stack-buffer aspect is the specific trigger, but the supported weakness is the unbounded buffer write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the transfer destination is the caller's stack buffer (per the commit, a stack-allocated DMA scatterlist), and size is a caller/device-controlled length passed straight to usb_control_msg with no validation. Trigger: a size larger than the destination buffer causes the USB core to write past the buffer's end during the control transfer. Consequence: out-of-bounds write, leading to stack corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
SCCP: Use int datatype for offset to prevent infinite loops

Fields are 16-bit values and large 16-bit values can be incorrectly
treated as negative, causing infinite loops in offset calculations.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-sccp.c had an infinite loop that was addressed by using a correct integer data type.

code_evidence: offset is declared guint16 [7]. VARIABLE_POINTER adds the parsed 16-bit pointer value to the 16-bit offset at [23], then advances offset by ptr_size at [26]; the accumulated value wraps modulo 65536 when a large pointer field is added. offset is returned at [491] and later reused at [469] to locate optional parameters, so the wrapped/incorrect offset can point backward and cause repeated traversal.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function supports CWE-835 because the miscalculated offset can make the surrounding parameter/optional-parameter iteration fail to reach its exit condition, producing an unreachable exit condition and infinite loop. This is a loop-termination/availability issue, not merely an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a 16-bit unsigned offset accumulates attacker-controlled 16-bit pointer values, so large values wrap instead of being treated as a large/negative delta. Trigger: a crafted SCCP message with a large variable-pointer value. Consequence: the offset calculations no longer advance monotonically, allowing an infinite loop and CPU resource exhaustion (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix a UAF resulting from a bug in BIO_new_NDEF

If the aux->asn1_cb() call fails in BIO_new_NDEF then the "out" BIO will
be part of an invalid BIO chain. This causes a "use after free" when the
BIO is eventually freed.

Based on an original patch by Viktor Dukhovni and an idea from Theo
Buehler.

Thanks to Octavio Galland for reporting this issue.

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    BIO_asn1_set_prefix(asn_bio, ndef_prefix, ndef_prefix_free);', '    BIO_asn1_set_suffix(asn_bio, ndef_suffix, ndef_suffix_free);', '     * Now let callback prepends any digest, cipher etc BIOs ASN1 structure', '     * needs.', '    if (aux->asn1_cb(ASN1_OP_STREAM_PRE, &val, it, &sarg) <= 0)', '    BIO_ctrl(asn_bio, BIO_C_SET_EX_ARG, 0, ndef_aux);', ''], 'added_lines': ['    BIO *pop_bio = NULL;', '    pop_bio = asn_bio;', '    if (BIO_asn1_set_prefix(asn_bio, ndef_prefix, ndef_prefix_free) <= 0', '            || BIO_asn1_set_suffix(asn_bio, ndef_suffix, ndef_suffix_free) <= 0', '            || BIO_ctrl(asn_bio, BIO_C_SET_EX_ARG, 0, ndef_aux) <= 0)', '        goto err;', "     * Now let the callback prepend any digest, cipher, etc., that the BIO's", '     * ASN1 structure needs.', '    /*', '     * The asn1_cb(), must not have mutated asn_bio on error, leaving it in the', '     * middle of some partially built, but not returned BIO chain.', '     */', '    if (aux->asn1_cb(ASN1_OP_STREAM_PRE, &val, it, &sarg) <= 0) {', '        /*', '         * ndef_aux is now owned by asn_bio so we must not free it in the err', '         * clean up block', '         */', '        ndef_aux = NULL;', '    }', '', '    /*', '     * We must not fail now because the callback has prepended additional', '     * BIOs to the chain', '     */', '    /* BIO_pop() is NULL safe */', '    (void)BIO_pop(pop_bio);']}
description:
The public API function BIO_new_NDEF is a helper function used for streaming
ASN.1 data via a BIO. It is primarily used internally to OpenSSL to support the
SMIME, CMS and PKCS7 streaming capabilities, but may also be called directly by
end user applications.

The function receives a BIO from the caller, prepends a new BIO_f_asn1 filter
BIO onto the front of it to form a BIO chain, and then returns the new head of
the BIO chain to the caller. Under certain conditions, for example if a CMS
recipient public key is invalid, the new filter BIO is freed and the function
returns a NULL result indicating a failure. However, in this case, the BIO chain
is not properly cleaned up and the BIO passed by the caller still retains
internal pointers to the previously freed filter BIO. If the caller then goes on
to call BIO_pop() on the BIO then a use-after-free will occur. This will most
likely result in a crash.



This scenario occurs directly in the internal function B64_write_ASN1() which
may cause BIO_new_NDEF() to be called and will subsequently call BIO_pop() on
the BIO. This internal function is in turn called by the public API functions
PEM_write_bio_ASN1_stream, PEM_write_bio_CMS_stream, PEM_write_bio_PKCS7_stream,
SMIME_write_ASN1, SMIME_write_CMS and SMIME_write_PKCS7.

Other public API functions that may be impacted by this include
i2d_ASN1_bio_stream, BIO_new_CMS, BIO_new_PKCS7, i2d_CMS_bio_stream and
i2d_PKCS7_bio_stream.

The OpenSSL cms and smime command line applications are similarly affected.

code_evidence: BIO_push() links asn_bio into the caller's BIO chain at line 15, so 'out' now holds an internal reference back to asn_bio (and asn_bio to out).
If aux->asn1_cb() fails at line 23, control jumps to err at line 32.

The error block only frees asn_bio (line 33) and ndef_aux (line 34); it never detaches asn_bio from the chain via BIO_pop(). The caller's out BIO therefore retains a dangling pointer to the freed asn_bio.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is a dangling chain pointer to memory freed in the error path, later reused by the caller — exactly CWE-416. It is not a mere double-free or leak: the freed BIO is referenced through the surviving chain rather than freed twice.

evidence_lines.code:
if (aux->asn1_cb(ASN1_OP_STREAM_PRE, &val, it, &sarg) <= 0)
goto err;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: after BIO_push() succeeds, a later asn1_cb() failure frees asn_bio without unlinking it from the chain. Trigger: a callback failure such as an invalid CMS recipient key. Consequence: caller's BIO still references freed memory, and a subsequent BIO_pop()/chain traversal dereferences it, yielding a use-after-free (crash or worse).

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in reconn_set_ipaddr_from_hostname in fs/cifs/connect.c in the Linux kernel. The issue occurs when it forgets to set the free pointer server->hostname to NULL, leading to an invalid pointer request.

commit_msg:
Unsquashfs: fix write outside destination directory exploit

An issue on Github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
shows how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and ..) can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by checking all names for
validity.

In doing so I have also added checks for '.' and for names that
are shorter than they should be (names in the file system should
not have '\0' terminators).

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t\t/* check name for invalid characters (i.e /, ., ..) */', '\t\t\tif(check_name(dire->name, dire->size + 1) == FALSE) {', '\t\t\t\tERROR("File system corrupted: invalid characters in name\\n");', '\t\t\t\tgoto corrupted;', '\t\t\t}', '']}
description: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-1.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 stores the filename in the directory entry; this is then used by unsquashfs to create the new file during the unsquash. The filename is not validated for traversal outside of the destination directory, and thus allows writing to locations outside of the destination.

code_evidence: The directory entry name is copied from the on-disk directory table into dire->name using the attacker-controlled length dire->size + 1; no validation of the name content occurs at this point.

The unvalidated name is then copied into dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name with strcpy, so the raw on-disk filename (which may contain '/' or '..') is retained for later use in path construction during unsquash.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-22 fits because external input (the on-disk filename) is used to construct a pathname under a restricted destination directory without neutralizing '/' or '..', enabling escape from that directory. This is relative path traversal rather than a mere buffer issue.

evidence_lines.code: strcpy(dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name, dire->name);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accepts a filesystem-supplied filename without checking for path separators or '..' components. Trigger: a crafted Squashfs image whose directory entry name contains traversal elements. Consequence: downstream unsquash file creation uses the name to build a path, allowing writes outside the destination directory.

commit_msg:
Currently, locking of ->session is very inconsistent; most places
protect it using the legacy tty mutex, but disassociate_ctty(),
__do_SAK(), tiocspgrp() and tiocgsid() don't.
Two of the writers hold the ctrl_lock (because they already need it for
->pgrp), but __proc_set_tty() doesn't do that yet.

On a PREEMPT=y system, an unprivileged user can theoretically abuse
this broken locking to read 4 bytes of freed memory via TIOCGSID if
tiocgsid() is preempted long enough at the right point. (Other things
might also go wrong, especially if root-only ioctls are involved; I'm
not sure about that.)

Change the locking on ->session such that:

 - tty_lock() is held by all writers: By making disassociate_ctty()
   hold it. This should be fine because the same lock can already be
   taken through the call to tty_vhangup_session().
   The tricky part is that we need to shorten the area covered by
   siglock to be able to take tty_lock() without ugly retry logic; as
   far as I can tell, this should be fine, since nothing in the
   signal_struct is touched in the `if (tty)` branch.
 - ctrl_lock is held by all writers: By changing __proc_set_tty() to
   hold the lock a little longer.
 - All readers that aren't holding tty_lock() hold ctrl_lock: By
   adding locking to tiocgsid() and __do_SAK(), and expanding the area
   covered by ctrl_lock in tiocspgrp().

Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Jiri Slaby <jirislaby@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttty->session = get_pid(task_session(current));'], 'added_lines': ['\ttty->session = get_pid(task_session(current));']}
description: A locking inconsistency issue was discovered in the tty subsystem of the Linux kernel through 5.9.13. drivers/tty/tty_io.c and drivers/tty/tty_jobctrl.c may allow a read-after-free attack against TIOCGSID, aka CID-c8bcd9c5be24.

code_evidence: __proc_set_tty() acquires tty->ctrl_lock with spin_lock_irqsave at line 4, updates ->pgrp and releases the lock at line 8, then assigns tty->session outside the protected region at line 9. The commit's purpose is to keep ctrl_lock held while writing ->session so all writers serialize consistently with readers like tiocgsid().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to hold the required lock across all accesses to the shared ->session resource, which is precisely improper locking (CWE-667): inconsistent lock coverage leads to unpredictable shared-state modification. This is a locking-scope defect, not a separate missing-check or lifetime bug, so CWE-667 fits the target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ->session write is performed after ctrl_lock is dropped, so a concurrent reader holding ctrl_lock can observe or race on a stale/freed session pointer. Trigger: preemption between unlock and the session assignment allows another thread to read ->session via TIOCGSID. Supported consequence: read-after-free of the session field and inconsistent shared state.

+++ func_after
@@ -21,7 +21,7 @@

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      y < 0 || y > img->height)'], 'added_lines': ['      y < 0 || y >= img->height)']}
description: A heap buffer overflow in image_set_mask function of HTMLDOC before 1.9.15 allows an attacker to write outside the buffer boundaries.

code_evidence: Bounds check rejects only y < 0 or y > img->height; y == img->height passes because the comparison uses > instead of >=, while x uses the correct >= img->width.
When maskscale == 8, the passing y value indexes img->mask[y * img->maskwidth + x], writing one row past the allocated mask buffer.

When maskscale != 8, y is multiplied by maskscale and the nested loops compute maskptr = img->mask + y * img->maskwidth + x / 8, so the off-by-one row also produces an out-of-bounds write via *maskptr |= masks[x & 7].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing >= constraint allows both the direct and scaled mask assignments to write beyond the intended buffer. This is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the indexed mask locations are modified.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an off-by-one boundary check: y == img->height satisfies the guard because only y > img->height is rejected. Triggering image_set_mask with y equal to the image height reaches the mask write paths, causing a heap out-of-bounds write past the mask buffer and potential memory corruption.

Ignore certain messages in plugin broker process if they are not sent by the
browser.

BUG=610600
CQ_INCLUDE_TRYBOTS=tryserver.chromium.linux:linux_site_isolation

description: The PPAPI implementation in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.82 does not validate the origin of IPC messages to the plugin broker process that should have come from the browser process, which allows remote attackers to bypass a sandbox protection mechanism via an unexpected message type, related to broker_process_dispatcher.cc, ppapi_plugin_process_host.cc, ppapi_thread.cc, and render_frame_message_filter.cc.
