code_evidence: getvvcol() is called on top and bot at lines 57-58; per the patch comment, this call flushes (frees) rex.line. Line 65 then dereferences the stale rex.line pointer by passing it to win_linetabsize() and computing rex.input - rex.line, so the buffer is used after being released.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a heap pointer (rex.line) after the call that frees it, which is precisely use-after-free (CWE-416). This is not merely a null/dangling check omission; the stale pointer is actively passed to win_linetabsize() and used in pointer arithmetic.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: rex.line is invalidated by getvvcol() but the code continues to use the old pointer in win_linetabsize() and the offset computation. Trigger: matching a visual-block (Ctrl_V) region where getvvcol() runs. Consequence: read of freed memory, potentially crash or disclosure; the fix re-fetches the line via reg_getline() before use.

commit_msg:
Commit a23740ec43ba ("bpf: Track contents of read-only maps as scalars") is
checking whether maps are read-only both from BPF program side and user space
side, and then, given their content is constant, reading out their data via
map->ops->map_direct_value_addr() which is then subsequently used as known
scalar value for the register, that is, it is marked as __mark_reg_known()
with the read value at verification time. Before a23740ec43ba, the register
content was marked as an unknown scalar so the verifier could not make any
assumptions about the map content.

The current implementation however is prone to a TOCTOU race, meaning, the
value read as known scalar for the register is not guaranteed to be exactly
the same at a later point when the program is executed, and as such, the
prior made assumptions of the verifier with regards to the program will be
invalid which can cause issues such as OOB access, etc.

While the BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG map flag is always fixed and required to be
specified at map creation time, the map->frozen property is initially set to
false for the map given the map value needs to be populated, e.g. for global
data sections. Once complete, the loader "freezes" the map from user space
such that no subsequent updates/deletes are possible anymore. For the rest
of the lifetime of the map, this freeze one-time trigger cannot be undone
anymore after a successful BPF_MAP_FREEZE cmd return. Meaning, any new BPF_*
cmd calls which would update/delete map entries will be rejected with -EPERM
since map_get_sys_perms() removes the FMODE_CAN_WRITE permission. This also
means that pending update/delete map entries must still complete before this
guarantee is given. This corner case is not an issue for loaders since they
create and prepare such program private map in successive steps.

However, a malicious user is able to trigger this TOCTOU race in two different
ways: i) via userfaultfd, and ii) via batched updates. For i) userfaultfd is
used to expand the competition interval, so that map_update_elem() can modify
the contents of the map after map_freeze() and bpf_prog_load() were executed.
This works, because userfaultfd halts the parallel thread which triggered a
map_update_elem() at the time where we copy key/value from the user buffer and
this already passed the FMODE_CAN_WRITE capability test given at that time the
map was not "frozen". Then, the main thread performs the map_freeze() and
bpf_prog_load(), and once that had completed successfully, the other thread
is woken up to complete the pending map_update_elem() which then changes the
map content. For ii) the idea of the batched update is similar, meaning, when
there are a large number of updates to be processed, it can increase the
competition interval between the two. It is therefore possible in practice to
modify the contents of the map after executing map_freeze() and bpf_prog_load().

One way to fix both i) and ii) at the same time is to expand the use of the
map's map->writecnt. The latter was introduced in fc9702273e2e ("bpf: Add mmap()
support for BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY") and further refined in 1f6cb19be2e2 ("bpf:
Prevent re-mmap()'ing BPF map as writable for initially r/o mapping") with
the rationale to make a writable mmap()'ing of a map mutually exclusive with
read-only freezing. The counter indicates writable mmap() mappings and then
prevents/fails the freeze operation. Its semantics can be expanded beyond
just mmap() by generally indicating ongoing write phases. This would essentially
span any parallel regular and batched flavor of update/delete operation and
then also have map_freeze() fail with -EBUSY. For the check_mem_access() in
the verifier we expand upon the bpf_map_is_rdonly() check ensuring that all
last pending writes have completed via bpf_map_write_active() test. Once the
map->frozen is set and bpf_map_write_active() indicates a map->writecnt of 0
only then we are really guaranteed to use the map's data as known constants.
For map->frozen being set and pending writes in process of still being completed
we fall back to marking that register as unknown scalar so we don't end up
making assumptions about it. With this, both TOCTOU reproducers from i) and
ii) are fixed.

Note that the map->writecnt has been converted into a atomic64 in the fix in
order to avoid a double freeze_mutex mutex_{un,}lock() pair when updating
map->writecnt in the various map update/delete BPF_* cmd flavors. Spanning
the freeze_mutex over entire map update/delete operations in syscall side
would not be possible due to then causing everything to be serialized.
Similarly, something like synchronize_rcu() after setting map->frozen to wait
for update/deletes to complete is not possible either since it would also
have to span the user copy which can sleep. On the libbpf side, this won't
break d66562fba1ce ("libbpf: Add BPF object skeleton support") as the
anonymous mmap()-ed "map initialization image" is remapped as a BPF map-backed
mmap()-ed memory where for .rodata it's non-writable.

Fixes: a23740ec43ba ("bpf: Track contents of read-only maps as scalars")
Reported-by: w1tcher.bupt@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Andrii Nakryiko <andrii@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\tif ((cmd == BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_BATCH ||', '\t     cmd == BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_AND_DELETE_BATCH) &&', '\t    !(map_get_sys_perms(map, f) & FMODE_CAN_READ)) {', '', '\tif (cmd != BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_BATCH &&', '\t    !(map_get_sys_perms(map, f) & FMODE_CAN_WRITE)) {', ''], 'added_lines': ['\tbool has_read  = cmd == BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_BATCH ||', '\t\t\t cmd == BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_AND_DELETE_BATCH;', '\tbool has_write = cmd != BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_BATCH;', '\tif (has_write)', '\t\tbpf_map_write_active_inc(map);', '\tif (has_read && !(map_get_sys_perms(map, f) & FMODE_CAN_READ)) {', '\tif (has_write && !(map_get_sys_perms(map, f) & FMODE_CAN_WRITE)) {', '\tif (has_write)', '\t\tbpf_map_write_active_dec(map);']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernel's ebpf verifier between bpf_map_update_elem and bpf_map_freeze due to a missing lock in kernel/bpf/syscall.c. In this flaw, a local user with a special privilege (cap_sys_admin or cap_bpf) can modify the frozen mapped address space. This flaw affects kernel versions prior to 5.16 rc2.

code_evidence: The function checks FMODE_CAN_READ via map_get_sys_perms() for lookup-style batch commands and jumps to err_put with -EPERM on failure.
It separately checks FMODE_CAN_WRITE for write-style batch commands (update/delete) before dispatch.
After the permission checks, it dispatches to map->ops->map_lookup_batch, map_lookup_and_delete_batch, map_update_batch or map_delete_batch based on cmd.
err_put only does fdput(f) and returns; there is no accounting of an in-flight write phase or serialization with map_freeze().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic TOCTOU: the resource state (map writability/frozen status) is checked at lines 15-25 but can change before the write is used at lines 26-33. CWE-367 directly captures the check-then-use race; a plain permission-check weakness would not require the concurrent state change that makes the check stale.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The capability check (FMODE_CAN_READ/WRITE) is performed before the batch operation executes, but nothing marks the map as having an active write or prevents a concurrent BPF_MAP_FREEZE from completing between the check and the map_update/delete_batch call. A user can therefore pass the writability check on an unfrozen map, have the map frozen, and still complete a pending update, invalidating the verifier's assumption that read-only map contents are constant.

commit_msg:
Use new libostree APIs to reject world-writable/suid content

This uses the new libostree APIs that landed recently to ensure
that we reject any files with mode outside of `0775` for system
helper pulls, and we also mask directory modes during checkout.

However, this does *not* fix up any already downloaded content.
For that, one could uninstall/reinstall; or a future patch could
do a one-time fixup pass.

Note that I am not aware of a way for flatpak applications to escalate their
privileges directly with this flaw; the bubblewrap `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` turns
of setuid. However, in combination with code execution on the host via another
mechanism (e.g. unsandboxed app), a setuid app injected could be used to gain
full host privileges.

At this time we're not aware of any flatpak content exploiting this issue.

Closes: https://github.com/flatpak/flatpak/issues/845
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  options.bareuseronly_dirs = TRUE; /* https://github.com/ostreedev/ostree/pull/927 */']}
description: In Flatpak before 0.8.7, a third-party app repository could include malicious apps that contain files with inappropriate permissions, for example setuid or world-writable. The files are deployed with those permissions, which would let a local attacker run the setuid executable or write to the world-writable location. In the case of the "system helper" component, files deployed as part of the app are owned by root, so in the worst case they could be setuid root.

code_evidence: OstreeRepoCheckoutAtOptions options is zero-initialized at line 26, so bareuseronly_dirs defaults to FALSE. The function then sets options.mode to OSTREE_REPO_CHECKOUT_MODE_USER and passes options unmodified to ostree_repo_checkout_at for both the full-tree and subpath checkouts (lines 116-119, 163-166), so checked-out files retain repository mode bits rather than being masked to 0775.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function assigns permissions to deployed app content without constraining them, letting unintended actors execute or modify security-critical files; this is incorrect permission assignment for a critical resource (CWE-732), not merely a missing authorization check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the checkout options never request bareuseronly_dirs, and OSTREE_REPO_CHECKOUT_MODE_USER does not strip setuid/world-writable bits from file entries. Trigger: a malicious third-party repository commit containing files with mode outside 0775 is deployed. Consequence: the files land with those permissions, and under the root-owned system helper they can become setuid root or world-writable, enabling privilege escalation or tampering.

commit_msg: imap_quote_string make room for quotes
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  /* save room for trailing quote-char */', '  dlen -= 2;'], 'added_lines': ['  /* save room for quote-chars */', '  dlen -= 3;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Mutt before 1.10.1 and NeoMutt before 2018-07-16. imap_quote_string in imap/util.c does not leave room for quote characters, leading to a stack-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Line 8 writes the opening quote after advancing pt, and line 9 reserves only two bytes (dlen -= 2) for the opening quote and the trailing quote/null terminator.
The loop at line 10 consumes dlen, and lines 26-27 unconditionally write the closing quote and NUL after the loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the code writes past the end of the intended destination buffer due to an off-by-one under-reservation. It is an out-of-bounds write rather than mere improper input validation, since the defect is the write past the buffer boundary.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function reserves two bytes but must accommodate the opening quote already written, the closing quote, and the NUL terminator. When src fills the remaining budget, the loop exits with dlen exhausted, yet lines 26-27 still write '*pt++' and '*pt', placing bytes past the destination buffer end. The trigger is a long source string that saturates dlen; the supported consequence is a stack-based out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
Affected are ProcRRChangeProviderProperty and ProcRRChangeOutputProperty.
See also xserver@8f454b79 where this same bug was fixed for the core
protocol and XI.

This fixes an OOB read and the resulting information disclosure.

Length calculation for the request was clipped to a 32-bit integer. With
the correct stuff->nUnits value the expected request size was
truncated, passing the REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE check.

The server then proceeded with reading at least stuff->num_items bytes
(depending on stuff->format) from the request and stuffing whatever it
finds into the property. In the process it would also allocate at least
stuff->nUnits bytes, i.e. 4GB.

CVE-2023-6478, ZDI-CAN-22561

This vulnerability was discovered by:
Jan-Niklas Sohn working with Trend Micro Zero Day Initiative
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int totalSize;'], 'added_lines': ['    uint64_t totalSize;']}
description: A flaw was found in xorg-server. A specially crafted request to RRChangeProviderProperty or RRChangeOutputProperty can trigger an integer overflow which may lead to a disclosure of sensitive information.

code_evidence: Line 9 declares totalSize as signed int. Line 24 reads attacker-controlled 32-bit stuff->nUnits into unsigned long len; line 25 bounds len only against 0xffffffff minus the request header size, permitting values near 4GB. Line 27 computes sizeInBytes as format>>3 (1,2,4). Line 28 multiplies len*sizeInBytes into the int totalSize, which overflows/wraps for large len, yielding a small or negative value. Line 29 then passes the truncated totalSize to REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE, so the length check passes despite the oversized request.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is an integer multiplication whose result is stored in a narrower signed type, producing wraparound that bypasses a size check; this is precisely CWE-190. The consequence is OOB read/disclosure rather than the integer error itself, distinguishing cause from impact.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the 32-bit signed int totalSize receiving the product of a large attacker-controlled len and sizeInBytes, causing integer wraparound. Trigger is a crafted request with a huge nUnits that survives the line 25 check; the wrapped totalSize defeats the REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE validation, after which the handler reads at least nUnits bytes from the request, causing OOB read and information disclosure (and large allocation).

commit_msg:
Added stack overflow check for hermes::vm:: hermesBuiltinApply

Summary: This adds a missing check for stack overflow.

Reviewed By: tmikov

Differential Revision: D20104955

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (LLVM_UNLIKELY(newFrame.overflowed()))', '    return runtime->raiseStackOverflow(Runtime::StackOverflowKind::NativeStack);', '']}
description: A stack overflow vulnerability in Facebook Hermes 'builtin apply' prior to commit 86543ac47e59c522976b5632b8bf9a2a4583c7d2 (https://github.com/facebook/hermes/commit/86543ac47e59c522976b5632b8bf9a2a4583c7d2) allows attackers to potentially execute arbitrary code via crafted JavaScript. Note that this is only exploitable if the application using Hermes permits evaluation of untrusted JavaScript. Hence, most React Native applications are not affected.

code_evidence: A ScopedNativeCallFrame is allocated with len taken directly from the attacker-controlled array length at line 13.
No overflow check is performed on newFrame before the loop writes each argument into the frame's argument slots.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing overflow check allows the argument-copy loop to write past the end of the intended call-frame buffer, which is precisely an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an unbounded resource issue; the writes target memory beyond the allocated frame.

ScopedNativeCallFrame newFrame{
runtime, len, *fn, isConstructor, thisVal.getHermesValue()};

for (uint32_t i = 0; i < len; ++i) {
newFrame->getArgRef(i) = argArray->at(runtime, i);

Trigger: apply() called with a very large array length causes the stack frame allocation to overflow its bounds. commit_msg:
If L1 disables VMLOAD/VMSAVE intercepts, and doesn't enable
Virtual VMLOAD/VMSAVE (currently not supported for the nested hypervisor),
then VMLOAD/VMSAVE must operate on the L1 physical memory, which is only
possible by making L0 intercept these instructions.

Failure to do so allowed the nested guest to run VMLOAD/VMSAVE unintercepted,
and thus read/write portions of the host physical memory.

Fixes: 89c8a4984fc9 ("KVM: SVM: Enable Virtual VMLOAD VMSAVE feature")

Suggested-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Maxim Levitsky <mlevitsk@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tvmcb_set_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_VMLOAD);', '\tvmcb_set_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_VMSAVE);']}
description: A flaw was found in the KVM's AMD code for supporting SVM nested virtualization. The flaw occurs when processing the VMCB (virtual machine control block) provided by the L1 guest to spawn/handle a nested guest (L2). Due to improper validation of the "virt_ext" field, this issue could allow a malicious L1 to disable both VMLOAD/VMSAVE intercepts and VLS (Virtual VMLOAD/VMSAVE) for the L2 guest. As a result, the L2 guest would be allowed to read/write physical pages of the host, resulting in a crash of the entire system, leak of sensitive data or potential guest-to-host escape.

code_evidence: The loop copies the L1 host intercepts into the effective control area, establishing the L1 baseline for the nested guest.
The loop then ORs in the L2 (nested) intercepts from g->intercepts, so the nested guest's requests are merged without any restriction.
Only SMI is conditionally cleared; there is no enforcement that VMLOAD/VMSAVE remain intercepted when L1 has not enabled virtual VMLOAD/VMSAVE.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function omits an authorization/containment check on nested intercept configuration, allowing the L1 guest to grant L2 access to operations that should remain under L0 control. This missing restriction on the L2 action matches CWE-862 rather than a mere validation error, since the defect is failure to enforce a required intercept constraint.

evidence_lines.code:
for (i = 0; i < MAX_INTERCEPT; i++)
c->intercepts[i] = h->intercepts[i];

for (i = 0; i < MAX_INTERCEPT; i++)
c->intercepts[i] |= g->intercepts[i];

if (!intercept_smi)
vmcb_clr_intercept(c, INTERCEPT_SMI);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: recalc_intercepts merges L2-provided intercept bits into the effective VMCB without requiring VMLOAD/VMSAVE to stay intercepted when L1 disabled them and no virtual VMLOAD/VMSAVE support is available. Trigger: a malicious L1 supplies a nested VMCB whose virt_ext disables both intercepts. Consequence: L2 executes VMLOAD/VMSAVE unintercepted against host physical memory, enabling read/write of host pages.

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tq->bins[slot].perturbation = prandom_u32();'], 'added_lines': ['\tget_random_bytes(&q->bins[slot].perturbation,', '\t\t\t sizeof(q->bins[slot].perturbation));']}
description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: Line 3 seeds the per-slot perturbation value with prandom_u32(), a non-cryptographic PRNG output, rather than a cryptographically strong random source.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because the function supplies a security-relevant value from an insufficiently random source; the fix replaces prandom_u32() with get_random_bytes(), confirming the weakness is the randomness source, not a separate hashing flaw.

evidence_lines.code: q->bins[slot].perturbation = prandom_u32();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the perturbation used for hashing/flow classification is derived from prandom_u32(), whose outputs are predictable and not cryptographically strong. Trigger: an attacker who observes or infers the perturbation-dependent hashes can predict or correlate the per-slot value. Supported consequence: weakened unpredictability of the perturbation in the security context described by the commit, enabling inference of device/flow characteristics rather than a direct memory-safety impact.

commit_msg:
Fix potential double-free() in Interactive Service (CVE-2018-9336)

Malformed input data on the service pipe towards the OpenVPN interactive
service (normally used by the OpenVPN GUI to request openvpn instances
from the service) can result in a double free() in the error handling code.

This usually only leads to a process crash (DoS by an unprivileged local
account) but since it could possibly lead to memory corruption if
happening while multiple other threads are active at the same time,
CVE-2018-9336 has been assigned to acknowledge this risk.

Fix by ensuring that sud->directory is set to NULL in GetStartUpData()
for all error cases (thus not being free()ed in FreeStartupData()).

Rewrite control flow to use explicit error label for error exit.

Discovered and reported by Jacob Baines <jbaines@tenable.com>.

CVE: 2018-9336

Signed-off-by: Gert Doering <gert@greenie.muc.de>
Acked-by: Selva Nair <selva.nair@gmail.com>
Message-Id: <20180414072617.25075-1-gert@greenie.muc.de>
URL: https://www.mail-archive.com/search?l=mid&q=20180414072617.25075-1-gert@greenie.muc.de

Signed-off-by: Gert Doering <gert@greenie.muc.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    BOOL ret = FALSE;', '        goto out;', '        goto out;', '        goto out;', '        goto out;', '        goto out;', '        goto out;', '        goto out;', "    data = NULL; /* don't free data */", '    ret = TRUE;', 'out:', '    return ret;'], 'added_lines': ['        goto err;', '        goto err;', '        goto err;', '        goto err;', '        goto err;', '        goto err;', '        goto err;', '    return TRUE;', 'err:', '    sud->directory = NULL;\t\t/* caller must not free() */', '    return FALSE;']}
description: openvpnserv.exe (aka the interactive service helper) in OpenVPN 2.4.x before 2.4.6 allows a local attacker to cause a double-free of memory by sending a malformed request to the interactive service. This could cause a denial-of-service through memory corruption or possibly have unspecified other impact including privilege escalation.

code_evidence: After the NULL-terminated check, sud->directory is assigned the malloc'd data pointer; if the working-directory length check fails (size <= 0), control jumps to out: where free(data) runs, yet sud->directory still aliases that freed block.
Similarly, when the command-line options check fails after sud->options is set, the error path frees data while sud->directory still points to it.

The out: label unconditionally calls free(data); on success data is set to NULL before the label so no double free occurs, but on these mid-parse error paths the pointer is not cleared and remains reachable through sud->directory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The same heap address (data, also stored in sud->directory) is freed in GetStartupData and then freed again by the caller, matching CWE-415's definition of calling free() twice on one address. This is distinct from a simple use-after-free; the defect is the duplicated deallocation through two retained pointers.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: error exits after sud->directory = data leave the caller-visible pointer aliasing the block that the local error handler frees, without nulling it. Trigger: a malformed pipe request whose directory or options length exhausts the buffer. Consequence: the caller later frees sud->directory again, a double free (crash/DoS, possible memory corruption).

commit_msg:
journalctl: verify sealed log epochs are continuous

Currently empty epochs are not sealed. This allows an attacker to truncate
a sealed log and continue it without any problems showing when verifying the
log.

This partially addresses CVE-2023-31438. One way to extend this change to
address CVE-2023-31438 completely, would be to verify that there is exactly
one seal per epoch (and not sealing when the epoch has not ended yet).

the change also adds a journal-file flag: HEADER_COMPATIBLE_SEALED_CONTINUOUS
this flag indicates that a journal file is sealed continuously and decides whether
any missing crypto epochs should trigger a warning or an error.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (!f->hmac_running)', '                return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['        if (!f->hmac_running) {', '                r = journal_file_hmac_start(f);', '                if (r < 0)', '                        return r;', '        }']}
description: An issue was discovered in systemd 253. An attacker can truncate a sealed log file and then resume log sealing such that checking the integrity shows no error, despite modifications. NOTE: the vendor reportedly sent "a reply denying that any of the finding was a security vulnerability."

code_evidence: Early exits return 0 when the header is not sealed or when hmac is not running, so tag appending is skipped without any integrity value being produced or checked.
After the header check, the code only asserts f->hmac is non-null; it does not verify that the HMAC state corresponds to a continuous sealed epoch before writing a tag.
The computed HMAC tag is copied into o->tag.tag and hmac_running is cleared, producing a seal value but with no validation that prior epochs were continuous.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-354 covers improper validation of integrity check values. Here the sealing/HMAC integrity mechanism is applied without validating that the chain of sealed epochs is continuous, so the integrity check cannot detect truncation, fitting the target weakness rather than a generic checksum bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function emits tag/HMAC values for a sealed journal without validating continuity of sealed epochs, and silently skips sealing when hmac is not running. Trigger: an attacker truncates a sealed log and resumes sealing; verification still passes because missing epochs are not detected. Consequence: integrity verification fails to detect modification/truncation of the sealed log.

commit_msg:
Commit 326587b84078 ("sched: fix goto retry in pick_next_task_rt()")
removed any path which could make pick_next_rt_entity() return NULL.
However, BUG_ON(!rt_se) in _pick_next_task_rt() (the only caller of
pick_next_rt_entity()) still checks the error condition, which can
never happen, since list_entry() never returns NULL.
Remove the BUG_ON check, and instead emit a warning in the only
possible error condition here: the queue being empty which should
never happen.

Fixes: 326587b84078 ("sched: fix goto retry in pick_next_task_rt()")
Signed-off-by: Pietro Borrello <borrello@diag.uniroma1.it>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Reviewed-by: Phil Auld <pauld@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Steven Rostedt (Google) <rostedt@goodmis.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230128-list-entry-null-check-sched-v3-1-b1a71bd1ac6b@diag.uniroma1.it
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (SCHED_WARN_ON(list_empty(queue)))', '\t\treturn NULL;']}
description: In the Linux kernel, pick_next_rt_entity() may return a type confused entry, not detected by the BUG_ON condition, as the confused entry will not be NULL, but list_head.The buggy error condition would lead to a type confused entry with the list head,which would then be used as a type confused sched_rt_entity,causing memory corruption.

code_evidence: queue is derived from array->queue + idx, and next is unconditionally produced by list_entry(queue->next, struct sched_rt_entity, run_list). The container_of-style cast assumes queue->next points to a real sched_rt_entity.run_list; if the queue is empty, queue->next is the list head itself, which is reinterpreted as a sched_rt_entity rather than rejected.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-843 fits because a list_head object is accessed through an incompatible struct sched_rt_entity type via list_entry, and the caller consumes the confused pointer. A NULL-return/error-handling issue alone would not capture the incompatible-type access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unguarded list_entry cast treats whatever queue->next points to as a struct sched_rt_entity without verifying the queue is non-empty. Trigger: an empty active queue yields a list_head that is type-confused into a sched_rt_entity; the caller then accesses it as a scheduling entity, causing memory corruption/logical errors rather than a NULL check failure.

commit_msg:
vhost: fix FD leak with inflight messages

Even if unlikely, a buggy vhost-user master might attach fds to inflight
messages. Add checks like for other types of vhost-user messages.

Fixes: d87f1a1cb7b6 ("vhost: support inflight info sharing")

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (validate_msg_fds(dev, ctx, 1) != 0)', '\t\treturn RTE_VHOST_MSG_RESULT_ERR;']}
description: A flaw was found in dpdk. This flaw allows a malicious vhost-user master to attach an unexpected number of fds as ancillary data to VHOST_USER_GET_INFLIGHT_FD / VHOST_USER_SET_INFLIGHT_FD messages that are not closed by the vhost-user slave. By sending such messages continuously, the vhost-user master exhausts available fd in the vhost-user slave process, leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: Line 14 reads ctx->fds[0] and line 15 only checks message size and fd < 0. The function never verifies how many fds the master attached to the inflight message, so extra ancillary fds delivered by the vhost-user master are neither validated nor closed.
Lines 53-54 pass fd to mmap; lines 59-63 close only the previously stored dev->inflight_info->fd and then store the single fd. Any additional attached fds are dropped without close(), leaking them.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function fails to restrict and release a limited OS resource (file descriptors), and repeated requests exhaust it. This is a missing-close resource leak leading to exhaustion, not merely a memory-safety bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation of the number of ancillary fds on VHOST_USER_SET_INFLIGHT_FD, so only ctx->fds[0] is consumed. Trigger: a malicious vhost-user master repeatedly sends inflight messages with extra fds; each call leaks those unclosed fds. Consequence: the slave process exhausts its fd table, causing denial of service.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['unsigned int GetUVarBE(int nPos, int nSize, bool *pbSuccess)', '            if ( nPos < 0 || nPos + nSize > m_nLen )'], 'added_lines': ['unsigned int GetUVarBE(const unsigned int& nPos, const unsigned int& nSize, bool *pbSuccess)', '            if ( m_nLen < nSize || nPos > (m_nLen - nSize) )']}
description: Onlyoffice Document Server v6.0.0 and below and Core 6.1.0.26 and below were discovered to contain a heap overflow via the component DesktopEditor/fontengine/fontconverter/FontFileBase.h.

code_evidence: Bounds check uses signed int nPos and nSize; condition nPos < 0 || nPos + nSize > m_nLen can overflow when nPos + nSize wraps, bypassing the guard.
After the check, the loop indexes m_sFile[nPos + nIndex] up to nSize bytes; if the guard is bypassed by integer overflow, these reads/writes go past m_sFile's m_nLen buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The out-of-bounds indexing of m_sFile writes/reads past the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. The integer overflow is the enabling cause, but the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds buffer access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the signed-integer overflow in the bounds expression nPos + nSize, which can wrap negative and pass the > m_nLen test. Trigger: caller supplies large nPos/nSize. Consequence: the loop indexes m_sFile out of bounds, producing memory corruption/overflow.

commit_msg:
Path traversal vulnerability

Do not extract files with relative paths.

[bug #794337]
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tprefix_len = p + 2 - file_name;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\treturn NULL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in GNOME file-roller before 3.29.91. It allows a single ./../ path traversal via a filename contained in a TAR archive, possibly overwriting a file during extraction.

code_evidence: The loop scans the caller-supplied file_name and, on encountering a '..' component (ISDOT(p[0]) && ISDOT(p[1]) with slash or terminator at p[2]), records prefix_len = p + 2 - file_name instead of rejecting the name.

After the scan the function returns file_name + prefix_len with leading slashes skipped, so a '..' component is stripped from the returned pointer but the remaining path is still used by the caller for extraction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the pathname-neutralization step for archive member names, and it fails to properly neutralize '..' elements, allowing resolution outside the restricted extraction directory, which matches CWE-22. This is the relative-traversal form rather than an absolute-path issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sanitizer only advances past a detected '..' segment rather than rejecting it, so the returned path can still resolve relative to the extraction root in a way that escapes it (as the commit message notes, a single ./../ traversal). Trigger: a TAR member whose filename contains a '..' path element. Consequence: files may be written outside the intended extraction directory, overwriting existing files.

commit_msg:
Fix range issues in ZRANDMEMBER and HRANDFIELD (CVE-2023-22458) (#11674)

missing range check in ZRANDMEMBER and HRANDIFLD leading to panic due
to protocol limitations
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        } else if (c->argc == 4)'], 'added_lines': ['        } else if (c->argc == 4) {', '            if (l < LONG_MIN/2 || l > LONG_MAX/2) {', '                addReplyError(c,"value is out of range");', '                return;', '            }', '        }']}
description: Redis is an in-memory database that persists on disk. Authenticated users can issue a `HRANDFIELD` or `ZRANDMEMBER` command with specially crafted arguments to trigger a denial-of-service by crashing Redis with an assertion failure. This problem affects Redis versions 6.2 or newer up to but not including 6.2.9 as well as versions 7.0 up to but not including 7.0.8. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

code_evidence: Line 7 parses the user-supplied count into signed long l without bounds. Line 11-12 sets withvalues=1 when argc==4, then line 13 passes l directly to hrandfieldWithCountCommand with no range check, so an extreme l (e.g. near LONG_MAX) reaches the count logic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the missing range constraint allows a signed integer calculation on the attacker-controlled count to overflow or wrap, which is the documented cause of the crash. The consequence is availability loss (DoS), consistent with CWE-190's scope; the weakness is the unchecked arithmetic, not merely an input-validation gap.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the count l is accepted from the client and forwarded to the count command without validating it against LONG_MIN/2 and LONG_MAX/2. Trigger: an authenticated client issues HRANDFIELD with an extreme count and 'WITHVALUES'. The downstream count code performs arithmetic on l (e.g. negating or scaling the count) that overflows signed long, producing a wrong/negative value and ultimately an assertion failure that crashes the server.

Moonlight-common-c is vulnerable to buffer overflow starting in commit f57bd745b4cbed577ea654fad4701bea4d38b44c. avcodec/gif: Fix lzw buffer size

Fixes out of array access
Fixes: aaa479088e6fb40b04837b3119f47b04/asan_heap-oob_e38c68_8576_9d653078b2470700e2834636f12ff557.tga

Found-by: Mateusz "j00ru" Jurczyk and Gynvael Coldwind
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ff_lzw_encode_init(s->lzw, s->buf, 2 * width * height,'], 'added_lines': ['    ff_lzw_encode_init(s->lzw, s->buf, s->buf_size,']}
description: libavcodec/gif.c in FFmpeg before 2.8.6 does not properly calculate a buffer size, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds array access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted .tga file, related to the gif_image_write_image, gif_encode_init, and gif_encode_close functions.

code_evidence: height and width come from avctx, but when GF_OFFSETTING trims the frame (lines 27, 52) only the local width/height shrink; the encode buffer passed to ff_lzw_encode_init is sized as 2 * width * height using these variables, while the encoder later consumes width*height bytes per row loop (lines 94-107). The buffer bound is thus computed from the possibly-reduced dimensions rather than the actual allocated buffer size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: ff_lzw_encode_init accepts a buffer length that does not bound the region the encoder writes into, permitting writes beyond the buffer's intended boundary. This is a memory-buffer out-of-bounds access consistent with CWE-119 (the fix switches to the correct s->buf_size).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the LZW output buffer length is derived from a product of width*height that does not match the buffer actually allocated for encoding, so the encoder can write past the end of s->buf. Trigger: a crafted frame whose offset-trimmed dimensions yield an underestimated product. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap write, leading to crash/DoS or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
gnttab: split maptrack lock to make it fulfill its purpose again

The way the lock is currently being used in get_maptrack_handle(), it
protects only the maptrack limit: The function acts on current's list
only, so races on list accesses are impossible even without the lock.

Otoh list access races are possible between __get_maptrack_handle() and
put_maptrack_handle(), due to the invocation of the former for other
than current from steal_maptrack_handle(). Introduce a per-vCPU lock
for list accesses to become race free again. This lock will be
uncontended except when it becomes necessary to take the steal path,
i.e. in the common case there should be no meaningful performance
impact.

When in get_maptrack_handle adds a stolen entry to a fresh, empty,
freelist, we think that there is probably no concurrency.  However,
this is not a fast path and adding the locking there makes the code
clearly correct.

Also, while we are here: the stolen maptrack_entry's tail pointer was
not properly set.  Set it.

This is CVE-2017-12136 / XSA-228.

Reported-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <Ian.Jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    spin_lock(&v->maptrack_freelist_lock);', '', '', '    spin_unlock(&v->maptrack_freelist_lock);']}
description: Race condition in the grant table code in Xen 4.6.x through 4.9.x allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (free list corruption and host crash) or gain privileges on the host via vectors involving maptrack free list handling.

code_evidence: put_maptrack_handle() writes the handle into the target vCPU's freelist: it sets the entry's ref to MAPTRACK_TAIL, reads v->maptrack_tail atomically, then loops with cmpxchg on that tail, and finally links the old tail via write_atomic(&maptrack_entry(t, prev_tail).ref, handle). The tail update and the separate prev_tail link update are not performed under any lock in this function; the shared maptrack_tail and the freelist entries can be concurrently accessed by __get_maptrack_handle()/steal_maptrack_handle() operating on another vCPU's list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a non-atomic read-modify-write/link sequence on a shared freelist concurrently reachable by another code path, violating exclusivity and atomicity; this matches CWE-362. The added spin_lock/unlock in the patch confirms the missing synchronization rather than a pure memory-ordering issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the freelist tail and entry links are modified without holding the per-vCPU maptrack_freelist_lock, so the cmpxchg loop and the subsequent write_atomic link are not atomic with respect to concurrent steal-path access. Trigger: concurrent get/put operations on the same vCPU freelist. Consequence: freelist corruption leading to host crash or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
In the error path, 'new_apdu->a_data' is not freed.
This can be triggered by the guest continuely.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liqiang6-s@360.cn>
Reviewed-by: Marc-André Lureau <marcandre.lureau@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        g_free(new_apdu);', '        g_free(new_apdu);'], 'added_lines': ['        vcard_apdu_delete(new_apdu);', '        vcard_apdu_delete(new_apdu);']}
description: Memory leak in the vcard_apdu_new function in card_7816.c in libcacard before 2.5.3 allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host memory consumption) via vectors related to allocating a new APDU object.

code_evidence: Line 11 allocates new_apdu->a_data with g_memdup, so the struct owns a heap buffer. On failure of vcard_apdu_set_class (lines 14-16) only g_free(new_apdu) runs, freeing the struct but not a_data. The same partial free occurs at lines 19-21 when vcard_apdu_set_length fails, again leaving a_data allocated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because an allocated resource (a_data) is not released after its effective lifetime ends on the error paths. The leak is of an owned heap buffer, not a use-after-free or double free, so it is a missing-release weakness rather than CWE-415/416.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error paths release the VCardAPDU struct with g_free instead of a destructor that also frees the owned a_data buffer. Trigger: a guest supplies an APDU that passes the length check but fails class or length validation, repeatedly exercising these branches. Consequence: each failed call leaks a_data, accumulating host memory and enabling denial of service.

commit_msg:
vfio/pci: Fix integer overflows, bitmask check

The VFIO_DEVICE_SET_IRQS ioctl did not sufficiently sanitize
user-supplied integers, potentially allowing memory corruption. This
patch adds appropriate integer overflow checks, checks the range bounds
for VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_NONE, and also verifies that only single element
in the VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_TYPE_MASK bitmask is set.
VFIO_IRQ_SET_ACTION_TYPE_MASK is already correctly checked later in
vfio_pci_set_irqs_ioctl().

Furthermore, a kzalloc is changed to a kcalloc because the use of a
kzalloc with an integer multiplication allowed an integer overflow
condition to be reached without this patch. kcalloc checks for overflow
and should prevent a similar occurrence.

Signed-off-by: Vlad Tsyrklevich <vlad@tsyrklevich.net>
Signed-off-by: Alex Williamson <alex.williamson@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tint ret = 0;', '\t\tif (!(hdr.flags & VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_NONE)) {', '\t\t\tsize_t size;', '\t\t\tint max = vfio_pci_get_irq_count(vdev, hdr.index);', '', '\t\t\tif (hdr.flags & VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_BOOL)', '\t\t\t\tsize = sizeof(uint8_t);', '\t\t\telse if (hdr.flags & VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_EVENTFD)', '\t\t\t\tsize = sizeof(int32_t);', '\t\t\telse', '\t\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '', '\t\t\tif (hdr.argsz - minsz < hdr.count * size ||', '\t\t\t    hdr.start >= max || hdr.start + hdr.count > max)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tsize_t size;', '\t\tint max, ret = 0;', '\t\t    hdr.count >= (U32_MAX - hdr.start) ||', '\t\tmax = vfio_pci_get_irq_count(vdev, hdr.index);', '\t\tif (hdr.start >= max || hdr.start + hdr.count > max)', '\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '', '\t\tswitch (hdr.flags & VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_TYPE_MASK) {', '\t\tcase VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_NONE:', '\t\t\tsize = 0;', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tcase VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_BOOL:', '\t\t\tsize = sizeof(uint8_t);', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tcase VFIO_IRQ_SET_DATA_EVENTFD:', '\t\t\tsize = sizeof(int32_t);', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tdefault:', '\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t\t}', '', '\t\tif (size) {', '\t\t\tif (hdr.argsz - minsz < hdr.count * size)']}
description: drivers/vfio/pci/vfio_pci.c in the Linux kernel through 4.8.11 allows local users to bypass integer overflow checks, and cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or have unspecified other impact, by leveraging access to a vfio PCI device file for a VFIO_DEVICE_SET_IRQS ioctl call, aka a "state machine confusion bug."

code_evidence: The VFIO_DEVICE_SET_IRQS branch copies a user-controlled struct vfio_irq_set header (line 150) and only validates argsz, index, and flags (lines 152-155). hdr.count, hdr.start, and hdr.argsz are attacker-controlled integers. The size is chosen from flags (lines 159-164), then line 165 computes hdr.count * size without overflow checking and compares it to hdr.argsz - minsz; line 166 checks hdr.start + hdr.count > max, which can also overflow. A crafted count/size causes the multiplication to wrap, passing the size check, and line 168-169 then memdup_user copies hdr.count * size bytes into a heap buffer allocated with the same wrapped size, leading to a buffer over-read/over-write relative to intended bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked count*size leads memdup_user to operate beyond the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The underlying arithmetic overflow is the root cause, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds buffer read/write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unvalidated multiplication and addition of attacker-controlled hdr.count, hdr.start, and size can integer-overflow, so bounds checks pass while memdup_user at line 169 uses the wrapped count*size. Trigger: a local user with a VFIO PCI device file issues VFIO_DEVICE_SET_IRQS with a large count. Supported consequence: memory corruption/out-of-bounds heap access.

commit_msg:
Bugs 698804/698810/698811: Keep PDF object numbers below limit.

This ensures that:
 * xref tables with objects pointers do not grow out of bounds.
 * other readers, e.g. Adobe Acrobat can parse PDFs written by mupdf.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif (num <= 0 || num > MAX_OBJECT_NUMBER)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif (num <= 0 || num > PDF_MAX_OBJECT_NUMBER)']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the ensure_solid_xref function in pdf/pdf-xref.c in Artifex MuPDF 1.12.0 allows a remote attacker to potentially execute arbitrary code via a crafted PDF file, because xref subsection object numbers are unrestricted.

code_evidence: The object-number guard rejects num<=0 or num>MAX_OBJECT_NUMBER, but the crafted PDF can still supply very large object numbers within that bound; num comes from the parsed integer token and is stored in list[listlen].num.
Accepted entries are appended to the growing list, and maxnum is advanced to the largest num, so maxnum is attacker-controlled up to the object-number limit.
pdf_ensure_solid_xref(ctx, doc, maxnum) and the loop for (i = 1; i < maxnum; i++) size/iterate the xref by maxnum, so a large maxnum drives xref allocation.

The second loop indexes pdf_get_populating_xref_entry(ctx, doc, list[i].num) for each stored num, writing entry fields at that index; if the xref was sized below list[i].num, this is an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs xref-entry writes at attacker-influenced object-number indices without ensuring the buffer is large enough, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. This is the buffer-boundary failure itself, not merely an integer parsing issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that xref subsection object numbers are not restricted tightly enough before being used to size and index the xref table. A crafted PDF with a large but accepted object number makes maxnum large and later indexes the xref entry array with that number, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
KVM: x86: Check lapic_in_kernel() before attempting to set a SynIC irq

When KVM_CAP_HYPERV_SYNIC{,2} is activated, KVM already checks for
irqchip_in_kernel() so normally SynIC irqs should never be set. It is,
however,  possible for a misbehaving VMM to write to SYNIC/STIMER MSRs
causing erroneous behavior.

The immediate issue being fixed is that kvm_irq_delivery_to_apic()
(kvm_irq_delivery_to_apic_fast()) crashes when called with
'irq.shorthand = APIC_DEST_SELF' and 'src == NULL'.

Signed-off-by: Vitaly Kuznetsov <vkuznets@redhat.com>
Message-Id: <20220325132140.25650-2-vkuznets@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (KVM_BUG_ON(!lapic_in_kernel(vcpu), vcpu->kvm))', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s KVM when attempting to set a SynIC IRQ. This issue makes it possible for a misbehaving VMM to write to SYNIC/STIMER MSRs, causing a NULL pointer dereference. This flaw allows an unprivileged local attacker on the host to issue specific ioctl calls, causing a kernel oops condition that results in a denial of service.

code_evidence: vcpu->arch.apic is passed as the source APIC to kvm_irq_delivery_to_apic; if no in-kernel LAPIC exists, this pointer is NULL. With irq.shorthand set to APIC_DEST_SELF (line 12), the delivery path dereferences the NULL src.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function passes a potentially NULL vcpu->arch.apic into kvm_irq_delivery_to_apic, which dereferences it for APIC_DEST_SELF delivery. This is a direct NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476), not merely a missing input validation issue; the missing lapic_in_kernel check is the cause, and the NULL dereference is the supported weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
struct kvm_vcpu *vcpu = hv_synic_to_vcpu(synic);
ret = kvm_irq_delivery_to_apic(vcpu->kvm, vcpu->arch.apic, &irq, NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: synic_set_irq does not verify that the vCPU has an in-kernel LAPIC before building a self-directed IPI and calling kvm_irq_delivery_to_apic with vcpu->arch.apic as src. Trigger: a misbehaving VMM writes SYNIC/STIMER MSRs to invoke this path when no in-kernel irqchip/LAPIC exists. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference in the APIC delivery path, causing a kernel oops/DoS on the host.

description: An issue has been found in libIEC61850 v1.3. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in prepareGooseBuffer in goose/goose_publisher.c.

code_evidence: Line 4 declares a fixed-size stack struct ifreq buffer; line 6 zeroes it. Line 7 copies the caller-supplied interfaceId into buffer.ifr_name using strcpy with no length bound, so an interfaceId longer than IFNAMSIZ overflows the fixed ifr_name field and adjacent stack memory. Line 8 then passes the corrupted buffer to ioctl.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unbounded copy writes beyond the intended ifr_name buffer boundary. The commit's switch to strncpy with IFNAMSIZ confirms the missing bound; this is an out-of-bounds write rather than merely a string-handling issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unbounded strcpy into the fixed-size ifr_name field of a stack-allocated ifreq. Trigger: a caller passes an interfaceId string longer than IFNAMSIZ. Consequence: the copy writes past ifr_name into adjacent stack memory, corrupting the stack and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.5122: lisp indenting my run over the end of the line

Problem:    Lisp indenting my run over the end of the line.
Solution:   Check for NUL earlier.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t    if (*that == NUL)', '\t\t\tbreak;']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.

code_evidence: The inner scan loop at line 31 iterates over the heap line buffer returned by ml_get_curline() while *that != NUL. When a quote is seen, the loop at line 47 advances that via *++that until a closing quote or NUL, but after the quote block ends (line 59) execution continues to lines 61-64, which read and increment parencount based on *that without re-checking for NUL. Since the quote loop can leave that pointing at the terminating NUL, the subsequent post-increment at line 65 can move that one past the end of the heap buffer, and the next iteration of the for loop at line 31 dereferences *that out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The pointer walks past the end of a heap-allocated line buffer obtained from ml_get_curline(), matching CWE-122's heap buffer overflow. It is not merely an off-by-one read; the loop continues incrementing and dereferencing past the allocation bound.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the quote-scanning path advances the pointer to the line's terminating NUL but does not stop the surrounding loop before the pointer is incremented past the end. Trigger: a Lisp line containing a quote whose scan reaches the end of the line. Consequence: the next iteration dereferences and iterates beyond the heap-allocated line buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds read/overflow (CWE-122).

description: An out-of-bounds (OOB) memory write flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s watch_queue event notification subsystem. This flaw can overwrite parts of the kernel state, potentially allowing a local user to gain privileged access or cause a denial of service on the system.

code_evidence: Line 5 sets len to the coherency length, and line 11 allocates a buffer of exactly len bytes. Line 16 reads len bytes into that buffer via vfs_getxattr, and line 17 requires xlen == len.
Line 27 then calls memcmp(buf->data, p, len), where buf->data is a member offset inside the allocated buffer, so the comparison reads len bytes starting past the buffer's beginning.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 covers writes past the intended buffer; here the analogous out-of-bounds access is a read at line 27 due to the missing struct-size adjustment, matching the memory-safety root cause the patch corrects by resizing the buffer and the comparison length.

evidence_lines.code: } else if (memcmp(buf->data, p, len) != 0) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The buffer is sized to the coherency length but the memcmp at line 27 starts at buf->data, a member inside the struct, and copies len bytes. This reads len bytes from an offset within a len-byte allocation, extending past the end of the buffer. Triggered whenever the xattr read succeeds (xlen == len) and reaches the comparison, producing an out-of-bounds read of adjacent kernel memory. The fix adds sizeof(*buf) to the allocation and subtracts it from the memcmp length.

commit_msg:
RDMA/rtrs-clt: Fix possible double free in error case

Callback function rtrs_clt_dev_release() for put_device() calls kfree(clt)
to free memory. We shouldn't call kfree(clt) again, and we can't use the
clt after kfree too.

Replace device_register() with device_initialize() and device_add() so that
dev_set_name can() be used appropriately.

Move mutex_destroy() to the release function so it can be called in
the alloc_clt err path.

Fixes: eab098246625 ("RDMA/rtrs-clt: Refactor the failure cases in alloc_clt")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220217030929.323849-1-haris.iqbal@ionos.com
Reported-by: Miaoqian Lin <linmq006@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Md Haris Iqbal <haris.iqbal@ionos.com>
Reviewed-by: Jack Wang <jinpu.wang@ionos.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@nvidia.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmutex_destroy(&clt->paths_ev_mutex);', '\tmutex_destroy(&clt->paths_mutex);', '\t/* release callback will free clt in last put */'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/*', '\t * release callback will free clt and destroy mutexes in last put', '\t */']}
description: drivers/infiniband/ulp/rtrs/rtrs-clt.c in the Linux kernel before 5.16.12 has a double free related to rtrs_clt_dev_release.

code_evidence: free_clt() frees permits and the per-CPU path, then destroys the paths mutexes and calls device_unregister(&clt->dev). The comment removed in the patch stated the release callback frees clt on the last put; device_unregister() drops the device reference and can invoke rtrs_clt_dev_release(), which kfree()s clt. Nothing in this function prevents that release path from freeing clt while the caller may also free it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly participates in the double-free flow: device_unregister() can trigger the release callback that frees clt, and the same object may be freed again by the caller. This matches CWE-415 (freeing the same address twice) rather than a mere leak or null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: free_clt() delegates final memory release to the device release callback via device_unregister(), but the surrounding error path can additionally free clt, yielding two frees of the same object. Trigger: an allocation/error path that calls free_clt() and then also kfree(clt). Consequence: double free and potential use-after-free of clt, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg:
Fixed break instruction in a try-catch block.

Previously, JUMP offset for a break instruction inside a try-catch
block was not set to a correct offset during code generation
when a return instruction was present in inner try-catch block.

The fix is to update the JUMP offset appropriately.

This closes #553 issue on Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            /*', '             * block can be NULL when &ctx->try_exit_label is "@return"', '             * for outermost try-catch block.', '             */', '', '                }', '', '            } else {', '', '                /*', '                 * when block == NULL, we still want to patch the "finally"', '                 * instruction break_offset.', '                 */', '', '                block = njs_generate_find_block(vm, generator->block,', '                                                NJS_GENERATOR_ALL,', '                                                &no_label);', '', '                if (block != NULL) {', '                    patch = njs_generate_make_exit_patch(vm, block, &no_label,', '                                njs_code_offset(generator, finally)', '                                + offsetof(njs_vmcode_finally_t, break_offset));', '                    if (njs_slow_path(patch == NULL)) {', '                        return NJS_ERROR;', '                    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Nginx NJS v0.7.5. The JUMP offset for a break instruction was not set to a correct offset during code generation, leading to a segmentation violation.

code_evidence: When try_block->exit is set, the code searches for a block via njs_generate_find_block with NJS_GENERATOR_ALL and &ctx->try_exit_label, then only patches the finally break_offset inside 'if (block != NULL)'. If no matching block is found (block == NULL, e.g. the outermost try-catch where the label is "@return"), the break_offset of the finally instruction remains unpatched and the failure is silently skipped rather than handled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-754 fits because the code fails to check/handle the unusual condition of a NULL block during code generation, silently ignoring the unpatched jump offset; the consequence is a crash from the invalid jump, matching the DoS/instability scope. This is a missing-condition check rather than a memory-safety primitive like CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The generator assumes a block will always be found for the exit label; when the lookup returns NULL for an outermost try-catch, the break_offset is left at its default instead of being set to the correct jump target. Executing the break then jumps to an invalid offset, producing a segmentation violation (crash).

commit_msg:
Fix string format vulnerability

If the message in g_log_structured itself
contained format sequences like %d or %n they
were applied again, leading to leaked stack contents
and possibly memory corruption. It can be triggered
e.g. by a volume label containing format sequences.

Print the message argument itself into a "%s" string
to avoid intepreting format sequences.

https://github.com/storaged-project/udisks/issues/578
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -14,7 +14,7 @@
 
 #if GLIB_CHECK_VERSION(2, 50, 0)
   g_log_structured ("udisks", (GLogLevelFlags) level,
-                    "MESSAGE", message, "THREAD_ID", "%d", (gint) syscall (SYS_gettid),
+                    "MESSAGE", "%s", message, "THREAD_ID", "%d", (gint) syscall (SYS_gettid),
                     "CODE_FUNC", function, "CODE_FILE", location);
 #else
   g_log ("udisks", level, "[%d]: %s [%s, %s()]", (gint) syscall (SYS_gettid), message, location, function);
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    "MESSAGE", message, "THREAD_ID", "%d", (gint) syscall (SYS_gettid),'], 'added_lines': ['                    "MESSAGE", "%s", message, "THREAD_ID", "%d", (gint) syscall (SYS_gettid),']}
description: UDisks 2.8.0 has a format string vulnerability in udisks_log in udiskslogging.c, allowing attackers to obtain sensitive information (stack contents), cause a denial of service (memory corruption), or possibly have unspecified other impact via a malformed filesystem label, as demonstrated by %d or %n substrings.

code_evidence: The varargs format is expanded once into message via g_strdup_vprintf, so message may contain attacker-influenced text such as a filesystem label.
On the GLib >= 2.50 path, message is passed directly as the value for the "MESSAGE" field without a constant format specifier, so g_log_structured reinterprets any %d or %n sequences in it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-134 fits because a format-string-consuming function receives an externally influenced string as its format, enabling %n/%d interpretation. This is distinct from the initial g_strdup_vprintf use, which legitimately applies the caller's format; the weakness is the second, uncontrolled formatting of message.

Line 7 detects a backslash and line 8 increments src to skip the escaped character, but that increment is not guarded by the end bound. If the backslash is the last byte before end, src advances past end, and line 24 (++src) or the next line 5 dereference reads beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads memory beyond the valid range delimited by end, and the patch's heap-buffer-overflow fix targets that over-read. It is not CWE-787, since the defect is an out-of-bounds read, not a write.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the end boundary is enforced only after *src is dereferenced, and the escape-skip increment at line 8 is not bounded. Trigger: input ending in a backslash, or src reaching end, causes line 5 or the post-increment dereference to read past the intended buffer. Consequence: an out-of-bounds heap read, matching the reported heap-buffer-overflow/over-read.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn -EFAULT;', '', '\tif (trace.rx_traces > RDS_MSG_RX_DGRAM_TRACE_MAX)']}

commit_msg:
We're holding the request reference, but we need to go one higher
to ensure that the ctx remains valid after the request has finished.
If the ring is closed with pending task_work inflight, and the
given io_kiocb finishes sync during issue, then we need a reference
to the ring itself around the task_work execution cycle.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v5.7+
Reported-by: syzbot+9b260fc33297966f5a8e@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tpercpu_ref_get(&req->ctx->refs);', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.8.2. fs/io_uring.c has a use-after-free related to io_async_task_func and ctx reference holding, aka CID-6d816e088c35.

code_evidence: The function initializes req->task_work and registers it via io_req_task_work_add(req, &req->task_work) without taking a reference on the request's io_uring context (req->ctx). The callback io_rw_resubmit may run asynchronously after the request completes, so the ctx can be released while the task_work is still pending, leaving the deferred callback to operate on freed ring state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the deferred resubmit path accesses req->ctx after the ring (and its context) may have been freed; the missing percpu_ref_get on req->ctx->refs is exactly the lifetime constraint that prevents this. This is a lifetime/ownership defect, not a mere null-pointer or logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the deferred task_work is queued without holding a ctx reference, so the ring may be torn down while the callback is still pending. Trigger: a request reissued via io_rw_reissue finishes synchronously during issue while the ring closes with task_work inflight. Consequence: the resubmit callback dereferences freed ctx memory, yielding a use-after-free.

babeld: fix #10502 #10503 by repairing the checks on length

This patch repairs the checking conditions on length in four functions:
babel_packet_examin, parse_hello_subtlv, parse_ihu_subtlv, and parse_update_subtlv

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if(i + 1 > bodylen) {', '        if(i + len > bodylen) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if(i + 2 > bodylen) {', '        if(i + len + 2 > bodylen) {']}
description: A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in FRRouting through 8.1.0 due to a wrong check on the input packet length in the babel_packet_examin function in babeld/message.c.

code_evidence: The loop walks message TLVs starting at packet + 4 + i while i < bodylen, but bodylen is the declared payload length without accounting for the 4-byte header, so message indexing is offset from the bounded region.
The length checks compare i + 1 and i + len against bodylen instead of i + 1 + 2 and i + len + 2; they permit a TLV whose type/len bytes and payload extend past the declared body.
The cursor advances by len + 2, so an under-checked TLV can push indexing past the packet buffer on the next iteration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs reads through message beyond the intended packet buffer boundary because the length constraint is wrong; this is an improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer, matching CWE-119. It is not merely an integer issue since the direct consequence is out-of-bounds memory access.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the truncation guards omit the two-byte TLV header and the four-byte packet header offset, so i + len + 2 may exceed bodylen while the check passes. Trigger: a crafted Babel packet with a TLV length near bodylen causes message[1] and the next iteration's message[0] to be read past the packet buffer, yielding out-of-bounds reads (and potential crash) rather than writes.

commit_msg:
a/ulaw: fix multiple buffer overflows

i2ulaw_array() and i2alaw_array() fail to handle ptr [count] = INT_MIN
properly, leading to buffer underflow. INT_MIN is a special value
since - INT_MIN cannot be represented as int.

In this case round - INT_MIN to INT_MAX and proceed as usual.

f2ulaw_array() and f2alaw_array() fail to handle ptr [count] = NaN
properly, leading to null pointer dereference.

In this case, arbitrarily set the buffer value to 0.

This commit fixes #429 (CVE-2018-19661 and CVE-2018-19662) and
fixes #344 (CVE-2017-17456 and CVE-2017-17457).

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Don't have %cr4.fsgsbase active behind a guest kernels back

Currently, a 64bit PV guest can appear to set and clear FSGSBASE in %cr4, but
the bit remains set in hardware.  Therefore, the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE are usable
even when the guest kernel believes that they are disabled.

The FSGSBASE feature isn't currently supported in Linux, and its context
switch path has some optimisations which rely on userspace being unable to use
the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions.  Xen's current behaviour undermines this
expectation.

In 64bit PV guest context, always load the guest kernels setting of FSGSBASE
into %cr4.  This requires adjusting how Xen uses the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE
instructions.

 * Delete the cpu_has_fsgsbase helper.  It is no longer safe, as users need to
   check %cr4 directly.
 * The raw __rd{fs,gs}base() helpers are only safe to use when %cr4.fsgsbase
   is set.  Comment this property.
 * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}{base,shadow}() and read_msr() helpers are updated to use
   the current %cr4 value to determine which mechanism to use.
 * toggle_guest_mode() and save_segments() are update to avoid reading
   fs/gsbase if the values in hardware cannot be stale WRT struct vcpu.  A
   consequence of this is that the write_cr() path needs to cache the current
   bases, as subsequent context switches will skip saving the values.
 * write_cr4() is updated to ensure that the shadow %cr4.fsgsbase value is
   observed in a safe way WRT the hardware setting, if an interrupt happens to
   hit in the middle.
 * load_segments() is updated to use the VMLOAD optimisation if FSGSBASE is
   unavailable, even if only gs_shadow needs updating.  As a minor perf
   improvement, check cpu_has_svm first to short circuit a context-dependent
   conditional on Intel hardware.
 * pv_make_cr4() is updated for 64bit PV guests to use the guest kernels
   choice of FSGSBASE.

This is part of XSA-293.

Reported-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( cpu_has_fsgsbase )'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( read_cr4() & X86_CR4_FSGSBASE )']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges because a guest can manipulate its virtualised %cr4 in a way that is incompatible with Linux (and possibly other guest kernels).

code_evidence: The function decides whether to use the raw __rdgsbase() instruction based on cpu_has_fsgsbase, a cached/global feature flag rather than the current hardware %cr4.FSGSBASE state.
If the flag is set it returns the hardware GS base via __rdgsbase(); otherwise it reads MSR_GS_BASE and returns that value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the code processes base state using a feature flag without validating the required current-state property (live %cr4.FSGSBASE). The patch replaces the unchecked capability check with read_cr4() & X86_CR4_FSGSBASE, confirming the missing validation of actual hardware state rather than a mere transformation error.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( cpu_has_fsgsbase )
return __rdgsbase();

rdmsrl(MSR_GS_BASE, base);
return base;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the choice of mechanism trusts a static feature capability instead of validating the live %cr4.FSGSBASE bit that actually governs whether the WRGSBASE/RDGSBASE instructions are permitted. Trigger: a 64-bit PV guest clears FSGSBASE in its virtual %cr4, but the hardware bit stays set, so cpu_has_fsgsbase remains true and __rdgsbase() is used. This lets guest userspace access GS base state the guest kernel believes is disabled, undermining kernel context-switch assumptions and enabling privilege/DoS impact.

commit_msg:
Currently the arm64 kernel ignores the top address byte passed to brk(),
mmap() and mremap(). When the user is not aware of the 56-bit address
limit or relies on the kernel to return an error, untagging such
pointers has the potential to create address aliases in user-space.
Passing a tagged address to munmap(), madvise() is permitted since the
tagged pointer is expected to be inside an existing mapping.

The current behaviour breaks the existing glibc malloc() implementation
which relies on brk() with an address beyond 56-bit to be rejected by
the kernel.

Remove untagging in the above functions by partially reverting commit
ce18d171cb73 ("mm: untag user pointers in mmap/munmap/mremap/brk"). In
addition, update the arm64 tagged-address-abi.rst document accordingly.

Link: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/1797052
Fixes: ce18d171cb73 ("mm: untag user pointers in mmap/munmap/mremap/brk")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # 5.4.x-
Cc: Florian Weimer <fweimer@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Reported-by: Victor Stinner <vstinner@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Will Deacon <will@kernel.org>
Acked-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Catalin Marinas <catalin.marinas@arm.com>
Signed-off-by: Will Deacon <will@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\taddr = untagged_addr(addr);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel 5.4 and 5.5 through 5.5.6 on the AArch64 architecture. It ignores the top byte in the address passed to the brk system call, potentially moving the memory break downwards when the application expects it to move upwards, aka CID-dcde237319e6. This has been observed to cause heap corruption with the GNU C Library malloc implementation.

code_evidence: Line 7 applies untagged_addr() to the user-supplied addr, stripping the top byte before any validation. The sanitized addr is then passed unmodified to vm_mmap_pgoff() at line 33, so the kernel maps/validates at the aliased lower address rather than the address the caller supplied.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the untagged address causes memory to be written/established at a location outside the region the caller intended, corrupting memory (observed heap corruption). The missing constraint (rejecting out-of-range addresses) permits writes past the intended mapping boundary; this is the out-of-bounds write consequence rather than a mere information leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ksys_mmap_pgoff silently untags the caller's address instead of rejecting addresses exceeding the 56-bit limit. Trigger: a user passes a tagged address (top byte set) to mmap. Consequence: the operation targets an aliased address, so the kernel returns success where an error was expected, breaking callers such as glibc malloc that rely on rejection and enabling address aliasing in user space.

commit_msg:
Fix heap OOB read in macho.iterate_chained_fixups ##crash

* Reported by peacock-doris via huntr.dev
* Reproducer 'tests_65305'

mrmacete:
* Return early if segs_count is 0
* Initialize segs_count also for reconstructed fixups

Co-authored-by: pancake <pancake@nopcode.org>
Co-authored-by: Francesco Tamagni <mrmacete@protonmail.ch>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tbin->segs_count = bin->nsegs;']}
description: Heap Buffer Overflow in iterate_chained_fixups in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.6.6.

code_evidence: When BIND_SUBOPCODE_THREADED_APPLY is processed, cur_seg is loaded from bin->chained_starts[seg_idx] at line 57; seg_idx comes from the attacker-controlled immediate byte at line 105 and is only validated to be < bin->nsegs. If chained_starts[seg_idx] is NULL, a new segment is allocated and stored at bin->chained_starts[seg_idx], then page_start is sized by page_count derived from bin->segs[seg_idx].vmsize. Line 80 then writes cur_seg->page_start[page_index] using page_index = seg_off/ps, where seg_off is attacker-controlled from ULEB opcodes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes data past the end of the intended heap buffer via an incorrect bounds check. The write at line 80 with an oversized page_index is the direct unsafe operation, consistent with an out-of-bounds write rather than a read-only over-read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check at line 79 compares page_index (a page index) against maxsize = page_count * sizeof(ut16) (a byte count), so the check is too permissive. Trigger: crafted chained-fixup bind opcodes set seg_idx and a large seg_off, yielding a page_index that passes the faulty check. Consequence: page_start[page_index] writes past the allocated heap buffer, causing an out-of-bounds heap write and potential crash or memory corruption.

There is a bunch of cases where we can grab req->fs but not put it, this
can be used to cause a controllable overflow with further implications.

to be sure we don't do it twice.
