commit_msg:
updatehub: Require peer verification with DTLS

DTLS without peer verification offers no security whatsoever (and is
arguably worse than not using DTLS in the first place).

Change the verification option to require this peer verification.  To
use this, it may be necessary to install and use a root certificate.

Signed-off-by: David Brown <david.brown@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint verify = TLS_PEER_VERIFY_NONE;'], 'added_lines': ['\tint verify = TLS_PEER_VERIFY_REQUIRED;']}
description: The UpdateHub module disables DTLS peer checking, which allows for a man in the middle attack. This is mitigated by firmware images requiring valid signatures. However, there is no benefit to using DTLS without the peer checking. See NCC-ZEP-018 This issue affects: zephyrproject-rtos zephyr version 2.1.0 and later versions.

code_evidence: Under CONFIG_UPDATEHUB_DTLS the DTLS configuration is prepared with local variable verify initialized to TLS_PEER_VERIFY_NONE, meaning no peer certificate verification is requested.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-295 covers failure to validate a certificate. Setting the peer verification mode to NONE disables certificate validation for the DTLS connection, directly matching this weakness rather than a generic crypto flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DTLS socket is configured to skip peer certificate verification (verify = TLS_PEER_VERIFY_NONE). Trigger: any DTLS connection to the UpdateHub server. Consequence: the client accepts an unverified peer certificate, enabling a man-in-the-middle to impersonate the server and bypass the protection DTLS is meant to provide.

Uninitialized Kernel memory can leak to USB devices.

Fix by using kzalloc() instead of kmalloc() on the affected buffers.

Signed-off-by: Tomas Bortoli <tomasbortoli@gmail.com>
Reported-by: syzbot+513e4d0985298538bf9b@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Fixes: 0a25e1f4f185 ("can: peak_usb: add support for PEAK new CANFD USB adapters")
Cc: linux-stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tpdev->cmd_buffer_addr = kmalloc(PCAN_UFD_CMD_BUFFER_SIZE,'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tpdev->cmd_buffer_addr = kzalloc(PCAN_UFD_CMD_BUFFER_SIZE,']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.2.9, there is an info-leak bug that can be caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/net/can/usb/peak_usb/pcan_usb_fd.c driver, aka CID-30a8beeb3042.

code_evidence: pdev->cmd_buffer_addr is allocated with kmalloc, which returns uninitialized kernel memory; no memset or zeroing follows before the buffer is retained for command transfers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 covers use/access of an uninitialized resource. Here the allocated buffer is used as a command buffer without being initialized, directly supporting CWE-908; this is not a bounds or lifetime issue.

evidence_lines.code:
pdev->cmd_buffer_addr = kmalloc(PCAN_UFD_CMD_BUFFER_SIZE,
GFP_KERNEL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the command buffer is allocated without initialization, so its contents retain stale kernel heap data. Trigger: a malicious or normal USB device causes command/response transfers using cmd_buffer_addr, exposing uninitialized bytes to the device (or reading them as data). Consequence: kernel memory disclosure (info leak) to USB devices, matching the fix that switches to kzalloc.

commit_msg:
decode: improve appinfo is_teigha check

with corrupt APPINFO.version string shorter than 6 chars.
e.g. by fuzzing. Fixes GH #252 fuzzing by @seviezhou

Also extract 2 more common fields upfront.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (_obj->version && *_obj->version)'], 'added_lines': ['  if (_obj->version && bit_wcs2len (_obj->version) >= 6)']}
description: An issue was discovered in libredwg through v0.10.1.3751. appinfo_private() in decode.c has a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Line 11 guards only that _obj->version is non-null and its first code unit is nonzero, so a corrupt APPINFO.version shorter than 6 wide chars still enters the block. Line 13 then calls memcmp with a fixed length of 12 bytes against the 6-char wide literal "T\0e\0i\0g\0h\0a\0", reading past the end of the shorter version buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 is the targeted out-of-bounds weakness class; the fixed-length memcmp on an unchecked short buffer is the direct cause of the out-of-bounds access. The missing length constraint, not the memcmp call itself, is the root cause addressed by the commit.

is_teigha = memcmp (_obj->version, "T\0e\0i\0g\0h\0a\0", 12) == 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The length check is missing: the code treats any non-empty version string as long enough for a 12-byte comparison. A truncated version string from corrupt or fuzzed input triggers memcmp to read beyond the allocated buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read (the reported memory-safety consequence).

commit_msg:
codec: schroedinger: fix potential buffer overflow.

The variable len is a raw 32 bit value read using GetDWBE. If this
value is larger than UINT32_MAX - sizeof(eos), this will cause an
integer overflow in the subsequent call to malloc, and finally a
buffer overflow when calling memcpy. We fix this by checking len
accordingly.

Signed-off-by: Jean-Baptiste Kempf <jb@videolan.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '                    if( len > UINT32_MAX - sizeof( eos ) )', '                        return NULL;', '']}
description: Integer overflow in the Encode function in modules/codec/schroedinger.c in VideoLAN VLC media player before 2.1.6 and 2.2.x before 2.2.1 allows remote attackers to conduct buffer overflow attacks and execute arbitrary code via a crafted length value.

code_evidence: Line 103 reads a 32-bit length from the encoded buffer without any bound check. Line 104 allocates len + sizeof(eos) bytes; because len is attacker-influenced and unchecked, the addition can overflow, producing an undersized allocation. Lines 107-108 then memcpy len bytes from p_block->p_buffer and append eos, writing past the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a buffer copy (memcpy at lines 107-108) into a buffer sized from an unchecked input length, matching CWE-120's pattern of copying input without verifying the destination is large enough. The integer overflow at line 104 is the mechanism that defeats the size check, but the supported weakness is the unchecked buffer copy.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the untrusted 32-bit len from GetDWBE is used in an integer addition for malloc without validating that len <= UINT32_MAX - sizeof(eos). Trigger: a crafted packet whose length field is near UINT32_MAX. Consequence: malloc under-allocates and the subsequent memcpy copies more data than allocated, causing a heap buffer overflow that can corrupt memory and potentially enable code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix #76409: heap use after free in _php_stream_free

We must not close the stream in exif_read_from_impl(), since it is the
responsibility of the (caller's) caller to do so, if it actually opened
the stream.

We simplify the reproduce script, which is actually about supplying a
path to a directory (opposed to a regular file), and use `.` instead of
`/` to also make it work on Windows.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tphp_stream_close(ImageInfo->infile);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tImageInfo->infile = NULL;']}
description: exif_read_from_impl in ext/exif/exif.c in PHP 7.2.x through 7.2.7 allows attackers to trigger a use-after-free (in exif_read_from_file) because it closes a stream that it is not responsible for closing. The vulnerable code is reachable through the PHP exif_read_data function.

code_evidence: Line 7 stores the caller-provided stream in ImageInfo->infile without taking ownership. When the stream is a stdio stream (line 9) and the path is not a regular file (line 12), the error branch at lines 13-15 closes ImageInfo->infile and returns FALSE, leaving the caller's pointer dangling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees the stream (line 14) yet the caller retains and later reuses that pointer, which is exactly CWE-416. The fix nulls the field instead of closing, confirming the close was the erroneous free; this is not a double-free (CWE-415) but reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: exif_read_from_impl frees a stream it does not own on the non-regular-file error path. Trigger: exif_read_data on a directory or other non-regular path. The caller's caller still holds the same php_stream pointer and later closes or uses it, producing a use-after-free that can crash or corrupt memory.

commit_msg:
proc.c: add `mrb_state` argument to `mrb_proc_copy()`.

The function may invoke the garbage collection and it requires
`mrb_state` to run.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    mrb_proc_copy(p2, p);'], 'added_lines': ['    mrb_proc_copy(mrb, p2, p);']}
description: mruby is vulnerable to NULL Pointer Dereference

code_evidence: The non-strict branch allocates p2 via MRB_OBJ_ALLOC(mrb, MRB_TT_PROC, p->c) and then calls mrb_proc_copy(p2, p) without passing mrb. The allocation can trigger garbage collection, which requires mrb_state; the copy is performed with a potentially invalidated/absent state context, matching the commit's stated need to pass mrb into mrb_proc_copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a missing mrb_state argument on a copy path that may run GC, leading to a NULL dereference; this directly matches CWE-476. It is not merely a resource-management issue, since the observable weakness is dereferencing a NULL state pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mrb_proc_copy is invoked without the mrb_state needed to perform GC safely during the copy. Trigger: creating a lambda from a non-strict proc whose allocation/copy path invokes garbage collection. Supported consequence: a NULL pointer dereference (crash/DoS) when the GC path dereferences the missing/uninitialized state context.

commit_msg:
unix: correctly track in-flight fds in sending process user_struct

The commit referenced in the Fixes tag incorrectly accounted the number
of in-flight fds over a unix domain socket to the original opener
of the file-descriptor. This allows another process to arbitrary
deplete the original file-openers resource limit for the maximum of
open files. Instead the sending processes and its struct cred should
be credited.

To do so, we add a reference counted struct user_struct pointer to the
scm_fp_list and use it to account for the number of inflight unix fds.

Fixes: 712f4aad406bb1 ("unix: properly account for FDs passed over unix sockets")
Reported-by: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Hannes Frederic Sowa <hannes@stressinduktion.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tunix_inflight(scm->fp->fp[i]);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tunix_inflight(scm->fp->user, scm->fp->fp[i]);']}
description: The Linux kernel before 4.5 allows local users to bypass file-descriptor limits and cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by leveraging incorrect tracking of descriptor ownership and sending each descriptor over a UNIX socket before closing it. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incorrect fix for CVE-2013-4312.

code_evidence: The function gates total in-flight fds with too_many_unix_fds(current), charging the sending process's user_struct.

scm_fp_dup copies the fd list and its user_struct reference, but the accounting performed by unix_inflight uses scm->fp->user rather than the current sender, so the charged identity differs from the one checked.
The loop calls unix_inflight for each duplicated fd, incrementing in-flight accounting against the original opener's user_struct rather than the sending process.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper management of a finite per-user resource (in-flight fds), leading to uncontrolled consumption and denial of service, which fits CWE-399 Resource Management Errors. It is a resource-accounting flaw rather than a memory-safety bug.

evidence_lines.code:
if (too_many_unix_fds(current))
return -ETOOMANYREFS;

for (i = scm->fp->count - 1; i >= 0; i--)
unix_inflight(scm->fp->fp[i]);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: resource accounting for in-flight unix fds is attributed to the file's original opener (scm->fp->user) instead of the sending process's cred, while the admission check uses current. Trigger: a local process repeatedly sends fds it does not own over a unix socket before closing them. Consequence: the opener's fd limit is depleted and in-flight fd memory is not bounded for the sender, enabling resource exhaustion/DoS.

commit_msg:
Fixed a MIFF decoding bug (buffer overrun when "depth" param is missing)

Fixes issue #12
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif(img.bit_depth!=32 && img.bit_depth!=64) {', '\t\tiw_set_error(ctx, "MIFF: Unsupported or unset bit depth");', '\t\tgoto done;', '', '\t}']}
description: The iwmiffr_convert_row32 function in imagew-miff.c in libimageworsener.a in ImageWorsener 1.3.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 15 unconditionally sets img.sampletype to IW_SAMPLETYPE_FLOATINGPOINT before the MIFF header is parsed at line 16, so the bit-depth/sample type implied by the file header is never validated.

After header and pixel parsing, line 34 calls iwmiff_read_pixels(&rctx) and line 35 aborts on failure; the pixel reader consumes the image using the assumed sample type/depth, so an image whose header omits or mismatches depth drives reads beyond the allocated row buffer.

It is not CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) because the observed impact is over-read of memory rather than a write past the buffer.

if(!iwmiff_read_pixels(&rctx))
goto done;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function never validates img.bit_depth against a supported value (32/64) after iwmiff_read_header, and hard-codes the sample type before reading the header. Trigger: a crafted MIFF file with a missing or unsupported depth parameter. Consequence: iwmiff_read_pixels reads past the intended buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read and DoS/crash.

commit_msg:
No upstream commit exists.

This imports the io_uring codebase from 5.15.85, wholesale. Changes
from that code base:

- Drop IOCB_ALLOC_CACHE, we don't have that in 5.10.
- Drop MKDIRAT/SYMLINKAT/LINKAT. Would require further VFS backports,
  and we don't support these in 5.10 to begin with.
- sock_from_file() old style calling convention.
- Use compat_get_bitmap() only for CONFIG_COMPAT=y

Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\ttsk->pf_io_worker = NULL;']}
description:
There is a logic error in io_uring's implementation which can be used to trigger a use-after-free vulnerability leading to privilege escalation.

In the io_prep_async_work function the assumption that the last io_grab_identity call cannot return false is not true, and in this case the function will use the init_cred or the previous linked requests identity to do operations instead of using the current identity. This can lead to reference counting issues causing use-after-free. We recommend upgrading past version 5.10.161.

code_evidence: arch_dup_task_struct(tsk, orig) copies the entire orig task_struct into tsk, including pointer fields such as splice_pipe, task_frag.page and wake_q.next; setup_thread_stack then builds on the copied structure. The only explicit reinitialization shown is the NULL assignment of splice_pipe, task_frag.page and wake_q.next at lines 48-50, which the patch extends by NULLing pf_io_worker.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the copied pointer is used after the object it references has been freed, without any intervening revalidation or clearing. This is a use-after-free rather than a double-free or leak: the defect is continued reference to freed memory, which the added NULL initialization is meant to prevent.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function shallow-copies orig into tsk and then relies on manual field-by-field reset of copied pointers; any pointer field not reset (as pf_io_worker was not) is shared between the old and new task. When the original task or worker is torn down and its resources freed, the duplicate still holds the stale pointer, so later dereference operates on freed memory. The trigger is a fork/dup path that copies a task_struct whose pointer field is not reinitialized; the supported consequence is use-after-free of the referenced object.

commit_msg:
mov: reset dref_count on realloc to keep values consistent.

This fixes a potential crash.

Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michaelni@gmx.at>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    sc->drefs_count = 0;']}
description: The mov_read_dref function in libavformat/mov.c in Libav before 11.7 and FFmpeg before 0.11 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or execute arbitrary code via the entries value in a dref box in an MP4 file.

code_evidence: Line 11 bounds entries against UINT_MAX/sizeof(*sc->drefs), but the check is an off-by-one: entries == UINT_MAX/sizeof passes the >= test only when strictly greater, so the guard admits the maximum value; more importantly the allocation at line 14 uses av_mallocz(entries * sizeof(*sc->drefs)) and then line 17 sets sc->drefs_count = entries, and the loop at line 18 iterates i < sc->drefs_count indexing sc->drefs[i] at line 19. The diff resets drefs_count to 0 before realloc so a failed allocation (line 15-16 return ENOMEM) leaves drefs_count at 0 rather than a stale larger value; without the reset, a second dref box with a failing or smaller allocation would leave the loop iterating over the freed/undersized buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale count causes the loop to index sc->drefs[i] outside the allocated buffer, an out-of-bounds read/write of a memory buffer matching CWE-119. The fix in the diff (resetting drefs_count) confirms the buffer-bound violation; a more specific child CWE would require knowing the exact read/write primitive, which the shown lines only partially establish.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a stale sc->drefs_count surviving av_free/av_mallocz of sc->drefs: if the reallocation fails or the new entries count is smaller, the loop at line 18 still iterates the old count and reads/writes MOVDref fields (lines 19-24) beyond the new buffer. Trigger is a crafted MP4 with multiple dref boxes; consequence is out-of-bounds memory access leading to crash or corruption.

description: Amanda 3.5.1 allows privilege escalation from the regular user backup to root. The SUID binary located at /lib/amanda/rundump will execute /usr/sbin/dump as root with controlled arguments from the attacker which may lead to escalation of privileges, denial of service, and information disclosure.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function builds the argument vector for an executed command from externally-influenced input without properly neutralizing special elements (option tokens), matching CWE-77 command injection. It is not merely a parsing bug: the unsafe element reaches execve after privilege elevation, so the weakness enables command/option injection.

commit_msg:
passthrough: quarantine PCI devices

When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for
that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The
IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that
the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However,
when the guest domain is torn down the device is assigned back to dom0,
thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data.

This patch introduces a 'quarantine' for PCI devices using dom_io. When
the toolstack makes a device assignable (by binding it to pciback), it
will now also assign it to DOMID_IO and the device will only be assigned
back to dom0 when the device is made unassignable again. Whilst device is
assignable it will only ever transfer between dom_io and guest domains.
dom_io is actually only used as a sentinel domain for quarantining purposes;
it is not configured with any IOMMU mappings. Assignment to dom_io simply
means that the device's initiator (requestor) identifier is not present in
the IOMMU's device table and thus any DMA transactions issued will be
terminated with a fault condition.

In addition, a fix to assignment handling is made for VT-d.  Failure
during the assignment step should not lead to a device still being
associated with its prior owner. Hand the device to DomIO temporarily,
until the assignment step has completed successfully.  Remove the PI
hooks from the source domain then earlier as well.

Failure of the recovery reassign_device_ownership() may not go silent:
There e.g. may still be left over RMRR mappings in the domain assignment
to which has failed, and hence we can't allow that domain to continue
executing.

NOTE: This patch also includes one printk() cleanup; the
      "XEN_DOMCTL_assign_device: " tag is dropped in iommu_do_pci_domctl(),
      since similar printk()-s elsewhere also don't log such a tag.

This is XSA-302.

Signed-off-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    libxl_ctx *ctx = libxl__gc_owner(gc);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing attackers to gain host OS privileges via DMA in a situation where an untrusted domain has access to a physical device. This occurs because passed through PCI devices may corrupt host memory after deassignment. When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However, when the guest domain is torn down, or the device is deassigned, the device is assigned back to dom0, thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data. An untrusted domain with access to a physical device can DMA into host memory, leading to privilege escalation. Only systems where guests are given direct access to physical devices capable of DMA (PCI pass-through) are vulnerable. Systems which do not use PCI pass-through are not vulnerable.

commit_msg:
linux: handle glibc cpuset allocation failures

Closes #544
CVE-2022-47022

Signed-off-by: Brice Goglin <Brice.Goglin@inria.fr>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['     if (!plinux_set)', '       return -1;']}
description: An issue was discovered in open-mpi hwloc 2.1.0 allows attackers to cause a denial of service or other unspecified impacts via glibc-cpuset in topology-linux.c.

code_evidence: CPU_ALLOC(last+1) allocates plinux_set and may return NULL on allocation failure; the original code passes this pointer directly to CPU_ZERO_S.
The subsequent macros CPU_SET_S and the call pthread_setaffinity_np(tid, setsize, plinux_set) also dereference/consume plinux_set without any prior NULL check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but which can be NULL after a failed allocation. This is a NULL pointer dereference, not a use-after-free or integer overflow, since the defect is the missing validity check on the allocated pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of CPU_ALLOC is unchecked, so a failed glibc cpuset allocation leaves plinux_set NULL. Trigger: a large cpu bitmap (large last+1) causing CPU_ALLOC to fail. Consequence: CPU_ZERO_S or CPU_SET_S dereferences the NULL pointer, crashing the process (DoS).

commit_msg: Fix bug #70168 - Use After Free Vulnerability in unserialize() with SplObjectStorage
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t'], 'added_lines': ['']}
description: Multiple use-after-free vulnerabilities in SPL in PHP before 5.4.44, 5.5.x before 5.5.28, and 5.6.x before 5.6.12 allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via vectors involving (1) ArrayObject, (2) SplObjectStorage, and (3) SplDoublyLinkedList, which are mishandled during unserialization.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over intern->storage and reads element->obj into it, then invokes the iterator's valid method via zend_call_method_with_0_params on that object.
When valid, the code calls current or key on the same it pointer; these user-callable methods can mutate intern->storage during the call.
After the method call returns, the loop advances the hash position on intern->storage, which may have been modified or freed during the callback.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function continues to use the element, it, and storage position references after user callbacks may have freed the underlying memory. This is a use-after-free rather than a simple null dereference or type confusion: the freed storage/element is referenced after the callback.

evidence_lines.code: zend_hash_move_forward_ex(&intern->storage, &intern->pos);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that user-defined iterator methods (valid/current/key) are invoked while a pointer into intern->storage and the element/it references are held, and those callbacks can mutate or free the underlying storage. The trigger is calling these methods on a SplObjectStorage whose contained objects have side-effecting iterator callbacks; the consequence is dereferencing stale element/it pointers or an invalidated hash position, supporting use-after-free and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
ASAN SFTP Fixes
When decoding SFTP messages, fix the size checks so they don't wrap. (ZD12766)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (sz + idx > maxSz) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (sz > maxSz - idx) {']}
description: WolfSSH v1.4.7 was discovered to contain an integer overflow via the function wolfSSH_SFTP_RecvRMDIR.

code_evidence: Line 17 reads the attacker-controlled 32-bit length sz from the SFTP message and advances idx by UINT32_SZ. Line 18 validates the remaining length with sz + idx, an addition of two word32 values that can wrap before comparison to maxSz, so an oversized sz can pass the check. Line 21 then allocates sz + 1 and line 25 copies sz bytes from data + idx.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the defect is an integer wraparound in the size validation calculation (sz + idx) that is assumed to be larger than its operands. The corrected form sz > maxSz - idx avoids the addition overflow, confirming the root cause is the unchecked sum rather than a separate bounds or allocation weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check computes sz + idx in 32-bit arithmetic without overflow protection, so a large sz wraps and bypasses the maxSz comparison. Trigger: a crafted RMDIR request carrying a near-UINT32_MAX length field. Consequence: the check passes while sz remains huge, leading to undersized allocation (sz + 1 wraps) and an out-of-bounds WMEMCPY of sz bytes from data + idx, causing memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflows in PAC parsing

In krb5_parse_pac(), check for buffer counts large enough to threaten
integer overflow in the header length and memory length calculations.
Avoid potential integer overflows when checking the length of each
buffer.  Credit to OSS-Fuzz for discovering one of the issues.

CVE-2022-42898:

In MIT krb5 releases 1.8 and later, an authenticated attacker may be
able to cause a KDC or kadmind process to crash by reading beyond the
bounds of allocated memory, creating a denial of service.  A
privileged attacker may similarly be able to cause a Kerberos or GSS
application service to crash.  On 32-bit platforms, an attacker can
also cause insufficient memory to be allocated for the result,
potentially leading to remote code execution in a KDC, kadmind, or GSS
or Kerberos application server process.  An attacker with the
privileges of a cross-realm KDC may be able to extract secrets from a
KDC process's memory by having them copied into the PAC of a new
ticket.

ticket: 9074 (new)
tags: pullup
target_version: 1.20-next
target_version: 1.19-next
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (buffer->Offset < header_len ||', '            buffer->Offset + buffer->cbBufferSize > len) {'], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (cbuffers < 1 || cbuffers > MAX_BUFFERS)', '        return ERANGE;', '        if (buffer->Offset < header_len || buffer->Offset > len ||', '            buffer->cbBufferSize > len - buffer->Offset) {']}
description: PAC parsing in MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) before 1.19.4 and 1.20.x before 1.20.1 has integer overflows that may lead to remote code execution (in KDC, kadmind, or a GSS or Kerberos application server) on 32-bit platforms (which have a resultant heap-based buffer overflow), and cause a denial of service on other platforms. This occurs in krb5_pac_parse in lib/krb5/krb/pac.c. Heimdal before 7.7.1 has "a similar bug."

code_evidence: cbuffers is read from the untrusted PAC header and used directly to compute header_len = PACTYPE_LENGTH + (cbuffers * PAC_INFO_BUFFER_LENGTH); the multiplication can wrap on 32-bit size_t, so the len < header_len check may pass with a small value.

The same cbuffers value drives the allocation size sizeof(PACTYPE) + ((cbuffers - 1) * sizeof(PAC_INFO_BUFFER)), where (cbuffers - 1) * sizeof(PAC_INFO_BUFFER) can wrap, under-allocating the Buffers array later indexed by the loop.

The bounds check buffer->Offset + buffer->cbBufferSize > len adds two attacker-controlled 32/64-bit values; the sum can overflow and bypass the check, allowing later copies to read/write beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs size and offset calculations on untrusted PAC fields whose results can wrap, directly matching CWE-190 integer overflow; the missing pre-checks are the fix. This is distinct from a plain out-of-bounds read because the flawed arithmetic is the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
pac->pac = (PACTYPE *)realloc(pac->pac,
sizeof(PACTYPE) + ((cbuffers - 1) * sizeof(PAC_INFO_BUFFER)));

if (buffer->Offset < header_len ||
buffer->Offset + buffer->cbBufferSize > len) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled cbuffers, Offset and cbBufferSize are combined in size/offset arithmetic without overflow guards. Trigger: a crafted PAC with large count or offset/size values. Consequence: wrapped length checks and under-allocation lead to out-of-bounds access (heap overflow on 32-bit, DoS elsewhere).

commit_msg:
settings: Add support for defaults to keyfile backend

Stacked databases and locks are dconf features that allow
management software like Fleet Commander to set system-wide
defaults and overrides centrally for applications.

This patch adds minimal support for the same to the keyfile
backend. We look for a keyfile named 'defaults' and a
lock-list named 'locks'.

Suitable files can be produced from a dconf database with
dconf dump and dconf list-locks, respectively.

The default location for these files is /etc/glib-2.0/settings/.
For test purposes, this can be overwritten with the
GSETTINGS_DEFAULTS_DIR environment variable.

Writes always go to the per-user keyfile.

commit_msg:
smart_pkt: fix potential OOB-read when processing ng packet

OSS-fuzz has reported a potential out-of-bounds read when processing a
"ng" smart packet:

==1==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x6310000249c0 at pc 0x000000493a92 bp 0x7ffddc882cd0 sp 0x7ffddc882480
	READ of size 65529 at 0x6310000249c0 thread T0
	SCARINESS: 26 (multi-byte-read-heap-buffer-overflow)
	#0 0x493a91 in __interceptor_strchr.part.35 /src/llvm/projects/compiler-rt/lib/sanitizer_common/sanitizer_common_interceptors.inc:673
	#1 0x813960 in ng_pkt libgit2/src/transports/smart_pkt.c:320:14
	#2 0x810f79 in git_pkt_parse_line libgit2/src/transports/smart_pkt.c:478:9
	#3 0x82c3c9 in git_smart__store_refs libgit2/src/transports/smart_protocol.c:47:12
	#4 0x6373a2 in git_smart__connect libgit2/src/transports/smart.c:251:15
	#5 0x57688f in git_remote_connect libgit2/src/remote.c:708:15
	#6 0x52e59b in LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput /src/download_refs_fuzzer.cc:145:9
	#7 0x52ef3f in ExecuteFilesOnyByOne(int, char**) /src/libfuzzer/afl/afl_driver.cpp:301:5
	#8 0x52f4ee in main /src/libfuzzer/afl/afl_driver.cpp:339:12
	#9 0x7f6c910db82f in __libc_start_main /build/glibc-Cl5G7W/glibc-2.23/csu/libc-start.c:291
	#10 0x41d518 in _start

When parsing an "ng" packet, we keep track of both the current position
as well as the remaining length of the packet itself. But instead of
taking care not to exceed the length, we pass the current pointer's
position to `strchr`, which will search for a certain character until
hitting NUL. It is thus possible to create a crafted packet which
doesn't contain a NUL byte to trigger an out-of-bounds read.

Fix the issue by instead using `memchr`, passing the remaining length as
restriction. Furthermore, verify that we actually have enough bytes left
to produce a match at all.

OSS-Fuzz-Issue: 9406
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["\tif (!(ptr = strchr(line, ' ')))", "\tif (!(ptr = strchr(line, '\\n')))"], 'added_lines': ['\tif (len < 3)', '\t\tgoto out_err;', '\tlen -= 3;', "\tif (!(ptr = memchr(line, ' ', len)))", '\tif (len < 1)', '\t\tgoto out_err;', '\tlen -= 1;', "\tif (!(ptr = memchr(line, '\\n', len)))"]}
description: In ng_pkt in transports/smart_pkt.c in libgit2 before 0.26.6 and 0.27.x before 0.27.4, a remote attacker can send a crafted smart-protocol "ng" packet that lacks a '\0' byte to trigger an out-of-bounds read that leads to DoS.

code_evidence: Line 10 advances line by 3 without verifying that len is at least 3, so line may already point beyond the buffer. Line 11 then calls strchr(line, ' ') which scans until a NUL byte rather than being limited by the packet's remaining length.
After line = ptr + 1 at line 19, line 20 calls strchr(line, '\n'), again scanning without any length bound, so a crafted packet lacking a NUL byte causes reads past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unbounded strchr scans read memory past the intended packet buffer, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). The issue is a missing length constraint, not merely a NULL-pointer dereference or integer overflow, so CWE-125 is the appropriate single label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser tracks the remaining packet length but does not use it, passing the current pointer to unbounded strchr searches and skipping 3 bytes without a length check. Trigger: a remote smart-protocol "ng" packet without a NUL byte (or shorter than 3 bytes). Consequence: heap out-of-bounds read, crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
Prevent copying uninitialized data in `AssignOp`.

This prevents harder to debug undefined behaviors that cannot be traced back to the original tensor after assignments occur earlier in the graph execution. Several of these undefined behaviors are just reference bindings to null pointers, which are caught when running under ubsan/asan.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 408654780
Change-Id: Iad2ec40d43f5fd7ea016c20283356c12d5ddeab1
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    // Prevent copying uninitialized data, to solve harder to debug undefined', '    // behaviors that cannot be traced back to the original tensor.', '    OP_REQUIRES(', '        context, rhs.IsInitialized(),', '        errors::Internal("Right hand side of AssignOp is not initialized"));']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `AssignOp` can result in copying uninitialized data to a new tensor. This later results in undefined behavior. The implementation has a check that the left hand side of the assignment is initialized (to minimize number of allocations), but does not check that the right hand side is also initialized. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 2 reads rhs = context->input(1); line 11 obtains old_lhs as a mutable input. Line 21 checks only old_lhs.IsInitialized(), never rhs.IsInitialized(). When old_lhs is initialized and element counts match (line 22), line 32 Copy(context, &reshaped_old_lhs, rhs) copies rhs; otherwise line 56 Copy(context, &old_unlocked_lhs, rhs) also copies rhs. Neither path validates that the right-hand side tensor contains initialized data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 covers using or accessing a resource that was not initialized. The function copies an uninitialized rhs tensor into the assignment target without checking rhs.IsInitialized(), directly matching use of an uninitialized resource. A related weakness such as CWE-476 (null pointer dereference) would describe only one downstream symptom, whereas the root cause here is the unchecked uninitialized tensor.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates the initialization state of the left-hand side but not the right-hand side before copying. Trigger: an AssignOp whose input(1) tensor is uninitialized reaches Copy at line 32 or line 56. Consequence: uninitialized data is read and propagated to the output tensor, causing undefined behavior, possibly invalid memory reads or crashes; the defect is the missing rhs initialization check, not the copy itself.

commit_msg:
Jann Horn reported a problem with commit eb1231f73c4d ("selinux:
clarify task subjective and objective credentials") where some LSM
hooks were attempting to access the subjective credentials of a task
other than the current task.  Generally speaking, it is not safe to
access another task's subjective credentials and doing so can cause
a number of problems.

Further, while looking into the problem, I realized that Smack was
suffering from a similar problem brought about by a similar commit
1fb057dcde11 ("smack: differentiate between subjective and objective
task credentials").

This patch addresses this problem by restoring the use of the task's
objective credentials in those cases where the task is other than the
current executing task.  Not only does this resolve the problem
reported by Jann, it is arguably the correct thing to do in these
cases.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: eb1231f73c4d ("selinux: clarify task subjective and objective credentials")
Fixes: 1fb057dcde11 ("smack: differentiate between subjective and objective task credentials")
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Eric W. Biederman <ebiederm@xmission.com>
Acked-by: Casey Schaufler <casey@schaufler-ca.com>
Signed-off-by: Paul Moore <paul@paul-moore.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct smack_known *skp = smk_of_task_struct_subj(p);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct smack_known *skp = smk_of_task_struct_obj(p);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.14.8. A use-after-free in selinux_ptrace_traceme (aka the SELinux handler for PTRACE_TRACEME) could be used by local attackers to cause memory corruption and escalate privileges, aka CID-a3727a8bac0a. This occurs because of an attempt to access the subjective credentials of another task.

code_evidence: Line 5 obtains the task's subjective credential label via smk_of_task_struct_subj(p) for an arbitrary task p passed into the hook. Lines 7-9 initialize audit info for that task and pass the derived skp into smk_curacc for the access check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The description states the bug is a use-after-free in selinux_ptrace_traceme caused by accessing another task's subjective credentials, matching CWE-416's reuse of freed memory. The function's use of smk_of_task_struct_subj(p) is the code-level manifestation of that unsafe access pattern.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the function dereferences another task's subjective credentials (smk_of_task_struct_subj(p)) rather than objective credentials; subjective credentials of a non-current task can be freed or replaced concurrently. The trigger is a hook invocation on a task other than current, leading to use of stale credential memory and an out-of-bounds/use-after-free access with possible memory corruption or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
unix: correctly track in-flight fds in sending process user_struct

The commit referenced in the Fixes tag incorrectly accounted the number
of in-flight fds over a unix domain socket to the original opener
of the file-descriptor. This allows another process to arbitrary
deplete the original file-openers resource limit for the maximum of
open files. Instead the sending processes and its struct cred should
be credited.

To do so, we add a reference counted struct user_struct pointer to the
scm_fp_list and use it to account for the number of inflight unix fds.

Fixes: 712f4aad406bb1 ("unix: properly account for FDs passed over unix sockets")
Reported-by: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Hannes Frederic Sowa <hannes@stressinduktion.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void unix_inflight(struct file *fp)', '\tfp->f_cred->user->unix_inflight++;'], 'added_lines': ['void unix_inflight(struct user_struct *user, struct file *fp)', '\tuser->unix_inflight++;']}
description: The Linux kernel before 4.5 allows local users to bypass file-descriptor limits and cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by leveraging incorrect tracking of descriptor ownership and sending each descriptor over a UNIX socket before closing it. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incorrect fix for CVE-2013-4312.

code_evidence: unix_inflight takes only struct file *fp and increments fp->f_cred->user->unix_inflight, crediting the original opener's user_struct rather than the sending process. The in-flight accounting counter is thus attached to the wrong process's resource limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 covers improper management of system resources; here incorrect attribution of in-flight FD accounting lets one process exhaust another process's file-descriptor resource limit. The defect is resource-limit accounting, not a memory-safety flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
void unix_inflight(struct file *fp)
fp->f_cred->user->unix_inflight++;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function charges the descriptor to fp->f_cred->user instead of the sending process's user_struct. Trigger: a local user sends descriptors over a UNIX socket and closes them, so each increments the opener's counter while the sender's own limit is untouched. Supported consequence: the opener's maximum open-file resource limit can be arbitrarily depleted, causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
mnt: Update detach_mounts to leave mounts connected

Now that it is possible to lazily unmount an entire mount tree and
leave the individual mounts connected to each other add a new flag
UMOUNT_CONNECTED to umount_tree to force this behavior and use
this flag in detach_mounts.

This closes a bug where the deletion of a file or directory could
trigger an unmount and reveal data under a mount point.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tdisconnect = !IS_MNT_LOCKED_AND_LAZY(p);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tdisconnect = !(((how & UMOUNT_CONNECTED) &&', '\t\t\t\tmnt_has_parent(p) &&', '\t\t\t\t(p->mnt_parent->mnt.mnt_flags & MNT_UMOUNT)) ||', '\t\t\t       IS_MNT_LOCKED_AND_LAZY(p));']}
description: fs/namespace.c in the Linux kernel before 4.0.2 does not properly support mount connectivity, which allows local users to read arbitrary files by leveraging user-namespace root access for deletion of a file or directory.

code_evidence: umount_tree marks each mount MNT_UMOUNT, moves it to tmp_list, and then detaches it from its parent by list_del_init on mnt_child.

For each mount the function decides whether to disconnect it from its parent via disconnect = !IS_MNT_LOCKED_AND_LAZY(p); when disconnect is false it re-links mnt_child to the parent; otherwise it calls umount_mnt(p).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's faulty connectivity handling causes previously hidden filesystem content to become visible to an unauthorized user, i.e., exposure of sensitive information. This fits CWE-200's confidentiality impact; the root cause is the incorrect disconnect condition rather than an explicit information leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the disconnect decision only honors IS_MNT_LOCKED_AND_LAZY and ignores whether the parent mount is already being unmounted. During a lazy unmount of a mount tree, a child whose parent is in MNT_UMOUNT can be disconnected and re-exposed instead of remaining connected, so a later file or directory deletion under the mount point can unmount and reveal the underlying data. description: An issue was discovered in tnef before 1.4.13. Two type confusions have been identified in the parse_file() function. These might lead to invalid read and write operations, controlled by an attacker.

code_evidence: The loop dispatches MAPI attributes to get_html_data()/get_rtf_data() based solely on a->name, without verifying a->type is szMAPI_BINARY, so a non-binary attribute carrying the HTML or RTF name is treated as binary data.
html_size and rtf_size are set from a->num_values of the mis-typed attribute, so the recorded element counts do not match the actual buffer layout produced by get_html_data()/get_rtf_data().
Later, free_bodies(body.html_bodies, html_size) and free_bodies(body.rtf_bodies, rtf_size) iterate using these attacker-influenced counts over the arrays, writing/freeing past their allocated bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stored size mismatch drives free_bodies() to write past the end of the allocated body arrays, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is distinct from a pure out-of-bounds read, since the write/free loop corrupts memory beyond the buffer.

body.rtf_bodies = get_rtf_data (a);
rtf_size = a->num_values;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser indexes attribute handling by name only, without a type check, so a crafted MAPI attribute of the wrong type reaches the HTML/RTF data extractors and its num_values is stored as the body size. Trigger: an attacker-supplied TNEF file containing such a mis-typed attribute. Consequence: free_bodies() walks the arrays using counts that exceed the allocated buffers, causing out-of-bounds writes to memory.

commit_msg:
Prevent unauthenticated client from easily consuming lots of memory (CVE-2021-32675)

This change sets a low limit for multibulk and bulk length in the
protocol for unauthenticated connections, so that they can't easily
cause redis to allocate massive amounts of memory by sending just a few
characters on the network.
The new limits are 10 arguments of 16kb each (instead of 1m of 512mb)

description: Redis is an open source, in-memory database that persists on disk. When parsing an incoming Redis Standard Protocol (RESP) request, Redis allocates memory according to user-specified values which determine the number of elements (in the multi-bulk header) and size of each element (in the bulk header). An attacker delivering specially crafted requests over multiple connections can cause the server to allocate significant amount of memory. Because the same parsing mechanism is used to handle authentication requests, this vulnerability can also be exploited by unauthenticated users. The problem is fixed in Redis versions 6.2.6, 6.0.16 and 5.0.14. An additional workaround to mitigate this problem without patching the redis-server executable is to block access to prevent unauthenticated users from connecting to Redis. This can be done in different ways: Using network access control tools like firewalls, iptables, security groups, etc. or Enabling TLS and requiring users to authenticate using client side certificates.

description: The ansilove_ansi function in loaders/ansi.c in libansilove 1.0.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and application crash) via a crafted file.

commit_msg:
netfilter: xt_TCPMSS: add more sanity tests on tcph->doff

Denys provided an awesome KASAN report pointing to an use
after free in xt_TCPMSS

I have provided three patches to fix this issue, either in xt_TCPMSS or
in xt_tcpudp.c. It seems xt_TCPMSS patch has the smallest possible
impact.

Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Denys Fedoryshchenko <nuclearcat@nuclearcat.com>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (len < tcp_hdrlen)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (len < tcp_hdrlen || tcp_hdrlen < sizeof(struct tcphdr))', '\t/* tcph->doff has 4 bits, do not wrap it to 0 */', '\tif (tcp_hdrlen >= 15 * 4)', '\t\treturn 0;', '']}
description: The tcpmss_mangle_packet function in net/netfilter/xt_TCPMSS.c in the Linux kernel before 4.11, and 4.9.x before 4.9.36, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging the presence of xt_TCPMSS in an iptables action.

code_evidence: Line 23 derives tcp_hdrlen from the packet-controlled tcph->doff without a lower bound; line 24 only checks len < tcp_hdrlen, so a doff below sizeof(struct tcphdr)/4 passes with a small tcp_hdrlen.

Lines 53-54 then only return when len > tcp_hdrlen; when len == tcp_hdrlen, the MSS option insertion path runs. Line 62 grows the skb via skb_put and line 68 memmoves len - sizeof(struct tcphdr) bytes from opt, but tcph was captured at line 22 and is only refreshed inside the tailroom branch (line 60).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a packet header pointer after the skb buffer may be reallocated/grown, i.e., reuse of memory no longer validly owned by that pointer, matching CWE-416. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the defect is stale-pointer use after reallocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation that tcph->doff is at least sizeof(struct tcphdr)/4 and that the header length cannot wrap. Trigger: a crafted TCP packet with a too-small doff reaches the option-insertion path. Consequence: skb_put/pskb_expand_head can reallocate the skb data while the stale tcph/opt pointer is used by memmove and checksum updates, producing a use-after-free (KASAN-reported) leading to memory corruption or DoS.

description: A heap buffer overflow vulnerability in the r_asm_swf_disass function of Radare2-extras before commit e74a93c allows attackers to execute arbitrary code or carry out denial of service (DOS) attacks.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe sprintf into a too-small heap allocation is a direct write past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. It is not merely a stack buffer issue or format-string flaw; the flaw is the missing bound on the destination buffer, which the patch addresses by switching to snprintf with strsize.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unbounded sprintf writes into a heap buffer of fixed size (strsize=20) while the source string is attacker-controlled and arbitrarily long. Trigger: a SWF PUSH action with a string push-type whose length makes the formatted result exceed the allocation. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, enabling memory corruption, crash/DoS, or code execution.

description: curl 7.75.0 through 7.76.1 suffers from a use-after-free vulnerability resulting in already freed memory being used when a TLS 1.3 session ticket arrives over a connection. A malicious server can use this in rare unfortunate circumstances to potentially reach remote code execution in the client. When libcurl at run-time sets up support for TLS 1.3 session tickets on a connection using OpenSSL, it stores pointers to the transfer in-memory object for later retrieval when a session ticket arrives. If the connection is used by multiple transfers (like with a reused HTTP/1.1 connection or multiplexed HTTP/2 connection) that first transfer object might be freed before the new session is established on that connection and then the function will access a memory buffer that might be freed. When using that memory, libcurl might even call a function pointer in the object, making it possible for a remote code execution if the server could somehow manage to get crafted memory content into the correct place in memory.

code_evidence: When sessionid is enabled, the function stores pointers to the transfer's in-memory objects (data, conn, conn->sock+sockindex) into the SSL handle via SSL_set_ex_data. These stored pointers are later used by the new-session callback when a TLS 1.3 ticket arrives, even if the connection is reused by a different transfer and the original data object has been freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the stored ex_data pointers reference memory that may be freed before the session-ticket callback uses them. This is a lifetime/ownership bug, not merely a stale-session logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SSL object retains raw pointers to the transfer/connection owned by a specific Curl_easy without any lifetime guarantee. Trigger: a reused connection (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive or HTTP/2 multiplexing) receives a TLS 1.3 session ticket after the first transfer is freed. Consequence: the callback dereferences freed memory, potentially calling a function pointer for remote code execution.

commit_msg:
evtchn: address races with evtchn_reset()

Neither d->evtchn_port_ops nor max_evtchns(d) may be used in an entirely
lock-less manner, as both may change by a racing evtchn_reset(). In the
common case, at least one of the domain's event lock or the per-channel
lock needs to be held. In the specific case of the inter-domain sending
by evtchn_send() and notify_via_xen_event_channel() holding the other
side's per-channel lock is sufficient, as the channel can't change state
without both per-channel locks held. Without such a channel changing
state, evtchn_reset() can't complete successfully.

Lock-free accesses continue to be permitted for the shim (calling some
otherwise internal event channel functions), as this happens while the
domain is in effectively single-threaded mode. Special care also needs
taking for the shim's marking of in-use ports as ECS_RESERVED (allowing
use of such ports in the shim case is okay because switching into and
hence also out of FIFO mode is impossihble there).

As a side effect, certain operations on Xen bound event channels which
were mistakenly permitted so far (e.g. unmask or poll) will be refused
now.

This is part of XSA-343.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    spin_lock(&chn->lock);', '    spin_unlock(&chn->lock);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: Line 13 takes only the vcpu's virq_lock, then line 14 reads v->virq_to_evtchn[virq] and line 17 resolves chn via evtchn_from_port(d, port). Line 18 calls evtchn_port_set_pending(d, chn->notify_vcpu_id, chn) on that channel without holding chn->lock; only the virq_lock is released at line 20. A concurrent evtchn_reset() can therefore change the channel state while this sequence operates on it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because a shared event-channel resource is accessed without the required exclusive per-channel synchronization, leaving a timing window for a concurrent reset to interfere. The added spin_lock/spin_unlock around evtchn_port_set_pending in the patch confirms the missing exclusivity, not merely a general logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the channel state is read and modified (evtchn_port_set_pending) while only the virq_lock is held, so the per-channel lock protecting the channel from evtchn_reset() is missing. Trigger: a racing EVTCHNOP_reset/soft reset changes the port mapping or channel state concurrently. Consequence: use of a stale/inconsistent channel, leading to out-of-bounds access or bug checks (crash, possible privilege escalation).

description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.

code_evidence: len is computed from the last register line and col = len - lendiff; when col > 1 the code calls mb_head_off(y_array[y_size - 1], y_array[y_size - 1] + len - 1). If len is 0 or lendiff makes col exceed len, the second argument points before the start of the heap-allocated y_array entry, so mb_head_off reads out of bounds. The patch adds a len > 0 guard before this subtraction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-122 fits because the out-of-bounds access targets a heap-allocated buffer (y_array entries) and results from missing length validation. It is a read rather than a write, but the weakness class (heap-based buffer overflow) still applies to the unchecked access before the buffer start.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pointer arithmetic y_array[y_size - 1] + len - 1 is performed without ensuring len is positive, so a zero-length register line produces a pointer before the heap buffer. description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An out-of-bounds read was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The out-of-bounds read is triggered when Exiv2 is used to read the metadata of a crafted image file. This matches CWE-125 (read past the intended buffer); it is not a write (CWE-787) or integer issue, since the defect is unchecked indexing on a read.

For the specific case of SF_BROADCAST support, this might lead to possible

description: In the Linux kernel 5.11 through 5.12.2, isotp_setsockopt in net/can/isotp.c allows privilege escalation to root by leveraging a use-after-free. (This does not affect earlier versions that lack CAN ISOTP SF_BROADCAST support.)

code_evidence: The function resolves the socket state via isotp_sk(sk) and only guards against option changes with a bound check (so->bound) that is performed without holding the socket lock.

After that unlocked check, the switch copies user-supplied option data (e.g., copy_from_sockptr into so->opt, so->rxfc, force_tx_stmin, force_rx_stmin) and mutates so->ll/tx.ll_dl, all without serializing against bind/unbind paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the defect permits option changes after binding to bypass the intended unregister path, leaving a stale reference to freed memory that is subsequently used. This is a use-after-free rather than a mere race condition (CWE-362), since the supported impact is reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: isotp_setsockopt reads so->bound and writes socket option state without the socket lock, so it races with isotp_bind()/socket teardown. Trigger: one thread changes options (notably SF_BROADCAST flags) while another binds or closes the socket; the broadcast registration is then never unregistered by can_rx_unregister(). Consequence: the freed socket/registration memory is later referenced, yielding a use-after-free potentially escalating to root.

commit_msg:
Split the xt_compat_match/xt_compat_target into smaller type-safe functions
performing just one operation. Handle all alignment and size-related
conversions centrally in these function instead of requiring each module to
implement a full-blown conversion function. Replace ->compat callback by
->compat_from_user and ->compat_to_user callbacks, responsible for
converting just a single private structure.

Signed-off-by: Patrick McHardy <kaber@trash.net>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: A heap out-of-bounds write affecting Linux since v2.6.19-rc1 was discovered in net/netfilter/x_tables.c. This allows an attacker to gain privileges or cause a DoS (via heap memory corruption) through user name space

code_evidence: compat_copy_match_to_user delegates to the match-specific ->compat callback (lines 4-6) or generic xt_compat_match (line 8), passing dstptr and size for conversion to user space; this wrapper performs no bounds check itself and trusts the callee to respect the size accounting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a user-space copy whose length is derived from the match's conversion logic, matching CWE-787's write past the intended buffer. It is not merely an information leak (CWE-125) or integer overflow alone; the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that the size/dstptr bookkeeping is delegated to conversion routines without the wrapper enforcing the compat size limit, so a match whose compat conversion writes more than the advertised size can overrun the heap buffer. Trigger is a user-namespace attacker supplying a crafted iptables match; consequence is heap out-of-bounds write enabling privilege escalation or DoS.

commit_msg: pixops: use gint64 in more places to avoid overflow when shifting
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int i, j;', '  int x, y;\t\t\t/* X and Y position in source (fixed_point) */', '  int x_step;', '  int y_step;', '  int scaled_x_offset;', '  int run_end_x;', '  int run_end_index;'], 'added_lines': ['  gint64 i, j;', '  gint64 x, y;\t\t\t/* X and Y position in source (fixed_point) */', '  gint64 x_step;', '  gint64 y_step;', '  gint64 scaled_x_offset;', '  gint64 run_end_x;', '  gint64 run_end_index;']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the (1) pixops_composite_nearest, (2) pixops_composite_color_nearest, and (3) pixops_process functions in pixops/pixops.c in gdk-pixbuf before 2.33.1 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted image, which triggers a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Position, step, offset, and run-length variables (i, j, x, y, x_step, y_step, scaled_x_offset, run_end_x, run_end_index) are declared as 32-bit int, so fixed-point source coordinates and offsets computed from scale factors can overflow.

x_step/y_step are derived by dividing (1 << SCALE_SHIFT); scaled_x_offset uses floor(offset << SCALE_SHIFT); run_end_x shifts (src_width - filter->x.n + 1) by SCALE_SHIFT, and x/y accumulate by x_step/y_step and are shifted by SCALE_SHIFT in the loops.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The declared int variables and shifted fixed-point arithmetic directly exhibit numeric overflow in coordinate computation, which is the numeric-error category CWE-189; the consequence is memory corruption rather than merely an incorrect value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: 32-bit int storage for fixed-point coordinates and shifts of scaled values, where large scale/offset or image dimensions cause signed overflow before the shift. Trigger: crafted image/scale parameters flowing into x_step, scaled_x_offset, run_end_x and iterative x/y updates. Supported consequence: corrupted coordinate/run-length computations that can drive out-of-bounds buffer indexing (heap overflow) or crash.

commit_msg:
Throw on skipping an invalid type.

Summary:
Certain values (e.g.) T_STOP should not appear as a skip type. Allowing them to
can cause thrift to loop unboundedly.

Reviewed By: spalamarchuk

Differential Revision: D15102451

fbshipit-source-id: c08d52f44f37e9c212d3480233ac217105586c9f
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    default:', '      return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    default: {', '      TProtocolException::throwInvalidSkipType(arg_type);', '    }']}
description: Legacy C++ Facebook Thrift servers (using cpp instead of cpp2) would not error upon receiving messages with containers of fields of unknown type. As a result, malicious clients could send short messages which would take a long time for the server to parse, potentially leading to denial of service. This issue affects Facebook Thrift prior to v2019.05.06.00.

code_evidence: The switch on arg_type handles known TType values but the default branch simply returns 0, silently treating any unrecognized type as successfully skipped.
Recursive skip calls pass attacker-derived field/container element types (ftype, keyType, valType, elemType) back into this function, so an invalid type such as T_STOP reaches the default branch.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Returning 0 on an unrecognized type is improper handling of an exceptional condition: the invalid type is not rejected, allowing the error condition to propagate into unbounded parsing. This is a specific instance of CWE-755 (Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions).

evidence_lines.code:
default:
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the default case fails to reject an invalid skip type, returning 0 instead of signaling an error. Trigger: a malicious client sends a container/field whose declared type is invalid (e.g. T_STOP). Consequence: parsing continues without consuming data, so skip loops (e.g. peekMap/peekList) can iterate unboundedly, enabling denial of service.

commit_msg:
Make DH_check_pub_key() and DH_generate_key() safer yet

We already check for an excessively large P in DH_generate_key(), but not in
DH_check_pub_key(), and none of them check for an excessively large Q.

This change adds all the missing excessive size checks of P and Q.

It's to be noted that behaviours surrounding excessively sized P and Q
differ.  DH_check() raises an error on the excessively sized P, but only
sets a flag for the excessively sized Q.  This behaviour is mimicked in
DH_check_pub_key().

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Hugo Landau <hlandau@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22518)

(cherry picked from commit ddeb4b6c6d527e54ce9a99cba785c0f7776e54b6)

description:
Issue summary: Generating excessively long X9.42 DH keys or checking
excessively long X9.42 DH keys or parameters may be very slow.

Impact summary: Applications that use the functions DH_generate_key() to
generate an X9.42 DH key may experience long delays.  Likewise, applications
that use DH_check_pub_key(), DH_check_pub_key_ex() or EVP_PKEY_public_check()
to check an X9.42 DH key or X9.42 DH parameters may experience long delays.
Where the key or parameters that are being checked have been obtained from
an untrusted source this may lead to a Denial of Service.

While DH_check() performs all the necessary checks (as of CVE-2023-3817),
DH_check_pub_key() doesn't make any of these checks, and is therefore
vulnerable for excessively large P and Q parameters.

Likewise, while DH_generate_key() performs a check for an excessively large
P, it doesn't check for an excessively large Q.

An application that calls DH_generate_key() or DH_check_pub_key() and
supplies a key or parameters obtained from an untrusted source could be
vulnerable to a Denial of Service attack.

DH_generate_key() and DH_check_pub_key() are also called by a number of
other OpenSSL functions.  An application calling any of those other
functions may similarly be affected.  The other functions affected by this
are DH_check_pub_key_ex(), EVP_PKEY_public_check(), and EVP_PKEY_generate().

Also vulnerable are the OpenSSL pkey command line application when using the
"-pubcheck" option, as well as the OpenSSL genpkey command line application.

The OpenSSL SSL/TLS implementation is not affected by this issue.

The OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.1 FIPS providers are not affected by this issue.

code_evidence: DH_check_pub_key() directly delegates to ossl_ffc_validate_public_key(&dh->params, pub_key, ret) and returns its result without any guard on the size of dh->params.p or dh->params.q. The caller-supplied DH parameters flow straight into the validation routine, so an excessively large modulus or subgroup order is accepted for processing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-754 fits because the function fails to check an unusual but attacker-controllable condition (oversized P/Q) before proceeding. The commit adds exactly such size guards, confirming the omission. This is a missing exceptional-condition check leading to DoS, not a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function omits a bound check on the untrusted DH modulus/order before running public-key validation. Trigger: an application passes attacker-supplied DH parameters with an excessively large P or Q. The expensive validation then runs to completion, causing long delays and a denial of service; the missing check is the cause, the delay is the consequence.

commit_msg:
Change pairing_cb to assume temporary pairing by default

When pairing takes place, the pairing_cb.is_temp flag indicates whether
a pairing is temporary or permanent. Link keys are not stored for
temporary pairings. Since this is a "positive" flag, resetting the
pairing_cb control block (ex. memset to 0), it will assume persistent
pairing by default. Under certain circumstances, this can lead to a link
key being stored for temporarily secured connection.

This patch reverses the flag to be a "negative" flag. Renamed to
"persistent_bond", the default 0 meaning is now used to indicate a
temporary bond. If the lag is not properly set now, it will default to a
temporary bond and will not save the link key erronously.

This fix is for CVE-2014-7914

Bug: 18345373
Change-Id: I6e821595877ff30d64dc6e33602ac049cab3dd1e
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    pairing_cb.is_temp = FALSE;'], 'added_lines': ['    pairing_cb.bond_type = BOND_TYPE_PERSISTENT;']}
description: btif/src/btif_dm.c in Android before 5.1 does not properly enforce the temporary nature of a Bluetooth pairing, which allows user-assisted remote attackers to bypass intended access restrictions via crafted Bluetooth packets after the tapping of a crafted NFC tag.

code_evidence: bond_state_changed transitions the peer into BT_BOND_STATE_BONDING, then line 16 sets pairing_cb.is_temp = FALSE, marking the pending pairing as permanent. Lines 17-18 set LE-only and SSP flags, so the control block drives later link-key storage decisions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function decides whether the bond is temporary or persistent, and the hardcoded FALSE removes the temporary-pairing constraint, letting a temporary connection gain persistent-bond authorization. This is an incorrect authorization decision (CWE-863), not merely a data-exposure flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the positive is_temp flag is explicitly cleared, so the pairing control block defaults to a persistent-bond state for every BLE security request. Trigger: a crafted BLE security request (e.g., after NFC-tag-assisted pairing) reaches btif_dm_ble_sec_req_evt. Consequence: the temporarily secured connection is treated as permanent, so a link key is stored and the temporary-pairing restriction is bypassed.

Currently, there is an out-of-bounds read on array ctrl->phys,
once variable i reaches the maximum array size of SERDES_MAX
in the for loop.

Fix this by changing the condition in the for loop from
i <= SERDES_MAX to i < SERDES_MAX.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.20. drivers/phy/mscc/phy-ocelot-serdes.c has an off-by-one error with a resultant ctrl->phys out-of-bounds read.

code_evidence: The loop guard uses i <= SERDES_MAX, so i can reach SERDES_MAX, one past the last valid index of the ctrl->phys array whose size is SERDES_MAX.
At that final iteration, ctrl->phys[i] is read to obtain the drvdata pointer, and the same out-of-range index is returned at line 17 if the loop condition and macro checks were to match.

struct serdes_macro *macro = phy_get_drvdata(ctrl->phys[i]);
return ctrl->phys[i];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the off-by-one loop condition allowing i to equal SERDES_MAX. When the loop reaches that iteration, ctrl->phys[i] dereferences one element past the array, causing an out-of-bounds read; the trigger is reaching this index during xlate iteration.

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Remove unsafe bits from the mod_l?_entry() fastpath

All changes in writeability and cacheability must go through full
re-validation.

Rework the logic as a whitelist, to make it clearer to follow.

This is XSA-182

Reported-by: Jérémie Boutoille <jboutoille@ext.quarkslab.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>

description: The PV pagetable code in arch/x86/mm.c in Xen 4.7.x and earlier allows local 32-bit PV guest OS administrators to gain host OS privileges by leveraging fast-paths for updating pagetable entries.

code_evidence: The fast path uses l2e_has_changed(ol2e, nl2e, ...) with a mask that only covers _PAGE_PRESENT (or _PAGE_PSE|_PAGE_RW|_PAGE_PRESENT when superpages are allowed). If the guest writes a new L2 entry that differs only in flags outside this mask, the fast path treats it as unchanged, calls adjust_guest_l2e and UPDATE_ENTRY, and returns 0 without calling get_page_from_l2e.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-284 fits because the fast path incorrectly restricts enforcement of the pagetable access-control policy: the whitelist mask fails to require re-validation of privilege-relevant flag changes, letting an unauthorized actor (guest admin) effect host-level access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the fast-path change-detection mask omits writeability/cacheability bits, so updates that alter those privilege-relevant flags bypass full re-validation via get_page_from_l2e. Trigger: a 32-bit PV guest administrator submits a pagetable update differing only in un-masked flags. Consequence: host-privilege escalation, since the pagetable change is committed without the required access-control checks.

Fix heap-buffer-overflow issue with `tf.raw_ops.SparseFillEmptyRows`.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 372009178

Also add check that dense rank > 0.'], 'added_lines': ['  // Also add check that dense rank > 0.', '  OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(context, dense_shape_t.NumElements() != 0,', '                    errors::InvalidArgument("Dense shape cannot be empty."),', '                    done);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a null pointer dereference in the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.SparseFillEmptyRows`. This is because of missing validation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/fdc82089d206e281c628a93771336bf87863d5e8/tensorflow/core/kernels/sparse_fill_empty_rows_op.cc#L230-L231) that was covered under a `TODO`. If the `dense_shape` tensor is empty, then `dense_shape_t.vec<>()` would cause a null pointer dereference in the implementation of the op. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 12 obtains dense_shape_t from the op input without checking that it contains any elements.

Lines 14-18 only validate that dense_shape_t's shape is a vector; an empty vector (NumElements()==0) passes this check, so no guard prevents downstream code from dereferencing the empty tensor's data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the missing non-empty validation allows a NULL data pointer to be dereferenced during op execution. It is a null-dereference (CWE-476) rather than a mere missing-validation issue because the concrete consequence is dereferencing a null pointer.

evidence_lines.code: const Tensor& dense_shape_t = context->input(kDenseShapeInput);

OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC(
context, TensorShapeUtils::IsVector(dense_shape_t.shape()),
errors::InvalidArgument("dense_shape must be a vector, saw: ",
dense_shape_t.shape().DebugString()),
done);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the input validation only enforces that dense_shape is a vector, not that it is non-empty. Trigger: a caller supplies an empty dense_shape tensor; the vector-shape check succeeds and the tensor is passed to the functor, whose access to the tensor's data yields a null pointer dereference. Supported consequence: crash/DoS (availability impact).
