commit_msg:
Use spinlocks to deal with workers introducing a wrapper
asus_schedule_work(), and several spinlock checks.
Otherwise, asus_kbd_backlight_set() may schedule led->work after the
structure has been freed, causing a use-after-free.

Fixes: af22a610bc38 ("HID: asus: support backlight on USB keyboards")
Signed-off-by: Pietro Borrello <borrello@diag.uniroma1.it>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230125-hid-unregister-leds-v4-5-7860c5763c38@diag.uniroma1.it
Signed-off-by: Benjamin Tissoires <benjamin.tissoires@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tschedule_work(&led->work);'], 'added_lines': ['\tasus_schedule_work(led);']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. A use-after-free may be triggered in asus_kbd_backlight_set when plugging/disconnecting in a malicious USB device, which advertises itself as an Asus device. Similarly to the previous known CVE-2023-25012, but in asus devices, the work_struct may be scheduled by the LED controller while the device is disconnecting, triggering a use-after-free on the struct asus_kbd_leds *led structure. A malicious USB device may exploit the issue to cause memory corruption with controlled data.

code_evidence: Under the LED lock, the callback stores brightness then releases the lock; the work item is queued unconditionally afterward via schedule_work(&led->work), with no check that the led structure is still registered/alive.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function queues work referencing led without a lifetime guard, so led->work can be scheduled after the containing structure is freed and later executed against stale memory, matching CWE-416. A plain race condition is the mechanism, but the supported consequence is use of freed memory, which is the target weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: scheduling led->work is not protected against concurrent teardown of the asus_kbd_leds structure. Trigger: a malicious USB device disconnecting while the LED controller calls asus_kbd_backlight_set causes the work to be queued after led is freed. Consequence: the worker later dereferences freed memory, yielding use-after-free and possible memory corruption.

commit_msg:
DICOM: Prevent infinite loop (dissect_dcm_tag)

uint32 value could wrap around, resulting in infinite loop.

Bug: 14411
Change-Id: I26c73f74adc65c7a5acf22970a54c93a7f7a2344
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/25873
Petri-Dish: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
(cherry picked from commit b6328eba6a3d33930489709ee1e47140dcc30dfb)
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/25877
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        else if (offset + vl <= endpos) {'], 'added_lines': ['        else if ((offset + vl <= endpos) &&', '                 (offset + vl > offset)) { /* Ensure no wraparound */']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.12, epan/dissectors/packet-dcm.c had an infinite loop that was addressed by checking for integer wraparound.

code_evidence: Line 141 gates the item branch on offset + vl <= endpos; both offset and vl are guint32, so the addition can wrap and pass this check with a small wrapped sum. Lines 142-144 then compute offset + vl - offset_tag and set vl_max = vl from the wrapped value.

Lines 180-205: when is_sequence or is_item and vl > 0, line 196 computes endpos_item = offset + vl_max, and lines 197-198 loop while offset < endpos_item, recursing via dissect_dcm_tag. A wrapped vl_max can make endpos_item <= offset, so the loop body never advances or the recursion re-enters the same tag, yielding an unreachable exit condition.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's loop exit relies on endpos_item derived from a wraparound-prone sum, so the exit condition offset < endpos_item can never become false, matching CWE-835's unreachable loop exit. The wraparound is the cause; the infinite loop is the supported consequence, not a separate integer weakness label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is unchecked 32-bit addition of attacker-controlled value length vl to offset in the length check and endpos_item computation. Trigger: a DICOM tag with a large vl causing offset + vl to wrap below endpos. Consequence: the item loop in lines 197-204 never terminates (or recursion repeats), consuming CPU and hanging the dissector.

commit_msg:
The bg_flags field in the block group descripts is only valid if the
uninit_bg or metadata_csum feature is enabled.  We were not
consistently looking at this field; fix this.

Also block group #0 must never have uninitialized allocation bitmaps,
or need to be zeroed, since that's where the root inode, and other
special inodes are set up.  Check for these conditions and mark the
file system as corrupted if they are detected.

This addresses CVE-2018-10876.

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=199403

Cc: stable@kernel.org

commit_msg:
Currently CONFIG_TIMER_STATS exposes process information across namespaces:

kernel/time/timer_list.c print_timer():

        SEQ_printf(m, ", %s/%d", tmp, timer->start_pid);

/proc/timer_list:

 #11: <0000000000000000>, hrtimer_wakeup, S:01, do_nanosleep, cron/2570

Given that the tracer can give the same information, this patch entirely
removes CONFIG_TIMER_STATS.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['#ifdef CONFIG_TIMER_STATS', '\tchar tmp[TASK_COMM_LEN + 1];', '#endif', '#ifdef CONFIG_TIMER_STATS', '\tSEQ_printf(m, ", ");', '\tprint_name_offset(m, timer->start_site);', '\tmemcpy(tmp, timer->start_comm, TASK_COMM_LEN);', '\ttmp[TASK_COMM_LEN] = 0;', '\tSEQ_printf(m, ", %s/%d", tmp, timer->start_pid);', '#endif'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The time subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.9.9, when CONFIG_TIMER_STATS is enabled, allows local users to discover real PID values (as distinguished from PID values inside a PID namespace) by reading the /proc/timer_list file, related to the print_timer function in kernel/time/timer_list.c and the __timer_stats_timer_set_start_info function in kernel/time/timer.c.

code_evidence: Under CONFIG_TIMER_STATS, print_timer() emits timer->start_site, a copy of timer->start_comm, and timer->start_pid into the seq_file. These values describe the process that armed the timer, including its real PID, and are written to /proc/timer_list without any namespace translation or access check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly writes sensitive process identifiers into a world-readable proc file, matching CWE-200's exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor. It is not a memory-safety flaw; the weakness is the intentional disclosure of PID-namespace-spanning data.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The seq_file output is generated from kernel-global timer metadata rather than namespace-scoped state; a local user reading /proc/timer_list therefore receives the real PID and comm of processes outside its PID namespace. The cause is unsanitized disclosure of start_pid/start_comm; the consequence is cross-namespace process information exposure.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

Reviewed-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Fam Zheng <famz@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Daniel P. Berrange <berrange@redhat.com>
Message-id: 20170213135235.12274-8-pbonzini@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    nbd_coroutine_end(client, &request);'], 'added_lines': ['    nbd_coroutine_end(bs, &request);']}
description: An assertion-failure flaw was found in Qemu before 2.10.1, in the Network Block Device (NBD) server's initial connection negotiation, where the I/O coroutine was undefined. This could crash the qemu-nbd server if a client sent unexpected data during connection negotiation. A remote user or process could use this flaw to crash the qemu-nbd server resulting in denial of service.

code_evidence: The function asserts bytes <= NBD_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE and assert(!flags) at entry, aborting the client process if the read request size or flags violate these preconditions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because the function contains assert() statements that can be triggered by request parameters, producing a crash more severe than a graceful error return. This is a reachable-assertion availability issue, not a memory-safety flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
assert(bytes <= NBD_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE);
assert(!flags);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: reachable assert() statements in the read path abort the process instead of returning an error for oversized reads or unexpected flags. Trigger: a request reaching this path with bytes exceeding NBD_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE or nonzero flags. Consequence: process exit/crash, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
ASAN SFTP Fixes
When decoding SFTP messages, fix the size checks so they don't wrap. (ZD12766)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (sz > maxSz - idx) {', '            return WS_BUFFER_E;', '        }', '        if (sz > maxSz - idx) {', '            return WS_BUFFER_E;', '        }']}
description: WolfSSH v1.4.7 was discovered to contain an integer overflow via the function wolfSSH_SFTP_RecvRMDIR.

code_evidence: Line 19 reads attacker-controlled sz from data; line 20 checks sz + idx > maxSz, but sz + idx can wrap when sz is near UINT32_MAX, so the bounds check can be bypassed.

Lines 29-31 advance idx by the handle size plus two UINT32_SZ offset fields and read a second sz without validating it against maxSz; line 32 then passes data + idx and sz to WPWRITE, so idx and sz may exceed the actual buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an integer wraparound in the size check (sz + idx) that invalidates the bounds constraint, matching CWE-190. This is not merely a logic error; the arithmetic overflow directly enables the unsafe buffer access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The length validation at line 20 performs sz + idx without overflow protection, allowing a large attacker-supplied sz to wrap and pass the check. The later unchecked write length and offset indexing then permit out-of-bounds reads/writes via WPWRITE, causing memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
nsfs: mark dentry with DCACHE_RCUACCESS

Andrey reported a use-after-free in __ns_get_path():

  spin_lock include/linux/spinlock.h:299 [inline]
  lockref_get_not_dead+0x19/0x80 lib/lockref.c:179
  __ns_get_path+0x197/0x860 fs/nsfs.c:66
  open_related_ns+0xda/0x200 fs/nsfs.c:143
  sock_ioctl+0x39d/0x440 net/socket.c:1001
  vfs_ioctl fs/ioctl.c:45 [inline]
  do_vfs_ioctl+0x1bf/0x1780 fs/ioctl.c:685
  SYSC_ioctl fs/ioctl.c:700 [inline]
  SyS_ioctl+0x8f/0xc0 fs/ioctl.c:691

We are under rcu read lock protection at that point:

        rcu_read_lock();
        d = atomic_long_read(&ns->stashed);
        if (!d)
                goto slow;
        dentry = (struct dentry *)d;
        if (!lockref_get_not_dead(&dentry->d_lockref))
                goto slow;
        rcu_read_unlock();

but don't use a proper RCU API on the free path, therefore a parallel
__d_free() could free it at the same time.  We need to mark the stashed
dentry with DCACHE_RCUACCESS so that __d_free() will be called after all
readers leave RCU.

Fixes: e149ed2b805f ("take the targets of /proc/*/ns/* symlinks to separate fs")
Cc: Alexander Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Cc: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tdentry->d_flags |= DCACHE_RCUACCESS;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the __ns_get_path function in fs/nsfs.c in the Linux kernel before 4.11. Due to a race condition when accessing files, a Use After Free condition can occur. This also affects all Android releases from CAF using the Linux kernel (Android for MSM, Firefox OS for MSM, QRD Android) before security patch level 2018-07-05.

code_evidence: Under rcu_read_lock(), the stashed dentry is read from ns->stashed and its lockref is taken; the reader relies on RCU grace period to keep the dentry alive until rcu_read_unlock().

The slow path publishes a freshly instantiated dentry into ns->stashed via atomic_long_cmpxchg without setting DCACHE_RCUACCESS, so __d_free() may release the dentry immediately rather than after an RCU grace period.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a race condition: concurrent reader and free code sequences access the shared stashed dentry without proper synchronization, violating exclusivity and causing a use-after-free. CWE-362 captures the improper synchronization root cause; the use-after-free is its consequence rather than a separate weakness here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The stashed dentry is published to a shared location and later dereferenced by concurrent readers holding only rcu_read_lock(). Because the dentry is not marked DCACHE_RCUACCESS, the free path can free it without waiting for RCU readers, so a reader between the atomic_long_read and lockref_get_not_dead can obtain a pointer to freed memory.

commit_msg:
Bug 698042: xps: fix glyph index and index bounds check.

If a gs_glyph has the GS_MIN_GLYPH_INDEX offset, we need to remove the offset
before we try to use it.

Secondly, using a unsigned variable for a value from which we subtract 1, and
which can be zero doesn't work well. Switch to a signed value.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    uint numGlyphs;', '    numGlyphs = u16(postp + 32);', '    if (glyph > numGlyphs - 1)'], 'added_lines': ['    int numGlyphs;', '', '    if (glyph >= GS_MIN_GLYPH_INDEX) {', '        glyph -= GS_MIN_GLYPH_INDEX;', '    }', '    numGlyphs = (int)u16(postp + 32);', '    if ((int)glyph > numGlyphs - 1)']}
description: The xps_true_callback_glyph_name function in xps/xpsttf.c in Artifex Ghostscript GhostXPS 9.21 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (Segmentation Violation and application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: numGlyphs is unsigned (line 7), and the bounds check compares glyph against numGlyphs - 1 (line 41). If numGlyphs is 0, the subtraction wraps to a huge value, so the check passes for any glyph.
Line 45 then indexes postp + 34 + (glyph * 2) using the unchecked glyph, reading a glyph_name_index outside the post table.

The pascal-string walk (lines 57,61) advances pascal_stringp by attacker-controlled string lengths, and the range check at line 66 occurs only after pstr->data and pstr->size are derived from the out-of-bounds pascal_stringp.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads from memory locations outside the post-table buffer because the index and length checks are ineffective, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds read/write operations. This is a buffer-bounds violation rather than merely an integer issue, since the integer underflow is the cause and the out-of-bounds access is the direct weakness.

evidence_lines.code: glyph_name_index = u16(postp + 34 + (glyph * 2));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unsigned underflow in numGlyphs - 1 disables the glyph bounds check, and the GS_MIN_GLYPH_INDEX offset is not removed, so an oversized glyph reaches the post-table index. Trigger: a crafted XPS file with a zero-glyph post table or large glyph id. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads at lines 45/61 and a subsequent memcpy from a pointer past the buffer, causing a segmentation violation/crash (CWE-119).

commit_msg:
xfs_attr3_leaf_create may have errored out before instantiating a buffer,
for example if the blkno is out of range.  In that case there is no work
to do to remove it, and in fact xfs_da_shrink_inode will lead to an oops
if we try.

This also seems to fix a flaw where the original error from
xfs_attr3_leaf_create gets overwritten in the cleanup case, and it
removes a pointless assignment to bp which isn't used after this.

Bugzilla: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=199969
Reported-by: Xu, Wen <wen.xu@gatech.edu>
Tested-by: Xu, Wen <wen.xu@gatech.edu>
Signed-off-by: Eric Sandeen <sandeen@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Darrick J. Wong <darrick.wong@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\terror = xfs_da_shrink_inode(args, 0, bp);', '\t\tbp = NULL;', '\t\tif (error)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* xfs_attr3_leaf_create may not have instantiated a block */', '\t\tif (bp && (xfs_da_shrink_inode(args, 0, bp) != 0))']}
description: An issue was discovered in fs/xfs/libxfs/xfs_attr_leaf.c in the Linux kernel through 4.17.3. An OOPS may occur for a corrupted xfs image after xfs_da_shrink_inode() is called with a NULL bp.

code_evidence: xfs_attr3_leaf_create is called with &bp, and bp was set to NULL at line 26. If creation fails before instantiating a buffer, the error branch still passes bp to xfs_da_shrink_inode(args, 0, bp) without checking it is non-NULL, so the NULL buffer pointer is consumed by the shrink path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences/uses a pointer expected to be valid but NULL, matching CWE-476. This is not merely improper error handling; the concrete defect is the unchecked NULL bp passed downstream.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path assumes xfs_attr3_leaf_create always produced a buffer, but on failure (e.g., out-of-range blkno) bp remains NULL. Trigger: a corrupted xfs image causes leaf creation to fail; xfs_da_shrink_inode then operates on NULL bp, leading to a crash/oops. The original error may also be overwritten.

commit_msg: fixed potential heap buffer overflow - cf #1272
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (nbBytes>DescSize) break;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (nbBytes + 16 > DescSize) return GF_ODF_INVALID_DESCRIPTOR;']}
description: An issue was discovered in gpac 0.8.0. The gf_odf_del_ipmp_tool function in odf_code.c has a heap-based buffer over-read.

code_evidence: The loop reads num_alternate entries of 16 bytes into ipmpt->specificToolID[i] via gf_bs_read_data before checking nbBytes against DescSize. The bound check at line 18 occurs after the read and only breaks; the descriptor-size limit is not enforced before consuming each 16-byte block, so reads can exceed the declared descriptor size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads data past the intended buffer boundary before validating the remaining size. It is an out-of-bounds read, not an out-of-bounds write, since the unsafe operation is gf_bs_read_data consuming input beyond DescSize.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-iteration size check is placed after the 16-byte read, so the descriptor boundary is not validated before reading. Trigger: a crafted descriptor with is_alt set and a num_alternate value large relative to DescSize causes gf_bs_read_data to consume data beyond the intended descriptor extent. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read of the bitstream buffer, potentially disclosing memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
vgacon: remove software scrollback support

Yunhai Zhang recently fixed a VGA software scrollback bug in commit
ebfdfeeae8c0 ("vgacon: Fix for missing check in scrollback handling"),
but that then made people look more closely at some of this code, and
there were more problems on the vgacon side, but also the fbcon software
scrollback.

We don't really have anybody who maintains this code - probably because
nobody actually _uses_ it any more.  Sure, people still use both VGA and
the framebuffer consoles, but they are no longer the main user
interfaces to the kernel, and haven't been for decades, so these kinds
of extra features end up bitrotting and not really being used.

So rather than try to maintain a likely unused set of code, I'll just
aggressively remove it, and see if anybody even notices.  Maybe there
are people who haven't jumped on the whole GUI badnwagon yet, and think
it's just a fad.  And maybe those people use the scrollback code.

If that turns out to be the case, we can resurrect this again, once
we've found the sucker^Wmaintainer for it who actually uses it.

Reported-by: NopNop Nop <nopitydays@gmail.com>
Tested-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: 张云海 <zhangyunhai@nsfocus.com>

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

description: The vgacon subsystem in the Linux kernel before 5.8.10 mishandles software scrollback. There is a vgacon_scrolldelta out-of-bounds read, aka CID-973c096f6a85.

commit_msg:
Fix info leak vulnerability of IDrm

bug: 26323455
Change-Id: I25bb30d3666ab38d5150496375ed2f55ecb23ba8
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            DrmPlugin::KeyRequestType keyRequestType;'], 'added_lines': ['            DrmPlugin::KeyRequestType keyRequestType = DrmPlugin::kKeyRequestType_Unknown;']}
description: media/libmedia/IDrm.cpp in mediaserver in Android 6.x before 2016-04-01 does not initialize a certain key-request data structure, which allows attackers to obtain sensitive information from process memory, and consequently bypass an unspecified protection mechanism, via unspecified vectors, as demonstrated by obtaining Signature or SignatureOrSystem access, aka internal bug 26323455.

code_evidence: The local keyRequestType is declared without initialization and passed by address to getKeyRequest; the callee may leave it unset.
After the call, the value is written to the reply unconditionally, carrying any uninitialized stack content to the caller.
The declared type is a bare local whose value depends entirely on whether getKeyRequest assigns it; no default or check guards the write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in managing security features used for access control. Here uninitialized key-request metadata is leaked across the Binder boundary, undermining the DRM protection mechanism rather than merely producing garbage, matching the permissions/access-control category.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an uninitialized stack variable is returned to the remote caller because the code does not default or validate keyRequestType before writing it. Trigger: a GET_KEY_REQUEST transaction where getKeyRequest does not set the out-parameter. Consequence: process memory contents leak into the reply, potentially exposing data that enables bypassing protection mechanisms.

commit_msg:
Disallow namespace nodes in XPointer ranges

Namespace nodes must be copied to avoid use-after-free errors.
But they don't necessarily have a physical representation in a
document, so simply disallow them in XPointer ranges.

Found with afl-fuzz.

Fixes CVE-2016-4658.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ret = (xmlXPathObjectPtr) xmlMalloc(sizeof(xmlXPathObject));', '    if (ret == NULL) {', '        xmlXPtrErrMemory("allocating range");', '\treturn(NULL);', '    }', '    memset(ret, 0 , (size_t) sizeof(xmlXPathObject));', '    ret->type = XPATH_RANGE;', '    ret->user = start;', '    ret->index = -1;', '    ret->user2 = end->user;', '    ret->index2 = end->index;'], 'added_lines': ['    ret = xmlXPtrNewRangeInternal(start, -1, end->user, end->index);']}
description: xpointer.c in libxml2 before 2.9.5 (as used in Apple iOS before 10, OS X before 10.12, tvOS before 10, and watchOS before 3, and other products) does not forbid namespace nodes in XPointer ranges, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (use-after-free and memory corruption) via a crafted XML document.

code_evidence: The function validates start and end pointer objects and their types, but never inspects whether the node/point refers to a namespace node.
After validation, a range object is allocated and populated with the caller-supplied start and end->user pointers, with index -1 and end->index, and then ordered.
No constraint rejects namespace nodes before these pointers are stored in the range object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing namespace-node restriction allows invalid node pointers into range structures, leading to memory corruption/use-after-free; this is an improper restriction of operations within memory bounds, matching CWE-119. The root cause is the absent node-type constraint, not merely allocation failure.

evidence_lines.code:
if (start->type != XPATH_POINT)
return(NULL);

if (end->type != XPATH_POINT)
return(NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accepts namespace nodes as range endpoints without a guard, so pointers to namespace nodes lacking a physical document representation are stored in the range. Trigger: a crafted XML/XPointer expression creates a range over namespace nodes. Supported consequence: later range processing dereferences/copies these nodes, causing use-after-free and memory corruption, consistent with out-of-bounds memory operations.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12897/ISO CLNS: Use ND_TTEST() for the bounds checks in isoclns_print().

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kamil Frankowicz.

Don't pass the remaining caplen - that's too hard to get right, and we
were getting it wrong in at least one case; just use ND_TTEST().

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            isoclns_print(ndo, p + 1, l2info.length - 1, l2info.caplen - 1);'], 'added_lines': ['            isoclns_print(ndo, p + 1, l2info.length - 1);']}
description: The ISO CLNS parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isoclns.c:isoclns_print().

code_evidence: When p[0]==0x03, the function calls isoclns_print with p+1 and a length of l2info.length-1, but also passes l2info.caplen-1 as the remaining capture length. The length and caplen are decremented independently of the actual bytes available after p+1, so the callee's bounds checks can be computed from an incorrect caplen and read past the captured buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the defect is an out-of-bounds read of captured packet memory driven by an incorrect length passed to the parser, not a write or a missing free. The fix removes the hand-computed caplen so the callee uses ND_TTEST() against the real snapshot end, confirming the over-read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller derives the sub-buffer caplen by subtracting 1 from l2info.caplen without verifying that caplen is nonzero or that p+1 leaves that many captured bytes. Trigger: a truncated Juniper ATM1 frame whose first byte is 0x03 reaches the ISO CLNS parser. Consequence: isoclns_print performs bounds checks against an overstated capture length and reads past the end of the packet buffer (CWE-125).

commit_msg:
Add missing validations in dillation ops.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 372037158
Change-Id: I4ee304c84a02550c030288a6534000b934fc1599
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            filter_backprop(h_max, w_max, d) +=', '                out_backprop(b, h_out, w_out, d);'], 'added_lines': ['            if (h_max < filter_rows && w_max < filter_cols) {', '              filter_backprop(h_max, w_max, d) +=', '                  out_backprop(b, h_out, w_out, d);', '            }']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can write outside the bounds of heap allocated arrays by passing invalid arguments to `tf.raw_ops.Dilation2DBackpropInput`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/afd954e65f15aea4d438d0a219136fc4a63a573d/tensorflow/core/kernels/dilation_ops.cc#L321-L322) does not validate before writing to the output array. The values for `h_out` and `w_out` are guaranteed to be in range for `out_backprop` (as they are loop indices bounded by the size of the array). However, there are no similar guarantees relating `h_in_max`/`w_in_max` and `in_backprop`. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: h_max and w_max are initialized to 0 and only reassigned inside the val > cur_val branch; if no valid (h_in, w_in) position qualifies, they retain 0 or stale values rather than a guaranteed in-range filter index.

The comparison and assignments to h_max/w_max occur only when the input coordinate passes the bounds checks at lines 27 and 30; otherwise no valid filter position is recorded for this output/depth iteration.

The write filter_backprop(h_max, w_max, d) += ... uses h_max/w_max as indices into the filter-sized buffer without validating them against filter_rows/filter_cols, so invalid argument combinations can produce out-of-range indices.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes through unvalidated indices past the intended filter_backprop buffer bounds. It is a direct out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
int h_max = 0;
int w_max = 0;

filter_backprop(h_max, w_max, d) +=
out_backprop(b, h_out, w_out, d);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the computed filter indices h_max/w_max are used to index filter_backprop without a range check against filter_rows/filter_cols. Trigger: invalid stride/rate/padding arguments cause no valid input position to be selected, leaving h_max/w_max unbounded relative to the filter. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap write to filter_backprop, corrupting memory.

commit_msg:
Use specified ciphers for outgoing STARTLS connections

Perdition(8) says:

        --ssl_outgoing_ciphers STRING:

              Cipher list when making outgoing SSL or TLS connections as
              per ciphers(1). If empty ("") then openssl's default will
              be used.  (default "")

However, this is only the case for outgoing connections that do not use
STARTTLS (the perdition terminology is confusing here, since what it
calls "TLS" actually means "start as cleartext, negotiate to encrypted
via STARTTLS" and what it calls "SSL" actually means "start SSL or TLS
session, run service inside that").


This is a security concern because it means that perdition is not
obeying the specifications of the administrator, and may accept weaker
ciphersuites than instructed on its backhaul connections.

Consider the case where an administrator wants to offer relatively
promiscuous IMAP connections to their end users -- if the user's MUA
only has some weak cipher suite or cleartext IMAP, we want to accept the
weak ciphersuite as better than nothing.  However, the admin's backend
IMAP servers are all under her control, and she knows that they are
capable of stronger ciphersuites.  in this case, ssl_listen_ciphers will
allow weak ciphers, and ssl_outgoing_ciphers will be strict and require
high security, to at least protect the link between perdition and the
backend IMAP server.

However, if this outgoing connection happens to use IMAP+STARTTLS
instead of IMAPS, the bug described here will offer weak ciphersuites to
the backend IMAP server.

This is CVE-2013-4584
This is Debian Bug #729028

Signed-off-by: Simon Horman <horms@verge.net.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t      opt.ssl_ca_path, opt.ssl_listen_ciphers, servername);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t      opt.ssl_ca_path, opt.ssl_outgoing_ciphers, servername);']}
description: Perdition before 2.2 may have weak security when handling outbound connections, caused by an error in the STARTTLS IMAP and POP server. ssl_outgoing_ciphers not being applied to STARTTLS connections

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function is a large main() whose only relevant change swaps ssl_listen_ciphers for ssl_outgoing_ciphers; nothing in the function demonstrates improper handling of an exceptional condition, so the function does not support CWE-755.

commit_msg:
check_chain_extensions: Do not override error return value by check_curve

The X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT flag enables additional security checks of the
certificates present in a certificate chain. It is not set by default.

Starting from OpenSSL version 1.1.1h a check to disallow certificates with
explicitly encoded elliptic curve parameters in the chain was added to the
strict checks.

An error in the implementation of this check meant that the result of a
previous check to confirm that certificates in the chain are valid CA
certificates was overwritten. This effectively bypasses the check
that non-CA certificates must not be able to issue other certificates.

If a "purpose" has been configured then a subsequent check that the
certificate is consistent with that purpose also checks that it is a
valid CA. Therefore where a purpose is set the certificate chain will
still be rejected even when the strict flag has been used. A purpose is
set by default in libssl client and server certificate verification
routines, but it can be overriden by an application.

Affected applications explicitly set the X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT
verification flag and either do not set a purpose for the certificate
verification or, in the case of TLS client or server applications,
override the default purpose to make it not set.

CVE-2021-3450

Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if ((ctx->param->flags & X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT) && num > 1) {', '            if (ret < 0)', '            else if (ret == 0)', '        if ((x->ex_flags & EXFLAG_CA) == 0'], 'added_lines': ['        if (ret > 0', '            && (ctx->param->flags & X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT) && num > 1) {', '            if (ret < 0) {', '                ret = 0;', '            } else if (ret == 0) {', '            }', '        if (ret > 0', '            && (x->ex_flags & EXFLAG_CA) == 0']}
description: The X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT flag enables additional security checks of the certificates present in a certificate chain. It is not set by default. Starting from OpenSSL version 1.1.1h a check to disallow certificates in the chain that have explicitly encoded elliptic curve parameters was added as an additional strict check. An error in the implementation of this check meant that the result of a previous check to confirm that certificates in the chain are valid CA certificates was overwritten. This effectively bypasses the check that non-CA certificates must not be able to issue other certificates. If a "purpose" has been configured then there is a subsequent opportunity for checks that the certificate is a valid CA. All of the named "purpose" values implemented in libcrypto perform this check. Therefore, where a purpose is set the certificate chain will still be rejected even when the strict flag has been used. A purpose is set by default in libssl client and server certificate verification routines, but it can be overridden or removed by an application. In order to be affected, an application must explicitly set the X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT verification flag and either not set a purpose for the certificate verification or, in the case of TLS client or server applications, override the default purpose. OpenSSL versions 1.1.1h and newer are affected by this issue. Users of these versions should upgrade to OpenSSL 1.1.1k. OpenSSL 1.0.2 is not impacted by this issue. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1k (Affected 1.1.1h-1.1.1j).

code_evidence: Under X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT with num > 1, check_curve(x) overwrites the prior ret from the must_be_ca switch; the error paths (ret<0, ret==0) set ctx->error but do not force ret to a failing value.

The subsequent ret==0 gate at line 72 is the only point where verify_cb_cert is invoked, so a non-failing ret from check_curve lets an earlier INVALID_CA/INVALID_NON_CA result pass through as success.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the certificate-chain validation routine, and the flaw causes a CA-validity check result to be lost, so an invalid chain is accepted. This is improper certificate validation (CWE-295); it is not merely an unchecked return value, since the defect is that the certificate validation decision is incorrectly computed and trusted.

evidence_lines.code:
if (ret == 0 && !verify_cb_cert(ctx, x, i, X509_V_OK))
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the strict-mode curve check reuses the ret variable holding the CA-validity result and overwrites it with check_curve's return, so a successful curve check discards a prior failed CA check. Trigger: a chain where a non-CA certificate issues another certificate, with X509_V_FLAG_X509_STRICT set and num > 1. Consequence: the INVALID_CA/INVALID_NON_CA failure is not propagated and the chain is accepted, bypassing certificate validation.

commit_msg:
epan: Fix a memory leak.

Make sure _proto_tree_add_bits_ret_val allocates a bits array using the
packet scope, otherwise we leak memory. Fixes #17032.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tbytes = tvb_get_bits_array(NULL, tvb, bit_offset, no_of_bits, &bytes_length);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tbytes = tvb_get_bits_array(wmem_packet_scope(), tvb, bit_offset, no_of_bits, &bytes_length);']}
description: Memory leak in the dissection engine in Wireshark 3.4.0 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file.

code_evidence: In the FT_BYTES case, line 99 calls tvb_get_bits_array with a NULL scope, so the allocated bits array is not tied to any wmem scope and has no owner to release it. Line 100 passes that buffer to proto_tree_add_bytes_with_length, but the function never frees bytes afterward.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the function allocates memory that is not released after its effective lifetime, matching a missing-release weakness with availability impact. It is not a buffer overflow or use-after-free; the buffer is used correctly but never reclaimed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the temporary bit array is allocated with no wmem scope, so no lifetime manages it. Trigger: dissection of an FT_BYTES field with no_of_bits > 64 reaches this branch for each packet. Consequence: the allocation is never released, leaking memory per packet and enabling resource-consumption denial of service via crafted capture files or injected packets.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4968: reading past end of the line when C-indenting

Problem:    Reading past end of the line when C-indenting.
Solution:   Check for NUL.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["\t    if (p[i] == '\\'')\t\t    // check for trailing '"], 'added_lines': ["\t    if (p[i - 1] != NUL && p[i] == '\\'')    // check for trailing '"]}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.4968.

code_evidence: After an escaped quote, i is advanced past a backslash and any digits; the code then reads p[i] without ensuring that position lies within the NUL-terminated string. The patch guards this by checking p[i - 1] != NUL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences past the end of a heap-allocated buffer, matching CWE-122 (heap-based buffer overflow). It is an out-of-bounds read rather than an out-of-bounds write, so a plain 'buffer overflow' label is less precise.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the index i can point at or beyond the terminating NUL (for example a trailing backslash or digit run at end of line), yet p[i] is dereferenced unconditionally. Trigger: C-indenting a line ending in an incomplete quoted or escaped sequence. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read past the end of the heap-allocated line buffer.

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Fix leak in SNDRV_TIMER_IOCTL_PARAMS

The stack object “tread” has a total size of 32 bytes. Its field
“event” and “val” both contain 4 bytes padding. These 8 bytes
padding bytes are sent to user without being initialized.

Signed-off-by: Kangjie Lu <kjlu@gatech.edu>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tmemset(&tread, 0, sizeof(tread));']}
description: The snd_timer_user_params function in sound/core/timer.c in the Linux kernel through 4.6 does not initialize a certain data structure, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel stack memory via crafted use of the ALSA timer interface.

code_evidence: A stack-allocated struct snd_timer_tread tread is declared at line 79 without initialization; only event, tstamp.tv_sec, tstamp.tv_nsec and val are assigned (80-83), leaving the padding bytes in the event/val fields uninitialized. The whole struct, including padding, is then passed to snd_timer_user_append_to_tqueue at line 84, which queues it for user consumption.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly transfers a partially initialized structure containing uninitialized padding into a user-accessible queue, exposing kernel stack data to an unauthorized local actor. This is a direct information exposure matching CWE-200, not merely an indirect confidentiality impact of another primitive.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the tread stack object is partially initialized and its uninitialized padding is copied into the timer event queue that is readable by user space. Trigger: a local user enables the early-event flag and tread mode via SNDRV_TIMER_IOCTL_PARAMS, causing this branch to run. Consequence: kernel stack memory contents are disclosed to the user, a confidentiality loss.

commit_msg:
During shutdown the IOAPIC trigger mode is reset to edge triggered
while the vfio-pci INTx is still registered with a resampler.
This allows us to get into an infinite loop:

ioapic_set_irq
  -> ioapic_lazy_update_eoi
  -> kvm_ioapic_update_eoi_one
  -> kvm_notify_acked_irq
  -> kvm_notify_acked_gsi
  -> (via irq_acked fn ptr) irqfd_resampler_ack
  -> kvm_set_irq
  -> (via set fn ptr) kvm_set_ioapic_irq
  -> kvm_ioapic_set_irq
  -> ioapic_set_irq

Commit 8be8f932e3db ("kvm: ioapic: Restrict lazy EOI update to
edge-triggered interrupts", 2020-05-04) acknowledges that this recursion
loop exists and tries to avoid it at the call to ioapic_lazy_update_eoi,
but at this point the scenario is already set, we have an edge interrupt
with resampler on the same gsi.

Fortunately, the only user of irq ack notifiers (in addition to resamplefd)
is i8254 timer interrupt reinjection.  These are edge-triggered, so in
principle they would need the call to kvm_ioapic_update_eoi_one from
ioapic_lazy_update_eoi, but they already disable AVIC(*), so they don't
need the lazy EOI behavior.  Therefore, remove the call to
kvm_ioapic_update_eoi_one from ioapic_lazy_update_eoi.

This fixes CVE-2020-27152.  Note that this issue cannot happen with
SR-IOV assigned devices because virtual functions do not have INTx,
only MSI.

Fixes: f458d039db7e ("kvm: ioapic: Lazy update IOAPIC EOI")
Suggested-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Alex Williamson <alex.williamson@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Vitaly Kuznetsov <vkuznets@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t * EOI for this vetor.', '\t\tkvm_ioapic_update_eoi_one(vcpu, ioapic,', '\t\t\t\t\t  entry->fields.trig_mode,', '\t\t\t\t\t  irq);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t * EOI for this vector.']}
description: An issue was discovered in ioapic_lazy_update_eoi in arch/x86/kvm/ioapic.c in the Linux kernel before 5.9.2. It has an infinite loop related to improper interaction between a resampler and edge triggering, aka CID-77377064c3a9.

code_evidence: The kvm_for_each_vcpu loop skips vCPUs that do not match the destination or have a pending EOI, then calls rtc_irq_eoi and kvm_ioapic_update_eoi_one for the matching vCPU. kvm_ioapic_update_eoi_one passes entry->fields.trig_mode and irq onward, which can invoke the resampler ack path that re-enters ioapic_set_irq and returns here while the entry is still edge-triggered, so the loop body never terminates.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the kvm_for_each_vcpu iteration cannot reach its exit condition: the re-entrant EOI path keeps the loop active via the resampler, producing an infinite loop. This is a reachability/termination flaw rather than a memory-safety issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ioapic_lazy_update_eoi re-enters EOI notification for an edge-triggered entry still registered with a resampler. The trigger is an INTx ack that reaches this function after trigger-mode reset during shutdown; the resampler callback re-queues the interrupt, causing unbounded recursion and CPU consumption (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix #78559: Heap buffer overflow in mb_eregi

We backport kkos/oniguruma@d3e402928b6eb3327f8f7d59a9edfa622fec557b.

Lines 70-71 derive src_offset = row * img_rowsize + col_offset from that too-small stride, placing later rows earlier than their real positions.
Line 75 copies full_bytes from src_buff + src_offset, so the undersized stride shifts the read bound.
Lines 85-87 compute offset1/offset2 from the same img_rowsize stride for the sub-byte branch.
Line 108 copies full_bytes from src_buff + offset1 using the wrong stride.
Lines 145-149 index src_buff[offset1 + j] and src_buff[offset1 + j + 1] up to full_bytes+1 using the incorrect row base.

row_offset = row * img_rowsize;
src_offset = row_offset + col_offset;
_TIFFmemcpy (sect_buff + dst_offset, src_buff + src_offset, full_bytes);
_TIFFmemcpy (sect_buff + dst_offset, src_buff + offset1, full_bytes);

commit_msg:
floppy_revalidate() doesn't perform any error handling on lock_fdc()
result. lock_fdc() might actually be interrupted by a signal (it waits for
fdc becoming non-busy interruptibly). In such case, floppy_revalidate()
proceeds as if it had claimed the lock, but it fact it doesn't.

In case of multiple threads trying to open("/dev/fdX"), this leads to
serious corruptions all over the place, because all of a sudden there is
no critical section protection (that'd otherwise be guaranteed by locked
fd) whatsoever.

While at this, fix the fact that the 'interruptible' parameter to
lock_fdc() doesn't make any sense whatsoever, because we always wait
interruptibly anyway.

Most of the lock_fdc() callsites do properly handle error (and propagate
EINTR), but floppy_revalidate() and floppy_check_events() don't. Fix this.

Spotted by 'syzkaller' tool.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (lock_fdc(drive, true))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (lock_fdc(drive))']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernels implementation of the floppy disk drive controller driver software. The impact of this issue is lessened by the fact that the default permissions on the floppy device (/dev/fd0) are restricted to root. If the permissions on the device have changed the impact changes greatly. In the default configuration root (or equivalent) permissions are required to attack this flaw.

code_evidence: do_format() calls lock_fdc(drive, true) and returns -EINTR when it fails, so it does check the lock result. The lock is interruptible; when interrupted, the function returns before set_floppy(), so no unprotected critical section is entered here. The diff only drops the redundant 'interruptible' argument; the error check on line 4 remains.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 requires a concurrent sequence missing exclusive access to a shared resource. Here lock_fdc() failure is detected and the function returns, so the shared fdc state is not used without the lock; the race described in the commit is not supported by this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The target race involves a caller proceeding without the fdc lock after an interrupted lock_fdc(). In do_format() the lock failure is handled by returning -EINTR, so the unprotected critical-section path described in the commit is not present in this function. The changed argument only removes a redundant parameter.

description: compile in regexp.c in Artifex MuJS through 1.2.0 results in stack consumption because of unlimited recursion, a different issue than CVE-2019-11413.

code_evidence: count() recurses unconditionally into node->x and node->y for P_CAT/P_ALT without any depth bound.
P_REP also recurses into node->x with no depth limit; only the computed program size n is checked against REG_MAXPROG afterward.
P_PAR/P_PLA/P_NLA likewise recurse into node->x without tracking recursion depth.

case P_ALT: return count(g, node->x) + count(g, node->y) + 2;

Trigger: compiling a crafted regexp whose Renode tree is deep enough. Consequence: stack exhaustion/overflow during regexp compilation, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
If the server sends a reply in which even the first string would
overflow the transmitted bytes, list[0] (or flist[0]) will be set to
NULL and a count of 0 is returned.

If the resulting list is freed with XFreeExtensionList or
XFreeFontPath later on, the first Xfree call:

    Xfree (list[0]-1)
 turns into
    Xfree (NULL-1)

which will most likely trigger a segmentation fault.

I have modified the code to return NULL if the first string would
overflow, thus protecting the freeing functions later on.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t} else if (i == 0) {', '\t\t    Xfree(flist);', '\t\t    Xfree(ch);', '\t\t    flist = NULL;', '\t\t    break;']}
description: An issue was discovered in XListExtensions in ListExt.c in libX11 through 1.6.5. A malicious server can send a reply in which the first string overflows, causing a variable to be set to NULL that will be freed later on, leading to DoS (segmentation fault).

code_evidence: The reply length rep.length from the server is used to size the buffer: nbytes = rep.length << 2 and ch = Xmalloc(nbytes + 1); only the overflow of the shift itself is guarded, not the consistency of the string data inside the buffer.

The first string length is read from the buffer (length = *(unsigned char *)ch), then the loop checks ch + length < chend; for i == 0 a too-long first string falls into the else branch and sets flist[0] = NULL without freeing the allocated list.
count is only incremented for accepted strings, so *npaths = count does not reflect the NULL first entry, and the partially-initialized flist is returned to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the defect is missing validation of untrusted server reply data (the string length versus available bytes) before it is used to build the returned list; the crash is the downstream consequence of that unvalidated input, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code: *npaths = count;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the server-supplied reply layout and does not validate that the first string length fits within nbytes before accepting it. Trigger: a malicious server sends a reply whose first string length overflows the transmitted bytes; flist[0] becomes NULL while the list is still returned. Consequence: callers such as XFreeFontPath later free list[0]-1, dereferencing NULL-1 and causing a segmentation fault (DoS).

commit_msg:
Add guest mode functionality (3/3)

Add a flag to enable() to start Bluetooth in restricted
mode. In restricted mode, all devices that are paired during
restricted mode are deleted upon leaving restricted mode.
Right now restricted mode is only entered while a guest
user is active.

Bug: 27410683
Change-Id: If4a8855faf362d7f6de509d7ddc7197d1ac75cee
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static jboolean enableNative(JNIEnv* env, jobject obj) {', '', '    int ret = sBluetoothInterface->enable();'], 'added_lines': ['static jboolean enableNative(JNIEnv* env, jobject obj, jboolean isGuest) {', '    int ret = sBluetoothInterface->enable(isGuest == JNI_TRUE ? 1 : 0);']}
description: Bluetooth in Android 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-07-01 allows local users to gain privileges by establishing a pairing that remains present during a session of the primary user, aka internal bug 27410683.

code_evidence: enableNative forwards the caller-supplied isGuest flag to sBluetoothInterface->enable() as 1 or 0, selecting restricted (guest) mode for the Bluetooth service. The function performs no synchronization and does not verify whether the guest-mode transition is coordinated with the primary user's existing pairing state. The return value only maps BT_STATUS_SUCCESS/DONE to JNI_TRUE and carries no information about the mode actually applied.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a timing/atomicity violation over a shared resource (the paired-device set and enable state) because the mode change and pairing operations are not mutually exclusive, matching CWE-362's improper synchronization definition. It is not merely a missing authorization check (CWE-862) since the flaw depends on concurrent access ordering.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guest-mode flag is passed to the interface without any lock, state check, or atomic transition relative to the paired-device set shared with the primary user's session. Trigger: a local user initiates pairing while a guest-mode enable is in flight or while the primary user session is active. Consequence: the pairing is not removed when restricted mode ends, allowing the local user to retain elevated pairing privileges.

commit_msg:
passthrough: quarantine PCI devices

When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for
that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The
IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that
the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However,
when the guest domain is torn down the device is assigned back to dom0,
thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data.

This patch introduces a 'quarantine' for PCI devices using dom_io. When
the toolstack makes a device assignable (by binding it to pciback), it
will now also assign it to DOMID_IO and the device will only be assigned
back to dom0 when the device is made unassignable again. Whilst device is
assignable it will only ever transfer between dom_io and guest domains.
dom_io is actually only used as a sentinel domain for quarantining purposes;
it is not configured with any IOMMU mappings. Assignment to dom_io simply
means that the device's initiator (requestor) identifier is not present in
the IOMMU's device table and thus any DMA transactions issued will be
terminated with a fault condition.

In addition, a fix to assignment handling is made for VT-d.  Failure
during the assignment step should not lead to a device still being
associated with its prior owner. Hand the device to DomIO temporarily,
until the assignment step has completed successfully.  Remove the PI
hooks from the source domain then earlier as well.

Failure of the recovery reassign_device_ownership() may not go silent:
There e.g. may still be left over RMRR mappings in the domain assignment
to which has failed, and hence we can't allow that domain to continue
executing.

NOTE: This patch also includes one printk() cleanup; the
      "XEN_DOMCTL_assign_device: " tag is dropped in iommu_do_pci_domctl(),
      since similar printk()-s elsewhere also don't log such a tag.

This is XSA-302.

Signed-off-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( ret )'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( ret || is_system_domain(d) )']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing attackers to gain host OS privileges via DMA in a situation where an untrusted domain has access to a physical device. This occurs because passed through PCI devices may corrupt host memory after deassignment. When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However, when the guest domain is torn down, or the device is deassigned, the device is assigned back to dom0, thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data. An untrusted domain with access to a physical device can DMA into host memory, leading to privilege escalation. Only systems where guests are given direct access to physical devices capable of DMA (PCI pass-through) are vulnerable. Systems which do not use PCI pass-through are not vulnerable.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function is Xen IOMMU domain initialization; it contains no OS command construction or execution, so it cannot support CWE-78.

commit_msg:
drbg: ensure fork-safety without using a pthread_atfork handler

When the new OpenSSL CSPRNG was introduced in version 1.1.1,
it was announced in the release notes that it would be fork-safe,
which the old CSPRNG hadn't been.

The fork-safety was implemented using a fork count, which was
incremented by a pthread_atfork handler. Initially, this handler
was enabled by default. Unfortunately, the default behaviour
had to be changed for other reasons in commit b5319bdbd095, so
the new OpenSSL CSPRNG failed to keep its promise.

This commit restores the fork-safety using a different approach.
It replaces the fork count by a fork id, which coincides with
the process id on UNIX-like operating systems and is zero on other
operating systems. It is used to detect when an automatic reseed
after a fork is necessary.

To prevent a future regression, it also adds a test to verify that
the child reseeds after fork.

CVE-2019-1549

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <paul.dale@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/9802)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (drbg->fork_count != rand_fork_count) {', '        drbg->fork_count = rand_fork_count;'], 'added_lines': ['    int fork_id;', '    fork_id = openssl_get_fork_id();', '', '    if (drbg->fork_id != fork_id) {', '        drbg->fork_id = fork_id;']}
description: OpenSSL 1.1.1 introduced a rewritten random number generator (RNG). This was intended to include protection in the event of a fork() system call in order to ensure that the parent and child processes did not share the same RNG state. However this protection was not being used in the default case. A partial mitigation for this issue is that the output from a high precision timer is mixed into the RNG state so the likelihood of a parent and child process sharing state is significantly reduced. If an application already calls OPENSSL_init_crypto() explicitly using OPENSSL_INIT_ATFORK then this problem does not occur at all. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1d (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1c).

code_evidence: The function decides whether to reseed the DRBG by comparing drbg->fork_count against the global rand_fork_count; reseed_required is set only when these differ.
If reseed_required is false and prediction_resistance is false, RAND_DRBG_reseed is not called and drbg->meth->generate produces output from the existing state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is a reseed decision that fails to detect a forked process, causing reuse of insufficiently fresh random state; this directly matches CWE-330, use of insufficiently random values. It is not merely a state-management bug because the supported consequence is predictable/correlated RNG output.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The fork-detection relies on a fork count that is not incremented by default (the atfork handler is disabled), so a child process after fork() can retain the parent's DRBG state: fork_count equals rand_fork_count, reseed_required stays 0, and the child generates output without reseeding. The consequence is that parent and child may emit identical or correlated random values, weakening security contexts depending on unpredictability.

commit_msg:
Add recursion limit for ASN.1 indefinite lengths

The libkrb5 ASN.1 decoder supports BER indefinite lengths.  It
computes the tag length using recursion; the lack of a recursion limit
allows an attacker to overrun the stack and cause the process to
crash.  Reported by Demi Obenour.

CVE-2020-28196:

In MIT krb5 releases 1.11 and later, an unauthenticated attacker can
cause a denial of service for any client or server to which it can
send an ASN.1-encoded Kerberos message of sufficient length.

ticket: 8959 (new)
tags: pullup
target_version: 1.18-next
target_version: 1.17-next
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        const uint8_t **remainder_out, size_t *rlen_out)', '            ret = get_tag(p, len, &t, &c, &clen, &p, &len);'], 'added_lines': ['        const uint8_t **remainder_out, size_t *rlen_out, int recursion)', '        if (recursion >= 32)', '            return ASN1_OVERFLOW;', '            ret = get_tag(p, len, &t, &c, &clen, &p, &len, recursion + 1);']}
description: MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) before 1.17.2 and 1.18.x before 1.18.3 allows unbounded recursion via an ASN.1-encoded Kerberos message because the lib/krb5/asn.1/asn1_encode.c support for BER indefinite lengths lacks a recursion limit.

code_evidence: For an indefinite-length tag (o == 0x80 on line 35), the function enters a loop that recursively calls get_tag on the remaining buffer (line 40) for each nested element until a two-byte zero terminator is found; there is no recursion-depth counter or bound on nesting depth.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 covers missing recursion control leading to stack/resource exhaustion. The recursive get_tag call at line 40 is bounded only by input structure, and the patch's added recursion >= 32 check confirms the missing constraint; this is uncontrolled recursion, not merely a length-overflow issue (CWE-674 fits over CWE-787).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the indefinite-length BER branch recursively parses nested constructed elements with no depth limit. Trigger: an unauthenticated attacker supplies an ASN.1-encoded Kerberos message containing deeply nested indefinite-length constructed tags. Consequence: unbounded recursion consumes the program stack, crashing the process (denial of service).

commit_msg:
perf: Fix race in swevent hash

There's a race on CPU unplug where we free the swevent hash array
while it can still have events on. This will result in a
use-after-free which is BAD.

Simply do not free the hash array on unplug. This leaves the thing
around and no use-after-free takes place.

When the last swevent dies, we do a for_each_possible_cpu() iteration
anyway to clean these up, at which time we'll free it, so no leakage
will occur.

Reported-by: Sasha Levin <sasha.levin@oracle.com>
Tested-by: Sasha Levin <sasha.levin@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Arnaldo Carvalho de Melo <acme@redhat.com>
Cc: Frederic Weisbecker <fweisbec@gmail.com>
Cc: Jiri Olsa <jolsa@redhat.com>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Stephane Eranian <eranian@google.com>
Cc: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: Vince Weaver <vincent.weaver@maine.edu>
Signed-off-by: Ingo Molnar <mingo@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct swevent_htable *swhash = &per_cpu(swevent_htable, cpu);', '', '', '\tmutex_lock(&swhash->hlist_mutex);', '\tswhash->online = false;', '\tswevent_hlist_release(swhash);', '\tmutex_unlock(&swhash->hlist_mutex);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: Race condition in kernel/events/core.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (use-after-free) by leveraging incorrect handling of an swevent data structure during a CPU unplug operation.

code_evidence: Under hlist_mutex, the function marks swhash->online = false and then calls swevent_hlist_release(swhash), freeing the per-CPU swevent hash while the CPU is being unplugged. The mutex only serializes this path against itself, not against concurrent swevent event processing that may still hold references to the hash.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a release of a shared resource (swevent hash) without ensuring exclusive access against concurrent interfering code sequences, which is precisely a race condition violating exclusivity/atomicity (CWE-362). The use-after-free is the downstream consequence, not the weakness category itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the CPU-exit path frees the per-CPU swevent hash even though concurrent swevent code may still access it. Trigger: CPU unplug races with swevent events on that CPU. Consequence: use-after-free of the swevent hash, leading to crash, privilege escalation, or DoS.

commit_msg:
jpeg: Fix another possible buffer overrun

Found via the clang libfuzzer
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                block_length = data[i] * 256 + data[i+1];'], 'added_lines': ['                if (i + 1 < data_size)', '                    block_length = data[i] * 256 + data[i+1];']}
description: jpeg_size in pdfgen.c in PDFGen before 2018-04-09 has a heap-based buffer over-read.

code_evidence: The while loop is guarded only by i<data_size. After i+=block_length and the check (i+1)>=data_size, the code reads data[i], data[i+1], and for 0xC0 reads data[i+5]..data[i+8] without verifying those indices are within data_size. Line 24 then reads data[i] and data[i+1] after only i+=2, with no bound check before dereferencing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the supplied data buffer due to missing bounds validation, which is exactly CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). The patch adds an i+1<data_size guard before the line 24 read, confirming the out-of-bounds read; this is not a write (CWE-787) or integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing upper-bound checks on indices derived from attacker-controlled block_length and i before multiple data[] reads. Trigger: a crafted JPEG whose block_length advances i near data_size, or whose 0xC0 marker occurs near the buffer end. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read of up to several bytes past data_size, potentially leaking adjacent memory or crashing.

commit_msg: core(persistence): add more checks for implementation limitations
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                        if( i >= CV_FS_MAX_LEN )', '                            CV_PARSE_ERROR_CPP( "Too long string literal" );'], 'added_lines': ['                                        if (len + 2 + i >= CV_FS_MAX_LEN)', '                                            CV_PARSE_ERROR_CPP("string is too long");', '                        if (i + 1 >= CV_FS_MAX_LEN)', '                            CV_PARSE_ERROR_CPP("Too long string literal");']}
description: An exploitable heap buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the data structure persistence functionality of OpenCV, before version 4.2.0. A specially crafted JSON file can cause a buffer overflow, resulting in multiple heap corruptions and potentially code execution. An attacker can provide a specially crafted file to trigger this vulnerability.

code_evidence: At line 163, memcpy copies len + 2 bytes into strbuf + i, then i is advanced by len + 2; the length check only occurs afterward at line 172, so the copy can exceed CV_FS_MAX_LEN.
Line 171 writes strbuf[i++] before the bounds check on line 172, allowing a one-byte out-of-bounds write when i is already at the limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of the strbuf array, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write; the missing pre-write length constraint is the direct cause, not merely a parsing error.

evidence_lines.code:
memcpy( strbuf + i, ptr-1, len + 2 );
i += len + 2;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the fixed-size strbuf is written before validating that the write fits. A crafted entity name (long symbol) or accumulated string length makes i + len + 2 or i exceed CV_FS_MAX_LEN, overflowing the heap buffer. Trigger: parsing a malicious string literal in a file. Consequence: heap corruption and potential code execution.

commit_msg: fixes https://github.com/nu774/fdkaac/issues/55
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (count < 0)', '        return -1;']}
description: fdkaac before 1.0.5 was discovered to contain a stack overflow in read_callback function in src/main.c.

code_evidence: Line 3 declares a fixed 8192-byte stack buffer. Line 6 returns early only when count==0 or pcm_seek succeeds, so a negative count falls through. Line 9 passes count to vp->read as the size argument (count > 8192 ? 8192 : count); with negative count the ternary yields the negative value, and the read callback writes into buff based on that size, overflowing the stack buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the write length derived from an unchecked negative count causes a write beyond the buffer's bounds. It is not merely an integer issue; the integer value directly produces an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the fallback path lacks a lower-bound check on the signed count before using it as a read length into a fixed stack buffer. Trigger: a negative count reaching pcm_skip with a failing seek. Consequence: the callback writes past buff, causing stack memory corruption (the issue's stack overflow).

commit_msg:
module: Fix NULL vs IS_ERR checking for module_get_next_page

The module_get_next_page() function return error pointers on error
instead of NULL.
Use IS_ERR() to check the return value to fix this.

Fixes: b1ae6dc41eaa ("module: add in-kernel support for decompressing")
Signed-off-by: Miaoqian Lin <linmq006@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Dmitry Torokhov <dmitry.torokhov@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Luis Chamberlain <mcgrof@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!page) {', '\t\t\tretval = -ENOMEM;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (IS_ERR(page)) {', '\t\t\tretval = PTR_ERR(page);']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 6.1.2, kernel/module/decompress.c misinterprets the module_get_next_page return value (expects it to be NULL in the error case, whereas it is actually an error pointer).

code_evidence: module_get_next_page() returns an error pointer on failure, but line 27 tests only for NULL; an error pointer such as ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM) passes the check.
Line 31 then passes that error pointer to kmap_local_page() and line 32 sets avail_out, treating the invalid pointer as a valid page.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses an unchecked/incorrectly checked pointer that is not valid in the error path and then dereferences it, matching CWE-476's invalid-pointer dereference. The defect is the wrong error test, distinct from a plain missing allocation check.

evidence_lines.code:
s.next_out = kmap_local_page(page);
s.avail_out = PAGE_SIZE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error return of module_get_next_page() is validated with a NULL test instead of IS_ERR(), so error-pointer values are not recognized as failures. Trigger: allocation failure inside module_get_next_page(). Consequence: the error pointer is dereferenced/used as a page via kmap_local_page(), leading to invalid memory access and a crash (DoS).

Fixes: out of array read
Fixes: poc-2017.avi

description: The decode_frame function in libavcodec/utvideodec.c in FFmpeg through 3.2 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out of array read) via a crafted AVI file.

commit_msg:
settings: Make the keyfile backend parameterless

Make it possible to instantiate a keyfile settings backend
without specifying parameters, by turning the arguments to
the new() function into construct-only properties. If no
filename is specified, default to
$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/glib-2.0/settings/keyfile
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  GKeyfileSettingsBackend *kfsb;', '', '  kfsb = g_object_new (G_TYPE_KEYFILE_SETTINGS_BACKEND, NULL);', '  kfsb->keyfile = g_key_file_new ();', '  kfsb->permission = g_simple_permission_new (TRUE);', '', '  kfsb->file = g_file_new_for_path (filename);', '  kfsb->dir = g_file_get_parent (kfsb->file);', '  g_file_make_directory_with_parents (kfsb->dir, NULL, NULL);', '', '  kfsb->file_monitor = g_file_monitor (kfsb->file, 0, NULL, NULL);', '  kfsb->dir_monitor = g_file_monitor (kfsb->dir, 0, NULL, NULL);', '', '  kfsb->prefix_len = strlen (root_path);', '  kfsb->prefix = g_strdup (root_path);', '', '  if (root_group)', '    {', '      kfsb->root_group_len = strlen (root_group);', '      kfsb->root_group = g_strdup (root_group);', '    }', '', '  compute_checksum (kfsb->digest, NULL, 0);', '', '  g_signal_connect (kfsb->file_monitor, "changed",', '                    G_CALLBACK (file_changed), kfsb);', '  g_signal_connect (kfsb->dir_monitor, "changed",', '                    G_CALLBACK (dir_changed), kfsb);', '', '  g_keyfile_settings_backend_keyfile_writable (kfsb);', '  g_keyfile_settings_backend_keyfile_reload (kfsb);', '', '  return G_SETTINGS_BACKEND (kfsb);'], 'added_lines': ['  return G_SETTINGS_BACKEND (g_object_new (G_TYPE_KEYFILE_SETTINGS_BACKEND,', '                                           "filename", filename,', '                                           "root-path", root_path,', '                                           "root-group", root_group,', '                                           NULL));']}
description: The keyfile settings backend in GNOME GLib (aka glib2.0) before 2.60.0 creates directories using g_file_make_directory_with_parents (kfsb->dir, NULL, NULL) and files using g_file_replace_contents (kfsb->file, contents, length, NULL, FALSE, G_FILE_CREATE_REPLACE_DESTINATION, NULL, NULL, NULL). Consequently, it does not properly restrict directory (and file) permissions. Instead, for directories, 0777 permissions are used; for files, default file permissions are used. This is similar to CVE-2019-12450.

code_evidence: g_file_new_for_path(filename) and g_file_get_parent build the settings file and its directory from the caller-supplied path. g_file_make_directory_with_parents(kfsb->dir, NULL, NULL) then creates the directory tree without any permissions argument, so the backend never constrains who can access the configuration directory it creates.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-732 covers assigning permissions to a security-critical resource that grant access to a wider set of actors than required. Here the settings directory is created with default 0777 permissions instead of owner-only, matching incorrect permission assignment; this is a permission-assignment flaw, not a missing authorization check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the backend creates its configuration directory via g_file_make_directory_with_parents with NULL permission arguments, leaving directory mode at the permissive default (0777) rather than restricting it to the owner. Trigger: any caller instantiating the keyfile backend with a filename whose parent directory does not yet exist. Consequence: the directory, and files later written into it, may be readable or writable by unintended local actors, exposing or allowing modification of settings data.

commit_msg:
Fixed memory overrun bug in gdImageScaleTwoPass

_gdContributionsCalc would compute a window size and then adjust
the left and right positions of the window to make a window within
that size.  However, it was storing the values in the struct *before*
it made the adjustment.  This change fixes that.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tres->ContribRow[u].Left = iLeft;', '\t\tres->ContribRow[u].Right = iRight;', ''], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\tres->ContribRow[u].Left = iLeft;', '\t\tres->ContribRow[u].Right = iRight;']}
description: gd_interpolation.c in the GD Graphics Library (aka libgd) before 2.1.1, as used in PHP before 5.5.36, 5.6.x before 5.6.22, and 7.x before 7.0.7, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted image that is mishandled by the imagescale function.

code_evidence: Lines 23-24 store the unclamped iLeft and iRight into res->ContribRow[u] before any window adjustment.
Lines 25-31 then shrink the window when iRight - iLeft + 1 exceeds windows_size, but only the local iLeft/iRight are modified; the stored struct values remain the original wider range.
Lines 32-33 iterate and index Weights[iSrc-iLeft] using the adjusted locals, while downstream consumers rely on the stale stored Left/Right for the same row.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the defect lets code read past the end of the intended Weights buffer due to inconsistent persisted bounds; the primary supported impact is out-of-bounds memory read (DoS), not a write.

evidence_lines.code:
res->ContribRow[u].Left = iLeft;
res->ContribRow[u].Right = iRight;

description: An infinite loop vulnerability exists in Gpac 1.0.1 in gf_get_bit_size.
