commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn skb_get_hash_perturb(skb, q->perturbation) & (q->divisor - 1);'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn skb_get_hash_perturb(skb, &q->perturbation) & (q->divisor - 1);']}
description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: sfq_hash passes q->perturbation, a persisted per-queue value, to skb_get_hash_perturb() and masks the result with (q->divisor - 1) to select a bucket. The perturbation is the only secret input to the hash; the function neither refreshes nor supplies fresh randomness.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-330 fits because the security-relevant hash uses an insufficiently random, long-lived perturbation value as its secret. Related CWE-338 (weak PRNG) would require a specific generator flaw, which is not shown here; the issue is the non-random perturbation input.

evidence_lines.code: return skb_get_hash_perturb(skb, q->perturbation) & (q->divisor - 1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bucket selection depends on a static perturbation value rather than a cryptographically strong random source. Trigger: an attacker observing or inferring the perturbation can predict which queue a flow maps to. Consequence: flow-to-queue assignment becomes predictable, supporting traffic analysis or targeted queue manipulation.

commit_msg:
When __unmap_hugepage_range() calls to huge_pmd_unshare() succeed, a TLB
flush is missing.  This TLB flush must be performed before releasing the
i_mmap_rwsem, in order to prevent an unshared PMDs page from being
released and reused before the TLB flush took place.

Arguably, a comprehensive solution would use mmu_gather interface to
batch the TLB flushes and the PMDs page release, however it is not an
easy solution: (1) try_to_unmap_one() and try_to_migrate_one() also call
huge_pmd_unshare() and they cannot use the mmu_gather interface; and (2)
deferring the release of the page reference for the PMDs page until
after i_mmap_rwsem is dropeed can confuse huge_pmd_unshare() into
thinking PMDs are shared when they are not.

Fix __unmap_hugepage_range() by adding the missing TLB flush, and
forcing a flush when unshare is successful.

Fixes: 24669e58477e ("hugetlb: use mmu_gather instead of a temporary linked list for accumulating pages)" # 3.6
Signed-off-by: Nadav Amit <namit@vmware.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Kravetz <mike.kravetz@oracle.com>
Cc: Aneesh Kumar K.V <aneesh.kumar@linux.vnet.ibm.com>
Cc: KAMEZAWA Hiroyuki <kamezawa.hiroyu@jp.fujitsu.com>
Cc: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

We', '\t * could defer the flush until now, since by holding i_mmap_rwsem we', '\t * guaranteed that the last refernece would not be dropped. But we must', '\t * do the flushing before we return, as otherwise i_mmap_rwsem will be', '\t * dropped and the last reference to the shared PMDs page might be', '\t * dropped as well.', '\t *', '\t * In theory we could defer the freeing of the PMD pages as well, but', '\t * huge_pmd_unshare() relies on the exact page_count for the PMD page to', '\t * detect sharing, so we cannot defer the release of the page either.', '\t * Instead, do flush now.', '\t */', '\tif (force_flush)', '\t\ttlb_flush_mmu_tlbonly(tlb);']}

description: Rizin is a UNIX-like reverse engineering framework and command-line toolset. Versions 0.4.0 and prior are vulnerable to an out-of-bounds write when getting data from Luac files. A user opening a malicious Luac file could be affected by this vulnerability, allowing an attacker to execute code on the user's machine. Commits 07b43bc8aa1ffebd9b68d60624c9610cf7e460c7 and 05bbd147caccc60162d6fba9baaaf24befa281cd contain fixes for the issue.

code_evidence: Line 53 sizes upvalue_names from only proto->upvalue_entries, but line 62 iterates proto->dbg_upvalue_entries and line 63 writes upvalue_names[i] while incrementing i at line 69 with no bound relative to the allocation. If dbg_upvalue_entries is longer than upvalue_entries, the write at line 63 runs past the RZ_NEWS0 buffer allocated at line 56.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through upvalue_names[i] beyond the allocated array, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The missing constraint is that the loop index must be bounded by the allocated length, fixed by taking the max of both list lengths.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: allocation length is derived from one list (upvalue_entries) while the loop that indexes the buffer is driven by a different, independently parsed list (dbg_upvalue_entries). A malicious Luac file with more debug upvalue entries than upvalue entries triggers writes past the heap buffer, corrupting memory and potentially enabling code execution (CWE-787).

supply proper input buffer to X509_check_host

CVE-2020-7042 use of uninitialized memory in X509_check_host is fixed with
this commit

the uninitialized buffer common_name was passed as argument to X509_check_host
which prevented proper host name validation when openssl >= 1.0.2 was in use.
This came in with #282 which went into openfortivpn 1.7.1.
Unfortunately, this problem has stayed unnoticed because the return value
was not properly checked either (which is a separate issue, with CVE-2020-7041,
and which has been fixed by the previous commit)

description: An issue was discovered in openfortivpn 1.11.0 when used with OpenSSL 1.0.2 or later. tunnel.c mishandles certificate validation because the hostname check operates on uninitialized memory. The outcome is that a valid certificate is never accepted (only a malformed certificate may be accepted).

code_evidence: common_name is declared at line 12 but never assigned before line 21. Under HAVE_X509_CHECK_HOST, X509_check_host(cert, common_name, FIELD_SIZE, 0, NULL) is called with this uninitialized stack buffer as the hostname argument, and its result gates cert_valid at line 22. The #else branch at lines 25-26 is the only place common_name is populated, and it is not compiled when HAVE_X509_CHECK_HOST is defined.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because a stack resource (common_name) is used without initialization, and the uninitialized value is consumed by X509_check_host as the expected hostname, producing incorrect validation behavior. This is use of an uninitialized resource, not an out-of-bounds or format-string issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the host-validation path reads the uninitialized common_name buffer instead of tunnel->config->gateway_host. Trigger: building with OpenSSL >= 1.0.2, where HAVE_X509_CHECK_HOST is defined, and verifying a peer certificate. Consequence: X509_check_host compares against indeterminate stack contents, so valid certificates are rejected and matching is not tied to the intended gateway hostname.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. In versions of PJSIP prior to 2.13 the PJSIP parser, PJMEDIA RTP decoder, and PJMEDIA SDP parser are affeced by a buffer overflow vulnerability. Users connecting to untrusted clients are at risk. This issue has been patched and is available as commit c4d3498 in the master branch and will be included in releases 2.13 and later. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: Bounds check uses pointer arithmetic scanner->curptr + N > scanner->end, which can overflow or be bypassed when N is large relative to the buffer; syntax_err is invoked and returns on failure.
On success, pj_strset copies N bytes and curptr advances by N; the subsequent dereference *scanner->curptr reads at curptr without an EOF guard.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a bounded copy of N bytes into out (pj_strset) with a size check that can be evaded by pointer arithmetic overflow, matching CWE-120's buffer copy without adequate size validation. The post-copy dereference is an out-of-bounds read, but the primary defect is the copy without reliable input-size checking.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size check on N relies on unchecked pointer addition and the copy of N bytes proceeds without a robust size verification against the destination/remaining buffer. Trigger: a caller-supplied or parser-derived N that exceeds the valid input region. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read/write of the scanner buffer, leading to memory corruption or crash.

description: A potential memory leak issue was discovered in SDL2 in GLES_CreateTexture() function in SDL_render_gles.c. The vulnerability allows an attacker to cause a denial of service attack. The vulnerability affects SDL2 v2.0.4 and above. SDL-1.x are not affected.

code_evidence: For streaming textures, data->pixels is allocated via SDL_calloc at line 27 and stored in the GLES_TextureData struct.
On glGenTextures error, the handler frees only data (line 47), leaving data->pixels allocated when texture->access is SDL_TEXTUREACCESS_STREAMING.
On glTexImage2D error, the handler likewise frees only data (line 70), orphaning the streaming pixel buffer allocated earlier.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated memory (data->pixels) is not released after its effective lifetime ends when the error path discards its only reference. This is a missing-release leak, not a use-after-free or double-free, since the buffer is never freed at all on these paths.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that error-exit paths free the container struct data but not the separately allocated data->pixels buffer for streaming textures. Triggered when glGenTextures or glTexImage2D reports a GL error, each failed texture creation leaks the pixel buffer; repeated failures exhaust memory, causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
kvm: fix kvm_ioctl_create_device() reference counting (CVE-2019-6974)

kvm_ioctl_create_device() does the following:

1. creates a device that holds a reference to the VM object (with a borrowed
   reference, the VM's refcount has not been bumped yet)
2. initializes the device
3. transfers the reference to the device to the caller's file descriptor table
4. calls kvm_get_kvm() to turn the borrowed reference to the VM into a real
   reference

The ownership transfer in step 3 must not happen before the reference to the VM
becomes a proper, non-borrowed reference, which only happens in step 4.
After step 3, an attacker can close the file descriptor and drop the borrowed
reference, which can cause the refcount of the kvm object to drop to zero.

This means that we need to grab a reference for the device before
anon_inode_getfd(), otherwise the VM can disappear from under us.

Fixes: 852b6d57dc7f ("kvm: add device control API")
Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tkvm_get_kvm(kvm);'], 'added_lines': ['\tkvm_get_kvm(kvm);', '\t\tkvm_put_kvm(kvm);']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 4.20.8, kvm_ioctl_create_device in virt/kvm/kvm_main.c mishandles reference counting because of a race condition, leading to a use-after-free.

code_evidence: The device is published into kvm->devices and its fd is installed via anon_inode_getfd() at line 31 before kvm_get_kvm(kvm) at line 39 turns the borrowed VM reference into a real one.
Between the fd installation and line 39, a concurrent process can close the returned fd, dropping the borrowed reference and racing the kvm_get_kvm() call.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes a timing window where an interfering concurrent sequence modifies the shared VM refcount, violating exclusivity/atomicity of the reference-transfer sequence; this is a race condition (CWE-362). The resulting use-after-free is the consequence, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code:
list_add(&dev->vm_node, &kvm->devices);
mutex_unlock(&kvm->lock);

commit_msg: Lock down search_path in SPI calls
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* Lock down search_path */', '\tres = SPI_exec("SET LOCAL search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp", 0);', '\tif (res < 0)', '\t\tereport(ERROR, (errcode(ERRCODE_INTERNAL_ERROR), (errmsg("could not set search_path"))));']}
description:
TimescaleDB, an open-source time-series SQL database, has a privilege escalation vulnerability in versions 2.8.0 through 2.9.2. During installation, TimescaleDB creates a telemetry job that is runs as the installation user. The queries run as part of the telemetry data collection were not run with a locked down `search_path`, allowing malicious users to create functions that would be executed by the telemetry job, leading to privilege escalation. In order to be able to take advantage of this vulnerability, a user would need to be able to create objects in a database and then get a superuser to install TimescaleDB into their database. When TimescaleDB is installed as trusted extension, non-superusers can install the extension without help from a superuser.

Version 2.9.3 fixes this issue. As a mitigation, the `search_path` of the user running the telemetry job can be locked down to not include schemas writable by other users. The vulnerability is not exploitable on instances in Timescale Cloud and Managed Service for TimescaleDB due to additional security provisions in place on those platforms.

code_evidence: SPI_connect() opens an SPI session and the function proceeds directly to construct and execute materialization updates without ever constraining search_path.

The subsequent calls spi_update_materializations(...) execute SQL under the ambient search_path of the invoking (telemetry) session, so name resolution of referenced objects is not pinned to trusted schemas.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is improper management of the executing session's privilege context: the code runs privileged SQL without constraining the schema resolution scope, letting an unprivileged actor influence code executed under higher privilege. This is a privilege-management root cause, not merely a symptom, consistent with CWE-269.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function executes SPI-based SQL without locking search_path, so object names resolve against schemas writable by other users. Trigger: a low-privileged user creates a function/object shadowing a name used by the telemetry job, which then runs as the installation user. Supported consequence: the attacker-controlled object executes with the job's privileges, yielding privilege escalation.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.1. There is a memory leak in register_queue_kobjects() in net/core/net-sysfs.c, which will cause denial of service.

code_evidence: Lines 5-8 allocate dev->queues_kset via kset_create_and_add and return -ENOMEM on failure.
Lines 12-14 call net_rx_queue_update_kobjects; on error control jumps to the error label.
The error path at lines 21-24 unregisters queue kobjects but never releases dev->queues_kset before returning error.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory in kset_create_and_add but fails to release it on the error return, matching CWE-401's missing release after effective lifetime. This is a resource-lifetime leak, not a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path omits kset_unregister(dev->queues_kset), so the kset allocated at line 5 is leaked when net_rx_queue_update_kobjects or netdev_queue_update_kobjects fails. Trigger: a queue-update failure after the kset is created. Consequence: the allocation remains unreferenced, causing a memory leak and potential DoS.

Adding missing requirement on inputs for MirrorPadGrad op and updating arithmetic to account for int32 padding values.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 480691952
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      const Tpaddings before = paddings(d, 0);  // Pad before existing elements.', '      const Tpaddings after = paddings(d, 1);   // Pad after existing elements.', '      const int64_t out_size = in0.dim_size(d) - (before + after);'], 'added_lines': ['      const int64_t before = paddings(d, 0);  // Pad before existing elements.', '      const int64_t after = paddings(d, 1);   // Pad after existing elements.', '      const int64_t in_size = in0.dim_size(d);', '      const int64_t total_padding = before + after;', '      OP_REQUIRES(', '          context, total_padding < in_size && total_padding >= 0,', '          errors::InvalidArgument(', '              "Total paddings must be less than the input dimension size: ",', '              total_padding, " was not less than ", in_size));', '', '      const int64_t out_size = in_size - total_padding;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. If `MirrorPadGrad` is given outsize input `paddings`, TensorFlow will give a heap OOB error. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 717ca98d8c3bba348ff62281fdf38dcb5ea1ec92. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.11. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.10.1, 2.9.3, and TensorFlow 2.8.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: `before` and `after` are read from the paddings tensor and only checked for non-negativity (line 23), so values larger than the input dimension pass. Line 26 then computes `out_size = in0.dim_size(d) - (before + after)`, which becomes negative when padding exceeds the input size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing bound check on `before + after` against `in0.dim_size(d)` allows an invalid (negative) output dimension that later drives reads past the intended buffer, matching CWE-125. It is not merely an integer issue; the unchecked arithmetic leads to an out-of-bounds read of input/scratch memory.

evidence_lines.code:
const Tpaddings before = paddings(d, 0);        const Tpaddings after = paddings(d, 1);         OP_REQUIRES(context, before >= 0 && after >= 0,
const int64_t out_size = in0.dim_size(d) - (before + after);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-dimension sum of paddings is not constrained to be less than the input dimension, so `out_size` can become negative. This negative size flows into output/scratch tensor allocation and the MirrorPadGrad functor, whose indexing assumes a valid non-negative output extent, producing an out-of-bounds heap read. Trigger: a caller-supplied paddings matrix with large positive values for some dimension.

description: res_query in libresolv in glibc before 2.25 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and process crash).

code_evidence: Line 17 sizes the stack buffer from the caller-supplied type, and line 29 branches into the dual-query path when type equals T_UNSPEC. In that path line 31 builds the A query into query1; lines 38-40 may jump to unspec_nomem, and lines 45-49 may also jump there leaving n negative. The label at line 61 is reached with n possibly <= 0, yet nquery1/nquery2 were only partially assigned, so the second AAAA query at lines 52-58 is skipped.

When n <= 0, lines 74-79 allocate a heap buffer and goto again, but the same T_UNSPEC branch re-executes and can fail identically; control then falls to line 82, returns at line 99, or reaches __libc_res_nsend at lines 102-104 with inconsistent query lengths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function can proceed to dereference answer/header pointers it assumes are valid after a failed query path, causing a NULL pointer dereference and process crash. This is a null-dereference availability flaw, not a buffer overflow: the issue is unvalidated pointer state, not merely size arithmetic.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The T_UNSPEC branch can leave n non-positive after an internal query-build failure, and the retry path re-enters the same failing branch without correcting state. The subsequent send/answer handling proceeds with an invalid or unset query state, and the answer pointers (hp/hp2) are only asserted non-NULL at line 129 rather than validated, so a NULL dereference can occur and crash the resolver (DoS).

avcodec/webp: Always set pix_fmt

Fixes: 1435/clusterfuzz-testcase-minimized-6483783723253760

Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>

description: libavcodec/webp.c in FFmpeg before 2.8.12, 3.0.x before 3.0.8, 3.1.x before 3.1.8, 3.2.x before 3.2.5, and 3.3.x before 3.3.1 does not ensure that pix_fmt is set, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted file, related to the vp8_decode_mb_row_no_filter and pred8x8_128_dc_8_c functions.

code_evidence: The function derives frame geometry and buffer layout from the decoder context s and curframe without validating that avctx->pix_fmt has been set to a supported format; the patch adds an assertion confirming only YUVA420P/YUV420P are expected.
curframe is obtained via vp8_find_free_buffer and allocated by vp8_alloc_frame using the context's pixel format, so an unset or unexpected pix_fmt yields a mismatched allocation.
Linesize and uvlinesize are then read from the allocated frame and used by the later macroblock row decode routines, which index sub-sampled planes according to the assumed 4:2:0 layout.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a read/write outside an allocated frame buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The added assertion documents the missing pix_fmt constraint that permits the mismatched buffer layout.

evidence_lines.code:
VP8Context *s = avctx->priv_data;
VP8Frame *av_uninit(curframe), *prev_frame;

curframe->tf.f->key_frame = s->keyframe;
goto err;

s->linesize   = curframe->tf.f->linesize[0];
s->uvlinesize = curframe->tf.f->linesize[1];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pixel format is not guaranteed before frame allocation, so buffer dimensions/linesizes may not match the chroma layout the decoder's row and prediction functions assume. Trigger: a crafted WebP file decoded with an unset or unexpected pix_fmt. Consequence: macroblock row decoding indexes beyond the intended plane buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds access and crash.

commit_msg:
ucount:  Make get_ucount a safe get_user replacement

When the ucount code was refactored to create get_ucount it was missed
that some of the contexts in which a rlimit is kept elevated can be
the only reference to the user/ucount in the system.

Ordinary ucount references exist in places that also have a reference
to the user namspace, but in POSIX message queues, the SysV shm code,
and the SIGPENDING code there is no independent user namespace
reference.

Inspection of the the user_namespace show no instance of circular
references between struct ucounts and the user_namespace.  So
hold a reference from struct ucount to i's user_namespace to
resolve this problem.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/YZV7Z+yXbsx9p3JN@fixkernel.com/
Reported-by: Qian Cai <quic_qiancai@quicinc.com>
Reported-by: Mathias Krause <minipli@grsecurity.net>
Tested-by: Mathias Krause <minipli@grsecurity.net>
Reviewed-by: Mathias Krause <minipli@grsecurity.net>
Reviewed-by: Alexey Gladkov <legion@kernel.org>
Fixes: d64696905554 ("Reimplement RLIMIT_SIGPENDING on top of ucounts")
Fixes: 6e52a9f0532f ("Reimplement RLIMIT_MSGQUEUE on top of ucounts")
Fixes: d7c9e99aee48 ("Reimplement RLIMIT_MEMLOCK on top of ucounts")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tget_user_ns(new->ns);']}
description: kernel/ucount.c in the Linux kernel 5.14 through 5.16.4, when unprivileged user namespaces are enabled, allows a use-after-free and privilege escalation because a ucounts object can outlive its namespace.

code_evidence: alloc_ucounts() allocates a new ucounts via kzalloc and stores the caller's user_namespace pointer in new->ns at line 13, then publishes it into the hash table with hlist_add_head at line 21 and returns it at line 23. No reference to new->ns is acquired before the object becomes reachable to other users.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the ucounts object retains and later dereferences a pointer (new->ns) to memory whose lifetime was not extended, so the namespace can be freed before use. This is a missing lifetime/reference constraint enabling a use-after-free; the added get_user_ns in the patch confirms the missing reference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the new ucounts object records a raw pointer to its user_namespace without taking a namespace reference, so nothing keeps that namespace alive. Trigger: the ucounts object is inserted into the hash and handed out to contexts (POSIX mqueue, SysV shm, SIGPENDING) that hold no independent user_namespace reference, allowing the namespace to be freed while the ucounts object persists. Consequence: later ucount operations dereference new->ns after free, yielding use-after-free and potential privilege escalation.

curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);

commit_msg: fix unchecked length in stb_vorbis that could crash on corrupt/invalid files
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['         int n_read = r->end - r->begin;'], 'added_lines': ['         unsigned int actual_size = f->blocksize_1 / 2;', '         unsigned int limit_r_begin = r->begin < actual_size ? r->begin : actual_size;', '         unsigned int limit_r_end   = r->end   < actual_size ? r->end   : actual_size;', '         int n_read = limit_r_end - limit_r_begin;', '      // maximum reasonable partition size is f->blocksize_1', '']}
description: Sean Barrett stb_vorbis version 1.12 and earlier contains a Buffer Overflow vulnerability in All vorbis decoding paths. that can result in memory corruption, denial of service, comprised execution of host program. This attack appear to be exploitable via Victim must open a specially crafted Ogg Vorbis file. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in 1.13.

code_evidence: r->begin and r->end are read as 24-bit values from the file; only r->end < r->begin is rejected, so both may be far larger than the decoder's block size.

The pre-fix loop computes n_read = r->end - r->begin and divides by r->part_size to derive max_part_read, which sizes classify_mem and temp_memory_required; the patch clamps both bounds to blocksize_1/2 before subtracting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length produces an out-of-bounds buffer operation during residue decoding, matching CWE-119. The integer overflow is the root cause; the out-of-bounds access is the supported consequence, so CWE-119 rather than the integer-overflow child fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: residue begin/end are attacker-controlled and unbounded relative to blocksize_1, so n_read and part_read can be arbitrarily large. Trigger: a crafted Ogg Vorbis setup header with large residue bounds. Consequence: the derived max_part_read and classify_mem overflow or under-size the classification buffer, so later residue decoding reads/writes outside its intended boundary, causing memory corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
nfsd: encoders mustn't use unitialized values in error cases

In error cases, lgp->lg_layout_type may be out of bounds; so we
shouldn't be using it until after the check of nfserr.

This was seen to crash nfsd threads when the server receives a LAYOUTGET
request with a large layout type.

GETDEVICEINFO has the same problem.

Reported-by: Ari Kauppi <Ari.Kauppi@synopsys.com>
Reviewed-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: J. Bruce Fields <bfields@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tconst struct nfsd4_layout_ops *ops =', '\t\tnfsd4_layout_ops[gdev->gd_layout_type];'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst struct nfsd4_layout_ops *ops;', '\t\tops = nfsd4_layout_ops[gdev->gd_layout_type];']}
description: The NFSv4 server in the Linux kernel before 4.11.3 does not properly validate the layout type when processing the NFSv4 pNFS GETDEVICEINFO or LAYOUTGET operand in a UDP packet from a remote attacker. This type value is uninitialized upon encountering certain error conditions. This value is used as an array index for dereferencing, which leads to an OOPS and eventually a DoS of knfsd and a soft-lockup of the whole system.

code_evidence: At function entry, ops is initialized by indexing nfsd4_layout_ops with the attacker-supplied gdev->gd_layout_type before any error check.
Lines 11-12 jump to out when nfserr is set, but the out-of-bounds array access at line 7 has already occurred.
The later use of ops at line 19 is only reached after the nfserr check, but the index computation itself is unguarded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-129 fits because an untrusted input value is used directly as an array index without validation, causing an out-of-bounds access. This is not merely a null-pointer or uninitialized-variable issue: the index itself is not checked against the array bounds before use.

evidence_lines.code:
const struct nfsd4_layout_ops *ops =
nfsd4_layout_ops[gdev->gd_layout_type];

if (nfserr)
goto out;

if (gdev->gd_maxcount != 0) {
nfserr = ops->encode_getdeviceinfo(xdr, gdev);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: gdev->gd_layout_type from the remote GETDEVICEINFO request is used as an array index into nfsd4_layout_ops without bounds validation, and this happens before the nfserr error check. Trigger: a request with a large layout type causes an out-of-bounds read of a function pointer, which is then dereferenced; the consequence is a kernel OOPS that crashes the nfsd thread and can soft-lock the system (DoS).

commit_msg:
RDMA/rtrs-clt: Fix possible double free in error case

Callback function rtrs_clt_dev_release() for put_device() calls kfree(clt)
to free memory. We shouldn't call kfree(clt) again, and we can't use the
clt after kfree too.

Replace device_register() with device_initialize() and device_add() so that
dev_set_name can() be used appropriately.

Move mutex_destroy() to the release function so it can be called in
the alloc_clt err path.

Fixes: eab098246625 ("RDMA/rtrs-clt: Refactor the failure cases in alloc_clt")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220217030929.323849-1-haris.iqbal@ionos.com
Reported-by: Miaoqian Lin <linmq006@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Md Haris Iqbal <haris.iqbal@ionos.com>
Reviewed-by: Jack Wang <jinpu.wang@ionos.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@nvidia.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tclt->dev.class = rtrs_clt_dev_class;', '\tclt->dev.release = rtrs_clt_dev_release;', '\t\tgoto err;', '\terr = device_register(&clt->dev);', '\tif (err) {', '\t\tput_device(&clt->dev);', '\t\tgoto err;', '\t}', '\t\tgoto err_dev;', '\t\tgoto err_dev;', 'err_dev:', '\tdevice_unregister(&clt->dev);', 'err:', '\tkfree(clt);'], 'added_lines': ['\tclt->dev.class = rtrs_clt_dev_class;', '\tclt->dev.release = rtrs_clt_dev_release;', '\tdevice_initialize(&clt->dev);', '\t\tgoto err_put;', '', '\terr = device_add(&clt->dev);', '\tif (err)', '\t\tgoto err_put;', '\t\tgoto err_del;', '\t\tgoto err_del;', 'err_del:', '\tdevice_del(&clt->dev);', 'err_put:', '\tput_device(&clt->dev);']}
description: drivers/infiniband/ulp/rtrs/rtrs-clt.c in the Linux kernel before 5.16.12 has a double free related to rtrs_clt_dev_release.

code_evidence: device_register() failure path: put_device() invokes rtrs_clt_dev_release (which kfree()s clt), then goto err falls through to kfree(clt) again.
err_dev/err labels: device_unregister() also triggers release and kfree(clt), after which free_percpu and a second kfree(clt) run on the already-freed object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly frees clt in its error labels while the device core already frees it via the release callback, matching CWE-415's double free of one address. This is distinct from a simple use-after-free because the second free is the primary defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The release callback rtrs_clt_dev_release frees clt through put_device()/device_unregister(), but the error paths additionally call kfree(clt). Triggering any failure after dev_set_name (device_register error, kobject_create_and_add failure, or sysfs file creation failure) frees the same allocation twice, corrupting the allocator and enabling potential use-after-free memory corruption.

commit_msg: Address DSA/ECDSA side channel
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['   const BigInt k_inv = m_group.inverse_mod_order(k);', '   const BigInt xrm = m_group.mod_order(m_group.multiply_mod_order(m_x, r) + m);', '   const BigInt s = m_group.multiply_mod_order(k_inv, xrm);'], 'added_lines': ['   const BigInt k_inv = m_group.inverse_mod_order(k);', '', '   /*', '   * Blind the input message and compute x*r+m as (x*r*b + m*b)/b', '   */', '   m_b = m_group.square_mod_order(m_b);', '   m_b_inv = m_group.square_mod_order(m_b_inv);', '', '   m = m_group.multiply_mod_order(m_b, m);', '   const BigInt xr = m_group.multiply_mod_order(m_x, m_b, r);', '', '   const BigInt s = m_group.multiply_mod_order(k_inv, xr + m, m_b_inv);']}
description: Botan 2.5.0 through 2.6.0 before 2.7.0 allows a memory-cache side-channel attack on ECDSA signatures, aka the Return Of the Hidden Number Problem or ROHNP, related to dsa/dsa.cpp, ec_group/ec_group.cpp, and ecdsa/ecdsa.cpp. To discover an ECDSA key, the attacker needs access to either the local machine or a different virtual machine on the same physical host.

code_evidence: raw_sign computes k_inv via m_group.inverse_mod_order(k), then derives r from blinded_base_point_multiply_x(k,...). It then computes xrm = mod_order(multiply_mod_order(m_x, r) + m) and s = multiply_mod_order(k_inv, xrm) using unblinded message and private scalar m_x in the modular arithmetic, with no blinding of the message-dependent intermediate values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is that sensitive signing state (nonce inverse and private-scalar products) is exposed through observable timing/cache behavior, enabling unauthorized recovery of the ECDSA private key; this is an exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor, matching CWE-200.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The ECDSA signing arithmetic processes k_inv and the x*r+m product without blinding the message or the private-scalar multiplication. An attacker with local/co-resident access can exploit cache timing on these unblinded modular operations to recover information correlated with the nonce/private key, leading to key disclosure.

commit_msg:
ALSA: hrtimer: Fix stall by hrtimer_cancel()

hrtimer_cancel() waits for the completion from the callback, thus it
must not be called inside the callback itself.  This was already a
problem in the past with ALSA hrtimer driver, and the early commit
[fcfdebe70759: ALSA: hrtimer - Fix lock-up] tried to address it.

However, the previous fix is still insufficient: it may still cause a
lockup when the ALSA timer instance reprograms itself in its callback.
Then it invokes the start function even in snd_timer_interrupt() that
is called in hrtimer callback itself, results in a CPU stall.  This is
no hypothetical problem but actually triggered by syzkaller fuzzer.

This patch tries to fix the issue again.  Now we call
hrtimer_try_to_cancel() at both start and stop functions so that it
won't fall into a deadlock, yet giving some chance to cancel the queue
if the functions have been called outside the callback.  The proper
hrtimer_cancel() is called in anyway at closing, so this should be
enough.

Reported-and-tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\thrtimer_cancel(&stime->hrt);'], 'added_lines': ['\thrtimer_try_to_cancel(&stime->hrt);']}
description: sound/core/hrtimer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 does not prevent recursive callback access, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock) via a crafted ioctl call.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's defect is calling hrtimer_cancel() from a context that can be the hrtimer callback itself, causing a deadlock; there is no unvalidated input processing supporting CWE-20.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* Notify request callbacks */', '\tqueue_remove_all(att->req_queue, NULL, NULL, disc_att_send_op);', '\tqueue_remove_all(att->ind_queue, NULL, NULL, disc_att_send_op);', '\tqueue_remove_all(att->write_queue, NULL, NULL, disc_att_send_op);', ''], 'added_lines': ['\tatt->in_disc = true;', '', '\t/* Notify request callbacks */', '\tqueue_remove_all(att->req_queue, NULL, NULL, disc_att_send_op);', '\tqueue_remove_all(att->ind_queue, NULL, NULL, disc_att_send_op);', '\tqueue_remove_all(att->write_queue, NULL, NULL, disc_att_send_op);', '', '\tatt->in_disc = false;', '']}
description: In BlueZ before 5.55, a double free was found in the gatttool disconnect_cb() routine from shared/att.c. A remote attacker could potentially cause a denial of service or code execution, during service discovery, due to a redundant disconnect MGMT event.

code_evidence: The function removes the channel, drains att->req_queue, att->ind_queue and att->write_queue with disc_att_send_op callbacks, then separately frees chan->pending_req and chan->pending_ind via disc_att_send_op before calling bt_att_chan_free(chan). The callback disc_att_send_op may free the client that owns these requests, and per the commit trace, queue draining and disconnect notification can free the same client objects, causing bt_att_cancel to operate on already-freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch moves queue draining behind an in_disc guard to prevent re-entrant freeing of the same request memory. This directly targets double free of request/client objects during disconnect, matching CWE-415 rather than a generic use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Pending request callbacks are notified while the owning client can be freed during the same disconnect processing; the channel's pending_req/pending_ind are then freed again through disc_att_send_op, and the freed client later calls bt_att_cancel. The trigger is a disconnect with pending requests during service discovery, leading to a use-after-free/double-free and possible crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4647: "source" can read past end of copied line

Problem:    "source" can read past end of copied line.
Solution:   Add a terminating NUL.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t    if (ga_grow(&ga, 1) == FAIL)', '\t\tbreak;', '\t    buf[ga.ga_len++] = NUL;']}
description: heap buffer overflow in get_one_sourceline in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.4647.

code_evidence: When source_from_buf is set, ga_concat appends the stored line into the heap-grown ga buffer; buf is then set to ga.ga_data and ga.ga_len is not advanced by a NUL terminator.
len is computed as ga.ga_len + STRLEN(buf + ga.ga_len), and buf[len - 1] is written at line 79; without a terminating NUL the STRLEN scan and later indexing can run past the allocated heap buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-122 fits because the overflow targets a heap-allocated buffer (ga.ga_data grown via ga_grow/ga_concat) and the missing NUL lets indexing exceed the allocation. This is a heap buffer overflow rather than a stack overflow, as the affected buffer is dynamically allocated.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the copied source line is concatenated into the heap buffer without ensuring a NUL terminator, so STRLEN(buf + ga.ga_len) and buf[len - 1] operate beyond the valid line data. Triggering sourcing from a buffer line lacking a NUL within the allocation causes an out-of-bounds heap read/write, leading to memory corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow (CVE-2021-21309). (#8522)

On 32-bit systems, setting the proto-max-bulk-len config parameter to a high value may result with integer overflow and a subsequent heap overflow when parsing an input bulk (CVE-2021-21309).

This fix has two parts:

Set a reasonable limit to the config parameter.
Add additional checks to prevent the problem in other potential but unknown code paths.

(cherry picked from commit d32f2e9999ce003bad0bd2c3bca29f64dcce4433)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    ASSERT_NO_SIZE_OVERFLOW(size);']}
description: Redis is an open-source, in-memory database that persists on disk. In affected versions of Redis an integer overflow bug in 32-bit Redis version 4.0 or newer could be exploited to corrupt the heap and potentially result with remote code execution. Redis 4.0 or newer uses a configurable limit for the maximum supported bulk input size. By default, it is 512MB which is a safe value for all platforms. If the limit is significantly increased, receiving a large request from a client may trigger several integer overflow scenarios, which would result with buffer overflow and heap corruption. We believe this could in certain conditions be exploited for remote code execution. By default, authenticated Redis users have access to all configuration parameters and can therefore use the “CONFIG SET proto-max-bulk-len” to change the safe default, making the system vulnerable. **This problem only affects 32-bit Redis (on a 32-bit system, or as a 32-bit executable running on a 64-bit system).** The problem is fixed in version 6.2, and the fix is back ported to 6.0.11 and 5.0.11. Make sure you use one of these versions if you are running 32-bit Redis. An additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent clients from directly executing `CONFIG SET`: Using Redis 6.0 or newer, ACL configuration can be used to block the command. Using older versions, the `rename-command` configuration directive can be used to rename the command to a random string unknown to users, rendering it inaccessible. Please note that this workaround may have an additional impact on users or operational systems that expect `CONFIG SET` to behave in certain ways.

code_evidence: zcalloc computes size+PREFIX_SIZE for calloc without checking whether the addition wraps; the patch adds ASSERT_NO_SIZE_OVERFLOW(size) before this allocation, confirming the unchecked addition on line 2 is the overflow site.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an unchecked integer addition whose wrapped result is used directly as an allocation size, matching CWE-190's key characteristic of size-determining arithmetic that can overflow. The later buffer overflow is a consequence; the root cause is the missing overflow constraint at the addition.

evidence_lines.code: void *ptr = calloc(1, size+PREFIX_SIZE);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation-size arithmetic size+PREFIX_SIZE can wrap when size is near SIZE_MAX, so calloc receives a tiny size while the caller assumes a large buffer. Trigger: a large attacker-influenced bulk length (e.g., via proto-max-bulk-len on 32-bit builds) reaches zcalloc. Consequence: undersized heap allocation followed by out-of-bounds writes, corrupting the heap.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Reported-by: syzbot+f427adf9324b92652ccc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (is_bad_inode(inode))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (fuse_is_bad(inode))']}
description: An issue was discovered in the FUSE filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.10.6, aka CID-5d069dbe8aaf. fuse_do_getattr() calls make_bad_inode() in inappropriate situations, causing a system crash. NOTE: the original fix for this vulnerability was incomplete, and its incompleteness is tracked as CVE-2021-28950.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only checks is_bad_inode and dispatches writes; it contains no cleanup or resource-release logic, so it does not directly support CWE-459 (the cleanup defect resides in fuse_do_getattr/make_bad_inode).

commit_msg: Add height check for Graphics.createArrayBuffer(...vertical_byte:true) (fix #1421)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      assert(ptr>=gfx->backendData && ptr<((char*)gfx->backendData + graphicsGetMemoryRequired(gfx)));']}
description: Espruino before 1.98 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) with a user crafted input file via an Out-of-bounds Read during syntax parsing in which certain height validation is missing in libs/graphics/jswrap_graphics.c.

code_evidence: The function computes ptr from gfx->backendData plus a bit offset derived from lcdGetPixelIndex_ArrayBuffer(gfx,x,y,pixelCount); no bound on the resulting pointer is verified before use.
Line 22 reads existing = *ptr and line 24 writes *ptr, both using the unvalidated pointer; the added assert in the patch confirms the intended bound was previously missing.
Lines 25-29 advance ptr (either directly for VERTICAL_BYTE or via idx) across pixel iterations, potentially walking past the allocated buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the code dereferences *ptr at line 22 without validating that ptr lies within the intended backendData buffer, reading memory past the allocated region. The missing bound check is the direct cause of the OOB read; it is not merely an OOB write because the read of existing precedes the in-bounds-only store.

evidence_lines.code:
unsigned int existing = (unsigned int)*ptr;
*ptr = (char)((existing&~(mask<<bitIdx)) | ((col&mask)<<bitIdx));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: lcdSetPixels_ArrayBuffer_flat derives the write/read pointer solely from a pixel index without checking it against the backendData buffer size. A crafted graphics configuration (e.g. vertical byte layout) yields an index beyond the allocated array, so the loop reads *ptr past the buffer end, causing an out-of-bounds read and application crash.

commit_msg:
avcodec/mpeg4videoenc: Use 64 bit for times in mpeg4_encode_gop_header()

Fixes truncation
Fixes Assertion n <= 31 && value < (1U << n) failed at libavcodec/put_bits.h:169
Fixes: ffmpeg_crash_2.avi

Found-by: Thuan Pham <thuanpv@comp.nus.edu.sg>, Marcel Böhme, Andrew Santosa and Alexandru RazvanCaciulescu with AFLSmart

Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
(cherry picked from commit e1182fac1afba92a4975917823a5f644bee7e6e8)
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int hours, minutes, seconds;'], 'added_lines': ['    int64_t hours, minutes, seconds;']}
description: An improper integer type in the mpeg4_encode_gop_header function in libavcodec/mpeg4videoenc.c in FFmpeg 2.8 and 4.0 may trigger an assertion violation while converting a crafted AVI file to MPEG4, leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: Line 3 declares hours, minutes, seconds as 32-bit int while time is int64_t. Line 7 derives time from the picture pts; line 10 multiplies it by time_base.num, so a crafted AVI can supply a large pts that overflows the 32-bit seconds value at line 12 (FFUDIV). Lines 13-15 then compute minutes/hours from the truncated seconds, and lines 16,17,19 feed hours/minutes/seconds into put_bits with fixed widths (5,6,6 bits).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts an externally influenced timestamp and fails to validate that the derived hours/minutes/seconds fit the expected ranges before encoding, matching improper input validation. The truncation is a contributing derivation error; the DoS consequence follows from unvalidated input reaching put_bits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pts-derived time is converted into 32-bit seconds without range checking, so a large attacker-controlled timestamp truncates. The truncated values are then written via put_bits with narrow bit fields, violating the n <= 31 && value < (1U << n) assertion and crashing the encoder (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix crash in lexer refill (reported by Agostino Sarubbo).

The crash happened in a rare case of a very long lexeme that doen't fit
into the buffer, forcing buffer reallocation.

The crash was caused by an incorrect calculation of the shift offset
(it was smaller than necessary). As a consequence, the data from buffer
start and up to the beginning of the current lexeme was not discarded
(as it should have been), resulting in less free space for new data than
expected.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        shift_ptrs_and_fpos(buf - bot);'], 'added_lines': ['        shift_ptrs_and_fpos(buf - tok);', '    DASSERT(lim + free <= bot + BSIZE);']}
description: re2c 1.3 has a heap-based buffer overflow in Scanner::fill in parse/scanner.cc via a long lexeme.

code_evidence: On the reallocation path, BSIZE is grown and a new buffer of BSIZE+YYMAXFILL is allocated, but the shift offset is computed as buf - bot rather than buf - tok. The stale offset leaves pointers positioned for the old buffer, so the free-space value at line 20 (BSIZE - copy) does not match the actual room after the moved lexeme.
The subsequent read(free) uses that inflated free count, allowing more bytes to be written than the buffer's remaining capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes an incorrect free-space size and then writes that many bytes via read into the allocated buffer, exceeding its bounds. This is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); the incorrect offset is the root cause enabling the overwrite, not merely an arithmetic error.

evidence_lines.code: if (!read(free)) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the incorrect shift offset (buf - bot instead of buf - tok) fails to discard the prefix before the current lexeme, so free is overestimated. Trigger: a lexeme long enough to force reallocation. Consequence: read writes past the end of the heap buffer, causing a heap-based buffer overflow/crash.

in another subsystem]
Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190124063514.8571-2-houtao1@huawei.com
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: 7549ae3e81cc ("9p: Use the i_size_[read, write]() macros instead of using inode->i_size directly.")
Reported-by: Xing Gaopeng <xingaopeng@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Hou Tao <houtao1@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Dominique Martinet <dominique.martinet@cea.fr>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tloff_t i_size;', '\tspin_lock(&inode->i_lock);', '\ti_size = inode->i_size;', '\tv9fs_stat2inode(st, inode, inode->i_sb);', '\tif (v9ses->cache == CACHE_LOOSE || v9ses->cache == CACHE_FSCACHE)', '\t\tinode->i_size = i_size;', '\tspin_unlock(&inode->i_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned int flags;', '\tflags = (v9ses->cache == CACHE_LOOSE || v9ses->cache == CACHE_FSCACHE) ?', '\t\tV9FS_STAT2INODE_KEEP_ISIZE : 0;', '\tv9fs_stat2inode(st, inode, inode->i_sb, flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. The 9p filesystem did not protect i_size_write() properly, which causes an i_size_read() infinite loop and denial of service on SMP systems.

code_evidence: Under inode->i_lock, the function snapshots i_size into a local, calls v9fs_stat2inode (which writes inode->i_size), then restores inode->i_size directly at line 19 rather than via i_size_write(). Concurrent generic_fillattr() readers use i_size_read()/seqcount; the direct write leaves the seqcount state inconsistent so readers can spin in read_seqcount_begin().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is an unbounded loop whose exit condition (seqcount retry) never becomes reachable because of the improper i_size update, matching CWE-835's infinite loop/availability impact. This is not merely a race on data value; the loop itself is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: inode->i_size is modified by plain assignment (line 19) instead of the i_size_write() accessor that updates the seqcount on 32-bit SMP. Trigger: concurrent v9fs_vfs_getattr()/getattr_dotl() calls restore i_size while generic_fillattr() reads it. Consequence: i_size_read() loops in read_seqcount_begin(), causing CPU soft lockup and DoS.

commit_msg:
PR/454: Fix memory corruption when the continuation level jumps by more than
20 in a single step.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tlen = (ms->c.len += 20) * sizeof(*ms->c.li);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tlen = (ms->c.len = 20 + level) * sizeof(*ms->c.li);']}
description: The file_check_mem function in funcs.c in file before 5.23, as used in the Fileinfo component in PHP before 5.5.34, 5.6.x before 5.6.20, and 7.x before 7.0.5, mishandles continuation-level jumps, which allows context-dependent attackers to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted magic file.

code_evidence: When level >= ms->c.len, the buffer is grown by a fixed increment of 20 (ms->c.len += 20) rather than to accommodate the requested level.
After reallocation, the code unconditionally indexes ms->c.li[level] (lines 15 and 17) without verifying that level < ms->c.len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to ms->c.li[level] after an insufficient reallocation, an out-of-bounds write within a memory buffer, matching CWE-119. It is not merely an integer overflow: the capacity arithmetic (len) is correct for the wrong size, and the missing constraint is that level must be less than the grown capacity before indexing.

evidence_lines.code:
ms->c.li[level].got_match = 0;
ms->c.li[level].last_match = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the growth step only adds 20 to the current capacity, so a continuation level that jumps by more than 20 in one step leaves level >= ms->c.len. Because lines 15/17 then write ms->c.li[level] unconditionally, the write lands past the allocated array, corrupting adjacent heap memory. Trigger: a crafted magic file whose continuation level jumps by more than 20; consequence is a heap out-of-bounds write, causing crash/DoS and potentially code execution.

commit_msg:
For the case where both s32_{min,max}_value bounds are positive, the
__reg_assign_32_into_64() directly propagates them to their 64 bit
counterparts, otherwise it pessimises them into [0,u32_max] universe and
tries to refine them later on by learning through the tnum as per comment
in mentioned function. However, that does not always happen, for example,
in mov32 operation we call zext_32_to_64(dst_reg) which invokes the
__reg_assign_32_into_64() as is without subsequent bounds update as
elsewhere thus no refinement based on tnum takes place.

Thus, not calling into the __update_reg_bounds() / __reg_deduce_bounds() /
__reg_bound_offset() triplet as we do, for example, in case of ALU ops via
adjust_scalar_min_max_vals(), will lead to more pessimistic bounds when
dumping the full register state:

Before fix:

  0: (b4) w0 = -1
  1: R0_w=invP4294967295
     (id=0,imm=ffffffff,
      smin_value=4294967295,smax_value=4294967295,
      umin_value=4294967295,umax_value=4294967295,
      var_off=(0xffffffff; 0x0),
      s32_min_value=-1,s32_max_value=-1,
      u32_min_value=-1,u32_max_value=-1)

  1: (bc) w0 = w0
  2: R0_w=invP4294967295
     (id=0,imm=ffffffff,
      smin_value=0,smax_value=4294967295,
      umin_value=4294967295,umax_value=4294967295,
      var_off=(0xffffffff; 0x0),
      s32_min_value=-1,s32_max_value=-1,
      u32_min_value=-1,u32_max_value=-1)

Technically, the smin_value=0 and smax_value=4294967295 bounds are not
incorrect, but given the register is still a constant, they break assumptions
about const scalars that smin_value == smax_value and umin_value == umax_value.

After fix:

  0: (b4) w0 = -1
  1: R0_w=invP4294967295
     (id=0,imm=ffffffff,
      smin_value=4294967295,smax_value=4294967295,
      umin_value=4294967295,umax_value=4294967295,
      var_off=(0xffffffff; 0x0),
      s32_min_value=-1,s32_max_value=-1,
      u32_min_value=-1,u32_max_value=-1)

  1: (bc) w0 = w0
  2: R0_w=invP4294967295
     (id=0,imm=ffffffff,
      smin_value=4294967295,smax_value=4294967295,
      umin_value=4294967295,umax_value=4294967295,
      var_off=(0xffffffff; 0x0),
      s32_min_value=-1,s32_max_value=-1,
      u32_min_value=-1,u32_max_value=-1)

Without the smin_value == smax_value and umin_value == umax_value invariant
being intact for const scalars, it is possible to leak out kernel pointers
from unprivileged user space if the latter is enabled. For example, when such
registers are involved in pointer arithmtics, then adjust_ptr_min_max_vals()
will taint the destination register into an unknown scalar, and the latter
can be exported and stored e.g. into a BPF map value.

Fixes: 3f50f132d840 ("bpf: Verifier, do explicit ALU32 bounds tracking")
Reported-by: Kuee K1r0a <liulin063@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Reviewed-by: John Fastabend <john.fastabend@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t\t\t__update_reg_bounds(dst_reg);', '\t\t\t\t__reg_deduce_bounds(dst_reg);', '\t\t\t\t__reg_bound_offset(dst_reg);']}
description: The check_alu_op() function in kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through v5.16-rc5 did not properly update bounds while handling the mov32 instruction, which allows local users to obtain potentially sensitive address information, aka a "pointer leak."

code_evidence: In the 32-bit BPF_MOV register-copy path, the source scalar is copied into dst_reg and then zext_32_to_64(dst_reg) is called at line 75. The function returns without invoking __update_reg_bounds/__reg_deduce_bounds/__reg_bound_offset, so the 64-bit smin/smax and umin/umax fields are not refined from the 32-bit bounds and tnum. Consequently, for a constant scalar the invariant smin==smax and umin==umax is broken; the register is still constant but its 64-bit bounds are pessimistic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing bounds update causes verifier-tracked constant scalars to be misclassified as unknown, so pointer-derived values escape the verifier's intended control sphere and reach unprivileged user space. This exposes sensitive kernel address information to the wrong party, matching CWE-668; the underlying mistake is incomplete bounds refinement, not an authorization check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the mov32 path zero-extends the 32-bit register but omits the bounds-refinement triplet, leaving stale/pessimistic 64-bit min/max values on a constant scalar. Trigger: an unprivileged BPF program performs a 32-bit register move on a constant. Consequence: the verifier's bound tracking is inconsistent, and later pointer arithmetic taints the register as an unknown scalar, allowing kernel pointers to be leaked to user space via a BPF map value.

commit_msg:
candump: check for a too-long frame length.

If the frame length is longer than the maximum, report an error in the
file.

Fixes #19062, preventing the overflow on a buffer on the stack (assuming
your compiler doesn't call a bounds-checknig version of memcpy() if the
size of the target space is known).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    candump_write_packet(rec, buf, &msg);', '', '    return TRUE;'], 'added_lines': ['    return candump_write_packet(rec, buf, &msg, err, err_info);']}
description: Candump log parser crash in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.5 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.13 allows denial of service via crafted capture file

code_evidence: The function declares a stack-local msg_t msg and fills it via candump_parse(wth->fh, &msg, ...), so parsed frame data, including its length, lands in this fixed stack buffer before any bounds validation.

After parsing, the old code calls candump_write_packet(rec, buf, &msg) and unconditionally returns TRUE; it does not propagate an error and does not check whether the frame length exceeds the buffer capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing length constraint allows data to be written past the end of the intended fixed-size buffer. This is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the oversized length drives a copy into msg.

evidence_lines.code:
candump_write_packet(rec, buf, &msg);
return TRUE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parsed frame length from a crafted capture file is trusted when writing into the fixed stack msg buffer, without a check that it fits. Trigger: a candump file specifying an oversized frame length. Consequence: candump_write_packet copies the too-long frame past msg's bounds, corrupting the stack and crashing the parser (DoS).

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.5 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.11, the WBXML dissector could go into an infinite loop, triggered by packet injection or a malformed capture file. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-wbxml.c by adding length validation.

code_evidence: The while loop at line 17 advances off only through token handlers; the ENTITY handler (0x02) reads a length via tvb_get_guintvar at line 35 and unconditionally does off += 1+len at line 39, without checking len against tvb_len.
The LITERAL handler (0x04) similarly reads len at line 50 and advances off += 1+len at line 58 with no bound check on len.
The STR_T handler (0x83) reads len at line 94 and advances off += 1+len at line 100, again unvalidated.
The OPAQUE handler (0xC3) computes off += 1+len+idx at line 141 from attacker-controlled len/idx without validating against tvb_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's loop exit condition depends on off reaching tvb_len, but unchecked length-based increments can prevent that, matching CWE-835's unreachable exit condition. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read; the supported consequence is a non-terminating iteration causing resource exhaustion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: length values parsed from the packet are used to advance the loop index off without ensuring they stay within tvb_len. A malformed WBXML attribute with an oversized length causes off to jump past or not progress toward tvb_len, so the while (off < tvb_len) condition may never be reached, leaving the dissector spinning and consuming CPU (DoS).

Commit 086d49058cd8 ("ipv6: annotate some data-races around sk->sk_prot")
fixed some data-races around sk->sk_prot but it was not enough.

Some functions in inet6_(stream|dgram)_ops still access sk->sk_prot
without lock_sock() or rtnl_lock(), so they need READ_ONCE() to avoid
load tearing.

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
Signed-off-by: Kuniyuki Iwashima <kuniyu@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn sk->sk_prot->getsockopt(sk, level, optname, optval, optlen);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* IPV6_ADDRFORM can change sk->sk_prot under us. */', '\treturn READ_ONCE(sk->sk_prot)->getsockopt(sk, level, optname, optval, optlen);']}
description: A vulnerability has been found in Linux Kernel and classified as problematic. This vulnerability affects the function inet6_stream_ops/inet6_dgram_ops of the component IPv6 Handler. The manipulation leads to race condition. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-211090 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: Line 4 copies sock->sk into local sk; line 5 dereferences sk->sk_prot and immediately invokes its getsockopt handler. No lock_sock() or rtnl_lock() is taken before the read, and the protocol pointer is read once without READ_ONCE(), so the load is not atomic with respect to concurrent writers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits: a shared resource (sk->sk_prot) is accessed without exclusive access or atomic read, creating a timing window in which an interfering code sequence mutates it before use. This is improper synchronization of concurrent access rather than a missing bounds or type check.

evidence_lines.code:
struct sock *sk = sock->sk;
return sk->sk_prot->getsockopt(sk, level, optname, optval, optlen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sk->sk_prot is shared socket state that IPV6_ADDRFORM can reassign under the socket while this path reads it without synchronization. Trigger: another thread changes sk->sk_prot concurrently with sock_common_getsockopt, so the unprotected load can tear or observe a stale/inconsistent protocol pointer. Supported consequence: the call through the torn/stale pointer dispatches to an unexpected or invalid getsockopt implementation, causing instability or a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
ipsec: Fix aborted xfrm policy dump crash

An independent security researcher, Mohamed Ghannam, has reported
this vulnerability to Beyond Security's SecuriTeam Secure Disclosure
program.

The xfrm_dump_policy_done function expects xfrm_dump_policy to
have been called at least once or it will crash.  This can be
triggered if a dump fails because the target socket's receive
buffer is full.

This patch fixes it by using the cb->start mechanism to ensure that
the initialisation is always done regardless of the buffer situation.

Change-Id: Id41cdd41c4e43e0c3ac30c5d03c15b8046d70845
Fixes: 12a169e7d8f4 ("ipsec: Put dumpers on the dump list")
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
Signed-off-by: Steffen Klassert <steffen.klassert@secunet.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct xfrm_policy_walk *walk = (struct xfrm_policy_walk *) &cb->args[1];'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct xfrm_policy_walk *walk = (struct xfrm_policy_walk *)cb->args;']}
description: A vulnerability classified as problematic has been found in flar2 ElementalX up to 6.x on Nexus 9. Affected is the function xfrm_dump_policy_done of the file net/xfrm/xfrm_user.c of the component ipsec. The manipulation leads to denial of service. Upgrading to version 7.00 is able to address this issue. The name of the patch is 1df72c9f0f61304437f4f1037df03b5fb36d5a79. It is recommended to upgrade the affected component. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-217152.

code_evidence: Line 3 casts &cb->args[1] to struct xfrm_policy_walk *, but the dump state was initialized at cb->args by xfrm_dump_policy; line 4 then passes this misaligned pointer to xfrm_policy_walk_done, which operates on uninitialized/incorrect walk data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The done handler releases walk resources through an invalid pointer whose state was never properly established, i.e., improper shutdown/release of a resource across an abort path, matching CWE-404. A pure NULL-dereference label would miss the release-path misuse, but the crash is the consequence, not the cause.

evidence_lines.code:
struct xfrm_policy_walk *walk = (struct xfrm_policy_walk *) &cb->args[1];
xfrm_policy_walk_done(walk);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a wrong offset for the walk state: when a policy dump aborts before xfrm_dump_policy initializes the walk, done() still dereferences the bogus pointer and tears down an uninitialized walk. Trigger is a full receive buffer aborting the dump; the supported consequence is a crash/denial of service rather than a controlled resource leak.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.4+
Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!test_bit(KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE, &key->flags))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (key_is_positive(key))']}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.10 does not correctly synchronize the actions of updating versus finding a key in the "negative" state to avoid a race condition, which allows local users to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls.

commit_msg:
Initialize eh_generation of struct ext4_extent_header to prevent leaking
info to userspace. Fixes KMSAN kernel-infoleak bug reported by syzbot at:
http://syzkaller.appspot.com/bug?id=78e9ad0e6952a3ca16e8234724b2fa92d041b9b8

Cc: stable@kernel.org
Reported-by: syzbot+2dcfeaf8cb49b05e8f1a@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Fixes: a86c61812637 ("[PATCH] ext3: add extent map support")
Signed-off-by: Anirudh Rayabharam <mail@anirudhrb.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210506185655.7118-1-mail@anirudhrb.com
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\teh->eh_generation = 0;']}
description: A vulnerability was found in linux kernel, where an information leak occurs via ext4_extent_header to userspace.

code_evidence: ext4_ext_tree_init initializes the on-disk extent header fields eh_depth, eh_entries, eh_magic and eh_max but never sets eh_generation; the header is written to the inode via ext4_mark_inode_dirty. The uninitialized eh_generation field therefore persists in the inode's on-disk extent header.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly manages a persistent on-disk structure and fails to set one field, causing uninitialized kernel data to be exposed to userspace. This is a confidentiality error in code that manages/stores information, matching CWE-200 rather than a memory-safety root cause like out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the extent header's eh_generation field is left uninitialized when the tree is initialized, while the rest of the same structure is explicitly zeroed/set. Trigger: the inode is written out and later read back to userspace (e.g., via stat/getxattr or raw inode read), exposing the stale/uninitialized bytes. Consequence: kernel memory contents leak to userspace (KMSAN kernel-infoleak).

description: EOSIO/eos eos version after commit f1545dd0ae2b77580c2236fdb70ae7138d2c7168 contains a stack overflow vulnerability in abi_serializer that can result in attack eos network node. This attack appear to be exploitable via network request. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in after commit cf7209e703e6d3f7a5413e0cb1fe88a4d8e4b38d .

code_evidence: add() recurses into fc::reflector<M>::visit with an abi_to_variant_visitor but passes no depth counter or bound, so nested/recursive ABI type definitions re-enter add() without any limit until the stack is exhausted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs recursion on attacker-influenced ABI structure with no control over recursion depth, directly matching CWE-674 Uncontrolled Recursion. A generic resource-exhaustion label would be less precise since the specific mechanism is missing recursion control, not merely large allocations.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursive ABI-to-variant conversion has no recursion depth accounting or termination guard. Trigger: a network-supplied ABI with self-referential or deeply nested type definitions causes repeated add() re-entry. Consequence: unbounded stack consumption leading to stack overflow and node crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via
/home/fred/keepalived.data.

There doesn't appear to be a way around this backward incompatibility,
since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

description: MmsValue_decodeMmsData in mms/iso_mms/server/mms_access_result.c in libIEC61850 through 1.4.0 has a heap-based buffer overflow when parsing the MMS_BIT_STRING data type.

code_evidence: Line 51 reads the padding byte from the attacker-controlled MMS buffer without validating it. Line 52 computes bitStringLength = (8 * (dataLength - 1)) - padding; an unchecked padding (e.g., >7 or large) makes this length exceed the actual bit-string capacity. Line 53 allocates a bit string of that derived length, and line 54 memcpy's dataLength - 1 bytes into value->value.bitString.buf, so the copy size is decoupled from the padding-derived allocation size, enabling an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe memcpy into a buffer whose size was computed from unvalidated padding is a write beyond the intended heap buffer, matching CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write). It is not merely an integer issue; the direct consequence is an out-of-bounds heap write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the padding value from the wire is used to size the destination buffer without a plausibility bound, while the memcpy length is fixed by dataLength. A crafted MMS_BIT_STRING with an oversized padding yields a negative/undersized bitStringLength and a mismatched allocation, so memcpy writes past the heap buffer, causing memory corruption or crash.

before use in order to avoid NULL pointer dereference.

Acked-by: Srinivas Pandruvada <srinivas.pandruvada@linux.intel.com>
