commit_msg:
net_processing: Boost inv trickle rate

If transactions are being added to the mempool at a rate faster than 7tx/s
(INVENTORY_BROADCAST_PER_SECOND) then peers' inventory_to_send queue can
become relatively large. If this happens, increase the number of txids
we include in an INV message (normally capped at 35) by 5 for each 1000
txids in the queue.

This will tend to clear a temporary excess out reasonably quickly; an
excess of 4000 invs to send will be cleared down to 1000 in about 30
minutes, while an excess of 20000 invs would be cleared down to 1000 in
about 60 minutes.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    while (!vInvTx.empty() && nRelayedTransactions < INVENTORY_BROADCAST_MAX) {'], 'added_lines': ['                    size_t broadcast_max{INVENTORY_BROADCAST_MAX + (tx_relay->m_tx_inventory_to_send.size()/1000)*5};', '                    broadcast_max = std::min<size_t>(1000, broadcast_max);', '                    while (!vInvTx.empty() && nRelayedTransactions < broadcast_max) {']}
description: Bitcoin Core before 24.1, when debug mode is not used, allows attackers to cause a denial of service (e.g., CPU consumption) because draining the inventory-to-send queue is inefficient, as exploited in the wild in May 2023.

code_evidence: The trickle loop iterates over the heap of pending txids (lines 200-205) and erases each processed entry from m_tx_inventory_to_send (line 208), but the loop is bounded by the fixed INVENTORY_BROADCAST_MAX (line 202). When the queue grows faster than this fixed per-trickle cap, only a constant number of entries are drained per call, so the backlog in m_tx_inventory_to_send persists and the heap operations plus mempool lookups (lines 212-214) repeat on an ever-growing set. nRelayedTransactions only increments for entries that pass the filters (line 224), and the loop exits at the fixed cap regardless of queue size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to throttle/scale its resource (queue) consumption: a fixed output cap lets an input-driven queue grow without proportionally faster draining, matching CWE-400's lack of throttling for allocated resources causing CPU exhaustion. Contrast CWE-770 (allocation without limits) — here the entry cap exists but is not adaptive, so it is a consumption/throttling failure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-send drain rate is a constant (INVENTORY_BROADCAST_MAX) independent of the pending m_tx_inventory_to_send size, so when transactions are added faster than the drain rate the queue grows unboundedly. Trigger: a peer/attacker flooding tx inventory. Consequence: sustained CPU consumption from repeated heap and mempool processing of a large, slowly draining queue (CWE-400 DoS).

commit_msg:
evtchn: evtchn_reset() shouldn't succeed with still-open ports

While the function closes all ports, it does so without holding any
lock, and hence racing requests may be issued causing new ports to get
opened. This would have been problematic in particular if such a newly
opened port had a port number above the new implementation limit (i.e.
when switching from FIFO to 2-level) after the reset, as prior to
"evtchn: relax port_is_valid()" this could have led to e.g.
evtchn_close()'s "BUG_ON(!port_is_valid(d2, port2))" to trigger.

Introduce a counter of active ports and check that it's (still) no
larger then the number of Xen internally used ones after obtaining the
necessary lock in evtchn_reset().

As to the access model of the new {active,xen}_evtchns fields - while
all writes get done using write_atomic(), reads ought to use
read_atomic() only when outside of a suitably locked region.

Note that as of now evtchn_bind_virq() and evtchn_bind_ipi() don't have
a need to call check_free_port().

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( d->evtchn_fifo )', '    return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    int rc = 0;', '    if ( d->active_evtchns > d->xen_evtchns )', '        rc = -EAGAIN;', '    else if ( d->evtchn_fifo )', '    return rc;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The loop closes each valid port via evtchn_close() while no lock is held, so the port set is scanned and mutated without exclusive access.
Only after the unlocked close loop does the function take d->event_lock, and it then returns unconditionally 0 without verifying that no new ports were opened during the loop.
The unconditional success return reports a completed reset even if concurrent bind requests reopened ports.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a shared-resource (event-channel port table) operation without holding a lock across the whole sequence, and a concurrent code sequence can interfere, which is exactly CWE-362. The missing active-port recheck before returning success is the concrete exclusivity/atomicity violation.

evidence_lines.code:
for ( i = 0; port_is_valid(d, i); i++ )
evtchn_close(d, i, 1);
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the close-all-ports sequence is not atomic with respect to concurrent EVTCHNOP_bind requests, which can open new ports between the port_is_valid() scan and the lock acquisition. The reset then succeeds despite still-open ports, violating internal assumptions (e.g. port_is_valid() checks, port-number limits after FIFO-to-2-level switch), enabling out-of-bounds accesses, BUG_ON triggers, DoS, or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fix seqset iterator when it ends in a comma.

If the seqset ended with a comma, the substr_end marker would be just
before the trailing nul.  In the next call, the loop to skip the
marker would iterate right past the end of string too.

The fix is simple: place the substr_end marker and skip past it
immediately.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    while (!*(iter->substr_cur))', '      iter->substr_cur++;', "      *(iter->substr_end) = '\\0';"], 'added_lines': ["      *(iter->substr_end++) = '\\0';"]}
description: Mutt 1.11.0 through 2.0.x before 2.0.7 (and NeoMutt 2019-10-25 through 2021-05-04) has a $imap_qresync issue in which imap/util.c has an out-of-bounds read in situations where an IMAP sequence set ends with a comma. NOTE: the $imap_qresync setting for QRESYNC is not enabled by default.

code_evidence: After advancing substr_cur to substr_end, the code checks only for equality with eostr; the loop then dereferences *substr_cur while skipping NUL bytes without any bound against eostr.
strchr searches from substr_cur and, when a comma is found, writes a NUL at substr_end and leaves substr_end pointing at that NUL rather than past it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences memory beyond the intended string buffer, matching CWE-125. This is a read overrun, not a write, so out-of-bounds read rather than out-of-bounds write applies.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a sequence set ends with a comma, substr_end is set to the NUL just before eostr. On the next call substr_cur becomes that NUL, the equality check with eostr passes, and the skip loop reads *substr_cur past the end of the buffer. The root cause is the unbounded NUL-skipping loop; the trigger is a trailing comma, and the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
x86/pod: prevent infinite loop when shattering large pages

When populating pages, the PoD may need to split large ones using
p2m_set_entry and request the caller to retry (see ept_get_entry for
instance).

p2m_set_entry may fail to shatter if it is not possible to allocate
memory for the new page table. However, the error is not propagated
resulting to the callers to retry infinitely the PoD.

Prevent the infinite loop by return false when it is not possible to
shatter the large mapping.

This is XSA-246.

Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <julien.grall@linaro.org>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfn_aligned, INVALID_MFN, PAGE_ORDER_2M,', '                      p2m_populate_on_demand, p2m->default_access);', '        return true;', '    p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfn_aligned, mfn, order, p2m_ram_rw,', '                  p2m->default_access);', '    /* Remap this 2-meg region in singleton chunks */', '    for ( i = 0; i < (1UL << order); i++ )', '        p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfn_add(gfn_aligned, i), INVALID_MFN, PAGE_ORDER_4K,', '                      p2m_populate_on_demand, p2m->default_access);'], 'added_lines': ['        return !p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfn_aligned, INVALID_MFN, PAGE_ORDER_2M,', '                              p2m_populate_on_demand, p2m->default_access);', '    if ( p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfn_aligned, mfn, order, p2m_ram_rw,', '                       p2m->default_access) )', '    {', '        p2m_pod_cache_add(p2m, p, order);', '        goto out_fail;', '    }', '     * Remap this 2-meg region in singleton chunks. See the comment on the', '     * 1G page splitting path above for why a single call suffices.', '     *', '    if ( p2m_set_entry(p2m, gfn_aligned, INVALID_MFN, PAGE_ORDER_4K,', '                       p2m_populate_on_demand, p2m->default_access) )', '        return false;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing HVM guest OS users to cause a denial of service (infinite loop and host OS hang) by leveraging the mishandling of Populate on Demand (PoD) errors.

code_evidence: The 1G path calls p2m_set_entry to shatter into 2M pages but discards its return value and unconditionally returns true, so a failed shatter (e.g., page-table allocation failure) is reported as success.
The normal populate path likewise ignores p2m_set_entry's return value and proceeds to update mfn/gpfn mappings as if the entry were installed.
The remap_and_retry path ignores p2m_set_entry return values for each 4K remap and returns true, signaling the caller to retry even when shattering failed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-755 fits because the function fails to handle the exceptional p2m_set_entry error condition, treating failure as success. The consequence (infinite retry loop) is the downstream effect, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: p2m_set_entry failures during large-page shattering are not propagated. Trigger: a PoD populate requiring a split where allocating the new page table fails. The caller sees success and retries, causing an infinite loop and host hang (DoS).

description: Espruino before 1.99 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) and potential Information Disclosure with a user crafted input file via a Buffer Overflow during syntax parsing because strncpy is misused in jslex.c.

code_evidence: Each switch case copies a fixed string literal into caller-supplied buffer str using strncpy with the caller's len, without verifying len is large enough for the literal; if len is smaller than the literal, strncpy truncates and does not NUL-terminate, leaving str unterminated (e.g. "UNFINISHED TEMPLATE LITERAL" needs 25 bytes).

The operator-name path computes p by scanning tokenNames until n reaches 0, then strncpy(str, &tokenNames[p], len) copies a NUL-terminated operator name into str again bounded only by len; a short len truncates without terminating, and p is bounded only by sizeof(tokenNames), not by len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 covers writing past the intended buffer; here the writes into str are governed by an unvalidated caller length and lack of termination guarantee, the same unsafe bounded-copy pattern. It is not CWE-125 (over-read) because the defect is in the bounded write/termination contract, though the downstream effect may be an over-read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy length is the caller's len rather than a size checked against the source literal and destination capacity, and the function never guarantees NUL termination. Trigger: a caller passing a len smaller than the literal/operator name. Consequence: buffer content past the intended copy is not written here, but truncation leaves an unterminated buffer that later string operations may read past, and the missing bound check is the underlying unsafe write pattern; the description reports overflow/DoS/information disclosure during syntax parsing.

code_evidence: Line 10 computes bitmap->length as DstWidth * DstHeight * GetBytesPerPixel(bitmap->format) in UINT32 arithmetic without validating the multiplication; the result is passed to _aligned_malloc at line 11 as the heap allocation size.

Lines 14-53 then decode into bitmap->data using DstWidth/DstHeight (interleaved_decompress, planar_decompress, freerdp_image_copy) with no check that the allocated bitmap->length matches the pixel count implied by those dimensions.

bitmap->data = (BYTE*) _aligned_malloc(bitmap->length, 16);

commit_msg:
Doing a "get_user_pages()" on a copy-on-write page for reading can be
ambiguous: the page can be COW'ed at any time afterwards, and the
direction of a COW event isn't defined.

Yes, whoever writes to it will generally do the COW, but if the thread
that did the get_user_pages() unmapped the page before the write (and
that could happen due to memory pressure in addition to any outright
action), the writer could also just take over the old page instead.

End result: the get_user_pages() call might result in a page pointer
that is no longer associated with the original VM, and is associated
with - and controlled by - another VM having taken it over instead.

So when doing a get_user_pages() on a COW mapping, the only really safe
thing to do would be to break the COW when getting the page, even when
only getting it for reading.

At the same time, some users simply don't even care.

For example, the perf code wants to look up the page not because it
cares about the page, but because the code simply wants to look up the
physical address of the access for informational purposes, and doesn't
really care about races when a page might be unmapped and remapped
elsewhere.

This adds logic to force a COW event by setting FOLL_WRITE on any
copy-on-write mapping when FOLL_GET (or FOLL_PIN) is used to get a page
pointer as a result.

The current semantics end up being:

 - __get_user_pages_fast(): no change. If you don't ask for a write,
   you won't break COW. You'd better know what you're doing.

 - get_user_pages_fast(): the fast-case "look it up in the page tables
   without anything getting mmap_sem" now refuses to follow a read-only
   page, since it might need COW breaking.  Which happens in the slow
   path - the fast path doesn't know if the memory might be COW or not.

 - get_user_pages() (including the slow-path fallback for gup_fast()):
   for a COW mapping, turn on FOLL_WRITE for FOLL_GET/FOLL_PIN, with
   very similar semantics to FOLL_FORCE.

If it turns out that we want finer granularity (ie "only break COW when
it might actually matter" - things like the zero page are special and
don't need to be broken) we might need to push these semantics deeper
into the lookup fault path.  So if people care enough, it's possible
that we might end up adding a new internal FOLL_BREAK_COW flag to go
with the internal FOLL_COW flag we already have for tracking "I had a
COW".

Alternatively, if it turns out that different callers might want to
explicitly control the forced COW break behavior, we might even want to
make such a flag visible to the users of get_user_pages() instead of
using the above default semantics.

But for now, this is mostly commentary on the issue (this commit message
being a lot bigger than the patch, and that patch in turn is almost all
comments), with that minimal "enable COW breaking early" logic using the
existing FOLL_WRITE behavior.

[ It might be worth noting that we've always had this ambiguity, and it
  could arguably be seen as a user-space issue.

  You only get private COW mappings that could break either way in
  situations where user space is doing cooperative things (ie fork()
  before an execve() etc), but it _is_ surprising and very subtle, and
  fork() is supposed to give you independent address spaces.

  So let's treat this as a kernel issue and make the semantics of
  get_user_pages() easier to understand. Note that obviously a true
  shared mapping will still get a page that can change under us, so this
  does _not_ mean that get_user_pages() somehow returns any "stable"
  page ]

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Tested-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Acked-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Kirill Shutemov <kirill@shutemov.name>
Acked-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Cc: Matthew Wilcox <willy@infradead.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tgup_pgd_range(addr, end, gup_flags, pages, &nr_pinned);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/*', '\t * The FAST_GUP case requires FOLL_WRITE even for pure reads,', '\t * because get_user_pages() may need to cause an early COW in', '\t * order to avoid confusing the normal COW routines. So only', '\t * targets that are already writable are safe to do by just', '\t * looking at the page tables.', '\t */', '\t\tgup_pgd_range(addr, end, gup_flags | FOLL_WRITE, pages, &nr_pinned);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.7.3, related to mm/gup.c and mm/huge_memory.c. The get_user_pages (aka gup) implementation, when used for a copy-on-write page, does not properly consider the semantics of read operations and therefore can grant unintended write access, aka CID-17839856fd58.

code_evidence: The fast GUP path calls gup_pgd_range() with the caller's gup_flags after only disabling local IRQs; it does not force FOLL_WRITE, so a read-only COW page can be pinned without breaking COW.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because pinning the page and the later COW/unmap/remap by a concurrent code sequence are not made exclusive or atomic, allowing the shared page to change under the pinner.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A caller pins a COW page for reading without breaking COW. The page can later be COW'ed or taken over by another VM concurrently, so the returned page pointer no longer corresponds to the original VM; the window between pinning and later use is the race.

commit_msg:
Correctly load/initialize classes when using ConstantPool

- do not load classes in the "ifLoaded" calls
- never intitialize classes in the natives
- do not update the constant pool when querying from the natives

Fixes: #12016

[ci skip]

Signed-off-by: Graham Chapman <graham_chapman@ca.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn getFieldAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_JIT_COMPILE_TIME | J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL);'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn getFieldAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CLASS_LOAD);']}
description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: The native getFieldAtIfLoaded0 resolves the field by calling getFieldAt with J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_JIT_COMPILE_TIME | J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL, which permits resolution without ensuring the declaring class has been initialized before its static field is exposed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-909 fits because a resource (class state) is exposed before its required initialization; the missing constraint is the absence of a class-initialization step during resolution, not merely a wrong flag value or a race.

evidence_lines.code: return getFieldAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_JIT_COMPILE_TIME | J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the resolve flags allow the constant-pool entry to be resolved/JIT-compiled without triggering class initialization, so a static field can be read before its class initializer runs. Trigger: a caller invokes the ConstantPool API on an uninitialized class. Consequence: uninitialized static values may be observed, contradicting JVM initialization guarantees.

Fix segfault when attempting to convert string to float16.

To make sure this gets fixed, add test for converting string to any numeric type.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 286650886
Change-Id: I81f770ec2bbd33a863e8057ce198c679912fa8e0
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (TF_PREDICT_FALSE(sizeof(T) < sizeof(double) && std::isinf(*out) &&', '                         std::isfinite(as_double))) {', '    *out = PyInt_AS_LONG(v);', '    *out = PyLong_AsDouble(v);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (TF_PREDICT_FALSE(CheckForOverflow<T>(as_double, out))) {', '    *out = static_cast<T>(PyInt_AS_LONG(v));', '    *out = static_cast<T>(PyLong_AsDouble(v));']}
description: In TensorFlow before 1.15.2 and 2.0.1, converting a string (from Python) to a tf.float16 value results in a segmentation fault in eager mode as the format checks for this use case are only in the graph mode. This issue can lead to denial of service in inference/training where a malicious attacker can send a data point which contains a string instead of a tf.float16 value. Similar effects can be obtained by manipulating saved models and checkpoints whereby replacing a scalar tf.float16 value with a scalar string will trigger this issue due to automatic conversions. This can be easily reproduced by tf.constant("hello", tf.float16), if eager execution is enabled. This issue is patched in TensorFlow 1.15.1 and 2.0.1 with this vulnerability patched. TensorFlow 2.1.0 was released after we fixed the issue, thus it is not affected. Users are encouraged to switch to TensorFlow 1.15.1, 2.0.1 or 2.1.0.

code_evidence: PyFloat_Check guards the float path; the double is narrowed via static_cast<T> and only an overflow check (isinf of narrowed value with finite double) is performed before returning success.

PyLong path casts PyLong_AsDouble result directly to T; the only check is PyErr_Occurred, not whether the value fits T, so a large integer or a string-convertible object can be narrowed without range validation.

If no type branch matches, ErrorMixedTypes is returned; but the conversion branches accept inputs and narrow them without validating that the input's type/value is compatible with T before writing *out.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the converter receives input and fails to validate its type/value properties (representability as T) before processing, leading to unsafe narrowing and a crash. This is improper input validation rather than a pure overflow-only weakness, since the missing check is the type/range compatibility of the incoming value.

evidence_lines.code: return ErrorMixedTypes;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates only some properties of the input (float overflow, Python error) but does not validate that the input type/value can be safely represented as T before narrowing and writing *out. Trigger: calling tf.constant("hello", tf.float16) or similar string-to-float16 conversion in eager mode reaches this converter, which mishandles the input instead of rejecting it. Supported consequence: memory corruption/segfault, enabling denial of service.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

Reviewed-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Fam Zheng <famz@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Daniel P. Berrange <berrange@redhat.com>
Message-id: 20170213135235.12274-8-pbonzini@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>

description: An assertion-failure flaw was found in Qemu before 2.10.1, in the Network Block Device (NBD) server's initial connection negotiation, where the I/O coroutine was undefined. This could crash the qemu-nbd server if a client sent unexpected data during connection negotiation. A remote user or process could use this flaw to crash the qemu-nbd server resulting in denial of service.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no assert() or similar statement; the only yield and error-setting logic does not establish a reachable assertion, so CWE-617 is not supported.

commit_msg:
analysisd: fix off-by-one in OS_CleanMSG.

When removing the '[ID xx facility.severity]' substring of a syslog
message in `OS_CleanMSG` care needs to be taken to stay within the
bounds of the msg buffer when advancing past the `] ` in the msg.

Prev. to this commit the `pieces` pointer is incremented by 2 when there
may be only 1 character remaining before the null terminator.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                /* Going after the ] */', "                pieces = strchr(pieces, ']');"], 'added_lines': ['                /* Going after the "] " */', '                pieces = strstr(pieces, "] ");']}
description: In OSSEC-HIDS 2.7 through 3.5.0, the server component responsible for log analysis (ossec-analysisd) is vulnerable to an off-by-one heap-based buffer overflow during the cleaning of crafted syslog msgs (received from authenticated remote agents and delivered to the analysisd processing queue by ossec-remoted).

code_evidence: Lines 210-213 check only that pieces starts with "[ID " (pieces[0..3]) after the earlier loglen>26 branch; the subsequent strchr at line 215 locates the ']' and line 217 advances pieces by 2 unconditionally when a match is found. If the ']' is the final character before the NUL terminator (or followed by only one byte), pieces+2 moves past the end of the allocated buffer, and line 218 stores that out-of-bounds pointer into lf->log for later dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked pieces += 2 writes/positions a pointer past the intended heap buffer boundary, allowing memory beyond the allocation to be modified. This is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the resulting pointer is stored and used for subsequent writes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code advances the pointer by a fixed 2 bytes after locating ']' without verifying that both a ']' and a following space exist before the NUL terminator. Trigger: a crafted syslog message (e.g. "[ID 1]" with no trailing space) reaching this branch. Consequence: lf->log points one byte past the buffer end, causing an off-by-one out-of-bounds write/read on the heap during later processing.

commit_msg:
It's really bad when the allocation bitmaps and the inode table
overlap with the block group descriptors, since it causes random
corruption of the bg descriptors.  So we really want to head those off
at the pass.

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=199865

Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\text4_fsblk_t last_bg_block = sb_block + ext4_bg_num_gdb(sb, 0) + 1;', '\t\tif (block_bitmap >= sb_block + 1 &&', '\t\t    block_bitmap <= last_bg_block) {', '\t\t\text4_msg(sb, KERN_ERR, "ext4_check_descriptors: "', '\t\t\t\t "Block bitmap for group %u overlaps "', '\t\t\t\t "block group descriptors", i);', '\t\t\tif (!sb_rdonly(sb))', '\t\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t\t}', '\t\tif (inode_bitmap >= sb_block + 1 &&', '\t\t    inode_bitmap <= last_bg_block) {', '\t\t\text4_msg(sb, KERN_ERR, "ext4_check_descriptors: "', '\t\t\t\t "Inode bitmap for group %u overlaps "', '\t\t\t\t "block group descriptors", i);', '\t\t\tif (!sb_rdonly(sb))', '\t\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t\t}', '\t\t\tif (!sb_rdonly(sb))', '\t\t\t\treturn 0;', '\t\t}', '\t\tif (inode_table >= sb_block + 1 &&', '\t\t    inode_table <= last_bg_block) {', '\t\t\text4_msg(sb, KERN_ERR, "ext4_check_descriptors: "', '\t\t\t\t "Inode table for group %u overlaps "', '\t\t\t\t "block group descriptors", i);']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's ext4 filesystem. A local user can cause an out-of-bounds write and a denial of service or unspecified other impact is possible by mounting and operating a crafted ext4 filesystem image.

code_evidence: Descriptor-derived block_bitmap, inode_bitmap and inode_table are read from the on-disk group descriptor via ext4_block_bitmap/ext4_inode_bitmap/ext4_inode_table into local ext4_fsblk_t variables.

The block_bitmap is only rejected when it equals sb_block or falls outside [first_block,last_block]; a crafted image can place it inside the block group descriptor region, which is later written as bitmap data.
Similarly inode_bitmap is validated only against sb_block and the group range, so a descriptor overlapping the bg descriptor area is accepted.
inode_table is checked only for equality with sb_block and against the group bounds; an inode table overlapping the block group descriptors passes validation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing overlap constraint permits metadata writes to land on the block group descriptor region, i.e. writes outside the intended bitmap/inode-table buffers, matching CWE-787. It is a missing-validation cause rather than merely an integer miscalculation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ext4_check_descriptors does not reject allocation bitmaps or the inode table that overlap the block group descriptor blocks, relying only on equality with sb_block and range checks. Trigger: mounting and operating a crafted ext4 image whose group descriptor places these metadata blocks over the bg descriptor area. Consequence: subsequent bitmap/inode-table writes corrupt the block group descriptors, yielding an out-of-bounds write and possible denial of service or memory corruption.

description: GNW dissector crash in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.2 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.10 and allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

commit_msg:
Fix heap-buffer-overflow in getString

getString is allocating a 4-bytes buffer to store an 'R' and an
8-bit number.

t=malloc(4); /* Rdd */
sprintf(t,"R%d", act->p.RegisterNumber );
return t;

Since up to three digits can be required to store the 8-bit
number, the buffer has to be 5 bytes long.

In this commit we also fix the PUSH_DOUBLE case by dynamically
computing the required buffer size.

This commit fixes #116 (CVE-2018-7867).

+++ func_after
@@ -26,7 +26,7 @@

 #if 0
 	  case 4: /* REGISTER */
-                t=malloc(4); /* Rdd */
+		t=malloc(5); /* Rddd */
   		sprintf(t,"R%d", act->p.RegisterNumber );
   		return t;
 #endif

When len is zero, the len < caplen test at line 12 can be false (e.g., caplen also zero), so validation passes and res is returned at line 18 with a zero-length packet accepted.

description: In Wireshark 3.0.0, the Rbm dissector could go into an infinite loop. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/file-rbm.c by handling unknown object types safely.

and provide the correct length.

description: The IKEv2 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isakmp.c, several functions.

code_evidence: The function copies the IKEv2 header into e, derives len as ntohs(e.len) - 4, and bounds-checks only vid (the bytes after the header) with ND_TCHECK2(*vid, len).
Later, when 2 < ndo->ndo_vflag and 4 < len, rawprint reads ntohs(e.len) - 4 bytes starting at ext + 1.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the parser reads memory beyond the intended buffer; the weakness is an unchecked length driving a read, not a write or integer overflow per se.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the header length e.len is attacker-controlled and the check covers vid but not the rawprint read region; if the captured packet is shorter than the length claimed in e.len, the earlier ND_TCHECK2 may pass for vid while rawprint still reads past the end of the captured buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read and possible crash or disclosure.

description: A vulnerability in the Android media framework (ex) related to composition of frames lacking a color map. Product: Android. Versions: 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2, 8.0, 8.1. Android ID: A-68399117.

code_evidence: The color map is taken from gif->SColorMap and overridden by frame.ImageDesc.ColorMap when present, so cmap may be NULL for a frame lacking a color map.
The only check on cmap is a warning: if cmap is NULL or ColorCount mismatches, it merely logs 'potentially corrupt color map' and continues.
Execution then unconditionally dereferences cmap by passing it to copyLine inside the loop over copyHeight, with no guard preventing the NULL/incorrect color map from being used.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts attacker-controlled GIF color-map metadata but fails to validate it (NULL, inconsistent ColorCount/BitsPerPixel) before processing, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The missing constraint on cmap directly enables unsafe use; this is a validation failure rather than an encoding or filtering issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the frame's color map (or global color map) is not validated before use; a NULL or inconsistent cmap is only logged. Trigger: a crafted GIF whose frame lacks a color map and no usable global map. Consequence: copyLine dereferences an invalid/NULL color map during composition, causing memory corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
Limit the number of HTTP requests processed from a connection in I/O cycle

Signed-off-by: Yan Avlasov <yavlasov@google.com>

Signed-off-by: Ryan Northey <ryan@synca.io>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '  filter_manager_.decodeData(data, end_stream);'], 'added_lines': ['  if (!state_.deferred_to_next_io_iteration_) {', '    filter_manager_.decodeData(data, end_stream);', '  } else {', '    if (!deferred_data_) {', '      deferred_data_ = std::make_unique<Buffer::OwnedImpl>();', '    }', '    deferred_data_->move(data);', '    state_.deferred_end_stream_ = end_stream;', '  }']}
description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

code_evidence: decodeData unconditionally adds received bytes to streamInfo and immediately forwards every data buffer to filter_manager_.decodeData(data, end_stream); there is no per-connection or per-I/O-cycle cap on how many data frames or bytes are processed in one dispatcher turn.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the code lacks throttling over the number of resources (data buffers/streams) processed per cycle, allowing a remote peer to drive excessive consumption. The patch defers data to the next I/O iteration, confirming the missing per-cycle limit; this is resource exhaustion, not a memory-safety defect.

evidence_lines.code:
filter_manager_.streamInfo().addBytesReceived(data.length());
filter_manager_.decodeData(data, end_stream);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function processes each incoming data buffer synchronously without limiting the number of requests/streams handled per I/O iteration. Trigger: a peer rapidly resets many streams or floods data frames within one event-loop cycle. Consequence: unbounded CPU/memory consumption during that cycle, degrading or exhausting server resources (DoS).

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can trigger a null pointer dereference in the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.EditDistance`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/79865b542f9ffdc9caeb255631f7c56f1d4b6517/tensorflow/core/kernels/edit_distance_op.cc#L103-L159) has incomplete validation of the input parameters. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: ValidateShapes checks matrix/vector rank and that hypothesis_shape.NumElements matches hypothesis_indices.dim_size(1) [30], but never verifies hypothesis_values.NumElements() equals hypothesis_indices.dim_size(0). Likewise it validates truth_shape rank [36] and truth_indices.dim_size(1) [41], but omits any check that truth_values.NumElements() matches truth_indices.dim_size(0). The function returns Status::OK() [53] for sparse tensor triples whose values vector length disagrees with the index row count, so downstream code indexing values by row index can read out of bounds or dereference invalid memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing cardinality constraint permits later code to dereference a pointer it assumes valid, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. It is not merely a shape mismatch (CWE-20/1284) because the supported impact is a crash from an invalid pointer access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: incomplete shape validation in ValidateShapes accepts mismatched values/index cardinalities. Trigger: a crafted SparseTensor where values.NumElements() differs from indices.dim_size(0). Consequence: downstream EditDistance code performs an invalid access, yielding a null pointer dereference and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Add support for different number of page table levels dependent
on the highest address used for a process. This will cause a 31 bit
process to use a two level page table instead of the four level page
table that is the default after the pud has been introduced. Likewise
a normal 64 bit process will use three levels instead of four. Only
if a process runs out of the 4 tera bytes which can be addressed with
a three level page table the fourth level is dynamically added. Then
the process can use up to 8 peta byte.

Signed-off-by: Martin Schwidefsky <schwidefsky@de.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (unlikely(prev == next))', '\t\treturn;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The fork implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.5 on s390 platforms mishandles the case of four page-table levels, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted application, related to arch/s390/include/asm/mmu_context.h and arch/s390/include/asm/pgalloc.h.

code_evidence: The function unconditionally updates next->cpu_vm_mask and calls update_mm(next, tsk) without checking whether prev and next refer to the same mm, so the previous early-return guard on prev == next is gone.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code fails to validate/guard the input condition prev == next before processing, which is the required safety property for this path; this missing check matches CWE-20's improper validation of input properties before processing. It is not a memory-corruption root cause like CWE-119, but a missing precondition check enabling unsafe processing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the switch_mm path no longer short-circuits when prev == next, so mm state is re-applied even when no address-space switch is needed. On s390 with dynamically added page-table levels, this re-execution during fork can operate on an mm whose page-table level configuration is inconsistent, leading to a system crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Correctly load/initialize classes when using ConstantPool

- do not load classes in the "ifLoaded" calls
- never intitialize classes in the natives
- do not update the constant pool when querying from the natives

Fixes: #12016

[ci skip]

Signed-off-by: Graham Chapman <graham_chapman@ca.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (ramCPEntry != NULL) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif ((NULL != ramCPEntry) && J9_ARE_NO_BITS_SET(resolveFlags, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE)) {']}
description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: Class initialization is skipped only when J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CLASS_INIT is set; otherwise initializeClass is invoked when initStatus is not succeeded, and on failure staticAddress is nulled and the function exits without writing the CP entry.
When Java code cannot run, the function aborts via done with staticAddress NULL rather than caching a resolved static-field entry.

The CP entry is populated (flagsAndClass and valueOffset) using localClassAndFlags only when ramCPEntry is non-NULL; the patched guard adds J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE so the entry is not updated when the caller requested a query-only resolution.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is failure to gate resource (class/CP entry) publication on initialization state, matching CWE-909 missing initialization of a critical resource. The patched check prevents updating the CP entry when CP updates are disallowed, keeping resolution from exposing a class before initialization.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the RAM constant-pool static-field entry was written even when the caller requested resolution without CP update (e.g. ConstantPool queries), publishing a resolved field reference before the defining class initialization completed. Trigger: a caller using J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE on a not-yet-initialized class. Consequence: later resolution finds a cached entry and can access static members while class init has not run, exposing uninitialized/default values.

commit_msg:
problem: zeromq connects peer before handshake is completed

Solution: delay connecting the peer pipe until the handshake is completed
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '            if (_mechanism == NULL && _has_handshake_stage)', '                _session->engine_ready ();']}
description: In ZeroMQ before version 4.3.3, there is a denial-of-service vulnerability. Users with TCP transport public endpoints, even with CURVE/ZAP enabled, are impacted. If a raw TCP socket is opened and connected to an endpoint that is fully configured with CURVE/ZAP, legitimate clients will not be able to exchange any message. Handshakes complete successfully, and messages are delivered to the library, but the server application never receives them. This is patched in version 4.3.3.

code_evidence: When _handshaking is true, handshake() is called; on success _handshaking is set false and execution falls through to message processing, otherwise the function returns false.
After decoding, _session->flush() is invoked unconditionally, so session processing continues even before an engine_ready notification exists.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function lacks a constraint/state transition needed to bound connection processing, so completed-but-unusable connections persist and consume limited resources, matching CWE-400's uncontrolled maintenance of a limited resource. The consequence is availability impact, not merely a protocol error.

evidence_lines.code: _session->flush ();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The engine begins normal message flow as soon as the handshake returns, without signaling the session that the engine is ready (the added engine_ready call is absent). A peer can complete handshakes and deliver messages that are decoded but never surfaced to the application, leaving connections and queued state maintained; with many such peers, server resources are retained, denying legitimate clients.

The fields are allocated up to MAX_USAGE, meaning that potentially, we do
not have enough fields to fit the incoming values.
Add checks and silence KASAN.

Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>

description: The hid_input_field function in drivers/hid/hid-core.c in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows physically proximate attackers to obtain sensitive information from kernel memory or cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) by connecting a device, as demonstrated by a Logitech DJ receiver.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4009: reading one byte beyond the end of the line

Problem:    Reading one byte beyond the end of the line.
Solution:   Check for NUL byte first.
description: vim is vulnerable to Out-of-bounds Read

code_evidence: cmd is set to ea.cmd, the whitespace-skipped command pointer. The condition evaluates cmd[0] == cmd[1] to detect a doubled ''+'' or ''-'' range character. If cmd[0] is the terminating NUL (empty command), cmd[1] reads one byte past the end of the allocated line buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 covers reading data past the end of an intended buffer. The cmd[1] access beyond the NUL terminator is exactly such an out-of-bounds read; the patch adds the cmd[0] != NUL guard, confirming the missing bound.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the doubled-character test accesses cmd[1] without first confirming cmd[0] is a non-NUL character, so for an empty/short command the index 1 lies beyond the string terminator. Trigger: a Vim9 def function line whose command position is empty. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of one byte past the line buffer, matching the commit's reported over-read.

commit_msg:
Always set context node before calling XPath iterators

The xmlXPathNext* iterators rely on the XPath context node being set to
the start node of the iteration. Some parts of the code base like the
xsl:key functions also leave the context node in an unspecified state.
Make sure that the context node is reset before invoking the XPath
iterators. Also backup and restore the context node in
xsltNumberFormatGetMultipleLevel for good measure.

This bug could also lead to type confusion and invalid reads in
connection with namespace nodes.

Fixes #13. Also see the Chromium bug report:

https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=930663

Thanks to Nicolas Grégoire for the report.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    context->xpathCtxt->node = node;', '\tfor (ancestor = node;', '\t     (ancestor != NULL) && (ancestor->type != XML_DOCUMENT_NODE);', '\t     ancestor = xmlXPathNextAncestor(parser, ancestor)) {', '', '\t\tfor (preceding =', '                        xmlXPathNextPrecedingSibling(parser, ancestor);', '\t\t     preceding != NULL;', '\t\t     preceding =', '\t\t        xmlXPathNextPrecedingSibling(parser, preceding)) {', ''], 'added_lines': ['    xmlNodePtr oldCtxtNode;', '    oldCtxtNode = context->xpathCtxt->node;', '\tancestor = node;', '\twhile ((ancestor != NULL) && (ancestor->type != XML_DOCUMENT_NODE)) {', '            /*', '             * The xmlXPathNext* iterators require that the context node is', '             * set to the start node. Calls to xsltTestCompMatch* may also', '             * leave the context node in an undefined state, so make sure', '             * that the context node is reset before each iterator invocation.', '             */', '', '                context->xpathCtxt->node = ancestor;', '                preceding = xmlXPathNextPrecedingSibling(parser, ancestor);', '                while (preceding != NULL) {', '                    context->xpathCtxt->node = ancestor;', '                    preceding =', '                        xmlXPathNextPrecedingSibling(parser, preceding);', '            context->xpathCtxt->node = node;', '            ancestor = xmlXPathNextAncestor(parser, ancestor);', '    context->xpathCtxt->node = oldCtxtNode;']}
description: Type confusion in xsltNumberFormatGetMultipleLevel prior to libxslt 1.1.33 could allow attackers to potentially exploit heap corruption via crafted XML data.

code_evidence: Line 14 sets the XPath context node once before constructing the parser; the ancestor loop at 17-19 advances via xmlXPathNextAncestor without re-establishing the context node between iterations.

The preceding-sibling loop at 25-29 calls xmlXPathNextPrecedingSibling(parser, ancestor) and then continues from the returned node, again without resetting the context node after any intervening call.
Inside that loop, xsltTestCompMatchCount at 30-32 may mutate the shared xpathCtxt state, so the subsequent iterator call operates on a context node inconsistent with the node being iterated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The shared XPath context node is treated as one node type by the iterator while actually referencing an incompatible node left by a prior match call, which is exactly accessing a resource using an incompatible type. This is not merely a null dereference; the wrong typed node drives the iterator's memory access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: XPath iterators require the context node to equal the iteration start node, but xsltTestCompMatch* calls leave context->xpathCtxt->node in an unspecified state and the pre-patch code never restores it. Trigger: crafted XML/XSLT number formatting with count/from patterns so an intervening match test runs before the next iterator call. Consequence: the iterator interprets a namespace or other node as the expected node kind, yielding type confusion and invalid reads/heap corruption.

commit_msg:
Prevent division by 0 in `fully_connected.cc`

PiperOrigin-RevId: 385137282
Change-Id: If201e69b6e0048f0be001330b4b977e2b46db2cb
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, filter->dims->data[1] != 0);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the implementation of fully connected layers in TFLite is [vulnerable to a division by zero error](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/fully_connected.cc#L226). We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 718721986aa137691ee23f03638867151f74935f. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: input_size is computed by multiplying input dimensions [24-27]; after checking filter rank is 2 [28], the code computes batch_size = input_size / filter->dims->data[1] [29] without verifying that the filter's second dimension (data[1]) is nonzero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly performs a division whose divisor is a model-supplied dimension lacking a nonzero check, which is precisely CWE-369 (Divide By Zero). The patch adds the missing guard, confirming the divisor is the unsafe operand; this is not merely an out-of-bounds read but an arithmetic division by zero.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the divisor filter->dims->data[1] comes from an attacker-controllable filter tensor shape and is not constrained to be nonzero before the division at line 29. Trigger: a fully connected model whose filter has a zero-sized second dimension. Consequence: integer division by zero, crashing the PrepareImpl path (denial of service).

commit_msg:
[lite] Update TfLiteIntArrayCreate to return size_t

PiperOrigin-RevId: 416439896
Change-Id: I847f69b68d1ddaff4b1e925a09b8b69c1756653b
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int alloc_size = TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(size);'], 'added_lines': ['  size_t alloc_size = TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(size);']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. An attacker can craft a TFLite model that would cause an integer overflow in `TfLiteIntArrayCreate`. The `TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes` returns an `int` instead of a `size_t. An attacker can control model inputs such that `computed_size` overflows the size of `int` datatype. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 2 stores the result of TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(size) in an int alloc_size; the helper itself returns int, so a large attacker-controlled size can wrap to a small or negative value before the check on line 3. Line 4 then passes the wrapped alloc_size to malloc.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size calculation that can wrap because the result is stored in int, matching CWE-190 integer overflow/wraparound used in a memory-allocation size. It is not merely a bad bounds check; the arithmetic overflow is the root cause enabling the undersized allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the byte-size computation is performed and held in a signed int, so a crafted TFLite model size overflows/wraps to a small positive value that passes the <=0 guard. The trigger is an attacker-controlled array size; the supported consequence is an undersized heap allocation followed by writes to ret->size and later array elements, causing heap corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Harden slave timer list handling

A slave timer instance might be still accessible in a racy way while
operating the master instance as it lacks of locking.  Since the
master operation is mostly protected with timer->lock, we should cope
with it while changing the slave instance, too.  Also, some linked
lists (active_list and ack_list) of slave instances aren't unlinked
immediately at stopping or closing, and this may lead to unexpected
accesses.

This patch tries to address these issues.  It adds spin lock of
timer->lock (either from master or slave, which is equivalent) in a
few places.  For avoiding a deadlock, we ensure that the global
slave_active_lock is always locked at first before each timer lock.

Also, ack and active_list of slave instances are properly unlinked at
snd_timer_stop() and snd_timer_close().

Last but not least, remove the superfluous call of _snd_timer_stop()
at removing slave links.  This is a noop, and calling it may confuse
readers wrt locking.  Further cleanup will follow in a later patch.

Actually we've got reports of use-after-free by syzkaller fuzzer, and
this hopefully fixes these issues.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tlist_del_init(&timeri->ack_list);', '\t\t\tlist_del_init(&timeri->active_list);']}
description: sound/core/timer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 employs a locking approach that does not consider slave timer instances, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (race condition, use-after-free, and system crash) via a crafted ioctl call.

code_evidence: For a slave timer instance, the code clears SNDRV_TIMER_IFLG_RUNNING under slave_active_lock but does not unlink timeri->ack_list or timeri->active_list, so the slave's list nodes remain linked after stopping and can be reached concurrently through the master instance.
For a master timer, ack_list and active_list are unlinked only while holding timer->lock, so the slave path lacks the corresponding list removal and the master/slave locking is not coordinated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's operations on shared timer lists and flags are not consistently serialized between slave and master paths, creating a timing window where concurrent code accesses the same shared resource; this is CWE-362. The resulting use-after-free is a consequence, not the race itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: slave timer instances stop without unlinking their ack_list/active_list entries, and the slave path does not take the timer lock used by master operations, so a concurrent master operation can traverse a slave list node that is being freed or reused. Trigger: a local ioctl stops/closes a slave timer while the master instance operates concurrently, producing a race and use-after-free that can crash the system (DoS).

commit_msg: imgcodecs: remove assert() usage
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            assert( swap_rb );'], 'added_lines': ['            CV_Assert(swap_rb);']}
description: In OpenCV 3.3.1, an assertion failure happens in cv::RBaseStream::setPos in modules/imgcodecs/src/bitstrm.cpp because of an incorrect integer cast.

code_evidence: Line 9 derives swap_rb from caller-controlled flags via flags & CV_CVTIMG_SWAP_RB, so an external caller can set it to 0. Line 38 enters the conversion block when src_cn != dst_cn or (src_cn == 3 && swap_rb); with src_cn==3 and dst_cn==3 the condition only holds when swap_rb is nonzero. However, code is computed as src_cn*10+dst_cn (line 42), so code 33 is reachable for 3-to-3 conversion, and line 59 asserts swap_rb.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because an assert() in cvConvertImage is reachable from caller-controlled flags and terminates the process instead of returning a recoverable error. The change from assert to CV_Assert does not remove the reachable assertion; it only changes the error mechanism, so the weakness remains.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function relies on assert(swap_rb) at line 59 in the case-33 branch to guard the RGB2BGR conversion. The assertion is reachable with swap_rb==0 through the 3-channel to 3-channel path (code 33), so a caller passing flags without CV_CVTIMG_SWAP_RB can trigger an abort. The root cause is a reachable assertion rather than a validated error return; the supported consequence is process termination (denial of service).

commit_msg:
usb: gadget: don't release an existing dev->buf

dev->buf does not need to be released if it already exists before
executing dev_config.

Acked-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Signed-off-by: Hangyu Hua <hbh25y@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20211231172138.7993-2-hbh25y@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tgoto fail;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tspin_unlock_irq(&dev->lock);', '\t\treturn value;']}
description: drivers/usb/gadget/legacy/inode.c in the Linux kernel through 5.16.8 mishandles dev->buf release.

code_evidence: At lines 30-33, when dev->buf already exists, kbuf is freed but the code jumps to fail instead of returning; fail then kfree()s dev->buf at line 78 and sets it NULL.
The fail label is reached both after dev->buf was assigned (line 34 onward) and in this pre-existing-buf path, so the same cleanup releases two different pointers and mutates dev->buf state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-763 fits because the code performs resource release incorrectly: it invokes the shared kfree cleanup path on a pointer (dev->buf) that should not be released in this branch, releasing an invalid/live reference rather than the intended kbuf.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pre-existing dev->buf branch frees the newly allocated kbuf yet routes to the shared fail cleanup, which releases dev->buf and clears it. Trigger: calling dev_config when dev->buf is already set. Consequence: an existing buffer/reference is released and dev->buf is nulled, causing use-after-free or double-free on later access and possible memory corruption or crash; the fix unlocks and returns without touching dev->buf.

commit_msg:
(for 4.9.3) CVE-2018-14461/LDP: Fix a bounds check

In ldp_tlv_print(), the FT Session TLV length must be 12, not 8 (RFC3479)

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Konrad Rieck and
Bhargava Shastry.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).

Moreover:
Add and use tstr[].
Add a comment.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tTLV_TCHECK(8);', '    ND_PRINT((ndo, "\\n\\t\\t packet exceeded snapshot"));'], 'added_lines': ['\tTLV_TCHECK(12);', '\t/* 16 bits (FT Flags) + 16 bits (Reserved) */', '    ND_PRINT((ndo, "%s", tstr));']}
description: The LDP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.3 has a buffer over-read in print-ldp.c:ldp_tlv_print().

code_evidence: TLV_TCHECK(8) only verifies 8 bytes are available before parsing the FT Session TLV body.
After the flags, tptr+=4 skips 4 bytes, then EXTRACT_32BITS(tptr) reads 4 bytes at offset 4 (bytes 4-7).
tptr+=4 again, then EXTRACT_32BITS(tptr) reads 4 more bytes at offset 8 (bytes 8-11), beyond the 8-byte check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code reads beyond the buffer bounds established by its own check, which is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). This is not merely an integer issue; the constraint on required length is missing, so a short TLV triggers the read.

TLV_TCHECK(8);
ft_flags = EXTRACT_16BITS(tptr);

tptr+=4;
ui = EXTRACT_32BITS(tptr);

tptr+=4;
ui = EXTRACT_32BITS(tptr);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The length check validates only 8 bytes of the FT Session TLV, but parsing consumes flags (4 bytes), Reconnect Timeout (4 bytes) and Recovery Time (4 bytes), requiring 12. A captured packet with a short TLV passes TLV_TCHECK(8) and the second EXTRACT_32BITS reads past the validated snapshot, causing an out-of-bounds read (and potential crash).

description: Heap-based buffer overflow in content/renderer/media/canvas_capture_handler.cc in Google Chrome before 51.0.2704.63 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted web site.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs buffer read/write operations whose indices are not restricted to the actual source buffer bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory access. The root cause is missing size validation between source and destination, not a stride/alignment defect alone, so CWE-119 is the supported class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The copy loop bounds and source indexing are derived from the destination frame's coded size, with no verification that the source buffer actually contains that many RGBA pixels. When the caller supplies a source smaller than the destination's coded size (e.g., mismatched/odd or visible-rect-derived dimensions), the reads source[p*4+3] and src_ptr[pixel+3] walk past the source buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read; the writes can similarly exceed the intended destination region.

description: The ZipCommon::isValidPath() function in Zip/src/ZipCommon.cpp in POCO C++ Libraries before 1.8 does not properly restrict the filename value in the ZIP header, which allows attackers to conduct absolute path traversal attacks during the ZIP decompression, and possibly create or overwrite arbitrary files, via a crafted ZIP file, related to a "file path injection vulnerability".

code_evidence: isValidPath only rejects the exact name ".." and the prefixes "../" and "..\\" (lines 5-8), and searches for the bare substrings "/.." and "\\.." (lines 9,11). It never rejects absolute paths such as "/etc/passwd" or "C:\\...", and the substring checks do not cover a trailing ".." component or mixed separators like "/..\\". The function returns true for any path not matching these narrow patterns (line 13).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the restriction check that is supposed to keep extracted paths under the parent directory, but it fails to neutralize absolute path elements and some parent-directory sequences, which is exactly the improper pathname limitation described by CWE-22. The weakness is the incomplete blacklist, not a separate issue such as link following.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The filename taken from the ZIP header is validated only against a small set of hard-coded traversal patterns. A crafted archive entry with an absolute path or a traversal sequence not matching those literals passes validation and is later used to build the extraction target, so the resolved path can fall outside the intended extraction directory, permitting arbitrary file creation or overwrite.

commit_msg:
rtmpt: limit the number of iterations in rtmpt_get_amf_length().

This prevents a infinite-loop caused by crafted packets.

Fix: #17813.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['rtmpt_get_amf_param(tvbuff_t *tvb, gint offset, gint param, const gchar *prop)', '                itemlen = rtmpt_get_amf_length(tvb, offset);', '                                itemlen = rtmpt_get_amf_length(tvb, offset+2+iPropLength);'], 'added_lines': ['rtmpt_get_amf_param(tvbuff_t *tvb, gint offset, proto_item* pi, gint param, const gchar *prop)', '                itemlen = rtmpt_get_amf_length(tvb, offset, pi);', '                if (itemlen == 0)', '                        break;', '                                itemlen = rtmpt_get_amf_length(tvb, offset+2+iPropLength, pi);', '                                if (itemlen == 0)', '                                        break;']}
description: Infinite loop in RTMPT protocol dissector in Wireshark 3.6.0 to 3.6.1 and 3.4.0 to 3.4.11 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: The outer loop continues while remain > 0 && param > 0. itemlen comes from rtmpt_get_amf_length; if it returns 0, offset and remain do not change, so the loop condition never progresses and the loop spins forever.

The inner loop continues while remain > 2. If rtmpt_get_amf_length returns 0 at line 36, offset advances only by 2+iPropLength while remain decreases by the same amount; a value of 0 for itemlen still lets the loop iterate with an unchanged state relation, and crafted lengths can keep remain > 2 indefinitely without reaching the exit path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits: the iteration has an exit condition that crafted input prevents from being reached because the loop-progress variable itemlen can be zero. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the supported consequence is an infinite loop.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loops advance offset/remain using itemlen returned from rtmpt_get_amf_length without ensuring itemlen is non-zero. A crafted packet yielding zero-length AMF items leaves loop state unchanged (or non-decreasing), so the exit condition remain <= 0 / param == 0 is never reached. Consequence is CPU exhaustion (DoS) in the dissector.

commit_msg:
pam_tacplus.c: Fallback to using PID as task ID

If there is a failure obtaining a random task ID for the session
accounting request then fallback to using the PID, as this is unique
for the lifetime of the PAM application and therefore session.

description: libtac in pam_tacplus through 1.5.1 lacks a check for a failure of RAND_bytes()/RAND_pseudo_bytes(). This could lead to use of a non-random/predictable session_id.

code_evidence: The function formats the global task_id into buf with sprintf and adds it as the TACACS+ accounting "task_id" attribute; no check verifies that task_id was successfully randomized before it is sent as the session identifier.

tac_add_attrib(&attr, "task_id", buf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the accounting session identifier is taken directly from task_id without validating that random generation succeeded. Trigger: RAND_bytes()/RAND_pseudo_bytes() fails, leaving task_id zero or predictable. Consequence: the TACACS+ accounting request carries a non-random session_id, weakening session identification and accounting integrity.

commit_msg:
Kafka: Limit our decompression size.

Don't assume that the Internet has our best interests at heart when it
gives us the size of our decompression buffer. Assign an arbitrary limit
of 50 MB.

This fixes #16739 in that it takes care of

** (process:17681): WARNING **: 20:03:07.440: Dissector bug, protocol Kafka, in packet 31: ../epan/proto.c:7043: failed assertion "end >= fi->start"

which is different from the original error output. It looks like *that*
might have taken care of in one of the other recent Kafka bug fixes.

The decompression routines return a success or failure status. Use
gbooleans instead of ints for that.

commit_msg:
Fix oobread crash in java parser ##crash

* Reported by @bet4it via @huntrdev
* BountyID: 229a2e0d-9e5c-402f-9a24-57fa2eb1aaa7
* Reproducer: poc4java

description: Out-of-bounds Read in r_bin_java_constant_value_attr_new function in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.7.0. The bug causes the program reads data past the end 2f the intented buffer. Typically, this can allow attackers to read sensitive information from other memory locations or cause a crash. More details see [CWE-125: Out-of-bounds read](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/125.html).

code_evidence: offset is initialized to 6, and the buffer size is passed in as sz. Line 6 reads a ushort via R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) without checking that offset+2 is within sz, so the read can extend past the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads 2 bytes from buffer at a fixed offset without validating the buffer length, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not an out-of-bounds write, since no memory is modified past the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constant_value_idx read at offset 6 is performed unconditionally, with no bounds check against the caller-supplied sz. Trigger: a Java class attribute whose buffer is shorter than 8 bytes. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read, leading to disclosure of adjacent memory or a crash.

commit_msg: Bug 698050: xps: bounds check offset for requested cmap table
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void', '        return;'], 'added_lines': ['int', '        return 0;', '    if (font->cmapsubtable >= font->length) {', '        font->cmapsubtable = 0;', '        return 0;', '    }', '    return 1;']}
description: The xps_select_font_encoding function in xps/xpsfont.c in Artifex Ghostscript GhostXPS 9.21 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted document, related to the xps_encode_font_char_imp function.

code_evidence: The function computes cmapdata from font->cmaptable and entry as cmapdata + 4 + idx*8 without verifying that these offsets lie within font->length. It then reads u16(entry+0), u16(entry+2) and u32(entry+4) and derives font->cmapsubtable = font->cmaptable + u32(entry+4), all from attacker-controlled font data. Only idx is bounds-checked against font->cmapsubcount; the byte offset (cmaptable) and the derived subtable offset are not validated before being dereferenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the code directly dereferences u16/u32 at entry offsets derived from untrusted cmap data without ensuring they fall inside the allocated font buffer, causing a read past the intended buffer. This is a read-only over-read, not a write (CWE-787) or integer overflow (CWE-190) alone.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cmap table offset and the subtable offset read from the crafted cmap are used to index font->data without a bounds check against font->length. Trigger: a crafted document supplies a cmaptable or entry offset pointing beyond the font buffer. Consequence: the u16/u32 reads at entry+0..entry+4 over-read the heap buffer, enabling a crash (DoS) or disclosure of adjacent memory, and the unchecked cmapsubtable propagates the out-of-range offset to later cmap lookups.

commit_msg:
udmabuf: add back sanity check

Check vm_fault->pgoff before using it.  When we removed the warning, we
also removed the check.

Fixes: 7b26e4e2119d ("udmabuf: drop WARN_ON() check.")
Reported-by: zdi-disclosures@trendmicro.com
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tvmf->page = ubuf->pages[vmf->pgoff];'], 'added_lines': ['\tpgoff_t pgoff = vmf->pgoff;', '\tif (pgoff >= ubuf->pagecount)', '\t\treturn VM_FAULT_SIGBUS;', '\tvmf->page = ubuf->pages[pgoff];']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's udmabuf device driver. The specific flaw exists within a fault handler. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a memory access past the end of an array. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the kernel.

code_evidence: Line 4 retrieves ubuf from vma->vm_private_data without any bounds context. Line 5 indexes ubuf->pages directly with vmf->pgoff, a fault offset supplied by the faulting process, and stores the result in vmf->page. Line 6 then calls get_page on that pointer, so an out-of-range pgoff yields an out-of-bounds array read whose value is used as a page pointer. No check compares pgoff against ubuf->pagecount before the index use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-129 fits because an untrusted input (vmf->pgoff) is used to index the pages array without a range check, allowing an out-of-bounds access. This is an index-validation weakness rather than a general integer overflow: the missing constraint is the comparison of the index against pagecount.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the user-influenced fault offset vmf->pgoff is used as an array index into ubuf->pages without validating it against ubuf->pagecount. Trigger: a fault on the udmabuf mapping with a pgoff at or beyond pagecount. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read selects an attacker-influenced 'page' pointer that is dereferenced by get_page, supporting memory corruption and possible kernel privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
[tf2xla] Validate that stride and window size are positive

PiperOrigin-RevId: 504866231
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  for (size_t i = 0; i < input_dimensions.size(); ++i) {', '    if (window_dimensions[i] <= 0) {', '      return InvalidArgument("Window dimension %u has non-positive size %d", i,', '                             window_dimensions[i]);', '    }', '    if (window_strides[i] <= 0) {', '      return InvalidArgument("Window dimension %u has non-positive stride %d",', '                             i, window_strides[i]);', '    }', '  }']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.12.0 and 2.11.1, if the stride and window size are not positive for `tf.raw_ops.AvgPoolGrad`, it can give a floating point exception. A fix is included in TensorFlow version 2.12.0 and version 2.11.1.

code_evidence: The function only verifies that input_dimensions, window_dimensions and window_strides have equal sizes via the `ok` boolean; when sizes match it falls through to `return OkStatus()` at line 13 without examining the actual values of window_dimensions or window_strides.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is an incorrect comparison in a security-relevant validation context: the equality comparison of sizes is the only check, and the missing positivity check is a comparison that should consider additional factors but does not. CWE-697 (Pillar) captures this incomplete/incorrect validation comparison; the more specific downstream integer-division effect is a consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the validation comparison checks only array-length equality and never tests whether window_dimensions and window_strides entries are positive. Trigger: a caller supplies equal-length spans whose window or stride values are zero or negative. Supported consequence: the function reports OkStatus, allowing downstream AvgPoolGrad shape computation to perform division/modulo by a non-positive window or stride, yielding a floating point exception.

commit_msg: Fix the crash caused by get_long_object()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tsize = ndigits * 15;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t// the explicit cast is safe since ndigits is positive', '\t\tsize = (size_t)ndigits * 15;']}
description: Rizin v0.4.0 and below was discovered to contain an integer overflow via the function get_long_object(). This vulnerability allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via a crafted binary.

code_evidence: ndigits is read as a signed 32-bit value and its magnitude is taken for negative inputs, so it can be large. At line 27 the multiplication ndigits * 15 is performed in signed 32-bit arithmetic before assignment to size_t, allowing wraparound to a small or negative value. The wrapped size then feeds malloc at line 30.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size calculation assuming the product is always larger, but a large input wraps the signed multiplication, exactly CWE-190. The fix's explicit (size_t) cast confirms the intended overflow-free computation; the under-allocation is the downstream effect of the integer wraparound rather than a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size computation ndigits * 15 occurs in the signed int type of ndigits, so a crafted large ndigits overflows. Trigger: a malicious binary supplying a large digit count. Consequence: size becomes small/incorrect, malloc allocates too little, and the subsequent writes (memset and the hex-digit loop) exceed the buffer, causing a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
sctp: do not peel off an assoc from one netns to another one

Now when peeling off an association to the sock in another netns, all
transports in this assoc are not to be rehashed and keep use the old
key in hashtable.

As a transport uses sk->net as the hash key to insert into hashtable,
it would miss removing these transports from hashtable due to the new
netns when closing the sock and all transports are being freeed, then
later an use-after-free issue could be caused when looking up an asoc
and dereferencing those transports.

This is a very old issue since very beginning, ChunYu found it with
syzkaller fuzz testing with this series:

  socket$inet6_sctp()
  bind$inet6()
  sendto$inet6()
  unshare(0x40000000)
  getsockopt$inet_sctp6_SCTP_GET_ASSOC_ID_LIST()
  getsockopt$inet_sctp6_SCTP_SOCKOPT_PEELOFF()

This patch is to block this call when peeling one assoc off from one
netns to another one, so that the netns of all transport would not
go out-sync with the key in hashtable.

Note that this patch didn't fix it by rehashing transports, as it's
difficult to handle the situation when the tuple is already in use
in the new netns. Besides, no one would like to peel off one assoc
to another netns, considering ipaddrs, ifaces, etc. are usually
different.

Reported-by: ChunYu Wang <chunwang@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Marcelo Ricardo Leitner <marcelo.leitner@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Neil Horman <nhorman@tuxdriver.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
