description: The sctp_do_peeloff function in net/sctp/socket.c in the Linux kernel before 4.14 does not check whether the intended netns is used in a peel-off action, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls.

code_evidence: sctp_do_peeloff resolves the association by id and prepares a new socket without checking that the caller's netns matches the socket's netns.
The function creates a socket, copies the association's addresses, and calls sctp_sock_migrate to move the association and its transports to the new socket.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is reuse of freed transport objects after the sock is closed, matching CWE-416. The root cause is the absent netns constraint, not a missing bounds check or type confusion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Missing netns equality check lets an association be peeled off into a socket whose netns differs from the transports' original hash key. On close those transports are not unhashed, so later association lookup dereferences freed transports, producing a use-after-free crash.

commit_msg:
A lack of range checks in libXtst allows out of boundary accesses.
The checks have to be done in-place here, because it cannot be done
without in-depth knowledge of the read data.

If XRecordStartOfData, XRecordEndOfData, or XRecordClientDied
without a client sequence have attached data, an endless loop would
occur. The do-while-loop continues until the current index reaches
the end. But in these cases, the current index would not be
incremented, leading to an endless processing.

description: Multiple integer overflows in X.org libXtst before 1.2.3 allow remote X servers to trigger out-of-bounds memory access operations by leveraging the lack of range checks.

code_evidence: datum_bytes is extracted from the untrusted reply buffer, then datum_bytes+8 is shifted left by 2 with no upper bound; a large value wraps to a small or negative int before use as data_len.
In the XRecordFromClient path datum_bytes is extracted from the reply (32-bit or 16-bit) and shifted left by 2 without checking against INT_MAX, so the multiplication can overflow.
datum_bytes+2 is shifted left by 2 with no range check, allowing the length computation to wrap.

The bounds test current_index + datum_bytes > rep->length << 2 is itself an addition that can overflow when datum_bytes is large, letting the check pass while data->data points to an undersized buffer and data_len is attacker-controlled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unsafe operations are integer arithmetic ((datum_bytes+8)<<2, datum_bytes<<2, (datum_bytes+2)<<2, current_index+datum_bytes) on attacker-supplied values that can wrap before being used as a buffer length/offset. The patch adds explicit INT_MAX range checks, confirming the overflow is the root cause rather than a plain out-of-bounds read.

if (current_index + datum_bytes > rep->length << 2)
(long)rep->length << 2, current_index + datum_bytes,

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled datum_bytes is added to a constant and shifted left by 2 without an upper-bound check, and the subsequent bounds check adds current_index+datum_bytes which can also wrap. Trigger: a remote X server sends a reply whose embedded length field is near INT_MAX. Consequence: wrapped datum_bytes yields an incorrect data_len and passes the range check, so the callback reads out of bounds.

commit_msg: Lock down search_path in SPI calls
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Lock down search_path */', '\trc = SPI_exec("SET LOCAL search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp", 0);', '\tif (rc < 0)', '\t\tereport(ERROR, (errcode(ERRCODE_INTERNAL_ERROR), (errmsg("could not set search_path"))));', '']}
description:
TimescaleDB, an open-source time-series SQL database, has a privilege escalation vulnerability in versions 2.8.0 through 2.9.2. During installation, TimescaleDB creates a telemetry job that is runs as the installation user. The queries run as part of the telemetry data collection were not run with a locked down `search_path`, allowing malicious users to create functions that would be executed by the telemetry job, leading to privilege escalation. In order to be able to take advantage of this vulnerability, a user would need to be able to create objects in a database and then get a superuser to install TimescaleDB into their database. When TimescaleDB is installed as trusted extension, non-superusers can install the extension without help from a superuser.

Version 2.9.3 fixes this issue. As a mitigation, the `search_path` of the user running the telemetry job can be locked down to not include schemas writable by other users. The vulnerability is not exploitable on instances in Timescale Cloud and Managed Service for TimescaleDB due to additional security provisions in place on those platforms.

code_evidence: SPI_connect_ext establishes an SPI connection and the function then calls chunk_copy without setting a restricted search_path. The diff adds a SET LOCAL search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp after connect, confirming the pre-patch code executed SPI calls under the caller's mutable search_path, so attacker-controlled functions in writable schemas could be resolved.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing search_path lockdown lets an attacker influence which functions execute under a higher-privileged actor, an improper privilege-management flaw. CWE-269 fits; the technical impact is privilege escalation, but the root cause is failure to constrain the execution context's privileges.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: SPI operations run with the session search_path, which may include schemas writable by untrusted users. Trigger: a low-privileged user creates a function shadowing a name used by chunk_copy; when the privileged telemetry/copy job runs, the malicious function executes. Consequence: privilege escalation to the job's (installation) user.

description: An integer overflow issue exists in Godot Engine up to v3.2 that can be triggered when loading specially crafted.TGA image files. The vulnerability exists in ImageLoaderTGA::load_image() function at line: const size_t buffer_size = (tga_header.image_width * tga_header.image_height) * pixel_size; The bug leads to Dynamic stack buffer overflow. Depending on the context of the application, attack vector can be local or remote, and can lead to code execution and/or system crash.

code_evidence: Lines 8-9 read attacker-controlled width/height from the TGA header as uint32_t; line 36 computes width * height * sizeof(uint32_t) in 32-bit arithmetic for image_data.resize, so a crafted header can wrap the product to a small allocation.

Lines 45,56,79-81,92-95 then index p_buffer using a monotonically increasing i without any bounds check against the actual buffer length, so the pixel loops read past the undersized/actual input buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unsafe operation is an integer multiply used as a memory allocation size that can wrap to a small value. The missing size check is a consequence of the wrapped size, but the primary defect is the unchecked integer arithmetic; this distinguishes it from a pure OOB read (CWE-125) or allocation-size error alone.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation size width*height*4 is computed in 32-bit arithmetic and can wrap when the TGA header declares large dimensions, producing an undersized PoolVector. The loops still iterate over width*height pixels and dereference p_buffer[i]/p_buffer[i+3] with no length validation, so a malformed TGA triggers an out-of-bounds read (and the write macro can corrupt memory), leading to a crash or potential code execution.

description: libs/binder/IMemory.cpp in the IMemory Native Interface in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-04-01 does not properly consider the heap size, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, as demonstrated by obtaining Signature or SignatureOrSystem access, aka internal bug 26877992.

code_evidence: BpMemory::getMemory reads an attacker-controlled binder heap handle, offset o and size s from the reply Parcel, then assigns mOffset/mSize without checking them against the heap's actual size.

Because offsets and sizes are never validated, a crafted remote IMemory can describe a region outside the shared heap; the same unvalidated mOffset/mSize are later returned to callers via the offset/size out-parameters and mHeap is returned unconditionally.

It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the security impact is the cross-privilege access-control failure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation of the offset/size pair received from an untrusted binder peer against the backing heap bounds. Trigger: a malicious application supplies an IMemory whose offset/size exceed the real heap. Consequence: callers map or access memory outside the intended region, enabling privileged data access or corruption of other processes' mappings.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.4 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.10, there is a NetScaler file parser infinite loop, triggered by a malformed capture file. This was addressed in wiretap/netscaler.c by validating record sizes.

commit_msg:
Fix error condition for SC and CS

The SC and CS PDF operators correctly checked the return code from the
underlying setcolor and setcolorspace code, but we had already
set up the exec stack for handling a non-error return.

We have to do this before calling the underlying code, as that also
uses a state machine, and alters the exec stack. We must push our
own execution context first.

Ordinarily this isn't a problem, but if we have a custom error handler
which doesn't stop the interpreter, then we would continue on to try
and use what we'd pushed onto the exec stack, with predictably dire
results.

Here we avoid this by saving the exec stack pointer on entry, and if
an error occurs, restoring back to that point before returning control
to the PostScript interpreter.

A minor point, but we now also reset the space/color on an error as
well, previously it would have been left with the wrong space set.

commit_msg:
Avoid negative integer overflow when `chunkLength == 0`.

This fixes #789.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    while (iccOffset < 80 && iccOffset < chunkLength) {', '                         if (chunkData.pData_[iccOffset++] ==  0x00) {', '                            break;', '                         }', '                    }'], 'added_lines': ['                    do {', '                      enforce(iccOffset < 80 && iccOffset < chunkLength,', '                              Exiv2::kerCorruptedMetadata);', '                    } while(chunkData.pData_[iccOffset++] != 0x00);', '']}
description: An integer overflow in Exiv2 through 0.27.1 allows an attacker to cause a denial of service (SIGSEGV) via a crafted PNG image file, because PngImage::readMetadata mishandles a zero value for iccOffset.

code_evidence: iccOffset is initialized to 0 and incremented in the loop condition at line 49 while bounded by iccOffset < 80 && iccOffset < chunkLength; the loop exits when a NUL byte is found or the bound is reached.
Line 53 builds profileName_ using iccOffset-1, then line 54 increments iccOffset and enforces iccOffset <= chunkLength before line 55 calls zlibToDataBuf with chunkLength - iccOffset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is unsigned integer wraparound on iccOffset (0-1) and on chunkLength - iccOffset when chunkLength is zero, matching CWE-190's increment/wraparound-to-large-value pattern. This is not merely a bounds-check omission; the arithmetic itself produces the invalid size/offset used downstream.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When chunkLength is 0, the loop at lines 48-52 never executes because iccOffset < chunkLength is false, leaving iccOffset at 0. Line 53 then computes iccOffset-1 as an unsigned wraparound to a huge value used as the string length, and line 54's increment plus the subtraction chunkLength - iccOffset at line 55 also wrap. The malformed PNG chunk thus drives out-of-bounds reads/size computations and a crash.

openjpeg: Prevent integer overflows during calculation of |l_nb_precinct_size|

BUG=625541

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2124073003

description: Multiple integer overflows in the opj_tcd_init_tile function in tcd.c in OpenJPEG, as used in PDFium in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.116, allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted JPEG 2000 data.

l_nb_precincts is then multiplied by sizeof(opj_tcd_precinct_t) into l_nb_precinct_size, which drives opj_malloc/opj_realloc and the memset lengths at [169,173] and [177].

commit_msg:
When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via
/home/fred/keepalived.data.

There doesn't appear to be a way around this backward incompatibility,
since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

Signed-off-by: Quentin Armitage <quentin@armitage.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif ((fifo->fd = open(fifo->name, O_RDWR | O_CLOEXEC | O_NONBLOCK)) == -1) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif ((fifo->fd = open(fifo->name, O_RDWR | O_CLOEXEC | O_NONBLOCK | O_NOFOLLOW)) == -1) {']}
description: keepalived 2.0.8 didn't check for pathnames with symlinks when writing data to a temporary file upon a call to PrintData or PrintStats. This allowed local users to overwrite arbitrary files if fs.protected_symlinks is set to 0, as demonstrated by a symlink from /tmp/keepalived.data or /tmp/keepalived.stats to /etc/passwd.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only opens a notify FIFO for read/write and does not read, expose, or disclose sensitive information; the symlink-following open is a file-overwrite/arbitrary-file-access concern, not a CWE-200 information exposure.

commit_msg:
x86: Guard against corrupted PLT

There should be only one entry in PLT for a given symbol.  Set howto to
NULL after processing a PLT entry to guard against corrupted PLT so that
the duplicated PLT entries are skipped.

	PR binutils/22170
	 * elf32-i386.c (elf_i386_get_synthetic_symtab): Guard against
	 corrupted PLT.
	 * elf64-x86-64.c (elf_x86_64_get_synthetic_symtab): Likewise.

(cherry picked from commit 61e3bf5f83f7e505b6bc51ef65426e5b31e6e360)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* There should be only one entry in PLT for a given', '\t\t   symbol.  Set howto to NULL after processing a PLT', '\t\t   entry to guard against corrupted PLT.  */', '\t\tp->howto = NULL;']}
description: The *_get_synthetic_symtab functions in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, do not ensure a unique PLT entry for a symbol, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted ELF file, related to elf32-i386.c and elf64-x86-64.c.

code_evidence: The loop only emits a symbol when the located relocation matches got_vma and p->howto is non-NULL with an accepted relocation type; without consuming the relocation, a corrupted PLT with duplicate entries pointing at the same got_vma matches the same dynrelbuf entry repeatedly.
Each match copies the symbol into *s, computes name length, increments n and advances s, so repeated matches for one relocation inflate the count and the size budget for names.
offset increments per PLT entry, so a crafted PLT with many entries resolving to one relocation drives repeated writes through s and later name copies beyond the allocated buffers.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes symbols and name strings into buffers sized from a count that a corrupted PLT can inflate, so operations exceed the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119. The underlying cause is missing uniqueness validation, but the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds memory write.

evidence_lines.code:
if (got_vma == p->address
&& p->howto != NULL
&& (p->howto->type == R_386_JUMP_SLOT
|| p->howto->type == R_386_GLOB_DAT
|| p->howto->type == R_386_IRELATIVE))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the synthetic-symbol loop does not enforce a unique PLT entry per symbol; a relocation matched by got_vma remains available for subsequent PLT entries. Trigger: a crafted ELF whose PLT has duplicate entries resolving to the same dynamic relocation. Consequence: count/name-size accounting is inflated relative to actual distinct symbols, leading to out-of-bounds writes on the asymbol array and names buffer (heap-based buffer overflow).

commit_msg: tentative libsais safety patches
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    bz3_state->sais_array = malloc((block_size + 128) * sizeof(s32));', '    memset(bz3_state->sais_array, 0, sizeof(s32) * (block_size + 128));'], 'added_lines': ['    bz3_state->sais_array = malloc(BWT_BOUND(block_size) * sizeof(s32));', '    memset(bz3_state->sais_array, 0, sizeof(s32) * BWT_BOUND(block_size));']}
description: An issue was discovered in libbzip3.a in bzip3 before 1.3.0. A bz3_decode_block out-of-bounds write can occur with a crafted archive because bzip3 does not follow the required procedure for interacting with libsais.

code_evidence: sais_array is allocated with (block_size + 128) * sizeof(s32) and zeroed for the same size, but libsais requires its own BWT bound (BWT_BOUND(block_size)) which is larger than block_size + 128 for the supported block sizes; the buffer is therefore undersized relative to what the SA construction writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The undersized sais_array causes writes beyond the allocated buffer during BWT/SA construction, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an integer overflow (CWE-190) because the size computation is explicit and the defect is the insufficient bound versus libsais's required capacity.

evidence_lines.code:
bz3_state->sais_array = malloc((block_size + 128) * sizeof(s32));
memset(bz3_state->sais_array, 0, sizeof(s32) * (block_size + 128));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SA index array is sized with an ad-hoc block_size + 128 formula instead of the libsais-required BWT bound, so downstream libsais calls write indices past the allocation. Trigger: decoding a crafted archive with block_size near the permitted maximum. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write into heap memory, corrupting adjacent data and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix handling of stored error in a negatively instantiated user key

If a user key gets negatively instantiated, an error code is cached in the
payload area.  A negatively instantiated key may be then be positively
instantiated by updating it with valid data.  However, the ->update key
type method must be aware that the error code may be there.

The following may be used to trigger the bug in the user key type:

    keyctl request2 user user "" @u
    keyctl add user user "a" @u

which manifests itself as:

Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct trusted_key_payload *p = key->payload.data[0];'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct trusted_key_payload *p;', '\tif (test_bit(KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE, &key->flags))', '\t\treturn -ENOKEY;', '\tp = key->payload.data[0];']}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (BUG) via crafted keyctl commands that negatively instantiate a key, related to security/keys/encrypted-keys/encrypted.c, security/keys/trusted.c, and security/keys/user_defined.c.

code_evidence: The function dereferences key->payload.data[0] into p before any validation, then reads p->migratable. For a negatively instantiated key, payload contains a cached error code rather than a trusted_key_payload pointer, so this read treats the error value as a valid structure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing negative-state check lets an actor with update access operate on a key whose payload is an error code, violating the intended privilege/state boundary between negatively and positively instantiated keys. This improper privilege/state management is the root cause rather than the resulting crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the update method assumes payload.data[0] is a valid trusted_key_payload and never checks KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE. Trigger: a user negatively instantiates a trusted key via keyctl request2, then updates it with valid data through keyctl add. The error code is dereferenced as a structure pointer, leading to a kernel oops/DoS and potentially privilege impact as described.

commit_msg:
xen/rwlock: Add missing memory barrier in the unlock path of rwlock

The rwlock unlock paths are using atomic_sub() to release the lock.
However the implementation of atomic_sub() rightfully doesn't contain a
memory barrier. On Arm, this means a processor is allowed to re-order
the memory access with the preceeding access.

In other words, the unlock may be seen by another processor before all
the memory accesses within the "critical" section.

The rwlock paths already contains barrier indirectly, but they are not
very useful without the counterpart in the unlock paths.

The memory barriers are not necessary on x86 because loads/stores are
not re-ordered with lock instructions.

So add arch_lock_release_barrier() in the unlock paths that will only
add memory barrier on Arm.

Take the opportunity to document each lock paths explaining why a
barrier is not necessary.

This is XSA-314.

Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Acked-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    arch_lock_release_barrier();']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.13.x, allowing guest OS users to cause a denial of service or possibly gain privileges because of missing memory barriers in read-write unlock paths. The read-write unlock paths don't contain a memory barrier. On Arm, this means a processor is allowed to re-order the memory access with the preceding ones. In other words, the unlock may be seen by another processor before all the memory accesses within the "critical" section. As a consequence, it may be possible to have a writer executing a critical section at the same time as readers or another writer. In other words, many of the assumptions (e.g., a variable cannot be modified after a check) in the critical sections are not safe anymore. The read-write locks are used in hypercalls (such as grant-table ones), so a malicious guest could exploit the race. For instance, there is a small window where Xen can leak memory if XENMAPSPACE_grant_table is used concurrently. A malicious guest may be able to leak memory, or cause a hypervisor crash resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leak and privilege escalation cannot be excluded.

code_evidence: The unlock path performs atomic_sub(_QR_BIAS, &lock->cnts) to release the reader lock, then calls preempt_enable(); there is no arch_lock_release_barrier() before the counter is decremented, so the release of the shared counter can be observed before preceding critical-section memory accesses complete.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the unlock sequence fails to enforce exclusivity on the shared rwlock resource: a timing window lets an interfering code sequence modify the shared resource concurrently with the supposedly protected critical section. The missing release barrier is the synchronization defect causing the race, not merely a memory-ordering bug in isolation.

evidence_lines.code:
atomic_sub(_QR_BIAS, &lock->cnts);
preempt_enable();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reader unlock decrements the shared reader count without a release memory barrier. Trigger: on weakly ordered architectures (Arm) a concurrent writer/reader observes the decremented count while earlier critical-section accesses are still pending, so a writer can enter and modify data that readers still assume protected. Supported consequence: concurrent modification of shared state, violating exclusivity/atomicity and enabling memory leak, crash/DoS, or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Generating strings for XKB data used a single shared static buffer,
which offered several opportunities for errors. Use a ring of
resizable buffers instead, to avoid problems when strings end up
longer than anticipated.

Reviewed-by: Michal Srb <msrb@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Keith Packard <keithp@keithp.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Cristau <jcristau@debian.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    char *rtrn;', '    if (size >= BUFFER_SIZE)', '        return NULL;', '    if ((BUFFER_SIZE - tbNext) <= size)', '        tbNext = 0;', '    rtrn = &textBuffer[tbNext];', '    tbNext += size;', '    return rtrn;'], 'added_lines': ['    struct textBuffer *tb;', '    tb = &textBuffer[textBufferIndex];', '    textBufferIndex = (textBufferIndex + 1) % NUM_BUFFER;', '', '    if (size > tb->size) {', '        free(tb->buffer);', '        tb->buffer = xnfalloc(size);', '        tb->size = size;', '    }', '    return tb->buffer;']}
description: In X.Org Server (aka xserver and xorg-server) before 1.19.4, a local attacker authenticated to the X server could overflow a global buffer, causing crashes of the X server or potentially other problems by injecting large or malformed XKB related atoms and accessing them via xkbcomp.

The wrap check uses `(BUFFER_SIZE - tbNext) <= size` and resets tbNext to 0, then `rtrn = &textBuffer[tbNext]`; tbNext is advanced by size without a bound guaranteeing the write region stays within textBuffer, so a size near the limit can place the returned pointer at the buffer edge.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function returns a pointer into a fixed buffer without ensuring the requested size keeps subsequent operations within that buffer's bounds, enabling out-of-bounds memory access.

evidence_lines.code:
if (size >= BUFFER_SIZE)
return NULL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shared static textBuffer is indexed by tbNext with an off-by-one/insufficient boundary check, so a large size can yield a pointer whose region extends past textBuffer. Trigger: XKB atom data causing large string generation requests; consequence: out-of-bounds writes to global memory, crashing or corrupting the X server.

commit_msg:
internal redirect: fix a lifetime bug (#785)

Signed-off-by: Alyssa Wilk <alyssar@chromium.org>
Signed-off-by: Matt Klein <mklein@lyft.com>
Signed-off-by: Pradeep Rao <pcrao@google.com>

Generally this should consist of all downstream related', '  // data, and not include upstream related data.', '  (*connection_manager_.streams_.begin())', '      ->filter_manager_.streamInfo()', '      .setFromForRecreateStream(filter_manager_.streamInfo());']}
description: Envoy is a cloud-native high-performance edge/middle/service proxy. In versions prior to 1.22.1 if Envoy attempts to send an internal redirect of an HTTP request consisting of more than HTTP headers, there’s a lifetime bug which can be triggered. If while replaying the request Envoy sends a local reply when the redirect headers are processed, the downstream state indicates that the downstream stream is not complete. On sending the local reply, Envoy will attempt to reset the upstream stream, but as it is actually complete, and deleted, this result in a use-after-free. Users are advised to upgrade. Users unable to upgrade are advised to disable internal redirects if crashes are observed.

code_evidence: Line 11 removes the callback registration from the old encoder's stream, and line 12 calls connection_manager_.doEndStream(*this), ending/freeing the current ActiveStream while the function continues to operate on its members.

Line 13 creates a replacement stream and lines 19-22 decode headers and data into it; if decoding triggers a local reply, the downstream stream state handling can attempt to reset an upstream stream that is already complete and deleted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is referencing an already-freed upstream stream during local-reply/reset after doEndStream; operations on that stale stream are use-after-free (CWE-416), not merely a logic/state error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function ends the original stream (doEndStream) and then continues replaying headers/data on the new stream. When processing redirect headers causes a local reply, code resets the upstream stream even though it is complete and freed, yielding a use-after-free. Trigger: internal redirect with many headers causing a local reply during replay. Consequence: crash/DoS and possible memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Prevent unauthenticated client from easily consuming lots of memory (CVE-2021-32675)

This change sets a low limit for multibulk and bulk length in the
protocol for unauthenticated connections, so that they can't easily
cause redis to allocate massive amounts of memory by sending just a few
characters on the network.
The new limits are 10 arguments of 16kb each (instead of 1m of 512mb)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            return C_ERR;', '        } else if (ll > 10 && authRequired(c)) {', '            addReplyError(c, "Protocol error: unauthenticated multibulk length");', '            setProtocolError("unauth mbulk count", c);', '                return C_ERR;', '            } else if (ll > 16384 && authRequired(c)) {', '                addReplyError(c, "Protocol error: unauthenticated bulk length");', '                setProtocolError("unauth bulk length", c);']}
description: Redis is an open source, in-memory database that persists on disk. When parsing an incoming Redis Standard Protocol (RESP) request, Redis allocates memory according to user-specified values which determine the number of elements (in the multi-bulk header) and size of each element (in the bulk header). An attacker delivering specially crafted requests over multiple connections can cause the server to allocate significant amount of memory. Because the same parsing mechanism is used to handle authentication requests, this vulnerability can also be exploited by unauthenticated users. The problem is fixed in Redis versions 6.2.6, 6.0.16 and 5.0.14. An additional workaround to mitigate this problem without patching the redis-server executable is to block access to prevent unauthenticated users from connecting to Redis. This can be done in different ways: Using network access control tools like firewalls, iptables, security groups, etc. or Enabling TLS and requiring users to authenticate using client side certificates.

code_evidence: The multibulk length is parsed from the client query buffer into ll and only rejected when it exceeds a fixed 1MB cap; ll is then stored as c->multibulklen and used at line 28 to zmalloc an argv array of that many pointers.

The bulk length ll is parsed and only rejected when negative or above server.proto_max_bulk_len; ll is then stored as c->bulklen and later drives allocation via sdsMakeRoomFor (line 65) and createStringObject.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code allocates reusable memory per connection based on user-supplied lengths without per-actor limits or throttling for unauthenticated clients, matching CWE-770. It is not a simple integer overflow, since the missing control is the absence of allocation bounds rather than arithmetic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser accepts attacker-controlled element counts and element sizes and allocates memory proportional to them before any authentication check. A client sending a few small RESP headers can force large argv allocations and query-buffer growth, exhausting server memory and degrading availability.

description: NULL Pointer Dereference in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.8.2.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a direct NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): the code follows reloc_map without a NULL check, and the fix adds && map->reloc_map. It is not a general input-validation issue; the specific flaw is dereferencing an unchecked pointer.

evidence_lines.code:
if (map->perm & R_PERM_RELOC) {
return map->reloc_map->read (io, map, addr, buf, read_len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A map can carry the R_PERM_RELOC permission while its reloc_map pointer is unset; the guard on line 29 does not validate that pointer. Triggering a read at an address in such a submap reaches line 30 and dereferences NULL, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
app: fix #8230 crash in gimp_layer_invalidate_boundary when channel is NULL

gimp_channel_is_empty returns FALSE if channel is NULL. This causes
gimp_layer_invalidate_boundary to crash if the mask channel is NULL.

With a NULL channel gimp_channel_is_empty should return TRUE, just like
the similar gimp_image_is_empty does, because returning FALSE here
suggests we have a non empty channel.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  g_return_val_if_fail (GIMP_IS_CHANNEL (channel), FALSE);'], 'added_lines': ['  g_return_val_if_fail (GIMP_IS_CHANNEL (channel), TRUE);']}
description: An issue in gimp_layer_invalidate_boundary of GNOME GIMP 2.10.30 allows attackers to trigger an unhandled exception via a crafted XCF file, causing a Denial of Service (DoS).

code_evidence: Line 4 guards the input with g_return_val_if_fail (GIMP_IS_CHANNEL (channel), FALSE): when channel is NULL or not a GimpChannel, the macro returns FALSE, which asserts the channel is non-empty rather than treating the invalid argument as empty. Line 5 then dereferences channel via GIMP_CHANNEL_GET_CLASS (channel), which is reached only when the guard passes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function mishandles the exceptional NULL/invalid-channel condition by returning a semantically wrong value that propagates to callers, matching CWE-755 (Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions). A NULL-pointer dereference is the downstream consequence, not the weakness in this guard logic.

evidence_lines.code:
g_return_val_if_fail (GIMP_IS_CHANNEL (channel), FALSE);
return GIMP_CHANNEL_GET_CLASS (channel)->is_empty (channel);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the invalid/NULL channel case is mapped to FALSE (non-empty) instead of TRUE (empty), so callers such as gimp_layer_invalidate_boundary proceed as if a mask channel exists. Trigger: a crafted XCF yielding a NULL mask channel. Supported consequence: the caller dereferences the absent channel and crashes, causing a denial of service.

commit_msg:
When route4_change() is called on an existing filter, the whole
tcf_result struct is always copied into the new instance of the filter.

This causes a problem when updating a filter bound to a class,
as tcf_unbind_filter() is always called on the old instance in the
success path, decreasing filter_cnt of the still referenced class
and allowing it to be deleted, leading to a use-after-free.

Fix this by no longer copying the tcf_result struct from the old filter.

Fixes: 1109c00547fc ("net: sched: RCU cls_route")
Reported-by: valis <sec@valis.email>
Reported-by: Bing-Jhong Billy Jheng <billy@starlabs.sg>
Signed-off-by: valis <sec@valis.email>
Signed-off-by: Jamal Hadi Salim <jhs@mojatatu.com>
Reviewed-by: Victor Nogueira <victor@mojatatu.com>
Reviewed-by: Pedro Tammela <pctammela@mojatatu.com>
Reviewed-by: M A Ramdhan <ramdhan@starlabs.sg>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230729123202.72406-4-jhs@mojatatu.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tf->res = fold->res;'], 'added_lines': []}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's net/sched: cls_route component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

When route4_change() is called on an existing filter, the whole tcf_result struct is always copied into the new instance of the filter. This causes a problem when updating a filter bound to a class, as tcf_unbind_filter() is always called on the old instance in the success path, decreasing filter_cnt of the still referenced class and allowing it to be deleted, leading to a use-after-free.

We recommend upgrading past commit b80b829e9e2c1b3f7aae34855e04d8f6ecaf13c8.

code_evidence: On update (fold non-NULL), the new filter f copies fold->res verbatim, including the bound class reference held in the tcf_result, so f and fold both reference the same class.
The old fold is unlinked from the hash bucket, then *arg is replaced by f, and the success path calls tcf_unbind_filter(tp, &fold->res) on the old instance only.
Unbinding fold->res decrements the class's filter_cnt even though f->res still points to that class, so the class can be freed while f retains a dangling reference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale class reference in f->res is used after the referenced object is freed, matching CWE-416 (use after free). A mere refcount imbalance would be CWE-911, but here the supported consequence is use of freed memory, so CWE-416 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: copying fold->res into the replacement filter duplicates the class binding, but only the old instance is unbound, so the class reference count is decremented despite remaining referenced by f. Trigger: updating an existing route4 filter that is bound to a class. Consequence: the class may be deleted while f->res still points to it, yielding a use-after-free that can escalate to local privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Defend against bad PT_DYNAMIC

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/391
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
	modified:   p_lx_elf.h
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    dynseg = dyn; invert_pt_dynamic(dynseg);'], 'added_lines': ['                    dynseg = dyn; invert_pt_dynamic(dynseg, get_te32(&udynhdr->p_filesz));']}
description: A heap-based buffer over-read was discovered in the acc_ua_get_be32 function in miniacc.h in UPX 4.0.0 via a crafted Mach-O file.

code_evidence: dyn_len is taken from the untrusted PT_DYNAMIC p_filesz (line 218); dyn_off from p_offset (219). The file_size bound check (220-224) validates dyn_len+dyn_off against file_size, but not against the allocated ibuf size. dyn is computed as ibuf + (dyn_off - load_off) (227-228) and passed to invert_pt_dynamic (229), which the patch now bounds by p_filesz. The subsequent loop (230-232) reads dyn->d_tag and dyn->d_val while advancing by sizeof(*dyn) up to dyn_len, without verifying that dyn_off - load_off + dyn_len remains within the ibuf allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences dyn entries beyond the intended ibuf buffer, matching CWE-125 (read past the end of the intended buffer). This is distinct from CWE-787 (write) since only reads of d_tag/d_val and the dynamic inversion occur; the patch's added p_filesz bound confirms the missing read constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the PT_DYNAMIC extent is validated only against file_size, not against the size of the buffer ibuf actually holds. Trigger: a crafted ELF with a large p_filesz/p_offset relative to the loaded segment. Consequence: invert_pt_dynamic and the dynamic-entry loop read past the end of ibuf, yielding a heap-based out-of-bounds read (crash or memory disclosure).

commit_msg: Fix possible integer overflow
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '   if (digs < 0) {', '      return MP_VAL;', '   }']}
description: Integer Overflow vulnerability in mp_grow in libtom libtommath before commit beba892bc0d4e4ded4d667ab1d2a94f4d75109a9, allows attackers to execute arbitrary code and cause a denial of service (DoS).

code_evidence: `digs` is an attacker-influenced `int` used without any lower-bound check; `pa` is computed as `a->used + b->used`, and the loop `for (ix = digs; ix < pa; ix++)` begins at the unvalidated `digs`.
Inside the loop, `ty`/`tx`/`iy` and the `a->dp + tx` / `b->dp + ty` pointers are derived from `ix`, so a negative or oversized `digs` skews the index arithmetic and the `W[ix]` write.

The copy loop writes `W[ix]` into `c->dp + digs` via `tmpc`, and `MP_ZERO_DIGITS(tmpc, olduse - ix)` computes a length from the loop index, so a bad `digs` propagates into out-of-bounds indexing and size arithmetic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an unchecked integer input feeding size/offset arithmetic (`pa`, `olduse - ix`) whose result is assumed valid, matching CWE-190 integer overflow/wraparound affecting allocation and copy bounds. It is not merely a missing bounds check on a buffer; the arithmetic assumption is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function trusts the caller-supplied `digs` as a loop start and pointer offset without validating it. A negative or overflowing `digs` makes `pa`, `ix`, and `olduse - ix` inconsistent, so index and size calculations wrap or go negative, leading to out-of-bounds writes and possible memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
smtpd's filter state machine can prematurely release resources
leading to a crash.  From gilles@
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\tcase IO_DISCONNECTED:', '\t\tio_free(fs->io);', '\t\tfs->io = NULL;', '\t\tbreak;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: smtpd/lka_filter.c in OpenSMTPD before 6.8.0p1, in certain configurations, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and daemon crash) via a crafted pattern of client activity, because the filter state machine does not properly maintain the I/O channel between the SMTP engine and the filters layer.

code_evidence: The IO_DISCONNECTED handler calls io_free(fs->io) and then sets fs->io = NULL, unconditionally releasing the channel object referenced by the session.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a pointer expected to remain valid being freed and set to NULL while subsequent state-machine paths still dereference it, matching CWE-476. It is not merely a use-after-free because the code explicitly nulls the pointer, making the dereference a NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The disconnect path frees fs->io and nulls it, but filter_data and later IO_DATAIN handling still use fs->io (e.g., io_getline(fs->io, &len)). If a crafted sequence of client activity delivers or queues data after the channel is torn down, the stale/NULL fs->io is dereferenced, causing a crash. Root cause is premature release of the I/O channel in the filter state machine; the supported consequence is a NULL pointer dereference and daemon DoS, not code execution.

commit_msg:
If nilfs_attach_log_writer() failed to create a log writer thread, it
frees a data structure of the log writer without any cleanup.  After
commit e912a5b66837 ("nilfs2: use root object to get ifile"), this causes
a leak of struct nilfs_root, which started to leak an ifile metadata inode
and a kobject on that struct.

In addition, if the kernel is booted with panic_on_warn, the above
ifile metadata inode leak will cause the following panic when the
nilfs2 kernel module is removed:

  kmem_cache_destroy nilfs2_inode_cache: Slab cache still has objects when
  called from nilfs_destroy_cachep+0x16/0x3a [nilfs2]
  WARNING: CPU: 8 PID: 1464 at mm/slab_common.c:494 kmem_cache_destroy+0x138/0x140
  ...
  RIP: 0010:kmem_cache_destroy+0x138/0x140
  Code: 00 20 00 00 e8 a9 55 d8 ff e9 76 ff ff ff 48 8b 53 60 48 c7 c6 20 70 65 86 48 c7 c7 d8 69 9c 86 48 8b 4c 24 28 e8 ef 71 c7 00 <0f> 0b e9 53 ff ff ff c3 48 81 ff ff 0f 00 00 77 03 31 c0 c3 53 48
  ...
  Call Trace:
   <TASK>
   ? nilfs_palloc_freev.cold.24+0x58/0x58 [nilfs2]
   nilfs_destroy_cachep+0x16/0x3a [nilfs2]
   exit_nilfs_fs+0xa/0x1b [nilfs2]
    __x64_sys_delete_module+0x1d9/0x3a0
   ? __sanitizer_cov_trace_pc+0x1a/0x50
   ? syscall_trace_enter.isra.19+0x119/0x190
   do_syscall_64+0x34/0x80
   entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x63/0xcd
   ...
   </TASK>
  Kernel panic - not syncing: panic_on_warn set ...

This patch fixes these issues by calling nilfs_detach_log_writer() cleanup
function if spawning the log writer thread fails.

Fixes: e912a5b66837 ("nilfs2: use root object to get ifile")
Signed-off-by: Ryusuke Konishi <konishi.ryusuke@gmail.com>

Tested-by: Ryusuke Konishi <konishi.ryusuke@gmail.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (err) {', '\t\tkfree(nilfs->ns_writer);', '\t\tnilfs->ns_writer = NULL;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (unlikely(err))', '\t\tnilfs_detach_log_writer(sb);', '']}
description: A vulnerability, which was classified as problematic, has been found in Linux Kernel. This issue affects the function nilfs_attach_log_writer of the file fs/nilfs2/segment.c of the component BPF. The manipulation leads to memory leak. The attack may be initiated remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier VDB-211961 was assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: nilfs_segctor_start_thread() may fail after nilfs->ns_writer was allocated at line 8; on error the code only kfree()s the writer struct and nulls the pointer, without invoking nilfs_detach_log_writer() cleanup that releases the associated nilfs_root, ifile metadata inode and kobject.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers failing to properly release resources on a path; here the failed thread-start path releases the writer incorrectly and leaves dependent resources un-released, matching improper resource shutdown/release.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path of thread creation frees only the top-level writer object, skipping the structured teardown that releases resources owned by the writer (root/ifile inode/kobject). Trigger: nilfs_segctor_start_thread() returns nonzero. Consequence: leaked inode and kobject, slab objects remain at module unload, causing warning/panic under panic_on_warn (DoS).

commit_msg:
[media] dvb-usb-v2: avoid use-after-free

I ran into a stack frame size warning because of the on-stack copy of
the USB device structure:

drivers/media/usb/dvb-usb-v2/dvb_usb_core.c: In function 'dvb_usbv2_disconnect':
drivers/media/usb/dvb-usb-v2/dvb_usb_core.c:1029:1: error: the frame size of 1104 bytes is larger than 1024 bytes [-Werror=frame-larger-than=]

Copying a device structure like this is wrong for a number of other reasons
too aside from the possible stack overflow. One of them is that the
dev_info() call will print the name of the device later, but AFAICT
we have only copied a pointer to the name earlier and the actual name
has been freed by the time it gets printed.

This removes the on-stack copy of the device and instead copies the
device name using kstrdup(). I'm ignoring the possible failure here
as both printk() and kfree() are able to deal with NULL pointers.

Signed-off-by: Arnd Bergmann <arnd@arndb.de>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@s-opensource.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tconst char *name = d->name;', '\tstruct device dev = d->udev->dev;', '\tdev_info(&dev, "%s: \'%s\' successfully deinitialized and disconnected\\n",', '\t\t\tKBUILD_MODNAME, name);'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst char *devname = kstrdup(dev_name(&d->udev->dev), GFP_KERNEL);', '\tconst char *drvname = d->name;', '\tpr_info("%s: \'%s:%s\' successfully deinitialized and disconnected\\n",', '\t\tKBUILD_MODNAME, drvname, devname);', '\tkfree(devname);']}
description: drivers/media/usb/dvb-usb-v2/dvb_usb_core.c in the Linux kernel 4.9.x and 4.10.x before 4.10.12 interacts incorrectly with the CONFIG_VMAP_STACK option, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash or memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging use of more than one virtual page for a DMA scatterlist.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only copies a device structure onto the stack and later prints a stale name pointer; it performs no out-of-bounds buffer read/write, so CWE-119 is not directly supported.

commit_msg:
C12.22: Track our allocation sizes.

Add an allocated size element to the TOP_ELEMENT_CONTROL struct and use
it to make sure we're not trying to read past the end of a buffer in
canonify_unencrypted_header. Fixes #17636.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  guint32 len;'], 'added_lines': ['  guint32 len, allocated;', '    allocated = *(t->allocated);', "      /* bail out if our we're trying to read past the end of our element */", '      /* the network is always hostile */', '      if (allocated < len) {', '        return FALSE;', '      }']}
description: Buffer overflow in the C12.22 dissector in Wireshark 3.4.0 to 3.4.9 and 3.2.0 to 3.2.17 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: len is taken from *(t->length), the recorded element length, and may exceed the actual allocation of the source element *(t->element).
The truncate branch replaces len with a computed BER length (3+2*get_ber_len_size(len)), a value unrelated to the real buffer size.
The only bound check compares against the destination buffsize, not the source element allocation.
memcpy copies len bytes from *(t->element) into buff with no check that the source element actually holds len bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because memcpy performs a buffer copy whose input size is not verified against the actual source buffer size, allowing the copy to overrun. It is distinct from CWE-125 since the mechanism is an unchecked copy length rather than a direct indexed read.

evidence_lines.code: len = *(t->length);

memcpy(&buff[*offset], *(t->element), len);
(*offset) += len;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy length is trusted from table metadata while the source element's allocated size is never validated. Trigger: a crafted C12.22 packet causes a length field to exceed the element allocation, and memcpy reads past the source buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
binding: Moves the check for the first access to the initial document into BindingSecurity.

Checks the access to the initial document and reports it not only at
securityCheck() in V8Window.cpp but also at every call to
BindingSecurity::shouldAllowAccessTo() because V8 only calls back
securityCheck() on property lookups, and not for function invocation.

BindingSecurity::shouldAllowAccessTo() is called with every possible
cross-origin window, which means every possible new window.  Thus,
shouldAllowAccessTo() should be the right place to check the access
to the initial document.

TBR=benwells@chromium.org

commit_msg:
Make class "type" for USB conversations.

USB dissectors can't assume that only their class type has been passed around in the conversation.  Make explicit check that class type expected matches the dissector and stop/prevent dissection if there isn't a match.

Bug: 12356
Change-Id: Ib23973a4ebd0fbb51952ffc118daf95e3389a209
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/15212
Petri-Dish: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
Reviewed-by: Martin Kaiser <wireshark@kaiser.cx>
Petri-Dish: Martin Kaiser <wireshark@kaiser.cx>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot <buildbot-no-reply@wireshark.org>
Reviewed-by: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        usb_conv_info->class_data_type = USB_CONV_U3V;', '    } else if (usb_conv_info->class_data_type != USB_CONV_U3V) {', "        /* Don't dissect if another USB type is in the conversation */", '        return 0;']}
description: The USB subsystem in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.12 and 2.x before 2.0.4 mishandles class types, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: data is cast to usb_conv_info_t and its class_data field is read into u3v_conv_info. Only when class_data is NULL is a new u3v_conv_info_t allocated and stored. No check validates that data or usb_conv_info is non-NULL before dereferencing class_data at line 20, and class_data_type is not inspected before this dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences usb_conv_info->class_data while it may be NULL, and the added class_data_type guard is absent before this access. The crash stems from a NULL/invalid pointer dereference rather than an out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dissector dereferences usb_conv_info->class_data without verifying the conversation's class type or that the class_data pointer belongs to U3V. Trigger: a crafted USB packet causing dissect_u3v to run on a conversation whose class_data is NULL or of another class type. Consequence: NULL or type-confused pointer dereference leading to an application crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Do stricter error checking when parsing path nodes

The SVG spec mandates that path parsing should terminate on the first
error encountered, and an error be reported. To improve the handling
of corrupt files, implement such error handling, and also limit the
number of QPainterPath elements to a reasonable range.

commit_msg:
Fix security vulnerability with UnbatchGradKernel

PiperOrigin-RevId: 460992964
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    const Tensor& batch_key_t = context->input(3);', '    if (batch_key_t.NumElements() != 1) {', '      return errors::InvalidArgument("Expected `id` to be scalar. Received ",', '                                     batch_key_t.DebugString());', '    }', '      if (batch_index_t.NumElements() != batch_index_t.dim_size(0) * 3) {', '        return errors::InvalidArgument(', '            "batch_index should contain ", batch_index_t.dim_size(0) * 3,', '            " elements. Received ", batch_index_t.NumElements());', '      }']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. The `UnbatchGradOp` function takes an argument `id` that is assumed to be a scalar. A nonscalar `id` can trigger a `CHECK` failure and crash the program. It also requires its argument `batch_index` to contain three times the number of elements as indicated in its `batch_index.dim_size(0)`. An incorrect `batch_index` can trigger a `CHECK` failure and crash the program. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 5f945fc6409a3c1e90d6970c9292f805f6e6ddf2. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: Line 7 calls context->input(3).scalar<int64_t>()() without verifying that input 3 (`id`/batch_key) has exactly one element; a nonscalar tensor violates the scalar() precondition, which in TensorFlow triggers a CHECK failure.

Lines 12-19: after only checking that batch_index is non-empty, line 18 reshapes batch_index_t to {dim_size(0), 3} and line 19 iterates dim_size(0) rows; if NumElements() is not dim_size(0)*3, the shaped access precondition fails and triggers a CHECK.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked inputs reach assertion-style CHECKs that terminate the program, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion) with availability impact. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the observed failure is an assertion-triggered crash; the added guards confirm the preconditions were unvalidated.

evidence_lines.code:
mutex_lock ml(mu_);
const int64_t batch_key = context->input(3).scalar<int64_t>()();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing shape/size validation before calling scalar() on input 3 and before shaped<>() on batch_index. Trigger: a caller supplies a nonscalar `id` or a batch_index whose element count is not three times dim_size(0). Consequence: the internal CHECK/assertion fires, aborting the process (denial of service) rather than returning an InvalidArgument error.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (count > xsize) {'], 'added_lines': ['    int x = 0;', '        if (x + count > xsize) {', '        x += count;']}
description: In libImaging/SgiRleDecode.c in Pillow through 7.0.0, a number of out-of-bounds reads exist in the parsing of SGI image files, a different issue than CVE-2020-5311.

code_evidence: The bounds check compares only the current run length count against xsize, ignoring how many pixels have already been written in prior runs of this row.
With RLE_COPY_FLAG set, memcpy(dest, src, 2) copies count times, advancing src by 2 each iteration, so src is read beyond the input buffer when accumulated runs exceed xsize.
The literal-run branch also loops count times copying from src and then advances src by 2, reading past the supplied data without any cumulative limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe memcpy loops read from src beyond the intended input buffer due to a missing cumulative bound, which is precisely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a write overflow because dest advancement is bounded by the same unchecked count but the demonstrated defect is reading past src.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-run check count > xsize does not account for previously expanded pixels, so total output/input consumption can exceed the row width. Trigger: a crafted SGI RLE stream with several runs whose individual counts are each <= xsize but sum beyond it. Consequence: memcpy reads past the src buffer, yielding out-of-bounds reads (crash or memory disclosure).

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions due to incomplete validation in MKL implementation of requantization, an attacker can trigger undefined behavior via binding a reference to a null pointer or can access data outside the bounds of heap allocated arrays. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/core/kernels/mkl/mkl_requantization_range_per_channel_op.cc) does not validate the dimensions of the `input` tensor. A similar issue occurs in `MklRequantizePerChannelOp`. The [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/core/kernels/mkl/mkl_requantize_per_channel_op.cc) does not perform full validation for all the input arguments. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 9e62869465573cb2d9b5053f1fa02a81fce21d69 and in the Github commit 203214568f5bc237603dbab6e1fd389f1572f5c9. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Compute reads input, input_min, and input_max from the context and derives depth from input_max.NumElements(); the only pre-patch checks compare input_min.dim_size(0) and input_max.dim_size(0) to depth. The input tensor's rank, element count, and channel dimension are never validated, so a malformed input passes these guards.

A vector ranges is sized depth, and the loop indexes transposed_input.chip<0>(i) and input_min_data[i]/input_max_data[i]. Because input's shape was not checked against depth, the chip index and the per-channel array reads rely on unvalidated dimensions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the kernel processes input tensors without validating required shape and size properties before use. The missing checks on input rank, element count, and channel alignment are improper input validation; the resulting out-of-bounds access is the consequence, distinct from the validation gap itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the kernel trusts the caller-supplied input tensor shape and only partially checks the min/max tensors, so depth can disagree with input's channel count or input can be empty/rank-mismatched. Trigger: a crafted input tensor with an unexpected rank, zero elements, or a channel count different from depth. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap reads or undefined behavior when the loop indexes chips and min/max data arrays.

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflows.

The data structures linkhash and printbuf are limited to 2 GB in size
due to a signed integer being used to track their current size.

If too much data is added, then size variable can overflow, which is
an undefined behaviour in C programming language.

Assuming that a signed int overflow just leads to a negative value,
like it happens on many sytems (Linux i686/amd64 with gcc), then
printbuf is vulnerable to an out of boundary write on 64 bit systems.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Prevent signed integer overflows with large buffers. */', '\tif (size > INT_MAX - p->bpos - 1)', '\t\treturn -1;']}
description: json-c through 0.14 has an integer overflow and out-of-bounds write via a large JSON file, as demonstrated by printbuf_memappend.

code_evidence: The bounds check computes p->bpos + size + 1 and passes it to printbuf_extend without checking whether that signed int addition wraps.
After the check, memcpy writes size bytes at p->buf + p->bpos and bpos is incremented by size, so a wrapped negative length feeds into the copy and index update.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is an unchecked signed integer addition whose wraparound defeats the size check and drives a memory write, matching CWE-190. The out-of-bounds write is the consequence, not the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
if (p->size <= p->bpos + size + 1)
if (printbuf_extend(p, p->bpos + size + 1) < 0)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: p->bpos + size + 1 is evaluated as a signed int with no overflow guard, so a large size makes the sum wrap negative. The extend check then passes and memcpy/terminator writes use the unvalidated size and bpos, causing an out-of-bounds write when a large JSON input is appended.

description: A heap-based buffer overflow in WritePCXImage in coders/pcx.c in ImageMagick 7.0.6-8 Q16 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or code execution via a crafted file.

code_evidence: The bytes_per_line field is computed from image->columns and bits_per_pixel, then truncated to unsigned short; large columns wrap the value.
The truncated bytes_per_line is written to the header and used as the allocation length for the pixel buffer.

The DirectClass loop iterates x < pcx_info.bytes_per_line, writing one byte per iteration into the buffer sized from that same truncated value, so the write count matches the truncated length rather than the true row width.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the narrowed row length leads to operations on a buffer whose intended boundary is inconsistent with the actual data, permitting out-of-bounds reads/writes. A related integer-truncation weakness could be cited, but the supported consequence is the memory-buffer boundary violation.

pcx_info.bytes_per_line=(unsigned short) (((size_t) image->columns*
pcx_info.bits_per_pixel+7)/8);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the row length is narrowed to unsigned short without a bound check, so a large image width produces a wrapped bytes_per_line. Trigger: a crafted image with columns large enough that columns*bits_per_pixel/8 exceeds 65535. Consequence: the header and buffer length no longer represent the real row width, allowing out-of-bounds memory operations during pixel serialization.

commit_msg:
evtchn: address races with evtchn_reset()

Neither d->evtchn_port_ops nor max_evtchns(d) may be used in an entirely
lock-less manner, as both may change by a racing evtchn_reset(). In the
common case, at least one of the domain's event lock or the per-channel
lock needs to be held. In the specific case of the inter-domain sending
by evtchn_send() and notify_via_xen_event_channel() holding the other
side's per-channel lock is sufficient, as the channel can't change state
without both per-channel locks held. Without such a channel changing
state, evtchn_reset() can't complete successfully.

Lock-free accesses continue to be permitted for the shim (calling some
otherwise internal event channel functions), as this happens while the
domain is in effectively single-threaded mode. Special care also needs
taking for the shim's marking of in-use ports as ECS_RESERVED (allowing
use of such ports in the shim case is okay because switching into and
hence also out of FIFO mode is impossihble there).

As a side effect, certain operations on Xen bound event channels which
were mistakenly permitted so far (e.g. unmask or poll) will be refused
now.

This is part of XSA-343.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    evtchn_port_set_pending(d, v->vcpu_id, evtchn_from_port(d, port));'], 'added_lines': ['    struct evtchn *chn;', '    chn = evtchn_from_port(d, port);', '    spin_lock(&chn->lock);', '    evtchn_port_set_pending(d, v->vcpu_id, chn);', '    spin_unlock(&chn->lock);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: Line 8 reads v->virq_to_evtchn[virq] under only v->virq_lock, then lines 11-12 resolve and use evtchn_from_port(d, port) without holding the per-channel lock; a racing evtchn_reset() can change the port-to-channel mapping between the lookup and use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: A shared resource (the event-channel port mapping) is accessed with a timing window in which a concurrent reset can modify it, matching CWE-362; the missing per-channel lock is the improper synchronization, not merely a memory-safety bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function resolves the event channel from the port and passes it to evtchn_port_set_pending while only the virq lock is held; evtchn_reset() can concurrently alter d->evtchn_port_ops/max_evtchns, so the stale channel reference is used against changed state, violating internal assumptions and leading to out-of-bounds access or bug checks (host/guest crash, possible privilege escalation).

commit_msg: - fix - server crashes when presentation message has no user data (LIB61850-291)(#368)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    bool hasUserData = false;', '', '', '        if (bufPos == endPos) {', '            if (DEBUG_PRES)', '                printf("PRES: invalid message\\n");', '            return -1;', '        }', '            if (self->nextPayload.size > 0)', '                hasUserData = true;', '', '    if (hasUserData == false) {', '        if (DEBUG_PRES)', '            printf("PRES: user-data is missing\\n");', '', '        return -1;', '    }', '']}
description: A NULL pointer dereference in AcseConnection_parseMessage at src/mms/iso_acse/acse.c of libiec61850 v1.5.0 can lead to a segmentation fault or application crash.

code_evidence: The loop reads a tag and length, then dispatches on tag; the 0x61 branch invokes parseFullyEncodedData with the user-data contents and checks only the returned position.
If user-data is absent or empty, the 0x61 case is never reached, so the parse completes without populating self->nextPayload; the 0x00 case simply breaks and the loop exits.
No check exists after parsing that user-data was actually present before returning bufPos to the caller.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is dereferencing a pointer expected to be valid but left unset because the required user-data element was never parsed. This is a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476); it is not an out-of-bounds read, since the defect is the missing validity check on the user-data payload rather than an index error.

case 0x00: 
break;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: parseNormalModeParameters returns success even when no user-data element (tag 0x61) was parsed, leaving self->nextPayload unset. A presentation message lacking user data triggers this path, and the caller subsequently dereferences the missing/empty user-data structure, producing a NULL pointer dereference and crash.

commit_msg: iso9660: validate directory record length
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tchild = parse_file_info(a, parent, p);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tchild = parse_file_info(a, parent, p, b - p);']}
description: An out-of-bounds read flaw exists in parse_file_info in archive_read_support_format_iso9660.c in libarchive 3.3.2 when extracting a specially crafted iso9660 iso file, related to archive_read_format_iso9660_read_header.

code_evidence: Line 37 reads a block of length step into buffer b via __archive_read_ahead. Line 51 iterates directory records with a bound check p + *p <= b, but parse_file_info is called at line 59 with only pointer p and no record-length/remaining-bytes argument. The patch adds b - p to convey the remaining buffer length, indicating the callee previously parsed fields beyond the record boundary.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's caller-side omission of a length bound lets downstream parsing read beyond the intended buffer, which is exactly CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. It is not merely an integer issue; the missing constraint directly enables reading past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: read_children passes only the record pointer to parse_file_info without the remaining buffer length, so the callee cannot validate that the directory record's declared/accessed fields stay within the read block. A crafted iso9660 image with a malformed record triggers reads past the end of buffer b, yielding out-of-bounds memory access (crash or information disclosure).

description: A vulnerability was found in the Linux kernel, where accessing a deallocated instance in printer_ioctl() printer_ioctl() tries to access of a printer_dev instance. However, use-after-free arises because it had been freed by gprinter_free().

code_evidence: gprinter_free() resolves the printer_dev from the usb_function and then immediately releases it with kfree(dev), without any reference-counting or synchronization guarding other holders of the same object.

commit_msg: Safer std::vector indexing.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            for (unsigned i = 5; i < head.size(); ++i) {'], 'added_lines': ['            for (size_t i = 5; i < head.size(); ++i) {']}
description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. An out-of-bounds read was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The out-of-bounds read is triggered when Exiv2 is used to read the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: A fixed 80-byte stack buffer is declared and filled by two reads: xmlHdrCnt+1 bytes then len-xmlHdrCnt-1 bytes, where len=80. The reads are not checked against the actual number of bytes returned, only iIo.error()/eof().

start is set to 3 when the buffer begins with a UTF-8 BOM, and head is constructed from buf+start with length len-start. The string length is derived from the constant len, not from the bytes actually read, so uninitialized or out-of-range buffer contents can be treated as string data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the code reads beyond the intended buffer/content boundary during metadata type detection; the fix in the diff hardens indexing, consistent with an out-of-bounds read rather than a write or injection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The reader trusts the constant len rather than the number of bytes actually read. When input is shorter than expected or a BOM shifts the start offset, head can be built with a length exceeding the valid buffer content, and subsequent indexing/substr operations read past the intended data. The supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read, e.g. a crash/DoS when parsing a crafted image.

At [160-172] color_image_info/color_image are allocated and a unique filename acquired; if OpenBlob fails, return NULL leaks these resources.

commit_msg:
It turns out that currently we rely only on sysfs attribute
permissions:

  $ ll /sys/bus/rbd/{add*,remove*}
  --w------- 1 root root 4096 Sep  3 20:37 /sys/bus/rbd/add
  --w------- 1 root root 4096 Sep  3 20:37 /sys/bus/rbd/add_single_major
  --w------- 1 root root 4096 Sep  3 20:37 /sys/bus/rbd/remove
  --w------- 1 root root 4096 Sep  3 20:38 /sys/bus/rbd/remove_single_major

This means that images can be mapped and unmapped (i.e. block devices
can be created and deleted) by a UID 0 process even after it drops all
privileges or by any process with CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE in its user namespace
as long as UID 0 is mapped into that user namespace.

Be consistent with other virtual block devices (loop, nbd, dm, md, etc)
and require CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the initial user namespace for mapping and
unmapping, and also for dumping the configuration string and refreshing
the image header.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Ilya Dryomov <idryomov@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!capable(CAP_SYS_ADMIN))', '\t\treturn -EPERM;', '']}
description: The rbd block device driver in drivers/block/rbd.c in the Linux kernel through 5.8.9 used incomplete permission checking for access to rbd devices, which could be leveraged by local attackers to map or unmap rbd block devices, aka CID-f44d04e696fe.

code_evidence: The sysfs store handler rbd_image_refresh derives rbd_dev from dev and immediately calls rbd_dev_refresh(rbd_dev) with no capability or privilege check. The only control flow is the error propagation from rbd_dev_refresh; any caller that can write the sysfs attribute reaches the refresh operation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-863 fits because the function implements an access-controlled operation but omits the authorization check entirely, so the check is performed incorrectly (not at all); the missing CAP_SYS_ADMIN gate is the incorrect authorization, not a mere input-validation flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the handler performs a privileged device operation (refreshing the image header) without validating that the caller holds the required capability in the initial user namespace. Trigger: a process able to write the attribute, e.g. UID 0 in a user namespace or one with CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, invokes the store. Consequence: unauthorized refresh/mapping-related actions bypass the intended administrative restriction.
