commit_msg:
x86/pv: Don't have %cr4.fsgsbase active behind a guest kernels back

Currently, a 64bit PV guest can appear to set and clear FSGSBASE in %cr4, but
the bit remains set in hardware.  Therefore, the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE are usable
even when the guest kernel believes that they are disabled.

The FSGSBASE feature isn't currently supported in Linux, and its context
switch path has some optimisations which rely on userspace being unable to use
the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions.  Xen's current behaviour undermines this
expectation.

In 64bit PV guest context, always load the guest kernels setting of FSGSBASE
into %cr4.  This requires adjusting how Xen uses the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE
instructions.

 * Delete the cpu_has_fsgsbase helper.  It is no longer safe, as users need to
   check %cr4 directly.
 * The raw __rd{fs,gs}base() helpers are only safe to use when %cr4.fsgsbase
   is set.  Comment this property.
 * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}{base,shadow}() and read_msr() helpers are updated to use
   the current %cr4 value to determine which mechanism to use.
 * toggle_guest_mode() and save_segments() are update to avoid reading
   fs/gsbase if the values in hardware cannot be stale WRT struct vcpu.  A
   consequence of this is that the write_cr() path needs to cache the current
   bases, as subsequent context switches will skip saving the values.
 * write_cr4() is updated to ensure that the shadow %cr4.fsgsbase value is
   observed in a safe way WRT the hardware setting, if an interrupt happens to
   hit in the middle.
 * load_segments() is updated to use the VMLOAD optimisation if FSGSBASE is
   unavailable, even if only gs_shadow needs updating.  As a minor perf
   improvement, check cpu_has_svm first to short circuit a context-dependent
   conditional on Intel hardware.
 * pv_make_cr4() is updated for 64bit PV guests to use the guest kernels
   choice of FSGSBASE.

This is part of XSA-293.

Reported-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges because a guest can manipulate its virtualised %cr4 in a way that is incompatible with Linux (and possibly other guest kernels).

code_evidence: In the CONFIG_PV && CONFIG_HVM block, the decision to call svm_load_segs() is gated on is_pv_domain(nd), !is_pv_32bit_domain(nd), !is_idle_domain(nd), !cpu_has_fsgsbase and cpu_has_svm; the guest's virtualised %cr4.fsgsbase state is never consulted. The hardware FSGSBASE capability is used as the sole proxy for whether the guest kernel has FSGSBASE enabled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate the guest-controlled %cr4.fsgsbase state before deciding whether the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions are usable, treating an unvalidated hardware capability as equivalent to guest intent; this is improper validation of security-relevant guest input.

evidence_lines.code:
#if defined(CONFIG_PV) && defined(CONFIG_HVM)
if ( is_pv_domain(nd) && !is_pv_32bit_domain(nd) && !is_idle_domain(nd) &&
!cpu_has_fsgsbase && cpu_has_svm )
svm_load_segs(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0);
#endif

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the context-switch path assumes the guest's %cr4.fsgsbase matches hardware capability, ignoring that a 64-bit PV guest can clear the bit in its virtualised %cr4 while the hardware bit remains set. Trigger: a guest kernel disables FSGSBASE, then userspace executes WR{FS,GS}BASE. Supported consequence: the guest kernel's context-switch assumptions are violated, enabling privilege escalation or denial of service.

commit_msg:
Decoder: Fixes an out of bound write in bitstream buffer

[for mnc-dr-dev and later;  mnc-dev gets a different patch]

After emulation prevention, data is written as an int,
so at least 3 additional bytes should be available.
And since bitstream functions read 8 bytes ahead, 8 extra bytes
should be available in the bitstream buffer.

Bug: 33934721

Change-Id: I444ec6f85d01b0bade9f827e15c4b476779d6c69
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        buflen = MIN(buflen, buf_size);'], 'added_lines': ['        /* Since 8 bytes are read ahead, ensure 8 bytes are free at the', '        end of the buffer, which will be memset to 0 after emulation prevention */', '        buflen = MIN(buflen, buf_size - 8);']}
description: A remote code execution vulnerability in libavc in Mediaserver could enable an attacker using a specially crafted file to cause memory corruption during media file and data processing. This issue is rated as Critical due to the possibility of remote code execution within the context of the Mediaserver process. Product: Android. Versions: 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1.1. Android ID: A-33934721.

code_evidence: At line 258 buflen is bounded only by buf_size, the intermediate bitstream buffer size, without reserving trailing read-ahead space. Line 298 copies buflen bytes into pu1_bitstrm_buf, and the subsequent memset at lines 300-303 is guarded by (buflen + 8) < buf_size, so when buflen equals or nearly equals buf_size the copy fills the buffer to its end and the 8-byte zero padding is skipped.

buf_size derives from the dynamic allocation at lines 236-237 or the static buffer at line 250; the copy target pu1_bitstrm_buf is set at lines 244/249, so the destination capacity is exactly buf_size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The memcpy/memset operate on the intermediate buffer but the length constraint fails to preserve the intended read-ahead boundary, allowing operations outside it; this is a buffer-boundary restriction failure matching CWE-119. The fix MIN(buflen, buf_size - 8) confirms the missing headroom; the specific out-of-bounds read is a child-level manifestation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the start-code-derived buflen is clamped to buf_size without subtracting the 8 bytes that bitstream parsing reads ahead. Trigger: a crafted stream whose NAL length reaches the intermediate buffer size causes memcpy to fill the buffer and the memset read-ahead padding to be conditionally skipped. Consequence: bitstream functions read past the buffer's end, causing out-of-bounds memory access and potential memory corruption.

commit_msg: Fix #289: Memory leaks at parser.c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  /* Check memory access */', '  if (mprotect(gerec, nmalloc, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE) != 0) {', '    printf("Inaccessible Memory Address");', '    exit(-1);', '  }', '']}
description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability in libming version 0.4.8, allows attackers to execute arbitrary code and obtain sensitive information via parser.c component.

code_evidence: Line 5 computes nmalloc from glyphbits as ((glyphbits+31)/32)*sizeof(UI32); line 6 allocates exactly that many bytes for GlyphIndex and line 7 writes index 0.

The loop at lines 8-16 writes gerec->GlyphIndex[i] using readBits results; the only bound is i < nmalloc/sizeof(UI32) at line 9, which is derived from the same glyphbits value, so the write count is tied to allocation size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 requires a buffer copy without checking input size, writing past the destination. Here the copy into GlyphIndex is bounded by nmalloc/sizeof(UI32), computed from the same glyphbits used for allocation, so the classic unchecked-copy pattern is not demonstrated by this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation size and the loop bound both derive from glyphbits via the same rounding expression, so the buffer is sized consistently with the number of 32-bit chunks written. Trigger: a malformed glyphbits value would need to make the rounding produce fewer chunks than writes, but no such mismatch is present in this function. The mprotect addition in the patch is unrelated to buffer copying and does not address a size check.

commit_msg:
secvar: fix endian conversion

unpack_timestamp() calls le32_to_cpu() for endian conversion of
uint16_t "year" value. This patch fixes the code to use le16_to_cpu().

Signed-off-by: Nayna Jain <nayna@linux.ibm.com>
Reviewed-by: Daniel Axtens <dja@axtens.net>
Signed-off-by: Vasant Hegde <hegdevasant@linux.vnet.ibm.com>

description: An issue was discovered in OpenPOWER 2.6 firmware. unpack_timestamp() calls le32_to_cpu() for endian conversion of a uint16_t "year" value, resulting in a type mismatch that can truncate a higher integer value to a smaller one, and bypass a timestamp check. The fix is to use the right endian conversion function.

code_evidence: Line 4 reads timestamp->year with le32_to_cpu(), a 32-bit endian conversion, and assigns the result to a uint16_t 'year'. Line 11 then shifts this uint16_t into the packed 64-bit timestamp value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an incorrect conversion between numeric types: a 32-bit-converted value is narrowed into a uint16_t, matching CWE-681's description of data omission/translation during type conversion. The endian mismatch is the cause; the truncation and resulting wrong timestamp are the conversion-consequence.

uint16_t year = le32_to_cpu(timestamp->year);
val |= ((uint64_t) year) << (6*8);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The year field is a 16-bit value but is converted using a 32-bit little-endian helper, and the result is truncated when stored in uint16_t. This produces an incorrect year in the packed timestamp, which can cause a timestamp validity check to be evaluated against the wrong value.

commit_msg:
The VT_DISALLOCATE ioctl can free a virtual console while tty_release()
is still running, causing a use-after-free in con_shutdown().  This
occurs because VT_DISALLOCATE considers a virtual console's
'struct vc_data' to be unused as soon as the corresponding tty's
refcount hits 0.  But actually it may be still being closed.

Fix this by making vc_data be reference-counted via the embedded
'struct tty_port'.  A newly allocated virtual console has refcount 1.
Opening it for the first time increments the refcount to 2.  Closing it
for the last time decrements the refcount (in tty_operations::cleanup()
so that it happens late enough), as does VT_DISALLOCATE.

Reproducer:
	#include <fcntl.h>
	#include <linux/vt.h>
	#include <sys/ioctl.h>
	#include <unistd.h>

	int main()
	{
		if (fork()) {
			for (;;)
				close(open("/dev/tty5", O_RDWR));
		} else {
			int fd = open("/dev/tty10", O_RDWR);

			for (;;)
				ioctl(fd, VT_DISALLOCATE, 5);
		}
	}

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (vc[i] && i >= MIN_NR_CONSOLES) {', '\t\t\ttty_port_destroy(&vc[i]->port);', '\t\t\tkfree(vc[i]);', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (vc[i] && i >= MIN_NR_CONSOLES)', '\t\t\ttty_port_put(&vc[i]->port);']}
description: A race condition in the Linux kernel before 5.6.2 between the VT_DISALLOCATE ioctl and closing/opening of ttys could lead to a use-after-free.

code_evidence: The first loop checks vt_busy(i) under console_lock and stores the result of vc_deallocate(i) in vc[i]; if not busy, the vc_data pointer is cached for later freeing.

The second loop runs after console_unlock(), outside the lock, and unconditionally calls tty_port_destroy(&vc[i]->port) and kfree(vc[i]) on each cached non-NULL pointer without re-validating that the console is still unused or that no concurrent close/open is in progress.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The cached pointer is freed after console_unlock() without holding exclusive access, allowing an interfering close sequence to access the same shared vc_data concurrently; this is a classic improper synchronization race (CWE-362), whose downstream effect is use-after-free (CWE-416), but the target weakness is the race window.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decision that a console is deletable (vt_busy check) and the actual free (kfree) are separated by a lock release, so another thread can still be closing the tty and referencing the vc_data. Trigger: a concurrent tty close/cleanup path while vt_disallocate_all frees the struct. Consequence: the freed vc_data is later dereferenced, yielding a use-after-free in con_shutdown.

commit_msg:
Fix Heap-use-after-free in MDnsSdListener::Monitor::run

Use thread join to avoid thread exiting after instance
recycled.

Prior to implementing this patch, fuzzing would lead to a segmentation fault after approximately 500 rounds. With the addition of the patch, the fuzzing process can now be repeated for over 30,000 rounds.

Test: m, fuzzing
Fuzzing: mma mdns_service_fuzzer && adb sync data && adb shell /data/fuzz/arm64/mdns_service_fuzzer/mdns_service_fuzzer

(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:75e5e2e1faec7aa2812fc6fba30d6fe80558bacd)

description: In run of MDnsSdListener.cpp, there is a possible memory corruption due to a use after free. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: mPollFds and mPollRefs are heap buffers allocated once at run() entry and used throughout the loop.
The while(1) loop has no exit condition, so these buffers are never freed inside the loop; they are only freed after the infinite loop.
The POLLIN branch reads the control socket and may call rescan(), which can resize/reallocate the poll arrays while the loop continues.
Because the loop never terminates, the free() calls at the end are unreachable in normal operation, leaving the buffers and the thread's lifetime tied to the object instance.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the run loop keeps referencing heap buffers after the owning instance is destroyed; the fix adds a POLLHUP exit path that frees the buffers and returns, and the commit joins the thread to prevent it running after recycling. This is a lifetime/use-after-free issue, not merely a null dereference.

evidence_lines.code:
mPollFds = (struct pollfd *)calloc(sizeof(struct pollfd), mPollSize);
mPollRefs = (DNSServiceRef **)calloc(sizeof(DNSServiceRef *), mPollSize);

while (1) {
int pollResults = poll(mPollFds, pollCount, 10000000);

switch (mPollFds[0].revents) {
mPollFds[0].revents = 0;

free(mPollFds);
free(mPollRefs);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The monitor thread loops indefinitely over heap-allocated mPollFds/mPollRefs. When the MDnsSdListener instance is recycled while the thread is still running, the thread can continue to dereference or rescan into freed memory, causing a use-after-free and possible memory corruption.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ((prefix->majorVersion != X_PROTOCOL) ||'], 'added_lines': ['', '    if ((client->req_len << 2) != sz_xReq + sz_xConnClientPrefix +', '\tpad_to_int32(prefix->nbytesAuthProto) +', '\tpad_to_int32(prefix->nbytesAuthString))', '        reason = "Bad length";', '    else if ((prefix->majorVersion != X_PROTOCOL) ||']}
description: xorg-x11-server before 1.19.5 was missing extra length validation in ProcEstablishConnection function allowing malicious X client to cause X server to crash or possibly execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: prefix, auth_proto and auth_string are derived from the client-supplied request buffer using prefix->nbytesAuthProto without checking that these lengths fit within the received request.
The only validation compares protocol version; the request length is never checked against the declared auth field sizes before ClientAuthorized consumes the pointers and lengths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is missing validation of a client-supplied length/consistency property before using it to derive buffer offsets, matching CWE-20's improper input validation of size/length metadata. It is not a transformation or filtering flaw, so CWE-20 fits the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts client-declared nbytesAuthProto/nbytesAuthString and computes auth_proto/auth_string offsets without verifying the request length. A malicious client can supply inconsistent lengths so the derived pointers extend beyond the request buffer, which can crash the X server or, per the advisory, potentially enable code execution.

commit_msg:
Similarly as b02709587ea3 ("bpf: Fix propagation of 32-bit signed bounds
from 64-bit bounds."), we also need to fix the propagation of 32 bit
unsigned bounds from 64 bit counterparts. That is, really only set the
u32_{min,max}_value when /both/ {umin,umax}_value safely fit in 32 bit
space. For example, the register with a umin_value == 1 does /not/ imply
that u32_min_value is also equal to 1, since umax_value could be much
larger than 32 bit subregister can hold, and thus u32_min_value is in
the interval [0,1] instead.

Before fix, invalid tracking result of R2_w=inv1:

  [...]
  5: R0_w=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv(id=0) R10=fp0
  5: (35) if r2 >= 0x1 goto pc+1
  [...] // goto path
  7: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2=inv(id=0,umin_value=1) R10=fp0
  7: (b6) if w2 <= 0x1 goto pc+1
  [...] // goto path
  9: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2=inv(id=0,smin_value=-9223372036854775807,smax_value=9223372032559808513,umin_value=1,umax_value=18446744069414584321,var_off=(0x1; 0xffffffff00000000),s32_min_value=1,s32_max_value=1,u32_max_value=1) R10=fp0
  9: (bc) w2 = w2
  10: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv1 R10=fp0
  [...]

After fix, correct tracking result of R2_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=1,var_off=(0x0; 0x1)):

  [...]
  5: R0_w=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv(id=0) R10=fp0
  5: (35) if r2 >= 0x1 goto pc+1
  [...] // goto path
  7: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2=inv(id=0,umin_value=1) R10=fp0
  7: (b6) if w2 <= 0x1 goto pc+1
  [...] // goto path
  9: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2=inv(id=0,smax_value=9223372032559808513,umax_value=18446744069414584321,var_off=(0x0; 0xffffffff00000001),s32_min_value=0,s32_max_value=1,u32_max_value=1) R10=fp0
  9: (bc) w2 = w2
  10: R0=inv1337 R1=ctx(id=0,off=0,imm=0) R2_w=inv(id=0,umax_value=1,var_off=(0x0; 0x1)) R10=fp0
  [...]

Thus, same issue as in b02709587ea3 holds for unsigned subregister tracking.
Also, align __reg64_bound_u32() similarly to __reg64_bound_s32() as done in
b02709587ea3 to make them uniform again.

Fixes: 3f50f132d840 ("bpf: Verifier, do explicit ALU32 bounds tracking")
Reported-by: Manfred Paul (@_manfp)
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>

description: This vulnerability allows local attackers to escalate privileges on affected installations of Linux Kernel 5.11.15. An attacker must first obtain the ability to execute low-privileged code on the target system in order to exploit this vulnerability. The specific flaw exists within the handling of eBPF programs. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied eBPF programs prior to executing them. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to escalate privileges and execute arbitrary code in the context of the kernel. Was ZDI-CAN-13661.

code_evidence: __reg64_bound_u32 tests whether the u64 argument a lies strictly inside (U32_MIN, U32_MAX) using a single comparison chain and returns the boolean result directly; no clamping or truncation is applied to a before the check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a bound-classification calculation whose result feeds verifier range tracking; an incorrect result yields wrong security-critical bounds, matching CWE-682 Incorrect Calculation. The patch only simplifies the same expression, so the weakness in this function is the unsound boundary test rather than a separate memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The helper decides whether a 64-bit value can be safely propagated into 32-bit unsigned bounds, but the strict-inequality test and lack of a range clamp mean values near the 32-bit boundaries are classified imprecisely. When the verifier uses this result to set u32_min/u32_max from 64-bit umin/umax, it can conclude a subregister range is tighter than reality, corrupting tracked bounds and enabling out-of-bounds eBPF access that escalates privileges.

commit_msg:
Prevent division by 0

PiperOrigin-RevId: 370979352
Change-Id: Ic79191c316d986fc6072ecaebfec9d5f2b924d00
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, block_shape[dim] != 0);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The implementation of the `BatchToSpaceNd` TFLite operator is vulnerable to a division by zero error(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/b5ed552fe55895aee8bd8b191f744a069957d18d/tensorflow/lite/kernels/batch_to_space_nd.cc#L81-L82). An attacker can craft a model such that one dimension of the `block` input is 0. Hence, the corresponding value in `block_shape` is 0. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Loop iterates over spatial dimensions using block_shape[dim] as a divisor: line 20 checks output_batch_size % block_shape[dim] and line 21 computes output_batch_size / block_shape[dim]. block_shape comes from tensor data (line 4) with no zero guard in this function, so a crafted model with block_shape[dim]==0 reaches the modulo/division.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an unchecked division (and modulo) by a value derived from input tensor data, matching CWE-369 Divide By Zero; the missing block_shape[dim] != 0 check is the specific gap the fix adds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: block_shape[dim] is attacker-controlled model data and is used directly as a divisor without a non-zero constraint. Trigger: a model whose block_shape entry is 0. Consequence: division/modulo by zero causes a crash, an availability DoS.

commit_msg:
system/Error: truncate the snprintf() return value

snprintf() does not return the (truncated) length actually written,
but the length that would be needed if the buffer were large enough.
This API usage mistake in FormatLastError() can lead to overflow of
the stack buffer, crashing the process (Windows only).

Closes https://github.com/MusicPlayerDaemon/MPD/issues/1676
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsize_t length = snprintf(buffer, sizeof(buffer) - 128,'], 'added_lines': ['\tconstexpr std::size_t max_prefix = sizeof(buffer) - 128;', '\tsize_t length = snprintf(buffer, max_prefix,', '\tif (length >= max_prefix)', '\t\tlength = max_prefix - 1;']}
description: An issue in MPD (Music Player Daemon) v0.23.10 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via a crafted input.

code_evidence: snprintf() is called with a bound of sizeof(buffer)-128, but its return value is the length that would have been written if untruncated, not the bytes actually stored. That untruncated length is assigned to `length` and used directly to compute `p = buffer + length`, which can point past the 512-byte stack buffer before the two writes `*p++ = ':'` and `*p++ = ' '`.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the end of the intended stack buffer `buffer`, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The truncation mishandling is the cause; the resulting out-of-bounds write is the weakness. This is not merely an integer or format-string issue, since the concrete impact is memory written beyond the buffer bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the snprintf() return value is treated as a written length without clamping. Trigger: a crafted format/argument producing output longer than the 384-byte bound. Consequence: `p` is derived from an oversized `length`, so the subsequent writes at [9,10] (and the later FormatMessageA write) land out of bounds, corrupting the stack and crashing the process (Windows-only DoS).

commit_msg:
net: check packet payload length

While computing IP checksum, 'net_checksum_calculate' reads
payload length from the packet. It could exceed the given 'data'
buffer size. Add a check to avoid it.

Reported-by: Liu Ling <liuling-it@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Signed-off-by: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (plen < csum_offset+2)', '\treturn;'], 'added_lines': ['', '    /* Ensure data has complete L2 & L3 headers. */', '    if (length < 14 + 20) {', '        return;', '    }', '    if (plen < csum_offset + 2 || 14 + hlen + plen > length) {', '        return;', '    }']}
description: The net_checksum_calculate function in net/checksum.c in QEMU allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds heap read and crash) via the payload length in a crafted packet.

code_evidence: The function reads header fields without first verifying that the buffer is long enough: data[14] at line 5, data[16]/data[17] at line 8, and data[23] at line 9 (proto). With a short 'length', these reads go past the end of the buffer.

hlen and plen are taken directly from the packet. The only bound check at line 20 is plen < csum_offset+2; there is no check that 14+hlen+plen is within 'length'. Lines 22-23 write at data[14+hlen+csum_offset], and line 24 passes data+14+hlen with length plen to net_checksum_tcpudp, so an oversized plen makes that helper read past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes memory offsets from unvalidated packet lengths and then reads and writes through them without keeping them inside the 'data' buffer, which matches CWE-119. CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read) is a narrower child weakness, but the same missing length check also drives out-of-bounds writes at the checksum offsets, so the class-level CWE-119 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the payload and header lengths come from the packet, but the function never checks them against the actual buffer size 'length'. Trigger: a crafted packet with a short buffer or a large hlen/plen value. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap reads (and writes at the checksum offsets), leading to a crash or denial of service.

commit_msg: updateDevice() remove element from the list when realloc fails

commit_msg:
spi: lpspi: fix memory leak in fsl_lpspi_probe

In fsl_lpspi_probe an SPI controller is allocated either via
spi_alloc_slave or spi_alloc_master. In all but one error cases this
controller is put by going to error handling code. This commit fixes the
case when pm_runtime_get_sync fails and it should go to the error
handling path.

Fixes: 944c01a889d9 ("spi: lpspi: enable runtime pm for lpspi")
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20190930034602.1467-1-navid.emamdoost@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Mark Brown <broonie@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\treturn ret;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tgoto out_controller_put;']}
description: A memory leak in the fsl_lpspi_probe() function in drivers/spi/spi-fsl-lpspi.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering pm_runtime_get_sync() failures, aka CID-057b8945f78f. NOTE: third parties dispute the relevance of this because an attacker cannot realistically control these failures at probe time

code_evidence: The probe allocates an SPI controller via spi_alloc_slave or spi_alloc_master, giving ownership of a reference that must be released on error.
When pm_runtime_get_sync fails, the error branch logs and does return ret directly, bypassing the shared error path.
The out_controller_put label calls spi_controller_put(controller), which is the release site all other error paths jump to.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a controller and omits spi_controller_put on one error path, matching CWE-401's missing release of allocated memory. It is a leak rather than a use-after-free (CWE-416) because the object is simply never freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pm_runtime_get_sync failure path returns without releasing the controller reference acquired at allocation. Trigger: pm_runtime_get_sync returns a negative value during probe. Consequence: the spi_controller allocation is never freed, leaking memory; repeated probe attempts can exhaust memory.

Detect bogus DT_SYMENT.

commit_msg:
x86emul: honor guest CR0.TS and CR0.EM

We must not emulate any instructions accessing respective registers
when either of these flags is set in the guest view of the register, or
else we may do so on data not belonging to the guest's current task.

Being architecturally required behavior, the logic gets placed in the
instruction emulator instead of hvmemul_get_fpu(). It should be noted,
though, that hvmemul_get_fpu() being the only current handler for the
get_fpu() callback, we don't have an active problem with CR4: Both
CR4.OSFXSR and CR4.OSXSAVE get handled as necessary by that function.

This is XSA-190.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if ( (curr->arch.hvm_vcpu.guest_cr[0] & X86_CR0_EM) ||', '             !(curr->arch.hvm_vcpu.guest_cr[4] & X86_CR4_OSFXSR) )'], 'added_lines': ['    case X86EMUL_FPU_wait:', '        if ( !(curr->arch.hvm_vcpu.guest_cr[4] & X86_CR4_OSFXSR) )']}
description: Xen 4.7.x and earlier does not properly honor CR0.TS and CR0.EM, which allows local x86 HVM guest OS users to read or modify FPU, MMX, or XMM register state information belonging to arbitrary tasks on the guest by modifying an instruction while the hypervisor is preparing to emulate it.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only chooses whether FPU/MMX/XMM emulation is permitted based on guest CR0/CR4/XCR0 feature flags; it contains no concurrent access to a shared resource, no synchronization, and no timing window, so it does not support a race-condition (CWE-362) claim.

[tfg] Fix null type attribute

commit_msg: Fix write heap buffer overflow in opj_mqc_byteout(). Discovered by Ke Liu of Tencent's Xuanwu LAB (#835)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    l_data_size = (OPJ_UINT32)((p_code_block->x1 - p_code_block->x0) *', '                               (p_code_block->y1 - p_code_block->y0) * (OPJ_INT32)sizeof(OPJ_UINT32));'], 'added_lines': ['    /* The +1 is needed for https://github.com/uclouvain/openjpeg/issues/835 */', '    l_data_size = 1 + (OPJ_UINT32)((p_code_block->x1 - p_code_block->x0) *', '                                   (p_code_block->y1 - p_code_block->y0) * (OPJ_INT32)sizeof(OPJ_UINT32));']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the opj_mqc_byteout function in mqc.c in OpenJPEG before 2.2.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted bmp file.

opj_malloc(l_data_size + 1) allocates l_data_size+1 bytes and data_size is set to l_data_size, but data is advanced by one (data += 1), leaving only l_data_size usable bytes for encoder writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes an undersized buffer and exposes it to out-of-bounds writes, directly matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operations. The specific write overflow is a child weakness, but the target label is the buffer-boundary class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the computed l_data_size omits the sentinel byte required by opj_mqc_byteout, so the effective buffer after data += 1 is one byte short. Trigger: a crafted BMP producing code-block dimensions whose product fills the buffer. Consequence: opj_mqc_byteout writes past the heap allocation (heap buffer overflow), causing a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
gvariant-serialiser: Check offset table entry size is minimal

The entries in an offset table (which is used for variable sized arrays
and tuples containing variable sized members) are sized so that they can
address every byte in the overall variant.

The specification requires that for a variant to be in normal form, its
offset table entries must be the minimum width such that they can
address every byte in the variant.

That minimality requirement was not checked in
`g_variant_is_normal_form()`, leading to two different byte arrays being
interpreted as the normal form of a given variant tree. That kind of
confusion could potentially be exploited, and is certainly a bug.

Fix it by adding the necessary checks on offset table entry width, and
unit tests.

Spotted by William Manley.

Signed-off-by: Philip Withnall <pwithnall@endlessos.org>

Fixes: #2794
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  return offset_ptr == offset;'], 'added_lines': ['  gsize offset_table_size;', '  /* @offset_ptr has been counting backwards from the end of the variant, to', '   * find the beginning of the offset table. @offset has been counting forwards', '   * from the beginning of the variant to find the end of the data. They should', '   * have met in the middle. */', '  if (offset_ptr != offset)', '    return FALSE;', '', '  offset_table_size = value.size - offset_ptr;', '  if (value.size > 0 &&', '      gvs_calculate_total_size (offset, offset_table_size / offset_size) != value.size)', '    return FALSE;  /* offset size not minimal */', '', '  return TRUE;']}
description: A flaw was found in GLib. GVariant deserialization fails to validate that the input conforms to the expected format, leading to denial of service.

code_evidence: For each G_VARIANT_MEMBER_ENDING_OFFSET member, the loop reads an offset-table entry from value.data+offset_ptr after decrementing offset_ptr by offset_size, and bounds end to offset_ptr.

The final check only verifies offset_ptr == offset; it never verifies that offset_size is the minimal width needed to address every byte, so a larger-than-necessary offset table is accepted as normal form.
Because of the missing minimality check, the same variant tree can have multiple accepted byte encodings, weakening the normal-form invariant.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to enforce a constraint on how much offset-table space the variant format consumes, allowing inputs that keep an oversized offset table while still being accepted as normal form. This uncontrolled resource/format consumption directly supports CWE-400 within the deserialization path.

evidence_lines.code:
if (end < offset || end > offset_ptr)
return FALSE;
return offset_ptr == offset;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: gvs_tuple_is_normal validates offset table consistency but not that offset table entries use the minimal width required by the spec. Trigger: an attacker supplies a serialized variant whose offset table entries are wider than necessary; the function still returns TRUE. Consequence: multiple byte arrays are accepted as the normal form of one variant tree, causing confusion in consumers that rely on normal-form uniqueness and enabling denial-of-service conditions.

commit_msg: Thumbnail size range check
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  }', '', '  if (T.tlength < 64u)', '  {', '      if (errcode)', '          *errcode = EINVAL;', '      return NULL;', '  }', '', '  if (INT64(T.tlength) > 1024ULL * 1024ULL * LIBRAW_MAX_THUMBNAIL_MB)', '  {', '      if (errcode)', '          *errcode = LIBRAW_TOO_BIG;', '      return NULL;']}
description: LibRaw before 0.20-RC1 lacks a thumbnail size range check. This affects decoders/unpack_thumb.cpp, postprocessing/mem_image.cpp, and utils/thumb_utils.cpp. For example, malloc(sizeof(libraw_processed_image_t)+T.tlength) occurs without validating T.tlength.

code_evidence: For BITMAP thumbnails, malloc size is computed as sizeof(libraw_processed_image_t) + T.tlength, then T.tlength bytes are copied via memmove; the size and copy length derive directly from the thumbnail metadata T.tlength with no bounds check in this function.
For JPEG thumbnails, dsize = T.tlength + mk_exif*(...) is used for malloc; T.thumb+6 is passed to strcmp and T.tlength-2 is used as a copy length, again using unvalidated T.tlength.

The copy at T.thumb+2 with length T.tlength-2 relies on T.tlength being at least 2 and consistent with the allocated buffer; an attacker-controlled small or oversized value corrupts the size arithmetic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes the input-derived metadata field T.tlength but does not validate its required range before using it for allocation and copying, which is exactly improper input validation (CWE-20). The fix commit adds lower and upper bounds, confirming the missing validation is the root cause rather than a separate arithmetic or overflow weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
memmove(ret->data + (2 + sizeof(exif) + sizeof(th)), T.thumb + 2,
T.tlength - 2);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the thumbnail length field T.tlength is used in allocation size arithmetic and memmove lengths without a range check. Trigger: a crafted image sets T.tlength to a very large or very small value, so the malloc/memmove size is wrong. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read/write or excessive allocation, leading to memory corruption or denial of service.

commit_msg:
When converting from an inode from storing the data in-line to a data
block, ext4_destroy_inline_data_nolock() was only clearing the on-disk
copy of the i_blocks[] array.  It was not clearing copy of the
i_blocks[] in ext4_inode_info, in i_data[], which is the copy actually
used by ext4_map_blocks().

This didn't matter much if we are using extents, since the extents
header would be invalid and thus the extents could would re-initialize
the extents tree.  But if we are using indirect blocks, the previous
contents of the i_blocks array will be treated as block numbers, with
potentially catastrophic results to the file system integrity and/or
user data.

This gets worse if the file system is using a 1k block size and
s_first_data is zero, but even without this, the file system can get
quite badly corrupted.

This addresses CVE-2018-10881.

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=200015

Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tmemset(ei->i_data, 0, EXT4_MIN_INLINE_DATA_SIZE);']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's ext4 filesystem. A local user can cause an out-of-bound access in ext4_get_group_info function, a denial of service, and a system crash by mounting and operating on a crafted ext4 filesystem image.

code_evidence: The function clears only the on-disk inode's inline data region via ext4_raw_inode(&is.iloc)->i_block, then marks the inode as no longer having inline data and resets i_inline_off/i_inline_size.
The in-memory copy ei->i_data is never cleared before the inode is converted to a block-mapped layout.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because stale, uninitialized index data is used as block numbers, causing writes/addressing beyond the intended data region. The defect is an out-of-bounds write via corrupted block mapping, not merely a missing initialization.

evidence_lines.code:
memset((void *)ext4_raw_inode(&is.iloc)->i_block,
0, EXT4_MIN_INLINE_DATA_SIZE);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the conversion path zeroes the on-disk i_block buffer but leaves the stale in-memory ei->i_data contents intact while clearing EXT4_INODE_INLINE_DATA. Trigger: an inode that previously stored inline data is converted to indirect-block mapping, so ext4_map_blocks() later interprets stale i_data entries as block numbers. Supported consequence: the filesystem treats garbage as block pointers, corrupting filesystem integrity and user data (CVE-2018-10881).

commit_msg: Issue #287: made CSR/CSC readers more robust against invalid input (case #1).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if ( sscanf(l_line, "%u %u %u", o_row_count, o_column_count, o_element_count) == 3 ) {', '        l_row--;', '        l_column--;'], 'added_lines': ['        if (3 == sscanf(l_line, "%u %u %u", o_row_count, o_column_count, o_element_count) &&', '            0 != *o_row_count && 0 != *o_column_count && 0 != *o_element_count)', '        {', '        LIBXSMM_ASSERT(0 != l_row && 0 != l_column);', '        l_row--; l_column--;']}

Header values from sscanf size the heap allocations for o_row_idx, o_column_idx, o_values and l_column_idx_id; the column-index fill loop runs l_i <= *o_column_count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-influenced column indices past the end of heap buffers, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely a read overflow (CWE-125) because the offending accesses at lines 78-79 are stores into allocated arrays.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: element lines are trusted without validating l_column (and l_row) against the header-declared dimensions. A file whose element column index exceeds *o_column_count causes l_column_idx_id[l_column] and (*o_column_idx)[l_column+1] to write past the malloc'd buffers; a zero index underflows via l_column-- to a huge unsigned index. Trigger: malformed CSC input. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, memory corruption/crash.

commit_msg:
Don't change the state of the ETM flags until CCS processing

Changing the ciphersuite during a renegotiation can result in a crash
leading to a DoS attack. ETM has not been implemented in 1.1.0 for DTLS
so this is TLS only.

The problem is caused by changing the flag indicating whether to use ETM
or not immediately on negotiation of ETM, rather than at CCS. Therefore,
during a renegotiation, if the ETM state is changing (usually due to a
change of ciphersuite), then an error/crash will occur.

Due to the fact that there are separate CCS messages for read and write
we actually now need two flags to determine whether to use ETM or not.

CVE-2017-3733

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (!SSL_USE_ETM(s) && EVP_MD_CTX_md(s->read_hash) != NULL)'], 'added_lines': ['        if (!SSL_READ_ETM(s) && EVP_MD_CTX_md(s->read_hash) != NULL)']}
description: During a renegotiation handshake if the Encrypt-Then-Mac extension is negotiated where it was not in the original handshake (or vice-versa) then this can cause OpenSSL 1.1.0 before 1.1.0e to crash (dependent on ciphersuite). Both clients and servers are affected.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The changed line only switches the ETM flag accessor used to compute mac_size; the function contains no input-validation check or missing validation of an input property, so CWE-20 is not supported.

commit_msg:
Call strlen() if name length provided is 0, like OpenSSL does.
Issue notice by Christian Heimes <christian@python.org>
ok deraadt@ jsing@
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (name != NULL && namelen == 0)', '\t\tnamelen = strlen(name);']}
description: The int_x509_param_set_hosts function in lib/libcrypto/x509/x509_vpm.c in LibreSSL 2.7.0 before 2.7.1 does not support a certain special case of a zero name length, which causes silent omission of hostname verification, and consequently allows man-in-the-middle attackers to spoof servers and obtain sensitive information via a crafted certificate. NOTE: the LibreSSL documentation indicates that this special case is supported, but the BoringSSL documentation does not.

code_evidence: When name is non-NULL but namelen is 0, the early-return branch treats it as an empty name and returns success without storing any host, so no hostname entry is added to id->hosts.
The embedded-NUL check uses memchr(name, '\0', namelen); with namelen==0 it inspects nothing, so the zero-length case bypasses the only validation before the silent return.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Silently dropping the hostname constraint causes certificate validation to be performed without the intended hostname check, i.e. incorrect validation of the peer certificate, matching CWE-295 rather than a memory-safety issue.

evidence_lines.code:
if (name == NULL || namelen == 0)
return 1;

if (name && memchr(name, '\0', namelen))
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function silently accepts a zero name length as success instead of deriving length via strlen, so the requested hostname constraint is never recorded in id->hosts. Trigger: a caller sets a host name with namelen 0. Consequence: hostname verification is silently omitted, enabling a crafted certificate to spoof a server (man-in-the-middle).

commit_msg:
Add additional check returned from flb_malloc

This PR tries to address the issue raised in 3044 where
memory pointer returned from flb_malloc was not checked for NULL.
Credit to raminfp.

This PR fixes the 3044.

Signed-off-by: Yong Tang <yong.tang.github@outlook.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (!out_buff) {', '        flb_errno();', '        return NULL;', '    }']}

code_evidence: Line 6 allocates out_buff via flb_malloc without checking for NULL; the pointer is then passed to avro_writer_memory at line 44.
Line 103 passes out_buff to flb_sds_create_len; lines 106-108 dereference the returned ret (via flb_sds_len/alloc/avail) without a NULL check.

awriter = avro_writer_memory(out_buff, avro_buffer_size);

flb_sds_t ret =  flb_sds_create_len(out_buff, bytes_written);

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Don't have %cr4.fsgsbase active behind a guest kernels back

Currently, a 64bit PV guest can appear to set and clear FSGSBASE in %cr4, but
the bit remains set in hardware.  Therefore, the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE are usable
even when the guest kernel believes that they are disabled.

The FSGSBASE feature isn't currently supported in Linux, and its context
switch path has some optimisations which rely on userspace being unable to use
the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions.  Xen's current behaviour undermines this
expectation.

In 64bit PV guest context, always load the guest kernels setting of FSGSBASE
into %cr4.  This requires adjusting how Xen uses the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE
instructions.

 * Delete the cpu_has_fsgsbase helper.  It is no longer safe, as users need to
   check %cr4 directly.
 * The raw __rd{fs,gs}base() helpers are only safe to use when %cr4.fsgsbase
   is set.  Comment this property.
 * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}{base,shadow}() and read_msr() helpers are updated to use
   the current %cr4 value to determine which mechanism to use.
 * toggle_guest_mode() and save_segments() are update to avoid reading
   fs/gsbase if the values in hardware cannot be stale WRT struct vcpu.  A
   consequence of this is that the write_cr() path needs to cache the current
   bases, as subsequent context switches will skip saving the values.
 * write_cr4() is updated to ensure that the shadow %cr4.fsgsbase value is
   observed in a safe way WRT the hardware setting, if an interrupt happens to
   hit in the middle.
 * load_segments() is updated to use the VMLOAD optimisation if FSGSBASE is
   unavailable, even if only gs_shadow needs updating.  As a minor perf
   improvement, check cpu_has_svm first to short circuit a context-dependent
   conditional on Intel hardware.
 * pv_make_cr4() is updated for 64bit PV guests to use the guest kernels
   choice of FSGSBASE.

This is part of XSA-293.

Reported-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@
 static inline void wrgsbase(unsigned long base)
 {
-    if ( cpu_has_fsgsbase )
+    if ( read_cr4() & X86_CR4_FSGSBASE )
 #ifdef HAVE_AS_FSGSBASE
         asm volatile ( "wrgsbase %0" :: "r" (base) );
 #else
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( cpu_has_fsgsbase )'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( read_cr4() & X86_CR4_FSGSBASE )']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges because a guest can manipulate its virtualised %cr4 in a way that is incompatible with Linux (and possibly other guest kernels).

code_evidence: wrgsbase() chooses between the WRGSBASE instruction (lines 4-8) and a wrmsrl() MSR write (line 10) based solely on cpu_has_fsgsbase (line 3), a static capability flag rather than the actual current %cr4.fsgsbase bit. The patch replaces this check with read_cr4() & X86_CR4_FSGSBASE, showing the guard did not reflect the guest kernel's runtime CR4 setting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function validates the wrong property (static capability) rather than the required runtime CR4 state before executing a privileged instruction, i.e. improper validation of the condition governing the operation, matching CWE-20. It is not a mere transformation/filtering issue; the missing check on the actual CR4 bit is the defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the helper trusts a cached capability flag instead of the live CR4 state to decide whether the WRGSBASE instruction is permitted. Trigger: a 64-bit PV guest kernel clears FSGSBASE in its virtual CR4 while hardware keeps the bit set, so this path still emits WRGSBASE. Consequence: the guest can write FS/GS base behind the kernel's back, undermining context-switch assumptions and enabling privilege escalation or DoS.

commit_msg:
Fix comparison between different name types

Signed-off-by: Manuel Pégourié-Gonnard <manuel.pegourie-gonnard@arm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if( x509_crt_check_cn( &cur->buf, cn, cn_len ) == 0 )'], 'added_lines': ['            if( x509_crt_check_san( &cur->buf, cn, cn_len ) == 0 )']}
description: An issue was discovered in Mbed TLS before 2.24.0. The verification of X.509 certificates when matching the expected common name (the cn argument of mbedtls_x509_crt_verify) with the actual certificate name is mishandled: when the subjecAltName extension is present, the expected name is compared to any name in that extension regardless of its type. This means that an attacker could impersonate a 4-byte or 16-byte domain by getting a certificate for the corresponding IPv4 or IPv6 address (this would require the attacker to control that IP address, though).

code_evidence: When the subjectAltName extension is present, the loop iterates over every subject_alt_names entry and calls x509_crt_check_cn on cur->buf without inspecting the entry's type; on a match it breaks and does not set the mismatch flag.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs hostname verification of an X.509 certificate but incorrectly validates SAN entries, accepting a name of the wrong type; this is improper certificate validation (CWE-295). It is not merely a comparison bug because the consequence is a bypass of certificate identity checks.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: SAN entries are matched by value only, so an IPv4/IPv6 address entry is compared against the expected DNS name. Trigger: a certificate whose SAN contains an address encoding equal to the expected hostname. Consequence: the expected name is accepted and impersonation is possible, bypassing name verification.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.4+
Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>

description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.10 does not correctly synchronize the actions of updating versus finding a key in the "negative" state to avoid a race condition, which allows local users to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's only relevant change replaces a negative-flag test with key_is_negative(); the described race is a synchronization/atomicity issue in the KEYS subsystem, not improper input validation of the update payload, and the function itself contains no input-validation defect supporting CWE-20.

avcodec/vqavideo: Set video size

description: FFmpeg before 4.2 has a heap-based buffer overflow in vqa_decode_chunk because of an out-of-array access in vqa_decode_init in libavcodec/vqavideo.c.

code_evidence: Width and height are read directly from attacker-controlled extradata (lines 23-24) and only checked with av_image_check_size (line 25), which validates generic image dimensions but does not constrain them to the codec's buffer sizing assumptions.
The only subsequent size constraint (lines 36-39) merely requires dimensions to be multiples of vector_width/vector_height; it does not bound them relative to the later allocations.
decode_buffer_size is computed as (width/vector_width)*(height/vector_height)*2 (lines 47-48) and allocated at line 49, establishing the buffer whose bounds later decode paths rely on.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit fixes an out-of-array access caused by unconstrained dimensions, and the description identifies a heap-based buffer overflow from an out-of-array access; this is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) rather than a mere read or integer overflow, since the recorded consequence is writing past the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the init path accepts dimensions validated only by av_image_check_size, which is insufficient for this codec's later indexing and allocation arithmetic. Trigger: crafted VQA extradata supplying large width/height. Consequence: inconsistent sizing leads to an out-of-array write in vqa_decode_chunk, i.e., a heap-based buffer overflow.

description: FreeRDP is a free implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), released under the Apache license. commit_msg:
avformat/cinedec: Fix DoS due to lack of eof check

Fixes: loop.cine

Found-by: Xiaohei and Wangchu from Alibaba Security Team
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    for (i = 0; i < st->duration; i++)'], 'added_lines': ['    for (i = 0; i < st->duration; i++) {', '        if (avio_feof(pb))', '            return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;', '', '    }']}
description: In FFmpeg 3.3.3, a DoS in cine_read_header() due to lack of an EOF check might cause huge CPU and memory consumption. When a crafted CINE file, which claims a large "duration" field in the header but does not contain sufficient backing data, is provided, the image-offset parsing loop would consume huge CPU and memory resources, since there is no EOF check inside the loop.

code_evidence: Line 23 reads st->duration directly from the file via avio_rl32(pb), an attacker-controlled 32-bit count with no bound check. Line 139 seeks to offImageOffsets, then the loop at lines 140-141 iterates i from 0 to st->duration, calling avio_rl64 and av_add_index_entry on each iteration without any check on remaining input or a cap on iterations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 covers loops whose iteration count is not sufficiently limited and is attacker-influenced, matching the duration-driven loop at lines 140-141 that consumes resources per iteration. It is not CWE-835 (infinite loop) because the loop terminates when i reaches duration; the weakness is an unbounded, attacker-controlled iteration count.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the image-offset parsing loop is bounded only by the untrusted st->duration field, so a crafted CINE header declaring a huge duration while providing little backing data forces avio_rl64/av_add_index_entry to run for the full declared count. Trigger: a malicious file with a large duration. Consequence: excessive CPU and memory consumption (index entries) leading to denial of service.

commit_msg: [http2] delay processing requests upon observing suspicious behavior
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    conn->dos_mitigation.process_delay.cb = on_dos_process_delay;', '    conn->dos_mitigation.reset_budget = conn->super.ctx->globalconf->http2.max_concurrent_requests_per_connection;']}
description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

code_evidence: The added lines initialize the connection's DoS-mitigation state: a process-delay callback is registered and reset_budget is set from the configured max_concurrent_requests_per_connection. This is the only resource-throttling state established in create_conn; no other per-connection limit is set here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function configures a mechanism that limits how many requests are processed per connection, addressing uncontrolled resource consumption from rapid stream cancellation. It is not a memory-safety issue; the weakness is missing/limited throttling of resource allocation.

evidence_lines.code:
conn->received_any_request = 0;
return conn;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the absence of a bound on concurrently processed HTTP/2 streams, which the DoS mitigation counters by delaying processing. The added initialization arms that throttle with a configured budget; without it, a client canceling many streams quickly could drive repeated request processing and consume server resources (CPU/memory). Consequence is resource exhaustion/denial of service; the cause is unthrottled request processing, not the initialization itself.

commit_msg:
sched/fair: Fix infinite loop in update_blocked_averages() by reverting a9e7f6544b9c

Zhipeng Xie, Xie XiuQi and Sargun Dhillon reported lockups in the
scheduler under high loads, starting at around the v4.18 time frame,
and Zhipeng Xie tracked it down to bugs in the rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
manipulation.

Do a (manual) revert of:

  a9e7f6544b9c ("sched/fair: Fix O(nr_cgroups) in load balance path")

It turns out that the list_del_leaf_cfs_rq() introduced by this commit
is a surprising property that was not considered in followup commits
such as:

  9c2791f936ef ("sched/fair: Fix hierarchical order in rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list")

As Vincent Guittot explains:

 "I think that there is a bigger problem with commit a9e7f6544b9c and
  cfs_rq throttling:

  Let take the example of the following topology TG2 --> TG1 --> root:

   1) The 1st time a task is enqueued, we will add TG2 cfs_rq then TG1
      cfs_rq to leaf_cfs_rq_list and we are sure to do the whole branch in
      one path because it has never been used and can't be throttled so
      tmp_alone_branch will point to leaf_cfs_rq_list at the end.

   2) Then TG1 is throttled

   3) and we add TG3 as a new child of TG1.

   4) The 1st enqueue of a task on TG3 will add TG3 cfs_rq just before TG1
      cfs_rq and tmp_alone_branch will stay  on rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.

  With commit a9e7f6544b9c, we can del a cfs_rq from rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.
  So if the load of TG1 cfs_rq becomes NULL before step 2) above, TG1
  cfs_rq is removed from the list.
  Then at step 4), TG3 cfs_rq is added at the beginning of rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
  but tmp_alone_branch still points to TG3 cfs_rq because its throttled
  parent can't be enqueued when the lock is released.
  tmp_alone_branch doesn't point to rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list whereas it should.

  So if TG3 cfs_rq is removed or destroyed before tmp_alone_branch
  points on another TG cfs_rq, the next TG cfs_rq that will be added,
  will be linked outside rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list - which is bad.

  In addition, we can break the ordering of the cfs_rq in
  rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list but this ordering is used to update and
  propagate the update from leaf down to root."

Instead of trying to work through all these cases and trying to reproduce
the very high loads that produced the lockup to begin with, simplify
the code temporarily by reverting a9e7f6544b9c - which change was clearly
not thought through completely.

This (hopefully) gives us a kernel that doesn't lock up so people
can continue to enjoy their holidays without worrying about regressions. ;-)

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.3.9. ksmbd does not validate the SMB request protocol ID, leading to an out-of-bounds read.

code_evidence: The pre-patch function returns conn->request_buf[0] == 0 without validating the SMB protocol identifier; the buffer is later interpreted as an SMB2 message by downstream code such as init_smb2_rsp_hdr.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing protocol-ID validation lets malformed requests reach code that reads beyond the buffer bounds, as confirmed by the KASAN slab-out-of-bounds report in init_smb2_rsp_hdr. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write, so CWE-125 rather than CWE-787 applies.

evidence_lines.code: return conn->request_buf[0] == 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ksmbd_smb_request accepts any request whose first byte is zero, without checking the full 32-bit protocol ID against known SMB constants, so malformed or truncated requests pass validation. Trigger: a crafted SMB request with a matching leading byte but invalid/absent protocol header is processed as SMB2. Consequence: downstream SMB2 header parsing reads past the intended buffer, producing the reported slab-out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
mm: Tighten x86 /dev/mem with zeroing reads

Under CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM, reading System RAM through /dev/mem is
disallowed. However, on x86, the first 1MB was always allowed for BIOS
and similar things, regardless of it actually being System RAM. It was
possible for heap to end up getting allocated in low 1MB RAM, and then
read by things like x86info or dd, which would trip hardened usercopy:

usercopy: kernel memory exposure attempt detected from ffff880000090000 (dma-kmalloc-256) (4096 bytes)

This changes the x86 exception for the low 1MB by reading back zeros for
System RAM areas instead of blindly allowing them. More work is needed to
extend this to mmap, but currently mmap doesn't go through usercopy, so
hardened usercopy won't Oops the kernel.

Reported-by: Tommi Rantala <tommi.t.rantala@nokia.com>
Tested-by: Tommi Rantala <tommi.t.rantala@nokia.com>
Signed-off-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (pagenr < 256)', '\t\treturn 1;', '\tif (iomem_is_exclusive(pagenr << PAGE_SHIFT))', '\tif (!page_is_ram(pagenr))', '\t\treturn 1;', '\treturn 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (page_is_ram(pagenr)) {', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * For disallowed memory regions in the low 1MB range,', '\t\t * request that the page be shown as all zeros.', '\t\t */', '\t\tif (pagenr < 256)', '\t\t\treturn 2;', '', '\t}', '', '\t/*', '\t * This must follow RAM test, since System RAM is considered a', '\t * restricted resource under CONFIG_STRICT_IOMEM.', '\t */', '\tif (iomem_is_exclusive(pagenr << PAGE_SHIFT)) {', '\t\t/* Low 1MB bypasses iomem restrictions. */', '\t\tif (pagenr < 256)', '\t\t\treturn 1;', '', '\t\treturn 0;', '\t}', '', '\treturn 1;']}
description: The mm subsystem in the Linux kernel through 3.2 does not properly enforce the CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM protection mechanism, which allows local users to read or write to kernel memory locations in the first megabyte (and bypass slab-allocation access restrictions) via an application that opens the /dev/mem file, related to arch/x86/mm/init.c and drivers/char/mem.c.

code_evidence: Lines 3-4 unconditionally return 1 (access allowed) for any page number below 256, i.e., the first 1MB, before any RAM or exclusivity check is performed.
Lines 5-6 only deny access when iomem_is_exclusive() is true, after the low-1MB early return has already granted access.
Lines 7-8 return 1 for non-RAM pages, and line 9 returns 0 only for RAM pages above the low-1MB cutoff.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function assigns read permission to a critical resource (/dev/mem) more broadly than intended: the low-1MB bypass grants access to System RAM, a resource that should be restricted, matching incorrect permission assignment for a critical resource. It is not merely a missing authorization check but an explicit overly permissive grant.

evidence_lines.code:
if (pagenr < 256)
return 1;

if (iomem_is_exclusive(pagenr << PAGE_SHIFT))
return 0;

if (!page_is_ram(pagenr))
return 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The permission check for the /dev/mem security-critical resource returns 'allowed' for the entire low 1MB before consulting page_is_ram() or iomem_is_exclusive(), so System RAM that happens to be allocated there is exposed regardless of CONFIG_STRICT_DEVMEM. A local user opening /dev/mem and reading low addresses triggers the exposure, leaking kernel heap contents.

commit_msg:
More checks for correct header sizes

Reported-by: "P. Amsuo, Purdue University"
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        return;', '', '    if ((*idx + PICO_TCPOPTLEN_MSS) > len)']}
description: VirtualSquare picoTCP (aka PicoTCP-NG) through 2.1 lacks certain size calculations before attempting to set a value of an mss structure member.

code_evidence: The function validates the option via tcpopt_len_check at line 4, then unconditionally sets t->mss_ok = 1 at line 6 and reads a 16-bit MSS with short_from(opt + *idx) at line 7, advancing *idx by sizeof(uint16_t) at line 8. The function contains no check that *idx + PICO_TCPOPTLEN_MSS stays within len, so the offset arithmetic used to locate the MSS field is not bounded.

This is a calculation error rather than a pure missing length check; the incorrect offset drives subsequent out-of-bounds access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the offset calculation for reading the MSS value ignores the total option length. Trigger: a TCP MSS option with a length/idx combination that passes the earlier check but places *idx near or beyond len. commit_msg:
dbus: validate parameters of all calls

SetElement and DeleteElement were missing check for valid dump directory
path.

FindProblemByElementInTimeRange was not reporting invalid element names.

Related: #1214451

Signed-off-by: Jakub Filak <jfilak@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (!allowed_problem_dir(problem_id))', '        {', '            return_InvalidProblemDir_error(invocation, problem_id);', '            return;', '        }', '', '', '        if (!allowed_problem_dir(problem_id))', '        {', '            return_InvalidProblemDir_error(invocation, problem_id);', '            return;', '        }', '        if (!str_is_correct_filename(element))', '        {', '            log_notice("\'%s\' is not a valid element name", element);', '            char *error = xasprintf(_("\'%s\' is not a valid element name"), element);', '            g_dbus_method_invocation_return_dbus_error(invocation,', '                                              "org.freedesktop.problems.InvalidElement",', '                                              error);', '', '            free(error);', '            return;', '        }', '']}
description: Directory traversal vulnerability in abrt-dbus in Automatic Bug Reporting Tool (ABRT) allows local users to read, write to, or change ownership of arbitrary files via unspecified vectors to the (1) NewProblem, (2) GetInfo, (3) SetElement, or (4) DeleteElement method.

code_evidence: SetElement extracts attacker-controlled problem_id, element and value from the D-Bus parameters, then only validates element via str_is_correct_filename; problem_id is passed unchecked to open_directory_for_modification_of_element, which builds the directory path.
DeleteElement likewise takes problem_id and element from parameters and validates only element before passing problem_id into open_directory_for_modification_of_element.
FindProblemByElementInTimeRange reads element from the caller and forwards it into get_problem_dirs_for_element_in_time without validating it as a filename.

It is not merely missing authorization, since the defect is path construction from untrusted names.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: caller-supplied problem_id/element strings are concatenated into dump-directory paths without checking that they stay within the configured dump location. A local D-Bus caller can supply values containing '../' or absolute paths, causing file operations to resolve outside the restricted directory and allowing read, write, deletion or ownership changes of arbitrary files.

description: When processing certain files, PHP EXIF extension in versions 7.1.x below 7.1.28, 7.2.x below 7.2.17 and 7.3.x below 7.3.4 can be caused to read past allocated buffer in exif_process_IFD_TAG function. This may lead to information disclosure or crash.

The only bound check compares 2+NumDirEntries*12 to value_len, ignoring how far dir_start lies into the buffer. The loop then passes dir_start + 2 + 12*de to exif_process_IFD_TAG, which reads tag data relative to dir_start.

commit_msg: Fix #12239 - crash in the x86.nz assembler ##asm (#12252)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\twhile (begin && isspace ((ut8)str[*begin])) {', '\t} else if (isalpha ((ut8)str[*begin])) {   // word token', '\t\twhile (end && isalnum ((ut8)str[*end])) {', '\t} else if (isdigit ((ut8)str[*begin])) {   // number token'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (*begin > strlen (str)) {', '\t\treturn TT_EOF;', '\t}', '\twhile (begin && str[*begin] && isspace ((ut8)str[*begin])) {', '\t}', '\tif (isalpha ((ut8)str[*begin])) {   // word token', '\t\twhile (end && str[*end] && isalnum ((ut8)str[*end])) {', '\t}', '\tif (isdigit ((ut8)str[*begin])) {   // number token']}
description: getToken in libr/asm/p/asm_x86_nz.c in radare2 before 3.1.0 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer over-read) via crafted x86 assembly data, as demonstrated by rasm2.

code_evidence: Whitespace loop indexes str[*begin] and increments *begin without checking that *begin is below strlen(str), so a begin at or past the terminator reads beyond the string.
Word-token loop tests str[*end] with isalnum but only guards end != NULL; it never bounds *end against the string length, so scanning can advance past the terminator.
Number-token loop has the same defect: str[*end] is dereferenced and incremented while *end is unbounded relative to the buffer size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe operation is reading str[*begin]/str[*end] beyond the buffer's end, not writing to it. Contrast CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) would require a store past bounds, which is absent here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loops advance *begin/*end by one and dereference str at the new offset without any length check; the only guard is a NULL pointer test on begin/end. Crafted assembly input lacking a terminator within the scanned region (or with begin already at the end) drives the index past the allocated string, producing an out-of-bounds read that can crash the assembler.

commit_msg: Fix codestyle.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    if (width1 > 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t    if (width1 > 0)', '\t    {']}
description: Divide By Zero in vim/vim from 9.0.1367-1 to 9.0.1367-3

code_evidence: Line 103 computes width1 as window width minus column offset; line 104 guards the branch with width1 > 0. Inside, line 105 computes width2 = width1 + curwin_col_off2(). Line 107 divides (curwin->w_skipcol - width1) by width2. The guard only constrains width1, not width2; if col_off2 is negative and cancels width1, width2 becomes zero and the division on line 107 divides by zero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because line 107 performs a division whose divisor width2 is not validated against zero; the preceding guard only validates width1. This is a direct divide-by-zero, not merely an off-by-one or overflow issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the condition checks width1 > 0 but does not ensure the divisor width2 (width1 + col_off2) is nonzero. Trigger: a window configuration where width1 + curwin_col_off2() evaluates to 0 while w_skipcol > width1. Consequence: integer division by zero on line 107, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
shorten: pad the internal bitstream buffer

Fixes invalid reads.

Found-by: Mateusz "j00ru" Jurczyk and Gynvael Coldwind
CC:libav-stable@libav.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                                  s->max_framesize);'], 'added_lines': ['                                  s->max_framesize + FF_INPUT_BUFFER_PADDING_SIZE);']}
description: A vulnerability was found in FFmpeg 2.0. It has been classified as problematic. Affected is the function shorten_decode_frame of the component Bitstream Buffer. The manipulation leads to memory corruption. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

code_evidence: When max_framesize is zero, the bitstream buffer is allocated with av_fast_realloc sized only to s->max_framesize (1024), without FF_INPUT_BUFFER_PADDING_SIZE.

Later, buf_size is clamped to max_framesize - bitstream_size and memcpy writes buf_size bytes at bitstream_index+bitstream_size; the decoder's bit reading can then access/overrun beyond the allocated region because no padding exists.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch adds FF_INPUT_BUFFER_PADDING_SIZE to the allocation, directly fixing an out-of-bounds access on the bitstream buffer, matching CWE-787 (write/access past intended buffer end). It is not merely an integer overflow; the missing padding constraint is the defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the internal bitstream buffer is allocated without the input padding the bitstream reader assumes. Trigger: a remote packet causes decoding that reads/writes near the buffer end, exceeding the allocation. Supported consequence: invalid reads/out-of-bounds access leading to memory corruption.

commit_msg:

Convert this device to use vmstate for its save/load, including
providing a post_load function that sanitizes inbound data to

relying on the security properties of most of the unmaintained

work on this board due to issues in other device models).

commit_msg:
tcp: take care of truncations done by sk_filter()

With syzkaller help, Marco Grassi found a bug in TCP stack,
crashing in tcp_collapse()

Root cause is that sk_filter() can truncate the incoming skb,
but TCP stack was not really expecting this to happen.
It probably was expecting a simple DROP or ACCEPT behavior.

description: mruby through 2.1.2-rc has a heap-based buffer overflow in the mrb_yield_with_class function in vm.c because of incorrect VM stack handling. It can be triggered via the stack_copy function.

code_evidence: ci->argc is stored as the raw argc and n is computed as argc+2 for C functions, then mrb->c->stack is advanced by n before mrb_stack_extend(mrb, n) is called; the extension therefore applies to the already-shifted stack rather than the frame needing space.

With argc > 0, stack_copy writes argc values starting at mrb->c->stack+1, and mrb->c->stack[argc+1] is assigned afterward; when argc is large or the extension did not cover the shifted frame, these writes go past the allocated stack.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes caller-supplied argument values and a terminator into the VM stack at offsets computed from argc without ensuring the shifted frame fits, which is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is a missing bounds/size constraint on a memory write, not merely an incorrect stack-depth value.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stack pointer is advanced before stack extension and the frame size is derived from an unchecked argc, so the extend call does not guarantee room for the shifted frame. Trigger: calling mrb_yield_with_class with a large argc (or variadic argument count) reaches stack_copy and the nil terminator write beyond the stack buffer. Supported consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds write corrupting memory, potentially leading to crash or code execution.

This originated from an integer overflow: If mp4config.frame.ents
would be read-in with a value of (uint32t)(-1), it would overflow to 0

Merge pull request from GHSA-8hcp-hm38-mfph

* Check hostname during TLS transport selection

* revision based on feedback

* remove the code in create_request that has been moved
