description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In version 2.10 and earlier, PJSIP transport can be reused if they have the same IP address + port + protocol. However, this is insufficient for secure transport since it lacks remote hostname authentication. Suppose we have created a TLS connection to `sip.foo.com`, which has an IP address `100.1.1.1`. If we want to create a TLS connection to another hostname, say `sip.bar.com`, which has the same IP address, then it will reuse that existing connection, even though `100.1.1.1` does not have certificate to authenticate as `sip.bar.com`. The vulnerability allows for an insecure interaction without user awareness. It affects users who need access to connections to different destinations that translate to the same address, and allows man-in-the-middle attack if attacker can route a connection to another destination such as in the case of DNS spoofing.

code_evidence: In the UAC branch of dlg_update_routeset, the function records the initial destination hostname by copying rdata->tp_info.transport->remote_name.host into dlg->initial_dest when it is empty. This hostname is the identity later needed to bind a reused TLS transport to the dialog's destination, rather than relying only on the transport's IP address and port.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper certificate validation in the sense that the TLS peer identity is not tied to the expected hostname when reusing transports. Recording initial_dest supplies the hostname needed for that validation; the function itself only stores it, so the evidence is the identity binding required to prevent accepting a certificate for the wrong host.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: transport reuse was previously selected by IP address, port and protocol without recording or comparing the requested remote hostname. This change captures the initial destination host so a later TLS transport selection can verify the hostname matches before reusing the connection. Without this binding, a connection established to one hostname could be reused for a different hostname resolving to the same IP, enabling a man-in-the-middle to impersonate the peer.

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = table->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = xt_table_get_private_protected(table);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: Line 6 caches table->private into a local pointer without any synchronization, then line 12 calls alloc_counters(table) and line 17 dereferences the cached private->entries through xt_entry_foreach. The local snapshot is never refreshed after alloc_counters, so it can refer to table info that a concurrent xt_replace_table has already freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because line 17 dereferences a pointer to table info that the concurrent replacement frees before use. This is a stale-pointer lifetime defect, not merely a race or information leak; the supported consequence is reading freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function snapshots table->private into a local pointer before alloc_counters, with no ordering or protected access relative to the concurrent replacement path. Trigger: a CAP_NET_ADMIN namespace user runs concurrent iptables rules replacement while another context iterates entries; the replacement frees the old table info, and line 17 walks the stale private->entries. Consequence: use-after-free during entry copying, leading to read of freed memory or crash.

commit_msg:
Blink-in-JS should not run micro tasks

If Blink-in-JS runs micro tasks, there's a risk of causing a UXSS bug
(see 645211 for concrete steps).

This CL makes Blink-in-JS use callInternalFunction (instead of callFunction)
to avoid running micro tasks after Blink-in-JS' callbacks.

BUG=645211

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2330843002
Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#417874}

description: Blink in Google Chrome prior to 54.0.2840.59 for Windows, Mac, and Linux; 54.0.2840.85 for Android permitted execution of v8 microtasks while the DOM was in an inconsistent state, which allowed a remote attacker to inject arbitrary scripts or HTML (UXSS) via crafted HTML pages.

The size calculation in `build_open_gop_key_points()` goes through all entries in the loop and adds `sc->ctts_data[i].count` to `sc->sample_offsets_count`. The accumulated count is passed as the element count to av_calloc; a wrapped small value yields a small allocation.
The second loop writes sc->ctts_data[i].duration into sample_offsets[k++] for each count, so the write index exceeds the undersized allocation.
Similarly, open_key_samples_count accumulates sc->sync_group[i].count for the matching index without an overflow check.

Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, enabling memory corruption and potentially code execution.

commit_msg:
Fixed bugs of stack reallocation x GC

Macro 'checkstackGC' was doing a GC step after resizing the stack;
the GC could shrink the stack and undo the resize. Moreover, macro
'checkstackp' also does a GC step, which could remove the preallocated
CallInfo when calling a function. (Its name has been changed to
'checkstackGCp' to emphasize that it calls the GC.)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      CallInfo *ci = next_ci(L);', '      checkstackp(L, LUA_MINSTACK, func);  /* ensure minimum stack size */', '      L->ci = ci;', '      CallInfo *ci = next_ci(L);', '      checkstackp(L, fsize, func);', '      checkstackp(L, 1, func);  /* space for metamethod */'], 'added_lines': ['      CallInfo *ci;', '      checkstackGCp(L, LUA_MINSTACK, func);  /* ensure minimum stack size */', '      L->ci = ci = next_ci(L);', '      CallInfo *ci;', '      checkstackGCp(L, fsize, func);', '      L->ci = ci = next_ci(L);', '      checkstackGCp(L, 1, func);  /* space for metamethod */']}
description: Lua through 5.4.0 mishandles the interaction between stack resizes and garbage collection, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow, heap-based buffer over-read, or use-after-free.

code_evidence: C-function path: ci is obtained via next_ci(L) at line 12 before checkstackp(L, LUA_MINSTACK, func) at line 13. checkstackp can trigger a GC step that shrinks the stack, invalidating the preallocated CallInfo; ci is then written at lines 14-17 and stored to L->ci at line 18.
Lua-function path: same ordering, ci = next_ci(L) at line 32, then checkstackp at line 37; fields are written at lines 38-42 and L->ci assigned at line 43, after the GC-capable call.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing ci->nresults, callstatus, top and func through a pointer invalidated by the intervening stack resize is an out-of-bounds write into stack memory, matching CWE-787. The use-after-free is a secondary consequence of the same stale-pointer write rather than the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The CallInfo is allocated before a checkstackp call that may run garbage collection and reallocate/shrink the stack, so the stale ci pointer is written to after the resize. This corrupts stack memory (out-of-bounds write) or yields a use-after-free; the trigger is calling a function where checkstackp performs a GC step.

commit_msg:
A lack of range checks in libXtst allows out of boundary accesses.
The checks have to be done in-place here, because it cannot be done
without in-depth knowledge of the read data.

If XRecordStartOfData, XRecordEndOfData, or XRecordClientDied
without a client sequence have attached data, an endless loop would
occur. The do-while-loop continues until the current index reaches
the end. But in these cases, the current index would not be
incremented, leading to an endless processing.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t    UnlockDisplay(dpy);', '\t    SyncHandle();', '\t    return 0;', '\t}', '', '\tif (rep.length > INT_MAX >> 2) {']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in X.org libXtst before 1.2.3 allow remote X servers to trigger out-of-bounds memory access operations by leveraging the lack of range checks.

code_evidence: At line 24 the server-controlled reply length is used without an upper-bound check; line 25 computes rep.length<<2 as the allocation size for alloc_reply_buffer, and line 31 uses the same shifted value as the read size for _XRead. The shift truncates the length, so the size passed to allocation and the size passed to the read derive from a wrapped 32-bit value rather than the actual reply length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is an integer shift that can overflow the size computation used for allocation and copying, which matches CWE-190. The flaw is the wraparound in the size calculation itself, not a generic missing bounds check on an index.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: rep.length is a wire-supplied 32-bit value shifted left by 2 without validating it against INT_MAX>>2, so the computed byte count wraps to a small or negative value. Trigger: a remote X server returns a large reply length. Consequence: the undersized allocation is followed by a read of the shifted length, causing out-of-bounds memory access driven by the mismatch between allocation and copy size.

commit_msg:
Adds a new configuration proxy.config.http.allow_multi_range

This is needed to prevent potential abuse with well formed multi-
range requests.

description: When there are multiple ranges in a range request, Apache Traffic Server (ATS) will read the entire object from cache. This can cause performance problems with large objects in cache. This affects versions 6.0.0 to 6.2.2 and 7.0.0 to 7.1.3. To resolve this issue users running 6.x users should upgrade to 6.2.3 or later versions and 7.x users should upgrade to 7.1.4 or later versions.

code_evidence: Lines 156-157 load the existing cache range lookup/write configuration bytes, showing this startup routine governs range-request cache behavior. Line 173 reads proxy.config.http.send_http11_requests and is the insertion point adjacent to the added allow_multi_range setting, which gates whether multiple ranges in one request cause the whole cached object to be read.
The function itself only registers configuration values; the resource-control decision lives in the range-handling code that consumes oride.allow_multi_range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the weakness is failure to control consumption of a limited resource (cache read/memory) under attacker-controlled multi-range requests. It is not a memory-corruption issue; the supported impact is resource exhaustion/DoS.

evidence_lines.code:
HttpEstablishStaticConfigByte(c.oride.cache_range_lookup, "proxy.config.http.cache.range.lookup");
HttpEstablishStaticConfigByte(c.oride.cache_range_write, "proxy.config.http.cache.range.write");
HttpEstablishStaticConfigByte(c.oride.send_http11_requests, "proxy.config.http.send_http11_requests");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the proxy lacks throttling/restriction on multi-range requests, so a well-formed request with many ranges forces reading the entire large cached object. Trigger: a client sends a multi-range request against a large cached object. Supported consequence: excessive memory/CPU consumption, a resource-exhaustion availability impact.

The UAF is because:

 mount(pid: 921)               | cifsd(pid: 923)
-------------------------------|-------------------------------
                               | cifs_demultiplex_thread
SMB2_negotiate                 |
 cifs_send_recv                |
  compound_send_recv           |
   smb_send_rqst               |
    wait_for_response          |
     wait_event_state      [1] |
                               |  standard_receive3
                               |   cifs_handle_standard
                               |    handle_mid
                               |     mid->resp_buf = buf;  [2]
                               |     dequeue_mid           [3]

    resp_iov[i].iov_base = buf |

1. After send request to server, wait the response until
    mid->mid_state != SUBMITTED;
2. Receive response from server, and set it to mid;
3. Set the mid state to RECEIVED;
4. Kill the process, the mid state already RECEIVED, get 0;

The sock_llcp_release error path at lines 87-89 similarly calls nfc_llcp_local_put(llcp_sock->local) without clearing the pointer afterward.

commit_msg:
The internal VM "mmap()" interfaces are based on the mmap target doing
everything using page indexes rather than byte offsets, because
traditionally (ie 32-bit) we had the situation that the byte offset
didn't fit in a register.  So while the mmap virtual address was limited
by the word size of the architecture, the backing store was not.

So we're basically passing "pgoff" around as a page index, in order to
be able to describe backing store locations that are much bigger than
the word size (think files larger than 4GB etc).

But while this all makes a ton of sense conceptually, we've been dogged
by various drivers that don't really understand this, and internally
work with byte offsets, and then try to work with the page index by
turning it into a byte offset with "pgoff << PAGE_SHIFT".

Which obviously can overflow.

Adding the size of the mapping to it to get the byte offset of the end
of the backing store just exacerbates the problem, and if you then use
this overflow-prone value to check various limits of your device driver
mmap capability, you're just setting yourself up for problems.

The correct thing for drivers to do is to do their limit math in page
indices, the way the interface is designed.  Because the generic mmap
code _does_ test that the index doesn't overflow, since that's what the
mmap code really cares about.

HOWEVER.

Finding and fixing various random drivers is a sisyphean task, so let's
just see if we can just make the core mmap() code do the limiting for
us.  Realistically, the only "big" backing stores we need to care about
are regular files and block devices, both of which are known to do this
properly, and which have nice well-defined limits for how much data they
can access.

So let's special-case just those two known cases, and then limit other
random mmap users to a backing store that still fits in "unsigned long".
Realistically, that's not much of a limit at all on 64-bit, and on
32-bit architectures the only worry might be the GPU drivers, which can
have big physical address spaces.

To make it possible for drivers like that to say that they are 64-bit
clean, this patch does repurpose the "FMODE_UNSIGNED_OFFSET" bit in the
file flags to allow drivers to mark their file descriptors as safe in
the full 64-bit mmap address space.

[ The timing for doing this is less than optimal, and this should really
  go in a merge window. But realistically, this needs wide testing more
  than it needs anything else, and being main-line is the only way to do
  that.

  So the earlier the better, even if it's outside the proper development
  cycle        - Linus ]

Cc: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
Cc: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Cc: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: Dave Airlie <airlied@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\tif (!file_mmap_ok(file, inode, pgoff, len))', '\t\t\treturn -EOVERFLOW;']}
description: The Linux kernel through 5.3.13 has a start_offset+size Integer Overflow in cpia2_remap_buffer in drivers/media/usb/cpia2/cpia2_core.c because cpia2 has its own mmap implementation. This allows local users (with /dev/video0 access) to obtain read and write permissions on kernel physical pages, which can possibly result in a privilege escalation.

code_evidence: len is page-aligned at line 19; line 22 computes pgoff + (len >> PAGE_SHIFT) in unsigned long and compares to pgoff to detect wraparound, returning -EOVERFLOW at line 23. This core mmap code already guards the page-index addition, so the pgoff+size overflow described for driver-level byte-offset math is not present here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 requires an unchecked calculation that can wrap. The only relevant arithmetic (line 22) is a deliberate overflow check that returns -EOVERFLOW, so this function does not itself exhibit the integer overflow; it mitigates it. The described overflow lives in driver mmap implementations, not here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the commit context concerns drivers that convert pgoff to byte offsets via pgoff << PAGE_SHIFT and add mapping size, overflowing. In this function the arithmetic stays in page indices and is explicitly bounds-checked at line 22 before get_unmapped_area/mmap_region use pgoff. Trigger would require the check to be absent or bypassed; here it rejects wrapped values. No overflow consequence is supported by this function.

commit_msg:
[CVE-2023-29469] Hashing of empty dict strings isn't deterministic

When hashing empty strings which aren't null-terminated,
xmlDictComputeFastKey could produce inconsistent results. This could
lead to various logic or memory errors, including double frees.

For consistency the seed is also taken into account, but this shouldn't
have an impact on security.

Found by OSS-Fuzz.

Fixes #510.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (name == NULL) return(0);'], 'added_lines': ['    if ((name == NULL) || (namelen <= 0))', '        return(value);']}
description: An issue was discovered in libxml2 before 2.10.4. When hashing empty dict strings in a crafted XML document, xmlDictComputeFastKey in dict.c can produce non-deterministic values, leading to various logic and memory errors, such as a double free. This behavior occurs because there is an attempt to use the first byte of an empty string, and any value is possible (not solely the '\0' value).

code_evidence: Only a NULL name is rejected; an empty string (namelen <= 0) still reaches line 5, which dereferences *name and reads an arbitrary first byte when the string is not null-terminated.
When namelen > 10, line 8 reads name[namelen - 1] without validating the length against the actual buffer.
The switch on namelen adds name[9]..name[1] for the corresponding cases, so negative or empty lengths reach the default and skip the loop, leaving value dependent on the uninitialized *name byte.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit and code show that empty-string hashing is non-deterministic, which the description states can lead to double free, matching CWE-415. The function itself does not call free twice; it supplies the inconsistent hash that enables the double free, so it supports CWE-415 as the disclosed consequence rather than an unrelated weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (name == NULL) return(0);
value += *name;

if (namelen > 10) {
value += name[namelen - 1];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accepts empty strings (namelen <= 0) and still consumes *name, producing a hash derived from an arbitrary byte rather than a deterministic value. Trigger: a crafted XML document containing an empty non-null-terminated dict string. Consequence: inconsistent hash values break dictionary lookups and can lead to logic or memory errors such as double free.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: fix unconditional helper

Ben Hawkes says:

 In the mark_source_chains function (net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c) it
 is possible for a user-supplied ipt_entry structure to have a large
 next_offset field. This field is not bounds checked prior to writing a
 counter value at the supplied offset.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static inline bool unconditional(const struct ipt_ip *ip)', '\treturn memcmp(ip, &uncond, sizeof(uncond)) == 0;'], 'added_lines': ['static inline bool unconditional(const struct ipt_entry *e)', '\treturn e->target_offset == sizeof(struct ipt_entry) &&', '\t       memcmp(&e->ip, &uncond, sizeof(uncond)) == 0;']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

code_evidence: The helper takes only the embedded ipt_ip and returns true whenever its bytes equal a zeroed ipt_ip. It never inspects target_offset or the presence of matches, so a rule entry with a large user-controlled next_offset/target_offset and no matches is classified as an unconditional verdict rule.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The misclassification lets a caller operate on a memory location outside the intended rule buffer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds operation. The missing constraint is on entry layout (target_offset), not merely an integer overflow, so CWE-119 fits the resultant memory-buffer violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unconditional() decides 'unconditional rule' from address bytes alone, ignoring the entry's target_offset and match layout. Trigger: a crafted IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE entry with wildcard addresses but an oversized next_offset passes this test, so callers such as mark_source_chains proceed past a non-existent next entry and write a counter at the supplied offset. Consequence: out-of-bounds write into the rule blob, i.e., heap memory corruption leading to privilege escalation or DoS.

	by Alfred Farrugia & Sandro Gauci (Enable Security)

case PARA_VALUE_QUOTED:
switch (*(tmp+1))
{
case '\r':

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: parse_to_param walks attacker-controlled SIP To header bytes with a state machine but does not bound-check the lookahead at the backslash case and does not reject the header when the loop terminates still in the PARA_VALUE_QUOTED state. commit_msg:
[ Upstream commit ad0f75e5f57ccbceec13274e1e242f2b5a6397ed ]

When we clone a socket in sk_clone_lock(), its sk_cgrp_data is
copied, so the cgroup refcnt must be taken too. And, unlike the
sk_alloc() path, sock_update_netprioidx() is not called here.
Therefore, it is safe and necessary to grab the cgroup refcnt
even when cgroup_sk_alloc is disabled.

sk_clone_lock() is in BH context anyway, the in_interrupt()
would terminate this function if called there. And for sk_alloc()
skcd->val is always zero. So it's safe to factor out the code
to make it more readable.

The global variable 'cgroup_sk_alloc_disabled' is used to determine
whether to take these reference counts. It is impossible to make
the reference counting correct unless we save this bit of information
in skcd->val. So, add a new bit there to record whether the socket
has already taken the reference counts. This obviously relies on
kmalloc() to align cgroup pointers to at least 4 bytes,
ARCH_KMALLOC_MINALIGN is certainly larger than that.

This bug seems to be introduced since the beginning, commit
d979a39d7242 ("cgroup: duplicate cgroup reference when cloning sockets")
tried to fix it but not compeletely. It seems not easy to trigger until
the recent commit 090e28b229af
("netprio_cgroup: Fix unlimited memory leak of v2 cgroups") was merged.

Fixes: bd1060a1d671 ("sock, cgroup: add sock->sk_cgroup")

Reported-by: Peter Geis <pgwipeout@gmail.com>

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (cgroup_sk_alloc_disabled)', '\t\treturn;', '', '\t/* Socket clone path */', '\tif (skcd->val) {', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * We might be cloning a socket which is left in an empty', "\t\t * cgroup and the cgroup might have already been rmdir'd.", "\t\t * Don't use cgroup_get_live().", '\t\t */', '\t\tcgroup_get(sock_cgroup_ptr(skcd));'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (cgroup_sk_alloc_disabled) {', '\t\tskcd->no_refcnt = 1;']}
description: The Linux kernel 4.9.x before 4.9.233, 4.14.x before 4.14.194, and 4.19.x before 4.19.140 has a use-after-free because skcd->no_refcnt was not considered during a backport of a CVE-2020-14356 patch. This is related to the cgroups feature.

code_evidence: When cgroup_sk_alloc_disabled is set, the function returns at line 4 without recording that no reference was taken. For a cloned socket whose skcd->val is already populated (line 5), it calls cgroup_get(sock_cgroup_ptr(skcd)) at line 6 and returns at line 7; in the disabled path this get is skipped entirely, so the cloned socket's copied cgroup pointer is never refcounted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked refcount on the copied cgroup pointer leaves the socket holding a dangling reference to freed cgroup memory, matching CWE-416 rather than a simple leak; the consequence is use of freed memory, not merely a missing reference count.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the disabled-cgroup early return skips the cgroup reference acquisition that must accompany the copied sk_cgrp_data during socket cloning, and no no_refcnt flag is set to later suppress a matching put. Trigger: a socket is cloned while cgroup_sk_alloc is disabled; the clone's cgroup can be freed while the socket still points at it, and later access or release of that pointer is a use-after-free.

Specify type for matching Subject Alternative Name. (#18628)

description: Envoy is an open source edge and service proxy, designed for cloud-native applications. The default_validator.cc implementation used to implement the default certificate validation routines has a "type confusion" bug when processing subjectAltNames. This processing allows, for example, an rfc822Name or uniformResourceIndicator to be authenticated as a domain name. This confusion allows for the bypassing of nameConstraints, as processed by the underlying OpenSSL/BoringSSL implementation, exposing the possibility of impersonation of arbitrary servers. As a result Envoy will trust upstream certificates that should not be trusted.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over each configured subjectAltName matcher and wraps it directly with Matchers::StringMatcherImpl(matcher) at line 11, without inspecting matcher.san_type(). This differs from a mere missing validation check: the matcher's type information is discarded, causing the value to be interpreted under the wrong type.

Trigger: a certificate presents a value in a non-DNS SAN (e.g., URI or rfc822Name) that equals a configured matcher. The value is then matched as if it were a DNS name, so nameConstraints enforced by BoringSSL for the actual type are bypassed, enabling impersonation of arbitrary servers.

commit_msg:
RDS: fix race condition when sending a message on unbound socket

Sasha's found a NULL pointer dereference in the RDS connection code when
sending a message to an apparently unbound socket.  The problem is caused
by the code checking if the socket is bound in rds_sendmsg(), which checks
the rs_bound_addr field without taking a lock on the socket.  This opens a
race where rs_bound_addr is temporarily set but where the transport is not
in rds_bind(), leading to a NULL pointer dereference when trying to
dereference 'trans' in __rds_conn_create().

Vegard wrote a reproducer for this issue, so kindly ask him to share if
you're interested.

I cannot reproduce the NULL pointer dereference using Vegard's reproducer
with this patch, whereas I could without.

Complete earlier incomplete fix to CVE-2015-6937:

  74e98eb08588 ("RDS: verify the underlying transport exists before creating a connection")

Cc: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org

Reviewed-by: Vegard Nossum <vegard.nossum@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Sasha Levin <sasha.levin@oracle.com>
Acked-by: Santosh Shilimkar <santosh.shilimkar@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Quentin Casasnovas <quentin.casasnovas@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* racing with another thread binding seems ok here */'], 'added_lines': ['\tlock_sock(sk);', '\t\trelease_sock(sk);', '\trelease_sock(sk);']}
description: Race condition in the rds_sendmsg function in net/rds/sendmsg.c in the Linux kernel before 4.3.3 allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by using a socket that was not properly bound.  NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2015-6937.

code_evidence: rds_sendmsg reads rs->rs_bound_addr (and daddr) to decide whether the socket is bound, without holding the socket lock around this check; the comment removed by the patch confirms the check was expected to race with another thread binding.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is a missing synchronization constraint on a shared resource (the socket's bound state) checked and modified by concurrent code sequences, matching CWE-362. It is not merely a NULL dereference; the NULL dereference is the consequence of the race window.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bind-state check of rs->rs_bound_addr is performed without lock_sock(sk), so a concurrent bind can set rs_bound_addr while the transport is not yet established. Trigger: a local thread sends on an unbound socket while another thread binds it. The check passes with a partially initialized binding, and the subsequent connection creation dereferences a NULL transport, causing a crash (DoS).

  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call

  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

commit_msg:
mac80211: Fix NULL ptr deref for injected rate info

The commit cb17ed29a7a5 ("mac80211: parse radiotap header when selecting Tx
queue") moved the code to validate the radiotap header from
ieee80211_monitor_start_xmit to ieee80211_parse_tx_radiotap. This made is
possible to share more code with the new Tx queue selection code for
injected frames. But at the same time, it now required the call of
ieee80211_parse_tx_radiotap at the beginning of functions which wanted to
handle the radiotap header. And this broke the rate parser for radiotap
header parser.

The radiotap parser for rates is operating most of the time only on the
data in the actual radiotap header. But for the 802.11a/b/g rates, it must
also know the selected band from the chandef information. But this
information is only written to the ieee80211_tx_info at the end of the
ieee80211_monitor_start_xmit - long after ieee80211_parse_tx_radiotap was
already called. The info->band information was therefore always 0
(NL80211_BAND_2GHZ) when the parser code tried to access it.

For a 5GHz only device, injecting a frame with 802.11a rates would cause a
NULL pointer dereference because local->hw.wiphy->bands[NL80211_BAND_2GHZ]
would most likely have been NULL when the radiotap parser searched for the
correct rate index of the driver.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Ben Greear <greearb@candelatech.com>
Fixes: cb17ed29a7a5 ("mac80211: parse radiotap header when selecting Tx queue")
Signed-off-by: Mathy Vanhoef <Mathy.Vanhoef@kuleuven.be>
[sven@narfation.org: added commit message]
Signed-off-by: Sven Eckelmann <sven@narfation.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210530133226.40587-1-sven@narfation.org
Signed-off-by: Johannes Berg <johannes.berg@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* Sanity-check and process the injection radiotap header */', '\tif (!ieee80211_parse_tx_radiotap(skb, dev))'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Sanity-check the length of the radiotap header */', '\tif (!ieee80211_validate_radiotap_len(skb))', '\t/*', '\t * Process the radiotap header. This will now take into account the', '\t * selected chandef above to accurately set injection rates and', '\t * retransmissions.', '\t */', '\tif (!ieee80211_parse_tx_radiotap(skb, dev))', '\t\tgoto fail_rcu;', '']}
description: The mac80211 subsystem in the Linux kernel before 5.12.13, when a device supporting only 5 GHz is used, allows attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference in the radiotap parser) by injecting a frame with 802.11a rates.

code_evidence: The radiotap parser is invoked before any chandef/band selection, so info->band is still 0 (NL80211_BAND_2GHZ) when the 802.11a/b/g rate parser runs.
chandef is only assigned from the channel context or _oper_chandef here; on 5 GHz-only devices the 2 GHz band entry may be absent, and this band value is not yet available to the earlier parser call.
info->band = chandef->chan->band is set only after the parser has already been called, confirming the parser consumed a stale/default band.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's ordering defect leads directly to dereferencing a NULL band pointer in the rate parser, matching CWE-476. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the crash stems from a pointer expected to be valid being NULL.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!ieee80211_parse_tx_radiotap(skb, dev))
goto fail;
info->band = chandef->chan->band;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is ordering: ieee80211_parse_tx_radiotap runs at line 15 before info->band is populated at line 63. An injected frame carrying 802.11a rates makes the rate parser look up local->hw.wiphy->bands[NL80211_BAND_2GHZ], which is NULL on 5 GHz-only hardware, causing a NULL pointer dereference and denial of service.

commit_msg:
IndexedDB: Avoid side effects by evaluating key paths w/ HasOwnProperty

Although key path evaluation is always done against clones (so getters
are flattened into simple data properties), property lookups were
not restricted to inherited properties, allowing getters on prototypes
to be executed. This allows evaluation to be observable, and cause
side effects.

Restrict the lookup to own properties, and introduce special-case code
for those non-own values identified in the spec[1] as special cases.

[1] https://w3c.github.io/IndexedDB/#key-path-construct

BUG=637963
R=haraken@chromium.org

commit_msg:
syzbot reported a memory leak [0] related to IPV6_ADDRFORM.

The scenario is that while one thread is converting an IPv6 socket into
IPv4 with IPV6_ADDRFORM, another thread calls do_ipv6_setsockopt() and
allocates memory to inet6_sk(sk)->XXX after conversion.

Then, the converted sk with (tcp|udp)_prot never frees the IPv6 resources,
which inet6_destroy_sock() should have cleaned up.

setsockopt(IPV6_ADDRFORM)                 setsockopt(IPV6_DSTOPTS)
+-----------------------+                 +----------------------+
- do_ipv6_setsockopt(sk, ...)
  - sockopt_lock_sock(sk)                 - do_ipv6_setsockopt(sk, ...)
    - lock_sock(sk)                         ^._ called via tcpv6_prot
  - WRITE_ONCE(sk->sk_prot, &tcp_prot)          before WRITE_ONCE()
  - xchg(&np->opt, NULL)
  - txopt_put(opt)
  - sockopt_release_sock(sk)
    - release_sock(sk)                      - sockopt_lock_sock(sk)
                                              - lock_sock(sk)
                                            - ipv6_set_opt_hdr(sk, ...)
                                              - ipv6_update_options(sk, opt)
                                                - xchg(&inet6_sk(sk)->opt, opt)
                                                  ^._ opt is never freed.

                                            - sockopt_release_sock(sk)
                                              - release_sock(sk)

Since IPV6_DSTOPTS allocates options under lock_sock(), we can avoid this
memory leak by testing whether sk_family is changed by IPV6_ADDRFORM after
acquiring the lock.

This issue exists from the initial commit between IPV6_ADDRFORM and
IPV6_PKTOPTIONS.

description: A vulnerability was found in Linux Kernel. It has been declared as problematic. Affected by this vulnerability is the function ipv6_renew_options of the component IPv6 Handler. The manipulation leads to memory leak. The attack can be launched remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier VDB-211021 was assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: The function locks the socket and enters the optname switch without verifying that sk->sk_family is still AF_INET6.
The IPV6_ADDRFORM case later changes sk->sk_family to PF_INET (lines 68/78) and clears np->opt, so a concurrent setsockopt on another thread can run after conversion.
The IPV6_DSTOPTS/IPV6_RTHDR/IPV6_HOPOPTS cases delegate to ipv6_set_opt_hdr, and IPV6_2292PKTOPTIONS allocates opt via sock_kmalloc and installs it through ipv6_update_options.
Because the converted IPv4 protocol no longer invokes inet6_destroy_sock cleanup, options allocated here after conversion are never freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The allocated option resource is never released on the converted socket, matching CWE-404 (improper resource shutdown/release with resource-consumption impact). This is a leak rather than a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function does not re-check sk->sk_family after acquiring the socket lock, allowing IPV6_DSTOPTS/PKTOPTIONS to allocate IPv6 option memory on a socket another thread is converting to IPv4. Trigger: concurrent IPV6_ADDRFORM and option setsockopt. Consequence: the allocated txoptions object is leaked, causing unbounded memory consumption.

description: Heap-based buffer overflow in enhance.c in ImageMagick before 7.0.6-6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Buffers black, white, histogram and stretch_map are sized from GetPixelChannels(image) at allocation time; histogram and stretch_map use (MaxMap+1)*GetPixelChannels(image) elements.
Histogram indexing uses GetPixelChannels(image)*ScaleQuantumToMap(ClampToQuantum(pixel))+i, so the channel count read here must match the allocation.
stretch_map writes and subsequent reads use GetPixelChannels(image)*j+i with j up to MaxMap, again depending on the same channel count.
Pixel loop iterates j < GetPixelChannels(image) and indexes stretch_map with GetPixelChannels(image)*ScaleQuantumToMap(q[j])+j.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes into heap buffers (histogram, stretch_map) at indices derived from a channel count that can exceed the size used at allocation, which is a write past the end of the intended buffer. This matches CWE-787; a mere out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) would not describe the histogram increment and stretch_map assignment writes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-pixel channel count used to size black/white/histogram/stretch_map can change after allocation (the patch adds SyncImagePixelCache before these allocations to force cache/channel synchronization). If the effective channel count grows, the histogram and stretch_map accesses at lines 74-75, 119/125-126 and 199-200 compute indices beyond the allocated buffers, producing a heap-based out-of-bounds write that can crash or corrupt memory (DoS, per the description).

For PREP_WRITE_REQ, send_write is invoked with device and desc->proxy after the trust checks, so a D-Bus write proceeds asynchronously while the attribute/device may be torn down.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function continues to use device/attribute data after a concurrent disconnect may free it; this is not merely a missing input check but a lifetime violation.

desc->req_prep_authorization)
send_write(device, attrib, desc->proxy,

offset, bt_att_get_link_type(att),
false, true);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write path dereferences device and desc state during asynchronous D-Bus processing without a pending-disconnect cleanup callback, so a client disconnect can free those objects while send_write still uses them. commit_msg:
upstream: disallow empty incoming filename or ones that refer to the

current directory; based on report/patch from Harry Sintonen

OpenBSD-Commit-ID: f27651b30eaee2df49540ab68d030865c04f6de9

description: In OpenSSH 7.9, scp.c in the scp client allows remote SSH servers to bypass intended access restrictions via the filename of . or an empty filename. The impact is modifying the permissions of the target directory on the client side.

code_evidence: Lines 126-129 reject filenames containing '/' or equal to '..', but accept an empty filename (cp=="") and a bare '.'; the check does not reject these, so the remote-supplied name passes validation.
Lines 140-142 build np from targ and cp and assign curfile=cp at line 145; an empty or '.' cp therefore yields a target path that resolves to the target directory itself.
Lines 163-172 recurse into sink with the constructed path and then chmod/utimes it, so the name that passed validation is used to alter permissions of the target directory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-863 fits because the function's check is meant to authorize which server-supplied filenames may be used, but it performs the check incompletely: empty and '.' names slip through and reach chmod/utimes on the directory. This is a flawed authorization check, not merely a path-traversal (CWE-22) issue, since the accepted name is the target directory itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the filename authorization check omits empty names and '.', so a malicious server's C/D record can name the target directory itself. Trigger: the server sends an empty or '.' filename; the client builds np pointing at the directory and, for a 'D' record, recurses and applies chmod/utimes to it. Supported consequence: the client's target directory permissions are modified, bypassing the intended restriction on the server-supplied name.

commit_msg:
GetCountedString did a check for the whole string to be within the
request buffer but not for the initial 2 bytes that contain the length
field. A swapped client could send a malformed request to trigger a
swaps() on those bytes, writing into random memory.

Signed-off-by: Peter Hutterer <peter.hutterer@who-t.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (client->req_len <', '        bytes_to_int32(wire + 2 - (char *) client->requestBuffer))', '        return BadValue;', '']}
description: A vulnerability classified as critical was found in X.org Server. Affected by this vulnerability is the function _GetCountedString of the file xkb/xkb.c. The manipulation leads to buffer overflow. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The associated identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211051.

code_evidence: wire is dereferenced at line 7 to read the 2-byte length field and conditionally byte-swapped at lines 8-10, but no check confirms those initial two bytes lie within client->requestBuffer before the read.
The bounds check at lines 11-14 computes next from the untrusted len and only validates up to next; it does not validate the length-field bytes themselves that were already consumed.
The validated len then drives malloc(len + 1) and memcpy(*str, &wire[2], len) at lines 15-18, copying from the request buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs read/write operations on wire/requestBuffer without ensuring the accessed region (the 2-byte length field and the copied string) stays within the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. The missing pre-read bounds check is the specific root cause rather than a mere logic error.

evidence_lines.code:
*str = malloc(len + 1);
memcpy(*str, &wire[2], len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the initial 2-byte length prefix is read and swapped before any request-buffer bounds check, so a malformed request can point wire at the buffer edge. Trigger: a swapped client sends a request where the length field straddles or exceeds the request buffer. Consequence: swaps() and the subsequent memcpy operate outside the intended buffer, giving out-of-bounds read/write of memory.

commit_msg:
tjLoadImage(): Fix FPE triggered by malformed BMP

In rdbmp.c, it is necessary to guard against 32-bit overflow/wraparound
when allocating the row buffer, because since BMP files have 32-bit
width and height fields, the value of biWidth can be up to 4294967295.
Specifically, if biWidth is 1073741824 and cinfo->input_components = 4,
then the samplesperrow argument in alloc_sarray() would wrap around to
0, and a division by zero error would occur at line 458 in jmemmgr.c.

If biWidth is set to a higher value, then samplesperrow would wrap
around to a small number, which would likely cause a buffer overflow
(this has not been tested or verified.)

--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -211,6 +211,12 @@
     }
   }
 
+  /* Ensure that biWidth * cinfo->input_components doesn't exceed the maximum
+     value of the JDIMENSION type.  This is only a danger with BMP files, since
+     their width and height fields are 32-bit integers. */
+  if ((unsigned long long)biWidth *
+      (unsigned long long)cinfo->input_components > 0xFFFFFFFFULL)
+    ERREXIT(cinfo, JERR_WIDTH_OVERFLOW);
   /* Allocate one-row buffer for returned data */
   source->pub.buffer = (*cinfo->mem->alloc_sarray)
     ((j_common_ptr)cinfo, JPOOL_IMAGE,

description: libjpeg-turbo 1.5.90 is vulnerable to a denial of service vulnerability caused by a divide by zero when processing a crafted BMP image.

code_evidence: biWidth is an int parsed from the attacker-controlled 32-bit BMP header field via GET_4B [59], so it can be very large.
row_width derives from biWidth (e.g. biWidth*3 or biWidth*4) [126,137,148] without any upper-bound check before allocation.
The row buffer is allocated with alloc_sarray using (JDIMENSION)(biWidth * cinfo->input_components) [181-183]; this product can wrap around to 0 because JDIMENSION is 32-bit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function feeds an overflowed, zero-valued size into the allocator, leading to division by zero in allocation logic; this matches CWE-369. It is not merely an integer overflow because the supported consequence is the zero divisor crash.

int biWidth;
biWidth = (int)GET_4B(bmpinfoheader, 4);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the width*components product is computed in a 32-bit type without overflow checking, so a crafted biWidth (e.g. 1073741824 with 4 components) wraps to 0. Trigger: alloc_sarray receives samplesperrow = 0 and later divides by it, causing a divide-by-zero FPE and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
IB/security: Restrict use of the write() interface

The drivers/infiniband stack uses write() as a replacement for
bi-directional ioctl().  This is not safe. There are ways to
trigger write calls that result in the return structure that
is normally written to user space being shunted off to user
specified kernel memory instead.

For the immediate repair, detect and deny suspicious accesses to
the write API.

For long term, update the user space libraries and the kernel API
to something that doesn't present the same security vulnerabilities
(likely a structured ioctl() interface).

The impacted uAPI interfaces are generally only available if
hardware from drivers/infiniband is installed in the system.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jann@thejh.net>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgunthorpe@obsidianresearch.com>
[ Expanded check to all known write() entry points ]
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Doug Ledford <dledford@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* FIXME: This interface cannot continue out of staging */', '\tif (WARN_ON_ONCE(!ib_safe_file_access(fp)))', '\t\treturn -EACCES;']}
description: The InfiniBand (aka IB) stack in the Linux kernel before 4.5.3 incorrectly relies on the write system call, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (kernel memory write operation) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a uAPI interface.

code_evidence: The write handler accepts a user-controlled command header via copy_from_user into cmd and then acts on cmd.type and cmd.addr without any file-access safety check.
For commands with a copy payload, copy_from_user(dest, (void __user *)cmd.addr, copy) reads a user-supplied pointer from cmd.addr, so the caller controls the source address used by the kernel.
fp->private_data is dereferenced into fd and fd->uctxt before any validation, showing the handler operates on the file's private state as the basis for privileged operations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper access control: write() is used in place of a controlled ioctl-style interface, and the handler lacks the ib_safe_file_access() restriction that the fix adds, so unprivileged callers can reach privileged kernel operations. This fits CWE-264's permissions/privileges/access-control category rather than a pure memory-safety CWE.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write() entry point trusts the user-supplied command header (type, addr, len) and performs kernel copy operations and context operations without verifying that the file was opened through the intended uAPI path. Trigger: a local user issues write() with a crafted hfi1_cmd, reaching the switch and the copy_from_user at line 66. Consequence: kernel memory writes/reads driven by user-controlled addresses, enabling denial of service or unspecified impact.

commit_msg:
When a nested page fault is taken from an address that does not have
a memslot associated to it, kvm_mmu_do_page_fault returns RET_PF_EMULATE
(via mmu_set_spte) and kvm_mmu_page_fault then invokes svm_need_emulation_on_page_fault.

The default answer there is to return false, but in this case this just
causes the page fault to be retried ad libitum.  Since this is not a
fast path, and the only other case where it is taken is an erratum,
just stick a kvm_vcpu_gfn_to_memslot check in there to detect the
common case where the erratum is not happening.

This fixes an infinite loop in the new set_memory_region_test.

Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/*', '\t * If RIP is invalid, go ahead with emulation which will cause an', '\t * internal error exit.', '\t */', '\tif (!kvm_vcpu_gfn_to_memslot(vcpu, kvm_rip_read(vcpu) >> PAGE_SHIFT))', '\t\treturn true;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.8. arch/x86/kvm/svm/svm.c allows a set_memory_region_test infinite loop for certain nested page faults, aka CID-e72436bc3a52.

code_evidence: Function returns false by default (line 13), causing the caller to retry the page fault; only the SEV erratum branch (lines 8-11) returns true or requests a triple fault. When a nested page fault occurs at an address without a memslot, no branch forces emulation termination, so the fault is retried indefinitely.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing memslot check leaves the retry exit condition unreachable for such faults, matching CWE-835's unreachable loop exit. Contrasts with CWE-674 (uncontrolled recursion), which is not present here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the default return false makes kvm_mmu_page_fault retry the fault instead of emulating/terminating. Trigger: a nested page fault at a GFN lacking a memslot, which reaches this function. Consequence: unbounded retry loop causing CPU consumption (DoS).

commit_msg:
avformat/nutdec: Add check for avformat_new_stream

Check for failure of avformat_new_stream() and propagate
the error code.

Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>

The flaw occurs because the function lacks check of the return value of avformat_new_stream() and triggers the null pointer dereference error, causing an application to crash.

commit_msg:
BLIP: Fix decompression buffer bug

Until now, mistakenly, the buffer for decompressing compressed BLIP messages
has been statically allocated as 16 Kb, but that is not valid behavior.
16 Kb is the maximum size of a _compressed_ frame.  In theory, due to the
ability to zipbomb, there is virtually no upper bound on what the maximum
size of an uncompressed frame could be.  However, to keep sanity, it has
been made into a preference with a reasonable default that is not likely to
be exceeded (64 Kb).  The behavior before for this was that wireshark would
crash because the dissector would return NULL for a decompressed buffer due
to error and then try to deference it later.  A null check has been added,
so that the behavior is now that the packet will show
'<Error decompressing message>' instead, and log why it couldn't handle the
compressed message.  Closes #16866.

commit_msg:
Avoid races between check and use of the nested VMCB controls.  This
for example ensures that the VMRUN intercept is always reflected to the
nested hypervisor, instead of being processed by the host.  Without this
patch, it is possible to end up with svm->nested.hsave pointing to
the MSR permission bitmap for nested guests.

This bug is CVE-2021-29657.

Reported-by: Felix Wilhelm <fwilhelm@google.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: 2fcf4876ada ("KVM: nSVM: implement on demand allocation of the nested state")
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!nested_vmcb_checks(svm, vmcb12)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tload_nested_vmcb_control(svm, &vmcb12->control);', '', '\tif (!nested_vmcb_check_save(svm, vmcb12) ||', '\t    !nested_vmcb_check_controls(&svm->nested.ctl)) {']}
description: arch/x86/kvm/svm/nested.c in the Linux kernel before 5.11.12 has a use-after-free in which an AMD KVM guest can bypass access control on host OS MSRs when there are nested guests, aka CID-a58d9166a756. This occurs because of a TOCTOU race condition associated with a VMCB12 double fetch in nested_svm_vmrun.

code_evidence: vmcb12 is the host-mapped guest page from kvm_vcpu_map at line 14; lines 22-25 pass that same pointer to nested_vmcb_checks, which validates fields of vmcb12->control.

Later, line 62 copies the control area from the live vmcb12 into hsave, and lines 64-66 use that copied state in enter_svm_guest_mode and nested_svm_vmrun_msrpm. Because vmcb12 is guest-controlled shared memory, the control fields can be rewritten after the check at line 25 but before the copy at line 62.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function checks vmcb12->control at line 25 and then uses that same guest-shared resource at lines 62-66; the state can change between check and use, matching CWE-367's TOCTOU definition. The fix loads and validates a private snapshot, confirming the double-fetch race rather than a simple missing-validation weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guest-supplied VMCB control area is validated through one pointer but consumed later through a separate read/copy, with no single consistent snapshot. Trigger: a nested guest modifies the mapped VMCB12 control fields (e.g., MSR permission bitmap or intercepts) after nested_vmcb_checks passes but before copy_vmcb_control_area. Consequence: host uses unvalidated controls, allowing the VMRUN intercept to be processed by the host and svm->nested.hsave to reference the nested guest's MSR permission bitmap, bypassing host MSR access control.

commit_msg:
avformat/rmdec: Fix DoS due to lack of eof check

Found-by: Xiaohei and Wangchu from Alibaba Security Team
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            for (j = 0; j < len; j++)'], 'added_lines': ['            for (j = 0; j < len; j++) {', '                if (avio_feof(pb))', '                    return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;', '            }']}
description: In libavformat/rmdec.c in FFmpeg 3.3.3, a DoS in ivr_read_header() due to lack of an EOF (End of File) check might cause huge CPU consumption. When a crafted IVR file, which claims a large "len" field in the header but does not contain sufficient backing data, is provided, the first type==4 loop would consume huge CPU resources, since there is no EOF check inside the loop.

code_evidence: Line 46 reads attacker-controlled 32-bit len from the file. For type==4 (line 50), line 52 loops j from 0 to len, calling avio_r8(pb) once per iteration with no EOF or bound check, so a large claimed len keeps the loop iterating while the input is exhausted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits because the iteration count is derived from an untrusted length and is not sufficiently limited, enabling resource-consumption DoS. The missing EOF check is the mechanism; the excessive iteration is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the type==4 loop count comes from the file's len field and is not bounded or validated against available input. Trigger: a crafted IVR header claiming a large len with insufficient backing data. Consequence: the loop keeps iterating, consuming excessive CPU (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix return value check for openssl API used during pubkey validation.

Found thanks to bug report by Michael Scheibel <m.Scheibel (at) tuvit (dot) de>
ok patrick@, markus@, tb@
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (peerkey && !EVP_PKEY_cmp(peerkey, localkey)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (peerkey && EVP_PKEY_cmp(peerkey, localkey) != 1) {']}
description: iked in OpenIKED, as used in OpenBSD through 6.7, allows authentication bypass because ca.c has the wrong logic for checking whether a public key matches.

code_evidence: The peer public-key comparison negates EVP_PKEY_cmp and treats only a zero return as a mismatch. EVP_PKEY_cmp returns 1 for a match, 0 for a mismatch, and negative values on error; the negation makes a match (1) evaluate true, logging a mismatch and jumping to done with ret still -1.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to properly verify that the claimed peer identity's public key matches the configured key, so an invalid key can be accepted as authentic. This is insufficient proof of identity, matching CWE-287. It is not merely a resource or memory error; the consequence is improper authentication.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: wrong logic interpreting EVP_PKEY_cmp's tri-state return. When peerkey is present and matches localkey, the condition !1 is false and processing continues to ret=0; but the check conflates error (-1) and match, since !(-1) is also false, so a comparison error is treated as success. Trigger: a peer key that fails comparison (error return) passes validation, leading to authentication bypass.

commit_msg: GatherNd verifies that an index is valid before reading. (#1286)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      return GatherNd<float, IndicesT>(params, indices, output);', '      return GatherNd<int8_t, IndicesT>(params, indices, output);'], 'added_lines': ['  TfLiteStatus status = kTfLiteError;', '      status = GatherNd<float, IndicesT>(params, indices, output);', '      status = GatherNd<int8_t, IndicesT>(params, indices, output);', '  if (status != kTfLiteOk) {', '    TF_LITE_KERNEL_LOG(context, "gather_nd index out of bounds");', '  }', '  return status;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. The `GatherNd` function takes arguments that determine the sizes of inputs and outputs. If the inputs given are greater than or equal to the sizes of the outputs, an out-of-bounds memory read or a crash is triggered. This issue has been patched in GitHub commit 4142e47e9e31db481781b955ed3ff807a781b494. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: EvalGatherNd dispatches directly to GatherNd<float, IndicesT> or GatherNd<int8_t, IndicesT> and returns its status without any prior validation of the index values relative to the params/output dimensions. The function itself performs no bounds check on indices before the templated read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an unchecked index causing reads past the intended params buffer, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. It is not merely a missing error return; the read itself exceeds buffer bounds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the indices tensor is passed unvalidated into GatherNd, which reads params at index-derived offsets. Trigger: an index that is greater than or equal to the input/output size. Consequence: an out-of-bounds memory read or crash, consistent with the fix adding an out-of-bounds status check.

commit_msg:
fix a fencepost error in pipe_advance()

The logics in pipe_advance() used to release all buffers past the new
position failed in cases when the number of buffers to release was equal
to pipe->buffers.  If that happened, none of them had been released,
leaving pipe full.  Worse, it was trivial to trigger and we end up with
pipe full of uninitialized pages.  IOW, it's an infoleak.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.9
Reported-by: "Alan J. Wylie" <alan@wylie.me.uk>
Tested-by: "Alan J. Wylie" <alan@wylie.me.uk>
Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct pipe_buffer *buf;', '\tint idx = i->idx;', '\tsize_t off = i->iov_offset, orig_sz;', '\t', '\torig_sz = size;', '', '\t\t\tsize += off - pipe->bufs[idx].offset;', '\t\t\tif (size <= buf->len)', '\t\t\tsize -= buf->len;', '\t\tbuf->len = size;', '\t\toff = i->iov_offset = buf->offset + size;', '\tif (off)', '\t\tidx = next_idx(idx, pipe);', '\tif (pipe->nrbufs) {', '\t\tint unused = (pipe->curbuf + pipe->nrbufs) & (pipe->buffers - 1);', '\t\t/* [curbuf,unused) is in use.  Free [idx,unused) */', '\t\twhile (idx != unused) {', '\t\t\tpipe_buf_release(pipe, &pipe->bufs[idx]);', '\t\t\tidx = next_idx(idx, pipe);', '\t\t\tpipe->nrbufs--;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '\ti->count -= orig_sz;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tstruct pipe_buffer *buf;', '\t\tsize_t off = i->iov_offset, left = size;', '\t\tint idx = i->idx;', '\t\t\tleft += off - pipe->bufs[idx].offset;', '\t\t\tif (left <= buf->len)', '\t\t\tleft -= buf->len;', '\t\ti->iov_offset = buf->offset + left;', '\ti->count -= size;', '\t/* ... and discard everything past that point */', '\tpipe_truncate(i);']}
description: Off-by-one error in the pipe_advance function in lib/iov_iter.c in the Linux kernel before 4.9.5 allows local users to obtain sensitive information from uninitialized heap-memory locations in opportunistic circumstances by reading from a pipe after an incorrect buffer-release decision.

code_evidence: The loop walks pipe buffers while size > buf->len, subtracting each buffer length and advancing idx; it then sets buf->len = size on the final buffer.

The release loop computes unused = (curbuf + nrbufs) & (buffers-1) and frees [idx, unused) while decrementing nrbufs; when the number of buffers to release equals pipe->buffers, idx == unused before any release, so the loop body never executes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is disclosure of uninitialized kernel heap pages to a local reader, which is exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor. The off-by-one is the underlying mistake; CWE-200 captures the resulting infoleak that the commit explicitly describes.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the fencepost in the release-loop bound leaves buffers past the new position unreleased when the count to discard equals the full ring size, and the earlier 'buf->len = size' shrinks the current buffer without releasing the rest. Trigger: a pipe read/advance that consumes exactly pipe->buffers worth of buffers; the stale buffers stay marked in use. Consequence: later reads return page contents that were never initialized, leaking heap memory to the reader (infoleak).

commit_msg: Fix crash in fuzzed wasm r2_hoobr_consume_init_expr
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint buflen = bin->buf->length;', '\tif (sec->payload_data + 32 > buflen) {', '\t\treturn NULL;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tint buflen = bin->buf->length - (ut32)sec->payload_data;']}

buf is derived by adding the attacker-controlled payload_data offset to the buffer base, while len is the section payload_len and the loop condition only requires len < buflen.
consume_u8/consume_init_expr are called with buf+i and buf+len bounds that are not validated against the true remaining buffer size, so parsing can read past the buffer end.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds are computed against the full buffer length rather than the remaining bytes after payload_data, so payload_len and offsets can exceed the real buffer. A crafted WASM section triggers consume_* to read beyond the allocated buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and crash.

commit_msg:
9pfs: fix memory leak in v9fs_link

The v9fs_link() function keeps a reference on the source fid object. This
causes a memory leak since the reference never goes down to 0. This patch
fixes the issue.

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liqiang6-s@360.cn>
Reviewed-by: Greg Kurz <groug@kaod.org>
[groug, rephrased the changelog]
Signed-off-by: Greg Kurz <groug@kaod.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    put_fid(pdu, oldfidp);']}
description: Memory leak in the v9fs_link function in hw/9pfs/9p.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via vectors involving a reference to the source fid object.

code_evidence: oldfidp is acquired via get_fid at line 28, which takes a reference on the source fid. After v9fs_co_link at line 33, control falls through to label out (line 37) and then put_fid is called only for dfidp at line 38; oldfidp is never released on this path. The patch adds put_fid(pdu, oldfidp) before out, confirming the acquired reference was leaked on the success path (and on the oldfidp==NULL path no reference exists).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because a resource (the fid reference) is acquired and its effective lifetime ends after the link operation, yet it is never released, matching missing release after effective lifetime with an availability/memory-consumption impact. This is a leak of an acquired reference rather than a use-after-free, since the object is retained, not freed prematurely.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reference obtained by get_fid(pdu, oldfid) is not dropped on the normal completion path, where only dfidp is put. Trigger: a guest administrator issues a link operation that reaches v9fs_co_link and completes. Consequence: the fid reference count never returns to zero, so memory tied to the source fid is never freed, enabling resource-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121

The trusted flag and shallow check are the missing validation constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function constructs a serialised GVariant from caller-supplied bytes with only a shallow g_variant_serialised_check, and the trusted flag controls whether expensive ordering validation is skipped. Trigger: untrusted serialised bytes with overlapping variable-size array frame offsets. Consequence: a crafted GVariant normalises to a much larger type, causing excessive processing and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Set init processes as non-dumpable

This sets the init processes that join and setup the container's
namespaces as non-dumpable before they setns to the container's pid (or
any other ) namespace.

This settings is automatically reset to the default after the Exec in
the container so that it does not change functionality for the
applications that are running inside, just our init processes.

This prevents parent processes, the pid 1 of the container, to ptrace
the init process before it drops caps and other sets LSMs.

This patch also ensures that the stateDirFD being used is still closed
prior to exec, even though it is set as O_CLOEXEC, because of the order
in the kernel.

https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v4.9/fs/exec.c#L1290-L1318

The order during the exec syscall is that the process is set back to
dumpable before O_CLOEXEC are processed.

Signed-off-by: Michael Crosby <crosbymichael@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* make the process non-dumpable */', '\tif (prctl(PR_SET_DUMPABLE, 0, 0, 0, 0) != 0) {', '\t\tbail("failed to set process as non-dumpable");', '\t}']}
description: RunC allowed additional container processes via 'runc exec' to be ptraced by the pid 1 of the container.  This allows the main processes of the container, if running as root, to gain access to file-descriptors of these new processes during the initialization and can lead to container escapes or modification of runC state before the process is fully placed inside the container.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no concurrent code sequence or shared-resource timing window; the diff only adds a prctl(PR_SET_DUMPABLE,0) call, which is a dumpability/permission control, not a race condition.

commit_msg:
crypto: user - fix memory leak in crypto_reportstat

In crypto_reportstat, a new skb is created by nlmsg_new(). This skb is
leaked if crypto_reportstat_alg() fails. Required release for skb is
added.

Fixes: cac5818c25d0 ("crypto: user - Implement a generic crypto statistics")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (err)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (err) {', '\t\tkfree_skb(skb);', '\t}']}
description: A memory leak in the crypto_reportstat() function in crypto/crypto_user_stat.c in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering crypto_reportstat_alg() failures, aka CID-c03b04dcdba1.

code_evidence: Line 16 allocates an skb via nlmsg_new() and stores it in skb; on failure of allocation the code jumps to drop_alg without an skb to free.

Line 23 sets err from crypto_reportstat_alg(); if it fails, control falls to drop_alg, where crypto_mod_put(alg) releases only the algorithm reference, and lines 26-27 return err without freeing the skb allocated at line 16.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the allocated skb is not released on the error path, so memory remains unavailable for reuse. This is a missing release of allocated memory, distinct from a use-after-free since no dangling pointer is dereferenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path after crypto_reportstat_alg() failure returns without releasing the nlmsg_new() skb. Trigger: an attacker causes crypto_reportstat_alg() to fail (e.g., malformed statistics request) after allocation succeeds. Consequence: each failed request leaks an skb, and repeated requests exhaust kernel memory, causing denial of service.

A setusercontext(3) call with flags to change the UID, primary GID, and secondary GIDs was replaced (on certain platforms: Linux and possibly NetBSD) with a single setuid(2) call. Fix PPB_Flash_MessageLoop.

This CL suspends script callbacks and resource loads while running nested message loop using PPB_Flash_MessageLoop.

BUG=569496

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1559113002

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#374529}

description: The PPB_Flash_MessageLoop_Impl::InternalRun function in content/renderer/pepper/ppb_flash_message_loop_impl.cc in the Pepper plugin in Google Chrome before 49.0.2623.75 mishandles nested message loops, which allows remote attackers to bypass the Same Origin Policy via a crafted web site.

commit_msg:
Made some changes to the I/O stream library for memory streams.
There were a number of potential problems due to the possibility
of integer overflow.
Changed some integral types to the larger types size_t or ssize_t.
For example, the function mem_resize now takes the buffer size parameter
as a size_t.
Added a new function jas_stream_memopen2, which takes a
buffer size specified as a size_t instead of an int.
This can be used in jas_image_cmpt_create to avoid potential
overflow problems.

Added a new function jas_deprecated to warn about reliance on
deprecated library behavior.

Consequence: mem_resize receives a bogus size and the subsequent memcpy/position arithmetic can underflow, leading to an undersized buffer and out-of-bounds write or use-after-free (DoS).
