commit_msg:
net: sockets: getaddrinfo() buffer overflow, etc. fixes

The existing implementation assumed DNS resolv callback will be
called just once, but that's not always the case (apparently,
for multi-homes hosts or something). So, apply array bounds
checking (and do pointer arithmetic only after it, as the C
standard otherwise warns of "undefined behavior"). In such a case,
the port number wasn't set in each entry too, so rework how it's
done.

The issues discovered while resolving archive.ubuntu.com.

Signed-off-by: Paul Sokolovsky <paul.sokolovsky@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct zsock_addrinfo *ai = ai_arr + state->idx;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct zsock_addrinfo *ai;', '\tif (state->idx >= ARRAY_SIZE(ai_arr)) {', '\t\tNET_DBG("getaddrinfo entries overflow");', '\t\treturn;', '\t}', '', '\tai = ai_arr + state->idx;', '\tnet_sin(&ai->_ai_addr)->sin_port = state->port;']}
description: A buffer overflow has been found in the Zephyr Project's getaddrinfo() implementation in 1.9.0 and 1.10.0.

code_evidence: Line 5 computes ai = ai_arr + state->idx before any bounds check, so ai can point past the ai_arr buffer when state->idx is already out of range.
Lines 17-22 then memcpy into ai->_ai_addr and ai->_ai_canonname and write ai->ai_addr, ai->ai_addrlen, ai->ai_canonname, ai->ai_family through that out-of-bounds pointer.
Line 35 increments state->idx unconditionally, so repeated DNS callback invocations increase idx without limit, eventually exceeding ARRAY_SIZE(ai_arr).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through a pointer derived from an unchecked index into a fixed-size array, producing an out-of-bounds memory write, which is the core of CWE-119. The root cause is the missing bounds check on state->idx, distinct from a type or integer-conversion error.

evidence_lines.code: struct zsock_addrinfo *ai = ai_arr + state->idx;
state->idx++;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The callback assumes it runs only once, so state->idx is never checked against ARRAY_SIZE(ai_arr) before being used as an array offset. When the resolver invokes the callback multiple times (e.g., multi-homed hosts), ai points beyond ai_arr and the subsequent memcpy/writes corrupt adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
When going through execve(), zero out the NUMA fault statistics instead of
freeing them.

During execve, the task is reachable through procfs and the scheduler. A
concurrent /proc/*/sched reader can read data from a freed ->numa_faults
allocation (confirmed by KASAN) and write it back to userspace.
I believe that it would also be possible for a use-after-free read to occur
through a race between a NUMA fault and execve(): task_numa_fault() can
lead to task_numa_compare(), which invokes task_weight() on the currently
running task of a different CPU.

Another way to fix this would be to make ->numa_faults RCU-managed or add
extra locking, but it seems easier to wipe the NUMA fault statistics on
execve.

Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Petr Mladek <pmladek@suse.com>
Cc: Sergey Senozhatsky <sergey.senozhatsky@gmail.com>
Cc: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: Will Deacon <will@kernel.org>
Fixes: 82727018b0d3 ("sched/numa: Call task_numa_free() from do_execve()")
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190716152047.14424-1-jannh@google.com
Signed-off-by: Ingo Molnar <mingo@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void task_numa_free(struct task_struct *p)', '\tvoid *numa_faults = p->numa_faults;', '\tp->numa_faults = NULL;', '\tkfree(numa_faults);'], 'added_lines': ['void task_numa_free(struct task_struct *p, bool final)', '\tunsigned long *numa_faults = p->numa_faults;', '', '\tif (!numa_faults)', '\t\treturn;', '\tif (final) {', '\t\tp->numa_faults = NULL;', '\t\tkfree(numa_faults);', '\t} else {', '\t\tp->total_numa_faults = 0;', '\t\tfor (i = 0; i < NR_NUMA_HINT_FAULT_STATS * nr_node_ids; i++)', '\t\t\tnuma_faults[i] = 0;', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.6. On NUMA systems, the Linux fair scheduler has a use-after-free in show_numa_stats() because NUMA fault statistics are inappropriately freed, aka CID-16d51a590a8c.

code_evidence: Line 4 captures the pointer p->numa_faults into a local; lines 17-18 then set p->numa_faults to NULL and immediately kfree the captured allocation, destroying the shared NUMA fault statistics buffer while the live task remains reachable through procfs and the scheduler.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the freed numa_faults allocation remains referenced by concurrent readers of the still-live task; the fix avoids the free by zeroing in place for non-final cleanup. This is a dangling-reference use-after-free, not merely a double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: task_numa_free unconditionally frees the task's numa_faults buffer during execve while the task is still concurrently observable. Trigger: a parallel /proc/*/sched reader or a NUMA fault path accesses the now-freed buffer. Consequence: use-after-free read (confirmed by KASAN, leaking freed data to userspace) and potential memory corruption.

commit_msg:
vfs: make AIO use the proper rw_verify_area() area helpers

We had for some reason overlooked the AIO interface, and it didn't use
the proper rw_verify_area() helper function that checks (for example)
mandatory locking on the file, and that the size of the access doesn't
cause us to overflow the provided offset limits etc.

Instead, AIO did just the security_file_permission() thing (that
rw_verify_area() also does) directly.

This fixes it to do all the proper helper functions, which not only
means that now mandatory file locking works with AIO too, we can
actually remove lines of code.

Reported-by: Manish Honap <manish_honap_vit@yahoo.co.in>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tret = security_file_permission(file, MAY_READ);', '\t\tif (unlikely(ret))', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tret = aio_setup_single_vector(kiocb);', '\t\tret = security_file_permission(file, MAY_WRITE);', '\t\tif (unlikely(ret))', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tret = aio_setup_single_vector(kiocb);', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tret = security_file_permission(file, MAY_READ);', '\t\tif (unlikely(ret))', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tret = security_file_permission(file, MAY_WRITE);', '\t\tif (unlikely(ret))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tret = aio_setup_single_vector(READ, file, kiocb);', '\t\tret = aio_setup_single_vector(WRITE, file, kiocb);']}
description: Integer overflow in fs/aio.c in the Linux kernel before 3.4.1 allows local users to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via a large AIO iovec.

code_evidence: For IOCB_CMD_PREAD, access_ok is called with kiocb->ki_left as the length but no rw_verify_area() bounds/overflow check on the offset+length is performed before dispatching to aio_setup_single_vector(kiocb).

The PWRITE branch likewise checks access_ok(VERIFY_READ, kiocb->ki_buf, kiocb->ki_left) and only calls security_file_permission, then aio_setup_single_vector, without validating the offset/size range.
PREADV calls aio_setup_vectored_rw(READ, kiocb, compat) after only a file-mode check and security_file_permission; the iovec total length is not overflow-checked against the offset.
PWRITEV similarly invokes aio_setup_vectored_rw(WRITE, kiocb, compat) with no rw_verify_area-style size/offset validation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the missing constraint permits integer overflow/wraparound in the offset-plus-length computation that rw_verify_area() would normally guard. The weakness is the unchecked arithmetic, not merely a missing permission check (access control).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the AIO submission path validates buffer accessibility and file permission but never calls rw_verify_area(), so the combined offset and access size (ki_left or summed iovec lengths) can wrap past the representable offset limit. Trigger: a local user submits an AIO iovec with a large length/offset; the unchecked arithmetic yields a small or negative value used later in the read/write path. Supported consequence: denial of service or unspecified memory impact from the wrapped size.

code_evidence: After PString is allocated at line 56, the loop reads plen bytes; if ReadBlobByte returns EOF at line 66, the function returns -1 without freeing PString.

commit_msg:
Correctly handle dup() failure in Parcel::readNativeHandle

bail out if dup() fails, instead of creating an invalid native_handle_t

Bug: 28395952

Change-Id: Ia1a6198c0f45165b9c6a55a803e5f64d8afa0572
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (h->data[i] < 0) err = BAD_VALUE;'], 'added_lines': ['        if (h->data[i] < 0) {', '            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {', '                close(h->data[j]);', '            }', '            native_handle_delete(h);', '            return 0;', '        }']}
description: libs/binder/Parcel.cpp in the Parcels Framework APIs in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-07-01 does not validate the return value of the dup system call, which allows attackers to bypass an isolation protection mechanism via a crafted application, aka internal bug 28395952.

code_evidence: The function reads attacker-influenced counts numFds and numInts from the parcel via readInt32 and only checks the read status, never validating that the values are non-negative or bounded before passing them to native_handle_create and using numFds as the dup loop bound.

In the loop, each dup(readFileDescriptor()) result is stored into h->data[i]; the return value is checked only by assigning err = BAD_VALUE but the loop condition err==NO_ERROR stops iteration, leaving a partially populated handle with negative fd entries.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of input-derived values (numFds/numInts and the dup result) before processing, which matches CWE-20. It is not merely a resource-leak issue (CWE-404); the core defect is accepting unvalidated parcel data as a valid handle.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: numFds/numInts read from the parcel are not validated, and the dup() failure is not treated as a hard error. Trigger: a crafted parcel supplies unvalidated counts or a readFileDescriptor() that causes dup to fail, so the function returns a native_handle containing invalid/negative descriptor entries instead of failing. Consequence: callers operate on an invalid handle, bypassing the intended isolation/protection and risking unsafe descriptor use.

commit_msg:
ptrace: Check PTRACE_O_SUSPEND_SECCOMP permission on PTRACE_SEIZE

Setting PTRACE_O_SUSPEND_SECCOMP is supposed to be a highly privileged
operation because it allows the tracee to completely bypass all seccomp
filters on kernels with CONFIG_CHECKPOINT_RESTORE=y. It is only supposed to
be settable by a process with global CAP_SYS_ADMIN, and only if that
process is not subject to any seccomp filters at all.

However, while these permission checks were done on the PTRACE_SETOPTIONS
path, they were missing on the PTRACE_SEIZE path, which also sets
user-specified ptrace flags.

Move the permissions checks out into a helper function and let both
ptrace_attach() and ptrace_setoptions() call it.

Cc: stable@kernel.org
Fixes: 13c4a90119d2 ("seccomp: add ptrace options for suspend/resume")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20220319010838.1386861-1-jannh@google.com
Signed-off-by: Eric W. Biederman <ebiederm@xmission.com>

description: The Linux kernel before 5.17.2 mishandles seccomp permissions. The PTRACE_SEIZE code path allows attackers to bypass intended restrictions on setting the PT_SUSPEND_SECCOMP flag.

code_evidence: The function validates the requested data against PTRACE_O_MASK (lines 4-5) and, when PTRACE_O_SUSPEND_SECCOMP is set, requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN (lines 10-11) and a disabled seccomp mode plus no existing PT_SUSPEND_SECCOMP (lines 12-14). These checks gate the privileged option before flags are applied to child->ptrace at lines 16-19.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the weakness is a missing authorization check on an action (setting the privileged suspend-seccomp option) via PTRACE_SEIZE, allowing a privilege/protection bypass. This function shows the checks that should have been shared, confirming the intended authorization requirement rather than an input-validation flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the required CAP_SYS_ADMIN and seccomp-state authorization checks for PTRACE_O_SUSPEND_SECCOMP exist only on this PTRACE_SETOPTIONS path and are absent from the PTRACE_SEIZE path that also sets ptrace flags. Trigger: an attacker uses PTRACE_SEIZE with PTRACE_O_SUSPEND_SECCOMP. Consequence: the tracee can bypass all seccomp filters, a protection-mechanism bypass.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In version 2.11.1 and prior, there are various cases where it is possible that certain incoming RTP/RTCP packets can potentially cause out-of-bound read access. This issue affects all users that use PJMEDIA and accept incoming RTP/RTCP. A patch is available as a commit in the `master` branch. There are no known workarounds.

code_evidence: offset is computed from the RTP header and CSRC count, then, when the extension bit x is set, dec_hdr->ext_hdr is formed at pkt+offset and its length field is read at line 19 without first checking that offset+sizeof(pjmedia_rtp_ext_hdr) is within pkt_len. The ext_len read is then used to advance offset. The only length check (line 26) occurs after the extension header has already been dereferenced, so it cannot prevent the read at line 19.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads the extension header length past the end of the supplied packet buffer, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not a write or integer-only issue; the direct consequence is reading memory outside the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the extension-header pointer/length are dereferenced before any bounds validation against pkt_len. Trigger: an incoming RTP packet with the x bit set whose offset (header plus CSRCs) leaves fewer than sizeof(pjmedia_rtp_ext_hdr) bytes. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of the extension length field, enabling memory disclosure or crash.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language. In versions prior to and including 2.12 PJSIP there is a stack-buffer overflow vulnerability which only impacts PJSIP users who accept hashed digest credentials (credentials with data_type `PJSIP_CRED_DATA_DIGEST`). This issue has been patched in the master branch of the PJSIP repository and will be included with the next release. Users unable to upgrade need to check that the hashed digest data length must be equal to `PJSIP_MD5STRLEN` before passing to PJSIP.

code_evidence: In the PJSIP_CRED_DATA_DIGEST branch, the code only asserts that cred_info->data.slen equals 32; assertions may be compiled out and do not enforce a constraint at runtime.

The subsequent pj_memcpy copies cred_info->data.slen bytes from the attacker-influenced credential data pointer into the fixed-size stack buffer ha1[PJSIP_MD5STRLEN] (32 bytes); no length check guards the copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a buffer copy of input data into a fixed-size output buffer without verifying the input length is smaller than the destination, matching CWE-120. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the flaw is the unchecked write past ha1.

evidence_lines.code:
char ha1[PJSIP_MD5STRLEN];
char ha2[PJSIP_MD5STRLEN];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the digest credential length is trusted and copied into ha1 without a runtime bound check, since pj_assert is not a validation mechanism. Trigger: a user accepting hashed digest credentials supplies a PJSIP_CRED_DATA_DIGEST with data.slen > 32. Consequence: the copy writes past ha1 on the stack, corrupting adjacent stack memory (the patched code shows the intended guard is data.slen != 32 returning PJ_EINVAL).

commit_msg:
bn/bn_exp.c: constant-time MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_FROM_PREBUF.

Performance penalty varies from platform to platform, and even
key length. For rsa2048 sign it was observed to reach almost 10%.

CVE-2016-0702

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
(cherry picked from master)

Resolved conflicts:
	crypto/bn/bn_exp.c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_TO_PREBUF(&tmp, top, powerbuf, 0, numPowers))', '            goto err;', '        if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_TO_PREBUF(&am, top, powerbuf, 1, numPowers))', '            if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_TO_PREBUF', '                (&tmp, top, powerbuf, 2, numPowers))', '                if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_TO_PREBUF', '                    (&tmp, top, powerbuf, i, numPowers))', '        if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_FROM_PREBUF', '            (&tmp, top, powerbuf, wvalue, numPowers))', '            if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_FROM_PREBUF', '                (&am, top, powerbuf, wvalue, numPowers))'], 'added_lines': ['        if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_TO_PREBUF(&tmp, top, powerbuf, 0, window))', '            goto err;', '        if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_TO_PREBUF(&am, top, powerbuf, 1, window))', '            if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_TO_PREBUF(&tmp, top, powerbuf, 2,', '                                              window))', '                if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_TO_PREBUF(&tmp, top, powerbuf, i,', '                                                  window))', '        if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_FROM_PREBUF(&tmp, top, powerbuf, wvalue,', '                                            window))', '            if (!MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_FROM_PREBUF(&am, top, powerbuf, wvalue,', '                                                window))']}
description: The MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_FROM_PREBUF function in crypto/bn/bn_exp.c in OpenSSL 1.0.1 before 1.0.1s and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2g does not properly consider cache-bank access times during modular exponentiation, which makes it easier for local users to discover RSA keys by running a crafted application on the same Intel Sandy Bridge CPU core as a victim and leveraging cache-bank conflicts, aka a "CacheBleed" attack.

code_evidence: The constant-time path builds the precomputed table with MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_TO_PREBUF(..., numPowers) even though the table is only filled up to numPowers/2 entries (window bits, so numPowers = 1<<window and index i stops before numPowers).

The exponentiation loop then fetches entries with MOD_EXP_CTIME_COPY_FROM_PREBUF(..., wvalue, numPowers), so the copy routine's loop bound and cache-line access pattern depend on numPowers rather than the actual number of populated table entries.

Because the table access layout is sized/iterated by numPowers while real indices are bounded by the window, the memory access pattern during table lookup correlates with the secret exponent bits wvalue.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function handles a private RSA exponent and leaks it through timing-observable memory access patterns, exposing sensitive information to an unauthorized local observer. This is a confidentiality exposure of secret key material, matching CWE-200; the timing side channel is the mechanism, not a separate label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The prebuffer is populated and traversed using numPowers as the count, but the actual table only needs the window-indexed entries. The lookup of wvalue therefore touches a cache footprint whose timing depends on the secret exponent; a local attacker sharing the core can observe cache-bank conflicts and infer RSA key bits. The root cause is the secret-dependent access pattern, with key disclosure as the consequence.

commit_msg:
* src/cff/cffparse.c (cff_parser_run): Add one more stack size
check.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        FT_UInt                   num_args = (FT_UInt)', '                                             ( parser->top - parser->stack );', '        code = v;'], 'added_lines': ['        FT_UInt                   num_args;', '        if ( (FT_UInt)( parser->top - parser->stack ) >= parser->stackSize )', '          goto Stack_Overflow;', '', '        num_args     = (FT_UInt)( parser->top - parser->stack );', '        code         = v;', '']}
description: FreeType 2 before 2016-12-16 has an out-of-bounds write caused by a heap-based buffer overflow related to the cff_parser_run function in cff/cffparse.c.

code_evidence: The stack push at line 21 now checks the current depth against parser->stackSize before writing *parser->top++, preventing overflow.
Before the fix, num_args is derived from parser->top - parser->stack and *parser->top = p is written at line 149 without a bounds check, so a long operand sequence can push top past the stack end.
The old-engine loop similarly writes *parser->top++ at line 81; the added guard at line 79 bounds it against stackSize.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked *parser->top++ writes past the intended stack buffer, which is a classic out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). A stack-overflow label alone would not capture the memory-corruption write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: operand pushes to parser->stack were not bounded by stackSize before writing through parser->top. Trigger: a crafted CFF font with enough operands to fill the stack. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds write past the stack buffer, corrupting adjacent memory.

data. If it overcomes the ends of the packet we hit a crash. In this case
add an expert info and stop the dissection

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.13, 2.6.0 to 2.6.7, and 3.0.0, the DCERPC SPOOLSS dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-dcerpc-spoolss.c by adding a boundary check.

code_evidence: Reads a 32-bit length field from the packet into the unvalidated size variable.
Passes size directly to dissect_ndr_uint8s to read that many bytes, without checking against remaining packet length.
Uses offset - size and size as the item's length, assuming size bytes were actually present.
Creates a child tvb of length size from data, propagating the oversized read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unchecked size leads directly to reading beyond the intended buffer boundary. It is not CWE-787 (write) since the excess is consumed as read data and copied into a child tvb, not written out of bounds.

evidence_lines.code:
offset = dissect_ndr_uint32(tvb, offset, pinfo, tree, di, drep,
hf_buffer_size, &size);

offset = dissect_ndr_uint8s(tvb, offset, pinfo, NULL, di, drep,
hf_buffer_data, size, &data);

tree, hf_buffer_data, tvb, offset - size,
size, ENC_NA);
b->tvb = tvb_new_child_real_data(tvb, data, size, size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the packet-supplied size is used as a read length without verifying it fits within the tvb; the added boundary check is absent here. Trigger: a crafted DCERPC SPOOLSS packet declaring a size larger than remaining data. Consequence: dissect_ndr_uint8s and the subsequent item/tvb creation read past the end of the buffer, causing a crash (DoS) or memory disclosure.

description: A heap buffer overflow in ExtractImageSection function in tiffcrop.c in libtiff library Version 4.3.0 allows attacker to trigger unsafe or out of bounds memory access via crafted TIFF image file which could result into application crash, potential information disclosure or any other context-dependent impact

code_evidence: In the unaligned branch, the loop runs j from 0 through full_bytes inclusive and writes sect_buff[dst_offset + j] for each iteration, so it writes full_bytes+1 bytes into the destination while only full_bytes complete bytes are accounted for per row.
The trailing-bits path then writes sect_buff[dst_offset] after dst_offset was advanced by full_bytes, and src_buff[offset1 + full_bytes] is read without a bound check on the source buffer size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes sect_buff[dst_offset + j] beyond the intended per-row destination region because the loop bound and offset arithmetic do not match the allocated buffer size, which is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the primary supported consequence is memory corruption via the destination store.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The destination row stride is computed as full_bytes, but the unaligned copy loop writes full_bytes+1 bytes (j <= full_bytes), and the trailing-bit store adds one more byte at dst_offset. With crafted section/image dimensions, dst_offset advances past the allocated section buffer, producing a heap out-of-bounds write; the source read at offset1+full_bytes can also exceed src_buff.

description: There is a heap-buffer-overflow at lit-strings.c:431 in lit_read_code_unit_from_utf8 in JerryScript 2.2.0.

code_evidence: In the default case, when the token is a high surrogate in unicode mode, the code calls lit_cesu8_peek_next(re_ctx_p->input_curr_p) without first checking that input_curr_p is still before input_end_p. The diff adds exactly this end-of-string guard to the condition; the before-version reaches the peek when the high surrogate is the last input unit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 covers out-of-bounds memory writes; here the missing end-of-string check causes an out-of-bounds access past the intended buffer. The patch adds the missing boundary constraint, consistent with an out-of-bounds memory-safety defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unicode surrogate-pair branch reads the next code unit via lit_cesu8_peek_next after lit_cesu8_read_next has advanced input_curr_p to input_end_p, with no bounds check. Trigger: a regex ending in a high surrogate in unicode mode. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read past the input buffer (heap-buffer-overflow reported in lit_read_code_unit_from_utf8).

commit_msg:
Fix infinite loop in LZMA decompression

Check the liblzma error code more thoroughly to avoid infinite loops.

Closes: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/libxml2/issues/13
Closes: https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=794914

This is CVE-2018-9251 and CVE-2018-14567.

Thanks to Dongliang Mu and Simon Wörner for the reports.

description: libxml2 2.9.8, if --with-lzma is used, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via a crafted XML file that triggers LZMA_MEMLIMIT_ERROR, as demonstrated by xmllint, a different vulnerability than CVE-2015-8035 and CVE-2018-9251.

code_evidence: The do-while loop at line 10 continues while strm->avail_out is nonzero and ret != LZMA_STREAM_END (line 56). ret is set by lzma_code at line 43.

Only LZMA_MEM_ERROR, LZMA_DATA_ERROR and LZMA_PROG_ERROR are explicitly handled (lines 44-54); other non-OK, non-STREAM_END codes such as LZMA_MEMLIMIT_ERROR fall through without returning or breaking the loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's do-while loop has an exit condition that cannot be reached for certain liblzma error returns, matching CWE-835's iteration with an unreachable exit. This is a loop-construction flaw rather than a memory-safety weakness like CWE-787, which the code does not exhibit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: lzma_code can return an error code (e.g. LZMA_MEMLIMIT_ERROR) that is neither LZMA_STREAM_END nor one of the three handled codes. The loop condition only checks avail_out and STREAM_END, so when the decoder makes no progress and leaves avail_out nonzero, the exit condition is never reached, causing repeated calls and an infinite loop (CPU DoS). Root cause is the incomplete error-code check; consequence is resource consumption.

commit_msg:
coredump: fix race condition between mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and core dumping

The core dumping code has always run without holding the mmap_sem for
writing, despite that is the only way to ensure that the entire vma
layout will not change from under it.  Only using some signal
serialization on the processes belonging to the mm is not nearly enough.
This was pointed out earlier.  For example in Hugh's post from Jul 2017:

  https://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.LSU.2.11.1707191716030.2055@eggly.anvils

  "Not strictly relevant here, but a related note: I was very surprised
   to discover, only quite recently, how handle_mm_fault() may be called
   without down_read(mmap_sem) - when core dumping. That seems a
   misguided optimization to me, which would also be nice to correct"

In particular because the growsdown and growsup can move the
vm_start/vm_end the various loops the core dump does around the vma will
not be consistent if page faults can happen concurrently.

Pretty much all users calling mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and then
taking the mmap_sem had the potential to introduce unexpected side
effects in the core dumping code.

Adding mmap_sem for writing around the ->core_dump invocation is a
viable long term fix, but it requires removing all copy user and page
faults and to replace them with get_dump_page() for all binary formats
which is not suitable as a short term fix.

For the time being this solution manually covers the places that can
confuse the core dump either by altering the vma layout or the vma flags
while it runs.  Once ->core_dump runs under mmap_sem for writing the
function mmget_still_valid() can be dropped.

Allowing mmap_sem protected sections to run in parallel with the
coredump provides some minor parallelism advantage to the swapoff code
(which seems to be safe enough by never mangling any vma field and can
keep doing swapins in parallel to the core dumping) and to some other
corner case.

In order to facilitate the backporting I added "Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6"
however the side effect of this same race condition in /proc/pid/mem
should be reproducible since before 2.6.12-rc2 so I couldn't add any
other "Fixes:" because there's no hash beyond the git genesis commit.

Because find_extend_vma() is the only location outside of the process
context that could modify the "mm" structures under mmap_sem for
reading, by adding the mmget_still_valid() check to it, all other cases
that take the mmap_sem for reading don't need the new check after
mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm().  The expand_stack() in page fault
context also doesn't need the new check, because all tasks under core
dumping are frozen.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190325224949.11068-1-aarcange@redhat.com
Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6 ("userfaultfd: add new syscall to provide memory externalization")
Signed-off-by: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Peter Xu <peterx@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Rapoport <rppt@linux.ibm.com>
Reviewed-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@mellanox.com>
Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!mmget_still_valid(mm))', '\t\tgoto skip_mm;', 'skip_mm:']}
description: The coredump implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10 does not use locking or other mechanisms to prevent vma layout or vma flags changes while it runs, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information, cause a denial of service, or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a race condition with mmget_not_zero or get_task_mm calls. This is related to fs/userfaultfd.c, mm/mmap.c, fs/proc/task_mmu.c, and drivers/infiniband/core/uverbs_main.c.

code_evidence: userfaultfd_release() obtains the mm reference via mmget_not_zero() [9] and then takes mm->mmap_sem for writing [11], walking the vma list [13] and mutating vm_flags/vm_userfaultfd_ctx [21,31,32].
The vma traversal and mutation [12-33] proceed without any check that the mm is still valid for core dumping, so a concurrent core dump can observe or be confused by these layout/flag changes.
The lock is released via up_write() [34] and the mm reference dropped with mmput() [35]; the write lock does not serialize against the coredump path that runs without the write lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper locking: the write-lock-protected mutation of shared mm/vma state is not synchronized with the concurrent coredump reader, matching CWE-667's lock-acquisition/coverage failure. It is not merely a missing check; the lock does not cover the competing accessor, causing unpredictable shared-resource state changes.

evidence_lines.code:
up_write(&mm->mmap_sem);
mmput(mm);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the vma layout/flags are modified under mmap_sem for writing while the coredump path traverses the same vma structures without holding the write lock, and no mmget_still_valid() guard gates the mutation. Trigger: a local user causes userfaultfd_release() to run concurrently with a core dump, mutating vma fields mid-traversal. Supported consequence: inconsistent vma state during dumping, enabling information disclosure or denial of service.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.11.11. The user mode driver (UMD) has a copy_process() memory leak, related to a lack of cleanup steps in kernel/usermode_driver.c and kernel/bpf/preload/bpf_preload_kern.c, aka CID-f60a85cad677.

code_evidence: fini_umd is the exit/cleanup path for the user-mode driver. It kills the UMD via kill_pid(umd_ops.info.tgid,...), then immediately sets umd_ops.info.tgid to NULL, and calls umd_unload_blob without waiting for the killed process to exit or releasing the pipe/file and pid resources. The tgid pointer is overwritten before any wait/cleanup of the exited thread group occurs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to release allocated memory (pid and pipe file objects) after their effective lifetime, matching CWE-401's missing release of memory. This is a lifetime/cleanup omission, not a use-after-free: the pointers are dropped without freeing the underlying resources.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the teardown path does not wait for the killed UMD process to terminate before discarding its tgid and unloading, so the pipe_to_umh/pipe_from_umh file objects and pid/tgid allocated at clone time are never released. Trigger: loading the UMD then invoking fini_umd (module exit or setup error), causing the asynchronous exit cleanup to be skipped; the consequence is leaked kernel memory (DoS resource consumption).

commit_msg:
iio: imu: adis16400: fix memory leak

In adis_update_scan_mode_burst, if adis->buffer allocation fails release
the adis->xfer.

Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Alexandru Ardelean <alexandru.ardelean@analog.com>
Signed-off-by: Jonathan Cameron <Jonathan.Cameron@huawei.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!adis->buffer)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!adis->buffer) {', '\t\tkfree(adis->xfer);', '\t\tadis->xfer = NULL;', '\t}']}
description: A memory leak in the adis_update_scan_mode_burst() function in drivers/iio/imu/adis_buffer.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.9 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption), aka CID-9c0530e898f3.

code_evidence: Line 9 allocates adis->xfer with kcalloc and stores it in the device structure. Lines 12-14 then allocate adis->buffer with kzalloc; when that allocation fails, the function returns -ENOMEM at line 14 without freeing the previously allocated adis->xfer, and the pointer is not cleared. The xfer memory therefore remains referenced but is never released on this error path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because memory allocated at line 9 is not released when the subsequent allocation fails at lines 12-14, leaving it unavailable for reuse. This is a missing-release-on-error-path leak rather than a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path taken when kzalloc for adis->buffer fails abandons the earlier kcalloc result for adis->xfer. Trigger: memory pressure causing the buffer allocation to return NULL. Consequence: the xfer allocation is leaked, and repeated failures accumulate unreleased memory, supporting a resource-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg:
h264dec: check for overflows when calculating allocation size.

Bug: 27855419
Change-Id: Idabedca52913ec31ea5cb6a6109ab94e3fb2badd
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void* H264SwDecMalloc(u32 size)', '    return malloc(size);'], 'added_lines': ['void* H264SwDecMalloc(u32 size, u32 num)', '    if (size > UINT32_MAX / num) {', '        return NULL;', '    }', '    return malloc(size * num);']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the h264dec component in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-06-01 allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file that triggers a large memory allocation, aka internal bug 27855419.

code_evidence: H264SwDecMalloc takes a single u32 size and passes it directly to malloc(size); the allocation size is derived from caller-supplied dimensions without any overflow or range check. The patch adds a num multiplier and a UINT32_MAX/num guard, confirming the original lacked this constraint.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked allocation size leads to an undersized heap buffer that is written beyond its intended boundary, which is the memory-buffer out-of-bounds operation described by CWE-119. The integer overflow is the root cause; CWE-119 captures the resultant out-of-bounds access rather than a separate integer-handling label.

evidence_lines.code:
void* H264SwDecMalloc(u32 size)
return malloc(size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is an unchecked, attacker-influenced size (and later size*num product) used as the malloc length. A crafted H.264 media file can drive a size computation that overflows 32 bits, producing a small allocation; subsequent writes based on the intended large dimensions then exceed the heap buffer, causing memory corruption and potential code execution or denial of service.

commit_msg: Fixed bug #71323 - Output of stream_get_meta_data can be falsified by its input
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t', '\t\t\tadd_assoc_stringl_ex(meta, key, plen + 1, sep + 1, vlen, 1);'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t\tif (plen != sizeof("mediatype")-1 || memcmp(key, "mediatype", sizeof("mediatype")-1)) {', '\t\t\t\tadd_assoc_stringl_ex(meta, key, plen + 1, sep + 1, vlen, 1);', '\t\t\t}']}
description: In PHP before 5.5.32, 5.6.x before 5.6.18, and 7.x before 7.0.3, all of the return values of stream_get_meta_data can be controlled if the input can be controlled (e.g., during file uploads). For example, a "$uri = stream_get_meta_data(fopen($file, "r"))['uri']" call mishandles the case where $file is data:text/plain;uri=eviluri, -- in other words, metadata can be set by an attacker.

code_evidence: The while loop parses each RFC 2397 parameter: [63] computes plen as the key length from sep-path, [64] computes vlen, [65] duplicates the attacker-supplied key, and [66] writes it directly into the meta array via add_assoc_stringl_ex without checking whether the key is a reserved metadata name such as "mediatype".
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts caller-supplied parameter keys without validating them against reserved metadata names, an improper-input-validation flaw (CWE-20). It is distinct from CWE-116 output encoding: the defect is accepting unsafe input keys as-is, not escaping them for output.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the data: URL parameter key is copied verbatim into the metadata array, so a caller-controlled URI like data:text/plain;mediatype=evil,... can overwrite the genuine "mediatype" entry that the wrapper sets earlier. Trigger: any attacker-controlled data: URI passed to a stream-open function. Consequence: stream_get_meta_data() returns falsified metadata, letting untrusted input control values consumers rely on.

commit_msg:
FreeBSD: Fix UNIX permissions checking

Reviewed-by: Ryan Moeller <ryan@iXsystems.com>
Reviewed-by: Brian Behlendorf <behlendorf1@llnl.gov>
Signed-off-by: Matt Macy <mmacy@FreeBSD.org>
Closes #10727
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['#ifdef HAVE_KSID', '\tconst char *domain;', '\tuid_t id;', '\tdomain = zfs_fuid_find_by_idx(zfsvfs, index);', '\tASSERT(domain != NULL);', '', '\tif (type == ZFS_OWNER || type == ZFS_ACE_USER) {', '\t\t(void) kidmap_getuidbysid(crgetzone(cr), domain,', '\t\t    FUID_RID(fuid), &id);', '\t} else {', '\t\t(void) kidmap_getgidbysid(crgetzone(cr), domain,', '\t\t    FUID_RID(fuid), &id);', '\t}', '\treturn (id);', '#else', '\t/*', '\t * The Linux port only supports POSIX IDs, use the passed id.', '\t */', '\treturn (fuid);', '#endif /* HAVE_KSID */'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn (UID_NOBODY);']}
description: OpenZFS before 2.0.0-rc1, when used on FreeBSD, allows execute permissions for all directories.

code_evidence: When FUID_INDEX(fuid) is zero the raw fuid is returned unchanged; otherwise the SID-to-ID mapping path is taken.

For a non-zero index, the domain is looked up and zfs_fuid_find_by_idx's result is only ASSERTed non-NULL; the return values of kidmap_getuidbysid/kidmap_getgidbysid are ignored and id is returned regardless of whether the mapping succeeded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an incorrectly performed authorization check: the identity used for permission evaluation is not correctly resolved, so access decisions are made against the wrong actor. This is a flawed authorization decision (CWE-863), not merely a NULL-pointer or input-validation defect.

evidence_lines.code:
if (index == 0)
return (fuid);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function derives a POSIX uid/gid used for UNIX permission checks from an untrusted on-disk FUID without verifying that the SID-to-ID translation succeeded. If the mapping fails, the unchecked id (uninitialized or stale) is returned and used as the acting identity, so ownership/execute checks can be evaluated against the wrong principal, allowing execute permission on directories to all users on FreeBSD.

commit_msg: Issue #287: made CSR/CSC readers more robust against invalid input (case #1).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if ( sscanf(l_line, "%u %u %u", o_row_count, o_column_count, o_element_count) == 3 ) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (3 == sscanf(l_line, "%u %u %u", o_row_count, o_column_count, o_element_count) &&', '            0 != *o_row_count && 0 != *o_column_count && 0 != *o_element_count)', '        {']}
description: There is a heap-based buffer overflow in libxsmm_sparse_csc_reader at generator_spgemm_csc_reader.c in LIBXSMM 1.10, a different vulnerability than CVE-2018-20542 (which is in a different part of the source code and is seen at different addresses).

code_evidence: Header line is parsed into o_row_count/o_column_count/o_element_count; only the sscanf return count is checked, so values can be zero or arbitrary. Buffers are then sized from these counts and o_row_idx is written up to o_row_count+1 at [44,45,46].

Per-element lines parse l_row/l_column, decrement them at [60,61], then index o_column_idx[l_i], l_row_idx_id[l_row] and o_row_idx[l_row+1] without validating l_row < o_row_count or l_column < o_column_count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs unchecked index-based writes into heap-allocated arrays, directly matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. The missing bounds validation is the cause; the heap corruption is the consequence, not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reader trusts the header and element indices, allocating buffers from the declared counts and then indexing with unvalidated l_row/l_column and a running l_i. A malformed file with out-of-range row/column indices or a zero/oversized element count triggers writes past the allocated o_row_idx, o_column_idx or l_row_idx_id buffers, corrupting the heap.

commit_msg:
Unpack: Phdrs must be within expansion of first compressed block

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/388
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ((MAX_ELF_HDR - sizeof(Elf32_Ehdr))/sizeof(Elf32_Phdr) < u_phnum) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if ((umin(MAX_ELF_HDR, ph.u_len) - sizeof(Elf32_Ehdr))/sizeof(Elf32_Phdr) < u_phnum) {']}
description: A heap buffer overflow read was discovered in upx 4.0.0, because the check in p_lx_elf.cpp is not perfect.

code_evidence: Line 33 reads attacker-controlled ph.u_len from b_info; line 39 allocates a buffer u of exactly ph.u_len bytes and line 40 views it as Elf32_Ehdr. Line 56 reads u_phnum from the decompressed header, and line 62's bound only uses the fixed MAX_ELF_HDR (512) rather than the actual decompressed size ph.u_len, throwing only if u_phnum exceeds (512-sizeof(Ehdr))/sizeof(Phdr).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads program-header structures past the end of the ph.u_len-sized buffer because the e_phnum bound is decoupled from the real allocation size, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds write, as the flaw manifests as reading memory beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the e_phnum validation assumes the decompressed header buffer is at least MAX_ELF_HDR bytes, but the buffer is only ph.u_len bytes. When ph.u_len is smaller than 512 while u_phnum passes the check, later program-header iterations (lines 112, 124, 134, 177, 182, 205, 214) dereference phdr entries beyond the allocated u buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read of heap memory.

commit_msg:
x86/mm: Add barriers and document switch_mm()-vs-flush synchronization

When switch_mm() activates a new PGD, it also sets a bit that
tells other CPUs that the PGD is in use so that TLB flush IPIs
will be sent.  In order for that to work correctly, the bit
needs to be visible prior to loading the PGD and therefore
starting to fill the local TLB.

Document all the barriers that make this work correctly and add
a couple that were missing.

Signed-off-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Cc: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Andy Lutomirski <luto@amacapital.net>
Cc: Borislav Petkov <bp@alien8.de>
Cc: Brian Gerst <brgerst@gmail.com>
Cc: Dave Hansen <dave.hansen@linux.intel.com>
Cc: Denys Vlasenko <dvlasenk@redhat.com>
Cc: H. Peter Anvin <hpa@zytor.com>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Rik van Riel <riel@redhat.com>
Cc: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: linux-mm@kvack.org
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Ingo Molnar <mingo@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (current->active_mm != mm)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (current->active_mm != mm) {', '\t\t/* Synchronize with switch_mm. */', '\t\tsmp_mb();', '', '\t}', '', '\t\t/* Synchronize with switch_mm. */', '\t\tsmp_mb();', '', '\t/*', '\t * Both branches below are implicit full barriers (MOV to CR or', '\t * INVLPG) that synchronize with switch_mm.', '\t */']}
description: Race condition in arch/x86/mm/tlb.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 allows local users to gain privileges by triggering access to a paging structure by a different CPU.

code_evidence: The early-exit path checks current->active_mm against mm and jumps to out without any memory barrier, so the decision can be observed before switch_mm's PGD-in-use bit is visible.
When current->mm is NULL, leave_mm() is called and control goes to out with no synchronization barrier between the CR3 switch and the subsequent flush decision.
The flush branches rely on local_flush_tlb() or __flush_tlb_single() as implicit full barriers, but the two preceding early exits provide no such ordering with switch_mm on another CPU.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function coordinates a shared resource (the PGD/TLB state) across CPUs, and the missing barriers create a timing window where concurrent switch_mm() and flush_tlb_mm_range() interleave incorrectly. This is improper synchronization of concurrent access, matching CWE-362 rather than a memory-safety flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
if (current->active_mm != mm)
goto out;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: flush_tlb_mm_range() makes decisions about the active PGD and issues TLB flushes without ordering them against switch_mm() setting the PGD-in-use bit on another CPU. Trigger: a CPU switches mm while a concurrent flush observes stale state and skips or misorders the flush, leaving a stale TLB entry usable. Consequence: access to a paging structure by a different CPU, enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
floppy: check FDC index for errors before assigning it

Jordy Zomer reported a KASAN out-of-bounds read in the floppy driver in
wait_til_ready().

Which on the face of it can't happen, since as Willy Tarreau points out,
the function does no particular memory access.  Except through the FDCS
macro, which just indexes a static allocation through teh current fdc,
which is always checked against N_FDC.

Except the checking happens after we've already assigned the value.

The floppy driver is a disgrace (a lot of it going back to my original
horrd "design"), and has no real maintainer.  Nobody has the hardware,
and nobody really cares.  But it still gets used in virtual environment
because it's one of those things that everybody supports.

The whole thing should be re-written, or at least parts of it should be
seriously cleaned up.  The 'current fdc' index, which is used by the
FDCS macro, and which is often shadowed by a local 'fdc' variable, is a
prime example of how not to write code.

But because nobody has the hardware or the motivation, let's just fix up
the immediate problem with a nasty band-aid: test the fdc index before
actually assigning it to the static 'fdc' variable.

Reported-by: Jordy Zomer <jordy@simplyhacker.com>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>

commit_msg:
tcp: mark skbs with SCM_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS

SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS can be enabled and disabled
while packets are collected on the error queue.
So, checking SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS in sk->sk_tsflags
is not enough to safely assume that the skb contains
OPT_STATS data.

Add a bit in sock_exterr_skb to indicate whether the
skb contains opt_stats data.

Fixes: 1c885808e456 ("tcp: SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS option for SO_TIMESTAMPING")
Reported-by: JongHwan Kim <zzoru007@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Soheil Hassas Yeganeh <soheil@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Willem de Bruijn <willemb@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: The TCP stack in the Linux kernel through 4.10.6 mishandles the SCM_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS feature, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from the kernel's internal socket data structures or cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via crafted system calls, related to net/core/skbuff.c and net/socket.c.

code_evidence: The function checks only skb_may_tx_timestamp(sk, false) and then unconditionally copies hwtstamps and forwards skb to __skb_complete_tx_timestamp with SCM_TSTAMP_SND. It does not verify whether the skb actually carries OPT_STATS data before the timestamp completion path processes it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing per-skb OPT_STATS marker lets the timestamp completion code interpret a shorter skb as containing stats and read past its buffer. This is an out-of-bounds read, not merely a logic error, since the observable impact is reading unintended kernel memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decision to include OPT_STATS is based on the mutable sk->sk_tsflags state rather than a per-skb marker, so a packet queued while the option was enabled can be completed after the flag is cleared and the skb lacks the expected stats. Trigger: userspace toggles SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS while packets are pending on the error queue. Consequence: the completion path reads beyond the skb's intended stats buffer, leaking kernel memory or causing an out-of-bounds read/DoS.

commit_msg:
Rewrite url::recvline to be nonrecursive

This function processes network input. It's semi-trusted, because the
PAC ought to be trusted. But we still shouldn't allow it to control how
far we recurse. A malicious PAC can cause us to overflow the stack by
sending a sufficiently-long line without any '\n' character.

Also, this function failed to properly handle EINTR, so let's fix that
too, for good measure.

Fixes #134
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static inline string recvline(int fd) {', '\t// Read a character.', "\t// If we don't get a character, return empty string.", '\t// If we are at the end of the line, return empty string.', "\tchar c = '\\0';", '\t', "\tif (recv(fd, &c, 1, 0) != 1 || c == '\\n')", '\t\treturn "";', '\treturn string(1, c) + recvline(fd);'], 'added_lines': ['static string recvline(int fd) {', '\tstring line;', '\tint ret;', '\t// Reserve arbitrary amount of space to avoid small memory reallocations.', '\tline.reserve(128);', '', '\tdo {', '\t\tchar c;', '\t\tret = recv(fd, &c, 1, 0);', '\t\tif (ret == 1) {', "\t\t\tif (c == '\\n')", '\t\t\t\treturn line;', '\t\t\tline += c;', '\t\t}', '\t} while (ret == 1 || (ret == -1 && errno == EINTR));', '', '\treturn line;']}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is unbounded self-recursion: each received non-newline byte triggers exactly one recursive call, so recursion depth equals the line length. A remote HTTP server (or malicious PAC) sending an endless stream without '\n' drives the stack to exhaustion, crashing the process; the network input controls recursion depth.

commit_msg:
Fix NULL dereference in SSL_check_chain() for TLS 1.3

In the tls1_check_sig_alg() helper function, we loop through the list of
"signature_algorithms_cert" values received from the client and attempt
to look up each one in turn in our internal table that maps wire
codepoint to string-form name, digest and/or signature NID, etc., in
order to compare the signature scheme from the peer's list against what
is used to sign the certificates in the certificate chain we're
checking.  Unfortunately, when the peer sends a value that we don't
support, the lookup returns NULL, but we unconditionally dereference the
lookup result for the comparison, leading to an application crash
triggerable by an unauthenticated client.

Since we will not be able to say anything about algorithms we don't
recognize, treat NULL return from lookup as "does not match".

We currently only apply the "signature_algorithm_cert" checks on TLS 1.3
connections, so previous TLS versions are unaffected.  SSL_check_chain()
is not called directly from libssl, but may be used by the application
inside a callback (e.g., client_hello or cert callback) to verify that a
candidate certificate chain will be acceptable to the client.

CVE-2020-1967

Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (sig_nid == sigalg->sigandhash)'], 'added_lines': ['        if (sigalg != NULL && sig_nid == sigalg->sigandhash)']}
description: Server or client applications that call the SSL_check_chain() function during or after a TLS 1.3 handshake may crash due to a NULL pointer dereference as a result of incorrect handling of the "signature_algorithms_cert" TLS extension. The crash occurs if an invalid or unrecognised signature algorithm is received from the peer. This could be exploited by a malicious peer in a Denial of Service attack. OpenSSL version 1.1.1d, 1.1.1e, and 1.1.1f are affected by this issue. This issue did not affect OpenSSL versions prior to 1.1.1d. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1g (Affected 1.1.1d-1.1.1f).

code_evidence: When TLS 1.3 is active and the peer supplied certificate signature algorithms, sigalg is assigned via tls1_lookup_sigalg() for each peer value; that lookup can return NULL for an unrecognized codepoint.
The loop then unconditionally evaluates sigalg->sigandhash without any NULL check on the lookup result.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the code dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but which is NULL for unrecognized peer algorithms. The added 'sigalg != NULL' guard confirms the missing NULL constraint; this is a NULL dereference rather than an out-of-bounds or type-confusion issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the tls1_lookup_sigalg() result is dereferenced without verifying it is non-NULL. Trigger: an unauthenticated peer sends a signature_algorithms_cert value not present in the internal table, so the lookup returns NULL. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference crashes the application (DoS) when SSL_check_chain()/tls1_check_sig_alg() processes the peer list.

commit_msg:
p2m: Always check to see if removing a p2m entry actually worked

The PoD zero-check functions speculatively remove memory from the p2m,
then check to see if it's completely zeroed, before putting it in the
cache.

Unfortunately, the p2m_set_entry() calls may fail if the underlying
pagetable structure needs to change and the domain has exhausted its
p2m memory pool: for instance, if we're removing a 2MiB region out of
a 1GiB entry (in the p2m_pod_zero_check_superpage() case), or a 4k
region out of a 2MiB or larger entry (in the p2m_pod_zero_check()
case); and the return value is not checked.

The underlying mfn will then be added into the PoD cache, and at some
point mapped into another location in the p2m.  If the guest
afterwards ballons out this memory, it will be freed to the hypervisor
and potentially reused by another domain, in spite of the fact that
the original domain still has writable mappings to it.

There are several places where p2m_set_entry() shouldn't be able to
fail, as it is guaranteed to write an entry of the same order that
succeeded before.  Add a backstop of crashing the domain just in case,
and an ASSERT_UNREACHABLE() to flag up the broken assumption on debug
builds.

While we're here, use PAGE_ORDER_2M rather than a magic constant.

This is part of XSA-247.

Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

commit_msg:
gnttab: correct maptrack table accesses

In order to observe a consistent (limit,pointer-table) pair, the reader
needs to either hold the maptrack lock (in line with documentation) or
both sides need to order their accesses suitably (the writer side
barrier was removed by commit dff515dfea ["gnttab: use per-VCPU
maptrack free lists"], and a read side barrier has never been there).

Make the writer publish a new table page before limit (for bounds
checks to work), and new list head last (for racing maptrack_entry()
invocations to work). At the same time add read barriers to lockless
readers.

Additionally get_maptrack_handle() must not assume ->maptrack_head to
not change behind its back: Another handle may be put (updating only
->maptrack_tail) and then got or stolen (updating ->maptrack_head).

This is part of XSA-218.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>

GQUIC: make sure our tag offset advances.

Make sure gquic tag offset advances so that we don't infinitely loop.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                tag_offset += tag_len;'], 'added_lines': ['                goto end;', '', '    end:', '    if (offset + total_tag_len <= offset) {', '        expert_add_info_format(pinfo, gquic_tree, &ei_gquic_length_invalid,', '                                "Invalid total tag length: %u", total_tag_len);', '        return offset + tvb_reported_length_remaining(tvb, offset);', '    }']}
description: In Wireshark 3.2.0 to 3.2.7, the GQUIC dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-gquic.c by correcting the implementation of offset advancement.

code_evidence: tag_len is computed as offset_end - tag_offset (line 19) and accumulated into total_tag_len (line 20); if offset_end is less than tag_offset, tag_len becomes negative and total_tag_len becomes incorrect.
Lines 25-27 only clamp tag_len when it exceeds the remaining reported length; a negative tag_len passes this check and offset_end is set consistently with the bad value.

In the TAG_CCS loop, tag_offset advances by 8 while tag_len may be negative or inconsistent, so the loop bound offset_end - tag_offset can remain satisfied without progress or with mismatched arithmetic.
The default case adds tag_len bytes (line 264) and advances tag_offset by tag_len (line 269); when tag_len is negative this moves the offset backwards, breaking the offset_end comparison.
Lines 272-275 reset tag_offset to offset_end whenever the comparison fails, so the returned offset plus total_tag_len can be computed from a corrupted length value.

total_tag_len += tag_len;

commit_msg:
Fix error condition for SC and CS

The SC and CS PDF operators correctly checked the return code from the
underlying setcolor and setcolorspace code, but we had already
set up the exec stack for handling a non-error return.

We have to do this before calling the underlying code, as that also
uses a state machine, and alters the exec stack. We must push our
own execution context first.

Ordinarily this isn't a problem, but if we have a custom error handler
which doesn't stop the interpreter, then we would continue on to try
and use what we'd pushed onto the exec stack, with predictably dire
results.

Here we avoid this by saving the exec stack pointer on entry, and if
an error occurs, restoring back to that point before returning control
to the PostScript interpreter.

A minor point, but we now also reset the space/color on an error as
well, previously it would have been left with the wrong space set.

description: An issue was discovered in Artifex Ghostscript before 9.24. Incorrect exec stack handling in the "CS" and "SC" PDF primitives could be used by remote attackers able to supply crafted PDFs to crash the interpreter or possibly have unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: After check_estack(1) and push_op_estack(setstrokecolorspace_cont), the code calls zsetcolorspace, which may alter the exec stack; on error (code < 0) the function returns code without restoring esp, so the earlier pushed continuation remains and is later consumed out of order.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale exec-stack entry causes operations on an internal buffer beyond its intended bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory access; it is not merely a logic error because the corrupted stack pointer leads to memory misuse.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function pushes an execution-stack entry before a call that can fail and change the exec stack, but on the error path it returns without restoring the saved stack pointer. Trigger: a crafted PDF drives SC/CS through zsetcolorspace with a negative return code under a custom error handler. Consequence: the interpreter resumes with a mismatched exec stack, causing stack corruption, crashes, or unspecified impact.

commit_msg:
Fix OOB read in TS_OBJ_print_bio().

TS_OBJ_print_bio() misuses OBJ_txt2obj: it should print the result
as a null terminated buffer. The length value returned is the total
length the complete text reprsentation would need not the amount of
data written.

CVE-2016-2180

Thanks to Shi Lei for reporting this bug.

Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int len = OBJ_obj2txt(obj_txt, sizeof(obj_txt), obj, 0);', '    BIO_write(bio, obj_txt, len);', '    BIO_write(bio, "\\n", 1);'], 'added_lines': ['    OBJ_obj2txt(obj_txt, sizeof(obj_txt), obj, 0);', '    BIO_printf(bio, "%s\\n", obj_txt);']}
description: The TS_OBJ_print_bio function in crypto/ts/ts_lib.c in the X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Time-Stamp Protocol (TSP) implementation in OpenSSL through 1.0.2h allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and application crash) via a crafted time-stamp file that is mishandled by the "openssl ts" command.

code_evidence: obj_txt is a fixed 128-byte stack buffer. OBJ_obj2txt writes the text representation into it, bounded by sizeof(obj_txt), and returns the total length the full representation would need, not the number of bytes actually written. The return value is stored in len and passed directly to BIO_write as the read length from obj_txt.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: BIO_write reads len bytes from obj_txt while only sizeof(obj_txt) bytes were valid, which is a read past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-125. It is not an out-of-bounds write because the write into obj_txt is properly bounded by sizeof.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer is truncated to 128 bytes but the returned full-length value is used as the number of bytes to read, so BIO_write reads beyond the 128-byte obj_txt buffer. Trigger: a crafted time-stamp file whose object text representation exceeds 128 bytes. Consequence: out-of-bounds stack read, potentially leaking adjacent memory or crashing the application (DoS).

commit_msg: Set pixel cache to undefined if any resource limit is exceeded
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [''], 'added_lines': []}
description: The WPG parser in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-4 and 7.x before 7.0.1-5, when a memory limit is set, allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via vectors related to the SetImageExtent return-value check, which trigger (1) a heap-based buffer overflow in the SetPixelIndex function or an invalid write operation in the (2) ScaleCharToQuantum or (3) SetPixelIndex functions.

code_evidence: SetImageExtent is called and its MagickFalse status only breaks the record loop; the pixel cache is left unallocated/undefined while processing continues to the colormap and raster code below.
After the failed extent, image->colors is derived from bpp (one << bpp) and AcquireImageColormap is invoked, then the default palette is written.
The loop writes image->colormap[i] for i up to min(image->colors,256) without verifying the colormap buffer was successfully allocated for that many entries.
In the else branch, ResizeQuantumMemory may return NULL for image->colormap, but the result is stored without any NULL check before later colormap accesses.
UnpackWPGRaster is called unconditionally on the image whose extent allocation failed, so raster insertion writes pixels through the invalid cache.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked failure of the extent allocation followed by writes into the colormap and raster buffers produces memory accesses outside the intended buffer bounds, matching CWE-119. The root cause is the missing abort on SetImageExtent failure and unchecked allocation results, not merely a NULL dereference; the buffer-boundary violation is the direct observable effect.

commit_msg:
The X protocol uses CARD16 values to represent the length so
this would overflow.

CVE-2021-31535

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["    if (l < 2 || name[l - 1] != '*' || name[l - 2] != '-')"], 'added_lines': ["    if (l < 2 || name[l - 1] != '*' || name[l - 2] != '-' || l >= USHRT_MAX)"]}
description: LookupCol.c in X.Org X through X11R7.7 and libX11 before 1.7.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The libX11 XLookupColor request (intended for server-side color lookup) contains a flaw allowing a client to send color-name requests with a name longer than the maximum size allowed by the protocol (and also longer than the maximum packet size for normal-sized packets). The user-controlled data exceeding the maximum size is then interpreted by the server as additional X protocol requests and executed, e.g., to disable X server authorization completely. For example, if the victim encounters malicious terminal control sequences for color codes, then the attacker may be able to take full control of the running graphical session.

code_evidence: Line 14 computes l = strlen(name) from the caller-supplied font name; lines 15-16 only reject names not ending in '-*' and impose no upper bound on l.

Lines 29-30 bound the combined length against sizeof(buf)-1 before the copies at lines 31-32, so the local stack buffer buf[256] is protected; the unchecked length is passed into XLoadQueryFont at line 33.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fix adds the missing l >= USHRT_MAX constraint before the request is built, matching an unchecked input length that overflows a length field and corrupts the protocol stream. This is not the classic buf copy overflow since lines 29-32 bound buf; the weakness is the absent size check on the copied/forwarded input.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function accepts a font name of arbitrary length and forwards it into the X protocol request via XLoadQueryFont without enforcing the CARD16 length limit. A name exceeding USHRT_MAX yields a wrapped length field, so the server treats the excess bytes as additional protocol requests. The copy into buf is itself bounded, so the supported consequence is malformed request framing, not a stack overflow here.

description: A Null Pointer Deference issue exists in Academy Software Foundation OpenEXR 2.3.0 in generatePreview in makePreview.cpp that can cause a denial of service via a crafted EXR file.

code_evidence: Lines 18–19 compute fx and fy using a guard of previewWidth/previewHeight > 0, so when the preview dimension equals exactly 1 the divisor (previewWidth-1 or previewHeight-1) is zero. Line 26 then indexes pixels with int(y*fy+.5f) and int(x*fx+.5f), which become non-finite/undefined when fx or fy is derived from division by zero, yielding an out-of-bounds index into the pixels buffer rather than a valid element.

Consequence: the computed index at line 26 addresses outside the pixel buffer, causing a crash/denial of service.

description: DCTStream::getChars in DCTStream.cc in Poppler 20.12.1 has a heap-based buffer overflow via a crafted PDF document. NOTE: later reports indicate that this only affects builds from Poppler git clones in late December 2020, not the 20.12.1 release. In this situation, it should NOT be considered a Poppler vulnerability. However, several third-party Open Source projects directly rely on Poppler git clones made at arbitrary times, and therefore the CVE remains useful to users of those projects

This is a classic CWE-787 out-of-bounds write; it is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the overflow occurs on the destination of the copy.

commit_msg:
The purpose of this patch is to streamline error propagation and in particular
to propagate retrieve_ptr_limit() errors for pointer types that are not defining
a ptr_limit such that register-based alu ops against these types can be rejected.

The main rationale is that a gap has been identified by Piotr in the existing
protection against speculatively out-of-bounds loads, for example, in case of
ctx pointers, unprivileged programs can still perform pointer arithmetic. This
can be abused to execute speculatively out-of-bounds loads without restrictions
and thus extract contents of kernel memory.

Fix this by rejecting unprivileged programs that attempt any pointer arithmetic
on unprotected pointer types. The two affected ones are pointer to ctx as well
as pointer to map. Field access to a modified ctx' pointer is rejected at a
later point in time in the verifier, and 7c6967326267 ("bpf: Permit map_ptr
arithmetic with opcode add and offset 0") only relevant for root-only use cases.
Risk of unprivileged program breakage is considered very low.

Fixes: 7c6967326267 ("bpf: Permit map_ptr arithmetic with opcode add and offset 0")
Fixes: b2157399cc98 ("bpf: prevent out-of-bounds speculation")
Signed-off-by: Piotr Krysiuk <piotras@gmail.com>
Co-developed-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (retrieve_ptr_limit(ptr_reg, &alu_limit, opcode, off_is_neg))', '\t\treturn 0;', '\tif (update_alu_sanitation_state(aux, alu_state, alu_limit))', '\t\treturn -EACCES;'], 'added_lines': ['\tint err;', '\terr = retrieve_ptr_limit(ptr_reg, &alu_limit, opcode, off_is_neg);', '\tif (err < 0)', '\t\treturn err;', '', '\terr = update_alu_sanitation_state(aux, alu_state, alu_limit);', '\tif (err < 0)', '\t\treturn err;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.11.8. kernel/bpf/verifier.c performs undesirable out-of-bounds speculation on pointer arithmetic, leading to side-channel attacks that defeat Spectre mitigations and obtain sensitive information from kernel memory, aka CID-f232326f6966. This affects pointer types that do not define a ptr_limit.

code_evidence: The function calls retrieve_ptr_limit() and returns 0 on any nonzero result, including error values, so pointer types without a defined ptr_limit silently skip ALU sanitation and proceed to the do_sim speculative simulation path instead of being rejected.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing rejection produces a behavioral discrepancy: sanitized versus unsanitized paths differ observably, and the residual speculative execution leaks data via a side channel, matching CWE-203's observable-discrepancy/confidentiality impact. The patch makes error returns explicit and rejects the operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: retrieve_ptr_limit() errors are treated as a benign 'already sanitized' condition, so unprivileged pointer arithmetic on ctx/map pointers bypasses the alu_limit clamp. Trigger: an unprivileged BPF program performs ALU ops on a pointer type lacking ptr_limit. Consequence: speculative out-of-bounds loads proceed unrestricted, enabling side-channel leakage of kernel memory.

commit_msg:
Currently, we have a bug where a simultaneous DROPTAG ioctl and socket
close may race, as we attempt to remove a key from lists twice, and
perform an unref for each removal operation. This may result in a uaf
when we attempt the second unref.

This change fixes the race by making __mctp_key_remove tolerant to being
called on a key that has already been removed from the socket/net lists,
and only performs the unref when we do the actual remove. We also need
to hold the list lock on the ioctl cleanup path.

This fix is based on a bug report and comprehensive analysis from
butt3rflyh4ck <butterflyhuangxx@gmail.com>, found via syzkaller.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: 63ed1aab3d40 ("mctp: Add SIOCMCTP{ALLOC,DROP}TAG ioctls for tag control")
Reported-by: butt3rflyh4ck <butterflyhuangxx@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jeremy Kerr <jk@codeconstruct.com.au>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\thlist_del(&key->hlist);', '\t\thlist_del(&key->sklist);', '', '\t\t/* unref for the lists */', '\t\tmctp_key_unref(key);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!hlist_unhashed(&key->hlist)) {', '\t\t\thlist_del_init(&key->hlist);', '\t\t\thlist_del_init(&key->sklist);', '\t\t\tmctp_key_unref(key);', '\t\t}']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel MCTP (Management Component Transport Protocol) functionality. This issue occurs when a user simultaneously calls DROPTAG ioctl and socket close happens, which could allow a local user to crash the system or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: In the non-manual_alloc path, the code unconditionally calls hlist_del on key->hlist and key->sklist under keys_lock, then unlocks and calls mctp_key_unref once for the list references [17,18,20]. A second mctp_key_unref follows at line 22 for the local reference. If this function runs concurrently with socket close/DROPTAG teardown that already removed the key, the unconditional hlist_del and the list-reference unref execute again, dropping an extra reference and freeing the key while it is still in use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits a key to be freed via redundant unref while other paths still hold/use it, matching CWE-416 (referencing memory after free). It is a use-after-free rather than a plain double-free because the supported consequence is subsequent use of the freed key.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: removal and the list-reference unref are not guarded by a hashed/already-removed check, so a racing teardown path can perform the remove and unref twice. Trigger: simultaneous DROPTAG ioctl and socket close on the same key. Consequence: double unref frees the key prematurely; later access to the freed key is a use-after-free leading to crash or potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
net/appletalk: fix minor pointer leak to userspace in SIOCFINDIPDDPRT

Fields ->dev and ->next of struct ipddp_route may be copied to
userspace on the SIOCFINDIPDDPRT ioctl. This is only accessible
to CAP_NET_ADMIN though. Let's manually copy the relevant fields
instead of using memcpy().

BugLink: http://blog.infosectcbr.com.au/2018/09/linux-kernel-infoleaks.html
Cc: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (rp)', '\t\t\t\tmemcpy(&rcp2, rp, sizeof(rcp2));'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (rp) {', '\t\t\t\tmemset(&rcp2, 0, sizeof(rcp2));', '\t\t\t\trcp2.ip    = rp->ip;', '\t\t\t\trcp2.at    = rp->at;', '\t\t\t\trcp2.flags = rp->flags;', '\t\t\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.18.11. The ipddp_ioctl function in drivers/net/appletalk/ipddp.c allows local users to obtain sensitive kernel address information by leveraging CAP_NET_ADMIN to read the ipddp_route dev and next fields via an SIOCFINDIPDDPRT ioctl call.

code_evidence: When a route is found, the entire struct ipddp_route is copied from kernel memory (rp) into the local rcp2 with memcpy of sizeof(rcp2), including padding and the ->dev and ->next pointer fields.
rcp2 is then copied verbatim to the user-supplied ifr_data buffer via copy_to_user with sizeof(struct ipddp_route), so all copied bytes, including kernel pointers, reach userspace.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly transfers sensitive kernel internal state (pointer fields and padding) into a user-accessible resource, matching CWE-200's information-exposure behavior rather than a memory-corruption root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
if (rp)
memcpy(&rcp2, rp, sizeof(rcp2));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the kernel reuses a full-struct memcpy into a userspace-bound buffer without zeroing or field-selecting, so uninitialized padding and internal pointer fields (dev, next) are transferred. Trigger: a caller with CAP_NET_ADMIN issues SIOCFINDIPDDPRT for an existing route; the consequence is disclosure of kernel address values to the caller.
