The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/656e7673b14acd7835dc778867f84916c6d1cac2/tensorflow/core/kernels/sparse_add_op.cc) has a large set of validation for the two sparse tensor inputs (6 tensors in total), but does not validate that the tensors are not empty or that the second dimension of `*_indices` matches the size of corresponding `*_shape`. This allows attackers to send tensor triples that represent invalid sparse tensors to abuse code assumptions that are not protected by validation. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: num_dims is taken from a_shape->dim_size(0) and only checked to be >0; nothing ties it to the second dimension of a_indices_mat/b_indices_mat.
DimComparator::cmp is called with num_dims, so the comparison reads num_dims columns from each indices matrix even though those matrices may have a different dim_size(1).
Output rows are allocated with TensorShape({sum_nnz, num_dims}) and filled by chip<0> copies from the input index matrices, propagating the mismatched width.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked dimension mismatch lets the code read/operate beyond the bounds of the index buffer, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds memory access past the intended buffer; it is not merely a logic error, since the consequence is memory corruption/undefined behavior.

evidence_lines.code:
switch (sparse::DimComparator::cmp(a_indices_mat, b_indices_mat, i, j,
num_dims)) {

out_indices_mat.chip<0>(i) =
from_a ? a_indices_mat.chip<0>(idx) : b_indices_mat.chip<0>(idx);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the index matrices' second dimension is never validated against num_dims derived from a_shape. When an input provides fewer columns than num_dims, DimComparator::cmp reads past the end of the index matrix rows, and the output index copy assumes matching widths, yielding out-of-bounds memory access. Trigger: a sparse tensor whose indices matrix width differs from its shape length.

commit_msg:
can: bcm: delay release of struct bcm_op after synchronize_rcu()

can_rx_register() callbacks may be called concurrently to the call to
can_rx_unregister(). The callbacks and callback data, though, are
protected by RCU and the struct sock reference count.

So the callback data is really attached to the life of sk, meaning
that it should be released on sk_destruct. However, bcm_remove_op()
calls tasklet_kill(), and RCU callbacks may be called under RCU
softirq, so that cannot be used on kernels before the introduction of
HRTIMER_MODE_SOFT.

However, bcm_rx_handler() is called under RCU protection, so after
calling can_rx_unregister(), we may call synchronize_rcu() in order to
wait for any RCU read-side critical sections to finish. That is,
bcm_rx_handler() won't be called anymore for those ops. So, we only
free them, after we do that synchronize_rcu().

Fixes: ffd980f976e7 ("[CAN]: Add broadcast manager (bcm) protocol")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210619161813.2098382-1-cascardo@canonical.com
Cc: linux-stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Reported-by: syzbot+0f7e7e5e2f4f40fa89c0@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Reported-by: Norbert Slusarek <nslusarek@gmx.net>
Signed-off-by: Thadeu Lima de Souza Cascardo <cascardo@canonical.com>
Acked-by: Oliver Hartkopp <socketcan@hartkopp.net>
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tsynchronize_rcu();']}
description: .A flaw was found in the CAN BCM networking protocol in the Linux kernel, where a local attacker can abuse a flaw in the CAN subsystem to corrupt memory, crash the system or escalate privileges. This race condition in net/can/bcm.c in the Linux kernel allows for local privilege escalation to root.

code_evidence: can_rx_unregister() detaches the bcm_rx_handler callback for op, but the handler may still be executing concurrently under RCU protection. Immediately after list_del(), bcm_remove_op(op) frees op without waiting for those in-flight RCU read-side critical sections to finish.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The deletion sequence requires exclusive access to op, but a concurrent RCU callback can still touch it, violating atomicity. The missing synchronize_rcu() between unregister and free is a classic concurrent shared-resource race, matching CWE-362 rather than a mere lifetime bug alone.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: op is freed while bcm_rx_handler can still access it through RCU, because the unregister and free are not separated by a grace period. Trigger: a concurrent receive path invokes the callback for op during or just after bcm_delete_rx_op() unregisters and deletes it. Consequence: use-after-free of op, leading to memory corruption, crash, or privilege escalation.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        return NO_MEMORY;', '    }', '', '    if (numRects > (UINT32_MAX / sizeof(Rect))) {', '        android_errorWriteWithInfoLog(0x534e4554, "29983260", -1, NULL, 0);']}
description: Integer overflow in the Region::unflatten function in libs/ui/Region.cpp in mediaserver in Android 6.x before 2016-09-01 and 7.0 before 2016-09-01 allows attackers to obtain sensitive information via a crafted application, aka internal bug 29983260.

code_evidence: numRects is read from the untrusted buffer at line 6, then line 7 computes numRects * sizeof(Rect) in 32-bit arithmetic for the size check. The check at line 9 (added by the patch) rejects numRects > UINT32_MAX / sizeof(Rect), which is exactly the wraparound guard the pre-patch code lacked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer wraparound in a size calculation used as a bounds check, matching CWE-190. The patch's UINT32_MAX/sizeof(Rect) guard confirms the multiplication at line 7 was the overflow point; this is not a plain out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), since the missing constraint is the arithmetic overflow itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check multiplies the attacker-controlled numRects by sizeof(Rect) without guarding against 32-bit wraparound, so a large numRects wraps the product to a small value and passes the size check. The loop at line 12 then iterates numRects times, reading past the buffer and pushing rects into mStorage, exposing out-of-bounds data.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif((unsigned)mainc + (unsigned)sidec > (len - 8) / 4) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst unsigned int possibleMaxLength = (len - 8) / 4;', '\tif((unsigned)mainc > possibleMaxLength || (unsigned)sidec > possibleMaxLength || (unsigned)mainc + (unsigned)sidec > possibleMaxLength) {']}
description: An integer overflow was discovered in YGOPro ygocore v13.51. Attackers can use it to leak the game server thread's memory.

code_evidence: mainc and sidec are attacker-influenced int32 values read from the packet buffer deckbuf. The bounds check casts both to unsigned and sums them before comparing to (len - 8) / 4; the sum of two unsigned values can wrap to a small number, passing the check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The validating expression (unsigned)mainc + (unsigned)sidec is exactly an integer wraparound in a size check, matching CWE-190's cause and its confidentiality impact. It is not merely a missing-bounds check (CWE-1284) because the check exists but is defeated by arithmetic overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size validation adds two unsigned quantities without guarding the addition against wraparound. Trigger: a packet supplying large mainc/sidec whose unsigned sum wraps below the length limit. Consequence: the check is bypassed and the oversized counts flow into LoadDeck at line 14, enabling out-of-bounds reads that leak server thread memory as described in the CVE.

commit_msg:
tcp: mark skbs with SCM_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS

SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS can be enabled and disabled
while packets are collected on the error queue.
So, checking SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS in sk->sk_tsflags
is not enough to safely assume that the skb contains
OPT_STATS data.

Add a bit in sock_exterr_skb to indicate whether the
skb contains opt_stats data.

Fixes: 1c885808e456 ("tcp: SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS option for SO_TIMESTAMPING")
Reported-by: JongHwan Kim <zzoru007@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Soheil Hassas Yeganeh <soheil@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Willem de Bruijn <willemb@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbool tsonly;', '\t\t    sk->sk_type == SOCK_STREAM)', '\t\telse', '\t__skb_complete_tx_timestamp(skb, sk, tstype);'], 'added_lines': ['\tbool tsonly, opt_stats = false;', '\t\t    sk->sk_type == SOCK_STREAM) {', '\t\t\topt_stats = true;', '\t\t} else', '\t__skb_complete_tx_timestamp(skb, sk, tstype, opt_stats);']}
description: The TCP stack in the Linux kernel through 4.10.6 mishandles the SCM_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS feature, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from the kernel's internal socket data structures or cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via crafted system calls, related to net/core/skbuff.c and net/socket.c.

code_evidence: When tsonly is set, the code decides whether an skb carries OPT_STATS solely from the live sk->sk_tsflags bit, protocol and type. If that flag was cleared after the skb was queued, it falls through to alloc_skb(0,...), producing an skb lacking OPT_STATS data.
The resulting skb is passed to __skb_complete_tx_timestamp without any marker recording whether stats were actually included.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing per-skb opt_stats marker causes consumers to read beyond the intended buffer when parsing absent statistics; the consequence is an out-of-bounds read. This is a missing-constraint/state-tracking flaw, not a write overflow.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((sk->sk_tsflags & SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS) &&
sk->sk_protocol == IPPROTO_TCP &&
sk->sk_type == SOCK_STREAM)
skb = tcp_get_timestamping_opt_stats(sk);
else
#endif
skb = alloc_skb(0, GFP_ATOMIC);
__skb_complete_tx_timestamp(skb, sk, tstype);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the OPT_STATS decision is made at completion time from mutable socket flags rather than from a per-skb marker set when stats were gathered. Trigger: a local user disables SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS between queuing and completion, so a zero-length skb with no stats is delivered. Downstream consumers then parse OPT_STATS from an skb that lacks them, yielding an out-of-bounds read of kernel socket data (info leak) or a crash.

description: Muhammara is a node module with c/cpp bindings to modify PDF with js for node or electron (based/replacement on/of galkhana/hummusjs). The package muhammara before 2.6.0; all versions of package hummus are vulnerable to Denial of Service (DoS) when supplied with a maliciously crafted PDF file to be appended to another. This issue has been patched in 2.6.0 for muhammara and not at all for hummus. As a workaround, do not process files from untrusted sources.
